questions.f: Bees turn nectar into honey by fanning it with their wings until most of the water evaporates.

questions.q: What do we call the fine yellow dust from flowers that sticks to a bee's body?
questions.f: A bee packs pollen into little baskets on its back legs to carry home to the hive.

questions.q: What do we call it when animals move pollen from flower to flower?
questions.f: About one in three mouthfuls of our food depends on animal pollinators, mostly insects.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist whose job is studying animals?
questions.f: Zoologist comes from the Greek zoon, meaning living creature.

questions.q: The word 'mammal' comes from a root referring to what?
questions.f: It comes from the Latin mamma, meaning breast, since feeding milk is what defines the group.

questions.q: The word 'reptile' comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: It comes from the Latin repere, meaning to creep, which is also the root of the word reptation.

questions.q: The 'noct' in the word 'nocturnal' means what?
questions.f: From the Latin nox, meaning night, the same root behind the word nocturne, a piece of night music.

questions.q: What do we call an animal whose diet is mainly insects?
questions.f: Anteaters, swifts, and many bats are insectivores, and a single bat can eat thousands of insects a night.

questions.q: What do we call the place where a group of birds settles down to sleep?
questions.f: Some starling roosts hold a million birds, which whirl in huge shapes before settling for the night.

questions.q: What do we call the wooden home where a pet rabbit lives?
questions.f: Pet rabbits still love to dig and hide, so a good hutch has a dark corner for them to tuck into.

questions.q: What do we call an otter's home on a riverbank?
questions.f: An otter's holt is often hidden among tree roots with an underwater entrance for a secret door.

questions.q: What do we call the dome of sticks and mud a beaver lives in?
questions.f: A beaver lodge is entered from underwater, which keeps wolves and bears firmly outside.

questions.q: What do we call a male cat?
questions.f: A female cat is called a queen, especially when she is raising kittens.

questions.q: What do we call a male honeybee in a hive?
questions.f: Drones have no sting and do no work in the hive; their only job is to mate with a queen.

questions.q: What do we call an adult female lion?
questions.f: Lionesses do most of the hunting for the pride and often work together to surround their prey.

questions.q: What do we call the sharp, curved claws of an eagle or hawk?
questions.f: An eagle grips so hard with its talons that it can carry prey almost as heavy as itself.

questions.q: What do we call all the feathers covering a bird's body?
questions.f: A swan has more than 25,000 feathers in its plumage, most of them on its head and long neck.

questions.q: An octopus is a kind of fish.
questions.f: An octopus is a mollusc, a soft-bodied relative of snails and squid, with no bones or gills like a fish's.

questions.q: Camels can close their nostrils to keep sand out during a storm.
questions.f: Camels can shut their nostrils to slits and even trap moisture from their own breath as it leaves.

questions.q: Besides the platypus, which spiny mammal also lays eggs?
questions.f: The echidna and the platypus are the only mammals in the world that lay eggs instead of giving birth.

questions.q: Which desert reptile can squirt a jet of blood from its own eyes to scare predators?
questions.f: The horned lizard shoots the foul-tasting blood up to a metre to drive off hungry coyotes and foxes.

questions.q: Which living bird has the largest wingspan of all?
questions.f: A wandering albatross can have wings stretching over three metres, letting it glide for hours without a single flap.

questions.q: Which fish can climb out of the water and even scoot across mud on land?
questions.f: A mudskipper carries water in its gill chambers like a portable air tank while it is out of the water.

questions.q: Which insect has its 'ears' located on its legs?
questions.f: A cricket hears through thin patches on its front legs that pick up the chirps of other crickets.

questions.q: Which animal has the thickest, densest fur of any creature to stay warm in cold water?
questions.f: A sea otter can have a million hairs in a single square inch of fur, far more than any other animal.

questions.q: Which whale has a heart so large it can weigh as much as a small car?
questions.f: A blue whale's heartbeat can be sensed from over three kilometres away using special instruments.

questions.q: Which male bird builds and decorates a fancy stage to impress a mate?
questions.f: A male bowerbird arranges berries, shells, and even bottle caps by colour to attract a female.

questions.q: Which is the largest amphibian in the world, found in the rivers of Asia?
questions.f: The Chinese giant salamander can grow to nearly two metres, longer than most adult humans are tall.

questions.q: Which pig-like animal has a short, bendy snout and striped babies?
questions.f: Baby tapirs are covered in stripes and spots that fade as they grow, helping them hide in dappled forest light.

questions.q: Which insect is light enough to walk across the surface of a pond?
questions.f: Tiny water-repelling hairs on its legs let the water strider stand on the water's springy surface without sinking.

questions.q: Which sea creature can turn back into a younger form, earning the nickname 'immortal'?
questions.f: When hurt or starving, this tiny jellyfish can rewind its whole body to an earlier stage and start life over.

questions.q: Which bird can sleep while flying, resting half its brain at a time?
questions.f: A frigatebird can stay airborne for weeks, catching short naps on the wing high above the ocean.

questions.q: Which snake flattens its body and glides between trees, seeming to 'fly'?
questions.f: This snake launches itself, flattens like a ribbon, and slithers through the air to glide to a lower branch.

questions.q: Which biologist's job is described by the word 'ornithology'?
questions.f: Ornithology comes from the Greek word ornis, meaning bird, joined with logos, meaning study.

questions.q: The science called 'entomology' is the study of which creatures?
questions.f: Entomology comes from the Greek entomon, meaning insect, a word that also hints at their 'cut-in' segmented bodies.

questions.q: In the word 'zoology', the root 'zoo' means what?
questions.f: Zoology traces back to the Greek zoon, meaning living being or animal, plus logos, meaning study.

questions.q: The word 'octopus' is built from parts that mean what?
questions.f: Octopus comes from the Greek okto, meaning eight, and pous, meaning foot.

questions.q: The name 'dinosaur' was created from words meaning what?
questions.f: Dinosaur comes from the Greek deinos, meaning terrible or fearfully great, and sauros, meaning lizard.

questions.q: The word 'hippopotamus' is made from parts meaning what?
questions.f: Hippopotamus comes from the Greek hippos, meaning horse, and potamos, meaning river.

questions.q: The word 'rhinoceros' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: Rhinoceros comes from the Greek rhino, meaning nose, and keras, meaning horn.

questions.q: In words like 'octopus' and 'arthropod', the root 'pod' or 'pous' means what?
questions.f: This root comes from Greek and shows up in many animal words, from gastropod to cephalopod.

questions.q: The word 'amphibian' comes from roots meaning what?
questions.f: Amphibian comes from the Greek amphi, meaning both, and bios, meaning life, since they live in water and on land.

questions.q: A caterpillar changing into a butterfly is called 'metamorphosis', a word meaning what?
questions.f: Metamorphosis comes from the Greek meta, meaning change, and morphe, meaning form or shape.

questions.q: A 'carnivore' is named from a root meaning what kind of food?
questions.f: Carnivore comes from the Latin caro, meaning flesh, joined with vorare, meaning to devour.

questions.q: A 'herbivore' is named from a root meaning what kind of food?
questions.f: Herbivore comes from the Latin herba, meaning plant or grass, plus vorare, meaning to devour.

questions.q: The word 'marsupial' comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: Marsupial comes from the Latin marsupium, meaning pouch, the cosy place a joey grows up in.

questions.q: What is the unusual name for a group of jellyfish drifting together?
questions.f: A large smack of jellyfish drifting into shallow water is called a bloom.

questions.q: The word 'insect' comes from a Latin word meaning 'cut into', describing their segmented bodies.
questions.f: An insect's body is divided into three main sections, looking as if it was neatly cut into parts.

questions.q: A seahorse is actually a type of fish.
questions.f: Despite its horse-like head, a seahorse breathes with gills and has fins, making it a true fish.

questions.q: All mammals give birth to live babies.
questions.f: The platypus and echidna break this rule by laying eggs, yet they are still mammals that make milk.

questions.q: Why do most vultures have bare, featherless heads?
c: It keeps them clean while feeding
questions.f: A bald head is far easier to keep clean, and the bare skin also helps a vulture shed heat while soaring.

questions.q: Why do many birds deliberately swallow small stones and grit?
c: To help grind up their food
To store minerals in the crop
questions.f: The grit sits in the gizzard, a muscular pouch that mashes seeds since birds have no teeth to chew with.

questions.q: What is a rattlesnake's rattle actually made of?
questions.f: A new ring is added at each moult, so a longer rattle usually means an older snake.

questions.q: A woodpecker's very long tongue is stored where when not in use?
questions.f: The tongue wraps around the back of the skull like a seatbelt, which may also cushion the brain while hammering.

questions.q: What makes an owl's flight almost completely silent?
questions.f: Tiny fringes break up the rush of air over the wing, so a mouse never hears the owl coming.

questions.q: What is the job of the swim bladder inside a bony fish?
questions.f: By adding or removing gas, a fish can hover at any depth without wasting energy swimming.

questions.q: What does the 'lateral line' running along a fish's side do?
c: Senses movement and vibration in water
questions.f: The lateral line lets a fish in a school feel its neighbours turn, so a whole shoal can flick round as one.

questions.q: Why does a shark never run out of teeth?
c: Rows of new teeth move forward to replace old ones
Its teeth regrow from the root
questions.f: A shark may get through tens of thousands of teeth in a lifetime, like a conveyor belt in its jaws.

questions.q: A shark has no swim bladder, so what helps stop it sinking?
questions.f: A shark's liver can be a quarter of its whole body weight, packed with oil that is lighter than water.

questions.q: What special food turns a honeybee larva into a queen instead of a worker?
questions.f: Every larva gets a little royal jelly, but only future queens are fed it richly for their whole development.

questions.q: How long does a worker honeybee usually live during the busy summer?
questions.f: Summer workers literally wear out their wings, while bees born in autumn can live through the whole winter.

questions.q: Which insect has the fastest wingbeat of all, over 1,000 beats per second?
questions.f: Its muscles cannot fire that fast one beat at a time, so the whole thorax vibrates like a plucked string.

questions.q: How does a desert ant find its way straight back to its nest?
c: By tracking the sun and counting its steps
questions.f: Desert sand is too hot to hold a scent trail, so the ant keeps a running tally of distance and direction.

questions.q: Where does most of a reef coral's food actually come from?
c: Tiny algae living inside its tissues
questions.f: The algae make sugars by photosynthesis and share them, while the coral gives the algae a safe home.

questions.q: What happens during 'coral bleaching'?
c: Stressed coral expels the algae that feed it
Coral is stained white by salt
questions.f: Without its colourful algae the coral turns ghostly white and slowly starves unless conditions improve.

questions.q: Why can a clownfish sit among an anemone's stinging tentacles unharmed?
c: A special mucus coating protects it
It is too fast to be stung
questions.f: A clownfish builds up its protective slime layer gradually, brushing the tentacles a little at a time.

questions.q: What service do cleaner wrasse provide to much bigger reef fish?
c: They eat parasites off their skin
questions.f: Big fish queue up at 'cleaning stations' and hold still, even opening their mouths for a clean.

questions.q: Which animal produces the loudest clicks in the ocean to find food in the dark?
questions.f: A sperm whale's clicks pass through a huge oil-filled organ in its forehead that focuses the sound like a lens.

questions.q: Which shrimp-like animals are the main food of the largest whales?
questions.f: Antarctic krill may be the most abundant animal on Earth by total weight, gathering in swarms visible from space.

questions.q: Which is the heaviest bony fish in the world?
questions.f: An ocean sunfish can weigh over two tonnes and may release more eggs at once than any other vertebrate.

questions.q: What do we call the colour-changing cells in an octopus's skin?
questions.f: Each of these tiny sacs of pigment is pulled open by muscles, so an octopus can change pattern in a heartbeat.

questions.q: What hard structure sits hidden at the centre of an octopus's arms?
questions.f: An octopus's beak is the only hard part of its body, which is why it can squeeze through such tiny gaps.

questions.q: How does a scallop escape a hungry starfish?
c: It claps its shells to swim away
questions.f: A scallop also has dozens of tiny eyes along its shell edge, each with a mirror instead of a lens.

questions.q: How does a barnacle glued to a rock get its food?
c: It combs the water with feathery legs
It absorbs food through its shell
questions.f: A barnacle is really a crustacean lying on its back inside a shell, kicking food into its mouth.

questions.q: Which living animals are the closest relatives of the dinosaurs?
questions.f: Birds are not just relatives but living dinosaurs, descended from small feathered meat-eaters.

questions.q: Whales evolved from ancestors that lived where?
questions.f: Fossils show four-legged whale ancestors that walked on land before returning to the water.

questions.q: Which land animal is the closest living relative of whales and dolphins?
questions.f: Hippos and whales share an ancestor from about 55 million years ago, which is why both have almost no body hair.

questions.q: Why does a kangaroo lick its own forearms on a hot day?
questions.f: Blood vessels run close to the skin there, so wet forearms work rather like a radiator.

questions.q: How does a koala manage to digest tough, toxic eucalyptus leaves?
c: Helpful microbes in its long gut
questions.f: A joey gets its starter set of microbes by eating a special soft food its mother produces.

questions.q: Which animal has a pouch that opens backwards, towards its tail?
questions.f: A backwards pouch means a digging wombat does not shovel soil straight onto its baby.

questions.q: A platypus hunts with its eyes, ears, and nose shut, so what does it use?
questions.f: Thousands of sensors in the platypus's bill pick up the faint electricity made by a shrimp's twitching muscles.

questions.q: What lets fish such as gouramis gulp air at the water's surface?
questions.f: The maze-like labyrinth organ absorbs oxygen from air, so these fish survive in warm, stagnant pools.

questions.q: How is a turtle's shell attached to the rest of its body?
c: It is fused to its ribs and backbone
It is glued by thick skin
It is held by strong muscles
questions.f: A turtle can never leave its shell, because the shell is part of its skeleton.

questions.q: Why does a sea turtle appear to be crying salty tears?
c: Special glands flush out extra salt
It is straining to lay eggs
It keeps its eyes wet on land
questions.f: Drinking seawater loads a turtle with salt, and glands beside the eyes squeeze the excess out.

questions.q: Which is the largest turtle in the world?
questions.f: A leatherback can weigh 700 kg and has a rubbery shell instead of a hard one, letting it dive very deep.

questions.q: Why does a crocodile lie with its mouth wide open on a riverbank?
c: To lose heat and cool down
questions.f: A crocodile cannot sweat, so gaping lets heat escape through the wet lining of its mouth.

questions.q: Why do crocodiles swallow stones?
c: They help with balance and grinding food
questions.f: These swallowed stones are called gastroliths, and some dinosaurs used them in the very same way.

questions.q: How can a chameleon's tongue shoot out faster than a car accelerates?
c: Stored spring energy is released at once
questions.f: The tongue works like a stretched catapult: collagen is wound up tight, then released in a fraction of a second.

questions.q: Which is the longest venomous snake in the world?
questions.f: A king cobra can reach five metres and mostly eats other snakes, which is what its name really refers to.

questions.q: How does a snake pick up sounds without any outer ears?
c: It senses vibrations through its jaw
questions.f: Vibrations pass from the jawbone to the inner ear, so a snake feels footsteps as much as hears them.

questions.q: What do we call the pouch where a bird stores food before digesting it?
questions.f: Pigeons even make a milky food in the crop to feed their squabs.

questions.q: The word 'orangutan' comes from words meaning what?
questions.f: From Malay orang, meaning person, and hutan, meaning forest.

questions.q: The scientific name of the ostrich comes from words meaning what?
questions.f: Struthio camelus reflects an old idea that the long-necked, long-legged bird resembled a camel.

questions.q: The word 'flamingo' comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: The same root gives us the word flame, and young flamingos are grey until their diet turns them pink.

questions.q: The word 'porpoise' is built from roots meaning what?
questions.f: From the Latin porcus, meaning pig, and piscis, meaning fish, thanks to its blunt, snouty face.

questions.q: The word 'walrus' comes from old roots meaning what?
questions.f: Old Norse and Dutch words for whale and horse combined into the name we use today.

questions.q: The word 'lemur' comes from a Latin word for what?
questions.f: Naturalists chose lemures, the Roman word for restless spirits, because of the animals' wide night-time stare.

questions.q: The word 'caterpillar' comes from old roots meaning what?
questions.f: Old French chatepelose meant hairy cat, which fits the fuzzy caterpillars people saw on their crops.

questions.q: The word 'mosquito' literally means what?
questions.f: From Spanish and Portuguese, where mosca means fly and the ending makes it small.

questions.q: The word 'cobra' comes from a phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Portuguese sailors called it cobra de capelo, meaning snake with a hood.

questions.q: The spider called the 'tarantula' takes its name from what?
questions.f: It is named after Taranto in southern Italy, where a local wolf spider was blamed for a frenzied dancing illness.

questions.q: The word 'pangolin' comes from a Malay word meaning what?
questions.f: From penggulung, meaning roller, describing exactly what a frightened pangolin does.

questions.q: The name 'axolotl' comes from an Aztec word meaning what?
questions.f: From Nahuatl atl, water, and xolotl, a dog-like creature, and it lives in lakes near Mexico City.

questions.q: The name 'wildebeest' comes from Dutch words meaning what?
questions.f: Dutch settlers in southern Africa coined it, and the animal is also called the gnu.

questions.q: The bird name 'nightingale' literally means what?
questions.f: From old roots for night and to sing, since the male often sings loudest after dark.

questions.q: The word 'salmon' comes from a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: From salire, meaning to leap, which is exactly what a salmon does at a waterfall.

questions.q: The word 'vulture' comes from a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: From vellere, meaning to pluck or tear, describing how the bird feeds.

questions.q: The word 'falcon' comes from a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: From falx, meaning sickle, because of the curved shape of its talons and wings.

questions.q: The word 'spider' comes from an old root meaning what?
questions.f: It shares an ancestor with the word spin, from Old English spithra.

questions.q: The word 'cheetah' comes from a Sanskrit root meaning what?
questions.f: From chitraka, meaning spotted one, borrowed into English through Hindi.

questions.q: The snake called the 'python' takes its name from what?
questions.f: Python was a great serpent of Greek legend, slain by the god Apollo at Delphi.

questions.q: The fish name 'piranha' comes from roots meaning what?
questions.f: From the Tupi language of Brazil, combining words for fish and tooth.

questions.q: The name 'gecko' came into English by copying what?
questions.f: Malay and Javanese words imitated the loud 'gek-ko' call of the tokay gecko.

questions.q: What is the scientific term for an animal's whiskers?
questions.f: Vibrissae come from a Latin root meaning to vibrate, and each one sits in a nerve-packed follicle.

questions.q: What do we call the two bony, skin-covered horns on a giraffe's head?
questions.f: Ossicones are covered in skin and fur, and males use them like clubs when they spar.

questions.q: What do we call the partly digested food a cow brings back up to chew again?
questions.f: Chewing the cud grinds tough grass finer so that gut microbes can break it down.

questions.q: What do we call the chisel-shaped front teeth a beaver gnaws with?
questions.f: A beaver's incisors have iron in the front enamel, which makes them orange and very hard.

questions.q: What do we call the organ a spider uses to produce silk?
questions.f: Most spiders have several spinnerets and can make different silks for webs, wrapping, and safety lines.

questions.q: What do we call the pair of feelers on an insect's head?
questions.f: Antennae smell, taste, and feel; a male moth can detect a female's scent from kilometres away.

questions.q: An insect's eye made of hundreds of tiny units is called what?
questions.f: Each unit sees a tiny patch of the world, and a dragonfly has around 30,000 of them per eye.

questions.q: What is the middle section of an insect's three-part body called?
questions.f: All six legs and any wings attach to the thorax, which is packed with flight muscle.

questions.q: What do we call the bony plates in a crocodile's or turtle's skin?
questions.f: Scutes are reinforced with bone underneath, making crocodile skin something like living chain mail.

questions.q: What do we call the fleshy flap of skin hanging from a turkey's throat?
questions.f: A turkey's wattle flushes bright red when the bird is excited and helps it shed heat.

questions.q: All spiders build webs to catch their food.
questions.f: Many spiders, such as jumping and wolf spiders, stalk their prey and never build a web at all.

questions.q: A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage rather than bone.
questions.f: Cartilage is lighter and more flexible than bone, which helps a shark turn sharply and save energy.

questions.q: Which bird lays the largest egg compared with the size of its own body?
questions.f: A kiwi egg can be a fifth of the mother's weight, roughly like a human baby weighing 15 kg at birth.

questions.q: Why can penguins not fly, even though they have wings?
c: Their bones are solid and heavy
questions.f: Heavy bones would be terrible for flying but are perfect for diving, since they stop the penguin bobbing up.

questions.q: Which bird can dive deeper than any other?
questions.f: An emperor penguin has been recorded over 500 metres down, staying under for more than 20 minutes.

questions.q: What is the easiest way to tell most butterflies from most moths?
questions.f: Moth antennae are often feathery or thread-like, and most moths also rest with their wings spread flat.

questions.q: How can you tell an African elephant from an Asian elephant?
c: African elephants have much larger ears
African elephants have no trunk ridges
questions.f: An African elephant's ear is even said to resemble the shape of Africa itself.

questions.q: What is a reliable way to tell a crocodile from an alligator?
c: A crocodile has a narrower, V-shaped snout
An alligator has no teeth showing
A crocodile has no tail ridges
questions.f: An alligator's wide U-shaped snout hides its lower teeth when the mouth is shut, while a crocodile's stick out.

questions.q: How do newborn hares differ from newborn rabbits?
c: Hares are born furry with open eyes
Rabbits are born able to run
questions.f: Hares are born ready to bolt above ground, while rabbit kits stay hidden and helpless in a burrow.

questions.q: What visible feature separates a sea lion from a true seal?
c: Sea lions have external ear flaps
questions.f: Sea lions can also turn their back flippers forward and walk on land, while true seals must wriggle.

questions.q: What is the key difference between horns and antlers?
c: Antlers are bone and are shed each year
Horns are made of bone only
questions.f: Antlers are grown fresh and dropped annually, whereas horns have a bony core with a permanent keratin sheath.

questions.q: How many chambers does a typical fish's heart have?
questions.f: Two chambers are enough because a fish's blood makes a single loop: heart to gills to body and back.

questions.q: Which insect can live the longest, sometimes for decades?
questions.f: A queen termite may lay eggs for 30 years or more, making her the longest-lived insect known.

questions.q: Which spider has the widest leg span in the world?
questions.f: Its legs can span 30 cm, wide enough to cover a dinner plate, though its body stays fairly small.

questions.q: Which is the heaviest spider in the world?
questions.f: It can weigh as much as a small apple, and its name is misleading since it mainly eats insects and worms.

questions.q: What happens when ultraviolet light shines on a scorpion?
questions.f: Something in the outer layer of shell fluoresces, which is why researchers hunt scorpions at night with UV torches.

questions.q: How many hearts does an earthworm have?
questions.f: An earthworm has five pairs of pumping vessels along its body that push blood in a simple loop.

questions.q: Roughly how many tiny teeth does a garden snail have on its feeding ribbon?
questions.f: The ribbon of teeth is called a radula, and the snail scrapes it over leaves like a rasp.

questions.q: Which African animal makes a call that sounds like wild laughter?
questions.f: Hyena 'laughter' is really a nervous signal used when the clan is squabbling over food.

questions.q: Which hoofed animal can climb almost vertical rock and dam walls?
questions.f: An ibex has soft, rubbery hoof pads with hard rims that grip stone like climbing shoes.

questions.q: Which Arctic animal grows an underwool warmer than sheep's wool?
questions.f: Musk ox underwool, called qiviut, is eight times warmer than sheep's wool by weight and does not shrink.

questions.q: Which South American animal grows the finest, most valuable wool?
questions.f: Vicuna fibre is finer than a human hair, and Inca law once reserved it for royalty alone.

questions.q: Farm chickens were domesticated from which wild bird?
questions.f: Red junglefowl still live wild in Asian forests and look strikingly like a slim farmyard rooster.

questions.q: House cats are descended from which wild ancestor?
questions.f: African wildcats probably moved in beside early farmers to hunt the mice attracted to stored grain.

questions.q: How does a homing pigeon find its way back over hundreds of kilometres?
c: It senses the Earth's magnetic field and uses the sun
questions.f: Pigeons also use smell and low-frequency sound, combining several senses into one built-in map.

questions.q: Which animal was the first to orbit the Earth?
questions.f: Laika, a stray dog from Moscow, flew aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957 and opened the way for human spaceflight.

questions.q: Which animal is the emblem of the World Wide Fund for Nature?
questions.f: The panda was chosen partly because its black-and-white pattern printed cheaply in the 1960s.

questions.q: Which flightless bird is the national symbol of New Zealand?
questions.f: Kiwis have nostrils at the very tip of the beak, which is unique among birds, and they sniff out worms.

questions.q: Which animal is a national symbol of Canada?
questions.f: The beaver appeared on Canada's first postage stamp in 1851, honouring the fur trade that built early trade routes.

questions.q: About how much does a blue whale's tongue weigh?
questions.f: Yet a blue whale's throat is too narrow to swallow anything much bigger than a beach ball.

questions.q: Which mammal has one of the shortest pregnancies, under two weeks?
questions.f: Opossum babies are born the size of a bee and crawl into the pouch to finish developing.

questions.q: Which bird buries its eggs in a mound of rotting leaves to keep them warm?
questions.f: The male tests the mound with his beak like a thermometer and adds or removes soil to hold the heat steady.

questions.q: Which bird builds its nest almost entirely out of its own hardened saliva?
questions.f: Cave swiftlets also echolocate in total darkness, one of very few birds able to do so.

questions.q: Why does a rhinoceros roll about in mud?
c: The dried mud blocks sun and insects
questions.f: A crust of dried mud works as both sunscreen and insect repellent on the rhino's surprisingly sensitive skin.

questions.q: Which of these animals sleeps the least each day?
questions.f: A giraffe may sleep only around half an hour a day, often in short standing naps.

questions.q: Which is the longest insect in the world?
questions.f: One stick insect from China measures 62 cm with its legs stretched out, longer than your arm.

questions.q: Which is among the heaviest insects in the world?
questions.f: A Goliath beetle grub can weigh 100 grams, about the same as a small apple.

questions.q: How do millipedes differ from centipedes?
c: Millipedes have two pairs of legs per segment
Centipedes have four pairs per segment
questions.f: Centipedes have one pair per segment and are fast hunters, while millipedes trundle along eating dead leaves.

questions.q: Which is the largest crustacean that lives on land?
questions.f: A coconut crab can span a metre from claw to claw and climbs trees to reach fruit.

questions.q: Which bird has a beak longer than the rest of its body?
questions.f: It must perch with its bill tilted upwards, and it preens with its feet because its beak cannot reach.

questions.q: Which moth has one of the largest wing areas of any insect?
questions.f: An adult atlas moth never eats; it lives just a week or two on energy stored as a caterpillar.

questions.q: What do we call a group of crocodiles resting together in the sun?
questions.f: The word comes from basking, exactly what the crocodiles are doing as they soak up heat.

questions.q: What do we call a group of hyenas?
questions.f: A hyena clan can hold 80 members and is led by the females.

questions.q: What do we call a group of zebras?
questions.f: The name captures how a mass of moving stripes dazzles a predator trying to pick out one animal.

questions.q: What do we call a group of foxes?
questions.f: Skulk comes from an old word meaning to lurk, which suits a fox creeping through the hedges.

questions.q: What do we call a group of otters?
questions.f: The name fits their play, and river otters slide down muddy banks again and again for fun.

questions.q: What do we call a group of porcupines?
questions.f: Porcupines are mostly solitary, so a prickle is a rare sight outside a family group.

questions.q: What do we call a group of butterflies?
questions.f: They are also called a flutter, and some species gather in their millions at overwintering sites.

questions.q: What do we call a group of peacocks displaying together?
questions.f: Ostentation means showing off, which is precisely what a fanned peacock tail is for.

questions.q: What do we call a baby hare?
questions.f: Leveret comes from the French lievre, meaning hare.

questions.q: What do we call a baby llama or alpaca?
questions.f: Cria comes from a Spanish word meaning baby, and a newborn can stand within an hour.

questions.q: What do we call a young pigeon still in the nest?
questions.f: Squabs are fed 'crop milk', a rich paste made in both parents' throats.

questions.q: What do we call a young hawk or falcon taken for training?
questions.f: Eyas comes through French from a Latin root meaning nest, so it literally means a nestling.

questions.q: What do we call a young eel that has swum in from the sea?
questions.f: Elvers arrive at river mouths almost transparent and wriggle upstream in their thousands.

questions.q: What do we call a young frog that has just lost its tail?
questions.f: A froglet keeps a stub of tail for a while and absorbs it as extra food while it learns to hop.

questions.q: What do we call an adult male horse kept for breeding?
questions.f: A stallion's neck is thicker and more arched than a mare's, a difference riders spot at a glance.

questions.q: What do we call an adult male pig?
questions.f: Wild boars have tusks that keep growing and are sharpened each time the jaws move.

questions.q: What do we call a female donkey?
questions.f: A male donkey is called a jack, which is where the word jackass comes from.

questions.q: What do we call an adult male deer of a large species?
questions.f: An adult female of these species is called a hind, and a stag's antlers can carry a dozen points.

questions.q: What do we call a female peafowl?
questions.f: Only the male, the peacock, grows the huge decorated train of feathers.

questions.q: What do we call the ribbon of tiny teeth a snail feeds with?
questions.f: Radula comes from a Latin word meaning scraper, and some sea snails use theirs to drill through shells.

questions.q: What do we call the forked breastbone of a bird, often called the wishbone?
questions.f: Furcula means little fork in Latin, and it springs back with each wingbeat to help a bird breathe in flight.

questions.q: A 'prehensile' tail is one that can do what?
questions.f: Prehensile comes from a Latin root meaning to seize, and only some New World monkeys have truly gripping tails.

questions.q: 'Retractable' claws, like a cat's, are able to do what?
questions.f: Cheetahs are the odd ones out among cats, since their claws stay out to grip the ground like running spikes.

questions.q: An animal with 'cloven' hooves has feet that are what?
questions.f: Cattle, sheep, goats, and deer all walk on two weight-bearing toes with a hoof on each.

questions.q: What do we call the tiny breathing holes along the sides of an insect's body?
questions.f: Air travels from the spiracles through a branching network of tubes straight to the insect's tissues.

questions.q: What do we call the woolly coat shorn from a sheep in one piece?
questions.f: One fleece can weigh several kilograms and is sorted by fineness before it is spun.

questions.q: What do we call the stiff, hollow spines of a porcupine?
questions.f: Quills are modified hairs made of keratin, and they detach easily when a predator gets too close.

questions.q: The word 'giraffe' came into English from an Arabic word meaning what?
questions.f: From zarafah, and the giraffe's smooth, gliding stride does look like effortless walking.

questions.q: The word 'elephant' comes from an ancient root connected to what?
questions.f: The Greek elephas meant both the animal and ivory, the material its tusks provide.

questions.q: The word 'ferret' comes from a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: From fur, meaning thief, because ferrets sneak into burrows after rabbits.

questions.q: The word 'hamster' comes from a German root meaning what?
questions.f: Wild hamsters really do hoard, stuffing kilograms of seeds into underground stores for winter.

questions.q: The bird we call the 'turkey' got its English name from what?
c: A country it was traded through
questions.f: Europeans first met the bird via traders linked to Turkey, though it actually comes from North America.

questions.q: A hare is simply another name for a rabbit.
questions.f: Hares are a different group: longer-legged, faster, and born furry above ground rather than in a burrow.

questions.q: A starfish has a simple eye at the tip of each of its arms.
questions.f: Each arm-tip eye sees only blurry patches of light and dark, but that is enough to steer back to the reef.

questions.q: Which whale has a single long spiral tusk, earning it the nickname 'unicorn of the sea'?
questions.f: A narwhal's tusk is actually an overgrown tooth packed with millions of nerve endings that sense the water.

questions.q: Which bird sneakily lays its eggs in other birds' nests for them to raise?
questions.f: A newly hatched cuckoo chick often pushes the host's own eggs out so it can hog all the food.

questions.q: Which egg-laying mammal has a venomous spur on the male's hind leg?
questions.f: The male platypus is one of very few venomous mammals, with a sharp spur near each ankle.

questions.q: Which colourful reef fish can change from male to female during its life?
questions.f: In a clownfish group the largest becomes the female, and if she dies, a male changes sex to replace her.

questions.q: Which small bird makes the longest known nonstop flight, crossing an entire ocean?
questions.f: A bar-tailed godwit has flown over 13,000 km from Alaska to New Zealand without stopping to rest or eat.

questions.q: Which is the largest primate in the world?
questions.f: A silverback gorilla can weigh over 200 kg yet eats mostly leaves, shoots, and fruit.

questions.q: Which reptile has a light-sensing 'third eye' on top of its head?
questions.f: The tuatara of New Zealand is the last survivor of a reptile group that lived alongside the dinosaurs.

questions.q: Which sea mammal uses rocks as tools to crack open shellfish?
questions.f: A sea otter often keeps a favourite stone tucked in a pouch of loose skin under its arm.

questions.q: Which is the smallest bird in the world, weighing about two grams?
questions.f: The bee hummingbird is so tiny that its eggs are about the size of a coffee bean.

questions.q: Which bird has been recorded flying at the highest altitude, near jet-cruising height?
questions.f: A Ruppell's vulture was once struck by a plane at about 11,000 metres above the ground.

questions.q: Which land snake is considered the most venomous in the world?
questions.f: A single bite from the inland taipan carries enough venom to affect many adults, yet it is shy and rarely seen.

questions.q: Which animal has the longest pregnancy of any land mammal, nearly two years?
questions.f: An elephant is pregnant for around 22 months before its huge calf is finally born.

questions.q: Which sea creature has blue blood used by scientists to test medicines for safety?
questions.f: A horseshoe crab's blood is blue because it uses copper, not iron, to carry oxygen.

questions.q: Which fish swims powerfully upstream, leaping waterfalls, to lay its eggs?
questions.f: A salmon can find its way back to the exact stream where it hatched by using its keen sense of smell.

questions.q: Which insects build papery nests by chewing wood into a pulp?
questions.f: Wasps invented paper-making from wood pulp long before humans ever did.

questions.q: Which animals have front teeth that never stop growing, so they must gnaw to wear them down?
questions.f: A beaver's orange front teeth are so tough because they contain iron, and they grow all its life.

questions.q: Which lizard can sprint across the surface of water on its hind legs?
questions.f: The basilisk is nicknamed the Jesus Christ lizard for its ability to dash across water before it sinks.

questions.q: Which animal makes the loudest sound of any creature, louder than a jet engine?
questions.f: A blue whale's low calls can travel across hundreds of kilometres of ocean to reach other whales.

questions.q: Which big cat often drags its prey high up into a tree to eat in peace?
questions.f: A leopard is strong enough to haul prey heavier than itself several metres up a tree trunk.

questions.q: In many turtles, what decides whether the eggs hatch into males or females?
questions.f: Warmer nests often produce more female turtles, while cooler nests produce more males.

questions.q: The pufferfish carries a deadly toxin, prized in the Japanese delicacy 'fugu', called what?
questions.f: Tetrodotoxin is many times deadlier than cyanide with no antidote, so only specially licensed chefs are trusted to prepare fugu.

questions.q: Which animals sense the tiny electric signals of hidden prey using special pores in their skin?
questions.f: These jelly-filled pores, called ampullae of Lorenzini, let a shark find a fish buried under the sand.

questions.q: The talons of the powerful harpy eagle can grow as large as the claws of which animal?
questions.f: A harpy eagle's rear talons can top 12 cm, rivalling a grizzly's claws, and it snatches monkeys and sloths right out of the rainforest canopy.

questions.q: Which reptile travels across entire oceans to lay eggs on the same beach where it hatched?
questions.f: Scientists think sea turtles navigate using the Earth's magnetic field like a built-in compass.

questions.q: Which insect is often called the strongest for its size, rolling balls many times its weight?
questions.f: A dung beetle can pull a load over a thousand times its own body weight.

questions.q: Which land animal has the most genes for sense of smell, sniffing out water kilometres away?
questions.f: An elephant has around 2,000 smell-detecting genes, roughly five times as many as a dog.

questions.q: Which is the largest arthropod, with legs that can span nearly four metres?
questions.f: Despite its huge, spindly legs, the Japanese spider crab is gentle and feeds on scraps on the seafloor.

questions.q: Which deep-sea fish has a see-through head that lets it look straight up through its own skull?
questions.f: The barreleye's glowing green eyes can rotate inside its transparent, dome-shaped head.

questions.q: Which tree-dwelling animal sleeps up to 22 hours a day to save energy?
questions.f: Koalas sleep so much because eucalyptus leaves give very little energy and take ages to digest.

questions.q: Which is the most venomous fish, lying camouflaged as a rock on the reef?
questions.f: The stonefish hides its venomous spines so well that swimmers may step on it by accident.

questions.q: Which monkey uses its tail like an extra hand to grip branches?
questions.f: A spider monkey's gripping tail is so strong it can hang from a branch by the tail alone.

questions.q: Which bird balances its single egg on top of its feet through the freezing Antarctic winter?
questions.f: Male emperor penguins huddle together, sharing warmth, while keeping the egg off the icy ground.

questions.q: Which is the fastest-moving snake, able to slither faster than a person can run?
questions.f: A black mamba can move at around 20 km/h in short bursts across open ground.

questions.q: Killer whales are actually the largest members of which animal family?
questions.f: An orca is really a giant dolphin, hunting in coordinated family groups called pods.

questions.q: Which lizard flares a wide, umbrella-like frill of skin around its neck to look fierce?
questions.f: When bluffing fails, the frilled lizard folds up its frill and dashes off on its two back legs.

questions.q: Which is the heaviest snake in the world?
questions.f: A green anaconda can weigh over 200 kg, squeezing its prey rather than using venom.

questions.q: Which black-and-white seabird is nicknamed the 'sea parrot' for its colourful beak?
questions.f: A puffin's bright beak fades to a dull grey in winter and glows orange again for the breeding season.

questions.q: Which fish makes natural antifreeze so it can live in near-freezing polar seas?
questions.f: An icefish also has clear, pale blood because it survives without the red pigment most fish use.

questions.q: Which is the largest cat species in the world?
questions.f: A Siberian, or Amur, tiger can weigh over 300 kg and has thick fur for the freezing forests it roams.

questions.q: Which lizard sticks out a bright blue tongue to startle would-be attackers?
questions.f: The sudden flash of a vivid blue tongue can make a predator hesitate long enough for the skink to escape.

questions.q: Which nearly hairless rodent lives underground in insect-like colonies with a single breeding queen?
questions.f: Naked mole-rats barely feel some kinds of pain and can survive with very little oxygen underground.

questions.q: The science of 'herpetology' studies which two groups of animals?
questions.f: Herpetology comes from the Greek herpeton, meaning a creeping thing that crawls low to the ground.

questions.q: The science of 'ichthyology' is the study of which animals?
questions.f: Ichthyology comes from the Greek ichthys, meaning fish.

questions.q: The science of 'arachnology' is the study of which creatures?
questions.f: Arachnology takes its name from Arachne, a weaver in Greek myth who was turned into a spider.

questions.q: The science of 'mammalogy' is the study of which animals?
questions.f: Mammals are named for the mammary glands that produce milk to feed their young.

questions.q: The science of 'primatology' is the study of which animals?
questions.f: Primatology studies apes, monkeys, and their relatives, whose name comes from a Latin word meaning first or foremost.

questions.q: In words like 'pterodactyl', the root 'ptero' means what?
questions.f: This root comes from the Greek pteron, meaning wing or feather, and also appears in Lepidoptera.

questions.q: The word 'pterodactyl' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: Pterodactyl comes from the Greek pteron, meaning wing, and daktylos, meaning finger.

questions.q: The word 'chameleon' comes from roots that surprisingly mean what?
questions.f: Chameleon comes from Greek roots meaning lion of the ground, khamai plus leon.

questions.q: The word 'platypus' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: Platypus comes from the Greek platys, meaning flat, and pous, meaning foot.

questions.q: The word 'porcupine' comes from roots meaning what?
questions.f: Porcupine comes from Latin roots meaning pig with spines, though it is really a large rodent.

questions.q: The word 'squirrel' comes from an old root meaning what?
questions.f: Squirrel traces to the Greek skiouros, from skia meaning shadow and oura meaning tail.

questions.q: The word 'crocodile' comes from an old root meaning what?
questions.f: Crocodile comes from a Greek word meaning worm of the pebbles, from the way they bask on stony riverbanks.

questions.q: The name 'leopard' was formed by combining words for which two animals?
questions.f: People once thought the leopard was a cross between a lion, leo, and a panther, called a pard.

questions.q: Snakes flick their forked tongues to carry scent particles to which specialised sense organ?
questions.f: Also called the vomeronasal organ, it lets a snake 'taste' the air, and the two fork tips deliver a sense of direction to the scent.

questions.q: The 'panda's thumb' that lets a giant panda grip bamboo is not a real thumb but an enlarged what?
questions.f: Biologist Stephen Jay Gould made this famous: the panda's 'thumb' is a stretched wrist bone repurposed to strip bamboo.

questions.q: The word 'bovine' describes animals related to which farm creature?
questions.f: Bovine comes from the Latin bos, meaning ox or cow.

questions.q: The word 'porcine' describes animals related to which creature?
questions.f: Porcine comes from the Latin porcus, meaning pig or swine.

questions.q: The word 'vulpine' describes animals related to which creature?
questions.f: Vulpine comes from the Latin vulpes, meaning fox, and often describes someone clever or crafty.

questions.q: The word 'ursine' describes animals related to which creature?
questions.f: Ursine comes from the Latin ursus, meaning bear, which also gave the star pattern Ursa Major its name.

questions.q: The word 'lupine' describes animals related to which creature?
questions.f: Lupine comes from the Latin lupus, meaning wolf.

questions.q: A freshwater eel begins life as a strange, transparent, leaf-shaped larva called what?
questions.f: Leptocephalus means 'slim head'; these see-through larvae drift on ocean currents for months before becoming young eels called elvers.

questions.q: In names like 'Stegosaurus', the root 'saur' means what?
questions.f: This root comes from the Greek sauros, meaning lizard, and appears in almost every dinosaur name.

questions.q: The word 'pachyderm', once used for elephants, comes from roots meaning what?
questions.f: Pachyderm comes from the Greek pachys, meaning thick, and derma, meaning skin.

questions.q: What is the fitting name for a group of leopards?
questions.f: Leopards are mostly solitary, so a leap of leopards together in the wild is a rare sight.

questions.q: What is the name for a group of giraffes?
questions.f: The name tower suits giraffes perfectly, since they are the tallest animals on land.

questions.q: What is the striking name for a group of ravens?
questions.f: Ravens are remarkably clever and can solve puzzles and even mimic human speech.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a venomous animal and a poisonous one?
c: Venom is injected, poison harms if touched or eaten
questions.f: A snake that bites to inject toxin is venomous, while a frog whose skin is toxic to touch is poisonous.

questions.q: The word 'predator' comes from a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: Predator comes from the Latin praedari, meaning to seize prey or plunder.

questions.q: The word 'cephalopod', the group of octopuses and squid, means what?
questions.f: Cephalopod comes from the Greek kephale, meaning head, and pous, meaning foot, since their arms attach near the head.

questions.q: The word 'gastropod', the group that includes snails, means what?
questions.f: Gastropod comes from the Greek gaster, meaning stomach, and pous, meaning foot, describing a snail's muscular underside.

questions.q: The Canary Islands were named after the little canary bird.
questions.f: It is the other way round; the islands were named first, from a Latin word for dogs, and the bird took their name.

questions.q: Butterflies and moths belong to the same group of insects.
questions.f: Both are members of Lepidoptera, the insect order whose name means scaly-winged.

questions.q: Bats are completely blind.
questions.f: All bats can see, and many also use echolocation to hunt in total darkness.

questions.q: Sharks have existed on Earth longer than trees have.
questions.f: Sharks appeared well over 400 million years ago, before the first trees ever grew.

questions.q: A rhinoceros horn is made of keratin, the same material as your hair and fingernails.
questions.f: Unlike a cow's horn, a rhino's horn has no bony core and is built entirely from packed keratin fibres.

questions.q: An octopus has more than one brain.
questions.f: An octopus has a central brain plus a cluster of nerve cells in each arm, so its arms can act almost on their own.

questions.q: Seahorses and pipefish are the only animals in which the father becomes pregnant.
questions.f: The male seahorse carries the developing young in a special pouch and gives birth to them.

questions.q: 'Bergmann's rule' observes that, within a group, animals living in colder climates tend to have what?
questions.f: A bigger body loses heat more slowly, which is why Arctic animals often out-size their warm-climate relatives; a related idea, Allen's rule, predicts shorter limbs.

questions.q: Which group of dinosaurs contained the largest land animals that have ever lived?
questions.f: Long-necked sauropods such as Argentinosaurus may have reached 70 tonnes, held up by bones full of air spaces.

questions.q: Which extinct bird of Madagascar laid the largest eggs known from any animal?
questions.f: An elephant bird egg held about as much as 150 chicken eggs, and its closest living relative is the little kiwi.

questions.q: Which pouched predator, last seen alive in a Hobart zoo in 1936, is now extinct?
questions.f: Nicknamed the Tasmanian tiger, the thylacine had a pouch in both sexes and could open its jaws remarkably wide.

questions.q: Which huge sea mammal was hunted to extinction within 30 years of being described in 1741?
questions.f: Steller's sea cow grew to nine metres, grazing kelp in the cold North Pacific, and was gone by about 1768.

questions.q: Which flightless North Atlantic seabird became extinct in 1844?
questions.f: The great auk stood 80 cm tall and swam superbly, filling much the same role in the north as penguins do in the south.

questions.q: Which living bird is the dodo's closest relative?
questions.f: DNA showed the dodo was a giant flightless pigeon that lost the need to fly on predator-free Mauritius.

questions.q: Which horse is the only one alive today that was never domesticated?
questions.f: Przewalski's horse was saved from extinction by zoos and now roams the Mongolian steppe and the Chernobyl exclusion zone.

questions.q: Which antelope became the first animal ever moved off the 'extinct in the wild' list?
questions.f: Operation Oryx bred the last few in captivity, and released herds now number in the thousands in Oman and beyond.

questions.q: Which small porpoise of the Gulf of California is the world's rarest marine mammal?
questions.f: Fewer than a dozen vaquitas may remain, and the species was not even described by scientists until 1958.

questions.q: Which flightless New Zealand parrot attracts mates with a deep booming call?
questions.f: A male kakapo digs a bowl in the earth to amplify his boom, which can carry five kilometres across the hills.

questions.q: Which lemur taps on branches and listens for grubs moving inside the wood?
questions.f: The aye-aye then hooks the grub out with a long, thin middle finger that it keeps curled up while walking.

questions.q: Which antelope of the Central Asian steppe has a strange, bulbous, trunk-like nose?
questions.f: The saiga's odd nose warms freezing winter air and filters out summer dust before it reaches the lungs.

questions.q: Which is the only primate that lives almost entirely on grass?
questions.f: Geladas graze the high meadows of Ethiopia and have the strongest fingers of any primate for plucking grass blades.

questions.q: Which monkey is the only one living wild in Europe?
questions.f: A famous troop lives on the Rock of Gibraltar, the only wild monkeys anywhere on the European mainland.

questions.q: The Rh factor in human blood types is named after which animal?
questions.f: The factor was first identified in experiments with rhesus monkey blood, which is why it is called Rh.

questions.q: Which mammal is the most capable glider, sailing over 100 metres between trees?
questions.f: The colugo's gliding membrane stretches even between its fingers and toes, making it a living kite.

questions.q: Which tree-dwelling carnivore of Asia is famous for smelling like hot popcorn?
questions.f: The scent comes from a chemical also produced when popcorn is cooked, and the binturong uses it to mark its territory.

questions.q: Which animal has the strongest bite force relative to its body size among mammals?
questions.f: A Tasmanian devil's jaws can crush bone, letting it eat every scrap of a carcass and waste nothing.

questions.q: Which small striped marsupial eats almost nothing but termites?
questions.f: A numbat gets through around 20,000 termites a day using a tongue longer than half its head.

questions.q: Which lizard glides between trees on wings supported by its own ribs?
questions.f: The Draco spreads elongated ribs to open flaps of skin, gliding up to 30 metres between trunks.

questions.q: Which beetle defends itself by spraying a boiling-hot chemical jet?
questions.f: It mixes two chemicals in a hardened chamber, and the reaction fires the spray out at around 100 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Which desert beetle collects drinking water from morning fog on its own back?
questions.f: Bumps on its shell gather fog droplets that roll down to its mouth, and the design now inspires water-harvesting materials.

questions.q: The deep red food dye carmine is made from which creature?
questions.f: Cochineal insects are dried and crushed to make carmine, for centuries one of the most valuable exports of Mexico after silver.

questions.q: Iron gall ink, used for centuries of European documents, needed growths made by which insect?
questions.f: Oak galls grown by wasp larvae were crushed and mixed with iron salts, making the ink used by Bach and Leonardo.

questions.q: Which animals were the first living creatures sent into space, in 1947?
questions.f: Fruit flies rode a captured V-2 rocket to about 100 km up and parachuted back alive.

questions.q: Dolbear's law says you can estimate the air temperature by counting what?
questions.f: Count a cricket's chirps for 14 seconds and add 40 to get a rough temperature in Fahrenheit.

questions.q: Which insect has the fastest self-powered strike of any animal, its jaws snapping shut in a flash?
questions.f: The jaws close in about 0.1 milliseconds, and the ant can even fire them at the ground to catapult itself away.

questions.q: In a honeypot ant colony, what job do certain swollen workers perform?
c: They act as living food stores
questions.f: These workers hang from the ceiling swollen with sugary liquid and feed the colony from their own bodies in hard times.

questions.q: How do army ants cross a gap in their path?
c: They link their bodies into a living bridge
questions.f: Ants join legs to build a bridge, and it automatically widens or shifts to make the whole column's journey shortest.

questions.q: Which animals' mounds inspired the natural cooling design of the Eastgate Centre in Zimbabwe?
questions.f: The building copies the way termite mounds move air through chimneys and vents, cutting its cooling energy dramatically.

questions.q: Bumblebees can sense which surprising signal given off by flowers?
questions.f: A flower's electric field changes after a visit, so bees can tell which blooms have already been emptied.

questions.q: Charles Darwin predicted that a Madagascan orchid with a 30 cm nectar tube must be pollinated by what?
c: A moth with a very long tongue
questions.f: Decades later a hawk moth with a tongue that long was found, exactly as he had predicted.

questions.q: How do tiger moths defend themselves against hunting bats?
c: They click to jam the bat's sonar
They fold their wings and drop
They glow to warn them off
questions.f: The ultrasonic clicks confuse the bat's echoes, one of the oldest known arms races in the animal world.

questions.q: Why did dark-coloured peppered moths become common in industrial England?
c: Soot-blackened trees hid dark moths better
questions.f: When air cleaned up, pale moths returned to dominance, making this one of the clearest examples of evolution watched in real time.

questions.q: The word 'kangaroo' entered English from which source?
questions.f: It comes from gangurru in the Guugu Yimithirr language, recorded by Captain Cook's crew in 1770.

questions.q: Despite its name, the 'mongoose' has nothing to do with geese, because its name comes from what?
c: An Indian word borrowed into English
questions.f: It comes from the Marathi word mangus; English speakers simply reshaped the ending into a familiar bird name.

questions.q: The name 'moose' comes from an Algonquian word meaning what?
questions.f: The name describes exactly how a moose feeds, stripping twigs and bark from trees with its lips.

questions.q: The name 'raccoon' comes from a Powhatan word describing what?
c: One that scratches with its hands
questions.f: From aroughcun, and a raccoon's front paws really are packed with touch sensors for feeling out food.

questions.q: The name 'opossum' comes from a Powhatan word meaning what?
questions.f: Early English colonists borrowed the word directly, and the animal's pale, pointed face does look rather dog-like.

questions.q: The name 'chipmunk' comes from an Ojibwe word describing an animal that does what?
questions.f: The original word describes the head-first way a chipmunk scurries down a trunk.

questions.q: The name 'caribou' comes from a Mi'kmaq word meaning what?
questions.f: Caribou paw through deep snow with broad hooves to reach the lichen buried beneath.

questions.q: The name 'woodchuck' surprisingly has nothing to do with wood, coming instead from what?
questions.f: English speakers reshaped a native name such as wuchak into words they already knew: wood and chuck.

questions.q: The word 'albatross' came into English from a Portuguese word for which bird?
questions.f: Portuguese alcatraz meant pelican, and the same word later named a famous island prison in San Francisco Bay.

questions.q: The word 'penguin' may come from roots meaning what?
questions.f: The Welsh pen gwyn, white head, was probably first used for the great auk and later transferred to penguins.

questions.q: The word 'pelican' comes from a Greek root meaning what?
questions.f: From pelekan, linked to pelekys, an axe, most likely describing the bird's great chopping bill.

questions.q: The word 'condor' entered English from which language of South America?
questions.f: From the Quechua kuntur; the Andean condor was sacred in Inca belief as a messenger of the upper world.

questions.q: The word 'coyote' came into English from which language?
questions.f: From the Aztec word coyotl, passed through Spanish; in Aztec stories the coyote was a clever trickster.

questions.q: The word 'jaguar' comes from a Tupi word describing what?
c: A beast that kills with one leap
questions.f: From yaguara; a jaguar really does dispatch prey with one sudden pounce rather than a long chase.

questions.q: The word 'iguana' came into English from which people's language?
questions.f: From the Taino word iwana, one of the first animal names Europeans borrowed from the Americas.

questions.q: The word 'manatee' came into English from a Caribbean language, probably meaning what?
questions.f: From the Carib manattoui; manatees nurse their calves from teats under the flippers, which may explain the name.

questions.q: The animal name 'gnu' came from a southern African language and imitates what?
questions.f: Khoikhoi speakers named the wildebeest for the sound it makes, a nasal snort that carries across the plains.

questions.q: The name 'badger' probably comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: The white blaze on its face looks like a heraldic badge, and the French name blaireau also refers to the marking.

questions.q: The word 'lynx' comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: The root also gives us the Greek for lamp, and the lynx has long been a symbol of sharp eyesight.

questions.q: What do we call the membrane of skin that lets a bat, sugar glider, or colugo fly or glide?
questions.f: In bats the patagium stretches between hugely elongated finger bones, making the wing a webbed hand.

questions.q: What do we call the transparent 'third eyelid' that sweeps across the eye of a bird or crocodile?
questions.f: A diving bird uses it as built-in goggles, and it also shields a hawk's eye as it crashes into cover.

questions.q: What do we call the ability of sharks and platypuses to detect prey by its electrical activity?
questions.f: Every twitching muscle leaks a tiny electric field, so a shark can find a flatfish completely buried in sand.

questions.q: What do we call an animal's ability to sense the Earth's magnetic field for navigation?
questions.f: Sea turtles, robins, and salmon all seem to use it, and in some birds it may involve light-sensitive proteins in the eye.

questions.q: What do we call light produced by a living animal's own body chemistry?
questions.f: Most of the animals on Earth that make their own light live in the deep sea, where sunlight never reaches.

questions.q: A mule is the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse.
questions.f: The reverse pairing, a male horse with a female donkey, produces a smaller animal called a hinny.

questions.q: Owls have no sense of smell whatsoever.
questions.f: Owls do smell, though weakly; they simply rely far more on their extraordinary hearing and night vision.

questions.q: Which Australian turtle can stay underwater for days by absorbing oxygen through its rear end?
questions.f: It also grows a green mohawk of algae on its head, earning it the nickname the punk turtle.

questions.q: How does an alligator snapping turtle attract fish to its mouth?
c: It wiggles a worm-like lure on its tongue
questions.f: The turtle lies motionless with its mouth open, twitching a pink tongue extension that looks exactly like a wriggling worm.

questions.q: Jonathan, hatched around 1832 and living on St Helena, is the oldest known living land animal of which kind?
questions.f: This Seychelles giant tortoise has outlived every human who has ever met him and still enjoys bananas.

questions.q: Which reptile dives deeper than any other, reaching more than a kilometre down?
questions.f: Its shell is flexible and oily rather than hard and bony, so it can squash slightly instead of cracking under pressure.

questions.q: Which is the only snake known to build a nest for its eggs?
questions.f: The female king cobra gathers leaves into a mound with her coils and guards it fiercely until the eggs hatch.

questions.q: What is unusual about every known Brahminy blind snake?
questions.f: They reproduce without males, so a single snake carried in a plant pot can start a whole new population.

questions.q: What does a hognose snake do when threatened and its bluffing fails?
c: Sprays a smell like a skunk
questions.f: It flops upside down with its tongue hanging out, and will even flip back over if you right it.

questions.q: How does the tentacled snake catch fish so reliably?
c: It twitches to make the fish dart into its jaws
It stuns them with venom first
It uses its tentacles as nets
questions.f: The snake fakes a movement that triggers the fish's escape reflex, so the fish flees straight into the waiting mouth.

questions.q: Why does a marine iguana of the Galapagos sneeze so often?
c: To fire out excess salt from its glands
questions.f: During harsh El Nino years marine iguanas can also shrink their skeletons slightly to need less food.

questions.q: A medicine for type 2 diabetes was developed from the venom of which animal?
questions.f: A protein in Gila monster venom keeps blood sugar steady for hours, inspiring a whole family of modern drugs.

questions.q: Which pale, blind cave amphibian of Europe can live for around a century?
questions.f: Locals once thought olms washing out of caves were baby dragons, and one was recorded staying still for seven years.

questions.q: Which frog has skin so clear that you can see its organs through its belly?
questions.f: While it sleeps, a glass frog tucks most of its red blood cells into its liver so it becomes even harder to spot.

questions.q: How does a male Darwin's frog protect its developing young?
c: It carries them in its vocal sac
It glues them to its back
It guards them in a bubble nest
questions.f: The tadpoles grow inside their father's throat pouch and hop out of his mouth as tiny frogs.

questions.q: Which is the largest frog in the world?
questions.f: The Goliath frog of West Africa grows to 32 cm and shifts heavy stones to build nursery pools for its eggs.

questions.q: Which animal is the smallest known vertebrate, small enough to sit on a fingertip?
questions.f: Paedophryne amauensis measures about 7.7 mm and was found by tracking its insect-like call in leaf litter.

questions.q: Cane toads were released into Australia in 1935 in an attempt to control what?
questions.f: The toads barely touched the beetles, spread across the continent, and became one of history's worst invasive species.

questions.q: Which is the only fish known to be fully warm-blooded throughout its body?
questions.f: The opah circulates warm blood using a heat exchanger in its gills, letting it hunt actively in cold, deep water.

questions.q: Much of the white sand on a tropical beach has passed through which animal?
questions.f: A parrotfish scrapes coral for algae and grinds the rock in its gut, producing hundreds of kilograms of sand a year.

questions.q: Which reef fish has been seen recruiting a moray eel to help it hunt?
questions.f: A grouper signals with a head shake, and the eel flushes prey out of crevices the grouper cannot reach.

questions.q: How does the Hawaiian bobtail squid produce its glow?
c: It farms glowing bacteria in a light organ
questions.f: The squid glows downwards to erase its own shadow, and it evicts most of the bacteria each dawn to start again.

questions.q: Which shark is the only one known to be omnivorous, digesting seagrass as well as prey?
questions.f: Seagrass makes up more than half a bonnethead's diet, and it has the gut enzymes to actually digest it.

questions.q: Which small shark can walk across exposed reef and survive hours with almost no oxygen?
questions.f: It uses its fins like legs between tide pools and can shut down parts of its brain to save oxygen.

questions.q: What is remarkable about a goblin shark's jaws?
c: They shoot forward like a slingshot
questions.f: Elastic ligaments fling the jaws out of the mouth, one of the fastest bites measured in any shark.

questions.q: A zebra shark named Leonie surprised scientists in 2016 by doing what?
questions.f: After years apart from any male, Leonie switched to reproducing on her own, a first recorded in her species.

questions.q: Which fish has the largest brain relative to its body size?
questions.f: Manta rays have been filmed inspecting their own reflection, behaviour that hints at self-awareness.

questions.q: Which giant Amazon fish must breathe air at the surface and has famously tough scales?
questions.f: Its layered scales are so hard that piranha teeth cannot pierce them, and engineers study them for body armour.

questions.q: A clam-like animal that bores through wood inspired Marc Brunel's tunnelling shield. Which one?
questions.f: Brunel watched a shipworm rasp into timber while lining its tunnel behind it, then used the same idea under the Thames.

questions.q: Which sea slug keeps working algae parts in its body so it can live partly on sunlight?
questions.f: It swallows algae, stores their photosynthesis machinery, and can then survive for months on light alone.

questions.q: How does a giant tube worm at a deep-sea vent feed, given it has no mouth or gut?
c: Bacteria inside it turn chemicals into food
questions.f: Billions of bacteria inside the worm live on hydrogen sulfide from the vent, feeding the worm from within.

questions.q: Which sea creature's tadpole-like larva reveals it as a close relative of animals with backbones?
questions.f: A young sea squirt has a stiffening rod like a simple backbone, then settles down and absorbs its own brain.

questions.q: King Henry I of England is said to have died in 1135 after eating too many of which animals?
questions.f: Lampreys were a royal delicacy, and these jawless fish have changed little in 350 million years.

questions.q: An animal nicknamed 'Ming', found in 2006 and aged at 507 years, was which creature?
questions.f: Scientists counted the growth rings in the ocean quahog's shell, only to find they had ended the oldest known animal's life.

questions.q: How many eyes does a box jellyfish have?
questions.f: Some of those eyes have lenses and retinas like ours, yet the animal has no brain to process the pictures.

questions.q: Which is the only bird known to go into true, long-lasting hibernation?
questions.f: A poorwill can spend weeks tucked among rocks with its body cooled right down, something no other bird does.

questions.q: What do we call the swirling evening cloud formed by thousands of starlings?
questions.f: Each bird tracks about seven neighbours, and that simple rule produces the whole shifting shape.

questions.q: What do we call a group of apes?
questions.f: The old term nods to how clever apes are, and chimpanzees can outperform people at some memory tasks.

questions.q: What do we call a group of vultures feeding together on the ground?
questions.f: Vultures circling in the air have their own name too: a kettle.

questions.q: What do we call a group of larks?
questions.f: Exaltation means a lifting up, fitting a bird that sings while climbing high into the sky.

questions.q: What do we call a group of ferrets?
questions.f: It probably began as a busyness, describing how restlessly ferrets bustle about.

questions.q: What do we call a group of alligators?
questions.f: Alligators gather in shrinking dry-season pools, and big males bellow so hard the water dances above their backs.

questions.q: What do we call a young oyster that has just settled onto a surface?
questions.f: Oyster farmers collect spat on old shells, giving the young oysters somewhere solid to cement themselves.

questions.q: What do we call a young turkey?
questions.f: Poult comes from the same root as poultry and the French poulet, meaning young fowl.

questions.q: What do we call a litter of piglets born together?
questions.f: To farrow also means to give birth, and a sow may farrow twice a year.

questions.q: What do we call an animal at the very top of its food chain, hunted by nothing else?
questions.f: Apex comes from the Latin for peak or summit, and removing an apex predator can reshape a whole ecosystem.

questions.q: What do we call a species whose presence holds an entire ecosystem together?
questions.f: Sea otters are the classic example: without them, urchins strip the kelp forests bare.

questions.q: If an animal is 'endemic' to an island, what does that mean?
c: It is found naturally nowhere else
questions.f: Endemic comes from Greek roots meaning in the people or in a place, and islands are full of endemic species.

questions.q: What do we call a species that spreads into a new region and harms the wildlife already there?
questions.f: Invasive species are among the biggest causes of extinction, because local animals have no defences against them.

questions.q: What do we call a domesticated animal that has gone back to living wild?
questions.f: Feral comes from the Latin fera, meaning wild beast; feral pigeons and cats live in cities worldwide.

questions.q: The two-part scientific naming system for animals was created by which scientist?
questions.f: Linnaeus gave every species a genus and species name in Latin, so Homo sapiens and Panthera leo work in any language.

questions.q: In the scientific name Panthera leo, what does the first word 'Panthera' represent?
questions.f: Sharing a genus shows close kinship: Panthera also covers tigers, leopards, and jaguars.

questions.q: An 'ectothermic' animal gets its body heat from where?
questions.f: Ectotherms such as lizards need far less food than mammals of the same size, since they do not pay to stay warm.

questions.q: What do we call it when a lizard deliberately drops its own tail to escape?
questions.f: Autotomy means self-cutting, and the tail keeps thrashing to hold a predator's attention while the lizard slips away.

questions.q: What is the scientific name for the shedding of an insect's or crab's outgrown exoskeleton?
questions.f: Ecdysis comes from a Greek word meaning to strip off, and a freshly moulted crab is soft for days.

questions.q: What do we call the short-term deep sleep a hummingbird enters overnight to save energy?
questions.f: A hummingbird's heart rate can fall from over 1,000 beats a minute to about 50 while it is in torpor.

questions.q: What do we call the winter dormancy of reptiles, which is not quite hibernation?
questions.f: A brumating tortoise still wakes on mild days to drink, unlike a truly hibernating mammal.

questions.q: What is the name of the vocal organ a bird sings with?
questions.f: The syrinx sits where the windpipe splits in two, so some birds can sing two notes at once.

questions.q: What is an 'owl pellet'?
c: A coughed-up parcel of bones and fur
questions.f: Owls swallow prey whole and bring up the indigestible parts, so scientists can read an owl's diet from its pellets.

questions.q: What does a bird's preen gland, near the base of its tail, produce?
questions.f: A bird spreads the oil through its feathers while preening, keeping them supple and shedding rain.

questions.q: Crocodiles are more closely related to birds than to lizards.
questions.f: Crocodiles and birds are the last survivors of the archosaurs, the group that also included the dinosaurs.

questions.q: An elephant's tusks are enormously enlarged canine teeth.
questions.f: They are actually incisors, the front teeth, which is why they sit at the very front of the upper jaw.

questions.q: Which insect pollinates cacao flowers, making it the creature the world chocolate supply depends on?
questions.f: Cacao flowers are so awkwardly shaped that only these millimetre-long flies can reach in, and most flowers still fail.

questions.q: Which animal has the highest blood pressure of any creature, needed to pump blood up to its brain?
questions.f: A giraffe's heart must generate enormous pressure, and special valves in its neck stop blood rushing to its head when it bends down to drink.

questions.q: A raptor that stains its pale feathers orange in iron-rich mud, a Spanish name meaning bone-breaker, and food dropped from a height onto rocks?
questions.f: Roughly 85% of a lammergeier's diet is bone, dissolved by stomach acid strong enough to handle it.

questions.q: A paper-thin shell secreted by two specialised arms, a female that traps air at the surface to control her depth, and a name shared with Greek sailors?
questions.f: The argonaut, or paper nautilus, is an octopus, and it makes its shell itself rather than inheriting one.

questions.q: Swivelling hooks instead of suckers, the first intact adult hauled from the Ross Sea in 2007, and a beak bigger than any other squid's?
questions.f: It also has the largest eyes of any animal that has ever lived, each roughly the size of a dinner plate.

questions.q: A toxin also found in the feathers of a New Guinea bird, a home in Colombia's Choco rainforest, and a name taken from a hunting weapon?
questions.f: Batrachotoxin turns up in both this frog and the pitohui bird, probably built from beetles both of them eat.

questions.q: Two tusk-like teeth that erupt only in males, a life almost never glimpsed at the surface, and breath-holds of over three hours?
questions.f: It holds the mammal record for both depth and duration, diving nearly three kilometres down.

questions.q: Which bird has passed the mirror test, appearing to recognise itself in a reflection?
questions.f: When a mark was placed on a magpie, it tried to remove the mark while looking in a mirror, a sign of self-awareness.

questions.q: Life cycles of 13 or 17 years, both prime numbers, broods labelled with Roman numerals, and emergences of over a million insects an acre?
