questions.f: Prime-numbered cycles are hard for predators to breed in step with, so the strategy keeps the swarm safe.

questions.q: Which flatworm can be cut into pieces that each regrow into a complete new animal, brain included?
questions.f: Planarians are packed with stem cells, letting them rebuild any body part, even a whole new head.

questions.q: A museum curator named Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, a hinged joint inside the skull, and a name meaning hollow spine?
questions.f: Her 1938 find off South Africa revealed a fish known only from 66-million-year-old fossils.

questions.q: Which snake has the longest fangs of any venomous snake?
questions.f: A Gaboon viper's fangs can reach about five centimetres, the longest of any snake, folding back when not in use.

questions.q: Which small sea animal has teeth made of the strongest known natural material?
questions.f: Limpet teeth are reinforced with mineral fibres that outmatch even spider silk in strength for their size.

questions.q: A hollow helmet of spongy keratin, the lowest-frequency call recorded in any bird, and a role as chief gardener of the rainforest?
questions.f: Its booming call sits at the edge of human hearing, and its droppings spread the seeds of dozens of rainforest trees.

questions.q: Which sea slug steals the stinging cells of its prey and reuses them for its own defence?
questions.f: The blue dragon eats venomous jellyfish, then stores their unfired stingers in its own body to sting attackers.

questions.q: Which small, rock-dwelling animal is one of the elephant's closest living relatives?
questions.f: Despite looking like a plump rodent, the hyrax shares an ancient ancestor with elephants and manatees.

questions.q: A tail nearly as long as the rest of its body, a hunting whip that stuns whole shoals, and eyes enlarged for dawn dives?
questions.f: It is the only fish known to hunt by whipping its tail overhead like a bullwhip, cracking through the water.

questions.q: Which insect has been shown to navigate in a straight line using the light of the Milky Way?
questions.f: On a clear night a dung beetle uses the glowing band of our galaxy as a compass to roll its ball away in a straight line.

questions.q: Which fish holds one of the largest genomes, with far more DNA than a human?
questions.f: The marbled lungfish carries about 40 times more DNA than a person, the largest genome known in any animal.

questions.q: Which tiny mammal has the fastest heartbeat, racing over 1,000 beats a minute?
questions.f: The Etruscan shrew must eat almost constantly, since its blazing metabolism would otherwise starve it within hours.

questions.q: Which fish 'walks' along the seafloor using leg-like fins instead of swimming?
questions.f: The rare handfish uses its front fins like little hands to amble across the seabed.

questions.q: Which spider weaves the toughest silk known and spins webs across entire rivers?
questions.f: Darwin's bark spider silk is tougher than any other known, and its webs can span more than 25 metres over water.

questions.q: Which amphibian has no lungs at all and breathes entirely through its skin?
questions.f: Lungless salamanders make up the largest salamander family, absorbing oxygen straight through their moist skin.

questions.q: Which desert rodent can live its whole life without ever drinking a drop of water?
questions.f: The kangaroo rat makes water inside its body from the dry seeds it eats and has kidneys that waste almost none of it.

questions.q: Which bird's chicks have working claws on their wings, a trait from ancient ancestors?
questions.f: Young hoatzins use the claws on their wings to clamber through branches, then lose them as they grow up.

questions.q: An animal described by science only in 1998 off Sulawesi, six arms hidden in a burrow while two trail as a 'snake', and a swimming style copied from a poisonous flatfish?
questions.f: It is the only animal known to impersonate this many different species, picking whichever suits the threat.

questions.q: Haemoglobin that grips oxygen more tightly than any other bird's, muscle packed with extra capillaries, and a climb made at night in denser air?
questions.f: It crosses the Himalaya where the air holds a third of the oxygen at sea level, and it does so in a single day.

questions.q: A snout lined with pores that sense electric fields, a blade swung sideways through schools of fish, and an animal that is really a ray, not a shark?
questions.f: The saw carries thousands of tiny sensors, so it works as both a detector and a weapon.

questions.q: Which insect grows its own food by farming fungus in underground gardens?
questions.f: Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry; they use them to grow a fungus that becomes their food.

questions.q: A species that once made up a quarter of all North American birds, nesting colonies kilometres wide, and a captive female named Martha?
questions.f: Martha died in Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, ending a species whose flocks had darkened the sky for hours.

questions.q: Which small Caribbean mammal is one of the few that delivers venom through grooved teeth?
questions.f: The solenodon is a living fossil, little changed since it shared the Earth with the last dinosaurs.

questions.q: Which deep-sea fish has a jelly-like body suited to the crushing pressure far below the surface?
questions.f: In its deep home the blobfish looks like a normal fish; it only appears droopy when brought up to the low-pressure surface.

questions.q: A bird that keeps a favourite tool tucked under its foot, a hook whittled from a twig with its beak, and a home on one Pacific island?
questions.f: It makes and stores tools, ranks them by usefulness, and passes designs on: skills once thought unique to primates.

questions.q: Which nocturnal primate has eyes so large that each one is bigger than its brain?
questions.f: A tarsier cannot move its huge fixed eyes, so it swivels its head almost all the way around like an owl.

questions.q: Which toad carries its developing young embedded in the skin of its own back?
questions.f: Baby Surinam toads emerge fully formed straight from little pockets in their mother's back, skipping the free-swimming tadpole stage.

questions.q: An animal the Vatican once ruled could be eaten during Lent as though it were fish, a habit of re-digesting its own droppings, and teeth that never stop growing?
questions.f: Colonial settlers in South America wanted to eat it on fast days, so it was officially reclassified as 'fish'.

questions.q: Which sea snail hunts fish by firing a venomous harpoon-like tooth?
questions.f: A cone snail's harpoon strikes in a flash, and some species carry venom powerful enough to be dangerous to people.

questions.q: Which reptile gives birth to live young at sea and may never touch land in its life?
questions.f: The yellow-bellied sea snake drifts on ocean currents and bears its young in the open water, never coming ashore.

questions.q: Which eel-shaped fish defends itself by producing huge amounts of slime and tying itself in knots?
questions.f: A hagfish can turn a bucket of water into slime in seconds, then slide out of its own slime by knotting its body.

questions.q: A forehead melon it can visibly reshape, no dorsal fin at all, and neck vertebrae left unfused so it can turn its head?
questions.f: Nicknamed the sea canary, the beluga has such a wide range of chirps and whistles that whalers heard them through hulls.

questions.q: Which sea animal can change not only its colour but also the texture of its skin to match surroundings?
questions.f: A cuttlefish can raise bumps and ridges on its skin and flash colours in waves, all while being colour-blind itself.

questions.q: Which shrimp snaps a claw so fast it creates a bubble hot enough to stun its prey?
questions.f: The collapsing bubble from a pistol shrimp's snap makes a bang louder than a jet engine and a flash of light.

questions.q: Which fish knocks insects off overhanging leaves by spitting a precise jet of water?
questions.f: An archerfish adjusts its aim for the way light bends between air and water, hitting targets a metre away.

questions.q: Which bat has a tongue longer than its whole body, perfect for reaching deep into flowers?
questions.f: Its tongue is about 1.5 times its body length, the longest tongue relative to body size of any mammal.

questions.q: Which desert lizard drinks by channelling dew along grooves in its skin straight to its mouth?
questions.f: The thorny devil's skin acts like blotting paper, pulling water from damp sand up to its mouth against gravity.

questions.q: Which whale is believed to be the longest-lived mammal, reaching over 200 years?
questions.f: Old stone harpoon tips have been found in living bowhead whales, hinting they were hunted well over a century earlier.

questions.q: Which African bird builds massive shared nests that can house hundreds of birds for generations?
questions.f: A sociable weaver colony's giant thatched nest can last a hundred years and be seen from far across the desert.

questions.q: Which is the only primate known to have a venomous bite?
questions.f: A slow loris mixes a substance from a gland on its arm with its saliva to give its bite a venomous punch.

questions.q: A coat that fades to near-white in the hottest months, widely splayed hooves for soft sand, and a Saharan antelope down to a few dozen in the wild?
questions.f: The addax takes every drop of water it needs from desert plants, and its pale summer coat reflects the sun.

questions.q: Which flightless bird is the largest bird in the Americas?
questions.f: The male greater rhea raises the chicks alone, guarding eggs laid by several different females in one nest.

questions.q: Which mole has a star of 22 fleshy feelers on its snout and is the fastest-eating mammal?
questions.f: The star-nosed mole can find, identify, and gulp down a morsel of food in under a quarter of a second.

questions.q: The science of 'cetology' is the study of which animals?
questions.f: Cetology comes from the Greek ketos, meaning a great sea monster or whale.

questions.q: The science of 'malacology' is the study of which animals?
questions.f: Malacology comes from the Greek malakos, meaning soft, describing the soft bodies of snails, clams, and squid.

questions.q: The science of 'lepidopterology' is the study of which creatures?
questions.f: The name shares the root lepis, meaning scale, referring to the tiny scales that coat their wings.

questions.q: The science of 'myrmecology' is the study of which insects?
questions.f: Myrmecology comes from the Greek myrmex, meaning ant, and studies one of Earth's most numerous creatures.

questions.q: The science of 'apiology' is the study of which insects?
questions.f: Apiology comes from the Latin apis, meaning bee, and helps beekeepers understand their hives.

questions.q: The science of 'oology' is the study of which part of animal life?
questions.f: Oology comes from the Greek oion, meaning egg, and once involved collecting birds' eggs to study them.

questions.q: The bat order 'Chiroptera' has a name that means what?
questions.f: Chiroptera comes from the Greek cheir, meaning hand, and pteron, meaning wing, since a bat's wing is a webbed hand.

questions.q: The butterfly-and-moth order 'Lepidoptera' has a name meaning what?
questions.f: Lepidoptera comes from the Greek lepis, meaning scale, and pteron, meaning wing.

questions.q: The beetle order 'Coleoptera' has a name meaning what?
questions.f: Coleoptera comes from the Greek koleos, meaning sheath, since a beetle's hard front wings cover the delicate flying wings.

questions.q: The order 'Hymenoptera', which includes bees, wasps, and ants, has a name meaning what?
questions.f: Hymenoptera comes from the Greek hymen, meaning membrane, describing their thin, clear wings.

questions.q: The fly order 'Diptera' has a name meaning what?
questions.f: Diptera comes from the Greek di, meaning two, and pteron, meaning wing, since true flies have a single pair of wings.

questions.q: The word 'proboscis', the long feeding tube of a butterfly or elephant, comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: Proboscis comes from Greek roots meaning a means for taking food, from pro plus boskein, to feed.

questions.q: An animal described as 'oviparous' does what?
questions.f: Oviparous comes from the Latin ovum, meaning egg, and covers birds, most reptiles, and fish.

questions.q: An animal described as 'viviparous' does what?
questions.f: Viviparous comes from the Latin vivus, meaning alive, and describes most mammals.

questions.q: In 'ovoviviparous' animals, what happens to the eggs?
c: They hatch inside the mother's body
They are carried by the father
questions.f: Many sharks are ovoviviparous, keeping eggs safe inside the body until the pups hatch and are then born live.

questions.q: The word 'parthenogenesis' describes reproduction that happens how?
questions.f: Parthenogenesis comes from Greek roots meaning virgin origin, and some lizards, insects, and sharks can do it.

questions.q: An animal that is 'crepuscular' is most active at what time?
questions.f: Crepuscular comes from the Latin crepusculum, meaning twilight, the dim light favoured by deer and rabbits.

questions.q: An animal described as 'fossorial' is adapted for what?
questions.f: Fossorial comes from the Latin fossor, meaning digger, and describes moles and many burrowing animals.

questions.q: An animal described as 'saltatorial' is built for what?
questions.f: From the Latin saltare, to leap; kangaroos, jerboas, and frogs are all saltatorial.

questions.q: An animal described as 'cursorial' is specially adapted for what?
questions.f: Cursorial comes from the Latin currere, meaning to run, and fits cheetahs, ostriches, and greyhounds.

questions.q: An animal that is 'plantigrade' walks in which way?
c: On the soles of its feet
questions.f: Plantigrade comes from the Latin planta, meaning sole, and describes bears, raccoons, and humans.

questions.q: An animal that is 'digitigrade' walks in which way?
questions.f: Digitigrade comes from the Latin digitus, meaning finger or toe, and describes cats and dogs, which stand on their toes.

questions.q: An animal that is 'unguligrade' walks in which way?
c: On the tips of its hooves
questions.f: Unguligrade comes from the Latin ungula, meaning hoof, and describes horses and deer, which walk on hoof tips.

questions.q: What defines a 'eusocial' animal?
c: Castes, shared brood care, and overlapping generations
Simply living in a large herd
questions.f: Ants, termites, and naked mole-rats are eusocial, the most tightly organised societies in the animal world.

questions.q: The term 'aposematism' describes an animal using what?
questions.f: Aposematism comes from Greek roots meaning a sign that keeps away, like the bold colours of a poison dart frog.

questions.q: The term 'crypsis' describes an animal's ability to do what?
c: Blend in and avoid being seen
questions.f: Crypsis comes from the Greek kryptos, meaning hidden, the same root as in the word cryptic.

questions.q: In 'Batesian mimicry', what does a harmless animal do?
c: Copies the look of a dangerous one
questions.f: A harmless hoverfly with wasp-like stripes uses Batesian mimicry to trick predators into leaving it alone.

questions.q: What does 'kleptoparasitism' describe?
c: Stealing food another animal has caught
questions.f: Frigatebirds harry boobies until they drop their catch, and hyenas rob wild dogs the same way.

questions.q: An 'anadromous' fish does what?
c: Migrates from the sea into fresh water to breed
Migrates from rivers to the sea to breed
questions.f: Salmon are the classic example; eels do the reverse, which is called catadromous.

questions.q: In 'commensalism', how are the two species affected?
c: One benefits and the other is unaffected
questions.f: A barnacle riding on a whale gets a free trip through food-rich waters while the whale barely notices it.

questions.q: A 'brood parasite' such as the cuckoo does what?
c: Lays its eggs in another bird's nest
questions.f: By tricking other birds into raising its chicks, a brood parasite avoids all the hard work of parenting.

questions.q: An 'altricial' animal is born in what condition?
questions.f: Altricial chicks, like those of robins, hatch blind and featherless and depend completely on their parents.

questions.q: A 'precocial' animal is born in what condition?
questions.f: Precocial young, like ducklings and foals, can walk and feed themselves within hours of being born.

questions.q: The word 'pinniped', the group of seals and walruses, means what?
questions.f: Pinniped comes from the Latin pinna, meaning fin, and pes, meaning foot.

questions.q: A 'coprolite' is the fossilised remains of what?
questions.f: Coprolites reveal what extinct animals actually ate, right down to fish scales and bone fragments.

questions.q: The word 'monotreme' refers to a group of mammals named for what feature?
c: A single opening for waste and eggs
questions.f: From Greek roots meaning one hole; the platypus and echidnas are the only monotremes left.

questions.q: A 'ruminant' is an animal known for doing what?
c: Chewing cud from a multi-chambered stomach
questions.f: Ruminants like cows and deer bring food back up to chew again, breaking down tough grasses more fully.

questions.q: What are 'zooxanthellae'?
questions.f: These algae feed their coral hosts, and losing them is exactly what turns a bleached reef white.

questions.q: The tough material 'chitin' forms which part of an insect?
questions.f: Chitin is a strong, lightweight substance that also forms the shells of crabs and the beaks of squid.

questions.q: The name 'aardvark' comes from words meaning 'earth pig'.
questions.f: Aardvark comes from an old Afrikaans phrase for earth pig, describing the burrowing animal's pig-like snout.

questions.q: Octopuses can edit their own genetic instructions to help them cope with cold water.
questions.f: Octopuses and their relatives can rewrite their RNA on the fly, a rare ability that helps their nerves work in the cold.

questions.q: 'Aestivation' is like hibernation, but it is a deep rest to survive hot, dry summers instead of cold winters.
questions.f: Some lungfish aestivate by burrowing into mud and slowing their bodies right down until the rains return.

questions.q: A shrimp's heart is located in its head.
questions.f: A shrimp's heart sits in its thorax, just behind the head, near its stomach and other organs.

questions.q: A starfish has no brain and no blood.
questions.f: Instead of blood, a sea star pumps filtered seawater through its body to move nutrients around.

questions.q: The word 'alligator' comes from a Spanish phrase meaning 'the lizard'.
questions.f: Spanish explorers called it el lagarto, meaning the lizard, and English speakers ran the words together into alligator.

questions.q: Elephants are naturally terrified of mice.
questions.f: This is a long-standing myth; elephants may be startled by sudden movement, but they are not specially afraid of mice.

questions.q: Snakes have no eyelids and sleep with their eyes open.
questions.f: A clear scale called a brille covers and protects each eye, so a snake never blinks or shuts its eyes.

questions.q: No stomach at all, milk that seeps through the skin instead of teats, and ten sex chromosomes rather than two: which animal?
questions.f: All that, and it is also one of the only mammals that lays eggs and glows faintly under ultraviolet light.

questions.q: Grandmothers who lead hunts decades after their last calf, a dialect unique to each family, and a taste for shark liver point to which animal?
questions.f: Orcas are one of very few animals besides humans whose females live long past breeding age, passing on knowledge.

questions.q: Grazing trails visible on the seabed, an order named after mythical sea maidens, and a snout used to root up seagrass: which animal?
questions.f: Dugongs and manatees make up the Sirenia, named for the sirens whose songs sailors mistook them for.

questions.q: A saliva protein studied as a stroke treatment, food shared with hungry neighbours who once shared with it, and legs strong enough to run: which animal?
questions.f: The anticoagulant in its saliva was actually named draculin, and vampire bats keep track of who has repaid a favour.

questions.q: Teeth used to saw breathing holes through sea ice, dives past 600 metres, and eerie trills recorded beneath Antarctica: which animal?
questions.f: Weddell seals wear their teeth down so badly on ice that dentistry, not hunger, often limits their lives.

questions.q: A nose that works as a booming resonator, dives beyond 1,500 metres, and months of fasting ashore describe which animal?
questions.f: Elephant seals spend most of the year at sea, sleeping as they glide downwards in long, spiralling dives.

questions.q: A neck flexible enough to look backwards, colour that deepens to pink with age, and swims through flooded forest: which animal?
questions.f: Unfused neck vertebrae let the boto twist through submerged branches where ocean dolphins could never follow.

questions.q: Swimming habitually on its side, eyes that cannot form an image, and a life in silty rivers point to which animal?
questions.f: It has no lens in its eye at all and 'sees' entirely by echoes, so its blindness costs it nothing.

questions.q: A creature nicknamed goddess of the Yangtze, a survey in 2006 that found none, and the first large animal humans drove extinct in 50 years?
questions.f: The baiji, a Chinese river dolphin, was declared functionally extinct after a six-week search turned up nothing.

questions.q: Claws that never fully retract, skin grafts between individuals that are rarely rejected, and a chirp more like a bird's than a growl: which animal?
questions.f: Yes, the fastest land animal, and its low genetic variety comes from a population crash thousands of years ago.

questions.q: A heart and lungs far larger than its size requires, a refusal to jump fences it could clear, and speed built to outrun a predator extinct for millennia?
questions.f: The pronghorn can hold 60 km/h for kilometres, outclassing even a cheetah over distance.

questions.q: A red oily secretion once called blood sweat, a stomach of several chambers, and closest living relatives that live in the sea: which animal?
questions.f: The red ooze works as sunscreen and antiseptic, and the hippo's nearest kin really are the whales.

questions.q: Eyes that turn from gold in summer to deep blue in winter, tendons that click over bone as it walks, and vision extending into ultraviolet?
questions.f: Blue winter eyes scatter light inside the eye, boosting sensitivity in the long polar night.

questions.q: A big cat that cannot roar, a tail long enough to wrap round itself as a scarf, and paws that spread like snowshoes: which animal?
questions.f: Snow leopards lack the specialised throat tissue needed to roar, so they chuff and yowl instead.

questions.q: Africa's smallest wild cat, light enough to fit in a shoebox, yet the most successful hunter of any cat by strike rate?
questions.f: It succeeds in around 60% of hunts, taking more prey in a night than a leopard does in months.

questions.q: Ankles that rotate to let it climb down trunks head-first, the longest canine teeth relative to size of any cat, and a coat of blotchy 'clouds'?
questions.f: It can even hang upside down from a branch by its back feet while feeding.

questions.q: Partly webbed toes, a habit of tapping the water surface to imitate insects, and a cat that dives after its dinner?
questions.f: The fishing cat's double-layered coat keeps its skin dry even after a long swim in a mangrove creek.

questions.q: More English names than any other animal, a range stretching from Canada to Patagonia, and vocal cords that purr but cannot roar?
questions.f: Cougar, mountain lion, panther, catamount: over 40 names in English alone for one adaptable cat.

questions.q: A fold of skin along the belly, a mane noticeably thinner than its African cousin's, and a last wild home in the Gir Forest?
questions.f: Every wild Asiatic lion on Earth descends from a few dozen animals protected by a local ruler in the 1900s.

questions.q: A striped hyena relative with jaws too weak for bone, a tongue that laps up 300,000 insects a night, and no interest in meat?
questions.f: The aardwolf is the only hyena that lives almost entirely on termites, licking them off the ground.

questions.q: Skin loose enough to twist round inside a grip, resistance to snake venom, and a willingness to raid bees despite hundreds of stings?
questions.f: Its skin is also rubbery enough to blunt quills and stings, which is why the honey badger fears almost nothing.

questions.q: An individual tracked 3,500 km from Norway to Canada in 76 days, fur that changes with the season, and paws warm at minus 40 degrees?
questions.f: That young female crossed the sea ice averaging 46 km a day, astonishing the researchers following her collar.

questions.q: A ten-year boom and crash preserved in old fur-trade ledgers, feet like snowshoes, and numbers that drag a predator's up and down with them?
questions.f: The hare and lynx cycle, reconstructed from Hudson's Bay Company records, is the classic textbook case of linked populations.

questions.q: A rabbit relative that builds haystacks for winter, a shrill whistle from mountain scree, and a body so heat-sensitive that a warm afternoon can kill it?
questions.f: A pika gathers up to 30 kg of dried plants into stores wedged among the rocks.

questions.q: Ears roughly a third of its body length, hairy 'snowshoe' feet for loose sand, and a hopping gait like a miniature kangaroo?
questions.f: It has the largest ears relative to body size of any mammal, all the better for hearing insects in the Gobi night.

questions.q: Twins that swap cells in the womb and stay part-chimera for life, a father who carries the babies, and a monkey that fits in a hand?
questions.f: Some marmosets carry their twin's cells in their own blood and tissues, blurring the line between individuals.

questions.q: A female named Imo who invented washing food, bathing in volcanic hot springs, and the northernmost wild monkeys on Earth?
questions.f: Imo's habit of rinsing sweet potatoes spread through her troop and down the generations: culture, in monkeys.

questions.q: Arms longer than body and legs together, hand-over-hand swinging faster than a person can run, and pairs that sing loud daily duets?
questions.f: That arm-swinging travel is called brachiation, and a gibbon can cross 15 metres between branches in one swing.

questions.q: The most vividly coloured mammal alive, troops that can exceed 800 members, and a rump patterned to be followed through dark forest?
questions.f: The mandrill is also the largest monkey, and the brightest males hold the highest rank.

questions.q: A flexible little snout, cleared trails patrolled like a racetrack, and a closer kinship to elephants than to shrews?
questions.f: Also called elephant shrews, sengis belong to Afrotheria, the African group that also gave us elephants and hyraxes.

questions.q: An eyeless burrower that 'swims' through loose sand, iridescent fur despite a life in darkness, and hearing tuned to termite footsteps?
questions.f: Nobody is sure why an animal that cannot see should shimmer, making golden mole fur one of biology's odder puzzles.

questions.q: An island a Dutch captain named 'rat nest', a marsupial that climbs trees despite its build, and a face that seems permanently cheerful?
questions.f: Willem de Vlamingh mistook the quokkas of Rottnest Island for giant rats in 1696.

questions.q: Rabbit-like ears, a pouch that opens backwards, and an Easter mascot Australians promote instead of the rabbit?
questions.f: Chocolate Easter Bilbies raise money for conservation, since real rabbits are a pest across Australia.

questions.q: An alarm call that sounds like a dog barking, tiny tusk-like upper teeth, and the fewest chromosomes of any deer?
questions.f: The Indian muntjac has just six or seven chromosomes in total, remarkably few for a mammal.

questions.q: Dives of four metres for pond plants, antlers that reflect sound towards the ears, and nostrils that seal underwater?
questions.f: Moose dive for sodium-rich water plants, and their broad antlers may work as a hearing aid in dense forest.

questions.q: Upper tusks that grow up straight through the top of the snout, an Indonesian island home, and a name meaning pig-deer?
questions.f: A babirusa's tusks keep curving and can eventually grow back towards its own forehead.

questions.q: Corkscrew-spiralling horns, a climb up near-vertical cliffs, and the national animal of Pakistan?
questions.f: Markhor horns can twist more than a metre, and the name may come from words meaning snake-eater.

questions.q: A forest-dwelling bovine described only in 1992, two long straight horns, and an animal no biologist has yet seen alive in the wild?
questions.f: Nicknamed the Asian unicorn, the saola of Vietnam and Laos is known mostly from camera traps and local reports.

questions.q: An antelope that stands upright on its hind legs to browse, a neck earning it the name giraffe-gazelle, and a life without ever drinking?
questions.f: The gerenuk takes all its water from leaves and can reach food two metres up while standing on two legs.

questions.q: A stiff-legged bounce with all four feet at once, a back fold that flashes white when raised, and a national rugby emblem?
questions.f: That bounce is called pronking, and nobody is certain whether it signals fitness, confuses predators, or both.

questions.q: A herd rebuilt from roughly two dozen survivors in Yellowstone, a shoulder hump of muscle for shovelling snow, and a jump of nearly two metres?
questions.f: Tens of millions once roamed North America; by 1900 only a few hundred wild animals were left anywhere.

questions.q: A half-striped southern African animal shot out by the 1880s, a Latin name imitating its call, and a project breeding lookalikes today?
questions.f: DNA showed the quagga was a subspecies of plains zebra, so selective breeding can recreate its coat if not the animal.

questions.q: A name usually explained as a mistranslation of 'wide', a squared lip for cropping grass, and a last northern male named Sudan who died in 2018?
questions.f: The name has nothing to do with colour: it is thought to describe the wide mouth that crops grass like a lawnmower.

questions.q: The only Asian rhino with two horns, a coat of reddish hair, and song-like calls used to find mates in thick forest?
questions.f: Its whistles and whale-like songs travel through dense jungle where sight is useless.

questions.q: Recognised as its own species only in 2021, straighter downward tusks, and a role as the rainforest's chief seed-spreader?
questions.f: Forest elephants disperse the seeds of huge rainforest trees, so losing them changes the forest itself.

questions.q: Madagascar's largest carnivore, ankles that swivel for head-first descents, and a cat-like hunter that is really a mongoose relative?
questions.f: With no cats on Madagascar, the fossa evolved into the island's cat, a textbook case of convergent evolution.

questions.q: Pups taught to handle scorpions in graded lessons, calls that differ for airborne and ground threats, and a group where one female breeds?
questions.f: Adults bring pups disabled scorpions first, then live ones: one of the clearest cases of animal teaching.

questions.q: A pack that decides when to set off by sneezing, coats patterned differently on every individual, and a hunting success rate above any big cat's?
questions.f: Researchers found the more sneezes recorded, the sooner the pack moved: a kind of vote.

questions.q: A South American animal on stilt-like legs, neither wolf nor fox despite its name, and a diet half made of a fruit called the wolf apple?
questions.f: The maned wolf is its own genus, and the wolf apple it depends on will not germinate as well without passing through it.

questions.q: A canid that truly hibernates, a Japanese folklore shapeshifter called tanuki, and an animal that is neither raccoon nor dog?
questions.f: The raccoon dog is the only member of the dog family known to sleep through the winter.

questions.q: The animal that carried the name 'panda' first, a false thumb formed from a wrist bone, and a tail used as a blanket?
questions.f: The red panda was named around 50 years before the giant panda, which borrowed the name for its similar diet.

questions.q: The smallest of all bears, a tongue up to 25 cm long, and a golden crescent marking its chest?
questions.f: That long tongue reaches deep into hives and termite nests, earning the sun bear the nickname honey bear.

questions.q: A shaggy bear that carries its cubs on its back, a gap in its front teeth, and termites slurped up with a vacuum-like suck?
questions.f: The sloth bear is the only bear that regularly rides its young piggyback, sometimes two at a time.

questions.q: A whistle answered by a wild bird, a partnership with Tanzanian hunters older than farming, and a diet that includes beeswax?
questions.f: Honeyguides lead people to bees' nests and wait for the wax; the birds even learn each community's particular call.

questions.q: A researcher named Irene Pepperberg, an animal that answered 'none' when asked about a colour that was absent, and a working vocabulary of over 100 labels?
questions.f: Alex the parrot appeared to grasp the idea of zero, something once thought far beyond any bird.

questions.q: Up to 30,000 seed stores remembered across a mountainside, a pouch under the tongue for carrying pine seeds, and nesting in midwinter snow?
questions.f: Its memory for cache sites is so good that whole forests of whitebark pine depend on the seeds it forgets.

questions.q: A password note sung to eggs before they hatch, chicks that must repeat it to be fed, and a defence against imposter chicks?
questions.f: Cuckoo chicks hatch too late to learn the password, so the parents can tell their own young apart by sound.

questions.q: Feet too short to launch from flat ground, ten months airborne without landing, and sleep snatched in flight?
questions.f: Tracking tags showed young swifts stay aloft from leaving the nest until they first breed, nearly two years later.

questions.q: A cave-nesting bird that clicks to navigate in the dark, chicks once boiled down for lamp fuel, and a diet of fruit gathered at night?
questions.f: The oilbird is one of only a handful of birds that echolocate, and it is the only nocturnal fruit-eating bird.

questions.q: A bird ringed in 1956, still hatching chicks in her seventies, and a nesting ground on Midway Atoll?
questions.f: Wisdom is the oldest known wild bird, and she has flown an estimated eight million kilometres in her life.

questions.q: Ears set at slightly different heights on its skull, a face shaped like a shallow dish, and a strike accurate in complete darkness?
questions.f: The height difference lets a barn owl pinpoint sound vertically as well as sideways, building a sound map of the field.

questions.q: A bird that plunges head-first through crusted snow, the largest facial disc of any owl, and hearing that finds voles 30 cm under the surface?
questions.f: It can punch through snow strong enough to hold a person's weight, guided entirely by sound.

questions.q: A bill that clatters like a machine gun, an hour spent standing utterly motionless, and a chick that pants to cool in papyrus swamps?
questions.f: The shoebill's 24 cm bill ends in a sharp hook, and its greeting display is pure percussion.

questions.q: Quill-like crest feathers behind the head, legs used to stamp prey on the ground, and a bird of prey that hunts on foot across grassland?
questions.f: It appears on South Africa's coat of arms, and its stamp lands with a force several times its body weight.

questions.q: A nest of over 8,000 sticks strong enough to hold a person, and African folklore that calls it a lightning bird?
questions.f: The hamerkop's domed nest is so sturdy that eagles, owls, and even genets move in after it is abandoned.

questions.q: The largest wing area of any living bird, five hours of soaring without one flap, and bare skin that flushes colour with mood?
questions.f: One tracked condor flew over 170 km without flapping once, riding mountain updraughts like an invisible staircase.

questions.q: A parrot that lives among alpine snow, a talent for opening bins and car windows, and play calls that spread through a flock like laughter?
questions.f: The kea is the world's only alpine parrot, and hearing a recording of its warble makes other keas start playing.

questions.q: A species where the male's beak was short and stout while the female's was long and curved, feathers reserved for Maori chiefs, and a last sighting in 1907?
questions.f: No other bird is known to have differed so drastically in beak shape between the sexes.

questions.q: A Galapagos bird that trims a cactus spine to length, a beak too short to reach grubs, and a species central to ideas about adaptation?
questions.f: It is one of very few birds that make tools, shortening a spine until it fits the crevice.

questions.q: Toes long enough to walk across lily pads, males who incubate the eggs alone, and females who defend a harem of mates?
questions.f: A male jacana can tuck two chicks under each wing and carry them off, legs dangling.

questions.q: Wings rubbed together to make a violin-like tone, solid bones unlike any other bird's, and a courtship display performed at blurring speed?
questions.f: It sings with its wings, knocking a clubbed feather against a ridged one over 100 times a second.

questions.q: A fish that spawns on dry sand by the light of a full moon, eggs that wait in the beach for the next high tide, and a run watched by crowds in California?
questions.f: Grunion wriggle out of the surf, bury their eggs above the waterline, and catch the next wave back out.

questions.q: The longest bony fish in the world, a body that swims upright rippling like a ribbon, and a Japanese legend calling it a messenger of the sea god?
questions.f: Oarfish can reach eight metres, and folklore claims their appearance in shallow water warns of earthquakes.

questions.q: Teeth so long the fish needs sockets in its own skull to shut its mouth, and a home a kilometre down in the dark?
questions.f: The fangtooth is only about 15 cm long, yet it has the largest teeth for its body size of any fish in the sea.

questions.q: A fish filmed 8,000 metres down, a jelly-like body without scales, and flesh stabilised by a chemical that resists crushing pressure?
questions.f: Below about 8,400 m even that chemical fails, which may set the hard limit on how deep any fish can live.

questions.q: A chin organ that reads electric fields, a brain-to-body ratio rivalling a human's, and a hunter that 'sees' in muddy African rivers?
questions.f: It uses nearly 60% of its oxygen just to run that huge brain, the highest share known in any vertebrate.

questions.q: An animal that regrows damaged heart muscle, embryos clear enough to watch organs form, and a laboratory favourite from Indian streams?
questions.f: Zebrafish rebuild heart tissue that mammals can only scar, so researchers study them hoping to copy the trick.

questions.q: A vertebrate that matures in about 14 days, eggs that survive a completely dried-out pond, and a life measured in weeks?
questions.f: It is the fastest-maturing vertebrate known, racing through a whole life cycle before its puddle dries again.

questions.q: A gape that opens in six milliseconds, fins used to walk along the seabed, and a lure grown from the first spine of its back fin?
questions.f: Its strike is among the fastest feeding movements ever filmed in any animal, too quick for the eye to follow.

questions.q: A relative of the seahorse decked in leaf-shaped flaps, a male that carries eggs on his tail, and a home only in southern Australian waters?
questions.f: The leafy flaps are useless for swimming; they exist purely so the fish looks like drifting seaweed.

questions.q: A frightening name attached to an animal that mostly eats 'marine snow', a cloak of webbed arms, and light organs at the arm tips?
questions.f: Despite the name, it is a gentle drifter that collects falling flakes of debris on sticky filaments.

questions.q: A shell divided into gas-filled chambers, an eye that works as a pinhole with no lens, and up to 90 tentacles without a single sucker?
questions.f: The nautilus has drifted through the oceans almost unchanged for hundreds of millions of years.

questions.q: An animal that carries two shell halves to hide beneath, stilt-walks across the seabed on two arms, and was the first invertebrate seen using a portable tool?
questions.f: It tucks the shells together like a suitcase and runs off with them, ready to hide anywhere.

questions.q: Females thousands of times heavier than the males, a cape unfurled to look enormous, and arms that carry torn-off stinging tentacles as weapons?
questions.f: The tiny male is the size of a walnut; the female can be two metres long, one of the most extreme size gaps in nature.

questions.q: An animal known for centuries only from beaks in whale stomachs, first filmed alive in 2004, and eyes the size of a human head?
questions.f: Sailors' tales of the kraken were probably built on rare glimpses of this animal, unseen alive until this century.

questions.q: An animal that breathes through its rear end, defends itself by ejecting its own internal organs, and can loosen its body wall almost to liquid?
questions.f: It regrows the ejected organs in weeks, and its shape-shifting skin inspires research into changeable materials.

questions.q: A predator with up to 21 arms, an outbreak that can strip a reef bare, and a body covered in venomous spines?
questions.f: One of these starfish can eat its own body area of coral in a day, and outbreaks have devastated parts of the Great Barrier Reef.

questions.q: A five-part jaw named after a Greek philosopher, teeth that grind solid rock, and an animal that walks on tube feet between its spines?
questions.f: The jaw apparatus is called Aristotle's lantern, and urchin teeth self-sharpen as they wear.

questions.q: Not one animal but a colony of specialised individuals, a gas-filled float that catches the wind, and a name borrowed from an old warship?
questions.f: Each part of it is a separate zooid; none could survive alone, yet together they sail the open ocean.

questions.q: A rope-like colony filmed off Australia in 2020, an outer ring estimated at 45 metres, and a body built from thousands of clones?
questions.f: That Apolemia may be the longest animal ever recorded, hunting in a spiral like a vast living fishing net.

questions.q: A freshwater animal whose cells are constantly replaced, no measurable signs of ageing, and a name taken from a many-headed monster?
questions.f: Cut a hydra in pieces and each can regrow, which is exactly why it was named after the beast Hercules fought.

questions.q: A microscopic animal revived after 24,000 years in Siberian permafrost, no known males at all, and a genome stitched with borrowed bacterial genes?
questions.f: Bdelloids have gone without males for millions of years, patching their DNA with genes picked up from other kingdoms.

questions.q: An animal that fires two jets of instant glue, stubby unjointed legs, and a lineage barely changed in 500 million years?
questions.f: The glue squirts from two nozzles beside its mouth and sets in seconds, trapping insects where they stand.

questions.q: A creature living on a chimney wall at around 80 degrees Celsius, a fleece of bacteria on its back, and a home beside a deep-sea vent?
questions.f: It may be the most heat-tolerant complex animal known, and the bacterial fleece probably insulates it.

questions.q: An animal whose gut and reproductive organs extend into its legs, almost no body to speak of, and males that carry the eggs?
questions.f: With so little body space, a sea spider stores its organs in its legs, and it breathes straight through its skin.

questions.q: A crab covered in bristles that farm bacteria, a home beside hydrothermal vents, and a rhythmic arm-waving 'dance' to feed its crop?
questions.f: It waves its hairy claws through vent chemicals so the bacteria growing there can thrive, then eats them.

questions.q: A dome of silk filled with air carried down from the surface, a hunter that lives entirely submerged, and eggs laid underwater?
questions.f: It is the only spider known to spend its whole life underwater, refilling its silk bubble like a scuba tank.

questions.q: An animal smaller than a grain of rice, a courtship dance of raised coloured flaps, and vibrations drummed through a leaf?
questions.f: Males of these Australian spiders wave patterned flaps and legs in a routine that must be performed perfectly.

questions.q: A silk-hinged lid over a burrow, tripwires that betray passing insects, and an Australian female tracked to the age of 43?
questions.f: The spider known as Number 16 is the oldest individual spider ever recorded.

questions.q: A larva that digs a funnel-shaped pit in sand and flicks grains at escaping prey, and an adult that looks like a delicate damselfly?
questions.f: The larva may wait months in its pit, and it walks only backwards, which is why its old name means backwards-goer.

questions.q: A jaw snap clocked at 90 metres per second, the fastest movement known in any animal, and a hunter of Madagascan leaf litter?
questions.f: Instead of snapping open jaws shut, it presses the tips together and lets them slide past like a finger-snap.

questions.q: Workers who hold leaf edges together while others squeeze a larva to release silk, and colonies rented to guard orchards for 1,700 years?
questions.f: Chinese farmers were tying weaver ant nests into citrus trees as living pest control long before modern chemicals.

questions.q: An insect that changes colour, shape, and behaviour when crowded, a switch triggered by touch on its hind legs, and swarms recorded in ancient texts?
questions.f: A solitary green grasshopper can transform into a gregarious swarming locust within hours of being jostled.

questions.q: An insect crossing the Indian Ocean in relays between generations, a round trip near 14,000 km, and wings built for hours of gliding?
questions.f: No insect is known to migrate further, and it breeds in temporary rain pools along the way.

questions.q: A butterfly whose round trip takes several generations, a route from the Sahara to the Arctic Circle, and flight at up to 500 metres up?
questions.f: No individual completes the whole journey; the butterfly that returns is the great-grandchild of the one that set out.

questions.q: Long twisted hindwing tails, an adult with no working mouth, and a trick that makes a hunting bat strike empty air?
questions.f: Experiments showed the spinning tails throw off bat sonar, so the bat aims at the tail instead of the body.

questions.q: The source of the first chemical messenger ever identified in any animal, antennae sensitive to a handful of molecules, and an insect too heavy to fly?
questions.f: Bombykol, isolated in 1959 after processing half a million moths, opened the whole science of pheromones.

questions.q: A moth that squeaks when handled, raids beehives while smelling like the bees themselves, and carries a skull-like mark behind its head?
questions.f: Chemical camouflage lets it steal honey almost unchallenged, and its squeak may mimic a queen bee's call.

questions.q: An insect that pollinates just one species of tree, a whole life cycle spent inside the fruit, and a partnership around 75 million years old?
questions.f: Nearly every kind of fig has its own species of wasp, and neither partner can reproduce without the other.

questions.q: Pits on its body that sense infrared, an attraction to forest fires, and larvae that develop in freshly burnt wood?
questions.f: Some can detect a blaze from tens of kilometres away and fly towards it while everything else flees.

questions.q: A jump that accelerates harder than a flea's, a nymph hidden in froth known as cuckoo spit, and a leap 70 times its body length?
questions.f: Its take-off pulls over 400 times the force of gravity, among the highest accelerations of any animal.

questions.q: A famous engraving in Robert Hooke's 'Micrographia' of 1665, a spring made of the protein resilin, and a leap over 100 times its own height?
questions.f: Hooke's giant fold-out drawing of the flea astonished readers who had never seen what a microscope could reveal.

questions.q: An insect fitted with tiny 3D glasses by scientists, true stereo vision found in no other insect, and a strike completed in 60 milliseconds?
questions.f: The glasses proved mantises judge depth by comparing the two eyes' views, but in a way quite unlike ours.

questions.q: What colour is a robin's chest?
questions.f: A robin's reddish-orange breast helps it stand out, which is why it appears on so many winter cards.

questions.q: Which bird says 'coo' and is common in towns and parks?
questions.f: City pigeons are descended from rock doves that once nested on sea cliffs.

questions.q: What sound does a rooster make to greet the morning?
questions.f: Roosters can crow at almost any hour, not just at sunrise.

questions.q: Which small brown bird is one of the most common garden visitors?
questions.f: House sparrows have lived close to people for thousands of years.

questions.q: Which white seabird is often seen at the beach?
questions.f: Gulls are clever and can even learn to open bins to find food.

questions.q: What colour is a crow?
questions.f: Crows are among the smartest birds and can use simple tools.

questions.q: Which white bird is used as a symbol of peace?
questions.f: Doves and pigeons belong to the same bird family.

questions.q: Which farm bird gobbles and is famous at big feasts?
questions.f: Wild turkeys can actually fly short distances and roost in trees.

questions.q: What do we call a mother chicken?
questions.f: A hen may cluck softly to her chicks to keep them close.

questions.q: What do we call an adult male chicken?
questions.f: A rooster is also called a cockerel when it is young.

questions.q: Which black garden bird is often seen pulling worms from the lawn?
questions.f: Blackbirds are famous for their beautiful flute-like song.

questions.q: What do birds do with their eggs to keep them warm?
questions.f: Sitting on eggs to warm them is called incubation.

questions.q: A duckling is a baby duck.
questions.f: Ducklings can swim just hours after they hatch.

questions.q: Which small yellow bird is often kept as a singing pet?
questions.f: Canaries were once carried into coal mines to warn miners of bad air.

questions.q: What do owls mostly hunt at night?
questions.f: Owls swallow small prey whole and later cough up the bones as pellets.

questions.q: What is the name for a baby owl?
questions.f: Owlets are covered in soft fluffy down before their real feathers grow.

questions.q: What colour are the stripes on a bumblebee?
questions.f: The bold stripes warn hungry animals that a bee can sting.

questions.q: Which insect has big colourful wings and was once a caterpillar?
questions.f: Many butterflies taste with sensors on their feet.

questions.q: Which tiny biting insects buzz around and leave itchy bumps in summer?
questions.f: Only female mosquitoes bite, and they can smell you from far away.

questions.q: Which insects often live together in a hill made of soil?
questions.f: An ant hill can reach far underground with many tunnels and rooms.

questions.q: Which insect has a hard shiny shell over its wings?
questions.f: Beetles are the largest group of animals on Earth.

questions.q: What sound does a crow make?
questions.f: Crows have many different calls to warn each other of danger.

questions.q: Which insect is often called a 'creepy-crawly' and spins silk (but is not really an insect)?
questions.f: Spiders are arachnids, with eight legs instead of an insect's six.

questions.q: A caterpillar has more legs than a grown butterfly.
questions.f: A caterpillar has many little gripping legs, while a butterfly has just six.

questions.q: Which insect flutters to flowers by day and looks like a butterfly's cousin at night?
questions.f: Most moths fly at night while most butterflies fly by day.

questions.q: What do we call the thin feelers on top of an insect's head?
questions.f: Insects use their antennae to smell and feel the world around them.

questions.q: A baby spider is called a…?
questions.f: Some spiderlings float away on silk threads in a trip called ballooning.

questions.q: The word 'butterfly' begins with the name of which food?
questions.f: One old idea is that people thought butterflies liked to sip butter and milk.

questions.q: The word 'dragonfly' begins with the name of which mythical beast?
questions.f: Dragonflies are fierce hunters that snatch other insects in mid-air.

questions.q: In America, a 'ladybird' is usually called a lady…?
questions.f: Both names honour the 'lady', an old religious link to this lucky little beetle.

questions.q: A person who enjoys watching wild birds is a bird…?
questions.f: Serious birdwatchers are also called 'birders'.

questions.q: Finish the saying: 'as busy as a ___'.
questions.f: Bees really are busy, visiting thousands of flowers every day.

questions.q: Someone who loves staying up late is called a 'night ___'.
questions.f: The saying fits because most owls hunt after dark.

questions.q: What is a small house built for birds in a garden called?
questions.f: A birdhouse gives small birds a safe, dry place to raise their chicks.

questions.q: When a bird taps at food with its beak, we say it does what?
questions.f: Woodpeckers can peck a tree many times each second without hurting their heads.

questions.q: What do we call the two limbs a bird flaps to fly?
questions.f: A bird's wing is shaped to push air down so the bird lifts up.

questions.q: Which insect lives in a hive and can give a painful sting?
questions.f: Unlike a honeybee, a wasp can sting more than once.

questions.q: Which creepy-crawly has many, many legs and lives in damp places?
questions.f: 'Centipede' means 'a hundred feet', though most have far fewer than that.

questions.q: A bird uses its beak to pick up food.
questions.f: Beaks come in many shapes for cracking seeds, tearing meat or sipping nectar.

questions.q: Which brightly striped insect is known for making sweet honey?
questions.f: A whole hive of honeybees may hold tens of thousands of bees.

questions.q: What do we call the home where honeybees live and store honey?
questions.f: Inside a hive, bees build neat six-sided cells out of wax.

questions.q: Which large bird has a very long neck and often lives on farms in flocks by ponds?
questions.f: Geese honk loudly and can be good guards, warning of strangers.

questions.q: What is a baby goose called?
questions.f: Goslings follow the first thing they see move, usually their mother.

questions.q: Which garden bird is famous for copying the songs of other birds?
questions.f: Some birds, like starlings, can even copy phone ringtones and car alarms.

questions.q: Which insect can jump high and far using strong back legs, and lives in grass?
questions.f: A grasshopper can leap many times the length of its own body.

questions.q: Bees help flowers grow by carrying pollen between them.
questions.f: Without pollinators like bees, we would have far fewer fruits and vegetables.

questions.q: What do we call the fine yellow powder bees carry from flower to flower?
questions.f: Pollen sticks to a bee's fuzzy body and rubs off on the next flower.

questions.q: Which insect slowly munches leaves before turning into a butterfly?
questions.f: A hungry caterpillar can eat many times its own weight in leaves.

questions.q: Which colourful garden insect has spotted wings and is thought to bring good luck?
questions.f: Ladybirds are helpful in gardens because they eat pests that harm plants.

questions.q: Finish the saying: 'a little bird ___ me'.
questions.f: 'A little bird told me' is a playful way to say you heard a secret.

questions.q: What do we call a group of chicks and their mother together?
questions.f: A hen fluffs up her feathers to keep her whole brood warm.

questions.q: Which insect quickly lands on food indoors and rubs its front legs together?
questions.f: A housefly tastes food with its feet before it eats.

questions.q: Which bird bobs on ponds and dabbles its bill in the water for food?
questions.f: A duck's feathers are so oily that water rolls right off them.

questions.q: What is a baby bird that has just hatched and cannot yet fly called?
questions.f: Newly hatched chicks of many songbirds are naked and need lots of feeding.

questions.q: The word 'beehive' names the home of which insect?
questions.f: A busy hive smells sweet and warm from all the honey inside.

questions.q: What do we call the sound a small songbird makes?
questions.f: Many birds chirp most in the early morning, called the dawn chorus.

questions.q: Which insect can be a pretty green or brown and holds its front legs as if praying?
questions.f: A praying mantis can turn its head to look right over its shoulder.

questions.q: Most spiders have eight legs and are not insects.
questions.f: Insects have six legs and three body parts; spiders have eight legs and two.

questions.q: Which insect flies fast over ponds and has long see-through wings?
questions.f: Dragonflies are among the fastest flying insects in the world.

questions.q: What do we call a bird's mouth part used for eating?
questions.f: A beak, also called a bill, is made of the same stuff as your fingernails.

questions.q: Which brightly coloured bird can learn to whistle tunes and copy speech?
questions.f: Some parrots can live for more than fifty years.

questions.q: Which bird has a big stretchy pouch under its beak for scooping up fish?
questions.f: A pelican's throat pouch can hold more water than its own stomach.

questions.q: Feathers, hair and fingernails are all made of the same tough material called what?
questions.f: Keratin makes feathers both light and surprisingly strong.

questions.q: Which bird is the national symbol of the United States?
questions.f: Despite its name, the bald eagle is not bald; it has white head feathers.

questions.q: What do we call birds like eagles, hawks and owls that hunt other animals?
questions.f: Birds of prey are also known as raptors, from a Latin word meaning to seize.

questions.q: Which small bird arrives in spring and is often seen swooping to catch insects in the air?
questions.f: Swallows fly thousands of kilometres and famously return to the same nests each year.

questions.q: What is it called when a bird sheds old feathers and grows new ones?
questions.f: Some birds change to brighter feathers at moulting time to attract a mate.

questions.q: Which body part does a bird mainly use to steer and balance while flying?
questions.f: A bird can spread or twist its tail feathers like a rudder to turn.

questions.q: Birds are the only living animals that have feathers.
questions.f: Feathers are a feature unique to birds, though scientists think some dinosaurs had them too.

questions.q: Which word means an animal that is awake and active at night?
questions.f: Owls have huge eyes to gather what little light there is at night.

questions.q: Which Australian bird is famous for copying almost any sound it hears?
questions.f: A lyrebird can mimic chainsaws, camera clicks and other birds' songs perfectly.

questions.q: What do we call a person who studies birds?
questions.f: The word comes from the Greek 'ornis', meaning bird.

questions.q: What do we call a person who studies insects?
questions.f: 'Entomon' is the Greek word for insect, meaning something notched or cut into.

questions.q: A baby swan is called a…?
questions.f: Cygnets are grey and fluffy before they grow their bright white feathers.

questions.q: A baby eagle is called an…?
questions.f: Eaglets can be nearly as large as their parents before they first fly.

questions.q: Which insects live in huge colonies and can chew through wood in houses?
questions.f: Termites help nature by breaking down dead wood, but they can damage buildings.

questions.q: Which insect is famous for being one of the loudest, buzzing from trees in summer?
questions.f: A group of cicadas can be as loud as a passing motorbike.

questions.q: What do we call a butterfly's long coiled feeding tube for sipping nectar?
questions.f: When not in use, the proboscis curls up neatly like a party blower.

questions.q: Which insects can skate across the surface of a pond without sinking?
questions.f: Tiny hairs on their feet trap air and let them stand on the water's surface.

questions.q: How many wings does a typical butterfly have?
questions.f: A butterfly's two pairs of wings often lock together and beat as one.

questions.q: What do we call an animal, like an insect, that has no backbone?
questions.f: More than nine in ten animal species on Earth are invertebrates.

questions.q: Why do fireflies flash their glowing lights?
questions.f: Different firefly species flash in their own special patterns, like a code.

questions.q: What is the collective name for a group of flamingos?
questions.f: A flamboyance of flamingos can number in the thousands at a single lake.

questions.q: What is the collective name for a group of larks?
questions.f: 'Exaltation' fits the way larks sing while soaring high into the sky.

questions.q: A group of butterflies is playfully called a…?
questions.f: The name matches the swirl of shifting colours when they gather.

questions.q: Finish the simile: 'as free as a ___'.
questions.f: The saying pictures a bird able to fly wherever it wishes.

questions.q: Finish the simile: 'as light as a ___'.
questions.f: Feathers are so light because they are mostly hollow shafts and thin barbs.

questions.q: Finish the idiom: 'the early bird catches the ___'.
questions.f: The saying means people who start early often get the best results.

questions.q: Finish the idiom: 'birds of a ___ flock together'.
questions.f: It means people with similar interests tend to stick together.

questions.q: Finish the idiom: 'to kill two birds with one ___'.
questions.f: It means getting two things done with a single action.

questions.q: If someone has 'a bee in their bonnet', what does it mean?
c: They keep going on about one idea
questions.f: A real bee trapped in a hat would certainly be hard to ignore.

questions.q: What does it mean to call someone 'a social butterfly'?
c: They mingle happily with lots of people
questions.f: Like a butterfly flitting between flowers, they move easily from person to person.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'to wing it' mean?
questions.f: The phrase may come from actors performing a play with little rehearsal.

questions.q: Which insect stage comes straight after the egg in a butterfly's life?
questions.f: The caterpillar's main job is to eat and grow as fast as it can.

questions.q: A spider can have more than eight eyes.
questions.f: Most spiders have eight eyes, though some cave spiders have none at all.

questions.q: Which bird lays famously blue eggs in a neat cup-shaped nest?
questions.f: The blue colour may help protect the eggs from too much sunlight.

questions.q: What do we call the trip a bird makes flying south for winter and back in spring?
questions.f: Some birds cross entire oceans without stopping during migration.

questions.q: Which insect is a helpful garden hunter, eating pests like aphids and greenfly?
questions.f: A single ladybird can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime.

questions.q: Which bird can hang upside down at feeders and is a small, bold garden visitor with a blue cap?
questions.f: Blue tits are acrobatic and often cling to nut feeders upside down.

questions.q: What does the word 'aviary' mean?
c: A large cage or place for keeping birds
questions.f: 'Aviary' comes from the Latin 'avis', meaning bird.

questions.q: The Latin root 'avis', seen in words like 'aviation', means what?
questions.f: Early aeroplane inventors were inspired by watching birds fly.

questions.q: Which insect can leap and is famous for eating crops in huge swarms?
questions.f: A giant locust swarm can contain billions of insects and darken the sky.

questions.q: Which sea bird 'flies' underwater with its wings to chase fish and lives in the far south?
questions.f: Penguins are such strong swimmers that their wings work like flippers.

questions.q: What do we call the round nest-like case some caterpillars spin from silk?
questions.f: Moth caterpillars often spin a silk cocoon, while butterflies form a hard chrysalis.

questions.q: Which insect can beat its wings so fast that it hums, and drinks nectar while hovering like a tiny bird?
questions.f: The hummingbird hawk-moth is often mistaken for a real hummingbird.

questions.q: What do we call a bird's front limbs, changed over time for flying?
questions.f: A bird's wing has the same basic bones as your own arm and hand.

questions.q: Which large white bird with a long neck glides on lakes and mates for life?
questions.f: A swan pair often stays together for many years.

questions.q: Some insects can taste and smell using their antennae.
questions.f: Antennae are covered in tiny sense organs that pick up scents in the air.

questions.q: Which insect rolls and buries balls of dung, helping to clean up and feed the soil?
questions.f: Ancient Egyptians honoured the dung beetle, or scarab, as a lucky symbol.

questions.q: What is a young bird that has left the nest but is still learning to fly called?
questions.f: You should usually leave a fledgling alone, as its parents are often nearby.

questions.q: Which insect can appear in enormous swarms called plagues in some parts of the world?
questions.f: Locusts are simply grasshoppers that change behaviour when they crowd together.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'to take someone under your wing' mean?
questions.f: The image is of a mother bird sheltering her chicks beneath a wing.

questions.q: Which bird of prey is famous for hovering in one spot over fields, hunting mice below?
questions.f: A kestrel holds its head perfectly still while its wings beat fast.

questions.q: What do we call the season when many birds build nests and raise their young?
questions.f: Many birds sing most loudly in the breeding season to claim a territory.

questions.q: Which insect's larva lives in water before it grows wings and flies over ponds?
questions.f: A young dragonfly can spend years underwater before it takes to the air.

questions.q: What does the word 'flock' mean when talking about birds?
questions.f: Birds often flock together for safety, as many eyes spot danger sooner.

questions.q: Which brightly coloured bird can hover, dart and even fly backwards while sipping nectar?
questions.f: A hummingbird's heart can beat well over a thousand times a minute.

questions.q: What do we call a group of bees that leaves a hive together to find a new home?
questions.f: A swarm may cluster on a branch while scout bees search for a new nest site.

questions.q: An insect's body is divided into three main parts.
questions.f: The three parts are the head, the thorax and the abdomen.

questions.q: Which insect has clear, net-like wings and is sometimes called a 'darning needle'?
questions.f: Old folk tales wrongly claimed dragonflies could sew, giving them that nickname.

questions.q: What do we call the low, sheltered platform or branch a bird rests on?
questions.f: Birds have a special tendon that locks their toes around a perch as they sleep.

questions.q: Which word describes an animal that eats both plants and other animals, like many birds do?
questions.f: Many garden birds eat seeds, berries and insects, making them omnivores.

questions.q: In the word 'ornithology', the root 'ornith' means…?
questions.f: 'Ornith' comes from Greek, so ornithology is literally the study of birds.

questions.q: The 'ptero' in 'pterodactyl' and 'helicopter' means…?
questions.f: This Greek root turns up wherever the idea of a wing appears.

questions.q: Butterflies and moths belong to the order Lepidoptera; the root 'lepido' means…?
questions.f: From Greek, it points to the tiny overlapping scales that coat their wings.

questions.q: In 'apiary', the root 'api' refers to which creature?
questions.f: 'Apis' is the Latin word for bee, so an apiary is a home for kept bees.

questions.q: The word 'metamorphosis' contains 'morph', which means…?
questions.f: From Greek, it describes an insect completely changing its form as it grows.

questions.q: The writing tool 'pen' takes its name from a root meaning…?
questions.f: The Latin 'penna' means feather, because early pens were sharpened quills.

questions.q: In the word 'nocturnal', the root 'noct' means…?
questions.f: From Latin, it explains why nocturnal animals are active after sunset.

questions.q: The word 'raptor', used for birds of prey, comes from a root meaning to…?
questions.f: The same Latin root gives us words like 'rapture' and 'rapid'.

questions.q: The 'ova' in 'oval' and 'ovary' means…?
questions.f: From Latin, 'ovum' means egg, and eggs gave the oval its shape and name.

questions.q: A parent bird settling onto its eggs is doing what the Latin root of 'incubate' describes, namely to…?
questions.f: From Latin 'incubare', it describes a parent bird sitting on its eggs.

questions.q: The word 'chrysalis' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek 'chrysos', gold, because some butterfly pupae gleam with golden spots.

questions.q: A person who keeps and cares for bees is called a…?
questions.f: An apiarist is also simply known as a beekeeper.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for a group of ravens?
questions.f: Ravens gathered together have long been given this gloomy-sounding name.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for a group of eagles?
questions.f: Seeing a convocation of eagles soaring together is a rare sight.

questions.q: What does it mean when a bird 'preens'?
c: It cleans and arranges its feathers
questions.f: Birds spread oil from a special gland while preening to keep feathers waterproof.

questions.q: What are the sharp gripping claws of a bird of prey called?
questions.f: An eagle's grip with its talons can be far stronger than a human hand.

questions.q: Which bird can stay in the air for months, even sleeping while flying?
questions.f: Young swifts may fly non-stop for years before they first land to nest.

questions.q: Which birds are famous for the males weaving intricate hanging nests from grass?
questions.f: A male weaver builds nest after nest, hoping a female will approve of one.

questions.q: Which male bird collects colourful objects to decorate a structure called a 'bower'?
questions.f: Some bowerbirds sort their treasures by colour to impress a mate.

questions.q: Which male birds of New Guinea perform dazzling dances with bright plumes?
questions.f: Some birds of paradise can raise their feathers into astonishing shapes.

questions.q: What is the muscular stomach part birds use to grind up food, often with swallowed grit?
questions.f: Because birds have no teeth, the gizzard does the chewing inside them.

questions.q: What is the pouch in a bird's throat used to store food for later called?
questions.f: Pigeons even make a special 'crop milk' to feed their young.

questions.q: Birds sing using a special organ that mammals do not have, called the…?
questions.f: The syrinx lets some birds sing two notes at exactly the same time.

questions.q: What do we call the hard, protective wing cases that cover a beetle's flying wings?
questions.f: When a beetle flies, it lifts the elytra out of the way of its real wings.

questions.q: Insects like grasshoppers grow without a pupa stage; this is called…?
questions.f: Their young, called nymphs, look like small versions of the adults.

questions.q: What do we call the large eyes made of many tiny lenses that many insects have?
questions.f: A dragonfly's compound eyes can have tens of thousands of separate lenses.

questions.q: Which insects surprisingly have their 'ears' on their front legs?
questions.f: A cricket's leg 'ears' pick up the chirps of other crickets.

questions.q: The word 'larva' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: The idea is that the adult insect is 'masked' inside the young larva.

questions.q: An insect resting inside a hard case reminded naturalists of a wrapped-up toy; 'pupa' therefore means…?
questions.f: A pupa can look like a tiny wrapped doll while the insect changes inside.

questions.q: The 'aqua' in 'aquatic bird' means…?
questions.f: From Latin, it marks birds like ducks and swans that live on water.

questions.q: Which small bird can walk head-first down tree trunks looking for insects?
questions.f: The nuthatch is one of the few birds able to climb downward with ease.

questions.q: Which bird has a tongue so long it wraps around the back of its skull?
questions.f: The coiled tongue helps cushion the woodpecker's brain from all that hammering.

questions.q: What do we call a bird that eats mainly insects?
questions.f: Swallows and swifts are insectivores, scooping up bugs as they fly.

questions.q: What is the special waxy oil a bird spreads on its feathers to waterproof them?
questions.f: The oil comes from a gland near the base of the bird's tail.

questions.q: A worker honeybee is female.
questions.f: All the busy workers in a hive are females; the males are the lazy drones.

questions.q: Which insects can carry a scent trail so well that thousands follow the same path?
questions.f: Ants lay down chemical trails called pheromones to guide the colony.

questions.q: Which bird was once used to carry written messages over long distances?
questions.f: Homing pigeons can find their way back home from hundreds of kilometres away.

questions.q: What do we call the neat, six-sided wax cells bees build in a hive?
questions.f: The six-sided shape stores the most honey using the least wax.

questions.q: Which flightless bird from New Zealand is nearly blind but has an excellent sense of smell?
questions.f: A kiwi's nostrils sit at the very tip of its long beak, unusual among birds.

questions.q: The 'plume' in 'plumage' means…?
questions.f: 'Plumage' is the word for all of a bird's feathers taken together.

questions.q: What is the study and collecting of birds' eggs called?
questions.f: The name uses the Greek root for egg; collecting wild eggs is now illegal in many places.

questions.q: Which bird's chicks are famously fed a red spot on their parent's beak to beg for food?
questions.f: A gull chick pecks the red spot to make its parent bring up a meal.

questions.q: What is a swarm of locusts able to do that makes farmers fear them?
c: Eat entire fields of crops in hours
questions.f: A large swarm can eat as much food in a day as tens of thousands of people.

questions.q: Which insect's young is called a 'nymph' and looks like a small wingless adult?
questions.f: Nymphs shed their skin several times, growing wings only as they mature.

questions.q: Some birds swallow small stones to help grind up their food.
questions.f: These stones, called gastroliths, sit in the gizzard and crush tough seeds.

questions.q: Which insect tastes with its feet and unrolls a long tube to feed?
questions.f: Standing on food lets a butterfly tell instantly whether it is good to eat.

questions.q: What is the term for an animal, like most owls, that is active mainly at night?
questions.f: Owls' huge, forward-facing eyes make the most of dim night light.

questions.q: What is the word for animals, like most songbirds, that are active in the daytime?
questions.f: From the Latin for day, it is the opposite of nocturnal.

questions.q: Which large wading bird stands still in shallow water and spears fish with its beak?
questions.f: A heron can wait motionless for a long time before its lightning-fast strike.

questions.q: The 'coleo' in 'Coleoptera', the beetle order, means…?
questions.f: From Greek, it describes the sheath-like wing cases beetles fold over their wings.

questions.q: Which insects live in colonies with a queen, and build mounds that stay cool inside?
questions.f: Some termite mounds have clever air shafts that work like natural air conditioning.

questions.q: Which bird can rotate its neck far around because it has many more neck bones than a human?
questions.f: An owl has about twice as many neck bones as we do, letting it look behind itself.

questions.q: A butterfly and a moth both belong to the same insect order.
questions.f: Both are Lepidoptera, though moths usually fly at night and butterflies by day.

questions.q: Which brightly coloured insect warns predators it tastes bad with its red and black colours?
questions.f: Bright warning colours used this way are called aposematic colours.

questions.q: What do we call a bird's ability to find its way home over huge distances?
questions.f: Birds navigate using the sun, the stars and even the Earth's magnetic field.

questions.q: Which insect can fold its four wings flat and is often mistaken for a leaf or stick?
questions.f: A stick insect's camouflage is so good it can vanish against a twig.

questions.q: What do we call the flap of skin or feathers over a bird's ear opening?
questions.f: Birds have no outer ears; feathers called coverts protect the ear holes.

questions.q: Which insect can jump using a built-in catapult in its legs, storing energy like a spring?
questions.f: For its size, a flea's leap is one of the highest jumps in the animal world.

questions.q: The word 'diurnal' shares its 'di/diur' root, meaning day, with which other word?
questions.f: A diary records the events of each day, from the same Latin root for day.

questions.q: Which bird is known to store thousands of nuts and remember where it hid them?
questions.f: Some nutcrackers can recall thousands of hiding spots months later.

questions.q: 'Passerine' birds are the perching songbirds; the root 'passer' means…?
questions.f: From Latin, 'passer' is the sparrow, the model for this huge group of birds.

questions.q: An 'aquiline' nose is hooked like a bird's; the root 'aquila' means…?
questions.f: From Latin, 'aquila' is the eagle, whose curved beak inspired the term.

questions.q: Birds of the 'corvid' family are named from 'corvus', meaning…?
questions.f: Crows, ravens, magpies and jays are all corvids, from the Latin for crow.

questions.q: Formic acid, the sting of some ants, is named from 'formica', meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin, 'formica' is the ant, which sprays this acid to defend itself.

questions.q: An insect's 'exoskeleton' has the prefix 'exo', meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek, 'exo' shows the skeleton is worn on the outside of the body.

questions.q: The insect body part called the 'thorax' takes its name from a Greek word for…?
questions.f: The thorax is the middle section where an insect's legs and wings attach.

questions.q: A 'lepidopterist' is a scientist who studies which creatures?
questions.f: The name joins the Greek roots for 'scale' and 'wing'.

questions.q: The word 'apterous', describing some insects, means…?
questions.f: The 'a' means 'without' and 'pter' means wing, both from Greek.

questions.q: An insect's egg-laying tube is an 'ovipositor'; the 'ovi' part means…?
questions.f: 'Ovi' is egg and 'positor' is placer, so it literally places eggs.

questions.q: The word 'crepuscular' describes animals active at…?
