questions.f: From Latin 'crepusculum', twilight; many moths and bats are crepuscular.

questions.q: A 'murmuration' is the name for a swirling group of which birds?
questions.f: Thousands of starlings can wheel together in shape-shifting clouds at dusk.

questions.q: A 'charm' is the collective noun for a group of which small birds?
questions.f: The tinkling song of many goldfinches together suits the name 'charm'.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for a group of herons?
questions.f: Herons standing statue-still by the water gave rise to the word 'siege'.

questions.q: Chicks that hatch well-developed and can walk and feed almost at once are called…?
questions.f: Ducklings and chicks are precocial, unlike helpless, naked songbird chicks.

questions.q: Chicks that hatch blind, naked and helpless, needing much care, are called…?
questions.f: Most songbirds are altricial and depend fully on their parents at first.

questions.q: The clear fluid that acts as an insect's 'blood' is called…?
questions.f: Haemolymph is usually greenish or yellowish, not red, because it carries no haemoglobin.

questions.q: Which flightless, nocturnal parrot from New Zealand is one of the world's rarest birds?
questions.f: The kakapo is the heaviest parrot and cannot fly, so it climbs and walks instead.

questions.q: Which South American bird has chicks that grow tiny claws on their wings to climb?
questions.f: Hoatzin chicks lose the claws as they grow, but they hint at ancient bird ancestors.

questions.q: A bird eggshell is made mostly of which mineral?
questions.f: It is the same mineral found in chalk and seashells.

questions.q: Which powerful rainforest eagle has talons as large as a bear's claws?
questions.f: The harpy eagle can snatch monkeys and sloths right out of the treetops.

questions.q: What special feature lets birds take in fresh oxygen even as they breathe out?
questions.f: Air sacs keep air flowing one way through the lungs, ideal for high-altitude flight.

questions.q: What decides whether a female honeybee larva grows into a queen rather than a worker?
questions.f: A rich diet of royal jelly switches on the larva's development into a queen.

questions.q: Which arrangement of toes, two pointing forward and two back, do parrots and woodpeckers have?
questions.f: Zygodactyl feet give a strong grip for climbing and holding food.

questions.q: What is the practice of birds laying eggs in another species' nest to be raised called?
questions.f: The cuckoo is the most famous brood parasite, tricking other birds into feeding its chick.

questions.q: Which African bird holds the record for the highest confirmed bird flight, over 11 km up?
questions.f: One was famously struck by an aircraft at that astonishing height.

questions.q: Which beetle can spray a boiling-hot, foul chemical to defend itself?
questions.f: It mixes chemicals inside its body to fire the spray with a popping sound.

questions.q: Insects that undergo complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult) are called…?
questions.f: Butterflies, beetles and bees are all holometabolous insects.

questions.q: Which colours, invisible to humans, can bees see to find nectar guides on flowers?
questions.f: Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that act like landing lights for bees.

questions.q: How does a male moth detect a female from far away in the dark?
questions.f: A male moth's plume-like antennae can sense a few scent molecules on the breeze.

questions.q: The word 'entomophagy' means the practice of eating…?
questions.f: Insects are a common, protein-rich food for billions of people worldwide.

questions.q: 'Chitin', the tough material of an insect's shell, is named from a Greek word for…?
questions.f: Chitin also stiffens the beaks of squid and the shells of crabs.

questions.q: An 'ornithologist' studies birds; the matching 'ology' word for the study of bees is…?
questions.f: 'Apiology', from the Latin 'apis', is the scientific study of honeybees.

questions.q: Which bird is famous for the enormous shoe-shaped bill it uses to catch fish and even young crocodiles?
questions.f: The shoebill often stands frozen for long periods, then strikes with its huge bill.

questions.q: The name of the bird order 'Strigiformes' comes from 'strix', an old word for a…?
questions.f: 'Strix' was a screeching night bird in Roman legend, linked to owls.

questions.q: The 'mel' in 'mellifluous' and 'melliferous' means…?
questions.f: From Latin, 'mel' is honey; a melliferous plant is one that yields nectar for it.

questions.q: An insect breathes through tiny openings along its body rather than through a nose.
questions.f: These openings, called spiracles, lead to tubes that carry air straight to the tissues.

questions.q: What are the tiny breathing holes along the sides of an insect's body called?
questions.f: Because they rely on spiracles, insects cannot grow as large as big animals.

questions.q: Which tiny wasp is essential to the life cycle of the fig, pollinating it from the inside?
questions.f: Most kinds of fig depend on their own special species of fig wasp.

questions.q: Which insect spends the longest time as a nymph underwater before a brief adult life?
questions.f: A mayfly may live years as a nymph but only a day or so as a winged adult.

questions.q: The prefix 'antho', as in 'anthophilous' insects, means…?
questions.f: From Greek, anthophilous means flower-loving, describing many pollinators.

questions.q: Which group of dinosaurs are modern birds believed to have descended from?
questions.f: Theropods included two-legged meat-eaters like Velociraptor, close cousins of birds.

questions.q: 'Archaeopteryx', an ancient link between dinosaurs and birds, has a name meaning 'ancient…'?
questions.f: 'Archaeo' means ancient and 'pteryx' means wing, both from Greek.

questions.q: Among living animals, which are birds' closest relatives?
questions.f: Birds and crocodilians are the only survivors of the group called archosaurs.

questions.q: Which bird has a beak longer than the rest of its body, used to reach deep flowers?
questions.f: It must perch and preen with its feet because its beak is too long to reach.

questions.q: The 'vespi' in 'vespiary' names which stinging insect?
questions.f: From Latin 'vespa', wasp; a vespiary is a wasps' nest, and gave a scooter its name.

questions.q: What do we call the sound-making method used by crickets rubbing body parts together?
questions.f: A cricket scrapes a rough edge of one wing across the other to stridulate.

questions.q: Which insects have a caste system that includes a queen, workers and sometimes soldiers?
questions.f: Such highly organised insects are described as 'eusocial', meaning truly social.

questions.q: The word describing highly cooperative insects like ants and honeybees is…?
questions.f: In eusocial colonies, only a few members reproduce while the rest help raise young.

questions.q: Which bird can drink seawater thanks to special glands that remove the salt?
questions.f: Salt glands near the eyes drip the extra salt out through the nostrils.

questions.q: What do we call the yearly two-way journey some butterflies, like the monarch, undertake?
questions.f: No single monarch makes the whole round trip; it takes several generations.

questions.q: What is the resting, paused state some insects enter to survive winter or drought called?
questions.f: During diapause an insect's growth and activity almost completely stop.

questions.q: 'Eclosion' is the name for the moment an insect does what?
c: Emerges from its pupa or egg
questions.f: A newly eclosed butterfly must pump fluid into its crumpled wings before it can fly.

questions.q: Which bird is thought to have the most feathers, especially in winter, sometimes over 25,000?
questions.f: Swans grow extra downy feathers to stay warm on icy water.

questions.q: The 'psittac' root, as in 'psittacine', refers to which birds?
questions.f: From the Greek 'psittakos', parrot; psittacine simply means parrot-like.

questions.q: The 'gallus' root, seen in 'gallinaceous', refers to which farm bird?
questions.f: From Latin, 'gallus' is the rooster; gallinaceous birds include chickens and pheasants.

questions.q: Which garden bird is known to solve puzzles and even use bread as bait to catch fish?
questions.f: Members of the crow family are among the most intelligent of all birds.

questions.q: What do we call a female bird's colouring that blends into the nest, unlike the bright male?
questions.f: Dull female feathers help hide her and the eggs from hungry predators.

questions.q: Some cicadas spend more than a decade underground before emerging as adults.
questions.f: Periodical cicadas in North America appear together after exactly 13 or 17 years.

questions.q: Which insect performs a figure-eight 'waggle dance' to share the direction of food?
questions.f: The angle of the dance tells other bees which way to fly relative to the sun.

questions.q: What do we call an animal, like the hummingbird, whose diet is mainly flower nectar?
questions.f: Nectarivores often have long tongues or beaks to reach deep into blossoms.

questions.q: What do we call a bird whose diet is mainly seeds, like a finch?
questions.f: From Latin 'granum', grain; granivores often have short, strong, cone-shaped beaks.

questions.q: Which insect uses polarised light and the sun to steer a straight line while rolling dung?
questions.f: On moonless nights, dung beetles have even been shown to steer by the Milky Way.

questions.q: What is the fan-shaped bundle of long feathers a peacock raises called?
questions.f: A peacock's shimmering 'train' is not its tail but very long feathers above it.

questions.q: Which insect can detect a flower's faint electric field to tell if it still holds nectar?
questions.f: Tiny hairs on a bee's body bend in a flower's electric field, giving it a clue.

questions.q: What is the word for a bird's overall pattern and colour of feathers?
questions.f: Many birds switch to brighter breeding plumage in spring.

questions.q: Which bird, now extinct, was a large flightless pigeon relative from Mauritius?
questions.f: The dodo vanished within about a century of people arriving on its island.

questions.q: The 'culex' root, as in 'culicine', names which biting insect?
questions.f: From Latin, 'culex' is the gnat or mosquito, whose bites can spread disease.

questions.q: Which insects 'herd' aphids, protecting them to harvest their sweet honeydew?
questions.f: Some ants even carry their aphids to fresh plants, like farmers moving cattle.

questions.q: What sweet substance, given off by aphids, do ants and some bees collect?
questions.f: Honeydew is the sugary waste aphids leave after feeding on plant sap.

questions.q: Which sense allows the kiwi to find worms underground, unusual for a bird?
questions.f: The kiwi's nostrils are at the beak's tip, letting it sniff out prey in soil.

questions.q: What is the protective, jelly-like food fed to all young bee larvae for their first days?
questions.f: Only future queens keep eating royal jelly; workers switch to honey and pollen.

questions.q: What sticky plant resin do honeybees gather to seal and protect their hive?
questions.f: Propolis, sometimes called bee glue, even helps keep germs out of the hive.

questions.q: Which bird can hover in place and dive to snatch fish, then shake off water in flight?
questions.f: A kingfisher's dazzling blue comes from the way its feathers scatter light.

questions.q: The blue and green shimmer of a peacock feather is not from pigment but from what?
questions.f: Such 'structural colour' shifts and glitters as the viewing angle changes.

questions.q: Which insect can rotate its head almost fully around and is a patient ambush hunter?
questions.f: A mantis grabs prey with spiny front legs faster than the eye can follow.

questions.q: Male mosquitoes do not bite; only females feed on blood.
questions.f: Females need the protein in blood to make their eggs; males sip only nectar.

questions.q: What is the term for the yearly regrowth in which a bird replaces all its flight feathers?
questions.f: Some ducks moult so many feathers at once that they cannot fly for weeks.

questions.q: Which insect's caterpillar produces the silk used to weave fine cloth?
questions.f: A single silkworm cocoon can unwind into a thread over a kilometre long.

questions.q: Which flightless bird once stood over three metres tall in New Zealand before dying out?
questions.f: The giant moa was hunted to extinction not many centuries ago.

questions.q: What is the term for the loss of a species forever, as happened to the dodo and the moa?
questions.f: From Latin, it means 'quenched', like a flame that is put out for good.

questions.q: A springy bone that stores energy on every wingbeat, a Latin name meaning 'little fork', and a Thanksgiving table tradition converge on which everyday word?
questions.f: The furcula is a fused pair of collarbones, and it flexes like a tiny spring in flight.

questions.q: A Latin word for a raft, a breastbone with no ridge down it, and birds that traded flight for running converge on which group?
questions.f: Ostrich, emu, rhea, cassowary and kiwi are all ratites, and none can fly.

questions.q: A tuft on the wing's 'thumb', a device aircraft designers copied as a leading-edge slat, and the trick that stops a stall on landing converge on which feature?
questions.f: Raise a bird's alula and you can watch the airflow stay glued to the wing at low speed.

questions.q: A Latin word for oarsmen, feathers moulted a few at a time so flight is never lost, and the ten primaries of a wing converge on which term?
questions.f: The tail's flight feathers, by contrast, are the rectrices, the 'steerers'.

questions.q: Tiny hooks called 'hamuli' on a feather serve what purpose?
c: To zip the barbs into a smooth vane
questions.f: When barbs unhook, a bird re-zips them by preening, restoring a windproof surface.

questions.q: The fleshy area at the base of the upper beak, seen on parrots and pigeons, is the…?
questions.f: In budgerigars the cere's colour can even reveal whether the bird is male or female.

questions.q: A cave-nesting South American bird that clicks to fly in the dark, whose oil-rich chicks were once boiled for lamp fuel, is the…?
questions.f: It is the only nocturnal fruit-eating bird in the world.

questions.q: A wader that shrinks its own gut before departure, eleven days aloft without food or rest, and a track from Alaska to New Zealand converge on which bird?
questions.f: One tagged godwit flew over 13,000 km non-stop, the longest flight ever recorded.

questions.q: A nightjar the Hopi called 'the sleeping one', a bird found cold and torpid in a rock crevice for weeks, and a heart slowed almost to nothing converge on which species?
questions.f: The common poorwill is the only bird known to hibernate in the full sense.

questions.q: A German compound joining 'migration' and 'restlessness', caged birds fluttering toward one horizon, and an urge that appears exactly on schedule converge on which term?
questions.f: Even birds raised indoors show Zugunruhe when their wild cousins would be leaving.

questions.q: A failed northern seed crop, waxwings turning up hundreds of miles south of normal, and a word normally used of volcanoes converge on 'irruption', which means what?
c: An irregular mass movement of birds outside their normal range
A burst of song at dawn
questions.f: Unlike migration, an irruption is irregular, driven by hunger rather than the calendar.

questions.q: A Latin word for 'form', a stage counted between one shed skin and the next, and five such steps in a caterpillar's life converge on which term?
questions.f: A caterpillar can grow thousands of times heavier across its instars.

questions.q: A Latin word for 'image', the form reached after the final moult, and the partner term to 'larva' converge on which word?
questions.f: The imago is the only stage of most insects that can mate and, usually, fly.

questions.q: A Greek word for stripping off, a pale soft insect for a few hours afterwards, and a hormone named from the same root converge on which process?
questions.f: Ecdysis leaves behind a perfect hollow shell of the animal, called the exuvia.

questions.q: A bird that plunges through crusted snow at prey it can only hear, and whose facial disc is the widest of any owl, is the…?
questions.f: It can punch through snow crust hard enough to bear a person, guided by sound alone.

questions.q: Hind wings shrunk into vibrating clubs, an organ that works like an aircraft's gyroscope, and the reason a fly is so hard to swat converge on which structures?
questions.f: Halteres beat in antiphase with the wings and sense every twist of the body.

questions.q: Bees, wasps and ants form the order Hymenoptera; the root 'hymen' means…?
questions.f: The name points to their thin, membrane-like wings, from Greek.

questions.q: Dragonflies belong to the order 'Odonata', a name built from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek 'odonto', for their strongly toothed jaws that grip prey.

questions.q: Fleas make up the order 'Siphonaptera'; the '-aptera' ending tells us they are…?
questions.f: 'Siphon' points to their sucking mouthparts and 'aptera' to their lack of wings.

questions.q: Grasshoppers and crickets form the order 'Orthoptera'; 'ortho' means…?
questions.f: From Greek, the name refers to their straight, narrow forewings.

questions.q: Museum curators keep colonies of which beetles to clean delicate animal skeletons?
questions.f: The larvae nibble away every scrap of dried tissue without scratching the bone.

questions.q: A Greek word for ant, the lifelong specialism of E. O. Wilson, and a field with its own international society converge on which science?
questions.f: Wilson began by studying fire ants in Alabama as a teenager.

questions.q: A Latin name for China, a craft over 4,000 years old, and caterpillars reared on mulberry leaves converge on which practice?
questions.f: 'Sericum' meant silk, and 'Seres' was the Roman name for the people who made it.

questions.q: When a harmless hoverfly mimics a wasp's warning colours to avoid being eaten, this is called…?
questions.f: It is named after Henry Bates, who studied Amazon butterflies in the 1800s.

questions.q: The use of bold warning colours to signal that an animal is toxic is called…?
questions.f: From Greek meaning 'away-signal'; the black-and-yellow of wasps is a classic example.

questions.q: Which ant has formed a European 'supercolony' thousands of kilometres long, whose members never fight one another?
questions.f: Ants from Italy and Spain treat each other as nestmates, as though one vast colony.

questions.q: Workers hanging motionless from a nest ceiling, abdomens swollen into translucent globes, and a desert colony's living pantry converge on which ants?
questions.f: Nestmates tap a replete to make it bring up a drop of stored food.

questions.q: Bodies linked into living bridges, a raft that floats a whole colony through a flood, and a nest made of nothing but ants converge on which insects?
questions.f: Their temporary living nest is called a bivouac, and it moves on every few days.

questions.q: Adults holding a larva as though it were a glue gun, leaves drawn together in a team effort, and a nest built with neither wax nor mud converge on what material?
c: Silk squeezed from their own larvae
questions.f: The larvae give up their silk, which would otherwise have spun their own cocoons.

questions.q: A self-experimenting scientist's four-point sting index, and a pain likened to walking on hot coals, converge on which 2.5 cm ant?
questions.f: Justin Schmidt rated hundreds of stings on himself to build the scale.

questions.q: A bird that answers a particular human whistle, a partnership recorded for centuries in Mozambique, and an appetite for beeswax converge on the bird leading people to what?
questions.f: The honey-hunters take the honey and leave the wax and grubs as payment.

questions.q: A molecule named 'light-bringer', an enzyme now used to make living cells glow in laboratories, and a reaction that wastes almost no heat explain which insect's light?
c: A chemical reaction of luciferin and luciferase
questions.f: The chemistry is so efficient that firefly light is called cold light.

questions.q: Periodical cicadas emerge together only after 13 or 17 years; scientists think these prime numbers help them…?
questions.f: Prime-number cycles make it hard for any predator boom to line up with them.

questions.q: Which butterfly family has caterpillars that ants guard in exchange for sugary droplets?
questions.f: Some blues go further and are carried into the nest, where the ants rear them.

questions.q: The viceroy butterfly looks almost identical to the toxic monarch; this shared-warning resemblance is…?
questions.f: Since both are actually distasteful, each reinforces the other's warning to predators.

questions.q: Which bird uniquely digests leaves by fermenting them in an enlarged crop, rather like a cow?
questions.f: This fermentation gives the hoatzin a smell that earns it the nickname 'stinkbird'.

questions.q: A heart-shaped facial dish, ear openings set at slightly different heights, and a strike made in total darkness converge on which hunting method?
c: Slightly offset ears that time sound to each side
questions.f: The height difference lets the owl judge whether a rustle is above or below it.

questions.q: A Madagascan giant whose eggs are still found in dune sand, a creature probably behind the legend of the roc, and an extinction within the last thousand years converge on which bird?
questions.f: One elephant bird egg could hold the contents of well over a hundred hen's eggs.

questions.q: A parrot that strips rubber from car windscreens, birds filmed cooperating on multi-step puzzles, and the world's only true mountain parrot converge on which species?
questions.f: Keas will even work together to pull a rope so a distant food box opens.

questions.q: The fused bones of a bird's 'hand', which carry the main flight feathers, form the…?
questions.f: Fusing the hand bones into one strut keeps the wingtip rigid under load.

questions.q: The three simple eyes on the top of many insects' heads are called…?
questions.f: Ocelli likely sense light and dark and help keep the insect level in flight.

questions.q: 'True bugs' such as shield bugs belong to the order 'Hemiptera'; 'hemi' means…?
questions.f: The name refers to forewings that are half-hardened, half-membranous.

questions.q: Food passed mouth to mouth, a route by which chemical signals reach every nestmate, and a word built from Greek for 'nourishment exchange' converge on which behaviour?
questions.f: Trophallaxis makes a colony share one stomach as well as one scent.

questions.q: Tomato and blueberry flowers that refuse to let go of pollen, a bee gripping a blossom and vibrating hard, and a knack honeybees simply lack converge on which process?
questions.f: Growers keep bumblebee colonies in greenhouses purely for this shaking service.

questions.q: A researcher who painted numbers on the backs of bees, a Nobel Prize shared with Lorenz and Tinbergen, and the reading of a figure-of-eight dance converge on whom?
questions.f: He proved the dance encodes both the distance and the compass bearing to food.

questions.q: A giant's name from the Bible, a grub that can outweigh a small bird, and an African rainforest beetle converge on which insect?
questions.f: Adults are gentle giants that feed mainly on tree sap and ripe fruit.

questions.q: Which moth boasts one of the largest wing areas of any insect, named after a Greek Titan?
questions.f: Its wingtips even mimic a snake's head to scare off predators.

questions.q: A butterfly named after a British queen, restricted to a small corner of Papua New Guinea, and a wingspan approaching 25 cm converge on which insect?
questions.f: It was named in 1907 in honour of Queen Alexandra, wife of Edward VII.

questions.q: How do dragonfly nymphs make a quick escape underwater?
c: By squirting water from the rear like a jet
questions.f: They draw water into the gut and blast it out to shoot forward.

questions.q: Adult dragonflies are astonishing hunters, catching roughly what share of the prey they chase?
questions.f: They intercept prey by predicting where it will be, not just chasing it.

questions.q: Which wingless midge, able to survive being frozen solid, is the largest purely land animal native to Antarctica?
questions.f: At about 6 mm long, this midge outranks every other land animal on the continent.

questions.q: The gigantic prehistoric dragonfly relative 'Meganeura' could grow so large partly because of what?
c: Higher oxygen levels in the ancient air
questions.f: Insects breathe through tubes, so richer air once allowed far bigger bodies.

questions.q: Tubes instead of lungs, side openings called spiracles, and the reason no insect today grows dog-sized converge on which system?
questions.f: Air seeps in passively, so body size is limited by how far oxygen can travel.

questions.q: An African grassland bird that walks far more than it flies, a male reaching about 20 kg, and a display that inflates a great white throat converge on which species?
questions.f: The kori bustard is the heaviest living animal capable of sustained flight.

questions.q: A bird that rides on giraffe and buffalo, grooms out ticks and earwax, and will keep a small wound open for a drink converge on which species?
questions.f: Its relationship with big grazers sits somewhere between helper and freeloader.

questions.q: The 'falco' in falcon may derive from a Latin word 'falx', meaning…?
questions.f: It likely refers to the sickle-like curve of the falcon's wings or talons.

questions.q: Ducks and geese belong to 'Anseriformes'; the root 'anser' means…?
questions.f: From Latin, it is why goose-like traits are described as 'anserine'.

questions.q: Pigeons and doves form 'Columbiformes'; the root 'columba' means…?
questions.f: From Latin; a 'columbarium' can even mean a dovecote for keeping them.

questions.q: A term shared with human anatomy, a toe that points the wrong way, and the grip that lets a bird sleep without falling converge on which part?
questions.f: In humans the hallux is the big toe; in birds it closes the perching grip from behind.

questions.q: A Latin word for a summit, a measurement taken with callipers, and a clue for separating look-alike species converge on which feature?
questions.f: Ringers record culmen length as routinely as they record wing length.

questions.q: A Swedish word for play, a patch of ground used by males year after year, and females who visit only to choose converge on which term?
questions.f: At a lek the same few central males may father most of the chicks.

questions.q: Feathers shed on purpose, warm skin pressed against a clutch, and a seasonal change ringers use to sex a bird converge on which structure?
questions.f: Some ducks pluck their own down to line the nest as the patch develops.

questions.q: A group name shared with the solemn gathering held after a funeral, and used for scavenging birds crowded on the ground, is which collective noun?
questions.f: The same birds soaring in a rising thermal are instead called a kettle.

questions.q: A bird that punches a row of holes with its bill, threads plant fibre or spider silk through them, and draws two leaves into a cradle is doing what?
c: Sewing a leaf cradle with plant fibre or silk
questions.f: The stitching is so neat that early naturalists refused to believe a bird had done it.

questions.q: Which woodpecker drills thousands of holes in a single 'granary tree' to store acorns?
questions.f: A family group guards its granary all year, refitting acorns as they shrink and loosen.

questions.q: A pigment that both darkens a feather and toughens it, the reason so many white birds have black wingtips, and a chemical shared with human hair converge on which substance?
questions.f: Melanin-rich feathers resist abrasion, so they last where pale ones would fray.

questions.q: A bird's feather colour can come purely from structure, with no coloured pigment at all.
questions.f: Blue in most birds is 'structural colour', made by light scattering, not blue pigment.

questions.q: The block of fused hip and backbone unique to birds, giving the body a rigid frame, is the…?
questions.f: Welding the spine to the pelvis stops a bird twisting apart under flight forces.

questions.q: A Greek word for bee, a specialism inside entomology, and a field covering some 20,000 species converge on which science?
questions.f: Only about a dozen of those species are honey-making hive bees.

questions.q: A Greek word for hidden, a stick insect swaying like a twig in the breeze, and the exact opposite of warning colours converge on which strategy?
questions.f: Crypsis works by never being noticed at all, rather than by scaring anything off.

questions.q: An insect that never touches land, striding over waves hundreds of miles from any shore, and the only truly marine insect group converge on which creature?
questions.f: Halobates lays its eggs on floating feathers, seeds and even plastic debris.

questions.q: A Latin root meaning winged, wings snapped off after one single flight, and the founders of brand new colonies converge on which caste?
questions.f: A queen ant chews or rubs her own wings away before starting to dig.

questions.q: A stubby fusion of the last few vertebrae, the loss of a long bony ancestral tail, and the anchor for a spreading fan converge on which structure?
questions.f: Archaeopteryx still had the long bony tail that modern birds have traded away.

questions.q: A word borrowed from shipbuilding, a ridge missing entirely in the ostrich, and the anchor for the muscles that power a wingbeat converge on which structure?
questions.f: The bigger the keel, the more muscle a bird can pack in for powered flight.

questions.q: A swift of eastern Asia, a tail ending in bare feather spines, and speeds over 100 km/h without a dive converge on which bird?
questions.f: In a stooping dive the peregrine wins, but in flapping flight this needletail leads.

questions.q: The word 'vespertine', describing creatures active in the evening, shares a root with which word?
questions.f: From Latin 'vesper', evening; vespers are evening prayers.

questions.q: Which butterfly or moth family name, 'Sphingidae', gives the hawkmoths a link to which mythical creature?
questions.f: A startled hawkmoth caterpillar rears up in a pose said to recall the Sphinx.

questions.q: Cockroaches belong to the order 'Blattodea', from 'blatta', a Latin word for…?
questions.f: The order now includes termites, which are essentially social cockroaches.

questions.q: Earwigs form the order 'Dermaptera'; the root 'derma' means…?
questions.f: It refers to their leathery, skin-like forewings that cover folded hind wings.

questions.q: A name built from 'wing' and 'mark', a weighted dark patch near a wingtip, and steadier gliding converge on which structure?
questions.f: Removing the pterostigma makes a dragonfly's glide noticeably less stable.

questions.q: The first small crack a chick makes when it starts to break out of its shell is called…?
questions.f: From that first pip it can take a day or more of rest and effort to get out.

questions.q: An owl that wades into freezing rivers after salmon, a bird revered by the Ainu of Hokkaido, and the heaviest owl alive converge on which species?
questions.f: It nests in trees so vast that logging alone can end a local population.

questions.q: Which Neotropical birds make a living by following army ant swarms and snatching the insects that flee?
questions.f: They rarely eat the ants at all; they feast on the panic the ants create.

questions.q: The scientific name 'Apis mellifera' for the honeybee roughly means…?
questions.f: 'Apis' is bee and 'mellifera' means honey-bearing, both from Latin.

questions.q: Scout bees performing rival dances, a swarm hanging from a branch, and a slow build-up of votes decide what?
c: Which new nest site the swarm will take
questions.f: Scouts dance for competing sites until enough agree, then the swarm lifts off together.

questions.q: Which duck lines its nest with down so warm that people have gathered it for bedding for centuries?
questions.f: Collectors take eiderdown from the nests only after the ducklings have safely left.

questions.q: A Latin root meaning tender, wings that have not yet hardened, and colours that are still washed-out converge on which term?
questions.f: A teneral dragonfly is easy prey until its cuticle sets, which can take days.

questions.q: Which bird species is famous for the male incubating the eggs alone through the Antarctic winter?
questions.f: He balances the egg on his feet under a warm belly fold for about two months.

questions.q: Some hoverflies mimic the black-and-yellow bands of wasps yet cannot sting at all.
questions.f: This harmless disguise, called Batesian mimicry, fools predators into leaving them be.

questions.q: Which wasp paralyses a tarantula to feed its single larva, and delivers one of the most painful stings known?
questions.f: The sting is agonising but brief; the spider becomes living food for the grub.

questions.q: Greek roots meaning 'home-loving', a seabird returning to the exact ledge where it hatched, and rings recovered at the very colony of birth converge on which concept?
questions.f: Strong philopatry means island colonies can be genetically distinct from neighbours.

questions.q: The obsolete order name 'Isoptera', meaning 'equal wings', once covered which insects, now grouped with cockroaches?
questions.f: Genetic work showed termites are social cockroaches, so the old order was dissolved.

questions.q: A Latin word for the palm of a hand, skin stretched between three toes, and a paddle that folds on the forward stroke converge on which foot type?
questions.f: Grebes and coots instead have lobed toes, with flaps on each toe separately.

questions.q: Which bird stores surplus food impaled on thorns and barbed wire, keeping a larder for lean days?
questions.f: Its old country name, butcher bird, comes from that thorny pantry.

questions.q: The 'strid' in 'stridulation' and 'strident' carries the sense of…?
questions.f: From Latin 'stridere', to creak or screech, fitting a cricket's rasping song.

questions.q: What colour is the front of a penguin?
questions.f: A dark back and pale belly make a swimming penguin hard to spot from above or below.

questions.q: Which bright red bird is a favourite winter visitor in North American gardens?
questions.f: Only the male cardinal is scarlet; the female is a soft brown with red touches.

questions.q: Which black-and-white bird is famous for picking up shiny objects?
questions.f: Magpies are so clever they can recognise themselves in a mirror.

questions.q: Which Australian bird sounds as if it is laughing out loud?
questions.f: A family of kookaburras will laugh together to tell others whose patch of forest it is.

questions.q: Which small seabird has a big colourful beak and nests on northern cliffs?
questions.f: A puffin can hold a dozen little fish crosswise in its beak at once.

questions.q: Which tall bird in old stories builds its nest on a rooftop or chimney?
questions.f: Real white storks do nest on roofs and poles, and people often build platforms for them.

questions.q: Which big bird has a bare head and circles high in the sky looking for food?
questions.f: A vulture's bare head stays cleaner than a feathery one when it feeds.

questions.q: Which owl is snowy white and lives where it is very cold?
questions.f: A snowy owl's thick feathers cover even its toes to keep out the Arctic cold.

questions.q: Which little insect can nibble holes in woollen clothes in a cupboard?
questions.f: It is the tiny caterpillars, not the adult moths, that chew the wool.

questions.q: Which insect has pincers at the end of its body and hides under stones?
questions.f: Despite the scary name, earwigs do not crawl into ears; many are caring mothers.

questions.q: Which tiny green insect sits in crowds on rose stems, sipping plant juice?
questions.f: Aphids are the favourite food of ladybirds and their hungry young.

questions.q: Which flat brown insect scuttles away as soon as you turn on a light?
questions.f: Cockroaches can squeeze through a gap no thicker than a coin.

questions.q: Which tiny insect jumps out of a dog's fur and is very hard to catch?
questions.f: A flea can leap more than a hundred times its own height.

questions.q: Which long creepy-crawly has lots of legs and curls up when touched?
questions.f: 'Millipede' means 'thousand feet', but even the leggiest have far fewer.

questions.q: Which small garden animal carries a shell and leaves a shiny trail?
questions.f: A snail can pull its whole soft body inside its shell to stay safe and damp.

questions.q: Which long pink garden animal helps plants by making tunnels in the soil?
questions.f: Worm tunnels let air and rain reach plant roots underground.

questions.q: What does a stink bug do if something frightens it?
questions.f: The smelly spray teaches birds to leave shield bugs alone next time.

questions.q: What colours is a monarch butterfly?
questions.f: Those bold orange wings warn birds that a monarch tastes horrible.

questions.q: What colour is a grasshopper hiding in a meadow most likely to be?
questions.f: Being green makes a grasshopper almost invisible among the grass blades.

questions.q: What colour are most swans that swim on park lakes?
questions.f: Australia does have black swans, which surprised European explorers.

questions.q: How many legs does a butterfly have?
questions.f: Some butterflies keep their tiny front pair tucked up, so they look four-legged.

questions.q: How many legs does an ant have?
questions.f: Six legs let an ant keep three feet on the ground at all times, so it never wobbles.

questions.q: How many antennae does an ant have?
questions.f: An ant waves its two antennae to smell trails and greet nestmates.

questions.q: How many wings does a housefly have?
questions.f: Most insects have four wings, but flies have just one pair.

questions.q: What does a hummingbird use to reach the sweet liquid deep inside a flower?
questions.f: The tongue splits at the tip and flicks in and out many times a second.

questions.q: What food do people usually put in a garden bird feeder?
questions.f: Sunflower seeds are a favourite because they are full of energy-rich oil.

questions.q: What is a woodpecker looking for when it taps at tree bark?
questions.f: Its long, sticky tongue can reach deep into a tunnel to hook out a grub.

questions.q: What does a farmyard chicken peck at in the yard?
questions.f: Chickens also swallow tiny stones on purpose, to help grind up their food.

questions.q: What does a duck dabble for under the water of a pond?
questions.f: A dabbling duck tips tail-up so it can reach food just below the surface.

questions.q: Where does a woodpecker usually make its nest?
c: In a hole in a tree
questions.f: Old woodpecker holes are later used by owls, bats and squirrels.

questions.q: Where would you most likely find a garden spider's web?
c: Between plants or in a corner
questions.f: A garden spider often rebuilds its whole web fresh each morning.

questions.q: On which part of its body does a honeybee carry lumps of pollen home?
questions.f: Those pollen bundles are sometimes called pollen baskets or 'trousers'.

questions.q: What do spiders make their webs out of?
questions.f: A spider makes several kinds of silk, some sticky and some strong as rope.

questions.q: What can you put in a garden so birds can splash and drink?
questions.f: Bathing helps birds keep their feathers clean so they fly better.

questions.q: What happens to rain when it lands on a duck's oily feathers?
questions.f: That is where the saying 'like water off a duck's back' comes from.

questions.q: Why do so many birds sing loudly early in the morning?
questions.f: So many birds sing at once at first light that we call it the dawn chorus.

questions.q: What colour is a ladybird's shiny shell most often?
questions.f: Some ladybirds are yellow or orange, and a few are black with red spots.

questions.q: What do most small birds build their nests out of?
questions.f: Some birds line the nest with soft moss, feathers or even animal fur.

questions.q: Which part of a bird holds tight to a branch?
questions.f: A perching bird's toes lock shut automatically, so it will not fall while asleep.

questions.q: In which season do most garden birds build nests and lay eggs?
questions.f: Spring brings lots of caterpillars, just the food hungry chicks need.

questions.q: Birds do not have any teeth.
questions.f: Instead of chewing, birds swallow food and grind it up inside their bodies.

questions.q: Every kind of bird in the world can fly.
questions.f: Ostriches, penguins, kiwis and many others get about without ever flying.

questions.q: A ladybird can open its shell and fly away.
questions.f: The spotted shell lifts up to free a pair of delicate flying wings underneath.

questions.q: A caterpillar has no wings.
questions.f: Wings appear only after the caterpillar changes inside its case.

questions.q: Spiders have wings and can fly.
questions.f: Spiders cannot fly, though tiny ones float on silk threads in the breeze.

questions.q: Butterflies begin their lives as tiny eggs.
questions.f: A butterfly usually lays each egg on the exact plant its caterpillar will eat.

questions.q: Owls have large eyes that help them see when it is dark.
questions.f: An owl's eyes are so big they cannot roll, so it turns its whole head instead.

questions.q: An earthworm has lots of tiny legs.
questions.f: A worm has no legs at all; it grips the soil with rings of tiny bristles.

questions.q: A bee visits flowers to collect food.
questions.f: Bees gather both sweet nectar for energy and pollen for protein.

questions.q: Which animal's name is hidden inside the word 'ladybird'?
questions.f: Ladybirds are beetles, not birds, but the old name has stuck for centuries.

questions.q: The word 'honeybee' is made from 'bee' and which sweet word?
questions.f: It takes a huge amount of flower nectar to make one spoonful of honey.

questions.q: 'Grasshopper' joins the word 'grass' with which jumping action?
questions.f: The name fits perfectly: it hops, and it lives in grass.

questions.q: 'Woodpecker' joins the word 'wood' with which action?
questions.f: A woodpecker can hammer wood many times a second without a headache.

questions.q: Which colour word begins the bird name 'blackbird'?
questions.f: Only the male blackbird is truly black; the female is dark brown.

questions.q: A 'songbird' is a bird that is good at doing what?
questions.f: Songbirds learn their tunes when young, a bit like children learning to talk.

questions.q: A 'seabird' is a bird that lives near what?
questions.f: Many seabirds spend months over open water, only coming ashore to nest.

questions.q: A 'nestling' is a young bird that is still in its…?
questions.f: A nestling is younger than a fledgling, which has already hopped out.

questions.q: Which small flying word finishes off 'butterfly'?
questions.f: In German a butterfly is a 'Schmetterling', and in French a 'papillon'.

questions.q: Which hot word begins the insect name 'firefly'?
questions.f: A firefly's light is cool to touch, even though its name says fire.

questions.q: A dusty old spider web in the corner of a room is called a…?
questions.f: 'Cob' comes from an old English word for spider, 'coppe'.

questions.q: A 'silkworm' is named after the soft thread it makes, which is…?
questions.f: A silkworm is really the caterpillar of a moth, not a worm at all.

questions.q: An 'anteater' is an animal that eats which insect?
questions.f: A giant anteater can flick its long tongue in and out many times a second.

questions.q: A 'beekeeper' is a person who looks after which creatures?
questions.f: Beekeepers wear pale clothing because dark colours can make bees nervous.

questions.q: 'Birdseed' is food made for which animals?
questions.f: Different seeds attract different birds, so mixed seed brings a crowd.

questions.q: An 'eggshell' is the hard outside of an…?
questions.f: An eggshell has thousands of tiny holes so the chick inside can breathe.

questions.q: If something is 'featherlight', it is very…?
questions.f: All the feathers on a small bird together weigh less than its bones do.

questions.q: A 'flightless' bird is one that cannot do what?
questions.f: Flightless birds often have strong legs instead, for running or swimming.

questions.q: A bird's 'wingspan' is measured from one wingtip to…?
questions.f: The biggest seabird wingspans are wider than a car is long.

questions.q: Someone with very sharp eyesight is said to have an 'eagle ___'.
questions.f: An eagle really can spot a rabbit from high above the ground.

questions.q: Finish the saying: 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the ___'.
questions.f: It means what you already have is safer than what you only hope for.

questions.q: To upset someone slightly is to 'ruffle their ___'.
questions.f: A cross bird really does fluff up its feathers to look bigger.

questions.q: An 'anthill' is a home built by which insects?
questions.f: The mound you see is only the roof of a much bigger underground city.

questions.q: 'Beeswax' is a useful material made by which creatures?
questions.f: Bees ooze wax from their bodies in tiny flakes, then chew it into shape.

questions.q: A 'mockingbird' gets its name because it copies, or mocks, other birds'…?
questions.f: One mockingbird can run through dozens of different borrowed tunes.

questions.q: A 'kingfisher' is named after what it is brilliant at catching.
questions.f: A kingfisher dives like an arrow and closes its eyes just before the splash.

questions.q: A 'roadrunner' gets its name from what it loves to do?
questions.f: A real roadrunner can sprint faster than most people can run.

questions.q: A 'lacewing' insect is named after the pattern on its…?
questions.f: Its clear wings really do look like fine green lace held up to the light.

questions.q: A 'stick insect' is named because it looks just like a…?
questions.f: Some even sway gently, as if a twig were moving in the breeze.

questions.q: A 'leafcutter' ant is named because it cuts up and carries…?
questions.f: A line of leafcutters looks like a tiny parade of green umbrellas.

questions.q: A 'bumblebee' is named after the humming, bumbling sound it makes when it does what?
questions.f: Bumblebees were once called 'humble-bees' because of that deep hum.

questions.q: A 'swallowtail' butterfly is named for tails on its wings like which bird's?
questions.f: Swallowtails are among the largest and most graceful garden butterflies.

questions.q: A 'hummingbird' is named after the sound its fast wings make, which is a…?
questions.f: The hum is the sound of wings beating far too fast for your eye to follow.

questions.q: The little bumps you get on cold skin are named after which bird?
questions.f: They are called goose bumps because they look like a plucked goose's skin.

questions.q: The bird name 'peacock' ends with an old word for which kind of bird?
questions.f: The female is a peahen, and the chicks are peachicks.

questions.q: The word 'beetle' comes from an old word meaning 'little ___'.
questions.f: The name points to a beetle's strong little jaws.

questions.q: If a person is 'chirpy', they are…?
questions.f: The word borrows the bright, happy sound of a small bird's chirp.

questions.q: A 'henhouse' is a small building for keeping which birds?
questions.f: A good henhouse has a perch inside, because hens like to roost off the ground.

questions.q: Which seabird can glide for hours over the ocean without flapping its wings?
questions.f: An albatross locks its wings straight and rides the wind, using hardly any energy.

questions.q: Which bird has a huge hollow horn-like ridge on top of its beak?
questions.f: Some hornbill mothers seal themselves inside a tree hole while raising chicks.

questions.q: Which bird has a fan-shaped crest and a name that copies its soft call?
questions.f: The hoopoe raises its striped crest like an opening fan when it lands.

questions.q: Which colourful bird catches bees and knocks the sting out before eating them?
questions.f: A bee-eater rubs the insect against a branch to make it safe to swallow.

questions.q: Which bird has such tiny legs that it almost never lands on the ground?
questions.f: Swifts eat, drink and even sleep on the wing, landing mainly to nest.

questions.q: What does a swallow build its nest from?
questions.f: A pair of swallows may carry over a thousand beakfuls of mud to build one nest.

questions.q: Which bird is famous for singing beautifully after dark?
questions.f: A single nightingale can perform hundreds of different musical phrases.

questions.q: Which tiny brown bird holds its short tail cocked upright and sings very loudly?
questions.f: For its size the wren has one of the loudest songs of any bird.

questions.q: Which is the second-tallest bird in the world, after the ostrich?
questions.f: Emus can cover huge distances across Australia in search of food and water.

questions.q: Which large flightless bird of New Guinea wears a tall helmet on its head?
questions.f: The helmet, called a casque, may help the cassowary push through thick forest.

questions.q: Which large flightless bird runs wild across the grasslands of South America?
questions.f: Male rheas do all the sitting on the eggs and raise the chicks alone.

questions.q: Which enormous bird soars on rising air high over the Andes mountains?
questions.f: A condor can travel over 150 km barely flapping, riding warm rising air.

questions.q: Which large, brilliantly coloured parrot lives in South American rainforests?
questions.f: Macaws crack the hardest nuts with a beak strong enough to break a broom handle.

questions.q: Which small Australian parrot is one of the world's most popular pet birds?
questions.f: Wild budgerigars fly in huge green flocks across the Australian outback.

questions.q: Which parrot can raise and lower a showy crest of feathers on its head?
questions.f: A cockatoo raises its crest when excited, curious or cross.

questions.q: Which bird changes to white feathers in winter to hide against the snow?
questions.f: In summer the same bird is speckled brown, matching the bare mountain rocks.

questions.q: Why does a woodpecker drum fast on a hollow branch?
c: To send a message to other woodpeckers
questions.f: Drumming works like a song, announcing 'this patch of wood is mine'.

questions.q: What do we call the bundle of bones and fur an owl coughs back up?
questions.f: Scientists pull pellets apart to discover exactly what an owl has been eating.

questions.q: Why do geese fly in a V shape?
c: It saves energy for the birds behind
questions.f: Each goose rides the swirl of air from the wingtip ahead, so the flock tires less.

questions.q: How does a small bird keep warm on a freezing day?
c: It fluffs up its feathers to trap air
questions.f: Trapped air works just like the padding in a winter coat.

questions.q: How many eyes does a honeybee have altogether?
questions.f: Two big compound eyes are joined by three tiny simple eyes on top of its head.

questions.q: What material do bees build honeycomb from?
questions.f: Bees must eat plenty of honey to make the wax that oozes from their bodies.

questions.q: How do honeybees cool a hive that is getting too warm?
questions.f: Bees also fetch water and spread droplets inside so the fanning cools better.

questions.q: What are young ants called before they become adults?
questions.f: Worker ants carry the larvae around the nest to keep them at the perfect temperature.

questions.q: Which butterfly travels from Africa all the way to northern Europe each year?
questions.f: It takes several generations of painted ladies to complete the round trip.

questions.q: Grasshoppers scrape a leg on a wing, but a cricket makes its song by rubbing together its…?
questions.f: One wing carries a file of ridges and the other a hard scraper, like a tiny bow and string.

questions.q: Which insect's young builds a tiny tube case from sand grains and sticks underwater?
questions.f: Each caddisfly species has its own favourite building material and design.

questions.q: Which beetle has huge antler-shaped jaws?
questions.f: The 'antlers' are really enormous mandibles, used by males to wrestle rivals.

questions.q: Which beetle can flip itself upright with a loud snap?
questions.f: A click beetle bends its body and releases it like a spring, popping into the air.

questions.q: Which strong beetle has a great curved horn on its head?
questions.f: Rhinoceros beetles can shift objects many times their own weight.

questions.q: Which harmless fly is striped like a wasp and hovers over flowers?
questions.f: Its wasp costume is a bluff, since a hoverfly has no sting at all.

questions.q: Which spider builds a round, wheel-shaped web with spokes?
questions.f: An orb weaver often eats its old web at dawn and spins a fresh one.

questions.q: Which small spider stalks prey and pounces, using two very large front eyes?
questions.f: A jumping spider trails a safety line of silk in case it misses.

questions.q: Which eight-legged relative of spiders carries a curled tail?
questions.f: Many scorpions glow an eerie blue-green under ultraviolet light.

questions.q: Which small grey shelled creature under a plant pot is a crab relative, not an insect?
questions.f: Woodlice breathe with gill-like parts, so they must stay in damp places.

questions.q: Which has just one pair of legs on each body ring: a centipede or a millipede?
questions.f: Millipedes have two pairs per ring, which is why they seem to ripple as they walk.

questions.q: Which common bird can copy car alarms and phone ringtones?
questions.f: A starling collects sounds all its life and weaves them into its rambling song.

questions.q: Which bird sweeps its flat, spoon-shaped beak through shallow water to find food?
questions.f: It walks forward swinging its bill side to side, snapping shut on anything it touches.

questions.q: Which bird has crossed beak tips for prising seeds out of pine cones?
questions.f: Young crossbills are born with straight beaks that cross over as they grow.

questions.q: Which black-and-white wading bird has a slender beak curving upwards?
questions.f: The avocet sweeps its upturned bill through mud like a tiny scythe.

questions.q: Which tall bird performs a leaping courtship dance with its partner?
questions.f: Dancing cranes bow, jump and toss grass into the air together.

questions.q: Which insect is one of the fastest fliers in the insect world?
questions.f: A dragonfly can hover, fly backwards and turn on the spot in mid-air.

questions.q: Which insect can leap higher for its size: a flea or an ant?
questions.f: A flea's jump is powered by a springy pad of stored energy in its legs.

questions.q: Spiders have antennae just like insects do.
questions.f: Spiders sense the world with hairy legs and short feelers called pedipalps instead.

questions.q: A tick is an eight-legged creature that clings to an animal's skin.
questions.f: Ticks are arachnids, closer cousins to spiders than to any insect.

questions.q: Male mosquitoes feed on flower nectar rather than blood.
questions.f: Only females need a blood meal, and they use it to make their eggs.

questions.q: An owl's feathers have soft fringed edges that make its flight very quiet.
questions.f: The fringes break up the rush of air so prey never hears the owl coming.

questions.q: Butterflies and moths both have scales covering their wings.
questions.f: Rub a wing and the 'dust' on your finger is thousands of tiny scales.

questions.q: Bees can see the colour red as clearly as people do.
questions.f: Bees are poor at red but brilliant at blue, violet and ultraviolet.

questions.q: A bird's feathers weigh more than its skeleton.
questions.f: Birds' bones are so light and airy that the plumage often outweighs them.

questions.q: Ants can lift and carry objects heavier than themselves.
questions.f: Small bodies have proportionally thicker muscles, so tiny animals are mighty.

questions.q: All bees live in big hives with a queen.
questions.f: Most of the world's bee species are solitary, each female nesting alone.

questions.q: A grasshopper's ears are not on its head.
questions.f: Grasshoppers and crickets hear through organs on their bodies and front legs.

questions.q: What are the soft fluffy feathers closest to a bird's body called?
questions.f: Down traps warm air so well that people use it to fill winter jackets.

questions.q: What was an old pen made from a bird's feather called?
questions.f: Goose feathers made the best quills, and writers trimmed them with a penknife.

questions.q: Which bird has webbed feet: a duck or a sparrow?
questions.f: Webbing spreads out to push water, then folds on the forward stroke.

questions.q: Another everyday word for a bird's beak is a…?
questions.f: Both words mean the same thing, though 'bill' suits flat duck beaks best.

questions.q: What is a bird's 'crest'?
c: A tuft of feathers on its head
questions.f: Many birds raise a crest to signal alarm or excitement.

questions.q: What is the soft red flap of skin hanging under a chicken's beak called?
questions.f: Blood flowing through the wattle helps a chicken lose heat and stay cool.

questions.q: What is the red crown on top of a rooster's head called?
questions.f: A bright red comb is usually a sign that a chicken is healthy.

questions.q: What does it mean when a bird 'roosts'?
questions.f: Some birds roost in huge crowds for warmth and safety at night.

questions.q: What does 'hatch' mean?
c: To break out of an egg
questions.f: Chicks can take many hours, and sometimes days, to hatch fully.

questions.q: What does it mean when a young bird 'fledges'?
c: It grows flight feathers and leaves the nest
questions.f: A newly fledged bird is often clumsy and follows its parents around, begging.

questions.q: What does 'camouflage' mean?
questions.f: A sitting nightjar looks so much like bark that you can walk right past it.

questions.q: What does the word 'predator' mean?
questions.f: Predators keep other animal numbers in balance in a healthy habitat.

questions.q: In nature, what does the word 'prey' mean?
questions.f: Many prey animals have eyes on the sides of their heads to watch all around.

questions.q: What does 'pollinate' mean?
c: To carry pollen so a plant can make seeds
questions.f: About three in four of our food crops do better when insects pollinate them.

questions.q: In an insect's life cycle, what is the 'larva'?
questions.f: A larva's whole job is to eat and grow before it changes shape.

questions.q: When we say ants live in a 'colony', we mean they live…?
questions.f: A single ant colony can hold millions of individuals working as one team.

questions.q: The word 'insect' comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: An insect's body looks notched into three sections, which is how it got its name.

questions.q: The word 'spider' comes from an old word meaning to…?
questions.f: Spinning silk really is the spider's defining skill.

questions.q: 'Mosquito' is a Spanish word meaning 'little ___'.
questions.f: The word travelled into English from Spanish and Portuguese sailors.

questions.q: The word 'cockroach' came into English from which Spanish word?
questions.f: English speakers reshaped 'cucaracha' into the familiar 'cock' plus 'roach'.

questions.q: The bird name 'nightingale' means 'night ___'.
questions.f: The second half comes from an old word for singing, related to 'yell'.

questions.q: The bird name 'starling' means 'little ___'.
questions.f: The name may come from the pale speckles that dot its winter feathers.

questions.q: A flamingo's fiery colour, not its shape, gave it its name; the root behind it means…?
questions.f: The bird's fiery colour, not its shape, gave it the name.

questions.q: A group of geese standing on the ground is called a…?
questions.f: Geese are noisy in a gaggle, which is probably how the word was invented.

questions.q: A baby peacock is called a…?
questions.f: Peachicks look plain and brown; the male's train takes years to grow.

questions.q: Someone who fusses over everyone is called a 'mother ___'.
questions.f: Real hens are devoted parents, gathering chicks under their wings at any hint of danger.

questions.q: To learn something 'parrot fashion' means to repeat it…?
questions.f: Real parrots do better than that: some genuinely link words to objects.

questions.q: Someone who cannot sit still is said to have 'ants in their ___'.
questions.f: Anyone who has stood on a nest of ants will understand the picture.

questions.q: Finish the cosy saying: 'snug as a bug in a ___'.
questions.f: The rhyme has been comforting children since at least the 1700s.

questions.q: Something 'moth-eaten' is old and…?
questions.f: The holes are chewed by moth caterpillars feeding on wool.

questions.q: A 'bookworm' is someone who loves to…?
questions.f: Real book-eating insects, like silverfish, nibble the paste in old bindings.

questions.q: A 'nest egg' means money that you…?
questions.f: Farmers once left one egg in a nest to encourage a hen to keep laying there.

questions.q: Someone described as 'no spring chicken' is…?
questions.f: Chicks hatched in spring fetched the best prices, so older birds were less prized.

questions.q: Which bird bobs and dips as it walks along a stream and can swim underwater?
questions.f: A dipper walks right along the stream bed hunting insects among the stones.

questions.q: Which brown-and-cream bird has a booming call heard far across reed beds?
questions.f: A bittern's boom can carry several kilometres across the marsh.

questions.q: Which bird is nicknamed a 'sea parrot'?
questions.f: The nickname comes from the puffin's bright, oddly parrot-like beak.

questions.q: Which insect can be recognised by its long, dangling legs and clumsy flight indoors?
questions.f: Crane flies are harmless, and their nickname is 'daddy longlegs' in some places.

questions.q: Which insect makes a papery nest that looks like grey scribbled layers?
questions.f: Wasps chew wood into a pulp, so their nest really is a kind of homemade paper.

questions.q: What is inside a small round swelling, or 'gall', on an oak leaf?
questions.f: The tree grows the gall in response to a tiny wasp laying an egg there.

questions.q: Which insect can carry pollen even better than the honeybee for tomato flowers?
questions.f: A bumblebee grips the flower and vibrates, shaking pollen loose.

questions.q: Which insect's larva is an underwater hunter with a mask-like grabbing lip?
questions.f: The lip shoots out in a flash to seize a passing tadpole or insect.

questions.q: Which insect is famous for being able to survive in almost any city on Earth?
questions.f: Cockroaches can eat almost anything, including glue and paper.

questions.q: What do we call the outer shell an insect must shed in order to grow?
questions.f: A freshly moulted insect is soft and pale until its new shell hardens.

questions.q: Which small bird can be seen clinging to a tree trunk and spiralling upwards?
questions.f: A treecreeper works up one trunk, then flies down to the base of the next.

questions.q: Which bird's nest is a floating raft of weeds on a lake?
questions.f: Grebe chicks often ride on a parent's back, tucked among the feathers.

questions.q: Which insect is often the very first pollinator seen on a warm day in early spring?
questions.f: She has slept all winter underground and must find flowers fast to start a nest.

questions.q: The root 'nid' in 'nidification' means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'nidus'; nidification is simply the science of nest-building.

questions.q: An aeroplane's 'aileron' is named from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From French and Latin 'ala', wing; ailerons tilt a plane much as a bird twists its wingtips.

questions.q: The Latin root 'rostrum', used in bird descriptions, means…?
questions.f: A ship's beak-like prow gave the Roman speaking platform, and later the lectern, its name.

questions.q: The root 'vol' in 'volatile' and 'volley' means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'volare'; birds in some languages are literally 'the flying ones'.

questions.q: 'Arthropod', the group that includes insects and spiders, is built from roots meaning…?
questions.f: Every arthropod, from a shrimp to a butterfly, has jointed legs.

questions.q: 'Hexapod', another word for an insect, means…?
questions.f: From Greek 'hex' and 'pous'; six legs is the insect trademark.

questions.q: The 'pede' in 'centipede' and 'millipede' means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'pes'; the same root gives us 'pedal' and 'pedestrian'.

questions.q: The word 'millipede' literally means…?
questions.f: One record-breaking species finally passed a thousand legs, discovered in 2021.

questions.q: The root 'crypt' in 'cryptic colouring' means…?
questions.f: From Greek; the same root hides inside 'crypt' and 'cryptogram'.

questions.q: The root in 'mimicry' means…?
questions.f: From Greek 'mimos', a performer, the same source as 'mime'.

questions.q: The word 'proboscis' is built from roots meaning 'in front' plus…?
questions.f: From Greek; the name suits a butterfly's forward-reaching feeding tube perfectly.

questions.q: The root in 'mandible' means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'mandere'; the same root gives us 'manger', where animals chew their feed.

questions.q: Before it named an insect's feeler, the word 'antenna' meant a ship's…?
questions.f: A naturalist borrowed the long spar's name for the long feelers of insects.

questions.q: The word 'nectar' originally named the drink of…?
questions.f: In Greek myth nectar and ambrosia kept the gods forever young.

questions.q: The root 'migr' in 'migration' means…?
c: To move from place to place
questions.f: From Latin 'migrare'; the same root gives 'emigrate' and 'immigrant'.

questions.q: A 'papilionaceous' flower, such as a pea blossom, is shaped like which insect?
questions.f: From Latin 'papilio', butterfly, which also gave French 'papillon'.

questions.q: The keeping of bees for their honey is called…?
questions.f: 'Culture' here means cultivation, as in 'agriculture'.

questions.q: The keeping and breeding of birds is called…?
questions.f: From Latin 'avis', bird; zoos and breeders rely on skilled aviculture.

questions.q: A feather that seems to change colour as you tilt it is described as…?
questions.f: The word honours Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow.

questions.q: A set of eggs laid by one bird in a single nesting attempt is called a…?
questions.f: Once they hatch, the same group of chicks becomes a brood.

questions.q: An eagle's nest built high on a crag is called an…?
questions.f: Some eyries are used and enlarged by pair after pair for a century.

questions.q: A small building or box for keeping doves is called a…?
questions.f: Medieval estates kept dovecotes as a reliable source of eggs and meat.

questions.q: A baby pigeon is called a…?
questions.f: Squabs grow so fast on rich 'crop milk' that they double in weight in days.

questions.q: A baby turkey is called a…?
questions.f: Turkey poults can fly up to roost in trees within a couple of weeks.

questions.q: A group of partridges is called a…?
questions.f: A covey stays together all winter, exploding into flight if surprised.

questions.q: A group of woodpeckers is called a…?
questions.f: The name may refer to the way woodpeckers work their way down a trunk.

questions.q: A group of rooks nesting together high in the trees is called a…?
questions.f: Their treetop nest colony is also known as a rookery.

questions.q: The bird name 'robin' began as a pet form of which human name?
questions.f: 'Robin Redbreast' was such a familiar garden visitor that people gave it a first name.

questions.q: Which bird's name comes from an Australian Aboriginal word imitating its laughing call?
questions.f: The name comes from the Wiradjuri language of New South Wales.

questions.q: Which North American bird is named after the sound of its own call, 'chick-a-dee'?
questions.f: Chickadees vary the call, and other birds listen in for its danger warnings.

questions.q: The word 'locust' comes from a Latin word that also meant which sea creature?
questions.f: 'Locusta' covered both the leaping insect and the long-bodied lobster.

questions.q: The word 'cricket' entered English from an old French word imitating…?
questions.f: The bat-and-ball game's name comes from a different root entirely.

questions.q: A 'nit' is properly the name for the egg of which creature?
questions.f: Combing out nits one by one is where the word 'nitpicking' comes from.

questions.q: To 'open a can of worms' means to start something that is…?
questions.f: Anglers really did carry tins of bait worms, easily spilled.

questions.q: A 'glow-worm' is really not a worm at all, but which insect?
questions.f: In many species the glowing adult is a wingless female signalling to flying males.

questions.q: Which feathers give a bird its smooth, streamlined outer shape?
questions.f: Contour feathers overlap like roof tiles to shed wind and rain.

questions.q: Which sense is generally weakest in most birds?
questions.f: Kiwis, vultures and albatrosses are striking exceptions with keen noses.

questions.q: Why are guillemot eggs sharply pointed at one end?
c: So they roll in a tight circle instead of off the ledge
To fit more in a nest
questions.f: Guillemots lay on bare cliff ledges with no nest at all.

questions.q: Why are the eggs of hole-nesting birds like owls usually plain white?
c: They are hidden, so camouflage is not needed
questions.f: Pale eggs are also easier for a parent to see in a dark cavity.

questions.q: What is a 'scrape' nest?
c: A shallow hollow scratched in the ground
A mud cup on a wall
questions.f: Plovers and terns lay in scrapes, relying entirely on camouflage.

questions.q: In most European songbirds, which bird does the loud territorial singing?
questions.f: In many tropical species, though, pairs sing complicated duets together.

questions.q: Roughly how many species of bee live worldwide?
questions.f: Only a handful of those make honey; most are solitary and stingless in practice.

questions.q: About how long does a honeybee worker live during a busy summer?
questions.f: Workers born in autumn live far longer, surviving the whole winter in the hive.

questions.q: What happens to most wasps in a nest when winter comes?
c: They die, and only mated queens survive
questions.f: Each spring, a lone surviving queen must start a brand new paper nest.

questions.q: Which butterfly commonly survives winter as a sleeping adult in a shed or hollow tree?
questions.f: If disturbed, it flashes its big eye-spots and hisses by rubbing its wings.

questions.q: Mosquito larvae live in water and are nicknamed…?
questions.f: They hang below the surface, breathing through a little snorkel-like tube.

questions.q: How can you tell a resting damselfly from a resting dragonfly?
c: The damselfly usually folds its wings along its body
questions.f: Dragonflies hold their wings spread flat like a tiny aeroplane.

questions.q: Where do ladybirds usually spend the winter?
questions.f: Dozens may pack into a window frame or under bark until spring.

questions.q: Which spider carries her newly hatched young about on her back?
questions.f: She first carries the egg sac attached to her body, then the spiderlings themselves.

questions.q: Which spider builds a silk-hinged lid over its burrow and waits underneath?
questions.f: It leaves trip-lines of silk around the door to feel prey walking past.

questions.q: The long-legged 'harvestman' found on walls in autumn is…?
c: Not a spider, though it is an arachnid
questions.f: A harvestman has one body section and no silk glands, unlike a spider.

questions.q: A millipede is not an insect.
questions.f: Millipedes belong to their own group, with far more than six legs.

questions.q: Most bird species have a poor sense of taste compared with humans.
questions.f: A chicken has a few dozen taste buds; you have several thousand.

questions.q: An insect's blood does not carry oxygen around its body.
questions.f: Air tubes deliver oxygen directly, so insect blood is free to do other jobs.

questions.q: Which bird digs a long burrow in a cliff top to raise its single chick?
questions.f: Puffin burrows can run more than a metre back into the turf.

questions.q: Which seabird plunges into the sea from high up like a folded arrow?
questions.f: A gannet has air sacs in its face to cushion the shock of hitting the water.

questions.q: Which bird spreads its wings wide after fishing, as if hanging them out to dry?
questions.f: Its feathers are less waterproof than a duck's, which helps it dive deep.

questions.q: Which penguin is named after a French explorer's wife?
questions.f: Dumont d'Urville named the little Antarctic penguin after Adele, his wife.

questions.q: Which seabird is famous for chasing other birds to make them drop their catch?
questions.f: This food-stealing behaviour has a name of its own: kleptoparasitism.

questions.q: Which bird can inflate a huge scarlet throat pouch to impress a mate?
questions.f: The balloon-like pouch can stay puffed up for hours during display.

questions.q: Which insect is a major pollinator of the cacao tree that gives us chocolate?
questions.f: Tiny biting midges are almost the only visitors small enough for cacao flowers.

questions.q: Which bird builds its nest almost entirely from its own hardened saliva?
questions.f: These cave nests are the main ingredient of the famous bird's nest soup.

questions.q: Which insect group provides beeswax, honey and propolis all from one nest?
questions.f: Beekeepers can harvest all three without harming a healthy colony.

questions.q: What is the frothy egg case laid by a praying mantis called?
questions.f: The foam hardens like polystyrene, protecting dozens of eggs through winter.

questions.q: Which bird is known for lining its nest cup with mud and grass and singing from wires?
questions.f: Swallows often return to the very same barn rafter year after year.

questions.q: How does a bird's 'crop' help it feed its chicks?
c: It stores food that can be brought back up
questions.f: Pigeons even produce a special cheesy 'crop milk' for their squabs.

questions.q: Why do many birds swallow grit along with their seeds?
c: To help grind the seeds inside them
questions.f: Grit stays in the muscular gizzard and does the work of teeth.

questions.q: Which large bird is famous for dropping bones onto rocks to crack them open?
questions.f: Its old name, ossifrage, means 'bone-breaker'.

questions.q: Which bird of prey hunts by day but has ear tufts, unlike most falcons?
questions.f: Those 'ears' are just feather tufts; the real ear openings are hidden lower down.

questions.q: Which insect's adult stage often has no working mouth at all?
questions.f: With only a day or two to live, an adult mayfly has no need to eat.

questions.q: How do aphids multiply so fast in summer?
c: Females give birth to live young without mating
questions.f: A single aphid can become an army in a fortnight.

questions.q: Which insects can farm a fungus underground for food?
questions.f: Their fungus combs break down tough plant material the insects cannot digest.

questions.q: Which spider spins a silk sheet underwater and fills it with air?
questions.f: It carries air down on its body hairs to top up its private diving bell.

questions.q: How do firefly larvae differ from most other beetle grubs?
c: They glow in the dark too
questions.f: Even firefly eggs can give off a faint light.

questions.q: Which insect can be identified by its 'song' alone, so scientists record them at night?
questions.f: Each cricket species has its own tempo and pitch, like a signature tune.

questions.q: What do we call the shed, empty skin an insect leaves behind after moulting?
questions.f: A dragonfly's split exuvia is often left clinging to a reed by the water.

questions.q: Which of these is a true measure of an insect's growth stage?
c: The number of moults it has completed
The number of wings it has
questions.f: Each period between moults is called an instar.

questions.q: Which bird can be recognised in flight by a deeply forked tail and a red patch?
questions.f: Red kites twist that forked tail like a rudder to steer while soaring.

questions.q: Which bird hovers over reed beds with wings held in a shallow V?
questions.f: Harriers fly low and slow, listening as much as looking for prey.

questions.q: Which is the smallest bird of prey found in Britain?
questions.f: A merlin is little bigger than a blackbird but chases small birds at high speed.

questions.q: What is a bird's 'preen gland' also known as?
questions.f: 'Uropygial' comes from Greek roots meaning 'tail rump'.

questions.q: What is the third, see-through eyelid many birds blink sideways called?
questions.f: It works like a windscreen wiper, cleaning the eye without blocking the view.

questions.q: How does a bird lose heat on a hot day, having no sweat glands?
c: By panting and fluttering its throat
questions.f: Rapid throat fluttering is called gular fluttering.

questions.q: Why can a duck stand on ice without its feet freezing?
c: Warm and cool blood flow side by side in its legs
It has fur on its toes
It keeps one foot up always
questions.f: This clever heat-swapping system is called countercurrent exchange.

questions.q: What waste do birds produce instead of liquid urine?
c: A white paste of uric acid
questions.f: Saving water this way keeps birds light enough for easy flight.

questions.q: Which insect has been used by scientists for over a century to study inheritance?
questions.f: Fruit flies breed fast, so generations of genetics can be watched in weeks.

questions.q: Which insect can walk across a spider's web without getting stuck?
questions.f: A spider steps only on the non-sticky spokes and has oily, hairy feet.

questions.q: What is the name for the fine, hair-like feathers that sense air flow on a wing?
questions.f: They act like tiny whiskers, telling a bird how the air is moving.

questions.q: Which insect's larva is called a 'leatherjacket' and lives in lawns?
questions.f: Leatherjackets chew grass roots, which is why lawn birds probe for them.

questions.q: Which of these is a real reason moths are important at night?
c: They pollinate flowers that open after dark
questions.f: Pale, scented night flowers are designed to attract moths, not bees.

questions.q: A butterfly's wings are covered in overlapping scales, not hairs.
questions.f: The scales are flattened hairs, arranged like tiles on a roof.

questions.q: Birds are the only animals with a bone called the furcula, or wishbone.
questions.f: The springy wishbone helps store and release energy on every wingbeat.

questions.q: Most spiders can eat only liquid food.
questions.f: A spider softens its meal first, then sips, since it cannot chew solid pieces.

questions.q: Bees can be trained to detect certain smells.
questions.f: Trained bees will stick out their tongues at a scent they have learnt to expect.

questions.q: The root 'phile' in 'anthophile', a flower-lover, means…?
questions.f: The same Greek root sits inside 'bibliophile', a book lover.

questions.q: The word 'chrysalis' and the metal name 'chrysanthemum' share a root meaning…?
questions.f: 'Chrysanthemum' means golden flower, from the same Greek root.
