questions.q: The word 'thorax' names an insect's middle section and in humans names the…?
questions.f: Doctors still use 'thoracic' for anything to do with the chest.

questions.q: The word 'abdomen' names an insect's rear section and means…?
questions.f: In insects the abdomen holds the digestive system and, in females, the eggs.

questions.q: The prefix 'ex' in 'exuvia' and 'exoskeleton' carries the sense of…?
questions.f: An exuvia is literally what an insect has stripped off and left outside itself.

questions.q: The 'meta' in 'metamorphosis' means…?
questions.f: Joined with 'morph', shape, it names one of nature's greatest transformations.

questions.q: The word 'pupate' means to…?
questions.f: A caterpillar often wanders far from its food plant before it pupates.

questions.q: The word 'brood', as a verb, means to…?
c: Sit on eggs to keep them warm
questions.f: 'Brooding' later came to mean sitting deep in thought.

questions.q: 'Insectivorous' plants, like the sundew, are ones that…?
questions.f: Such plants grow in poor soil and get extra nutrients from their catch.

questions.q: The word 'apterous', used for some insects, is the opposite of…?
questions.f: Worker ants are apterous, while queens keep their wings until after mating.

questions.q: A word meaning 'bird-like' or 'of birds' is…?
questions.f: 'Avian' turns up in phrases like avian anatomy and avian flu.

questions.q: To 'take wing' means to…?
questions.f: English is full of flight phrases, from 'on the wing' to 'winging it'.

questions.q: A person who studies and rescues injured wild birds works in wildlife…?
questions.f: Rehabilitators aim to return every patient to the wild if they can.

questions.q: The word 'swarm' can be used as a verb meaning to…?
questions.f: Bees swarm when a hive gets crowded and half the colony leaves with a queen.

questions.q: A 'bird of passage' is an old-fashioned term for a bird that…?
questions.f: The phrase is now also used for people who never settle in one place.

questions.q: The word 'hive' used as a verb, as in 'to hive off', means to…?
questions.f: Beekeepers really do 'hive off' a swarm into a new box.

questions.q: Which insect's name is used for a computer fault?
questions.f: Engineers once taped a real moth into a logbook after it jammed an early computer.

questions.q: Which bird's name became a word for a wonderfully happy song, as in 'a lark of a day'?
questions.f: 'Larking about' means having harmless fun, like a skylark tumbling in the air.

questions.q: In golf, a score of one under par on a hole is called a…?
questions.f: American slang once used 'bird' for anything excellent, and golfers borrowed it.

questions.q: Which insect is used in the phrase 'to have a ___ in your bonnet' about a fixed idea?
questions.f: English has more bee sayings than for almost any other insect.

questions.q: Which is the correct term for an insect that spreads pollen between plants?
questions.f: Bees, moths, beetles, flies and even some wasps are pollinators.

questions.q: What do we call an animal that eats dead animals it did not kill?
questions.f: Vultures and carrion beetles are nature's clean-up crew.

questions.q: Which term describes a creature active mainly at dawn and dusk?
questions.f: Many moths and bats do their best hunting in that half-light.

questions.q: Which word describes a bird that stays in one region all year?
questions.f: Birders use 'vagrant' for a bird blown far outside its normal range.

questions.q: A rare bird found far outside its usual range is called a…?
questions.f: A single storm can carry an American songbird right across the Atlantic.

questions.q: Which bird's beak works like a pair of tweezers for picking insects off leaves?
questions.f: Beak shape is such a good clue to diet that experts can guess a bird's food at a glance.

questions.q: The word 'bug' originally meant something quite different: a…?
questions.f: The same old sense survives in 'bugbear' and 'bugaboo'.

questions.q: The bird name 'booby' comes from a Spanish word meaning…?
questions.f: Sailors thought the tame seabirds were simple; the same word gave us 'booby prize'.

questions.q: The name 'dodo' is usually traced to a Portuguese word meaning…?
questions.f: Sailors mistook the fearless dodo's tameness for stupidity.

questions.q: The word 'vulture' comes from a Latin root meaning to…?
questions.f: The same root idea appears in 'convulsion', a violent tearing motion.

questions.q: The word 'cocoon' comes from a Provençal word meaning…?
questions.f: It reached English through French in the 1600s, along with the silk trade.

questions.q: The garden flower 'columbine' takes its name from which bird?
questions.f: Its curved petals were thought to look like a ring of doves' heads.

questions.q: The flower 'cranesbill' is named after the resemblance of its seed pods to a bird's…?
questions.f: 'Geranium' likewise comes from the Greek for crane.

questions.q: The flower name 'larkspur' refers to a resemblance to a lark's…?
questions.f: Plant names are a hidden museum of bird and insect words.

questions.q: A 'penknife' was originally a small blade used for…?
questions.f: Writers reshaped the nib every few paragraphs as the feather wore down.

questions.q: 'Coccinellidae', the ladybird family name, comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin 'coccineus', scarlet, the colour of the classic ladybird.

questions.q: A baby hawk or falcon taken for training in falconry is called an…?
questions.f: The word comes from French, where the initial 'n' drifted onto the article.

questions.q: An artificial ant nest kept for study is called a…?
questions.f: Built from the Latin 'formica', ant, on the pattern of 'aquarium'.

questions.q: To be 'the bee's knees' means to be…?
questions.f: It was 1920s American slang, invented for its silly sound rather than any real fact.

questions.q: To 'eat crow' means to…?
questions.f: The phrase suggests being forced to swallow something extremely unpleasant.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for a group of turkeys?
questions.f: The name may come from roof timbers, where turkeys liked to roost.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for swans flying in formation?
questions.f: On the water the same birds are simply called a bevy.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for a group of pheasants?
questions.f: Medieval hunting books delighted in inventing a special word for every creature.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for a group of snipe?
questions.f: 'Wisp' catches the way a few snipe flick up out of the marsh and vanish.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for a group of nightingales?
questions.f: A 'watch' fits birds that sing through the small hours of the night.

questions.q: What is the traditional collective noun for a group of caterpillars?
questions.f: Some moth caterpillars really do march in columns, nose to tail.

questions.q: What is the collective noun for a group of cockroaches?
questions.f: English collective nouns often carry an opinion about the animal.

questions.q: What is a bird's 'pinion'?
c: The outer part of its wing
questions.f: To 'pinion' a bird meant to clip that outer section so it could not fly.

questions.q: Dark above and pale below colouring, seen in penguins and many fish, is called…?
questions.f: It makes an animal hard to see from above against the deep and from below against the light.

questions.q: The partnership between acacia trees and the ants that defend them is an example of…?
questions.f: The tree grows hollow thorns for the ants to live in and feeds them sugar.

questions.q: Which insect nymph makes the frothy 'cuckoo spit' seen on plant stems?
questions.f: The nymph blows bubbles from plant sap to hide itself inside a wet foam.

questions.q: Which small insect accelerates harder than a flea when it jumps?
questions.f: A froghopper's launch subjects it to hundreds of times the force of gravity.

questions.q: Which Australian bird buries its eggs in a huge mound of leaves and sand to incubate them?
questions.f: The male tests the mound's warmth with his beak and adds or removes material all season.

questions.q: Which material do hummingbirds use to make their tiny nests stretchy?
questions.f: The silk lets the cup expand as the chicks grow inside it.

questions.q: Which bird sits motionless on a broken stump, disguising itself as part of the wood?
questions.f: A potoo even has notches in its eyelids so it can peep while apparently asleep.

questions.q: Which African bird hunts on foot across the grasslands and has quill-like head feathers?
questions.f: The name may come from those head plumes, like quills tucked behind a clerk's ear.

questions.q: Which African bird builds a giant domed stick nest strong enough to bear a person's weight?
questions.f: A single hamerkop nest can contain thousands of sticks and take months to build.

questions.q: Relative to the size of its body, which bird lays the largest egg?
questions.f: A kiwi egg can be a fifth of the mother's weight, an extraordinary burden.

questions.q: A toucan's enormous bill also works as an excellent…?
questions.f: Thermal cameras show the bill glowing warm as the bird dumps excess heat.

questions.q: How does a flamingo feed?
c: With its head upside down, filtering water
questions.f: Its bill is built back-to-front for the job, with the big lower half held still.

questions.q: Which bird feeds its chick a bright red 'crop milk' produced inside its body?
questions.f: The colour comes from the same pigments that make the adults pink.

questions.q: Which bird is known to drop stones onto ostrich eggs to break them open?
questions.f: It is one of the few birds documented using a tool as a hammer.

questions.q: Some birds deliberately rub ants through their feathers, a behaviour called…?
questions.f: The formic acid from the ants may help control feather parasites.

questions.q: Which insect can detect a distant forest fire using infrared sensors?
questions.f: Fire-loving Melanophila beetles fly toward burnt wood to lay their eggs.

questions.q: Which desert beetle collects drinking water by standing in fog with its body tilted?
questions.f: Droplets condense on its back and trickle straight down to its mouth.

questions.q: Which insect runs so fast that it must stop to let its eyes catch up?
questions.f: At full sprint its world blurs, so it dashes, pauses, then dashes again.

questions.q: Which water beetle has each eye divided in two, watching above and below the surface at once?
questions.f: Whirligigs spin in dizzying circles on the surface film in sunny weather.

questions.q: Which is the largest family of animals on Earth by number of species?
questions.f: Around 90,000 weevil species have been described, and many more await names.

questions.q: How long can a queen ant of some species live?
questions.f: One captive queen was recorded living close to 30 years.

questions.q: What causes a solitary grasshopper to turn into a swarming locust?
c: Crowding, which changes its colour and behaviour
questions.f: Touch alone can trigger the switch; crowded nymphs jostle and transform.

questions.q: Which moth has long hind-wing tails thought to confuse hunting bats?
questions.f: The spinning tails give a false echo, so the bat grabs at empty air.

questions.q: Which moths answer a bat's hunting calls with rapid clicks of their own?
questions.f: The clicks both warn that the moth tastes bad and jam the bat's sonar.

questions.q: Which moth can squeak when handled and is named for a skull-like mark?
questions.f: It even raids beehives, apparently using a chemical disguise to pass unnoticed.

questions.q: Why do groups of butterflies gather on damp mud or sand, a habit called 'puddling'?
c: To take up salts and minerals
questions.f: Males often need those minerals to pass on to a mate with their sperm packet.

questions.q: Which butterfly has wings so transparent you can read print through them?
questions.f: Its wing surface is covered in tiny pillars that stop light reflecting.

questions.q: Which insect swims upside down just beneath the surface of a pond?
questions.f: It rows with hair-fringed hind legs and carries a bubble of air on its belly.

questions.q: How does a water scorpion breathe while staying underwater?
questions.f: The 'tail' is a snorkel, not a sting; water scorpions are harmless to people.

questions.q: Which wingless insect has changed so little that its relatives predate winged insects?
questions.f: Silverfish and their kin never evolved wings at all, unlike almost all other insects.

questions.q: Roughly how many insect species have been described and named by scientists?
questions.f: Estimates suggest several million more are still waiting to be discovered.

questions.q: Which insect holds the record as the world's longest, at over half a metre with legs outstretched?
questions.f: A Chinese species described in 2016 stretched to about 64 cm.

questions.q: A queen honeybee mates during a single flight period and stores sperm for years.
questions.f: She may mate with a dozen or more drones high in the air, then never again.

questions.q: Some worker honeybees act as 'heater bees', shivering to warm the brood nest.
questions.f: They keep the nursery within about a degree of 35C, like a living incubator.

questions.q: Termites are more closely related to cockroaches than to ants.
questions.f: Modern classification places termites inside the cockroach order Blattodea.

questions.q: A bird has only one working ovary, which helps save weight.
questions.f: Almost everything about a bird's body is built to be as light as possible.

questions.q: Some birds can see the Earth's magnetic field information through their eyes.
questions.f: Light-sensitive proteins in the eye seem to give migrating birds a compass reading.

questions.q: A tiny wasp that lays its eggs inside a caterpillar belongs to which group?
questions.f: Gardeners welcome them, since they keep plant-eating caterpillars in check.

questions.q: A name possibly meaning 'white head', a title borrowed from the great auk, and a paperback publisher's logo all point to which bird?
questions.f: European sailors first used the name for the northern great auk, then moved it south.

questions.q: A fruit renamed in the 1950s to help it sell abroad, a nickname for New Zealanders, and nostrils at a beak's tip converge on which bird?
questions.f: The Chinese gooseberry was rebranded 'kiwifruit' after the shy national bird.

questions.q: A Latin name meaning 'sparrow-camel', a habit of swallowing pebbles, and the largest egg of any living bird point to which species?
questions.f: Old naturalists called it Struthocamelus, half sparrow and half camel.

questions.q: A church official's scarlet robes, a bird whose female is a modest brown, and a familiar American garden visitor converge on which name?
questions.f: The bird was named for the red-robed cardinals of the Catholic Church.

questions.q: A folk dance from an Italian port, a fever once blamed on a spider bite, and a big hairy pet-shop favourite point to which creature?
questions.f: Both the spider and the tarantella dance are named after the town of Taranto.

questions.q: A Greek word for a prophet or diviner, forelegs folded as if in prayer, and a head that swivels to watch you converge on which insect?
questions.f: 'Mantis' means seer, because the pose looked like someone at prayer.

questions.q: Two Norse birds named Thought and Memory, protected residents of the Tower of London, and a bird that mimics speech point to which species?
questions.f: Legend says the kingdom falls if the Tower's ravens ever leave.

questions.q: A 1962 book that opens with a spring in which no birds sing, written by a marine biologist, helped bring about a ban on which chemical?
questions.f: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring showed DDT was thinning birds' eggshells.

questions.q: A Norwegian schoolboy's 1921 study of hens in a farmyard gave offices and playgrounds which phrase?
questions.f: Thorleif Schjelderup-Ebbe noticed hens formed a strict ladder of rank.

questions.q: A Paris market of second-hand goods, known as the 'marche aux puces', gave English which phrase?
questions.f: The name hinted that the old furniture might come with tiny lodgers.

questions.q: The dead-straight route a loaded forager flies back to its nest gave English which phrase for going directly?
questions.f: Bee hunters once followed that straight line to find wild honey trees.

questions.q: A Tudor horse-riding game in which riders followed a leader in scattered formation gave us which phrase for a pointless search?
questions.f: Shakespeare used the phrase in Romeo and Juliet.

questions.q: An ancient belief that a normally silent bird bursts into song as it dies gives us which phrase for a final performance?
questions.f: Real mute swans do not sing at the end, but the poetic image has lasted 2,000 years.

questions.q: Rows of small compartments in an old writing desk, named after a bird's nesting boxes, gave us which verb?
questions.f: To pigeonhole an idea is to file it away in a narrow slot.

questions.q: A carpenter's joint with flaring interlocking pins takes its name from which bird's spread tail?
questions.f: A dovetail joint is so strong it needs no nails at all.

questions.q: American settlers held 'quilting' and 'husking' gatherings; the same word now names which kind of contest?
questions.f: A 'bee' meant neighbours working busily together, just like insects in a hive.

questions.q: Which flower attracts male bees by mimicking the look and scent of a female bee?
questions.f: The disappointed visitor flies off dusted with pollen, which is the orchid's plan.

questions.q: Which insect larva digs a funnel-shaped pit in dry sand to trap passing ants?
questions.f: It lies buried at the bottom and flicks sand to make the walls collapse.

questions.q: Which insects are the only pollinators of yucca plants, whose seeds their young then eat?
questions.f: Plant and moth depend so completely on each other that neither survives alone.

questions.q: How do some stick insects get ants to carry their eggs to safety?
c: The eggs mimic seeds with an edible cap
The eggs stick to ants' legs
questions.f: Ants take the 'seed' home, eat the cap and leave the egg safe underground.

questions.q: Which insects are famous for shapes that mimic thorns, seeds and even ants on their backs?
questions.f: That strange 'helmet' is a wildly reshaped part of the thorax.

questions.q: Which pale pink insect resembles an orchid flower so closely that pollinators come to it?
questions.f: It is a hunter in disguise, waiting in plain sight among real blossom.

questions.q: Which mother insect famously guards her eggs and cleans them of mould?
questions.f: An earwig mother licks each egg to stop fungus taking hold.

questions.q: Which wasp builds a delicate mud jug and stocks it with food for its grub?
questions.f: Each little pot is sealed with the egg hanging inside on a thread.

questions.q: Which insect queen can live for decades and lay an egg every few seconds?
questions.f: Her swollen body may be thousands of times the mass of a worker.

questions.q: Which group of mosquitoes carries the parasite that causes malaria?
questions.f: You can spot many Anopheles resting with their bodies tilted nose-down.

questions.q: Which caterpillar puffs up a false face with big eyespots to look like a small snake?
questions.f: Birds veer away from the bluff, giving the caterpillar precious seconds.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the huge eyespots on an owl butterfly's wings?
questions.f: A sudden 'stare' can make a hungry bird hesitate just long enough.

questions.q: Which wasp has an extremely long, thread-like egg-laying tube for reaching grubs inside wood?
questions.f: The tube can be longer than the wasp's whole body, yet it drills through timber.

questions.q: Which seabird has been recorded sleeping in short bursts while gliding for days at a time?
questions.f: Instruments showed it dozing with half its brain while still airborne.

questions.q: Which penguin species lives farthest north, right on the equator?
questions.f: Cold ocean currents let this small penguin survive in the tropics.

questions.q: How does a young songbird learn its song?
c: By listening to adults and practising
questions.f: Young birds even 'babble' a rough subsong before getting it right.

questions.q: Birds of the same species in different regions can sing in different local…?
questions.f: Researchers can sometimes tell where a bird grew up by its song pattern.

questions.q: Which American bird was nicknamed the 'buffalo bird' because it followed roaming bison and never settled to build a nest?
questions.f: With the herd always moving, it took to leaving its eggs in other birds' nests instead.

questions.q: How does a cuckoo reduce the chance that its egg is thrown out of the nest?
c: Its egg closely matches the host's own eggs
It lays a much larger egg
It removes all the other eggs
questions.f: Different cuckoo lines specialise in different host species and egg patterns.

questions.q: Which birds' fine white plumes were once so prized by hat makers that protection laws were passed?
questions.f: The campaign against the feather trade helped create the first modern bird charities.

questions.q: Which bird performs a booming display flight in which air rushing past its tail feathers makes a bleating sound?
questions.f: The eerie noise is called 'drumming', and it is made by feathers, not the voice.

questions.q: Which small tropical bird makes a violin-like sound by rubbing club-shaped wing feathers together?
questions.f: Its wing bones are unusually solid, helping the sound carry through the forest.

questions.q: What is 'iridescent structural colour' most likely to disappear if you do what to a feather?
questions.f: Crush the microscopic layers and the colour vanishes, since no pigment made it.

questions.q: Which insect group has 'asynchronous' flight muscles that vibrate faster than nerve signals arrive?
questions.f: The muscle fires like a plucked elastic band, allowing hundreds of beats a second.

questions.q: How do many insects survive freezing winters without turning to ice inside?
c: They make natural antifreeze in their blood
questions.f: Sugars and special proteins keep ice crystals from forming in their cells.

questions.q: The word 'venom' differs from 'poison' because venom must be…?
c: Injected by a bite or sting
questions.f: So a bee is venomous, while a plant you must not eat is poisonous.

questions.q: What does the word 'carrion', in the diet of vultures and burying beetles, mean?
questions.f: From a Latin root for flesh, the same source as 'carnival' and 'carnivore'.

questions.q: The 'gena' and 'clypeus' are parts of an insect's…?
questions.f: Entomologists name every plate of an insect's armour, right down to the cheeks.

questions.q: What is the term for the second segment of an insect's leg, nearest the body after the coxa?
questions.f: An insect leg runs coxa, trochanter, femur, tibia, then the foot-like tarsus.

questions.q: An insect's foot section, which touches the ground, is called the…?
questions.f: Many insects taste with sensors on the tarsus, which is why flies dance on food.

questions.q: What does 'phoresy' describe when a tiny mite rides on a beetle?
c: Travelling on another animal without feeding on it
questions.f: It is simply hitchhiking, a free ride to fresh habitat.

questions.q: Which term describes a bird species found naturally in only one small region?
questions.f: Islands are full of endemic birds, which is also why they are so vulnerable.

questions.q: What does 'extirpated' mean when used about a bird?
c: Lost from one region but alive elsewhere
questions.f: Some birds have been extirpated locally and later reintroduced successfully.

questions.q: What is the practice of releasing captive-bred young birds gradually into the wild called?
questions.f: Falconers' word 'hacking' was borrowed by conservationists reintroducing peregrines.

questions.q: A hawk kept and flown by a falconer is fitted with soft leather straps called…?
questions.f: Falconry has given English a whole vocabulary, from 'hoodwink' to 'haggard'.

questions.q: In falconry, what does it mean when a bird 'stoops'?
questions.f: A peregrine's stoop is the fastest movement any animal makes.

questions.q: Some birds can recognise individual human faces.
questions.f: Crows and magpies remember a person who once bothered them, sometimes for years.

questions.q: Insects have a heart, but their blood does not travel in closed veins.
questions.f: A tube-like heart pumps fluid that simply washes around the body cavity.

questions.q: A ladybird can release a bitter yellow fluid from its leg joints when threatened.
questions.f: The fluid tastes so foul that a bird usually spits the beetle straight out.

questions.q: Butterflies can see more colours than humans can.
questions.f: Some butterflies have many more types of colour receptor than our three.

questions.q: Owls swallow prey whole because they cannot chew.
questions.f: Whatever cannot be digested is later coughed up as a neat pellet.

questions.q: Feathers evolved before birds could fly.
questions.f: Fossils show feathered dinosaurs that used them for warmth and display.

questions.q: Which bird's scientific name, 'Troglodytes', means 'cave dweller' and suits its habit of creeping into crevices?
questions.f: The tiny wren pokes into holes and cracks like a mouse hunting spiders.

questions.q: Which bird family name, 'Trochilidae', belongs to the hummingbirds and comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: Spanish speakers call them 'picaflor', flower-pecker, and Portuguese 'beija-flor', flower-kisser.

questions.q: A Portuguese sailors' word for a pelican, an island prison in San Francisco Bay, and a burden hung round a mariner's neck in Coleridge converge on which seabird?
questions.f: 'Alcatraz' became both the prison's name and, reshaped, the word albatross.

questions.q: Islands the Romans named for their large dogs, a small green finch bred for centuries, and a cage carried down a mine converge on which bird?
questions.f: The bird is named after the islands, and the islands after dogs, not the other way round.

questions.q: A bird Turks call 'hindi', Franklin praised in a letter to his daughter, and English named after a trading nation is which species?
questions.f: Traders muddled its origins so badly that several languages name it after the wrong country.

questions.q: A name inherited from a Latin 'bone-breaker', a reversible outer toe, and spiny pads that grip slippery scales point to which raptor?
questions.f: It is the only raptor with a toe it can swing backwards, perfect for carrying fish.

questions.q: A Greek word for 'axe', a heraldic bird said to feed its chicks from its own breast, and a stretchy throat converge on which bird?
questions.f: 'Pelekan' likened the huge bill to an axe blade.

questions.q: A Latin phrase meaning 'sea raven', birds tethered by Japanese ukai fishers, and wings held wide to dry converge on which bird?
questions.f: 'Corvus marinus' became 'cormorant' as the words wore down over centuries.

questions.q: A saint who stepped out onto water, sailors' name 'Mother Carey's chickens', and a bird that patters over the waves converge on which family?
questions.f: 'Petrel' is usually linked to Peter, who walked on the sea in the Bible story.

questions.q: A pet form of the name Margaret, an old word meaning black-and-white, and a bird that passed the mirror mark test converge on which species?
questions.f: 'Mag' plus 'pie', meaning pied, produced the name of this brilliant corvid.

questions.q: A Guatemalan banknote, an Aztec feathered-serpent god, and tail streamers longer than the bird itself converge on which species?
questions.f: Its feathers were so sacred that killing one was once a capital offence.

questions.q: A weaver punished by Athena, a class name for eight-legged animals, and a common '-phobia' converge on which mythological name?
questions.f: Ovid tells how the boastful weaver Arachne was changed into a spider.

questions.q: An acid first distilled from crushed ants, a Latin word for ant, and a 1910s laminate invented to replace mica converge on which name?
questions.f: The laminate's name literally means 'for mica', the mineral it substituted.

questions.q: A scale insect farmed on cactus pads in Oaxaca, a cargo Spain guarded like bullion, and the colouring E120 converge on which red?
questions.f: It takes roughly 70,000 insects to make a pound of the dye.

questions.q: A resin secreted by an Asian scale insect, French polish for furniture, and the brittle material of early gramophone records converge on which substance?
questions.f: 'Lac' comes from a Sanskrit word for a hundred thousand, hinting at the swarms needed.

questions.q: A scale insect living on Mediterranean oaks, an Arabic-derived word 'qirmiz', and a deep red converge on which colour word?
questions.f: The insect dye gave its name to the colour long before chemistry made cheaper reds.

questions.q: Oak swellings caused by tiny wasps, iron sulphate, and the writing on medieval charters converge on which product?
questions.f: Many of Europe's oldest documents are written in ink that began as an insect's nursery.

questions.q: A caterpillar that can no longer survive in the wild, a mulberry-only diet, and a craft secret guarded for millennia converge on which insect?
questions.f: Bombyx mori adults cannot even fly properly after thousands of years of breeding.

questions.q: A Greek girl's name meaning 'bee', the Hebrew name Deborah with the same sense, and the Latin 'apis' converge on which creature?
questions.f: Melissa, Deborah and Apis all quietly carry the same buzzing meaning.

questions.q: A word built from Greek for 'before the city', resin gathered from tree buds, and a germ-fighting seal at a nest entrance converge on which substance?
questions.f: The name pictures the sticky barricade standing in front of the bee city.

questions.q: A Latin word for fine flour, a substance counted in 'grains', and the misery of hay fever converge on which word?
questions.f: The dust-like grains are among the toughest objects in nature, surviving for millennia.

questions.q: A Victorian name 'humble-bee', a verb meaning to boom or drone, and Darwin's studies of clover converge on which insect?
questions.f: Darwin used the older name 'humble-bee' throughout his own writings.

questions.q: An 1897 formula by an American physicist, counting chirps for 14 seconds and adding 40, gives a rough reading of what?
questions.f: Crickets chirp faster when warm, so Dolbear's law turns an insect into a thermometer.

questions.q: A Madagascan orchid with a nectar spur nearly 30 cm deep, a prediction Darwin published in 1862, and a moth later named 'praedicta' converge on which feature?
questions.f: The moth Darwin predicted was found about forty years later, exactly as described.

questions.q: Soot-blackened trunks, a Victorian shift from pale to dark forms, and a return to pale after clean-air laws converge on which insect?
questions.f: Its story became the best-known school example of natural selection in action.

questions.q: Specimens lost when a ship burned, a letter posted from Ternate in 1858, and a faunal boundary through Indonesia converge on which naturalist?
questions.f: His letter prompted Darwin to publish his own long-delayed theory at last.

questions.q: A 1699 voyage to Surinam, plates showing caterpillars beside their food plants, and a German artist later honoured on a banknote converge on which pioneer?
questions.f: She showed insects as living creatures in their habitats, a revolution in its day.

questions.q: A stony Provencal garden called the 'harmas', ten volumes of insect 'Souvenirs', and Darwin's praise as an incomparable observer point to whom?
questions.f: Fabre watched wasps and beetles for decades rather than collecting dead specimens.

questions.q: A line of goslings following a man in rubber boots, a Nobel Prize shared in 1973, and the idea of imprinting converge on which scientist?
questions.f: He shared that prize with von Frisch, who decoded the honeybee's dance.

questions.q: A thirty-year study by Irene Pepperberg, a creature that named colours and shapes, and a farewell of 'you be good, I love you' converge on whom?
questions.f: Alex could count, compare and even use the concept of 'none'.

questions.q: A bird that died at Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, flocks once said to darken the sky for hours, and a name honouring a first lady converge on which species?
questions.f: The last of her kind was called Martha, after Martha Washington.

questions.q: A flightless North Atlantic diver, a last confirmed pair taken in Iceland in 1844, and a name later borrowed by southern seabirds converge on which species?
questions.f: European sailors called it 'penguin' long before they ever saw an Antarctic one.

questions.q: A Laysan albatross ringed on Midway Atoll in 1956 and still raising chicks in her seventies is known by which name?
questions.f: She is the oldest known wild bird, and has outlived the scientist who ringed her.

questions.q: A 2019 measurement of roughly 125 decibels, and a habit of shouting point-blank at a perched mate, belong to which bird?
questions.f: It is the loudest bird ever measured, louder than a pneumatic drill.

questions.q: An African weaver whose adult numbers may exceed 1.5 billion, forming clouds that farmers dread, is which bird?
questions.f: It is generally reckoned the most numerous wild bird on Earth.

questions.q: A cone-shaped cage with an inked floor, a planetarium sky overhead, and scratch marks showing which way a bird hops test which ability?
questions.f: Stephen Emlen's simple funnel showed caged birds orienting to an artificial night sky.

questions.q: A Pacific island corvid, twigs trimmed into hooks, and a captive bird named Betty bending wire converge on which species?
questions.f: These crows make different tool designs in different valleys, like local traditions.

questions.q: A bird that re-hides food if a rival was watching, and recovers its perishable stores first, belongs to which group?
questions.f: Such planning suggests these jays keep track of what others know.

questions.q: A Chinese fossil whose preserved pigment structures revealed a ginger-and-white striped tail belongs to which animal?
questions.f: It was the first dinosaur whose real colours scientists could reconstruct.

questions.q: A fossil seabird with bony 'pseudo-teeth' along its jaws and a wingspan over six metres is called?
questions.f: It is the largest flying bird known, dwarfing even the wandering albatross.

questions.q: A raptor weighing up to about 15 kg that vanished from New Zealand along with its giant prey is named after which man?
questions.f: Haast's eagle had a wingspan of around three metres and hunted the flightless moa.

questions.q: The extinct 'phorusrhacids', tall flightless South American hunters with great hooked beaks, are nicknamed…?
questions.f: Some stood taller than a person and could probably outrun one easily.

questions.q: Geese on the ground make a gaggle; the same birds flying in formation make a…?
questions.f: A tight V is a skein, while a loose, scattered line is sometimes called a plump.

questions.q: A falconer who keeps and flies hawks rather than falcons is properly called an…?
questions.f: The word comes from Old French for a keeper of goshawks.

questions.q: A falconry word for a wild-caught adult hawk now describes someone looking worn and exhausted; which word?
questions.f: A haggard hawk was harder to tame, and the word drifted into everyday English.

questions.q: A falconry verb for a hawk beating its wings in agitation gave Shakespeare which phrase about anxious waiting?
questions.f: 'Bate' meant to flutter and struggle on the perch, so 'bated' means held back.

questions.q: The royal buildings where hawks were kept while moulting gave which name to narrow London back streets?
questions.f: The King's Mews at Charing Cross later became stables, and the word followed.

questions.q: A decoy bird once tied to a stool to lure others, later American slang for a police informer, is which term?
questions.f: Wildfowlers really did use tethered live birds as living decoys.

questions.q: An old verb meaning to trick or cheat, taken from a seabird thought easily fooled, survives in which adjective?
questions.f: To 'gull' someone was to make a gull of them, an easy dupe.

questions.q: A lookout barrel high on a mast, said to have once held caged birds released to find land, is which nautical term?
questions.f: Released corvids fly straight toward the nearest shore, giving sailors a bearing.

questions.q: Louse eggs glued to hair, a fine-toothed comb, and hours of tedious work converge on which word for fussy fault-finding?
questions.f: The nits are so firmly cemented in place that only patient picking removes them.

questions.q: A 1972 talk title about a flap in Brazil and a tornado in Texas, and Edward Lorenz's weather model, converge on which phrase?
questions.f: Lorenz found that rounding a number slightly changed a whole simulated forecast.

questions.q: A claim made by Pappus in the 4th century and finally proved by Thomas Hales in 1999 says a hexagon is best at what?
c: Enclosing area with the least total wall
questions.f: Honeybees had the answer millions of years before mathematicians proved it.

questions.q: Sealed jars found in ancient Egyptian tombs, very low water content, and natural acidity explain why which food does not spoil?
questions.f: Bees also add an enzyme that produces a tiny amount of natural preservative.

questions.q: A drink fermented from honey and water, older in northern Europe than either wine or beer, is called…?
questions.f: A 'honeymoon' may recall the old custom of drinking mead for a month after a wedding.

questions.q: A parasitic mite named 'destructor', a syndrome first reported in 2006, and hives found empty of workers converge on which crisis?
questions.f: The mite weakens bees and spreads viruses, making colonies far likelier to fail.

questions.q: A V-2 rocket launched from White Sands in 1947 carried which creatures to become the first animals in space?
questions.f: The flies were recovered alive by parachute after crossing the boundary of space.

questions.q: A New Zealand cave ceiling like a starry sky, larvae of a fungus gnat, and sticky dangling fishing lines converge on which creature?
questions.f: Each Arachnocampa larva glows to lure midges onto its beaded silk snares.

questions.q: An insect a few millimetres long that has been recorded at about 99 decibels, the loudest animal for its size, is which?
questions.f: It makes the noise underwater, yet passers-by on the bank can hear it clearly.

questions.q: A dragonfly found on every continent but Antarctica, riding monsoon winds across the Indian Ocean, is the…?
questions.f: Its multi-generation journey may be the longest migration of any insect.

questions.q: Mandibles snapping shut at over 200 km/h, filmed in 2018 as the fastest known animal movement, belong to which insect?
questions.f: It does not swing the jaws shut but presses their tips together until one slides free.

questions.q: A closed loop of scent trail, a column of blind army ants, and a doomed spiral first described in 1936 is called an ant…?
questions.f: Each ant follows the one in front, so the circle keeps turning until they tire.

questions.q: Insects that weed their crop, carry antibiotic-making bacteria on their bodies, and cut leaves they never eat are which?
questions.f: They eat the fungus their leaf clippings feed, making them the world's oldest farmers.

questions.q: Japanese honeybees defend a hive by smothering a giant hornet inside a ball of bodies, defeating it with which weapon?
questions.f: The bees shiver until the centre of the ball is hotter than the hornet can survive.

questions.q: Male honeybees gather year after year at the same aerial meeting places, which beekeepers call drone…?
questions.f: Some of these spots have been used by generation after generation of bees.

questions.q: A ribbed plate buckled in and out thousands of times a second gives a cicada its song; the organ is a…?
questions.f: Hollow chambers in the cicada's body amplify the clicks into a piercing chorus.

questions.q: A word that names both a bird's wishbone and a spring-loaded jumping fork belongs to which tiny animal?
questions.f: A springtail's furcula is latched under its body and released to flip it into the air.

questions.q: The hormone that triggers an insect to shed its exoskeleton is called…?
questions.f: Its name shares a root with 'ecdysis', the technical word for moulting.

questions.q: Whether a moulting caterpillar stays a caterpillar or turns into a pupa depends on the level of which hormone?
questions.f: As juvenile hormone fades, the next moult takes the insect toward adulthood.

questions.q: An insect's kidney-like excretory tubes are named after which 17th-century Italian anatomist?
questions.f: Malpighian tubules pull waste from the body fluid and pass it to the gut.

questions.q: Each separate lens-and-cell unit of a compound eye is called an…?
questions.f: A dragonfly's eye can pack in around 30,000 of these tiny units.

questions.q: A spider's fang-bearing mouthparts are properly called the…?
questions.f: The short leg-like pedipalps beside them are used for sensing and handling food.

questions.q: Young spiders drifting for miles on silk threads, recently shown to sense atmospheric electric fields, are doing what?
questions.f: Darwin recorded spiderlings landing on the Beagle far out at sea.

questions.q: A jumping spider that waves its front legs like antennae and walks in a jerky zigzag is imitating which creature?
questions.f: Ant-mimicking spiders gain safety, since many predators avoid biting ants.

questions.q: A spider that holds a small rectangular web between its front legs and casts it over prey is the…?
questions.f: It has enormous night-adapted eyes, which is why it is also called the ogre-faced spider.

questions.q: Tiny Australian jumping spiders that raise a brilliantly patterned flap and dance for a female are known as…?
questions.f: Most are smaller than a grain of rice yet flash colours worthy of a bird of paradise.

questions.q: A dozen groves of oyamel fir in Michoacan, a roost science located only in 1975, and a sun-based compass converge on which insect?
questions.f: Millions cluster so thickly that fir branches bend under their weight.

questions.q: Australian moths that migrate to cool alpine caves each summer and appear to steer by the Earth's magnetic field are the…?
questions.f: They were an important seasonal food for Aboriginal peoples of the high country.

questions.q: Wing scales shaped like microscopic Christmas trees, scattering light rather than holding pigment, give which butterfly its flash of blue?
questions.f: The flash is visible from far off, then vanishes when the wings close to show dull brown.

questions.q: A ladybird introduced as a pest controller that now crowds out native species across Europe is the…?
questions.f: It can come in dozens of colour patterns, which makes it tricky to identify.

questions.q: The world's largest bee, rediscovered in Indonesia in 2019 and nesting inside termite mounds, is named after which naturalist?
questions.f: Wallace's giant bee has a wingspan wider than a human thumb is long.

questions.q: A veterinary painkiller given to cattle caused a catastrophic crash in which South Asian birds during the 1990s?
questions.f: Diclofenac in carcasses proved fatal to the birds, and over 95% were lost.

questions.q: A recovery programme that began with just 27 surviving birds in 1987 concerns which species?
questions.f: Every condor alive today descends from that tiny group of founders.

questions.q: Ultralight aircraft leading young birds along a migration route, and a wild flock once down to about 20 individuals, involve which species?
questions.f: Handlers even wore crane costumes so the chicks would not imprint on people.

questions.q: Every living member of which species descends from one female, nicknamed Old Blue, saved by cross-fostering in the 1980s?
questions.f: The population fell to five birds, with just one fertile female, and now numbers hundreds.

questions.q: A large flightless New Zealand rail declared extinct in 1898 and rediscovered in 1948 is the…?
questions.f: A doctor who had searched for years finally found a surviving population in a remote valley.

questions.q: An elusive Australian bird known from a few old specimens and photographed alive again in 2013 is the…?
questions.f: For most of the 20th century, ornithologists could not prove it still existed.

questions.q: A 1900 alternative to a festive shooting contest, now the longest-running citizen science project, is called the…?
questions.f: Frank Chapman suggested counting the birds instead of shooting them.

questions.q: A Danish schoolteacher, Hans Christian Mortensen, began which practice in 1899 to trace migration?
c: Putting numbered rings on birds' legs
questions.f: Millions of ringed birds have since revealed the hidden maps of migration.

questions.q: A campaign begun in 1889 by women who refused to wear feathered hats grew into which organisation?
questions.f: Their protest against the plume trade became one of the world's largest bird charities.

questions.q: A frontier artist who painted birds life-size in a 'double elephant folio' lends his name to which American society?
questions.f: His huge book, The Birds of America, is among the most valuable ever printed.

questions.q: A 1934 guide that grouped look-alike birds together and made field identification simple was written by whom?
questions.f: His system of pointing out key marks with little arrows changed birdwatching forever.

questions.q: Island birds whose beak shapes differ from island to island, named for a naturalist who barely noticed them at the time, are called…?
questions.f: Darwin failed to label which island each came from, and had to reconstruct it later.

questions.q: In British birding slang, someone who travels a long way to see a rare bird already found by others is a…?
questions.f: The name comes from the nervous excitement of chasing a rarity before it flies off.

questions.q: An Egyptian heron-like god of creation and rebirth also names which asteroid sampled by a NASA mission?
questions.f: OSIRIS-REx brought material from Bennu back to Earth in 2023.

questions.q: A World War II aircraft built largely of plywood and nicknamed the 'Wooden Wonder' was named after which insect?
questions.f: Because it used little metal, furniture makers helped build it.

questions.q: A 1915 novella whose travelling salesman wakes transformed into a giant creeping creature was written by whom?
questions.f: Kafka never let the illustrator show the creature, and the German word is deliberately vague.

questions.q: In the oldest Greek version of Aesop's fable about a summer singer and a grain-storing ant, the singer is which insect?
questions.f: Later translators swapped the Mediterranean cicada for a grasshopper their readers knew.

questions.q: A Liverpool band respelled an insect's name so a music word hid inside it; which insect?
questions.f: The Beatles built 'beat' into the name of a beetle, following Buddy Holly's Crickets.

questions.q: Leonardo da Vinci's sketched flying machine, copied from the anatomy of a wing, is called an…?
questions.f: Working ornithopters exist today, though none can yet carry a person far.

questions.q: A Crimean War nurse's surname, a bird famed for singing after dark, and 'The Lady with the Lamp' converge on which name?
questions.f: Florence Nightingale was named after the Italian city, not the bird.

questions.q: A famous naval architect's name, a wartime aircraft, and Britain's wartime women's naval service share a name with which tiny bird?
questions.f: Sir Christopher Wren, the Wren aircraft and the WRNS 'Wrens' all echo the little bird.

questions.q: Which bird's name became a verb meaning to abandon a bad habit abruptly, from an old phrase about plain speaking?
questions.f: 'Talk turkey' meant to speak plainly, and 'cold turkey' followed the same idea.

questions.q: An 1860s craze for keeping which insect's cocoons at home briefly threatened the silk trade of Europe?
questions.f: A disease of silkworms was solved by Louis Pasteur, saving the French silk industry.

questions.q: A queen that produces a scent controlling her whole colony, workers that build with paper, and a nest abandoned each autumn belong to which insect?
questions.f: Only a young mated queen survives the winter to start the cycle again.

questions.q: Which insect's wingbeat frequency is matched by a partner in a mid-air duet before mating?
questions.f: Male and female adjust their whine until the two tones harmonise.

questions.q: A gland at the base of a bird's tail, a Greek name meaning 'tail rump', and daily grooming converge on which structure?
questions.f: Its oil conditions feathers and may help fight feather-degrading bacteria.

questions.q: A duck sleeping at the edge of a group with one eye open is using which unusual ability?
c: Resting one brain half at a time
questions.f: Unihemispheric sleep lets the exposed birds keep watch while still resting.

questions.q: A bird that carries water many kilometres to its chicks, soaked in specially shaped belly feathers, is the…?
questions.f: The male's breast feathers work like a sponge, holding water even in dry desert air.

questions.q: Which structure in a bird's leg lets it stand on ice without losing much body heat?
questions.f: Warm outgoing blood heats the cold returning blood, so little warmth escapes.

questions.q: Which term describes an insect population that has two separate generations in one year?
questions.f: Silk producers prize bivoltine strains, since two harvests beat one.

questions.q: The Canary Islands are named after dogs, and the bird is named after the islands.
questions.f: Roman writers described large dogs there, and 'canis' gave the islands their name.

questions.q: The word 'penguin' was used for a northern seabird before it was ever applied to Antarctic birds.
questions.f: It first named the great auk, and sailors transferred it to the look-alike southern divers.

questions.q: Some ants keep a bacterium on their bodies that produces an antibiotic.
questions.f: Fungus-farming ants use it to protect their crop from mould, a natural pesticide.

questions.q: A hummingbird can enter a state so deep that its body temperature falls close to the air around it.
questions.f: This nightly torpor saves energy, and the bird takes many minutes to warm up again.

questions.q: Insects were flying tens of millions of years before the first birds appeared.
questions.f: Insects took to the air in the Devonian and Carboniferous, long before feathers existed.

questions.q: Which bird was once believed to be born from a barnacle on driftwood, a myth that shaped medieval fasting rules?
questions.f: Because nobody found its nest, some clergy classed it as seafood, not meat.

questions.q: A seahorse is a type of fish.
questions.f: Seahorses are bony fish that swim upright and are among the slowest swimmers in the sea.

questions.q: Which black-and-white sea bird swims well but cannot fly?
questions.f: Penguins use their wings like flippers to 'fly' through the water instead of the air.

questions.q: Which sea animal has a round shell covered in sharp spikes?
questions.f: Sea urchins walk very slowly on hundreds of tiny tube feet between their spines.

questions.q: Which sea bird often visits the beach and may try to grab your food?
questions.f: Gulls are clever scavengers that will happily snatch an unguarded snack.

questions.q: What is left behind on the rocks when the sea goes out, where crabs can hide?
questions.f: Tide pools are tiny sea worlds that empty at low tide and fill again when the tide returns.

questions.q: Which is warmer, the top of the ocean or the deep bottom?
questions.f: Sunlight warms the surface, so the deep sea stays cold and dark all year round.

questions.q: Most kinds of fish lay eggs.
questions.f: A single fish can lay thousands of tiny eggs at one time.

questions.q: The sea creature that looks like a flower but is really an animal is the...?
questions.f: A sea anemone's soft 'petals' are really stinging arms that catch tiny food.

questions.q: What do seals and sea lions mostly eat?
questions.f: Seals are meat-eaters that feast on fish and squid.

questions.q: A group of penguins gathered on the ice is called a colony.
questions.f: Emperor penguin colonies can hold thousands of birds that huddle together to stay warm.

questions.q: What colour is a blue whale's skin?
questions.f: A blue whale can look bright blue underwater because of how light shines through the sea.

questions.q: Do fish sleep?
c: Yes, but usually with their eyes open
questions.f: Many fish rest quietly while staying alert, since they have no eyelids to close.

questions.q: Sea otters often rest among tall underwater plants called...?
questions.f: Kelp is a giant seaweed that grows in underwater 'forests' where otters like to float.

questions.q: The sea is salty, but most lakes and rivers are not.
questions.f: Rivers carry tiny amounts of salt to the sea, where it slowly builds up over ages.

questions.q: What do we call a large, curved part of the coast where boats can shelter?
questions.f: A bay is a scooped-out part of the coast that shields boats from big waves.

questions.q: An octopus has a soft body with no bones at all.
questions.f: With no bones, an octopus can squeeze into surprisingly tight spaces.

questions.q: Which of these sounds would you hear at the seaside?
questions.f: The rush of a breaking wave is the sound of air being trapped and bubbling free.

questions.q: What do we call the far line where the sea seems to meet the sky?
questions.f: The horizon looks like a straight line, but it is really the gentle curve of the round Earth.

questions.q: After hatching on the beach, baby sea turtles hurry toward the...?
questions.f: Hatchlings head for the bright, open horizon over the water to find the sea.

questions.q: Coral reefs are home to many colourful fish.
questions.f: Coral reefs are like busy underwater cities, home to about a quarter of all sea creatures.

questions.q: Which of these is the odd one out because it does NOT live in the sea?
questions.f: Camels live in dry deserts, while crabs, clams, and cod all live in water.

questions.q: Dolphins talk to each other using clicks and...?
questions.f: Each dolphin has its own special whistle, a little like having its own name.

questions.q: What is the biggest kind of sea turtle?
questions.f: A leatherback can grow as big as a small car and has a soft, leathery shell.

questions.q: Seahorses hold on to seaweed using their curly...?
questions.f: A seahorse wraps its grippy tail around plants so it doesn't drift away in the current.

questions.q: What do polar bears hunt for near the icy sea?
questions.f: Polar bears wait patiently by holes in the sea ice for seals to come up for air.

questions.q: How does a penguin zoom quickly across flat ice?
questions.f: Penguins 'toboggan' on their bellies, using their feet and flippers to push along.

questions.q: Some kinds of crabs can live on land near the sea, not only in the water.
questions.f: Land crabs and coconut crabs live on shore but often return to the sea to lay their eggs.

questions.q: Whales feed their babies with...?
questions.f: Like all mammals, mother whales make milk to feed their growing calves.

questions.q: What do fish use to swim and steer through the water?
questions.f: Fish wave their fins and tails to push forward and turn in the water.

questions.q: Which large animal uses long tusks and lives on icy northern coasts?
questions.f: A walrus uses its long tusks to help haul its heavy body out onto the ice.

questions.q: Which sea creature has a fan-shaped shell and buries itself in the sand?
questions.f: Clams dig into the sand and strain tiny bits of food from the water.

questions.q: What helps keep a fish upright so it does not roll over?
questions.f: Fins on the back and sides act like keels to keep a fish steady.

questions.q: You can often find crabs, shells, and seaweed washed up on a beach.
questions.f: Waves and tides push all sorts of sea treasures onto the sand.

questions.q: When seals leave the sea to rest, where do they usually go?
questions.f: Seals 'haul out' onto land or ice to rest, warm up, and stay safe from ocean hunters.

questions.q: What do sea turtles use their flippers for?
questions.f: Sea turtles glide gracefully in water but move slowly and clumsily on land.

questions.q: Which small sea animal has ten legs and can shoot backwards by flicking its tail?
questions.f: A shrimp snaps its tail under its body to dart quickly away from danger.

questions.q: Where do most seals have their babies?
c: In a cave under the sea
questions.f: A seal pup must learn to swim after it is born, so its mother needs solid ground or ice.

questions.q: Which cold-water animal has the thickest fur and floats on its back?
questions.f: Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal to stay warm, since they have no blubber.

questions.q: A place with big glass tanks where people go to see fish and sea animals is an...?
questions.f: The word 'aquarium' comes from the Latin word 'aqua', meaning water.

questions.q: A person whose job is to catch fish is called a...?
questions.f: People have fished the seas for food for tens of thousands of years.

questions.q: A baby shark is called a...?
questions.f: Some sharks give birth to live pups instead of laying eggs.

questions.q: A long journey across the sea by ship is called a...?
questions.f: The word 'voyage' comes from a Latin word meaning a journey or road.

questions.q: The word 'seashell' is made by joining which two smaller words?
questions.f: Two words joined to make one, like 'sea' plus 'shell', form a compound word.

questions.q: The name 'starfish' tells you the animal is shaped like a...?
questions.f: Scientists now often call them 'sea stars' because they are not true fish.

questions.q: The animal called a 'seahorse' has a head shaped a bit like a...?
questions.f: Its scientific name, Hippocampus, comes from Greek words for 'horse' and 'sea monster'.

questions.q: A 'swordfish' is named after its long, pointy...?
questions.f: A swordfish uses its sword-like bill to slash at the smaller fish it hunts.

questions.q: A hard-shelled sea food such as a crab or clam is called a...?
questions.f: 'Shellfish' is a food word for shelled sea animals, even though they are not true fish.

questions.q: A boat that can travel under the sea is called a...?
questions.f: 'Sub' means under and 'marine' means sea, so a submarine goes 'under the sea'.

questions.q: The salty water of the sea is called...?
questions.f: Seawater is far too salty for people to drink safely.

questions.q: A person who works on and helps sail a ship is a...?
questions.f: The word 'sailor' comes from the sails that once powered every ship.

questions.q: Even though its name ends in 'fish', a jellyfish is really which kind of animal?
questions.f: Jellyfish have no bones, no brain, and no heart, so they are not true fish at all.

questions.q: What do we call the sandy or rocky land right next to the sea?
questions.f: The coast is the strip of land where the ground meets the ocean.

questions.q: The word 'octopus' hints that the animal has how many arms?
questions.f: 'Octo' means eight, the same as in 'octagon', a shape with eight sides.

questions.q: A 'seabird' is a bird that lives near and finds its food in the...?
questions.f: Seabirds such as gulls and puffins spend much of their lives out over the ocean.

questions.q: A 'lifeboat' is a special boat used mainly to...?
questions.f: Lifeboats rush out even in storms to save people who are in danger at sea.

questions.q: A 'lighthouse' by the sea shines a bright light to...?
questions.f: Its spinning light warns passing ships about rocks and shallow water near the shore.

questions.q: A 'reef' is an underwater ridge that is often built by tiny...?
questions.f: Coral reefs grow very slowly, sometimes only a finger's width in a whole year.

questions.q: The word 'ocean' first came from Okeanos, which the ancient Greeks pictured as a great...?
questions.f: The Greeks imagined Okeanos as a mighty river that flowed all the way around the world.

questions.q: A 'flipper' is the wide, flat limb that seals and turtles use to...?
questions.f: Flippers work like paddles to push these animals smoothly through the water.

questions.q: A 'sandcastle' at the beach is built from wet...?
questions.f: Wet sand sticks together because thin films of water hold the grains in place.

questions.q: A 'mermaid' is a make-believe creature that is half person and half...?
questions.f: Old sailors' tales of mermaids may have begun with sightings of gentle manatees.

questions.q: A 'harbour' is a sheltered place by the coast where...?
questions.f: Harbours protect boats from rough seas, often behind a strong wall.

questions.q: A shiny, round 'pearl' grows inside which sea animal?
questions.f: An oyster slowly coats a bit of grit with smooth layers to make a pearl.

questions.q: Which word means to move through water using your arms and legs?
questions.f: People must learn to swim, but most sea animals can swim from the moment they are born.

questions.q: A 'beachcomber' is a person who walks the beach looking for...?
questions.f: Beachcombers hunt for shells, driftwood, and smooth sea glass along the shore.

questions.q: The colour 'aquamarine' looks most like the...?
questions.f: 'Aqua' means water and 'marine' means sea, so aquamarine is a sea-blue-green colour.

questions.q: A 'buoy' floating in the water is used to...?
c: Mark a spot or guide boats
questions.f: Buoys bob on the surface to mark safe paths or warn about hidden dangers.

questions.q: A baby penguin is called a...?
questions.f: A penguin chick is kept warm on its parents' feet, safely off the freezing ice.

questions.q: The giant sea plant that otters rest in, called kelp, is a kind of...?
questions.f: Kelp is a fast-growing seaweed that can grow up to half a metre in a single day.

questions.q: A 'porthole' on a ship or submarine is a small, round...?
questions.f: Round portholes are strong and keep water out better than square windows would.

questions.q: What do we call the fin you see sticking up out of the water above a swimming shark?
questions.f: That triangle on a shark's back is its dorsal fin, and it helps the shark swim straight.

questions.q: Which sea bird has a big stretchy pouch under its beak for scooping up fish?
questions.f: A pelican's pouch can hold about three times as much as its stomach can.

questions.q: Which simple sea animal has no brain, no heart, and soaks up water like a bath sponge?
questions.f: A sea sponge really is an animal, and it feeds by pumping water through tiny holes.

questions.q: Which flat sea animal rests on the sandy bottom and has a long, thin tail?
questions.f: A ray flicks sand over its body so it can hide from hungry hunters.

questions.q: What must a crab do so it can grow bigger?
questions.f: A crab wriggles out of its old shell, then hides while its new soft shell hardens.

questions.q: What do sea stars have on the very tips of their arms?
questions.f: Each arm has a simple eye that can tell light from dark, so a sea star has five eyes.

questions.q: Which of these is a shellfish you might find on a rock at the beach?
questions.f: Mussels hold on to rocks with strong little threads so waves cannot wash them away.

questions.q: Which sea snail clings so tightly to a rock that it is very hard to pull off?
questions.f: A limpet clamps down with a suction grip that can be stronger than glue.

questions.q: Which reef fish has long, striped, feathery spines all around its body?
questions.f: A lionfish's beautiful spines are actually a warning that they are venomous.

questions.q: Which reef fish is bright orange with white stripes?
questions.f: There are about 30 kinds of clownfish, and not all of them are orange.

questions.q: Do all fish live in salty ocean water?
c: No, some live in rivers and lakes
questions.f: Goldfish and trout live in fresh water, while cod and tuna live in the salty sea.

questions.q: Which of these is a fish?
questions.f: Tuna breathe with gills, while dolphins, seals, and penguins all breathe air.

questions.q: What do we call the spray of air and water a whale blows up when it surfaces?
questions.f: Experts can tell whale species apart just by the shape of their spout.

questions.q: Where is the coldest ocean water found?
c: Near the North and South Poles
questions.f: Polar seas can be so cold that they are covered with floating ice for much of the year.

questions.q: What is the very top of a wave called?
questions.f: When a wave's crest tumbles forward and breaks, it turns into white, foamy surf.

questions.q: What happens at the beach when the tide goes out?
questions.f: Low tide is the best time to explore for shells and crabs on the wet sand.

questions.q: What do fishers use to catch many fish at once?
questions.f: Fishing nets have been made from plant fibres and rope for thousands of years.

questions.q: What does an anchor do for a boat?
questions.f: A heavy anchor digs into the seabed so the boat does not drift away.

questions.q: If a small boat has no engine or sail, what can you use to move it?
questions.f: Rowing with oars turns your own muscles into the boat's engine.

questions.q: What pushes a sailing boat along?
questions.f: A sail works a bit like a wing, catching the wind to pull the boat forward.

questions.q: Which of these things would float in the sea?
questions.f: A beach ball floats because it is full of light air.

questions.q: What do baby sea turtles come out of?
questions.f: A mother turtle can bury over 100 eggs in one warm, sandy nest.

questions.q: What does a crab mainly use its claws for?
questions.f: Many crabs have one big crushing claw and one smaller claw for picking up bits of food.

questions.q: Which sea animal often leaps right out of the water while swimming beside boats?
questions.f: Leaping may help dolphins save energy, since air is easier to move through than water.

questions.q: Which animal is much bigger, a dolphin or a blue whale?
questions.f: A blue whale can be over 20 metres long, while most dolphins are only 2 or 3 metres.

questions.q: Which of these would you expect to find lying on a sandy beach?
questions.f: Each empty shell on the sand was once the home of a living sea creature.

questions.q: What do we call a shark or a seal that hunts other animals for its food?
questions.f: Every healthy ocean needs predators to keep the numbers of other animals in balance.

questions.q: What do we call a group of gulls flying together?
questions.f: Gulls in a flock call loudly to each other when one of them finds food.

questions.q: A group of walruses resting together on the ice is called a...?
questions.f: Walruses pile up in big herds, sometimes resting their heads on each other.

questions.q: Why do swimmers wear goggles in the sea?
c: To see clearly and protect their eyes
questions.f: Goggles trap a pocket of air in front of your eyes so the water looks sharp, not blurry.

questions.q: What is a big ship that carries people on holidays across the sea called?
questions.f: The biggest cruise ships carry more people than live in some small towns.

questions.q: What are most beaches made of?
questions.f: Most sand grains are tiny bits of rock and shell worn smooth over many years.

questions.q: Which sea animal has a soft body and a hard, chalky shell in two halves?
questions.f: A scallop can swim by clapping the two halves of its shell together.

questions.q: Some sea animals, like sponges and coral, stay in one place their whole lives.
questions.f: Because they cannot chase food, they simply wait for it to drift past them.

questions.q: You can find shells on a beach that no animal lives in any more.
questions.f: Empty shells often become new homes for hermit crabs looking to move house.

questions.q: Fish do not have eyelids, so they cannot close their eyes.
questions.f: Most fish sleep with their eyes wide open because they have no lids to shut.

questions.q: An octopus can change the colour of its skin.
questions.f: An octopus can shift colour in less than a second to match a rock or a patch of sand.

questions.q: Whales are the loudest animals in the ocean.
questions.f: A whale's call can travel for many kilometres through the water.

questions.q: A sea turtle cannot pull its head and legs inside its shell like a pond turtle can.
questions.f: Sea turtles trade that safety for big flippers that make them fast, graceful swimmers.

questions.q: What do we call fish eggs, which look like tiny clear balls?
questions.f: Some fish guard their roe carefully, while others leave the eggs to drift away.

questions.q: Which sea creature has a shell, two eyes on stalks, and crawls slowly over the rocks?
questions.f: A sea snail scrapes food off rocks with a tongue covered in hundreds of tiny teeth.

questions.q: Which of these is used to help a diver see underwater?
questions.f: A diving mask keeps a layer of air over your eyes and nose so you can see clearly.

questions.q: Why is it important not to leave plastic rubbish on the beach?
c: Sea animals can be harmed by it
questions.f: Turtles sometimes mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish and try to eat them.

questions.q: Which sea animal can swim backwards very fast by squirting out water?
questions.f: A squid shoots a jet of water out of a tube called a siphon to zoom away.

questions.q: What do we call the small waves that ripple over the surface on a windy day?
questions.f: Even the tiniest ripples are made by wind pushing on the water's surface.

questions.q: The word 'iceberg' is built from words meaning 'ice' plus...?
questions.f: From Dutch and German roots meaning 'ice mountain', which suits these floating giants.

questions.q: The hammerhead shark is named after its head, which is shaped like a...?
questions.f: Its wide head lets a hammerhead see and sense in almost every direction at once.

questions.q: A sailfish is named after its huge fin, which looks like a boat's...?
questions.f: A sailfish raises its sail-like fin to look bigger and to help herd small fish.

questions.q: A sawfish gets its name from its long snout, which is lined with teeth like a...?
questions.f: A sawfish swipes its toothy snout sideways through a school of fish.

questions.q: A stingray is named for the way its tail can...?
questions.f: A stingray only uses the sharp spine in its tail to defend itself, never to hunt.

questions.q: A sand dollar is named because its round, flat shell looks like an old...?
questions.f: A living sand dollar is covered in tiny moving spines and is not white at all.

questions.q: The sea lion got its name because the males have a thick mane like a...?
questions.f: Male sea lions also roar loudly, which makes the name fit even better.

questions.q: The sea cucumber is named after a...?
questions.f: This soft, lumpy animal really does look like a bumpy cucumber lying on the seabed.

questions.q: The 'jelly' in 'jellyfish' describes the animal's...?
questions.f: Scientists often prefer the name 'sea jelly', because a jellyfish is not a fish.

questions.q: The word 'seagull' is made by joining 'sea' with which word?
questions.f: Bird experts usually just say 'gull', since many gulls live far from the sea.

questions.q: If you feel 'seasick', you feel unwell because of the...?
questions.f: Seasickness happens when your eyes and your ears disagree about how you are moving.

questions.q: The 'seaside' means the land right beside the...?
questions.f: Trips to the seaside became a popular holiday when trains first reached the coast.

questions.q: Something described as 'waterproof' does what?
questions.f: A duck's feathers are naturally waterproof thanks to a coat of oil.

questions.q: A 'snorkel' is a tube that lets you...?
c: Breathe with your face in the water
questions.f: The word 'snorkel' comes from a German word for a submarine's air pipe.

questions.q: The 'seafloor' is the...?
questions.f: More of the seafloor has been mapped from space than has ever been visited by people.

questions.q: 'Deep-sea' animals are ones that live...?
questions.f: Deep-sea animals are built to survive crushing pressure and total darkness.

questions.q: A 'lifejacket' is worn on a boat to help you...?
questions.f: Lifejackets are filled with foam or air, both of which are lighter than water.

questions.q: The 'captain' of a ship is the person who...?
questions.f: 'Captain' comes from a Latin word for head, since the captain is head of the ship.

questions.q: The 'crew' of a ship means...?
c: The people who work on it
questions.f: On old sailing ships, the crew slept in swinging cloth beds called hammocks.

questions.q: A 'seafarer' is a person who...?
questions.f: 'Farer' comes from an old word meaning traveller, as in 'wayfarer'.

questions.q: A 'shipwreck' is a ship that has been...?
questions.f: There may be over three million shipwrecks resting on the world's seabeds.

questions.q: 'Driftwood' on a beach is wood that has...?
questions.f: Driftwood is worn smooth and pale by months of tumbling in salty water.

questions.q: A 'sea breeze' is a wind that blows...?
c: From the sea toward the land
questions.f: Sea breezes form on sunny days because the land warms up faster than the sea.

questions.q: 'Sea salt' is salt that comes from...?
questions.f: Sea salt is made by letting seawater dry up in the sun until only salt is left.

questions.q: 'Seagrass' is a plant that grows...?
questions.f: Seagrass meadows are the favourite food of both turtles and manatees.

questions.q: A 'pearl diver' is someone who dives to collect...?
questions.f: Pearl divers once held their breath for minutes at a time, with no air tanks at all.

questions.q: A baby sea turtle is called a...?
questions.f: Hatchlings dig up out of the sand together, usually under cover of night.

questions.q: A 'shipmate' is someone who...?
c: Sails on the same ship as you
questions.f: 'Mate' means companion, so shipmates are companions at sea.

questions.q: To 'set sail' means to...?
questions.f: The phrase comes from the days when raising the sails was the first step of any voyage.

questions.q: 'Ashore' means...?
questions.f: Sailors coming ashore after a long voyage sometimes feel the ground swaying.

questions.q: The ocean sunfish is named for its habit of...?
c: Lying at the surface in the sun
questions.f: This giant fish basks flat on the surface, perhaps to warm up after a deep, cold dive.

questions.q: A 'catfish' is named for having long whiskers like a...?
questions.f: Those whiskers, called barbels, help the fish taste and feel its way in murky water.

questions.q: When something is 'afloat', it is...?
questions.f: Anything less dense than water, from a cork to a giant steel ship, can stay afloat.

questions.q: A 'seascape' is a picture or view of the...?
questions.f: Painters love seascapes because the water's colour changes with every hour of the day.

questions.q: Which is the second-largest ocean on Earth?
questions.f: The Atlantic Ocean sits between the Americas and Europe and Africa.

questions.q: Which ocean lies between Africa, Asia, and Australia?
questions.f: The Indian Ocean is the warmest of the world's major oceans.

questions.q: Which gas do fish pull out of the water using their gills?
questions.f: Gills work like tiny sieves, letting fish take in oxygen that is dissolved in water.

questions.q: Which shark is famous for being the fastest-swimming shark?
questions.f: A shortfin mako can burst through the water at over 40 miles per hour.

questions.q: Which is the largest toothed whale, known for diving deep to hunt squid?
questions.f: A sperm whale can hold its breath for over an hour on a deep hunting dive.

questions.q: What do we call a group of jellyfish drifting together?
questions.f: A large gathering of jellyfish is called a 'bloom' or sometimes a 'smack'.

questions.q: Which warm ocean current flows from the Gulf of Mexico north and across the Atlantic?
questions.f: The Gulf Stream carries warm water that helps keep western Europe milder than it would be.

questions.q: Which flat fish rests on the sea floor with both eyes on the same side of its head?
questions.f: A young flounder has one eye on each side, but one eye slowly moves as it grows flat.

questions.q: Coral reefs get much of their bright colour from tiny algae living inside the coral.
questions.f: When the water gets too warm, coral pushes out these algae and turns pale, or 'bleaches'.

questions.q: The killer whale, or orca, is actually the largest kind of...?
questions.f: Orcas belong to the dolphin family and hunt in clever, coordinated groups called pods.

questions.q: What do we call sea animals that have no backbone, such as jellyfish and crabs?
questions.f: About 95 percent of all animal species, on land and sea, are invertebrates.

questions.q: Which is bigger: the Pacific Ocean or all of Earth's land put together?
questions.f: The Pacific Ocean alone is larger than all the continents combined.

questions.q: An octopus has a surprising number of hearts. How many?
questions.f: Two hearts pump blood to the gills, and one pumps it to the rest of the body.

questions.q: About how long can a large sea turtle live?
questions.f: Some sea turtles are thought to live longer than most humans do.

questions.q: Which giant shark swims with its mouth wide open to filter tiny plankton from the water?
questions.f: The basking shark is the second-largest fish, gentle and harmless despite its huge mouth.

questions.q: Which cold-water bird 'flies' underwater and carries several small fish crosswise in its beak?
questions.f: A puffin can hold a dozen or more small fish in its colourful beak at once.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who studies the ocean and its waters, floor, and currents?
questions.f: Oceanographers use ships, robots, and satellites to explore the seas.

questions.q: Which sea has no land coastline, is ringed by ocean currents, and is full of floating seaweed?
questions.f: The Sargasso Sea, in the Atlantic, is named after the sargassum seaweed floating in it.

questions.q: Which fish famously swims upstream from the sea into rivers to lay its eggs?
questions.f: Salmon can leap up waterfalls to reach the exact river where they were born.

questions.q: Which large, gentle, plant-eating sea mammal is sometimes called a 'sea cow'?
questions.f: Manatees graze slowly on sea grass and can eat a tenth of their weight each day.

questions.q: A blue whale weighs more than ten elephants put together.
questions.f: A blue whale can weigh about 150 tonnes, far more than ten large elephants.

questions.q: What do we call the shallow, gently sloping seabed just off a continent's coast?
questions.f: The sunlit continental shelf is where much of the ocean's sea life is found.

questions.q: Which small, striped fish sets up 'cleaning stations' and eats pests off bigger fish?
questions.f: Even big predators wait in line for a cleaner wrasse to nibble away their parasites.

questions.q: Wild penguins live mostly in the southern half of the world, not near the North Pole.
