questions.f: Polar bears live in the Arctic north, while nearly all penguins live in the south.

questions.q: Which long-bodied fish hides in reef holes and opens and closes its mouth to breathe?
questions.f: A moray eel opens its mouth to pump water over its gills, not because it is angry.

questions.q: Which fish can leave the water and skip across mud, breathing air for a while?
questions.f: Mudskippers live along muddy coasts and can even climb roots with their fins.

questions.q: Coral polyps are close cousins of which other stinging sea animal?
questions.f: Corals and anemones both have stinging cells and belong to the same animal group.

questions.q: Which sea creature has eight arms plus two longer tentacles and a torpedo-shaped body?
questions.f: A squid uses its two longer tentacles to grab prey and its eight arms to hold it.

questions.q: Which whale is famous for singing long, complex songs that can last for hours?
questions.f: Male humpback whales in the same area often sing the same slowly changing song.

questions.q: A sea star can push its stomach out through its mouth to eat food outside its body.
questions.f: A sea star wraps its stomach around a clam, digests it, then pulls its stomach back in.

questions.q: In the word 'marine life', the word 'marine' means having to do with the...?
questions.f: 'Marine' traces back to the Latin word 'mare', meaning sea.

questions.q: In words like 'aquatic' and 'aquarium', the part 'aqua' means...?
questions.f: 'Aqua' is the Latin word for water and appears in many ocean-related words.

questions.q: Crabs, shrimp, and clams are all grouped as 'shellfish' because they share what feature?
questions.f: Shellfish belong to different animal families but are grouped by their protective shells.

questions.q: A young oyster that has settled onto a surface and begun to grow is called a...?
questions.f: Oyster spat glue themselves to a hard spot and stay there for the rest of their lives.

questions.q: A group of sharks is sometimes playfully called a...?
questions.f: English has many odd collective nouns, and a group of sharks is a 'shiver'.

questions.q: The word 'tide' grew from an old word for 'time'. Why does that fit the tides?
c: Tides rise and fall on a regular schedule
Tides only happen once a year
questions.f: The Old English word 'tid' meant 'time', and tides follow the clock-like pull of the Moon.

questions.q: A 'peninsula' is a piece of land that is almost surrounded by...?
questions.f: 'Peninsula' comes from Latin words meaning 'almost an island'.

questions.q: An 'island' is a piece of land completely surrounded by...?
questions.f: Greenland is the world's largest island that is not itself a continent.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who studies the plants and animals of the sea?
questions.f: Marine biologists study everything from microscopic plankton to giant whales.

questions.q: When people say 'coral', they often mean the stony reef made from the...?
questions.f: A reef is built layer by layer from the hard skeletons of countless tiny coral polyps.

questions.q: The word 'crustacean', used for crabs and lobsters, points to their hard outer...?
questions.f: 'Crustacean' comes from the Latin word 'crusta', meaning crust or hard shell.

questions.q: The 'pod' in 'octopus' and 'tripod' means...?
questions.f: 'Octopus' comes from Greek words meaning 'eight-foot'.

questions.q: A young eel that travels from the open sea into rivers is called an...?
questions.f: Tiny see-through elvers drift for thousands of miles before reaching river mouths.

questions.q: The word 'seashore' names the land right along the edge of the...?
questions.f: The seashore constantly changes shape as tides and storms move the sand.

questions.q: A 'whirlpool' is water that moves in a fast-spinning...?
questions.f: Strong tides squeezing through narrow channels can create swirling whirlpools.

questions.q: The word 'seafood' means food that comes from the...?
questions.f: Fish, shrimp, clams, and seaweed are all types of seafood.

questions.q: The word 'shoal' can mean a large group of fish or a shallow, hidden...?
questions.f: A shoal of sand just below the surface can be a danger to passing boats.

questions.q: The 'sea' in 'seahorse', 'seaweed', and 'seashell' tells us they all belong to the...?
questions.f: 'Sea' is a handy prefix that flags creatures and objects found in the ocean.

questions.q: A jellyfish body feels mostly...?
questions.f: A jellyfish is about 95 percent water, giving it a soft, see-through, wobbly body.

questions.q: A 'lagoon' is a calm, shallow pool of seawater cut off from the open ocean by a...?
questions.f: 'Lagoon' comes from a Latin word meaning a pond or pool.

questions.q: When a sailor falls off a ship into the sea, we say the person has gone...?
questions.f: The old cry 'man overboard!' still means someone has fallen into the water.

questions.q: A 'castaway' is a person left alone on a distant shore after being...?
questions.f: Tales of castaways surviving on lonely islands have thrilled readers for centuries.

questions.q: The sea anemone borrowed its name from a...?
questions.f: Because it looks like a blossom, the animal took the name of the wind-flower called anemone.

questions.q: A 'nautical' mile is a unit used to measure distance at...?
questions.f: 'Nautical' comes from the Greek word 'nautes', meaning sailor.

questions.q: Which sea lies between Europe and Africa?
questions.f: The name 'Mediterranean' means 'in the middle of the land', which suits this almost-enclosed sea.

questions.q: Which of Earth's five oceans is the smallest?
questions.f: Much of the small, shallow Arctic Ocean is capped by floating sea ice.

questions.q: What narrow stretch of sea separates England from France?
questions.f: At its narrowest the Channel is only about 33 kilometres across.

questions.q: About how much of seawater is actually salt?
questions.f: That small share still adds up to enough salt to bury all the land under a thick layer.

questions.q: About how much of an iceberg sticks up above the water?
questions.f: Because most of it is hidden below, we say the visible part is just 'the tip of the iceberg'.

questions.q: Which seabird has the largest wingspan of any living bird?
questions.f: Its wings can stretch about 3.5 metres, letting it glide for hours without a single flap.

questions.q: Which sea turtle is named after a bird because of its narrow, pointed beak?
questions.f: That beak lets a hawksbill reach into reef crevices to pull out sponges.

questions.q: What can scientists learn by counting the rings on a fish's scales?
questions.f: Like tree rings, scale and ear-bone rings record each year a fish has lived.

questions.q: Which gas do we breathe out that ocean plankton use to make food?
questions.f: The ocean soaks up around a quarter of the carbon dioxide people put into the air.

questions.q: Which of these ocean animals is a reptile?
questions.f: Sea turtles and sea snakes are the ocean's reptiles, with scaly skin and air-breathing lungs.

questions.q: What is the largest predatory fish in the ocean?
questions.f: The bigger whale shark and basking shark are gentle filter feeders, not hunters.

questions.q: Which two oceans does the Panama Canal connect?
questions.f: Before the canal opened in 1914, ships had to sail all the way around South America.

questions.q: Which famous ship sank in 1912 after striking an iceberg in the North Atlantic?
questions.f: The wreck lay lost for 73 years until it was found in 1985, nearly 4 km down.

questions.q: Which instrument helps sailors know which way is north?
questions.f: A compass needle swings to line up with Earth's own magnetic field.

questions.q: Before compasses, sailors in the north found their way using which star?
questions.f: The North Star sits almost exactly above the North Pole, so it barely seems to move.

questions.q: Which seabird dives from high in the air, hitting the water like an arrow?
questions.f: A gannet can plunge at over 80 km/h, with air sacs cushioning the impact.

questions.q: Which bird travels between the Arctic and the Antarctic every year?
questions.f: Over a long life, an Arctic tern may fly a distance equal to three trips to the Moon.

questions.q: Coral reefs grow best in which kind of seawater?
questions.f: Reef corals need sunlight for their algae partners, so they stay in the sunlit shallows.

questions.q: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of which country?
questions.f: It stretches over 2,300 kilometres along Australia's north-east coast.

questions.q: Salty seawater freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water does.
questions.f: Fresh water freezes at 0 C, but seawater must drop to about -2 C before it turns to ice.

questions.q: Which huge ray feeds by filtering plankton from the water as it swims?
questions.f: A manta ray can be 7 metres across yet eats only tiny drifting food.

questions.q: What do we call sea animals that eat only plants, such as manatees?
questions.f: From Latin roots meaning 'plant eater'; a manatee can munch grass for seven hours a day.

questions.q: What do we call an animal, like a crab, that feeds on dead things it finds?
questions.f: Scavengers are the ocean's clean-up crew, recycling anything that sinks to the bottom.

questions.q: Nearly every ocean food chain begins with which kind of living thing?
questions.f: These drifting plant-like specks use sunlight to make the food that feeds the whole sea.

questions.q: Which giant sea creature makes the ocean's biggest 'footprint' as a filter feeder?
questions.f: A whale shark can be 12 metres long yet swallows nothing bigger than small fish and plankton.

questions.q: About how long can a bottlenose dolphin hold its breath underwater?
questions.f: A dolphin can replace most of the air in its lungs in a single quick breath.

questions.q: Which sea has such salty, mineral-rich water that swimmers bob like corks?
questions.f: The Dead Sea is really a salty lake, nearly ten times saltier than the ocean.

questions.q: How does an animal use camouflage to stay safe?
c: By blending in with its surroundings
questions.f: A flatfish can change its pattern in minutes to match the seabed beneath it.

questions.q: When animals travel long distances at the same time each year, this is called...?
questions.f: Some whales migrate thousands of kilometres between cold feeding seas and warm nurseries.

questions.q: In the water cycle, what turns seawater into water vapour that rises into the sky?
questions.f: When seawater evaporates, the salt is left behind, so rain that falls later is fresh.

questions.q: Which of these seas is famous for being almost entirely surrounded by land?
questions.f: The Black Sea links to the Mediterranean only through a narrow, winding passage.

questions.q: There are more than 400 different kinds of shark living in the world's oceans.
questions.f: Scientists count over 500 shark species, and new ones are still being discovered.

questions.q: The seafloor is part of Earth's rocky outer layer, the crust.
questions.f: Oceanic crust is thinner than the crust under the continents but made of denser rock.

questions.q: Which large gulf lies on the southern coast of the United States?
questions.f: The warm waters of this gulf help feed the powerful Gulf Stream current.

questions.q: Which of these animals is at the very top of many ocean food chains?
questions.f: Orcas have no natural predators, which makes them an apex predator of the sea.

questions.q: When a kind of animal has died out completely and none are left, it is...?
questions.f: The Steller's sea cow, a huge relative of the manatee, went extinct in the 1700s.

questions.q: An animal at serious risk of dying out, like some sea turtles, is called...?
questions.f: Protecting nesting beaches has helped several endangered turtle populations recover.

questions.q: What do we call the place where a particular animal naturally lives?
questions.f: A single coral reef contains dozens of tiny habitats, from sandy patches to shady caves.

questions.q: The front of a ship is called the...?
questions.f: A ship's bow is shaped to slice through waves with as little splash as possible.

questions.q: The back of a ship is called the...?
questions.f: A ship's name is traditionally painted across its stern.

questions.q: On a ship, 'starboard' means which side?
questions.f: 'Starboard' comes from the old steering oar, which was fixed on the right-hand side.

questions.q: On a ship, 'port' means which side?
questions.f: It is the side once turned toward the dock, since the steering oar was on the other side.

questions.q: At sea, a 'knot' is a unit used to measure a ship's...?
questions.f: Sailors once timed knots on a rope paid out behind the ship to measure how fast it went.

questions.q: The 'hull' of a ship is its...?
questions.f: A hull works only if it stays watertight, so sailors patch every leak at once.

questions.q: The 'mast' on a sailing ship is the...?
c: Tall pole that holds the sails
questions.f: Some old sailing ships carried three or four masts covered in dozens of sails.

questions.q: A ship's 'rudder' is used to...?
questions.f: A rudder is a flat blade at the stern that swings to push the ship's tail sideways.

questions.q: The 'deck' of a ship is its...?
questions.f: Big ships have many decks stacked up, like the floors of a building.

questions.q: A group of ships sailing together is called a...?
questions.f: 'Fleet' comes from an old word meaning to float or swim.

questions.q: A 'ferry' is a boat that...?
c: Carries people back and forth on a set route
questions.f: 'Ferry' comes from an old word meaning to carry or to travel.

questions.q: A whale's tail is made of two wide blades called...?
questions.f: Unlike a fish's upright tail, a whale's flukes lie flat and beat up and down.

questions.q: A fin described as 'dorsal' is found on an animal's...?
questions.f: From Latin 'dorsum' (back); a dolphin's dorsal fin shape is unique enough to identify it.

questions.q: An animal described as a 'vertebrate', such as a shark, has a...?
questions.f: From Latin 'vertebra' (joint of the spine): fish, whales, and turtles are all vertebrates.

questions.q: A 'filter feeder' is an animal that gets food by...?
c: Straining it out of the water
questions.f: Sponges, clams, and even the giant whale shark are all filter feeders.

questions.q: An animal that is another animal's food is called its...?
questions.f: Herring are prey for almost everything bigger, from cod to seals to seabirds.

questions.q: Are fish warm-blooded or cold-blooded?
questions.f: A cold-blooded fish's body matches the water's temperature, so it saves lots of energy.

questions.q: Which of these sea animals is a mollusc?
questions.f: Molluscs have soft bodies, and many, but not all, protect themselves with a shell.

questions.q: Which of these sea animals is an echinoderm, a spiny-skinned animal?
questions.f: Sea urchins, sea stars, and sea cucumbers are all echinoderms with five-part bodies.

questions.q: What is 'sea level'?
c: The average height of the ocean's surface
questions.f: Mountains are measured in metres above sea level, so it is the world's shared measuring line.

questions.q: What is a 'rip current' at the beach?
c: A strong narrow flow pulling away from shore
questions.f: Rip currents are the reason lifeguards fly warning flags on many beaches.

questions.q: If a swimmer is caught in a rip current, what is the safest thing to do?
c: Stay calm and swim sideways out of it
questions.f: Rips are narrow, so swimming across the flow gets you free far faster than fighting it.

questions.q: Which is the largest penguin in the world?
questions.f: An emperor penguin stands over a metre tall and can dive deeper than any other bird.

questions.q: In emperor penguins, which parent keeps the single egg warm through the polar winter?
questions.f: The father balances the egg on his feet for about two months while the mother feeds at sea.

questions.q: Where do puffins usually make their nests?
questions.f: A pair of puffins often returns to the very same burrow year after year.

questions.q: The Southern Ocean, around Antarctica, is also known as the...?
questions.f: It was officially recognised as the world's fifth ocean, the youngest name on the map.

questions.q: Which is the world's largest bay?
questions.f: The Bay of Bengal, in the Indian Ocean, touches India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Sri Lanka.

questions.q: Which continent is completely surrounded by the Southern Ocean?
questions.f: Antarctica holds about 90 percent of all the ice on Earth.

questions.q: When is the Arctic sea ice at its largest?
questions.f: The ice cap grows and shrinks each year, breathing in and out with the seasons.

questions.q: What is an 'oil spill'?
questions.f: Spilled oil coats seabirds' feathers so they can no longer stay warm or waterproof.

questions.q: What is a 'marine reserve'?
c: A protected part of the sea
questions.f: Inside reserves where fishing is limited, fish grow bigger and more plentiful.

questions.q: How do scientists follow a shark or turtle on its long journeys?
questions.f: Tags beam a signal to satellites each time the animal surfaces, drawing its route on a map.

questions.q: What kind of machine explores the deep sea with no people aboard?
questions.f: Remote-controlled robots can stay down for hours in water that would crush a diver.

questions.q: What does a sea star use its hundreds of tiny 'tube feet' for?
questions.f: Each tube foot works by water pressure, like a tiny hydraulic machine.

questions.q: What do wild penguins mostly eat?
questions.f: Backward-pointing spines on a penguin's tongue stop slippery fish from escaping.

questions.q: Which is the largest inland body of salt water on Earth?
questions.f: The Caspian is called a sea because of its size and salt, but it has no link to the ocean.

questions.q: Waves in a storm are much bigger and more powerful than waves in calm weather.
questions.f: The stronger the wind and the longer it blows, the larger the waves it can build.

questions.q: Sea otters and seals both keep warm in cold water, but in completely different ways.
questions.f: Seals rely on thick fat, while otters trap warm air in the densest fur of any animal.

questions.q: Some fish can change colour to match the seabed they are resting on.
questions.f: Flatfish shift their spots and speckles within minutes to vanish against sand or gravel.

questions.q: Sea turtles must come up to the surface to breathe air.
questions.f: Turtles have lungs, not gills, so every dive ends with a trip back to the surface.

questions.q: Which sea creature travels in enormous swarms that can be seen from space?
questions.f: A single krill swarm can stretch for kilometres and tint the sea pink.

questions.q: Why does the sea get colder as you dive deeper?
c: Sunlight cannot warm the deep water
questions.f: Below about 1,000 metres, almost all seawater sits close to 4 C, everywhere on Earth.

questions.q: A large group of krill swarming together is called a...?
questions.f: Antarctic krill may be the most numerous single animal species on the planet by weight.

questions.q: A group of oysters growing together on the seabed is called an oyster...?
questions.f: Oyster beds shelter young fish and filter huge amounts of seawater every day.

questions.q: A 'gulf' is a very large...?
questions.f: A gulf is a big bite taken out of a coastline, often nearly enclosed by land.

questions.q: The word 'strait', as in the Bering Strait, tells you the passage of water is...?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'straitjacket', which means a tight, narrow jacket.

questions.q: A 'cape' on a map is a piece of land that...?
questions.f: Sailors once dreaded the storms around the Cape of Good Hope at Africa's tip.

questions.q: A 'cove' is a...?
questions.f: Coves are often ringed by rocks, which makes their water calm and inviting.

questions.q: An ocean 'trench' is a...?
c: Long, very deep valley in the seabed
questions.f: Every one of the ocean's deepest spots lies in a trench near the edge of a continent or islands.

questions.q: The word 'current', as in an ocean current, comes from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'currere' (to run): the same root gives us 'courier' and 'corridor'.

questions.q: The 'salinity' of seawater means its...?
questions.f: From Latin 'sal' (salt): scientists measure salinity to trace where a body of water came from.

questions.q: 'Desalination' is the process of...?
c: Taking the salt out of seawater
questions.f: Some dry countries get most of their drinking water from desalination plants.

questions.q: 'Evaporation' is when water...?
questions.f: From Latin 'vapor' (steam): evaporation from the sea supplies almost all of the world's rain.

questions.q: An 'exoskeleton', like a crab's shell, is a skeleton that is...?
questions.f: From Greek 'exo' (outside): the drawback is that the animal must shed it to grow.

questions.q: The 'urchin' in 'sea urchin' is an old English word for which animal?
questions.f: 'Urchin' once meant hedgehog, which suits this round, prickly sea creature perfectly.

questions.q: A 'mariner' is another word for a...?
questions.f: From Latin 'mare' (sea): 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' is a famous poem of the sea.

questions.q: The word 'navy' comes from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'navis' (ship): the same root gives us 'navigate' and 'naval'.

questions.q: The 'galley' on a ship is the...?
questions.f: A ship's galley must have raised edges on the stove so pots do not slide in rough seas.

questions.q: The 'bridge' of a ship is the place where the ship is...?
questions.f: The name comes from an old walkway bridging the paddle boxes of early steamships.

questions.q: The 'keel' runs along which part of a ship?
questions.f: A keel is like a ship's backbone and stops it from being blown sideways.

questions.q: 'Ballast' is heavy material carried low in a ship to...?
questions.f: Empty cargo ships take on seawater as ballast so they do not ride dangerously high.

questions.q: 'Cargo' means the...?
questions.f: About 90 percent of the world's traded goods travel by sea as cargo.

questions.q: A 'crow's nest' high on a ship's mast was used as a...?
questions.f: The name may come from the caged crows that early sailors released to point toward land.

questions.q: A 'tugboat' is a small, powerful boat that...?
questions.f: A tug's engines are enormous for its size, so it can nudge a giant ship into its berth.

questions.q: A 'trawler' is a fishing boat that works by...?
questions.f: 'Trawl' means to drag; trawlers can pull a net wide enough to swallow a jumbo jet.

questions.q: A 'stowaway' is a person who...?
c: Hides aboard a ship to travel secretly
questions.f: 'Stow' means to pack away, so a stowaway is someone packed out of sight.

questions.q: A ship's 'maiden voyage' is its...?
questions.f: The Titanic sank on its maiden voyage, before it ever completed a single crossing.

questions.q: What do we call the very deepest ocean zone, found only in the great trenches?
questions.f: The hadal zone is named after Hades, the Greek underworld, because it is so deep and dark.

questions.q: Which climate pattern warms the eastern Pacific and shifts weather worldwide, meaning 'the boy'?
questions.f: Fishermen in Peru named El Nino because its warm water often arrives around Christmas.

questions.q: What is it called when the ocean slowly turns more acidic by soaking up carbon dioxide?
questions.f: More acidic seawater makes it harder for shells and corals to build their hard parts.

questions.q: Which fish was thought extinct with the dinosaurs until one was caught alive in 1938?
questions.f: The coelacanth is called a 'living fossil' because it has changed little in millions of years.

questions.q: Which small sea creature can throw one of the fastest punches in nature?
questions.f: A mantis shrimp's strike is so fast it can crack the glass of an aquarium tank.

questions.q: What do we call the layer where warm surface water meets the cold deep water?
questions.f: The thermocline can act like a barrier that many animals rarely cross.

questions.q: Which is the longest mountain range on Earth, hidden almost entirely under the sea?
questions.f: The mid-ocean ridge winds around the globe for over 65,000 kilometres.

questions.q: Which metal in an octopus's blood makes it appear blue instead of red?
questions.f: Copper-based blood carries oxygen well in cold, low-oxygen deep water.

questions.q: Clownfish are all born male; what can the largest one in a group become?
questions.f: If the female of the group dies, the biggest male changes sex to take her place.

questions.q: About how much seawater can a single oyster filter and clean in one day?
questions.f: Beds of oysters act like natural water filters, keeping bays clearer and cleaner.

questions.q: Which is the most venomous fish in the sea, well camouflaged on the reef floor?
questions.f: A stonefish looks just like a lump of rock, so swimmers must watch where they step.

questions.q: Which soft sea animal can push out its own insides to distract a predator, then regrow them?
questions.f: A sea cucumber can eject sticky threads or organs and slowly grow them back later.

questions.q: Which colourful reef fish eats coral and then produces fine white sand?
questions.f: A single parrotfish can create hundreds of kilograms of soft sand each year.

questions.q: What do scientists call animals and plants that live on or in the ocean floor?
questions.f: 'Benthos' comes from a Greek word for the depths, meaning the bottom-dwellers.

questions.q: What do we call sea animals, like fish and squid, that swim freely against the current?
questions.f: Unlike drifting plankton, nekton are strong swimmers that choose where they go.

questions.q: Which shark is the longest-living vertebrate, reaching ages of several centuries?
questions.f: Some Greenland sharks alive today may have been born hundreds of years ago.

questions.q: The dim 'twilight zone' of the ocean has which scientific name?
questions.f: 'Meso' means middle, so the mesopelagic zone sits between the sunlit and midnight layers.

questions.q: What is the largest invertebrate (animal without a backbone) on Earth?
questions.f: The colossal squid has the largest eyes of any animal, about the size of a dinner plate.

questions.q: When a clownfish and an anemone help each other survive, this partnership is called...?
questions.f: The clownfish is protected by the stinging anemone and keeps it clean in return.

questions.q: Much of the soft white sand on tropical beaches was once eaten and produced by parrotfish.
questions.f: Parrotfish grind up coral to reach algae, then release the leftover coral as fine sand.

questions.q: Which colourful sea slug can steal stinging cells from its prey and use them for defence?
questions.f: A nudibranch can borrow the jellyfish stingers it eats and store them in its own body.

questions.q: What mainly pulls the ocean into the bulges that create the tides?
questions.f: The Sun helps too, but the closer Moon has the strongest pull on Earth's seas.

questions.q: Each night huge numbers of tiny sea animals swim up to feed, then sink by day. This is Earth's largest...?
questions.f: This daily up-and-down journey moves more living things than any other migration on the planet.

questions.q: Sharks can sense the tiny electric signals of hidden prey using special jelly-filled...?
questions.f: These sensing pores are named the ampullae of Lorenzini after the scientist who described them.

questions.q: The stiff bristles that baleen whales use to strain food are made of the same material as our...?
questions.f: Baleen is made of keratin, the same tough protein found in nails and hair.

questions.q: Some deep-sea fish can swallow prey larger than their own bodies.
questions.f: With stretchy stomachs and loose jaws, food is scarce enough that they cannot be picky.

questions.q: Which cooler ocean pattern is the opposite of El Nino, bringing colder eastern Pacific water?
questions.f: La Nina means 'the girl' and often flips the weather patterns that El Nino brings.

questions.q: The sinking of cold, salty water helps drive a slow global 'conveyor belt' of ocean currents. What is this circulation called?
questions.f: This deep current moves heat around the planet and can take 1,000 years to complete a loop.

questions.q: Corals get much of their food from tiny algae that live inside them, called...?
questions.f: These algae make food from sunlight and share it with the coral, which gives them a home.

questions.q: A scientist who studies fish is called an...?
questions.f: 'Ichthyologist' comes from the Greek word 'ichthys', meaning fish.

questions.q: The root 'hydro-' in words like 'hydrothermal' means...?
questions.f: 'Hydro' comes from the Greek word 'hydor', meaning water.

questions.q: An animal described as 'pelagic' lives in the...?
c: Open sea, away from the bottom
questions.f: 'Pelagic' comes from the Greek word 'pelagos', meaning the open sea.

questions.q: An animal described as 'benthic' lives on or near the ocean's...?
questions.f: 'Benthic' comes from the Greek 'benthos', meaning the depths.

questions.q: The word 'abyss', as in the abyssal zone, means...?
questions.f: 'Abyss' comes from a Greek word meaning 'without a bottom'.

questions.q: A 'cetacean' is any animal in the whale and dolphin group; the root 'cetus' means...?
questions.f: 'Cetus' comes from the Greek 'ketos', an ancient word for a great sea creature.

questions.q: The word 'mollusc', used for snails, clams, and octopuses, comes from a word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Mollusc' comes from the Latin 'mollis', meaning soft, describing their soft bodies.

questions.q: The prefix 'amphi-' in 'amphibious' means...?
questions.f: An amphibious animal or vehicle works both on land and in water; 'amphi' is Greek for 'both'.

questions.q: An 'estuary' is a place where a river's fresh water meets and mixes with the...?
questions.f: 'Estuary' comes from the Latin 'aestus', meaning tide, which sweeps in and out of it.

questions.q: An 'archipelago' is a...?
questions.f: 'Archipelago' comes from Greek words meaning 'chief sea'.

questions.q: The word 'tsunami' literally means...?
questions.f: 'Tsunami' is a Japanese word, since these waves grow tallest as they reach harbours.

questions.q: The word 'aquaculture' means the farming of...?
c: Fish and sea plants in water
questions.f: 'Aqua' means water and 'culture' means growing, so aquaculture is water farming.

questions.q: The word 'sonar', used to find things underwater with sound, is short for...?
questions.f: Sonar sends out sound and listens for the echo bouncing back off objects.

questions.q: The word 'scuba' is really an acronym standing for...?
questions.f: Scuba gear lets a diver carry their own air supply in a tank on their back.

questions.q: The suffix '-logy', as in 'biology' and 'oceanology', means the...?
questions.f: '-logy' comes from the Greek 'logos', meaning word, reason, or study.

questions.q: A person who studies shells and the molluscs that make them is a...?
questions.f: 'Conchologist' comes from the Greek 'konche', meaning shell.

questions.q: The word 'porpoise' comes from old words meaning 'pig fish'. A porpoise is a close cousin of the...?
questions.f: Porpoises are smaller than most dolphins and have rounder faces and flatter teeth.

questions.q: Something 'littoral' has to do with the...?
questions.f: 'Littoral' comes from the Latin 'litus', meaning shore.

questions.q: If seawater is described as 'saline', it is...?
questions.f: 'Saline' comes from the Latin 'sal', meaning salt.

questions.q: A 'regatta' is a...?
questions.f: The word 'regatta' first described gondola races held on the canals of Venice.

questions.q: If an object is 'buoyant', it...?
questions.f: The word 'buoyant' is linked to the floating markers called buoys.

questions.q: In sailing and cooking, 'brine' means...?
questions.f: Brine has long been used to preserve fish and other food by keeping germs out.

questions.q: A 'fathom' is an old unit used to measure a body of water's...?
questions.f: One fathom is about the span of a person's outstretched arms, roughly 1.8 metres.

questions.q: A 'delta' is the fan of land where a river drops its mud as it flows into the...?
questions.f: A river delta is named after the triangle-shaped Greek letter delta.

questions.q: How do dolphins and whales sleep without drowning?
c: They rest one half of the brain at a time
They do not sleep at all
questions.f: With half the brain awake, they keep one eye open and remember to surface for air.

questions.q: Why does shark skin feel like sandpaper?
c: It is covered in tiny tooth-like scales
It is made of dry bone
It has no covering at all
questions.f: These scales are so good at cutting drag that swimsuit designers copied their shape.

questions.q: In sea turtles, what decides whether the eggs in a nest hatch as males or females?
questions.f: Warmer sand produces more females, so a hotter climate can tip whole beaches one way.

questions.q: In an ocean wave, what actually travels across the sea?
questions.f: Water in a wave circles in place, which is why a floating gull just bobs up and down.

questions.q: Why does a wave finally break and tumble over near the shore?
questions.f: As the seabed rises, the wave slows and steepens until its crest topples forward.

questions.q: What do we call the flattest, most featureless region on the surface of the Earth?
questions.f: Thick layers of fine sediment have buried the deep-sea floor into an almost perfect flatness.

questions.q: Between the shallow shelf and the deep abyss, the seabed drops away down the continental...?
questions.f: Underwater avalanches have carved huge canyons into the continental slope.

questions.q: How does a sea cave, and eventually a sea arch, form in a cliff?
questions.f: When the roof of a sea arch finally collapses, a lone pillar called a sea stack is left standing.

questions.q: Which coiled fossil shell, common in old sea rocks, belonged to a relative of the squid?
questions.f: Ammonites ruled ancient seas for over 300 million years before dying out with the dinosaurs.

questions.q: Which of these ancient sea reptiles swam in the same age as the dinosaurs?
questions.f: Plesiosaurs rowed with four broad flippers and gave birth to live young at sea.

questions.q: Which sand dunes at the coast are most important for protecting the land behind them?
c: Dunes held together by grass roots
Wet dunes at the tide line
questions.f: Marram grass roots knit the sand together, turning a dune into a natural sea wall.

questions.q: Which is the correct name for the huge floating platforms of ice attached to Antarctica?
questions.f: When a chunk breaks off an ice shelf and floats free, it becomes an iceberg.

questions.q: Why is a sponge from the sea good for washing?
c: Its skeleton is a soft maze of holes
questions.f: For centuries divers harvested natural sponges from the Mediterranean for bathing.

questions.q: When a young animal changes body shape completely as it grows, like a crab larva, this is called...?
questions.f: From Greek roots meaning 'change of form'; a crab larva looks nothing like an adult crab.

questions.q: When fish release eggs and sperm into the water together, this is called...?
questions.f: Many reef fish spawn at dusk, when the eggs are less likely to be spotted and eaten.

questions.q: When two different species both benefit from living together, that is a kind of symbiosis called...?
questions.f: A goby fish and a blind shrimp share a burrow: the shrimp digs, the goby watches for danger.

questions.q: An animal that lives on another animal and harms it, like a fish louse, is a...?
questions.f: From Greek 'parasitos', meaning one who eats at another's table.

questions.q: Many open-ocean fish are dark on top and pale underneath. What is this pattern called?
questions.f: Seen from above they blend with dark depths; from below they vanish against bright sky.

questions.q: When a harmless animal copies the look of a dangerous one to stay safe, that is...?
questions.f: The harmless mimic octopus can even imitate the shape and swimming style of a venomous sole.

questions.q: Which ocean is named after a Greek Titan who held up the sky?
questions.f: Atlas gave his name to the Atlantic, to the Atlas Mountains, and to books of maps.

questions.q: The Pacific Ocean's name comes from a word meaning...?
questions.f: Magellan's crew named it 'peaceful' after escaping the wild storms of the southern tip of America.

questions.q: The word 'Arctic' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'arktos' (bear), for the Great Bear constellation that circles the northern sky.

questions.q: 'Antarctic' is built from a prefix meaning 'opposite' plus a root meaning...?
questions.f: So 'Antarctic' literally means 'opposite the bear', the far side of the world from the Arctic.

questions.q: Something 'maritime', like a maritime museum, has to do with the...?
questions.f: From Latin 'mare' (sea): a maritime nation is one whose life depends on the ocean.

questions.q: To 'circumnavigate' the globe means to...?
c: Sail or travel all the way around it
questions.f: From Latin 'circum' (around) + 'navigare' (to sail): Magellan's expedition first did it by 1522.

questions.q: A 'transatlantic' voyage is one that goes...?
questions.f: From Latin 'trans' (across): the first transatlantic telegraph cable was laid in the 1860s.

questions.q: To 'submerge' something means to...?
questions.f: From Latin 'sub' (under) + 'mergere' (to dip): 'emerge' is its opposite, to come back out.

questions.q: A 'submersible' is a craft designed to...?
questions.f: Unlike a submarine, a small submersible usually needs a support ship nearby.

questions.q: A 'periscope' takes its name from roots meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'peri' (around) + 'skopein' (to look): mirrors let a submarine peek above the waves.

questions.q: A 'hydrophone' is an instrument used to...?
questions.f: From Greek roots for water and sound; hydrophones let scientists eavesdrop on whale songs.

questions.q: An 'anemometer' measures the speed of the...?
questions.f: From Greek 'anemos' (wind), the same root behind the flower-like sea anemone.

questions.q: The Roman god of the sea, whose name is also a planet, is...?
questions.f: His Greek counterpart was Poseidon, who was said to stir up storms when angered.

questions.q: A 'trident', the sea god's weapon, is a spear with how many prongs?
questions.f: From Latin 'tri' (three) + 'dens' (tooth): real tridents were once used for spearing fish.

questions.q: The distress call 'Mayday' has nothing to do with May; it comes from a French phrase meaning...?
questions.f: From French 'm'aidez' (help me), chosen because it is clear over a crackly radio.

questions.q: A 'decapod', such as a crab or shrimp, is an animal with how many legs?
questions.f: From Greek 'deka' (ten) + 'pous' (foot): count a crab's legs and you will find ten, claws included.

questions.q: A 'bivalve', such as a clam or mussel, has a shell made of how many parts?
questions.f: From Latin 'bi' (two) + 'valva' (folding door): a strong muscle pulls the two halves shut.

questions.q: The hard shell covering the back of a crab or turtle is called its...?
questions.f: A turtle's carapace is fused to its ribs and spine, so it can never crawl out of it.

questions.q: The pair of long feelers on a lobster's head are its...?
questions.f: From Latin 'antenna' (sail yard): a lobster uses them to smell and feel its way in the dark.

questions.q: A 'rookery' is a place where seals or penguins gather to...?
questions.f: A crowded rookery can hold tens of thousands of noisy, squabbling birds.

questions.q: A group of eggs laid together in one nest is called a...?
questions.f: A single loggerhead turtle can lay several clutches of about 100 eggs in one season.

questions.q: When a crab or lobster sheds its shell to grow, the process is called...?
questions.f: A freshly moulted lobster is so soft it hides in a crevice for days until its shell hardens.

questions.q: An animal's blubber works mainly as insulation, keeping body heat from escaping into the water.
questions.f: Blubber also stores energy, so a fasting whale can live off it for months.

questions.q: Water conducts heat away from a body far faster than air does.
questions.f: That is why sea mammals need thick blubber or dense fur even in water above freezing.

questions.q: Nearly all of the ocean floor has been mapped in the same fine detail as the surface of Mars.
questions.f: Only a modest share of the seabed has been mapped in high detail; Mars is better charted.

questions.q: The ocean has absorbed most of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases.
questions.f: Over 90 percent of that extra heat has gone into the sea, not the air.

questions.q: What makes a shipping container that falls off a cargo ship dangerous to other boats?
c: It can float just below the surface
questions.f: Thousands of containers are lost at sea each year, and some drift half-submerged for weeks.

questions.q: Why is a coral reef sometimes called the 'rainforest of the sea'?
c: It packs enormous variety into a small area
questions.f: Reefs cover under one percent of the seafloor yet shelter around a quarter of marine species.

questions.q: How do scientists use a 'sediment core' drilled from the seabed?
c: To read the ocean's past like pages in a book
questions.f: Deeper layers are older, so a single core can reveal climates from millions of years ago.

questions.q: Which of these best explains why fish schools twist and turn as one body?
c: Each fish reacts fast to its nearest neighbours
questions.f: There is no leader: simple copying of neighbours creates those beautiful swirling shapes.

questions.q: How does an ocean current help drifting animals like young crabs and fish?
c: It carries them to new homes
questions.f: Larvae can ride currents hundreds of kilometres before settling on a distant reef.

questions.q: Why does ice float on the sea instead of sinking?
c: Ice is less dense than liquid water
questions.f: Water is one of the very few substances that expands when it freezes, and so floats.

questions.q: Why can a heavy steel ship float?
c: It pushes aside more water than it weighs
questions.f: This is buoyancy: a hollow hull displaces a huge volume of water for its weight.

questions.q: What does the 'density' of seawater describe?
c: How much mass is packed into a volume
questions.f: Cold, salty water is dense and sinks, which is what drives the deep ocean currents.

questions.q: What happens to water pressure as a diver goes deeper?
questions.f: Pressure rises by about one atmosphere for every ten metres of seawater.

questions.q: Which sense do many sea creatures rely on most, since sound travels so well in water?
questions.f: Sound moves about four and a half times faster in seawater than in air.

questions.q: Which best explains why the deep sea has so few large plants?
c: There is no sunlight for photosynthesis
questions.f: Below the sunlit zone, life must live on food that sinks from above or on chemical energy.

questions.q: Why do many deep-sea animals have red or black bodies?
c: Red looks black in the deep, hiding them
questions.f: Red light never reaches those depths, so a red shrimp is effectively invisible there.

questions.q: What is the main reason coral reefs are in danger from warming seas?
c: Heat makes corals expel their algae partners
questions.f: Without their algae, corals lose both colour and their main source of food.

questions.q: What are 'microplastics' in the ocean?
questions.f: Microplastics have been found from the deepest trenches to Arctic sea ice.

questions.q: Why are 'ghost nets' a serious problem in the sea?
c: Lost fishing nets keep trapping animals for years
questions.f: Modern nets are made of plastics that can drift and keep catching for decades.

questions.q: What is 'overfishing'?
c: Catching fish faster than they can breed
questions.f: When fishing is paused, some collapsed fish populations have bounced back within a decade.

questions.q: Which of these is the best example of a 'keystone' role in the sea?
c: One species whose loss changes a whole habitat
questions.f: The name comes from the central stone that holds an arch together.

questions.q: What do we call the total variety of living things in a habitat?
questions.f: From Greek 'bios' (life) + 'diversus' (varied): reefs and rainforests top the biodiversity lists.

questions.q: The 'biomass' of krill in the Southern Ocean means the total...?
c: Weight of all the living krill
questions.f: Antarctic krill biomass is estimated in the hundreds of millions of tonnes.

questions.q: What is a 'cuttlebone', the chalky plate inside a cuttlefish, used for?
questions.f: The cuttlefish pumps gas and liquid through the bone's tiny chambers to rise or sink.

questions.q: Which is the largest living reptile, found in coastal seas and river mouths?
questions.f: A big saltwater crocodile can top six metres and swim far out between islands.

questions.q: How does a seal find food in dark or muddy water?
c: It feels water movements with its whiskers
questions.f: Seal whiskers are so sensitive they can trace the swirling wake a fish left behind.

questions.q: Which starfish is famous for eating coral and can damage whole reefs when it swarms?
questions.f: One crown-of-thorns can eat its own body-width of coral in a single day.

questions.q: How big can a giant clam grow?
c: About the size of a coin
questions.f: Giant clams can live for a century, and their fleshy lips glow with colourful algae.

questions.q: Why is the sea sometimes green rather than blue?
c: Blooms of tiny plant-like plankton tint it
questions.f: Satellites measure that greenness to map where the ocean's tiny plants are thriving.

questions.q: What causes the thick sea foam that piles up on some beaches?
c: Wind churning natural substances in the water
questions.f: Bits of algae and other organic matter act like the whisked white of an egg.

questions.q: A narwhal's famous 'horn' is really a very long...?
questions.f: It is an overgrown left front tooth, packed with millions of nerve endings.

questions.q: The ancestors of whales and dolphins once walked on land.
questions.f: Fossils show four-legged, deer-sized ancestors that gradually took to the water.

questions.q: About how big is a blue whale's heart?
c: Roughly the size of a small car
About the size of a football
About the size of a bus
About the size of a fist
questions.f: That giant heart beats as slowly as twice a minute during a deep dive.

questions.q: How do seabirds like gulls drink seawater without getting sick?
questions.f: Salt glands near the eyes drip concentrated brine out of the bird's nostrils.

questions.q: Which of these is a true difference between a manta ray and a stingray?
c: A manta has no stinging tail spine
questions.f: Mantas are harmless plankton eaters that often somersault while feeding.

questions.q: Why do cormorants stand with their wings spread wide after fishing?
c: To dry their partly wettable feathers
questions.f: Slightly wettable feathers make cormorants less buoyant, so they dive more easily.

questions.q: How does an elephant seal get its name?
questions.f: A male inflates that nose to make a booming roar that carries down the beach.

questions.q: Which best describes what a sea otter pup can do soon after birth?
questions.f: A pup's baby fur is so buoyant it bobs like a cork while its mother dives for food.

questions.q: Which of these best explains how a hermit crab chooses a new home?
c: It tries on empty shells for the right fit
questions.f: Hermit crabs sometimes queue up by size and swap shells down the whole line at once.

questions.q: Why do many reef fish have bold, clashing patterns?
c: The patterns break up their outline among coral
questions.f: Against a busy, colourful reef, a bold stripe can hide a fish better than plain grey would.

questions.q: What is unusual about how a flatfish such as a plaice swims?
c: It swims on its side, along the bottom
questions.f: As a young flatfish grows, one eye migrates around its head so both end up facing up.

questions.q: Which of these lets a whale hold its breath far longer than a human can?
c: It stores extra oxygen in its muscles
It has larger lungs than a house
questions.f: Whale muscle is dark with myoglobin, a protein that stockpiles oxygen for long dives.

questions.q: How does a puffin's beak change during the breeding season?
questions.f: The colourful outer plates are shed after breeding, leaving a duller winter beak.

questions.q: Which ocean feature is created where two different currents meet?
c: A front, often rich in food
questions.f: Seabirds and whales gather at these fronts, where prey is swept together in long lines.

questions.q: Which of these best describes 'plankton nets' used by scientists?
c: Very fine mesh nets towed slowly
questions.f: The mesh must be finer than a hair to trap creatures smaller than a grain of rice.

questions.q: Why is the Mediterranean's tidal range unusually small?
c: It is nearly cut off from the open ocean
questions.f: With only the narrow Strait of Gibraltar to fill it, its tides shift by mere centimetres.

questions.q: What happens to a river's sediment when it meets the still, salty water of the sea?
c: It settles out and builds up land
questions.f: That settling is how deltas and mudflats slowly grow at a river's mouth.

questions.q: Which is the best reason coral reefs shelter coastlines during storms?
c: The reef breaks waves before they reach shore
questions.f: A healthy reef can absorb most of a wave's energy before it hits the beach.

questions.q: Which best describes 'upwelling' zones for fishing?
c: Rich fishing grounds fed by deep nutrients
questions.f: A few small upwelling regions supply a surprisingly large share of the world's fish catch.

questions.q: Sound is used more than light for long-distance communication in the ocean.
questions.f: Light fades within tens of metres of seawater, while sound can carry for many kilometres.

questions.q: Sea ice reflects sunlight better than open, dark ocean water does.
questions.f: That is why melting ice speeds up warming: dark water soaks up the heat white ice bounced away.

questions.q: Some jellyfish can sting even after they have washed up and died on a beach.
questions.f: The stinging cells fire on contact by themselves, so a broken tentacle is still risky.

questions.q: Every seahorse species swims upright, using a fin on its back rather than its tail.
questions.f: A seahorse's dorsal fin flutters up to 35 times a second to push it slowly along.

questions.q: The word 'walrus' is thought to come from old northern words meaning...?
questions.f: From Old Norse and Dutch roots: 'whale-horse' suits this huge, tusked swimmer well.

questions.q: A 'sea shanty' takes the 'shanty' part of its name from a word meaning...?
questions.f: From French 'chanter' (to sing): shanties gave sailors a shared rhythm for heavy work.

questions.q: A 'flotilla' is a...?
questions.f: From Spanish, meaning 'little fleet', it is the diminutive form of 'flota'.

questions.q: The word 'kayak' comes from which people's language?
questions.f: A traditional kayak was a sealskin-covered frame built to fit its owner's body exactly.

questions.q: The word 'canoe' entered English from the language of which people?
questions.f: Spanish explorers borrowed the local word 'canoa' and carried it back to Europe.

questions.q: The 'equator' takes its name from a word meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'aequare' (to make equal): it splits the globe into two equal halves.

questions.q: The word 'horizon' comes from a Greek root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'horizein' (to divide or bound), because it marks the limit of what we can see.

questions.q: 'Latitude' lines on a sea chart tell a sailor how far they are...?
c: North or south of the equator
questions.f: From Latin 'latus' (wide): latitude was easy to find from the Sun, unlike longitude.

questions.q: 'Longitude' lines tell a sailor how far they are...?
c: East or west of a starting line
questions.f: From Latin 'longus' (long): fixing longitude at sea was one of history's hardest problems.

questions.q: Which word means a scientist's careful record of a ship's daily voyage?
questions.f: It is named after the wooden log sailors threw overboard to measure the ship's speed.

questions.q: To 'fathom' a mystery means to understand it. The word first meant to measure the...?
questions.f: Sounding the depth 'fathomed' the sea, so understanding something deeply borrowed the word.

questions.q: 'Sea legs' means the ability to...?
c: Walk steadily on a moving ship
questions.f: It takes a day or two at sea for the brain to adjust and give a sailor their sea legs.

questions.q: The word 'harpoon' comes from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'harpe' (hook), through French; the barbed head is what makes a harpoon hold.

questions.q: A 'lagoon' and a 'lake' share a root meaning...?
questions.f: Both trace back to Latin 'lacus' (basin, pool).

questions.q: 'Aquatic' plants live in water; what does 'semi-aquatic' mean?
c: Living partly in water and partly on land
questions.f: From Latin 'semi' (half): otters, seals, and crocodiles all lead semi-aquatic lives.

questions.q: The word 'reef', when used about a sail, means to...?
c: Reduce the sail's area in strong wind
questions.f: Sailors 'reef' a sail by folding and tying part of it away, spilling some of the wind.

questions.q: An 'atlas' of maps and the Atlantic Ocean share a name from...?
questions.f: Early map books showed Atlas holding up the world, and the name stuck to the collection.

questions.q: The word 'gulf' also gives us the phrase 'a gulf between them', meaning a...?
questions.f: A geographic gulf is a wide opening, so the word came to mean any wide separation.

questions.q: To be 'marooned' means to be...?
c: Left stranded in a lonely place
questions.f: The word traces to escaped islanders called 'maroons', and became a pirate punishment.

questions.q: To 'jettison' something means to...?
questions.f: From Old French 'getaison' (a throwing): the words 'jettison' and 'jetsam' are cousins.

questions.q: A ship described as 'seaworthy' is...?
questions.f: Before any long voyage, a ship must be inspected and declared seaworthy.

questions.q: A 'landlubber' is a...?
c: Person unused to life at sea
questions.f: 'Lubber' is an old word for a clumsy fellow, so it is a gently teasing sailors' nickname.

questions.q: The 'bilge' of a ship is the...?
questions.f: Water always seeps into the bilge, so pumps must run to keep it dry.

questions.q: A 'hold' on a ship is the space used to...?
questions.f: The word comes from 'hollow', describing the great empty belly of the ship.

questions.q: 'Amidships' means...?
c: In the middle of the ship
questions.f: The most comfortable cabins are amidships, where a ship rolls and pitches the least.

questions.q: To go 'aloft' on a sailing ship means to climb...?
questions.f: Sailors sent aloft in a gale worked dozens of metres above a heaving deck.

questions.q: The 'rigging' of a sailing ship is its...?
c: Ropes and lines that work the sails
questions.f: A large square-rigged ship could carry many kilometres of rope in its rigging.

questions.q: A 'lookout' on a ship is the crew member whose job is to...?
questions.f: Even with radar, big ships still post a human lookout in busy or foggy waters.

questions.q: The word 'archipelago' and the word 'pelagic' share a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'pelagos' (open sea), which also gives us 'epipelagic' and 'bathypelagic'.

questions.q: 'Seismic' waves that can trigger a tsunami take their name from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'seismos' (a shaking): an undersea quake shoves the whole water column upward.

questions.q: The 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific is a zone famous for...?
questions.f: Most of the world's tsunamis are born along this restless horseshoe of plate boundaries.

questions.q: A 'volcanic island' such as Iceland or Hawaii is built up from...?
questions.f: Hawaii's Mauna Kea, measured from its seabed base, is taller than Mount Everest.

questions.q: What is 'sea spray' made of?
c: Tiny droplets of seawater carried by wind
questions.f: Salt from sea spray can be found in the air hundreds of kilometres inland.

questions.q: Roughly how deep is the ocean on average, across the whole planet?
questions.f: Though the Mariana Trench plunges nearly 11 km, the ocean averages only about 3,700 metres deep.

questions.q: The slowly spreading Mid-Atlantic Ridge is making which ocean gradually wider?
questions.f: New seafloor forms at the ridge, pushing the Americas and Europe apart a few centimetres a year.

questions.q: Which is the second-deepest ocean trench in the world?
questions.f: The Tonga Trench in the Pacific plunges to over 10,000 metres deep.

questions.q: At deep-sea vents, life makes food from chemicals instead of sunlight. What is this called?
questions.f: Bacteria at vents use chemicals like hydrogen sulfide to build food in total darkness.

questions.q: Which strange animals cluster around deep-sea vents, having no mouth or gut and relying on bacteria inside them?
questions.f: Giant tube worms can grow over two metres tall in the darkness near hot vents.

questions.q: Which is the heaviest bony fish in the ocean, shaped like a giant swimming head?
questions.f: An ocean sunfish, or mola, can weigh more than a small car.

questions.q: How do icefish survive in freezing polar seas without turning to ice inside?
questions.f: Special proteins stop ice crystals from growing in an icefish's blood and body.

questions.q: What is 'marine snow' in the deep ocean?
c: Falling bits of dead matter and waste
questions.f: This constant drift of particles feeds many animals living far below the sunlit surface.

questions.q: What do we call water that is a mix of fresh water and salt water?
questions.f: Brackish water is common in estuaries where rivers empty into the sea.

questions.q: The Coriolis effect makes large ocean currents curve because of Earth's...?
questions.f: As the planet spins, currents in the north curve right and those in the south curve left.

questions.q: Which mammal holds the record for the deepest dive, plunging nearly 3 kilometres down?
questions.f: Cuvier's beaked whales can stay underwater for over two hours on a single dive.

questions.q: Which tiny deep-sea fish is thought to be the most numerous vertebrate on Earth?
questions.f: Bristlemouths are small glowing fish, and there may be quadrillions of them in the deep sea.

questions.q: When a whale dies and sinks, feeding deep-sea life for years, this event is called a...?
questions.f: A single whale fall can support a whole community of deep-sea creatures for decades.

questions.q: How does a chambered nautilus control whether it floats or sinks?
c: By adjusting gas in its shell chambers
questions.f: The nautilus pumps gas and liquid between the sealed chambers of its spiral shell.

questions.q: Living light in the sea comes from a chemical reaction between luciferin and a helper called...?
questions.f: The enzyme luciferase speeds up the reaction that makes cold, glowing light with almost no heat.

questions.q: The 'electric eel' is not really an eel at all. It is actually a type of...?
questions.f: An electric eel can deliver a strong shock to stun prey or defend itself.

questions.q: How do sea turtles find the very beach where they hatched, years and oceans later?
questions.f: Turtles seem to read the beach's unique magnetic 'signature' like a home address.

questions.q: Which cold current off western South America powers one of the world's richest fishing grounds?
questions.f: The Humboldt Current drives upwelling that brings up nutrients feeding huge shoals of fish.

questions.q: The 'midnight zone', below about 1,000 metres, has which scientific name?
questions.f: In the bathypelagic zone the only light comes from animals that make their own.

questions.q: What do scientists call the layer where water density changes sharply with depth?
questions.f: The pycnocline can trap animals, sound, and even submarines above or below it.

questions.q: Coral reefs are built mostly from which hard mineral that polyps take from seawater?
questions.f: Calcium carbonate is the same mineral found in chalk and in many seashells.

questions.q: How can you tell a dugong from its cousin the manatee?
c: A dugong has a dolphin-like fluked tail
questions.f: A manatee's tail is a rounded paddle, while a dugong's is split into two flukes.

questions.q: European eels travel thousands of kilometres to breed in which mysterious sea?
questions.f: For a long time no one knew where eels bred until their trip to the Sargasso was discovered.

questions.q: The blue-green sparkle in breaking night waves is usually made by glowing...?
questions.f: These tiny plankton flash light when the water around them is disturbed.

questions.q: Which of these fish can keep its body warmer than the surrounding seawater?
questions.f: A few fast hunters, like the great white and tuna, are partly warm-bodied for extra speed.

questions.q: Which sense organ, a line of tiny receptors along a fish's side, detects movement and vibrations?
questions.f: The lateral line lets fish in a school turn together as if they were one body.

questions.q: The Japanese spider crab is the largest arthropod by leg span, reaching roughly...?
questions.f: Though its legs span a car's width, the spider crab is a gentle, slow-moving scavenger.

questions.q: Which land animal is the largest arthropod on land and can crack open coconuts?
questions.f: The coconut crab can climb trees and grow to nearly a metre across its legs.

questions.q: Which sea creature has the largest brain of any animal on Earth?
questions.f: A sperm whale's brain can weigh around 8 kilograms, the heaviest of any animal.

questions.q: A remora rides on a shark, eating scraps without harming it. What is this one-sided relationship called?
questions.f: In commensalism one animal benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed.

questions.q: What do we call a swirling, rotating ring of water that spins off from a large ocean current?
questions.f: Ocean eddies can be tens of kilometres wide and carry heat and life across the sea.

questions.q: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch collects inside which rotating current system?
questions.f: Slow-spinning gyres gather floating plastic into vast, patchy zones of debris.

questions.q: What do we call the science of measuring the depth and shape of the ocean floor?
questions.f: Bathymetric maps reveal underwater mountains, canyons, and plains we cannot see from above.

questions.q: The Atlantic Ocean is slowly getting wider while the Pacific Ocean is slowly shrinking.
questions.f: Seafloor spreading widens the Atlantic, while the Pacific narrows as its edges dive under continents.

questions.q: Most of the salt dissolved in seawater is made of sodium and which other element?
questions.f: Sodium and chloride together form common salt, the same kind we sprinkle on food.

questions.q: How do octopuses and squid bite their food?
questions.f: Their beak looks and works much like a parrot's and is one of their few hard parts.

questions.q: Which ambush fish 'walks' along the sea floor on leg-like fins and lures prey with a fishing rod?
questions.f: A frogfish can gulp prey in a fraction of a second, faster than the eye can follow.

questions.q: Seals, sea lions, and walruses belong to a group called 'pinnipeds', which means...?
questions.f: 'Pinniped' comes from Latin words for 'fin' and 'foot', describing their flipper limbs.

questions.q: Which deep-sea creature has an enormous, loose mouth like a pelican's pouch?
questions.f: The gulper eel's huge mouth lets it swallow prey much larger than its thin body.

questions.q: Which small shrimp snaps its claw so fast it makes a bubble that can stun nearby prey?
questions.f: The snapping bubble collapses with a loud pop and a tiny flash of light and heat.

questions.q: Which sea is the saltiest of the open seas because of its heat and high evaporation?
questions.f: The hot, dry climate around the Red Sea makes its water especially salty.

questions.q: When hunted, small fish like sardines swirl tightly together into a defensive sphere called a...?
questions.f: Swirling in a bait ball confuses predators, making it hard to pick out a single fish.

questions.q: Which deep-sea fish has a see-through head with tube-shaped eyes that look straight up?
questions.f: The barreleye can rotate its eyes to look up for prey and then forward to eat it.

questions.q: The waxy substance once taken from the sperm whale's head, used to make candles, is called...?
questions.f: Whalers prized spermaceti oil, which may help the whale focus sound for echolocation.

questions.q: The Portuguese man o' war looks like a single jellyfish, but it is really...?
questions.f: A man o' war is made of many specialised animals living and working together as one.

questions.q: An iceberg is frozen freshwater from a glacier, but 'pack ice' forms directly from frozen...?
questions.f: As seawater freezes, most of the salt is squeezed out, leaving fairly fresh sea ice.

questions.q: The study called 'cetology' focuses on which group of animals?
questions.f: 'Cetology' comes from the Greek 'ketos', an old word for a great sea creature.

questions.q: The root 'therm', found in 'thermocline', means...?
questions.f: 'Therm' comes from a Greek word for heat, as also seen in 'thermometer'.

questions.q: The root 'halo-', as in 'halocline', refers to...?
questions.f: 'Halo' comes from the Greek 'hals', meaning salt; a halocline is a salt-change layer.

questions.q: The ending '-cline' in 'thermocline' and 'halocline' describes a...?
questions.f: '-cline' comes from a Greek word meaning to lean or slope.

questions.q: The word 'bioluminescence' breaks down to mean...?
questions.f: 'Bio' means life and 'lumen' means light, so it is light made by living things.

questions.q: The word 'estuary' is built from the Latin 'aestus', which means...?
questions.f: From Latin 'aestus' (tide, surge): an estuary is a river mouth swept twice daily by the tides.

questions.q: The word 'plankton' comes from a root meaning...?
questions.f: Plankton are named for the way they drift wherever the currents carry them.

questions.q: The word 'nekton', for free-swimming sea animals, comes from a root meaning...?
questions.f: Unlike drifting plankton, nekton such as fish and squid actively swim where they choose.

questions.q: A salmon is 'anadromous', living in the sea but breeding in rivers. The root 'dromos' means...?
questions.f: 'Ana' means up and 'dromos' means running, so the fish 'runs up' rivers to spawn.

questions.q: 'Diurnal' tides happen once each...?
questions.f: 'Diurnal' comes from the Latin 'dies', meaning day.

questions.q: 'Semidiurnal' tides occur how often each day?
questions.f: 'Semi' means half, so a semidiurnal cycle brings two highs and two lows a day.

questions.q: The word 'archipelago' first named which specific body of water?
questions.f: 'Archipelago' meant 'chief sea', the Aegean, before it came to mean any group of islands.

questions.q: An 'isthmus' is a narrow strip of land that connects two larger areas across...?
questions.f: 'Isthmus' comes from a Greek word for a narrow passage, like the Isthmus of Panama.

questions.q: A 'fjord' is a deep, narrow sea inlet that was carved out by...?
questions.f: 'Fjord' comes from an Old Norse word; Norway is famous for its steep glacial fjords.

questions.q: The word 'maelstrom' means a powerful...?
questions.f: 'Maelstrom' comes from Dutch words meaning 'grinding stream'.

questions.q: Sailors call the calm belt near the equator, where winds often die, the...?
questions.f: Sailing ships could be stuck in the windless doldrums for days or even weeks.

questions.q: On a ship, the 'leeward' side is the side that is...?
questions.f: Sailors say 'leeward' for the calmer, downwind side, the opposite of 'windward'.

questions.q: The 'windward' side of a ship or island is the side that...?
questions.f: Storms hit the windward side first, so it often gets the most rain and waves.

questions.q: In sea law, 'flotsam' means wreckage or cargo that...?
questions.f: Flotsam floats away by accident, while jetsam is deliberately tossed overboard.

questions.q: The word 'jetsam' means goods that were deliberately...?
questions.f: 'Jetsam' comes from 'jettison', meaning to throw cargo overboard to lighten a ship.

questions.q: An 'aquanaut' is a person who lives and works...?
questions.f: 'Aqua' means water and '-naut' means sailor, so an aquanaut is an underwater explorer.

questions.q: Sonar works by sending out sound and then measuring the returning...?
questions.f: By timing how long the echo takes, sonar can map the seabed and find shoals of fish.

questions.q: In words like 'bathysphere' and 'bathyscaphe', the root 'bathy' means...?
questions.f: 'Bathy' comes from the Greek 'bathys', meaning deep, used for deep-diving craft.

questions.q: The '-naut' in 'aquanaut' and 'astronaut' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Nautes' meant sailor, so an astronaut is really a 'star-sailor'.

questions.q: A 'demersal' fish, unlike a pelagic one, lives mainly near the...?
questions.f: Demersal fish such as flatfish and cod feed close to the bottom of the sea.

questions.q: The sea anemone is named after a wind-flower whose name means 'daughter of the...'?
questions.f: 'Anemos' is the Greek word for wind, and the anemone flower nods in the breeze.

questions.q: Krill, the tiny food of great whales, are a kind of...?
questions.f: 'Krill' comes from a Norwegian word for tiny young fish, but krill are shrimp-like crustaceans.

questions.q: Baleen whales are also called 'mysticetes', a name hinting they are 'moustached...'?
questions.f: Their fringed baleen plates hang like a giant moustache used to strain tiny food.

questions.q: Toothed whales are called 'odontocetes'; the root 'odonto' means...?
questions.f: 'Odonto' is Greek for tooth, as in the word 'orthodontist'.

questions.q: The free-swimming bell stage of a jellyfish is called a 'medusa', named after a mythical figure with...?
questions.f: Medusa of Greek myth had snakes for hair, like the trailing tentacles of a jellyfish.

questions.q: The word 'polyp', as in a coral polyp, comes from words meaning 'many...'?
questions.f: 'Poly' means many and 'pous' means foot, describing the tentacle-ringed little animals.

questions.q: The tiny, hugely abundant plankton called a 'copepod' has a name meaning '...-foot'?
questions.f: From Greek 'kope' (oar) + 'pous' (foot): copepods row through the sea and may be the most numerous animals on Earth.

questions.q: In 'phytoplankton', the part 'phyto' means...?
questions.f: 'Phyto' comes from the Greek for plant; phytoplankton make food and oxygen from sunlight.

questions.q: The 'subtidal' zone is the part of the shore that is...?
c: Always underwater, below the low tide line
questions.f: 'Sub' means below, so the subtidal zone stays submerged even at the lowest tide.

questions.q: The 'intertidal' zone is the stretch of shore found between the high and low...?
questions.f: Intertidal animals like barnacles must survive both underwater and in open air each day.

questions.q: Water described as 'hypersaline' is...?
questions.f: 'Hyper' means over or excess, so hypersaline water is saltier than normal seawater.

questions.q: Octopuses and squid are 'cephalopods', a name meaning '...-foot'?
questions.f: 'Kephale' means head and 'pous' means foot; their arms attach right to their heads.

questions.q: Snails and sea slugs are 'gastropods', a name that literally means '...-foot'?
questions.f: 'Gaster' means stomach; gastropods glide along on a single muscular belly-foot.

questions.q: Despite its name, the horseshoe crab is most closely related to which group of animals?
questions.f: Its body plan has barely changed in 450 million years, long before the first dinosaurs.

questions.q: Which bay boasts the highest tides in the world, with a range of about 16 metres?
questions.f: The bay's funnel shape and length let each tide slosh in rhythm, amplifying it enormously.

questions.q: Which jawless fish defends itself by turning the water around it into thick slime?
questions.f: One hagfish can fill a bucket with slime in seconds, choking the gills of an attacker.

questions.q: The crabeater seal of Antarctica actually eats almost entirely which food?
questions.f: Its teeth interlock into a sieve for straining krill, and there are no crabs in its range.

questions.q: Which venomous sea snail hunts fish by firing a harpoon-like tooth?
questions.f: A painkiller drug many times stronger than morphine was developed from cone snail venom.

questions.q: What is the closest living land relative of whales and dolphins?
questions.f: Whales and hippos share an ancestor that lived around 55 million years ago.

questions.q: Which animal makes the loudest sound of any creature on Earth?
questions.f: A sperm whale's echolocating click can top 230 decibels underwater, sharp as a rifle crack.

questions.q: Which mammal is believed to be the longest-lived, with individuals passing 200 years?
questions.f: Old stone harpoon tips found in living bowheads first hinted at their extreme age.

questions.q: The right whale got its unfortunate name because whalers thought it was the 'right' whale to...?
questions.f: It swam slowly and floated when killed, and today it is among the rarest of all whales.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the fatty 'melon' in a dolphin's forehead?
questions.f: The melon acts like an acoustic lens, sharpening clicks into a narrow scanning beam.

questions.q: How do seabirds such as albatrosses cope with drinking salt water?
c: A gland above the beak drips out brine
questions.f: You can often see a salty drop hanging from a seabird's bill after it drinks.

questions.q: Which seabird can stay airborne for weeks and cannot take off from the water's surface?
questions.f: Its feathers are not waterproof, so a frigatebird snatches food without ever landing.

questions.q: Which bird holds the diving record among all birds, plunging beyond 500 metres?
questions.f: Emperor penguins can stay under for more than 20 minutes on the deepest dives.

questions.q: How does an albatross fly thousands of kilometres while barely flapping its wings?
c: It rides wind speed differences above the waves
questions.f: This trick is called dynamic soaring, and it lets one bird circle the globe in weeks.

questions.q: What can scientists learn from the layered wax plug in a whale's ear canal?
questions.f: Each band records months of the whale's life, even revealing periods of stress.

questions.q: Which small deep-sea animal bores into sunken whale bones to feed?
questions.f: Nicknamed 'zombie worms', they have no mouth and rely on bacteria to digest bone fat.

questions.q: The White Cliffs of Dover are made almost entirely from the shells of ancient...?
questions.f: Chalk is built from countless microscopic plates and shells that rained down on an ancient seabed.

questions.q: Which single-celled ocean drifters build tiny, intricate shells out of glassy silica?
questions.f: Diatom shells are so fine that their fossil dust is used as a gentle industrial filter.

questions.q: What are the potato-sized lumps of metal-rich rock scattered across parts of the abyssal plain?
questions.f: They grow just millimetres per million years, which makes any mining of them permanent.

questions.q: The scalding chimneys at some hydrothermal vents are nicknamed...?
questions.f: Water gushing from them can reach 400 C without boiling, because the pressure is so great.

questions.q: Which vent-dwelling worm can tolerate some of the hottest conditions known for a complex animal?
questions.f: The Pompeii worm lives with its tail in water near 80 C and its head in far cooler water.

questions.q: Which deep-sea snail armours its foot with scales containing iron?
questions.f: It is the only known animal to build iron sulfide minerals into its own body armour.

questions.q: A 'sea squirt', or tunicate, is surprisingly closely related to which group?
questions.f: Its tadpole-like larva has a stiffening rod along its back, the hallmark of our own family tree.

questions.q: The animal group containing jellyfish, corals, and anemones is named from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'knide' (nettle): cnidarians all sting, and 'cnidarian' begins with a silent C.

questions.q: The microscopic stinging capsule that fires from a jellyfish tentacle is called a...?
questions.f: It fires in under a millisecond, one of the fastest movements known in all of biology.

questions.q: Which clam, dredged off Iceland in 2006, was found to be over 500 years old?
questions.f: Nicknamed Ming, its age was counted from more than 500 growth rings in its shell.

questions.q: Deep-sea black corals are remarkable for being able to live for how long?
questions.f: Some deep black coral colonies have been dated at over 4,000 years old.

questions.q: Which region, spanning Indonesia and the Philippines, holds the greatest variety of reef life on Earth?
questions.f: Over 600 coral species live in the Coral Triangle, more than anywhere else in the world.

questions.q: What is a 'tidal bore'?
c: A wave of incoming tide that surges up a river
questions.f: On China's Qiantang River the bore can run several metres high and outrun a person.

questions.q: The stormy belt of westerly winds near 40 degrees south is nicknamed the...?
questions.f: Sailing ships once rode the Roaring Forties eastward, and modern round-the-world racers still do.

questions.q: Which wind belt did sailing ships rely on to cross the Atlantic westward?
questions.f: They were named 'trade' winds because reliable trade routes depended on them.

questions.q: The Northwest Passage is a sea route through the Arctic that links which two oceans?
questions.f: Explorers searched for it for centuries; melting sea ice has recently made it navigable.

questions.q: Which is the roughest and stormiest stretch of sea a ship can cross?
questions.f: Between South America and Antarctica, no land blocks the waves, so they circle the globe unchecked.

questions.q: Which canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean with the Red Sea?
questions.f: It cut the sea journey from Europe to India by thousands of kilometres, avoiding Africa entirely.

questions.q: The wind-force scale used at sea, running from calm to hurricane, is named after which figure?
questions.f: Beaufort defined each force by what the sails and the sea's surface actually looked like.

questions.q: Which navigational instrument measures the angle between a star and the horizon?
questions.f: It is called a sextant because its arc is one sixth of a circle, exactly 60 degrees.

questions.q: The magnetic compass used for navigation was first developed in which country?
questions.f: Chinese navigators were using magnetic compasses at sea by around the 11th century.

questions.q: The line of zero longitude, from which all sea charts are measured, runs through which place?
questions.f: Nations agreed on Greenwich in 1884, partly because most sea charts already used it.

questions.q: Which ship carried Charles Darwin on the voyage that shaped his ideas about life?
questions.f: Darwin was seasick for much of the five-year voyage, yet it changed science forever.
