questions.q: Which vessel became famous when it was crushed by pack ice, stranding Shackleton's crew in 1915?
questions.f: Every one of the 28 men survived, and the wreck was finally found in 2022, superbly preserved.

questions.q: What is a 'diving bell', used long before modern equipment?
c: An air-filled chamber lowered to divers
A warning bell on a buoy
questions.f: Air trapped inside let divers work below the surface, breathing from a bubble of their own.

questions.q: Which flag, showing a skull and crossbones, was flown by pirates?
questions.f: Real pirates used many different designs, hoping their flag would scare ships into surrendering.

questions.q: In sailors' folklore, 'Davy Jones's locker' means...?
questions.f: To be sent to Davy Jones's locker was to be lost at sea, a legend at least 300 years old.

questions.q: Which fish is prepared as the Japanese dish fugu, requiring a specially licensed chef?
questions.f: Parts of the pufferfish carry tetrodotoxin, so chefs train for years to prepare it safely.

questions.q: The jelly-like laboratory growing medium called agar is made from...?
questions.f: Agar came into science through a cook's recipe, and it still grows bacteria in labs worldwide.

questions.q: The dark seaweed sheet wrapped around sushi rolls is called...?
questions.f: Nori production once failed unpredictably until a British scientist worked out its hidden life cycle.

questions.q: Off Newfoundland, the Grand Banks became famous for a fishery that collapsed in 1992. Which fish?
questions.f: Cod were once so thick that sailors claimed a basket lowered over the side came up full.

questions.q: Which sea creature's blood is used to test that medicines and vaccines are free of bacteria?
questions.f: Its copper-based blue blood clots instantly around bacterial traces, an alarm no lab could match.

questions.q: Which sea creature inspired the ridged edges now added to some wind turbine blades?
questions.f: The bumps along a humpback's flippers, called tubercles, smooth the flow of water and air.

questions.q: A tsunami in the open ocean may be less than a metre high and pass unnoticed by a ship.
questions.f: Its energy is spread through the whole water column, and only piles up on reaching shallow water.

questions.q: Sea level is rising partly because warming seawater expands as it heats up.
questions.f: Thermal expansion accounts for a large share of the rise, alongside melting ice on land.

questions.q: The word 'cnidarian' begins with a silent letter, and the group is named after a stinging plant.
questions.f: From Greek 'knide' (nettle), the C is silent, and every cnidarian carries stinging cells.

questions.q: Coral reefs also exist in cold, deep water far from any sunlight.
questions.f: Cold-water reefs off Norway thrive in darkness, catching food from the current instead of using algae.

questions.q: The word 'baleen' comes from a Latin root meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'balaena' (whale), which also survives in the name of the balaenid whale family.

questions.q: The name 'killer whale' is thought to be a flipped version of an older name meaning...?
questions.f: Whalers saw orcas attacking large whales, and the phrase 'whale killer' gradually swapped around.

questions.q: The name 'beluga' comes from a Russian word meaning...?
questions.f: Its pale skin earned the name, and its chirping calls earned it the nickname 'sea canary'.

questions.q: The word 'narwhal' is built from old northern roots meaning 'whale' plus...?
questions.f: From Old Norse 'nar' (corpse), likely for its pale, blotchy skin, said to resemble a drowned sailor.

questions.q: The colour name 'sepia' comes from the Greek word for which animal?
questions.f: Artists once wrote and painted with real cuttlefish ink, and the brown shade kept the animal's name.

questions.q: The pigment name 'ultramarine' literally means...?
questions.f: The precious blue stone lapis lazuli was shipped from beyond the sea, making it costlier than gold.

questions.q: Roughly two thirds of an octopus's nerve cells are found where?
questions.f: Each arm can explore and grab on its own, so an octopus almost thinks with its limbs.

questions.q: An octopus's suckers can do something surprising besides gripping. What?
questions.f: An octopus reaching blindly into a crevice can taste a crab before it ever sees one.

questions.q: What is unusual about the shape of a cuttlefish's pupil?
c: It is shaped like a W
questions.f: Cuttlefish are colour-blind, yet the odd pupil may let them read colour from how light bends.

questions.q: Which is the largest species of octopus in the world?
questions.f: An arm span of over four metres has been recorded, yet it can squeeze through a small hole.

questions.q: The 'dumbo octopus' of the deep sea earned its nickname from...?
questions.f: It flaps those fins to hover, and it lives deeper than almost any other octopus.

questions.q: Why does a blobfish look saggy and strange in photographs?
c: Its body only holds shape under deep pressure
It has no bones at all
questions.f: Down where it lives, a blobfish is a perfectly normal-looking fish.

questions.q: What does a remora use to hitch a ride on a shark?
c: A suction disc that was once a fin
questions.f: Its front dorsal fin evolved into a ridged plate that grips like a suction cup.

questions.q: The 'boxer crab' defends itself in an unusual way. How?
c: It waves a stinging anemone in each claw
questions.f: The crab gets weapons, and the anemones get carried to fresh feeding spots.

questions.q: What does a 'decorator crab' do?
c: Sticks living sponges and algae onto its shell
questions.f: Its shell is covered in hooked bristles that work rather like natural Velcro.

questions.q: How does a kelp plant stay anchored against the pull of waves?
questions.f: A holdfast grips rock but takes in no food, since the kelp feeds through its whole surface.

questions.q: About how far can a flying fish glide above the waves in one leap?
questions.f: With repeated tail flicks at the surface, a flying fish can string glides together for 400 metres.

questions.q: How does a sea otter carry stones and food while swimming?
c: In loose pouches of skin under its forelimbs
questions.f: An otter often keeps a favourite anvil stone in that pouch for cracking shells later.

questions.q: Manatees cope with their gritty diet by having teeth that...?
c: Move forward and are replaced through life
questions.f: Worn front teeth drop out while new ones push forward, a rare 'conveyor belt' of molars.

questions.q: The pale patches on a gray whale's skin are largely made up of...?
questions.f: A single gray whale can carry hundreds of kilograms of hitchhiking barnacles.

questions.q: What have researchers discovered about the calls of different orca pods?
c: Each pod has its own dialect
questions.f: Calves learn their family's dialect, so an orca's accent reveals which clan it belongs to.

questions.q: Which seal can hold its breath the longest, staying down for over an hour under Antarctic ice?
questions.f: It gnaws breathing holes in the ice with its teeth to keep its own private air supply open.

questions.q: Which sea creature is called a 'sea butterfly' and is threatened by acidifying water?
questions.f: Their paper-thin shells are among the first things to dissolve as seawater turns more acidic.

questions.q: Great milky-white blooms visible from space are made by which shelled plankton?
questions.f: Their chalky plates scatter light, turning thousands of square kilometres of sea a pale turquoise.

questions.q: What is the ocean's 'biological pump'?
c: Sinking life that carries carbon to the deep
questions.f: Without this steady rain of carbon into the deep, the air would hold far more carbon dioxide.

questions.q: How do whales help fertilise the ocean's surface waters?
c: They feed deep and release nutrients near the surface
questions.f: Scientists call it the whale pump, and it helps plankton bloom where whales gather.

questions.q: Which sea is the world's largest area of brackish water, only lightly salty?
questions.f: So many rivers pour into the shallow Baltic that its northern end is nearly fresh.

questions.q: Where does the coldest, densest water in the world ocean form?
questions.f: Antarctic Bottom Water sinks to the seafloor and creeps north for centuries along the abyss.

questions.q: Which glowing bay in Puerto Rico is one of the brightest bioluminescent sites on Earth?
questions.f: Millions of dinoflagellates per litre make every paddle stroke flash electric blue.

questions.q: What is the main worry about mining the deep-sea floor for metals?
c: It destroys habitats that recover extremely slowly
questions.f: Tracks left by a test mining machine in the 1970s were still clearly visible decades later.

questions.q: Which fish famously has the largest teeth relative to its body size of any fish?
questions.f: Its teeth are so long that special sockets in its skull make room for them when it shuts its mouth.

questions.q: Which of these best describes a 'brine pool' on the deep seafloor?
c: A dense, extra-salty lake under the sea
questions.f: So salty it will not mix with the water above, a brine pool even has its own shoreline.

questions.q: A 'mesophotic' coral reef is one found at which depth?
c: Roughly 30 to 150 metres, in dim light
questions.f: From Greek roots for 'middle light', these twilight reefs may act as refuges for shallow species.

questions.q: Which whale-sized shark's mouth can be over a metre wide yet takes only tiny prey?
questions.f: The megamouth was completely unknown to science until one was accidentally caught in 1976.

questions.q: A ship's speed in knots and a nautical mile are both tied to the size of the Earth.
questions.f: A nautical mile equals one minute of latitude, so one knot is one minute of latitude per hour.

questions.q: Antarctic icefish have almost colourless blood because they lack red blood pigment.
questions.f: In their icy, oxygen-rich water they get by with clear blood, unique among vertebrates.

questions.q: Sound bends toward layers where it travels more slowly, which is why deep sound channels exist.
questions.f: This bending traps whale calls and lets them travel for thousands of kilometres.

questions.q: The word 'admiral' entered European languages from an Arabic phrase meaning...?
questions.f: From Arabic 'amir al-bahr': the Latin ending was added later by Mediterranean sailors.

questions.q: The word 'monsoon' comes from an Arabic word meaning...?
questions.f: From Arabic 'mawsim' (season): the wind reverses with the seasons, which traders relied on for centuries.

questions.q: The word 'hurricane' came into English from the language of which people?
questions.f: Their storm spirit was called Hurakan; 'canoe', 'hammock', and 'barbecue' came from the same language family.

questions.q: The word 'catamaran' comes from a Tamil term meaning...?
questions.f: From Tamil 'kattumaram': European sailors met these lashed-log craft off the coast of India.

questions.q: The word 'yacht' came from a Dutch word meaning...?
questions.f: Dutch 'jacht' boats were built to chase down pirates before they became pleasure craft.

questions.q: The word 'cruise' comes from a Dutch word meaning...?
questions.f: From Dutch 'kruisen' (to cross): warships once cruised back and forth across shipping lanes.

questions.q: The word 'atoll' entered English from the language of which island nation?
questions.f: From Dhivehi 'atolhu': the Maldives are made almost entirely of coral atolls.

questions.q: The word 'hammock', used by generations of sailors, came from which language family?
questions.f: Columbus's crews saw woven hanging beds in the Caribbean and adopted both the bed and the word.

questions.q: A 'league', the old sea distance in Jules Verne's title, is roughly how far?
questions.f: 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea' measures the journey's length, not its depth.

questions.q: A ship's 'tonnage' originally measured how many of what it could carry?
questions.f: From 'tun', a large cask: tonnage began as a count of barrels, not a weight in tonnes.

questions.q: The word 'skipper', for a boat's captain, comes from a Dutch word meaning...?
questions.f: From Dutch 'schipper': English borrowed a whole fleet of sea words from Dutch sailors.

questions.q: The 'bitter end' of a rope originally meant the end that was...?
c: Fastened inside the ship at the bitts
questions.f: Reaching the bitter end meant no cable was left to pay out, and the ship could drop no deeper.

questions.q: For a sailing ship, being 'taken aback' originally meant that the wind had...?
c: Blown the sails backwards against the mast
questions.f: A ship taken aback could stop dead or even be driven backwards, which is why the phrase means shocked.

questions.q: The phrase 'above board' comes from anything visible above a ship's...?
questions.f: Cargo or dealings hidden below the boards were suspect; honest business happened in plain view.

questions.q: 'Three sheets to the wind' refers to loose ropes that left a ship...?
questions.f: A 'sheet' is a rope controlling a sail; with three flapping free, the ship staggered like a sailor.

questions.q: The phrase 'the seven seas' is best understood today as meaning...?
questions.f: Different ages listed different sevens, so it has long been a poetic way of saying 'everywhere at sea'.

questions.q: 'Salvage' at sea means to...?
c: Rescue a ship or its cargo
questions.f: From Latin 'salvare' (to save): salvage crews can claim a reward for saving an abandoned vessel.

questions.q: A ship described as 'derelict' has been...?
questions.f: From Latin 'derelinquere' (to forsake entirely): a derelict drifting hull is a hazard to other ships.

questions.q: The order 'pipe down' came from a signal on a ship's...?
questions.f: The final pipe of the day sent the crew below decks for silence, so 'pipe down' came to mean be quiet.

questions.q: The 'gunwale', the upper edge of a boat's side, was named because it once supported...?
questions.f: Pronounced 'gunnel', it is the plank where a ship's guns were once mounted.

questions.q: A 'sampan', the small Asian boat, has a name meaning...?
questions.f: From Chinese roots for 'three planks', describing how simply the earliest ones were built.

questions.q: The word 'anchor' traces back to a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'ankura' (hook): the same root gives us 'angle' and even 'ankle'.

questions.q: A 'clipper' ship, famous for carrying tea and wool, was named for the way it...?
questions.f: Clippers raced home with the new tea crop, and the fastest could top 20 knots.

questions.q: The Pharos of Alexandria, one of the ancient wonders, was an early...?
questions.f: It stood for over 1,500 years, and its name still means 'lighthouse' in several languages.

questions.q: The 'Bermuda Triangle' became famous through 20th-century magazine stories about...?
c: Ships and planes said to vanish there
questions.f: Careful checks show no more losses there than in other busy, storm-prone stretches of sea.

questions.q: In diving, 'the bends' is a sickness caused by...?
c: Gas bubbles forming in the body on fast ascent
questions.f: Divers rise slowly, or sit in a pressure chamber, to let the dissolved gas leave safely.

questions.q: A survey ship's weighted sounding line, an 1875 depth reading that astonished Victorian science, and a name later given to the sea's lowest spot converge on which vessel?
questions.f: Her 1872-76 voyage founded oceanography, and the Challenger Deep still carries her name.

questions.q: A geochemist's 1987 essay, a warning that the Atlantic's overturning might stall, and the phrase 'the great ocean conveyor' converge on which scientist?
questions.f: Broecker's conveyor image warned that Earth's climate can lurch rather than drift.

questions.q: A gelatinous body with no swim bladder, footage shot at 8,336 metres in 2022, and a depth close to the theoretical limit for any fish converge on which animal?
questions.f: Below roughly 8,400 m a fish's cells could no longer hold seawater out, so none live deeper.

questions.q: Below the 'carbonate compensation depth', shells and coral fragments falling from above will...?
questions.f: Below the CCD, roughly 4-5 km deep, cold high-pressure water dissolves calcium carbonate faster than it arrives.

questions.q: When all land was joined as the supercontinent Pangaea, it was surrounded by a single vast ocean called...?
questions.f: 'Panthalassa' means 'all sea'; the smaller Tethys Sea lay in a bay along Pangaea's eastern edge.

questions.q: A current with no continent in its path, a flow greater than every river on Earth combined, and the reason Antarctica froze over converge on which current?
questions.f: By walling Antarctica off from warm water about 34 million years ago, it helped build the ice sheet.

questions.q: The small but deadly blue-ringed octopus defends itself with which powerful toxin?
questions.f: The same tetrodotoxin is found in pufferfish; a single blue-ringed octopus carries enough to be dangerous to humans.

questions.q: The coelacanth, thought extinct for 66 million years, was famously rediscovered alive in 1938 off which country?
questions.f: Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted the strange fish in a trawler's catch near East London, South Africa.

questions.q: A rising spiral of bubbles, a coordinated lunge up through the middle, and a trick spreading between individuals in the Gulf of Maine converge on which behaviour?
questions.f: Humpbacks learn it from each other, making it one of the clearest cases of animal culture.

questions.q: The nightly rise and dawn descent of countless small sea animals, the largest migration on Earth, is known as...?
questions.f: 'Diel' means daily; these animals hide in the dark deep by day and rise to feed near the surface at night.

questions.q: The mantis shrimp has one of nature's most complex eyes, with roughly how many types of colour receptor?
questions.f: Humans have three colour receptors; the mantis shrimp's dozen-plus may let it process colour with less brainpower.

questions.q: A jelly barely 4 millimetres across, a life cycle that can be run in reverse under stress, and cells that turn back into an earlier body form converge on which claim?
c: It may never die of old age
questions.f: Turritopsis dohrnii reverts to its polyp stage and starts over, in theory without limit.

questions.q: In deep-sea anglerfish, the tiny male survives by doing what to the much larger female?
questions.f: The dwarf male latches on and their tissues merge, so he becomes a lifelong attached mate and sperm source.

questions.q: A single night after a spring full moon, water thickened by pink and orange bundles, and whole reefs acting in perfect unison converge on which event?
questions.f: Corals cannot move to find partners, so they all release at once and let the currents do the rest.

questions.q: A gas given off by stressed plankton, particles that seed droplets in the air above the sea, and the sharp tang people call the smell of the seaside converge on which effect?
questions.f: That bracing seaside smell is largely dimethyl sulfide, and it helps build marine clouds.

questions.q: A shark recorded thousands of kilometres up the Amazon, kidneys that retune to fresh water, and a reputation for shallow, murky estuaries converge on which species?
questions.f: Few sharks can survive the switch; the bull shark simply adjusts how much salt it keeps.

questions.q: Megalodon, the largest shark that ever lived, is known to science almost entirely from its fossil...?
questions.f: Sharks have cartilage skeletons that rarely fossilize, but megalodon's teeth could be over 17 cm long.

questions.q: Discovered in 2021, the kitefin shark earned which record?
questions.f: Its belly glows with blue-green light, giving it a soft outline that hides it from predators below.

questions.q: The 'SOFAR channel' lets whale calls travel across whole oceans because it is a layer where sound...?
c: Travels at its slowest, so it bends back and stays trapped
questions.f: Sound rays bend toward this slow layer instead of escaping, so a call can carry for thousands of kilometres.

questions.q: Calls pitched near 10 to 40 hertz, songs that have been sliding lower in pitch for decades, and a voice that can cross a whole ocean basin converge on which animal?
questions.f: Their calls are so deep that people feel them rather than hear them.

questions.q: To sleep safely at night, some parrotfish surround themselves with a self-made...?
questions.f: The slime cocoon masks their scent from night hunters and may block biting parasites.

questions.q: Some sea stars can regrow an entire new body from just one severed...?
questions.f: In the 'comet' form, a single arm with a piece of the central disc slowly sprouts a whole new star.

questions.q: The deep-sea cephalopod Vampyroteuthis infernalis has a Latin name meaning 'vampire squid from...'?
questions.f: Despite the fearsome name, it is a gentle drifter that feeds on marine snow, not blood.

questions.q: The ocean sunfish (mola) holds which reproductive record among vertebrates?
c: Most eggs, up to about 300 million
questions.f: A female mola can carry hundreds of millions of tiny eggs, more than any other backboned animal.

questions.q: The 'yeti crab' near deep-sea vents grows and 'farms' colonies of bacteria on its hairy...?
questions.f: It waves its bristly arms over the vent flow to feed the bacteria, then eats them like a living garden.

questions.q: At the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the water pressure is roughly how many times that at the surface?
questions.f: That is over a tonne pressing on every square centimetre, yet snailfish and amphipods still live there.

questions.q: Red light gone within 20 metres, orange soon after, and a diver's cut that appears dark green converge on which fact about seawater?
questions.f: Only blue survives to a few hundred metres, which is why the open sea looks blue.

questions.q: The stoplight loosejaw is a rare deep-sea fish that produces which colour of light most others cannot even see?
questions.f: Its hidden red 'searchlight' lets it spot prey that are blind to red, like using invisible night-vision.

questions.q: An extinct volcano that never broke the surface, currents forced upward around its flanks, and a gathering of fish that draws distant trawlers converge on which feature?
questions.f: There may be over 100,000 seamounts, and each is an isolated island of deep-sea life.

questions.q: A seamount with a curiously flat top, planed off by ancient waves before it sank, is called a...?
questions.f: Guyots are named after 19th-century geographer Arnold Guyot; their flat tops mark old, wave-cut sea level.

questions.q: A sudden, towering wall of water that appears without warning in the open sea, not from an earthquake, is a...?
questions.f: Once dismissed as sailors' tales, a rogue wave over 25 m high was finally measured off Norway in 1995.

questions.q: Fertiliser washing into the sea can fuel algal blooms that create oxygen-starved 'dead zones' through a process called...?
questions.f: As the bloom dies and rots, bacteria use up the oxygen, suffocating fish and creating a dead zone.

questions.q: A fur trade that reduced them to a few thousand, barren rock where urchins ate everything, and kelp forests that returned with their protection converge on which animal?
questions.f: Ecologists coined the term 'keystone species' partly from watching otters remake whole coastlines.

questions.q: Up to 200 bright blue eyes along one shell rim, images focused by living mirrors instead of lenses, and an optical design echoing a reflecting telescope converge on which animal?
questions.f: Each eye grows a mirror of guanine crystals, a trick engineers only worked out much later.

questions.q: The fin whale is unique among whales for having colouring that is...?
c: Asymmetrical, with white only on the right jaw
questions.f: This one-sided white jaw may help herd fish, and no one is completely sure why it evolved.

questions.q: Skin that flickers red and white in a rippling wave, packs that hunt together off Peru, and a Spanish nickname meaning red devil converge on which animal?
questions.f: The flashes come from skin cells called chromatophores and may be a way of signalling the pack.

questions.q: Sensing pores spread across a head nearly a metre wide, prey detected while buried in sand, and a silhouette shared by nine living species converge on which shark?
questions.f: The wide head works like a broader metal detector, sweeping for the faint sparks of hidden prey.

questions.q: Charles Darwin correctly explained that a ring-shaped coral 'atoll' forms as a reef grows upward around a slowly sinking...?
questions.f: As the volcano sinks, the reef keeps growing toward the light, leaving a ring of coral around a central lagoon.

questions.q: A marker disc still visible 80 metres down, water almost as transparent as the distilled kind, and a sea named after a British sealing captain converge on which place?
questions.f: Its water is so clear because the freezing Antarctic surface supports very little plankton.

questions.q: Sea snakes must surface to breathe air, but they can also absorb some oxygen directly through their...?
questions.f: This skin-breathing lets some sea snakes stay submerged for a couple of hours between breaths.

questions.q: Twenty-four eyes with working lenses, a cube-shaped bell, and stinger nets strung across Australian beaches each summer converge on which animal?
questions.f: It is also among the most venomous animals known, with tentacles trailing three metres.

questions.q: Roots that breathe through pegs poking above the mud, seeds that sprout while still hanging on the parent, and a coastal barrier that blunts a storm surge converge on which trees?
questions.f: Their thickets are nurseries for young fish and lock away carbon faster than a rainforest.

questions.q: The carbon captured and stored by mangroves, seagrasses, and salt marshes is nicknamed...?
questions.f: Coastal 'blue carbon' habitats can lock away carbon many times faster than a forest on land.

questions.q: An order named after mythical singers, the only fully plant-eating sea mammals, and Florida springs crowded with them each winter converge on which group?
questions.f: Lonely sailors' reports of these gentle grazers may lie behind centuries of mermaid stories.

questions.q: El Nino paired with its linked seesaw of air pressure over the Pacific is together known by which name?
questions.f: ENSO, the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, is the single biggest driver of year-to-year climate swings worldwide.

questions.q: A 1977 dive in the submersible Alvin, two-metre worms thriving in total darkness, and proof that life can run on chemistry rather than sunlight converge on which place?
questions.f: The geologists aboard had no biologist with them, and had to preserve specimens in vodka.

questions.q: A nose inflated into a booming drum, four tonnes of blubber hauled onto a beach, and dives beyond 1,500 metres converge on which animal?
questions.f: It is the largest carnivoran alive, and it can stay submerged for nearly two hours.

questions.q: The deep-sea 'giant isopod' is an oversized relative of which familiar small land creature?
questions.f: Deep-sea gigantism can make this cousin of the pill bug grow to the size of a small cat.

questions.q: The veined, or 'coconut', octopus stunned scientists by carrying and reassembling which item as a portable shelter?
questions.f: Toting shells to hide in later is seen as one of the first clear cases of tool use by an invertebrate.

questions.q: The ocean helps steady Earth's climate largely because water has an unusually high...?
questions.f: Water absorbs and releases huge amounts of heat with little change in temperature, buffering the whole planet.

questions.q: Old seafloor is destroyed and recycled back into the mantle where oceanic plates dive down at deep-sea...?
questions.f: This 'subduction' at trenches is why the seafloor is nowhere older than about 200 million years.

questions.q: The root 'thalasso-', seen in 'Panthalassa' and 'thalassophobia', means...?
questions.f: From Greek 'thalassa' (sea): thalassophobia is the fear of the vast open ocean.

questions.q: The 'abyssopelagic' zone, from roots meaning 'bottomless open sea', spans roughly which depth?
questions.f: Below it lies only the hadal zone of the deepest trenches; the abyssopelagic is pitch black and near freezing.

questions.q: The 'hadal' zone of the deepest trenches takes its name from...?
questions.f: From Hades: fittingly, it is the darkest, deepest, most hidden realm of the sea.

questions.q: In 'pycnocline', the layer of fast-changing water density, the root 'pycno' means...?
questions.f: From Greek 'pyknos' (dense, thick): the pycnocline is where density changes sharply with depth.

questions.q: The sunlit 'euphotic' zone gets its name from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'eu' (good, well) + 'photic' (light): enough light for photosynthesis reaches this top layer.

questions.q: The dim twilight or 'dysphotic' zone is named with a prefix meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'dys' (bad, difficult): just enough light filters down to see, but far too little for plants to grow.

questions.q: The pitch-dark 'aphotic' zone is named for a prefix meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'a-' (without) + 'photic' (light): below about 1,000 m no sunlight remains at all.

questions.q: The 'neritic' zone refers to the relatively shallow water lying over the continental...?
questions.f: Sunlit and nutrient-rich, the neritic zone over the shelf holds most of the ocean's fisheries.

questions.q: The 'oceanic' zone, in contrast to the neritic, is the open water lying beyond the edge of the...?
questions.f: Past the shelf break the seafloor plunges away, and the vast, deep oceanic zone begins.

questions.q: A barnacle or coral is described as 'sessile', meaning it is...?
questions.f: From Latin 'sedere' (to sit): sessile animals stay anchored for life and let food drift to them.

questions.q: An animal described as 'motile' is one that is able to...?
questions.f: From Latin 'motus' (moved): motile animals such as fish and squid actively swim, unlike sessile ones.

questions.q: The rain of 'detritus' that feeds the deep sea consists of...?
questions.f: From Latin 'detritus' (worn away): this drifting debris is the deep sea's main food supply.

questions.q: A 'detritivore', such as a sea cucumber, is an animal that eats...?
questions.f: Sea cucumbers vacuum up detritus on the seabed, recycling nutrients back into the food web.

questions.q: A 'planktivore' is an animal whose diet is mainly...?
questions.f: The largest planktivores, like whale sharks and baleen whales, strain tiny plankton by the tonne.

questions.q: A 'piscivore' is an animal that mainly eats...?
questions.f: From Latin 'piscis' (fish): barracuda and many seabirds are classic piscivores.

questions.q: The zodiac sign Pisces and the word 'piscine' both come from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'piscis' (fish): 'piscine' simply means fish-like.

questions.q: Cuttlefish change colour using skin cells called 'chromatophores'; the root 'chroma' means...?
questions.f: From Greek 'chroma' (colour): a cuttlefish can flash rippling colours across its body in a fraction of a second.

questions.q: In 'phosphorescence', the root 'phosphor' means...?
questions.f: From Greek 'phos' (light) + 'phoros' (bearer): the planet Venus as morning star was the original 'phosphoros'.

questions.q: The light-making molecule 'luciferin' takes its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'lucifer' (light-bringer): luciferin plus the enzyme luciferase make living, glowing light.

questions.q: A 'photophore' is a light-producing organ; the ending '-phore' means...?
questions.f: From Greek 'phoros' (bearer): countless deep-sea animals wear rows of photophores like living lanterns.

questions.q: The Portuguese man o' war is a 'siphonophore'; the root 'siphon' refers to a...?
questions.f: From Greek 'siphon' (tube): a siphonophore is a colony of specialized bodies strung together like one animal.

questions.q: A snail scrapes food using a tongue-like ribbon of tiny teeth called a 'radula', from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'radere' (to scrape): a limpet's radula is tipped with one of the hardest materials known in nature.

questions.q: A mussel anchors itself to rock with tough 'byssus' threads, also known as its...?
questions.f: Ancient weavers spun the fine golden byssus of large mussels into a rare cloth called 'sea silk'.

questions.q: The tough material forming crab shells and squid beaks is called...?
questions.f: Chitin is a strong natural polymer; it also builds insect exoskeletons on land.

questions.q: A sea urchin's rigid internal skeleton, revealed once its spines drop off, is called a...?
questions.f: From Latin 'testa' (shell): the beautiful patterned 'test' of a sand dollar is its bare skeleton.

questions.q: Sea stars move on hundreds of 'ambulacral' tube feet; the root 'ambul' means...?
questions.f: From Latin 'ambulare' (to walk): the same root gives us 'ambulance' and 'amble'.

questions.q: When a sea star deliberately drops an arm to escape a predator, this self-amputation is called 'autotomy', meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'auto' (self) + 'tome' (cutting): the shed arm can distract a hunter while the animal escapes and regrows it.

questions.q: 'Osmosis', key to how sea animals handle salt, is the movement of what across a membrane?
questions.f: From Greek 'osmos' (a push): water flows toward the saltier side, which sea life must constantly manage.

questions.q: 'Osmoregulation' is an animal's control of its internal balance of...?
questions.f: Salmon completely re-tune their osmoregulation when moving between salt sea and fresh river water.

questions.q: A 'euryhaline' animal, like a bull shark, can tolerate a wide range of...?
questions.f: From Greek 'eurys' (wide) + 'hals' (salt): euryhaline species thrive from the open sea into rivers.

questions.q: A 'stenohaline' animal is one that can survive only a narrow range of...?
questions.f: From Greek 'stenos' (narrow) + 'hals' (salt): most open-ocean fish are stenohaline and quickly stressed by change.

questions.q: Eels are 'catadromous', a term describing fish that migrate down to the sea in order to...?
questions.f: From Greek 'kata' (down): eels spend life in rivers, then run down to the sea to spawn, the reverse of salmon.

questions.q: A 'diadromous' fish is one that migrates between...?
questions.f: From Greek 'dia' (across): salmon and eels are famous diadromous travellers between rivers and the sea.

questions.q: The sunlit surface layer, the 'epipelagic' zone, is named with a prefix meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'epi' (upon): reaching to about 200 m, the epipelagic is the only layer with enough light for plants.

questions.q: A great rotating system of ocean currents is a 'gyre', from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'gyros' (circle): five great gyres slowly whirl the surface of the world's oceans.

questions.q: A 'halophyte', such as a mangrove or marsh grass, is a plant that tolerates...?
questions.f: From Greek 'hals' (salt) + 'phyton' (plant): halophytes have clever ways to shed or store excess salt.

questions.q: 'Coralline' algae, which help cement reefs together, are named because they are...?
questions.f: These pink, chalky algae lay down limestone, acting as a natural mortar binding a reef into solid rock.

questions.q: The algae 'zooxanthellae' that live inside corals are named partly for the Greek 'xanthos', meaning...?
questions.f: Their golden-yellow pigment gives many corals their warm colour and feeds the coral through photosynthesis.

questions.q: 'Ambergris', the prized waxy substance from sperm whales once used in perfume, literally means...?
questions.f: From Old French 'ambre gris' (grey amber): lumps of it were once worth more than their weight in gold.

questions.q: A 'nudibranch', the often dazzling sea slug, has a name that literally means '...gills'?
questions.f: From Latin 'nudus' (naked) + Greek 'branchia' (gills): its breathing organs sit exposed on its back.

questions.q: A comb jelly is a 'ctenophore', a name meaning '...-bearer'?
questions.f: From Greek 'ktenos' (comb): rows of beating comb-like hairs shimmer with rainbow colours as it swims.

questions.q: In 1960 the first crewed descent to the deepest point of the ocean was made aboard which vessel?
questions.f: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh rode Trieste to the Challenger Deep, a feat not repeated by anyone for 52 years.

questions.q: Across vast 'high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll' waters, phytoplankton growth is held back mainly by a shortage of which element?
questions.f: Sprinkling a little iron dust on these seas can spark a huge plankton bloom, an idea called the iron hypothesis.

questions.q: A map dismissed by a colleague as 'girl talk', the discovery of a rift valley running down the Atlantic floor, and a partnership with Bruce Heezen converge on which scientist?
questions.f: Her hand-drawn seafloor maps became key evidence for seafloor spreading and plate tectonics.

questions.q: Complaints that westbound mail ships ran two weeks late, a thermometer lowered over the side on Atlantic crossings, and the first printed chart of a warm current converge on which figure?
questions.f: As deputy postmaster he charted the Gulf Stream in the 1770s; British captains ignored it for years.

questions.q: A campaigner called 'the sailor's friend', an 1876 law against overloaded 'coffin ships', and a rubber-soled shoe with a matching band converge on which marking?
questions.f: Samuel Plimsoll's circle-and-line mark still shows how deeply a loaded ship may safely sit.

questions.q: A Yorkshire carpenter, a government prize worth a fortune, and a sea clock the size of a large pocket watch called H4 converge on which man?
questions.f: His clock finally let a ship fix its longitude, solving navigation's most deadly puzzle.

questions.q: Cliffs at Lyme Regis, the first ichthyosaur skeleton to reach London, and a tongue-twister often linked to her converge on which fossil hunter?
questions.f: She found plesiosaurs too, yet as a woman she could not join the Geological Society.

questions.q: An admiral nicknamed for his grogram cloak, a 1740 order to water down the navy's rum ration, and the word for feeling dazed converge on which drink?
questions.f: Edward 'Old Grog' Vernon's diluted rum gave English both 'grog' and 'groggy'.

questions.q: Jellyfish netted by the hundred thousand in Puget Sound, a protein that makes living cells glow, and a 2008 Nobel Prize converge on which laboratory tool?
questions.f: Osamu Shimomura's jellyfish protein now lets biologists watch genes switch on inside living cells.

questions.q: An unusually thick nerve fibre, Hodgkin and Huxley's 1952 equations, and a 1963 Nobel for how nerve signals travel converge on which sea animal?
questions.f: The squid's giant axon was wide enough to push an electrode into, unlocking the nerve impulse.

questions.q: Thousands of crushed sea snails per few grams of dye, a colour Roman law reserved for emperors, and the Greek word behind our 'purple' converge on which creature?
questions.f: From Greek 'porphura', the snail's name: Tyrian purple was once worth more than its weight in silver.

questions.q: A 1908 experiment on a broth made from kelp, crystals of glutamate on a dish, and the naming of a fifth basic taste converge on which seaweed?
questions.f: Kikunae Ikeda called the taste 'umami', meaning delicious, after isolating it from kombu stock.

questions.q: A spot where the nearest humans are usually orbiting overhead, a graveyard for retired spacecraft, and a name borrowed from a Jules Verne captain converge on which place?
questions.f: This oceanic pole of inaccessibility lies about 2,700 km from the nearest land in any direction.

questions.q: A Scottish tidal race, a boating accident that nearly drowned George Orwell while he was writing '1984', and one of the world's great whirlpools converge on which strait?
questions.f: Orwell was staying on Jura, finishing his novel, when his boat capsized in the Gulf of Corryvreckan.

questions.q: A container swept overboard in 1992, plastic bath toys washing up on Alaskan beaches for years afterwards, and a new way to test current models converge on which objects?
questions.f: Nearly 29,000 toys spilled, and oceanographers tracked them to map the North Pacific Gyre.

questions.q: Mammoth bones and stone tools dredged up in fishing nets, a plain that once joined Britain to Europe, and flooding some 8,000 years ago converge on which lost land?
questions.f: Trawlers still haul up harpoons and hand axes from what is now the floor of the North Sea.

questions.q: A 1958 Alaskan earthquake, a rockfall into a narrow inlet, and trees stripped bare 524 metres up the far slope converge on which record?
questions.f: Two fishermen in Lituya Bay rode the wave over a forest and lived to describe it.

questions.q: Stone markers carved on Japanese hillsides, warnings not to build below them, and villages spared in 2011 converge on which objects?
questions.f: Some stones are over 600 years old; the hamlet of Aneyoshi obeyed its marker and survived.

questions.q: Sea nomads of Southeast Asia, spleens about half again larger than average, and dives lasting over ten minutes converge on which people?
questions.f: A larger spleen releases an extra reserve of oxygen-rich blood cells during a long breath-hold.

questions.q: Women divers of Jeju Island, a fishing tradition led by grandmothers, and a whistling exhale called sumbisori converge on which divers?
questions.f: Many haenyeo still free-dive into their seventies and eighties, carrying no air tanks.

questions.q: A noodle-shop owner's son, an 1896 patent for seeding oysters, and the collapse of a trade that once demanded thousands of dives converge on which invention?
questions.f: Kokichi Mikimoto's method made pearls affordable and ended the hunt for wild ones.

questions.q: A jelly made from fish swim bladders, centuries of use in clearing cloudy beer, and the reason some beers are not vegan converge on which substance?
questions.f: Isinglass makes yeast clump and settle, leaving the beer above it bright and clear.

questions.q: Stone vats unearthed at Pompeii, a sauce made by fermenting fish in salt, and the ancestor of the anchovy in Worcestershire sauce converge on which condiment?
questions.f: Romans splashed garum on nearly everything; a good vintage could cost as much as fine perfume.

questions.q: A food once fed to prisoners and servants, shells spread on fields as fertiliser in colonial New England, and a reputation transformed by railway dining cars converge on which animal?
questions.f: Lobster was so cheap that serving it too often was once considered a mark of poverty.

questions.q: Greenland shark flesh buried and dried for weeks, a powerful smell of ammonia, and a traditional Icelandic delicacy converge on which food?
questions.f: Fresh Greenland shark is toxic, so fermenting it for months is what makes it safe to eat.

questions.q: A naturalist's notes from an 1741 shipwreck, a nine-metre relative of the manatee, and extinction within 27 years of its discovery converge on which animal?
questions.f: Georg Steller described it while stranded on Bering Island; hunters wiped it out by 1768.

questions.q: A flightless North Atlantic seabird, the last known pair killed on an Icelandic islet in 1844, and museum eggs now worth fortunes converge on which bird?
questions.f: Standing nearly a metre tall, it filled the penguin's role in the northern hemisphere.

questions.q: A small porpoise of the northern Gulf of California, nets set illegally for a fish called totoaba, and a population now in single figures converge on which animal?
questions.f: 'Vaquita' means little cow; it is the most endangered marine mammal in the world.

questions.q: A hydrophone recording made off Bermuda in the 1960s, a surprise best-selling 1970 album of animal sounds, and a campaign that helped end commercial whaling converge on which discovery?
questions.f: Roger Payne's album 'Songs of the Humpback Whale' sold millions and fuelled Save the Whales.

questions.q: A voice tracked by navy listening arrays since 1989, a call pitched far higher than any known whale species, and the nickname 'the loneliest whale' converge on which mystery?
questions.f: No answering call has ever been recorded, though its route matches a normal whale migration.

questions.q: An ultra-low sound detected across thousands of kilometres in 1997, early speculation about a vast unknown animal, and an eventual answer involving cracking ice converge on which sound?
questions.f: Scientists later matched the Bloop to icequakes as huge Antarctic icebergs split apart.

questions.q: A steel ball with quartz windows, a 1934 dive to 923 metres, and radio broadcasts made live from the deep converge on which craft?
questions.f: William Beebe and Otis Barton hung from a cable, with no way to steer or propel themselves.

questions.q: An engineer named Emile Gagnan, a valve adapted from a wartime gas-powered car, and a 1943 device that freed divers from surface hoses converge on which invention?
questions.f: Gagnan and Jacques Cousteau's demand valve became the heart of all modern scuba gear.

questions.q: A nuclear-powered submarine, a 1958 voyage beneath the Arctic ice cap, and the first crossing of the North Pole underwater converge on which vessel?
questions.f: Its name honoured Captain Nemo's fictional submarine from Jules Verne's novel.

questions.q: A one-man wooden craft shaped like a barrel, hand-cranked propellers, and a failed 1776 attack in New York Harbour converge on which vessel?
questions.f: David Bushnell's Turtle was the first submarine ever used in war.

questions.q: A 1979 walk on the seabed at 381 metres in an armoured suit, the nickname 'Her Deepness', and decades of leading undersea missions converge on which scientist?
questions.f: She walked untethered on the ocean floor, still a record for that kind of dive.

questions.q: A researcher nicknamed the Shark Lady, a flatfish whose milky secretion makes a shark's jaws clamp shut, and decades of Red Sea diving converge on which scientist?
questions.f: Eugenie Clark's work on the Moses sole hinted at a natural shark repellent.

questions.q: A naturalist working in Sicily, the invention of the glass aquarium in the 1830s, and proof that the argonaut octopus makes its own shell converge on which pioneer?
questions.f: She built tanks to watch sea life alive, and Charles Darwin later cited her work.

questions.q: A 1951 bestseller called 'The Sea Around Us', years as a biologist for the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and a later book that transformed pesticide law converge on which writer?
questions.f: Her ocean books made her famous long before 'Silent Spring' changed environmental law.

questions.q: Curved palm ribs lashed into a frame, small shells marking islands, and a record of how ocean swells bend converge on which navigational tool?
questions.f: Navigators memorised the chart on land, then read the real swells with their bodies at sea.

questions.q: A double-hulled canoe launched in 1975, a 1976 crossing from Hawaii to Tahiti with no instruments, and the revival of star-path navigation converge on which vessel?
questions.f: Micronesian navigator Mau Piailug guided her using stars, swells, and birds alone.

questions.q: A 1569 world map, straight lines that let a sailor hold one compass bearing, and wildly stretched polar regions converge on which projection?
questions.f: It distorts area badly but is still ideal for plotting a steady course across the sea.

questions.q: A rock guarding the Mediterranean's mouth, a name from the Arabic for 'Tariq's mountain', and one of the ancient Pillars of Hercules converge on which place?
questions.f: From 'Jabal Tariq', for the commander who landed there in 711.

questions.q: A strait whose name means 'ox ford', a myth of Io swimming across as a cow, and water splitting two continents inside one city converge on which channel?
questions.f: Istanbul is the only city in the world that straddles two continents across this strait.

questions.q: A strait named for a girl who fell from a golden ram, Leander's nightly swim to Hero, and Byron's imitation of that swim in 1810 converge on which waterway?
questions.f: Today it is called the Dardanelles, but 'Hellespont' means 'sea of Helle'.

questions.q: A headland first named for its storms, renamed by a Portuguese king in a burst of optimism, and rounded by Vasco da Gama in 1497 converge on which landmark?
questions.f: Bartolomeu Dias called it the Cape of Storms before the king rebranded it for good luck.

questions.q: A sea tinted by silt, a name shared with the great river that colours it, and shallow water between China and Korea converge on which sea?
questions.f: The Yellow River carries so much fine loess that it stains the sea at its mouth.

questions.q: Thick salt beds drilled from beneath the Mediterranean floor, a sea nearly dried out 5.5 million years ago, and a flood through Gibraltar that refilled it converge on which event?
questions.f: The refilling Zanclean flood may have poured in a thousand times faster than the Amazon.

questions.q: A landmass 94 percent underwater, a crust too thick and light to be ocean floor, and New Zealand as its highest ground converge on which continent?
questions.f: Geologists formally described Zealandia as Earth's eighth continent in 2017.

questions.q: A near-perfect circular sinkhole off Belize, a limestone cave drowned as the sea rose, and a dark ring visible from the air converge on which feature?
questions.f: It formed as a dry cave during the ice ages, then flooded when meltwater raised the sea.

questions.q: A 1953 North Sea flood that killed over 1,800 people, a nation a quarter of which lies below sea level, and vast storm-surge barriers converge on which project?
questions.f: Its Maeslant barrier has two arms each as long as the Eiffel Tower is tall.

questions.q: An island abbey, a tidal range that can reach 14 metres, and pilgrims who once crossed only at low water converge on which landmark?
questions.f: The tide there was said to rush in 'at the speed of a galloping horse'.

questions.q: A machine of brass gears and pulleys, sums of tidal harmonics turned by a crank, and secret predictions for the 1944 Normandy landings converge on which device?
questions.f: Arthur Doodson's machines gave the D-Day planners the tides and moonlight they needed.

questions.q: A mythical bird said to nest on the winter sea, a spell of calm around the solstice, and a phrase meaning happier days gone by converge on which word?
questions.f: Alcyone was turned into a kingfisher, and the gods calmed the sea while she nested.

questions.q: Orkney and Shetland folklore, seals that shed their skins to walk as humans, and a hidden sealskin that traps a bride converge on which creature?
questions.f: In the tales, a selkie wife always finds her skin at last and returns to the sea.

questions.q: White flowers cast into the surf on New Year's Eve in Brazil, an African orisha of the sea, and little boats of offerings pushed out on the waves converge on which goddess?
questions.f: Millions dressed in white gather on Brazilian beaches to ask her blessing for the year.

questions.q: An Inuit goddess of the sea, a story of a girl who fell into the ocean and became its ruler, and a dwarf planet named in 2004 converge on which name?
questions.f: Astronomers chose her name for a frigid, distant world far beyond Pluto's orbit.

questions.q: An Irish sea god, a cloak of mist that hid an island, and a British island that still bears his name converge on which figure?
questions.f: The Isle of Man is named for Manannan, who was said to guard it behind a wall of fog.

questions.q: A sea god who calms the waves by blowing a twisted shell, the largest moon of Neptune, and a name given to a giant conch converge on which figure?
questions.f: Neptune's moon Triton is one of the few in the solar system that orbits backwards.

questions.q: A shape-shifting sea god, a herdsman who tended Poseidon's seals, and an adjective meaning endlessly adaptable converge on which name?
questions.f: Grab hold of Proteus and he changes form; that legend gave English the word 'protean'.

questions.q: A monster perched on a rock, a whirlpool churning across the channel, and a phrase for being caught between two evils converge on which strait's legends?
questions.f: Odysseus had to choose between Scylla's rock and Charybdis's whirlpool in these narrows.

questions.q: A king who leapt from a cliff, black sails mistaken for news of his son's death, and Theseus's forgotten promise converge on which sea's name?
questions.f: Aegeus threw himself into the water, and by legend the sea has carried his name ever since.

questions.q: A dragon god's palace of coral, a rescued turtle repaying a kindness, and a fisherman who returns home to find three centuries gone converge on which tale?
questions.f: He opens a forbidden box and his lost years catch up with him all at once.

questions.q: The first avatar of Vishnu, a warning of a world-drowning flood, and a boat towed to safety by a horn converge on which figure?
questions.f: Matsya takes the form of a giant fish, and 'matsya' is simply the Sanskrit word for fish.

questions.q: A Norse god of the sea and of wealth, a home called Noatun, and a marriage that failed because of noisy gulls converge on which deity?
questions.f: His giantess wife Skadi missed her mountains; he could not bear her wolves' howling.

questions.q: A Maori god who fled to the water after a quarrel among brothers, an ancestor claimed by all fish, and a name shared with a research ship converge on which deity?
questions.f: Because Tangaroa's children fled to sea, Maori tradition says the forest and the ocean still feud.

questions.q: A Norwegian tidal current off Lofoten, an Edgar Allan Poe tale about a descent into it, and the word Jules Verne borrowed for a giant vortex converge on which whirlpool?
questions.f: 'Maelstrom' comes from Dutch words meaning 'grinding current', first used of this very spot.

questions.q: A cable-laying voyage by the largest ship of its age, a failed first attempt in 1858, and instant messages between continents from 1866 converge on which achievement?
questions.f: Cyrus Field's cable cut the time for a message across the Atlantic from ten days to minutes.

questions.q: A brigantine found sailing crewless in 1872, an intact cargo of alcohol, and a missing lifeboat converge on which ship?
questions.f: Every theory from fumes to waterspouts has been offered; not one crew member was ever found.

questions.q: A whaleship rammed and sunk by a sperm whale in 1820, months adrift in open boats, and a first mate's account that Melville later read converge on which vessel?
questions.f: The Essex disaster gave Melville the ending for 'Moby-Dick' three decades later.

questions.q: A balsa-log raft, five men and a parrot, and a 1947 drift of nearly 7,000 km from Peru to Polynesia converge on which expedition?
questions.f: Thor Heyerdahl wanted to show ancient South Americans could have reached the Pacific islands.

questions.q: Sailors' teeth marked by tiny black spots, bleeding gums on long voyages, and a 1747 experiment with lemon juice converge on which shipboard disease?
questions.f: James Lind's citrus trials eventually gave British sailors their nickname, 'limeys'.

questions.q: Carved whale teeth and bone, long idle hours on 19th-century whaleships, and inked pictures of ships and sweethearts converge on which folk art?
questions.f: Sailors scratched designs with a needle then rubbed in lampblack or tobacco juice.

questions.q: A stiffening strip in Victorian corsets and umbrellas, a substance harvested from a whale's mouth, and a market that collapsed once spring steel arrived converge on which material?
questions.f: Baleen bends and springs back like plastic, and it was known in the trade as whalebone.

questions.q: Islands buried in seabird droppings, an 1856 American law claiming them, and a fertiliser boom that reshaped world farming converge on which substance?
questions.f: Guano was so valuable that nations fought over barren, waterless rocks to mine it.

questions.q: A jawless fish with a rasping round mouth, a sucker used to cling to hosts, and a species that invaded the Great Lakes converge on which animal?
questions.f: Lampreys are among the most ancient vertebrates alive, older than jaws themselves.

questions.q: A single-celled organism the size of an apple, a body of many nuclei in one cell, and abundance on the abyssal plain converge on which giant?
questions.f: Among the largest single cells known, xenophyophores build shells from grains they glue together.

questions.q: A five-toothed chewing structure named after a Greek philosopher, an animal that grazes algae from rock, and a mouth that faces downward converge on which creature?
questions.f: 'Aristotle's lantern' is the urchin's jaw, named for the philosopher who first described it.

questions.q: A network of fine blood vessels running side by side, warm blood passing its heat to cold, and the reason a tuna's muscles stay hot converge on which structure?
questions.f: Latin for 'wonderful net': the same trick keeps a penguin's feet from freezing its whole body.

questions.q: A false seabed on a ship's echo sounder, a reading that rises at dusk and sinks at dawn, and wartime confusion about the ocean's depth converge on which phenomenon?
questions.f: Sonar operators were baffled until they realised they were bouncing sound off billions of small animals.

questions.q: A white disc lowered on a rope, a measure of how far light penetrates, and a method from an 1865 Vatican-backed cruise converge on which instrument?
questions.f: Angelo Secchi's simple disk is still used worldwide to gauge water clarity.

questions.q: A unit equal to a million cubic metres of water per second, a scale for measuring whole currents, and a Norwegian-American oceanographer converge on which unit?
questions.f: The Gulf Stream moves at roughly 30 sverdrups, more than all the world's rivers combined.

questions.q: A wind-driven spiral of water layers turning with depth, a puzzle first noticed in drifting Arctic ice, and a Swedish scientist's 1905 theory converge on which effect?
questions.f: Fridtjof Nansen noticed ice drifting at an angle to the wind, and Ekman worked out why.

questions.q: A circle of clear water seen when looking up from below, an unbroken ring beyond which the surface turns mirror-like, and the bending of light converge on which phenomenon?
questions.f: A diver sees the entire sky squeezed into a cone about 97 degrees wide.

questions.q: A chemical that props up proteins under pressure, a level found to rise steadily with depth, and a possible reason no fish live below about 8,400 metres converge on which substance?
questions.f: Past that depth a fish would need so much of it that water would flood into its cells.

questions.q: Nearly 4,000 drifting robots, a ten-day cycle of sinking and surfacing, and a global temperature record begun in 2000 converge on which programme?
questions.f: Named after the ship of Jason's Argonauts, the fleet reports from two kilometres down.

questions.q: A sudden standing sloshing of water in an enclosed basin, a rhythm set by the basin's own shape, and a Swiss lake that gave the effect its name converge on which phenomenon?
questions.f: Lake Geneva's sloshing was studied first, but seiches strike harbours and bays worldwide.

questions.q: A point in the sea where the tidal range falls to almost nothing, a pattern of tides rotating around it, and lines on a chart radiating outward converge on which feature?
questions.f: Tides swing around these hubs like the hands of a clock, driven by the shape of each basin.

questions.q: Sharks and rays share a group name built from roots meaning 'beaten metal plate' and...?
questions.f: 'Elasmobranch' points to their exposed plate-like gill slits, with no bony cover over them.

questions.q: The class name uniting sharks, rays, and chimaeras is built from roots meaning 'cartilage' plus...?
questions.f: From Greek 'chondros' (cartilage) + 'ichthys' (fish): not one true bone among them.

questions.q: A shark's skin is covered in 'placoid' scales, a term from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'plax' (plate): each tiny scale is built like a tooth, with enamel and a pulp cavity.

questions.q: The bony flap covering a fish's gills is the 'operculum', from a Latin root meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'operire' (to cover): a fish pumps water past its gills by flaring this lid.

questions.q: The pearly inner shell layer prized in jewellery is called 'nacre'; the same material forms...?
questions.f: An oyster lays down the same nacre around an irritant, layer by layer, to make a pearl.

questions.q: An 'amphipod', the shrimp-like animal swarming at whale falls, has a name meaning '...-footed'?
questions.f: From Greek 'amphi' (both): its legs point in two directions, some for walking, some for swimming.

questions.q: An 'isopod', such as the deep-sea giant, has a name meaning '...-footed'?
questions.f: From Greek 'isos' (equal): unlike an amphipod, all its legs are much the same shape.

questions.q: A 'brachiopod', the shelled creature common in ancient sea fossils, has a name meaning '...-foot'?
questions.f: From Greek 'brachion' (arm): they look like clams but belong to a wholly separate branch of life.

questions.q: The head-and-chest section fused together in a crab or shrimp is called the...?
questions.f: From Greek roots for head and chest: the carapace is the shield that covers it.

questions.q: A lobster's large pincer is properly called a 'chela', from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'chele' (claw): the same root names the 'chelicerae' of spiders and horseshoe crabs.

questions.q: A 'chiton', the armoured sea creature clinging to rocks, borrows the name of an ancient Greek...?
questions.f: Its eight overlapping plates reminded naturalists of a layered Greek garment.

questions.q: The stalked, flower-like relatives of sea stars called crinoids take their name from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'krinon' (lily): sea lilies were far more abundant in ancient seas than today.

questions.q: Sea otters belong to the 'mustelid' family, which also includes...?
questions.f: The sea otter is the heaviest mustelid and the only one that lives its whole life at sea.

questions.q: A 'piezophile' is an organism that thrives under high...?
questions.f: From Greek 'piezein' (to press): some deep-trench bacteria will not grow at surface pressure at all.

questions.q: A 'psychrophile' is an organism that thrives in conditions that are extremely...?
questions.f: From Greek 'psychros' (cold): psychrophiles keep working in briny channels inside sea ice.

questions.q: 'Abyssal', 'abysmal', and the 'abyssopelagic' zone all descend from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'abyssos' (bottomless), which is why 'abysmal' came to mean hopelessly bad.

questions.q: The term 'thalassocracy' describes a state whose power rests on its...?
questions.f: From Greek 'thalassa' (sea) + 'kratos' (power): Minoan Crete is often called the first thalassocracy.

questions.q: 'Limnology' is the study of inland waters, while its saltwater counterpart is...?
questions.f: From Greek 'limne' (lake): limnologists study lakes and rivers, oceanographers the sea.

questions.q: 'Malacology' is the branch of zoology devoted to...?
questions.f: From Greek 'malakos' (soft), the same root behind 'mollusc' itself.

questions.q: 'Carcinology' is the study of which animals?
questions.f: From Greek 'karkinos' (crab), a word that also named the constellation Cancer.

questions.q: 'Phycology' is the scientific study of...?
questions.f: From Greek 'phykos' (seaweed): phycologists study everything from plankton to giant kelp.

questions.q: The word 'scuttle', as in to scuttle a ship, first referred to a...?
c: Small opening cut in the hull or deck
questions.f: A 'scuttle' was a hatch; to scuttle a ship was to open her up and let the sea in.

questions.q: 'Scuttlebutt', meaning gossip, originally named a ship's...?
questions.f: Sailors traded rumours around the water cask, exactly as offices later did at the water cooler.

questions.q: To 'careen' a ship meant to...?
c: Tip it on its side to clean the hull
questions.f: From a root meaning 'keel': a careened ship lay on a beach so barnacles could be scraped off.

questions.q: A 'jury-rigged' mast is one that has been...?
questions.f: Nothing to do with courtroom juries; 'jury' here meant makeshift, for temporary sea repairs.

questions.q: 'Chock-a-block' described two pulley blocks that had been...?
questions.f: With the blocks touching, no rope was left to pull, so the phrase came to mean crammed full.

questions.q: Judging someone by 'the cut of their jib' compares them to a ship's...?
questions.f: A vessel's nationality could be guessed from the shape of its jib, long before its flag was visible.

questions.q: A ship's 'painter' is a...?
c: Rope at the bow for tying up
questions.f: Probably from an old word for a hanging cord; every small boat still has its painter.

questions.q: A 'hawser' on a ship is a...?
questions.f: The hawsehole in the bow, through which the anchor cable runs, shares the same root.

questions.q: The 'freeboard' of a ship is the distance from the waterline up to the...?
questions.f: Too little freeboard and waves sweep the deck, which is exactly what the Plimsoll line guards against.

questions.q: What do astronauts shout at the end of a countdown: 'Three, two, one, ___!'
questions.f: Rocket countdowns were made famous by a 1929 space movie before real rockets ever used them!

questions.q: What do we call the round holes and dents all over the Moon?
questions.f: 'Crater' comes from a Greek word for a big mixing bowl, which is just what they look like.

questions.q: You can sometimes see the Moon in the sky during the daytime.
questions.f: The Moon is often up in daylight - it is just harder to spot against the bright blue sky.

questions.q: Sun + flower spells the name of which tall yellow plant?
questions.f: Young sunflowers really do turn their heads to follow the Sun across the sky all day.

questions.q: What do we call the soft silvery light that comes from the Moon?
questions.f: Moonlight is really sunlight bouncing off the Moon, like light bouncing off a giant mirror.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of 'sunrise'?
questions.f: At sunset the sky can glow orange and pink as sunlight bends through the thick evening air.

questions.q: What sits at the very center of our solar system?
questions.f: The Sun sits in the middle while all eight planets travel around it in giant circles.

questions.q: How many Suns can you see in Earth's sky?
questions.f: Some faraway worlds circle two stars at once, so they would see two suns in their sky!

questions.q: A starfish gets its name because its body is shaped like a what?
questions.f: Real stars are giant balls of glowing gas, but a starfish is a sea animal with five arms.

questions.q: What do we call the dark time of day when the stars come out?
questions.f: Even at night the Sun keeps shining - it is busy lighting up the other side of Earth.

questions.q: In space, astronauts keep their drinks in what so they do not float away?
questions.f: Spilled water in space floats around as round, wobbly bubbles that astronauts can chase and sip!

questions.q: The Moon is really made of yellow cheese.
questions.f: Moon rocks carried home by astronauts show the Moon is made of gray rock and dust - no cheese!

questions.q: Which word means the same as 'blast-off'?
questions.f: 'Launch' first meant to throw a spear - today we 'throw' whole rockets into the sky!

questions.q: The Sun is much, much bigger than the Moon.
questions.f: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon - it only looks small because it is so far away.

questions.q: Astronauts went 'moonwalking' when they walked on the what?
questions.f: Twelve astronauts have walked on the Moon, and many hopped like kangaroos in the low gravity.

questions.q: What color does Earth mostly look when you see it from space?
questions.f: Astronauts call Earth the Blue Marble because its huge oceans shine blue from space.

questions.q: How do astronauts keep from drifting around while they sleep?
c: They strap their sleeping bags to the wall
They hold the ceiling all night
They tie balloons to their feet
questions.f: Some astronauts say sleeping while floating feels like snoozing on a soft cloud.

questions.q: Which word means the bright, warm light of the Sun?
questions.f: Sunshine feels warm because it carries energy all the way from the Sun to your skin.

questions.q: What does the Sun give plants so they can grow?
questions.f: Plants catch sunlight with their leaves and use it to make their own food.

questions.q: What did Moon astronauts push into the ground to celebrate their visit?
questions.f: The flags have a stiff wire along the top so they look like they are waving in the windless air.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who studies the stars?
questions.f: 'Astronomer' is built from Greek word parts that mean 'star arranger'.

questions.q: What do rockets burn to fly up into space?
questions.f: Big rockets gulp their fuel so fast they could empty a swimming pool in less than a minute!

questions.q: A rocket countdown counts which way?
questions.f: Counting down builds excitement - when the count hits zero, the engines roar to life.

questions.q: Where does a rocket's journey into space begin?
questions.f: Launch pads spray out huge fountains of water to soften the rocket's mighty roar.

questions.q: A 'moonbeam' is a thin ray of what?
questions.f: Poets love moonbeams, and some flowers only open their petals under the light of the Moon.

questions.q: What kind of food do astronauts eat in space?
questions.f: Tortillas are astronaut favorites because they do not make floating crumbs like bread does.

questions.q: Stars come in different colors, like red, yellow, and blue.
questions.f: Blue stars are the hottest and red stars are the coolest - the opposite of a water tap!

questions.q: The Sun, the Moon, and the stars all shine in the ___?
questions.f: The word 'sky' comes from an old Norse word that actually meant 'cloud'.

questions.q: Long ago, sailors at sea found their way at night using what?
questions.f: Sailors steered by star patterns long before there were maps or compasses for the open sea.

questions.q: A 'stargazer' is someone who loves to do what?
questions.f: 'Gazing' means looking at something for a long time - stargazers can watch the sky for hours.

questions.q: 'Spacecraft' means a craft, or vehicle, that travels where?
questions.f: 'Craft' is a very old word for a vessel - so a spacecraft is truly a 'space ship'.

questions.q: The Sun is so bright that you should never do what?
questions.f: Even sunglasses are not enough - scientists use special dark filters to study the Sun safely.

questions.q: What do we call the Sun's first light in the early morning?
questions.f: 'Dawn' and 'day' both grew from the same very old word for brightness.

questions.q: Which word names the dim, dusky time just after sunset?
questions.f: 'Dusk' comes from an old word meaning dark - it is when the first stars peek out.

questions.q: A rocket can reach space in less than ten minutes.
questions.f: Rockets zoom to space faster than most school bus rides - under ten minutes to leave the air behind!

questions.q: Which word names the huge, dark, airless place where the stars and planets are?
questions.f: Space is so empty that a chunk of it the size of your school would hold almost nothing at all.

questions.q: Where can you watch a star show projected on a big dome ceiling?
questions.f: A planetarium machine can paint thousands of stars indoors, even on a rainy afternoon.

questions.q: How do astronauts in space talk with people back on Earth?
questions.f: Astronauts can even make video calls home and wave to their families from orbit.

questions.q: What do we call made-up stories about spaceships and aliens?
questions.f: Many real astronauts say science fiction stories made them fall in love with space as kids.

questions.q: The Big Dipper star pattern looks most like which kitchen object?
questions.f: In England the same stars are called the Plough, and in India the Saptarishi - seven sages.

questions.q: Which word means to fly up high, like a rocket?
questions.f: 'Soar' comes from old words meaning 'to rise into the air' - eagles and rockets both do it.

questions.q: Where can you see the most stars at night?
questions.f: Far from city glow you can see a couple of thousand stars instead of just a handful.

questions.q: How do astronauts wash their hair in space?
questions.f: Water will not pour in space, so astronauts rub in special shampoo and towel it out.

questions.q: In space, an astronaut's hair floats around their head.
questions.f: With nothing pulling it down, long hair spreads out like a fluffy halo in every direction.

questions.q: Owls and bats are awake under the Moon at night. Night-time animals are called what?
questions.f: 'Nocturnal' comes from a Latin word for night - moths even use the Moon to find their way.

questions.q: Finish the rhyme: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you ___.'
questions.f: The tune of this rhyme is the same one used for the alphabet song - try singing both!

questions.q: In the rhyme 'Hey Diddle Diddle', which animal jumped over the Moon?
questions.f: This funny rhyme is over 250 years old - and the dish ran away with the spoon!

questions.q: Some people imagine they see a friendly face on the full Moon. What is it called?
questions.f: People in different countries see different pictures - many in Asia see a rabbit on the Moon!

questions.q: The stars are still in the sky during the day - we just cannot see them.
questions.f: Daylight is too bright for starlight, but the stars never go away - they are shining right now!

questions.q: What do we call it when a spaceship comes back down and touches the ground gently?
questions.f: Some capsules land under parachutes so softly that small rockets puff at the last second to cushion them.

questions.q: What do we call it when astronauts float outside their ship to fix things?
questions.f: A single spacewalk can last more than six hours - astronauts even have a snack bar in their helmet!

questions.q: Which of these is a real space job?
questions.f: Thousands of engineers work together for years to build one rocket that flies in minutes.

questions.q: Some rockets can fly to space, land back on Earth, and be used again.
questions.f: Reusable rockets land standing up on their tails, just like rockets in old cartoons!

questions.q: How many stars are there in the night sky?
questions.f: There are more stars in space than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches.

questions.q: What do we call the light that reaches us from the stars?
questions.f: Starlight travels for years to reach your eyes - you are seeing the past when you look up!

questions.q: Which two smaller words are hiding inside 'spaceship'?
questions.f: English loves gluing words together - moonlight, starfish, and sunflower are all made this way.

questions.q: What did the first Moon visitors carry home in special boxes?
questions.f: Apollo astronauts brought back hundreds of kilograms of Moon rocks for scientists to study.

questions.q: Where does an astronaut sit during a rocket launch?
questions.f: Astronauts lie on their backs at launch so the big push presses them safely into their seats.

questions.q: Which word means a make-believe creature from another planet?
questions.f: 'Alien' really just means 'from somewhere else' - scientists have not found any real ones yet.

questions.q: A small round window on a spaceship or ship is called a what?
questions.f: Astronauts say looking out the window at Earth is their favorite way to spend free time.

questions.q: About how long did it take astronauts to travel from Earth to the Moon?
questions.f: The Moon is so far away that driving there by car would take about six months without stopping!

questions.q: What do we call the faraway line where the sky seems to touch the ground?
questions.f: 'Horizon' comes from a Greek word meaning 'the limit' - you can never walk to it!

questions.q: Which game did an astronaut once play on the Moon with a club and two balls?
questions.f: Astronaut Alan Shepard smuggled a golf club head to the Moon and watched his ball sail far in the low gravity.

questions.q: Which takes longer: one day or one year?
questions.f: A year holds about 365 days - that is one whole trip for Earth around the Sun.

questions.q: The thin curved Moon shape seen on many flags is called a what?
questions.f: The croissant pastry is named after the very same curved moon shape!

questions.q: What sits at the very top of a rocket that carries astronauts?
questions.f: The pointy top also has a tiny escape rocket that can whisk the crew away to safety.

questions.q: What color are the big puffy suits astronauts wear on spacewalks?
questions.f: White bounces away the fierce sunlight and keeps the astronaut cooler inside.

questions.q: The Moon really follows your car when you ride at night.
questions.f: It only looks that way - the Moon is so far off that moving down a road barely changes your view of it.

questions.q: Too much time playing in strong sunlight can give your skin a what?
questions.f: Sunscreen works like a shield, bouncing away the strong rays that cause sunburn.

questions.q: What crunchy space treat is made by taking all the water out of ice cream?
questions.f: Freeze-dried ice cream crunches instead of melting - no freezer needed!

questions.q: Inside the space station there is no real up or down.
questions.f: Astronauts can work on the ceiling as easily as the floor - every wall can be a floor!

questions.q: Which grand word means the whole of space and everything in it?
questions.f: 'Cosmos' is a Greek word that means beautiful order - the opposite of chaos.

questions.q: Which word means super-duper big, like the universe?
questions.f: 'Gigantic' comes from the giants of Greek stories - beings of enormous size.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the word for the vehicle that flies to space?
questions.f: 'Rocket' ends in -et, like 'jacket' and 'bucket' - a handy pattern to remember.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'moon'?
questions.f: Moon and spoon have rhymed in songs and poems for hundreds of years.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'star'?
questions.f: Rhymes helped people remember songs and stories long before books were common.

questions.q: When the Sun is at its highest point in the sky, what time is it about?
questions.f: 'Noon' once meant a different hour - the word slowly slid to midday over the centuries.

questions.q: In which season are the nights the longest and the starry skies the darkest?
questions.f: In midwinter near the poles, the Sun barely rises at all - stars shine almost all day!

questions.q: Which day of the week is named after the Sun?
questions.f: People long ago gave each day of the week to a bright sky object or a god.

questions.q: Which day of the week is named after the Moon?
