questions.f: Monday means 'Moon day' - in French it is lundi, from luna, the Latin word for Moon.

questions.q: The Moon can sometimes look big and orange when it is low in the sky.
questions.f: Near the horizon, moonlight passes through lots of air, which paints the Moon orange.

questions.q: 'Goodnight Moon' is a famous what?
questions.f: In this classic book, a little bunny says goodnight to everything - even the Moon.

questions.q: On a spacewalk, where do astronauts carry the air they breathe?
questions.f: The life-support backpack is like a wearable mini-spaceship, with air, water, and power.

questions.q: 'Blast' in 'blast-off' means a sudden, powerful what?
questions.f: A rocket blast is so loud that birds and people must stay far away from the pad.

questions.q: Long ago, people told the time using the Sun's shadow on a what?
questions.f: A sundial's pointer casts a moving shadow that sweeps around like a clock hand.

questions.q: Astronauts can eat fresh apples and oranges when a supply ship arrives.
questions.f: Cargo ships bring fresh fruit as a treat - astronauts eat it quickly before it spoils.

questions.q: Which word means totally dark, with no light at all - like deep space?
questions.f: 'Pitch' is a sticky black tar - so pitch-black means as black as tar.

questions.q: Finish the cheerful saying: 'Reach for the ___!'
questions.f: This saying means aim as high as you can - even if the stars are far away, try!

questions.q: What is the see-through part of a space helmet that flips down over the face?
questions.f: Spacewalk visors are coated with a whisper-thin layer of real gold to block the Sun's glare.

questions.q: Sunlight on your skin helps your body make which vitamin?
questions.f: Vitamin D helps build strong bones - one more gift from our star, the Sun.

questions.q: Which of these can you really find on the Moon?
questions.f: Some lunar mountains are taller than many mountains on Earth, and they never wear down in the still air.

questions.q: Our planet's name, 'Earth', also means the ___ under your feet.
questions.f: Earth is the only planet whose name does not come from a Greek or Roman god.

questions.q: Which word means 'to shine softly in the dark', like the Moon?
questions.f: Some sea creatures and mushrooms glow too - their light is called living light.

questions.q: What sticky strips do astronauts use so tools do not float away?
questions.f: Velcro patches line the station walls - even food trays stick on with it.

questions.q: What is the biggest and brightest thing in our night sky?
questions.f: The full Moon is bright enough to read a book by on a clear night.

questions.q: When we say 'half-moon', how much of the Moon's circle can we see shining?
questions.f: Astronomers call it a 'quarter moon' because the Moon is a quarter of the way through its monthly trip.

questions.q: Many rockets launch near the sea so falling parts splash safely into the water.
questions.f: Launch sites by the ocean give rockets a huge, empty splash zone with no houses below.

questions.q: What do we call the front control room of a spaceship or plane?
questions.f: A spaceship cockpit is also called the flight deck - it is packed with screens and switches.

questions.q: Robot explorers built by people are driving around on Mars right now.
questions.f: Wheeled robots called rovers study Mars every day and send their photos home to Earth.

questions.q: A 'moonquake' is what kind of event on the Moon?
c: A shaking of the Moon's ground
questions.f: The Moon really does quake gently - astronauts left instruments there that felt the wobbles.

questions.q: What helps your eyes see more stars after you step outside at night?
questions.f: After about twenty minutes in darkness, your eyes become hundreds of times better at seeing stars.

questions.q: Which is the only planet we know of where people live?
questions.f: Earth sits in the perfect warm zone where water can stay liquid - just right for life.

questions.q: What do we call the blanket of air wrapped all around our planet?
questions.f: 'Atmosphere' is built from Greek word parts meaning 'vapour ball'.

questions.q: Which word means the study of stars and planets?
questions.f: Astronomy is the oldest science of all - people have been sky-watching for thousands of years.

questions.q: Stars make their very own light, but planets do not.
questions.f: Planets only glow because sunlight bounces off them, like a bicycle reflector at night.

questions.q: Which is the smallest: the Sun, Earth, or the Moon?
questions.f: About four Moons side by side would stretch across the width of Earth.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT found in space?
questions.f: Space is full of rocks, dust, and ice - but nobody has ever spotted a pool up there!

questions.q: What does a rover do on Mars?
questions.f: Mars rovers roll very slowly - some travel less than the length of a football field in a day.

questions.q: What shape is the Sun?
questions.f: The Sun is one of the roundest objects ever measured in nature.

questions.q: Which word means 'very, very far away'?
questions.f: 'Distant' comes from Latin words meaning 'standing apart' - stars stand very far apart indeed.

questions.q: What must a space helmet always keep inside it?
questions.f: A helmet also has a tiny sponge pad astronauts can rub against to scratch an itchy nose.

questions.q: When people say 'It's not rocket science', they mean something is not very ___?
questions.f: Building rockets is so tricky that its name became a byword for hard work everywhere.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the word for a machine that orbits Earth?
questions.f: Remember double-l in the middle: sa-TEL-lite, from a Latin word for a companion.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the word for a space traveller?
questions.f: Astro plus naut: two Greek pieces meaning 'star' and 'sailor'.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the word for a far-seeing sky instrument?
questions.f: Tele means far and scope means to look - so a telescope is a 'far-looker'.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'night'?
questions.f: Poets love the night-light-bright rhyme family for writing about the sky.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'space'?
questions.f: The 1960s contest to reach the Moon really was called the Space Race.

questions.q: 'Sunrise' is built from which two words?
questions.f: On the space station, astronauts see about sixteen sunrises every single day.

questions.q: What do we call a giant cloud of gas and dust in space where new stars are born?
questions.f: 'Nebula' is simply the Latin word for cloud or mist.

questions.q: Which is hotter: the Sun or a campfire?
questions.f: The Sun's surface is thousands of degrees - far hotter than any fire you could build.

questions.q: What do we call the machines we send to explore planets with no people aboard?
questions.f: 'Probe' means something that pokes ahead to find out what is there.

questions.q: What kind of weather makes stargazing hard?
questions.f: That is why big telescopes are built on high, dry mountains where clouds are rare.

questions.q: Before flying to space, astronauts must spend years doing what?
questions.f: Astronaut training includes swimming, flying jets, and even learning another language.

questions.q: 'Countdown' is built from which two words?
questions.f: At the end of the count, engineers shout 'we have lift-off' - a phrase everyone knows.

questions.q: Which of these is a real planet in our solar system?
questions.f: Neptune is so far away that it has completed only one orbit since it was discovered.

questions.q: How many letters are in the planet name 'Mars'?
questions.f: Mars has the shortest name of all eight planets - and it is the fourth one from the Sun.

questions.q: Which planet's name begins with the letter J?
questions.f: Jupiter is the only planet whose name starts with J - and it is the biggest of them all.

questions.q: Which planet's name ends with the letters '-urn'?
questions.f: Saturn was named after a Roman god of harvests, whose festival became a winter party.

questions.q: Glowing green and pink curtains of light near the North Pole are called the northern ___?
questions.f: They appear when tiny particles from the Sun crash into the air high above the poles.

questions.q: Which is farther away from you: the Moon or the stars?
questions.f: Even the nearest star is about a hundred million times farther away than the Moon.

questions.q: How many hours does one Earth day last?
questions.f: One day is one full spin of Earth - and that spin is very slowly getting slower.

questions.q: What do we call twelve o'clock at night, when the sky is darkest?
questions.f: 'Midnight' means the middle of the night - the halfway point between sunset and sunrise.

questions.q: Which scientist studies rocks, including the rocks brought back from the Moon?
questions.f: One Apollo astronaut, Harrison Schmitt, was a real geologist who studied Moon rocks himself.

questions.q: The 'uni' at the start of 'universe' means what?
questions.f: 'Universe' means 'turned into one' - everything there is, gathered into a single whole.

questions.q: What do astronauts usually wear inside the space station?
questions.f: Bulky spacesuits are only needed outside - inside, the station is warm and full of air.

questions.q: Which animal name belongs to a real constellation?
questions.f: Leo the Lion is one of the oldest named star patterns, listed by astronomers long ago.

questions.q: Which is usually bigger: a planet or the moon that circles it?
questions.f: Earth's Moon is unusually large for its planet - about one quarter of Earth's width.

questions.q: 'Weightless' means having no what?
questions.f: Astronauts are not truly weightless - they are falling around Earth, which feels the same.

questions.q: A rocket does not need air to push against in order to fly in space.
questions.f: A rocket pushes on its own hot exhaust, so it works even better where there is no air.

questions.q: What do we call a sudden bright burst of light and energy from the Sun?
questions.f: A big flare can release more energy in minutes than people use in a whole year.

questions.q: Which word means a journey made to explore somewhere new?
questions.f: Space station crews are officially called Expeditions, and they are numbered in order.

questions.q: What do we call the room where scientists test things and do experiments?
questions.f: The space station is really a floating laboratory with several science rooms joined together.

questions.q: Earth takes one year to circle the Sun. What do we call the four parts of that year?
questions.f: Seasons happen because Earth leans over as it travels - not because it moves nearer the Sun.

questions.q: What do engineers use on Earth to send messages to faraway spacecraft?
questions.f: Some of these dishes are as wide as a football pitch, listening for whisper-faint signals.

questions.q: What does the space station use to grab arriving cargo ships?
questions.f: The station's long robot arm can inch its way along the outside like a giant caterpillar.

questions.q: About how many sunrises do space station astronauts see each day?
questions.f: The station laps the whole planet every 90 minutes, so day and night flash past constantly.

questions.q: How many stars are there in our solar system?
questions.f: Our single star is the Sun - but most star systems in the galaxy have two or more.

questions.q: What do we call the dark shape you make when you stand in the way of sunlight?
questions.f: Eclipses are just very big shadows - one sky object's shadow landing on another.

questions.q: What do we call the old broken pieces of rockets and satellites still circling Earth?
questions.f: Even a tiny fleck of space junk can crack a window, so spacecraft are built extra tough.

questions.q: Some rockets carry only cargo, with no people on board at all.
questions.f: Robot cargo ships deliver food, water, and science kit - some can even dock all by themselves.

questions.q: Which planet shines so brightly at dusk that people nicknamed it the 'evening star'?
questions.f: Venus outshines every true star because its thick clouds bounce back most of the sunlight that hits them.

questions.q: What are the colorful stripes that wrap around the planet Jupiter?
questions.f: Jupiter's cloud stripes race in opposite directions, stirred by winds faster than any hurricane on Earth.

questions.q: Which two planets have no moons at all?
questions.f: Every other planet has at least one moon - Saturn and Jupiter have well over a hundred between them!

questions.q: Deep-blue Neptune is named after the Roman god of what?
questions.f: Neptune's ocean-blue color made the sea god's name a perfect fit - though its 'blue' comes from methane gas.

questions.q: Where on Earth do astronauts practice their spacewalks?
questions.f: Floating underwater beside a sunken model of the space station feels a lot like floating in space.

questions.q: What do we call it when a returning space capsule lands in the ocean?
questions.f: Ships with helicopters wait nearby to scoop up the capsule and its crew within minutes.

questions.q: What is the team on the ground called that guides astronauts through their mission?
questions.f: Rows of experts watch every heartbeat of the flight - each desk has its own special job.

questions.q: Satellites circling Earth help scientists do which everyday job?
questions.f: Weather satellites photograph storms from above, so warnings can reach people days early.

questions.q: The International Space Station is about as big as what?
questions.f: It took more than 40 rocket flights to carry the station up piece by piece, like giant LEGO.

questions.q: You can sometimes see the space station from your backyard, looking like a bright moving star.
questions.f: It looks like a fast, silent star gliding across the sky - websites can tell you exactly when to look!

questions.q: What mainly makes the ocean rise and fall in tides each day?
c: The Moon's gravity pulling on the water
questions.f: The Moon pulls Earth's water into gentle bulges, so shores see high tide about twice a day.

questions.q: What sits at the north and south poles of Mars?
questions.f: Mars's polar caps hold water ice plus frozen carbon dioxide - the same stuff as dry ice.

questions.q: What is Ingenuity, which made history on Mars in 2021?
c: A tiny helicopter that flew there
questions.f: Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet - and its first hop lasted just 39 seconds.

questions.q: Why must astronauts exercise about two hours every day in space?
c: To keep their muscles and bones strong
questions.f: Without gravity to push against, muscles and bones weaken - so astronauts run on special treadmills.

questions.q: About how far above Earth does outer space begin?
questions.f: That invisible boundary is only about an hour's highway drive away - straight up!

questions.q: Which organization builds and launches India's rockets?
questions.f: The Indian Space Research Organisation once carried rocket parts by bicycle and bullock cart in its early days!

questions.q: NASA is the famous space agency of which country?
questions.f: NASA was created in 1958, the year after the very first satellite reached orbit.

questions.q: What do we call a mountaintop building with a rolling roof, built for giant telescopes?
questions.f: 'Observatory' comes from a Latin word meaning 'to watch' - and its dome slides open at night.

questions.q: Which time word is an old cousin of the word 'moon'?
questions.f: A month was originally one full cycle of the Moon - 'moon' and 'month' grew from the same word.

questions.q: If you 'space out' during class, what are you doing?
questions.f: English borrows space words for feelings - you can also be 'starry-eyed' or 'over the moon'.

questions.q: Finish the saying: 'Shoot for the Moon - even if you miss, you will land among the ___.'
questions.f: The saying is a favorite of teachers and coaches - aiming high pays off even when you fall short.

questions.q: An aquanaut explores under the sea. The word part 'naut' means what?
questions.f: An astronaut is literally a 'star sailor' - sailing the sea of space instead of water.

questions.q: In space stories, what do aliens often call a person from Earth?
questions.f: The ending '-ling' means a small member of a group - like duckling, seedling, and Earthling.

questions.q: A telescope studies faraway things. Which tool studies tiny things instead?
questions.f: 'Micro' means small and 'tele' means far - the ending 'scope' means an instrument for looking.

questions.q: What do we call the imaginary line through Earth that it spins around?
questions.f: Earth's axis is tilted like a leaning spinning top - that tilt is why we have seasons.

questions.q: What opens above a returning space capsule to slow its fall?
questions.f: Capsule parachutes are huge - some could cover half a basketball court each, and three open together.

questions.q: What do we call a night when dozens of shooting stars streak across the sky?
questions.f: Meteor showers happen when Earth flies through a trail of dust left behind by a comet.

questions.q: Solar panels on rooftops and spaceships turn what into electricity?
questions.f: The space station's solar wings stretch wider than a passenger jet's wingspan.

questions.q: The word 'solar' means anything to do with the ___?
questions.f: It comes from 'sol', the Latin name for the Sun - which also hides inside the word 'parasol'.

questions.q: The word 'lunar' means anything to do with the ___?
questions.f: It comes from 'luna', the Latin name for the Moon - the Romans pictured Luna driving a silver chariot.

questions.q: How many planets have human beings walked on so far?
questions.f: People have only walked on the Moon - and the Moon is a moon, not a planet!

questions.q: Our Sun is actually a medium-sized star, not a giant one.
questions.f: Some stars are so huge that a million Suns could line up across them - ours is comfortably average.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the word for an icy space visitor with a glowing tail?
questions.f: One m, one t - 'comet' comes from a Greek word meaning 'long-haired star'.

questions.q: What protects a space capsule from fierce heat as it returns to Earth?
questions.f: Rubbing against the air makes a returning capsule glow hotter than lava - the shield takes the heat.

questions.q: Why do rockets drop off big empty sections as they climb?
c: To get lighter and go faster
questions.f: Dropping empty fuel tanks is like a runner tossing away empty water bottles mid-race.

questions.q: If something happens 'once in a blue moon', how often does it happen?
questions.f: A 'blue moon' is a rare second full moon in one calendar month - the Moon does not actually turn blue.

questions.q: What are the darker, cooler patches that appear on the Sun's surface called?
questions.f: A single sunspot can be bigger than the whole Earth - they mark tangles in the Sun's magnetism.

questions.q: Jupiter takes its name from the Roman god who ruled as what?
questions.f: Fittingly, the planet named for the king of the gods is bigger than all the others put together.

questions.q: The constellation name 'Ursa Major' means the Great ___?
questions.f: 'Ursa' is Latin for bear - and 'Ursa Minor' next to it is the Little Bear.

questions.q: Why does the Hubble Space Telescope take sharper pictures than telescopes on the ground?
c: It sits above Earth's blurry air
questions.f: Hubble has been orbiting since 1990 and has taken well over a million observations.

questions.q: What do astronomers call the Moon when its bright part is growing each night?
questions.f: 'Wax' here is an old word meaning to grow - the opposite of 'wane', to shrink.

questions.q: If the Moon's lit part is shrinking each night, the Moon is said to be doing what?
questions.f: 'Wane' also survives in the phrase 'her interest waned' - meaning it faded away.

questions.q: Which planet is circled by a huge orange-hazed moon called Titan?
questions.f: Titan has rivers and lakes - but they are filled with liquid methane, not water.

questions.q: Which of these is the real science of studying stars and planets?
questions.f: Astronomy uses telescopes and measurements; astrology is an old belief system, not science.

questions.q: The word part 'geo' in 'geology' and 'geography' means what?
questions.f: So a geologist studies Earth's rocks, and a geographer maps Earth's places.

questions.q: Which scientist worked out the laws of gravity after wondering about a falling apple?
questions.f: Newton realised the same force pulling the apple down also holds the Moon in its orbit.

questions.q: Which is closer to Earth: the space station or the Moon?
questions.f: The Moon is around a thousand times farther out than the space station.

questions.q: Travelling from Earth toward the Sun, which planet would you reach first?
questions.f: Venus comes closer to Earth than any other planet ever does.

questions.q: All the other planets in the solar system could fit inside Jupiter.
questions.f: Jupiter is so vast that its mass is more than twice that of all the other planets combined.

questions.q: Which mission first carried humans down onto the Moon's surface?
questions.f: Six Apollo missions landed people on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

questions.q: What does a GPS receiver in a phone or car use satellites to work out?
questions.f: GPS needs signals from several satellites at once to pin down your spot on Earth.

questions.q: In 'GPS', what does the letter P stand for?
questions.f: GPS means Global Positioning System - it works anywhere on the planet, day or night.

questions.q: What is a space probe?
c: A robot spacecraft with no crew aboard
questions.f: Probes can survive journeys of many years - far longer than a human crew could manage.

questions.q: The word 'planet' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: Ancient sky-watchers noticed these few bright dots wandered against the fixed stars.

questions.q: The word 'galaxy' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: That is why our galaxy's hazy band across the sky is called the Milky Way.

questions.q: The word 'asteroid' was built to mean '___-like'?
questions.f: Through early telescopes asteroids looked like tiny points of light, just like stars.

questions.q: The word 'satellite' comes from a Latin word for what?
questions.f: Romans used it for the followers who trailed after an important person - just as moons trail planets.

questions.q: A cosmonaut's title literally means a sailor of the ___?
questions.f: 'Cosmos' means the ordered universe, so cosmonauts are 'universe sailors'.

questions.q: In everyday English, calling a number 'astronomical' means it is what?
questions.f: Space distances are so huge that the word for sky science became a word for hugeness.

questions.q: India's 'Chandrayaan' missions have a name that means what?
questions.f: 'Chandra' means Moon and 'yaan' means vehicle - a beautifully literal mission name.

questions.q: India's Mars mission was nicknamed 'Mangalyaan'. What does 'Mangal' mean?
questions.f: Mangal is the Sanskrit name for the planet Mars - and also gives Tuesday its Hindi name.

questions.q: Which sea creature also gives its name to a constellation of the zodiac?
questions.f: Cancer means crab in Latin - and Pisces, the fishes, is another watery star pattern.

questions.q: Which lasts longer: one day on Earth or one day on Mars?
questions.f: A Martian day runs about 37 minutes longer, so rover teams slowly drift out of step with Earth clocks.

questions.q: More than a million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
questions.f: About 1.3 million Earths would pack into the Sun's volume - our star is a true giant.

questions.q: Which four planets are the small rocky ones nearest the Sun?
questions.f: Astronomers call them the terrestrial planets, from a Latin word meaning earthy.

questions.q: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are known together as the ___ planets?
questions.f: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, while Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants.

questions.q: What do we call the invisible layer high above us that blocks harmful rays from the Sun?
questions.f: Ozone is a special form of oxygen - a thin shield only millimetres thick if squeezed together.

questions.q: Earth behaves like a giant magnet, which is why compasses work.
questions.f: Earth's magnetic field also deflects particles from the Sun, protecting life below.

questions.q: An Apollo astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather together on the Moon. What happened?
c: They hit the ground at the same moment
questions.f: With no air to slow the feather, both fell at exactly the same rate - just as Galileo predicted.

questions.q: What do we call a spacecraft built to circle a planet and study it from above?
questions.f: Missions often send an orbiter and a lander together - one maps, one touches down.

questions.q: The word 'rover', used for Mars robots, means one who does what?
questions.f: 'Roving' once described wandering travellers - a perfect name for a wheeled explorer.

questions.q: Which planet is named after the swift Roman messenger god with winged sandals?
questions.f: It suits the planet perfectly - Mercury races around the Sun faster than any other.

questions.q: Which planet is named after the Roman goddess of love and beauty?
questions.f: Venus is the only planet named after a goddess rather than a god.

questions.q: The word 'gravity' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: That same root gives us 'grave' for serious matters - things with real weight.

questions.q: One year on Jupiter lasts about twelve Earth years.
questions.f: Jupiter's slow, wide orbit means a child born there would not have a first birthday until age twelve!

questions.q: Which planet pulls with the strongest gravity?
questions.f: On Jupiter's cloud tops you would feel more than twice as heavy as you do at home.

questions.q: Which is bigger: the Sun or Jupiter?
questions.f: About a thousand Jupiters would fit inside the Sun - and Jupiter is the largest planet.

questions.q: Saturn is not the only planet with rings.
questions.f: Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune all have faint rings - Saturn's are simply bright and showy.

questions.q: How many bright stars line up to make Orion's Belt?
questions.f: Those three stars are a favourite signpost - a line drawn through them points toward Sirius.

questions.q: Which famous constellation is pictured as a hunter wearing a belt?
questions.f: Orion is visible from nearly everywhere on Earth, which is why so many cultures named it.

questions.q: The sparkling star cluster called the Pleiades is also known by which nickname?
questions.f: In India the same cluster is Krittika, and in Japan it lends its name to a famous car badge.

questions.q: Halley's Comet is famous because it does what?
questions.f: Because of that timing, most people get only one chance in a lifetime to see it.

questions.q: How do astronauts brush their teeth in space?
c: They use a little water and swallow the toothpaste
questions.f: Swallowing is easier than chasing floating blobs of foam around the cabin!

questions.q: What happens if an astronaut cries in space?
c: Tears cling to their eyes in wobbly blobs
questions.f: With no gravity to pull them down, tears pool up and have to be wiped away.

questions.q: Why do astronauts use liquid salt and pepper instead of shakers?
c: Loose grains would float away and get in their eyes
questions.f: Almost everything on the station comes in squeeze bottles or sealed pouches for this reason.

questions.q: The space station toilet does its job using what instead of flushing water?
questions.f: Waste water is even cleaned and recycled - astronauts joke that yesterday's coffee is today's coffee.

questions.q: Which country built and operates the Tiangong space station?
questions.f: 'Tiangong' means 'heavenly palace' - a name from old Chinese stories.

questions.q: Which star pattern is most often used to help find the Pole Star?
questions.f: Follow the two stars at the end of the Dipper's bowl and they point almost exactly at Polaris.

questions.q: The word 'stellar' describes something to do with what?
questions.f: 'Stella' is Latin for star - which is why a brilliant performance is called stellar.

questions.q: 'Interstellar' travel means travelling between what?
questions.f: The prefix 'inter' means between - as in international, meaning between nations.

questions.q: There are more stars in the Milky Way than there are people on Earth.
questions.f: Our galaxy holds well over a hundred billion stars - many times the human population.

questions.q: The Sun has enough fuel to keep shining for billions more years.
questions.f: Our star is roughly middle-aged, with around five billion years of steady shining still ahead.

questions.q: Which Indian scientist is remembered as the father of India's space programme?
questions.f: India's Moon lander Vikram was named in his honour.

questions.q: What do we call the dusty, powdery soil that covers the Moon's surface?
questions.f: Moon dust is sharp and clingy - it scratched Apollo visors and stuck to everything.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the word for the study of the sky?
questions.f: It ends like 'economy' and 'anatomy' - the '-nomy' part means arranging or ordering.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the name of our galaxy's shape?
questions.f: Spiral galaxies have curving arms of stars that wind outward from a bright centre.

questions.q: Which word means a machine that lands gently on another world?
questions.f: India's Vikram lander touched down near the Moon's south pole in 2023.

questions.q: When astronauts say 'Roger', what do they mean?
questions.f: 'Roger' was once the radio codeword for the letter R, short for 'received'.

questions.q: What does the flight term 'Copy that' mean?
questions.f: Space radio talk is full of short, clear phrases so nothing gets misheard.

questions.q: The word part 'aero' in 'aerospace' and 'aeroplane' means what?
questions.f: 'Aerospace' joins air and space - the two places flying machines travel.

questions.q: The word 'orbit' comes from a Latin word for what?
questions.f: Roman carts left curved ruts in the road - and planets trace curved tracks around the Sun.

questions.q: Venus can appear as both a morning star and an evening star.
questions.f: Ancient Greeks thought they were two different objects and gave each its own name.

questions.q: Who first turned a telescope on the night sky and saw mountains on the Moon?
questions.f: Galileo's rough sketches of the Moon's shadows proved it was a rugged world, not a smooth lamp.

questions.q: What do we call the powerful bottom section of a rocket that lifts it off the pad?
questions.f: Boosters do the hardest work in the first two minutes, then fall away once they are empty.

questions.q: What do engineers call the forward push that a rocket engine makes?
questions.f: A rocket only rises when its thrust beats its weight - otherwise it just sits there rumbling.

questions.q: What do we call the cargo that a rocket is built to carry into space?
questions.f: A payload can be a satellite, a telescope, or a whole crew capsule.

questions.q: What do we call it when two spacecraft join together in orbit?
questions.f: Docking must be gentle - the two ships close in at little more than walking pace.

questions.q: What do we call the small sealed room astronauts pass through to go outside?
questions.f: The air is pumped out first so none is wasted when the outer door opens.

questions.q: What do we call each big section that is joined together to build a space station?
questions.f: Modules arrive folded up inside rockets and are bolted on like train carriages.

questions.q: Astronauts get slightly taller during a long stay in space.
questions.f: Without gravity squashing them, the discs in their spine spread out - and shrink again back home.

questions.q: Why do astronauts' faces often look puffy during their first days in orbit?
c: Body fluids drift upward without gravity
questions.f: Astronauts nickname it 'puffy face, bird legs' - fluid shifts up and the legs go thin.

questions.q: In space, sunlight is fiercer than on Earth because there is no air to soften it.
questions.f: That is why spacesuit visors carry a gold coating and station windows have shutters.

questions.q: Which planet has the largest canyon system in the solar system?
questions.f: Valles Marineris is so long it would stretch right across the United States.

questions.q: Which planet is the second largest in our solar system?
questions.f: Saturn is wide but light - it is the only planet less dense than water.

questions.q: The word 'hemisphere' means what?
questions.f: 'Hemi' means half and 'sphere' means ball - so Earth has northern and southern halves.

questions.q: What is the distance straight across a circle or a planet called?
questions.f: Earth's diameter is about 12,742 kilometres - just over three times the Moon's.

questions.q: You must never look at a solar eclipse without special eclipse glasses.
questions.f: Ordinary sunglasses are far too weak - eclipse filters block almost all of the Sun's light.

questions.q: What do we call a printed map that shows where the stars are in the night sky?
questions.f: Star charts have guided sailors, farmers, and festival-planners for thousands of years.

questions.q: What do radio telescopes collect from space?
questions.f: Radio dishes can study clouds of gas that are completely invisible to ordinary telescopes.

questions.q: Astronauts have grown and eaten fresh lettuce on the space station.
questions.f: Space-grown lettuce, and even chilli peppers, have been served up in orbit.

questions.q: What happens to the space station's rubbish and dirty laundry?
c: It burns up in a cargo ship on the way down
It is buried on the Moon
questions.f: Old cargo ships are packed with waste and deliberately burn up high over the ocean.

questions.q: The word part 'micro' in 'microgravity' means what?
questions.f: Scientists say microgravity, not zero gravity - there is still a whisper of gravity up there.

questions.q: What are the glowing lights near the South Pole called?
questions.f: They are the twin of the northern lights, and both are named after Aurora, goddess of dawn.

questions.q: Which planet has dust storms that can grow to cover the entire world?
questions.f: One giant Martian storm in 2018 blotted out the sunlight and ended a rover's mission.

questions.q: Besides Earth, which planet has clearly tilted seasons that scientists can watch?
questions.f: Mars leans about 25 degrees, close to Earth's 23.5 - so its polar caps grow and shrink each year.

questions.q: When a launch is called off at the last minute, engineers say it has been what?
questions.f: Launches get scrubbed for tiny reasons - a stray boat, a gust of wind, or one stubborn valve.

questions.q: What do we call the pointed nose cone that shields a satellite during launch?
questions.f: Once the rocket is above the thick air the fairing splits open like a clam and drops away.

questions.q: Which gas is often burned with liquid oxygen to power powerful rocket engines?
questions.f: Hydrogen and oxygen burn so cleanly that the exhaust is mostly plain water vapour.

questions.q: What is the dome-shaped window room on the space station called?
questions.f: With seven windows, the cupola gives the best view of Earth anywhere in the solar system.

questions.q: Which of these does a weather satellite watch from orbit?
questions.f: Satellites spotted the eye of hurricanes long before any plane could safely fly into one.

questions.q: Which word describes a spacecraft with no people aboard?
questions.f: Most spacecraft ever launched have been uncrewed - robots reach places people cannot.

questions.q: What do we call the small embroidered badge designed for each space mission?
questions.f: Crews help design their own patch, often hiding little jokes and symbols in the artwork.

questions.q: The Russian spacecraft 'Soyuz' has a name that means what?
questions.f: Soyuz capsules have carried crews for over fifty years - the longest-serving spaceship design.

questions.q: About how long does the space station stay in Earth's shadow each orbit?
questions.f: Night lasts under an hour up there, so the station's solar wings must charge batteries fast.

questions.q: Which of these is a real Moon landing site name?
questions.f: Early astronomers mistook the Moon's dark plains for seas, and the poetic names stuck.

questions.q: Why did early astronomers name dark patches on the Moon 'seas'?
c: They thought the smooth dark areas held water
questions.f: They are really vast plains of hardened lava - the Latin word for them, 'maria', means seas.

questions.q: What do we call the huge assembly building where rockets are stacked upright?
questions.f: NASA's assembly building is so tall that clouds have formed near its ceiling.

questions.q: Which word means to send a spacecraft up into space?
questions.f: Watch the spelling: launch has 'au' - lunch is what you eat afterwards!

questions.q: Which planet is nearest to Earth's size and mass?
questions.f: Venus is Earth's near-twin in size, yet its surface is hot enough to melt lead.

questions.q: The word 'terrestrial' describes something belonging to what?
questions.f: So an 'extraterrestrial' would be something from beyond Earth.

questions.q: What do we call an object from space that is smaller than an asteroid, just a speck of dust?
questions.f: Millions of these specks hit Earth's air daily, adding tonnes of space dust to our planet.

questions.q: Earth gains many tonnes of space dust every single day.
questions.f: Most of it burns to powder high up and drifts down so gently that nobody notices.

questions.q: Which is a real name of one of Saturn's moons?
questions.f: Enceladus shoots icy fountains from cracks near its south pole.

questions.q: What do we call the point in the sky directly above your head?
questions.f: 'Zenith' also means the highest point of anything - the zenith of a career, for example.

questions.q: What do we call a group of satellites working together, like the GPS fleet?
questions.f: Astronomers use 'constellation' for star patterns; engineers borrowed it for satellite teams.

questions.q: Which is bigger: the Milky Way or the solar system?
questions.f: The solar system is one tiny speck among hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way.

questions.q: Which of these is a dwarf planet?
questions.f: Eris is so far out and so icy that it takes about 557 years to circle the Sun once.

questions.q: Which word describes rocks and dust that orbit between Mars and Jupiter?
questions.f: Even if you gathered every asteroid together, they would not make one decent-sized moon.

questions.q: What do scientists call a moon or planet that always keeps the same face toward its partner?
questions.f: Many big moons in the solar system are tidally locked to their planets, just like ours.

questions.q: Which planet's name comes last in alphabetical order?
questions.f: Alphabetically the planets run Earth, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Neptune, Saturn, Uranus, Venus.

questions.q: What do we call a very bright meteor that outshines the planets?
questions.f: A really brilliant fireball can cast shadows on the ground for a second or two.

questions.q: Which everyday invention was improved by space research on lightweight materials?
questions.f: Memory foam was developed to cushion aircraft and spacecraft seats before it reached mattresses.

questions.q: What is the job of a flight controller in Mission Control?
c: Watching one system and advising the crew
questions.f: Each controller has a call sign for their speciality, like 'Guidance' or 'Comms'.

questions.q: Which word means the height of something above the ground?
questions.f: Confusingly, spacecraft engineers use 'attitude' too - it means which way the craft is pointing.

questions.q: What do we call a satellite that always stays above the same spot on Earth?
questions.f: Television dishes can point at one fixed patch of sky because the satellite never seems to move.

questions.q: Sound cannot travel through space, but radio signals can.
questions.f: Radio waves are not sound - they need no air, which is why we can talk to distant probes.

questions.q: What do we call the huge cloud of glowing gas thrown off by a dying star?
questions.f: Confusingly they have nothing to do with planets - early observers just thought they looked round.

questions.q: Which of these jobs would help design a spacesuit?
questions.f: A modern spacesuit has more than a dozen layers and costs as much as a small house.

questions.q: What does the 'tele' in 'telescope' and 'television' mean?
questions.f: So television literally means 'far seeing' - and a telescope is a far-looker.

questions.q: What do we call the shining trail of gas and dust a comet leaves as it nears the Sun?
questions.f: Big comets can grow tails millions of kilometres long, yet they weigh almost nothing.

questions.q: The word 'constellation' is built from Latin parts meaning what?
questions.f: 'Con' means with and 'stella' means star - a constellation is literally a company of stars.

questions.q: The word 'equinox' is built from Latin parts meaning what?
questions.f: On the two equinoxes, day and night are almost exactly the same length everywhere on Earth.

questions.q: A 'heliocentric' model of the solar system puts what at the centre?
questions.f: 'Helios' is the Greek Sun - Copernicus published this Sun-centred idea in 1543.

questions.q: Which astronomer argued that Earth circles the Sun, not the other way round?
questions.f: His book appeared in the year he died - a quiet ending to a world-changing idea.

questions.q: An old 'geocentric' model of the universe placed which body at the centre?
questions.f: Ptolemy's Earth-centred system was used for well over a thousand years.

questions.q: Scientists call a single Martian day by which short name?
questions.f: Rover teams live on 'sol time', drifting 37 minutes later each day relative to Earth.

questions.q: In China, people who fly to space are often called taikonauts, from a word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Taikong' means outer space - so a taikonaut is a space sailor, just like an astronaut.

questions.q: India's crewed spaceflight programme 'Gaganyaan' has a name meaning what?
questions.f: 'Gagan' means sky and 'yaan' means vehicle - the same 'yaan' as in Chandrayaan.

questions.q: India's solar observatory Aditya-L1 is named after a word meaning what?
questions.f: Aditya is an ancient Sanskrit name for the Sun - fitting for a Sun-watching spacecraft.

questions.q: In the Indian calendar, 'Purnima' refers to which lunar phase?
questions.f: 'Amavasya' is the opposite - the dark night of the new moon.

questions.q: Which is the brightest star in Earth's night sky?
questions.f: Sirius looks so bright partly because it is close - only about 8.6 light-years away.

questions.q: About how old is the universe?
questions.f: Astronomers measure it from the faint afterglow of heat left over from the universe's first moments.

questions.q: About how old is planet Earth?
questions.f: The oldest bits of Earth we can date are tiny crystals of the mineral zircon.

questions.q: What do astronomers call the band around a star where liquid water could survive?
questions.f: It is nicknamed the Goldilocks zone - not too hot, not too cold, but just right.

questions.q: Which colour of star is the hottest?
questions.f: It feels backwards, but blue flames and blue stars are both hotter than red ones.

questions.q: Which of Jupiter's moons is most likely to hide a salty ocean under its icy crust?
questions.f: Europa's ice is crisscrossed with cracks, hinting at a moving ocean beneath.

questions.q: About how long is one full day-and-night cycle on the Moon?
questions.f: That means a Moon base would face roughly two weeks of unbroken darkness at a time.

questions.q: If you weigh 60 kg on Earth, roughly what would you weigh on Mars?
questions.f: Martian gravity is about 38 percent of Earth's, so a high jump there would be spectacular.

questions.q: India's Chandrayaan-3 lander touched down in 2023 near which part of the Moon?
questions.f: That made India the first nation to land successfully so near the lunar south pole.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere holds most of our weather?
questions.f: 'Tropo' comes from a Greek word for turning - this is the churning, cloud-making layer.

questions.q: Airliners cruise mostly in which calm atmospheric layer?
questions.f: 'Strato' means layer - the air here sits in smooth bands with very little turbulence.

questions.q: What is the difference between a meteor and a meteorite?
c: A meteorite is one that reaches the ground
A meteorite is bigger in space
A meteor is made of ice only
questions.f: In space it is a meteoroid, in the sky a meteor, and on the ground a meteorite.

questions.q: Why is the study of weather called 'meteorology' when meteors are space rocks?
c: 'Meteor' once meant anything high in the air
questions.f: Ancient Greeks lumped clouds, rainbows, and shooting stars together as 'things up high'.

questions.q: How far away is Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun?
questions.f: Even at the speed of today's fastest probes, the journey would take tens of thousands of years.

questions.q: The word 'celestial' describes things belonging to what?
questions.f: It comes from 'caelum', the Latin word for sky - the same root as the ceiling above you.

questions.q: Which mission was the first to carry humans all the way around the Moon?
questions.f: Its crew took the famous Earthrise photograph on Christmas Eve, 1968.

questions.q: Which spacecraft carried the first crew to visit the International Space Station in 2000?
questions.f: People have now lived aboard the station without a break for over two decades.

questions.q: Why does a candle flame look round and blue in orbit?
c: Hot gas cannot rise without gravity
questions.f: On Earth rising hot air stretches a flame into a teardrop; in orbit it spreads out as a ball.

questions.q: Which was the first spacecraft to photograph the far side of the Moon?
questions.f: Its 1959 pictures were grainy and streaky, yet they revealed a landscape no human had seen.

questions.q: What is the roughly 11-year pattern in the Sun's activity called?
questions.f: At solar maximum sunspots crowd the surface and auroras spread far from the poles.

questions.q: The Moon is slowly drifting farther from Earth each year.
questions.f: It creeps away about 3.8 centimetres a year - measured by bouncing lasers off Apollo mirrors.

questions.q: Where does most of the Moon's surface get its craters from?
questions.f: With no air or rain to erase them, lunar craters can survive for billions of years.

questions.q: Temperatures on the Moon swing between roughly what extremes?
c: Around 120 C in sun and -130 C in shade
questions.f: With no atmosphere to spread the heat, sunlit and shadowed ground differ wildly.

questions.q: Which telescope, launched in 1990, needed a repair mission for its blurry mirror?
questions.f: Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993 - like giving the telescope a pair of glasses.

questions.q: Which force actually keeps the space station from flying off into deep space?
questions.f: The station is really falling around Earth forever - it just keeps missing the ground.

questions.q: What do we call a spacecraft manoeuvre that uses a planet's gravity to gain speed?
questions.f: It works like a tennis ball bouncing off a moving racquet - the planet lends a little speed.

questions.q: Which planet's rings are made of countless separate chunks, not solid hoops?
questions.f: If Saturn's rings were solid, tides from the planet would tear them apart.

questions.q: Which everyday device grew out of the need to make spacecraft computers small and light?
questions.f: The Apollo guidance computer helped drive the rush to shrink electronics down to chips.

questions.q: What does a spacecraft's 'attitude' describe?
c: How fast it spins its wheels
questions.f: Small thrusters or spinning wheels nudge a craft's attitude so its cameras aim correctly.

questions.q: What are the two main things a rocket must carry besides its fuel?
questions.f: There is no air in space, so rockets carry their own oxygen supply to burn the fuel.

questions.q: The Sun does not sit still - it orbits the centre of the Milky Way.
questions.f: One lap takes roughly 230 million years, so the Sun has circled about twenty times since it formed.

questions.q: Which of these best describes a comet's make-up?
questions.f: Astronomer Fred Whipple nicknamed comets 'dirty snowballs' - and the name stuck.

questions.q: Roughly how much of the Moon's surface can we ever see from Earth?
questions.f: The Moon rocks gently as it orbits, letting us peek slightly around both edges over time.

questions.q: What do we call the point on Earth's surface where a satellite passes directly overhead?
questions.f: Plotted over hours, a satellite's ground track traces a wavy line across the world map.

questions.q: Which word means the study of the physical nature of stars and galaxies?
questions.f: Astrophysics grew when scientists realised the same physics rules Earth and the stars alike.

questions.q: What is 'astrobiology' the search for?
questions.f: Astrobiologists study extreme deserts and deep vents on Earth to guess what alien life might need.

questions.q: Which planet did Mariner 4 photograph up close for the first time in 1965?
questions.f: Its 21 grainy pictures dashed old hopes of finding canals and forests on Mars.

questions.q: How do astronauts sleep during a long flight without floating into equipment?
c: Zipped into bags anchored in small crew cabins
questions.f: Each cabin is about the size of a phone booth, with a laptop, a light, and photos from home.

questions.q: What do we call the huge cloud from which our Sun and planets formed?
questions.f: Leftovers from that cloud became asteroids and comets - fossils of the solar system's birth.

questions.q: Which is heavier: all the planets together, or the Sun?
questions.f: The Sun holds more than 99 percent of everything in the solar system.

questions.q: What do we call a telescope that uses curved mirrors instead of lenses?
questions.f: Newton built one of the first reflectors, and nearly all giant telescopes today use mirrors.

questions.q: Why are the biggest observatories built on high mountains?
questions.f: Some sit above 4,000 metres, where astronomers need extra oxygen just to work comfortably.

questions.q: What does 'light pollution' make harder to do?
questions.f: Over a third of people on Earth can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live.

questions.q: Which prefix in 'exoplanet' tells you the planet is outside our solar system?
questions.f: 'Exo' means outside - the same root as 'exoskeleton', a skeleton worn on the outside.

questions.q: About how many exoplanets have astronomers confirmed so far?
questions.f: The first was confirmed in the 1990s - now new ones are announced almost every week.

questions.q: How do astronomers most often detect an exoplanet passing in front of its star?
c: The star changes colour to green
questions.f: That tiny dip is called a transit, and it can reveal a planet smaller than Earth.

questions.q: Which word describes a moon or planet moving in front of a more distant object?
questions.f: 'Occult' simply means hidden - so an occultation is a hiding event, nothing spooky.

questions.q: You could safely watch a partial eclipse using the shadow made by a pinhole in card.
questions.f: A pinhole projects a small image of the Sun onto the ground - safe because you look away from the Sun.

questions.q: Which of these is a real Indian observatory site famous for high-altitude astronomy?
questions.f: Hanle sits over 4,500 metres up in a cold desert - one of the world's darkest, driest skies.

questions.q: What is a 'space elevator' in engineering ideas?
c: A cable from Earth to orbit
A stairway on a launch tower
questions.f: No known material is strong enough yet - but the idea dates back to a Russian thinker in 1895.

questions.q: The word 'astral' describes something relating to what?
questions.f: 'Astral' shares its root with asterisk - the little star-shaped mark on your keyboard.

questions.q: An 'asterisk' gets its name from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: Printers named the symbol for its star shape - and 'aster' flowers are named the same way.

questions.q: The 'photo' in 'photograph' and 'photosphere' means what?
questions.f: The Sun's photosphere is its visible 'light sphere' - the layer whose glow we actually see.

questions.q: What does the prefix 'multi' tell you about a 'multistage' rocket?
c: It has many parts that separate
It launches many times a day
It uses many fuels at once
questions.f: Dropping empty stages is why rockets can reach orbit at all - a single-stage design struggles.

questions.q: The word 'lunar module' uses 'lunar' from the Latin word for what?
questions.f: Luna was also the Roman goddess who drove a silver chariot across the night sky.

questions.q: A 'circumlunar' flight does what?
questions.f: 'Circum' means around - the same prefix as in circumference and circumnavigate.

questions.q: The word 'antenna', used for radio dishes, was borrowed from a word for what?
questions.f: Early radio pioneers thought their wires looked like the delicate feelers of an insect.

questions.q: Which pair of Greek roots build the word 'microgravity'?
questions.f: 'Gravitas' meant heaviness in Latin, and 'micro' means small - a whisper of weight.

questions.q: What does the term 'spacefaring' describe?
c: Being able to travel in space
questions.f: 'Faring' is an old word for travelling - it survives in 'wayfarer' and 'farewell'.

questions.q: What does a 'gibbous' moon look like?
c: More than half lit but not full
questions.f: 'Gibbous' comes from a Latin word for hump-backed - it describes the bulging lit shape.

questions.q: The word 'crescent' comes from a Latin verb meaning what?
questions.f: That is why 'crescendo' in music means growing louder - the same root exactly.

questions.q: Which planet's family of moons is named after characters from Shakespeare's plays?
questions.f: Titania, Oberon, Puck, and Miranda all circle Uranus - a very literary planet.

questions.q: Which spacecraft flew past Pluto and sent back the first sharp pictures of it?
questions.f: It raced past in 2015 after a nine-year journey, then took over a year to send all its data home.

questions.q: Which astronomer discovered Pluto in 1930?
questions.f: He was 24 and compared photographic plates by flicking between them, hunting for a moving dot.

questions.q: What did the Great Dark Spot on Neptune turn out to be?
questions.f: When Hubble looked years later the spot had vanished - Neptune's storms come and go.

questions.q: Which planet has the fastest winds ever measured in the solar system?
questions.f: Neptune's winds can scream past at over 2,000 kilometres per hour - faster than a jet fighter.

questions.q: Which is the most volcanically active world in the solar system?
questions.f: Jupiter's pull squeezes and stretches Io, keeping its insides molten and its volcanoes erupting.

questions.q: What is unusual about the shape of Saturn's north polar storm?
questions.f: The hexagon is wider than Earth and has held its neat shape for decades.

questions.q: Which spacecraft spent 13 years studying Saturn before diving into the planet in 2017?
questions.f: It was deliberately destroyed so it could never crash into a moon that might host life.

questions.q: Saturn's rings are extremely thin compared with how wide they are.
questions.f: In many places they are only tens of metres thick - like a sheet of paper the size of a city.

questions.q: Which was the first rover to drive on Mars, back in 1997?
questions.f: It was the size of a microwave oven and travelled barely a hundred metres in total.

questions.q: Which Mars rover was designed for 90 days but kept working for about 14 years?
questions.f: Its last message came during a planet-wide dust storm that blocked the sunlight it needed.

questions.q: What powers the Curiosity rover through cold Martian nights?
c: Heat from a nuclear power source
questions.f: A nuclear generator keeps it warm and working even when dust dims the sunlight.

questions.q: What did NASA's MOXIE experiment do on Mars?
questions.f: It split carbon dioxide to make breathable oxygen - a first step toward crewed missions.

questions.q: India's Chandrayaan-1 mission made which important lunar discovery?
c: Signs of water molecules on the Moon
questions.f: Its instruments spotted water clinging to the soil, especially near the poles.

questions.q: India's Chandrayaan-3 rover was named 'Pragyan', a word meaning what?
questions.f: Its partner lander was named Vikram, honouring the founder of India's space programme.

questions.q: Which country's rover 'Zhurong' explored Mars starting in 2021?
questions.f: Zhurong is named after a fire god from ancient Chinese stories - fitting for the red planet.

questions.q: Which was the first spacecraft to land safely on Mars and send back pictures?
questions.f: Its first photo in 1976 showed rocky orange ground and its own footpad resting on the soil.

questions.q: Why does Venus have a runaway greenhouse effect?
c: It is closest to the Sun
questions.f: Venus's surface stays around 465 C day and night - hot enough to melt lead.

questions.q: What surprising thing did radar mapping reveal beneath Venus's clouds?
questions.f: Venus has more volcanoes than any other planet we know, though most seem long quiet.

questions.q: Why does Mercury have almost no atmosphere?
c: Its weak gravity and the Sun's heat strip gas away
Its magnetic field blows air off
questions.f: With no air blanket, Mercury swings from scorching daytime heat to bitter night-time cold.

questions.q: What do astronomers call the swirling disc of matter falling toward a black hole?
questions.f: Friction heats that disc until it glows brighter than entire galaxies of ordinary stars.

questions.q: What is the 'event horizon' of a black hole?
c: The boundary beyond which nothing can escape
The ring of dust around it
questions.f: Cross it and even light cannot turn back - which is exactly why black holes look black.

questions.q: In 2019 astronomers released the first direct image of what?
questions.f: Telescopes on several continents worked as one giant instrument to capture that fiery orange ring.

questions.q: What remains after a medium-sized star like the Sun runs out of fuel?
questions.f: A white dwarf is Earth-sized but incredibly dense, slowly cooling for billions of years.

questions.q: What do astronomers call the process that makes the Sun shine?
questions.f: Each second the Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium.

questions.q: Which two elements make up the great majority of the Sun?
questions.f: Those two are also the most common elements in the whole universe.

questions.q: Astronomers believe the universe is still expanding today.
questions.f: Distant galaxies are racing away from us - and the more distant they are, the faster they go.

questions.q: What do astronomers call the stretching of light from galaxies rushing away from us?
questions.f: Stretched light waves look redder - the same idea as a siren's pitch dropping as it passes.

questions.q: Which invisible substance seems to hold galaxies together with extra gravity?
questions.f: It appears to outweigh all the ordinary matter in the universe several times over.

questions.q: What is the Local Group?
c: The cluster of galaxies our Milky Way belongs to
questions.f: It holds dozens of galaxies, but the Milky Way and Andromeda are by far the two giants.

questions.q: About how wide is the Milky Way galaxy?
questions.f: Light itself needs a thousand centuries just to cross our home galaxy.

questions.q: Which two small galaxies orbit the Milky Way and are visible from the southern sky?
questions.f: They are named after Ferdinand Magellan, whose crew recorded them on their voyage.

questions.q: What will eventually happen to the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies?
c: They will swap stars and separate
questions.f: The merger is billions of years away, and stars are so far apart that few would ever crash.

questions.q: Which of these is a real space telescope built to hunt exoplanets?
questions.f: Kepler stared at one patch of sky for years and found thousands of candidate worlds.

questions.q: What does the term 'gas giant' tell you about a planet?
c: It has no solid surface to stand on
It is filled with helium balloons
It is made of solid ice
questions.f: Descend into Jupiter and the gas simply gets thicker and hotter until it acts like liquid.

questions.q: Why are Uranus and Neptune called 'ice giants' rather than gas giants?
c: They hold more water, ammonia, and methane ices
questions.f: Astronomers use 'ices' loosely here - deep inside, those materials are hot, dense fluids.

questions.q: What is the Kuiper Belt?
c: A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune
A band of hot dust near the Sun
questions.f: Pluto is one of its largest members - it was the belt's first resident to be discovered.

questions.q: Which of these is the correct order, from smallest to largest?
questions.f: Each step up in that list is a huge jump - the Milky Way holds hundreds of billions of suns.

questions.q: Which fact best explains why we have never heard sound from a rocket in space?
c: Sound needs a material like air to travel through
Rockets are silent in vacuum by design
questions.f: Astronauts do hear their ship rumble from the inside, carried through the metal itself.

questions.q: What do we call the imaginary line on Earth's surface directly below the Sun at noon?
questions.f: That point wanders between the tropics through the year as Earth's tilt shifts the seasons.

questions.q: What causes the Sun's apparent path across our sky to shift through the year?
questions.f: That tilt of about 23.5 degrees is the single reason seasons exist at all.

questions.q: Which term describes a full turn of a planet on its own axis?
questions.f: Rotation gives you a day; revolution around the Sun gives you a year.

questions.q: Which term describes one complete trip of a planet around the Sun?
questions.f: Mixing these two up is one of the commonest slips in astronomy exams.

questions.q: Why can astronauts see stars but not a blue sky from orbit?
c: There is no air to scatter sunlight into blue
questions.f: Earth's blue sky is really sunlight bouncing off air molecules - no air, no blue.

questions.q: What was the Space Shuttle's most unusual feature compared with earlier spacecraft?
c: It landed on a runway like a glider
questions.f: The Shuttle came home unpowered, gliding down for a dead-stick landing every single time.

questions.q: What is a 'solar sail' designed to catch?
questions.f: Sunlight's push is feather-faint, but it never stops - so a sail can build up huge speed.

questions.q: An object in orbit keeps circling largely because there is no air to slow it down.
questions.f: Low satellites do meet faint traces of air, which is why the space station needs regular boosts.

questions.q: What does a spacecraft's 'heat shield' actually do during re-entry?
c: Absorbs and carries away enormous heat
questions.f: Some shields are designed to char and flake away on purpose, taking the heat with them.

questions.q: Which term describes the practice of studying Earth's land and seas from satellites?
questions.f: Remote sensing tracks crops, floods, and forests across whole countries in a single pass.

questions.q: What do we call the fine ash-like dust that Apollo crews found clinging to everything?
c: Lunar dust that smelled of gunpowder
questions.f: Astronauts said the dust, once inside the cabin, gave off a faint burnt-gunpowder smell.

questions.q: The word 'orbiter', 'lander', and 'rover' all end in a suffix that means what?
questions.f: The '-er' ending turns a verb into a doer: a lander lands, a rover roves, an orbiter orbits.

questions.q: 'Extraterrestrial' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: 'Extra' means outside or beyond - the same prefix as in 'extraordinary'.

questions.q: A 'perigee' is the point where the Moon is what?
questions.f: 'Peri' means near and 'gee' comes from Gaia, the Earth - so perigee means near-Earth.

questions.q: What does the word 'supermoon' describe?
c: A full moon at its closest point to Earth
A moon twice its normal size
questions.f: A supermoon looks around 14 percent wider than a full moon at its farthest - subtle but real.

questions.q: What is the word for the shadow's dark inner core during an eclipse?
questions.f: 'Umbra' is Latin for shade - the same root as umbrella, a little shade-maker.

questions.q: Which word describes something shaped like a slightly squashed circle, as orbits are?
questions.f: Kepler showed that planets travel in ellipses, not perfect circles - a revolutionary idea.

questions.q: The 'aster' in 'disaster' and 'asteroid' refers to what?
questions.f: 'Disaster' once meant an ill-starred event - people blamed bad luck on the positions of the stars.

questions.q: Which word means a huge cloud of interstellar gas and dust, from the Latin for mist?
questions.f: Its plural is 'nebulae' - one of the loveliest plurals in all of science.

questions.q: Which word names the point in the sky directly beneath your feet, opposite the zenith?
questions.f: Both 'nadir' and 'zenith' came into European languages from Arabic star science.

questions.q: What does the term 'first light' mean for a new telescope?
c: Its very first observation of the sky
questions.f: First light is a huge moment - years of building end with one long-awaited image.

questions.q: Which word describes a star that suddenly brightens enormously, from the Latin for 'new'?
questions.f: Early observers thought a nova was a brand-new star appearing where none had been.

questions.q: What does the word 'apollo' refer to in Greek and Roman stories?
c: A god linked with light and the Sun
questions.f: NASA chose the name because Apollo drove his chariot across the sky - a fine image for Moon flights.

questions.q: NASA's Artemis Moon programme is named after Apollo's what?
questions.f: The name signals a plan to land the first woman on the Moon.

questions.q: Which word describes an object that circles a star and has cleared its orbital neighbourhood?
questions.f: That third condition is exactly the rule Pluto fails, since it shares its zone with icy neighbours.

questions.q: Which of these best describes a 'light-second'?
c: The distance light travels in one second
questions.f: It is about 300,000 kilometres - roughly the distance from Earth to the Moon in just over a second.

questions.q: Roughly how long does a radio message take to travel one way from Earth to Mars?
questions.f: That delay means rovers must handle emergencies alone - no one can steer them live.

questions.q: Why do Mars rover drivers send a whole day's instructions at once?
c: Radio delay makes live driving impossible
Rovers only work once a day
questions.f: Teams plan each move on 3D models before uploading the day's whole plan in one go.

questions.q: What is 'terraforming' an idea about?
c: Changing a planet to be more Earth-like
questions.f: 'Terra' means Earth - the word means literally 'Earth-shaping'.

questions.q: Which resource would be most valuable to a future Moon base?
questions.f: Water can be split into breathable oxygen and rocket fuel - which is why the poles matter so much.

questions.q: Why are craters near the Moon's poles especially interesting to scientists?
c: Sunlight never reaches their floors, so ice can survive
questions.f: Some crater floors have sat in permanent shadow for billions of years - cold traps for ice.

questions.q: How do scientists think Earth's Moon most likely formed?
c: A huge collision blasted debris into orbit
It was captured from another star
questions.f: The impacting body is often nicknamed Theia, after the mother of the Moon goddess in Greek stories.

questions.q: The same side of the Moon always faces Earth because it spins once per orbit.
questions.f: That neat match-up is called synchronous rotation, and it took billions of years to settle.

questions.q: Which mission gathered the very first samples ever returned from an asteroid to Earth?
questions.f: Japan's Hayabusa brought back mere specks in 2010 - and every grain was priceless.

questions.q: In 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into an asteroid to test what?
c: Whether a nudge can change an asteroid's orbit
How loud a crash sounds in space
questions.f: The impact shortened the little moonlet's orbit by far more than engineers had hoped.

questions.q: Which spacecraft landed a small probe on a comet's surface in 2014?
questions.f: Its lander Philae bounced twice before settling in shadow, running on batteries alone.

questions.q: What did astronomers name the first confirmed visitor from beyond our solar system?
questions.f: The Hawaiian name means 'a messenger from far away arriving first'.

questions.q: Which meteor shower reliably peaks every August?
questions.f: The Perseids are named for the constellation Perseus, where their streaks seem to start.

questions.q: Where does the name of a meteor shower usually come from?
c: The constellation the streaks seem to come from
questions.f: That apparent starting point is called the radiant - it shifts slightly night by night.

questions.q: What is the main reason so few meteoroids ever reach the ground?
c: They burn up from friction with the air
questions.f: Most are the size of a grain of sand and vanish more than 70 kilometres up.

questions.q: Which of these is the largest known impact crater visible on Earth's surface today?
questions.f: Vredefort's scar is so vast that you can only make out its full ring from space.

questions.q: India's Lonar Lake in Maharashtra was formed by what?
questions.f: It is one of very few impact craters in the world formed in ancient volcanic basalt rock.

questions.q: What causes the tail of a meteor to glow so brightly?
c: Air heated to glowing by the speeding rock
questions.f: The rock compresses the air ahead of it so violently that the air itself lights up.

questions.q: Which astronomer's calculations correctly predicted a comet's return, earning it his name?
questions.f: He never lived to see it come back - it returned 16 years after his death, right on schedule.

questions.q: What did Charles Messier's famous catalogue list?
c: Fuzzy objects that were not comets
questions.f: Messier was a comet hunter, so he listed these smudges mainly to avoid being fooled by them.

questions.q: Which sky object is catalogued as M31?
questions.f: At about 2.5 million light-years away, it is the farthest thing most people can see unaided.

questions.q: Why do we say looking at distant galaxies is looking back in time?
c: Their light left them long ago
questions.f: Light from Andromeda set out when our ancestors were only beginning to walk upright.

questions.q: Which telescope, launched in 1999, studies the universe in X-rays?
questions.f: It honours Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, the Indian-born scientist who explained dying stars.

questions.q: Why must X-ray telescopes be placed in space?
c: They need cold vacuum to focus
questions.f: Our air shields us from cosmic X-rays - wonderful for life, frustrating for astronomers.

questions.q: What does an infrared telescope detect?
c: Heat radiation invisible to our eyes
questions.f: Infrared sees straight through dust clouds, revealing stars being born inside them.

questions.q: Why does the James Webb Space Telescope carry a huge tennis-court-sized sunshield?
c: Its instruments must stay extremely cold
questions.f: The shield keeps one side near room temperature while the other side chills below -220 C.

questions.q: Which term describes a place where a spacecraft can hover in balance between two gravities?
questions.f: India's Aditya-L1 and the Webb telescope both park at such points to keep steady views.

questions.q: What is India's Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle usually shortened to?
questions.f: In 2017 a single PSLV flight carried a record 104 satellites into orbit at once.

questions.q: What was Aryabhata, launched by India in 1975?
questions.f: It honoured the ancient mathematician who calculated the length of the year with startling accuracy.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian astronomer explained eclipses as shadows rather than as monsters?
questions.f: Writing around 499 CE, he said the Moon simply passes into Earth's shadow - correct and bold.

questions.q: What is the giant stone instrument complex Jantar Mantar in Jaipur used for?
c: Measuring positions of the Sun and stars
questions.f: Its huge sundial can show the time to within about two seconds - built entirely of masonry.

questions.q: Ancient people built stone monuments aligned with sunrise on the solstice.
questions.f: From Stonehenge to Konark, builders across the world used the Sun itself as a giant calendar.

questions.q: What is a 'blue moon' by the most common modern definition?
c: A second full moon within one calendar month
questions.f: It happens roughly every two and a half years - hence the phrase for something rare.

questions.q: What is a 'harvest moon'?
c: The full moon nearest the autumn equinox
A moon that turns orange in spring
The first full moon of the year
A moon seen only from farms
questions.f: Its early rise gave farmers extra light for bringing in crops after sunset.

questions.q: During a total lunar eclipse, why does the Moon often glow coppery red?
c: Sunlight bends through Earth's atmosphere onto it
questions.f: You are seeing every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once, painted onto the Moon.

questions.q: Which lasts longer: a total solar eclipse or a total lunar eclipse?
questions.f: Earth's shadow is huge, so the Moon can stay inside it for over an hour.

questions.q: Why does a total solar eclipse only sweep across a narrow strip of Earth?
c: The Moon's dark shadow is small when it reaches us
questions.f: The path of totality is usually just a couple of hundred kilometres wide.

questions.q: Which of the Sun's features can be seen with the naked eye only during a total eclipse?
questions.f: 'Corona' means crown - and that pearly halo is a million times fainter than the Sun's face.

questions.q: What is the solar wind?
c: A stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun
questions.f: It blows past Earth at hundreds of kilometres per second, day and night, without stopping.

questions.q: How does Earth's magnetic field protect life from the solar wind?
c: It deflects charged particles around the planet
questions.f: Mars lost most of its magnetic shield long ago - and lost most of its atmosphere too.

questions.q: What is a 'geomagnetic storm' able to disrupt on Earth?
questions.f: Operators sometimes power down equipment on purpose when a big solar storm is forecast.

questions.q: Which colour do oxygen atoms high in our atmosphere usually glow during an aurora?
questions.f: Higher up, oxygen glows red instead, while nitrogen adds blue and pink fringes.

questions.q: Why is space described as a vacuum?
c: It contains almost no particles of matter
questions.f: Even the emptiest lab vacuum on Earth is crowded compared with the space between stars.

questions.q: Which of these would happen to an unprotected astronaut's water bottle in a vacuum?
c: The water would boil at room temperature
The water would freeze instantly and stay solid
questions.f: With no pressure holding it in, water boils away fiercely - even when it is cold.

questions.q: What is the main job of the space station's Canadarm2?
c: Moving cargo and astronauts outside the station
questions.f: It can walk end over end along the station's outside like an inchworm with hands at both ends.

questions.q: The word 'solstice' is built from Latin parts meaning what?
questions.f: For a few days the Sun's noon height barely changes - it seems to pause before turning back.

questions.q: The word 'zodiac' comes from a Greek phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Most zodiac signs are creatures - though Libra the scales sneaks in as an object.

questions.q: An 'astrolabe', the great medieval sky instrument, has a name meaning what?
questions.f: With one brass disc a navigator could tell the time, find latitude, and locate stars.

questions.q: 'Albedo', used for how much light a world reflects, comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Fresh snow has a high albedo; charcoal-dark comet crusts have among the lowest known.

questions.q: The word 'regolith' is built from Greek parts meaning what?
questions.f: It describes loose crushed rock over solid bedrock - the Moon, Mars, and Earth all have it.

questions.q: When a planet appears to move 'retrograde', the word literally means what?
questions.f: The apparent backtrack is an illusion caused by Earth overtaking the planet on the inside.

questions.q: 'Perihelion' is built from Greek parts meaning what?
questions.f: Earth reaches perihelion in early January - so northern winters happen when we are closest!

questions.q: What does 'aphelion' describe?
c: An orbit's farthest point from the Sun
questions.f: 'Apo' means away from - the same prefix as in apogee, the point farthest from Earth.

questions.q: A 'sidereal' day is measured against what?
questions.f: 'Sidus' is Latin for star - and a sidereal day is about four minutes shorter than a solar one.

questions.q: Why is the Sun's yearly path across our sky called the 'ecliptic'?
c: Eclipses happen only when the Moon crosses it
It marks the edge of the sky
It was named after a Greek king
questions.f: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so eclipses need it to sit almost exactly on that line.

questions.q: The cheerful word 'jovial' comes from the belief that people born under which planet were merry?
questions.f: Jove was another Roman name for Jupiter - so a jovial person was Jupiter-blessed.

questions.q: Someone described as 'mercurial' changes mood quickly - named after which planet's god?
questions.f: Mercury was the quicksilver messenger, and the liquid metal quicksilver bears his name too.

questions.q: The word 'martial', as in martial arts, comes from which planet's namesake god?
questions.f: Mars was the Roman god of war, and March - the old campaigning season - is named for him too.

questions.q: Which element's name honours the Greek Sun god because it was first found in sunlight?
questions.f: Helium was spotted as a mystery yellow line in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, years before it was found on Earth.

questions.q: 'Cryogenic' rocket fuel takes its name from Greek parts meaning what?
questions.f: Cryogenic engines chill hydrogen below -250 C so it will fit into the tank as a liquid.

questions.q: The aurora is named after which Roman goddess?
questions.f: 'Aurora borealis' pairs her name with Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind.

questions.q: In 'aurora australis', what does 'australis' mean?
questions.f: The same Latin word gave Australia its name - the great southern land.

questions.q: The study of the Moon is sometimes called 'selenology', after which goddess?
questions.f: The element selenium is named after her too, because it was found alongside 'moon-like' tellurium.

questions.q: In words like 'meteoroid' and 'asteroid', what does the suffix '-oid' mean?
