questions.f: So an asteroid is star-resembling and a meteoroid is meteor-resembling - both borrowed shapes.

questions.q: A comet's glowing head is called its 'coma', from a word meaning what?
questions.f: Comet and coma share that hairy idea - the ancients saw these objects as long-haired stars.

questions.q: What is the 'penumbra' during an eclipse?
c: The bright ring around the Sun
questions.f: 'Paene' means almost - so penumbra is 'almost shadow', where only part of the Sun is hidden.

questions.q: An 'annular' solar eclipse takes its name from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: The Moon sits too far to cover the Sun fully, leaving a blazing ring of fire around a black disc.

questions.q: What is the 'Kármán line' commonly used to mark?
c: The edge of the Moon's shadow
questions.f: Named after engineer Theodore von Kármán, it sits about 100 kilometres up, where wings stop working.

questions.q: One 'astronomical unit' is defined as roughly what distance?
questions.f: About 150 million kilometres - a handy ruler for measuring the solar system.

questions.q: On the star brightness scale, what does a lower magnitude number mean?
questions.f: The scale runs backwards because the Greeks ranked the brightest stars as 'first class'.

questions.q: Which type of star is by far the most common in the Milky Way?
questions.f: Red dwarfs are so faint that not one of them can be seen from Earth without a telescope.

questions.q: What is a 'brown dwarf'?
c: An object too small to sustain normal fusion
questions.f: They sit in the gap between the biggest planets and the smallest true stars.

questions.q: A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh roughly as much as what?
questions.f: Neutron stars pack more than the Sun's mass into a ball the size of a city.

questions.q: What is a pulsar?
c: A spinning neutron star sweeping beams past us
questions.f: Some spin hundreds of times a second, keeping better time than many atomic clocks.

questions.q: Which astronomer proved that Andromeda lies far outside our own galaxy?
questions.f: Overnight the universe grew from one galaxy to countless galaxies - and kept growing.

questions.q: Which astronomer discovered Uranus in 1781, the first planet ever found with a telescope?
questions.f: He was a professional musician who ground his own mirrors as a hobby.

questions.q: Kepler's laws describe planetary orbits as which shape?
c: Ellipses with the Sun at one focus
questions.f: He also found that planets speed up when nearer the Sun and slow down when farther away.

questions.q: Which four moons are known together as the Galilean moons?
questions.f: Their steady dance around Jupiter was the first proof that not everything orbits Earth.

questions.q: Which moon in the solar system has a thick atmosphere richer in nitrogen than Earth's air?
questions.f: Its air is so dense and gravity so weak that a person with strapped-on wings could flap and fly.

questions.q: Which large moon orbits its planet backwards, hinting it was captured?
questions.f: Triton also erupts icy geysers, making it one of the coldest active worlds we know.

questions.q: Pluto's largest moon Charon is named after which figure from Greek stories?
c: A giant who held the sky
questions.f: Pluto's other moons follow the theme: Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra.

questions.q: What is the huge pale heart-shaped feature that New Horizons photographed on Pluto?
c: A vast plain of nitrogen ice
questions.f: Named Tombaugh Regio, its ice slowly churns and turns over like a lava lamp in slow motion.

questions.q: Which pair of Martian moons have names meaning 'fear' and 'dread'?
questions.f: They were the horse-tending sons of Mars in Greek stories - a fittingly warlike pair.

questions.q: What does the name 'Sputnik' mean?
questions.f: The world's first satellite was a metal sphere with four whip antennas and a simple beeping radio.

questions.q: Who performed the first spacewalk in 1965?
questions.f: His suit ballooned so stiffly that he had to bleed out air just to squeeze back through the hatch.

questions.q: Who became the first woman to fly in space, in 1963?
questions.f: She was a textile worker and amateur parachutist before being chosen from over four hundred applicants.

questions.q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module that landed on the Moon?
questions.f: 'The Eagle has landed' became one of the most quoted sentences of the twentieth century.

questions.q: During Apollo 13's crisis, what did the crew use as a lifeboat?
questions.f: The little Moon lander was never designed to keep three men alive for four days - but it did.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission was the last to land people on the Moon?
questions.f: Its crew included Harrison Schmitt, the only professional geologist to walk on another world.

questions.q: Which astronaut orbited alone in the command module while two crewmates walked on the Moon?
questions.f: Passing behind the Moon he was cut off from every other human being - the loneliest place ever occupied.

questions.q: When Rakesh Sharma was asked in 1984 how India looked from orbit, what did he reply?
questions.f: His answer quoted a beloved patriotic poem and became one of India's most famous space moments.

questions.q: Which Indian-American astronaut ran a marathon while orbiting Earth?
questions.f: She ran the Boston Marathon distance on a treadmill in 2007, strapped down so she would not float off.

questions.q: What was remarkable about the cost of India's Mars Orbiter Mission?
c: It cost less than many Hollywood films
It was the most expensive Mars mission
It was funded entirely by donations
questions.f: At roughly 450 crore rupees, it worked out cheaper per kilometre than many city taxi rides.

questions.q: India's Mars Orbiter Mission made India the first nation to do what?
c: Reach Mars orbit on its first attempt
questions.f: Many earlier Mars missions by other nations failed on the first try - India's succeeded straight away.

questions.q: Which Indian president and scientist led the team behind the SLV-3 launch vehicle?
questions.f: SLV-3 put the Rohini satellite in orbit in 1980, making India the world's seventh spacefaring nation.

questions.q: What did America's first satellite, Explorer 1, unexpectedly discover in 1958?
c: Belts of trapped radiation around Earth
questions.f: They are named the Van Allen belts, after the scientist whose simple detector found them.

questions.q: At what height above the equator must a satellite orbit to stay above one spot on Earth?
questions.f: At that altitude one orbit takes exactly one day, so the satellite seems to hang motionless.

questions.q: Which famous science-fiction author first popularised the idea of geostationary communications satellites?
questions.f: He set out the idea in a 1945 magazine article, decades before the first one flew.

questions.q: Roughly what speed must a spacecraft reach to escape Earth's gravity entirely?
questions.f: That is around 40,000 kilometres per hour - fast enough to cross India in about four minutes.

questions.q: Who built and flew the world's first liquid-fuelled rocket in 1926?
questions.f: His rocket rose just 12 metres and flew for two and a half seconds - the start of everything.

questions.q: Which Russian schoolteacher worked out the mathematics of rocket flight decades before rockets flew?
questions.f: He wrote that Earth is humanity's cradle, but we cannot stay in the cradle forever.

questions.q: Which rocket carried every Apollo crew that flew to the Moon?
questions.f: Standing 111 metres tall, it burned about 20 tonnes of fuel every second at lift-off.

questions.q: Which mathematician's hand calculations helped check the flight paths of early American spaceflights?
questions.f: John Glenn asked for her to recheck the computer's numbers before he would fly.

questions.q: Who led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for the Apollo missions?
questions.f: Her code spotted an overload during the Moon landing and kept the vital tasks running.

questions.q: Who became the first American woman to fly in space, in 1983?
questions.f: She later co-founded a company to get science lessons about space into schools.

questions.q: Who was the first African-American woman to travel into space?
questions.f: She carried a poster from a dance troupe into orbit, saying science and art both belong there.

questions.q: Which of these was NOT one of NASA's Space Shuttle orbiters that flew in space?
questions.f: Enterprise was a test article used for glide landings - it never had engines for orbital flight.

questions.q: The Soviet space station 'Mir' had a name that means what?
questions.f: Mir hosted crews for 15 years and was deliberately brought down into the Pacific in 2001.

questions.q: Which was the world's first space station, launched in 1971?
questions.f: 'Salyut' means salute - a tribute to Yuri Gagarin ten years after his historic flight.

questions.q: Which atmospheric layer does the International Space Station actually orbit within?
questions.f: The thermosphere is scorching hot yet so thin that a thermometer there would read cold.

questions.q: About how much bone mass can an astronaut lose per month without countermeasures?
questions.f: That is why the station has a weight machine using vacuum cylinders instead of heavy plates.

questions.q: What was special about NASA's study of astronaut Scott Kelly and his brother Mark?
c: They are identical twins, one in space and one on Earth
They both walked on the Moon
questions.f: Comparing twins let scientists separate spaceflight effects from ordinary ageing.

questions.q: What do engineers call the moment of greatest aerodynamic stress on a climbing rocket?
questions.f: Rockets often throttle down through max Q, then push hard again once the air thins.

questions.q: In mission control language, what does the word 'nominal' mean?
questions.f: Controllers avoid excited words on the loop - 'nominal' is the highest praise a rocket can get.

questions.q: Why do many countries prefer launch sites close to the equator?
c: Earth's spin gives rockets a bigger free head start
questions.f: At the equator the ground is already moving east at about 1,670 kilometres per hour.

questions.q: India's main launch site, Satish Dhawan Space Centre, is on which island?
questions.f: Its east-coast position lets rockets drop spent stages harmlessly into the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: From which historic cosmodrome did Yuri Gagarin launch, still in use today?
questions.f: Baikonur sits in Kazakhstan, and Russia still rents the site for its launches.

questions.q: Which bright star in Orion is a red supergiant nearing the end of its life?
questions.f: It is so vast that if it replaced the Sun, it would swallow the orbit of Mars.

questions.q: Which brilliant blue-white supergiant marks the hunter's foot in Orion?
questions.f: Rigel pumps out tens of thousands of times more light than the Sun.

questions.q: What is the Orion Nebula?
c: A vast nursery where new stars are forming
questions.f: It is one of the few nebulae bright enough to be glimpsed without a telescope.

questions.q: Which famous Hubble image shows towering columns of gas in the Eagle Nebula?
questions.f: Each pillar is several light-years tall, being slowly eroded by the light of nearby young stars.

questions.q: Besides spirals, which are the two other main galaxy shapes astronomers classify?
questions.f: Giant ellipticals are thought to grow by swallowing smaller galaxies over billions of years.

questions.q: What is gravitational lensing?
c: Massive objects bending light from things behind them
Light being trapped in a lens
questions.f: It can smear a distant galaxy into arcs or rings - a natural magnifying glass in space.

questions.q: What did the LIGO detectors first observe directly in 2015?
c: Gravitational waves from two merging black holes
questions.f: The stretch they measured was smaller than a thousandth the width of a proton.

questions.q: What is Sagittarius A*?
c: The supermassive black hole at our galaxy's centre
questions.f: It holds about four million times the Sun's mass, yet stays hidden behind thick dust.

questions.q: Named for a Titan, hiding rivers of liquid methane, and the only moon beyond ours where a probe has landed - which world?
questions.f: The Huygens probe parachuted down in 2005 and heard the wind before its batteries faded.

questions.q: A Roman god of the underworld, a name suggested by a schoolgirl in Oxford, and a plain of nitrogen ice shaped like a heart: which world?
questions.f: Eleven-year-old Venetia Burney's suggestion beat hundreds of others sent in from around the world.

questions.q: A flattened forest in Siberia, thousands of square kilometres of destruction, and no crater at all point to which 1908 event?
questions.f: An object probably exploded high in the air, which is why no impact hole was ever found.

questions.q: Which meteor shower comes from an asteroid rather than a comet?
questions.f: Its parent, Phaethon, behaves oddly - a rock that sheds dust like a comet when it nears the Sun.

questions.q: The Moon has a very slight atmosphere, far too thin to breathe.
questions.f: A whisper-thin veil of gases like helium and argon clings to the surface - technically an exosphere.

questions.q: Which planet has the strongest magnetic field in the solar system?
questions.f: If we could see Jupiter's magnetic bubble from Earth, it would look larger than the full Moon.

questions.q: What is remarkable about the density of Saturn compared with water?
c: Saturn is less dense than water
Saturn is exactly as dense as water
questions.f: Its huge volume of light hydrogen and helium makes it the only planet that would float.

questions.q: Which planet is the densest in the solar system?
questions.f: Earth's heavy iron core wins narrowly over Mercury, which is squeezed less by its own weight.

questions.q: Which planet has the coldest measured temperatures in the solar system?
questions.f: Uranus once dipped to about -224 C, colder even than far more distant Neptune.

questions.q: How long does one day last on Venus, measured against the stars?
questions.f: Venus turns so slowly and backwards that its sunrise comes in the west.

questions.q: Roughly how crushing is the air pressure at Venus's surface?
questions.f: That is like the pressure nearly a kilometre deep in Earth's ocean - it crushed early landers fast.

questions.q: What are Venus's clouds mostly made of?
questions.f: Those clouds reflect so much sunlight that Venus is the brightest planet in our sky.

questions.q: What did radar find hiding in permanently shadowed craters at Mercury's poles?
questions.f: Astonishing, given daytime temperatures nearby soar past 400 C.

questions.q: Which spacecraft was the first to orbit Mercury, arriving in 2011?
questions.f: Its name was a neat backronym, and Mercury was the messenger of the Roman gods.

questions.q: Jupiter's Great Red Spot has been shrinking over the past century of observations.
questions.f: It was once wide enough to swallow three Earths; now it is closer to just one.

questions.q: What powers Io's relentless volcanoes?
c: Tidal squeezing by Jupiter and neighbouring moons
questions.f: Io is stretched and released constantly, kneading its insides into molten rock.

questions.q: Which moon of Jupiter is the only known moon with its own magnetic field?
questions.f: Ganymede is bigger than Mercury and probably has a churning liquid iron core.

questions.q: Which icy moon's south-polar geysers feed one of Saturn's outer rings?
questions.f: A spacecraft flew straight through the plumes and tasted salt and simple organic molecules.

questions.q: Which mission first landed a probe on the surface of a moon of another planet?
questions.f: Huygens survived the descent and sent back images of pebbles rounded as if by flowing liquid.

questions.q: What is unusual about the way the planet Uranus is tilted?
c: Its axis lies nearly in its orbital plane
It has no tilt at all
questions.f: That extreme lean gives each pole about 21 years of continuous sunlight, then 21 years of night.

questions.q: The star name 'Antares' was built to mean what?
questions.f: Its reddish glow really can be mistaken for Mars - hence the boastful name.

questions.q: The star name 'Regulus' in Leo means what?
questions.f: Copernicus popularised the name - a small ruler sitting at the heart of the lion.

questions.q: The name of the star 'Sirius' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: Its summer appearance before dawn gave us the phrase 'the dog days' of high summer.

questions.q: The star name 'Arcturus' was built from Greek parts meaning what?
questions.f: It trails behind Ursa Major, the Great Bear, as though keeping watch over it.

questions.q: The constellation name 'Cygnus' means what?
questions.f: Its brightest star, Deneb, marks the swan's tail - and 'deneb' means tail.

questions.q: The constellation 'Lyra' is named after which object?
questions.f: In Greek stories it was the lyre of Orpheus, whose music could charm anything alive.

questions.q: The constellation name 'Aquila' means what?
questions.f: Its brightest star, Altair, comes from an Arabic phrase for 'the flying one'.

questions.q: The zodiac name 'Aquarius' describes a person doing what?
questions.f: 'Aqua' means water - and its neighbour Pisces, the fishes, keeps the watery theme going.

questions.q: The constellation name 'Sagittarius' means what?
questions.f: 'Sagitta' is Latin for arrow - and a small constellation named Sagitta means just that.

questions.q: The constellation 'Draco' takes its name from which creature?
questions.f: Its star Thuban was the pole star when the Egyptian pyramids were being built.

questions.q: The word 'galaxy' and the Latin phrase 'Via Lactea' both refer to what?
c: A road of milk across the sky
questions.f: Greek stories said spilt milk from a goddess left the pale band across the heavens.

questions.q: The word 'zenith' reached English through a garbled copy of an Arabic phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Medieval scribes miscopied the word, and the mistake became permanent English.

questions.q: The word 'almanac', a book of sky and calendar tables, entered European languages from which language?
questions.f: Medieval Europe learned much of its practical astronomy from Arabic scholarship.

questions.q: In navigation, 'azimuth' comes from an Arabic word meaning what?
questions.f: Azimuth tells you the compass direction of an object; altitude tells you how high it sits.

questions.q: In Sanskrit tradition the pole star is called 'Dhruva Tara' - what does 'dhruva' mean?
questions.f: Every other star wheels around it, so calling it the fixed star is exactly right.

questions.q: In Indian tradition, which planet is called 'Shani'?
questions.f: Saturday is Shanivar in Hindi - the same planet-and-day pairing found across many cultures.

questions.q: Which planet is known in Indian tradition as 'Brihaspati' or 'Guru'?
questions.f: Guruvar, or Thursday, is named after it - just as Thursday honours a thunder god in English.

questions.q: In Sanskrit-derived usage, what does 'antariksh' mean?
questions.f: India's early spaceflight vocabulary drew on old Sanskrit words for sky and space.

questions.q: What does the Sanskrit term 'nakshatra' refer to in classical Indian astronomy?
c: A lunar mansion or star grouping
questions.f: Twenty-seven nakshatras divide the Moon's monthly path, one for roughly each night.

questions.q: When people say a career has reached its 'apogee', they borrow a term meaning what?
questions.f: 'Perigee' has not caught on as a word for low points - but it logically should have.

questions.q: A planet is said to be 'at opposition' when what happens?
c: It sits opposite the Sun in our sky
It passes in front of the Sun
questions.f: Opposition is the best time to observe an outer planet - closest, brightest, and up all night.

questions.q: What is a 'transit of Venus'?
c: Venus crossing the Sun's face as seen from Earth
questions.f: Transits come in pairs about eight years apart, then not again for over a century.

questions.q: What is 'earthshine'?
c: Sunlight reflected off Earth faintly lighting the Moon's dark part
The glow of city lights in space
questions.f: Leonardo da Vinci worked out the cause centuries before anyone could check it.

questions.q: What is a 'moonbow'?
c: A ring of ice around the Moon
questions.f: Moonbows look ghostly white because moonlight is too faint for our colour vision.

questions.q: Which is the darkest stage of evening twilight, used by astronomers?
questions.f: Only after astronomical twilight ends does the sky reach its faintest natural darkness.

questions.q: Why do we need leap years?
c: Earth's orbit takes about a quarter day more than 365 days
Calendars lose a day to rounding
questions.f: Without leap days, our calendar would drift by about 24 days every century.

questions.q: Why was the Gregorian calendar introduced in 1582?
c: The old calendar had drifted out of step with the seasons
questions.f: Ten dates were simply skipped that October to snap the calendar back into place.

questions.q: What is the 'midnight sun'?
c: Sunlight at midnight inside the polar circles in summer
A solar flare seen at night
questions.f: At the poles the Sun can circle the horizon for weeks without ever setting.

questions.q: How does an ion thruster differ from a chemical rocket?
c: It gives a tiny push for years instead of a huge push for minutes
It works only in an atmosphere
questions.f: Its faint blue glow could not lift a sheet of paper, yet over years it reaches astonishing speeds.

questions.q: What is 'aerobraking'?
c: Using a planet's upper air to slow a spacecraft
questions.f: It saves precious fuel, but demands dozens of careful skims through the thin outer air.

questions.q: Why do spacecraft usually lose radio contact briefly during re-entry?
c: Superheated glowing gas blocks radio signals
questions.f: That silence is called the communications blackout, and it can last several tense minutes.

questions.q: How were the Spirit and Opportunity rovers cushioned as they reached the Martian surface?
questions.f: They bounced dozens of times across the plains before rolling to a stop and unfolding.

questions.q: How was the heavy Curiosity rover lowered onto Mars?
c: On cables from a hovering sky crane
questions.f: Engineers nicknamed the sequence 'seven minutes of terror' because they could only watch and wait.

questions.q: What is NASA's Deep Space Network?
c: Giant radio dishes on three continents for talking to distant probes
A telescope array on the Moon
questions.f: Spaced roughly evenly around the globe, at least one dish can always see any distant spacecraft.

questions.q: How do probes heading far from the Sun usually generate electricity?
questions.f: Sunlight at Saturn is about a hundred times weaker than at Earth - solar panels struggle there.

questions.q: What is a CubeSat?
c: A tiny standard-sized satellite built from small cubes
questions.f: Universities and schools have flown CubeSats no bigger than a loaf of bread.

questions.q: What device lets a spacecraft turn without using any fuel?
questions.f: Spinning a heavy wheel one way makes the craft rotate the other - conservation of momentum at work.

questions.q: The Sun's light we see today left its core many thousands of years ago.
questions.f: Energy takes ages to bounce out from the core, though only eight minutes to cross to Earth.

questions.q: Which layer of the Sun lies just above the visible surface and glows red during eclipses?
questions.f: 'Chromo' means colour - it appears as a thin rosy rim at the very start of a total eclipse.

questions.q: Which strange fact about the Sun's corona still puzzles physicists?
c: It is far hotter than the surface below it
questions.f: The corona reaches millions of degrees while the surface sits near 5,500 C - heat flowing the wrong way.

questions.q: What is a coronal mass ejection?
c: A huge cloud of magnetised plasma flung off the Sun
A hole in the Sun's surface
questions.f: When one sweeps past Earth it can light up auroras and rattle power grids.

questions.q: Which spacecraft has flown closest to the Sun, dipping inside its corona?
questions.f: It shelters behind a carbon heat shield while reaching speeds near 700,000 kilometres per hour.

questions.q: What is the source of the Sun's energy according to modern physics?
questions.f: About four million tonnes of matter becomes pure energy in the Sun every single second.

questions.q: Which particles stream from the Sun in such numbers that trillions pass through you each second?
questions.f: They interact so weakly that almost all of them pass straight through the whole Earth.

questions.q: Which term describes two stars that orbit one another?
questions.f: Astronomers reckon most stars are born in pairs or larger families - our lone Sun is unusual.

questions.q: What is the nearest star system to the Sun, containing three stars?
questions.f: Its faint third member, Proxima, is the closest single star to us - and has planets.

questions.q: Which term describes a star's true total output of light, whatever its distance?
questions.f: A dim-looking star can be enormously luminous if it happens to lie very far away.

questions.q: What do astronomers call the long stable phase when a star fuses hydrogen in its core?
questions.f: Our Sun is roughly halfway through its own main-sequence life of about ten billion years.

questions.q: Which term describes the apparent shift of a nearby star as Earth moves around the Sun?
questions.f: Measuring that tiny wobble is still the most direct way to find a star's distance.

questions.q: Which spacecraft mapped the precise positions of nearly two billion stars?
questions.f: Its catalogue is so detailed that it has redrawn our map of the Milky Way's shape and history.

questions.q: A fireball over a Russian city in 2013, thousands of shattered windows, and a fragment hauled from a frozen lake: which event?
questions.f: Caught on hundreds of dashboard cameras, it became the best-recorded meteor fall in history.

questions.q: A hole in the Arizona desert long thought volcanic, an engineer who drilled for iron ore and found none, and Apollo crews training on its rim: what is it?
questions.f: Daniel Barringer spent decades and a fortune proving it was an impact - and he was right.

questions.q: Named for a Hawaiian goddess, spinning so fast it is squashed into an egg shape, and ringed as well as mooned: which dwarf planet?
questions.f: It rotates once every four hours - the fastest spin of any large body in the solar system.

questions.q: Which asteroid is occasionally bright enough to glimpse without a telescope?
questions.f: Vesta has a mountain near its south pole about twice the height of Everest.

questions.q: Which mission returned samples from the asteroid Bennu to Earth in 2023?
questions.f: The spacecraft touched the surface for only seconds, puffing gas to blow up dust into its collector.

questions.q: What is a 'near-Earth object'?
c: An asteroid or comet whose orbit brings it close to Earth's
A comet inside the asteroid belt
questions.f: Sky surveys now find thousands each year, and none of the large known ones threaten us.

questions.q: Which comet became a spectacular naked-eye sight for months during 1997?
questions.f: It was visible to the unaided eye for a record 18 months as it swung past the Sun.

questions.q: What happened to Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 in July 1994?
c: It broke apart and crashed into Jupiter
questions.f: Its fragments left dark bruises in Jupiter's clouds, some as wide as Earth, for months.

questions.q: What are the two distinct tails a bright comet often shows?
c: A curved dust tail and a straight ion tail
A hot tail and a cold tail
A north tail and a south tail
A gas tail and a rock tail
questions.f: The ion tail always points directly away from the Sun; the heavier dust lags behind in a curve.

questions.q: What is the Oort cloud believed to be?
c: A vast shell of icy bodies far beyond the planets
A ring inside the asteroid belt
A dust cloud circling the Sun's poles
questions.f: It is named after Jan Oort, and it may reach a thousand times farther out than Neptune.

questions.q: How long did Yuri Gagarin's historic first spaceflight last?
questions.f: He completed just one orbit, singing to himself on the way down, and landed by parachute.

questions.q: Which spacecraft carried the first human into orbit?
questions.f: The capsule was a sphere so that it would tumble to a safe attitude no matter how it re-entered.

questions.q: Who became the oldest person to fly in space when he returned to orbit at 77?
questions.f: He had also been the first American to orbit Earth, 36 years earlier.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of NASA's Gemini programme?
questions.f: Without Gemini's two-man rehearsals, Apollo would never have been ready by 1969.

questions.q: What happened during the Apollo-Soyuz mission of 1975?
c: American and Soviet crews docked and shook hands in orbit
Two crews raced to the Moon
A joint Mars flyby was attempted
questions.f: They needed a special adapter module because the two ships' hatches were entirely incompatible.

questions.q: Who made the first untethered spacewalk, flying free of his spacecraft in 1984?
questions.f: The resulting photograph of a lone figure against black space is one of spaceflight's most famous.

questions.q: Which spacecraft used radar to map almost the whole surface of Venus?
questions.f: Radar was essential - Venus's clouds hide the surface completely from ordinary cameras.

questions.q: What did NASA's InSight lander measure on Mars?
questions.f: It detected hundreds of quakes, revealing that Mars has a surprisingly large liquid core.

questions.q: Which country's 'Hope' probe entered Mars orbit in 2021?
questions.f: It was built in under six years, making the UAE the fifth space power to reach Mars.

questions.q: Which mission achieved the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon?
questions.f: Because the far side never faces us, the mission needed a relay satellite to send signals home.

questions.q: Which lunar crater near the south pole is a prime target for future bases?
questions.f: Its rim gets almost constant sunlight while its floor stays in permanent freezing shadow.

questions.q: What did NASA's Artemis I mission do in 2022?
c: Sent an uncrewed capsule around the Moon
questions.f: The Orion capsule travelled farther from Earth than any crew-rated spacecraft before it.

questions.q: Which milestone did SpaceX achieve for the first time in December 2015?
c: Landing an orbital-class booster upright for reuse
questions.f: Reusing boosters cut launch costs dramatically and changed the whole industry's economics.

questions.q: Why is heat lost from a spacecraft only by radiation?
c: There is no air to carry heat away by convection
questions.f: That is why spacecraft need big radiator panels - shedding heat in space is surprisingly hard.

questions.q: Which of Newton's laws most directly explains how a rocket engine works?
c: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Objects at rest stay at rest
questions.f: Throw mass hard out the back and the rocket is pushed just as hard forward.

questions.q: In orbit, how does a spacecraft catch up with one ahead of it?
c: By dropping to a lower, faster orbit first
questions.f: Orbital mechanics is famously counter-intuitive: speeding up actually makes you fall behind.

questions.q: What is a sun-synchronous orbit useful for?
c: Passing over each place at the same local time every day
questions.f: Consistent lighting makes it perfect for comparing satellite images taken months apart.

questions.q: What worrying scenario is named the 'Kessler syndrome'?
c: Collisions creating debris that causes still more collisions
Astronauts losing their sense of balance
Satellites falling to Earth at once
questions.f: Even a bolt travelling at orbital speed carries the punch of a hand grenade.

questions.q: A spacecraft window can be cracked by a paint fleck travelling at orbital speed.
questions.f: Shuttle windows really were chipped by tiny flecks - which is why debris tracking matters so much.

questions.q: Which term describes a spacecraft designed to shield against tiny high-speed impacts with spaced layers?
questions.f: The first thin layer shatters the particle into vapour, which the second layer easily stops.

questions.q: What is 'space weather'?
c: Conditions in space driven by solar activity
questions.f: Forecasters now issue space weather warnings for airlines, satellite operators, and power companies.

questions.q: Which everyday technology came from NASA research into digital image sensors?
questions.f: The compact CMOS sensor was developed to shrink cameras for spacecraft, then it went everywhere.

questions.q: Which navigation satellite system was developed by India?
questions.f: NavIC covers India and the surrounding region with its own independent set of satellites.

questions.q: Which of these best explains why the Moon has 'mascons'?
c: Denser rock beneath ancient impact basins tugs harder on orbiters
questions.f: These mass concentrations were discovered when early lunar orbiters wobbled unexpectedly.

questions.q: What did Apollo astronauts leave behind that scientists still use today?
c: Mirrors for bouncing lasers off the Moon
questions.f: Those reflectors let us measure the Earth-Moon distance to within a few centimetres.

questions.q: Which force gradually slows Earth's spin and pushes the Moon outward?
questions.f: Corals and ancient shells record days that were noticeably shorter hundreds of millions of years ago.

questions.q: Days on Earth were significantly shorter when dinosaurs lived.
questions.f: Late Cretaceous days ran about half an hour shorter, so their year held more of them.

questions.q: Which effect makes a sunset appear slightly later than it geometrically should?
c: Refraction bending light over the horizon
questions.f: When you watch the Sun touch the horizon, it has geometrically already set.

questions.q: Why does the Moon look larger near the horizon than high overhead?
c: It is an illusion in how our brains judge size
questions.f: Photographs prove the size is identical - the famous Moon illusion happens entirely in the mind.

questions.q: What is the 'terminator' on a planet or moon?
c: The dividing line between day and night
questions.f: Shadows are longest there, which is why photographs along the terminator show the best detail.

questions.q: Which term describes a moon keeping the same face toward its planet while slowly rocking side to side?
questions.f: That gentle rocking is why we can glimpse a little more than half the Moon's surface over time.

questions.q: Which of these best explains why the Milky Way looks like a band rather than a sphere of stars?
c: We sit inside a flat disc and look along it
Stars are arranged in a ring
Our eyes cannot see faint stars
questions.f: Looking along the disc, countless stars pile up into a glowing stripe across the sky.

questions.q: What do astronomers call the dark lanes that split the Milky Way's glow?
questions.f: Andean and Australian cultures gave those dark shapes names of their own, seeing animals in them.

questions.q: Roughly how long does the Sun take to complete one orbit of the galaxy?
questions.f: The last time the Sun was here, the earliest dinosaurs were only just appearing.

questions.q: What is the 'habitable zone' of a red dwarf star like compared with the Sun's?
c: Much closer in, because the star is far dimmer
questions.f: Planets there orbit in days, and are usually locked with one face permanently sunlit.

questions.q: Which system of seven Earth-sized planets around one small star excited astronomers in 2017?
questions.f: Several of its worlds sit in the star's habitable zone, packed closer than Mercury is to our Sun.

questions.q: What is a 'hot Jupiter'?
c: A giant planet orbiting very close to its star
questions.f: The first exoplanet found around a normal star was one, and it stunned theorists who thought it impossible.

questions.q: Which pioneering pair announced the first planet orbiting another Sun-like star in 1995?
questions.f: They shared a Nobel Prize for a discovery that opened up an entire new field of astronomy.

questions.q: What is SETI?
c: The search for signals from intelligent life beyond Earth
questions.f: Radio astronomers have listened for decades - so far, the universe has stayed silent.

questions.q: What does the Drake equation try to estimate?
c: How many communicating civilisations might exist in our galaxy
questions.f: Frank Drake wrote it as an agenda for discussion, not a formula with a fixed answer.

questions.q: A trained soprano who left the concert stage, the first woman in Britain paid a royal salary for science, and finder of eight comets: who?
questions.f: She swept the sky for hours in freezing English nights, calling out notes to be written down by lamplight.

questions.q: A Harvard 'computer' paid a few cents an hour, a rule linking a star's pulse rate to its true brightness, and the yardstick that first measured the distance to other galaxies: who?
questions.f: She was profoundly deaf, and her law is still the first rung on the cosmic distance ladder.

questions.q: A thesis rejected as too radical in 1925, a demonstration that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen, and a career spent at Harvard without a proper title for decades: who?
questions.f: Her supervisor later admitted she had been right all along - it is now called the most brilliant astronomy thesis ever written.

questions.q: Galaxy edges that spin far too fast, a career of patient measurements at Kitt Peak, and the strongest early case for unseen mass: who?
questions.f: She showed that stars at a galaxy's rim orbit as fast as those near the centre - impossible without extra hidden mass.

questions.q: Squiggles on a chart recorder nicknamed 'little green men', a Cambridge graduate student's stubbornness, and a Nobel Prize awarded to her supervisors: who made the discovery?
questions.f: The steady radio pulses she refused to dismiss turned out to be the first known pulsar.

questions.q: A long sea voyage from Madras to England spent calculating, a limit of about 1.4 solar masses, and a bitter public argument with a famous knight of astronomy: who?
questions.f: He was proved right decades later, and an X-ray observatory now carries his name.

questions.q: An equation describing how hot gas loses its electrons, work that let astronomers read stellar spectra properly, and a scientist who later helped plan India's river projects: who?
questions.f: His ionisation equation turned starlight into a thermometer for measuring stellar temperatures.

questions.q: A duel that cost him part of his nose, a private island observatory funded by a king, and twenty years of naked-eye measurements that another man turned into ellipses: who?
questions.f: He wore a prosthetic nose and kept a pet elk - and his data was the finest before telescopes.

questions.q: A legal defence written for a mother accused of witchcraft, an early tale of a voyage to the Moon, and a discarded model of nested geometric solids: who?
questions.f: His story 'Somnium' is sometimes called the first work of science fiction ever written.

questions.q: A pendulum clock design, discoveries announced first as scrambled anagrams, and the first moon ever found beyond our own: who?
questions.f: He also worked out that Saturn's puzzling 'ears' were a flat ring encircling the planet.

questions.q: Timing errors in the eclipses of a Jovian moon, a Danish astronomer's stubborn arithmetic, and the first proof that light does not travel instantly: who?
questions.f: He noticed Io's eclipses ran late when Earth was farther away - light was taking time to cross the gap.

questions.q: A tiny annual wobble in star positions, an explanation involving Earth's own motion through space, and confirmation that Earth truly orbits: which effect?
questions.f: James Bradley found it while hunting for parallax - and accidentally proved Earth's motion instead.

questions.q: Unexplained wobbles in the path of a newly found planet, a prediction posted to a Berlin observatory, and a discovery made within a degree of the calculated spot: who did the sums?
questions.f: Neptune was found the very night the letter arrived - mathematics had located a world nobody had seen.

questions.q: A faint companion inferred from a wobble long before it was seen, a mass like the Sun's squeezed into an Earth-sized ball, and the nickname 'the Pup': which star?
questions.f: It was the first white dwarf ever recognised, hiding in the glare of the sky's brightest star.

questions.q: A star in Cygnus, a painstaking measurement of a shift smaller than a coin seen kilometres away, and the first true distance ever found to another star: which star was measured?
questions.f: Friedrich Bessel published the result in 1838, finally giving humanity a measured yardstick to the stars.

questions.q: A persistent hiss from every direction, pigeons evicted and their droppings scrubbed from a horn antenna, and a Nobel Prize awarded for unexplained noise: what had they found?
questions.f: That faint hiss is the cooled afterglow of the universe's fiery beginning, filling all of space.

questions.q: A radio broadcast mocking a rival theory, decades of work on how stars forge elements, and the accidental coining of cosmology's most famous phrase: who?
questions.f: He never accepted the theory he named - yet 'Big Bang' is the label that stuck forever.

questions.q: A Belgian priest with a physics doctorate, a paper on an expanding universe published two years before a famous law, and the idea of a 'primeval atom': who?
questions.f: Astronomers now often credit him alongside Hubble for the discovery of cosmic expansion.

questions.q: A mule driver turned night assistant, spectra of faint galaxies gathered on Mount Wilson, and the redshift measurements behind a famous distance-velocity law: who?
questions.f: He had no formal degree at all, yet became one of the finest observers of his generation.

questions.q: A designer whose identity was a state secret while he lived, years lost in a Siberian labour camp, and the driving force behind the first satellite and first human flight: who?
questions.f: He was known publicly only as 'the Chief Designer' - his name was revealed after his death in 1966.

questions.q: A bishop who lent his church as a workshop, rocket parts carried on bicycles and bullock carts, and a fishing village chosen for sitting on the magnetic equator: which site?
questions.f: India's space age began in 1963 with a small sounding rocket launched from that quiet coastal village.

questions.q: A mother whose maiden name happened to be Moon, a doctoral thesis on orbital rendezvous, and the second pair of boots to press into lunar dust: who?
questions.f: His rendezvous mathematics was so respected that colleagues nicknamed him 'Dr. Rendezvous'.

questions.q: Five hundred seeds packed in a small canister, a forester who became an astronaut, and saplings planted across a country for its bicentennial: what were the results called?
questions.f: Stuart Roosa carried the seeds around the Moon on Apollo 14, and the trees grew normally.

questions.q: An artist who mixed lunar boot dust into his paints, the fourth man on the Moon, and canvases textured with a geology hammer: who?
questions.f: He left NASA to paint full time, saying he was the only artist who had actually been there.

questions.q: Two lightning strikes seconds after lift-off, a flight controller's snap decision to reset the power system, and a crew that carried on to the Moon anyway: which mission?
questions.f: A young engineer remembered an obscure test procedure and called out the fix from memory.

questions.q: An old robot probe revisited on foot, pieces cut away to study space weathering, and the only spacecraft ever inspected by humans on another world: which craft?
questions.f: Apollo 12 landed deliberately within walking distance of the earlier lander.

questions.q: A geologist who never flew in space, a comet that struck Jupiter bearing his name, and ashes carried to the Moon aboard a small orbiter: who?
questions.f: He is the only person whose remains rest on the Moon, scattered there by the Lunar Prospector probe.

questions.q: An ounce of a discoverer's ashes aboard, the fastest launch speed ever achieved, and a flyby of a snowman-shaped rock beyond Pluto: which spacecraft?
questions.f: It carried some of Clyde Tombaugh's ashes past the very world he discovered.

questions.q: A shape often described as a snowman, a name from a Powhatan word meaning 'sky', and the most distant object ever visited by a spacecraft: what is it?
questions.f: Its two lobes settled together so gently that they preserve the earliest stages of planet building.

questions.q: A hidden Soviet camera, a mission whose photographs were developed in space aboard the craft, and humanity's first look at a face no one had seen: which probe's images?
questions.f: The film was developed, fixed, dried, and then scanned onboard before being radioed home.

questions.q: A capsule that survived 23 minutes on a crushing surface, the first data ever radioed from another planet's ground, and a 1970 Soviet triumph: which mission?
questions.f: Its parachute partly melted on the way down, yet it still transmitted temperature readings from the surface.

questions.q: A probe that recorded the sound of wind on another world, colour photographs of orange rock, and a drill that sampled soil before the heat killed it: which mission?
questions.f: It lasted 127 minutes on Venus, more than four times its design life.

questions.q: A spacecraft that used one planet's gravity to reach another, the first ever to try that trick, and the only craft to visit Mercury in the twentieth century: which one?
questions.f: Its Venus swingby proved gravity assists worked, and no probe returned to Mercury until MESSENGER flew past in 2008.

questions.q: A craft that dropped a probe into a giant planet's clouds, an antenna that never fully unfurled, and a deliberate plunge to protect an icy moon: which mission?
questions.f: Its probe survived nearly an hour inside Jupiter's atmosphere, measuring winds and lightning.

questions.q: A spacecraft carrying three small aluminium figurines, an orbit that dives over a giant planet's poles, and a name from the Roman queen of the gods: which mission?
questions.f: In the old stories Juno peered through the clouds to see what Jupiter was hiding - a perfect fit.

questions.q: An ion-drive probe, the first craft ever to orbit two different worlds, and visits to both the largest asteroid and the brightest one: which mission?
questions.f: Its gentle ion engines let it enter orbit around Vesta, leave again, and settle at Ceres.

questions.q: An asteroid with its own tiny moon, the first such pair ever confirmed, and a discovery made during a Jupiter-bound flyby: which asteroid?
questions.f: Its little companion was named Dactyl, after mythical beings who lived on Mount Ida.

questions.q: A name meaning 'dragon palace' from a Japanese folk tale, a spinning-top shape, and pristine grains delivered to Earth in 2020: which asteroid?
questions.f: In the tale, a fisherman returns from an undersea palace with a mysterious box - like a sample capsule.

questions.q: Satellites built to watch for secret nuclear tests, flashes coming from the wrong direction entirely, and a discovery kept classified for years: which phenomenon?
questions.f: The Vela satellites found the brightest explosions in the universe while policing a test-ban treaty.

questions.q: Two dead stars spiralling together in 2017, gravitational ripples followed by a visible glow, and fresh evidence for where heavy elements like gold come from: what merged?
questions.f: Telescopes worldwide swung round within hours, watching newly forged heavy elements light up.

questions.q: A star whose Arabic name means 'the ghoul', a brightness that dips every 2.87 days, and the first eclipsing binary ever understood: which star?
questions.f: Ancient sky-watchers may have noticed its winking - it marks the demon's head in Perseus.

questions.q: A red star in Cetus that fades and returns over about eleven months, a name meaning 'wonderful', and the first variable star ever recorded: which one?
questions.f: Its discovery in 1596 shattered the old belief that the heavens never change.

questions.q: A Chinese record of a 'guest star' in 1054, Native American rock art from the same era, and a shredded cloud powered by a spinning core: what do they describe?
questions.f: The exploding star was bright enough to see in daylight for weeks before fading away.

questions.q: A star whose Arabic name means 'the follower', an orange giant marking a bull's eye, and the star a famous space probe will drift near in two million years: which star?
questions.f: It was called the follower because it trails the Pleiades cluster across the sky each night.

questions.q: A name from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the flying eagle', a star spinning so fast it is visibly squashed, and one corner of the Summer Triangle: which star?
questions.f: It rotates in about nine hours, bulging out at its equator like a slightly flattened ball.

questions.q: The brightest star of the northern summer's harp, a former pole star of the distant past, and the first star ever photographed: which one?
questions.f: An 1850 daguerreotype at Harvard captured it - the first stellar portrait in history.

questions.q: A star with the largest known proper motion across our sky, a red dwarf only six light-years away, and a long history of false planet claims: which star?
questions.f: It shifts by about the width of the Moon every 180 years - a sprinter among the fixed stars.

questions.q: An unexpected dimming in 2019 that made headlines, a surface so lumpy it changes shape, and a dust cloud rather than an imminent explosion: which star?
questions.f: Astronomers concluded the star had simply belched out dust that briefly veiled its own light.

questions.q: Timing wobbles in a spinning stellar corpse, an announcement in 1992, and the very first planets ever confirmed beyond our solar system: what did they orbit?
questions.f: Planets around a dead star came as a shock - three years before the first around a Sun-like star.

questions.q: A cluster catalogued as M45, the name Krittika in Indian tradition, and a badge on millions of Japanese cars: which star group?
questions.f: 'Subaru' is the Japanese name for the cluster - which is why the badge shows six stars.

questions.q: A star that will one day mark the pole, a 26,000-year wobble of Earth's axis, and the reason the pyramids' pole star was not Polaris: what is that wobble called?
questions.f: Around 2600 BCE the pole pointed near Thuban in Draco - Polaris was then just another star.

questions.q: A cycle of 18 years, 11 days, and about 8 hours, a pattern used by ancient astronomers to anticipate eclipses, and a family of repeats stretching over centuries: what is it called?
questions.f: Because of the extra eight hours, each repeat lands about a third of the way around the world.

questions.q: A corroded bronze mechanism raised from a Greek shipwreck, dozens of interlocking gears, and a device that predicted eclipses and planet positions: what is it?
questions.f: Nothing of comparable complexity is known for the next thousand years of human history.

questions.q: The word 'quasar' was shortened from a longer scientific phrase meaning what?
questions.f: They looked like stars on photographic plates but blazed with the power of whole galaxies.

questions.q: The word 'pulsar' was coined by shortening which description?
questions.f: A British newspaper is credited with popularising the snappy contraction in 1968.

questions.q: The astronomical term 'syzygy' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: It describes the Sun, Earth, and Moon lining up - the arrangement behind eclipses and spring tides.

questions.q: The distance unit 'parsec' is a contraction of which two words?
questions.f: It is the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond - about 3.26 light-years.

questions.q: The star name 'Betelgeuse' descends from an Arabic phrase meaning what?
questions.f: A medieval misreading of the first letter is why we say 'Bet-' rather than 'Yad-' today.

questions.q: The star name 'Fomalhaut' comes from an Arabic phrase meaning what?
questions.f: It sits in Piscis Austrinus, the southern fish, right where the constellation's mouth is drawn.

questions.q: The bright star 'Capella' has a Latin name meaning what?
questions.f: In the old stories she is Amalthea, the goat that suckled the infant Zeus.

questions.q: The star name 'Procyon' was built from Greek parts meaning what?
questions.f: It rises just before Sirius, the great Dog Star - so it heralds the dog's arrival.

questions.q: The star name 'Spica' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Virgo is often drawn holding a sheaf of wheat, with Spica marking the grain in her hand.

questions.q: The star name 'Bellatrix' in Orion means what?
questions.f: It marks the hunter's left shoulder, and its name has since been borrowed by storytellers.

questions.q: The star name 'Denebola' in Leo means what?
questions.f: 'Deneb' means tail, and it turns up in several star names across different constellations.

questions.q: The star name 'Achernar' comes from an Arabic phrase meaning what?
questions.f: It marks the far end of Eridanus, the celestial river winding across the southern sky.

questions.q: Ptolemy's great astronomical work is known as the 'Almagest', a title meaning what?
questions.f: Arabic scholars called it 'al-majisti', from a Greek word for greatest - and that name replaced the original.

questions.q: An 'orrery', the clockwork model of the solar system, is named after what?
questions.f: The Earl of Orrery received an early example, and his title became the name of the whole device.

questions.q: An 'ephemeris' is named from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: It is a day-by-day table of where each sky object will be - a diary of the heavens.

questions.q: The word 'ellipse' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: The same root gives 'ellipsis', the three dots that show words have been left out.

questions.q: In orbital mechanics, the word 'apsis' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: Perihelion and aphelion are the two apsides of an orbit - the arch's low and high ends.

questions.q: Which element is named after the dwarf planet Ceres?
questions.f: Both the asteroid and the element were found in the same decade, and the namers were feeling cosmic.

questions.q: Which element takes its name from the asteroid Pallas?
questions.f: Pallas was discovered in 1802 and the metal named soon after, in the same burst of enthusiasm.

questions.q: Which element's name honours the goddess of the Earth, as a companion to moon-named selenium?
questions.f: 'Tellus' meant Earth in Latin, and selenium was named after Selene, the Moon.

questions.q: Which three consecutive elements in the periodic table are named after planets or dwarf planets?
questions.f: They were named in order of discovery, echoing the order of the outer worlds themselves.

questions.q: India's proposed term 'vyomanaut' is built from a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Vyoma' means sky, so the word matches astronaut and cosmonaut in structure exactly.

questions.q: ISRO's humanoid robot 'Vyommitra' has a name meaning what?
questions.f: 'Mitra' means friend - the half-humanoid is designed to ride uncrewed test flights.

questions.q: In classical Indian astronomy, 'Rohini' is the name given to which bright star?
questions.f: India's first satellite series was named Rohini, quietly borrowing a star name thousands of years old.

questions.q: In Indian tradition, the star called 'Chitra' is which star in Western naming?
questions.f: The state of Chittirai's festival month and the star share the same ancient name.

questions.q: The Chinese crewed spacecraft 'Shenzhou' has a name meaning what?
questions.f: It sounds almost identical to an old poetic name for China itself - a deliberate double meaning.

questions.q: China's lunar programme is named 'Chang'e' after what?
c: A goddess who flew to the Moon
questions.f: Her companion in the tale is a jade rabbit - which is why the rovers are named Yutu.

questions.q: China's far-side relay satellite 'Queqiao' is named after what?
c: A bridge of magpies from a folk tale
questions.f: In the story, magpies form a bridge across the heavens for two separated lovers to meet.

questions.q: Japan's asteroid missions are named 'Hayabusa' after which creature?
questions.f: The name suits a craft that swoops down, snatches a sample, and climbs away again.

questions.q: Japan's lunar orbiter 'Kaguya' took its name from what?
c: A princess from a bamboo tale who returns to the Moon
questions.f: In the story a baby found inside a bamboo stalk grows up and departs for the Moon.

questions.q: Israel's lunar lander 'Beresheet' had a name meaning what?
questions.f: It is the opening word of the Hebrew Bible - a bold choice for a nation's first Moon attempt.

questions.q: The Soviet shuttle 'Buran' had a name meaning what?
questions.f: It flew once, in 1988, and did so entirely uncrewed and under automatic control.

questions.q: The first module of the International Space Station, 'Zarya', has a name meaning what?
questions.f: Fittingly, it was the dawn of a station that has now been continuously crewed for over two decades.

questions.q: The Japanese laboratory module on the space station, 'Kibo', has a name meaning what?
questions.f: It is the station's largest single module, complete with an outdoor porch for experiments.

questions.q: The motto 'Ad astra per aspera' means what?
questions.f: Kansas adopted it as a state motto, and it is engraved at NASA in memory of lost crews.

questions.q: A crew capsule named for a folk song about a magic dragon, a booster named after a fictional starship, and a company motto about occupying Mars: whose vehicles?
questions.f: Dragon takes its name from 'Puff the Magic Dragon' - a jab at early sceptics of the company.

questions.q: A suborbital rocket named after the first American in space, a heavier one named after the first American to orbit, and a Latin motto meaning 'step by step, ferociously': whose?
questions.f: 'Gradatim Ferociter' captures a company that tests patiently and then pushes hard.

questions.q: A launch site chosen because it sits almost on the equator, a European spaceport in South America, and rockets named after a Cretan princess: where is it?
questions.f: Ariane takes its name from Ariadne, who gave Theseus the thread out of the labyrinth.

questions.q: A satellite whose name means 'search', another meaning 'star', and a Russian segment full of such names: which station are they part of?
questions.f: Poisk means search and Zvezda means star - the station is a museum of Russian nouns.

questions.q: A cosmonaut's shout of 'Poyekhali!' at lift-off translates as what?
questions.f: Yuri Gagarin's cheerful one-word send-off became a national catchphrase overnight.

questions.q: A first flight in 1961 lasting 15 minutes, a golf swing a decade later, and a rocket family later named in his honour: who?
questions.f: He was grounded for years by an inner-ear problem, then came back to walk on the Moon.

questions.q: A record 437 continuous days in orbit, a stay long enough to cover a Mars round trip, and a doctor who studied himself: who?
questions.f: He walked from the capsule after landing, on purpose, to prove a Mars crew could arrive on their feet.

questions.q: A cosmonaut in orbit while his country changed its name, an extended mission with no clear way home, and the nickname 'the last Soviet citizen': who?
questions.f: He launched from the Soviet Union in 1991 and came home to a Russia that had replaced it.

questions.q: An October 2019 first, two Americans working outside together, and a task involving a failed battery charger: what milestone?
c: The first repair of a solar wing
questions.f: Christina Koch and Jessica Meir made the walk, and Koch went on to set a record for women in space.

questions.q: A Cuban pilot, a 1980 flight aboard a Soyuz, and the first person of African descent to reach orbit: who?
questions.f: He flew as part of the Interkosmos programme, which took citizens of allied nations into space.

questions.q: A 1978 flight, a Czechoslovak air force pilot, and the first person in space from neither the USSR nor the USA: who?
questions.f: He later joked that he was told not to touch anything aboard, so he kept his hands to himself.

questions.q: A pair of dogs who orbited and came home alive in 1960, a flight that carried mice and a rabbit too, and a puppy later given to a president's family: who were they?
questions.f: One of Strelka's puppies was sent to the Kennedy family as a diplomatic gift.

questions.q: A 1963 French flight, electrodes and a suborbital hop, and the only cat ever to travel to space: what was her name?
questions.f: A statue honouring her was finally unveiled at the International Space University in 2019.

questions.q: Two spiders named Arabella and Anita, a 1973 experiment aboard an American station, and webs that started messy and grew neat: which station?
questions.f: The spiders adjusted within days, spinning near-normal webs despite weightlessness.

questions.q: A 1968 Soviet flight, two tortoises aboard, and the first living creatures to loop around the Moon and return: which mission?
questions.f: The tortoises came home having lost a little weight, but otherwise perfectly healthy.

questions.q: Which creatures were the first animals ever sent into space, aboard a captured rocket in 1947?
questions.f: They were flown to study radiation at high altitude, and their capsule parachuted safely back.

questions.q: A creature that can survive vacuum, dehydration, and heavy radiation, and which has been flown outside a spacecraft to prove it: what is it?
questions.f: Nicknamed water bears, they curl into a dried-out 'tun' state and simply wait for better conditions.

questions.q: Which human-made object still in orbit is the oldest, launched in 1958?
questions.f: Its radio fell silent in 1964, but the little grapefruit-sized sphere is still quietly circling.

questions.q: A physicist's vivid nickname adopted at a 1967 lecture, a term replacing the clumsy phrase 'gravitationally collapsed object', and a name that critics called vulgar: what was named?
questions.f: John Wheeler popularised the phrase, and its punchiness helped the idea spread worldwide.

questions.q: A radius named after a German physicist who solved Einstein's equations while serving in the First World War: what does it mark?
c: A black hole's event horizon size
questions.f: Karl Schwarzschild sent his solution from the front and died of illness months later.

questions.q: A theoretical trickle of particles escaping from a black hole's edge, a process that makes small black holes evaporate, and a prediction from the 1970s: what is it called?
questions.f: The smaller the black hole, the faster it glows away - the tiniest would vanish in a flash.

questions.q: A grim nickname for what tidal forces would do to anything falling into a small black hole: what is the term?
questions.f: Gravity would pull your feet far harder than your head, stretching you like pulled dough.

questions.q: A strong X-ray source in the swan, the subject of a famous friendly bet between two physicists, and one of the first black holes ever identified: what is it called?
questions.f: Stephen Hawking bet against it being a black hole - a hedge, he joked, in case his life's work was wrong.

questions.q: A star tracked for decades as it whipped around an invisible mass, an orbit completed in about 16 years, and a Nobel Prize for mapping our galaxy's centre: which star is it?
questions.f: Watching S2 swing past at thousands of kilometres per second proved a supermassive object lurks there.

questions.q: A giant elliptical galaxy in Virgo, a jet of matter spotted as early as 1918, and the subject of the first image of a black hole's shadow: which galaxy?
questions.f: Its central black hole is so vast that light needs about a day to cross its horizon.

questions.q: A 1998 result from two rival supernova teams, exploding stars used as standard candles, and evidence that cosmic expansion is speeding up: what did they infer exists?
questions.f: It appears to make up most of the universe's energy - and nobody yet knows what it is.

questions.q: A puzzle asking why the night sky is dark if the universe is infinite and eternal, and a paradox named after a nineteenth-century German astronomer: what is it called?
questions.f: The answer is that the universe has a finite age, so light from the farthest places has not arrived.

questions.q: Balloon flights to measure air's mysterious ionisation, radiation that increased with altitude rather than decreasing, and a 1912 discovery: what had been found?
questions.f: Victor Hess rode balloons up to 5,000 metres to prove the radiation came from above, not from the ground.

questions.q: A burst of ghostly particles detected hours before the visible light in 1987, a nearby exploding star, and the birth of a new kind of astronomy: which event?
questions.f: Neutrinos escape a collapsing core immediately, while light takes hours to fight its way out.

questions.q: A detector buried in ice at the South Pole, a cubic kilometre of instrumented glacier, and a hunt for particles that barely interact with anything: what is it called?
questions.f: When a neutrino does hit, it makes a faint blue flash that thousands of buried sensors can catch.

questions.q: A stubborn shortfall in expected particles from the Sun, a puzzle solved by particles changing identity in flight, and a Nobel Prize in 2015: what was the problem called?
questions.f: Neutrinos come in three flavours, and they morph between them as they travel - so detectors missed some.

questions.q: A nebula in Centaurus chilled by rapidly expanding gas, a temperature colder than the background of space itself, and a bow-tie shape: what is remarkable about it?
c: It is the coldest known natural place in the universe
It has the strongest magnetic field
It is the fastest spinning object
It is the oldest known nebula
questions.f: The Boomerang Nebula sits at about one degree above absolute zero - colder than empty space nearby.

questions.q: A star so vast its surface would engulf Jupiter's orbit, a red hypergiant in Scutum, and a longtime contender for largest known star: which one?
questions.f: Its outer layers are so thin that much of it is less dense than the air in your room.

questions.q: A crowded cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a star of roughly two hundred solar masses, and the current record holder for stellar heft: which star?
questions.f: It pours out millions of times more light than the Sun and burns through its fuel with reckless speed.

questions.q: A neutron star spinning over 700 times each second, a beam sweeping past us faster than a kitchen blender, and a record for rotation: what class of object?
questions.f: Its equator moves at a good fraction of the speed of light, yet the star holds together.

questions.q: A neutron star with a magnetic field trillions of times Earth's, a 2004 flare that disturbed our atmosphere from across the galaxy, and a name coined in the 1990s: what is it?
questions.f: Its field is so intense it would wipe a credit card from farther away than the Moon.

questions.q: Millisecond radio flashes from far outside our galaxy, a phenomenon first spotted in archived data in 2007, and one source that repeats: what are they called?
questions.f: At least some appear to come from magnetars - but the full story is still being written.

questions.q: A star in Cygnus with baffling irregular dips in brightness, a wave of speculation about giant alien structures, and a likely answer involving dust: which star?
questions.f: Officially KIC 8462852, it is named after Tabetha Boyajian, who led the study of its odd flickers.

questions.q: A hypothetical shell built to capture a star's whole output, a scale of civilisations ranked by energy use, and a staple of speculative astronomy: whose sphere?
questions.f: Freeman Dyson meant it as a thought experiment about detecting advanced technology, not a blueprint.

questions.q: A ranking of civilisations by the energy they can harness, proposed by a Soviet astronomer in 1964: whose scale is it?
questions.f: On his scale, humanity has not yet reached Type I - full command of one planet's energy.

questions.q: A 72-second signal in 1977, a note scribbled in the margin of a printout, and a source never detected again: what is it known as?
questions.f: Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled the data and wrote one word - and the name stuck forever.

questions.q: A 1974 radio transmission aimed at a globular cluster 25,000 light-years away, a picture drawn in binary, and a demonstration rather than a serious call: what was it?
questions.f: It coded our numbers, our chemistry, a stick figure, and a sketch of the dish that sent it.

questions.q: A gold-anodised plaque bolted to a 1972 probe, a diagram of hydrogen's spin flip, and a map based on pulsar frequencies: which spacecraft carried it first?
questions.f: The pulsar map works as a cosmic address, pinpointing when and where the craft came from.

questions.q: A far-off world where astronomers suspect silicate clouds rain down, a gas giant whose deep blue colour comes from scattering not water, and one of the best-studied hot Jupiters: which planet?
questions.f: Winds there may top 8,000 kilometres per hour, whipping glassy droplets sideways.

questions.q: A super-Earth orbiting its star in under 18 hours, a surface likely covered in molten rock, and early speculation that its carbon might form diamond: which planet?
questions.f: Later studies cooled the diamond idea, but the world remains a lava-covered oddity.

questions.q: A predicted distant world invoked to explain the clustered orbits of far-flung icy bodies, and a search that has so far come up empty: what is the hypothesis called?
questions.f: If it exists it may be several times Earth's mass and take over ten thousand years to orbit.

questions.q: A distant object named after an Inuit sea goddess, an orbit stretching hundreds of times Earth's distance from the Sun, and a discovery in 2003: which body?
questions.f: Its orbit takes over eleven thousand years, and it may never come near the known planets.

questions.q: A small distant world found to have a ring where theory says one should not survive, and a 2023 announcement from telescope occultation data: which body?
questions.f: Its ring sits well outside the distance where rings were thought to be possible.

questions.q: Objects orbiting between Jupiter and Neptune, behaving partly like asteroids and partly like comets, and named after mythical half-horse beings: what are they called?
questions.f: Like their namesakes they are hybrids - rocky bodies that sometimes sprout comet-like activity.

questions.q: A mission named after a fossil skeleton, a tour of asteroids sharing Jupiter's orbit, and a plan to visit more bodies than any previous spacecraft: which mission?
questions.f: Just as the fossil Lucy illuminated human origins, these ancient asteroids should illuminate the planets'.

questions.q: A slow push from sunlight re-radiated unevenly by a spinning asteroid, an effect that shifts orbits over centuries, and a factor in tracking hazardous rocks: what is it called?
questions.f: It is feeble, but over millennia it can move an asteroid thousands of kilometres off its expected path.

questions.q: A ten-point public scale for rating impact hazard, named after an Italian city where it was adopted in 1999: what is it called?
questions.f: Almost every object ever rated has dropped back to zero once more observations came in.

questions.q: An asteroid named after an Egyptian god of chaos, a very close pass due in April 2029, and a rock that will be visible to the naked eye that night: which one?
questions.f: It will pass closer than our geostationary satellites - and pose no danger at all.

questions.q: A faint cone of light along the ecliptic after dusk, sunlight scattered by dust in the plane of the planets, and a sight needing very dark skies: what is it called?
questions.f: It is sometimes called false dawn, because a similar glow appears before sunrise.

questions.q: A faint oval glow directly opposite the Sun in the night sky, caused by dust backscattering light, and known by a German name: what is it called?
questions.f: 'Gegenschein' means counter-glow - and spotting it is a badge of honour among dark-sky observers.

questions.q: A faint natural glow of the night atmosphere itself, visible in photographs from orbit as a thin green line, and present even with no Moon or aurora: what is it?
questions.f: Oxygen atoms recombining high above us keep the night sky from ever being truly black.

questions.q: Bright spots flanking the Sun at 22 degrees, ice crystals acting as prisms, and a phenomenon recorded in medieval chronicles: what are they called?
questions.f: Their proper name is parhelia, meaning 'beside the sun' - hexagonal ice crystals do the bending.

questions.q: A pinkish band above the horizon opposite the setting Sun, sitting atop Earth's own rising shadow, and named after a goddess: what is it called?
questions.f: The dark blue-grey band below it is the shadow of Earth itself, projected onto our own air.

questions.q: The highest clouds in Earth's atmosphere, glowing electric blue on summer nights near the poles, and made of ice around meteor dust: what are they called?
questions.f: They form near 80 kilometres up, so high that they shine long after the ground is dark.

questions.q: A purple ribbon in the night sky discovered by amateur photographers, later given a friendly backronym by scientists, and not a true aurora: what is it called?
questions.f: It stands for Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement - the joke name came first.

questions.q: A figure-eight traced by the Sun's noon position over a year, visible in long-exposure photographs, and named from a Greek word for a sundial's pedestal: what is it?
questions.f: Its shape comes from Earth's tilt combined with the slightly uneven speed of our orbit.

questions.q: The difference between clock time and sundial time, varying by about a quarter of an hour across the year: what is it called?
questions.f: Old sundials often carried a small table so users could convert shadow time to clock time.

questions.q: A star's first pre-dawn reappearance after weeks of invisibility, an event ancient Egyptians tied to the Nile's flood, and a term still used by astronomers: what is it called?
questions.f: Sirius's heliacal rising once marked the Egyptian new year with remarkable reliability.

questions.q: A 19-year period after which Moon phases fall on the same calendar dates, used to set festival calendars worldwide: what is it called?
questions.f: It is why lunar-solar calendars insert an extra month in certain years to stay in step.

questions.q: A bronze disc dug up in Germany, gold inlays showing a crescent and a cluster of seven dots, and possibly the oldest concrete depiction of the sky: what is it?
questions.f: Those seven dots are widely read as the Pleiades - a star cluster on a 3,600-year-old object.

questions.q: Thirteen stone towers in a line in coastal Peru, a viewing platform aligned with sunrise, and possibly the oldest solar observatory in the Americas: what is the site?
questions.f: The towers mark sunrise positions across the whole year, working like a giant stone calendar.

questions.q: A Maya manuscript surviving in a German library, tables tracking one planet's appearances over centuries, and astonishing accuracy without telescopes: which planet did it track?
questions.f: The Dresden Codex's Venus tables stay accurate to within a couple of hours per cycle.

questions.q: A Greek scholar in Egypt, shadows in two cities at noon, and a startlingly good estimate of Earth's circumference around 240 BCE: who?
questions.f: He needed only a well, a stick, and the distance between Alexandria and Syene.

questions.q: A Greek thinker who put the Sun at the centre roughly 1,800 years before Copernicus, and whose idea was mostly ignored in his own time: who?
questions.f: He also tried to measure the relative distances of Sun and Moon using the geometry of eclipses.

questions.q: A Persian astronomer's tenth-century book of stars, the first written record of a 'little cloud' in Andromeda, and a description of the Large Magellanic Cloud: who?
questions.f: That 'little cloud' was our neighbouring galaxy, noted centuries before telescopes existed.

questions.q: A ruler who built giant masonry instruments in five Indian cities, a keen reader of Persian and European star tables, and the founder of Jaipur: who?
questions.f: He sent scholars abroad to gather astronomical books before building his stone observatories.

questions.q: An Indian city long treated as the reference meridian for classical Indian astronomy, and the site of an old observatory still standing: which city?
questions.f: Ancient Indian texts measured longitudes from Ujjain much as modern maps measure from Greenwich.

questions.q: A seventh-century Indian mathematician who wrote that objects fall because the Earth attracts them, centuries before Newton: who?
questions.f: He also gave rules for zero and negative numbers in the same remarkable treatise.

questions.q: A twelfth-century Indian astronomer whose 'Siddhanta Shiromani' discussed instantaneous motion, and who wrote a famous chapter addressed to his daughter: who?
questions.f: That chapter, the Lilavati, teaches mathematics through charming puzzles about bees and lotuses.

questions.q: India's largest radio telescope array sits near which city?
questions.f: The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope spreads thirty huge dishes across the countryside in a Y shape.

questions.q: An observatory at Kavalur in Tamil Nadu is named after which Indian astronomer?
questions.f: He co-discovered a comet as a young researcher, and it carries his name to this day.

questions.q: What was Astrosat, launched by India in 2015?
questions.f: It observes the same object in visible, ultraviolet, and X-ray light at the same time.

questions.q: Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, what is the legal status of the Moon?
c: No nation may claim sovereignty over it
It belongs to whoever lands first
It is divided among the major powers
It is owned by the United Nations
questions.f: Over a hundred countries have signed - it also bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit.

questions.q: An improbable paperwork story: what did the Apollo 11 crew declare on a customs form on returning?
c: Moon rock and moon dust samples
questions.f: The form, filed in Honolulu, lists the departure point as 'Moon' - and it really was submitted.

questions.q: What were the actual first words spoken from the lunar surface after touchdown?
c: Houston, Tranquility Base here - the Eagle has landed
That's one small step for man
We came in peace for all mankind
questions.f: The famous 'small step' line came later, as Armstrong stepped off the ladder.

questions.q: A small aluminium figure and a plaque bearing fourteen names, left quietly on the Moon in 1971 to honour those lost in spaceflight: which mission left it?
