questions.f: The little sculpture is called Fallen Astronaut, and it still lies beside Hadley Rille.

questions.q: A pale chunk of rock collected in 1971, thought to be a piece of the Moon's original crust, and nicknamed after the first book of the Bible: what is it called?
questions.f: It turned out to be around four billion years old - nearly as old as the Moon itself.

questions.q: Startling orange soil found on the Moon in 1972, evidence of ancient volcanic fire fountains, and a geologist's excited shouting: which mission found it?
questions.f: The orange beads are tiny glass droplets, frozen sprays from eruptions billions of years ago.

questions.q: A lunar module nicknamed after a cartoon dog, cast adrift in 1969, and the only such craft still orbiting the Sun today: which mission's lander?
questions.f: Snoopy was jettisoned into solar orbit, and amateur astronomers have hunted for it ever since.

questions.q: A falling space station, debris scattered across Western Australia, and a small local council fine for littering that went unpaid for decades: which station?
questions.f: The shire of Esperance issued a 400-dollar fine in 1979 - it was finally paid by a fundraiser in 2009.

questions.q: A dead, tumbling station with frozen water inside, a manual docking flown with a laser rangefinder, and one of spaceflight's greatest rescues in 1985: which station was saved?
questions.f: The crew entered in fur coats and hats, chipping ice off the walls to bring the station back to life.

questions.q: Which cosmonaut holds the record for the most spacewalks ever performed?
questions.f: He made sixteen excursions, totalling more than three full days outside a spacecraft.

questions.q: Which astronaut became the first woman to command a Space Shuttle mission?
questions.f: She had already been the first woman to pilot a Shuttle, six years earlier.

questions.q: A smuggled harmonica, a handful of sleigh bells, and a 1965 prank radio report of an unidentified craft in a red suit: which mission's crew?
questions.f: They then played 'Jingle Bells' - the first music ever performed live in space.

questions.q: A commander who recorded a music video aboard the space station, a Canadian with a guitar, and a song about a fictional stranded astronaut: who?
questions.f: His orbital cover of 'Space Oddity' has been watched tens of millions of times.

questions.q: A pressurised espresso machine delivered to orbit in 2015, developed with an Italian coffee company: what was it nicknamed?
questions.f: Astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti drank the first proper espresso in orbit from a specially designed cup.

questions.q: Velcro was invented by NASA for the space programme.
questions.f: A Swiss engineer patented it in the 1950s after noticing burrs sticking to his dog - NASA merely used it a lot.

questions.q: Teflon was created specifically for spacecraft heat shields.
questions.f: It was discovered accidentally in a chemistry lab in 1938, long before any spacecraft existed.

questions.q: A privately developed pen with a pressurised ink cartridge, sold to both American and Soviet space programmes, and the subject of a persistent cost myth: whose pen?
questions.f: The company funded its own development - NASA simply bought the pens at a modest unit price.

questions.q: Which of these technologies genuinely grew out of space programme research?
questions.f: A coating developed for astronaut visors was adapted to make everyday spectacle lenses tougher.

questions.q: Which crew travelled faster relative to Earth than any humans before or since?
questions.f: Their return speed touched about 39,900 kilometres per hour - still the human speed record.

questions.q: Which crew holds the record for travelling farthest from Earth?
questions.f: Their looping free-return path around the far side carried them a little beyond any other crew.

questions.q: What was the first human-made object to reach the edge of space, back in 1944?
questions.f: A vertical test flight of an early liquid-fuelled rocket crossed roughly 175 kilometres altitude.

questions.q: When was the first photograph of Earth taken from above the boundary of space?
questions.f: A 35mm camera on a captured rocket snapped grainy black-and-white frames of the curving horizon.

questions.q: The famous 'Blue Marble' photograph of the whole Earth was taken during which mission?
questions.f: It became one of the most reproduced images in history and a symbol of the environmental movement.

questions.q: A telescope pointed at a seemingly empty patch of sky for ten days in 1995, an image revealing thousands of galaxies, and a gamble many called a waste of time: what was it?
questions.f: The director spent his own discretionary observing time on it - and changed cosmology forever.

questions.q: A giant wooden-mounted telescope in Ireland, the largest in the world for seventy years, and the first instrument to reveal a galaxy's spiral shape: what was it nicknamed?
questions.f: Lord Rosse sketched the whirlpool pattern of M51 in 1845, decades before anyone knew what galaxies were.

questions.q: Which is the most massive globular cluster orbiting our galaxy, possibly the core of a devoured dwarf galaxy?
questions.f: It holds millions of stars, and unlike normal clusters its stars vary in age and composition.

questions.q: A nearby star so old that early estimates awkwardly exceeded the age of the universe, nicknamed after a long-lived biblical figure: which star?
questions.f: Refined measurements brought its age safely under the universe's - but only just.

questions.q: A disagreement between two careful methods of measuring how fast the universe expands: what is this puzzle usually called?
questions.f: One method reads the early universe's afterglow; the other counts nearby stars - and they disagree.

questions.q: A vast concentration of mass pulling our whole galaxy group across space, hidden behind the Milky Way's dust: what is it called?
questions.f: We are drifting toward it at hundreds of kilometres per second without being able to see it clearly.

questions.q: The supercluster of galaxies our Milky Way belongs to was named in 2014 with a Hawaiian phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Laniakea contains an estimated hundred thousand galaxies, all flowing in a common direction.

questions.q: Which term describes the moment, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe first became transparent?
questions.f: Electrons finally joined nuclei, letting light travel freely - that released light is what we see as the microwave background.

questions.q: Which term describes the brief, enormous expansion proposed for the universe's first fraction of a second?
questions.f: It neatly explains why the universe looks so uniform and so nearly flat in every direction.

questions.q: A traditional pre-launch breakfast for American astronauts since 1961: what is it?
questions.f: Alan Shepard ate it before the first American flight, and the custom simply never stopped.

questions.q: A Russian launch tradition holds that crews watch which film the night before flying?
questions.f: The habit began in the 1970s and is now considered essential good luck at Baikonur.

questions.q: What is a 'zero-gravity indicator' on a spacecraft?
c: A small toy that floats when weightlessness begins
questions.f: Crews often choose something personal - plush toys, knitted dolls, or a child's favourite figure.

questions.q: Which award, shaped like a cartoon beagle, is given by American astronauts to outstanding ground staff?
questions.f: Every Silver Snoopy pin is flown in space before being presented, making each one a real spaceflown object.

questions.q: Astronauts must wear their launch suits for spacewalks as well.
questions.f: Launch and re-entry suits are quite different garments from the bulky, self-contained spacewalking suits.

questions.q: Why do American and Russian spacewalk suits use different pressures and preparation routines?
c: Different designs need different pre-breathing to avoid gas bubbles
One uses helium instead of oxygen
questions.f: Lower suit pressure aids movement but demands breathing pure oxygen beforehand, like a diver decompressing.

questions.q: Which award-winning phrase describes the boundary dispute over where 'astronaut' status begins?
questions.f: American military and civil authorities long used 50 miles, while international bodies favour the higher line.

questions.q: A sample of Martian rock found in Antarctica in 1984, a 1996 announcement that split scientists, and structures argued to be fossil microbes: what is it called?
questions.f: Most researchers now think the tiny shapes formed without life - but the debate reshaped astrobiology.

questions.q: A meteorite that fell in Australia in 1969, packed with amino acids, and evidence that life's building blocks form in space: which one?
questions.f: Dozens of amino acids have been identified in it, several unknown in Earth's biology.

questions.q: The largest single meteorite ever found still lies where it fell in Namibia. What is it called?
questions.f: It weighs over 60 tonnes, and remarkably no impact crater was ever found around it.

questions.q: Cut and etched iron meteorites reveal a distinctive interlocking crystal pattern. What is it called?
questions.f: The crystals grew over millions of years of achingly slow cooling - impossible to fake on Earth.

questions.q: Tiny meteorite grains can be collected from ordinary rooftop gutters by careful hobbyists.
questions.f: Amateur scientists have confirmed genuine micrometeorites among city roof dust using magnets and microscopes.

questions.q: A crewed spacecraft designed for gliding runway landings that flew only one uncrewed mission, and then was cancelled: which vehicle?
questions.f: Its single 1988 flight was fully automatic - no crew ever rode it, and none ever will.

questions.q: What do we call the flat inside part of your hand?
questions.f: Your palm has no hair and helps you grip toys, spoons and swings tightly.

questions.q: What is the joint between your hand and your arm called?
questions.f: Your wrist bends and twists so your hand can wave, turn and point.

questions.q: What is the joint between your foot and your leg called?
questions.f: Your ankle lets your foot tip up and down when you walk or jump.

questions.q: What is the back part of your foot called?
questions.f: Your heel touches the ground first each time you take a step.

questions.q: What is the bony bump where your finger bends called?
questions.f: You have knuckles on each finger so it can fold up to make a fist.

questions.q: What is the bottom of your foot called, the part you stand on?
questions.f: The sole of your foot can feel grass, sand and warm floors.

questions.q: What is the soft pink part around your teeth called?
questions.f: Your gums hold your teeth firmly in place, like soil around a plant.

questions.q: What is the small hole in your nose that you breathe through called?
questions.f: You have two nostrils, and tiny hairs inside them help catch dust.

questions.q: What are the tiny hairs on the edge of your eyelid called?
questions.f: Eyelashes help keep dust and bright light out of your eyes.

questions.q: What is the soft flap of skin that closes over your eye called?
questions.f: Your eyelids sweep across your eyes when you blink to keep them wet.

questions.q: What is the soft, dangly bottom part of your ear called?
questions.f: The earlobe is the squishy part at the bottom where earrings often go.

questions.q: What do we call the pointed part of your face just below your mouth?
questions.f: Your chin is at the very bottom of your face and moves when you chew.

questions.q: What is the soft, round part of your face below each eye called?
questions.f: Your cheeks turn pink when you run around or feel shy.

questions.q: What is the front of your head, above your eyes, called?
questions.f: Your forehead is where a thermometer often checks if you feel hot.

questions.q: What is the smallest finger on your hand called?
questions.f: The pinky is the littlest finger, sitting on the outside of your hand.

questions.q: What do we call the middle part of your body where a belt goes?
questions.f: Your waist is the narrower part between your ribs and your hips.

questions.q: What is the joint at the top of your leg, where it meets your body, called?
questions.f: Your hips let your legs swing forward and back as you walk.

questions.q: What is the hard front part of your lower leg called?
questions.f: Bumping your shin hurts because the bone sits right under thin skin.

questions.q: What is the soft, curved back of your lower leg called?
questions.f: Your calf is a strong muscle that helps you stand on your tiptoes.

questions.q: What is the upper part of your leg, above the knee, called?
questions.f: Your thigh holds the longest bone in your whole body.

questions.q: What is the little dent in the middle of your tummy called?
questions.f: Your belly button is left over from a tube that fed you before you were born.

questions.q: Which body part do you rotate to swing your arm in a big circle?
questions.f: Your shoulder is the most freely moving joint in the whole body.

questions.q: What do we call your hand when all the fingers are curled up tight?
questions.f: Making a fist tucks your fingers safely inside your hand.

questions.q: A doctor who looks after your teeth is called a…?
questions.f: A dentist checks your teeth and shows you how to keep them clean.

questions.q: A person who helps you when you are sick or hurt is a…?
questions.f: Doctors listen to your heart and help your body get better.

questions.q: What do we call the very end of one of your fingers?
questions.f: Your fingertips are super sensitive and can feel tiny bumps and edges.

questions.q: What do we call your two lower limbs that you walk on?
questions.f: Your two legs take you thousands of steps every single day.

questions.q: What do we call your two upper limbs, with a hand on each end?
questions.f: Your arms can lift, carry, throw and hug all day long.

questions.q: How many ears does a person usually have?
questions.f: Having two ears helps you tell which side a sound is coming from.

questions.q: How many arms does a person usually have?
questions.f: Two arms let you carry something in one hand and wave with the other.

questions.q: How many legs does a person usually have?
questions.f: Humans walk on two legs, which is called walking upright.

questions.q: Which body part do you mainly use to walk and run?
questions.f: Your leg muscles push against the ground to move you forward.

questions.q: Which body parts do you bring together to clap?
questions.f: Clapping makes a sound as your two palms slap together.

questions.q: Which body part do you use to kick a ball?
questions.f: Your foot has 26 little bones that help you kick and balance.

questions.q: Which body parts do you wrap around someone to give a hug?
questions.f: A warm hug can help you feel calm and happy.

questions.q: Which body part connects your head to your shoulders?
questions.f: Your neck lets your head turn side to side and nod up and down.

questions.q: Which body part do you move up and down to nod 'yes'?
questions.f: Nodding your head is a way to say yes without any words.

questions.q: Which part of your face do you use to talk and to eat?
questions.f: Your mouth shapes words with help from your lips and tongue.

questions.q: Which body parts do you close when you fall asleep?
questions.f: Closing your eyes helps block out light so you can rest.

questions.q: Which body part do you use to point at something far away?
questions.f: People often point with the index finger, next to the thumb.

questions.q: On which part of his face does a man grow a beard?
questions.f: Beard hair grows on the lower face when a boy becomes a grown man.

questions.q: Which body part do you wave to say hello?
questions.f: A friendly wave uses your hand and a big smile.

questions.q: Which body part do you use to blow out birthday candles?
questions.f: You push air out of your lungs and through your mouth to puff out flames.

questions.q: Which body part do you brush to keep it clean and shiny?
questions.f: Brushing twice a day sweeps away bits of food and keeps teeth strong.

questions.q: Which part of you gets a haircut?
questions.f: You can cut hair without any pain because the strands are not alive.

questions.q: Which body parts do you bend when you kneel down?
questions.f: Your knees are the biggest joints in your whole body.

questions.q: Which body parts do you lift in a shrug when you say 'I don't know'?
questions.f: A shrug is a little body signal that means you are not sure.

questions.q: How many thumbs does a person usually have?
questions.f: Your thumbs can touch every other finger, which helps you grab things.

questions.q: Which round body part sits on top of your neck?
questions.f: Your head holds your brain, eyes, ears, nose and mouth.

questions.q: Drinking milk helps make which body parts strong?
questions.f: Milk is full of calcium, which helps build strong bones and teeth.

questions.q: Which body parts should you wash before you eat a meal?
questions.f: Washing your hands rinses away tiny germs before they reach your food.

questions.q: What does your tummy sometimes do when you are very hungry?
questions.f: A rumble is the sound of air and juices moving in your empty tummy.

questions.q: What might your teeth do when you feel very cold?
questions.f: Chattering teeth are part of shivering, which helps warm your body up.

questions.q: When you run fast, your heart beats faster than when you rest.
questions.f: Your heart speeds up to send more oxygen to your busy muscles.

questions.q: A person usually has two hands.
questions.f: Each hand has five fingers, giving you ten fingers in total.

questions.q: Most people have ten fingers in total.
questions.f: Five fingers on each hand add up to ten handy helpers.

questions.q: Your two feet are found at the bottom of your legs.
questions.f: Your feet spread your weight so you can stand without toppling over.

questions.q: A person usually has just one nose.
questions.f: Your one nose has two nostrils to breathe and smell through.

questions.q: A person has one heart inside their chest.
questions.f: Your single heart works day and night without ever taking a break.

questions.q: Your fingernails are found at the tips of your fingers.
questions.f: Fingernails act like little shields for the sensitive tips of your fingers.

questions.q: What colour do healthy, clean teeth usually look?
questions.f: The hard outer layer of a tooth, called enamel, is naturally whitish.

questions.q: What do you do many times every minute to take in air?
questions.f: You breathe in and out all the time, even while you are asleep.

questions.q: How many eyes do you use to see?
questions.f: Using two eyes helps you judge how near or far things are.

questions.q: On which body part do you wear a warm hat?
questions.f: A hat keeps your head warm because you lose heat from the top of you.

questions.q: On which body parts do you wear gloves?
questions.f: Gloves keep your fingers cosy and warm on a chilly day.

questions.q: On which body parts do you wear socks and shoes?
questions.f: Shoes protect the soles of your feet from sharp and hot ground.

questions.q: In front of which body parts do glasses sit to help you see?
questions.f: Glasses bend the light so blurry things look nice and sharp.

questions.q: On which body parts do people wear earrings?
questions.f: Earrings usually clip or hang on the soft earlobe.

questions.q: Which body part does a bike helmet protect?
questions.f: A helmet guards your head, which holds your very important brain.

questions.q: On which finger do people often wear a ring?
questions.f: A ring slides onto a finger and can be a symbol of a promise.

questions.q: Which body part do you use to hold a pencil and write?
questions.f: Your fingers and thumb work together to grip a pencil just right.

questions.q: Which body parts do you use to carry a heavy bag?
questions.f: Strong arm muscles help you lift and carry things from place to place.

questions.q: What is the front part of your body, below your neck, called?
questions.f: Your chest is a bony box that keeps your heart and lungs safe inside.

questions.q: What do we call the part of your body behind your chest?
questions.f: You can feel the bumpy line of your backbone running down your back.

questions.q: What do we call the hollow spot underneath your arm?
questions.f: Your armpit is one of the warmest and most ticklish places on your body.

questions.q: How many fingers are on one hand?
questions.f: Four fingers plus a thumb make five, which is why we count in fives.

questions.q: How many toes are on one foot?
questions.f: Your five toes spread out to help you balance when you stand still.

questions.q: How many nostrils does your nose have?
questions.f: Air goes in through both nostrils, but often one is a little clearer than the other.

questions.q: How many knees does a person have?
questions.f: Your two knees bend so you can climb stairs, jump and sit cross-legged.

questions.q: What do we call the small brown dots that appear on some people's skin?
questions.f: Freckles often grow darker in summer when the sun shines on your skin.

questions.q: What do we call the little dents that show in some people's cheeks when they smile?
questions.f: Dimples happen when a small muscle under the cheek is shaped a bit differently.

questions.q: What do we call the hair that grows on a man's upper lip?
questions.f: A moustache sits just above the lip, while a beard covers the chin.

questions.q: What do we call the nails that grow on your feet?
questions.f: Toenails grow more slowly than fingernails because your toes get less blood flow.

questions.q: What word describes a person who has no hair on their head?
questions.f: A bald head still has tiny hair roots, they just stop growing long hairs.

questions.q: What do you do with your mouth when you feel happy?
questions.f: A smile uses more than a dozen muscles pulling at the corners of your mouth.

questions.q: What do we call it when you shut just one eye quickly at a friend?
questions.f: A wink uses one eyelid, while a blink closes both eyes at the same time.

questions.q: What noise do you make when your throat feels tickly and scratchy?
questions.f: A cough is a fast puff of air that pushes tickly dust out of your airway.

questions.q: What do you do with your mouth when you are sleepy and open it wide?
questions.f: A yawn pulls in a big gulp of air and stretches your jaw at the same time.

questions.q: What do you do to your food with your teeth before you swallow it?
questions.f: Chewing mashes food into small soft pieces that slide down easily.

questions.q: What do we call the noisy air that comes back up from your tummy?
questions.f: A burp is mostly air you swallowed along with your food and fizzy drinks.

questions.q: Which sense do you use with your tongue?
questions.f: Your tongue can pick out sweet, salty, sour and bitter flavours.

questions.q: Which sense do you use with your skin?
questions.f: Your skin can tell the difference between a soft feather and a rough rock.

questions.q: Which sense do you use with your nose?
questions.f: Your nose can recognise thousands of different smells, from bread to rain.

questions.q: What does your body need every night so you wake up feeling fresh?
questions.f: While you sleep, your body quietly repairs itself and grows.

questions.q: Which drink is best for your body when you feel thirsty?
questions.f: Your body is mostly water, so you need to top it up all day long.

questions.q: What do we stick over a small cut to keep it clean?
questions.f: A plaster keeps dirt out while your skin quietly knits itself back together.

questions.q: Which tool does a grown-up use to check if you have a temperature?
questions.f: A thermometer shows if your body is hotter than its usual 37 degrees.

questions.q: Which kind of picture lets a doctor see the bones inside you?
questions.f: Bones show up bright white on an X-ray because they block the rays.

questions.q: Where is the best place to sneeze so you do not spread germs?
questions.f: Sneezing into your elbow traps the germs instead of putting them on your hands.

questions.q: What do you rub on your skin to stop the sun from burning it?
questions.f: Sunscreen works like a shield, bouncing away the sun's strongest rays.

questions.q: What do you squeeze onto your toothbrush before you clean your teeth?
questions.f: Toothpaste has a mineral called fluoride that helps make teeth tougher.

questions.q: Which food helps keep your teeth strong, cheese or sweets?
questions.f: Cheese is full of calcium, while sticky sweets feed the germs that cause holes.

questions.q: How many times a day do dentists say you should brush your teeth?
questions.f: Brushing morning and night keeps germs from settling on your teeth.

questions.q: About how many hours of sleep does a child need each night?
questions.f: Children need more sleep than grown-ups because their bodies are still growing.

questions.q: Which part of your foot do you stand on when you go up on tiptoe?
questions.f: Your strong calf muscles lift your heels to push you onto your toes.

questions.q: Your heart sits slightly to which side of your chest?
questions.f: That is why people place a hand on the left side to feel their heartbeat.

questions.q: What do we call the skin on the top of your head, under your hair?
questions.f: Your scalp holds about a hundred thousand tiny hair roots.

questions.q: What do we call the blue or purple mark left on your skin after a bump?
questions.f: A bruise is a tiny bit of blood trapped just under the skin.

questions.q: Which word describes hair that is full of curls?
questions.f: Whether hair grows curly or straight depends on the shape of each hair root.

questions.q: What do we call someone who writes with their left hand?
questions.f: About one person in ten is left-handed, so lefties are quite special.

questions.q: Who is the person whose job is to cut and style your hair?
questions.f: A hairdresser trims the ends of hairs, which does not hurt at all.

questions.q: Who looks after you in hospital and helps the doctors?
questions.f: Nurses check your temperature and make sure you take your medicine.

questions.q: Which word means the same as your 'tummy'?
questions.f: Your stomach is the stretchy bag inside that holds your dinner.

questions.q: How do your legs usually feel after a very long walk?
questions.f: Tired legs are your muscles telling you they need a rest and a drink.

questions.q: Your two feet are usually about the same size as each other.
questions.f: For most people one foot is a tiny bit bigger, which is why shoes feel different.

questions.q: You need both your eyes and a light to see the colours in a picture.
questions.f: In the dark your eyes still work, but colours fade away to shades of grey.

questions.q: Washing your hands with soap gets rid of more germs than water alone.
questions.f: Soap grabs onto germs and grease so the water can rinse them away.

questions.q: Your fingernails keep growing all through your life.
questions.f: Nails grow from a soft base hidden under your skin, pushing outward.

questions.q: Every person's face looks a little bit different.
questions.f: Even twins have small differences, which is how we tell people apart.

questions.q: Which two smaller words are joined to make the word 'fingernail'?
questions.f: English loves joining two small words to name a body part.

questions.q: The word 'footprint' joins 'foot' with which other word?
questions.f: A footprint is the mark your foot prints onto sand, mud or snow.

questions.q: The word 'heartbeat' joins 'heart' with which other word?
questions.f: Each heartbeat is one squeeze of the muscle pushing blood on its way.

questions.q: The word 'toothbrush' joins 'tooth' with which other word?
questions.f: The first toothbrushes had bristles made from animal hair.

questions.q: The word 'eyelash' joins 'eye' with which other word?
questions.f: An old meaning of 'lash' was a thin, whip-like strand, just like an eyelash.

questions.q: The word 'handshake' joins 'hand' with which other word?
questions.f: People have shaken hands as a friendly greeting for thousands of years.

questions.q: The word 'backbone' joins 'back' with which other word?
questions.f: Your backbone is not one bone but a stack of many small ones.

questions.q: The word 'eyeball' joins 'eye' with which other word?
questions.f: Your eyeball really is almost perfectly round, like a small ball.

questions.q: The word 'eyebrow' joins 'eye' with which other word?
questions.f: 'Brow' is an old English word for the ridge above your eye.

questions.q: The word 'earache' joins 'ear' with a word meaning what?
questions.f: So a toothache is a pain in a tooth and a headache is a pain in your head.

questions.q: The word 'sunburn' joins 'sun' with which other word?
questions.f: Sunburn is your skin telling you it had too much strong sunshine.

questions.q: Which body part's name begins with a silent letter 'k'?
questions.f: Long ago people really did say the 'k' in words like knee and knife.

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'thumb'?
questions.f: The silent 'b' is a leftover from the way the word was spelled centuries ago.

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'wrist'?
questions.f: Several English words about twisting begin with a silent 'wr', like wring and wrap.

questions.q: Which body part rhymes with the word 'toes'?
questions.f: Rhyming words end with the same sound, even when they are spelled differently.

questions.q: Which body part rhymes with the word 'sweet'?
questions.f: 'Feet' and 'sweet' share the same long 'ee' sound at the end.

questions.q: Which body part rhymes with the word 'pie'?
questions.f: 'Eye' has just three letters but only one sound, rhyming neatly with pie.

questions.q: Which body part rhymes with the word 'chair'?
questions.f: Watch out, because 'hair' also sounds exactly like the animal called a hare.

questions.q: Which body part rhymes with the word 'win'?
questions.f: Chin, shin and skin all rhyme with win, which makes them handy for poems.

questions.q: Which body part rhymes with the word 'lung'?
questions.f: 'Tongue' has a surprising spelling, ending in 'gue' but sounding like 'ung'.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the joint where your arm meets your body?
questions.f: 'Shoulder' keeps a tricky silent 'u' right in the middle.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the stretchy organ that holds your dinner?
questions.f: 'Stomach' ends in 'ch' but sounds like a 'k', which trips up many spellers.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the stretchy tissue that pulls your bones?
questions.f: The 'c' in muscle is silent, hiding quietly between the s and the l.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the taster inside your mouth?
questions.f: Remember it as 'ton' plus 'gue' to get this famously tricky word right.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the bony bump on a finger?
questions.f: 'Knuckle' starts with a silent 'k' just like knee and knit.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the joint just above your foot?
questions.f: 'Ankle' rhymes with uncle but is spelled with an 'a' and a 'k'.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the joint in the middle of your arm?
questions.f: 'Elbow' is built from two old words meaning arm and bend.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the flap that closes over your eye?
questions.f: An eyelid is simply a 'lid' that closes over your eye like a pot lid.

questions.q: With which letter does the body part you hear with begin?
questions.f: Ear, elbow and eye all begin with the letter E.

questions.q: How many letters are there in the word 'elbow'?
questions.f: E-L-B-O-W spells the joint in the middle of your arm.

questions.q: What do we call the part of your body you sit down on?
questions.f: You sit on the body's biggest muscle, which is padded to keep you comfy.

questions.q: What do the strong cords called tendons connect together?
questions.f: The Achilles tendon at your heel is the thickest tendon in your body.

questions.q: What do the tough bands called ligaments connect?
questions.f: Ligaments hold your joints together so bones do not slip apart.

questions.q: Which blood cells are your body's soldiers that fight off germs?
questions.f: White blood cells swarm to a cut or infection to attack invaders.

questions.q: Which tiny blood cells help your blood clot and form a scab?
questions.f: Platelets rush to a cut and stick together to plug the leak.

questions.q: What is the clear dome at the very front of your eye called?
questions.f: The cornea is like a window that lets light into your eye.

questions.q: What is the light-sensing layer at the back of your eye called?
questions.f: The retina turns light into signals your brain reads as pictures.

questions.q: Which stretchy organ stores your urine until you visit the toilet?
questions.f: An adult bladder can hold about two cups of liquid before it feels full.

questions.q: What do we call the tiny living building blocks that make up your body?
questions.f: Your body is built from trillions of cells, far too small to see.

questions.q: Which gas do you mostly breathe OUT when you exhale?
questions.f: Plants soak up the carbon dioxide you breathe out and use it to grow.

questions.q: What is a healthy human body temperature very close to?
questions.f: Your body works hard to stay near 37C, even on cold or hot days.

questions.q: What do we call the whole frame of bones that holds up your body?
questions.f: Without your skeleton you would flop down like a jellyfish.

questions.q: Which body system uses nerves to carry messages to and from the brain?
questions.f: Messages zip along your nerves faster than a racing car.

questions.q: Which part of your ear helps you keep your balance?
questions.f: Tiny loops of fluid in your inner ear tell your brain which way is up.

questions.q: Which red blood cells carry oxygen to every part of your body?
questions.f: Red blood cells get their colour from iron that grabs onto oxygen.

questions.q: Your brain is divided into a left and a right what?
questions.f: The two halves of your brain are joined by a bundle of nerve fibres.

questions.q: What is the doctor's tool used to listen to your heart and lungs?
questions.f: A stethoscope makes the quiet lub-dub of your heart loud enough to hear.

questions.q: What do we call the smallest, thinnest blood vessels in your body?
questions.f: Capillaries are so narrow that blood cells must line up one by one to pass.

questions.q: Muscles work by pulling, not by pushing.
questions.f: Muscles often come in pairs so one pulls a bone one way and the other pulls it back.

questions.q: The heart is a special kind of muscle.
questions.f: Your heart muscle never gets tired, squeezing and relaxing all your life.

questions.q: White blood cells and red blood cells both float in your blood.
questions.f: Red cells carry oxygen while white cells hunt for germs, all in the same blood.

questions.q: Which part of your eye can you feel a gentle blink protecting?
questions.f: Blinking spreads a thin layer of tears to keep the cornea clean and moist.

questions.q: What do we call the study of the parts of the body?
questions.f: Doctors learn anatomy so they know where every bone and organ belongs.

questions.q: A person who cannot hear is described as…?
questions.f: Many deaf people communicate quickly and clearly using sign language.

questions.q: Which word describes someone who has lost their sight?
questions.f: Blind people can read with their fingertips using raised dots called braille.

questions.q: What is the special name for a doctor who cares for children?
questions.f: A pediatrician measures how tall and healthy you grow as you get older.

questions.q: A molar is which kind of body part?
questions.f: Flat, wide molars crush and grind your food before you swallow it.

questions.q: What is the correct plural of the word 'tooth'?
questions.f: English keeps a few old plurals, so one tooth becomes many teeth.

questions.q: What is the correct plural of the word 'foot'?
questions.f: Like tooth to teeth, foot changes its middle to become feet.

questions.q: The word part 'cardio', as in cardiologist, refers to which organ?
questions.f: This word part comes from an old Greek word for the heart, kardia.

questions.q: The word part 'derma', as in dermatologist, refers to which body covering?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for skin, which is your largest organ.

questions.q: The 'dent' in the word 'dentist' points to which body part?
questions.f: This root comes from a Latin word for tooth, dens.

questions.q: The prefix 'bi-' in the muscle name 'biceps' means…?
questions.f: The biceps in your upper arm has two ends that anchor onto bone.

questions.q: The word 'muscle' first meant a small…?
questions.f: People thought a flexing muscle looked like a little mouse under the skin.

questions.q: What is the throb of blood that you can feel at your wrist called?
questions.f: Each pulse beat matches one squeeze of your heart pushing blood along.

questions.q: A word ending in '-ologist' names someone who does what?
questions.f: So a biologist studies life, and a zoologist studies animals.

questions.q: What do we call the stack of small bones that make up your backbone?
questions.f: You have 33 vertebrae stacked like beads to protect your spinal cord.

questions.q: What do we call an eye doctor who tests your sight and fits glasses?
questions.f: An optometrist checks how sharply each eye can read a chart of letters.

questions.q: The muscle in your upper arm that you flex to show strength is the…?
questions.f: Bending your elbow makes the biceps bunch up into a little hill.

questions.q: Which food group does your body use most to build and repair muscle?
questions.f: Meat, beans, eggs and nuts are all packed with muscle-building protein.

questions.q: Which vitamin, found in oranges, helps cuts heal and keeps gums healthy?
questions.f: Sailors long ago fell ill on long voyages because their food had no vitamin C.

questions.q: Which mineral does your blood need to carry oxygen properly?
questions.f: Spinach, red meat and beans all help top up your body's iron.

questions.q: Which vitamin, found in carrots, helps you see in dim light?
questions.f: Vitamin A helps make the light-sensing pigment at the back of your eye.

questions.q: Where on your body can you most easily feel your pulse?
questions.f: Press gently at these spots and an artery lies just under the skin.

questions.q: About how many times does a resting child breathe in one minute?
questions.f: Children breathe faster than adults because their lungs are smaller.

questions.q: What is a fever?
c: A body temperature higher than normal
questions.f: A fever is your body deliberately turning up the heat to make germs uncomfortable.

questions.q: What is a vaccine designed to do?
c: Teach your body to fight a germ
questions.f: A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless preview so it is ready to fight.

questions.q: Which organ sits on the right, tucked just under your lower ribs?
questions.f: The liver is your heaviest internal organ, weighing over a kilogram in adults.

questions.q: After the stomach, which part of the gut does food travel into next?
questions.f: Most of the goodness in your food is soaked up in the small intestine.

questions.q: Which two organs work together as your body's main air-and-blood team?
questions.f: Your heart sends blood to the lungs to pick up a fresh load of oxygen.

questions.q: About how much of the air you breathe in is oxygen?
questions.f: Most of the air is actually nitrogen, which your lungs simply breathe back out.

questions.q: What is the small dangly organ at the back of your throat called?
questions.f: Your uvula helps stop food from sneaking up into your nose when you swallow.

questions.q: What is the roof of your mouth called?
questions.f: The front of your palate is hard and bony, while the back part is soft.

questions.q: Which body parts make the sound of your voice?
questions.f: Air rushing past your vocal cords makes them flutter, creating sound.

questions.q: What makes a person's voice sound high or low?
c: How fast the vocal cords vibrate
questions.f: Longer, thicker cords vibrate more slowly, which is why they make deeper voices.

questions.q: How many basic tastes were traditionally listed for the tongue?
questions.f: Sweet, salty, sour and bitter were the classic four, and umami later joined them.

questions.q: Which parts of your body are the most sensitive to a light touch?
questions.f: These areas are crowded with touch sensors, which is why they feel so much.

questions.q: What is the tiny pit in your skin that each hair grows out of called?
questions.f: You are born with all the hair follicles you will ever have.

questions.q: What is the job of the sticky mucus inside your nose?
questions.f: Tiny moving hairs then sweep the trapped dirt away toward your throat.

questions.q: Why do you have two ears instead of one?
c: To work out where a sound comes from
To hear two songs at once
questions.f: A sound reaches the nearer ear a whisker sooner, and your brain notices.

questions.q: What is colour blindness?
questions.f: Red and green are the pair most often confused, and it affects more boys than girls.

questions.q: What is the doctor's word for the sudden kick your leg gives when your knee is tapped?
questions.f: A reflex is so fast that the message never has to reach your brain first.

questions.q: Which organ decides to blink before you even notice something coming?
questions.f: A protective blink can happen in about a tenth of a second.

questions.q: How many hours does food usually take to pass right through your body?
questions.f: Most of that time is spent in the large intestine, soaking up water.

questions.q: What is the small pouch that hangs off the start of your large intestine called?
questions.f: Scientists now think the appendix may store useful gut bacteria.

questions.q: What are the two soft lumps at the back of your throat that help fight germs?
questions.f: Tonsils sit like guards where germs first arrive in your mouth and nose.

questions.q: What was your belly button once joined to before you were born?
questions.f: The cord delivered food and oxygen, so you did not need to eat or breathe.

questions.q: Which twins look almost exactly alike because they came from one cell?
questions.f: Identical twins share the same genes, but even they have different fingerprints.

questions.q: Roughly how much does an adult human brain weigh?
questions.f: Although it is only about 2% of your weight, the brain uses about 20% of your energy.

questions.q: Which part of a bone is hollow and filled with soft marrow?
questions.f: This clever design keeps bones strong but light enough to carry around.

questions.q: Which of these keeps your heart muscle strongest over time?
questions.f: Exercise makes the heart pump more blood with each beat, so it can rest more between beats.

questions.q: What is the bowl-shaped ring of bone at the bottom of your spine called?
questions.f: Your pelvis carries your body's weight down into your legs.

questions.q: Which muscles are in your chest, used when you do a push-up?
questions.f: People often shorten the name of these chest muscles to 'pecs'.

questions.q: What is the sticky film of germs that builds up on unbrushed teeth called?
questions.f: If plaque is left alone it hardens into a crust that only a dentist can scrape off.

questions.q: What is a cavity in a tooth?
questions.f: Germs turn sugar into acid, and the acid slowly eats a hole through the enamel.

questions.q: What is dental floss used for?
questions.f: A brush cannot reach the tight gaps where floss slides through easily.

questions.q: Veins have small one-way valves that stop blood from sliding backward.
questions.f: These valves matter most in your legs, where blood must climb upward.

questions.q: Your body cannot make its own vitamin C, so you must get it from food.
questions.f: Many animals make their own, but humans lost that ability long ago.

questions.q: Exercise makes your muscles grow stronger, not fewer in number.
questions.f: You keep roughly the same muscles all your life, but each fibre can thicken.

questions.q: Bones are lighter than they look because they are not solid all the way through.
questions.f: Inside, bone has a honeycomb structure, like the frame of a bridge.

questions.q: The whole of your gut, stretched out, is much longer than you are tall.
questions.f: It fits inside you because it is folded and coiled up many times over.

questions.q: The word part 'stetho' in 'stethoscope' refers to which part of the body?
questions.f: From Greek stethos, meaning chest, joined to skopein, to look at or examine.

questions.q: In words like 'microscope' and 'telescope', the part 'scope' means…?
questions.f: So a stethoscope is really a tool for 'examining the chest'.

questions.q: What does the word 'biology' mean the study of?
questions.f: From Greek bios, life, so a biologist studies everything that lives.

questions.q: A pedicure is a treatment for which part of the body?
questions.f: From Latin pes, foot, plus cura, care, so it literally means foot care.

questions.q: In the word 'antiseptic', the prefix 'anti-' means…?
questions.f: An antiseptic works against the germs that could grow in a wound.

questions.q: In a 'blood transfusion', the part 'trans-' tells you the blood is…?
c: Poured across from one person to another
questions.f: From Latin trans, across, plus fundere, to pour.

questions.q: What does the word 'bruise' describe?
questions.f: A bruise changes colour as your body slowly clears away the trapped blood.

questions.q: What is a blister?
c: A bubble of fluid under the skin
questions.f: That fluid cushion is your body protecting rubbed skin while it repairs.

questions.q: What does the word 'fracture' mean when a doctor uses it?
questions.f: From Latin frangere, to break, which also gives us 'fragile'.

questions.q: What has happened if you 'sprain' your ankle?
c: You have stretched or torn a ligament
questions.f: That is why a sprained ankle swells up and needs rest and ice.

questions.q: What is a scar?
c: The mark left where skin has healed
questions.f: Scar skin is tough but does not grow hair or sweat like normal skin.

questions.q: If part of your body feels 'numb', what does that mean?
questions.f: Numbness happens when nerve messages from that spot cannot get through.

questions.q: What does it mean to feel 'dizzy'?
c: Feeling like the room is spinning
questions.f: Dizziness often starts in the balance loops of your inner ear.

questions.q: Which word sounds just like 'heel' but means to get better?
questions.f: Homophones like heel and heal sound the same but mean quite different things.

questions.q: The word 'waist' sounds exactly like which other word?
questions.f: One is the middle of your body, the other means rubbish, so spelling matters.

questions.q: The body word 'muscle' sounds exactly like the name of which sea creature?
questions.f: Both words trace back to a Latin word for a little mouse.

questions.q: The word 'sole' of your foot sounds like which other word?
questions.f: Confusingly, 'sole' is also the name of a flat fish that lies on the seabed.

questions.q: Which health worker helps you move again after an injury, using exercises?
questions.f: Physiotherapists coach you through stretches that gently rebuild strength.

questions.q: Which health worker prepares and hands out your medicines?
questions.f: Pharmacists check that different medicines are safe to take together.

questions.q: What do we call a doctor who carries out operations?
questions.f: The word comes from Greek roots meaning 'hand work'.

questions.q: Who is specially trained to help a mother when her baby is being born?
questions.f: The word midwife comes from old English words meaning 'with woman'.

questions.q: Who rushes to an emergency in an ambulance to give first aid?
questions.f: The prefix 'para' here means working alongside doctors.

questions.q: Which body system includes your stomach, intestines and liver?
questions.f: The digestive system turns a sandwich into fuel your cells can actually use.

questions.q: Which body system includes your nose, windpipe and lungs?
questions.f: Its whole job is swapping the oxygen you need for the waste gas you do not.

questions.q: Which body system includes your heart and blood vessels?
questions.f: It is called circulatory because the blood goes round and round in a loop.

questions.q: Which body system is made up of all your bones together?
questions.f: Your skeleton gives you shape, protects your organs and stores minerals.

questions.q: Which body system defends you against germs?
questions.f: Your immune system remembers old enemies, so you rarely catch the same illness twice.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of your body's organs?
questions.f: The femur is a bone, while organs are made of soft tissues doing a special job.

questions.q: Which travels through your body inside blood vessels?
questions.f: Air goes through airways and food through the gut, each with its own pipes.

questions.q: Which is bigger, one of your kidneys or your heart?
questions.f: A kidney is about the size of a computer mouse, while a heart is fist-sized.

questions.q: Which grows faster, the hair on your head or the nails on your toes?
c: They grow at the same rate
questions.f: Scalp hair grows several times faster than the slowest-growing toenails.

questions.q: Which of these organs is protected by your ribcage?
questions.f: Your ribs form a springy cage that flexes every time you take a breath.

questions.q: Which of these is the correct order for food going down?
questions.f: Muscles in the food pipe squeeze in waves, so you could even swallow upside down.

questions.q: Which of these is made of muscle rather than bone?
questions.f: Your tongue is a bundle of muscles that never gets tired of talking.

questions.q: Which is the correct name for the bone in your upper arm?
questions.f: It sounds like 'humorous', which is why the nearby nerve became the 'funny bone' joke.

questions.q: Which sense do you lose most of when you have a blocked-up nose?
questions.f: Most of what we call flavour is really smell drifting up from the back of the mouth.

questions.q: What does your body make more of when you exercise in the heat?
questions.f: As sweat dries off your skin it carries heat away, cooling you down.

questions.q: Why does your face sometimes go red when you are hot or embarrassed?
c: Tiny blood vessels in the skin widen
questions.f: Wider vessels bring more red blood close to the surface of your skin.

questions.q: Why do your eyes make tears even when you are not sad?
c: To keep the eye clean and wet
questions.f: You produce a thin layer of tears with every single blink.

questions.q: What is the main reason your body needs oxygen?
questions.f: Without oxygen, your cells cannot unlock the energy stored in your dinner.

questions.q: Which part of your body keeps growing new cells to replace old skin?
c: The lower layer of your skin
questions.f: Fresh cells are pushed slowly upward and become the surface you can touch.

questions.q: What happens to your pupils when a doctor shines a torch in your eye?
questions.f: Doctors use this quick reflex to check that your nerves are working well.

questions.q: Why do your muscles feel warm after running about?
questions.f: Only about a quarter of a muscle's energy becomes movement; the rest is heat.

questions.q: What is a cramp in a muscle?
c: A muscle squeezing tight and not letting go
questions.f: Gently stretching the muscle and drinking water usually helps a cramp settle.

questions.q: What do doctors call the water and salts your body loses in sweat?
questions.f: That is why sports drinks include a pinch of salt as well as water.

questions.q: Which is the healthiest way to keep your heart and lungs strong?
questions.f: Running, swimming and cycling all give your heart a good workout.

questions.q: What does the word 'organ' mean when we talk about the body?
c: A body part with a special job
questions.f: The heart, liver and lungs are all organs, each with its own important task.

questions.q: What does the word 'tissue' mean in the body?
c: A group of similar cells working together
questions.f: Muscle tissue, nerve tissue and bone tissue each build different organs.

questions.q: What does the word 'digest' mean?
questions.f: Digestion starts the moment you begin chewing your first mouthful.

questions.q: What does the word 'inhale' mean?
questions.f: Its opposite is 'exhale', from Latin words meaning to breathe in and out.

questions.q: If a person is described as 'right-handed', what does that mean?
c: They prefer their right hand for tasks
questions.f: About nine out of ten people around the world are right-handed.

questions.q: What does the medical word 'pulse' actually count?
questions.f: From Latin pulsare, to beat or to push.

questions.q: Which word means the tiny living things that can make you ill?
questions.f: Bacteria and viruses are the two most common kinds of germ.

questions.q: What is a 'symptom'?
c: A sign that you are unwell
questions.f: A cough, a rash and a headache are all symptoms doctors listen out for.

questions.q: What does the word 'appetite' describe?
questions.f: Hormones from your stomach and brain work together to switch appetite on and off.

questions.q: What does 'hygiene' mean?
questions.f: The word comes from Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health.

questions.q: What is the medical word for the body's outer covering?
questions.f: An adult's skin, laid flat, would cover roughly two square metres.

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'knuckle' and also in 'knee'?
questions.f: Old English speakers pronounced that 'k', but over centuries it fell quiet.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the body's framework of bones?
questions.f: Remember three e-sounds: skel-e-ton, with an 'o' near the end.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the long tube that absorbs your food?
questions.f: It ends like 'fine' and 'nine', with a silent 'e' on the end.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of one of the two openings of your nose?
questions.f: 'Nostril' comes from old words meaning nose-hole.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the tiny hairs along your eyelids?
questions.f: Words ending in 'sh' add '-es' to make a plural, like brush and brushes.

questions.q: What is the correct plural of the word 'vertebra'?
questions.f: Latin words ending in '-a' often make their plural with '-ae'.

questions.q: Which word describes a person who can use both hands equally well?
questions.f: From Latin ambi, both, and dexter, right hand, so it means 'right-handed on both sides'.

questions.q: What is the word for a person who has a very good sense of taste and smell for food?
questions.f: Professional tea and coffee tasters train their tongues for years.

questions.q: What is a 'joint' in the language of the body?
questions.f: Your body has hundreds of joints, from big hips to tiny finger knuckles.

questions.q: What is the medical name for the whole of your gut?
questions.f: The intestines are divided into a small one and a large one.

questions.q: Which word describes the body's ability to fight off a germ it has met before?
questions.f: From Latin immunis, meaning exempt or safe from something.

questions.q: What is a 'gland' in the body?
c: An organ that makes and releases a substance
questions.f: Sweat glands, tear glands and salivary glands each release a different liquid.

questions.q: What is the medical word for spit?
questions.f: You make around a litre of saliva every single day without noticing.

questions.q: What is the medical word for sweat?
questions.f: From Latin per, through, and spirare, to breathe, as if your skin were breathing.

questions.q: What does the word 'nutrient' mean?
c: Something in food that your body needs
questions.f: Proteins, vitamins and minerals are all nutrients hidden in your meals.

questions.q: What does the word 'skeleton' name in the body?
questions.f: An adult skeleton makes up roughly a seventh of a person's total weight.

questions.q: Your left and right hands are mirror images of each other.
questions.f: That is why a left glove will never fit comfortably on your right hand.

questions.q: Sneezing and coughing are two different ways your body clears out irritants.
questions.f: A sneeze clears the nose while a cough clears the airway lower down.

questions.q: Your bones are joined to your muscles so that when a muscle shortens, a bone moves.
questions.f: Tendons pass the pull from muscle to bone, like a rope tugging a lever.

questions.q: Your body can repair a broken bone by growing new bone tissue.
questions.f: A plaster cast simply holds the pieces still while your body does the mending.

questions.q: Which of your senses works even while you are fast asleep?
questions.f: Your ears keep listening, which is how an alarm clock manages to wake you.

questions.q: What do we call the clear liquid part of blood left when the cells are removed?
questions.f: Plasma is straw-coloured, not red, because the red cells have been taken out.

questions.q: Which body part contains your voice box, food pipe and windpipe all together?
questions.f: That is a lot of important plumbing packed into a very narrow space.

questions.q: Which is the largest muscle in the human body?
questions.f: The gluteus maximus in your buttock powers you up stairs and out of chairs.

questions.q: The Achilles tendon, the body's thickest tendon, is found at your…?
questions.f: It links your calf muscle to your heel bone so you can push off the ground.

questions.q: The right lung has three lobes while the left lung has only two.
questions.f: The left lung is smaller to leave a cosy notch for the heart.

questions.q: What is the name of the largest artery in your body?
questions.f: The aorta carries fresh blood straight out of the heart to the whole body.

questions.q: Which organ makes insulin to help control the sugar in your blood?
questions.f: The pancreas sits behind your stomach and also makes juices for digestion.

questions.q: Which small pouch stores the bile your liver makes?
questions.f: The gallbladder squeezes bile into your gut to help break down fatty food.

questions.q: Which organ filters out old, worn-out red blood cells?
questions.f: The spleen also stores blood and helps your body fight infection.

questions.q: How many bones, called vertebrae, are stacked in a human backbone?
questions.f: These vertebrae protect the spinal cord, a thick bundle of nerves.

questions.q: What is the medical name for your kneecap?
questions.f: The patella is a small shield of bone that guards the front of your knee.

questions.q: What is the medical name for your collarbone?
questions.f: The clavicle links your arm to the rest of your skeleton at the shoulder.

questions.q: What is the medical name for your breastbone, in the middle of your chest?
questions.f: Your ribs curve around and join the sternum at the front.

questions.q: What is the medical name for your shoulder blade?
questions.f: The flat, triangular scapula slides across your back as your arm moves.

questions.q: A red blood cell lives for only about four months before being replaced.
questions.f: Your bone marrow builds millions of fresh red blood cells every second.

questions.q: More than half of the human body is made of water.
questions.f: About 60 percent of an adult body is water, found inside and around cells.

questions.q: What is the largest part of the brain, used for thinking and memory, called?
questions.f: The wrinkled cerebrum is split into a left and a right half.

questions.q: Which little flap stops food from going down your windpipe when you swallow?
questions.f: The epiglottis snaps shut over your airway so food heads to the stomach instead.

questions.q: What are the tiny finger-like bumps that soak up nutrients in your small intestine?
questions.f: Millions of villi give the gut a huge surface to absorb food into the blood.

questions.q: What is one main job of your large intestine?
questions.f: The large intestine reclaims water from leftovers before you go to the toilet.

questions.q: Digestion of starchy food begins in your mouth thanks to an enzyme in your…?
questions.f: An enzyme called amylase in spit starts turning bread into simple sugars.

questions.q: What is the common name for the last set of molars, which appear in your late teens?
questions.f: They were named wisdom teeth because they arrive when you are older and wiser.

questions.q: How many different types of teeth does an adult mouth have?
questions.f: Incisors, canines, premolars and molars each do a different job on your food.

questions.q: Which teeth at the front of your mouth are shaped for cutting and biting?
questions.f: Your sharp, chisel-shaped incisors are perfect for biting into an apple.

questions.q: Which snail-shaped part of the inner ear turns sound into nerve signals?
questions.f: The spiral cochlea is filled with fluid and thousands of tiny hair cells.

questions.q: The three tiny bones inside your ear are nicknamed the hammer, anvil and…?
questions.f: These three smallest bones pass sound vibrations deep into your ear.

questions.q: What is the outer layer of your skin called?
questions.f: The epidermis is the tough top layer you can see and touch.

questions.q: What is the iron-rich substance in red blood cells that carries oxygen called?
questions.f: Hemoglobin turns bright red when it grabs oxygen in your lungs.

questions.q: Where inside a cell is your DNA, the body's instruction book, kept?
questions.f: The nucleus is like the control room at the centre of most of your cells.

questions.q: How many chromosomes does a typical human body cell contain?
questions.f: You inherit 23 chromosomes from each parent, giving you 46 in all.

questions.q: Which mineral is stored in your bones to keep them hard and strong?
questions.f: Bones act as a storehouse, lending calcium to the body when it is needed.

questions.q: The liver can grow back even if part of it is removed.
questions.f: The liver is the only human organ that can regrow to its full size.

questions.q: The word part 'osteo', as in osteoporosis, refers to which body part?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for bone, osteon.

questions.q: The word part 'neuro', as in neuroscience, refers to which body part?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for nerve or sinew, neuron.

questions.q: The word part 'gastro', as in gastritis, refers to which organ?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for the stomach or belly, gaster.

questions.q: The word part 'optic', as in optician, is all about which sense?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word linked to seeing and the eye.

questions.q: The word part 'audi', as in auditory, refers to which sense?
questions.f: It comes from a Latin word meaning to hear, audire.

questions.q: The root 'manu', as in 'manual', refers to which body part?
questions.f: It comes from a Latin word for hand, manus, so manual means done by hand.

questions.q: A podiatrist is a doctor who takes special care of your…?
questions.f: The root 'pod' comes from a Greek word for foot.

questions.q: The word part 'cephal', as in cephalic, refers to which body part?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for head, kephale.

questions.q: An orthodontist straightens which part of your body?
questions.f: The root 'odont' comes from a Greek word for tooth.

questions.q: In words like arthritis and tonsillitis, the ending '-itis' means…?
questions.f: So arthritis means swollen, sore joints.

questions.q: The word part 'arthro', as in arthritis, refers to what part of the body?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for joint, arthron.

questions.q: A neurologist is a doctor who specialises in which body system?
questions.f: Neurologists treat problems in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.

questions.q: The word 'cornea', the clear front of the eye, comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Early scholars thought this tough, clear layer was a bit like thin horn.

questions.q: The word 'pupil', the dark centre of the eye, comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: You can see a tiny doll-sized reflection of yourself in someone's pupil.

questions.q: The 'iris', the coloured ring of your eye, is named after a word meaning…?
questions.f: The Greek goddess Iris was linked to the rainbow, matching the eye's many colours.

questions.q: The tooth called a 'molar' takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Like a heavy millstone, flat molars grind your food into a paste.

questions.q: Your pointed 'canine' teeth are named after which animal?
questions.f: These sharp teeth look like a dog's fangs, made for gripping and tearing.

questions.q: The word 'skeleton' comes from an old word meaning…?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek phrase for a dried-up body, all bones and no flesh.

questions.q: In the muscle name 'triceps', the prefix 'tri-' tells you it has how many heads?
questions.f: The triceps at the back of your arm anchors onto bone in three places.

questions.q: What is the medical name for the bony case that protects your brain?
questions.f: The cranium is made of several flat bones fused firmly together.

questions.q: If something is described as 'cardiac', it relates to which organ?
questions.f: A cardiac surgeon is a doctor who operates on the heart.

questions.q: If something is described as 'pulmonary', it relates to which organs?
questions.f: The pulmonary arteries carry blood from your heart to your lungs.

questions.q: If something is described as 'renal', it relates to which organs?
questions.f: It comes from a Latin word for kidney, renes.

questions.q: The sense described by the word 'olfactory' is your sense of…?
questions.f: Your olfactory nerve carries scent messages from your nose to your brain.

questions.q: The humerus is the long bone found in which part of your body?
questions.f: Its rounded top slots into your shoulder blade to form a ball-and-socket joint.

questions.q: Which two bones make up your forearm, between elbow and wrist?
questions.f: The radius rolls over the ulna, which is how you can turn your palm upward.

questions.q: Which two bones make up your lower leg, between knee and ankle?
questions.f: The thick tibia carries your weight while the slim fibula steadies the ankle.

questions.q: What is the collective name for the eight small bones in your wrist?
questions.f: These eight little blocks slide against each other to let your wrist bend and twist.

questions.q: What is the collective name for the three tiny bones inside your middle ear?
questions.f: All three ossicles together would fit comfortably on a single fingernail.

questions.q: What type of joint in your neck lets you shake your head 'no'?
questions.f: The top vertebra pivots around a peg on the one below, like a wheel on an axle.

questions.q: What are the wiggly, unmoving seams between the bones of your skull called?
questions.f: They interlock like jigsaw pieces, which makes the skull far stronger.

questions.q: Which muscles run down the back of your thigh?
questions.f: Sprinters must warm up their hamstrings carefully, as they pull easily.

questions.q: The deltoid muscle, shaped like a triangle, sits on which part of your body?
questions.f: It is named after the triangular Greek letter delta.

questions.q: Which side of your heart receives blood arriving back from the body?
questions.f: The right side then sends that tired blood on a short trip to the lungs.

questions.q: What is the wall of muscle that divides the left and right sides of your heart called?
questions.f: You also have a septum of cartilage separating your two nostrils.

questions.q: Which nerve carries pictures from your eye to your brain?
questions.f: Over a million nerve fibres are bundled into each optic nerve.

questions.q: What are the two main parts of the central nervous system?
questions.f: Nerves outside these two form the peripheral nervous system.

questions.q: Which part of the brain is essential for forming new memories?
questions.f: You have one hippocampus curled deep inside each side of the brain.

questions.q: What is the middle layer of your skin, beneath the epidermis, called?
questions.f: The dermis is where your sweat glands, hair roots and touch sensors live.

questions.q: What is the thin, clear membrane covering the white of your eye called?
questions.f: When it gets inflamed and pink, doctors call the condition conjunctivitis.

questions.q: Which tube carries urine from a kidney down to the bladder?
questions.f: You have two ureters, one running down from each kidney.

questions.q: What are the two large airways that branch off the bottom of your windpipe called?
questions.f: One bronchus heads into each lung before splitting again and again.

questions.q: What is the thin double membrane wrapped around each of your lungs called?
questions.f: A slippery film between its layers lets your lungs glide as they inflate.

questions.q: What is the sac of membrane that surrounds and protects your heart called?
questions.f: The name simply means 'around the heart'.

questions.q: Where in the body does gas exchange, swapping oxygen for carbon dioxide, take place?
c: In the alveoli of the lungs
questions.f: The walls there are so thin that gases slip straight through into the blood.

questions.q: Which organ produces bile, the greenish liquid that helps digest fat?
questions.f: The liver makes bile continuously and the gallbladder simply stores it.

questions.q: What is the medical name for your voice box's neighbour, the tube behind your nose and mouth?
questions.f: The pharynx is a shared crossroads for both air and food.

questions.q: Which structure in your throat is commonly known as the Adam's apple?
questions.f: It is a ridge of cartilage that grows more prominent in boys during their teens.

questions.q: Which part of the large intestine is the longest section?
questions.f: The colon travels up, across and down your abdomen in a big question-mark shape.

questions.q: Which teeth sit between your canines and your molars?
questions.f: Premolars have two points on top, making them good at both tearing and grinding.

questions.q: Which cells in your skin make it possible to feel pain from a scratch?
questions.f: Pain sensors are the most numerous kind of sensor in your skin.

questions.q: About what percentage of your body weight does your skeleton make up?
questions.f: Bone is surprisingly light because it is a honeycomb inside rather than a solid block.

questions.q: Which mineral, alongside calcium, is packed into bone to keep it rigid?
questions.f: Calcium and phosphorus combine into a crystal that gives bone its hardness.

questions.q: How many muscles work together to move each of your eyeballs?
questions.f: These six muscles let your eye look up, down, sideways and roll slightly.

questions.q: Which gland in front of your ears produces most of your saliva?
questions.f: Thinking about a lemon is enough to set your parotid glands flowing.

questions.q: How many pairs of salivary glands does the human mouth have?
questions.f: Together they keep your mouth wet enough to talk, taste and swallow.

questions.q: Cartilage has no blood vessels of its own, which is why it heals slowly.
questions.f: Nutrients must seep in from surrounding tissue, so a torn knee cartilage takes ages to mend.

questions.q: Your body has more bacteria cells living in and on it than you might expect.
questions.f: Most of them live harmlessly in your gut, and many actively help you digest food.

questions.q: Nerve messages travel as tiny electrical signals along the nerve fibres.
questions.f: At each gap between neurons the electrical signal switches to a chemical one.

questions.q: Your tongue is anchored to the floor of your mouth by a thin fold of tissue.
questions.f: That little fold is called the frenulum, and you can feel it with your fingertip.

questions.q: A person can live a healthy life with only one kidney.
questions.f: The remaining kidney simply grows a little larger and takes on the extra work.

questions.q: What is the medical word for your internal organs taken as a group?
questions.f: From a Latin word for the soft parts inside the body.

questions.q: What is the anatomical term for your arms and legs together?
questions.f: Doctors also call them the extremities, because they extend from the trunk.

questions.q: What is the anatomical name for the main part of the body, without head or limbs?
questions.f: Your trunk holds nearly all your vital organs in two big cavities.

questions.q: The root 'spir' in 'respiration' and 'inspire' means…?
questions.f: From Latin spirare, so 'inspire' once meant to breathe a thought into someone.

questions.q: The root 'ocul' in 'binoculars' and 'oculist' refers to which body part?
questions.f: From Latin oculus, eye, so binoculars are literally 'for two eyes'.

questions.q: If something is described as 'nasal', it relates to which body part?
questions.f: From Latin nasus, nose, which also gives us the word 'nostril'.

questions.q: If something is described as 'oral', it relates to which body part?
questions.f: From Latin os, oris, meaning mouth, so oral hygiene means mouth care.

questions.q: If something is described as 'lingual', it relates to which body part?
questions.f: From Latin lingua, tongue, the same root behind 'language' and 'linguist'.

questions.q: If something is described as 'dorsal', it relates to which side of the body?
questions.f: From Latin dorsum, back, which is why a shark's back fin is its dorsal fin.

questions.q: In anatomy, 'lateral' means positioned toward the…?
questions.f: Its opposite is 'medial', meaning closer to the body's midline.

questions.q: The prefix 'hypo-' in a medical word tells you something is…?
questions.f: So hypothermia means your body temperature has dropped too low.

questions.q: The prefix 'hyper-' in a medical word tells you something is…?
questions.f: So a hyperactive muscle is one that is working more than it should.

questions.q: If a person is 'dehydrated', what is their body short of?
questions.f: The root 'hydro' comes from a Greek word for water.

questions.q: The root 'vit' in 'vitamin' and 'vital' means…?
questions.f: From Latin vita, life, so vital organs are the ones you cannot live without.

questions.q: The prefix 'mono-' in a word like 'monocular' means…?
questions.f: A monocle is a single lens for one eye, from the same root.

questions.q: The word 'tendon' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin tendere, to stretch, the same root behind 'extend' and 'tense'.

questions.q: The word 'ligament' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin ligare, to bind, which also gives us the word 'oblige'.

questions.q: The word 'nerve' comes from an old word meaning…?
questions.f: Early anatomists lumped nerves, tendons and cords together as stringy things.

questions.q: The word 'elbow' is built from two old words meaning…?
questions.f: An 'ell' was an old measure based on the length of a forearm.

questions.q: The word 'nostril' is built from 'nose' plus a word meaning…?
questions.f: From Old English nosthyrl, literally a nose-hole.

questions.q: The word 'wrist' comes from an old root meaning…?
questions.f: The same twisting root gives us 'wring', 'wrap' and 'wrestle'.

questions.q: The word 'digit', used for a finger or toe, also came to mean…?
questions.f: People counted on their fingers, so the word for finger became the word for numeral.

questions.q: The 'palm' of your hand shares its name with which plant?
questions.f: The tree was named for its broad, flat, hand-shaped leaves.

questions.q: What does an anaesthetist do in a hospital?
c: Sends patients safely to sleep for surgery
questions.f: The word means 'without feeling', from Greek an- plus aisthesis, sensation.

questions.q: Which kind of pictures does a radiologist study?
questions.f: Radiologists can spot a hairline crack in a bone that others would miss.

questions.q: What does a physiologist study?
questions.f: Anatomy is about the body's parts; physiology is about what those parts do.

questions.q: Which organ of the body can regrow lost tissue, making living donation possible?
questions.f: A donor can give away part of their liver and both halves will grow back.

questions.q: What is the name for the automatic muscle wave that pushes food along your gut?
questions.f: Because the squeeze travels in one direction, an astronaut can swallow in zero gravity.

questions.q: Roughly how long does an adult's large intestine measure?
questions.f: It is shorter but much wider than the small intestine, hence the name.

questions.q: Which chemicals in your body speed up reactions such as digestion?
questions.f: Each enzyme fits only one job, like a key that opens a single lock.

questions.q: What do we call the ball of chewed food you swallow in one gulp?
questions.f: From Latin bolus, meaning a lump or a ball.

questions.q: Which sense organ contains both hearing and balance equipment?
questions.f: The cochlea handles sound while the looping canals beside it handle balance.

questions.q: What happens to the lens of your eye as you look from a book to a distant hill?
questions.f: A ring of muscle relaxes and the lens flattens, sharpening far-away things.

questions.q: Which structure controls how much light enters your eye?
questions.f: The iris is a ring of muscle that widens or narrows the pupil in its middle.

questions.q: Where are your tear glands located?
questions.f: Tears drain away through a tiny hole near your nose, which is why crying makes you sniff.

questions.q: What is the name of the pigment in the retina that reacts to light?
questions.f: Bright light bleaches rhodopsin, which is why you are dazzled for a moment.

questions.q: Roughly how many taste buds does an adult tongue carry?
questions.f: Each bud holds dozens of taste cells, and they are replaced every couple of weeks.

questions.q: Which body organ contains sensors for both smell and the moistening of air?
questions.f: Your nose warms and dampens every breath before it reaches your lungs.

questions.q: What are the microscopic moving hairs that sweep mucus out of your airways called?
questions.f: Millions of cilia beat in waves, like a field of wheat in the wind.

questions.q: Which white blood cells are named after the lymph system they patrol?
questions.f: Lymphocytes are the cells that remember germs long after you recover.

questions.q: What is the name for a substance that triggers your immune system to react?
questions.f: Antibodies are the body's reply; antigens are the messages that start the argument.

questions.q: What is the thin fluid that drains from your tissues into lymph vessels called?
questions.f: Unlike blood, lymph has no pump; it is squeezed along by your ordinary movements.

questions.q: Which body fluid is produced by your liver and stored ready for use?
questions.f: An adult liver makes up to a litre of bile every day.

questions.q: What is the outer layer of a kidney called?
questions.f: From a Latin word for bark, because it wraps the organ like bark on a tree.

questions.q: Which nutrients does your small intestine pass straight into the bloodstream?
