questions.f: Fibre is one of the few things that travels on through, keeping your gut moving.

questions.q: Which food part cannot be digested but keeps your gut healthy?
questions.f: Fibre gives the muscles of your gut something to push against.

questions.q: Which of these does your body produce to fight a specific germ it has met?
questions.f: Each antibody is shaped to lock onto one particular invader.

questions.q: Which two body systems work together to control almost everything you do?
questions.f: Nerves send fast electrical messages while hormones send slower chemical ones.

questions.q: How long does it usually take for a simple broken bone in a child to knit together?
questions.f: Children's bones mend faster than adults' because they are still growing.

questions.q: Which part of a long bone is where growth in length happens in children?
c: The growth plate near each end
questions.f: Growth plates harden into solid bone once you stop growing taller.

questions.q: How many bones does an adult human hand contain, including the wrist?
questions.f: All those small bones are what let your hand make so many precise shapes.

questions.q: Your body sheds and rebuilds its outer layer of skin over and over throughout life.
questions.f: Much of household dust is made of the skin flakes people quietly shed.

questions.q: Your left and right lungs contain different numbers of sections, or lobes.
questions.f: Three on the right, two on the left, because the heart takes up room.

questions.q: Blood in your veins is dark red, never blue, even though veins look blue through skin.
questions.f: Skin scatters light in a way that makes the vessels underneath look bluish.

questions.q: Your heart pumps blood through two separate circuits, one to the lungs and one to the body.
questions.f: That double loop is why the heart needs four chambers instead of two.

questions.q: The word part 'hema' or 'haem' at the start of a word points to which body fluid?
questions.f: From Greek haima, blood, which gives us haemoglobin and haematology.

questions.q: The word part 'melan' in 'melanin' means which colour?
questions.f: From Greek melas, black, because the pigment darkens skin and hair.

questions.q: The word 'keratin', the protein in nails and hair, comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek keras, horn, because animal horn is made of the very same protein.

questions.q: The word 'sebum', your skin's natural oil, comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: That is why the glands producing it are called sebaceous glands.

questions.q: The word 'follicle' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin folliculus, a small sack, because each one is a tiny pouch in the skin.

questions.q: The word 'cuticle' at the base of your nail comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin cutis, skin, so a cuticle is a thin fold of skin.

questions.q: The word 'saliva' has always meant which body fluid?
questions.f: The Latin word saliva passed into English almost completely unchanged.

questions.q: The word 'enamel' on your teeth comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: The name comes from the craft of melting glassy coatings onto metal.

questions.q: The tooth word 'incisor' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin incidere, to cut, the same root behind 'incision' and 'scissors'.

questions.q: The word 'gingivitis' tells you which part of the mouth is inflamed?
questions.f: From Latin gingiva, gum, plus the ending meaning inflammation.

questions.q: The word 'thorax', used for the chest, originally meant…?
questions.f: Ancient armour covered the chest, so the armour's name became the body part's name.

questions.q: The word 'pelvis' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: The ring of hip bones really is shaped like a shallow basin.

questions.q: The word 'sternum' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Doctors sometimes call its pointed lower tip the 'xiphoid', meaning sword-shaped.

questions.q: The word 'appendix' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: That is also why extra pages hanging at the back of a book are called an appendix.

questions.q: The word 'rectum' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Early anatomists named it for its fairly straight path, unlike the coiling gut above.

questions.q: The word 'alveolus', one tiny air sac, comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin alveus, a basin or trough, so each one is a small cavity.

questions.q: The word 'bronchus' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: The airways do branch like a tree, but the name came from the pipe itself.

questions.q: The word part 'cyto' in 'cytoplasm' refers to…?
questions.f: So cytoplasm is the jelly filling the inside of a cell.

questions.q: The prefix 'sub-' in 'sublingual' tells you the position is…?
questions.f: A sublingual tablet is one you tuck under your tongue to dissolve.

questions.q: The prefix 'peri-' in 'pericardium' means…?
questions.f: So the pericardium is the sac that goes around the heart.

questions.q: The prefix 'intra-' in 'intravenous' means…?
questions.f: An intravenous drip delivers fluid directly within a vein.

questions.q: The prefix 'inter-' in 'intervertebral' means…?
questions.f: The intervertebral discs are cushions sitting between the bones of your spine.

questions.q: In the word 'symmetry', used to describe the body, 'sym-' means…?
questions.f: Your body is roughly symmetrical, with a matching left and right side.

questions.q: What does a dietitian advise people about?
questions.f: Dietitians plan meals for people whose bodies need very particular nutrition.

questions.q: What does a chiropodist look after?
questions.f: The name is built from Greek roots meaning hand and foot.

questions.q: What is the term for a doctor who specialises in the care of older people?
questions.f: From Greek geras, old age, the mirror image of paediatrics for children.

questions.q: A person who studies the shape and structure of the body is an…?
questions.f: The word anatomy literally means 'cutting up', which is how early study was done.

questions.q: What does the term 'vital signs' mean in a hospital?
c: Basic measures like pulse and temperature
questions.f: Pulse, breathing rate, temperature and blood pressure are the classic four.

questions.q: What is the medical word for a joint being forced out of its normal position?
questions.f: Shoulders dislocate most easily because their socket is so shallow.

questions.q: What is 'posture'?
c: The way you hold your body
questions.f: Good posture spreads your weight so no single muscle has to strain.

questions.q: What does the word 'reflex' literally suggest is happening?
questions.f: From Latin reflectere, to bend back, because the signal turns around at the spinal cord.

questions.q: What is the medical term for the sense of your body's position and balance combined?
questions.f: Your inner ear, your eyes and your muscles all report in to keep you steady.

questions.q: Which of these describes 'metabolism'?
c: All the chemical reactions keeping you alive
The number of bones you have
questions.f: From a Greek word meaning change, because your body is always transforming things.

questions.q: What is the medical name for the tube that carries urine out of your body?
questions.f: The ureters run down from the kidneys, while the single urethra is the final exit.

questions.q: Which muscle, running across the thigh, is the longest in the human body?
questions.f: The ribbon-like sartorius helps you cross one leg over the other.

questions.q: The muscles that move your eyes are among the fastest-reacting muscles in your body.
questions.f: Eye muscles make quick darting movements called saccades many times a second.

questions.q: Which is the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body?
questions.f: The stapedius braces the tiniest ear bone against very loud sounds.

questions.q: Which tiny gland is often called the body's 'master gland'?
questions.f: The pea-sized pituitary bosses other glands and even controls how you grow.

questions.q: In which part of the body is the thyroid gland found?
questions.f: The butterfly-shaped thyroid sets how fast your body burns energy.

questions.q: Your adrenal glands sit on top of your kidneys.
questions.f: These little glands pump out adrenaline when you get a fright or a thrill.

questions.q: What is the main job of the hormone insulin?
questions.f: Insulin lets your cells take in sugar from the blood to use for energy.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood out to the whole body?
questions.f: The left ventricle has the thickest walls because it works the hardest.

questions.q: What is the main job of the valves inside your heart?
questions.f: Heart valves snapping shut make the familiar lub-dub sound.

questions.q: Which patch of special cells acts as the heart's natural pacemaker?
questions.f: The sinoatrial node fires tiny electric signals that set your heartbeat.

questions.q: After the main bronchi, air travels into ever-smaller tubes called…?
questions.f: Bronchioles branch like a tree until they reach tiny air sacs called alveoli.

questions.q: Which hard layer of a tooth lies just beneath the outer enamel?
questions.f: Dentine is slightly softer than enamel and gives teeth their off-white colour.

questions.q: What is found in the soft pulp at the very centre of a tooth?
questions.f: The pulp is why a deep cavity can cause a sharp toothache.

questions.q: Which cells are responsible for building new bone tissue?
questions.f: Osteoblasts lay down fresh bone, which is how a broken bone mends.

questions.q: Yellow bone marrow mainly stores fat, while red marrow makes blood cells.
questions.f: When you lose a lot of blood, yellow marrow can switch back to making cells.

questions.q: What is the slippery fluid that lubricates and cushions your joints called?
questions.f: Synovial fluid lets bones glide smoothly instead of grinding together.

questions.q: Your hip and shoulder are examples of which type of joint?
questions.f: A ball-and-socket joint lets the limb swing in almost any direction.

questions.q: Your elbow and knee are examples of which type of joint?
questions.f: A hinge joint bends and straightens like the hinge on a door.

questions.q: Rods in your retina work best in dim light, while cones handle colour.
questions.f: That is why colours fade to grey when you look around a dark room.

questions.q: What is the 'blind spot' in your eye?
c: Where the optic nerve leaves the retina
questions.f: There are no light sensors there, but your brain quietly fills in the gap.

questions.q: How many types of colour-sensing cones does a typical human eye have?
questions.f: Cones tuned to red, green and blue light mix to make every colour you see.

questions.q: How does the lens of your eye help you focus on near and far objects?
questions.f: Tiny muscles squeeze the lens fatter for close-up things, a trick called accommodation.

questions.q: What is the tough white part of your eye called?
questions.f: The sclera is a strong outer coat that holds the eyeball's round shape.

questions.q: Which savoury flavour is counted as the fifth basic taste?
questions.f: Umami is the rich, savoury taste found in cheese, mushrooms and broth.

questions.q: What are the small bumps on your tongue that hold your taste buds called?
questions.f: Most papillae are far too small to see clearly without a magnifier.

questions.q: What is the deepest layer of your skin, made largely of fat, called?
questions.f: This fatty layer helps keep you warm and cushions the body underneath.

questions.q: Which skin cells produce the pigment that colours your skin and protects it from the sun?
questions.f: Melanocytes make more pigment in sunlight, which is how a tan forms.

questions.q: Which glands in your skin produce an oil called sebum?
questions.f: Sebum keeps your skin and hair from drying out and cracking.

questions.q: Which of these is a common pattern found in human fingerprints?
questions.f: Fingerprint experts sort prints into loops, whorls and arches.

questions.q: What is the pale half-moon shape at the base of your fingernail called?
questions.f: The lunula gets its name because it looks like a tiny crescent moon.

questions.q: What is the pale, liquid part of blood that carries cells and nutrients called?
questions.f: Plasma is mostly water and makes up more than half of your blood.

questions.q: Which system is used to sort human blood into groups such as A, B, AB and O?
questions.f: Your blood group depends on tiny markers sitting on your red blood cells.

questions.q: Which blood type is often called the 'universal donor'?
questions.f: O-negative blood can be given safely to almost anyone in an emergency.

questions.q: What is the long fibre of a nerve cell that carries signals away from it called?
questions.f: Some axons running down to your toes are nearly a metre long.

questions.q: What is the tiny gap between two nerve cells, where signals jump across, called?
questions.f: Chemicals leap across the synapse to pass the message to the next neuron.

questions.q: What is the fatty coating that speeds up signals along a nerve called?
questions.f: Myelin works like insulation on a wire, letting signals race along.

questions.q: Which lobe at the front of the brain helps with planning and decisions?
questions.f: The frontal lobe is one of the last parts of the brain to fully develop.

questions.q: Which lobe at the back of the brain mainly handles vision?
questions.f: Signals from your eyes travel all the way to the back of your head to be seen.

questions.q: The left side of your brain mainly controls the right side of your body.
questions.f: Nerve pathways cross over, so each brain half steers the opposite side.

questions.q: What is the clear liquid that cushions and protects your brain called?
questions.f: Your brain floats in this fluid, which softens knocks and bumps.

questions.q: What are the protective membranes that wrap around your brain and spinal cord called?
questions.f: Three layers of meninges form a tough, cushioning cover for your nerves.

questions.q: How do endocrine glands send their messages around the body?
c: By releasing hormones into the blood
questions.f: Hormones travel in the bloodstream to reach faraway organs.

questions.q: Each of your kidneys contains about a million tiny filters called nephrons.
questions.f: Nephrons clean waste from your blood and turn it into urine.

questions.q: What is the first part of the small intestine, just after the stomach, called?
questions.f: The duodenum is where bile and pancreas juices join to digest food.

questions.q: Bile helps digestion by breaking large blobs of fat into tiny droplets.
questions.f: Splitting fat into droplets gives enzymes more surface to work on.

questions.q: Where do the helpful bacteria of your gut microbiome mostly live?
questions.f: Trillions of friendly microbes there help you digest food and stay healthy.

questions.q: What is the job of the antibodies your immune system makes?
c: To target and fight specific germs
questions.f: Once you beat an illness, matching antibodies can guard you next time.

questions.q: What is the main job of the small lumps called lymph nodes?
questions.f: Lymph nodes can swell up when they are busy fighting an infection.

questions.q: Which part of the brain acts as the body's thermostat, keeping your temperature steady?
questions.f: The hypothalamus triggers shivering when cold and sweating when hot.

questions.q: What is the smallest kind of blood vessel, where oxygen passes into the tissues?
questions.f: Capillary walls are just one cell thick, so gases slip through easily.

questions.q: Which two Toronto researchers first isolated insulin in the early 1920s, saving countless diabetics?
questions.f: Frederick Banting and Charles Best purified it from pancreas extract, and it revived dying patients almost overnight.

questions.q: The word part 'nephro', as in nephron, refers to which organ?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for kidney, nephros.

questions.q: The word part 'pulmo', as in pulmonary, refers to which organ?
questions.f: It comes from a Latin word for lung, pulmo.

questions.q: The word part 'haemo' or 'hemo', as in hemoglobin, refers to what?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for blood, haima.

questions.q: The word part 'dactyl', as in polydactyl, refers to which body parts?
questions.f: A polydactyl person or cat is born with extra fingers or toes.

questions.q: What is the reflex where a baby's big toe curls upward when the sole of its foot is stroked?
questions.f: Named after neurologist Joseph Babinski, it is normal in babies but a warning sign if it appears in adults.

questions.q: The word part 'cost', as in intercostal, refers to which body parts?
questions.f: Your intercostal muscles sit between the ribs and help you breathe.

questions.q: The word part 'gloss', as in glossitis, refers to which body part?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for tongue, glossa.

questions.q: The word part 'rhino', as in rhinoplasty, refers to which body part?
questions.f: A rhinoceros is literally a 'nose-horn' animal, sharing the same root.

questions.q: What is the name of the roughly 24-hour internal body clock that governs sleep and alertness?
questions.f: The name comes from Latin 'circa diem', meaning 'about a day', matching one spin of the Earth.

questions.q: Wilhelm Roentgen won the first-ever Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering what, first imaging his wife's hand?
questions.f: In 1895 the ghostly picture of Anna Roentgen's finger bones and ring became the first medical X-ray ever taken.

questions.q: A hematologist is a doctor who specialises in which part of the body?
questions.f: Hematologists study conditions like anaemia and clotting problems.

questions.q: A nephrologist is a doctor who specialises in which organs?
questions.f: Nephrologists help patients whose kidneys are not filtering well.

questions.q: A gastroenterologist is a doctor who specialises in which system?
questions.f: They care for the stomach, intestines and other digestive organs.

questions.q: A pulmonologist is a doctor who specialises in which organs?
questions.f: Pulmonologists help patients with asthma and other breathing troubles.

questions.q: An endocrinologist is a doctor who specialises in which part of the body?
questions.f: They treat conditions linked to hormones, such as diabetes.

questions.q: The word part 'ophthalmo', as in ophthalmologist, refers to which organ?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for eye, ophthalmos.

questions.q: An audiologist is a specialist who helps with which sense?
questions.f: Audiologists test hearing and can fit tiny hearing aids.

questions.q: In the word 'orthopedic', the prefix 'ortho-' means…?
questions.f: Orthopedic doctors help straighten and mend bones and joints.

questions.q: The windpipe's name, 'trachea', comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Ridges of cartilage give the trachea a slightly rough, bumpy feel.

questions.q: The breathing muscle called the 'diaphragm' takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The diaphragm forms a wall between your chest and your belly.

questions.q: The 'thyroid' gland is named after a word meaning…?
questions.f: The gland was thought to look like an ancient warrior's shield.

questions.q: The first part of the small intestine, the 'duodenum', is named for the number…?
questions.f: It was measured as about twelve finger-widths long by early anatomists.

questions.q: The 'retina' at the back of the eye takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Its web of tiny blood vessels reminded early scholars of a net.

questions.q: The 'clavicle', or collarbone, has a name meaning…?
questions.f: The bone's gentle S-curve reminded people of an old-fashioned door key.

questions.q: The kneecap's medical name, 'patella', comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The flat, rounded bone looks a bit like a tiny shallow plate.

questions.q: Each backbone bone, a 'vertebra', is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Stacked vertebrae let your spine twist and turn in many directions.

questions.q: If a sense is described as 'gustatory', it relates to your sense of…?
questions.f: It comes from a Latin word meaning to taste, gustare.

questions.q: If something is described as 'tactile', it relates to your sense of…?
questions.f: It comes from a Latin word meaning to touch, tangere.

questions.q: The word part 'cyto', as in cytology, refers to what?
questions.f: Cytology is the study of the tiny cells that make up living things.

questions.q: Histology is the microscopic study of the body's…?
questions.f: The 'hist' root comes from a Greek word for tissue or web.

questions.q: In a word like 'appendectomy', the ending '-ectomy' means…?
questions.f: So an appendectomy is an operation to take out the appendix.

questions.q: In the word 'subcutaneous', the prefix 'sub-' tells you the layer is…?
questions.f: A doctor can give some medicines by a subcutaneous injection under the skin.

questions.q: In the word 'epidermis', the prefix 'epi-' means…?
questions.f: The epidermis is the layer sitting on top of the deeper dermis.

questions.q: A 'hypodermic' needle gets its name because it goes where?
questions.f: The prefix 'hypo' means under, and 'derma' means skin.

questions.q: In the word 'intercostal', the prefix 'inter-' means…?
questions.f: Intercostal muscles sit between the ribs to help your chest expand.

questions.q: What does it mean if a muscle is described as 'involuntary'?
c: It works without you thinking about it
questions.f: Your heart and gut muscles are involuntary, working while you sleep.

questions.q: Which phrase best describes cartilage?
questions.f: Cartilage cushions your joints and shapes your bendy nose and ears.

questions.q: The outer flap of your ear, the 'pinna', takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The pinna funnels sound waves into the ear canal toward the eardrum.

questions.q: The word part 'somato', as in somatic, refers to what?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for body, soma, so somatic cells are body cells.

questions.q: Who invented the stethoscope in 1816 after rolling a sheet of paper into a tube?
questions.f: Laennec was too shy to press his ear to a patient's chest, so he invented a polite alternative.

questions.q: Which English doctor used matter from cowpox to create the first vaccine?
questions.f: The word vaccine itself comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.q: Who first used the word 'cell' for living things after peering at cork through a microscope?
questions.f: The tiny empty boxes reminded Hooke of the bare cells monks slept in.

questions.q: Which surgeon performed the world's first successful human heart transplant in 1967?
questions.f: The operation took place in Cape Town, South Africa, and made headlines worldwide.

questions.q: What is the Heimlich manoeuvre used to treat?
questions.f: A firm inward push under the ribs uses trapped air in the lungs to pop the blockage free.

questions.q: What does the Apgar score check, moments after a birth?
questions.f: Devised by Virginia Apgar in 1952, it scores things like breathing and colour out of ten.

questions.q: A shortage of which vitamin causes scurvy, with bleeding gums and loose teeth?
questions.f: Long sea voyages without fresh fruit made scurvy the terror of old sailing fleets.

questions.q: A shortage of which vitamin causes rickets, softening a child's growing bones?
questions.f: Sunlight on skin makes vitamin D, so rickets spread in smoky, sunless industrial cities.

questions.q: A swelling of the thyroid called a goitre is usually caused by a lack of which mineral?
questions.f: Adding a trace of iodine to table salt wiped out goitre across whole countries.

questions.q: A shortage of which vitamin causes the nerve illness beriberi?
questions.f: It appeared when polished white rice replaced brown rice, whose husks held the vitamin.

questions.q: What do the two numbers in a blood pressure reading such as 120 over 80 describe?
c: Pressure when the heart squeezes and when it rests
questions.f: The higher number is the push of each beat; the lower one is the pressure between beats.

questions.q: What does the term 'basal metabolic rate' measure?
questions.f: Even lying perfectly still, your body burns most of its daily energy just staying alive.

questions.q: What is the medical term for the volume of air moved in one ordinary breath?
questions.f: A relaxed adult breath moves only about half a litre of air.

questions.q: Roughly how many protein-coding genes does the human genome contain?
questions.f: Scientists once guessed 100,000, so the real answer was a genuine surprise.

questions.q: Which parent passes mitochondrial DNA on to a child?
questions.f: Because it passes down the female line, it lets scientists trace ancient ancestry.

questions.q: What are the protective caps at the ends of your chromosomes called?
questions.f: They shorten slightly each time a cell divides, like a fuse burning down.

questions.q: Which chemical does the body release that causes the itching and sneezing of an allergy?
questions.f: That is why allergy medicines are called antihistamines.

questions.q: Which large white blood cell surrounds and swallows germs whole?
questions.f: Its name means 'big eater', and a single one can gobble up a hundred bacteria.

questions.q: Which protein forms the tough mesh that holds a blood clot together?
questions.f: Fibrin threads criss-cross a wound like scaffolding, trapping cells in a plug.

questions.q: Which blood type is described as the 'universal recipient'?
questions.f: People with AB positive blood carry all the markers, so no donor type looks foreign.

questions.q: Which hormone from the kidneys tells bone marrow to make more red blood cells?
questions.f: Living at high altitude raises it, which is why athletes train in the mountains.

questions.q: Which cells are responsible for breaking down and recycling old bone?
questions.f: Building cells and breaking cells work as a team, rebuilding your whole skeleton over years.

questions.q: Your entire skeleton is gradually replaced and renewed over the course of about ten years.
questions.f: Bone is living tissue, constantly demolished and rebuilt in tiny patches.

questions.q: Which type of joint in your thumb lets it swing and rotate like a rider on a saddle?
questions.f: This joint is a big reason human hands can grip tools so precisely.

questions.q: What are the small fluid-filled cushions that reduce friction near joints called?
questions.f: From Latin bursa, a purse, because each one is a small flattened bag.

questions.q: What is the thin living membrane that covers the outer surface of a bone called?
questions.f: It is richly supplied with nerves, which is why a knock to the shin hurts so much.

questions.q: What is the anatomical name for the calf muscle whose name means 'belly of the leg'?
questions.f: From Greek gaster, belly, plus kneme, leg, describing its bulging shape.

questions.q: The broad muscle across your upper back and shoulders is named after which shape?
questions.f: The left and right trapezius muscles together form that four-sided shape.

questions.q: Which muscle name means 'the broadest of the back'?
questions.f: Swimmers develop it strongly, which gives them a wide V-shaped back.

questions.q: In the muscle name 'rectus abdominis', the word 'rectus' means…?
questions.f: Its fibres run straight up the front of the abdomen, unlike the oblique muscles beside it.

questions.q: The hormone 'adrenaline' is named for glands positioned where?
questions.f: Its other name, epinephrine, says the same thing using Greek roots instead of Latin.

questions.q: The word 'artery' comes from an ancient root meaning…?
questions.f: Arteries empty after death, so early anatomists concluded they must carry air.

questions.q: The eye's 'lens' is named after which food?
questions.f: From Latin lens, lentil, because a lentil seed has that same double-curved shape.

questions.q: The word 'vertigo' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'vertex' and the spinning of a vortex.

questions.q: The word 'cortex', used for the brain's outer layer, means…?
questions.f: From Latin cortex, tree bark, because it wraps the organ as bark wraps a trunk.

questions.q: The branching arms of a nerve cell, its 'dendrites', are named after…?
questions.f: From Greek dendron, tree, because they spread out like twigs from a branch.

questions.q: The word 'synapse' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: It names the tiny junction where one nerve cell hands its message to the next.

questions.q: The 'uvula' hanging at the back of your throat is named after which small fruit?
questions.f: From Latin uvula, little grape, which is just what it looks like.

questions.q: The forearm bone called the 'radius' shares its name with which everyday object?
questions.f: It pivots around the ulna, sweeping like a spoke turning on a hub.

questions.q: The slender lower leg bone, the 'fibula', is named after which object?
questions.f: Beside the tibia it looked like the pin of a clasp holding a cloak.

questions.q: The boat-shaped bone in your foot is called the…?
questions.f: From Latin navis, ship, the same root behind 'navy' and 'navigate'.

questions.q: The heel bone's medical name is…?
questions.f: It is the largest bone in the foot and takes the first thump of every step.

questions.q: The pea-shaped bone in the wrist is called the…?
questions.f: From Latin pisum, pea, and yes, another wrist bone is named for the moon.

questions.q: Which Latin name for an ear bone means 'anvil'?
questions.f: The hammer bone strikes it, which is how the blacksmith names arose.

questions.q: The maze-like inner ear is often called the 'labyrinth' because…?
c: Its winding passages resemble a maze
It is shaped like a shell only
questions.f: Getting lost in it is a real risk for surgeons, so they operate with great care.

questions.q: The medical word 'cerumen' refers to which substance?
questions.f: From Latin cera, wax, and it slowly carries dust out of the ear canal.

questions.q: In the eye, the 'macula' is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: This small yellowish spot on the retina is where your sharpest vision sits.

questions.q: The word 'astigmatism' is built from roots meaning…?
questions.f: An unevenly curved cornea spreads light into a smear instead of a sharp point.

questions.q: The word 'caries', used for tooth decay, means…?
questions.f: Acid made by mouth bacteria is what starts the rotting process.

questions.q: The 'caecum' at the start of the large intestine has a name meaning…?
questions.f: It is a blind-ended pouch, closed at one end like a cul-de-sac.

questions.q: The middle section of the small intestine, the 'jejunum', is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Early anatomists always found it empty in dissections, hence the odd name.

questions.q: The word 'lymph' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: Lymph really is a pale, watery fluid, quite unlike red blood.

questions.q: The word 'plexus', as in a nerve plexus, means…?
questions.f: Nerves in a plexus weave together like strands plaited into a braid.

questions.q: A 'ganglion' in the nervous system takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: A ganglion is a knot-like cluster of nerve cell bodies.

questions.q: The word 'foramen', as in the holes of the skull, means…?
questions.f: The largest is the foramen magnum, where the spinal cord leaves the skull.

questions.q: The word 'suture', used for skull seams and stitches, means…?
questions.f: Surgical stitches and skull joints share the same sewing image.

questions.q: The word 'papilla', as in the bumps on your tongue, means…?
questions.f: Anything nipple-shaped or bump-like in the body tends to be called a papilla.

questions.q: The medical prefix 'dys-', as in 'dyslexia', means…?
questions.f: So dyslexia describes difficulty with reading words, not a lack of intelligence.

questions.q: In the word 'polydactyl', the prefix 'poly-' means…?
questions.f: A famous colony of polydactyl cats with extra toes lived at Hemingway's house.

questions.q: The prefix 'exo-', as in 'exoskeleton', means…?
questions.f: Insects wear their skeleton on the outside, while ours is an endoskeleton.

questions.q: In anatomy, 'proximal' describes a position that is…?
questions.f: Its opposite, 'distal', means farther away, as your fingertips are distal to your wrist.

questions.q: In anatomy, what does 'ventral' mean?
questions.f: It shares a root with 'ventricle', the little belly-shaped chamber of the heart.

questions.q: What does the medical word 'benign' mean when describing a lump?
questions.f: From Latin benignus, kindly, so a benign lump is the reassuring kind.

questions.q: What does 'chronic' mean when a doctor describes a condition?
questions.f: From Greek chronos, time, so its opposite is 'acute', meaning sudden and short.

questions.q: What does the term 'congenital' mean?
questions.f: From Latin roots meaning 'born with'.

questions.q: Goose bumps are a leftover reflex from ancestors whose body hair fluffed up for warmth.
questions.f: The tiny muscles still fire, but with thin human hair the effect is mostly wasted.

questions.q: About how much air can a healthy adult push out in one deepest possible breath?
questions.f: Doctors call this the vital capacity and measure it with a spirometer.

questions.q: Roughly how much blood does an adult heart pump every minute at rest?
questions.f: That means your entire blood supply completes a full circuit in about a minute.

questions.q: Which organ uses about a fifth of your body's oxygen despite being only 2% of your weight?
questions.f: That is why even a brief loss of blood flow to the brain makes you faint.

questions.q: Which element makes up the greatest share of the human body by mass?
questions.f: Most of it is locked up in water, which is roughly two-thirds of your body.

questions.q: About how much calcium does an adult body contain, nearly all of it in bone?
questions.f: Your bones act as a bank, lending calcium out whenever blood levels drop.

questions.q: How many muscles work together inside your tongue?
questions.f: Four anchor it to nearby bone and four run entirely within the tongue itself.

questions.q: Roughly how much saliva does an adult produce in a day?
questions.f: Over a lifetime that adds up to enough to fill several swimming pools.

questions.q: Which structure in the brain relays almost all incoming sensory signals?
questions.f: Nearly everything you see, hear or feel passes through this central switchboard.

questions.q: What are the ridges on the wrinkled surface of the brain called?
questions.f: The grooves between them are sulci, and the folding packs far more surface inside the skull.

questions.q: Which cells wrap around nerve fibres outside the brain to form their fatty sheath?
questions.f: Named after Theodor Schwann, who also helped establish that all tissue is built of cells.

questions.q: What is the medical name for the sac of membrane lining your abdominal cavity?
questions.f: It is the largest membrane of its kind in the body, with a huge folded surface.

questions.q: Which valve sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle of the heart?
questions.f: It is also called the bicuspid valve, and its name comes from a bishop's mitre hat.

questions.q: How many cusps, or flaps, does the tricuspid valve of the heart have?
questions.f: It guards the doorway between the right atrium and the right ventricle.

questions.q: Which blood vessels are the only arteries in an adult that carry oxygen-poor blood?
questions.f: They are heading to the lungs to collect oxygen, so they break the usual rule.

questions.q: Which arteries supply the heart muscle itself with blood?
questions.f: They branch off the aorta and wrap the heart like a crown, hence the name.

questions.q: Which large arteries carry blood up the neck to the brain?
questions.f: You can feel a strong pulse from them on either side of your windpipe.

questions.q: The liver receives blood from the gut before that blood reaches the rest of the body.
questions.f: This detour lets the liver check and clean everything you absorb from a meal.

questions.q: How many types of muscle tissue does the human body contain?
questions.f: Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle each have a completely different job.

questions.q: Which type of muscle tissue lines the walls of your gut and blood vessels?
questions.f: It works without you thinking about it, squeezing food and blood steadily along.

questions.q: Which type of muscle can generate its own rhythm without any nerve signal?
questions.f: A heart removed and kept alive in the lab will keep beating all by itself.

questions.q: Which pair of long neck muscles turns your head from side to side?
questions.f: Its mouthful of a name simply lists the three bones it attaches to.

questions.q: Which ring-shaped muscle closes your eyelids?
questions.f: A matching ring, the orbicularis oris, purses your lips for a whistle.

questions.q: Which muscle of the forehead lifts your eyebrows in surprise?
questions.f: It is the muscle responsible for the horizontal lines that appear on a forehead.

questions.q: The 'oblique' muscles of your abdomen are named because their fibres run…?
questions.f: Their slanting pull is what lets you twist your torso from side to side.

questions.q: What does the medical term 'atrophy' describe?
questions.f: Astronauts must exercise hard in orbit, or weightlessness lets their muscles atrophy.

questions.q: What does 'hypertrophy' mean when talking about muscle?
c: Growth in the size of fibres
questions.f: Training does not add new fibres; it thickens the ones you already have.

questions.q: Which branch of the nervous system prepares the body for 'fight or flight'?
questions.f: It floods you with adrenaline, widening pupils and speeding the heart in an instant.

questions.q: Which branch of the nervous system handles 'rest and digest'?
questions.f: It slows the heart and switches digestion back on once danger has passed.

questions.q: What is the 'grey matter' of the brain mostly made of?
questions.f: White matter, by contrast, is mostly bundles of fibres wrapped in pale myelin.

questions.q: What are the two main types of lymphocyte in your immune system?
questions.f: B cells make antibodies while T cells hunt down infected cells directly.

questions.q: What does the term 'autoimmune' mean?
c: The immune system attacks the body's own tissue
The body has no immune system
questions.f: The immune system is normally very good at telling 'self' from 'invader'.

questions.q: What is anaemia?
c: Too few healthy red blood cells
questions.f: It often leaves a person tired and pale, because less oxygen reaches their tissues.

questions.q: Which yellowish pigment, left over from worn-out red blood cells, colours bile?
questions.f: The same pigment is why a fading bruise turns yellow-green before it disappears.

questions.q: Which vitamin is produced by helpful bacteria living in your large intestine?
questions.f: Vitamin K is essential for making your blood clot properly.

questions.q: Which hormone from the thyroid gland helps lower the calcium level in blood?
questions.f: It works in opposition to parathyroid hormone, keeping calcium finely balanced.

questions.q: What are endorphins?
questions.f: They are behind the pleasant glow athletes call a runner's high.

questions.q: What is the valve between your small and large intestine called?
questions.f: It stops the contents of the large intestine from washing back the wrong way.

questions.q: Which layer of your skin contains no blood vessels at all?
questions.f: That is why a very shallow graze can hurt without bleeding a single drop.

questions.q: What is the anatomical name for the long shaft in the middle of a limb bone?
questions.f: The rounded end of the bone is the epiphysis, from Greek roots meaning 'growing upon'.

questions.q: What is 'ossification'?
questions.f: Much of a baby's skeleton starts as cartilage and slowly ossifies into true bone.

questions.q: Which forearm bone forms the bony point of your elbow?
questions.f: Rest your elbow on a table and the knob you feel is the top of the ulna.

questions.q: Tooth enamel is built mostly from crystals of which mineral compound?
questions.f: Packed tightly, those crystals make enamel the hardest substance your body builds.

questions.q: The word part 'phag', as in 'macrophage', means…?
questions.f: So a macrophage is literally a 'big eater' among your white blood cells.

questions.q: The word part 'troph', as in 'atrophy' and 'hypertrophy', relates to…?
questions.f: From Greek trophe, food, so hypertrophy is 'over-nourishment' of a muscle.

questions.q: Which is the largest single cell in the human body?
c: A nerve cell in the ear
questions.f: The female egg cell, or ovum, is just about visible to the naked eye as a tiny dot.

questions.q: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body.
questions.f: This tough, ropey protein gives strength to skin, tendons, bones and cartilage.

questions.q: Roughly how many nerve cells are thought to be in the human brain?
questions.f: Each neuron may link to thousands of others, forming a vast web of connections.

questions.q: Which is the longest single cell in the human body?
questions.f: A motor neuron can stretch from the base of the spine all the way to the toe.

questions.q: How many separate bones are fused together to form an adult human skull?
questions.f: The skull's flat bones knit together along wiggly seams called sutures.

questions.q: The human body has 12 pairs of cranial nerves.
questions.f: These nerves branch straight from the brain to control the face, eyes and more.

questions.q: How many pairs of spinal nerves branch from the human spinal cord?
questions.f: Each pair serves a different band of the body, from neck to toes.

questions.q: The vagus is the longest of the cranial nerves, reaching down to organs in the belly.
questions.f: Its name means 'wandering', because it roams so far from the brain.

questions.q: What is the thick band of nerve fibres connecting the brain's two hemispheres called?
questions.f: The corpus callosum lets the left and right sides of the brain share messages.

questions.q: Which part of the brainstem controls automatic actions like your heartbeat and breathing?
questions.f: Even while you sleep, the medulla keeps these life-support jobs running.

questions.q: The fovea is the tiny spot on the retina that gives you your sharpest vision.
questions.f: You aim the fovea at whatever you read, packed with tightly spaced cones.

questions.q: Roughly how many cells is an adult human body estimated to contain?
questions.f: That is thousands of times more cells than there are stars in our galaxy.

questions.q: About how many base pairs make up the complete human genome?
questions.f: If you read one letter per second, spelling it out would take nearly a century.

questions.q: What is the small ball of capillaries in a nephron that first filters the blood called?
questions.f: The glomerulus works like a sieve, holding back blood cells and big proteins.

questions.q: Roughly how much blood do the kidneys filter in a single day?
questions.f: Almost all of it is reabsorbed, so you only pass a litre or two of urine.

questions.q: What is the name for the mushy, partly digested food that leaves your stomach?
questions.f: The stomach churns food with acid for hours to turn it into soupy chyme.

questions.q: Which stomach enzyme mainly digests proteins?
questions.f: Pepsin only works well in the stomach's strong acid, which suits it perfectly.

questions.q: Which digestive enzyme is responsible for breaking down fats?
questions.f: Lipase from the pancreas snips fats into fatty acids your body can absorb.

questions.q: The acid inside your stomach has a very low pH of roughly…?
questions.f: This acid is strong enough to dissolve metal, yet a lining of mucus protects you.

questions.q: In what form does your liver store spare glucose for later energy?
questions.f: When blood sugar drops, the liver breaks glycogen back down into glucose.

questions.q: The islets of Langerhans in the pancreas produce insulin and which other hormone?
questions.f: Insulin lowers blood sugar and glucagon raises it, keeping levels balanced.

questions.q: What is the substance that coats the air sacs and stops them collapsing called?
questions.f: Surfactant lowers surface tension so tiny alveoli can stay open for air.

questions.q: Which fluid-filled structures of the inner ear sense when your head spins or turns?
questions.f: Fluid sloshing in these loops tells your brain you are rotating.

questions.q: Which hormone, released by the adrenal glands, is often called the 'stress hormone'?
questions.f: Cortisol helps your body cope with stress but stays high if you worry too long.

questions.q: Red blood cells, or erythrocytes, have no nucleus.
questions.f: Losing the nucleus leaves more room for oxygen-carrying hemoglobin.

questions.q: What is the basic repeating unit of a muscle that shortens when it contracts?
questions.f: Thousands of sarcomeres line up end to end inside every muscle fibre.

questions.q: Which two proteins slide past each other to make a muscle contract?
questions.f: Myosin filaments grab and haul on actin filaments, shortening the muscle.

questions.q: Fast-twitch muscle fibres are best suited to quick, powerful bursts of effort.
questions.f: Sprinters rely on fast-twitch fibres, while marathon runners use slow-twitch ones.

questions.q: In an adult, most new red blood cells are made in the red marrow of which bones?
c: Flat bones like the breastbone and hip
questions.f: In babies, almost every bone helps make blood, but that shrinks with age.

questions.q: What is the X-shaped point where the two optic nerves partly cross called?
questions.f: At the optic chiasm, signals swap sides so each brain half gets both eyes' views.

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries most of the feeling from your face?
questions.f: The trigeminal nerve splits into three branches spreading across the face.

questions.q: Which gland releases growth hormone to help your body grow taller?
questions.f: Too little growth hormone in childhood can slow growth, while too much speeds it.

questions.q: Which hormone from the thyroid gland sets the speed of your metabolism?
questions.f: Thyroxine is one of the few body chemicals that contains the element iodine.

questions.q: What is the name for the body's ability to keep its inner conditions steady?
questions.f: Homeostasis keeps things like temperature and water levels within safe limits.

questions.q: Human blood is slightly alkaline, with a pH of around 7.4.
questions.f: The body works hard to hold blood pH in a very narrow, safe range.

questions.q: Which large vessel returns most of the body's lymph fluid back into the bloodstream?
questions.f: The thoracic duct empties lymph into a big vein near the base of the neck.

questions.q: Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles in your skin help you sense what?
questions.f: Different receptors respond to a light stroke, a firm press or a buzzing vibration.

questions.q: Which hard tissue covers and protects the root of a tooth below the gum?
questions.f: Cementum anchors fibres that hold the tooth firmly in its socket.

questions.q: Which ring of muscle guards the exit where food leaves the stomach?
questions.f: The pyloric sphincter opens now and then to let chyme trickle into the gut.

questions.q: What is the proper name for the bones that make up your fingers and toes?
questions.f: Each finger has three phalanges, but the thumb has only two.

questions.q: In the instrument name 'sphygmomanometer', the part 'sphygmo' refers to your…?
questions.f: A sphygmomanometer is the cuff a nurse uses to measure your blood pressure.

questions.q: The word part 'laryngo', as in laryngitis, refers to which body part?
questions.f: Laryngitis is a swelling of the voice box that can leave you croaky.

questions.q: In medical words, the ending '-aemia' or '-emia' refers to a condition of the…?
questions.f: So leukaemia is a disease affecting the white cells of the blood.

questions.q: The word part 'thrombo', as in thrombosis, refers to a…?
questions.f: A thrombosis is a blood clot blocking the flow inside a vessel.

questions.q: In words like erythrocyte and leukocyte, the ending '-cyte' means…?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for a hollow vessel, later used to mean cell.

questions.q: In the word 'rhinoplasty', the ending '-plasty' means…?
questions.f: A rhinoplasty is an operation to reshape the nose.

questions.q: A name like 'Achilles tendon', taken from the figure it honours, is an example of a(n)…?
questions.f: Dozens of body parts carry the names of the anatomists who first described them.

questions.q: What is the term for the vivid feeling that a limb is still present after it has been amputated?
questions.f: The brain's body map keeps a slot for the missing limb, so it still 'feels' fingers or toes that are gone.

questions.q: The word part 'sarco', as in sarcomere, refers to which body tissue?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek word for flesh, sarx.

questions.q: The word part 'adipo', as in adipose, refers to which body tissue?
questions.f: Adipose tissue stores energy and helps keep the body warm.

questions.q: If something is described as 'lacrimal', it relates to which watery product?
questions.f: Your lacrimal glands, tucked above each eye, keep it bathed in tears.

questions.q: In the muscle name 'quadriceps', the prefix 'quadri-' means…?
questions.f: The quadriceps at the front of your thigh is a team of four muscles.

questions.q: The white of the eye, the 'sclera', takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The sclera is a tough, fibrous coat that protects the delicate eyeball.

questions.q: The jelly-like 'vitreous' humour of the eye is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Its clear, glass-like look lets light pass straight through to the retina.

questions.q: The watery 'aqueous' humour at the front of the eye is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: This thin fluid feeds the lens and cornea, which have no blood supply.

questions.q: The 'fovea', the eye's spot of sharpest sight, is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The fovea is a tiny dip in the retina, packed with colour-sensing cones.

questions.q: The 'vagus' nerve gets its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: It wanders from the brainstem all the way down to the heart and gut.

questions.q: The word 'hormone' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: Hormones are chemical messengers that stir organs into action.

questions.q: The hormone 'insulin' takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: It is made in the pancreas by clusters of cells called the islets, or little islands.

questions.q: The protein 'collagen' has a name built from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Boiling collagen-rich tissue makes a sticky glue, which inspired the name.

questions.q: The liquid part of blood, 'plasma', takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The same root gives us words like 'plastic', meaning easily shaped.

questions.q: The tiniest blood vessels, the 'capillaries', are named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: They are as fine as a hair, so blood cells squeeze through one by one.

questions.q: The body's largest artery, the 'aorta', is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The aorta arches upward out of the heart before curving down through the body.

questions.q: Each pumping lower chamber of the heart, a 'ventricle', is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The word shares a root with 'ventral', meaning the belly side of the body.

questions.q: Each upper receiving chamber of the heart, an 'atrium', is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: In old Roman houses, the atrium was the open hall you first stepped into.

questions.q: The heartbeat phase called 'systole' comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: During systole the heart muscle squeezes together to push blood out.

questions.q: The muscle wave called 'peristalsis' comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Ring-like squeezes wrap around the gut to push food along, even upside down.

questions.q: The food pipe, the 'oesophagus', has a name built from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Its muscles carry each mouthful down toward the stomach.

questions.q: The stomach's exit valve, the 'pylorus', is named from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Like a gatekeeper, the pylorus decides when food may leave the stomach.

questions.q: A 'sphincter' is a ring of muscle whose name comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: Sphincters tighten to close an opening and relax to let things through.

questions.q: What is the small vertical groove between your nose and upper lip called?
questions.f: Almost everyone has a philtrum, though its exact shape varies from person to person.

questions.q: In anatomy, which body part is called the 'hallux'?
questions.f: The hallux is the sturdy big toe that helps you balance and push off when walking.

questions.q: In anatomy, which body part is called the 'pollex'?
questions.f: The pollex, or thumb, can touch each fingertip, giving humans a strong grip.

questions.q: In anatomy, which part of the body is the 'axilla'?
questions.f: The axilla is a warm, sheltered hollow where lymph nodes can often be felt.

questions.q: If something is described as 'buccal', it relates to which part of the mouth?
questions.f: It comes from a Latin word for cheek, bucca.

questions.q: If something is described as 'plantar', it relates to which body surface?
questions.f: A plantar wart is one that grows on the sole where you press when walking.

questions.q: If something is described as 'tympanic', it relates to a body part shaped like a…?
questions.f: The tympanic membrane, or eardrum, vibrates like a drumskin when sound hits it.

questions.q: Which is the longest and widest single nerve in the human body?
questions.f: The sciatic nerve runs from the lower back down through each leg toward the foot.

questions.q: A bone that is just a ring with no body, a Titan sentenced to an endless burden, and the reason you can nod 'yes' point to which vertebra?
questions.f: The same mythological name is why a book of maps became known as an atlas.

questions.q: Four fused leftovers at the spine's base, a name borrowed from a bird's beak, and the last trace of a human tail converge on which bone?
questions.f: From Greek kokkyx, cuckoo, whose curved beak the bone was thought to resemble.

questions.q: A gap a midwife checks with a fingertip, a name meaning 'little fountain', and the reason a newborn's head can be squeezed at birth all point to what?
questions.f: You can feel a pulse beating there, which is exactly why it earned the fountain name.

questions.q: A bone ancient writers believed would never decay, a triangular keystone locking spine to hips, and a name meaning 'holy' identify which structure?
questions.f: Its reputation for surviving in graves gave it that sacred-sounding name.

questions.q: A bone the size of a grain of rice, a name taken from a rider's footrest, and the final relay before the cochlea describe which bone?
questions.f: It is the smallest bone in the body, and it completes a three-bone chain of levers.

questions.q: A bone named after a seed, floating inside a tendon rather than joining two bones, with the kneecap as its largest example: what is this class of bone?
questions.f: Small sesamoids also hide in your hands and feet, acting as tiny pulleys for tendons.

questions.q: A pair of crescent-shaped cartilage pads, a name meaning 'little moon', and the injury footballers dread most in the knee point to what?
questions.f: Because cartilage has almost no blood supply, a torn meniscus heals painfully slowly.

questions.q: An iron rod fired through a Vermont railway worker's skull in 1848, a survivor whose personality changed, and the first great lesson about the frontal lobe: who was he?
questions.f: Gage lived another dozen years, and his skull is still studied at Harvard today.

questions.q: A patient nicknamed 'Tan' who could utter almost no other syllable, a French surgeon's 1861 autopsy, and a patch of the left frontal lobe converge on what?
questions.f: Paul Broca's discovery was the first solid proof that a mental skill lives in a specific place.

questions.q: Cells taken without permission in Baltimore in 1951, the first human line that would grow forever in glass, and a family told the truth decades later: what are they called?
questions.f: They came from Henrietta Lacks, and her cells have since travelled into space and into millions of experiments.

questions.q: A doctor who drank a beaker of bacteria to prove his own theory, an ulcer blamed for a century on worry, and a 2005 Nobel Prize point to which scientist?
questions.f: He fell ill within days, proving that Helicobacter pylori, not stress, caused most stomach ulcers.

questions.q: A Padua professor who dissected in front of crowds, a lavishly illustrated book of 1543, and the man who dared correct Galen's animal-based errors: who was he?
questions.f: His book 'De Humani Corporis Fabrica' is often called the first modern anatomy textbook.

questions.q: A Delft cloth merchant who ground his own tiny lenses, the first person to glimpse red blood cells, and a man who called what he saw 'animalcules': who was he?
questions.f: He never trained as a scientist, yet he opened the whole microscopic world to view.

questions.q: A surgeon who sprayed carbolic acid over operating tables, a sharp fall in deaths after surgery, and a mouthwash later named in his honour identify whom?
questions.f: Listerine was named after him, though he never had anything to do with making it.

questions.q: A hairpin bend named after a German anatomist, a plunge deep into the kidney's inner zone, and the reason your urine can be saltier than your blood: what is it?
questions.f: Desert animals have extra-long loops, which lets them survive on remarkably little water.

questions.q: A cup-shaped filter named after an English surgeon, the very first step in making urine, and a sieve that holds back blood cells describe what?
questions.f: Around a million of these microscopic cups sit inside each of your kidneys.

questions.q: Gaps in a nerve's fatty insulation named after a French histologist, and a leaping style of conduction called 'saltatory', point to what?
questions.f: By jumping gap to gap, a signal can travel over a hundred metres per second.

questions.q: A bundle of fibres named after a Swiss anatomist, a relay carrying the beat from atria to ventricles, and the wiring that follows the pacemaker: what is it?
questions.f: Wilhelm His junior found it in 1893, completing the map of the heart's electrical circuit.

questions.q: A law named for an English physiologist stating that the fuller the heart, the harder it squeezes: what is this principle called?
questions.f: It is why your heart automatically matches its output to the blood returning from your veins.

questions.q: A manoeuvre named after an Italian anatomist, used by divers to clear their ears and by doctors to slow a racing heart: what is it called?
questions.f: You perform it by trying to breathe out hard while keeping mouth and nose shut.

questions.q: A tube named after a 16th-century Italian anatomist, a link between throat and middle ear, and the reason a yawn can unblock a plane-sore ear: what is it?
questions.f: Children's tubes are shorter and flatter, which is why they get more ear infections.

questions.q: A Spanish histologist who drew nerve cells by hand, a Nobel Prize shared in 1906 with a scientific rival, and proof that neurons are separate units: who was he?
questions.f: Cajal and Golgi shared the prize while flatly disagreeing about what they had each seen.

questions.q: A chemical whose crucial experiment came to a scientist in a dream on Easter night, the first messenger ever found between nerve cells: what is it?
questions.f: Otto Loewi woke, scribbled the idea down, and could not read his own handwriting the next morning.

questions.q: A messenger first found in blood serum where it tightened vessels, of which about nine tenths actually lives in your gut: which chemical is it?
questions.f: Its name comes from 'serum' plus 'tone', and it is now best known for affecting mood.

questions.q: A hormone whose name means 'swift birth', released during a hug, and nicknamed the cuddle chemical: which is it?
questions.f: From Greek oxys, swift, and tokos, birth, because it makes the womb contract.

questions.q: A German-born biochemist's spinning wheel of reactions, also called the citric acid cycle, turning inside every mitochondrion: what is it named?
questions.f: Hans Krebs worked it out in Sheffield after fleeing Nazi Germany, and won a Nobel for it.

questions.q: An X-ray image labelled 'Photo 51', a laboratory at King's College London, and a 1962 Nobel that came four years too late for her: who was she?
questions.f: Her diffraction photograph gave Watson and Crick the crucial clue to DNA's double helix.

questions.q: A Scottish naval surgeon's controlled trial of 1747, bleeding gums aboard long voyages, and the nickname 'limey' all trace back to which doctor?
questions.f: Lind proved citrus cured scurvy decades before the navy finally acted on his findings.

questions.q: A Scottish missionary in Japan who noticed marks on ancient pottery, a letter to Nature in 1880, and the claim that no two fingers match: who was he?
questions.f: He even used prints to clear a wrongly accused man, years before police adopted the idea.

questions.q: A German polymath who first measured how fast a nerve signal travels, and who in 1851 invented a mirrored device for peering into a living eye: who was he?
questions.f: His ophthalmoscope meant doctors could suddenly see a living retina for the very first time.

questions.q: A Boston dentist, an operation at Massachusetts General in October 1846, and a word suggested by the poet Oliver Wendell Holmes converge on what?
questions.f: Holmes coined the term from Greek roots meaning 'without sensation'.

questions.q: A graduate student watching his sleeping son's eyelids flicker in 1953, and a stage of sleep in which the body lies still but the brain races: what was found?
questions.f: Eugene Aserinsky's observation revealed that dreaming has its own measurable stage.

questions.q: A Dutch eye doctor's chart from 1862, a single huge letter at the top, and the reason 'twenty-twenty' means ordinary vision point to whom?
questions.f: On his chart, 20/20 simply means you read at 20 feet what a normal eye reads at 20 feet.

questions.q: Numbers hidden in fields of coloured dots, a Japanese army doctor's test of 1917, and a quick way to reveal red-green confusion: what is this test called?
questions.f: Some plates are designed so that only people with colour blindness can see the hidden figure.

questions.q: A soldier's clumsy night-writing code, a blind fifteen-year-old's brilliant simplification, and a six-dot cell you read with a fingertip: what did he create?
questions.f: Louis Braille lost his sight at three and had finished his system before he turned sixteen.

questions.q: A German paper of 1901 badly mistranslated into English, a schoolbook diagram putting 'sweet' at the tongue's tip, and a myth finally overturned: what was it?
questions.f: Every part of your tongue can in fact detect every basic taste.

questions.q: A Tokyo chemist's 1908 study of kelp broth, a crystal of glutamate scraped from the dish, and a savoury taste the West ignored for eighty years: who was he?
questions.f: He named the taste umami, and it took until 2000 for tongue receptors to prove him right.

questions.q: A sneeze set off by stepping into bright sunshine, affecting roughly a quarter of people, and running in families: what is this reflex called?
questions.f: Scientists think the light signal and the nose signal cross wires in a shared nerve.

questions.q: A physician to Roman gladiators, dissections carried out on Barbary apes, and errors that went unchallenged for fourteen centuries point to whom?
questions.f: Because Rome forbade human dissection, his animal-based anatomy quietly misled Europe for over a millennium.

questions.q: A Persian scholar's five-volume Canon of Medicine, a text taught in European universities for six centuries, and a bridge from Greek learning to Renaissance doctors: who was he?
questions.f: Known in the West as Avicenna, he wrote his medical encyclopedia in the early 11th century.

questions.q: A woman who used wedge diagrams to prove that filth killed more soldiers than wounds, and who published 'Notes on Nursing' in 1859: who was she?
questions.f: Remembered as the lady with the lamp, she was in fact a pioneering statistician.

questions.q: A factor named after a monkey, discovered in 1940, and the reason blood is labelled 'positive' or 'negative': what is it?
questions.f: Rh is short for rhesus, the macaque whose blood was used in the original experiments.

questions.q: Cells whose name means 'glue', outnumbering neurons in the brain, and long dismissed as mere packing material: what are they?
questions.f: Far from being padding, they feed neurons, insulate them and tidy up their waste.

questions.q: A structure Descartes called the seat of the soul, shaped like a tiny pine cone, releasing its hormone only in darkness: what is it?
questions.f: Its name comes from Latin pinea, pine cone, and it helps set your daily sleep clock.

questions.q: A gland named after a bunch of herb flowers, busiest in childhood, and the school where immune T-cells are trained: which is it?
questions.f: It shrinks steadily after puberty, having already trained a lifetime's supply of cells.

questions.q: An organ whose name means 'all flesh', tucked behind the stomach, doing two utterly different jobs at once: which is it?
questions.f: It pours enzymes into the gut and hormones into the blood, an unusual double life.

questions.q: A word coined in 1912, a mistaken belief that these substances all contained amines, and a name literally meaning 'life substance': what was named?
questions.f: Casimir Funk's slight error is why we still spell it 'vitamin' rather than 'vita'.

questions.q: A word borrowed from the Greek for a ship, a queasiness sailors knew all too well, and a feeling that has nothing to do with the sea today: what is it?
questions.f: From Greek naus, ship, the very same root that gives us 'navy' and 'nautical'.

questions.q: An eye complaint sharing its name with a waterfall, treated in antiquity by pushing the clouded lens aside with a needle: what is it?
questions.f: That risky ancient operation, called couching, was performed as long ago as 800 BC.

questions.q: A Greek phrase meaning 'to shut the eye', a habit of squinting at distant signs, and an eyeball slightly too long from front to back: what condition is this?
questions.f: Because light focuses just short of the retina, faraway objects blur while close work stays sharp.

questions.q: An eyeball that has grown a fraction too short, a struggle to read small print, and a Greek name meaning 'old man's eye': which is it?
questions.f: It creeps up on almost everyone past forty, as the lens slowly loses its flexibility.

questions.q: A word from the Greek for 'falling away', like leaves dropping from a tree, describing cells that die on purpose: what is it?
questions.f: Around fifty billion of your cells quietly bow out this way every single day.

questions.q: Muscles a few people can still twitch to wiggle their ears, a fold at the inner corner of the eye, and a tailbone are all examples of what?
questions.f: From Latin vestigium, a footprint, because they are traces left by our ancestors.

questions.q: A membrane whose name means 'tough mother', translated from Arabic by medieval scholars, and the outermost of the brain's three wrappings: what is it?
questions.f: The innermost layer is the pia mater, the 'tender mother', hugging the brain's every fold.

questions.q: A brain membrane named for a spider, a fluid-filled space crossed by fine strands, and a position between the tough mother and the tender mother: which is it?
questions.f: Cerebrospinal fluid flows through this cobweb layer, cushioning the brain against knocks.

questions.q: A structure named after a sea horse, curled inside the temporal lobe, and the part whose loss left one famous patient unable to form new memories: what is it?
questions.f: Patient H.M. lived for decades in a permanent present after surgery removed his.

questions.q: A pair of almond-shaped nodes deep in the temporal lobes, acting as the brain's alarm bell for fear: what are they called?
questions.f: From Greek amygdale, almond, a shape that matches them almost perfectly.

questions.q: A structure holding more neurons than all the rest of the brain, a name meaning 'little brain', and the smoother of every movement you make: what is it?
questions.f: It is barely a tenth of the brain's volume yet contains over half of its neurons.

questions.q: A bulge on the brainstem named after a bridge, carrying fibres across from side to side, sitting just above the medulla: what is it?
questions.f: It also holds the switches that flip you into and out of dreaming sleep.

questions.q: A wrist bone named after a boat, the one most often broken in a fall onto the palm, and a notoriously slow healer: which bone is it?
questions.f: Its blood supply enters from one end only, which is why a break there mends so reluctantly.

questions.q: A U-shaped bone joined to no other bone, anchoring the tongue, and a key to why humans can speak so clearly: which bone is it?
questions.f: It floats in the throat, held only by muscles and ligaments, like a hammock's ring.

questions.q: A hip socket named after a Roman vinegar saucer, a deep cup of three fused bones, and the joint that carries your whole weight: what is it?
questions.f: Its depth is why hips dislocate far less often than shallow-socketed shoulders.

questions.q: A bone named after an ancient flute, the shin's weight-bearing pillar, and the second longest bone in the body: which is it?
questions.f: Hollow animal leg bones really were carved into the earliest simple flutes.

questions.q: A muscle named after tailors, the longest in the body, running diagonally across the thigh: which is it?
questions.f: It helps you sit cross-legged, the very posture in which tailors once worked all day.

questions.q: A calf muscle named after a flatfish, lying beneath its bulkier neighbour, and a tireless helper in standing still: which is it?
questions.f: From Latin solea, sole, both the fish and the flat sole of a sandal.

questions.q: A jaw muscle whose name simply means 'chewer', capable of a bite force of several hundred newtons: which muscle is it?
questions.f: For its small size it is among the strongest muscles anywhere in the body.

questions.q: A network of arteries at the brain's base, named after a 17th-century English physician, able to reroute blood when one vessel narrows: what is it?
questions.f: Thomas Willis mapped it in 1664, and it works as the brain's built-in emergency detour.

questions.q: Four glands each the size of a grain of rice, hidden behind a butterfly-shaped neighbour, guarding the calcium level of your blood: what are they?
questions.f: They were only recognised in the 1880s, having been mistaken for part of the thyroid.

questions.q: A term for pain felt far from its true source, the reason a heart attack can ache in the jaw or arm: what is this phenomenon called?
questions.f: Nerves from skin and organs share spinal routes, so the brain misreads the return address.

questions.q: A sense with no organ you can point to, letting you touch your nose with closed eyes, sometimes called the sixth sense: what is it?
questions.f: Sensors buried in your muscles and joints constantly report your limbs' positions.

questions.q: A spiral cavity holding rows of hair cells, an Italian anatomist's name, and the place where vibration finally becomes a nerve signal: what is it?
questions.f: Around 16,000 hair cells sit inside it, and once damaged by loud noise they never regrow.

questions.q: A network of fibres named after a Czech anatomist, spreading the electrical signal through the ventricle walls almost instantly: what are they?
questions.f: Jan Purkinje's fibres conduct so fast that both ventricles contract as though they were one.

questions.q: An effect described by a Danish physiologist in 1904, whereby rising carbon dioxide loosens hemoglobin's hold on oxygen: what is it called?
questions.f: It cleverly ensures that the hardest-working, most acidic tissues receive the most oxygen.

questions.q: A 1628 book of just 72 pages, a claim that blood travels in a closed circle, and the overthrow of 1,400 years of teaching: whose work was this?
questions.f: Before Harvey, physicians believed the liver made fresh blood which the body simply consumed.

questions.q: A Viennese scientist's discovery of 1901, the reason a transfusion stopped being a gamble, and the letters A, B and O: who was he?
questions.f: He also helped identify the rhesus factor, and won his Nobel Prize in 1930.

questions.q: A cavity behind the cheekbone, a name meaning 'a bend or hollow', and the ache that follows a heavy cold all point to which air-filled space?
questions.f: Four pairs of these hollows lighten the skull and add resonance to your voice.

questions.q: A structure named from the Greek for 'snail', a spiral filled with fluid, and the place where pitch is sorted from low to high converge on what?
questions.f: Different points along its spiral respond to different notes, like keys on a piano.

questions.q: Three fluid-filled loops set at right angles, an organ that reports every tilt of your head, and the reason spinning makes you giddy point to what?
questions.f: Because they sit at right angles, they can sense rotation in all three dimensions.

questions.q: A word meaning 'without a point', an unevenly curved cornea, and light smeared into a streak rather than a dot describe which condition?
questions.f: A cornea shaped more like a rugby ball than a football is the usual culprit.

questions.q: A gap in the retina where no light sensors sit, the exit door of a million nerve fibres, and a hole your brain quietly paints over: what is it?
questions.f: Close one eye and the missing patch never appears, because your brain invents the details.

questions.q: A dip in the retina named from the Latin for 'small pit', packed with cones, and the spot you unknowingly aim at every word you read: what is it?
questions.f: It is barely a millimetre wide, yet it delivers nearly all of your detailed vision.

questions.q: A pigment bleached by bright light, a reason it takes minutes to see inside a dark cinema, and a molecule built with vitamin A: what is it?
questions.f: Rebuilding it is exactly what 'getting your night vision' means.

questions.q: A word from the Greek for 'thin skin', the wrapping around every one of your muscles, and the tissue a surgeon must part to reach them: what is it?
questions.f: This tough sheeting also forms the tough band that can inflame under the heel.

questions.q: A term from the Latin for 'little belly', a chamber with the thickest wall in the heart, and the pump that fills your aorta: which chamber is it?
questions.f: Its wall is roughly three times thicker than the right ventricle's, because it pushes blood everywhere.

questions.q: Fine cords called 'heart strings', flaps that would otherwise blow inside out, and the reason a valve holds firm under pressure point to what?
questions.f: Their name translates literally as 'tendinous cords', and they act like a parachute's lines.

questions.q: A valve named after a bishop's pointed hat, guarding the left atrium's doorway, also known by a word meaning 'two-pointed': which valve is it?
questions.f: Its two flaps together look strikingly like the tall mitre worn by a bishop.

questions.q: A patch of tissue near the top of the right atrium, a rhythm of about seventy per minute, and the true origin of every heartbeat: what is it called?
questions.f: It fires an electrical spark without being told to, which is why it earned the name pacemaker.

questions.q: A phase of the heartbeat named from a Greek word for 'drawing apart', when chambers relax and refill: what is it called?
questions.f: It is the lower of the two numbers in a blood pressure reading.

questions.q: An organ once believed to be the seat of courage and laughter, sitting under the left ribs, and the graveyard of tired red blood cells: which is it?
questions.f: Old writers spoke of 'venting your spleen', because they blamed it for bad temper.

questions.q: A duct named after a Wirsung, a gland doing two jobs at once, and the pipe that pours enzymes into the duodenum belongs to which organ?
questions.f: It joins the bile duct just before both empty into the gut through a shared opening.

questions.q: Clusters of cells named after a German pathologist, scattered like islands through a larger gland, and the only source of your insulin: what are they?
questions.f: They make up only one or two per cent of the pancreas, yet without them you could not use sugar.

questions.q: Patches of immune tissue named after a Swiss anatomist, lining the small intestine, and standing guard where food meets the body: what are they?
questions.f: They let your immune system sample your dinner and check it for dangerous passengers.

questions.q: Cells named after a 19th-century German anatomist, stationed in the liver, devouring worn-out blood cells and bacteria: what are they?
questions.f: They are the largest population of resident macrophages anywhere in your body.

questions.q: A vessel that carries blood from the gut straight to the liver, a name meaning 'gateway', and a detour that checks your meal before it circulates: what is it?
questions.f: It is unusual because it starts in capillaries and ends in capillaries too.

questions.q: A duct named from the Greek for chest, the main drain of the lymph system, emptying into a vein near the collarbone: what is it?
questions.f: It returns several litres of lymph to the bloodstream every single day.

questions.q: A hormone whose name means 'sweet-making', released when blood sugar dips, and the mirror twin of insulin: which is it?
questions.f: It tells your liver to unpack stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood.

questions.q: A hormone named from words meaning 'to work at', made by the outer adrenal layer, and the chemical that lingers when worry drags on: which is it?
questions.f: Its level normally peaks in the early morning to help wake you up.

questions.q: A hormone named after the Greek word for 'shield', containing atoms of iodine, and the dial that sets how fast you burn energy: which is it?
questions.f: It is one of the very few molecules in the human body built around iodine.

questions.q: A rhythm named from Latin words meaning 'about a day', reset each morning by light hitting the retina, and the reason jet lag exists: what is it?
questions.f: Left in constant darkness, the human clock still ticks at roughly 24 hours.

questions.q: A protein whose name means 'glue-producer', the most plentiful protein in your body, and the scaffold inside skin and tendon: what is it?
questions.f: Boiling collagen-rich tissue makes gelatine, which is how it earned its glue-like name.

questions.q: A protein whose name comes from the Greek for 'horn', found in nails, hair and rhino horn alike: what is it?
