questions.f: Grass grows from a base near the soil, so cutting the tips does not kill it.

questions.q: Flax stems can be turned into linen cloth.
questions.f: Long fibres inside flax stems are separated, spun, and woven into linen.

questions.q: The root "sylva" in "silviculture" and "Pennsylvania" means...?
questions.f: Silviculture is the growing of forest trees; "sylva" is Latin for wood.

questions.q: What do we call a single thick main root that drives straight down, as in a carrot?
questions.f: A taproot anchors deeply and can reach water far below the surface.

questions.q: The word "dandelion" comes from a French phrase meaning the tooth of a...?
questions.f: From "dent de lion" - the leaf edges are jagged like sharp teeth.

questions.q: Which root system spreads as a dense mat of thin roots, as in grasses?
questions.f: Fibrous roots grip the topsoil tightly and help stop it washing away.

questions.q: The word "daisy" grew from an old English phrase meaning the eye of the...?
questions.f: From "daeges eage," day’s eye, because the flower opens each morning.

questions.q: What do we call two different living things that help each other survive?
questions.f: In symbiosis both partners benefit, as with bees and the flowers they feed on.

questions.q: The root "carp" in "pericarp," the wall of a fruit, means...?
questions.f: From Greek "karpos," fruit; the pericarp is the fruit wall around the seed.

questions.q: Which term describes a flower that has both male and female parts?
questions.f: Perfect, or bisexual, flowers carry both stamens and a pistil in one bloom.

questions.q: The word "rhododendron" is built from Greek roots meaning rose and...?
questions.f: From "rhodon" (rose) and "dendron" (tree) - literally the rose tree.

questions.q: What do we call the green outer whorl of a flower, taken as a whole?
questions.f: The calyx is all the sepals together, protecting the bud before it opens.

questions.q: Which plant group has vascular tubes but reproduces with spores, not seeds?
questions.f: Ferns have proper water-carrying tubes yet still scatter spores like mosses.

questions.q: The word "corolla" names all the petals of a flower taken together, from Latin for a small...?
questions.f: A ring of petals sits like a little crown at the top of the stem.

questions.q: Which farming method grows plants in stacked layers indoors under lights?
questions.f: Vertical farms stack crops in racks, saving land and water in cities.

questions.q: The root "sperm" in "angiosperm" and "spermatophyte" means...?
questions.f: From Greek "sperma," seed; spermatophytes are all the seed-bearing plants.

questions.q: What do we call the tough, stringy material that forms plant cell walls?
questions.f: Cellulose is the world’s most common organic material, and it makes plants firm.

questions.q: Which tree family does the coffee plant belong to, sharing it with gardenias?
questions.f: Coffee and gardenia both sit in the Rubiaceae, or madder, family.

questions.q: The prefix "mono-" in "monoculture" tells you a field is planted with how many crops?
questions.f: Monoculture grows a single crop over a large area, which can invite disease.

questions.q: What do we call a plant that has been moved to a new region and spreads harmfully?
questions.f: Invasive plants outcompete local ones because their usual controls are absent.

questions.q: Which layer of a leaf is packed with chloroplasts and does most photosynthesis?
questions.f: Tall palisade cells sit near the top surface to catch the most light.

questions.q: The word "annual rings" and the word "annual" both come from a root meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin "annus," year - one ring usually forms each growing year.

questions.q: Which sugar-rich liquid is drawn from maple trees in early spring?
questions.f: Maple sap runs when cold nights are followed by mild days.

questions.q: What do we call a plant native only to one particular place on Earth?
questions.f: Endemic plants are found nowhere else, which makes them easy to lose.

questions.q: The word "herbivore" is built from "herba" plus "vorare," meaning to...?
questions.f: Herbivores devour plants; "vorare" is Latin for to swallow up.

questions.q: Which process breaks down dead leaves and wood back into soil nutrients?
questions.f: Fungi and bacteria decompose litter, recycling its nutrients into the soil.

questions.q: The root "xer" in "xeriscaping," a dry-climate garden style, means...?
questions.f: From Greek "xeros," dry; xeriscaping uses plants that need little water.

questions.q: What do we call the swollen base of a flower that becomes the fruit?
questions.f: After pollination the ovary swells around the developing seeds.

questions.q: Which family includes cabbage, broccoli, kale, and Brussels sprouts?
questions.f: All are forms of one species, Brassica oleracea, bred into different shapes.

questions.q: The word "photoperiod" describes how a plant responds to the length of...?
questions.f: Many plants flower only when days reach a certain length.

questions.q: What do we call the waxy coating on grapes and plums that rubs off?
questions.f: That dusty bloom is natural wax that slows water loss from the fruit.

questions.q: Which term names the whole above-ground leafy structure of a tree?
questions.f: A tree’s crown is its spread of branches and leaves.

questions.q: The root "gen" in "genus" and "genetics" carries the idea of...?
questions.f: From Latin "genus," birth or kind - a genus groups closely related species.

questions.q: What do we call farming that uses no synthetic pesticides or fertilisers?
questions.f: Organic growers rely on compost, rotation, and natural pest control.

questions.q: Which structure lets water pass from soil into a root against the pull of gravity?
questions.f: Root hairs vastly increase the surface soaking up soil water.

questions.q: The word "conifer" is built from Latin roots meaning to bear...?
questions.f: From "conus" (cone) and "ferre" (to bear) - the cone-bearing trees.

questions.q: What do we call a plant’s response of growing toward or away from a stimulus?
questions.f: Tropisms bend a plant toward light, water, or with gravity.

questions.q: Which tissue layer just under a tree’s bark carries sugars up and down?
questions.f: The inner bark holds the phloem, the tree’s food pipeline.

questions.q: The word "agronomy" combines "agros" (field) with "nomos," meaning...?
questions.f: Agronomy is the science of managing fields and soil for crops.

questions.q: What do we call the natural spread of seeds away from the parent plant?
questions.f: Dispersal by wind, water, or animals stops seedlings crowding the parent.

questions.q: Which plant family includes tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, and aubergines?
questions.f: These crops are all Solanaceae, once feared because some relatives are toxic.

questions.q: The word "dormant" describes a seed or plant that is...?
questions.f: Dormancy lets seeds wait safely until conditions are right to sprout.

questions.q: What do we call the tiny pores in bark that let a woody stem breathe?
questions.f: Lenticels are small raised pores that let gases move through bark.

questions.q: Which crop is the world’s most important source of vegetable oil by volume?
questions.f: Oil palms produce more oil per hectare than any other oil crop.

questions.q: The word "botanical garden" names a collection of plants kept mainly for...?
questions.f: Botanical gardens grow labelled collections for science and education.

questions.q: What do we call the point on a stem where a leaf or bud is attached?
questions.f: Nodes are the joints of a stem; the gaps between them are internodes.

questions.q: Which trees make up most of the vast cold forests circling the far north?
questions.f: The boreal forest, or taiga, is dominated by hardy conifers.

questions.q: The root "phyto" in "phytology" and "phytochemical" means...?
questions.f: From Greek "phyton," plant; phytochemicals are plant-made compounds.

questions.q: What do we call a fruit formed from many separate flowers fused together?
questions.f: A pineapple is a multiple fruit, built from dozens of small flowers.

questions.q: Which gas, breathed out by plants at night, do they take in for respiration?
questions.f: Plants respire like animals, using oxygen to release energy from sugar.

questions.q: The word "arable" describes land that is suitable for...?
questions.f: Arable land can be ploughed and sown; the word comes from Latin for to plough.

questions.q: What do we call the study of pollen grains, useful for dating ancient soils?
questions.f: Pollen grains survive for millennia, so palynology reveals past plant life.

questions.q: Which part of a grass plant grows from the base, letting it survive mowing?
questions.f: A grass grows from near the soil, so cutting the tips does not stop it.

questions.q: The word "cultivar" is a blend of "cultivated" and...?
questions.f: A cultivar is a plant variety produced and named by growers.

questions.q: What do we call the thick, fleshy leaf or stem tissue that stores water?
questions.f: Succulent tissue swells with stored water for use in dry spells.

questions.q: Which pigment change makes a banana skin turn from green to yellow?
questions.f: As green chlorophyll fades, the yellow pigments underneath show through.

questions.q: The root "flori" in "floriculture" points to the growing of...?
questions.f: Floriculture is the business of growing flowers and ornamental plants.

questions.q: What do we call a plant organ that stores food and can grow a new plant?
questions.f: Bulbs, tubers, and corms all store food and can sprout new plants.

questions.q: Which term describes trees and shrubs that lose leaves in a dry season, not winter?
questions.f: In monsoon climates many trees drop leaves to survive the dry months.

questions.q: The word "vegetation" is a general term for all the...?
questions.f: Vegetation describes the plant cover of a landscape as a whole.

questions.q: What do we call the practice of cutting off a shoot and rooting it as a new plant?
questions.f: A cutting placed in soil or water can grow roots and become a clone.

questions.q: Which nutrient, often shown as "K" on fertiliser bags, helps plants resist disease?
questions.f: The three main plant nutrients are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.

questions.q: The word "orchard" and the word "horticulture" both trace to a root meaning...?
questions.f: Latin "hortus," garden, lies behind both words.

questions.q: What do we call the tough fibres inside a celery stalk or a leaf?
questions.f: Vascular bundles are the plumbing that carries water and food.

questions.q: Which region’s plants are adapted to hot dry summers and mild wet winters?
questions.f: Mediterranean plants like olive and lavender have tough, oily leaves.

questions.q: The word "pollinator" names any animal that carries...?
questions.f: Bees, birds, bats, and beetles all act as pollinators.

questions.q: What do we call a plant that survives fire and resprouts from its base?
questions.f: Resprouters keep buds protected below the bark or soil.

questions.q: Which term names the tiny stalk that attaches a single flower to a cluster?
questions.f: A pedicel holds one flower; a peduncle holds a whole cluster.

questions.q: The root "chrys" in "chrysanthemum" and "chrysalis" means...?
questions.f: From Greek "chrysos," gold - a chrysalis often gleams golden.

questions.q: Which plant is grown on terraces cut into steep hillsides across Asia?
questions.f: Terraces hold flooded paddies level on slopes and stop soil washing away.

questions.q: The word "biodiversity" describes the variety of...?
questions.f: Rainforests hold the greatest plant biodiversity on Earth.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who classifies and names living things?
questions.f: Taxonomists sort plants into families, genera, and species.

questions.q: Which flower opens only at night and is pollinated by moths and bats?
questions.f: Pale, strongly scented night flowers are easy for moths to find in the dark.

questions.q: The word "sylvan," meaning of the woods, shares its root with...?
questions.f: Both come from Latin "sylva," meaning wood or forest.

questions.q: What do we call the ability of some seeds to survive years before sprouting?
questions.f: Some buried seeds stay alive for decades, waiting for light and water.

questions.q: Which plant tissue makes cork, and on which tree is it thickest?
questions.f: A special cork cambium builds the thick spongy bark of the cork oak.

questions.q: The word "hedgerow" names a line of shrubs that traditionally marks...?
questions.f: Hedgerows divide fields and shelter huge numbers of birds and insects.

questions.q: What do we call plants that grow in the cracks and ledges of rock faces?
questions.f: Lithophytes root on stone; "lithos" is Greek for rock.

questions.q: Which crop, native to the Andes, is a seed eaten like a grain and is high in protein?
questions.f: Quinoa is not a true cereal but its seeds are cooked and eaten like grain.

questions.q: The word "fertiliser" names material added to soil to supply...?
questions.f: Fertilisers replace the nutrients that growing crops remove from soil.

questions.q: What do we call the way ivy holds onto a wall as it climbs?
questions.f: Ivy grows tiny clinging rootlets that grip brick and bark.

questions.q: Which term describes a fruit that develops without fertilisation, like some bananas?
questions.f: Parthenocarpic fruit forms with no seeds, which is why bananas are seedless.

questions.q: The root "hydro" plus "ponos" (labour) gives "hydroponics," meaning work with...?
questions.f: Hydroponic growers feed plants in water instead of soil.

questions.q: What do we call the loose, crumbly structure of healthy garden soil?
questions.f: Good tilth means soil that crumbles nicely and lets roots and air through.

questions.q: Which tall tropical grass is harvested and crushed for its sweet juice?
questions.f: Sugarcane stores sucrose in its thick, juicy stalks.

questions.q: The word "greenhouse gas" borrows its name from a glasshouse because both...?
questions.f: A greenhouse traps warmth inside, just as certain gases warm the planet.

questions.q: What do we call the small, dry, one-seeded fruit of a sunflower?
questions.f: What we call a sunflower seed is really a small dry fruit with the seed inside.

questions.q: Which nutrient shortage most often turns a plant’s older leaves pale yellow?
questions.f: Without enough nitrogen, plants cannot build the green pigment properly.

questions.q: The word "perianth" names the petals and sepals together, from roots meaning around the...?
questions.f: From "peri" (around) and "anthos" (flower).

questions.q: What do we call plants that complete their whole life cycle very quickly after rain?
questions.f: Desert ephemerals sprout, flower, and seed within weeks of a downpour.

questions.q: Which structure in a pine cone shelters the developing seeds?
questions.f: Woody cone scales close in wet weather and open to release seeds when dry.

questions.q: The word "arbour," a shady garden shelter, shares its root with...?
questions.f: Both trace to Latin "arbor," tree.

questions.q: What do we call the practice of growing two crops together for mutual benefit?
questions.f: Beans climbing maize stalks is a classic companion planting pair.

questions.q: Which part of a fern uncurls as it grows, resembling the head of a violin?
questions.f: Young fern shoots called fiddleheads unroll slowly into full fronds.

questions.q: The word "photosynthate" names the product a plant makes, chiefly...?
questions.f: Photosynthate is the sugary food produced by photosynthesis.

questions.q: What do we call soil that has been washed or blown away from farmland?
questions.f: Erosion by wind and rain strips the precious topsoil crops depend on.

questions.q: Which plant hormone group makes stems stretch longer between leaves?
questions.f: Gibberellins were discovered from a fungus that made rice seedlings grow too tall.

questions.q: The word "legume" comes from a Latin word connected with...?
questions.f: From "legere," to gather - legume pods are gathered by hand.

questions.q: What do we call the outer skin of cells covering a leaf?
questions.f: The leaf epidermis is a protective skin, pierced by tiny pores.

questions.q: Which crop family fixes nitrogen and so is often sown to enrich tired soil?
questions.f: Clover and beans host bacteria that put nitrogen back into the soil.

questions.q: The word "sclerotic," meaning hardened, shares a root with which plant tissue?
questions.f: From Greek "skleros," hard - sclerenchyma cells have hard, thick walls.

questions.q: What do we call the way desert plants shrink their leaves to spines to save water?
questions.f: Cactus spines are leaves adapted to lose almost no water at all.

questions.q: A taproot is a single dominant root that grows straight downward.
questions.f: Carrots and dandelions both drive one thick taproot deep into the soil.

questions.q: Ferns have vascular tubes even though they reproduce with spores.
questions.f: Ferns are vascular plants, which is why they can grow far taller than mosses.

questions.q: Cellulose in plant cell walls is one of the most common materials on Earth.
questions.f: Nearly every plant builds its walls from cellulose, making it hugely abundant.

questions.q: A monoculture field is planted with a single crop.
questions.f: Growing one crop over a wide area is efficient but can spread disease fast.

questions.q: All parts of every plant in the nightshade family are safe to eat.
questions.f: Tomato and potato leaves contain compounds that make them unsafe to eat.

questions.q: Plants use oxygen for respiration, not just carbon dioxide for food.
questions.f: Like animals, plants respire day and night to release energy from sugar.

questions.q: Seeds can stay dormant for years and still sprout later.
questions.f: Dormancy lets seeds wait out drought or cold until conditions improve.

questions.q: The word "arable" describes land fit for growing crops.
questions.f: Arable land can be ploughed and sown, from Latin meaning to plough.

questions.q: A pineapple grows from many small flowers fused into one fruit.
questions.f: Dozens of flowers merge on a single stalk to form a pineapple.

questions.q: A monk in Brno, 28,000 pea plants, and a paper ignored for 34 years point to which scientist?
questions.f: Mendel’s pea experiments founded genetics, but the world only noticed in 1900.

questions.q: Thin slices of cork under a 1665 microscope reminded one Englishman of monks’ rooms, giving biology which word?
questions.f: Robert Hooke saw tiny empty boxes in cork and called them cells, after monastery cells.

questions.q: A duke’s glasshouse at Chatsworth and a fungus that destroyed the Gros Michel explain the name of which banana?
questions.f: Nearly every supermarket banana is a Cavendish clone, named for the Dukes of Devonshire.

questions.q: A French pharmacist posted armed guards around a field so the crop would seem worth stealing. Which crop?
questions.f: Parmentier’s trick made suspicious Parisians finally accept the potato as food.

questions.q: The word "aspirin" was built from "acetyl" plus a letter-shortening of which plant name?
questions.f: Meadowsweet was once Spiraea; the bark of willow gave the related salicylic acid.

questions.q: The Latin word "liber," meaning the inner bark used for writing, gives us which everyday word?
questions.f: Romans wrote on bark, so the word for bark came to mean book, then library.

questions.q: The English word "book" is thought to descend from a Germanic word for which tree?
questions.f: Early runes were carved on beech tablets, so the wood’s name became the word for book.

questions.q: Sea-route traders carried the Min Nan word "te" while overland caravans carried "cha," splitting the world’s names for which drink?
questions.f: Countries supplied by sea say tea or thé; those supplied by land say chai or cha.

questions.q: The fruit was named first and the colour second, from a Sanskrit word "naranga." Which word is it?
questions.f: English had no word for the colour until the fruit arrived and lent it one.

questions.q: Which tree’s genus name, Sequoia, is traditionally said to honour the inventor of a writing system?
questions.f: The name is usually credited to Sequoyah, who devised the Cherokee syllabary.

questions.q: A 1667 treaty swapped a nutmeg island in the Bandas for Manhattan. Which island?
questions.f: The Dutch kept nutmeg-rich Run and handed New Amsterdam to the English.

questions.q: Which spice did Alaric reportedly demand by the pound, alongside gold, to spare Rome in 408?
questions.f: Pepper was so valuable it served as ransom, rent, and even wages.

questions.q: Carbonised filaments of which plant lit Edison’s early long-lasting light bulbs?
questions.f: Edison’s team tested thousands of fibres; Japanese bamboo burned longest.

questions.q: The densest commercial wood, lignum vitae, was once used for ship propeller-shaft bearings because it is naturally...?
questions.f: Its oily resin let it run underwater without grease, even in early submarines.

questions.q: Which tree provided the wood for the English longbow, often imported by the shipload?
questions.f: Yew’s springy sapwood and stiff heartwood made a natural composite bow.

questions.q: The word "canvas" comes from the Latin name of which fibre plant?
questions.f: From "cannabis," because sailcloth was originally woven from hemp.

questions.q: Which fibre plant gives us both linen cloth and linseed oil, and the word "line"?
questions.f: Latin "linum" lies behind linen, line, and linoleum alike.

questions.q: A deposed Mexican general in exile, sapodilla tree latex, and Thomas Adams led to which product?
questions.f: Santa Anna brought chicle north; Adams turned the failed rubber substitute into gum.

questions.q: 70,000 seeds shipped to Kew in 1876 and plantations in Malaya ended the Amazon boom in which product?
questions.f: Henry Wickham’s seeds broke Brazil’s monopoly, stranding Manaus and its opera house.

questions.q: Sealed glass cases invented by Nathaniel Ward let live plants survive long sea voyages. What were they called?
questions.f: Wardian cases moved tea to India and rubber to Asia, reshaping world agriculture.

questions.q: Which crop disease, named for the country of the scientists who identified it rather than its origin, devastated a favourite street tree?
questions.f: Two Dutch women first described the fungus, so the name points to the lab, not the source.

questions.q: An aphid from America devastated French vineyards in the 1860s and was beaten by grafting. What is it?
questions.f: Nearly every European vine now grows on American rootstock resistant to phylloxera.

questions.q: A blight arriving around 1904 killed billions of which once-dominant American forest tree?
questions.f: A fungus from Asia reduced a giant of eastern forests to sprouting stumps.

questions.q: Six trees within 2 km of the 1945 Hiroshima blast survived, and its fan leaf earns it the name "maidenhair tree". Which is it?
questions.f: Ginkgo has no living wild relatives, a lone survivor of an ancient lineage.

questions.q: A parasite with no leaves, stems, or roots that lives inside a grape-family vine bears the name of Singapore’s founder. Which plant?
questions.f: Rafflesia grows entirely within its host until the giant bloom bursts out.

questions.q: Which plant did Darwin call "one of the most wonderful in the world," and whose Latin name means "mousetrap"?
questions.f: Dionaea muscipula grows wild only near Wilmington, North Carolina.

questions.q: A 2,000-year-old seed from Masada was sprouted in 2005 and named Methuselah. What kind of tree is it?
questions.f: The ancient Judean date seed germinated after two millennia in dry storage.

questions.q: Seeds from a squirrel’s burrow frozen in Siberian permafrost for 32,000 years were regrown into which kind of plant?
questions.f: Silene stenophylla is the oldest plant ever regenerated from natural seed tissue.

questions.q: Which vault at 78 degrees north, cut into permafrost, made its first withdrawal in 2015 for Syria?
questions.f: The "doomsday vault" holds spare copies of the world’s crop seeds.

questions.q: Staff of a Leningrad seed bank starved during the 872-day siege rather than eat what they guarded. What was it?
questions.f: They died protecting Vavilov’s irreplaceable collection of crop varieties.

questions.q: Semi-dwarf rust-resistant wheat bred in Mexico won which agronomist the Nobel Peace Prize?
questions.f: His Green Revolution wheat is credited with saving perhaps a billion lives.

questions.q: Maize plants, "jumping genes," and a long-delayed 1983 Nobel Prize belong to which scientist?
questions.f: She discovered transposons in corn decades before others accepted the idea.

questions.q: A mouse, a sealed jar, and a sprig of mint in 1771 showed that plants could do what?
questions.f: Joseph Priestley’s mint kept a candle burning, hinting at oxygen release.

questions.q: A willow weighed for five years beside soil that barely lost weight led van Helmont to wrongly conclude trees are built from...?
questions.f: He was wrong about soil but right that most mass does not come from the ground.

questions.q: Pollen grains jittering in water in 1827 revealed a motion later explained by Einstein. Who watched them?
questions.f: Brown also named the cell nucleus; the jittering is now called Brownian motion.

questions.q: Which US crop scientist promoted legume rotation to restore worn-out soil and published scores of peanut uses?
questions.f: Carver taught farmers that peanuts and cowpeas could heal exhausted cotton fields.

questions.q: A frontier nurseryman planted apple seeds for cider, not eating apples, across Ohio and Indiana. By what nickname is he known?
questions.f: John Chapman’s seedling apples were mostly small and sour, destined for cider.

questions.q: A cooking apple called Flower of Kent grew at the Woolsthorpe manor of which thinker?
questions.f: The famous falling apple was this old English cooking variety.

questions.q: A 1637 crash in Haarlem and a name from a word for turban belong to which flower?
questions.f: The prized streaked petals of tulip mania were actually caused by a virus.

questions.q: Which flower is named after Joel Roberts Poinsett, an early US envoy to Mexico?
questions.f: Poinsett sent the plant home in the 1820s and it became a Christmas fixture.

questions.q: A French navigator who circumnavigated the globe lent his name to which climbing plant?
questions.f: The papery coloured "flowers" of bougainvillea are really bracts.

questions.q: Which shrub genus is named for Joseph Banks, the botanist aboard the Endeavour?
questions.f: Banksias have brush-like flower spikes and woody cones that open after fire.

questions.q: Nicotine takes its name from Jean Nicot, a French ambassador who promoted which plant?
questions.f: Nicot sent the plant to the French court, and the chemical later took his name.

questions.q: Which heart medicine came from foxglove, described by William Withering in 1785?
questions.f: Withering learned of the foxglove remedy from a local herbal healer.

questions.q: A cancer drug called paclitaxel was first isolated from the bark of which tree?
questions.f: Harvesting bark was so destructive that chemists learned to make the drug another way.

questions.q: The Madagascar periwinkle gave medicine two drugs that transformed the treatment of...?
questions.f: Vincristine and vinblastine raised survival rates dramatically.

questions.q: Bandages of absorbent bog moss dressed wounds in the First World War. Which moss?
questions.f: Sphagnum holds many times its weight in liquid and is naturally acidic.

questions.q: A spice-bearing plant stamped on the coins of ancient Cyrene was harvested to extinction. What was it?
questions.f: Its heart-shaped seed pod may even be the ancestor of the heart symbol.

questions.q: Which fruit did 18th-century English hosts sometimes rent for a single evening as a status symbol?
questions.f: Pineapples were so costly that guests admired one centrepiece for weeks.

questions.q: Which vegetable is neither from Jerusalem nor an artichoke, its name likely twisted from "girasole"?
questions.f: It is a sunflower relative grown for knobbly tubers.

questions.q: The avocado’s huge seed suits animals that no longer exist, making it an example of what?
questions.f: Giant ground sloths and other megafauna probably swallowed the seeds whole.

questions.q: Which thorny American tree, planted in living fences before barbed wire, drops grapefruit-sized fruit almost nothing eats?
questions.f: Its likely dispersers, the great Ice Age mammals, died out long ago.

questions.q: Bamboo flowering across Mizoram roughly every 48 years triggers a rat plague locals call...?
questions.f: Mass seeding feeds an explosion of rats that then devour the rice crop.

questions.q: Which Andean plant waits 80 to 100 years, then throws up a flower spike over 8 m tall and dies?
questions.f: It produces thousands of flowers in one final, spectacular effort.

questions.q: Cones that stay sealed until fire heats them show an adaptation called...?
questions.f: Lodgepole pine cones pop open in a blaze, seeding fresh bare ground.

questions.q: Which buds, hidden under eucalyptus bark, let the tree resprout straight after a bushfire?
questions.f: Epicormic buds sit deep in the bark, shielded from the flames.

questions.q: Washington DC’s 1912 cherry trees replaced a 1910 shipment that was destroyed because it carried...?
questions.f: Tokyo sent over 3,000 healthy replacements, still celebrated each spring.

questions.q: Which tree, sacred at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka, is often called the oldest planted tree with a known planting date?
questions.f: Tradition dates its planting to the third century BC.

questions.q: A tree appears on the flag of which country, whose ancient forests supplied Phoenician shipbuilders?
questions.f: The cedar of Lebanon is a national emblem and a biblical symbol of strength.

questions.q: Each species of fig depends on its own species of tiny insect to pollinate it. Which insect?
questions.f: Fig and fig wasp are so entwined that neither can reproduce without the other.

questions.q: Which vine, shown at the 1876 Philadelphia exposition and later planted to stop erosion, became known as the vine that ate the South?
questions.f: Kudzu can grow 30 cm a day and smother whole forests.

questions.q: The tumbleweed rolling through Western films is a Eurasian invader properly called...?
questions.f: It arrived in the 1870s, probably as a contaminant in imported flaxseed.

questions.q: Which flowering plant has the largest known genome, roughly fifty times the size of a human’s?
questions.f: Its enormous genome would stretch far longer than the plant itself if unwound.

questions.q: Dendrochronology, the dating of wood by tree rings, was developed by an astronomer studying...?
questions.f: A. E. Douglass sought a sunspot record in tree rings and founded a new science.

questions.q: A bristlecone pine felled in 1964, later found to have almost 5,000 rings, is remembered as...?
questions.f: Its cutting helped inspire stronger protection for ancient trees.

questions.q: Which staple crop was bred from a scruffy Mexican grass called teosinte?
questions.f: Teosinte’s few hard kernels became the fat cobs of modern corn.

questions.q: The "Three Sisters" of Indigenous American farming are maize, beans, and...?
questions.f: Corn gives beans a pole, beans feed the soil, and squash leaves shade out weeds.

questions.q: Which was the first genetically modified whole food approved for sale, in 1994?
questions.f: It was engineered to soften more slowly after picking.

questions.q: Golden rice was engineered to help prevent deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.f: Its grains make beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A.

questions.q: Which citrus-linked deficiency disease drove navies to stock lemon and lime juice?
questions.f: Vitamin C in citrus cured the sailors’ scourge and earned Britons the name "limeys".

questions.q: The word "vanilla" comes from a Spanish word meaning a little...?
questions.f: Vanilla pods are the cured seed capsules of a climbing orchid.

questions.q: A twelve-year-old on Réunion in 1841 worked out how to hand-pollinate which crop?
questions.f: Edmond Albius’s technique is still used on vanilla farms worldwide.

questions.q: Cacao’s scientific name, Theobroma, translates as food of the...?
questions.f: Linnaeus gave chocolate’s tree a name fit for its status among the Aztecs.

questions.q: Which blue dye, long extracted from a plant, gives denim its traditional colour?
questions.f: Indigo was so valuable it was nicknamed blue gold before synthetic dyes arrived.

questions.q: Which trees supply most of the world’s cork, harvested without felling them?
c: cork oaks of Portugal and Spain
questions.f: Bark is stripped every nine years or so and simply grows back.

questions.q: Roughly how much maple sap must be boiled to make one part of syrup?
questions.f: Sap is only a few percent sugar, so most of the water is boiled away.

questions.q: Which lightweight wood, prized for model aircraft, comes from a fast-growing tropical tree?
questions.f: Balsa trees shoot up quickly, producing very light but surprisingly stiff wood.

questions.q: Dense, close-grained spruce from a cold period may explain the tone of instruments by which maker?
questions.f: Slow growth in the Little Ice Age produced unusually tight, even rings.

questions.q: The word "papyrus," source of the word "paper," names a plant that is a kind of...?
questions.f: Strips of papyrus pith were pressed into sheets along the Nile.

questions.q: The word "cabbage" traces back to a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From "caput," head - a cabbage is a tight head of leaves.

questions.q: The word "broccoli" comes from an Italian word meaning little...?
questions.f: From "brocco," a shoot or sprout, describing its flower stalks.

questions.q: The word "coconut" is thought to come from a Portuguese word for a...?
questions.f: The three marks on the shell reminded sailors of a face.

questions.q: Which flower’s name comes from the Greek word for a rainbow?
questions.f: The iris was named for its dazzling range of colours.

questions.q: The "sycamore" of the Bible is a fig relative, but the name literally means fig-...?
questions.f: From "sykon" (fig) and "moron" (mulberry).

questions.q: Roughly how tall can water be lifted in a tree before physics sets a limit?
questions.f: Cohesion of water in xylem fails beyond roughly this height, capping tree size.

questions.q: Which theory explains sap rising as water pulled upward by evaporation from leaves?
questions.f: Evaporating leaves tug on unbroken water columns all the way to the roots.

questions.q: Gibberellin, the stem-stretching hormone, was first found in a fungus that made rice seedlings grow...?
questions.f: Japanese farmers called it foolish seedling disease before the hormone was isolated.

questions.q: Photoperiodism was discovered in the 1920s using a tobacco variety called Maryland...?
questions.f: It refused to flower in long summer days, revealing day-length control.

questions.q: Which parasitic vine finds its host by sensing airborne chemicals, then grows toward the smell?
questions.f: Dodder seedlings sniff out tomato plants and lean toward them before touching.

questions.q: Which African desert plant grows just two leaves that keep lengthening for over a thousand years?
questions.f: Fog rolling off the Atlantic supplies much of its water in the Namib.

questions.q: Which Socotran tree oozes a red resin traded for centuries as dragon’s blood?
questions.f: Its upturned branches form a crown shaped like an umbrella.

questions.q: The Calvin cycle, the sugar-building stage of photosynthesis, was traced using which tool?
questions.f: Melvin Calvin followed carbon-14 through algae and won a Nobel Prize in 1961.

questions.q: Which plant compound gives freshly cut grass its smell and is a distress signal to neighbours?
questions.f: Damaged leaves puff out these chemicals, and nearby plants raise their defences.

questions.q: Acacias in Africa can summon which insects to attack browsing animals?
questions.f: The trees house ants in swollen thorns and reward them with nectar.

questions.q: What do we call the swollen thorns and nectar glands that house a tree’s insect bodyguards?
questions.f: Domatia are living quarters plants build for their defenders.

questions.q: Which term describes a plant whose flowers open before its leaves appear in spring?
questions.f: Magnolias and redbuds bloom on bare branches, making the display more visible.

questions.q: What do we call the shedding of bark in plates or strips, as in a plane tree?
questions.f: Exfoliating bark sheds soot and grime, which helps plane trees thrive in cities.

questions.q: What is the name for the seed-bearing "wing" of an ash or maple that spins as it falls?
questions.f: A samara is a dry winged fruit built for a long, spinning glide.

questions.q: What do we call the study of the relationship between climate and the timing of leafing and flowering?
questions.f: Phenology records show many plants now leaf out earlier than a century ago.

questions.q: What do we call the hard inner stone of a peach, properly the seed’s protective layer?
questions.f: The endocarp is the innermost fruit wall, hardened into a pit.

questions.q: Robert Hooke coined the biological word "cell" after looking at cork.
questions.f: The empty boxes in cork reminded him of the small rooms monks lived in.

questions.q: Nearly all supermarket bananas are clones of a single variety.
questions.f: Cavendish bananas are propagated from cuttings, so they are genetically identical.

questions.q: Every fig species is pollinated by its own particular species of wasp.
questions.f: This tight partnership means neither fig nor wasp can breed without the other.

questions.q: The tumbleweed of Western films is native to North America.
questions.f: Russian thistle arrived from Eurasia in the 1870s and spread across the plains.

questions.q: Some pine cones stay sealed until the heat of a fire opens them.
questions.f: This adaptation, called serotiny, seeds bare ground right after a blaze.

questions.q: The word "canvas" comes from the Latin name for hemp.
questions.f: Sailcloth was originally woven from hemp fibre, giving canvas its name.

questions.q: Cork can be harvested from a cork oak without killing the tree.
questions.f: Strippers take only the outer bark, which regrows over about nine years.

questions.q: Ginkgo trees have many close wild relatives alive today.
questions.f: The ginkgo is the sole survivor of its entire order, with no living cousins.

questions.q: A Madagascan orchid with a 30 cm nectar spur, a prediction published in 1862, and a hawkmoth finally identified in 1903 make up which famous vindication?
questions.f: Darwin insisted a moth with a foot-long tongue must exist; it was named praedicta in his honour.

questions.q: A gardener who measured the ribbed underside of a giant water-lily leaf went on to design which 1851 building?
questions.f: Joseph Paxton copied the leaf’s radiating ribs to hold acres of glass on slender iron.

questions.q: Fossil leaves carried back by Scott’s dying polar party became key evidence for a vanished supercontinent. Which fossil plant?
questions.f: The same leaf turns up in Africa, India, and Australia, tracing the outline of Gondwana.

questions.q: Sap that stayed infectious after every bacterium was filtered out, mottled tobacco leaves, and a new word coined in 1898 mark the discovery of the first...?
questions.f: Tobacco mosaic disease revealed a whole invisible class of agents smaller than bacteria.

questions.q: A children’s author studied spore germination, had her paper read aloud by a man because women could not attend, and received an apology a century later. Who was she?
questions.f: The Linnean Society formally apologised in 1997 to the creator of Peter Rabbit.

questions.q: A curator climbing the shattered stairs of a burning academy in 1906 saved nearly 1,500 irreplaceable specimens. Who was she?
questions.f: She saved the type specimens and left her own belongings to burn in the San Francisco fire.

questions.q: A botanist’s assistant who sailed disguised as a man became the first woman to circumnavigate the globe. Who was she?
questions.f: She served on Bougainville’s voyage; a nightshade, Solanum baretiae, now carries her name.

questions.q: A Scot in disguise, twenty thousand smuggled seedlings, and the founding of Indian plantations belong to which crop’s history?
questions.f: Robert Fortune shipped China’s guarded tea plants to the Himalayas for the East India Company.

questions.q: A leaf rust that ruined Ceylon’s estates from 1869 pushed the island to switch to which replacement crop?
questions.f: Coffee rust bankrupted the planters, and Sri Lanka became famous for tea instead.

questions.q: A voyage to carry saplings to the Caribbean, a mutiny in 1789, and plants tipped into the sea point to which ship?
questions.f: Bligh was transporting breadfruit when his crew seized the ship, dumping the cargo overboard.

questions.q: An Australian bay was named in 1770 for the enormous haul of specimens two naturalists gathered there. What name did it get?
questions.f: Banks and Solander collected so many new plants that Cook renamed the inlet for botany.

questions.q: A geneticist who mapped where the world’s crops were born died of malnutrition in a Soviet prison in 1943. Who was he?
questions.f: He had assembled the largest seed collection on Earth while his rival Lysenko denied genetics existed.

questions.q: A shrub found only in New Caledonia sits on the very oldest branch of the flowering-plant family tree. Which is it?
questions.f: Amborella is the sister lineage to every other flowering plant alive.

questions.q: Darwin used the phrase "an abominable mystery" in an 1879 letter about the sudden rise of which group?
questions.f: Their explosive appearance in the fossil record still puzzles botanists today.

questions.q: Silica from ancient Scottish hot springs preserved the world’s finest window on the first land plants. What is the site called?
questions.f: Cells and even fungi are preserved in three dimensions in this Devonian deposit.

questions.q: A single male plant taken from a South African forest, cloned worldwide, and no female ever found makes which cycad the "loneliest plant"?
questions.f: Every specimen on Earth is a cutting of the same male, so it cannot breed naturally.

questions.q: A tree extinct in the wild since the 1800s survives only because one collector’s seeds were shared, and it honours an American statesman. Which tree?
questions.f: John Bartram’s garden kept Franklinia alatamaha alive after it vanished from the wild.

questions.q: Seeds gathered by Thor Heyerdahl in 1956 are the reason which Easter Island tree still exists at all?
questions.f: Toromiro is extinct in the wild and survives only in botanical collections.

questions.q: A Mauritian tree was once thought to need a vanished bird’s gut to germinate its stones. Which tree?
questions.f: The dodo theory of 1977 is now doubted, but it made the tree world-famous.

questions.q: A grove named by settlers for a figure raising its arms in prayer depends on a single moth species. Which plant?
questions.f: Yucca moths deliberately pack pollen into the flower, then lay eggs in the ovary.

questions.q: The only tree for hundreds of kilometres in the Sahara, used as a caravan landmark, was destroyed by a truck in 1973. What was it called?
questions.f: Its metal replacement still marks the spot; the trunk sits in a museum in Niamey.

questions.q: Five hundred seeds flown around the Moon in an astronaut’s kit in 1971 were later planted across America. What are the results called?
questions.f: Stuart Roosa carried them on Apollo 14; the seedlings grew normally back on Earth.

questions.q: A sealed biosphere canister, a cotton seed watered on the lunar far side in 2019, and a sprout killed by the two-week night belong to which mission?
questions.f: It was the first seed ever to germinate on another world, if only briefly.

questions.q: A rye fungus, convulsions in 1690s Massachusetts, and a much-argued medical theory converge on which organism?
questions.f: Ergot poisoning has been proposed, though never proven, as a cause of the Salem accusations.

questions.q: A French official who smuggled cloves and nutmeg out of the Dutch islands had a surname meaning "pepper". Who was he?
questions.f: Poivre broke the spice monopoly by planting the stolen seedlings on Mauritius.

questions.q: A clove tree on Ternate nicknamed Afo mattered because it survived a campaign to...?
c: destroy all trees outside a monopoly
questions.f: The Dutch uprooted clove trees to control supply; Afo’s seedlings escaped them.

questions.q: Bark smuggled from the Andes by Charles Ledger and Manuel Incra Mamani founded plantations in Java for which medicine?
questions.f: The seeds Mamani gathered yielded unusually rich bark, and Java came to supply most of the world.

questions.q: A fourth-century Chinese text, a sweet wormwood plant, and a 2015 Nobel Prize belong to which anti-malarial drug?
questions.f: Tu Youyou found the cold-extraction hint in Ge Hong’s ancient recipe book.

questions.q: A star-shaped pod from southern China, a compound called shikimic acid, and a bottleneck in making the flu drug oseltamivir point to which spice?
questions.f: For years global Tamiflu output was limited by the star anise harvest.

questions.q: An extract of autumn crocus, a spindle that fails to pull chromosomes apart, and giant blooms prized by breeders point to which drug?
questions.f: By doubling chromosome sets, colchicine created many of our garden varieties.

questions.q: Candlelit sheds, a Yorkshire triangle, and a crop that pops audibly as it grows describe which forced vegetable?
questions.f: Forced rhubarb grows so fast in the dark that you can hear the stalks creak.

questions.q: A pseudocereal ground into Breton pancakes, a close cousin of rhubarb and sorrel, and a flour with no gluten at all point to which seed?
questions.f: Despite its name it is no relation of wheat and is not even a grass.

questions.q: A grain sacred to the Aztecs was suppressed by Spanish colonisers and has since been revived. Which is it?
questions.f: Amaranth was tied to religious ritual, so its cultivation was discouraged after the conquest.

questions.q: A seedless mutation spotted in Bahia, two trees shipped to Riverside in 1873, and a fruit that can only ever be cloned describe which orange?
questions.f: Every navel orange on Earth is a graft-descendant of one Brazilian mutant.

questions.q: A Californian postman’s backyard seedling of 1926 became the ancestor of nearly every avocado sold today. Which variety?
questions.f: Rudolph Hass patented the tree in 1935; every Hass avocado is a graft from it.

questions.q: A self-taught Californian breeder, a russet-skinned potato released in 1902, and the standard chip of the fast-food age point to whom?
questions.f: The Russet Burbank still dominates the world’s french fries.

questions.q: A hybrid-corn seed company founder later served as a United States vice-president. Who was he?
questions.f: Wallace’s Pioneer Hi-Bred helped hybrid maize transform American yields.

questions.q: A chance seedling on Maria Ann Smith’s Australian property gave the world which apple?
questions.f: The tart green apple grew from discarded French crab-apple cores near her Ryde farm.

questions.q: An ornamental prized at Victorian flower shows, spread only by broken fragments, and a British invasion behaving as one plant describe which weed?
questions.f: Britain’s knotweed is essentially a single female clone, so it sets no seed.

questions.q: Sixty million hectares of Australian cactus, a caterpillar imported from Argentina, and one of history’s great biological-control victories involve which agent?
questions.f: Cactoblastis larvae bored the prickly pear out from the inside.

questions.q: A plant that thrives on burnt ground, pink spires across cleared London rubble, and a nickname born of the Blitz belong to which weed?
questions.f: Rosebay willowherb colonised the ruins so fast it earned a wartime name.

questions.q: A chance hybrid of an American and an Oriental parent, bark shed in plates to slough off soot, and avenues across a smoky capital describe which tree?
questions.f: Shedding its skin lets the plane survive air that would kill other trees.

questions.q: An annual gift from Oslo since 1947, a thank-you for wartime support, and a spruce watched by crowds each December stands in which square?
questions.f: Norway has sent a tree every single year for over seventy-five years.

questions.q: A Kenyan scheme paying village women per surviving seedling, tens of millions of trees, and a 2004 prize never before given to an African woman point to whom?
questions.f: Her Green Belt Movement tied forest restoration to women’s livelihoods.

questions.q: Himalayan villagers surrounding trees in 1973, a Hindi word meaning to cling, and the origin of a now-common English nickname describe which movement?
questions.f: The Chipko protests gave the world the phrase tree hugger.

questions.q: A man who planted a forest single-handedly on an Indian sandbar is known as the Forest Man of...?
questions.f: Jadav Payeng turned bare silt into woodland now big enough for elephants and tigers.

questions.q: A wheat stem rust strain found in 1999 and named for the country where it appeared is called...?
questions.f: Ug99 broke resistance genes that had protected wheat for decades.

questions.q: A textbook two-partner definition, a 2016 genetic study of look-alike lichens, and an extra fungus hiding in the outer layer point to which organism?
questions.f: Many lichens turn out to be three-way partnerships rather than two.

questions.q: A 1997 Nature paper on linked forest fungi gave popular science which nickname?
questions.f: Underground fungal threads shuttle carbon and signals between neighbouring trees.

questions.q: A pitcher holding litres of fluid on Mount Kinabalu, a lid smeared with nectar, and tree shrews paying for the meal with droppings describe which plant?
questions.f: It gains more nitrogen from shrew dung than from the insects it drowns.

questions.q: An underwater bladder held under tension, a trapdoor buckling inward in under a millisecond, and prey sucked in before it can react describe which plant?
questions.f: Utricularia’s trap is among the fastest movements known in any plant.

questions.q: A flower burning stored starch to stay above freezing, a hole melted up through late snow, and a stench that draws the first flies describe which plant?
questions.f: It can hold itself around twenty degrees warmer than the air around it.

questions.q: A pair of flat leaf tips flush with the gravel, translucent windows letting light below ground, and near-perfect stone mimicry describe which plants?
questions.f: Buried almost entirely, they photosynthesise through windows in their leaf tops.

questions.q: Some passionflowers grow small yellow bumps on their leaves that mimic butterfly...?
questions.f: A female butterfly avoids laying where eggs already appear to be, sparing the leaf.

questions.q: A palm that waits decades in leaf, a flower cluster carrying millions of blooms, and death immediately after fruiting describe which tree?
questions.f: Its inflorescence is the largest branched flower cluster of any plant.

questions.q: A Chinese valley yielded living trees of a genus known only from fossils in the 1940s. Which tree?
questions.f: Metasequoia had been described from fossils years before anyone found it alive.

questions.q: A bushwalker named David Noble rappelling into a canyon in 1994 discovered which conifer?
questions.f: Fewer than a hundred wild Wollemi pines are known, and their location is kept secret.

questions.q: A Western Australian bay, one clone spanning some 180 km of seabed, and an age measured in thousands of years describe which organism?
questions.f: Genetic tests showed the entire meadow grew from a single seedling.

questions.q: A Swedish spruce called Old Tjikko is remarkable because its trunk is young but its...?
questions.f: The roots have cloned new trunks for roughly 9,500 years on that mountainside.

questions.q: A pod too hard for most jaws, a bee strong enough to force the flower open, and a rodent that buries what it cannot eat explain why which crop resists farming?
questions.f: Only the agouti can crack the pod, and the nuts it forgets become trees.

questions.q: The cashew is awkward to process because its shell contains an irritant related to the oil in...?
questions.f: Cashews, mangoes, and poison ivy all belong to the same family.

questions.q: A Queensland rainforest native, a shell needing enormous force to crack, and an industry built up in Hawaii describe which nut?
questions.f: Hawaiian growers selected the cultivars that made this Australian tree a world crop.

questions.q: Cassava must be soaked, grated, or fermented before eating because it contains compounds that release...?
questions.f: Traditional processing removes the toxins, making a staple for hundreds of millions.

questions.q: A West African berry contains miraculin, a protein that briefly makes sour foods taste...?
questions.f: Miraculin latches onto sweet receptors and switches them on when acid arrives.

questions.q: Which fruit, the heaviest borne on any tree, can exceed 30 kg?
questions.f: A single jackfruit can feed a large family and grows straight from the trunk.

questions.q: Which fruit is banned from Singapore’s trains and many hotels because of its smell?
questions.f: Durian’s aroma comes from a cocktail of sulphur compounds that lingers for hours.

questions.q: Saffron’s crocus cannot set seed and must be propagated by hand because it is a sterile...?
questions.f: Every saffron corm is a clone, split and replanted by growers each year.

questions.q: Cyanobacteria performing photosynthesis are blamed for which vast ancient change to the planet?
questions.f: Their waste oxygen poisoned much of early life and rusted the oceans.

questions.q: Which fossil is generally regarded as among the earliest known vascular land plants?
questions.f: Cooksonia was a few centimetres tall, with simple stems tipped by spore cases.

questions.q: Which Devonian plant is often called the first "modern" tree, with a trunk and true leaves?
questions.f: Its deep roots helped weather rock and build the first proper forest soils.

questions.q: Towering scale trees called Lepidodendron dominated swamps that became today’s...?
questions.f: Their bark left diamond-patterned fossils in Carboniferous coal measures.

questions.q: Which enormous Silurian and Devonian organism, up to 8 m tall, is now thought to have been a fungus, not a plant?
questions.f: For a time these spires were the tallest living things on land.

questions.q: A monastery garden in Padua, a 1753 book that still fixes the starting date for plant names, and a clock told by opening flowers point to whom?
questions.f: Species Plantarum set the baseline for every botanical name we use today.

questions.q: A climb up Chimborazo, sketches of plants banded by altitude, and the founding of plant geography belong to which explorer?
questions.f: He showed that climbing a mountain passes through the same zones as travelling to the poles.

questions.q: A Himalayan rhododendron haul, decades of letters to Darwin, and a long directorship of Kew describe which botanist?
questions.f: Hooker was the friend Darwin trusted with his theory years before publishing.

questions.q: An Indian cytologist who improved sugarcane and had a magnolia named in her honour was...?
questions.f: Her chromosome studies helped India breed far sweeter cane.

questions.q: A woman who began serious plant collecting at fifty-one and gathered some 150,000 specimens was...?
questions.f: Mexia explored remote Mexico and South America on collecting trips lasting years.

questions.q: Which crop’s "centres of origin" idea holds that a crop’s wild diversity is richest where it was first domesticated?
questions.f: Vavilov used the rule to hunt for the wild relatives that breeders still rely on.

questions.q: Which Soviet agronomist rejected genetics, promised harvests from "training" seeds, and wrecked his country’s crop science?
questions.f: Lysenko’s political favour let him silence and imprison real geneticists.

questions.q: Fungal threads branching into bushy tufts inside a root cell, a partnership traceable back over 400 million years, and a name meaning little tree describe what?
questions.f: This alliance may be what allowed plants to colonise dry land at all.

questions.q: A dense sheath cloaking a pine rootlet, threads that never break into the cells, and a truffle at the far end of the network describe which partnership?
questions.f: The prefix means outside, describing the mantle around each rootlet.

questions.q: Dogs replacing pigs on Piedmont hillsides, a fungus nobody can farm reliably, and a price per kilo beyond any vegetable describe which delicacy?
questions.f: Pigs were banned in places because they ate the prize before the hunter arrived.

questions.q: Winter wheat sown in autumn, a Latin root meaning spring, and seedlings that refuse to bloom until weeks of cold have passed describe which requirement?
questions.f: The cold check stops a plant flowering in the mild spell before winter arrives.

questions.q: Seeds layered between damp sand in a cold frame, a term borrowed from the language of rock layers, and a deliberate fake winter describe which treatment?
questions.f: Gardeners imitate the months a seed would normally lie outdoors.

questions.q: An agave hoarding starch for decades, a talipot palm’s single colossal flower spike, and death immediately after seeding describe which strategy?
questions.f: Everything the plant has saved is spent on one enormous reproductive gamble.

questions.q: A fatty parcel glued to a seed, a trail of ants hauling it underground, and a Greek word for ant name which dispersal method?
questions.f: Ants eat the treat and dump the seed in a nutrient-rich waste chamber.

questions.q: A coconut adrift for months, mangrove seedlings riding an outgoing tide, and a Greek root for water describe which dispersal method?
questions.f: Waterproof, buoyant seeds can cross open ocean and still sprout on landfall.

questions.q: A pale oily parcel fused to a bloodroot seed, an ant nest’s refuse pile, and a Greek word for oil point to which structure?
questions.f: The seed is carried, stripped of its treat, and left in perfect compost.

questions.q: The one part of a yew that is not poisonous, the lacy scarlet coat sold as mace, and a fleshy overcoat on a seed all describe which structure?
questions.f: Birds swallow the yew’s red aril and pass the toxic seed unharmed.

questions.q: Mistletoe tapping an apple branch, leaves still green and working, and a prefix meaning half describe which kind of plant?
questions.f: It steals water and minerals but still makes some of its own sugar.

questions.q: Dodder with not a trace of green, Rafflesia hidden entirely inside a vine, and a prefix meaning whole describe which category?
questions.f: Having abandoned photosynthesis, these plants cannot survive alone at all.

questions.q: A waxy white woodland stem, sugar siphoned from a fungus that trades with nearby trees, and no chlorophyll whatsoever describe which lifestyle?
questions.f: The ghost plant is really a thief taxing the forest’s underground market.

questions.q: Chicory roots roasted as a wartime coffee substitute, a sugar humans can barely digest, and a favourite food of gut bacteria point to which polymer?
questions.f: Daisy-family plants store inulin where most plants would store starch.

questions.q: Needle-sharp crystals of calcium oxalate, a houseplant nicknamed dumb cane, and a mouth left numb and swollen point to which structures?
questions.f: The needles jab soft tissue, delivering irritants exactly where they hurt.

questions.q: The silver sheen of a desert sage, the sting of a nettle, and the glue drops of a sundew are all built from which structures?
questions.f: One structure, endlessly redesigned, for shade, defence, and trapping prey.

questions.q: Red kidney beans left too long in a slow cooker, a protein that makes blood cells clump, and advice to always boil hard first point to which compound?
questions.f: Just a few undercooked beans can cause hours of misery.

questions.q: A scar sealed before the leaf lets go, a Latin root meaning to cut away, and a tidy autumn parting describe which layer?
questions.f: The tree amputates its own leaves deliberately, closing the wound first.

questions.q: Which internal tree tissue, sealed off and often dark, is created to block decay after injury?
questions.f: Trees compartmentalise damage rather than healing it the way animals do.

questions.q: A leaning conifer pushing from beneath, a broadleaf hauling from above, and timber notorious for warping on the saw describe which wood?
questions.f: Conifers make compression wood; broadleaves make tension wood instead.

questions.q: Lichen crusting fresh lava, birch scrub shading the lichen out, and oak woodland centuries later describe which process?
questions.f: Each stage builds the soil and shade that dooms it and favours the next.

questions.q: Fireweed on a bombsite, lichen on cooling lava, and the first thin crust of soil describe which kind of species?
questions.f: Pioneers make the ground habitable for the very plants that will replace them.

questions.q: A wood that persists until fire or storm resets the clock, the last stage of succession, and a name borrowed from drama describe which community?
questions.f: It is stable only until the next big disturbance starts the sequence again.

questions.q: Birch sprinting into a new clearing, seedlings that die beneath their own parents, and a species doomed as the canopy closes are called what?
questions.f: Such trees are gamblers, betting everything on finding an opening.

questions.q: Which soil-dwelling group converts ammonia into nitrates that plant roots can absorb?
questions.f: Nitrification is a key step returning nitrogen to a usable form for plants.

questions.q: Which genus of bacteria fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of alders rather than legumes?
questions.f: Alders can therefore colonise raw gravel where nitrogen is almost absent.

questions.q: A bird’s nest fern perched on a branch, leaves funnelling falling debris inward, and a plant making its own compost aloft use which arrangement?
questions.f: The fern farms a private soil bed metres above the forest floor.

questions.q: Tree frogs breeding many metres above the ground, a bromeliad’s cupped leaves brimming with rain, and a Greek phrase meaning plant pond name which habitat?
questions.f: Whole food chains run their course in a puddle held by a single plant.

questions.q: Which growth form lets a strangler fig start in the canopy and end up standing alone?
c: it germinates on a host and roots downward
it climbs from the forest floor
it grows only from seed in soil
questions.f: The host eventually dies and rots away inside a hollow lattice of fig roots.

questions.q: Which enormous Indian banyan is famous for a canopy covering well over a hectare?
c: the Bodhi tree of Bodh Gaya
questions.f: Its main trunk rotted away, leaving a forest of prop roots that is still one tree.

questions.q: Which tree of the Namib, whose name means "quiver", provided San hunters with arrow holders?
questions.f: Hollowed branches of this tree aloe made light, tough quivers.

questions.q: Which Madagascan tree is named for how its huge leaf bases collect drinkable rainwater?
questions.f: It is not a true palm but a relative of the bird of paradise flower.

questions.q: Which African genus of baobabs is named after the naturalist Michel Adanson?
questions.f: Adanson described the tree in Senegal, and Linnaeus honoured him in the name.

questions.q: Which palm produces the world’s longest leaves, sometimes over 20 m, used for weaving?
questions.f: Raffia fibre from the leaf skin is a staple of basketry and horticulture.

questions.q: Which pale, thick, tannin-rich bark helps a giant sequoia shrug off forest fires?
c: bark up to about 60 cm thick
questions.f: The spongy bark insulates so well that fire scars often heal over.

questions.q: Coast redwoods supplement their water supply by absorbing fog directly through their...?
questions.f: Foliar uptake lets the crown drink from cloud when the soil is dry.

questions.q: Which tallest known living tree, its exact site kept secret, is a coast redwood named...?
questions.f: Trampling by visitors grew so bad that the area was legally closed in 2022.

questions.q: Which species is the tallest flowering plant on Earth, topping 100 m in Tasmania?
questions.f: Eucalyptus regnans is the tallest angiosperm, though conifers grow taller still.

questions.q: Which New Zealand conifer, revered for its vast trunk girth, includes a giant called Tane Mahuta?
questions.f: Kauri dieback disease now threatens these ancient forest giants.

questions.q: Which plant family, with about 28,000 species, is generally reckoned the largest of all?
questions.f: Orchids grow on every continent except Antarctica, mostly as tropical epiphytes.

questions.q: Orchid seeds are dust-like because they contain almost no...?
questions.f: They must meet the right fungus to feed them or they simply never grow.

questions.q: Which orchid genus dupes male insects into mating with a flower that mimics a female?
questions.f: The flower even copies the insect’s scent, not just its shape and fuzz.

questions.q: Which Australian orchid flings a visiting wasp against its pollen with a hinged, decoy-tipped arm?
questions.f: The wasp grabs the decoy, the hinge swings, and pollen is slapped onto its back.

questions.q: Pale blooms opening only after dark, a heavy musky odour, and a Greek term meaning hand-wing describe which pollination syndrome?
questions.f: Bat-pollinated flowers are often sturdy enough to take a landing mammal.

questions.q: Scarlet tubes with no scent at all, thin nectar in generous volume, and visitors with sharp eyes but poor noses describe which syndrome?
questions.f: Perfume would be wasted on a hummingbird, so these flowers shout in colour.

questions.q: A bloom reeking of rotting meat, flies tricked into laying doomed eggs, and a Greek root meaning putrid describe which syndrome?
questions.f: The flower offers no food at all, only a convincing and costly lie.

questions.q: A bumblebee clamped to a tomato flower, flight muscles vibrating without the wings moving, and pollen shaken from sealed tubes describe what?
questions.f: Honeybees cannot do this, which is why glasshouses hire bumblebees.

questions.q: A short-tongued bumblebee at a long-tubed flower, a hole chewed near the base, and a reward taken with no pollen moved describe what?
questions.f: The flower pays the price and gets nothing whatever in return.

questions.q: An orchid promising a mate it cannot provide, another mimicking food it does not hold, and insects leaving empty-handed describe which strategy?
questions.f: Roughly a third of orchid species cheat their pollinators entirely.

questions.q: A lawn of dandelions all genetically identical, seed set with no fertilisation at all, and clones by the thousand describe which process?
questions.f: The flower goes through the motions but skips the mixing of genes.

questions.q: Oaks across a whole county fruiting in the same autumn, more acorns than any squirrel can hide, and lean years in between describe which tactic?
questions.f: Boom and bust starves the seed predators, then swamps the survivors.

questions.q: Poppies erupting over churned battlefield soil, seeds that had waited decades in the dark, and light reaching them at last describe which reserve?
questions.f: Disturb old ground and you may wake a garden that has slept for a century.

questions.q: What is the name for the leaf mosaic arrangement that minimises shading between a plant’s own leaves?
questions.f: Leaves shuffle their angles and stalk lengths so each catches some light.

questions.q: Which measurement compares total leaf area to the ground area beneath a canopy?
questions.f: A dense rainforest canopy can carry several square metres of leaf per square metre of soil.

questions.q: Jigsaw channels of sky above a Malaysian plantation, crowns halting just short of contact, and a name suggesting bashfulness describe what?
questions.f: Wind-whipped branch tips and light-sensing may both keep the neighbours apart.

questions.q: A gardener pinching out a tip to get a bushier plant, side buds held in check by the leader, and a hormone flowing downward describe what?
questions.f: Remove the tip and the suppressed buds are released within days.

questions.q: A potato sprouting in a dark cupboard, stems long, pale, and weak, and everything gambled on reaching the light describe which condition?
questions.f: The seedling stops making leaves and spends all it has on stem length.

questions.q: Which pigment protein lets plants sense red and far-red light and so detect shade from rivals?
questions.f: Leaves absorb red but reflect far-red, so neighbours betray themselves by their glow.

questions.q: Which blue-light receptor family controls a plant’s bending toward a window?
questions.f: Phototropins trigger the hormone shifts that curve the growing stem.

questions.q: Which internal cycle keeps a plant opening its leaves on schedule even in constant darkness?
questions.f: Plants run their own daily clock and anticipate dawn rather than merely reacting.

questions.q: Chrysanthemums timed for autumn shows, growers hanging blackout cloth, and a plant that is really measuring the length of the night is called what?
questions.f: A single flash of light in the small hours can cancel the whole signal.

questions.q: Which hormone-like signal, long sought and finally identified as a protein, triggers flowering?
questions.f: Botanists hunted the mystery flowering signal for over seventy years.

questions.q: Every plant of the "loneliest cycad" alive today is a clone of a single male specimen.
questions.f: No female Encephalartos woodii has ever been found, so it cannot reproduce sexually.

questions.q: Orchid seeds usually need a partner fungus in order to germinate successfully.
questions.f: The dust-like seeds carry almost no food, so a fungus must feed the seedling.

questions.q: Tobacco mosaic disease led to the discovery of the first known virus.
questions.f: Filtered sap stayed infectious, revealing agents far smaller than bacteria.

questions.q: Crown shyness describes tree crowns that grow into and through each other.
questions.f: It is the opposite: neighbouring crowns stop short, leaving gaps between them.

questions.q: Trees seal off and compartmentalise wounds rather than healing them as animals do.
questions.f: Damaged wood is walled away behind chemical barriers and simply grown over.

questions.q: A locked Dutch garden, a stolen cutting, and the coffee plants of the entire Americas trace back to a handful of seedlings from which city’s botanic garden?
questions.f: Nearly all New World arabica is said to descend from a few closely guarded Dutch plants.

questions.q: A pineapple-shaped stone finial, an 18th-century hothouse arms race, and a fruit rented by the evening reflect the status of which crop in Georgian Britain?
questions.f: Gardeners burned tons of coal in "pineries" to ripen a single showpiece fruit.

questions.q: A wardrobe of specimens pressed onto paper, a sheet that fixes a species name forever, and a global lending network describe which collection?
questions.f: The single sheet that anchors a species name is called its type specimen.

questions.q: A single pressed sheet in a locked cabinet, the final court of appeal when a name is disputed, and a label outranking any photograph describe what?
questions.f: Names are anchored to physical objects, not to descriptions or pictures.

questions.q: Which principle states that the earliest validly published name for a plant takes precedence?
questions.f: It is why a familiar name sometimes has to be dropped for an older, forgotten one.

questions.q: Two names published for one plant, a rule awarding victory to the older, and a familiar label quietly retired describe what?
questions.f: Much of taxonomy is housekeeping, deciding which of several names must win.

questions.q: In the name Quercus robur, the word "robur" is properly called the specific...?
questions.f: The genus is Quercus; together with the epithet it forms the full species name.

questions.q: The standard ending "-aceae" on a botanical name tells you the rank is a...?
questions.f: Poaceae, Fabaceae, and Asteraceae are all plant families.

questions.q: Which group of flowering plants, once split into monocots and dicots, is now known to be an unnatural grouping?
questions.f: The old dicots turn out to include several separate early lineages, so the label was retired.

questions.q: Which large lineage contains most familiar broadleaf trees and about three-quarters of flowering species?
questions.f: The "true dicots" share distinctive three-grooved pollen.

questions.q: Which flowering-plant group includes magnolias, laurels, and black pepper, outside both monocots and eudicots?
questions.f: Magnoliids branch off early and keep several ancient floral features.

questions.q: Which two-word term describes wood from broadleaved trees, regardless of how soft it actually is?
questions.f: Balsa is a hardwood botanically, even though you can dent it with a thumbnail.

questions.q: Which vessel-free water-conducting cells make conifer wood structurally different from broadleaf wood?
questions.f: Conifers move water through narrow tracheids rather than wide open vessels.

questions.q: Which cells sit beside phloem sieve tubes and keep them loaded with sugar?
questions.f: Sieve tubes lose most of their contents, so companion cells do the metabolic work.

questions.q: Two cells bowing apart as they swell with water, a pore slammed shut in drought, and the gateway for every molecule of carbon dioxide describe what?
questions.f: Every atom of carbon in a tree once passed between a pair of these cells.

questions.q: The waterproofing of a champagne cork, the sealing band inside a root, and rot resistance measured in decades point to which substance?
questions.f: Suberin is why a cork keeps a bottle sealed for years without decaying.

questions.q: The shine on a holly leaf, a skin that slows water loss to a trickle, and a polymer named from the Latin for skin point to what?
questions.f: Without this waxy skin, land plants would dry out within hours.

questions.q: Which ring of cells with a waterproof band forces water to pass through root cell membranes?
questions.f: The Casparian strip blocks the gaps, letting the plant filter what it admits.

questions.q: A waterproof band cementing a ring of root cells, a checkpoint water cannot slip around, and a name honouring a 19th-century German botanist describe what?
questions.f: It forces every drop through a living membrane, so the root can filter it.

questions.q: Droplets ranged along a strawberry leaf edge at dawn, water pushed from below rather than pulled from above, and something often mistaken for dew describe what?
questions.f: The result is guttation, and unlike dew it comes from inside the plant.

questions.q: An audible click from a drought-stressed trunk, an air bubble snapping a thread of water, and a vessel permanently out of service describe what?
questions.f: Enough broken columns and the tree can no longer lift water at all.

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of the water a plant absorbs is lost again through transpiration?
questions.f: Only a tiny remainder is actually built into the plant’s tissues.

questions.q: Which crop uses the C4 pathway, giving it an advantage in hot, bright, dry conditions?
questions.f: Maize, sorghum, and sugarcane are all C4 champions of the tropics.

questions.q: An enzyme confusing oxygen for carbon dioxide, up to a quarter of fixed carbon thrown away on a hot day, and the flaw C4 plants sidestep describe what?
questions.f: A 3-billion-year-old error in the world’s commonest enzyme still costs harvests.

questions.q: Pores that open only at midnight, malic acid banked until dawn, and a pineapple’s astonishing thrift with water describe which pathway?
questions.f: Taste a succulent leaf at sunrise and it really is more sour than at dusk.

questions.q: A pathway first pinned down in a family of fleshy-leaved succulents, an acid named after that same family, and cacti that later borrowed the trick point to which family?
questions.f: Crassulaceae gave the process its mouthful of a name.

questions.q: A plant flourishing on nickel-rich serpentine rock, leaves loaded with metal that would poison its neighbours, and a possible tool for cleaning land describe what?
questions.f: One New Caledonian tree even bleeds a blue-green, nickel-laden sap.

questions.q: A crop sown on mine waste, an ash heap richer in metal than some natural ores, and a harvest measured in kilograms of nickel describe what?
questions.f: The plants are burned and the metal is simply smelted from the ash.

questions.q: Glassy shapes moulded inside living grass cells, grains still sitting in a Neolithic floor, and evidence of a crop long after every seed rotted describe what?
questions.f: Because they are effectively glass, they outlast almost everything else.

questions.q: Charred seeds swept from a hearth, silica bodies moulded into a clay floor, and the dinner of a vanished village are the business of which field?
questions.f: Rubbish and ash tell us what people actually grew, not just what they wrote down.

questions.q: Einkorn, emmer, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch, and flax are together called the founder crops of which region?
questions.f: These eight species underwrote the first farming villages on Earth.

questions.q: Wild ears flinging their grain to the ground, a rare mutant that stubbornly holds on, and the trait early farmers selected without knowing it describe what?
questions.f: Domestication began when the plants that would not let go were the ones harvested.

questions.q: Which crop was domesticated from a wild grass in the Yangtze region and feeds much of Asia?
questions.f: Paddy cultivation transformed the landscape as well as the diet of the region.

questions.q: Andean nights of hard frost, days of thin bright sun, tubers trodden underfoot and dried, and a store lasting years point to which crop?
questions.f: Chuño let Andean states stockpile food against famine and feed armies.

questions.q: A stick pushed into damp soil that roots almost eagerly, orchards of genetically identical trees, and one of the first crops ever cloned point to which fruit?
questions.f: Figs root so readily that growers could copy a favourite tree millennia ago.

questions.q: Which grafting-dependent fruit means every commercial tree of a variety is genetically identical?
questions.f: Apple seeds never breed true, so orchards are built entirely from grafts.

questions.q: Which rootstock choice mainly determines a modern orchard apple tree’s final...?
