questions.q: The word 'sustenance' means…?
questions.f: From Latin words meaning to hold up from beneath, as food holds up the body.

questions.q: The coffee drink 'macchiato' takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The espresso is 'stained' with just a spot of milk.

questions.q: The Italian dessert 'affogato', ice cream under hot espresso, means…?
questions.f: The scoop of ice cream really is drowned in a shot of hot coffee.

questions.q: The Japanese tea 'matcha' takes its name from words meaning…?
questions.f: Because you drink the whole powdered leaf, matcha is far stronger than steeped tea.

questions.q: Wild rice is not actually a true rice.
questions.f: It is the seed of a different water grass, harvested from lakes and marshes.

questions.q: A pineapple keeps ripening and growing sweeter after it is picked.
questions.f: Unlike bananas, pineapples stop sweetening once cut from the plant, so pick a ripe one.

questions.q: Olive oil labelled 'extra virgin' is pressed without using heat or chemicals.
questions.f: Only mechanical pressing counts, which is why extra virgin keeps such a fresh flavour.

questions.q: Most of the world's saffron is grown in Iran.
questions.f: Iran produces the vast majority of the global saffron harvest each year.

questions.q: Salmon get their pink colour from the food they eat.
questions.f: Pigments in the shrimp and krill they eat tint the fish's flesh pink.

questions.q: Boiling an egg makes its proteins unfold and set into a solid.
questions.f: Heat unravels the coiled proteins so they link up into a firm mesh.

questions.q: A mug of filter coffee usually holds more caffeine than one small espresso.
questions.f: Espresso is more concentrated, but a big filter coffee delivers more caffeine overall.

questions.q: Pouring oil into pasta water is the best way to stop the pasta sticking.
questions.f: The oil just floats on top; stirring the pasta early is what really works.

questions.q: The browning reaction in seared meat and toast is named after which chemist?
questions.f: Maillard described the reaction in 1912, but its role in flavor was only understood decades later.

questions.q: The French 'mother sauce' béchamel is a white sauce thickened with…?
c: A roux of flour and butter
questions.f: A roux is flour cooked in fat; whisked with milk it becomes smooth béchamel.

questions.q: The dessert Peach Melba was created by chef Escoffier to honor which opera singer?
questions.f: Escoffier served peaches and ice cream on an ice swan, echoing a swan in Melba's opera.

questions.q: Beef Wellington is popularly said to be named after which British figure?
questions.f: The pastry-wrapped beef may have been named to celebrate Wellington's victory at Waterloo.

questions.q: Nachos were invented by a man whose nickname 'Nacho' was short for which name?
questions.f: Ignacio Anaya threw together the snack for hungry customers in Mexico in 1943.

questions.q: The Granny Smith apple is named after Maria Ann Smith, a grower from which country?
questions.f: She reportedly grew the first tree from discarded French crab apples near Sydney in the 1860s.

questions.q: The Hass avocado, the world's most common variety, is named after Rudolph Hass, who was a…?
questions.f: Nearly every Hass avocado traces back to a single tree Hass patented in California in 1935.

questions.q: Earl Grey tea gets its distinctive flavor from oil of which citrus fruit?
questions.f: Bergamot is a fragrant, sour citrus grown mostly in the Calabria region of Italy.

questions.q: The Margherita pizza's red, white, and green toppings were meant to match…?
questions.f: Legend says it was made in 1889 for Queen Margherita of Italy, hence the patriotic colors.

questions.q: The thin raw-beef dish carpaccio was named after a painter famous for using which color?
questions.f: A Venetian chef named it after Vittore Carpaccio, whose paintings glowed with red tones.

questions.q: Vitamin K took its letter from a German word for which body process?
questions.f: A Danish scientist named it 'K' because it helps blood coagulate, or clot.

questions.q: Tahini, the paste in hummus and halva, is made from ground…?
questions.f: Sesame is one of humanity's oldest oilseed crops, grown for over 3,000 years.

questions.q: The additive MSG (monosodium glutamate) mainly boosts which taste?
questions.f: MSG delivers the same glutamate that gives tomatoes, cheese, and broth their savory depth.

questions.q: Scientists say the 'five-second rule' is a myth because bacteria transfer…?
questions.f: Studies show germs can jump to dropped food in well under a second.

questions.q: Chili peppers only reached Asian and African cooking after explorers brought them from…?
questions.f: Before Columbus, no cuisine in the Old World had ever tasted a chili pepper.

questions.q: Which preservation method removes water by freezing food and then using a vacuum?
questions.f: Freeze-drying keeps flavor and shape so well it is used for astronaut meals and instant coffee.

questions.q: The Maillard browning reaction needs heat plus which two ingredients?
questions.f: Proteins provide the amino acids and starches or sugars provide the reducing sugars.

questions.q: Which technique cooks food slowly in a sealed bag in precisely warm water?
questions.f: 'Sous vide' is French for 'under vacuum'; it cooks food evenly edge to edge.

questions.q: To 'flambé' a dish, a cook briefly sets fire to its…?
questions.f: The flames burn off the harsh alcohol while leaving behind its flavor.

questions.q: The world's priciest coffee, kopi luwak, is collected from the droppings of which animal?
questions.f: The civet eats ripe coffee cherries, and its digestion is said to smooth the beans' flavor.

questions.q: Traditional balsamic vinegar comes only from which Italian city?
questions.f: Real aged balsamic is boiled grape juice matured in wooden barrels for years.

questions.q: By law, true Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese can only be made in a region of…?
questions.f: Each wheel is stamped and inspected; failures are sold under plainer names.

questions.q: The famous Bramley is a variety of which fruit, prized for cooking?
questions.f: Bramley apples stay sharp and fluff up when cooked, perfect for pies and sauce.

questions.q: Which acid makes rhubarb leaves toxic, even though the stalks are safe?
questions.f: Oxalic acid in the leaves can bind calcium in the body, so only the stalks are eaten.

questions.q: The Scottish dish haggis is traditionally cooked inside a sheep's…?
questions.f: Today many haggis are cooked in artificial casings instead of a natural stomach lining.

questions.q: Tempeh, a firm high-protein cake, is made by fermenting which bean?
questions.f: Tempeh comes from Indonesia, where a mold binds the beans into a solid cake.

questions.q: The spicy fermented red paste gochujang is a staple of which country's cooking?
questions.f: Gochujang blends chili powder, fermented soybeans, and rice, aged in earthenware pots.

questions.q: Which everyday seasoning is the only rock or mineral that humans eat directly?
questions.f: Salt was once so valuable it was traded ounce for ounce and used as money.

questions.q: The 'Spice Islands' that Europeans raced to reach for nutmeg and cloves are the…?
questions.f: For centuries the Moluccas, now part of Indonesia, were the world's only source of these spices.

questions.q: Capsaicin makes chilies feel hot by triggering a receptor that normally senses…?
questions.f: The TRPV1 receptor is fooled into signaling burning even though nothing is actually hot.

questions.q: Theobromine, the stimulant in chocolate, has a scientific name meaning…?
questions.f: Cacao's genus 'Theobroma' joins Greek 'theos' (god) and 'broma' (food).

questions.q: Which nutrient provides the most energy per gram, about 9 calories?
questions.f: Carbohydrates and protein give about 4 calories per gram, less than half as much as fat.

questions.q: Ristretto, lungo, and doppio are all variations of which drink?
questions.f: They differ by how much water passes through the coffee: short, long, or a double shot.

questions.q: The frozen 'TV dinner' ready meal was first sold in which country?
questions.f: Swanson launched it in 1953, reportedly to use up a huge surplus of Thanksgiving turkey.

questions.q: Traditional Worcestershire sauce gets its savory tang from a fermented base of which fish?
questions.f: The recipe was based on a sauce brought back from India in the 1830s.

questions.q: Unlike baking soda, baking powder can work alone because it already contains its own…?
questions.f: Baking soda needs an outside acid like lemon or buttermilk to make bubbles rise.

questions.q: Today's exported bananas are mostly the Cavendish, which replaced which earlier variety?
questions.f: A fungus called Panama disease wiped out the tastier Gros Michel in the 1950s.

questions.q: The savory jelly called aspic is set using which protein?
questions.f: Gelatin comes from collagen in animal bones and skin simmered into a clear broth.

questions.q: Fruit jam sets into a spreadable gel thanks to a natural substance called…?
questions.f: Under-ripe fruit and apple peels are especially rich in gel-forming pectin.

questions.q: The common sweet orange is a natural hybrid of a mandarin and which larger citrus?
questions.f: Most familiar citrus fruits are blends of just a few wild ancestors, including the pomelo.

questions.q: In an 1893 case, the US Supreme Court legally ruled the tomato to be a…?
questions.f: The court sided with cooks over botanists so tomatoes could be taxed as vegetables.

questions.q: Ghee, common in Indian cooking, is a form of clarified…?
questions.f: Simmering butter and straining out the milk solids leaves pure golden fat that keeps for months.

questions.q: The sweetener aspartame is roughly how much sweeter than ordinary sugar?
questions.f: Because so little is needed, aspartame adds almost no calories to diet drinks.

questions.q: Plant-based 'Impossible' burgers get their meaty look and taste from which molecule?
questions.f: The heme is made by fermenting yeast, giving the patty a bloody, beefy quality.

questions.q: Prized Kobe beef comes from cattle raised in which country?
questions.f: Real Kobe beef comes only from Tajima-strain cattle in Japan's Hyogo region.

questions.q: Which prized fungus grows underground and is hunted using trained dogs or pigs?
questions.f: White truffles from Alba, Italy, can sell for thousands of dollars per pound.

questions.q: The fresh herb cilantro comes from the very same plant as which spice?
questions.f: Some people carry a gene that makes cilantro leaves taste like soap.

questions.q: Dietary fiber belongs to which class of nutrients?
questions.f: Fiber is a carbohydrate our bodies cannot digest, which is exactly why it aids digestion.

questions.q: Keeping oil and water mixed in mayonnaise or vinaigrette is called…?
questions.f: An emulsifier like egg yolk coats the droplets so the oil and water cannot separate.

questions.q: Tempura, the light Japanese batter-fry, was introduced by traders from which country?
questions.f: Portuguese missionaries brought the frying technique to Japan in the 1500s.

questions.q: The word 'restaurant' comes from a French word meaning to…?
questions.f: Early Paris 'restaurants' sold restoring broths said to bring strength back to the weary.

questions.q: 'Companion' and 'company' share a Latin root meaning literally 'one who shares…'?
questions.f: From Latin 'com' (with) and 'panis' (bread), a companion is someone you break bread with.

questions.q: The word 'ketchup' originally named a fermented sauce made from…?
questions.f: The name likely comes from Hokkien Chinese 'kê-tsiap', a briny fish or shellfish sauce.

questions.q: The word 'spice' comes from a Latin word 'species' that meant…?
questions.f: Merchants listed valuable spices as special 'kinds' of trade goods.

questions.q: The word 'biscuit' literally means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'bis' (twice) and 'coctus' (cooked); biscuits were baked twice to keep for voyages.

questions.q: The word 'vinegar' literally means…?
questions.f: From French 'vin' (wine) and 'aigre' (sour), since vinegar forms when wine sours.

questions.q: The word 'pretzel' traces back to a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: The looped shape was said to resemble arms folded in prayer.

questions.q: The word 'sugar' traces back through Arabic and Persian to a Sanskrit word meaning…?
questions.f: Sanskrit 'sharkara' described sugar in coarse, gritty crystals.

questions.q: The word 'candy' comes from an Arabic and Persian word 'qand' meaning…?
questions.f: 'Sugar candy' once meant sugar boiled and set into hard crystals.

questions.q: The word 'chocolate' comes from the Aztec 'xocolatl', usually translated as…?
questions.f: The Aztecs drank cacao unsweetened, often frothy and spiced with chili.

questions.q: The word 'tomato' comes from the Aztec 'tomatl', meaning roughly a…?
questions.f: The Spanish carried both the fruit and its Nahuatl name back to Europe.

questions.q: The word 'avocado' was later confused in Spanish with a word meaning…?
questions.f: The Nahuatl 'ahuacatl' shifted to Spanish 'aguacate', close to 'abogado', meaning lawyer.

questions.q: 'Cappuccino' is named because its color resembled the robes of which monks?
questions.f: The brown Capuchin habit matched the shade of coffee softened with a little milk.

questions.q: The word 'espresso' describes coffee that is…?
questions.f: Hot water is forced under pressure through the grounds, making each cup fresh to order.

questions.q: The word 'barbecue' comes from a Caribbean word 'barbacoa' for a…?
questions.f: Spanish explorers borrowed the Taíno word for the raised wooden grill.

questions.q: The word 'lasagne' originally referred to the…?
questions.f: It comes from a Greek and Latin word 'lasanum' for a cooking pot.

questions.q: When pasta is cooked 'al dente', it is…?
questions.f: 'Al dente' is Italian for 'to the tooth', pasta with a slight, pleasant chew.

questions.q: The word 'pasta' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'paste', since pasta begins as a soft dough.

questions.q: In a professional kitchen, 'mise en place' means…?
questions.f: Chefs prep and arrange every ingredient before service so cooking flows smoothly.

questions.q: Vegetables cut 'julienne' are shaped into…?
questions.f: The precise matchstick cut helps vegetables cook quickly and evenly.

questions.q: The knife cut 'brunoise' produces food in the form of…?
questions.f: A brunoise starts from a julienne, then cut crosswise into miniature cubes.

questions.q: The root 'frig' in 'refrigerate' means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'frigus', cold; to refrigerate is literally to make cold again.

questions.q: The root 'coagul' in 'coagulate' means to…?
questions.f: Adding rennet makes milk coagulate, the first step in turning it into cheese.

questions.q: The word 'yogurt' comes from a Turkish word meaning to…?
questions.f: Turkish 'yoğurmak' describes kneading or thickening, just as bacteria thicken milk into yogurt.

questions.q: The word 'cereal' honors Ceres, the Roman goddess of…?
questions.f: Romans prayed to Ceres for good harvests, and her name still tops the breakfast bowl.

questions.q: The fruit name 'nectarine' means a fruit as sweet as…?
questions.f: A nectarine is simply a smooth-skinned peach without the fuzz.

questions.q: The 'cantaloupe' melon is named after an Italian estate whose name means 'wolves…'?
questions.f: Cantalupo, near Rome, is where the melon was first grown in Europe.

questions.q: 'Flour' and 'flower' were once the same word, because flour is the 'flower', or finest part, of the…?
questions.f: Milling separates the fine white 'flower of the meal' from the coarser bran.

questions.q: The root 'gran' in 'granary' and 'granola' means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'granum', grain; a granary stores grain and granola is packed with it.

questions.q: The word 'pasteurize' honors Louis Pasteur, who proved that food spoils because of…?
questions.f: Gently heating milk kills most of these microbes, so it stays fresh far longer.

questions.q: Words like 'sandwich' and 'graham cracker', named after people, are called…?
questions.f: An eponym is a word taken from the name of a real or mythical person.

questions.q: The graham cracker is named after Sylvester Graham, who was a…?
questions.f: Graham preached that plain whole-grain foods led to a healthier, calmer life.

questions.q: In classic French dining, the word 'entrée' originally meant the…?
questions.f: 'Entrée' means 'entrance', so in France it is a starter, not the main course as in the US.

questions.q: Ordering 'à la carte' means choosing dishes…?
questions.f: 'À la carte' is French for 'from the card', letting diners pick and pay per item.

questions.q: A 'table d'hôte' menu offers a meal that is…?
c: A fixed price with set courses
questions.f: 'Table d'hôte' means 'host's table', a complete meal at one set price.

questions.q: The word 'gourmand' describes a person who…?
questions.f: A gourmand relishes eating in quantity, while a gourmet prizes fine quality.

questions.q: A 'gourmet' is distinguished from a 'gourmand' by valuing…?
questions.f: 'Gourmet' once meant a wine merchant's assistant with a finely trained palate.

questions.q: The word 'delicatessen' comes from a German and French word meaning…?
questions.f: A deli was originally a shop selling ready-made 'delicacies'.

questions.q: The wasabi served in most sushi restaurants is often dyed horseradish, not real wasabi.
questions.f: True wasabi is costly and fades fast, so cheaper horseradish paste usually stands in.

questions.q: Cashews and mangoes belong to the same plant family as poison ivy.
questions.f: That is why raw cashew shells contain an irritating oil and must be roasted before eating.

questions.q: The prestigious 'Bocuse d'Or' cooking contest is named after a legendary chef from which country?
questions.f: Paul Bocuse helped launch nouvelle cuisine and founded the contest in 1987.

questions.q: The dish Chicken Marengo was supposedly made to celebrate a victory in which battle?
questions.f: Legend says Napoleon's cook improvised it from whatever he could find after the 1800 fight.

questions.q: Hollandaise, the sauce on eggs Benedict, is an emulsion of egg yolk and…?
questions.f: Warm yolks hold melted butter in a rich, silky suspension seasoned with lemon.

questions.q: Which French 'mother sauce' is a deep brown sauce built on meat stock?
questions.f: Espagnole is the base for many rich gravies and demi-glace.

questions.q: Which pale French 'mother sauce' is a light stock thickened with a blond roux?
questions.f: 'Velouté' means 'velvety', describing its smooth, coating texture.

questions.q: A Russian ballerina on tour, a crisp shell of baked meringue, and a lasting rivalry between two nations point to which dessert?
questions.f: Both Australia and New Zealand still claim they invented it to honor Anna Pavlova.

questions.q: The rich chocolate 'Sachertorte' cake originated in which European city?
questions.f: A famous court battle in Vienna decided who could call their cake the 'Original Sacher-Torte'.

questions.q: The pink-and-yellow checkerboard 'Battenberg' cake is associated with which country?
questions.f: It is said to have been made for a royal wedding linking Britain and the Battenberg family.

questions.q: Beef Stroganoff is named after a wealthy noble family from which country?
questions.f: The dish of beef in a sour-cream sauce first appeared in 19th-century Russian cookbooks.

questions.q: The Caprese salad of tomato, mozzarella, and basil takes its name from which Italian island?
questions.f: Its colors echo the Italian flag, just like the Margherita pizza.

questions.q: Spicy 'Buffalo wings' are named after a city in which US state?
questions.f: They were first served at the Anchor Bar in Buffalo, New York, in 1964.

questions.q: Vitamin C is also known by which chemical name?
questions.f: 'Ascorbic' literally means 'anti-scurvy', the disease it prevents.

questions.q: Which vitamin also goes by the name riboflavin?
questions.f: Riboflavin glows yellow-green and colors the water when you rinse vitamin pills.

questions.q: Cured meats like ham stay pink and safe thanks to a small amount of…?
questions.f: Nitrites block harmful bacteria and lock in the rosy color of cured meat.

questions.q: Browning pure sugar with heat, without any protein, is the process called…?
questions.f: Unlike the Maillard reaction, caramelization needs only sugar and heat.

questions.q: Cornstarch thickens a sauce as its granules swell and burst with heat, a process called…?
questions.f: That is why a sauce suddenly thickens only once it nears a simmer.

questions.q: Fresh cheeses like paneer and ricotta are made by curdling hot milk with an…?
questions.f: A splash of lemon juice or vinegar makes the milk proteins clump instantly.

questions.q: The stretching-and-stacking step named 'cheddaring' is used to make which cheese?
questions.f: Cheddaring presses out whey and gives the cheese its firm, dense body.

questions.q: The blue veins in Stilton and Roquefort come from a mold of which genus?
questions.f: It is a cousin of the mold that gave us the antibiotic penicillin.

questions.q: The fiery curry 'vindaloo' blends Portuguese and local cooking from which country?
questions.f: It grew in Goa from a Portuguese dish of meat in wine and garlic.

questions.q: Chili heat is now measured in labs by machines instead of tasters, using a method called…?
questions.f: High-performance liquid chromatography measures capsaicin far more precisely than a tongue can.

questions.q: A lack of which mineral causes goiter, a swelling of the thyroid gland?
questions.f: Adding iodine to table salt has nearly wiped out goiter in many countries.

questions.q: The childhood bone disease rickets is caused by a shortage of which vitamin?
questions.f: Sunlight and fortified milk both help the body make and get enough vitamin D.

questions.q: Which is generally the world's most expensive nut, grown mainly in Australia and Hawaii?
questions.f: Macadamia trees take years to bear, and the shells are famously hard to crack.

questions.q: An enzyme called papain, taken from which fruit, is used to tenderize meat?
questions.f: Papain breaks down tough muscle proteins, softening the meat before cooking.

questions.q: A chemist's unwashed hands in 1879, a name hinting at 'sugar', and the pink packet on diner tables point to which sweetener?
questions.f: Constantin Fahlberg noticed his fingers tasted sweet after a day in the lab.

questions.q: The classic Reuben sandwich stacks corned beef, Swiss cheese, sauerkraut, and which dressing?
questions.f: The whole sandwich is then grilled until the cheese melts and the bread crisps.

questions.q: Studies suggest which food is the most shoplifted item in the world?
questions.f: Its high value and easy resale make cheese a surprisingly common target for thieves.

questions.q: A price once higher than gold, a tiny island traded for Manhattan, and warm eggnog all point to which spice?
questions.f: The Dutch swapped the nutmeg island of Run for New York's Manhattan in 1667.

questions.q: In the Columbian Exchange, the potato went to Europe while which grain traveled to the Americas?
questions.f: Europeans brought wheat, cattle, and sugar cane across the Atlantic in return.

questions.q: Japanese 'dashi' broth is made from kelp and flakes of dried, smoked…?
questions.f: The kelp and bonito each add glutamates and inosinates that make umami soar.

questions.q: Which common fruit carries its seeds on the outside rather than hidden inside?
questions.f: Each tiny 'seed' on a strawberry is really a separate small fruit of its own.

questions.q: The real wasabi plant belongs to the same family as which vegetables?
questions.f: Its sharp bite comes from the same kind of compounds found in mustard and horseradish.

questions.q: The 'glycemic index' of a food measures how quickly it raises your…?
questions.f: Slow-digesting, low-GI foods give steadier energy than a sugary snack.

questions.q: The dish of melted cheese dipped with bread cubes, 'fondue', comes from which country?
questions.f: 'Fondue' comes from the French word for 'melted'.

questions.q: 'Raclette', both a cheese and a dish scraped off as it melts, comes from which region?
questions.f: 'Raclette' comes from a French word meaning 'to scrape'.

questions.q: The tangy, deep-red spice 'sumac' adds a lemony sourness to which cuisine?
questions.f: Ground sumac is a key part of the spice blend called za'atar.

questions.q: The tannins in strong tea and unripe fruit create which sensation in the mouth?
questions.f: Tannins bind to proteins in your saliva, which is what makes your mouth feel dry.

questions.q: The four fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and…?
questions.f: Because they are stored in body fat, taking too much of them can be harmful.

questions.q: Which country grows the most cocoa beans in the world?
questions.f: West Africa produces most of the world's cocoa, though it eats very little chocolate.

questions.q: The Middle Eastern sweet 'halva' is most often made from sesame paste and…?
questions.f: Halva can be crumbly from sesame or gel-like when made from flour and syrup.

questions.q: Which serious illness can grow in improperly home-canned foods?
questions.f: The bacterium thrives without air, so sealed low-acid jars are canned with great care.

questions.q: The French dish 'coq au vin' translates literally as…?
questions.f: Slow simmering turns a tough old rooster tender and flavorful.

questions.q: The hairy tropical fruit 'rambutan' takes its name from a Malay word meaning…?
questions.f: Its soft, spiky covering does look a bit like a tuft of red hair.

questions.q: The word 'cauliflower' combines a word for cabbage with the word…?
questions.f: So a cauliflower is literally the 'cabbage flower', its unopened white buds.

questions.q: The word 'zucchini' means, in Italian, a little…?
questions.f: From 'zucca', gourd or squash; the British call the same vegetable a courgette.

questions.q: The words 'broth' and 'brew' share an ancient root meaning to…?
questions.f: Both begin with heating water until it seethes and bubbles.

questions.q: The word 'toast' comes from a Latin word meaning to…?
questions.f: From 'torrere', to dry with heat, the same root as 'torrid'.

questions.q: The word 'raisin' comes from a Latin word meaning a…?
questions.f: From 'racemus', a bunch of grapes, since raisins are simply dried grapes.

questions.q: The 'muscat' grape and 'muscatel' wine take their name from a word for…?
questions.f: The grapes were named for their heavy, musky perfume.

questions.q: The word 'pomegranate' means an apple full of…?
questions.f: From Latin 'pomum granatum', the 'seeded apple'.

questions.q: In French, potato is 'pomme de terre', which literally means apple of the…?
questions.f: Many languages named the strange new tuber after a more familiar fruit.

questions.q: The word 'chowder' comes from a French word 'chaudière' for a…?
questions.f: Fishermen tossed the day's catch into one big pot to make the soup.

questions.q: The word 'casserole' originally referred to the…?
questions.f: From a French word for a small pan; the food later took the container's name.

questions.q: An 'aperitif' drink is named from a Latin word meaning to…?
questions.f: It is meant to 'open' the appetite before a meal begins.

questions.q: A 'digestif', taken after a meal, is meant to aid…?
questions.f: It pairs with the aperitif that opens the meal at the other end.

questions.q: The word 'relish' originally meant a…?
questions.f: From an Old French word for aftertaste, it now names a tangy condiment.

questions.q: The word 'chutney' comes from a Hindi word meaning to…?
questions.f: From 'chatni', linked to 'chatna', to lick, because the relish is so tasty.

questions.q: The word 'biryani' comes from a Persian word meaning to…?
questions.f: The rice and spices are often fried before being layered and steamed with meat.

questions.q: A dish called 'pilaf' or 'pilau' is made mainly of seasoned…?
questions.f: The rice is toasted in fat, then simmered in flavorful stock.

questions.q: The word 'yeast' comes from an ancient root meaning to…?
questions.f: Fittingly, active yeast makes dough and brewing liquids froth and bubble.

questions.q: The word 'flavor' traces back through French to a Latin word linked to…?
questions.f: Much of what we call flavor is really aroma sensed by the nose.

questions.q: The word 'aroma' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Only later did 'aroma' come to mean any pleasant smell.

questions.q: A 'savory' flavor is one that is…?
questions.f: Savory dishes are the opposite of sweet ones, rich in salt and umami.

questions.q: A person's 'palate' refers to their sense of…?
questions.f: The palate is literally the roof of the mouth, long thought to be where taste lived.

questions.q: The root 'gust', in 'gustatory' and 'disgust', means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'gustare', to taste; 'disgust' is literally 'bad taste'.

questions.q: The 'olfactory' sense, which shapes how food tastes, is the sense of…?
questions.f: Block your nose and a jellybean loses most of its flavor, leaving only sweetness.

questions.q: An old-fashioned word, a 'viand', means an item of…?
questions.f: From Latin 'vivenda', things needed for living.

questions.q: The old word 'victuals', said as 'vittles', means…?
questions.f: It shares its root with 'victual' and even 'vital', all about sustaining life.

questions.q: When travelers pack 'provisions', they are carrying…?
questions.f: To 'provide' and 'provision' both mean to look ahead and prepare.

questions.q: A 'larder' in an old house was a cool room for storing…?
questions.f: It was named for lard, the fat and cured meats once kept there.

questions.q: The word 'pantry' comes from a French word for…?
questions.f: From 'pain', bread; the pantry was first where the household bread was kept.

questions.q: A household 'butler' was originally the servant in charge of the…?
questions.f: 'Butler' comes from the same word as 'bottle'.

questions.q: A 'steward' of a great house originally kept watch over the…?
questions.f: 'Steward' comes from 'sty-ward', the keeper of the hall and its provisions.

questions.q: In a baked Alaska, ice cream survives the hot oven because its meringue coat is packed with…?
questions.f: Air is a poor conductor of heat, so the whipped meringue shields the ice cream.

questions.q: The kitchen hierarchy of head chef, sous chef, and station cooks is a system called…?
questions.f: Escoffier borrowed the idea from the army, giving each cook one clear post.

questions.q: In a classic kitchen brigade, the 'garde manger' is responsible for…?
questions.f: The name means 'keeper of the food', from the days of cold larders.

questions.q: A 'chiffonade' of basil is a cut whose French name literally means made of…?
questions.f: The leaves are stacked, rolled, and sliced into fine shreds like torn cloth.

questions.q: To 'braise' food comes from a French word for…?
questions.f: From 'braise', embers; braising means searing then simmering in a covered pot.

questions.q: The word 'poach', as in a poached egg, comes from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: The set white forms a little pouch around the yolk.

questions.q: A dish served 'au gratin' is finished with a…?
questions.f: 'Gratin' comes from a French word meaning to scrape, for the crust scraped from the dish.

questions.q: The word 'roux', for the flour-and-butter thickener, comes from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: The longer you cook a roux, the redder-brown and nuttier it becomes.

questions.q: A clear consomme is traditionally clarified using a 'raft' made from…?
questions.f: As the egg white cooks it rises, trapping every cloudy particle in a floating mat.

questions.q: The French sauce 'beurre blanc' has a name meaning…?
questions.f: It is butter whisked into a reduction of wine and shallots until silky.

questions.q: The word 'wagyu', for the prized Japanese beef, literally means…?
questions.f: 'Wa' means Japanese and 'gyu' means cattle, so wagyu is any Japanese breed.

questions.q: In beef, the fine white flecks of fat inside the muscle are called…?
questions.f: Marbling melts as the steak cooks, basting the meat from the inside.

questions.q: The Chinese dumpling name 'wonton' is often translated as swallowing a…?
questions.f: The thin, ruffled wrappers really do float in broth like little clouds.

questions.q: The Cantonese term 'dim sum' is usually translated as…?
questions.f: The little dishes are meant to touch the heart rather than fill the stomach.

questions.q: The Japanese word 'teriyaki' combines words meaning grill and…?
questions.f: The sugary glaze is brushed on so the finished dish gleams.

questions.q: The Japanese snack name 'edamame' literally means…?
questions.f: The soybeans were traditionally sold and steamed still attached to the branch.

questions.q: The Korean dish name 'bibimbap' literally means…?
questions.f: Everything is stirred together at the table, mixing rice, vegetables, and egg.

questions.q: The Korean dish name 'bulgogi' literally means…?
questions.f: The thin marinated slices are cooked fast over a fierce flame.

questions.q: Spanish 'tapas' take their name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: One story says a slice of bread was laid over a glass as a lid, then topped with food.

questions.q: An Italian 'antipasto' course takes its name from words meaning…?
questions.f: 'Pasto' means meal, so antipasto comes before it, unrelated to pasta.

questions.q: The Italian dish 'bruschetta' takes its name from a verb meaning to…?
questions.f: The bread is charred over embers first, which is where the name comes from.

questions.q: The folded pizza called a 'calzone' takes its name from an Italian word for a…?
questions.f: The stuffed, folded shape reminded Italians of a rolled-up trouser leg.

questions.q: The pastry called an 'eclair' takes its name from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: One theory says it is eaten in a flash, another that its glaze gleams like lightning.

questions.q: The Austrian pastry 'strudel' takes its name from a German word meaning…?
questions.f: Slice it open and the coiled layers look just like a swirling eddy.

questions.q: The word 'souffle' comes from a French verb meaning to…?
questions.f: Trapped air in the whipped egg whites expands in the oven and lifts the dish.

questions.q: The word 'bagel' comes from a Yiddish word meaning a…?
questions.f: From 'beygl', related to a German word for a ring or bow.

questions.q: Tiny French cakes called 'petits fours' are named for being baked in a…?
questions.f: 'Four' means oven; the little cakes went in as the big brick oven cooled.

questions.q: The tea grade 'orange pekoe' refers to the…?
c: Size and style of the leaf
questions.f: Despite the name, orange pekoe tea contains no orange at all.

questions.q: The tea name 'oolong' is usually translated as…?
questions.f: Oolong is partly oxidized, sitting between green and black tea.

questions.q: Chocolate is 'tempered' by carefully controlling the crystals of its…?
questions.f: Correct tempering is what gives a chocolate bar its glossy shine and clean snap.

questions.q: The dull white film that appears on old chocolate is called…?
questions.f: Bloom is just fat or sugar migrating to the surface, and it is harmless to eat.

questions.q: The sugar content of fruit juice and syrup is commonly measured on the…?
questions.f: Growers test grapes and melons with a refractometer that reads degrees Brix.

questions.q: Roughly how many of the twenty amino acids are 'essential', meaning we must eat them?
questions.f: A 'complete' protein such as egg or quinoa supplies all nine at once.

questions.q: Oily fish such as mackerel and sardines are especially rich in…?
questions.f: The fish get their omega-3s from the algae at the base of the ocean food web.

questions.q: Salting sliced aubergine draws out water by osmosis.
questions.f: Salt outside the cells pulls water across their walls, firming and seasoning the flesh.

questions.q: A fur trader watching Inuit freeze fish in seconds, a surname that splits into a bird and an eye, and a familiar box of frozen peas point to which inventor?
questions.f: Birdseye pioneered flash-freezing, which locks in flavor by making tiny ice crystals.

questions.q: A rescued French silk industry, swan-neck flasks that sank the idea of life from nothing, and a rabies vaccine point to which scientist?
questions.f: The gentle heating that keeps milk fresh, pasteurization, is named after him.

questions.q: A prize from Napoleon III for cheap army rations, a pearly sheen that earned it a Greek name, and old laws forcing it to be sold white point to which food?
questions.f: 'Margarine' comes from Greek 'margarites', pearl, for the shimmer of its first crystals.

questions.q: A health sanitarium in Battle Creek, a batch of forgotten boiled grain rolled thin, and a feud with a sugar-loving brother point to which man?
questions.f: The accident of stale, rolled wheat led to the first breakfast flakes.

questions.q: A wounded pharmacist's search for a tonic, a bookkeeper's flowing script that became a logo, and a formula once locked in a bank vault point to which drink?
questions.f: Its early recipe drew flavor from the kola nut and the coca leaf.

questions.q: A model town with its own amusement park, a fortune first built on caramels, and a lucky cancelled Titanic ticket point to which chocolate maker?
questions.f: Hershey built a whole Pennsylvania town, complete with a free school for orphans.

questions.q: Candy-coated chocolate spotted with soldiers in the Spanish Civil War and two surnames joined by an ampersand point to which sweet?
questions.f: The letters stand for Mars and Murrie; the shell famously melts in your mouth, not your hand.

questions.q: A 1937 naming contest, a canned meat that flooded the Pacific in wartime, and a Monty Python sketch that renamed junk email point to which product?
questions.f: Hawaii still eats more of it per person than anywhere else in the US.

questions.q: A leftover from beer brewing, a homegrown reply after WWI cut off a British import, and a jingle about 'happy little' children point to which spread?
questions.f: Vegemite is a dark, salty paste made from spent brewer's yeast.

questions.q: A Paris confectioner, food sealed in champagne bottles and boiled, and a prize from an emperor who said armies march on their stomachs point to which inventor?
questions.f: Appert's sealed-and-heated jars were the birth of modern canning.

questions.q: A prisoner of war fed only potatoes, guarded fields left unguarded at night on purpose, and a French dish that still bears his name point to which man?
questions.f: Parmentier's clever tricks convinced wary French people the potato was safe and good.

questions.q: A 12-year-old enslaved boy on an Indian Ocean island, a quick pinch of a toothpick-thin flower, and the reason your ice cream isn't rare point to which person?
questions.f: Albius devised hand-pollination in 1841, making vanilla farming possible worldwide.

questions.q: A Spanish seaside restaurant open only half the year, juice turned into bursting spheres, and a waiting list a million names long point to which chef?
questions.f: His restaurant elBulli made 'molecular gastronomy' famous before closing in 2011.

questions.q: An army field ration bearing his initial, a Seven Countries study of heart disease, and the diet named for the Mediterranean point to which scientist?
questions.f: The wartime 'K-ration' is widely said to carry the K of Ancel Keys.

questions.q: A Polish-born biochemist, a coined word blending 'vital' with a nitrogen compound, and the hunt for what cured beriberi point to which scientist?
questions.f: Funk's 1912 term 'vitamine' gave us the everyday word 'vitamin'.

questions.q: A ship's surgeon's 1747 trial dividing sick sailors into groups, and citrus beating cider and vinegar point to which physician?
questions.f: Lind's test, an early controlled experiment, showed citrus cures scurvy.

questions.q: A formerly enslaved scientist, hundreds of uses for a humble legume to rescue worn-out soil, and a myth crediting him with peanut butter point to which man?
questions.f: Carver promoted peanuts and sweet potatoes to restore soil drained by cotton.

questions.q: Short, sturdy rust-resistant wheat bred in Mexico, a rare Nobel Peace Prize for a scientist, and credit for saving perhaps a billion lives point to whom?
questions.f: Borlaug is called the father of the Green Revolution in farming.

questions.q: Pulling fertilizer out of thin air, a process that now feeds roughly half the planet, and a darker wartime legacy point to which chemist?
questions.f: The Haber process turns nitrogen from the air into the fertilizer that grows our crops.

questions.q: The 'father of the fertilizer industry', a concentrated beef extract sold as a cube, and the law of the minimum point to which chemist?
questions.f: Liebig's beef extract became the famous Oxo stock cube.

questions.q: Towering edible centerpieces of spun sugar, cooking for a tsar and for kings, and the title 'king of chefs and chef of kings' point to which cook?
questions.f: Carême was among the first to organize the classic French mother sauces.

questions.q: A tall American who once worked in wartime intelligence, a cookbook that demystified boeuf bourguignon, and a beloved TV kitchen point to which cook?
questions.f: Her show 'The French Chef' taught a generation of Americans to cook French food.

questions.q: A friendly signature on flour-company replies, a soothing radio voice, and a face that was painted but never truly existed point to which 'person'?
questions.f: Betty Crocker was invented in 1921 by a milling company as a trusted brand persona.

questions.q: A Fourth of July rush at a Tijuana restaurant, a tableside toss of romaine from dwindling supplies, and a dish wrongly linked to a Roman point to which chef?
questions.f: The Caesar salad is named for restaurateur Caesar Cardini, not the emperor.

questions.q: A late-night raid on a Hollywood restaurant's icebox, a chopped jumble of leftovers, and a salad named for the owner point to which dish?
questions.f: Bob Cobb of the Brown Derby is said to have thrown it together after hours.

questions.q: A maitre d' nicknamed for a grand New York hotel, an 1896 mix of apple, celery, and mayonnaise, and later a handful of walnuts point to which salad?
questions.f: It was created by Oscar Tschirky, 'Oscar of the Waldorf', for the hotel's opening.

questions.q: A Kentucky roadside gas-station cafe, an honorary title with no real army, and eleven herbs and spices point to which man?
questions.f: Kentucky's governor made Sanders an honorary 'colonel' for his cooking.

questions.q: A milkshake-mixer salesman, two brothers in San Bernardino with a speedy service system, and golden arches point to which businessman?
questions.f: Kroc bought out the McDonald brothers and grew the chain worldwide.

questions.q: A postwar noodle stall, oil-flash-drying that lets noodles revive in hot water, and even a cup you eat straight from point to which inventor?
questions.f: Ando invented instant ramen in 1958 and cup noodles in 1971.

questions.q: A machine left running by accident over a weekend in Bern, a smoothing process called conching, and a Swiss name on truffle boxes point to which chocolatier?
questions.f: Lindt's conching machine gave chocolate its melt-in-the-mouth smoothness.

questions.q: A German-born Swiss pharmacist, an 1867 milk food credited with saving a sick baby, and a little bird's-nest logo point to which founder?
questions.f: His surname means 'little nest', which is why a nest appears on the logo.

questions.q: A cold soup older than the tomato it now holds, an Andalusian laborer's lunch of stale bread and oil, and a name meaning 'soaked' point to which dish?
questions.f: Before tomatoes reached Europe, gazpacho was just bread, garlic, oil, and vinegar.

questions.q: A chilled potato-and-leek soup born not in France but at a New York hotel, a chef's memory of his mother's cooking, and a name from a spa town point to which dish?
questions.f: Chef Louis Diat created it at the Ritz-Carlton, naming it for nearby Vichy.

questions.q: A soup once soured with fermented hogweed, a UNESCO cultural listing tied to Ukraine, and a deep beet-red bowl point to which dish?
questions.f: Its ruby color comes from beetroot, added in most modern recipes.

questions.q: Hungarian cattle-herders whose very name the dish borrows, dried red peppers stirred through, and a hearty paprika stew point to which food?
questions.f: 'Gulyás' means herdsman, the cowboys of the Hungarian plains who first made it.

questions.q: Soybeans fermented until they pull into slimy threads, a bacterium named for hay, and a breakfast that divides even Japan point to which food?
questions.f: The sticky strands are prized, and the bacterium behind it is Bacillus subtilis.

questions.q: A shark whose fresh flesh is toxic, months of burial and hanging to cure it, and a dish Icelanders dare tourists to try point to which food?
questions.f: Curing breaks down the toxins that make fresh Greenland shark unsafe to eat.

questions.q: An egg cured for weeks in clay, ash, and lime, a jelly-black translucent look, and a name suggesting an age it doesn't really have point to which food?
questions.f: The alkaline cure transforms the egg in weeks, not the centuries its name suggests.

questions.q: A Baltic herring fermented inside a bulging tin, a stench so fierce it is opened outdoors, and a Swedish August tradition point to which food?
questions.f: The can keeps fermenting on the shelf, which is why it bulges before opening.

questions.q: Dried cod revived in a lye bath, a jelly-textured Nordic Christmas dish, and Scandinavian immigrant church suppers point to which food?
questions.f: 'Lutefisk' means 'lye fish', for the alkaline soak that turns it gelatinous.

questions.q: Salmon once buried in the sand to cure, a name meaning 'buried fish', and a modern dill-and-salt version point to which dish?
questions.f: 'Grav' means grave; fishermen once fermented salmon in pits above the tide line.

questions.q: A Mexican sauce that can carry thirty ingredients, including chile and chocolate, a name that simply means 'sauce', and convent-kitchen legends in Puebla point to which dish?
questions.f: From Nahuatl 'molli', sauce; mole poblano is its most famous version.

questions.q: Dried meat pounded with fat and berries, a food that fueled polar expeditions, and a Cree word for 'manufactured grease' point to which food?
questions.f: Its mix of fat and protein packs huge energy into a light, long-lasting cake.

questions.q: A jelly set firm with starch and sugar, a fragrance of rosewater under powdered sugar, and a snowy Narnia temptation point to which sweet?
questions.f: Its Turkish name, 'lokum', comes from an Arabic word for 'morsel'.

questions.q: A confection once whipped from the sap of a wetland plant, a name that is literally that plant's, and a stick over a campfire point to which treat?
questions.f: Early marshmallows really used mucilage from the marsh-mallow plant's root.

questions.q: A sugared confection named after a 17th-century French diplomat, a New Orleans version made with pecans, and a cook's happy accident point to which sweet?
questions.f: It is said to be named for the Marechal du Plessis-Praslin, whose cook made it.

questions.q: No fire ever touches the fish, an acid unravels its proteins until they turn white, and a June national holiday point to which dish?
questions.f: Peru so loves ceviche that it celebrates a national ceviche day each June.

questions.q: A protein rendered from boiled bones and skin, the wobble in a molded dessert, and the reason gummy bears aren't vegetarian point to which substance?
questions.f: Gelatin is cooked-down collagen, the body's most abundant protein.

questions.q: The main protein of milk, the solid curd left when milk sours, and an old-fashioned wood glue and button plastic point to which substance?
questions.f: Casein plastic, called galalith, once made buttons and jewelry.

questions.q: The watery liquid drained off in cheesemaking, the 'curds and ___' of a nursery rhyme, and a powder scooped by bodybuilders point to which byproduct?
questions.f: Once a waste product, whey is now a valuable high-protein powder.

questions.q: An emulsifier hiding in egg yolks and soybeans, the reason chocolate flows smoothly, and the secret to stable mayonnaise point to which substance?
questions.f: Lecithin's molecules grab both oil and water, keeping mixtures from separating.

questions.q: A gelling agent pulled from red seaweed, the jelly in a scientist's petri dish, and a vegetarian stand-in for animal gelatin point to which substance?
questions.f: Agar sets firmer than gelatin and stays solid even at room temperature.

questions.q: A thickener made by feeding sugar to bacteria, the glue that binds gluten-free bread, and a word on many ice-cream labels point to which additive?
questions.f: It is named after the bacterium Xanthomonas that ferments it into being.

questions.q: A red-orange dye from the seeds of the achiote tree, the reason many cheddars look orange, and a colorant in lipstick point to which additive?
questions.f: Cheddar is naturally pale; annatto gives it that familiar orange color.

questions.q: The single molecule behind most 'vanilla' flavor, a compound once pulled from wood-pulp waste, and the frosting on cheap cakes point to which flavoring?
questions.f: Most vanilla flavor today is synthetic vanillin, not from the costly orchid pod.

questions.q: The oil that gives cloves their punch, a numbing scent of the dentist's office, and a spice in mulled cider point to which compound?
questions.f: Eugenol is used in dentistry both to numb and to soothe sore teeth.

questions.q: A crystal from mint that fools a cold-sensing nerve, a rub for a stuffy nose, and after-dinner sweets point to which compound?
questions.f: Menthol triggers the TRPM8 receptor, the same one that senses actual cold.

questions.q: The compound behind black pepper's bite, a molecule that helps the body absorb turmeric's curcumin, and the sneeze in a pepper mill point to which substance?
questions.f: Piperine can boost curcumin absorption many times over.

questions.q: A compound that doesn't exist until you crush the clove, the source of garlic's smell and folk-medicine fame, and an enzyme reaction point to which substance?
questions.f: Crushing garlic lets an enzyme build allicin, which fades again as it cooks.

questions.q: The pungent compound in fresh ginger, a molecule that grows even hotter when the root is dried, and a settler of upset stomachs point to which substance?
questions.f: Drying turns gingerol into shogaol, which tastes noticeably spicier.

questions.q: An amino acid blamed for holiday drowsiness, a building block of the mood chemical serotonin, and a share of turkey no greater than chicken's point to which substance?
questions.f: The post-feast sleepiness owes far more to the huge meal than to the turkey itself.

questions.q: A bitter alkaloid a plant makes to poison insects, the world's most used stimulant, and a shared ingredient of coffee, tea, and cacao point to which compound?
questions.f: Plants evolved caffeine as a pesticide, but it wakes humans up instead.

questions.q: Three crimson threads from each flower, a spice once forge-proofed against fakes on pain of death, and a weight that can outprice gold point to which spice?
questions.f: It takes many thousands of hand-picked crocus flowers to make a single kilogram.

questions.q: A northern Italian city that lends its name to both a dry-cured ham and a hard grating cheese, protected-origin laws, and violet perfume history point to which place?
questions.f: Only ham from this area may be sold as true Prosciutto di Parma.

questions.q: An English village beside a dramatic limestone gorge, caves once used to ripen a cheese, and a name now copied worldwide point to which place?
questions.f: The cool, damp gorge caves were ideal for aging the cheese named after the village.

questions.q: A Dutch market town with a famous weigh-house for trading cheese, a waxed rind, and a name that labels the cheese but not where it must be made point to which place?
questions.f: 'Gouda' is a style, so it can legally be made almost anywhere in the world.

questions.q: A Burgundian city, a sharp condiment made with verjuice instead of vinegar, and a name now used generically for a mustard style point to which place?
questions.f: Dijon mustard's smooth heat comes from using sour grape juice, or verjuice.

questions.q: An Italian city nicknamed 'the fat one' for its rich cooking, a meat sauce the world calls by its name, and a pink mortadella sausage point to which place?
questions.f: 'Bologna la grassa', the fat, is the home of true ragu alla bolognese.

questions.q: A Himalayan hill town, a prized 'champagne of teas' picked in spring flushes, and a toy railway that climbs to it point to which place?
questions.f: Its high altitude and cool mist give Darjeeling tea a delicate, floral flavor.

questions.q: A Normandy village, a soft bloomy cheese said to be perfected by a farmer's wife sheltering a priest, and a round wooden box point to which cheese?
questions.f: Marie Harel is traditionally credited with perfecting Camembert in the 1790s.

questions.q: A region east of Paris, a soft cheese crowned 'king of cheeses' at an 1815 diplomatic congress, and a white bloomy rind point to which cheese?
questions.f: At the Congress of Vienna, Brie was voted the finest cheese by the diplomats.

questions.q: A German city on the river Main, a thin smoked sausage that carried its name abroad, and a rival claim from Vienna point to which namesake city?
questions.f: The frankfurter sausage lent its name to the American hot dog.

questions.q: An Italian port city, a basil sauce crushed in a mortar, and a namesake salami point to which place?
questions.f: Pesto alla genovese comes from Genoa, capital of the Liguria region.

questions.q: The capital of French Guiana, a ground red pepper that shares its name, and a former prison colony nearby point to which place?
questions.f: Cayenne pepper is named after the region, though it is now grown around the world.

questions.q: A city in the Mexican state of Veracruz, a popular chili named after it though grown elsewhere, and a state-capital status point to which place?
questions.f: The jalapeno takes its name from Xalapa (Jalapa), where it was once chiefly grown.

questions.q: A Spanish city, bitter oranges too sour to eat raw, and the classic British breakfast marmalade point to which place?
questions.f: Seville oranges are prized precisely for the sharp bitterness that suits marmalade.

questions.q: An English town legally protected for its hand-raised pork pies, a famous blue cheese made nearby, and old fox-hunting fame point to which town?
questions.f: Only pies made around Melton Mowbray may use that name in the UK.

questions.q: A Thai coastal town's name, a rooster on a green-capped bottle made by a Vietnamese refugee, and a chili-garlic squeeze point to which sauce?
questions.f: David Tran's Huy Fong sauce is named after the town of Si Racha in Thailand.

questions.q: A fiery paste of roasted chilies and caraway, a staple pounded up across Tunisia, and a tube squeezed into couscous point to which condiment?
questions.f: Harissa is often called the national condiment of Tunisia.

questions.q: A noodle soup simmered from charred onion and star anise, a name perhaps echoing a French 'pot on the fire', and Hanoi street stalls point to which dish?
questions.f: One theory links pho to the French pot-au-feu brought during colonial times.

questions.q: Wheat noodles brought from China, an alkaline salt that makes them springy and yellow, and styles from miso to tonkotsu point to which dish?
questions.f: The alkaline water, called kansui, gives ramen noodles their distinctive bite.

questions.q: Noodles milled from a seed that is not a true grain, a New Year's Eve tradition for long life, and a nutty gray strand point to which food?
questions.f: Soba is made from buckwheat, which is related to rhubarb, not to wheat.

questions.q: A Quebec dish said to be named from slang for 'a mess', fresh cheese curds that squeak, and hot gravy over fries point to which food?
questions.f: The dish began in rural Quebec in the 1950s and is now a Canadian icon.

questions.q: A watery rice porridge eaten across Asia for the sick, a breakfast topped with pickles or pork, and a name from a Tamil word point to which dish?
questions.f: 'Congee' comes through Portuguese from the Tamil word 'kanji'.

questions.q: A Southern US breakfast of ground hominy, a dish rooted in Native American treated maize, and a partner to shrimp point to which food?
questions.f: Hominy is corn soaked in an alkali, the same nixtamalization used for tortillas.

questions.q: Tiny rolled balls of steamed semolina, a Berber staple of North Africa, and a shared UNESCO heritage listing point to which food?
questions.f: Couscous is rolled by hand from moistened durum wheat and steamed over a stew.

questions.q: A spongy sour flatbread that doubles as plate and spoon, a batter fermented from the tiny grain teff, and Ethiopian communal dining point to which food?
questions.f: Diners tear off pieces of injera to scoop up stews piled on top of it.

questions.q: A crisp South Indian crepe from a fermented rice-and-lentil batter, a spiced potato filling, and a giant version longer than the table point to which dish?
questions.f: The overnight fermentation gives a dosa its lacy crispness and tang.

questions.q: A corn-dough parcel steamed in a leaf wrapper, an ancient Mesoamerican portable meal, and a Christmas gathering in Mexico point to which food?
questions.f: Families still gather for a 'tamalada' to make hundreds of tamales together.

questions.q: A griddled corn cake split and stuffed like a pocket, a daily bread of Venezuela and Colombia, and a pre-Columbian maize origin point to which food?
questions.f: Arepas were being made long before Europeans arrived in South America.

questions.q: A dense German Christmas loaf shaped to suggest a swaddled infant, a thick blanket of powdered sugar, and hidden marzipan point to which food?
questions.f: The fold of the loaf is said to represent the baby Jesus in swaddling clothes.

questions.q: A tall domed sweet bread from Milan, a legend of a baker's helper named Toni, and candied fruit at Christmas point to which food?
questions.f: One legend says 'pan de Toni', Toni's bread, gave panettone its name.

questions.q: A loaf whose length and weight are fixed by French law, a crackly crust from steam-injected ovens, and a 2022 UNESCO listing point to which bread?
questions.f: French tradition sets the classic baguette at about 250 grams and 65 centimeters.

questions.q: A dense black rye baked up to a day at low heat, a dark color from slow browning rather than cocoa, and a blunt old German name point to which bread?
questions.f: The long, gentle bake caramelizes the bread's own sugars to near-black.

questions.q: A flat unleavened bread baked in under 18 minutes so it cannot rise, a symbol of a hurried exodus, and crumbs for soup balls point to which food?
questions.f: During Passover, matzo recalls the flight from Egypt with no time for dough to rise.

questions.q: Which vitamin comes almost entirely from animal foods, making it the one vegans most need to supplement?
questions.f: B12 is made by bacteria, and plants simply do not store it the way animal foods do.

questions.q: Which country eats the most instant noodles in total each year?
questions.f: China and Hong Kong together get through more than 40 billion servings a year.

questions.q: Which spice is the most traded in the world by volume?
questions.f: Black pepper alone accounts for a fifth of the world's whole spice trade.

questions.q: Which of these is a true botanical nut, not a drupe seed or a legume?
questions.f: Hazelnuts, chestnuts, and acorns are true nuts; almonds and cashews are seeds of drupes.

questions.q: One food Calorie is the heat needed to raise a kilogram of water by how much?
questions.f: The food 'Calorie' is really a kilocalorie, a thousand of the tiny science calories.

questions.q: The root 'sacchar', as in 'saccharin', means…?
questions.f: From Greek 'sakkharon', also giving 'saccharide', the science word for a sugar.

questions.q: An 'oenophile' is a devoted lover of…?
questions.f: From Greek 'oinos', wine, also the root of 'oenology', the study of winemaking.

questions.q: A 'turophile' is a passionate lover of…?
questions.f: From Greek 'tyros', cheese, the same root behind the amino acid tyrosine.

questions.q: The amino acid 'tyrosine' takes its name from the Greek word for…?
questions.f: It was first isolated from the protein in cheese back in 1846.

questions.q: The root 'ov', as in 'ovum' and 'oval', relates to…?
questions.f: From Latin 'ovum', egg, which is why an egg shape is called oval.

questions.q: The root 'lip', as in 'lipid', means…?
questions.f: From Greek 'lipos', fat; lipids include the oils and butter in our food.

questions.q: The word 'gluten' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Gluten really is the gluey protein network that makes bread dough stretchy.

questions.q: The word 'protein' comes from a Greek word 'proteios' meaning…?
questions.f: A chemist chose the name in 1838 to stress how essential proteins are to life.

questions.q: The '-amine' in the coined word 'vitamin' originally referred to a type of…?
questions.f: The final 'e' was dropped once scientists found not all vitamins are amines.

questions.q: The word 'carbohydrate' literally means carbon combined with…?
questions.f: Early chemists saw these molecules had hydrogen and oxygen in water's 2-to-1 ratio.

questions.q: The word 'sirloin' comes from an Old French term meaning…?
questions.f: The tale that a king knighted the cut 'Sir Loin' is a fun but false legend.

questions.q: The words 'porridge' and 'pottage' both come from a word for food cooked in a…?
questions.f: Pottage was the everyday thick stew simmered in the family cooking pot.

questions.q: The word 'sushi' actually describes the seasoned…?
questions.f: Sushi first meant sour rice used to preserve fish, and the name stuck to the rice.

questions.q: The word 'sashimi' literally means 'pierced…'?
questions.f: One theory says fins were once pinned to the slices to show which fish it was.

questions.q: The word 'tofu' comes from Chinese words meaning 'bean' plus…?
questions.f: Tofu is literally curdled bean milk, pressed into blocks much like cheese.

questions.q: The word 'curry' likely comes from the Tamil word 'kari', meaning…?
questions.f: There is no single 'curry powder' in India; the word describes a saucy dish.

questions.q: The words 'sherbet', 'sorbet', and 'syrup' all trace to an Arabic word meaning to…?
questions.f: They descend from 'shariba', to drink, since all began as sweet beverages.

questions.q: In 'artichoke', from Arabic 'al-kharshuf', the 'al-' part means…?
questions.f: That same Arabic 'al' hides inside 'alcohol', 'algebra', and 'apricot'.

questions.q: The word 'apricot' shares a root with 'precocious', both pointing to ripening…?
questions.f: The apricot ripens earlier in the year than the peach it resembles.

questions.q: 'A norange' became 'an orange' in English through a shift linguists call…?
questions.f: The same slip turned 'a napron' into 'an apron' and 'an ewt' into 'a newt'.

questions.q: The edible 'mussel' and the body's 'muscle' share a Latin root meaning little…?
questions.f: A flexing muscle reminded Romans of a small mouse moving under the skin.

questions.q: The word 'pumpkin' traces to a Greek word 'pepon' meaning…?
questions.f: A 'pepon' was a large melon considered ready to eat once fully ripened.

questions.q: The word 'melon' comes from a Greek word that also meant…?
questions.f: Greek 'melon' meant apple or any tree fruit before it narrowed to the melon.

questions.q: Before it named the tropical fruit, the English word 'pineapple' referred to…?
questions.f: Explorers thought the spiky fruit looked like a pine cone, so the old name shifted.

questions.q: The word 'grocer' originally meant a merchant who sold goods in…?
questions.f: A 'grosser' dealt by the gross, in bulk, rather than in small retail amounts.

questions.q: The word 'butcher' comes from an Old French word linked to which animal?
questions.f: From 'bouc', a billy goat, hinting at the animals early butchers prepared.

questions.q: The word 'lard' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: The same root gives 'larder', once the room for storing cured fatty meats.

questions.q: The words 'salami', 'salsa', 'sauce', and 'sausage' all descend from the Latin word for…?
questions.f: Salt preserved and seasoned food, seeding a whole family of tasty words.

questions.q: The sauce 'mayonnaise' is popularly linked to the port of Mahon on which island?
questions.f: One story says a French chef discovered the sauce there after a 1756 battle.

questions.q: The dish 'steak tartare' is popularly named after which historical people?
questions.f: A legend claimed Tatar riders tenderized raw meat under their saddles.

questions.q: The 'kaiser roll' takes its name from a word that means…?
questions.f: 'Kaiser', like 'tsar', comes from the name Caesar and means emperor.

questions.q: The word 'coleslaw' comes from the Dutch 'koolsla', meaning literally…?
questions.f: So spelling it 'cold slaw' is a tasty misunderstanding of the Dutch.

questions.q: The pasta name 'spaghetti' means little…?
questions.f: From 'spago', string or twine, made small and plural for the thin strands.

questions.q: The pasta name 'vermicelli' literally means little…?
questions.f: These very thin noodles were thought to resemble tiny wriggling worms.

questions.q: The pasta name 'linguine' means little…?
questions.f: The flat, narrow strands were said to look like little tongues, from 'lingua'.

questions.q: The pasta name 'orecchiette' means little…?
questions.f: Their small ear-like cups are perfect for catching a chunky sauce.

questions.q: The pasta name 'farfalle' comes from the Italian word for…?
questions.f: Pinched in the middle, each piece spreads out like butterfly wings.

questions.q: The dumpling name 'gnocchi' comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The bumpy little dumplings were named for their knuckle-like shape.

questions.q: The bread name 'ciabatta' is the Italian word for…?
questions.f: This flat, wide loaf was thought to resemble a well-worn slipper.

questions.q: The flatbread 'focaccia' takes its name from a Latin word 'focus' meaning…?
questions.f: It was 'hearth bread', baked in the ashes and embers of the fireplace.

questions.q: The spice name 'paprika' ultimately comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: It reached English through Hungarian, tracing back to the word for pepper.

questions.q: The word 'symposium' comes from a Greek word meaning a…?
questions.f: A Greek symposium was a lively gathering with wine, music, and conversation.

questions.q: A 'macedoine' of diced fruit or vegetables is named after which ancient realm's mix of peoples?
questions.f: Alexander's Macedonian empire was famed as a jumble of many nations.

questions.q: The word 'schnitzel' comes from a German word meaning a…?
questions.f: A schnitzel is a thin slice of meat, pounded flat and fried.

questions.q: The Swedish word 'smorgasbord' literally means a…?
questions.f: It joins words for buttered bread and table, now meaning a buffet spread.

questions.q: The word 'fudge', before it named a candy, first meant to…?
questions.f: 'To fudge' meant to put together clumsily, perhaps how the sweet was first made.

questions.q: The word 'pudding' comes from an old word for a…?
questions.f: That is why blood sausage is still called 'black pudding'.

questions.q: The word 'custard' comes from 'crustade', a tart made with a…?
questions.f: Only later did custard come to mean the soft egg-and-milk filling itself.

questions.q: The dessert 'trifle' takes its name from a word originally meaning something…?
questions.f: A trifle was seen as a light, whimsical 'trifle' of a dish.

questions.q: The word 'jelly' comes from a Latin word 'gelare' meaning to…?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'gelatin', 'gel', and 'congeal'.

questions.q: The word 'gelato' shares the root 'gelare' with 'jelly', meaning…?
questions.f: Gelato is literally 'frozen', churned slower and warmer than ice cream.

questions.q: The dessert 'blancmange' literally means…?
questions.f: The medieval version was a pale dish of pounded chicken, almonds, and rice.

questions.q: The word 'fricassee' comes from French words meaning to…?
questions.f: A fricassee is meat cut up, lightly fried, then simmered in sauce.

questions.q: The word 'ragout' comes from a French word meaning to…?
questions.f: A ragout was meant to wake up the taste buds with rich flavor.

questions.q: An Italian 'ragu', cousin of the French 'ragout', is a…?
questions.f: Ragu alla bolognese is the slow-cooked meat sauce for tagliatelle.

questions.q: The soup called 'consomme' gets its name because it has been…?
questions.f: A consomme is a broth simmered and cleared until it is crystal clear.

questions.q: The word 'bouillon' comes from a French word meaning to…?
questions.f: A bouillon is simply a clear broth made by boiling meat or vegetables.

questions.q: A 'bisque' is best described as a smooth…?
questions.f: Classic bisque is a rich, creamy soup made from crab, lobster, or shrimp.

questions.q: Traditional 'mincemeat' pie filling historically contained fruit along with…?
questions.f: Old recipes mixed dried fruit with real minced meat and beef fat, or suet.

questions.q: The odd spelling of 'sundae' is thought to dodge naming which day?
questions.f: The treat may have been sold on Sundays, with the spelling changed to avoid offense.

questions.q: The word 'scone' may come from a Dutch word 'schoonbrood', meaning…?
questions.f: Its exact origin is debated, but the Dutch link is a leading theory.

questions.q: The word 'cookie' comes from a Dutch word 'koekje' meaning…?
questions.f: Dutch settlers in New York brought both the treat and the word to America.

questions.q: The word 'waffle' comes from a Dutch word linked to a…?
questions.f: The grid pattern recalls a honeycomb, and 'waffle' relates to 'weave'.

questions.q: The word 'brioche' comes from a French word meaning to…?
questions.f: The rich, buttery dough must be worked hard, from Norman French 'brier', to pound.

questions.q: The word 'baguette' comes from a word meaning a…?
questions.f: From Italian 'bacchetta', a little rod, describing the loaf's slim shape.

questions.q: The word 'croissant' literally means…?
questions.f: The pastry is shaped like a crescent moon, which is what the French word means.

questions.q: The words 'macaron' and 'macaroni' come from an Italian word for a…?
questions.f: Both trace to 'maccarone', a word for a fine paste or dumpling.

questions.q: The word 'biscotti' means…?
questions.f: Like 'biscuit', it comes from 'bis coctus'; biscotti are baked twice for crunch.

questions.q: The word 'mustard' comes from 'must', or grape juice, plus a word meaning…?
questions.f: Early mustard mixed the ground seeds with grape must, giving 'mustum ardens', burning must.

questions.q: The sauce 'aioli' takes its name directly from its two main ingredients: garlic and…?
questions.f: From Provencal 'ai' (garlic) and 'oli' (oil), pounded into a creamy sauce.

questions.q: The word 'pesto' comes from a word meaning to…?
questions.f: It shares its root with 'pestle', the tool used to crush the basil and pine nuts.

questions.q: The word 'guacamole' comes from the Aztec 'ahuacamolli', meaning avocado…?
questions.f: From Nahuatl, joining the words for avocado and sauce, or 'molli'.

questions.q: The word 'tortilla' is a Spanish diminutive meaning a little…?
questions.f: From 'torta', cake; the Spanish named the flat corn round a 'little cake'.

questions.q: The word 'burrito' literally means little…?
questions.f: One idea is that the stuffed roll resembled the packs a little donkey carried.

questions.q: The word 'taco' may come from a Mexican word for a…?
questions.f: Miners used 'tacos', little paper-wrapped charges, which the food may resemble.

questions.q: The word 'enchilada' describes something that has been…?
questions.f: It comes from a Spanish verb meaning 'to season with chile'.

questions.q: The word 'pepperoni' in Italian actually refers to…?
questions.f: In Italy, 'peperoni' means bell peppers; the sausage sense is American.

questions.q: The word 'prosciutto' comes from a Latin phrase meaning…?
questions.f: The ham is 'dried out' by long salting and months of air-drying.

questions.q: The word 'bacon' originally meant…?
questions.f: It comes from an old Germanic word for the back and sides of a pig.

questions.q: On an Italian menu, 'scampi' are a kind of…?
questions.f: Scampi are langoustines, small lobster-like shellfish, not simply large shrimp.

questions.q: The word 'caviar' comes through Italian from a Persian and Turkish word for…?
questions.f: The most prized caviar is the roe of the sturgeon fish.

questions.q: The word 'nougat' comes from an Occitan word rooted in the Latin 'nux', meaning…?
questions.f: Fittingly, nougat is a chewy sweet packed with nuts such as almonds or pistachios.

questions.q: A Massachusetts inn on an old toll road, a chocolate bar chopped instead of melted, and a recipe traded for a lifetime supply point to which invention?
questions.f: Ruth Wakefield's Toll House recipe was printed on Nestle bags in return for free chocolate.

questions.q: Inspectors who never admit their jobs, a top rating meaning 'worth a special journey', and a booklet once handed out free at garages point to which award?
questions.f: It was created by a tire company hoping motorists would drive, and wear out tires, further.

questions.q: An 1867 land purchase mocked as a folly, a meringue shell that shields ice cream from a hot oven, and Delmonico's in New York point to which dessert?
questions.f: The dish was reportedly named to celebrate the United States buying Alaska.

questions.q: Two French sisters running a hotel in the Loire, an apple tart assembled in the wrong order, and a dish always served upside down point to which dessert?
questions.f: The Tatin sisters' happy accident is now a classic of French pastry.

questions.q: A Rome restaurant owner soothing his wife after childbirth, a Hollywood couple's honeymoon in the 1920s, and butter beaten into cheese point to which dish?
questions.f: Alfredo di Lelio's simple pasta became famous when Douglas Fairbanks and Mary Pickford raved about it.

questions.q: A Wall Street broker with a morning appetite, a request for toast with poached eggs and bacon at the Waldorf, and hollandaise point to which dish?
questions.f: Lemuel Benedict's 1894 special order was adopted onto the hotel's menu.

questions.q: An English chemist whose wife could not eat eggs, a powder based on cornflour, and a yellow tin still on British shelves point to which product?
questions.f: Alfred Bird invented egg-free custard in 1837, then went on to help perfect baking powder too.

questions.q: A Louisiana island sitting atop a salt dome, three years of aging in oak barrels under a salt cap, and a pepper named for a Mexican state point to which sauce?
questions.f: The McIlhenny family has made it on Avery Island since the 1860s.

questions.q: A steward of a French royal household, a name attached to one of the five mother sauces, and milk thickened with a pale roux point to which man?
questions.f: The marquis lent his name to bechamel, though he likely never cooked it himself.

questions.q: A West African shrub, a protein that switches on sweet receptors only when acid is present, and lemons that taste like lemonade point to which berry?
questions.f: Its protein, miraculin, can make vinegar taste sugary for up to an hour.

questions.q: Bark from a South American tree that once fought malaria, a faint blue glow under ultraviolet light, and a famously bitter mixer point to which drink?
questions.f: The quinine that makes it bitter also makes tonic water fluoresce in the dark.

questions.q: A spice that numbs rather than burns, a molecule that makes lips vibrate at about 50 cycles a second, and a numbing-and-hot Chinese flavour pairing point to which spice?
questions.f: Its compound tricks touch nerves, creating a fizzing tingle called 'ma la' with chili.

questions.q: A resin with a sulphurous raw smell, a pinch that mellows into onion and garlic when fried, and a staple of Indian cooking without alliums point to which spice?
questions.f: Its Latin-derived name warns of the smell, but cooking transforms it completely.

questions.q: A seed that makes sweat smell of syrup, a bitter note in curry powder, and the fake maple flavour in cheap syrups point to which spice?
questions.f: Fenugreek contains sotolon, the same compound that gives maple syrup its aroma.

questions.q: A Moroccan blend whose name means 'head of the shop', a mix that can run past thirty spices, and no two versions alike point to which seasoning?
questions.f: The name suggests the shopkeeper's finest blend, kept behind the counter.

questions.q: A squeaky Cypriot cheese with mint folded in, an unusually high melting point, and slices that grill without collapsing point to which cheese?
questions.f: Halloumi is heated during making, which sets its proteins so it holds shape on the grill.

questions.q: Milk from Balkan donkeys, a herd of only a few hundred animals, and a price of hundreds of dollars for a small wheel point to which cheese?
questions.f: Serbian pule is widely reported as the world's most expensive cheese.

questions.q: An Icelandic dairy food strained until it is nearly solid, a technically cheese-not-yogurt classification, and Viking-era origins point to which product?
questions.f: Skyr is made with rennet, which is why dairy scientists class it as a fresh cheese.

questions.q: Melons grown one to a vine under careful pruning, a perfect netted rind, and pairs auctioned in Japan for thousands of dollars point to which fruit?
questions.f: Growers in Hokkaido sacrifice every other fruit so one melon gets all the sugar.

questions.q: An orchid-family crop grown mainly in Madagascar today, pods that must be killed and sweated for months, and the world's second-priciest spice point to which flavour?
questions.f: Curing develops the vanillin, which barely exists in the freshly picked green pod.

questions.q: A French base named after an 18th-century duke, a trio of diced onion, carrot, and celery, and the flavour foundation of countless stocks point to which mixture?
questions.f: It is said to honour the Duke of Mirepoix, whose cook popularized the blend.

questions.q: Finely chopped mushrooms cooked down with shallots, a stuffing sealed inside Beef Wellington, and a name honouring a 17th-century marquis point to which preparation?
questions.f: It is credited to the cook of the Marquis d'Uxelles, hence the name.

questions.q: A dish of thin pancakes flamed at the table, a name honouring a young girl in a French dining room, and orange butter point to which dessert?
questions.f: The classic story credits a young assistant waiter at Monte Carlo with the happy accident.
