questions.f: Archers typically shoot ends of three or six arrows, then walk down together to score and collect.

questions.q: 'Draughts' is the British name for which game?
questions.f: Same board, same discs: Americans say checkers while Britons say draughts.

questions.q: 'Noughts and crosses' is the British name for which game?
questions.f: A 'nought' is a zero, so the name literally lists the game's two symbols, O and X.

questions.q: The martial art 'kendo' is literally the way of the what?
questions.f: From Japanese 'ken' (sword) and 'do' (way), kendo is fenced with bamboo swords and armor.

questions.q: A martial arts teacher is a 'sensei', literally meaning one who...?
questions.f: 'Sen' (before) plus 'sei' (born): a sensei has simply traveled the path ahead of you.

questions.q: The winner's 'podium' comes from a Greek word meaning a little what?
questions.f: Greek 'podion', little foot, named a low footing or base; 'podiatrist' shares the root.

questions.q: The word 'champion' grew from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Latin 'campus' meant field; a 'campio' was the fighter who took the field.

questions.q: 'Agile' comes from a Latin root meaning to...?
questions.f: Latin 'agere', to do or drive, also powers 'agent', 'action', and 'agitate'.

questions.q: Rubber-soled shoes were nicknamed 'sneakers' because they let wearers do what?
questions.f: Unlike clacking leather heels, rubber soles were so quiet you could sneak up on anyone.

questions.q: In Britain the playing field is called a 'pitch'; as a verb, 'pitch' also means to...?
questions.f: One little word covers throwing a ball, a soccer field, a tent, and even a musical note.

questions.q: The two small wooden pieces balanced on top of cricket stumps are called...?
questions.f: The ball must usually knock a bail off for a batter to be bowled; in wind, umpires may remove them.

questions.q: Ice climbers strap 'crampons' onto their boots; what are they?
questions.f: Crampon points bite into ice so climbers can walk up frozen waterfalls.

questions.q: In climbing, to 'belay' a partner means to...?
c: Manage their rope to catch any fall
questions.f: The belayer feeds rope through a friction device, ready to lock it the instant a climber slips.

questions.q: Tennis borrowed 'grand slam' from a term for winning every trick in...?
questions.f: In whist and bridge, a grand slam takes all thirteen tricks; tennis applied it to winning all four majors.

questions.q: In racket sports, a 'rally' is...?
c: The final point of a match
questions.f: 'Rally' also means to recover or regroup, which is why comebacks are called rallies too.

questions.q: Why are top tournament players called 'seeds'?
c: They are scattered through the draw like planted seeds
Early prizes were bags of grain
questions.f: Officials 'sow' the best players apart so the biggest stars can only meet in late rounds.

questions.q: Before it meant bouncing a basketball, 'dribble' meant to...?
questions.f: A dribbling tap drips slowly; soccer and basketball borrowed the word for small, controlled touches.

questions.q: How do the two riders sit on a tandem bicycle?
questions.f: 'Tandem' is Latin for 'at length'; scholars joked the riders sat lengthwise, and the pun stuck.

questions.q: A 3-0 soccer score is read 'three-nil'; 'nil' is squeezed from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Nil' clips Latin 'nihil', nothing, the same root hiding in 'annihilate'.

questions.q: In golf slang, a 'duffer' is...?
questions.f: 'Duff' means to botch a shot, so a duffer is someone who duffs rather often.

questions.q: What does golf's 'handicap' system do?
c: Lets players of different skill compete fairly
Limits how many clubs you carry
questions.f: The term traces to 'hand-in-cap', an old wagering game with forfeits drawn from a cap.

questions.q: The athlete's 'biceps' muscle has a name that literally means...?
questions.f: Latin 'bi' (two) plus 'caput' (head): the biceps attaches at two points, hence two heads.

questions.q: In chess notation, '!' marks a strong move while '?' marks a mistake.
questions.f: Annotators even award '!!' for brilliancies and '??' for blunders.

questions.q: 'Racket' is an accepted spelling for both the tennis bat and a loud noise.
questions.f: Both racket and racquet are used for the bat, while the noisy 'racket' has just one spelling.

questions.q: 'Referee' and 'umpire' are interchangeable titles used identically in every sport.
questions.f: Each sport picks its own tradition: soccer has referees, cricket and tennis have umpires.

questions.q: A runner nicknamed the 'Czech Locomotive', a grimacing style coaches hated, and a 1952 marathon gold won on debut in the same week as two track golds converge on which athlete?
questions.f: Zatopek's Helsinki triple, the 5,000 m, 10,000 m, and marathon at one Games, has never been repeated.

questions.q: An emperor's palace guard, the cobblestones of Rome by torchlight, and a world record set without shoes all point to which marathon champion?
questions.f: Ethiopia's Bikila ran the 1960 Olympic marathon barefoot, then won again in 1964, in shoes.

questions.q: A medical student squeezing training into lunch breaks, two pacemaker friends, and a windy Oxford evening in May 1954 combine in which running milestone?
c: The first mile run under four minutes
questions.f: Roger Bannister's 3:59.4 stood as a record for just 46 days, but the barrier-breaking made history.

questions.q: A childhood leg brace after illness, a Tennessee college track club, and three sprint golds at Rome 1960 tell the story of which athlete?
questions.f: Rudolph, once told she might never walk unaided, became the fastest woman in the world.

questions.q: A 19-year-old coated in grease against the cold, a zigzag course forced by storms, and a 1926 crossing nearly two hours faster than any man's converge on which swimmer?
questions.f: Ederle's English Channel swim earned her a New York ticker-tape parade before two million people.

questions.q: Thin air at 2,240 meters, a leap so far the optical measurer ran off its rail, and a record that survived 23 years all describe whose 1968 jump?
questions.f: Beamon's 8.90 m stunned Mexico City; officials needed an old-fashioned tape to confirm it.

questions.q: A borrowed tip about takeoff boards, a friendship begun mid-competition in 1936, and four gold medals at one Games point to which sprinter and long jumper?
questions.f: German jumper Luz Long befriended and advised Owens in Berlin, a sporting friendship still celebrated.

questions.q: An army recruit discovered in training races, a heartbreaking fourth place in Rome by a tenth of a second, and a nickname bestowed in Pakistan identify which Indian runner?
questions.f: After a 1960 race in Lahore, Pakistan's president dubbed Milkha Singh 'The Flying Sikh'.

questions.q: A railway-town athletics prodigy called the 'Payyoli Express', four golds at the 1986 Asian Games, and a 1984 Olympic final lost by one-hundredth of a second describe which athlete?
questions.f: Usha missed the 400 m hurdles bronze in Los Angeles by 0.01 s, the closest miss in Indian Olympic history.

questions.q: A ball said to stick to his stick like glue, officials abroad who once examined that stick for magnets, and a Berlin 1936 captaincy converge on which hockey legend?
questions.f: Dhyan Chand led India to its third straight Olympic hockey gold; his birthday is India's National Sports Day.

questions.q: A rice farmer's daughter from Manipur, six world championships in the ring, and the nickname 'Magnificent Mary' identify which boxer?
questions.f: Mary Kom won a world title in six different weight classes and an Olympic bronze in 2012.

questions.q: A Chennai prodigy nicknamed the 'Lightning Kid', a 2000 world title won in Tehran, and five world championship reigns in three formats point to which chess player?
questions.f: Anand was India's first grandmaster and carried the world title across knockout, tournament, and match play.

questions.q: A Norwegian toddler who memorized the world's flags, a draw against Kasparov at age 13, and a world title won in 2013 in Chennai converge on which player?
questions.f: Carlsen dethroned Anand in Anand's home city and later held world titles in three formats at once.

questions.q: A Reykjavik hall in 1972, a forfeited second game over television cameras, and a Cold War duel dubbed the Match of the Century converge on which contest?
questions.f: Bobby Fischer's win ended 24 years of Soviet world champions and set off a global chess boom.

questions.q: A 1997 New York rematch, a move 44 that unnerved a world champion, and a machine dismantled soon after its victory point to which milestone?
questions.f: IBM's Deep Blue became the first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion in a match.

questions.q: An 18th-century touring 'automaton' in a turban, hidden sliding panels and a concealed human master, and games against Napoleon converge on which famous hoax?
questions.f: The Turk fooled Europe for decades; a chess expert crouched inside worked its arm by levers.

questions.q: An unemployed architect, letter counts tallied from newspaper front pages, and a game first called Lexiko converge on the birth of which pastime?
questions.f: Alfred Butts priced Scrabble's letters from frequency tables; that is why Q and Z score ten.

questions.q: A 1904 patent by Lizzie Magie, a board designed to warn against greedy landlords, and rules later famous under another name converge on the ancestor of which game?
questions.f: Magie's Landlord's Game preached against monopolies; the hit version ironically celebrates them.

questions.q: A 1948 polio ward, a schoolteacher designing for children who could not yet read, and a rainbow trail of colored squares converge on which board game?
questions.f: Eleanor Abbott invented Candy Land while recovering from polio, for young patients on her ward.

questions.q: A 4,500-year-old board from a Mesopotamian tomb, rules deciphered from a cuneiform tablet, and a British Museum curator's detective work identify which game?
questions.f: Curator Irving Finkel matched a Babylonian tablet to the board, reviving rules unread for millennia.

questions.q: An Irish linen merchant's son, a goalkeeper weary of deliberate fouls, and an 1891 proposal for a 12-yard kick converge on the invention of what?
questions.f: William McCrum's 'death penalty' outraged purists but became soccer's most dramatic moment.

questions.q: A referee stuck at a London traffic light, a language muddle at the 1966 World Cup, and a debut at Mexico 1970 combine in the story of what?
questions.f: Ken Aston dreamed up the cards after a signal: yellow for caution, red for stop.

questions.q: A trophy stolen from a London exhibition in 1966, a ransom note, and a dog named Pickles sniffing under a garden hedge converge on which recovery?
questions.f: Pickles found the Jules Rimet Trophy wrapped in newspaper a week before the World Cup began.

questions.q: A Welsh major's 1874 patent, an hourglass-shaped court, and a tongue-twisting Greek name that nobody used converge on the birth of which sport?
questions.f: Walter Wingfield sold his 'Sphairistike' in boxed sets; buyers kept the game and dropped the name.

questions.q: A volcanic islet in a Scottish firth, a bird sanctuary quarried by one firm under license, and two granites called Common Green and Blue Hone converge on which sporting supply?
questions.f: Nearly every Olympic curling stone is cut from Ailsa Craig granite, prized because it never chips.

questions.q: A shepherd... actually a water-carrier from a village near Athens, an 1896 course from a famous battlefield, and a nation's ecstatic king converge on which champion?
questions.f: Louis won the first modern Olympic marathon; Greeks showered him with offered gifts for life.

questions.q: A plasterer from Cheltenham, fogged-up glasses under his goggles, and a last-place finish that charmed Calgary 1988 identify which Olympian?
questions.f: Britain's first Olympic ski jumper in 60 years became so beloved the closing ceremony saluted him.

questions.q: A push-cart derby heritage, sleds borrowed from other nations, and a crash at Calgary 1988 followed by a walk to the finish line describe which team?
questions.f: The Jamaican bobsledders carried their sled over the line to applause and inspired the film Cool Runnings.

questions.q: A beekeeper from Auckland, a Sherpa mountaineer on his seventh expedition, and sweets buried in the snow as an offering at the top converge on which 1953 achievement?
c: The first ascent of Mount Everest
questions.f: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached Everest's summit at 11:30 am on 29 May 1953.

questions.q: A Tokyo choir member turned climber, an avalanche survived at 6,300 meters, and a 1975 summit no woman had reached before identify which mountaineer?
questions.f: Tabei, dug from the snow by her Sherpa guide days earlier, became the first woman atop Everest.

questions.q: An unbeaten 175 that no camera filmed because of a BBC strike, a balcony at Lord's, and 1983 underdogs toppling twice-reigning champions converge on which triumph?
c: India's first cricket World Cup win
questions.f: Kapil Dev's rescue innings against Zimbabwe survives only in memory; weeks later India stunned the West Indies at Lord's.

questions.q: A Bengaluru leg-spinner, a Delhi scoreboard reading ten wickets to one name, and a feat matched only by Jim Laker converge on which bowler?
questions.f: Kumble took all ten Pakistani wickets in an innings in 1999; teammates ensured no one else got one.

questions.q: A boy practicing with a golf ball and a cricket stump against a water tank, a final-innings duck, and an average frozen at 99.94 converge on which batsman?
questions.f: Bradman needed just four runs in his last Test innings to average 100; he was bowled for nought.

questions.q: A Harris hawk named Rufus, dawn patrols over show courts, and pigeons banished from strawberry-scented lawns converge on which sporting venue?
questions.f: Rufus the hawk is Wimbledon's official bird-scarer, flying before the gates open each morning.

questions.q: A 1936 winner's request for buttermilk, a delighted dairy industry, and a chilled bottle handed over in victory lane converge on the tradition of which race?
questions.f: Since Louis Meyer's buttermilk, Indy 500 winners have celebrated with milk, choosing their type in advance.

questions.q: A courtship contest of 1588 according to legend, a ring of sand behind a Sussex pub, and Good Friday finals converge on which world championship?
questions.f: The World Marbles Championship has been held at Tinsley Green's Greyhound pub for generations.

questions.q: A 1980 argument in a Welsh pub, a 22-mile course over moor and bog, and rare human victories in the hottest years converge on which event?
questions.f: In Llanwrtyd Wells, runners race horses cross-country; a human first won outright in 2004.

questions.q: Post-station courier horses of old Japan, a sash called a tasuki passed instead of a baton, and a Tokyo-to-Kyoto relay of 1917 converge on which race format?
questions.f: Ekiden road relays grip Japan each New Year, when the Hakone Ekiden empties the streets.

questions.q: A 1925 diphtheria serum run to an icebound town, a statue of the dog Balto in Central Park, and a thousand-mile race founded in 1973 converge on which event?
questions.f: The Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race honors the relay of mushers who saved Nome, Alaska.

questions.q: A start and finish at Les Sables-d'Olonne, a rule forbidding stopovers and outside help, and three months alone in the Southern Ocean converge on which race?
questions.f: The Vendee Globe is sailing's solo, nonstop lap of the planet, nicknamed the Everest of the seas.

questions.q: A race around the Isle of Wight in 1851, a queen told 'there is no second', and sport's oldest still-contested international trophy converge on which prize?
questions.f: The schooner America won the cup later named for her; it predates the modern Olympics by 45 years.

questions.q: An azalea-lined course in Georgia, a champions-only wardrobe rule, and a garment that traditionally may leave the grounds for just one year converge on which prize?
questions.f: Masters champions keep their green jacket for a year, then store it at Augusta National forever.

questions.q: A stadium built for 1950 with room for a fifth of a million, a hush nicknamed the 'Maracanazo', and a neighbor's upset in the deciding match converge on which venue?
questions.f: Uruguay's 1950 win over Brazil before nearly 200,000 fans remains soccer's most famous silence.

questions.q: A constitution's centenary, thirteen teams arriving by steamship, and a final played with a different ball in each half converge on which tournament?
questions.f: Hosts Uruguay won the first World Cup 4-2 over Argentina after each side's favored ball got one half.

questions.q: An Indian prince who dazzled England with the leg glance, a county career at Sussex, and a domestic trophy named in his honor in 1934 converge on which cricketer?
questions.f: India's Ranji Trophy is named for Ranjitsinhji, whose wristy strokes changed batting forever.

questions.q: Which ball is covered in black and white patches?
questions.f: The classic black-and-white pattern was designed so the ball showed up clearly on old TV sets.

questions.q: In hopscotch, what do you toss into a square before you hop?
questions.f: Players skip over the square holding their stone, which makes each turn a little trickier.

questions.q: In archery, what do you aim your arrow at?
questions.f: Archery targets have colored rings, and the tiny gold center is worth the most points.

questions.q: What do boxers punch when they train in the gym?
questions.f: Heavy punching bags can weigh as much as a grown-up, so they barely swing when hit.

questions.q: Where do soccer players sit while they wait for their turn to play?
c: On the grass in the middle
questions.f: Coaches sit by the bench too, ready to send a substitute onto the field.

questions.q: What do skaters wear to protect their knees?
questions.f: Pads on knees, elbows, and wrists let skaters try new tricks without getting scraped.

questions.q: In Snakes and Ladders, what carries you up the board?
questions.f: Ladders lift you up while snakes slide you down, so every roll of the dice is exciting.

questions.q: What shape is a hula hoop?
questions.f: Because a hoop is one smooth circle, it can spin around and around without stopping.

questions.q: In a game of tag, what is the spot where you cannot be tagged called?
questions.f: Reaching base means a quick rest, but you cannot stay there forever!

questions.q: What do you use to put air back into a flat ball?
questions.f: A pump pushes air through a tiny needle poked into the ball's valve.

questions.q: Which sport is played in a bowling alley?
questions.f: Bowling lanes are coated in slippery oil so the heavy ball can glide toward the pins.

questions.q: On a golf course, what marks the spot where each hole is?
questions.f: Golfers look for the flag in the distance to know which way to aim their shot.

questions.q: In a race, who is the winner?
questions.f: In photo-finish races, cameras help judges see exactly who crossed the line first.

questions.q: What should you drink lots of after running around?
questions.f: You lose water when you sweat, so drinking water helps your body cool down.

questions.q: Where does a running race begin?
questions.f: Runners line up carefully, because starting even a step early is against the rules.

questions.q: What do you do when a teammate calls for the ball?
questions.f: Good passing wins games, because a ball travels faster than any player can run.

questions.q: What does a baseball catcher wear to protect their face?
questions.f: Catchers crouch close behind the batter, so they wear a mask, helmet, and chest padding.

questions.q: What is it called when you turn sideways over your hands in gym class?
questions.f: A cartwheel is named after a spinning wagon wheel, since your arms and legs are the spokes.

questions.q: What is it called when you balance upside down on your hands?
questions.f: Gymnasts learn handstands early, because almost every other move begins from one.

questions.q: Which one is a winter sport?
questions.f: Winter sports need ice or snow, which is why many are played indoors in warm countries.

questions.q: What is the flat board behind a basketball hoop called?
questions.f: Smart players bounce the ball off the backboard so it drops neatly into the hoop.

questions.q: In table tennis, what stretches across the middle of the table?
questions.f: The little net is only about 15 centimeters tall, but it still catches plenty of shots.

questions.q: In a jigsaw puzzle, what do you fit together?
questions.f: Every jigsaw piece has just one perfect place, so you must look closely at each shape.

questions.q: In dominoes, what must you match when you lay down a tile?
questions.f: Matching dots keeps the line growing, and clever players save their doubles for later.

questions.q: Which word means to run slowly for exercise?
questions.f: Jogging is gentler than sprinting, so you can keep going much longer.

questions.q: Which sport is played in a ring by two people wearing big gloves?
questions.f: A boxing round often lasts three minutes, then fighters rest in their corners.

questions.q: What do skiers hold in their hands as they slide downhill?
questions.f: Ski poles help with balance and give a little push along flat patches of snow.

questions.q: Which two words make up the word 'cartwheel'?
questions.f: A cart is a wagon, and its wheel spins round, just like your body in a cartwheel.

questions.q: Which two words make up 'handstand'?
questions.f: You really do stand on your hands, so the word says exactly what it means.

questions.q: The word 'playground' joins 'play' with which word?
questions.f: A playground is simply ground for playing, and compound words like this are everywhere.

questions.q: Which word joins with 'suit' to name what you wear in a pool?
questions.f: A swimsuit is smooth and stretchy so it does not drag in the water.

questions.q: The tall posts on either side of a soccer goal are called goal...?
questions.f: A shot that clangs off the goalpost and stays out is every striker's worst luck.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'win'?
questions.f: Words with opposite meanings, like win and lose, are called antonyms.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'start'?
questions.f: Races have a start line and a finish line, one at each end of the track.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'fast'?
questions.f: Three of these words all mean fast, which makes them synonyms of each other.

questions.q: To 'toss' a ball means to throw it...?
questions.f: You toss a coin before a match, letting it flip gently through the air.

questions.q: What is more than one match called?
questions.f: Words ending in ch add '-es' to become plural: matches, coaches, and benches.

questions.q: What is more than one trophy called?
questions.f: When a word ends in y after a consonant, the y becomes 'ies': trophy, trophies.

questions.q: If you are the 'fastest' in your class, that means you are...?
questions.f: The ending '-est' means the most of something: fastest, tallest, strongest.

questions.q: Someone who kicks the ball in a team is called a...?
questions.f: Add '-er' to an action and you get the doer: kick, kicker; throw, thrower.

questions.q: 'Runner' means a person who...?
questions.f: In baseball, a player racing between bases is called a runner.

questions.q: What is the short, friendly word for a referee?
questions.f: Fans shout 'come on, ref!' because short words are easier to yell across a stadium.

questions.q: The word 'bat' can mean a flying animal and also what?
c: A stick for hitting a ball
questions.f: Words with the same spelling but different meanings, like bat, are called homonyms.

questions.q: Which word means a long seat and also the place substitutes wait?
questions.f: Coming off the bench means being sent on as a substitute during a game.

questions.q: What do we call the ground where races are run: a race...?
questions.f: 'Racetrack' is another compound word, joining race and track into one.

questions.q: In archery you shoot arrows, and in bowling you roll a ball.
questions.f: Both sports are about aiming carefully, one at a target and one at ten pins.

questions.q: A cartwheel is done with your hands touching the floor.
questions.f: Your hands land one at a time as your legs sweep over in a big circle.

questions.q: Kite flying works best on a windy day.
questions.f: Wind pushes against the kite's surface and lifts it high into the sky.

questions.q: You need two people to play a game of tug of war.
questions.f: Tug of war needs pullers on both ends, and big teams can have eight players a side.

questions.q: Ice is slippery, which is why skates glide across it so easily.
questions.f: A thin film of water forms under the blade, letting skaters slide almost without friction.

questions.q: The word 'goals' is the plural of 'goal'.
questions.f: Most English words just add s to become plural: goal, goals; game, games.

questions.q: Which sport uses a helmet, a bat, and a big mitt to catch?
questions.f: A catcher's mitt has extra padding because pitches arrive incredibly fast.

questions.q: How many players from one netball team are on court at once?
questions.f: Each netball player wears letters like GS or GK showing which zones they may enter.

questions.q: How many lanes does an Olympic swimming pool have?
questions.f: Ten lanes are built but only eight are raced, so the outer lanes soak up the waves.

questions.q: How many players in total are on court during a tennis doubles match?
questions.f: Doubles players use the wider court, including the side alleys closed off in singles.

questions.q: In chess, how many pawns does each player start with?
questions.f: Eight pawns form a wall in front of the more valuable pieces at the start.

questions.q: Where do the rooks stand at the start of a chess game?
questions.f: Rooks begin boxed into corners, then become powerful once the board opens up.

questions.q: How many players are in a cricket team on the field?
questions.f: Eleven fielders spread out, and captains give the positions names like slip and mid-off.

questions.q: What is a bowler in cricket trying to hit with the ball?
questions.f: Knocking the stumps and dislodging a bail means the batter is out, bowled.

questions.q: How many players from one American football team are on the field at once?
questions.f: Squads carry over 50 players because attack, defense, and kicking units all differ.

questions.q: In basketball, what is a 'dunk'?
c: Pushing the ball down through the hoop while touching it
A shot from behind the arc
questions.f: Dunking needs a huge leap, since players must reach above a hoop three meters up.

questions.q: Which swimming stroke is swum lying on your back?
questions.f: Backstrokers watch flags above the pool to know when the wall is coming.

questions.q: Which winter sport combines skating with spins, jumps, and music?
questions.f: Figure skating got its name from the patterns, or figures, skaters once traced on the ice.

questions.q: What is the special outfit worn for judo practice called?
questions.f: The heavy cotton gi is built to be gripped and pulled during throws.

questions.q: In most martial arts, which belt color does a complete beginner wear?
questions.f: Students start with white and work through colors as they learn new skills.

questions.q: In athletics, which event has athletes jumping over a bar using a long pole?
questions.f: Bendy fiberglass poles fling vaulters more than five meters into the air.

questions.q: Which throwing event uses a long, thin, spear-shaped implement?
questions.f: A men's javelin weighs 800 grams and can sail more than 90 meters.

questions.q: In which athletics event do competitors leap into a pit of sand?
questions.f: Officials rake the sand flat after each jump so every landing mark shows clearly.

questions.q: Which sport is played in a pool with goals at each end and a ball?
questions.f: Water polo players may hold the ball with only one hand at a time.

questions.q: Which water sport involves standing on a board and riding waves?
questions.f: Surfing joined the Olympics in 2020, with heats judged on the best waves ridden.

questions.q: Which sport is played on a flat lawn called a 'green', rolling heavy balls?
questions.f: Bowls are shaped slightly lopsided on purpose, so they curve as they slow down.

questions.q: The Tour de France is a famous long race in which sport?
questions.f: Riders cover over 3,000 kilometers across three weeks of daily stages.

questions.q: In weightlifting, what is the long bar loaded with weights called?
questions.f: A men's competition barbell alone weighs 20 kilograms before any plates go on.

questions.q: In the game Twister, what do you place your hands and feet on?
questions.f: A spinner decides each move, so players end up tangled in knots of arms and legs.

questions.q: In Connect Four, what are you trying to line up?
questions.f: Rows can be up and down, across, or diagonal, so watch every direction.

questions.q: In charades, how do you give your team clues?
questions.f: Charades players mime signals for book, film, or song before acting out the title.

questions.q: In Pictionary, how do you get teammates to guess the word?
questions.f: Speed matters in Pictionary, so quick scribbles usually beat careful artwork.

questions.q: In Sudoku, which numbers do you use to fill the grid?
questions.f: Each row, column, and small box must hold every digit from one to nine exactly once.

questions.q: In the game of marbles, what are players trying to do?
c: Knock other marbles out of the ring
questions.f: Marbles were once made of real marble stone, which is how the game got its name.

questions.q: The Olympic Games come in two main kinds. Which are they?
questions.f: The Winter Games began in 1924 and feature only sports played on snow or ice.

questions.q: How many dots are on the blank half of a domino tile?
questions.f: A blank counts as zero, and a double-blank is the lowest tile in the whole set.

questions.q: In water polo, players may hold the ball with both hands at once.
questions.f: Only the goalkeeper may use two hands; everyone else plays one-handed.

questions.q: A hurdler must jump over every hurdle in the race.
questions.f: Running around a hurdle means disqualification, so athletes must clear all ten.

questions.q: Figure skaters perform to music during their routines.
questions.f: Judges score both the jumps and how well the skating matches the music.

questions.q: A person who bowls in cricket is called a...?
questions.f: 'Bowler' is also a kind of round hat, another word doing two jobs at once.

questions.q: In baseball, the player who catches behind home plate is the...?
questions.f: Catchers use secret hand signals to tell the pitcher which pitch to throw.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'victory'?
questions.f: Athletes learn from defeat, and many champions lost plenty of games first.

questions.q: What is the short, friendly form of the word 'champion'?
questions.f: Clipping long words is common in sport: champ, ref, sub, and gym.

questions.q: A game that ends with the scores level can be called a tie or a...?
questions.f: British fans usually say draw while American fans say tie, for the same result.

questions.q: Which word names the very last game that decides the champion?
questions.f: Finals often follow semifinals, and losing semifinalists sometimes play for third place.

questions.q: Which spelling names the person who trains a team: coach or couch?
questions.f: A coach trains you, but a couch is for sitting; just one letter separates them.

questions.q: Which spelling fits the sentence 'Our team will ____ them today'?
questions.f: 'Beat' means to defeat, while a 'beet' is a purple root vegetable.

questions.q: Which spelling fits 'She ____ the ball to me': threw or through?
questions.f: 'Threw' is the past tense of throw; 'through' means going from one side to the other.

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'wrestling'?
questions.f: English keeps silent letters from older spellings, as in write, wrong, and wrap.

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'muscle'?
questions.f: The c stays because the word came from Latin 'musculus', meaning little mouse!

questions.q: What does it mean to 'compete'?
c: To take part in a contest against others
questions.f: Compete comes from Latin words meaning to strive together, side by side.

questions.q: In sports, what does 'defend' mean?
c: To stop the other team scoring
questions.f: Defenders block shots and steal passes, protecting their own goal or basket.

questions.q: A 'substitute' in a match is a player who...?
questions.f: Substitutes stay warmed up on the bench so they can enter the game instantly.

questions.q: 'Equipment' in sport means...?
c: The gear you need to play
questions.f: Equipment lists vary hugely: chess needs a board, while ice hockey needs a whole kit bag.

questions.q: Which sport uses a 'birdie', another name for the shuttlecock?
questions.f: The nickname fits, since a feathered shuttle really does flutter like a small bird.

questions.q: Which two sports divide their play into 'innings'?
questions.f: Cricket usually says innings even for one turn, while baseball counts nine separate innings.

questions.q: In basketball, what is a 'foul'?
c: Breaking a rule, often by illegal contact
questions.f: Collect too many fouls and a player must leave the game for good.

questions.q: How many periods, called 'chukkas', does a polo match usually have?
questions.f: Ponies get swapped between chukkas because galloping is exhausting work.

questions.q: How many players from one field hockey team are on the pitch at once?
questions.f: Field hockey sticks have a flat side and a round side, and only the flat side may hit the ball.

questions.q: What is the sport of moving quickly through obstacles by vaulting and climbing?
questions.f: Parkour grew out of military obstacle training in France in the 1980s.

questions.q: Which sport is played by teams paddling a long boat to a drumbeat?
questions.f: A drummer sits at the bow so every paddler strokes at exactly the same instant.

questions.q: In cycling, what is a 'velodrome'?
c: An indoor track with steeply banked sides
questions.f: The banking is so steep that riders would slide down it if they stopped pedaling.

questions.q: What is the sport of climbing indoor walls with ropes and grips called?
questions.f: Sport climbing joined the Olympics in 2020, mixing speed, bouldering, and endurance routes.

questions.q: In gymnastics, what do judges give for a routine?
questions.f: Judges add difficulty and execution scores together, subtracting for wobbles and falls.

questions.q: Which sport features a 'goal' guarded by a keeper wearing a helmet and huge pads?
questions.f: Hockey goalies wear over 20 kilograms of padding to stop shots that fly over 150 km/h.

questions.q: In sports, what is a 'timeout'?
c: A short break a team can call
questions.f: Coaches use timeouts to change tactics or stop the other team's winning run.

questions.q: What do we call the schedule showing who plays whom and when?
questions.f: League fixture lists are planned months ahead so every team plays every rival.

questions.q: In cricket, what is the strip of hard ground in the middle called?
questions.f: Groundskeepers roll the pitch flat, and how much grass they leave changes the whole match.

questions.q: In basketball, what happens after a team scores?
c: The other team gets the ball
questions.f: Restarting fast after a basket is called a transition, and it often catches defenders napping.

questions.q: How many players are in a beach volleyball team?
questions.f: With only two players covering the sand, beach volleyball demands enormous fitness.

questions.q: Which board game's pieces are called 'stones'?
questions.f: Go stones are black and white discs, and once placed they never move again.

questions.q: In a chess game, which player moves first?
c: The one with the white pieces
The one with the black pieces
questions.f: Moving first is a small advantage, so tournaments give players equal turns with white.

questions.q: In field hockey, players may hit the ball with either side of the stick.
questions.f: Only the flat face is legal, which is why beginners learn to flip the stick quickly.

questions.q: Beach volleyball players usually play barefoot.
questions.f: Bare feet grip the sand better than shoes, though players wear socks on very hot sand.

questions.q: In Go, a stone once placed stays where it is unless it gets captured.
questions.f: Because stones never move, Go is a game of building shapes rather than shifting pieces.

questions.q: Someone who dives from a board is called a...?
questions.f: Divers train on dry-land trampolines with harnesses before trying new twists over water.

questions.q: Someone who rides a horse in a race is called a...?
questions.f: Jockeys are among the lightest athletes in sport, because less weight helps the horse run faster.

questions.q: The word 'racehorse' is made by joining 'race' with which word?
questions.f: 'Horse' and 'hoarse' sound the same, so read carefully before you spell.

questions.q: What is the correct plural of 'coach'?
questions.f: Words ending in ch, sh, s, or x take '-es': coaches, dashes, buses, boxes.

questions.q: What does 'athletic' mean?
questions.f: 'Athletic' describes the person, while 'athletics' names the sport of running, jumping, and throwing.

questions.q: Which word means very tired after a hard game?
questions.f: Athletes recover from exhaustion with rest, food, and plenty of water.

questions.q: The word 'undefeated' describes a team that has...?
questions.f: The prefix 'un-' plus 'defeated' says it plainly: not defeated, not even once.

questions.q: A game played away from your own home ground is called an...?
questions.f: Home teams often win more often, a boost fans call home advantage.

questions.q: Which word describes a player who can use both hands equally well?
questions.f: The fancy word for this is ambidextrous, and it is rare and very useful in sport.

questions.q: What is a 'goal drought'?
questions.f: A drought means a dry spell without rain, so a goal drought is a dry spell without goals.

questions.q: If a match is 'postponed', what has happened?
c: It has been moved to a later date
questions.f: The prefix 'post-' means after, so the game will be played after the original date.

questions.q: What does the word 'tournament' describe?
c: A series of games to find a winner
questions.f: Knockout tournaments send losers home, while league tournaments let everyone play everyone.

questions.q: In sports, what is a 'record'?
questions.f: World records must be set under official conditions before they can be recognized.

questions.q: What is a 'spectacular' goal?
questions.f: 'Spectacular' and 'spectator' share a root about watching and seeing.

questions.q: To 'qualify' for a final means to...?
questions.f: Qualifying rounds thin big fields down to the fastest or strongest few.

questions.q: Which word means one full circle of a track?
questions.f: An outdoor athletics track is 400 meters, so a 1500 m race is nearly four laps.

questions.q: A 'stadium' is best described as...?
c: A large sports ground surrounded by seats
questions.f: The biggest stadiums seat over 100,000 fans, more people than live in many towns.

questions.q: What is a 'trophy cabinet'?
c: Where a club displays its prizes
questions.f: Some famous clubs need whole rooms to show off decades of cups and shields.

questions.q: What does the '-ics' ending in 'gymnastics' and 'athletics' signal?
questions.f: The same ending appears in mathematics, physics, and acrobatics.

questions.q: Which spelling names the swimming contest: heat or heet?
questions.f: A heat is an early race that decides who makes the final; the word also means warmth.

questions.q: The word 'sportsmanship' contains three smaller words: sports, man, and ship.
questions.f: The '-ship' ending means a quality or state, as in friendship and leadership.

questions.q: 'Practice makes perfect' means repeating something helps you improve.
questions.f: Athletes repeat basic skills thousands of times until they happen without thinking.

questions.q: In golf, finishing a hole one stroke under par is called a...?
questions.f: Golf named its under-par scores after birds, with the rare three-under called an albatross.

questions.q: In tennis, what is a 'double fault'?
c: Missing both serves, losing the point
Two players calling the same shot
questions.f: Double faults are the only way to hand your opponent a point without them touching the ball.

questions.q: In ice hockey, where must a penalized player sit?
questions.f: While one team is short-handed, the other enjoys a 'power play' with an extra attacker.

questions.q: In tennis, what is played when a set reaches six games each?
questions.f: Tiebreaks are usually first to seven points, and players must win by two.

questions.q: In basketball, what does an 'assist' record?
c: A pass that leads directly to a basket
questions.f: Great playmakers rack up assists, proving that passing is as valuable as scoring.

questions.q: In cricket, what is a 'wide'?
c: A ball bowled too far from the batter to hit
A wide gap in the field
questions.f: A wide costs the bowling team a run and the ball must be bowled again.

questions.q: In cricket, what is an 'all-rounder'?
c: A player good at both batting and bowling
A fielder who circles the boundary
questions.f: All-rounders are precious because they do two jobs, giving captains extra choices.

questions.q: In baseball, what is the 'strike zone'?
c: The area over the plate where a pitch counts as a strike
questions.f: The zone stretches from a batter's knees to the middle of their chest, so it changes per player.

questions.q: In athletics, what happens to a sprinter who makes a false start?
c: They are disqualified from the race
They must run in lane one
questions.f: Sensors in the blocks detect movement faster than any human reaction time could be.

questions.q: In swimming, what is a 'flip turn'?
c: A somersault turn at the wall
questions.f: Flip turns save swimmers precious tenths of a second on every single lap.

questions.q: From what height do Olympic platform divers make their highest dives?
questions.f: Divers hit the water at around 50 km/h, which is why they enter hands or feet first.

questions.q: In ski jumping, judges score athletes on distance and what else?
c: Style in the air and on landing
How fast they climb back up
questions.f: Jumpers spread their skis into a V shape, a style that adds lift and distance.

questions.q: How many people ride in the largest Olympic bobsled?
questions.f: Bobsled crews sprint and push together before leaping in, and the brakeman boards last.

questions.q: How many colored faces does a standard Rubik's Cube have?
questions.f: A cube has 43 quintillion possible arrangements, yet any of them can be solved in 20 moves or fewer.

questions.q: How many sets must a player win to take a men's Grand Slam tennis match?
questions.f: Best-of-five matches can last over four hours, so stamina matters as much as skill.

questions.q: To how many points is a standard volleyball set played?
questions.f: Teams must also lead by two, and the deciding fifth set is played only to 15.

questions.q: How many numbered scoring segments does a dartboard have?
questions.f: The numbers are arranged so a slightly missed throw usually lands on a low score.

questions.q: How many red balls are on the table at the start of a snooker frame?
questions.f: Players must alternate red and colored balls, which is why breaks build up so fast.

questions.q: In eight-ball pool, which ball must be potted last?
questions.f: Sinking the eight ball too early loses the game instantly, so patience wins.

questions.q: At the Olympic closing ceremony, what is handed to the next host city?
questions.f: The mayor of the current host passes the flag on, a tradition begun in 1920.

questions.q: In the Paralympic sport of goalball, how do players track the ball?
c: By listening for bells inside it
By feeling vibrations in the floor
By following a teammate's voice only
questions.f: All goalball players wear eyeshades, so the whole arena stays silent during play.

questions.q: In rugby, what is the kick taken after a try called?
questions.f: A successful conversion adds two points, and the kick is taken in line with where the try was scored.

questions.q: Which item of clothing does Wimbledon famously require players to wear?
questions.f: The all-white rule dates from Victorian times, when visible sweat marks were thought improper.

questions.q: How often is the men's FIFA World Cup held?
questions.f: The tournament has been held every four years since 1930, apart from a gap in the 1940s.

questions.q: In archery and darts, what is the very center of the target called?
questions.f: Archers call the center the gold, since the innermost ring is colored gold.

questions.q: In snooker, potting the black ball is worth more than potting the pink.
questions.f: The colors rise in value from yellow at two up to black at seven.

questions.q: In goalball, every player wears eyeshades so nobody can see the ball.
questions.f: Because sight is removed for all, sighted and blind athletes compete on equal terms.

questions.q: A tennis tiebreak is won by the first player to reach exactly seven points.
questions.f: You must also lead by two, so tiebreaks sometimes stretch to 15-13 or beyond.

questions.q: The root 'ped' in 'pedometer', a step counter, means...?
questions.f: Latin 'pes' or 'pedis' means foot, and gives us pedal, pedestrian, and centipede.

questions.q: The 'kilo' in 'kilometer' means...?
questions.f: A 10,000-meter track race is ten kilometers, or 25 laps of a standard track.

questions.q: The 'centi' in 'centimeter' tells you it is...?
questions.f: High jump records are measured in centimeters, so one small unit can decide a medal.

questions.q: The 'meter' in 'thermometer' and 'kilometer' comes from a word meaning...?
questions.f: Greek 'metron' means measure, hiding in speedometer, diameter, and geometry.

questions.q: In a 'photo finish', the root 'photo' means...?
questions.f: Greek 'phos' means light, and photo-finish cameras capture thousands of light images per second.

questions.q: The 'tele' in 'television', where fans watch matches, means...?
questions.f: Television literally means seeing far, from Greek 'tele' plus Latin 'visio'.

questions.q: In 'autograph', the parts mean self plus...?
questions.f: So an autograph is literally self-writing, which is why only the star can give you one.

questions.q: The 'cycl' in 'cycling' and 'cyclone' means...?
questions.f: Greek 'kyklos' means circle, so cyclists really do travel by circles.

questions.q: In tennis, the score word 'deuce' comes from a word meaning...?
questions.f: From French 'deux', two: at deuce a player must win two points in a row to take the game.

questions.q: The 'cent' in cricket's 'century' means...?
questions.f: The same root builds cent, percent, and centenary, all about hundreds.

questions.q: A cricket 'wicketkeeper' is so named because they keep, or guard, the...?
questions.f: 'Wicket' once meant a small gate, which is just what three stumps and two bails resemble.

questions.q: In golf, what is a 'caddie'?
c: A person who carries a player's clubs and gives advice
questions.f: Top caddies read wind and slopes so well that players rarely ignore their advice.

questions.q: A word for a horse race over jumps is a...?
questions.f: Athletics has a steeplechase too, complete with barriers and a water jump.

questions.q: What does the term 'underdog' mean?
questions.f: Underdog victories are sport's best stories, precisely because nobody expects them.

questions.q: Which word describes moves practiced so often they feel automatic?
questions.f: Gymnasts perform a routine, a fixed sequence rehearsed hundreds of times.

questions.q: What is a 'spectacle' in the world of sport?
c: An impressive show for the crowd
questions.f: Opening ceremonies are designed as spectacles, packed with music, color, and light.

questions.q: In sport, 'stamina' means...?
c: The strength to keep going a long time
questions.f: Cyclists in three-week races need extraordinary stamina, riding daily for hours.

questions.q: What does it mean to 'clinch' a title?
questions.f: Teams can clinch a league with games to spare when no rival can catch them.

questions.q: 'Semifinal' and 'quarterfinal' both use fraction words to show how far along a tournament is.
questions.f: Quarter means one fourth and semi means half, describing the shrinking field of teams.

questions.q: In a knockout soccer match, how long is extra time in total?
questions.f: Extra time is two halves of 15 minutes, and a penalty shootout follows if scores stay level.

questions.q: How many hurdles must a sprinter clear in the 110 meter hurdles?
questions.f: The hurdles stand about waist-high, and top runners take exactly three strides between each.

questions.q: Over how many days is an Olympic decathlon contested?
questions.f: Day one ends with the 400 meters; day two finishes with the exhausting 1500 meters.

questions.q: What is the 'sweet spot' on a bat or racket?
c: The place that gives the best hit with least vibration
questions.f: Hit the sweet spot and the ball flies with almost no sting in your hands.

questions.q: Why do snooker players rub chalk on the tip of their cue?
c: To stop the tip slipping off the ball
questions.f: A slip is called a miscue, and even a tiny one can ruin a perfect shot.

questions.q: In rowing, a 'sculler' uses how many oars?
questions.f: Rowers who sweep hold a single long oar, while scullers work two shorter ones.

questions.q: In basketball, what is a 'double dribble'?
c: Bouncing the ball again after stopping your dribble
questions.f: Once you stop your dribble you must pass or shoot, so ball handlers think fast.

questions.q: In volleyball, what is a 'dig'?
c: A desperate save of a hard-driven ball
questions.f: Diggers often dive full length, sacrificing their knees to keep the ball alive.

questions.q: In soccer, what is a 'clean sheet'?
c: A game in which a team concedes no goals
questions.f: Goalkeepers treasure clean sheets, and league awards are given for collecting the most.

questions.q: A goalless draw is a game in which...?
questions.f: The suffix '-less' means without, as in fearless, endless, and goalless.

questions.q: An 'invincible' team is one that...?
questions.f: Latin 'vincere' means to conquer, so invincible means unconquerable.

questions.q: What is a 'spectator sport'?
questions.f: Soccer is the world's biggest spectator sport, watched by billions of people.

questions.q: In sport, 'flexibility' means...?
c: How far you can bend and stretch
How long you can hold your breath
questions.f: Gymnasts and divers stretch daily, because flexibility lets them shape the air.

questions.q: The athletics word 'javelin' originally meant a...?
questions.f: From Old French 'javelot', a light throwing spear; the sport keeps the hunting shape.

questions.q: The word 'somersault' is built from older words meaning...?
questions.f: From Old French 'sombresaut': 'sobre' (over) plus 'saut' (jump), nothing to do with summer!

questions.q: In figure skating, a 'quad' jump has how many mid-air turns?
questions.f: 'Quad' means four, and skaters spin four full rotations in under a second of airtime.

questions.q: In chess, the capture called 'en passant' can only be made against what?
c: A pawn that has just moved two squares
questions.f: The move must be played immediately or the right vanishes; 'en passant' means 'in passing'.

questions.q: The machine that resurfaces an ice rink between periods is named after whom?
questions.f: Zamboni built the first machine in 1949 to shave, wash, and re-ice a rink in minutes.

questions.q: The figure-skating jump called the 'salchow' is named after a skater from which country?
questions.f: Ulrich Salchow won ten world titles and gave his name to a takeoff from the back inside edge.

questions.q: In the Tour de France, what does the polka-dot jersey mark its wearer as?
questions.f: Riders chase 'King of the Mountains' points at the top of each categorized climb.

questions.q: How long is a professional boxing round?
questions.f: A one-minute rest follows each round, when trainers give advice in the corner.

questions.q: How heavy is the men's competition discus?
questions.f: The women's discus is 1 kg, which is why their throws travel a good deal further.

questions.q: How heavy is the men's shot in the Olympic shot put?
questions.f: That odd figure is exactly 16 pounds, the weight of an old British cannonball.

questions.q: Which Olympic running event includes a water jump on every lap?
questions.f: Runners hit the barrier with one foot and land in a pit of water almost 70 cm deep.

questions.q: How long is the Olympic open water swimming marathon?
questions.f: Swimmers race for around two hours in lakes or the sea, feeding from poles held out by coaches.

questions.q: The Olympic sport now called artistic swimming was previously known as what?
questions.f: The name changed in 2017; competitors are not allowed to touch the bottom of the pool.

questions.q: In sumo, what is the raised clay ring called?
questions.f: The dohyo is rebuilt for each tournament and swept with brooms between bouts.

questions.q: In kabaddi, how long does a raider have to complete a raid?
questions.f: The raider must tag opponents and return across the midline before the clock runs out.

questions.q: Chess's 'fifty-move rule' allows a player to claim what?
questions.f: If fifty moves pass with no capture and no pawn move, the game is declared drawn.

questions.q: How many tiles are in a standard mahjong set?
questions.f: Players build walls from the tiles, and the clacking sound is called the twittering of sparrows.

questions.q: How many tricks are played in each deal of contract bridge?
questions.f: Four players each hold 13 cards, so every deal produces exactly 13 tricks.

questions.q: How many letter tiles are in a standard English Scrabble set?
questions.f: Two of the 100 tiles are blanks, wild cards worth zero points but able to be any letter.

questions.q: How many clubs may a golfer carry in their bag during a competition round?
questions.f: Carrying a fifteenth club brings a penalty, so caddies count carefully before teeing off.

questions.q: How many overs does each team bowl in a One Day International cricket match?
questions.f: A full ODI innings is 300 legal balls, which usually takes about three and a half hours.

questions.q: How far apart are the bases on a professional baseball diamond?
questions.f: Ninety feet between bases has barely changed since the 1850s, balancing hitting and fielding.

questions.q: How many points does a Formula 1 race winner score under the modern system?
questions.f: Points run 25, 18, 15 down to one for tenth place, with a bonus for the fastest lap in some seasons.

questions.q: In boxing, what does the abbreviation TKO stand for?
questions.f: A TKO is called when a fighter cannot safely continue, even without being counted out.

questions.q: The Latin word 'harena', the origin of 'arena', actually means what?
questions.f: Roman arenas were floored with sand, which soaked up spills and gave sure footing.

questions.q: The 'ambi' in 'ambidextrous' means...?
questions.f: 'Dexter' meant right hand, so an ambidextrous player has two 'right' hands.

questions.q: The word 'record' comes from Latin parts meaning to bring back to the...?
questions.f: Latin 'cor' means heart; to record was to learn by heart before it meant to write down.

questions.q: The word 'trophy' comes from a Greek word describing what?
c: The turning back of an enemy
questions.f: Greeks built a 'tropaion' where a foe turned and fled; today the cup marks the same triumph.

questions.q: Sport's 'hat-trick' began in cricket, where a bowler taking three wickets in three balls won what?
questions.f: Clubs really did buy the bowler a new hat, and the phrase spread to every other sport.

questions.q: The sport 'polo' takes its name from a Himalayan word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Pulu' means ball in Balti, spoken in the mountains where British players first saw the game.

questions.q: The word 'rookie' is thought to be a worn-down form of which word?
questions.f: Army slang chewed 'recruit' into 'rookie', and sport borrowed it for first-year players.

questions.q: Rowing's 'coxswain' is built from old words meaning what?
questions.f: A 'cock' was a small boat and a 'swain' a servant, so the coxswain served the boat.

questions.q: The word 'regatta' first described boat races held where?
questions.f: Venetian 'regata' meant a contest or struggle, and gondola races made the word famous.

questions.q: In Olympic tradition, an 'Olympiad' is properly what?
questions.f: That is why Games are numbered by Olympiad even when a scheduled Games is not held.

questions.q: In Monopoly's original London edition, which is the most expensive property?
questions.f: American sets swapped in Boardwalk and Park Place, but the dark blue corner stayed priciest.

questions.q: In Le Mans-style endurance racing, drivers take turns sharing the same car.
questions.f: Teams of two or three drivers swap during pit stops, since nobody can race for 24 hours.

questions.q: At the Olympics the decathlon is contested by men and the heptathlon by women.
questions.f: Men tackle ten events over two days; women contest seven, including the javelin and 800 m.

questions.q: A few dollars earned playing summer baseball, medals stripped in 1913, and a family finally handed them back decades later converge on which athlete?
questions.f: Thorpe won both the pentathlon and decathlon at Stockholm 1912, and a king called him the world's greatest athlete.

questions.q: A 30-year-old mother of two told she was past it, a coach she had married, and the nickname 'the Flying Housewife' point to which sprinter?
questions.f: Blankers-Koen won four golds at London 1948 while holding world records she could not even enter.

questions.q: Six Olympic Games spanning 28 years, a coach who once told him he was too old, and a fitness test he answered by beating the whole national squad describe which fencer?
questions.f: Gerevich won six consecutive team sabre golds from 1932 to 1960, a feat unmatched in any sport.

questions.q: A Swedish marksman shooting at moving deer targets, a first Games entered at 60, and a final medal collected at 72 identify which Olympian?
questions.f: Swahn remains the oldest Olympic medalist ever, and his son competed alongside him.

questions.q: A diabetes diagnosis at 35, a vow after Atlanta that anyone seeing him near a boat should shoot him, and a Sydney comeback converge on which rower?
questions.f: Redgrave won rowing gold at five consecutive Olympic Games between 1984 and 2000.

questions.q: A Hawaiian whose flutter kick baffled 1912 officials, an eight-man rescue made with a board, and demonstration waves ridden in Australia point to whom?
questions.f: Kahanamoku won Olympic swimming gold and is celebrated as the man who carried surfing to the world.

questions.q: A swimmer who won five golds, then swung through Hollywood jungles for two decades, is which athlete?
questions.f: Weissmuller set dozens of world records before playing Tarzan in twelve films.

questions.q: A torn cartilage in 1964, a neck brace worn in warm-up, and four straight Olympic titles in one throwing event belong to which athlete?
questions.f: Oerter won discus gold at four consecutive Games, each time as an underdog against the favorite.

questions.q: A Ukrainian gymnast who competed in three Games in the 1950s and 60s and held the record of 18 Olympic medals until 2012 is who?
questions.f: Latynina's 18 medals stood as the all-time record for 48 years, until Michael Phelps passed her.

questions.q: A dental student, a mustache he joked warmed his upper lip, and seven finals in eight Munich days converge on which swimmer?
questions.f: Spitz won seven golds in 1972, a single-Games record that lasted until Beijing 2008.

questions.q: A Kenyan police officer racing in pain from gallstones, a stadium traffic jam he escaped by jogging the last mile, and thin Mexican air converge on whom?
questions.f: Keino won 1500 m gold in 1968 and launched Kenya's long reign in distance running.

questions.q: A hooded full-body racing suit, a cauldron lit by the same athlete who later won the 400 meters, and 1997 world silver point to which runner?
questions.f: Freeman lit the Sydney 2000 flame and then won gold before her home crowd.

questions.q: The Olympic torch relay from Olympia to the host city was staged for the very first time at which Games?
questions.f: The relay was invented for 1936 and has opened every Games since, carried by thousands of runners.

questions.q: Tennis at the sprawling 1900 Paris Games, a player deaf since her twenties, and a milestone for women's sport converge on which champion?
questions.f: Cooper became the first individual female Olympic champion, five years before women's events were common.

questions.q: A Spartan princess who never entered the stadium, a team of chariot horses she owned, and victories in 396 and 392 BC identify whom?
questions.f: Chariot crowns went to the owner, so Kyniska became the first woman recorded as an Olympic victor.

questions.q: Twelve olive crowns, four consecutive ancient Games, and victories in three separate running events belong to which athlete of antiquity?
questions.f: Leonidas swept the stadion, diaulos, and armored race four Games running in the 2nd century BC.

questions.q: A cook from Elis, a single footrace, and the year 776 BC converge on which figure?
c: Coroebus, the first recorded Olympic champion
questions.f: Coroebus won the stadion sprint, the only event at the earliest recorded ancient Games.

questions.q: Legends of a young bull carried on his shoulders and a diet of enormous daily meals surround which ancient wrestler?
questions.f: Milo won six Olympic wrestling crowns, and stories of his strength grew taller with every retelling.

questions.q: Bronze statues at Olympia called the 'Zanes' were paid for using what?
questions.f: Each statue carried the cheat's name, so competitors walked past a wall of shame into the stadium.

questions.q: The ancient Greek 'hoplitodromos' was a footrace run while carrying what?
questions.f: The armored race let athletes show they were ready to defend their city, not just win laurels.

questions.q: The ancient Greek 'ekecheiria' declared before each Olympics was what?
c: A sacred truce allowing safe travel to the Games
questions.f: The truce let competitors and spectators cross warring territories unharmed on the way to Olympia.

questions.q: The ancient Heraean Games at Olympia were footraces held for whom?
questions.f: Winners received olive crowns and portions of a sacrificed cow, honoring the goddess Hera.

questions.q: An 1892 speech at the Sorbonne, a committee founded in 1894, and a lifelong belief in education through sport point to which figure?
questions.f: Coubertin revived the Olympics and later designed the five-ring symbol himself.

questions.q: A Scottish missionary who refused to run on a Sunday, an English sprinter facing prejudice, and Paris 1924 inspired which famous film?
questions.f: Eric Liddell switched to the 400 m and won it; Harold Abrahams took the 100 m at the same Games.

questions.q: A dusty, boiling 1904 marathon, a runner who rode part of the way in a car, and a hastily returned trophy converge on which host city's Games?
questions.f: Fred Lorz was disqualified after his lift, and the true winner finished in around three and a half hours.

questions.q: Athletes asked to bring their own towels, no new venues built, and rationing still in force describe which Olympics, nicknamed the Austerity Games?
questions.f: Britain hosted just three years after the war, housing competitors in colleges and army camps.

questions.q: An archer, a flaming arrow, and an opening ceremony in 1992 converge on which host city?
questions.f: Paralympic archer Antonio Rebollo shot his arrow over the cauldron, igniting the gas as it passed.

questions.q: Which Games were the first at which every competing nation included at least one female athlete?
questions.f: Women's boxing also debuted in 2012, meaning every sport on the program finally included women.

questions.q: A neurologist at an English spinal hospital, an archery contest for wheelchair patients in 1948, and a movement that grew into a global Games point to whom?
questions.f: Guttmann's Stoke Mandeville Games grew directly into the modern Paralympic Games.

questions.q: A backyard summer camp in Maryland, a sister who had intellectual disabilities, and a 1968 Chicago event founded which movement?
questions.f: Eunice Kennedy Shriver's camp grew into a movement now serving millions of athletes worldwide.

questions.q: Which multi-sport event began in 1930 at Hamilton, Canada under the name the British Empire Games?
questions.f: Renamed several times, it is now the Commonwealth Games, held every four years.

questions.q: The very first Asian Games, held in 1951, took place in which city?
questions.f: Eleven nations competed in New Delhi, with India topping the medal table's second place.

questions.q: A wrestler from a Maharashtra village, a bronze at Helsinki 1952, and independent India's first individual Olympic medal identify whom?
questions.f: Jadhav wrestled in the bantamweight class; villagers sold belongings to fund his trip.

questions.q: A weightlifter from Andhra Pradesh, a bronze in the 69 kg class at Sydney 2000, and a first for Indian women converge on whom?
questions.f: Malleswari became the first Indian woman ever to win an Olympic medal.

questions.q: A 10-meter air rifle, a home range built by his family, and Beijing 2008 point to which athlete?
questions.f: Bindra's win was India's first individual Olympic gold medal in any sport.

questions.q: A Haryana farmer's son, a throw of 87.58 meters in Tokyo, and India's first Olympic gold in athletics belong to whom?
questions.f: Chopra's javelin gold in 2021 was India's first athletics medal of any color at the Olympics.

questions.q: A doubles specialist who won an unlikely singles bronze at Atlanta 1996 for India is which player?
questions.f: Paes ended a 44-year wait for an individual Indian Olympic medal in any sport.

questions.q: Five goals in the 1952 Olympic hockey final, a policeman's career in Punjab, and three golds converge on which player?
questions.f: His five goals in one Olympic final remain a record for the men's hockey gold medal match.

questions.q: How many Olympic gold medals has India's men's field hockey team won in total?
questions.f: India won six golds in a row from 1928 to 1956, and its eighth arrived in Moscow in 1980.

questions.q: The Greek word 'agon', meaning a contest, is the hidden root of which English word?
questions.f: The struggle of a contest gave us agony, protagonist, and antagonist alike.

questions.q: The ancient 'palaestra' was a school built for training in which discipline?
questions.f: Greek 'pale' means wrestling, and the palaestra's sandy courtyard sat beside the gymnasium.

questions.q: Victors at the ancient Olympic Games were crowned with wreaths cut from a wild olive tree at Olympia.
questions.f: A golden sickle cut branches from a sacred tree said to have been planted by Heracles himself.

questions.q: The chess rook's name traces to a Persian word 'rukh' meaning what?
questions.f: Indian and Persian armies fielded chariots, and only later did European carvers turn them into castles.

questions.q: In the older Indian and Persian forms of chess, the piece we call the bishop represented what?
questions.f: Sanskrit chaturanga fielded four arms of an army: infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots.

questions.q: In chess, 'zugzwang' describes a position in which a player...?
c: Would be better off not having to move at all
questions.f: German for 'move compulsion', zugzwang decides countless endgames, since passing your turn is illegal.

questions.q: In chess, a 'fianchetto' is named from an Italian word meaning what?
questions.f: The bishop slides to the flank behind an advanced pawn, sniping along the long diagonal.

questions.q: In 'stalemate', the older meaning of 'stale' is closest to which idea?
questions.f: The word arrived from Anglo-French for a standstill; only later did 'stale' come to mean old bread.

questions.q: A retired Indiana architect's puzzle called Number Place, a Japanese magazine's rename, and a New Zealander's program that hooked British papers converge on which pastime?
questions.f: Howard Garns devised it in 1979; the Japanese name shortens a phrase meaning 'the digits must be single'.

questions.q: A Moscow computer scientist, childhood pentomino puzzles, and a name blending the Greek for four with his favorite sport point to which game?
questions.f: Alexey Pajitnov combined 'tetra' with 'tennis' in 1984; his falling blocks are still everywhere.

questions.q: An Ohio barber, a family argument over the rules of crazy eights, and decks sold from his shop in 1971 gave the world which card game?
questions.f: Merle Robbins printed the first 5,000 decks himself and sold them to customers between haircuts.

questions.q: A solicitor's clerk on wartime fire-watching duty, a love of murder-mystery parlour games, and a 1947 patent produced which board game?
questions.f: Anthony Pratt's game reached shops in 1949, and Americans know it simply as Clue.

questions.q: A missing Scrabble set, a Montreal photo editor and a sports journalist, and six colored wedges converge on which 1981 game?
questions.f: Chris Haney and Scott Abbott designed it in 45 minutes; it went on to sell tens of millions of copies.

questions.q: A German dental technician, Viking voyages that shaped an earlier design, and sheep traded for wood point to which modern board game?
questions.f: Klaus Teuber's 1995 game of roads and resources launched the boom in modern German-style board games.

questions.q: A gaming board among a boy king's grave goods, thirty squares in three rows, and throwing sticks used instead of dice describe which ancient game?
questions.f: Senet boards appear in Egyptian tombs for over 2,000 years, including four found with Tutankhamun.

questions.q: In Go, the extra points given to the white player are called 'komi'. Why?
c: To offset black's advantage in moving first
questions.f: Modern rules usually set komi at six and a half points, so draws become impossible.

questions.q: The Chinese board game xiangqi has a distinctive feature running across the middle of its board. What is it?
questions.f: Only some pieces may cross the river, and the two generals must never face each other along an open file.

questions.q: In playing cards, the figure we now call the jack was traditionally called what?
questions.f: Printers switched to 'jack' so the corner index J could not be confused with K for king.

questions.q: The playing-card suit name 'spade' comes from an Italian word meaning what?
questions.f: Italian 'spada' means sword; the French later redrew the suit as a black pointed leaf shape.

questions.q: The card called the 'ace' takes its name from a word meaning what?
c: A small Roman coin or unit
questions.f: Latin 'as' meant a unit of one, which is why the ace originally counted lowest, not highest.

questions.q: The joker was added to standard card decks in the 1860s specifically for which game?
questions.f: American euchre players needed a top trump card, and the grinning joker was invented to fill the role.

questions.q: The word 'domino' probably came into gaming from the name of what?
questions.f: The masquerade domino was a black hood with a white lining, matching the tiles' colors.

questions.q: In tennis, the game's name is thought to come from a French call meaning what?
questions.f: Servers in the old indoor game shouted 'tenez!' as they struck, and English ears heard 'tennis'.

questions.q: The word 'racquet' traces back to an Arabic word meaning what?
questions.f: Early players batted the ball with a bare palm; 'rahat al-yad' means the palm of the hand.

questions.q: In golf, a seaside course is called a 'links' because the word originally meant what?
c: Ridged ground between beach and farmland
questions.f: Old English 'hlinc' meant a rise or ridge; sandy links land was useless for farming but perfect for golf.

questions.q: A music-hall song of 1890 about an unseen opponent, a phantom standard score for a hole, and a golf term for one over par converge on which word?
questions.f: Golfers played against the mysterious 'Bogey Man' of the song; his score later became one over par.

questions.q: Golf's word 'caddie' comes from a French word meaning what?
questions.f: French 'cadet' passed into Scots as 'cawdy', a general errand-runner, before it meant a club carrier.

questions.q: In cricket, the delivery called a 'yorker' most likely takes its name from what?
questions.f: Yorkshire bowlers were famous for the trick of pitching right at a batter's toes.

questions.q: In cricket, a score of 111 is nicknamed a 'Nelson'. What do superstitious players do about it?
c: Lift their feet off the ground until the score changes
questions.f: Umpire David Shepherd famously hopped on the spot whenever the score reached Nelson.

questions.q: In Australian cricket, what is the 'baggy green'?
questions.f: Players receive one cap for a whole career, and wearing a battered old one is a badge of honor.

questions.q: A club disbanded in 1878, silver rupees withdrawn from an Indian bank, and three king cobras forming the handles describe which trophy?
questions.f: The Calcutta Football Club melted its funds into a cup now contested by England and Scotland at rugby.

questions.q: A chief hidden in a food pit, a chant composed about escaping capture, and a challenge performed before matches since 1905 converge on what?
questions.f: Te Rauparaha composed Ka Mate, now performed by New Zealand's All Blacks before kickoff.

questions.q: Rugby's word 'scrum' is a shortening of which longer word?
questions.f: 'Scrimmage' itself came from 'skirmish', so the scrum's name has a battlefield past.

questions.q: The word 'gymkhana' is built from a borrowed word meaning what kind of building?
questions.f: Persian and Urdu 'gend-khana' meant ball house; British India reshaped it into a sports meeting.

questions.q: Polo's 'chukka' comes from a Hindi word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Chakkar' means a turn or round, and each chukka lasts about seven and a half minutes.

questions.q: In the Tour de France, what is the 'lanterne rouge'?
questions.f: The name recalls the red lamp on a train's last carriage, and fans cheer the survivor who wears it.

questions.q: In professional cycling, what is a 'domestique'?
c: A rider whose job is to help the team leader
A rider in their first season
questions.f: French for servant, domestiques fetch bottles, block wind, and even give up their own bikes.

questions.q: The martial art name 'sambo' is a shortened Russian phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Sambo blends judo and folk wrestling styles from across the former Soviet republics.

questions.q: In martial arts ranking, what is the difference between 'kyu' and 'dan' grades?
c: Kyu grades come before black belt, dan grades after
Kyu grades are for weapons only
questions.f: Kyu numbers count downward toward first dan, then dan numbers count upward from there.

questions.q: In sumo, what is a 'yokozuna'?
c: The highest rank a wrestler can hold
questions.f: Only a handful of yokozuna are named each century, and one can never be demoted, only retire.

questions.q: The Southeast Asian sport 'sepak takraw' is played with a ball made of what?
questions.f: Players spike the light ball over a net with bicycle kicks, never using their hands.

questions.q: In the Basque sport of jai alai, players catch and hurl the ball using what?
c: A curved wicker basket strapped to the arm
questions.f: The name means 'merry festival', and its pelota can travel faster than 250 km/h.

questions.q: In the Irish sport of hurling, what is the ball called?
questions.f: The stick is a hurley, and skilled players can balance the sliotar on it while sprinting.

questions.q: Curling is nicknamed 'the roaring game' because of the sound stones make sliding over pebbled ice.
questions.f: Sprayed water droplets freeze into 'pebbles', and stones rumble across them like distant thunder.

questions.q: Frozen shell craters, carols traded between opposing trenches in December 1914, and a kickabout in no-man's-land are remembered as what?
questions.f: Soldiers in several places laid down arms to play football, a story still marked with memorial matches.

questions.q: A munitions factory team from Preston, crowds of 50,000 in 1920, and an English ban that lasted 50 years converge on which pioneers?
questions.f: The FA banned women from its grounds in 1921, calling the game unsuitable; the ban ended in 1971.

questions.q: Who scored the first goal in the history of the football World Cup, in 1930?
questions.f: Laurent volleyed France's opener against Mexico; he later said nobody realized it would matter so much.

questions.q: A shootout in Belgrade in 1976, a chipped penalty straight down the middle, and a goalkeeper diving early gave which technique its name?
questions.f: Antonin Panenka's cheeky chip won the European Championship for Czechoslovakia.

questions.q: A Dutch winger at the 1974 World Cup, a Swedish defender left facing the wrong way, and a drag-back still taught today converge on which move?
questions.f: Johan Cruyff faked a cross, dragged the ball behind his standing leg, and accelerated away.

questions.q: A childhood illness that left his legs curved, a nickname meaning 'little bird', and two World Cup wins in the late 1950s describe which player?
questions.f: Garrincha's bent legs made his dribbling impossible to read, and Brazil never lost when he and Pele both played.

questions.q: Which change to football's offside law in 1925 caused goal totals to leap almost overnight?
c: Needing two opponents ahead instead of three
Allowing offside only in the penalty area
Letting the goalkeeper be counted twice
questions.f: Teams responded by inventing the centre-back, and English league goals jumped by over a thousand that season.

questions.q: In which city was FIFA, football's world governing body, founded in 1904?
questions.f: Seven European associations signed the founding statutes; FIFA moved to Zurich only in 1932.

questions.q: A 1932-33 cricket tour of Australia, fast bowling aimed to cramp a great batsman, and a diplomatic row between governments are known as what?
questions.f: England's leg-side tactics against Don Bradman were so controversial that the laws were later changed.

questions.q: A Swansea ground in 1968, a Glamorgan bowler named Malcolm Nash, and one over that cost 36 runs converge on which batsman?
questions.f: Sobers became the first player to hit six sixes in a single over of first-class cricket.

questions.q: Which batsman holds the record for the highest individual score in a Test innings?
