questions.f: Lara reclaimed the record in 2004 in Antigua, six months after Hayden had taken it from him.

questions.q: An Old Trafford pitch in 1956, a Surrey off-spinner, and 19 wickets in a single Test match converge on whom?
questions.f: Laker took nine wickets in the first innings and all ten in the second, a record still unmatched.

questions.q: A Barbados Test of 1958, an innings lasting over 16 hours, and a nickname 'the Little Master' point to which batsman?
questions.f: Hanif batted 970 minutes to save the match, the longest innings ever played in first-class cricket.

questions.q: A Manchester Test in 1993, a ball that drifted then spun sharply behind Mike Gatting's legs, and a first delivery in Ashes cricket converge on whom?
questions.f: Warne's leg-break is remembered as the Ball of the Century, and he went on to over 700 Test wickets.

questions.q: Which bowler holds the record for the most wickets in Test cricket history?
questions.f: Muralitharan's unusually flexible wrist let him spin the ball both ways with the same action.

questions.q: How many Test cricket matches in history have finished as a tie, with the scores exactly level?
questions.f: Only 1960 at Brisbane and 1986 at Madras have ended level in nearly 2,500 Test matches.

questions.q: A Hershey, Pennsylvania arena in 1962, a game finished by a 100-point performance, and no video footage surviving converge on which player?
questions.f: Chamberlain also averaged over 50 points per game that whole season, a record nobody has approached.

questions.q: A team founded in Chicago in 1926 that toured with comedy routines, yet took its name from a New York neighborhood, is which side?
questions.f: The name suggested a Black team and worldwide travel; the Globetrotters have since played in over 120 countries.

questions.q: Which basketball team, assembled for Barcelona 1992, is remembered as the 'Dream Team'?
c: The United States men's Olympic squad
questions.f: It was the first Olympics open to NBA professionals, and the team won by an average of 44 points.

questions.q: A Brooklyn debut in April 1947, a number 42 now retired by every team, and a college career in four sports converge on which athlete?
questions.f: Robinson broke baseball's colour barrier and was named Rookie of the Year that same season.

questions.q: A 1932 World Series game, a gesture toward the outfield still argued over, and a home run on the very next pitch belong to which player?
questions.f: Ruth's 'called shot' may have been aimed at the pitcher or the crowd; the ball landed in the bleachers either way.

questions.q: Baseball's award for the best pitcher is named after a man who won how many games?
questions.f: Cy Young's 511 career wins are so far ahead of everyone else that the record is considered unbreakable.

questions.q: Why did tennis switch from white balls to yellow ones in 1972?
c: Yellow shows up better on television
questions.f: Wimbledon held on to white balls until 1986, long after the rest of the tennis world changed.

questions.q: A Houston arena in 1973, a 55-year-old former champion's challenge, and 30,000 spectators converge on which famous match?
questions.f: Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs in straight sets, a huge moment for women's professional sport.

questions.q: Which tennis player is the only one to win all four Grand Slam titles in the same calendar year twice?
questions.f: Laver did it as an amateur in 1962 and again as a professional in 1969, seven years apart.

questions.q: In 1988 one tennis player won all four majors plus Olympic gold in a single year. Who?
questions.f: Graf's feat was christened the Golden Slam, and no singles player has repeated it since.

questions.q: Which player holds the record for the most Grand Slam singles titles in tennis history?
questions.f: Court won 11 of her titles at the Australian Open, in an era when many rivals skipped the trip.

questions.q: A 1967 Boston race, a bib entered under initials, and an official who tried to pull a runner off the course converge on which athlete?
questions.f: Switzer finished the marathon; women were officially allowed to enter Boston five years later.

questions.q: A Ukrainian vaulter who set 35 outdoor and indoor world records and was first over six meters is who?
questions.f: Bubka broke his own record centimeter by centimeter, collecting a bonus for each new mark.

questions.q: Which athlete has held the high jump world record since 1993, clearing 2.45 meters?
questions.f: Sotomayor's mark has stood longer than almost any other athletics record on the books.

questions.q: Why was the men's javelin redesigned in 1986?
c: Throws were getting dangerously long for stadiums
The old javelin broke too easily
questions.f: Shifting the centre of gravity forward made javelins dip sooner, cutting distances by around ten percent.

questions.q: Why did swimming's governing body ban polyurethane bodysuits from 2010?
c: They added buoyancy and speed unfairly
They were too expensive to make
questions.f: Over 100 world records fell in 2008 and 2009 while the suits were legal, so the rules were rewritten.

questions.q: A 1970 crash at Oberstdorf, a tumble replayed weekly for decades on American television, and the phrase 'the agony of defeat' converge on which athlete?
questions.f: Bogataj walked away with only a mild concussion, and later attended an awards show as a celebrity.

questions.q: A Sarajevo ice rink in 1984, a Ravel composition, and a set of perfect sixes for artistic impression describe which pair?
questions.f: Torvill and Dean's Bolero earned nine perfect 6.0 marks, still the most famous routine in ice dance.

questions.q: A Norwegian skater who won three Olympic titles and then starred in Hollywood ice films is who?
questions.f: Henie also introduced short skirts and white boots to figure skating, changing the sport's look forever.

questions.q: The winter sliding sport 'skeleton' is thought to be named after what?
c: The bony look of its early metal sled
questions.f: Riders on the Cresta Run at St Moritz began going head-first in the 1880s, and the name stuck.

questions.q: The word 'bobsleigh' comes from early riders doing what to go faster?
c: Bobbing their bodies back and forth
Bobbing their heads under the wind
questions.f: The bobbing turned out not to help much, but the name outlasted the technique.

questions.q: An amateur who won all four of golf's majors in 1930 and retired at 28, later helping design a Georgia course, was who?
questions.f: Jones's clean sweep is called the Impregnable Quadrilateral, and he co-founded Augusta National.

questions.q: Golf's oldest major, first played in 1860, awards which trophy?
questions.f: The winner of The Open first received a red leather Challenge Belt; the Claret Jug arrived in 1872.

questions.q: A stolen bicycle reported to a Louisville policeman, an Olympic light-heavyweight gold in 1960, and a name changed in 1964 converge on which athlete?
questions.f: The officer who took the bicycle report was a boxing coach who invited young Cassius Clay to train.

questions.q: Formula One's Nurburgring Nordschleife was nicknamed 'the Green Hell' by Jackie Stewart.
questions.f: The 20-kilometer forest circuit has more than 70 corners, and Stewart's nickname stuck for good.

questions.q: A Cambridge college wall, a rulebook of 1848 pinned up for students, and an attempt to settle arguments between old schoolboys converge on which document?
questions.f: The Cambridge Rules shaped the Football Association's laws of 1863, the ancestor of today's game.

questions.q: A Sheffield club founded in 1857, a corner kick invented locally, and the world's oldest football club still playing converge on which side?
questions.f: Sheffield FC's early code gave football the corner kick, the throw-in, and the crossbar.

questions.q: A ban on tampering with the pitch, the 1744 Laws fixing the length at 22 yards, and an old surveyor's unit converge on which cricket measurement?
c: The length of a cricket pitch
questions.f: Twenty-two yards is exactly one chain, a surveying unit of 100 links used to lay out fields.

questions.q: A tavern keeper's field in London, a club that moved twice taking its turf along, and laws of cricket published in 1788 converge on which institution?
questions.f: The MCC still owns and rewrites the Laws of Cricket, and its home is Lord's in London.

questions.q: A Victorian doctor with a huge beard, first-class runs scored across five decades, and the first double century in cricket describe whom?
questions.f: Grace was so popular that crowds paid double when he played, and he captained England at 50.

questions.q: A cricket-mad Melbourne athlete, a winter game invented in 1858 to keep players fit, and an oval-shaped field converge on which sport's founding?
questions.f: Tom Wills proposed the game so cricketers could train in winter, which is why it is played on cricket ovals.

questions.q: A Massachusetts college in 1895, a game designed for businessmen who found basketball too rough, and a net raised above head height converge on which sport?
questions.f: William Morgan borrowed from tennis, handball, and baseball, and his net was just two meters high.

questions.q: An English boarding-school teacher's 1890s adaptation of basketball, hoops without backboards, and zones players may not leave converge on which sport?
questions.f: Netball spread across the British Empire and is now played by millions, mostly women and girls.

questions.q: A Dutch teacher's 1902 game, mixed teams by design, and a basket on a pole with no backboard describe which sport?
questions.f: 'Korf' means basket in Dutch, and korfball remains one of very few sports played by mixed teams throughout.

questions.q: A Canadian physical trainer in 1891, a game for the space between football and baseball seasons, and an indoor court converge on which invention?
questions.f: James Naismith wrote 13 rules in about an hour, and the first game ended 1-0.

questions.q: A Brazilian sport played on hard courts with a heavier, low-bouncing ball, born on the streets of 1930s Uruguay, is known as what?
questions.f: Futsal's name blends Spanish and Portuguese words for 'indoor football', and it trains dazzling close control.

questions.q: A Mexican businessman's 1969 court, walls kept from squash, and doubles played with stringed bats converge on which fast-growing racket sport?
questions.f: Enrique Corcuera walled in his court to stop balls escaping, and padel now has millions of players.

questions.q: A Washington state island in 1965, an improvised game using a badminton court and table tennis paddles, and a family dog often blamed for the name converge on which sport?
questions.f: The founders' dog Pickles may have chased the ball, though some say the name came from boat crews.

questions.q: A Scottish loch village's winter pastime, granite from an offshore islet, and brooms once made of corn straw converge on which sport's origins?
questions.f: Curling stones were first hauled from Scottish riverbeds, and matches date to at least the 1540s.

questions.q: A Montreal skating rink in 1875, a wooden disc used to stop the ball flying into spectators, and the first organized indoor game converge on what?
c: The invention of the hockey puck
questions.f: Players sliced a rubber ball flat so it would stay on the ice, creating the puck we know today.

questions.q: A frozen fen in the Netherlands, races between villages on natural ice, and a 200-kilometer route ridden only in the coldest winters describe which event?
questions.f: The Eleven Cities Tour has been held only 15 times since 1909, whenever the canals freeze thick enough.

questions.q: A 1922 Swedish race retracing a 16th-century royal escape on skis is known as what?
questions.f: Nearly 16,000 skiers cover 90 kilometers, and the winner is showered with a wreath of birch.

questions.q: In archery, what does an 'end' of arrows shot at a longer distance require competitors to do first?
c: Score and collect arrows before the next end
questions.f: Modern Olympic recurve archers shoot at 70 meters, where the gold ring looks the size of a drawing pin.

questions.q: A rattan pole planted in a courtyard, wrestlers building strength through aerial poses, and a Maratha training tradition converge on which Indian sport?
questions.f: 'Mallakhamb' means wrestler's pole, and gymnasts spin around it in poses held for seconds at a time.

questions.q: A pit of red earth mixed with oil and turmeric, daily routines called 'jor', and a training hall known as an akhara belong to which sport?
questions.f: Indian pehlwani wrestlers train in mud pits, and the soil is treated to keep it soft and clean.

questions.q: A hundred rowers in a single canoe, songs sung to keep time, and a Kerala festival on the Pamba river describe which race?
questions.f: Kerala's snake boats can carry over 100 paddlers and are among the longest watercraft used in sport.

questions.q: A wooden stick struck in mid-air, a smaller tapered peg, and a village game seen as an ancestor of cricket converge on which Indian pastime?
questions.f: Players flick the small gilli into the air with the danda stick, then hit it as far as they can.

questions.q: A pile of seven flat stones, a rubber ball thrown to scatter them, and a race to rebuild the tower name which Indian street game?
questions.f: Known as pittu or seven stones in different regions, the game needs only stones and a ball.

questions.q: In carrom, the red disc that must be pocketed and then 'covered' by another piece is called what?
questions.f: Pocket the queen and you must sink one of your own pieces next, or the queen returns to the centre.

questions.q: In kabaddi, what is the 'bonus line'?
c: A line a raider can cross for an extra point
questions.f: A raider must touch beyond the bonus line with one foot in the air to claim the extra point.

questions.q: In kho-kho, how do the chasers in the sitting line face?
questions.f: Because neighbors face opposite ways, a tagged teammate can spring up and sprint in either direction.

questions.q: In the ancient Roman world, what was a 'ludus'?
c: A training school for public contests
questions.f: The Latin word covered both play and school, and it gives us 'ludicrous' and the game name Ludo.

questions.q: The word 'athletics' as a sport name covers three families of events. Which are they?
questions.f: Americans call the same sport 'track and field', while world championships use 'athletics'.

questions.q: The word 'pentathlon' at the ancient Games covered which set of events?
c: Running, jumping, discus, javelin, and wrestling
Boxing, running, swimming, riding, and archery
Chariot racing and four foot races
questions.f: The modern pentathlon, invented in 1912, swapped in fencing, swimming, riding, shooting, and running.

questions.q: The word 'discipline', used for each branch of a sport, comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Latin 'discere' means to learn, so a discipline was first a subject taught, not a punishment.

questions.q: The word 'stamina' originally referred to what, in Latin?
c: Threads of life spun by the Fates
questions.f: Latin 'stamina' were threads; the idea of a thread of life stretched into meaning lasting strength.

questions.q: The word 'tournament' shares a root with which everyday word?
questions.f: Old French 'tornoiement' came from turning, describing knights wheeling their horses to charge again.

questions.q: The word 'prize' and the word 'price' both descend from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Latin 'pretium' meant worth or reward, and the two English spellings drifted apart over centuries.

questions.q: The word 'gauntlet', as in 'running the gauntlet', came into English from a word meaning what?
questions.f: Swedish 'gatlopp' meant lane-run; English ears reshaped it into the name of an armored glove.

questions.q: An athlete's 'quadriceps' muscle group is named for the fact that it has what?
c: Four times the strength of the hamstring
questions.f: Latin 'quadri' plus 'caput' means four heads, three from the thigh bone and one from the hip.

questions.q: The 'Achilles tendon', famous among sprinters, is named after a hero said to be vulnerable where?
questions.f: The tendon is the thickest in the human body, and a sprinter's push-off puts huge force through it.

questions.q: Why does the marathon's official distance carry the odd figure of 42.195 kilometers?
c: It matched a lengthened 1908 course in London
It was the exact distance from Marathon to Athens
It was set by a coin toss in 1921
questions.f: The 1908 course ran 26 miles 385 yards, and that measurement was adopted as standard in 1921.

questions.q: What does the 'Fosbury' name describe in high jumping, in technical terms?
c: Clearing the bar head-first on your back
questions.f: Deep foam landing pits made the backwards technique safe, and it swept away the old straddle roll.

questions.q: The chess term 'grandmaster' was made an official international title by FIDE in 1950.
questions.f: The first list of 27 grandmasters included Mikhail Botvinnik, Max Euwe, and Samuel Reshevsky.

questions.q: FIDE, the world chess federation, uses the Latin motto 'Gens una sumus', meaning 'we are one people'.
questions.f: The motto has appeared on the federation's emblem since 1924, when FIDE was founded in Paris.

questions.q: A 'bonspiel' is the name for a curling tournament.
questions.f: Curling has its own vocabulary, from the skip who calls shots to the hog line the stone must cross.

questions.q: Which instrument do many kids learn first at school by blowing into it?
questions.f: Recorders are very old—one found in a castle moat in Holland is more than 600 years old!

questions.q: A person who plays the piano is called a…?
questions.f: Adding '-ist' to a word often means 'a person who does it,' like artist and cyclist.

questions.q: What do you call a person who plays the drums?
questions.f: The ending '-er' turns an action into a person, like teach into teacher.

questions.q: A woman who dances in a ballet is called a…?
questions.f: 'Ballerina' is an Italian word—ballet uses words from Italy and France.

questions.q: What is a short, catchy tune in a TV advert called?
questions.f: Jingles are written to get stuck in your head so you remember the product.

questions.q: A joyful song that people sing at Christmas time is called a…?
questions.f: Long ago, a carol was a circle dance with singing, not just a song.

questions.q: What is the main tune of a song called?
questions.f: 'Melody' comes from old Greek words for song and singing.

questions.q: In which dance do you lean back and pass under a low stick?
questions.f: Limbo dancing comes from the island of Trinidad, and champions can pass under sticks lower than a chair seat!

questions.q: What do ballet dancers wear on their feet?
questions.f: Ballet slippers are soft and thin so dancers can point and bend their feet easily.

questions.q: A triangle is a metal instrument you strike with a small metal rod.
questions.f: The triangle hangs from a loop so it can ring freely when you tap it.

questions.q: What do you call the singer who stands at the front of a band?
questions.f: The lead singer is also called the 'front man' or 'front woman' of the band.

questions.q: Marching bands play music while walking in parades.
questions.f: Marching band members practice playing and stepping in patterns at the same time.

questions.q: Which big drum in a drum kit is played with a foot pedal?
questions.f: The bass drum makes the deep 'boom' you can feel in your chest at concerts.

questions.q: A show where the actors sing and dance to tell the story is called a…?
questions.f: Famous musicals like The Lion King are performed on stages all over the world.

questions.q: Where do people usually go to watch an orchestra perform?
questions.f: Concert halls are specially shaped so the music sounds clear in every seat.

questions.q: What is the raised platform where singers and dancers perform called?
questions.f: The word 'stage' comes from an old French word for a standing place.

questions.q: What is the special word for clapping to show you loved a show?
questions.f: 'Applause' comes from a Latin word meaning to clap—Romans clapped at shows too!

questions.q: In the song 'B-I-N-G-O', what kind of animal is Bingo?
questions.f: The song spells Bingo's name, then swaps letters for claps—great spelling practice!

questions.q: In 'The Wheels on the Bus', what do the wheels do?
questions.f: In the song, it's the people who go up and down and the wipers that go swish!

questions.q: 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little…' what?
questions.f: The tune is from an old French song and was around before the star words were added.

questions.q: In freeze dance, what should you do the moment the music stops?
questions.f: Freeze dance is also called 'musical statues' because you freeze like a statue.

questions.q: In musical chairs, what do players race to grab when the music stops?
questions.f: One chair is taken away each round, so the game gets harder and harder.

questions.q: A music box plays a tune all by itself when you wind it up.
questions.f: Inside, tiny bumps on a turning drum pluck the teeth of a metal comb to play the tune.

questions.q: Who plays the songs and music at a party?
questions.f: DJ is short for 'disc jockey'—someone who 'rides' the records!

questions.q: Moving your body in time with the beat of music is called…?
questions.f: People have danced for thousands of years—ancient cave paintings show dancers!

questions.q: How many performers are on stage during a solo?
questions.f: 'Solo' means 'alone' in Italian, the language of many music words.

questions.q: A duet is a song performed by how many people?
questions.f: 'Duet' comes from 'duo,' a Latin word meaning two.

questions.q: 'Do, re, mi, fa, sol' are special names we sing for musical…?
questions.f: Singers use these note names to learn tunes before adding the real words.

questions.q: Which party dance has everyone flapping their arms like a bird?
questions.f: The Chicken Dance song was written in Switzerland and is played at parties worldwide.

questions.q: In the movie Happy Feet, what kind of dancing does the penguin Mumble love?
questions.f: Real emperor penguins can't dance, but they do sing special calls to find each other!

questions.q: In the old story, the Pied Piper leads the rats away by playing a…?
questions.f: 'Pied' means wearing patchwork clothes of many colors.

questions.q: Which Disney character is the sorcerer's apprentice in the musical film Fantasia?
questions.f: In Fantasia, cartoons are drawn to match famous classical music.

questions.q: Elsa sings the song 'Let It Go' in which movie?
questions.f: 'Let It Go' has been recorded in more than 40 different languages.

questions.q: Who sings 'Under the Sea' in The Little Mermaid?
questions.f: 'Under the Sea' won the Oscar for Best Original Song in 1990.

questions.q: In 'Baby Shark', which family member comes right after Mommy Shark?
questions.f: The 'Baby Shark' video became one of the most-watched videos ever on YouTube.

questions.q: In the famous Beatles song, what color is the submarine?
questions.f: The Beatles even made a cartoon movie called Yellow Submarine in 1968.

questions.q: In 'Hey Diddle Diddle', which instrument does the cat play?
questions.f: 'Fiddle' is a friendly nickname for the violin.

questions.q: In 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat', life is but a…?
questions.f: This song is often sung as a 'round,' with groups starting one after another.

questions.q: What does a snake charmer play to make the cobra sway?
questions.f: Snakes can't hear the tune well—they actually follow the moving pipe with their eyes!

questions.q: What are the fluffy shakers that cheerleaders wave called?
questions.f: Cheerleaders shake pom-poms in time with chants, like colorful silent music.

questions.q: 'Happy Birthday to You' is one of the most-sung songs in the whole world.
questions.f: The birthday song has been sung in space by astronauts too!

questions.q: What do you call a book full of songs?
questions.f: Joining two words like 'song' and 'book' makes a compound word.

questions.q: What is the part of a song that repeats after every verse called?
questions.f: The chorus is usually the catchiest part—the bit everyone sings along to.

questions.q: Which instrument do you play by blowing while sliding it along your lips?
questions.f: A harmonica is small enough to fit in your pocket, so cowboys loved carrying one.

questions.q: What is the part that swings inside a bell to make it ring?
questions.f: It's called a clapper because it claps against the sides of the bell.

questions.q: The djembe, a drum from West Africa, is played with bare hands.
questions.f: Djembe players make deep or sharp sounds by hitting different parts of the drum skin.

questions.q: Which of these makes gentle music when the wind blows through it?
questions.f: Wind chimes have hung in gardens in China and Japan for hundreds of years.

questions.q: A person who dances is a dancer. A person who sings is a…?
questions.f: English often adds '-er' to an action word to name the person who does it.

questions.q: What is the small flat tool used to pluck guitar strings called?
questions.f: Its fancy name is 'plectrum,' but most players just say pick.

questions.q: Which part of a guitar is named after a part of your body?
questions.f: A guitar also has a 'head' at the top of its neck and a 'body' below!

questions.q: In 'If You're Happy and You Know It', what do you do first?
questions.f: Action songs like this one help little kids learn to keep a steady beat.

questions.q: Which letters are famously sung in 'Old MacDonald Had a Farm'?
questions.f: People have sung versions of this farm song for about 100 years.

questions.q: In the song, the itsy bitsy spider climbed up the water…?
questions.f: This finger-play song is sung in many countries with different spider names.

questions.q: What do we call the special song a country sings at big events like the Olympics?
questions.f: When athletes win gold, their country's anthem is played at the medal ceremony.

questions.q: Which loud horn wakes everyone up at summer camp?
questions.f: The wake-up tune played on a bugle is called 'Reveille.'

questions.q: Which funny little instrument buzzes when you hum into it?
questions.f: A kazoo only works if you hum—just blowing air makes no sound at all!

questions.q: Which word means music that is quiet and gentle?
questions.f: Music can whisper or roar—composers choose soft and loud sounds on purpose.

questions.q: Which word means how loud or quiet a sound is?
questions.f: 'Volume' comes from a Latin word—turning it up makes music fill the room.

questions.q: In which dance does everyone form a long line and hold the person in front?
questions.f: The conga line dance came from Cuba and is loved at parties everywhere.

questions.q: In ballet, boys and men dance too.
questions.f: Male ballet dancers do huge leaps and lift their partners high in the air.

questions.q: What do you call the name of a song, shown at the top of the page?
questions.f: Some song titles are just one word—like 'Happy' by Pharrell Williams.

questions.q: Which body part do you snap to make a clicking beat?
questions.f: Finger snaps are used instead of drums in some famous songs.

questions.q: What do you call the little tune your phone plays when someone calls?
questions.f: 'Ringtone' is a new compound word—phones once could only ring one way.

questions.q: Which huge sea animal is famous for singing long songs underwater?
questions.f: A humpback whale's song can travel for many miles through the ocean.

questions.q: Which bird is famous for copying the songs of other birds?
questions.f: The mockingbird's name means it 'mocks,' or copies, other birds' songs.

questions.q: Rock, pop, and jazz are all kinds of…?
questions.f: There are hundreds of music styles, and new ones are invented all the time.

questions.q: What do we call the music-like sounds birds make at sunrise?
questions.f: The early-morning concert of many birds singing is called the dawn chorus.

questions.q: You can make music by tapping two wooden sticks together.
questions.f: Tapping sticks called claves make the click-clack beat in lots of Latin music.

questions.q: A 'trio' is a group of how many musicians?
questions.f: 'Tri-' means three—the same beginning as triangle and tricycle.

questions.q: When a crowd shouts 'Encore!' at the end of a concert, what do they want?
questions.f: 'Encore' means 'again' in French—funnily, French audiences shout a different word: 'Bis!'

questions.q: What is the big final number of a show called?
questions.f: 'Finale' is Italian for 'final'—often the whole cast returns to the stage for it.

questions.q: A singer in a band can also be called a…?
questions.f: 'Vocal' relates to the voice—the same root appears in 'vocabulary,' words you can voice.

questions.q: What is a tryout called where singers perform hoping to win a part?
questions.f: An audition is where judges listen—the root 'audi' is all about hearing.

questions.q: What is a practice session before a concert called?
questions.f: A 'dress rehearsal' is the last practice, done in full costume as if it were the real show.

questions.q: What is the funny name for a catchy tune stuck in your head?
questions.f: 'Earworm' was borrowed from the German word 'Ohrwurm,' which means the same thing.

questions.q: What kind of song is a 'sea shanty'?
questions.f: Sailors sang shanties to pull ropes in rhythm—the strong beat kept everyone heaving together.

questions.q: Which instrument is nicknamed the 'mouth organ'?
questions.f: Inside a harmonica, tiny metal reeds vibrate as you breathe in and out.

questions.q: 'Fiddle' is a folk nickname for which instrument?
questions.f: Same instrument, different style—classical players say violin, folk players often say fiddle.

questions.q: When everyone sings the exact same notes together, they sing in…?
questions.f: 'Uni-' means one—in unison, many voices sound like a single voice.

questions.q: A line that keeps coming back in a song is called the…?
questions.f: 'Refrain' can also mean 'to hold back'—the two meanings arrived by different word paths.

questions.q: Rock, jazz, and hip-hop are each a different musical…?
questions.f: 'Genre' means a kind or type—books and movies are sorted into genres too.

questions.q: What do you call a whole collection of songs released together by an artist?
questions.f: Early records came in book-like sleeves that looked like photo albums—the name stuck.

questions.q: When a band plays its own version of another artist's song, that version is called a…?
questions.f: Some covers become more famous than the original recording of the song.

questions.q: A piece of music with no singing at all is called an…?
questions.f: Movie soundtracks are mostly instrumentals, so the music never talks over the actors.

questions.q: Making drum and beat sounds using only your mouth is called…?
questions.f: Skilled beatboxers can sound like a whole drum kit and a DJ at the same time.

questions.q: Where does the orchestra sit during a ballet or musical?
c: In a sunken pit in front of the stage
questions.f: The orchestra pit keeps the players low so the audience can see the dancers above.

questions.q: Why is a grand piano called 'grand'?
questions.f: In a grand piano the strings lie flat and long; in an upright piano they stand vertically.

questions.q: What are the little metal discs that rattle around a tambourine's rim called?
questions.f: A tambourine can be shaken, tapped, or hit on your hip—all at once in some dances!

questions.q: What is it called when a performer mouths the words without really singing?
questions.f: 'Sync' is short for 'synchronize,' which means to match timing exactly.

questions.q: What do you call a list of songs you save to play in a row?
questions.f: Before playlists, people recorded 'mixtapes' of favorite songs on cassette tapes.

questions.q: What do you call the one musician who plays a special part alone in front of the group?
questions.f: Adding '-ist' to 'solo' names the person who performs the solo.

questions.q: Inside a piano, pressing a key makes a soft felt hammer strike the strings.
questions.f: That's why a piano is officially a percussion instrument—something gets struck!

questions.q: What is the round opening in the middle of an acoustic guitar called?
questions.f: The sound hole lets the vibrating air inside the hollow body escape as rich sound.

questions.q: K-pop is a world-famous pop music style from which country?
questions.f: The 'K' in K-pop stands for Korea, and its fans stream billions of songs a year.

questions.q: Reggae music, made famous by Bob Marley, began on which island?
questions.f: Reggae's relaxed off-beat rhythm is recognized by UNESCO as a world cultural treasure.

questions.q: Which US city is nicknamed 'Music City' for its country music?
questions.f: Nashville's Grand Ole Opry radio show has broadcast country stars since 1925.

questions.q: Steel drums from Trinidad were first hammered out of what?
questions.f: Steelpan makers tune each dent in the barrel's surface to play a different note.

questions.q: Which twangy string instrument is the star of bluegrass music?
questions.f: The banjo's design came to America with enslaved Africans and their gourd instruments.

questions.q: How many basic positions of the feet are there in ballet?
questions.f: Every ballet step begins and ends in one of the five positions.

questions.q: Most ballet steps have French names.
questions.f: Ballet grew up in the French royal court, so its dictionary stayed French worldwide.

questions.q: In square dancing, who shouts out which moves to do next?
questions.f: Dancers must listen fast—the caller can mix moves in any order they like!

questions.q: In line dancing, dancers stand in rows and all do…?
c: The same steps at the same time
questions.f: Line dances are popular at country music parties because no partner is needed.

questions.q: In a traditional maypole dance, what do dancers hold as they circle the pole?
questions.f: As they weave in and out, the ribbons braid a pattern down the pole.

questions.q: 'The Nutcracker' ballet is traditionally performed around which holiday?
questions.f: In the story, a nutcracker doll comes to life on Christmas Eve and battles the Mouse King.

questions.q: In the famous ballet 'Swan Lake', the main dancer plays a princess turned into a…?
questions.f: The same ballerina often dances both the white swan and the tricky black swan.

questions.q: French horn players keep one hand inside the bell of the horn while playing.
questions.f: Moving the hand in the bell changes the horn's tone—players 'steer' the sound.

questions.q: Which huge metal disc from East Asia makes a deep crash when struck?
questions.f: Some orchestra gongs are taller than the player who strikes them.

questions.q: A cowbell is a real instrument used in pop and Latin music.
questions.f: The cowbell really did start life around the necks of grazing cows.

questions.q: The vuvuzela, a long plastic horn, buzzed loudly at the 2010 soccer World Cup in…?
questions.f: Thousands of vuvuzelas together sounded like a giant swarm of bees on TV.

questions.q: The song 'Do-Re-Mi' comes from which famous musical?
questions.f: In the movie, a governess teaches seven children to sing using the note names.

questions.q: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart began composing music at about what age?
questions.f: By age six, young Mozart was performing for empresses and kings across Europe.

questions.q: The Beatles came from which English city?
questions.f: Liverpool's Cavern Club, where the Beatles played early shows, is now a landmark.

questions.q: Which singer is known as the 'King of Rock and Roll'?
questions.f: Elvis's home, Graceland, gets hundreds of thousands of music fans visiting each year.

questions.q: What is the national anthem of the United States called?
questions.f: Its words were written in 1814 while a huge flag flew over a fort during a battle.

questions.q: Mariachi bands, with trumpets, violins, and fancy suits, come from which country?
questions.f: Mariachi musicians wear decorated 'charro' suits with silver buttons down the legs.

questions.q: Traditional opera singers perform without microphones, even in huge theaters.
questions.f: Opera singers train for years to project their voices over a whole orchestra.

questions.q: Why can't people hear a dog whistle?
c: Its sound is too high for human ears
It makes no sound at all
questions.f: Dogs hear much higher sounds than we do, so the whistle is loud and clear to them.

questions.q: What do you really hear when you hold a seashell to your ear?
c: Nearby noise echoing inside the shell
questions.f: The shell's curved inside catches sounds around you and blends them into a soft 'whoosh.'

questions.q: If you tap glasses of water with a spoon, what does adding MORE water do to the note?
questions.f: Extra water slows the glass's vibrations, so a fuller glass rings out a deeper note.

questions.q: Trumpets and trombones have a small valve to empty water that collects inside.
questions.f: It's nicknamed the 'spit valve,' but the drips are mostly condensed breath—like fog on a window.

questions.q: Yodeling, singing that flips quickly between low and very high notes, comes from which mountains?
questions.f: Alpine herders once yodeled to call cows and to send messages across valleys.

questions.q: What is the funny name for the stool a drummer sits on?
questions.f: Drummers really do call it a throne—the drummer rules the beat, after all.

questions.q: What does an electric guitar need to be heard across a big room?
questions.f: Unplugged, an electric guitar is quiet—its solid body barely makes any sound alone.

questions.q: Dancers in dazzling feathered costumes samba through the streets at Carnival in which city?
questions.f: Rio's samba schools spend all year building floats and practicing for the parade.

questions.q: Michael Jackson made which gliding dance move world-famous?
questions.f: In the moonwalk, the dancer slides backward while appearing to walk forward.

questions.q: A one-man band is a single performer playing several instruments at the same time.
questions.f: Classic one-man bands strap cymbals between their knees and a drum on their back.

questions.q: Pretending to play an invisible guitar to your favorite song is called playing…?
questions.f: There is a real Air Guitar World Championship held every year in Finland.

questions.q: A new band that practices in someone's home is often called a…?
questions.f: Some of the world's biggest rock bands really did start out practicing in garages.

questions.q: Dances like the waltz and foxtrot, done by pairs in a big hall, are called…?
questions.f: 'Ballroom' literally means a room for balls—'ball' once meant a big dancing party.

questions.q: Singing a tune with your lips closed is called…?
questions.f: When you hum, the sound buzzes out through your nose instead of your mouth.

questions.q: A song that becomes hugely popular is called a…?
questions.f: Charts like the Hot 100 rank each week's biggest hit songs.

questions.q: What is the general word for any person who plays music?
questions.f: 'Musician' keeps the word 'music' inside it—just add a person ending.

questions.q: At a concert, who sits at a desk of sliders making sure every instrument sounds right?
questions.f: Sound engineers 'mix' the show live, balancing voices and instruments for the crowd.

questions.q: What does a 'tribute band' do?
c: Performs the songs of one famous band
questions.f: Some tribute bands dress and move exactly like the famous band they honor.

questions.q: The root 'phon' in symphony, microphone, and headphone means…?
questions.f: From Greek 'phone' meaning sound or voice—a telephone is literally 'far sound.'

questions.q: The word 'symphony' breaks into roots that literally mean…?
questions.f: 'Sym-' means together and 'phon' means sound—dozens of players sounding as one.

questions.q: The root 'oct' in octave and octopus means…?
questions.f: An octave spans eight note names, and October was the eighth Roman month.

questions.q: The root 'audi' in audience, audition, and auditorium means…?
questions.f: An audience is literally 'the hearers'—the Latin root also gives us 'audio.'

questions.q: Based on its roots, an 'auditorium' is a place for…?
questions.f: The Latin ending '-orium' means 'a place for,' just like in 'aquarium.'

questions.q: The old root 'cant' in 'chant' and 'enchant' means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'cantare'—an 'enchanted' object has literally had a spell sung over it!

questions.q: The 'phil' in 'philharmonic' orchestra means…?
questions.f: A philharmonic is a 'music-loving' society—'phil' also starts 'philosophy,' love of wisdom.

questions.q: The word 'percussion' comes from a Latin root meaning…?
questions.f: Every percussion instrument is struck, tapped, or hit—the name says exactly that.

questions.q: In ancient Greek theaters, the 'orchestra' was originally…?
c: The space where the chorus danced
questions.f: 'Orchestra' comes from a Greek verb meaning 'to dance'—musicians took over the space later.

questions.q: The old Italian root 'ballare' behind ballet, ballerina, and ballroom means…?
questions.f: 'Ball,' an old word for a dancing party, comes from the very same root.

questions.q: What does a choreographer do?
c: Designs the dance steps for a show
questions.f: Choreographers write dances the way authors write books—some even use special step notation.

questions.q: A 'lyricist' is the person who writes a song's…?
questions.f: 'Lyrics' trace back to the lyre, the small Greek harp that accompanied ancient poems.

questions.q: What is a 'busker'?
c: A musician who performs on the street for tips
questions.f: Some superstars, including Ed Sheeran, began their careers busking on sidewalks.

questions.q: A great conductor is respectfully called 'maestro', a word that means…?
questions.f: Italian for master—related to words like 'mastery' and 'maestoso,' meaning majestically.

questions.q: In music, the Italian term 'allegro' tells players to go…?
questions.f: 'Allegro' literally means cheerful—fast music and happy moods go together in Italian.

questions.q: The musical term 'adagio' tells players to play…?
questions.f: 'Adagio' comes from 'ad agio'—at ease, taking the music gently.

questions.q: Notes marked 'staccato' should sound…?
questions.f: 'Staccato' means detached in Italian—the opposite marking, legato, means bound together.

questions.q: The name of the piccolo, the tiny flute, is Italian for…?
questions.f: Its full name was once 'flauto piccolo'—literally 'small flute.'

questions.q: The word 'music' itself honors the Muses. Who were they?
questions.f: A 'museum' is also named for the Muses—a temple to the arts, just like music.

questions.q: What is a 'troupe'?
questions.f: Watch the spelling—'troupe' with a U-P-E performs; a 'troop' is soldiers or scouts.

questions.q: The 'barre' in a ballet studio is…?
c: A rail dancers hold while practicing
questions.f: Dancers warm up 'at the barre' every day, from beginners to world-famous stars.

questions.q: A 'matinee' is a performance held at what time?
questions.f: It comes from 'matin,' French for morning—though most matinees now happen after lunch.

questions.q: What is an 'intermission'?
c: A break in the middle of a show
questions.f: 'Inter-' means between—an intermission is literally 'a sending between' the acts.

questions.q: The root 'pod' in 'podium', the platform a conductor stands on, means…?
questions.f: The same root appears in 'tripod' (three feet) and 'podiatrist' (a foot doctor).

questions.q: The 'metron' in 'metronome', the ticking practice tool, means…?
questions.f: A metronome measures out the beat—'thermometer' and 'kilometer' share the root.

questions.q: A child with an amazing, adult-level talent for music is called a…?
questions.f: From a Latin word for an omen or marvel—prodigies seemed like wonders of nature.

questions.q: A 'serenade' is traditionally a song performed…?
c: In the evening beneath someone's window
questions.f: It traces to 'sera,' Italian for evening—the morning version is called an aubade.

questions.q: A small group of musicians who perform together is called an…?
questions.f: 'Ensemble' is French for 'together'—actors in a play can form an ensemble too.

questions.q: When jazz players invent music on the spot as they play, it is called…?
questions.f: 'Improvise' comes from Latin for 'unforeseen'—music made without seeing it coming.

questions.q: What is a 'jam session'?
c: Musicians playing together informally for fun
questions.f: At jam sessions, players trade solos and invent grooves with no script at all.

questions.q: A performer's very first public appearance is called their…?
questions.f: French for 'beginning'—the tricky silent T makes 'debut' a spelling-bee favorite.

questions.q: The pianist who plays supporting music for a singer is called an…?
questions.f: To 'accompany' literally means to go along with someone—musically, note by note.

questions.q: Jazz music was born around 1900 in which American city?
questions.f: New Orleans brass bands even play joyful jazz parades through the streets.

questions.q: Mozart was born in which European country?
questions.f: His birthplace, Salzburg, holds a music festival in his honor every summer.

questions.q: Vivaldi's famous set of violin concertos 'The Four Seasons' paints pictures of…?
questions.f: Vivaldi wrote poems for each season and made the violins imitate birds and storms.

questions.q: Which Russian composer wrote both 'Swan Lake' and 'The Nutcracker'?
questions.f: Tchaikovsky doubted Swan Lake at first—today it is the world's best-known ballet.

questions.q: The 'concertmaster', the orchestra's lead player, plays which instrument?
questions.f: The concertmaster sits closest to the conductor and walks on to a special round of applause.

questions.q: Which orchestra drums are tuned to exact notes using foot pedals?
questions.f: Timpani are nicknamed kettledrums because their big copper bowls look like kettles.

questions.q: Which clef marks the staff where LOW notes are written?
questions.f: Cellos, tubas, and left-hand piano parts all read the curly bass clef.

questions.q: Musical notes are named using which letters of the alphabet?
questions.f: After G the note names start over at A—that repeating span is the octave.

questions.q: Which note lasts the LONGEST when played?
questions.f: One whole note equals four quarter notes, like one dollar equals four quarters.

questions.q: A 'sharp' raises a note a tiny step. What does a 'flat' do?
questions.f: The flat symbol looks like a small letter b, and the sharp looks like a hashtag.

questions.q: Which Latin dance shares its name with a spicy tomato sauce?
questions.f: 'Salsa' means sauce—the dance is a zesty mix of Cuban and Puerto Rican styles.

questions.q: The polka, a bouncy hopping dance for couples, first became a craze in…?
questions.f: Polka fever swept Europe in the 1840s—newspapers called it 'polkamania.'

questions.q: 'Bollywood', famous for spectacular song-and-dance scenes, is the film industry of…?
questions.f: The name blends Bombay, the old name of Mumbai, with Hollywood.

questions.q: Rapping is speaking rhyming words in rhythm over a musical beat.
questions.f: Great rappers juggle rhyme, rhythm, and wordplay at high speed—true word athletes.

questions.q: Gospel music, full of powerful group singing and clapping, grew up in…?
questions.f: Gospel choirs helped shape soul, R&B, and much of today's pop singing style.

questions.q: Blues music got its name because 'feeling blue' means feeling…?
questions.f: Blues singers turned hard times into powerful songs—then blues gave birth to rock and roll.

questions.q: Rock and roll exploded into worldwide popularity during which decade?
questions.f: Teens with new transistor radios and jukeboxes powered the rock and roll craze.

questions.q: What does a synthesizer do?
questions.f: 'Synthesize' means to build by combining—synths build brand-new sounds from electric waves.

questions.q: A vinyl record is played by a tiny needle riding along a spiral groove.
questions.f: The groove's microscopic wiggles are the actual shape of the music's sound waves.

questions.q: Blind musicians can read music written in braille.
questions.f: Braille music uses raised dot patterns for notes—Stevie Wonder learned music this way.

questions.q: How does a harpsichord, the piano's older cousin, make its sound?
c: Its strings are plucked by little quills
questions.f: Because the quills pluck at one strength, a harpsichord can't play louder or softer like a piano.

questions.q: What do you get when you strike a tuning fork?
questions.f: Its two prongs vibrate at an exact speed, giving musicians a perfectly reliable note.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four main choir voice parts?
questions.f: The four choir parts—soprano, alto, tenor, bass—are remembered by the letters SATB.

questions.q: The dragon dance, where a team carries a long dragon puppet on poles, celebrates…?
questions.f: Longer dragons are luckier—some parade dragons stretch over 100 meters.

questions.q: English Morris dancers traditionally tie rows of bells below their knees.
questions.f: Morris dancers also wave handkerchiefs or clash sticks in time with the music.

questions.q: The hopak, a dance with deep squat kicks and huge leaps, comes from…?
questions.f: The hopak began among Cossack warriors celebrating after battles.

questions.q: Kabuki, a centuries-old theater of dance, song, and bold makeup, comes from…?
questions.f: Kabuki actors train from childhood, and famous stage names pass down through families.

questions.q: Johann Strauss II, the 'Waltz King' who wrote 'The Blue Danube', filled which city with waltzes?
questions.f: 'The Blue Danube' is so loved that Vienna's New Year concert plays it every year.

questions.q: Which part of your ear vibrates like a tiny drum skin when sound arrives?
questions.f: The eardrum passes vibrations to three tiny bones—the smallest bones in your body.

questions.q: In an opera, the story is mostly sung rather than spoken.
questions.f: Even simple lines like 'pass the salt' get gloriously sung in opera.

questions.q: The pop group ABBA comes from Sweden.
questions.f: ABBA's name is built from the first letters of the four members' first names.

questions.q: What is printed music that performers read from called?
questions.f: Before printing, monks copied music by hand—one songbook could take months.

questions.q: The steady four-beats-per-measure time signature 4/4 is nicknamed…?
questions.f: It's so common that composers often just write a big 'C' instead of 4/4.

questions.q: An artist remembered for only one big hit song is called a…?
questions.f: Some one-hit wonders, like 'Take On Me,' are still sung by stadiums decades later.

questions.q: When a band plays an 'unplugged' concert, they play…?
questions.f: MTV's Unplugged shows made stripped-down acoustic concerts world-famous in the 1990s.

questions.q: A 'flash mob' is when a crowd in a public place suddenly…?
c: Breaks into a planned dance or song
questions.f: Flash mobs are secretly rehearsed, then look totally spontaneous to surprised shoppers.

questions.q: The Grammy Award trophy is shaped like which old music machine?
questions.f: The gramophone's big horn amplified records before electric speakers existed.

questions.q: When a leader sings a line and the group answers back, the pattern is called…?
questions.f: Call and response powers sea shanties, gospel choirs, and stadium chants alike.

questions.q: In a jazz band, which instrument usually plucks the steady 'walking' low notes?
questions.f: A 'walking' bassline strolls up and down the scale, one note per beat.

questions.q: Breaking (breakdancing) made its debut as an official Olympic event at which Games?
questions.f: Olympic breakers are called b-boys and b-girls and battle one-on-one, judged like gymnasts.

questions.q: The root 'xylo' in xylophone means…?
questions.f: A xylophone is literally a 'wood sound'—its metal cousin is properly a glockenspiel.

questions.q: Singing 'a cappella' is unaccompanied because the phrase literally means…?
c: In the style of the chapel
questions.f: Church chapels of old allowed only voices, so chapel-style came to mean instrument-free.

questions.q: The Japanese word 'karaoke' literally translates to…?
questions.f: 'Kara' means empty—the orchestra is there on tape, but its singer is missing: that's you.

questions.q: In Hawaiian, 'ukulele' is usually translated as…?
questions.f: One story says a nimble-fingered player nicknamed 'the jumping flea' made the instrument famous.

questions.q: A harsh, clashing mixture of sounds is a 'cacophony'. Its root 'kakos' means…?
questions.f: Its pleasant opposite is 'euphony'—'eu' means good, as in eulogy, good words.

questions.q: The Greek root behind 'acoustic', 'akouein', means…?
questions.f: Acoustics—the science of sound—decides whether a concert hall sounds glorious or muddy.

questions.q: By their roots, a 'sonata' is played on instruments while a 'cantata' is…?
questions.f: Latin 'sonare' means to sound and 'cantare' to sing—the two words split music neatly in half.

questions.q: The text of an opera is called the 'libretto', which literally means…?
questions.f: Some composers wrote their own librettos; others hired poets, sparking famous feuds.

questions.q: The highest voice is the 'soprano', from an Italian root meaning…?
questions.f: 'Sopra' means above—the soprano line floats on top of all the other voices.

questions.q: 'Falsetto', the airy voice men use to sing very high notes, literally means…?
questions.f: The Bee Gees built chart-topping hits almost entirely from falsetto singing.

questions.q: A 'virtuoso' is a musician who…?
questions.f: From Italian for 'skilled'—virtuoso violinist Paganini played so fast fans swore it was magic.

questions.q: 'Choreography' combines Greek roots that literally mean…?
questions.f: 'Khoreia' is dance and 'graphein' to write—a choreographer writes with moving bodies.

questions.q: The ballet spin called a 'pirouette' takes its name from a French word for a…?
questions.f: Elite ballerinas can chain thirty-two spins in a row in Swan Lake's famous fouetté sequence.

questions.q: The ballet knee-bend 'plié' literally means…?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'pliers' and 'pliable'—things that bend.

questions.q: In ballet, an 'arabesque' is a pose balanced on one leg with the other…?
questions.f: The name once described swirling 'Arabian-style' ornament patterns in art.

questions.q: 'Glockenspiel', the small metal-bar instrument, is German for…?
questions.f: 'Glocke' means bell—marching bands carry lyre-shaped glockenspiels that ring like tiny bells.

questions.q: In film and opera music, a 'leitmotif' is…?
c: A theme that returns with a certain character or idea
The final chord of a scene
questions.f: Think of Darth Vader's march—composer John Williams borrowed the trick from Wagner's operas.

questions.q: An 'aria' is an opera's showpiece solo song. The word is Italian for…?
questions.f: In English too, old songbooks called a melody an 'ayre'—a tune as light as breath.

questions.q: 'Diva', the title for a celebrated female opera star, literally means…?
questions.f: Its male counterpart, 'divo,' exists too—both come from the Latin for divine.

questions.q: A musician's 'repertoire' is…?
c: All the pieces they are ready to perform
The order of bows at the end
questions.f: It traces to a Latin word for an inventory—literally the shelf of works a player can 'find again.'

questions.q: 'Rhapsody' comes from Greek roots meaning songs that are…?
questions.f: Ancient rhapsodes 'stitched' epic poems together—Queen's Bohemian Rhapsody stitches five styles.

questions.q: A 'nocturne', like those Chopin wrote for piano, is a piece evoking…?
questions.f: 'Nox' is Latin for night—painter Whistler borrowed the word back for his misty night scenes.

questions.q: The 'overture' comes first in an opera because the word literally means…?
questions.f: Rossini famously wrote some overtures at the last minute—one allegedly the night before the premiere.

questions.q: The 'bel' hidden inside the loudness unit 'decibel' honors which inventor?
questions.f: A whole 'bel' proved too large for everyday sounds, so we measure in tenths—decibels.

questions.q: The frequency unit 'hertz' is named after a German physicist.
questions.f: Heinrich Hertz proved radio waves exist in 1887; one hertz is one vibration per second.

questions.q: The cochlea, the spiral organ that turns sound into nerve signals, is named after a…?
questions.f: Unrolled, your cochlea's spiral would stretch about 3 centimeters—a snail-sized marvel.

questions.q: 'Tympanum', the anatomical name for the eardrum, is also the root of which orchestra instrument?
questions.f: Both come from the Greek for drum—your ear literally contains a tiny kettledrum skin.

questions.q: SONAR, which 'sings' pulses through the sea, is an acronym standing for…?
c: Signal Output with No Audible Return
questions.f: Sonar was developed after the Titanic disaster to detect icebergs and, later, submarines.

questions.q: The oboe's name comes from the French 'hautbois', meaning…?
questions.f: 'Haut' means high and 'bois' wood—English speakers respelled the French sound as o-b-o-e.

questions.q: 'Cello' is actually a shortened form of which full Italian name?
questions.f: For centuries it was politely written with an apostrophe—'cello—to show the missing letters.

questions.q: With the Italian ending '-one' meaning 'big', the word 'trombone' literally means…?
questions.f: 'Tromba' is trumpet—add '-one' and you get the trumpet's stretched-out big brother.

questions.q: The clarinet's name means 'little trumpet', from the Latin root 'clarus', meaning…?
questions.f: Its bright upper notes reminded listeners of the clarino trumpet register—hence the name.

questions.q: The waltz takes its name from the German 'walzen', meaning…?
questions.f: When the turning waltz arrived around 1800, scandalized critics called the close hold shocking.

questions.q: 'Disco' is short for 'discothèque', a French coinage that literally means…?
questions.f: It was modeled on 'bibliothèque' (library)—a library of discs instead of books.

questions.q: 'Opera' is the plural of the Latin word 'opus', so an opera is literally…?
questions.f: Composers still number pieces as Opus 1, Opus 2—opera bundles many 'works' into one show.

questions.q: The saxophone is named after Adolphe Sax, who was…?
c: The Belgian instrument maker who invented it
questions.f: Sax patented it in 1846; rivals sued him so often he twice went bankrupt defending his horns.

questions.q: The sousaphone, the big wrap-around marching tuba, is named after…?
questions.f: Sousa, the 'March King,' asked for a tuba whose sound would lift over the band's heads.

questions.q: 'Syncopation' is the rhythmic trick of…?
c: Accenting off-beats where you least expect them
questions.f: Syncopation powers ragtime, jazz, and funk—your foot taps the beat, the music dodges it.

questions.q: 'Prima donna', now slang for a demanding star, originally meant the opera's…?
c: First lady, its leading female singer
questions.f: The leading man was the 'primo uomo'—but only 'prima donna' entered everyday English.

questions.q: An 'impresario' is the person who…?
c: Organizes and finances concerts and shows
questions.f: From Italian 'impresa,' an undertaking—impresarios gambled fortunes on stars and spectacles.

questions.q: A 'conservatory' can be a greenhouse—or, in music, it is a…?
questions.f: Italian 'conservatorio' orphanages taught music so well they became the first great music schools.

questions.q: A musician with 'perfect pitch' can…?
c: Name any note they hear without a reference
questions.f: It's also called absolute pitch and is far more common among people who start music very young.

questions.q: The 'amphi' in 'amphitheater', the round open-air venue, means…?
c: On both sides or all around
questions.f: An amphibian likewise lives 'on both sides'—in water and on land.

questions.q: By its Greek roots, Edison's 'phonograph' of 1877 is literally a…?
questions.f: The first words Edison recorded on it were 'Mary had a little lamb.'

questions.q: 'Stereo' sound takes its name from the Greek 'stereos', meaning…?
questions.f: Two speakers build a 'solid,' three-dimensional image of sound between them.

questions.q: Surprisingly, the slow storytelling 'ballad' shares its root with which word?
questions.f: Both come from 'ballare,' to dance—medieval ballads were originally dancing songs.

questions.q: The most treasured violins in the world were made around 1700 in Cremona, Italy, by…?
questions.f: Around 650 'Strads' survive; one sold at auction for more than 15 million dollars.

questions.q: A full symphony orchestra typically has about how many musicians?
questions.f: Roughly sixty of them are string players—the strings outnumber everyone else combined.

questions.q: The roof of the Sydney Opera House is designed to look like…?
questions.f: Architect Jørn Utzon reportedly cracked the sail geometry while peeling an orange.

questions.q: Jazz legend Louis Armstrong, nicknamed 'Satchmo', was a master of which instrument?
questions.f: 'Satchmo' is short for 'satchel mouth'—and his gravelly singing became as famous as his horn.

questions.q: Ella Fitzgerald dazzled audiences with 'scat' singing, which means…?
c: Repeating the last word of each line
questions.f: The 'First Lady of Song' could trade fast scat choruses with trumpet players—and win.

questions.q: Motown Records, hit factory of the Supremes and Stevie Wonder, was founded in which city?
questions.f: 'Motown' blends 'motor town'—Detroit was the capital of America's car industry.

questions.q: The legendary 1969 Woodstock festival took place on a dairy farm in which US state?
questions.f: Around 400,000 people showed up—organizers had printed tickets for far fewer.

questions.q: Sony's Walkman, launched in 1979, was the first hugely popular way to…?
c: Carry your music and listen through headphones anywhere
questions.f: Early Walkmans had two headphone jacks so friends could share the music.

questions.q: The Beatles' 'Yesterday' is among the most re-recorded songs in music history.
questions.f: Paul McCartney says the melody came to him in a dream—thousands of cover versions followed.

questions.q: The twinkling solo in Tchaikovsky's 'Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy' features which rare instrument?
questions.f: Tchaikovsky secretly imported the brand-new celesta from Paris so rivals couldn't copy it first.

questions.q: Ballet was born in the courts of which country during the Renaissance?
questions.f: Italian court spectacles moved to France with Catherine de' Medici—then France named the steps.

questions.q: Which French king, a keen dancer who performed as the sun in a ballet, founded the first ballet academy?
questions.f: His golden Sun role earned him the nickname the Sun King; his academy opened in 1661.

questions.q: Moscow's world-famous Bolshoi Ballet takes its name from a Russian word meaning…?
questions.f: Its rival in St. Petersburg, the Mariinsky, is named after an empress, Maria.

questions.q: The hard toe box of a ballerina's pointe shoe is traditionally stiffened with…?
c: Layers of fabric and paper hardened with glue
questions.f: Principal dancers can soften and wear out a pair of pointe shoes in a single performance.

questions.q: In ballet, a 'pas de deux' is literally a…?
questions.f: 'Pas' means step—a grand pas de deux has a set recipe: duet, two solos, and a fiery finale.

questions.q: The 'corps de ballet' is…?
c: The group of dancers who perform together behind the stars
questions.f: French for 'body of the ballet'—in Swan Lake they move as one, like a single flock of swans.

questions.q: La Scala, one of the world's most famous opera houses, stands in which city?
questions.f: Singers fear La Scala's picky 'loggione' fans in the cheap seats, who boo even stars.

questions.q: Broadway earned the nickname 'The Great White Way' because of its…?
questions.f: It was one of the first American streets fully lit by electric bulbs in the 1890s.

questions.q: The musical 'West Side Story' retells which Shakespeare play among New York street gangs?
questions.f: Leonard Bernstein's score famously mixes Latin dance rhythms with opera-sized drama.

questions.q: 'The Sound of Music' is based on the real singing family named…?
questions.f: The real von Trapps toured as a family choir after leaving Austria in the 1930s.

questions.q: The musical 'Hamilton' tells the story of a US founding father largely through…?
questions.f: Lin-Manuel Miranda got the idea reading Hamilton's biography on vacation.

questions.q: Johann Sebastian Bach had twenty children.
questions.f: Four of Bach's sons became renowned composers themselves—music ran in the family business.

questions.q: Why did Haydn hide a sudden fortissimo crash in his 'Surprise' Symphony?
c: To jolt drowsy audience members awake
questions.f: Haydn joked it would 'make the ladies jump'—the loud chord lands mid-lullaby in movement two.

questions.q: Tchaikovsky's '1812 Overture' is scored to include real cannon fire.
questions.f: Outdoor performances use actual artillery—sixteen cannon shots are written into the score.

questions.q: 'In the Hall of the Mountain King', which speeds up into a frantic chase, was written by…?
questions.f: Grieg wrote it for the play Peer Gynt—and privately joked that he could hardly bear the tune.

questions.q: 'Flight of the Bumblebee', with its furious buzzing runs, comes from an opera by…?
questions.f: In the opera, a prince is magically transformed into a bee—the music is his takeoff.

questions.q: Scott Joplin, composer of 'The Entertainer', was crowned the king of which style?
questions.f: 'Ragtime' likely comes from 'ragged time'—the melody's syncopated, torn-up rhythm.

questions.q: Healthy young humans can hear frequencies in roughly what range?
questions.f: The top of the range fades with age—teens can hear ringtones many adults cannot.

questions.q: Bats hunt using 'echolocation', a word built from roots meaning…?
questions.f: Bat clicks are ultrasonic—pitched far above the highest note a human can hear.

questions.q: Elephants keep in touch across kilometers using 'infrasound', which is sound…?
questions.f: Elephants can sense these deep rumbles arriving through the ground with their feet.

questions.q: Which tiny sea creature stuns prey with a snap louder than most gunshots?
questions.f: Its snapping claw shoots a bubble that collapses with a flash of light and a deafening crack.

questions.q: Soldiers are ordered to break step when marching across bridges.
questions.f: Rhythmic marching can resonate with a bridge's natural swing—in 1831 it helped wreck one in England.

questions.q: The Doppler effect explains why a passing ambulance siren seems to…?
c: Drop in pitch as it goes by
questions.f: Christian Doppler predicted the effect in 1842; scientists tested it with trumpeters on a train.

questions.q: A sonic boom happens when an aircraft…?
c: Flies faster than the speed of sound
Breaks the sound barrier of radio
questions.f: The plane outruns its own sound waves, which pile up into one thunderous shockwave.

questions.q: The larynx, home of your vocal cords, is commonly called the…?
questions.f: Your vocal folds can flutter hundreds of times per second when you sing a high note.

questions.q: In recording studios, Auto-Tune software is used to…?
questions.f: Cranked to extremes, it creates the robotic warble that became a pop sound of its own.

questions.q: A vinyl LP album is designed to spin at which speed?
questions.f: LP stands for 'long play'—the slower spin squeezed over twenty minutes onto each side.

questions.q: A compact disc is read by a laser beam, with nothing touching the disc's surface.
questions.f: The laser reads billions of microscopic pits—no needle, so a CD never wears out from playing.

questions.q: Fittingly, the first video ever played on MTV in 1981 was…?
questions.f: The Buggles' song title proved half-true—radio survived, but video changed pop forever.

questions.q: ABBA shot to world fame by winning the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest with which song?
questions.f: Eurovision, running since 1956, is one of the longest-running TV music contests on Earth.

questions.q: The swing dance 'Lindy Hop' is said to be named after Charles Lindbergh's famous…?
questions.f: Headlines read 'Lindy Hops the Atlantic'—Harlem dancers borrowed the phrase for their new steps.

questions.q: The kicking, arm-swinging dance craze of the 1920s takes its name from which US city?
questions.f: The Charleston's signature rhythm came from a 1923 Broadway song of the same name.

questions.q: The 'cha-cha-cha' is said to be named after…?
c: The shuffling sound of the dancers' feet
questions.f: Composer Enrique Jorrín noticed dancers' feet whispering 'cha-cha-cha' on the triple step.

questions.q: Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' is the best-selling album of all time.
questions.f: Thriller's 14-minute zombie video was so cinematic it premiered like a Hollywood film.

questions.q: The official anthem of the European Union is a melody known as…?
questions.f: The EU anthem has no official words—every country hears it in its own language of music.

questions.q: The erhu, whose bow is trapped between its two strings, is a fiddle from…?
questions.f: The erhu's snakeskin-covered sound box helps it 'sing' almost like a human voice.

questions.q: A person who plays the guitar is called a…?
questions.f: The ending '-ist' names the player, just like in pianist and violinist.

questions.q: When a song slowly gets quieter and quieter at the end, that ending is called a…?
questions.f: Radio hits often fade out because the band just kept playing in the studio!

questions.q: In the song 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes', what comes right after shoulders?
questions.f: The song speeds up each round, turning singing into a giggly workout.

questions.q: At the end of 'Ring Around the Rosie', everyone…?
questions.f: Kids have played this circle-dance singing game for well over a hundred years.

questions.q: In the 'Hokey Pokey', after you put your arm in and out, you…?
questions.f: In England the same dance is called the 'Hokey Cokey.'

questions.q: What do we call all the people watching and listening at a concert?
questions.f: 'Audience' comes from a word meaning to hear—they're literally 'the listeners.'

questions.q: In 'Jingle Bells', what is dashing through the snow?
questions.f: 'Jingle Bells' was actually written for Thanksgiving, not Christmas!

questions.q: Which big purple dinosaur sings the 'I Love You' song on TV?
questions.f: Barney's 'I Love You' song borrows the tune of 'This Old Man.'

questions.q: The happy song 'Hakuna Matata' comes from which movie?
questions.f: 'Hakuna matata' is a real Swahili phrase meaning 'no worries.'

questions.q: Which Disney character sings 'How Far I'll Go' by the ocean?
questions.f: Moana's songs were co-written by Lin-Manuel Miranda, who also wrote Hamilton.

questions.q: In the movie Encanto, the family sings 'We Don't Talk About…' who?
questions.f: 'We Don't Talk About Bruno' became a bigger chart hit than 'Let It Go.'

questions.q: What is it called when the whole crowd is invited to sing together?
questions.f: At sing-alongs the words are often shown on a big screen so no one gets lost.

questions.q: Frogs croak at night to sing to other frogs.
questions.f: Some frogs puff up a throat pouch like a balloon to make their croak louder.

questions.q: The rooster's loud morning song is called a…?
questions.f: Funny English: a rooster crows, but a crow is also a bird—words can wear two hats!

questions.q: In the song, Mary had a little lamb with fleece as white as…?
questions.f: 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' was the first thing ever played back on a recording machine.

questions.q: The special song that starts your favorite TV show is called its…?
questions.f: A good theme song tells you what show is on before you even look at the screen.

questions.q: What music does a big clock tower play to mark the hour?
questions.f: London's famous Big Ben is actually the name of the giant bell inside the tower.

questions.q: Words like 'boom', 'crash', and 'ding' are words that copy real sounds.
questions.f: Sound-copying words have a fancy name—onomatopoeia—one of the trickiest words to spell!

questions.q: Which fairy-tale girl dances at the royal ball until the clock strikes midnight?
questions.f: A 'ball' is a grand dancing party—the word comes from an old verb meaning to dance.

questions.q: Which shiny golden instrument has a curved neck and buttons, and is played by blowing?
questions.f: The saxophone is one of the few instruments named after the person who invented it.

questions.q: The picture on the front of an album is called the album…?
questions.f: Some album covers are so famous that people hang them on walls like art.

questions.q: 'You've Got a Friend in Me' is the theme song of which movie?
questions.f: Randy Newman wrote and sang it—his voice opens every Toy Story film.

questions.q: The letters CD stand for 'compact disc'.
questions.f: 'Compact' means small—CDs replaced much bigger vinyl records and reels.

questions.q: The special clothes a performer wears on stage are called a…?
questions.f: 'Costume' and 'custom' were once the same word—both about what people usually wear.

questions.q: Where do people usually drop coins for a street musician?
questions.f: An open guitar case with a few coins inside is the busker's friendly invitation.

questions.q: What is the conductor's big book showing every instrument's part at once called?
questions.f: A conductor's score can show more than twenty lines of music stacked on every page.

questions.q: The sections of a song that tell the story with new words each time are the…?
questions.f: Most pop songs alternate: verse, chorus, verse, chorus—new story, same big hook.

questions.q: The 'bridge' of a song is…?
c: A middle section that sounds different from the rest
questions.f: Songwriters add a bridge to surprise your ears before the final chorus returns.

questions.q: The singers who support the star with harmonies from behind are called…?
questions.f: Many pop stars, including Whitney Houston's mom, started out as backup singers.

questions.q: The weekly list ranking the most popular songs is called the…?
questions.f: When a song is number one, musicians say it 'topped the charts.'

questions.q: One song released on its own, not with an album, is called a…?
questions.f: The name comes from vinyl days—one single song pressed on each side of a small record.

questions.q: A new version of a song made by re-arranging its recording is called a…?
questions.f: DJs invented remixing—stretching and swapping parts so crowds could dance longer.

questions.q: Musicians call a paid performance a…?
questions.f: 'Gig' started as jazz slang about a century ago—now even office workers use it.

questions.q: The crew member who hauls and sets up a band's equipment on tour is a…?
questions.f: 'Roadie' is short for 'road crew'—they build a concert stage in hours, city after city.

questions.q: Music with a strong steady beat made for parading in step is called a…?
questions.f: March composer John Philip Sousa wrote 'The Stars and Stripes Forever,' the US national march.

questions.q: The nervous, shaky feeling before going on stage is called…?
questions.f: Even superstars get stage fright—many say a little nervousness makes them perform better.

questions.q: A singer who drifts away from the correct notes is said to be singing…?
questions.f: 'Key' here means the set of notes a song lives in—wander outside and ears notice fast.

questions.q: The company that records and releases an artist's music is called a record…?
questions.f: The name comes from the round paper label glued to the middle of vinyl records.

questions.q: In square dancing, what happens in a 'do-si-do'?
c: Partners circle around each other back-to-back
questions.f: 'Do-si-do' comes from the French 'dos-à-dos,' meaning back-to-back.

questions.q: When the whole cast returns at the end to bow, it is called the curtain…?
questions.f: Record-breaking opera curtain calls have lasted over an hour of applause.

questions.q: A school club where students meet to sing together is often called a…?
questions.f: 'Glee' is an old English word for entertainment and joy—glee clubs date back to the 1700s.

questions.q: What is a jukebox?
c: A machine that plays the song you pick for a coin
questions.f: Classic diner jukeboxes let you flip through song cards and watch the record load.

questions.q: Which ridged instrument do you play by scraping a stick along its bumps?
questions.f: The guiro began as a dried hollow gourd—its scrape drives Latin dance rhythms.

questions.q: The kalimba, played by plucking metal tongues with your thumbs, is nicknamed the…?
questions.f: It is based on the African mbira, an instrument more than a thousand years old.

questions.q: Which instrument is a row of pipes of different lengths that you blow across?
questions.f: It is named after Pan, the Greek nature god who played pipes in myths.

questions.q: Which pair of small drums is held between the knees and tapped with the hands?
questions.f: Bongos come from Cuba—one drum is slightly bigger and deeper than its twin.

questions.q: On a drum kit, what are the two cymbals that open and close with a foot pedal called?
questions.f: Drummers keep time on the hi-hat—closed it ticks, open it sizzles.

questions.q: In 'Peter and the Wolf', each character is played by a different instrument.
questions.f: The duck is an oboe, the cat a clarinet, the bird a flute—and Peter is the strings.

questions.q: The Mexican folk song 'La Cucaracha' is about which creature?
questions.f: 'Cucaracha' means cockroach—singers invent endless funny verses about it.

questions.q: The French round 'Frère Jacques' asks a sleepy person to wake up and ring the…?
questions.f: In English he became 'Brother John,' and the tune is sung as a round worldwide.

questions.q: 'Kookaburra sits in the old gum tree' celebrates a laughing bird from which country?
questions.f: A kookaburra's call really does sound like loud human laughter echoing through the bush.

questions.q: Modern piano keys are usually topped with…?
questions.f: Pianos switched from ivory to plastic to protect elephants.

questions.q: Most guitar strings today are made of…?
questions.f: Classical guitars hum with soft nylon; rock guitars ring with bright steel.

questions.q: The stretched hair on a violin bow traditionally comes from which animal?
questions.f: One bow uses around 150 to 200 hairs, usually from horses' tails.

questions.q: Which toy instrument changes pitch when you pull its plunger in and out?
questions.f: Cartoon sound artists love the slide whistle for falling and boinging noises.

questions.q: Which composer wrote the famous movie music for both Star Wars and Harry Potter?
questions.f: John Williams has earned more than fifty Oscar nominations—a record for any living person.

questions.q: In a handbell choir, each ringer is responsible for just a few bells.
questions.f: The melody hops from person to person, so the whole team plays one tune together.

questions.q: Many songbirds learn their songs by copying their parents.
questions.f: Young birds even 'babble' quietly at first, practicing like human babies learning to talk.
