questions.q: Which insect is famous for making the loudest buzzing 'summer soundtrack'?
questions.f: Some cicadas hit around 100 decibels—about as loud as a motorcycle.

questions.q: Who leads a marching band down the street, often wearing a tall hat?
questions.f: The drum major sets the tempo with a long mace and dramatic signals.

questions.q: The prefix 'mega' in 'megaphone' means…?
questions.f: A megaphone makes a 'great sound'—cheer captains and film directors both swear by it.

questions.q: The prefix 'semi' in 'semitone', music's smallest step, means…?
questions.f: A semitone is a half step—the distance from a piano key to its closest neighbor.

questions.q: To 'transpose' a song literally means to…?
c: Shift it across to higher or lower notes
questions.f: 'Trans' means across—singers ask for songs transposed to fit their comfortable range.

questions.q: The 'pre' in 'prelude' tells you this piece of music comes…?
questions.f: From Latin 'ludere,' to play—a prelude literally 'plays before' the show begins.

questions.q: With the Italian ending '-etta' meaning small, an 'operetta' is literally a…?
questions.f: Operettas are light and funny—Gilbert and Sullivan's 'H.M.S. Pinafore' is a famous one.

questions.q: Shouting 'Bravo!' after a performance tells the performer…?
questions.f: Italian-speaking fans fine-tune it: 'brava' for a woman, 'bravi' for the whole cast.

questions.q: When the whole audience rises to its feet clapping, the performer has earned a standing…?
questions.f: In ancient Rome, an 'ovatio' was a victory parade—today the victory is artistic.

questions.q: The 'downbeat' of each measure is…?
questions.f: It's named for the conductor's baton, which literally moves down on beat one.

questions.q: Music passed down by ordinary people for generations, often with no known author, is called…?
questions.f: 'Folk' simply means people—the same word appears in 'folklore,' the people's stories.

questions.q: In music, the louds and softs of a performance are together called its…?
questions.f: From the Greek for power—dynamics turn the same notes into a whisper or a storm.

questions.q: Writing music down in symbols so others can play it is called…?
questions.f: An Italian monk named Guido invented the note-line system musicians still use today.

questions.q: The treble clef is nicknamed after the note whose line it curls around. Which note?
questions.f: Its swirl wraps the G line—the bass clef's two dots hug the F line, so it's the F clef.

questions.q: The distance in pitch between any two notes is called an…?
questions.f: 'Inter' means between—time between school classes is called an interval too.

questions.q: 'Chamber music' is written for a few players because 'chamber' means…?
questions.f: It was music for a palace room rather than a grand hall—every player gets their own part.

questions.q: A concert where music students each perform for family and friends is called a…?
questions.f: 'Recital' comes from reciting—performing from memory, just like a poem.

questions.q: The 'gale' hidden in 'nightingale' comes from an old English word meaning…?
questions.f: A nightingale is literally a 'night singer'—males sing in the dark to attract mates.

questions.q: Clog dancing hammers out rhythms using what kind of footwear?
questions.f: Factory workers in clogs invented steps during breaks—the machines gave them the beat.

questions.q: The vertical lines that slice written music into equal time chunks create…?
questions.f: Musicians also call a measure a 'bar'—as in the phrase 'a twelve-bar blues.'

questions.q: What do brass players slide into the bell of the instrument to hush and color its tone?
questions.f: Jazz trumpeters wave a plunger mute to make the horn 'talk'—wah-wah-wah.

questions.q: What is the clamp guitarists fasten across the neck to raise every string at once?
questions.f: 'Capo' is Italian for head—it becomes the strings' new starting point.

questions.q: Instead of sticks, jazz drummers often sweep the snare softly with wire…?
questions.f: Brushes give ballads their gentle 'sssh-tick' pulse, quiet as a whisper.

questions.q: Which handheld instrument has piano-style keys but sounds only when you blow into it?
questions.f: Reggae legend Augustus Pablo made the humble melodica the lead voice of hit records.

questions.q: The 1930s and 40s, when huge bands made ballrooms bounce, are called the ___ era.
questions.f: Swing bandleaders like Duke Ellington and Benny Goodman were the pop stars of their day.

questions.q: The word 'sonic', as in sonic boom and supersonic, means relating to…?
questions.f: From Latin 'sonus'—'supersonic' literally means 'above sound,' faster than sound travels.

questions.q: Why do string players rub sticky rosin on their bow hair?
c: So the bow grips the string enough to make it vibrate
To keep the hair from tangling
questions.f: Rosin is hardened tree resin—without it, a bow slides silently across the string.

questions.q: A player piano can perform a song by itself, reading holes punched in a paper roll.
questions.f: Each hole triggers one note—families gathered around pianos that 'played themselves' a century ago.

questions.q: Bharatanatyam, a classical dance rich in hand gestures and stamping feet, comes from…?
questions.f: Its hand shapes, called mudras, can narrate whole stories without a single word.

questions.q: Afrobeats, one of today's fastest-growing pop styles, boomed out of Nigeria and…?
questions.f: Afrobeats stars now sell out stadiums from Lagos to London and New York.

questions.q: Hip-hop music was born in the 1970s at block parties in which New York borough?
questions.f: DJ Kool Herc looped the drum breaks of records—and dancers 'broke' during those breaks.

questions.q: The three tiny bones that pass sound through your ear are the hammer, the anvil, and the…?
questions.f: The stirrup is the smallest bone in your body—smaller than a grain of rice.

questions.q: When a boy's voice deepens in his teens, people say his voice 'breaks'.
questions.f: The larynx grows quickly, and for a while the voice can squeak and dive without warning.

questions.q: Which animal's whooping chorus is often called the loudest of any land animal?
questions.f: Howler monkey calls can carry roughly five kilometers through dense rainforest.

questions.q: Australia's lyrebird is astonishing because it can imitate…?
c: Almost any sound it hears, even camera shutters
questions.f: Lyrebirds have mimicked car alarms and chainsaws—their tail resembles a Greek lyre.

questions.q: Why does a performing DJ use two turntables?
c: To blend one song into the next without a gap
To have a spare if one breaks
questions.f: Crossfading between decks keeps the dance floor moving—silence is a DJ's enemy.

questions.q: In the days of silent movies, live musicians played along in the theater.
questions.f: Pianists improvised chase music and love themes live, matching the screen scene by scene.

questions.q: The Highland fling, danced solo with arms raised like antlers, comes from…?
questions.f: Legend says warriors danced it on their small round shields after victories.

questions.q: The hora, where dancers circle with linked arms and guests are lifted on chairs, is danced at…?
questions.f: The circling hora is also a national dance in Romania and Israel.

questions.q: A powwow is a festival of drumming, singing, and dancing held by…?
questions.f: The big powwow drum is played by several drummers at once, all sharing one heartbeat.

questions.q: Frédéric Chopin, whose piano pieces include dances called mazurkas, was born in…?
questions.f: Chopin wrote almost nothing but piano music—and folded Polish folk dances into it.

questions.q: Using songs and rhythm to help patients heal and communicate is called music…?
questions.f: Music therapists help stroke patients who cannot speak to sing words instead.

questions.q: On an electric guitar, which part 'listens' to the vibrating strings and turns them into signal?
questions.f: A pickup is a magnet wrapped in wire—the steel string's wiggle writes itself into electricity.

questions.q: In rap music, the letters 'MC' originally stood for…?
questions.f: The MC's job was hyping the crowd for the DJ—then the rhymes became the main event.

questions.q: Queen's stadium anthem 'We Will Rock You' is built on the crowd pattern stomp, stomp,…?
questions.f: The band wanted a beat an entire stadium could play with feet and hands—no drums needed.

questions.q: 'Take Me Out to the Ball Game' is traditionally sung during which sport's seventh-inning stretch?
questions.f: The songwriters had reportedly never attended a big-league game when they wrote it.

questions.q: Which song do crowds join hands and sing as the clock strikes midnight on New Year's Eve?
questions.f: The words are old Scots by poet Robert Burns—'auld lang syne' means 'old long since.'

questions.q: A short, showy trumpet blast announcing someone important is called a…?
questions.f: Fanfares once announced royalty; today they open the Olympics and movie studio logos.

questions.q: A 'barbershop quartet' performs…?
questions.f: The style truly began in barbershops, where customers harmonized while they waited.

questions.q: Humming through a comb wrapped in paper turns it into a simple kazoo.
questions.f: The paper buzzes against your hum exactly like a kazoo's membrane.

questions.q: Flattening a drinking straw and snipping its tip lets you play it like which instrument family?
questions.f: The flattened tip becomes a double reed—snip the straw shorter and the pitch climbs.

questions.q: A medieval traveling poet-musician who sang of love and heroes was called a…?
questions.f: Troubadour comes from a root meaning 'to find'—they were 'finders' of songs.

questions.q: An honored poet-singer is called a 'bard'. Which writer is famous as simply 'The Bard'?
questions.f: Celtic bards sang a tribe's history from memory—a living library with a harp.

questions.q: In rap battles, inventing rhymes on the spot with no script is called…?
questions.f: Great freestylers weave things they see in the room straight into their rhymes.

questions.q: Borrowing a slice of an old recording to build a new song is called…?
questions.f: A two-second drum break from 1969, the 'Amen break,' lives inside thousands of songs.

questions.q: In old-time jug bands, players made rhythm by strumming thimbled fingers across a…?
questions.f: Jug bands turned laundry boards and whiskey jugs into a whole rhythm section.

questions.q: Two ordinary spoons can be played as a folk percussion instrument.
questions.f: Spoon players clack the backs of nested spoons between palm and knee at blazing speed.

questions.q: How do you play a musical saw?
c: Bend the blade and stroke it with a bow
Tap its teeth with a hammer
questions.f: Bending changes the pitch, giving an eerie gliding voice—like a ghost singing opera.

questions.q: The Greek root 'harmonia', source of 'harmony', originally meant…?
questions.f: Greek carpenters used it for well-fitted joints—music borrowed the idea of parts that fit.

questions.q: 'Rhythm' descends from the Greek 'rhythmos', which meant…?
questions.f: The Greeks pictured time flowing like a river—rhythm is how music rides that current.

questions.q: The tempo marking 'andante' tells musicians to play at the pace of…?
questions.f: It comes from Italian 'andare,' to walk—music that strolls rather than runs.

questions.q: The tempo word 'presto' means very fast—which entertainers borrowed it as a magic word?
questions.f: 'Presto!' means 'quickly!' in Italian—the trick happens faster than the eye can see.

questions.q: The tempo marking 'largo' asks for playing that is…?
questions.f: From the Latin for wide—the same root gives English the word 'large.'

questions.q: British musicians call an eighth note a 'quaver', a word that also means…?
questions.f: A voice that quavers trembles—fitting for a note that flutters by so quickly.

questions.q: The British name for a quarter note, 'crotchet', comes from a French word for a…?
questions.f: Early crotchets were drawn with hooks—'crochet' needlework uses the same little hook.

questions.q: The word 'clef', as in treble clef, is French for…?
questions.f: A clef is the 'key' that unlocks the staff—without it, the lines name no notes at all.

questions.q: 'Chord' began as a shortened form of which English word meaning agreement?
questions.f: Notes in agreement sound as one—its spelling later borrowed the H from Greek 'chorda,' string.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Echo was a mountain nymph who could only…?
c: Repeat the last words others spoke
questions.f: Cursed by Hera, Echo faded until only her voice remained—bouncing back our own words.

questions.q: Emergency 'sirens' are named after the Sirens of Greek myth, whose singing…?
questions.f: Odysseus had his crew plug their ears with beeswax so they could row safely past.

questions.q: The whirling Italian folk dance 'tarantella' is tangled up with the name of which creature?
questions.f: Folk belief claimed frantic dancing sweated out a tarantula's venom—both names honor Taranto.

questions.q: The stretchy one-piece 'leotard' worn by dancers is named after Jules Léotard, a French…?
questions.f: Léotard invented the flying trapeze act—and the daring outfit that let him soar.

questions.q: The canary, the classic singing pet, is named after islands that were themselves named after…?
questions.f: Rome called them 'Canariae Insulae,' isles of dogs—so the bird is accidentally named for dogs.

questions.q: A 'concerto' is a piece that spotlights…?
c: One soloist backed by the whole orchestra
questions.f: The soloist often gets a 'cadenza'—a flashy solo moment where the orchestra falls silent.

questions.q: Several songs stitched into one continuous performance are called a…?
questions.f: 'Medley' and 'meddle' share a root meaning to mix—a medley meddles tunes together.

questions.q: 'Vibrato', the expressive shimmer in a singer's long notes, is technically a rapid…?
questions.f: From Latin 'vibrare,' to shake—string players rock a fingertip to make notes shimmer.

questions.q: A 'glissando' instructs the player to…?
c: Slide smoothly through all the notes in between
questions.f: From French 'glisser,' to slide—harpists sweep whole rainbows of notes in one gesture.

questions.q: Playing a chord's notes one after another instead of together is an 'arpeggio', literally…?
c: Playing in the manner of a harp
questions.f: From Italian 'arpa,' harp—whose strings are almost always sounded one by one.

questions.q: The Greek 'khoros', ancestor of 'chorus' and 'choir', originally named a group that…?
questions.f: Greek choruses danced as they sang—so our biggest singing words secretly come from dance.

questions.q: Which music word contains no A, E, I, O, or U—getting by with only a Y?
questions.f: R-H-Y-T-H-M is a spelling-bee classic—six letters, and Y does all the vowel work.

questions.q: In 'psalm', a sacred song, which letter is silent?
questions.f: Greek loanwords hid their P sounds in English—'psalm' rhymes with 'calm.'

questions.q: A 'ceilidh'—spelled C-E-I-L-I-D-H—is a Scottish and Irish evening of…?
questions.f: Pronounced 'KAY-lee'—the Gaelic spelling makes it a spelling-bee boss battle.

questions.q: In a stage show, the performer who has learned a starring role in case the star cannot go on is the…?
questions.f: Broadway legends have been born overnight when an understudy stepped in and dazzled.

questions.q: 'Reverberation' is the technical name for…?
c: Sound lingering as it bounces around a room
questions.f: From Latin for 'beat back'—cathedrals can reverberate for six seconds or more.

questions.q: With 'poly' meaning many, 'polyphony' is music where…?
c: Several independent melodies weave at once
Every instrument plays the same note
questions.f: Renaissance composers braided four or more singing lines—each one a tune on its own.

questions.q: The Greek 'organon', root of 'organ', originally meant…?
questions.f: Your body's organs are 'tools' of life—the pipe organ is simply 'the instrument.'

questions.q: The snare drum crackles because of what stretched across its bottom head?
c: A rattling band of coiled wires
questions.f: Those wires are the 'snares'—flip a lever to lift them and the crack becomes a thud.

questions.q: With 'penta' meaning five, a pentatonic scale uses how many different notes?
questions.f: Play only a piano's black keys and you get a pentatonic scale—it's nearly impossible to sound bad.

questions.q: The chromatic scale, which uses all twelve semitones, borrows 'chroma', the Greek word for…?
questions.f: Musicians heard the in-between notes as 'coloring' the plain scale—chromatic means colorful.

questions.q: A 'mezzo-soprano' sits between soprano and alto because 'mezzo' means…?
questions.f: The same word hides in 'mezzanine'—the half-floor between two storeys of a building.

questions.q: Backstage, performers relax before showtime in a lounge traditionally called the…?
questions.f: Theaters have used the name since the 1600s, though nobody is sure the first one was green.

questions.q: Old theater stages sloped toward the audience, which is why walking away from the crowd is called moving…?
questions.f: An actor who lurked uphill forced others to turn their backs—'upstaging' still means stealing focus.

questions.q: In showbiz, an 'EGOT' winner has collected an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar, and a…?
questions.f: The Tony crowns Broadway—fewer than two dozen people have ever completed the EGOT.

questions.q: MIDI, the standard that lets keyboards talk to computers, stands for Musical Instrument…?
questions.f: Since 1983, rival companies' gear has spoken MIDI—one of tech's rare universal handshakes.

questions.q: Holst's orchestral suite 'The Planets' includes no movement for which planet?
questions.f: Holst followed astrology, not astronomy—and Pluto wasn't even discovered until 1930.

questions.q: In Saint-Saëns' 'Carnival of the Animals', the graceful 'Swan' glides on which solo instrument?
questions.f: The dying-swan ballet solo, created for Anna Pavlova, floats on this very cello melody.

questions.q: The galloping finale of Rossini's 'William Tell Overture' became the theme of which masked hero?
questions.f: Conductor Arturo Toscanini joked that fans could no longer hear the opera without shouting 'Hi-yo Silver!'

questions.q: 'Ride of the Valkyries', with its soaring warrior-maiden theme, was composed by…?
questions.f: It opens Act Three of Die Walküre—one opera in Wagner's four-night Ring cycle.

questions.q: Audiences traditionally stand during the 'Hallelujah Chorus' of Handel's Messiah.
questions.f: Legend says King George II rose to his feet at it in 1743—and everyone has stood since.

questions.q: Antonio Vivaldi, nicknamed 'The Red Priest' for his hair, taught music for decades at a Venice…?
questions.f: His all-girl orchestra at the Pietà became one of Europe's most famous ensembles.

questions.q: Hildegard of Bingen, one of the earliest composers we know by name, was a medieval…?
questions.f: Writing in the 1100s, she composed chants, wrote on medicine, and founded monasteries.

questions.q: Pianist Franz Liszt drove crowds so wild that newspapers coined which word for the frenzy?
questions.f: Fans fought over his gloves and broken piano strings—rock-star worship, 1840s style.

questions.q: Which pianist and composer appeared on Germany's 100 Deutsche Mark banknote?
questions.f: Clara toured Europe for six decades and premiered much of Robert Schumann's and Brahms's music.

questions.q: Luciano Pavarotti earned which royal nickname for nailing opera's most feared high notes?
questions.f: He once hit nine high Cs in a single aria—the crowd stopped the show mid-scene.

questions.q: The Three Tenors first sang together in 1990 on the eve of which world event?
c: The soccer World Cup final in Rome
questions.f: Their 'Nessun dorma' turned an opera aria into a global sports anthem.

questions.q: Which Beatles album cover shows the four simply walking across a London crosswalk?
questions.f: Tourists still queue daily to recreate the photo—the crossing is officially protected as a landmark.

questions.q: The Beatles gave their final live performance in 1969 from…?
c: The rooftop of their London office
questions.f: Police stopped the surprise lunchtime gig after about 42 minutes of traffic chaos.

questions.q: Guitar icon Jimi Hendrix famously played…?
c: A right-handed guitar flipped over and restrung, left-handed
questions.f: His school-era cheap guitars forced the flip—and helped create a sound no one could copy.

questions.q: Which singer, famous for 'Respect', is honored as the 'Queen of Soul'?
questions.f: In 1987 Aretha became the first woman inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

questions.q: In 2016, songwriter Bob Dylan received which surprising honor?
questions.f: The Swedish Academy praised his song poetry—he skipped the ceremony, then accepted quietly later.

questions.q: In the United States, an album 'goes platinum' when it sells…?
questions.f: Gold comes first at half a million—'diamond' waits at the ten-million summit.

questions.q: France's stirring national anthem is called…?
questions.f: Volunteer soldiers from Marseille sang it marching into Paris in 1792—the name stuck.

questions.q: In Australia's beloved song 'Waltzing Matilda', 'Matilda' is actually…?
questions.f: 'Waltzing Matilda' means tramping the outback with your bundle—no ballroom involved.

questions.q: Which giant woodwind rumbles out the lowest notes in a symphony orchestra?
questions.f: Its folded tube stretches about five meters—unrolled, taller than a giraffe.

questions.q: Roughly how many strings are stretched inside a full-size piano?
questions.f: Most notes get three strings each, pulled to a combined tension of about 20 tons.

questions.q: The piano was invented around 1700 by Bartolomeo Cristofori, an instrument keeper for a powerful family in…?
questions.f: He worked for the Medici—only three of his original pianos survive today.

questions.q: The two curly sound slots carved into a violin's front are called…?
questions.f: They're shaped like italic letter fs—their exact length helps tune the violin's voice.

questions.q: The classic blues song structure repeating the same chord journey is called the…?
questions.f: Learn twelve bars and three chords, and you can jam along to thousands of songs.

questions.q: The lightning-fast, complex jazz style pioneered in the 1940s by Charlie Parker is called…?
questions.f: The name may echo scat syllables—musicians simply sang 'be-bop' to describe its jumps.

questions.q: What was visually unmistakable about Dizzy Gillespie's trumpet?
c: Its bell bent upward at an angle
questions.f: A dancer fell on it in 1953—Dizzy liked the tilted sound and kept it bent forever.

questions.q: Ravel's 'Boléro' is famous for being essentially one long…?
questions.f: At its premiere a woman cried that Ravel was mad—he said she'd understood the piece perfectly.

questions.q: In John Cage's famous piece '4′33″', the performer…?
questions.f: Cage's point: the coughs, shuffles, and hum of the hall become the music.

questions.q: The oldest known musical instruments are roughly 40,000-year-old flutes made from…?
questions.f: Found in German caves, they show Ice Age humans made music with five-note precision.

questions.q: Astronaut Chris Hadfield went viral by recording which David Bowie song aboard the Space Station?
questions.f: His floating guitar performance was the first music video ever shot in orbit.

questions.q: The two Voyager space probes launched in 1977 each carry Earth's music on a…?
questions.f: The playlist spans Bach, Chuck Berry, and songs from dozens of cultures—with playing instructions.

questions.q: The pavlova, a meringue dessert beloved in Australia and New Zealand, is named after a famous…?
questions.f: Chefs said the dessert was 'light as Pavlova'—both countries still claim they invented it.

questions.q: In 2015, Misty Copeland became the first African American woman promoted to principal dancer at…?
questions.f: Copeland started ballet at 13—late for ballet—and rose to the very top in one decade.

questions.q: Dancer Ginger Rogers was praised for doing everything Fred Astaire did, but…?
questions.f: The famous line began as a caption in a 1982 comic strip and became her motto.

questions.q: Gene Kelly filmed the famous 'Singin' in the Rain' dance while running a high fever.
questions.f: Reports say he had a temperature of around 103°F—yet the joyful take made history.

questions.q: Which 2012 dance hit became the first video ever to reach one billion YouTube views?
questions.f: Psy's horse-riding dance racked up views so fast YouTube had to upgrade its view counter.

questions.q: Apple launched the iPod in 2001 with which famous promise?
questions.f: The first iPod's spinning hard drive held five gigabytes—laughably small today.

questions.q: MP3 files shrink music mainly by…?
c: Discarding sounds human ears barely notice
questions.f: The trick, called perceptual coding, can cut a file to a tenth of its size.

questions.q: What really exists beneath the Paris Opera house, echoing the Phantom's underground lake?
questions.f: Firefighters train by diving in it—Gaston Leroux spun the tank into the Phantom's lair.

questions.q: Mandolins are strung with their eight strings arranged…?
questions.f: Paired 'courses' make the mandolin shimmer—each pluck strikes twins in unison.

questions.q: An Arabic name meaning 'the wood', a pear-shaped body, and a bent-back pegbox arrived in Europe with the Moors and became which Renaissance instrument?
questions.f: 'Al-'ud' fused into 'lute'—the oud itself still reigns across Middle Eastern music.

questions.q: The 'kithara', a concert instrument of professional ancient Greek musicians, survives today mainly as…?
c: The name of a Greek dance
questions.f: From kithara through Arabic 'qitara' and Spanish 'guitarra'—a 2,500-year word journey.

questions.q: Clicked overhead in Spanish dance and demanded by Bizet's 'Carmen', this instrument's name literally means 'little chestnuts'. What is it?
questions.f: Spanish 'castaña' means chestnut—the polished clickers resemble two glossy nut halves.

questions.q: A sweet-potato shape, a name meaning 'little goose', and fame from a Zelda video game all point to which vessel flute?
questions.f: Italian 'oca' means goose—its inventor thought the shape looked like a goose without a head.

questions.q: The Greek 'kymbe' behind 'cymbal' originally named a…?
questions.f: Flip a cymbal over and the ancient logic appears—it really is a shallow metal bowl.

questions.q: Its name welds Latin 'dulce' to Greek 'melos'—literally 'sweet song'. Which hammered string instrument is it?
questions.f: Hammered dulcimers shimmer from Iran's santur to China's yangqin—one family, many names.

questions.q: Portugal's melancholy guitar-backed song style takes its name from the Latin 'fatum', meaning…?
questions.f: Fado's signature emotion is 'saudade'—a bittersweet longing Portuguese swears no other word can translate.

questions.q: The cool 1950s Brazilian style 'bossa nova' translates roughly as…?
questions.f: 'Bossa' was Rio slang for a knack or flair—'The Girl from Ipanema' carried it worldwide.

questions.q: The slow Cuban dance rhythm that opens Bizet's most famous aria is the 'habanera', literally meaning…?
questions.f: The tune itself was borrowed from Spanish composer Yradier—Bizet thought it was a folk song.

questions.q: Chopin's beloved 'mazurka' dances are named after Mazovia, which is…?
questions.f: Exiled in Paris, Chopin folded Mazovian village rhythms into some sixty piano mazurkas.

questions.q: In Indian classical music, a 'raga' is a melodic framework whose Sanskrit name means…?
questions.f: Ragas are matched to times of day—some are strictly sunrise music, others belong to midnight.

questions.q: The Italian opera ideal of agile, ornamented, gorgeous singing is called 'bel canto', literally…?
questions.f: Rossini quipped the style needs just three things: voice, voice, and voice.

questions.q: A soprano who specializes in fast, high, ornamental runs is called a 'coloratura', from an Italian word for…?
questions.f: Coloratura parts 'color' the melody with trills and leaps—like calligraphy for the voice.

questions.q: A 'countertenor' is a male singer whose range…?
c: Rises into alto or soprano territory
Only works in falsetto-free chest voice
questions.f: The name means he sings 'against' (above) the tenor line—a sound prized in baroque opera.

questions.q: The springy little ballet jump 'pas de chat' is literally the…?
questions.f: Dancers' knees snap up sideways mid-air—exactly like a startled cat hopping.

questions.q: A ballet 'jeté' is a leap whose French name literally means…?
questions.f: In a grand jeté the dancer 'throws' one leg forward and seems to hang in the air.

questions.q: The turning ballet step 'fouetté', famous from Swan Lake's 32-spin sequence, literally means…?
questions.f: The working leg 'whips' around to power each turn—like an ice skater pulling in their arms.

questions.q: In an opera house, the 'répétiteur' is the specialist who…?
c: Coaches singers through their roles at the piano
questions.f: French for 'repeater'—they drill every phrase until opening night, then the conductor gets the bow.

questions.q: The 'proscenium', the grand arch framing a stage, is built from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: In Greek theaters the 'skene' was the backdrop building—our word 'scene' walked out of it.

questions.q: Stretching a single sung syllable across a long run of notes—a gospel and chant specialty—is called…?
questions.f: From Greek for 'song'—Whitney Houston's 'I' in 'I Will Always Love You' is a textbook melisma.

questions.q: A short musical figure repeated stubbornly under changing music is an 'ostinato', Italian for…?
questions.f: Ravel's Boléro rides one snare-drum ostinato for a quarter of an hour.

questions.q: Playing 'rubato' lets a soloist bend the tempo expressively. The word literally means…?
questions.f: Time 'stolen' from one note is repaid to another—Chopin was the technique's great master.

questions.q: The playful symphonic movement called a 'scherzo' takes its name from the Italian for…?
questions.f: Composers swapped the stately minuet for the scherzo—trading a bow at court for a wink.

questions.q: In the alphabet song, which letter do you sing right after G?
questions.f: The alphabet song helps kids remember letter order by turning spelling into music.

questions.q: How many letters do you sing in the alphabet song?
questions.f: The song squeezes all 26 English letters into about 20 seconds of singing.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'song'?
questions.f: Songwriters hunt for rhymes so the ends of lines chime together.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'beat'?
questions.f: Handy for songwriters: you tap your feet to the beat, and the words rhyme too.

questions.q: In 'Baa, Baa, Black Sheep', what does the sheep have three bags full of?
questions.f: This rhyme is sung to the same tune as the alphabet song and 'Twinkle, Twinkle.'

questions.q: In the rhyme, Old King Cole called for his fiddlers — how many?
questions.f: He also called for his pipe and his bowl before the music started.

questions.q: In 'Rock-a-Bye Baby', where is the baby's cradle?
questions.f: It is one of the best-known lullabies in the English language.

questions.q: In 'This Old Man', he played knick-knack on my…?
questions.f: Each verse moves to a new number and a new body part—great counting practice.

questions.q: In 'The Ants Go Marching', how do the ants march first?
questions.f: The tune is borrowed from an old marching song, so it is easy to stomp along to.

questions.q: In the nursery song, London Bridge is…?
questions.f: Children play it as a singing game where two players make an arch with their arms.

questions.q: In the song, where does the Muffin Man live?
questions.f: Drury Lane is a real street in London, famous for its theater.

questions.q: Which brass instrument has a long tube you push and pull?
questions.f: Players learn seven slide positions and find them by feel, without looking.

questions.q: Which instrument is bigger: a violin or a cello?
questions.f: A cello is so big that players sit down and rest it on the floor on a metal spike.

questions.q: Which small yellow pet bird is famous for its singing?
questions.f: Male canaries do most of the singing, and some are bred just for their song.

questions.q: Which food shares its name with the stick a drummer holds?
questions.f: The chicken leg got the name because it looks like a stick for beating a drum.

questions.q: The word 'drumstick' is made by joining which two words?
questions.f: Two words joined into one make a compound word, like 'football' or 'sunshine.'

questions.q: Which two words are joined to make 'songbird'?
questions.f: A songbird is any bird that sings—there are thousands of songbird kinds worldwide.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'loud'?
questions.f: Music needs both—the quiet bits make the loud bits feel even bigger.

questions.q: If you clap once for each beat in the word 'but-ter-fly', how many claps?
questions.f: Word beats are called syllables—clapping them is how musicians learn rhythm.

questions.q: Yesterday I ___ a song. Which word fits?
questions.f: Sing, sang, sung—English changes the whole word instead of just adding '-ed.'

questions.q: Add '-er' to 'dance' and you get which word?
questions.f: The silent E is dropped before adding '-er'—a handy spelling rule.

questions.q: A person who plays the flute is called a…?
questions.f: In Britain they often say 'flautist' instead—two spellings, one player.

questions.q: A person who plays the violin is called a…?
questions.f: The '-ist' ending shows up all over music: pianist, cellist, harpist, organist.

questions.q: What do you call a person who plays the trumpet?
questions.f: Some instruments take '-er' and others take '-ist'—English likes to keep you guessing.

questions.q: What do musicians rest their sheet music on while they play?
questions.f: Music stands fold up flat so players can carry them to every rehearsal.

questions.q: What are the shoes with metal plates on the bottom called?
questions.f: The metal plates are called taps, and they turn the whole floor into a drum.

questions.q: Dancers practice in a big room with mirrors called a dance…?
questions.f: Mirrors let dancers check their own shapes without a teacher saying a word.

questions.q: Which dance move has you wriggling along the floor like a wiggly animal?
questions.f: The worm became a breakdancing favorite in the 1980s.

questions.q: Ballet slippers are most often which color?
questions.f: Pale pink makes the dancer's legs and feet look like one long line.

questions.q: What should dancers do before they start dancing hard?
questions.f: Warm muscles bend more easily, which helps dancers avoid getting hurt.

questions.q: If you listen to music with headphones on, who can hear it?
questions.f: Headphones send the sound straight into your ears instead of into the room.

questions.q: What do earplugs do at a very loud concert?
c: Make the sound quieter and safer
questions.f: Loud noise can harm your ears for good, so many musicians wear earplugs on stage.

questions.q: Which is quieter: a lullaby or a rock concert?
questions.f: Lullabies are sung softly on purpose, to help a baby drift off.

questions.q: In music class, what do you tap together to practice a steady beat?
questions.f: Rhythm sticks are one of the simplest instruments—two pieces of wood and a beat.

questions.q: Which jingling bells are tied to horses pulling a winter sleigh?
questions.f: Sleigh bells warned people that a quiet horse-drawn sleigh was coming through the snow.

questions.q: Which drum does a marching band player wear strapped in front of them?
questions.f: Marching snare drums have a crisp crack that carries far down a parade route.

questions.q: In most bands, which player keeps the beat for everyone else?
questions.f: Musicians say the drummer is the band's engine room.

questions.q: Which large instrument often plays in a church as a bride walks in?
questions.f: A church organ can be as loud as a whole orchestra all by itself.

questions.q: In 'Five Little Speckled Frogs', where do the frogs sit?
questions.f: One frog jumps into the pool in each verse, so the counting goes down.

questions.q: In 'I'm a Little Teapot', the teapot is short and…?
questions.f: 'Stout' means round and sturdy—and it rhymes neatly with 'spout' and 'out.'

questions.q: Which tiny instruments are worn on the fingers and chinked together while dancing?
questions.f: Also called zills, they have been used by dancers for hundreds of years.

questions.q: The steady beat of music is often compared to which body sound?
questions.f: Musicians call the steady beat the 'pulse'—the very same word used for your heartbeat.

questions.q: Which bird is named after the sound of its own call?
questions.f: Cuckoo clocks copy the bird, popping out a wooden bird to sing the hour.

questions.q: Which word copies a real sound?
questions.f: Comic books are full of sound-copying words like ZAP, POW, and SPLASH.

questions.q: What do we call the team of drummers in a marching band?
questions.f: Drumline players often spin their sticks and toss them mid-beat.

questions.q: Which of these can be blown like a horn?
questions.f: Conch shell horns have been blown as signals and in ceremonies for thousands of years.

questions.q: 'Pop Goes the ___' — which animal completes this song title?
questions.f: Jack-in-the-boxes usually play this tune, popping open on the word 'pop.'

questions.q: In the song, how many men did the Grand Old Duke of York have?
questions.f: Children stand up and sit down as the song marches the men up and down the hill.

questions.q: Which pet makes a soft rumbling purr?
questions.f: A cat's purr vibrates about 25 times a second—you can feel it with your hand.

questions.q: Which bird calls 'hoo-hoo' in the night?
questions.f: Owls have soft feather edges, so they fly almost silently while calling loudly.

questions.q: Which animal makes a mighty roar?
questions.f: A lion's roar can be heard from about eight kilometers away.

questions.q: Which word best copies the sound of thunder?
questions.f: Thunder is the sound of air heated so fast by lightning that it bangs.

questions.q: What does a band leader usually count before the music starts?
questions.f: That count-in is called a 'four count'—it gets everyone starting on the same beat.

questions.q: Which of these plays a little tune or chime when a visitor presses it?
questions.f: Some doorbells play tunes—one popular chime is called the Westminster chime.

questions.q: What is a nursery rhyme?
c: A short song or poem for young children
questions.f: Many nursery rhymes are hundreds of years old and were passed on by singing.

questions.q: What do you call words that a crowd shouts over and over in rhythm?
questions.f: Sports crowds chant so loudly that stadiums seem to shake.

questions.q: Which animal gives its name to the hopping party dance, the '___ Hop'?
questions.f: The Bunny Hop is danced in a line, with two hops at the end of every step pattern.

questions.q: What does a 'quintet' tell you about the group?
questions.f: 'Quint' means five, just as it does in quintuplets—five babies born at once.

questions.q: A 'sextet' is a group of how many musicians?
questions.f: Latin number words fill music: duet, trio, quartet, quintet, sextet, septet, octet.

questions.q: A 'septet' has how many players?
questions.f: 'Sept' means seven—which is why September was once the seventh Roman month.

questions.q: Which word means a very short piece of music, especially for beginners?
questions.f: Musicians often call these pieces 'etudes,' from the French word for study.

questions.q: What do we call the list of songs a band plans to play at a concert?
questions.f: Bands tape the setlist to the stage floor so they never lose their place.

questions.q: A series of concerts in different cities is called a…?
questions.f: Big tours travel with dozens of trucks carrying the stage, lights, and speakers.

questions.q: What do you call the huge outdoor event where many bands play over several days?
questions.f: 'Festival' comes from a word meaning feast day—music turned it into a summer tradition.

questions.q: What do we call the room where songs are recorded?
questions.f: Recording studios have padded walls so no echo or street noise sneaks onto the track.

questions.q: What is a 'medley' in a school concert?
c: Several songs joined into one performance
questions.f: Medleys let a choir squeeze five favorite tunes into one showstopper.

questions.q: What does it mean to sing 'in harmony'?
c: Singing different notes that sound good together
questions.f: Two singers in harmony can sound richer than ten singers on the same note.

questions.q: What does an 'a cappella' group perform without?
questions.f: A cappella groups often imitate drums and bass with their voices instead.

questions.q: What is the 'hook' of a pop song?
c: The catchiest part that grabs your ear
questions.f: Songwriters say the hook has to land in the first fifteen seconds to catch listeners.

questions.q: Which word describes music with a smooth, flowing feel?
questions.f: Composers write the Italian word 'legato' when they want notes joined smoothly.

questions.q: What is a 'lyric' in a song?
c: A line of the words being sung
questions.f: Song lyrics are printed inside album covers so fans can sing every word.

questions.q: What does the word 'tune' mean in music?
c: A melody you can sing or hum
questions.f: 'Tune' is also a verb—to tune an instrument is to make its notes correct.

questions.q: What does a 'karaoke' machine remove from a song?
questions.f: The words scroll on a screen with a bouncing marker to keep you on the beat.

questions.q: What is a 'boy band'?
c: A pop group of young male singers
questions.f: Boy bands usually sing and dance in tight formation rather than play instruments.

questions.q: What does a 'fan club' do?
c: Brings together admirers of a musician
questions.f: Fan clubs once ran on posted newsletters; now they run on social media.

questions.q: What is a 'talent show'?
c: A tour of a music factory
questions.f: Many famous singers were discovered in school or television talent shows.

questions.q: Which word means the special sound that makes one singer's voice recognizable?
questions.f: You can spot a favorite singer in a second—the human ear is amazing at tone.

questions.q: What is a lullaby's job?
questions.f: Lullabies exist in nearly every culture, and most are slow, low, and repetitive.

questions.q: Which instrument family does the violin belong to?
questions.f: Its four strings can also be plucked—players call that pizzicato.

questions.q: Which instrument sits between the violin and the cello in size and pitch?
questions.f: Violists are proud of their warm middle voice—and famously good at viola jokes.

questions.q: Which woodwind instrument is longer and lower than a clarinet and has a curved metal mouth pipe?
questions.f: A bassoon's tube is over two meters long, folded in half to make it holdable.

questions.q: Which instrument's name means 'English horn' even though it is a woodwind, not brass?
questions.f: It is neither English nor a horn—it is a bigger, mellower cousin of the oboe.

questions.q: Which drum from Ireland is played with a short wooden beater called a tipper?
questions.f: Bodhran players change the drum's pitch by pressing a hand against the inside skin.

questions.q: Japanese taiko drumming is famous for its…?
c: Huge drums played with big sticks and whole-body movement
questions.f: The biggest taiko drums can weigh as much as a small car.

questions.q: Which country is home to the balalaika, a string instrument with a triangular body?
questions.f: Its three strings and pointed shape make it instantly recognizable on stage.

questions.q: The banjo-like shamisen, played with a large plectrum, comes from which country?
questions.f: Shamisen players strike the strings so firmly that the whole body thumps like a drum.

questions.q: The charango, a tiny high-pitched guitar, is played in the mountains of…?
questions.f: Andean musicians pair the charango with panpipes for their bright mountain sound.

questions.q: Which African instrument is a large harp-lute with a gourd body, played by griot musicians?
questions.f: Kora players pluck 21 strings with just their thumbs and index fingers.

questions.q: What is the 'bow' of a violin made to do?
c: Draw across the strings to make them vibrate
Hit the strings like a hammer
questions.f: Great bows are made of springy wood, and their stick curves inward, not outward.

questions.q: An orchestra usually tunes and warms up before the conductor walks on stage.
questions.f: That jumble of scales and squeaks is one of the most exciting sounds in a concert hall.

questions.q: Where does the choir usually stand in a big concert performance?
c: At the back of the audience
questions.f: Choirs stand on stepped platforms called risers so every voice reaches the room.

questions.q: Why do stage performers often wear microphones taped near their hairline?
c: So their hands stay free to dance
questions.f: These tiny 'headset mics' let dancers sing while leaping across the stage.

questions.q: What is a 'spotlight' used for in a show?
c: To shine a bright beam on one performer
questions.f: 'To be in the spotlight' now means to be the center of everyone's attention.

questions.q: What does a 'stage manager' do?
c: Runs the backstage side of a show
questions.f: The stage manager calls every lighting and scenery cue over a headset, unseen.

questions.q: What is a 'dance-off'?
c: A friendly contest of dance moves
A day when dancing is banned
questions.f: Dance-offs are judged on creativity and control—not just speed.

questions.q: Which dance style is famous for spins, freezes, and floor moves?
questions.f: Breakers invent their own signature moves and give them nicknames.

questions.q: In the Irish dance called stepdance, the arms are usually…?
c: Held still while the feet fly
questions.f: Hard shoes make the famous thundering rhythm, seen worldwide in Riverdance.

questions.q: Which Greek circle dance speeds up as it goes and is danced with linked shoulders?
questions.f: Sirtaki was actually created for a 1964 film and became a symbol of Greece.

questions.q: Belly dancing, with its rippling hip movements, is traditionally associated with which region?
c: The Middle East and North Africa
questions.f: Dancers often play finger cymbals while dancing, becoming their own percussion section.

questions.q: Which dance involves two long bamboo poles clapped together while dancers hop between them?
questions.f: Tinikling copies the way a heron hops between grass stems—one slip and your ankles know it.

questions.q: Why do many singers avoid ice-cold drinks before a performance?
c: Cold can tighten the muscles they sing with
questions.f: Most singers sip room-temperature water and hum gently to warm up first.

questions.q: Which of these helps a singer's voice most?
questions.f: Vocal folds need moisture to vibrate smoothly, so singers carry water everywhere.

questions.q: Why does a guitar go out of tune when a room gets much hotter or colder?
c: The strings and wood expand or shrink
questions.f: Touring musicians retune constantly—stage lights can heat a guitar in minutes.

questions.q: What does a 'tuner' app on a phone do?
c: Shows if a note is too high or too low
questions.f: It counts the vibrations per second and compares them with the correct pitch.

questions.q: Sound is caused by things vibrating.
questions.f: Put a hand on a speaker while music plays and you can feel the vibration directly.

questions.q: Which travels through a wall more easily: high squeaky notes or deep bass notes?
questions.f: That's why you hear the neighbors' thumping bass but not their singing.

questions.q: What is a 'soundtrack'?
c: The music that goes with a film or game
questions.f: Game soundtracks often change as you play, growing tense when danger appears.

questions.q: Which of these classic games is famous for its short, catchy background tunes?
questions.f: Composer Koji Kondo had so little memory to work with that every note had to count.

questions.q: Which instrument is Ludwig van Beethoven best known for playing himself?
questions.f: Beethoven was famous as a piano superstar in Vienna before he was famous as a composer.

questions.q: Which composer wrote a piece nicknamed 'Für Elise', one of the most-played piano tunes ever?
questions.f: Nobody is certain who Elise was—the manuscript's messy handwriting hides the answer.

questions.q: What did the composer Johann Sebastian Bach work as for much of his life?
questions.f: Bach wrote a fresh piece nearly every week for church services—by hand.

questions.q: Which instrument did the famous musician Yo-Yo Ma make world-famous?
questions.f: Yo-Yo Ma played for a US president at age seven and has recorded over 100 albums.

questions.q: Which nickname belongs to Michael Jackson?
questions.f: Nicknames like these are called honorifics—music loves crowning its stars.

questions.q: What is the 'Billboard Hot 100'?
c: A weekly chart of the most popular songs in the US
A list of the loudest bands
questions.f: It has been counting hits since 1958, blending sales, radio play, and streams.

questions.q: Streaming means listening to music over the internet without downloading the whole file first.
questions.f: Streaming now provides most of the world's recorded music listening.

questions.q: Which of these is a percussion instrument you scrape rather than strike?
questions.f: Washboard players wear metal thimbles to scratch out a rattling rhythm.

questions.q: The root 'melo' in 'melody' and 'melodrama' means…?
questions.f: A melodrama was literally a play with songs—later it came to mean an over-the-top drama.

questions.q: The 'micro' in 'microphone' means…?
questions.f: A microphone catches small sounds; a microscope shows small things.

questions.q: 'Saxophone' is built from an inventor's surname plus a root meaning…?
questions.f: Adolphe Sax's name plus Greek 'phone' gives us literally 'Sax's sound.'

questions.q: To 'amplify' music comes from a Latin root meaning…?
questions.f: An amplifier makes the sound 'larger'—the same root gives us 'ample,' meaning plenty.

questions.q: A 'theatre' is, by its Greek root, a place for…?
questions.f: Neat pair: a theatre is for seeing, an auditorium for hearing—two senses, two words.

questions.q: The word 'drama' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek drama was performed with masks, choruses, and dancing—action first, words second.

questions.q: The word 'concert' grew from a root meaning…?
questions.f: That's why we also say people act 'in concert'—they're working in agreement.

questions.q: The word 'lullaby' is thought to be built from…?
questions.f: Both halves are soothing sounds—the word almost rocks the baby by itself.

questions.q: In music, 'diminuendo' tells performers to…?
questions.f: Same root as 'diminish'—the sound shrinks note by note.

questions.q: The marking 'forte' tells a player to play…?
questions.f: 'Forte' means strong—and in English, your forte is your strong point.

questions.q: In 'fortissimo', the Italian ending '-issimo' means…?
questions.f: So fortissimo is 'very loud' and pianissimo is 'very soft'—one ending, opposite extremes.

questions.q: The word 'tempo' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: The same root gives 'temporary' and 'contemporary'—all about time.

questions.q: A 'hymn' is a song of…?
questions.f: 'Hymn' keeps a silent N at the end—but 'hymnal' brings the sound back to life.

questions.q: If a sound is 'inaudible', the prefix 'in-' tells you it…?
questions.f: 'In-' flips a word's meaning: visible/invisible, audible/inaudible.

questions.q: A stage performer called a 'ventriloquist' has a name literally meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin 'venter' (belly) and 'loqui' (to speak)—the voice seems to come from elsewhere.

questions.q: A 'chorister' is…?
questions.f: Cathedral choristers often start training at seven or eight years old.

questions.q: The music format called a 'cassette' takes its name from a word meaning…?
questions.f: French 'cassette' is a little case—inside, two reels wound the tape past the player's head.

questions.q: The word 'podcast' was made by blending 'broadcast' with…?
questions.f: Words built by mashing two others together are called blends, or portmanteau words.

questions.q: The brass instrument called a 'cornet' has a name meaning…?
questions.f: Latin 'cornu' means horn—the same root hides inside 'unicorn,' the one-horned beast.

questions.q: In written music, a 'coda' comes at the end because the word means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'cauda,' tail—the coda is the piece's wagging finish.

questions.q: Songs written in a minor key usually sound…?
questions.f: Swap a few notes and a happy major tune turns instantly gloomy—the same melody, new mood.

questions.q: Guitar 'tab' notation shows players…?
c: Which string and fret to press
questions.f: Tab uses six lines for six strings—handy for players who never learned to read notes.

questions.q: What does a repeat sign in sheet music tell a musician?
questions.f: Repeat signs save paper—composers avoided writing the same page out twice.

questions.q: About how many strings does a full concert harp have?
questions.f: Harpists memorize the colors: red strings are Cs and black or blue strings are Fs.

questions.q: How many pedals does a concert harp have?
questions.f: Each pedal controls one note name across the whole instrument, changing sharps and flats.

questions.q: The alphorn, a wooden horn several metres long, is played in the mountains of…?
questions.f: Herders once used its huge tone to call cattle and signal across Alpine valleys.

questions.q: How does a hurdy-gurdy make its sound?
c: A hand-cranked wheel rubs against the strings
questions.f: It's a fiddle that plays itself—the crank does the bowing while fingers work the keys.

questions.q: The koto, a long zither played kneeling on the floor, comes from…?
questions.f: Koto players wear picks on three fingers to pluck its thirteen silk or nylon strings.

questions.q: The harmonium, common in Indian music, makes sound when the player…?
c: Pumps a bellows with one hand and plays keys with the other
questions.f: It arrived from Europe in the 1800s and became a fixture of Indian devotional singing.

questions.q: 'The Magic Flute', an opera full of fairy-tale magic, was written by…?
questions.f: Its Queen of the Night aria climbs to a high F—one of opera's most feared notes.

questions.q: Handel's 'Water Music' got its name because it was first performed…?
c: On boats on the River Thames
questions.f: King George I loved it so much in 1717 that he asked for it three times in one evening.

questions.q: Which 1990s dance hit has a fixed arm routine followed by a jump and hip turn?
questions.f: Its Spanish creators, Los del Río, sang it for years before it swept the world.

questions.q: In the party song 'Y.M.C.A.', dancers spell the four letters using their…?
questions.f: Fans invented the arm-spelling on a TV show—the band then copied it back.

questions.q: In many music classes, each solfa note (do, re, mi) also has its own…?
questions.f: The hand signs let a teacher 'conduct' a melody silently for the class to sing.

questions.q: What is unusual about the song 'Cha Cha Slide'?
c: Its lyrics call out the dance moves as you go
questions.f: A Chicago fitness instructor wrote it as a workout routine for his gym classes.

questions.q: Besides the melody pipe, what do a bagpipe's other pipes play?
questions.f: The drones never change, which is why bagpipe tunes float over a constant hum.

questions.q: Why are a piano's black keys grouped in twos and threes?
c: So players can find their place by touch
questions.f: Blindfolded pianists can find middle C by feeling for those groups alone.

questions.q: On a piano score, the 'grand staff' is…?
c: Treble and bass staves joined together
questions.f: The right hand usually reads the treble stave while the left reads the bass.

questions.q: Why do you see lightning before you hear the thunder?
c: Light travels much faster than sound
questions.f: Count the seconds and divide by three for a rough distance in kilometres.

questions.q: Why does cupping a hand behind your ear help you hear better?
c: It gathers more sound waves toward your ear
questions.f: Many animals swivel big ear flaps to do the same job automatically.

questions.q: Why do singers hum quietly before a performance?
c: It warms up the voice gently
questions.f: Humming vibrates the vocal folds without strain—like stretching before a race.

questions.q: The band name 'The Beatles' is a play on the spelling of which word?
questions.f: They swapped the second E for an A to smuggle the word 'beat' into the insect's name.

questions.q: What is a 'stage name'?
c: A performing name that is not the artist's birth name
questions.f: Countless stars perform under invented names that are catchier than their real ones.

questions.q: What makes an album a 'live' album?
c: It was recorded at a concert
questions.f: You can usually hear the crowd cheering between the tracks.

questions.q: What is 'sight-reading'?
c: Playing a piece well the very first time you see it
questions.f: Professional session players are hired for it—they record music minutes after seeing it.

questions.q: A musician who plays 'by ear' performs…?
questions.f: Many legendary blues and folk players never read a note of written music.

questions.q: What is a 'chord progression'?
c: The order the chords move in through a song
questions.f: A handful of progressions power thousands of pop songs—which is why so many sound alike.

questions.q: Why is an acoustic guitar's body hollow?
c: The air inside vibrates to make the sound louder
To make it lighter to hold
questions.f: The hollow space is a resonating chamber—shrink it and the guitar gets quieter.

questions.q: What does the small wooden 'bridge' on a violin do?
c: Carries the strings' vibrations into the body
questions.f: It isn't glued on at all—string pressure alone holds a violin bridge upright.

questions.q: What is a drum key used for?
c: Tightening the bolts that stretch a drumhead
questions.f: Tighter heads mean higher pitch—drummers tune by ear around the whole rim.

questions.q: What happens at a 'sound check'?
c: The crew tests and balances levels before the show
questions.f: Sound checks can take longer than the concert itself at big outdoor venues.

questions.q: A modern flute is called a 'transverse' flute because it is held…?
questions.f: 'Trans' means across—recorders, by contrast, are end-blown and point downward.

questions.q: The 'bugle' owes its name to an animal, because early ones were made from the horn of a…?
questions.f: From Latin 'buculus,' a young bullock—soldiers literally blew through cattle horns.

questions.q: Concert 'arenas' take their name from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Roman arena floors were sanded—today's arenas host stadium tours instead.

questions.q: The glass harmonica, played by touching spinning glass bowls, was invented by…?
questions.f: Mozart and Beethoven both wrote for Franklin's eerie invention.

questions.q: The whirling dancers known as dervishes, who spin with one palm up and one down, come from…?
questions.f: Their spinning is a Sufi form of prayer, tied to the poet Rumi's followers in Konya.

questions.q: Which time signature gives an Irish jig its lilting swing?
questions.f: Say 'jiggety-jig' and you have felt 6/8—two groups of three quick beats.

questions.q: The instruction 'da capo' sends a performer back to the beginning because it literally means…?
questions.f: Italian 'capo' means head—a company's 'capo' is its head, too.

questions.q: A 'fermata' over a note tells the player to…?
questions.f: From Italian 'fermare,' to stop—a railway 'fermata' in Italy is simply a stop.

questions.q: A 'paradiddle' is a drummer's practice pattern of…?
c: Alternating and doubled sticking, like R-L-R-R
One stick spun in the air
questions.f: Drummers drill dozens of these patterns, called rudiments, with names like flam and ratamacue.

questions.q: Modern orchestras tune to an A vibrating at how many times per second?
questions.f: It's written A440; some orchestras nudge it to 442 or 443 for extra brilliance.

questions.q: On an old vinyl single, what was the 'B-side'?
c: The flip side, holding the less-promoted song
questions.f: Some B-sides outgrew their A-sides and became the bigger hits by accident.

questions.q: Why did the band Led Zeppelin spell 'Led' without an A?
c: So people would not pronounce it 'leed'
questions.f: The name came from a joke that the band would go down like a lead balloon.

questions.q: Besides Swan Lake and The Nutcracker, which is Tchaikovsky's third great ballet?
questions.f: Its 1890 premiere was so lavish that the sets nearly bankrupted the theatre.

questions.q: In ballet, 'turnout' means rotating the legs outward from the…?
questions.f: Forcing turnout from the knees injures dancers—teachers watch for it constantly.

questions.q: How is a jaw harp (mouth harp) played?
c: Held against the teeth while a metal tongue is plucked
questions.f: Your mouth becomes the resonating chamber—change its shape and the note's colour shifts.

questions.q: The word 'radio', which carried music into homes, comes from a Latin root meaning…?
questions.f: Signals 'radiate' outward like rays—the same root as radius and radiant.

questions.q: 'Tinnitus', a ringing in the ears, takes its name from a Latin verb meaning…?
questions.f: Musicians guard against it with earplugs—loud sound can leave the ringing permanent.

questions.q: The Suzuki method teaches young children music mainly by…?
c: Listening and imitating before reading notes
questions.f: Shinichi Suzuki called it the mother-tongue method—kids learn music the way they learn speech.

questions.q: The 'Mach' number, used for speeds beyond sound, honors physicist Ernst Mach of…?
questions.f: Mach photographed shockwaves around speeding bullets long before jets existed.

questions.q: Medical ultrasound scanners work using sound that is…?
c: Too high-pitched for humans to hear
questions.f: Echoes bouncing off tissue are turned into a picture—sonar for the human body.

questions.q: Gershwin's 'Rhapsody in Blue' famously opens with a swooping solo on which instrument?
questions.f: Gershwin wrote a plain scale; the band's clarinettist smeared it into a glissando at rehearsal.

questions.q: Which composer's 'Canon in D' has become a wedding-ceremony staple?
questions.f: It sat forgotten for two centuries before a 1960s recording made it inescapable.

questions.q: The synthesizer that made electronic music mainstream in the 1960s was built by…?
questions.f: Moog's keyboards purred on hit records within a few years of leaving his workshop.

questions.q: Chubby Checker's 'The Twist' is remarkable for reaching number one in the US…?
c: On the same day as its release
questions.f: It topped the chart in 1960, faded, then climbed all the way back in 1962.

questions.q: The solemn US bugle call played at military funerals and at lights-out is called…?
questions.f: Just 24 notes long, it was reworked during the American Civil War.

questions.q: The dance style 'voguing', full of sharp poses and hand performance, is named after…?
questions.f: Dancers struck poses like magazine models in Harlem ballroom competitions.

questions.q: A normal speaking conversation measures roughly how many decibels?
questions.f: Every 10 decibels means ten times more sound energy—120 dB is a painful roar.

questions.q: How many sharps are in the key signature of G major?
questions.f: Just F sharp—which is why G major is one of the first keys guitarists learn.

questions.q: What does the 'whammy bar' on an electric guitar do?
c: Bends the pitch of the notes
questions.f: Its proper name is the vibrato arm—Jimi Hendrix used it to make guitars howl and dive.

questions.q: On an orchestral score's page, which family is written on the bottom staves?
questions.f: The order runs top to bottom: woodwinds, brass, percussion, then strings anchoring the page.

questions.q: The word 'Muzak', now slang for bland background music, began as…?
questions.f: The firm piped soothing music into factories and lifts—hence 'elevator music.'

questions.q: The so-called 'Mozart effect' was the popular claim that hearing Mozart could…?
c: Briefly boost performance on spatial puzzles
questions.f: The 1993 study measured a small, short-lived effect—then the newspapers made it magic.

questions.q: In musical theatre, an 'eleven o'clock number' is…?
c: A big showstopper late in the second act
A song cut before opening night
questions.f: The name dates from when Broadway curtains rose at 8:30 and the show peaked near 11.

questions.q: London's great theatre district, the rival of Broadway, is known as the…?
questions.f: Some West End musicals have run for decades without a single night off.

questions.q: A violin prodigy stopped by tendon trouble, a career built on 'aerial fingering', and concerts played without touching the instrument point to which virtuoso?
questions.f: Rockmore's precision turned the theremin from a novelty gadget into a true concert instrument.

questions.q: A physicist who demonstrated a new instrument to Lenin, and a listening device hidden inside a carved wooden seal in a US embassy, point to which inventor?
questions.f: His bug, nicknamed 'The Thing', needed no batteries—and his instrument is played in mid-air.

questions.q: A 1968 album of Bach realized entirely on Moog synthesizers, plus the score for Disney's 'Tron', are the work of which composer?
questions.f: 'Switched-On Bach' outsold nearly every classical record of its year and made synths respectable.

questions.q: Hand-spliced tape loops, a plucked string re-pitched in a BBC workshop, and test-tone oscillators instead of synthesizers created which famous TV theme?
questions.f: Delia Derbyshire assembled it in 1963, note by note, years before synthesizers reached Britain.

questions.q: Engineers testing early MP3 compression used which singer's bare, unaccompanied recording as their toughest trial?
questions.f: 'Tom's Diner' was so exposed that every flaw showed—Vega is now nicknamed the mother of the MP3.

questions.q: Before he built pitch-correction software for singers, the engineer behind Auto-Tune used the same mathematics to…?
questions.f: Andy Hildebrand analyzed seismic echoes—then pointed the same trick at wobbly vocals.

questions.q: A crash that left one arm permanently set at a playing angle, tape experiments called 'sound on sound', and a legendary solid-body guitar point to whom?
questions.f: He asked surgeons to fix his elbow at an angle that would still let him cradle a guitar.

questions.q: A caravan fire that damaged two fretting fingers, a rebuilt left-hand technique, and 1930s Paris point to which guitarist?
questions.f: He invented 'gypsy jazz' using mostly two fingers—and could outplay anyone with five.

questions.q: A soloist who performs barefoot to feel the stage, and who pushed a London academy to change its admission rules, is which percussionist?
questions.f: Profoundly deaf since childhood, Glennie hears through her whole body—her feet do the listening.

questions.q: Manuscripts found in 2009 in an abandoned Illinois house, and a 1933 Chicago Symphony premiere, restored the reputation of which composer?
questions.f: Price was the first African American woman to have a symphony played by a major US orchestra.

questions.q: Songs published under a brother's name, and a piece Queen Victoria praised as her favourite that he then admitted was not his, point to which composer?
questions.f: Felix confessed the truth to the Queen—the song was written by his gifted sister.

questions.q: A champion fencer, a colonel in the French army, and the conductor who premiered Haydn's Paris symphonies were all the same 18th-century composer. Who?
questions.f: Born in Guadeloupe, he was Europe's finest swordsman and one of Paris's finest violinists.

questions.q: An open-air concert for 75,000 at the Lincoln Memorial in 1939, and the Metropolitan Opera's first Black soloist in 1955, describe which singer?
questions.f: Barred from a Washington hall, she sang on the steps instead—and made history.

questions.q: A teacher whose pupils included Aaron Copland, Quincy Jones and Astor Piazzolla, and the first woman to conduct the Boston Symphony, was who?
questions.f: For half a century, aspiring composers crossed oceans just to study in her Paris apartment.

questions.q: Invented in Germany as a portable substitute for a church organ, carried to Buenos Aires by sailors, and now tango's sobbing voice — which instrument?
questions.f: Its buttons are in no logical order, so pushing and pulling produce completely different notes.

questions.q: In Indian classical music, which instrument's entire job is to hold a shimmering drone behind the soloist?
questions.f: Its strings are plucked in a slow, endless cycle, wrapping the raga in a cushion of sound.

questions.q: A single wire on a wooden bow, a gourd resonator, and a stone pressed against the string set the rhythm of a capoeira circle. Which instrument?
questions.f: Tradition says the berimbau, not the players, decides how fast the capoeira game will go.

questions.q: Which Brazilian drum 'laughs' and 'squeals' because a stick fixed inside it is rubbed with a damp cloth?
questions.f: Samba schools use the cuíca's chattering voice as the parade's comic conversation.

questions.q: The cajón — a box drum the player sits astride and slaps — originated with enslaved communities in which country?
questions.f: Shipping crates became drums when other instruments were forbidden; flamenco adopted it in the 1970s.

questions.q: Which national instrument of Sweden is a fiddle fitted with rows of wooden keys and extra resonating strings?
questions.f: Its name means 'key harp', and carvings suggest it has been played for over 600 years.

questions.q: What makes Norway's Hardanger fiddle different from an ordinary violin?
c: Extra understrings that ring without being played
Six tuning pegs on the tailpiece
questions.f: Those sympathetic strings give it a haunting halo—film composers borrow it for wild landscapes.

questions.q: An instrument swung on a long cord to make a pulsing roar, used in Aboriginal Australian ceremony, is called a…?
questions.f: Versions have been found on nearly every continent—it may be among humanity's oldest instruments.

questions.q: An 'Aeolian harp' produces music when…?
c: The wind blows across its strings
questions.f: It is named for Aeolus, the Greek keeper of the winds—nature plays it, not a musician.

questions.q: A musician who plays a tower of bells from a keyboard of heavy wooden batons is called a…?
questions.f: Carillonneurs play with fists and feet—some instruments weigh more than a hundred tonnes.

questions.q: The study of bells and bell-ringing is known as…?
questions.f: From Latin 'campana', a bell—English change-ringers give their patterns names like Grandsire Triples.

questions.q: The scholarly study of musical instruments and how they are classified is called…?
questions.f: Its name comes from 'organon', the Greek word for tool or instrument.

questions.q: A researcher who studies the music of the world's different cultures is an…?
questions.f: Early ethnomusicologists hauled wax-cylinder recorders up mountains to capture village songs.

questions.q: In instrument science, a xylophone counts as an 'idiophone' because its sound comes from…?
questions.f: 'Idio' means one's own—an idiophone needs no strings, skins, or reeds to sing.

questions.q: A drum is classed as a 'membranophone' because its sound begins with…?
questions.f: The Hornbostel-Sachs system sorts every instrument on Earth into just a handful of such families.

questions.q: In that same system, a violin is a chordophone and a flute is an…?
questions.f: Electrophones were added later for instruments whose sound begins as electricity.

questions.q: A 'lithophone' is an instrument made of…?
questions.f: Ancient stone chimes have been unearthed in Vietnam and China—rock music, quite literally.

questions.q: A craftsman who builds and repairs violins, lutes and guitars is called a…?
questions.f: The word comes straight from 'lute', the instrument such makers once built above all others.

questions.q: Ringing hammers, a string divided exactly in half, and a brotherhood convinced numbers ruled the universe point to whose musical discovery?
questions.f: Halving a string raises it exactly one octave—simple ratios turn out to rule harmony.

questions.q: Two notes spelled differently but sounding identical, like F sharp and G flat, are described as…?
questions.f: On a piano they share one key; on a violin a player can shade them ever so slightly apart.

questions.q: The solfège syllables come from a Latin hymn's opening words. Which original syllable was later replaced by 'do'?
questions.f: Guido of Arezzo took each syllable from the hymn's line beginnings; singers found 'ut' too clipped.

questions.q: The squiggle-like symbols used to write down medieval chant before modern notation are called…?
questions.f: Neumes showed the shape of a melody but not exact pitches—singers filled the rest from memory.

questions.q: In British note naming, a whole note is called a…?
questions.f: A breve is twice as long again—and the longa, longer still, has all but vanished from music.

questions.q: A Dutch inventor's ticking machine, a showman who toured a chess-playing automaton, and ear trumpets built for Beethoven converge on which man?
questions.f: Winkel built the ticking device first; Maelzel patented it, marketed it, and got his name on the beat.

questions.q: A choreographer shouting counts from the wings, a bassoon opening pitched so high players dread it, and Fantasia's dinosaurs all point to which work?
questions.f: Its 1913 Paris premiere caused such an uproar that dancers could not hear the orchestra.

questions.q: A Vienna court Kapellmeister who taught Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt, then had his reputation wrecked by a 1979 play, was who?
questions.f: The play and film 'Amadeus' invented his poisonous rivalry with Mozart—history clears him.

questions.q: A composer who kept driving a taxi and fixing pipes long after his operas were famous, and whose scores repeat tiny patterns for hours, is who?
questions.f: A critic once found Glass under a sink, plumbing—he politely insisted he was also a composer.

questions.q: A piece instructing 840 repetitions, 'furniture music' written to be ignored, and a wardrobe of identical velvet suits point to which composer?
questions.f: A 1963 performance of his 'Vexations' relayed pianists for over 18 hours.

questions.q: In which Haydn symphony do the players snuff out their candles and leave the stage one by one?
questions.f: It was a polite hint to Prince Esterházy that the musicians were overdue a holiday—it worked.

questions.q: An organ performance in Halberstadt, Germany that began in 2001 and is scheduled to end in 2640 uses a piece by which composer?
questions.f: The score is marked 'as slow as possible'—volunteers change the notes every few years.

questions.q: A festival theatre designed by one composer, with a hidden orchestra pit and no side boxes, stands in which German town?
questions.f: Wagner sank the orchestra out of sight so nothing would break the audience's illusion.

questions.q: Mahler's colossal Eighth Symphony is nicknamed the 'Symphony of a…'?
questions.f: Its premiere used two choirs, a children's choir, eight soloists, and a vast orchestra.

questions.q: Schubert's 'Unfinished' Symphony earns its nickname because it has only…?
questions.f: He sketched a third movement, set the score aside, and never returned to it.

questions.q: A set of variations dedicated 'to my friends pictured within', a hidden theme nobody has proved, and an organist's bulldog falling into a river point to which composer?
questions.f: Variation XI portrays the dog paddling to shore—the 'Enigma' itself is still unsolved.

questions.q: Six symphonic poems about a homeland, the opening of Prague's National Theatre, and total deafness in his last years describe which composer?
questions.f: He could no longer hear a note of 'Má vlast', whose river music is now a national treasure.

questions.q: A summer spent in the Czech-speaking village of Spillville, Iowa, and a New York conservatory directorship, belong to which composer?
questions.f: He urged American composers to build a national style on spirituals and Indigenous melodies.

questions.q: Which composer's patriotic tone poem was so stirring that Russian censors forced concerts to list it under harmless fake titles?
questions.f: 'Finlandia' toured as 'Impromptu' and 'A Scandinavian Choral March' to slip past the censors.

questions.q: The whirlwind 'Sabre Dance', a favourite of ice-skating routines, comes from a ballet by which composer?
questions.f: It closes his ballet 'Gayane'—the xylophone player has one of music's most feared workouts.

questions.q: Copland's fiddling 'Hoedown' from the ballet 'Rodeo' became famous decades later in adverts for…?
questions.f: 'Beef. It's What's for Dinner.' turned a concert-hall hoedown into a national jingle.

questions.q: Cryptic crosswords written for a New York magazine, a mentor named Oscar Hammerstein, and lyrics for a 1957 gang musical point to whom?
questions.f: He loved puzzles all his life—his lyrics fit together with the same clockwork cleverness.

questions.q: A songwriter who never learned to read music and used a special lever-fitted piano to shift keys wrote which of America's most-recorded catalogues?
questions.f: He composed mostly in F sharp; his trick piano transposed for him—and he wrote 'White Christmas.'

questions.q: A childhood in Zanzibar, an art-school training used to design his band's heraldic crest, and a boyhood stamp album point to which singer?
questions.f: Queen's crest features the band members' zodiac signs—his stamp album is in a British museum.

questions.q: A debut album on which one Minneapolis teenager played all 27 instruments points to which artist?
questions.f: For years he was billed by an unpronounceable symbol instead of a name.

questions.q: Two of country music's most famous songs written on a single day, and a song sealed in a vault until 2045, belong to which singer?
questions.f: She has said 'Jolene' and 'I Will Always Love You' came to her on the very same day.

questions.q: A battered Martin guitar with a hole worn clean through it, named after a film cowboy's horse, belongs to which musician?
questions.f: The guitar 'Trigger' has been played for over fifty years and carries dozens of signatures.

questions.q: In the music business, what is a 'master recording'?
c: The original recording all copies are made from
The loudest mix of a song
questions.f: Owning the masters means owning the money—artists have fought long battles for them.

questions.q: Which song set the record for the most weeks at number one on the US Billboard Hot 100?
questions.f: Nineteen weeks at the top—remixes kept it climbing all through 2019.

questions.q: A gospel singer playing distorted electric guitar in the 1940s, decades before rock guitar heroes, was who?
questions.f: Elvis and Chuck Berry both studied her records—she is now called rock's godmother.
