questions.q: A crouching 'duck walk' first used to smooth over a crumpled suit, and a song later launched into space, point to which guitarist?
questions.f: 'Johnny B. Goode' is the only rock song on the Voyager probes' record of Earth.

questions.q: A rectangular guitar built to his own design, and a hambone rhythm named after him, belong to which musician?
questions.f: That 'shave-and-a-haircut' beat turns up in songs by Buddy Holly, U2, and George Michael.

questions.q: Which insect-named 1950s band's name inspired a British group to pick an insect name with a musical pun in it?
questions.f: Buddy Holly's Crickets gave the Beatles both the idea and the courage to misspell it.

questions.q: An uncredited Detroit house band that played on more number-one hits than the Beatles, Elvis and the Beach Boys combined were known as the…?
questions.f: They recorded by day in a basement studio nicknamed the Snakepit—and were left off the labels.

questions.q: A Motown bass legend who played almost everything with one finger nicknamed 'The Hook' was who?
questions.f: His basslines walked and sang so much that later players transcribed them like classical solos.

questions.q: The Los Angeles session players who anonymously recorded countless 1960s hits are remembered as the…?
questions.f: Bassist Carol Kaye alone is thought to have played on thousands of released tracks.

questions.q: Production of the famous Roland TR-808 drum machine ended mainly because…?
c: The supply of a specific faulty transistor ran out
questions.f: That flawed chip gave the 808 its sizzly, unrepeatable noise—hip-hop was built on the accident.

questions.q: A three-and-a-quarter-second piece, composed on an Apple computer for a rival company's software, was written by which musician?
questions.f: Eno wrote the Windows 95 startup sound after being asked for something 'inspiring, universal, optimistic.'

questions.q: The swelling cinema logo sound called 'Deep Note' was created by…?
c: A computer program blending about thirty sliding voices
A pipe organ recorded in a cathedral
questions.f: Its creator wrote 20,000 lines of code; every performance of the program came out slightly different.

questions.q: The world's most-heard mobile ringtone was lifted from an 1902 guitar piece by which composer?
questions.f: Nokia borrowed 13 notes from his 'Gran Vals'—heard billions of times a day at its peak.

questions.q: 'Happy Birthday to You' became free for everyone to use after…?
c: A 2016 court settlement ended its copyright claim
questions.f: For decades films had to pay to use it—so characters sang 'For He's a Jolly Good Fellow' instead.

questions.q: The long-running musical 'Cats' sets to music a book of poems by which writer?
questions.f: 'Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats' was written for Eliot's godchildren.

questions.q: A choreographer who put a story-telling 'dream ballet' into a 1943 Broadway hit, changing musicals forever, was who?
questions.f: Her dream sequence in 'Oklahoma!' proved dance could carry a plot, not just decorate it.

questions.q: Bowler hats worn to hide thinning hair, turned-in knees, and rolled shoulders became the signature style of which choreographer?
questions.f: His angular look defines 'Chicago' and 'Cabaret'—dancers still call the style pure Fosse.

questions.q: A Russian-born choreographer who founded an American company and created the plotless ballet 'Serenade' was who?
questions.f: He said ballet needed no story: 'See the music, hear the dance.'

questions.q: An impresario who commissioned Stravinsky's ballets and hired Picasso to paint his sets ran which company?
questions.f: Sergei Diaghilev never danced or composed—he simply had an unbeatable eye for genius.

questions.q: A dancer whose leaps were said to defy gravity, and who choreographed 'The Afternoon of a Faun', was who?
questions.f: Audiences swore he paused in mid-air—photographers of the time could not catch him.

questions.q: A technique built on 'contraction and release', and a collaboration with Aaron Copland on 'Appalachian Spring', belong to which dancer?
questions.f: Graham's technique starts from the breath and the belly—the opposite of ballet's lifted lightness.

questions.q: A dancer who threw away shoes and corsets to perform barefoot in flowing Greek-style tunics was who?
questions.f: She said she took her steps from waves, clouds, and wind rather than from a ballet book.

questions.q: Whirling metres of silk under coloured electric lights, several stage-lighting patents, and a friendship with Marie Curie point to which dancer?
questions.f: She was elected to a French astronomical society and experimented with glowing chemical effects.

questions.q: A choreographer who ordered his movements by tossing coins, working alongside composer John Cage, was who?
questions.f: Music and dance were made separately and met for the first time at the performance.

questions.q: Which choreographer's signature work 'Revelations' is danced to African American spirituals?
questions.f: 'Revelations' has been performed for more people than almost any other modern dance work.

questions.q: A trained anthropologist who researched Caribbean dance, then built it into American stage choreography, was who?
questions.f: Her fieldwork in Haiti and Jamaica turned dance research into a whole new theatrical language.

questions.q: A pet cheetah named Chiquita, Parisian stardom, and later burial honours in the Panthéon belong to which performer?
questions.f: Baker was the first American-born woman honoured in France's Panthéon, in 2021.

questions.q: A staircase routine, and a US national dance day held on his birthday, honour which tap dancer?
questions.f: National Tap Dance Day falls on 25 May because that is the day he was born.

questions.q: A leapfrog descent of a grand staircase, landing in full splits on every step, was the trademark of which act?
questions.f: Fred Astaire called their 'Stormy Weather' number the greatest dance sequence ever filmed.

questions.q: A seven-minute interval act at the 1994 Eurovision Song Contest in Dublin grew into which global stage show?
questions.f: The interval slot exists to fill voting time—this one accidentally launched a worldwide phenomenon.

questions.q: A Lindy Hop pioneer who invented airborne partner moves, then worked at a post office for thirty years before being rediscovered, was who?
questions.f: The swing revival tracked him down in the 1980s—he taught and danced into his nineties.

questions.q: Which singer's velvet voice made tango a worldwide craze in the 1920s and is honoured by statues across Buenos Aires?
questions.f: Fans still say 'Gardel sings better every day'—a joke about how his legend keeps growing.

questions.q: In the Indian classical dance kathak, what are 'chakkars'?
questions.f: Dancers strap on 'ghungroo'—strings of up to a hundred ankle bells—and still spin dozens of times.

questions.q: Kathakali, whose performers wear towering headdresses and vivid painted faces, comes from which region?
questions.f: Traditional shows once ran all night; the makeup alone can take several hours to apply.

questions.q: The Balinese 'kecak' performance is remarkable because its music is made entirely by…?
c: A large chorus of chanting voices
questions.f: Dozens of men chant interlocking 'chak' patterns—a gamelan built from human voices alone.

questions.q: A room lined with sound-absorbing wedges, where a visiting composer reported hearing two mysterious hums from inside his own body, is called an…?
questions.f: John Cage left convinced silence does not exist—he had heard his nerves and his blood.

questions.q: A dome where a murmur against the wall travels 33 metres to a listener opposite made which London building famous for its 'whispering gallery'?
questions.f: The curved wall guides the sound around the ring instead of letting it scatter.

questions.q: An engineer who built synchronous electric clocks and an early 3D-glasses system also invented which instrument beloved of gospel and rock bands?
questions.f: Laurens Hammond used spinning metal tonewheels—clockmaking skills turned into music history.

questions.q: A teacher who built a tiny keyboard from aircraft parts to give recovering servicemen something to play gave his name to which electric piano?
questions.f: Harold Rhodes's bedside 'lap piano' grew into the bell-like keyboard of countless soul records.

questions.q: A film sound specialist who recreates footsteps, rustling coats and crunching snow in a studio is named after Jack Foley and called a…?
questions.f: Foley artists smash celery for breaking bones and shake gloves full of rice for rain.

questions.q: A 1951 western, a soldier character's name, and a sound designer's running joke gave film history which reused stock effect?
questions.f: Once you know it, you hear the same yelp in Star Wars, Indiana Jones, and hundreds more.

questions.q: A medieval teaching trick that mapped musical notes onto the joints of the left hand is known as the…?
questions.f: Guido of Arezzo's hand let a teacher point to a knuckle and have a whole choir sing that note.

questions.q: A whistled language loud enough to cross deep ravines, now protected by UNESCO, survives on which island?
questions.f: Silbo Gomero whistles Spanish itself—vowels and consonants become pitches and glides.

questions.q: A shepherd's song about a folk hero, sung by Valya Balkanska, carried which country's music aboard the Voyager probes?
questions.f: Its wailing bagpipe accompaniment is now the farthest-travelled folk song in history.

questions.q: Twenty-four fiendish violin caprices, a fine second career on the guitar, and a legend about playing on a single string point to whom?
questions.f: Audiences whispered his skill was supernatural; he was happy to let the rumour sell tickets.

questions.q: A ring worn on the finger, sliding along a wire beside a keyboard, controls the pitch of which 1928 French instrument?
questions.f: Fewer than 400 were ever built; Radiohead's Jonny Greenwood plays one on stage.

questions.q: Wartime scrambling of telephone speech at Bell Labs led to which device, later used to give singers robot voices?
questions.f: 'Voice coder' was built to hide conversations, then borrowed by funk and electronic bands.

questions.q: Flat spinning discs replaced Edison's wax cylinders thanks to which inventor's gramophone?
questions.f: Discs could be stamped by the thousand from one master—cylinders had to be recorded almost singly.

questions.q: In 19th-century opera houses, a 'claque' was a group paid to…?
questions.f: Claque leaders sold their services to singers—and sometimes threatened to boo instead.

questions.q: Inside a violin stands a small wooden dowel that Italian makers call the 'anima', or soul. What is its English name?
questions.f: Move it a millimetre and the whole voice of the instrument changes—it is glued to nothing.

questions.q: The violin chin rest, now standard, was invented around 1820 by which composer-violinist?
questions.f: Before it, players gripped the instrument against the collarbone and could not shift so freely.

questions.q: One leading theory explains the density of Stradivari's spruce by pointing to…?
c: A long cold spell that slowed tree growth
questions.f: Narrow, even growth rings from the Little Ice Age may be part of the violins' secret.

questions.q: A keyboard that played short loops of recorded tape supplied the famous flute sound on 'Strawberry Fields Forever'. What was it?
questions.f: Each key dragged its own tape strip past a playback head—a sampler built from sticky tape.

questions.q: A cabinet with a motor-driven rotating horn, giving organ chords their swirling wobble, is called a…?
questions.f: The swirl is real Doppler effect—the sound source is physically spinning around inside the cabinet.

questions.q: A famous 1972 piece for two performers, in which one claps a pattern and the other slowly shifts it by one beat, was written by…?
questions.f: 'Clapping Music' needs no instruments at all—just two pairs of very disciplined hands.

questions.q: A 'prepared piano' is one where the player has…?
c: Placed screws, bolts and rubber between the strings
Bowed the strings with fishing line
questions.f: John Cage started doing it when a dance studio had no room for a percussion ensemble.

questions.q: Which composer devised the twelve-tone method, in which all twelve notes are used before any repeats?
questions.f: He described it as a way to organize music once traditional keys had been abandoned.

questions.q: The overtone-rich style called 'khoomei', in which a singer sounds two pitches at once, comes from…?
questions.f: Herders imitate wind, rivers, and animals—one throat producing a drone and a whistle together.

questions.q: 'Katajjaq', a breathy throat-singing game usually played face-to-face by two women until one laughs, belongs to which people?
questions.f: It is a contest as much as a song—the loser is whoever runs out of breath or giggles first.

questions.q: The instruction 'col legno' asks a string player to…?
c: Strike the strings with the wooden stick of the bow
Play with the bow upside down
questions.f: Italian for 'with the wood'—it sounds like tiny dry bones tapping and shocked early audiences.

questions.q: 'Sul ponticello' tells a player to bow…?
questions.f: 'Ponticello' means little bridge; bowing there gives a thin, glassy, shivering sound.

questions.q: 'Portamento' describes a singer or player…?
c: Sliding smoothly from one pitch to the next
questions.f: From Italian 'portare', to carry—the voice is carried between the notes rather than jumping.

questions.q: A 'hemiola' happens when a passage briefly fits…?
c: Three beats into the space of two
questions.f: Its Greek root means 'one and a half'—Baroque composers loved this rhythmic sleight of hand.

questions.q: In an orchestral score, 'tutti' means…?
questions.f: Italian for 'all'—the opposite instruction, for one player alone, is 'solo'.

questions.q: When a score is marked 'divisi', a section must…?
c: Split into separate groups playing different notes
questions.f: Violinists sharing a stand simply take a line each—one plays the upper, one the lower.

questions.q: The marking 'attacca' at the end of a movement tells performers to…?
c: Begin the next movement at once, with no pause
questions.f: It stops an audience from clapping and breaking the music's spell.

questions.q: 'Sotto voce' literally means…?
questions.f: It asks for a hushed, confidential tone—used in novels for muttered asides too.

questions.q: The phrase 'ad libitum', shortened in English to 'ad lib', literally means…?
questions.f: In music it invites the player to improvise; on stage it means inventing your own lines.

questions.q: The letters 'V.S.' scribbled at the bottom of a page of music warn a player to…?
questions.f: It stands for 'volti subito'—every accompanist dreads the mid-phrase page turn.

questions.q: If a player's part is marked 'tacet' for a movement, they should…?
questions.f: Latin for 'it is silent'—triangle players have been known to wait three movements for one ding.

questions.q: An 'anacrusis' is…?
c: A note or notes before the first full bar
questions.f: Singers call it a pick-up—'Happy Birthday' begins with one before the first strong beat.

questions.q: A singer's 'tessitura' is…?
c: The part of the range where the voice sits most comfortably
The highest note they can reach
questions.f: Italian for texture—two sopranos may share a top note but have very different tessituras.

questions.q: A 'requiem' takes its name from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: The service's opening words ask for eternal rest—composers from Mozart to Fauré set them.

questions.q: The large sung work called an 'oratorio' is named after…?
questions.f: Performances in Rome's oratory gave the form its name—Handel's 'Messiah' is the most famous.

questions.q: The choral form called the 'motet' takes its name from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: 'Mot' means word—the motet grew from adding fresh words to existing chant lines.

questions.q: In a synagogue or church, a 'cantor' is the person who…?
questions.f: From Latin 'cantare', to sing—the same root as chant, cantata, and incantation.

questions.q: The Renaissance ancestor of the trombone was called the 'sackbut', a name thought to describe…?
questions.f: From Old French words for pull and push—exactly what the slide still does today.

questions.q: The Renaissance wind instrument called the 'crumhorn' has a name meaning…?
questions.f: Its curled-up end makes it look like a walking stick that hums.

questions.q: The brass instrument named 'ophicleide' is built from Greek words meaning…?
questions.f: It replaced the coiled bass horn called the serpent, then lost its own job to the tuba.

questions.q: The 'euphonium' has a name meaning…?
questions.f: 'Eu' means good and 'phon' means sound—brass bands treasure it as their tenor singer.

questions.q: The 'flugelhorn' takes the German word 'Flügel', meaning…?
questions.f: It was named for a horn used to signal the 'wings' of a hunting party.

questions.q: The word 'clavichord' is built from roots meaning…?
questions.f: Latin 'clavis' plus 'chorda'—Bach's 'Well-Tempered Clavier' uses the same key-word root.

questions.q: A Viennese maker's grand piano adds nine extra bass keys, their tops darkened so pianists do not reach for them by mistake. Which maker?
questions.f: Its Imperial model has 97 keys instead of 88—those low notes mostly just add resonance.

questions.q: A New York street packed with song publishers, whose clattering upright pianos reminded a reporter of banging kitchenware, became known as…?
questions.f: Writers worked in tiny cubicles, churning out sheet music hits before radio even existed.

questions.q: A Broadway office block where teams of young songwriters wrote 1960s pop hits floor by floor is remembered as the…?
questions.f: Carole King and other teenagers wrote future classics in its cramped piano cubicles.

questions.q: A singer hired to perform the same handful of songs nightly for years to soothe a melancholy Spanish king was known as…?
questions.f: Farinelli became so trusted at court that he ended up advising on state affairs.

questions.q: A keyboard prodigy who toured Europe billed alongside her younger brother, then stopped performing as she came of age, was who?
questions.f: Their father's letters praise her playing as the equal of Wolfgang's—then history mislaid her.

questions.q: A 'Gaelic' symphony premiered in Boston in 1896 made which composer the first American woman to have a symphony performed by a major orchestra?
questions.f: She was largely self-taught in composition, working from textbooks she translated herself.

questions.q: A composer who wrote a marching anthem for the women's suffrage movement, then conducted its singing with a toothbrush through a prison window, was who?
questions.f: Fellow campaigners sang 'The March of the Women' in the courtyard while she beat time above.

questions.q: A trumpeter who trained like a boxer and recorded jazz's best-selling album mostly in first takes was who?
questions.f: 'Kind of Blue' was built from sketches handed out in the studio—the band improvised the rest.

questions.q: A saxophonist who practised so relentlessly that friends found him asleep still holding his horn wrote which fearsome jazz obstacle course?
questions.f: John Coltrane's chord cycle moves so fast that students still use it as a rite of passage.

questions.q: A pianist of spiky, off-kilter harmonies is, after Duke Ellington, the second most-recorded jazz composer. Who?
questions.f: 'Round Midnight' alone has been recorded well over a thousand times.

questions.q: A classically trained pianist rejected by a Philadelphia conservatory, who played bar piano under an invented name so her family would not find out, was who?
questions.f: The conservatory awarded her an honorary degree decades later, days before she died.

questions.q: A gospel singer standing behind Martin Luther King Jr. in 1963 called out 'Tell them about the dream!' Who was she?
questions.f: He set his notes aside and improvised the most famous passage of the speech.

questions.q: A trumpeter who arranged for Frank Sinatra, became a major label's first Black vice-president, and later produced history's best-selling album is who?
questions.f: He was 32 when Mercury Records promoted him—and 49 when he produced 'Thriller'.

questions.q: A car-plant worker who applied assembly-line thinking to making hit records founded which label?
questions.f: Berry Gordy moved singers from grooming to choreography to studio like cars down a line.

questions.q: A pianist who used a low folding chair built by his father, hummed audibly while recording, and taped the same Bach work 26 years apart was who?
questions.f: Engineers could never edit out the humming—so it stayed on the finished records.

questions.q: A pianist whose hand could stretch a twelfth, who left Russia in 1917 and rebuilt his life touring America, was who?
questions.f: That giant reach let him write chords most pianists must break into two grabs.

questions.q: Paper rolls that make a player piano work inspired a wartime radio patent co-invented by which film star?
questions.f: With composer George Antheil she designed frequency hopping—an ancestor of modern wireless.

questions.q: A teenager who played almost every instrument himself made the first album released by Virgin Records. What was it called?
questions.f: Mike Oldfield overdubbed dozens of parts alone; a famous 1973 film then made its theme unforgettable.

questions.q: A Düsseldorf group's train-themed electronic track was later looped into hip-hop's 'Planet Rock'. Who were they?
questions.f: Their robotic pulse shaped techno, electro, and synth-pop across three continents.

questions.q: A trained electronics technician who worked out how to cut precisely between two spinning records is remembered as which DJ pioneer?
questions.f: He marked records with crayon and practised for hours to hit the break exactly on time.

questions.q: A DJ technique was invented by accident when a teenager, holding a record still while his mother shouted at him to turn the volume down, liked the sound. What technique?
questions.f: Grand Wizzard Theodore was about 13—he spent months turning the accident into a skill.

questions.q: A composer of whistling western themes who refused to move to Hollywood finally won a competitive Oscar in 2016, aged 87. Who?
questions.f: He scored more than 400 films while living in Rome and rarely speaking English.

questions.q: A singer whose recordings for Indian cinema spanned some seven decades and dozens of languages was who?
questions.f: Indian films use 'playback' singers, so her voice emerged from hundreds of different actresses.

questions.q: In Indian cinema, the vocalist who records songs for actors to mime on screen is called a…?
questions.f: Top playback singers become bigger household names than many of the actors they sing for.

questions.q: A cellist complaining about a 'wolf tone' is describing…?
c: An unwanted howling wobble on one particular note
questions.f: The note fights the body's own resonance; players fit a small metal 'wolf eliminator' to tame it.

questions.q: When tuning a piano, what does a technician listen for to know two strings match?
c: The disappearance of a wavering pulse
questions.f: Those pulses are called beats; when the wobble stops, the two pitches are locked together.

questions.q: Piano tuners deliberately use 'stretched' tuning, which means…?
c: High notes are tuned slightly sharp and low notes slightly flat
Only the middle octave is tuned
The black keys are tuned last
questions.f: Real strings produce slightly sharp overtones, so a mathematically perfect piano sounds wrong.

questions.q: Which part of a piano actually radiates most of the sound into the room?
questions.f: Strings alone are far too thin to move much air—the big wooden board does the shouting.

questions.q: On a violin bow, the part gripping the hair at the player's hand end is called the…?
questions.f: Nobody is certain why it is called a frog—one guess is a mistranslation of an old word for spool.

questions.q: The thin inlaid stripe running around the edge of a violin's front and back is called…?
questions.f: It is not just decoration—it helps stop a knock at the edge from splitting the whole plate.

questions.q: The diagram arranging all keys so that neighbours differ by one sharp or flat is called the circle of…?
questions.f: Travel all twelve steps around it and you arrive back where you began, like a clock face.

questions.q: Medieval theorists nicknamed which interval 'the devil in music' for its restless, unsettled sound?
questions.f: Today it opens 'The Simpsons' theme and countless suspense scores—unease on demand.

questions.q: Bach wrote preludes and fugues in all 24 keys mainly to demonstrate…?
c: A tuning system that made every key usable
questions.f: Older tunings left some keys sounding sour—'The Well-Tempered Clavier' celebrated the fix.

questions.q: A string player produces a glassy 'harmonic' by…?
c: Touching the string lightly instead of pressing it down
Tuning the string down an octave
questions.f: The light touch silences part of the string's vibration, leaving a pure, flute-like overtone.

questions.q: In Afro-Cuban music, the pattern called 'clave' gets its name because the word means…?
questions.f: It is the key that unlocks the groove—every other part must line up with it.

questions.q: A 'polyrhythm' happens when musicians play…?
c: Two conflicting rhythms at once, like three beats against two
The same rhythm twice as fast
questions.f: West African drumming layers several at once—your ear can flip between them like an optical illusion.

questions.q: In Baroque music, the numbers written under a bass line, telling a keyboard player which chords to build, are called…?
questions.f: It is musical shorthand—two performers could read the same page and never play it identically.

questions.q: In film scoring, 'Mickey Mousing' means…?
c: Matching the music note-for-note to on-screen action
questions.f: Every footstep gets its own note—brilliant in cartoons, unintentionally comic in serious films.

questions.q: Film music described as 'diegetic' is music that…?
c: The characters in the scene can hear too
questions.f: A car radio in the shot is diegetic; a swelling orchestra only the audience hears is not.

questions.q: Why do studio musicians record while listening to a 'click track'?
c: To keep perfectly steady time for later editing
questions.f: A steady click lets engineers stitch together takes recorded weeks and continents apart.

questions.q: In music collecting, a 'bootleg' is…?
c: An unofficial recording released without permission
questions.f: Fans once smuggled tape recorders into concerts inside coats and boots—hence the name.

questions.q: At a record company, what does the department called 'A&R' do?
c: Finds new artists and chooses their material
questions.f: It stands for artists and repertoire—A&R scouts spend their lives in small, loud venues.

questions.q: Records that spin at 78 revolutions per minute were made mostly from…?
questions.f: Shellac comes from an insect resin—and shatters like a biscuit if you drop the disc.

questions.q: Which double-headed barrel drum, slung from the shoulder, drives the Punjabi dance music bhangra?
questions.f: One stick is curved and one is thin, so a single player produces both boom and crack.

questions.q: Which performer has won more Grammy Awards than any other artist in history?
questions.f: She passed a record that had stood since 1997, when a classical conductor held the top spot.

questions.q: Which musical held the record as Broadway's longest-running show when it finally closed in 2023?
questions.f: It ran for 35 years and more than 13,000 performances at the same theatre.

questions.q: In West African stories, the clever trickster Anansi is which small creature?
questions.f: In the Akan language of Ghana, the name Anansi means spider.

questions.q: In Russian folk tales, Baba Yaga's little house stands on a pair of what?
questions.f: Storytellers say her hut can spin around and even run through the forest.

questions.q: In a famous Japanese tale, the boy Momotaro was found inside a giant what?
questions.f: Momotaro means peach boy, and he travels with a dog, a monkey and a pheasant.

questions.q: Which Egyptian goddess was pictured as a friendly cat?
questions.f: Bastet was believed to guard homes and families, so many Egyptians kept little cat statues.

questions.q: In Norse myth, the goddess Freyja rides in a chariot pulled by two what?
questions.f: A chariot pulled by cats may be the most unusual ride in all of myth.

questions.q: Two birds sit on Odin's shoulders and whisper the news to him. What birds are they?
questions.f: Their names, Huginn and Muninn, mean thought and memory.

questions.q: In Chinese legend, which lady lives on the moon with a jade rabbit?
questions.f: Families look for her at the Mid-Autumn Festival, when the moon is roundest.

questions.q: The Hindu god Vishnu flies through the sky on a giant bird called what?
questions.f: Garuda is so loved that airlines and national symbols in Asia still use his name.

questions.q: Which Hindu god is often shown with a snake around his neck and a moon in his hair?
questions.f: The snake is called Vasuki, and Shiva is also honoured as the lord of dance.

questions.q: Saraswati, the Hindu goddess of learning, sits beside which graceful white bird?
questions.f: She also holds a stringed instrument called a veena, because music is part of learning.

questions.q: The Hindu goddess Durga is often shown riding which big cat?
questions.f: Her lion shows courage, and she is celebrated for nine nights during the Navaratri festival.

questions.q: Kartikeya, a brave Hindu god, rides which colourful bird?
questions.f: His peacock is named Paravani, and in south India he is loved as Murugan.

questions.q: A stone statue of Nandi the bull sits outside temples of which Hindu god?
questions.f: Nandi always faces the temple door, as if waiting patiently for his master.

questions.q: The Egyptian god Sobek had the head of which river animal?
questions.f: Egyptians even kept sacred crocodiles in temple pools in Sobek's honour.

questions.q: Egyptians told of a beetle rolling the sun across the sky. Which beetle was it?
questions.f: Real scarab beetles roll balls of dung, which is why the story got started.

questions.q: Which looped Egyptian symbol stood for life?
questions.f: Gods in paintings hold the ankh by its loop, like carrying a little key to life.

questions.q: Which bird was the special symbol of Zeus, king of the Greek gods?
questions.f: Greeks thought an eagle flying by was a message straight from Zeus.

questions.q: Which showy bird belonged to Hera, queen of the Greek gods?
questions.f: Old stories say the eyes in a peacock's tail feathers were a gift from Hera.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Athena gave the city of Athens which useful tree?
questions.f: Olives gave the Greeks food, oil and lamp fuel, so it was a truly great gift.

questions.q: Artemis, Greek goddess of the hunt, carries which weapon?
questions.f: Her twin brother Apollo carries a bow too, but he is better known for his lyre.

questions.q: Hephaestus, the Greek god of making things, works at what?
questions.f: Greeks imagined his hammer ringing inside volcanoes, where his fires burned.

questions.q: The Greek god Pan is famous for playing which instrument?
questions.f: Rows of hollow reeds tied together are still called panpipes today.

questions.q: Which fruit belongs to Dionysus, the Greek god of feasts and vines?
questions.f: Greek art shows him crowned with grape leaves and carrying a pinecone-tipped staff.

questions.q: Which Roman god of love is drawn as a boy with a bow?
questions.f: His Greek name is Eros, and the word cupid comes from a Latin word for longing.

questions.q: In the Chinese zodiac story, which small animal won the great animal race?
questions.f: The rat rode on the ox's head and jumped off at the finish line to win.

questions.q: In Australian Aboriginal stories, the Rainbow Serpent is a giant what?
questions.f: Storytellers say the Rainbow Serpent's winding body carved out rivers and waterholes.

questions.q: In Polynesian legend, the hero Maui used a magic fish-hook to pull up what?
questions.f: New Zealand's North Island is nicknamed Te Ika-a-Maui, the fish of Maui.

questions.q: The legendary lost city of El Dorado was said to be made of what?
questions.f: Explorers searched South America for years, but El Dorado was never found.

questions.q: American folk hero Johnny Appleseed walked the land planting what?
questions.f: He was a real man named John Chapman, and the tall tales grew up around him.

questions.q: Which wise old wizard helps King Arthur in the legends?
questions.f: Legend says Merlin knew what would happen before it happened.

questions.q: King Arthur's famous table had which shape, so no knight sat at the head?
questions.f: Sitting in a circle meant every knight was equally important.

questions.q: Arthur's knights went searching for the Holy Grail, which was a magical what?
questions.f: The word grail comes from an old word for a wide dish or bowl.

questions.q: In the tale of Aladdin, where was the genie hiding?
questions.f: In the oldest versions Aladdin also has a magic ring with a second helpful spirit.

questions.q: In Arabian tales, what did people use to fly across the desert sky?
questions.f: Flying carpets appear in old Middle Eastern stories about King Solomon too.

questions.q: In legends, where does a dragon usually make its home?
c: In a nest in a tree
questions.f: Caves suited storytellers well, since they are dark, echoey and perfect for hiding treasure.

questions.q: Which real animal does a unicorn look most like?
questions.f: Very old descriptions gave the unicorn a goat's beard and a lion's tail as well.

questions.q: Paul Bunyan, the giant lumberjack of American tall tales, had a blue ox named what?
questions.f: Tall tales say Babe's footprints filled with water and became Minnesota's lakes.

questions.q: In the legend of Hamelin, the Pied Piper led the rats away by playing what?
questions.f: Pied means having two colours, and the piper wore a patchy coat of many colours.

questions.q: In many Native American stories, Coyote is a clever trickster.
questions.f: Coyote tales are told from California to the Great Plains, often to explain how the world works.

questions.q: Leprechauns come from the folklore of Ireland.
questions.f: Old Irish tales describe them as tiny shoemakers who guard their coins carefully.

questions.q: Which little folklore creature is often made into a garden statue with a red pointy hat?
questions.f: Garden gnomes were first made in Germany in the 1800s and quickly spread worldwide.

questions.q: In Native American legends, the giant Thunderbird makes thunder by doing what?
questions.f: Some stories add that lightning flashes when the Thunderbird blinks its eyes.

questions.q: Sun Wukong, the hero of a famous Chinese story, is which animal?
questions.f: He is called the Monkey King, and he can turn a single hair into a copy of himself.

questions.q: In stories, fairies are usually much smaller than people.
questions.f: Older folk tales sometimes described fairies as human-sized; the tiny winged kind became popular later.

questions.q: In Hawaiian legend, Pele is the goddess of what?
questions.f: Hawaiians say Pele lives in the crater of Kilauea, one of Earth's busiest volcanoes.

questions.q: In old European tales, which little creature helps a shoemaker overnight?
questions.f: In the Grimm story the shoemaker thanks the elves by sewing them tiny clothes.

questions.q: Which sweet dumpling is said to be Ganesha's favourite treat?
questions.f: Families make piles of modak for the Ganesh Chaturthi festival every year.

questions.q: Norse stories say the goddess Idunn keeps a basket of magic what?
questions.f: One bite of her apples keeps the Norse gods young and strong.

questions.q: In Japanese folklore, which waving cat figure is put in shops for good luck?
questions.f: Maneki-neko means beckoning cat, and a raised left paw is said to invite customers in.

questions.q: Which Greek goddess of the harvest taught people to grow grain?
questions.f: Greeks thanked Demeter at harvest time with the very first loaf of new bread.

questions.q: In Norse myth, which god sails a magic ship that folds up small enough to carry?
questions.f: His ship Skidbladnir always finds a fair wind, then folds away like cloth.

questions.q: In folk tales, dwarves are famous for digging in mines.
questions.f: Old German tales made dwarves master miners and smiths who knew every gem in the rock.

questions.q: Which Egyptian goddess wore cow horns and was loved as a goddess of music and joy?
questions.f: Dancers shook a rattle called a sistrum in Hathor's temples.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Hestia looked after which part of the home?
questions.f: Cities kept a public fire burning for Hestia so her flame never went out.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, which goddess repaired the sky and made people out of clay?
questions.f: Nuwa is often shown with a woman's upper body and a long snake tail.

questions.q: In Norse tales, a mischievous squirrel named Ratatoskr runs up and down what?
questions.f: Ratatoskr carries messages between an eagle at the top and a dragon at the roots.

questions.q: In fairy tales, a magic mirror can show things that are far away.
questions.f: Magic mirrors turn up in tales from Europe, Persia and China alike.

questions.q: In legends about vampires, which smelly plant is used to keep them away?
questions.f: Folk cures often used garlic against illness, which is how it got into the stories.

questions.q: Which Greek goddess is the twin sister of Apollo?
questions.f: Greeks linked Apollo with the sun and Artemis with the moon.

questions.q: In old tales a mermaid often sits on a rock doing what?
questions.f: Sailors' stories almost always gave the mermaid a comb and a small mirror.

questions.q: A very old story about gods and heroes is called what?
questions.f: The word myth comes from the Greek word mythos, meaning a spoken story.

questions.q: The 'uni' at the start of 'unicorn' tells you the animal has how many horns?
questions.f: From Latin unus, one, plus cornu, horn: a one-horn.

questions.q: The word 'mermaid' is built from an old word for sea plus 'maid'. So it means a maid of the what?
questions.f: The old English word mere meant sea or lake, and it survives in the name Windermere.

questions.q: The word 'dragon' comes from an old word for a huge what?
questions.f: From Greek drakon, a giant serpent; wings and fire were added by later storytellers.

questions.q: What do we call the big pot a witch stirs in stories?
questions.f: Cauldron comes from a Latin word for a hot bath, calidarium.

questions.q: Which magic word do stage magicians famously shout?
questions.f: Abracadabra was written on charms in Roman times, long before top hats and rabbits.

questions.q: A magic drink brewed in a fairy tale is called a what?
questions.f: Potion comes from the Latin potio, a drink, which is also behind the word poison.

questions.q: Most fairy tales in English begin with which four words?
questions.f: Storytellers in other languages have their own openings, like Spanish erase una vez.

questions.q: A story about a hero that people retell as if it really happened is called a what?
questions.f: Legend comes from Latin legenda, meaning things to be read aloud.

questions.q: All the myths of one people gathered together are called their what?
questions.f: The ending -logy means the study of something, so mythology is the study of myths.

questions.q: If a god is 'immortal', what does that mean?
questions.f: Greek gods were said to stay immortal by eating ambrosia and drinking nectar.

questions.q: A brave girl or woman at the centre of a legend is called a what?
questions.f: Heroine is simply the word hero with an ending that once marked a female form.

questions.q: In stories, baby dragons come out of what?
questions.f: Because dragons were imagined as giant reptiles, storytellers gave them eggs like lizards.

questions.q: What do we call an animal that only exists in stories, like a unicorn?
questions.f: Mythical creatures often mix real animals together, like an eagle joined to a lion.

questions.q: If a forest in a tale is 'enchanted', it has been touched by what?
questions.f: Enchant comes from Latin incantare, to sing a spell over something.

questions.q: In 'fairy tale', the word 'tale' means a what?
questions.f: Tale is related to tell, so a tale is simply something that is told.

questions.q: Aztec legend says the people built their city where they saw an eagle sitting on which plant?
questions.f: That eagle on a cactus still sits in the middle of the flag of Mexico.

questions.q: In Maya stories, people were finally made out of which food plant?
questions.f: The Maya book called the Popol Vuh says the first successful humans were shaped from maize dough.

questions.q: Who is the father of the Norse thunder god Thor?
questions.f: Thor's mother is the earth goddess Jord, whose name simply means earth.

questions.q: Egyptians said the night sky was the goddess Nut, and her body was covered with what?
questions.f: Painted coffin lids often show Nut arching over the earth, dotted with golden stars.

questions.q: Which Greek goddess was the rainbow, carrying messages between gods and people?
questions.f: Her name lives on in the flower called an iris and in the coloured ring of your eye.

questions.q: In Greek myth, the nine sisters who inspire music, poetry and dance are called the what?
questions.f: Their name gave us both museum and music.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, dragons are believed to control which part of the weather?
questions.f: Farmers once prayed at dragon temples for rain in a dry summer.

questions.q: Amaterasu, one of the most important gods of Japan, is the goddess of what?
questions.f: Japan's nickname, land of the rising sun, fits her story perfectly.

questions.q: In Japanese folklore, where does the creature called a kappa live?
questions.f: A kappa is said to carry a dish of water on its head, and it loves cucumbers.

questions.q: What is the name of King Arthur's castle and court?
questions.f: Camelot appears in French tales of Arthur written about 800 years ago.

questions.q: In the Robin Hood legends, which very tall friend is called Little John?
questions.f: Calling a giant of a man Little John is an old English joke that stuck.

questions.q: In the Ramayana, who is Rama's wife?
questions.f: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana spend fourteen years in the forest together in the story.

questions.q: Baby Krishna is famous in Indian stories for stealing what from the kitchen?
questions.f: Village women hung their butter pots from the ceiling, and he still found a way up.

questions.q: Who is the Greek god of war?
questions.f: The Romans called him Mars, and they liked him far more than the Greeks did.

questions.q: In Scandinavian folklore, what happens to a troll caught in sunlight?
questions.f: Norwegians point at odd rocky hills and joke that those are sunlit trolls.

questions.q: In Russian folk tales, the feathers of the Firebird do what?
questions.f: One glowing feather is enough to light a whole room in the stories.

questions.q: In Scottish legend, a selkie can change from a person into which animal?
questions.f: Selkie tales come from Orkney and Shetland, where grey seals watch the shore all year.

questions.q: Which Norse creatures are famous as underground smiths who forged the gods' treasures?
questions.f: Norse tales say two dwarf brothers made Thor's hammer in their workshop.

questions.q: The Inca honoured a sun god named Inti.
questions.f: Their midwinter festival for Inti, called Inti Raymi, is still celebrated in Peru today.

questions.q: Mami Wata is a water spirit in stories told across West and Central Africa.
questions.f: Her name means mother water, and she is often pictured with a large snake.

questions.q: In stories, an ogre is a huge, clumsy, greedy giant.
questions.f: The word ogre first appeared in French fairy tales in the 1690s.

questions.q: Chinese dragons are usually shown as long and snake-like rather than fat and winged.
questions.f: Artists gave them deer antlers, fish scales and eagle claws, but almost never bat wings.

questions.q: A shape-shifter in folklore is a being that can change its shape.
questions.f: Shape-shifters appear worldwide, from Japanese fox spirits to Irish selkies.

questions.q: Shango, a powerful god in Yoruba stories from Nigeria, rules over what?
questions.f: His symbol is a double-headed axe, and his colours are red and white.

questions.q: Which Hindu god has four faces and is honoured as the creator?
questions.f: His four faces are said to look in all four directions at once.

questions.q: Which Hindu goddess of good fortune is welcomed into homes at Diwali?
questions.f: Families light lamps by the door so Lakshmi can find her way in.

questions.q: In legends, what does a knight usually ride?
questions.f: A knight's warhorse was called a destrier, and it was worth as much as a small farm.

questions.q: Which Greek god is the messenger who guides travellers?
questions.f: Greeks piled stones by the roadside as little markers for Hermes.

questions.q: In Norse myth, what colour is the goddess Hel's kingdom said to be?
questions.f: Her cold, foggy hall lies in Niflheim, whose name means house of mists.

questions.q: In Greek myth, what does the giant Argus have an amazing number of?
questions.f: Hera set the hundred-eyed Argus to guard something, since some of his eyes always stayed open.

questions.q: Which sea animal often pulls the chariot of the Greek sea god in old artwork?
questions.f: Greeks thought dolphins rescued sailors, so they made fine helpers for a sea god.

questions.q: In Egyptian myth, which goddess wore a feather on her head as a sign of truth?
questions.f: Maat's ostrich feather stood for balance and fairness in everything.

questions.q: In Greek stories, what are nymphs?
questions.f: Different nymphs looked after trees, springs, mountains and meadows.

questions.q: Which shiny metal do fairy-tale dwarves and dragons both love to collect?
questions.f: Gold never rusts or tarnishes, which is one reason old stories treat it as magical.

questions.q: In folklore, what does a wishing well ask you to drop in?
questions.f: People have thrown coins into springs as gifts to water spirits for thousands of years.

questions.q: In the story of the Trojan War, which beautiful city did the Greek army camp outside?
questions.f: The ruins of Troy were found in Turkey in the 1870s, proving the city was real.

questions.q: In Egyptian belief, what did people become after being wrapped in linen bandages?
questions.f: Bandaging kept the body safe so its owner could enjoy the afterlife.

questions.q: In Greek myth, what is a satyr's lower half like?
questions.f: Satyrs love music and dancing, and they follow the god Dionysus everywhere.

questions.q: Which Norse god is the watchman with hearing so sharp he can hear grass grow?
questions.f: Heimdall's horn, the Gjallarhorn, can be heard through all nine worlds.

questions.q: In Greek myth, who is the god of sleep?
questions.f: His name gave us the word hypnosis, and his son Morpheus ruled dreams.

questions.q: How many Pandava brothers are there in the Mahabharata?
questions.f: They are Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva, and each has his own talent.

questions.q: Which fierce Egyptian goddess had the head of a lioness?
questions.f: Egyptians held a yearly festival to calm Sekhmet down and keep her friendly.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which winged goddess stands for victory?
questions.f: A famous armless statue of her, the Winged Victory, stands in the Louvre in Paris.

questions.q: In many myths, what do gods use to travel across the sky?
questions.f: Greek, Hindu and Norse myths all put their sun god in a chariot.

questions.q: Which Greek creature is half man and half goat and plays the pipes?
questions.f: Fauns come from Roman stories, while the Greeks told of very similar satyrs.

questions.q: In Irish legend, where would you find the fairy folk living?
questions.f: Irish people called them the people of the mounds, and left those hills alone.

questions.q: What do we call a person in a story who does brave and noble deeds?
questions.f: Hero is a Greek word, and Greeks used it for someone halfway between human and god.

questions.q: 'Goddess' is the word for a female what?
questions.f: English adds -ess to a few old words, as in lion and lioness.

questions.q: In myths, the 'underworld' is a place found where?
questions.f: Greeks, Egyptians and Maya all imagined the land of the dead somewhere below.

questions.q: The word 'thunderbolt' is made by joining 'thunder' to which word?
questions.f: A bolt once meant an arrow, so a thunderbolt is an arrow made of storm.

questions.q: A 'trickster' in a myth is a character who loves to play what?
questions.f: Nearly every culture has one, from Anansi in Ghana to Coyote in North America.

questions.q: In Greek myth, 'nectar' was the gods' special what?
questions.f: Today nectar means the sweet juice inside a flower that bees turn into honey.

questions.q: If we call a ship 'titanic', we mean it is very what?
questions.f: The word honours the Titans, the giant gods who ruled before Zeus.

questions.q: 'Wizardry' means the work of a what?
questions.f: Wizard began as an ordinary word for a wise person before it turned magical.

questions.q: A 'quest' in a legend is a long what?
questions.f: Quest comes from a Latin word meaning to seek, the same root as question.

questions.q: In fairy tales, a 'curse' is the opposite of a what?
questions.f: In tales the cure for a curse is often something small and kind, like a promise kept.

questions.q: A 'charm' can be a small object worn to bring what?
questions.f: Charm comes from the Latin carmen, a song, because charms were once sung aloud.

questions.q: A 'riddle' in a legend is a puzzling what?
questions.f: Riddle contests appear in Greek, Norse and Indian stories alike.

questions.q: 'Legendary' describes someone so famous that they seem like a what?
questions.f: We say a legendary player, meaning stories will still be told about them later.

questions.q: 'Mythical' is the describing word made from which noun?
questions.f: Something mythical belongs to myth, so it never really existed.

questions.q: A 'temple' is a building where people do what?
questions.f: Temple comes from a Latin word for a space marked out for the gods.

questions.q: A 'chariot' in myth is a light cart pulled by what?
questions.f: Some myth chariots swap the horses for stranger teams, like Freyja's pair of cats.

questions.q: 'Spellbound' describes someone so amazed that they cannot do what?
questions.f: It began as a real idea in tales: a spell that binds you where you stand.

questions.q: The 'fire' in 'Firebird' tells you the bird looks like it is what?
questions.f: Russian storytellers say a Firebird feather still glows after it falls.

questions.q: A 'giant' in a story is someone who is very what?
questions.f: Giant comes from the Greek gigas, the name of an ancient race of huge beings.

questions.q: If a hero is 'invisible', what can nobody do?
questions.f: Invisible splits into in-, not, plus a root meaning able to be seen.

questions.q: 'Werewolf' names a person who turns into which animal?
questions.f: The were part comes from an old English word for man, so it means man-wolf.

questions.q: 'Sacred' describes something treated as very what?
questions.f: Egyptian cats, Indian cows and Greek olive trees were all called sacred.

questions.q: A story creature that is part one animal and part another is best described as what?
questions.f: The griffin, the centaur and the mermaid are all built by mixing two creatures.

questions.q: A 'prophecy' in a myth is a message about what?
questions.f: Greeks travelled to Delphi to hear prophecies from the priestess called the Pythia.

questions.q: Which word means the same as 'ghost'?
questions.f: Phantom comes from a Greek word meaning to show or appear.

questions.q: A 'giant-killer' in a folk tale is a hero who defeats what?
questions.f: The English tale Jack the Giant Killer was already popular over 300 years ago.

questions.q: Which word names a big group of gods worshipped together by one people?
questions.f: Pantheon is built from Greek pan, all, plus theos, god.

questions.q: In stories, what does a hero wear to protect their head?
questions.f: Greek helmets often had a bristling horsehair crest along the top.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which Titan was the father of Zeus?
questions.f: Romans called him Saturn, and gave him a midwinter festival called the Saturnalia.

questions.q: How many main gods lived on Mount Olympus in Greek belief?
questions.f: Ancient lists disagree slightly, so Hestia and Dionysus sometimes swap places in the twelve.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Circe turned Odysseus's sailors into which animals?
questions.f: A magic herb called moly protected Odysseus from her potion.

questions.q: Which Greek god gave Odysseus a bag holding all the winds?
questions.f: His crew opened the bag out of curiosity and blew the ship straight back to where it started.

questions.q: In the Odyssey, who waits at home weaving and unweaving the same cloth?
questions.f: She promised to choose a new husband when the weaving was done, so she never finished it.

questions.q: Which fruit tree did Hercules have to find in the garden of the Hesperides?
questions.f: A hundred-headed dragon named Ladon coiled around the trunk to guard it.

questions.q: What was special about the skin of the Nemean lion in Hercules' first labour?
questions.f: Hercules wore the lion skin afterwards, which is why art shows him in a lion's head hood.

questions.q: One of Hercules' labours was cleaning enormous stables. How did he do it?
c: He redirected a river through them
He asked the gods for wind
questions.f: Those were the stables of King Augeas, and they had not been cleaned in thirty years.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Orpheus almost rescued his wife from the underworld but broke which rule?
questions.f: He turned to check she was following, one step too early, and lost her.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Sisyphus was given the endless task of pushing what?
questions.f: The rock always rolls back down, which is why we call hopeless work Sisyphean.

questions.q: Which wise centaur taught heroes like Achilles and Jason?
questions.f: Chiron was skilled in medicine and music, and the constellation Sagittarius honours him.

questions.q: Which Greek nymph turned into a laurel tree to escape Apollo?
questions.f: Apollo then wore laurel leaves, and winners at Greek games were crowned with them.

questions.q: Where in Greece did people travel to hear the most famous oracle?
questions.f: The priestess there was called the Pythia, and kings waited weeks for her answers.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Helios drove which glowing vehicle across the sky each day?
questions.f: His son Phaethon begged for a turn at the reins, and the ride ended badly.

questions.q: In Norse myth, how many Norns spin the threads of fate?
questions.f: Their names mean roughly what has become, what is becoming, and what shall be.

questions.q: In Norse belief, how many worlds hang on the branches and roots of the world tree?
questions.f: They include Midgard for humans, Asgard for gods and Jotunheim for giants.

questions.q: In Norse myth, the great wolf Fenrir was finally held by a ribbon made of what?
c: Impossible things like a bird's spit
questions.f: The dwarves' ribbon Gleipnir also contained the sound a cat makes when it moves.

questions.q: In Norse myth, what chases the sun and moon across the sky?
questions.f: The wolves Skoll and Hati explain eclipses in the old stories.

questions.q: What is unusual about the handle of Thor's hammer in the myth?
c: It is shaped like a snake
questions.f: Loki, as a fly, pestered the dwarf working the bellows, so the handle came out stubby.

questions.q: In Norse stories, who is Odin's wife and the queen of the gods?
questions.f: Frigg is said to know everyone's fate but to keep it to herself.

questions.q: In Egyptian myth, who is the wife and sister of Osiris?
questions.f: Isis was such a famous magician that Egyptians called on her name in healing spells.

questions.q: Egyptians stored a mummy's organs in four special containers called what?
questions.f: Each jar had a different head on the lid: human, baboon, jackal and falcon.

questions.q: What did Egyptians call the dangerous underworld a soul had to travel through?
questions.f: Spells to help with the journey were written on coffin walls and papyrus scrolls.

questions.q: Which Egyptian god was said to shape babies on a potter's wheel?
questions.f: Khnum had a ram's head, and his workshop was imagined right beside the Nile's clay.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, Vishnu's very first avatar was which animal?
questions.f: As the fish Matsya he towed a boat to safety through a great flood.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, which animal form did Vishnu take to support a mountain on his back?
questions.f: As Kurma the turtle he became the pivot for the churning of the cosmic ocean.

questions.q: Which river is said to flow from the hair of the Hindu god Shiva?
questions.f: Shiva caught the falling river in his hair so its force would not smash the earth.

questions.q: Which three-pronged weapon does Shiva carry?
questions.f: Trishula means three spears, and its points stand for creation, protection and change.

questions.q: In the Ramayana, which loyal brother goes with Rama into the forest?
questions.f: Bharata, another brother, refuses the throne and waits for Rama to come home.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, whose body became the mountains and rivers of the world?
questions.f: Pangu is said to have held the sky and earth apart for 18,000 years first.

questions.q: In Chinese legend, the archer Houyi shot down extra what?
questions.f: Ten suns were scorching the crops, so he left just the one we have.

questions.q: Chinese New Year customs are said to scare off which legendary beast?
questions.f: Red decorations and loud firecrackers are exactly what the Nian is said to hate.

questions.q: In a Chinese love legend, a bridge across the sky is made of which birds?
questions.f: The weaver girl and the cowherd meet on that bridge once a year at the Qixi festival.

questions.q: In Japanese myth, Susanoo defeated a monster with how many heads?
questions.f: Inside its tail he found a famous sword, one of Japan's three imperial treasures.

questions.q: In Japanese myth, what coaxed the sun goddess out of the cave she was hiding in?
questions.f: Curious about the laughter outside, she peeked out, and light returned to the world.

questions.q: At the Japanese festival of Setsubun, what do people throw to drive out oni?
questions.f: They shout demons out, good luck in, then eat one bean for each year of their age.

questions.q: In Japanese folklore, the tengu is known for its very long what?
questions.f: Tengu are mountain spirits, and old masks give them a bright red face too.

questions.q: In West African tales, Anansi bargains with the sky god to become the keeper of what?
questions.f: That is why story collections in Ghana are called Anansesem, meaning spider tales.

questions.q: In Yoruba stories, Ogun is the powerful god of iron and which craft?
questions.f: Even today Nigerian metalworkers and drivers may honour Ogun for safety with tools.

questions.q: In Yoruba belief, Oshun is the goddess of which kind of water?
questions.f: A sacred grove on the Osun River in Nigeria is now a World Heritage Site.

questions.q: Which Aztec god of rain was prayed to for good harvests?
questions.f: Tlaloc is easy to spot in Aztec art because of his round goggle-like eyes.

questions.q: In Inca legend, the first Inca couple came out of which high lake?
questions.f: Titicaca sits 3,800 metres up and is the highest large lake ships can sail.

questions.q: In Inuit stories, Sedna rules over what?
questions.f: Hunters asked Sedna's permission before a hunt, since she owned the seals and whales.

questions.q: In American tall tales, Pecos Bill used which unusual lasso?
questions.f: Tall tales also say he rode a tornado across three states.

questions.q: In Irish legend, Fionn mac Cumhaill gained all knowledge by tasting which fish?
questions.f: He burned his thumb on the cooking salmon and sucked it, and the wisdom went to him.

questions.q: In Arthurian legend, who gives Arthur his sword from the water?
questions.f: When Arthur's last battle is over, the sword is thrown back to her waiting hand.

questions.q: Which knight of the Round Table finally achieves the quest for the Grail?
questions.f: Legend makes Galahad the son of Lancelot and the purest knight of all.

questions.q: In Russian tales, Baba Yaga flies about riding in what?
c: A mortar, steering with a pestle
questions.f: A mortar and pestle are kitchen tools for grinding, which makes her ride wonderfully odd.

questions.q: Who is the thunder god of the old Slavic peoples?
questions.f: Perun's symbol was the oak tree, and axe-shaped charms were worn in his honour.

questions.q: The oldest long poem we know tells of a king of Uruk. What is his name?
questions.f: The Epic of Gilgamesh was written on clay tablets over 4,000 years ago.

questions.q: In Australian folklore, the bunyip is said to lurk where?
questions.f: Bunyip comes from the Wemba-Wemba language of Victoria.

questions.q: According to legend, the Flying Dutchman is a ghostly what?
questions.f: Sailors said seeing her glowing sails meant a storm was coming.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek writer first described the lost island of Atlantis?
questions.f: Plato used Atlantis in a lesson about pride; no evidence of the island has ever been found.

questions.q: In Maori tradition, a taniwha is a powerful creature that guards rivers and lakes.
questions.f: Some New Zealand road and building plans have been redesigned out of respect for taniwha sites.

questions.q: The Epic of Gilgamesh includes a story about a great flood.
questions.f: A man named Utnapishtim survives it in a boat, centuries before similar stories were written down elsewhere.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Hades is one of the three brothers who divided the world with Zeus and Poseidon.
questions.f: They drew lots: Zeus got the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Hades the world below.

questions.q: Norse myth says the gods and the giants were often related to each other.
questions.f: Thor's mother and Odin's mother were both giantesses, which makes the family tree tangled.

questions.q: Guanyin is honoured across East Asia as a figure of mercy and kindness.
questions.f: Guanyin's name means the one who hears the cries of the world.

questions.q: Egyptian myth says the sky goddess Nut swallowed the sun each evening.
questions.f: She then gave birth to it again at dawn, which explained sunrise beautifully.

questions.q: What is a 'fable'?
c: A short story with animals that teaches a lesson
questions.f: Aesop's fables are the most famous, and most end with a clear moral.

questions.q: What does the word 'epic' mean when it names a kind of story?
c: A long poem about heroic deeds
questions.f: From Greek epos, a word or song; the Iliad and the Mahabharata are both epics.

questions.q: The word 'folklore' is made of 'folk' plus 'lore'. What does 'lore' mean?
questions.f: So folklore is the knowledge of ordinary people, learned by listening rather than reading.

questions.q: In myths, what is an 'omen'?
c: A sign of what is to come
questions.f: Romans watched birds for omens before making big decisions.

questions.q: What is a 'labyrinth'?
questions.f: True labyrinths have one winding path, while mazes have branching choices.

questions.q: A 'mortal' in a Greek myth is someone who what?
questions.f: From Latin mors, death; add in- and you get immortal, the opposite.

questions.q: What does the word 'deity' mean?
questions.f: Deity, divine and even the name Zeus all trace back to an old root meaning shining sky.

questions.q: The 'hydr' in the monster Hydra, and in 'hydrant', means what?
questions.f: The Hydra was a water snake living in a marsh, so its name fits perfectly.

questions.q: If something is 'colossal', it is what?
questions.f: The word honours the Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze statue about 33 metres tall.

questions.q: What does the word 'oracle' describe?
c: Someone who answers questions for a god
questions.f: Oracle comes from the Latin orare, to speak.

questions.q: A 'saga' is a long story of families and heroes. The word originally meant what?
questions.f: From Old Norse; Icelanders wrote down their sagas about 800 years ago.

questions.q: If a task is called 'Herculean', what is it?
questions.f: It recalls the twelve labours, any one of which would exhaust a normal person.

questions.q: What does the word 'petrify' literally mean?
questions.f: From Greek petra, rock; Medusa's stare is the most famous example in myth.

questions.q: An 'idol' in old stories is what?
c: A statue treated as a god
questions.f: From Greek eidolon, an image or likeness.

questions.q: What does the word 'Olympian' mean when talking about Greek gods?
questions.f: The modern Olympic Games are named after Olympia, a different place used for festivals.

questions.q: The word 'naga', used for serpent beings in Indian myth, simply means what?
questions.f: Nagas guard treasure and rain in Indian and Southeast Asian stories alike.

questions.q: The word 'Ramayana' means the journey of whom?
questions.f: Ayana means going or journey, so the title tells you the whole shape of the story.

questions.q: The festival name 'Deepavali', or Diwali, means a row of what?
questions.f: Deepa means lamp and vali means row, so families line their walls with little lights.

questions.q: A 'monster' in a myth is best described as what?
c: A frightening creature unlike any real animal
questions.f: Monster comes from a Latin word meaning a warning or a strange sign.

questions.q: What does 'legendary hero' mean?
c: A hero known from old stories
A hero who is still alive
A hero who was a king
questions.f: Some legendary heroes really existed, like the outlaw behind the Robin Hood tales.

questions.q: A 'seer' in a myth is someone who can do what?
questions.f: Seer is simply the word see plus -er, an English word for a Greek idea.

questions.q: What does the word 'sphinx-like' mean today?
questions.f: The Greek Sphinx asked riddles, so her name became a byword for a puzzle.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Perseus rescued Andromeda from which danger?
questions.f: Andromeda, Perseus and the monster Cetus all became constellations side by side.

questions.q: Who gave Theseus the ball of thread that saved him in the maze?
questions.f: Ariadne was the daughter of King Minos, who owned the maze.

questions.q: In Greek myth, how did the huntress Atalanta lose her famous race?
questions.f: Three rolling golden apples were enough to slow the fastest runner in Greece.

questions.q: In Greek myth, who ferries souls across the river into the underworld?
questions.f: Greeks placed a coin with the dead so they could pay Charon's fare.

questions.q: What was the name of the happy meadow where good souls rested in Greek belief?
questions.f: The grand Champs-Elysees avenue in Paris is named after those Elysian Fields.

questions.q: In Greek myth, after a great flood how did Deucalion and Pyrrha make new people?
questions.f: The stones they tossed over their shoulders became the next generation of humans.

questions.q: In Greek myth, King Midas was given the ears of which animal?
questions.f: He hid them under a hat, but his barber could not keep the secret.

questions.q: Which boy was carried to Olympus to become cupbearer to the gods?
questions.f: Jupiter's largest moon is named Ganymede, and it is bigger than the planet Mercury.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which goddess punished people who were far too proud?
questions.f: We still call a rival who keeps beating us our nemesis.

questions.q: Who were the Amazons in Greek myth?
questions.f: A Spanish explorer named South America's great river after them in the 1540s.

questions.q: In Greek myth, the harpies kept stealing food from which unlucky king?
questions.f: Two of Jason's crewmates, who could fly, finally chased the harpies away.

questions.q: What guarded the Golden Fleece in the grove at Colchis?
questions.f: Medea's sleeping potion did what no sword could and closed the dragon's eyes.

questions.q: In Norse myth, who chooses brave warriors and leads them to Odin's hall?
questions.f: Valkyrie means chooser of the fallen, and they ride through the sky on horseback.

questions.q: In Norse myth, the first cow Audhumla fed the first giant by giving what?
questions.f: She also licked salty ice, uncovering the ancestor of the gods hidden inside.

questions.q: Which Norse god owns a golden-bristled boar that can run over air and water?
questions.f: Dwarves made the boar Gullinbursti, whose bristles light up the night.

questions.q: In Norse myth, which plant was the one thing that could hurt Baldur?
questions.f: His mother made everything else promise not to harm him, but skipped the small mistletoe.

questions.q: In Norse myth, whose head did Odin keep so he could ask it for advice?
questions.f: Mimir was the wisest being in the nine worlds, and his well held all knowledge.

questions.q: In Egyptian myth, which sacred bird was said to rise from the fire at Heliopolis?
questions.f: Greek travellers heard the bennu story and retold it as the phoenix.

questions.q: Which Egyptian god was worshipped in the form of a living bull named Apis?
questions.f: When an Apis bull died, Egypt held a national funeral and searched for its successor.

questions.q: Which cheerful, dwarf-like Egyptian god protected families and newborn babies?
questions.f: Bes appears on mirrors, beds and headrests, sticking out his tongue to scare off trouble.

questions.q: Which Egyptian goddess who protected mothers was shaped like a hippopotamus?
questions.f: Egyptians feared real hippos, so a friendly hippo goddess was an especially strong guardian.

questions.q: Which cobra goddess guarded the crown of Egyptian kings?
questions.f: The rearing cobra on a pharaoh's forehead is called a uraeus.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, Indra rides which magnificent white animal?
questions.f: The elephant Airavata is said to have several trunks and to bring rain clouds.

questions.q: How many horses pull the chariot of the Hindu sun god Surya?
questions.f: The seven horses are often explained as the seven colours hidden inside sunlight.

questions.q: Which weapon does the Vedic god Indra hurl, whose name means thunderbolt?
questions.f: Vajra also means diamond, since both are unbreakable.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, which god keeps records and rules over what happens after death?
questions.f: Yama rides a buffalo, and his name means restraint or the one who binds.

questions.q: In the Mahabharata, which sage is said to have dictated the epic while Ganesha wrote it down?
questions.f: Legend says Ganesha broke off his own tusk to use as a pen and never paused.

questions.q: In the Ramayana, which giant brother of Ravana is famous for sleeping for months?
questions.f: Waking him took drums, elephants and a feast, according to the story.

questions.q: Which collection of Indian animal fables was written to teach princes wisdom?
questions.f: Its stories travelled to Persia, Arabia and Europe, shaping fables everywhere.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, who rules the heavens as the highest of the gods?
questions.f: Chinese New Year customs include reporting the year's news to the Jade Emperor.

questions.q: In Chinese legend, the Queen Mother of the West grows a garden of what?
questions.f: Her peach trees are said to ripen only once every few thousand years.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, Yu the Great became a hero by doing what?
questions.f: Instead of walls he dug channels, and stories say he worked for thirteen years.

questions.q: In Chinese folklore, Mazu is a goddess who protects which people?
questions.f: Temples to Mazu line the coasts of Fujian, Taiwan and Southeast Asia.

questions.q: In a Japanese tale, Urashima Taro was rewarded for rescuing which animal?
questions.f: The turtle carried him to a palace under the sea, where time ran differently.

questions.q: In an old Japanese story, Princess Kaguya was discovered inside a glowing what?
questions.f: At the end of the tale she returns to the moon, her true home.

questions.q: In Japanese belief, Inari is the god of rice and is served by which messenger animals?
questions.f: Stone foxes guard thousands of Inari shrines, often with a key or a rice sheaf in the mouth.

questions.q: In Japanese myth, the thunder god Raijin makes storms using a ring of what?
questions.f: His companion Fujin, the wind god, carries a big bag of winds on his shoulders.

questions.q: Which West African epic tells the story of the founder of the Mali Empire?
questions.f: Griots, the storytelling musicians of Mali, have passed Sundiata's story on for 700 years.

questions.q: In Akan belief from Ghana, Nyame is the god of what?
questions.f: Anansi the spider is called Nyame's son in many of the tales.

questions.q: In San stories of southern Africa, the trickster creator Kaggen takes the form of which insect?
questions.f: San rock paintings in the Drakensberg mountains still show his stories.

questions.q: In Maya myth, the Hero Twins beat the lords of the underworld at which sport?
questions.f: Maya cities had stone ball courts shaped like a capital I for that very game.

questions.q: Which Aztec god was honoured as the god of the sun and of their capital city?
questions.f: His name means hummingbird of the south, one of the loveliest god names anywhere.

questions.q: In Inca myth, which creator god is said to have made the sun, moon and stars at Lake Titicaca?
questions.f: Inca legend says Viracocha then walked across the ocean without sinking.

questions.q: In stories from the Pacific Northwest, which clever bird brought light to the world?
questions.f: Haida and Tlingit carvings show Raven holding the sun in his beak.

questions.q: In Iroquois tradition, the earth was built on the back of which animal?
questions.f: That is why North America is called Turtle Island in many Indigenous stories.

questions.q: Which made-up American animal is a jackrabbit with antlers?
questions.f: Postcards of jackalopes have been sold in Wyoming since the 1930s.

questions.q: In Irish legend, Tir na nOg is a land where people never do what?
questions.f: Visitors who return home from Tir na nOg find that centuries have passed.

questions.q: Which creature appears on the flag of Wales?
questions.f: Welsh kings used the red dragon as a battle standard over a thousand years ago.

questions.q: In Slavic tales, the dragon Zmey Gorynych is famous for having how many heads?
questions.f: Russian storytellers say each head breathes its own fire.

questions.q: In Mesopotamian myth, which goddess of love and war was linked to the planet Venus?
questions.f: Her sacred animal was the lion, and her star had eight points.

questions.q: Egyptian myth says Thoth invented writing.
questions.f: Scribes poured out a drop of ink for Thoth before starting work.

questions.q: In Greek myth, the Furies chased people who had broken solemn promises.
questions.f: Greeks nervously called them the Kindly Ones, hoping flattery would help.

questions.q: Norse myth says the gods built their wall around Asgard entirely by themselves.
questions.f: A builder and his amazing stallion did the work, and the gods nearly lost their bargain.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, every god has an animal companion or mount called a vahana.
questions.f: Vahana means vehicle: a swan for Saraswati, a bull for Shiva, a mouse for Ganesha.

questions.q: The Japanese Seven Lucky Gods travel together on a treasure ship.
questions.f: Children put a picture of that ship under their pillow at New Year for lucky dreams.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Iris travelled between gods and people using the rainbow as her road.
questions.f: That is why iridescent things, which flash with rainbow colours, carry her name.

questions.q: A 'demigod' in myth is someone who is half what?
questions.f: Demi- means half, from French; Hercules is the most famous demigod of all.

questions.q: The word 'trident' is built from parts meaning three plus what?
questions.f: From Latin tres and dens, tooth, the same root as dentist.

questions.q: If something is 'gigantic', it is named after which mythical beings?
questions.f: The Greek Gigantes fought the Olympian gods in a famous battle called the Gigantomachy.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'elf'?
questions.f: English swaps f for v in a handful of old words: leaf and leaves, wolf and wolves.

questions.q: What does the word 'serpent' mean?
questions.f: From Latin serpere, to creep; that is also where creepy-crawly ideas come from.

questions.q: A griffin's front feet end in 'talons'. What are talons?
questions.f: Talon comes from a Latin word for heel, then shifted to mean a bird's grabbing claw.

questions.q: What does the word 'shrine' mean?
questions.f: Shrine comes from a Latin word for a box, since shrines often held a treasured object.

questions.q: In myths, what is an 'altar'?
questions.f: From Latin altus, high, because offerings were placed up where the gods could see.

questions.q: What does the word 'divine' mean?
questions.f: Divine, deity and even the Roman name Jupiter all come from one ancient root.

questions.q: A story's 'moral' is what?
questions.f: Aesop's fables put the moral right at the end so nobody could miss it.

questions.q: What does a 'spell' originally mean in old English?
questions.f: That older meaning survives in gospel, which means good spell or good news.

questions.q: What does the word 'immortality' name?
questions.f: Many myths, from Gilgamesh to the Chinese elixir tales, are quests for immortality.

questions.q: An 'amulet' is a small object worn to do what?
questions.f: Egyptians wore scarab and ankh amulets by the thousand.

questions.q: What does 'monstrous' mean?
questions.f: Monstrous once simply meant unnatural, before it grew to mean enormous.

questions.q: A 'heroic' deed is one that is what?
questions.f: Greek poets sang of the heroic age, the time when heroes and gods still mingled.

questions.q: In a myth, a 'quest object' like the Golden Fleece or the Grail is best described as what?
c: The prize the hero must find
questions.f: Storytellers in every land use this shape: a hard journey towards one shining thing.

questions.q: What is a 'prophet' in old stories?
c: Someone who speaks for a god
questions.f: From Greek pro, before, plus phanai, to speak: one who speaks beforehand.

questions.q: What does the word 'underworld' mean in Greek myth?
questions.f: The Greeks named it after Hades, its ruler, then used the name for the place itself.

questions.q: What does 'sacrifice' mean in ancient religion?
c: An offering given to a god
questions.f: From Latin sacer, holy, plus facere, to make: to make something holy.

questions.q: If a hero is described as 'fated', what does that mean?
