questions.f: Greek myth gave fate to three sisters who measured and cut each life's thread.

questions.q: What is a 'bard' in Celtic tradition?
c: A poet and singer of tales
questions.f: Welsh bards competed at gatherings called eisteddfodau, a custom that continues today.

questions.q: A 'winged' creature in a myth has what?
questions.f: Sculptors loved winged beings: Nike, Pegasus and Assyrian bull-men all fly.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'mythical beast' tell you about the animal?
questions.f: Some mythical beasts were inspired by real bones, like elephant skulls and fossil teeth.

questions.q: In Greek myth, the goddess Eris started the Trojan War trouble by tossing in what?
questions.f: It was labelled for the fairest, and three goddesses each thought it meant her.

questions.q: Which goddess did Paris choose as the fairest, setting the Trojan War in motion?
questions.f: Hera offered power and Athena offered wisdom, but Aphrodite promised love.

questions.q: Which Trojan princess could see the future but was never believed?
questions.f: We still call someone a Cassandra when they give warnings that nobody heeds.

questions.q: Which Trojan hero escaped the burning city and, in Roman legend, led his people to Italy?
questions.f: The Roman poet Virgil made his journey the subject of the Aeneid.

questions.q: What clever name did Odysseus give the cyclops so he could not be blamed later?
questions.f: When the cyclops shouted that Nobody had tricked him, his neighbours simply laughed.

questions.q: How did Odysseus's crew survive sailing past the Sirens?
questions.f: Odysseus left his own ears open but had himself tied to the mast so he could listen safely.

questions.q: Sailing between Scylla and Charybdis meant choosing between a monster and what?
questions.f: The phrase now describes any choice where both options are bad.

questions.q: In Greek myth, what was left at the bottom of Pandora's jar?
questions.f: Ancient Greek called the container a pithos, a big storage jar, not a box.

questions.q: Which Greek goddess of crossroads and magic carried torches?
questions.f: Greeks left food at crossroads for Hecate on the night of the new moon.

questions.q: Which Greek healer god carries a staff with a single snake curled round it?
questions.f: That rod of Asclepius is still the symbol used by ambulances and medical groups.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which princess was carried to Crete by Zeus in the form of a bull?
questions.f: A whole continent ended up bearing her name.

questions.q: Which Greek hero founded the city of Thebes after sowing dragon's teeth?
questions.f: Greeks also credited Cadmus with bringing them the alphabet.

questions.q: Which shining metal creature made by Hephaestus guarded the island of Crete?
questions.f: Talos circled Crete three times a day, making him one of myth's first robots.

questions.q: In Norse myth, what did Odin sacrifice hanging on the world tree for nine nights?
c: He gave himself up to gain the runes
questions.f: He came back with the secret of writing, which he shared with gods and people.

questions.q: In Norse myth, whose child is the eight-legged horse Sleipnir?
questions.f: Loki, shape-shifting as usual, is Sleipnir's parent, which makes Odin's horse his nephew.

questions.q: Which two wolves sit at Odin's side while he feasts?
questions.f: Odin gives them his own food and takes only wine himself.

questions.q: In Norse myth, the first world was made from the body of which being?
questions.f: His bones became mountains and his skull the dome of the sky.

questions.q: Which dragon gnaws at the roots of the Norse world tree?
questions.f: A squirrel carries insults between Nidhogg below and an eagle up top.

questions.q: In Egyptian myth, Shu the air god separated which two gods?
questions.f: Paintings show Shu kneeling, holding up Nut the sky while Geb the earth lies below.

questions.q: What is the Egyptian Eye of Horus best known as?
c: A charm for protection and healing
questions.f: Egyptians also used its parts as fractions in their measurements.

questions.q: Which Egyptian collection of spells was written to guide a soul safely through the afterlife?
questions.f: Its Egyptian name means the book of coming forth by day.

questions.q: Which Egyptian god is the brother of Osiris and the rival who wants his throne?
questions.f: Set is drawn as an unknown creature with a curved snout, which puzzles scholars still.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, gods and asuras churned the ocean using which mountain as a stick?
questions.f: The serpent Vasuki was the rope, and Vishnu as a turtle steadied the mountain's base.

questions.q: What were the gods and asuras hoping to win by churning the cosmic ocean?
questions.f: Fourteen treasures rose from the sea before the amrita finally appeared.

questions.q: How many main avatars, or descents, of Vishnu are usually counted?
questions.f: They run from a fish through a turtle, a boar and a lion up to Krishna and Kalki.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, why did young Krishna lift Mount Govardhan?
c: To shelter villagers from a storm
questions.f: He held it up like an umbrella for seven days until the rain stopped.

questions.q: According to legend, Ganesha broke off one of his own tusks to use as what?
questions.f: That is why he is often shown with one whole tusk and one snapped short.

questions.q: In Hindu tradition, which three gods make up the Trimurti?
questions.f: Their roles are usually given as creating, protecting and transforming the world.

questions.q: In Chinese legend, how many Immortals travel together across the sea?
questions.f: Each of the Eight Immortals carries a different magic tool, from a flute to a gourd.

questions.q: In Journey to the West, which animal companion is called Zhu Bajie?
questions.f: The travelling group also includes a monk, a monkey, a river ogre and a dragon-horse.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, why does Chang'e live on the moon?
c: She swallowed an elixir of immortality
She was banished by a dragon
She flew there on a crane
questions.f: China's real moon missions are named Chang'e in her honour.

questions.q: Which Chinese mythical bird, often called the Chinese phoenix, stands for peace and the empress?
questions.f: Unlike the western phoenix it does not burn; it simply appears in times of peace.

questions.q: In the Chinese Legend of the White Snake, what is Bai Suzhen able to do?
questions.f: The tale is one of China's four great folk legends and is retold in opera every year.

questions.q: Chinese dragon boat races remember which loyal poet?
questions.f: Rice dumplings called zongzi are eaten at the same festival in his memory.

questions.q: In Japanese myth, which pair of gods created the islands of Japan?
questions.f: They are said to have stirred the sea with a jewelled spear, and drops formed the first island.

questions.q: In Japanese folklore, the tanuki is a shape-shifting version of which real animal?
questions.f: Statues of tanuki outside restaurants usually show one with a straw hat and a sake flask.

questions.q: In the Japanese tale, how big was the hero Issun-boshi?
c: About the size of a thumb
As small as a grain of rice
As big as a doll's house
questions.f: He used a needle as a sword and a rice bowl as a boat.

questions.q: In Korea's founding legend, which animal became a woman and mothered Dangun?
questions.f: The story says she stayed in a cave eating garlic and mugwort for a hundred days.

questions.q: In Polynesian legend, why did Maui catch the sun with ropes?
questions.f: He wanted more daylight so his mother would have time to dry her cloth.

questions.q: Which Maya book preserves the stories of the Hero Twins and the creation of people?
questions.f: It was written down in the 1500s in the Kiche Maya language using Latin letters.

questions.q: In Maya belief, what was Xibalba?
questions.f: Maya guides today still point out caves said to be entrances to Xibalba.

questions.q: In Inca legend, who was the first Inca, sent by the sun to found Cusco?
questions.f: Legend says he carried a golden staff and settled where it sank into the ground.

questions.q: In Mesopotamian epic, who becomes Gilgamesh's closest friend?
questions.f: Enkidu starts as a wild man of the steppe and ends as the king's equal.

questions.q: In the Old English poem, which hero comes to Denmark to help against the monster Grendel?
questions.f: Beowulf is the oldest long poem in English, written over a thousand years ago.

questions.q: Which legendary saint is famous for facing a dragon and is the patron of England?
questions.f: The dragon story was attached to George by European storytellers in the Middle Ages.

questions.q: Swiss legend says William Tell was forced to shoot an arrow at what?
c: An apple on his son's head
questions.f: He is a national hero of Switzerland, though historians cannot prove he existed.

questions.q: In Norse myth, the Vanir and the Aesir were two different families of gods.
questions.f: After a long quarrel they exchanged hostages, which is how Freyr and Freyja joined Asgard.

questions.q: The Aztecs believed the world had already been created and destroyed several times.
questions.f: Their Sun Stone records earlier ages that ended in wind, fire, flood and jaguars.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Prometheus's brother Epimetheus was married to Pandora.
questions.f: Their names mean forethought and afterthought, which tells you who thought things through.

questions.q: Egyptian myth says the sun god had to fight a giant serpent every night.
questions.f: The serpent Apep tried to swallow the sun boat, and every sunrise was a victory.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, an eclipse was explained by a shadow demon swallowing the sun.
questions.f: Rahu and Ketu, the two lunar nodes, are the astronomy behind that story.

questions.q: Homer's Iliad tells the whole story of the Trojan War from beginning to end.
questions.f: It actually covers only a few weeks near the end, and the wooden horse is not even in it.

questions.q: The alarm called a 'siren' is named after Greek beings famous for what?
questions.f: A French engineer named his warning instrument after them in the early 1800s.

questions.q: The word 'panic' comes from the name of which Greek god?
questions.f: Lonely travellers blamed sudden fear in the woods on Pan leaping out for fun.

questions.q: Why is a book of maps called an 'atlas'?
c: Early ones showed the Titan holding up the world
questions.f: Mercator put a picture of Atlas in his 1595 map collection, and the name stuck.

questions.q: The word 'volcano' comes from the name of which god of fire and forges?
questions.f: Italy's island of Vulcano was thought to sit above his workshop chimney.

questions.q: Break the name 'Cyclops' into its Greek parts and you get what?
questions.f: From kyklos, circle, plus ops, eye; the same kyklos gives us cycle and bicycle.

questions.q: The name 'Minotaur' literally means what?
questions.f: Tauros means bull, and it is also behind the star name Taurus.

questions.q: January is named after Janus, a Roman god shown with what?
questions.f: One face looks back at the old year and one forward to the new.

questions.q: Wednesday is named after which god?
questions.f: Old English Wodnesdaeg matched the Latin day of Mercury, since both gods were travellers.

questions.q: Saturday takes its name from which Roman god?
questions.f: It is the only English weekday name still borrowed straight from a Roman god.

questions.q: The word 'ocean' comes from Oceanus, who in Greek myth was what?
c: A Titan of the great river circling the world
questions.f: Greeks pictured Oceanus as an endless stream wrapping the whole earth.

questions.q: A 'museum' originally meant a place belonging to whom?
questions.f: The famous Museum of Alexandria was a research home dedicated to those nine goddesses.

questions.q: In Greek myth the word 'chaos' first meant what?
questions.f: Only later did chaos come to mean total disorder.

questions.q: The 'geo' in geography comes from the name of which earth goddess?
questions.f: So geography is literally earth-writing and geology is earth-study.

questions.q: An 'odyssey' means what kind of experience?
questions.f: Odysseus took ten years to sail home, which is quite a benchmark for a long trip.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word 'karma' literally means what?
questions.f: The idea is simple: actions have results, the way seeds have plants.

questions.q: The Atlantic Ocean is named after which mythical figure?
questions.f: Greeks called the water beyond the Atlas Mountains the sea of Atlas.

questions.q: Which study is named from Greek words meaning gods plus study?
questions.f: Theos means god, and it also hides inside names like Theodore, meaning gift of god.

questions.q: What does the word 'polytheism' mean?
questions.f: Poly means many; a monotheist believes in one, since mono means single.

questions.q: If a computer program hides its true purpose, we call it a Trojan. Why?
c: It recalls the trick of the wooden horse
questions.f: The name was first used for sneaky software in the 1970s.

questions.q: Which strong cord at the back of your ankle is named after a Greek hero?
questions.f: Anatomists gave it that name in the 1690s because of the hero's famous weak spot.

questions.q: The Roman goddess Fortuna gave English which everyday word?
questions.f: She was often shown with a wheel, which is where a wheel of fortune comes from.

questions.q: What does the word 'nymph' mean in Greek?
questions.f: Insect scientists borrowed the word for the young stage of insects like dragonflies.

questions.q: An 'oracle bone' from ancient China was used for what?
questions.f: Cracks in heated ox bones were read as answers, and the marks carved on them are China's earliest writing.

questions.q: What does the word 'immortalise' mean?
questions.f: Poets said they immortalised heroes, keeping them alive in words rather than in bodies.

questions.q: A 'pantheon' can mean all a people's gods, or what kind of building?
c: A temple to all the gods
questions.f: Rome's Pantheon still stands, with a wide open hole in its dome to let in the sky.

questions.q: What does the word 'invulnerable', used of heroes like Achilles, mean?
questions.f: From Latin vulnus, a wound; add in- for not.

questions.q: A 'demigoddess' would be described as what?
questions.f: Greek writers also used the word heroine for such figures.

questions.q: What does the word 'mythical' contrast with?
questions.f: Historians work hard to sort the mythical Troy from the real ruins under it.

questions.q: What is a 'bestiary'?
c: A book describing real and imagined animals
questions.f: Medieval bestiaries put unicorns and phoenixes right beside elephants and bees.

questions.q: Which word describes a story that explains why something in nature is the way it is?
questions.f: Why the moon has phases and why bears have short tails are both classic origin myths.

questions.q: What does 'supernatural' mean?
questions.f: Super means above, so supernatural events sit above the ordinary rules.

questions.q: In folklore studies, what is a 'variant'?
c: A different version of the same tale
questions.f: Cinderella has hundreds of variants worldwide, including a ninth-century Chinese one.

questions.q: What does the word 'incantation' literally describe?
c: Words sung or chanted as a spell
questions.f: From Latin in- plus cantare, to sing, which also gives us chant and enchant.

questions.q: A 'talisman' differs from an ordinary charm because it is believed to do what?
questions.f: The word travelled into English through Arabic tilsam.

questions.q: What does the term 'shape-shifter' describe in myth studies?
c: A being that changes form at will
questions.f: Zeus, Loki, kitsune and selkies are all shape-shifters in their own traditions.

questions.q: In Greek, 'Hades' names both a god and what?
questions.f: The Greeks were nervous of saying his name, so they often called him the Rich One instead.

questions.q: Which word means a very old story that gives a made-up reason for a real custom?
questions.f: Storytellers explained everything this way, from wedding rings to why cats wash after eating.

questions.q: What does 'divination' mean?
c: Trying to learn hidden things or the future
questions.f: Methods have included bird flight, ox bones, coins, cards and dreams.

questions.q: What does 'sacred grove' mean?
c: A group of trees treated as holy
questions.f: Greeks, Celts and Yoruba all kept sacred groves, and some still stand today.

questions.q: What is a 'culture hero' in the study of myth?
c: A figure who gives people a vital skill or gift
questions.f: Prometheus with fire and Shennong with farming are both culture heroes.

questions.q: What does the word 'primordial' mean in creation stories?
questions.f: Egyptians called their primordial waters Nun, and everything rose out of them.

questions.q: What is the difference between a myth and a legend, as scholars usually use the words?
c: Myths involve gods; legends involve people believed to be real
questions.f: So Zeus belongs to myth while Robin Hood belongs to legend.

questions.q: What does 'anthropomorphic' mean when describing a god?
c: Shaped or acting like a human
questions.f: From Greek anthropos, human, plus morphe, form.

questions.q: In Norse myth, how did Thor get his hammer back from the giant Thrym?
questions.f: Loki went along as the bridesmaid, and the wedding feast gave the disguise away.

questions.q: In Norse belief, what is Fimbulwinter?
c: A terrible winter before the end of the world
questions.f: Three winters in a row with no summer between them is how the sagas describe it.

questions.q: Which giant Norse sea being brews ale for the gods in an enormous kettle?
questions.f: Norse poets called the sea Aegir's brewing pot when the waves were foaming.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which giant hunter was placed among the stars after his death?
questions.f: Orion's belt of three bright stars is one of the easiest patterns to spot in winter.

questions.q: In Greek myth, the nymph Callisto was turned into which animal before becoming a constellation?
questions.f: That is why the Great Bear, Ursa Major, wheels around the northern sky.

questions.q: Which Greek goddess drives the moon across the night sky?
questions.f: Her brother Helios drove the sun, and their sister Eos opened the dawn.

questions.q: In Greek myth, who is the goddess of the dawn?
questions.f: Poets called her rosy-fingered, because dawn light seems to reach across the sky.

questions.q: In Greek myth, the sculptor Pygmalion fell in love with what?
questions.f: Aphrodite brought the statue to life, and the story inspired countless plays and films.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Psyche had to complete impossible tasks to win back whom?
questions.f: Her hardest task was sorting a mountain of mixed grain, and helpful ants did it for her.

questions.q: Which Egyptian afterlife place was imagined as a perfect farmland?
questions.f: Egyptians hoped for endless good harvests and cool water there.

questions.q: In Egyptian belief, what were the ka and the ba?
c: Two parts of a person's spirit
questions.f: The ba was drawn as a bird with a human head so it could fly out of the tomb and return.

questions.q: Which Egyptian city was the great centre for the cat goddess Bastet?
questions.f: Archaeologists there found cat cemeteries holding thousands of carefully wrapped cats.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, why is Shiva called Neelkanth, the blue-throated one?
c: He held poison in his throat to protect the world
He swam in a blue river
He was born under a blue moon
questions.f: The poison rose from the churning of the ocean, and Shiva stopped it spreading.

questions.q: Which mountain is described as the home of Shiva and Parvati?
questions.f: The real Kailash in Tibet is climbed by nobody, out of respect for its sacredness.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, which goddess is the wife of Shiva and mother of Ganesha?
questions.f: Parvati means she of the mountains, fitting for a goddess at home on Kailash.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, Garuda the eagle is the sworn enemy of which creatures?
questions.f: Statues often show Garuda gripping a snake, a scene carved from India to Indonesia.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, how many Dragon Kings rule the waters?
questions.f: Each guards one of the four seas around the world as Chinese storytellers pictured it.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, which god-emperor tasted hundreds of plants to find medicines?
questions.f: He is honoured as the founder of Chinese farming and herbal medicine.

questions.q: In Chinese legend, why did the giant Kuafu chase the sun?
c: To catch it and end a drought
questions.f: The story says he drank two rivers dry along the way.

questions.q: In Japanese myth, which three treasures are the emperor's sacred symbols?
c: A mirror, a sword and a jewel
A fan, a crown and a bell
A drum, a rope and a mask
A bow, a coin and a comb
questions.f: They come straight from the stories of Amaterasu and Susanoo.

questions.q: In Japanese folklore, what did people blame for earthquakes?
c: A giant catfish under the islands
questions.f: Prints of the catfish Namazu became hugely popular after the 1855 Edo earthquake.

questions.q: In Japanese folklore, the more tails a kitsune has, the more what?
questions.f: Nine tails is the top rank, said to be reached only after a thousand years.

questions.q: In Yoruba belief, who is the messenger god who stands at the crossroads?
questions.f: No prayer is complete without greeting Eshu first, since he carries messages upward.

questions.q: In Yoruba stories, Yemoja is the motherly goddess of what?
questions.f: Her name is linked to the Ogun River, and she is honoured across the Atlantic too.

questions.q: In Maya belief, which god of rain carried a lightning axe?
questions.f: Maya farmers dropped offerings into deep natural wells called cenotes for Chaac.

questions.q: At the Maya pyramid of Kukulkan, what appears on the steps at the equinox?
c: A shadow shaped like a snake
questions.f: Thousands of visitors gather at Chichen Itza twice a year to watch the serpent slither down.

questions.q: In Irish legend, which young hero is the greatest warrior of Ulster?
questions.f: His name means the hound of Culann, earned when he guarded a smith's gate as a boy.

questions.q: In Arthurian legend, where is Arthur taken to be healed after his last battle?
questions.f: Avalon means the isle of apples, and legend says Arthur waits there still.

questions.q: In Russian tales, the villain Koschei keeps his life hidden inside what?
c: A needle inside a series of nested containers
questions.f: The needle is in an egg, in a duck, in a hare, in a chest, buried under an oak.

questions.q: In Slavic folklore, the domovoi is a spirit that looks after what?
questions.f: Families left him porridge behind the stove to keep him friendly.

questions.q: In Persian myth, the Simurgh is an enormous what?
questions.f: She is said to be so old that she has seen the world destroyed three times.

questions.q: Which Persian epic poem tells the deeds of the hero Rostam?
questions.f: Its title means the book of kings, and it runs to about 50,000 rhyming lines.

questions.q: In Finnish myth, what is the Sampo that everyone fights over?
c: A magic mill that makes riches
questions.f: The Kalevala, Finland's national epic, was collected from village singers in the 1800s.

questions.q: In German legend, Siegfried gains great power after defeating which dragon?
questions.f: Wagner turned the tale into a huge cycle of four operas.

questions.q: Jewish legend from Prague tells of a golem, a helper made of what?
questions.f: Stories say the golem was woken by a word written on paper and placed in its mouth.

questions.q: In German legend, the Lorelei is a maiden whose singing lured boats onto what?
c: A rocky bend of the Rhine
questions.f: The real Lorelei rock echoes strangely, which probably started the story.

questions.q: Which legendary sea monster of Norwegian tales was said to be as big as an island?
questions.f: Sailors were warned that if the sea boiled and bubbled, the kraken was rising.

questions.q: Which real animal probably inspired sailors' mermaid sightings?
questions.f: Columbus recorded seeing three mermaids in 1493 and noted they were not as pretty as painted.

questions.q: Which Greek writer's poems are our main source for Greek myths of the gods' family tree?
questions.f: His Theogony, meaning birth of the gods, sorts hundreds of gods into order.

questions.q: Which Roman poet retold hundreds of Greek myths in a long poem about transformations?
questions.f: His Metamorphoses is why we know so many myth details, from Arachne to Midas.

questions.q: Which Icelandic writer of the 1200s wrote down much of what we know about Norse myth?
questions.f: His Prose Edda was written partly as a handbook for poets.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Selene and Helios were sister and brother.
questions.f: Their parents were the Titans Hyperion and Theia.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, the Monkey King was once made a minor official in heaven.
questions.f: He was put in charge of the heavenly stables, which he found deeply insulting.

questions.q: Egyptian myth gave the god Thoth two forms: an ibis and a baboon.
questions.f: Baboons greet the sunrise with noise, which Egyptians read as morning worship.

questions.q: In Norse myth, Loki is described as a blood brother of Odin.
questions.f: That sworn bond is why the gods put up with Loki for so long.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, the god Kubera is the keeper of treasures and wealth.
questions.f: He is described as the guardian of the north and the lord of the yakshas.

questions.q: Ancient Greeks believed all their myths were literally true in every detail.
questions.f: Greek writers argued about them constantly, and some openly called the stories inventions.

questions.q: The 'hippo' in both 'hippopotamus' and the myth creature 'hippocampus' means what?
questions.f: So hippopotamus means river horse, and a hippocampus is a horse with a fish tail.

questions.q: Taken apart, Pandora's name describes her as what?
questions.f: Every god gave her a gift, which is exactly how her name describes her.

questions.q: The word 'Trimurti' means three what?
questions.f: Tri is three in Sanskrit as in Latin, so tricycle and Trimurti share a root idea.

questions.q: If a set of tunnels is described as 'labyrinthine', what is it like?
questions.f: The word comes straight from the Cretan Labyrinth of Greek myth.

questions.q: A 'necropolis' is a what?
questions.f: From Greek nekros, dead, plus polis, city; Egypt's Valley of the Kings is one.

questions.q: What does 'metamorphosis' mean?
questions.f: From meta, change, plus morphe, form; it also names how caterpillars become butterflies.

questions.q: In myth studies, what is a 'ritual'?
c: A set of actions repeated in a fixed order
questions.f: Rituals often act out a myth, which is why the two are studied together.

questions.q: What is a 'hymn'?
c: A song of praise to a god
questions.f: The Homeric Hymns are Greek songs to individual gods, some nearly 2,700 years old.

questions.q: What is a 'pilgrimage'?
c: A journey to a holy place
questions.f: Pilgrims have walked to Delphi, Varanasi, Ise and Santiago for centuries.

questions.q: In stories, what is a 'trial' that a hero faces?
c: A test that must be passed
questions.f: Folklorists noticed heroes usually face three trials, each harder than the last.

questions.q: What does the word 'Amazonian' suggest about a person?
c: Tall and strong like a warrior woman
questions.f: The word can also just mean of the Amazon River, which was itself named from the myth.

questions.q: What is 'personification' in myth?
c: Turning an idea into a character
Naming a god after a place
questions.f: Victory, Sleep, Fear and Memory all became Greek characters this way.

questions.q: A 'sacred oath' in myth is best described as what?
c: A solemn promise made before the gods
questions.f: Greek gods swore their strongest oaths on the underworld river Styx.

questions.q: What does the word 'guardian' mean when we speak of a guardian of a treasure?
questions.f: Dragons, giants and sleepless serpents are myth's favourite guardians.

questions.q: What does 'legendary' mean when a place is called legendary, like Camelot?
c: Known from stories, not proven real
questions.f: Archaeologists have proposed several English sites for Camelot, but none is certain.

questions.q: A 'firebird' and a 'phoenix' both belong to which group of words?
c: Compound and borrowed names for bird myths
questions.f: Firebird is built from two English words, while phoenix was borrowed whole from Greek.

questions.q: What does the word 'hero-cult' describe in ancient Greece?
c: Honouring a dead hero at his tomb
questions.f: Greek cities competed for the bones of famous heroes, believing they brought protection.

questions.q: What is a 'foundation myth'?
c: A story of how a city or people began
A story about the first god
questions.f: Rome's she-wolf and Mexico's eagle on a cactus are both foundation myths.

questions.q: What does 'cosmology' mean?
c: An account of how the universe is arranged
questions.f: Norse cosmology stacks nine worlds on one tree; Greek cosmology stacks sky, earth and underworld.

questions.q: What is an 'epithet' in epic poetry?
questions.f: Homer keeps repeating them: grey-eyed Athena, swift-footed Achilles, rosy-fingered dawn.

questions.q: What does the word 'mortal' tell you about the heroes of Greek epic?
questions.f: Greek poets called humans simply the mortals, which says a lot about how they saw life.

questions.q: If a god is called 'zoomorphic', how is that god shown?
questions.f: Egyptian gods are the champions of zoomorphic art, with heads of falcons, jackals and cats.

questions.q: What is a 'libation' in ancient worship?
c: A drink poured out as an offering
A loaf left at a shrine
questions.f: Greeks poured wine on the ground before drinking, sharing the first sip with the gods.

questions.q: What does the word 'nectar' mean today, and where did it come from?
c: Flower juice, from the gods' drink
A honey cake, from a Greek feast
A rare gem, from a Norse tale
questions.f: Botanists borrowed the Greek word for the drink of the gods and gave it to flowers.

questions.q: What is a 'monster-slayer' story pattern?
c: A hero frees a place from a beast
questions.f: Perseus, Beowulf, Susanoo and Rama all star in monster-slayer tales.

questions.q: What does 'invoke' mean when a poet invokes a Muse?
questions.f: Both the Iliad and the Odyssey open by asking a goddess to tell the story.

questions.q: What is a 'dynasty of gods' in a creation story?
c: One family of gods replacing another
questions.f: Greek myth has three: sky gods, then Titans, then Olympians.

questions.q: What does the word 'sacrilege' mean?
questions.f: In myth, sacrilege is almost always the fastest way to attract a god's attention.

questions.q: What does 'ancestral' mean when a people trace themselves to a legendary founder?
questions.f: Greek families claimed descent from heroes, and Japanese emperors from Amaterasu.

questions.q: Which word describes a story feature that appears again and again, like a magic ring?
questions.f: Folklorists index thousands of motifs so they can compare tales across the world.

questions.q: What does the word 'twilight' mean in the phrase twilight of the gods?
questions.f: It translates the Norse idea of Ragnarok, which German gave as Gotterdammerung.

questions.q: What does the word 'nether' mean in 'netherworld'?
questions.f: Nether survives in the Netherlands, a country of low-lying land.

questions.q: What is a 'winged messenger' called in Greek art?
questions.f: Both Hermes and Iris served as heralds, and both were shown with wings.

questions.q: What does the word 'ambrosia' mean by its parts?
questions.f: The a- means not and the rest is related to mortal, so it is the food of the deathless.

questions.q: In storytelling, what is a 'boon'?
questions.f: Folklorists say the classic hero's journey ends with bringing a boon back home.

questions.q: What does 'ancient' mean when we speak of ancient myths?
questions.f: The oldest written myths we have, from Sumer, are over 4,000 years old.

questions.q: Which word names the study of how words came to have their forms and meanings?
questions.f: Etymology explains why so many English words secretly hide a Greek god's name.

questions.q: What does 'legend' mean on a map, and how is that linked to legends in stories?
c: The key explaining symbols, since both mean things to be read
questions.f: Latin legenda means things to be read, which suits both uses perfectly.

questions.q: Which labour sent Hercules after birds with feathers of bronze?
questions.f: He scared them into the air with a bronze rattle made by Hephaestus.

questions.q: Hercules had to capture a deer with golden antlers that was sacred to which goddess?
questions.f: Because harming it would offend Artemis, he chased the Ceryneian hind for a whole year instead.

questions.q: Which Amazon queen owned the belt that Hercules was sent to fetch?
questions.f: The belt was a gift from Ares, which is why it was worth a whole labour.

questions.q: Three grey sisters in Greek myth shared a single what between them?
questions.f: Perseus snatched the eye of the Graeae and refused to hand it back until they gave directions.

questions.q: On Mount Helicon, a spring sacred to the Muses was said to have opened when what happened?
c: Pegasus struck the rock with a hoof
questions.f: That spring, Hippocrene, means horse fountain, and poets said drinking from it brought inspiration.

questions.q: What is the name of the ten-year war between the Olympians and the Titans?
questions.f: The suffix -machy means battle, and it also shows up in the giants' war, the Gigantomachy.

questions.q: Which Muse was said to inspire epic poetry, and is called the chief of the nine?
questions.f: Her name means beautiful-voiced, and a steam organ was later named a calliope after her.

questions.q: Which two rocks at the entrance to the Mediterranean were called the Pillars of Hercules?
c: Gibraltar and a peak in Morocco
questions.f: Legend said Hercules split a mountain in two on his way to fetch Geryon's cattle.

questions.q: In Greek myth, the herdsman Geryon was remarkable because he had what?
c: Three bodies joined at the waist
questions.f: His cattle were guarded by a two-headed dog, making the tenth labour doubly difficult.

questions.q: Which Roman priestesses kept a sacred flame burning and were chosen as children?
questions.f: Letting Vesta's fire go out was treated as a national emergency in Rome.

questions.q: Roman families honoured household gods of the store cupboard and hearth called what?
questions.f: Small shrines called lararia stood in Roman homes, complete with tiny statues.

questions.q: Roman legend says which animals raised the alarm when enemies crept up the Capitol at night?
questions.f: The geese were sacred to Juno, and Rome kept honouring them for the warning.

questions.q: In the Aeneid, whom does Aeneas carry out of burning Troy on his shoulders?
questions.f: Roman artists loved the image, and it became a symbol of duty to family.

questions.q: Which queen of Carthage does Aeneas meet on his voyage in Roman legend?
questions.f: Virgil made her story so moving that Roman readers wept over a queen from Rome's old enemy.

questions.q: In Norse myth, how did the giantess Skadi choose her husband among the gods?
c: By looking only at their feet
questions.f: She picked the finest feet expecting Baldur, and got Njord the sea god instead.

questions.q: On a fishing trip in Norse myth, what did Thor hook on his line?
questions.f: His companion Hymir cut the line in terror, which the poems treat as a real tragedy.

questions.q: At the hall of Utgard-Loki, Thor failed a drinking contest because the horn was joined to what?
questions.f: He also wrestled an old woman who was really old age, so losing was no disgrace.

questions.q: What is the name of the horn Heimdall will blow to warn the Norse gods?
questions.f: Its name means the yelling horn, and it is kept beside the world tree.

questions.q: Beside which well do the Norse Norns sit to shape fate?
questions.f: They water the world tree from it daily to keep the tree from rotting.

questions.q: In Norse myth, which fire giant guards the burning land of Muspelheim?
questions.f: His flaming sword is said to be brighter than the sun.

questions.q: In Egyptian belief, where did a soul face the weighing of the heart?
questions.f: Forty-two judges lined the hall, each asking about one kind of wrongdoing.

questions.q: Egyptians placed a special carved scarab over the chest of a mummy to protect what?
questions.f: Spells on the heart scarab politely asked the heart not to give evidence against its owner.

questions.q: Which two Egyptian gods were combined into one supreme god called Amun-Ra?
c: A hidden god and the sun god
questions.f: Amun means the hidden one, so joining him to visible Ra covered both sides of divinity.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, which weapon is Vishnu's spinning discus?
questions.f: He also carries a conch called Panchajanya, whose sound is said to scatter fear.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, which wish-granting cow is the mother of all cattle?
questions.f: Art shows Kamadhenu with many gods living inside her body, one in each part.

questions.q: Which king's centuries of effort finally brought the river Ganga down to earth?
questions.f: His name lives on in the Bhagirathi, one of the Ganga's Himalayan headstreams.

questions.q: Which avatar of Vishnu appears as half lion and half man?
questions.f: The form was designed to slip through a very cleverly worded promise.

questions.q: In the Ramayana, which flying chariot belongs to Ravana?
questions.f: Pushpaka means flowery, and the story says it could grow to hold any number of passengers.

questions.q: Which brother of Ravana leaves Lanka to join Rama's side?
questions.f: He is remembered as an example of choosing what is right over family loyalty.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, how many transformations is the Monkey King famous for mastering?
questions.f: His cloud somersault was said to cover 34,000 miles in a single leap.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, the young hero Nezha is given a new body made of what?
questions.f: He fights with a fire-tipped spear and rides on wheels of wind and fire.

questions.q: In Chinese legend, the bird Jingwei spends forever trying to do what?
questions.f: Chinese has a saying about Jingwei filling the sea, meaning stubborn determination.

questions.q: In Japanese myth, what is the name of the land of the dead that Izanagi visits?
questions.f: He escapes by blocking the entrance with an enormous boulder.

questions.q: Which legendary Japanese sword was found inside the tail of an eight-headed serpent?
questions.f: Its name means grass-cutter, earned when a prince used it to escape a burning field.

questions.q: In Japanese folklore, the yuki-onna appears as a woman made of what?
questions.f: Her tales come mostly from the deep-snow regions of northern Japan.

questions.q: In Japanese tales, the boy Kintaro grew up in the mountains wrestling with whom?
questions.f: He carries an axe and is often drawn on children's banners as a symbol of strength.

questions.q: In Yoruba creation stories, which god shapes human bodies before Olodumare gives them breath?
questions.f: Obatala's colour is white, and his followers wear it in his honour.

questions.q: In Zulu tradition, Unkulunkulu is honoured as what?
questions.f: The name means the very great one or the ancient one.

questions.q: Ethiopian legend says the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon had a son who became which emperor?
questions.f: The story is told in the Kebra Nagast, the book of the glory of kings.

questions.q: In Aztec belief, how many earlier suns, or world ages, came before the present one?
questions.f: The great Sun Stone in Mexico City records each one and how it ended.

questions.q: What did the Aztecs call the layered underworld a soul journeyed through?
questions.f: The journey took four years and included a river crossed with the help of a dog.

questions.q: In Maya myth, what are the names of the Hero Twins?
questions.f: At the end of their story they rise into the sky as the sun and the moon.

questions.q: Which Inca goddess of the moon was said to be the wife of the sun god Inti?
questions.f: Incas believed a lunar eclipse meant an animal was attacking her, so they made noise to help.

questions.q: In Andean belief, who is Pachamama?
questions.f: Offerings to Pachamama are still made in August across Peru and Bolivia.

questions.q: In Anishinaabe stories, which culture hero is known for shaping the land and outwitting others?
questions.f: He often takes the shape of a great rabbit in the tales.

questions.q: Which humpbacked flute player appears in rock art across the American Southwest?
questions.f: Hopi and Zuni traditions link him with fertility, music and travelling traders.

questions.q: In Lakota tradition, who brought the sacred pipe to the people?
questions.f: The birth of a white buffalo calf is still treated as a hugely important event.

questions.q: In Irish myth, which goddess of battle appears as a crow?
questions.f: Her name is often translated as phantom queen or great queen.

questions.q: Which Irish god gave his name to the harvest festival of Lughnasadh?
questions.f: Lugh was said to be brilliant at every skill, which is why his name means shining.

questions.q: In Irish myth, which race of gods arrived in Ireland and later became the fairy folk?
questions.f: Defeated in battle, they were said to withdraw into the hills and mounds.

questions.q: In Irish legend, the Children of Lir were turned into which birds?
questions.f: The story gives them 900 years on the lakes and seas of Ireland, still able to sing.

questions.q: Which Arthurian knight accepts a beheading game from a mysterious green stranger?
questions.f: The poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight was written in the late 1300s by an unknown poet.

questions.q: In Arthurian legend, which castle is named as Arthur's birthplace?
questions.f: Real ruins at Tintagel in Cornwall draw thousands of visitors, though they are later than Arthur's supposed date.

questions.q: British legend credits Merlin with moving which stones by magic?
questions.f: Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote that Merlin brought them from Ireland in the 1130s.

questions.q: In Mesopotamian myth, which god defeats the sea goddess Tiamat and makes the world?
questions.f: The story is told in the Enuma Elish, recited each year at Babylon's New Year festival.

questions.q: Which brightly tiled Babylonian gate was decorated with dragons and bulls for a goddess?
questions.f: Its blue glazed bricks were rebuilt in a Berlin museum, and they still glow.

questions.q: The Greek Muses were said to be daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, the goddess of memory.
questions.f: Memory is the perfect mother for poetry in a world where poems were performed, not read.

questions.q: Norse myth says Odin's spear Gungnir never misses its target.
questions.f: Dwarves made it, and oaths sworn on its point were considered unbreakable.

questions.q: Egyptian myth gave the sun god a different name at each stage of the day.
questions.f: Khepri at dawn, Ra at noon and Atum at sunset describe one god in three moments.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, Hanuman is described as a son of the wind god Vayu.
questions.f: That parentage explains his ability to leap enormous distances.

questions.q: A bronze man circling an island three times a day, a single vein sealed with a plug, and Medea's cunning point to which guardian?
questions.f: Talos is arguably literature's first robot, built by Hephaestus to patrol Crete.

questions.q: A jealous goddess, a wandering island, and twins born under a palm tree on Delos point to which pair?
questions.f: Delos was said to float until it was anchored to reward it for sheltering their mother.

questions.q: A cave on Crete, a stone swallowed instead of a baby, and a goat nurse called Amaltheia converge on the childhood of which god?
questions.f: Amaltheia's broken horn became the cornucopia, the horn of plenty.

questions.q: A pair of dice-like lots, three brothers, and a helmet that hid its wearer point to which division of the Greek world?
questions.f: Zeus, Poseidon and Hades drew lots, and Hades' helmet came from the Cyclopes.

questions.q: A wedding nobody wanted, a hammer hidden by a giant, and Loki in a bridesmaid's veil converge on which Norse object?
questions.f: Thor's appetite at the feast nearly gave the disguise away before the hammer reappeared.

questions.q: Golden apples, a kidnapping by an eagle-shaped giant, and gods suddenly turning grey converge on which Norse goddess?
questions.f: Without Idunn's apples the gods aged fast, so they made Loki fetch her back.

questions.q: Your breakfast cereal quietly honours which goddess?
questions.f: Ceres was the Roman goddess of grain, and her name still sits in your breakfast bowl.

questions.q: If something is described as 'martial', it relates to what?
questions.f: From Mars, the Roman war god, who also lent his name to March, the campaigning season.

questions.q: The 'aurora' in aurora borealis is the name of the Roman goddess of what?
questions.f: Borealis comes from Boreas, the Greek north wind, so the phrase means northern dawn.

questions.q: The word 'music' traces back to which group of Greek beings?
questions.f: Mousike meant the art of the Muses, which covered poetry and dance as well as tunes.

questions.q: The name of the monster called a 'harpy' comes from a Greek verb meaning what?
questions.f: From harpazein, to seize; the harpies were always described as stealing food away.

questions.q: A 'dryad' is a tree nymph, and the 'dry' part of her name means which tree?
questions.f: From Greek drys, oak, which also hides inside the word druid.

questions.q: Which sea creature's adult, bell-shaped stage is scientifically called a 'medusa'?
questions.f: Naturalists thought the trailing tentacles looked like the Gorgon's snaky hair.

questions.q: The snake called a python takes its name from a creature killed by which god?
questions.f: Apollo defeated the serpent Python at Delphi and took over its oracle.

questions.q: The 'lycanthrope' in werewolf stories combines Greek words meaning what?
questions.f: From lykos, wolf, plus anthropos, human, the same root as in anthropology.

questions.q: The word 'poltergeist' literally means what?
questions.f: From German poltern, to make a racket, plus Geist, ghost.

questions.q: In German folklore, a 'doppelganger' is literally a what?
questions.f: German folklore treated meeting your own double as a very bad sign indeed.

questions.q: The word 'kamikaze' means divine what?
questions.f: It first named the storms that wrecked Mongol invasion fleets heading for Japan in 1274 and 1281.

questions.q: The English word 'taboo' came from a Pacific word meaning what?
questions.f: Captain Cook recorded tapu in Tonga in 1777, and English adopted it almost at once.

questions.q: The word 'hurricane' comes from the name of a storm god worshipped where?
questions.f: Taino and Maya traditions both name a storm power close to Huracan.

questions.q: The word 'totem' entered English from an Ojibwe word describing what?
questions.f: Doodem referred to one's clan, so a totem is really a family badge.

questions.q: Norse warriors called berserkers got their name from words probably meaning what?
questions.f: Whether it was bear-shirt or bare-shirt is still argued, but the bear reading is favoured.

questions.q: The word 'valkyrie' means chooser of the what?
questions.f: Valr means the fallen in battle, and it appears again in Valhalla, their hall.

questions.q: The Norse word 'rune' originally meant what?
questions.f: That older sense survives in words like rune-craft and in the German raunen, to whisper.

questions.q: The 'mare' in 'nightmare' originally meant what?
c: A crushing spirit that sat on sleepers
questions.f: Old folk belief blamed the feeling of a weight on the chest on that mare.

questions.q: The word 'fairy' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: From fata, the Fates, so fairies began as beings who decided destinies.

questions.q: In Roman belief, what was a 'genius' before the word meant a clever person?
c: A guardian spirit that accompanied a person
questions.f: Romans celebrated a birthday by honouring the person's genius with wine and cake.

questions.q: In Sanskrit, what does 'avatar' describe?
questions.f: A god descending into the world became, much later, your descended image on a screen.

questions.q: 'Guru' began life as a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: A teacher is weighty with knowledge, which is a rather beautiful image.

questions.q: Take 'mantra' apart and its two pieces mean what?
questions.f: So a mantra is literally a tool for the mind.

questions.q: 'Yoga' shares an ancient root with the English word yoke. What does that root mean?
questions.f: That root is a distant cousin of the English word yoke itself.

questions.q: The name 'Himalaya' is built from Sanskrit words meaning what?
questions.f: Hima is snow, related to the Latin hiems, winter; alaya means dwelling.

questions.q: The title 'Mahabharata' means the great story of whom?
questions.f: Maha means great, and India's official name Bharat comes from the same ancestor figure.

questions.q: The word 'hieroglyph' is built from Greek words meaning what?
questions.f: Greeks saw the signs on temple walls and assumed they must all be holy.

questions.q: The word 'pharaoh' comes from an Egyptian phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Per-aa first described the palace, then came to mean the person inside it.

questions.q: A grand tomb is called a 'mausoleum' after a ruler buried where?
questions.f: The tomb of Mausolus was so splendid it became one of the seven wonders.

questions.q: Before it meant a long race, 'marathon' was the name of what?
questions.f: Legend says a messenger ran from Marathon to Athens with news of the victory in 490 BC.

questions.q: In ancient Greece, what exactly was an 'Olympiad'?
questions.f: Greeks dated events by counting Olympiads, using the games as a shared calendar.

questions.q: We call a trusted adviser a 'mentor' because of a character in which story?
questions.f: Athena disguised herself as Mentor to guide Odysseus's son, so the adviser was a goddess.

questions.q: A task described as 'Sisyphean' is what?
c: Endless and repeated with no progress
questions.f: Any job that undoes itself the moment you finish qualifies.

questions.q: To 'cut the Gordian knot' means to do what?
c: Solve a tangled problem with one bold stroke
questions.f: Alexander the Great is said to have sliced the famous knot rather than pick at it.

questions.q: If a room is described as 'spartan', what is it like?
questions.f: Sparta's reputation for tough simple living turned its name into an adjective.

questions.q: The name 'basilisk' means what?
questions.f: From Greek basileus, king; a crest on its head was described as a crown.

questions.q: The word 'leviathan' is used today to mean what?
questions.f: It began as the name of a huge sea creature in Hebrew scripture.

questions.q: Which word, from the same tradition as leviathan, names a gigantic land beast?
questions.f: Behemoth is now used for anything vast, from a lorry to a company.

questions.q: Which element is named after the Titans of Greek myth?
questions.f: Its discoverer named it for the Titans because of its enormous strength.

questions.q: Which element is named after the planet Uranus, itself named for a Greek sky god?
questions.f: Uranium was found in 1789, just eight years after the planet was discovered.

questions.q: Which element takes its name from the Greek sun god?
questions.f: Helium was spotted in sunlight before anyone found it on Earth, so Helios was perfect.

questions.q: Which liquid metal shares its name with a swift Roman messenger god?
questions.f: Alchemists linked the quick-moving metal to the quick-moving god and the planet alike.

questions.q: 'Galaxy' translates out of Greek as what?
questions.f: Greek myth said the Milky Way was a splash of spilled milk across the sky.

questions.q: Hidden inside 'arctic' is the Greek word for which animal?
questions.f: Arktos means bear, and the Great Bear constellation wheels above the north pole.

questions.q: The Greek word 'psyche' meant both soul and which creature?
questions.f: Greek artists drew the soul as a butterfly leaving the body, and Psyche is shown with wings.

questions.q: Which flower's name comes from a Greek youth loved by Apollo?
questions.f: Myth says the flower sprang up where the youth fell during a discus game.

questions.q: The fruit called a nectarine is named after what?
c: Nectar, the drink of the gods
questions.f: It simply means sweet as nectar, and it is a smooth-skinned peach.

questions.q: Hermes' winged sandals have their own name in Greek. What is it?
questions.f: His winged hat was the petasos and his snake staff the kerykeion, or caduceus.

questions.q: Which staff, wrongly used as a medical symbol, actually belongs to Hermes and has two snakes?
questions.f: Hermes guided souls and guarded traders, so his staff really means messages and trade.

questions.q: The word 'bard', 'druid' and 'ovate' all name ranks in which tradition?
questions.f: Roman writers described these three grades among the Celts of Gaul and Britain.

questions.q: The Japanese word 'kami' is best translated as what?
questions.f: Shinto counts eight million kami, a poetic way of saying countless.

questions.q: Vampire bats got their name in which order of events?
c: The legend came first, then the bats were named
questions.f: European vampire tales were famous by the 1730s; naturalists named the bats afterwards.

questions.q: What does the word 'kraken' come from in Norwegian?
questions.f: Krake also means a sickly animal, which suits a beast said to be all tentacles.

questions.q: Which Greek word gives us both 'chthonic' and the idea of underground gods?
questions.f: Chthonic gods like Hades were worshipped with offerings poured into pits, not on high altars.

questions.q: The word 'titan' is used today for what kind of person?
c: Someone hugely powerful in their field
questions.f: We speak of a titan of industry, quietly recalling gods who ruled before Zeus.

questions.q: What does the Greek word 'daimon' originally mean, before it became demon?
questions.f: Socrates said his daimon warned him when he was about to do something foolish.

questions.q: What does the word 'epic simile' describe in Homer?
c: A long comparison spun out over several lines
questions.f: Homer compares warriors to lions, waves and wildfire, sometimes for six lines at a time.

questions.q: In myth studies, what is a 'monomyth'?
c: The single shared pattern behind many hero stories
questions.f: Joseph Campbell popularised the idea in 1949, and film-makers have used it ever since.

questions.q: What does the word 'pantheon' mean when a writer speaks of the Egyptian pantheon?
c: All its gods as a group
questions.f: Egypt's pantheon numbered well over 1,500 named gods across three thousand years.

questions.q: What is a 'psychopomp' in the study of religion?
c: A guide who leads souls onward
questions.f: Hermes, Anubis and the Valkyries all do this job in their own traditions.

questions.q: What does 'apotheosis' mean?
c: Being raised to the rank of a god
questions.f: Roman emperors were sometimes voted an apotheosis by the senate after death.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'sword of Damocles' describe?
c: A constant danger hanging over someone
A gift with a hidden cost
questions.f: The story has a king hang a sword by a single hair above a courtier's dinner seat.

questions.q: In Greek thought, what was 'hubris'?
questions.f: Bellerophon trying to fly Pegasus up to Olympus is the classic example.

questions.q: What is a 'grimoire'?
c: A book of spells and magical instructions
questions.f: The word is related to grammar, since both once meant obscure book-learning.

questions.q: The word 'phoenix' was used by Greek writers before the Roman period.
questions.f: Herodotus described the bird in the 400s BC, saying Egyptian priests had told him about it.

questions.q: Several chemical elements are named after figures from Norse myth.
questions.f: Thorium honours Thor and vanadium honours Vanadis, another name for Freyja.

questions.q: The words 'jovial' and 'Jupiter' are related.
questions.f: Astrologers said people born under Jupiter were cheerful, so jovial came to mean merry.

questions.q: The English word 'panic' and the word 'pandemonium' come from the same root.
questions.f: Panic is from the god Pan, while pandemonium was coined by Milton from pan, all, plus demon.

questions.q: A stolen mirror, a cave, and a dance that made the gods roar with laughter converge on the return of which deity?
questions.f: The mirror used to lure her out is echoed by the mirror kept at Ise Shrine today.

questions.q: A woven contest, a torn tapestry, and a body shrinking as fingers turn to legs point to which figure?
questions.f: Zoologists later named the spider class Arachnida after her.

questions.q: A poisoned churning, a throat held tight, and the name blue-throated converge on which god?
questions.f: Shiva swallowed the halahala poison and held it in his throat, which turned blue.

questions.q: A wooden bridge of magpies, a cowherd and a weaving girl, and a festival on the seventh night of the seventh month point to which star pair?
questions.f: The Milky Way is the river that keeps the two stars apart the rest of the year.

questions.q: A mill grinding out salt at the bottom of the sea, a stolen treasure, and a national epic collected from village singers point to which object?
questions.f: Finns say the sea is salty because the broken Sampo keeps grinding down there.

questions.q: A plant of youth lost to a snake, a mourned friend, and a boatman named Utnapishtim converge on which king?
questions.f: His story survives on twelve clay tablets, and new fragments still turn up today.

questions.q: A hundred unblinking eyes, a lullaby played on a reed pipe, and the pattern of a peacock's tail converge on which watchman?
questions.f: Hera set his eyes into the peacock's feathers after Hermes sang every one of them to sleep.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which goddess of the night was so ancient that even Zeus was careful with her?
questions.f: Homer says Zeus once held back because he feared to upset Nyx.

questions.q: Which Greek goddess was born fully grown from the head of Zeus?
questions.f: Hephaestus is credited with opening the way, and Athena stepped out already armoured.

questions.q: Which Titan of light was the father of the sun, the moon and the dawn?
questions.f: His name means the one who goes above, which suits a family of sky-travellers.

questions.q: Which Greek goddess of justice is the ancestor of the blindfolded figure with scales?
questions.f: Themis carried scales, and her daughter Dike stood for justice in action.

questions.q: Which Greek sea god had to be held tight while he changed shape, to make him answer questions?
questions.f: That is why anything endlessly adaptable is called protean.

questions.q: Which Greek sea god blows a conch shell to raise or calm the waves?
questions.f: A statue of Triton with his shell stands in Rome's Piazza Barberini, still spouting water.

questions.q: On whose island was Odysseus kept for seven years before the gods ordered his release?
questions.f: Calypso offered him immortality and he still chose to sail home.

questions.q: Who recognised Odysseus first when he returned home in disguise after twenty years?
questions.f: The dog Argos wagged his tail and could not get up; Homer makes it one of the saddest scenes in the poem.

questions.q: What test did Penelope set to choose a husband in the Odyssey?
questions.f: None of the suitors could even bend it, and the disguised beggar strung it easily.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which cupbearer of the gods was the goddess of youth?
questions.f: She poured nectar until Ganymede took over the job.

questions.q: In Norse myth, which golden ring of Odin's drips eight new rings every ninth night?
questions.f: Its name means the dripper, and dwarves made it alongside Thor's hammer.

questions.q: Which famous necklace belongs to the Norse goddess Freyja?
questions.f: Loki once stole it, and Heimdall had to wrestle him in the shape of a seal to get it back.

questions.q: Which Norse god is the poet of Asgard, whose name is linked to poetry itself?
questions.f: Norse poets swore oaths over a cup called the bragarfull, the cup of Bragi.

questions.q: How many roots does the Norse world tree have, according to the Prose Edda?
questions.f: One reaches the gods, one the frost giants and one the misty world of the dead.

questions.q: In Norse cosmology, which world is home to the light elves?
questions.f: The dwarves' world, Nidavellir, means dark fields, forming a neat pair with Alfheim.

questions.q: Which four Egyptian gods, the Sons of Horus, protected a mummy's organs?
questions.f: Their heads appear on the four canopic jars: human, baboon, jackal and falcon.

questions.q: Which Egyptian god was worshipped as a sun disc with rays ending in tiny hands?
questions.f: Pharaoh Akhenaten made Aten the chief god for a short, dramatic time around 1350 BC.

questions.q: In Egyptian myth, Shu is the god of air and Tefnut is the goddess of what?
questions.f: They were the first pair created by Atum, so air and water came before everything else.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, who won the race around the world by circling his own parents?
questions.f: He argued that his parents were his whole world, and the mango prize was his.

questions.q: What is the name of Shiva's famous dancing form, shown inside a ring of fire?
questions.f: Nataraja means lord of the dance, and the ring of fire stands for the whole universe.

questions.q: Which avatar of Vishnu appears as a small brahmin who asks for three steps of land?
questions.f: Two steps covered the whole world, which made the third step rather awkward for the king.

questions.q: Which avatar of Vishnu is still expected, riding a white horse?
questions.f: Kalki is described as the tenth and final avatar, arriving at the end of the age.

questions.q: In Hindu myth, on which serpent does Vishnu rest between world ages?
questions.f: Shesha has many hoods, and the name means the remainder, what is left when all else ends.

questions.q: In Hindu tradition, who is the divine architect and craftsman of the gods?
questions.f: Builders and engineers in India still mark Vishwakarma Puja by honouring their tools.

questions.q: In Chinese myth, which mountain range is described as the home of gods and immortals?
questions.f: The Queen Mother of the West is said to keep her peach garden there.

questions.q: In Chinese legend, Penglai is an island where what can be found?
questions.f: Emperors sent real expeditions east to look for Penglai, and none came back with the elixir.

questions.q: In Japanese myth, which goddess danced to lure Amaterasu out of the cave?
questions.f: She is honoured as the goddess of joy and of the performing arts.

questions.q: In Japanese myth, who is the moon god and brother of the sun goddess?
questions.f: His name comes from words meaning moon counter, since the moon marked the months.

questions.q: In a well-known Japanese folk tale, a rescued crane repays kindness by doing what?
questions.f: The tale is called Tsuru no Ongaeshi, the crane's return of a favour.

questions.q: In Yoruba belief, Oya is the powerful goddess of what?
questions.f: She is linked with the Niger River and with sudden, sweeping change.

questions.q: In an Anansi story, what happens when he tries to keep all the wisdom in one pot?
c: The pot breaks and wisdom spreads to everyone
He hides it in a tree forever
He forgets where he put it
questions.f: That is the storytellers' way of explaining why everybody has a little wisdom.

questions.q: In stories of the Wabanaki peoples, which culture hero shapes the land and outwits giants?
questions.f: Glooscap tales are told across the Maritimes and Maine, often explaining local landmarks.

questions.q: Which Welsh collection of medieval tales includes Pwyll, Branwen and Rhiannon?
questions.f: Rhiannon rides a white horse that nobody can catch, however fast they gallop.

questions.q: Which Irish epic tells of a great cattle raid and a magical brown bull?
questions.f: The full title is Tain Bo Cuailnge, and Cu Chulainn defends Ulster almost single-handed.

questions.q: In Irish myth, the Dagda owns a cauldron that does what?
questions.f: He also owns a harp that plays the seasons and a club that can undo its own damage.

questions.q: In European folklore, what is the Wild Hunt?
c: A ghostly troop of riders across the winter sky
A hunt for a golden stag
questions.f: Leaders named for the hunt include Odin, King Arthur and Herne the Hunter.

questions.q: Which German nobleman's name became a byword for wildly exaggerated tall tales?
questions.f: The real baron did tell traveller's tales, and a writer turned them into famous fiction in 1785.

questions.q: Greek myth says Athena and Poseidon competed to become the patron god of Athens.
questions.f: Poseidon offered a saltwater spring and a horse, but the olive tree won the vote.

questions.q: In Norse myth, Hel's realm is guarded by a dog named Garm.
questions.f: Garm is chained by a cave called Gnipahellir, howling until the world's last day.

questions.q: In Hindu tradition, apsaras are heavenly dancers described in the epics.
questions.f: Carvings of apsaras cover the walls of Angkor Wat in Cambodia by the thousand.

questions.q: The Roman god Janus gave his name to a month and to a kind of two-faced door god.
questions.f: His temple doors in Rome were kept open in wartime and shut in peace, which was rare.

questions.q: A woman weeping for her children turned to stone, a mountain in Turkey that seems to trickle water, and a bragging contest with a goddess point to whom?
questions.f: Mount Sipylus has a weathered rock face that locals still call the weeping Niobe.

questions.q: A crab sent to help a monster, a hero counting heads, and a summer constellation converge on which labour?
questions.f: Hera rewarded the crab by placing it in the sky as Cancer.

questions.q: A ribbon of nine impossible ingredients, a lake island, and a god who kept his word converge on which chained creature?
questions.f: Gleipnir looked like a silk ribbon, which is exactly why the wolf agreed to be tested by it.

questions.q: A god of writing, a set of scales, and a feather light enough to balance a life converge on which Egyptian scene?
questions.f: Thoth wrote down the result while Anubis worked the scales.

questions.q: The name 'Heracles' is usually explained as meaning what?
questions.f: Odd, since Hera spent the myths making his life difficult.

questions.q: To a Greek astronomer, a 'planet' was literally what?
questions.f: Planets wander against the fixed stars, and each got a god's name.

questions.q: Split 'disaster' into its old parts and you find what?
questions.f: It comes from the belief that a badly placed star could ruin your plans.

questions.q: Why does 'lunatic' contain the Latin word for moon?
c: People once blamed the moon for changing moods
It meant pale as the moon
questions.f: Luna was the Roman moon goddess, and the old belief lingers in the word to this day.

questions.q: Which month is named after the Roman queen of the gods?
questions.f: Juno protected marriage, which is one reason June weddings became popular.

questions.q: Tuesday is named after which Norse god?
questions.f: Old English Tiwesdaeg matched the Roman day of Mars, since both were war gods.

questions.q: Friday takes its name from which Norse goddess?
questions.f: It replaced the Roman day of Venus, matching a goddess of love with a goddess of marriage.

questions.q: Sunday and Monday are named after what?
c: A god and a goddess of light
questions.f: Both translate Latin names, dies Solis and dies Lunae, straight into English.

questions.q: Which spring flower is named after a Greek youth who gazed into a pool?
questions.f: Daffodils belong to the genus Narcissus, so the myth is in every florist's shop.

questions.q: What does the word 'necromancy' mean?
questions.f: From nekros, dead, plus manteia, prophecy; Odysseus performs one in the Odyssey.

questions.q: What does the word 'oracular' mean?
questions.f: Oracles were famously vague, which meant they were never quite wrong.

questions.q: What does the Greek suffix in 'theogony' mean?
questions.f: Hesiod's Theogony is literally the birth of the gods, from gonos, offspring.

questions.q: A vat named Odrerir, a giantess guarding a hollowed mountain, and Odin's escape in eagle shape converge on which Norse prize?
questions.f: Skalds called their own verses Odin's booty, because poetry was literally stolen goods.

questions.q: 540 doors wide enough for 800 to march through, a goat whose milk runs as mead, and a roof of golden shields describe which hall?
questions.f: The goat Heidrun stands on the roof, browsing the leaves of a tree above it.

questions.q: A hull built from untrimmed nails of the dead, a launch on a flooded shore, and a giant at the tiller point to which vessel?
questions.f: Norse people trimmed the nails of the dead carefully, to delay the ship's completion.

questions.q: Two pieces of driftwood, three gods handing out breath, wits and warmth, and the names Ask and Embla open which story?
c: The making of the first humans in Norse myth
questions.f: Ask means ash tree, and Embla is usually read as elm, so people began as trees.

questions.q: A blue glass pigment, ore that yielded no copper, and miners blaming a mischievous mine spirit point to which element?
questions.f: German miners blamed the kobold, and the sprite's name is now stamped on the periodic table.

questions.q: An ore nicknamed after a devil, a coin worth five cents, and Swedish chemistry of the 1750s point to which metal?
questions.f: Kupfernickel meant Old Nick's copper, a miner's grumble at ore that gave no copper at all.

questions.q: A figure punished with food forever out of reach, a metal that shrugs off almost every acid, and element 41 named for his daughter point to which element?
questions.f: Tantalum resists acids the way Tantalus could never reach the fruit, and niobium honours Niobe.

questions.q: A moon goddess, the light-sensitive drums of early photocopiers, and a neighbour element named for the earth point to which element?
questions.f: Berzelius named selenium after Selene because it turned up beside tellurium, named for the earth.

questions.q: An asteroid found in 1802, another name for Athena, and the metal inside catalytic converters converge on which element?
questions.f: Wollaston named it in 1803 after the newly discovered asteroid Pallas.

questions.q: An asteroid spotted on New Year's Day 1801, a Roman grain goddess, and the sparking flint in a lighter point to which element?
questions.f: Lighter flints are ferrocerium, so a grain goddess lights your candles.

questions.q: A second name for the Norse goddess Freyja, tough spanner steel, and a Swedish discovery of 1830 point to which element?
questions.f: Vanadis was Freyja's byname, and vanadium salts glow in a whole rainbow of colours.

questions.q: The rainbow goddess, salts of many colours, and one of the densest metals known converge on which element?
questions.f: A thin worldwide layer of iridium in the rocks helped prove a huge asteroid struck Earth.

questions.q: Twin-bladed symbols carved all over the ruins at Knossos, a Cretan word borrowed by Greek speakers, and the name 'labyrinth' converge on which object?
questions.f: Labrys was the name of that axe, so the maze may have begun as simply the place of the axe.

questions.q: A spring that opened on Mount Helicon, poets who swore a drink from it brought inspiration, and a winged horse's name converge on which meaning?
questions.f: It fits neatly, since his hoof was said to open the Hippocrene spring.

questions.q: A monster who let nobody pass without an answer, an Egyptian phrase meaning living image, and a Greek verb converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Greeks may have named her for the tight grip of a question you cannot escape.

questions.q: A Lycian mountainside whose natural flames still burn, an ordinary Greek farm word, and a monster stitched from three creatures converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Turkey's Yanartas has burned for thousands of years and was tied to the monster's story.

questions.q: A Greek adjective used of terrifying storms and war cries, three sisters known together by it, and an English word for a fearsome stare converge on which meaning?
questions.f: So the three sisters were, quite simply, the Grim Ones.

questions.q: A tree still placed in the genus Phoenix, a Greek word for deep purple-red, and a bird Herodotus was told about in Egypt converge on which plant?
questions.f: One word covered palm, purple and bird alike, which is why translators still argue over it.

questions.q: Hook-beaked beasts in Scythian goldwork, a Greek word used for anything curved, and a lion-bodied guardian converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Gryps described the fierce curved beak, which is the creature's most striking feature.

questions.q: Law tablets set up in Athens around 621 BC, a name that only sounds reptilian, and a modern term for harsh rules converge on whom?
questions.f: Draco's laws of about 621 BC were famously harsh, and dragons have nothing to do with it.

questions.q: A roadside host on the road to Athens, a bed that every single guest fitted, and a name describing exactly what he did converge on which meaning?
questions.f: He forced guests to fit his bed exactly, which is why the word means brutally forced to fit.

questions.q: 'Halcyon days' originally described what?
c: Calm winter days when a kingfisher nested at sea
questions.f: Alcyone became a kingfisher, and the winds were said to drop so she could brood.

questions.q: Water that emptied a soul's memory, a medical word for heavy drowsiness, and a name meaning forgetting converge on which stream?
questions.f: Lethe means forgetfulness, and its water erased memories in a single sip.

questions.q: 'Stygian' darkness takes its name from a river whose name means what?
questions.f: Even the gods swore their most binding oaths by the Styx.

questions.q: The verb 'to tantalize' comes from a figure punished how?
c: With water and fruit that drew away
questions.f: Tantalus was the father of Niobe, and both gave their names to elements.

questions.q: The mother of the nine Muses, memory palaces drilled into Roman speakers, and a trick for remembering a list converge on whose name?
questions.f: Memory was the mother of the Muses, which is a poet's idea of how art works.

questions.q: The Greek name for Ursa Minor, the tail-tip star sailors steered by, and a phrase for whatever everyone is watching converge on which literal meaning?
questions.f: It was the Greek name for Ursa Minor, whose tail-tip star is Polaris.

questions.q: A Flemish chemist hunting a name for airy matter, Hesiod's yawning emptiness, and the label on your cooker converge on which borrowed word?
questions.f: The chemist Van Helmont borrowed the Greek word for the primordial void.

questions.q: The word 'pandemonium' was invented by John Milton as the name of what?
c: A palace of all the demons
questions.f: Only later did it come to mean any wild uproar.

questions.q: A drink that kept Olympians from dying, a root that also hides inside the word for death, and the sweet liquid bees gather converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Nek relates to death and tar to overcoming, so nectar defeats dying.

questions.q: Enormous public feasts described by Homer, a Greek number word, and a count of oxen converge on which literal meaning?
questions.f: Homer uses the word for enormous public feasts of offering.

questions.q: Two eagles released to find the world's middle, a carved stone kept beside Apollo's shrine, and a Greek word for the body's centre converge on what that stone marked?
questions.f: Omphalos means navel, and Zeus was said to have marked the spot with eagles.

questions.q: Officials who studied the sky before any public business, a Latin pairing of bird with looking, and a word for a promising start converge on which practice?
questions.f: An auspex was a bird-watcher, from avis, bird, plus specere, to look.

questions.q: A forge imagined beneath Mount Etna, a sulphur-and-heat process patented in 1844, and the rubber in your tyres converge on which god's name?
questions.f: Charles Goodyear's heat-and-sulphur process was named for the god of the forge in 1844.

questions.q: Airtight glassware in alchemists' workshops, an Egyptian sage merged with a Greek god, and a jar label promising a perfect seal converge on which figure?
c: Hermes, in his form as a master of secrets
questions.f: Alchemists honoured Hermes Trismegistus, and airtight sealing was one of their arts.

questions.q: A limestone quarried at Assos and said to consume whatever it held, a Greek pairing of flesh with eating, and a stone coffin in a museum converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Pliny the Elder passed on the stone's alarming reputation, and the name stuck to coffins everywhere.

questions.q: A pointed item on a Greek baker's list, a borrowed word applied to Egypt's tombs, and monuments their builders actually called mer converge on what pyramis first named?
questions.f: It seems the Greeks named Egypt's tombs after a pointed cake from their own bakeries.

questions.q: Mountain pitch sold by apothecaries as medicine, a Persian word for wax, and wrapped bodies shipped to Europe converge on which substance?
questions.f: Mumiya described dark pitch, and Europeans thought Egyptian bodies were preserved with it.

questions.q: A headdress drawn as a seat, a name written with that very sign, and a goddess whose Greek spelling we still use converge on which meaning?
questions.f: That is why her headdress is drawn as a throne, spelling her name in a picture.

questions.q: A first mound said to rise from the waters at Heliopolis, a sacred stone kept in a temple court, and a shape repeated at the very top of Egyptian stonework point to what the benben shaped?
c: The tips of obelisks and pyramids
questions.f: Priests at Heliopolis said the benben was the first mound to rise from the waters.

questions.q: A yearly festival at Puri, chariots so vast that crowds are needed to haul them, and an English word for an unstoppable lorry converge on which deity?
questions.f: European travellers saw the huge festival chariots and turned the god's name into a word for unstoppable force.

questions.q: A lamp going out rather than a place arrived at, a Sanskrit verb for blowing, and a word borrowed by a famous rock band converge on which literal sense?
c: Blowing out, as of a flame
questions.f: The image is a lamp going out quietly, not a place you travel to.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word 'amrita' breaks down into parts meaning what?
questions.f: The same root sits inside the Latin mors and the English mortal.

questions.q: Grammar codified by Panini, sister tongues labelled Prakrit or natural, and a name deliberately set against them converge on which meaning?
