questions.f: Its everyday cousin languages were called Prakrit, meaning natural or ordinary.

questions.q: A word coined to mark off older island customs from newly arrived Buddhism, a phrase joining gods to a road, and the name over a shrine gateway converge on which meaning?
questions.f: It was coined to distinguish Japan's older beliefs from newly arrived Buddhism.

questions.q: The Japanese word 'torii', naming a shrine gateway, is usually explained as meaning what?
questions.f: One story says birds were placed on the gate as messengers of the kami.

questions.q: A term anthropologists carried home from Melanesia in 1891, a quality a chief could win or forfeit, and a blue bar that empties when a game character casts a spell converge on which idea?
c: Spiritual power that can be gained or lost
questions.f: Anthropologists borrowed the word, and video games later borrowed it again.

questions.q: Translated, the name 'Quetzalcoatl' means what?
questions.f: The quetzal is a real bird with tail feathers over half a metre long.

questions.q: The Maya name 'Xibalba' means roughly what?
questions.f: Kiche Maya storytellers made it a place of tests rather than punishment.

questions.q: Irish words for woman and for mound, certain families said to have their own attendant spirit, and a name for a wailing warning converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Bean is woman and sidhe is the mound where the fairy folk live.

questions.q: An Irish word pairing small with body, a solitary craftsman among the fairy folk, and a modern parade mascot converge on which original meaning?
questions.f: From lu, small, plus corp, body; the shoemaking came later.

questions.q: Roman writers describing ceremonies in oak groves, a Celtic root joining a tree to knowing, and a grade still awarded at the Welsh eisteddfod converge on which meaning?
questions.f: From roots for oak and knowledge, matching Roman reports of oak-grove rituals.

questions.q: A Celtic year cut into a bright half and a dark half, a feast marking the changeover, and a name joining a season to its close converge on which meaning?
questions.f: It marked the start of the dark half of the Celtic year, around the first of November.

questions.q: Reindeer herders of the Evenki, Russian travellers' reports reaching Europe in the 1600s, and a word now used across the world converge on which original sense?
questions.f: It came from Evenki, spoken across a huge stretch of Siberia.

questions.q: A cheeky Greek spirit called kobalos, German mine sprites blamed for worthless ore, and a Halloween decoration converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Kobalos named a cheeky trickster spirit, and it may also lie behind kobold.

questions.q: Unexplained engine faults in the 1920s, crew slang decades before the word reached the cinema, and a creature invented to take the blame converge on which group?
questions.f: Pilots blamed unexplained faults on gremlins long before the word reached films.

questions.q: A Roman punisher of broken oaths, a name worn down through French fairy tales of the 1690s, and a giant in a children's story converge on which god?
questions.f: Orcus was a punisher of broken oaths in the Roman underworld.

questions.q: A physician who renamed diseases and gave each element its own spirit, four coinages fantasy writers still use, and a garden statue in a red hat converge on whom?
questions.f: His four elementals were gnome for earth, undine for water, sylph for air and salamander for fire.

questions.q: 'Wyvern' grew out of an older word for which animal?
questions.f: That is why heraldry gives a wyvern two legs and a snaky tail.

questions.q: Persian words joining man to eating, Greek writers copying a traveller's report, and a page in a medieval bestiary converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Greek writers borrowed the Persian description and passed it into every bestiary.

questions.q: A Persian poem of 1177 in which birds set out to find their king, a pun counting the searchers, and a giant bird who raised a foundling converge on which phrase?
questions.f: In Attar's poem thirty birds seek the Simurgh and discover they are it.

questions.q: Beings said to share the world unseen, a word Europeans respelled as genie, and an Arabic root converge on which meaning?
questions.f: So jinn are the hidden ones, which explains why they are so rarely seen.

questions.q: Desert tales of travellers lured off the road, an Arabic verb, and a modern word for someone drawn to grim scenes converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Old tales placed ghouls in the desert, waylaying travellers who left the road.

questions.q: A single puzzling word in the Book of Psalms, Prague legends of a clay servant, and a modern term for a mindless helper converge on which meaning?
questions.f: It appears once in the Book of Psalms, meaning something unformed.

questions.q: Three sisters who measured out every life, Shakespeare's trio on a blasted heath, and an Old English noun behind a very common adjective converge on which meaning?
questions.f: Shakespeare's weird sisters are really the Fates, not merely odd women.

questions.q: Who is credited in Greek myth with building the wooden horse?
questions.f: Odysseus had the idea, but Epeius the carpenter did the work, and he hid inside it too.

questions.q: Which Trojan priest warned his city not to trust the Greeks' parting gift?
questions.f: A marble group of Laocoon, found in Rome in 1506, astonished Renaissance artists.

questions.q: Which small statue of Athena was believed to keep Troy safe while it remained inside?
questions.f: Romans later claimed the Palladium had been carried to Italy and kept in Vesta's temple.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which three judges decided a soul's fate in the underworld?
questions.f: Two of the three had been kings of Crete before taking the job.

questions.q: What endless task were the Danaids given in the Greek underworld?
questions.f: Artists loved the image of women carrying water in vessels full of holes.

questions.q: What did the Argonauts release to test the Clashing Rocks before rowing through?
questions.f: The bird lost only its tail feathers, and the Argo lost only its stern ornament.

questions.q: A blind seer given inner sight, a warning not to touch a sun god's cattle, and counsel offered in the land of the dead point to whom?
questions.f: Greek writers said he had lived as both a man and a woman, so he knew everything twice over.

questions.q: A bowl of warm water, an old scar above the knee, and a nurse who nearly gave the game away point to which servant?
questions.f: She had raised Odysseus, and she knew that scar from a boyhood boar hunt.

questions.q: A princess washing linen at a river, a stranger asleep under olive branches, and ships that steer themselves point to which people?
questions.f: Their king gave Odysseus the ride home he had spent ten years failing to earn.

questions.q: A boar sent by an angry goddess, a huntress praised for the first strike, and a log kept safe in a chest point to whose story?
questions.f: The Fates had said he would live as long as the log stayed unburned.

questions.q: Walls that built themselves, a lyre with strings given by Hermes, and the seven gates of Thebes point to which musician?
questions.f: The stones were said to rise and settle into place in time with his playing.

questions.q: A king who trapped Death in a sack, an unfinished funeral used as an excuse, and a return trip from the underworld point to whom?
questions.f: Nobody in the world could die while Death was tied up, which annoyed the gods immensely.

questions.q: A guest who broke every rule of hospitality, a cloud shaped like a goddess, and a wheel that never stops turning point to whom?
questions.f: His punishment gave poets an image of guilt that spins on forever.

questions.q: A wooden chest set adrift, a shower of gold, and a grandfather frightened by a prophecy point to which mother?
questions.f: The chest washed up on Seriphos, where a fisherman took in mother and baby.

questions.q: A queen's boast about her own beauty, a sea monster sent in reply, and a W of five bright stars point to whom?
questions.f: Her constellation circles the pole upside down for half the night, which Greeks read as a rebuke.

questions.q: A crown set among the stars, a wedding on Naxos, and a bride left behind by a departing ship point to whom?
questions.f: Corona Borealis, the northern crown, is said to be her wedding diadem.

questions.q: A mother who asked to see a god's true glory, a baby carried to term by Zeus himself, and the title twice-born point to which deity?
questions.f: Greeks called him Dithyrambos, the twice-born, and named a kind of song after it.

questions.q: Gold, silver, bronze, a race of heroes and iron are the five stages in which Greek scheme?
questions.f: Hesiod put his own hard times in the age of iron, which suggests he was having a rough century.

questions.q: A torch-lit procession from Athens, a barley drink, and a ceremony no initiate would ever describe point to which rites?
questions.f: They ran for nearly two thousand years, and the secret was kept so well we still do not know it.

questions.q: A prince taught to plough, a chariot drawn by winged serpents, and the gift of grain to humankind point to whom?
questions.f: Demeter chose him as her messenger of farming after her daughter was returned.

questions.q: A cousin who handed out twelve impossible jobs, and who is said to have hidden in a storage jar when the cattle arrived, was who?
questions.f: Greek vase painters loved drawing him peeping out of the jar in terror.

questions.q: A nephew with a burning torch, a crab underfoot, and heads that suddenly stopped growing back point to which helper?
questions.f: Because he had help, Eurystheus refused to count that labour, which seems rather unfair.

questions.q: A water jar, the nymphs of a spring in Mysia, and a hero the Argonauts had to sail away without point to whom?
questions.f: Heracles searched so long for him that the Argo left them both behind.

questions.q: A golden ram, two children fleeing across the water, and a strait later named after the girl who fell point to which pair?
questions.f: That fleece became the Golden Fleece, and the strait became the Hellespont.

questions.q: An African king who fought at Troy, a mother who was the dawn, and two singing statues in Egypt point to whom?
questions.f: Greeks named the Colossi of Memnon after him because one cracked statue moaned at sunrise.

questions.q: A hero abandoned on Lemnos, the bow of Heracles, and a prophecy that Troy could not fall without him point to whom?
questions.f: The Greeks had to sail back and apologise to a man they had left behind for ten years.

questions.q: Nine books offered to a king, leaves scattered before the answer could be read, and a golden bough point to which prophetess?
questions.f: Rome bought only three of her books and kept them for emergencies for centuries.

questions.q: A king who claimed nightly advice from a spring nymph, Rome's earliest calendar reform, and a grove outside the walls point to whom?
questions.f: The nymph Egeria was, in effect, Rome's first constitutional adviser.

questions.q: A Roman goddess of orchards, a suitor who changed shape to reach her, and a pruning knife point to whom?
questions.f: Her name is simply the Latin word for fruit, and pomme in French still carries it.

questions.q: Roman spring games, a goddess of blossom, and the scientific word for a region's plant life point to whom?
questions.f: Her partner in modern science is Faunus, whose name gives us fauna.

questions.q: Rome's third great god beside Jupiter and Mars, and the name given to Romulus after he was made divine, was what?
questions.f: One of Rome's hills, the Quirinal, still carries his name.

questions.q: Underground chapels, a following of Roman soldiers, and a midwinter birthday feast point to which god?
questions.f: Over a hundred mithraea have been dug up, from Syria to the banks of the Thames.

questions.q: A taste of a dragon's heart, the sudden ability to understand birds, and two nuthatches giving a warning point to which hero?
questions.f: The Norse Sigurd is the same figure as the German Siegfried.

questions.q: A ring taken from a dwarf in fish shape, a curse on every later owner, and a hoard sunk in the Rhine point to which ring?
questions.f: Wagner turned this cursed ring into the centre of a sixteen-hour opera cycle.

questions.q: A god who saves leather scraps his whole life, an unusually thick shoe, and one final duty at the world's end point to whom?
questions.f: Norse people were told to throw away leather offcuts so his shoe would be finished in time.

questions.q: A nine-night ride on an eight-legged horse, a leap over the gates of the dead, and a plea for a brother point to whom?
questions.f: Hermod's errand failed on a technicality, because one being refused to weep.

questions.q: Which Norse eagle at the world's edge is said to make the wind with the beating of its wings?
questions.f: Its name means corpse-swallower, which Norse poets seem to have thought was a good title.

questions.q: According to the Poetic Edda, how many mothers does Heimdall have?
questions.f: He is called the son of nine mothers, and nobody has ever fully explained it.

questions.q: In skaldic poetry, what did the kenning 'whale road' mean?
questions.f: Kennings are riddling nicknames: sky candle for the sun, wound sea for a battle.

questions.q: A snake bite, a goddess bargaining for a hidden name, and a cure given only in exchange point to which Egyptian pair?
questions.f: Knowing a god's true name meant sharing that god's power, which is why Ra guarded his.

questions.q: Which Egyptian book divides the sun god's night journey into twelve hours, one per chapter?
questions.f: Amduat means that which is in the underworld, and it decorates royal tomb walls.

questions.q: Which Egyptian ceremony used special tools to touch a mummy's mouth?
questions.f: It was meant to let the dead eat, drink and speak again in the next life.

questions.q: A creator god at Heliopolis plus his descendants, a Greek number word, and a rival group of eight at Hermopolis converge on how many gods the Ennead held?
questions.f: Ennea is Greek for nine; Hermopolis had an Ogdoad instead, a group of eight.

questions.q: A pillar raised upright at festivals, a symbol read as stability, and a link to Osiris point to which Egyptian sign?
questions.f: Raising the djed was performed by the pharaoh himself in a great public ceremony.

questions.q: Small servant figures packed into tombs by the hundred, spells to wake them, and a name meaning answerer point to what?
questions.f: One tomb held 401 of them: one worker for each day of the year plus overseers.

questions.q: A god designed under Egypt's Greek rulers, a great temple at Alexandria, and a blend of Osiris with a sacred bull point to whom?
questions.f: Serapis was meant to give Greeks and Egyptians one god they could share.

questions.q: A Greek god of shadow, a polar expedition ship, and an Antarctic volcano all share which name?
questions.f: James Ross named the smoking mountain after his ship in 1841.

questions.q: Seven sages, a fixed star called Dhruva, and the seven bright stars of the Great Bear point to which Indian group?
questions.f: Indian astronomers matched each sage to one star of the Big Dipper.

questions.q: In the Mahabharata, who learned archery by watching lessons from outside and practising alone?
questions.f: His story is told as a hard lesson about who was allowed to learn in that world.

questions.q: A spiral battle formation, a young warrior who knew how to enter but not how to leave, and a father away fighting point to whom?
questions.f: The chakravyuha is still used as a word for a trap you can walk into but not out of.

questions.q: A vessel that fed any number of guests until its owner had eaten, and a sun god's gift for exile, point to which object?
questions.f: Akshaya means never-ending, and patra means bowl.

questions.q: A sage who watched the world dissolve into ocean, a floating banyan leaf, and a baby holding the universe point to whom?
questions.f: He is described as deathless, which is handy if you want to watch the end of an age.

questions.q: A king left dangling halfway to heaven, a rival heaven built by an angry sage, and a phrase for being stuck in between point to whom?
questions.f: In Indian languages a trishanku situation still means caught between two worlds.

questions.q: A princess who chose a husband fated to die young, a year of vows, and an argument that won him back point to whom?
questions.f: She out-argued Yama himself, using his own rules of fairness against him.

questions.q: An ageing vulture who challenged a flying chariot and lived just long enough to give directions points to whom?
questions.f: His brother Sampati later helped the search party work out where Lanka was.

questions.q: A bear king older than the epic itself, a wrestling match with Krishna, and help at the ocean bridge point to whom?
questions.f: He appears in both the Ramayana and stories of Krishna, which makes him remarkably long-lived.

questions.q: Berries tasted first to check they were sweet, years of waiting in a forest hut, and a lesson about love over ritual point to whom?
questions.f: Rama accepted the half-eaten berries gladly, which is the whole point of the story.

questions.q: A physician rising from the churned ocean with a pot in his hands, and the patron figure of Indian medicine, is who?
questions.f: India marks National Ayurveda Day on the festival day named after him.

questions.q: Four eyes, the tracks of birds and beasts in mud, and the invention of Chinese writing point to whom?
questions.f: Legend says that when he finished, the sky rained millet and ghosts wailed all night.

questions.q: A real monk of the 600s, seventeen years of travel to India, and a novel written 900 years later point to whom?
questions.f: Journey to the West turned his very real expedition into a fantasy with a monkey.

questions.q: A water god who cracked a mountain holding up the sky, a tilted heaven, and rivers all running east point to whom?
questions.f: Chinese storytellers used the tilt to explain why the great rivers flow the way they do.

questions.q: A cup of soup at the last bridge, an old woman at the gate, and rebirth with no memories point to whom?
questions.f: Her soup of forgetting is why, in Chinese belief, nobody arrives remembering the last life.

questions.q: A scholar who failed an examination, a wild-bearded figure painted on New Year doors, and a demon-catcher point to whom?
questions.f: His portrait was hung to guard the household, a job usually given to a fierce general.

questions.q: A third eye in the forehead, a faithful hound, and a rival who could also change into seventy-two shapes point to whom?
questions.f: He is the one god who finally out-changes the Monkey King in Journey to the West.

questions.q: An old man in the moonlight, a ledger of marriages, and a red thread tied between two ankles point to whom?
questions.f: Couples in China and Taiwan still leave offerings at his shrines before a wedding.

questions.q: A princess of blossom, a shrine at the foot of Mount Fuji, and a name meaning the flowers that make trees bloom point to whom?
questions.f: She is honoured as the calmer of Fuji, which is still an active volcano.

questions.q: A Heian court diviner, a five-pointed star still called his seal, and a legend that his mother was a fox point to whom?
questions.f: His shrine in Kyoto still sells charms marked with the Seimei star.

questions.q: A dragon king's palace under the sea, two jewels that raise and lower the tides, and a borrowed rescue point to which Japanese god?
questions.f: The tide jewels appear in tales of empresses and in shrine treasures alike.

questions.q: Which of Japan's Seven Lucky Gods is the only one who began in Japan itself?
questions.f: The other six arrived from Chinese and Indian traditions, which is why Ebisu is special.

questions.q: In Japanese folklore, what is a tsukumogami?
c: An everyday object that comes alive with age
questions.f: Tales set the age of awakening at a hundred years, so old umbrellas are worth watching.

questions.q: Two farmers arguing about a hat, a road between their fields, and a lesson about seeing only one side point to which god?
questions.f: Eshu's hat was red on one side and white on the other, and he walked between them once.

questions.q: In Dogon tradition of Mali, who are the Nommo?
c: Ancestral water spirits who taught humankind
questions.f: Dogon carvings show them with fish-like lower bodies and raised arms.

questions.q: A spider trickster carried across the Atlantic, a name softened to Aunt Nancy, and rabbit tales of the American South point to which figure?
questions.f: Scholars trace the Br'er Rabbit stories partly back to those travelling Anansi tales.

questions.q: A city that prospered thanks to a bargain with a great serpent named Bida points to which African legend?
questions.f: Wagadu is remembered in Soninke tradition as the beginning of the Ghana Empire.

questions.q: A smoking mirror, a jaguar shape, and a rival tricked into leaving the city of Tula point to which god?
questions.f: His name means smoking mirror, and polished obsidian mirrors were used for divination.

questions.q: The best-preserved copies of the Epic of Gilgamesh came from the library of an Assyrian king at Nineveh.
questions.f: Ashurbanipal's tablet collection, dug up in the 1850s, is why we can read the epic at all.

questions.q: The element tellurium is named after a myth figure, while selenium is named after the earth.
questions.f: It is the other way round: selenium honours the moon goddess Selene, tellurium the earth.

questions.q: The Popol Vuh survives because a Spanish friar copied it out in the Kiche language with a translation.
questions.f: Francisco Ximenez made his copy around 1701, and the original manuscript is now lost.

questions.q: The Great Sphinx of Giza has a male royal head, unlike the Greek Sphinx, which was female.
questions.f: Egyptian sphinxes were guardian kings; the Greeks made theirs a winged woman who asked riddles.

questions.q: Rahu and Ketu of Hindu myth correspond to the two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's.
questions.f: Those crossing points are exactly where eclipses can happen, which is why the myth fits so well.

questions.q: In Roman Egypt, Anubis and the Greek Hermes were merged into a single god called Hermanubis.
questions.f: Both were guides of souls, so combining them was an obvious move for their worshippers.

questions.q: Finland's national epic, the Kalevala, was assembled by a doctor who collected songs from villagers.
questions.f: Elias Lonnrot walked thousands of miles gathering verses, publishing the epic in 1835.

questions.q: The Iliad and the Odyssey are written in a mixed poetic dialect that nobody ever spoke day to day.
questions.f: It blends forms from different regions and centuries, a special language built for singing epic.

questions.q: A dog-headed god, a hairless breed still bred in Mexico, and a guide across the last river point to whom?
questions.f: The xoloitzcuintli dog carries his name, and dogs were buried with the dead to guide them.

questions.q: A ceremony held once every fifty-two years, every household fire put out, and a new flame carried from a hilltop point to which people?
questions.f: The New Fire ceremony calmed fears that the sun might not return at the end of a cycle.

questions.q: Walls once sheathed in gold plate, a garden of golden maize, and the exact centre of Cusco point to which building?
questions.f: Its name means golden enclosure, and Inca roads were measured from its walls.

questions.q: A great law binding five nations, a tree of peace, and a poem by Longfellow that borrowed the name for the wrong hero point to whom?
questions.f: The real Hiawatha helped found the Iroquois Confederacy, centuries before the poem.

questions.q: A weaver of the first web, a guide up from the underworld, and a grandmother figure in Hopi and Navajo stories is who?
questions.f: Navajo tradition credits Spider Woman with teaching people to weave on a loom.

questions.q: In Maya myth, which boastful bird-being claimed to be both the sun and the moon?
questions.f: The Hero Twins deal with him early in the Popol Vuh, using a blowpipe and a clever trick.

questions.q: A smith who forges a magic mill, an unwilling marriage bargain, and a rival singer from the north point to which Finnish hero?
questions.f: Ilmarinen also forged the sky itself, according to some Kalevala verses.

questions.q: In the Kalevala, Louhi is the powerful mistress of which land?
questions.f: She is a shape-shifting ruler who sets impossible bride-tasks for visiting heroes.

questions.q: A baby left on a mountain, a giant bird that raises him, and a son who becomes Persia's greatest hero point to whom?
questions.f: The Simurgh gave Zal a feather to burn whenever he needed her help.

questions.q: In Persian legend, what could the Cup of Jamshid show its owner?
questions.f: Persian poets used the cup as an image for the wise heart that sees everything.

questions.q: Five legs when seen from the corner, a human face on a bull's body, and Assyrian palace doorways point to what?
questions.f: Sculptors carved an extra leg so the guardian looked right from the front and the side.

questions.q: In Mesopotamian myth, how many gates did Inanna pass through on her journey below?
questions.f: At each gate she gave up one ornament, so she arrived with nothing at all.

questions.q: In Mesopotamian myth, which storm-bird stole the tablet of destinies?
questions.f: The god Ninurta won it back, and the story was copied out by scribes for centuries.

questions.q: Which Mesopotamian king is described as flying up on the back of an eagle?
questions.f: Cylinder seals show the flight, making it one of the world's oldest pictures of a person airborne.

questions.q: In Geoffrey of Monmouth's history, what name is given to Arthur's sword?
questions.f: French writers turned Caliburn into Excalibur, and the newer name stuck.

questions.q: At the Round Table, what was the Siege Perilous?
c: An empty seat reserved for the Grail knight
questions.f: Siege here is an old word for a seat, not a battle, which confuses many readers.

questions.q: Which English abbey announced in 1191 that it had found the grave of Arthur and Guinevere?
questions.f: The abbey had just suffered a fire and badly needed pilgrims, which historians find suspicious.

questions.q: In Welsh myth, what could the cauldron of Bran the Blessed do?
c: Restore the fallen to life, though silent
Fill with any food wished for
questions.f: Bran's story ends with his own head giving advice for years, which is very Welsh.

questions.q: A woman conjured out of oak, broom and meadowsweet, a betrayal, and a change into an owl point to whom?
questions.f: Her name means flower face, and the owl still carries her name in Welsh.

questions.q: A cauldron brewed for a year and a day, three drops on a boy's thumb, and a chase through shape after shape point to whom?
questions.f: The boy who tasted the drops became Taliesin, the greatest of the Welsh bards.

questions.q: A lost stained-glass window, a town record naming the year 1284, and 130 missing children point to which legend?
questions.f: The rats were added to the story centuries later; the earliest versions have only the children.

questions.q: Which naturalist listed the kraken among real animals in an early edition of his great classification?
questions.f: He quietly dropped it from later editions, which was probably wise.

questions.q: The word 'Bigfoot' was coined in 1958 by whom?
c: A newspaper reporting on found tracks
questions.f: A logging crew's story reached a local paper, and the catchy name spread from there.

questions.q: The Himalayan name behind 'yeti' is usually translated as what?
questions.f: Yeh-teh describes a creature of rocky ground, not a snowman, despite the famous nickname.

questions.q: A ten-foot figure dug up on a New York farm in 1869, tickets sold to see it, and a carver's confession point to which hoax?
questions.f: P. T. Barnum could not buy it, so he made a copy and exhibited that instead.

questions.q: In Slavic folklore, who is the shape-shifting master of the forest who can grow as tall as the trees?
questions.f: Travellers said you could break his spell by wearing your shoes on the wrong feet.

questions.q: A merchant musician, a court beneath a lake, and a gusli played for a water tsar point to which Russian hero?
questions.f: Rimsky-Korsakov turned his tale into an opera full of underwater dances.

questions.q: In Russian folklore, what are Alkonost and Sirin?
c: Birds with women's faces whose songs enchant
questions.f: They are close cousins of the Greek sirens, arriving through Byzantine art.

questions.q: A freshwater serpent-woman of French legend, a promise never to look on Saturdays, and a noble family's claimed ancestor point to whom?
questions.f: The counts of Lusignan proudly claimed descent from her, tail and all.

questions.q: A mountain spirit of the Silesian ranges, a name nobody dared say to his face, and weather that punished rude travellers point to whom?
questions.f: Politeness mattered: call him by his nickname on his own mountain and a storm was said to follow.

questions.q: An Alpine winter figure who inspects children's spinning work, a name meaning the bright one, and a midwinter procession point to whom?
questions.f: Frau Perchta's midwinter parades still take place in Austria and Bavaria today.

questions.q: An Italian gift-bringer who arrives on 6 January carrying a broom points to whom?
questions.f: Her name is worn down from Epifania, the Italian word for Epiphany.

questions.q: In Inuit tradition, one explanation for the northern lights is what?
c: Spirits playing a ball game in the sky
questions.f: Some versions say the players use a walrus skull for a ball, which is wonderfully specific.

questions.q: A goatskin worn over one shoulder in Greek art, a gorgon's head set at its centre, and a modern phrase about working under someone's protection converge on what an aegis first was?
questions.f: Athena's aegis carried a gorgon's head, and it made anyone who saw it think again.

questions.q: A city known by two names, a poem covering only weeks of a ten-year siege, and a title built from a place name converge on what 'Iliad' means?
questions.f: So the Iliad is the Troy poem and the Odyssey is the Odysseus poem, plain and simple.

questions.q: An 'Aeolian harp' plays when what happens?
c: The wind blows across its strings
It is placed near the sea
questions.f: It is named for Aeolus, keeper of the winds, and it needs no player at all.

questions.q: The slowest-moving planet known to the ancients, a cold temperament in old medicine, and an adjective that is the exact opposite of jovial converge on which description?
questions.f: Astrologers blamed slow, cold Saturn; jovial, from Jupiter, is its cheerful opposite.

questions.q: If someone is 'mercurial', what are they like?
questions.f: Both the swift god and the restless metal stand behind the word.

questions.q: A 'stentorian' voice is named after a character in the Iliad who was what?
c: A herald with an enormous voice
questions.f: Homer says Stentor could shout as loudly as fifty other men together.

questions.q: To call a wise old adviser 'a Nestor' recalls a king of where?
questions.f: He was the oldest Greek at Troy and the one everyone asked for advice.

questions.q: Greeks who refused to believe humans built Mycenae's walls, a legendary set of one-eyed smiths, and a term archaeologists still use converge on which kind of building?
questions.f: Greeks found Mycenaean walls so massive they assumed the Cyclopes had built them.

questions.q: An 'Augean task' is one that is what?
questions.f: It recalls the stables that Hercules cleaned by rerouting a river through them.

questions.q: Something described as 'Promethean' involves what?
questions.f: Mary Shelley subtitled Frankenstein The Modern Prometheus for exactly this reason.

questions.q: What did the Greeks mean by 'Hyperborean'?
questions.f: They imagined a happy land past Boreas where the sun shone all summer long.

questions.q: The word 'gargantuan' comes from a giant invented by which writer?
questions.f: Rabelais published his tale of the giant Gargantua in the 1530s.

questions.q: 'Archetype' unpacks into Greek words for what?
questions.f: So an archetype is the original mould from which copies are pressed.

questions.q: The word 'allegory' comes from Greek parts meaning what?
questions.f: An allegory says one thing on the surface and another underneath, on purpose.

questions.q: A German chemist naming a new medicine in 1817, a god whose whole realm was dreams, and a hospital painkiller converge on which substance?
questions.f: Named for Morpheus in 1817 by a German chemist, because of the sleep it brings.

questions.q: A healer god with a family of daughters, one sister whose name became hygiene, and a word for a cure-all converge on whose child?
questions.f: Her sister was Hygieia, and the word hygiene comes from that sister's name.

questions.q: A Titan holding up a weight forever, the bone that lets you nod, and a partner bone that lets you shake your head converge on which vertebra?
questions.f: Below it sits the axis, and together they let you nod and shake your head.

questions.q: Which flowering plant's name comes from the Greek for wind flower?
questions.f: Greeks said the petals opened when the spring wind blew across them.

questions.q: Which garden flower's name honours Paeon, a healer in Greek myth?
questions.f: Peony roots were used as medicine for centuries, which is how the name fits.

questions.q: The name 'Delphinium' and the place name Delphi both connect to which animal?
questions.f: Apollo was worshipped at Delphi under the title Delphinios, the dolphin one.

questions.q: Which reddish laboratory dye is named after the Greek goddess of dawn?
questions.f: Eos gave her name to the pink stain that shows up in almost every biology lab.

questions.q: A plant described as 'heliotropic' does what?
questions.f: Helios plus trope, a turning; Greek myth explained it with the story of Clytie.

questions.q: Which small freshwater animal is named for a myth monster because it regrows lost parts?
questions.f: Cut a hydra in pieces and each piece can grow into a whole animal, just like the myth.

questions.q: In biology, what is a 'chimera'?
c: One organism with cells from two different beginnings
questions.f: Some cats with split-coloured faces are natural chimeras, formed from two merged embryos.

questions.q: Which lizard, able to sprint across water, carries the name of a myth monster?
questions.f: Basiliscus lizards run upright on the surface, which earned them the nickname Jesus lizards.

questions.q: The paper nautilus octopus has the scientific name Argonauta, which recalls what?
questions.f: Nautilus itself simply means sailor, so the name means Argo-sailor.

questions.q: Irrigation canals dug by the Hohokam and long abandoned, a settler's suggestion in 1868, and a bird on the city seal converge on why the name was chosen?
c: A new city was rising from an older one's ruins
It was founded on a burnt plain
questions.f: Canals built by the ancient Hohokam people lay under the new town, so the name fit.

questions.q: Two attendants of the war god in the Iliad, names chosen by Asaph Hall in 1878, and a pair of tiny lumpy satellites converge on which meanings?
questions.f: In the Iliad they are the war god's own attendants, so the moons keep him company.

questions.q: Which planet's moons are named mostly after Shakespeare's characters rather than myth figures?
questions.f: Titania, Oberon, Miranda and Ariel all come from plays, breaking the usual rule.

questions.q: Which country is famous for kangaroos and koalas?
questions.f: Kangaroos live in the wild only in Australia and nearby New Guinea.

questions.q: Which country is the home of the giant panda?
questions.f: Wild giant pandas live in cool bamboo forests in the mountains of central China.

questions.q: Which country is famous for pizza, pasta and gondola boats?
questions.f: Italy has more than 7,000 kilometres of coastline and thousands of pasta shapes.

questions.q: Which country has a red maple leaf on its flag?
questions.f: Canada chose the maple leaf because maple trees grow all across its eastern forests.

questions.q: Which country in the Alps is famous for chocolate and cheese?
questions.f: Swiss makers invented milk chocolate in the 1870s by stirring milk powder into cocoa.

questions.q: Which country is famous for windmills and fields of tulips?
questions.f: Dutch windmills once pumped water off the land so farmers could use it.

questions.q: In which city would you visit Central Park?
questions.f: Central Park is so big that about 40 million people visit it every year.

questions.q: What is the name of the famous giant bell in London's clock tower?
questions.f: Big Ben is the bell inside; the tower itself is called the Elizabeth Tower.

questions.q: What do we call a round model of the Earth that you can spin?
questions.f: The oldest globe still around was made in Germany in 1492 and has no America on it.

questions.q: What do we call the very highest point of a mountain?
questions.f: Climbers often reach a peak early in the morning, before the wind picks up.

questions.q: What do we call a small mountain?
questions.f: In Britain a bump under about 600 metres is usually called a hill, not a mountain.

questions.q: What runs down the side of a volcano when it erupts?
questions.f: Lava can be hotter than 1,000 degrees Celsius - hot enough to glow bright orange.

questions.q: What do we call the bowl-shaped hole at the top of a volcano?
questions.f: Some old craters fill with rain and turn into beautiful round lakes.

questions.q: On most maps, which direction is at the top?
questions.f: Old maps often put east at the top, which is why we say we 'orient' a map.

questions.q: On a compass, which direction is opposite to north?
questions.f: A compass needle is a tiny magnet that lines up with the Earth's own magnetism.

questions.q: What do we call a shelter built from blocks of snow?
questions.f: Snow traps air, so inside an igloo it can be much warmer than the freezing air outside.

questions.q: Which is the biggest bird in Africa, too heavy to fly?
questions.f: An ostrich cannot fly but it can run faster than a racing bicycle.

questions.q: Which big striped cat is the national animal of India?
questions.f: India is home to most of the world's remaining wild tigers.

questions.q: What does a camel store inside its hump?
questions.f: The stored fat gives a camel energy when there is nothing to eat for days.

questions.q: What do we call sandy land beside the sea where people play?
questions.f: Beach sand is made of tiny pieces of rock and shell smashed up by waves.

questions.q: What do we call a big area where many trees grow together?
questions.f: About a third of all the land on Earth is still covered by forest.

questions.q: Which is bigger, a city or a village?
questions.f: Tokyo's wider city area holds more people than the whole of Canada.

questions.q: What do we call a very tall building in a big city?
questions.f: The word skyscraper was first used for tall ships' masts before it meant buildings.

questions.q: What do we call the faraway line where the sky seems to meet the land?
questions.f: Standing on a beach, your horizon is only about five kilometres away.

questions.q: What language do most people speak in France?
questions.f: French is an official language in nearly 30 countries around the world.

questions.q: What language do most people speak in Spain?
questions.f: Spanish is spoken by more people as a first language than English is.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the sport of sumo wrestling?
questions.f: Sumo matches begin with wrestlers tossing salt to make the ring clean and lucky.

questions.q: In which country were Lego bricks invented?
questions.f: The name Lego comes from Danish words meaning 'play well'.

questions.q: What do we call the coloured cloth that stands for a country?
questions.f: Nepal is the only country whose flag is not a rectangle - it has two triangles.

questions.q: What do we call a road that goes through a mountain or under a river?
questions.f: The Channel Tunnel between England and France runs under the sea for 50 kilometres.

questions.q: Which prickly plant is famous for growing in hot deserts?
questions.f: A giant saguaro cactus can hold hundreds of litres of water in its thick stem.

questions.q: What do we call the low land lying between two hills or mountains?
questions.f: Many valleys were carved out slowly by rivers or by ancient moving ice.

questions.q: What do we call a wide, flat, grassy stretch of land?
questions.f: Huge grassy plains in North America are called prairies.

questions.q: Which continent are Kenya and Nigeria in?
questions.f: Africa has more than a billion people and over a thousand different languages.

questions.q: Which continent is France in?
questions.f: France shares land borders with eight other European countries.

questions.q: What do we call people who visit another country for a holiday?
questions.f: France welcomes more holiday visitors each year than any other country.

questions.q: What is the name of the planet we all live on?
questions.f: Earth is the only planet we know of with liquid water on its surface.

questions.q: Which country is famous for football and the city of Rio de Janeiro?
questions.f: Brazil has won the football World Cup five times, more than any other country.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the giant stone Sphinx with a lion's body?
questions.f: The Great Sphinx was carved from one enormous piece of limestone rock.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the dance called flamenco?
questions.f: Flamenco dancers clap and stamp to keep the beat instead of using a drum.

questions.q: Which animals often pull sleds across the snow in the cold Arctic?
questions.f: Husky dogs have two layers of fur, so they can nap outside in freezing weather.

questions.q: Which country is famous for its huge, colourful carnival parades in February?
questions.f: Rio's carnival parade is so big it has its own stadium with room for 70,000 fans.

questions.q: In which country would you find the famous city of Paris?
questions.f: Paris grew up around an island in the middle of the River Seine.

questions.q: What do we call the sea water that tastes salty?
questions.f: Rivers wash tiny bits of salt off the land into the sea, year after year.

questions.q: Camels can walk a long way across hot deserts without drinking.
questions.f: A thirsty camel can gulp down over 100 litres of water in just a few minutes.

questions.q: Every country in the world has its own flag.
questions.f: A country's flag is one of the first things it chooses when it becomes independent.

questions.q: A village is bigger than a city.
questions.f: Villages are small settlements, while cities can hold millions of people.

questions.q: You can find snow on some mountain tops even in hot countries.
questions.f: Air gets colder the higher you go, so tall tropical peaks stay snowy all year.

questions.q: The Earth is shaped roughly like a ball.
questions.f: Earth bulges slightly at the middle, so it is a tiny bit squashed, not a perfect ball.

questions.q: Everybody in the world speaks the same language.
questions.f: People speak around 7,000 different languages across the world today.

questions.q: A book full of maps is called an...?
questions.f: It is named after Atlas, a giant in Greek stories who held the sky on his shoulders.

questions.q: A person who travels to find out about unknown places is an...?
questions.f: The word explore comes from Latin explorare, meaning to search out.

questions.q: The word 'geography' means the study of...?
questions.f: From Greek geo, meaning earth, and graphein, meaning to write.

questions.q: In the word 'island', which letter is silent?
questions.f: The S sneaked in centuries ago because writers copied the spelling of 'isle'.

questions.q: A small flow of water that joins a bigger river is called a...?
questions.f: Every big river in the world begins as a tiny stream somewhere uphill.

questions.q: A country's capital is the city where its...?
questions.f: Capital comes from Latin caput, meaning head - the head city of a country.

questions.q: The little box on a map that explains what the symbols mean is called the...?
questions.f: Mapmakers also call it a legend, from a Latin word meaning 'to be read'.

questions.q: Which word means a long journey, especially across the sea?
questions.f: Voyage comes from Latin viaticum, the food and money you packed for a trip.

questions.q: The word 'igloo' comes from an Inuit word meaning...?
questions.f: In Inuktitut, iglu means any kind of home, not only one made of snow.

questions.q: Long ago the word 'desert' meant a place that had been...?
questions.f: It comes from Latin desertus, meaning abandoned - the same root as 'deserted'.

questions.q: The word 'volcano' comes from the name of a Roman god of...?
questions.f: Vulcan was the Roman blacksmith god, said to keep his forge under an Italian island.

questions.q: Which word means all the people who live in a place?
questions.f: The world's population passed eight billion people in the year 2022.

questions.q: A trip to watch wild animals in Africa is often called a...?
questions.f: Safari is a Swahili word that simply means 'journey'.

questions.q: A 'canyon' is a deep valley with...?
questions.f: Canyon comes from Spanish canon, meaning a tube or pipe.

questions.q: Which word means a very small village?
questions.f: Hamlet shares its root with 'home', and once meant a little cluster of houses.

questions.q: The word 'jungle' describes land thickly covered with...?
questions.f: Jungle came into English from Hindi jangal, meaning wild uncleared ground.

questions.q: What do we call the person who guides a ship using maps and stars?
questions.f: Navigator comes from Latin navis, a ship, and agere, to drive.

questions.q: Which word means the very top of a mountain that climbers aim for?
questions.f: Summit comes from Latin summus, meaning highest.

questions.q: The imaginary line where one country stops and another begins is the...?
questions.f: The longest border between two countries runs between Canada and the United States.

questions.q: What do we call a big group of islands lying close together?
questions.f: Indonesia is made of more than 17,000 islands sitting side by side.

questions.q: The word 'continent' is used for very large areas of...?
questions.f: Continent comes from Latin terra continens, meaning 'continuous land'.

questions.q: The word 'atlas' comes from the name of a giant in Greek stories.
questions.f: Early mapmakers printed a picture of Atlas holding the world on the first page.

questions.q: A 'harbour' is a sheltered place where boats can safely stop.
questions.f: Harbour comes from old words meaning 'army shelter' - a safe place to rest.

questions.q: Which word means a picture of the whole world drawn flat on paper?
questions.f: No flat map can show the round Earth perfectly, so every world map stretches something.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the wide sun hat called a sombrero?
questions.f: Sombrero comes from the Spanish word sombra, meaning shade.

questions.q: Which country is famous for bagpipes and kilts?
questions.f: A piper blows air into a bag, then squeezes it to keep the sound going without stopping.

questions.q: Which country's lucky symbol is a green three-leaved shamrock?
questions.f: Ireland is nicknamed the Emerald Isle because rain keeps its fields so green.

questions.q: In which country were painted nesting dolls, one inside the other, made famous?
questions.f: They are called matryoshka dolls, and the biggest sets have dozens of layers.

questions.q: Which fluffy animal is a famous helper in the mountains of Peru?
questions.f: Llamas can carry heavy packs up steep mountain paths where trucks cannot go.

questions.q: Which round, brown bird that cannot fly is a symbol of New Zealand?
questions.f: A kiwi lays one of the biggest eggs for its body size of any bird on Earth.

questions.q: In which country was coffee first discovered growing wild?
questions.f: An old story says a goat herder noticed his goats dancing after eating coffee berries.

questions.q: Which island country is the home of reggae music?
questions.f: Reggae's steady off-beat rhythm grew up in Jamaica in the 1960s.

questions.q: Which country is famous for waffles and delicious chocolates?
questions.f: Belgium has more than 2,000 chocolate shops for a country smaller than many US states.

questions.q: Which country is famous for its steep sea inlets called fjords?
questions.f: Fjords were carved by slow-moving ice, then filled up by the sea.

questions.q: In which northern country is the region called Lapland, full of reindeer?
questions.f: In Lapland the winter Sun can stay below the horizon for weeks.

questions.q: In which city would you visit the ancient Colosseum?
questions.f: The Colosseum could seat about 50,000 people, more than many stadiums today.

questions.q: In which country is the snow-topped Mount Fuji?
questions.f: Mount Fuji is a volcano, and thousands of people climb it every summer.

questions.q: In which country is the Golden Gate Bridge?
questions.f: Its famous orange-red paint colour is called International Orange.

questions.q: In which country is the Sydney Opera House?
questions.f: Its white roof is covered with more than a million shiny tiles.

questions.q: Which country celebrates Diwali, the festival of lights?
questions.f: Families light rows of little clay lamps called diyas along their doorways.

questions.q: In which country do crowds gather each spring to see cherry blossom?
questions.f: Watching the pink blossom is called hanami, meaning flower viewing.

questions.q: In which country do people perform dragon dances at New Year?
questions.f: A single dragon costume can be over 30 metres long and need many dancers.

questions.q: Which pair of sticks is used for eating meals in China and Japan?
questions.f: Chopsticks have been used for eating in China for more than 3,000 years.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the sport of baseball?
questions.f: Baseball is also hugely popular in Japan, Cuba and the Dominican Republic.

questions.q: Which hot drink is Britain especially famous for enjoying?
questions.f: Britain drinks around 100 million cups of tea every single day.

questions.q: Which elephant has bigger ears, the African or the Asian one?
questions.f: Big ears help African elephants cool down by letting heat escape from the blood inside.

questions.q: Which is the biggest land animal on Earth?
questions.f: A big male African elephant can weigh as much as six family cars.

questions.q: Do polar bears live near the North Pole or the South Pole?
questions.f: Under their white fur, polar bears actually have black skin to soak up sunshine.

questions.q: Which continent do wild lions live on?
questions.f: A tiny group of wild lions also survives in the Gir forest in India.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the tango dance?
questions.f: Tango grew up in the busy port neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires.

questions.q: In which country were the very first Olympic Games held long ago?
questions.f: The ancient games were held at Olympia every four years for a thousand years.

questions.q: Which country is famous for growing lots of the world's coffee today?
questions.f: Brazil has grown more coffee than any other country for over 150 years.

questions.q: Which country is famous for pretzels and big brass bands?
questions.f: Germany bakes over a thousand different kinds of bread and roll.

questions.q: Which country is famous for elephants, temples and spicy noodle soups in Asia?
questions.f: The elephant is a national symbol of Thailand and appears in many festivals.

questions.q: Which African country is famous for wildlife parks full of zebras and giraffes?
questions.f: Each year over a million wildebeest cross Kenya's plains in a huge migration.

questions.q: Iceland has hot springs where steamy water bursts out of the ground.
questions.f: Iceland heats most of its homes with natural hot water from underground.

questions.q: Wild penguins and wild polar bears live in the same place.
questions.f: Penguins live in the far south while polar bears live only in the far north.

questions.q: Some countries have no sea coast at all.
questions.f: There are more than 40 landlocked countries, including Switzerland and Nepal.

questions.q: People in different countries use different kinds of money.
questions.f: There are around 180 different official currencies used around the world.

questions.q: Africa is one single country.
questions.f: Africa is a continent made up of 54 separate countries.

questions.q: Camels are sometimes called the ships of the desert.
questions.f: They earned the nickname because they carry goods steadily across sandy 'seas'.

questions.q: What do we call the edge of the land where it meets the sea?
questions.f: Coast comes from Latin costa, meaning rib or side.

questions.q: What do we call water tumbling down over a cliff edge?
questions.f: Some waterfalls are so tall that the water breaks into mist before it lands.

questions.q: The word 'map' comes from a Latin word that meant...?
questions.f: Latin mappa meant a napkin or sheet of cloth, and early maps were drawn on cloth.

questions.q: A person whose job is drawing maps is called a...?
questions.f: From Greek chartes, a sheet of paper, plus graphein, to write.

questions.q: Which word means a country's own special song?
questions.f: Japan's anthem has only 32 words, one of the shortest in the world.

questions.q: Which word means the kind of money a country uses?
questions.f: Currency comes from Latin currere, to run - money 'runs' from hand to hand.

questions.q: Which word means a huge city?
questions.f: Metropolis is Greek for 'mother city'.

questions.q: The 'geo' at the start of 'geography' and 'geology' means...?
questions.f: So geology is 'earth study' and geography is 'earth writing'.

questions.q: A 'rainforest' is a forest that gets lots and lots of...?
questions.f: Some rainforests get more than four metres of rain in a single year.

questions.q: Which word means the shaking of the ground?
questions.f: Millions of tiny earthquakes happen every year, but most are far too small to feel.

questions.q: Warm 'tropical' countries are the ones close to the...?
questions.f: Tropical places get strong sunshine all year, so they never really have winter.

questions.q: Which word means a long line of mountains standing together?
questions.f: The word range once meant a row of soldiers standing in line.

questions.q: In 'kilometre', which part means one thousand?
questions.f: Kilo comes from the Greek word khilioi, meaning thousand.

questions.q: Which word means all the food, clothes, music and customs of a group of people?
questions.f: Culture comes from Latin cultura, meaning to grow or tend, like a garden.

questions.q: Which word means land far away from the sea, in the middle of a country?
questions.f: The farthest inland spot from any sea is in northwest China.

questions.q: Which word describes a town that sits right beside the sea?
questions.f: About four in ten people on Earth live within 100 kilometres of a coast.

questions.q: The word 'globe' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Latin globus meant a round lump or ball of anything.

questions.q: Which word means the top layer of ground where plants grow?
questions.f: It can take hundreds of years for nature to build a single centimetre of soil.

questions.q: Which direction is exactly between north and east?
questions.f: A full compass rose can show 32 different named directions.

questions.q: Which word means somebody who has always lived in a place?
questions.f: Local comes from Latin locus, meaning place.

questions.q: Which word names the wide grassy land in Africa where zebras graze?
questions.f: African grasslands are also called savanna, a word borrowed from the Caribbean.

questions.q: Which word means a special day when a whole country celebrates together?
questions.f: Holiday began as 'holy day', a day off for religious festivals.

questions.q: Which word means the path a ship or plane follows?
questions.f: Route comes from a Latin phrase meaning a 'broken' or cut-through way.

questions.q: Which word means a person who has come to live in a new country?
questions.f: Around one in every 30 people on Earth lives in a country they were not born in.

questions.q: What do we call the big picture of Earth taken from high in the sky?
questions.f: Satellites circle Earth taking pictures that help make today's maps.

questions.q: Which country is partly in Europe and partly in Asia?
questions.f: Istanbul is a city with one half in Europe and the other half in Asia.

questions.q: Which country's flag is green, white and orange stripes?
questions.f: India's flag also has orange, white and green, but with a blue wheel in the middle.

questions.q: Which country is famous for beautiful white houses with blue roofs on its islands?
questions.f: Greece has around 6,000 islands, but only about 200 have people living on them.

questions.q: Which large, cold country has the city of Moscow as its capital?
questions.f: Moscow's underground railway stations are decorated like palaces.

questions.q: Which country is famous for tacos and a spicy sauce called salsa?
questions.f: Chocolate, tomatoes and maize were all first grown by peoples of Mexico.

questions.q: Which country would you visit to see wild giant tortoises on the Galapagos Islands?
questions.f: Some Galapagos tortoises live for well over a hundred years.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the beautiful Angkor Wat temple?
questions.f: Angkor Wat is the largest religious building in the world by area.

questions.q: In which country would you find the city of Cape Town?
questions.f: Cape Town sits under a mountain with a top so flat it is called Table Mountain.

questions.q: Which country is famous for its beautiful old temples in the city of Kyoto?
questions.f: Kyoto was Japan's capital city for more than a thousand years.

questions.q: Which country has a flag with a picture of a tree on it?
questions.f: The tree is a cedar, which has grown in Lebanon's mountains for thousands of years.

questions.q: Which country is famous for cuckoo clocks and yodelling in the mountains?
questions.f: Yodelling started as a way for herders to call across wide mountain valleys.

questions.q: Which country grows more olives for oil than any other?
questions.f: Spain has more than 300 million olive trees, many of them over a century old.

questions.q: Which country is home to the tall, spotted giraffe in the wild?
questions.f: A giraffe's neck has just seven bones, the same number as yours.

questions.q: Some countries are made up only of islands.
questions.f: Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines are all island countries with thousands of islands.

questions.q: Which continent has no countries and no permanent towns?
questions.f: Scientists from many nations share Antarctica under a treaty signed in 1959.

questions.q: Which river flows through the middle of Paris?
questions.f: Paris began as a settlement on an island in the Seine called the Ile de la Cite.

questions.q: Which river flows through London?
questions.f: The Thames has more than 200 bridges along its length.

questions.q: Which is the longest river in Europe?
questions.f: The Volga does not reach an ocean - it empties into the Caspian Sea.

questions.q: Which is the longest river in Asia?
questions.f: The Yangtze runs about 6,300 kilometres across China from the Tibetan highlands to the sea.

questions.q: Which canal lets ships cut between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans?
questions.f: Ships are lifted up 26 metres by giant water locks and then lowered again.

questions.q: Which canal joins the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea?
questions.f: It saves ships from Europe to Asia a journey of thousands of kilometres around Africa.

questions.q: Which mountain range is used as the dividing line between Europe and Asia?
questions.f: The Urals run north to south across Russia for about 2,500 kilometres.

questions.q: Which is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea?
questions.f: Sicily is home to Mount Etna, one of the most active volcanoes on Earth.

questions.q: In which country is Mount Kilimanjaro?
questions.f: Kilimanjaro stands alone on a plain, so it looks even taller than it is.

questions.q: In which country is the ancient stone circle of Stonehenge?
questions.f: Some of its stones were dragged all the way from Wales, over 200 kilometres away.

questions.q: In which country does the giant Christ the Redeemer statue stand?
questions.f: It stands on Corcovado mountain, 700 metres above the city of Rio de Janeiro.

questions.q: In which country are four presidents' faces carved into Mount Rushmore?
questions.f: Each carved face is about 18 metres tall - as high as a five-storey building.

questions.q: In which city does the ancient temple called the Parthenon stand?
questions.f: The Parthenon has stood on the Acropolis hill for about 2,500 years.

questions.q: In which city would you find the small Little Mermaid statue by the harbour?
questions.f: She is only 1.25 metres tall, and honours a story by Hans Christian Andersen.

questions.q: Which city is nicknamed the Big Apple?
questions.f: The nickname was spread in the 1920s by a sports writer covering horse racing.

questions.q: Which city is nicknamed the Eternal City?
questions.f: Romans believed their city would last forever, no matter what happened elsewhere.

questions.q: Which country is known as the Land of the Rising Sun?
questions.f: Japan's own name, Nippon, means 'origin of the sun'.

questions.q: Which country is nicknamed the Land of Fire and Ice?
questions.f: Iceland has around 130 volcanoes and hundreds of glaciers side by side.

questions.q: Which is the largest lake in Africa?
questions.f: Lake Victoria touches three countries: Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya.

questions.q: In which country is the Serengeti, famous for its huge herds?
questions.f: Serengeti comes from a Maasai word meaning 'endless plains'.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain in North America?
questions.f: Denali means 'the tall one' in the language of Alaska's Koyukon people.

questions.q: Which is the highest peak in the Alps?
questions.f: Mont Blanc means 'white mountain' in French, because snow sits on it all year.

questions.q: Which country has more active volcanoes than any other?
questions.f: Indonesia sits where several giant plates of the Earth's crust grind together.

questions.q: Which country contains more lakes than the rest of the world put together?
questions.f: Canada has around two million lakes, most of them scooped out by ancient ice.

questions.q: Which is the largest country in Africa by area?
questions.f: Most of Algeria is Sahara Desert, so nearly everyone lives near the north coast.

questions.q: Which is the largest country in South America?
questions.f: Brazil borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.

questions.q: Which is the smallest continent?
questions.f: Australia is sometimes counted together with nearby islands as Oceania.

questions.q: Which two countries share a land border with the United States?
questions.f: The US-Canada border is the longest land border between any two countries.

questions.q: Which ocean surrounds Antarctica?
questions.f: The Southern Ocean was officially named the fifth ocean in the year 2000.

questions.q: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
questions.f: Seasonal monsoon winds once carried trading ships back and forth across it.

questions.q: Which language has the most people speaking it as their first language?
questions.f: Around 900 million people grow up speaking Mandarin Chinese.

questions.q: Which language do people speak in Brazil?
questions.f: Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country in the world.

questions.q: What is the money used in Japan called?
questions.f: The word yen means 'round object', because coins are round.

questions.q: Which money is shared by many countries in Europe?
questions.f: Twenty countries use the euro, and its notes show bridges and doorways, not real people.

questions.q: What is the money used in India called?
questions.f: Rupee comes from a Sanskrit word for wrought silver.

questions.q: Which desert covers much of Botswana and Namibia in southern Africa?
questions.f: Kalahari comes from a Tswana word meaning 'the great thirst'.

questions.q: On which continent is the Danube River?
questions.f: The Danube flows through or touches ten countries, more than any other river.

questions.q: Which country is directly south of the United States?
questions.f: The border between them runs for about 3,100 kilometres.

questions.q: Which hemisphere is Australia in?
questions.f: That is why Christmas in Australia falls in the middle of summer.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Italy?
questions.f: Rome contains a whole separate country inside it: Vatican City.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Germany?
questions.f: Berlin has more bridges than Venice - over 900 of them.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Spain?
questions.f: Madrid sits on a high plateau, making it one of Europe's highest capitals.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Kenya?
questions.f: Nairobi has a national park with wild lions right on the city's edge.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Mexico?
questions.f: Mexico City was built on the site of the Aztec island city of Tenochtitlan.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Argentina?
questions.f: Buenos Aires means 'good airs' in Spanish.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Thailand?
questions.f: Bangkok's full Thai ceremonial name is the longest city name in the world.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Greece?
questions.f: Athens is named after Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Norway?
questions.f: Oslo sits at the end of a long fjord, surrounded by forest and hills.

questions.q: What is the capital city of South Korea?
questions.f: Around half of all South Koreans live in or around Seoul.

questions.q: What is the capital city of New Zealand?
questions.f: Wellington is the southernmost capital city of any independent country.

questions.q: Vatican City is completely surrounded by the city of Rome.
questions.f: It covers less than half a square kilometre, smaller than many city parks.

questions.q: The Pacific Ocean touches both Asia and North America.
questions.f: Only about 80 kilometres of sea separate Russia from Alaska at the Bering Strait.

questions.q: Every country in Europe uses the euro.
questions.f: Countries such as Poland, Sweden and Switzerland keep their own money.

questions.q: Switzerland has no coastline on any sea.
questions.f: It is landlocked, but big lakes and rivers still carry boats through the country.

questions.q: There are more countries in Asia than in Antarctica.
questions.f: Asia has about 49 countries; Antarctica has none at all.

questions.q: The Alps stretch across several countries, not just one.
questions.f: The Alps run through eight countries, from France all the way to Slovenia.

questions.q: The word 'equator' comes from a Latin word meaning to make...?
questions.f: The equator splits the Earth into two equal halves, north and south.

questions.q: The Pacific Ocean's name means...?
questions.f: Magellan named it Mar Pacifico after finding calm water there in 1520.

questions.q: The word 'hemisphere' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek hemi, half, and sphaira, ball.

questions.q: A person from Denmark is called a...?
questions.f: The country's name means 'the borderland of the Danes'.

questions.q: A person from Sweden is called a...?
questions.f: Sweden's own name for itself is Sverige, meaning 'realm of the Svear'.

questions.q: A person from Finland is called a...?
questions.f: Finns call their country Suomi, and their language is unlike its neighbours' languages.

questions.q: People from the Netherlands are called...?
questions.f: 'Dutch' and 'Deutsch' come from the same old word meaning 'of the people'.

questions.q: Which word describes an area with towns, buildings and busy streets?
questions.f: Urban comes from Latin urbs, meaning city.

questions.q: Which word describes the quiet countryside with farms and fields?
questions.f: Rural comes from Latin rus, meaning open land or countryside.

questions.q: A green spot with water in the middle of a desert is called an...?
questions.f: Oasis came into Greek from an ancient Egyptian word for a fertile spot.

questions.q: The word 'Netherlands' literally means...?
questions.f: About a quarter of the country lies below sea level, protected by dykes.

questions.q: The word 'Norway' comes from words meaning...?
questions.f: It described the sailing route hugging Norway's long, island-dotted coast.

questions.q: Which word means a country with no coast on the sea?
questions.f: Two countries, Uzbekistan and Liechtenstein, are surrounded only by other landlocked countries.

questions.q: 'Antarctic' means the region opposite the...?
questions.f: The prefix ant- means 'opposite', so Antarctic is 'the opposite of the Arctic'.

questions.q: The word 'tropical' is used for places between the two lines called the...?
questions.f: The Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn mark where the Sun can be straight overhead.

questions.q: What do we call the study of the world's peoples, their customs and beliefs?
questions.f: From Greek anthropos, meaning human being.

questions.q: Which word means a language somebody learns after their first language?
questions.f: More people speak English as a second language than as a first one.

questions.q: A traveller's book about the places they visited is called a...?
questions.f: The ending -logue comes from Greek logos, meaning word or account.

questions.q: Which word names a large farm in a hot country growing crops like tea or sugar?
questions.f: Plantation comes straight from Latin plantare, to plant.

questions.q: Which word describes a place where two rivers meet and join?
questions.f: From Latin con, together, and fluere, to flow.

questions.q: The word 'Nippon', Japan's name for itself, means...?
questions.f: Japan sits east of China, so from China it lay in the direction of the sunrise.

questions.q: Which word means a group of people who share a language and traditions?
questions.f: Nation comes from Latin natio, meaning birth or a people born in one place.

questions.q: The words 'Dutch' and 'Deutsch' grew from the very same old root word.
questions.f: Both come from a word meaning 'of the people', which is why they look so alike.

questions.q: The word 'oasis' was borrowed into English from ancient Egyptian through Greek.
questions.f: It first described the fertile hollows dotted across Egypt's western desert.

questions.q: The Maori are the first people of which country?
questions.f: Maori navigators reached New Zealand in ocean-going canoes around 700 years ago.

questions.q: Which people traditionally herd reindeer in the far north of Europe?
questions.f: Sami reindeer herders live across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.

questions.q: Which desert covers part of the southwestern United States?
questions.f: Death Valley, one of the hottest places on Earth, sits at the Mojave's edge.

questions.q: Which is the largest state of the United States by area?
questions.f: Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas, but has far fewer people.

questions.q: Which is the windiest continent on Earth?
questions.f: Winds pour downhill off Antarctica's ice dome and can top 300 kilometres an hour.

questions.q: Which continent has the most people living on it?
questions.f: More than half of all the people on Earth live in Asia.

questions.q: Which country has three different capital cities for different jobs?
questions.f: Pretoria runs the government, Cape Town makes the laws and Bloemfontein hosts the top court.

questions.q: Which country stretches the longest distance from north to south?
questions.f: Chile is over 4,000 kilometres long but on average only about 180 kilometres wide.

questions.q: Which sea lies between Australia and New Zealand?
questions.f: It is named after Abel Tasman, the Dutch sailor who crossed it in 1642.

questions.q: Which narrow stretch of water separates Asia from North America?
questions.f: During the last ice age, dry land here let people walk from Asia into America.

questions.q: Greenland is a self-governing part of which European kingdom?
questions.f: Greenlandic, related to Inuit languages of Canada, is its official language.

questions.q: Which is the largest of North America's Great Lakes?
questions.f: Lake Superior holds enough water to cover both North and South America knee-deep.

questions.q: Which US city is famous for hilly streets, cable cars and thick sea fog?
questions.f: Locals nicknamed the summer fog rolling through the bay 'Karl'.

questions.q: In which country would you ride the Trans-Siberian Railway?
questions.f: The full journey from Moscow to Vladivostok takes about a week.

questions.q: Which European river is famous for the castles lining its banks in Germany?
questions.f: More than 40 castles and fortresses stand along one 65-kilometre stretch of the Rhine.

questions.q: In which city are the headquarters of the United Nations?
questions.f: The land it sits on is international territory, not part of any single country.

questions.q: How many stripes are on the flag of the United States?
questions.f: The stripes stand for the 13 original colonies that became the first states.

questions.q: Which country's flag is red with one large yellow star?
questions.f: China's red flag is similar but has five stars, one big and four small.

questions.q: Which country's flag shows a white dragon holding jewels?
questions.f: Bhutan's name for itself, Druk Yul, means 'land of the thunder dragon'.

questions.q: Which flag is a plain red cross on a white background?
questions.f: It honours Saint George, and has flown over English ships since the Middle Ages.

questions.q: Which is the largest island in Asia?
questions.f: Borneo is shared by three countries: Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei.

questions.q: Which island is shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic?
questions.f: It is the only Caribbean island split between two separate countries.

questions.q: Which country has more World Heritage sites than any other?
questions.f: Italy has around 60 protected sites, from Roman ruins to whole historic towns.

questions.q: Which country is home to the ancient Inca people's descendants and the city of Cusco?
questions.f: Cusco was the Inca capital, and its name means 'navel' or centre of the world.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the ancient Maya pyramid at Chichen Itza?
questions.f: When you clap near its steps, the echo sounds like the call of a sacred bird.

questions.q: Which is the world's largest country that lies entirely in Europe?
questions.f: Russia is bigger but most of it lies in Asia, not Europe.

questions.q: Which mountain range separates France from Spain?
questions.f: Tucked in the Pyrenees is tiny Andorra, one of Europe's smallest countries.

questions.q: Which country lies between France and the Netherlands on the North Sea coast?
questions.f: Belgium has three official languages: Dutch, French and German.

questions.q: Which country produces the most tea in the world?
questions.f: Tea plants originally grew wild in the hills where China, Myanmar and India meet.

questions.q: Which sport is the most popular in the world by number of fans?
questions.f: Football's rules were written down in England in 1863 and spread worldwide by sailors.

questions.q: Which country hosted the very first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
questions.f: They were held in Athens to echo the ancient games at Olympia.

questions.q: Which imaginary lines run east to west around the globe like belts?
questions.f: The equator is the longest line of latitude, at zero degrees.

questions.q: Which country is famous for the ancient rock-cut churches of Lalibela?
questions.f: Eleven churches were carved downwards into solid rock, roofs first.

questions.q: Antarctica is a desert, because so little rain or snow falls there each year.
questions.f: Some Antarctic valleys have had almost no precipitation for millions of years.

questions.q: The Great Lakes of North America hold fresh water, not salt water.
questions.f: Together they hold about a fifth of all the fresh surface water on Earth.

questions.q: Some countries lie on both sides of the equator.
questions.f: Brazil, Indonesia, Kenya and several others are crossed by the equator.

questions.q: New Zealand is made up of two main islands.
questions.f: They are simply called the North Island and the South Island.

questions.q: Africa and Asia are joined by a narrow strip of land in Egypt.
questions.f: The Suez Canal was dug straight through that strip, the Isthmus of Suez.

questions.q: There are more people living in Asia than in all the other continents together.
questions.f: Asia's population is around 4.7 billion, well over half the world's total.

questions.q: A person a country sends to represent it in another country is called an...?
questions.f: An ambassador's home abroad is called an embassy, and it counts as their country's ground.

questions.q: The '-land' ending in England, Iceland and Thailand simply means...?
questions.f: So Thailand means 'land of the Thai', a word meaning free.

questions.q: Which official booklet lets you travel between countries?
questions.f: Passport comes from French passer, to pass, and port, a harbour gate.

questions.q: 'England' means the land of which ancient people?
questions.f: The Angles sailed to Britain from what is now northern Germany and Denmark.

questions.q: The word 'safari' came into English from which African language?
questions.f: Swahili is spoken by over a hundred million people across East Africa.

questions.q: 'Iceland' and 'Greenland' were named by sailors who spoke which old language?
questions.f: Curiously, Greenland is the icier of the two, and Iceland the greener.

questions.q: Which word means the whole world seen as one connected place?
questions.f: That is where 'global' and 'globalisation' come from.

questions.q: What do we call a country ruled by a king or queen?
questions.f: From Greek monos, one, and archein, to rule - rule by one person.

questions.q: What do we call a country where the people vote to choose their leaders?
questions.f: From Greek demos, the people, and kratos, power.

questions.q: The word 'chocolate' came into Spanish from the language of which people?
questions.f: The Aztec word xocolatl described a bitter drink made from cocoa beans.

questions.q: The word 'canoe' came to Europe from the Caribbean word...?
questions.f: Columbus's crew recorded the Taino word kanoa for a dug-out boat.

questions.q: The word 'boomerang' comes from a language of which country's first peoples?
