questions.f: It was recorded from the Dharug language spoken near what is now Sydney.

questions.q: The word 'sauna' was borrowed into English from which language?
questions.f: Finland has around three million saunas for just five and a half million people.

questions.q: A 'bazaar' is a word from Persian meaning a...?
questions.f: Istanbul's Grand Bazaar has around 4,000 shops under one roof.

questions.q: 'Origami' is built from Japanese words meaning...?
questions.f: From ori, to fold, and kami, paper.

questions.q: Which word means a picture-writing symbol used in ancient Egypt?
questions.f: Hieroglyph is Greek for 'sacred carving'.

questions.q: Which word means a group of countries working together as partners?
questions.f: Alliance comes from Latin ligare, to bind or tie together.

questions.q: A 'frankfurter' sausage is named after which city?
questions.f: The hamburger takes its name from Hamburg in the same way.

questions.q: Brussels sprouts are named after the capital city of which country?
questions.f: They were grown in fields around Brussels as early as the 1500s.

questions.q: Which small dog breed shares its name with a Mexican state?
questions.f: Chihuahua is Mexico's largest state and mostly desert.

questions.q: The word 'marathon' is the name of a place in which country?
questions.f: A messenger was said to have run from the town of Marathon to Athens with news.

questions.q: Which word describes a person who is travelling on a ship or plane, not working on it?
questions.f: Passenger comes from the same root as 'passage', a way through.

questions.q: Which word names the line of hills or mountains you see against the sky?
questions.f: City skylines are shaped by their tallest towers instead of hills.

questions.q: A road built to go around a busy city rather than through it is a...?
questions.f: Some ring roads, like Beijing's, are stacked in several loops one outside the other.

questions.q: What do we call a place where a river finally flows into the sea?
questions.f: Rivers are described with body words: they have a mouth, a bed and banks.

questions.q: Which word means the beginning point of a river, high in the hills?
questions.f: Explorers spent centuries arguing about the true source of the Nile.

questions.q: Which word means a curved stretch of coast where the sea comes inland?
questions.f: Hudson Bay in Canada is so big that ships can sail into it for days.

questions.q: Which word means a language everybody in a country is taught in school?
questions.f: India has 22 languages listed in its constitution for official use.

questions.q: The word 'pyjamas' came into English from India and Persia, where it meant...?
questions.f: Persian pay-jama meant 'leg garment', loose trousers tied at the waist.

questions.q: The word 'shampoo' came into English from India, from a word meaning to...?
questions.f: Hindi champo meant to knead and massage the head.

questions.q: The word 'safari' means 'journey' in the language it came from.
questions.f: So a safari park is really a 'journey park'.

questions.q: 'Democracy' is built from Greek words meaning 'people power'.
questions.f: Ancient Athens let thousands of citizens vote on laws in an open-air meeting.

questions.q: Sausages and cheeses are often named after the towns where they were first made.
questions.f: Frankfurter, cheddar and parmesan are all named after places.

questions.q: Which word means the number of people living in each square kilometre?
questions.f: Monaco is the most crowded country, with over 19,000 people per square kilometre.

questions.q: Which word means the weather a place usually has over many years?
questions.f: Climate comes from a Greek word meaning 'slope', because sunlight slants differently on Earth.

questions.q: Which word means a huge city area where several towns have grown together?
questions.f: Built from Latin con, together, and urbs, city.

questions.q: What do we call the study of the Earth's rocks and how they formed?
questions.f: Geologists can read a canyon wall like the pages of a very old book.

questions.q: Which word names the flat land beside a river that floods after heavy rain?
questions.f: Floodplain soil is rich, which is why ancient farmers settled on it.

questions.q: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
questions.f: Lesotho is the only country in the world lying entirely above 1,000 metres in altitude.

questions.q: Which city, at about 3,600 metres up, is the world's highest seat of government?
questions.f: Visitors often need a day of rest in La Paz because the thin air leaves them breathless.

questions.q: Which two rivers gave ancient Mesopotamia its name?
questions.f: Mesopotamia is Greek for 'between the rivers'.

questions.q: Which high, wide plateau in Asia is nicknamed the Roof of the World?
questions.f: It averages over 4,500 metres high - higher than most of the Alps.

questions.q: Which country is the world's largest archipelago, with over 17,000 islands?
questions.f: Indonesia's islands stretch about 5,000 kilometres from end to end.

questions.q: Which narrow strait separates Spain from Morocco?
questions.f: At its narrowest the two continents are only about 14 kilometres apart.

questions.q: Which is the driest inhabited continent?
questions.f: Around 70 per cent of Australia is arid or semi-arid land.

questions.q: Which African country contains more ancient pyramids than Egypt?
questions.f: The Nubian kingdom of Kush built over 200 steep, narrow pyramids along the Nile.

questions.q: On which river do the mighty Victoria Falls thunder down?
questions.f: The falls form the largest single sheet of falling water on the planet.

questions.q: Which volcano buried the Roman town of Pompeii?
questions.f: Ash preserved loaves of bread and even footprints for almost 2,000 years.

questions.q: Which is the highest active volcano in Europe?
questions.f: Etna erupts so often that Sicilian farmers plant crops in its rich volcanic soil.

questions.q: Which country built a brand-new inland capital in 1960, laid out in the shape of an aeroplane?
questions.f: Brasilia rose from empty scrubland in just 41 months, designed by Lucio Costa.

questions.q: Which is the largest landlocked country in the world?
questions.f: Kazakhstan is bigger than all of western Europe put together.

questions.q: Which is the northernmost capital city of any independent country?
questions.f: Reykjavik means 'smoky bay', named after steam rising from its hot springs.

questions.q: The word HOMES helps you remember the names of what?
questions.f: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior - one letter each.

questions.q: In which country is the red-walled Alhambra palace with its fountain courtyards?
questions.f: Alhambra comes from Arabic al-hamra, meaning 'the red one'.

questions.q: In which country is the fairy-tale castle of Neuschwanstein?
questions.f: Built in the 1800s, it inspired the look of several film and theme-park castles.

questions.q: In which city does the great domed Hagia Sophia stand?
questions.f: When finished in 537 it had the largest dome in the world, and held that record for centuries.

questions.q: In which country was an army of thousands of life-size clay soldiers discovered?
questions.f: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an in 1974 struck the Terracotta Army by accident.

questions.q: In which country is the huge red rock called Uluru?
questions.f: Uluru is sacred to the Anangu people, and most of the rock lies buried underground.

questions.q: Which lake high in the Andes is the world's highest large navigable lake?
questions.f: Local families build floating islands on it out of woven reeds.

questions.q: In which country is the Atacama Desert?
questions.f: Some Atacama weather stations have never once recorded rainfall.

questions.q: The huge Iguazu Falls sit on the border between which two countries?
questions.f: The falls are made of around 275 separate drops spread over nearly three kilometres.

questions.q: Which is the largest bay in the world?
questions.f: Rivers pouring into it make its northern waters surprisingly fresh.

questions.q: The ancient Silk Road linked China to which region?
questions.f: Silk, paper and gunpowder travelled west along it while glass and horses travelled east.

questions.q: Which flower is the national flower of India?
questions.f: Lotus leaves are so water-repellent that engineers copy them to make self-cleaning paint.

questions.q: Which country contains the world's longest railway tunnel, deep under the Alps?
questions.f: The Gotthard Base Tunnel runs 57 kilometres beneath the mountains.

questions.q: Which island nation lies just southeast of India across a narrow strait?
questions.f: A chain of sandbanks called Adam's Bridge almost connects the two.

questions.q: Which is the world's fourth-largest island, lying off the coast of Mozambique?
questions.f: Around nine in ten of Madagascar's wild species live nowhere else on Earth.

questions.q: Which mountain range stretches across northern India, Nepal and Bhutan?
questions.f: The name means 'abode of snow' in Sanskrit.

questions.q: Which mountain range runs along the northwest edge of Africa?
questions.f: They shield the coast from the Sahara, so one side is green and the other bone dry.

questions.q: Which sea is slowly shrinking because rivers feeding it were diverted for farming?
questions.f: Old fishing boats now sit rusting on dry sand kilometres from any water.

questions.q: Which vast wetland in Botswana is a delta that never reaches the sea?
questions.f: Its water spreads out across the Kalahari sands and simply evaporates away.

questions.q: Which country's Great Rift Valley is slowly splitting the continent apart?
questions.f: In millions of years the valley may fill with sea, cutting off a new landmass.

questions.q: Which country has the most people living in cities rather than countryside, at nearly 100%?
questions.f: Singapore is a city that is also an entire country, so it is virtually all urban.

questions.q: Which two countries are separated by the Pyrenees plus a tiny country between them?
questions.f: Andorra sits high in the Pyrenees and has two heads of state at once.

questions.q: Which country's coastline is dotted with over 1,000 islands along the Adriatic Sea?
questions.f: Croatia's clear Adriatic waters make it one of Europe's favourite sailing coasts.

questions.q: Which desert stretches across Mongolia and northern China?
questions.f: The Gobi is a cold desert where winter temperatures can drop below minus 30 Celsius.

questions.q: Which continent contains the countries Suriname, Guyana and Uruguay?
questions.f: Suriname is the smallest country in South America by area.

questions.q: Which country's national parks protect the volcanic hot pools of Rotorua?
questions.f: Rotorua's ground bubbles with mud pools and smells faintly of sulphur.

questions.q: Which mountain, straddling Italy and Switzerland, has a famously pyramid-shaped peak?
questions.f: Its four steep faces point almost exactly at the four compass directions.

questions.q: Which country has more than 400 volcanoes and sits on the Pacific plate's edge in the Americas?
questions.f: Chile's volcanoes rise along the Andes, formed as one plate dives beneath another.

questions.q: Which country's people first domesticated the potato, high in the Andes?
questions.f: Andean farmers grow thousands of potato varieties, in colours from purple to blue.

questions.q: Which country is home to the ancient rose-red Persepolis ruins?
questions.f: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire 2,500 years ago.

questions.q: Which two Asian countries have the most people of any nations on Earth?
questions.f: Each has well over a billion people - together, more than a third of humanity.

questions.q: Russia has territory in both Europe and Asia.
questions.f: The Ural Mountains run through Russia and mark the traditional dividing line.

questions.q: The Sahara receives more rain each year than the Amazon rainforest.
questions.f: Parts of the Amazon get over three metres of rain a year; the Sahara often gets a few centimetres.

questions.q: Istanbul was once known as Constantinople.
questions.f: It was renamed after the Roman emperor Constantine, who made it his capital in 330.

questions.q: Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and China.
questions.f: Climbers can reach the top from the Nepali south side or the Tibetan north side.

questions.q: A country can have more than one official language.
questions.f: Bolivia officially recognises dozens, including Spanish, Quechua and Aymara.

questions.q: The Dead Sea shore is the lowest dry land on the surface of the Earth.
questions.f: Its shores sit around 430 metres below sea level and keep dropping.

questions.q: The word 'peninsula' is built from Latin words meaning...?
questions.f: From paene, almost, and insula, island - land nearly cut off by water.

questions.q: A river 'delta' is named after a letter of which alphabet?
questions.f: The Nile's fan-shaped mouth looks like the triangular Greek letter delta.

questions.q: The name 'Mediterranean' literally means...?
questions.f: From Latin medius, middle, and terra, land - a sea almost ringed by continents.

questions.q: The word 'Sahara' is simply the Arabic word for...?
questions.f: So 'Sahara Desert' really says 'Desert Desert'.

questions.q: The name 'Gobi' comes from a Mongolian word meaning...?
questions.f: Much of the Gobi is bare rock and gravel rather than sand dunes.

questions.q: The word 'geyser' comes from an Icelandic verb meaning to...?
questions.f: It comes from Geysir, the name of one famous spouting spring in Iceland.

questions.q: The word 'fjord' shares an ancient root with which English word?
questions.f: Both come from a root meaning a place where you can cross water.

questions.q: The word 'prairie' was borrowed from French, where it means...?
questions.f: French explorers used it for the wide grasslands of North America.

questions.q: A 'plateau' takes its name from a French word meaning...?
questions.f: The same French word gives us 'plate' and even 'platter'.

questions.q: The word 'strait' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'strict' and 'restrict'.

questions.q: A 'cape' of land gets its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From caput, head - the same root as 'captain' and 'capital'.

questions.q: 'Latitude' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Longitude comes from longus, meaning length, so the pair means 'width and length'.

questions.q: The word 'ocean' comes from the name of a Greek...?
questions.f: Okeanos was believed to be a vast river encircling the whole world.

questions.q: The word 'suburb' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin sub, below or near, and urbs, city.

questions.q: The Latin root 'terra', found in 'territory' and 'terrain', means...?
questions.f: Terra also hides inside Mediterranean, terrace and extraterrestrial.

questions.q: An 'aqueduct' is built from Latin parts meaning...?
questions.f: Roman aqueducts carried water gently downhill for up to 90 kilometres.

questions.q: The word 'monsoon' came into English from an Arabic word meaning...?
questions.f: Sailors named the winds mawsim because they changed direction with the seasons.

questions.q: The word 'tsunami' is built from Japanese words meaning...?
questions.f: Fishermen at sea often felt nothing, then returned to find their harbour wrecked.

questions.q: A 'nomad' takes their name from a Greek word about people who...?
questions.f: Greek nomas described herders roaming with their animals in search of grass.

questions.q: The name 'Singapore' comes from Sanskrit words meaning...?
questions.f: From simha, lion, and pura, city - though no lions ever lived there.

questions.q: The country name 'Argentina' comes from a Latin word for which metal?
questions.f: Early explorers hoped to find mountains of silver up the River Plate.

questions.q: 'Costa Rica' means...?
questions.f: Puerto Rico, meaning 'rich port', was named in the same hopeful style.

questions.q: 'Sierra Leone' means...?
questions.f: A Portuguese sailor named its hills after distant thunder that sounded like roaring.

questions.q: Which continent's name comes from Latin words meaning 'southern land'?
questions.f: Mapmakers drew an imagined Terra Australis long before Europeans reached it.

questions.q: The country 'Colombia' is named after which explorer?
questions.f: Curiously, Columbus never set foot in the country that carries his name.

questions.q: 'Bolivia' is named after a leader called...?
questions.f: Bolivar helped free several South American countries from Spanish rule.

questions.q: The Philippines is named after a 16th-century king of which country?
questions.f: The islands were named for King Philip II by a Spanish explorer in 1543.

questions.q: The ending '-stan' in country names such as Kazakhstan means...?
questions.f: It comes from an old Persian root, so Uzbekistan is 'land of the Uzbeks'.

questions.q: The name 'Los Angeles' is Spanish for...?
questions.f: Its original 1781 name was much longer, mentioning a river and a queen of angels.

questions.q: Which US state's name is Spanish for 'mountain'?
questions.f: Nevada means 'snow-covered' and Colorado means 'coloured red'.

questions.q: The Egyptian city Alexandria was named after...?
questions.f: He founded around 20 cities and named many of them after himself.

questions.q: Which word means a wide plain of grass with scattered trees, from a Caribbean language?
questions.f: Spanish sailors borrowed zabana from the Taino people of the Caribbean.

questions.q: Which word describes a deep, narrow, rocky valley with a stream at the bottom?
questions.f: Gorge comes from a French word for throat, the same root as 'gargle'.

questions.q: Which word means the raised bank of soil built to hold back a river or sea?
questions.f: Levee comes from French lever, to raise.

questions.q: 'Cartography' is the art and science of making...?
questions.f: From Greek chartes, a sheet of papyrus, and graphein, to write.

questions.q: Which word means the study of place names and where they came from?
questions.f: From Greek topos, place, and onoma, name.

questions.q: Which word names the special word for a person from a place, like 'Parisian'?
questions.f: From Greek demos, people, plus onoma, name.

questions.q: The word 'Sahara' and the word 'desert' in that name mean nearly the same thing.
questions.f: Sahara comes from Arabic sahra, meaning desert, so the phrase repeats itself.

questions.q: 'Longitude' and 'long' come from the same Latin root.
questions.f: Latin longus gives us long, longitude, elongate and even 'lunge'.

questions.q: The Arctic is named after an animal, while the Antarctic is named after the Arctic.
questions.f: Arktos means bear, and 'ant-' means opposite, so Antarctic is 'opposite the bear'.

questions.q: Which is the largest city in South America?
questions.f: Greater Sao Paulo is home to over 20 million people.

questions.q: Which Nigerian city, built partly on lagoon islands, is one of Africa's biggest?
questions.f: Lagos means 'lakes' in Portuguese, after the lagoon it grew around.

questions.q: Which sacred river flows past the ancient city of Varanasi?
questions.f: The Ganges basin is the most crowded river basin on Earth, feeding hundreds of millions.

questions.q: In which country does the Mekong River spread into its great rice-growing delta?
questions.f: The delta grows enough rice to feed much of Southeast Asia.

questions.q: Which river flows through Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade?
questions.f: The Danube passes more capital cities than any other river in the world.

questions.q: In which country is the Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat?
questions.f: After rain it becomes a mirror so perfect that the sky and ground look identical.

questions.q: In which country is the Pantanal, the world's largest tropical wetland?
questions.f: In the wet season it floods to an area larger than England.

questions.q: Which country covers most of the Iberian Peninsula?
questions.f: Portugal and tiny Gibraltar share the peninsula with Spain.

questions.q: Which three countries make up Scandinavia?
questions.f: Add Finland and Iceland and the group is called the Nordic countries instead.

questions.q: Which line of latitude crosses right through Australia?
questions.f: It runs through Alice Springs, near the country's red centre.

questions.q: Which river forms much of the border between Texas and Mexico?
questions.f: Mexicans call the same river the Rio Bravo del Norte.

questions.q: Which African lake is the second deepest lake in the world?
questions.f: It plunges about 1,470 metres down, second only to Lake Baikal.

questions.q: Which country grows more bananas than any other?
questions.f: India grows them mostly for people at home, while Ecuador exports the most.

questions.q: Which West African country produces the most cocoa beans in the world?
questions.f: Around two in every five chocolate bars start life in Ivory Coast.

questions.q: Which country's flag shows a white crescent moon and star on red?
questions.f: Tunisia's flag also has a crescent and star, but inside a white circle.

questions.q: What is the blue wheel in the middle of India's flag called?
questions.f: It has 24 spokes and is copied from a pillar built by Emperor Ashoka.

questions.q: Which country celebrates the Day of the Dead with marigolds and sugar skulls?
questions.f: Families build home altars called ofrendas to welcome relatives' spirits back for a night.

questions.q: In which country do people throw bright coloured powders at the festival of Holi?
questions.f: Holi welcomes spring, and for one day almost everyone ends up rainbow-coloured.

questions.q: Which country celebrates its new year, Songkran, with a giant water fight?
questions.f: Splashing water is meant to wash away the troubles of the old year.

questions.q: In which country is the tomato-throwing festival La Tomatina held?
questions.f: The town of Bunol uses over 100 tonnes of overripe tomatoes each year.

questions.q: Which country celebrates Bastille Day on the 14th of July?
questions.f: It marks the day in 1789 when crowds stormed a Paris prison-fortress.

questions.q: The lively samba is the national dance of which country?
questions.f: Samba schools in Rio spend all year preparing costumes for one parade.

questions.q: The didgeridoo, a long wooden drone pipe, comes from which country?
questions.f: Skilled players use circular breathing to hold one note for many minutes.

questions.q: In which country was the sport of cricket first played?
questions.f: The earliest known reference to cricket dates from the 1500s in southeast England.

questions.q: In which country did the martial art of judo begin?
questions.f: Judo means 'the gentle way', and became an Olympic sport in 1964.

questions.q: In which country did taekwondo begin?
questions.f: Taekwondo means roughly 'the way of the foot and fist'.

questions.q: In which country did yoga first develop, thousands of years ago?
questions.f: The word yoga means 'to join' or 'yoke' in Sanskrit.

questions.q: Which country has more languages spoken in it than any other, over 800?
questions.f: Steep mountain valleys kept neighbouring groups apart for centuries, so each kept its own tongue.

questions.q: Which US state lies closest to Russia?
questions.f: Two small islands in the Bering Strait, one Russian and one American, are 4 kilometres apart.

questions.q: Which country would you visit to walk the ancient Inca Trail?
questions.f: The Inca built about 40,000 kilometres of stone roads without using the wheel.

questions.q: Which sea, bordered by Turkey and Ukraine, is famous for being almost enclosed?
questions.f: Its deep water holds almost no oxygen, so shipwrecks there stay astonishingly well preserved.

questions.q: Which country is home to the sandstone towers of Cappadocia and its cave homes?
questions.f: People carved entire underground cities there, some big enough for thousands of residents.

questions.q: Which country is home to the ancient Mayan city of Tikal, deep in the rainforest?
questions.f: Tikal's tallest temple rises about 70 metres above the jungle floor.

questions.q: Which country's coast is warmed by a current that keeps its ports ice-free all winter?
questions.f: The North Atlantic Drift carries warm water all the way from the Gulf of Mexico.

questions.q: Which desert, on Africa's southwest coast, is thought to be the world's oldest?
questions.f: Its dunes have been dry for around 55 million years, and some tower 300 metres high.

questions.q: Which country has more than 6,000 named islands and the city of Bergen?
questions.f: Bergen sits between seven mountains and is one of Europe's rainiest cities.

questions.q: Which two continents are joined by the narrow country of Panama?
questions.f: Panama is so twisty that in places the sun rises over the Pacific.

questions.q: Which mountain in Tanzania and Kenya gave Kenya its name?
questions.f: Mount Kenya is Africa's second highest peak and has glaciers almost on the equator.

questions.q: Which country was formed by joining Tanganyika and the island of Zanzibar?
questions.f: Its name is a blend of the two: Tan-Zan-ia.

questions.q: Which country's people call their homeland Deutschland?
questions.f: Deutschland means roughly 'land of the people', from an old word for the common tongue.

questions.q: Which country's people traditionally call their land Hellas?
questions.f: That is why we still say 'Hellenic' when we mean Greek.

questions.q: Which country is also officially called Bharat?
questions.f: Bharat comes from the name of a legendary king in ancient Indian texts.

questions.q: Quito, a high city sitting almost on the equator, is the capital of which country?
questions.f: Quito is cool all year despite the equator, because it stands 2,850 metres up.

questions.q: Which country contains the world's largest known cave passage, Son Doong?
questions.f: Its biggest chamber could hold a whole New York city block, skyscrapers included.

questions.q: Which country is home to the Great Blue Hole, a giant round sea sinkhole?
questions.f: It is over 300 metres across and about 125 metres deep.

questions.q: Some rivers form the border between two different countries.
questions.f: The Danube, Rio Grande and Mekong all act as borders along parts of their length.

questions.q: Egypt has land on two continents.
questions.f: The Sinai Peninsula, east of the Suez Canal, counts as part of Asia.

questions.q: Every continent has at least one desert.
questions.f: Even Europe has one: the Tabernas desert in southern Spain.

questions.q: There are countries where more than half the land is below sea level.
questions.f: The Netherlands comes closest, with about a quarter of its land below sea level.

questions.q: Mount Kilimanjaro has glaciers even though it stands close to the equator.
questions.f: Its ice fields have shrunk sharply over the last century as the climate warms.

questions.q: The word 'compass' is built from Latin parts meaning...?
questions.f: The idea was measuring by stepping out equal paces, as with a pair of compasses.

questions.q: The word 'orient' originally meant the direction of the...?
questions.f: From Latin oriens, rising - which is why lining up a map is called orienting it.

questions.q: The Atlantic Ocean is named after...?
questions.f: Ancient Greeks called the sea beyond the Atlas Mountains the Atlantic.

questions.q: The word 'kayak' was borrowed from the language of which people?
questions.f: An Inuit qajaq was built by stretching sealskin over a driftwood or bone frame.

questions.q: The word 'hammock' came into English from a language of which region?
questions.f: Taino people slept in woven nets slung between trees, safely off the ground.

questions.q: The word 'barbecue' came from the Caribbean word 'barbacoa', meaning a...?
questions.f: Spanish sailors recorded barbacoa as a frame of sticks for drying or cooking food.

questions.q: The word 'tomato' came into Europe from the Aztec word...?
questions.f: Tomatoes reached Italy in the 1500s and only later became a pasta favourite.

questions.q: The word 'llama' was borrowed from which South American language?
questions.f: Quechua was the language of the Inca and is still spoken by millions today.

questions.q: The word 'coffee' travelled into English from an Arabic word, 'qahwa', through which language?
questions.f: Arabic qahwa became Turkish kahve, then Italian caffe, then English coffee.

questions.q: A 'caravan' of camels takes its name from a Persian word meaning a...?
questions.f: Roadside inns for them were called caravanserais, and some still stand today.

questions.q: The word 'guru' comes from Sanskrit and originally meant...?
questions.f: Its older sense is 'heavy' - someone weighty with knowledge.

questions.q: The Olympic Games take their name from...?
questions.f: The games were held in the sacred grove at Olympia every four years.

questions.q: Which word means a country's people all belonging to one large family group by descent?
questions.f: From Greek ethnos, meaning nation or people.

questions.q: Which word means a language that different peoples use to talk to each other in trade?
questions.f: Lingua franca is Italian for 'Frankish tongue', a trade language of Mediterranean sailors.

questions.q: A word borrowed from another language, like 'safari', is called a...?
questions.f: English has borrowed words from more than 350 different languages.

questions.q: Which word means the ordinary local form of a language, different from place to place?
questions.f: From Greek dialektos, meaning way of speaking.

questions.q: 'Geothermal' energy uses heat from where?
questions.f: Iceland heats about nine in ten of its homes with geothermal water.

questions.q: Which word describes rock, soil or land worn away slowly by wind and water?
questions.f: Erosion carved the world's canyons grain by grain over millions of years.

questions.q: Which word means all the plant life growing naturally in a region?
questions.f: From Latin vegetare, to enliven or grow.

questions.q: Which word means an animal or plant found naturally in only one place on Earth?
questions.f: Lemurs are endemic to Madagascar - they live wild nowhere else.

questions.q: The root 'hydro' in 'hydroelectric' and 'hydrography' means...?
questions.f: Norway makes almost all its electricity from falling water - true hydro power.

questions.q: The prefix 'trans-' in 'transatlantic' and 'transcontinental' means...?
questions.f: So the Trans-Siberian Railway is the one that runs right across Siberia.

questions.q: The prefix 'sub-' in 'subtropical' and 'subcontinent' means...?
questions.f: The Indian subcontinent hangs 'below' the main mass of Asia on the map.

questions.q: 'Circumnavigate' means to...?
questions.f: From Latin circum, around, plus navigare, to sail.

questions.q: Which word means an official count of everyone living in a country?
questions.f: Ancient Rome held censuses over 2,000 years ago to count its citizens.

questions.q: Which word means a journey made for scientific study or discovery?
questions.f: From Latin expedire, to free the feet - to get moving.

questions.q: Which word means the natural home where a plant or animal lives?
questions.f: Habitat is simply Latin for 'it dwells'.

questions.q: Which word means moving from one country or region to another to live?
questions.f: From Latin migrare, to move house.

questions.q: Which word means the map lines that join places of equal height?
questions.f: Closely packed contour lines mean the slope is very steep.

questions.q: Which word means the height of land above sea level?
questions.f: From Latin altus, high - the same root as 'altar' and 'exalt'.

questions.q: Which word names the shape and features of the land, like hills and valleys?
questions.f: From Greek topos, place, plus graphein, to write.

questions.q: Which word means the amount by which one map shrinks the real world?
questions.f: A scale of 1 to 50,000 means one centimetre on paper equals half a kilometre.

questions.q: Which word means a place's usual pattern of temperature and rainfall through the year?
questions.f: Geographers group the world into climate zones, from polar to equatorial.

questions.q: The word 'volcano' and the name of the Italian island Vulcano share the same origin.
questions.f: Both come from Vulcan, the Roman god believed to work his forge beneath the island.

questions.q: 'Lingua franca' is Italian for 'Frankish tongue'.
questions.f: It began as a mixed trading speech used in Mediterranean ports.

questions.q: The words 'orient' and 'orientation' are related.
questions.f: Old maps put east at the top, so lining a map up correctly meant finding the orient.

questions.q: Quechua, the language of the Inca, is still spoken by millions of people today.
questions.f: It is an official language in Peru and Bolivia, alongside Spanish.

questions.q: Which word names a piece of a country cut off from the main part by other territory?
questions.f: Alaska is a US exclave, separated from the other states by Canada.

questions.q: Which is the largest country lying entirely within the Southern Hemisphere?
questions.f: Brazil is bigger overall, but part of it pokes north of the equator.

questions.q: Which is the largest peninsula in the world?
questions.f: It covers about 3 million square kilometres, and holds the vast Empty Quarter sand sea.

questions.q: An 1896 victory at Adwa helped which African country avoid ever becoming a European colony?
questions.f: Ethiopia also uses its own calendar, with 13 months in a year.

questions.q: Which two countries each share land borders with 14 other nations, more than any others?
questions.f: Brazil comes next with 10, touching every South American country but two.

questions.q: Which is the only African country with coastline on both the Atlantic and Indian Oceans?
questions.f: The two oceans are often said to meet near Cape Agulhas, Africa's true southern tip.

questions.q: Which is the only country whose English name begins with the letter Q?
questions.f: Quebec and Queensland are big, but they are provinces, not countries.

questions.q: Which large country has no permanent rivers at all?
questions.f: It relies on wells and on huge plants that take the salt out of seawater.

questions.q: The blisteringly hot Danakil Depression, with its acid pools, lies mainly in which country?
questions.f: Yellow, green and orange salt crusts make it look more like another planet.

questions.q: Oymyakon, often called the coldest permanently inhabited place, is in which country?
questions.f: Temperatures there have dropped below minus 67 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Yellowstone National Park contains roughly half of the world's...?
questions.f: Underneath sits a giant magma chamber that keeps the water boiling.

questions.q: What is the name of the research station standing at the geographic South Pole?
questions.f: It honours the two rival explorers who raced for the pole in 1911 and 1912.

questions.q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
questions.f: Amundsen's team used skis and dog teams, and beat Scott by about five weeks.

questions.q: Whose expedition completed the first sailing voyage all the way around the world?
questions.f: Magellan died en route, so Juan Sebastian Elcano brought the last ship home in 1522.

questions.q: Which is the only sea on Earth with no land coastline, bounded instead by ocean currents?
questions.f: Floating seaweed there shelters baby sea turtles and young eels.

questions.q: Roughly a quarter of the world's traded goods squeeze through which narrow strait?
questions.f: At its narrowest it is only about 2.7 kilometres wide.

questions.q: Which major shipping canal has no locks at all along its length?
questions.f: The seas at each end sit at almost the same level, so no lifting is needed.

questions.q: Which country contains the Three Gorges Dam, the largest power station on Earth?
questions.f: Its reservoir is so heavy that it very slightly slows the Earth's spin.

questions.q: Which is the most populous country in Africa?
questions.f: Nigeria has over 200 million people and more than 500 languages.

questions.q: Which is the world's second-largest rainforest, after the Amazon?
questions.f: It is home to forest elephants, bonobos and okapis.

questions.q: Which river is the only major river to cross the equator twice?
questions.f: Its curving course means part of its basin is having a wet season year-round.

questions.q: Which river carries the second-greatest volume of water to the sea, after the Amazon?
questions.f: It is also the deepest river in the world, with spots over 220 metres deep.

questions.q: Which is the world's second-highest mountain?
questions.f: K2 got its plain name from a surveyor's list: Karakoram peak number two.

questions.q: Which is the highest volcano in the world?
questions.f: It sits on the Chile-Argentina border and holds a tiny crater lake near its summit.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain in Antarctica?
questions.f: It was not even spotted by humans until 1958, as planes flew over the ice.

questions.q: An 1883 eruption heard nearly 5,000 kilometres away destroyed most of which island volcano?
questions.f: For years afterwards its dust made sunsets around the world glow strange colours.

questions.q: Mauna Loa, the largest active volcano on Earth by volume, is in which country?
questions.f: It rises from the sea floor, so most of its enormous bulk is hidden underwater.

questions.q: The International Date Line roughly follows which line of longitude?
questions.f: It zigzags around islands so no country is split into two different dates.

questions.q: Which Pacific island nation is among the very first places to see each new year?
questions.f: Kiribati's Line Islands run 14 hours ahead of Greenwich time.

questions.q: Which enormous country runs on just one single time zone?
questions.f: In China's far west the Sun can rise around 10 in the morning by the clock.

questions.q: Which is the largest country in the Caribbean?
questions.f: Cuba is longer than the whole of England from end to end.

questions.q: Which is the least densely populated country in the world?
questions.f: Mongolia averages about two people per square kilometre of grassland and desert.

questions.q: Which country's flag is the only one to show a building?
questions.f: The building is Angkor Wat, drawn in white against a red band.

questions.q: Which country's flag shows a map of the country itself?
questions.f: Kosovo's flag does too, making them a rare pair.

questions.q: Which country's flag features a bird of paradise?
questions.f: It also shows the Southern Cross, the constellation used to find south.

questions.q: Which country has a national anthem with no official words at all?
questions.f: Crowds hum along to the Marcha Real, or simply chant 'lo-lo-lo'.

questions.q: Which country flies the oldest national flag still in use?
questions.f: The Dannebrog's red-and-white cross design goes back to at least the 1300s.

questions.q: Which country changed its name from Swaziland in 2018?
questions.f: Eswatini means 'land of the Swazis' in the siSwati language.

questions.q: Which country was formerly known as Ceylon?
questions.f: Its own name, Sri Lanka, means 'resplendent island'.

questions.q: Which country was officially renamed from Persia in 1935?
questions.f: Iran means 'land of the Aryans', a name its people had used for centuries.

questions.q: Which country was once called Siam?
questions.f: Thailand's own name means 'land of the free'.

questions.q: Which African country took its modern name from a great stone-walled ruin?
questions.f: Great Zimbabwe's name means 'houses of stone', built without any mortar.

questions.q: Which country was known as the Gold Coast until 1957?
questions.f: It took its new name from a powerful medieval West African empire.

questions.q: Which island did European sailors long call Formosa, meaning 'beautiful'?
questions.f: Portuguese sailors reportedly cried 'Ilha Formosa' as they passed its green mountains.

questions.q: Which city was called Saigon before 1976?
questions.f: Locals still often call the central district Saigon today.

questions.q: Which Indian city was renamed from Bombay in 1995?
questions.f: The name honours Mumbadevi, a goddess of the local Koli fishing community.

questions.q: Which Russian city was called Leningrad for most of the 20th century?
questions.f: The city has had three names in a hundred years: Petrograd, Leningrad, then Saint Petersburg again.

questions.q: Which world capital was known as Edo until 1868?
questions.f: Its new name, Tokyo, means 'eastern capital'.

questions.q: Which is the flattest country in the world, with its highest point under 3 metres?
questions.f: Most Maldivian islands rise barely a metre above the waves.

questions.q: Which country is the smallest in Africa by land area?
questions.f: The Seychelles' 115 islands add up to less than 500 square kilometres.

questions.q: A Dutch navigator of the 1640s, an island south of Australia, and a sea between two countries all carry which sailor's name?
questions.f: Tasmania, the Tasman Sea and even a Tasmanian devil all trace back to him.

questions.q: A month mistaken for a river's name, a bay taken for an estuary, and a statue on Corcovado point to which city?
questions.f: Portuguese sailors reached the bay in January 1502 and called it 'river of January'.

questions.q: A Swahili phrase meaning 'house of peace', a former Tanzanian capital, and a busy Indian Ocean port name which city?
questions.f: Tanzania later moved its official capital inland to Dodoma.

questions.q: A Spanish Easter feast called Pascua Florida, a 1513 landing, and a peninsula of swamps and springs name which place?
questions.f: Florida means 'flowery', from the feast of flowers at Easter.

questions.q: The Caspian Sea is bordered by five countries.
questions.f: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan all touch its shores.

questions.q: There is a country where the lowest point of land is still over 1,000 metres above sea level.
questions.f: Lesotho's lowest ground sits about 1,400 metres up, earning it the nickname Kingdom in the Sky.

questions.q: Some capital cities of neighbouring countries sit within sight of each other across a river.
questions.f: Brazzaville and Kinshasa face each other across the Congo, the closest capital pair.

questions.q: Antarctica has an active volcano with a lake of molten lava inside it.
questions.f: Mount Erebus has kept a bubbling lava lake going for decades.

questions.q: There is a country that has territory on every continent except Antarctica.
questions.f: France governs overseas regions in South America, Africa, Oceania and the Indian Ocean.

questions.q: The word 'archipelago' comes from Greek roots meaning...?
questions.f: It first described the Aegean Sea, then came to mean the islands scattered in it.

questions.q: An 'isthmus' takes its name from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: A narrow neck of land joining two bigger pieces, like the Isthmus of Panama.

questions.q: The word 'atoll' was borrowed into English from the language of which island nation?
questions.f: Dhivehi atolhu described the ring-shaped coral islands of the Maldive chain.

questions.q: A volcanic 'caldera' is named from a Spanish word meaning...?
questions.f: A caldera forms when a volcano's roof collapses into the emptied chamber below.

questions.q: The word 'tundra' entered English from northern Europe, where it meant...?
questions.f: Below the surface lies permafrost, ground that stays frozen all year round.

questions.q: The word 'taiga' names the vast northern belt of what?
questions.f: The taiga is the largest land biome on Earth, ringing the whole northern world.

questions.q: 'Steppe' came into English from Russian, describing...?
questions.f: The Eurasian steppe stretches from Hungary almost to China.

questions.q: A flat-topped desert hill called a 'mesa' takes its name from Spanish for...?
questions.f: A smaller, narrower one is called a butte.

questions.q: The 'pampas' of Argentina take their name from a Quechua word meaning...?
questions.f: The same root appears in Peruvian place names such as Pampas de Nazca.

questions.q: The word 'kiosk' came into English from Turkish, where it meant a...?
questions.f: Ottoman kosk pavilions were open summer houses in palace gardens.

questions.q: The colour name 'turquoise' literally means...?
questions.f: The stone reached Europe through Turkey, so French called it pierre turquoise.

questions.q: The flower name 'tulip' comes from a Turkish word for a...?
questions.f: The petals were thought to look like the folds of a turban.

questions.q: The word 'paradise' comes from an Old Persian word meaning...?
questions.f: Persian kings built enclosed pleasure gardens called pairidaeza.

questions.q: The title 'admiral' comes from an Arabic phrase meaning...?
questions.f: From amir al-bahr; the extra 'd' crept in from Latin admirari, to admire.

questions.q: The word 'hurricane' comes from a Caribbean people's name for a...?
questions.f: Spanish sailors recorded the Taino name Hurakan.

questions.q: The word 'ketchup' most likely came from a Chinese dialect word for a...?
questions.f: Hokkien ke-tsiap was a salty fish brine; tomatoes were added much later in America.

questions.q: Why do some languages say 'tea' while others say 'chai'?
c: Sea traders and land traders used different Chinese words
One word is older than the other
One means green and one black
Chai came from India, tea from Japan
questions.f: Coastal Min Chinese te travelled by ship, while Mandarin cha travelled overland.

questions.q: The business word 'tycoon' came from a Japanese title meaning...?
questions.f: American visitors picked up taikun, a title used for Japan's shogun.

questions.q: 'Karaoke' is built from Japanese parts meaning...?
questions.f: From kara, empty, plus oke, a clipped form of the English word orchestra.

questions.q: The word 'kimono' literally means...?
questions.f: From ki, to wear, and mono, thing.

questions.q: 'Rickshaw' is shortened from a Japanese word meaning...?
questions.f: Jinrikisha breaks into jin, person, riki, power, and sha, vehicle.

questions.q: The word 'robot' was coined in a 1920 Czech play, from a word meaning...?
questions.f: Karel Capek's brother suggested robota, an old word for drudgery.

questions.q: The Russian title 'tsar' developed from the name of which Roman?
questions.f: The German title Kaiser comes from exactly the same source.

questions.q: The word 'utopia', invented in 1516 for an imaginary island, literally means...?
questions.f: Thomas More built it from Greek ou, not, and topos, place.

questions.q: To live a 'spartan' life is named after a city in which country?
questions.f: Sparta's citizens were famous for plain food, hard training and few comforts.

questions.q: The Canary Islands are most likely named after which animals?
questions.f: Latin canis means dog; the little yellow canary bird was named after the islands, not the reverse.

questions.q: Why is the turkey bird named after a country it does not come from?
c: It reached Europe through Turkish trade routes
Its call sounds like the word Turkey
questions.f: The bird is American; several languages instead name it after India by mistake.

questions.q: The spotted Dalmatian dog is named after a region in which modern country?
questions.f: Dalmatia is Croatia's rugged Adriatic coast.

questions.q: The Labrador retriever's name comes from a region of which country?
questions.f: Confusingly, the breed was developed from dogs of nearby Newfoundland.

questions.q: The Siamese cat is named after the old name of which country?
questions.f: They were once kept in the royal palaces of Siam and rarely seen abroad.

questions.q: The words 'jeans' and 'denim' come from the names of two cities in...?
questions.f: Jeans from Genoa, and denim from serge de Nimes - cloth of Nimes.

questions.q: The fruit name 'peach' traces back to a Latin phrase meaning 'apple of...'?
questions.f: Persica travelled into French as pesche and then English peach - though peaches began in China.

questions.q: The 'tangerine' is named after which port city?
questions.f: The fruit was shipped to Europe from Tangier in Morocco.

questions.q: The scented water called 'cologne' is named after a city in which country?
questions.f: An Italian perfumer created it in Koln, which the French call Cologne.

questions.q: The place-name ending '-grad', as in Volgograd, means...?
questions.f: Its cousin '-gorod' appears in Novgorod, meaning 'new town'.

questions.q: The ending '-burg' or '-borough' in place names originally meant a...?
questions.f: Edinburgh, Hamburg and Peterborough all began as strongholds.

questions.q: English towns ending in '-chester' or '-caster' grew from what kind of site?
questions.f: From Latin castra, a military camp - hence Manchester, Lancaster and Chester.

questions.q: In Scottish place names such as Ben Nevis, 'ben' means...?
questions.f: Loch means lake, and glen means narrow valley.

questions.q: In Spanish place names, a 'sierra' is a mountain range named after which tool?
questions.f: Jagged peaks reminded Spanish speakers of the teeth of a saw.

questions.q: The Canadian city name 'Montreal' comes from words meaning...?
questions.f: Jacques Cartier named the hill Mont Royal in 1535.

questions.q: The name 'Canada' most likely came from an Iroquoian word meaning...?
questions.f: Explorers heard kanata and used it for the whole country.

questions.q: The name 'Mississippi' comes from an Ojibwe phrase meaning...?
questions.f: Misi-ziibi - and its nickname 'Old Man River' echoes the same idea.

questions.q: The state name 'Texas' comes from a Caddo word meaning...?
questions.f: Spanish visitors heard teysha used as a greeting and thought it was a place name.

questions.q: In Arabic place names, a 'wadi' is a...?
questions.f: Wadis stay bone dry for years, then flood in minutes after a storm.

questions.q: The name 'Hong Kong' means...?
questions.f: The scent may have come from incense wood once shipped through its bay.

questions.q: 'Beijing' means 'northern capital'. What does 'Nanjing' mean?
questions.f: Bei means north, nan means south, and jing means capital.

questions.q: 'Casablanca' is Spanish for...?
questions.f: Its Arabic name, ad-Dar al-Bayda, means exactly the same thing.

questions.q: Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, has a name meaning...?
questions.f: Empress Taytu named it in 1886 after the mimosa flowers on the hillside.

questions.q: China's own name for itself, Zhongguo, means...?
questions.f: The idea was of a central realm with other lands arranged around it.

questions.q: Which is usually counted as the highest mountain in Europe?
questions.f: Elbrus, in Russia's Caucasus, is a dormant volcano with two snowy summits.

questions.q: Which country is often said to have more islands than any other, over 200,000?
questions.f: Most Swedish islands are tiny rocks, and only a few hundred have people on them.

questions.q: The wettest inhabited places on Earth, Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, are in which country?
questions.f: They can receive over 11 metres of rain a year, most of it in a few monsoon months.

questions.q: The Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, lies in India and which other country?
questions.f: Its tangled roots shelter the only tigers on Earth that regularly swim between islands.

questions.q: Which two animals hold up Australia's coat of arms?
questions.f: Both are said to struggle to walk backwards, suggesting a nation that only moves forward.

questions.q: Which two countries officially include the word 'The' in their names?
questions.f: The Gambia keeps its 'The' to avoid confusion with nearby Zambia.

questions.q: Which is the only country named after a woman?
questions.f: French sailors named the Caribbean island after Saint Lucy of Syracuse.

questions.q: Saudi Arabia is named after...?
questions.f: It is one of very few countries named after a family, the House of Saud.

questions.q: Which country's older English name came from a valuable material it once exported?
questions.f: Nearby stretches were named the Gold Coast and the Pepper Coast in the same way.

questions.q: Which sea is named for the silt that a great river dumps into it?
questions.f: The Yellow River carries so much fine soil that the water turns golden-brown.

questions.q: Which country has roughly five sheep for every person?
questions.f: Sheep numbers there peaked at over 70 million in the 1980s.

questions.q: Which continent's mainland has no active volcanoes?
questions.f: Australia's last mainland eruptions were thousands of years ago in Victoria.

questions.q: Which country contains both the highest and the lowest points of North America?
questions.f: Denali reaches 6,190 metres while Death Valley dips 86 metres below sea level.

questions.q: Which is the world's oldest surviving republic, completely surrounded by Italy?
questions.f: San Marino claims a founding date of the year 301.

questions.q: Which country abolished its army in 1948 and has had none since?
questions.f: It spends the money on schools and health care instead, and is famous for its wildlife.

questions.q: Which country was the first to give women the right to vote in national elections?
questions.f: New Zealand women voted in 1893, decades ahead of most of the world.

questions.q: Which country has the oldest parliament still meeting today?
questions.f: Iceland's Althing first gathered in the open air at Thingvellir in the year 930.

questions.q: The historic centre of Venice is built across roughly how many small islands?
questions.f: They are linked by about 400 bridges and separated by 150 canals.

questions.q: Which city has long been nicknamed the City of Light?
questions.f: The nickname began with its early street lighting and its reputation for learning.

questions.q: Which US city is nicknamed the Windy City?
questions.f: Some say the nickname mocked its boastful speakers, not just its lake breezes.

questions.q: The Pacific region names Micronesia, Polynesia and Melanesia mean...?
questions.f: All three share the Greek word nesos, meaning island.

questions.q: Which country produces the most natural rubber in the world?
questions.f: Rubber trees are native to the Amazon, but most now grow in Southeast Asia.

questions.q: Which country harvests the most wheat each year?
questions.f: China grows the most, but Russia usually exports the largest amount.

questions.q: Which mountain's local names are Sagarmatha in Nepal and Chomolungma in Tibet?
questions.f: Its English name honours George Everest, a surveyor who never even saw it.

questions.q: The local name for Victoria Falls, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means...?
questions.f: Spray rises so high that it can be seen from 50 kilometres away.

questions.q: Uluru was known for decades by which other English name?
questions.f: It now carries both names officially, honouring the Anangu people's original word.

questions.q: 'Tierra del Fuego' at South America's tip means...?
questions.f: Magellan's crew saw campfires along the shore and named the region for them.

questions.q: The Cape of Good Hope was first named by Portuguese sailors as the Cape of...?
questions.f: The king renamed it hopefully, because rounding it opened a sea route to India.

questions.q: A ship's speed in 'knots' is named after knots once tied in a...?
questions.f: Sailors counted the knots slipping through their hands as sand ran through a timer.

questions.q: The Amazon River was named by Spanish explorers after...?
questions.f: They reported being attacked by fighters they compared to the Amazons of myth.

questions.q: Brazil takes its name from...?
questions.f: Brazilwood gave a glowing red dye that was Europe's first big prize from the coast.

questions.q: The Caribbean Sea is named after...?
questions.f: The same people's name also lies behind the word 'Caribbean' cuisine and culture.

questions.q: Which explorer's name is carried by a Canadian city, an island and a Washington state town?
questions.f: Hudson likewise gave his name to a river, a bay and a strait.

questions.q: Which Pacific island nation is named after the British explorer who charted it?
questions.f: Its own Maori name is Kuki Airani, a local version of Cook's name.

questions.q: Which country's name comes from a Greek word for islands, joined to the name of India?
questions.f: It means roughly 'the Indian islands', coined by European geographers in the 1800s.

questions.q: The name 'Montenegro' means...?
questions.f: Its own people call it Crna Gora, which means exactly the same.

questions.q: 'Venezuela' is thought to mean...?
questions.f: Explorers saw stilt houses over water and were reminded of Venice.

questions.q: 'Liberia' takes its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: It was founded in the 1820s as a home for freed people from the Americas.

questions.q: New Zealand is named after a province of which country?
questions.f: Dutch mapmakers used Nieuw Zeeland, after the coastal Dutch province of Zeeland.

questions.q: 'Bangladesh' means...?
questions.f: Its name uses desh, a word for country that appears across South Asia.

questions.q: The island of Trinidad was named after...?
questions.f: Columbus reportedly named it for three hilltops he saw on the horizon.

questions.q: The name 'Ukraine' is usually explained as meaning...?
questions.f: The idea of a frontier land fits its long, open plains.

questions.q: 'Mexico' comes from the name of which people?
questions.f: The Mexica are the people we more often call the Aztecs.

questions.q: There is a country with no standing army at all.
questions.f: Costa Rica, Iceland and several small island states manage without one.

questions.q: Some countries lie in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres and in both the Eastern and Western.
questions.f: Kiribati manages all four, since the equator and the date line both cross it.

questions.q: The Caspian Sea is bigger than all five of the Great Lakes put together.
questions.f: At around 371,000 square kilometres it dwarfs them, which is why it is called a sea.

questions.q: Australia is wider from east to west than the distance from London to Moscow.
questions.f: Australia spans about 4,000 kilometres; London to Moscow is around 2,500.

questions.q: Africa's tallest mountain and its lowest land point are both in the same country.
questions.f: Kilimanjaro is in Tanzania, while Africa's lowest point, Lake Assal, is in Djibouti.

questions.q: Some countries are named after their own rivers.
questions.f: Niger, Gambia, Jordan, Paraguay and India all share names with major rivers.

questions.q: The word 'occident', meaning the west, comes from a Latin word for...?
questions.f: The Sun 'falls' in the west, so occidens meant setting, opposite oriens.

questions.q: A 'meridian' line takes its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: At local noon the Sun crosses your meridian - hence a.m. and p.m., before and after.

questions.q: The word 'tropic' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: At the tropics the Sun seems to stop and turn back, ending its journey north or south.

questions.q: 'Cosmopolitan' is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: From kosmos, world, and polites, citizen.

questions.q: The word 'indigenous' comes from Latin roots meaning...?
questions.f: From indu, within, and gignere, to be born.

questions.q: The word 'aboriginal' comes from a Latin phrase meaning...?
questions.f: Ab origine - from the origin, from the very start.

questions.q: A 'hinterland' takes its name from a German word meaning...?
questions.f: It means the inland region served by a port or city.

questions.q: 'Alluvial' soil is named from a Latin verb meaning to...?
questions.f: Alluvial plains are built from mud a river washed down and dropped.

questions.q: An 'estuary' takes its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From aestus, the surge of the tide that pushes seawater up into the river.

questions.q: The word 'lagoon' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Latin lacuna also gives us 'lacuna', a gap or missing piece.

questions.q: 'Permafrost' describes ground that...?
questions.f: About a quarter of the northern hemisphere's land sits on permafrost.

questions.q: The word 'tectonic', as in tectonic plates, comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Greek tekton, a carpenter or builder - the plates that build the world's surface.

questions.q: The word 'seismic' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: So a seismograph is literally a 'shaking writer'.

questions.q: The word 'tornado' most likely came from a Spanish word meaning...?
questions.f: Spanish tronada, a thunderstorm, was probably reshaped by tornar, to turn.

questions.q: The word 'anorak' was borrowed into English from which language?
questions.f: An annoraaq was a hooded sealskin jacket built to keep out sea spray.

questions.q: The word 'moccasin' came from the languages of which region's first peoples?
questions.f: Algonquian-speaking peoples gave English moccasin, moose, raccoon and toboggan.

questions.q: The word 'tepee' comes from a Lakota word meaning to...?
questions.f: From ti, to dwell, and pi, used for - a thing used for living in.

questions.q: The word 'bungalow' comes from a word meaning 'of Bengal', describing a...?
questions.f: British officials copied the low, wide-roofed houses of Bengal across the world.

questions.q: The colour word 'khaki' comes from an Urdu and Persian word meaning...?
questions.f: Khak means dust, which is exactly what the colour blends into.

questions.q: The soft wool called 'cashmere' is named after which region?
questions.f: It is combed from the fine undercoat of goats bred in high, cold pastures.

questions.q: The word 'typhoon' is usually linked to a Chinese phrase meaning...?
questions.f: Greek Typhon, a storm monster, may have nudged the English spelling too.

questions.q: Which region name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'the west'?
questions.f: The Maghreb covers Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and their neighbours.

questions.q: The 'Sahel' belt south of the Sahara has a name meaning...?
questions.f: Arabic sahil, shore - the grassy 'coast' of the great desert 'sea'.

questions.q: Which word means the study of how people, places and environments interact, split into human and physical branches?
questions.f: Physical geography studies rivers and rocks; human geography studies cities and cultures.

questions.q: Which projection makes Greenland look almost as big as Africa on flat maps?
questions.f: Mercator keeps directions true for sailors, but stretches land near the poles hugely.

questions.q: What is the name for a map that shows height and relief using shading and contour lines?
questions.f: Walkers rely on them, because closely spaced contours warn of a steep climb ahead.

questions.q: Which word describes two places on exactly opposite sides of the globe?
questions.f: From Greek anti, opposite, and podes, feet - people whose feet point towards yours.

questions.q: What is the term for a lake, sea or basin whose water never reaches the ocean?
questions.f: The Caspian Sea and Great Salt Lake are both endorheic - water only leaves by evaporating.

questions.q: What word describes the half-salty water found where a river meets the sea?
questions.f: Brackish water suits special fish such as mullet, which move between river and sea.

questions.q: Which term describes a country's rocky underwater shelf, gently sloping before the deep ocean?
questions.f: Most of the world's fishing happens over these shallow shelves.

questions.q: What is the term for a landscape of caves, sinkholes and underground rivers in limestone?
questions.f: The word comes from the Kras region on the Slovenia-Italy border.

questions.q: Which word names a ridge of rock and rubble left behind by a melting glacier?
questions.f: Whole hills across northern Europe are old moraines dropped by vanished ice sheets.

questions.q: Which word describes a long, steep slope or cliff at the edge of a plateau?
questions.f: South Africa's Great Escarpment separates its high inland plateau from the coast.

questions.q: What do geographers call an isolated hill of hard rock rising abruptly from a plain?
questions.f: Inselberg is German for 'island mountain'; Uluru is a famous example.

questions.q: Which term describes the belt of calm winds near the equator that once stalled sailing ships?
questions.f: That is why being stuck and gloomy is called being 'in the doldrums'.

questions.q: Which winds, blowing steadily towards the equator, carried sailing ships west for centuries?
questions.f: Columbus rode them west, then sailed north to catch the westerlies home.

questions.q: Sailors named the stormy southern latitudes near 40 degrees south the...?
questions.f: With almost no land to slow them, winds there race right around the globe.

questions.q: Which term describes a city so large and important that it dominates its whole country?
questions.f: Bangkok is a classic example, many times bigger than Thailand's next city.

questions.q: What is the word for the movement of people from countryside into cities?
questions.f: More than half of humanity has lived in cities since around 2007.

questions.q: Which word describes the gradual turning of fertile land into desert?
questions.f: Planting belts of trees, as in Africa's Great Green Wall, can slow it down.

questions.q: What is a 'megacity'?
c: A city of over 10 million people
questions.f: There are now more than 30 megacities, most of them in Asia.

questions.q: On a Mercator map, countries near the equator look larger than they really are.
questions.f: Mercator stretches the poles, so equatorial countries look relatively smaller.

questions.q: The word 'karst' comes from a place name in Europe.
questions.f: The Kras plateau near Trieste gave its name to limestone landscapes worldwide.

questions.q: 'Cosmopolitan' and 'metropolis' both contain a Greek word for city.
questions.f: Polis, city, also hides in 'police', 'policy' and 'politics'.

questions.q: Ducie Island, Motu Nui and Maher Island as its three nearest neighbours, and a name borrowed from a Jules Verne captain, identify which spot?
questions.f: Space agencies aim retired stations and cargo ships at Point Nemo, the loneliest water on Earth.

questions.q: Phosphate mining on Banaba, 33 low atolls, and a 1995 decision to shift the date line eastwards point to which country?
questions.f: That date-line shift is why Kiribati's Line Islands now greet each new year before anyone else.

questions.q: A switch of driving side in 2009, a calendar with no 30 December 2011, and a trade turn away from California name which nation?
questions.f: Samoa jumped the date line to share working days with Australia and New Zealand.

questions.q: Africa's only ski resort, the Katse Dam selling water to a neighbour, and a conical straw hat on the flag identify which country?
questions.f: Nicknamed the Kingdom in the Sky, Lesotho sits entirely above 1,000 metres.

questions.q: An island stripped for seabird droppings, a largest settlement called Yaren that is only a district, and a ring road 19 km long name which country?
questions.f: Phosphate made Nauru briefly one of the richest places per person on Earth.

questions.q: Television legalised only in 1999, a capital with no traffic lights, and archery as the national sport point to which country?
questions.f: Bhutan measures Gross National Happiness and absorbs more carbon than it releases.

questions.q: A burning gas crater in the sand, a record for the densest cluster of white marble buildings, and the Karakum covering most of the land name which country?
questions.f: The Darvaza crater has burned since a drilling accident in the 1970s.

questions.q: A failed 1802 climb by Alexander von Humboldt, a peak once believed the world's highest, and Ecuador's tallest summit all name which mountain?
questions.f: Because Earth bulges at the equator, Chimborazo's top is the farthest surface point from the planet's centre.

questions.q: A US pilot whose plane stuck fast on a tabletop mountain in 1937, a Pemon name meaning 'waterfall of the deepest place', and Auyan-tepui identify what?
questions.f: Jimmie Angel's plane sat on the summit for 33 years before being lifted off by helicopter.

questions.q: A tripoint of Venezuela, Brazil and Guyana, sheer 400-metre cliffs, and the setting that inspired a 1912 Conan Doyle novel name which mountain?
questions.f: Its flat top is a tepui, a sandstone island in the sky with plants found nowhere else.

questions.q: A Norwegian claim, a surface about 93 per cent glacier, and a position roughly 1,700 km from Antarctica identify which island?
questions.f: Bouvet Island is generally reckoned the most remote island on the planet.

questions.q: A village called Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, a whole population evacuated to England in 1961, and just a handful of shared surnames name which place?
questions.f: It is the most remote inhabited archipelago in the world, with no airstrip at all.

questions.q: A population of about 50, descendants of the Bounty's crew, and Britain's least populated overseas territory point to which islands?
questions.f: Pitcairn's people once earned much of their income from selling postage stamps.

questions.q: A 1920 treaty letting citizens of many nations settle visa-free, more polar bears than people, and the world's northernmost commercial airport name where?
questions.f: A vault dug into Svalbard's permafrost stores backup seeds for crops worldwide.

questions.q: A military signals post on Ellesmere Island, a site 817 km from the North Pole, and a name taken from a Royal Navy ship identify which settlement?
questions.f: Alert is the northernmost permanently inhabited place on Earth.

questions.q: A port on the Beagle Channel, a former prison colony, and the main departure point for Antarctic cruises identify which city?
questions.f: Ushuaia calls itself the city at the end of the world, the southernmost city anywhere.

questions.q: A Peruvian gold-mining town at about 5,100 metres, homes without piped water, and thin air with half the usual oxygen identify which settlement?
questions.f: La Rinconada is the highest permanent human settlement in the world.

questions.q: Dragon's blood trees, part of Yemen, and around a third of its plants growing nowhere else identify which island?
questions.f: Socotra split from mainland Arabia millions of years ago, leaving its plants to evolve alone.

questions.q: Twenty-two Belgian patches inside the Netherlands, borders painted across pavements, and two town halls in one small town name which place?
questions.f: Some front doors there have two house numbers, one for each country.

questions.q: A Spanish town encircled by France, and a 1659 treaty that handed over villages but not towns, identify which enclave?
questions.f: Llivia's lawyers argued it was a villa, not a village, and so it stayed Spanish.

questions.q: Two islands under 4 km apart, one Russian and one American, with a clock difference of about 21 hours, are called what?
questions.f: The date line runs between them, so locals call them Tomorrow Island and Yesterday Isle.

questions.q: A troop of Barbary macaques, a name from Arabic meaning 'mountain of Tariq', and a main road that crosses an airport runway identify which place?
questions.f: Traffic on Winston Churchill Avenue stops with barriers every time a plane lands.

questions.q: A country smaller than New York's Central Park, an Oceanographic Museum founded by a prince, and citizens barred from its own casino identify where?
questions.f: Monaco is the second-smallest country, yet has the world's densest population.

questions.q: A country with two heads of state, one a French president and the other a Spanish bishop, is which nation?
questions.f: Andorra's odd double rule dates from a medieval agreement made in 1278.

questions.q: A principality with no airport, an accidental 2007 border crossing by lost Swiss soldiers, and neighbours that are themselves landlocked identify where?
questions.f: Liechtenstein is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world.

questions.q: Liquid water sealed for millions of years, four kilometres of ice above it, and radar surveys near a Russian research base reveal what?
questions.f: Lake Vostok is the largest of more than 400 lakes hidden under Antarctic ice.

questions.q: A West Antarctic hollow 2,540 metres below sea level, buried under ice yet not under sea, is called what?
questions.f: It is the lowest point on any land surface on Earth that no ocean covers.

questions.q: A flow driven by the westerlies, unbroken by any continent, carrying more water than any other current, is called the...?
questions.f: It moves over 100 times as much water as all the world's rivers combined.

questions.q: Peruvian fishers noticing warm water around Christmas, collapsing anchovy catches, and a Spanish name meaning 'the boy' describe which phenomenon?
questions.f: El Nino shifts rainfall worldwide, bringing floods to some regions and drought to others.

questions.q: A downslope wind east of the Rockies, temperature jumps of 20 degrees in an hour, and a nickname meaning 'snow eater' describe which wind?
questions.f: One Chinook in Montana in 1972 raised the temperature by 57 degrees Celsius in a day.

questions.q: A dry season wind off the Sahara, dust that grounds West African flights, and a local nickname of 'the doctor' describe which wind?
questions.f: Harmattan dust from Africa regularly drifts all the way across the Atlantic.

questions.q: A Persian tale of three travelling princes, an old Arabic name for Sri Lanka, and a letter written by Horace Walpole in 1754 gave English which word?
questions.f: Sarandib was the Arab traders' name for Sri Lanka, and it means happy accidents to this day.

questions.q: A twisting river in western Turkey, the nearby ancient port of Miletus, and a looping border pattern in Greek pottery gave English which word?
questions.f: The river is now called the Buyuk Menderes, still winding exactly as it always did.

questions.q: An eastern Mediterranean island rich in ore, the Latin phrase 'aes Cyprium', and the chemical symbol Cu explain the name of which metal?
questions.f: Cyprus supplied so much of it that the island's name became the metal's name.

questions.q: A district of ancient Thessaly, hillside stones that tugged at iron, and a Greek adjective built from that place name give us which word?
questions.f: The stones were lodestones, and Magnesia's name also lives on in magnesium.

questions.q: Toquilla straw woven in Montecristi, canal workers buying them by the crate, and a 1906 photograph of a US president explain the misleading name of what?
questions.f: Panama hats are made in Ecuador; they only got their name from where they were sold.

questions.q: Which country controls the largest exclusive economic zone of ocean in the world?
questions.f: Its scattered overseas islands give France rights over more than 10 million square kilometres of sea.

questions.q: Which national capital lies closest to the equator?
questions.f: Quito sits about 25 kilometres from the line, with a monument marking the spot.

questions.q: Which two capital cities are the closest together anywhere on Earth?
questions.f: You can walk from one to the other in minutes, since one sits inside the other.

questions.q: Which two countries are usually said to share the world's shortest land border, about 150 metres?
questions.f: They meet near Kazungula, where four countries almost touch at one point on the Zambezi.

questions.q: Which country's flag has a completely different emblem on its front and back?
questions.f: One side shows the national coat of arms, the other the seal of the treasury.

questions.q: Which country's flag has 14 red and white stripes plus a 14-pointed star?
questions.f: The 14 points stand for its 13 states plus the federal territories.

questions.q: Which country once flew the world's only flag that was a single plain colour with no design?
questions.f: Libya's flag was solid green from 1977 until 2011, when the older tricolour returned.

questions.q: Which country's official national animal is the unicorn?
questions.f: The unicorn appears chained on the royal arms, a symbol of untameable pride.

questions.q: Which country contains the world's tallest statue, standing about 182 metres high?
questions.f: The Statue of Unity rises from an island in the Narmada River in Gujarat.

questions.q: Which country contains the longest bridge in the world, a rail viaduct over 160 km long?
questions.f: The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge carries high-speed trains across low, wet farmland.

questions.q: Which country has the world's largest airport by land area, bigger than a small nation?
questions.f: King Fahd International near Dammam covers about 780 square kilometres.

questions.q: Which Greek scholar worked out the Earth's circumference around 240 BC using shadows and a well?
questions.f: He also invented the word 'geography', and his answer was within a few per cent of the truth.

questions.q: Whose ancient 'Geographia', rediscovered in the 1400s, gave Renaissance mapmakers their grid of coordinates?
questions.f: His maps also badly underestimated the size of the ocean, which encouraged Columbus to sail west.

questions.q: On whose 1507 world map did the name 'America' appear in print for the first time?
questions.f: He later regretted it and dropped the name, but by then it had already stuck.

questions.q: Which traveller from Tangier journeyed roughly 120,000 kilometres across Africa and Asia in the 1300s?
questions.f: His written account covers about 40 modern countries, from Mali to China.

questions.q: Which admiral led China's huge treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean in the early 1400s?
questions.f: Some of his ships may have been several times longer than Columbus's flagship.

questions.q: Which German geographer coined the term 'Silk Road' in 1877?
questions.f: The traders themselves never used the name; it is barely 150 years old.

questions.q: Which explorer completed the first sea voyage from Europe to India around the southern tip of Africa?
questions.f: Dias rounded the Cape first, but da Gama pushed on and reached Calicut in 1498.

questions.q: Which lake is thought to contain more islands than any other lake on Earth?
questions.f: Lake Huron has around 30,000 islands, including the world's largest lake island.

questions.q: Which country records more tornadoes for its size than anywhere else on Earth?
questions.f: They are usually small and brief, but Britain averages around 30 to 50 a year.

questions.q: Which strait's name means 'ox ford', from a Greek story about a girl turned into a cow?
questions.f: Io, fleeing Hera, was said to have swum across it.

questions.q: The strait Bab-el-Mandeb, between Africa and Arabia, has a name meaning...?
questions.f: Sailors named it for the danger of its currents and reefs.

questions.q: The Latin name Helvetia, still printed on stamps and coins, belongs to which country?
questions.f: Using Latin avoids favouring any one of Switzerland's four official languages.

questions.q: Hibernia was the Roman name for which land?
questions.f: Caledonia meant Scotland and Cambria meant Wales in the same Roman style.
