questions.q: Aotearoa, the Maori name for New Zealand, is usually translated as...?
c: Land of the long white cloud
questions.f: Early navigators may have spotted the islands first as cloud banked over unseen mountains.

questions.q: Shqiperia, Albania's own name for itself, is often explained as meaning...?
questions.f: A black double-headed eagle has flown on its flag for centuries.

questions.q: Misr is the local name of which country?
questions.f: The name is thousands of years old and appears in ancient Semitic records.

questions.q: Algeria's Arabic name, al-Jaza'ir, means...?
questions.f: It refers to small islands that once lay off the coast of Algiers harbour.

questions.q: In South Asian city names such as Islamabad and Hyderabad, the ending '-abad' means...?
questions.f: It comes from a Persian word, so Hyderabad is roughly 'Haydar's settled place'.

questions.q: In Chinese place names such as Tian Shan, the element 'shan' means...?
questions.f: Tian Shan means 'heavenly mountains', a range stretching across Central Asia.

questions.q: In place names such as Aberdeen and Inverness, 'aber' and 'inver' both mean...?
questions.f: So Inverness is the mouth of the River Ness, and Aberdeen the mouth of the Dee.

questions.q: English town names ending in '-by', such as Grimsby and Whitby, were left by which settlers?
questions.f: A Norse 'by' was a farm or village, and hundreds still dot northern England.

questions.q: In Japanese place names, the ending 'jima' or 'shima' means...?
questions.f: So Hiroshima means 'broad island' and Iwo Jima means 'sulphur island'.

questions.q: An 1815 eruption on Sumbawa, a summerless 1816 in Europe, and a gloomy lakeside holiday that produced a monster novel point to which volcano?
questions.f: Tambora's dust cooled the whole planet, and the wet, dark summer inspired Frankenstein.

questions.q: A 1783 Icelandic fissure eruption, a sulphurous haze that ruined harvests across Europe, and a possible nudge towards revolution in France name which volcano?
questions.f: Laki poured out lava for eight months, the largest such flow in recorded history.

questions.q: A name meaning 'island mountain glacier', a bigger neighbour called Katla, and an ash plume that cost airlines billions in 2010 identify which volcano?
questions.f: Its eruption grounded around 100,000 flights across Europe in a single week.

questions.q: A Bronze Age blast that hollowed out a Minoan island, a crescent of cliffs around a flooded crater, and one theory about Atlantis point to which island?
questions.f: Its caldera is so deep that cruise ships anchor in what was once a mountain's heart.

questions.q: An island that rose out of the sea in 1963, a name taken from a Norse fire giant, and a ban on all visitors but a few scientists identify which place?
questions.f: Scientists watch Surtsey to see exactly how life colonises brand-new land.

questions.q: Matching fossils on facing coasts, a theory laughed at in 1912, and a fatal Greenland expedition in 1930 point to which scientist?
questions.f: Wegener's drifting continents were only accepted decades after his death.

questions.q: A Flemish mapmaker imprisoned in 1544, a 1569 chart letting sailors rule straight compass lines, and swollen polar regions point to whom?
questions.f: Mercator also coined the modern use of the word 'atlas' for a book of maps.

questions.q: A 1714 act of parliament, a prize for solving longitude at sea, and a watch called H4 tested on a voyage to Jamaica point to which craftsman?
questions.f: Harrison's clocks let sailors finally know how far east or west they had travelled.

questions.q: A silver planisphere made for King Roger II of Sicily, maps drawn with south at the top, and a 12th-century Muslim geographer point to whom?
questions.f: His Tabula Rogeriana stayed the most accurate world map for about 300 years.

questions.q: A New Zealand beekeeper, a Sherpa from the Khumbu valley, and news that reached London on a coronation morning point to which pair?
questions.f: They stood on Everest's summit on 29 May 1953; Britain heard on 2 June.

questions.q: A lifeboat named the James Caird, a mountain range crossed on foot in 1916, and a crew rescued after nearly two years point to which explorer?
questions.f: Shackleton lost his ship but not a single member of his expedition.

questions.q: A ship deliberately frozen into the Arctic ice, a travel document for refugees, and the 1922 Nobel Peace Prize point to which Norwegian?
questions.f: Nansen passports let stateless people travel when no country would issue them papers.

questions.q: A Scottish sailor marooned for over four years, a Chilean island group renamed in 1966, and a novel of 1719 point to which archipelago?
questions.f: Alexander Selkirk's real ordeal helped inspire Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe.

questions.q: A missionary lost in central Africa, a New York newspaper's funded search, and a famously stiff greeting in 1871 point to which explorer?
questions.f: His four words - 'Dr Livingstone, I presume' - became the most quoted line in exploration.

questions.q: A Victorian Englishwoman canoeing the Ogowe river, a long skirt worn through swamps, and a book called Travels in West Africa point to whom?
questions.f: She insisted her heavy skirt once saved her by cushioning a fall into a game pit.

questions.q: Desert journeys mapped by camel, a hand in drawing Iraq's borders, and the founding of the Baghdad museum point to which traveller?
questions.f: Bell knew Arabic, Persian and archaeology, and was nicknamed the Desert Queen.

questions.q: An African American explorer fluent in Inuktitut, a 1909 polar expedition, and a reburial at Arlington in 1988 point to whom?
questions.f: Henson was the expedition's most skilled dog driver and sledge builder.

questions.q: A line drawn on a map in 1494, a pope's ruling between two kingdoms, and the reason one huge South American country speaks Portuguese identify which agreement?
questions.f: The line fell just far enough west to hand Portugal the eastern bulge of Brazil.

questions.q: A nutmeg island signed away in 1667, a Dutch claim swapped for a North American settlement, and the Banda archipelago describe the deal that secured which place for England?
questions.f: The Dutch kept tiny Run and its spice trees; England kept the island that became New York.

questions.q: A sale for 7.2 million dollars in 1867, a purchase mocked as one secretary's Folly, and later strikes of gold and oil describe which land deal?
questions.f: It worked out at about two cents an acre for territory twice the size of Texas.

questions.q: A failed French dig of the 1880s, a doctor named Gorgas fighting mosquitoes, and a 1914 opening overshadowed by war in Europe describe what?
questions.f: Controlling mosquitoes was what finally made the crossing possible.

questions.q: A 32-kilometre dam finished in 1932, an inland sea turned into a freshwater lake, and a brand-new province called Flevoland describe which project?
questions.f: The Dutch have reclaimed so much land that their maps genuinely keep changing shape.

questions.q: The world's largest reservoir by volume, a dam on the Zambezi, and a 1958 animal rescue named Operation Noah identify which lake?
questions.f: Rangers ferried thousands of stranded animals off shrinking islands as the water rose.

questions.q: A Yale lecturer led uphill by a local farmer in 1911, a set of overgrown terraces, and world fame from 1913 magazine photographs point to whom?
questions.f: Local families already knew the ruins well; Bingham brought them to global attention.

questions.q: A Swiss traveller disguised as a pilgrim in 1812, a narrow gorge called the Siq, and the first European account of a rose-red city point to whom?
questions.f: He was only 27, and had learned Arabic well enough to pass as a Syrian trader.

questions.q: A German businessman digging at a Turkish mound called Hisarlik in the 1870s, convinced an ancient poem described a real city, was who?
questions.f: Schliemann's rough digging destroyed layers, but he did find a real city under the myth.

questions.q: Shapes visible in full only from the air, a Peruvian plateau where it almost never rains, and a German mathematician who swept them for decades identify what?
questions.f: Maria Reiche protected the lines with a broom and a stepladder for over 40 years.

questions.q: An Irish mound older than the Egyptian pyramids, a stone-lined passage, and a roof-box that lets sunrise in at midwinter identify which site?
questions.f: For a few minutes each winter solstice, sunlight creeps down the passage to the inner chamber.

questions.q: Carved stone pillars on a Turkish hilltop, deliberately buried around 8000 BC, and a date older than farming itself identify which site?
questions.f: It suggests people gathered to build monuments before they settled down to grow crops.

questions.q: A Cappadocian underground city rediscovered in 1963 behind a house wall, eighteen levels deep, with wells and stables, is called what?
questions.f: It could shelter perhaps 20,000 people, plus their food stores and animals.

questions.q: A Polish mine worked for 700 years, chapels carved from rock salt, and chandeliers made of salt crystals identify which place?
questions.f: Miners carved statues underground for centuries, purely to decorate their workplace.

questions.q: A capital opened in 2005, roads up to 20 lanes wide that stand almost empty, and a country once called Burma identify which city?
questions.f: Naypyidaw covers several times the area of New York City with a fraction of the people.

questions.q: A capital moved 1,200 km north in 1997, winter temperatures near minus 40, and a country stretching from the Caspian to China identify which city?
questions.f: It is reckoned the second-coldest capital city in the world, after Ulaanbaatar.

questions.q: A capital built from scratch in the 1980s at a country's geographic centre, beside a granite dome called Aso Rock, is which city?
questions.f: It replaced Lagos, which had grown far too crowded to serve as a capital.

questions.q: A capital moved to a president's home village, and the largest church building in the world, identify which city?
questions.f: The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace was modelled on St Peter's, but built even taller.

questions.q: Which country's official legislative capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte?
questions.f: Colombo is bigger and busier, but parliament sits in Kotte just outside it.

questions.q: Which city is Switzerland's federal seat of government, despite not being its largest?
questions.f: Switzerland calls it a 'federal city' rather than a capital, to keep the cantons equal.

questions.q: Which tiny Indonesian island group was for centuries the world's only source of nutmeg?
questions.f: Nutmeg was once worth more than its weight in gold in European markets.

questions.q: Which reservoir has the largest surface area of any artificial lake in the world?
questions.f: Ghana's Akosombo Dam flooded about 3.6 per cent of the whole country.

questions.q: Which woman was the first to reach the summit of Everest, in 1975?
questions.f: Tabei later became the first woman to climb the highest peak on every continent.

questions.q: Which vessel carried two men to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 1960?
questions.f: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh spent about 20 minutes at nearly 11 kilometres down.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain in South America?
questions.f: At 6,961 metres, Aconcagua is the highest peak outside Asia.

questions.q: Which is the highest peak in Oceania, rising from the mountains of New Guinea?
questions.f: Also called Carstensz Pyramid, it has small glaciers despite sitting near the equator.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain on the Australian mainland?
questions.f: At 2,228 metres it is the easiest of the Seven Summits to walk up.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain in the British Isles?
questions.f: Ben Nevis is the collapsed remains of an ancient volcano, 1,345 metres high.

questions.q: The legend of 'El Dorado' originally described not a city but a...?
questions.f: Spanish reports told of a chief dusted with gold powder before diving into a lake.

questions.q: The word 'Shangri-La' for a hidden paradise was invented in a 1933 novel called...?
questions.f: James Hilton set it in a hidden Himalayan valley where nobody grew old.

questions.q: The poetic word 'Xanadu' comes from the real summer capital of which ruler?
questions.f: Shangdu's ruins still stand in Inner Mongolia; Coleridge made the name famous.

questions.q: 'Cathay', used by medieval European travellers, was a name for which country?
questions.f: It came from the Khitan people who once ruled northern China.

questions.q: Calling a set of rules 'byzantine' means they are needlessly complicated, from the old name of which city?
questions.f: Byzantium became Constantinople and then Istanbul, but the adjective stuck.

questions.q: The word 'laconic', meaning using very few words, comes from a region of ancient...?
questions.f: Laconia was Sparta's region, and its people were famous for blunt one-line replies.

questions.q: The word 'vandalism' comes from a people who journeyed from central Europe to rule which region?
questions.f: The Vandals crossed Spain and set up a kingdom around Carthage in the 400s.

questions.q: Calling an artist 'bohemian' comes from the name of a region in which modern country?
questions.f: The French wrongly believed travelling Roma people had come from Bohemia.

questions.q: The word 'arcadian', meaning peaceful and rural, comes from a mountainous region of...?
questions.f: Poets pictured Arcadia's shepherds living a simple, perfect country life.

questions.q: The spider name 'tarantula' comes from a town in which country?
questions.f: Taranto also gave its name to the tarantella, a dance once thought to cure spider bites.

questions.q: The neckwear called a 'cravat' takes its name from soldiers of which nationality?
questions.f: French troops copied the knotted scarves of Croatian cavalry in the 1600s.

questions.q: The soft leather called 'suede' is named after which country?
questions.f: French shops sold gants de Suede - Swedish gloves - made from the skin's rough side.

questions.q: To 'canter' on horseback is named after pilgrims riding to which English city?
questions.f: The easy pace was called the Canterbury gallop, then shortened.

questions.q: The five-line comic poem called a 'limerick' shares its name with a city in which country?
questions.f: Nobody is quite sure how the Irish city's name became attached to the verse form.

questions.q: The 'Jerusalem' in Jerusalem artichoke is thought to be a mangled version of which word?
questions.f: Girasole is Italian for sunflower, which is what the plant actually is.

questions.q: The root vegetable called a 'swede' in Britain is named after which country?
questions.f: Elsewhere it is called a rutabaga, from a Swedish word meaning 'root bag'.

questions.q: The satsuma orange is named after a former province of which country?
questions.f: Satsuma is now part of Kagoshima, at the southern end of Kyushu.

questions.q: The kiwifruit was renamed for marketing in the 1960s. What was it called before?
questions.f: New Zealand growers renamed it after their national bird to help it sell abroad.

questions.q: The word 'mocha', used for coffee, comes from a port in which country?
questions.f: Al Mokha on the Red Sea shipped the world's coffee for nearly 200 years.

questions.q: Riding trousers called 'jodhpurs' are named after a city in which country?
questions.f: A maharaja of Jodhpur wore them at Queen Victoria's jubilee and started a fashion.

questions.q: The word 'juggernaut', meaning an unstoppable force, comes from a temple festival in which country?
questions.f: European visitors watched the enormous chariot of Jagannath rolling through Puri.

questions.q: The word 'academy' comes from the name of a grove on the edge of which city?
questions.f: Plato taught in a grove sacred to a hero called Akademos.

questions.q: A hat-maker is called a 'milliner' after traders from which city?
questions.f: Milaners sold fine ribbons, gloves and straw goods across Renaissance Europe.

questions.q: Which fine cotton cloth is named after the Iraqi city of Mosul?
questions.f: Damask comes from Damascus and calico from Calicut in the very same way.

questions.q: Which sauce is traditionally said to be named after Mahon, a port on Menorca?
questions.f: French forces are said to have brought the recipe home after taking the port in 1756.

questions.q: Water alkaline enough to turn dead birds into stone-like statues, a nearby volcano that erupts black lava, and millions of nesting flamingos identify which lake?
questions.f: Ol Doinyo Lengai beside it erupts the coolest, runniest lava on Earth.

questions.q: Sandstone layered like a cake, iron and mineral bands laid down over 20 million years, and a Gansu park nicknamed the rainbow mountains identify what?
questions.f: The stripes are old seabed and desert sands, tipped on their side by colliding plates.

questions.q: Around 40,000 interlocking hexagonal basalt columns, a legend about a giant building a bridge to Scotland, and the Antrim coast identify which place?
questions.f: The columns formed as thick lava cooled and cracked into neat six-sided blocks.

questions.q: Snow-white terraces of mineral rock, warm pools stepping down a hillside, and the ruined Roman city of Hierapolis above them identify which site?
questions.f: Pamukkale means 'cotton castle' in Turkish, and the white rock is travertine.

questions.q: A Mauritanian bull's-eye 40 km wide, layers of rock worn into rings, and a landmark astronauts use to find their place identify which feature?
questions.f: Once thought an impact crater, it is now read as a deeply eroded dome of rock.

questions.q: Around 1,200 grassy mounds on the island of Bohol that turn brown in the dry season are known as what?
questions.f: They are the eroded remains of ancient coral limestone lifted above the sea.

questions.q: Some 1,600 limestone towers rising from green water, and a Vietnamese name meaning 'descending dragon', identify which bay?
questions.f: Legend says dragons spat jewels into the sea to shield the coast from invaders.

questions.q: Sixteen lakes stepping downhill, natural dams built by moss and algae, and a Croatian national park identify which site?
questions.f: The travertine barriers are still growing about a centimetre a year.

questions.q: Dead camelthorn trees standing 900 years after they died, a white clay pan, and orange dunes 300 metres high identify which place?
questions.f: The air is so dry that the trees cannot rot; they simply bleach in the sun.

questions.q: A fog-bound Namibian shore, seal colonies in their thousands, and the rusting hulls of stranded ships give which coast its grim name?
questions.f: Cold ocean water meeting hot desert air brews the fog that trapped so many ships.

questions.q: Limestone needles too sharp to walk on barefoot, a Malagasy name saying exactly that, and lemurs leaping between spikes identify which reserve?
questions.f: Rain slowly dissolved the limestone downward, leaving a forest of stone blades.

questions.q: A river that blooms deep red for a few months each year thanks to an underwater plant, in Colombia's Serrania de la Macarena, is called what?
questions.f: Locals call it the liquid rainbow, because red plants, green algae and yellow sand mix.

questions.q: A bubble-gum pink lake on Middle Island that stays pink even in a bottle identifies which Australian curiosity?
questions.f: Salt-loving microbes and algae make a pigment that colours the whole lake.

questions.q: A Nevada mound spraying water in bright green and red, growing from a well drilled by accident in 1964, is called what?
questions.f: Heat-loving algae paint the growing mineral cone its startling colours.

questions.q: Rocks that leave long trails across a dry lake bed, finally filmed moving in 2013, are found at which place?
questions.f: Thin sheets of night ice break up and shove the stones along in a light breeze.

questions.q: A rusty red waterfall pouring from a glacier, iron-rich brine sealed away for a million years, and the Taylor Valley identify which Antarctic oddity?
questions.f: The salty water stays liquid at temperatures well below freezing point.

questions.q: An Ethiopian settlement with the world's highest average yearly temperature, salt terraces and sulphur springs, is called what?
questions.f: Its average temperature over a year is above 34 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: A Jordanian sandstone valley used as Mars in many films, with 2,000-year-old Nabataean inscriptions on its cliffs, is called what?
questions.f: Its name is often translated as the Valley of the Moon.

questions.q: Beehive-striped sandstone domes in Western Australia, little known to outsiders until 1983, are called what?
questions.f: Local Aboriginal peoples had known the range, now called Purnululu, for millennia.

questions.q: A New Zealand valley of over 6 metres of rain a year, cliffs dropping straight into deep water, and a place named a sound but really a fiord is which place?
questions.f: Its Maori name, Piopiotahi, refers to a single thrush in an old legend.

questions.q: Tides rising and falling up to 16 metres twice a day, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, happen in which bay?
questions.f: About 100 billion tonnes of water flow in and out of the bay each tide.

questions.q: A rocky island abbey cut off by tides of up to 14 metres, once reached only by a causeway of sand, is which site?
questions.f: Locals warned that the tide came in 'at the speed of a galloping horse'.

questions.q: A 55-kilometre sea crossing with a 6.7-km undersea tunnel, opened in 2018, links Hong Kong, Macau and which city?
questions.f: The tunnel lets ships pass overhead without needing a bridge tall enough for them.

questions.q: A railway crossing a pass over 5,000 metres high, with extra oxygen piped into the carriages, runs in which country?
questions.f: The Qinghai-Tibet railway is the highest railway in the world.

questions.q: A road running roughly 30,000 km from Alaska towards Argentina, broken only by a roadless rainforest gap, is called what?
questions.f: The missing stretch, the Darien Gap, has never been bridged by any road.

questions.q: A paved international road crossing the Khunjerab Pass at 4,714 metres links China with which country?
questions.f: The Karakoram Highway is the highest paved road border crossing in the world.

questions.q: Which country's Seikan Tunnel holds the record for the longest undersea section of any tunnel?
questions.f: About 23 kilometres of its length runs beneath the Tsugaru Strait.

questions.q: Which is the most powerful waterfall in Europe by volume of water?
questions.f: Meltwater from Iceland's biggest glacier feeds Dettifoss all summer long.

questions.q: Which Caribbean island holds a huge naturally boiling lake in a volcanic valley?
questions.f: Dominica's Boiling Lake is a flooded crack in the ground heated by molten rock below.

questions.q: A cave system in New Zealand lit by the glow of thousands of fungus gnat larvae is at which place?
questions.f: Visitors drift through in boats in total silence, since noise makes the glow switch off.

questions.q: Which waterfall in Guyana is famous for having one of the world's greatest single drops by volume?
questions.f: Its single plunge is about 226 metres, nearly five times the height of Niagara.

questions.q: The name 'Amsterdam' describes a dam built on which river?
questions.f: Rotterdam is named the same way, after a dam on the little river Rotte.

questions.q: 'Copenhagen' comes from Danish words meaning...?
questions.f: Kobenhavn grew rich taxing ships passing through its narrow strait.

questions.q: The name 'Dublin' comes from Irish words meaning...?
questions.f: Dubh linn was a dark tidal pool where Viking ships once moored.

questions.q: Serbia's capital, Belgrade, has a name meaning...?
questions.f: Its white limestone fortress sits where the Sava joins the Danube.

questions.q: Budapest was created in 1873 by joining Pest with which other town?
questions.f: Buda sits on the hilly west bank and Pest on the flat east bank of the Danube.

questions.q: The Russian port name 'Vladivostok' means...?
questions.f: It sits closer to Tokyo and Beijing than to Moscow.

questions.q: Mongolia's capital, Ulaanbaatar, has a name meaning...?
questions.f: It is the coldest national capital city in the world.

questions.q: Nepal's capital, Kathmandu, takes its name from a...?
questions.f: Kasthamandap was a huge pavilion said to be built from a single tree.

questions.q: Bangkok's older name, Bang Makok, is usually translated as...?
questions.f: Its full ceremonial Thai name runs to over 160 letters.

questions.q: 'Kuala Lumpur' means...?
questions.f: The city grew up where two rivers meet, at the heart of a tin-mining district.

questions.q: Vietnam's capital, Hanoi, has a name meaning...?
questions.f: It sits in a bend of the Red River, ringed by water on several sides.

questions.q: 'Shanghai' means...?
questions.f: It began as a fishing town on the mudflats of the Yangtze delta.

questions.q: Egypt's capital, Cairo, has an Arabic name meaning...?
questions.f: Al-Qahira was founded in 969 as a walled royal city beside older settlements.

questions.q: Sudan's capital, Khartoum, is usually said to be named after the shape of...?
questions.f: The strip of land where the Blue and White Nile meet curves like a trunk.

questions.q: Kenya's capital, Nairobi, takes its name from a Maasai phrase meaning...?
questions.f: It began in 1899 as a railway depot beside a cool stream.

questions.q: Morocco's capital, Rabat, has a name meaning...?
questions.f: A ribat was a fortified religious outpost, often guarding a frontier.

questions.q: Libya's capital, Tripoli, has a Greek-derived name meaning...?
questions.f: There is another Tripoli in Lebanon, named in exactly the same way.

questions.q: Bolivia's La Paz has a name meaning...?
questions.f: Its full original name celebrated peace after a Spanish civil conflict in Peru.

questions.q: Uruguay's capital, Montevideo, is traditionally explained as meaning...?
questions.f: A lookout is said to have spotted the low hill of the Cerro and shouted it out.

questions.q: Canada's Toronto takes its name from an Iroquoian phrase meaning...?
c: Where there are trees in the water
questions.f: It described fish weirs made of stakes driven into a narrow channel.

questions.q: Which US city's name comes from a Miami-Illinois word for a wild onion or leek?
questions.f: Shikaakwa described the smelly wild garlic growing along the riverbank.

questions.q: The city name 'Detroit' comes from a French word meaning...?
questions.f: It guards the narrow channel linking Lake Huron to Lake Erie.

questions.q: 'Baton Rouge' in Louisiana means...?
questions.f: French explorers reported a reddened pole marking a boundary between peoples.

questions.q: Which country calls itself Suomi?
questions.f: Finnish is unrelated to Swedish or Russian, but is a cousin of Estonian and Hungarian.

questions.q: Which country calls itself Magyarorszag?
questions.f: It means 'land of the Magyars', the people who settled the Danube plain in the 800s.

questions.q: Which country calls itself Sakartvelo?
questions.f: Its alphabet, with 33 rounded letters, is used for almost no other language.

questions.q: Which country calls itself Hayastan?
questions.f: The name traces back to Hayk, a legendary founding ancestor.

questions.q: In Scottish and English place names, the ending '-ness', as in Inverness, means...?
questions.f: Skegness and Sheerness are both coastal headlands too.

questions.q: In Irish and Scottish place names, 'kil' as in Kilkenny usually means...?
questions.f: From cill, a monk's cell or small church.

questions.q: In Welsh place names, 'llan' as in Llandudno means...?
questions.f: Hundreds of Welsh villages begin with llan followed by a saint's name.

questions.q: In York, streets ending in '-gate', such as Micklegate, come from a Norse word meaning...?
questions.f: Confusingly, York's actual gates are called bars, not gates.

questions.q: In Arabic place names, 'ras' as in Ras al-Khaimah means...?
questions.f: Jebel means mountain and ain means spring in the same naming system.

questions.q: The knitted headgear called a 'balaclava' is named after a village in which region?
questions.f: British troops in the freezing winter of 1854 were sent knitted hoods to wear.

questions.q: The words 'spa' and 'duffel' both come from town names in which country?
questions.f: Spa gave its name to health resorts, and Duffel to thick woollen cloth.

questions.q: Angora wool and the Angora rabbit are named after the older name of which capital city?
questions.f: Angora cats, goats and rabbits all take their name from the same city.

questions.q: Despite its name, the Great Dane dog breed was mainly developed in which country?
questions.f: German breeders called it the Deutsche Dogge; a French writer's label stuck in English.

questions.q: The dried fruit called a 'currant' is named after which Greek city?
questions.f: Raisins of Corinth were shipped across medieval Europe under that name.

questions.q: The melon called a 'cantaloupe' is named after an estate near which city?
questions.f: Cantalupo was a papal country estate where the seeds were first grown in Europe.

questions.q: The water of the Caspian Sea is slightly salty rather than fresh.
questions.f: It is about a third as salty as the open ocean, a leftover of an ancient sea.

questions.q: Lake Chad has shrunk to a small fraction of the size it covered in the 1960s.
questions.f: Drought and irrigation have cut it by more than 90 per cent in living memory.

questions.q: Which strong farm animal pulled the plow in olden days?
questions.f: Oxen are trained cattle, and farmers used them to pull plows for thousands of years.

questions.q: Before electric lights, what did people burn for light at night?
questions.f: Candles were often made from beeswax, and big houses needed hundreds of them.

questions.q: What pushed old sailing ships across the sea?
questions.f: Big cloth sails caught the wind, so sailors watched the weather very carefully.

questions.q: Long, long ago Earth had a freezing cold time called the ___ Age.
questions.f: During the Ice Age, giant sheets of ice called glaciers covered huge parts of the land.

questions.q: What did cave people make warm clothes from?
questions.f: They stitched furs together using needles carved from bone.

questions.q: The very first trains were powered by what?
questions.f: Burning coal boiled water into steam, and the steam pushed the train's engine.

questions.q: On sunny days long ago, what did people use to tell the time?
questions.f: A sundial's shadow slowly moves as the sun crosses the sky.

questions.q: Royal crowns long ago were usually made of which shiny yellow metal?
questions.f: Gold never rusts, so ancient golden treasures still shine today.

questions.q: Which humped animal carried explorers across hot deserts?
questions.f: Camels can travel for days across the desert without a drink of water.

questions.q: Which animals pulled sleds for explorers in snowy lands?
questions.f: Teams of strong sled dogs helped explorers reach the icy ends of the Earth.

questions.q: Which bird carried rolled-up messages for people long ago?
questions.f: Homing pigeons can find their way home from hundreds of kilometres away.

questions.q: Which snappy animal swam in Egypt's great river long ago?
questions.f: Crocodiles still live in African rivers today, just like in ancient times.

questions.q: Stone Age people made sewing needles out of animal bone.
questions.f: Bone needles more than 20,000 years old have been found by scientists.

questions.q: The first Olympic champions won crowns made of leaves, not gold medals.
questions.f: Ancient Greek winners were crowned with a wreath of olive leaves.

questions.q: Children long ago played with dolls and spinning tops.
questions.f: Toy dolls and tops thousands of years old have been dug up in ancient cities.

questions.q: What did ancient Greeks usually wear on their feet?
questions.f: Greek sandals were made of leather and tied on with straps.

questions.q: In stories, pirates lock their treasure inside a big wooden what?
questions.f: Real pirates usually spent their treasure fast — buried chests are mostly from storybooks!

questions.q: A person who travels far to discover new places is called an...?
questions.f: The word 'explorer' comes from a Latin word meaning 'to search out.'

questions.q: A person who robs treasure from ships at sea is called a...?
questions.f: Pirates flew scary flags so other ships would give up without a fight.

questions.q: A king's son is called a...?
questions.f: 'Prince' comes from a Latin word meaning 'first person.'

questions.q: What do we call the funny joker who entertained kings and queens?
questions.f: Jesters often wore floppy hats with jingling bells on the ends.

questions.q: Sunday is named after what bright thing in the sky?
questions.f: Monday got its name from the Moon — it means 'Moon day.'

questions.q: A person who bakes bread for a village is called a...?
questions.f: Long ago people got last names from their jobs — that is why Baker is a common name!

questions.q: Who hammers hot iron into horseshoes and tools?
questions.f: The 'black' in blacksmith comes from the dark color of the iron they hammered.

questions.q: The group of workers who sail a ship together is called the...?
questions.f: Every crew member had a job, from cook to lookout.

questions.q: The word 'breakfast' means to break your nighttime...?
questions.f: A 'fast' is a time of not eating — breakfast ends the fast you kept while sleeping.

questions.q: A made-up old story about gods and heroes is called a...?
questions.f: The Greek myths about Zeus and Hercules are thousands of years old.

questions.q: The land a king rules is called his...?
questions.f: 'Kingdom' is simply 'king' plus '-dom,' an old ending that means his land and power.

questions.q: A grand, fancy home where a king and queen live is called a...?
questions.f: Some royal palaces have more than a thousand rooms!

questions.q: A long trip across the sea is called a...?
questions.f: 'Bon voyage' is French for 'have a good trip!'

questions.q: A brave person who does great deeds in old stories is called a...?
questions.f: 'Hero' comes from an ancient Greek word for a mighty protector.

questions.q: A big fancy feast with music at a castle was called a...?
questions.f: Castle banquets could last for hours, with course after course of food.

questions.q: What do we call the horse-pulled coach that carried kings and queens?
questions.f: In the fairy tale, Cinderella's carriage was made from a magic pumpkin.

questions.q: A very large group of soldiers is called an...?
questions.f: 'Army' goes back to 'arma,' the Latin word for tools of war.

questions.q: A legend is a famous old story told for many, many years.
questions.f: Some legends, like King Arthur, mix real history with make-believe.

questions.q: Who is the leader in charge of a whole ship?
questions.f: 'Captain' comes from 'caput,' the Latin word for 'head.'

questions.q: In old stories, what fire-breathing beast guarded piles of treasure?
questions.f: Dragon stories were told long ago in both Europe and China.

questions.q: What tall tower shines a bright light to guide ships at night?
questions.f: Before electricity, lighthouse keepers kept big oil lamps burning all night.

questions.q: Where did a sailor climb to look far out to sea?
questions.f: The lookout's spot high on the mast is called the crow's nest.

questions.q: Long ago, letters traveled by horse and ship — there was no email.
questions.f: Mail riders swapped tired horses for fresh ones so letters kept moving day and night.

questions.q: What game with little rolling glass or clay balls did children play even in ancient times?
questions.f: Marbles thousands of years old have been found in ancient children's tombs.

questions.q: Which up-and-down toy on a string is more than 2,000 years old?
questions.f: Ancient Greek paintings show children playing with yo-yo-like toys on strings.

questions.q: Ancient artists carved statues from which smooth white stone?
questions.f: Many ancient statues that look white today were once painted in bright colors!

questions.q: Which big Ice Age cat had two huge, curved front teeth?
questions.f: A saber-toothed cat's fangs could grow longer than your hand.

questions.q: The Vikings sailed from cold northern lands we now call...?
questions.f: Norway, Sweden and Denmark together are known as Scandinavia.

questions.q: What kept a castle's great hall warm on cold nights?
questions.f: Thick woven wall hangings called tapestries also helped keep the warmth in.

questions.q: What did school children write on long ago instead of paper notebooks?
questions.f: Children wrote on slates with chalk, then wiped them clean for the next lesson.

questions.q: Before fridges were invented, how did people keep food cold?
questions.f: Ice cut from frozen winter lakes was stored in icehouses and lasted into summer.

questions.q: Silk cloth was first made from threads spun by little silkworms.
questions.f: Ancient China kept the secret of silk-making hidden for hundreds of years.

questions.q: Where did villagers long ago fetch their water?
questions.f: People tossed coins into wells for luck — that is where wishing wells come from.

questions.q: In an old Greek story, sneaky soldiers hid inside a giant wooden ___?
questions.f: We still call a sneaky trick a 'Trojan horse' because of this famous tale.

questions.q: What did towns ring loudly from a tall tower to share big news?
questions.f: Town bells told people when to wake, work, pray, or run to safety.

questions.q: A straw figure that frightens birds away from a farmer's field is called a...?
questions.f: The name says its job: it is there to scare the crows!

questions.q: Castle windows were often narrow slits instead of big open squares.
questions.f: Thin window slits let defenders peek out while staying safe inside.

questions.q: What do we call the seat a rider straps onto a horse's back?
questions.f: Saddles were invented thousands of years ago to make long rides easier.

questions.q: Viking ships moved using a big sail and lots of what?
questions.f: When the wind stopped, the whole crew rowed together to keep the ship moving.

questions.q: Which of these toys did children long ago NOT have?
questions.f: An Egyptian board game called senet is more than 4,000 years old.

questions.q: Which home could people who traveled with their animals pack up and move?
questions.f: People who move from place to place with their herds are called nomads.

questions.q: What hidden surprise did some old castles have?
questions.f: Some castles had hidden tunnels so people could slip out unseen.

questions.q: What did explorers often plant in the ground when they reached a new land?
questions.f: Explorers even planted a flag on the Moon in 1969.

questions.q: Before most people had books, where did bedtime stories come from?
questions.f: Favorite stories were passed from grandparents to children for hundreds of years.

questions.q: What is the metal hat that protected a knight's head called?
questions.f: Many knight helmets had a visor that flipped up so the knight could see and breathe.

questions.q: A person who takes care of sheep is called a...?
questions.f: 'Shepherd' is really just 'sheep' + 'herder' squashed into one word.

questions.q: 'Farewell' is an old word people say when someone is...?
questions.f: It began as 'fare well,' a wish that your journey goes well.

questions.q: On old farms, what is a baby cow called?
questions.f: A baby horse is a foal, and a baby sheep is a lamb.

questions.q: Which word means 'very old — from a time long, long ago'?
questions.f: 'Ancient' grew out of a Latin word meaning 'before.'

questions.q: A person who catches fish for a living is called a...?
questions.f: Fishing villages are some of the oldest kinds of towns in the world.

questions.q: Sailors shouted 'Land ___!' when they finally spotted the shore.
questions.f: 'Ho!' was an old-fashioned shout to make everyone look up and pay attention.

questions.q: What are the colorful picture windows in very old buildings called?
questions.f: The glowing glass pictures told stories to people who could not read.

questions.q: Both castles and palaces were homes for kings and queens.
questions.f: A castle was built strong for safety; a palace was built to look grand.

questions.q: Which word means to dig something up out of the ground?
questions.f: Scientists unearth fossils, old coins, and even buried cities.

questions.q: Before big bridges were built, people often crossed rivers on what?
questions.f: The earliest rafts were simply logs tied tightly together.

questions.q: Some dinosaurs were as small as chickens.
questions.f: Compsognathus was a mini dinosaur about the size of a turkey.

questions.q: What was the fastest way to cross the ocean 200 years ago?
questions.f: Later, speedy sailing ships called clippers raced across oceans carrying tea and mail.

questions.q: Which volcano erupted almost 2,000 years ago and buried the Roman town of Pompeii?
questions.f: The ash preserved streets, shops, and even loaves of bread for archaeologists to find.

questions.q: Which artist painted the famous Mona Lisa?
questions.f: Leonardo kept the painting with him and carried it on his travels for years.

questions.q: Which giant 'unsinkable' ship sank on its very first voyage in 1912?
questions.f: The Titanic's wreck was not found on the ocean floor until 1985.

questions.q: In 1953, Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the top of which mountain?
questions.f: The two climbers always said they reached the summit together, as a team.

questions.q: What did Galileo point at the night sky to make amazing discoveries?
questions.f: With his telescope, Galileo saw mountains on the Moon for the first time.

questions.q: Which code of dots and dashes carried messages along telegraph wires?
questions.f: The distress call SOS is three dots, three dashes, three dots.

questions.q: Louis Braille invented a way for blind people to read using...?
c: Raised dots felt with the fingers
questions.f: Louis Braille was only 15 years old when he invented his reading system.

questions.q: The sandwich is named after an English earl who wanted to eat without leaving his card game.
questions.f: The Earl of Sandwich asked for meat between bread slices in the 1700s — the name stuck.

questions.q: The ice pop was invented by accident by an 11-year-old boy.
questions.f: Frank Epperson left a drink with a stirring stick outside on a freezing night in 1905.

questions.q: The old penny-farthing bicycle had one giant wheel and one tiny wheel.
questions.f: It was named after two British coins — a big penny and a small farthing.

questions.q: Why did ancient China build the Great Wall?
c: To keep out invaders from the north
As a giant road for traders
questions.f: Soldiers on the wall's watchtowers sent warnings using smoke signals.

questions.q: Which people built the mountaintop city of Machu Picchu?
questions.f: The city sits so high in the Andes that clouds often drift below it.

questions.q: Which beetle was a lucky symbol in ancient Egypt?
questions.f: Carved scarab charms were worn like lucky jewelry.

questions.q: Besides people, what else did ancient Egyptians often turn into mummies?
questions.f: Archaeologists have found millions of animal mummies, from cats to crocodiles.

questions.q: In ancient Egypt, both men and women wore black eye makeup.
questions.f: The dark makeup, called kohl, may also have cut down the desert sun's glare.

questions.q: Where did ancient Romans go to wash, relax, and meet their friends?
questions.f: Roman baths had steamy hot rooms, cold pools, and even exercise yards.

questions.q: What language did the ancient Romans speak?
questions.f: French, Spanish, and Italian all grew out of Latin over many centuries.

questions.q: What slowly trickles through an hourglass to measure time?
questions.f: Sailors used sandglasses to time their turns on night watch.

questions.q: What was the first hot-air balloon's passenger crew in 1783?
c: A sheep, a duck, and a rooster
questions.f: The Montgolfier brothers' animal passengers floated over France and landed safely.

questions.q: The 'tele' in telescope and telephone means...?
questions.f: In Greek, a telescope is literally a 'far-seer' and a telephone a 'far-sound.'

questions.q: The 'sub' in submarine means...?
questions.f: Submarine puts together Latin words for 'under' and 'the sea.'

questions.q: The 'bi' in bicycle tells you it has how many wheels?
questions.f: A one-wheeler is a unicycle — 'uni' means one.

questions.q: How many years long is a century?
questions.f: The root 'cent' means hundred — just like the 100 cents in a dollar.

questions.q: 'Prehistoric' describes the time ___ writing was invented.
questions.f: The prefix 'pre-' means before — prehistory left no written records at all.

questions.q: 'Nine o'clock' began as a short way of saying nine ___ the clock.
questions.f: People said 'of the clock' to show they meant clock time, not sun time.

questions.q: The word 'alphabet' is built from alpha and beta, the first two letters used by the ancient...?
questions.f: Alpha and beta slowly became our letters A and B.

questions.q: Long ago, a person whose job was copying out documents by hand was called a...?
questions.f: In ancient Egypt, scribes trained for years and were highly respected.

questions.q: A Roman floor picture made from thousands of tiny colored tiles is called a...?
questions.f: Some Roman mosaics used more than a million little tiles.

questions.q: A traveling musician who sang songs in castles was called a...?
questions.f: Minstrels also carried news and gossip from town to town.

questions.q: Who rang a bell and shouted 'Hear ye! Hear ye!' to announce the news?
questions.f: Criers began with 'Oyez!' — an old word meaning 'Listen!'

questions.q: A young person learning a craft from a master was called an...?
questions.f: After years of training, an apprentice became a 'journeyman,' paid by the day.

questions.q: A knight's special family symbol, painted on his shield, was called his coat of...?
questions.f: No two families were supposed to use the same coat of arms.

questions.q: Thursday is named after which hammer-carrying Norse god?
questions.f: 'Thursday' literally means 'Thor's day.'

questions.q: The word 'month' is closely related to which object in the sky?
questions.f: A month began as the time of one full cycle of the Moon.

questions.q: The letters the Vikings carved into wood and stone are called...?
questions.f: Tall carved runestones still stand across Scandinavia today.

questions.q: A large Spanish sailing ship that carried treasure across the ocean was called a...?
questions.f: Sunken galleons full of silver coins are still being discovered today.

questions.q: The short burst of trumpet music announcing a king's arrival is called a...?
questions.f: Heralds blew fanfares so crowds knew something important was coming.

questions.q: The marathon race is named after Marathon, a place in which country?
questions.f: Legend says a messenger ran about 40 kilometres from Marathon to Athens with big news.

questions.q: Aesop of ancient Greece was famous for short animal stories called...?
questions.f: 'The Tortoise and the Hare' is one of Aesop's fables from over 2,500 years ago.

questions.q: A Viking family home — one big shared wooden hall — was called a...?
questions.f: The whole family gathered around one fire pit in the middle of the longhouse.

questions.q: People in China have eaten with chopsticks for thousands of years.
questions.f: Early chopsticks were probably used for cooking before they were used for eating.

questions.q: Which ocean did the Vikings cross to reach Iceland and Greenland?
questions.f: They made these bold trips in open wooden ships with no cabins.

questions.q: Pepper and other spices were once so costly that only rich people could afford them.
questions.f: Spices traveled for months by ship and camel before reaching Europe's markets.

questions.q: What job did old-fashioned windmills mostly do?
questions.f: In the Netherlands, windmills also pumped water off low farmland.

questions.q: In castle times, what did most people eat with instead of forks?
questions.f: Forks only became common in Europe a few hundred years ago.

questions.q: Knights showed off their skills at big festival contests called...?
questions.f: A grand tournament could last for days, with games, feasts, and parades.

questions.q: A big picture woven from colored thread and hung on a castle wall is a...?
questions.f: A single grand tapestry could take a team of weavers years to finish.

questions.q: What did ancient Greek actors wear so people far away could see their characters?
questions.f: Happy and sad theater masks are still a symbol of acting today.

questions.q: In old villages, where did people gather to buy and sell goods?
questions.f: Market day was the big weekly event where the whole village met.

questions.q: What lit big city streets before electric streetlights?
questions.f: Every evening, lamplighters walked the streets lighting each lamp by hand.

questions.q: Which color did Roman emperors famously wear?
questions.f: Purple dye was so rare and costly that it became the color of rulers.

questions.q: What is the front end of a ship called?
questions.f: The back end of a ship is called the stern.

questions.q: The 'micro' in microscope means...?
questions.f: A microscope is literally a 'small-looker' in Greek.

questions.q: A book of maps is called an...?
questions.f: It is named after Atlas, the giant in Greek myth who held up the sky.

questions.q: What did kings press into hot wax to seal an important letter?
questions.f: A royal wax seal proved the letter really came from the king.

questions.q: What is the dark underground room of a castle called?
questions.f: 'Dungeon' first meant the castle's great tower before it meant a cellar prison.

questions.q: The royal child who will be the NEXT king or queen is called the...?
questions.f: 'Heir' is related to the word 'inherit' — to receive something passed down.

questions.q: What did a lighthouse keeper do every single night?
questions.f: Keepers climbed hundreds of stairs to tend the lamp, even in storms.

questions.q: The world's first cities grew in Mesopotamia between the Euphrates and which other river?
questions.f: This river valley is often called the cradle of civilization.

questions.q: After the age of pyramids, many pharaohs were buried in rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the...?
questions.f: More than 60 royal tombs have been discovered in the valley so far.

questions.q: The Americas are named after which explorer?
questions.f: A mapmaker printed 'America' on a 1507 map in Vespucci's honor, and the name stuck.

questions.q: The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, was amazingly built where?
c: On an island in a lake
questions.f: Mexico City stands today on the very spot where Tenochtitlan once floated.

questions.q: The Aztecs sometimes paid for goods using what as money?
questions.f: In the Aztec world, money for chocolate really did grow on trees.

questions.q: How did the Inca keep detailed records without any writing?
questions.f: The knotted string records, called quipu, still hold secrets experts are untangling.

questions.q: Which food did Inca farmers first grow high in the Andes mountains?
questions.f: The Inca even freeze-dried potatoes in the cold mountain air to store them for years.

questions.q: The game of chess was first played in which land?
questions.f: An early version was called chaturanga, meaning the 'four parts' of an army.

questions.q: Which country printed the world's first paper money?
questions.f: European travelers could hardly believe that printed paper could work as money.

questions.q: What was the famous network of trade routes linking China with Europe called?
questions.f: The catchy name was invented centuries later by a German geographer.

questions.q: The first modern Olympic Games were held in 1896 in which city?
questions.f: Athens was chosen to honor the games' ancient Greek birthplace.

questions.q: Which Greek thinker supposedly leaped from his bath shouting 'Eureka!'?
questions.f: 'Eureka' is Greek for 'I have found it!'

questions.q: In Homer's Odyssey, which hero spends ten long years trying to sail home?
questions.f: Thanks to him, we now call any long, adventurous journey an 'odyssey.'

questions.q: Athens' great rival city-state in ancient Greece was...?
questions.f: The two cities disagreed about almost everything, from schooling to government.

questions.q: Erik the Red named icy Greenland 'green' partly to attract settlers.
questions.f: A lovely-sounding name, he figured, would tempt more Vikings to move there.

questions.q: Old mapmakers drew sea monsters on parts of the ocean no one had explored.
questions.f: Monsters and swirling whirlpools marked the scary edges of the known world.

questions.q: Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly alone across which ocean?
questions.f: Her 1932 solo flight took nearly 15 hours through storms and fog.

questions.q: Lewis and Clark led a famous expedition across which continent?
questions.f: Their team hiked and paddled to the Pacific Ocean and back, helped by the guide Sacagawea.

questions.q: Edison's phonograph of 1877 was the first machine that could...?
questions.f: The first words it ever played back were 'Mary had a little lamb.'

questions.q: The can opener was invented about 50 years after canned food.
questions.f: Early instructions said to open cans with a hammer and chisel!

questions.q: The inventor of Velcro got the idea from what?
c: Burrs sticking to his dog's fur
questions.f: He put the prickly burrs under a microscope and copied their tiny hooks.

questions.q: The ice cream cone became popular at a World's Fair in 1904.
questions.f: When an ice cream stand ran out of dishes, a waffle seller rolled cones to the rescue.

questions.q: Gently heating milk to kill germs is called 'pasteurization' after which scientist?
questions.f: Pasteur's heating trick made milk and juice far safer to drink.

questions.q: The first Ferris wheel, star of the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, was named after...?
questions.f: George Ferris's giant wheel lifted 60 people in each of its 36 cabins.

questions.q: The root 'circum' in 'circumnavigate' means...?
questions.f: To circumnavigate the globe is to travel all the way around it.

questions.q: Explorers named the Pacific Ocean with a word that means...?
questions.f: After weeks of rough seas, the calm new ocean seemed wonderfully 'pacific.'

questions.q: The word 'astronaut' is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: Russia's 'cosmonaut' means 'sailor of the universe' instead.

questions.q: The word 'robot' comes from a Czech word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Robot' first appeared in a 1920 play about factory machines that looked human.

questions.q: The toy name 'LEGO' comes from Danish words meaning...?
questions.f: 'Leg godt' is Danish for 'play well' — a fitting name for a toy company.

questions.q: The word 'pen' comes from 'penna,' a Latin word for...?
questions.f: For centuries, pens really were feathers — sharpened goose quills dipped in ink.

questions.q: A 'manuscript' is literally a document that was...?
questions.f: It joins the Latin words 'manu' (by hand) and 'scriptum' (written).

questions.q: The root 'chrono' in 'chronology' means...?
questions.f: A chronology lines up events in time order — and a chronometer measures time.

questions.q: The Greek root 'polis' in 'metropolis' and 'acropolis' means...?
questions.f: Even 'politics' began as a word for the business of the city.

questions.q: In 'democracy,' the Greek root 'demos' means...?
questions.f: Add 'kratos' (power) and democracy literally means 'people power.'

questions.q: Soldiers who rode and fought on horseback were called the...?
questions.f: 'Cavalry' traces back to 'caballus,' a Latin word for horse.

questions.q: The grand ceremony where a new king or queen is crowned is called a...?
questions.f: It comes from 'corona,' the Latin word for crown.

questions.q: A line of rulers who all belong to the same family is called a...?
questions.f: Ancient Egypt's pharaohs are grouped into about 30 dynasties.

questions.q: 'Goodbye' began long ago as a squashed way of saying...?
questions.f: Over centuries, the whole blessing melted down into one little word.

questions.q: The heavy iron gate that slid down to seal a castle entrance was the...?
questions.f: Its name comes from old French for 'sliding door.'

questions.q: Who announced royal news and kept careful track of knights' coats of arms?
questions.f: The heralds' special skill is still called 'heraldry' today.

questions.q: At a medieval feast, a 'trencher' was a plate made of...?
questions.f: After dinner, the gravy-soaked bread plates were given to the poor or the dogs.

questions.q: The 5,300-year-old 'Iceman' found frozen in the Alps in 1991 is nicknamed...?
questions.f: Named for the Otztal Alps where hikers found him, he still carried his copper axe and arrows.

questions.q: The country of Sudan has more ancient pyramids than Egypt.
questions.f: Nubian kings of Kush built over 200 steep, narrow pyramids at Meroe along the Nile.

questions.q: King Hammurabi of Babylon is remembered for one of the world's first written...?
questions.f: His 282 laws were carved on a stone pillar taller than a person — it now stands in the Louvre.

questions.q: The wedge-shaped writing pressed into wet clay tablets in Mesopotamia is called...?
questions.f: 'Cuneus' is Latin for wedge — scribes pressed the marks with a cut reed.

questions.q: The massive stepped temple-towers of ancient Mesopotamia are called...?
questions.f: The Great Ziggurat of Ur rose in giant terraces, with a shrine at the very top.

questions.q: The Phoenicians made their famous purple dye from...?
questions.f: Thousands of murex snails went into dyeing a single royal robe — hence 'royal purple.'

questions.q: Which seafaring traders spread an early alphabet around the Mediterranean?
questions.f: The Greeks adapted their letters — our 'A' began as aleph, the sign of an ox's head.

questions.q: Petra, the ancient city carved into rose-red cliffs, lies in which modern country?
questions.f: Its Nabataean builders carved whole temple fronts straight into the canyon walls.

questions.q: Angkor Wat, the world's largest temple complex, stands in which country?
questions.f: The temple is such a national treasure that it appears on Cambodia's flag.

questions.q: Mansa Musa, possibly the richest person in all of history, ruled which empire?
questions.f: He handed out so much gold on one journey that prices in Cairo sagged for years.

questions.q: In the Middle Ages, the desert city of Timbuktu was world-famous for its...?
questions.f: Families in Timbuktu guarded hundreds of thousands of handwritten manuscripts.

questions.q: Aboriginal Australians have the oldest continuous living culture on Earth.
questions.f: Their stories, art, and traditions stretch back tens of thousands of years, unbroken.

questions.q: Polynesian sailors crossed the vast Pacific guided by...?
questions.f: Master navigators could read islands beyond the horizon from the shape of the swells.

questions.q: The Lascaux cave paintings were discovered in 1940 by teenagers following their dog.
questions.f: The dog, fittingly named Robot, nosed at a hole that led to a 17,000-year-old gallery.

questions.q: Emperor Hadrian built his famous coast-to-coast wall across which Roman frontier?
questions.f: Letters dug up at a wall fort include a soldier being sent warm socks from home.

questions.q: Some Roman concrete could harden underwater — and Roman sea walls still stand today.
questions.f: The secret was volcanic ash; modern engineers still study the recipe.

questions.q: Archaeologists have found everyday graffiti scribbled on the walls of Pompeii.
questions.f: Ancient Romans doodled jokes, greetings, and 'I was here' notes just like people today.

questions.q: On scorching days, spectators in the Colosseum could be shaded by...?
questions.f: Sailors from the Roman fleet worked the ropes of the huge awning, called the velarium.

questions.q: Which philosopher was the boyhood tutor of Alexander the Great?
questions.f: Alexander was said to sleep with a copy of Homer's Iliad tucked under his pillow.

questions.q: The greatest library of the ancient world stood in which city?
questions.f: Ships docking in the harbor were searched for scrolls so the library could copy them.

questions.q: Which water-lifting device, still used on farms today, is named after Archimedes?
questions.f: Turn the screw's handle and water climbs the spiral — no electricity needed.

questions.q: During the ancient Olympic Games, Greek city-states observed a special...?
c: Truce, so athletes could travel safely
questions.f: The sacred truce, the ekecheiria, let rivals compete side by side in peace.

questions.q: Knights sometimes dressed their horses in colorful cloth coats.
questions.f: The flowing horse-coats, called caparisons, matched the knight's own colors.

questions.q: Which animal gave people wool for warm clothes long ago?
questions.f: Sheep were sheared with big hand scissors, then the wool was spun into yarn.

questions.q: On old farms, which animal was milked to make butter and cheese?
questions.f: Butter was made by churning milk up and down in a wooden barrel.

questions.q: What long, flowing garment did kings wear over their shoulders?
questions.f: Royal robes were often trimmed with soft white fur and shiny thread.

questions.q: What did old ships drop into the water to stay in one place?
questions.f: The first anchors were simply big heavy stones tied to ropes.

questions.q: Where did villagers take their grain to be ground into flour?
questions.f: The person who ran the mill was the miller — another job that became a last name.

questions.q: What turned the big wheel of a watermill?
questions.f: The rushing water spun the wheel, and the wheel turned heavy grinding stones.

questions.q: Swapping your eggs for a neighbor's apples, with no money at all, is called...?
questions.f: Before coins were invented, people traded goods with each other all the time.

questions.q: Real pirates made prisoners walk the plank all the time.
questions.f: Walking the plank is mostly a storybook idea — real records of it are very rare.

questions.q: Sailors long ago told stories of which creature, half woman and half fish?
questions.f: Some sailors may have really been seeing sleepy sea animals called manatees.

questions.q: People in cold northern lands have used skis for thousands of years.
questions.f: Ancient wooden skis have been found preserved in icy bogs.

questions.q: Which golden grain did ancient Egyptians grow beside their river?
questions.f: Egyptian bakers turned the wheat into many different shapes of bread.

questions.q: What round toy did children long ago roll along with a stick?
questions.f: Hoop-rolling races were popular with kids for hundreds of years.

questions.q: Where did people long ago usually wash their clothes?
c: In the bathtub... of a robot
questions.f: Clothes were scrubbed on rocks or wooden washboards and dried in the sun.

questions.q: Which bright star did sailors use to find their way north at night?
questions.f: The North Star barely moves in the sky, so it made a trusty guide.

questions.q: What warm drink have people in China sipped for thousands of years?
questions.f: A legend says tea began when leaves blew into an emperor's cup of hot water.

questions.q: Which bird's feathers made the best writing quills long ago?
questions.f: A small blade for sharpening quills is why we still say 'pen knife.'

questions.q: A person who sews clothes to fit you is called a...?
questions.f: 'Tailor' comes from an old word meaning 'to cut.'

questions.q: A person who makes and mends shoes is called a...?
questions.f: Funnily enough, 'cobbler' is also the name of a fruity baked dessert.

questions.q: A person who builds things out of wood, like doors and tables, is a...?
questions.f: Carpenters built almost everything in old villages, from cradles to carts.

questions.q: The book where a captain writes down each day's sailing events is the ship's...?
questions.f: Captains still keep logbooks today — even astronauts keep them in space!

questions.q: Who guarded the town gate at night and called out 'All's well!'?
questions.f: Night watchmen called out the hour so people knew the time in bed.

questions.q: The word 'unicorn' means 'one horn.'
questions.f: 'Uni' means one and 'cornu' means horn — a one-horned wonder.

questions.q: The biggest, most important ship in a king's fleet was called the...?
questions.f: The admiral flew his special flag from it — that is how it got its name.

questions.q: A person who carries important letters for a king is called a...?
questions.f: Royal messengers rode fast horses and swapped them at stations along the road.

questions.q: The kitchen on board a ship is called the...?
questions.f: 'Galley' was also the name of an ancient ship rowed by many oarsmen.

questions.q: The steering area of a ship, where the wheel is, is called the...?
questions.f: 'Taking the helm' now means taking charge of anything.

questions.q: A book that tells the true story of one person's whole life is a...?
questions.f: 'Bio' means life and 'graphy' means writing — life-writing.

questions.q: A period of 1,000 years is called a...?
questions.f: 'Mille' is Latin for thousand — the same root hiding in 'millimeter.'

questions.q: The small tower on the corner of a castle is called a...?
questions.f: 'Turret' literally means 'little tower.'

questions.q: The golden rod a king or queen holds at grand ceremonies is a...?
questions.f: Scepters have been symbols of royal power since ancient Egypt.

questions.q: A woman who rules an empire is called an...?
questions.f: Empress Wu Zetian ruled China's mighty Tang empire on her own.

questions.q: Saturday is named after which Roman god, who also names a ringed planet?
questions.f: In English, Saturday is the only weekday still keeping its Roman god's name.

questions.q: In olden days, the light evening meal was called...?
questions.f: 'Supper' is related to 'soup' — evening meals were often a pot of it.

questions.q: A group of traders and camels crossing the desert together is called a...?
questions.f: Camels in a caravan were nicknamed the 'ships of the desert.'

questions.q: The skull-and-crossbones pirate flag has the nickname 'Jolly...?'
questions.f: No one knows for sure how the flag got its cheerful-sounding name.

questions.q: The 'auto' in automobile means...?
questions.f: An automobile 'moves by itself' — no horse required, which amazed people.

questions.q: The 'phon' in telephone and phonograph means...?
questions.f: A phonograph is literally a 'sound-writer.'

questions.q: A soldier standing guard at a gate or door is called a...?
questions.f: A sentry's famous challenge was 'Halt! Who goes there?'

questions.q: The old word 'fortnight' means...?
questions.f: It is squashed down from 'fourteen nights.'

questions.q: The sea god's three-pronged spear is a 'trident' — 'tri' plus 'dent,' meaning three...?
questions.f: 'Dens' is Latin for tooth — the same root as 'dentist.'

questions.q: Ancient Greeks and Romans wrote school notes on tablets coated with...?
questions.f: Flip your stylus and rub — the flat end erased the wax for reuse.

questions.q: The Great Fire of London in 1666 began in a...?
questions.f: It started in Pudding Lane, and the rebuilt city rose grander than before.

questions.q: Big Ben is actually the name of a giant bell, not the clock tower.
questions.f: The great bell weighs about as much as two elephants; the tower is called the Elizabeth Tower.

questions.q: Which old Italian city has canals for streets, where boats take the place of cars?
questions.f: For centuries, sleek black boats called gondolas have been its taxis.

questions.q: The Pilgrims crossed the Atlantic in 1620 aboard which famous ship?
questions.f: Their stormy crossing took about 66 days.

questions.q: Which flightless bird, met by sailors on the island of Mauritius, is now extinct?
questions.f: The dodo had no fear of people because it had never had enemies before.

questions.q: Which frozen continent did explorers race to reach in the early 1900s?
questions.f: Even today, Antarctica has no towns — only visiting scientists.

questions.q: Before pumpkins, people carved spooky lanterns out of turnips.
questions.f: The custom came from Ireland, where big turnips were easier to find than pumpkins.

questions.q: Wealthy ancient Romans often ate dinner while lying down on couches.
questions.f: Diners leaned on their left elbow and ate with the right hand.

questions.q: The Maya built their great stone cities mostly in...?
questions.f: Laser scanners flown over the jungle keep finding whole Maya cities hidden under the trees.

questions.q: Who was the first human to travel into space, in 1961?
questions.f: His single trip around the Earth lasted just 108 minutes.

questions.q: The ancient Greeks and Romans both sailed which sea at the center of their world?
questions.f: Its name means 'in the middle of the lands' — exactly how they saw it.

questions.q: What was the famous horseback mail relay across the American West called?
questions.f: It lasted only about 18 months before the telegraph put it out of business.

questions.q: Camel caravans crossed which desert to reach the golden city of Timbuktu?
questions.f: Traders there once swapped salt for gold, weight for weight.

questions.q: Traditional Japanese homes used sliding paper screens instead of glass windows.
questions.f: The screens, called shoji, let in soft glowing light.

questions.q: The teddy bear is named after which US president?
questions.f: A 1902 cartoon of 'Teddy' Roosevelt sparing a bear cub gave toymakers the idea.

questions.q: Ice skates long ago were made from animal bones.
questions.f: Skaters glided on polished bone blades tied to their shoes.

questions.q: The Statue of Liberty was a gift to the United States from which country?
questions.f: The statue crossed the ocean packed in 350 pieces and was rebuilt like a puzzle.

questions.q: Which castle building stored the grain and food supplies?
questions.f: A full granary meant a castle could hold out for months if trouble came.

questions.q: Legend says the Aztecs built their capital where they saw an eagle perched on a...?
questions.f: That eagle-on-a-cactus scene appears on Mexico's flag today.

questions.q: The first animal to orbit the Earth, in 1957, was...?
questions.f: Laika flew aboard Sputnik 2 — Ham, Felicette, and Albert were real space animals too.

questions.q: Coal miners long ago carried which small bird underground as a safety helper?
questions.f: Canaries noticed bad air first — which is why we still say 'canary in a coal mine.'

questions.q: Roman numerals have no symbol for zero.
questions.f: Try writing 105 without a zero — Romans wrote CV and just did without.

questions.q: Hannibal famously crossed the snowy Alps to surprise Rome, bringing along...?
questions.f: Getting dozens of elephants over icy mountain passes stunned the ancient world.

questions.q: Europeans once believed tomatoes were poisonous.
questions.f: Tomatoes belong to the same plant family as deadly nightshade, which scared people off.

questions.q: Some of the oldest known musical instruments are 40,000-year-old flutes made from...?
questions.f: Found in German caves — and modern copies of them can still be played.

questions.q: What was the jolting early bicycle with iron-banded wheels nicknamed?
questions.f: Iron tires plus cobblestone streets made every ride a full-body workout.

questions.q: Roman soldiers built a complete fortified camp almost every night while marching.
questions.f: Camps used the same layout every time, so every soldier knew his way in the dark.

questions.q: Pencil 'lead' is actually graphite and contains no lead at all.
questions.f: Ancient Romans really did write with lead sticks — the old name simply stuck.

questions.q: The Wright brothers' whole first flight was shorter than a jumbo jet's wingspan.
questions.f: That first hop covered about 37 metres — a 747's wings stretch farther.

questions.q: Alchemists of long ago worked for centuries trying to turn ordinary metals into...?
questions.f: They never managed it — but their experiments helped give birth to chemistry.

questions.q: The Hundred Years' War actually lasted more than one hundred years.
questions.f: It ran on and off for 116 years — the name rounds down.

questions.q: Which British queen ruled for so long that a whole era is named after her?
questions.f: Victoria reigned 63 years; 'Victorian' now describes everything from houses to manners.

questions.q: The Eiffel Tower was originally meant to be temporary.
questions.f: Built for an 1889 fair, it was saved partly because it made a superb radio mast.

questions.q: What color was the Statue of Liberty when it was brand new?
questions.f: Weather slowly turned the copper skin the famous green we see today.

questions.q: For their famous ballgame, the Maya made balls out of...?
questions.f: They tapped rubber trees centuries before Europeans had ever seen rubber bounce.

questions.q: In English legend, which forest was Robin Hood's hideout?
questions.f: The oldest surviving Robin Hood ballads were written down in the 1400s.

questions.q: In the legends of King Arthur, what is the name of his famous sword?
questions.f: In some tales, the sword in the stone and Excalibur are two different swords.

questions.q: Why was King Arthur's legendary table famously round?
c: So no knight sat at the head above the others
To fit the castle's round hall
So food could be spun to each seat
To honor the shape of the sun
questions.f: A giant painted 'Round Table' still hangs in Winchester Castle in England.

questions.q: Pirates' famous 'pieces of eight' were coins made of which metal?
questions.f: The Spanish coin could be cut into eight 'bits' — why a US quarter is still 'two bits.'

questions.q: The Maori people, famous for the haka, are the first people of which country?
questions.f: Their ancestors reached New Zealand by open ocean canoe — a stunning feat of navigation.

questions.q: Bronze, the metal that named an age, is a mix of copper and...?
questions.f: The blend is harder than either metal alone — perfect for early tools.

questions.q: What was Sputnik, launched in 1957?
questions.f: It beeped radio signals as it circled Earth — its name means 'traveling companion.'

questions.q: The Romans called the Greek sea god Poseidon by which name?
questions.f: The planet Neptune's deep sea-blue color suits its name perfectly.

questions.q: Which sport, played on seaside 'links,' did Scotland give the world centuries ago?
questions.f: A Scottish king once tried to ban it because men were skipping archery practice.

questions.q: The old city of Venice stands on top of...?
questions.f: Millions of timber piles hold it up — starved of air underwater, the wood barely rots.

questions.q: Why did sailing ships almost always carry a cat?
c: To hunt the rats that ate supplies
To warn the crew of storms
questions.f: Ship's cats were working crew members — some became famous mascots.

questions.q: The board game Snakes and Ladders first came from which country?
questions.f: It began as Moksha Patam, a game teaching that good deeds lift you up.

questions.q: Which animal hauled loads for the Inca along their mountain roads?
questions.f: With no horses or wheeled carts, sure-footed llama trains kept the empire supplied.

questions.q: The month of July is named after which Roman leader?
questions.f: The very next month, August, honors his heir Augustus.

questions.q: In Roman numerals, the letter C stands for which number?
questions.f: C is for 'centum' — the same root as century and percent.

questions.q: Nike, whose name now appears on sports shoes, was the Greek goddess of...?
questions.f: The famous winged statue in the Louvre is Nike landing on a ship's prow.

questions.q: Volcanoes are named after Vulcan, the Roman god of...?
questions.f: Romans pictured his underground forge sending up the smoke of Mount Etna.

questions.q: The root 'biblio' in 'bibliography' means...?
questions.f: A bibliophile is a book lover, and a bibliography is a list of books.

questions.q: A person who makes maps is called a...?
questions.f: 'Charta' meant a sheet of paper — a cartographer fills that sheet with the world.

questions.q: The art of beautiful, decorative handwriting is called...?
questions.f: 'Calli' means beautiful — medieval monks spent lifetimes perfecting it.

questions.q: The glowing gold-decorated letters in medieval books are called ___ letters.
questions.f: 'Lumen' means light — real gold leaf made the pages flash by candlelight.

questions.q: The room in a monastery where monks copied books by hand was the...?
questions.f: Copying one large book by hand could take a monk a whole year.

questions.q: 'Kindergarten,' a word from German, literally means...?
questions.f: Its inventor thought young minds should be tended like growing plants.

questions.q: Sailors' signal system of two hand-held flags is called...?
questions.f: 'Sema' means sign — each flag position spells a different letter.

questions.q: The notched stone tops of castle walls, where defenders could duck, are the...?
questions.f: The gaps are 'crenels' and the solid teeth are 'merlons.'

questions.q: The word 'Renaissance' literally means...?
questions.f: Europe felt ancient art and knowledge being 'born again' after the Middle Ages.

questions.q: 'Navigate' comes from 'navis,' the Latin word for...?
questions.f: The same root sails on in 'navy' and 'naval.'

questions.q: A 'decade' is a period of how many years?
questions.f: 'Deka' is Greek for ten — a decathlon packs ten events into one contest.

questions.q: The Old Norse word for a long tale of heroes and feuding families is a...?
questions.f: Iceland's medieval sagas still name real farms you can visit today.

questions.q: The steep-sided sea inlets of Norway, carved by glaciers, are called...?
questions.f: 'Fjord' is one of the few Norwegian words used all over the world.

questions.q: The study of family trees and ancestors is called...?
questions.f: 'Genea' means family line — some royal family trees stretch back a thousand years.

questions.q: A settlement ruled from a distant 'mother country' is called a...?
questions.f: From Latin 'colonus,' a settler-farmer working new land.

questions.q: A 'pilgrim' is best described as a person who...?
c: Travels to a place that is special to them
questions.f: From 'peregrinus,' Latin for a wanderer far from home.

questions.q: In pioneer days, the 'frontier' meant...?
c: The far edge of settled land
questions.f: Beyond the frontier, maps simply ran out.

questions.q: A craftsman called a 'cooper' spent his days making...?
questions.f: Barrels stored everything from apples to nails — and Cooper became a common last name.

questions.q: On an old sailing ship, the 'figurehead' was...?
c: A carved statue at the bow
