questions.f: Today a 'figurehead' also means a leader with no real power — all show, like the statue.

questions.q: A 'mason' is a builder who works mainly with...?
questions.f: Cathedral masons carved their personal marks into blocks — you can still spot them.

questions.q: Ada Lovelace, often called the first computer programmer, wrote about whose 'Analytical Engine'?
questions.f: Ada was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron — and saw further than the engine's own inventor.

questions.q: In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee invented which world-changing system?
questions.f: He gave the Web away for free — no patent, no royalties.

questions.q: Wilhelm Rontgen called his mysterious new rays 'X-rays' because...?
questions.f: His first X-ray picture showed his wife's hand — bones, wedding ring, and all.

questions.q: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 after what drifted into his dish of germs?
questions.f: He came back from vacation to find the mold clearing a germ-free ring around itself.

questions.q: Alfred Nobel, founder of the Nobel Prizes, made his fortune by inventing...?
questions.f: A newspaper printed his obituary too early — reading it pushed him to fund the prizes.

questions.q: Henry Ford joked that Model T buyers could pick any color, as long as it was...?
questions.f: Black paint dried fastest, keeping his assembly line racing along.

questions.q: The world's first postage stamp, issued in Britain in 1840, is known as the...?
questions.f: The Twopenny Blue followed just days later — both showed young Queen Victoria.

questions.q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
questions.f: Amundsen secretly switched his goal from north to south after the North Pole was claimed.

questions.q: The narrow sea gap between Asia and Alaska is named after which explorer?
questions.f: Bering was a Danish captain who explored the strait while sailing for Russia.

questions.q: Which explorer gave his name to both a New York river and a huge Canadian bay?
questions.f: Hudson vanished in 1611 after his crew set him adrift — his fate is still a mystery.

questions.q: Spanish explorers named Florida with a word meaning...?
questions.f: Ponce de Leon arrived around the Spanish 'festival of flowers' at Easter time.

questions.q: Sailors once measured a ship's speed by paying out a rope and counting its...?
questions.f: The rope's knots slipping past per sandglass-turn gave us the speed unit 'knots.'

questions.q: British sailors got the nickname 'limeys' from eating limes to prevent...?
questions.f: The vitamin C in citrus kept crews healthy on months-long voyages.

questions.q: The rock-hard biscuit that fed sailors on long voyages was called...?
questions.f: Sailors nicknamed the biscuits 'tooth dullers' and often dunked them to survive them.

questions.q: The small, nimble Portuguese ship that opened the age of exploration was the...?
questions.f: Its slanted lateen sails let it zigzag against the wind along Africa's coasts.

questions.q: What did old-time navigators measure with an astrolabe?
c: The height of the sun or stars above the horizon
The depth of the water below
questions.f: From a star's height a sailor could work out how far north or south the ship lay.

questions.q: The Terracotta Army stands guard at the tomb of which ruler?
questions.f: No two of the thousands of clay soldiers have the same face.

questions.q: For about 500 years, ordinary people could not set foot in Beijing's palace, called the ___ City.
questions.f: Legend claims it has 9,999 rooms — one fewer than heaven's palace.

questions.q: The Mongol Empire became the largest connected land empire in history.
questions.f: Its pony-express-style relay system could speed a message hundreds of kilometres a day.

questions.q: The Japanese word 'samurai' originally meant...?
questions.f: Samurai served great lords called daimyo — service was the heart of the job.

questions.q: Emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a...?
questions.f: Some 20,000 workers and 1,000 elephants labored on it for about two decades.

questions.q: Legend says Rome was founded by twin brothers named...?
questions.f: The story goes that the abandoned twins were rescued and raised by a she-wolf.

questions.q: Ancient Roman cities had fast-food counters serving hot meals to passersby.
questions.f: Dozens of these 'thermopolia,' with jars sunk into marble counters, survive at Pompeii.

questions.q: A Roman mile was defined as one thousand...?
c: Double steps of a marching soldier
questions.f: 'Mille passus' — a thousand paces — shrank over time into our word 'mile.'

questions.q: The word 'plumbing' comes from 'plumbum,' the Latin name of which metal?
questions.f: Roman water pipes were lead — and that is why lead's chemical symbol is Pb.

questions.q: Rome's 'Senate' takes its name from 'senex,' meaning...?
questions.f: The Senate began as a council of elders — gray hair was the entry ticket.

questions.q: The royal titles 'tsar' and 'kaiser' both come from the name of...?
questions.f: One family name became the word for 'emperor' in languages across Europe.

questions.q: 'Gladiator' comes from 'gladius,' the Latin word for...?
questions.f: The gladiolus flower is a 'little sword' — named for its blade-shaped leaves.

questions.q: The word 'arena' comes from 'harena,' the Latin word for the ___ spread on the floor.
questions.f: Every sports 'arena' today is named after that ancient layer of sand.

questions.q: The 'amphi' in amphitheater means...?
questions.f: An amphitheater wraps seats entirely around the action — a theater doubled into a ring.

questions.q: 'Metropolis' literally means...?
questions.f: Greek colonies called their founding city their 'mother' — metropolis.

questions.q: The 'acro' in acropolis — and in acrobat — means...?
questions.f: An acropolis is the 'high city,' and an acrobat 'walks on high.'

questions.q: 'Chivalry,' the code of knights, traces back to 'cheval,' the French word for...?
questions.f: A knight in French is a 'chevalier' — literally a horseman.

questions.q: The noble title 'duke' comes from 'dux,' Latin for...?
questions.f: Rome's frontier generals were each called a 'dux' — the title outlived the empire.

questions.q: 'Curfew' comes from the old French 'couvre-feu,' an evening signal to...?
questions.f: An evening bell told townsfolk to damp their hearths so houses would not burn at night.

questions.q: A 'freelance' worker was originally a knight whose lance was...?
questions.f: The word was popularized by Sir Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe in 1820.

questions.q: The word 'journey' originally meant the distance you could travel in...?
questions.f: From French 'journee' (a day) — and journeymen were craftsmen paid by the day.

questions.q: 'Window' comes from an Old Norse word meaning...?
questions.f: Before glass, a window really was just an eye-hole for the wind.

questions.q: 'Going berserk' recalls Norse warriors called berserkers, named for their...?
questions.f: 'Serkr' meant shirt — the name may literally mean 'bear-shirt.'

questions.q: 'Ransack' comes from Old Norse words that mean to...?
questions.f: 'Rann' (house) plus 'saka' (search) — a word the Vikings left behind in English.

questions.q: The English word 'law' was borrowed from Old Norse.
questions.f: Viking settlers in England also left behind everyday words like sky, egg, and knife.

questions.q: Wednesday is named after which one-eyed Norse god?
questions.f: 'Woden's day' — while Tuesday belongs to Tyr and Friday to the goddess Frigg.

questions.q: January is named for Janus, the Roman god pictured with...?
questions.f: One face looks back at the old year, the other gazes into the new.

questions.q: The 'sept-' in September means seven — so why is it our NINTH month?
c: The Roman year once began in March
Two extra months were squeezed in ahead of it
questions.f: October, November, and December are 'eight, nine, ten' for the same old reason.

questions.q: 'Vaccine' comes from 'vacca' — because the first vaccine used a mild pox caught from...?
questions.f: Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox never caught smallpox.

questions.q: 'Quarantine' originally meant a waiting period of exactly how many days?
questions.f: Venice held arriving ships offshore for 'quaranta giorni' — forty days.

questions.q: 'Camera' is the Latin word for...?
questions.f: The camera obscura — 'dark room' — projected the outside world onto its wall.

questions.q: 'Helicopter' is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: The split is helico-pter, not heli-copter — 'helix' plus 'pteron,' a wing.

questions.q: Nobel coined 'dynamite' from 'dynamis,' the Greek word for...?
questions.f: The same root powers the words dynamic, dynamo, and dynasty.

questions.q: 'Algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr,' meaning roughly...?
questions.f: It headlines a 9th-century Baghdad textbook that taught the world equations.

questions.q: 'Mesopotamia' is Greek for the land...?
questions.f: 'Meso' (between) + 'potamos' (river) — the Tigris and Euphrates hug it on both sides.

questions.q: The title 'pharaoh' originally meant...?
questions.f: Egyptians named the ruler after the palace — as we say 'the White House decided.'

questions.q: 'Hieroglyph' is Greek for...?
questions.f: 'Hieros' (sacred) + 'glyphein' (to carve) — writing fit for temple walls.

questions.q: Describing a room as 'spartan' means it is...?
questions.f: The Spartans made toughness and bare-bones living a point of civic pride.

questions.q: The word 'mentor' comes from Mentor, a wise adviser in which ancient epic?
questions.f: The goddess Athena borrowed Mentor's shape to guide Odysseus' young son.

questions.q: 'Colossal' comes from the Colossus of Rhodes, a towering harbor statue of which god?
questions.f: It stood about 33 metres tall — and an earthquake felled it after only ~54 years.

questions.q: A grand tomb is called a 'mausoleum' after King Mausolus, who ruled in what is now...?
questions.f: His tomb at Halicarnassus was so splendid it made the Seven Wonders list.

questions.q: 'Bank' comes from the Italian 'banca' — the ___ where medieval money changers worked.
questions.f: A money changer's smashed bench — 'banca rotta' — gave us the word 'bankrupt.'

questions.q: Surprisingly, the Greek word 'schole,' the root of 'school,' first meant...?
questions.f: Only people with leisure time could sit around discussing ideas — so leisure became school.

questions.q: 'Graduate' and 'grade' both come from 'gradus,' Latin for...?
questions.f: To graduate is literally to take a step up.

questions.q: 'Artifact' combines Latin words meaning...?
questions.f: 'Arte factum' — a thing made by craft, whether a gold mask or a clay marble.

questions.q: 'Excavate' literally means to...?
questions.f: 'Ex' + 'cavare' shares its root with 'cave' — to make hollow.

questions.q: 'Monument' comes from 'monere,' a Latin verb meaning to...?
questions.f: A monument's whole job is to make passersby remember.

questions.q: 'Civilization' grows from 'civis,' the Latin word for...?
questions.f: The same root builds 'city,' 'civic,' and 'civil.'

questions.q: 'Nomad' traces to a Greek word connected with...?
questions.f: Nomads moved with their grazing animals — the pasture set the calendar.

questions.q: 'Eavesdropping' originally meant listening from where?
c: The strip where rain drips off a roof
questions.f: Lurking in the 'eavesdrip' close to the wall put you near enough to hear secrets.

questions.q: 'Sheriff' is squashed together from 'shire reeve' — the king's officer of the...?
questions.f: The reeve of each shire kept the king's peace centuries before the Wild West.

questions.q: In the Middle Ages, the word 'villain' simply meant a...?
questions.f: A 'villanus' worked at a villa — snobbery slowly turned the word into an insult.

questions.q: 'Companion' literally means a person you share ___ with.
questions.f: 'Com' (with) + 'panis' (bread) — friendship measured in shared loaves.

questions.q: A medieval 'bonfire' was originally a fire of...?
questions.f: The 'bon' looks French but isn't — midsummer 'bone fires' burned the year's animal bones.

questions.q: A 'clue' — originally spelled 'clew' — was literally a...?
questions.f: Theseus followed an unwound thread out of the labyrinth — the first 'clue' ever followed.

questions.q: Slanted 'italic' printing type takes its name from...?
c: Italy, where it was first cut
questions.f: A Venice printer designed it around 1500 to squeeze classics into pocket-sized books.

questions.q: Capital letters are called 'uppercase' because printers stored them in the upper of two type cases.
questions.f: Small letters lived in the handier lower case — hence 'lowercase.'

questions.q: Diesel fuel and the diesel engine are named after...?
c: The engineer who invented the engine
The firm that first sold it
questions.f: Rudolf Diesel patented his engine in the 1890s; his name now sits on fuel pumps everywhere.

questions.q: Giant rigid airships were called 'zeppelins' after...?
c: The German count who built them
The town of their first flight
questions.f: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin's airships carried paying passengers before airplanes did.

questions.q: The power unit 'watt' honors James Watt, famous for transforming the...?
questions.f: Watt also coined 'horsepower' — comparing engines to horses helped him sell them.

questions.q: Cardigan sweaters and wellington boots are both named after British...?
questions.f: An earl and a duke lent their titles to knitwear and rubber boots alike.

questions.q: The saxophone is named after...?
questions.f: Sax invented it in the 1840s — long before jazz made it a star.

questions.q: A wandering knight who roamed in search of adventure was called a knight-...?
questions.f: 'Errant' means wandering — from the same root as 'error,' a wandering off course.

questions.q: The ancient Egyptian calendar's new year began with the dawn rising of which star?
questions.f: The Dog Star's return warned farmers the Nile's life-giving flood was coming.

questions.q: Aluminum was once so difficult to produce that it cost more than gold.
questions.f: France's emperor served his most honored guests with aluminum cutlery — gold for the rest.

questions.q: In medieval Europe, rent could sometimes be paid in which spice?
questions.f: A token 'peppercorn rent' is still a legal term for a tiny symbolic payment.

questions.q: Napoleon was unusually short for a man of his time.
questions.f: He was about average height — British cartoons and mixed-up French units built the myth.

questions.q: Who first sighted the Pacific Ocean after crossing the jungles of Panama in 1513?
questions.f: He waded into the surf in full armor and claimed the entire sea on the spot.

questions.q: Which town was buried by Vesuvius along with Pompeii?
questions.f: Its hot mud sealed wooden furniture, food, and even a library of scrolls.

questions.q: The shortest war on record lasted less than one hour.
questions.f: The 1896 clash between Britain and Zanzibar was over in well under 45 minutes.

questions.q: The cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde were built by which people?
questions.f: They tucked multi-story stone villages into canyon walls, reached by ladders and toeholds.

questions.q: Before alarm clocks were common, a 'knocker-upper' earned wages by...?
c: Tapping on windows to wake workers
Drumming the town awake at dawn
questions.f: Some used long poles, others pea-shooters aimed at upstairs windows.

questions.q: A Victorian 'mudlark' scraped together a living by...?
c: Searching river mud for things to sell
questions.f: Mudlarks combed the Thames at low tide — today it's a licensed hobby that finds real treasures.

questions.q: By trade, a 'fletcher' made...?
questions.f: 'Fletching' is the feather work that makes an arrow fly straight.

questions.q: A 'chandler' originally earned his living making...?
questions.f: Later, 'ship's chandlers' sold supplies to sailors — the name drifted with the trade.

questions.q: An American businessman bought London Bridge in 1968 and rebuilt it in Arizona.
questions.f: The granite bridge was shipped stone by numbered stone to Lake Havasu City.

questions.q: Which province did Rome lean on as its 'breadbasket' of grain?
questions.f: Giant grain ships from Alexandria kept the city of Rome fed.

questions.q: The brilliant red dye treasured in Aztec markets — and later Europe — came from...?
questions.f: Cochineal bugs still tint some foods and lipsticks today.

questions.q: Instead of soap, Roman bathers cleaned themselves with...?
c: Olive oil scraped off with a curved tool
questions.f: The bronze scraper was called a strigil — oil on, grime off.

questions.q: Most of the brick-and-stone Great Wall that tourists visit today was built under which dynasty?
questions.f: Earlier walls were mostly packed earth; the Ming rebuilt in brick over 200 years.

questions.q: The Egyptian 'shaduf' was a simple machine for...?
c: Lifting river water to the fields
questions.f: A bucket on a counterweighted pole — farmers along the Nile still use them.

questions.q: In dates, the letters 'AD' stand for 'anno Domini,' Latin for...?
c: In the year of the Lord
questions.f: Many historians now write 'CE' — Common Era — for the same years.

questions.q: Before rubber erasers, people rubbed out pencil marks with bread.
questions.f: Moist bread crumbs lifted the marks — the discovery of rubber's powers came later.

questions.q: The Persian kings' 'Royal Road' was built to speed up...?
c: Royal mail carried by relay riders
questions.f: Herodotus' praise of its unstoppable couriers inspired the US postal motto.

questions.q: The Aztecs required children — girls as well as boys — to attend school.
questions.f: Historians count the Aztecs among the first societies with schooling for everyone.

questions.q: Pineapples were once so precious in Europe that people rented them as party decorations.
questions.f: An 18th-century pineapple could cost as much as a coach — far too dear to actually eat.

questions.q: The world's first traffic light, installed in London in 1868, ran on gas.
questions.f: It stood outside Parliament, guiding horse carriages with red and green gas lamps.

questions.q: 'Ballot' comes from the Italian 'ballotta,' meaning a little...?
questions.f: Venetians voted by dropping colored balls into urns — 'blackballing' comes from the same custom.

questions.q: 'Disaster' literally means a...?
questions.f: 'Dis' + 'astro' — misfortune once got blamed on unlucky stars.

questions.q: A 'Herculean' task recalls Hercules, who myth says completed how many great labors?
questions.f: One labor: cleaning vast stables in a single day — by rerouting two rivers through them.

questions.q: The phrase 'Achilles' heel' comes from the tale that baby Achilles was dipped into...?
questions.f: His mother held him by the heel — the one spot the waters never touched.

questions.q: In Greek myth, sailors blocked their ears with wax to resist the Sirens'...?
questions.f: Odysseus had himself tied to the mast so he could listen and still sail safely past.

questions.q: Pandora's famous 'box' was actually a jar in the original Greek story.
questions.f: A translation slip centuries later turned the great jar into a little box.

questions.q: In every Roman town, the 'forum' was the...?
questions.f: 'Forum' now means any place where ideas are traded instead of goods.

questions.q: Rome's 'circus' buildings took their name from the Latin word for...?
questions.f: Modern circus rings still keep both the shape and the name.

questions.q: 'Hygiene' honors Hygieia, who in Greek belief was...?
questions.f: She was the daughter of Asclepius, the god of medicine — wellness ran in the family.

questions.q: 'Museum' literally means a temple of the...?
questions.f: The nine Muses of art and learning also hide inside the word 'music.'

questions.q: 'Pajamas' comes from Persian words describing a...?
questions.f: They began as loose daytime trousers in South Asia; Europeans adopted them for sleep.

questions.q: 'Shampoo' entered English from a Hindi word meaning to...?
questions.f: The first 'shampooing' was a head massage — the soap came later.

questions.q: 'Hurricane' comes from Huracan, who in Caribbean Taino belief was a...?
questions.f: The Maya told of a storm god with a strikingly similar name.

questions.q: 'Canoe' and 'hammock' both entered European languages from the peoples of...?
questions.f: Taino words picked up by Spanish sailors — along with 'barbecue.'

questions.q: 'Tomato' and 'coyote' come from Nahuatl, the tongue of which empire?
questions.f: 'Tomatl' and 'coyotl' — 'chocolate' is usually traced to Nahuatl, too.

questions.q: 'Kayak' and 'anorak' were both borrowed from the language of which Arctic people?
questions.f: Skin-covered boats and hooded jackets — gear built for ice, names built to last.

questions.q: 'Safari' is a Swahili word that simply means...?
questions.f: Swahili borrowed it from the Arabic 'safar' — travel.

questions.q: 'Alarm' comes from the old Italian cry 'all'arme!', meaning...?
questions.f: A shout to grab weapons slowly mellowed into your morning beep.

questions.q: 'Biscuit' literally means...?
questions.f: 'Bis coctus' — baked, then baked again so it would keep on long voyages.

questions.q: The Greeks coined 'barbarian' to tease how foreigners...?
questions.f: To Greek ears, unfamiliar speech was just 'bar-bar-bar.'

questions.q: 'Vandalism' recalls the Vandals, who were...?
c: A tribe that raided ancient Rome
questions.f: Their name became a word for wreckers only centuries later, coined during the French Revolution.

questions.q: Every 'palace' echoes the Palatine, a famous hill in which city?
questions.f: Emperors' homes on the Palatine grew so grand that the hill's name became the word.

questions.q: The perfume 'cologne' is named after a city in which country?
questions.f: 'Eau de Cologne' was first mixed in Koln in 1709.

questions.q: The hamburger takes its name from the German city of Hamburg.
questions.f: The frankfurter is named for Frankfurt the same way.

questions.q: The Canary Islands are named after dogs, not birds.
questions.f: Romans called them 'Canariae Insulae' — islands of dogs; the canary bird is named after the islands.

questions.q: In 1215, English barons forced King John to accept a charter of rights called...?
questions.f: 'The Great Charter' — a few of its clauses are still law after 800 years.

questions.q: Stranded in 1504, Columbus persuaded local leaders to feed his crew by predicting...?
questions.f: His almanac gave him the date — the red Moon appeared right on schedule.

questions.q: Roughly how many of Magellan's ~270 crewmen completed the first voyage around the world?
questions.f: One battered ship, the Victoria, limped home carrying enough spices to pay for the voyage.

questions.q: Which leader's calendar reform introduced the leap year?
questions.f: An Alexandrian astronomer, Sosigenes, did the math behind the famous reform.

questions.q: The prime meridian — longitude zero — passes through which London district?
questions.f: An 1884 conference in Washington picked it as the world's starting line for time and maps.

questions.q: Standard time zones were created largely because of railroads.
questions.f: Every town once kept its own sun time — timetables forced the clocks to agree.

questions.q: Thomas Edison's famous laboratory earned him the nickname 'The Wizard of...?'
questions.f: His New Jersey lab promised a minor invention every ten days — and roughly delivered.

questions.q: The QWERTY keyboard layout was designed in the 1870s partly to...?
questions.f: Legend adds that salesmen loved that 'TYPEWRITER' can be tapped out on the top row alone.

questions.q: The first recorded computer 'bug' was an actual moth.
questions.f: In 1947, engineers taped the moth into the logbook: 'First actual case of bug being found.'

questions.q: The Post-it note grew out of a 3M glue experiment that...?
questions.f: A colleague's church-choir bookmarks kept falling — weak glue turned out to be the answer.

questions.q: Bubble wrap was originally invented to be wallpaper.
questions.f: Textured plastic wallpaper flopped — then someone needed padding for delicate electronics.

questions.q: Play-Doh was first sold not as a toy but as a...?
questions.f: It scrubbed coal soot off walls until home heating changed and a toy was born.

questions.q: A sponge diver's haul off an Aegean islet in 1900, thirty corroded bronze gears, and a dial tracking eclipse cycles point to which ancient device?
questions.f: It modelled the movements of the sun, moon and planets — nothing so complex is known for the next 1,000 years.

questions.q: An Indonesian volcano, a rainy Swiss holiday spent writing ghost stories indoors, and failed harvests across Europe gave 1816 which nickname?
questions.f: Tambora's ash dimmed the sky — and that gloomy holiday produced Mary Shelley's Frankenstein.

questions.q: A lightning strike she survived as a baby, a seaside shop selling 'curiosities', and a tongue-twisting song point to which fossil hunter?
questions.f: 'She sells seashells by the seashore' is said to be about Anning, who found the first complete plesiosaur.

questions.q: Who coined the word 'dinosaur' in 1842?
questions.f: Owen built London's Natural History Museum — and named the creatures 'terrible lizards' before anyone had a full skeleton.

questions.q: Red lead pigment called minium, monks painting glowing initials, and a modern word for something tiny converge on which word?
questions.f: Miniature had nothing to do with size at first — small pictures simply happened to be painted in minium.

questions.q: Broken pottery shards, ten years of exile, and a show of hands in ancient Athens converge on which modern word?
questions.f: Athenians scratched a name on a potshard — an ostrakon — to vote someone out of the city.

questions.q: A temple of Juno on Rome's Capitoline Hill, the city's coin workshop, and the word 'mint' all trace to which everyday word?
questions.f: Juno's title was Moneta — the goddess whose temple housed the coin presses.

questions.q: Silver from a Bohemian valley, coins nicknamed thaler, and Dutch traders in old New York gave which currency its name?
questions.f: Joachimsthal's coins became 'thaler', then 'daler', then dollar — used in dozens of countries today.

questions.q: A chequered counting cloth, medieval tax clerks moving markers across squares, and a chess-like grid named which government office?
questions.f: Britain's finance chief is still the Chancellor of the Exchequer — named after a tablecloth.

questions.q: Arabic words for 'house of manufacture', a Venetian shipyard that could finish a galley in a day, and a London football club share which word?
questions.f: The club began as a team of workers at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich.

questions.q: A clumsy wooden shoe, angry French factory workers, and a word for deliberately wrecking machinery converge on which term?
questions.f: From 'sabot' — the peasant clog that also gave dancers their clattering 'sabot' steps.

questions.q: A goat, a singing chorus, and a springtime Greek song contest converge on which word for a sorrowful drama?
questions.f: 'Tragos' (goat) plus 'oide' (song) — nobody is quite sure why the goat was there.

questions.q: Tree bark, the Latin word 'liber', and rooms lined with shelves converge on which building's name?
questions.f: Romans wrote on the inner bark of trees, so 'liber' came to mean book.

questions.q: 'Sarcophagus' is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: Greeks believed a certain limestone slowly consumed what was placed inside it.

questions.q: The Greek word 'pyramis', ancestor of 'pyramid', originally named a...?
questions.f: Greek visitors seem to have nicknamed Egypt's monuments after a pointed little cake.

questions.q: 'Draconian' honours Draco, an Athenian remembered for...?
c: Writing the city's first written law code
questions.f: His penalties were famously severe — later reformers replaced almost all of them.

questions.q: 'Laconic' — using very few words — comes from Laconia, the homeland of which people?
questions.f: Warned an enemy would enter their city, the Spartans reportedly replied with a single word: 'If.'

questions.q: 'Parchment' takes its name from Pergamon, an ancient city in what is now...?
questions.f: Legend says Pergamon developed animal-skin pages when a rival cut off its papyrus supply.

questions.q: 'Encyclopedia' is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: The idea was a complete ring of education, with no gaps left open.

questions.q: The military title 'marshal' began as a word meaning...?
questions.f: The royal stable boy climbed the ranks until 'marshal' outranked almost everyone.

questions.q: 'Constable' comes from Latin words meaning...?
questions.f: Like 'marshal', the title began among the horses and ended up commanding armies.

questions.q: Roman office-seekers gave us 'candidate' because they wore...?
questions.f: 'Candidus' means shining white — and 'candid' and 'candle' are its cousins.

questions.q: 'Cipher' and 'zero' both descend from an Arabic word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Sifr' translated an Indian term for the empty place in a column of numbers.

questions.q: The word 'algorithm' preserves the name of which 9th-century Baghdad mathematician?
questions.f: Latin readers turned his name into 'algorismi' — and every computer since has run on it.

questions.q: 'Admiral' comes from Arabic words meaning...?
questions.f: 'Amir al-bahr' sailed into European languages through Sicily and Spain.

questions.q: 'Denim' and 'jeans' are named after which pair of cities?
questions.f: 'De Nimes' meant the sturdy French cloth; Genoese sailors' trousers gave us 'jeans'.

questions.q: 'Tycoon' entered English from a Japanese title meaning...?
questions.f: American visitors picked up 'taikun' in the 1850s; newspapers soon aimed it at business barons.

questions.q: A Swedish warship, a maiden voyage of barely 1,300 metres in 1628, and a salvage in 1961 gave the world which museum ship?
questions.f: Top-heavy and over-armed, she capsized in Stockholm harbour — and 98 percent of her survives.

questions.q: A ship crushed by pack ice in 1915, an 800-mile open-boat voyage to South Georgia, and a crew who all came home point to which leader?
questions.f: His ship Endurance was finally found on the seabed, upright and remarkably intact, in 2022.

questions.q: A Yorkshire carpenter, a working clock built of wood at nineteen, and a sea watch called H4 solved which problem?
questions.f: John Harrison's clocks beat the astronomers — H4 lost only seconds on an Atlantic crossing.

questions.q: A kite-lifted aerial in Newfoundland, the letter S tapped three times, and a Nobel Prize in 1909 belong to which inventor?
questions.f: Experts insisted radio waves could not bend around the Earth — that faint 1901 signal proved otherwise.

questions.q: Carved pillars raised about 11,000 years ago in southeastern Turkey — before farming or pottery — make up which site?
questions.f: It is older than Stonehenge by roughly 6,000 years, built by people who had not yet planted a field.

questions.q: The oldest surviving great story in world literature tells of a Mesopotamian king named...?
questions.f: Half the epic was lost until clay tablets turned up in a buried Assyrian library.

questions.q: China's earliest known writing survives as questions scratched onto 'oracle bones' from which dynasty?
questions.f: Diviners heated the bones until they cracked, then read the cracks as answers.

questions.q: Which Bronze Age Greek script did the architect Michael Ventris decipher in 1952?
questions.f: The tablets turned out to be warehouse lists — proof that the Mycenaeans spoke early Greek.

questions.q: Who finally cracked Egyptian hieroglyphs in the early 1820s?
questions.f: Knowing Coptic was his secret weapon — it preserved echoes of the ancient Egyptian language.

questions.q: A shepherd tossing a stone into a cave, jars of ancient scrolls, and cliffs above the Dead Sea point to which site?
questions.f: The scrolls found there in 1947 pushed the oldest known biblical manuscripts back a thousand years.

questions.q: A landowner's hunch, a Suffolk mound opened weeks before war broke out in 1939, and the ghostly print of a 27-metre ship point to which site?
questions.f: The wood had rotted away entirely, leaving only rivets and a ship-shaped stain in the sand.

questions.q: A 70-metre embroidery, a comet blazing over frightened onlookers, and Latin captions naming Harold describe which artwork?
questions.f: That comet is Halley's, and this is one of the earliest pictures ever made of it.

questions.q: William the Conqueror's vast survey of English land and livestock, finished in 1086, is known as the ___ Book.
questions.f: Nicknamed for judgment day because, like it, there was no appealing its verdict.

questions.q: Which admiral commanded enormous Chinese treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean in the early 1400s?
questions.f: His flagships dwarfed European vessels of the day — and one voyage brought a giraffe home to court.

questions.q: Which medieval Moroccan traveller covered roughly 120,000 km — far more than Marco Polo?
questions.f: He wandered for about 29 years, from Mali to China, and dictated it all as a book of travels.

questions.q: The first woman known to have sailed around the world did so disguised as a valet — who was she?
questions.f: A botanist's assistant on a French voyage, she has a South American nightshade, Solanum baretiae, named in her honour.

questions.q: Which vast stone-walled complex, the largest ancient ruin south of the Sahara, gave a modern nation its name?
questions.f: Its mortar-free walls were built so precisely that they still stand after 700 years.

questions.q: Which ancient city near modern St Louis raised an earthen mound covering a wider area than the Great Pyramid?
questions.f: At its height around 1100 CE, Cahokia may have held more people than London did.

questions.q: How were the giant Nazca lines of Peru actually made?
c: By clearing dark stones to expose pale ground
By planting lines of pale grasses
questions.f: The desert is so dry and windless that lines swept aside 2,000 years ago have barely blurred.

questions.q: An Etruscan word for a hooded cloak, a Roman gate at the edge of a marketplace, and a modern shopping walkway share which term?
questions.f: An arcade is a row of arches — the word arrived through arches long before shops moved in.

questions.q: A Roman soldier's marching pace, a thousand of them counted out, and a modern road sign converge on which unit?
questions.f: 'Mille passus' meant a thousand double paces — about 1,479 metres, a little short of today's mile.

questions.q: Feeding a plough team, an Anglo-Saxon field length, and horse racing in England converge on which old unit of distance?
questions.f: A 'furrow long' was how far oxen could pull before resting — eight of them make a mile.

questions.q: A rope stretched between a man's outspread arms, sailors calling out depths, and a lead weight converge on which unit?
questions.f: From an Old English word for the embrace of two arms — about 1.8 metres of sounding line.

questions.q: A pebble used for counting, a Roman reckoning board, and a branch of mathematics feared by students converge on which word?
questions.f: 'Calculus' is Latin for little stone — and 'calculate' literally means to shuffle pebbles.

questions.q: A notched wooden stick, a tax record split in half so neither side could cheat, and cricket scores converge on which word?
questions.f: Britain kept its accounts on tally sticks until the 1820s; burning the old pile set Parliament on fire.

questions.q: An Old English word for a notch, a shepherd's count of twenty sheep, and a Gettysburg speech opening converge on which word?
questions.f: 'Four score and seven years ago' means 87 — a score is 20, from the notch cut at every twentieth animal.

questions.q: Coarse brown cloth spread over a clerk's writing table gave English which word for an office?
questions.f: The cloth named the desk, the desk named the room, and the room named 'bureaucracy'.

questions.q: 'Salt' hides inside which everyday English word connected with work?
questions.f: Roman soldiers received a salt allowance — 'worth his salt' still praises a good worker.

questions.q: The prefix in 'palaeolithic' and 'palaeontology' means...?
questions.f: 'Palaios' is Greek for ancient — 'lithos' adds the stone, making it the Old Stone Age.

questions.q: 'Neolithic' describes the age when people first...?
questions.f: 'Neos' means new — the New Stone Age brought villages, pottery and planted fields.

questions.q: 'Mesolithic' sits between which two ages?
questions.f: 'Mesos' means middle — the same root as in Mesopotamia, the land in the middle of rivers.

questions.q: The term 'prehistory' was needed because history, strictly speaking, begins with...?
questions.f: Everything before writing has to be read from objects and bones instead of documents.

questions.q: Scholars call the study of writing systems and old handwriting...?
questions.f: Epigraphy is its cousin — the study of inscriptions carved into stone and metal.

questions.q: The study of coins and medals is called...?
questions.f: Philately collects stamps and vexillology studies flags — every hobby gets a Greek name.

questions.q: Which term describes an object that is out of its proper time, like a wristwatch in a Roman film?
questions.f: 'Ana' (against) plus 'chronos' (time) — literally something set against its own time.

questions.q: Tree rings, a Greek word for wood, and dating a wooden roof beam to an exact year converge on which science?
questions.f: Overlapping ring patterns from old timbers now stretch the calendar back thousands of years.

questions.q: Reading the layers of soil in a dig, deepest is oldest, is the principle of...?
questions.f: Each layer, or stratum, is a page — archaeologists read the ground from the bottom up.

questions.q: In museum work, an object's 'provenance' is its...?
c: Recorded history of ownership and findspot
questions.f: Without provenance, even a genuine treasure loses most of what it can tell us.

questions.q: A cliff-edge Greek monastery, a hidden storeroom, and a fragile document read by X-ray converge on which word for a reused manuscript?
questions.f: Scraped-clean parchment was written over — but modern imaging can still recover the erased text beneath.

questions.q: The oval frame drawn around a royal name in Egyptian inscriptions is called a...?
questions.f: French soldiers named it after a gun cartridge, which the loop resembled.

questions.q: An Egyptian tomb's small servant figurines, meant to work for the dead, are called...?
questions.f: One royal burial held over 400 of them — a full workforce, plus overseers.

questions.q: Egyptian jars that held a mummy's organs are called ___ jars.
questions.f: Each of the four lids showed a different protective spirit — jackal, baboon, falcon and human.

questions.q: The flat-topped, bench-shaped tombs that came before Egypt's pyramids are called...?
questions.f: 'Mastaba' is Arabic for bench — local workers thought the ruins looked like mud benches.

questions.q: Which pharaoh's architect Imhotep designed the first pyramid, built in steps?
questions.f: Imhotep was so admired that Egyptians later worshipped him as a god of healing.

questions.q: A female pharaoh, statues showing her in a king's false beard, and a terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri point to whom?
questions.f: She ruled for about two decades — then a later pharaoh tried to chisel her out of the record.

questions.q: A pharaoh who moved his capital to open desert, a switch to worshipping the sun disc, and a famous painted bust of his queen point to whom?
questions.f: His new city, Amarna, was abandoned within a generation — and his son was Tutankhamun.

questions.q: A Mesopotamian invention shaped like a cylinder, rolled across wet clay, served as a...?
questions.f: Rolling the carved stone printed a whole scene — the world's first repeatable image.

questions.q: Ancient Sumer's people invented which farming machine that let one worker sow seed in straight rows?
questions.f: A funnel behind the blade dropped seed straight into the furrow it had just cut.

questions.q: Which ancient wonder was a giant lighthouse, one of the tallest buildings of its age?
questions.f: 'Pharos' became the word for lighthouse in French, Spanish and Italian.

questions.q: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes used shadows in two Egyptian cities to measure the Earth's...?
questions.f: His answer was within a few percent of the true figure — with nothing but shadows, a well and geometry.

questions.q: Which Greek thinker proposed that everything is made of tiny indivisible pieces, about 2,400 years ago?
questions.f: He called them 'atomos' — uncuttable — and modern chemistry kept the name.

questions.q: Which ancient astronomer argued the Earth circles the sun, roughly 1,800 years before Copernicus?
questions.f: His idea was rejected for centuries because no one could feel the Earth moving.

questions.q: A vanished 4th-century mathematician of Alexandria, famous for teaching astronomy and geometry, was...?
questions.f: She is the first woman mathematician whose life and work are reliably recorded.

questions.q: Which Roman writer's encyclopedia, Natural History, survived to become a model for later ones?
questions.f: He died investigating the eruption of Vesuvius — curiosity to the very last.

questions.q: 'Herodotus' is remembered with which nickname?
questions.f: His rival Thucydides checked facts more strictly — but Herodotus told better stories.

questions.q: A stolen fig, a Greek word for informer, and a person who flatters the powerful converge on which word?
questions.f: 'Sykophantes' means 'fig-shower' — the reason behind the fig is still debated.

questions.q: Barrel-dwelling philosophers of ancient Greece, a Greek word for dog-like, and modern distrust of motives converge on which word?
questions.f: The Cynics were nicknamed 'dogs' for living rough and shameless in public.

questions.q: A painted porch in Athens, a school that taught calm endurance, and a modern word for uncomplaining converge on which term?
questions.f: 'Stoa' means porch — the philosophy is named after the place its founder taught.

questions.q: An enslaved attendant who walked children to school gave us which word for a teacher?
questions.f: 'Paidagogos' means child-leader — his job was the walk, not the lesson.

questions.q: Which word for a public speaking place comes from the Latin for 'beaks of captured ships'?
questions.f: Rome decorated its speakers' platform with ships' prows, and speakers have stood at a 'rostrum' ever since.

questions.q: 'Forum', 'agora' and 'plaza' all originally named a city's...?
questions.f: Democracy, shopping and gossip all began in the same open square.

questions.q: A wax writing tablet, a Roman pointed tool, and a modern word for a writer's manner converge on which term?
questions.f: 'Stilus' was the writing tool — a person's stylus-work became their 'style'.

questions.q: 'Tabula rasa', praised by philosophers, literally describes a...?
questions.f: Smooth the wax flat and yesterday's lesson is gone — the mind as a fresh tablet.

questions.q: Which Roman emperor's wall-to-wall building projects included the Pantheon's vast unreinforced concrete dome?
questions.f: Nearly 1,900 years on, it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth.

questions.q: Rome's aqueducts moved water using nothing but...?
questions.f: Some channels drop only a few centimetres per kilometre — surveyed by hand, with no lasers.

questions.q: A Roman road's name for its top layer of dressed paving stones gave us which word?
questions.f: 'Pavire' meant to beat down — road-makers pounded each layer solid before adding the next.

questions.q: Which everyday word comes from the Roman practice of dividing land into 'centuriae'?
questions.f: A centurion commanded roughly a hundred men — the same 'hundred' hiding in century and percent.

questions.q: Excavators at Vindolanda on Rome's British frontier found which remarkable everyday objects?
c: Ink letters written on thin wood
questions.f: One tablet is a birthday party invitation — the earliest known writing by a woman in Latin.

questions.q: Byzantine defenders were famous for a mysterious burning weapon known as...?
questions.f: The recipe was such a closely held secret that it has never been reconstructed.

questions.q: Which empress rose from the Constantinople stage to rule beside Justinian and reshape the law?
questions.f: Laws passed in her time expanded women's rights to property and inheritance.

questions.q: Hagia Sophia's builders solved a hard problem: how to set a round dome on a square room, using...?
questions.f: The trick made huge domed churches and mosques possible for the next 1,500 years.

questions.q: Which 6th-century Byzantine writer secretly composed a scathing 'Secret History' of his own emperor?
questions.f: He wrote flattering official histories by day — and the unpublishable version in private.

questions.q: An Old Norse word for law-speaker, an open-air assembly on Iceland's lava plain, and the world's oldest surviving parliament name converge on which body?
questions.f: Iceland's Althing first met around 930 CE and still governs the country today.

questions.q: Which Viking settlement in Newfoundland proved Norse sailors reached North America around 1000 CE?
questions.f: A cloak pin, iron nails and a smithy sealed the case — Norse tools 5,000 km from Norway.

questions.q: A sunstone, a rowed vessel with a shallow keel, and burial mounds in Norway converge on which craft?
questions.f: Its shallow draught let crews sail up rivers and land on any beach — no harbour needed.

questions.q: Which broad-bellied Norse ship, not the longship, carried families and cargo across the open Atlantic?
questions.f: Slower but far roomier, the knarr was the moving van of the Viking world.

questions.q: 'Husband' originally meant...?
questions.f: From Old Norse 'husbondi' — and 'husbandry' still means managing a farm or household.

questions.q: 'Lord' and 'lady' come from Old English words about which food?
questions.f: A lord was the loaf-warden and a lady the loaf-kneader — power measured in bread.

questions.q: A woman who spun thread for a living gave English which word?
questions.f: Spinning was one of the few trades open to unmarried women, so the job name became a label.

questions.q: A cloth-stretching frame with hooks, a Yorkshire mill, and a phrase for nervous waiting converge on which expression?
questions.f: Wet wool was hooked onto a 'tenter' frame and stretched taut to dry — as tense as it sounds.

questions.q: Which word for something passed down through a family originally named a tool bolted into the house?
questions.f: A loom was a household's most valuable fixture — so the family loom became the family heirloom.

questions.q: A worker who dyed cloth blue in medieval Europe used which plant, before indigo arrived?
questions.f: Woad-dyers' vats smelled so foul that Queen Elizabeth I reportedly banned them near her palaces.

questions.q: An 18-year-old chemist, a failed attempt to make a malaria drug, and the first bright synthetic dye converge on which colour?
questions.f: William Perkin's 1856 accident launched the entire synthetic dye and chemical industry.

questions.q: Nutmeg once grew naturally only on which tiny island group?
questions.f: The spice was so precious that the Dutch once traded away Manhattan to secure the islands.

questions.q: A flower bulb, wild prices in 1630s Amsterdam, and the first famous market crash converge on which craze?
questions.f: At the peak, a single rare bulb could reportedly cost more than a canal-side house.

questions.q: Which Italian banking family of Florence funded artists, produced popes, and gave Europe modern accounting habits?
questions.f: Their double-entry bookkeeping was as world-changing as the art they paid for.

questions.q: A Venetian coin worth little, a cheap news-sheet sold for it, and a modern newspaper title converge on which word?
questions.f: The 'gazeta' bought you the news — so the paper took the coin's name.

questions.q: Which German trading alliance of northern port cities dominated the Baltic in the Middle Ages?
questions.f: Its name survives in Lufthansa and in the 'H' on cars from Hamburg and Bremen.

questions.q: A ceremony where Venice's ruler threw a gold ring into the sea celebrated the city's...?
questions.f: The Doge repeated the wedding every year for some 800 years.

questions.q: Which 15th-century Korean king oversaw the creation of the Hangul alphabet so ordinary people could read?
questions.f: Hangul is so logical that its letter shapes copy the shape of the mouth making each sound.

questions.q: Movable metal type was in use in Korea about two centuries before Gutenberg — printed by order of which dynasty?
questions.f: Korea cast bronze type in the 1200s; Europe reached the same idea independently around 1450.

questions.q: Before he printed books, Johannes Gutenberg trained in which craft?
questions.f: Metalworking is exactly the skill needed to cast thousands of identical letters.

questions.q: A printer's collection of one letter, an upper and a lower storage box, and modern keyboard shortcuts converge on which pair of terms?
questions.f: Compositors reached up for capitals and down for the rest, all day long.

questions.q: In printing, the small crossbar strokes finishing a letter's stems are called...?
questions.f: Roman stonecutters' chisels left them — 'sans serif' simply means without them.

questions.q: A note at the end of an old book naming its printer and date is called a...?
questions.f: From Greek for 'finishing touch' — publishers still print a colophon symbol today.

questions.q: Books printed before 1501, in the very first decades of European printing, are called...?
questions.f: The word means 'swaddling clothes' — books still in their cradle.

questions.q: An illegible illustrated book, a Yale library vault, and centuries of failed code-breaking converge on which manuscript?
questions.f: Its plants match no known species, and no cipher expert has read a single sentence.

questions.q: A German field, a 3,600-year-old bronze disc, and the oldest known picture of the night sky converge on which find?
questions.f: Its cluster of seven gold dots is thought to be the Pleiades — a Bronze Age star map.

questions.q: Which extraordinarily well-preserved Neolithic village sits on Orkney, uncovered by a storm in 1850?
questions.f: Its stone beds, shelves and hearths are all still in place after 5,000 years.

questions.q: At Newgrange in Ireland, sunlight floods the inner chamber only around...?
questions.f: The builders aimed a stone passage at the sunrise 5,000 years before telescopes existed.

questions.q: Bog bodies from Denmark and Ireland survive so well because peat bogs are...?
questions.f: Tollund Man's face and eyelashes survive so vividly that he looks asleep, 2,400 years on.

questions.q: A Beatles song playing at camp, a hominin skeleton found in Ethiopia in 1974, and the name 'Lucy' converge on which species?
questions.f: Lucy walked upright about 3.2 million years ago — long before big brains evolved.

questions.q: Neanderthals are named after...?
questions.f: The Neander valley bones, found in 1856, were the first ancient human species ever recognised.

questions.q: The Denisovans, a cousin of Neanderthals, were first identified from...?
c: DNA in a single finger bone
questions.f: A whole human population was discovered by genetics before anyone found much of its skeleton.

questions.q: A 1938 South African fishing net, a museum curator's sketch, and a fish thought extinct for 66 million years converge on which animal?
questions.f: Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer refused to let the strange catch be thrown away — and rewrote biology.

questions.q: Roy Chapman Andrews' 1920s Gobi expeditions made which famous first?
c: Digging up the first T. rex
questions.f: His khaki-and-adventure reputation is often said to have helped inspire movie explorers.

questions.q: Archaeopteryx, found in German limestone in the 1860s, mattered so much because it showed...?
questions.f: Discovered two years after Darwin's book, it arrived like a fossil on cue.

questions.q: An accidental spark of static, a Chinese silk cloth, and a Greek word for amber converge on which everyday word?
questions.f: 'Elektron' meant amber — rub it and it crackles, the first electricity anyone noticed.

questions.q: Ancient shepherds in a Turkish region, stones that tugged at iron, and a modern compass converge on which word?
questions.f: Magnesia's iron-attracting rocks gave the phenomenon its name thousands of years ago.

questions.q: A frog's leg, an Italian anatomist's laboratory, and the unit on every AA battery converge on which name?
questions.f: Volta built the first true battery in 1800 — and got the volt named after him.

questions.q: A blackened photographic plate, a Paris shed, and an element named after a homeland converge on which scientist?
questions.f: She named polonium after Poland — and remains the only person to win Nobels in two sciences.

questions.q: A London pump handle, a street map dotted with cases, and the birth of epidemiology converge on which doctor?
questions.f: By plotting deaths on a map in 1854, he proved cholera came from water, not bad air.

questions.q: A Crimean hospital, a rose-shaped statistical diagram, and a lifelong campaign for clean wards converge on whom?
questions.f: Her real weapon was data: her charts showed most deaths came from disease, not the fighting.

questions.q: A garden of pea plants, a monastery in Brno, and rules ignored for 35 years converge on which scientist?
questions.f: He counted about 28,000 pea plants — and founded genetics before anyone knew what a gene was.

questions.q: A Welsh-born naturalist collecting in the Malay Archipelago, a letter posted in 1858, and a joint scientific paper converge on whom?
questions.f: Wallace reached the idea of natural selection independently — and his letter pushed Darwin to publish.

questions.q: A Prussian explorer, a climb up a South American volcano, and hundreds of places named after him converge on whom?
questions.f: More things are named for Humboldt than almost any other person — a current, a squid, even a Moon sea.

questions.q: A Bletchley Park hut, a machine called the Bombe, and a wartime code-breaking triumph point to whom?
questions.f: His earlier paper on 'computable numbers' had already sketched the idea of a universal computer.

questions.q: The world's first programmable electronic computer, built to break wartime codes, was named...?
questions.f: It stayed an official secret for decades, so American machines got the credit for years.

questions.q: Six women hired to program ENIAC in the 1940s were long mistaken by the public for...?
questions.f: They programmed by rewiring the machine by hand — and mostly went uncredited for decades.

questions.q: A NASA mathematician whose hand calculations checked an early orbital flight, later celebrated in film, was...?
questions.f: John Glenn asked for her to verify the computer's numbers before he would fly.

questions.q: The first message sent over ARPANET, ancestor of the internet, was cut short — arriving as...?
questions.f: They were typing LOGIN when the system crashed — an accidentally poetic first word.

questions.q: A Finnish paper mill founded in 1865 grew into which famous phone company?
questions.f: It made paper, then rubber boots, then cables — then the world's best-selling phones.

questions.q: A pharmacist's syrup, a marble soda fountain in Atlanta, and an 1886 ledger of five-cent sales converge on which drink's origin?
questions.f: Its distinctive contoured bottle came later, designed to be recognisable by touch in the dark.

questions.q: Two brothers running a health sanatorium, a batch of boiled wheat left out too long, and flakes rolled thin converge on which food?
questions.f: The Kellogg brothers' accident with stale wheat became the world's breakfast.

questions.q: Commercially sliced bread first went on sale in 1928 in which country?
questions.f: An inventor spent 16 years on the slicing machine — hence 'the greatest thing since sliced bread'.

questions.q: A New York restaurant, a customer complaining his potatoes were too thick, and a chef's sarcastic reply converge on which snack's legend?
questions.f: The story credits chef George Crum in 1853 — the 'insult' became the world's favourite snack.

questions.q: A dentist, chewy tree sap from Central America, and a failed attempt to make rubber tyres converge on which product?
questions.f: Thomas Adams could not vulcanise chicle into rubber — so he sold it as gum instead.

questions.q: A game designed to teach the unfairness of land rents, a Quaker teacher's board, and a bestselling family game converge on which title?
questions.f: Lizzie Magie patented The Landlord's Game in 1904, decades before Monopoly's official invention story.

questions.q: A 1913 New York newspaper puzzle called a 'word-cross' grew into which pastime?
questions.f: Arthur Wynne's diamond-shaped grid became the square puzzle within a few years.

questions.q: A Budapest architecture teacher, a wooden model that twisted without falling apart, and a 1980 toy award converge on which invention?
questions.f: Erno Rubik built it to explain 3D geometry, and it took him a month to solve it himself.

questions.q: A naval engineer's spring falling off a shelf, a Philadelphia toy shop demonstration, and 1945 Christmas shoppers converge on which toy?
questions.f: Richard James was designing ship instruments when the spring walked down a stack of books.

questions.q: A Yale student's pie-tin toss, a company called Wham-O, and a name respelled from a pie company's converge on which toy?
questions.f: Students had been throwing Frisbie Pie Company tins for years; the spelling was tweaked for the trademark.

questions.q: The oldest known complete set of board-game rules, on a Babylonian tablet, belongs to the Royal Game of...?
questions.f: Five thousand years old — and modern players can and do still play it.

questions.q: Which strategy game, played on a 19x19 grid, is thought to be the oldest board game still played with unchanged rules?
questions.f: Legend has a Chinese emperor inventing it to teach his son; it is at least 2,500 years old.

questions.q: A peach basket nailed to a gymnasium balcony, a Massachusetts winter, and 13 hand-written rules in 1891 gave us which sport?
questions.f: James Naismith's first baskets had no hole — someone had to fetch the ball out each time.

questions.q: A Massachusetts gym teacher wanting a gentler indoor game than basketball invented which sport in 1895?
questions.f: William Morgan first called it 'mintonette' before someone noticed players were volleying the ball.

questions.q: Modern football's rules were codified in 1863 by which newly formed body?
questions.f: Its main argument was whether handling the ball should be allowed — the answer split football from rugby.

questions.q: The claim that Abner Doubleday invented baseball is best described as...?
c: A myth invented by a 1900s commission
A finding of careful archive research
A rule change credited to him
questions.f: The game grew out of older bat-and-ball games; Doubleday appears never to have mentioned baseball at all.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek athletic event combined running, jumping, throwing and wrestling into one contest?
questions.f: 'Penta' means five — its winners were considered the most complete athletes of all.

questions.q: The Greek foot race that gave 'stadium' its name covered roughly how far?
questions.f: The 'stade' was one length of the track, and the building took its name from the race.

questions.q: A Greek word for dancing ground, seats cut into a hillside, and a modern group of musicians converge on which word?
questions.f: The orchestra was the flat circle where the chorus danced — the players moved in much later.

questions.q: In Greek theatre, a crane lowering a god onto the stage gave us which phrase for a convenient plot rescue?
questions.f: Literally 'god from the machine' — critics were complaining about lazy endings 2,400 years ago.

questions.q: Which Latin phrase describing a work's date means 'in the year of the founding of the city'?
questions.f: Romans sometimes counted years from Rome's legendary founding, traditionally 753 BCE.

questions.q: Archaeologists use 'in situ' to mean an object is...?
c: Still in the exact place it was found
questions.f: Recording an object in situ preserves the information its position carries — dig it up and that is gone.

questions.q: 'Tumulus' and 'barrow' both describe a...?
questions.f: Britain alone has tens of thousands of them, from the Stone Age to the Vikings.

questions.q: A 'megalith' is, by the word's own parts, a...?
questions.f: 'Menhir' names a single upright stone and 'dolmen' a stone table — all from megalithic builders.

questions.q: An 'artesian' well is named after a region in France because there...?
c: Wells were first lined with brick
questions.f: Trapped underground pressure pushes the water up on its own — no bucket needed.

questions.q: A 'guillotine' window and 'sandwich' both belong to which category of word?
questions.f: An eponym is a word made from a person's name — history is stuffed with them.

questions.q: 'Boycott' comes from the name of a 19th-century land agent in which country?
questions.f: Tenants in County Mayo refused all dealings with Captain Boycott in 1880 — and named a tactic.

questions.q: 'Silhouette' is named after a French official remembered for...?
questions.f: Etienne de Silhouette's penny-pinching became a joke — cheap shadow portraits took his name.

questions.q: 'Pasteurise', 'galvanise' and 'mesmerise' are all verbs built from...?
questions.f: Pasteur, Galvani and Mesmer each ended up as a verb — a rare kind of immortality.

questions.q: 'Maverick', meaning an independent thinker, began as a word for...?
questions.f: Texas rancher Samuel Maverick famously left his cattle unbranded, so unmarked strays took his name.

questions.q: 'Gerrymander' blends a governor's surname with the shape of a...?
questions.f: An 1812 Massachusetts voting district was so contorted that cartoonists drew it as a lizard.

questions.q: 'Nicotine' is named after Jean Nicot, a French diplomat who...?
c: Sent tobacco plants to his queen
questions.f: Nicot shipped the plant from Portugal in the 1500s and the whole chemical family carries his name.

questions.q: 'Lynx-eyed', 'panic' and 'siren' all entered English from...?
questions.f: Panic is the fright caused by the god Pan — his sudden appearances terrified travellers.

questions.q: A Greek goddess of retribution gave English which word for a persistent rival?
questions.f: Nemesis punished pride — which is why she now means the enemy you cannot shake off.

questions.q: 'Titanic', 'titan' and 'titanium' all recall the Titans, who in Greek myth were...?
c: Gods who ruled before the Olympians
questions.f: Titanium was named for their strength — the element resists almost everything.

questions.q: 'Chaos', in the earliest Greek accounts, meant...?
questions.f: The modern sense of disorder came much later; at first chaos was simply the great gap before everything.

questions.q: 'Cosmos' is the Greek opposite of chaos, meaning...?
questions.f: 'Cosmetic' shares the root — both are about putting things in good order.

questions.q: Which word for a wandering people comes from a Greek term for pasture?
questions.f: The herd chose the route — 'nomos' meant the pasture where animals were put out to graze.

questions.q: 'Peninsula' is built from Latin words meaning...?
questions.f: 'Paene' (almost) plus 'insula' (island) — the same 'insula' hides inside 'isolate' and 'insulate'.

questions.q: 'Archipelago' first named which specific sea before it meant any island chain?
questions.f: 'Chief sea' was the Aegean's nickname; its scatter of islands stretched the word's meaning.

questions.q: 'Mediterranean' literally means...?
c: In the middle of the lands
questions.f: To Rome it was simply 'our sea' — everything important happened around its edges.

questions.q: The Latin term 'terra incognita' on old maps marked land that was...?
questions.f: Mapmakers wrote it where knowledge ran out — and sometimes filled the space with imagined beasts.

questions.q: Australia's name comes from a Latin phrase meaning the unknown ___ land.
questions.f: 'Terra Australis Incognita' was theorised long before Europeans reached the continent.

questions.q: A 1607 English settlement, a 'starving time', and America's first permanent English colony converge on which name?
questions.f: Roanoke came earlier but vanished; Plymouth came later — Jamestown was the one that lasted.

questions.q: An abandoned English colony, the word CROATOAN carved into a post, and a mystery unsolved since 1590 converge on which site?
questions.f: Historians now suspect the colonists joined nearby Indigenous communities.

questions.q: Which Shoshone woman guided part of the Lewis and Clark expedition while carrying her infant son?
questions.f: She appears on a US dollar coin — one of the few people on money who never held office.

questions.q: The Underground Railroad's most famous conductor, who guided many groups to freedom, was...?
questions.f: She later served as a scout and nurse, and became the first woman to lead an armed US expedition.

questions.q: Which country was the first to grant women the vote in national elections, in 1893?
questions.f: A petition with nearly 32,000 signatures — a quarter of the country's adult women — won the day.

questions.q: A 240-mile walk to the sea, a handful of evaporated salt, and a protest against a tax converge on which leader?
questions.f: By making salt from seawater in 1930, he broke a law with a gesture the whole world understood.

questions.q: A lime quarry that damaged his eyesight, prisoner number 466/64, and 27 years of confinement converge on which future president?
questions.f: Robben Island's most famous prisoner walked free in 1990 and led South Africa four years later.

questions.q: A seamstress, a Montgomery bus, and a boycott lasting 381 days converge on which figure?
questions.f: Teenager Claudette Colvin had refused to move nine months earlier, a case less widely remembered.

questions.q: A misread press conference, crowds at checkpoints, and pickaxes sold as souvenirs converge on which 1989 event?
c: The fall of the Berlin Wall
questions.f: An official's muddled answer about travel rules sent thousands to the gates that very night.

questions.q: Which everyday word for a hidden listening device shares its origin with a real moth in a 1947 logbook?
questions.f: 'Bug' meant a machine fault long before it meant an insect in a computer — but the moth made it famous.

questions.q: A hilltop signal chain, an Old French word for beckoning, and a lighthouse's flash converge on which word?
questions.f: England's beacon hills could pass a warning the length of the country in a matter of hours.

questions.q: A ship's rope trailing a wooden board, half-minute sandglasses, and modern aviation speeds converge on which practice?
questions.f: The log line's knots gave both the speed unit and the ship's daily 'log' of progress.

questions.q: Which navigational instrument replaced the astrolabe at sea by using mirrors to measure angles?
questions.f: Its arc is one sixth of a circle — hence 'sextant', from the Latin for sixth.

questions.q: 'Starboard' comes from an Old English word describing the side where the ___ was fixed.
questions.f: Ships docked with the other side to shore for loading — which is why it is called 'port'.

questions.q: A merchant's insurance certificate, a Latin word meaning 'reward', and a policy on a cargo ship converge on which word?
questions.f: From Latin praemium, a reward — and marine insurance at London coffee houses grew into the modern industry.

questions.q: A 17th-century London coffee house, ships' news read aloud to merchants, and the world's most famous insurance market converge on which name?
questions.f: Edward Lloyd's coffee house was where shipowners and insurers met — the market kept his name.

questions.q: 'Curriculum' comes from a Latin word originally describing a...?
questions.f: A course of study is literally a course to be run — as in 'curriculum vitae', the course of a life.

questions.q: A hollow bronze bird, a Greek engineer's steam-spun toy, and a temple door that opened by itself point to which ancient inventor?
questions.f: His spinning steam ball, the aeolipile, worked about 1,700 years before practical steam engines.

questions.q: Which ancient people are credited with striking the first true coins, around 600 BCE?
questions.f: Lydia's king Croesus grew so wealthy that 'rich as Croesus' is still a saying.

questions.q: Egyptian scribes measured the Nile's flood height using a stepped structure called a...?
questions.f: The flood reading set the year's taxes — too low meant famine, too high meant washed-out villages.

questions.q: The standard Egyptian unit of length, based on the forearm, was the...?
questions.f: A royal cubit rod kept in the temple was the master ruler every builder had to match.

questions.q: Which two crops did the earliest farmers of the Fertile Crescent first domesticate?
questions.f: Wild wheat shatters and scatters its seed; farmers slowly bred plants that held on to it.

questions.q: Maize, beans and squash grown together by Indigenous American farmers are known as the Three...?
questions.f: Beans feed the soil, corn gives them a pole to climb, and squash leaves shade out weeds.

questions.q: Which ancient civilisation of Mexico carved the colossal stone heads that predate the Maya?
questions.f: Some heads weigh over 20 tonnes and were moved dozens of kilometres without wheels or draught animals.

questions.q: Which mathematical idea did the Maya develop independently for their calendar counts?
questions.f: Their zero, often drawn as a shell, was worked out separately from the zeros of Babylon and India.

questions.q: Which crop's arrival in Europe from the Americas eventually helped populations grow rapidly?
questions.f: One field of potatoes could feed several times as many people as the same field of grain.

questions.q: Which Inca engineering feat crossed deep gorges and was rewoven by hand each year?
questions.f: One such bridge in Peru is still rebuilt from twisted grass every year by local communities.

questions.q: The Inca called their vast road system by a name meaning the ___ road.
questions.f: Qhapaq Nan ran some 40,000 km — with relay runners instead of wheeled carts.

questions.q: Aztec farmers grew crops on 'chinampas', which were...?
c: Raised garden beds built in shallow lake water
questions.f: Canals between the beds watered the crops and doubled as roads for canoes.

questions.q: Which Chinese invention let sailors keep steering in rough seas and is still on ships today?
questions.f: Chinese ships also pioneered watertight compartments — the idea modern hulls still use.

questions.q: The 'four great inventions' traditionally credited to ancient China are papermaking, printing, gunpowder and...?
questions.f: Early Chinese compasses were spoon-shaped lodestones that spun on polished bronze plates.

questions.q: Fine ceramic ware became known in English simply as 'china' because...?
c: It was first imported from China
A merchant named China sold it
The clay came from a place called China
It was painted with Chinese scenes
questions.f: Europe spent centuries trying to reverse-engineer the recipe for true porcelain.

questions.q: Which medieval Islamic scholar's optics work explained that we see by light entering the eye?
questions.f: He tested his ideas with dark rooms and pinholes — early scientific method in action.

questions.q: Which physician's 'Canon of Medicine' was a standard European textbook for around 600 years?
questions.f: Known in Europe as Avicenna, he reportedly wrote well over a hundred books.

questions.q: Baghdad's great centre of translation and learning was called the House of...?
questions.f: Scholars there rescued Greek science by translating it into Arabic, centuries before Europe reread it.

questions.q: Which university, founded in Morocco in 859 CE, is often called the oldest still-running degree-granting institution?
questions.f: It was founded by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, who spent her inheritance on it.

questions.q: Which everyday timekeeper did medieval European monasteries drive the development of?
questions.f: Monks needed to know prayer hours in the dark — and bells had to ring on time.

questions.q: Gothic cathedrals could hold huge windows thanks to which invention?
questions.f: External props took the roof's outward push, so the walls could become glass.

questions.q: Medieval cathedral builders used a 'trebuchet'-like machine called a treadwheel crane, powered by...?
questions.f: Some of these wooden wheels still sit in cathedral roof spaces, hundreds of years later.

questions.q: Which farming change of the Middle Ages let heavier soils be ploughed and boosted harvests?
questions.f: Paired with the horse collar, it turned northern Europe's clay into breadbasket.

questions.q: The horse collar mattered because, unlike an ox yoke, it...?
c: Let a horse pull hard without choking
Could be used on any animal
questions.f: Horses plough faster than oxen — the collar unlocked roughly a 50 percent speed gain.

questions.q: Which medieval organisation set training rules, prices and standards for a town's craftsmen?
questions.f: Guild inspectors could smash substandard goods in the street — quality control, medieval style.

questions.q: A guild's finished proof of skill, submitted to become a master, was called a...?
questions.f: The word now means any great work of art — but it started as a trade exam.

questions.q: Medieval European towns often had strict rules about how far a baker's loaf could fall short in weight.
questions.f: Bakers added an extra roll to every dozen to stay safe — hence the 'baker's dozen' of 13.

questions.q: Which Chinese engineering project, begun over 1,400 years ago, is the world's longest artificial waterway?
questions.f: It runs some 1,700 km, linking the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, and is still in use.

questions.q: Japan's long period of near-total isolation from foreign trade is known as...?
questions.f: 'Closed country' lasted over 200 years, with one small Dutch trading post as the keyhole.

questions.q: Which Japanese era, beginning in 1868, saw rapid modernisation of industry and schools?
questions.f: Japan built railways, factories and a national school system in barely a generation.

questions.q: Which structure did the Romans build to bring a legion's water across a valley near Nimes?
questions.f: Its stones were cut so precisely that most of it needed no mortar at all.

questions.q: Which mountain-crossing invention let medieval merchants haul goods over Alpine passes year-round?
questions.f: Monks ran shelters at the top — and bred the big rescue dogs named after St Bernard Pass.

questions.q: Which everyday building material did the Romans use so well that its recipe was largely lost for centuries?
questions.f: Medieval Europe rebuilt in stone because nobody could match Roman concrete any more.

questions.q: Which pigment, mined in Afghanistan, was once more expensive than gold for painters?
questions.f: Ground from lapis lazuli, it was saved for the most important robes in a painting.

questions.q: Which technique let Renaissance painters make flat panels look deep and three-dimensional?
questions.f: Brunelleschi and Alberti worked out the geometry — art suddenly had a vanishing point.

questions.q: Which Florentine architect solved how to dome the city's cathedral without huge wooden supports?
questions.f: He laid bricks in a herringbone pattern so each ring held itself up as it rose.

questions.q: Which invention of the 1590s let people see disease-causing detail for the first time, though not identified yet?
questions.f: A century later Leeuwenhoek's lenses revealed a whole world he called 'animalcules'.

questions.q: Which ancient Egyptian board game, played with sticks instead of dice, was buried with pharaohs?
questions.f: Boards have been found in royal tombs — including several belonging to Tutankhamun.

questions.q: The Romans borrowed most of their gods from which earlier people?
questions.f: Zeus became Jupiter, Ares became Mars, and Aphrodite became Venus.

questions.q: Which Greek myth figure flew too near the sun on wax wings?
questions.f: His father Daedalus built the wings — and the labyrinth they were escaping from.

questions.q: In Greek myth, the labyrinth on Crete was built to hold which creature?
questions.f: Theseus found his way out by following a thread — the original 'clue'.

questions.q: Which Egyptian god, with a jackal's head, was linked to mummy-making?
questions.f: Priests wore Anubis masks while preparing a mummy for burial.

questions.q: Which Egyptian god was pictured with the head of an ibis and credited with inventing writing?
questions.f: Scribes poured a drop of ink for Thoth before starting work.

questions.q: The Norse afterlife hall for brave warriors was called...?
questions.f: Bifrost was the rainbow bridge, and Asgard the home of the gods.

questions.q: In Norse myth, what was the name of the rainbow bridge to the gods' realm?
questions.f: Yggdrasil was the world tree and Mjolnir was Thor's hammer.

questions.q: Which ancient people gave us the words 'Druid' and built hill forts across Europe?
questions.f: Celtic languages survive today in Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Breton.

questions.q: Which Roman building has a great round hole open to the sky at the top of its dome?
questions.f: The opening is called an oculus — Latin for eye — and rain simply drains away through the floor.

questions.q: Roman soldiers were paid partly in salt-money and were nicknamed after which weapon?
questions.f: The gladius was so tied to soldiering that 'gladiator' comes from it.

questions.q: A Roman legion was made up of roughly how many soldiers?
questions.f: Each legion was split into centuries, and each century had its own standard to follow.

questions.q: Which structure did Rome build across its cities to carry sewage away?
questions.f: Rome's main sewer, the Cloaca Maxima, still drains part of the city today.

questions.q: Which everyday Roman invention is still built into most modern buildings' doorways?
questions.f: An arch turns a heavy load into a squeeze — so stone can span a wide gap without breaking.

questions.q: What did medieval Europe use before paper became common?
questions.f: A single large Bible could take the skins of more than 200 animals.

questions.q: What was the main job of a medieval castle's 'moat' besides holding water?
questions.f: Diggers could not tunnel under a wall if the ground was flooded above them.

questions.q: What was a 'squire' expected to do for his knight?
c: Care for his armour, horse and weapons
questions.f: Squires trained for years before a knighting ceremony called the accolade.

questions.q: Which large bird did medieval nobles train for hunting?
questions.f: Falconry rules were so strict that different ranks were allowed different species of bird.

questions.q: What did medieval Europeans use to sweeten food, before sugar was widely available?
