questions.f: Monasteries kept beehives, which also supplied wax for church candles.

questions.q: Why did medieval spices matter so much for food?
c: They added flavour that plain preserved food lacked
questions.f: The old story that spices hid spoiled meat is mostly a myth — spices cost far more than fresh meat.

questions.q: Which ancient wonder was a huge temple to Artemis, in what is now Turkey?
c: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
The Statue of Zeus at Olympia
questions.f: Its columns were so tall that a few surviving fragments still dwarf visitors.

questions.q: What did the ancient Greeks call their independent cities, each with its own laws?
questions.f: There were hundreds of them, and they argued constantly — but shared a language and games.

questions.q: Ancient Greek homes were often built around an open central...?
questions.f: The courtyard was the family's light, air and workspace all in one.

questions.q: Which Greek city gave its name to a style of tall, leafy-topped column?
questions.f: Corinthian columns are the fanciest of the three classical styles, with carved acanthus leaves.

questions.q: Where did ancient Greeks travel to hear prophecies from a priestess?
questions.f: Delphi was thought to be the world's centre, marked by a stone called the omphalos, or navel.

questions.q: Which sea people of Crete are famous for palace ruins and bull-leaping paintings?
questions.f: They are named after King Minos of the Minotaur legend.

questions.q: The famous Trojan Horse story is told in poems about the city of Troy, located in modern...?
questions.f: Excavations at Hisarlik have revealed at least nine cities stacked on the same hill.

questions.q: How did ancient Egyptians move enormous stone blocks across sand?
c: By wetting the sand ahead of their sledges
By rolling them on wooden balls
questions.f: A tomb painting shows a worker pouring water in front of a sledge — and experiments show it halves the effort.

questions.q: What did Egyptian workers who built royal tombs live in?
questions.f: Records from one village even list days off — including for a worker's family celebrations.

questions.q: Which writing tool did Mesopotamian scribes press into clay?
questions.f: The reed's wedge-shaped tip is what makes cuneiform look like rows of little arrows.

questions.q: Why have so many clay tablets survived from Mesopotamia?
c: Fire hardened them instead of destroying them
questions.f: Burning archives baked the clay — disaster for the owners, luck for historians.

questions.q: Which invention let ancient farmers water fields far from a river?
questions.f: Whole societies organised themselves around digging and sharing the canals.

questions.q: Which animal was domesticated first, long before cats, cows or horses?
questions.f: Dogs joined humans while everyone was still hunting — thousands of years before farming.

questions.q: Where were horses first tamed for riding, according to most evidence?
questions.f: Riding transformed travel, trade and warfare across whole continents.

questions.q: Which everyday container, invented in the ancient Mediterranean, carried oil and wine by ship?
questions.f: Their pointed bases let sailors stack them upright in sand or racks in the hold.

questions.q: How did ancient people usually preserve fish and meat for winter?
questions.f: Salt was so vital that whole trade routes and towns grew up around it.

questions.q: What did ancient Romans call the large country estates where wealthy families lived?
questions.f: City Romans lived in apartment blocks called insulae — 'islands' of housing.

questions.q: Which technology allowed ancient Rome to heat floors and walls with hot air?
questions.f: Floors sat on little pillars so hot air from a furnace could flow underneath.

questions.q: What is a 'palisade' in early forts?
c: A fence of sharpened wooden stakes
questions.f: Quick to build and surprisingly strong — many later stone castles began as palisades.

questions.q: What is the historical term for a large farm estate worked by villagers under a lord?
questions.f: The lord's own fields were the 'demesne', worked as part of the villagers' dues.

questions.q: What is a 'chronicle'?
c: A record of events in the order they happened
questions.f: Monks wrote chronicles year by year — sometimes leaving blank lines for the future.

questions.q: An object made and used by people in the past is called an...?
questions.f: A natural object like a seed or bone found on a site is called an 'ecofact' instead.

questions.q: A person who studies ancient plants and pollen to learn about past climates is a kind of...?
questions.f: Pollen grains survive for thousands of years — and each plant's grain has its own shape.

questions.q: The word 'fossil' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From 'fossilis' — anything obtained by digging, long before it meant ancient remains.

questions.q: The 'saur' in dinosaur, plesiosaur and stegosaur means...?
questions.f: So 'stegosaur' means roof lizard — named for the plates along its back.

questions.q: 'Tyrannosaurus rex' translates roughly as...?
questions.f: 'Rex' is Latin for king, tacked onto Greek words for tyrant and lizard.

questions.q: 'Triceratops' is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: Its frilled skull is one of the largest heads of any land animal ever.

questions.q: 'Pterodactyl' comes from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: One enormously long finger held out the whole wing membrane.

questions.q: 'Mammoth' now means huge — but the animal's name probably came from a word for...?
questions.f: Siberian tusks turned up in the soil, so early names linked the beast to the ground itself.

questions.q: The word 'era' means...?
c: A long distinct period of time
questions.f: Geologists slice the past into eras, periods and epochs, each longer than a human lifetime.

questions.q: 'Medieval' is built from Latin words meaning...?
questions.f: 'Medium' plus 'aevum' — a name given by later writers who felt they lived in a newer age.

questions.q: 'Antique' and 'antiquity' both come from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Ante' means before — the same 'ante' in anticipate and antechamber.

questions.q: A 'relic' is best described as...?
c: Something left behind from the past
A copy of an old object
questions.f: From 'relinquere', to leave behind — the same root as 'relinquish'.

questions.q: A 'dynamo', 'dynasty' and 'dynamite' all share a root meaning...?
questions.f: Greek 'dynamis' — power — links a generator, a ruling family and an explosive.

questions.q: 'Monarch' is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: 'Mono' plus 'arkhein' — the same 'arch' as in architect, the chief builder.

questions.q: 'Republic' comes from Latin words meaning the ___ thing.
questions.f: 'Res publica' — the public affair, in contrast with a king's private property.

questions.q: 'Empire' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Imperium' was a Roman official's power to give orders — the same root as 'imperative'.

questions.q: 'Barbarian', 'Vandal' and 'Goth' were all names Romans used for...?
questions.f: Two of those names later became insults, and one became a style of cathedral.

questions.q: A 'crusade' takes its name from a Latin word for...?
questions.f: 'Crux' means cross — marchers sewed cloth crosses onto their clothes.

questions.q: 'Pilgrimage' and 'peregrine falcon' share a root meaning...?
questions.f: 'Peregrinus' meant foreign or wandering — and that falcon was caught while migrating.

questions.q: A 'treaty' is best described as...?
questions.f: From Latin 'tractare', to handle or discuss — the same root as 'treat' and 'tractable'.

questions.q: An 'archive' is a place that keeps...?
questions.f: From Greek 'arkheion', the town hall where public records were kept.

questions.q: 'Museum' pieces are catalogued by a 'curator', whose title means one who...?
questions.f: From Latin 'curare', to care for — the same root as 'cure'.

questions.q: A 'century' of Roman soldiers was commanded by a...?
questions.f: Centurions were the experienced professionals who actually held the army together.

questions.q: 'Colosseum' is thought to come from a nearby giant...?
questions.f: A colossal bronze figure once stood beside it, lending the amphitheatre its nickname.

questions.q: 'Renaissance man' describes a person who...?
c: Has skills in many different fields
questions.f: Leonardo painted, engineered, studied anatomy and designed flying machines — the model for the phrase.

questions.q: The word 'utopia', coined in 1516, means literally...?
questions.f: Thomas More's joke: his perfect island's name admits it does not exist.

questions.q: The 'compass rose' on old maps shows...?
questions.f: It is called a rose because its points fan out like petals.

questions.q: On old ships, 'ballast' was heavy material carried to...?
questions.f: Ballast stones dumped in harbours have helped archaeologists trace old trade routes.

questions.q: A ship's 'keel' is the...?
c: Backbone along the bottom of the hull
questions.f: 'Even keel' now means steady and balanced, on ships or off.

questions.q: What is 'cartography'?
questions.f: Some of the oldest surviving maps are Babylonian clay tablets nearly 3,000 years old.

questions.q: Which invention let ancient cities store and move water uphill using pressure?
questions.f: Pipes running down and up a valley let water climb the far side by itself.

questions.q: What made the Bronze Age possible in places with no local tin?
questions.f: Tin sometimes travelled thousands of kilometres to reach a copper-rich workshop.

questions.q: Why did iron eventually replace bronze for tools and weapons?
c: Iron ore was far more common
questions.f: Bronze needed scarce tin; iron ore lies almost everywhere, once you can work it hot enough.

questions.q: Which ancient people are credited with the earliest known alphabet with letters for consonants only?
questions.f: Vowel letters were the Greeks' addition, and every European alphabet followed.

questions.q: Which ancient library was destroyed in stages, losing countless irreplaceable scrolls?
questions.f: Ashurbanipal's clay-tablet library survived far better, because fire only baked it harder.

questions.q: Which everyday object did the Chinese first make from bamboo and gunpowder for celebrations?
questions.f: Early rockets were bamboo tubes — the bang came before the beautiful colours.

questions.q: Which invention allowed messages to travel faster than a horse for the first time?
questions.f: Suddenly news could cross a country in minutes instead of days.

questions.q: What powered the earliest factories before steam engines?
questions.f: That is why the first mill towns hug fast-flowing rivers.

questions.q: Which invention of the 1800s let ordinary families keep food fresh far longer at home?
questions.f: A block of delivered ice in an insulated cabinet was the fridge's direct ancestor.

questions.q: Which 19th-century invention made tall buildings practical for the first time?
questions.f: Elisha Otis demonstrated his safety brake by having his own lift's rope cut on stage.

questions.q: Why were early photographs' subjects rarely smiling?
c: Long exposure times made holding a smile hard
questions.f: Sitters had to hold still for many seconds — a serious face was simply easier to keep.

questions.q: What was the very first thing photographed successfully, around 1826?
questions.f: Joseph Nicephore Niepce's rooftop view needed hours of exposure on a treated plate.

questions.q: Which invention let people first hear recorded music in their own homes?
questions.f: Flat discs beat cylinders because they were far easier to stack and copy.

questions.q: Which sea creature's shell did ancient people use as money in many parts of the world?
questions.f: Cowrie shells were used as money across Africa and Asia for centuries.

questions.q: What did the ancient Greeks call their marketplace and meeting square?
questions.f: 'Agoraphobia', the fear of crowded open places, is named after it.

questions.q: What did Roman children use for counting at school?
questions.f: Skilled abacus users can still beat someone with a calculator on simple sums.

questions.q: What are the ruins of an ancient building or city called?
questions.f: The word comes from Latin 'ruere', to fall down.

questions.q: Which large flat stone marks the top of an ancient stone doorway?
questions.f: Stonehenge's famous crosspieces are lintels, lifted into place with no cranes.

questions.q: What is a very old handwritten book, made before printing, called?
questions.f: Some medieval manuscripts still smell faintly of the beeswax used on the leather covers.

questions.q: What did knights wear over their armour to show their colours?
questions.f: Without it, two armoured knights looked much the same on a dusty field.

questions.q: Which weapon did medieval archers in England famously use?
questions.f: Skilled archers trained from boyhood — some skeletons show enlarged bones in their bow arm.

questions.q: What was the wooden lance-barrier in a jousting arena called?
questions.f: That barrier is why jousting is also called 'tilting'.

questions.q: What does a 'coat of mail' protect a wearer from?
questions.f: A single mail shirt could contain over 20,000 riveted rings.

questions.q: Who ran a medieval castle's kitchen and cooked for hundreds?
questions.f: Big castle kitchens had spits large enough to roast a whole ox.

questions.q: Which room in a castle held the family's chapel?
c: A small private chapel inside the walls
questions.f: Grand castles often had two chapels, one for the family and one for the household.

questions.q: What did a medieval village usually build at its centre?
questions.f: The church tower was often the tallest structure for miles around.

questions.q: What is a very long boat paddled by many rowers in ancient Greece called?
questions.f: The most famous Greek warship, the trireme, had three banks of oars.

questions.q: Which country's ancient warriors were known as samurai?
questions.f: A samurai's sword was considered part of his soul and was cared for daily.

questions.q: What is the traditional Japanese cloth garment with wide sleeves called?
questions.f: 'Kimono' simply means 'thing to wear'.

questions.q: What is the traditional draped Indian garment called?
questions.f: A sari can be several metres of unstitched cloth, wrapped without a single button.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek city gave the world the first theatres?
questions.f: The theatre of Dionysus in Athens seated thousands on a hillside.

questions.q: What did the ancient Egyptians use to grind grain into flour?
questions.f: Tiny bits of grit in the bread wore Egyptian teeth flat — mummies show it clearly.

questions.q: Which large ancient city was the capital of the Roman Empire?
questions.f: At its height, Rome may have been the first city anywhere to hold a million people.

questions.q: Which ancient empire was ruled from the city of Persepolis?
questions.f: Persepolis had a hall of a hundred columns for receiving visitors from across the empire.

questions.q: Which people built stone cities in the Andes mountains of South America?
questions.f: Inca builders shaped stones to fit together so tightly that a knife blade cannot slip between them.

questions.q: Which ancient people wrote using picture symbols on stone monuments in Central America?
questions.f: Maya glyphs were only fully understood in the last few decades.

questions.q: Which continent were the pyramids of Giza built on?
questions.f: Egypt sits in the northeast corner of Africa, with a slice across into Asia.

questions.q: What did the ancient Romans call Britain?
questions.f: Britannia later became a symbol of Britain, shown as a woman with a shield and trident.

questions.q: What did Roman soldiers wear on their feet for long marches?
questions.f: Iron studs in the soles gripped the road — and made a marching legion audible from far off.

questions.q: Which drink did ancient Egyptians make from barley?
questions.f: Workers were sometimes paid in bread and beer — both counted as everyday food.

questions.q: Which everyday Egyptian object was often shaped like a small headrest?
questions.f: A curved wooden headrest kept elaborate hairstyles from being flattened overnight.

questions.q: Which useful tool did the ancient Egyptians use to keep walls perfectly straight?
questions.f: A weight on a string always hangs straight down — the simplest test of true vertical there is.

questions.q: What did people use before matches to carry a flame from house to house?
questions.f: Keeping the household fire alive was a daily chore, and neighbours borrowed embers.

questions.q: What did old-fashioned bakers use to slide loaves into a hot oven?
questions.f: Pizza bakers still use exactly the same tool today.

questions.q: What was a medieval town's 'guildhall' used for?
questions.f: Many guildhalls were the grandest buildings in town after the church.

questions.q: Where did people go to see plays in Shakespeare's London?
questions.f: The cheapest ticket meant standing in the yard in all weathers — those watchers were 'groundlings'.

questions.q: In Shakespeare's day, who played the female parts on stage?
questions.f: Women appeared on the English public stage only from the 1660s.

questions.q: Which sweet food did the Aztecs make from cacao and chilli?
questions.f: Sugar and milk were added much later — the original was bitter and frothy.

questions.q: Which everyday vegetable did Europeans first see in the Americas?
questions.f: Potatoes, maize, peppers and cocoa all made the same journey east.

questions.q: Which grain has been grown in flooded fields across Asia for thousands of years?
questions.f: Terraced rice fields in some places are more than a thousand years old and still worked.

questions.q: What did people once use to whiten and clean their clothes before modern soap powders?
questions.f: Ash mixed with water makes lye, the key ingredient of old-fashioned soap.

questions.q: What is a 'quill' pen made from?
questions.f: A single goose feather might write a few pages before needing resharpening.

questions.q: What did writers use to soak up wet ink on a page?
questions.f: Old letters sometimes still have grains of sand caught in the folds.

questions.q: How did people once send a letter without an envelope?
c: Folded the paper and sealed it with wax
Rolled it in a leather tube
questions.f: Clever folding, called letterlocking, meant the letter could not be opened without leaving a trace.

questions.q: What is the name for a very old, valuable object collected today?
questions.f: Many dealers call an object antique once it is over 100 years old.

questions.q: What do we call the family of a king or queen and their household?
questions.f: 'Courtier' means a person who spends their time at the royal court.

questions.q: Which word describes a queen or king ruling on their own?
questions.f: 'Sovereign' was also the name of an English gold coin.

questions.q: Which title belongs to a person who rules for a young king until he grows up?
questions.f: From Latin 'regere', to rule — the same root as 'regime' and 'regal'.

questions.q: What is a 'chronicle' writer's job?
questions.f: Some monastery chronicles were kept going by different writers for centuries.

questions.q: 'Prehistory' means the time before...?
questions.f: Everything we know from that time comes from objects, not documents.

questions.q: An 'archaeologist' digs, but a 'historian' mostly studies...?
questions.f: The best history often comes from putting both kinds of evidence side by side.

questions.q: Which word means 'happening at the same time'?
questions.f: Historians love finding events that were simultaneous but on opposite sides of the world.

questions.q: 'BCE' in dates stands for...?
questions.f: BCE and CE label the same years as BC and AD, without a religious reference.

questions.q: Which of these came first: the wheel, the printing press, or the telephone?
questions.f: Wheels are around 5,500 years old; printing about 600; telephones under 150.

questions.q: Which was invented most recently: paper, glass, or plastic?
questions.f: Glass and paper are ancient; the first fully synthetic plastic dates from around 1907.

questions.q: Which is older: the Colosseum or the Eiffel Tower?
questions.f: The Colosseum opened around 80 CE, about 1,800 years before the Eiffel Tower.

questions.q: Which invention came first: the bicycle or the car?
questions.f: Bicycle chains, gears and ball bearings all helped make early cars possible.

questions.q: Roman roads were built in layers, with big stones at the bottom and smaller ones on top.
questions.f: Some Roman roads are still under modern highways, holding them up.

questions.q: Egypt's pyramids were built by teams of paid workers, not by wandering strangers.
questions.f: Records list workers' names, rations and even their sick days.

questions.q: The Vikings were traders and farmers as well as sailors.
questions.f: Viking silver from Baghdad has been dug up in Sweden — proof of long trading journeys.

questions.q: Ancient Greeks held athletic contests at religious festivals.
questions.f: Besides Olympia, big games were held at Delphi, Corinth and Nemea.

questions.q: Knights had to be wealthy, because armour and warhorses were very costly.
questions.f: A full set of armour could cost as much as a small farm.

questions.q: Medieval castles were often painted white on the outside.
questions.f: Limewash both brightened and protected the stone — the Tower of London got its name from it.

questions.q: Explorers used to bring back plants and seeds as well as gold.
questions.f: Ships carried potted plants in special glass cases so they survived the voyage.

questions.q: Some ancient Egyptian paint colours are still bright after 3,000 years.
questions.f: Egyptian blue, made by heating sand, copper and natron, is the oldest known synthetic pigment.

questions.q: Woolly mammoths lived in North America as well as in Europe and Asia.
questions.f: Mammoths crossed between continents when low sea levels exposed a land bridge.

questions.q: Dinosaur footprints can be fossils, just like bones.
questions.f: Trackways show how fast dinosaurs walked and whether they travelled in groups.

questions.q: Which invention let people read at night without candles or oil?
questions.f: Bulbs also removed the smoke and soot that once coated ceilings.

questions.q: Which machine made cloth much faster during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.f: One power loom could out-produce many hand weavers, changing whole towns.

questions.q: Which sweet food did people collect from beehives long ago?
questions.f: Beekeepers have kept hives for at least 4,500 years.

questions.q: What did people ride before cars were invented?
questions.f: Horses were the fastest way to travel over land for thousands of years.

questions.q: What did knights carry a shield for?
questions.f: A knight's shield was often painted with his family's colours and pictures.

questions.q: What is a very old, ruined building called?
questions.f: Ruins tell us how buildings were made, even after the roof is gone.

questions.q: What did cave artists use to paint on rock?
questions.f: They blew powdered colour through hollow bones to make soft, sprayed shapes.

questions.q: Which big grey animal helped people carry heavy loads in India long ago?
questions.f: Elephants can lift logs weighing hundreds of kilograms with their trunks.

questions.q: What did old windmills have that spun in the wind?
questions.f: The miller turned the whole top of the mill to face the wind.

questions.q: What did people long ago keep water in at home?
questions.f: Clay jars keep water cool because a little seeps out and evaporates.

questions.q: What did people use to see themselves before glass mirrors?
questions.f: A well-polished bronze mirror gives a warm, golden reflection.

questions.q: What did a knight's horse wear on its feet?
questions.f: Horseshoes protect hooves on hard roads, and a blacksmith nailed them on.

questions.q: Which building had a big bell that told the village the time?
questions.f: Before clocks in homes, everyone shared the same bell.

questions.q: What did people spin from wool to make cloth?
questions.f: A spinning wheel twists loose wool into strong thread.

questions.q: What did people put on a horse's back to carry bags?
questions.f: Traders loaded pack horses and mules with goods for market.

questions.q: What was the very first kind of boat probably made from?
questions.f: Dugout canoes thousands of years old have been found in lakes and bogs.

questions.q: Where did ancient Greek children go to learn?
questions.f: Greek boys learned reading, music and sport; girls were usually taught at home.

questions.q: What did ancient Romans throw into a fountain for good luck?
questions.f: People still toss coins into fountains today — an ancient habit that never stopped.

questions.q: What are the very old drawings on cave walls pictures of, mostly?
questions.f: Horses, bulls and deer show up again and again in the oldest cave art.

questions.q: What did ancient people use a spear for?
questions.f: Stone spear tips were tied to wooden shafts with animal sinew.

questions.q: What did people build to cross a river on foot?
questions.f: The oldest bridges were flat stones or fallen logs laid across streams.

questions.q: What did people long ago use to catch fish?
questions.f: Fish hooks made from bone are more than 20,000 years old.

questions.q: What is a very big, old ship's steering handle called?
questions.f: Before wheels, ships were steered with a long wooden bar called a tiller.

questions.q: Which ancient people wore a long cloth called a toga?
questions.f: Putting a toga on properly took help — there were no buttons or pins.

questions.q: What did the ancient Egyptians build boats out of, besides wood?
questions.f: Reed boats float beautifully and were used for fishing on the Nile.

questions.q: What is a group of camels walking together across the desert called?
questions.f: Caravans travelled at night to avoid the fierce daytime heat.

questions.q: What did people write on before paper reached Europe?
questions.f: Those thin, scraped skins are called parchment.

questions.q: Which building is the home of a king's soldiers and guards in a castle?
questions.f: Guards took turns keeping watch through the night.

questions.q: What did a knight promise to do?
questions.f: That promise was part of a code of behaviour called chivalry.

questions.q: What did people burn in old lamps to make light?
questions.f: Olive oil lamps lit ancient Greek and Roman homes.

questions.q: What did ancient people wear on their heads to keep off the hot sun?
questions.f: Loose cloth is cooler than bare skin in a desert, and keeps out the sand.

questions.q: Long ago, most people walked everywhere they went.
questions.f: Only wealthier people could afford a horse, so most journeys were on foot.

questions.q: Ancient people used shells and beads as jewellery.
questions.f: Beads made from shells over 40,000 years ago have been found in caves.

questions.q: Very old money was sometimes made from metal shaped like a coin.
questions.f: Before coins, people also used shells, salt blocks and even cocoa beans.

questions.q: A castle's tallest tower was a good place to watch for visitors.
questions.f: From the top of a tall tower you can see for many kilometres.

questions.q: Ancient Egyptians kept cats as pets.
questions.f: Cats were so loved in Egypt that many families had them, and some were mummified.

questions.q: Old wooden ships could sink in a bad storm.
questions.f: That is why sailors watched the sky so closely and told so many weather sayings.

questions.q: What do we call a story about the past that grown-ups tell children?
questions.f: 'Once upon a time' has been used to begin tales for hundreds of years.

questions.q: A person who studies old bones and buildings is called an...?
questions.f: Archaeologists brush away dirt with tiny tools so nothing gets broken.

questions.q: A very long time — one hundred years — is called a...?
questions.f: Ten years is a decade, and a hundred years is a century.

questions.q: A ruler's special seat is a throne. What is his special hat?
questions.f: Some crowns are so heavy that kings and queens only wear them briefly.

questions.q: Which word means 'in the past, a long time ago'?
questions.f: Historians divide 'long ago' into ages, like the Stone Age and the Bronze Age.

questions.q: What is a picture of a person, painted long ago, called?
questions.f: Before cameras, a painted portrait was the only way to remember a face.

questions.q: What do we call a big journey to find new places?
questions.f: Expeditions took months of planning and huge amounts of food.

questions.q: What word means a place where old things are shown to visitors?
questions.f: Some museums display objects thousands of years old.

questions.q: A treasure map shows where treasure is buried. What do we call the drawing of the land?
questions.f: Old maps often drew sea monsters where no one had sailed yet.

questions.q: A person who rules a country with a crown is a king or a...?
questions.f: Some countries have had ruling queens for hundreds of years.

questions.q: What do we call the soldiers who guarded a castle gate?
questions.f: Guards worked in shifts so the gate was never left alone.

questions.q: What is a baby sheep on an old farm called?
questions.f: A baby goat, on the other hand, is called a kid.

questions.q: What do we call the long pole with a sail on a ship?
questions.f: Big sailing ships had three or more masts, each with several sails.

questions.q: Which word means the people who lived before you in your family?
questions.f: Your ancestors go back further than anyone can count.

questions.q: Which body part pumps blood around your body?
questions.f: Your heart beats about 100,000 times every day.

questions.q: What do you use to smell things?
questions.f: Your nose can tell apart thousands of different smells.

questions.q: What covers a bird's body?
questions.f: Feathers keep birds warm and help them fly.

questions.q: What is the fastest animal on land?
questions.f: A cheetah can run as fast as a car on a highway.

questions.q: Which part of a plant is usually underground?
questions.f: Roots soak up water and hold the plant in the ground.

questions.q: What do bees make inside their hive?
questions.f: Bees make honey from the sweet nectar of flowers.

questions.q: What do we use to look at very tiny things?
questions.f: A microscope makes tiny things look much bigger.

questions.q: What do we use to look at faraway stars?
questions.f: Telescopes gather light so we can see distant space.

questions.q: What gas do green plants give off that we breathe?
questions.f: Plants make oxygen while they turn sunlight into food.

questions.q: What do we call frozen rain that falls as little ice balls?
questions.f: Hailstones form high in storm clouds before falling.

questions.q: What comes out of clouds when it rains?
questions.f: Rain is water that falls from clouds back to the ground.

questions.q: Plants grow from what tiny thing you plant in soil?
questions.f: A single seed holds everything a plant needs to start growing.

questions.q: Which part of a plant is often bright and colourful to attract bees?
questions.f: Colourful flowers help attract bees and butterflies.

questions.q: Which animal has a long trunk?
questions.f: An elephant uses its trunk to drink, smell, and grab food.

questions.q: What is at the centre of our solar system?
questions.f: Everything in our solar system orbits the Sun.

questions.q: What part of your body do you think with?
questions.f: Your brain controls almost everything your body does.

questions.q: Which of these is a mammal?
questions.f: Mammals have fur or hair and feed their babies milk.

questions.q: What do your lungs help you do?
questions.f: You have two lungs that fill with air when you breathe in.

questions.q: What do we call the air that surrounds our planet?
questions.f: The atmosphere is a blanket of air that keeps Earth just right for life.

questions.q: What do caterpillars turn into?
questions.f: A caterpillar changes inside a chrysalis before becoming a butterfly.

questions.q: How many bones does an adult human body have?
questions.f: Babies are born with even more bones that later join together.

questions.q: What do we call rain that has turned to ice crystals in the sky?
questions.f: Every snowflake has its own six-sided pattern.

questions.q: Which of these animals can fly?
questions.f: A bat is the only mammal that can truly fly.

questions.q: What do plants need to make their own food?
questions.f: Plants use sunlight, water, and air to make food.

questions.q: Which liquid do cows give us to drink?
questions.f: Milk is full of calcium that helps bones grow strong.

questions.q: What is the hard white part inside your mouth used for chewing?
questions.f: Teeth help you bite and chew your food.

questions.q: Which of these lives in water its whole life?
questions.f: Most fish cannot survive out of water for long.

questions.q: What do we call the coldest season of the year?
questions.f: In winter it is cold, and some places get snow.

questions.q: What shines in the sky at night and gives no heat of its own?
questions.f: The Moon reflects sunlight, which is why it glows at night.

questions.q: A person who studies stars and planets is called an...?
questions.f: 'Astronomer' comes from a Greek word meaning 'star.'

questions.q: The study of living things is called...?
questions.f: 'Bio' means 'life,' so biology is the study of life.

questions.q: A baby frog is called a...?
questions.f: Tadpoles have tails and live in water before growing legs.

questions.q: A baby dog is called a...?
questions.f: Puppies are born unable to see or hear.

questions.q: A baby cat is called a...?
questions.f: Kittens are born with their eyes closed.

questions.q: A baby cow is called a...?
questions.f: A young cow is called a calf.

questions.q: A baby kangaroo is called a...?
questions.f: A joey rides inside its mother's pouch.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the weather is called a...?
questions.f: Meteorologists help predict rain, storms, and sunshine.

questions.q: A doctor who takes care of your teeth is called a...?
questions.f: Dentists help keep your teeth healthy and clean.

questions.q: The word 'telescope' has 'tele' in it, which means...?
questions.f: 'Tele' means 'far,' so a telescope helps you see far away.

questions.q: The word 'microscope' starts with 'micro,' which means...?
questions.f: 'Micro' means 'small,' perfect for viewing tiny things.

questions.q: A group of stars that makes a picture in the sky is called a...?
questions.f: People long ago named constellations after animals and heroes.

questions.q: An animal that only eats plants is called a...?
questions.f: 'Herbi' comes from a Latin word for plants.

questions.q: An animal that only eats meat is called a...?
questions.f: 'Carni' comes from a Latin word meaning 'flesh.'

questions.q: An animal that is awake at night and sleeps by day is called...?
questions.f: Owls and bats are nocturnal animals.

questions.q: A person who studies rocks is called a...?
questions.f: 'Geo' means 'Earth,' so geologists study the Earth's rocks.

questions.q: A person who studies animals is called a...?
questions.f: 'Zoo' comes from a Greek word meaning 'animal.'

questions.q: A person who studies plants is called a...?
questions.f: Botanists study everything from tiny mosses to giant trees.

questions.q: The 'aqua' in 'aquarium' means...?
questions.f: An aquarium is a water home for fish and other creatures.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who works in a laboratory doing experiments?
questions.f: Scientists ask questions and test ideas with experiments.

questions.q: A young horse is called a...?
questions.f: A newborn horse can stand and walk within hours.

questions.q: The special coat scientists wear in a lab is called a...?
questions.f: A white lab coat helps protect a scientist's clothes.

questions.q: The word 'dinosaur' means 'terrible' what?
questions.f: 'Dinosaur' comes from Greek words meaning 'terrible lizard.'

questions.q: A place where scientists do experiments is called a...?
questions.f: 'Laboratory' comes from a Latin word meaning 'to work.'

questions.q: A person who explores space in a spaceship is called an...?
questions.f: 'Astronaut' means 'star sailor' in Greek.

questions.q: A young swan is called a...?
questions.f: A grey cygnet grows into a graceful white swan.

questions.q: 'Photo' in the word 'photograph' means...?
questions.f: A camera captures a picture using light.

questions.q: The colourful arc in the sky after rain is called a...?
questions.f: A rainbow forms when sunlight bends through raindrops.

questions.q: A person who flies planes and studies flight is called a...?
questions.f: Pilots use science to keep planes safely in the air.

questions.q: What is the name for a baby chicken?
questions.f: A chick pecks its own way out of its shell.

questions.q: A group of wolves is called a...?
questions.f: Wolves live and hunt together in a family pack.

questions.q: A group of fish swimming together is called a...?
questions.f: A school of fish moves together to stay safe.

questions.q: The 'thermo' in 'thermometer' has to do with...?
questions.f: A thermometer measures how hot or cold something is.

questions.q: A person who studies the human body to keep people healthy is a...?
questions.f: Doctors use science to help our bodies stay well.

questions.q: A young cat, dog, and rabbit are all examples of an animal's...?
questions.f: Many baby animals have their own special names.

questions.q: The Sun is a star.
questions.f: Our Sun is a medium-sized star that looks big because it is close.

questions.q: Spiders are insects.
questions.f: Spiders are arachnids; they have eight legs, not six.

questions.q: A butterfly begins its life as a caterpillar.
questions.f: This amazing change is called metamorphosis.

questions.q: Plants need water to grow.
questions.f: Water travels up from the roots to every part of the plant.

questions.q: Fish can breathe underwater using gills.
questions.f: Gills pull oxygen out of the water so fish can breathe.

questions.q: Humans breathe out a gas called carbon dioxide.
questions.f: Plants can use the carbon dioxide we breathe out.

questions.q: The Moon makes its own bright light like the Sun.
questions.f: The Moon only reflects light from the Sun.

questions.q: A whale is a fish.
questions.f: A whale is a mammal; it breathes air and feeds its babies milk.

questions.q: Your skin is the largest organ of your body.
questions.f: Skin protects everything inside your body.

questions.q: Bees help flowers by carrying pollen from one to another.
questions.f: This pollination helps plants make seeds and fruit.

questions.q: All birds can fly.
questions.f: Penguins and ostriches are birds that cannot fly.

questions.q: How many wings does a butterfly have?
questions.f: A butterfly's four wings are covered in tiny coloured scales.

questions.q: What do bees collect from flowers to take back to the hive?
questions.f: Bees turn sweet nectar into honey inside the hive.

questions.q: Which hard part of your body protects your brain?
questions.f: The skull is like a strong helmet made of bone.

questions.q: What is the biggest animal in the ocean?
questions.f: A blue whale's heart alone can be as big as a small car.

questions.q: Which tool would you use to measure how long a pencil is?
questions.f: Rulers are marked in centimetres and millimetres.

questions.q: Which creature spins a web to catch its food?
questions.f: Spider silk is stretchier than most human-made threads.

questions.q: What do birds lay in their nests?
questions.f: Baby birds grow inside the egg before hatching.

questions.q: What is the hot melted rock that flows out of a volcano called?
questions.f: Lava can glow bright orange because it is so hot.

questions.q: Which of these is a bird that hunts at night?
questions.f: An owl can turn its head very far around to look behind it.

questions.q: Which animal has black and white stripes and looks like a horse?
questions.f: Every zebra's stripe pattern is different, like a fingerprint.

questions.q: In which season do most flowers start to bloom?
questions.f: Warmer spring days and rain wake up sleeping plants.

questions.q: What do we call the shape of an animal or plant left in rock from long ago?
questions.f: Some fossils are millions of years old.

questions.q: Which star is closest to Earth?
questions.f: The Sun is so close that it lights up our whole daytime sky.

questions.q: What do we call a large group of trees growing together?
questions.f: Forests are home to more animals than almost any other place.

questions.q: Which animal can change colour to blend in with its surroundings?
questions.f: A chameleon's eyes can look in two directions at once.

questions.q: What loud rumbling sound comes after a flash of lightning?
questions.f: Thunder is the sound of air heated so fast that it bangs.

questions.q: What is the hard part on the outside of an egg called?
questions.f: The shell keeps the growing chick safe inside.

questions.q: Which tool tells you how heavy something is?
questions.f: Scientists weigh things carefully before an experiment.

questions.q: What do we call the pointy sticks of ice that hang from a roof in winter?
questions.f: Icicles grow as dripping water freezes bit by bit.

questions.q: Which tool does a doctor use to listen to your heartbeat?
questions.f: A stethoscope makes quiet body sounds easier to hear.

questions.q: Which part of an apple holds the seeds?
questions.f: Plant an apple seed and it could grow into a whole tree.

questions.q: What are the tiny water drops you find on grass early in the morning?
questions.f: Dew forms when cool air cannot hold all its water vapour.

questions.q: Which small creature carries its shell on its back and moves very slowly?
questions.f: A snail can pull its whole body inside its shell.

questions.q: What do plants take in from the soil along with water?
questions.f: Nutrients in soil work like vitamins for plants.

questions.q: What do we call Earth's one natural satellite?
questions.f: The Moon takes about a month to travel around Earth.

questions.q: What does a caterpillar make around itself before it changes?
questions.f: Inside, the caterpillar's body changes completely.

questions.q: What are the white fluffy shapes floating in the sky made of?
questions.f: Clouds hold millions of droplets too light to fall.

questions.q: Which lab container is a wide cup with a little lip for pouring?
questions.f: Beakers have lines on the side to show how much liquid is inside.

questions.q: What do scientists wear on their hands to keep them safe in a lab?
questions.f: Gloves stop chemicals from touching a scientist's skin.

questions.q: Which is bigger, the Sun or the Earth?
questions.f: Over a million Earths could fit inside the Sun.

questions.q: Which part of a carrot plant do we eat?
questions.f: Carrots store sugary food in their fat orange root.

questions.q: What do fireflies make in the dark?
questions.f: A firefly makes cold light inside its own body.

questions.q: Which animal has no legs and moves by sliding along?
questions.f: Snakes push against the ground with their strong muscles.

questions.q: What do we call the Sun together with all the planets going around it?
questions.f: Our solar system has eight planets circling one star.

questions.q: Which glass tool do scientists use to stir a liquid?
questions.f: Gentle stirring helps things dissolve faster.

questions.q: What do we call a very tall pile of rock that rises high above the land?
questions.f: Some mountains are so tall that snow stays on top all year.

questions.q: A young tree is called a...?
questions.f: A sapling is thin and bendy compared with a grown tree.

questions.q: A group of birds flying together is called a...?
questions.f: Flying in a flock helps birds save energy.

questions.q: A group of cows is called a...?
questions.f: Cows in a herd stay close together for safety.

questions.q: A group of ants living and working together is called a...?
questions.f: One ant colony can have millions of ants.

questions.q: A group of insects flying together is called a...?
questions.f: A swarm of bees moves like one huge cloud.

questions.q: Puppies or kittens born at the same time are called a...?
questions.f: A litter of puppies can have six or more babies.

questions.q: A scientist who studies sea animals and plants is called a...?
questions.f: 'Marine' means to do with the sea.

questions.q: The home that bees build and live in is called a...?
questions.f: A hive holds neat wax rooms shaped like hexagons.

questions.q: An underground home dug by a rabbit is called a...?
questions.f: Rabbit burrows join up into big underground tunnels.

questions.q: Which tool is a round lens with a handle that makes small things look bigger?
questions.f: A magnifying glass bends light to enlarge what you see.

questions.q: The word part 'meter' at the end of 'thermometer' means...?
questions.f: You will spot 'meter' in many measuring tools.

questions.q: The word part 'astro' in 'astronaut' means...?
questions.f: From Greek astron, meaning star.

questions.q: The word 'science' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin scientia, meaning knowledge.

questions.q: When scientists carefully try something out to test an idea, it is called an...?
questions.f: Good experiments can be repeated by other scientists.

questions.q: Tiny living things too small to see that can make you ill are called...?
questions.f: Washing your hands helps wash germs away.

questions.q: The word 'zoo' is short for a longer name meaning a garden of...?
questions.f: 'Zoo' is short for zoological garden.

questions.q: A tiny young plant that has just come up from a seed is called a...?
questions.f: A seedling's first leaves feed it until real leaves grow.

questions.q: The notebook a scientist writes results in during an experiment is called a...?
questions.f: Scientists record everything so they do not forget a detail.

questions.q: A person who studies the tiny living things seen only under a microscope needs a...?
questions.f: Microscopes reveal a whole world too small for our eyes.

questions.q: Not all insects have wings.
questions.f: Worker ants and fleas are insects with no wings at all.

questions.q: Rocks are living things.
questions.f: Rocks do not grow, eat, or breathe, so they are not alive.

questions.q: Seeds need water to start growing.
questions.f: Water wakes the seed up and softens its hard coat.

questions.q: Fireflies can make their own light.
questions.f: A chemical reaction inside their bodies creates a cool glow.

questions.q: A snail is faster than a cheetah.
questions.f: A cheetah is one of the fastest animals; a snail creeps slowly.

questions.q: Which sense do you use to feel whether something is rough or smooth?
questions.f: Your skin is packed with tiny sensors that feel texture.

questions.q: Which part of a plant carries water up from the roots to the leaves?
questions.f: Tiny tubes inside the stem act like drinking straws for the plant.

questions.q: What is the powdery yellow dust inside flowers called?
questions.f: Bees carry pollen between flowers so plants can make seeds.

questions.q: Which blood cells help your body fight off germs?
questions.f: White blood cells are like tiny soldiers inside your body.

questions.q: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
questions.f: Jupiter is so big that all the other planets could fit inside it.

questions.q: What do we call an animal without a backbone?
questions.f: Worms, insects, and jellyfish are all invertebrates.

questions.q: Which gas do plants take in to make their food?
questions.f: Plants breathe in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.

questions.q: What is the closest planet to the Sun?
questions.f: Mercury zips around the Sun faster than any other planet.

questions.q: How many legs does a crab have?
questions.f: A crab has ten legs, and the front two are its claws.

questions.q: Which tube carries food from your mouth down to your stomach?
questions.f: Muscles squeeze food along it, so you could swallow upside down.

questions.q: Which part of the body makes sound so you can speak?
questions.f: Your vocal cords vibrate to create the sound of your voice.

questions.q: What do we call the path a planet takes around the Sun?
questions.f: Earth takes one year to complete a single orbit of the Sun.

questions.q: Which of these is a reptile?
questions.f: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and most lay eggs.

questions.q: What do we call all the water vapour rising, cooling, and falling as rain?
questions.f: The Sun powers the water cycle by heating up the oceans.

questions.q: Which animal group do frogs and toads belong to?
questions.f: Amphibians live part of their life in water and part on land.

questions.q: What is the green substance in leaves that traps sunlight?
questions.f: Chlorophyll gives plants their green colour.

questions.q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.f: Mars looks red because its soil is full of rusty iron.

questions.q: How many teeth does a typical adult human have?
questions.f: This includes four wisdom teeth at the very back.

questions.q: What simple machine is a see-saw an example of?
questions.f: A lever balances on a point called a fulcrum.

questions.q: Which sense organ helps you keep your balance?
questions.f: Tiny fluid-filled tubes in your inner ears sense movement.

questions.q: What do we call animals that eat both plants and meat?
questions.f: Humans, bears, and pigs are all omnivores.

questions.q: Which force slows down a bike when you stop pedalling and hit the brakes?
questions.f: Friction happens when two surfaces rub against each other.

questions.q: What do we call an animal that hunts another animal for food?
questions.f: Lions, hawks, and sharks are all predators.

questions.q: Which part of a flower makes the seeds?
questions.f: After a flower is pollinated, its ovary can grow into a fruit.

questions.q: What kind of energy does a moving windmill turn into electricity?
questions.f: Windmills, or wind turbines, spin to make clean electricity.

questions.q: Which layer of the Earth do we live on?
questions.f: The crust is the thin, rocky outer layer of our planet.

questions.q: What tool would you use to measure the temperature of water?
questions.f: Thermometers often use coloured liquid that rises with heat.

questions.q: Which of these animals is a marsupial that carries its baby in a pouch?
questions.f: Marsupial babies are tiny at birth and grow inside the pouch.

questions.q: What is the main gas that makes up the Sun?
questions.f: The Sun turns hydrogen into helium, releasing huge amounts of energy.

questions.q: Which body system includes the brain and the nerves?
questions.f: The nervous system sends messages all around your body.

questions.q: What do we call the tiny living units that make up all living things?
questions.f: Your body is made of trillions of tiny cells.

questions.q: What causes day and night on Earth?
questions.f: Earth turns all the way around once about every 24 hours.

questions.q: Which of these is a source of light that we do not make ourselves?
questions.f: The Sun is a natural light source; the others are made by people.

questions.q: What do we call an animal's home that it builds, like a bird's?
questions.f: Birds build nests to keep their eggs safe and warm.

questions.q: Which of these do decomposers do in nature?
questions.f: Fungi and worms recycle dead plants and animals into soil.

questions.q: What do we call the study of the weather over a long time in a place?
questions.f: Climate describes the usual weather a place has year after year.

questions.q: The word part 'ovi' in 'oviparous' and 'oval' means...?
questions.f: From Latin ovum, meaning egg.

questions.q: A scientist who studies insects is called an...?
questions.f: 'Entomon' is the Greek word for insect.

questions.q: The prefix 'bi' in 'bicycle' and 'binoculars' means...?
questions.f: Binoculars use two eyepieces, one for each eye.

questions.q: A word meaning 'to eat plants' is 'herbivore.' The part 'vore' means...?
questions.f: You can spot 'vore' in carnivore and omnivore too.

questions.q: The root 'therm' in 'thermometer' means...?
questions.f: A thermos keeps drinks hot by trapping heat.

questions.q: A collective noun for a group of lions is a...?
questions.f: A pride of lions usually shares one large territory.

questions.q: A collective noun for a group of whales or dolphins is a...?
questions.f: Dolphins in a pod work together to find food.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the heart is a...?
questions.f: 'Cardio' comes from the Greek word for heart.

questions.q: The 'geo' in 'geography' and 'geology' means...?
questions.f: Geography is the study of the Earth's features.

questions.q: A baby kangaroo, born very small, is called a...?
questions.f: A newborn joey is about the size of a jellybean.

questions.q: The prefix 'tri' in 'triangle' means...?
questions.f: A triangle has three sides and three corners.

questions.q: A group of crows is often called a...?
questions.f: 'A murder of crows' is one of the oddest collective nouns.

questions.q: The 'micro' in 'microphone' means small, and 'phone' means...?
questions.f: A microphone picks up small sounds and makes them louder.

questions.q: A young deer is called a...?
questions.f: A spotted fawn hides in tall grass to stay safe.

questions.q: The root 'lun' in 'lunar' refers to the...?
questions.f: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth's shadow covers the Moon.

questions.q: The root 'sol' in 'solar' refers to the...?
questions.f: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity.

questions.q: An animal that comes out mainly during the daytime is called...?
questions.f: Diurnal is the opposite of nocturnal.

questions.q: A scientist who studies birds is called an...?
questions.f: 'Ornis' is the Greek word for bird.

questions.q: The word 'planet' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Planets seem to wander across the night sky among the stars.

questions.q: A place that keeps and studies live sea creatures is an...?
questions.f: 'Aquarium' combines 'aqua' (water) with a place ending.

questions.q: A glass tank for keeping land plants and small animals is a...?
questions.f: 'Terra' is the Latin word for land or earth.

questions.q: A dome-shaped room where you can watch the stars projected is a...?
questions.f: A planetarium shows the night sky on a curved ceiling.

questions.q: A baby bear is called a...?
questions.f: Bear cubs stay with their mother for a year or two.

questions.q: The prefix 'octo' in 'octopus' means...?
questions.f: An octopus has eight arms.

questions.q: A group of bees living and working together is called a...?
questions.f: A bee colony can hold tens of thousands of bees.

questions.q: The 'ology' at the end of words like 'biology' means...?
questions.f: Almost any '-ology' word names a field of study.

questions.q: Sound needs something like air or water to travel through.
questions.f: Sound travels as vibrations, so it cannot cross empty space.

questions.q: A spider is a type of insect.
questions.f: Spiders are arachnids with eight legs, not insects.

questions.q: The Earth travels around the Sun once each year.
questions.f: This journey around the Sun is what gives us a year.

questions.q: All metals are attracted to magnets.
questions.f: Only some metals, like iron and steel, are magnetic.

questions.q: Plants make their own food using sunlight in a process called photosynthesis.
questions.f: 'Photo' means light and 'synthesis' means putting together.

questions.q: Bats find their way in the dark using sound.
questions.f: Bats use echolocation, listening for echoes of their own squeaks.

questions.q: A tomato is scientifically a fruit.
questions.f: Botanically, a fruit holds the seeds, which tomatoes do.

questions.q: Human beings are mammals.
questions.f: Like all mammals, humans have hair and feed their babies milk.

questions.q: The Moon is bigger than the Sun.
questions.f: The Sun is far larger; it only looks smaller because it is so far away.

questions.q: Ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why it floats.
questions.f: Water is unusual because it expands when it freezes.

questions.q: What is the name of the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.f: The Pacific is so wide it covers about a third of the planet.

questions.q: Which vitamin, found in oranges and lemons, helps keep you healthy?
questions.f: Sailors long ago ate citrus fruit to avoid a disease called scurvy.

questions.q: The prefix 'sub' in 'submarine' and 'subway' means...?
questions.f: A submarine travels under the surface of the sea.

questions.q: Which organ uses strong acid to help break down the food you swallow?
questions.f: A layer of mucus stops the acid harming the stomach itself.

questions.q: What is the largest organ inside the human body?
questions.f: The liver does hundreds of jobs, including cleaning your blood.

questions.q: Which part of a plant makes most of its food?
questions.f: Leaves are flat and wide to catch as much sunlight as possible.

questions.q: Which planet is the only one not named after a god or goddess?
questions.f: 'Earth' comes from old words simply meaning ground or soil.

questions.q: What do we call a space rock that burns up as a bright streak in our sky?
questions.f: Most meteors are no bigger than a grain of sand.

questions.q: What do we call a huge group of stars held together by gravity?
questions.f: There are likely more galaxies in the universe than people on Earth.

questions.q: What are the round dents covering the Moon's surface called?
questions.f: Craters were made by space rocks crashing into the Moon.

questions.q: What mainly causes the ocean's tides to rise and fall?
questions.f: The Sun's gravity pulls on the oceans too, but more weakly.

questions.q: What do we call a ball of ice and dust that grows a bright tail near the Sun?
questions.f: Halley's Comet returns to our skies about every 76 years.

questions.q: What do we call the imaginary line that Earth spins around?
questions.f: Earth's axis is tilted, which is what gives us seasons.

questions.q: Which body system includes the stomach and the intestines?
questions.f: Food can take a whole day to travel through it.

questions.q: Which is the longest bone in the human body?
questions.f: The femur is your thigh bone, and it is very strong.

questions.q: What are the tiny patterns of ridges on your fingertips called?
questions.f: No two people have exactly the same fingerprints.

questions.q: What is the name for the natural place where an animal or plant lives?
questions.f: A habitat gives an animal food, water, and shelter.

questions.q: What do we call rain, snow, sleet, and hail all together?
questions.f: Precipitation is the part of the water cycle that falls to Earth.

questions.q: What is the hard outer covering of a beetle or crab called?
questions.f: An insect must shed its exoskeleton in order to grow.

questions.q: Which is the largest land animal alive today?
questions.f: A big male African elephant can weigh as much as six cars.

questions.q: Which bird can hover in place and even fly backwards?
questions.f: A hummingbird's wings can beat over 50 times a second.

questions.q: Which bird is the fastest animal on Earth when diving?
questions.f: In a dive it can pass 300 kilometres per hour.

questions.q: Which unusual mammal lays eggs instead of giving birth?
questions.f: The platypus also has a bill like a duck's.

questions.q: What do we call the long winter sleep some animals take?
questions.f: A hibernating animal's heartbeat slows right down.

questions.q: What do we call the long seasonal journeys some animals make each year?
questions.f: Arctic terns migrate nearly pole to pole every year.

questions.q: What is a snake mostly doing when it flicks its tongue in and out?
questions.f: The tongue carries scent particles to a special organ in the mouth.

questions.q: Which is the tallest kind of tree in the world?
questions.f: The tallest known redwood stands over 115 metres high.

questions.q: What can the rings inside a tree trunk tell you?
questions.f: Each ring is usually one year of growth.

questions.q: Which simple machine is a rope running over a grooved wheel?
questions.f: Pulleys let you lift heavy loads with less effort.

questions.q: Which unit is used to measure electrical power?
questions.f: A bright room lamp might use about 10 watts today.

questions.q: Which instrument measures how fast the wind is blowing?
questions.f: Most anemometers have spinning cups that catch the wind.

questions.q: Which type of rock forms when layers of sand and mud are pressed together?
questions.f: Most fossils are found in sedimentary rock.

questions.q: What is the name for melted rock still underneath the Earth's surface?
questions.f: Once magma flows out onto the surface, we call it lava.

questions.q: At what temperature does water freeze on the Fahrenheit scale?
questions.f: Water freezes at 32 F, which is the same as 0 C.

questions.q: What does a seismograph measure?
questions.f: A seismograph draws a jagged line as the ground shakes.

questions.q: What is the name for the amount of space that an object takes up?
questions.f: Volume is often measured in cubic centimetres or litres.

questions.q: Which lab tool is a tall tube with markings, used to measure liquid volume?
questions.f: You read the level at the bottom of the curve, called the meniscus.

questions.q: What is the deepest known place in the ocean?
questions.f: Its deepest point is nearly 11 kilometres down.

questions.q: Besides oxygen, what do plants make during photosynthesis?
questions.f: Plants use that sugar as food and store some as starch.

questions.q: Which group do mushrooms belong to?
questions.f: Fungi cannot make their own food the way plants do.

questions.q: Which is the largest of the four inner rocky planets?
questions.f: Earth is just slightly larger than Venus.

questions.q: What is the name for a scientist's careful, testable guess?
questions.f: An experiment either supports a hypothesis or shows it is wrong.

questions.q: A scientist who studies chemicals and how they react is called a...?
questions.f: Chemists work out what substances are made of.

questions.q: A scientist who studies forces, energy, and motion is called a...?
questions.f: A physicist might study anything from atoms to galaxies.

questions.q: The word part 'scope' in 'telescope' and 'microscope' means...?
questions.f: From Greek skopein, meaning to look or examine.

questions.q: A group of geese resting on the ground is called a...?
questions.f: In the air, a group of geese is often called a skein.

questions.q: A group of frogs is called an...?
questions.f: An army of frogs can be very noisy on a spring night.

questions.q: A baby seal is called a...?
questions.f: Seal pups are often born with soft white fur.

questions.q: A baby owl is called an...?
questions.f: Owlets have fluffy down before their flight feathers grow.

questions.q: What is the hard case a caterpillar forms around itself before becoming a butterfly?
questions.f: Moths spin a silk cocoon; butterflies form a hard chrysalis.

questions.q: The word 'chrysalis' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Some chrysalises really do shimmer with a golden sheen.

questions.q: The word part 'arthro' in 'arthropod' means...?
questions.f: Arthropods, like insects and crabs, have jointed legs.

questions.q: The word 'amphibian' is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: Amphibians live both in water and on land.

questions.q: The word 'mammal' comes from a Latin word linked to...?
questions.f: All mammals feed their young on milk.

questions.q: The word 'reptile' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin reptilis, from repere, to creep.

questions.q: The word 'insect' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: An insect's body looks cut into three sections.

questions.q: The word 'pollen' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Pollen grains really are as fine as flour.

questions.q: In Greek myths, 'nectar' was the drink of the...?
questions.f: Flowers offer their own sweet nectar to insects.

questions.q: The word 'orbit' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: A planet's path really is like a wheel's rut in the sky.

questions.q: The word 'satellite' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: A satellite keeps company with the planet it circles.

questions.q: The word 'cell' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Cells reminded their discoverer of small rooms in a building.

questions.q: A 'vertebra' is a single bone of the...?
questions.f: Your backbone is a stack of vertebrae.

questions.q: The word part 'aero' in 'aeroplane' and 'aerobic' means...?
questions.f: Aerobic exercise gets more air into your lungs.

questions.q: The word part 'sphere' in 'atmosphere' and 'hemisphere' means...?
questions.f: A sphere is perfectly round in every direction.

questions.q: The prefix 'kilo' in 'kilogram' and 'kilometre' means...?
questions.f: A kilometre is one thousand metres.

questions.q: The prefix 'milli' in 'millimetre' means...?
questions.f: There are one thousand millimetres in a metre.

questions.q: A scientist who studies how living things and their surroundings fit together is an...?
questions.f: Ecologists study whole habitats, not just single animals.

questions.q: Jupiter has more mass than all the other planets in our solar system combined.
questions.f: Jupiter is about two and a half times the mass of everything else combined.

questions.q: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived.
questions.f: It is larger than any dinosaur scientists have found.

questions.q: Insects have three main body parts.
questions.f: They are the head, the thorax, and the abdomen.

questions.q: The Moon has a thick atmosphere like Earth's.
questions.f: The Moon has almost no atmosphere at all.

questions.q: Sharks are mammals.
questions.f: Sharks are fish, and they breathe using gills.

questions.q: Your heart is a muscle.
questions.f: It is a muscle that never takes a day off.

questions.q: A year on Mars is longer than a year on Earth.
questions.f: Mars takes about 687 Earth days to orbit the Sun once.

questions.q: Which scientist is famous for the theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.f: Darwin developed his ideas after a voyage on the ship HMS Beagle.

questions.q: What is the powerhouse of the cell, where energy is made?
questions.f: Mitochondria turn food and oxygen into usable energy.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered that white light is made of many colours?
questions.f: Newton split sunlight into a rainbow using a glass prism.

questions.q: What is the process by which plants lose water vapour through their leaves?
questions.f: Transpiration helps pull water all the way up a tall tree.

questions.q: How many bones are in an adult human hand and wrist together?
questions.f: Your hands have many small bones that let you move with great precision.

questions.q: Which planet spins on its side, almost like a rolling ball?
questions.f: Uranus is tilted so far that its poles take turns facing the Sun.

questions.q: What do we call an animal that has cold blood and its body temperature changes with its surroundings?
questions.f: Reptiles bask in the sun to warm up their ectothermic bodies.

questions.q: Which part of the human eye controls how much light gets in?
questions.f: The iris makes the black pupil grow larger or smaller.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for water?
questions.f: Water is two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.

questions.q: Which gas makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.f: Even though we need oxygen, most of the air is actually nitrogen.

questions.q: What is the name for a material that lets electricity pass through it easily, like copper?
questions.f: Metals are good conductors because their electrons move freely.

questions.q: What do we call the change of a gas directly into a solid, without becoming liquid?
questions.f: Frost forms by deposition when water vapour turns straight to ice.

questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.f: Arteries have thick walls to handle the strong push of the heart.

questions.q: What is the study of the forces that make objects move called?
questions.f: Mechanics is a major branch of physics.

questions.q: Which scientist is credited with discovering gravity after watching a falling apple?
questions.f: Newton's laws explain how gravity pulls objects toward each other.

questions.q: What do we call a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up?
questions.f: Enzymes in your body are natural catalysts.

questions.q: Which organ in the human body filters waste out of the blood to make urine?
questions.f: Most people have two kidneys, each about the size of a fist.

questions.q: What is the boiling process that separates a liquid from a mixture and collects it again?
questions.f: Distillation can turn salty seawater into fresh drinking water.

questions.q: Which type of rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens?
questions.f: Igneous comes from a Latin word for fire.

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of an element that still has its properties?
questions.f: Atoms are so small that millions could fit on the tip of a pin.

questions.q: Which scientist developed the process of pasteurisation to kill germs in milk?
questions.f: Pasteur's work helped prove that germs cause many diseases.

questions.q: What is the name of the force that pulls objects toward the centre of the Earth?
questions.f: Gravity is what gives objects their weight.

questions.q: Which part of a plant cell gives it a firm, boxy shape?
questions.f: Plant cells have a stiff cell wall that animal cells lack.

questions.q: What do we call animals with a backbone?
questions.f: Fish, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and mammals are all vertebrates.

questions.q: Which planet has the shortest day, spinning around in under 11 hours?
questions.f: Despite being the biggest planet, Jupiter spins the fastest.

questions.q: What do we call the pathway that shows what eats what in nature?
questions.f: A food chain usually starts with a plant that captures sunlight.

questions.q: What is the name of the pigment that makes human skin, hair, and eyes darker?
questions.f: Melanin also helps protect skin from the Sun's rays.

questions.q: Which simple machine is a ramp an example of?
questions.f: An inclined plane makes it easier to move a load upward.

questions.q: What do we call the middle layer of the Earth, between the crust and the core?
questions.f: The mantle is made of hot, slowly flowing rock.

questions.q: Which scientist created the first widely used polio vaccine?
questions.f: Salk's vaccine helped protect millions of children from polio.

questions.q: What is the red protein in blood that carries oxygen?
questions.f: Haemoglobin contains iron, which is why blood turns bright red with oxygen.

questions.q: Which scientist accidentally discovered penicillin from a mould?
questions.f: Fleming noticed a mould killing bacteria in his lab dish.

questions.q: What do we call a solid that turns straight into a gas, like dry ice?
questions.f: Dry ice sublimes into a foggy carbon dioxide gas.

questions.q: Which of Newton's laws says that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction?
questions.f: This law explains how rockets push themselves into space.

questions.q: What do we call the tiny particles that orbit the nucleus of an atom?
questions.f: Electrons carry a negative electric charge.

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
questions.f: The cerebellum sits at the back of your brain.

questions.q: What is the name for animals that are active at twilight, at dawn and dusk?
questions.f: Rabbits and deer are often crepuscular.

questions.q: Which unit is used to measure electric current?
questions.f: The ampere is often shortened to 'amp.'

questions.q: What is the process by which a caterpillar transforms into a butterfly called?
questions.f: Complete metamorphosis has four stages: egg, larva, pupa, adult.

questions.q: In 'photosynthesis,' the part 'synthesis' means...?
questions.f: Photosynthesis puts together sugar from water and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: The root 'hydro' in 'hydrogen' and 'hydroelectric' means...?
questions.f: Hydrogen was named because burning it produces water.

questions.q: The prefix 'micro' means small; what does 'macro' mean?
questions.f: 'Macro' is the opposite of 'micro.'

questions.q: A scientist who studies fossils and ancient life is a...?
questions.f: 'Palaeo' comes from Greek meaning 'ancient.'

questions.q: The word 'atom' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: The Greeks thought atoms could not be split into anything smaller.

questions.q: The 'chloro' in 'chlorophyll' refers to the colour...?
questions.f: 'Chloros' is Greek for a pale green colour.

questions.q: A scientist who studies earthquakes is a...?
questions.f: 'Seismos' is the Greek word for shaking or earthquake.

questions.q: The root 'vor' in 'carnivore' and 'omnivore' means...?
questions.f: 'Voro' is Latin for 'I eat' or 'devour.'

questions.q: In the word 'omnivore,' the prefix 'omni' means...?
questions.f: 'Omni' means all, so omnivores eat all kinds of food.

questions.q: The word 'nucleus' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: The nucleus sits at the centre of a cell, like a kernel.

questions.q: The root 'derm' in words like 'epidermis' means...?
questions.f: A dermatologist is a doctor who treats the skin.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the tiny world of germs and microbes is a...?
questions.f: Microbiologists study life too small to see with the naked eye.

questions.q: The word 'gravity' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Gravis' is Latin for heavy, and gravity gives weight.

questions.q: The 'cardi' in 'cardiovascular' refers to the...?
questions.f: Your cardiovascular system includes the heart and blood vessels.

questions.q: A word for the young of an insect, like a young beetle grub, is a...?
questions.f: Larvae later change form as they grow up.

questions.q: The prefix 'trans' in 'transpiration' and 'transparent' means...?
questions.f: Light passes through something transparent.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the ocean is an...?
questions.f: Oceanographers explore currents, waves, and deep-sea life.

questions.q: The root 'therm' appears in 'thermal.' A 'thermostat' controls...?
questions.f: A thermostat keeps a room at a steady temperature.

questions.q: The word 'element' in chemistry means a substance that...?
c: Cannot be broken into simpler substances
questions.f: Gold, oxygen, and iron are all elements.

questions.q: A group of stars named after a mythical hunter is the constellation...?
questions.f: Orion is easy to spot by the three stars of his 'belt.'

questions.q: The 'ped' in 'centipede' and 'pedal' means...?
questions.f: A centipede's name means 'hundred feet.'

questions.q: In 'centipede,' the part 'centi' means...?
questions.f: 'Centi' also appears in 'century,' a hundred years.

questions.q: A scientist who classifies and names living things studies...?
questions.f: Taxonomy sorts life into groups like kingdom, class, and species.

questions.q: The root 'anatomy' contains 'tomy,' which means...?
questions.f: Anatomy originally meant cutting things open to study them.

questions.q: A word for a substance dissolved in a liquid is the...?
questions.f: In salty water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent.

questions.q: The liquid that dissolves another substance is called the...?
questions.f: Water is often called the universal solvent.

questions.q: A word describing plants that shed all their leaves each autumn is...?
questions.f: 'Deciduous' comes from a Latin word meaning 'to fall down.'

questions.q: An electric current is a flow of tiny charged particles called electrons.
questions.f: When electrons flow through a wire, they carry electrical energy.

questions.q: Sound travels faster through solids than through air.
questions.f: Particles are packed closer in solids, so vibrations pass quickly.

questions.q: The heart has four chambers.
questions.f: Two atria receive blood and two ventricles pump it out.

questions.q: Whales breathe through gills like fish do.
questions.f: Whales are mammals that breathe air through blowholes.

questions.q: A leap year happens because Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun.
questions.f: We add a day every four years to catch up with those extra quarters.

questions.q: Diamond and graphite are both made of the element carbon.
questions.f: The atoms are arranged differently, giving very different results.

questions.q: All bacteria are harmful to humans.
questions.f: Many bacteria are helpful, such as those that aid digestion.

questions.q: Light can travel through the vacuum of empty space.
questions.f: That is how sunlight reaches Earth across empty space.

questions.q: The chemical symbol 'Fe' stands for iron.
questions.f: It comes from 'ferrum,' the Latin word for iron.

questions.q: Which planet is the hottest in the solar system, even hotter than Mercury?
questions.f: Venus's thick clouds trap heat like a giant greenhouse.

questions.q: What is the name of the windpipe that carries air toward the lungs?
questions.f: Rings of cartilage keep the trachea from collapsing.

questions.q: Which inventor is widely credited with creating a practical, long-lasting light bulb?
questions.f: Edison tested thousands of materials before finding a lasting filament.

questions.q: The root 'audi' in 'audible' and 'auditory' means...?
questions.f: An auditory nerve carries sound signals to the brain.

questions.q: The root 'opt' in 'optics' and 'optical' relates to...?
questions.f: Optics is the branch of physics that studies light and vision.

questions.q: A doctor who studies and treats the skin is a...?
questions.f: 'Derma' is the Greek word for skin.

questions.q: The prefix 'de' in 'dehydrate' means...?
questions.f: To dehydrate is to remove water from something.

questions.q: Which scientist first used a telescope to discover four moons of Jupiter?
questions.f: Those four are still called the Galilean moons today.

questions.q: Who was the first human to walk on the Moon?
questions.f: He stepped onto the surface in July 1969.

questions.q: Who was the first person to travel into space?
questions.f: Gagarin orbited Earth once in 1961 in Vostok 1.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to fly in space?
questions.f: She flew solo aboard Vostok 6 in 1963.

questions.q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite launched into orbit?
questions.f: Its steady radio beep could be heard by amateur radio fans worldwide.

questions.q: Which planet has the tallest volcano in the solar system?
questions.f: Olympus Mons on Mars is about three times the height of Everest.

questions.q: How many moons does Mars have?
questions.f: They are named Phobos and Deimos.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere contains the ozone layer?
questions.f: Aeroplanes often cruise in the calm lower stratosphere.
