questions.q: What does the ozone layer protect life on Earth from?
questions.f: Ozone absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light.

questions.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
c: Gases in the air trapping heat
questions.f: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth would be far too cold for us.

questions.q: What is the giant long-lasting storm on Jupiter called?
questions.f: This storm is wider than the whole Earth.

questions.q: What colour does blue litmus paper turn when dipped in an acid?
questions.f: In a base, red litmus turns blue instead.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula for common table salt?
questions.f: One sodium atom joins one chlorine atom.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Pb?
questions.f: Pb comes from 'plumbum', the Latin word for lead.

questions.q: Which metal is used in most household wiring because it conducts well?
questions.f: Copper is drawn into thin wires without snapping.

questions.q: Bronze is an alloy made mainly of copper and which other metal?
questions.f: The Bronze Age is named after this useful mixture.

questions.q: Steel is made by mixing iron with a small amount of which element?
questions.f: Just a little carbon makes iron far stronger.

questions.q: What do we call a mixture that looks completely the same throughout, like salt water?
questions.f: In a solution the particles are far too small to see.

questions.q: Which method separates an undissolved solid from a liquid using filter paper?
questions.f: The solid left on the paper is called the residue.

questions.q: Which technique separates the different coloured dyes in an ink?
questions.f: The colours travel up the paper at different speeds.

questions.q: Which piece of lab equipment heats things using an adjustable gas flame?
questions.f: Turning its collar changes the flame from yellow to hot blue.

questions.q: Which lab tool is a slender tube used to transfer small, exact volumes of liquid?
questions.f: Pipettes let scientists measure drops very precisely.

questions.q: In an experiment, what do we call the one thing you deliberately change?
questions.f: Changing only one thing at a time makes results trustworthy.

questions.q: In an experiment, what do we call the thing you measure as your result?
questions.f: It 'depends' on what you changed.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a control in an experiment?
c: To give something unchanged to compare against
questions.f: Without a control you cannot tell what caused a change.

questions.q: What are the smallest blood vessels in the body called?
questions.f: Capillary walls are just one cell thick so gases pass easily.

questions.q: What are the tiny air sacs in your lungs called?
questions.f: Your lungs hold hundreds of millions of alveoli.

questions.q: Which part of the digestive system absorbs most of the nutrients from food?
questions.f: Its inner surface is folded into millions of tiny villi.

questions.q: Which sheet of muscle below the lungs helps you breathe in?
questions.f: When the diaphragm flattens, air rushes into your lungs.

questions.q: What connects a muscle to a bone?
questions.f: You can feel a tendon behind your ankle.

questions.q: What connects one bone to another at a joint?
questions.f: Ligaments are tough but slightly stretchy.

questions.q: Which mineral is most needed to build strong bones and teeth?
questions.f: Dairy foods and leafy greens are rich in calcium.

questions.q: What do we call the organisms at the start of a food chain that make their own food?
questions.f: Green plants and algae are the main producers on Earth.

questions.q: What do we call many food chains linked together in one habitat?
questions.f: Food webs show that most animals eat more than one thing.

questions.q: What is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth?
questions.f: The Amazon holds about a tenth of all known species.

questions.q: What causes a solar eclipse?
c: The Moon passing between Earth and the Sun
questions.f: A total solar eclipse can turn day briefly into twilight.

questions.q: What causes the changing phases of the Moon?
c: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits
questions.f: The Moon is always half lit; we just see it from different angles.

questions.q: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
questions.f: At that speed light could circle Earth over seven times in a second.

questions.q: Roughly how fast does sound travel through air?
questions.f: That is why you hear thunder seconds after you see lightning.

questions.q: Which unit measures the frequency of a wave?
questions.f: One hertz means one wave cycle every second.

questions.q: Ohm's law links voltage, current, and which third quantity?
questions.f: Voltage equals current multiplied by resistance.

questions.q: What do we call a circuit in which all the components sit in a single loop?
questions.f: In a series circuit, one break stops everything.

questions.q: Which safety device protects a circuit by melting when the current is too high?
questions.f: A blown fuse breaks the circuit before wires overheat.

questions.q: What do we call a material that conducts electricity only partly, used in computer chips?
questions.f: Silicon is the most widely used semiconductor.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation LED stand for?
questions.f: LEDs turn most of their energy into light rather than heat.

questions.q: What is the pivot point of a lever called?
questions.f: Moving the fulcrum changes how much effort you need.

questions.q: What do we call an object's resistance to any change in its motion?
questions.f: A heavier object has more inertia than a light one.

questions.q: Which of Newton's laws explains why an object at rest stays at rest unless pushed?
questions.f: It is often called the law of inertia.

questions.q: What do we call the steady maximum speed a falling object reaches?
questions.f: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity when drag balances gravity.

questions.q: What does density describe?
c: How much mass is packed into a space
questions.f: Density is mass divided by volume.

questions.q: What do we call the upward force a fluid exerts on an object placed in it?
questions.f: Upthrust is why you feel lighter in a swimming pool.

questions.q: How many bones make up the adult human skull?
questions.f: Most of them are firmly locked together at wiggly seams.

questions.q: What is the term for the variety of different living things in an area?
questions.f: High biodiversity usually means a healthier habitat.

questions.q: What do we call heat that travels by the movement of a warm liquid or gas?
questions.f: Convection currents make warm air rise and cool air sink.

questions.q: Which of these is the correct name for the study of the cell?
questions.f: Cytologists study cell structure under microscopes.

questions.q: The word part 'cyto' in 'cytoplasm' means...?
questions.f: From Greek kytos, meaning a hollow vessel or cell.

questions.q: The word part 'hepat' in 'hepatic' refers to the...?
questions.f: Hepatic arteries carry blood to the liver.

questions.q: The word part 'gastro' in 'gastric' refers to the...?
questions.f: Gastric juices help digest your dinner.

questions.q: The word part 'pulmo' in 'pulmonary' refers to the...?
questions.f: The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs.

questions.q: The word part 'haemo' in 'haemoglobin' means...?
questions.f: From Greek haima, meaning blood.

questions.q: The word 'equinox' is built from Latin words meaning...?
questions.f: At an equinox, day and night are almost the same length.

questions.q: The word 'solstice' is built from Latin words meaning...?
questions.f: At a solstice the Sun seems to pause before reversing its path.

questions.q: The word 'eclipse' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: The Sun seemed to 'fail' when it vanished at midday.

questions.q: The word 'crater' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Greek kraters were wide bowls for mixing drinks.

questions.q: The word 'comet' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: The tail looked like flowing hair to ancient sky-watchers.

questions.q: The word 'asteroid' means...?
questions.f: Through early telescopes asteroids looked like faint stars.

questions.q: The 'atmos' in 'atmosphere' means...?
questions.f: So 'atmosphere' is literally a sphere of vapour.

questions.q: The word part 'baro' in 'barometer' means...?
questions.f: A barometer weighs the air pressing down on us.

questions.q: The word part 'anemo' in 'anemometer' means...?
questions.f: From Greek anemos, meaning wind.

questions.q: The word part 'hygro' in 'hygrometer' means...?
questions.f: A hygrometer measures humidity in the air.

questions.q: The word part 'stetho' in 'stethoscope' means...?
questions.f: So a stethoscope is literally a chest-viewer.

questions.q: The word 'microbe' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Microbes are living things too small to see unaided.

questions.q: The word 'antibiotic' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Antibiotics act against bacteria, not against viruses.

questions.q: The word 'antiseptic' contains 'septic', which means...?
questions.f: An antiseptic works against decay-causing microbes.

questions.q: The word 'pupa' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: A wrapped pupa did look like a little swaddled doll.

questions.q: The word 'vitamin' contains 'vita', which means...?
questions.f: Vitamins were first thought to be vital amines.

questions.q: The word 'molecule' comes from a Latin phrase meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin moles, a mass, plus a 'little' ending.

questions.q: The element helium is named after the Greek god of the...?
questions.f: Helium was spotted in sunlight before it was found on Earth.

questions.q: The element phosphorus has a name meaning...?
questions.f: White phosphorus glows faintly in air.

questions.q: The element carbon takes its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin carbo, meaning charcoal.

questions.q: The element calcium takes its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin calx, the lime made by roasting limestone.

questions.q: The metal copper takes its name from which Mediterranean island?
questions.f: Romans called it 'aes cyprium', metal of Cyprus.

questions.q: The word 'magnet' comes from the name of an ancient region called...?
questions.f: Naturally magnetic stones were found near Magnesia.

questions.q: The word 'electric' comes from a Greek word for...?
questions.f: Rubbed amber attracts dust, an early clue to static charge.

questions.q: The word 'algae' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin alga, meaning seaweed.

questions.q: The word 'virus' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Early scientists knew something harmful passed through filters.

questions.q: The temperature unit 'Celsius' is named after a scientist from which country?
questions.f: Anders Celsius proposed his scale in 1742.

questions.q: The unit 'volt' is named after which scientist?
questions.f: Volta built one of the first batteries, the voltaic pile.

questions.q: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum, but light can.
questions.f: Light needs no medium, while sound needs particles to vibrate.

questions.q: The Sun is closer to Earth in some months than in others.
questions.f: Earth's orbit is slightly oval, so the distance changes a little.

questions.q: Antibiotics are effective against viruses such as the common cold.
questions.f: Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses.

questions.q: Arteries generally carry blood away from the heart.
questions.f: The pulmonary artery is the exception carrying blood to the lungs.

questions.q: A conifer is a tree that produces its seeds inside cones.
questions.f: Pines, spruces, and firs are all conifers.

questions.q: Mass and weight mean exactly the same thing in science.
questions.f: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the force of gravity on it.

questions.q: An insect breathes through tiny holes along its body rather than lungs.
questions.f: Those openings are called spiracles.

questions.q: Glass is a better conductor of heat than metal.
questions.f: Metals conduct heat far better, which is why metal feels colder.

questions.q: Which scientist proposed the theory of general relativity?
questions.f: General relativity describes gravity as a bending of space and time.

questions.q: What is the process by which a cell divides to make two identical cells?
questions.f: Mitosis lets your body grow and repair itself.

questions.q: Which particle in the atomic nucleus has no electric charge?
questions.f: Neutrons help hold the nucleus together despite proton repulsion.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered radioactivity elements polonium and radium?
questions.f: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry.

questions.q: What is the pH value of a neutral solution like pure water?
questions.f: Values below 7 are acidic and above 7 are basic, or alkaline.

questions.q: What are the tiny pores on a leaf that open and close to control gas exchange?
questions.f: Two guard cells swell or shrink to open each stoma.

questions.q: What do we call the movement of water molecules across a membrane from low to high solute?
questions.f: Osmosis helps plant roots pull water from the soil.

questions.q: Which scientist is known as the father of modern genetics for his work with pea plants?
questions.f: Mendel discovered how traits pass from parents to offspring.

questions.q: What is the name for the change of state from a gas directly to a liquid?
questions.f: Dew forms overnight when water vapour condenses on cool grass.

questions.q: Which unit measures the amount of energy or work done?
questions.f: The joule is named after physicist James Prescott Joule.

questions.q: What is the most abundant element in the universe?
questions.f: Hydrogen makes up roughly three-quarters of all normal matter.

questions.q: Which part of a plant cell captures light energy for photosynthesis?
questions.f: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll.

questions.q: What do we call the resistance of a fluid to flowing, thick like honey?
questions.f: Honey has a much higher viscosity than water.

questions.q: Which scientist first observed cells and gave them their name?
questions.f: Hooke saw box-like cork cells that reminded him of monks' rooms.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.f: One newton is roughly the weight of a small apple.

questions.q: Which type of chemical bond involves atoms sharing electrons?
questions.f: Water molecules are held together by covalent bonds.

questions.q: What do we call an animal or plant that can make its own food?
questions.f: Plants are autotrophs because they photosynthesise.

questions.q: Which planet has the fastest winds in the solar system, reaching supersonic speeds?
questions.f: Neptune's storms can blow faster than the speed of sound.

questions.q: What is the study of heredity and genes called?
questions.f: Genetics explains why children resemble their parents.

questions.q: Which scientist developed the modern periodic table, arranging elements by pattern?
questions.f: Mendeleev even left gaps for elements not yet discovered.

questions.q: What is the term for the amount of matter in an object, which never changes with location?
questions.f: Weight can change on the Moon, but mass stays the same.

questions.q: Which blood cells help the blood to clot when you get a cut?
questions.f: Platelets rush to a wound and form a protective plug.

questions.q: What is the name of the largest artery in the human body?
questions.f: The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood away from the heart.

questions.q: Which scientist's laws describe the motion of planets in elliptical orbits?
questions.f: Kepler showed planets move in ellipses, not perfect circles.

questions.q: What do we call the temperature at which a solid turns to liquid?
questions.f: The melting point of ice is 0 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
questions.f: Alpha particles are the least penetrating type of radiation.

questions.q: What is the name of the molecule that carries genetic instructions in living things?
questions.f: DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder called a double helix.

questions.q: Which scientist is credited with discovering the electron?
questions.f: Thomson found that atoms contain even smaller charged particles.

questions.q: What do we call the process where rock is worn away by wind, water, or ice?
questions.f: Erosion carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years.

questions.q: Which gland controls many body processes and is called the 'master gland'?
questions.f: The pituitary is only about the size of a pea.

questions.q: What is the name for a reaction that releases heat energy to the surroundings?
questions.f: Burning fuel is an exothermic reaction.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere contains most weather and clouds?
questions.f: Almost all weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere.

questions.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body, found in the ear?
questions.f: The stapes is smaller than a grain of rice.

questions.q: Which scientist demonstrated that lightning is a form of electricity?
questions.f: Franklin's famous kite experiment linked lightning to electric sparks.

questions.q: What is the process by which living things release energy from food using oxygen?
questions.f: Cellular respiration happens inside the mitochondria.

questions.q: Which force must be overcome for an aircraft to rise into the air?
questions.f: Wings generate lift to fight against gravity's pull.

questions.q: What do we call organisms that break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil?
questions.f: Fungi and bacteria are important decomposers.

questions.q: Which scientist built an early model of the atom with electrons in fixed orbits?
questions.f: Bohr pictured electrons circling the nucleus like planets.

questions.q: What is the term for a trait that appears only when two copies of a gene are present?
questions.f: A recessive trait can be hidden by a dominant one.

questions.q: Which instrument measures atmospheric pressure to help forecast weather?
questions.f: A falling barometer reading often warns of stormy weather.

questions.q: What is the name for the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing escapes?
questions.f: Not even light can escape once it crosses the event horizon.

questions.q: Which process turns nitrogen from the air into forms plants can use?
questions.f: Certain bacteria in soil and roots carry out nitrogen fixation.

questions.q: What is the hardest known naturally occurring substance, scoring 10 on the Mohs scale?
questions.f: The Mohs scale ranks minerals by how they scratch one another.

questions.q: Which scientist first measured the speed of light with reasonable accuracy?
questions.f: Romer studied the timing of Jupiter's moons to estimate light's speed.

questions.q: What is the name for the energy stored in an object because of its position or height?
questions.f: A raised weight stores gravitational potential energy.

questions.q: Which part of the neuron carries signals away from the cell body?
questions.f: A single axon can be over a metre long in humans.

questions.q: What is the name of the process by which unstable atomic nuclei break apart, releasing energy?
questions.f: Fission powers nuclear reactors on Earth.

questions.q: Which vitamin does human skin produce when exposed to sunlight?
questions.f: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones.

questions.q: What do we call the sudden change of a gene that can create new traits?
questions.f: Mutations are the raw material for evolution.

questions.q: The word 'mitosis' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: It refers to the thread-like chromosomes seen during cell division.

questions.q: The prefix 'endo' in 'endothermic' and 'endoskeleton' means...?
questions.f: An endoskeleton is a skeleton found inside the body.

questions.q: The prefix 'exo' in 'exoskeleton' means...?
questions.f: Insects wear their skeletons on the outside as exoskeletons.

questions.q: The word 'photosynthesis' combines 'photo' (light) with 'synthesis,' meaning...?
questions.f: Plants put together sugars using light energy.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the atmosphere and forecasts weather relies on 'meteor,' which means...?
questions.f: 'Meteoron' referred to anything high in the sky.

questions.q: The root 'genes' in 'genetics' and 'generate' means...?
questions.f: 'Genesis' means the origin or beginning of something.

questions.q: The word 'chromosome' contains 'chromo,' which means...?
questions.f: Chromosomes were named because they take up coloured stains.

questions.q: The prefix 'iso' in 'isotope' and 'isosceles' means...?
questions.f: Isotopes have the same number of protons.

questions.q: The root 'phago' in 'phagocyte' means...?
questions.f: Phagocytes are cells that engulf and eat invading germs.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the nervous system and the brain is a...?
questions.f: 'Neuron' is the Greek word for nerve.

questions.q: The 'osteo' in 'osteology' and 'osteoporosis' refers to...?
questions.f: An osteopath treats problems of the bones and joints.

questions.q: The word 'vaccine' comes from a Latin word for...?
questions.f: Early smallpox vaccines used the related cowpox virus.

questions.q: The root 'lys' in 'analysis' and 'lysosome' means...?
questions.f: A lysosome breaks down waste inside a cell.

questions.q: The prefix 'hemi' in 'hemisphere' means...?
questions.f: Earth is divided into northern and southern hemispheres.

questions.q: A scientist who studies fungi practises...?
questions.f: 'Mykes' is the Greek word for mushroom or fungus.

questions.q: The word 'planet' pairs with 'nebula,' a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: A nebula is a giant cloud of gas and dust in space.

questions.q: The 'therm' in 'thermodynamics' pairs with 'dynamics,' which relates to...?
questions.f: Thermodynamics studies how heat and energy move.

questions.q: A word meaning the scientific study of heredity's molecular basis uses 'DNA.' What does the 'D' stand for?
questions.f: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid.

questions.q: The prefix 'ambi' in 'ambidextrous' means...?
questions.f: An ambidextrous person can use both hands equally well.

questions.q: The root 'morph' in 'metamorphosis' means...?
questions.f: 'Morph' also appears in 'amorphous,' meaning without shape.

questions.q: In 'metamorphosis,' the prefix 'meta' suggests...?
questions.f: 'Meta' often signals a change or transformation.

questions.q: The '48' element gold uses the symbol Au from the Latin word 'aurum,' meaning...?
questions.f: 'Aurum' evoked the glow of sunrise.

questions.q: The element sodium uses the symbol Na, from the Latin word...?
questions.f: Many symbols come from a Latin or Greek name.

questions.q: The word 'laboratory' shares its root with 'labour,' meaning...?
questions.f: A laboratory is literally a place of work and experiment.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the kidneys is a...?
questions.f: 'Nephros' is the Greek word for kidney.

questions.q: The root 'volv' in 'evolve' and 'revolve' means...?
questions.f: Species change, or 'roll onward,' as they evolve.

questions.q: The 'helio' in 'heliocentric' refers to the...?
questions.f: A heliocentric model places the Sun at the centre.

questions.q: The root 'centr' in 'heliocentric' and 'centrifuge' means...?
questions.f: A centrifuge spins samples around a central point.

questions.q: A word for the study of the origin and structure of the universe is...?
questions.f: 'Cosmos' is the Greek word for the ordered universe.

questions.q: The prefix 'poly' in 'polymer' means...?
questions.f: A polymer is a chain built from many repeating units.

questions.q: In 'polymer,' the part 'mer' means...?
questions.f: A monomer is a single unit; many make a polymer.

questions.q: The word 'symbiosis' contains 'sym,' meaning...?
questions.f: Symbiosis is a close relationship between two living things.

questions.q: The root 'bio' in 'symbiosis' and 'biology' means...?
questions.f: 'Bios' is the Greek word for life.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the relationships between living things and their environment studies...?
questions.f: 'Oikos' is Greek for house or home, the root of 'eco.'

questions.q: Weight is a force, while mass is the amount of matter in an object.
questions.f: Weight depends on gravity, but mass stays constant everywhere.

questions.q: In the periodic table, elements in the same column tend to have similar properties.
questions.f: These vertical columns are called groups or families.

questions.q: DNA is made of two strands twisted into a double helix.
questions.f: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images helped reveal this shape.

questions.q: Nuclear fusion is the process that powers the Sun.
questions.f: The Sun fuses hydrogen nuclei into helium, releasing energy.

questions.q: Sound waves are longitudinal, meaning the particles vibrate along the direction of travel.
questions.f: This is different from the up-and-down motion of many light waves.

questions.q: An object in free fall is weightless because gravity has stopped acting on it.
questions.f: Gravity is still acting; the feeling of weightlessness comes from falling freely.

questions.q: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions in living things.
questions.f: Most enzymes are proteins with very specific jobs.

questions.q: All acids have a pH greater than 7.
questions.f: Acids have a pH below 7; bases are above 7.

questions.q: What is the term for water rising up narrow tubes in a plant against gravity?
questions.f: Capillary action, aided by transpiration, lifts water to treetops.

questions.q: Which even smaller particles combine to form protons and neutrons?
questions.f: Protons and neutrons are each made of three quarks.

questions.q: The suffix 'tropism' in 'phototropism' refers to...?
questions.f: In phototropism, a plant grows and turns toward light.

questions.q: The prefix 'super' in 'supersonic' means...?
questions.f: Supersonic speeds are faster than the speed of sound.

questions.q: Which famous puzzle asks why, with billions of stars, we have found no clear sign of aliens, summed up as 'Where is everybody?'
questions.f: Physicist Enrico Fermi reportedly raised it casually over lunch in 1950.

questions.q: The Fermi paradox is named after which physicist?
questions.f: Fermi also built the first controlled nuclear chain reaction.

questions.q: What is the name of the equation used to estimate how many communicating alien civilizations might exist in our galaxy?
questions.f: Astronomer Frank Drake wrote it in 1961 to guide the search for alien signals.

questions.q: In physics, what famous experiment shows that light and tiny particles can behave like both waves and particles?
questions.f: Sent through two slits, particles form a striped wave pattern on the screen.

questions.q: What do we call the effect where a fast-moving clock ticks more slowly than a clock at rest?
questions.f: Time dilation comes from Einstein's theory of relativity.

questions.q: Einstein called which strange quantum link between two particles 'spooky action at a distance'?
questions.f: Measuring one entangled particle seems to instantly affect its partner.

questions.q: Why can we only see part of the universe, a region called the observable universe?
c: Light from farther away has not had time to reach us
The rest is hidden by clouds
questions.f: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, limiting how far we can see.

questions.q: In discussions of the Fermi paradox, what is the name of a proposed barrier that might stop life from becoming a space-faring civilization?
questions.f: The Great Filter idea asks whether the hardest step is behind us or ahead.

questions.q: In Schrödinger's famous thought experiment, the cat is imagined to be in what odd condition until it is observed?
c: Both states at once, called superposition
questions.f: Superposition means a quantum system holds several possibilities at once.

questions.q: Which scientist predicted that black holes can slowly glow and lose energy, a glow now named after him?
questions.f: This faint glow is called Hawking radiation.

questions.q: The 'dark forest' idea, a proposed answer to the Fermi paradox, was made famous by novels from which author?
questions.f: It suggests civilizations stay quiet to avoid being noticed by others.

questions.q: A light-year is a measure of what?
questions.f: It is how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

questions.q: When distant galaxies move away from us, their light is stretched toward which colour?
questions.f: This stretching, called redshift, is a clue that the universe is expanding.

questions.q: The ability of light to act as both a wave and a particle is called...?
questions.f: Both light and matter show this dual behaviour on tiny scales.

questions.q: What does the acronym SETI stand for?
questions.f: SETI projects scan the skies for signals from alien civilizations.

questions.q: The faint heat left over from the Big Bang that fills all of space is called the...?
questions.f: It was discovered by accident in 1965 as a hiss in a radio antenna.

questions.q: A black hole's point of no return, beyond which not even light escapes, is called the...?
questions.f: Stephen Hawking showed this boundary can slowly emit faint radiation.

questions.q: What do we call the interference pattern of bright and dark stripes made when waves pass through two slits?
questions.f: These fringes are the fingerprint of wave behaviour.

questions.q: According to relativity, a twin who travels near light speed and returns will be...?
c: Younger than the twin who stayed
Older than the twin who stayed
questions.f: This is the famous 'twin paradox' of time dilation.

questions.q: The word 'galaxy' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: It refers to the milky band of our own Milky Way galaxy.

questions.q: Newton's second law is usually written as force equals mass multiplied by what?
questions.f: It explains why a heavier trolley needs a bigger push.

questions.q: Roughly 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd is known as which constant?
questions.f: It is the number of particles in one mole of a substance.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered the neutron in 1932?
questions.f: The neutron explained why atoms weigh more than their protons suggest.

questions.q: Which type of bond between water molecules gives water its high boiling point?
questions.f: These weak attractions make water behave far stranger than it should.

questions.q: What do we call a molecule with a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end?
questions.f: Water's polarity lets it dissolve an enormous range of substances.

questions.q: What is an ion with a positive electrical charge called?
questions.f: Cations form when an atom loses one or more electrons.

questions.q: What do we call the reaction between an acid and a base?
questions.f: It usually produces a salt and water.

questions.q: Which law of thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or destroyed?
questions.f: Energy only ever changes from one form into another.

questions.q: What do we call the energy needed to raise one kilogram of a substance by one degree?
questions.f: Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity.

questions.q: What do we call the energy absorbed during a change of state, with no temperature change?
questions.f: Melting ice soaks up latent heat while staying at 0 degrees.

questions.q: On a wave diagram, what do we call the height from the middle line to a crest?
questions.f: A louder sound has a larger amplitude.

questions.q: What is the distance between one wave crest and the next called?
questions.f: Wavelength is usually measured in metres.

questions.q: What do we call the change in a sound's pitch as its source races past you?
questions.f: It is why a siren drops in pitch as an ambulance passes.

questions.q: What do we call the splitting of white light into its colours by wavelength?
questions.f: Each colour bends by a slightly different amount.

questions.q: What do we call light waves that vibrate in only one plane?
questions.f: Polarising sunglasses cut glare bouncing off water.

questions.q: What is the usual range of human hearing?
questions.f: The upper limit tends to drop as people get older.

questions.q: What do we call the total number of protons and neutrons in an atom?
questions.f: Carbon-14 has a mass number of 14.

questions.q: What is the name for the group 18 elements, which barely react at all?
questions.f: Their outer electron shells are already full.

questions.q: What is the name for the very reactive group 1 metals such as sodium?
questions.f: They are soft enough to cut with a knife.

questions.q: Which element is the most abundant in the Earth's crust?
questions.f: Most crustal rock is built from oxygen-containing minerals.

questions.q: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
questions.f: Aluminium is locked up in clays and ores like bauxite.

questions.q: Which organelle assembles proteins inside a cell?
questions.f: A single cell may hold millions of ribosomes.

questions.q: What is the name for a cell that has no nucleus, such as a bacterium?
questions.f: Prokaryotes keep their DNA loose in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: How do bacteria usually reproduce?
questions.f: One bacterium simply splits into two identical cells.

questions.q: In DNA, which base always pairs with adenine?
questions.f: Cytosine pairs with guanine, completing the rungs of the ladder.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body cell?
questions.f: They come as 23 matching pairs.

questions.q: What do we call the complete set of an organism's genetic material?
questions.f: The human genome was first drafted in 2001.

questions.q: What do we call all the populations of different species living in one area?
questions.f: Add the non-living surroundings and you have an ecosystem.

questions.q: What do we call the particular role a species plays within its habitat?
questions.f: Two species rarely share exactly the same niche for long.

questions.q: What do we call a relationship where both species benefit?
questions.f: Bees and flowering plants are a classic example.

questions.q: What do we call a relationship where one species benefits and the other is unaffected?
questions.f: Barnacles riding on a whale are often given as an example.

questions.q: What word describes a species found naturally in only one place on Earth?
questions.f: Lemurs are endemic to Madagascar.

questions.q: What do we call it when unrelated species separately evolve similar features?
questions.f: Bats and birds both evolved wings independently.

questions.q: A bat's wing and a human arm share the same underlying bone plan. Such structures are called...?
questions.f: Homologous structures point to a shared ancestor.

questions.q: During which era did the dinosaurs live?
questions.f: The Mesozoic is often called the age of reptiles.

questions.q: In which period did Tyrannosaurus rex live?
questions.f: T. rex lived closer to us in time than to Stegosaurus.

questions.q: What is the name of the supercontinent that existed about 250 million years ago?
questions.f: Pangaea later split into the continents we know.

questions.q: What do we call the point on the Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's origin?
questions.f: The origin underground is called the focus.

questions.q: Which earthquake waves arrive at a seismograph first?
questions.f: P stands for primary, because they travel fastest.

questions.q: About how old is the Earth?
questions.f: Radioactive dating of ancient rocks and meteorites gives this age.

questions.q: In science, what is a theory?
c: A well-tested explanation supported by evidence
questions.f: In everyday speech 'theory' means a guess, but not in science.

questions.q: What do we call a fluid whose thickness changes when you stir or squeeze it?
questions.f: Cornflour mixed with water goes firm when you hit it.

questions.q: What do we call an animal that gives birth to live young rather than laying eggs?
questions.f: Most mammals are viviparous.

questions.q: What word describes an animal that lives mainly in trees?
questions.f: From Latin arbor, meaning tree.

questions.q: What word describes an animal that eats mainly fruit?
questions.f: Fruit bats and many monkeys are frugivorous.

questions.q: The word part 'ophthalmo' in 'ophthalmology' refers to the...?
questions.f: Ophthalmologists are doctors who treat eye conditions.

questions.q: The word part 'paed' in 'paediatrics' means...?
questions.f: Paediatricians are doctors for children.

questions.q: The word 'anaesthesia' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Anaesthetics let surgery happen without any feeling.

questions.q: The word 'diagnosis' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: A diagnosis identifies what is wrong by looking right through the clues.

questions.q: The word 'prognosis' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: A prognosis is a forecast of how an illness will go.

questions.q: The word 'epidemic' is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: A pandemic, by contrast, means 'all the people'.

questions.q: The word 'quarantine' comes from an Italian word for...?
questions.f: Ships once waited forty days before crews could land.

questions.q: The word 'pathogen' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek pathos, suffering, plus the root for producing.

questions.q: The word part 'cryo' in 'cryogenics' means...?
questions.f: Cryogenics studies materials at extremely low temperatures.

questions.q: The word 'acoustics' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Acoustics is the science of sound.

questions.q: The word 'chemistry' grew out of an older word, 'alchemy', partly from Arabic. What did the 'al' mean?
questions.f: Arabic 'al-kimiya' gave us both alchemy and chemistry.

questions.q: The word 'alkali' comes from an Arabic phrase meaning...?
questions.f: Early alkalis were made by leaching wood ash.

questions.q: LASER is an acronym. What does the first word, 'light', join with?
c: Amplification by stimulated emission of radiation
questions.f: Every letter of 'laser' stands for a word.

questions.q: The word part 'vector' in disease spread comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Mosquitoes are vectors that carry malaria parasites.

questions.q: When Wilhelm Roentgen named his new rays, why did he choose the letter X?
questions.f: Physicists still call them X-rays over a century later.

questions.q: The unit 'decibel' contains 'bel', named in honour of which inventor?
questions.f: A decibel is one tenth of a bel.

questions.q: The hormone name 'insulin' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: It is made in the pancreatic islets, or little islands.

questions.q: The word 'muscle' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: A flexing bicep reminded Romans of a mouse under the skin.

questions.q: The word 'artery' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Ancient anatomists found arteries empty after death and thought they held air.

questions.q: The word 'skeleton' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek skeletos, meaning dried or withered.

questions.q: A drooling dog, a bell rung before feeding, and a 1904 Nobel Prize for digestion research converge on which scientist?
questions.f: Pavlov's conditioned reflex became one of psychology's foundations.

questions.q: A scale where 0 once meant boiling, a 1742 Swedish thermometer, and a unit renamed in 1948 converge on which temperature scale?
questions.f: Celsius originally ran upside down; others later flipped it.

questions.q: A brine-and-ice zero point, a German glassblower's precise mercury tubes, and 212 for boiling converge on which temperature scale?
questions.f: Daniel Fahrenheit made the first reliable mercury thermometers.

questions.q: A mischievous goblin blamed by German miners, a deep blue glass pigment, and element 27 converge on which metal?
questions.f: Miners named it after the 'kobold' they blamed for worthless ore.

questions.q: A Greek word meaning 'lazy', Ramsay and Rayleigh's 1894 discovery, and the gas inside old filament bulbs converge on which element?
questions.f: Argon was named 'lazy' because it refuses to react.

questions.q: A Greek word meaning 'hidden', a gas found in leftover liquid air in 1898, and element 36 converge on which noble gas?
questions.f: Ramsay and Travers found it hiding after the other gases boiled away.

questions.q: A Greek sun god's name, a yellow line seen in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, and party balloons converge on which element?
questions.f: Helium is the only element first detected in space before on Earth.

questions.q: Greek words meaning 'water-silver', the symbol Hg, and a planet's name converge on which element?
questions.f: Its old name, hydrargyrum, gives us the odd symbol Hg.

questions.q: Burdock burrs stuck to a dog's coat, a Swiss engineer's microscope, and the French for 'velvet' and 'hook' converge on which invention?
questions.f: George de Mestral turned a walk in the woods into a fastener.

questions.q: A gas Priestley made from ashes, the second most common element in the crust, and computer chips converge on which element?
questions.f: Silicon's name comes from Latin silex, meaning flint.

questions.q: A catalyst changes the products of a chemical reaction.
questions.f: A catalyst only speeds the reaction up; the products stay the same.

questions.q: All isotopes of an element have the same number of protons.
questions.f: They differ only in how many neutrons they carry.

questions.q: Sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air.
questions.f: Warmer particles move faster, passing vibrations on more quickly.

questions.q: Every chemical reaction that gives out light must also give out heat.
questions.f: Some reactions glow coolly, a process called chemiluminescence.

questions.q: Plants carry out respiration as well as photosynthesis.
questions.f: Plants respire day and night to release energy from their sugars.

questions.q: Diamond conducts heat better than most metals.
questions.f: Its rigid carbon lattice carries heat vibrations extremely well.

questions.q: A virus can reproduce entirely on its own, without a host cell.
questions.f: Viruses must hijack a living cell's machinery to make copies.

questions.q: A hay-fever escape to the treeless island of Helgoland, the invention of matrix mechanics in 1925, and a solo Nobel in 1932 converge on which physicist?
questions.f: On Helgoland he worked out the maths behind his uncertainty principle.

questions.q: A silver-staining method that finally made nerve cells visible, a Nobel shared with a bitter rival in 1906, and a stack of flattened sacs converge on which scientist's name?
questions.f: The Golgi apparatus, the cell's packaging depot, still carries his name.

questions.q: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix during replication?
questions.f: Helicase 'unzips' the two strands so they can be copied.

questions.q: What is the term for the point in a chemical titration where the reaction is just complete?
questions.f: Indicators change colour near the equivalence point.

questions.q: A 1964 paper first rejected as being of no obvious relevance, a mechanism explaining why W and Z particles are heavy, and a nickname its namesake disliked converge on which particle?
questions.f: Higgs hated the tabloid nickname 'the God particle'.

questions.q: What is the SI base unit of luminous intensity?
questions.f: One candela is roughly the light of a single candle.

questions.q: Research on the microscopic pores of coal, later work on tobacco mosaic virus, and a King's College darkroom converge on which scientist?
questions.f: Her 'Photo 51' revealed the double helix to Watson and Crick.

questions.q: An Italian Jesuit's posthumous 1665 book, light creeping into a geometric shadow, and faint bright bands beside a razor's edge converge on which phenomenon?
questions.f: Francesco Grimaldi coined the word 'diffraction' for this effect.

questions.q: Which blood protein binds oxygen in muscle tissue, distinct from haemoglobin?
questions.f: Myoglobin gives red meat its colour and stores oxygen in muscle.

questions.q: What is the term for an animal that maintains a constant body temperature internally?
questions.f: Mammals and birds are endotherms, often called warm-blooded.

questions.q: An air pump built with Hooke's help, a 1661 book called 'The Sceptical Chymist', and a J-shaped tube of mercury converge on which scientist?
questions.f: Boyle's law says squeezing a gas into half the space doubles its pressure.

questions.q: What is the name of the process by which certain bacteria convert nitrogen compounds back into nitrogen gas?
questions.f: Denitrification completes part of the nitrogen cycle.

questions.q: Thirty years of work in a Berlin institute, a Christmas walk in Swedish exile spent doing sums with her nephew, and element 109 converge on which physicist?
questions.f: She explained the splitting of the atom; her colleague took the Nobel.

questions.q: What is the term for a solution that resists changes in pH when acid or base is added?
questions.f: Blood contains buffers that keep its pH remarkably steady.

questions.q: A torsion balance shielded from draughts in a garden shed, two lead spheres, and an experiment nicknamed 'weighing the world' converge on whom?
questions.f: His 1798 measurement let scientists work out Earth's mass.

questions.q: A dye streak injected into a glass pipe in 1883, a dimensionless number bearing his name, and the switch from smooth to swirling flow converge on which engineer?
questions.f: His number still tells engineers whether a flow will be smooth or turbulent.

questions.q: A career studying polar air masses, matching fossil ferns on facing Atlantic coasts, and a 1912 lecture mocked for offering no mechanism converge on whom?
questions.f: Wegener's continental drift was vindicated by plate tectonics decades later.

questions.q: What is the term for a chemical reaction in which a substance loses electrons?
questions.f: A handy memory aid is 'OIL RIG': oxidation is loss.

questions.q: Which organelle in plant cells is responsible for storing water and maintaining pressure?
questions.f: When the vacuole loses water, a plant wilts.

questions.q: A Belfast-born baron, the triumph of the transatlantic telegraph cable, and the only major temperature unit written without a degree sign converge on whom?
questions.f: William Thomson became Lord Kelvin, named after a river in Glasgow.

questions.q: A colour photograph of a tartan ribbon, a prize-winning study of the stability of Saturn's rings, and a set of four equations converge on which physicist?
questions.f: His equations revealed that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.

questions.q: A 1926 letter to Nature proposing a new word, an American chemist better remembered for acid-base theory, and a massless carrier of energy converge on which term?
questions.f: Gilbert Lewis coined 'photon' for the particle of light.

questions.q: Which cellular process produces the most ATP, taking place across the mitochondrial membrane?
questions.f: This electron-transport process yields the bulk of a cell's energy.

questions.q: An 1887 interferometer floating on a bath of mercury, the hunt for a headwind of 'ether', and a famous null result converge on which experiment?
questions.f: Its failure to find the ether cleared the way for special relativity.

questions.q: Oddly speckled maize kernels, findings dismissed for three decades, and an unshared 1983 Nobel converge on which geneticist?
questions.f: Her 'jumping genes' are now known to shape genomes everywhere.

questions.q: Which fundamental force is responsible for radioactive beta decay?
questions.f: The weak force can change one type of quark into another.

questions.q: Inge Lehmann's 1936 study of odd seismic echoes, a boundary about 5,150 km down, and iron held solid by crushing pressure converge on which layer?
questions.f: Lehmann spotted the inner core using earthquake waves alone.

questions.q: A well at Syene where the noon Sun cast no shadow, the chief librarianship at Alexandria, and a sieve for sifting prime numbers converge on whom?
questions.f: His shadow measurement gave Earth's circumference to within a few percent.

questions.q: Mercury chilled to 4.2 kelvin in a Leiden laboratory in 1911, a small magnet hovering above a cooled ceramic disc, and the total expulsion of magnetic fields converge on which phenomenon?
questions.f: Kamerlingh Onnes found resistance vanish completely, not merely fall.

questions.q: Karl Lohmann's 1929 discovery, three phosphate groups in a row, and a body that recycles its own weight of the stuff each day converge on which molecule?
questions.f: You make and spend your own body weight in ATP daily.

questions.q: An unpublished Dutch manuscript of 1621, a constant ratio of two sines, and a spoon that looks broken in a glass of water converge on whose law?
questions.f: Snell's law lets us design every lens and fibre-optic cable.

questions.q: A young man's expedition through Lapland, a slim 1735 book that grew edition by edition, and a garden laid out as a living catalogue converge on whom?
questions.f: His 'Systema Naturae' gave every species a two-part Latin name.

questions.q: What is the name of the theoretical boundary where a rocket must reach to leave Earth's gravity, about 11.2 km per second?
questions.f: Below escape velocity, an object falls back or enters orbit.

questions.q: A gas Priestley once called 'marine acid air', a fluid near pH 1 held back by a mucus shield, and the parietal cells of the stomach lining converge on which acid?
questions.f: Your stomach makes fresh acid strong enough to dissolve metal.

questions.q: What is the name for a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction reaching steady output?
questions.f: A reactor is 'critical' when its reaction is exactly self-sustaining.

questions.q: A bookbinder's apprentice with almost no schooling, a series of Christmas lectures for children, and a mesh cage that blocks electric fields converge on whom?
questions.f: His discovery of induction underlies every generator in the world.

questions.q: A tube of mercury sealed at one end, an empty space at the top that scholars insisted was impossible, and the first barometer converge on which scientist?
questions.f: He proved that air has weight and that a vacuum can exist.

questions.q: Which part of the brain regulates hunger, thirst, and body temperature?
questions.f: The tiny hypothalamus links the nervous and hormonal systems.

questions.q: What is the name for the maximum number of electrons in the third electron shell of an atom?
questions.f: The formula 2n squared gives 18 for the third shell.

questions.q: A converted squash court beneath a Chicago stadium, a 1938 Nobel for work with slow neutrons, and element 100 converge on which physicist?
questions.f: He also gave his name to the famous paradox about missing aliens.

questions.q: What is the term for a substance that exists in a state between liquid and gas above a critical temperature and pressure?
questions.f: Supercritical carbon dioxide is used to decaffeinate coffee.

questions.q: What is the term for the study of the interactions of matter and light, often used to identify elements?
questions.f: Each element gives off its own signature set of spectral lines.

questions.q: A wave equation published in 1926, the founding of a Dublin institute, and a short book asking 'What Is Life?' converge on which physicist?
questions.f: His little book on life inspired a generation of molecular biologists.

questions.q: Two copper half-spheres pressed together, teams of horses that could not pull them apart, and a 1654 demonstration for an emperor converge on which apparatus?
questions.f: Otto von Guericke used them to show the crushing strength of air pressure.

questions.q: A bitter priority quarrel between a Swiss father and son, a 1738 book titled 'Hydrodynamica', and faster flow meaning lower pressure converge on which principle?
questions.f: Daniel Bernoulli's insight helps explain how wings and carburettors work.

questions.q: A 67-metre wire hung in the Pantheon, a pin tracing arcs in sand, and a slowly turning plane of swing converge on which device?
questions.f: In 1851 it gave the first simple proof that the Earth rotates.

questions.q: A tax collector's private laboratory, tin heated in sealed vessels and weighed to the grain, and the naming of a gas Priestley had already made converge on whom?
questions.f: His careful weighing showed that matter is never lost in a reaction.

questions.q: What is the term for the angle above which light undergoes total internal reflection?
questions.f: Total internal reflection makes fibre-optic cables work.

questions.q: A Toronto laboratory in the summer of 1921, a patent sold to the university for one dollar, and the islets of Langerhans converge on which discovery?
questions.f: Banting and Best refused to profit from a life-saving hormone.

questions.q: A German geologist's 1812 list of ten reference minerals, a test done with a fingernail and a steel file, and talc at one end converge on which property?
questions.f: Friedrich Mohs ranked minerals by which could scratch which.

questions.q: The word 'entropy' was coined from a Greek root meaning...?
questions.f: Clausius chose it to parallel the word 'energy.'

questions.q: The prefix 'endo' contrasts with 'ecto.' In biology, 'ecto' means...?
questions.f: An ectoparasite lives on the outside of its host.

questions.q: The term 'isomer' contains 'iso' (equal) and 'mer,' meaning...?
questions.f: Isomers share the same parts but differ in arrangement.

questions.q: The word 'catalyst' comes from a Greek term meaning...?
questions.f: 'Katalysis' meant a dissolving or breaking down.

questions.q: The 'plasm' in 'cytoplasm' and 'protoplasm' means...?
questions.f: 'Plasma' comes from a Greek word for something shaped.

questions.q: The root 'phyll' in 'chlorophyll' and 'mesophyll' means...?
questions.f: 'Phyllon' is the Greek word for leaf.

questions.q: The word 'meiosis' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Meiosis lessens the chromosome number by half in sex cells.

questions.q: The 'som' in 'chromosome,' 'ribosome,' and 'lysosome' means...?
questions.f: 'Soma' is the Greek word for body.

questions.q: The prefix 'anti' in 'antibody' and 'antioxidant' means...?
questions.f: Antibodies act against invading pathogens.

questions.q: The word 'protein' derives from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Proteins were seen as of first importance to life.

questions.q: The suffix 'phobia' means fear, so 'hydrophobic' molecules seem to...?
questions.f: Oils are hydrophobic and do not mix with water.

questions.q: The opposite of hydrophobic is 'hydrophilic,' where 'philic' means...?
questions.f: Hydrophilic substances dissolve readily in water.

questions.q: The root 'troph' in 'autotroph' and 'heterotroph' means...?
questions.f: An autotroph provides its own nourishment.

questions.q: In 'heterotroph,' the prefix 'hetero' means...?
questions.f: Heterotrophs get nourishment from other organisms.

questions.q: The term 'allotrope' shares 'tropos,' meaning...?
questions.f: Diamond and graphite are allotropes, different forms of carbon.

questions.q: The word 'diffusion' comes from a Latin root meaning...?
questions.f: Diffusion spreads particles from high to low concentration.

questions.q: The 'gen' in 'oxygen,' 'hydrogen,' and 'antigen' means...?
questions.f: Lavoisier named oxygen thinking it produced acids.

questions.q: The 'oxy' in 'oxygen' originally referred to...?
questions.f: 'Oxys' is Greek for sharp or sour, linking to acids.

questions.q: The word 'nucleus' has the plural form...?
questions.f: Latin words ending in '-us' often take '-i' in the plural.

questions.q: The scientific plural of 'fungus' is...?
questions.f: Like 'cactus' to 'cacti,' the ending shifts to '-i.'

questions.q: The plural of the science word 'phenomenon' is...?
questions.f: Greek-derived '-on' words often pluralise to '-a.'

questions.q: The plural of 'bacterium' is...?
questions.f: 'Bacteria' is already plural; a single one is a bacterium.

questions.q: A scientist who studies the structure and evolution of the universe as a whole is a...?
questions.f: Cosmologists study the origin and fate of the cosmos.

questions.q: The root 'stasis' in 'homeostasis' and 'metastasis' means...?
questions.f: 'Stasis' refers to a standing still or standstill.

questions.q: The prefix 'homeo' in 'homeostasis' means...?
questions.f: Homeostasis keeps conditions similar and steady.

questions.q: The term 'valence' in chemistry comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Valence describes an atom's combining power.

questions.q: The word 'viscosity' comes from a Latin word for...?
questions.f: 'Viscum' was a sticky substance made from mistletoe.

questions.q: The 'seismo' in 'seismograph' and 'seismic' means...?
questions.f: A seismograph records the shaking of earthquakes.

questions.q: The root 'lumen' in 'luminous' and 'luminescence' means...?
questions.f: 'Lumen' is the Latin word for light.

questions.q: The term 'osmosis' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Osmos' meant a pushing, fitting how water is driven across membranes.

questions.q: The prefix 'peri' in 'perihelion' and 'perimeter' means...?
questions.f: A planet is at perihelion when nearest the Sun.

questions.q: The opposite of 'perihelion' is 'aphelion,' where 'ap' or 'apo' means...?
questions.f: Aphelion is the point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.

questions.q: The word 'element' entered science from a Latin term that meant...?
questions.f: Ancient thinkers spoke of the basic elements of matter.

questions.q: The term 'quantum' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: A quantum is the smallest discrete amount of a quantity.

questions.q: The root 'chrom' appears in 'monochromatic,' where 'mono' means...?
questions.f: Monochromatic light is a single pure colour.

questions.q: The word 'crystal' comes from a Greek word originally meaning...?
questions.f: The Greeks thought clear quartz was permanently frozen ice.

questions.q: The plural of the word 'stimulus' in biology is...?
questions.f: A stimulus triggers a response; several are stimuli.

questions.q: The prefix 'a-' or 'an-' in 'anaerobic' and 'asexual' means...?
questions.f: Anaerobic organisms live without oxygen.

questions.q: Entropy, a measure of disorder, tends to increase in an isolated system.
questions.f: This is the essence of the second law of thermodynamics.

questions.q: In a redox reaction, oxidation and reduction always occur together.
questions.f: Electrons lost by one substance are gained by another.

questions.q: The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of their motion.
questions.f: This is a cornerstone of Einstein's special relativity.

questions.q: Enzymes are consumed and used up permanently during the reactions they catalyse.
questions.f: Catalysts, including enzymes, emerge unchanged and can be reused.

questions.q: A catalyst works by lowering the activation energy of a reaction.
questions.f: It provides an easier pathway without changing the final products.

questions.q: Mitochondria contain their own small loop of DNA, separate from the nucleus.
questions.f: This supports the idea that they were once free-living bacteria.

questions.q: Neutron stars are so dense that a teaspoon of their material would weigh billions of tonnes.
questions.f: They pack more than the Sun's mass into a city-sized sphere.

questions.q: In a covalent bond, electrons are transferred completely from one atom to another.
questions.f: That describes an ionic bond; covalent bonds share electrons.

questions.q: What is the name of the deep puzzle over whether information that falls into a black hole is destroyed forever?
questions.f: It pits general relativity against a core rule of quantum mechanics.

questions.q: Hawking radiation is explained using pairs of what appearing near a black hole's event horizon?
questions.f: One partner escapes as radiation while the other falls in.

questions.q: In the Drake equation, the letter N stands for the number of what in our galaxy?
questions.f: The other terms estimate factors like star formation and habitable planets.

questions.q: A virtual-reality game about a world with three suns, a Hugo Award in 2015, and a chilling answer to Fermi's question converge on which novel series?
questions.f: Its 'dark forest' argues that quiet civilizations are the surviving ones.

questions.q: A 1964 paper written while on leave from CERN, an inequality that experiments can actually violate, and a challenge to Einstein's 'hidden variables' converge on whose theorem?
questions.f: Bell turned a philosophical argument into a testable experiment.

questions.q: Gravitational time dilation means clocks tick more slowly when they are...?
c: Closer to a strong gravitational field
questions.f: GPS satellites must correct for this to stay accurate.

questions.q: Because space itself expands, the observable universe now has a radius of roughly how many billion light-years?
questions.f: Though the universe is 13.8 billion years old, expansion stretches the horizon much wider.

questions.q: A 1998 essay about a barrier life must pass, advocacy of prediction markets, and the claim that finding alien fossils would be terrible news converge on which economist?
questions.f: If the filter still lies ahead of us, silence in the sky is reassuring.

questions.q: Which interpretation of quantum mechanics says a wavefunction collapses to one outcome only when measured?
questions.f: Schrödinger's cat was designed to highlight how strange this idea is.

questions.q: In the double-slit experiment, what happens to the interference pattern if you detect which slit each particle goes through?
questions.f: Measuring the path forces particle-like behaviour and erases the wave pattern.

questions.q: What is the term for the loss of quantum behaviour as a system interacts with its surroundings?
questions.f: Decoherence helps explain why big objects don't show obvious superposition.

questions.q: Hawking radiation implies smaller black holes are ______ than larger ones.
questions.f: A black hole's temperature is inversely related to its mass.

questions.q: Impossible staircases drawn with his father, singularity theorems published in 1965, and a pair of tiles that never repeat converge on which mathematician?
questions.f: His 2020 Nobel honoured the mathematics that made black holes inevitable.

questions.q: The cosmological redshift of distant galaxies is caused mainly by...?
questions.f: Space stretching lengthens the light's wavelength as it travels.

questions.q: What is the name for the smallest meaningful length in physics, about 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 35 metres?
questions.f: Below the Planck length, our current physics no longer applies.

questions.q: Einstein's 1905 explanation of the photoelectric effect showed that light delivers energy in packets called...?
questions.f: This work, not relativity, earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.q: A 'quasar' takes its name from the phrase 'quasi-stellar' object, meaning it looks almost like a...?
questions.f: Quasars are blazingly bright cores of distant young galaxies.

questions.q: The word 'singularity,' used for the centre of a black hole, comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: At a singularity, our equations predict density becoming infinite.

questions.q: Schrödinger coined the German word 'Verschränkung' for which quantum phenomenon?
questions.f: English speakers translated it as 'entanglement.'

questions.q: The observable universe's edge is sometimes called the particle ______, the farthest distance light could have travelled to us.
questions.f: Beyond the particle horizon, light has simply not had time to arrive.

questions.q: A laboratory at Colorado Springs, a 1943 court ruling that overturned Marconi's radio patents, and the SI unit of magnetic flux density converge on which inventor?
questions.f: He also championed the alternating-current system that lights our homes.

questions.q: A translation of an Italian engineer's lecture notes, seven appended notes labelled A to G, and an algorithm for Bernoulli numbers converge on whom?
questions.f: Note G is often called the first published computer program.

questions.q: An unfinished Difference Engine, a public campaign against street musicians, and a punched-card machine never built converge on which Victorian?
questions.f: His Analytical Engine anticipated the modern computer by a century.

questions.q: A codebreaking machine called the Bombe, a 1936 paper on computable numbers, and an 'imitation game' converge on whom?
questions.f: The Turing test still frames debates about machine intelligence.

questions.q: Unpaid lectures given under Hilbert's name at Gottingen, a theorem tying symmetries to conservation laws, and Einstein's public praise converge on which mathematician?
questions.f: Noether's theorem underpins much of modern theoretical physics.

questions.q: A 1956 experiment with chilled cobalt-60, the overturning of parity conservation, and the nickname 'First Lady of Physics' converge on which physicist?
questions.f: Her colleagues won the Nobel for the theory; she was left out.

questions.q: X-ray studies of penicillin, a structure of vitamin B12, and the mapping of insulin in 1969 converge on which crystallographer?
questions.f: She remains the only British woman to win a Nobel in a science.

questions.q: A Harvard 'computer' paid by the hour, 1,777 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds, and a law linking brightness to period converge on whom?
questions.f: Her law gave astronomers their first reliable cosmic measuring stick.

questions.q: A 1925 doctoral thesis once called the most brilliant in astronomy, and the then-shocking claim that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen, converge on whom?
questions.f: She was talked out of publishing her conclusion, which proved correct.

questions.q: Spectrograph nights at Kitt Peak, rotation curves that stubbornly refused to fall off, and galaxies spinning too fast converge on which astronomer?
questions.f: Her measurements turned dark matter from a curiosity into a crisis.

questions.q: A signal nicknamed LGM-1, metres of chart-recorder paper read by hand in 1967, and a 'bit of scruff' converge on which discovery?
questions.f: Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the regular pulses of a spinning neutron star.

questions.q: A 1924 measurement of Cepheids in Andromeda, the end of the 'Great Debate', and a law relating distance to recession speed converge on whom?
questions.f: He proved that other galaxies lie far beyond our own.

questions.q: A Belgian Catholic priest, a 1927 solution predicting an expanding cosmos, and a 'primeval atom' converge on which scientist?
questions.f: His primeval atom grew into what we now call the Big Bang theory.

questions.q: A 1933 study of the Coma Cluster, a prediction of gravitational lensing, and the coining of a now-famous German term converge on which astronomer?
questions.f: Zwicky gave us the phrase 'dark matter' decades before it was accepted.

questions.q: A limit of about 1.4 solar masses, a bruising public clash with Eddington, and a NASA X-ray observatory's name converge on which astrophysicist?
questions.f: Above his limit, a white dwarf cannot hold itself up.

questions.q: Clumping seen when serum met foreign cells, a 1901 paper describing three groups, and the Rh factor of 1940 converge on which scientist?
questions.f: His work on blood groups made safe transfusion possible.

questions.q: A Delft cloth merchant, hand-ground beads of glass magnifying over 250 times, and creatures he called 'animalcules' converge on whom?
questions.f: He was the first person to see bacteria and protozoa.

questions.q: Tobacco leaves with mottled patterns, a porcelain filter that held back every bacterium yet still passed the disease, and a Latin word for poison converge on the discovery of what?
questions.f: Dmitri Ivanovsky's 1892 filter experiments opened up virology.

questions.q: A 1960 radio search called Project Ozma, the 1974 Arecibo message, and an equation with seven terms converge on which astronomer?
questions.f: His equation still frames every serious discussion of alien life.

questions.q: A 1974 paper titled 'Black hole explosions?', a long-running bet with Kip Thorne over Cygnus X-1, and singularity theorems co-authored with Penrose converge on whom?
questions.f: His radiation prediction showed black holes are not quite forever.

questions.q: Bongo drums, diagrams of particle interactions, and an O-ring dipped in iced water at a 1986 hearing converge on which physicist?
questions.f: His iced-water demonstration explained the Challenger disaster in seconds.

questions.q: A milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes, a gardener's son inoculated in 1796, and a farmer called Benjamin Jesty who got there first converge on which pioneer?
questions.f: Jenner's cowpox trials began the science of vaccination.

questions.q: A dot map of Soho streets, a pump handle removed in 1854, and a brewery whose workers stayed well converge on which physician?
questions.f: His detective work founded modern epidemiology.

questions.q: A 'coxcomb' diagram of wedges, election as the first woman fellow of the Royal Statistical Society, and a campaign for clean hospital wards converge on whom?
questions.f: She used statistics as persuasively as any general used maps.

questions.q: Cliffs at Lyme Regis, the first complete Plesiosaurus skeleton, and stony objects she called 'bezoar stones' converge on which fossil hunter?
questions.f: Her bezoar stones turned out to be fossilised droppings.

questions.q: Beetles collected along the Amazon, a line dividing Asian from Australian wildlife, and an 1858 letter posted from Ternate converge on which naturalist?
questions.f: His letter pushed Darwin to publish at last.

questions.q: Mealworm chromosomes counted under a microscope, a 1905 paper on X and Y, and credit long handed to E. B. Wilson converge on which biologist?
questions.f: She showed that chromosomes determine an organism's sex.

questions.q: A five-year voyage through the Americas from 1799, the first maps drawn with isotherms, and more species named after him than anyone else converge on whom?
questions.f: He saw nature as one connected web long before ecology existed.

questions.q: A husband-and-wife laboratory in St Louis, the cycle of glycogen and lactate, and the third woman ever to win a science Nobel converge on whom?
questions.f: In 1947 she became the first woman to win the Nobel in Medicine.

questions.q: Bulletins urging farmers to rotate their crops, a Tuskegee laboratory, and hundreds of uses found for a single legume converge on which scientist?
questions.f: He helped exhausted southern soils recover by promoting peanuts.

questions.q: Hand-computed launch windows, a 1960 report on orbital equations, and an astronaut who asked for the electronic answer to be checked converge on whom?
questions.f: John Glenn trusted her arithmetic more than the new computers.

questions.q: A moth taped into a logbook, the first compiler, and the committee behind COBOL converge on which computing pioneer?
questions.f: She argued that programs should be written in words, not numbers.

questions.q: A remedy in a 4th-century Chinese text, an extraction redesigned to use low temperatures, and sweet wormwood converge on which Nobel laureate?
questions.f: Her artemisinin has saved millions of lives from malaria.

questions.q: Chimpanzees poking twigs into termite mounds, a decision to give study subjects names rather than numbers, and a 1960 arrival at Gombe converge on whom?
questions.f: Her termite-fishing observation forced a rethink of what makes us human.

questions.q: A trilogy about the sea, a 1962 book that took its title from birdless mornings, and hearings that led to a pesticide ban converge on which writer?
questions.f: 'Silent Spring' helped launch the modern environmental movement.

questions.q: A screen coated with barium platinocyanide glowing behind cardboard, a photograph of his wife's hand, and the first Nobel Prize in Physics converge on whom?
questions.f: He called his mysterious rays 'X' because their nature was unknown.

questions.q: An island observatory named Uraniborg, a metal nose piece, and twenty years of measurements made without any telescope converge on which astronomer?
questions.f: His data let Kepler work out that orbits are ellipses.

questions.q: An eleventh-century 'Book of Optics', experiments with a darkened room and a pinhole, and the argument that we see because light enters the eye converge on whom?
questions.f: He insisted on testing ideas by experiment centuries before Galileo.

questions.q: Bronze balls held in dragons' mouths, a device of 132 CE that dropped one when the ground trembled, and a Han-dynasty armillary sphere converge on whom?
questions.f: His seismoscope could show which direction a distant quake came from.

questions.q: A dream of a snake seizing its own tail, six carbon atoms in a closed loop, and the chemical meaning of 'aromatic' converge on which molecule?
questions.f: August Kekule said the ring's structure came to him in a daydream.

questions.q: A geodesic-dome architect's name, sixty carbon atoms arranged like a football, and the nickname 'buckyball' converge on which class of molecule?
questions.f: Their 1985 discovery opened up a whole new chemistry of carbon.

questions.q: Sticky tape peeled across graphite, Friday-evening side projects in Manchester, and a sheet one atom thick converge on which material?
questions.f: Geim and Novoselov won the 2010 Nobel for their tape trick.

questions.q: A refrigerant sample that seemed to vanish from its cylinder in 1938, a slippery white powder found coating the inside, and non-stick pans converge on which material?
questions.f: Roy Plunkett's 'failed' experiment produced PTFE by accident.

questions.q: Radioactive labels on protein coats and on genetic material, a kitchen blender, and viruses stripped from bacteria in 1952 converge on which experiment?
questions.f: It confirmed that DNA, not protein, carries the genetic message.

questions.q: A 1964 Soviet paper on energy budgets, three numbered types, and a way of ranking how much power a civilization can harness converge on which scale?
questions.f: A Type II civilization would command the entire output of its star.

questions.q: A goddess of the rainbow, brightly coloured salts, and a strange abundance in a thin clay layer 66 million years old converge on which element?
questions.f: That iridium spike is key evidence for the asteroid impact theory.

questions.q: A Greek word for 'smell', a pungent oxide used to stain microscope samples, and the densest naturally occurring element converge on which metal?
questions.f: A cupful of osmium would weigh about as much as a small child.

questions.q: A Greek word for 'stranger', a gas found in the residue of liquid air in 1898, and bright car headlamps converge on which element?
questions.f: Xenon also produced the first noble-gas compound, upsetting textbooks.

questions.q: A name taken from the Moon goddess, discovery beside an element named for the Earth, and early photocopier drums converge on which element?
questions.f: Berzelius named selenium after Selene when he found it with tellurium.

questions.q: A mythical king punished with fruit forever out of reach, an oxide that stubbornly refuses to absorb acid, and tiny capacitors converge on which metal?
questions.f: Tantalum capacitors sit inside almost every mobile phone.

questions.q: A Norse goddess of beauty, compounds spanning a rainbow of oxidation states, and the tough steel in good spanners converge on which element?
questions.f: Vanadium's colourful salts earned it a goddess's name.

questions.q: A Norse thunder god, an 1828 discovery by Berzelius in a Norwegian mineral, and a proposed alternative reactor fuel converge on which element?
questions.f: Thorium reactors remain an active area of research.

questions.q: The first asteroid ever discovered, the most abundant of the rare-earth elements, and the sparking flint of a cigarette lighter converge on which element?
questions.f: Cerium is named after Ceres, found in 1801.

questions.q: An asteroid spotted in 1802, a metal that soaks up hydrogen like a sponge, and catalytic converters converge on which element?
questions.f: Palladium can absorb hundreds of times its own volume of hydrogen.

questions.q: A Greek word for 'rose', salts of a rose-red colour, and a metal that has at times outpriced gold many times over converge on which element?
questions.f: Rhodium plating keeps white gold jewellery from tarnishing.

questions.q: A Latin word for sky-blue, two blue lines seen by Bunsen and Kirchhoff in 1860, and the atomic clock that defines the second converge on which element?
questions.f: One second is 9,192,631,770 vibrations of a caesium atom.

questions.q: A Latin word for deepest red, the second element ever found by flame spectroscopy, and a softer cousin of caesium converge on which metal?
questions.f: Bunsen and Kirchhoff found it in 1861, a year after caesium.

questions.q: An indigo-blue spectral line, a metal soft enough to mark paper, and the transparent conducting film on touchscreens converge on which element?
questions.f: Indium tin oxide lets your phone screen be both clear and conductive.

questions.q: A Greek word for a green shoot, a vivid green flame line spotted by Crookes in 1861, and element 81 converge on which element?
questions.f: Its green spectral line gave thallium its budding name.

questions.q: A Greek word for a strong smell, the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature, and the silver salts of old photographic film converge on which element?
questions.f: Bromine and mercury are the only two elements liquid at room temperature.

questions.q: A Greek word for violet, purple fumes rising from burnt seaweed ash, and Courtois's accidental 1811 discovery converge on which element?
questions.f: Iodine's violet vapour gave the element its name.

questions.q: A Swedish phrase meaning 'heavy stone', the highest melting point of any metal, and the glowing filament of an old light bulb converge on which element?
questions.f: Tungsten melts at about 3,422 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: The symbol Sb, an ancient black eye cosmetic ground from its ore, and a brittle metalloid converge on which element?
questions.f: Sb comes from 'stibium', the Latin name for the mineral stibnite.

questions.q: A German miners' term joining 'copper' with a mischievous sprite, an ore that yielded no copper at all, and Cronstedt's 1751 isolation converge on which metal?
questions.f: Kupfernickel roughly meant 'Old Nick's copper'.

questions.q: A Spanish word meaning 'little silver', a metal early colonists discarded as a nuisance, and a very high melting point converge on which element?
questions.f: 'Platina' was a dismissive nickname before platinum became precious.

questions.q: A Greek word for 'artificial', the first element ever made in a laboratory rather than found, and element 43 converge on which element?
questions.f: No isotope of technetium is stable, so almost none occurs naturally.
