questions.f: Golden-angle spacing of about 137.5 degrees packs seeds most efficiently - hence Fibonacci counts.

questions.q: The 'golden angle' of roughly 137.5 degrees comes from dividing a full turn by...?
questions.f: It is the most 'irrational' turn possible - so new leaves never shade the ones below.

questions.q: A rectangle whose leftover piece stays the same shape after you remove a square is called...?
questions.f: Repeat the trick forever and the corners trace a logarithmic spiral.

questions.q: Which numbers, defined by their own recursive addition rule, were described in India by Pingala centuries before Fibonacci?
questions.f: Pingala studied poetic metres - short and long syllables generate the same sequence.

questions.q: Every even number up to about four quintillion has been checked to be a sum of two primes, yet Goldbach's conjecture remains unproven.
questions.f: Verification, however far it runs, can never cover an infinite set - only a proof would.

questions.q: Cantor proved that the rational numbers, though densely packed, are the same size of infinity as the counting numbers.
questions.f: His clever zigzag listing pairs every fraction with a counting number - none is missed.

questions.q: The four colour theorem's first accepted proof relied on a computer checking nearly 2,000 cases.
questions.f: Some mathematicians refused to accept it - a proof no human could read in full.

questions.q: There are exactly five Platonic solids, and Euclid's Elements ends by proving no others exist.
questions.f: Book XIII closes the whole work with that proof - a deliberate grand finale.

questions.q: Hardy considered number theory beautifully useless - yet it now secures the world's internet traffic.
questions.f: In 1940 he boasted his work had 'no practical use'; prime-based cryptography proved him wrong.

questions.q: The word 'hundred' descends from a root meaning ten, plus an old suffix for a count.
questions.f: Proto-Germanic 'hund' plus 'rad' (count) - literally 'a count of tens'.

questions.q: The sky often glows orange and pink as the Sun goes down. What is this time called?
questions.f: Sunset light travels through extra air, which scatters away blue and leaves warm orange and pink.

questions.q: At what time of day does the Sun rise?
c: In the middle of the night
questions.f: The Sun seems to rise because our Earth is always slowly spinning toward it.

questions.q: On a windy day, what toy can you fly high on a string?
questions.f: Kites have flown for over 2,000 years — they were first made long ago in China.

questions.q: What do you build outside after a big snowfall and give a carrot nose?
questions.f: The biggest snowman ever built was taller than a ten-storey building!

questions.q: What twinkles high in the sky on a clear night?
questions.f: Stars twinkle because their light wiggles as it passes through Earth's moving air.

questions.q: A raincoat is a special coat that keeps off the what?
questions.f: The first rubber raincoats were made about 200 years ago and were called mackintoshes.

questions.q: Which season comes right after winter?
questions.f: In spring the days grow longer and warmer, waking up plants and animals.

questions.q: Which season comes right after summer?
questions.f: Autumn is also harvest time, when many fruits and vegetables are ready to pick.

questions.q: What shape does the full Moon look like in the sky?
questions.f: The Moon is really a giant ball of rock — it just looks like a flat circle from far away.

questions.q: The word 'snowball' joins 'snow' together with which little word?
questions.f: Joining two small words to make a new one, like snow + ball, makes a compound word.

questions.q: If your breath makes a tiny cloud outside, the air must be very what?
questions.f: Your warm, damp breath turns into tiny water droplets you can see when it hits cold air.

questions.q: A day when school closes because of deep snow is called a what?
questions.f: On snow days, snowplows work hard to clear the roads while kids go sledding.

questions.q: What word means the opposite of 'hot'?
questions.f: Words with opposite meanings, like hot and cold, are called antonyms.

questions.q: What word means the opposite of 'wet'?
questions.f: Deserts are the driest places on Earth — some get almost no rain for years.

questions.q: What warm drink do many kids love to sip after playing in the snow?
questions.f: People have been drinking chocolate for thousands of years — the Aztecs loved it too.

questions.q: What do you wear on your feet to splash in puddles?
questions.f: Rain boots are sometimes called wellies, after a duke named Wellington who made them popular.

questions.q: What do we call water when it freezes hard and solid?
questions.f: Ice floats on water — that is why ice cubes bob at the top of your drink.

questions.q: When the sky is full of grey clouds, we say the day is what?
questions.f: Grey clouds look dark because they are so thick that sunlight cannot shine through.

questions.q: The soft light that comes from the Moon at night is called what?
questions.f: Moonlight is really sunlight bouncing off the Moon like a giant mirror.

questions.q: 'Rainy', 'sunny' and 'windy' are all words that describe the what?
questions.f: Adding the letter 'y' to words like rain, sun and wind turns them into describing words.

questions.q: What do you wear on your hands to keep them toasty in the snow?
questions.f: Mittens keep fingers warmer than gloves because the fingers share their heat together.

questions.q: What lights up the night sky with a gentle silver glow?
questions.f: The Moon is Earth's closest neighbour in space, about 384,000 kilometres away.

questions.q: A 'sunny' day is a day full of what?
questions.f: Sunshine helps your body make vitamin D, which keeps your bones strong.

questions.q: What do we call the middle of the day, when the Sun is at its highest?
questions.f: At noon your shadow is at its shortest because the Sun is almost overhead.

questions.q: Clouds can move across the sky.
questions.f: The wind pushes clouds along — some race across the sky at over 100 kilometres per hour.

questions.q: The Moon makes its own light, just like the Sun does.
questions.f: The Moon has no light of its own — it only reflects light from the Sun.

questions.q: Snow melts faster on a warm day.
questions.f: Heat makes the tiny bits inside snow jiggle faster until the snow turns back into water.

questions.q: Wind can push a sailboat across the water.
questions.f: Sailors have used wind power to cross whole oceans for thousands of years.

questions.q: Stars shine only in winter.
questions.f: Stars shine all year round — daylight is just too bright for us to see them.

questions.q: The opposite of 'day' is 'night'.
questions.f: Day and night happen because the Earth spins — one full spin takes 24 hours.

questions.q: Rain makes the ground wet.
questions.f: Rain soaks into the soil, giving thirsty plants and trees a big drink.

questions.q: Which season is the best one for building sandcastles at a hot beach?
questions.f: Slightly wet sand sticks together best, which is why castles are built near the waves.

questions.q: Finish the rhyme: 'April showers bring May ____.'
questions.f: This old rhyme means spring rain helps flowers bloom — and 'showers' rhymes with 'flowers'.

questions.q: What is another name for the season called autumn?
questions.f: It is called fall in America because that is when the leaves fall from the trees.

questions.q: In winter, ponds can freeze so hard that people do what on top of them?
questions.f: Pond ice must be very thick before it is safe — and only when a grown-up says so.

questions.q: In which season are pumpkins picked, just in time for harvest fun?
questions.f: Pumpkins grow all summer long and turn orange and ready by autumn.

questions.q: 'Snow' plus 'storm' makes which big weather word?
questions.f: A snowstorm with fierce winds gets an even wilder name — a blizzard.

questions.q: What do you ride to slide down a snowy hill?
questions.f: Some Olympic sledders zoom down icy tracks faster than cars drive on a highway.

questions.q: A windmill gets its turning power from the what?
questions.f: Long ago, windmills used the wind to grind grain into flour for bread.

questions.q: The hottest part of a summer day is usually when the Sun is where?
questions.f: When the Sun is high, its rays hit the ground straight on and warm it fastest.

questions.q: Spring, summer, autumn and winter are the four what?
questions.f: Some tropical countries have just two seasons instead — a wet one and a dry one.

questions.q: What colour do storm clouds usually turn just before heavy rain?
questions.f: Storm clouds look dark because they are packed so full of water that light cannot get through.

questions.q: The sunflower got its name because its big round bloom looks like the what?
questions.f: Young sunflowers even turn their heads during the day to follow the Sun across the sky.

questions.q: On a snowy day, what can you catch on your tongue?
questions.f: Each snowflake you catch grew its shape inside a freezing cloud high above you.

questions.q: Splish, splash! What do we call a small pool of rainwater on the ground?
questions.f: Puddles slowly disappear in the sunshine as the water floats away into the air.

questions.q: What bright thing in the daytime sky should you never stare at?
questions.f: The Sun is so bright it can hurt your eyes — even special glasses are needed to view it safely.

questions.q: What word means the opposite of 'cloudy'?
questions.f: On a truly clear day you can sometimes see mountains more than 100 kilometres away.

questions.q: Too much time in strong sunshine can turn your skin red. This is called a what?
questions.f: Sunscreen, hats and shade are the superhero team that protects your skin outside.

questions.q: Which big machine pushes deep snow off the roads?
questions.f: Some snowplows also sprinkle salt, which helps melt the ice on the road.

questions.q: A scarf keeps which part of you warm on a freezing day?
questions.f: You lose lots of heat from your head and neck, so hats and scarves really do help.

questions.q: What playful word describes the sound of rain tapping on a roof?
questions.f: Words that copy sounds, like pitter-patter and splash, are called onomatopoeia.

questions.q: In winter, the days are short and the nights are very what?
questions.f: Near the North Pole, a winter night can last for weeks without any sunrise at all.

questions.q: The word 'daytime' is the opposite of what?
questions.f: When it is daytime where you live, it is nighttime on the other side of the world.

questions.q: On what kind of day does an ice pop melt the fastest?
questions.f: Heat always flows into colder things, so a hot day melts an icy treat extra fast.

questions.q: 'Splash', 'drip' and 'plop' are all sounds made by what?
questions.f: Rain sounds different on every surface — try listening to it on a tent, a window and a tin roof.

questions.q: After a rainy night, which wiggly creature often appears on the sidewalk?
questions.f: Worms come up when soil gets soggy, and moving is easier for them on wet ground.

questions.q: What do we call a round house built from blocks of packed snow?
questions.f: Snow traps lots of air, so a well-built igloo can stay cosy even in a polar wind.

questions.q: When farm fields turn dusty and dry, what do farmers hope will come?
questions.f: A good soaking rain can wake up thirsty crops in just a day or two.

questions.q: If you play in the rain without a coat, you will get soaking what?
questions.f: Your skin is waterproof, but your clothes are not — that is what raincoats are for!

questions.q: A big beach umbrella protects you from the hot sun by making cool what?
questions.f: Shade can feel around 10 degrees cooler than standing in the direct sunshine.

questions.q: What can you fold from paper to wave cool air onto your face?
questions.f: Moving air helps sweat dry from your skin, and that is what cools you down.

questions.q: The word 'nightfall' means the time when what begins?
questions.f: Nightfall is a poetic word — as if the darkness gently falls over the sky like a blanket.

questions.q: A weather report on TV tells you what tomorrow's what will be?
questions.f: Weather reporters use pictures from space to see storms coming days away.

questions.q: A 'shower' of rain means rain that falls how?
questions.f: A shower can end so fast that the Sun comes back out while the ground is still wet.

questions.q: In which season do many birds fly away to warmer places?
questions.f: This big trip is called migration — some birds fly thousands of kilometres.

questions.q: What word means 'a little bit wet', like grass in the early morning?
questions.f: Morning grass is damp because water from the night air settles on it in tiny drops.

questions.q: When thunder starts to boom, where is the safest place to be?
questions.f: A good rule: when thunder roars, go indoors!

questions.q: Adding the letter 'y' to 'wind' makes which describing word?
questions.f: English loves this trick — sun becomes sunny, rain becomes rainy, snow becomes snowy.

questions.q: What colour do most kids use to draw the Sun?
questions.f: The Sun actually shines white — Earth's air just makes it look yellow to us.

questions.q: What do you wear on your head to keep the hot sun off your face?
questions.f: A wide brim shades your face, ears and neck all at once.

questions.q: On a rainy day, what small creature hops happily in the puddles?
questions.f: Frogs love damp weather because their skin needs to stay wet.

questions.q: What do we call the white stuff that covers the ground after a snowfall?
questions.f: A thick snow blanket keeps the soil underneath warmer than the freezing air above.

questions.q: Which word describes a day with no clouds at all?
questions.f: On clear nights you can see the most stars, because nothing blocks their light.

questions.q: What sound does thunder make?
questions.f: Thunder is the sound of air jumping out of the way of a lightning bolt.

questions.q: Which season has Christmas in many cold countries?
questions.f: In Australia, Christmas lands in summer — some families barbecue on the beach!

questions.q: What warm woolly thing do you pull on when the air turns chilly?
questions.f: Wool keeps you warm because it traps lots of tiny pockets of air.

questions.q: What do we call the air moving fast outside?
questions.f: You cannot see the wind, but you can watch it push leaves and flags around.

questions.q: Which of these is a colour you find in a rainbow?
questions.f: A rainbow has red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

questions.q: What tiny bright dots make patterns in the night sky?
questions.f: People long ago joined stars into pictures like a bear, a lion and a hunter.

questions.q: When the ground is icy, how should you walk?
questions.f: Ice is slippery because a super-thin layer of water sits on top of it.

questions.q: What kind of clothes do you wear to swim on a hot summer day?
questions.f: Swimming is a great way to cool down because water carries heat away from your skin.

questions.q: What tall thing bends and sways in a strong wind?
questions.f: Bending helps trees survive storms — a stiff tree would snap instead.

questions.q: What do we call frozen water shaped into little cubes for drinks?
questions.f: Ice cubes float, so they keep the top of your drink cool.

questions.q: When it is very hot, what does your body do to help cool you down?
questions.f: As sweat dries off your skin, it carries heat away with it.

questions.q: When you are very cold, what does your body do?
questions.f: Shivering is your muscles wiggling fast to make extra heat.

questions.q: What season is it when snowdrops and daffodils first pop up?
questions.f: Snowdrops can push their shoots up right through a thin layer of snow.

questions.q: Which word means 'a lot of rain in a short time'?
questions.f: Heavy rain can fill a bucket left outside in less than an hour.

questions.q: What do we call the pretty white pattern frost makes on a cold window?
questions.f: Frost draws feathery shapes as water in the air freezes onto the cold glass.

questions.q: Adding 'ing' to 'rain' makes which word?
questions.f: 'It is raining' tells you the rain is happening right now.

questions.q: What do we call the picture of clouds and suns on a weather chart?
questions.f: A little cloud with lines under it means rain — no words needed!

questions.q: What do farmers grow with the help of sunshine and rain?
questions.f: Plants use sunlight to make their own food — that is how a tiny seed becomes a tall corn plant.

questions.q: Which animal is famous for loving cold, snowy places?
questions.f: A polar bear's thick fur and fat keep it cosy even swimming in icy water.

questions.q: What word describes air that is nice and not too hot or too cold?
questions.f: Mild days are perfect for playing outside without a coat or a fan.

questions.q: What do we call the time of year when school takes a long break in summer?
questions.f: Summer holidays began long ago so children could help on farms during the busiest months.

questions.q: Where do you look to see a rainbow?
questions.f: Look away from the Sun after a shower — that is where the bow appears.

questions.q: What do we call a very big wind storm with lots of rain?
questions.f: During a storm, staying inside with your family is the safest plan.

questions.q: What can you draw in the snow with a stick?
questions.f: Fresh snow is a giant blank page — and it wipes clean with the next snowfall.

questions.q: On which kind of day do you need an umbrella most?
questions.f: Umbrellas have been keeping people dry for more than 3,000 years.

questions.q: Ice is colder than warm water.
questions.f: Ice must be at freezing or colder, or it would melt right away.

questions.q: The Sun rises every morning.
questions.f: Even on cloudy days the Sun rises — the clouds just hide it from view.

questions.q: Umbrellas are used to keep you dry.
questions.f: Some umbrellas are so big they shade a whole café table.

questions.q: Leaves grow back on trees in spring.
questions.f: Trees keep tiny buds hidden all winter, ready to burst open when it warms up.

questions.q: Thunder can be very loud.
questions.f: Thunder can be heard many kilometres away from the lightning that made it.

questions.q: Snow is warm and dry.
questions.f: Snow is cold and wet — that is why you need gloves to play in it.

questions.q: A hot day makes many people want a cold drink.
questions.f: Drinking water on hot days keeps your body from getting too warm.

questions.q: What is the name of the season with the warmest weather in most places?
questions.f: Summer is warmest because your part of Earth leans toward the Sun.

questions.q: What do you call it when the wind blows very gently?
questions.f: A soft breeze is just enough to flutter a flag or spin a pinwheel.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'sun'?
questions.f: Rhyming words help poets write cheerful weather rhymes.

questions.q: What is the last thing to happen at the end of a rainstorm?
questions.f: After the rain stops, the air often smells wonderfully fresh.

questions.q: Which word means 'very, very cold'?
questions.f: When it is freezing, water outside turns into ice.

questions.q: Which word means 'very, very hot'?
questions.f: We say 'boiling' because water boils when it gets very hot indeed.

questions.q: Which bird is often seen splashing in a puddle or birdbath?
questions.f: Birds bathe to keep their feathers clean so they can fly well.

questions.q: What do you call the sky when it is full of dark rain clouds?
questions.f: 'Gloomy' means dim and grey — the perfect word for a rainy afternoon.

questions.q: When you plant a seed, what two things from the sky help it grow?
questions.f: Sunlight gives plants energy and rain gives them a drink.

questions.q: What is the big word for the fluffy shapes in the sky?
questions.f: Clouds come in many shapes — some look like animals if you watch long enough.

questions.q: Which of these keeps you dry: a raincoat or a paper hat?
questions.f: Paper soaks up water, but a raincoat lets it slide right off.

questions.q: In which season do you most often see snowmen?
questions.f: Snowmen last longest when the weather stays below freezing.

questions.q: What word describes a small amount of rain?
questions.f: A sprinkle barely wets the pavement before it dries again.

questions.q: What do we call the season word 'spring' when it means the time of year?
questions.f: The word 'spring' also means to jump — plants seem to spring up in that season!

questions.q: Which of these is a cold-weather treat you can only make outdoors in winter?
questions.f: You need packing snow — the slightly wet kind that sticks together.

questions.q: When rain and sunshine happen together, what might appear?
questions.f: You need the Sun behind you and rain in front for the bow to show up.

questions.q: What is the name of the star closest to Earth?
questions.f: The Sun looks huge to us only because it is so much nearer than other stars.

questions.q: What can wind do to a pile of dry autumn leaves?
questions.f: Wind scattering leaves helps spread seeds to new places.

questions.q: What do you call it when the wind blows so hard you must hold your hat?
questions.f: On very windy days, hats and balloons make a run for it!

questions.q: Which is the coldest: ice, warm soup or a sunny rock?
questions.f: Ice stays at freezing until it melts, no matter how long you wait.

questions.q: Where does snow land when it falls?
questions.f: Snow lands quietly — much softer than the pattering of rain.

questions.q: What do we call a very short, sudden rain that stops quickly?
questions.f: Some showers are so small that only half your street gets wet.

questions.q: What are you doing when you 'wrap up warm'?
questions.f: Layers of clothes trap warm air next to your body, like a cosy sandwich.

questions.q: On a foggy morning, how far can you see?
questions.f: Fog is a cloud sitting on the ground, and its droplets scatter light everywhere.

questions.q: What word goes with 'snow' to make the name of a snowy hat-wearing figure?
questions.f: Compound words like snowman join two smaller words together.

questions.q: What does a plant need lots of on a very dry day?
questions.f: Thirsty plants droop, then perk right up after a good watering.

questions.q: What word means 'wet from a small amount of rain'?
questions.f: Damp towels and damp grass both feel a little wet to touch.

questions.q: On a hot day, where is it cooler: in the shade or in the sunshine?
questions.f: Shade blocks the Sun's rays before they can warm you up.

questions.q: Which of these can you hear during a big storm?
questions.f: Sunshine and rainbows are silent — thunder is the loud one.

questions.q: How does the Sun help wet clothes on a washing line?
questions.f: The Sun's warmth turns the water in the cloth into invisible vapour.

questions.q: What kind of weather does a beach day need?
questions.f: Even on sunny beach days, a hat and sunscreen keep you safe.

questions.q: Which season comes right after autumn?
questions.f: Winter brings the shortest days of the whole year.

questions.q: What can you make with your hands in the snow to throw at a target?
questions.f: Snowballs stick together best when the snow is slightly melty.

questions.q: Which word describes the Sun's warm feeling on your skin?
questions.f: The Sun's warmth travels 150 million kilometres to reach your arm.

questions.q: What word means the same as 'chilly'?
questions.f: Words that mean nearly the same thing, like cool and chilly, are synonyms.

questions.q: What is at the top of the sky on a clear day?
questions.f: Straight up is where the sky looks its deepest blue.

questions.q: Which comes first in the day: sunrise or sunset?
questions.f: Sunrise starts the day and sunset ends it — the Sun's daily journey.

questions.q: Rainbows have many colours.
questions.f: A rainbow's colours blend into each other, so it really has countless shades.

questions.q: You should carry an umbrella in a thunderstorm with lightning.
questions.f: During lightning it is safest to go inside — not to hold anything up in the air.

questions.q: The Sun looks bigger than the other stars because it is much closer to us.
questions.f: Many stars are far bigger than the Sun, but they are unimaginably far away.

questions.q: You can see your breath more easily on cold days.
questions.f: The warm damp air from your lungs turns into a mini cloud in the cold.

questions.q: Trees lose their leaves in the summer.
questions.f: Most leaf-dropping trees are at their greenest in summer and bare in winter.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a season?
questions.f: Monday is a day of the week — there are seven days but only four seasons.

questions.q: Which weather word starts with the same sound as 'flag'?
questions.f: Fog and flag both begin with the letter f.

questions.q: At what temperature does water freeze into ice on the Celsius scale?
questions.f: On the Fahrenheit scale used in the USA, water freezes at 32 degrees instead.

questions.q: What is the striped cloth tube at airports that fills with wind to show its direction?
questions.f: Pilots glance at the windsock before take-off — a stiff, straight sock means strong wind.

questions.q: From which direction does the Sun rise each morning?
questions.f: Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun first peeks over the eastern horizon.

questions.q: What do we call a huge, slow-moving river of ice creeping down a mountain valley?
questions.f: Glaciers move so slowly that some travel less than a metre in a whole day.

questions.q: What is the imaginary line around Earth's warm middle called?
questions.f: Places on the equator get strong sunshine all year, so they never have a cold winter.

questions.q: Weather is what's happening today, but the usual pattern over many years is called the what?
questions.f: A handy saying: climate is what you expect, weather is what you get.

questions.q: What metal spike on tall buildings guides lightning safely into the ground?
questions.f: Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod, and it still protects buildings today.

questions.q: What do we call the tall towers with giant spinning blades that turn wind into electricity?
questions.f: One large wind turbine can power hundreds of homes when the wind blows well.

questions.q: Solar panels on rooftops make electricity from what?
questions.f: The word 'solar' comes from 'sol', the Latin word for the Sun.

questions.q: What do we call the faraway line where the sky seems to meet the land or sea?
questions.f: At the beach, the horizon is only about 5 kilometres away for someone standing at the shore.

questions.q: A 'shooting star' isn't a star at all. What is it really?
questions.f: Most meteors are smaller than a pea, yet they blaze bright enough to see from the ground.

questions.q: The Moon's changing shapes through the month are called its what?
questions.f: The Moon takes about 29 and a half days to go through all its phases.

questions.q: Which star looks the biggest and brightest to us because it is the closest?
questions.f: The next closest star is so far away its light takes over four years to reach us.

questions.q: What garden 'clock' tells the time using a shadow cast by the Sun?
questions.f: Sundials are among the oldest clocks — ancient Egyptians used them thousands of years ago.

questions.q: What do we call a stretch of many very hot days in a row?
questions.f: During heat waves, cities open cool public buildings so everyone can beat the heat.

questions.q: Harvest time, when farmers gather most of their crops, comes in which season?
questions.f: Harvest festivals around the world celebrate this season of plenty with feasts.

questions.q: A desert can turn freezing cold at night.
questions.f: With no clouds to trap heat, the Sahara can drop from baking hot to near freezing after dark.

questions.q: Every cloud in the sky brings rain.
questions.f: Most clouds never rain at all — their droplets are too small and light to fall.

questions.q: You can get a sunburn even on a cloudy day.
questions.f: Most of the Sun's burning UV rays pass right through thin clouds.

questions.q: A thermometer measures the speed of the wind.
questions.f: Thermometers measure temperature — 'thermo' means heat and 'meter' means measurer.

questions.q: The Moon can sometimes be seen in the daytime sky.
questions.f: The Moon is often up during the day — it is just easier to spot against a dark night sky.

questions.q: What is the invisible blanket of air wrapped all around Earth called?
questions.f: Without the atmosphere there would be no wind, no rain and no blue sky at all.

questions.q: The long winter sleep that animals like hedgehogs take is called what?
questions.f: A hibernating animal's heartbeat can slow from hundreds of beats a minute to just a few.

questions.q: A weather 'forecast' tells you the weather when?
questions.f: 'Fore' means ahead or before — just like the 'fore' in forehead, the front of your head.

questions.q: What is a 'downpour'?
questions.f: In a serious downpour, more rain can fall in an hour than some deserts see in a year.

questions.q: If the sky is 'overcast', what does it look like?
questions.f: 'Overcast' literally means 'cast over' — as if a grey blanket were thrown across the sky.

questions.q: What is a 'gust' of wind?
c: A sudden short burst of wind
questions.f: Weather stations report both the steady wind speed and the strongest gusts.

questions.q: What is 'slush'?
questions.f: Slush forms when snow starts melting — great for splashing, terrible for sledding.

questions.q: The root 'sol' in the word 'solar' means what?
questions.f: From Latin 'sol' we also get 'solstice' and 'parasol' — a shade against the sun.

questions.q: The word 'lunar', as in lunar eclipse, means 'to do with the' what?
questions.f: 'Luna' is the Latin name for the Moon — in Spanish the Moon is still called 'la luna'.

questions.q: What is a 'snowdrift'?
c: A deep pile of snow heaped up by wind
questions.f: Wind can sculpt snowdrifts taller than a grown-up against walls and fences.

questions.q: 'Twilight' is the name for the dim, dreamy light between what?
questions.f: There is a morning twilight too, in the quiet minutes just before sunrise.

questions.q: A 'tropical' place is usually what, all year round?
questions.f: The tropics are the sunny lands lying close to Earth's equator.

questions.q: 'Polar' weather is the kind found near Earth's what?
questions.f: Polar explorers face months of darkness, howling winds and air far below freezing.

questions.q: What is 'mist'?
questions.f: Mist and fog are the same thing — it is called fog when it is thick enough to hide faraway things.

questions.q: What word means the opposite of 'melt'?
questions.f: Water is amazing — it can melt, freeze and even float into the air as invisible vapour.

questions.q: In the word 'rainbow', the old word 'bow' means a what?
questions.f: The same curved 'bow' appears in 'bow and arrow' — a rainbow is an arch of rain-light.

questions.q: Something 'seasonal', like mangoes or snow boots, appears only at a certain what?
questions.f: Strawberries are seasonal in many countries — sweetest in late spring and summer.

questions.q: A 'weatherproof' jacket is one that does what?
questions.f: The suffix '-proof' means 'protected against' — like waterproof and fireproof.

questions.q: The ending '-ology' in 'meteorology' means the what of something?
questions.f: Meteorology is the study of weather; add '-ist' and you get the scientist who studies it.

questions.q: What is another popular name for a tornado?
questions.f: The nickname comes from the way the wild wind twists round and round in a funnel.

questions.q: A group of stars that makes a picture, like the Big Dipper, is called a what?
questions.f: Astronomers officially recognise 88 constellations covering the whole sky.

questions.q: A 'blustery' day is a day that is what?
questions.f: In the Winnie-the-Pooh stories, a very windy day is famously called a blustery day.

questions.q: 'Thermal' underwear and thermal flasks have to do with keeping in what?
questions.f: The Greek root 'therm' means heat — it hides in thermometer and thermostat too.

questions.q: The root 'aqua', as in aquarium, means what?
questions.f: 'Aqua' is Latin for water — an aqueduct is a bridge built to carry water.

questions.q: 'Rainfall' is the word for how much rain does what in a place?
questions.f: The rainfall of a whole year is often measured in just millimetres or inches.

questions.q: What is the hottest part of a sunny day, usually?
questions.f: The ground keeps soaking up heat after noon, so around 2 to 3 pm often feels hottest.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, spring begins around which month?
questions.f: South of the equator it is the opposite — March there is the start of autumn.

questions.q: What snowy shape do you make by lying down and sweeping your arms and legs?
questions.f: Thousands of people once made snow angels together in North Dakota to set a world record.

questions.q: What do we call the first soft light in the sky before the Sun rises?
questions.f: The French call it 'aube', poets call it daybreak — early birds simply call it singing time.

questions.q: What tool do you look through to see faraway stars and planets better?
questions.f: 'Tele' means far and 'scope' means to look — a telescope is literally a far-looker.

questions.q: What do people wear to protect their eyes on bright, glaring days?
questions.f: Snow reflects sunlight so strongly that skiers can get 'snow blindness' without eye protection.

questions.q: Which continent, at the bottom of the world, is the coldest of them all?
questions.f: Antarctica is so cold that scientists there wear layers upon layers, even in its summer.

questions.q: In which season are the days shortest and the nights longest?
questions.f: The year's very shortest day is called the winter solstice.

questions.q: What glow from city lamps and signs hides the stars at night?
questions.f: Far from city lights you can see thousands of stars — in a bright city, sometimes only a handful.

questions.q: Sunlight takes about how long to travel from the Sun to Earth?
questions.f: Sunshine is a time traveller — the light warming you left the Sun about eight minutes ago.

questions.q: What invisible force pulls raindrops down from the clouds to the ground?
questions.f: Gravity pulls everything down — rain, snowflakes, autumn leaves and dropped ice creams.

questions.q: What is a 'flurry' of snow?
questions.f: 'Flurry' also describes any quick burst of activity — like a flurry of birthday cards.

questions.q: A 'crescent' Moon has which shape?
questions.f: 'Crescent' comes from a Latin word meaning 'growing' — the young Moon is growing fuller.

questions.q: A 'gale' is a very strong what?
questions.f: Gales at sea can whip up waves taller than houses.

questions.q: Which weather is best for drying wet laundry outside?
questions.f: Warm sunshine plus moving air makes water evaporate from clothes much faster.

questions.q: If you are 'snowed under' with homework, what does it mean?
c: You have far too much to do
questions.f: English borrows weather for feelings — you can also be 'flooded' with messages.

questions.q: A 'hazy' sky looks what?
questions.f: Haze is caused by tiny bits of dust, salt or smoke floating in the air.

questions.q: How long does Earth take to spin around once, giving us day and night?
questions.f: That one spin is why the Sun seems to travel across the sky each day.

questions.q: How long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
questions.f: That journey is about 940 million kilometres — and we ride it every year.

questions.q: Which is bigger, the Sun or the Moon?
questions.f: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but also about 400 times farther away.

questions.q: What is a 'drought'?
c: A long period with far too little rain
questions.f: During droughts, rivers shrink and towns often ask everyone to save water.

questions.q: Which two things does a plant need from the weather to grow well?
questions.f: Plants also need carbon dioxide from the air to build their leaves and stems.

questions.q: What is the name of the science of the stars, planets and space?
questions.f: Astronomers use huge telescopes on mountaintops where the air is thin and clear.

questions.q: What is a 'crop' on a farm?
questions.f: Farmers watch the forecast closely — one bad hailstorm can flatten a whole crop.

questions.q: What is the word for the top layer of a lake when it freezes over?
questions.f: Ice floats on top because frozen water is lighter than liquid water.

questions.q: Which season is best for kite flying because of steady breezes?
questions.f: Spring winds are lively as warm and cold air take turns across the land.

questions.q: What do we call a wind that carries dust and makes the air hazy?
questions.f: Dust from the Sahara sometimes travels across the whole Atlantic Ocean.

questions.q: When water in a pot gets very hot, it turns into what?
questions.f: Steam is water in gas form — the same stuff that makes clouds when it cools.

questions.q: What word describes the amount of water vapour in the air?
questions.f: High humidity is why summer air can feel heavy and sticky.

questions.q: What do we call a place that gets almost no rain and has lots of sand?
questions.f: Not all deserts are sandy — some are rocky, and some are covered in ice.

questions.q: What is a 'rainforest'?
c: A forest that gets very heavy rainfall
A forest planted in the rain
A forest that never gets wet
questions.f: Some rainforests get more than 4 metres of rain a year — taller than a door!

questions.q: Which of these words describes the flat frozen land near the Arctic?
questions.f: On the tundra, the soil below the surface stays frozen all year round.

questions.q: When the wind and rain wear away rocks over many years, that is called what?
questions.f: Erosion carved the Grand Canyon — water and time are patient sculptors.

questions.q: What is the name for a long, gentle slope of sand shaped by desert wind?
questions.f: Some desert dunes slowly walk across the land as the wind pushes their sand.

questions.q: Which is heavier: cold air or warm air?
questions.f: Cold air sinks and warm air rises — the engine behind almost all weather.

questions.q: Why do you sometimes see your shadow only on sunny days?
c: A shadow needs bright light to form
questions.f: On overcast days light comes from every direction, so shadows blur away.

questions.q: When does the Moon look completely round?
questions.f: At full moon, the Sun is lighting the whole side of the Moon that faces us.

questions.q: What is the 'new moon'?
c: When the Moon's lit side faces away and we cannot see it
A moon seen only in spring
questions.f: A new moon is invisible — but it is the perfect time to go stargazing.

questions.q: Where does most of Earth's water sit?
questions.f: About 97 percent of Earth's water is salty ocean water.

questions.q: What do we call the salty water in the sea?
questions.f: Seawater got salty from minerals that rivers carried off the land over billions of years.

questions.q: What do we call it when the sea rises and falls twice a day?
questions.f: The Moon's gravity pulls the ocean, creating tides all around the world.

questions.q: Which of these might a strong wind do to an umbrella?
questions.f: Some modern umbrellas are designed to flip back without breaking.

questions.q: What piece of clothing has a hood to keep rain off your head?
questions.f: The word 'anorak' comes from the Greenlandic Inuit word 'annoraaq'.

questions.q: What does a snow shovel do?
c: Clears snow out of the way
questions.f: Wide plastic shovels are lighter than metal ones, which helps on big driveways.

questions.q: Why do roads sometimes get sprinkled with salt in winter?
c: Salt makes ice melt at lower temperatures
questions.f: Salty water freezes below zero, so the ice turns back to liquid.

questions.q: What is the study of the weather called?
questions.f: Meteorologists collect millions of measurements every day from land, sea, sky and space.

questions.q: What kind of shoes help you walk on deep snow without sinking?
questions.f: Snowshoes spread your weight over a bigger area, just like a duck's webbed foot.

questions.q: What is a 'sunbeam'?
questions.f: You can spot sunbeams best when dust or mist gives the light something to bounce off.

questions.q: What is the word for water drops on the outside of a cold glass?
questions.f: The water did not leak out — it came from the air touching the cold glass.

questions.q: Which word describes the wind's speed and direction together?
questions.f: Sailors and pilots always want both numbers — how fast and from where.

questions.q: When snow and ice on a mountain melt in spring, where does the water go?
questions.f: Snowmelt keeps many great rivers flowing through the whole summer.

questions.q: Why do many houses have gutters along the roof edge?
questions.f: Without gutters, rain would pour off the roof and soak the walls below.

questions.q: What do we call the mark on a wall or ground made when sunlight is blocked?
questions.f: Your shadow is longest in the early morning and late afternoon.

questions.q: What is the name for the water stored inside a cloud?
questions.f: A single big storm cloud can hold thousands of tonnes of water in tiny droplets.

questions.q: What do we call a bridge of colour that seems to touch the ground at both ends?
questions.f: Legends in many countries say something wonderful waits at a rainbow's end.

questions.q: The Earth spins as it travels around the Sun.
questions.f: Earth does both at once — spinning gives us days, orbiting gives us years.

questions.q: Fog is really a cloud that has formed near the ground.
questions.f: Walk into fog and you are literally walking inside a cloud.

questions.q: All deserts are hot.
questions.f: The Gobi Desert has freezing winters, and Antarctica is a cold desert too.

questions.q: Rainwater starts out as fresh water, not salty water.
questions.f: Evaporation leaves the salt behind in the sea — that is nature's water purifier.

questions.q: Wind can be used to make electricity.
questions.f: Some countries already get more than half their power from the wind on breezy days.

questions.q: Hot air balloons work because hot air sinks.
questions.f: Hot air rises, which is exactly what lifts the balloon into the sky.

questions.q: Snow can pile up deeper on the sides of buildings than in the open.
questions.f: Wind swirls around walls and drops its snow load there, building deep drifts.

questions.q: Which is warmer: a sunny windowsill or a shady corner?
c: It depends on the day only
questions.f: Glass lets sunlight in, and that trapped warmth is why cats love windowsills.

questions.q: What does an 'umbrella stand' by the door tell you about the local weather?
questions.f: Rainy cities like Bergen in Norway see rain on well over 200 days a year.

questions.q: The word 'sunflower' is made of which two words?
questions.f: Its French name, 'tournesol', means 'turns with the sun'.

questions.q: What does the prefix 'mid' mean in 'midsummer' and 'midnight'?
questions.f: Midnight is the middle of the night and midsummer the middle of summer.

questions.q: What does the word 'overcoat' tell you about where you wear it?
questions.f: The prefix 'over-' also gives us overshoes and overcast.

questions.q: A 'raindrop' is a drop of what?
questions.f: A typical raindrop is only about 2 millimetres across — smaller than a pea.

questions.q: 'Snowfall' means the snow is doing what?
questions.f: Cities measure snowfall in centimetres, using a flat board wiped clean each hour.

questions.q: 'Sunrise' and 'sunset' are opposites. What are opposite words called?
questions.f: Sunrise and sunset are antonyms, while dawn and daybreak are synonyms.

questions.q: Which word means the same as 'wind'?
questions.f: English has many wind words: breeze, gust, gale, draught and squall.

questions.q: A 'weathervane' shows the wind's what?
questions.f: Weathervanes point INTO the wind — a north wind swings the arrow to the north.

questions.q: What is a 'sunspot' on the Sun?
c: A cooler, darker patch on the Sun's surface
questions.f: Sunspots can be bigger than Earth, and they come and go over weeks.

questions.q: 'Skyline' usually means what?
c: The outline of buildings against the sky
questions.f: Every city has a skyline — some, like New York's, are famous worldwide.

questions.q: What does 'evergreen' tell you about a tree?
c: It keeps green leaves all year
questions.f: Pine needles are tough and waxy, which helps them survive freezing winters.

questions.q: 'Frostbite' is damage caused by what?
questions.f: Fingers, toes, ears and noses are most at risk — that is why mittens matter.

questions.q: A 'sunbather' is someone who does what?
questions.f: Sunbathers should always use sunscreen — the Sun's rays are strongest at midday.

questions.q: What does the word 'thundercloud' describe?
c: A cloud shaped like a drum
questions.f: Thunderclouds can grow taller than Mount Everest in under an hour.

questions.q: 'Sunscreen' works by doing what?
questions.f: Look for a high SPF number — and remember to reapply after swimming.

questions.q: What is a 'raincloud'?
questions.f: Rainclouds look dark because their thick water blocks the sunlight.

questions.q: 'Waterproof' means what?
questions.f: Waterproof fabrics often have millions of pores too small for water but big enough for air.

questions.q: What does a 'weather station' do?
questions.f: Some remote weather stations report automatically from mountaintops and buoys at sea.

questions.q: Which of these means 'a small amount of snow'?
questions.f: A dusting is just enough to whiten the grass but not to build a snowman.

questions.q: What is a 'monsoon' best described as?
c: A season of heavy rain brought by shifting winds
questions.f: Monsoon rains water the crops that feed billions of people in Asia.

questions.q: What is 'sleet' usually a mix of?
questions.f: Sleet stings when it hits your face — half rain, half ice.

questions.q: A 'heatproof' oven glove protects you from what?
questions.f: The suffix '-proof' means protected against, whether it is heat, water or wind.

questions.q: 'Sundown' is another word for what?
questions.f: 'Sunup' is the matching old word for sunrise.

questions.q: What does the '-graph' in 'barograph' tell you the machine does?
questions.f: A barograph traces a wiggly ink line of air pressure across a slowly turning drum.

questions.q: Which word describes weather that changes often and quickly?
questions.f: Island weather is famously changeable — sunshine and showers can swap in minutes.

questions.q: What is a 'cloudy' drink like lemonade compared to a 'clear' one?
questions.f: The same word describes the sky and a glass — both hard to see through.

questions.q: What does the word 'seasonal' describe about a job or fruit?
c: It happens only at certain times of year
questions.f: Ski instructors and beach lifeguards both have very seasonal jobs.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the weather scientist's title?
questions.f: Watch the middle: me-te-o-ro-lo-gist — the 'o-r-o' trips up many spellers.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the frozen-rain word?
questions.f: 'Hale' means healthy, as in 'hale and hearty' — a homophone trap!

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the coloured arc in the sky?
questions.f: Rain + bow — two easy words joined, so the spelling stays simple.

questions.q: The word 'temperature' contains which hidden smaller word?
questions.f: Both come from Latin 'temperare', to mix or moderate — even losing your temper!

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the word for a whirling storm?
questions.f: Its plural can be spelled tornadoes or tornados — both are accepted.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'sky'?
questions.f: When a word ends in a consonant plus y, the y changes to 'ies'.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'flash', as in a flash of lightning?
questions.f: Words ending in 'sh' take '-es' — flashes, splashes and washes.

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'freeze'?
questions.f: Freeze, froze, frozen — an irregular verb, like speak, spoke, spoken.

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'blow', as in the wind blew?
questions.f: 'Blew' and 'blue' sound the same but mean very different things.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
questions.f: 'Rain' is treated as a single thing, so it takes 'is'.

questions.q: What do the words 'weather' and 'whether' show us about English?
questions.f: Words that sound the same but differ in meaning and spelling are homophones.

questions.q: In the word 'thunderstorm', which two smaller words are joined?
questions.f: English builds long weather words from short ones: snowstorm, rainstorm, sandstorm.

questions.q: What is a group of stars named after a hunter with a bright belt?
questions.f: Orion's three belt stars are among the easiest to spot on winter nights.

questions.q: Which bright star sits almost exactly above the North Pole?
questions.f: Because Polaris barely moves, travellers used it as a compass for centuries.

questions.q: What is the brightest star in the night sky?
questions.f: Sirius is nicknamed the Dog Star because it sits in the constellation Canis Major.

questions.q: What is our galaxy called?
questions.f: On dark nights, its billions of distant stars blur into a pale band across the sky.

questions.q: What is the name for a cloud of glowing gas and dust in space?
questions.f: 'Nebula' is Latin for cloud — space has clouds too, just made of gas and dust.

questions.q: Which of these can you safely use to look at the stars?
c: A magnifying glass on the Sun
questions.f: Ordinary binoculars reveal moons around Jupiter and craters on the Moon.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin's famous kite experiment showed that lightning is a form of what?
questions.f: Franklin flew his kite in 1752 — and soon after invented the lightning rod to protect buildings.

questions.q: What is the ghostly ring of light sometimes seen around the Moon on cold nights?
questions.f: Moon halos form when moonlight bends through ice crystals floating high in thin clouds.

questions.q: What is the scientific name for the Northern Lights?
questions.f: The dancing colours appear when particles from the Sun crash into gases high above the poles.

questions.q: Which planet is famous for dust storms so huge they can wrap around the entire planet?
questions.f: In 2018 a global Mars dust storm blocked so much sunlight that the rover Opportunity fell silent.

questions.q: The ozone layer high in the atmosphere protects us from what?
questions.f: Nations agreed in 1987 to ban the chemicals that were damaging the ozone layer — and it is healing.

questions.q: The longest day of the year in the north is called the summer what?
questions.f: In parts of Scandinavia, the summer solstice sun barely sets at all — it is a huge festival day.

questions.q: The big, bright 'harvest moon' rises in which season?
questions.f: Its light once helped farmers keep gathering crops after sunset — hence the name.

questions.q: On February 2nd, which animal is said to predict the end of winter in North America?
questions.f: The most famous forecaster, Punxsutawney Phil, has been 'predicting' since the 1880s.

questions.q: On a hot afternoon at the coast, a cool wind often blows from sea to land. Its name?
questions.f: Land heats faster than water, so rising warm air over the beach pulls in cool sea air.

questions.q: Which steady winds once carried sailing ships across the oceans to trade?
questions.f: Columbus rode the trade winds west across the Atlantic in 1492.

questions.q: A huge mass of snow suddenly rushing down a mountainside is called an what?
questions.f: Rescue dogs can smell a person buried under metres of avalanche snow.

questions.q: What carries weather instruments many kilometres up into the sky twice a day worldwide?
questions.f: Hundreds of weather balloons are released around the world every single day, rain or shine.

questions.q: What are people called who follow tornadoes and big storms to study them?
questions.f: Storm chasers helped scientists place instruments right in a tornado's path.

questions.q: What is the name for the thin, almost invisible ice that makes winter roads slippery?
questions.f: Black ice is actually clear — it just shows the dark road beneath, so drivers cannot see it.

questions.q: A full moon that looks extra big because the Moon is closest to Earth is called a what?
questions.f: A supermoon can look about 14 percent bigger and noticeably brighter than the smallest full moons.

questions.q: When the Moon slides exactly between Earth and the Sun, we see a solar what?
questions.f: By lucky chance the Moon and Sun look the same size in our sky, so the Moon can cover the Sun exactly.

questions.q: Photographers call the warm, glowing light just after sunrise and before sunset the what?
questions.f: During golden hour the low Sun paints everything with soft, honey-coloured light.

questions.q: Which US state records the most tornadoes in a typical year?
questions.f: Texas is huge and sits at the meeting point of warm gulf air and cool northern air — tornado fuel.

questions.q: Why can't a flag flutter in the wind on the Moon?
questions.f: With no atmosphere there is no wind — Apollo flags had a stiff rod to hold them out.

questions.q: Greenland and Antarctica are buried under gigantic slabs of ice called ice what?
questions.f: The Antarctic ice sheet holds most of the fresh water on the entire planet.

questions.q: Which dazzling planet is often called the Evening Star?
questions.f: Venus outshines every true star in our sky because its thick clouds reflect sunlight brilliantly.

questions.q: A space rock that survives its fiery fall and actually lands on Earth is called a what?
questions.f: While it is still blazing through the sky it is a meteor — only once it lands does it become a meteorite.

questions.q: On a weather map, what does a big letter H stand for?
questions.f: High-pressure areas usually bring calm, clear skies, while the letter L warns of stormier low pressure.

questions.q: What trick of hot air makes a distant road look like it is covered in water?
questions.f: Light bends as it passes through layers of hot and cool air, painting a shimmering false pool.

questions.q: A forecast says '70% chance of rain'. That number is the probability of what?
questions.f: It means that in 7 out of 10 situations just like this one, measurable rain fell.

questions.q: In folklore, which frosty character is said to paint icy patterns on winter windows?
questions.f: The real artist is water vapour freezing into feathery crystals on cold glass.

questions.q: In which month does summer officially begin in the Northern Hemisphere?
questions.f: Summer starts at the June solstice, when the North Pole leans most toward the Sun.

questions.q: At solar noon, when the Sun is highest, your shadow is at its what?
questions.f: Ancient scientists used noon shadows of sticks to measure the size of the whole Earth.

questions.q: What is the 'snow line' on a tall mountain?
c: The height above which snow stays all year
questions.f: Near the equator the snow line sits very high — Kilimanjaro keeps ice near its 5,895-metre summit.

questions.q: Which famously breezy US city is nicknamed 'The Windy City'?
questions.f: Chicago sits beside Lake Michigan, where wind whistles between its skyscrapers.

questions.q: Which temperature scale is used for everyday weather reports in the United States?
questions.f: On this scale a comfortable room is about 70 degrees and water boils at 212.

questions.q: A huge floating mountain of ice that has broken off a glacier is called an what?
questions.f: About nine-tenths of an iceberg hides underwater — you truly see only the tip.

questions.q: The South Pole is colder than the North Pole.
questions.f: The South Pole sits on a high, icy continent, while the North Pole floats on sea ice over ocean water.

questions.q: Tornadoes have been recorded on every continent except Antarctica.
questions.f: Even the United Kingdom gets small tornadoes — dozens touch down there in some years.

questions.q: A rainbow always appears in the part of the sky opposite the Sun.
questions.f: To find a rainbow, put the Sun at your back — the bow forms around the shadow of your own head.

questions.q: The Moon gets gentle rain showers from time to time.
questions.f: With no atmosphere, the Moon has no rain, no wind and no weather at all.

questions.q: A glowing red sky at sunset often means fine weather the next day.
questions.f: The old rhyme 'red sky at night, sailor's delight' works because weather usually arrives from the west.

questions.q: Hurricanes are given people's names taken from lists prepared years in advance.
questions.f: The lists repeat every six years — but the names of terrible storms are retired forever.

questions.q: Snow can fall even when the thermometer reads slightly above freezing.
questions.f: Flakes falling through a shallow layer of mild air can reach the ground before melting.

questions.q: Lightning always travels from the cloud down to the ground.
questions.f: Most lightning never touches the ground at all — it flashes inside or between clouds.

questions.q: The word 'smog' was invented by squashing together which two words?
questions.f: Blended words like smog and brunch are called portmanteau words.

questions.q: 'Equinox', when day and night are equal, literally means what?
questions.f: From Latin aequus (equal) and nox (night) — it happens each March and September.

questions.q: 'Meteorology' comes from a Greek word meaning things that are what?
questions.f: Greek 'meteoros' meant 'lifted high' — the ancients grouped clouds, rain and shooting stars together.

questions.q: 'Cyclone' comes from the Greek word 'kyklos', meaning what?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'bicycle' — two circles! Cyclone winds spin in a giant circle.

questions.q: The root 'anemo' in 'anemometer', the wind-speed instrument, means what?
questions.f: From Greek 'anemos' — the wind-loving anemone flower shares the very same root.

questions.q: A hydrologist is a scientist who studies what?
questions.f: Hydrologists track rain, rivers and underground water — 'hydro' is Greek for water.

questions.q: 'Tempest' is a grand old word for what?
questions.f: Shakespeare named a whole play 'The Tempest' — it opens with a dramatic shipwreck storm.

questions.q: What is a 'squall'?
c: A sudden, brief storm of wind with rain or snow
questions.f: Sailors fear squalls because they can strike a calm sea in just minutes.

questions.q: Land described as 'arid' is extremely what?
questions.f: From Latin 'arere', to be parched — arid lands get very little rain.

questions.q: 'Frigid' air is air that is what?
questions.f: Latin 'frigus' means cold — the same root chills the word 'refrigerator'.

questions.q: A 'sweltering' afternoon is one that is what?
questions.f: 'Swelter' is an old word for suffering from heat — perfect for sticky midsummer days.

questions.q: 'Balmy' weather is what kind of weather?
questions.f: It comes from 'balm', a soothing ointment — balmy air feels soothing on your skin.

questions.q: A 'muggy' day feels what?
questions.f: Mugginess is high humidity — sweat cannot evaporate, so you feel hotter than the thermometer says.

questions.q: Gardeners call soil 'parched' when it is what?
questions.f: 'Parched' can describe dry throats too — the word paints instant thirst.

questions.q: 'Umbrella' comes from the Latin word 'umbra', meaning what?
questions.f: The first umbrellas were sunshades — rain protection came along later.

questions.q: Aurora, who gave her name to the polar lights, was the Roman goddess of what?
questions.f: Each morning Aurora was said to fly across the sky announcing the sunrise.

questions.q: The wispy cloud name 'cirrus' is Latin for a what?
questions.f: Cirrus clouds really do look like white curls brushed across the high sky.

questions.q: If you 'take a rain check' on a picnic, what are you doing?
c: Politely postponing it for another time
questions.f: The phrase comes from baseball — rained-out fans got a 'rain check' ticket for the next game.

questions.q: Someone feeling 'under the weather' is what?
questions.f: On old ships, seasick sailors were sent below deck — literally under the weather.

questions.q: 'Every cloud has a silver lining' means what?
c: Something good hides in every bad situation
questions.f: The 'lining' is the bright rim you see when sunlight glows behind a dark cloud.

questions.q: To 'weather the storm' means to do what?
questions.f: It is a sailing phrase — a ship that 'weathers' a storm survives it and sails on.

questions.q: The 'snowball effect' describes something that does what?
c: Keeps growing bigger as it goes
questions.f: Like a snowball rolling downhill, gathering more snow — small starts can grow huge.

questions.q: The prefix 'hemi' in 'hemisphere' means what?
questions.f: A hemisphere is half a sphere — the equator slices Earth into northern and southern halves.

questions.q: The root 'aero', as in aeroplane, means what?
questions.f: Greek 'aer' means air — it also floats inside 'aerial' and 'aerobics'.

questions.q: A scientist who studies long-term climate patterns is called a what?
questions.f: Climatologists read clues from tree rings, ice and mud to learn about weather long past.

questions.q: What are 'galoshes'?
questions.f: Galoshes slip on right over your normal shoes to keep them dry.

questions.q: What is a 'cold snap'?
c: A sudden short spell of cold weather
questions.f: A cold snap can drop temperatures overnight — gardeners rush to cover their plants.

questions.q: 'Hydrologic cycle' is the scientific name for which famous cycle?
questions.f: The same water has cycled between sky, sea and land for billions of years.

questions.q: The 'prevailing wind' of a place is what?
c: The direction the wind usually blows from
questions.f: Trees on windy coasts grow bent over, sculpted by the prevailing wind.

questions.q: 'March comes in like a lion and goes out like a lamb' means March begins how?
questions.f: The saying captures March's switch from winter's roar to spring's calm.

questions.q: Travellers who are 'snowbound' are what?
questions.f: The suffix '-bound' means stuck or held — like 'housebound' or 'fogbound'.

questions.q: The suffix '-less' in 'cloudless' and 'windless' means what?
questions.f: A cloudless sky is a sky without clouds — perfect for stargazing.

questions.q: 'Waterlogged' ground is ground that is what?
questions.f: Football matches get cancelled when waterlogged pitches turn to squelching mud.

questions.q: If smoke drifts 'downwind' of a campfire, where is it going?
c: The direction the wind is blowing toward
questions.f: Animals often stay downwind of danger so their scent is not carried toward it.

questions.q: Skiers call fresh, light, fluffy new snow what?
questions.f: Powder snow is full of air, so skis float through it like it is a cloud.

questions.q: A mild spell when winter snow melts for a while is called a what?
questions.f: A 'January thaw' can trick flowers into sprouting weeks too early.

questions.q: What is a 'cloudburst'?
questions.f: A single cloudburst can flood streets in minutes — then stop as suddenly as it began.

questions.q: What do we call the natural process by which plants release water vapour from their leaves?
questions.f: A single big oak can release hundreds of litres of water into the air on a hot day.

questions.q: Why is it colder at the poles than at the equator?
c: Sunlight strikes the poles at a low, slanting angle
The poles are farther from the Sun
questions.f: Slanting rays spread their energy over a wider patch of ground — the same light, thinly buttered.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere sits directly above the one where our weather happens?
questions.f: Airliners often cruise at the bottom of the stratosphere to escape bumpy weather below.

questions.q: What is a 'whiteout'?
c: When blowing snow makes everything look uniformly white
questions.f: In a whiteout, you can lose track of up and down — polar explorers rope themselves together.

questions.q: What causes the sound of a thunderclap to arrive as a long rumble in the mountains?
questions.f: Mountains reflect the sound again and again, stretching one bang into a drumroll.

questions.q: Why does a wet swimsuit feel cold when you step out of the pool on a breezy day?
c: Evaporating water takes heat from your skin
questions.f: That is evaporative cooling — the same trick that makes sweating work.

questions.q: What do we call the process where ice turns straight into water vapour without melting first?
questions.f: That is why a snowbank can shrink on a sunny, freezing day without leaving a puddle.

questions.q: Which weather condition makes flying an aeroplane bumpy?
questions.f: Clear-air turbulence can strike a cloudless sky, which is why seatbelt signs come on suddenly.

questions.q: What is the name for the mixture of gases that surrounds and protects Earth?
questions.f: Air also shields us from most meteors, which burn up long before reaching the ground.

questions.q: Which colour of visible light is scattered the most by air molecules?
questions.f: Scattered blue light bounces around the sky and reaches your eyes from every direction.

questions.q: What happens to air pressure as you climb a mountain?
questions.f: Thinner air is why mountaineers gasp for breath and why crisp packets puff up on planes.

questions.q: Why does water in a kettle boil at a lower temperature on a high mountain?
c: Lower air pressure lets water boil sooner
questions.f: On Everest, water boils at about 70 degrees Celsius — too cool to cook pasta properly.

questions.q: What is the highest mountain on Earth, whose summit reaches into fierce winds?
questions.f: Everest's summit is about 8,849 metres up, where air holds only a third of the usual oxygen.

questions.q: What kind of weather usually follows the arrival of a cold front?
questions.f: A cold front often marches through with a burst of showers, then a fresh, breezy clearance.

questions.q: What is the 'wind chill'?
c: How much colder the wind makes the air feel on your skin
questions.f: Wind strips away the thin layer of warm air hugging your skin, so you feel colder.

questions.q: Which type of rock is worn into strange shapes by desert wind and sand?
questions.f: Wind-carved sandstone arches and towers fill parks like Utah's Arches National Park.

questions.q: Which season do farmers usually plant most of their seeds in cool countries?
questions.f: Spring soil is warming and damp — ideal for germinating seeds.

questions.q: Why do many animals grow thicker fur in autumn?
questions.f: Some, like the Arctic fox, also swap brown coats for white winter camouflage.

questions.q: Why are there few clouds over hot deserts?
c: The air there is too dry for clouds to form
questions.f: Cloudless skies are why desert nights turn surprisingly cold — heat escapes straight to space.

questions.q: What is a 'reservoir' used for during dry spells?
questions.f: When droughts drag on, sunken villages sometimes reappear as reservoir levels drop.

questions.q: Why do cities sometimes flood faster than fields in a heavy storm?
c: Concrete and tarmac cannot absorb the water
questions.f: Rain-gardens and green roofs are now built to soak up city storm water.

questions.q: What is the water table?
c: The level below which the ground is saturated with water
questions.f: Wells must be dug below the water table, which rises and falls with the seasons.

questions.q: Which of these describes 'sea level'?
c: The average height of the ocean surface
The deepest point of the sea
The height of the highest wave
questions.f: Mountain heights, plane altitudes and air pressure are all measured from sea level.

questions.q: What is a 'basin' in weather and geography?
c: A low area where water collects
questions.f: Cold air pools in basins on still nights, so valleys can be frostier than hillsides.

questions.q: Why do many mountain villages get frost when nearby hillsides do not?
c: Cold air sinks and pools in the valley bottom
questions.f: Growers call these dips 'frost hollows' and plant tender fruit trees on slopes instead.

questions.q: What does a rain gauge need to work properly?
c: To sit in the open, away from trees and walls
To be filled with water first
questions.f: A sheltered gauge catches too little rain — position matters as much as the instrument.

questions.q: What are the four main points of a compass?
questions.f: Winds are always named for where they come FROM: a north wind blows from the north.

questions.q: What is 'latitude'?
c: How far north or south of the equator a place is
A place's height above the sea
How far east or west it is
questions.f: Latitude largely decides climate, which is why the tropics stay warm year-round.

questions.q: What causes the seasons to change on Earth?
c: Earth's tilted axis as it orbits the Sun
Earth speeding up and slowing down
questions.f: The tilt stays fixed, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun.

questions.q: What is a 'leap year' for, in terms of Earth and the Sun?
c: Keeping the calendar in step with Earth's orbit
questions.f: Earth's year is about 365.24 days, so we add a day every four years to catch up.

questions.q: Which of these best describes 'condensation trails' behind aircraft?
c: Lines of ice cloud from engine exhaust
questions.f: On busy days, contrails can spread and merge into a thin veil that dims the sunshine.

questions.q: What natural feature makes coastal weather milder than inland weather?
c: The nearby ocean's slow heating and cooling
questions.f: Water needs enormous energy to change temperature, so it steadies the air above it.

questions.q: What is an 'oasis'?
c: A watered, green spot in a desert
questions.f: Oases form where underground water reaches the surface — real palm trees, not illusions.

questions.q: Which of these is a real hazard of hiking in hot weather?
questions.f: Shade, water and rest are the cure — and the best hikers start early to beat the heat.

questions.q: Why do people in very hot countries often wear loose white clothing?
c: White reflects sunlight and loose cloth lets air move
questions.f: Dark clothes soak up more sunlight and can feel noticeably hotter.

questions.q: What does a lightning conductor need to work?
c: A path of metal leading safely into the ground
questions.f: The rod gives the bolt an easy route down, sparing the building's walls.

questions.q: Why should you not shelter under a lone tree during a thunderstorm?
c: Tall isolated objects are more likely to be struck
questions.f: A car with a metal roof is far safer — the shell guides current around the passengers.

questions.q: Which of these gases in the air do plants take in to grow?
questions.f: Plants breathe in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen — the opposite of us.

questions.q: Air weighs something, even though we cannot see it.
questions.f: The air in an average classroom weighs about as much as a grown-up person.

questions.q: A single thunderstorm can contain more energy than many power stations produce in an hour.
questions.f: Storms are enormous heat engines — condensation releases staggering amounts of energy.

questions.q: Fresh water freezes at a higher temperature than salty water.
questions.f: That is why the sea can stay liquid below zero and why salt clears icy paths.

questions.q: Deserts can be found on every continent.
questions.f: Even Europe has semi-desert, and Antarctica is the largest cold desert of all.

questions.q: The higher the humidity, the harder it is for sweat to evaporate.
questions.f: That is why 30 degrees in a damp climate feels far worse than 30 degrees in a dry one.

questions.q: Clouds always form at the same height above the ground.
questions.f: Fog hugs the ground while cirrus floats 10 km up — clouds occupy the whole depth of the sky.

questions.q: Ice can form on an aircraft's wings and change how it flies.
questions.f: That is why planes are sprayed with de-icing fluid on frosty mornings.

questions.q: Water expands when it freezes.
questions.f: That expansion cracks rocks, bursts pipes and makes ice float on ponds.

questions.q: The Moon's gravity is the main cause of ocean tides.
questions.f: The Sun helps too — when both pull together you get especially high spring tides.

questions.q: Weather forecasts have become far more accurate over the last fifty years.
questions.f: A modern five-day forecast is about as reliable as a one-day forecast was in the 1980s.

questions.q: The root 'therm' appears in 'thermos'. What does a thermos flask do?
questions.f: Its double walls with a vacuum between them stop heat travelling either way.

questions.q: The root 'photo' in 'photosynthesis' means what?
questions.f: Photosynthesis is literally 'putting together with light' — the Sun's gift to every leaf.

questions.q: 'Geothermal' energy combines roots meaning what?
questions.f: Iceland heats whole towns with geothermal water bubbling up from volcanic rock.

questions.q: The prefix 'sub' in 'subzero' and 'submarine' means what?
questions.f: Subzero temperatures are below zero — and a submarine travels below the waves.

questions.q: The prefix 'trans' in 'transparent' and 'transport' means what?
questions.f: Transparent things let light travel across them — like clear ice or a windowpane.

questions.q: A 'barometric' reading tells you about what?
questions.f: Falling barometric pressure often gives a few hours' warning of an approaching storm.

questions.q: 'Tropical' comes from a Greek word meaning what — the point where the Sun seems to turn back?
questions.f: 'Tropos' means turning — the Sun reaches the Tropic of Cancer then turns south again.

questions.q: The 'graph' in 'photograph' means to do what?
questions.f: A photograph is literally 'light writing' — the Sun signing its name on film.

questions.q: 'Antarctic' means the opposite of 'Arctic'. Which prefix tells you so?
questions.f: 'Arktos' is Greek for bear — the Arctic is 'the bear', named for the constellation overhead.

questions.q: A 'thermostat' does what in a house?
questions.f: Therm (heat) plus statos (standing) — it makes the heat stand still at your chosen setting.

questions.q: The suffix '-scope' in 'telescope' and 'microscope' means what?
questions.f: A periscope looks around corners, a stethoscope 'looks' at sounds inside your chest.

questions.q: What is an 'isotherm' on a weather map?
c: A line joining places of equal temperature
questions.f: Iso (equal) plus therm (heat) — isotherms bunch together where a front is sharpest.

questions.q: The word 'drizzle' is thought to come from an old word meaning what?
questions.f: Drizzle drops are under half a millimetre — small enough to hang in the air.

questions.q: Which word describes something 'to do with the seasons'?
questions.f: Seasonal winds, seasonal fruit and seasonal jobs all follow the calendar.

questions.q: 'Aquifer', an underground store of water, joins 'aqua' with a root meaning what?
questions.f: Aquifers are natural water carriers in rock — many towns drink from them daily.

questions.q: A 'reservoir' comes from a French word meaning what?
questions.f: Same root as 'reserve' — a reservoir keeps water in reserve for dry months.

questions.q: 'Evaporate' contains the Latin word 'vapor', meaning what?
questions.f: E- means out, so to evaporate is to go out as steam.

questions.q: A 'gauge' is a device that does what?
questions.f: Rain gauges, fuel gauges and pressure gauges all measure — with an unusually tricky spelling.

questions.q: 'Torrent' and 'torrential' share a root meaning what?
questions.f: A mountain torrent after heavy rain can roll boulders along its bed.

questions.q: 'Season's greetings' uses 'season' to mean what?
questions.f: The word does double duty: 'to season' food comes from the same root as ripening in due time.

questions.q: To 'brave the elements' means to face what?
questions.f: The ancient 'elements' were earth, air, fire and water — weather in shorthand.

questions.q: If plans are 'washed out', what has happened?
questions.f: Cricket matches are famously washed out — a whole day lost to rain.

questions.q: Someone described as a 'ray of sunshine' is what?
questions.f: English loves sunny metaphors — a warm welcome, a beaming smile, a bright idea.

questions.q: To 'be on cloud nine' means to feel what?
questions.f: One story links it to cumulonimbus, once ninth in a numbered cloud list — the towering giant.

questions.q: If you 'have your head in the clouds', what are you doing?
questions.f: Its opposite is 'down to earth' — weather words describe personalities too.

questions.q: A 'whirlwind tour' of a city means a visit that is what?
questions.f: The metaphor borrows the spinning speed of a real whirlwind.

questions.q: To 'take the wind out of someone's sails' means to do what?
questions.f: Sailing ships could steal a rival's wind by cutting in front — instant slowdown.

questions.q: A 'sunny disposition' describes what about a person?
questions.f: 'Disposition' means your usual mood — so a sunny one shines most days.

questions.q: To 'save for a rainy day' means to do what?
c: Put money aside for hard times
questions.f: For farmers and market traders, a rainy day literally meant no earnings.

questions.q: What does 'the tip of the iceberg' describe?
c: A small visible part of a much bigger problem
questions.f: About 90 percent of an iceberg hides below the waterline — hence the phrase.

questions.q: A person with a 'stormy temper' is what?
questions.f: Temperature and temper share a Latin root — both are about balance and mixture.

questions.q: To 'break the ice' at a party means to do what?
c: Ease the awkwardness and get people talking
questions.f: Ice-breaking ships smash a channel for others to follow — a perfect metaphor.

questions.q: If someone gives you 'the cold shoulder', what are they doing?
questions.f: Cold in English almost always signals distance — a chilly reply, an icy glare.

questions.q: A situation described as 'a perfect storm' means what?
c: Several bad things happening at once
questions.f: The phrase became famous after a 1991 Atlantic storm formed from three merging systems.

questions.q: What is a 'weather eye', as in 'keep a weather eye on it'?
questions.f: Sailors kept one eye on the windward horizon, where the next squall would appear.

questions.q: 'Chasing rainbows' means doing what?
questions.f: A rainbow always moves as you move — you can never actually reach it.

questions.q: 'A storm in a teacup' describes what?
c: A big fuss over something small
questions.f: Americans say 'a tempest in a teapot' — same idea, different crockery.

questions.q: To 'go with the flow' borrows its image from what?
questions.f: Weather and water fill our language — we also 'drift', 'freeze up' and 'blow hot and cold'.

questions.q: What is a 'sunbelt' region?
c: A warm, sunny part of a country
questions.f: America's Sun Belt stretches across its southern states, drawing millions of new residents.

questions.q: 'Frostbitten' fingers have been harmed by what?
questions.f: '-bitten' is a vivid old suffix — the cold is imagined as taking a bite.

questions.q: What is 'hail' called in the plural when you count each piece?
