questions.f: Most hailstones are pea-sized, but the biggest on record weighed nearly a kilogram.

questions.q: Which word correctly names a scientist who studies earthquakes, not weather?
questions.f: Greek 'seismos' means shaking — a useful word to keep separate from weather science.

questions.q: What is a 'microclimate'?
c: The special climate of a very small area
A climate that lasts a minute
questions.f: A south-facing garden wall can create a microclimate warm enough to ripen grapes.

questions.q: What does 'nocturnal' mean, as in nocturnal fog?
questions.f: Latin 'nox' means night — its daytime opposite is 'diurnal'.

questions.q: What is a 'squall line'?
c: A long row of thunderstorms travelling together
questions.f: Squall lines can stretch for hundreds of kilometres and arrive with a sudden wind shift.

questions.q: 'Torrid' weather is what?
questions.f: Old geographers called the tropics the 'torrid zone' — the burning belt of the world.

questions.q: 'Bleak' describes weather that is what?
questions.f: Charles Dickens chose the word for 'Bleak House' — instant atmosphere in one syllable.

questions.q: 'Inclement' weather means weather that is what?
questions.f: Its opposite, 'clement', means mild — the same root as the name Clementine.

questions.q: What are the 'dog days' of summer?
c: The hottest, stickiest days of the year
questions.f: Romans linked the heat to Sirius, the Dog Star, rising with the Sun in late summer.

questions.q: What does the word 'monsoonal' describe?
questions.f: Adding '-al' turns a noun into a describing word: seasonal, coastal, monsoonal.

questions.q: 'Sultry' weather is best described as what?
questions.f: 'Sultry' comes from an old form of 'swelter' — heat you can almost drink.

questions.q: What does 'crisp' mean when describing an autumn morning?
questions.f: Crisp air often follows a night of clear skies and light frost.

questions.q: What is a 'brolly' in British English?
questions.f: Shortened from 'umbrella' — English loves to trim long words down to friendly ones.

questions.q: An Irish hydrographer in the Royal Navy devised a 0-to-12 ladder for wind, from mirror-calm sea to hurricane. His name is on which scale?
questions.f: Francis Beaufort's 1805 scale let sailors judge wind from the look of the waves alone.

questions.q: A pupil of Galileo filled a glass tube with mercury in 1643 and accidentally invented which weather instrument?
questions.f: Evangelista Torricelli's mercury column rose and fell with air pressure — forecasting was born.

questions.q: The temperature scale with 0 for freezing and 100 for boiling is named after an astronomer from which country?
questions.f: Anders Celsius of Uppsala proposed it in 1742 — oddly, with the numbers running the other way.

questions.q: Which temperature scale begins at absolute zero and therefore has no negative numbers?
questions.f: Zero kelvin is about minus 273 degrees Celsius — the coldest anything can possibly be.

questions.q: Hurricane strength categories 1 to 5 come from which two-name scale?
questions.f: Engineer Herbert Saffir and meteorologist Robert Simpson created it around 1970.

questions.q: The dry area on the sheltered side of a mountain range, where rain rarely reaches, is called a what?
questions.f: Rising air rains out on the windward slopes, leaving deserts like Death Valley in the shadow.

questions.q: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water starts condensing out is called the what?
questions.f: When the dew point is high, the air feels tropical — sweat simply will not dry.

questions.q: An 'anticyclone' — a large area of sinking, high-pressure air — usually brings what weather?
questions.f: Summer anticyclones can park for weeks, bringing heat waves and cloudless skies.

questions.q: Seen from above, hurricanes in the Northern Hemisphere spin in which direction?
questions.f: Earth's rotation deflects the winds — south of the equator the same storms spin clockwise.

questions.q: The dome of seawater that a hurricane's winds push ashore is called the storm what?
questions.f: Storm surge, not wind, is often a hurricane's most dangerous weapon on the coast.

questions.q: What happens to a hurricane's name after the storm proves especially destructive?
c: It is retired from the lists forever
It is given to the next storm
It moves to the typhoon list
questions.f: Names like Katrina and Sandy will never be used for a storm again.

questions.q: The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June until the end of which month?
questions.f: Late summer's warm ocean water makes September the stormiest month of all.

questions.q: 'Hurricane hunters' are pilots who do what?
c: Fly aircraft straight into hurricanes to measure them
questions.f: Their planes punch through the eyewall into the calm eye — bumpy science at its bravest.

questions.q: El Nino has a cool opposite phase. What is it called?
questions.f: La Nina means 'the little girl' — it cools the tropical Pacific and reshuffles world weather.

questions.q: Smooth, lens-shaped clouds that hover over mountains are often mistaken for what?
questions.f: Lenticular clouds stay eerily still while wind flows through them like water over a stone.

questions.q: A mature thunderstorm's flat, spreading top is named after which blacksmith's tool?
questions.f: The rising air smashes into the stratosphere and flattens sideways into the anvil shape.

questions.q: What is 'thundersnow'?
c: A snowstorm with thunder and lightning
questions.f: It is rare because winter clouds are shallow — snow also muffles the thunder to a soft boom.

questions.q: 'Heat lightning' flickering silently on a summer horizon is really what?
c: A distant storm too far away to hear
questions.f: Thunder rarely carries more than about 15 kilometres — the flash outruns the sound.

questions.q: About how many lightning flashes strike somewhere on Earth every single second?
questions.f: That adds up to several million flashes a day, day and night, all year round.

questions.q: In polar cold, ice crystals can glitter in mid-air like floating sparkles. This is called what?
questions.f: Diamond dust can fall from a completely clear blue sky at far-below-freezing temperatures.

questions.q: The two bright spots that sometimes flank the low Sun on icy days are nicknamed what?
questions.f: Sun dogs 'follow' the Sun like loyal dogs — plate-shaped ice crystals bend the light.

questions.q: In a double rainbow, how do the colours of the second, fainter bow run?
questions.f: Light bounces twice inside each raindrop for the second bow, flipping red to the inside.

questions.q: The 'midnight sun' is a summer phenomenon in polar lands where the Sun does what?
questions.f: In far-north towns you can read a book outdoors at midnight under full sunshine.

questions.q: The Southern Hemisphere's answer to the northern lights is called aurora what?
questions.f: 'Australis' simply means southern — penguins get their own light show.

questions.q: A 'blue moon' is most commonly defined as what?
c: The second full moon in one calendar month
The closest moon of the year
questions.f: It happens only every two to three years — hence 'once in a blue moon' for something rare.

questions.q: Which famous meteor shower streaks across northern skies every August?
questions.f: The Perseids are dust from comet Swift-Tuttle burning up at 59 kilometres per second.

questions.q: 'Earthshine' is the faint glow that lets you see what?
c: The dark part of a crescent moon
questions.f: It is sunlight bouncing off Earth onto the Moon — Leonardo da Vinci explained it 500 years ago.

questions.q: Why do sunsets glow red and orange?
c: Sunlight crosses so much air that blue light scatters away
The Sun cools and reddens each evening
Dust burns in the evening air
Clouds soak up the blue light
questions.f: The longer path strips out the blues, letting the leftover reds flood the horizon.

questions.q: Stars twinkle when we watch them from Earth because of what?
questions.f: Above the atmosphere, telescopes like Hubble see stars shining perfectly steadily.

questions.q: Which planet, wrapped in thick carbon-dioxide clouds, is the hottest in the solar system?
questions.f: Venus's runaway greenhouse effect bakes its surface to about 460 degrees Celsius — hot enough to melt lead.

questions.q: Earth's axis is tilted by about how many degrees — the tilt that gives us seasons?
questions.f: No tilt would mean no seasons — every day everywhere would feel roughly the same.

questions.q: Ground that stays frozen year after year, found under Arctic lands, is called what?
questions.f: Some Siberian permafrost has stayed frozen since the age of the mammoths.

questions.q: Every cloud droplet needs a tiny floating speck — dust, salt or smoke — to form around. These specks are called what?
questions.f: No specks, no clouds — even sea salt tossed up by waves helps build the sky.

questions.q: The instrument package that dangles beneath a rising weather balloon, radioing back data, is a what?
questions.f: 'Sonde' is French for probe — each flight measures temperature, humidity and pressure up to 30 km.

questions.q: Which radar, named after an Austrian physicist, lets forecasters see wind and rain moving inside storms?
questions.f: Christian Doppler described in 1842 how waves shift with motion — the trick behind storm radar and speed cameras.

questions.q: A hygrometer is the instrument that measures what?
questions.f: Early hygrometers used a strand of human hair, which stretches as the air gets damper.

questions.q: The powerful winter storms that batter America's east coast are called nor'easters because of what?
c: Their winds blow from the northeast
Sailors from the north named them
questions.f: A nor'easter's counterclockwise swirl drags ocean air ashore from the northeast.

questions.q: The gigantic whirl of frigid air that circles high above each pole is called the polar what?
questions.f: When the polar vortex wobbles, lobes of Arctic air can spill south and freeze whole countries.

questions.q: The 'heat index' tells how hot it really feels by combining temperature with what?
questions.f: At high humidity, 32 degrees can feel like 40 — sweat stops cooling you when air is already damp.

questions.q: Crowds gather at Stonehenge every June to watch the sunrise line up on which day?
questions.f: The 4,500-year-old stones frame the solstice sunrise — Stone Age sky science.

questions.q: The scientific unit of pressure, used for air pressure, is named after which French thinker?
questions.f: Pascal had a barometer carried up a mountain in 1648, proving air grows thinner with height.

questions.q: Which gas, released by burning coal and oil, traps extra heat in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.f: Scientists read Antarctic ice bubbles to compare today's carbon dioxide with air from 800,000 years ago.

questions.q: 'Cloud seeding', used to coax rain from clouds, sprinkles them with crystals of what?
questions.f: Discovered in 1946, the crystals mimic ice, giving droplets something to freeze onto.

questions.q: In some fog-drenched deserts, people harvest drinking water using giant what?
c: Mesh nets that catch fog droplets
questions.f: In Morocco and Chile, fog nets on ridges collect thousands of litres from passing clouds.

questions.q: Fresh snow is a surprisingly good insulator because it is mostly made of what?
questions.f: Up to 95 percent of fresh snow is air — the secret behind warm igloos and safe snow dens.

questions.q: Why do distant hills look extra sharp and clear right after a rainstorm?
c: Rain has washed dust and haze out of the air
questions.f: Raindrops sweep floating dust to the ground, leaving the air rinsed clean like a window.

questions.q: Deep glacier ice glows blue because the ice does what?
c: Absorbs red light and reflects blue
questions.f: Ancient, air-squeezed ice swallows the red end of the spectrum — only the blue escapes to your eye.

questions.q: The famous 'hole' in the ozone layer opens each spring over which region?
questions.f: Discovered in 1985, it shocked the world into banning ozone-eating chemicals within two years.

questions.q: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January, during the northern winter.
questions.f: Seasons come from Earth's tilt, not distance — January's Earth is 5 million km nearer the Sun than July's.

questions.q: The white cloud above a boiling kettle is liquid water droplets, not water vapour.
questions.f: True water vapour is invisible — the visible puff is vapour that has already condensed back to droplets.

questions.q: Pine cones open their scales in dry weather and close them up in damp air.
questions.f: The scales bend as they absorb moisture — people once hung pine cones as natural weather gauges.

questions.q: Some weather satellites hover over one fixed spot on Earth all day long.
questions.f: Geostationary satellites orbit exactly as fast as Earth spins, 36,000 km up, staring at one hemisphere.

questions.q: Hurricanes usually weaken quickly once they move over land.
questions.f: Cut off from warm ocean water — their fuel — hurricanes wind down like unplugged machines.

questions.q: Dew forms most heavily on clear, calm nights.
questions.f: With no clouds to trap heat and no wind to stir the air, the ground cools fast and moisture settles out.

questions.q: The winds of the jet stream regularly rake the summit of Mount Everest.
questions.f: Everest pokes into jet-stream heights — climbers wait for brief windows when the ferocious winds lift.

questions.q: You can estimate the temperature on a summer night by counting cricket chirps.
questions.f: Dolbear's law, published in 1897: chirps in 14 seconds plus 40 roughly equals degrees Fahrenheit.

questions.q: The phase of the Moon decides whether or not it will rain tomorrow.
questions.f: The Moon rules tides, but careful studies find no meaningful lunar control over daily rain.

questions.q: 'Solstice' is built from Latin words meaning the Sun does what?
questions.f: From sol + sistere — for a few days the sunrise point pauses before drifting back along the horizon.

questions.q: 'Monsoon' comes from an Arabic word, 'mawsim', meaning what?
questions.f: Arab sailors timed their Indian Ocean voyages by these faithfully reversing seasonal winds.

questions.q: The word 'hurricane' traces back to Huracan, who was what in Caribbean and Maya belief?
questions.f: Spanish sailors borrowed the name from the Taino people in the 1500s.

questions.q: The puffy-cloud name 'cumulus' is Latin for what?
questions.f: 'Accumulate' shares the root — cumulus clouds are literally heaps of rising air.

questions.q: 'Precipitation' comes from a Latin verb meaning to do what?
questions.f: Praecipitare meant plunging from a height — exactly what rain, hail and snow do.

questions.q: 'Atmosphere' is built from the Greek word 'atmos', meaning what?
questions.f: Atmos + sphaira: a 'ball of vapour' — a surprisingly accurate name for our planet's airy shell.

questions.q: The root 'baro' in 'barometer' means what?
questions.f: From Greek 'baros' — a barometer literally weighs the column of air pressing down on it.

questions.q: 'Vernal', as in the vernal equinox, refers to which season?
questions.f: Latin 'ver' means spring — vernal ponds are pools that appear only in springtime.

questions.q: The Latin root 'hibernus', hiding inside 'hibernate', means what?
questions.f: Romans called winter quarters hiberna — and they punned on it when they Latinised Ireland's name as Hibernia.

questions.q: The Greek root 'bronto', found in Brontosaurus, means what?
questions.f: Brontosaurus is the 'thunder lizard' — and brontophobia is a fear of thunder.

questions.q: The Latin root 'pluvia', found in 'pluviometer', means what?
questions.f: A pluviometer is just a rain gauge in fancy dress — Spanish still says 'lluvia' for rain.

questions.q: A nephologist is a scientist devoted to studying what?
questions.f: Greek 'nephos' means cloud — Victorian nephologists sketched clouds from hilltops for hours.

questions.q: The Latin root 'glacies', behind 'glacier' and 'glacial', means what?
questions.f: A 'glacial pace' means moving as slowly as ice — some glaciers manage mere centimetres a day.

questions.q: 'Nebulous', meaning vague or unclear, comes from the Latin word 'nebula' for what?
questions.f: Astronomers still call fuzzy clouds of space gas 'nebulae' — clouds among the stars.

questions.q: Taken literally, the word 'parasol' means what?
questions.f: Para- (ward off) + sol (sun) — its rainy cousin, the French parapluie, wards off rain.

questions.q: 'Torrential' rain is rain that falls how?
questions.f: From Latin 'torrens', a rushing stream — a torrential downpour turns roads into rivers.

questions.q: A 'deluge' is what?
questions.f: From Latin 'diluvium', the great flood — you can also face a deluge of homework.

questions.q: A 'zephyr' is what kind of wind?
questions.f: Zephyrus was the Greek god of the mild west wind, herald of spring.

questions.q: The sirocco is a hot, dust-laden wind that blows from the Sahara toward where?
questions.f: A strong sirocco can dust Italian cars pink with Saharan sand — desert mail, airborne.

questions.q: In 'aurora borealis', the word 'borealis' means what?
questions.f: Boreas was the Greek god of the north wind — so the name means 'northern dawn'.

questions.q: Thursday is named after Thor, the Norse god of what?
questions.f: 'Thor's day' became Thursday — in German it is Donnerstag, literally 'thunder day'.

questions.q: On a weather map, an isobar is a line connecting places with equal what?
questions.f: Iso means equal, baros means weight — tightly packed isobars warn of strong winds.

questions.q: A 'sou'wester' is a famous piece of foul-weather gear. What is it?
questions.f: Its long back brim sends rain down your coat instead of down your neck.

questions.q: 'Corona', the name for the Sun's wispy halo seen during a total eclipse, is Latin for what?
questions.f: The pearly corona is the Sun's outer atmosphere — visible only when the Moon hides the glare.

questions.q: The word 'contrail', for a jet's white sky-line, is short for what?
questions.f: Jet exhaust moisture freezes instantly in the cold thin air, drawing a line of ice-cloud.

questions.q: On a ship or an island, the sheltered side facing away from the wind is called the what?
questions.f: Hawaii's leeward coasts are sunny and dry while windward slopes catch rain almost daily.

questions.q: Sailors dreaded the windless equatorial belt where ships could drift for weeks. Its name?
questions.f: 'Stuck in the doldrums' now describes any gloomy, stalled mood — straight from sailing days.

questions.q: The flat, blanket-like cloud name 'stratus' is Latin for what?
questions.f: The same root builds 'stratum' and 'strategy' — things laid out in layers or plans.

questions.q: A 'maritime' climate is a climate shaped mainly by what?
questions.f: Oceans heat and cool slowly, so maritime lands like Britain get mild winters and cool summers.

questions.q: Words like 'fahrenheit', 'pascal' and 'beaufort', coined from people's names, are called what?
questions.f: Weather science is packed with eponyms — a hall of fame hidden in its vocabulary.

questions.q: In cloud names like 'altocumulus', the prefix 'alto-' marks clouds at what height?
c: The very top of the sky
questions.f: From Latin 'altus' (high) — though in cloud science the alto- family floats in the middle storey.

questions.q: If guests get a 'frosty reception', how are they welcomed?
questions.f: English borrows temperature for feelings — a warm welcome, an icy stare, a heated argument.

questions.q: A 'tempestuous' friendship is one that is what?
questions.f: From 'tempest' — Latin 'tempestas' meant both weather and storm, fair or foul.

questions.q: 'Equator' comes from the Latin 'aequus', meaning what?
questions.f: The equator is the line that divides — equates — Earth into two equal halves.

questions.q: A 'lull' in a storm is what?
c: A quiet pause before it resumes
questions.f: The word may echo 'lullaby' — both hush things down, at least for a while.

questions.q: When a gale finally 'abates', what does it do?
questions.f: From Old French 'abattre', to beat down — storms, fevers and floods can all abate.

questions.q: The southern line where the noon Sun can stand directly overhead is the Tropic of what?
questions.f: It was named for the constellation the Sun occupied at the December solstice 2,000 years ago.

questions.q: The Arctic Circle marks the southern limit of what?
c: Places with at least one 24-hour day and night each year
questions.f: Stand north of it in June and the Sun simply circles the sky without setting.

questions.q: On an equinox, the Sun rises almost exactly due east from anywhere on Earth. Why?
c: The Sun is directly over the equator that day
questions.f: Architects use equinox sunrises to align buildings — an ancient trick still checked with a compass.

questions.q: Tropical cyclones generally need ocean water warmer than about what temperature to form?
questions.f: Below that threshold the sea cannot pump up enough warm, moist air to keep the engine running.

questions.q: The fastest wind ever measured on Earth, about 484 km/h, was clocked inside what?
questions.f: Mobile Doppler radar caught it near Bridge Creek, Oklahoma in 1999 — no instrument could survive there.

questions.q: 'Tornado Alley' is the nickname for a storm-prone stretch of which region?
c: The central plains of the United States
questions.f: Dry air off the Rockies rides over moist Gulf air there — a recipe for spinning storms.

questions.q: 'Lake-effect snow' happens when cold air crosses what?
questions.f: Buffalo, New York can be buried under a metre of lake-effect snow while nearby towns stay clear.

questions.q: Which is the key difference between freezing rain and sleet?
c: Freezing rain lands as liquid then freezes on contact
Freezing rain falls only at night
questions.f: That is why freezing rain glazes every branch in glass while sleet just rattles off the pavement.

questions.q: 'Snow water equivalent' tells scientists what?
c: How much water a snowpack would make if melted
questions.f: Western US states plan their whole summer water supply from spring snow-water measurements.

questions.q: Which type of fog forms when warm, moist air drifts over a cold surface?
questions.f: San Francisco's famous summer fog is advection fog rolling off a chilly ocean current.

questions.q: Radiation fog forms in which conditions?
c: Clear, calm nights when the ground cools quickly
questions.f: It usually burns off by mid-morning as the Sun warms the ground back up.

questions.q: A neat circular gap in a thin cloud layer, sometimes mistaken for a UFO trace, is called a fallstreak what?
questions.f: A passing aircraft can trigger the cloud's droplets to freeze and fall, punching a hole clean through.

questions.q: A menacing, low, wedge-shaped cloud that races out ahead of a thunderstorm's gust front is called a what cloud?
questions.f: It looks like the storm's plough — dramatic to photograph, and a signal to get indoors.

questions.q: Storm spotters watch for a lowered, rotating 'wall cloud' because it may signal what?
questions.f: It hangs beneath the storm's rain-free base, right where the updraft is spinning hardest.

questions.q: On radar, forecasters watch for a curled 'hook echo' because it suggests what?
c: Rotation that may produce a tornado
questions.f: The hook is rain wrapping around the storm's spinning core — a warning sign since the 1950s.

questions.q: Weather radar detects rain by bouncing radio waves off what?
c: Raindrops and ice in the cloud
questions.f: Bigger drops bounce back more signal, which is how radar maps rainfall intensity in colour.

questions.q: What is the difference between a tornado watch and a tornado warning?
c: A watch means conditions are possible; a warning means one is happening or imminent
questions.f: Watch means be ready, warning means take shelter now — the wording saves lives.

questions.q: A network of drifting ocean buoys reports sea temperatures and waves back to forecasters. Buoys matter because they cover what?
c: Vast ocean areas with no land stations
questions.f: Ocean data was so scarce before buoys and satellites that many storms arrived unannounced.

questions.q: 'Albedo' measures a surface's ability to do what?
questions.f: Fresh snow reflects up to 90 percent of sunlight; dark ocean reflects less than 10.

questions.q: Melting sea ice can speed up warming because dark water does what compared with ice?
questions.f: Scientists call this a feedback loop — the change nudges itself along.

questions.q: What is the key difference between sea ice and an iceberg?
c: Sea ice is frozen seawater; icebergs break off glaciers
questions.f: That is why melting sea ice barely raises sea level, but melting land ice does.

questions.q: When a chunk of glacier cracks off into the sea, the process is called what?
questions.f: Watching a glacier calve is thunderous — a wall of ice collapsing into the water.

questions.q: The 'treeline' on a mountain marks the altitude above which what happens?
questions.f: Cold, wind and short growing seasons stunt the last trees into twisted, knee-high shrubs.

questions.q: Cyclones in the North Indian Ocean, hurricanes in the Atlantic — what are the same storms called in the northwest Pacific?
questions.f: One physics, three passports: the name depends purely on which ocean the storm is born in.

questions.q: Which gas, released by wetlands, livestock and leaks, traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide?
questions.f: Methane does not last as long in the air, which is why cutting it cools things comparatively fast.

questions.q: 'Acid rain', which damaged forests and lakes in the 20th century, was caused mainly by what?
c: Sulphur and nitrogen gases from burning fuel
questions.f: Cleaner power stations and catalytic converters have cut it dramatically since the 1980s.

questions.q: Ozone is helpful high in the stratosphere but harmful near the ground, where it is part of what?
questions.f: Los Angeles pioneered ozone alerts — sunlight cooking traffic fumes creates it on hot afternoons.

questions.q: The eruption of Mount Pinatubo in 1991 cooled global temperatures for about two years because it injected what?
questions.f: A veil of tiny droplets reflected sunlight back to space — natural sunshade, roughly half a degree of cooling.

questions.q: The deadliest hurricane in United States history struck which Texas island city in 1900?
questions.f: Afterwards the whole city was raised on fill and shielded by a seawall — engineering born of tragedy.

questions.q: The Great Blizzard of March 1888 paralysed which region, hastening the move to put its wires underground?
questions.f: Snowdrifts buried New York City to second-storey windows — and buried the overhead telegraph tangle for good.

questions.q: Jet stream winds commonly blow at speeds of roughly what?
questions.f: That is why a flight from New York to London can arrive an hour earlier than the return trip.

questions.q: Why do aircraft take off and land into the wind whenever possible?
c: Headwind gives extra lift at lower ground speed
It saves fuel on the runway
questions.f: That is why big airports build their runways lined up with the prevailing wind.

questions.q: Why do very cold regions use alcohol thermometers rather than mercury ones?
c: Mercury freezes at about minus 39 degrees Celsius
questions.f: Dyed alcohol keeps flowing far below that, which is why polar thermometers are usually red.

questions.q: Infrared satellite images of clouds are especially useful because they can be taken when?
c: At night as well as by day
questions.f: Infrared senses temperature, so the coldest, highest storm tops glow brightest in the pictures.

questions.q: Air pressure is sometimes reported in 'inches of mercury'. A typical sea-level reading is about what?
questions.f: The unit is a fossil of Torricelli's tube — 30 inches of mercury balanced against the whole atmosphere.

questions.q: A 'wind rose' diagram shows what at a glance?
c: How often the wind blows from each direction
questions.f: Airport planners and wind-farm engineers both live by these petal-shaped charts.

questions.q: 'Alpenglow' is the rosy light seen on mountain peaks when?
c: Just after sunset or before sunrise
questions.f: The Sun has already set for the valley below, but its reddened light still reaches the summits.

questions.q: The pink band that hovers above your own shadow on the horizon after sunset is nicknamed the Belt of what?
questions.f: Beneath it lies the bluish shadow of the Earth itself, creeping up the sky as night falls.

questions.q: Photographers prize the 'blue hour'. When is it?
c: The deep-blue twilight just before sunrise or after sunset
questions.f: City lights and residual sky-blue balance perfectly for those few minutes — hence the name.

questions.q: In sky vocabulary, the 'zenith' is which point?
questions.f: Its opposite, straight down beneath your feet, is the nadir — both words came into English from Arabic.

questions.q: Why is solar noon usually not at exactly 12:00 on the clock?
c: Clock time uses wide standard time zones, and Earth's orbit is not a perfect circle
questions.f: Sundials and clocks can disagree by a quarter of an hour — the 'equation of time'.

questions.q: Aphelion is the point in Earth's orbit where our planet is what?
questions.f: Earth reaches aphelion in early July — northern summer happens despite being farther away.

questions.q: Slow changes in Earth's tilt, orbit shape and wobble that help pace ice ages are named after a Serbian scientist. They are called what cycles?
questions.f: Milutin Milankovitch calculated them by hand while interned during World War I.

questions.q: Which idea did William Willett campaign for in 1907 so people could enjoy more evening light?
questions.f: Britain adopted his clock-shifting scheme in 1916 — a golfer's annoyance turned national policy.

questions.q: In 1666 a young Isaac Newton used a prism in a darkened room to prove what about sunlight?
c: It is a mixture of all the colours
questions.f: He then recombined the colours back into white light — the experiment behind every rainbow explanation.

questions.q: When sunlight passes through a raindrop, which colour is bent the most?
questions.f: Because violet bends most, it ends up on the rainbow's inner edge and red on the outside.

questions.q: The United States national weather service began in 1870 under which unlikely department?
questions.f: Soldiers telegraphed observations across the country — storm warnings were a military mission first.

questions.q: World Meteorological Day is marked each March 23 by which global organisation?
questions.f: It grew out of an 1873 congress in Vienna, when nations agreed to share weather data freely.

questions.q: The '30-30 rule' for lightning safety says you should go inside if thunder follows the flash within how long?
questions.f: And wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before heading back out — the second 30.

questions.q: Which flat, featureless grey cloud sheet often thickens through the day before steady rain arrives?
questions.f: Nimbostratus can rain gently for many hours — no drama, just a soaked afternoon.

questions.q: A thin, milky-white cloud veil that turns the Sun watery and often carries a halo is called what?
questions.f: It usually rides in about a day ahead of a warm front, an early warning written in ice crystals.

questions.q: Meteorologists call the boundary at the top of the weather layer the 'tropopause'. Above it, temperature does what?
c: Stops falling and begins to rise
questions.f: That warming lid is why thunderstorm tops flatten out instead of climbing forever.

questions.q: The average drop in air temperature with height in the lower atmosphere is called the what rate?
questions.f: It averages about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre — the reason mountaintops wear snow in summer.

questions.q: 'Convection' comes from a Latin verb meaning what — describing how heat rides upward in the air?
questions.f: Convection puffs up every fair-weather cumulus cloud and every towering thunderhead.

questions.q: 'Latent heat' is called latent — meaning hidden — because it does what?
c: Changes water between states without changing its temperature
questions.f: That hidden heat, released when vapour condenses, is the fuel that powers hurricanes.

questions.q: An 'adiabatic' temperature change in rising air happens without what?
c: Any heat entering or leaving the air parcel
questions.f: Greek for 'not passable' — rising air cools simply because it expands, no heat needed.

questions.q: An 'anabatic' wind is one that does what during the day?
c: Blows up a warming mountain slope
Sinks into the valley at night
questions.f: Greek 'anabasis' means going up — its downhill night-time partner is the katabatic wind.

questions.q: 'Saturated' air is air that is what?
c: Holding all the water vapour it can at that temperature
questions.f: From Latin 'satur', full — the same root as 'satisfy'. Cool saturated air and clouds appear.

questions.q: 'Condense' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Condensed milk and condensing vapour share the idea: squeeze the same stuff into less space.

questions.q: When forecasters say a shower will 'dissipate', they mean it will do what?
questions.f: From Latin 'dissipare', to scatter — the same root as a 'dissipated' fortune.

questions.q: 'Precipitation' and 'precipice' share a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: Both come from 'praeceps' — head-first. Rain and cliffs are relatives in the dictionary.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'weathering' and 'erosion'?
c: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion carries the pieces away
questions.f: Frost, heat and rain do the weathering; rivers, wind and glaciers do the hauling.

questions.q: 'Boreal', as in the boreal forest ringing the Arctic, means what?
questions.f: From Boreas, the Greek north wind — the boreal forest is the largest land biome on Earth.

questions.q: The word 'meridian' comes from Latin words meaning what?
questions.f: 'Medius dies' — the Sun crosses your meridian at local noon, which is where a.m. and p.m. come from.

questions.q: The abbreviation 'a.m.' stands for a Latin phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Ante meridiem and post meridiem — noon itself is technically neither.

questions.q: 'Circadian', describing your body's daily rhythm, is built from Latin words meaning what?
questions.f: Circa (about) plus dies (day) — daylight resets the clock inside almost every living thing.

questions.q: 'Perihelion' contains the Greek word 'helios', meaning what?
questions.f: Helium was named after helios because it was spotted in the Sun's spectrum before being found on Earth.

questions.q: A 'heliocentric' model of the solar system places what at the centre?
questions.f: Copernicus published the idea in 1543 — and our seasons finally made proper sense.

questions.q: 'Photovoltaic' panels combine roots meaning what?
questions.f: Photo (light) plus volt, for Alessandro Volta — the word carries a scientist's name inside it.

questions.q: A 'pyranometer' measures incoming sunshine. The root 'pyr' means what?
questions.f: The same root heats up 'pyre' and 'pyrotechnics' — and 'ano' here points at the sky above.

questions.q: The 'hygro' in 'hygrometer' means what?
questions.f: Not to be confused with 'hydro' (water) — hygrometers measure dampness in the air, not liquid.

questions.q: The Latin word 'incus', used for a thunderstorm's flat top, means what?
questions.f: Cumulonimbus incus is the official name for a storm that has spread out into an anvil.

questions.q: Clouds labelled 'castellanus' get their name because their tops look like what?
questions.f: Castellanus turrets in the morning sky warn that the air is unstable — storms may follow by afternoon.

questions.q: 'Cumulonimbus' is built from two cloud words meaning what?
questions.f: Luke Howard's naming system lets you read a cloud's behaviour straight out of its Latin label.

questions.q: The word 'avalanche' entered English from Alpine French, from a verb meaning what?
questions.f: Alpine guides had the vocabulary long before scientists did — the mountains taught the words.

questions.q: 'Typhoon' has a tangled history, but is usually linked to a Chinese term meaning what?
questions.f: Greek myth's monster Typhon may have shaped the English spelling — two languages, one storm.

questions.q: The word 'icicle' is a curious doubling: the old English part 'gicel' already meant what?
questions.f: So an icicle is literally an 'ice-icicle' — English quietly said the same thing twice.

questions.q: The archaic word 'welkin', as in 'the welkin rang', means what?
questions.f: It is a cousin of the German 'Wolke', cloud — the sky was once named for what filled it.

questions.q: 'Firmament', a grand old word for the sky, carries the sense of what?
questions.f: Ancient writers pictured a solid dome overhead — the word froze that idea into the language.

questions.q: The colour word 'azure', used for a clear sky, traces back to the name of which blue stone?
questions.f: Traders' tongues dropped the first letter of 'lazuli' — a spelling accident that gave us azure.

questions.q: 'Cerulean' blue takes its name from the Latin word 'caelum', meaning what?
questions.f: The same root gives 'celestial' — a whole family of words born from looking up.

questions.q: 'Vespertine' describes something belonging to which part of the day?
questions.f: Vespers are evening prayers, and Venus as the evening star was once called Vesper.

questions.q: 'Matutinal' describes something belonging to which part of the day?
questions.f: Matins are morning prayers — its evening twin is vespertine.

questions.q: A 'weathercock' on a church spire is really what?
c: A weather vane shaped like a rooster
A bell that rings in storms
questions.f: A 9th-century papal decree is said to have put roosters on churches — weather science by way of poultry.

questions.q: A 'windfall' originally meant what?
c: Fruit or wood blown down by the wind
questions.f: Commoners could gather what the wind knocked down — free fruit became the word for unexpected luck.

questions.q: Sunday and Monday are named after which two things?
questions.f: Saturday keeps Saturn, while Tuesday to Friday belong to Norse gods — the week is a sky map.

questions.q: A 'draught' (or draft) of cold air in a house means what?
c: A current of air flowing through
questions.f: The word comes from 'draw' — a draught is air being drawn through a gap.

questions.q: 'Empyrean', a poetic name for the highest heaven, comes from a Greek root meaning what?
questions.f: Ancient thinkers imagined the topmost sky as pure fire — the same 'pyr' as in pyre.

questions.q: An old rhyme warns: 'Rainbow in the morning, shepherds take ____.' What word completes it?
questions.f: A morning rainbow sits in the west, where weather usually comes from — folklore with real physics.

questions.q: 'Ring around the moon, rain or snow soon' has some truth because a lunar halo means what?
c: High ice clouds are moving in ahead of a front
The Moon is closer than usual
questions.f: Cirrostratus often runs a day ahead of rain — the folklore was reading a genuine signal.

questions.q: Why is the saying 'red sky at night, sailor's delight' often reliable in mid-latitudes?
c: Clear western skies at sunset mean fair weather is heading your way
questions.f: Weather generally travels west to east there, so you are seeing tomorrow arriving.

questions.q: A metal car body helps protect passengers from lightning by carrying the current around the outside.
questions.f: It acts as a Faraday cage — the shell, not the rubber tyres, is what keeps you safe.

questions.q: Snow that looks pristine white can still contain traces of dust carried from thousands of kilometres away.
questions.f: Every flake formed around a speck — glaciologists identify Saharan and volcanic dust in polar layers.

questions.q: A hurricane's winds are strongest at its exact centre.
questions.f: The centre is the calm eye — the fiercest winds ring it in the eyewall just outside.

questions.q: The word 'monsoon' properly refers to a seasonal wind reversal, not just heavy rain.
questions.f: There is a dry monsoon season too — the wind turns around whether or not it brings rain.

questions.q: Thunderstorms can form over the ocean as well as over land.
questions.f: Ocean storms often peak overnight, while land storms peak in the afternoon — opposite schedules.

questions.q: Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas in Earth's atmosphere.
questions.f: It amplifies warming: warmer air holds more vapour, which traps still more heat.

questions.q: On average, air can hold about 7 percent more water vapour for every degree Celsius of warming.
questions.f: This is the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship — the reason a warmer world sees heavier downpours.

questions.q: Lightning can strike well away from the rain, out of a seemingly clear patch of sky.
questions.f: So-called 'bolts from the blue' can travel more than 15 km from their parent storm.

questions.q: Antarctica holds enough ice that its complete melting would raise global sea level by many metres.
questions.f: Estimates run to roughly 58 metres — which is why glaciologists watch its coastline so closely.

questions.q: Hailstones can be sliced open to reveal layers, a bit like tree rings.
questions.f: Each layer marks another journey up through the storm's freezing zone.

questions.q: Which pair of weather words are homophones — sounding alike but spelled and meaning differently?
questions.f: Spelling bees love these traps: hail falls from clouds, while hale means hearty and healthy.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the instrument that measures air pressure?
questions.f: One r, then 'meter' — from Greek baros, weight, and metron, measure.

questions.q: How is the polar light show correctly spelled?
questions.f: Two words, both from Latin: the dawn goddess and the north wind, side by side.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the swirling tropical storm word?
questions.f: Henry Piddington coined it in 1848 from Greek 'kyklos' while studying Indian Ocean storms.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'stratus', the flat cloud type?
questions.f: Latin plurals confuse everyone: one stratum of rock, many strata — but stratus clouds become strati.

questions.q: Which word means 'able to be seen through', as with thin cloud?
questions.f: Translucent lets light through but scatters it; transparent lets you see shapes clearly.

questions.q: Ox roasts on a frozen river, an elephant marched across the ice in 1814, and souvenir cards 'printed on the Thames' — which vanished London tradition?
questions.f: During the Little Ice Age the Thames froze solid many times — 1814 hosted the very last frost fair.

questions.q: An Indonesian eruption, June snow in New England, and a rain-soaked Geneva holiday that produced the novel Frankenstein all point to which year?
questions.f: Mount Tambora's 1815 blast dimmed the Sun worldwide — 1816 became the 'Year Without a Summer'.

questions.q: He captained Darwin's Beagle, coined the word 'forecast', and now names a sea area read out nightly on British radio. Who?
questions.f: FitzRoy founded what became the UK Met Office and issued the first public storm warnings.

questions.q: Launched in April 1960, it beamed back thousands of fuzzy TV pictures and proved storms could be watched from orbit. Which satellite?
questions.f: TIROS-1 worked only 78 days, yet it changed forecasting forever — no hurricane has gone unseen since.

questions.q: A Vermont farmer, a microscope bolted to a bellows camera, and 5,000 portraits of ice crystals earned which man the nickname 'Snowflake'?
questions.f: Bentley caught his first snowflake photo in 1885 and never charged scientists for his pictures.

questions.q: Around 340 BC a Greek philosopher wrote the book that still names weather science, filing rainbows and shooting stars together. Who?
questions.f: His 'Meteorologica' ruled the subject for nearly 2,000 years — 'meteorology' comes straight from its title.

questions.q: A Japanese scientist launching balloons from his observatory north-east of Tokyo in the 1920s published his great discovery in Esperanto, so few ever read it. He had found what?
questions.f: Wasaburo Oishi charted the ferocious high-altitude river of air from Tateno, Ibaraki, decades before Western pilots met it.

questions.q: In 1979 a Pacific storm grew wider than half the United States and set the record for lowest sea-level pressure ever measured. Its name?
questions.f: Tip spanned about 2,200 km and bottomed out at 870 hectopascals — both still world records.

questions.q: For three and a half hours in 1925, one tornado carved a record 350-kilometre path across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana. Its name in the record books?
questions.f: No tornado before or since has stayed on the ground so long or so far.

questions.q: When two hurricanes drift close together, they begin slowly circling each other like dance partners. This is called the what?
questions.f: Sakuhei Fujiwhara described the storm dance in 1921 by studying whirlpools in water.

questions.q: When a fast cold front catches the warm front ahead and lifts it off the ground, weather maps draw purple symbols. This front is called?
questions.f: 'Occluded' means shut off — the warm air is sealed away aloft, and the storm begins to wind down.

questions.q: Forecasters say 'bombogenesis' when a storm's central pressure plunges about 24 millibars in 24 hours. Such a storm is nicknamed a what?
questions.f: These explosive deepeners can turn an ordinary rainy day into a hurricane-force blizzard overnight.

questions.q: Average air pressure at sea level is about how many millibars?
questions.f: That is roughly a kilogram of air pressing on every square centimetre of you, all the time.

questions.q: The common halo around the Sun or Moon always has the same radius. How many degrees?
questions.f: Hexagonal ice crystals bend light by a minimum of 22 degrees — geometry drawn on the sky.

questions.q: A rainbow's main bow always forms at about what angle from the point directly opposite the Sun?
questions.f: Rene Descartes worked out the 42-degree geometry in 1637 by tracing rays through a glass ball of water.

questions.q: Legend says becalmed crews near 30 degrees latitude threw horses overboard to save water, naming which windless ocean belts?
questions.f: These are the sinking-air deserts of the sea — most of the world's great land deserts sit at the same latitudes.

questions.q: Clipper crews racing toward Australia dropped far south to ride howling westerlies known as the what?
questions.f: Further south still lie the Furious Fifties and the Screaming Sixties — sailors graded the roar.

questions.q: An 1835 paper on spinning machines by a French engineer now explains why cyclones rotate opposite ways in the two hemispheres. His name?
questions.f: Coriolis never studied weather — his rotating-frame maths was written for waterwheels.

questions.q: Letter codes like Af, Csa and ET sort every spot on Earth into climate types under whose classification?
questions.f: Koppen drew his first world climate map in 1884 — and geographers still argue over its letters today.

questions.q: The white slatted thermometer box on stilts at every weather station was designed by the father of the author of Treasure Island. Its name?
questions.f: Thomas Stevenson built lighthouses; his son Robert Louis chose stories over screens.

questions.q: A glass sphere on a stand slowly burns a scorch line across a curved paper card. What is this Victorian instrument recording?
questions.f: The Campbell-Stokes recorder, invented in 1853, still chars its daily cards at some stations.

questions.q: A ceilometer points its beam straight up to measure what?
c: The height of the cloud base
questions.f: Airports depend on ceilometers — pilots must know how low the cloud 'ceiling' hangs.

questions.q: Glacier scars in ancient rocks that once sat on the equator are key evidence for which deep-past scenario?
questions.f: Around 700 million years ago, ice may have gripped the planet from pole to pole.

questions.q: At one planet's north pole, clouds trace a six-sided jet-stream pattern wider than several Earths. Which planet?
questions.f: Voyager glimpsed Saturn's hexagon in 1981; Cassini later filmed it swirling in colour.

questions.q: On one moon of Saturn, clouds rain liquid methane into rivers and seas — the only other world known with a full rainfall cycle. Which moon?
questions.f: Titan's fat raindrops fall in slow motion through air thicker than Earth's.

questions.q: Rain tinted red or orange by desert dust carried thousands of kilometres has which dramatic folk name?
questions.f: Saharan dust rides the wind to Europe, sometimes turning snow on the Alps orange too.

questions.q: High mountain snowfields sometimes blush pink and smell faintly sweet. The cause?
c: Cold-loving algae blooming in the snow
questions.f: 'Watermelon snow' is coloured by algae with a built-in red sunscreen — explorers noted it for centuries.

questions.q: Dig beneath a lightning strike on a sandy beach and you may find a rough glassy tube nicknamed 'petrified lightning'. Its scientific name?
questions.f: The bolt melts sand along its path — some fulgurites branch underground like frozen roots.

questions.q: Magellan's sailors rejoiced when ghostly blue-violet flames danced harmlessly on the mast-tips during storms. The glow is called?
questions.f: It is a quiet electrical discharge — St. Elmo is the patron saint of sailors, so it read as protection.

questions.q: For decades pilots quietly reported red jellyfish-shaped flashes high above thunderstorms; a camera finally caught one in 1989. They are called?
questions.f: Sprites erupt 50-90 km up and last milliseconds — their cousins are named elves and blue jets.

questions.q: Patient sunset watchers over clear ocean horizons hope to catch a one-second emerald wink as the Sun's last sliver vanishes. It is called the what?
questions.f: The atmosphere acts as a weak prism, letting green light linger a heartbeat longer than red.

questions.q: Grapefruit-sized glowing orbs reported drifting through rooms during thunderstorms puzzled scientists for centuries. The phenomenon?
questions.f: Chinese researchers accidentally caught one on spectrograph video in 2012 — it contained vaporised soil.

questions.q: Ice crystals can paint an upside-down rainbow smiling near the top of the sky. Its tongue-twisting name?
questions.f: Sky-watchers call it 'the smile in the sky' — it never touches the horizon.

questions.q: An hour after sunset in the darkest spring skies, a faint pyramid of light climbs from the horizon — sunlight scattered by comet dust. Its name?
questions.f: Queen guitarist Brian May finished his doctoral thesis on zodiacal dust — 36 years late, in 2007.

questions.q: Between the two bows of a double rainbow lies a strip of noticeably darker sky, named after a Greek philosopher. It is called?
questions.f: Alexander of Aphrodisias described it around 200 AD — raindrops send no light back from that zone.

questions.q: A hiker above the fog meets a giant haloed shadow that copies every move, named for a German peak wrapped in witch legends. It is the?
questions.f: The rainbow ring around the shadow's head is called a glory — pilots see one around their plane's shadow.

questions.q: On bitterly cold nights, people hear booms and feel jolts as water-soaked frozen ground suddenly cracks. Scientists call these?
questions.f: Cryoseisms are loud enough that police sometimes field reports of explosions on the coldest nights.

questions.q: In freezing fog, summit huts and ships grow feathery white ice vanes that point INTO the wind. This deposit is called?
questions.f: Supercooled fog droplets freeze on contact — rime 'feathers' can grow a metre long on mountaintops.

questions.q: Children in one Siberian village stay home from school only when it is colder than about minus 52. The coldest inhabited place on Earth is?
questions.f: Oymyakon once recorded minus 67.7 degrees — eyelashes freeze there in minutes.

questions.q: The observatory that clocked a 231 mph gust in 1934 still advertises 'the World's Worst Weather'. Mount Washington stands in which US state?
questions.f: For 62 years that gust was the fastest wind ever measured at Earth's surface.

questions.q: A '100-year flood' actually means a flood with what chance of happening in any single year?
questions.f: Two '100-year floods' can strike in back-to-back years — the name misleads even adults.

questions.q: The northern line on the globe where the noon Sun can stand exactly overhead once a year is the Tropic of what?
questions.f: It is drifting: Earth's slow wobble moves the tropic about 15 metres every year.

questions.q: A rotating updraft called a mesocyclone, a flying-saucer profile, and the strongest tornadoes on record define which thunderstorm type?
questions.f: A supercell is one giant spinning engine that can outlive ordinary storms by hours.

questions.q: Window-seat passengers sometimes see rainbow rings around their aircraft's shadow on the cloud deck below. The optical effect is called a?
questions.f: Mountain climbers knew glories long before aviation — it is the same ring that crowns a Brocken spectre.

questions.q: From September to March a thunderstorm builds over Australia's Tiwi Islands nearly every afternoon — so reliably that WWII pilots gave it a name. Which?
questions.f: 'Hector the Convector' can tower 20 km and is one of the most studied storms on Earth.

questions.q: Each spring, glider pilots gather at Burketown, Australia, to surf a rolling cloud tube up to 1,000 km long. It is called the what?
questions.f: The Morning Glory is a travelling wave of air — pilots ride its rising front edge like surfers.

questions.q: Satellite photos show elegant swirling cloud pinwheels streaming downwind of ocean islands. Engineers call these vortex what?
questions.f: Von Karman vortex streets appear behind chimneys and bridge piers too — islands just draw them in cloud.

questions.q: On frigid nights, streetlights and the low Sun can stretch into glowing vertical beams as flat ice crystals drift down. These are called?
questions.f: Each pillar is millions of tiny mirrors — plate crystals reflecting one light source in mid-air.

questions.q: Castles hovering over the sea and ships sailing upside down in the sky belong to a mirage named after King Arthur's sorceress half-sister. It is called?
questions.f: Layered warm-over-cold air bends light into stacked images — likely fuel for Flying Dutchman legends.

questions.q: Polar navigators read the clouds: a bright white glare on their undersides warns of pack ice ahead. The glare is called?
questions.f: Its partner is 'water sky' — dark patches under cloud that promise open water for the ship.

questions.q: On newly frozen polar seas, millions of delicate frosty 'petals' can bloom across the surface overnight. They are called?
questions.f: Frost flowers are extra salty and host dense microbial life — gardens on brand-new ice.

questions.q: Silky white 'candy floss' ice curling from rotten logs on damp winter nights was proved in 2015 to need the help of what?
questions.f: Hair ice grows only on wood hosting the fungus Exidiopsis effusa — a century-old mystery solved.

questions.q: After certain snowfalls, fields wake up dotted with natural snow doughnuts that rolled themselves. These rarities are called?
questions.f: It takes wet snow, a crust beneath, and just the right wind — nature's own snowman starter kits.

questions.q: High in the dry Andes, sunlight carves snowfields into forests of tilted white blades named after kneeling monks. They are called?
questions.f: Sunlight sublimates hollows straight to vapour; the blades between can top a person's height.

questions.q: At Death Valley's Racetrack Playa, rocks leave long trails across the mud. In 2014 scientists filmed the movers: light wind plus what?
questions.f: On rare frozen mornings, ice panes shove the stones millimetre by millimetre — mystery solved after 70 years.

questions.q: 'Black blizzards', Black Sunday 1935, and a westward migration of farm families gave which nickname to the parched American plains of the 1930s?
questions.f: Ploughed-up grassland plus drought let the soil itself take flight — some dust reached New York City.

questions.q: African nations are growing a belt of trees and restored land thousands of kilometres long to hold back the Sahara's edge. The project is called?
questions.f: Launched in 2007, it aims to restore 100 million hectares across the width of Africa.

questions.q: On tropical mountains, some forests take much of their water not from rain but by combing it from passing mist. They are called what forests?
questions.f: In cloud forests, mossy branches drip constantly — trees literally drink from the sky.

questions.q: One beetle survives in a nearly rainless desert by doing dawn headstands so fog beads on its back and rolls to its mouth. Its home is the?
questions.f: Engineers copy the fog-basking beetle's bumpy shell to design water-harvesting surfaces.

questions.q: In hills drenched by some of Earth's heaviest rain, villagers train living fig-tree roots into bridges that ordinary wood could never survive. Which Indian state?
questions.f: Root bridges near rain-record villages grow stronger every year — some are centuries old.

questions.q: Loma, Montana once warmed 57 degrees Celsius in a single day as a wind the Blackfoot people call 'snow eater' poured off the Rockies. The wind?
questions.f: That 1972 swing from minus 48 to plus 9 remains the world-record 24-hour temperature change.

questions.q: Alpine valleys can jump 20 degrees in hours when a warm, dry wind spills down the mountains' lee side. Its classic Alpine name?
questions.f: 'Foehn effect' is now the general term — air dried and warmed by crossing any mountain range.

questions.q: Van Gogh grumbled that it shook his easel as he painted in Provence: a cold, dry northerly that funnels down the Rhone valley. Its name?
questions.f: The mistral can blow for days on end — but it also sweeps Provence's skies famously clear.

questions.q: A fierce, icy wind that tumbles from the mountains onto the Adriatic coast shares its name with the Greek god of the north wind. It is the?
questions.f: In Trieste, ropes and chains are strung along streets so pedestrians can hold on during bora blasts.

questions.q: A dusty Saharan trade wind that brings West Africa dry, hazy relief from December to February is called the?
questions.f: Harmattan haze can hide the Sun for days and carry Saharan dust far out over the Atlantic.

questions.q: Hot, dry autumn winds that rush from the high desert toward the southern California coast are named the what winds?
questions.f: Santa Anas can push humidity into single digits — surfers love the offshore breeze they bring.

questions.q: What is a 'williwaw'?
c: A sudden violent gust that plunges from mountains to the sea
questions.f: Sailors rounding Patagonia and the Aleutians coined it — Gore Vidal borrowed it for his first novel.

questions.q: The word 'haboob', for a towering wall of wind-driven dust, comes from an Arabic root meaning what?
questions.f: Sudanese haboobs can rise 1,500 metres and swallow whole cities in minutes.

questions.q: 'Derecho', the name for a windstorm that travels in a devastating straight line for hundreds of kilometres, is Spanish for what?
questions.f: It was coined in 1888 as the straight-line opposite of the twisting 'tornado'.

questions.q: What is 'graupel'?
c: Soft, crumbly snow pellets coated in frozen droplets
questions.f: Skiers call it styrofoam snow — snowflakes that collected a jacket of frozen cloud droplets on the way down.

questions.q: Antarctic travellers curse 'sastrugi'. What are they?
c: Hard wind-carved ridges in the snow surface
questions.f: The word is Russian — sledges judder over sastrugi like a road of frozen waves.

questions.q: Snow that has survived at least one summer and is compacting on its slow way to becoming glacier ice is called?
questions.f: From German for 'of last year' — squeeze firn long enough and it turns to blue glacier ice.

questions.q: In Australia, a playful rhyming name for a small spinning column of dust is a what?
questions.f: The word comes from Aboriginal languages — the same swirl Americans call a dust devil.

questions.q: Antarctica's ferocious gravity-driven winds that drain cold air downhill are 'katabatic' — from Greek meaning what?
questions.f: Katabatic winds at Cape Denison average gale force year-round — the windiest sea-level place on Earth.

questions.q: Rain forced when moist air is shoved up a mountainside is called 'orographic' — the root 'oro' means what?
questions.f: Orography explains why one side of a range drips with ferns while the other bakes.

questions.q: Someone with 'chionophobia' has an intense fear of what?
questions.f: Greek 'chion' means snow — chionophile animals, like snowshoe hares, love it instead.

questions.q: 'Ozone' was named in 1840 from a Greek verb meaning what — thanks to its sharp smell?
questions.f: You can sniff ozone near photocopiers and after lightning — the nose knew before the chemists.

questions.q: Taken apart into its Old Norse pieces, the everyday word 'window' literally means what?
questions.f: 'Vindauga' — early windows were unglazed eyes in the wall that let in wind along with light.

questions.q: In Old Norse, the word that became English 'sky' originally meant what?
questions.f: To Norse speakers, 'sky' meant the cloud cover itself — fitting for northern weather.

questions.q: Before it floated upward in meaning, the Old English word 'clud' — ancestor of 'cloud' — meant what?
questions.f: People saw billowing heaps in the sky and named them after rocky hills — the old sense survives in 'clod'.

questions.q: 'Tornado' is usually traced to the Spanish 'tronada', meaning what — reshaped by 'tornar', to turn?
questions.f: English sailors mangled the Spanish storm word until it spun — a word history with a twist.

questions.q: 'Climate' descends from the Greek 'klima', meaning what — from how the Earth tips away from the Sun?
questions.f: Greek geographers sliced the world into latitude bands by their 'slope' toward the Sun.

questions.q: The Latin root 'unda' inside 'inundate' — to flood — means what?
questions.f: The same wave rolls through 'undulate' and 'abundant' — originally 'overflowing like waves'.

questions.q: The 'hoar' in hoarfrost is an old word meaning what?
questions.f: A 'hoary' tale is grey-bearded with age — hoarfrost makes the world look ancient overnight.

questions.q: 'Petrichor', the smell of rain on dry ground, was coined in 1964 from Greek words meaning what?
c: Stone + the fluid of the gods
questions.f: Petra plus ichor — Australian scientists bottled the scent from baked rocks before naming it.

questions.q: Calm, golden 'halcyon days' are named after a mythical bird said to still the winter seas while nesting. Which bird?
questions.f: Greeks believed the halcyon nested on the waves around the winter solstice, charming the sea flat.

questions.q: A harp played only by the breeze, the geologist's word for wind-blown sand, and Odysseus's bag of winds all trace back to which figure?
questions.f: Aeolus was the Greek keeper of the winds — 'aeolian' processes still sculpt deserts and dunes.

questions.q: The alignment of Sun, Earth and Moon in a near-straight line — the setup for eclipses and king tides — is called a?
questions.f: Syzygy is a spelling-bee legend: three y's and not a single ordinary vowel.

questions.q: Sunbeams fanning out through gaps in cloud go by what name, from the Latin for twilight?
questions.f: Sailors call them 'the sun drawing water' — they actually converge, but perspective fans them out.

questions.q: The darkest central core of a shadow — where an eclipse turns total — shares its Latin name with a rainy-day accessory. It is the?
questions.f: Latin 'umbra' means shade — stand in the Moon's umbra and day becomes night for a few minutes.

questions.q: 'Eclipse' comes from the Greek 'ekleipsis', meaning what — as if the Sun had failed its post?
questions.f: To Greek skywatchers the Sun seemed to desert the sky — 'ekleipein', to leave out.

questions.q: Rippled rows of small high clouds that reminded sailors of fish scales are called a what sky?
questions.f: 'Mackerel scales, furl your sails' — the pattern often runs a day ahead of unsettled weather.

questions.q: Long streaming wisps of high cirrus, curling like something from a stable, are nicknamed what?
questions.f: Mares' tails show fierce winds aloft — old rhymes pair them with mackerel skies as storm warnings.

questions.q: Londoners nicknamed their thickest, yellowest, most infamous fogs after a food. They were called what?
questions.f: Coal smoke thickened the fog and tinted it yellow-green — streetlamps burned at midday.

questions.q: A flopped 1709 play, a new machine for stage sound effects, and a rival production of Macbeth using that machine gave English which idiom?
questions.f: Playwright John Dennis fumed that they had stolen his thunder — his invention outlived his play.

questions.q: Dendrochronology lets scientists read droughts and cold snaps of past centuries from what?
questions.f: Greek 'dendron' means tree — a wide ring records a kind year, a narrow ring a harsh one.

questions.q: Rare polar stratospheric clouds that shimmer like the inside of a seashell are called what clouds?
questions.f: 'Nacre' is mother-of-pearl — they glow 20 km up, before dawn and after sunset, in extreme cold.

questions.q: In 2017 the International Cloud Atlas accepted its first new cloud name in decades: a turbulent, upside-down-sea look called?
questions.f: Latin for 'roughness' — everyday photographers of the Cloud Appreciation Society got it recognised.

questions.q: Cloud crests that curl like perfect breaking surf — beloved by physics teachers — are named after which two scientists?
questions.f: Kelvin-Helmholtz waves roll up wherever fast air slides over slow — some think they inspired van Gogh's swirls.

questions.q: On dry, sunny, below-freezing days, snowbanks shrink without ever melting into puddles. The ice is escaping by which process?
questions.f: Ice jumps straight to invisible vapour — the same trick 'dry ice' performs on stage.

questions.q: Rows of smooth pouches sagging beneath a storm's anvil — a favourite of storm photographers — are called what clouds?
questions.f: Mammatus pouches are sinking blobs of cool, cloudy air — often a sign the worst has just passed.

questions.q: On the Beaufort scale, the term 'gale' officially begins at which force number?
questions.f: Force 8 means winds near 62-74 km/h — whole trees sway and walking becomes a struggle.

questions.q: A psychrometer finds humidity by comparing the readings of two thermometers — one dry and one what?
questions.f: Evaporation chills the wet bulb; the drier the air, the bigger the gap between the two.

questions.q: The rare adjective 'estival' describes things belonging to which season?
questions.f: From Latin 'aestas' — and 'aestivate' is to sleep away the summer, as desert snails do.

questions.q: Hawaiians blend two words to name the haze that drifts from Kilauea's craters: 'vog', short for what?
questions.f: When lava meets the sea there is even 'laze' — lava haze — to go with the vog.

questions.q: Towering clouds that build over wildfires and erupting volcanoes carry the Latin fire prefix in their name. They are called what clouds?
questions.f: Huge pyrocumulonimbus storms can make their own lightning — fire writing weather.

questions.q: The pocket 'aneroid' barometer, which needs no mercury, takes its name from Greek meaning what?
questions.f: Inside is a sealed metal capsule that flexes with pressure — invented by Lucien Vidie in 1844.

questions.q: On climate maps, a line joining places that receive equal rainfall is called an?
questions.f: Greek 'hyetos' means rain — iso-lines let one glance compare wet coasts with dry interiors.

questions.q: A 'synoptic' weather chart earns its name from Greek meaning what?
questions.f: One synoptic map shows simultaneous observations from thousands of stations — the whole sky at once.

questions.q: When meteorologists speak of 'advection', they mean heat or moisture being moved how?
questions.f: Warm advection ahead of a front can melt snow overnight without a ray of sunshine.

questions.q: 'Insolation' — nearly a homophone of insulation — is the technical term for what?
questions.f: From Latin 'insolare', to place in the sun — solar panel engineers live by insolation maps.

questions.q: The poetic Scots word 'gloaming' names which time of day?
questions.f: 'Roamin' in the gloamin'' — it shares an ancient root with 'glow', the last light of the sky.

questions.q: West Country English blends two damp words into 'mizzle', meaning what?
questions.f: Cornwall and Devon specialise in mizzle — too thick for mist, too fine for rain.

questions.q: The cold summer sea-fog that rolls off the North Sea onto Scottish coasts has which short local name?
questions.f: Edinburgh can shiver under haar while towns 20 km inland bask in sunshine.

questions.q: The smooth little cap of cloud that sometimes sits atop a growing storm tower is called 'pileus', Latin for a what?
questions.f: A pileus means the tower below is rocketing upward — it punches through its own cap minutes later.

questions.q: A 'supermoon' happens when the full Moon coincides with 'perigee'. Perigee is what?
c: The Moon's closest point to Earth
The Moon's highest point in the sky
questions.f: From Greek peri + ge, 'near the Earth' — the far point is the apogee.

questions.q: Aristophanes built a city in the air called Cloud Cuckoo Land; dictionary-makers borrowed its Greek name, 'nephelococcygia', for which pastime?
questions.f: Nephele (cloud) + kokkyx (cuckoo) — the fanciest possible word for spotting dragons in the sky.

questions.q: Word-watchers savour the irony in a 'meteoric rise' to fame, because real meteors only ever do what?
questions.f: The phrase borrows the meteor's speed and brilliance — and quietly ignores its direction.

questions.q: The storm petrel, the little seabird sailors read as a gale warning, is said to be named after which saint's feat?
questions.f: 'Petrel' echoes 'little Peter' — the bird patters across the waves as if walking on the sea.

questions.q: 'Hyperborean', a grand old word for the far frozen north, literally means living where?
questions.f: Greeks imagined the Hyperboreans in a sunny paradise on the far side of Boreas's icy blast.

questions.q: 'Orient', the old word for the East, literally refers to what daily sky event?
questions.f: Latin 'oriens', rising — maps were once drawn with sunrise-east at the top, hence 'to orient' yourself.

questions.q: 'Noon' comes from Latin 'nona hora', the ninth hour of daylight — meaning the word originally pointed to about what time?
questions.f: Monastery prayers at the ninth hour drifted earlier over the centuries, dragging the word to midday.

questions.q: 'Season' descends from the Latin 'satio', a word tied to which farm activity?
questions.f: A season was originally the right time to sow — the farming calendar named the year's chapters.

questions.q: Before it meant gathering crops, the Old English word 'haerfest' — our 'harvest' — was simply the name of what?
questions.f: English later borrowed 'autumn' and let 'harvest' shrink to mean the gathering itself.

questions.q: The stick or blade whose shadow tells the time on a sundial has a Greek name meaning 'one who knows'. It is the?
questions.f: The same root gives 'gnome' — originally a wise knower, not a garden ornament.

questions.q: In 1922 an English scientist imagined 64,000 human 'computers' in a vast hall calculating tomorrow's weather; his own first forecast, done by hand, took weeks. Who?
questions.f: Richardson's dream came true in 1950, when the ENIAC computer ran the first machine forecast.

questions.q: A rounded-off decimal in a 1961 computer run and a lecture titled after a butterfly in Brazil and a tornado in Texas launched whose 'chaos' revolution?
questions.f: Lorenz's butterfly effect explains why forecasts beyond about two weeks may stay impossible forever.

questions.q: A Scottish forecaster persuaded General Eisenhower to postpone history's largest sea invasion by one day to dodge a June 1944 storm. His name?
questions.f: Stagg's team spotted a brief calm window for June 6 — one of history's most important forecasts.

questions.q: Hours before the worst storm to hit southern England since 1703, a BBC weatherman famously reassured viewers there was no hurricane coming. Who?
questions.f: The Great Storm of October 1987 felled 15 million trees — and made his remark broadcasting legend.

questions.q: In 1919 the Bergen School likened clashing air masses to armies facing each other along a battle-line. Which everyday forecasting term did that metaphor give us?
questions.f: Vilhelm and Jacob Bjerknes had just lived through a war of trench lines — warm and cold air have been fighting on our maps ever since.

questions.q: The thickness of the ozone layer overhead is measured in units named after which Oxford scientist?
questions.f: Dobson built his ozone spectrometers in the 1920s; 300 Dobson units is a typical healthy reading.

questions.q: Around 1900, balloonist Leon Teisserenc de Bort discovered that above the weather lies a calm, layered zone. What did he name it?
questions.f: He also named the troposphere — the 'turning sphere' where all our weather churns.

questions.q: NASA's first spacecraft named after a living scientist flies ever closer to the Sun, studying the 'solar wind' he predicted in 1958. His surname?
questions.f: Eugene Parker watched the launch in 2018, aged 91 — the probe has since 'touched' the Sun's corona.

questions.q: Sparking telegraph wires, auroras seen from the tropics, and a British astronomer's sunspot sketch mark the greatest solar storm on record, in 1859. It is called the?
questions.f: Some telegraphs ran on aurora power alone — a repeat today could disrupt satellites worldwide.

questions.q: The number of sunspots freckling the Sun rises and falls in a cycle of roughly how many years?
questions.f: Heinrich Schwabe spotted the cycle in 1843 after 17 patient years of daily sunspot counts.

questions.q: A near-total disappearance of sunspots from about 1645 to 1715, overlapping Europe's coldest Little Ice Age decades, is called the?
questions.f: Astronomers of the era sometimes went years without logging a single spot.

questions.q: Aurora chasers photographed a mysterious purple ribbon, named it after a character in the film Over the Hedge, and scientists kept the name as an acronym. It is?
questions.f: Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement — a 3,000-degree river of gas, and officially still Steve.

questions.q: Photograph the noon Sun from the same spot every week for a year and its positions trace a graceful figure-8 called the?
questions.f: The 8 comes from Earth's tilt plus its slightly oval orbit — some old globes printed it in the Pacific.

questions.q: In 1441 Korea under King Sejong deployed standard bronze vessels so every province could report the same measurement. What did the 'cheugugi' measure?
questions.f: Korea's rain-gauge network predates most European ones by about two centuries.

questions.q: At the 1851 Great Exhibition, Dr George Merryweather displayed twelve leeches in bottles rigged to ring a bell before storms. He called his device the?
questions.f: He lobbied the government to install leech warning stations along the coast — it politely declined.

questions.q: Victorian captains carried sealed 'storm glasses' whose floating crystals supposedly foretold the weather. Which forecasting admiral popularised them?
questions.f: 'FitzRoy's storm glass' still sells as a curiosity — the crystals respond mostly to temperature.

questions.q: In the little Alpine weather-house toy, the rain-lady and sun-man swing outdoors because a cord inside twists in response to what?
questions.f: The cord — traditionally catgut or hair — coils and uncoils as damp air loosens it.

questions.q: Londoner Jonas Hanway endured decades of jeering from coachmen in the 1750s for carrying which then-outrageous accessory?
questions.f: Coachmen feared brollies would ruin their rainy-day trade — within 30 years every gentleman carried one.

questions.q: A Glasgow chemist sandwiched rubber dissolved in naphtha between layers of cloth in 1823, and Britons still wear his name in the rain. Who?
questions.f: The garment gained a 'k' — mackintosh — and 'mac' remains British slang for a raincoat.

questions.q: A Japanese physicist grew the world's first artificial snowflake in 1936 — on a strand of rabbit fur — and called snow crystals 'letters from the sky'. Who?
questions.f: Nakaya's diagram shows how temperature and moisture choose each snowflake's shape.

questions.q: Centuries before sunglasses, Arctic hunters carved bone and antler into slitted goggles to defeat which hazard?
questions.f: Thin slits cut the glare bouncing off snow — the same idea as a camera's narrow aperture.

questions.q: Winter campers can hollow a sleeping shelter out of a settled pile of snow. This snow-dome, from a Dene word, is called a?
questions.f: Unlike an igloo's cut blocks, a quinzhee is shovelled up as a heap first, then dug out.

questions.q: Satellites spot long, bright cloud lines tracing the world's shipping lanes. What creates these 'ship tracks'?
c: Exhaust particles seeding extra cloud droplets
questions.f: Each particle becomes a droplet seed — more, smaller droplets make the cloud brighter and whiter.

questions.q: Snowflakes are six-sided because of the shape water molecules take when they lock together. What geometry do the frozen molecules form?
questions.f: The 104.5-degree kink in every water molecule forces ice into honeycomb lattices — hence six arms.

questions.q: The science of nature's calendar — first flowering, leaf-fall, bird return dates — is called?
questions.f: Japan's cherry-blossom phenology records stretch back over 1,200 years — a climate archive in petals.

questions.q: Hibernation's mirror-twin — desert snails sealing up to sleep through scorching, dry months — is called what?
questions.f: From Latin 'aestas', summer — some African lungfish aestivate in dried mud for years.

questions.q: Grasses, oaks and pines skip the bees entirely: their pollen travels by wind. Botanists call this?
questions.f: Anemos (wind) + philos (loving) — wind-loving pollination is why breezy days trouble hay fever sufferers.

questions.q: The 1686 chart of the trade winds — often called the first meteorological map — was drawn by the astronomer far more famous for a what?
questions.f: Edmond Halley mapped the tropical winds decades before correctly predicting his comet's return.

questions.q: An octagonal marble tower in Athens, over 2,000 years old, is carved with eight flying wind gods and once bore a bronze Triton vane. It is the Tower of the?
questions.f: Part clock, part weather station, part compass — an ancient all-in-one forecast office.

questions.q: Shifts at the Ben Nevis summit observatory, a glory seen in the mist, and years spent bottling clouds in a lab led to a 1927 Nobel Prize for which Scot?
