questions.f: Wilson's cloud chamber, born from mountain mist, let physicists photograph particle tracks.

questions.q: During WWII, radar operators cursed the fuzzy clutter blurring their screens — until scientists realised the 'noise' was worth studying. It was?
questions.f: Those nuisance echoes became weather radar — swords to ploughshares on a glowing screen.

questions.q: German settlers in Pennsylvania swapped the badger of their old-country Candlemas lore for a local burrowing animal, founding which tradition?
questions.f: In Europe the shadow-watcher was a badger or bear; America supplied the groundhog.

questions.q: Dogger, Fisher, German Bight: millions of Britons drift to sleep hearing this nightly radio litany of sea areas. It is called the?
questions.f: Broadcast since 1925, its hypnotic place-names have inspired poems, songs and album tracks.

questions.q: Daniel Fahrenheit pinned the zero of his 1724 scale to the coldest mixture he could reliably brew: ice, water and what?
questions.f: Brine freezes far below plain water — his 'coldest reproducible cold' became 0 degrees F.

questions.q: Faint pastel fringes sometimes seen just inside a rainbow's violet edge — proof that light behaves as a wave — are called what bows?
questions.f: Drop-size interference paints them; classical ray optics simply cannot explain the extra stripes.

questions.q: Walkers in thick mist sometimes meet a ghostly white bow with almost no colour arcing before them. It is called a?
questions.f: Fog droplets are too tiny to split colours cleanly — sailors nicknamed it the sea-dog.

questions.q: Even far from any city, the night sky is never perfectly black: the upper air itself glows faintly green. This is called?
questions.f: Daytime sunlight energises the air's atoms, and all night long they slowly shed that energy as light.

questions.q: For months after Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, fine ash in the air made the Moon genuinely appear which colour from many places?
questions.f: Ash particles of just the right size scattered red light away — a literal blue moon, and lavender suns too.

questions.q: The rising full Moon looks enormous on the horizon, yet cameras show it is no bigger than when overhead. What causes the 'moon illusion'?
questions.f: Block the scenery by peeking through a tube and the giant Moon instantly shrinks — pure perception.

questions.q: Anders Celsius's original 1742 thermometer scale had one startling feature. What was it?
c: It ran backwards, with 0 at boiling and 100 at freezing
It used seawater instead of mercury
questions.f: Colleagues flipped the scale soon after his death — otherwise summer would read colder than winter.

questions.q: On frigid mornings, 'sea smoke' rises from harbours like steam off a bath. What is happening?
c: Very cold air is turning moisture off warmer water into instant fog
Salt is crystallising in the air
questions.f: Arctic sea smoke needs a big gap — bitter air over comparatively warm water — and vanishes metres up.

questions.q: Sailors call the small dark ripple-patches that a light breeze scatters across calm water what?
questions.f: Racing sailors hunt cat's paws to find the next puff — the sea prints the wind's footsteps.

questions.q: A rare 'heat burst' can send temperatures soaring in the middle of the night as a dying thunderstorm collapses.
questions.f: Sinking air compresses and heats; heat bursts have pushed night readings up more than 10 degrees in minutes.

questions.q: Hurricanes never form directly on the equator.
questions.f: The Coriolis effect vanishes at the equator, so storms there cannot gather their spin.

questions.q: Astronauts on the International Space Station see about 16 sunrises every 24 hours.
questions.f: Orbiting every 90 minutes, the ISS crosses from night to day again and again — sunrise on a loop.

questions.q: In 1887, ranchers in Montana reported snowflakes wider than a dinner plate — still the largest ever claimed.
questions.f: The Fort Keogh flakes were described as 38 cm across; Guinness still lists the report.

questions.q: Statistically, Groundhog Day forecasts turn out correct in most years.
questions.f: Analyses put Punxsutawney Phil's accuracy around 40 percent or lower — a coin flip does better.

questions.q: The word 'blizzard' appears in weather use as far back as Old English a thousand years ago.
questions.f: It only settled on snowstorms in 1870s America, spread by an Iowa newspaper's storm reports.

questions.q: Some valleys in Antarctica have seen no rain and almost no snow for a very, very long time.
questions.f: The McMurdo Dry Valleys, scoured by katabatic winds, are among the driest places on the planet.

questions.q: Auroras are statistically most frequent around the March and September equinoxes.
questions.f: Earth's magnetic tilt aligns favourably with the solar wind near the equinoxes — the 'Russell-McPherron effect'.

questions.q: The Empire State Building is struck by lightning around two dozen times in a typical year.
questions.f: Its lightning rod happily takes the hits — scientists once used the tower as a lightning laboratory.

questions.q: Researchers have recorded faint crackling and clapping sounds during strong auroral displays.
questions.f: Finnish scientists captured auroral sounds in 2012, vindicating a century of 'imagined' whispers.

questions.q: A rare class of lightning called superbolts can flash roughly a thousand times brighter than an ordinary stroke.
questions.f: Satellites find superbolts cluster oddly over oceans and in winter — still an open puzzle.

questions.q: On Saturn's moon Titan, raindrops fall far more slowly than they do on Earth.
questions.f: Low gravity plus thick air means Titan's fat methane drops drift down like snowflakes.

questions.q: Sunsets on Mars are blue.
questions.f: Martian dust scatters red light across the sky and lets blue linger around the setting Sun — rovers photographed it.

questions.q: Once the Sun climbs higher than about 42 degrees, no ordinary rainbow can be seen from flat ground.
questions.f: The bow's centre sits opposite the Sun — too high a Sun pushes the whole circle below the horizon.

questions.q: A Quaker chemist, an 1802 lecture to a London science club, and a Latin naming system copied from botany gave the world what?
questions.f: Luke Howard's cumulus, stratus and cirrus so moved Goethe that the poet wrote verses in his honour.

questions.q: Wet-bulb temperature matters because above roughly 35 degrees wet-bulb, the human body can no longer do what?
questions.f: At that point the air is so damp that sweat will not evaporate — shade and stillness stop helping.

questions.q: The Atlantic conveyor of warm water that keeps Britain milder than Labrador at the same latitude is called the?
questions.f: Benjamin Franklin, as a postmaster puzzled by slow mail ships, published one of its first charts.

questions.q: Cities run hotter than the countryside around them, especially at night. Climatologists call this the urban what effect?
questions.f: Dark roofs and roads store the day's heat and release it after dark — painting roofs white measurably helps.

questions.q: Ice cores drilled at Vostok and Dome C in Antarctica trap ancient air, letting scientists read the atmosphere back how far?
questions.f: Each bubble is a genuine sample of prehistoric sky, sealed the winter it fell as snow.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere is the coldest, where temperatures can dip near minus 90 degrees Celsius?
questions.f: The frigid mesosphere is also where meteors burn up and where noctilucent clouds shine.

questions.q: A sudden violent downdraft that slams straight out of a thunderstorm base — a genuine hazard for landing aircraft — is called a?
questions.f: Ted Fujita identified microbursts after investigating crashes; airports now watch for them with special radar.

questions.q: The scale rating tornado strength was upgraded in 2007 to judge damage more carefully. Its current name?
questions.f: The EF scale reads the wreckage backwards to estimate winds — nobody can safely hold an anemometer inside.

questions.q: A burning glass that chars a curved card, still logging daily sunshine hours, is named for John Francis Campbell and which Cambridge mathematician who redesigned it in 1879?
questions.f: Stokes also lent his name to a unit of kinematic viscosity — and to Stokes' law of settling droplets, pure cloud physics.

questions.q: When rain falls through freezing air and coats every twig in clear, heavy armour, forecasters call the event an ice what?
questions.f: Glaze ice can add so much weight that power lines and whole forests come down under it.

questions.q: Meteorologists call the invisible layer of atmosphere nearest the ground, stirred by friction and heat, the planetary what?
questions.f: It deepens with the day's heating, which is why afternoon winds usually blow stronger than dawn winds.

questions.q: A rain of frogs or fish is not folklore alone. What best explains genuine reported cases?
questions.f: Honduras marks an annual 'lluvia de peces' festival — waterspouts are the leading explanation.

questions.q: How does a hailstone's cross-section reveal its history inside a storm?
c: It has onion-like layers from repeated trips up and down
It records rings for each hour
Its colour maps the cloud's height
Its shape shows the wind direction
questions.f: Slice one open and count the milky and clear layers — each is another lap through the freezing zone.

questions.q: Vanilla, chocolate and 'nimbus' all appear in one 1802 naming scheme. In cloud Latin, what does nimbus mean?
questions.f: That is why the rain-bringing giants are cumulonimbus and the drizzle-sheets are nimbostratus.

questions.q: 'Anticyclonic gloom' is British forecasters' name for which counterintuitive winter situation?
c: High pressure trapping grey murk for days
questions.f: Sinking air puts a lid on the cold, damp surface layer — sunny high pressure turns dishwater grey.

questions.q: A 'temperature inversion' is unusual because in that layer the air does what with height?
c: Gets warmer as you go up
questions.f: Inversions trap smoke and sound — on inversion nights distant trains can be heard startlingly clearly.

questions.q: Balloons burst near 30 km up because air pressure there is roughly what fraction of sea level?
questions.f: That thin air is why the region is nicknamed 'near space' — the sky above looks nearly black.

questions.q: In 1783 two French brothers sent a sheep, a duck and a rooster aloft to test whether high air was safe. Their invention?
questions.f: The Montgolfiers' passengers landed unharmed — humans flew a few weeks later, and weather science took off.

questions.q: An 1852 balloon flight, a rival scale of air temperature, and pioneering studies of the aurora belong to which British scientist knighted for cold?
questions.f: Glaisher soared past 8 km without oxygen and nearly died — his assistant pulled the valve cord with his teeth.

questions.q: John Tyndall's 1859 laboratory experiment was the first to prove what about certain gases?
questions.f: Tyndall measured how water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb infrared — the greenhouse effect, in the lab.

questions.q: Some vast desert dunes hum and boom as sand avalanches down their slopes. These are called what dunes?
questions.f: Marco Polo blamed desert spirits; physicists now credit synchronised grains sliding in unison.

questions.q: The huge lens-shaped stack of clouds that forms downwind of a mountain range is nicknamed a what?
questions.f: Glider pilots ride these mountain waves to extraordinary heights — over 15 km in record flights.

questions.q: Which unit do aviators and mariners use for wind speed, equal to one nautical mile per hour?
questions.f: Sailors once timed knots on a rope paid out behind the ship — the counting device named the unit.

questions.q: Old almanacs promised a warm spell in late autumn named after which group of people?
questions.f: The phrase dates to the 1770s in New England; Britain's equivalent was long called St. Martin's summer.

questions.q: A brief mild spell around late January, folklore says, once let farmers glimpse spring. What is it usually called?
questions.f: Statisticians argue over whether it is real — but the phrase has warmed almanacs for centuries.

questions.q: A cold, dry, sinking-air belt at about 30 degrees latitude helps explain why most of the world's great deserts sit where?
c: In two bands north and south of the tropics
questions.f: Air that rose and rained at the equator descends here bone-dry — the Hadley cell's exhaust.

questions.q: The three-cell picture of global circulation names its tropical loop after an 18th-century English lawyer-scientist. He was?
questions.f: Hadley explained the trade winds in 1735 — his day job was law; meteorology was his hobby.

questions.q: The giant meandering waves in the jet stream that steer our storms bear the name of a Swedish-American scientist. Which?
questions.f: Carl-Gustaf Rossby's waves explain why a wobble over the Pacific can flood Europe a week later.

questions.q: In 1896 a Swedish chemist first calculated how much warming a doubling of carbon dioxide might cause. Who?
questions.f: He thought a warmer world might be pleasant — and got the basic physics remarkably close.

questions.q: Which machine turns slices of bread golden and crispy?
questions.f: A toaster's wires glow orange because electricity makes them heat up.

questions.q: Which kitchen machine boils water for a cup of tea?
questions.f: An electric kettle can boil a litre of water in under three minutes.

questions.q: Which machine keeps ice cream hard and frozen?
questions.f: A freezer pumps heat out of the food and blows it into the room behind.

questions.q: Which machine blows warm air to dry your hair?
questions.f: A hairdryer is really a small fan blowing over a hot wire.

questions.q: Which machine presses the wrinkles out of clothes?
questions.f: Irons use heat and a little steam to make cloth lie flat again.

questions.q: Which machine cuts the grass in a garden?
questions.f: Most lawnmowers spin a blade under the machine faster than you can see.

questions.q: Which vehicle rushes sick people to hospital?
questions.f: The word 'ambulance' comes from a French phrase for a moving hospital.

questions.q: Which truck empties the rubbish bins on your street?
questions.f: Many rubbish trucks squash the waste inside so they can carry much more.

questions.q: Which vehicle pulls a broken-down car away?
questions.f: Tow trucks use a winch, a motor that reels in a strong steel cable.

questions.q: Which farm machine pulls a plough across a field?
questions.f: Tractors have huge back wheels so they grip soft mud without sinking.

questions.q: Which machine tumbles wet clothes in warm air until they are dry?
questions.f: A tumble dryer turns the drum so warm air can reach every piece of cloth.

questions.q: Which machine stitches two pieces of cloth together very fast?
questions.f: A sewing machine makes a stitch by locking two threads together, over and over.

questions.q: Which machine helps you look at faraway stars?
questions.f: A telescope gathers much more starlight than your small eye can.

questions.q: Which machine spins a sharp bit to make a hole in wood?
questions.f: A drill bit has a spiral groove that carries the wood dust up and out.

questions.q: Which truck has a big drum that turns slowly to keep concrete runny?
questions.f: If the drum stopped turning for too long, the concrete inside would set solid.

questions.q: Which machine lifts heavy boxes onto high shelves in a warehouse?
questions.f: A forklift carries a heavy weight at the back so it does not tip forward.

questions.q: Which vehicle clears snow off a road with a big angled blade?
questions.f: The angled blade pushes snow sideways so it piles up beside the road.

questions.q: Which machine pushes soil around with a wide blade at the front?
questions.f: Bulldozers ride on metal tracks so they do not sink into soft ground.

questions.q: Which boat carries people and cars on a short trip across water?
questions.f: Many ferries have doors at both ends, so they never need to turn around.

questions.q: Which small strong boat pushes and pulls giant ships in a harbour?
questions.f: A tugboat is small but has an enormous engine for its size.

questions.q: Which ride carries you up a mountain hanging from a thick wire?
questions.f: Cable cars hang from a moving loop of steel rope pulled by a motor.

questions.q: Which machine wakes you in the morning with a ringing sound?
questions.f: The very first alarm clocks could only ring at one fixed time.

questions.q: Which little machine adds up numbers for you?
questions.f: A pocket calculator can do more sums in a second than a person can in a year.

questions.q: What do you slide around a desk to move the arrow on a screen?
questions.f: It was named a 'mouse' because its early cable looked like a tail.

questions.q: Which machine has skis at the front and an engine for riding on snow?
questions.f: Snowmobiles push themselves along with a wide rubber track, like a tank.

questions.q: Which machine cooks food with hot air inside a closed box?
questions.f: A fan oven blows the hot air around so food cooks evenly all over.

questions.q: Which machine warms up leftovers in about a minute using invisible waves?
questions.f: Microwaves shake the water inside food, and the shaking makes heat.

questions.q: A tractor is a machine built mainly for work on farms.
questions.f: Tractors can pull ploughs, trailers, mowers and dozens of other tools.

questions.q: A lawnmower is the machine you use to wash your clothes.
questions.f: A lawnmower cuts grass; a washing machine cleans clothes.

questions.q: Ambulances have flashing lights and a siren so other drivers move aside.
questions.f: Drivers must pull over to let an ambulance pass, because seconds matter.

questions.q: Which part of a bicycle do you sit on?
questions.f: A bicycle seat is called a saddle, a word borrowed from horse riding.

questions.q: What are the thin metal bars inside a bicycle wheel called?
questions.f: Thin spokes are light but together they hold up a rider many times their weight.

questions.q: What do you hold with both hands to steer a bicycle?
questions.f: Turning the handlebars turns the front wheel, and the bike leans into the curve.

questions.q: What do you ring on a bicycle to warn people you are coming?
questions.f: A bicycle bell works by flicking a tiny hammer against a metal dome.

questions.q: What should you wear on your head when riding a bike?
questions.f: A helmet's foam squashes on impact, soaking up energy instead of your head.

questions.q: What is the pointed front part of a boat called?
questions.f: A pointed bow slices through waves instead of pushing against them.

questions.q: What is the back part of a boat called?
questions.f: The steering rudder usually hangs at the stern, right behind the propeller.

questions.q: What is the small front room where an airplane pilot sits called?
questions.f: An airliner cockpit has hundreds of switches, dials and screens.

questions.q: What is the huge shed where airplanes are parked and repaired?
questions.f: Some hangars are so big that clouds can form near the ceiling.

questions.q: Where do trains stop so passengers can get on and off?
questions.f: The world's biggest station by platform count is Grand Central in New York, with 44.

questions.q: What is the small building at a house where a car is kept?
questions.f: The word 'garage' comes from a French word meaning to store or shelter.

questions.q: What do we call the sheltered place where ships tie up safely?
questions.f: Harbour walls break up big waves so boats inside stay calm.

questions.q: A person whose job is to repair cars and machines is called a…?
questions.f: 'Mechanic' comes from the same old word as 'machine' itself.

questions.q: A person riding a bicycle is called a…?
questions.f: 'Cyclist' comes from 'cycle', meaning a circle or wheel.

questions.q: A person who travels into space aboard a spacecraft is an…?
questions.f: 'Astronaut' is built from words meaning star and sailor.

questions.q: A person who designs and builds machines is called an…?
questions.f: Engineers plan a machine on paper long before anyone builds it.

questions.q: Who is in charge of a ship at sea?
questions.f: The captain gives the orders, and the helmsman turns the wheel.

questions.q: The everyday word 'bike' is a short way of saying…?
questions.f: 'Bike' became common in the 1880s, when bicycles were the newest craze.

questions.q: In the word 'bicycle', the part 'bi' means…?
questions.f: The same 'bi' gives us binoculars, which use two eyepieces.

questions.q: In the word 'tricycle', the part 'tri' means…?
questions.f: The same 'tri' appears in triangle, which has three corners.

questions.q: In the word 'unicycle', the part 'uni' means…?
questions.f: The same 'uni' gives us unicorn, an animal with a single horn.

questions.q: In the word 'submarine', the part 'sub' means…?
questions.f: 'Marine' means sea, so a submarine is simply an under-sea craft.

questions.q: In the word 'telephone', the part 'tele' means…?
questions.f: The same 'tele' appears in television and telescope.

questions.q: The word 'fridge' is a short way of saying…?
questions.f: 'Refrigerate' comes from a word meaning to make cool again.

questions.q: The word 'plane' is short for which longer machine name?
questions.f: 'Aeroplane' is built from words meaning air and flat surface.

questions.q: What is the metal rod that a pair of wheels spins around called?
questions.f: Grease on an axle lets the wheel spin freely instead of scraping.

questions.q: What is the rubber blade that sweeps rain off a car's windscreen?
questions.f: Wipers were invented after a driver had to keep stopping to clean the glass.

questions.q: What does a driver press to make a loud warning sound in a car?
questions.f: Early car horns were rubber bulbs you squeezed to honk.

questions.q: Which flashing light shows other drivers that a car is about to turn?
questions.f: Before indicators, drivers had to stick an arm out of the window to signal.

questions.q: What are the curved covers above bicycle wheels that stop mud splashing?
questions.f: In America mudguards are usually called fenders.

questions.q: Which machine is used to lift water up out of a well?
questions.f: A hand pump uses your muscles to make air push water up the pipe.

questions.q: Which old machine squeezes air out of leather bags to make a fire hotter?
questions.f: Blacksmiths pumped bellows for hours to get iron glowing hot.

questions.q: Which machine uses the wind to grind wheat into flour?
questions.f: The Netherlands still has over a thousand working historic windmills.

questions.q: Which machine uses a flowing river to turn a large wheel?
questions.f: Watermills ground grain for villages for well over two thousand years.

questions.q: A windmill needs moving air to turn its sails.
questions.f: On a still day a windmill simply stands quiet and does no work.

questions.q: Which giant farm machine cuts wheat and separates the grain as it drives?
questions.f: It is called a 'combine' because it combines several old jobs into one machine.

questions.q: Which truck lifts a worker high in a basket to fix a streetlight?
questions.f: It got its name from lifting fruit pickers up into tall orchard trees.

questions.q: Which machine on a dairy farm gently takes milk from cows?
questions.f: Some modern dairies use robots that milk cows whenever the cows choose.

questions.q: A ferry can carry cars as well as people across water.
questions.f: Car ferries drive vehicles straight on at one port and off at the other.

questions.q: Which machine keeps blowing air to cool a room, without making it cold?
questions.f: A fan does not cool the air; the moving air just carries heat off your skin.

questions.q: Which machine sharpens a pencil when you twist it round?
questions.f: A sharpener holds a tiny wedge-shaped blade at just the right angle.

questions.q: Which small machine opens metal tins of food?
questions.f: A can opener uses a sharp wheel that rolls around the rim, cutting as it goes.

questions.q: Which machine plays music and news out loud from the air?
questions.f: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, so news arrives instantly.

questions.q: What do we call a cart with two wheels that a horse pulls?
questions.f: Carts were among the first wheeled machines, used over 5,000 years ago.

questions.q: The word 'motor' describes something that makes a machine…?
questions.f: 'Motor' comes from a Latin word meaning mover.

questions.q: The word 'pedal' comes from an old word meaning…?
questions.f: The same root gives us pedestrian, someone travelling on foot.

questions.q: Which machine shows moving pictures on a screen in your living room?
questions.f: The word television is built from parts meaning far and seeing.

questions.q: Which pedal does a driver press with a foot to make a car speed up?
questions.f: The accelerator lets more fuel and air into the engine, so it works harder.

questions.q: Which small flying machine has no pilot on board and is steered from the ground?
questions.f: Most small drones use four spinning rotors, which is why they are called quadcopters.

questions.q: What do we call the part that stores power for a torch or a phone?
questions.f: A battery holds energy as chemicals and releases it as electricity.

questions.q: Which flat panel on a roof turns sunlight straight into electricity?
questions.f: Solar panels have no moving parts at all, so they can last for decades.

questions.q: Which tall machine spins three long blades in the wind to make electricity?
questions.f: The tips of a big turbine blade can travel faster than a racing car.

questions.q: Which tool bangs nails into wood?
questions.f: A hammer works because all the swing's energy lands on one tiny nail head.

questions.q: Which tool has sharp teeth for cutting through wood?
questions.f: Each tooth of a saw is a tiny wedge that chips out a little wood.

questions.q: Which tool grips a nut and turns it tight?
questions.f: In America a spanner is usually called a wrench.

questions.q: Which workshop tool clamps wood still while you cut it?
questions.f: A vice tightens using a screw, one of the six simple machines.

questions.q: Which tool rolls out of a case to measure how long something is?
questions.f: The springy steel tape curls into a shallow U so it stays stiff in the air.

questions.q: Which vehicle runs along one single rail instead of two?
questions.f: Monorail trains often sit astride the rail like a rider on a horse.

questions.q: Which vehicle runs on rails laid in a city street?
questions.f: Many trams take their power from an overhead wire through a metal arm.

questions.q: Which vehicle carries many passengers around a city on ordinary roads?
questions.f: 'Bus' is short for omnibus, a Latin word meaning 'for everyone'.

questions.q: Which car do you pay to ride in, with a meter showing the fare?
questions.f: The meter that counts the fare is called a taximeter, which gave the taxi its name.

questions.q: Which machine in a shop reads the black stripes on a price label?
questions.f: The scanner shines a light and measures which stripes bounce it back.

questions.q: Which machine in a wall hands out banknotes when you use a card?
questions.f: Inside, rubber rollers count out the notes one by one, very quickly.

questions.q: Which machine helps you brush your teeth by buzzing and spinning?
questions.f: Some electric brushes move their bristles thousands of times a minute.

questions.q: Which machine tells you how heavy something is?
questions.f: Kitchen scales usually squash a tiny spring or sensor to measure weight.

questions.q: Which instrument measures how hot or cold something is?
questions.f: 'Thermo' means heat, and 'meter' means measure.

questions.q: Which small instrument has a needle that always points north?
questions.f: The needle is a tiny magnet that lines up with the Earth's own magnetism.

questions.q: Which fairground machine spins round and round with painted horses?
questions.f: A carousel is also called a merry-go-round or a gallopers.

questions.q: Which machine lifts a car off the ground so someone can work underneath?
questions.f: A car jack uses a screw or oil pressure to turn a small push into a big lift.

questions.q: Which machine cools a whole room down on a hot day?
questions.f: An air conditioner works like a fridge, but it chills a room instead of food.

questions.q: Which tool is made of two sharp blades joined at a pin?
questions.f: Scissors are two levers and two wedges working together.

questions.q: Which machine pushes air into a bicycle tyre?
questions.f: You are squeezing air into a smaller space, which makes the tyre firm.

questions.q: What is the long strip of ground an airplane speeds along to take off?
questions.f: Big airport runways can be over three kilometres long.

questions.q: What do we call the wheels an airplane lands on?
questions.f: Landing gear folds up inside the plane in flight to help it fly faster.

questions.q: What is the tall pole that holds up a sailing boat's sail?
questions.f: Very old sailing ships sometimes carried three or four masts.

questions.q: Which vehicle floats along on a cushion of blown air?
questions.f: A hovercraft can cross water, mud and beach without stopping.

questions.q: Which boat is moved by a person pulling on two oars?
questions.f: Each oar works as a lever, with the boat's edge acting as the fulcrum.

questions.q: Which narrow boat is paddled with a blade on each end of one pole?
questions.f: Kayaks were first built with skin stretched over frames of wood and bone.

questions.q: What is the outer ring of a bicycle wheel, which the tyre sits on?
questions.f: The rim is usually made of light aluminium so the wheel spins up easily.

questions.q: What do we call the middle of a wheel, where the axle goes through?
questions.f: Bearings inside the hub let the wheel spin with almost no rubbing.

questions.q: Which metal fastener has a spiral groove and is turned into wood?
questions.f: That spiral groove is called the thread, and it pulls the screw in as it turns.

questions.q: What do we call it when you put oil on a machine so it moves smoothly?
questions.f: Oil separates two metal surfaces so they slide instead of grinding.

questions.q: In the word 'photograph', the part 'photo' means…?
questions.f: 'Photograph' means light-writing, because light draws the picture.

questions.q: In the word 'microscope', the part 'micro' means…?
questions.f: 'Scope' means to look at, so a microscope is a small-thing-looker.

questions.q: In the word 'automatic', the part 'auto' means…?
questions.f: An automatic machine acts by itself once you switch it on.

questions.q: The word 'aircraft' means a machine that travels through the…?
questions.f: 'Craft' is an old word for a vehicle, used for boats and spacecraft too.

questions.q: A machine built to travel beyond the sky is called a…?
questions.f: Spacecraft must carry everything they need, because space is empty.

questions.q: A drone can fly with nobody sitting inside it.
questions.f: The pilot stands on the ground holding a radio controller.

questions.q: Solar panels can make electricity in total darkness.
questions.f: No light means no power, which is why solar homes also use batteries.

questions.q: A city bus travels on metal rails like a train.
questions.f: Buses use rubber tyres on ordinary roads, so their route can change.

questions.q: A tugboat is smaller than the ships it pushes.
questions.f: Tugboats are small but pack a huge engine, like an ant lifting a crumb.

questions.q: Which machine cuts hair with tiny moving blades?
questions.f: Clippers have two combs; one stays still while the other slides sideways.

questions.q: Which machine sprays water to wash a car?
questions.f: A pressure washer squeezes water through a tiny hole so it comes out fast.

questions.q: Which machine at a building site carries away loads of soil?
questions.f: A dump truck tips its whole back up so the soil slides straight out.

questions.q: Which machine flattens a new road until it is smooth and hard?
questions.f: The roller's drum is so heavy it squeezes the surface flat by weight alone.

questions.q: Which vehicle carries fuel or milk inside a big round tank?
questions.f: Tanks are round because a curved wall is much stronger than a flat one.

questions.q: What do we call the metal tracks that a train runs along?
questions.f: Rails spread a train's huge weight across the wooden or concrete sleepers.

questions.q: What is the tunnel under a river or a city called that trains run through?
questions.f: 'Tunnel' comes from an old French word for a cask or barrel shape.

questions.q: What is the machine that carries you up a ski slope called?
questions.f: A ski lift is a giant loop of cable pulled around by a motor at one end.

questions.q: What machine do you use to talk to someone in another country?
questions.f: Your voice becomes an electric or light signal that races along a cable.

questions.q: What do we call a set of railway carriages joined behind an engine?
questions.f: 'Train' comes from an old word meaning something dragged along behind.

questions.q: Which machine keeps the air in a room from getting too dry?
questions.f: A humidifier adds tiny droplets of water into the air as mist.

questions.q: Which machine on a train's front pushes leaves and snow aside?
questions.f: Old American locomotives had a big wedge-shaped one called a cowcatcher.

questions.q: What is the moving belt at a shop checkout called?
questions.f: A conveyor belt is a loop of rubber pulled around by rollers.

questions.q: Which machine grinds coffee beans into powder?
questions.f: A grinder crushes beans between two hard surfaces called burrs.

questions.q: Which machine helps a swimmer breathe underwater by carrying air?
questions.f: The word 'scuba' is made from the first letters of a long name for the gear.

questions.q: Which machine helps a fisherman wind in his line?
questions.f: A fishing reel is a wheel and axle with a handle acting as a lever.

questions.q: Which vehicle has caterpillar tracks and a bucket for digging?
questions.f: Metal tracks spread the digger's weight so it does not sink in mud.

questions.q: What do we call the door at the back of a lorry that folds down?
questions.f: A folded-down tailgate makes a handy ramp for loading.

questions.q: What is the sound a steam train's whistle makes?
questions.f: Steam whistles work by forcing hot steam past a sharp edge.

questions.q: Which machine spins clothes very fast to fling the water out?
questions.f: Spinning throws the water outwards, so it escapes through tiny holes.

questions.q: Which machine turns and turns to lift a bucket from a well?
questions.f: A windlass is a wheel and axle: you turn a handle and rope winds on.

questions.q: An airplane's engines are usually fixed under or on its wings.
questions.f: Hanging engines under the wings makes them easier to service and replace.

questions.q: A pair of scissors has three blades.
questions.f: Scissors have exactly two blades that cross over each other.

questions.q: What do we call the little wheels on a suitcase or a chair leg?
questions.f: Castors swivel, which is why a shopping trolley can turn in any direction.

questions.q: What is the word for a machine used in the home, like an oven or a fridge?
questions.f: 'Appliance' comes from 'apply', meaning to put something to use.

questions.q: Which machine keeps a fish tank's water clean by pushing it through a sponge?
questions.f: The sponge traps dirt while helpful bacteria grow on it and clean the water.

questions.q: Which flying machine has a big balloon of gas and an engine underneath?
questions.f: Airships float because the gas inside is lighter than the air around it.

questions.q: Which machine bakes bread by mixing dough and heating it in one box?
questions.f: A bread maker has a paddle that kneads the dough before baking starts.

questions.q: What is the balance point of a lever called?
questions.f: Moving the fulcrum closer to a heavy load makes it far easier to lift.

questions.q: Which force makes machine parts get warm when they rub together?
questions.f: Engineers fight friction with oil, grease and smooth ball bearings.

questions.q: What is the main job of oil or grease inside a machine?
questions.f: A thin film of oil keeps metal surfaces from touching at all.

questions.q: What do the small steel balls inside a wheel hub do?
c: Let it spin with almost no rubbing
questions.f: Ball bearings replace sliding with rolling, which wastes far less energy.

questions.q: Which part of a submarine lets the crew see above the waves?
questions.f: A periscope uses angled mirrors or prisms to bend light down a tube.

questions.q: Sonar finds objects underwater by sending out what?
questions.f: The crew times the echo, because sound travels a known speed in water.

questions.q: Radar spots distant aircraft by bouncing what off them?
questions.f: Radar was rushed into use in the 1930s and changed air travel forever.

questions.q: Which fuel do jet airliners burn?
questions.f: Jet fuel is a kind of paraffin, oilier and safer to carry than petrol.

questions.q: What is the main job of a car's radiator?
questions.f: Water carries the engine's heat to the radiator, where air blows it away.

questions.q: What does a car's exhaust pipe carry away?
questions.f: The muffler in the pipe uses chambers to quiet the engine's banging.

questions.q: Which part of a car changes which gear the engine drives through?
questions.f: A gearbox is a case of different-sized cogs you can switch between.

questions.q: What do a car's springs and shock absorbers do?
questions.f: Together they are called the suspension, because the body hangs on them.

questions.q: Which car part holds the wheels, engine and body together?
questions.f: Many modern cars have no separate chassis; the body itself is the frame.

questions.q: What is the sliding metal part that moves up and down inside an engine cylinder?
questions.f: A car engine's pistons can move up and down 50 times every second.

questions.q: Which famous car, made from 1908, was the first that ordinary families could afford?
questions.f: Ford's moving assembly line cut the time to build one car from 12 hours to under 2.

questions.q: What is an assembly line?
c: Workers each add one part as the product moves past
One worker builds the whole machine
A line painted on a factory floor
questions.f: The idea came partly from watching meat-packing plants move carcasses on hooks.

questions.q: Which inventor's laboratory produced the first long-lasting electric light bulb in 1879?
questions.f: Edison's team tested thousands of materials before finding one that glowed for hours.

questions.q: Which train family is France's high-speed service known as?
questions.f: TGV stands for a French phrase meaning 'high-speed train'.

questions.q: Who became the first human to travel into space, in 1961?
questions.f: His flight lasted 108 minutes and circled the Earth just once.

questions.q: Sputnik 1, launched in 1957, was the world's first what?
questions.f: It was a metal ball the size of a beach ball that beeped as it circled Earth.

questions.q: Why are airliners built mostly from aluminium rather than steel?
c: It is much lighter for its strength
questions.f: Every kilogram saved means less fuel burned on every single flight.

questions.q: What does welding do to two pieces of metal?
c: Melts them so they join as one
questions.f: A welder's arc can reach several thousand degrees in a tiny spot.

questions.q: What is a rivet used for?
questions.f: A big airliner can be held together by more than a million rivets.

questions.q: What are the hinged flaps on an airplane's wings that make it roll called?
questions.f: When one aileron lifts, the other drops, tipping the plane into a turn.

questions.q: What is the tall fin on an airplane's tail mainly for?
questions.f: Without a tail fin a plane would swing side to side like a badly thrown dart.

questions.q: What do the flaps on the back of a wing do when a plane comes in to land?
c: Give extra lift at slow speed
questions.f: Extended flaps let a heavy jet fly slowly enough to touch down safely.

questions.q: Which machine turns movement into electricity?
questions.f: A generator is a motor working backwards: you turn it, and current flows out.

questions.q: An electric motor spins because of which invisible force?
questions.f: Coils of wire push against magnets, over and over, to keep the shaft turning.

questions.q: How does an electric car store the energy it needs?
questions.f: A big car battery pack can weigh as much as five adults.

questions.q: What turns inside a windmill to crush grain into flour?
questions.f: Two heavy stones grind grain between them, one still and one turning.

questions.q: What did the very first traffic lights, in 1868 London, run on?
questions.f: A police officer had to stand there and switch the gas-lit signal by hand.

questions.q: Why do heavy lorries have so many wheels?
c: To spread the weight over the road
questions.f: Too much weight on one wheel would crack the road surface underneath.

questions.q: An electric motor and a generator are built from very similar parts.
questions.f: Spin a motor by hand and it will actually produce a little electricity.

questions.q: A bicycle's chain must be oiled to work smoothly.
questions.f: A dry chain wears out fast and can waste a surprising amount of your effort.

questions.q: Jet engines work by pushing air backwards very fast.
questions.f: For every backwards push on the air, the air pushes the plane forwards.

questions.q: A car's battery is what makes the engine start turning.
questions.f: The battery spins a small starter motor, which gets the big engine going.

questions.q: The word 'automobile' is built from parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek autos plus Latin mobilis; it means a carriage that moves itself.

questions.q: The word 'periscope' comes from parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek peri and skopein; you look around a corner or above the sea.

questions.q: The word 'microphone' is built from parts meaning…?
questions.f: A microphone catches small sounds and turns them into an electric signal.

questions.q: The word 'megaphone' is built from parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek megas, meaning great or large, plus phone, meaning voice.

questions.q: The word 'propeller' comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin propellere, made of pro (forward) and pellere (to push).

questions.q: A helicopter's spinning blade unit is called a rotor because the word means…?
questions.f: 'Rotor' shares its root with rotate and rotation.

questions.q: The word 'barometer' means a device that measures…?
questions.f: From Greek baros, meaning weight; it senses the pressure of the atmosphere.

questions.q: The word 'cycle' in 'bicycle' and 'motorcycle' means…?
questions.f: From Greek kyklos, a circle; the same root gives us cyclone.

questions.q: Which spelling of this word for a car, van or lorry is correct?
questions.f: 'Vehicle' comes from Latin vehere, to carry, which explains the h.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the parts of a machine, taken all together?
questions.f: Keep the 'machine' and add -ry: machinery.

questions.q: You press a bicycle's ____ to slow down. Which spelling fits?
questions.f: A 'brake' stops a machine; to 'break' something is to snap it.

questions.q: A boat moves with the wind using a ____. Which spelling fits?
questions.f: A 'sale' is selling something; a 'sail' catches the wind.

questions.q: A rowing boat is pushed along with an ____. Which spelling fits?
questions.f: 'Ore' is rock containing metal, and 'or' joins two choices.

questions.q: Bridges and rails are built of ____, a strong metal. Which spelling fits?
questions.f: To 'steal' is to take without asking; 'steel' is iron mixed with carbon.

questions.q: What word means a small, clever, useful gizmo or tool?
questions.f: 'Gadget' appeared among sailors in the 1800s for any small handy fitting.

questions.q: What do we call a badly made, odd-looking machine cobbled together?
questions.f: 'Contraption' probably blends 'contrive', 'trap' and 'invention'.

questions.q: What is the person who steers a ship's wheel called?
questions.f: The wheel itself is called the helm, from an old word for a rudder handle.

questions.q: On a steam train, who shovelled coal into the firebox?
questions.f: A fireman could shovel several tonnes of coal on a single long journey.

questions.q: Who checks tickets and helps passengers on a train?
questions.f: 'Conductor' comes from a Latin word meaning one who leads along.

questions.q: What do we call the crew member who works out an aircraft's route?
questions.f: 'Navigate' comes from Latin navis, a ship, and agere, to drive.

questions.q: Which worker heats iron in a forge and hammers it into shape?
questions.f: 'Black' refers to the dark iron the smith works, as opposed to bright tin.

questions.q: A group of lorries or cars travelling together is called a…?
questions.f: 'Convoy' comes from an old French word meaning to accompany.

questions.q: A group of military aircraft flying as one unit is called a…?
questions.f: 'Squadron' comes from an Italian word for a square formation.

questions.q: A small group of little ships is called a…?
questions.f: 'Flotilla' is Spanish for 'little fleet'.

questions.q: Which word means the plan or drawing an engineer works from?
questions.f: Old copying methods printed white lines on blue paper, hence the name.

questions.q: Which of these machines does NOT use an engine to move?
questions.f: A sledge simply slides, pulled by gravity, animals or people.

questions.q: Which of these travels on water and needs no fuel at all?
questions.f: A sailing boat harvests energy the wind is giving away for free.

questions.q: Which of these was designed to work underground?
questions.f: A boring machine's spinning cutting head can be wider than a house.

questions.q: Which machine would a builder use to lift a load of bricks up a wall?
questions.f: A pulley lets you pull down, which is easier than lifting straight up.

questions.q: Which machine measures the amount of electricity a home uses?
questions.f: Old meters had a spinning aluminium disc you could watch through the glass.

questions.q: Why does a bicycle have a wide, ridged pattern on its tyres?
questions.f: The pattern is called tread, and the grooves push water out of the way.

questions.q: What happens inside a fridge to make it cold?
c: Heat is pumped out of it
questions.f: That is why the back of a fridge feels warm when you touch it.

questions.q: Which machine sorts and posts your letter along its journey?
questions.f: Modern sorting machines can read addresses and handle 30,000 letters an hour.

questions.q: What does a machine's 'horsepower' describe?
questions.f: James Watt invented the unit to show how many horses his engine replaced.

questions.q: Which of these needs a runway of water rather than land?
questions.f: A seaplane rests on floats or a boat-shaped hull instead of wheels.

questions.q: Which machine turns a strip of paper tape into a printed receipt?
questions.f: Many receipt printers use heat instead of ink to darken the special paper.

questions.q: Why is a shopping trolley easier to move than a heavy box you drag?
questions.f: Rolling friction can be twenty times smaller than sliding friction.

questions.q: Which household machine uses a spinning drum and hot air together?
questions.f: Sensors in modern dryers stop the machine as soon as the clothes are dry.

questions.q: Which of these did people use before electric refrigerators?
c: Ice boxes filled with blocks of ice
questions.f: Ice was cut from frozen lakes in winter and stored in sawdust all summer.

questions.q: What does a smoke alarm do when it senses smoke?
questions.f: Many smoke alarms sense smoke particles blocking a tiny beam of light.

questions.q: Which part of a plane holds the passengers and cargo?
questions.f: 'Fuselage' comes from a French word meaning spindle-shaped.

questions.q: Horsepower is a unit used to describe how powerful an engine is.
questions.f: One horsepower is about 746 watts of power.

questions.q: A glider has no engine and rises by riding warm air currents.
questions.f: Skilled glider pilots have flown thousands of kilometres without an engine.

questions.q: The word 'submarine' contains a part meaning 'sea'.
questions.f: Latin mare means sea, and marinus means of the sea.

questions.q: Which early bicycle had one huge front wheel and a tiny back one?
questions.f: It was named after two British coins of very different sizes.

questions.q: Air-filled rubber tyres were first made popular in 1888 by which Scotsman?
questions.f: He made them for his son's tricycle to give a smoother ride on cobbles.

questions.q: How does a canal lock move a boat between two water levels?
c: It seals a chamber and fills or empties it
It lifts the boat on a crane
It pumps the boat through a pipe
questions.f: Locks need no pumps: gravity alone lets water in and out of the chamber.

questions.q: What does a 3D printer do to build an object?
c: Cuts a shape from a block
questions.f: Because it adds material, this is called additive manufacturing.

questions.q: What is the room where a ship's officers steer and navigate called?
questions.f: It is called the bridge because early ones were walkways across the deck.

questions.q: On a ship, which side is 'port'?
questions.f: Ships once docked with the left side to port, so the loading side got the name.

questions.q: What is the long fin running along the bottom of a sailing boat called?
questions.f: The keel stops the boat sliding sideways and helps keep it upright.

questions.q: What does the word 'hull' mean on a boat?
c: The main body of the boat
questions.f: A boat with two hulls side by side is called a catamaran.

questions.q: Which machine at the top of a lighthouse spreads its beam far out to sea?
questions.f: The ringed Fresnel lens bends scattered light into one powerful beam.

questions.q: Which rocket carried astronauts to the Moon?
questions.f: Saturn V stood taller than a 30-storey building and is still the tallest rocket flown.

questions.q: Why do rockets drop parts of themselves as they climb?
c: Empty fuel tanks are dead weight
questions.f: Dropping used stages is why rockets get thinner as they rise.

questions.q: What protects a returning spacecraft from the fierce heat of re-entry?
questions.f: Air squashed in front of the capsule gets thousands of degrees hot.

questions.q: Which machine did astronauts drive on the Moon in the early 1970s?
questions.f: Three of these battery-powered buggies are still parked on the Moon today.

questions.q: What does the small fuse in a plug do?
c: Breaks the circuit if too much current flows
questions.f: A thin wire inside melts on purpose, cutting the power before wires overheat.

questions.q: What is a switch's job in an electrical machine?
c: To open or close the circuit
questions.f: When the switch is open there is a gap, and electricity cannot jump across.

questions.q: How does a hydroelectric dam make electricity?
questions.f: Hydro plants can switch on within minutes, faster than most power stations.

questions.q: Which part of a clock keeps it ticking at a steady rhythm?
questions.f: A pendulum's swing depends on its length, not on how far it swings.

questions.q: What keeps a modern wristwatch so accurate?
questions.f: The crystal vibrates 32,768 times a second, and the watch counts the beats.

questions.q: Who sent the first message across the Atlantic by radio, in 1901?
questions.f: The signal was just the letter S, three dots, but it changed the world.

questions.q: What did Samuel Morse's code use to spell out letters?
questions.f: The letter E is a single dot, because E is the commonest letter in English.

questions.q: Which Scot gave the first public demonstration of television, in 1926?
questions.f: His first moving TV picture was of a ventriloquist's dummy head.

questions.q: Why are the letters on a keyboard arranged as QWERTY?
c: It was designed for early typewriters
It was chosen by computer makers
questions.f: The layout spread common letter pairs apart so the metal bars jammed less.

questions.q: Which machine did Isaac Singer make a household name in the 1850s?
questions.f: Singer let families pay in instalments, which made machines affordable.

questions.q: Which early locomotive won the 1829 Rainhill Trials?
questions.f: Stephenson's Rocket reached about 30 mph, astonishing the crowd.

questions.q: What are the wooden or concrete beams under railway tracks called?
questions.f: In America they are called ties; they hold the rails exactly the right width apart.

questions.q: Why is crushed stone spread under railway tracks?
c: It spreads the weight and drains water
questions.f: That stone layer is called ballast, and it also lets the track be re-levelled.

questions.q: Which city opened the world's first underground railway, in 1863?
questions.f: The first Tube trains were pulled by steam engines in smoky tunnels.

questions.q: What does a tower crane use to stop it toppling over?
questions.f: Blocks of concrete sit on the short arm to balance the load on the long arm.

questions.q: What makes a pneumatic drill hammer up and down?
questions.f: 'Pneumatic' comes from a Greek word for breath or air.

questions.q: Which of the six simple machines is a bicycle wheel spinning on its axle?
questions.f: The wheel and axle turns a small strong twist into a long smooth roll.

questions.q: Why is a long screw with closely spaced threads easier to turn in?
c: Each turn moves it a smaller distance
questions.f: A screw is just a ramp wrapped around a pole; a gentler ramp is easier.

questions.q: What is a puncture in a bicycle tyre?
c: A hole letting the air escape
questions.f: A tiny thorn can flatten a tyre holding air at three times atmospheric pressure.

questions.q: A 3D printer can only print in plastic.
questions.f: Printers now build objects from metal powder, concrete, ceramics and even chocolate.

questions.q: Canal locks need electric pumps to move water in and out.
questions.f: Gravity does the work; the paddles simply let water flow the way it wants to.

questions.q: The London Underground was the first underground railway in the world.
questions.f: Its first line opened in 1863, decades before New York's subway.

questions.q: A ship's 'bridge' is a walkway for passengers to cross the deck.
questions.f: Today the bridge is the command room where the ship is steered.

questions.q: The word 'transport' is built from parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin trans and portare; a porter also carries things.

questions.q: In 'telegraph' and 'photograph', the part 'graph' means…?
questions.f: A telegraph writes at a distance; a photograph is written by light.

questions.q: In 'telescope' and 'periscope', the part 'scope' means…?
questions.f: From Greek skopein, to watch or examine.

questions.q: In 'telephone' and 'microphone', the part 'phone' means…?
questions.f: From Greek phone, meaning voice, which also gives us phonics.

questions.q: The word 'invent' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From invenire; inventors 'find' ideas nobody has come upon before.

questions.q: The word 'construct' contains a root meaning…?
questions.f: Latin struere, to build; the same root gives structure and destruction.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'assemble' a machine?
questions.f: 'Dismantle' once meant to strip off a cloak or mantle.

questions.q: The word 'ferry' comes from an old word meaning…?
questions.f: It shares an ancestor with the German fahren, to travel.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'aircraft'?
questions.f: Like 'sheep' and 'deer', aircraft keeps the same form in the plural.

questions.q: Which spelling of the two-wheeled pedal machine is correct?
questions.f: Both halves come from Greek: bi- for two and kyklos for wheel.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the width between railway rails?
questions.f: A standard-gauge track is 1,435 mm wide, set in the earliest railway days.

questions.q: Which spelling names a person who designs machines?
questions.f: 'Engineer' once meant a builder of siege engines and bridges.

questions.q: Which word describes a vehicle that can travel on both land and water?
questions.f: From Greek amphi (both) and bios (life), like a frog.

questions.q: Which word means 'to do with ships and sailing'?
questions.f: From Greek nautes, a sailor; the same root hides inside astronaut.

questions.q: What do we call a worker who shapes metal parts using a lathe?
questions.f: A lathe spins the metal while a fixed tool shaves it to shape.

questions.q: What is an old-fashioned word for a pilot, from the Latin for bird?
questions.f: Latin avis means bird, which also gives us aviary and aviation.

questions.q: Which machine's name literally tells you it measures the road you travel?
questions.f: From Greek hodos, a road or path, plus metron, a measure.

questions.q: Which of these words names a machine part that goes round and round?
questions.f: A crankshaft changes the pistons' up-and-down into round-and-round.

questions.q: Which of these is measured in volts?
questions.f: A common car battery supplies about 12 volts.

questions.q: Which machine turns fuel into movement by burning it inside itself?
questions.f: 'Internal' because the burning happens inside the cylinders, not in a separate firebox.

questions.q: Where does a steam engine burn its fuel?
c: Outside the cylinder, under a boiler
questions.f: That makes it an external combustion engine, the opposite of a car engine.

questions.q: Which of these machines works with no moving parts at all?
questions.f: That is why solar panels can sit on a roof for 25 years with no repairs.

questions.q: How does a parachute slow a falling person or capsule?
c: It pushes against a lot of air
questions.f: A big canopy grabs so much air that falling speed drops to a gentle walk-off.

questions.q: What is the moving handrail on an escalator for?
questions.f: The handrail moves at exactly the same speed as the steps.

questions.q: Why did Elisha Otis's 1854 invention make tall buildings practical?
c: It stopped a lift falling if the rope broke
It removed the need for stairs
questions.f: He demonstrated it by having his own hoist rope cut while he stood on it.

questions.q: Which machine is used to hoist a car engine out of the engine bay?
questions.f: A chain hoist multiplies your pull using several pulleys in a block.

questions.q: Which of these vehicles usually carries the most passengers at once?
questions.f: A London double-decker can carry around 80 people.

questions.q: What is the job of a car's windscreen washer pump?
questions.f: The fluid contains soap and antifreeze so it works in winter.

questions.q: Which machine helps a doctor see inside your body without cutting?
questions.f: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are blocked by dense bone.

questions.q: Which machine keeps a hospital patient breathing when they cannot?
questions.f: A ventilator gently pushes air into the lungs and lets it flow back out.

questions.q: Which machine cleans a swimming pool by crawling along the bottom?
questions.f: Pool robots use brushes and a filter bag, like a vacuum for water.

questions.q: Which machine did farmers use before combine harvesters to separate grain?
questions.f: Threshing beat the grain loose from the stalks, a job once done by hand with flails.

questions.q: What does a baler make on a farm?
c: Tight bundles of hay or straw
questions.f: A baler ties each bale with twine automatically as it moves along.

questions.q: Which machine draws water for crops from under the ground?
questions.f: Wind-powered pumps still dot farms in Australia and the American West.

questions.q: Why does a helicopter's rotor blade have a slightly twisted shape?
c: Its tip moves faster than its root
questions.f: The twist keeps lift even along the blade despite the huge speed difference.

questions.q: Which of these is a machine designed to go up but never come back down?
questions.f: Weather balloons burst high in the stratosphere, and the instruments parachute home.

questions.q: What does a car's alternator do while the engine runs?
questions.f: A belt from the engine spins the alternator, which generates electricity.

questions.q: Why do many machines have a flywheel?
c: Its spin smooths out uneven power
questions.f: A heavy spinning wheel keeps going between the engine's power pulses.

questions.q: An escalator's handrail travels at the same speed as its steps.
questions.f: If it drifted out of step, riders would be tugged off balance.

questions.q: A steam engine burns its fuel inside the cylinder, like a car engine.
questions.f: Steam engines burn fuel outside, under a boiler, to make steam first.

questions.q: The word 'nautical' comes from a Greek word for sailor.
questions.f: Greek nautes, sailor, plus astron, star, gives us astronaut.

questions.q: Which machine measures how deep the water is under a boat?
questions.f: It times how long a sound pulse takes to bounce off the seabed.

questions.q: Which instrument measures wind speed with little spinning cups?
questions.f: From Greek anemos, meaning wind.

questions.q: What does a machine's 'output' mean?
c: The useful work or product it gives
questions.f: Engineers compare output with input to work out efficiency.

questions.q: The word 'machine' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek mekhane also gives us 'mechanic' and, through Latin, 'machination'.

questions.q: The word 'engine' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Latin ingenium also gives us 'ingenious' — an engine was a clever device.

questions.q: The word 'robot' was coined from a Czech word meaning…?
questions.f: Karel Capek used it in his 1920 play R.U.R., and the word spread worldwide.

questions.q: The word 'tractor' is built on a Latin verb meaning…?
questions.f: Latin trahere also gives us tract, traction and attract.

questions.q: The word 'factory' is rooted in a Latin verb meaning…?
questions.f: Latin facere also gives us fact, manufacture and benefactor.

questions.q: 'Manufacture' literally means…?
questions.f: From Latin manus (hand) and factum (made) — long before factories existed.

questions.q: The word 'hydraulic' is built from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: Greek hydor plus aulos, a pipe or flute; hydraulic machines push oil or water through pipes.

questions.q: 'Pneumatic' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek pneuma; a pneumatic drill runs on compressed air.

questions.q: The word 'helicopter' is built from Greek words meaning…?
questions.f: From helix and pteron; the same pteron hides in pterodactyl.

questions.q: An airplane's 'aileron' takes its name from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: French aile means wing, so an aileron is a wing's small wing.

questions.q: A car's 'chauffeur' was originally a word for someone who…?
questions.f: Early steam cars needed the driver to keep the boiler hot, hence 'heater'.

questions.q: The word 'turbine' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Latin turbo, a spinning top; turbines whirl in water, steam or gas.

questions.q: The word 'piston' comes from a root meaning…?
questions.f: Related to pestle — a piston pounds up and down inside its cylinder.

questions.q: 'Cylinder' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek kylindros, from a verb meaning to roll.

questions.q: An engine's 'valve' is named from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Latin valva; a valve swings shut like a folding door leaf.

questions.q: The word 'lever' comes from a French verb meaning…?
questions.f: French lever, to lift; the same root gives us elevate and levitate.

questions.q: The word 'fulcrum' comes from a Latin word for…?
questions.f: Latin fulcire means to prop up — the fulcrum props up the lever.

questions.q: The word 'excavator' is built from a Latin root meaning…?
questions.f: Latin cavus, hollow, gives cave, cavity and excavate.

questions.q: The word 'foundry', where metal parts are cast, comes from a verb meaning…?
questions.f: Latin fundere, to pour — foundries pour molten metal into moulds.

questions.q: What does the acronym RADAR stand for?
questions.f: 'Ranging' means finding how far away something is.

questions.q: What does the acronym SONAR stand for?
questions.f: Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.

questions.q: What does the word SCUBA stand for?
questions.f: Jacques Cousteau and Emile Gagnan perfected the regulator that made it work.

questions.q: The word 'jet' comes from a French verb meaning…?
questions.f: French jeter; a jet engine literally throws air backwards.

questions.q: The Ferris wheel is named after…?
c: George Ferris, the engineer who designed it
the ferrous iron it was made from
questions.f: His 80-metre wheel was the star of the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.

questions.q: The diesel engine is named after…?
questions.f: His engine squeezed air so hard that fuel lit without any spark.

questions.q: The airship type called a Zeppelin was named after…?
questions.f: He was in his sixties when his first rigid airship flew in 1900.

questions.q: The unit of power called the watt honours which engineer?
questions.f: Watt also gave us the word horsepower to advertise his engines.

questions.q: The unit of electrical push, the volt, is named after…?
questions.f: Volta built the first true battery, a stack of metal discs and brine-soaked cloth.

questions.q: The unit of electric current is named after which scientist?
questions.f: Ampere worked out the rules linking electric currents and magnetism.

questions.q: Which unit, named after a German physicist, counts cycles per second?
questions.f: A quartz watch crystal vibrates at 32,768 hertz.

questions.q: What are the four strokes of a four-stroke engine, in order?
questions.f: Students remember it as suck, squeeze, bang, blow.

questions.q: How does a diesel engine light its fuel without a spark plug?
c: Air squeezed so hard it becomes very hot
questions.f: Squeezing air to a twentieth of its volume can heat it past 500 degrees C.

questions.q: What is a car's clutch for?
c: Connecting and disconnecting engine from gearbox
questions.f: Two friction plates press together; ease them apart and you can change gear.

questions.q: Why does a car need a differential between its driven wheels?
c: The outer wheel travels further in a turn
To keep the wheels the same size
questions.f: Without it, one tyre would have to skid every time you turned a corner.

questions.q: What does a turbocharger use to force extra air into an engine?
questions.f: Waste exhaust spins a turbine, which spins a compressor on the same shaft.

questions.q: What is regenerative braking on an electric car?
c: The motor works as a generator to slow the car
The brakes spray water to cool
questions.f: Braking energy that once became waste heat now flows back into the battery.

questions.q: What does an anti-lock braking system stop from happening?
questions.f: ABS releases and reapplies the brakes many times a second so you can still steer.

questions.q: Which steering mechanism turns a steering wheel's spin into side-to-side movement?
questions.f: A small toothed pinion rolls along a straight toothed bar called the rack.

questions.q: A bicycle's 'derailleur' is named for what it does to the chain?
questions.f: The French word means to derail, and that is exactly the trick it performs.

questions.q: What is 'torque' in a machine?
questions.f: From Latin torquere, to twist; the same root gives us torch and torment.

questions.q: If a small gear with 10 teeth drives a big gear with 40, the big gear turns…?
c: Four times slower, with more force
Four times faster, with less force
questions.f: Gears trade speed for turning force; you never get both for free.

questions.q: What ancient machine still used today raises water with a spiral inside a tube?
questions.f: Modern versions lift sewage in treatment plants and water in Dutch polders.

questions.q: Hero of Alexandria's aeolipile, from about 2,000 years ago, was an early…?
questions.f: Steam jets spun a metal ball — a toy that hinted at the steam age to come.

questions.q: The Antikythera mechanism, found in a Greek shipwreck, is the oldest known…?
questions.f: Its bronze gears predicted eclipses and the positions of the planets.

questions.q: Which engineer built the first steam locomotive to run on rails, in 1804?
questions.f: His engine hauled 10 tonnes of iron along a Welsh tramway, winning a bet.

questions.q: What did James Watt's spinning 'governor' do to a steam engine?
questions.f: As it spun faster, weights flew outward and closed the steam valve — early automation.

questions.q: What did the Jacquard loom of 1804 use to control its patterns?
questions.f: Those punched cards later inspired the very first computer programmers.

questions.q: Which railway is the longest single line in the world?
questions.f: It runs over 9,000 km and crosses eight time zones.

questions.q: A ship's speed in 'knots' means nautical miles per hour — why 'knots'?
c: Sailors counted knots on a line trailing behind
Ropes were knotted at the mast
questions.f: They timed a wooden log on a knotted rope with a sandglass to work out speed.

questions.q: Which instrument let sailors find latitude by measuring the Sun's angle?
questions.f: A sextant covers a sixth of a circle, which is where its name comes from.

questions.q: Why did screw propellers replace paddle wheels on ocean ships?
c: They stay underwater in rough seas
questions.f: A paddle wheel lifts clear of the water when a ship rolls, losing its bite.

questions.q: What is a bilge pump on a boat for?
c: Removing water that collects in the bottom
questions.f: The bilge is the very lowest inside part of a hull, where water gathers.

questions.q: A diesel engine has no spark plugs.
questions.f: Compression alone makes the air hot enough to ignite the fuel spray.

questions.q: The Antikythera mechanism was made in ancient Greek times, not the Middle Ages.
questions.f: It dates from roughly the 2nd century BC and stunned the divers who found it.

questions.q: A gear train can increase turning force without adding any energy.
questions.f: You gain force but lose speed; total energy can never increase.

questions.q: The word 'robot' is older than the word 'robotics'.
questions.f: 'Robot' arrived in 1920; Isaac Asimov coined 'robotics' about twenty years later.

questions.q: What is an 'automaton'?
c: A machine built to move by itself
questions.f: From Greek automatos, self-acting; 18th-century automata could write and play music.

questions.q: The word 'android' is built from a Greek root meaning…?
questions.f: Greek andros (man) plus -oid (like); an android is a human-shaped robot.

questions.q: What is a 'prototype', judging by its Greek parts?
questions.f: From protos (first) and typos (model or impression).

questions.q: What does it mean to say a machine is 'obsolete'?
c: No longer used because something better exists
questions.f: From a Latin word meaning worn out or fallen out of use.

questions.q: What does a patent give an inventor?
c: The sole right to make and sell the invention for a time
questions.f: 'Patent' comes from a Latin phrase meaning 'lying open' — the details are published.

questions.q: Which word describes a shape designed to slip through air easily?
questions.f: From Greek aer (air) and dynamis (power).

questions.q: What is a 'mechanism'?
c: The working parts that make something operate
questions.f: Watchmakers call a mechanism a movement.

questions.q: The word 'catamaran' comes from a Tamil phrase meaning…?
questions.f: From kattu (to tie) and maram (wood); English sailors borrowed it in the 1600s.

questions.q: The word 'yacht' comes from a Dutch word meaning…?
questions.f: Dutch jacht ships were fast hunters used to chase pirates.

questions.q: The word 'canoe' entered English from a Caribbean word for…?
questions.f: Spanish sailors borrowed the Carib word canoa in the 1490s.

questions.q: The word 'caravan' comes from a Persian word for…?
questions.f: Persian karwan; the towed holiday caravan borrowed the name much later.

questions.q: The word 'taxi' is short for 'taximeter', built from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The taximeter measured the fare, so the cab became a taxi.

questions.q: A 'coupe' car takes its name from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: A coupe carriage was 'cut' shorter than a full-size one.

questions.q: Which word means a machine or system worked by pressing on liquid?
questions.f: Liquids barely squash, so they pass a push along almost perfectly.

questions.q: Which of these machines is a first-class lever, with the pivot in the middle?
questions.f: In a first-class lever the fulcrum sits between the effort and the load.

questions.q: Which simple machine is hidden inside a flight of spiral stairs?
questions.f: Spiral stairs are a ramp wrapped round a pole — which is also what a screw is.

questions.q: What does 'mechanical advantage' measure?
c: How much a machine multiplies your force
questions.f: A machine with an advantage of 4 lets one unit of push move four units of load.

questions.q: Which of these did the Bessemer process transform in the 1850s?
questions.f: Blasting air through molten iron burned out impurities in minutes, not days.

questions.q: Which machine let one worker spin many threads at once from 1764?
questions.f: James Hargreaves reportedly named it after a spinning wheel knocked over on its side.

questions.q: What was the main advantage of Watt's separate condenser?
c: The cylinder stayed hot, saving fuel
questions.f: Older engines wasted fuel reheating the cylinder on every single stroke.

questions.q: How does a hot-air balloon pilot make the balloon descend?
c: Lets the air inside cool or vents it
questions.f: Cooler air inside is heavier, so lift falls and the balloon sinks gently.

questions.q: Why do many bridges and machine frames use triangles?
c: A triangle cannot be pushed out of shape
questions.f: Squares can squash into diamonds; triangles cannot without breaking a side.

questions.q: Which part of a jet engine squeezes air before fuel is added?
questions.f: Rows of small blades squeeze the air to many times its normal pressure.

questions.q: Roughly how fast does sound travel through air at sea level?
questions.f: That is Mach 1; sound moves faster on a warm day than a cold one.

questions.q: Which pilot first flew faster than sound in level flight, in 1947?
questions.f: He flew the Bell X-1 with two ribs broken from a horse-riding fall days earlier.

questions.q: What does an altimeter in an aircraft actually measure?
c: Air pressure, to work out height
Distance to the ground by radio
questions.f: Pilots reset the altimeter to the local pressure before each landing.

questions.q: Which machine part is a 'cam'?
c: A shaped wheel that lifts something as it turns
questions.f: Camshafts in engines open and close the valves in perfect rhythm.

questions.q: What does a ratchet allow a mechanism to do?
c: Turn one way but not back
questions.f: A springy pawl drops between teeth, which is what makes the clicking sound.

questions.q: Which type of gear lets a shaft drive another at right angles?
questions.f: Bevel gears in a car's differential turn the drive shaft's spin through 90 degrees.

questions.q: What is a worm gear especially good at?
c: Making a big speed reduction in a small space
questions.f: A worm gear usually cannot be driven backwards, so it locks a load in place.

questions.q: A machine's mechanical advantage can be less than one.
questions.f: A bicycle in a high gear trades force for speed, giving an advantage under one.

questions.q: 'Aerodynamic' contains a Greek root meaning air.
questions.f: Greek aer gives us aerial, aeroplane and aerobics too.

questions.q: Which group of small ships was famously called an 'armada'?
questions.f: 'Armada' is Spanish for an armed fleet, from Latin armata.

questions.q: Which machine did George Cayley's 1853 glider prove was possible?
questions.f: Cayley worked out lift, drag and thrust fifty years before the Wright brothers flew.

questions.q: Which part of a bicycle multiplies your leg force before the chain?
questions.f: Longer cranks give more leverage, just like a longer spanner.

questions.q: Which word means 'to do with movement', from a Greek verb meaning to move?
questions.f: Greek kinein also gives us cinema, because films are moving pictures.

questions.q: The word 'locomotive' is built from Latin parts meaning…?
questions.f: Latin loco (from a place) plus motivus (causing motion) — a self-moving machine.

questions.q: A 'dynamo' takes its name from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek dynamis also gives us dynamic and dynamite.

questions.q: The word 'thermostat' is built from parts meaning…?
questions.f: It holds the temperature steady, from Greek therme and statos.

questions.q: A 'gyroscope' is named from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: Leon Foucault coined the name because you could watch Earth's turn through it.

questions.q: The word 'accelerate' is built on a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Latin celer, swift; a car's accelerator makes it swifter.

questions.q: 'Aviation' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Latin avis; the same root gives aviary and the pilot's old title, aviator.

questions.q: Why is a ship's right-hand side called 'starboard'?
c: From 'steer board', the old steering oar's side
Because stars were watched from there
From a Spanish word for right
questions.f: Old ships steered with an oar over the right side, so that became the steer-board side.

questions.q: A car's 'dashboard' was originally a board that…?
c: stopped mud dashing up from the horses
questions.f: When engines replaced horses, the name stayed and the dials moved in.

questions.q: A car's 'chassis' takes its name from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: French chassis, a frame, from the same root as 'case'.

questions.q: The word 'anchor' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek ankyra, a hook or bend — the same idea as an angle.

questions.q: The lifting machine called a 'crane' is named after…?
questions.f: The jib and hook look just like the bird's neck and beak reaching out.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct — the tools that grip nuts and bolts?
questions.f: The silent w survives from Old English wrencan, to twist.

questions.q: Which machine word starts with a silent 'p'?
questions.f: Greek words beginning 'pn' keep the p in English but drop the sound.

questions.q: You ____ a bicycle with your feet. Which spelling fits?
questions.f: To 'peddle' is to sell things door to door; a 'petal' is part of a flower.

questions.q: Which spelling names the rod a wheel turns on?
questions.f: An 'axel' is a jump in figure skating, named after Axel Paulsen.

questions.q: A parachute's cloth canopy is spelled with which word part?
questions.f: French chute means a fall, so a parachute guards against a fall.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'axis', as in a machine's axis of rotation?
questions.f: A robot arm with six axes can reach almost any angle.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'radius', used for a wheel's measurement?
questions.f: Latin words ending in -us often take -i in the plural.

questions.q: In 'monorail', the part 'mono' means…?
