questions.f: Greek monos, alone or single; monopoly and monologue share it.

questions.q: A machine described as 'multi-purpose' can do…?
questions.f: Latin multus means many; a Swiss army knife is multi-purpose.

questions.q: Which word describes a small underwater craft that must stay near a mother ship?
questions.f: Submarines are independent; submersibles rely on support from a surface vessel.

questions.q: How long is the Channel Tunnel between England and France?
questions.f: Nearly 38 km of it lies under the sea, the longest undersea section anywhere.

questions.q: How do ships climb the hill in the middle of the Panama Canal?
c: Locks lift them to a high lake
questions.f: Ships rise 26 metres to Gatun Lake, then step back down on the other side.

questions.q: What made the 1885 Rover 'safety bicycle' safer than a penny-farthing?
c: Two equal wheels and a chain drive
questions.f: Its shape is basically the bicycle we still ride today.

questions.q: The 1817 'Draisine' running machine had no pedals — how did riders move?
c: Pushing along the ground with their feet
questions.f: Karl von Drais's invention taught the world that two wheels can balance.

questions.q: Percy Spencer discovered microwave cooking while working with which device?
questions.f: He noticed the magnetron's waves had softened something in his pocket.

questions.q: Josephine Cochrane's 1886 patent gave the world a practical…?
questions.f: She built it because she was tired of servants chipping her fine china.

questions.q: Hubert Cecil Booth's first vacuum cleaner of 1901 was so big it was…?
questions.f: Hoses were fed through windows while the machine growled outside.

questions.q: Which aircraft designer built the first practical single-rotor helicopter, flown in 1939?
questions.f: He had dreamt of it since boyhood, inspired by a Jules Verne story.

questions.q: Which spacecraft became the first reusable one to fly to orbit, in 1981?
questions.f: The Shuttle flew 135 missions before retiring in 2011.

questions.q: What does a Falcon 9 rocket do that older rockets could not?
c: Land its first stage upright to fly again
questions.f: Its boosters steer home on grid fins and land on a floating platform.

questions.q: Which machine tool is often called the 'mother of machine tools'?
questions.f: A lathe can even make the parts for another lathe.

questions.q: What does a CNC machine use to control its cutting?
questions.f: CNC stands for computer numerical control.

questions.q: Why does an incandescent light bulb waste so much energy?
c: Most of it leaves as heat, not light
questions.f: Only about 5% becomes light, which is why LEDs replaced them.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of an LED over an old filament bulb?
c: Far more light per unit of electricity
questions.f: A good LED lasts tens of thousands of hours instead of about a thousand.

questions.q: Why is a perpetual motion machine impossible?
questions.f: Energy can be moved and changed, but never created from nothing.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a block and tackle?
c: Several pulleys multiply your pulling force
questions.f: With four rope sections supporting the load, you pull with a quarter of the force.

questions.q: What does a car jack's screw thread do to your effort?
c: Turns a small turning force into a big lift
questions.f: You turn the handle many times to raise the car a few centimetres.

questions.q: Which part of a bicycle brake actually converts motion into heat?
c: Brake pads rubbing the rim or disc
questions.f: After a long descent, brake discs can get too hot to touch.

questions.q: Why does a spinning ice skater or flywheel resist changes to its speed?
questions.f: Engineers use heavy flywheels to smooth out jerky power in machines.

questions.q: How does a bicycle's freewheel let you coast without pedalling?
c: A ratchet lets the wheel outrun the pedals
questions.f: That familiar ticking sound is the ratchet pawls skipping over their teeth.

questions.q: What is the job of a governor on an old steam engine?
questions.f: It is one of the earliest examples of a machine controlling itself.

questions.q: How does an electric doorbell make its ringing sound?
c: An electromagnet snaps a hammer against a chime
A tiny motor spins a bell
Air is forced through a reed
questions.f: Some bells break their own circuit so the hammer springs back, over and over.

questions.q: Why do aircraft wings have upturned tips called winglets?
c: They cut the swirling air that causes drag
questions.f: Winglets can save a few percent of fuel on every flight.

questions.q: What does a pitot tube on an aircraft measure?
questions.f: It compares the pressure of air rushing in with still air pressure.

questions.q: What happens when an aircraft 'stalls' in flight?
c: The wings stop making enough lift
questions.f: A stall is about the angle of the wing to the air, not about the engine at all.

questions.q: Which part of a helicopter lets the pilot change the blades' bite in the air?
questions.f: Raising the collective tilts every blade at once and the helicopter rises.

questions.q: What is the main reason a submarine has a double hull on many designs?
c: An outer hull holds ballast around the strong inner hull
questions.f: The inner pressure hull is the one that must resist crushing depths.

questions.q: The Channel Tunnel contains three separate tunnels, not one.
questions.f: Two rail tunnels flank a smaller service tunnel used for maintenance and rescue.

questions.q: A worm gear can usually be driven backwards by its load.
questions.f: Its self-locking action is why worm gears are used in hoists and gates.

questions.q: An aircraft can stall even with its engines at full power.
questions.f: Stalling depends on the wing's angle to the airflow, not on thrust.

questions.q: LED lamps produce more light per watt than filament bulbs.
questions.f: That efficiency won its inventors a Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014.

questions.q: What is 'kinematics' the study of?
c: Motion of parts, without asking what causes it
questions.f: From Greek kinema, movement; the study of forces is called dynamics.

questions.q: What is a 'linkage' in a machine?
c: Bars joined by pivots that guide movement
questions.f: Windscreen wipers use a clever four-bar linkage to sweep back and forth.

questions.q: Which machine part seals a joint so oil or gas cannot escape?
questions.f: Head gaskets in engines must survive both furnace heat and huge pressure.

questions.q: What is a 'bushing' inside a machine?
c: A sleeve that a shaft turns inside
questions.f: Bushings are cheaper and quieter than ball bearings for slow-moving parts.

questions.q: What is the job of a heat sink in an electronic machine?
c: Carrying heat away from a hot chip
questions.f: Its fins give the air a huge surface to steal heat from.

questions.q: Why is a car's engine oil filter essential?
c: It traps grit that would grind the bearings
questions.f: A speck of metal a tenth of a millimetre wide can ruin a bearing.

questions.q: What does a spark plug actually do?
c: Jumps a spark to ignite the fuel and air
questions.f: That spark needs thousands of volts to leap the tiny gap.

questions.q: Which is measured in newton metres in a workshop?
questions.f: Mechanics use a torque wrench that clicks when the right tightness is reached.

questions.q: What is 'tyre pressure' usually measured in?
questions.f: A car tyre holds air at roughly twice the pressure of the air around you.

questions.q: Which machine converts electrical energy into sound?
questions.f: A coil in a magnetic field pushes a paper cone back and forth, shaking the air.

questions.q: A microphone and a loudspeaker are related because…?
c: Each is roughly the other working in reverse
questions.f: Shout into a small speaker and it really can act as a microphone.

questions.q: What does a transformer change in an electrical supply?
questions.f: Power lines carry electricity at high voltage because that wastes less energy.

questions.q: Why do power stations send electricity at very high voltage?
c: It loses less energy in the wires
questions.f: Higher voltage means smaller current, and smaller current heats the cable less.

questions.q: Which part of a wind turbine turns slow blade rotation into fast generator spin?
questions.f: Blades may turn 15 times a minute while the generator spins over 1,000.

questions.q: What does the yaw mechanism on a wind turbine do?
c: Turns the whole top to face the wind
questions.f: A small wind vane tells the controller which way to swing the machine.

questions.q: Which machine does a bicycle repairer use to true a buckled wheel?
questions.f: Tightening spokes on one side pulls the rim straight again.

questions.q: What is the 'gear inch' or gear ratio on a bike telling you?
c: How far one pedal turn moves you
How many teeth the chain has
questions.f: A high gear moves you further per pedal stroke but demands more push.

questions.q: Why do racing bicycles use very narrow, hard tyres?
c: Less of the tyre flexes, so less energy is lost
questions.f: Every squash and un-squash of rubber turns some of your effort into heat.

questions.q: What does a lift's counterweight do?
c: Balances the car so the motor works less
questions.f: The counterweight usually matches the car plus about 40% of a full load.

questions.q: Which safety device stops a lift if it descends too fast?
c: A governor-triggered brake on the guide rails
questions.f: Elisha Otis's spring-loaded pawls were the first version of this idea.

questions.q: What is 'ballast' on a ship for?
c: Weight low down to keep it steady
questions.f: Empty ships pump in seawater as ballast so they do not roll dangerously.

questions.q: What is the 'draught' of a ship?
c: How deep it sits in the water
questions.f: A ship with too deep a draught cannot enter a shallow harbour.

questions.q: Which machine keeps a ship's course steady without a human at the wheel?
questions.f: Ship autopilots have quietly steered vessels since the 1920s.

questions.q: What is a 'hydrofoil'?
c: A wing under a boat that lifts the hull clear of the water
questions.f: Lifting the hull out cuts drag hugely, so hydrofoils are very fast.

questions.q: Which vehicle uses an Archimedes-style screw or paddles to cross swamps?
questions.f: Screw-driven machines can crawl through mud where wheels sink hopelessly.

questions.q: Which of these machines was NOT invented in the 20th century?
questions.f: Practical sewing machines were selling well by the 1850s.

questions.q: Put these in order: which came FIRST?
questions.f: Trevithick's locomotive ran in 1804, Benz's car in 1886.

questions.q: Which of these machines does its work by removing material?
questions.f: That is called subtractive manufacturing, the opposite of 3D printing.

questions.q: How does an injection moulding machine make plastic toys?
c: Squirts melted plastic into a metal mould
questions.f: One mould can stamp out identical parts millions of times.

questions.q: What is a 'lathe' used for?
c: Spinning material while a tool shapes it
questions.f: Ancient Egyptians used a bow-driven lathe over 3,000 years ago.

questions.q: What does an air compressor store energy as?
questions.f: Release that air and it can drive drills, spray guns and tyre inflators.

questions.q: Which machine separates cream from milk by spinning it fast?
questions.f: Spinning throws heavier liquid outward, leaving lighter cream nearer the middle.

questions.q: Why do escalator steps flatten out at the top and bottom?
c: So passengers can step on and off safely
questions.f: The steps run on two sets of rails that gradually change the tread angle.

questions.q: What is 'tolerance' in engineering?
c: How much a part may differ from its exact size
questions.f: Jet engine parts are often made to within a hundredth of a millimetre.

questions.q: Which tool measures thickness far more precisely than a ruler?
questions.f: Its fine screw thread turns a tiny movement into a big, readable turn.

questions.q: A hydrofoil boat rises out of the water as it speeds up.
questions.f: Underwater wings generate lift just as an aeroplane's wings do in air.

questions.q: Which two engineers, working separately in Britain and Germany, developed the jet engine?
c: Frank Whittle and Hans von Ohain
Ernst Heinkel and Geoffrey de Havilland
questions.f: Von Ohain's engine flew first, in 1939; Whittle had patented the idea back in 1930.

questions.q: Robert Goddard's 1926 machine, which rose just 12 metres, was the first working…?
questions.f: Newspapers had mocked him for claiming a rocket could work in the vacuum of space.

questions.q: Christopher Cockerell tested his hovercraft idea in the 1950s using…?
c: Two tin cans and a hairdryer
A bathtub and a fan heater
A vacuum cleaner and a kite
questions.f: The air blown through the narrow gap between the cans proved his cushion theory.

questions.q: Unimate, installed at a General Motors plant in 1961, was the world's first…?
c: Industrial robot on a production line
questions.f: It weighed nearly two tonnes and stacked hot die-cast metal parts.

questions.q: Which writer coined the word 'robotics' and set out its famous Three Laws?
questions.f: He assumed the word already existed, and was surprised to learn he had invented it.

questions.q: Whose 1888 drive of 106 km became the first long journey by motor car?
questions.f: She cleaned a blocked fuel line with a hat pin and used a garter as insulation.

questions.q: Mary Anderson's 1903 patent covered an early version of which car device?
questions.f: Carmakers rejected it as a distraction; within 20 years it was standard.

questions.q: Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin designed which life-saving device, then let rivals use it free?
questions.f: Volvo opened the patent in 1959 because sharing it would save more lives.

questions.q: Percy Shaw's 1934 invention that made night driving safer is known as…?
questions.f: His rubber studs even wipe themselves clean when a tyre presses them down.

questions.q: Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot's 1769 machine is often called the first…?
questions.f: His steam wagon was built to haul cannon and moved at walking pace.

questions.q: Gottlieb Daimler's 1885 'Reitwagen' was essentially the first…?
questions.f: Its name means 'riding wagon', and it had two small outrigger wheels for balance.

questions.q: Which mathematician wrote what is regarded as the first computer program, for Babbage's Analytical Engine?
questions.f: Her notes described how the machine could compute Bernoulli numbers, and even make music.

questions.q: Which machine did Herman Hollerith build to speed up the 1890 US census?
questions.f: His company later became part of IBM.

questions.q: ENIAC, switched on in 1945, did its calculations using around 18,000…?
questions.f: Replacing burnt-out tubes was a daily chore for its operators.

questions.q: Which component, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, replaced the vacuum tube?
questions.f: It won Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.q: Douglas Engelbart demonstrated which machine at his 1968 'Mother of All Demos'?
questions.f: His prototype was a wooden box with two metal wheels underneath.

questions.q: The company name 'Xerox' comes from a process name meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek xeros (dry) and graphein (to write); Chester Carlson's copier used no wet ink.

questions.q: What does the acronym LASER stand for?
c: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Angle Scattering and Energy Reflection
questions.f: An earlier device using microwaves instead of light was called a maser.

questions.q: The unit of sound level, the decibel, is named in honour of which inventor?
questions.f: A decibel is one tenth of a bel, the larger unit named for him.

questions.q: The Mach number, used for supersonic speed, honours which physicist?
questions.f: Mach photographed shock waves around speeding bullets in the 1880s.

questions.q: An aircraft's 'empennage' means its tail unit, from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: Arrows are feathered for the same reason: it keeps them flying straight.

questions.q: Small wings mounted ahead of the main wing are called 'canards' because the word means…?
questions.f: Early aircraft with front wings looked like a duck flying with neck outstretched.

questions.q: An engine pod hung under a wing is a 'nacelle', from a word meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin navicella, a small ship — the shape reminded people of a hull.

questions.q: A 'monocoque' structure gets its strength from…?
questions.f: French for 'single shell'; an egg and a racing car chassis work the same way.

questions.q: A railway's overhead wire system is called the 'catenary', from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: A hanging chain forms the exact curve mathematicians call a catenary.

questions.q: The 'pantograph' on an electric train shares its name with a copying device meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek pan (all) and graphein (to write); both use hinged parallel arms.

questions.q: A 'funicular' railway takes its name from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Two cars balance on one cable, so each helps haul the other up the slope.

questions.q: 'Semaphore' signalling is built from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: From sema (sign) and phoros (bearing) — arms or flags that carry a message.

questions.q: The word 'juggernaut', now used for huge lorries, comes from…?
c: a great temple chariot in India
questions.f: English travellers borrowed it from Jagannath, whose festival cart is enormous.

questions.q: The word 'sabotage' is often traced to a French word for…?
questions.f: 'Sabot' means clog; the link to clumsy or deliberate damage stuck to the word.

questions.q: 'Escalator' began life as a trademark built from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From scala, stairs; because the brand name became generic, anyone can use it now.

questions.q: The road surface 'tarmac' takes half its name from which engineer?
questions.f: Tar was added to McAdam's crushed-stone roads to stop cars kicking up dust.

questions.q: The ballpoint pen is called a 'biro' in many countries after…?
questions.f: He noticed newspaper ink dried fast, and designed a pen to use a thicker ink.

questions.q: The vacuum flask brand 'Thermos' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: James Dewar invented the flask for laboratory work and never patented it.

questions.q: An absurdly complicated machine that does a simple job is called a…?
questions.f: In Britain the same idea is called a Heath Robinson contraption, after another cartoonist.

questions.q: The word 'cybernetics' is built on a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek kybernetes; the same root, through Latin, gives us the word 'govern'.

questions.q: A 'servo' motor takes its name from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: A servo obediently moves to whatever position it is commanded to hold.

questions.q: What is an 'actuator' in a machine?
c: The part that turns a signal into movement
questions.f: From Latin actuare, to put into action; muscles are the body's actuators.

questions.q: 'Telemetry' means…?
c: measuring at a distance and sending the data
questions.f: Formula 1 teams read hundreds of telemetry channels while the car is on track.

questions.q: 'Ergonomics' is built from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: From ergon (work) and nomos (law) — designing machines to suit human bodies.

questions.q: A machine described as 'autonomous' literally has…?
questions.f: From Greek autos (self) and nomos (law), so it governs itself.

questions.q: What is the difference between welding and soldering?
c: Welding melts the parts themselves; soldering melts only the filler
Welding uses glue; soldering uses heat
questions.f: Brazing sits in between, using a filler that melts hotter than solder.

questions.q: What is the true difference between an autogyro and a helicopter?
c: An autogyro's rotor is turned by airflow, not the engine
An autogyro has no engine at all
questions.f: An autogyro's engine drives a propeller; the rotor freewheels, so it cannot hover.

questions.q: Why can a rocket accelerate in space while a jet engine cannot work there?
c: A rocket carries its own oxidiser
questions.f: Jet engines must breathe outside air; rockets bring everything they burn.

questions.q: What does a turboprop engine use its turbine mainly to do?
questions.f: Turboprops are more efficient than jets at lower speeds and heights.

questions.q: In a high-bypass turbofan, most of the thrust comes from…?
c: Air pushed by the big front fan
questions.f: That is why modern airliner engines are so wide and comparatively quiet.

questions.q: What does Pascal's principle make possible in a hydraulic machine?
c: A small force on a small piston lifts a big load
questions.f: Press on 1 cm2 and a piston 100 times bigger gives 100 times the force.

questions.q: Which principle explains why an object floats when it displaces its own weight in water?
questions.f: Legend says Archimedes worked it out in his bath and ran out shouting 'Eureka!'.

questions.q: Why can no heat engine be 100% efficient, even in theory?
c: Some heat must always be dumped to a cooler place
questions.f: Sadi Carnot proved this limit in 1824, before engines were well understood.

questions.q: What is the key difference between power and torque?
c: Torque is twisting force; power is how fast work is done
Power is measured in newton metres
questions.f: Power equals torque multiplied by rotational speed.

questions.q: Which locomotive holds the world speed record for steam, set in 1938?
questions.f: It hit 126 mph down Stoke Bank and damaged a bearing doing it.

questions.q: In 2007 a modified French TGV set a wheeled-rail speed record of about…?
questions.f: The run used bigger wheels, a shortened train and an overhead wire at extra voltage.

questions.q: Japan's first Shinkansen line opened in which year?
questions.f: It opened days before the Tokyo Olympics and halved the Tokyo-Osaka journey.

questions.q: What was unusual about Concorde's nose?
c: It drooped down for take-off and landing
questions.f: The sharp nose was great for speed but blocked the pilots' view of the runway.

questions.q: Which aircraft is the fastest air-breathing crewed jet ever flown?
questions.f: Its panels fitted loosely on the ground, sealing only when heat expanded them in flight.

questions.q: Which cargo aircraft, with six engines, was the heaviest ever built?
questions.f: Only one was ever completed; its name means 'dream' in Ukrainian.

questions.q: How did the Harrier jump jet take off vertically?
questions.f: Four swivelling nozzles let the pilot point the engine's blast wherever it was needed.

questions.q: Which two aviators made the first non-stop flight across the Atlantic, in 1919?
questions.f: They flew a converted bomber and landed in an Irish bog, nose-first.

questions.q: Who flew solo from Britain to Australia in 1930 in a second-hand biplane?
questions.f: She had only about 85 hours of flying experience when she set off.

questions.q: Which pilot became the first African-American woman to earn a pilot's licence, in 1921?
questions.f: She had to travel to France to train, because US schools refused her.

questions.q: Which spacecraft made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet?
questions.f: Mars air is so thin its blades had to spin about 2,500 times a minute.

questions.q: Lunokhod 1, landed in 1970, was the first successful…?
questions.f: It was steered from Earth despite a radio delay of a couple of seconds.

questions.q: How does the Curiosity rover generate electricity on Mars?
questions.f: That is why it keeps working through dust storms and long Martian nights.

questions.q: What is an ion thruster's great advantage for deep-space missions?
c: Tiny thrust but astonishing fuel economy
questions.f: An ion engine's push feels like a sheet of paper resting on your hand, but it never stops.

questions.q: The Plimsoll line painted on a ship's hull shows…?
c: How deeply it may safely be loaded
questions.f: Samuel Plimsoll fought for it so hard he was nicknamed 'the sailor's friend'.

questions.q: Brunel's SS Great Britain of 1843 was the first ship to combine…?
c: An iron hull with a screw propeller for Atlantic crossings
A steel keel and paddle wheels
questions.f: She is now preserved in the very Bristol dock where she was built.

questions.q: Malcolm McLean's 1956 voyage of the Ideal X launched which idea?
questions.f: Standard boxes cut the cost of loading a ship by more than 90%.

questions.q: Which vessel carried two men to the deepest point of the ocean in 1960?
questions.f: They reached nearly 11 km down, and saw the window crack on the way.

questions.q: Which clockmaker's marine chronometer H4 finally solved the longitude problem?
questions.f: Knowing the exact time at home lets a sailor calculate how far east or west they are.

questions.q: An autogyro cannot hover in still air the way a helicopter can.
questions.f: Its rotor needs airflow through it, which means the machine must keep moving.

questions.q: Volvo gave away the patent for the three-point seat belt.
questions.f: The company decided the invention was too important to keep to itself.

questions.q: The word 'govern' and the word 'cybernetics' come from the same root.
questions.f: Both trace back to Greek kybernetes, a ship's steersman.

questions.q: A high-bypass turbofan gets most of its thrust from the burning core.
questions.f: Most thrust comes from cool air pushed round the core by the big front fan.

questions.q: Ion thrusters produce less push than the weight of a coin.
questions.f: But they can run for years, eventually reaching enormous speeds.

questions.q: What is a 'coxswain', a word built from older parts meaning…?
questions.f: A 'cock' was a small ship's boat; the swain was the lad who looked after it.

questions.q: The word 'pilot' traces back to a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek pedon; sea pilots existed centuries before anyone flew.

questions.q: A 'fathom' of depth, about 1.8 m, originally meant…?
questions.f: Sailors measured a sounding line by hauling it in arm-span by arm-span.

questions.q: On a ship, the 'binnacle' is the case that houses which instrument?
questions.f: From Latin habitaculum, a little dwelling — a small house for the compass.

questions.q: A car's 'boot' is named after which part of a horse-drawn coach?
c: The locker where the coachman sat and stored goods
questions.f: Americans kept a different image and call it the trunk, after strapped-on travel trunks.

questions.q: Which word describes a car body style whose name means 'little leap' in French?
questions.f: The original cabriolet was a light carriage that bounced along on its springs.

questions.q: The 'limousine' is thought to be named after…?
c: a French region whose cloaks resembled the roof
questions.f: Drivers of early ones sat outside under a hood shaped like a Limousin shepherd's cloak.

questions.q: What does the engineering term 'calibrate' mean?
c: Adjust an instrument against a known standard
questions.f: It comes from 'calibre', the exact bore of a tube or barrel.

questions.q: In machine design, what is 'redundancy'?
c: Spare systems that take over if one fails
questions.f: Airliners carry several independent hydraulic systems for exactly this reason.

questions.q: What does 'fail-safe' mean in engineering?
c: If it fails, it fails into a safe state
questions.f: Railway signals go red when power is lost, which is a classic fail-safe.

questions.q: What is a 'feedback loop' in a control system?
c: Output is measured and used to adjust the input
questions.f: Watt's steam governor was an early mechanical feedback loop.

questions.q: Which term describes designing a machine so it wears out sooner than it need?
questions.f: The phrase spread in the 1930s and is still argued about today.

questions.q: What is 'backlash' in a gear train?
c: The small free play between meshing teeth
questions.f: Precision machines use anti-backlash gears so a command moves the tool exactly.

questions.q: What does a 'Cardan' or universal joint let a drive shaft do?
questions.f: It is named after Gerolamo Cardano, who described the linkage in the 1500s.

questions.q: Which mechanism keeps a ship's compass or a camera level as its mount tilts?
questions.f: 'Gimbal' comes from a Latin word for twin, because the rings come in pairs.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a Watt or 'parallel motion' linkage?
c: Guiding a piston rod in a straight line
questions.f: Watt called it one of his most ingenious ideas, though not his most famous.

questions.q: What is 'cavitation', a problem for ship propellers?
c: Bubbles forming and collapsing, pitting the metal
questions.f: Collapsing bubbles hammer the surface hard enough to chew holes in steel.

questions.q: Why do engineers worry about 'metal fatigue' in aircraft?
c: Repeated flexing can crack metal below its normal strength
questions.f: Aircraft are inspected on a strict schedule of flight cycles for this reason.

questions.q: What is 'resonance' in a machine?
c: Vibration growing when driven at a natural frequency
questions.f: Engineers deliberately shift a machine's natural frequency away from its running speed.

questions.q: Which type of motor is easiest to control precisely, step by step?
questions.f: 3D printers and scanners rely on steppers to move exact fractions of a turn.

questions.q: What does an inverter do in an electric vehicle?
c: Turns battery DC into AC for the motor
Charges the battery from the brakes
questions.f: Changing the AC frequency is how the controller sets the motor's speed.

questions.q: Why do maglev trains have no wheels touching the track at speed?
c: Magnetic forces hold them above the guideway
questions.f: With no wheel contact, the main resistance left is the air itself.

questions.q: What is the main job of a 'flywheel energy storage' system?
questions.f: Some are spun in a vacuum on magnetic bearings to cut losses to almost nothing.

questions.q: How does a Stirling engine differ from a steam engine?
c: It seals the same gas inside and cycles it
It burns fuel in the cylinder
It uses no heat at all
questions.f: A Stirling engine will run on any heat source, even a cup of hot tea.

questions.q: What was unusual about the Wankel engine used in some cars?
c: A triangular rotor replaced the pistons
questions.f: The rotor sweeps a figure-of-eight chamber, giving very smooth running.

questions.q: What does a car's catalytic converter do?
c: Turns harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones
questions.f: It uses precious metals such as platinum as the catalyst — no fuel is burnt.

questions.q: How does a crumple zone protect people in a crash?
c: It folds up, spreading the stop over more time
questions.f: Bela Barenyi patented the idea in the 1950s, when stiff cars were thought safest.

questions.q: A Stirling engine can be powered by any source of heat.
questions.f: Working models will run on a mug of hot water or the warmth of a hand.

questions.q: Cavitation damages propellers by forming and collapsing bubbles.
questions.f: Ship designers shape blades carefully to delay it to higher speeds.

questions.q: A shipworm boring neat tunnels through timber, iron frames pushed forward inch by inch, and a twice-flooded crossing under the Thames gave engineering which invention?
questions.f: Marc Brunel copied the worm's protective tube; every big tunnel machine descends from it.

questions.q: A 1,500-tonne uninvited yacht, a royal naval review at Spithead in 1897, and a dash at 34 knots past every chasing launch announced which new machine?
questions.f: Charles Parsons' Turbinia embarrassed the Royal Navy into adopting turbines within years.

questions.q: An elephant-shaped water clock, a hand-washing figure that offered soap, and a Baghdad book of 'ingenious devices' point to which engineer?
questions.f: His 1206 treatise described about 50 machines, including early crankshafts and pumps.

questions.q: A poem by Robert Burns about a short garment, a race to bring the first tea of the season home, and a fast iron-framed hull identify which ship?
questions.f: 'Cutty sark' is Scots for a short shift; she is preserved in dry dock at Greenwich.

questions.q: A wingspan of 97 metres, mostly birch rather than the wood in its nickname, and a single one-mile hop in 1947 describe which aircraft?
questions.f: Nicknamed the Spruce Goose, it held the wingspan record for nearly 70 years.

questions.q: 5,127 prototypes, a frustration with clogged bags, and a spinning column of air borrowed from sawmills led to which machine?
questions.f: James Dyson took five years of models before the cyclone worked well enough to sell.

questions.q: Which businessman's name became the standard word for the machine that smooths ice rinks?
questions.f: He built the first one from a war-surplus tractor chassis in 1949.

questions.q: Which safety system, patented by George Westinghouse in 1869, transformed railways?
questions.f: Because it fails on when air is lost, a snapped pipe stops the whole train.

questions.q: Standard railway gauge, used on most of the world's tracks, measures…?
questions.f: Brunel's rival 7-foot broad gauge rode better but lost the battle for standardisation.

questions.q: What made Stephenson's Rocket so much better than earlier locomotives?
c: A multi-tube boiler that raised steam quickly
questions.f: Twenty-five copper tubes ran through the water, hugely increasing the heated surface.

questions.q: What is a 'bogie' on a railway vehicle?
c: A pivoting frame carrying a set of wheels
questions.f: Bogies let long carriages swing round curves that a rigid wheelbase could never take.

questions.q: Why does the Boeing 747 have a hump on its upper deck?
c: The nose was designed to open for cargo, so the cockpit sat above
questions.f: Boeing expected supersonic jets to take over passengers, leaving the 747 as a freighter.

questions.q: Which airliner, entering service in 1952, was the world's first jet-powered passenger aircraft?
questions.f: Its square windows taught engineers a hard lesson about metal fatigue at corners.

questions.q: What does 'fly-by-wire' mean in a modern aircraft?
c: Controls send electrical signals to computers, not cables to surfaces
The pilot flies using autopilot only
Radio commands come from the ground
questions.f: Computers can filter out commands that would overstress the aircraft.

questions.q: Who invented the flight data recorder, the so-called black box, in the 1950s?
questions.f: He was Australian, and his first unit was ignored for years before being adopted worldwide.

questions.q: Why is an aircraft cabin pressurised in flight?
c: Outside air is far too thin to breathe
To hold the fuselage shape only
questions.f: At cruising height the cabin feels like standing on a 2,000-metre mountain.

questions.q: What did the Apollo Guidance Computer store its permanent program in?
questions.f: Women at a Massachusetts factory literally wove the software by threading wires.

questions.q: How does an ablative heat shield protect a returning capsule?
c: It slowly burns and flakes away, carrying heat off
It conducts heat into the cabin
questions.f: Sacrificing the outer layer keeps the structure beneath surprisingly cool.

questions.q: Which crewed spacecraft design has flown longer than any other, since 1967?
questions.f: Soyuz has been repeatedly updated but keeps its original three-module layout.

questions.q: How does a hydrogen fuel cell make electricity?
c: Hydrogen and oxygen combine, giving current and water
Hydrogen is burned in a turbine
questions.f: The only exhaust is water vapour, which is why buses and trains are trying it.

questions.q: What does wireless charging use to pass energy to a phone?
questions.f: One coil's changing magnetic field makes a current flow in the other, with no contact.

questions.q: What does an engine's 'displacement' measure?
c: The total volume swept by all its pistons
questions.f: A 2.0-litre engine sweeps two litres of air and fuel every two turns.

questions.q: What does 'compression ratio' compare in an engine?
c: Cylinder volume at the bottom versus the top of the stroke
questions.f: Diesels run ratios around 20:1, which is why they need no spark.

questions.q: In an engine described as a 'V8', what does the V refer to?
c: Two banks of cylinders set at an angle
questions.f: A V layout makes an eight-cylinder engine much shorter than a straight one.

questions.q: What does a Venturi tube do to a fluid passing through its narrow throat?
c: Speeds it up and lowers its pressure
questions.f: Named after Giovanni Venturi; carburettors used the effect to draw in fuel.

questions.q: Which water turbine uses jets striking cups on a wheel's rim?
questions.f: Lester Pelton's split-cup design turns a high, narrow jet into remarkable efficiency.

questions.q: Which measuring device is named after the French mathematician who devised its sliding scale?
questions.f: Pierre Vernier's 1631 scale lets you read a fraction of the smallest division.

questions.q: The four-stroke petrol engine cycle is often named after which German engineer?
questions.f: Otto's 1876 engine made the four-stroke idea practical and commercially successful.

questions.q: A 'reciprocating' engine is one whose main parts…?
questions.f: From Latin reciprocus, moving to and fro; a rotary engine does not reciprocate.

questions.q: What does 'technology' literally mean, from its Greek roots?
c: the study of craft or skill
questions.f: From tekhne (craft, art) and logia (study of).

questions.q: 'Jettison' and 'jetsam' share a root with 'jet' that means…?
questions.f: Latin jactare, to throw; jetsam is cargo thrown overboard.

questions.q: 'Viaduct' literally means…?
questions.f: From Latin via (way) and ducere (to lead), on the pattern of aqueduct.

questions.q: 'Synchronous' machines are so called because the word means…?
questions.f: From Greek syn (together) and chronos (time).

questions.q: The root 'tract' in 'tractor', 'traction' and 'retract' means…?
questions.f: Latin trahere; a tractor draws a plough, and retracting draws something back.

questions.q: The root 'lev' in 'lever', 'elevator' and 'levitate' means…?
questions.f: Latin levis (light) and levare (to raise) sit behind all three words.

questions.q: The root 'rot' in 'rotor', 'rotate' and 'rotary' means…?
questions.f: Latin rota, a wheel; a rotunda is a round building for the same reason.

questions.q: 'Manual', 'manufacture' and 'manipulate' all contain a root meaning…?
questions.f: Latin manus; a manual was originally a handbook.

questions.q: A 'chronometer' is precisely what kind of machine?
questions.f: The name combines Greek chronos (time) and metron (measure).

questions.q: A railway air brake applies itself if the air pipe is broken.
questions.f: Westinghouse's design keeps brakes off with pressure, so losing pressure stops the train.

questions.q: The Spruce Goose flew more than a hundred times before being retired.
questions.f: It made a single short hop in 1947 and never flew again.

questions.q: A Pelton wheel is driven by water jets rather than submerged flow.
questions.f: That suits mountain schemes where water falls a long way down a narrow pipe.

questions.q: Modern airliner cabins are kept at the same pressure as sea level.
questions.f: They sit at roughly the pressure found 1,800-2,400 m up a mountain.

questions.q: Which lever class has the effort applied between the fulcrum and the load?
questions.f: Tweezers and a fishing rod are third-class levers; they trade force for reach.

questions.q: A nutcracker and a wheelbarrow are both examples of which lever class?
questions.f: In a second-class lever the load sits between the fulcrum and your effort.

questions.q: If a pulley system has four rope sections supporting a load, the ideal effort needed is…?
questions.f: You must pull four times as much rope, so total work stays the same.

questions.q: What is the ideal mechanical advantage of a ramp 5 m long rising 1 m?
questions.f: You push with a fifth of the force but over five times the distance.

questions.q: In physics, what does 'work' equal?
questions.f: Hold a heavy box still and, in this strict sense, you do no work at all.

questions.q: Power is best defined as…?
c: The rate at which work is done
questions.f: One watt is one joule of work every second.

questions.q: Why is a machine's real efficiency always below its ideal figure?
c: Friction and heat lose some energy
questions.f: Even superb gearboxes lose a couple of percent as warmth and noise.

questions.q: What does 'degrees of freedom' describe in a robot arm?
c: The number of independent ways it can move
questions.f: Six degrees of freedom lets a gripper reach any position at any angle.

questions.q: What is a robot's 'end effector'?
c: The tool or gripper at the tip of the arm
questions.f: Swap the end effector and the same arm can weld, paint or pack eggs.

questions.q: What is 'teleoperation'?
c: A human controlling a machine from a distance
questions.f: Bomb-disposal and deep-sea robots are usually teleoperated in real time.

questions.q: What does the Turing test try to judge?
c: Whether a machine's replies are indistinguishable from a person's
How much memory a machine needs
questions.f: Alan Turing proposed it in 1950 as a way round arguing about the word 'thinking'.

questions.q: Which surgical robot system lets a surgeon operate through tiny incisions from a console?
questions.f: The system scales the surgeon's hand movements down and cancels out tremor.

questions.q: What do warehouse robots such as the Kiva system famously do?
c: Carry whole shelving units to a human picker
questions.f: Instead of workers walking to shelves, the shelves come to the workers.

questions.q: Which of Asimov's Three Laws comes first?
c: A robot may not injure a human being
A robot must tell the truth
questions.f: Each later law is subordinate to the one before it, which drives all his plots.

questions.q: What is a 'cobot' designed to do?
questions.f: Cobots sense contact and stop, so they need no safety cage.

questions.q: Which sensor, spinning a laser to build a 3D map, is central to many self-driving cars?
questions.f: The name combines 'light' with 'radar'.

questions.q: What is an 'inertial measurement unit' used for on aircraft and rockets?
c: Sensing acceleration and rotation to track motion
questions.f: It can navigate with no outside signal at all, which matters in space.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a machine's 'governor', in modern terms?
questions.f: Governors on scooters and buses cap top speed for safety and legality.

questions.q: Why do submarines running quietly prefer electric propulsion underwater?
c: Electric motors are far quieter than engines
questions.f: Diesel engines also need outside air, which is impossible when submerged.

questions.q: What does a submarine's 'snorkel' allow it to do?
c: Run diesel engines while just below the surface
questions.f: A mast draws in air and vents exhaust while the hull stays hidden.

questions.q: How do icebreaker ships clear thick ice?
c: Their sloped bow rides up and crushes it with weight
They blast it with water jets
questions.f: Many can also rock side to side by pumping water between tanks.

questions.q: What is 'deadweight tonnage' a measure of?
c: How much cargo, fuel and crew a ship can carry
questions.f: It is quoted in tonnes and tells you a merchant ship's real earning capacity.

questions.q: Why is the Suez Canal built without locks, unlike Panama?
c: It crosses nearly flat land at sea level
questions.f: Both ends open onto seas of almost the same height, so ships sail straight through.

questions.q: What does a ship's 'azimuth thruster' or pod drive allow?
c: Thrust to be pointed in any direction
questions.f: Cruise ships can spin almost on the spot, so many need no tugs to dock.

questions.q: What is a 'gantry' crane?
c: A crane on a frame that straddles its load
A crane fixed to a wall
A crane inside a lift shaft
questions.f: Container ports use gantry cranes that stride over ships and railway tracks.

questions.q: What does a tower crane operator use the 'jib' for?
c: The horizontal arm that carries the load
questions.f: The trolley runs along the jib to move a load in and out.

questions.q: Why does an excavator use hydraulics rather than cables today?
c: Oil pressure gives huge, precise force in a small space
questions.f: Liquids barely compress, so a pump's push arrives almost instantly at the ram.

questions.q: What is a 'slew ring' on an excavator or crane?
c: The big bearing letting the top rotate on the base
questions.f: It carries the whole upper machine's weight while letting it spin freely.

questions.q: How does a tunnel boring machine support the tunnel behind it as it advances?
c: It erects curved concrete segments into a ring
It relies on the rock alone
questions.f: The machine also pushes off those completed rings to drive itself forward.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a car's 'limited-slip differential'?
c: Sending torque to the wheel with grip
questions.f: An ordinary differential would send power to whichever wheel spins uselessly.

questions.q: What does a continuously variable transmission use instead of fixed gears?
c: A belt running on cone-shaped pulleys
questions.f: Changing the pulley diameters gives an unlimited number of ratios.

questions.q: Why did the original Mini's designer put its engine sideways?
c: To leave more of the body for passengers
questions.f: Alec Issigonis even hid the gearbox in the sump to save more space.

questions.q: What is unusual about the Volkswagen Beetle's original engine?
c: It was air-cooled and mounted at the rear
questions.f: No radiator meant nothing to freeze, which suited cold-climate owners.

questions.q: How does a hybrid car's engine avoid wasting fuel in traffic?
c: It shuts off and the electric motor takes over
questions.f: City driving suits hybrids best, which is the opposite of most engines.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'wastegate' on a turbocharged engine?
c: Letting exhaust bypass the turbine to limit boost
questions.f: Without it, boost pressure could climb until the engine damaged itself.

questions.q: Which of these best describes an 'intercooler'?
c: A radiator that cools air after the turbocharger
questions.f: Cooler air is denser, so more oxygen fits into each cylinder.

questions.q: What does a car's 'crumple zone' deliberately sacrifice to protect people?
c: The structure at the front and rear
questions.f: The passenger cell stays rigid while everything around it folds up.

questions.q: How quickly must an airbag inflate to be useful?
c: In about 30 thousandths of a second
questions.f: A chemical reaction produces nitrogen gas almost explosively fast.

questions.q: What is 'brake fade'?
c: Loss of braking power as parts overheat
questions.f: Long descents are safer in a low gear, letting the engine do some braking.

questions.q: Why do heavy lorries often use compressed-air brakes rather than hydraulic ones?
c: Air is easy to store, pipe and top up along a long vehicle
Air brakes are cheaper to build
questions.f: That hiss when a lorry stops is air venting from the brake system.

questions.q: How does a 'jake brake' or engine brake slow a heavy truck?
c: It opens exhaust valves so the engine resists compression
It sprays water on the discs
questions.f: That loud staccato bark on a downhill road is the engine brake at work.

questions.q: Which of these did Ford's moving assembly line NOT change?
c: The time to build a car
questions.f: Ford famously doubled wages to $5 a day to keep workers on the fast line.

questions.q: What is 'just-in-time' manufacturing designed to reduce?
c: Stockpiles of parts waiting in the factory
questions.f: Toyota developed the idea so parts arrive exactly when they are needed.

questions.q: What is a 'jig' in a workshop?
c: A guide that holds work and directs the tool
questions.f: Jigs make the hundredth part as accurate as the first.

questions.q: What does electroplating do to a machine part?
c: Coats it in a thin metal layer using electricity
questions.f: Chrome bumpers and gold connector pins are both electroplated.

questions.q: Why are some steel parts 'quenched' after heating?
questions.f: Blacksmiths judged the moment by the colour of the glowing metal.

questions.q: What does a 'go/no-go gauge' tell a machinist?
c: Whether a part is within its allowed size range
questions.f: One end should slip on, the other should not — a fast, foolproof check.

questions.q: Which machine is used to bend sheet metal along a straight line?
questions.f: A long blade presses the sheet into a V-shaped die to make a crisp fold.

questions.q: What does an EDM (electrical discharge machining) tool cut with?
questions.f: Sparks erode metal so precisely that EDM can cut hardened steel into puzzle shapes.

questions.q: How does a water-jet cutter slice through steel plate?
c: Water at very high pressure carrying abrasive grit
questions.f: The jet can be thinner than a pencil lead and never heats the metal.

questions.q: An ordinary differential sends most torque to the wheel with the least grip.
questions.f: That is exactly why limited-slip and locking differentials were invented.

questions.q: Alan Turing's test judges a machine by its conversation, not its calculations.
questions.f: He suggested it in a 1950 paper that opened with the question 'Can machines think?'.

questions.q: The Suez Canal uses a series of locks to lift ships over high ground.
questions.f: Panama needs locks; Suez runs at sea level from end to end.

questions.q: A cobot is designed to share a workspace with people without a safety cage.
questions.f: Force sensors let it stop the instant it feels unexpected contact.

questions.q: What was the significance of the Ideal X, the Turbinia and the Rocket alike?
c: Each demonstrated a technology that transformed transport
Each set a world speed record
Each was built in the same decade
questions.f: Containers, turbines and multi-tube boilers each reshaped how goods and people move.

questions.q: A 200-guinea prize in a Piccadilly shop window, 67 years of failed attempts, and an American who needed 51 hours to win it all concern a lock made by which engineer?
questions.f: Bramah also invented the hydraulic press and the beer engine that pulls pints today.

questions.q: A bitter quarrel with a toolmaker, a machine meant to print error-free logarithm tables, and half a brain now on show in London point to which inventor?
questions.f: His Difference Engine was to calculate AND print, removing human copying mistakes.

questions.q: Bones softened for a Royal Society dinner, the very first safety valve, and a piston pulled down by condensing steam all credit which inventor?
questions.f: His 1679 'steam digester' was the ancestor of both the pressure cooker and the steam engine.

questions.q: A method of making a truly flat surface by rubbing three plates together, a measuring machine reading a millionth of an inch, and Britain's first standard screw thread belong to whom?
questions.f: His 1841 thread standard meant a nut from one workshop finally fitted a bolt from another.

questions.q: A bench micrometer nicknamed the 'Lord Chancellor', a screw-cutting lathe, and an apprentice list including Whitworth and Nasmyth describe which machine-tool pioneer?
questions.f: Maudslay's lathe let engineers cut accurate screw threads for the very first time.

questions.q: A wig-maker turned mill owner, a spinning frame too heavy for human muscle, and a village mill at Cromford working night and day point to which figure?
questions.f: Cromford Mill of 1771 is often called the world's first true factory.

questions.q: A machine named after a crossbred animal, because it combined two rivals' inventions, spun fine thread from around 1779. What was it?
questions.f: Samuel Crompton's mule crossed Hargreaves' jenny with Arkwright's water frame.

questions.q: A parson's knitting frame of 1589, a queen who refused him a patent, and a flight to France to find backers concern which inventor?
questions.f: Elizabeth I reportedly wanted finer silk stockings before she would grant protection.

questions.q: Parts borrowed from a church organ's soundboard, seed sown in tidy rows, and a Berkshire farmer's 1701 machine describe which invention?
questions.f: Jethro Tull adapted organ mechanisms so his drill dropped seed at an even rate.

questions.q: A three-point linkage still used on farms, a handshake deal with Henry Ford that ended in a huge lawsuit, and the first Irishman to fly his own aircraft point to whom?
questions.f: His linkage let a tractor and its implement act as one machine, transforming ploughing.

questions.q: Sticky prairie soil, a broken sawmill blade polished into a curved blade, and an 1837 Illinois blacksmith's shop gave farming which machine?
questions.f: John Deere's smooth steel shed the soil instead of clogging like cast iron.

questions.q: A loom that halted itself the instant a thread snapped, a patent sold to a Lancashire firm, and the money used to found a car company point to which family?
questions.f: Sakichi Toyoda's 'stop on fault' idea became a founding principle of Toyota production.

questions.q: Piston rings rejected as too rough, surplus engines strapped to bicycles in post-war Japan, and a company logo with wings describe which founder?
questions.f: He failed a supplier's quality test, went back to school, and got the rings right.

questions.q: A pair of overlapping herringbone gear teeth became the badge of which car maker?
questions.f: Andre Citroen's double chevron logo pictures the double-helical gears he first manufactured.

questions.q: Motors built into the wheel hubs, a petrol engine used only to generate current, and an 1900 Paris Exposition sensation describe which early machine?
questions.f: Ferdinand Porsche built a working series hybrid over a century before they became fashionable.

questions.q: A bronze vessel ringed with eight dragon heads, a ball released to show a distant tremor's direction, and an astronomer of the Han court gave us which machine?
questions.f: Zhang Heng's device of 132 AD is the earliest known earthquake detector.

questions.q: A water-driven tower in Kaifeng, a chain of buckets tipping in strict turn, and the earliest known escapement mechanism belong to which engineer?
questions.f: His 1088 clock tower kept time with an escapement 200 years before European clocks.

questions.q: A cart carrying a figure whose arm always pointed the same way, a gear train working out the difference between two wheels, and no magnet anywhere describe which machine?
questions.f: Chinese engineers achieved with gearing what a compass does with magnetism.

questions.q: A ninth-century Baghdad book of about a hundred devices, trick jugs, and a flute player driven by a rotating cylinder describe whose work?
questions.f: Their programmable flute machine is sometimes called the first mechanical sequencer.

questions.q: A Roman writer's ten books on architecture describe a cart that dropped a pebble into a box each time a wheel turned. What machine was that?
questions.f: Vitruvius's design counted distance mechanically about 2,000 years ago.

questions.q: A record of 70.86 mph on water in 1919, a tetrahedral kite big enough to lift a man, and a Boston school for deaf children all involve which inventor?
questions.f: His hydrofoil HD-4 held the world marine speed record for a decade.

questions.q: A wooden screw that snapped in half and made the boat go faster, and an 1845 tug-of-war that a paddle steamer lost, helped prove which invention?
questions.f: Francis Pettit Smith's accident showed a shorter, single-turn propeller worked far better.

questions.q: A passenger saloon slung on gimbals to cure seasickness, a converter blasting air through molten iron, and a knighthood for cheap steel describe whom?
questions.f: His swinging-saloon steamer of 1875 was a costly flop; his steel process changed the world.

questions.q: Relays clicking in a Berlin flat, punched instructions cut into old cinema film, and a machine finished in 1941 describe which computer?
questions.f: Konrad Zuse built the first programmable, automatic digital computer in his parents' living room.

questions.q: A telephone engineer who paid for valves out of his own pocket, 1,500 of them glowing at once, and a wartime machine kept secret for 30 years point to whom?
questions.f: His Colossus of 1943 was arguably the first large-scale electronic computer.

questions.q: A relay-built mouse called Theseus that remembered a maze, a juggling machine, and a thesis linking switches to logic all belong to which thinker?
questions.f: Shannon's mouse, built in 1950, was one of the first machines that could learn.

questions.q: Paper curling in a humid printing works, an idea that struck on a foggy railway platform, and a 1902 patent called 'Apparatus for Treating Air' gave us what?
questions.f: Willis Carrier's machine was invented to steady paper, not to cool people.

questions.q: A safety hood for smoke-filled rescues, a signal with a third 'all stop' position, and a 1923 patent sold to General Electric describe which inventor?
questions.f: That third position is the ancestor of today's amber light.

questions.q: An oil cup that fed lubricant to a moving steam engine, dozens of patents, and a phrase about genuine quality often linked to his name describe whom?
questions.f: His self-acting lubricator let trains run without stopping to be greased.

questions.q: A flat-bottomed bag that stands up on its own, a machine to fold it, and an 1871 court case against a man who said a woman could not have designed it describe whom?
questions.f: She won the case, and paper grocery bags have looked much the same ever since.

questions.q: Player-piano rolls, a wartime patent for hopping radio frequencies, and a Hollywood career all belong to which inventor?
questions.f: With composer George Antheil she patented an idea now echoed in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

questions.q: A daughter asking why she must wait to see the picture, a 1948 camera called the Model 95, and polarising film point to which inventor?
questions.f: Land's instant camera developed the print inside itself in about a minute.

questions.q: A patent lawyer working in a rented back room, rejection by around twenty companies, and a machine finally sold in 1959 as the '914' describe which invention?
questions.f: Chester Carlson's dry copying process took over twenty years to reach an office desk.

questions.q: Titanium quietly bought through intermediaries, panels that only sealed once hot, and a design office nicknamed after a comic-strip still describe whose team?
questions.f: The SR-71 leaked fuel on the ground until friction heat expanded it into a seal.

questions.q: A racing floatplane built for the Schneider Trophy, an elliptical wing chosen to bury guns in a thin section, and a designer who died in 1937 describe which aircraft's origins?
questions.f: R. J. Mitchell's Schneider racers taught British designers about high-speed flight.

questions.q: A lattice airframe woven like a basket, work on a giant airship called the R100, and later research into swinging wings describe which engineer?
questions.f: His geodetic structure let bombers keep flying with large sections shot away.

questions.q: A hinge added at each blade root to cure uneven lift, a Channel crossing in 1928, and a rotor that freewheels describe whose machine?
questions.f: His flapping hinge is now on virtually every helicopter rotor in the world.

questions.q: A wristwatch ordered from Cartier so he could read the time in flight, an airship moored outside a Paris restaurant, and a 1906 hop before official judges describe whom?
questions.f: Europe's first officially witnessed powered flight was made by his 14-bis.

questions.q: A designer known publicly only as 'the Chief Designer', a rocket derived from a missile still flying today, and a name kept secret until his death describe whom?
questions.f: His R-7 launched Sputnik and still carries crews to orbit as the Soyuz rocket.

questions.q: A stack of listings taller than its author, a phrase coined to make the work sound respectable, and code that saved a Moon landing describe whose team?
questions.f: She coined the term 'software engineering' when nobody took programming seriously.

questions.q: A shuttle-shaped spacecraft, a single flight in 1988 with nobody aboard, and a fully automatic runway landing describe which vehicle?
questions.f: Buran's automated landing in a crosswind was decades ahead of its time.

questions.q: Nylon bridles paying out from a hovering jet-powered stage, a rover too heavy for airbags, and 'seven minutes of terror' describe which landing system?
questions.f: After lowering Curiosity, the descent stage flew away to crash at a safe distance.

questions.q: Five kite-shaped layers the size of a tennis court, 344 things that could fail with no backup, and a mirror kept at -230 C describe which machine?
questions.f: Its sunshield drops the temperature by about 300 degrees from front to back.

questions.q: A mirror ground about two microns too flat at the edge, blurred first images in 1990, and corrective optics called COSTAR fitted by spacewalkers describe which machine?
questions.f: The error was smaller than a fiftieth of a hair's width, yet it ruined every image.

questions.q: A computer with under 70 kilobytes of memory, a 3.7-metre dish still whispering from beyond the heliopause, and instruments warmed by decaying plutonium describe which craft?
questions.f: It also carries a gold-plated record of Earth sounds, in case anyone ever finds it.

questions.q: A 17-metre arm with a hand at each end that walks end-over-end across a space station describes which machine?
questions.f: Because either end can grip, it moves around the station like an inchworm.

questions.q: A rotating boat lift in Scotland, two balanced caissons, and a design that spends only about the energy of boiling a few kettles per turn describes what?
questions.f: A floating boat displaces its own weight in water, so both caissons always balance.

questions.q: A railway hanging beneath its rail since 1901, a German city built along a river, and an elephant that once fell out and swam away describe which system?
questions.f: Tuffi the circus elephant leapt from a carriage in 1950 and survived with only scratches.

questions.q: Fifty-seven kilometres beneath the Alps, a boring machine crew working for 17 years, and an opening ceremony in 2016 describe which structure?
questions.f: It is the world's longest and deepest railway tunnel.

questions.q: A machine weighing 2,700 tonnes that travels at about 1.6 km/h and is measured in metres per litre of fuel served which programme?
questions.f: Two of these giants have been carrying rockets to the launch pad since the 1960s.

questions.q: A bucket wheel 21 metres across, a body weighing over 14,000 tonnes, and a German coal mine describe which record-holder?
questions.f: It is the heaviest land vehicle ever built, and it needs five people to operate it.

questions.q: A device with no moving parts that pushes water into a boiler using the boiler's own steam was patented in 1858 by which engineer?
questions.f: The injector puzzled physicists at first because it seemed to give something for nothing.

questions.q: A Belgian's valve gear, visible outside the wheels of many later steam locomotives, is named after…?
questions.f: His arrangement was easier to reach for maintenance than Stephenson's link motion.

questions.q: On old single-track railways, what did a driver have to carry to prove he alone could use the line?
questions.f: Only one token existed per section, so two trains could never be let in at once.

questions.q: Which steering geometry, patented in London in 1818, makes a car's inner front wheel turn more sharply than the outer?
questions.f: Rudolph Ackermann patented the design for a Munich carriage-maker, Georg Lankensperger.

questions.q: Which suspension component, now on most cars, is named after the American engineer who devised it in the 1940s?
questions.f: Combining spring, damper and steering pivot in one unit saved space and weight.

questions.q: Which engine design closes its valves mechanically instead of relying on springs?
questions.f: Ducati kept this Italian idea alive because springs cannot cope at extreme engine speeds.

questions.q: Rubber cones, fluid pipes connecting front and rear wheels, and a designer who also made a folding-framed bicycle describe which suspension?
questions.f: Alex Moulton's system linked the wheels so the car stayed level over bumps.

questions.q: Which French car famously rose on its suspension after starting, thanks to high-pressure fluid and gas spheres?
questions.f: Its hydropneumatic system also powered the brakes, steering and gear change.

questions.q: The Falkirk Wheel uses very little energy because its two water-filled caissons always weigh the same.
questions.f: A boat entering displaces exactly its own weight of water, so balance never changes.

questions.q: Konrad Zuse's Z3 used punched cinema film as its program tape.
questions.f: Paper tape was scarce in wartime Berlin, so he punched holes in discarded film stock.

questions.q: A steam injector contains no moving pumping parts.
questions.f: Cones of steam and water do the work, which is why it baffled early theorists.

questions.q: Buran, the Soviet shuttle, only ever flew with a crew aboard.
questions.f: Its single 1988 flight was entirely automatic, from launch to runway landing.

questions.q: What does 'specific impulse' tell a rocket engineer?
c: How efficiently the engine uses its propellant
questions.f: Higher specific impulse means more push from every kilogram of propellant.

questions.q: What are 'hypergolic' rocket propellants?
c: Ones that ignite on contact with each other
questions.f: Needing no ignition system makes them ideal for engines that must restart in space.

questions.q: In rocketry, what does 'ullage' refer to?
c: The empty space above liquid in a tank
questions.f: Small 'ullage motors' nudge the rocket so the propellant settles before the main engine lights.

questions.q: What is 'regenerative cooling' in a rocket engine?
c: Fuel is pumped through the nozzle walls before burning
Water is sprayed on the outside
questions.f: The propellant becomes the coolant, then the heat it absorbed goes back into the flame.

questions.q: The 'Karman line', often taken as the edge of space, sits about how high?
questions.f: Above it, an aircraft would need orbital speed to generate enough lift to stay up.

questions.q: What does a ship's 'metacentric height' tell naval architects?
c: How strongly it will right itself when it rolls
questions.f: Too little and the ship is tender; too much and it snaps back uncomfortably fast.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a ship's bulbous bow?
c: Cancelling out some of the ship's own bow wave
questions.f: The bulb makes a wave that partly cancels the hull's, cutting fuel use by several percent.

questions.q: What does a Kort nozzle, a ring around a ship's propeller, improve?
c: Thrust at low speed for tugs and trawlers
questions.f: The shroud stops water spilling sideways off the blade tips.

questions.q: Which propeller system uses vertical blades that change pitch as they orbit, letting a vessel thrust in any direction?
questions.f: Harbour tugs and ferries use it because they can go sideways without turning.

questions.q: A gilded copper bird that appeared to swallow grain, a silk-loom automation scheme, and a Frenchman praised by Voltaire point to which 18th-century machine?
questions.f: The 'digestion' was faked by a hidden compartment, but the mechanism astonished Europe.

questions.q: About 6,000 parts, a seated boy who dips his own quill and follows his letters with his eyes, and a family of Swiss watchmakers describe which automaton?
questions.f: Built by Pierre Jaquet-Droz around 1774, it still writes today and can be reprogrammed.

questions.q: A Hungarian courtier's cabinet, a machine that could also be made to say 'mama', and 84 years of touring describe which famous device?
questions.f: Wolfgang von Kempelen's chess player hid a human expert; his speaking machine was genuine.

questions.q: Twisting glass rods that imitate flowing water, a silver bird that catches a fish, and a museum in County Durham describe which automaton?
questions.f: Made in 1773, it still performs once a day at the Bowes Museum.

questions.q: A brass figure found in pieces in 1928, four drawings and three poems locked in its cams, and a message it wrote naming its own maker describe which machine?
questions.f: Its story inspired the book and film about Hugo Cabret.

questions.q: An aluminium figure lettered R.U.R. across its chest, a 1928 London exhibition it opened by rising and speaking, and Captain Richards' workshop describe which robot?
questions.f: Eric was Britain's first robot and toured the world before disappearing.

questions.q: A two-metre gold-coloured figure that walked, counted on its fingers, and had a mechanical dog called Sparko, appeared at which event?
questions.f: Westinghouse's Elektro responded to spoken commands using a telephone relay system.

questions.q: A wheeled cart trailing a radio link at Stanford, software that could plan how to shove boxes up a ramp, and a wobble that gave it its name describe which robot?
questions.f: Built between 1966 and 1972, it was the first mobile robot that could reason about its own actions.

questions.q: A 1966 program that turned your statements back into questions, a script called DOCTOR, and users who confided in it despite knowing better describe what?
questions.f: Joseph Weizenbaum was disturbed by how quickly people trusted his simple pattern-matcher.

questions.q: PVC electrical conduit, legs whose proportions were found by a computer search, and herds that walk on Dutch beaches using only wind describe whose creations?
questions.f: Some store wind in plastic bottles so they can keep walking when the breeze drops.

questions.q: A stack of old pennies balanced on a pendulum, a four-tonne clock frame, and adding one coin to gain two fifths of a second a day describe which machine?
questions.f: Keepers of Big Ben's clock still fine-tune its rate by adding or removing pennies.

questions.q: A gauze cylinder that lets air through but stops flame escaping, a rivalry with a self-taught colliery engineman, and 1815 mine trials describe which invention?
questions.f: Humphry Davy and George Stephenson each produced one, and argued about it for years.

questions.q: A Devon ironmonger, engines with efficiency under one percent, and cylinders cooled by a jet of water inside describe whose machine?
questions.f: Wasteful as it was, his 1712 atmospheric engine drained mines for over 70 years.

questions.q: A 1698 patent, a pump advertised as 'The Miner's Friend', and steam condensed to suck water up a pipe describe whose device?
questions.f: It could only lift water a short way before the vacuum failed, but it started an industry.

questions.q: A gauge of seven feet, a ship so long she had to be launched sideways into the Thames, and a stovepipe hat in a famous photograph describe which engineer?
questions.f: The SS Great Eastern was nearly 700 feet long, dwarfing every ship of her day.

questions.q: Concentric prism rings replacing a solid glass block, a French lighthouse engineer, and a beam visible from far out at sea describe which invention?
questions.f: Augustin-Jean Fresnel's design captures light that a normal lens would waste.

questions.q: A force pump, a water-powered organ, and a float-driven clock in ancient Alexandria describe whose inventions?
questions.f: Ctesibius worked around 250 BC and is often called the father of pneumatics.

questions.q: An inkpot described in ancient Byzantium that could be tipped any way without spilling is the earliest known use of what?
questions.f: Philo of Byzantium's nested rings are the same idea that keeps ships' compasses level.

questions.q: A 1551 description of a spit turned by a jet of steam, and a six-cylinder pump worked by a camshaft, belong to which Ottoman polymath?
questions.f: His steam turbine sketch predates European versions by well over a century.

questions.q: Rotating drums, a machine built to find each day's cipher settings, and huts in a Buckinghamshire park describe which device?
questions.f: Turing's Bombe tested thousands of possible wheel positions far faster than any human.

questions.q: A moth taped into a Harvard logbook in 1947 gave a famous illustration to which engineering term?
questions.f: Engineers had called faults 'bugs' since Edison's day; Grace Hopper's team found a literal one.

questions.q: A number comparing a fluid's inertia with its stickiness, dye streaks in glass tubes, and a Manchester professor of the 1880s describe which idea?
questions.f: It predicts whether flow will be smooth or turbulent, in pipes, rivers and around wings.

questions.q: An eight-page paper of 1904, a thin sticky film of air clinging to a surface, and a Gottingen professor describe which discovery?
questions.f: Ludwig Prandtl's short paper explained drag and made modern aerodynamics possible.

questions.q: A trail of alternating swirls behind a chimney, cables humming in a steady wind, and a Hungarian-American aerodynamicist describe which phenomenon?
questions.f: Bridges and chimneys are given helical strakes to break up these regular vortices.

questions.q: A ship with tall spinning cylinders instead of sails, the German vessel Buckau of 1924, and sideways force from spin all rely on which effect?
questions.f: Flettner rotors are being fitted to cargo ships again today to cut fuel use.

questions.q: A vehicle flying metres above the Caspian Sea, stubby wings trapping a cushion of air, and a shape western analysts nicknamed a 'monster' describe which machine?
questions.f: Ground effect gave it huge lift, but only within a few metres of a flat surface.

questions.q: A single-rail vehicle kept upright by two spinning gyroscopes, a 1907 demonstration carrying passengers, and an Irish-Australian inventor describe which machine?
questions.f: Louis Brennan's car could balance perfectly still on one rail with people aboard.

questions.q: A three-wheeled teardrop car of 1933, room for eleven passengers, and a designer better known for domes describe which vehicle?
questions.f: Buckminster Fuller's prototype could turn in its own length but was tricky in crosswinds.

questions.q: A boiler quietly hissing, a Florida beach in 1906, and a record of about 127 mph unbeaten by steam ever since describe which machine?
questions.f: Steam cars were once faster than petrol cars, and started with no crank or clutch.

questions.q: Two jet engines, a Nevada desert measured mile in 1997, and a shock wave heard across the valley describe which record-breaker?
questions.f: It became the first land vehicle officially to exceed the speed of sound.

questions.q: Steam-powered cars once held the world land speed record.
questions.f: A Stanley Steamer set a record of about 127 mph in 1906.

questions.q: Flettner rotor ships use spinning cylinders to generate thrust from the wind.
questions.f: Spin plus airflow creates sideways force, exactly as it does on a curving football.

questions.q: Prandtl's boundary layer paper of 1904 was fewer than ten pages long.
questions.f: Its brevity hid an idea that reshaped the whole science of flight.

questions.q: Eric, Britain's first robot, was built before the word 'robot' existed.
questions.f: Eric appeared in 1928, eight years after Capek's play introduced the word.

questions.q: What is 'Dutch roll' in an aircraft?
c: A coupled rocking and yawing wobble
questions.f: Airliners fit a yaw damper specifically to smooth this motion out.

questions.q: What is the 'coffin corner' in high-altitude flight?
c: Where stall speed and maximum speed almost meet
A blind spot behind the tail
A corner of the flight envelope with no fuel reserve
questions.f: Fly too slowly and you stall; too fast and you approach shock-wave problems.

questions.q: What does a 'thrust reverser' actually do after touchdown?
questions.f: Clamshell doors or sliding cowls deflect the flow so it pushes against the roll.

questions.q: What is 'flutter' that engineers test wings and bridges for?
c: Vibration that feeds on itself and grows rapidly
questions.f: Flutter can tear a structure apart in seconds if a natural frequency is hit.

questions.q: What is 'washout' in a wing's design?
c: The tips are set at a smaller angle than the roots
Fuel is dumped from the tips
questions.f: It makes the root stall first, so the ailerons keep working a moment longer.

questions.q: What does a high 'aspect ratio' wing look like?
questions.f: Gliders use very high aspect ratios because long thin wings make less drag for their lift.

questions.q: What does an aircraft's APU provide?
c: Electricity and air when the engines are off
questions.f: The auxiliary power unit is a small turbine, usually in the tailcone.

questions.q: What is 'bleed air' on a jet airliner used for?
c: Pressurising the cabin and de-icing wings
questions.f: It is hot, high-pressure air tapped from the engine compressors.

questions.q: What does FADEC do in a modern engine?
c: Controls fuel and engine settings digitally
questions.f: Full authority digital engine control means the pilot's lever is only a request.

questions.q: What is a 'compressor stall' in a jet engine?
c: Airflow through the compressor breaks down
questions.f: A violent version, called a surge, can bang loudly enough to be heard in the cabin.

questions.q: What are 'vortex generators', those small fins on some wings?
c: Tiny vanes that stir the boundary layer to delay separation
questions.f: By mixing fast air down to the surface, they keep the flow attached at higher angles.

questions.q: On railways, what is 'cant'?
c: The tilt of the track on a curve
questions.f: Tilting the outer rail up lets trains take curves faster without passengers sliding.

questions.q: What is a 'fishplate' on a railway?
c: A metal bar bolting two rail ends together
questions.f: The old clickety-clack of a train came from wheels crossing these joints.

questions.q: What does a locomotive's superheater do?
c: Heats steam beyond boiling point for more power
questions.f: Superheated steam holds more energy and does not condense so readily in the cylinder.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a steam locomotive's blastpipe?
c: Exhaust steam up the chimney to draw the fire
questions.f: Working harder makes a stronger draught, which is why a labouring engine barks.

questions.q: What is a Beyer-Garratt locomotive?
c: One boiler slung between two separate engine units
questions.f: The layout gave huge power while spreading weight over light, curving track.

questions.q: In a workshop, what is 'swarf'?
c: The chips and shavings cut from metal
questions.f: Swarf is razor sharp, which is why machinists never brush it away by hand.

questions.q: What does the 'kerf' of a saw mean?
c: The width of the slot the blade removes
The blade thickness at the spine
questions.f: Careful woodworkers allow for the kerf, or the finished piece ends up short.

questions.q: What is a 'collet' in a machine tool?
c: A sleeve that grips a tool or workpiece tightly
questions.f: Collets grip more evenly than jaws, so they suit delicate, precise work.

questions.q: What does 'knurling' do to a metal handle?
c: Rolls a criss-cross grip pattern into it
questions.f: No metal is removed; the pattern is squeezed up out of the surface.
