questions.q: What is 'investment casting' also known as?
questions.f: A wax model is coated in ceramic, melted out, and replaced with molten metal.

questions.q: What does 'sintering' do to metal or ceramic powder?
c: Heats it so grains bond without fully melting
questions.f: Many 3D-printed metal parts are finished by sintering in a furnace.

questions.q: What is 'case hardening'?
c: Making only the outer skin of a part hard
questions.f: A hard surface resists wear while the tough core stops the part snapping.

questions.q: What does 'annealing' do to metal?
c: Softens it by slow, controlled cooling
questions.f: Annealing relieves internal stresses so the metal can be bent without cracking.

questions.q: What is 'extrusion' in manufacturing?
c: Forcing material through a shaped die
questions.f: Aluminium window frames and even some pasta shapes are made this way.

questions.q: The word 'auger' arose because English speakers misheard 'a nauger'. What did the older word mean?
c: A borer for the nave of a wheel
questions.f: The same shifting of an 'n' turned 'a napron' into 'an apron'.

questions.q: In 'cotton gin', the word 'gin' is a shortened form of which word?
questions.f: So a cotton gin is simply a cotton engine, from the same root as 'ingenious'.

questions.q: The word 'tram' comes from an old northern European word meaning…?
questions.f: Wooden beams in mines guided wagons long before iron rails appeared.

questions.q: The word 'ballast' comes from old northern words meaning…?
questions.f: It is cargo that earns nothing, carried only for stability.

questions.q: The word 'sampan', a small Chinese boat, literally means…?
questions.f: From Chinese san (three) and ban (board or plank).

questions.q: The ship type called a 'junk' takes its name from a Malay or Javanese word meaning…?
questions.f: From jong; the English sense of 'junk' as rubbish is a completely separate word.

questions.q: A 'coracle' takes its name from a Welsh word meaning…?
questions.f: Welsh corwgl describes the round, one-person craft still used on some rivers.

questions.q: A 'gudgeon' pin in an engine shares its name with…?
questions.f: From French goujon; the fish and the pin both took the name from the same word.

questions.q: A 'ferrule', the metal band on a tool handle, took its spelling from the Latin word for…?
questions.f: Latin ferrum influenced the older word viriola, a little bracelet.

questions.q: A builder's 'plumb line' is named from the Latin word for which metal?
questions.f: Latin plumbum also gives us plumber, who once worked with lead pipes.

questions.q: The word 'cyborg', coined in 1960, is a shortening of which phrase?
questions.f: Clynes and Kline invented it for a paper about adapting humans to space travel.

questions.q: Pilotless aircraft became known as 'drones' partly because of an early target aircraft named…?
questions.f: A hive's male bee is a drone, so a radio-controlled 'Queen Bee' escort got the name.

questions.q: An artificial hill raised in a Berlin suburb, wing kits sold to enthusiasts, and roughly 2,000 glides in the 1890s describe which pioneer?
questions.f: The Wright brothers studied his published tables of lift before building anything.

questions.q: A silver medal engraved with the three forces of flight, a coachman sent aloft across a valley in 1853, and a Yorkshire baronet describe whom?
questions.f: Cayley identified lift, drag and thrust a full century before jet airliners flew.

questions.q: A V8-engined motorcycle timed at over 136 mph in 1907, flying boats for the US Navy, and a long patent war with Ohio brothers describe whom?
questions.f: He was called 'the fastest man on earth' before he ever built an aeroplane.

questions.q: Bellows and valves taken from a family organ factory, a windowless box on a stand, and pilots trained on the ground from 1929 describe which machine?
questions.f: Ed Link used his father's pipe-organ parts to make the cockpit pitch and roll.

questions.q: A fuselage pinched like a bottle at the waist, drag that fell away near the speed of sound, and a NASA engineer's rule describe which idea?
questions.f: Richard Whitcomb's rule turned a failing 1950s fighter into a supersonic success.

questions.q: An engine whose cylinders spun round with the propeller, castor oil as its lubricant, and gyroscopic forces that made turning easier one way describes which type?
questions.f: Pilots of 1917 had to learn that a right turn behaved quite differently from a left.

questions.q: Eighteen cylinders arranged in a triangle, three crankshafts, and a distinctive howl in British locomotives describe which engine?
questions.f: Its triangular layout packed enormous power into a very small space.

questions.q: A journey beneath the Arctic ice to the North Pole in 1958, and a reactor allowing months submerged, describe which machine?
questions.f: Nuclear power freed submarines from surfacing for air, changing naval design forever.

questions.q: An Ohio department-store janitor with a persistent cough, a soap box, a pillowcase and a fan motor, and a cousin's husband named Hoover invented what?
questions.f: James Murray Spangler sold his patent in 1908; the Hoover name did the rest.

questions.q: A patent held jointly by two famous physicists, no moving parts, and heat instead of a compressor describe which machine?
questions.f: Einstein and Leo Szilard patented an absorption fridge driven only by a heat source.

questions.q: A soldier's complaint about burnt canteen toast, a timer, and springs that fling the bread up led to which 1919 invention?
questions.f: Charles Strite's machine ejected the toast so nobody had to watch it.

questions.q: An Iowa jeweller, hat pins used to hold a loaf together, and bakers who feared the bread would go stale describe which machine?
questions.f: Otto Rohwedder's 1928 slicer led to the phrase 'the greatest thing since sliced bread'.

questions.q: An idea that came in the bath, a chocolate-bar dispenser as inspiration, and a code shortened to four digits because a wife could not recall six describe which machine?
questions.f: John Shepherd-Barron's first machine opened at a London bank in 1967.

questions.q: Morse code drawn in beach sand with a hand, dots and dashes stretched into lines, and a packet of chewing gum scanned in 1974 describe which invention?
questions.f: Norman Joseph Woodland's circular 'bullseye' code came first; the striped version won.

questions.q: A coin dropped onto a pan, a lever tipping open a valve, and a temple in Roman Egypt describe the ancestor of which machine?
questions.f: Hero of Alexandria's device dispensed a measure of holy water for a coin.

questions.q: An undertaker convinced the local operator sent callers to a rival, and a model built with collar studs, produced which machine?
questions.f: Almon Strowger's step-by-step switch removed the human operator entirely.

questions.q: A swinging pendulum, a clock keeping two machines in step, and an 1843 patent for sending pictures by wire describe whose invention?
questions.f: Bain's fax idea came about thirty years before the telephone was even patented.

questions.q: A teenager building gears for his tax-collector father, a carry mechanism that clicked digits over, and about twenty surviving machines describe which calculator?
questions.f: Blaise Pascal was only 19 when he began work on it in the 1640s.

questions.q: Brass pulleys, wires summing many separate rhythms, and a machine built to forecast the sea describe which Victorian invention?
questions.f: Lord Kelvin's machine added tidal cycles mechanically to draw the coming tide curve.

questions.q: A government memo about 'death rays' that was redirected towards detection, masts strung along a coast, and a Scottish meteorologist describe which system?
questions.f: Robert Watson-Watt showed that finding aircraft mattered far more than destroying them.

questions.q: A copper block drilled with circular cavities, a Birmingham laboratory in 1940, and centimetre-length waves describe which device?
questions.f: Randall and Boot's magnetron made compact radar possible, and later the microwave oven.

questions.q: A laboratory shut for the summer, a new employee with no holiday entitlement, and every part carved from one piece of germanium describe which invention?
questions.f: Jack Kilby built his in July 1958; Robert Noyce's planar version made chips manufacturable.

questions.q: Fifty spinning discs, a cabinet the size of two refrigerators, and about five megabytes of storage in 1956 describe which machine?
questions.f: Today a fingernail-sized card holds tens of thousands of times as much.

questions.q: A prototype named P2, a walk that recovers balance the way people do, and a name that is an acronym rather than a tribute describe which robot?
questions.f: Honda insists the name stands for Advanced Step in Innovative Mobility.

questions.q: A 12-year-old's winning essay, a rover weighing about 11 kg, and a 1997 landing cushioned by airbags describe which machine?
questions.f: Valerie Ambroise won the naming contest; the rover outlived its week-long mission plan.

questions.q: A 90-day mission plan, nearly 15 years of work, and a final message about failing batteries in a dust storm describe which machine?
questions.f: It drove more than 45 km across Mars, a distance nobody expected.

questions.q: A toaster-sized box that splits carbon dioxide, an experiment carried on a rover, and the first oxygen made on another planet describe which device?
questions.f: Perseverance's MOXIE showed astronauts could one day make their own air on Mars.

questions.q: Harpoons that failed to fire, a bounce across a comet, and a shadowed ledge that starved the solar panels describe which machine?
questions.f: It still sent home data before its batteries ran flat in 2014.

questions.q: An improvised parasol pushed through a scientific airlock, a torn shield, and an overheating station in 1973 describe which repair?
questions.f: Without the makeshift shade, the station's interior would have stayed too hot to use.

questions.q: A polished sphere designed to be visible from the ground, two radio transmitters, and a beep heard by amateur listeners describe which machine?
questions.f: Its aluminium ball was buffed to a mirror finish so observers could catch the sunlight.

questions.q: The cavity magnetron developed for radar later made the microwave oven possible.
questions.f: The same tube that found aircraft now heats leftovers in millions of kitchens.

questions.q: Lord Kelvin built a machine that predicted tides mechanically.
questions.f: Its pulleys and wires added together dozens of separate tidal rhythms.

questions.q: Sojourner, the first Mars rover, was named by a schoolchild.
questions.f: A 12-year-old won NASA's essay contest with a tribute to Sojourner Truth.

questions.q: Almon Strowger, who built the first automatic telephone exchange, was an undertaker.
questions.f: He suspected human operators of diverting his customers to a competitor.

questions.q: Which mechanism, essential to film projectors, turns steady rotation into precise stop-start motion?
questions.f: Its slotted wheel advances one frame at a time, then holds it still to be shown.

questions.q: What does a Scotch yoke mechanism produce from a rotating crank?
questions.f: It gives perfect sinusoidal movement, useful in test rigs and some pumps.

questions.q: A brake or gear cable in a flexible outer sheath is named after which inventor?
questions.f: Bowden cables now control everything from bicycle brakes to aircraft throttles.

questions.q: The cross-head screw and matching screwdriver widely used in the 20th century is named after…?
questions.f: Its shape lets a power driver slip out on purpose when the screw is tight enough.

questions.q: Which square-drive screw, popular in Canada, is named after its Canadian inventor?
questions.f: Peter Robertson's design lets you start a screw one-handed because it grips the driver.

questions.q: The British Standard Whitworth thread has a thread angle of…?
questions.f: Metric and American threads use 60 degrees, which is why the two never mix.

questions.q: In workshop talk, what is a 'thou'?
questions.f: A human hair is roughly two to three thou thick.

questions.q: What is 'hysteresis' in a mechanical or magnetic system?
c: The output lags behind the input, depending on history
questions.f: It is why a spring gauge can read slightly differently going up and coming down.

questions.q: What is 'creep' in a loaded metal component?
c: Slow permanent stretching under long steady stress
questions.f: Turbine blades are designed around creep, because they sit hot and loaded for years.

questions.q: What causes galvanic corrosion in a machine?
c: Two different metals touching in the presence of moisture
questions.f: That is why boatbuilders fit sacrificial zinc anodes to protect steel and bronze.

questions.q: What does anodising do to an aluminium part?
c: Grows a hard protective oxide layer electrically
questions.f: The porous oxide can be dyed, which is how coloured aluminium parts are made.

questions.q: What is a 'trunnion' in machinery?
c: A cylindrical pin on which something pivots
questions.f: Big telescopes and old cannon both rotate on trunnions.

questions.q: What is a Belleville washer designed to do?
c: Act as a spring under a bolt
questions.f: Its slight cone shape keeps tension on a bolt as parts expand and contract.

questions.q: On a ship, the 'gunwale' is…?
c: The top edge of the hull's side
questions.f: The name comes from the wale, a strengthening plank, once used to support guns.

questions.q: The word 'scuttlebutt', meaning gossip, originally named which piece of ship's equipment?
questions.f: Sailors gathered to drink and chat there, exactly like a modern water cooler.

questions.q: A ship's 'capstan' takes its name from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From capistrum, a halter; the drum was turned by bars pushed by the crew.

questions.q: A 'davit', the small crane that swings a boat out, probably takes its name from…?
questions.f: Sailors named the fitting after 'David', much as they said 'jack' for a helpful device.

questions.q: What is a ship's 'freeboard'?
c: The height from the waterline to the deck edge
The free space in the hold
questions.f: Too little freeboard and waves come aboard, which is what the Plimsoll line prevents.

questions.q: On a ship, the difference between 'list' and 'trim' is that list means…?
questions.f: Trim is fore-and-aft; crews adjust it by moving water between tanks.

questions.q: In railway language, what is a 'consist'?
c: The set of vehicles making up a train
questions.f: Freight staff talk about 'the consist' the way sailors talk about a ship's manifest.

questions.q: A 'Mallet' locomotive is characterised by…?
c: Two sets of driving wheels, one able to swing
questions.f: Anatole Mallet's articulated design let very long engines take tight curves.

questions.q: What are railway 'catch points' for?
c: Derailing a runaway vehicle before it reaches a main line
questions.f: Deliberately derailing one wagon is better than letting it run into traffic.

questions.q: What did a 'banker' locomotive do?
c: Helped push trains up a steep gradient
questions.f: Banking engines waited at the foot of famous inclines for the next heavy train.

questions.q: What is 'unsprung mass' in a vehicle?
c: The weight not supported by the springs, like wheels
The weight of the body shell
questions.f: Lower unsprung mass lets a wheel follow bumps faster, improving grip and comfort.

questions.q: What does 'toe-in' describe on a car's wheels?
c: The wheels pointing slightly towards each other
The tilt of the wheel from vertical
questions.f: A tiny amount keeps the steering feeling stable at speed.

questions.q: What does 'castor angle' give a bicycle or car?
questions.f: It is why a shopping trolley wheel swings round to trail behind its pivot.

questions.q: What is the Atkinson cycle, used in many hybrid engines, designed to gain?
c: Efficiency, by expanding gases longer than they were compressed
questions.f: You lose some power but recover more useful energy from each drop of fuel.

questions.q: What does variable valve timing let an engine do?
c: Change when valves open to suit engine speed
questions.f: Settings good for low-speed pulling are quite wrong for high-speed power.

questions.q: Why do racing engines sometimes use a 'dry sump'?
c: Oil is stored in a separate tank so it cannot slosh away
questions.f: Hard cornering can starve a normal sump's pump for a fatal fraction of a second.

questions.q: What is 'lapping' in precision manufacturing?
c: Rubbing two surfaces with fine abrasive to make them match
questions.f: Lapping produced the flat surfaces that made accurate steam engines possible.

questions.q: What does 'broaching' do to a hole?
c: Pulls a toothed tool through to cut an exact shape
questions.f: It is how square holes and internal splines are produced quickly.

questions.q: Which machine element is measured by its 'pitch circle diameter'?
questions.f: Two meshing gears effectively roll on their pitch circles without slipping.

questions.q: What is 'duty cycle' for a machine such as a welder or compressor?
c: The share of time it may run before it must rest
questions.f: A 20% duty cycle means about two minutes of work in every ten.

questions.q: What color is a ripe banana?
questions.f: Bananas start out green and slowly turn yellow as they ripen and get sweeter.

questions.q: Stop signs are painted which bright color?
questions.f: Red stands out from far away, so drivers can spot a stop sign quickly.

questions.q: What do you use to take a photograph?
questions.f: Some cameras can snap dozens of pictures in a single second.

questions.q: Which tool do you use to cut paper for a craft?
questions.f: Safety scissors have rounded tips so young artists can cut without getting hurt.

questions.q: A ripe pumpkin is usually which color?
questions.f: Some prize-winning pumpkins grow heavier than a horse!

questions.q: What can you wear over your clothes to keep paint off them?
questions.f: Artists' aprons often end up covered in colorful old paint splatters.

questions.q: Where do people go to look at famous paintings?
questions.f: Some museums are so big you could walk for days and still not see everything.

questions.q: Which drawing tool makes gray lines you can erase?
questions.f: Pencil marks erase because the soft gray graphite sits loosely on the paper.

questions.q: Where do kids usually draw with big sticks of colored chalk?
questions.f: Some cities hold chalk festivals where whole streets become giant pictures.

questions.q: What soft, squishy stuff do you roll and shape with your hands?
questions.f: The first play dough was actually invented to clean dirty wallpaper.

questions.q: Which shape is perfectly round like a ball?
questions.f: Artists practice by drawing smooth circles freehand, without tracing anything.

questions.q: What do you swish a paintbrush in to clean it?
questions.f: Clean brushes last longer and keep new colors from turning muddy.

questions.q: Pressing a paint-dipped potato onto paper makes a?
questions.f: You can carve a star or heart into a potato half to print any shape you like.

questions.q: What can appear in the sky when the sun shines during rain?
questions.f: To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and the rain in front of you.

questions.q: A zebra's stripes are black and which other color?
questions.f: Every zebra has its own stripe pattern, just like a fingerprint.

questions.q: What color is a bar of chocolate?
questions.f: Painters mix red, yellow and a touch of blue to make rich chocolate browns.

questions.q: What does glitter add to a craft project?
questions.f: Glitter sparkles because its tiny flat pieces bounce light in every direction.

questions.q: What holds a picture neatly on the wall?
questions.f: Some museum frames are carved from wood and covered in real gold.

questions.q: Which tool makes a dull pencil pointy again?
questions.f: Long ago, people sharpened their pencils by whittling them with a small knife.

questions.q: In finger painting, what do you use instead of a brush?
questions.f: Finger painting lets you feel the cool, slippery paint as you swirl it around.

questions.q: Flamingos are famous for feathers of which color?
questions.f: Flamingos turn pink from the tiny shrimp-like creatures they eat.

questions.q: On a traffic light, which color means GO?
questions.f: Traffic lights always keep the same color order so drivers can trust them.

questions.q: Threading colorful beads onto a string makes a?
questions.f: People have made beads from shells, seeds and stones for thousands of years.

questions.q: Cutting tiny shapes from folded paper and opening it up makes a paper?
questions.f: Like real snowflakes, folded-paper snowflakes come out different every time.

questions.q: Which little beetle is red with black spots?
questions.f: A ladybug's bright colors warn birds that it does not taste good.

questions.q: Which bird spreads a giant fan of colorful tail feathers?
questions.f: A peacock's train can hold more than 100 shimmering eye-spot feathers.

questions.q: In which season do many leaves turn red, orange and gold?
questions.f: Artists love autumn because whole forests look freshly painted.

questions.q: What do you blow through to make bubble-print art?
questions.f: Blowing into soapy paint makes bubbles that pop into flowery prints on paper.

questions.q: What happens to wet clay as it dries out?
questions.f: Dry clay becomes even harder when it is baked in a very hot oven.

questions.q: Besides sand, what do you need to shape a strong sandcastle?
questions.f: Damp sand sticks together, which is why castles built near the waves work best.

questions.q: Which cartoon mouse did Walt Disney help create?
questions.f: Early Mickey Mouse cartoons were drawn by hand, one picture at a time.

questions.q: Rubbing a crayon over paper placed on a leaf makes a leaf?
questions.f: The crayon catches the leaf's bumpy veins, so the pattern appears like magic.

questions.q: Who paints stars and butterflies on kids' cheeks at a fair?
questions.f: Face painters use special paints that are safe for skin and wash off easily.

questions.q: A circle has corners.
questions.f: A circle is one smooth curved line with no corners or straight sides at all.

questions.q: Leaving the cap off a marker can make it dry out.
questions.f: Marker ink contains liquid that evaporates into the air when the cap is off.

questions.q: You should wash your paintbrushes when you finish painting.
questions.f: Paint left to dry in a brush turns hard and ruins the soft bristles.

questions.q: Crayons can melt if you leave them in a hot car.
questions.f: Crayon wax starts to soften at around 40 degrees Celsius — some artists melt crayons on purpose!

questions.q: A rectangle has three sides.
questions.f: A rectangle has four sides — its opposite sides are the same length.

questions.q: A person who paints pictures is called a?
questions.f: Many famous painters, like Picasso, began painting when they were children.

questions.q: A person whose job is taking photos is a?
questions.f: 'Photographer' is a big word that simply means a person who takes photos.

questions.q: 'Paintbrush' is one word made by joining 'paint' and which word?
questions.f: Words glued together like this, such as 'paintbrush', are called compound words.

questions.q: 'Rainbow' joins the word 'rain' with which other word?
questions.f: A 'bow' is a curved arc — a rainbow really is a giant bow of colors.

questions.q: A book full of blank pages for drawing is called a?
questions.f: Leonardo da Vinci filled thousands of sketchbook pages with ideas and drawings.

questions.q: The word 'colorful' means full of what?
questions.f: The ending '-ful' means 'full of', so 'colorful' means full of color.

questions.q: A design that repeats again and again is called a?
questions.f: Stripes, spots and checkerboards are all patterns because they repeat.

questions.q: The long, thin bands of color on a candy cane are called?
questions.f: A repeated band of color is a stripe — tigers, bees and flags all wear them.

questions.q: A tiny round mark made with the tip of a marker is a?
questions.f: Some artists build whole pictures out of thousands of tiny dots.

questions.q: The opposite of a light color is a ____ color.
questions.f: Navy blue is a dark color, while sky blue is a light color.

questions.q: A silly, squiggly drawing you make while daydreaming is a?
questions.f: Even presidents doodle — some of their meeting doodles are kept in museums.

questions.q: A simple picture symbol that stands for a team or company is a?
questions.f: Good logos are so simple you can draw them from memory.

questions.q: 'Artwork' is a compound word made from 'art' and?
questions.f: 'Artwork' can mean one piece of art or all the art someone has made.

questions.q: The person who sits very still so an artist can draw them is the?
questions.f: Models must hold still a long time, so artists give them little rest breaks.

questions.q: A funny drawing in a comic strip or newspaper is called a?
questions.f: Cartoonists can show a whole joke in just one drawing.

questions.q: Which word means to make a picture using a pencil?
questions.f: 'Draw' is also used for luck — but artists draw pictures, not straws!

questions.q: Which word means pressing an inked shape onto paper to copy it?
questions.f: Your fingertips leave prints too — that is why they are called fingerprints.

questions.q: What is the correct plural of 'brush'?
questions.f: Words ending in 'sh' add '-es' to make more than one, like brushes and wishes.

questions.q: An artist's very best and most famous work is called their?
questions.f: 'Masterpiece' joins 'master' and 'piece' — a piece of work fit for a master.

questions.q: A line that curves gently up and down like the sea is called?
questions.f: 'Wavy' comes from 'wave', because the line moves like water waves.

questions.q: The 'tri' at the start of 'triangle' means which number?
questions.f: 'Tri' means three in old Greek and Latin — a tricycle has three wheels.

questions.q: In 'cut and paste' crafts, what does 'paste' mean to do?
questions.f: Long before computers, 'cut and paste' meant real scissors and real glue.

questions.q: Messy, loopy pencil marks made very fast are called?
questions.f: Most artists' first drawings as toddlers were happy scribbles.

questions.q: Which word means the same as 'picture'?
questions.f: 'Image' and 'imagine' are cousins — imagining is making pictures in your head.

questions.q: 'Craft' means making things skillfully with your?
questions.f: 'Handicraft' even puts the word 'hand' right inside it.

questions.q: A room where paintings are hung up for people to enjoy is a?
questions.f: Some galleries are free to visit, so anyone can walk in and enjoy the art.

questions.q: Colors that look nice together are said to do what?
questions.f: Artists test which colors match by putting little dabs side by side.

questions.q: To 'sparkle' means to shine with tiny flashes of?
questions.f: 'Sparkle' comes from 'spark' — a tiny flash, like from a campfire.

questions.q: The special way an artist writes their name on a painting is their?
questions.f: 'Signature' comes from 'sign' — artists usually sign in a bottom corner.

questions.q: The line that goes around the outside edge of a shape is its?
questions.f: 'Outline' joins 'out' and 'line' — the line on the outside.

questions.q: A very, very small painting or model is called a?
questions.f: Some miniature paintings are small enough to fit inside a locket.

questions.q: Which word means to add pretty things to make something lovely?
questions.f: We decorate cakes, classrooms and holiday trees — all to make them beautiful.

questions.q: Which artist painted water lilies floating on his garden pond again and again?
questions.f: Monet dug the lily pond himself at his home in Giverny, France, and painted it about 250 times.

questions.q: Twisting a shirt tight with rubber bands before dyeing it creates which art?
questions.f: The bands block the dye, leaving white sunbursts and spirals where they were tied.

questions.q: The 'lead' inside a pencil is really made of what?
questions.f: Graphite is a soft form of carbon — the same element that makes diamonds.

questions.q: How many colored rings link together on the Olympic flag?
questions.f: The five rings stand for five parts of the world joined together in sport.

questions.q: India's flag has stripes of saffron, green and which other color?
questions.f: In the white middle stripe sits a navy-blue wheel with exactly 24 spokes.

questions.q: What do artists look into when painting a picture of their own face?
questions.f: Before cameras existed, a mirror was the only way artists could see themselves to paint.

questions.q: What pushes the paint out of a can of spray paint?
questions.f: The rattle you hear when shaking the can is a little ball that mixes the paint.

questions.q: Knitting turns yarn into fabric using two long what?
questions.f: Speedy knitters can loop more than 100 stitches in a single minute.

questions.q: Mixing yellow paint into green makes which brighter color?
questions.f: In-between mixes like yellow-green are known as tertiary colors.

questions.q: Where would you most likely see huge glowing sculptures carved from ice?
questions.f: The ice festival in Harbin, China builds whole palaces of ice lit from inside.

questions.q: Which color appears at the very TOP of a rainbow?
questions.f: Rainbow colors always run red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

questions.q: Which juice works as invisible ink that appears when the paper is warmed?
questions.f: Gentle heat browns the dried lemon juice faster than the paper around it.

questions.q: Bees make which waxy material used in some crayons and polishes?
questions.f: Bees build their honeycomb from wax, and artists have drawn with it for centuries.

questions.q: Statues of which animals guard the steps of the New York Public Library?
questions.f: The two marble lions even have names — Patience and Fortitude.

questions.q: Whose giant faces are carved into Mount Rushmore?
questions.f: Each carved face on the mountain is about as tall as a six-story building.

questions.q: What does the Statue of Liberty hold high in her raised hand?
questions.f: Her other arm cradles a tablet marked with the date of American independence.

questions.q: Gingerbread artists build and decorate little edible what?
questions.f: Bakers use white icing as the 'glue' that holds gingerbread walls together.

questions.q: What color are London's famous double-decker buses?
questions.f: London buses have been painted bright red for over 100 years.

questions.q: Egypt's Great Sphinx statue has a lion's body and the head of a?
questions.f: The Sphinx was carved from one giant ridge of limestone rock.

questions.q: Totem poles of the Pacific Northwest are carved from what?
questions.f: The stacked animal figures on a totem pole tell a family's story.

questions.q: A quilt is a cozy blanket sewn together from many what?
questions.f: Classic quilt patterns have friendly names like 'log cabin' and 'flying geese'.

questions.q: Which famous sign spells a city's name in giant white letters on a hillside?
questions.f: Each letter of the Hollywood sign stands about as tall as a four-story building.

questions.q: The Crayola company is most famous for making what?
questions.f: Crayola makes about three billion crayons every single year.

questions.q: Which insect's colorful wing patterns often inspire artists' designs?
questions.f: Butterfly wings get their colors from thousands of tiny overlapping scales.

questions.q: What see-through paper lets you copy a drawing placed underneath it?
questions.f: Animators once traced characters onto clear sheets for every frame of a cartoon.

questions.q: Glowing Halloween faces are usually carved into which vegetable?
questions.f: The first jack-o'-lanterns in Ireland were carved from turnips, not pumpkins.

questions.q: San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge is painted which color?
questions.f: Its special shade, 'International Orange', helps the bridge show up in thick fog.

questions.q: What are the tiny colored paper bits tossed in the air at celebrations?
questions.f: At first, Italian crowds threw little candies — 'confetti' — before paper took over.

questions.q: Which tool helps you draw a perfectly straight line?
questions.f: Architects once used long wooden straightedges taller than themselves.

questions.q: Flipping the pages of a flip book quickly makes its drawings seem to move.
questions.f: Your brain blends the fast pictures together — the same trick behind movies.

questions.q: A sculptor is an artist who only paints on canvas.
questions.f: Sculptors shape statues from clay, stone, metal or wood — painting is a different job.

questions.q: Some paints glow brightly under ultraviolet 'black light'.
questions.f: Fluorescent paints soak up invisible UV light and shine it back as bright color.

questions.q: Adding more water to watercolor paint makes the color look lighter.
questions.f: Watercolor artists lighten colors with water instead of white paint.

questions.q: Oil paints dry faster than watercolors.
questions.f: Oil paint can stay wet for days or weeks, while watercolor dries in minutes.

questions.q: Sidewalk chalk drawings wash away in the rain.
questions.f: Chalk artists check the weather — one storm can erase a whole day's masterpiece.

questions.q: An artist who carves or shapes statues is called a?
questions.f: The word 'sculptor' is built from an old root meaning 'to carve'.

questions.q: An artist who draws the funny pictures in comic strips is a?
questions.f: The '-ist' ending turns 'cartoon' into the person who makes cartoons.

questions.q: The color 'orange' is named after which fruit?
questions.f: English speakers named the fruit first — the color name came later.

questions.q: Which color name is also the name of a small purple flower?
questions.f: Lavender and rose are also colors that borrowed their names from flowers.

questions.q: An artist's own special way of making art is called their?
questions.f: Experts can often name a painter just by recognizing the style of the brushwork.

questions.q: A special show where an artist's works are displayed is an?
questions.f: 'Exhibition' comes from a root meaning 'to hold out' — to show something to everyone.

questions.q: Which tube-shaped toy uses mirrors to show ever-changing colorful patterns?
questions.f: 'Kaleidoscope' is Greek for 'beautiful shape watcher' — a favorite spelling-bee word.

questions.q: Which word describes how a surface feels, like rough, silky or bumpy?
questions.f: Painters even fake texture, making flat paint look like fluffy fur or rough stone.

questions.q: A cut-out shape you paint through to copy a design perfectly is a?
questions.f: Street signs and road letters are often painted using giant metal stencils.

questions.q: A 'tricolor' flag is decorated with how many colors?
questions.f: France's blue, white and red flag is nicknamed the Tricolore.

questions.q: An artist who draws the pictures inside storybooks is an?
questions.f: 'Illustrate' comes from a root meaning 'to light up' — pictures light up a story.

questions.q: 'Dye', the liquid that colors cloth, sounds exactly like which word?
questions.f: Words that sound alike but are spelled differently are called homophones.

questions.q: The frame or machine used for weaving threads into cloth is a?
questions.f: Giant factory looms can weave cloth faster than a hundred hand weavers.

questions.q: The '-ist' ending in words like 'artist' and 'violinist' means?
questions.f: Add '-ist' to a word and you name the person: art, artist; cartoon, cartoonist.

questions.q: When one shape partly covers another in a drawing, the shapes?
questions.f: 'Overlap' means to lap over — overlapping shapes make pictures look deeper.

questions.q: A butterfly's two matching wings show which kind of balance?
questions.f: 'Symmetry' means the two sides mirror each other exactly.

questions.q: A line that turns sharply back and forth, like lightning, is a?
questions.f: 'Zigzag' is a fun word that sounds like the sharp turns it describes.

questions.q: A line that curls around and around a center point is a?
questions.f: Snail shells, cinnamon rolls and some galaxies are all natural spirals.

questions.q: The part of a picture that looks farthest away, behind everything, is the?
questions.f: Its opposite, the foreground, is the part that seems closest to you.

questions.q: The boxes that hold each scene of a comic strip are called?
questions.f: Comic artists change panel sizes to make big moments feel bigger.

questions.q: In comics, a character's spoken words float inside a speech?
questions.f: Thoughts get cloud-shaped bubbles, while shouts get spiky ones.

questions.q: A small statue you can hold in your hand is called a?
questions.f: 'Figurine' means 'little figure' — the '-ine' ending makes it small.

questions.q: Which of these words names a shade of green?
questions.f: Emerald green is named after the sparkling green gemstone.

questions.q: 'Waterproof' ink is special because water cannot do what to it?
questions.f: 'Proof' in 'waterproof' means protected against — safe from water.

questions.q: A person who shapes bowls, mugs and vases from clay is a?
questions.f: A potter's finished pieces are called pottery — the maker's name is inside the word.

questions.q: A picture made with a camera is called a?
questions.f: All those '-graph' words share an ancient root meaning 'to write or draw'.

questions.q: A 'weaver' is a craftsperson who makes what?
questions.f: Weavers criss-cross threads over and under each other to build fabric.

questions.q: An exact copy of a famous artwork, made honestly, is called a?
questions.f: Museums sometimes display replicas so the fragile originals can rest safely.

questions.q: The folder or case where an artist keeps their best work is a?
questions.f: 'Portfolio' comes from roots meaning 'to carry leaves' — pages carried around.

questions.q: Which Norwegian artist painted 'The Scream'?
questions.f: Munch said the idea came to him at sunset, when the sky turned blood-red over a fjord.

questions.q: 'The Thinker', a bronze statue of a man deep in thought, is by which sculptor?
questions.f: Rodin first made 'The Thinker' small, as part of a giant sculpted doorway.

questions.q: Which French artist made huge colorful paper cut-outs when illness kept him in bed?
questions.f: Matisse called his scissors technique 'drawing with scissors' and 'painting with paper'.

questions.q: The Terracotta Army of clay soldiers guards an ancient emperor's tomb in which country?
questions.f: Farmers digging a well in 1974 stumbled onto the buried army by accident.

questions.q: Andy Warhol became famous for painting cans of which food?
questions.f: Warhol painted 32 Campbell's soup cans — one for every flavor sold at the time.

questions.q: The Mona Lisa is painted not on canvas but on a panel of?
questions.f: Leonardo painted her on a plank of poplar wood, which has slowly warped with age.

questions.q: Which French artist is famous for paintings of ballet dancers?
questions.f: Degas made more than 1,000 works of dancers, often shown backstage rehearsing.

questions.q: Frida Kahlo, famous for bold portraits full of flowers, came from which country?
questions.f: Kahlo's blue family home in Mexico City is now a museum called La Casa Azul.

questions.q: Ancient Egyptian wall paintings usually show people's faces from which angle?
questions.f: Egyptian artists mixed views — side face, front eye and shoulders — in one figure.

questions.q: Madhubani folk painting, full of fish, suns and peacocks, comes from which country?
questions.f: Madhubani art began as wall paintings in villages of Bihar, in eastern India.

questions.q: Shaping melted glass by blowing air through a long pipe is called?
questions.f: Glassblowers work with glowing glass hotter than 1,000 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: In old stained-glass windows, the colored pieces are held together by strips of?
questions.f: The soft metal strips, called cames, form the black outlines you see in the window.

questions.q: The island of Murano, famous for centuries of glass art, belongs to which city?
questions.f: Venice moved its glass furnaces to Murano in 1291, partly to guard trade secrets.

questions.q: Before painting, artists stretch their canvas tightly over a wooden?
questions.f: The hidden support is called a stretcher — tight canvas keeps paint from cracking.

questions.q: Oil paint is made by mixing colored pigment with what?
questions.f: Most oil paints use linseed oil, which slowly hardens as it meets the air.

questions.q: Roughly how hot does a pottery kiln get when firing clay?
questions.f: That is far hotter than a kitchen oven — hot enough to make clay glow orange.

questions.q: Bronze, the classic statue metal, is a mixture of copper and which other metal?
questions.f: Adding tin makes copper harder — a discovery so big it named the Bronze Age.

questions.q: Leonardo da Vinci filled his notebooks using what unusual writing style?
questions.f: His backwards script reads normally when you hold the page up to a mirror.

questions.q: A 3-D printer builds a sculpture by adding material in thin stacked?
questions.f: Artists now 3-D print sculptures in plastic, metal and even chocolate.

questions.q: Paper, the artist's basic material, was invented about 2,000 years ago in?
questions.f: Early Chinese papermakers mashed tree bark, rags and old fishing nets into pulp.

questions.q: Painted barns, handmade quilts and weather vanes are examples of which art?
questions.f: Folk art is made by everyday people using skills passed down in families.

questions.q: What is the special dark room where film photographs are developed called?
questions.f: Photographers use dim red light there, because it will not spoil the film paper.

questions.q: Artist Yayoi Kusama covers giant pumpkins and whole rooms with which pattern?
questions.f: Kusama calls her endless dots 'infinity nets' and has painted them since childhood.

questions.q: Which Dutch artist drew impossible staircases that seem to climb forever?
questions.f: Mathematicians love Escher — his tricks are based on real geometry puzzles.

questions.q: Which white powder mixes with water and sets rock-hard, perfect for casting?
questions.f: Sculptors pour liquid plaster into molds to copy statues — doctors use it for casts too.

questions.q: A simple camera can be made from a closed box with just a tiny what?
questions.f: A pinhole camera projects an upside-down picture of the world inside the box.

questions.q: Mixing blue and green paint makes which ocean-like color?
questions.f: Teal is named after a small duck with a striking blue-green head stripe.

questions.q: What is the largest art museum in the world?
questions.f: The Louvre in Paris has around 35,000 artworks on display at any time.

questions.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States as a gift?
questions.f: The statue crossed the Atlantic in 1885, packed in 214 crates like a giant puzzle.

questions.q: Shaping wood on a fast-spinning machine called a lathe is known as?
questions.f: Woodturners hold sharp chisels against the spinning wood to carve bowls and legs.

questions.q: The giant mirror-shiny 'Bean' sculpture reflects the skyline of which city?
questions.f: Its real name is Cloud Gate, and its polished steel shows no visible seams.

questions.q: The famous Little Mermaid statue sits on a harbor rock in which city?
questions.f: The statue honors Hans Christian Andersen, the Danish author of the fairy tale.

questions.q: Dreamlike art such as Salvador Dali's belongs to which art movement?
questions.f: Surrealists painted straight from dreams and imagination instead of real life.

questions.q: Visitors toss coins over their shoulders into which sculpted Roman fountain?
questions.f: About a million euros in coins land in the Trevi each year and go to charity.

questions.q: Oil painting became hugely popular with European artists in the 1400s.
questions.f: Painters like Jan van Eyck showed how slow-drying oils could capture tiny details.

questions.q: A large bronze statue is usually solid metal all the way through.
questions.f: Big bronzes are hollow — a solid one would be too heavy and too expensive.

questions.q: Black is what we see when almost no light reaches our eyes.
questions.f: A truly black surface swallows nearly all the light that lands on it.

questions.q: The very first photographs could not capture color.
questions.f: Early photos were black and white; some studios hand-painted color on top.

questions.q: Clay shrinks a little as it dries and is fired in the kiln.
questions.f: Potters make pieces slightly oversized because clay can shrink by about a tenth.

questions.q: The Mona Lisa appears to have no eyebrows today.
questions.f: Experts think delicate painted eyebrows faded or were lost in old cleanings.

questions.q: Sculptures can be made by adding material, not only by carving it away.
questions.f: Building up clay or wax is called modeling; carving stone is called subtracting.

questions.q: Watercolor paper is usually much thicker than printer paper.
questions.f: Thick cotton papers soak up washes of water without wrinkling or tearing.

questions.q: The root 'chroma', found in 'monochrome', means?
questions.f: From Greek — a monochrome picture uses just one color, and chrome shines with color.

questions.q: The 'photo' in 'photograph' means?
questions.f: From Greek — a photograph is literally a picture drawn by light itself.

questions.q: The root 'graph', in 'photograph' and 'autograph', means?
questions.f: From Greek — an autograph is 'self-writing', your own name written by you.

questions.q: The prefix 'poly-' in 'polychrome' sculpture means?
questions.f: From Greek — polychrome statues are painted in many colors, and a polygon has many sides.

questions.q: The word 'Renaissance', the great age of Leonardo and Michelangelo, means?
questions.f: From French — Europe felt ancient art and learning were being 'born again'.

questions.q: 'Pigment' comes from the root 'pingere', meaning?
questions.f: From Latin — the same root also hides inside the word 'picture'.

questions.q: 'Sculpture' is built on an ancient root meaning?
questions.f: From Latin 'sculpere' — sculptors have been 'carvers' for over 2,000 years.

questions.q: 'Statue' comes from the root 'stare', meaning?
questions.f: From Latin — a statue stands in place, just like the words 'station' and 'stable'.

questions.q: The word 'museum' originally meant a temple of the?
questions.f: In Greek myth, the nine Muses inspired art, music and poetry.

questions.q: The word 'easel' originally meant which animal?
questions.f: From Dutch 'ezel' — like a donkey, the easel patiently carries the artist's load.

questions.q: The word 'canvas' originally referred to which plant fiber?
questions.f: From Latin 'cannabis' — early canvas cloth was woven from tough hemp fibers.

questions.q: 'Papier-mâché', the molded paper craft, literally means?
questions.f: It is French — soaked, mashed paper looks 'chewed' before it dries rock-hard.

questions.q: Which spelling names the artist's paint-mixing board?
questions.f: 'Palate' is the roof of your mouth and a 'pallet' is a shipping platform — tricky homophones!

questions.q: The word 'crayon' grew out of 'craie', a word meaning?
questions.f: From French — the first crayons were chalky drawing sticks, long before wax ones.

questions.q: An artist's 'studio' shares its ancient root with which school word?
questions.f: Both come from Latin 'studium', meaning eagerness — a place of devoted work.

questions.q: Paper turned so it is taller than it is wide is in which orientation?
questions.f: It is named 'portrait' because paintings of people are usually tall and narrow.

questions.q: 'Collage' comes from the root 'coller', meaning?
questions.f: From French — a collage is literally a 'gluing' of papers, photos and scraps.

questions.q: A person or idea that inspires an artist is called the artist's?
questions.f: The word comes from the nine Muses, the inspiration goddesses of Greek myth.

questions.q: An artist's 'medium' is the?
questions.f: Paint, clay, ink or even light can be a medium — the plural is 'media'.

questions.q: Shading a drawing with layers of crisscrossed lines is called?
questions.f: The closer the crossed lines, the darker the area appears to the eye.

questions.q: Which yarn craft is worked with one single hook?
questions.f: 'Crochet' comes from a French word meaning 'little hook' — say it 'kro-SHAY'.

questions.q: A heavy woven wall-hanging that shows pictures or scenes is a?
questions.f: Medieval castles hung tapestries partly as art and partly to block cold drafts.

questions.q: To 'gild' a frame or statue means to coat it with a thin layer of?
questions.f: Gilders lay on gold leaf so thin that a gentle breath can tear it.

questions.q: In color theory, a color's 'hue' means its?
questions.f: Light pink and deep wine are different, yet both share the hue 'red'.

questions.q: Adding white to a color creates a lighter version called a?
questions.f: Pink is simply a tint of red — red with white mixed in.

questions.q: Adding black to a color creates a darker version called a?
questions.f: Navy is a shade of blue — that is why 'shady' places are darker.

questions.q: Paint so thick and solid that you cannot see through it is called?
questions.f: Opaque comes from a Latin word for 'shaded' — light cannot pass through.

questions.q: To 'engrave' a design means to cut it into a?
questions.f: Engravers cut lines into metal or stone — coins are made from engraved dies.

questions.q: The arrangement of shapes, colors and figures in a picture is its?
questions.f: 'Composition' means 'putting together' — the same word used for writing music.

questions.q: Baking finished clay pots in a kiln is called?
questions.f: Firing changes clay forever — once fired, it can never turn soft again.

questions.q: The flat, bendy blade artists use to spread thick paint is a palette?
questions.f: Palette knives never need washing mid-painting — paint peels off once dry.

questions.q: The art and science of designing beautiful buildings is called?
questions.f: 'Architect' comes from Greek roots meaning 'chief builder'.

questions.q: The '-scope' ending in 'kaleidoscope' means something you?
questions.f: From Greek 'skopein', to look — telescopes and microscopes share the root.

questions.q: A 'monument' is a work of art built to help people do what?
questions.f: It comes from Latin 'monere', to remind — monuments keep memories alive in stone.

questions.q: Which Dutch master painted around 80 portraits of himself over his lifetime?
questions.f: Rembrandt tracked his own face from confident youth to weathered old age — a painted autobiography.

questions.q: The Impressionist movement was named after which Monet painting?
questions.f: Critic Louis Leroy used 'Impressionists' as an insult in 1874 — the artists proudly kept the name.

questions.q: 'The Starry Night' hangs in which New York institution?
questions.f: Van Gogh painted the view from his asylum window at Saint-Remy, adding an imaginary village.

questions.q: The famous portrait known as 'Whistler's Mother' shows her doing what?
c: Sitting in profile in a chair
questions.f: Whistler's actual title was 'Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1' — he saw it as a color study.

questions.q: In Grant Wood's 'American Gothic', the stern farmer grips which tool?
questions.f: The models were the artist's sister and his dentist, posed before a real Iowa farmhouse.

questions.q: Before oil paint took over, artists bound their pigments with which ingredient to make tempera?
questions.f: Egg tempera dries in minutes and can last a thousand years without darkening.

questions.q: The Bayeux Tapestry, which tells of the Battle of Hastings, is technically a work of?
questions.f: Despite its name it is not a woven tapestry — the 70-meter story is stitched in wool thread.

questions.q: Alexander Calder invented which type of gently moving, hanging sculpture?
questions.f: Marcel Duchamp coined the name 'mobile'; babies now sleep under Calder's invention worldwide.

questions.q: Grids of black lines filled with red, yellow and blue squares are the trademark of?
questions.f: Mondrian worked without rulers taped to the canvas, adjusting lines by eye for perfect balance.

questions.q: Which painter is most often credited with making the first purely abstract artworks?
questions.f: Kandinsky said he wanted paintings to work like music — color as sound, form as rhythm.

questions.q: About how tall is Michelangelo's marble 'David'?
questions.f: The block had been abandoned by two earlier sculptors before 26-year-old Michelangelo took it on.

questions.q: Earthy pigments like ochre and umber owe their reddish-browns to which compound?
questions.f: Iron oxide is basically rust — cave painters were drawing with rusty earth 30,000 years ago.

questions.q: One of humanity's oldest black pigments, lamp black, is collected from?
questions.f: Ancient makers burned oil lamps under plates and scraped off the velvety black soot.

questions.q: J. M. W. Turner was celebrated for dramatic paintings of what?
questions.f: Turner strapped paint boxes to his travels for decades — critics called him 'the painter of light'.

questions.q: Roughly how many paintings by Johannes Vermeer survive today?
questions.f: Vermeer worked slowly and died poor; his tiny surviving output is now beyond price.

questions.q: Which 'golden' mathematical proportion have artists used for pleasing designs since ancient times?
questions.f: The ratio, about 1.618, appears in the Parthenon, in seashells and in sunflower spirals.

questions.q: Which composition rule tells photographers to place subjects a third of the way into the frame?
questions.f: Camera grids overlay two lines each way — the four crossing points are the power spots.

questions.q: Which Mexican muralist, husband of Frida Kahlo, covered walls with scenes of workers and history?
questions.f: Rivera's murals were so popular that muralism became Mexico's national art form.

questions.q: What glass structure now marks the main entrance of the Louvre?
questions.f: Architect I. M. Pei's 1989 pyramid was hated at first — now it is a Paris icon.

questions.q: Visitors to New York's Guggenheim Museum view art while walking down a giant?
questions.f: Frank Lloyd Wright designed it so you take the lift up and drift down past the art.

questions.q: Rembrandt's enormous group portrait of a city militia is known as?
questions.f: Centuries of dark varnish earned it the nickname — cleaning revealed it is set in daylight.

questions.q: The huge round stained-glass windows of Gothic cathedrals are called what windows?
questions.f: The rose window of Notre-Dame in Paris spans about 13 meters and survived the 2019 fire.

questions.q: In Japanese kintsugi, broken pottery is repaired with lacquer dusted in?
questions.f: Kintsugi treats the cracks as part of the object's story, making repairs proudly visible.

questions.q: Indonesian batik creates cloth patterns by blocking the dye with?
questions.f: Artists draw hot wax with a pen-like tool called a canting, then dye and boil the wax away.

questions.q: A 'camera obscura' projects an image of the outside world into a dark room through a?
questions.f: Its Latin name means 'dark chamber' — the projected scene appears upside down on the wall.

questions.q: The most common form of color blindness makes it hard to tell apart which two colors?
questions.f: About 1 in 12 boys has some red-green color blindness; designers plan palettes around it.

questions.q: Roughly how many clay soldiers stand in China's Terracotta Army?
questions.f: Along with soldiers there are clay horses, chariots, acrobats and bronze waterbirds.

questions.q: Sculptors' beloved marble forms deep underground from which rock?
questions.f: Heat and pressure recrystallize limestone into marble — that is why marble glows softly.

questions.q: Traditional Asian lacquerware gets its glossy coating from the sap of a?
questions.f: Sap of the lacquer tree hardens into a waterproof shine — some pieces survive 2,000 years.

questions.q: The linseed oil that binds most oil paints is pressed from the seeds of which plant?
questions.f: Flax gives artists linseed oil and weavers linen — one plant serving art twice.

questions.q: The giant Nazca Lines, drawings visible only from the air, stretch across a desert in?
questions.f: A hummingbird, a monkey and a spider the size of stadiums were scraped into the desert floor.

questions.q: Before cheap paper, scribes wrote and painted on parchment, which is made from?
questions.f: The finest calf-skin version, vellum, was so valued that old books were scraped and reused.

questions.q: When white light passes through a prism, which color bends the most?
questions.f: Violet's short waves bend hardest, which is why it lands at the rainbow's inner edge.

questions.q: Since the 1950s, the Mona Lisa has been displayed behind what?
questions.f: After attacks with acid and a rock, she got sealed protective glass — now climate-controlled too.

questions.q: Seurat's famous painting made of tiny dots shows Parisians relaxing where?
questions.f: 'La Grande Jatte' took Seurat about two years and millions of hand-placed dots.

questions.q: Keith Haring first became famous for chalk drawings of dancing figures made where?
questions.f: Haring drew on empty black ad panels in the New York subway — fast, before police arrived.

questions.q: Artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude were famous for doing what to landmarks?
questions.f: In 1995 they wrapped Berlin's entire Reichstag in silvery fabric for two weeks.

questions.q: The 20-meter steel 'Angel of the North' spreads its wings in which country?
questions.f: Antony Gormley's angel has wings wider than a jumbo jet and greets drivers near Gateshead.

questions.q: Excavations showed that Easter Island's famous stone heads actually have?
questions.f: Many moai are full statues buried to the shoulders by centuries of soil.

questions.q: Old 'flake white' paint was dangerous for artists because it contained?
questions.f: Painters licked brushes to a point, slowly poisoning themselves; titanium white replaced it.

questions.q: Ancient Greek vases are instantly recognizable in which two-color scheme?
questions.f: Potters mastered a triple-firing trick that turned parts of the same clay black or red.

questions.q: Tiffany lamps, prized by collectors, have glowing shades made of?
questions.f: Louis Comfort Tiffany's workshop soldered thousands of glass pieces into dragonflies and wisteria.

questions.q: The jeweled Faberge eggs were Easter gifts made for the royal family of which country?
questions.f: Each imperial egg hid a surprise inside — one held a tiny working train of gold.

questions.q: Early Impressionist paintings were mocked by many critics when first shown.
questions.f: Rejected by the official Salon, the group ran its own show in a photographer's studio in 1874.

questions.q: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling lying flat on his back.
questions.f: A famous myth — he actually stood on a scaffold he designed, painting overhead for four years.

questions.q: The Statue of Liberty's inner iron framework was engineered by Gustave Eiffel.
questions.f: The same engineer raised his famous Paris tower a few years later.

questions.q: The Mona Lisa is a huge painting, taller than an adult person.
questions.f: Visitors are often shocked — the world's most famous painting is only about 77 by 53 centimeters.

questions.q: Acrylic paint was invented centuries before oil paint.
questions.f: Acrylics are a 20th-century invention; oil painting was already ancient by then.

questions.q: For most of history, good blue pigments were far rarer than earthy reds and browns.
questions.f: Reds and browns lay in the soil everywhere, but rich blue had to come from rare minerals.

questions.q: A fresco painter must finish each section before the wet plaster dries.
questions.f: Painters plaster only the patch they can finish that day — the day's patch is called a 'giornata'.

questions.q: 'Miniature' does not come from 'mini' — it comes from 'minium', the name of a?
questions.f: Latin 'minium' was the red lead used for small manuscript pictures — size came into it later.

questions.q: In Renaissance workshops, a 'cartoon' originally meant what?
questions.f: From Italian 'cartone', big paper — Raphael's tapestry cartoons still survive in London.

questions.q: The word 'pastel' comes from 'pastello', meaning a little?
questions.f: Italian for the paste of ground pigment rolled into those soft, chalky sticks.

questions.q: The 'silhouette' shadow portrait is named after Etienne de Silhouette, who was a?
questions.f: His penny-pinching made 'a la Silhouette' mean 'done cheaply' — like a portrait of plain shadow.

questions.q: The brownish photo tone 'sepia' takes its name from which sea creature?
questions.f: Greek 'sepia' means cuttlefish, whose ink filled artists' pens for centuries.

questions.q: The earth pigment 'ochre' comes from a root meaning which color?
questions.f: From Greek 'ochros', pale yellow — though ochres range from gold to rusty red.

questions.q: The warm pigment 'sienna' is named after a historic city in which country?
questions.f: Painters prized the iron-rich earth dug near Siena; 'burnt sienna' is that earth roasted.

questions.q: The color word 'cerulean' comes from 'caelum', meaning?
questions.f: Latin for sky — cerulean blue is literally 'sky blue' with a fancier name.

questions.q: 'Turquoise' literally means a stone from which land?
questions.f: French traders called it 'pierre turquoise' because the gems reached Europe through Turkey.

questions.q: 'Iridescent', for shifting rainbow shimmer, honors Iris, the Greek goddess of the?
questions.f: Iris carried messages across the sky on a rainbow — the colored part of your eye shares her name.

questions.q: The word 'pixel' in digital art is short for?
questions.f: Coined in the 1960s from 'pix' (pictures) plus 'element' — the atom of every screen image.

questions.q: 'Avant-garde' art borrows a military term that means?
questions.f: French for troops sent ahead of the army — avant-garde artists push ahead of taste.

questions.q: 'Abstract' comes from Latin roots meaning to?
questions.f: 'Abstrahere' — abstract art draws away from showing real objects, keeping only shape and color.

questions.q: 'Impasto', paint laid on thick and ridged, comes from a word meaning?
questions.f: Italian — Van Gogh's impasto is so thick that his brush grooves cast tiny shadows.

questions.q: 'Lithography', the printmaking technique, literally means writing on?
questions.f: From Greek 'lithos' — artists still draw on slabs of limestone with greasy crayons to print.

questions.q: An 'amateur' artist is, by the word's root, one who works for?
questions.f: From Latin 'amare', to love — an amateur creates purely for the love of it.

questions.q: A museum 'curator' is, by the word's root, a person who takes?
questions.f: From Latin 'cura', care — the same root gives us 'cure' and 'manicure'.

questions.q: A 'patron' who funds artists gets the name from 'pater', meaning?
questions.f: Latin — a patron protects artists the way a parent would; the Medici were history's most famous.

questions.q: 'Relief' sculpture, which rises from a flat wall, comes from a root meaning to?
questions.f: From Latin 'relevare' — the figures seem lifted from the surface, like faces on coins.

questions.q: 'Gargoyle' shares its gurgling root with 'gargle' — real gargoyles work as?
questions.f: Water gurgles through their throats and shoots clear of the cathedral walls.

questions.q: A 'tessellation' covers a surface with repeating shapes and leaves no?
questions.f: From the Latin for mosaic tiles — honeycombs and Escher's lizards tessellate perfectly.

questions.q: A 'triptych' is an artwork hinged or joined in how many panels?
questions.f: Greek 'tri' + 'ptyche', fold — medieval altarpieces folded shut like winged cabinets.

questions.q: An 'atelier' is a traditional name for an artist's?
questions.f: French — great ateliers were team studios where apprentices ground pigments and painted skies.

questions.q: A 'retrospective' exhibition surveys an artist's work by looking?
questions.f: Latin 'retro' (backward) + 'specere' (to look) — usually a living legend's victory lap.

questions.q: Two or more letters intertwined into a single design, like an artist's initials, form a?
questions.f: Albrecht Durer's famous 'AD' monogram was copied so much he went to court over it.

questions.q: A 'luminous' painting seems to do what?
questions.f: From Latin 'lumen', light — Turner achieved luminous skies with thin glowing glazes.

questions.q: 'Translucent' glass lets light pass through but is not fully?
questions.f: 'Trans' (through) + 'lucere' (to shine) — frosted glass glows without giving a clear view.

questions.q: 'Ceramic' comes from 'keramos', an ancient word for?
questions.f: Greek — Athens even had a potters' quarter called the Kerameikos.

questions.q: The hidden wire or metal skeleton that supports a clay sculpture is the?
questions.f: From the Latin for armor — without an armature, tall clay figures slump under their own weight.

questions.q: The museum specialist who repairs and protects aging artworks is a?
questions.f: Conservators use X-rays and microscopes, removing old varnish a few millimeters at a time.

questions.q: A trained guide who teaches visitors about a museum's art is called a?
questions.f: From Latin 'docere', to teach — the same root as 'doctor' and 'document'.

questions.q: Medieval manuscripts 'illuminated' with gold leaf were literally?
questions.f: From Latin 'illuminare' — the gold caught candlelight so pages truly flashed with light.

questions.q: 'Graffiti' comes from an Italian verb meaning to?
questions.f: 'Graffiare' — archaeologists use the same word for messages scratched on Pompeii's walls.

questions.q: Shading a drawing with thousands of tiny separate dots is called?
questions.f: Engravers perfected stippling because dots survive printing better than delicate lines.

questions.q: In perspective drawing, the spot where parallel lines seem to meet is the?
questions.f: Brunelleschi demonstrated it around 1415 with a painted panel and a peephole mirror trick.

questions.q: The soft green film that time gives to copper and bronze statues is called?
questions.f: From the Italian for a shallow dish coating — collectors prize patina as beauty earned by age.

questions.q: The sculpted band running along the top of a classical wall, sounding like 'freeze', is a?
questions.f: The Parthenon's frieze ran 160 meters around the temple — a marble parade of riders.

questions.q: Which spelling means asking people for votes or opinions — not the painter's cloth?
questions.f: One extra 's' turns the artist's canvas into the campaigner's door-knocking.

questions.q: A 'kinetic' sculpture is one designed to move.
questions.f: From Greek 'kinesis', motion — Calder's mobiles and wind-driven towers are kinetic art.

questions.q: The word 'photography' literally means 'drawing with light'.
questions.f: Coined in 1839 from Greek 'photos' and 'graphein' — light does the drawing on film.

questions.q: Insects scraped from cactus pads, a Spanish trade secret guarded for centuries, and the red in some modern yoghurts converge on which pigment?
questions.f: Cochineal red is still used as a food colouring — it takes about 70,000 insects to make a pound.

questions.q: A pigment new to the 1800s, museum sunflowers slowly turning brown, and chemists tracking the decay with X-rays converge on which colour?
questions.f: Van Gogh's blazing chrome yellow is chemically unstable, so his sunflowers are quietly wilting.

questions.q: A teenager's failed attempt to brew malaria medicine from coal tar, a purple stain left in the flask, and a fortune made in dye works describe which colour?
questions.f: William Perkin's 1856 mistake became mauve, the first synthetic dye, and made him rich by 18.

questions.q: A figure that would vanish under weeds within decades, villagers who 'scour' it by hand every few years, and 3,000 years of chalk turf describe which artwork?
questions.f: The Uffington White Horse survives only because people have kept weeding it since the Bronze Age.

questions.q: A sculptor overhearing his work credited to a rival, a night alone with a chisel, and the only signature he ever carved describe which statue?
questions.f: Michelangelo cut his name into Mary's sash — and reportedly never signed another work.

questions.q: A sculptor who used dynamite as his main carving tool, a granite ridge in South Dakota, and a son who finished the job in 1941 describe whom?
questions.f: About 90 percent of Mount Rushmore was blasted away with explosives, not chiselled.

questions.q: A process handed 'free to the world' in 1839 except in England, pictures on silvered copper that must be tilted to be seen, and exposures lasting minutes describe what?
questions.f: Sitters had to hold still so long that early portrait studios clamped their heads in braces.

questions.q: Faces painted in hot coloured beeswax on thin wooden boards, then bound onto Egyptian mummies, describe the portraits of which region?
questions.f: The Fayum portraits still stare out with startling realism after nearly 2,000 years.

questions.q: 340 leaves of calfskin, a page holding some 10,000 interlocking spirals, and monks who fled Viking raids describe which manuscript?
questions.f: It lives at Trinity College Dublin, where a different page is turned for display each day.

questions.q: Canvases ordered sealed away for two decades after their maker's death, diagrams from spiritual sittings, and abstraction before the men who got the credit describe whom?
questions.f: Hilma af Klint's huge 1907 paintings only became famous about a century after she made them.

questions.q: A painter's daughter admitted to Florence's drawing academy in 1616, life-size biblical heroines, and commissions from the Medici describe whom?
questions.f: Artemisia Gentileschi was the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of Design.

questions.q: A wax model melted out and thrown away, a hollow mould filled with molten metal, and 5,000 years of bronze statues describe which method?
questions.f: Because the wax is destroyed, every lost-wax cast begins with a brand-new model.

questions.q: An element whose name simply means 'colour', the green fire inside emeralds, and the pigment viridian converge on which metal?
questions.f: Chromium compounds also give rubies their red — the same metal, a different crystal.

questions.q: A faint green line along the edge of a pane, minerals added specially to cancel a tint, and extra cost for truly clear glass point to which element?
questions.f: Iron impurities tint almost all sand, so low-iron 'water white' glass is sold at a premium.

questions.q: Wasp-made growths on oak twigs, iron salts, and the ink in Leonardo's notebooks and the US Constitution describe which writing material?
questions.f: Iron gall ink bites into the paper, so it cannot be washed off — but it slowly eats the page too.

questions.q: A papier-mache maker's fevered dream in the 1930s, carved creatures with wings, horns and spots, and a made-up word he shouted describe what?
questions.f: Pedro Linares said the creatures in his dream all cried one nonsense word: 'alebrijes'.

questions.q: Zen monks who carried it from China, a bamboo stalk finished in three strokes, and black ink with no colour at all describe which art?
questions.f: In sumi-e a wrong stroke cannot be fixed, so painters rehearse for years before touching paper.

questions.q: A glaze coloured by iron fired without oxygen, kilns Chinese critics ranked 'first under heaven', and a jade-green sheen describe which ceramic?
questions.f: Korean Goryeo celadon was so admired that Chinese connoisseurs rated it above their own.

questions.q: An ore Chinese potters called 'Muhammadan blue', a Silk Road journey to the Jingdezhen kilns, and painting done before glazing describe which metal?
questions.f: Cobalt survives the kiln's heat, which is why blue-and-white porcelain never fades.

questions.q: A painter who spent 70 years painting a hometown he left as a young man, floating lovers, and a Paris Opera ceiling describe whom?
questions.f: Chagall never stopped painting Vitebsk, the town of his childhood, entirely from memory.

questions.q: An 11-centimetre figure found beside a Danube railway cutting in 1908, faint traces of red ochre, and an age of about 25,000 years describe which object?
questions.f: The Venus of Willendorf is carved from limestone not found anywhere near where she was buried.

questions.q: A bust left behind in an abandoned sculptor's workshop, one eye deliberately unfinished, and a century-long ownership argument describe which artwork?
questions.f: Found in 1912, the Nefertiti bust is now the star of Berlin's Neues Museum.

questions.q: A coating grown as a forest of microscopic tubes, 99.9 percent of light swallowed, and solid objects that read as flat holes describe which material?
questions.f: Vantablack is so dark that crumpled foil coated in it looks like a smooth black sheet.

questions.q: A 2009 lab experiment heating manganese oxide, an unexpectedly brilliant powder in the furnace, and the first new inorganic blue in 200 years describe what?
questions.f: YInMn blue reflects heat so well that it is being tested as a roof coating.

questions.q: A blue ground from cobalt glass, a cheap stand-in for a costly mineral, and old painted skies that have faded to grey describe which pigment?
questions.f: Smalt was affordable but unstable — many Renaissance heavens were far bluer when new.

questions.q: Birds diving at painted grapes, a rival's painted curtain that fooled the winner, and a boast about outdoing nature describe which Greek painter?
questions.f: Zeuxis lost the rematch: Parrhasius painted a curtain so real that Zeuxis asked him to draw it back.

questions.q: A building saved from demolition in the 1970s, giant gilded clocks looming over the galleries, and Impressionists hung under a glass barrel vault describe which museum?
questions.f: The Musee d'Orsay was a railway station whose platforms were too short for modern trains.

questions.q: Mulberry bark beaten into fibres, sliding screens that glow with soft light, and a craft on UNESCO's heritage list describe which paper?
questions.f: Washi is so tough that conservators use it to repair centuries-old European books.

questions.q: Jasper, jade and lapis cut so precisely the joints vanish, flowers that look painted from a few steps back, and a marble mausoleum at Agra describe which craft?
questions.f: Pietra dura inlay uses no paint at all — every petal is a shaped sliver of coloured stone.

questions.q: Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' was once cut down on all sides to fit a wall.
questions.f: Trimmed in 1715 for Amsterdam's town hall; AI recently reconstructed the missing strips.

questions.q: A Banksy artwork shredded itself moments after selling at auction.
questions.f: In 2018 'Girl with Balloon' slid into a hidden shredder — reborn as 'Love is in the Bin'.

questions.q: The Ghent Altarpiece is often called the most frequently stolen artwork in history.
questions.f: Stolen or seized about a dozen times; one panel taken in 1934 has never been found.

questions.q: Egyptian blue is considered the world's first synthetic pigment.
questions.f: Fired from sand, copper and natron 4,500 years ago, it glows infrared — useful to detectives today.

questions.q: Folk artist Grandma Moses only began painting seriously in her late seventies.
questions.f: Anna Mary Robertson Moses swapped embroidery for paint at 78 and made over 1,500 works.

questions.q: 'Vermilion' descends from 'vermiculus', meaning a little?
questions.f: Latin — medieval reds came from worm-like insects, so the wormy name stuck to the color.

questions.q: 'Crimson' traces back to 'kermes', the name of an?
questions.f: Dried kermes scale insects, gathered from Mediterranean oaks, dyed the robes of kings.

questions.q: Before naming a color, 'scarlet' originally referred to a luxurious type of?
questions.f: Medieval 'scarlet' was a costly fine fabric — so often dyed red that the color took the name.

questions.q: 'Azure' ultimately derives from the ancient name of which blue stone?
questions.f: Persian 'lazhward' named the lapis mines; French dropped the L and 'azur' was born.

questions.q: 'Gouache', the opaque cousin of watercolor, comes from 'guazzo', meaning a?
questions.f: Italian for a watering place or splash — fitting for paint that moves as liquid mud-thick color.

questions.q: Leonardo's hazy blending technique 'sfumato' comes from 'fumo', meaning?
questions.f: Italian — his edges vanish 'like smoke', with glazes thinner than a human hair.

questions.q: 'Gesso', the white primer brushed onto canvases, is literally the word for?
questions.f: Italian for gypsum chalk — Renaissance panels took up to fifteen polished gesso layers.

questions.q: To 'etch' a metal printing plate comes from an old root meaning to?
questions.f: Germanic 'etzen' — the acid literally eats the drawn lines into the copper plate.

questions.q: In 'intaglio' printmaking, where does the ink that prints the image sit?
c: In grooves cut below the surface
questions.f: Italian for 'cut in' — the plate is wiped clean, leaving ink only in the incised lines.

questions.q: 'Serigraphy', the fine-art name for screen printing, is built on a root meaning?
questions.f: Latin 'sericum' — the first stencil screens were stretched from real silk.

questions.q: 'Encaustic' painting with hot pigmented wax takes its name from a root meaning?
questions.f: Greek 'enkaustikos' — the Fayum mummy portraits were 'burned in' with heated wax.

questions.q: A 'grisaille' painting is executed entirely in tones of which color?
questions.f: From French 'gris' — sculptors' rivals painted grey fake statues so real they fooled the eye.

questions.q: 'Verdigris', the green crust on old copper, literally means 'green of'?
questions.f: Old French 'vert-de-Grece' — medieval traders credited the pigment to Greek workshops.

questions.q: A sculptor's small preliminary model for a larger work is called a?
questions.f: French for 'little model' — committees approve the maquette before marble is ever cut.

questions.q: A statue in 'contrapposto' stands with its weight shifted onto?
questions.f: Italian for 'counterpoise' — the relaxed S-curve made Greek statues suddenly look alive.

questions.q: The 'bas' in 'bas-relief' tells you the carving projects how far from the surface?
questions.f: French for 'low' — coins are bas-relief, while high relief figures nearly step off the wall.

questions.q: A 'vernissage', the private preview of an exhibition, literally means a day of?
questions.f: French — artists once used preview day to varnish and retouch paintings already on the wall.

questions.q: An artwork's 'provenance' is the documented record of its?
questions.f: From French 'provenir', to come from — gaps in provenance can expose fakes and stolen art.

questions.q: By its root, a 'connoisseur' of art is literally one who?
