questions.f: From Old French 'connoistre', to know — deep knowing, not deep pockets, makes the connoisseur.

questions.q: 'Aesthetic', concerning beauty in art, comes from a root meaning to?
questions.f: Greek 'aisthanesthai' — its opposite gives us 'anaesthetic', to feel nothing at all.

questions.q: The style name 'Baroque' likely comes from 'barroco', a jeweler's word for an irregular?
questions.f: Portuguese — critics meant it as a sneer at art they found lumpy and overdone.

questions.q: 'Rococo' derives from 'rocaille', ornamental work made of pebbles and?
questions.f: French garden grottoes crusted with shellwork lent their name to the frothiest of styles.

questions.q: Critics dubbed Matisse's circle 'Les Fauves', which translates as the?
questions.f: At the 1905 Salon, their savage colors made one critic cry 'Donatello among the wild beasts!'

questions.q: The art movement 'Dada' took its name from a nursery word for a?
questions.f: Legend says the founders stabbed a French dictionary with a paper knife and kept the word it hit.

questions.q: Japanese 'ukiyo-e' prints take their name from a phrase meaning pictures of the?
questions.f: The 'floating world' was the fleeting realm of theaters, fashion and pleasure in old Edo.

questions.q: The fine web of surface cracks on an aged oil painting is called?
questions.f: French — each region's old masters crack differently, so experts read craquelure like fingerprints.

questions.q: Drawing an arm aimed at the viewer far shorter than its real length is called?
questions.f: Mantegna's 'Dead Christ' shocked viewers with feet-first foreshortening around 1480.

questions.q: In weaving, the threads carried over and under across the loom's fixed threads are the?
questions.f: Remember it as 'weft goes left to right' — the fixed lengthwise threads are the warp.

questions.q: Pottery that has been fired once but not yet glazed is called?
questions.f: From French for 'twice-cooked' pastry — bisque ware waits chalky and porous for its glaze firing.

questions.q: 'Porcelain' comes from 'porcellana', an old Italian name for a type of?
questions.f: Marco Polo compared China's glossy ceramics to polished cowrie shells, and the name stuck.

questions.q: An 'aquarelle' is a work painted in which medium?
questions.f: French, from Latin 'aqua' — the water hiding in the word gives the medium away.

questions.q: Painting 'en plein air' means working where?
questions.f: French — paint sold in portable tin tubes from 1841 set the Impressionists loose outdoors.

questions.q: A 'vignette', the soft-edged small illustration, originally meant a design of little?
questions.f: French — printers framed chapter openings with curling vine ornaments.

questions.q: The individual small tiles that make up a mosaic are called?
questions.f: From Greek for 'four-cornered' — Roman floors used millions of hand-cut stone tesserae.

questions.q: A 'pentimento' in a painting is a visible trace of the artist's?
questions.f: Italian for 'repentance' — X-rays show a whale-sized pentimento hiding in many masterpieces.

questions.q: Mondrian's Dutch movement 'De Stijl' translates simply as?
questions.f: Its founders believed straight lines and primary colors could redesign the whole world.

questions.q: Marcel Duchamp's term for an ordinary manufactured object declared to be art is a?
questions.f: His 1913 bicycle wheel on a stool started a debate about what counts as art that never ended.

questions.q: 'Sgraffito' decorates pottery or plaster by scratching through a top layer to reveal?
questions.f: Italian for 'scratched' — Renaissance palace facades were sgraffito-carved like giant cameos.

questions.q: In Egyptian art, the oval frame enclosing a ruler's name in hieroglyphs is a?
questions.f: French soldiers thought the ovals looked like gun cartridges — 'cartouches' — and the name held.

questions.q: The word 'fresco' literally means 'fresh'.
questions.f: Italian — 'buon fresco' is painted on fresh wet plaster, locking pigment in as it cures.

questions.q: Engravers cut their lines into metal with a tool called a burin.
questions.f: The lozenge-tipped burin is pushed, never pulled — masters steer the plate, not the tool.

questions.q: In heraldry, the color red is called 'gules'.
questions.f: From Old French 'gueules' — heraldry keeps its own color names, like 'azure' and 'sable'.

questions.q: 'Achromatic' colors are those without any hue, such as black, white and grey.
questions.f: Greek 'a-' (without) plus 'chroma' (color) — the word literally spells out 'colorless'.

questions.q: What color is fresh grass?
questions.f: Grass is green because of a substance called chlorophyll that helps plants use sunlight.

questions.q: A ripe tomato is usually which color?
questions.f: Green tomatoes turn red as they ripen in the warm sun.

questions.q: What color is a carrot?
questions.f: Long ago most carrots were purple or white — orange ones were bred later.

questions.q: A juicy lemon is which color?
questions.f: Painters call bright, cool yellow 'lemon yellow' after the fruit.

questions.q: Fluffy fair-weather clouds usually look which color?
questions.f: Clouds look white because their tiny water droplets bounce back all the colors of sunlight.

questions.q: Tree trunks are usually which color?
questions.f: Artists mix red, yellow and a little blue to paint tree-bark brown.

questions.q: Most frogs in a pond are which color?
questions.f: Green skin helps a frog hide among the reeds and lily pads.

questions.q: A polar bear's thick fur looks which color?
questions.f: Polar bear hairs are really see-through, but they scatter light and look white as snow.

questions.q: Fire engines are usually painted which color?
questions.f: Bright red helps everyone spot a fire engine rushing to help.

questions.q: A glass of milk is which color?
questions.f: Artists use milky white to make any color look softer and paler.

questions.q: A checkerboard is made of squares of which two colors?
questions.f: Black-and-white patterns are so striking that many artists use nothing else.

questions.q: Road cones that warn drivers are usually which bright color?
questions.f: Orange stands out against grey roads better than almost any other color.

questions.q: A tiger's fur is orange with stripes of which color?
questions.f: Tiger stripes break up its shape so it seems to vanish in tall grass.

questions.q: A robin is famous for the red patch on its?
questions.f: That splash of red makes the robin one of the easiest birds to draw.

questions.q: Valentine hearts are usually colored?
questions.f: Red is often used for love and warmth in art all around the world.

questions.q: Diwali is the festival of what?
questions.f: Families light rows of little clay lamps called diyas and draw colorful floor patterns.

questions.q: Santa Claus is nearly always drawn wearing which color?
questions.f: Old pictures showed Santa in green and brown too, before red became his favorite.

questions.q: At Easter, which food do people decorate with paint and stickers?
questions.f: In Ukraine, artists decorate eggs with beeswax and dye in a craft called pysanky.

questions.q: Which vegetable is often used for a snowman's nose?
questions.f: A snowman is really a sculpture — it just melts when the sun comes out.

questions.q: A colorful kite needs what to fly?
questions.f: Whole festivals fill the sky with painted kites shaped like fish, birds and dragons.

questions.q: A decorated mask is worn over your?
questions.f: People have carved and painted masks for festivals for thousands of years.

questions.q: Folding a sheet of paper into something you can throw makes a paper?
questions.f: Paper airplanes are a simple kind of origami that really flies.

questions.q: Adding button eyes to an old sock makes a?
questions.f: Puppet shows can tell whole stories using nothing but sock characters.

questions.q: What do you fill with air to decorate a party?
questions.f: Balloon artists twist long balloons into dogs, swords and flowers.

questions.q: A book of black outline drawings for you to fill in is a?
questions.f: Coloring is great practice at keeping your hand steady inside the lines.

questions.q: What sticky strip holds a poster on the wall without glue?
questions.f: Artists use special low-stick tape so it peels off without tearing the paper.

questions.q: Which tool covers a big wall with paint fastest?
questions.f: A roller spreads paint in wide stripes, so walls get done in minutes.

questions.q: Dabbing paint with a sponge makes a pattern that looks?
questions.f: Sponge printing is a favorite way to paint clouds, leaves and stone walls.

questions.q: What is inside a pen that makes the marks?
questions.f: Ballpoint pens roll a tiny ball that picks up ink and leaves it on the paper.

questions.q: Chalk marks on a blackboard are usually which color?
questions.f: White chalk shows up best against dark boards, just like white paint on dark paper.

questions.q: Which shape looks like a circle that has been gently stretched?
questions.f: Artists draw an oval first when they want to sketch a face or an egg.

questions.q: How many points does a simple drawn star usually have?
questions.f: A five-pointed star can be drawn without lifting your pencil off the paper.

questions.q: Adding white paint to blue makes which color?
questions.f: Painters call a color mixed with white a 'tint' — light blue is a tint of blue.

questions.q: Mixing red and green paint together usually makes?
questions.f: Red and green sit opposite on the color wheel, so mixing them dulls both.

questions.q: Which artwork is bigger, a mural or a postcard?
questions.f: Some murals are so tall that artists paint them from cranes.

questions.q: What do you rub on paper to stick a shape down?
questions.f: Glue sticks were invented in the 1960s and were inspired by lipstick tubes.

questions.q: What do you dip your brush in to rinse the color off?
questions.f: When the water turns muddy, artists swap it for fresh water.

questions.q: Ripe strawberries are which color?
questions.f: Strawberry red is a warm color, so it seems to jump forward in a picture.

questions.q: A sunflower has yellow petals and a middle of which color?
questions.f: That dark middle is packed with hundreds of tiny seeds arranged in spirals.

questions.q: Most woolly sheep in a field are which color?
questions.f: Sheep wool can be dyed any color once it is spun into yarn.

questions.q: Which part of a carrot plant is green?
questions.f: Artists love carrots because they show two strong colors in one plant.

questions.q: What do you use to hold two pieces of paper together with a click?
questions.f: Staplers push a tiny metal staple through the paper and fold it flat.

questions.q: 'Paintbox' is made by joining 'paint' with which word?
questions.f: A paintbox is simply a box that holds your paints — the word says so.

questions.q: 'Chalkboard' joins 'chalk' with which word?
questions.f: Chalkboards used to be made from real slate rock.

questions.q: 'Handprint' is made from 'hand' and which word?
questions.f: Cave artists left handprints on rock walls more than 20,000 years ago.

questions.q: 'Snowman' joins 'snow' with which word?
questions.f: A snowman is one of the few sculptures that disappears all by itself.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'blue'?
questions.f: Blue and glue rhyme even though they are spelled differently at the start.

questions.q: If a color is 'bright', it looks?
questions.f: Bright colors reflect lots of light straight back to your eyes.

questions.q: The opposite of a bright color is a ____ color.
questions.f: Artists dull a color by adding a little grey or its opposite color.

questions.q: Which word best describes glue?
questions.f: Glue works by gripping tiny bumps on both surfaces as it dries.

questions.q: The opposite of a rough surface is a ____ surface.
questions.f: Artists sand wood smooth before painting so the brush glides along.

questions.q: Something 'shiny' does what to light?
questions.f: Gold paint looks shiny because tiny flecks in it bounce light like mirrors.

questions.q: What is the correct plural of 'box', as in paint boxes?
questions.f: Words ending in x take '-es' to become plural, like boxes and foxes.

questions.q: Yesterday I ____ a picture. Which word fits?
questions.f: 'Draw' becomes 'drew' in the past — just like 'grow' becomes 'grew'.

questions.q: Add '-ing' to 'paint' and you get the word for a?
questions.f: A painting is the picture; a painter is the person who made it.

questions.q: To 'trace' a picture means to?
questions.f: You can trace by holding paper against a sunny window.

questions.q: To 'blend' two colors means to?
questions.f: Blending with a soft brush makes one color melt gently into the next.

questions.q: The words printed under a picture to explain it are the?
questions.f: Newspaper photos almost always come with a caption underneath.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the cutting tool?
questions.f: 'Scissors' hides a silent c — a classic spelling-bee trap.

questions.q: Which spelling of the color made from red and blue is correct?
questions.f: Purple ends in '-ple', just like apple and simple.

questions.q: Which spelling of the color of a lemon is correct?
questions.f: Yellow has a double l right in the middle.

questions.q: Which spelling means a drawing or photograph?
questions.f: 'Picture' ends in '-ture', the same ending as nature and future.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for a carved figure?
questions.f: 'Statue' ends in '-ue', though it sounds like 'chew'.

questions.q: In 'multicolored', the beginning 'multi' means?
questions.f: 'Multi' means many, so a multicolored kite has many colors.

questions.q: A painting that shows one person's face is called a?
questions.f: Before cameras, a painted portrait was the only way to remember a face.

questions.q: The opposite of wet paint is ____ paint.
questions.f: Some paints dry in minutes; thick oil paint can take weeks.

questions.q: In 'colorless', the ending '-less' means?
questions.f: Colorless means without color — clear water and plain glass are colorless.

questions.q: To 'copy' a drawing means to?
questions.f: Art students learn a lot by copying great paintings before inventing their own.

questions.q: Something 'handmade' is made by?
questions.f: 'Handmade' hides the word 'hand' right at the front.

questions.q: A 'pale' color is one that looks?
questions.f: Painters make a color pale by stirring in plenty of white.

questions.q: A cloth or animal that is 'spotted' is covered in?
questions.f: Leopards are spotted, while zebras are striped.

questions.q: A person who makes art is called an?
questions.f: You can be an artist with paint, clay, thread or even sand.

questions.q: A very big statue can be described as?
questions.f: Huge means very large — some statues are taller than 20 grown-ups stacked up.

questions.q: The word 'rainbow' has seven letters.
questions.f: Seven letters and seven rainbow colors — an easy one to remember.

questions.q: The word 'scissors' ends with the letter s.
questions.f: 'Scissors' both starts and ends with s, and hides a silent c too.

questions.q: The color words 'pink' and 'purple' start with the same letter.
questions.f: Both begin with p — and mixing red with white or blue gets you to each one.

questions.q: You can make green paint by mixing blue and yellow.
questions.f: Yellow plus blue is the classic way to mix green in a paintbox.

questions.q: A statue is flat like a piece of paper.
questions.f: Statues are solid and three-dimensional, so you can walk around them.

questions.q: Paint spilled on your clothes is easier to clean while it is still wet.
questions.f: Wet paint rinses out, but dried paint grips the cloth fibers tightly.

questions.q: Japan's flag shows a red circle standing for what?
questions.f: Japan's name in Japanese means 'origin of the sun', so the red disc fits perfectly.

questions.q: Which leaf is drawn in the middle of Canada's flag?
questions.f: The design was chosen in 1965 after a long national argument about flags.

questions.q: Mixing red, green and blue LIGHT all together makes which color?
questions.f: Your TV screen builds every picture out of just those three colors of light.

questions.q: Which gas glows orange-red inside a bright advertising sign?
questions.f: Other gases glow other colors, but every glowing tube got nicknamed 'neon'.

questions.q: Which color is a ruby?
questions.f: Rubies and sapphires are the same mineral — a tiny bit of chromium turns one red.

questions.q: An emerald gemstone is which color?
questions.f: Painters named the pigment 'emerald green' after this glittering stone.

questions.q: An amethyst crystal is which color?
questions.f: Amethyst is a purple form of quartz, colored by traces of iron.

questions.q: Which chemical makes leaves green?
questions.f: Chlorophyll soaks up red and blue light and reflects green back at your eyes.

questions.q: Which country's artists are famous for tall wooden nesting dolls?
questions.f: The largest sets can hold more than 50 dolls, each hand-painted inside the next.

questions.q: A piñata is a decorated paper container filled with what?
questions.f: Piñatas are built from papier-mache and then covered in bright paper frills.

questions.q: Papel picado are Mexican decorations cut from what?
questions.f: Artists stack many sheets and cut them all at once with sharp chisels.

questions.q: Which color is considered lucky and is used everywhere at Chinese New Year?
questions.f: Red envelopes, red lanterns and red banners all invite good fortune.

questions.q: Which two colors decorate almost everything at Halloween?
questions.f: Orange stands for harvest pumpkins and black for the long autumn nights.

questions.q: Which nationality was the painter Claude Monet?
questions.f: Monet's garden at Giverny in northern France is still open to visitors today.

questions.q: Which nationality was Michelangelo?
questions.f: He was born in Tuscany and carved 'David' for the city of Florence.

questions.q: Rembrandt, master of light and shadow, came from which country?
questions.f: Rembrandt worked in Amsterdam, and his house there is now a museum.

questions.q: Which was the first full-length cartoon film Disney ever made?
c: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.f: Released in 1937, it needed over 250,000 hand-painted drawings.

questions.q: Films made by moving clay models a tiny bit at a time are called?
questions.f: One second of stop-motion may need 24 separate photographs.

questions.q: What is the drawing of a plan for a film or cartoon, scene by scene, called?
questions.f: Directors sketch storyboards before a single camera is switched on.

questions.q: What does a camera's flash add to a dark photograph?
questions.f: Early photographers used a burst of burning powder instead of an electric flash.

questions.q: What does a camera lens do to light before it reaches the film or sensor?
questions.f: A curved glass lens bends light rays so they meet and form a sharp picture.

questions.q: Drawing with a wax crayon and then painting over it with watercolor works because?
questions.f: This trick is called wax resist — the crayon lines stay clean and bright.

questions.q: Sprinkling salt onto wet watercolor paint makes what appear?
questions.f: Each salt grain drinks up water and pushes the pigment aside as it dries.

questions.q: Floating paint on water and dipping paper in makes swirly art called?
questions.f: Turkish artists have practised this floating-paint craft, called ebru, for centuries.

questions.q: About how many folded paper cranes make a traditional Japanese good-luck set?
questions.f: A set of 1,000 strung cranes is called senbazuru and is often given as a wish for health.

questions.q: How many sides does an octagon have?
questions.f: Stop signs are octagons so drivers recognize their shape even from behind.

questions.q: Which solid shape is shaped like a can of soup?
questions.f: Artists learn to draw cubes, cones, spheres and cylinders before anything else.

questions.q: Which solid shape rises to a single point, like an ice-cream cone?
questions.f: Sketching simple solids first is how artists build up complicated objects.

questions.q: The Eiffel Tower is repainted every few years to protect it from what?
questions.f: Each repaint uses about 60 tonnes of paint, and the color has changed several times.

questions.q: What are the ancient Egyptian picture-symbols used for writing called?
questions.f: Egyptian scribes could draw over 700 different picture-signs.

questions.q: What was the first material ancient Egyptians made writing sheets from?
questions.f: They sliced the reed's stem, layered the strips crosswise and pressed them flat.

questions.q: Which tool do you use to measure and draw an exact angle?
questions.f: Architects and designers use protractors so their plans fit together exactly.

questions.q: Which drawing tool helps you make a perfect circle?
questions.f: One leg pins the center while the pencil leg swings all the way around.

questions.q: Why do artists sketch lightly in pencil before painting?
questions.f: Light guide lines vanish under paint but keep everything in the right place.

questions.q: What kind of art is made using a computer, tablet and stylus?
questions.f: Digital artists can undo a mistake instantly — something painters cannot do.

questions.q: Museums keep their galleries cool and dim mainly to?
questions.f: Strong light slowly fades old paint and paper, so light levels are carefully limited.

questions.q: Which of these would a museum most likely put behind glass?
questions.f: Paper and ink are the most delicate things museums own.

questions.q: What do we call the stripes of color a shop shows so you can pick a paint?
questions.f: Paint companies invent thousands of names, from 'elephant grey' to 'apple crumble'.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the rainbow's first three colors?
questions.f: The name ROY G BIV helps you remember all seven in order.

questions.q: Which color of clothing keeps you coolest on a hot sunny day?
questions.f: White reflects sunlight away, while black soaks it up as heat.

questions.q: Glow-in-the-dark paint works because it first has to?
questions.f: The paint stores energy from light and then releases it slowly as a soft glow.

questions.q: A macaw parrot is famous for feathers that are?
questions.f: Scarlet macaws mix red, yellow and blue — the three primary colors in one bird.

questions.q: Which African cloth is famous for its bright woven strips of pattern?
questions.f: Kente weavers in Ghana give each pattern its own name and meaning.

questions.q: What is a large paper or printed sheet advertising a film or show called?
questions.f: Poster art became a serious art form in Paris in the 1890s.

questions.q: Which surface would be hardest to paint on with watery paint?
questions.f: Water beads up on plastic instead of soaking in, so the paint slides around.

questions.q: What do you call the small squares of colored glass or stone in a mosaic pattern?
questions.f: Roman mosaic makers cut their tiles with a hammer and a hardened blade.

questions.q: Which sea creature's shell is famous for a beautiful spiral shape artists love to draw?
questions.f: A nautilus shell's spiral gets wider at a steady rate — a favorite of mathematicians.

questions.q: Which of these is a job in a museum?
questions.f: Museum guides are often called docents, from a Latin word meaning 'to teach'.

questions.q: Blowing gently on wet ink through a straw makes lines that look?
questions.f: Ink blowing is a favorite way to draw spooky bare branches.

questions.q: Which is a 'cool' color pairing?
questions.f: Cool colors seem to sink back, which is why distant hills look bluish.

questions.q: An artist who paints in the open air outdoors is painting from?
questions.f: Portable paint tubes, invented in 1841, first let painters work outdoors easily.

questions.q: A person learning a craft by working beside a master is called an?
questions.f: Renaissance apprentices ground pigments for years before touching a canvas.

questions.q: A group of paintings by one artist all on the same subject is called a?
questions.f: Monet's haystack series shows the same field in dozens of different lights.

questions.q: The word 'artistic' describes someone who is?
questions.f: Adding '-ic' turns 'art' into a describing word, just like 'hero' becomes 'heroic'.

questions.q: Someone who thinks up brand-new ideas is described as?
questions.f: 'Creative' comes from 'create', meaning to make something that did not exist.

questions.q: The word 'imagination' means the power to?
questions.f: 'Imagination' hides the word 'image' — pictures in your head.

questions.q: A person who plans how a poster, chair or dress will look is a?
questions.f: 'Design' comes from a root meaning 'to mark out' a plan.

questions.q: A line that runs flat from side to side is?
questions.f: 'Horizontal' comes from 'horizon', the flat line where land meets sky.

questions.q: A line that runs straight up and down is?
questions.f: Artists check a drawing's verticals by holding a pencil up at arm's length.

questions.q: A line that leans across a shape from corner to corner is?
questions.f: Diagonal lines make a picture feel full of movement and energy.

questions.q: Two lines that never meet, however far you draw them, are?
questions.f: In perspective drawing, real parallel lines seem to meet far away — a clever illusion.

questions.q: '3-D' art is short for how many dimensions?
questions.f: Height, width and depth make three — a painting has only the first two.

questions.q: The brightest little spot of light an artist paints on a shiny apple is the?
questions.f: One tiny white highlight can make a flat circle suddenly look round and glossy.

questions.q: Placing a very dark shape next to a very light one creates strong?
questions.f: 'Contrast' comes from roots meaning 'to stand against'.

questions.q: The part of a picture that seems closest to you is the?
questions.f: 'Fore' means in front — the same 'fore' as in forehead and forecast.

questions.q: How the sizes of a drawing's parts compare to each other is called?
questions.f: Artists learn that an adult body is roughly seven and a half heads tall.

questions.q: The criss-cross of squares artists use to copy a picture accurately is a?
questions.f: Copying square by square is how muralists blow a small sketch up to wall size.

questions.q: The first, rough version of a design is called a?
questions.f: 'Draft' and 'draw' are cousins — both come from a root meaning to pull.

questions.q: The one and only first version of an artwork, not a copy, is the?
questions.f: Museums list 'after Rembrandt' when a painting is a copy by someone else.

questions.q: Which word means a picture stands for something bigger, like a dove for peace?
questions.f: Artists have used symbols for centuries so a picture can tell more than it shows.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for a painter's stand?
questions.f: 'Easel' looks odd because it began as a word for a donkey carrying a load.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the art of carving statues?
questions.f: 'Sculpture' needs its silent p, which comes from the Latin for carving.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for a place that shows art?
questions.f: 'Gallery' doubles its l — remember that galleries are long walkways.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the tool with soft bristles?
questions.f: 'Brush' shares its root with 'bristle', the stiff hairs it is made of.

questions.q: Which spelling of the blue-green color is correct?
questions.f: 'Turquoise' is a famous spelling-bee word — the 'oi' trips almost everyone up.

questions.q: To 'sew' means to join cloth using?
questions.f: 'Sew' sounds like 'so' but means something completely different.

questions.q: A single loop of yarn made in knitting is called a?
questions.f: 'Stitch' is used in sewing, knitting and even in the phrase 'a stitch in time'.

questions.q: To 'embroider' cloth means to decorate it with?
questions.f: Skilled embroiderers know dozens of named stitches, like chain and satin stitch.

questions.q: A shape or picture element that repeats through an artwork is called a?
questions.f: A single flower motif might repeat hundreds of times across one printed fabric.

questions.q: When something is 'iconic', it is?
questions.f: 'Icon' first meant a religious picture, then came to mean any famous image.

questions.q: A 'sculpture garden' is a garden filled with?
questions.f: Sculpture parks let big artworks stand in the open air all year.

questions.q: The word 'gigantic' describes a statue that is?
questions.f: 'Gigantic' comes from the giants of Greek myth.

questions.q: To 'restore' an old painting means to?
questions.f: 'Re-store' means to bring back — restorers return artworks to how they once looked.

questions.q: An artwork's 'title' is its?
questions.f: When an artwork has no title, museums label it 'Untitled'.

questions.q: To 'display' an artwork means to?
questions.f: 'Display' comes from a root meaning to unfold or spread out.

questions.q: The word 'photograph' contains the smaller word 'photo'.
questions.f: 'Photo' is short for photograph, and it also means light.

questions.q: Yellow and purple sit opposite each other on the color wheel.
questions.f: Each primary color faces the secondary color mixed from the other two.

questions.q: A pencil marked 'H' is harder and makes a lighter line than one marked 'B'.
questions.f: H stands for hard and B for black — 9H is faint and scratchy, 9B is soft and dark.

questions.q: Paper is made from wood fibers mashed into pulp.
questions.f: The finest artists' papers use cotton fibers instead, which last much longer.

questions.q: A sculpture made of ice can last for years in a warm room.
questions.f: Ice sculptors work in freezing halls, and their art may last only a single day.

questions.q: Cartoon films are still sometimes drawn by hand rather than by computer.
questions.f: Hand-drawn animation is now a specialty, prized for its warm, wobbly lines.

questions.q: Two people can look at the same painting and feel completely different things.
questions.f: Museums love this — one crowd finds calm in a painting while another finds drama.

questions.q: The word 'crayon' contains the word 'ray'.
questions.f: C-r-a-y-o-n hides r-a-y in the middle — a handy spelling clue.

questions.q: Which artist painted 'Nighthawks', showing a late-night diner through big glass windows?
questions.f: Hopper said the painting was about loneliness in a big city, not any real diner.

questions.q: Which fruit did Paul Cezanne paint over and over in his still lifes?
questions.f: Cezanne said he wanted to 'astonish Paris with an apple', and he did.

questions.q: Which artist filled canvases with Californian swimming pools and a splash?
questions.f: Hockney later took up drawing on an iPad and printed the results huge.

questions.q: Roy Lichtenstein made paintings that copied the look of which printed thing?
questions.f: He hand-painted the printer's dots, called Ben-Day dots, one by one.

questions.q: Alberto Giacometti's famous bronze figures are shaped how?
questions.f: He kept scraping his clay figures thinner until some were barely more than lines.

questions.q: Henry Moore's large stone and bronze figures often contain what surprising feature?
questions.f: Moore said a hole can give a sculpture as much shape as the solid parts.

questions.q: Which artist made huge outdoor works from ice, leaves, stones and twigs?
questions.f: Many of his sculptures melt or blow away, so photographs are all that remain.

questions.q: Which Italian artist painted 'The Last Supper' on a monastery wall in Milan?
questions.f: He painted on dry plaster instead of wet, so the mural started flaking within 20 years.

questions.q: Which three artists are often called the great trio of the Italian Renaissance?
questions.f: They all worked within a few decades of each other, sometimes in the same city.

questions.q: Albrecht Durer drew a famous woodcut of a rhinoceros without ever?
questions.f: He worked from a written description and a sketch, and his armored rhino was copied for 250 years.

questions.q: What is a 'kiln' used for?
questions.f: 'Kiln' comes from a Latin word for a kitchen or cooking place.

questions.q: What is the thin glassy coating that makes pottery shiny and waterproof?
questions.f: Glaze is powdered glass and minerals that melt smooth in the kiln's heat.

questions.q: A simple pot built from rolled ropes of clay stacked in circles is a?
questions.f: Coiling is older than the potter's wheel and still used by artists worldwide.

questions.q: Why do potters knead and pound clay before shaping it?
questions.f: Trapped air can expand in the kiln and crack a pot apart — kneading clay is called wedging.

questions.q: A print made by carving a picture into soft floor tile material is a?
questions.f: Lino is easier to carve than wood, so schools use it for printmaking.

questions.q: Screen printing pushes ink through a fine mesh using a rubber-edged?
questions.f: T-shirt printers use one screen for each color in the design.

questions.q: Which sculpture technique joins metal pieces by melting their edges together?
questions.f: Welded steel let 20th-century sculptors build huge open shapes full of air.

questions.q: An artwork assembled from everyday found objects is called an?
questions.f: Artists have built sculptures from bicycle parts, bottle tops and old typewriters.

questions.q: A whole room built as an artwork you walk into is called an?
questions.f: Installations can include light, sound, smell and even the visitors themselves.

questions.q: Why do artists spray finished charcoal drawings with fixative?
questions.f: Charcoal dust sits loose on the paper until a fine mist of resin glues it down.

questions.q: Which eraser can be squished into any shape to lift pencil out of a drawing?
questions.f: Artists knead it like putty, and it lifts graphite without scrubbing the paper.

questions.q: What tool do artists hold up at arm's length to compare sizes and angles?
questions.f: This trick, called sighting, turns your pencil into a simple measuring stick.

questions.q: Colors that sit next to each other on the color wheel are called?
questions.f: Analogous schemes, like blue-green-teal, feel calm because they share a family.

questions.q: Three colors spaced evenly around the color wheel form which scheme?
questions.f: Red, yellow and blue form the most famous triadic set of all.

questions.q: How strong or washed-out a color looks is called its?
questions.f: A fully saturated red screams; the same red with grey added whispers.

questions.q: Staring at a red shape then looking at white paper makes you see a ghostly?
questions.f: Your tired red-sensing cells hand over, so you see red's opposite — an afterimage.

questions.q: Why do faraway mountains look pale blue to a landscape painter?
questions.f: Painters copy this haze on purpose, a trick called atmospheric perspective.

questions.q: What gives human skin and hair its brown coloring?
questions.f: Portrait painters mix skin tones from reds, yellows, blues and white — never one 'skin' color.

questions.q: Digital pictures are built from tiny colored squares called?
questions.f: Zoom in far enough on any photo and the smooth image breaks into squares.

questions.q: Warli painting, made with simple white stick figures, comes from which country?
questions.f: Warli artists paint rice-paste figures on mud walls to celebrate harvests and weddings.

questions.q: The Ndebele people are famous for painting bold geometric patterns on what?
questions.f: Ndebele women in South Africa repaint the bright wall designs by hand each year.

questions.q: Inuit artists in the Arctic are famous for carving which soft stone?
questions.f: Soapstone is soft enough to shape with hand tools, yet takes a deep polish.

questions.q: Navajo artists of the American Southwest are world-famous for weaving what?
questions.f: Navajo weavers work on upright looms and often invent each pattern as they go.

questions.q: Pysanky are decorated eggs made with wax and dye by artists in which country?
questions.f: Each color is dyed in turn, with wax protecting the parts that must stay light.

questions.q: Maori artists of New Zealand are renowned for intricate carving in?
questions.f: Carved meeting houses tell a whole community's history in spirals and figures.

questions.q: Where would you find Michelangelo's original 'David' statue today?
questions.f: It stood outdoors for 369 years before moving into the Accademia Gallery.

questions.q: The Rijksmuseum, home to Dutch masterpieces, is in which city?
questions.f: Its long Gallery of Honour was designed so daylight falls on Rembrandt's biggest work.

questions.q: London's Tate Modern gallery is housed in a converted?
questions.f: Its vast Turbine Hall once held electricity generators and now holds giant artworks.

questions.q: Which artist made 'The Persistence of Memory', with clocks draped over a branch?
questions.f: The tiny painting is only about 24 by 33 centimetres — smaller than a sheet of paper.

questions.q: Which artist was known as a leader of the Impressionists' love of dappled sunlight and picnics?
questions.f: Renoir kept painting even when illness made him strap the brush to his hand.

questions.q: Which American artist painted mothers and children in soft Impressionist colors?
questions.f: Cassatt moved to Paris and helped American collectors discover Impressionism.

questions.q: What is a 'triptych' most likely to be found above?
questions.f: Three-panel altarpieces could be folded shut to protect the painting inside.

questions.q: Which is the softest and darkest of these pencil grades?
questions.f: B stands for black, and the higher the number, the softer and darker the line.

questions.q: An artist's 'thumbnail' is a?
questions.f: Designers often draw a dozen thumbnails before choosing one to develop.

questions.q: Which is the correct order for painting in watercolor?
c: Any order, it makes no difference
questions.f: Watercolor is see-through, so you cannot cover a dark patch with a light one.

questions.q: Cave artists sometimes blew powdered pigment through a hollow bone to make?
questions.f: Blown paint around a hand leaves a stencilled handprint — found on cave walls worldwide.

questions.q: A print can be an original artwork, not just a copy of a painting.
questions.f: Prints are made from a plate the artist carved, so each pull is an original.

questions.q: Mixing all three primary paint colors together makes a muddy brown or grey.
questions.f: Each pigment absorbs some light, so mixing many leaves very little light bouncing back.

questions.q: Michelangelo carved 'David' from a block that other sculptors had already given up on.
questions.f: The tall, narrow, part-cut block sat abandoned in a Florence yard for about 25 years.

questions.q: Charcoal is one of the oldest drawing materials in the world.
questions.f: Burnt sticks from the fire were drawing tools long before pencils existed.

questions.q: A single artwork can belong to more than one style or movement.
questions.f: Artists rarely fit neatly in one box — labels are invented by critics afterwards.

questions.q: Acrylic paint can be thinned with water but becomes waterproof once dry.
questions.f: That is why acrylic brushes must be washed before the paint sets hard.

questions.q: The word 'paper' takes its name from which ancient writing material?
questions.f: Real paper came from China, but Europe borrowed the older Egyptian name.

questions.q: The root 'morph' in 'zoomorphic' means?
questions.f: From Greek — a zoomorphic pot is one shaped like an animal.

questions.q: The root 'zoo' in 'zoomorphic' means?
questions.f: From Greek 'zoion' — a zoo is literally a place of animals.

questions.q: 'Plastic' arts, like clay modelling, take their name from a root meaning?
questions.f: From Greek 'plastikos' — the material was named after the property, not the reverse.

questions.q: 'Calligraphy' is built from Greek words meaning?
questions.f: 'Kallos' plus 'graphein' — some calligraphers spend years on a single alphabet.

questions.q: The root 'icon' in 'iconography' means?
questions.f: From Greek 'eikon' — the little pictures on your screen borrowed the same word.

questions.q: The root 'xylo' in 'xylography', an old word for woodblock printing, means?
questions.f: From Greek — a xylophone is literally a 'wood sound' instrument.

questions.q: The '-ism' ending in 'Impressionism' or 'Cubism' marks a?
questions.f: Art history is full of '-isms', and most began as insults from critics.

questions.q: 'Mural' comes from the Latin word 'murus', meaning?
questions.f: That root also gives us 'immure' — to shut inside walls.

questions.q: The word 'mosaic' is thought to come from a word connected to the?
questions.f: The Muses inspired art, and their name may hide in this patient tile craft.

questions.q: 'Tempera' paint takes its name from a root meaning to?
questions.f: From Latin 'temperare' — the same root as 'temper' and 'temperature'.

questions.q: 'Terracotta' literally means?
questions.f: From Italian — you can read the recipe right in the name.

questions.q: 'Graphite', the pencil mineral, is named from a root meaning to?
questions.f: From Greek 'graphein' — the mineral was named in 1789 for what it does best.

questions.q: The word 'design' comes from a root meaning to?
questions.f: From Latin 'designare' — a designer marks out a plan before anything is built.

questions.q: 'Mandala', the circular pattern used in Asian art, comes from a word meaning?
questions.f: From Sanskrit — mandalas are built outward from one still point at the centre.

questions.q: 'Rangoli' comes from a root meaning?
questions.f: From Sanskrit 'rang' — the word for color hides in many Indian art terms.

questions.q: 'Glaze', the shiny coat on pottery, is closely related to which everyday word?
questions.f: Both come from the same old root — glaze really is a thin skin of glass.

questions.q: The verb 'draw' originally meant to?
questions.f: That older sense survives in 'draw the curtains' and 'a horse-drawn cart'.

questions.q: The root 'sym' in 'symmetry' means?
questions.f: Greek 'sym' plus 'metron' means 'measured together' — both sides match.

questions.q: The prefix 'peri' in 'perimeter', the line around a shape, means?
questions.f: From Greek — a periscope looks around corners and a perimeter runs all the way round.

questions.q: The prefix 'macro' in 'macro photography' means?
questions.f: Macro lenses make tiny things look large, filling the frame with a single insect eye.

questions.q: The prefix 'proto' in 'prototype', the first model of a design, means?
questions.f: From Greek — designers build a prototype before making thousands of copies.

questions.q: A person who studies and writes about the history of art is an art?
questions.f: Art historians read paintings like documents, spotting clues in clothes and objects.

questions.q: A person whose job is judging and writing opinions about new art is a?
questions.f: From Greek 'krites', a judge — the same root as 'criticize' and 'criterion'.

questions.q: The person who runs the bidding when an artwork is sold is the?
questions.f: 'Auction' comes from a Latin word meaning 'increase', because the bids climb.

questions.q: An artist who designs jewellery works with a?
questions.f: 'Jewel' comes through French from a Latin word for a plaything or delight.

questions.q: Someone who designs the look of clothes is a fashion?
questions.f: Fashion designers draw flat sketches called technical drawings so makers can copy them.

questions.q: Which word describes an artwork's overall feeling, like calm or stormy?
questions.f: Artists change mood with color temperature, light and even brushstroke direction.

questions.q: 'Perspective' comes from a root meaning to?
questions.f: From Latin 'perspicere' — early artists literally looked through peepholes to check it.

questions.q: A 'genre' painting shows?
questions.f: Dutch artists made genre painting famous with kitchens, letters and card games.

questions.q: An 'anonymous' artwork is one whose maker is?
questions.f: Whole medieval cathedrals were carved by anonymous craftspeople.

questions.q: The word 'chisel' comes from a root meaning to?
questions.f: From Latin 'caedere', to cut — the same root hides in 'scissors' and 'decide'.

questions.q: A 'mallet' is a kind of?
questions.f: From Latin 'malleus', hammer — sculptors prefer wooden mallets so chisels last longer.

questions.q: The word 'chalk' comes from a root meaning?
questions.f: From Latin 'calx' — the same root that gives us calcium.

questions.q: Something described as 'ornate' is?
questions.f: 'Ornate' and 'ornament' both come from the Latin for 'to equip or adorn'.

questions.q: The 'gilded' frame of a mirror has been covered with?
questions.f: 'Gilded' comes straight from 'gold' — its old past form was 'gilt'.

questions.q: A 'facade' is which part of a building?
questions.f: From French — the word hides 'face', which is exactly what a facade is.

questions.q: An 'arch' in architecture is a curved opening that mainly?
questions.f: Romans built arches so well that many still carry roads and water today.

questions.q: A tall stone pillar holding up a roof is a?
questions.f: Greek columns came in three orders — Doric, Ionic and Corinthian.

questions.q: A 'dome' is a roof shaped like?
questions.f: 'Dome' comes from a word for 'house', the same root as 'domestic'.

questions.q: Which word means an artwork or building has been made to last a very long time?
questions.f: From Latin 'durare', to last — the same root as 'endure' and 'during'.

questions.q: To 'exhibit' an artwork means to?
questions.f: From Latin 'exhibere', to hold out — the museum holds the work out for all to see.

questions.q: A 'symmetrical' pattern would look the same if you did what to it?
questions.f: Butterflies, snowflakes and Taj Mahal facades are all famously symmetrical.

questions.q: The word 'sepia' now describes photographs that look?
questions.f: Old prints were toned brown on purpose because it helped them last longer.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the fast-drying plastic-based paint?
questions.f: 'Acrylic' keeps the tricky '-yl-' from the chemical name acrylic acid.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for a dark shadow-shaped portrait?
questions.f: A spelling-bee classic — the h hides silently after the l.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for the see-through paint?
questions.f: Both British and American spellings are correct, but the middle stays the same.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct for a picture made from small tiles?
questions.f: Remember it as mo-sa-ic, three neat syllables in a row.

questions.q: 'Photogenic' means someone tends to look good in photographs.
questions.f: It joins 'photo' (light) with a root meaning 'producing' — good light-making.

questions.q: The word 'canvas' and the word 'canvass', meaning to seek votes, are the same word.
questions.f: They share a surprising history — canvassing once meant tossing someone in a canvas sheet.

questions.q: 'Sculpt' and 'sculptor' both keep a silent p in their spelling.
questions.f: The p survives from Latin 'sculpere', to carve — sound it out in your head to spell it.

questions.q: The word 'artisan' means a skilled worker who makes things by hand.
questions.f: Artisan and artist share a root, but an artisan's work is usually useful as well as lovely.

questions.q: A Paris toll collector who never left France, jungles copied from a botanical garden, and 'The Sleeping Gypsy' point to which painter?
questions.f: Critics mocked his flat, dreamlike jungles until Picasso threw a banquet in his honour.

questions.q: A former wallpaper designer, bowler-hatted men falling like rain, and a painted pipe labelled 'this is not a pipe' point to whom?
questions.f: Magritte wanted viewers to notice that a picture of a thing is never the thing itself.

questions.q: A lollipop logo drawn in one afternoon, a dream sequence for a Hitchcock film, and a moustache modelled on Velazquez point to which artist?
questions.f: Dali insisted the sweet's logo sit on top of the wrapper so it always showed — and it still does.

questions.q: A gold engraver's son, a Vienna society crowned with a gilded dome of leaves, and a trip to Ravenna's mosaics point to which painter?
questions.f: Those Byzantine mosaics launched his 'Golden Phase', which produced 'The Kiss'.

questions.q: A man who moved house more than 90 times, used over 30 artist names, and signed himself 'Old Man Crazy to Paint' is which printmaker?
questions.f: He was about 70 when he made 'The Great Wave', his most famous print of all.

questions.q: A block nicknamed 'the Giant', abandoned for 25 years, a 1501 contract with a 26-year-old, and a move indoors in 1873 tell the story of which statue?
questions.f: Two sculptors had already hacked at the marble and quit before Michelangelo took it on.

questions.q: An empty frame still hanging on the wall, a 1990 overnight theft of 13 works, and a Boston mansion built to look Venetian point to which museum?
questions.f: Her will forbade rearranging anything, so the robbed frames hang empty to this day.

questions.q: A Long Island barn floor, a 1949 magazine asking 'is he the greatest living painter?', and fractal maths used to test fakes point to whom?
questions.f: He laid huge canvases flat on the floor and walked around them, dripping paint as he went.

questions.q: A pigment from a single Swedish chemist's lab, Napoleon's bedroom wallpaper on St Helena, and sick Victorian dressmakers point to which poison in green paint?
questions.f: Scheele's green was so cheap that it colored wallpaper, sweets wrappers and party dresses.

questions.q: A childhood among tapestry restorers, a giant bronze arachnid called 'Maman', and marble spirals point to which sculptor?
questions.f: She called the nine-metre spider a portrait of her mother, patient and endlessly repairing.

questions.q: A 1926 customs officer taxing a bronze as plain metal, a 1928 court ruling that abstraction counts as art, and 'Bird in Space' involve which sculptor?
questions.f: US customs wanted 40 percent duty on kitchen utensils; the court disagreed and freed modern art.

questions.q: Four teenagers and a dog named Robot in 1940, creeping green algae in the 1960s, and an exact concrete replica built nearby describe which cave?
questions.f: Visitors' breath fed the algae, so the real cave closed in 1963 and a copy took its place.

questions.q: A wager over a galloping horse's hooves, 24 trip-wire cameras beside a racetrack, and a machine called the zoopraxiscope point to which photographer?
questions.f: His 1878 photo sequence proved all four hooves do leave the ground — and pointed the way to film.

questions.q: A three-year-old's impatient question in 1943, a firm named after polarized light, and a print developing in your hand describe which invention?
questions.f: Edwin Land's daughter asked why she could not see the photo at once; he had an answer by 1948.

questions.q: A botanist's 1843 book of seaweeds, iron salts turning deep blue in sunlight, and the origin of architects' 'blueprints' describe which process?
questions.f: Anna Atkins made what many call the first book illustrated with photographs.

questions.q: Complaints about dull black threads at a Paris tapestry works, a law of simultaneous contrast, and Seurat's dots trace back to which chemist?
questions.f: The 'faulty' dyes were fine — neighbouring colors were fooling the weavers' eyes.

questions.q: A Berlin dye-maker's contaminated batch in about 1706, the waves of a Japanese print master, and a modern antidote for metal poisoning describe which pigment?
questions.f: Hokusai seized on the cheap new blue, and doctors still prescribe it as a medicine today.

questions.q: A Cumbrian sheep-marking discovery, guards posted at the mine, and a wartime blockade that forced clay to be mixed with powder gave us which everyday object?
questions.f: Nicolas-Jacques Conte's clay-and-graphite recipe of 1795 is still how pencils are graded today.

questions.q: Artists once rubbing out pencil with stale bread, a 1770 London shop mix-up, and a sap named for the job it does describe which invention?
questions.f: The material was literally named 'rubber' because it rubbed out marks.

questions.q: A soap company's wallpaper cleaner, a teacher's classroom idea, and a 1956 rebrand for children describe which modelling material?
questions.f: Sales of wallpaper cleaner were dying; renamed as a toy, the same dough sold by the tonne.

questions.q: A company that first sold carbon black for tyres, a name coined from the French for chalk plus a word for oily, and 1903 describe which product?
questions.f: Alice Binney, the founder's wife, blended 'craie' and 'oleaginous' into the famous name.

questions.q: Two concert musicians tinkering after hours, a 1935 Kodak triumph, and a 1973 pop song describe which colour film?
questions.f: Leopold Mannes and Leopold Godowsky Jr were professional musicians before they were chemists.

questions.q: Dyed grains of potato starch, three colour filters, and the Lumiere brothers in 1907 describe which early colour photograph process?
questions.f: Millions of microscopic dyed starch grains acted as a filter mosaic — the first easy colour photos.

questions.q: An Italian handyman hiding in a cupboard overnight, a painting carried out under a workman's smock, and Picasso questioned by police describe which crime?
questions.f: Vincenzo Peruggia kept the painting in his Paris room for two years before trying to sell it.

questions.q: A mural on dry wall instead of wet plaster, flaking within 20 years, sandbags in 1943, and a 21-year restoration describe which artwork?
questions.f: Leonardo's experiment failed almost at once, which is why so little original paint survives.

questions.q: A painter who designed the Uffizi, wrote 'Lives of the Artists', and turned 'Gothic' into an insult was?
questions.f: Vasari's gossipy book is why we know so many Renaissance artists' stories at all.

questions.q: A convex mirror reflecting two extra witnesses, a small dog, and a wall signature reading 'was here 1434' belong to which painting?
questions.f: Jan van Eyck signed the back wall like graffiti — unusual and cheeky for the 1400s.

questions.q: Plato pointing to the sky, Aristotle gesturing outward, and Michelangelo slipped in as a brooding philosopher describe which fresco?
questions.f: Raphael painted himself into the crowd too, peeking out near the right-hand edge.

questions.q: An alchemist locked in a Saxon castle to make gold, white clay from a nearby hill, and Europe's first true porcelain describe which factory?
questions.f: Johann Bottger never made gold, but crossed-swords Meissen marks became worth almost as much.

questions.q: A factory village called Etruria, a device invented to measure kiln heat, and a grandson named Charles Darwin describe which potter?
questions.f: His pale blue jasperware with white figures has been copied for over 200 years.

questions.q: A rushed Christmas poster for actress Sarah Bernhardt in 1894, a six-year contract, and swirling hair everywhere describe which artist?
questions.f: Overnight fame turned his flowing style into the look of Art Nouveau across Europe.

questions.q: A Brotherhood admiring painters from before Raphael, a model floating in a cold bathtub, and a poet who kept a pet wombat describe which group?
questions.f: Elizabeth Siddal caught a chill posing as Ophelia when the bath's warming lamps went out.

questions.q: A missionary in a coal-mining district, about 900 paintings in a single decade, and 650 letters to an art-dealer brother describe which artist?
questions.f: Theo's widow later published the letters, which is how the world learned to love the paintings.

questions.q: A Paris stockbroker who quit finance in his thirties, a stormy stay in Arles, and canvases of Tahiti describe which painter?
questions.f: He wanted colours 'from imagination', and his flat bright shapes shaped modern art.

questions.q: One hundred million hand-painted porcelain seeds, 1,600 artisans in Jingdezhen, and a hall visitors were told to stop walking on describe which work?
questions.f: Ai Weiwei's seeds looked identical from afar; every single one was individually painted.

questions.q: Which metal salt is used to make green fireworks and green glass?
questions.f: Strontium burns red, sodium yellow and copper blue — fireworks are chemistry as art.

questions.q: Egypt's Great Pyramid was originally covered in a smooth outer casing of?
questions.f: Most of the polished casing was later removed to build medieval Cairo.

questions.q: The Parthenon's marble sculptures were carved under the supervision of which sculptor?
questions.f: Phidias also made a giant gold-and-ivory Athena inside the temple, long since lost.

questions.q: Which classical column style is topped with carved acanthus leaves?
questions.f: Doric capitals are plain, Ionic have scrolls, and Corinthian burst into leaves.

questions.q: The Pantheon in Rome is famous for a dome with what at its very top?
questions.f: The nine-metre oculus is the building's only light source — and lets the rain in.

questions.q: Gothic cathedrals used flying buttresses mainly to?
questions.f: With the weight braced outside, builders could fill the walls with stained glass instead of stone.

questions.q: A column carved in the shape of a standing woman is called a?
questions.f: Six caryatids hold up a porch of the Erechtheion in Athens.

questions.q: Frank Gehry's swooping Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao is clad in which metal?
questions.f: The paper-thin titanium ripples in the light and gave rise to the phrase 'the Bilbao effect'.

questions.q: Christ the Redeemer in Rio is covered with thousands of small tiles of which stone?
questions.f: Soapstone resists weather well — handy for a statue struck by lightning most years.

questions.q: Which is the world's tallest statue, unveiled in India in 2018?
questions.f: It stands 182 metres tall and honours Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

questions.q: Antoni Gaudi covered Park Guell with mosaics made from broken tiles, a technique called?
questions.f: Using smashed offcuts let curved surfaces be tiled — and cost almost nothing.

questions.q: Which artist created 'Balloon Dog', a giant mirror-polished stainless steel sculpture?
questions.f: They look inflatable but weigh over a tonne, with no visible weld seams at all.

questions.q: Which artist's 45,500-year-old painting of a wild pig, found in Sulawesi, is among the world's oldest known?
questions.f: Cave art turns up on nearly every continent, made long before writing was invented.

questions.q: The oldest known drawing kit, a 73,000-year-old crosshatch on stone, was found in which country?
questions.f: The Blombos Cave hashtag was drawn in ochre — the earliest known deliberate drawing.

questions.q: Georgia O'Keeffe painted for decades at Ghost Ranch in which US state?
questions.f: She collected sun-bleached desert bones and painted them floating against blue skies.

questions.q: Which artist quit art for years to compete seriously in international chess?
questions.f: He played for France in chess olympiads while secretly building one last artwork.

questions.q: Velazquez's 'Las Meninas' surprises viewers by including which figure?
c: The painter himself at his easel
questions.f: A mirror at the back shows the king and queen, so we seem to stand exactly where they stood.

questions.q: Vincent van Gogh and Paul Gauguin once shared a house and painted side by side.
questions.f: They spent nine intense weeks together in Arles in 1888 before falling out.

questions.q: Photography's arrival pushed many painters toward styles a camera could not copy.
questions.f: Once cameras handled likenesses, painters chased light, feeling and pure abstraction instead.

questions.q: The Colosseum was originally decorated with painted plaster and marble facing.
questions.f: Almost all Roman monuments were brightly finished — bare stone is what time left behind.

questions.q: 'Pencil' comes from 'penicillus', a Latin word meaning a little?
questions.f: Romans used little brushes with tapered tips; the medicine penicillin shares the same root.

questions.q: The word 'style' comes from 'stilus', which was an ancient?
questions.f: Your handwriting came from your stilus, so your 'style' became your personal manner.

questions.q: 'Portrait' comes from a root meaning to?
questions.f: From Latin 'protrahere' — the painter draws the person's likeness out onto the panel.

questions.q: 'Caricature' comes from 'caricare', a word meaning to?
questions.f: Italian — a caricaturist 'loads up' the nose or chin until it nearly bursts.

questions.q: 'Grotesque' first described decorations discovered in?
questions.f: Renaissance artists crawled into Nero's buried palace and copied the odd painted creatures they found.

questions.q: 'Still life' entered English as a translation of a Dutch word meaning?
questions.f: Dutch 'stilleven' named a whole industry of painted fruit, flowers and gleaming glassware.

questions.q: 'Landscape' entered English as a painters' term originally meaning a?
questions.f: It arrived with Dutch landscape paintings in the 1600s and only later described real scenery.

questions.q: 'Sketch' comes from a root meaning?
questions.f: From Greek 'schedios' via Italian — a sketch was always meant to be quick and improvised.

questions.q: 'Enamel' comes from an old root meaning to?
questions.f: Enamel is powdered glass melted onto metal, so the name describes the method exactly.

questions.q: 'Cloisonne' enamel is named for the little metal?
questions.f: French 'cloison' means partition; thin wires fence off each pool of colored glass.

questions.q: 'Repousse' metalwork is made by hammering the design?
questions.f: French for 'pushed back' — the raised design appears on the front as you hammer behind.

questions.q: 'Filigree' is delicate metalwork built from twisted?
questions.f: Its name joins the Latin words for thread and grain, both used in the technique.

questions.q: 'Marquetry' decorates furniture with patterns made of?
questions.f: Cabinetmakers cut several woods at once so the pieces slot together like a jigsaw.

questions.q: 'Khaki', the dusty uniform color, comes from a word meaning?
questions.f: From Urdu and Persian — the color was chosen so uniforms matched dry ground.

questions.q: 'Maroon', the deep brownish red, comes from a French word for a?
questions.f: French 'marron' — the color of a roasted chestnut shell.

questions.q: 'Beige' originally described wool that was?
questions.f: French — the color of natural, unbleached, undyed wool straight off the sheep.

questions.q: 'Ecru', a pale cream color, comes from a word meaning?
questions.f: French 'ecru' — the shade of raw linen before any bleaching.

questions.q: 'Cyan' comes from 'kyanos', an old word for?
questions.f: Greek — the same root gives the mineral name for deep blue kyanite.

questions.q: 'Fuchsia', the vivid pinkish purple, is named after?
questions.f: The flower honours Leonhart Fuchs, and the color took the flower's name.

questions.q: 'Chartreuse', a yellow-green, is named after a?
questions.f: Carthusian monks have made the green liqueur since the 1700s, and its recipe is still secret.

questions.q: Which color word comes from the name of a Spanish city famous for fine leather?
questions.f: Cordoba's burgundy-brown leather was so prized that shoemakers still use the word.

questions.q: 'Damask', the patterned fabric artists love to paint, is named after which city?
questions.f: Trade names hide geography everywhere in art: muslin, calico and organdie all do the same.

questions.q: 'Calico' cotton takes its name from a port in?
questions.f: Kozhikode, once called Calicut, shipped the printed cottons that made the name famous.

questions.q: 'Vellum', the finest writing skin, comes from a root meaning?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'veal' — vellum was made from young calfskin.

questions.q: 'Parchment' takes its name from the ancient city of?
questions.f: Legend says Pergamon developed it when a rival cut off its supply of papyrus.

questions.q: The word 'ink' descends from a Greek word meaning?
questions.f: 'Enkauston' also gives us 'encaustic' — ancient purple inks were fixed with heat.

questions.q: 'Turpentine', the painter's solvent, is named after which tree?
questions.f: Most modern turpentine is distilled from pine resin instead.

questions.q: 'Varnish' is thought to be named after Berenice, an ancient?
questions.f: The Libyan city was linked with fragrant resin — the raw material of varnish.

questions.q: 'Kaolin', the white clay of porcelain, is named after a hill meaning?
questions.f: Chinese 'Gaoling' — the hill that supplied the clay gave its name to the material.

questions.q: 'Faience', the tin-glazed pottery, is named after the Italian town of?
questions.f: Delftware, majolica and faience are cousins — each named for where it was made.

questions.q: 'Mannequin' comes from a Dutch word meaning?
questions.f: Artists' jointed 'lay figures' were the first mannequins, used to arrange drapery.

questions.q: A 'mahlstick' (or maulstick) is a padded stick a painter uses to?
questions.f: One end rests on the canvas edge so the wrist never smudges wet paint.

questions.q: 'Sanguine' drawing chalk gets its name because its color resembles?
questions.f: From Latin 'sanguis' — red chalk was Leonardo's favourite for studies of muscles and faces.

questions.q: Drawing with a silver stylus that slowly tarnishes brown is called?
questions.f: Silverpoint cannot be erased, so Renaissance apprentices had to draw with total confidence.

questions.q: A 'Claude glass', carried by 18th-century landscape painters, was a small?
questions.f: Named after painter Claude Lorrain, it simplified a view into soft tones like his paintings.

questions.q: Painting a picture in one sitting, while everything is still wet, is called?
questions.f: Italian for 'at first' — it demands speed and nerve, with no chance to fix layers later.

questions.q: Brushing a thin see-through layer of color over dry paint is called?
questions.f: Old masters stacked dozens of glazes to get colours that seem lit from inside.

questions.q: Dragging a dry, stiff brush of light paint over a rough surface is called?
questions.f: Scumbled paint catches only the raised grain, giving mist, smoke and worn stone.

questions.q: Rubbing a pencil over paper laid on a textured surface is called?
questions.f: French for 'rubbing' — Max Ernst turned floorboard rubbings into whole imaginary forests.

questions.q: The brown spots that appear on old paper over time are called?
questions.f: Damp and traces of iron cause it — conservators can reduce foxing but rarely remove it.

questions.q: The rough, slightly toothy surface that helps paper grip pastel is called its?
questions.f: Slick paper cannot hold pastel dust, so pastellists choose papers with plenty of tooth.

questions.q: The soft, feathery natural edge on a sheet of handmade paper is the?
questions.f: Deckle edges prove a sheet was made by hand rather than cut by machine.

questions.q: A pigment made by fixing a dye onto a colourless powder is called a?
questions.f: The name comes from 'lac', the insect resin used in some of the earliest examples.

questions.q: Colours that fade badly in sunlight are described by artists as?
questions.f: From Latin 'fugere', to flee — many bright 19th-century pinks have already fled.

questions.q: In paint, the liquid that carries and glues the pigment together is the?
questions.f: Same pigment, different binder: oil, egg or gum arabic each make a different paint.

questions.q: 'Gum arabic', the binder in watercolor, is the sap of which tree?
questions.f: The same sap thickens fizzy drinks and sweets — and lets dry paint re-wet with one brushstroke.

questions.q: Which word describes a print run of a limited, numbered set of copies?
questions.f: '12/50' on a print means the twelfth sheet of an edition of fifty.

questions.q: A shape or figure placed at the edge of a painting to lead your eye inward is a?
questions.f: French for 'pushing back' — a dark tree at the corner can make distance feel vast.

questions.q: A painting or relief made in a circular format is called a?
questions.f: Italian for 'round' — Renaissance families hung tondi to celebrate a new baby.

questions.q: A two-panel hinged artwork is a?
questions.f: 'Di' means two, 'tri' three, and 'poly' many — the same counting roots as in geometry.

questions.q: 'Chinoiserie' describes European decoration that imitates the style of?
questions.f: 18th-century Europe went wild for pagodas, dragons and blue-and-white patterns.

questions.q: 'Japonisme' describes the 19th-century European craze for the art of?
questions.f: Cheap Japanese prints arrived as packing paper and changed Van Gogh and Degas forever.

questions.q: The word 'museum' and the word 'music' share the same ancient root.
questions.f: Both come from the Muses — nine goddesses who inspired every art at once.

questions.q: A 'palette' can mean both a mixing board and the range of colours an artist uses.
questions.f: Critics talk about a painter's 'restricted palette' meaning very few colours, not a small board.

questions.q: A painter whose entire known output would fit in one gallery, a suspected optical device in his studio, and a 1945 forger's confession trial converge on which artist?
questions.f: His 'Girl with a Pearl Earring' is now world famous, yet he was nearly forgotten for two centuries.

questions.q: A fake sold to a Nazi official, a treason charge, and a prison-cell painting made to prove the accused was only a forger describe whom?
questions.f: To escape the treason charge he had to prove his 'Vermeers' were his own — and he painted one under guard.

questions.q: A 1656 bankruptcy inventory of shells and armour, a son named Titus, and highlights scratched into wet paint with a brush handle point to which painter?
questions.f: He was a compulsive collector; the auction list of his belongings is now a treasure for historians.

questions.q: A 1401 competition for bronze doors, a rival who lost and went off to build a dome, and panels later nicknamed 'the Gates of Paradise' involve which sculptor?
questions.f: Michelangelo supposedly gave the doors their heavenly nickname.

questions.q: Herringbone brickwork, an ox-powered hoist, and building with no wooden framework beneath describe whose engineering triumph?
questions.f: His Florence cathedral dome is still the largest brick dome in the world.

questions.q: An elephant carrying an obelisk, a colonnade that embraces a Roman square, and marble hair that seems to lift in the wind point to which sculptor?
questions.f: He worked for eight popes and effectively designed the look of Baroque Rome.

questions.q: A painter who served as a diplomat, was knighted by two rival kings, and ran a studio of specialist assistants was?
questions.f: He spoke several languages and helped negotiate peace between Spain and England.

questions.q: A court painter who went deaf in his forties, murals painted straight onto his own house walls, and a print series called 'Los Caprichos' describe whom?
questions.f: The house murals were later peeled off the plaster and transferred to canvas.

questions.q: A painter born on Crete, trained among Venetian colourists, whose lasting Spanish nickname just means 'the Greek', is known as?
questions.f: He signed his paintings in Greek letters all his life, even while living in Toledo, Spain.

questions.q: A barber's son, a bequest of nearly 300 oils and 30,000 sketches to his nation, and Britain's most argued-about art prize point to which painter?
questions.f: The Turner Prize keeps his name in the headlines every single year.

questions.q: A critic's jibe about 'flinging a pot of paint in the public's face', an 1878 libel trial, and damages of one farthing involve which painter?
questions.f: He won the case but the costs ruined him — and he later published the whole transcript himself.

questions.q: Months of painting in only 20 minutes of dusk each evening, a scandal-causing portrait titled only 'Madame X', and some 900 oils describe whom?
questions.f: He chased the exact fading light for 'Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose', working a few minutes a day.

questions.q: Late canvases that turned muddy red-brown, an eye operation in 1923, and one garden pond returned to for a quarter century describe whose career?
questions.f: Cataracts yellowed his vision; after surgery he reworked paintings he had made almost blind.

questions.q: A banker father's allowance, a mountain painted over 30 times, and Picasso calling him 'the father of us all' point to which artist?
questions.f: His broken-up planes of colour led almost directly to Cubism.

questions.q: A father who handed over his brushes for good, a 1907 canvas that shocked even his friends, and an estate of roughly 50,000 works point to whom?
questions.f: He is credited with the largest output of any artist ever catalogued.

questions.q: A painter said to avoid the colour green entirely, a passion for boogie-woogie jazz, and an unfinished New York canvas describe whom?
questions.f: He reportedly asked to sit facing away from windows so he would not have to look at trees.

questions.q: A trained lawyer who said he heard colours as sounds, and a canvas seen sideways that looked better as pure shape, describe which painter?
questions.f: He wrote a whole book, 'Concerning the Spiritual in Art', about colour as music.

questions.q: A Bauhaus teacher who left about 9,000 works, a diary of colour experiments, and a picture called 'Twittering Machine' describe whom?
questions.f: He said a drawing is simply 'taking a line for a walk'.

questions.q: A series called 'Constellations' painted while fleeing in 1940, ladders and stars repeated for decades, and a Barcelona foundation point to whom?
questions.f: He said he wanted to 'assassinate painting' and start over with pure signs and symbols.

questions.q: Over 1,000 paintings left to one city in a will, canvases deliberately stored outdoors, and a cycle titled 'The Frieze of Life' describe whom?
questions.f: He called his paintings his children and believed a little weathering did them good.

questions.q: Fifty-three post stations along a coastal highway, rain drawn as straight black lines, and two prints Van Gogh copied in oil point to which printmaker?
questions.f: Van Gogh copied his bridge in the rain almost line for line, adding a border of invented characters.

questions.q: Born in Budapest to a Hungarian mother and Sikh father, trained in Paris, and dead at 28 — which pioneering modern Indian painter?
questions.f: India's National Gallery treats her paintings as national treasures that may not leave the country.

questions.q: A road inspector, 18 years of secret building from rubble and broken bangles, and a hidden kingdom in a Chandigarh forest describe which work?
questions.f: Officials found the illegal garden in 1975 and, instead of bulldozing it, made it a public park.

questions.q: An Italian tile-setter, 33 years of towers built from steel, mortar and broken bottles, and a walk away from it all describe which Los Angeles landmark?
questions.f: Simon Rodia gave the towers to a neighbour in 1955 and left town without explanation.

questions.q: A French postman who tripped on a stone in 1879, rocks carried home on his rounds for 33 years, and a palace admired by Picasso describe which work?
questions.f: Ferdinand Cheval's hand-built palace is now an official French historic monument.

questions.q: Three women renting an office in 1929, an opening show of Cezanne, Gauguin, Seurat and Van Gogh, and six rooms of borrowed art founded which museum?
questions.f: Abby Rockefeller, Lillie Bliss and Mary Sullivan were nicknamed 'the daring ladies'.

questions.q: A medieval fortress turned royal palace, a 1793 decision to open it to the public, and wartime crates hidden in country chateaux describe which museum?
questions.f: Its foundations still include the stone base of a 12th-century defensive tower.

questions.q: Thousands of flattened aluminium bottle tops, copper wire stitching, and hangings re-draped differently in every museum describe which sculptor's work?
questions.f: He deliberately lets each host museum decide the folds, so the work is never the same twice.

questions.q: A teacher who took up painting seriously at nearly 70, mosaic-like dabs of colour, and a 1972 Whitney solo show describe which artist?
questions.f: She was the first Black woman to have a solo exhibition at the Whitney Museum.

questions.q: Sixty panels laid out at once so each colour could be brushed across them all, a story told in captions, and 'The Migration Series' describe whom?
questions.f: Working colour by colour across all 60 panels kept the whole series perfectly consistent.

questions.q: Quilts with painted scenes and hand-written text, and a children's book called 'Tar Beach', describe which American artist?
questions.f: She turned to quilts partly because they could be rolled up and shipped cheaply to exhibitions.

questions.q: Dada puppets, abstract compositions, and the first woman to appear on a Swiss banknote describe which artist?
questions.f: Her portrait appeared on the Swiss 50-franc note, a rare honour for an abstract artist.

questions.q: An artist granted exclusive rights to the blackest known coating, and a rival's 'pinkest pink' sold to everyone except him, describe whom?
questions.f: Artist Stuart Semple made buyers promise they were not Kapoor before selling them the pink.

questions.q: Works sold as sets of written instructions, executed by museum staff on the wall, and repainted long after the artist's death describe whom?
questions.f: He argued the idea is the artwork, so any trained hand can carry out the drawing.

questions.q: A shy illustrator of shoe advertisements, 600-plus sealed cardboard 'time capsules', and a silver-foil-lined studio describe which artist?
questions.f: He filled the boxes with letters, pizza dough and even a mummified foot, then taped them shut.

questions.q: An 1877 accusation of casting a figure from a living model, an unfinished doorway commission, and hundreds of separately modelled hands describe whom?
questions.f: He kept a whole cupboard of spare modelled hands and feet to assemble into new figures.

questions.q: A judo master who wrote a manual on the sport, a patented shade of blue, and paintings made with a blowtorch describe which artist?
questions.f: His blue is so intensely velvety because the pigment was suspended in a nearly invisible binder.

questions.q: Returning a fortune to a restaurant that had commissioned murals, and 14 dark canvases in a Houston chapel, describe which painter?
questions.f: He decided diners should not eat under his paintings, so he gave the money back.

questions.q: A teenager tagging Manhattan with the signature SAMO, a joint show with Warhol, and paintings crowded with words describe whom?
questions.f: The crown he drew over his figures was his way of calling his heroes kings.

questions.q: Canvases that made 1960s gallery-goers feel seasick, and a 1965 New York show called 'The Responsive Eye', point to which painter?
questions.f: Fashion houses copied her stripes so fast that she tried, and failed, to stop them.
