questions.q: Staged photographs of small-town neighbours, a painting of a girl escorted to school in 1964, and 321 magazine covers describe which illustrator?
questions.f: 'The Problem We All Live With' showed a very different side of America from his cosy covers.

questions.q: A trained concert pianist turned photographer, an eleven-step exposure system, and a print called 'Moonrise, Hernandez' describe whom?
questions.f: He said he learned discipline at the piano and applied exactly the same rigour to the darkroom.

questions.q: Interlocking star tiles that stunned a Dutch printmaker in 1922, poems inscribed on the walls, and a fortress palace above Granada describe which building?
questions.f: Its patterns use nearly every mathematical way of tiling a flat surface.

questions.q: A 1560 building put up for magistrates' offices, a private corridor crossing a bridge of jewellers' shops, and a Medici bequest describe which gallery?
questions.f: The last Medici heiress left the whole collection to the city on condition it never leave Florence.

questions.q: A winter palace turned museum, a staff of cats on official mouse patrol, and Catherine the Great's bulk art purchases describe which museum?
questions.f: The cats have guarded the cellars since the 1700s and even have their own press day.

questions.q: Thirty caves cut into a horseshoe cliff, a thousand years lost to jungle, and rediscovery in 1819 by a hunting party describe which painted site?
questions.f: Its murals are among the finest surviving paintings of ancient India.

questions.q: A farmer's 1820 discovery on the island of Milos, a plinth inscription that soon vanished, and a French officer's swift purchase describe which statue?
questions.f: The missing plinth may have named the sculptor — which is why scholars still argue about her date.

questions.q: A diary note about a scream passing through nature, a 1994 theft timed to an Olympic opening, and a pencilled line calling the artist mad describe which work?
questions.f: Experts confirmed in 2021 that Munch himself wrote the 'painted by a madman' note.

questions.q: One of the first large Italian paintings on canvas rather than panel, a pose borrowed from an antique marble, and a Medici villa at Castello describe which work?
questions.f: Canvas was cheaper and travelled better than wooden panels — a practical choice that changed art.

questions.q: A vast canvas painted in a Paris attic in one month of 1937, a tour that raised refugee funds, and an exile that ended in 1981 describe which painting?
questions.f: Picasso refused to let it enter Spain until the country was a republic again.

questions.q: A school with three homes in fourteen years, a foundation course called the Vorkurs, and teachers who scattered to Chicago and Tel Aviv describe what?
questions.f: Tel Aviv's 'White City' has thousands of buildings in the style its exiled architects carried there.

questions.q: A blue that survives centuries of jungle humidity, indigo locked into a rare clay, and offerings dropped into a Yucatan sinkhole describe which pigment?
questions.f: Chemists spent decades working out how the Maya bonded dye to clay so permanently.

questions.q: A synthetic colour made by Chinese alchemists over 2,000 years ago, traces on the Terracotta Army, and a barium compound studied by physicists describe what?
questions.f: Cooled to near absolute zero, Han purple behaves in ways that still puzzle physicists.

questions.q: A plant fermented in vats, a 1577 German ban on its cheaper rival as 'the devil's dye', and Europe's main blue before ocean trade describe which dye plant?
questions.f: Woad and indigo yield the same blue chemical, but indigo plants give far more of it.

questions.q: Three threads plucked by hand from each crocus flower, the costliest spice by weight, and a yellow prized by medieval illuminators describe what?
questions.f: It takes roughly 150,000 flowers to make a single kilogram of saffron.

questions.q: A red resin tapped from trees on Socotra, a name born of a myth about a fight between beasts, and violin varnish describe which material?
questions.f: Medieval writers really believed the resin was the mingled blood of an elephant and a serpent.

questions.q: A mineral whose old Latin name means 'gold paint', a favourite of medieval illuminators, and a substance modern chemists handle with gloves is?
questions.f: Its glittering yellow crystals are an arsenic compound, so it has been retired from paint boxes.

questions.q: A copper ore ground up for ancient Egyptian eye paint, a green named after the mallow leaf, and banded green stone jewellery describe which pigment?
questions.f: Its Greek name comes from the mallow plant, whose leaves are the same soft green.

questions.q: A blue copper mineral that slowly turns green on old paintings, and Europe's workhorse blue before overseas trade, describe which pigment?
questions.f: Many medieval 'green' skies were originally blue — the pigment itself changed over centuries.

questions.q: A yellow resin whose name is a garbled version of a Southeast Asian country's, tapped from a tree, and used to dye monks' robes is?
questions.f: The word comes from Cambodia, where the resin was traditionally collected.

questions.q: A red drawn from a plant's roots, an Arabic word for 'juice' behind its name, and the first natural dye ever copied in a laboratory in 1868 describe?
questions.f: Synthetic alizarin wiped out Europe's huge madder-farming industry within a generation.

questions.q: A dark-furred animal, the heraldic word for black, and a prized artists' brush all share which single name?
questions.f: Sable brushes are actually made from a related weasel, but the name stuck to all three uses.

questions.q: A French word for a flea, a fashionable 18th-century court colour, and a brownish purple in modern paint charts all name which colour?
questions.f: French courtiers really did name the fashionable shade after the insect's colour.

questions.q: A word meaning 'biting', a dyer's alum bath, and the acid that eats into an etching plate all point to which term?
questions.f: Without a mordant, most natural dyes would simply rinse straight out of the cloth.

questions.q: A brown ink boiled from beechwood soot, a favourite for old master wash drawings, and a colour that fades in strong light describe which ink?
questions.f: Bistre gave Rembrandt's quick pen sketches their warm golden shadows.

questions.q: A red earth once shipped from a Black Sea port, a sketch drawn straight onto rough wall plaster, and a layer conservators uncover describe which term?
questions.f: When frescoes are removed from walls, the red underdrawing beneath is often revealed intact.

questions.q: A drawing pricked with hundreds of pinholes, a bag of charcoal dust tapped along the holes, and dotted guide lines found under frescoes describe which method?
questions.f: The dotted transfer marks are called spolvero, from the Italian for dust.

questions.q: Powdered resin dusted on copper and melted, acid biting the gaps into soft grey washes, and Goya's print series describe which technique?
questions.f: Aquatint gave printmakers their first easy way to print broad areas of tone instead of lines.

questions.q: A drypoint plate wears out after only a small number of good prints.
questions.f: The velvety line comes from a raised metal burr that the press flattens a little each time.

questions.q: A curved rocker tool roughening a copper plate all over, a name meaning 'half tone', and prints once called 'the English manner' describe which technique?
questions.f: The printmaker works from dark to light, burnishing the roughened plate smooth for highlights.

questions.q: A French word meaning 'squirt', a 1990s marketing coinage, and museum-quality inkjet prints converge on which term?
questions.f: Printer Jack Duganne invented the fancy name in 1991 so gallery buyers would take inkjets seriously.

questions.q: A chemistry graduate buying a small printing firm in 1962, a numbered book of ink swatches, and an annual 'Colour of the Year' describe which system?
questions.f: Numbered ink recipes let a designer in one country match a printer in another exactly.

questions.q: A Boston art teacher's 1905 'colour tree', three axes named hue, value and chroma, and a chart still used to describe soil converge on which system?
questions.f: Soil scientists worldwide still carry Munsell books into the field to name the exact brown.

questions.q: A Bauhaus teacher who fled to America, squares that change shade depending on their neighbours, and a 1963 book called 'Interaction of Color' describe whom?
questions.f: He proved one identical grey can look like two different colours side by side.

questions.q: A prism in a darkened Cambridge room, a wish to match the seven notes of a musical scale, and the odd extra colour in ROYGBIV point to whom?
questions.f: Most people cannot separate indigo from blue; it is there because seven felt more harmonious.

questions.q: A great German poet, a book of 1810 attacking Newton's optics, and careful studies of coloured shadows describe whose colour theory?
questions.f: His science was largely wrong but artists loved it, because it described what the eye actually feels.

questions.q: Two fabrics matching under shop lights but clashing in daylight, and a headache for car repair shops, describe which colour effect?
questions.f: Two colours can reflect light differently yet still look identical under one particular lamp.

questions.q: Colours such as magenta, which correspond to no single wavelength of light, are described as?
questions.f: Your brain invents magenta when red and blue cones fire together with no green in between.

questions.q: Tree rings counted in a poplar panel, a felling date, and an earliest possible painting date converge on which dating method?
questions.f: Panel rings can show that a 'medieval' painting sits on wood cut centuries too late.

questions.q: A stretched smear across the bottom of Holbein's 'The Ambassadors' that snaps into shape only from one side is an example of?
questions.f: Step to the right place and the flattened blur resolves into a crisp skull.

questions.q: A blue-black watercolour mixed rather than mined, sold ready-made in tubes, and named after an 18th-century English painter is?
questions.f: William Payne's recipe let landscape painters skip harsh black altogether.

questions.q: A botanical illustrator frustrated that no single tube matched a real leaf gave his name to which colour?
questions.f: William Hooker mixed gamboge with Prussian blue to capture living foliage.

questions.q: A glowing yellow said to come from mango-fed cattle, exported as smelly dried balls, and reportedly banned around 1908 describe which pigment?
questions.f: Turner and other watercolourists loved its warmth long before anyone questioned how it was made.

questions.q: An element discovered in 1817, brilliant paints on the market by the 1840s, and a warning label on modern tubes describe which pigment family?
questions.f: Cadmium reds and yellows are prized because they barely fade at all over centuries.

questions.q: Paintings where figures blaze out of near-total darkness, taken further than ordinary chiaroscuro, are said to use?
questions.f: From Italian 'tenebroso', gloomy — Caravaggio's followers were nicknamed the tenebrists.

questions.q: Roman portrait busts that honestly show wrinkles, warts and balding heads belong to which tradition?
questions.f: From Latin 'verus', true — Roman patricians treated a lived-in face as proof of experience.

questions.q: An early Greek statue of a standing youth, stiff-armed with one foot forward, is called a?
questions.f: The female version is a kore; both were carved before Greek sculptors learned to relax the pose.

questions.q: Greek builders gave columns a slight outward bulge, called entasis, in order to?
questions.f: Perfectly straight columns look pinched in the middle, so the Greeks curved them to look straight.

questions.q: A chubby winged child figure that swarms across Baroque ceilings is called a?
questions.f: The plural is putti — Italian for 'little boys'.

questions.q: A black metal paste rubbed into engraved silver lines is called?
questions.f: Its name comes from Latin 'nigellum', blackish — the dark filling makes fine engraving readable.

questions.q: Inlaying gold or silver wire into darkened steel, a craft named after a Syrian city, is called?
questions.f: Damascus was legendary for patterned steel, so its name attached to the decoration too.

questions.q: Ceilings painted so that fake architecture seems to soar upward beyond the real roof are examples of?
questions.f: Baroque churches used quadratura to make a flat ceiling appear to open straight onto heaven.

questions.q: The reddish clay layer brushed under gold leaf so it can be burnished to a mirror shine is called?
questions.f: Its warm red glows faintly through the gold, which is why old haloes look so rich.

questions.q: Conservators shine a lamp almost flat across a painting's surface in order to reveal?
questions.f: This 'raking light' throws long shadows, exposing every ripple, tear and past repair.

questions.q: Filling only the losses in a damaged painting, without touching the original paint, is called?
questions.f: Ethical conservators use paints that can be dissolved off later, so their work is reversible.

questions.q: The powdery pale green corrosion that can slowly eat away an ancient bronze is nicknamed bronze?
questions.f: Unlike a stable patina, this chloride corrosion keeps spreading until the metal is treated.

questions.q: Centuries of candle soot, a cleaning finished in 1994, and colours so bright that critics cried 'repainting' describe which project?
questions.f: Nobody had realised Michelangelo painted in such shocking pinks, limes and oranges.

questions.q: A well-meaning parishioner's 2012 touch-up, a mocking internet nickname, and a sudden tourist boom for a Spanish town describe which fresco?
questions.f: The ruined fresco now draws thousands of paying visitors a year — far more than the original ever did.

questions.q: A portrait retitled to hide its sitter's name, a niece's long legal battle, and a record-breaking 2006 sale describe which Klimt painting?
questions.f: For decades it hung under the neutral title 'Woman in Gold'.

questions.q: Six tonnes of fossilised resin panelling, a Prussian king's gift to a Russian tsar, and a disappearance in 1945 describe which lost artwork?
questions.f: A full replica was completed in 2003, but the original panels have never been found.

questions.q: An emperor's order in 1863 after thousands of rejections, a hall of the turned-away, and the show that made Manet notorious describe what?
questions.f: Napoleon III let the rejected artists exhibit so the public could judge the jury.

questions.q: A festival first held in Venice in 1895, national pavilions in a public garden, and a name meaning 'every two years' describe which event?
questions.f: Germany holds Documenta every five years, and many cities now run triennials too.

questions.q: Fifteen volumes of 'sketches at random' begun around 1814, a printmaker in his fifties, and a word now used worldwide for comics describe which title?
questions.f: Hokusai's 'Manga' was a drawing manual — Japanese comics borrowed the word much later.

questions.q: The word 'emoji' is built from Japanese elements meaning?
questions.f: 'E' means picture and 'moji' means written character — its likeness to 'emotion' is pure coincidence.

questions.q: 'Calotype', an early paper photograph process, is built from Greek elements meaning?
questions.f: Talbot's paper negatives could be reprinted many times, unlike one-off metal daguerreotypes.

questions.q: A view from a window needing hours of exposure, a plate coated in bitumen, and a process its inventor called 'sun-writing' describe whose photograph?
questions.f: His 1820s 'View from the Window at Le Gras' is the oldest surviving camera photograph.

questions.q: A spinning drum of slits, a strip of drawings inside, and a name meaning 'wheel of life' describe which Victorian animation toy?
questions.f: Spinning it makes the drawings appear to move, exactly as film would decades later.

questions.q: A disc with a bird on one side and a cage on the other, twisted on strings, is a toy named from Greek for?
questions.f: The thaumatrope proved that two images can fuse into one in the viewer's mind.

questions.q: 'Raster' graphics, made of rows of pixels, take their name from a Latin word meaning?
questions.f: Latin 'rastrum' — the scanning lines were compared to the parallel marks left by a rake.

questions.q: A parchment scraped clean and written over, with the older text still faintly showing, is called a?
questions.f: Ultraviolet light has recovered lost ancient works from beneath medieval writing.

questions.q: A Greek word for a little cooking skewer, tapering Egyptian monuments, and the stone needles now standing in Paris and New York converge on which term?
questions.f: Greek visitors to Egypt thought the monuments looked like giant spits, and the nickname stuck.

questions.q: A ruler's tomb at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and a word now used for any grand tomb converge on which term?
questions.f: King Mausolus gave his name to every mausoleum built since.

questions.q: A bronze giant that stood barely 54 years, an earthquake that felled it, and an English word for anything enormous converge on which harbour's statue?
questions.f: The Colossus of Rhodes lay in pieces for centuries, and sightseers still came to see them.

questions.q: 'Baldachin', the canopy over an altar, is named after a rich silk associated with which city?
questions.f: 'Baldacco' was the Italian name for Baghdad, source of the luxurious cloth.

questions.q: Portuguese and Spanish 'azulejo' tiles are named not from the word for blue but from an Arabic word meaning?
questions.f: The blue link is a coincidence — plenty of early azulejos were green, yellow and white.

questions.q: The honeycomb-like clusters of niches vaulting Islamic ceilings are called?
questions.f: Each cell mathematically supports the next, so a whole dome grows from one repeated unit.

questions.q: 'Mannerism', the style following the High Renaissance, is named from an Italian word meaning?
questions.f: From 'maniera' — critics used it to mean artists imitating a style rather than nature.

questions.q: A 'pastiche' takes its name from an Italian word for a?
questions.f: 'Pasticcio' was a pie of mixed ingredients — a pastiche mixes borrowed styles the same way.

questions.q: 'Decoupage', decorating an object with cut-out paper, comes from a word meaning to?
questions.f: 18th-century ladies imitated expensive lacquerware by gluing on prints and varnishing them.

questions.q: A yarn resist-dyed BEFORE it is woven, producing blurry-edged patterns, makes which fabric?
questions.f: The soft feathered edges are the giveaway — weavers can never line the threads up perfectly.

questions.q: Mali's bogolan cloth gets its patterns from fermented?
questions.f: 'Bogolanfini' literally means mud cloth, and the iron-rich mud sets the dye permanently.

questions.q: Adinkra cloth from Ghana is covered in stamped symbols that each carry a?
questions.f: The stamps are carved from calabash gourd, and each symbol has a name and a lesson.

questions.q: Guna artists of Panama make molas by cutting away layers of stacked cloth, a technique called?
questions.f: Instead of adding shapes on top, the maker snips down through several colours to reveal them.

questions.q: Japanese raku tea bowls are famous for being?
c: Pulled glowing hot from the kiln
questions.f: The sudden cooling crackles the glaze, so no two bowls can ever match.

questions.q: Netsuke are tiny Japanese carvings that originally worked as?
questions.f: Kimono had no pockets, so a carved toggle anchored a hanging purse to the belt.

questions.q: Shibori is the Japanese art of patterning cloth by?
questions.f: Stitching, folding, clamping and pole-wrapping each leave their own unmistakable pattern.

questions.q: The Ardabil Carpet, one of the world's oldest dated carpets, is a treasure of which museum?
questions.f: Woven around 1540, it holds roughly 30 million hand-tied knots.

questions.q: A flat woven rug with no knotted pile, common from Turkey to Central Asia, is a?
questions.f: Because there is no pile, a kilim shows the same crisp pattern on both faces.

questions.q: The soft squirrel-hair brush a gilder uses to lift and float gold leaf is called a gilder's?
questions.f: Gilders brush it against their hair first, so a whisper of static picks the leaf up.

questions.q: An artwork's 'condition report' lists every crack, loss and past repair before it travels.
questions.f: Couriers check the report at both ends, so any new damage is spotted immediately.

questions.q: 'Chrysography' means writing or drawing in gold.
questions.f: From Greek 'chrysos', gold — the same root as the chrysanthemum, the golden flower.

questions.q: A 'diorama' is named from roots meaning 'to see through'.
questions.f: Early dioramas were lit from behind so painted scenes seemed to change from day to night.

questions.q: Ultramarine blue can now be made synthetically far more cheaply than from lapis lazuli.
questions.f: A French prize in 1824 sparked the recipe, and the synthetic version arrived within four years.

questions.q: What is the fine colored powder that gives paint its color called?
questions.f: The same pigment powder can become oil paint, watercolor or crayon depending what it is mixed with.

questions.q: On Christmas Eve, Santa is said to enter houses through what?
questions.f: The chimney idea spread from the 1823 poem 'A Visit from St. Nicholas'.

questions.q: What round, leafy decoration do people hang on the front door at Christmas?
questions.f: A wreath is a ring of leaves, and a ring has no end, which is why it stands for never-ending cheer.

questions.q: What is often placed at the very top of a Christmas tree?
questions.f: Some families use an angel instead of a star at the top of the tree.

questions.q: What are the shiny, sparkly strands draped on a Christmas tree called?
questions.f: Tinsel was once made from real thin silver, which quickly went black.

questions.q: At a birthday party, which decoration do children love to pop?
questions.f: Party balloons are usually filled with helium, a gas lighter than air.

questions.q: In which blindfold party game do you attach a tail to an animal picture?
c: Pin the Tail on the Donkey
questions.f: Pin the Tail on the Donkey has been a birthday favourite for well over a hundred years.

questions.q: On New Year's Eve, what colourful lights are set off in the night sky?
questions.f: Fireworks get their colours from metal salts: copper burns blue-green, strontium burns red.

questions.q: Before blowing out birthday candles, what are you supposed to make?
questions.f: The custom says the wish comes true only if you keep it secret.

questions.q: What card do you send friends to ask them to come to your party?
questions.f: Many invitations end with R.S.V.P., a short way of asking guests to reply.

questions.q: Which lucky golden fruit is often given as a gift at Chinese New Year?
questions.f: Oranges are given because their round golden shape suggests coins and good fortune.

questions.q: Many families sweep the whole house before Chinese New Year to sweep away what?
questions.f: Sweeping stops on New Year's Day itself, so the fresh good luck is not brushed out.

questions.q: Which small animal is first in the Chinese zodiac cycle?
questions.f: A story says the clever rat rode on the ox's back and hopped off to win the race.

questions.q: What do many families buy to wear on the first day of Diwali?
questions.f: Wearing new clothes stands for a fresh start as the new season begins.

questions.q: During Diwali, what do families carry over to their neighbours' houses?
questions.f: Sharing sweets is how neighbours wish each other a bright year ahead.

questions.q: Which squirting toy do children use to spray coloured water at Holi?
questions.f: A pichkari works like a big syringe, pushing out a long jet of colour.

questions.q: Which flying night animal is a popular Halloween decoration?
questions.f: Real bats are helpful, gobbling up thousands of mosquitoes in a single night.

questions.q: Fake ones of what are strung in corners as spooky Halloween decorations?
questions.f: A real spider can spin a whole new web in under an hour.

questions.q: What do trick-or-treaters carry to hold all their candy?
questions.f: Plastic pumpkin buckets for trick-or-treating first appeared in the 1950s.

questions.q: Which tart red sauce is served beside the turkey at Thanksgiving?
questions.f: Cranberries bounce when they are fresh, which is how growers sort the good ones.

questions.q: At Thanksgiving dinner, families take turns saying what they are what?
questions.f: Thanksgiving began as a harvest feast, a thank-you for a good crop.

questions.q: Which jam-filled fried doughnut is a Hanukkah treat?
questions.f: Foods fried in oil are eaten at Hanukkah because the holiday remembers a miracle of oil.

questions.q: During Ramadan, the evening meal that breaks the day's fast is called what?
questions.f: Many families break the fast with dates, just as tradition says the Prophet did.

questions.q: At a wedding, what does the bride often carry in her hands?
questions.f: In many places the bride tosses her bouquet, and whoever catches it is said to be lucky.

questions.q: What do a bride and groom usually slip onto each other's fingers?
questions.f: The ring goes on the fourth finger because people once thought a vein ran from it to the heart.

questions.q: Your parents' parents are together called your what?
questions.f: In many families grandparents are the ones who pass down old recipes and stories.

questions.q: What do we call a very young child who has just learned to walk?
questions.f: The word toddler comes from 'toddle', meaning to walk with short wobbly steps.

questions.q: A baby who was born only days ago is called a what?
questions.f: Newborn babies sleep for about sixteen hours a day.

questions.q: Which shape is seen everywhere on Valentine's Day?
questions.f: Millions of Valentine's cards are sent every year, plus plenty to pets.

questions.q: In which month is Valentine's Day celebrated?
questions.f: Valentine's Day falls on 14 February, in the middle of the shortest month.

questions.q: What gift do children most often give on Mother's Day?
questions.f: More flowers are sold for Mother's Day than for almost any other day of the year.

questions.q: Which Christmas plant has spiky green leaves and bright red berries?
questions.f: Holly berries feed hungry winter birds, though they are not safe for people to eat.

questions.q: In the famous song, which reindeer has a shiny red nose?
questions.f: Rudolph was invented in 1939 for a department store's Christmas booklet.

questions.q: Where is Santa Claus said to live and make his toys?
questions.f: Finland claims Santa lives in Lapland, and children's letters really do arrive there.

questions.q: Besides cookies, which crunchy snack do children leave out for Santa's reindeer?
questions.f: Real reindeer love lichen, a crusty plant they dig out from under the snow.

questions.q: What is usually hidden behind the little doors of an Advent calendar?
questions.f: Advent calendars count down the days of December leading up to Christmas.

questions.q: In the Christmas nativity story, the baby was laid in a what?
questions.f: A manger is really a feeding trough for farm animals.

questions.q: At Easter, a fluffy yellow chick hatches out of what?
questions.f: A chick uses a tiny hard bump on its beak, called an egg tooth, to crack out.

questions.q: Which special sweet bread is baked in Mexico for the Day of the Dead?
questions.f: Pan de muerto is decorated with dough strips shaped like bones and a little ball on top.

questions.q: On Day of the Dead, whose photographs do families place on the home altar?
questions.f: The photos help families feel that loved ones are visiting for the night.

questions.q: In Japan, people gather in spring to picnic under which pretty blossoms?
questions.f: Japan's TV news reports a 'blossom front' moving north across the country each spring.

questions.q: On Japan's Children's Day, which fish-shaped streamers fly outside houses?
questions.f: Carp are chosen because they swim strongly upstream, a picture of a brave child.

questions.q: At Carnival parades, what do many dancers wear over their faces?
questions.f: Venice is famous for Carnival masks with long curved beaks and gold paint.

questions.q: What do guests often throw over a couple as they leave their wedding?
questions.f: Some places throw rice or petals instead, wishing the couple plenty and happiness.

questions.q: What is the birthday child usually most excited to open?
questions.f: Wrapping gifts in decorated paper became common only in the last hundred years or so.

questions.q: Which little green fairy man appears in St Patrick's Day stories?
questions.f: Stories say a leprechaun hides a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow.

questions.q: Which country celebrates its birthday on the Fourth of July?
questions.f: The Fourth of July is marked with parades, picnics and a great many fireworks.

questions.q: What are the long twisted paper decorations hung across a party room called?
questions.f: Paper streamers are also thrown from ships as they leave port in some countries.

questions.q: Which party toy unrolls with a squeak when you blow into it?
questions.f: A party blower works because your breath unrolls a tightly coiled paper tube.

questions.q: The number of candles on a birthday cake usually matches what?
questions.f: Some cakes add one extra 'candle to grow on' for the year ahead.

questions.q: Giant cartoon balloons float through New York streets for which holiday parade?
questions.f: The first giant balloons joined that parade in 1927, led by Felix the Cat.

questions.q: The word 'birthday' is simply made from which two smaller words?
questions.f: Old English speakers used a similar pairing, and the word has barely changed since.

questions.q: The word 'holiday' was first made from two words meaning what?
questions.f: Long ago every holiday really was a holy day set aside from work.

questions.q: The word 'Christmas' is a short way of saying what?
questions.f: The spelling 'Xmas' uses X for the Greek letter chi, the first letter of Christ.

questions.q: 'Halloween' is a shortened form of All Hallows' what?
questions.f: 'Hallow' is an old word for a saint, so the night comes before All Saints' Day.

questions.q: When a holiday's name has 'Eve' in it, that means the day just what?
questions.f: That is why Christmas Eve is 24 December and New Year's Eve is 31 December.

questions.q: The word 'twins' tells you how many babies were born together?
questions.f: About one in every eighty births around the world produces twins.

questions.q: How many babies does the word 'triplets' describe?
questions.f: The prefix 'tri' means three, just as it does in tricycle and triangle.

questions.q: When we call a meal a 'feast', we mean it is what?
questions.f: 'Feast' and 'festival' come from the very same Latin word for a joyful day.

questions.q: At a party, the person who invites the guests is called the what?
questions.f: 'Host' and 'guest' grew from the same ancient root, which once meant either one.

questions.q: The word 'sibling' means one of your what?
questions.f: 'Sibling' comes from an Old English word for kinship, and returned to use in the 1900s.

questions.q: Your mother and father together are called your what?
questions.f: 'Parent' comes from a Latin word meaning to bring forth.

questions.q: Your sister's daughter is your what?
questions.f: 'Niece' arrived in English from French, and its cousin word 'nephew' is the boy version.

questions.q: A child with no brothers or sisters is called an what?
questions.f: Being an only child is far more common today than it was a century ago.

questions.q: The sweet course served at the end of a festival meal is called what?
questions.f: 'Dessert' comes from a French word meaning to clear the table.

questions.q: A 'costume' is a set of special what?
questions.f: 'Costume' and 'custom' come from the same root, since clothing showed local customs.

questions.q: A festival 'mask' is worn over which part of you?
questions.f: The oldest known stone masks are about nine thousand years old.

questions.q: In a festival 'parade', people mostly do what?
questions.f: 'Parade' comes from a word meaning to prepare or show off.

questions.q: A 'wreath' is a decoration shaped like what?
questions.f: The word 'wreath' is related to 'writhe', meaning to twist.

questions.q: A 'bouquet' is a bunch of what?
questions.f: 'Bouquet' began as a French word for a little wood or clump of trees.

questions.q: 'Confetti' means tiny bits of what, showered over celebrating people?
questions.f: In Italy confetti once meant sugared sweets, which were thrown instead of paper.

questions.q: In 'Merry Christmas', the word 'merry' means what?
questions.f: 'Merry' is an old English word that once meant pleasant or short and sweet.

questions.q: 'Kin' is another word for the members of your family.
questions.f: That is why the old phrase 'kith and kin' means friends and family together.

questions.q: A 'banquet' is a tiny snack eaten alone.
questions.f: A banquet is a grand feast; the word comes from an Italian word for a long bench.

questions.q: A family 'reunion' is when relatives come together again after being apart.
questions.f: 'Re-union' literally means uniting once more.

questions.q: How many days does the celebration of Kwanzaa last?
questions.f: Each of the seven days honours a different idea, such as unity and creativity.

questions.q: What do families use to turn plain Easter eggs bright colours?
questions.f: Onion skins and beetroot juice make lovely natural egg dyes.

questions.q: Hot cross buns, eaten at Easter, have which shape marked on top?
questions.f: The cross is usually piped on in a paste of flour and water before baking.

questions.q: What are the shiny round balls hung on Christmas tree branches called?
questions.f: Glass baubles were first blown in the German town of Lauscha in the 1800s.

questions.q: A candy cane is shaped like which letter of the alphabet?
questions.f: Turn it the other way up and a candy cane looks like a shepherd's crook.

questions.q: Which spicy Christmas cookie is baked in the shape of a little person?
questions.f: Whole gingerbread houses are built from the same stiff, spicy dough.

questions.q: Which plant do people traditionally stand under to share a Christmas kiss?
questions.f: Mistletoe grows on tree branches instead of in the ground.

questions.q: On New Year's Eve, people count down the last seconds starting from which number?
questions.f: In New York a giant lighted ball drops during the final minute of the year.

questions.q: Which folded, filled food is eaten for luck at Chinese New Year in northern China?
questions.f: Dumplings are shaped like little money bags, so eating them hints at wealth.

questions.q: At the Chinese Mid-Autumn Festival, children walk about carrying what?
questions.f: Some children's lanterns are shaped like rabbits, because of a rabbit story about the moon.

questions.q: What do families do to their whole house in the days before Diwali?
questions.f: A spotless home is said to welcome good fortune at Diwali.

questions.q: At Eid and at weddings, what reddish-brown paste is used to draw patterns on hands?
questions.f: Henna comes from crushed leaves, and the stain fades away in a week or two.

questions.q: During Ramadan, the daily fast begins at which time of day?
questions.f: The pre-dawn meal eaten just before the fast starts is called suhoor.

questions.q: Which sweet is shaped like a tiny yellow-and-orange kernel at Halloween?
questions.f: Candy corn has been made since the 1880s and was first called chicken feed.

questions.q: What do people carve into the front of a Halloween pumpkin?
questions.f: The biggest pumpkins ever grown weigh more than a small car.

questions.q: Which kind of Mexican band, with trumpets and violins, often plays at fiestas?
questions.f: Mariachi musicians wear a fitted suit called a traje de charro.

questions.q: Which oil is traditionally used for the Hanukkah lamps and cooking?
questions.f: The Hanukkah story is all about one small jar of olive oil that lasted and lasted.

questions.q: At a Western wedding, what does the bride often wear over her face or hair?
questions.f: Roman brides wore veils over two thousand years ago.

questions.q: In Britain and America, which colour wedding dress is most traditional?
questions.f: White dresses became the fashion after Queen Victoria wore one in 1840.

questions.q: Which animal do people watch for a weather prediction on Groundhog Day?
questions.f: The custom came from Europe, where people watched badgers and bears instead.

questions.q: On which day of the year do people play harmless jokes on each other?
questions.f: In France the trick is to stick a paper fish on someone's back.

questions.q: April Fools' Day falls on which date?
questions.f: In Britain the joking is supposed to stop at noon.

questions.q: In which month is Christmas Day?
questions.f: Christmas Day is 25 December, near the shortest day in the northern half of the world.

questions.q: Halloween comes at the end of which month?
questions.f: Halloween is 31 October, the last night before All Saints' Day.

questions.q: Bonfire Night, with bonfires and fireworks on 5 November, is a tradition in which country?
questions.f: Children in Britain once made a stuffed figure and asked for 'a penny for the guy'.

questions.q: On Father's Day, which item of clothing is a classic gift?
c: A pair of socks with bells
questions.f: Father's Day was first held in Spokane, in the United States, in 1910.

questions.q: What do families set off or watch together to celebrate Diwali night?
questions.f: Many families now choose quieter, greener Diwali celebrations for the sake of pets.

questions.q: At Chinese New Year, dancers hold up a long cloth creature that snakes down the street. What is it?
questions.f: The longest festival dragons need dozens of dancers to hold them up.

questions.q: Which fizzy-looking treat do you put candles into at a birthday party?
questions.f: The custom of a candle-topped birthday cake grew from German Kinderfest parties.

questions.q: Which drink is often warmed with spices at winter festivals and markets?
questions.f: Warm spiced cider is flavoured with cinnamon sticks and cloves.

questions.q: What do people usually wear on their heads at a wedding in Britain called a 'hat party'?
questions.f: Big decorated hats are a long-standing tradition at British weddings and races.

questions.q: Which festival food is a whole roasted bird stuffed with breadcrumbs?
questions.f: The bready mixture inside is called stuffing in Britain and dressing in parts of the USA.

questions.q: At a party, what is put on a gift before you give it?
questions.f: Two brothers in Kansas started selling decorated gift wrap in 1917 when tissue ran out.

questions.q: What loopy decoration is tied around a present to finish it off?
questions.f: Curling ribbon springs into ringlets when you drag a scissor blade along it.

questions.q: Which festival treat is a stack of pancakes eaten on Pancake Day?
questions.f: Pancake Day used up eggs and butter before the fasting weeks of Lent began.

questions.q: At Chinese New Year, what do children say to grown-ups to wish them well?
questions.f: In Mandarin the greeting is 'Xin nian kuai le'.

questions.q: During Onam and other Indian feasts, food is often served on what instead of a plate?
questions.f: A banana leaf needs no washing up, and it is completely compostable.

questions.q: Which sticky sweet is pulled and twisted at fairs and festivals into a fluffy cloud?
questions.f: Cotton candy is spun sugar, blown into threads thinner than a human hair.

questions.q: At a fairground during a festival, what big wheel do you ride to see the view?
questions.f: The first Ferris wheel was built for the 1893 world's fair in Chicago.

questions.q: What does a family often make together to remember a holiday, using photos?
questions.f: The word 'album' comes from a Latin word meaning blank and white.

questions.q: 'Feliz Navidad', heard in songs each December, means happy what?
questions.f: 'Navidad' comes from a Latin word for birth, the same root as 'nativity'.

questions.q: The greeting 'Shalom', used at Jewish celebrations, means what?
questions.f: 'Shalom' works as hello, goodbye and a wish for peace, all in one word.

questions.q: In Hawaii, the word 'aloha' is used both to say hello and to say what?
questions.f: Visitors to Hawaii are often welcomed with a flower necklace called a lei.

questions.q: To greet someone with 'namaste', what do you do with your hands?
questions.f: A small bow of the head usually goes with the pressed palms.

questions.q: When people say 'Cheers!' at a celebration, what do they do with their glasses?
questions.f: The clink is a friendly signal that everyone is celebrating the same thing.

questions.q: Your 'surname' is which of your names?
questions.f: 'Sur' means over or above, so a surname sits above your personal name.

questions.q: A 'nickname' is what kind of name?
questions.f: 'Nickname' began as 'an eke-name', meaning an added name.

questions.q: The 'firstborn' in a family is which child?
questions.f: In many old traditions the firstborn inherited the family's land.

questions.q: 'Newlyweds' are people who have just done what?
questions.f: The trip newlyweds take is called a honeymoon.

questions.q: At a wedding, the two people getting married are called the bride and the what?
questions.f: 'Groom' comes from an old word 'guma', simply meaning man.

questions.q: A 'family tree' is a drawing that shows what?
questions.f: It is called a tree because the branches spread out just like a real one.

questions.q: Your 'ancestors' are family members who lived when?
c: At the same time as you
questions.f: 'Ancestor' comes from Latin words meaning one who goes before.

questions.q: An 'elder' in a family is someone who is what?
questions.f: Many cultures give elders the honour of starting the festival meal.

questions.q: A 'godmother' is a special grown-up chosen to do what for a child?
c: Help look after and guide them
questions.f: Godparents traditionally promise to help with a child's upbringing.

questions.q: If your parent marries again, their new wife becomes your what?
questions.f: 'Step' in these words comes from an old word meaning bereaved, not from stairs.

questions.q: The word 'breakfast' means to break your night-long what?
questions.f: A fast is a time without eating, so breakfast ends the overnight one.

questions.q: A 'potluck' party is one where guests each bring what?
questions.f: The old word 'potluck' meant taking your luck with whatever was in the pot.

questions.q: A 'picnic' is a meal eaten where?
questions.f: 'Picnic' comes from the French 'pique-nique', an old word for a shared meal.

questions.q: When you 'decorate' a room for a party, you make it look what?
questions.f: 'Decorate' comes from a Latin word meaning to add beauty or honour.

questions.q: A 'greeting card' is a folded card with what inside?
questions.f: The world's first printed Christmas cards were sold in London in 1843.

questions.q: The word 'candy' means the same as which British word?
questions.f: 'Candy' traces all the way back to the Sanskrit word 'khanda', meaning a piece of sugar.

questions.q: If someone is described as 'jolly' at a festival, they are what?
questions.f: 'Jolly' most likely comes from an old French word linked to Yule celebrations.

questions.q: A 'lantern' is a light with what around it?
c: A cover to shield the flame
questions.f: Paper lanterns can hold a candle safely because the flame sits well away from the paper.

questions.q: In a parade, a 'float' is what?
questions.f: Early parade floats were built on barges that really floated on water.

questions.q: A 'firecracker' is a small firework that mainly does what?
questions.f: Firecrackers were invented in China around a thousand years ago.

questions.q: When we say a family is 'related', we mean they what?
questions.f: 'Relative' and 'related' both come from a Latin word meaning to carry back.

questions.q: What word means a big gathering of relatives from near and far?
questions.f: Some family reunions gather hundreds of cousins in one park.

questions.q: A 'guest of honour' at a celebration is the person who is what?
questions.f: The guest of honour usually sits at the head of the table.

questions.q: The word 'gift' means the same as which other word?
questions.f: 'Gift' comes from an old Norse and Germanic word simply meaning a giving.

questions.q: If a party is 'annual', how often does it happen?
questions.f: 'Annual' comes from the Latin word 'annus', meaning year.

questions.q: What do we call the tune everyone sings while the cake is carried in?
questions.f: The birthday tune began life in 1893 as a classroom song called 'Good Morning to All'.

questions.q: 'Grandparents' are your parents' parents.
questions.f: Your grandparents' parents would be your great-grandparents.

questions.q: A 'niece' is a boy.
questions.f: A niece is a girl; the boy version of the word is nephew.

questions.q: At Chinese New Year, houses are often decorated with red paper.
questions.f: Red paper cuttings and banners are pasted on doors and windows for luck.

questions.q: On Halloween, people give out fruit instead of any candy at all.
questions.f: Candy is the classic treat, though some houses hand out satsumas or stickers too.

questions.q: The word 'festival' is related to the word 'feast'.
questions.f: Both grew from the Latin word 'festum', meaning a joyful holiday.

questions.q: Tet, a new-year festival with kumquat trees and sticky rice cakes, belongs to which country?
questions.f: Vietnamese families believe the first visitor of Tet sets the household's luck for the year.

questions.q: Chuseok, a harvest thanksgiving with songpyeon rice cakes, is celebrated in which country?
questions.f: Families travel home for Chuseok to share food at their ancestors' graves.

questions.q: Oktoberfest, the world's biggest folk fair, is held in which German city?
questions.f: Oktoberfest began in 1810 as a public party for a royal wedding, complete with horse races.

questions.q: Dancing around a flower-covered maypole is the heart of Midsummer in which country?
questions.f: Swedish Midsummer falls near the longest day, when the far north barely gets dark at all.

questions.q: On St Lucia's Day a girl wears a crown of candles in which country?
questions.f: Saffron buns called lussekatter are baked for the day, turning the dough golden.

questions.q: Dutch children leave out which item for Sinterklaas to fill with treats?
questions.f: Sinterklaas is said to arrive by steamboat, and his name gave us 'Santa Claus'.

questions.q: At Loy Krathong, people float little decorated baskets on rivers in which country?
questions.f: Each floating krathong carries a candle and often a coin as a thank-you to the water.

questions.q: During Obon, families float lanterns to guide ancestors' spirits home in which country?
questions.f: The circle dance performed at Obon is called Bon Odori.

questions.q: Naadam, a festival of wrestling, archery and horse racing, belongs to which country?
questions.f: Naadam's horse races are ridden by children, over courses many kilometres long.

questions.q: Inti Raymi, an ancient festival of the sun, is celebrated in which South American country?
questions.f: Inti Raymi was an Inca festival, and it falls in June because that is midwinter south of the equator.

questions.q: During Kwanzaa, what is placed in the special holder called a kinara?
questions.f: The kinara's candles are black, red and green, the colours of the Pan-African flag.

questions.q: Juneteenth, celebrated on 19 June, remembers the end of slavery in which country?
questions.f: The date marks 1865, when the news finally reached enslaved people in Galveston, Texas.

questions.q: Cinco de Mayo, a Mexican-American celebration, is named after which date?
questions.f: It remembers a surprise Mexican victory at Puebla in 1862, not Mexico's independence day.

questions.q: Bastille Day, celebrated on 14 July with parades and fireworks, is the national day of which country?
questions.f: In French it is simply called 'la Fete nationale' or 'le quatorze juillet'.

questions.q: Which flat, unleavened bread is eaten during the Jewish festival of Passover?
questions.f: Matzah must be baked in under eighteen minutes so the dough has no time to rise.

questions.q: The special Passover meal, with its set order of foods and readings, is called what?
questions.f: 'Seder' means 'order', because every step of the evening follows a set sequence.

questions.q: At Rosh Hashanah, which fruit is dipped in honey to wish for a sweet year?
questions.f: Round challah bread is also served, standing for the circle of the year.

questions.q: Which hollow ram's horn is blown at the Jewish New Year?
questions.f: A skilled blower can sound the shofar in four different patterns during the service.

questions.q: During Sukkot, families eat and sometimes sleep in a temporary hut called what?
questions.f: A sukkah's leafy roof must be loose enough to let you see the stars through it.

questions.q: Which triangular filled cookie is baked for the Jewish festival of Purim?
questions.f: Children in costume also shake noisemakers called groggers whenever the villain's name is read.

questions.q: Eid al-Adha falls at the time of which great journey to Mecca?
questions.f: Around two million pilgrims travel to Mecca for the Hajj in a normal year.

questions.q: Which Indian community celebrates Vaisakhi with harvest dances and processions?
questions.f: Vaisakhi also marks 1699, when the Sikh community of the Khalsa was founded.

questions.q: At Sikh festivals, the free meal served to everyone in the community is called what?
questions.f: In langar everyone sits on the floor in rows, to show that all people are equal.

questions.q: Lohri, celebrated with bonfires, popcorn and peanuts, marks the end of which season?
questions.f: Lohri falls in mid-January, the coldest stretch of the Punjabi year.

questions.q: Durga Puja, with huge decorated pavilions called pandals, is grandest in which Indian city?
questions.f: Kolkata's Durga Puja was added to UNESCO's heritage list in 2021.

questions.q: At the end of Ganesh Chaturthi, what happens to the clay statues?
c: They are locked in a museum
questions.f: Many families now use clay with seeds inside, so the statue grows into a plant.

questions.q: Janmashtami celebrates the birth of which Hindu god?
questions.f: In Mumbai teams build human pyramids to reach a hanging pot of curd, called dahi handi.

questions.q: During Nepal's Tihar festival, which loyal animal gets a garland and a special meal?
questions.f: Kukur Tihar honours dogs for their friendship and their sharp guarding noses.

questions.q: Bhutan's Tshechu festivals are famous for performances by dancers wearing what?
questions.f: Tshechu masked dances tell moral stories and are performed in monastery courtyards.

questions.q: At the Dragon Boat Festival, which sticky rice parcel wrapped in leaves is eaten?
questions.f: Teams race long narrow boats to the beat of a drummer sitting at the front.

questions.q: Qingming, in early April, is also known in English as which kind of day?
questions.f: Families tidy ancestors' graves and often fly kites afterwards in the spring wind.

questions.q: China's Double Ninth Festival is now especially a day to honour whom?
questions.f: Climbing a hill and drinking chrysanthemum tea are Double Ninth traditions.

questions.q: At Japan's Setsubun, what do families throw to chase bad luck out of the house?
questions.f: People shout 'Demons out, luck in!' as the beans fly out of the door.

questions.q: Japan's Hinamatsuri, on 3 March, is celebrated by displaying what?
questions.f: The dolls are arranged on red steps, with an emperor and empress on the top tier.

questions.q: At Japan's Tanabata festival, wishes are written on paper strips and tied to what?
questions.f: Tanabata tells of two stars, Orihime and Hikoboshi, allowed to meet just once a year.

questions.q: Japan's Shichi-Go-San festival celebrates children of which ages?
questions.f: Children receive a long thin sweet called chitose ame, meaning 'thousand-year candy'.

questions.q: The Sapporo Snow Festival in Japan is famous for what?
questions.f: Some Sapporo snow sculptures are as tall as a three-storey building.

questions.q: Quebec's Winter Carnival is led by a giant snowman mascot named what?
questions.f: Bonhomme wears a red cap and a woven sash called a ceinture flechee.

questions.q: Which song do crowds in Britain and beyond link arms to sing at midnight on New Year's Eve?
questions.f: Its words were written down by the Scottish poet Robert Burns in 1788.

questions.q: Burns Night suppers in Scotland famously begin with a poem addressed to what?
questions.f: Robert Burns wrote 'Address to a Haggis' in 1786, and it is still recited every 25 January.

questions.q: Which two plants are worn on St David's Day in Wales?
questions.f: Wales celebrates St David's Day on 1 March with parades and school concerts.

questions.q: Boxing Day, a holiday in Britain and many Commonwealth countries, falls on which date?
questions.f: The name may come from alms boxes opened to help the poor the day after Christmas.

questions.q: On Three Kings' Day, Spanish and Latin American children traditionally receive what?
questions.f: A ring-shaped rosca de reyes cake is shared, with a tiny figurine hidden inside.

questions.q: Mexico's Las Posadas is a procession held over how many nights before Christmas?
questions.f: The nine nights stand for the nine months before a birth in the Christmas story.

questions.q: Because of the seasons, Christmas in Australia falls in which time of year?
questions.f: Many Australian families celebrate with a barbecue or a beach picnic.

questions.q: Which red-leaved Christmas plant originally comes from Mexico?
questions.f: Its bright red parts are not petals at all but coloured leaves called bracts.

questions.q: In the Christmas story, the wise men bring gold, frankincense and what?
questions.f: Frankincense and myrrh are both fragrant tree resins, once worth as much as gold.

questions.q: How many Sundays make up the season of Advent before Christmas?
questions.f: Advent wreaths hold one candle for each of those Sundays.

questions.q: Wassailing, an old English winter custom, involves singing to what?
questions.f: Villagers sang and made noise in orchards to wish the apple trees a good crop.

questions.q: In the United States, Mother's Day falls in which month?
questions.f: Britain instead keeps Mothering Sunday, which moves each year with the date of Easter.

questions.q: A silver wedding anniversary marks how many years of marriage?
questions.f: Fifty years earns gold, and sixty years is called a diamond anniversary.

questions.q: At a Western wedding, the groom's chosen helper is called the what?
questions.f: The bride's helpers are her bridesmaids, and the youngest are often flower girls.

questions.q: A Jewish boy's coming-of-age ceremony, the bar mitzvah, happens at which age?
questions.f: A girl's bat mitzvah is usually held at twelve.

questions.q: A quinceanera celebrates a Latin American girl reaching which age?
questions.f: The party often includes a waltz with her father and a symbolic change into high heels.

questions.q: In Spain, a child's lost tooth is collected by a little mouse named what?
questions.f: He was invented in 1894 for a story written for a young Spanish king.

questions.q: At a Christian christening, what is poured or sprinkled on the baby's head?
questions.f: The ceremony is also called a baptism, from a Greek word meaning to dip.

questions.q: Your grandparent's parent is your what?
questions.f: Some lucky children today meet five living generations of their family.

questions.q: Your husband's or wife's mother is called your mother-in-what?
questions.f: 'In-law' once meant related by canon law, the rules of the church.

questions.q: The word 'carnival' comes from words meaning farewell to what?
questions.f: Carnival came just before Lent, when meat was traditionally given up.

questions.q: 'Mardi Gras' literally translates as which two words?
questions.f: It is the last rich, buttery day before the plain eating of Lent begins.

questions.q: The word 'pinata' comes from an Italian word for what?
questions.f: The first pinatas really were clay pots, covered in paper to look festive.

questions.q: The festival name 'Deepavali' is built from words meaning what?
questions.f: 'Deepa' means lamp and 'avali' means row, which is why homes are outlined in light.

questions.q: The festival name 'Navratri' means what?
questions.f: 'Nava' means nine and 'ratri' means night, exactly matching the festival's length.

questions.q: The name 'Nowruz' translates as what?
questions.f: Nowruz begins at the exact moment of the spring equinox, calculated to the minute.

questions.q: 'Rosh Hashanah' literally means which phrase?
questions.f: Calling New Year the 'head' of the year is a picture of the year having a body.

questions.q: The word 'Hanukkah' means what?
questions.f: The name recalls the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem long ago.

questions.q: The festival word 'Eid' simply means what?
questions.f: That is why there are two Eids, one after Ramadan and one at the time of the Hajj.

questions.q: The name 'Kwanzaa' comes from a Swahili phrase meaning what?
questions.f: It is drawn from 'matunda ya kwanza', and Kwanzaa was created in 1966.

questions.q: The holiday name 'Juneteenth' was made by squashing together which two words?
questions.f: Blended words like this are called portmanteau words, just like 'brunch'.

questions.q: The word 'Advent' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Advent' shares its root with 'adventure', something that comes your way.

questions.q: 'Epiphany', the festival on 6 January, comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: That is also why a sudden bright idea is called an epiphany.

questions.q: The Christmas word 'Noel' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: The same Latin root 'natalis' gives us the word 'nativity'.

questions.q: The word 'carol' originally meant which kind of activity?
questions.f: Early carols were danced in a circle, which is why they have a bouncy repeating chorus.

questions.q: The old greeting 'wassail' meant what?
questions.f: It comes from 'waes hael', an Old English toast to someone's good health.

questions.q: The word 'companion' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: From Latin 'com' plus 'panis', bread, which is what friends have always shared.

questions.q: The word 'family' comes from a Latin word for what?
questions.f: Latin 'familia' covered everyone living under one roof, not only blood relatives.

questions.q: A 'matriarch' is a family's what?
questions.f: 'Matri' means mother and 'arch' means ruler, as in monarch and architect.

questions.q: If a grandmother is your 'maternal' grandmother, she is whose mother?
questions.f: 'Maternal' comes from Latin 'mater' and 'paternal' from 'pater', father.

questions.q: An 'heirloom' is an object that is what?
questions.f: The word joins 'heir' with the old sense of 'loom', meaning a tool.

questions.q: 'Cornucopia', the horn overflowing with harvest food, literally means what?
questions.f: From Latin 'cornu', horn, and 'copia', abundance.

questions.q: Nyepi, a whole day of silence with no travel or noise, is observed on which Indonesian island?
questions.f: Even Bali's airport closes for Nyepi, making it one of the quietest days on Earth.

questions.q: Enkutatash, a new-year festival celebrated in September, belongs to which country?
questions.f: Ethiopia keeps its own calendar of thirteen months, so its year begins in our September.

questions.q: Crop Over, a summer festival in Barbados, celebrates the end of which harvest?
questions.f: Crop Over ends with a costumed parade called Grand Kadooment.

questions.q: Which drum-like instrument, made from an oil barrel, is the sound of Trinidad's Carnival?
questions.f: The steelpan is one of the few brand-new musical instruments invented in the 20th century.

questions.q: In Guatemala, giant handmade kites are flown over cemeteries on which festival?
questions.f: Some Sumpango kites are over ten metres across and take months to build from tissue paper.

questions.q: In Ecuador, what do families burn at midnight on New Year's Eve?
c: Life-size dolls of the old year
questions.f: The 'ano viejo' dolls are stuffed with sawdust and stand for leaving the old year behind.

questions.q: During Las Fallas in Valencia, Spain, what happens to the enormous sculptures?
c: They are floated out to sea
questions.f: The huge cardboard figures are called ninots, and one is pardoned from the flames each year.

questions.q: At the strange festival in Ivrea, Italy, townspeople playfully throw what?
questions.f: The Battle of the Oranges uses tonnes of fruit, and teams ride on horse-drawn carts.

questions.q: Which Italian city is famous for elaborate Carnival masks and canal parades?
questions.f: The plain white Venetian mask with a beaked chin is called a bauta.

questions.q: In Germany, children walk with homemade lanterns on the feast of which saint?
questions.f: They sing lantern songs on 11 November and share a sweet bread man called a Weckmann.

questions.q: At the Polish Christmas Eve supper called Wigilia, an extra place is set for whom?
questions.f: Wigilia traditionally has twelve meatless dishes and begins when the first star appears.

questions.q: Maslenitsa, a Russian week of feasting before Lent, is famous for eating what?
questions.f: The thin round blini are said to stand for the returning sun.

questions.q: In Bulgaria, a red-and-white thread bracelet is worn each March until the wearer sees what?
c: A stork or a blossoming tree
questions.f: The bracelet is called a martenitsa and is then tied to a tree branch.

questions.q: Greek families dye their Easter eggs which colour, then tap them together?
questions.f: The winner of the tapping game is the person whose egg stays uncracked.

questions.q: In Greece, the New Year cake called vasilopita hides what inside?
questions.f: Whoever finds the coin in their slice is promised luck for the whole year.

questions.q: On King's Day in the Netherlands, the whole country dresses in which colour?
questions.f: Orange honours the royal House of Orange-Nassau.

questions.q: In Iceland, Christmas stories feature thirteen mischievous characters known as what?
questions.f: Each Yule Lad has his own odd habit, like slamming doors or licking spoons.

questions.q: In Ireland, a ring baked inside the Halloween barmbrack loaf is said to predict what?
questions.f: Other charms baked into the bread included a coin for wealth and a pea for poverty.

questions.q: In the Scottish custom of first-footing, the first visitor of the new year brings what?
questions.f: Coal, shortbread and salt were carried in to promise warmth and food all year.

questions.q: At the Eisteddfod festival in Wales, the top prize is given for what?
questions.f: The winning poet is 'chaired' in a ceremony that goes back centuries.

questions.q: At Cooper's Hill in England, competitors chase which food down a steep slope?
questions.f: The cheese can reach speeds of over 100 kilometres an hour on the way down.

questions.q: In the town of Olney, England, Shrove Tuesday features a race carrying what?
c: A frying pan with a pancake
questions.f: Runners must toss the pancake at the start and the finish of the race.

questions.q: Pasadena's famous New Year's Day parade has floats that must be covered in what?
questions.f: A single Rose Parade float can use more flowers than a florist sells in a year.

questions.q: Matariki, now a public holiday, marks the Maori new year and the rising of what?
questions.f: Matariki is the star cluster many others call the Pleiades or the Seven Sisters.

questions.q: At a Hawaiian luau, guests are welcomed with a flower necklace called what?
questions.f: Giving a lei is a greeting, a farewell and a mark of respect all at once.

questions.q: A Maori hangi is a feast cooked how?
c: In a pit oven in the ground
In a clay pot on a fire
questions.f: Hot stones are buried with baskets of food, which steams underground for hours.

questions.q: A powwow is a celebration of which peoples' music and dance?
questions.f: Powwow dancers compete in styles such as jingle dress and fancy shawl.

questions.q: At Korea's Seollal new year, eating a bowl of tteokguk soup means what?
c: You have grown a year older
questions.f: Children also perform a deep bow called sebae and receive money afterwards.

questions.q: Japanese families welcome the new year with stacked lacquer boxes of food called what?
questions.f: Each osechi food carries a wish; black beans, for instance, stand for good health.

questions.q: At Chiang Mai's Yi Peng festival in Thailand, thousands of what are released?
questions.f: Yi Peng often overlaps with Loy Krathong, filling both sky and river with light.

questions.q: In the Philippines, the star-shaped Christmas lantern is called what?
questions.f: Parols were first made to light the way to the dawn Masses of Simbang Gabi.

questions.q: In Indonesia, the huge Eid homecoming journey, when cities empty out, is called what?
questions.f: Tens of millions travel for mudik, one of the largest yearly migrations anywhere.

questions.q: On the Iranian Nowruz table, the seven special items all begin with which letter sound?
questions.f: The spread is called haft-sin, meaning 'seven S things', and includes sprouted wheat and apples.

questions.q: Tu BiShvat is a Jewish festival often called the new year of what?
questions.f: Many families mark it by planting saplings or eating dried fruit and nuts.

questions.q: On Simchat Torah, people dance around the synagogue carrying what?
questions.f: It celebrates finishing the yearly reading of the Torah and starting again at once.

questions.q: In Egypt, a colourful metal-and-glass lantern called a fanous is hung up during which month?
questions.f: The Ramadan fanous tradition is said to date back over a thousand years in Cairo.

questions.q: The Islamic calendar, which sets the dates of Eid, has how many months?
questions.f: Its months follow the moon, so the year is about eleven days shorter than the solar one.

questions.q: The French Christmas dessert 'buche de Noel' is a cake shaped like what?
questions.f: It recalls the real Yule log families once burned slowly through the darkest nights.

questions.q: The carol 'Silent Night' was first performed in a village church in which country?
questions.f: It was sung in 1818 with a guitar, because the church organ was out of action.

questions.q: Surprisingly, the song 'Jingle Bells' was originally written for which holiday?
questions.f: It also became the first song broadcast from space, by Gemini 6 astronauts in 1965.

questions.q: What is inside a British Christmas cracker besides a small toy and a joke?
questions.f: The bang comes from a tiny strip of card with a trace of friction-sensitive chemical.

questions.q: By tradition, Christmas decorations are taken down on which night?
questions.f: Twelfth Night falls twelve days after Christmas, around 5 or 6 January.

questions.q: The wedding rhyme asks for something old, something new, something borrowed and something what?
questions.f: An older version adds 'and a silver sixpence in her shoe'.

questions.q: At a Greek wedding, guests are given sugared almonds called koufeta, always in what number?
questions.f: An odd number cannot be divided evenly, a wish that the couple stay together.

questions.q: In a Hindu wedding, the couple take seven steps together in a ritual called what?
questions.f: 'Sapta' means seven, and each step is a promise the couple makes.

questions.q: At a Jewish wedding, the couple stand beneath a canopy called what?
questions.f: The open sides of the chuppah stand for a home always welcoming to guests.

questions.q: In Mexico, the birthday custom of 'la mordida' invites the birthday person to do what?
c: Take the first bite of cake without hands
questions.f: Friends usually give a gentle nudge so the birthday nose touches the frosting.

questions.q: In Israel, a birthday person is often seated in a chair and then what?
questions.f: The chair is lifted once for each year, which gets tiring at big birthdays.

questions.q: In many Chinese families, a baby's first month is celebrated by giving out what?
questions.f: Red stands for luck, and the egg's round shape stands for a whole, harmonious life.

questions.q: The Hindu ceremony 'annaprasana' celebrates a baby's first taste of what?
questions.f: The baby is usually fed a spoonful of sweet rice by a grandparent.

questions.q: Fraternal twins begin when how many eggs are fertilised?
questions.f: Identical twins come from a single egg splitting, which is why they look so alike.

questions.q: In family history, one 'generation' is usually counted as roughly how many years?
questions.f: That is why four generations often live at the same time in one family.

questions.q: The word 'yuletide' ends with 'tide', which in old English meant what?
questions.f: The same sense survives in 'Christmastide' and 'Eastertide'.

questions.q: 'Shrove Tuesday' takes its name from an old word 'shrive', meaning to do what?
questions.f: People confessed before Lent, then used up rich food, which is why pancakes appeared.

questions.q: The name 'Lent' comes from an old word connected to what?
questions.f: Old English 'lencten' meant spring, when the daylight visibly lengthens.

questions.q: The English festival name 'Easter' is thought to come from what?
c: The name of a spring goddess
questions.f: An English monk called Bede wrote that a spring goddess named Eostre gave the month its name.

questions.q: In holiday names like Christmas and Candlemas, the ending '-mas' means what?
questions.f: That is why Michaelmas and Martinmas mark saints' days too.

questions.q: The word 'Sabbath' comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: Hebrew 'shabbat' means to cease or rest from work.

questions.q: The month name 'Ramadan' comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: The month originally fell in the hottest part of the Arabian year.

questions.q: The word 'jubilee', used for a big anniversary, traces back to a word for what?
questions.f: Hebrew 'yobel' was the horn blown to announce a special fiftieth year.

questions.q: 'Anniversary' is built from Latin parts meaning what?
questions.f: From 'annus', year, and 'vertere', to turn, because the year has come round again.

questions.q: A 'centenarian' is a person celebrating what?
questions.f: There are now over half a million centenarians alive in the world.

questions.q: The word 'banquet' comes from an Italian word meaning what?
questions.f: Guests once perched on benches, and 'banchetto' meant a small bench.

questions.q: 'Smorgasbord', a spread of many festive dishes, comes from a phrase meaning what?
questions.f: The Swedish word joins 'smorgas', an open sandwich, with 'bord', table.

questions.q: The word 'menu' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: A menu began as a 'detailed list' written out small for the host.

questions.q: A 'recipe' takes its name from a Latin word that means what?
questions.f: Old recipes began with 'Recipe...', an instruction meaning 'take these things'.

questions.q: The word 'chef' originally meant what?
questions.f: The full old title was 'chef de cuisine', head of the kitchen.

questions.q: A 'pantry', where festival food is stored, is named from a word for what?
questions.f: Latin 'panis' means bread, the same root found in 'companion'.

questions.q: The word 'hospitality' comes from a Latin word that meant both what?
questions.f: Latin 'hospes' covered both roles, and also gave us 'hotel' and 'hospital'.

questions.q: The word 'candle' comes from a Latin verb meaning what?
questions.f: The same root 'candere' hides in 'chandelier' and 'incandescent'.

questions.q: The word 'bonfire' was originally a compound meaning what?
questions.f: Medieval bonfires really did burn old animal bones along with the wood.

questions.q: The word 'festoon', a hanging chain of decorations, is a cousin of which word?
questions.f: Both grew from Latin 'festa', because festoons were made for feast days.

questions.q: 'Regalia', the grand dress worn in some festival parades, means things belonging to what?
questions.f: Latin 'regalis' means kingly, the same root as 'regal' and 'reign'.

questions.q: The word 'descendant' contains a root meaning what?
questions.f: Your descendants come down the family tree from you; your ancestors go before you.

questions.q: The word 'infant' comes from Latin parts meaning what?
questions.f: From 'in-', not, plus 'fans', speaking, since babies have not yet learned words.

questions.q: The word 'honeymoon' originally referred to what?
questions.f: 'Moon' here means month, and honey stood for the sweetness of the beginning.

questions.q: The word 'bridal' comes from an old term meaning what?
questions.f: 'Bride-ale' was the celebration drink and feast held at a wedding.

questions.q: The bird we call a 'turkey' was named after what?
c: A country it was traded through
questions.f: The bird is American, but Europeans first met it through Turkish traders.

questions.q: The words 'fiesta' and 'feast' are related.
questions.f: Both come from Latin 'festa', which also gives us festival and festoon.

questions.q: Nowruz, Songkran and Seollal are all new-year celebrations.
questions.f: They fall in spring, in April and in winter, because each follows a different calendar.

questions.q: At Ethiopia's Timkat festival, priests carry a covered replica of what?
questions.f: Timkat celebrates the baptism of Jesus, and the replica tabot is paraded to water and back.

questions.q: Malaysia's Thaipusam festival draws huge crowds to which famous limestone cave temple?
questions.f: Pilgrims climb 272 steps at Batu Caves carrying decorated frames called kavadi.

questions.q: Sri Lanka's grand Esala Perahera procession in Kandy honours which relic?
questions.f: Elephants in embroidered cloth parade by night, led by a tusker carrying the relic casket.

questions.q: At the Tibetan new year of Losar, families eat a soup with objects hidden in the dumplings to reveal what?
c: A playful hint about your character
questions.f: Finding wool suggests a kind heart, while a chilli hints that you are sharp-tongued.

questions.q: Cambodia's Bon Om Touk water festival celebrates a river that does something remarkable each year. What?
c: It reverses its direction of flow
questions.f: The Tonle Sap flows backwards when the Mekong floods, then drains again in November.

questions.q: Nagaland's Hornbill Festival is nicknamed the festival of what?
questions.f: It is called the Festival of Festivals because it gathers the traditions of many Naga tribes at once.

questions.q: At the Chhath Puja festival of Bihar, worshippers stand in water to honour which part of nature?
questions.f: Offerings are made at sunset and again at sunrise, one of the few festivals to thank the setting Sun.

questions.q: During Karva Chauth, the moon is traditionally first viewed through what?
questions.f: The sieve breaks the moonlight into many small points of light.

questions.q: The Ugadi dish 'pachadi' famously mixes how many different tastes?
questions.f: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, spicy and tangy together stand for the many flavours of a year.

questions.q: On Kerala's Vishu new year, the first thing you are meant to see on waking is what?
c: A lit lamp on the roof
questions.f: The vishukkani display holds golden konna flowers, fruit, coins and a mirror.

questions.q: Kerala's Thrissur Pooram festival is famous for a contest exchanging what atop elephants?
questions.f: The parasol-swapping display is called kudamattam, and crowds cheer each new design.

questions.q: The Kumbh Mela, one of the largest human gatherings on Earth, rotates between how many cities?
questions.f: Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nashik and Ujjain each host it in turn, all on sacred rivers.

questions.q: At the Mid-Autumn Festival, the salted duck egg yolk inside a mooncake stands for what?
questions.f: The richest mooncakes hide two yolks, and each cake is stamped with a lucky character.

questions.q: At China's Lantern Festival, which sweet food made of glutinous rice balls is eaten?
questions.f: The round white balls float in warm syrup, and their shape suggests family togetherness.

questions.q: Chinese New Year's sticky 'nian gao' cake is eaten because its name sounds like what?
questions.f: Chinese festival foods often work as puns, since 'gao' also means tall or high.

questions.q: In Japan, the pine-and-bamboo decoration placed at the entrance for New Year is called what?
questions.f: Kadomatsu means 'gate pine' and is meant to welcome good spirits to the home.

questions.q: Kyoto's Gion Matsuri is famous for parading enormous wheeled what?
questions.f: The largest yamaboko floats weigh over ten tonnes and are pulled entirely by hand.

questions.q: At Korea's Chuseok, women perform a circle dance under the full moon called what?
questions.f: Dancers link hands, sing and spin faster and faster as the circle grows.

questions.q: Vietnam's square Tet rice cake, banh chung, is said to represent what?
questions.f: Its round partner, banh giay, stands for the sky.

questions.q: At the Philippines' Pahiyas festival, houses are decorated with colourful wafers made from what?
questions.f: The thin kiping wafers are pressed from rice paste and hung in bright cascades.

questions.q: On Bali's Galungan festival, tall decorated bamboo poles are set outside homes. What are they called?
questions.f: A penjor arches over the street, laden with rice, fruit and coconut leaves.

questions.q: Before Eid al-Fitr prayers, Muslims are expected to give a charity payment called what?
questions.f: It is given as food or its value, so that everyone can share in the festival meal.

questions.q: Muslims seek Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, during which part of Ramadan?
questions.f: Many people stay awake in prayer, since the exact night is not known.

questions.q: The festival of Mawlid celebrates the birthday of whom?
questions.f: Streets are decorated and sweets are shared, and in Egypt a sugar doll is a Mawlid treat.

questions.q: Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, lasts for about how long?
questions.f: The fast runs from sunset to nightfall the next day, ending with a blast of the shofar.

questions.q: Which dairy dessert is traditional at the Jewish festival of Shavuot?
questions.f: Shavuot marks the giving of the Torah, and dairy foods are the customary way to celebrate.

questions.q: At the Passover seder, the hidden piece of matzah that children search for is called what?
questions.f: The word comes from Greek and means something like 'dessert' or after-dinner treat.

questions.q: On the Hanukkah menorah, the extra ninth candle used to light the others is called what?
