questions.f: 'Shamash' means servant or attendant, because its whole job is to serve the other flames.

questions.q: At Purim, the custom of 'mishloach manot' means sending friends what?
questions.f: Baskets usually hold at least two ready-to-eat foods, often including hamantaschen.

questions.q: The Christmas tree became fashionable in Britain after a picture appeared showing which royal family?
questions.f: An 1848 illustration of their decorated tree spread the custom across Britain and America.

questions.q: The now-familiar plump, red-suited Santa was popularised by 1930s adverts for which drink?
questions.f: Artist Haddon Sundblom painted him each year from 1931, but red-suited Santas existed before.

questions.q: In an Advent wreath, the pink or rose candle marks a Sunday named for which idea?
questions.f: It is called Gaudete Sunday, from a Latin word meaning 'rejoice'.

questions.q: The Twelve Days of Christmas begin on which day?
questions.f: Counting twelve days from 25 December brings you to Epiphany on 6 January.

questions.q: In Greece, Epiphany is celebrated with a custom in which people dive for what?
c: A cross thrown into the water
questions.f: Whoever surfaces with the cross is said to have luck for the year.

questions.q: Groundhog Day grew out of a European weather custom attached to which festival?
questions.f: An old rhyme said a bright, clear Candlemas meant winter still had a long way to run.

questions.q: Which flower did Anna Jarvis choose as the emblem of the American Mother's Day?
questions.f: Jarvis later fought against the holiday's commercialisation, unhappy at the profits made from it.

questions.q: US Thanksgiving became a fixed national holiday after a long campaign by which writer?
questions.f: Hale wrote letters for decades, and also wrote 'Mary Had a Little Lamb'.

questions.q: Canada's Thanksgiving is held on which day?
questions.f: Canada's harvest arrives earlier, so its Thanksgiving comes six weeks before the American one.

questions.q: The Halloween custom of 'souling' involved going door to door to do what?
c: Sing or pray in exchange for cakes
questions.f: Soul cakes were small spiced buns given out to the singers, an ancestor of trick-or-treating.

questions.q: On Day of the Dead altars, the cut-paper banners strung overhead are called what?
questions.f: The delicate tissue-paper flutters constantly, said to show that spirits are moving through.

questions.q: In Alpine tradition, which shaggy horned companion travels with St Nicholas?
questions.f: Whole parades of costumed Krampus figures with cowbells fill Austrian towns in early December.

questions.q: In Italian tradition, La Befana delivers gifts while riding what?
questions.f: She arrives on the eve of Epiphany, and children leave her a glass of wine and a snack.

questions.q: Shetland's Up Helly Aa festival ends with the ceremonial burning of what?
questions.f: Hundreds of torch-bearers march behind the galley before setting it alight.

questions.q: At Sweden's Midsummer, children famously dance around the pole imitating which animal?
questions.f: The song 'Sma grodorna' has dancers hop about pretending to be small frogs with no ears or tails.

questions.q: On Slavic Kupala Night, young people float what on the water to see their fortune?
questions.f: A wreath that floats far is a good sign; one that sinks is a joke about waiting a while longer.

questions.q: In Poland's Dozynki harvest festival, what is presented to the host of the celebration?
questions.f: The wreath is made from ears of wheat, rye and flowers from the finished fields.

questions.q: Dutch children leave a drawing or a poem for Sinterklaas, and often receive what letter-shaped treat?
questions.f: Each child gets the first letter of their own name, moulded in chocolate.

questions.q: 'Jumping the broom' is a wedding custom especially associated with which community?
questions.f: The broom-jump marks the sweeping away of the old and the start of a shared home.

questions.q: At a Korean paebaek ceremony, elders throw jujubes and chestnuts for the couple to catch. Why?
c: The number caught playfully predicts children
questions.f: Dates stand for daughters and chestnuts for sons in this good-humoured tradition.

questions.q: In a Japanese wedding, 'san-san-kudo' involves the couple taking how many sips in total?
questions.f: Three sips from each of three cups, since three is an unbreakable, indivisible number.

questions.q: Before an Indian wedding, the ceremony where turmeric paste is applied to the couple is called what?
questions.f: Turmeric is used because it is thought to brighten skin and ward off illness.

questions.q: A 70th wedding anniversary is traditionally called which anniversary?
questions.f: Sixty years is diamond, so the very rare seventy earns the tougher metal.

questions.q: In Japan, a child who loses a lower tooth is traditionally told to throw it where?
questions.f: Upper teeth are thrown down and lower teeth up, so the new tooth grows in the right direction.

questions.q: In Denmark, how do families announce that someone in the house has a birthday?
c: They fly the national flag outside
They ring a bell at noon
questions.f: Danish flags also appear on birthday cakes and table decorations.

questions.q: Nowruz begins at the exact moment of which astronomical event?
c: The first full moon of March
questions.f: Because the equinox is a precise instant, Nowruz can start in the middle of the night.

questions.q: The Chinese and Jewish calendars are both lunisolar, adding an extra month now and then.
questions.f: That leap month keeps their festivals from drifting out of their proper season.

questions.q: Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas are celebrated at the same time by Hindus and Sikhs.
questions.f: Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, the release of Guru Hargobind, on the same autumn nights.

questions.q: The Gaelic festival name 'Samhain' is generally taken to mean what?
questions.f: It marked the boundary between the light half and the dark half of the Celtic year.

questions.q: The May festival name 'Beltane' is usually explained as meaning what?
questions.f: Cattle were driven between two bonfires at Beltane to protect them for the summer.

questions.q: The name 'Kris Kringle' is a worn-down form of a word meaning what?
questions.f: German 'Christkindl' was the gift-bringer, and English speakers reshaped it into a name for Santa.

questions.q: 'Santa Claus' is an English reshaping of which name?
questions.f: Dutch settlers in New York brought Sinterklaas, and English tongues smoothed it to Santa Claus.

questions.q: The word 'mistletoe' comes from older words that literally mean what?
questions.f: Birds spread mistletoe seeds in their droppings, and old English speakers noticed.

questions.q: The poinsettia is named after Joel Poinsett, who was famous as what?
questions.f: He sent cuttings home in the 1820s, and the plant took his name.

questions.q: The word 'tinsel' comes from an old French word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Estincele' meant a spark, which is exactly what tinsel does to candlelight.

questions.q: 'Pyrotechnics', the proper name for the firework maker's craft, means what?
questions.f: From Greek 'pyr', fire, and 'techne', art or skill.

questions.q: A 'vigil' held on the eve of a festival takes its name from a word meaning what?
questions.f: The same root gives us 'vigilant', meaning wide awake and alert.

questions.q: A 'novena', nine days of prayers before some feasts, is named from the word for what?
questions.f: Latin 'novem' means nine, as in November, once the ninth month of the Roman year.

questions.q: The word 'quinceanera' is built from a Spanish word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Quince' is fifteen, and the whole word means a girl who has turned fifteen.

questions.q: The phrase 'bar mitzvah' means what?
questions.f: 'Bat mitzvah', for a girl, means daughter of the commandment.

questions.q: The Hebrew word 'menorah' simply means what?
questions.f: The Hanukkah lamp with nine branches is more precisely called a hanukkiah.

questions.q: The name of the Hanukkah 'dreidel' comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: Yiddish 'dreyen' means to spin, from the same family as German 'drehen'.

questions.q: The festival name 'Purim' means what?
questions.f: The story turns on lots being cast to pick a day, which is where the name comes from.

questions.q: 'Hamantaschen', the Purim pastries, takes its name from words meaning what?
questions.f: German 'Taschen' means pockets or pouches, describing the folded dough.

questions.q: The Hebrew word 'sukkah' means what?
questions.f: The festival Sukkot is therefore the Festival of Booths.

questions.q: The Passover book read aloud at the seder, the Haggadah, has a name meaning what?
questions.f: It fulfils the instruction to tell the story to your children, year after year.

questions.q: The word 'kosher' means what?
questions.f: It describes food that fits the rules, and in slang has come to mean 'above board'.

questions.q: The Sanskrit-derived word 'puja' means what?
questions.f: That is why Durga Puja and Ganesh Puja are named for the act, not the date.

questions.q: 'Prasad', shared out at Hindu festivals, is best described as what?
questions.f: The word carries the sense of grace or a gracious gift.

questions.q: The festival name 'Dussehra' is built from a word meaning which number?
questions.f: 'Dasha' is ten, and the festival follows the nine nights of Navratri.

questions.q: The harvest festival name 'Pongal' literally means what?
questions.f: Families cheer as the pot of rice and milk boils over, which is the moment of celebration.

questions.q: The word 'Songkran' comes from a Sanskrit term meaning what?
questions.f: It refers to the sun moving into a new zodiac position, which sets the date in mid-April.

questions.q: The Japanese word 'origami', used for festival decorations, is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: Strings of a thousand folded cranes, called senbazuru, are made as a wish for good fortune.

questions.q: The Japanese word 'kimono' literally means what?
questions.f: 'Ki' means wear and 'mono' means thing, so the name is delightfully practical.

questions.q: The word 'yukata', the light summer festival robe, originally described a garment for what?
questions.f: 'Yukatabira' meant bathing cloth, and today yukata are worn to fireworks displays.

questions.q: The Korean festival name 'Chuseok' means what?
questions.f: It falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, always at full moon.

questions.q: The word 'siesta', the rest after a big festival lunch, comes from a phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Romans counted from dawn, so the sixth hour was around midday.

questions.q: A 'ceilidh', an Irish or Scottish party with dancing, takes its name from a word meaning what?
questions.f: A ceilidh began as an evening visit with stories, songs and then dancing.

questions.q: To describe a warm, sociable feast, we can call it 'convivial', from a root meaning what?
questions.f: From Latin 'con', with, and 'vivere', to live; a convivium was a shared banquet.

questions.q: The word 'celebrate' comes from a Latin word that meant what?
questions.f: Latin 'celeber' described a busy, thronged place, and so a much-honoured event.

questions.q: 'Congratulations' contains a root meaning what?
questions.f: From Latin 'gratus', pleasing, the same root as 'gratitude' and 'grace'.

questions.q: The word 'commemorate' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: From 'com', together, and 'memorare', to bring to mind.

questions.q: Raising a glass is called a 'toast' because of what old custom?
c: Putting spiced toast in the cup
Toasting bread on the fire first
questions.f: A piece of spiced toast was floated in wine to flavour it, and the name stuck to the speech.

questions.q: The word 'genealogy', the study of family lines, is built from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Genea' plus 'logos' gives the study of descent, which is why 'gene' looks familiar.

questions.q: The family-tree word 'pedigree' is thought to come from a French phrase meaning what?
questions.f: The three-line mark used on old family charts looked just like a bird's footprint.

questions.q: 'Nepotism', favouring your own relatives, comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: It described powerful churchmen handing important jobs to their nephews.

questions.q: If a relationship is described as 'filial', it is the duty of a what?
questions.f: From Latin 'filius' and 'filia'; 'filial piety' is a central idea in Confucian family life.

questions.q: A surname like Johnson or Petersson is called a 'patronymic', meaning it is based on what?
questions.f: Iceland still uses them, with '-son' for a son and '-dottir' for a daughter.

questions.q: The word 'cousin' comes from a Latin term that originally meant what?
questions.f: Latin 'consobrinus' described that exact relation before the word widened out.

questions.q: Ghana's Homowo harvest festival has a name that means what?
questions.f: The Ga people celebrate surviving a long-ago famine by jeering at hunger itself.

questions.q: The Igbo New Yam Festival marks the moment when it becomes acceptable to do what?
questions.f: The oldest man traditionally tastes the first yam, thanking the earth for the crop.

questions.q: Cape Town's Minstrel Carnival, with its brightly dressed troupes, is held on which day?
questions.f: It is known in Afrikaans as Tweede Nuwe Jaar, the 'Second New Year'.

questions.q: Bolivia's Oruro Carnival is best known for the dramatic dance called what?
questions.f: Dancers wear enormous horned masks, and the festival is a UNESCO heritage event.

questions.q: In Oaxaca, Mexico, the Night of the Radishes features what?
questions.f: Carvers have just hours to work before their vegetable artworks wilt.

questions.q: The Bahamian festival Junkanoo bursts into the streets in the small hours of which day?
questions.f: Rushers dance to goombay drums and cowbells from about two in the morning.

questions.q: Trinidad's Carnival begins before dawn with a muddy, paint-splashed session called what?
questions.f: The name comes from a French phrase meaning 'day opens'.

questions.q: The purple, green and gold of Mardi Gras stand for justice, faith and what?
questions.f: Purple is justice, green is faith and gold is power, chosen by a Carnival krewe in 1872.

questions.q: Whoever finds the tiny figurine in a Mardi Gras king cake traditionally must do what?
c: Wear a paper crown all day
questions.f: The finder buys the next cake, which keeps the season's parties rolling along.

questions.q: Rio's Carnival parades take place in a purpose-built stadium designed by which architect?
questions.f: The Sambadrome opened in 1984 and seats around ninety thousand people.

questions.q: Basel's Carnival, in Switzerland, famously begins at four in the morning with what?
c: All the city lights being switched off
questions.f: The Morgestraich starts in total darkness, lit only by painted lanterns.

questions.q: In Cologne's Carnival, the crowd's traditional shout is which word?
questions.f: Neighbouring Dusseldorf shouts 'Helau' instead, and the rivalry is taken seriously.

questions.q: In Iceland, the Christmas Eve tradition of Jolabokaflod involves giving what?
questions.f: The 'Christmas book flood' means Icelanders spend the evening reading in bed with chocolate.

questions.q: In Catalonia, the Christmas character 'Tio de Nadal' is what?
c: A log that is looked after and gives out sweets
questions.f: Children feed the little log daily, cover it with a blanket, then tap it with sticks on Christmas Eve.

questions.q: In Provence, France, Christmas Eve supper traditionally ends with how many desserts?
questions.f: The thirteen desserts include nougat, dried figs and a flat olive-oil bread called pompe a huile.

questions.q: In Ukraine, the sheaf of wheat brought indoors at Christmas is called what?
questions.f: The name means 'grandfather spirit', and it honours the family's ancestors and the harvest.

questions.q: In Russian tradition, who brings New Year gifts, helped by his granddaughter Snegurochka?
questions.f: Ded Moroz means 'Grandfather Frost', and he wears a long blue or white coat.

questions.q: Ethiopia's Christmas, called Genna, falls on which date?
questions.f: Churches using the older Julian reckoning celebrate Christmas about two weeks after 25 December.

questions.q: Outside India, the largest Diwali celebrations in the world are held in which city?
questions.f: Leicester's Golden Mile switches on Diwali lights that draw tens of thousands of visitors.

questions.q: In Japan, the New Year money given to children in decorated envelopes is called what?
questions.f: Like Chinese red packets, otoshidama envelopes are chosen to suit the child's age and taste.

questions.q: In Japan, the first shrine or temple visit of the new year is known as what?
questions.f: Millions visit in the first three days, and many buy a paper fortune called omikuji.

questions.q: Japanese families eat long thin buckwheat noodles on New Year's Eve to wish for what?
questions.f: Toshikoshi soba means 'year-crossing noodles', and they are easy to bite, so the old year cuts off cleanly.

questions.q: At Mongolia's Tsagaan Sar, families serve a towering stack of what?
questions.f: Hundreds of buuz dumplings are folded in the days beforehand and frozen outdoors.

questions.q: For Nauryz, Kazakh families cook a soup called nauryz kozhe with how many ingredients?
questions.f: The seven ingredients stand for the seven days of the week and the seven ages of life.

questions.q: On the thirteenth day of Nowruz, Iranian families traditionally do what?
questions.f: On Sizdah Bedar the sprouted greens from the new-year table are thrown into running water.

questions.q: On the last Wednesday eve before Nowruz, Iranians celebrate by doing what?
questions.f: Chaharshanbe Suri means 'Red Wednesday', and jumpers chant a wish for health.

questions.q: On Shab-e Yalda, the longest night of the year, Iranian families eat which two red fruits?
questions.f: Red fruit stands for the returning sun, and families read poems by Hafez until late.

questions.q: In Greece, Clean Monday at the start of Lent is celebrated by doing what outdoors?
questions.f: Families picnic on flatbread and vegetables, and the sky fills with homemade kites.

questions.q: Israel's Purim street parade is known by which name?
questions.f: The name comes from a phrase about celebrating until you can hardly tell one thing from another.

questions.q: The Jewish festival of Lag BaOmer is celebrated with what?
questions.f: Children collect scrap wood for weeks, and families picnic beside the fires.

questions.q: In Turkey, Eid al-Fitr is popularly known as which feast?
questions.f: Seker Bayrami is named for the sweets children collect from neighbours' doors.

questions.q: Egypt's ancient spring festival Sham el-Nessim has a name meaning what?
questions.f: Families spend the whole day picnicking outdoors, the Monday after Coptic Easter.

questions.q: At the Hmong New Year, the ball-tossing game 'pov pob' is played mainly to do what?
questions.f: Players toss a cloth ball in two facing lines, and a dropped catch costs a small forfeit.

questions.q: During Cambodia's Pchum Ben, families rise before dawn to offer what at temples?
questions.f: The offerings are made for ancestors over fifteen days at the end of the rainy season.

questions.q: Assam's Bihu festival is celebrated how many times in a year?
questions.f: Rongali, Kongali and Bhogali Bihu mark sowing, tending and harvesting the rice crop.

questions.q: On Gudi Padwa, Maharashtrian families raise a decorated pole topped with what?
c: An upturned copper or silver pot
questions.f: The gudi is hung with neem leaves, mango leaves and a garland, then set at a window.

questions.q: During the monsoon festival of Teej, women traditionally enjoy what?
questions.f: Green clothes and bangles are worn for Teej, matching the freshly rain-washed fields.

questions.q: Rajasthan's Pushkar Fair is world-famous as a giant market for which animals?
questions.f: Thousands of camels arrive, decorated with pom-poms and shaved into patterns.

questions.q: The Rath Yatra festival in Puri involves pulling enormous wooden what?
questions.f: Each chariot is rebuilt from scratch every year and needs thousands of people to move it.

questions.q: At the Philippines' Sinulog and Ati-Atihan festivals, dancers honour an image known as what?
questions.f: The Santo Nino image was a gift brought to Cebu in 1521 and is the oldest Christian relic there.

questions.q: Simbang Gabi, the Filipino Christmas novena, consists of Masses held at what time?
questions.f: Nine consecutive dawn Masses lead up to Christmas, followed by rice cakes outside the church.

questions.q: At Myanmar's Thingyan new-year festival, what do people do?
questions.f: The water washes away the old year's bad luck, in the hottest month of the Burmese year.

questions.q: American Thanksgiving became a national holiday when which president proclaimed it in 1863?
questions.f: Lincoln set it on the last Thursday of November, and Congress fixed the fourth Thursday in 1941.

questions.q: Which dry chicken bone do people pull apart for a wish after Thanksgiving dinner?
questions.f: The wishbone is really the bird's furcula, which helps a flying bird's chest muscles work.

questions.q: America's Memorial Day was originally known by which name?
questions.f: The old name came from the custom of decorating graves with flowers each spring.

questions.q: International Workers' Day, celebrated with parades in many countries, falls on which date?
questions.f: The United States and Canada instead hold Labour Day in September.

questions.q: India's Republic Day parade in Delhi takes place on which date?
questions.f: Independence Day is 15 August, but Republic Day marks the constitution taking effect in 1950.

questions.q: Holi is celebrated on the full-moon night of the Hindu month of Phalguna.
questions.f: The bonfire comes on the full moon and the colour-throwing on the following day.

questions.q: The word 'Carnival' and the season of Lent are historically connected.
questions.f: Carnival was the last burst of feasting before the plain, meat-free weeks of Lent.

questions.q: Mongolia's new-year festival name 'Tsagaan Sar' means what?
questions.f: White stands for purity and for the dairy foods piled high on the holiday table.

questions.q: The word 'Pentecost' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: It falls fifty days after Easter, which is why the number is baked into the name.

questions.q: The harvest festival name 'Lammas' comes from words meaning what?
questions.f: A loaf baked from the first ripe wheat was brought to church on 1 August.

questions.q: In church calendars, the 'octave' of a feast means what?
questions.f: Latin 'octo' means eight, the same root as octopus and October.

questions.q: The word 'solstice', which fixes many midwinter festivals, literally means what?
questions.f: From Latin 'sol' and 'sistere'; the sun's rising point seems to pause before turning back.

questions.q: The word 'equinox', which sets the date of Nowruz and Easter, means what?
questions.f: From 'aequus', equal, and 'nox', night, when day and night are almost the same length.

questions.q: The month name 'January' honours a Roman god who was the god of what?
questions.f: Janus had two faces, one looking back at the old year and one forward to the new.

questions.q: The month name 'February' comes from a Roman festival of what?
questions.f: 'Februa' were cleansing rites held in the middle of the month.

questions.q: The word 'calendar' comes from the Roman 'kalends', which was what?
c: The first day of the month
questions.f: Debts were called in on the kalends, and 'calare' meant to call out or proclaim.

questions.q: The name 'December' shows that it was once which month of the Roman year?
questions.f: The old year began in March, which also explains September, October and November.

questions.q: The word 'tradition' comes from a Latin verb meaning what?
questions.f: A tradition is literally something handed across the generations.

questions.q: The word 'clan', used for extended families, comes from a Gaelic word meaning what?
questions.f: Gaelic 'clann' means children or offspring, so a clan is one big family of descendants.

questions.q: A ruling family that lasts for generations is a 'dynasty', from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: Greek 'dunastes' meant a lord or ruler, from 'dunamai', to be able.

questions.q: The word 'husband' originally meant what?
questions.f: From Old Norse for house-dweller, which is also why farming is called husbandry.

questions.q: The word 'matrimony' is built from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: From 'mater'; the parallel word 'patrimony' means what is inherited from a father.

questions.q: The word 'spouse' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: From 'sponsus'; the same root gives us 'sponsor' and 'respond'.

questions.q: Someone described as 'betrothed' has exchanged what?
questions.f: 'Be-' plus 'troth', an old form of 'truth', meaning a solemn promise.

questions.q: A bride's 'trousseau' takes its name from a French word meaning what?
questions.f: It was once the small bundle of linen and clothes a bride brought to her new home.

questions.q: The word 'progeny', meaning a person's children, contains a root meaning what?
c: To be born or brought forth
questions.f: The same root shows up in 'generation', 'genes' and 'genealogy'.

questions.q: 'Posterity' means what?
questions.f: From Latin 'posterus', coming after; speeches are often addressed 'to posterity'.

questions.q: In the old phrase 'kith and kin', what does 'kith' mean?
questions.f: 'Kith' is related to an old word for known, so the phrase means the known and the related.

questions.q: A word for members of a family group linked by descent, from Latin 'tribus', is what?
questions.f: Rome itself was traditionally divided into three tribus, which may be where the number hides.

questions.q: The word 'sorority' comes from a Latin word for what?
questions.f: 'Soror' means sister, and 'frater' gives us fraternity and fraternal twins.

questions.q: A 'septuagenarian' is a person celebrating birthdays in which decade?
questions.f: Octogenarian is eighties, nonagenarian is nineties, centenarian is a hundred and over.

questions.q: The word 'revel', meaning to make merry, comes from a Latin verb meaning what?
questions.f: Loud partying and rebellion looked similar enough to share a root.

questions.q: The word 'masquerade' traces back through Italian to an Arabic word for what?
questions.f: Arabic 'maskharah' meant a clown or a jest, which became 'maschera', a mask.

questions.q: An 'effigy', burned or paraded at some festivals, means what?
c: A likeness or model of someone
questions.f: From Latin 'effingere', to shape or form.

questions.q: The word 'pageant' comes from a Latin word that also gives us which everyday word?
questions.f: 'Pagina' meant a sheet or scene, and medieval pageants were played on movable stages.

questions.q: The word 'anthem' developed from 'antiphon', which described singing that is what?
questions.f: Two halves of a choir answered each other, from Greek 'anti', against, and 'phone', sound.

questions.q: The word 'sugar' can be traced back to an ancient Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Sharkara' described sugar's grainy look, and the word travelled through Persian and Arabic to Europe.

questions.q: The word 'barbecue', used for festival cookouts, comes from a Taino word for what?
c: A wooden framework over a fire
questions.f: Spanish explorers recorded 'barbacoa' in the Caribbean in the 1500s.

questions.q: The word 'potlatch', a great gift-giving feast of the Pacific Northwest, means what?
questions.f: At a potlatch a host's status came from how much they gave away, not what they kept.

questions.q: 'Fraternal twins' takes its name from a Latin word for brother.
questions.f: From 'frater'; the term is used for non-identical twins of any gender.

questions.q: A poet lost in a river, rice parcels dropped into the water to feed him, and crews paddling to a drumbeat all belong to which festival?
questions.f: Legend says villagers raced boats to save the poet Qu Yuan and threw zongzi to protect his body.

questions.q: A weaver girl, a cowherd, and two stars on opposite banks of the Milky Way are honoured at which festival?
questions.f: The lovers are the stars Vega and Altair, allowed to meet only on the seventh night of the seventh month.

questions.q: Which Indian festival's five days run from Dhanteras through Lakshmi Puja to Bhai Dooj?
questions.f: Each day has its own focus, from buying metal on Dhanteras to honouring brothers on the last day.

questions.q: Ganesh Chaturthi was transformed from a home ritual into a huge public festival in the 1890s by whom?
questions.f: Tilak saw public pandals as a way to bring people together across caste lines.

questions.q: In 1905, which writer promoted Raksha Bandhan as a way to unite a divided Bengal?
questions.f: Tagore had neighbours tie rakhis on each other as a public gesture of solidarity.

questions.q: Vesak is remarkable because it marks how many events in the Buddha's life on one day?
questions.f: Tradition holds that his birth, his enlightenment and his passing all fell on the same full-moon day.

questions.q: The Chinese zodiac's twelve animals combine with five elements to make a repeating cycle of how many years?
questions.f: The sexagenary cycle means a 'wood dragon' or 'metal rat' year returns only once in sixty years.

questions.q: At the Mid-Autumn Festival, which figure is said to live on the moon with a jade rabbit?
questions.f: China's lunar missions are named Chang'e, and one rover was called Yutu, 'jade rabbit'.

questions.q: Makar Sankranti marks the sun's entry into which zodiac sign?
questions.f: 'Makara' is Capricorn, and the festival is one of the few Hindu dates fixed by the solar calendar.

questions.q: Onam celebrates the yearly homecoming of which legendary king?
questions.f: Keralans say the good king Mahabali visits to check that his people are still happy.

questions.q: The Tamil harvest festival Pongal lasts four days, beginning with which one?
questions.f: Bhogi is for clearing out the old, Mattu Pongal honours cattle and Kaanum Pongal is for outings.

questions.q: How often does the full Kumbh Mela return to each of its four host cities?
questions.f: A half-size Ardh Kumbh comes at the six-year midpoint, still drawing tens of millions.

questions.q: Sukkot's 'four species' include a palm frond, myrtle, willow and which citrus fruit?
questions.f: A perfect etrog must have unblemished skin and its little stem tip intact.

questions.q: At the Passover seder, the youngest child traditionally recites what?
questions.f: The Ma Nishtana asks why this night is different from all other nights.

questions.q: The Hanukkah story centres on a revolt led by which family?
questions.f: Judah Maccabee's name is often explained as meaning 'the hammer'.

questions.q: On Ash Wednesday, the ashes marked on foreheads traditionally come from what?
c: Burnt palms from the previous Palm Sunday
questions.f: Nothing is wasted: last year's palms are saved, dried and burned for this year's ashes.

questions.q: Easter's date is set as the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after what?
questions.f: The calculation is called the computus, and it can move Easter across five weeks of the calendar.

questions.q: Orthodox Easter often falls later than Western Easter because those churches use which calendar?
questions.f: The Julian calendar now runs thirteen days behind the Gregorian one used in the West.

questions.q: The Easter Bunny came to America through the traditions of which settlers?
questions.f: The 'Osterhase' left eggs in nests of grass, the ancestor of today's Easter basket.

questions.q: Ukrainian Easter eggs called pysanky are decorated using which technique?
questions.f: A stylus called a kistka draws hot beeswax lines that stop the dye reaching the shell.

questions.q: The first commercial Christmas card, from 1843, was commissioned by which British figure?
questions.f: Cole also helped found the museum we now call the V and A.

questions.q: The printed Advent calendar with little doors was popularised in the early 1900s in which country?
questions.f: Gerhard Lang, who remembered his mother's cardboard version, began printing them around 1908.

questions.q: In Sweden, the town of Gavle builds a giant Christmas figure of which animal?
questions.f: The straw Yule goat has become famous partly because it so often fails to survive December.

questions.q: In 1600s England and Boston, Christmas celebrations were at times what?
questions.f: Puritans objected to the feasting, and Boston's ban lasted from 1659 to 1681.

questions.q: Tchaikovsky's Christmas ballet 'The Nutcracker' introduced audiences to which then-new instrument?
questions.f: Its bell-like keyboard sound became the voice of the Sugar Plum Fairy.

questions.q: Which tall, domed sweet bread studded with candied fruit is the Christmas cake of Milan?
questions.f: Panettone dough is hung upside down to cool so its airy structure does not collapse.

questions.q: Chaucer's poem 'The Parliament of Fowls' gave us the first clear link between 14 February and what?
questions.f: Written around 1382, it is the earliest known connection of St Valentine's Day with romance.

questions.q: Esther Howland earned the nickname 'Mother of the American Valentine' by doing what?
questions.f: She built a successful business in Worcester, Massachusetts, from the 1840s.

questions.q: The BBC's famous 1957 April Fools' hoax featured a harvest of what?
questions.f: So many viewers asked how to grow their own that the BBC advised placing a sprig in tomato sauce.

questions.q: Until 1752, the legal new year in England and its colonies began on which date?
questions.f: That is why some old documents write dates like 'February 1721/22'.

questions.q: The Times Square New Year's ball drop began in 1907 as a replacement for what?
questions.f: Fireworks had been banned after hot ash rained onto the streets.

questions.q: The Kwanzaa principle 'Umoja' stands for which of the seven ideas?
questions.f: The seven principles are called the Nguzo Saba, and one is highlighted on each day.

questions.q: Juneteenth commemorates the reading in Galveston of which announcement?
questions.f: It was read on 19 June 1865, two and a half years after the Proclamation was signed.

questions.q: Red foods such as strawberry soda and red velvet cake at Juneteenth are often said to stand for what?
questions.f: Hibiscus and kola, both red drink plants from West Africa, are part of the story.

questions.q: Which Wampanoag man, who spoke English, is linked to the 1621 harvest feast in Plymouth?
questions.f: Tisquantum had learned English after being taken to Europe years earlier.

questions.q: The shopping term 'Black Friday' is generally traced to 1950s police in which city?
questions.f: Officers used it for the traffic chaos before the annual Army-Navy football game.

questions.q: Until 1932, the giant balloons at Macy's Thanksgiving parade ended the day how?
c: Released into the sky with a reward label
questions.f: Finders who mailed a balloon back received a gift from the store.

questions.q: Punxsutawney's Groundhog Day ceremony has been held since which decade?
questions.f: The first official Punxsutawney Phil event is dated to 1887.

questions.q: Britain's Mothering Sunday originally involved returning to what?
questions.f: Servants were given the day off to travel home, often picking flowers on the way.

questions.q: The wedding phrase 'tie the knot' is generally traced to which old custom?
questions.f: In handfasting the couple's hands are bound together with ribbon or cloth.

questions.q: At Chinese weddings, which character is displayed everywhere as a lucky symbol?
questions.f: The 'double happiness' character is literally the word for joy written twice, side by side.

questions.q: At a Greek Orthodox wedding, the couple wear two crowns joined by what?
questions.f: The stefana are then kept at home, often framed, for the rest of the couple's life.

questions.q: A 40th wedding anniversary is traditionally linked to which gemstone?
questions.f: Sapphire is 45, gold is 50 and diamond is 60.

questions.q: In a Chinese 'zhuazhou' ceremony, a one-year-old is invited to do what?
c: Grab one of many objects laid out
questions.f: The chosen object is a playful hint at the child's future, much like the Korean doljabi.

questions.q: At an Aqiqah celebration, a baby's shaved hair is traditionally weighed against what?
c: Silver, which is then given to charity
questions.f: The custom joins a family's private joy with a public act of generosity.

questions.q: 'First cousin once removed' describes what relationship?
questions.f: 'Removed' counts generations; 'second cousin' means you share great-grandparents instead.

questions.q: A 'nuclear family' is best described as what?
c: Any family living in a city
A family with only one child
questions.f: The phrase became common in the 1900s, in contrast to the wider extended family.

questions.q: In Icelandic naming, a girl whose father is named Jon would have which surname?
questions.f: Iceland uses patronymics, so members of one family often have different last names.

questions.q: The word 'juggernaut' entered English from the name of which festival deity?
questions.f: European travellers saw the vast Rath Yatra chariots and the word came to mean an unstoppable force.

questions.q: The Spanish festival name 'posada' means what?
questions.f: Las Posadas re-enacts a search for lodging, going house to house singing at each door.

questions.q: The word 'nuptial', meaning to do with weddings, comes from a Latin verb meaning what?
questions.f: Roman brides wore a flame-coloured veil, and 'nubere' meant to take the veil for marriage.

questions.q: In the word 'wedlock', the ending has nothing to do with locks. What did it mean?
questions.f: Old English '-lac' formed nouns of activity, so wedlock is simply the act of pledging.

questions.q: The word 'gaudy', now meaning showily bright, comes from a Latin verb meaning what?
questions.f: The same root gives Gaudete Sunday its name and, some say, the word for a college feast.

questions.q: Someone with a 'jovial' festival mood is named after which Roman god?
questions.f: Astrologers thought people born under Jupiter, or Jove, were cheerful and generous.

questions.q: The word 'souvenir', brought home from a festival, means what in French?
questions.f: From Latin 'subvenire', to come up into the mind, so a souvenir is a memory-trigger.

questions.q: The 'maundy' in Maundy Thursday comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Mandatum novum', a new commandment, opens the ceremony of that evening.

questions.q: Lent's old Latin name 'Quadragesima' refers to which number?
questions.f: The forty days recall a forty-day fast, and the Spanish 'cuaresma' still shows the number.

questions.q: The word 'gingerbread' ends in 'bread' only because English speakers reshaped which earlier word?
questions.f: The Old French word meant preserved ginger; the '-bread' ending was a helpful mishearing.

questions.q: The word 'marigold', the flower of Day of the Dead altars, is generally explained as meaning what?
questions.f: The Aztec name for the same flower, cempasuchil, means something like 'twenty flower'.

questions.q: The campfire treat 's'mores' is a squashed form of which phrase?
questions.f: The first printed recipe, in a 1927 Girl Scout handbook, called them 'some mores'.

questions.q: The dessert 'pavlova' is named after a famous what?
questions.f: Anna Pavlova toured Australia and New Zealand in the 1920s, and both claim the meringue.

questions.q: Battenberg cake is said to have been created to celebrate what?
questions.f: It honoured the 1884 marriage of a granddaughter of Queen Victoria to Prince Louis of Battenberg.

questions.q: The word 'sandwich', now a picnic staple, comes from the title of what?
questions.f: The Earl of Sandwich reputedly asked for meat between bread so he need not leave the card table.

questions.q: The word 'avuncular' describes behaviour like that of a what?
questions.f: Latin 'avunculus' meant 'little grandfather', originally a mother's brother.

questions.q: 'Consanguinity' between family members refers to what?
questions.f: Relations by marriage are instead called 'affinity', from a word meaning bordering on.

questions.q: 'Primogeniture' is the custom of passing inheritance to whom?
questions.f: From Latin 'primus', first, and 'genitus', born.

questions.q: A family described as 'matrilineal' traces descent through whom?
questions.f: The Minangkabau of Indonesia form one of the largest matrilineal societies in the world.

questions.q: The Book of Esther, read at Purim, never once mentions God by name.
questions.f: It is the only book of the Hebrew Bible with that distinction, which scholars have long debated.

questions.q: The song 'Happy Birthday to You' was under copyright claim until a court settlement in the 2010s.
questions.f: A 2016 settlement finally placed the world's most-sung song firmly in the public domain.

questions.q: An indoor Caribbean party organised by Claudia Jones in 1959 and a neighbourhood fair in 1966 grew into which festival?
questions.f: Rhaune Laslett's 1966 street fair merged with the Caribbean celebrations to create Europe's biggest street carnival.

questions.q: In Zurich's Sechselauten festival, how quickly a snowman figure's head explodes is said to predict what?
c: The quality of the coming summer
The winner of a boat race
The date of the first snow
questions.f: The straw Booegg is packed with firecrackers; a quick bang means a fine warm summer.

questions.q: At Belgium's Binche Carnival, the costumed Gilles wear hats decorated with what?
questions.f: The Gilles also toss oranges into the crowd, and catching one is considered lucky.

questions.q: Catalonia's human tower festivals end when who climbs to the very top?
c: A small child called the enxaneta
questions.f: The enxaneta raises a hand with four fingers up, standing for the stripes of the Catalan flag.

questions.q: In Spain's Semana Santa processions, the bearers who carry the heavy floats are called what?
questions.f: They walk in step under the float, guided by a knock from the leader outside.

questions.q: During Valencia's Las Fallas, the daytime event called the mascleta is a display of what?
questions.f: A mascleta is judged by rhythm and the pressure you feel in your chest, not by colour.

questions.q: Spain's day for playing tricks, its version of April Fools' Day, falls on which date?
questions.f: It is called the Day of the Holy Innocents, and newspapers print joke stories.

questions.q: At Porto's Festa de Sao Joao in Portugal, revellers famously bop each other with what?
questions.f: Leeks were used in the old days, and the squeaky plastic hammer is the modern replacement.

questions.q: When the French galette des rois is shared, who traditionally hides under the table?
c: The youngest child, to call out who gets each slice
questions.f: Hiding means nobody can be accused of steering the lucky charm to a favourite.

questions.q: On France's Chandeleur, a crepe is flipped while the cook holds what?
questions.f: Landing the crepe cleanly while holding a coin is supposed to bring a prosperous year.

questions.q: France's Fete de la Musique, when anyone may play in the street, began in which decade?
questions.f: Launched in 1982, it now takes place in over a hundred countries on the June solstice.

questions.q: Denmark's Fastelavn includes children in costume striking a barrel to release what?
questions.f: The child who breaks it open is crowned 'cat king', a title from a much older version of the game.

questions.q: In Poland, Easter Monday is famous for a custom involving what?
questions.f: Smigus-Dyngus turns whole streets into a friendly water fight.

questions.q: Norway's Constitution Day on 17 May is celebrated with parades led by whom?
questions.f: Children march with flags and bands, and eat a famously large number of hot dogs and ice creams.

questions.q: In Finland, 1 May celebrations involve students wearing what?
questions.f: On Vappu Eve, statues in Helsinki are given caps of their own.

questions.q: Wales' Mari Lwyd midwinter custom involves a decorated horse figure doing what at doors?
c: Trading rhyming challenges to be let in
questions.f: The household must answer each verse in rhyme, and if they run out, the Mari Lwyd comes in for food.

questions.q: Philadelphia's Mummers Parade takes place on which day?
questions.f: The name comes from 'mum', meaning silent, because mummers once performed in disguise without speaking.

questions.q: Padstow's May Day 'Obby Oss' celebration in Cornwall features what?
c: A hooped horse figure danced through the streets
questions.f: Two rival Osses, Red and Blue, parade all day to their own drumbeats.

questions.q: Staffordshire's Abbots Bromley Horn Dance uses reindeer antlers that have been dated to roughly when?
questions.f: Radiocarbon dating placed the antlers in the 11th century, though reindeer had long vanished from Britain.

questions.q: Harbin's famous winter festival builds palaces and slides from ice cut where?
questions.f: Blocks are sawn from the frozen river and lit from within by coloured lights.

questions.q: In Lopburi, Thailand, an unusual annual banquet is laid out for which guests?
questions.f: Tonnes of fruit are stacked into pyramids for the town's macaques at the Monkey Buffet Festival.

questions.q: Which country hosts the World Wife Carrying Championships each July?
questions.f: The winner's prize is traditionally the carried partner's weight in beverages, and the course has a water hazard.

questions.q: Albuquerque's October fiesta is the world's largest gathering of what?
questions.f: Hundreds launch together in a 'mass ascension', helped by a wind pattern called the Albuquerque Box.

questions.q: The formal White House ceremony of pardoning a Thanksgiving turkey began under which president?
questions.f: Earlier presidents received turkeys as gifts, but the official pardon dates from 1989.

questions.q: Venice's Carnival was suppressed for many years and only fully revived in which decade?
questions.f: Napoleon's rule ended the old Carnival in 1797, and the city revived it in 1979.

questions.q: Siena's twice-yearly Palio horse race between city districts lasts roughly how long?
questions.f: Each contrada, or district, has its own colours, museum and even its own fountain.

questions.q: Italy's mid-August holiday 'Ferragosto' takes its name from a phrase meaning what?
questions.f: Emperor Augustus declared a rest period in 18 BC, and Italy still empties its cities in mid-August.

questions.q: In Greece and Hungary, many people celebrate 'name days'. What are these?
c: The feast day of the saint they are named after
The day their name was registered
questions.f: In some families the name day is celebrated more warmly than the birthday itself.

questions.q: Easter Island got its European name because a Dutch expedition arrived there on what?
questions.f: Jacob Roggeveen named it Paasch-Eyland; the Rapa Nui people call the island Rapa Nui.

questions.q: Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean was named for what reason?
c: A ship sighted it on Christmas Day
It is shaped like a tree
Its first settlers arrived in December
questions.f: An East India Company captain named it on 25 December 1643.

questions.q: The South African region Natal was named because Vasco da Gama's fleet passed it on which day?
questions.f: 'Natal' means birth, from the same root as 'nativity' and 'Navidad'.

questions.q: The words Paques, Pascua and Pasqua all name which festival?
questions.f: They come from Hebrew 'Pesach', Passover, which is why a paschal lamb belongs to both festivals.

questions.q: 'Stir-up Sunday', when British families traditionally make the Christmas pudding, is named after what?
c: The opening words of a church prayer
A market where spices were sold
questions.f: The prayer for that Sunday begins 'Stir up, we beseech thee', and cooks took the hint.

questions.q: The word 'guy', now meaning any person, began as a reference to whom?
questions.f: Effigies of Fawkes were called 'guys', then the word spread to shabby figures and finally to everyone.

questions.q: The drink name 'punch', served at parties, is thought to come from a word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Panch' referred to the five ingredients in the original Indian recipe: spirit, water, lemon, sugar and spice.

questions.q: In 'eggnog', what did the old word 'nog' originally mean?
questions.f: East Anglian 'nog' was a strong beer, which was the drink's earliest base.

questions.q: The words 'sherbet' and 'sorbet' both trace back to an Arabic word meaning what?
questions.f: 'Sharbat' was a cool sweetened drink, and Persian and Turkish carried the word into Europe.

questions.q: The Indian sweet name 'gulab jamun' literally refers to which two things?
questions.f: 'Gulab' is rose water and 'jamun' is a dark purple fruit the dumplings resemble.

questions.q: The name of the Indian sweet 'barfi' comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: Persian 'barf' means snow, describing the sweet's pale, dense look.

questions.q: Which word shares its Latin root with 'candle'?
questions.f: Latin 'candere', to shine or glow white, also hides inside 'incandescent'.

questions.q: A standing 'ovation' takes its name from a Latin verb meaning what?
questions.f: 'Ovare' meant to exult; in Rome an ovation was also a lesser form of a triumph parade.

questions.q: The '-cade' in 'motorcade' was borrowed from 'cavalcade', which originally involved what?
questions.f: Italian 'cavallo' means horse, so a cavalcade was a mounted procession.

questions.q: A 'serenade' outside someone's window is named from a word connected to what?
questions.f: Italian 'sera' means evening; a dawn version is called an aubade.

questions.q: Something described as 'auspicious' for a festival date originally involved what?
questions.f: Roman augurs studied birds, from 'avis' plus 'specere', to look.

questions.q: The word 'hilarious' comes from a Latin word that meant what?
questions.f: Latin 'hilaris' meant merry, and the Romans even had a spring festival called the Hilaria.

questions.q: A 'sabbatical' year off work takes its name from which festival idea?
questions.f: Ancient law set aside every seventh year as a sabbatical year for the land to rest.

questions.q: The word 'vacation' comes from a Latin verb meaning what?
questions.f: From 'vacare'; the same root gives 'vacant' and 'vacuum'.

questions.q: A 'cortege', the formal procession at some ceremonies, comes from a word connected to what?
questions.f: Italian 'corteggio' meant a courtly retinue, from the same root as 'courtesy'.

questions.q: The 'Mari' processions, morris dancing and mummers' plays are all examples of what kind of custom?
c: Folk performance passed on by tradition
questions.f: Folklorists call these 'calendar customs', tied to fixed dates in the farming year.

questions.q: The dance name 'morris' is generally thought to be a form of which word?
questions.f: Dancers once blackened or painted their faces as part of a disguise, which may explain the name.

questions.q: The word 'krewe', used for Mardi Gras clubs, is a deliberately old-fashioned spelling of which word?
questions.f: The Mistick Krewe of Comus chose the antique spelling in 1857 and it stuck.

questions.q: The word 'Hijri', naming the Islamic calendar's era, refers to what?
questions.f: The calendar counts from the journey from Mecca to Medina in 622.

questions.q: The Sikh term 'gurpurab' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: 'Purab' means a festival or holy day, so each guru's anniversary is a gurpurab.

questions.q: A 'Nagar Kirtan' procession at Sikh festivals is literally what?
questions.f: Hymns are sung through the streets, often with sweets and water offered to everyone watching.

questions.q: The word 'mangalsutra', worn by many married Hindu women, means what?
questions.f: 'Mangal' means auspicious and 'sutra' means thread, the same word behind 'suture'.

questions.q: A 'sangeet' evening before a wedding takes its name from a word meaning what?
questions.f: Families rehearse dances for weeks, and both sides often compete for the best performance.

questions.q: The word 'creche', the nativity scene set up at Christmas, originally meant what?
questions.f: St Francis of Assisi is credited with staging the first live nativity scene in 1223.

questions.q: 'Auld Lang Syne' translates most closely as what?
questions.f: It means something like 'days long past', which is why it suits the turn of the year.

questions.q: The name 'Hogmanay' is generally thought to come from an old French word for what?
questions.f: Forms like 'aguillanneuf' meant a new-year gift or the shout used when asking for one.

questions.q: Which word for a festival day comes from the Latin 'feria', a holiday?
questions.f: Spanish 'feria' still means both a fair and a public holiday.

questions.q: 'Corpus Christi' processions in Spain and Italy are famous for streets covered in what?
questions.f: In Genzano, Italy, the flower carpet stretches for hundreds of metres up a sloping street.

questions.q: The traditional English quarter day of 25 March is called what?
questions.f: Lady Day was also the old start of the legal year, which is why the tax year still begins in early April.

questions.q: On Ireland's Wren Day, 26 December, groups called wrenboys go from house to house doing what?
c: Playing music and collecting for a party
questions.f: They wear straw hats and masks, and the money collected pays for a village dance.

questions.q: A 'harvest home' supper marked the end of what?
c: Bringing in the last of the crop
questions.f: The last sheaf was often plaited into a corn dolly and kept until spring sowing.

questions.q: The word 'carnival' is related to 'carnivore'.
questions.f: Both contain Latin 'carnis', flesh or meat; Carnival was the farewell to meat before Lent.

questions.q: Ash Wednesday and Easter Sunday are always exactly forty days apart.
questions.f: Lent's forty days skip the Sundays, so the actual gap is forty-six days.

questions.q: The Mardi Gras throw known as a 'doubloon' is a stamped aluminium coin.
questions.f: Krewes began minting them in 1960, and collectors now trade rare designs.

questions.q: Trinidad's steelpan was developed from discarded oil drums in the 20th century.
questions.f: Tuners hammer the drum head into note-shaped facets, each one carefully sunk and shaped.

questions.q: A midwinter Roman feast where masters served their servants, a mock king chosen by lot, and gifts of small wax figures describe which festival?
questions.f: Saturnalia's role-reversal and gift-giving echo through later midwinter customs across Europe.

questions.q: A Spokane woman moved by a 1909 sermon, a widowed veteran raising six children, and official recognition only in 1972 lie behind which holiday?
questions.f: Sonora Smart Dodd campaigned for decades before President Nixon signed it into law.

questions.q: A village organ out of action, a priest's 1816 poem, and a schoolteacher named Franz Gruber produced which carol?
questions.f: It was sung with guitar in Oberndorf on Christmas Eve 1818 and is now UNESCO-listed heritage.

questions.q: A 1908 newspaper column, a coin slipped under a pillow, and a Spanish rival who is a mouse all point to which figure?
questions.f: An early mention appeared in the Chicago Tribune in 1908, decades after Spain's Ratoncito Perez.

questions.q: A professor's 1966 creation, a woven mat called an mkeka, and seven principles in Swahili describe which celebration?
questions.f: Maulana Karenga drew on African first-fruits harvest festivals when he designed it.

questions.q: On a Passover seder plate, the sweet brown paste called charoset represents what?
questions.f: It is usually made from apples, nuts and spices, and its name comes from a word for clay.

questions.q: Before Passover, some families search the house for crumbs of leaven using what?
questions.f: Any chametz found is burned the next morning, and the search is often a game for children.

questions.q: At the seder table, the extra cup of wine that is poured but not drunk is set aside for whom?
questions.f: Some families now add a cup of water for Miriam alongside Elijah's cup.

questions.q: On Shemini Atzeret, which special prayer is traditionally added to the service?
c: A prayer for the harvest moon
questions.f: The prayer comes just as Israel's rainy season should be starting.

questions.q: The Christingle, made for Advent services, is built around which fruit?
questions.f: A candle stands in the orange, with a red ribbon around it and sweets on four cocktail sticks.

questions.q: Christmas crackers were invented in the 1840s by which London tradesman?
questions.f: He first wrapped sweets in twists of paper, then added the bang after watching a fire crackle.

questions.q: The Christmas Eve service of 'Nine Lessons and Carols' is broadcast from which chapel?
questions.f: The Cambridge version dates from 1918 and always opens with a solo treble singing 'Once in Royal David's City'.

questions.q: A silver coin is traditionally hidden in which British festive dish?
questions.f: A sixpence was the usual coin, and finding it was supposed to bring a year of wealth.

questions.q: Britain's simnel cake, eaten at Easter, is decorated with how many marzipan balls?
questions.f: Eleven stand for the apostles without Judas; a twelfth is sometimes added for Jesus.

questions.q: Ashbourne's Shrovetide football match is played between goals set how far apart?
questions.f: Whole streets join in over two days, and shopkeepers board up their windows.

questions.q: The Lenten pretzel's twisted shape is traditionally said to represent what?
questions.f: Latin 'bracellus' means little arms, and pretzels were made with only flour, water and salt for Lent.

questions.q: At the British Royal Maundy ceremony, how many recipients receive the coins?
c: As many people as the monarch's years of age
Forty, for the days of Lent
questions.f: Two sets of purses are given, and the number of pence in one matches the sovereign's age.

questions.q: The White House Easter Egg Roll has been held on the South Lawn since which decade?
questions.f: It moved there in 1878 after Congress banned egg rolling on the Capitol grounds.

questions.q: On Epiphany, some families chalk letters and the year above a doorway. What do the letters traditionally stand for?
c: The names of the three kings
A Latin blessing for the house
questions.f: C, M and B stand for Caspar, Melchior and Balthazar, and also for a Latin blessing phrase.

questions.q: The seven points of a traditional Las Posadas pinata stand for what?
questions.f: Blindfolded, the hitter is meant to be striking out at temptation, with sweets as the reward.

questions.q: On Martinmas, 11 November, which roast bird is traditional in Germany and Scandinavia?
questions.f: A legend says geese gave St Martin away by honking when he tried to hide from being made bishop.

questions.q: During the Christmas Truce of 1914, soldiers famously did what between the trenches?
questions.f: Letters home described carols answered across no-man's-land and kickabouts in the frozen mud.

questions.q: The Rockefeller Center Christmas tree tradition began in 1931 with a tree put up by whom?
questions.f: Workers building the complex decorated a small tree with tin cans and paper garlands.

questions.q: In Charles Dickens' 'A Christmas Carol', the Cratchit family's dinner is upgraded from a goose to what?
questions.f: The book's popularity in 1843 helped make the turkey the British Christmas centrepiece.

questions.q: During the Hajj, pilgrims circle the Kaaba how many times?
questions.f: The circling is called tawaf, always performed anticlockwise.

questions.q: The extra night prayers offered during Ramadan are known as what?
questions.f: Over the month, many mosques recite the whole Quran across these nightly prayers.

questions.q: The word 'Eid al-Fitr' names the festival of what?
questions.f: 'Fitr' shares its root with 'iftar', the meal that breaks each day's fast.

questions.q: The Ramadan pre-dawn meal 'suhoor' takes its name from a word meaning what?
questions.f: Its partner 'iftar' comes from a root meaning to break something open.

questions.q: The Palm Sunday shout 'Hosanna' originally meant what?
questions.f: It began as a Hebrew plea for rescue and became a cry of celebration instead.

questions.q: The word 'hallelujah', sung at many festivals, means what?
questions.f: 'Amen', by contrast, means something close to 'so be it' or 'truly'.

questions.q: The name 'Christingle' is generally explained as meaning what?
questions.f: The custom began among Moravian Christians in 1747, when children were given lighted candles.

questions.q: The word 'biscuit', a staple of festival tea tables, literally means what?
questions.f: From French 'bis' and 'cuit', because biscuits were baked again to dry them for storage.

questions.q: Which word shares a root with 'confetti' and 'confection'?
questions.f: All come from Latin 'conficere', to put together; a comfit is a sugar-coated seed or nut.

questions.q: The word 'currant', found in festive cakes, comes from the name of which place?
questions.f: 'Raisins of Corauntz' were dried grapes shipped from the Greek city of Corinth.

questions.q: Traditional 'plum pudding' contains no plums because 'plum' once meant what?
questions.f: The same old sense survives in 'sugarplum', which was a sweet, not a fruit.

questions.q: The word 'spice' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Latin 'species' meant a type of merchandise, and spices were the most valuable type of all.

questions.q: The spice 'clove', used in festive baking and pomanders, is named from a word for what?
questions.f: Latin 'clavus' means nail, which is exactly what a dried clove looks like.

questions.q: The word 'nutmeg' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: From Old French 'nois muguede', musk-scented nut.

questions.q: The word 'canape', passed round at parties, is the same word as which piece of furniture?
questions.f: French 'canape' means couch, because the topping sits on its little bed of bread.

questions.q: The phrase 'hors d'oeuvre' literally means what?
questions.f: They sit outside the main sequence of the meal, like an architect's outbuilding.

questions.q: On a French festival menu, the 'entree' originally referred to which course?
questions.f: American usage moved it to the main course, which still confuses travellers.

questions.q: The dessert name 'trifle' comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: Early trifles were simply flavoured cream, before jelly, sponge and custard arrived.

questions.q: The word 'nougat', sold at fairs and Christmas markets, comes from a Latin word for what?
questions.f: From 'nux'; Provencal 'nougat' is still made with almonds and honey for the thirteen desserts.

questions.q: The word 'custard' is related to which other word?
questions.f: A medieval 'crustade' was a pie with a crust, filled with the egg mixture we now eat alone.

questions.q: An 'eponym' is what?
c: A person a thing is named after
questions.f: Poinsettia, sandwich and pavlova are all eponyms, named from real people.

questions.q: If someone is your 'namesake', what is true?
c: They were born on your birthday
They are named in your family tree only
questions.f: Children are often given a grandparent's name, making them that grandparent's namesake.

questions.q: A 'scion' of an old family originally meant what in gardening?
c: A shoot or twig for grafting
questions.f: The image is of a living shoot carrying the family's line onward.

questions.q: Marriage 'banns', read out in church, take their name from a word meaning what?
questions.f: The same root lies behind 'abandon' and 'banish', all involving a public proclamation.

questions.q: The word 'elope' comes from an old Dutch verb meaning what?
questions.f: 'Ontlopen' meant to run off, which is exactly what an eloping couple does.

questions.q: A 'legacy' left to descendants takes its name from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: The same root gives 'legate' and 'delegate', people appointed to act for others.

questions.q: To 'christen' a baby or a ship literally means what?
questions.f: That is why ship launches are still called christenings, complete with a bottle.

questions.q: A godparent's formal title at a baptism is what?
questions.f: 'Sponsor' comes from the same Latin root as 'spouse', meaning one who solemnly promises.

questions.q: The Hindu wedding ritual 'kanyadaan' involves what?
c: The parents formally giving the bride's hand
questions.f: Modern couples sometimes rework or skip the ritual, preferring shared vows.

questions.q: Which festival meal is traditionally eaten by Italian-American families on Christmas Eve?
c: The Feast of the Seven Fishes
questions.f: It grew from the Catholic custom of avoiding meat on the eve of a feast day.

questions.q: In Ukraine, a spider's web found on a Christmas tree is considered what?
c: A sign of an early spring
questions.f: A folk tale about a poor family's tree spun with silver webs is why Ukrainians hang spider ornaments.

questions.q: Which vegetable's carving competitions are the centrepiece of Ireland's older Halloween customs?
questions.f: Irish and Scottish emigrants found American pumpkins far easier to hollow out.

questions.q: In Japan, Setsubun's lucky sushi roll 'ehomaki' must be eaten how?
c: Whole, facing a lucky direction, in silence
questions.f: The lucky direction changes each year according to the zodiac.

questions.q: On Setsubun, people traditionally eat how many roasted soybeans?
c: One for each year of their age
questions.f: Some add one extra bean for the year ahead, which makes for a crunchy afternoon.

questions.q: Japan's Coming of Age Day is held on which day?
questions.f: Young women often wear a furisode, a kimono with long swinging sleeves.

questions.q: According to Japanese superstition, leaving the Hinamatsuri dolls out too long means what?
c: The family must buy new ones
questions.f: Families pack them away within a day or two, just in case.

questions.q: Mardi Gras and Carnival end on the same day each year.
questions.f: Both finish on Shrove Tuesday, the day before Ash Wednesday begins Lent.

questions.q: The Christmas tree custom reached Britain before it reached Germany.
questions.f: Decorated indoor trees were a German custom for centuries before they became fashionable in Britain.

questions.q: The word 'Sukkot' and the word 'sukkah' come from the same root.
questions.f: Sukkot is simply the plural of sukkah, so the name means 'booths'.

questions.q: A hood lost to the wind by a medieval lady, thirteen officials called Boggins, and a leather tube heaved by a crowd towards one of four pubs point to which custom?
questions.f: Lincolnshire's Haxey Hood is played every 6 January, and the winning pub keeps the hood behind the bar for a year.

questions.q: A tar-filled half-barrel carried blazing round a Moray fishing town, a date set by the old calendar, and embers taken home for luck describe which event?
questions.f: Burghead marks its new year on 11 January, the date that 1752's calendar reform took away.

questions.q: Uppies and Doonies, a ball thrown from the Mercat Cross, and a scrum that sometimes ends in the harbour belong to which game?
c: The Hurling of the Silver Ball
questions.f: Orkney plays the Ba' on Christmas Day and New Year's Day, and a match can last for hours.

questions.q: A Welsh valley that quietly ignored the calendar reform of 1752 still greets its new year on 13 January. What is the celebration called?
questions.f: The Gwaun Valley near Fishguard kept the old date, and children still call door to door for calennig.

questions.q: Children swinging paper balls on string, three circuits of a parish church, and a bell rung at six on 1 March point to which Scottish custom?
questions.f: Lanark's children race round St Nicholas Church, and coins are scattered for them afterwards.

questions.q: A man covered head to foot in thousands of sticky burdock burrs, walking miles in near silence with two attendants, appears at which festival?
questions.f: The Burry Man's suit takes hours to assemble, and he leans on two staves because he can barely bend.

questions.q: A man sewn entirely into a suit of straw, led through a Cambridgeshire town in January and stripped for a bonfire the next day, belongs to which festival?
questions.f: The custom was revived in 1980 after being stopped by police about a century earlier.

questions.q: Wooden discs strapped to hands, waist and knees, clapped in rhythm by dancers crossing a Lancashire town each Easter Saturday, identify which troupe?
questions.f: The Bacup 'Nutters' dance the whole length of the town, from boundary to boundary.

questions.q: Flower petals, seeds and bark pressed into panels of wet clay to make pictures beside village springs is the art of which Derbyshire custom?
questions.f: Tissington's wells have been dressed since at least the 18th century, and each panel takes a week.

questions.q: Tutti-men with flower-topped poles, an official called the Orange Scrambler, and a court held on the second Tuesday after Easter belong to which festival?
questions.f: Hocktide is one of the last surviving manorial courts still doing real business in England.

questions.q: A royal charter of 1284, birds driven to market from the fens, and a huge October funfair on Nottingham's Forest Recreation Ground name which event?
questions.f: Thousands of geese really were walked to Nottingham for the fair, which is over 700 years old.

questions.q: A charter of 1685, horses washed in the River Eden, and Europe's largest yearly gathering of Gypsy and Traveller families identify which fair?
questions.f: Appleby's fair fills a Cumbrian town each June, and the horse-washing in the river is its best-known scene.

questions.q: A mountain goat hoisted onto a high stand and crowned by a schoolgirl queen for three August days names which Irish fair?
questions.f: Killorglin's King Puck is returned to the hills afterwards, and the fair claims roots four centuries deep.

questions.q: Rushes woven into a four-armed cross, a feast on 1 February, and the old Gaelic quarter day of early spring point to which festival?
questions.f: St Brigid's crosses are hung over doors for the year, and 2023 made the day an Irish public holiday.

questions.q: Hilltop assemblies, the ceremonial cutting of the first grain, and a god's name that became the Irish word for August identify which festival?
questions.f: Irish 'Lunasa' still means August, and the Puck Fair is one of its living descendants.

questions.q: A mechanical dove running along a wire, flints said to be brought back from Jerusalem, and a cart of fireworks in a cathedral square identify which Easter custom?
questions.f: A smooth flight for the 'colombina' is taken as a promise of a good harvest.

questions.q: Four teams in Renaissance costume, a great square floored with sand, and a prize once said to be a cow name which Florentine festival sport?
questions.f: Each June the quarters of Florence play in colours worn since the 1500s.

questions.q: A man dressed as a red-and-yellow devil leaping over mattresses laid with babies, in a Castilian village at Corpus Christi, is which custom?
questions.f: Castrillo de Murcia has held its baby-jumping blessing since about 1620.

questions.q: A Zapotec word for the reciprocal exchange of gifts, delegations from eight regions, and the Dance of the Feather name which Mexican festival?
questions.f: Oaxaca's Guelaguetza takes its name from a whole system of mutual help between neighbours.

questions.q: A pot-bellied household figure loaded with miniature banknotes and tiny suitcases, bought exactly at noon on 24 January in La Paz, belongs to which fair?
questions.f: The little god is called Ekeko, and the miniatures are meant to become real during the year.

questions.q: Dancers in shaggy bear costumes called ukukus, a glacier pilgrimage above Cusco, and a name meaning 'snow star' identify which festival?
questions.f: Tens of thousands climb to nearly 5,000 metres for it, and UNESCO lists it as heritage.

questions.q: Bonfires in the middle of winter-free June, a comic mock village wedding, and a square dance called quadrilha identify which Brazilian celebration?
questions.f: The June festivals honour three saints, and the northeast holds the biggest ones, with corn dishes everywhere.

questions.q: A rope hundreds of metres long gripped by pilgrims, a small statue found by a cattle herder, and October in Belem name which procession?
questions.f: Around two million people join the Cirio, one of the largest religious processions on Earth.

questions.q: Masked dancers in towering peacock-feather headdresses, snare drum and whistle, and Bermuda's Boxing Day streets identify which tradition?
questions.f: Gombey blends African, Caribbean, British and Native American influences, and the troupes are family-based.

questions.q: Model tombs called tadjahs, tassa drumming, and Muharram marked in the Caribbean identify which festival?
questions.f: Indian indentured workers brought Hosay to Trinidad in the 1850s, and the name comes from 'Hussain'.

questions.q: White gowns called aropale, a strict ban on shoes and umbrellas, and processions on Lagos Island identify which Nigerian festival?
questions.f: Eyo is held only occasionally, usually to honour a departed chief, and turns the city white for a day.

questions.q: Thousands wading into a river with calabashes and hand nets, racing to land the biggest fish within an hour, describes which festival?
questions.f: Argungu's contest in Kebbi State has been held since 1934, when it marked a truce between neighbours.

questions.q: Horsemen in quilted armour cantering forward to salute an emir at the close of Ramadan identifies which West African celebration?
questions.f: Kano and Katsina hold the grandest Durbars, a tradition once used to review a city's cavalry.

questions.q: A bonfire called Demera, topped with a cross and yellow daisies, celebrates the finding of the True Cross at which Ethiopian festival?
questions.f: The direction the burnt cross falls is read as a sign for the year ahead.

questions.q: Wodaabe men in ochre face paint, admired for gleaming teeth and bright eyes, dance in long lines at which Sahel gathering?
questions.f: At Gerewol the men are the ones judged, and young women choose the winners.

questions.q: Stacks of thin mufleta pancakes, front doors thrown open to neighbours, and the very evening Passover ends identify which celebration?
questions.f: Mimouna is a Moroccan Jewish tradition, now widely celebrated in Israel with open-house visiting.

questions.q: A hillside reading of the Torah on the 29th of Cheshvan, fasting, and a festival of Ethiopian Jews now a national holiday in Israel is called what?
questions.f: 'Sigd' means prostration, and the day was traditionally kept on a mountain to feel closer to Jerusalem.

questions.q: Pockets turned out and crumbs cast into flowing water in the days after the Jewish new year describes which custom?
questions.f: 'Tashlich' means 'you will cast', and many communities walk to a river or the sea for it.

questions.q: A drummer walking the alleys before dawn, calling sleepers by name so they can eat before the fast, is known in Arabic as what?
questions.f: The mesaharati's rounds are centuries old, and in some cities the job passes down through one family.

questions.q: An Indonesian gathering held after Eid where colleagues and relatives formally ask one another's forgiveness is called what?
questions.f: The phrase was coined in Indonesia and exists nowhere else in the Muslim world.

questions.q: A tower of buns climbed for points, three meat-free days, and floats with children seemingly floating in mid-air identify which festival?
c: The Tai Hang Fire Dragon Dance
questions.f: Hong Kong's bun scramble was suspended for decades after a tower collapsed, then revived as a timed contest.

questions.q: Sticky sweets smeared on a paper portrait's mouth, a report carried up to heaven, and a send-off on the 23rd day of the last lunar month involve whom?
questions.f: Sweetening Zao Jun's mouth is meant to ensure only kind words about the household are reported.

questions.q: A congee of eight treasures cooked on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month gives its name to which Chinese festival?
questions.f: Laba garlic, pickled until it turns green, is prepared on the same day for the new year dumplings.

questions.q: Dumplings eaten so that ears do not freeze, the longest night of the year, and a saying that it matters as much as new year identify which festival?
questions.f: Southern China eats tangyuan and the north eats dumplings, and both count it as growing a year older.

questions.q: Three days with no fire lit and only cold food eaten, later absorbed into tomb-sweeping day, describes which old Chinese festival?
questions.f: The Cold Food Festival honours a loyal retainer, and its ban on cooking fires made cold rolls a speciality.

questions.q: Girls competing at threading needles by moonlight and praying for skill in weaving belongs to which Chinese festival?
questions.f: Qixi falls on the seventh night of the seventh month, and Japan's Tanabata grew from the same story.

questions.q: Pine torches carried in procession through fields in the sixth lunar month, among the Yi people of Liangshan, marks which festival?
questions.f: Torchlight is carried round crops to drive away pests, and whole valleys glow at once.

questions.q: Coloured glutinous rice hiding tokens, where a chilli means a polite refusal, is exchanged at which festival of the Miao?
questions.f: Guizhou's Sisters' Meal Festival is sometimes called one of the world's oldest ways of saying yes or no.

questions.q: A vast appliqued religious banner unrolled at dawn on a hillside, opera performances, and a name meaning 'yogurt banquet' identify which Tibetan festival?
questions.f: Yogurt was traditionally offered to monks ending their summer retreat, and the name stuck.

questions.q: Masked monastic dances in Ladakh and a giant thangka displayed only once every twelve years, in the Year of the Monkey, belong to which festival?
questions.f: Hemis honours Guru Padmasambhava, and the twelve-year cycle draws visitors from around the world.

questions.q: Two babies held up by sumo wrestlers while a referee urges them on, with victory to whoever cries first, is which Japanese event?
questions.f: Crying is thought to drive off bad spirits and promise healthy growth, and it is done at shrines each spring.

questions.q: Long bamboo poles hung with dozens of lit paper lanterns, balanced on foreheads, hips and shoulders, feature at which Japanese festival?
questions.f: An Akita kanto can carry 46 lanterns and weigh about 50 kilograms.

questions.q: A cucumber given matchstick legs to be a swift horse, and an aubergine made into a slow cow, are prepared for which Japanese festival?
questions.f: The horse brings ancestors home quickly and the cow carries them back slowly, laden with gifts.

questions.q: Giant characters set alight on the hillsides around Kyoto on 16 August form part of which observance?
