questions.f: The best known is the character for 'great', which is why locals call the event Daimonji.

questions.q: Japan's postal service holds back millions of items each December so they can all arrive on one morning. What are they?
questions.f: Nengajo are posted in advance and delivered on 1 January, and each carries a lottery number.

questions.q: A red cap and waistcoat, a sixtieth birthday, and the completion of one full turn of the zodiac-and-element cycle mark which Japanese celebration?
questions.f: Red is the colour of babyhood in Japan, so kanreki playfully treats the sixtieth year as being reborn.

questions.q: Nuts cracked between the teeth at dawn, kites deliberately cut loose, and the first full moon of the lunar year mark which Korean festival?
questions.f: Cutting the kite string is said to send away the year's misfortunes with it.

questions.q: Hundreds of thousands of women cooking rice pudding in clay pots along the streets of Thiruvananthapuram is which festival?
questions.f: Attukal Pongala has been recognised as the largest single gathering of women anywhere in the world.

questions.q: Flowers stacked into a tapering tower like a temple gopuram, then floated on a lake, belong to which Telangana festival?
questions.f: Each layer uses a different seasonal bloom, and the festival closes the nine nights of Navratri.

questions.q: Bamboo poles clapped in rhythm while dancers step nimbly between them belongs to the spring festival of which Indian state?
questions.f: Chapchar Kut features the Cheraw dance, whose bamboo clapping demands perfect timing.

questions.q: Eight days of fasting and reflection that end with everyone saying 'Micchami Dukkadam', asking forgiveness, describes which festival?
questions.f: Paryushana is the most important Jain observance, and the closing day is called Kshamavani, forgiveness day.

questions.q: A living child goddess drawn through the streets on a chariot, masked Lakhey dancers, and eight days in Kathmandu identify which festival?
questions.f: The Kumari, a young girl revered as a living goddess, appears publicly during Indra Jatra.

questions.q: Shopkeepers opening a fresh red account book and settling old debts marks which new year celebration?
questions.f: The ritual is called halkhata, and customers are offered sweets and a calendar.

questions.q: A procession carrying the 'behrana sahib' and devotion to Jhulelal mark the new year of which community?
questions.f: Cheti Chand falls on the second day of the Sindhi month of Chet, in spring.

questions.q: Neighbours taking turns to stir a huge cauldron of sprouted wheat paste all night, for a spring new year, are making what?
questions.f: Sumalak needs no sugar at all: the sweetness comes entirely from sprouting the wheat.

questions.q: Wishes written on paper and buried beneath a rose bush on the night of 5 May belong to which Turkish festival?
questions.f: Hidirellez marks the meeting of two figures, Hizir and Ilyas, and the arrival of spring.

questions.q: An autumn Persian festival honouring Mithra, with a table of marjoram, rosewater and a mirror, is called what?
questions.f: Mehregan was once as important as Nowruz, and it celebrates friendship and fair dealing.

questions.q: A midwinter Persian fire festival held fifty days before Nowruz is known by which name?
questions.f: 'Sadeh' means hundred, counting a hundred days and nights to the new year.

questions.q: Wooden towers on Pentecost Island, vines tied to the ankles, and a yam-harvest ritual that inspired bungee jumping identify which custom?
questions.f: A New Zealander who saw the ritual in the 1970s went on to develop commercial bungee jumping.

questions.q: A Hawaiian season honouring the god Lono, when warfare paused and games and feasting filled the calendar, was called what?
questions.f: Makahiki ran for about four months of the year, roughly from November, and taxes were paid in produce.

questions.q: Old fires extinguished and a new one kindled, debts and quarrels set aside, and the first ripe maize eaten describe which ceremony?
questions.f: Also called the busk, it is kept by Muscogee, Cherokee and other southeastern nations as a new year.

questions.q: A walrus-hide blanket held by dozens of people, tossing a person high into the air, celebrates a good spring season at which Alaskan festival?
questions.f: The Inupiat blanket toss began as a way to spot game far off across the flat sea ice.

questions.q: Masked riders in tall cone hats going farm to farm to beg ingredients for a communal gumbo describes which Louisiana tradition?
questions.f: The Cajun prairie 'run' is much older than the city parades, and a live chicken is often the prize.

questions.q: A New Orleans krewe's most prized throw, hand-decorated and by law handed over rather than thrown, is what?
questions.f: A 1988 law protected the krewe from injury claims, so the famous coconuts are passed to the crowd.

questions.q: A church, its patron saint's mass, and the fair that grew up in the churchyard gave Dutch and Flemish which word for a village festival?
questions.f: 'Kerk' plus 'mis' became kermis, and painters like Bruegel made the rowdy kermis scene famous.

questions.q: Pots and pans banged outside a newly married couple's window, a French word for a rough serenade, and an American spelling 'shivaree' all name which custom?
questions.f: A London magazine once used 'The Charivari' as its subtitle, because it was full of noisy mockery.

questions.q: A Greek phrase meaning 'at the bridal chamber', verses by Sappho and later by Spenser, and a poem written for a wedding define which term?
questions.f: Spenser's 'Epithalamion' of 1595 was written for his own wedding day.

questions.q: A French word for a petticoat, an 18th-century square dance for four couples, and a modern debutante ball share which name?
questions.f: Dancers' flicking petticoats gave the dance its name, long before it meant a formal ball.

questions.q: A southern Italian port, a spider blamed for fits of frenzied dancing, and a whirling festival dance in six-eight time point to which dance?
questions.f: Taranto gave its name to both the dance and the tarantula spider.

questions.q: A Trinidadian musician's 1970s blend, a name made by fusing two genre words, and Carnival's road-march sound produce which music?
questions.f: Lord Shorty is credited with the mix, and the name joins 'soul' with 'calypso'.

questions.q: An Italian verb meaning to tumble, a revolving drum of folded tickets, and a stall at a village fete give us which word?
questions.f: The tickets tumble in the drum, and in Naples tombola is a Christmas family game like bingo.

questions.q: A banner hung from a crossbar rather than a pole, carried at the head of Italian city-district parades, is called what?
questions.f: Florence's chief magistrate was the 'gonfaloniere', the standard-bearer of justice.

questions.q: A Greek hymn first addressed to Apollo the healer, later any song of triumph, gives us which word?
questions.f: 'Paian' was a cry used in the hymn itself, which became the name of the whole song.

questions.q: A wild choral hymn to Dionysus, sung and danced by a circle of fifty men, and the acknowledged ancestor of Greek drama is called what?
questions.f: Athens held dithyramb contests between the city's tribes, complete with prizes and a sponsor.

questions.q: Greek words for 'all' and 'assembly', a speech made at a national festival, and today's word for lavish praise combine in which term?
questions.f: A 'panegyris' was a full gathering of the people, exactly where such speeches were delivered.

questions.q: A Russian critic writing about Rabelais, a world briefly turned upside down, and a term for festive misrule in literature give us which word?
questions.f: Mikhail Bakhtin argued that carnival laughter temporarily levelled every rank in society.

questions.q: A 1909 book by the ethnographer Arnold van Gennep, three stages of separation, transition and return, and graduations today gave us which phrase?
questions.f: His French title 'Les rites de passage' is now everyday English.

questions.q: A Latin word for a doorstep, the awkward middle stage of a ceremony, and being 'betwixt and between' give us which adjective?
questions.f: From 'limen'; the anthropologist Victor Turner made liminality central to how rituals work.

questions.q: The Romans handled the extra day by doubling the sixth day before the March kalends. What is the proper adjective for such a year?
questions.f: 'Bis sextus' means 'twice sixth', and bissextile is still the technical term for a leap year.

questions.q: A day or month inserted into a calendar to keep festivals in their season is described by which adjective?
questions.f: From Latin 'calare', to proclaim, because such days were announced by the priests.

questions.q: Monastic tables of moons and Sundays, medieval manuscripts full of reckoning, and the fixing of one festival's date are all called what?
questions.f: Working out Easter drove much of medieval mathematics and astronomy in Europe.

questions.q: Which Sunday's name announces the number seventy and once opened the run-up to Lent?
questions.f: The trio Septuagesima, Sexagesima and Quinquagesima counted down the Sundays before Lent.

questions.q: A Latin word meaning 'rejoice', the fourth Sunday of Lent, and the day English tradition turned into Mothering Sunday name which day?
questions.f: Rose-coloured vestments are worn, marking a pause in the plainness of Lent.

questions.q: A German word often mistranslated as 'rose Monday', a dialect verb meaning to rave, and Carnival's biggest parade day give us which name?
questions.f: The 'rosen' comes from 'rasen', to rave about, not from flowers at all.

questions.q: A pope who died on the last day of December gave his name to New Year's Eve in Germany and Austria. Which name?
questions.f: Pope Sylvester I died on 31 December 335, so the whole evening is now called Silvester.

questions.q: A Hamburg pastor in 1839, a cartwheel fitted with twenty-four candles, and children counting off the days invented which item?
questions.f: Johann Hinrich Wichern used twenty small red candles and four large white ones for the Sundays.

questions.q: A cherry branch cut on 4 December, stood in water indoors, and timed to bloom at Christmas is known in Germany as what?
questions.f: If the twig flowers by Christmas Eve, tradition promises luck for the coming year.

questions.q: A teenage girl elected every two years, wearing a gold crown and ringlets, opens which famous German Christmas market?
questions.f: The Nuremberg Christkind gives a prologue from the church balcony to open the Christkindlesmarkt.

questions.q: A proclamation read out in a Finnish city square since the Middle Ages, warning against disorderly conduct, belongs to which tradition?
c: The Declaration of Christmas Peace in Turku
questions.f: Almost the whole country listens on radio or television at noon on Christmas Eve.

questions.q: An old Icelandic month name, tables of preserved and fermented foods, and a 19th-century revival name which midwinter feast?
questions.f: Thorrablot menus feature famously challenging dishes, eaten with much laughter and singing.

questions.q: Cream buns on Monday, salted mutton and peas on Tuesday, and costumes on Wednesday make up Iceland's version of which season?
questions.f: Bolludagur, Sprengidagur and Oskudagur run straight into the beginning of Lent.

questions.q: Paper hats, moon-faced lanterns and August evenings eating shellfish outdoors describe which Swedish party?
questions.f: The crayfish party season opened when the fishing ban lifted, and singing between courses is expected.

questions.q: Hutspot stew and herring with white bread mark a Dutch city's yearly party for the lifting of a siege in 1574. Which city?
questions.f: Leiden celebrates every 3 October, and the foods are said to be what the relief fleet brought in.

questions.q: A giant pretzel-shaped bread thrown to the crowd from a hilltop chapel belongs to the festival of which Flemish town?
questions.f: The Krakelingen festival ends with the throwing of thousands of ring-shaped breads.

questions.q: Women snipping off men's neckties, then symbolically storming the town hall, happens on which day of Cologne's Carnival?
questions.f: The custom began in 1824 with washerwomen in Beuel, near Bonn, and became an official Carnival day.

questions.q: Towering illuminated mitre-shaped headdresses, cowbells and whip-cracking through a Swiss village on 5 December belong to which festival?
questions.f: Kussnacht's biggest 'Iffele' headdresses stand nearly two metres tall and are lit from inside.

questions.q: Engadine schoolchildren ringing cowbells through their village on 1 March to drive out winter is which Swiss custom?
questions.f: The name comes from the Romansh for the kalends, or first day, of March.

questions.q: Twelve nights between Christmas and Epiphany, houses censed with juniper smoke, and Alpine weather omens are known as what?
questions.f: Each of the twelve nights is said to forecast the weather of one month of the coming year.

questions.q: In Chinese tradition, the coming-of-age ceremony 'guan li' centred on presenting a young man with what?
questions.f: Girls had a matching ceremony, the ji li, marked by pinning up the hair.

questions.q: The Hindu ceremony 'upanayana' marks a child receiving what?
c: A sacred thread worn over the shoulder
questions.f: It traditionally opened a student's years of formal study with a teacher.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word for the sequence of rites marking a Hindu life, from birth through marriage, is what?
questions.f: Classical texts list sixteen samskaras, of which weddings and naming ceremonies are the best known.

questions.q: In old legal English, 'cousin-german' means a first cousin because 'german' there means what?
c: Of the same parents or stock
questions.f: The surviving adjective 'germane', meaning closely relevant, comes from exactly this sense.

questions.q: The English custom called Borough English, in which the youngest son inherited the land, is known technically as what?
questions.f: It survived in some manors for centuries, on the logic that older sons had already been provided for.

questions.q: Which title belongs to someone whose claim to inherit could be displaced by the birth of a nearer relative?
questions.f: An heir apparent, by contrast, cannot be displaced by any later birth.

questions.q: The practice of marrying within one's own community or group is called what?
questions.f: 'Exogamy', its opposite, means marrying outside the group, from Greek 'exo', outside.

questions.q: The custom of addressing a parent as 'mother of' or 'father of' their child is known as what?
questions.f: It is common in Arabic naming, where a father may be known as Abu, meaning 'father of'.

questions.q: In ancient Rome, the male head of a household with legal authority over the family was called what?
questions.f: His authority, 'patria potestas', extended over adult children and household property alike.

questions.q: The most solemn form of ancient Roman wedding took its name from a shared cake made of which grain?
questions.f: 'Confarreatio' comes from 'far', spelt wheat, and the ceremony required ten witnesses.

questions.q: A nickname or assumed name, especially a colourful one, is properly called what?
questions.f: French 'sobriquet' once meant a chuck under the chin, a familiar and slightly cheeky gesture.

questions.q: In Hindu tradition, the lineage group inherited from the father's line, often considered in marriage, is called what?
questions.f: Many families still consult gotra when arranging a marriage, to keep the lines distinct.

questions.q: Chinese families have long kept 'jia pu'. What are they?
questions.f: Some jia pu trace dozens of generations, and they are still consulted at family reunions.

questions.q: In Spain and much of Latin America, a person traditionally carries how many surnames?
questions.f: The father's first surname is followed by the mother's, so neither family line disappears.

questions.q: On New Year's Eve, Danes traditionally do what to their neighbours' doorsteps?
questions.f: A big pile of broken china was a sign of how many friends you had.

questions.q: At Filipino New Year celebrations, why do families wear polka dots and serve round fruit?
questions.f: Twelve round fruits, one for each month, are often arranged on the table.

questions.q: In Colombia, an old New Year custom involves walking around the block carrying what?
questions.f: The empty case is a wish for a year full of travel.

questions.q: In Greece, what is smashed on the doorstep for luck at the turn of the year?
questions.f: The more seeds that scatter, the more abundance the household is promised.

questions.q: In Brazil, New Year revellers dress in white and traditionally do what at the beach?
questions.f: Each wave carries a wish, and offerings of white flowers are made to the sea goddess Iemanja.

questions.q: An Estonian New Year tradition encourages people to eat how many meals during the day?
questions.f: Each meal was thought to give the strength of that many men in the coming year.

questions.q: In Germany and Austria, molten metal poured into water at New Year was read to predict the future. The custom is called what?
questions.f: Lead was banned for safety, so families now use tin or wax for the same fortune-telling shapes.

questions.q: On New Year's Eve, German television traditionally shows a black-and-white British comedy sketch. Which one?
questions.f: Almost unknown in Britain, 'Dinner for One' has been a German New Year fixture since 1972.

questions.q: Which country celebrates a national Thanksgiving on the first Thursday of November?
questions.f: Liberia was founded partly by settlers from the United States, who brought the holiday with them.

questions.q: Norfolk Island's unusual Thanksgiving tradition arrived thanks to visits from whom in the 1890s?
questions.f: The tiny Pacific island still decorates its church with palm leaves, corn and lemons.

questions.q: Armenian Apostolic Christians celebrate Christmas on which date?
questions.f: They kept the older practice of marking the nativity and the baptism together on one day.

questions.q: Songkran was Thailand's official new year until the country moved the date in which decade?
questions.f: Thailand shifted the official new year to 1 January in 1941, but Songkran kept the celebrations.

questions.q: Which Chinese New Year taboo is traditionally observed on the first day of the festival?
questions.f: The word for hair sounds like the word for prosperity, so washing it seems like rinsing luck away.

questions.q: Diwali's main night falls on which lunar phase?
questions.f: Amavasya, the darkest night of the month, is exactly why the lamps matter so much.

questions.q: In Sri Lanka, public holidays fall on every 'Poya' day, which is which lunar phase?
questions.f: Twelve or thirteen Poya holidays a year make Sri Lanka's calendar unusually moon-driven.

questions.q: Which festival's name is derived from the Sanskrit for 'the ninth night' being completed, ending in a tenth day of victory?
questions.f: 'Vijaya' means victory and 'dashami' means tenth, so the count of nights runs straight into it.

questions.q: Which item is traditionally placed at the centre of a Japanese New Year decoration called kagami mochi?
questions.f: Two stacked rice cakes are topped with a daidai orange, whose name puns on 'generation after generation'.

questions.q: The 'Christmas pickle' ornament, often described as a German tradition, is largely an American invention.
questions.f: Surveys in Germany find few people have heard of it; the story seems to have been created to sell glass ornaments.

questions.q: The word 'germane' and the family term 'cousin-german' share the same origin.
questions.f: Both come from Latin 'germanus', meaning of the same parents, hence closely connected.

questions.q: Leap-day marriage proposals by women are tied to a tradition attributed to St Brigid and St Patrick.
questions.f: The story is legend rather than history, but it made 29 February 'Bachelor's Day' in Irish folklore.

questions.q: An eleven-day Babylonian spring festival, promises to the gods about repaying debts, and today's January habit all point to the ancestor of what?
questions.f: The festival was called Akitu, and its promises are the oldest known form of a new-year resolution.

questions.q: A Roman February festival of purification, a cave on the Palatine linked to a she-wolf, and a date later attached to lovers point to which festival?
questions.f: The Lupercal cave was where Rome's twin founders were said to have been suckled by a wolf.

questions.q: A Roman festival from 13 to 21 February honouring family ancestors, ending in a shared meal of reconciliation, was called what?
questions.f: Its closing day, the Caristia, was for settling family quarrels over dinner.

questions.q: On 1 March, Roman husbands gave gifts to their wives at a festival of Juno Lucina. What was it called?
questions.f: Slaves were given the day off by the mistress of the house, making it an ancient sort of Mothers' Day.

questions.q: The gift-giving day within Saturnalia, named after the little figurines exchanged, was called what?
questions.f: The 'sigilla' were small wax or pottery figures, an ancestor of the Christmas ornament.

questions.q: A hand-woven robe carried through Athens, a procession up to the Acropolis, and games held every four years belong to which festival?
questions.f: The peplos woven for Athena's statue is thought to be the scene shown on the Parthenon frieze.

questions.q: A monk writing in 725 recorded that the Anglo-Saxons called the night before Christmas 'Modraniht'. What does that mean?
questions.f: Bede mentions the name but not what was done, leaving one of the great puzzles of English folklore.

questions.q: Bede recorded that the Anglo-Saxon name for February meant the month of what?
questions.f: 'Solmonath' was explained as the month when cakes were offered, in the hungriest part of winter.

questions.q: An Aztec ceremony held once every 52 years extinguished every fire in the land and then relit them from one source. What was it called?
questions.f: The new flame was kindled on a hilltop and carried by runners to relight the whole valley.

questions.q: In ancient Egypt, the new year festival 'Wepet Renpet' was tied to the rising of which star?
questions.f: Sirius rose just before the Nile's flood, making it the natural marker of the Egyptian year.

questions.q: An Egyptian pharaoh's jubilee, traditionally held after thirty years on the throne, was known as which festival?
questions.f: The king had to run a course to prove his fitness to keep ruling.

questions.q: A print by Jose Guadalupe Posada, a skeleton in an enormous feathered hat, and a later Diego Rivera mural gave Mexico which figure?
questions.f: Posada's elegant skeleton mocked people who imitated European fashions, and Rivera gave her the name.

questions.q: A seed-filled clay pot broken by Chinese farmers, a traveller's report to Europe, and Spanish missionaries in Mexico converge on which party object?
questions.f: Missionaries turned the pot into a seven-pointed star to teach a lesson about temptation.

questions.q: An Edison company colleague, eighty hand-wired bulbs in red, white and blue in 1882, and a New York parlour window produced the first what?
questions.f: Edward H. Johnson wired them himself, and the tree revolved on a small motor for good measure.

questions.q: A German fairy tale published in 1812 and the bakers of Nuremberg together made which festive item popular?
questions.f: Hansel and Gretel's edible cottage sent German bakers straight to their spice cupboards.

questions.q: Two Kentucky sisters, a kindergarten song of 1893 titled 'Good Morning to All', and new words produced which famous tune?
c: For He's a Jolly Good Fellow
questions.f: Patty and Mildred Hill wrote the melody; the birthday words were attached later and made it world-famous.

questions.q: A Jewish immigrant songwriter, the 1942 film 'Holiday Inn', and the best-selling single ever recorded point to which song?
questions.f: Irving Berlin wrote it, and Bing Crosby's recording has sold an estimated 50 million copies.

questions.q: A 1939 booklet written for a department store by Robert May and a 1949 recording by Gene Autry launched which character?
questions.f: May's employer, Montgomery Ward, gave away millions of copies of the little book.

questions.q: A Scottish poet's 1788 letter, a Canadian bandleader's radio broadcasts from 1929, and midnight in New York made which song a fixture?
questions.f: Guy Lombardo's orchestra played it every New Year's Eve, cementing the custom in North America.

questions.q: A jeweller's Easter gift for a tsarina in 1885, a golden hen hidden inside a plain shell, and fifty imperial commissions describe what?
questions.f: Peter Carl Faberge's first egg opened to reveal a hen, which itself opened to reveal a tiny crown.

questions.q: A copywriter named Frances Gerety, a sleepless night in 1947, and four words changed which wedding custom forever?
questions.f: Her slogan 'A Diamond Is Forever' turned a rare gift into an expectation within a generation.

questions.q: A London baker's inspiration from the spire of St Bride's church is the traditional story behind which wedding item?
questions.f: St Bride's stepped spire does look remarkably like a stack of cake tiers.

questions.q: Which canonical hour of prayer takes its name from the evening star?
questions.f: 'Vesper' is Latin for evening, and the Greek Hesperus was the evening star.

questions.q: The study and practice of bell-ringing, heard at weddings and festivals, is called what?
questions.f: English change ringing sends bells through mathematical sequences called methods, some thousands of changes long.

questions.q: At the close of the Jewish Sabbath, the Havdalah ceremony uses wine, a braided candle and what else?
questions.f: The spices are sniffed to carry a little of the day's sweetness into the working week.

questions.q: 'Sheva Brachot' after a Jewish wedding refers to what?
c: Seven blessings repeated at festive meals for a week
Seven days of quiet at home
questions.f: Friends host the couple at dinners all week so the blessings can be said with a gathering present.

questions.q: At a Jewish wedding, the 'mezinke' dance honours whom?
c: Parents marrying off their last child
questions.f: The parents are crowned with wreaths and danced around while guests sweep the floor around them.

questions.q: The ceremony 'upsherin' marks a Jewish boy's what?
c: First haircut at the age of three
questions.f: The custom is compared to the rule of leaving a young fruit tree unharvested for three years.

questions.q: During Sukkot, the symbolic guests welcomed into the booth each night are called what?
questions.f: Seven biblical figures are invited in turn, and many families now name seven women as well.

questions.q: The Muslim marriage feast, which is a communal celebration hosted after the wedding contract, is called what?
questions.f: Sharing the walima widely, including with those who have little, is part of the tradition.

questions.q: In South Asia, the night before Eid, when markets stay open and hands are decorated, is popularly called what?
questions.f: 'Chaand Raat' means 'moon night', because the celebration begins the moment the crescent is sighted.

questions.q: The Bismillah ceremony in some Muslim families marks a child's what?
c: First formal lesson in reading the Quran
questions.f: The child is usually about four, and the family gathers as for any other rite of passage.

questions.q: A Sikh wedding ceremony is called 'Anand Karaj', a name meaning what?
questions.f: The couple walk four times around the Guru Granth Sahib, one round for each of the Lavan hymns.

questions.q: The Parsi ceremony 'Navjote' initiates a child by investing them with what?
questions.f: The sudreh and kusti are worn for life, the cord retied several times a day with prayers.

questions.q: Zoroastrian tradition marks six seasonal feasts of obligation known as what?
questions.f: Each Gahambar celebrates one of the six creations, and food is shared with the whole community.

questions.q: The Bahai calendar of nineteen months of nineteen days needs extra days, called what?
questions.f: These 'days of Ha' are set aside for hospitality and gift-giving before the fasting month.

questions.q: In Theravada Buddhist countries, the Kathina festival at the end of the rains retreat centres on offering monks what?
questions.f: Traditionally the cloth had to be cut and sewn within a single day by the community.

questions.q: At a Japanese matsuri, the portable shrine carried, jostled and paraded through the streets is called what?
questions.f: The rougher the ride, the better, because the shaking is believed to please the deity inside.

questions.q: The red paper 'chunlian' pasted around Chinese doorways at new year are what?
questions.f: The two vertical strips must match in rhythm and meaning, like a rhyming couplet for the house.

questions.q: Why is the character for 'fu' often pasted upside down on Chinese doors at new year?
c: It is easier to read from below
It marks a household in mourning
questions.f: 'Dao', upside down, is a pun on 'dao', to arrive, so upside-down luck means luck arriving.

questions.q: The Chinese new year custom of 'shousui' means what?
c: Staying up late to see the year in
questions.f: Children are told that staying awake adds years to their parents' lives.

questions.q: In Vietnam, the tall bamboo pole raised outside homes at Tet is called what?
questions.f: Charms hung at the top are meant to guard the house during the days when the kitchen gods are away.

questions.q: The Latin American system of co-parenthood, linking parents and godparents as 'compadres', is known as what?
questions.f: Anthropologists call such bonds fictive kinship: family ties created by ceremony rather than birth.

questions.q: In Islamic tradition, children nursed by the same woman are considered what?
questions.f: Milk kinship carries real family status in Islamic law, and it appears in medieval Europe too.

questions.q: A Roman citizen's three-part name consisted of a praenomen, a nomen and what?
questions.f: The nomen marked the clan, or gens, and the cognomen the particular family branch.

questions.q: In Balinese tradition, names such as Wayan, Made, Nyoman and Ketut indicate what?
c: The day of the week born
questions.f: A fifth child starts the cycle again, so families use 'Wayan Balik', meaning Wayan once more.

questions.q: Japanese names like Ichiro, Jiro and Saburo traditionally indicate what?
questions.f: 'Ichi', 'ji' and 'sabu' come from one, two and three, so Ichiro is simply 'first son'.

questions.q: In Russian naming, a middle name such as Ivanovich or Ivanovna is what?
c: A patronymic from the father's name
questions.f: Polite address in Russia often uses the first name plus patronymic, with no surname at all.

questions.q: In Ethiopian naming custom, a child's second name is usually what?
questions.f: Because there is no inherited family name, alphabetical lists in Ethiopia are made by first name.

questions.q: In Welsh naming tradition, what did 'ap' or 'ab' before a name mean?
questions.f: 'Ferch' meant daughter of, and 'ap Rhys' eventually contracted into the surname Price.

questions.q: In Gaelic naming, the prefix 'O' as in O'Brien originally meant what?
questions.f: 'Mac' means son, so MacDonald and O'Donnell mark different generations of the same idea.

questions.q: Hungarian and Chinese naming customs share which feature?
questions.f: That is why the composer known abroad as Franz Liszt is Liszt Ferenc in Hungary.

questions.q: In many Chinese families, a shared 'generation name' in the middle position shows what?
c: Which generation of the family you belong to
questions.f: Clan books sometimes set out a poem, with each generation taking the next character in turn.

questions.q: The Sikh names Singh and Kaur, given at the founding of the Khalsa, mean what?
questions.f: They were adopted so that everyone shared a name and caste distinctions in surnames disappeared.

questions.q: The word 'carousel', for a fairground ride, comes from an Italian and French word for what?
questions.f: Riders once speared rings while galloping, which is why some carousels still have a brass ring to grab.

questions.q: A 'raffle' at a village fete takes its name from an old French word for what?
questions.f: The medieval 'raffle' involved three dice, and the word slowly slid across to prize draws.

questions.q: The word 'gala' shares an origin with which other word?
questions.f: Old French 'gale' meant merrymaking or showing off, giving both a gala and a gallant.

questions.q: A 'fete champetre', once a fashionable form of party, was what?
questions.f: Watteau painted dozens of them, and the phrase means literally a country festival.

questions.q: Someone described as 'saturnine' at a festival is the opposite of jovial because of which planet's supposed influence?
questions.f: Old astrology gave us jovial from Jupiter, mercurial from Mercury and saturnine from cold, slow Saturn.

questions.q: The word 'epicure', for a lover of fine festival food, comes from the name of whom?
questions.f: Epicurus actually taught simple living, so his name has been rather unfairly borrowed.

questions.q: The sweet 'praline' is named after which kind of person?
questions.f: The cook of Marshal du Plessis-Praslin is credited with the first sugared almonds of that name.

questions.q: 'Caesar salad', a party-buffet classic, is named after whom?
questions.f: Cardini is said to have invented it in Tijuana in the 1920s when his kitchen was running low.

questions.q: The word 'chopsticks' is thought to come from a pidgin English phrase meaning what?
questions.f: 'Chop chop' meant hurry, and the Chinese term for the utensils, kuaizi, also suggests quickness.

questions.q: A 'nosegay', once carried at weddings, is literally what?
c: A small bunch of flowers that pleases the nose
questions.f: 'Gay' here has its old meaning of ornament, so a nosegay is a nose-ornament.

questions.q: The word 'corsage', worn at proms and weddings, originally referred to what?
questions.f: Flowers were pinned at the bodice, so the name of the garment slid onto the flowers.

questions.q: The word 'boutonniere' literally means what?
questions.f: The flower was threaded through the buttonhole of a lapel, which is where the name comes from.

questions.q: A 'triduum' in the church calendar covers how long?
questions.f: The Easter Triduum runs from the evening of Maundy Thursday to the evening of Easter Day.

questions.q: The Latin name 'Tenebrae', for a service in Holy Week, means what?
questions.f: Candles are extinguished one by one until the church is left in near-total darkness.

questions.q: The 'Magnificat', sung at Advent services, takes its name from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: The canticle opens 'My soul magnifies the Lord', and the first word became its title.

questions.q: The Arbaeen gathering in Iraq is reported to draw more people annually than the Hajj.
questions.f: Millions walk to Karbala, and volunteers line the route offering food, water and places to rest.

questions.q: The Roman festival Saturnalia and the modern Christmas share the custom of gift-giving, but not their dates.
questions.f: Saturnalia ran from 17 December for up to a week, ending before 25 December.

questions.q: The Bahai and Islamic calendars both begin their day at sunset.
questions.f: Days that begin at sunset are common to the Jewish, Islamic and Bahai calendars alike.

questions.q: 'Compline', the last prayer service of the day, takes its name from a word meaning 'complete'.
questions.f: It completes the round of daily hours, from Matins at night to Compline at bedtime.

questions.q: In The Princess and the Pea, what tiny thing is hidden under all the mattresses?
questions.f: The true princess feels the tiny pea even through twenty mattresses and twenty feather beds!

questions.q: Rapunzel lets her long hair down from the top of a tall what?
questions.f: Rapunzel's hair is so long and strong that visitors climb it like a rope ladder.

questions.q: In Peter Pan, the children fly away to which magical land?
questions.f: To reach Neverland, Peter says to fly toward the second star to the right and straight on till morning.

questions.q: What kind of pet is Dorothy's Toto in The Wizard of Oz?
questions.f: Little Toto rides all the way to Oz inside Dorothy's flying farmhouse.

questions.q: Winnie the Pooh's gloomy friend Eeyore is what kind of animal?
questions.f: Poor Eeyore is always losing his tail, so it is pinned back on with a nail.

questions.q: Which of Winnie the Pooh's friends loves bouncing on his springy tail?
questions.f: Tigger says that bouncing is what Tiggers do best!

questions.q: In The Elves and the Shoemaker, what do the elves make at night?
questions.f: The tiny elves sneak in while everyone sleeps and finish the poor shoemaker's work perfectly.

questions.q: Chicken Little runs around telling everyone that what is falling?
questions.f: An acorn bonks Chicken Little on the head, and she thinks the whole sky is tumbling down.

questions.q: In the story, what does the Little Red Hen bake all by herself?
questions.f: Since no one helped plant or grind the wheat, the Little Red Hen eats her fresh bread herself.

questions.q: Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jumps over the what?
questions.f: Long ago, jumping over a candle flame without putting it out was thought to bring good luck.

questions.q: In the rhyme, Little Boy Blue is supposed to blow his what?
questions.f: He needs to blow his horn because the sheep are in the meadow and the cows are in the corn.

questions.q: In the rhyme, the old woman with many children lives inside a giant what?
questions.f: The rhyme says she had so many children she didn't know what to do.

questions.q: Wee Willie Winkie runs through the town wearing his what?
questions.f: Wee Willie Winkie taps on windows to check that all the children are in bed by eight o'clock.

questions.q: In Sing a Song of Sixpence, which birds are baked in a pie?
questions.f: The rhyme says four and twenty blackbirds began to sing when the pie was opened.

questions.q: In the rhyme, where does the first little piggy go?
questions.f: Another little piggy stays home, and the littlest one cries 'wee wee wee' all the way home.

questions.q: In the rhyme Pussycat, Pussycat, whom did the cat go to London to see?
questions.f: While visiting the Queen, the pussycat frightens a little mouse under her chair.

questions.q: In The Enormous Turnip, how does the family finally pull the giant turnip out?
questions.f: Even the tiniest mouse joins the line, and teamwork pops the turnip out at last.

questions.q: In Wonderland, what does the White Rabbit keep worrying that he is?
questions.f: The hurrying White Rabbit cries, 'Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be too late!'

questions.q: The Cheshire Cat in Wonderland is famous for its big what?
questions.f: The Cheshire Cat fades away slowly until only its wide grin is left floating in the air.

questions.q: In The Wizard of Oz, what does the Cowardly Lion wish for?
questions.f: By the end of the journey, the Lion has been brave many times without noticing it.

questions.q: The Tin Man in Oz hopes the Wizard will give him a what?
questions.f: The kind Tin Man cries so often that his friends must oil his jaw so it won't rust shut.

questions.q: In Peter Pan, what part of himself does Peter chase around Wendy's room?
questions.f: Peter's shadow comes loose, and Wendy kindly sews it back onto his feet.

questions.q: The Pied Piper plays his pipe to lead away all the town's what?
questions.f: When the town refuses to pay him, the piper plays again and leads the children away instead.

questions.q: In Beatrix Potter's books, Peter Rabbit wears a little jacket of which color?
questions.f: Peter loses his blue jacket with brass buttons while escaping from the garden.

questions.q: In Stone Soup, what do the clever travelers start their soup with?
questions.f: Curious villagers each add a little food, and soon the 'stone soup' is a real feast.

questions.q: In the rhyme, where do the five little monkeys jump before falling off?
questions.f: One by one they bump their heads, and the doctor says, 'No more monkeys jumping on the bed!'

questions.q: Star light, star bright — what do you make when you see the first star?
questions.f: The old rhyme asks the first star of the night to grant the wish you wish tonight.

questions.q: Which four animals travel together in The Musicians of Bremen?
c: A donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster
A horse, a pig, a duck and a goat
A cow, a sheep, a hen and a fox
questions.f: The four old friends scare robbers away by making their loudest music all at once.

questions.q: What happens to Baby Bear's little chair when Goldilocks sits in it?
questions.f: The little chair was just right for sitting — but not strong enough to hold Goldilocks!

questions.q: Young King Arthur shows he is the true king by pulling a sword out of a what?
questions.f: Many strong knights tug at the sword, but only Arthur can slide it out of the stone.

questions.q: Robin Hood and his Merry Men live hidden in Sherwood what?
questions.f: Sherwood Forest is a real forest in England that you can still visit today.

questions.q: Ali Baba opens the secret treasure cave with the magic words 'Open ___!'
questions.f: Sesame is a real plant whose seed pods pop open all at once when they are ripe.

questions.q: In Edward Lear's poem, the Owl and the Pussycat go to sea in a beautiful pea-green what?
questions.f: They pack honey and plenty of money, wrapped up in a five-pound note.

questions.q: In Heidi, where does Heidi live with her grandfather?
questions.f: Heidi loves her grandfather's hut in the Alps, with goats to play with and hay to sleep on.

questions.q: In The Wind in the Willows, which animal goes crazy for shiny motorcars?
questions.f: Rich Mr. Toad of Toad Hall shouts 'Poop-poop!' whenever a motorcar zooms by.

questions.q: The Grand Old Duke of York marches his ten thousand men up to the top of a what?
questions.f: The rhyme jokes that when they were only halfway up, they were neither up nor down.

questions.q: Winnie the Pooh lives in the Hundred Acre Wood.
questions.f: The Hundred Acre Wood was based on a real forest in England called Ashdown Forest.

questions.q: Peter Pan is a boy who never wants to grow up.
questions.f: Peter Pan says, 'I want always to be a little boy and to have fun.'

questions.q: The Cowardly Lion in Oz goes to the Wizard to ask for a new hat.
questions.f: The Lion asks for courage — and learns he had plenty of it all along.

questions.q: In the famous rhyme, London Bridge is falling down.
questions.f: London Bridge is a real bridge, and the old rhyme suggests building it up again and again.

questions.q: The White Rabbit in Wonderland carries a pocket watch.
questions.f: Alice follows him because a rabbit with a waistcoat and a watch is far too curious to ignore.

questions.q: A person who writes a storybook is called an what?
questions.f: Some authors write a whole book with just a pencil and paper before anyone types it.

questions.q: The person who draws the pictures in a storybook is the what?
questions.f: Beatrix Potter was both author and illustrator — she painted every picture of Peter Rabbit herself.

questions.q: Words like 'cat' and 'hat' end with the same sound, so we say they do what?
questions.f: Nursery rhymes use rhyming words to make them easy and fun to remember.

questions.q: The name of a book printed on its front is called the what?
questions.f: Some famous titles are questions, jokes, or even a single word.

questions.q: A building full of books that you can borrow for free is a what?
questions.f: Some libraries even have special vans called bookmobiles that bring books to your street.

questions.q: The friendly helper who finds books for you at the library is a what?
questions.f: Librarians organize thousands of books so any story can be found in minutes.

questions.q: A made-up story that did not really happen is called what?
questions.f: Fiction can be about anything you can imagine — even talking bears and flying ships.

questions.q: A long book is divided into big parts — each part is called a what?
questions.f: Reading 'just one more chapter' at bedtime is a trick readers have used for ages.

questions.q: A soft, gentle song that helps a baby fall asleep is called a what?
questions.f: Rock-a-bye Baby is one of the most famous lullabies in the world.

questions.q: The people and animals that a story is about are called its what?
questions.f: A character can be anyone — a girl, a dragon, or even a talking teapot.

questions.q: The words 'happily ever after' usually come at which part of a fairy tale?
questions.f: Fairy tales in many languages end with their own special happy phrase.

questions.q: Cinderella gets her name because she sleeps near the cinders. Cinders are what?
questions.f: Poor Cinderella slept by the fireplace, so her clothes were always dusted with gray ash.

questions.q: A baby duck, like the little hero of The Ugly Duckling, is called a what?
questions.f: The ending '-ling' is a little word-tail that means 'small one.'

questions.q: Mary had a little lamb — and a lamb is a baby what?
questions.f: The rhyme was inspired by a real girl named Mary whose pet lamb followed her to school.

questions.q: The word 'unicorn' tells you the magical horse has exactly one what?
questions.f: 'Uni' means one — just like a unicycle has only one wheel.

questions.q: A mermaid in stories is half girl and half what?
questions.f: The 'mer' part of mermaid is a very old word for the sea.

questions.q: Someone who loves reading all the time is playfully called a book-what?
questions.f: Real 'bookworms' exist — tiny insects that nibble the pages of very old books!

questions.q: A silly sentence that is hard to say fast, like 'She sells seashells,' is a tongue-what?
questions.f: Tongue twisters trip up your mouth because so many words start with the same sounds.

questions.q: Words like 'buzz,' 'moo,' and 'pop' are special because they sound like what?
questions.f: Storybooks use sound words like CRASH and SPLASH to make pictures noisy in your head.

questions.q: The magic stick a fairy godmother waves is called a what?
questions.f: In Cinderella, one wave of the wand turns rags into a beautiful ball gown.

questions.q: The brave character who saves the day in a story is called the what?
questions.f: A story's hero can be anyone — even a small hobbit-sized person with a big heart.

questions.q: Storybook dragons are most famous for breathing what?
questions.f: In old tales, dragons guard piles of gold and sleep on top of their treasure.

questions.q: Which of these is a compound word made from two smaller words?
questions.f: Story + book = storybook! English loves gluing words together like this.

questions.q: A 'tale' is another word for a what?
questions.f: Watch the spelling: a fox's 'tail' and a fairy 'tale' sound the same but are different words.

questions.q: Puss in Boots is a clever cat. A baby cat is called a what?
questions.f: Kittens are born with their eyes closed and open them after about a week.

questions.q: Which of these words rhymes with 'king'?
questions.f: Poets collect rhyming words like 'king, ring, sing, wing' to build their verses.

questions.q: The hard outside part that protects a book's pages is called the what?
questions.f: The saying 'don't judge a book by its cover' reminds us to peek inside first.

questions.q: In stories a wizard casts a 'spell.' In a spelling bee, to 'spell' means to do what?
c: Say a word's letters in order
questions.f: Long ago 'spell' meant to tell or say — that is how magic words and letter-saying share one word.

questions.q: In fairy tales, a king and queen usually live in a what?
questions.f: Real castles had drawbridges that pulled up to keep unwanted visitors out.

questions.q: In storybooks, a king wears his golden crown on his what?
questions.f: Crowns in stories are often magic — some even let the wearer understand animals.

questions.q: In fairy tales, a princess is the daughter of a what?
questions.f: The word 'princess' comes from 'prince,' which long ago meant 'first person' in the land.

questions.q: The 'un-' at the start of 'unhappy' means what?
questions.f: Add 'un-' and a word flips: lucky becomes unlucky, and kind becomes unkind.

questions.q: Jack meets a giant at the top of the beanstalk. The word 'giant' means very what?
questions.f: We borrow the word for huge things today, like giant pandas and giant pumpkins.

questions.q: In The Golden Goose, what happens to everyone who touches the goose?
questions.f: A long line of stuck people looks so funny that a princess who never laughed bursts out laughing.

questions.q: In the rhyme, Simple Simon meets a pieman going to the what?
questions.f: Simple Simon wants to taste the pies — but he hasn't got a penny to pay.

questions.q: Polly puts the kettle on so everyone can have what?
questions.f: Right after Polly puts it on, Sukey takes the kettle off again!

questions.q: In Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary, what is Mary asked about?
questions.f: Her strange garden grows silver bells, cockle shells, and pretty maids all in a row.

questions.q: An author is the person who writes a book.
questions.f: The word 'author' is related to old words meaning someone who makes things grow.

questions.q: A library is a place where you buy shoes.
questions.f: A library lends books for free — some big libraries hold millions of them.

questions.q: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
questions.f: That is why 'moon' and 'spoon' rhyme, but 'moon' and 'star' do not.

questions.q: How long does Sleeping Beauty sleep in the fairy tale?
questions.f: The whole castle falls asleep with her, and a thorn hedge grows all around it.

questions.q: Why do the Three Billy Goats Gruff want to cross the bridge?
questions.f: The sweet grass on the far hillside is worth facing a grumpy troll for.

questions.q: Finish the rhyme: 'Rain, rain, go away, come again another ___.'
questions.f: Children have sung versions of this rhyme for hundreds of years.

questions.q: 'It's raining, it's pouring, the old man is ___.'
questions.f: He went to bed and bumped his head, the rhyme says, and couldn't get up in the morning.

questions.q: 'One, two, buckle my ___.'
questions.f: The counting rhyme goes all the way up: 'nine, ten, a big fat hen!'

questions.q: 'Ring-a-ring o' roses, a pocket full of ___.'
questions.f: Posies are little bunches of flowers, perfect for a pocket.

questions.q: 'I'm a little teapot, short and ___.'
questions.f: 'Stout' means sturdy and round — here is my handle, here is my spout!

questions.q: 'Pease porridge hot, pease porridge ___.'
questions.f: Some like it in the pot, nine days old — pease porridge was thick pea soup.

questions.q: Dorothy from The Wizard of Oz lives on a farm in which state?
questions.f: There's no place like home — and for Dorothy, home is gray, windy Kansas.

questions.q: Where does Cinderella lose her slipper as she runs from the ball?
questions.f: She has to run because the magic ends at the last stroke of midnight.

questions.q: What is the Scarecrow in The Wizard of Oz stuffed with?
questions.f: Crows soon learn the friendly Scarecrow isn't scary at all — one even sits on his shoulder.

questions.q: Little Miss Muffet sits on her tuffet eating curds and what?
questions.f: Curds and whey was a soft cheese snack, a bit like cottage cheese.

questions.q: 'Hot cross buns! One a penny, two a ___.'
questions.f: Street sellers in old London really did sing out this rhyme to sell their buns.

questions.q: In the rhyme, Doctor Foster stepped in a puddle right up to his middle.
questions.f: After his soggy trip to Gloucester, the rhyme says he never went there again.

questions.q: Which piece of writing usually has short lines and rhyming words?
questions.f: Poems are made to be heard — their beat and rhymes make them fun to say aloud.

questions.q: A tricky question like 'What has hands but cannot clap?' is called a what?
questions.f: The answer is a clock! Riddles appear in fairy tales all over the world.

questions.q: Baby Bear is a young bear. A baby bear is called a what?
questions.f: Lion, tiger, and fox babies are called cubs too.

questions.q: The Big Bad Wolf is a wolf. A baby wolf is called a what?
questions.f: Wolf pups live in a family group called a pack.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'frog,' like the one the princess kissed?
questions.f: Frog and log rhyme because they share the same '-og' ending sound.

questions.q: Pinocchio tells fibs. A 'fib' is a small what?
questions.f: Every fib makes Pinocchio's wooden nose grow a little longer.

questions.q: In stories, a fox's cozy underground home is called a what?
questions.f: Story foxes plan their tricks at home in their dens.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'bear,' like the three in Goldilocks?
questions.f: Bear and chair rhyme even though they are spelled differently at the start.

questions.q: The big letter that starts your name is called a what?
questions.f: Book titles and character names all start with capital letters.

questions.q: Putting words in ABC order, like in a dictionary, is called what?
questions.f: Libraries often shelve storybooks in alphabetical order by the author's name.

questions.q: A poet is a person who writes poems.
questions.f: Some poets write whole books of poems just for children.

questions.q: In The Nutcracker story, the toy nutcracker's job is to crack open what?
questions.f: Real nutcrackers shaped like little soldiers have been carved in Germany for centuries.

questions.q: Which animal is famous for being 'in sheep's clothing' in a fable?
questions.f: The fable warns that someone friendly-looking may not be friendly at all.

questions.q: In Beauty and the Beast, what magic flower does the Beast keep safe?
questions.f: In many tellings, the rose's falling petals count down the Beast's time.

questions.q: What did the three little kittens lose in the nursery rhyme?
questions.f: They find them again and then get pie — but they get the mittens all dirty.

questions.q: In Snow White, where do the seven dwarfs go every day?
questions.f: They dig for diamonds and gems, then march home singing over the hills.

questions.q: What magic word do fairy-tale magicians often say when something appears?
questions.f: 'Abracadabra' is over 1,800 years old — it was once written on charms as a healing word.

questions.q: In Hansel and Gretel, the house in the woods is made of what?
questions.f: Its gingerbread walls and sugar windows are a trap for hungry children.

questions.q: Which fairy-tale girl visits a house and tries three bowls, three chairs and three beds?
questions.f: Baby Bear's things are always the ones that suit her best.

questions.q: In Peter Pan, what does Tinker Bell sprinkle so the children can fly?
questions.f: Peter says you also need a happy thought to lift you off the ground.

questions.q: In the rhyme, what does Little Jack Horner pull out of his pie?
questions.f: He sits in a corner, sticks in his thumb, and says, 'What a good boy am I!'

questions.q: In the fable, what does the lion do that scares all the other animals?
questions.f: A lion's roar can be heard from five miles away — no wonder fables make him the king.

questions.q: In the story, the Little Engine keeps saying 'I think I ___.'
questions.f: The brave little engine puffs its way over the mountain by never giving up.

questions.q: Where does the Owl and the Pussycat's boat sail?
questions.f: They sail away for a year and a day to the land where the Bong-Tree grows.

questions.q: What kind of animal is Mowgli's friend Bagheera in The Jungle Book?
questions.f: Black panthers are really leopards whose coats are so dark the spots barely show.

questions.q: In fairy tales, what does a wicked witch usually fly on?
questions.f: Some tales give witches flying mortars, buckets, or even wooden spoons instead.

questions.q: In the rhyme, the mouse ran up the clock. What time did the clock strike?
questions.f: 'Hickory dickory dock' may just be nonsense counting words shepherds once used.

questions.q: What does Rapunzel's visitor call out from below her tower?
questions.f: Her braid works as a ladder — but it must have hurt quite a lot!

questions.q: In stories, an elf is usually what size?
questions.f: In the oldest tales elves were human-sized — storybooks shrank them later.

questions.q: In The Little Red Hen, which animals refuse to help her?
questions.f: They all want to eat the bread, though — until they remember they never helped.

questions.q: In the Winnie the Pooh stories, which little friend is a very small pig?
questions.f: Piglet is often scared but does brave things anyway — Pooh's best kind of friend.

questions.q: In Cinderella, whom does Cinderella dance with at the ball?
questions.f: The prince searches the whole kingdom afterward with nothing but a lost slipper.

questions.q: In the rhyme, what is the muffin man's job?
questions.f: Muffin men once walked London's streets with trays of muffins on their heads.

questions.q: Which nursery rhyme animal 'went to market' in the toe-counting rhyme?
questions.f: Grown-ups have counted babies' toes with this rhyme for over 250 years.

questions.q: In The Ugly Duckling, the other birds are unkind to him at first.
questions.f: He only feels sad because he is compared to ducklings — he was never a duck at all.

questions.q: In Jack and the Beanstalk, Jack's magic beans grow into a giant plant overnight.
questions.f: Real bean plants do climb fast, but they need weeks, not one night.

questions.q: Alice in Wonderland meets a talking caterpillar.
questions.f: The Caterpillar sits on a mushroom and asks Alice, 'Who are YOU?'

questions.q: The 'moral' of a fable comes at which point in the story?
questions.f: Aesop's morals are so short they often fit in a single line.

questions.q: A story about talking animals that teaches a lesson is called a what?
questions.f: Aesop's fables are more than 2,000 years old and still told everywhere.

questions.q: A very short story you read to a child at bedtime is called a bedtime what?
questions.f: Reading to children each night helps them learn hundreds of new words.

questions.q: What do we call the drawings inside a picture book?
questions.f: In a picture book, the pictures tell just as much of the story as the words.

questions.q: A baby fox, like the sly one in Aesop's fables, is called a what?
questions.f: Fox babies are also called kits, and a family lives together in a den.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'moon,' as in the cow jumping over it?
questions.f: In Hey Diddle Diddle the dish runs away with the spoon — a rhyme with the moon.

questions.q: 'Giant' and 'tiny' mean opposite things. Words like that are called what?
questions.f: Fairy tales love opposites: giants and dwarfs, kind sisters and unkind ones.

questions.q: The word 'fairy tale' has two words. How many words are in 'storybook'?
questions.f: 'Storybook' is a compound word — two words joined into one.

questions.q: A knight in a story rides a horse. A baby horse is called a what?
questions.f: A foal can stand up and walk within hours of being born.

questions.q: In stories, a 'cottage' is a what?
questions.f: Snow White finds a tiny cottage with seven little beds inside.

questions.q: In fairy tales, a 'forest' is a place with many what?
questions.f: Fairy-tale forests are where heroes get lost — and where the magic usually starts.

questions.q: Words that begin with the same sound, like 'Peter Piper,' are fun because they do what?
questions.f: Repeating a starting sound makes a line tricky and fun to say fast.

questions.q: When you read a story out loud to someone, you are doing what?
questions.f: Reading aloud helps you hear how a story sounds — poets do it all the time.

questions.q: Which one is a fairy-tale creature, not a real animal?
questions.f: Dragons appear in stories from China to England — but never in a zoo.

questions.q: An illustrator draws the pictures for a storybook.
questions.f: Some illustrators paint hundreds of pictures for a single book.

questions.q: 'Cat' and 'bat' rhyme with each other.
questions.f: Rhyming pairs like these are the building blocks of nursery rhymes.

questions.q: Every storybook must have exactly ten pages.
questions.f: Picture books are often 32 pages, while big novels can pass 500.

questions.q: In Oliver Twist, hungry Oliver bravely asks, 'Please, sir, I want some ___.'
questions.f: Oliver's simple request for more porridge shocks everyone in Charles Dickens's famous story.

questions.q: Who tells the story in the book Black Beauty?
questions.f: Anna Sewell wrote the whole book as if the horse himself were speaking.

questions.q: In The Secret Garden, which bird shows Mary the way to the hidden garden door?
questions.f: The friendly robin perches near the spot where the buried key is hidden.

questions.q: Tom Sawyer tricks his friends into doing which chore for him?
questions.f: Tom pretends painting is so much fun that his friends pay him for a turn.

questions.q: On a pirate treasure map, what letter usually marks the spot?
questions.f: The idea of 'X marks the spot' became famous through Treasure Island.

questions.q: In Treasure Island, what pet sits on Long John Silver's shoulder?
questions.f: The parrot squawks 'Pieces of eight!' — the name of old Spanish silver coins.

questions.q: Where is Robinson Crusoe stranded for many years?
questions.f: Crusoe builds his own shelter, grows food, and keeps a calendar carved on a post.

questions.q: When Gulliver wakes up in Lilliput, what has happened to him?
c: Tiny people have tied him down
He is floating in the air
questions.f: The six-inch Lilliputians use hundreds of tiny ropes and pegs to pin down the giant visitor.

questions.q: In Washington Irving's tale, how long does Rip Van Winkle sleep in the mountains?
questions.f: Rip wakes with a long white beard and finds his whole village changed.

questions.q: The story of Heidi takes place in which famous mountains?
questions.f: Author Johanna Spyri set Heidi in the Swiss Alps, where she spent her own summers.

questions.q: In The Wind in the Willows, Ratty says there is nothing half so much fun as messing about in what?
questions.f: Ratty is really a water vole who lives happily on the riverbank.

questions.q: Kipling's Just So story explains how the camel got his what?
questions.f: In the tale, the lazy camel keeps saying 'Humph!' — until he gets one.

questions.q: In Kipling's story, the Elephant's Child gets his long trunk from a tug-of-war with a what?
questions.f: Before that, the story says, elephants had only short, boot-sized noses.

questions.q: How many March sisters are there in Little Women?
questions.f: Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy were based on author Louisa May Alcott and her own sisters.

questions.q: In Aesop's fable, the fox flatters the crow so she will drop her piece of what?
questions.f: When the proud crow opens her beak to sing, the cheese falls right into the fox's mouth.

questions.q: In Aesop's fable, a wolf sneaks among the flock by wearing the skin of a what?
questions.f: 'A wolf in sheep's clothing' now describes anyone who pretends to be harmless.

questions.q: In the fable Belling the Cat, what do the mice want to hang around the cat's neck?
questions.f: The plan sounds perfect until one wise mouse asks, 'But who will do it?'

questions.q: In Aesop's Bundle of Sticks, sticks tied together in a bundle cannot be what?
questions.f: One stick snaps easily, but the bundle stays strong — a lesson about sticking together.

questions.q: In the old tale, what does Androcles gently pull from the lion's paw?
questions.f: Years later the grateful lion recognizes Androcles and refuses to harm him.

questions.q: In the Arabian Nights, how does Scheherazade keep the king listening night after night?
questions.f: She stops each story at the most exciting part, so the king must wait another day for the ending.

questions.q: In the Arabian Nights, how many amazing voyages does Sinbad the Sailor make?
questions.f: On one voyage Sinbad lands on what looks like an island — but it is a sleeping whale.

questions.q: King Arthur's knights famously sit at a table of which shape?
questions.f: At a round table there is no head seat, so no knight can claim to be more important.

questions.q: Merlin, King Arthur's wise helper, is famous for being a what?
questions.f: In some tales Merlin lives backwards through time, remembering the future instead of the past.

questions.q: Excalibur, King Arthur's famous treasure, is what kind of object?
questions.f: Legends say Excalibur's scabbard was even more precious than the sword itself.

questions.q: In Andersen's tale The Nightingale, the little bird sings for the emperor of which land?
questions.f: The emperor learns that the plain real bird sings more sweetly than his jeweled wind-up one.

questions.q: What is unusual about Andersen's Steadfast Tin Soldier?
questions.f: The toymaker ran out of tin, so the last little soldier was cast with a single leg.

questions.q: Mother Goose is the imaginary teller of what?
questions.f: Nobody knows if a real Mother Goose ever lived — her name has appeared on rhyme books for centuries.

questions.q: In the poem The Night Before Christmas, how many reindeer pull St. Nick's sleigh?
questions.f: This 1823 poem gave the reindeer their famous names, from Dasher to Blitzen.

questions.q: In Edward Lear's poem, who marries the Owl and the Pussycat?
questions.f: The turkey who lives on the hill marries them, and they dance by the light of the moon.

questions.q: What does the wooden puppet Pinocchio wish to become?
questions.f: After proving himself brave, truthful, and unselfish, his wish finally comes true.

questions.q: The Emerald City in The Wizard of Oz shines in which color?
questions.f: Emeralds are real green gemstones, which is how the city got its name.

questions.q: What carries Dorothy's house from Kansas all the way to Oz?
questions.f: Author L. Frank Baum used the old word 'cyclone' for what we usually call a tornado.

questions.q: In Wonderland, the Mad Hatter is famous for hosting an endless what?
questions.f: For the Hatter it is always six o'clock, so it is always time for tea.

questions.q: In Wonderland, the Queen of Hearts' gardeners are busy painting white roses what color?
questions.f: They planted white roses by mistake and hope the Queen will never notice.

questions.q: Beatrix Potter's washerwoman Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle is what kind of animal?
questions.f: Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle was named after Beatrix Potter's own pet hedgehog.

questions.q: In the Grimm tale The Fisherman and His Wife, what creature grants the wishes?
questions.f: The wife's wishes grow greedier and greedier — until the couple ends up back in their old hut.

questions.q: Mark Twain wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.
questions.f: Twain filled the book with memories of his own boyhood beside the Mississippi River.

questions.q: Treasure Island is a story about pirates and buried treasure.
questions.f: It gave us many pirate favorites, including the one-legged sea cook with a parrot.

questions.q: In Black Beauty, the story is told by a dog.
questions.f: Black Beauty is a horse — the book asked readers to treat horses kindly.

questions.q: Words that mean almost the same thing, like 'happy' and 'glad,' are called what?
questions.f: Writers use synonyms so they don't repeat the same word again and again.

questions.q: Words with opposite meanings, like 'brave' and 'scared,' are called what?
questions.f: The 'ant-' part comes from a root meaning 'against' — antonyms work against each other.

questions.q: The voice that tells you what happens in a story is called the what?
questions.f: In Black Beauty the narrator is a horse, and in other books it can even be the villain.

questions.q: The 'plot' of a story means what?
questions.f: Many fairy-tale plots follow a pattern: a problem, three tries, and a happy ending.

questions.q: The words characters speak, shown inside quotation marks, are called what?
questions.f: Reading dialogue aloud in funny voices is a favorite trick of great storytellers.

questions.q: A book that tells the true story of a real person's life is called a what?
questions.f: The 'bio' part means life, so a biography is literally 'life-writing.'

questions.q: A second book that continues the same story is called a what?
questions.f: L. Frank Baum wrote more than a dozen sequels about the Land of Oz.

questions.q: Stories with magic, dragons, and imaginary worlds belong to which kind of story?
questions.f: Fantasy worlds often come with their own maps printed inside the book's front cover.

questions.q: Which book lists words in ABC order and tells you what they mean?
questions.f: Big dictionaries can hold hundreds of thousands of words — perfect for spelling champions.

questions.q: A person who writes poems is called a what?
questions.f: A country's official poet is sometimes given the grand title 'poet laureate.'

questions.q: A made-up name an author uses instead of their real name is called a what?
questions.f: Mark Twain, the author of Tom Sawyer, was really named Samuel Clemens.

questions.q: The edge of a book that faces you on a shelf, showing its title, is the what?
questions.f: It is called the spine because it holds the book together — just like your backbone.

questions.q: The short line of words printed under a picture is called a what?
questions.f: Captions tell you what a picture shows, like a tiny story in one sentence.

questions.q: The ABC list at the back of a book that helps you find topics is the what?
questions.f: An index tells you the exact page — no flipping through the whole book needed.

questions.q: The person whose job is to check and improve an author's writing is the what?
questions.f: Editors catch spelling slips and mixed-up chapters before a book is printed.

questions.q: The ending '-ling' in 'duckling' and 'gosling' means what?
questions.f: English hides size-words in endings: a duckling is simply a little duck.

questions.q: The prefix 're-' in 'reread' and 'retell' means what?
questions.f: Rereading a favorite book means reading it again — some fans reread stories dozens of times.

questions.q: The prefix 'pre-' in 'preview' means what?
questions.f: A preview lets you peek at a story before it is fully out.

questions.q: The ending '-less' in 'fearless' means what?
questions.f: A fearless knight is without fear — and a sleepless night is a night without sleep.

questions.q: A group of geese, like Mother Goose's friends, is called a what?
questions.f: On the ground geese are a gaggle, but flying in a V they are often called a skein.

questions.q: Edward Lear made up the funny word 'runcible' to describe a what?
questions.f: Lear never explained what 'runcible' means — he just liked the sound of it.

questions.q: A short wise saying like 'Look before you leap' is called a what?
questions.f: Many proverbs began as the morals of fables told thousands of years ago.

questions.q: A group of lines in a poem, like a paragraph in a story, is called a what?
questions.f: Poets leave a blank line between stanzas, like taking a breath between thoughts.

questions.q: A 'kingdom' is the land that a king does what to?
questions.f: The '-dom' ending shows up in other words too, like 'freedom' and 'wisdom.'

questions.q: The list at the front of a book showing its chapters is called the table of what?
questions.f: It is a 'table' in the old sense of a list — no furniture involved.

questions.q: Very old stories about gods, heroes, and how the world began are called what?
questions.f: Greek myths gave us characters like Hercules and flying Pegasus.

questions.q: When authors 'revise' a story, what do they do?
questions.f: Famous authors often revise a story many times before anyone else sees it.

questions.q: Adding '-ly' to 'happy' makes 'happily' — as in happily ever what?
questions.f: The '-ly' ending turns describing words into how-words: brave becomes bravely.

questions.q: A baby goose, like the ones following Mother Goose, is called a what?
questions.f: The Ugly Duckling was really a cygnet — a baby swan — mixed in with the ducklings.

questions.q: An 'avid' reader is a reader who is very what?
questions.f: Avid readers are the ones who read under the covers with a flashlight.

questions.q: The '-er' ending in 'writer' and 'reader' turns an action into a what?
questions.f: Write becomes writer, tell becomes teller, dream becomes dreamer.

questions.q: The setting of a story is where and when it happens.
questions.f: Change the setting and everything changes — Cinderella on the Moon would be a new tale.

questions.q: 'Tale' and 'tail' sound the same but mean different things.
questions.f: Sound-alike words like these are called homophones — spelling-bee favorites!

questions.q: Adding '-s' to 'book' makes it mean more than one book.
questions.f: Watch out: some plurals break the rule, like 'mouse' becoming 'mice.'

questions.q: The syllables in a word are the beats you can clap, like el-e-phant.
questions.f: Haiku poets count syllables the same way to build their three-line poems.

questions.q: A nonfiction book is full of made-up magic adventures.
questions.f: Nonfiction means true facts — books about volcanoes, planets, or real explorers.

questions.q: In the Greek story of the golden touch, everything King Midas touches turns to what?
questions.f: Midas is delighted — until his breakfast and even his daughter turn to gold.

questions.q: American tall tales say Johnny Appleseed walked the land planting what?
questions.f: He was based on a real man, John Chapman, who really did plant apple orchards.

questions.q: In tall tales, Paul Bunyan's giant companion Babe is a big blue what?
questions.f: Stories say Babe was so huge that his footprints filled with water and became lakes.

questions.q: Winnie the Pooh gets stuck in Rabbit's front doorway. Why?
questions.f: Pooh has to wait until he gets thinner — his friends use his legs as a towel rack.

questions.q: In the rhyme, what does Tom, Tom, the Piper's Son steal and run away with?
questions.f: In the rhyme it was likely a pastry pig — a little pig-shaped treat sold at fairs.

questions.q: 'Ride a cock-horse to Banbury Cross, to see a fine lady upon a white ___.'
questions.f: With rings on her fingers and bells on her toes, she shall have music wherever she goes.

questions.q: In Grimm's The Star Money, what falls from the sky for the kind, giving girl?
questions.f: She gives away everything she owns — then the stars themselves shower her with silver.

questions.q: How does Dorothy finally travel home from Oz?
questions.f: The balloon leaves without her, so the magic shoes carry her home in three steps.

questions.q: After nibbling a magic cake, Alice grows so big she fills the White Rabbit's what?
questions.f: Stuck with an arm out the window, giant Alice hears the Rabbit's plans to smoke her out!

questions.q: What is the family name of Wendy, John, and Michael in Peter Pan?
questions.f: Barrie borrowed bits of the family from real friends of his, the Llewelyn Davies boys.

questions.q: In Charlotte's Web, who saves Wilbur the piglet first, even before Charlotte does?
questions.f: Eight-year-old Fern stops her father and raises the tiny runt piglet herself.

questions.q: In Heidi, what is the name of Heidi's friend the goatherd?
questions.f: Peter leads the village goats up the mountain every summer morning.

questions.q: In Black Beauty, Merrylegs is a favorite of the children. What is Merrylegs?
questions.f: The gentle gray pony gives rides to the children and never once loses his temper.

questions.q: In Aesop's fable, two stubborn goats meet in the middle of a narrow bridge. What won't they do?
c: Step back to let the other pass
questions.f: Neither will give way — and both end up tumbling into the stream below.

questions.q: Robin Hood's biggest, tallest friend has which joking name?
questions.f: Legend says John Little's name was flipped as a joke after he beat Robin in a quarterstaff duel.

questions.q: Robin Hood wins the Sheriff's archery contest with an amazing shot. What does his arrow do?
c: Splits the other arrow in the bullseye
questions.f: Splitting an arrow already in the bullseye is still called a 'Robin Hood' by archers today.

questions.q: King Arthur's famous castle and court are called what?
questions.f: Storytellers have placed Camelot all over Britain — no one knows where it 'really' was.

questions.q: Complete the famous story title: 'Ali Baba and the ___ Thieves.'
questions.f: The thieves hide inside giant oil jars to sneak into Ali Baba's house.

questions.q: In The Snow Queen, how is Kai carried away to the far north?
questions.f: Kai ties his little sled to her great white sledge — and it never stops.

questions.q: In Collodi's Pinocchio, which tiny creature keeps giving Pinocchio wise advice?
questions.f: The Talking Cricket has advised the puppet for over a century — long before any movie.

questions.q: What finally defeats the Wicked Witch of the West in The Wizard of Oz?
questions.f: Dorothy is only trying to rinse off a spill — and the astonished witch melts away.

questions.q: The rhyme 'Thirty days hath September' helps you remember the days in each month.
questions.f: People have leaned on this little memory rhyme since at least the 1500s.

questions.q: Pegasus, the flying creature of Greek stories, is a winged horse.
questions.f: Poets claimed a spring of inspiration bubbled up where Pegasus stamped his hoof.

questions.q: In The Jungle Book, Bagheera is a brown bear.
questions.f: Bagheera is a sleek black panther — his name comes from a Hindi word for tiger.

questions.q: In fables, taking 'the lion's share' means taking what?
questions.f: In Aesop's fable the lion claims every single portion of the hunt — that's the joke.

questions.q: In 'spelling bee,' the word 'bee' means what?
c: A gathering to do something together
questions.f: Old-time neighbors held quilting bees and husking bees — work parties with friends.

questions.q: 'Once, twice, thrice' — 'thrice' means how many times?
questions.f: 'Thrice' sounds old-fashioned now, but fairy tales love things that happen three times.

questions.q: The smaller second title under a book's main title is called the what?
questions.f: 'Sub-' means under — a subtitle sits under the main title on the cover.

questions.q: An author's messy first version of a story is called a rough what?
questions.f: Famous authors may write ten drafts before a story feels just right.

questions.q: The blank space around the edges of a book page is called the what?
questions.f: Long ago, students and monks scribbled notes — even doodles — in the margins.

questions.q: Which letters are the vowels of the English alphabet?
questions.f: The letter Y moonlights as a vowel too, in words like 'myth' and 'rhyme.'

questions.q: Which punctuation marks show the exact words a character speaks?
questions.f: In British books they're often single quotes; American books usually use double.

questions.q: A king's official joke-teller and entertainer is called the court what?
questions.f: Jesters wore belled caps and were often the only ones allowed to tease the king.
