questions.q: In the Middle Ages, a 'minstrel' was a person who did what?
c: Traveled about singing songs and tales
questions.f: Minstrels carried news and stories from castle to castle, like walking radio stations.

questions.q: A book where you write what happened in your own day is called a what?
questions.f: Some famous classic books are written as if they were a character's private diary.

questions.q: If something ends 'like a fairy tale,' how does it end?
questions.f: That's why weddings and lucky wins get called 'fairy-tale endings.'

questions.q: The 'nursery' in 'nursery rhyme' refers to what?
questions.f: Nursery rhymes were sung in children's rooms long before they were ever printed.

questions.q: 'Dragon' comes before 'dwarf' in alphabetical order.
questions.f: Both start with D, so you compare the next letters: R comes before W.

questions.q: In the story of Rumpelstiltskin, how does the queen learn the little man's secret?
c: She reads it in a book
questions.f: He dances round his fire singing his own name — the worst way to keep a secret.

questions.q: In Grimm's The Bremen Town Musicians, what do the animals want to become?
questions.f: None of them can really play — but their noise is enough to win them a home.

questions.q: In Andersen's The Princess and the Pea, how does the prince know she is a real princess?
c: She felt the pea through the mattresses
She knew all the royal names
questions.f: The bruised, sleepless princess proves her royalty by being extremely sensitive.

questions.q: In the Grimm tale, why do the twelve dancing princesses wear out their shoes each night?
c: They sneak away to a secret ball
They run races in the garden
questions.f: A clever soldier follows them through a trapdoor to an underground palace.

questions.q: In the tale of the Nightingale, what does the emperor prefer at first?
c: A painted picture of a bird
questions.f: When the clockwork bird breaks, only the real nightingale can help him.

questions.q: In Aesop's Lion and the Mouse, why does the lion let the tiny mouse go?
c: He is amused by the mouse's promise to help
The mouse is too small to eat
questions.f: Later the mouse gnaws through ropes to free the lion — small friends can do great things.

questions.q: In the fable of the Milkmaid, why does she spill all her milk?
c: She daydreams and tosses her head
questions.f: She is busy imagining the dress she'll buy — and the pail slides off her head.

questions.q: In Aesop's fable, the two travelers meet a bear. What does the boastful one do?
c: Climbs a tree and leaves his friend
questions.f: The other plays dead, then jokes the bear told him never to trust a false friend.

questions.q: Which Beatrix Potter character is a very naughty squirrel who teases an owl?
questions.f: Nutkin's riddles annoy Old Brown the owl so much that he loses his tail.

questions.q: In Beatrix Potter's tale, Jeremy Fisher goes fishing while sitting on a what?
questions.f: Jeremy is a frog in a mackintosh coat and shiny goloshes.

questions.q: In Alice in Wonderland, which creature recites the poem about the crocodile and hosts nothing at all?
questions.f: Mock turtle soup was a real Victorian dish made without any turtle — hence the sad creature.

questions.q: Who first tells the Emperor that his invisible new clothes are beautiful?
questions.f: Nobody wants to admit they see nothing, in case it means they are foolish.

questions.q: In Aladdin's story, the ring and the lamp each hold a what?
questions.f: The ring's genie is far less powerful than the mighty genie of the lamp.

questions.q: In the Grimm tale, what does the frog want in return for fetching the golden ball?
c: To eat and live with the princess
questions.f: The princess keeps her promise unwillingly — and the spell breaks anyway.

questions.q: In The Wizard of Oz, which of Dorothy's friends is afraid of getting wet?
questions.f: Rain would rust the Tin Man solid, so he carries his own oil can everywhere.

questions.q: In Peter Pan, why does Captain Hook fear the crocodile?
questions.f: It also swallowed a clock, so Hook always hears it ticking before it arrives.

questions.q: In the Panchatantra tale, how does the clever crow trick the snake?
c: By dropping a stolen necklace near its hole
questions.f: Servants come hunting for the missing necklace — and the snake gets found instead.

questions.q: In fables, which animal is most often shown as slow but wise?
questions.f: Tortoises can really live over 100 years, so 'old and wise' fits them well.

questions.q: In Robin Hood stories, the monk who joins the outlaws is called Friar who?
questions.f: Friar Tuck is famous for enjoying a good meal as much as a good fight.

questions.q: In The Secret Garden, who is the sickly boy Mary discovers in the great house?
questions.f: Colin believes he will never walk — until the garden and fresh air change everything.

questions.q: In Tom Sawyer, what does Tom find in the cave with Becky?
questions.f: He later returns and digs up a box holding thousands of dollars in gold coins.

questions.q: Where do the Lilliputians in Gulliver's Travels famously argue about how to break an egg?
c: At the big end or the little end
With a spoon or a knife
questions.f: Swift used the silly quarrel to poke fun at grown-ups fighting over small things.

questions.q: In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver later visits a land of giants.
questions.f: In Brobdingnag Gulliver is the tiny one, kept in a box and nearly eaten by a monkey.

questions.q: In Andersen's The Little Mermaid, the mermaid trades her voice away.
questions.f: The sea witch takes her beautiful voice in exchange for legs.

questions.q: Aesop's fable about the boy who cried wolf teaches that lying costs you trust.
questions.f: When the real wolf comes, nobody believes the boy's cries anymore.

questions.q: The word 'fairy' comes from an old word connected to what?
questions.f: Latin fata meant the Fates — the powers said to decide people's destinies.

questions.q: A 'troll' in folk tales is usually described as what?
questions.f: 'Troll' came into English from Norse tales, where they live in rocks and under bridges.

questions.q: A 'giant' is huge. The opposite word for a very small storybook person is a what?
questions.f: In old Norse tales dwarfs are master smiths who forge magical treasures.

questions.q: What does a 'chapter book' mean?
c: A book with no pictures allowed
questions.f: Moving up to chapter books is a big step for a young reader.

questions.q: An 'anthology' of poems is what?
questions.f: From Greek words for 'flower gathering' — an anthology is a bouquet of writing.

questions.q: The word 'nonsense' means what?
c: Words that make no sense on purpose
questions.f: Edward Lear made nonsense a proper art form with his silly verses.

questions.q: If a story is 'told from the point of view' of a character, that means what?
c: We see events as that character does
questions.f: Switching point of view can turn a hero into a villain and back again.

questions.q: A story's 'theme' is what?
questions.f: Kindness beats cleverness is a theme running through many Aesop fables.

questions.q: When a fairy tale calls someone 'wicked,' it means they are what?
questions.f: 'Wicked' shares an old root with 'witch' — both once meant twisted or bent.

questions.q: In the phrase 'nursery rhyme,' rhymes are helpful because they are easy to do what?
questions.f: Before books were common, rhyme and rhythm were how stories stayed alive.

questions.q: The word 'moral' in a fable means what?
questions.f: From Latin mores, meaning customs or manners — the way people ought to behave.

questions.q: Which is a plural formed the tricky way, not by adding -s?
questions.f: Old English changed vowels to make plurals — mouse/mice, goose/geese, foot/feet.

questions.q: 'Beauty and the Beast' both start with B. What is that repeated sound called?
questions.f: Titles use alliteration because repeated sounds are catchy and easy to recall.

questions.q: 'Aesop' is the name of a person. Names of people and places are called what nouns?
questions.f: Proper nouns always get a capital letter, wherever they appear in a sentence.

questions.q: 'The Tortoise and the Hare' — a hare is like a what, but bigger and faster?
questions.f: Hares are born with fur and open eyes, while rabbits are born bald and blind.

questions.q: A 'novelist' is a person who writes what?
questions.f: Some novelists write a book every year; others take a decade over one.

questions.q: A 'playwright' writes what?
questions.f: The '-wright' ending means maker — like a shipwright who builds ships.

questions.q: A word that reads the same forwards and backwards, like 'level,' is a what?
questions.f: From Greek for 'running back again' — 'racecar' and 'noon' work too.

questions.q: In a play, the words that tell actors what to do are called stage what?
questions.f: Shakespeare's most famous stage direction is 'Exit, pursued by a bear.'

questions.q: Words like 'their' and 'there' sound alike but mean different things.
questions.f: Homophones like these trip up even confident spellers.

questions.q: The word 'library' comes from a Latin word for book.
questions.f: Latin liber meant book, so a library is literally a book-place.

questions.q: An 'author' and a 'narrator' are always exactly the same person.
questions.f: The author writes the book; the narrator is the voice inside it — sometimes a horse or a mouse.

questions.q: Homer's epic poem the Odyssey follows which hero's long journey home?
questions.f: His trip home from the Trojan War takes ten whole years of storms, monsters, and detours.

questions.q: In the legend of Troy, what did Greek soldiers hide inside to sneak into the city?
c: A giant statue of a lion
questions.f: The Trojans wheeled the 'gift' inside themselves — with soldiers waiting in its hollow belly.

questions.q: Which ancient poet is credited with composing both the Iliad and the Odyssey?
questions.f: Ancient tradition says Homer was blind and recited his enormous poems from memory.

questions.q: In Jules Verne's novel, who races around the world in eighty days?
questions.f: Fogg wins his bet by one day, thanks to crossing the date line without realizing it.

questions.q: In Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, what is the Nautilus?
questions.f: Verne imagined an electric submarine decades before real ones ruled the deep.

questions.q: In Norse tales, Thor rides a chariot pulled across the sky by two what?
questions.f: Legends say the rumble of Thor's chariot wheels is the sound of thunder.

questions.q: The Headless Horseman gallops through which Washington Irving story?
questions.f: The nervous schoolmaster Ichabod Crane meets the Horseman on a dark ride home.

questions.q: 'Listen, my children, and you shall hear of the midnight ride of ___.'
questions.f: Longfellow's poem made Revere's 1775 warning ride one of America's most famous stories.

questions.q: In Wordsworth's poem that begins 'I wandered lonely as a cloud,' the poet sees a crowd of what?
questions.f: Wordsworth really did see those daffodils beside a lake in England's Lake District.

questions.q: William Blake's famous poem begins, 'Tyger Tyger, burning ___.'
questions.f: Blake spelled 'tyger' the old-fashioned way and printed the poem with his own artwork.

questions.q: In Robert Frost's famous poem, the traveler must choose between two what?
questions.f: He takes the road less traveled by — 'and that has made all the difference.'

questions.q: The famous American poem Casey at the Bat is about which sport?
questions.f: Crowds loved hearing the poem performed on stage in the 1880s, like a comedy show.

questions.q: Which writer is nicknamed 'the Bard of Avon'?
questions.f: 'Bard' is an old word for poet, and Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon.

questions.q: What was the Globe in Shakespeare's London?
questions.f: The round, open-air Globe has been rebuilt, and plays are performed there today.

questions.q: Puck, the mischievous fairy who loves pranks, appears in which Shakespeare play?
questions.f: Puck brags he can put a girdle round the earth in forty minutes.

questions.q: Jean de La Fontaine, who retold Aesop's fables as elegant poems, lived in which country?
questions.f: French schoolchildren still memorize La Fontaine's fables, like The Crow and the Fox.

questions.q: Anansi, the trickster hero of many West African tales, is what kind of creature?
questions.f: Anansi stories crossed the ocean with storytellers and are now told across the Caribbean too.

questions.q: Br'er Rabbit begs NOT to be thrown into the one place he secretly wants to go. Where?
questions.f: Born and bred in the briar patch, the trickster rabbit escapes through the thorns laughing.

questions.q: In the American tall tale, steel-driving John Henry races against what?
questions.f: Songs about John Henry's mighty race have been sung for well over a century.

questions.q: In Norse folk tales, what happens to trolls caught in sunlight?
questions.f: Some strange rock formations in Norway are said to be trolls who stayed out too late.

questions.q: In Greek myth, what does Pandora open, letting troubles loose upon the world?
questions.f: In the oldest Greek tellings it was actually a large jar — 'box' came from a later translation.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Icarus falls because he flies too close to what?
questions.f: The wax holding his feather wings melts, a story still told as a warning against overconfidence.

questions.q: The Greek hero Hercules is most famous for his amazing what?
questions.f: Stories say he completed twelve nearly impossible tasks, called the Labors of Hercules.

questions.q: In Andersen's tale, what does the Little Match Girl sell on the cold streets?
questions.f: Each match she strikes glows with a warm, wonderful vision in the winter night.

questions.q: In Andersen's The Wild Swans, Elisa's eleven brothers are turned into what?
questions.f: To break the spell, Elisa must knit eleven shirts from stinging nettles without saying a word.

questions.q: Kipling's brave Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, who guards a family's garden, is what kind of animal?
questions.f: Real mongooses are famously quick enough to battle cobras — just like Rikki-Tikki.

questions.q: In The Jungle Book, which animals raise the boy Mowgli as their own?
questions.f: Mowgli's wolf family calls him 'man-cub' and teaches him the Law of the Jungle.

questions.q: When the curtain is pulled back, the great Wizard of Oz turns out to be what?
questions.f: He calls himself a humbug — a faker — but still helps Dorothy's friends see their own strengths.

questions.q: Robin Hood's greatest enemy holds which title?
questions.f: Nottingham is a real English city, and its castle still celebrates the Robin Hood legend.

questions.q: The Dewey Decimal system, used in many libraries, is a way of doing what?
questions.f: Melvil Dewey invented it in 1876, giving every subject its own number range.

questions.q: In old legends, the phoenix is a bird reborn from its own what?
questions.f: Stories say only one phoenix lives at a time, bursting into flame and rising young again.

questions.q: Writers long ago used quill pens, which were made from what?
questions.f: Goose feathers worked best, and writers kept a knife handy to sharpen them — a 'pen knife.'

questions.q: In Wonderland, what happens when Alice drinks from the bottle labeled 'DRINK ME'?
questions.f: She shuts up like a telescope, shrinking to just ten inches tall.

questions.q: In Andersen's tale, the one-legged Steadfast Tin Soldier loves a paper what?
questions.f: The paper dancer stands on one leg too, which makes the soldier feel they are alike.

questions.q: In Aesop's fable, how does the reed survive the storm that topples the mighty oak?
questions.f: The fable teaches that flexible things can outlast the strong but stiff.

questions.q: In Andersen's The Snow Queen, what is the queen's faraway palace made of?
questions.f: Her great halls are lit by the northern lights, with a frozen lake at the very center.

questions.q: The ruins of Troy, the city from Homer's epics, were found by archaeologists in modern Turkey.
questions.f: For centuries people thought Troy was pure legend — until diggers uncovered it in the 1870s.

questions.q: Jules Verne wrote about a voyage to the Moon a century before real astronauts went there.
questions.f: His 1865 story even launched its travelers from Florida, close to where Apollo missions later left Earth.

questions.q: The poem Casey at the Bat ends with Casey hitting a mighty home run.
questions.f: The famous last line says there is no joy in Mudville — mighty Casey has struck out.

questions.q: The Cheshire Cat is a character in The Wizard of Oz.
questions.f: The grinning Cheshire Cat belongs to Alice's Wonderland, not Dorothy's Oz.

questions.q: How many lines does a sonnet have?
questions.f: Shakespeare wrote 154 of them, and poets still use the 14-line form today.

questions.q: A quatrain is a stanza made of how many lines?
questions.f: The 'quat-' root, meaning four, also shows up in 'quartet' and 'quarter.'

questions.q: A very long poem about a hero's great deeds, like the Odyssey, is called an what?
questions.f: We now call any huge adventure 'epic' thanks to these giant old poems.

questions.q: A poem that tells a story and was often sung is called a what?
questions.f: Old ballads about Robin Hood carried his legend for centuries before books did.

questions.q: 'Her smile was like sunshine' — comparing with 'like' or 'as' is called a what?
questions.f: 'Simile' is closely related to 'similar' — both come from a root meaning alike.

questions.q: 'The sea was an angry beast' — a comparison without 'like' or 'as' is a what?
questions.f: Its root idea is 'carrying across' — a metaphor carries meaning from one thing to another.

questions.q: 'The wind whispered secrets' gives human traits to the wind. That device is called what?
questions.f: Fables personify animals the same way, letting foxes flatter and lions rule.

questions.q: 'I've told you a MILLION times!' — huge exaggeration in writing is called what?
questions.f: Tall tales like Paul Bunyan's run entirely on hyperbole.

questions.q: 'Peter Piper picked a peck' repeats starting sounds. That trick is called what?
questions.f: Poets love alliteration because repeated sounds make lines almost sing.

questions.q: Sound-imitating words like 'buzz' and 'splash' are examples of what?
questions.f: Onomatopoeia is a spelling-bee classic — five vowels in a row near the end!

questions.q: When a poem is signed 'Anonymous,' what does that tell you?
questions.f: Its roots mean 'without a name' — many beloved nursery rhymes are anonymous.

questions.q: The prefix 'auto-' in 'autobiography' means what?
questions.f: An autobiography is self-life-writing — three Greek pieces glued together.

questions.q: The root 'biblio-' in 'bibliophile' means what?
questions.f: From Greek biblion — the ancient city of Byblos traded the papyrus books were made from.

questions.q: The word 'poet' comes from an ancient root meaning a what?
questions.f: From Greek poietes — the Greeks saw poets as makers who built things from words.

questions.q: Ordinary writing that is not poetry — like most storybooks — is called what?
questions.f: From Latin prosa, 'straightforward speech' — writing that marches ahead in plain lines.

questions.q: The word 'fable' comes from the Latin 'fabula,' meaning a what?
questions.f: From Latin fari, 'to speak' — a fable is simply 'a thing told.'

questions.q: The Ugly Duckling was really a baby swan all along. A baby swan is called a what?
questions.f: 'Cygnet' is a little Latin-based word meaning 'small swan' — with a soft g, like 'signet.'

questions.q: Which reference book do writers open to find synonyms?
questions.f: 'Thesaurus' comes from a Greek word for treasure — it is literally a treasury of words.

questions.q: The mini-dictionary of special terms at the back of a book is called a what?
questions.f: It grew from 'glosses' — little explanations scribes once wrote in the margins.

questions.q: In which kind of poem do the first letters of each line spell out a word?
questions.f: Poets have hidden names and secret messages in acrostics for thousands of years.

questions.q: A line or verse that repeats again and again through a poem or song is the what?
questions.f: Old ballads used refrains so listeners could join in on every chorus.

questions.q: The funny five-line 'limerick' poem takes its name from a what?
questions.f: An old party song invited guests to 'come up to Limerick' — the name stuck to the verse form.

questions.q: 'Genre' — as in the fantasy or mystery genre — means what?
c: A kind or category of story
questions.f: It is a French word for 'kind,' cousin to 'general' and 'gender.'

questions.q: 'Narrate' comes from a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: From Latin narrare — related to 'gnarus,' knowing, because a teller must know the tale.

questions.q: The word 'paper' comes from the name of what?
questions.f: Egyptians pressed strips of the papyrus reed into sheets five thousand years ago.

questions.q: The word 'alphabet' is built from what?
questions.f: Alpha and beta lead the Greek alphabet — like calling ours 'the ay-bee.'

questions.q: The root 'graph' in 'autograph' and 'paragraph' means what?
questions.f: Greek graphein first meant to scratch or carve — the earliest writing was scratched into clay and stone.

questions.q: When a story jumps back in time to show something that happened earlier, that is a what?
questions.f: Storytellers as old as Homer used flashbacks — the Odyssey starts in the middle and looks back.

questions.q: A 'wordsmith' is someone who does what?
questions.f: A smith shapes metal; a wordsmith hammers sentences into shape.

questions.q: Before printing presses, who copied books out by hand?
questions.f: From Latin scribere, 'to write' — one careful scribe could spend a year on a single book.

questions.q: An 'owlet' is a what?
questions.f: The '-et' and '-let' endings mean little — a booklet is a little book, a piglet a little pig.

questions.q: A poem's 'rhyme scheme,' written with letters like AABB, shows what?
c: Which lines rhyme with each other
questions.f: Matching letters mark matching sounds — AABB means the first two lines rhyme, then the next two.

questions.q: Poetry with no set rhyme or regular beat is called what?
questions.f: Walt Whitman helped make free verse famous — poems that flow like natural speech.

questions.q: A long invented story like Treasure Island is a 'novel' — a word that originally meant what?
questions.f: From Latin novus — when novels appeared, they were the 'new' kind of story.

questions.q: Which everyday word is a cousin of 'fable' and once meant 'like something from the old tales'?
questions.f: Calling dessert 'fabulous' literally calls it the stuff of fables.

questions.q: Which word shares its Latin root — 'to write' — with 'scribble'?
questions.f: Scribere gave English describe, scribe, script, and even prescription.

questions.q: Which word shares its Latin root — 'to say' — with 'dictionary'?
questions.f: Dicere, 'to say,' also built dictate, verdict, and contradict.

questions.q: Which word shares its 'singing' root with 'chant'?
questions.f: To enchant once meant to sing a spell over someone — magic and music in one word.

questions.q: The root of 'legible' — as in legible handwriting — means what?
questions.f: Latin legere, 'to read,' also hides inside 'lecture' and 'legend.'

questions.q: The 'audio' in 'audiobook' comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: Latin audire also gives us audience — literally 'the hearers' of a tale.

questions.q: A female hero of a story is called a what?
questions.f: Watch the spelling: the story heroine ends in '-ine,' one letter different from a medicine word.

questions.q: A book of maps is called an 'atlas' after a figure from Greek myth who did what?
questions.f: Early map books showed the Titan Atlas carrying the heavens, and his name stuck.

questions.q: A 'bibliography' at the end of a book lists what?
questions.f: Biblio + graphy: literally 'book-writing' — a written record of books.

questions.q: A poem written to praise or celebrate something, like 'Ode to Autumn,' is an what?
questions.f: From a Greek word for song — odes were once sung to music at festivals.

questions.q: A couplet is a pair of lines of poetry that rhyme with each other.
questions.f: Shakespeare ended his sonnets with a couplet — two rhyming lines that snap shut like a lid.

questions.q: The prefix 'tri-' in 'trilogy' means three.
questions.f: A trilogy is a story told in three books — the same 'tri-' as in triangle and tricycle.

questions.q: The word 'ballad' comes from an old root meaning 'to dance.'
questions.f: Ballads began as dancing songs — 'ballad,' 'ballet,' and 'ballroom' are all cousins.

questions.q: 'Read' (today) and 'read' (yesterday) are spelled the same but pronounced differently.
questions.f: Words spelled alike but said differently are called homographs — 'same writing' in Greek.

questions.q: An epilogue appears at the very beginning of a book.
questions.f: Epi- means 'after' — an epilogue follows the ending, while a prologue leads the way in.

questions.q: The word 'bookkeeper' has three double letters in a row.
questions.f: The oo-kk-ee run makes it a favorite oddity among spelling fans.

questions.q: In Aesop's Dog in the Manger, the dog cannot eat hay — yet he stops the ox from doing what?
questions.f: A 'dog in the manger' now means anyone who blocks others from what they can't use themselves.

questions.q: In the famous story, a Dutch boy saves his town by plugging a leak with his finger. A leak in what?
c: A dike holding back the sea
questions.f: The tale appears in the American book Hans Brinker — and Holland later put up statues of the boy.

questions.q: In the Nutcracker story, the toy nutcracker leads an army against the King of the what?
questions.f: E.T.A. Hoffmann's 1816 tale later inspired Tchaikovsky's beloved Christmas ballet.

questions.q: In A Christmas Carol, which character says, 'God bless us, every one!'
questions.f: Tiny Tim's cheerful blessing closes Dickens's story on its warmest note.

questions.q: In Twain's The Prince and the Pauper, two boys can swap lives because they look what?
questions.f: A poor boy and Prince Edward trade clothes for fun — and get trapped in each other's lives.

questions.q: Huckleberry Finn floats his raft down which great American river?
questions.f: Mark Twain piloted steamboats on the Mississippi before he ever wrote about it.

questions.q: What amazing thing can Doctor Dolittle do?
questions.f: His parrot Polynesia is the one who first teaches him animal languages.

questions.q: In Kenneth Grahame's The Reluctant Dragon, the dragon would rather do what than fight?
questions.f: The boy and St. George end up staging a pretend battle so everyone stays happy.

questions.q: In Oscar Wilde's The Happy Prince, what does the jeweled statue give away to help the poor?
questions.f: A loyal swallow delays flying south to carry the statue's treasures across the city.

questions.q: In Wilde's The Selfish Giant, what season refuses to leave the giant's garden?
questions.f: Spring returns only when the giant knocks down his wall and lets the children play again.

questions.q: In the Japanese tale, the hero Momotaro is discovered inside a giant what?
questions.f: His name means 'Peach Boy,' and he sets off with a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant.

questions.q: Stories from the Arabian Nights made famous a carpet that can do what?
questions.f: In the tale, Prince Husain buys the magic carpet at a market in Bisnagar.

questions.q: Before his long sleep, Rip Van Winkle joins strange mountain men playing which game?
questions.f: Their rolling ninepin balls were said to be the thunder echoing in the Catskills.

questions.q: In the fable, Mercury offers a woodcutter a golden axe. What does the honest man say?
questions.f: For his honesty he receives the gold, the silver, AND his own axe back.

questions.q: In Grimm's Snow-White and Rose-Red, the friendly bear at the door is really a what?
questions.f: The sisters brush snow from his fur all winter, never guessing his royal secret.

questions.q: Which Norse god is the famous shape-shifting trickster of the old tales?
questions.f: In one story Loki turns into a fly, in another a salmon — trouble in every shape.

questions.q: When Dorothy first arrives in Oz, whose small blue country does she land in?
questions.f: In Baum's book each region of Oz has its own color — Munchkin Country is blue.

questions.q: In the Queen of Hearts' croquet game, what do the players use as mallets?
questions.f: The balls are live hedgehogs, which keep unrolling and strolling away.

questions.q: Peter Pan leads a band of boys in Neverland known as the what?
questions.f: They fell out of their prams as babies, Peter says, and were never claimed.

questions.q: Kaa, who helps rescue Mowgli in The Jungle Book, is what kind of creature?
questions.f: In Kipling's book Kaa is wise and helpful — his hypnotic dance defeats the monkey tribe.

questions.q: Kipling's Just So story explains how the whale got his tiny what?
questions.f: A clever shipwrecked mariner wedges a grating in the whale's throat — so whales eat only small fish.

questions.q: In Eugene Field's lullaby poem, Wynken, Blynken, and Nod sail off in a what?
questions.f: They fish for herring in a river of dew among the stars — then turn out to be one sleepy child.

questions.q: In Edward Lear's limerick, what do the birds do in the Old Man's beard?
questions.f: Two owls and a hen, four larks and a wren — all nesting in one magnificent beard.

questions.q: In the old rhyme, on which day is Solomon Grundy born?
questions.f: The rhyme races through his whole life in a single week of days.

questions.q: The most famous library of the ancient world stood in Alexandria, in which country?
questions.f: Scholars there tried to collect a copy of every scroll in the known world.

questions.q: How do readers use braille to enjoy a story?
c: Feeling raised dots with their fingers
questions.f: Each braille letter fits in a six-dot cell small enough for one fingertip.

questions.q: Robinson Crusoe names his island companion after what?
questions.f: They meet on a Friday, so Crusoe calls his loyal friend Friday.

questions.q: In The Swiss Family Robinson, how does the family come to live on a wild island?
c: Their ship is wrecked in a storm
questions.f: They rescue tools and animals from the wreck and build a famous treehouse home.

questions.q: In Russian fairy tales, what is special about the Firebird's feathers?
questions.f: A single dropped feather keeps glowing — and tempts heroes into risky quests.

questions.q: In the fable of the Fox and the Cat, the cat escapes the hounds using its one trick. What is it?
questions.f: The fox brags of a hundred tricks but is caught deciding which to use — one good trick beats many.

questions.q: In Andersen's tale, tiny Thumbelina sleeps in a cradle made from a what?
questions.f: Her blanket is a rose petal and her mattress is made of violet leaves.

questions.q: Scrooge's famous catchphrase in A Christmas Carol is 'Bah! Humbug!'
questions.f: A 'humbug' was Victorian slang for a fraud — Scrooge thinks Christmas cheer is fake.

questions.q: In Russian tales, Baba Yaga's hut stands on giant chicken legs.
questions.f: The walking hut can turn to face visitors — who must know the polite words to make it open.

questions.q: Doctor Dolittle is famous for talking to plants.
questions.f: It's animals he talks with — from Gub-Gub the pig to the two-headed pushmi-pullyu.

questions.q: A 'fortnight' in old stories means how long?
questions.f: It squeezes 'fourteen nights' into one word — Britain still uses it daily.

questions.q: A knight's 'steed' in fairy tales is his what?
questions.f: 'Steed' is an Old English word saved from vanishing by storybooks and poems.

questions.q: When a storybook hero sets off on a 'quest,' what are they doing?
c: Making a long search for something
questions.f: From a Latin root meaning 'to seek' — the same root hiding in 'question.'

questions.q: A 'slumbering' princess is doing what?
questions.f: Slumber is a soft old word for sleep — perfect for hundred-year naps.

questions.q: In old tales, to 'dwell' in a cottage means to do what there?
questions.f: That's why a home is still called a 'dwelling' on official papers.

questions.q: When Jack and Jill 'fetch' a pail of water, what are they doing?
c: Going to get it and bring it back
questions.f: 'Fetch' packs a whole round trip into one small word — dogs know it well.

questions.q: A 'maiden' in old stories is a what?
questions.f: A ship's first trip is still called its 'maiden voyage' — its young journey.

questions.q: In old stories, your 'kin' are your what?
questions.f: 'Kin' hides inside 'king' — originally the leader of a family line.

questions.q: When a fairy-tale character cries 'Woe is me!' they are full of what?
questions.f: 'Woe' is one of English's oldest words — a cry of sorrow straight from Old English.

questions.q: Robin Hood's 'Merry' Men are what?
questions.f: 'Merry' meant pleasant and jolly — the same word we keep in 'Merry Christmas.'

questions.q: A 'cunning' fox in a fable is what?
questions.f: 'Cunning' originally just meant 'knowing' — foxes gave it its sneaky flavor.

questions.q: Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky opens with 'Twas brillig, and the slithy ___.'
questions.f: Carroll invented dozens of words here — 'chortle' and 'galumph' escaped into real English.

questions.q: A made-up word like Carroll's 'slithy' — blending 'slimy' and 'lithe' — is called a what?
questions.f: Humpty Dumpty explains the idea in Through the Looking-Glass: two meanings packed in one word.

questions.q: Which mirror-world sequel did Lewis Carroll write after Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
questions.f: Its chess-game structure means Alice starts as a pawn and ends up crowned a queen.

questions.q: Tweedledum and Tweedledee argue over a broken what?
questions.f: Their quarrel comes straight from an old nursery rhyme Carroll built a chapter around.

questions.q: In Through the Looking-Glass, which two creatures fight for the crown in the old rhyme?
questions.f: The lion and unicorn really do appear together on Britain's royal coat of arms.

questions.q: 'The Walrus and the Carpenter' is a poem recited inside which book?
questions.f: The pair persuade a crowd of young oysters to take a most unwise walk.

questions.q: In the Panchatantra frame story, why were the tales first told?
questions.f: A scholar promised to make three dull princes wise within six months — using stories.

questions.q: In Grimm's Hansel and Gretel, why do the breadcrumbs fail as a trail?
questions.f: Their first trail of white pebbles worked fine — bread was the fatal downgrade.

questions.q: In the Grimm tale, which bird helps Cinderella's cause instead of a fairy godmother?
questions.f: In the Grimms' version, birds at her mother's grave bring her gowns and sort her lentils.

questions.q: Andersen's tale The Emperor's New Clothes was published as part of a collection in which decade?
questions.f: It appeared in 1837, in the same little booklet as The Little Mermaid.

questions.q: In A Midsummer Night's Dream, what does Bottom's head get turned into?
questions.f: Puck's prank makes the fairy queen fall in love with a weaver wearing a donkey head.

questions.q: In Shakespeare's The Tempest, which spirit serves the magician Prospero?
questions.f: Ariel can whip up storms, turn invisible, and sing sailors to sleep.

questions.q: Which Greek storyteller's fables were passed on orally for centuries before being written down?
questions.f: The oldest surviving written collection dates from centuries after Aesop's supposed lifetime.

questions.q: In the Odyssey, what do the Sirens use to lure sailors?
questions.f: Odysseus plugs his crew's ears with wax and has himself tied to the mast to hear them safely.

questions.q: In the Odyssey, Penelope delays remarrying by promising to finish what first?
questions.f: Each night she secretly unravels the day's weaving, stretching the work for years.

questions.q: What is a 'chapbook,' sold cheaply in earlier centuries?
c: A small paper booklet of tales or ballads
questions.f: Chapbooks spread Jack the Giant Killer and Robin Hood to ordinary homes for a penny.

questions.q: Who compiled the first great Oxford-style English dictionary in 1755, almost single-handed?
questions.f: Johnson defined 'lexicographer' as 'a writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge.'

questions.q: William Caxton is remembered as the first person to do what in England?
questions.f: His press printed Chaucer's Canterbury Tales in the 1470s, spreading one spelling standard.

questions.q: An illuminated manuscript is a hand-made book decorated with what?
questions.f: 'Illuminated' means lit up — the gold really does glow in candlelight.

questions.q: Which storytelling tradition uses a 'griot' to keep a community's history in memory?
questions.f: A griot can recite generations of family history from memory, with music.

questions.q: Which epic of ancient India tells of Prince Rama's quest to rescue Sita?
questions.f: It is performed as dance and shadow-puppet theatre from India to Indonesia.

questions.q: In the Norse tales, what is Yggdrasil?
questions.f: Its branches hold up the worlds, and a squirrel named Ratatoskr runs messages along its trunk.

questions.q: Which epic is one of the oldest known works of literature, from ancient Mesopotamia?
questions.f: It was written on clay tablets around 4,000 years ago — and includes a great flood story.

questions.q: Which of these ancient works is a Roman epic about the founding of Rome?
questions.f: Virgil worked on it for over ten years and still called it unfinished.

questions.q: Lewis Carroll's real name was Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, and he taught mathematics.
questions.f: He lectured at Oxford, and his pen name was his real names translated and flipped around.

questions.q: Beatrix Potter first printed The Tale of Peter Rabbit herself after publishers turned it down.
questions.f: She printed 250 private copies in 1901; a publisher signed it the very next year.

questions.q: In Homer's Odyssey, the hero's faithful dog recognizes him after twenty years.
questions.f: Old Argos wags his tail at his disguised master — a scene readers still find moving.

questions.q: The word 'anthology' is built from Greek pieces meaning what?
questions.f: Ancient Greeks gathered short poems the way you'd gather blossoms for a bouquet.

questions.q: The root 'myth' in 'mythology' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: Greek mythos simply meant a tale told — the magic came later.

questions.q: The root 'phil' in 'bibliophile' means what?
questions.f: The same root builds 'philosophy' — love of wisdom.

questions.q: 'Manuscript' is built from Latin pieces meaning what?
questions.f: Manus (hand) plus scriptum (written) — every book was a manuscript before printing.

questions.q: The word 'volume' for a book comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Ancient books were scrolls you rolled up — hence volumen, a roll.

questions.q: The 'chapter' of a book comes from a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: Latin caput, head — a chapter is a 'heading,' the same root as 'captain' and 'capital.'

questions.q: 'Encyclopedia' is built from Greek pieces meaning roughly what?
questions.f: The idea is a circle of learning — everything a well-taught person should know.

questions.q: The word 'tragedy' in drama comes from a Greek word connected to what animal?
questions.f: Tragoidia means 'goat song' — scholars still argue about exactly why.

questions.q: The root 'nym' in 'pseudonym' and 'synonym' means what?
questions.f: A pseudonym is a false name; an anonymous writer has no name at all.

questions.q: 'Alliteration' contains a Latin root meaning what?
questions.f: Latin littera, letter — the same root behind 'literature' and 'literacy.'

questions.q: A 'protagonist' contains the prefix 'proto-', which means what?
questions.f: In Greek drama the protagonist was literally the first actor to compete alone on stage.

questions.q: The 'ant-' in 'antagonist' means what?
questions.f: Agon meant a contest, so the antagonist is the one struggling against the hero.

questions.q: What is a 'nom de plume'?
questions.f: It is French for 'pen name' — English borrowed the phrase whole.

questions.q: An author's short note thanking helpers at the front of a book is the what?
questions.f: It shares a root with 'know' — the author is publicly knowing who helped.

questions.q: When a story's ending is left unresolved to make you wait, it is called a what?
questions.f: Old magazine serials really did leave heroes hanging off cliffs to sell next month's issue.

questions.q: An 'idiom' like 'spill the beans' means what?
c: A phrase whose meaning isn't literal
A repeated line in a poem
questions.f: Idioms are the hardest part of any language — you cannot work them out word by word.

questions.q: A group of ravens, the birds of many old poems, is called an what?
questions.f: Collective nouns for birds are wonderfully odd: a murder of crows, an exaltation of larks.

questions.q: The word 'plot' can mean both a story's events and a patch of ground.
questions.f: One word, two lives — the story sense came later, from the idea of a mapped-out plan.

questions.q: In Poe's most famous poem, the visiting raven repeats which single word?
questions.f: Poe said he chose a raven because he needed a creature capable of speech but empty of reason.

questions.q: In A Christmas Carol, which former business partner visits Scrooge wrapped in chains?
questions.f: Marley's chain is forged from cash-boxes, keys, and ledgers — the things he cared for in life.

questions.q: Counting Marley, how many ghosts visit Scrooge in A Christmas Carol?
questions.f: Most people say three — forgetting Marley, who arrives first to announce the others.

questions.q: Don Quixote famously charges at windmills, mistaking them for what?
questions.f: 'Tilting at windmills' now means battling imaginary enemies.

questions.q: What is the name of Don Quixote's faithful, down-to-earth squire?
questions.f: Sancho rides a donkey named Dapple and dreams of governing his own island.

questions.q: Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote in which language?
questions.f: Spanish is still nicknamed 'la lengua de Cervantes' — the language of Cervantes.

questions.q: What were the first names of the two Brothers Grimm?
questions.f: Both were university librarians — collecting tales was their side project.

questions.q: A famous harbor statue in Copenhagen honors which Andersen character?
questions.f: The bronze mermaid, unveiled in 1913, is one of Denmark's most visited landmarks.

questions.q: In the original Arabian Nights text, the tale of Aladdin is set in which land?
questions.f: The storytellers set it in a fantasy 'China' — though everyone in it acts like they live in the Middle East.

questions.q: In the Old English epic, which monster does the hero Beowulf battle first?
questions.f: Beowulf fights the dragon too — but only fifty years later, as an old king.

questions.q: In The Canterbury Tales, why do the traveling pilgrims tell stories?
c: It is a contest with a prize
questions.f: The host promises the best storyteller a free supper at his inn.

questions.q: In Arthurian legend, Excalibur is finally returned to whom?
questions.f: A mysterious arm rises from the water, catches the thrown sword, and draws it under.

questions.q: Emily Dickinson wrote that 'Hope is the thing with ___.'
questions.f: Her tiny poem pictures hope as a bird that sings on without ever asking a crumb.

questions.q: Walt Whitman's poem 'O Captain! My Captain!' mourns which leader?
questions.f: Whitman pictures the nation as a ship that has weathered the storm — but lost its captain.

questions.q: Ivanhoe and Rob Roy are adventure novels by which Scottish writer?
questions.f: Scott was so popular that Edinburgh built him a 200-foot monument — the largest ever for a writer.

questions.q: Sherlock Holmes has an even more brilliant older brother. What is his name?
questions.f: Mycroft rarely leaves his armchair at the Diogenes Club — Sherlock says he sometimes IS the government.

questions.q: What is Sherlock Holmes's famous London address?
questions.f: Fans still mail letters to 221B — and a museum there answers some of them.

questions.q: In Jules Verne's novel, Professor Lidenbrock leads a journey to the center of what?
questions.f: The explorers climb down an Icelandic volcano and find an underground ocean.

questions.q: Who is the boy narrator of Treasure Island?
questions.f: Jim finds the treasure map in a dead pirate's sea chest at his family's inn.

questions.q: Anne of Green Gables insists her name be spelled a special way. What way?
questions.f: Anne says the E makes her name look 'so much more distinguished.'

questions.q: Anne of Green Gables is set on which Canadian island?
questions.f: Green Gables farm is a real place there that fans visit from around the world.

questions.q: In Baum's book, why does everything in the Emerald City look so green?
c: The city floats on a green lake
questions.f: The 'wizard' locks green glasses on every visitor — the city is no greener than any other.

questions.q: What is the name of Captain Hook's pirate ship in Peter Pan?
questions.f: 'Jolly Roger' is also the name for the skull-and-crossbones flag itself.

questions.q: How does Toad escape from prison in The Wind in the Willows?
c: Through a tunnel dug by Mole
By bribing the jailer with gold
questions.f: The jailer's daughter lends him the disguise — and Toad then steals a train ride home.

questions.q: Roughly how many tales did the Brothers Grimm's final edition contain?
questions.f: The seventh edition of 1857 held 210 tales — the brothers kept revising for forty years.

questions.q: What is the name of the lanky schoolmaster in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow?
questions.f: Irving named him Crane for his looks — long neck, long arms, and a nose like a beak.

questions.q: 'Mark Twain' was the pen name of which American writer?
questions.f: He tried other pen names first, including the wonderful 'Thomas Jefferson Snodgrass.'

questions.q: In Little Women, what does Jo March dream of becoming?
questions.f: Jo sells her first stories for pocket money — just as Louisa May Alcott really did.

questions.q: Little Women takes place during which war?
questions.f: The March girls' father is away serving as an army chaplain.

questions.q: E.B. White's small hero Stuart Little is what kind of creature?
questions.f: Stuart is born into an ordinary New York family — and sails a model boat in Central Park.

questions.q: How many Muses — goddesses of poetry and the arts — did the Greeks count?
questions.f: Both 'music' and 'museum' come from the Muses — a museum is literally their shrine.

questions.q: What are the names of Dorothy's aunt and uncle in The Wizard of Oz?
questions.f: Baum may have named Aunt Em after his own mother-in-law, Matilda 'Em' Gage's family.

questions.q: The Song of Hiawatha is a long poem by which American poet?
questions.f: Its drumming rhythm — 'By the shores of Gitche Gumee' — is instantly recognizable.

questions.q: Which Frost poem ends, 'And miles to go before I sleep'?
c: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
questions.f: Frost repeats the line twice, letting the poem drift off like the falling snow.

questions.q: Around 1455, Johannes Gutenberg printed Europe's first great movable-type book. What was it?
questions.f: About 49 copies of the Gutenberg Bible survive — each worth many millions today.

questions.q: The largest library in the world, the Library of Congress, is in which city?
questions.f: It holds over 170 million items on about 838 miles of shelves.

questions.q: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' is famous for being a what?
c: Sentence using every letter of the alphabet
questions.f: Typists and font designers have used this pangram to test every key since the 1880s.

questions.q: In The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, the sailor brings a curse on his ship by harming which bird?
questions.f: That's why a burden someone can't escape is called 'an albatross around the neck.'

questions.q: Charles Perrault published his famous 1697 fairy-tale collection in which language?
questions.f: His Paris collection gave us the classic versions of Cinderella and Puss in Boots.

questions.q: In Burnett's A Little Princess, which girl is left penniless at her boarding school?
questions.f: Sara keeps pretending she is a princess — 'It's easy to be one when everything is nice,' she says.

questions.q: Rip Van Winkle takes his twenty-year nap in which mountains?
questions.f: Irving set his tale in New York's Catskills, near the Hudson River villages he knew.

questions.q: What false name does Odysseus give the Cyclops to escape his cave?
questions.f: When blinded Polyphemus roars 'Nobody is hurting me!', his neighbors shrug and leave.

questions.q: Odin's two ravens fly the world gathering news. Their names mean what?
questions.f: Huginn and Muninn perch on Odin's shoulders each evening to whisper what they saw.

questions.q: Homer's Iliad takes its name from Ilium — another name for which city?
questions.f: 'Iliad' literally means 'the poem about Ilium.'

questions.q: Emily Dickinson published fewer than a dozen poems during her lifetime.
questions.f: After she died, her sister found nearly 1,800 poems hand-sewn into little booklets.

questions.q: The Canterbury Tales were written in Middle English.
questions.f: Chaucer's opening line — 'Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote' — still puzzles modern readers.

questions.q: Sherlock Holmes's loyal friend and chronicler is Dr. Watson.
questions.f: Almost all the stories are told in Watson's voice — he is the narrator, not Holmes.

questions.q: Beowulf is one of the oldest long poems in the English language.
questions.f: Its Old English is so different from ours that it must be translated like a foreign tongue.

questions.q: The word 'quixotic' means wildly idealistic. It is an eponym taken from what?
questions.f: Cervantes's windmill-charging hero gave English an adjective his own name now outlives.

questions.q: To 'pander' to someone comes from Pandarus, a go-between in tales about which city?
questions.f: Chaucer and Shakespeare both retold his story, and his name slid into English as a verb.

questions.q: A 'malapropism' — a comically wrong word choice — is named after a character in what?
questions.f: Mrs. Malaprop in Sheridan's play The Rivals mangles words in almost every speech.

questions.q: Calling a grumpy miser a 'Scrooge' is an example of which word-formation?
questions.f: Dickens invented the name in 1843; dictionaries now list 'scrooge' as a common noun.

questions.q: The word 'serendipity' was coined by Horace Walpole after a fairy tale set in which old land name?
questions.f: Serendip was an old name for Sri Lanka; Walpole minted the word in a 1754 letter.

questions.q: A 'catalogue' and a 'dialogue' share a Greek root meaning what?
questions.f: Logos, word — the same root behind 'logic,' 'prologue,' and 'monologue.'

questions.q: The 'stereo' in 'stereotype' originally described a printing plate that was what?
questions.f: Reusing one fixed plate is why a stereotype now means a rigid, unchanging image.

questions.q: The words 'cliche' and 'stereotype' both began as terms from which trade?
questions.f: A cliche was a ready-made printing block — literally a phrase cast to be used again.

questions.q: To 'read between the lines' and 'lower case' both come from technologies of what?
questions.f: Compositors kept capitals in the upper case of a type tray, small letters in the lower.

questions.q: An 'aside' in a play is a speech aimed at whom?
c: The audience, unheard by other characters
questions.f: Shakespeare's villains love asides — they let a schemer share plans with us alone.

questions.q: 'Soliloquy' is built from Latin pieces meaning what?
questions.f: Solus plus loqui — a character thinking aloud with nobody else on stage.

questions.q: In poetry, 'iambic pentameter' means each line has how many metrical feet?
questions.f: 'Penta' means five, and each iambic foot is a soft beat then a strong one: da-DUM.

questions.q: A poem's 'meter' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: Metron gave us both poetic meter and the metre you measure length with.

questions.q: An 'elegy' is a poem written for what purpose?
questions.f: Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard is among the most quoted poems in English.

questions.q: A 'villanelle' is a fixed poetic form with how many lines?
questions.f: Two repeating refrains weave through its five tercets and closing quatrain.

questions.q: A 'sestina' is a demanding poem form built on how many repeating end-words?
questions.f: The same six words end every stanza, shuffled in a strict spiral order.

questions.q: Which Japanese poetic form is a 31-syllable verse older than haiku?
questions.f: Its 5-7-5-7-7 pattern was the court poetry of Japan for over a thousand years.

questions.q: A 'senryu' looks like a haiku but differs how?
c: It is about human nature and often humorous
It never uses seasons words but must rhyme
questions.f: Haiku traditionally needs a season word; senryu skips nature and teases people instead.

questions.q: In haiku, a 'kigo' is what?
questions.f: 'Cherry blossom' signals spring; 'frog' points to summer — a kigo dates the poem instantly.

questions.q: A 'clerihew' is a short comic poem about what?
questions.f: E.C. Bentley invented the form as a schoolboy, poking fun at famous figures in four lines.

questions.q: 'Doggerel' describes verse that is what?
questions.f: Chaucer may have coined it as an insult — bad verse limping along like a mongrel.

questions.q: 'Bowdlerize' means to cut parts out of a book. It comes from what?
questions.f: Thomas Bowdler published a 'family' Shakespeare in 1807 with the awkward bits removed.

questions.q: A 'palimpsest' is a manuscript page that has been what?
c: Scraped clean and written on again
questions.f: Modern scanners can now read the erased under-layers, recovering lost ancient texts.

questions.q: A 'codex' differs from a scroll because it is what?
c: Bound in pages like a book
questions.f: The switch from scroll to codex around Roman times is why books have pages at all.

questions.q: 'Vellum,' used for the finest old manuscripts, was made from what?
questions.f: It shares a root with 'veal' — both trace back to a word for calf.

questions.q: A 'colophon' in a book is what?
c: A note about who printed it and when
questions.f: From a Greek word for 'summit' — the finishing touch at a book's very end.

questions.q: The 'incunabula' are books printed during which period?
questions.f: From Latin for 'swaddling clothes' — books from printing's infancy.

questions.q: A 'folio' book size gets its name from the sheet being folded how many times?
questions.f: Shakespeare's collected plays of 1623 are known simply as the First Folio.

questions.q: In storytelling, 'in medias res' means the tale begins where?
c: In the middle of the action
questions.f: Homer's Iliad starts nine years into the war — the classic example.

questions.q: A 'deus ex machina' ending is one where what happens?
c: An unlikely rescue arrives from nowhere
Everything is revealed as a dream
questions.f: Greek theatres used a crane to lower actors playing gods — 'god from the machine.'

questions.q: What does the term 'bildungsroman' describe?
questions.f: German for 'formation novel' — Anne of Green Gables and David Copperfield both qualify.

questions.q: An 'epistolary' novel is told through what?
questions.f: Latin epistola, letter — Dracula and Frankenstein both use the trick.

questions.q: A 'foil' character exists mainly to do what?
questions.f: Jewelers backed gems with shiny foil to make them sparkle — the metaphor stuck.

questions.q: In literature, 'pathos' refers to writing that does what?
questions.f: The same Greek root gives us 'sympathy' and 'pathetic.'

questions.q: An 'allegory' is a story in which what happens?
questions.f: Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress sends a man named Christian past a giant called Despair.

questions.q: 'Onomatopoeia' is built from Greek pieces meaning what?
questions.f: Greeks saw such words as freshly minted names for the noises themselves.

questions.q: An 'oxymoron' pairs two words that do what?
questions.f: 'Bittersweet' and 'deafening silence' are oxymorons — and the word itself is one: sharp-dull.

questions.q: 'Euphony' in poetry means what?
questions.f: Eu- means good, phone means sound — the opposite is the harsher cacophony.

questions.q: 'Enjambment' in poetry describes what?
c: A sentence running past the line break
questions.f: From French for 'striding over' — the meaning steps across into the next line.

questions.q: 'Assonance' repeats which sounds?
questions.f: 'The rain in Spain' leans on the long-a assonance to feel almost musical.

questions.q: A 'caesura' in a line of verse is what?
questions.f: Old English poems like Beowulf are built around a strong caesura in every line.

questions.q: In verse, a 'trochee' is a metrical foot with which pattern?
questions.f: 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright' hammers along in trochees — the reverse of an iamb.

questions.q: 'Blank verse' means poetry that is what?
questions.f: Most of Shakespeare's plays are in blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter.

questions.q: A 'kenning' in Old Norse and Old English poetry is what?
questions.f: Beowulf calls the sea a 'whale-road' and a king a 'ring-giver' — kennings all.

questions.q: A group of storytellers' term, 'anthropomorphism,' means giving animals what?
questions.f: Anthropos means human, morphe means shape — the engine of every talking-animal fable.

questions.q: 'Juvenilia' refers to what?
c: Works an author wrote when very young
questions.f: Jane Austen's teenage juvenilia survives — sharp, funny, and often absurd.

questions.q: A 'polyglot' reader of world folk tales is someone who does what?
questions.f: Poly plus glotta, tongue — the Grimms and Andersen were both read by polyglots first.

questions.q: A 'lexicon' is what?
questions.f: From Greek lexis, word — the same root inside 'lexicographer.'

questions.q: To 'gild the lily' means what?
questions.f: It is a friendly misquote of Shakespeare's King John, which spoke of painting the lily.

questions.q: The word 'novel' as a book and 'novel' meaning new share the same Latin root.
questions.f: Novus, new — early novels were sold as the newfangled kind of storytelling.

questions.q: A 'homograph' pair is spelled alike but may be pronounced differently.
questions.f: 'Bow' the ribbon and 'bow' the bend are homographs; 'bough' is only a homophone.

questions.q: The word 'anthology' originally referred to a collection of medicinal recipes.
questions.f: It meant a gathering of flowers — the metaphor was for short, pretty poems.

questions.q: Which award, first given in 1922, honors the year's best American children's book?
questions.f: It is named for John Newbery, the 18th-century London bookseller who made children's books a business.

questions.q: The Caldecott Medal is awarded specifically for excellence in what?
questions.f: It honors Randolph Caldecott, whose lively 1870s picture books changed the form forever.

questions.q: The Carnegie Medal for children's literature is awarded in which country?
questions.f: Andrew Carnegie funded thousands of public libraries, and British librarians named the prize for him.

questions.q: An old Cornish inn, a boy's lost map, and a marooned sailor eating cheese in his dreams all sail into which novel?
questions.f: Stevenson drew the treasure map first, to amuse his stepson — then wrote a book to fit it.

questions.q: A weaver's donkey head, a love potion squeezed from a flower, and a play-within-a-play about a wall belong to which comedy?
questions.f: The clumsy 'Pyramus and Thisbe' play at the end is Shakespeare cheerfully mocking bad theatre.

questions.q: A ninepin game in the Catskills, a musket rusted to powder, and a village that forgot a man's name point to which story?
questions.f: Irving wrote it while living in England, homesick for the Hudson Valley.

questions.q: A tin toymaker short of metal, a paper dancer, and a journey down a gutter in a folded boat belong to which tale?
questions.f: Andersen's soldier keeps his rigid salute the whole way — that steadfastness is the point.

questions.q: A mole, a badger, a caravan smashed in a ditch, and a chapter about a piper at dawn all belong to which book?
questions.f: Grahame first told these stories in bedtime letters to his son Alastair.

questions.q: A schoolteacher's spelling reform, a blue-backed speller sold by the million, and an 1828 American dictionary point to which man?
questions.f: Webster is why Americans write 'color' and 'center' while Britons keep 'colour' and 'centre.'

questions.q: A doctor's word lists, a lifelong habit of classifying everything, and an 1852 book of synonyms point to which name?
questions.f: Roget was a physician who organized words the way naturalists organized beetles.

questions.q: A Scottish editor, a corrugated-iron shed nicknamed the Scriptorium, and thousands of volunteer slips of paper built which book?
c: Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable
questions.f: James Murray worked on it for 36 years and never saw it finished — it took 70.

questions.q: A summer of storms by a Swiss lake, a ghost-story contest among friends, and an 18-year-old's nightmare produced which novel?
questions.f: Mary Shelley's monster is never named in the book — 'Frankenstein' is the scientist.

questions.q: A rabbit named after a family pet, a picture letter to a sick child, and a self-printed booklet of 1901 led to which classic?
questions.f: That illustrated letter to five-year-old Noel Moore is the seed of the whole book.

questions.q: A boy named Christopher Robin, a London Zoo bear from Winnipeg, and a bridge game played with sticks point to which book?
questions.f: The real bear at the zoo was named after the city of Winnipeg — hence 'Winnie.'

questions.q: A Kansas cyclone, a shop drawer labelled O-Z, and a road paved in yellow brick point to which author?
questions.f: Baum said he glanced at a filing cabinet drawer marked O-Z and had his country's name.

questions.q: A river picnic in 1862, a girl named Alice Liddell, and a mathematician's afternoon story led to which book?
c: At the Back of the North Wind
questions.f: Alice begged him to write it down, and he handed her a hand-lettered manuscript as a gift.

questions.q: A Danish cobbler's son, a failed singing career, and paper cuttings folded for children point to which writer?
questions.f: Andersen's intricate paper cuttings still survive in Danish museums.

questions.q: A pen name meaning 'two fathoms deep', a Mississippi pilot's licence, and a jumping frog contest point to which author?
questions.f: 'Mark twain' was the riverboat call meaning the water was safely twelve feet deep.

questions.q: An Italian newspaper serial, a talking cricket, and a puppet whose feet burn off point to which book?
questions.f: Collodi tried to end the serial early by killing off the puppet — readers demanded more.

questions.q: A game warden's son in India, a Vermont winter, and a wolf-raised boy point to which author?
questions.f: Kipling wrote much of The Jungle Book while living in snowy Vermont, remembering India.

questions.q: A childhood spent as a friend of orphans, a nurse who told grim stories, and 210 collected tales point to which pair?
questions.f: Their storyteller Dorothea Viehmann supplied dozens of the most famous tales.

questions.q: Asbjornsen and Moe played the Grimms' role for the folk tales of which country?
questions.f: Their collection gave the world Three Billy Goats Gruff and East of the Sun, West of the Moon.

questions.q: Aleksandr Afanasyev collected the great national fairy-tale corpus of which country?
questions.f: His nearly 600 tales are why Baba Yaga and the Firebird are known worldwide.

questions.q: Elias Lonnrot stitched together folk songs into which national epic?
questions.f: Finland's Kalevala later helped inspire Tolkien's invented languages and myths.

questions.q: Andrew Lang is remembered for editing a famous series of fairy books known by what?
questions.f: The Blue Fairy Book of 1889 was followed by red, green, yellow, and nine more colours.

questions.q: Charles Perrault's Cinderella has a detail the Grimms' version lacks. Which?
questions.f: The Grimms use helpful doves at a grave instead — no godmother anywhere in sight.

questions.q: Which classic children's novel was written by a woman using the initials E. Nesbit?
questions.f: Edith Nesbit's mix of ordinary children and everyday magic shaped a century of fantasy.

questions.q: Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote The Secret Garden and which other beloved book?
questions.f: Burnett was born in England but wrote most of her famous books in America.

questions.q: Which novel by Johanna Spyri became Switzerland's most famous children's book?
questions.f: Spyri wrote it in just four weeks, and it has never been out of print since 1881.

questions.q: Selma Lagerlof wrote a famous children's book about a boy flying across Sweden on what?
questions.f: She wrote it as a school geography reader — then won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

questions.q: Which poet wrote A Child's Garden of Verses as well as Treasure Island?
questions.f: Many of its poems, like 'The Land of Counterpane,' recall his childhood spent ill in bed.

questions.q: Christina Rossetti's long fairy poem about two sisters and forbidden fruit is called what?
questions.f: Rossetti also wrote the Christmas poem that became the carol 'In the Bleak Midwinter.'

questions.q: Which writer published the children's verse collection When We Were Very Young in 1924?
questions.f: Milne's verses came out in 1924, two years before Pooh ever appeared in a book.

questions.q: Which Beatrix Potter tale features a cat who bakes a pie with a rolling pin and a rat inside?
questions.f: Potter set it in her own farmhouse, Hill Top, whose staircase appears in the pictures.

questions.q: Aesop's fables were first put into Latin verse by which Roman writer?
questions.f: Phaedrus's neat Latin versions are how medieval Europe learned Aesop at all.

questions.q: The Panchatantra travelled west and became famous in Arabic as which book?
questions.f: Named for two jackal characters, it was translated into more than sixty languages.

questions.q: In the Ramayana, who is the monkey hero devoted to Prince Rama?
questions.f: Hanuman's leap across the sea to Lanka is one of the epic's most retold scenes.

questions.q: The Journey to the West, one of China's great novels, follows a monk and which mischievous companion?
questions.f: Sun Wukong can somersault 34,000 miles and turn a single hair into a copy of himself.

questions.q: Which very old Japanese story features a bamboo cutter finding a tiny girl from the Moon?
c: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
questions.f: Dating from around the 900s, it is often called Japan's oldest surviving prose tale.

questions.q: In Grimm's tale, what does the Pied Piper of Hamelin ask for as payment?
questions.f: A Hamelin chronicle records a real 1284 date for children leaving the town — nobody knows why.

questions.q: The Grimms' first edition was intended as a scholarly collection, not a children's book.
questions.f: It had footnotes and no pictures; only later editions were softened and illustrated for families.

questions.q: Aesop's fables were originally written down by Aesop himself.
questions.f: Nothing in Aesop's own hand exists — the fables circulated by word of mouth for generations.

questions.q: E.B. White, author of Charlotte's Web, also co-wrote a famous guide to writing style.
questions.f: He revised his old professor's booklet into Strunk and White's The Elements of Style.

questions.q: Kipling was the first English-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
questions.f: He won in 1907 and, at 41, is still the youngest literature laureate ever.

questions.q: The Little Prince was written by a working airmail pilot.
questions.f: Antoine de Saint-Exupery flew mail routes over deserts — which is where his story begins.

questions.q: Anne of Green Gables was rejected by publishers before it was finally printed.
questions.f: L.M. Montgomery put the manuscript in a hatbox for two years before trying again.

questions.q: In The Little Prince, what does the fox tell the boy is essential?
c: What is invisible to the eye
questions.f: The fox's line — one sees rightly only with the heart — is among the most quoted in modern literature.

questions.q: In The Little Prince, what does the narrator's first drawing look like to grown-ups?
questions.f: It is really a boa constrictor that has swallowed an elephant — grown-ups never see it.

questions.q: Which flower does the Little Prince leave behind on his tiny planet?
questions.f: He learns his rose is unique because of the time he spent caring for her.

questions.q: In Pinocchio, the puppet's nose grows because of what?
questions.f: Collodi's Blue Fairy scolds him: lies are the kind that have long noses or short legs.

questions.q: Which Grimm tale features a girl helped by a magical hazel tree at her mother's grave?
questions.f: Her tears water the twig she planted, and it grows into a wish-granting tree.

questions.q: A bell that never rang, a boy who cried out from a wooden horse, and a bundle of sticks all belong to whose collected tales?
questions.f: Belling the Cat, The Boy Who Cried Wolf, and The Bundle of Sticks all sit in the same ancient collection.

questions.q: In Andersen's The Snow Queen, what gets into Kai's eye and heart to change him?
c: Splinters of a broken magic mirror
questions.f: The shattered troll-mirror makes everything beautiful look ugly to whoever it pierces.

questions.q: In The Secret Garden, why has the garden been locked for ten years?
c: Mary's uncle shut it after his wife died there
questions.f: Archibald Craven buried the key rather than see the roses his wife planted.

questions.q: In Charlotte's Web, what does Charlotte leave behind at the fairground?
questions.f: Wilbur carries the sac home in his mouth, and Charlotte's daughters keep him company for life.

questions.q: In Charlotte's Web, which sly rat helps Wilbur only when there's food in it for him?
questions.f: He fetches scraps of newspaper words for Charlotte's web — for a price, of course.

questions.q: In Oliver Twist, the boy who befriends Oliver in London is nicknamed what?
questions.f: His real name is Jack Dawkins, but nobody in the book ever calls him that.

questions.q: In Dickens's David Copperfield, which cheerfully broke friend is always expecting something to turn up?
questions.f: 'Micawberism' entered English for hopeful, unrealistic optimism about money.

questions.q: In Robinson Crusoe, what discovery terrifies Crusoe most after years alone?
questions.f: One bare human footprint upends his whole solitary world in a single paragraph.

questions.q: In Moby-Dick, what is the name of the ship Ishmael sails on?
questions.f: Melville named it after a New England people, and its famous first line is just three words.

questions.q: Which novel opens with the line 'Call me Ishmael'?
questions.f: Those three words are among the most recognized openings in world literature.

questions.q: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' opens which novel?
questions.f: Dickens's two cities are London and Paris, on either side of the French Revolution.

questions.q: Which novel begins, 'It is a truth universally acknowledged...'?
questions.f: Austen's opening sentence is quoted so often it now works as a joke template.

questions.q: Which novel's famous line is 'Reader, I married him'?
questions.f: Charlotte Bronte's narrator speaks straight to us — startling readers in 1847.

questions.q: The Bronte sisters first published under which set of pen names?
questions.f: They kept their initials but chose names that hid whether the authors were women.

questions.q: Which novel features an orphan named Pip and a mysterious benefactor?
questions.f: Dickens rewrote the ending after a friend begged him for a gentler close.

questions.q: In The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, which building is practically a character itself?
questions.f: Hugo's novel was so popular it triggered a real restoration campaign for Notre-Dame.

questions.q: In Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days, what does Fogg's servant Passepartout do best?
c: Get into and out of scrapes
questions.f: His name means 'goes everywhere' — literally a master key in French.

questions.q: In The Three Musketeers, what is the group's famous motto?
c: All for one and one for all
questions.f: Dumas's hero d'Artagnan was loosely based on a real 17th-century soldier.

questions.q: In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Good Witch who first helps Dorothy rules which region?
questions.f: In Baum's book Glinda rules the South; the unnamed Witch of the North gives Dorothy her kiss of protection.

questions.q: How many books did L. Frank Baum himself write in the Oz series?
questions.f: He tried to end the series three times; readers' letters kept dragging him back to Oz.

questions.q: Which Aesop fable gave English the phrase 'sour grapes'?
questions.f: Nearly every European language has its own 'sour grapes' phrase from this one short fable.

questions.q: In Aesop's The Ass in the Lion's Skin, what gives the donkey away?
questions.f: The moral: a costume cannot hide what you truly are the moment you open your mouth.

questions.q: In La Fontaine's version, which two animals star in the fable about flattery and cheese?
questions.f: French children still recite 'Maitre Corbeau, sur un arbre perche' from memory.

questions.q: In the Odyssey, the enchantress Circe turns Odysseus's men into what?
questions.f: A herb called moly protects Odysseus himself from her potion.

questions.q: In Greek myth, which craftsman built the Labyrinth and the wings of wax and feathers?
questions.f: His name is the root of 'daedal,' a rare English word meaning skilfully made.

questions.q: In Norse mythology, what is the name of Thor's hammer?
questions.f: Its name is related to old words for 'crusher' — and possibly for lightning itself.

questions.q: The Poetic Edda and Prose Edda, our main sources for Norse tales, were written down in which country?
questions.f: Icelandic scholars preserved these poems on vellum in the 1200s, centuries after the Viking age.

questions.q: In the Arabian Nights, what does the fisherman find sealed inside a brass bottle?
questions.f: The jinni has been trapped so long that his gratitude has turned to fury.

questions.q: Which Robin Hood ballad character is his sweetheart in later tellings?
questions.f: Marian entered the legend centuries after the earliest ballads, from May Day plays.

questions.q: In Arthurian tales, which knight is famous for seeking the Holy Grail and being 'pure of heart'?
questions.f: 'A Galahad' still means an impossibly noble person in English.

questions.q: In Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, what does the Green Knight challenge the court to do?
questions.f: The poem survives in one single manuscript, alongside three other poems by an unknown author.

questions.q: Which long allegory follows a pilgrim named Christian to the Celestial City?
questions.f: Bunyan wrote it in prison, and it became one of the best-selling English books ever.

questions.q: Milton's Paradise Lost is written in which form?
questions.f: Milton dictated much of it after going blind, composing lines overnight in his head.

questions.q: Dante's Divine Comedy is written in three-line stanzas using which rhyme scheme?
questions.f: Its interlocking ABA BCB pattern chains the whole poem together like a braid.

questions.q: Which poet leads Dante as a guide through the first part of the Divine Comedy?
questions.f: Dante chose Virgil because the Aeneid also describes a journey to the underworld.

questions.q: The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel, was written by whom?
questions.f: A noblewoman at the Japanese court wrote it around the year 1000 — centuries before European novels.

questions.q: Which children's classic features a wooden Italian puppet, a fox and cat con-artist pair, and a field of buried coins?
c: The Nutcracker and the Mouse King
questions.f: The Fox and the Cat convince Pinocchio to plant his gold and wait for a money tree.

questions.q: Which famous library was carved from rock at Ephesus and once held thousands of scrolls?
questions.f: Its beautiful facade still stands in modern Turkey, though the scrolls are long gone.

questions.q: The House of Wisdom, a great centre for translating and copying books, stood in which city?
questions.f: Scholars there preserved Greek science and Indian mathematics for the whole world.

questions.q: The Bodleian Library, one of Europe's oldest, belongs to which university?
questions.f: By law it can claim a copy of every book published in Britain.

questions.q: Braille was invented by a teenager in France. What was his age when he devised the system?
questions.f: Louis Braille had been blind since a childhood accident and adapted a military night-writing code.

questions.q: Which technology made mass-market paperback storybooks affordable in the 1930s?
c: Cheap paperback binding and rotary presses
questions.f: Penguin's sixpenny paperbacks in 1935 put good books in coat pockets everywhere.

questions.q: Dickens published many of his novels in monthly instalments before they were books.
questions.f: Readers queued at docks in New York for the next instalment of The Old Curiosity Shop.

questions.q: Hans Christian Andersen wrote almost all of his fairy tales from older folk sources.
questions.f: Most, including The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling, were his own inventions.

questions.q: The Odyssey and the Iliad were composed to be performed aloud rather than read.
questions.f: Their repeated phrases — 'rosy-fingered dawn' — were memory aids for reciting poets.

questions.q: The Nobel Prize in Literature has been awarded for children's storybooks.
questions.f: Selma Lagerlof and Rudyard Kipling both wrote beloved children's classics and won it.

questions.q: The phrase 'once upon a time' has direct equivalents in dozens of other languages.
questions.f: Russian says 'there lived and there were'; Korean 'in the old days when tigers smoked.'

questions.q: Sleeping Beauty appears in Perrault's collection as well as the Grimms'.
questions.f: Perrault printed it in 1697; the Grimms collected their own version over a century later.

questions.q: Lewis Carroll invented the word 'chortle' in Jabberwocky.
questions.f: He blended 'chuckle' and 'snort' — and the word is now in every English dictionary.

questions.q: Some 450 watercolours of fungi, a spore-germination paper read aloud to the Linnean Society by a man, and prize-winning Herdwick sheep converge on which author?
questions.f: Peter Rabbit's creator was also a serious mycologist who left over 4,000 Lakeland acres to the National Trust.

questions.q: A word game called Doublets sold to Vanity Fair, a book titled Euclid and His Modern Rivals, and a pioneering portrait-photography hobby point to which writer?
questions.f: All of it was the work of Oxford mathematician Charles Dodgson — better known for a girl and a rabbit hole.
