questions.q: A coil of rope packed in every suitcase, a five-week visit that exhausted Charles Dickens, and exquisite paper cuttings belong to which storyteller?
questions.f: He carried the rope to escape hotel fires — and outstayed his welcome so badly that Dickens stopped writing back.

questions.q: A manual on breeding Hamburg chickens, a trade magazine for shop-window dressers, and a filing drawer labelled O-Z point to which author?
questions.f: Before Oz, Baum was a poultry expert and the founding editor of The Show Window.

questions.q: A senior post at the Bank of England, essays gathered as The Golden Age, and a stage version A.A. Milne titled Toad of Toad Hall point to which writer?
questions.f: Grahame rose to Secretary of the Bank of England while quietly writing about riverbank animals.

questions.q: An amateur cricket club called the Allahakbarries, a birthplace in Kirriemuir, and a copyright signed over to Great Ormond Street Hospital point to whom?
questions.f: Barrie's gift means the children's hospital has quietly earned from Peter Pan ever since 1929.

questions.q: An assistant editorship at Punch, a detective novel called The Red House Mystery, and an anti-war book titled Peace with Honour belong to which author?
questions.f: Milne resented that a bear of very little brain overshadowed his grown-up writing entirely.

questions.q: A patent for a self-pasting scrapbook, a fortune lost on the Paige typesetting machine, and two visits of Halley's Comet frame whose life?
questions.f: Twain was born in an 1835 comet year and died in 1910 as it returned, exactly as he had predicted.

questions.q: Service as a Union army nurse, a book called Hospital Sketches, and lurid thrillers signed 'A.M. Barnard' point to which novelist?
questions.f: The author of Little Women secretly wrote sensational potboilers under a man's name for money.

questions.q: A teenage folio of parrot lithographs, a job drawing the Earl of Derby's private menagerie, and drawing lessons for Queen Victoria point to whom?
questions.f: Lear was a first-rate natural-history artist long before anyone read his nonsense verse.

questions.q: A pet raven named Grip reviewed by Edgar Allan Poe, a fascination with mesmerism, and dummy book-spines bearing joke titles belong to which novelist?
questions.f: Poe reviewed Barnaby Rudge and its raven — and arguably borrowed the bird for a poem of his own.

questions.q: A donkey trek through the Cevennes, a grave on Mount Vaea, and the Samoan name Tusitala belong to which author?
questions.f: Tusitala means 'teller of tales' — the islanders' name for the man who wrote Treasure Island.

questions.q: A seat on the Amiens town council, and a rejected manuscript unlocked from a family safe in 1989, belong to which novelist?
questions.f: Paris in the Twentieth Century, refused as too gloomy in 1863, was finally published in 1994.

questions.q: A father who was a general, a vast dictionary of cookery, and a coffin carried into the Pantheon in 2002 belong to which author?
questions.f: France honoured the creator of the Three Musketeers 132 years after his death.

questions.q: Thousands of ink-wash drawings, nineteen years of exile on Guernsey, and a funeral procession watched by roughly two million people belong to whom?
questions.f: Hugo's body lay under the Arc de Triomphe before an enormous procession to the Pantheon in 1885.

questions.q: A herbarium of some 400 pressed plants, forty hand-sewn booklets found in a drawer, and a preserved white dress in Amherst point to which poet?
questions.f: Her sister found nearly 1,800 poems stitched into those little 'fascicles' after her death.

questions.q: Setting some of his own book's type by hand, a clerk's job lost to a scandalised superior, and years of hospital visiting point to which poet?
questions.f: Whitman self-published Leaves of Grass in 1855 and kept enlarging it for the rest of his life.

questions.q: A textbook on seashells, a newspaper column daring readers to send unbreakable ciphers, and a cosmological essay called Eureka belong to which writer?
questions.f: The Conchologist's First Book was the best-selling book Poe published in his own lifetime.

questions.q: A Harvard professorship, a Cambridge club that met weekly to check translations, and the first complete American rendering of Dante point to which poet?
questions.f: The Dante Club gathered at Longfellow's house while he finished the Divine Comedy in 1867.

questions.q: An apprenticeship to the engraver James Basire, a self-invented method called illuminated printing, and plates hand-tinted with his wife point to which poet?
questions.f: Blake etched text and picture together on one plate, making each copy of Songs of Innocence unique.

questions.q: An unfinished dream-poem, a blamed visitor 'on business from Porlock', and the coining of the phrase 'suspension of disbelief' point to which poet?
questions.f: Coleridge said the interruption cost him hundreds of remembered lines of Kubla Khan.

questions.q: A cottage at Grasmere, a sister's detailed journals, and seven years as a Poet Laureate who wrote no official verse point to which poet?
questions.f: Dorothy Wordsworth's journal recorded the lakeside daffodils two years before her brother's poem.

questions.q: A day job collecting excise taxes, a lifetime spent rescuing old Scots songs, and a supper held every 25 January point to which poet?
questions.f: Among the songs Burns saved and reshaped was the one the world now sings on New Year's Eve.

questions.q: A customs controller for the port of London, a stint as Clerk of the King's Works, and the first grave in Poets' Corner belong to which writer?
questions.f: Chaucer was buried in Westminster Abbey for his royal service; the poets clustered around him later.

questions.q: A law describing how consonants shifted across Germanic languages, and a German dictionary not finished until 1961, are the work of which fairy-tale collector?
questions.f: Grimm's Law is taught in linguistics classes that never mention Snow White at all.

questions.q: A high office under Louis XIV's minister Colbert, and a 1697 story collection published under his teenage son's name, belong to which author?
questions.f: Perrault may have hidden behind his son's name because fairy tales were beneath a royal official.

questions.q: A real surname of Lorenzini, a pen name borrowed from his mother's village, and an Italian translation of Perrault point to which author?
questions.f: Carlo Lorenzini took his pen name from Collodi in Tuscany — then created a puppet who wanted to be a boy.

questions.q: A title invented by a sick daughter, a satirical tax fable called Pomperipossa, and the world's richest children's-book prize point to which author?
questions.f: Karin Lindgren, home ill in bed, demanded a story about someone called Pippi Longstocking.

questions.q: A Finnish painter of public frescoes who wrote in Swedish and drew a daily comic strip for London's Evening News created which characters?
questions.f: Tove Jansson drew the Moomin strip for years before returning happily to painting and prose.

questions.q: A schoolboy job tasting chocolates for Cadbury, a co-invented medical valve, and the screenplay for a James Bond film belong to which writer?
questions.f: The Wade-Dahl-Till valve was designed to help children with fluid on the brain.

questions.q: A bet about writing a book with only fifty different words, and a special Pulitzer citation in 1984, belong to which author?
questions.f: He won the bet: Green Eggs and Ham uses exactly fifty distinct words.

questions.q: A notebook jotting about a couple who asked for an orphan boy and were sent a girl grew into which novel?
questions.f: That single line in L.M. Montgomery's notebook became a book beloved enough to be school reading in Japan.

questions.q: A craze for velvet suits and lace collars among 1880s boys was set off by which novel?
questions.f: Frances Hodgson Burnett's hero dressed so charmingly that a generation of boys suffered for it.

questions.q: A standard catalogue that numbers Aesop's fables for scholars is known as which index?
questions.f: Ben Edwin Perry numbered 584 fables, so scholars can cite 'Perry 24' and be understood anywhere.

questions.q: Folklorists classify Cinderella as tale type 510A in which international system?
questions.f: The ATU index lets researchers compare a Chinese Cinderella with a Scottish one in one glance.

questions.q: Which Russian scholar broke folktales down into 31 recurring narrative functions?
questions.f: His Morphology of the Folktale of 1928 quietly shaped how screenwriters plot films today.

questions.q: Which folklorist's English Fairy Tales gave us the familiar versions of Jack and the Beanstalk and The Three Little Pigs?
questions.f: Jacobs deliberately wrote in a voice children could hear read aloud, unlike scholarly rivals.

questions.q: Peter and Iona Opie spent their lives collecting what?
questions.f: They interviewed thousands of children, proving that skipping rhymes travel further than most poetry.

questions.q: Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book of about 1744 matters because it is the earliest surviving what?
questions.f: Only one volume of the original two survives, and it sits in the British Library.

questions.q: A Little Pretty Pocket-Book of 1744 was famously sold together with what?
questions.f: John Newbery's marketing trick — a toy with the book — helped invent children's publishing.

questions.q: Comenius's Orbis Sensualium Pictus of 1658 is often called the first what?
questions.f: Every Latin word sat beside a numbered picture — a teaching idea still used in phrasebooks.

questions.q: A hornbook, used to teach reading for centuries, was what?
c: A paddle-shaped board covered with thin horn
A bound book with horn clasps
questions.f: The translucent horn sheet protected the alphabet page from sticky fingers — early lamination.

questions.q: The New England Primer, an early American bestseller, taught reading mainly through what?
questions.f: 'In Adam's fall we sinned all' launched its alphabet — memorized by generations of colonial children.

questions.q: The McGuffey Readers, sold by the tens of millions in 19th-century America, were what?
questions.f: Their step-by-step passages taught reading, elocution, and morals to a whole continent.

questions.q: Struwwelpeter, a famous 1845 German picture book of cautionary tales, was written by a what?
c: Doctor, as a present for his son
questions.f: Heinrich Hoffmann couldn't find a good picture book to buy, so he made one himself.

questions.q: Wilhelm Busch's Max und Moritz of 1865 is often cited as an ancestor of what?
questions.f: Its picture-and-verse panels directly inspired the American strip The Katzenjammer Kids.

questions.q: In the world of old books, 'foxing' describes what?
questions.f: The rusty freckles come from traces of iron and damp reacting inside the paper over decades.

questions.q: A book's 'recto' page is which one?
questions.f: Recto faces you on the right; its reverse is the verso — Latin for 'turned.'

questions.q: In bookbinding, a 'signature' is what?
c: A folded sheet forming several pages
questions.f: Look at a hardback's top edge and you can see the folded signatures sewn side by side.

questions.q: The decorative papers glued inside a hardback's front and back covers are called what?
questions.f: Many classic children's books hide a map on the endpapers — the first thing a reader explores.

questions.q: A 'frontispiece' in an old storybook is what?
c: An illustration facing the title page
questions.f: For centuries it was the only picture in the whole book, so illustrators made it count.

questions.q: An 'errata slip' tucked into a book lists what?
c: Words too rare for the glossary
questions.f: Latin errata means 'errors' — a printer's confession pasted in at the last minute.

questions.q: A 'colophon' and an 'imprint' both tell a reader about what?
questions.f: Early printers signed off with elaborate colophons, sometimes including a little joke or prayer.

questions.q: An 'ex libris' label pasted inside a cover shows what?
questions.f: Latin for 'from the books of' — collectors have commissioned artists to design theirs for centuries.

questions.q: 'Marginalia' became a familiar literary term partly through a series of essays by whom?
questions.f: Poe published pieces titled Marginalia, pretending they were notes scribbled in his own books.

questions.q: A 'deckle edge' on a fine book's pages is what?
questions.f: It comes from the frame used in hand papermaking — now often faked to look luxurious.

questions.q: In a printed book, the 'gutter' is what?
c: The inner margin at the spine
The blank strip at the top
questions.f: Designers fight over gutter width — too narrow and the words vanish into the fold.

questions.q: A pedlar's pack of cheap booklets, an old English word for trade, and the man whose name hides inside 'chapbook' was called what?
questions.f: 'Chapbook' simply means the chapman's book — 'chap' comes from an old word for trade.

questions.q: Weekly instalments costing one penny, an American cousin priced at a dime, and thrilling serials devoured by apprentices describe what?
questions.f: Their American cousins were 'dime novels' — the same cheap thrills at a different price.

questions.q: A 'roman a clef' is a novel in which what happens?
c: Real people appear under invented names
The plot is a puzzle to solve
questions.f: French for 'novel with a key' — readers in the know can unlock who is really who.

questions.q: A 'Robinsonade' is a story of which kind?
questions.f: Defoe's castaway spawned so many imitations that the whole genre took his hero's name.

questions.q: A 'picaresque' novel follows what kind of central figure?
c: A roguish wanderer of low birth
An orphan raised in a palace
questions.f: From Spanish picaro, a rascal — the form was invented in 16th-century Spain.

questions.q: In Aristotle's terms, 'anagnorisis' means what?
questions.f: Odysseus's old nurse spotting his scar is a textbook anagnorisis, written centuries before Aristotle named it.

questions.q: Aristotle's 'peripeteia' refers to what?
questions.f: Greek for 'a falling around' — the pivot on which every good plot swings.

questions.q: The Greek term 'hamartia' in drama refers to what?
questions.f: It comes from an archer's word for missing the mark — a slip, not necessarily a wickedness.

questions.q: 'Denouement' comes from a French word meaning what?
questions.f: The plot's knots are literally untied — which is why a tangled ending feels unsatisfying.

questions.q: A word appearing exactly once in a whole body of writing, a Greek phrase meaning 'said once', and a translator's nightmare in Homer point to which term?
questions.f: Greek for 'said once' — Homer's poems are full of them, and they drive translators mad.

questions.q: A misfiled note about density, a nonexistent entry that survived years in Webster's, and a term for a word born from error describe what kind of word?
c: A word that exists only through an error
A word used solely in poetry
A word with no known origin
questions.f: 'Dord' famously haunted Webster's dictionary for years after a misfiled note about density.

questions.q: A Roman poet's complaint about words 'a foot and a half long', a jab in the Ars Poetica, and a very long word for very long words point to which poet?
questions.f: Horace mocked poets who used 'words a foot and a half long' — and gave us a foot-and-a-half word for it.

questions.q: A 1727 essay parodying a Greek work on the sublime, a Greek noun for depth, and a term for an accidental slide into the ridiculous point to which writer?
questions.f: Pope's 1727 essay Peri Bathous parodied a Greek work on the sublime — bathos is Greek for 'depth.'

questions.q: A word for a tiny person, a word for something enormous, and a word for a brutish lout were all minted by which two novelists?
questions.f: Lilliputian and Yahoo come from Gulliver's Travels; gargantuan from Rabelais's giant Gargantua.

questions.q: A 1516 Latin book by a lord chancellor, a Greek pun on 'good place', and a coined island name that literally means what?
questions.f: Thomas More built it from Greek ou-topos in 1516, punning on eu-topos, 'good place.'

questions.q: A tutor who insists all is for the best, the Lisbon earthquake dropped into a 1759 satire, and a byword for silly optimism point to which book?
questions.f: Voltaire's Dr. Pangloss insists all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds, whatever happens.

questions.q: A hypnotic music master in an 1894 bestseller, the hat style named after its stage version, and a word for a sinister controller point to which novel?
questions.f: George du Maurier's 1894 bestseller also gave English 'in the altogether' and the trilby hat.

questions.q: A plane lost over the Himalayas in 1933, the first name of the retreat now called Camp David, and hotels worldwide all borrow a place invented in which novel?
questions.f: James Hilton's name has since been given to hotels, a presidential retreat, and a real Chinese county.

questions.q: A poets' quarrel of the 1720s, a nickname built from the first name Ambrose, and a term for feeble sentimentality point to a mockery of which kind of writer?
c: A poet of dainty children's verses
questions.f: Rivals coined it from Ambrose Philips's first name to ridicule his sugary verses of the 1720s.

questions.q: A comic nurse in Martin Chuzzlewit, an enormously baggy umbrella, and Victorian slang in which the umbrella took her name point to which novelist?
questions.f: Mrs. Sarah Gamp in Martin Chuzzlewit carried such a famously baggy umbrella that her name became the object.

questions.q: A character in an 1798 comedy who never once appears on stage, the endlessly repeated question 'What will she say?', and a byword for disapproval mean what?
questions.f: She never appears on stage in Thomas Morton's 1798 play — characters only ask what she'd say.

questions.q: A calendar carved on a post, a companion named after the weekday they met, and an office term for an indispensable helper point to which novel?
questions.f: Defoe's castaway named his companion for the weekday they met, and offices borrowed the phrase.

questions.q: An old friend left in charge of a household in Ithaca, a goddess who borrows his shape to give advice, and a modern word for a wise guide point to which epic?
questions.f: Mentor guides Telemachus — and the goddess Athena often borrows his shape to give the advice.

questions.q: A herald said to shout as loudly as fifty men, a single passing mention among Greek ships, and an adjective for a booming voice point to which poem?
questions.f: Homer says Stentor could shout as loudly as fifty men together.

questions.q: A gift of true foresight, a curse that nobody will believe it, and a modern label for an ignored warner all describe what?
c: Someone who never tells the truth
questions.f: In the Troy legends she is given true foresight but cursed so that nobody believes her.

questions.q: A king of Epirus, a remark that one more such win would finish him, and a phrase for triumph that costs too much describe what?
questions.f: King Pyrrhus is said to have remarked that another such win would finish him entirely.

questions.q: The ancient regional name for Sparta's homeland, a reputation for one-word replies, and an adjective for terse speech point to which region?
questions.f: Laconia's Spartans were famous for one-word replies — the ultimate literary economy.

questions.q: A sea-god who must be gripped tight before he answers, Menelaus's wrestling match on a beach, and an adjective for endless versatility point to which epic?
questions.f: Proteus keeps shifting shape to escape questions — you must hold on until he turns back.

questions.q: A bird believed to nest on a calm winter sea, fourteen windless days at midwinter, and a phrase for golden untroubled times point to which bird?
questions.f: Legend said the kingfisher nested on calm winter seas, so those days were windless and bright.

questions.q: A hybrid slain by Bellerophon, a modern biology term for one body with two sets of cells, and an adjective meaning fanciful point to a beast built from how many animals?
questions.f: Lion, goat, and serpent in one — which is why a chimera means an impossible mix.

questions.q: Achilles's fiercely loyal troops, a name echoing the Greek word for ants, and a term for an unthinking underling point to which hero?
questions.f: Their name resembles the Greek word for ants, which suited their swarming loyalty.

questions.q: A goatskin cloak carried by Athena, a standing Homeric epithet for Zeus, and a modern phrase meaning 'under the protection of' point to which object?
questions.f: Zeus and Athena carry the aegis in Homer, so being under it meant divine protection.

questions.q: Fruit that draws back from a reaching hand, a metal so unreactive it resists acids, and a verb meaning to tease with the unreachable point to which name?
questions.f: His name also lurks in the metal tantalum, which stubbornly resists being dissolved.

questions.q: A boulder that never stays at the summit, a famous 1942 essay by Albert Camus, and an adjective for futile labour point to what kind of task?
questions.f: He rolls a boulder uphill forever, and it always rolls back — literature's oldest image of drudgery.

questions.q: A river whose oaths even gods could not break, a ferryman waiting for payment, and an adjective meaning pitch-dark point to which place?
questions.f: Oaths sworn on the Styx were unbreakable, even for gods — Homer says so plainly.

questions.q: A goat that nursed the infant Zeus, a favourite emblem on coins and coats of arms, and a Latin pair of words for abundance point to which meaning?
questions.f: The overflowing goat's horn appears in Greek myth and on coins and coats of arms ever since.

questions.q: The word 'narrative' and the word 'gnome' both connect to an ancient root meaning what?
questions.f: A 'gnomic' saying is a knowing one — and a narrator is literally one who knows the tale.

questions.q: A Latin word for a mixed dish, a false but ancient link to goat-legged spirits, and a genre perfected by Horace and Juvenal point to which original meaning?
questions.f: Romans thought of satire as a mixed plate of everything — the satyr link came later by accident.

questions.q: A weapon Aristophanes used against tragedians, a Greek prefix meaning beside, and a Greek noun for song point to which word's literal meaning?
questions.f: Para plus oide — a song sung alongside the original, deliberately out of step.

questions.q: A performer stitching Homeric episodes together, a Greek verb for sewing, and a term now used for free-flowing music point to which original action?
questions.f: A rhapsode literally stitched episodes of Homer together for an audience.

questions.q: An Italian word for a room, the blank line a poet leaves like a doorway, and the three-line units Dante built point to which meaning?
questions.f: Each stanza is a little room in the house of a poem — a metaphor poets still use.

questions.q: A ploughman's turn at the end of a furrow, the movement your eye makes at a line break, and a Latin noun behind 'reverse' point to which meaning?
questions.f: Versus meant turning at a furrow's end — exactly what your eye does at a line break.

questions.q: A Latin verb behind 'textile', the image of threads crossing, and a scholar's word for the words themselves point to which meaning?
questions.f: Texere gave us textile too — a text really is something woven from threads.

questions.q: A Scots word for occult learning, a dull schoolroom subject, and a modern word for dazzling charm all descend from one word — what did it involve?
questions.f: In Scots, grammarye meant occult learning — booklearning looked like enchantment to most people.

questions.q: Runes cut into pale wood, a Latin word for bark that came to mean a volume, and a smooth-barked forest tree point to which tree?
questions.f: Early runes may have been cut into beech wood, and the Latin for book, liber, first meant bark.

questions.q: A goose's wing plucked for writing, a small knife kept for sharpening, and a Latin noun behind 'pinnate' point to which original meaning?
questions.f: Penna, feather — while 'pencil' comes from penicillus, a little tail-shaped brush.

questions.q: A Greek word for something burnt in, imperial purple writing fluid, and a wax painting technique called encaustic point to which meaning?
questions.f: Enkauston described a purple ink burnt in by heat — the same root as 'encaustic' painting.

questions.q: A pointed tool for Roman wax tablets, a person's distinctive handwriting, and eventually a writer's manner all began as what?
questions.f: Romans wrote on wax with a stylus, so a person's handwriting — then their manner — became their style.

questions.q: A rolled papyrus sheet, a Latin verb behind 'revolve', and one book out of a matching set point to which meaning?
questions.f: Ancient volumes were rolled scrolls, and you revolved them as you read.

questions.q: An Arabic-derived word for a warehouse, a 1731 London periodical that borrowed it, and a compartment holding a supply point to which meaning?
questions.f: The Gentleman's Magazine of 1731 borrowed the word to mean a storehouse of writing.

questions.q: A Latin adjective for white, a Roman noticeboard coated in plaster, and a book of blank pages point to which original object?
questions.f: Latin albus, white — Romans posted notices on whitened boards called alba.

questions.q: A ligature squeezing the letters e and t together and a Latin phrase meaning 'by itself' gave this symbol a name slurred from which spoken phrase?
questions.f: Children reciting the alphabet ended with 'and per se and' — which slurred into ampersand.

questions.q: A Greek word for a small star, a mark ancient editors used to flag genuine lines, and a modern footnote signal point to which meaning?
questions.f: Ancient editors used the little star to flag a line they thought was genuine.

questions.q: A capital C standing for capitulum, a red mark starting a new thought, and the symbol revealed when you show formatting point to which mark?
questions.f: The pilcrow began as a C for capitulum, 'little head' — the ancestor of our word chapter.

questions.q: A Greek grammarian's short phrase, a word meaning something cut off, and the briefest pause in punctuation point to which meaning?
questions.f: Greek grammarians thought in cut-off phrases; the mark took the name of the phrase itself.

questions.q: A Venetian printer around 1500, a slanted face cut to squeeze more words onto a page, and a name honouring a country point to which country?
questions.f: Aldus Manutius of Venice cut the first italics around 1500 to fit more words on a page.

questions.q: A tiny finishing stroke, Roman letters carved in stone, and a French word for 'without' used to name its absence point to which feature?
c: A small finishing stroke on a letter
questions.f: Fonts without them are 'sans serif' — French for 'without serif.'

questions.q: A lone line stranded at the top of a page, a partner term borrowed from family words for a line left at the foot, and a typesetter's daily nuisance describe what?
c: A short last line stranded at the top of a page
questions.f: Its partner, an 'orphan', is a lone first line left dangling at the bottom of a page.

questions.q: A Greek phrase meaning 'useful learning', a schoolroom cousin of the poetic anthology, and passages picked to teach point to a book gathering what?
questions.f: Greek for 'useful learning' — a schoolroom cousin of the poetic anthology.

questions.q: A Latin phrase meaning flower-gathering, a monk's notebook of favourite lines, and the exact metaphor behind 'anthology' point to a collection of what?
questions.f: Latin for 'flower gathering' — the exact same metaphor as the Greek-built 'anthology.'

questions.q: 'Epigraph' and 'epitaph' differ how?
c: An epigraph opens a book; an epitaph marks a grave
An epigraph is spoken; an epitaph is sung
An epigraph closes a poem; an epitaph opens it
They are the same word spelled two ways
questions.f: Both share the Greek graphein, to write — one at a book's threshold, one at a life's.

questions.q: An 'epigram' is best described as what?
c: A short, witty pointed poem or saying
questions.f: The Roman poet Martial perfected the form: brief, sharp, and remembered.

questions.q: 'Metonymy' is at work in which phrase?
c: The pen is mightier than the sword
questions.f: Pen stands in for writing and sword for war — a name swapped for a closely linked thing.

questions.q: 'Synecdoche' is at work in which phrase?
questions.f: 'Hands' means whole sailors — a part standing for the whole thing.

questions.q: 'Litotes' is a figure of speech that does what?
c: States something by denying its opposite
questions.f: 'Not bad at all' is litotes — Old English and Old Norse poetry are stuffed with it.

questions.q: 'Chiasmus' arranges words in which pattern?
questions.f: Named for the Greek letter chi, X — the ideas cross over in the middle.

questions.q: In poetry, 'apostrophe' as a figure of speech means what?
c: Addressing an absent person or thing
questions.f: 'O Captain! My Captain!' is an apostrophe — nothing to do with the punctuation mark.

questions.q: An 'eye rhyme' is a pair of words that do what?
c: Look like they rhyme but do not sound alike
Rhyme in the middle of lines
questions.f: 'Love' and 'move' are the classic pair — they rhymed once, and the spelling kept the memory.

questions.q: The three joints of a finger, a galloping DUM-da-da beat, and the foot Homer's lines are built from take their name from a Greek word for what?
questions.f: One long joint then two short ones, exactly like the bones of a finger: DUM-da-da.

questions.q: Slow Greek libation chants, two heavy beats side by side, and a foot that halts a galloping line describe which syllable pattern?
questions.f: Its name comes from Greek libation chants, which were sung in slow, heavy beats.

questions.q: Six feet to a line, a finger-shaped rhythm, and a beat built for reciting from memory point to which metre?
questions.f: Six dactylic feet per line — a galloping rhythm built for reciting aloud from memory.

questions.q: 'Swift-footed' attached forever to one hero, 'wine-dark' attached forever to the sea, and a reciting poet needing to fill a line point to which device?
c: A fixed descriptive phrase attached to a name
questions.f: 'Swift-footed Achilles' and 'wine-dark sea' let a reciting poet fill a line without pausing.

questions.q: A Persian astronomer's quatrains, an 1859 English version that first sold in a penny box, and a Suffolk gentleman's loose paraphrase point to which translator?
questions.f: FitzGerald's loose 1859 version sold so slowly at first that copies were dumped in a penny box.

questions.q: Couplets that each stand alone, a repeated closing refrain, and centuries of Persian and Urdu singers point to a form built from what?
c: Rhyming couplets with a repeated refrain
questions.f: Beloved in Persian and Urdu poetry, each couplet can stand alone as a complete thought.

questions.q: An early 1700s French version, two famous tales missing from every Arabic manuscript, and Europe's first taste of Scheherazade point to which translator?
questions.f: Galland's early 1700s version added Aladdin and Ali Baba, which no surviving Arabic manuscript contains.

questions.q: A knight writing in prison, a text Caxton printed in 1485, and the first English prose gathering of Arthur's story point to which work?
questions.f: Thomas Malory finished it in prison, and Caxton printed it in 1485.

questions.q: A Neapolitan courtier's dialect tales of the 1630s, the oldest printed Cinderella, and a frame of fifty stories over five days point to which collection?
questions.f: Giambattista Basile's Neapolitan collection of the 1630s holds the oldest printed Cinderella and Rapunzel.

questions.q: Ten tellers, ten days, and a structure Chaucer later borrowed for his pilgrims: what are Boccaccio's young people doing?
questions.f: Boccaccio's structure — ten tellers, ten days — directly inspired Chaucer's pilgrims.

questions.q: A chain of changing shapes, the source of the Pyramus and Thisbe playlet in Midsummer, and a poet exiled to the Black Sea point to which work?
questions.f: Shakespeare mined it constantly — the Pyramus and Thisbe play in Midsummer comes straight from Ovid.

questions.q: A man turned into a donkey, a tale of Cupid and Psyche told by an old woman, and the oldest complete fairy tale on record point to which novel?
questions.f: Apuleius embeds the tale inside a story about a man turned into a donkey — the oldest fairy tale on record.

questions.q: The word 'pamphlet' may derive from the title of a popular medieval love poem.
questions.f: Scholars trace it to Pamphilus, a widely copied Latin poem circulated as loose unbound sheets.

questions.q: 'Palindrome' is built from Greek pieces meaning 'running back again'.
questions.f: One of the oldest known examples is a Greek fountain inscription reading the same both ways.

questions.q: Aesop's fable collection includes stories that also appear in India's Jataka tales.
questions.f: Scholars still argue over which tradition borrowed from which — the traffic ran both ways.

questions.q: A blocked-up window, a lifetime of unpaid dinners, and 'The Sketch Book' published under the name Geoffrey Crayon point to which writer?
questions.f: Irving also invented the mock-historian Diedrich Knickerbocker, whose name became slang for New Yorkers.

questions.q: A Norwich-born schoolmaster's dictionary of phrase and fable, a chapter on 'phrases and allusions', and generations of quiz answers point to which compiler?
questions.f: Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable of 1870 explains the stories hidden inside everyday sayings.

questions.q: A stolen printing of an unfinished poem, a translated Persian astronomer-poet, and a penny bargain box in London point to which famous 19th-century book?
questions.f: Copies dumped for a penny were snapped up by Rossetti and Swinburne, who made it a sensation.

questions.q: A dictionary that took a lone scholar nine years, a definition mocking his own trade, and a patron he skewered in a famous letter point to which man?
questions.f: Johnson defined 'oats' as food for horses and, in Scotland, for people — and got away with it.

questions.q: A Scottish farmer's son turned Congregational minister, a pioneering fantasy called Phantastes, and a friendship that pushed Lewis Carroll to publish Alice point to which author?
questions.f: MacDonald's children begged Carroll to print Alice, and MacDonald's own fantasies later inspired C.S. Lewis.

questions.q: A journalist's account of a real shipwrecked sailor, a Presbyterian dissenter's pamphlets, and a pen name change adding 'De' point to which novelist?
questions.f: Born Daniel Foe, he grandified his own name — and turned castaway Alexander Selkirk into fiction.

questions.q: A dean of a Dublin cathedral, an anonymous proposal about Ireland that scandalised readers, and a fictional land of talking horses point to which writer?
questions.f: Swift's Houyhnhnms, in Gulliver's fourth voyage, are rational horses who find humans absurd.

questions.q: A novel with a solid black page, marbled pages bound in by hand, and a squiggly line drawn to show a plot point to which 18th-century book?
questions.f: Laurence Sterne's typographic jokes are still cited as the first experimental novel in English.

questions.q: A Bengali polymath's Nobel Prize of 1913, a school founded at Santiniketan, and two national anthems written by one man point to whom?
questions.f: Tagore wrote the texts that became the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.

questions.q: A Nigerian novelist's 1958 debut, a title borrowed from a Yeats poem, and a challenge to colonial storytelling point to which book?
questions.f: Chinua Achebe took his title from Yeats's line 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold.'

questions.q: An 1866 novel about a Russian student, a magazine serialisation, and a title meaning literally 'transgression and punishment' point to which work?
questions.f: Dostoevsky wrote it under crushing deadlines to pay debts, chapter by chapter.

questions.q: A count who rewrote his own novel by hand many times, a school for peasant children, and a late renunciation of his own fiction point to which author?
questions.f: Tolstoy came to dismiss War and Peace and Anna Karenina as unimportant compared with his moral writings.

questions.q: A doctor who called medicine his lawful wife and literature his mistress, a journey to Sakhalin, and a rule about a gun on the wall point to whom?
questions.f: 'Chekhov's gun' says that if a rifle hangs in act one, it must be fired before the end.

questions.q: A whaling novel that sold poorly on publication in 1851, a dedication to Hawthorne, and a revival forty years after the author's death point to which book?
questions.f: Melville died nearly forgotten in 1891; his masterpiece was rediscovered in the 1920s.

questions.q: A poem published anonymously in a Troy newspaper in 1823 gave the world what?
questions.f: A Visit from St. Nicholas fixed Santa's sleigh team in print for the very first time.

questions.q: A children's magazine called St. Nicholas, an editor named Mary Mapes Dodge, and a story about silver skates produced which famous novel?
questions.f: Dodge had never visited the Netherlands when she wrote her Dutch classic in 1865.

questions.q: A clergyman-naturalist's tale of a chimney sweep who becomes a water creature is which Victorian book?
c: At the Back of the North Wind
questions.f: Charles Kingsley wrote it partly to argue for laws protecting child workers.

questions.q: A Punch cartoonist's precise line drawings, a quarrel over how Alice should look, and 92 wood-engraved illustrations point to which artist?
questions.f: Tenniel rejected the first print run for poor picture quality — and Carroll paid to have it redone.

questions.q: Which illustrator's misty, gnarled watercolours defined Edwardian gift editions of Grimm, Andersen and Peter Pan?
questions.f: Rackham's twisted trees with half-hidden faces set the visual style for fairy tales for a century.

questions.q: Which American illustrator and teacher shaped modern pictures of Robin Hood and King Arthur, and taught N.C. Wyeth?
questions.f: Pyle's Brandywine school of illustrators dominated American storybooks for decades.

questions.q: Which term describes the wordless double-page picture that opens many modern picture books?
questions.f: Illustrators plan a picture book as a sequence of spreads, thinking about each page turn.

questions.q: The 'Golden Age of children's literature' is usually dated to roughly which span?
questions.f: Alice, Treasure Island, The Jungle Book, Peter Pan and Pooh all appeared inside that window.

questions.q: Which honour is often called the 'little Nobel' for children's literature?
questions.f: Given every two years since 1956, it honours a writer's whole body of work, not one book.

questions.q: In Grimm scholarship, who was Dorothea Viehmann?
c: A gifted storyteller who supplied many tales
The illustrator of the first edition
questions.f: Her tellings are so polished that the Grimms held her up as their model informant.

questions.q: The tale type known as 'The Kind and the Unkind Girls' is best represented in English by which story?
questions.f: Reward and punishment are dealt out by a woman who shakes feather beds to make it snow on earth.

questions.q: 'The Juniper Tree' and 'Fitcher's Bird' belong to which collection?
questions.f: The Grimms kept many strange, dark tales that later editors quietly dropped from children's editions.

questions.q: In Norse literature, a 'saga' differs from an 'edda' how?
c: A saga is a prose narrative; an edda is a poetic or mythic handbook
A saga is sung; an edda is spoken
A saga is Danish; an edda is Icelandic
A saga is about gods; an edda about families
questions.f: Iceland's family sagas read like realist novels written 700 years before the novel existed.

questions.q: 'Skald' is the Norse word for what?
questions.f: Skaldic verse is so tightly packed with kennings that a single stanza can take a page to explain.

questions.q: In Welsh literature, what is the Mabinogion?
c: A collection of medieval Welsh tales
questions.f: Its eleven tales include Culhwch and Olwen, among the earliest surviving Arthurian prose in any language.

questions.q: In Irish tradition, a 'seanchai' is what?
questions.f: Seanchai carried hundreds of tales, and Irish collectors recorded them on wax cylinders in the 1930s.

questions.q: 'Kamishibai', a Japanese storytelling form, uses what?
c: Picture cards in a small wooden stage
questions.f: Street performers pedalled from town to town, sliding cards through a frame as they narrated.

questions.q: 'Dastangoi', a revived South Asian storytelling art, features what?
c: A solo narrator performing long romances
questions.f: Nineteenth-century dastangos in Delhi and Lucknow could keep an audience gripped for hours.

questions.q: 'Wayang kulit', which stages the Ramayana and Mahabharata, is which art form?
questions.f: Indonesian puppeteers can perform a single all-night show lasting nine hours without a script.

questions.q: The Sanskrit term 'katha' refers to what?
questions.f: The Kathasaritsagara, or 'ocean of streams of story', gathers hundreds of Indian tales in verse.

questions.q: Which enormous Sanskrit collection's title translates as 'Ocean of the Streams of Story'?
questions.f: Somadeva compiled it in the 11th century — it is several times longer than the Iliad and Odyssey combined.

questions.q: The Hitopadesha, a Sanskrit fable collection, differs from the Panchatantra how?
c: It is a later, independent work drawing on similar material
It is written in verse only
questions.f: Its title means 'beneficial advice' — it was among the first Sanskrit books printed in the West.

questions.q: In the Jataka tales, what is the being who appears in each story called?
questions.f: Each tale ends by revealing which character was the Buddha-to-be in a former life.

questions.q: Which term describes the framing device of a story inside a story, as in the Arabian Nights?
questions.f: Scheherazade's own survival is the frame that holds a thousand nights of tales together.

questions.q: The 'rule of three' in folk tales means what?
c: Events and characters come in threes
A moral is stated three times
questions.f: Three wishes, three bears, three little pigs — the pattern is easy to remember and satisfying to hear.

questions.q: In folklore studies, a 'motif' differs from a 'tale type' how?
c: A motif is a single recurring element; a type is a whole plot
A motif is regional; a type is universal
A motif is ancient; a type is modern
A motif belongs to poems; a type to prose
questions.f: Stith Thompson's Motif-Index catalogues thousands of them, from magic rings to grateful animals.

questions.q: 'Etiological' folk tales exist mainly to explain what?
c: How something came to be the way it is
Why a place has its name only
questions.f: Kipling's Just So Stories are deliberate literary imitations of the etiological folk tale.

questions.q: A 'cumulative tale' is one that does what?
c: Repeats and adds to a growing chain of events
Retells the same event three ways
questions.f: The House That Jack Built and The Enormous Turnip both pile detail on detail until it topples.

questions.q: A 'trickster' figure in world folklore typically does what?
c: Wins by cunning rather than strength
questions.f: Anansi, Br'er Rabbit, Reynard, and Coyote are all cousins in the same enormous family.

questions.q: Reynard the Fox is the trickster hero of a cycle of tales from which region?
questions.f: The tales were so popular that French replaced its old word for fox, goupil, with renard.

questions.q: A 'beast fable' differs from a 'beast epic' chiefly in what way?
questions.f: Aesop gives you a fable in ten lines; Reynard's beast epic runs for thousands.

questions.q: 'Bestiary' books of the Middle Ages described animals mainly to do what?
questions.f: They cheerfully mixed real lions with unicorns, since both carried a moral meaning.

questions.q: A 'psalter' and a 'book of hours' were medieval books used mainly for what?
questions.f: Their lavish margins are where medieval artists hid rabbits, dragons, and jokes.

questions.q: A red earth pigment, the Latin word behind 'rubric', and headings that guided a reader's eye point to which practice?
questions.f: Latin rubrica, red earth — which is why an instruction is still called a rubric.

questions.q: A medieval manuscript's 'illuminator' and 'scribe' usually differed how?
c: One worked in Latin, one in the local tongue
One bound the book, one sold it
One copied poems, one copied laws
questions.f: A single big book could pass through the hands of a parchment maker, scribe, illuminator, and binder.

questions.q: 'Uncial' and 'Carolingian minuscule' are types of what?
questions.f: Carolingian minuscule is the ancestor of our lower-case letters — Renaissance printers copied it directly.

questions.q: The invention of spaces between words in Latin writing mattered because it enabled what?
questions.f: Roman texts ran letters together, so reading aloud was the only practical way to decode them.

questions.q: A single word printed below the last line, a binder assembling folded sheets, and a check against pages in the wrong order point to a mark that did what?
c: Showing the first word of the next page
questions.f: It helped binders assemble the folded sheets in the right order.

questions.q: An 1809 book that diagnosed a disease and was itself avidly collected, auction fever among gentlemen, and shelves bought faster than they were read describe what?
questions.f: An 1809 book of that name diagnosed the disease and, of course, was itself avidly collected.

questions.q: A Japanese word joining 'piling up' with 'reading', a bedside tower of unopened spines, and a gentle joke about ambition describe what habit?
c: Buying books and letting them pile up unread
Lending books and never getting them back
questions.f: The Japanese word combines 'piling up' with 'reading' — a gentle joke about ambition.

questions.q: A Latin word for swaddling clothes, roughly 30,000 surviving editions, and printing's earliest years point to books made before which year?
questions.f: Fewer than 30,000 distinct editions survive from printing's cradle years.

questions.q: A dolphin curled round an anchor, italic type cut around 1500, and classics small enough for a saddlebag point to which innovation?
questions.f: Aldus Manutius made pocket-sized classics so readers could carry Virgil on horseback.

questions.q: Which printer's device famously showed a dolphin wrapped around an anchor?
questions.f: Aldus took the emblem from a Roman coin, pairing speed and steadiness.

questions.q: A wallpaper designer turned printer, a Chaucer of 1896 often called the century's most beautiful book, and hand-made paper point to which aim?
questions.f: Its Chaucer of 1896 is often called the most beautiful book printed in the 19th century.

questions.q: A 'variorum' edition of a classic story presents what?
c: Different versions and scholars' notes together
questions.f: Variorum editions let you watch an author changing their mind across decades of revisions.

questions.q: In textual scholarship, a 'crux' is what?
c: A passage whose correct wording is uncertain
questions.f: Latin for cross — editors say a crux 'tortures' them, which is exactly the metaphor intended.

questions.q: 'Galley proofs' are named after what?
c: The tray that held set type
The gallery where proofs were read
questions.f: Compositors slid finished type into a long metal galley, then printed a rough copy from it.

questions.q: Shared copying mistakes, a diagram shaped like a family tree, and a lost original nobody has ever seen point to which scholarly tool?
c: A family tree of manuscript copies
A list of an author's works
questions.f: By tracing shared mistakes, scholars can reconstruct a lost original nobody has ever seen.

questions.q: The Grimms' tale collection was among the first books printed with the modern term 'fairy tale' on the title page.
questions.f: Their German title means 'Children's and Household Tales' — no fairies mentioned anywhere.

questions.q: The phrase 'fairy tale' entered English as a translation of the French 'conte de fees'.
questions.f: Madame d'Aulnoy coined 'contes de fees' in the 1690s, and English took the label wholesale.

questions.q: Mother Goose first appeared in print on the frontispiece of Perrault's French tales.
questions.f: His 1697 volume was subtitled Contes de ma mere l'Oye — Tales of My Mother the Goose.

questions.q: Aesop's most famous fables all survive in his own original Greek verse.
questions.f: They come to us through later writers like Babrius and Phaedrus — no text by Aesop exists.

questions.q: Iceland's medieval sagas were written on parchment made from calfskin.
questions.f: Vellum was so precious that scribes scraped old pages clean and reused them.

questions.q: The word 'novel' entered English before the word 'novelist'.
questions.f: The books had to exist first — 'novelist' followed once writing them became a recognised job.

questions.q: Andersen's The Ugly Duckling is widely read as a disguised story about the author himself.
questions.f: A poor, awkward cobbler's son who became Denmark's most celebrated writer — the parallel is hard to miss.

questions.q: Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in a dialect based on the speech of northern England.
questions.f: He wrote in the London dialect, which is one reason it became the basis of standard English.

questions.q: A baby horse is called a...?
questions.f: A foal can trot beside its mother when it is only one day old.

questions.q: A baby kangaroo has a special name. What is it?
questions.f: A joey rides inside its mother's pouch for about six months.

questions.q: What is a baby pig called?
questions.f: The ending '-let' means small, and it also appears in 'booklet' and 'droplet.'

questions.q: A baby deer is called a...?
questions.f: Fawns are born with white spots that help them hide in the forest.

questions.q: What do we call a baby goat?
questions.f: That is why 'kid' also became a friendly word for a child.

questions.q: A baby chicken is called a...?
questions.f: A chick pecks its way out of the egg using a tiny bump called an egg tooth.

questions.q: What is a baby frog called?
questions.f: 'Tadpole' comes from old words meaning 'toad head' because it looks like a big head with a tail.

questions.q: You have one foot. You stand on two...?
questions.f: English changes the vowel instead of adding S, an old pattern from Old English.

questions.q: One tooth, but a mouth full of...?
questions.f: 'Tooth' and 'foot' change their middle letters the very same way.

questions.q: What is the word for more than one child?
questions.f: 'Children' is one of the very few English plurals that ends in '-ren.'

questions.q: One man, but three...?
questions.f: 'Man' becomes 'men' and 'woman' becomes 'women' by swapping just one vowel.

questions.q: What do we call more than one goose?
questions.f: Goose becomes geese, but more than one moose is still just moose!

questions.q: One leaf falls, then lots of...?
questions.f: The F turns into V, just like 'knife' becoming 'knives.'

questions.q: What is the correct word for more than one sheep?
questions.f: 'Sheep,' 'deer,' and 'fish' usually stay the same whether there is one or one hundred.

questions.q: One person waits, then many...?
questions.f: 'People' took the place of 'persons' in everyday talk long ago.

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'big'?
questions.f: 'Small' and 'little' are synonyms, which means they share the same meaning.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of 'fast'?
questions.f: Watch out: the other three all mean fast, not the opposite!

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'happy'?
questions.f: Words with opposite meanings, like happy and sad, are called antonyms.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of 'day'?
questions.f: 'Daytime' and 'nighttime' are both compound words built from smaller words.

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'wet'?
questions.f: 'Damp' and 'soggy' are sneaky choices because they both still mean a bit wet.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'open'?
questions.f: 'Shut' and 'closed' both work as opposites of 'open.'

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'up'?
questions.f: 'Up' and 'down' are two of the shortest antonyms in English.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of 'loud'?
questions.f: 'Quiet' has three vowels in a row: u, i, and e.

questions.q: Which animal word rhymes with 'dog'?
questions.f: Rhyming words share the same ending sound, like 'dog,' 'frog,' and 'log.'

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'cake'?
questions.f: 'Cake' and 'lake' rhyme even though a silent E hides at the end of each.

questions.q: Put 'cup' and 'cake' together. What treat do you get?
questions.f: Words made by joining two smaller words are called compound words.

questions.q: Which sea animal's name is made from 'star' and 'fish'?
questions.f: A starfish is not really a fish, but its name stuck anyway.

questions.q: 'Butter' plus 'fly' makes the name of which insect?
questions.f: Nobody is sure why butterflies got 'butter' in their name!

questions.q: Which sport's name is made from 'foot' and 'ball'?
questions.f: 'Basketball' and 'baseball' are compound words too.

questions.q: Joining 'snow' and 'man' makes which winter word?
questions.f: 'Snowball,' 'snowflake,' and 'snowstorm' are all built from 'snow' plus another word.

questions.q: Which bathroom item's name joins 'tooth' and 'brush'?
questions.f: 'Toothpaste' is another compound word starting with 'tooth.'

questions.q: Which snack name is made from 'pop' and 'corn'?
questions.f: The snack is named for the popping sound the corn makes when it bursts.

questions.q: Which glowing insect's name joins 'fire' and 'fly'?
questions.f: Some people call fireflies 'lightning bugs,' which is a compound word too.

questions.q: Which room's name is made from 'bed' and 'room'?
questions.f: 'Bathroom' and 'classroom' end with 'room' as well.

questions.q: What do we call the coat made for wearing in the rain?
questions.f: 'Rainbow,' 'raindrop,' and 'raincoat' all begin with the word 'rain.'

questions.q: Which fruit's name joins 'water' and 'melon'?
questions.f: The name fits: a watermelon is about nine-tenths water.

questions.q: Which tall yellow flower's name joins 'sun' and 'flower'?
questions.f: Young sunflowers slowly turn their heads to follow the sun across the sky.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound a bee makes?
questions.f: 'Buzz' even sounds buzzy because of its double Z.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound of a ticking clock?
questions.f: Words that copy real sounds, like 'tick-tock,' are fun to say out loud.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound of jumping into water?
questions.f: Sound-copying words like 'splash' make stories feel noisy and alive.

questions.q: Which word do we use for a cat's happy rumbling sound?
questions.f: 'Purr' stretches out its R sound, a little like the sound itself.

questions.q: A person who teaches at a school is called a...?
questions.f: Adding '-er' to an action word often names the person who does it.

questions.q: Someone whose job is baking bread is a...?
questions.f: 'Baker' is simply 'bake' plus '-er,' meaning a person who bakes.

questions.q: What do we call a person who sings songs?
questions.f: In 'singer,' the '-er' ending means 'one who sings.'

questions.q: A person who grows crops on a farm is a...?
questions.f: 'Farm' plus '-er' makes 'farmer,' the person who farms.

questions.q: What do we call a person who dances?
questions.f: French gave English the word 'dance' many hundreds of years ago.

questions.q: A person who runs in races is called a...?
questions.f: 'Run' doubles its N before adding '-er' to keep the short sound.

questions.q: Which word sounds like 'sun' but means a boy child?
questions.f: Words that sound alike but have different spellings are called homophones.

questions.q: Which word sounds like 'sea' but means to look with your eyes?
questions.f: 'See' and 'sea' sound exactly the same but mean totally different things.

questions.q: Which word sounds like 'two' but means 'also'?
questions.f: 'To,' 'too,' and 'two' are three spellings for the very same sound.

questions.q: Which word sounds like 'here' but means to listen with your ears?
questions.f: A trick to remember: 'hear' has the word 'ear' hiding inside it.

questions.q: Which little word sounds just like the insect 'bee'?
questions.f: 'Be' and 'bee' are homophones, words that sound the same but are spelled differently.

questions.q: Which word sounds like the color 'blue' and tells what the wind did?
questions.f: 'The wind blew' and 'the sky is blue' sound alike but use different spellings.

questions.q: Which fruit's name sounds exactly like 'pair'?
questions.f: 'Pair,' 'pear,' and 'pare' are three different words that all sound the same.

questions.q: Which word sounds like 'tail' but means a story?
questions.f: A fairy tale is a story, while a fairy's tail would be something else entirely!

questions.q: Which word sounds like 'right' but means to make words on paper?
questions.f: 'Write' starts with a silent W, like 'wrong' and 'wrap.'

questions.q: How many syllables are in the word 'banana'?
questions.f: Clap as you say ba-na-na and you will feel the three beats.

questions.q: How many syllables does the word 'dog' have?
questions.f: A syllable is one beat of a word, and 'dog' has just a single beat.

questions.q: How many syllables are in the word 'tiger'?
questions.f: Say ti-ger with a clap on each part to count its two syllables.

questions.q: Which letter comes right after M in the alphabet?
questions.f: M and N sit side by side in the very middle of the alphabet.

questions.q: Which letter comes right before D in the alphabet?
questions.f: The alphabet order helps us find words quickly in a dictionary.

questions.q: Which letter comes last in the alphabet?
questions.f: Z is also one of the rarest letters in English words.

questions.q: Which of these letters is a vowel?
questions.f: Vowels are open, singable sounds, and every English word needs at least one vowel sound.

questions.q: Which of these letters is a consonant?
questions.f: Consonants are made by blocking air with your lips, teeth, or tongue.

questions.q: The word 'don't' is a short way of saying...?
questions.f: The little mark in 'don't' is an apostrophe, and it shows where a letter is missing.

questions.q: 'Can't' is the short form of which words?
questions.f: Squashed-together words like 'can't' are called contractions.

questions.q: 'I'm' is a short way of writing...?
questions.f: The apostrophe in 'I'm' stands in for the missing letter A.

questions.q: What does 'it's' stand for?
questions.f: 'It's' with an apostrophe means 'it is,' while 'its' without one shows belonging.

questions.q: 'We're' is the short form of which words?
questions.f: 'We're,' 'you're,' and 'they're' all hide the little word 'are.'

questions.q: The word 'huge' means very...?
questions.f: 'Huge,' 'giant,' and 'enormous' are all bigger ways of saying big.

questions.q: The word 'tiny' means very...?
questions.f: 'Tiny,' 'mini,' and 'wee' all describe very small things.

questions.q: What do we call the first meal of the day, eaten in the morning?
questions.f: Its name means breaking the long 'fast,' the time you spent not eating overnight.

questions.q: Which word means the same as 'afraid'?
questions.f: Words with the same meaning, like 'afraid' and 'scared,' are called synonyms.

questions.q: When you shout, you are talking very...?
questions.f: 'Yell,' 'holler,' and 'shout' are all synonyms for talking loudly.

questions.q: Which word means the same as 'begin'?
questions.f: 'Begin,' 'start,' and 'commence' all mean the same thing.

questions.q: An 'exit' is the way...?
questions.f: 'Exit' comes from a Latin word meaning 'he goes out.'

questions.q: Which of these words names a color?
questions.f: Color words like 'purple' are describing words that tell us how things look.

questions.q: Which of these is an action word?
questions.f: Action words are called verbs, and every sentence needs one.

questions.q: Which of these words always needs a capital letter?
questions.f: Days of the week and people's names always start with capital letters.

questions.q: What letter do we usually add to a word to mean more than one?
questions.f: One cat becomes two cats just by adding the letter S.

questions.q: Which little word fits the blank: '___ orange, please!'
questions.f: We use 'an' instead of 'a' before words that start with a vowel sound.

questions.q: 'Phone' is a short way of saying which longer word?
questions.f: Chopping the front off a long word, like 'telephone' to 'phone,' is called clipping.

questions.q: 'Math' is short for which school subject?
questions.f: In Britain, people shorten 'mathematics' to 'maths' with an S.

questions.q: A baby dog is called a kitten.
questions.f: A baby dog is a puppy; a kitten is a baby cat.

questions.q: 'Won't' is the short way of writing 'will not.'
questions.f: It is a strange one: 'will not' squashes down to 'won't,' not 'willn't.'

questions.q: The word 'pizza' has two Zs in it.
questions.f: 'Pizza' kept its double Z when English borrowed it from Italian.

questions.q: In the alphabet, the letter B comes right after A.
questions.f: A and B start the alphabet, and their Greek cousins are alpha and beta.

questions.q: 'Happy' and 'glad' mean almost the same thing.
questions.f: Words that share a meaning, like 'happy' and 'glad,' are called synonyms.

questions.q: The word 'hiss' copies the sound a snake makes.
questions.f: 'Hiss' uses a stretchy S sound, just like a real snake.

questions.q: The plural of 'box' is 'boxes.'
questions.f: Words ending in X add '-es,' so one fox becomes two foxes.

questions.q: Every sentence should begin with a capital letter.
questions.f: Capital letters at the start help readers see where each new sentence begins.

questions.q: The word 'red' is the name of an animal.
questions.f: 'Red' names a color, though it does appear in animal names like 'red fox.'

questions.q: 'Grandmother' is made from the two words 'grand' and 'mother.'
questions.f: Two words joined into one, like 'grandmother,' make a compound word.

questions.q: What is a group of cows called?
questions.f: 'Herd' is used for many grazing animals, including elephants and deer.

questions.q: A group of bees flying together is called a...?
questions.f: A swarm can hold thousands of bees following one queen to a new home.

questions.q: What is a group of dolphins called?
questions.f: Whales also travel in pods, and a pod can hunt and play together for years.

questions.q: A group of sheep is called a...?
questions.f: 'Flock' works for sheep and for birds, two very different animals.

questions.q: The prefix 'un-' in 'unhappy' means...?
questions.f: Stick 'un-' on a word and it flips the meaning, like 'lock' and 'unlock.'

questions.q: The prefix 're-' in 'redo' means...?
questions.f: 'Replay,' 'rewrite,' and 'rebuild' all mean doing something again.

questions.q: The ending '-ful' in 'hopeful' means...?
questions.f: 'Joyful' means full of joy, and 'careful' means full of care.

questions.q: The ending '-less' in 'fearless' means...?
questions.f: 'Homeless,' 'endless,' and 'spotless' all use '-less' to mean 'without.'

questions.q: Which two words were blended to make 'motel'?
questions.f: Motels appeared along highways so drivers could park right by their rooms.

questions.q: A 'spork' is a blend of which two utensil words?
questions.f: Blended words like 'spork' are called portmanteau words.

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'knee'?
questions.f: Long ago English speakers really did pronounce the K in 'knee' and 'knight.'

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'lamb'?
questions.f: 'Comb,' 'thumb,' and 'climb' all end with the same silent B.

questions.q: In the word 'phone,' the letters 'ph' make the sound of which letter?
questions.f: The 'ph' spelling for the F sound comes from words borrowed from Greek.

questions.q: Big, bigger, and then...?
questions.f: The '-est' ending marks the superlative, the most of something.

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'run'?
questions.f: 'Run' is an irregular verb, so it changes its vowel instead of adding '-ed.'

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'go'?
questions.f: 'Went' was borrowed from a completely different old verb, 'wend.'

questions.q: Which word is a synonym of 'angry'?
questions.f: 'Furious' means extremely angry, an even stronger word than 'mad.'

questions.q: Which word is an antonym of 'ancient'?
questions.f: 'Ancient' means very old, so its opposite is 'modern' or 'new.'

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'knight'?
questions.f: 'Knight' and 'night' are homophones, and the K in 'knight' was once pronounced.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'whole'?
questions.f: A 'whole' pizza and a 'hole' in the ground sound the same when spoken.

questions.q: What does the short form 'Dr.' stand for?
questions.f: Shortened words with a period, like 'Dr.' and 'St.,' are called abbreviations.

questions.q: The letters 'TV' are short for which word?
questions.f: 'Television' mixes Greek 'tele' meaning far with a Latin word for seeing.

questions.q: A word that names a person, place, or thing is called a...?
questions.f: 'Teacher,' 'park,' and 'pencil' are all nouns.

questions.q: A word that shows an action, like 'swim,' is called a...?
questions.f: 'Verb' comes from a Latin word that simply means 'word.'

questions.q: In 'shiny coin,' what kind of word is 'shiny'?
questions.f: Adjectives describe nouns, telling us their size, color, shape, or feel.

questions.q: The word 'breakfast' means to 'break' your overnight...?
questions.f: A 'fast' is a stretch of time without eating, and breakfast ends it.

questions.q: How many syllables are in the word 'dictionary'?
questions.f: Say dic-tion-ar-y slowly and you can count all four beats.

questions.q: The word 'gym' is short for 'gymnasium.'
questions.f: 'Gymnasium' traces back to ancient Greek schools for exercise.

questions.q: 'Their,' 'there,' and 'they're' all sound the same.
questions.f: They are homophones, which is why spellers must think about meaning, not just sound.

questions.q: The silent letter in 'comb' is C.
questions.f: The silent letter in 'comb' is actually the B at the end.

questions.q: The Greek root 'tele' in 'telephone' means...?
questions.f: A telephone carries a voice 'far,' and a telescope lets you see far.

questions.q: The Latin root 'aqua' in 'aquarium' means...?
questions.f: 'Aqueduct' and 'aquatic' share the same watery root.

questions.q: The root 'bio' in 'biology' means...?
questions.f: A 'biography' is the story of someone's life.

questions.q: The root 'geo' in 'geography' means...?
questions.f: 'Geology' and 'geometry' also grew from the Greek word for Earth.

questions.q: The root 'micro' in 'microscope' means...?
questions.f: A microscope lets us 'see the small,' while a microphone picks up small sounds.

questions.q: The root 'octo' in 'octopus' means...?
questions.f: 'Octopus' means 'eight feet,' and an octagon has eight sides.

questions.q: The root 'cent' in 'century' means...?
questions.f: A centipede is named for its 'hundred feet,' and a cent is a hundredth of a dollar.

questions.q: The Latin root 'port' in 'transport' means...?
questions.f: 'Portable' means carryable, and a porter is someone who carries things.

questions.q: The Latin root 'audi' in 'audience' means...?
questions.f: 'Audio' and 'audible' come from the same hearing root.

questions.q: The Latin root 'dict' in 'predict' means...?
questions.f: To 'predict' is literally to 'say before,' and to 'dictate' is to say aloud.

questions.q: The root 'scrib' in 'scribble' means...?
questions.f: A 'manuscript' is literally something written by hand.

questions.q: The prefix 'sub-' in 'submarine' means...?
questions.f: A submarine goes under the sea, and a subway runs under the street.

questions.q: The prefix 'pre-' in 'preview' means...?
questions.f: A preview is a look before, and to preheat an oven is to heat it beforehand.

questions.q: The ending '-phobia' means...?
questions.f: 'Arachnophobia' is the fear of spiders, from the Greek word for fear.

questions.q: The ending '-ology' in 'biology' means...?
questions.f: 'Zoology,' 'geology,' and 'meteorology' are all fields of study.

questions.q: A scientist who studies stars and planets is an...?
questions.f: An astrologer reads horoscopes, but an astronomer does the science.

questions.q: The root 'dent' in 'dentist' means...?
questions.f: 'Dental' and 'dentures' share the Latin tooth root, 'dens.'

questions.q: The Latin root 'ped' in 'pedal' means...?
questions.f: A 'pedestrian' is a person traveling on foot.

questions.q: The root 'manu' in 'manual' means...?
questions.f: To 'manufacture' once meant to make something by hand.

questions.q: Which two words were blended to make 'sitcom'?
questions.f: Blends like 'sitcom' keep the front of one word and the back of another.

questions.q: The word 'kindergarten' literally means...?
questions.f: English borrowed it straight from German: 'Kinder' children plus 'Garten' garden.

questions.q: The dance word 'ballet' traces back to a word meaning...?
questions.f: English took 'ballet' from French, which got it from Italian 'balletto,' a little dance.

questions.q: The word 'spaghetti' literally means...?
questions.f: In Italian, 'spago' means string, so spaghetti are 'little strings.'

questions.q: A word built from first letters, like 'scuba,' is called an...?
questions.f: 'Scuba' stands for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus.

questions.q: Which is the traditional name for a group of crows?
questions.f: This spooky-sounding name appears in English lists of animal groups from the 1400s.

questions.q: The study of where words come from is called...?
questions.f: Mix them up and you switch subjects: entomology is the study of insects.

questions.q: The prefix 'uni-' in 'unicorn' means one.
questions.f: A unicorn has one horn, a unicycle one wheel, and a uniform is 'one form.'

questions.q: The hamburger is named after the German city of Hamburg.
questions.f: It has nothing to do with ham; 'Hamburg steak' came first.

questions.q: The root 'therm' in 'thermometer' means water.
questions.f: 'Therm' means heat, which is why a thermos keeps drinks warm.

questions.q: The word 'salary' comes from the Latin word for which substance?
questions.f: Roman soldiers received a 'salarium,' money linked to precious salt.

questions.q: 'Muscle' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Romans thought a flexing muscle looked like a small mouse moving under the skin.

questions.q: The sandwich is named after an English...?
questions.f: The 4th Earl of Sandwich reportedly ate meat between bread so he could keep playing cards.

questions.q: The word 'robot' was coined from an old word meaning...?
questions.f: It debuted in Karel Capek's 1920 Czech play R.U.R., from 'robota,' forced labor.

questions.q: Broken into its ancient roots, 'disaster' literally means...?
questions.f: People once blamed calamities on unlucky stars, 'dis' plus 'astrum.'

questions.q: By its Latin roots, a 'companion' is someone you share ___ with.
questions.f: 'Com' means with and 'panis' means bread, so companions break bread together.

questions.q: 'Candidate' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Romans seeking office wore chalk-whitened togas, 'candidus' meaning white.

questions.q: The Greek roots of 'tragedy' literally mean...?
questions.f: 'Tragoidia' may recall goats given as prizes or costumes in early Greek drama.

questions.q: The Latin roots of 'trivia' literally mean...?
questions.f: At a 'trivium,' a three-way crossroads, people swapped everyday chatter.

questions.q: 'Quarantine' comes from an Italian phrase meaning...?
questions.f: Ships reaching Venice during plague times waited 'quaranta giorni,' forty days.

questions.q: 'Dandelion' comes from a French phrase meaning...?
questions.f: 'Dent-de-lion' describes the flower's jagged, tooth-like leaves.

questions.q: 'Vaccine' comes from the Latin word for which animal?
questions.f: Edward Jenner's first vaccine used cowpox, so he built the name from 'vacca,' cow.

questions.q: The word 'malaria' comes from an Italian phrase meaning...?
questions.f: People blamed swamp air for the disease before mosquitoes were discovered.

questions.q: The fabric word 'denim' comes from the name of a city in...?
questions.f: 'Serge de Nimes,' cloth of Nimes, was shortened to 'de Nimes,' then denim.

questions.q: 'Jeans' takes its name from which Italian city?
questions.f: Sailors from Genoa wore sturdy cloth that the French called 'genes.'

questions.q: 'Ketchup' traces back to 'ke-tsiap,' originally a sauce made from...?
questions.f: The word came from Hokkien Chinese; tomatoes only joined the recipe centuries later.

questions.q: The word 'alphabet' is built from...?
questions.f: Alpha and beta, the Greek A and B, were squashed together to name the whole set.

questions.q: 'January' is named after Janus, the Roman god of...?
questions.f: Janus had two faces, one looking back at the old year and one ahead to the new.

questions.q: 'Cereal' comes from Ceres, the Roman goddess of...?
questions.f: Ceres watched over grain crops, so grain foods carry her name.

questions.q: 'Volcano' comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of...?
questions.f: Romans imagined Vulcan's blacksmith forge rumbling under a smoking island.

questions.q: The word 'echo' comes from Echo, who in Greek myth was...?
c: A nymph who could only repeat words
questions.f: In the myth, Echo lost her own voice and could only repeat what others said.

questions.q: A book of maps is called an 'atlas' after...?
c: A Titan holding up the sky
questions.f: Early map books showed the Titan Atlas carrying the heavens on their covers.

questions.q: The color word 'khaki' comes from a word meaning...?
questions.f: It reached English through Hindi and Urdu from the Persian 'khak,' meaning dust.

questions.q: The word 'shampoo' originally meant to...?
questions.f: It comes from the Hindi 'champo,' a command meaning 'massage!'

questions.q: 'Cookie' comes from 'koekje,' a word meaning...?
questions.f: Dutch settlers brought the word 'koekje' to America along with the treat.

questions.q: 'Alligator' comes from 'el lagarto,' a Spanish phrase meaning...?
questions.f: Spanish explorers in Florida saw huge 'lizards' and the name stuck.

questions.q: The word 'mosquito' literally means...?
questions.f: In Spanish, 'mosca' means fly, and '-ito' makes it little.

questions.q: 'Chocolate' traces back to 'xocolatl,' often translated as...?
questions.f: The word came from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, who drank it unsweetened.

questions.q: The word 'sofa' traces back to an Arabic word for...?
questions.f: Arabic 'suffa' named a raised, cushioned sitting platform.

questions.q: The original 'qajaq,' which gave us the word 'kayak,' was a...?
questions.f: The word comes from Inuit; a qajaq was built so a hunter could roll it upright if it flipped.

questions.q: Which spelling means writing paper and envelopes?
questions.f: Remember E for envelope; 'stationary' with an A means standing still.

questions.q: The head of a school is the...?
questions.f: A classic memory trick: the princiPAL is your pal; a princiPLE is a rule.

questions.q: Which spelling means a kind word of praise?
questions.f: 'Complement' with an E means something that completes, like colors that match.

questions.q: 'Fewer' is correctly used for things you can...?
questions.f: Careful writers say fewer cookies but less milk.

questions.q: If a speaker only hints at a meaning, the listener must do what?
questions.f: Speakers imply; listeners infer, reading between the lines.

questions.q: The sweet course after dinner is spelled...?
questions.f: Remember the double S because you always want seconds of dessert.

questions.q: In careful writing, 'affect' is usually which part of speech?
questions.f: The rain affects the game, and the effect is a cancellation: verb, then noun.

questions.q: To 'allude' to something means to...?
questions.f: Its near-twin 'elude' means to escape, as a fox eludes the hounds.

questions.q: An 'eminent' scientist is...?
questions.f: Its sound-alike 'imminent' means about to happen, a classic spelling-bee trap.

questions.q: Which spelling names the building where lawmakers meet?
questions.f: 'Capital' with an A is the city, the money, or the uppercase letter.

questions.q: 'Silent' and 'listen' use exactly the same letters. Such word pairs are...?
questions.f: Rearranging letters makes anagrams; 'astronomer' hides 'moon starer.'

questions.q: 'Jumbo shrimp' squeezes two clashing ideas together. What is this figure called?
questions.f: 'Deafening silence' and 'bittersweet' work the same contradictory magic.

questions.q: A word named after a real person, like 'sandwich,' is called an...?
questions.f: 'Watt,' 'braille,' and 'diesel' all honor real people.

questions.q: 'Edit' was created by trimming down 'editor.' This process is called...?
questions.f: 'Burgle' was carved out of 'burglar' the very same way.

questions.q: Which two words were blended to make 'podcast'?
questions.f: The blend was coined in 2004 and quickly outgrew the gadget it was named for.

questions.q: 'Emoticon' is a blend of which two words?
questions.f: The first smiley :-) was proposed on a computer message board in 1982.

questions.q: 'Bass' the fish and 'bass' the low sound share spelling but not sound. They are...?
questions.f: 'Homograph' means 'same writing'; homophones are the same in sound instead.

questions.q: In 'Swimming is fun,' the word 'swimming' acts as a noun. It is called a...?
questions.f: A gerund is an '-ing' verb form doing a noun's job in the sentence.

questions.q: Which is a correct plural of 'cactus'?
questions.f: 'Cactuses' is fine too; 'cacti' follows the word's Latin pattern.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'crisis'?
questions.f: Greek-style words flip '-is' to '-es,' like 'oasis' becoming 'oases.'

questions.q: What is the plural of 'ox'?
questions.f: The old '-en' plural survives in only a few words, like 'children' and 'brethren.'

questions.q: What are the three dots (...) that show a trailing-off thought called?
questions.f: 'Ellipsis' comes from Greek for 'falling short,' and its plural is 'ellipses.'

questions.q: Which punctuation mark can link two closely related complete sentences?
questions.f: A comma alone there causes an error editors call a comma splice.

questions.q: The prefix 'circum-' in 'circumnavigate' means...?
questions.f: To circumnavigate the globe is to sail all the way around it.

questions.q: The prefix 'mal-' in 'malfunction' means...?
questions.f: French 'mal' means badly, so a malfunction is a working-badly.

questions.q: The root 'bene' in 'benefactor' means...?
questions.f: A benefactor literally 'does good,' and a benefit is a good result.

questions.q: The word 'leotard' honors Jules Leotard, a 19th-century French...?
questions.f: Leotard invented the flying trapeze act in 1859 and performed it in the snug one-piece that took his name.

questions.q: The prefix 'pseudo-' in 'pseudonym' means...?
