questions.f: A pseudonym is a false name, like Dr. Seuss for Theodor Geisel.

questions.q: The prefix 'hyper-' in 'hyperactive' means...?
questions.f: Its opposite is 'hypo-,' meaning under, as in 'hypothermia.'

questions.q: The root 'chron' in 'chronological' means...?
questions.f: A chronometer measures time, and 'synchronize' means to match times.

questions.q: Sudden overwhelming fear is called 'panic' after which Greek god?
questions.f: Travelers blamed the goat-legged god Pan for the strange noises that spooked them in wild places.

questions.q: The word 'silhouette' honors Etienne de Silhouette, an 18th-century French...?
questions.f: His penny-pinching made his name a joke for anything done cheaply, like shadow portraits instead of paintings.

questions.q: 'Petrichor' is the scholarly name for...?
questions.f: Two Australian scientists coined it in 1964 from Greek 'petra' (stone) and 'ichor,' the fluid in the veins of the gods.

questions.q: Something 'ephemeral' lasts...?
questions.f: The Greek root means 'for a day,' and mayflies are called ephemera.

questions.q: What is an 'aglet'?
questions.f: 'Aglet' comes from an old French word for 'little needle.'

questions.q: Horace Walpole coined 'serendipity' in 1754 after a fairy tale about the princes of...?
questions.f: Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka; the tale's princes kept making lucky discoveries by accident.

questions.q: A 'tyro' is a beginner; the Latin original 'tiro' meant...?
questions.f: Rome's rawest soldiers were 'tirones,' so the word marched from the barracks into every field of learning.

questions.q: The 'mare' in 'nightmare' was an old word for a bad spirit in dreams.
questions.f: People once blamed a spooky visitor called a 'mare' for bad dreams, not a horse.

questions.q: 'Awful' originally meant 'full of awe.'
questions.f: It described things that inspired wonder before it came to mean terrible.

questions.q: 'Sincere' comes from a Latin phrase meaning 'without wax.'
questions.f: That story is a myth; it really comes from 'sincerus,' meaning pure or whole.

questions.q: The Latin root 'terra' means earth.
questions.f: It grounds words like 'territory,' 'terrain,' and 'terrarium.'

questions.q: The word 'decade' comes from a Greek word meaning ten.
questions.f: Greek 'deka' means ten, as in 'decathlon,' a contest of ten events.

questions.q: The word 'clue' comes from an old word for a ball of thread.
questions.f: In myth, Theseus followed a 'clew' of thread to escape the labyrinth.

questions.q: The flower name 'daisy' began as 'day's eye.'
questions.f: Daisies open at sunrise and close at night, like an eye of the day.

questions.q: The word 'butterfly' began as 'flutterby' and got flipped around.
questions.f: A fun myth: Old English already called the insect 'buttorfleoge,' butterfly.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'hat'?
questions.f: 'Hat,' 'bat,' 'cat,' and 'mat' all belong to the same rhyming family.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'bug'?
questions.f: Rhyming words share their ending sound, and 'bug' and 'rug' both end in '-ug.'

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'pig'?
questions.f: 'Pig,' 'wig,' 'dig,' and 'big' make a handy rhyming set for poems.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'box'?
questions.f: A rhyming pair like 'fox in a box' is easy to remember and fun to say.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'bee'?
questions.f: 'Bee,' 'tree,' 'see,' and 'key' all end with the same long E sound.

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'hot'?
questions.f: Watch out: 'warm' and 'boiling' are still on the hot side!

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of 'in'?
questions.f: 'In' and 'out' are opposites, and both are tiny two-letter or three-letter words.

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'soft'?
questions.f: A pillow is soft, but a rock is hard.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of 'old'?
questions.f: 'Old' has two opposites: 'young' for people and animals, and 'new' for things.

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'full'?
questions.f: A glass can be full, empty, or half of each.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of 'clean'?
questions.f: 'Clean' has lots of friends that mean nearly the same: 'tidy,' 'neat,' and 'spotless.'

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'near'?
questions.f: 'Near' and 'close' mean the same thing, so neither can be its own opposite.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of 'dark'?
questions.f: The word 'light' does two jobs: it means bright, and it also means not heavy.

questions.q: Put 'play' and 'ground' together. What place do you get?
questions.f: Two small words stuck together make one compound word.

questions.q: Which special day's name joins 'birth' and 'day'?
questions.f: 'Holiday' is a compound word too, from 'holy' plus 'day.'

questions.q: Which breakfast food's name joins 'pan' and 'cake'?
questions.f: The name says how it is made: a cake cooked in a pan.

questions.q: Which box gets letters and joins 'mail' and 'box'?
questions.f: All four choices are compound words, but only one holds your letters.

questions.q: Which beach treasure's name joins 'sea' and 'shell'?
questions.f: 'Seaweed,' 'seashore,' and 'seahorse' all start with the word 'sea.'

questions.q: Which spotted insect's name joins 'lady' and 'bug'?
questions.f: In Britain the same insect is called a ladybird.

questions.q: Which school item's name joins 'note' and 'book'?
questions.f: 'Bookshelf,' 'bookmark,' and 'notebook' all contain the word 'book.'

questions.q: Which splashy wonder of nature joins 'water' and 'fall'?
questions.f: 'Waterfall' packs the whole picture into one word: water that falls.

questions.q: Where does a dog sleep if the word joins 'dog' and 'house'?
questions.f: 'Doghouse' and 'kennel' mean the same thing, but only one is a compound word.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound a duck makes?
questions.f: Ducks say 'quack' in English but 'coin coin' in French books.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound of a balloon bursting?
questions.f: 'Pop' is short and sharp, just like the sound it copies.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound of food cooking in a hot pan?
questions.f: You can almost hear the pan in the S and Z sounds of 'sizzle.'

questions.q: Which word copies the sound of thunder?
questions.f: Thunder is the sound of air heated so fast by lightning that it bangs.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound of a leaky tap?
questions.f: Say 'drip, drip, drip' and you have made a tiny sound picture with words.

questions.q: A person who writes stories is called a...?
questions.f: Add '-er' to 'write' and you name the person who does it.

questions.q: Someone who drives a bus is a...?
questions.f: 'Drive' plus '-er' makes 'driver,' one who drives.

questions.q: Someone who builds houses is a...?
questions.f: 'Build' plus '-er' names the job, and so do 'teacher' and 'farmer.'

questions.q: The word 'unkind' means...?
questions.f: The little beginning 'un-' flips a word to mean the opposite.

questions.q: If you 'retell' a story, you tell it...?
questions.f: 'Re-' means again, so 'reread' means to read something one more time.

questions.q: How many letters are in the word 'cat'?
questions.f: Three letters, but only one syllable when you say it.

questions.q: Which letter comes first in the alphabet?
questions.f: A is first in English, and its Greek cousin 'alpha' starts the word 'alphabet.'

questions.q: How many syllables are in the word 'elephant'?
questions.f: Clap along: el-e-phant gives you three claps.

questions.q: How many syllables are in the word 'rainbow'?
questions.f: Compound words often have one syllable from each little word inside.

questions.q: Which of these should always begin with a capital letter?
questions.f: Months, days, and people's names always get a capital letter.

questions.q: Which mark do we put at the end of a telling sentence?
questions.f: In Britain this mark is called a full stop instead of a period.

questions.q: Which mark shows a shout or a surprise?
questions.f: Writers save exclamation marks for special moments so they keep their punch.

questions.q: One bus, but three...?
questions.f: Words ending in S add '-es,' so one kiss becomes two kisses.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like the number 'four'?
questions.f: 'For,' 'four,' and 'fore' are three spellings that all sound the same.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like the number 'one'?
questions.f: You 'won' the game, and that is 'one' win.

questions.q: A comma is used to show a short pause in a sentence.
questions.f: The word 'comma' comes from a Greek word meaning a piece cut off.

questions.q: Every word in a sentence needs a capital letter.
questions.f: Only the first word, names, and a few special words get capitals.

questions.q: The word 'moon' has two of the same letter side by side.
questions.f: Double letters show up everywhere: 'book,' 'tree,' 'grass,' and 'happy.'

questions.q: One baby, but a room full of...?
questions.f: When a word ends in a consonant plus Y, the Y changes to '-ies.'

questions.q: What is the plural of 'city'?
questions.f: 'Party' becomes 'parties' and 'story' becomes 'stories' by the same rule.

questions.q: Add '-ing' to 'hop'. What is the correct spelling?
questions.f: Doubling the P keeps the short O sound; 'hoping' with one P comes from 'hope.'

questions.q: Add '-ing' to 'hope'. What is the correct spelling?
questions.f: Drop the silent E before adding '-ing,' so 'bake' becomes 'baking.'

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of 'swim' plus '-ing'?
questions.f: Short-vowel words with one final consonant double it: 'run,' 'sit,' 'swim.'

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of 'make' plus '-ing'?
questions.f: The silent E has done its job, so it packs up and leaves before '-ing.'

questions.q: Which spelling follows the 'i before e' pattern correctly?
questions.f: The old rhyme says i before e except after c, as in 'receive.'

questions.q: After the letter C, which spelling follows the rule correctly?
questions.f: After the letter C, the pattern flips to 'ei,' as in 'ceiling' and 'deceive.'

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the day after Tuesday?
questions.f: That hidden D survives from Woden's day, an old name for the god Odin.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling of the second month of the year?
questions.f: Most people skip the first R when speaking, which is why it gets lost in writing.

questions.q: Which spelling of the word meaning 'for this reason' is correct?
questions.f: 'Because' began as the two words 'by cause.'

questions.q: How do you correctly spell the word for someone you like to play with?
questions.f: A handy trick: a friend sticks with you to the END.

questions.q: Which spelling of the word meaning 'very pretty' is correct?
questions.f: 'Beautiful' hides three vowels in a row at the start: e, a, u.

questions.q: How do you correctly spell the name for the day after today?
questions.f: One M, two Rs: 'tomorrow' grew out of the phrase 'to morrow,' meaning to morning.

questions.q: Which spelling of the word meaning 'needed' is correct?
questions.f: One collar and two sleeves: one C, then two Ss.

questions.q: How do you correctly spell the word meaning 'to keep apart'?
questions.f: There is 'a rat' in the middle of 'separate.'

questions.q: Which spelling of the word for a steady beat in music is correct?
questions.f: 'Rhythm' is famous for having no ordinary vowels, only Y doing vowel duty.

questions.q: How do you correctly spell the word meaning 'for certain'?
questions.f: It comes from 'definite,' which contains the word 'finite,' meaning having an end.

questions.q: Which word uses the 'ck' spelling correctly?
questions.f: After a short vowel at the end of a small word, English writes 'ck,' as in 'sock' and 'kick.'

questions.q: Which spelling of the word meaning 'to grab a ball' is correct?
questions.f: The 'tch' spelling follows a short vowel, as in 'match,' 'fetch,' and 'itch.'

questions.q: In which word does the letter C make an S sound?
questions.f: C goes soft before E, I, and Y, as in 'city,' 'cell,' and 'cycle.'

questions.q: In which word does the letter G make a J sound?
questions.f: G goes soft before E, I, and Y, as in 'gentle,' 'giraffe,' and 'gym.'

questions.q: How do you correctly add '-ful' to 'care'?
questions.f: The ending '-ful' always has just one L, even though 'full' has two.

questions.q: How do you correctly write 'careful' as an '-ly' word?
questions.f: Adding '-ly' to '-ful' gives you the double L, as in 'hopefully.'

questions.q: Which word is the correct plural of 'knife'?
questions.f: 'Wife,' 'life,' and 'knife' all swap F for V before adding S.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'mouse' when you mean the computer kind or the animal?
questions.f: 'Mouse' becomes 'mice,' but 'house' never becomes 'hice.'

questions.q: What is the plural of 'woman'?
questions.f: Only one letter changes in writing, but the first vowel sound changes when spoken.

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'catch'?
questions.f: 'Catch,' 'teach,' and 'buy' all take a surprising '-ght' or '-ught' past form.

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'teach'?
questions.f: 'Taught' and 'caught' rhyme and both use the old '-aught' pattern.

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'bring'?
questions.f: Some people say 'brang' by copying 'sing/sang,' but the standard form is 'brought.'

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'fly'?
questions.f: 'Flew' is the simple past, while 'flown' needs a helper word like 'has.'

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'island'?
questions.f: The S was added by writers who wrongly linked it to the word 'isle.'

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'castle'?
questions.f: 'Castle,' 'listen,' and 'whistle' all keep a silent T.

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'hour'?
questions.f: Because the H is silent, we write 'an hour,' not 'a hour.'

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'sword'?
questions.f: The W was pronounced in Old English, when the word sounded more like 'sweord.'

questions.q: Which letters are silent in the word 'science'?
questions.f: The 'sc' spelling makes one S sound in 'science,' 'scene,' and 'scissors.'

questions.q: Which letter is silent in the word 'receipt'?
questions.f: The silent P was added to show the word's link to Latin 'recipere,' to receive.

questions.q: 'Shouldn't' is the short form of which words?
questions.f: The apostrophe stands exactly where the O of 'not' used to be.

questions.q: 'They'll' is the short form of which words?
questions.f: '-'ll' contractions squash 'will' down to two letters.

questions.q: 'Let's' is a short way of writing...?
questions.f: Without the apostrophe, 'lets' is just an ordinary verb: she lets me go.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation 'etc.' stand for?
questions.f: 'Et cetera' is Latin for 'and the rest.'

questions.q: What does the abbreviation 'St.' stand for in 'Baker St.'?
questions.f: Confusingly, 'St.' can also stand for 'Saint,' as in St. Patrick.

questions.q: The letters 'ASAP' stand for...?
questions.f: A short form built from first letters, like ASAP, is called an initialism.

questions.q: What do the letters 'RSVP' on an invitation ask you to do?
questions.f: It stands for a French phrase meaning 'please respond.'

questions.q: 'Laser' is a short form built from the first letters of a long phrase. What is such a word called?
questions.f: An acronym is said as a word; 'laser' hides 'light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.'

questions.q: The prefix 'dis-' in 'disagree' means...?
questions.f: 'Dislike,' 'disappear,' and 'dishonest' all use 'dis-' to flip the meaning.

questions.q: The prefix 'mis-' in 'misspell' means...?
questions.f: 'Misspell' really does have a double S: 'mis' plus 'spell.'

questions.q: The prefix 'semi-' in 'semicircle' means...?
questions.f: A semicircle is half a circle, and semifinals come before the final.

questions.q: The prefix 'non-' in 'nonsense' means...?
questions.f: 'Nonstop,' 'nonfiction,' and 'nonsense' all mean 'not that thing.'

questions.q: The prefix 'bi-' in 'bicycle' means...?
questions.f: 'Bilingual' means speaking two languages, and 'binoculars' use two eyepieces.

questions.q: The prefix 'over-' in 'oversleep' means...?
questions.f: 'Overeat,' 'overload,' and 'overreact' all mean doing something too much.

questions.q: The suffix '-able' in 'washable' means...?
questions.f: 'Readable,' 'breakable,' and 'lovable' all describe what can be done to something.

questions.q: The suffix '-ness' in 'kindness' turns the word into...?
questions.f: '-ness' makes nouns out of adjectives, as in 'darkness' and 'sadness.'

questions.q: The suffix '-ist' in 'scientist' names...?
questions.f: 'Artist,' 'pianist,' and 'cyclist' all name people by what they do.

questions.q: The suffix '-ish' in 'reddish' means...?
questions.f: 'Sixish' can even mean around six o'clock.

questions.q: The suffix '-ward' in 'homeward' shows...?
questions.f: 'Backward,' 'upward,' and 'westward' all point somewhere.

questions.q: The suffix '-hood' in 'childhood' means...?
c: A state or time of being
questions.f: 'Neighbourhood' and 'brotherhood' use the same old English ending.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'plain'?
questions.f: A 'plain' can be flat land, while a 'plane' flies or smooths wood.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'week'?
questions.f: To remember which is which: a 'weak' arm has an A for 'ache.'

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'bare'?
questions.f: 'Bare' means uncovered, and 'bear' is both the animal and a word for carrying.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'sail'?
questions.f: Ships have sails; shops have sales.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'threw'?
questions.f: 'Thorough' looks similar but has an extra syllable and a different sound.

questions.q: 'Misspell' is correctly spelled with two Ss in the middle.
questions.f: It is a favourite joke among spellers that 'misspell' is often misspelled.

questions.q: When you add '-es' to 'box,' the plural is spelled 'boxs.'
questions.f: The correct plural is 'boxes,' because words ending in X need '-es.'

questions.q: The word 'listen' contains a silent T.
questions.f: Its Old English ancestor 'hlysnan' had no T at all; the letter crept in later.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'meat'?
questions.f: 'Meet' has two Es because two people come together.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'road'?
questions.f: She rode her bike along the road: same sound, two spellings.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'deer'?
questions.f: Letters begin with 'Dear' but a forest holds 'deer.'

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'cell'?
questions.f: A prison has a cell; a shop wants to sell.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'waist'?
questions.f: 'Waist' is part of your body, and 'waste' is something thrown away.

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like 'mail'?
questions.f: Both words came from different old languages and only later ended up sounding alike.

questions.q: A word that takes the place of a name, like 'she' or 'they,' is a...?
questions.f: 'Pro-' means 'for,' so a pronoun stands in for a noun.

questions.q: In 'She ran quickly,' what kind of word is 'quickly'?
questions.f: Adverbs often end in '-ly' and tell how, when, or where something happens.

questions.q: Words like 'and,' 'but,' and 'or' that join parts of a sentence are called...?
questions.f: 'Conjunction' comes from Latin words meaning 'joined together.'

questions.q: In 'the cat under the table,' what kind of word is 'under'?
questions.f: Prepositions show position or direction: under, over, beside, through.

questions.q: The words 'a,' 'an,' and 'the' are known as...?
questions.f: 'The' is the most common word in written English, and it is an article.

questions.q: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.f: Matching the verb to a singular or plural subject is called agreement.

questions.q: Which sentence talks about the future?
questions.f: English builds the future with helper words like 'will' and 'shall.'

questions.q: Which punctuation mark can introduce a list?
questions.f: The colon's two dots act like a little drum roll before the list arrives.

questions.q: Which mark joins words like 'well-known' together?
questions.f: A hyphen is short; the longer dash is used to break up a sentence.

questions.q: What do we call the curved marks ( ) around an extra note?
questions.f: 'Parenthesis' comes from Greek words meaning 'put in beside.'

questions.q: In 'Sam's book,' what job is the apostrophe doing?
c: Showing that the book belongs to Sam
questions.f: Apostrophes have two jobs: missing letters and belonging.

questions.q: What is the correct plural of 'potato'?
questions.f: 'Tomato,' 'hero,' and 'volcano' also like the '-oes' plural.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'wolf'?
questions.f: 'Wolf,' 'calf,' 'shelf,' and 'half' all swap F for V.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'deer'?
questions.f: 'Deer,' 'sheep,' 'moose,' and 'aircraft' stay the same in the plural.

questions.q: What is a group of ants living together called?
questions.f: One ant colony can hold millions of workers, all sisters.

questions.q: What is a group of monkeys called?
questions.f: 'Troop' is used for monkeys and also for baboons.

questions.q: What is a group of whales swimming together called?
questions.f: Some whale pods stay together for a lifetime and share their own calls.

questions.q: What do we call a group of horses kept together?
questions.f: A group of young racehorses in training is also called a string.

questions.q: What is a baby rabbit called?
questions.f: Baby rabbits are called kittens or kits, just like baby cats.

questions.q: What is a baby eagle called?
questions.f: The ending '-et' means small, as in 'owlet' and 'piglet.'

questions.q: Which two words blend together to make 'brainstorm'?
questions.f: 'Brainstorm' is a compound word that pictures ideas whirling like weather.

questions.q: Which two words were blended to make 'e-mail'?
questions.f: The first message between two computers was sent in 1971.

questions.q: Which two words were blended to make 'webinar'?
questions.f: Blends like this are called portmanteau words.

questions.q: Which two words were blended to make 'skateboard'?
questions.f: Early skateboarders nailed roller-skate wheels straight onto wooden boards.

questions.q: Which of these words is a palindrome?
questions.f: 'Noon,' 'eye,' 'radar,' and 'civic' all read the same in both directions.

questions.q: Rearranging the letters of 'star' gives which word?
questions.f: A word made by rearranging another word's letters is called an anagram.

questions.q: What is a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet at least once called?
questions.f: 'Pan' means all, so a pangram uses all the letters.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound of a bell?
questions.f: 'Ding-dong' doubles the sound word, a trick called reduplication.

questions.q: Which word copies the sound of paper tearing?
questions.f: Comic books are full of sound words like 'rip,' 'zap,' and 'thwack.'

questions.q: Which of these words means the MOST tired?
questions.f: Choosing exactly the right strength of word is called using precise diction.

questions.q: Which of these words describes the SMALLEST amount of rain?
questions.f: English has dozens of rain words, from 'mizzle' to 'cloudburst.'

questions.q: Which word is the strongest way to say 'happy'?
questions.f: Writers pick stronger synonyms to make feelings clearer.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'generous'?
questions.f: 'Generous' comes from a Latin word for noble birth, once thought to bring good manners.

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of 'brave'?
questions.f: Three of these choices are synonyms of 'brave,' not opposites.

questions.q: Which word means nearly the same as 'enormous'?
questions.f: 'Gigantic' comes from the giants of Greek myth, the Gigantes.

questions.q: The word 'bicycle' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: 'Bi' means two and 'cycle' means circle or wheel.

questions.q: The word 'telescope' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: 'Tele' means far, and Galileo's version could see the moons of Jupiter.

questions.q: 'Homework' literally means work done...?
questions.f: 'Homework' is a compound word: 'home' plus 'work.'

questions.q: A 'dictionary' is a book that explains what?
questions.f: An atlas maps places and an encyclopedia explains topics; a dictionary handles words.

questions.q: What is a book of synonyms called?
questions.f: 'Thesaurus' comes from a Greek word meaning treasure store.

questions.q: What do we call the alphabetical list of hard words at the back of a book?
questions.f: 'Glossary' comes from a Greek word for tongue or language.

questions.q: What is the base word inside 'unhelpful'?
questions.f: Strip off the prefix 'un-' and the suffix '-ful' and 'help' is left.

questions.q: Which word family does 'sign' belong to?
questions.f: They all grew from Latin 'signum,' a mark or token.

questions.q: Which word is spelled with a double L in the middle?
questions.f: 'Balloon' has both a double L and a double O.

questions.q: How do you correctly spell the name of a building full of books?
questions.f: It comes from Latin 'liber,' meaning book, which is why the R matters.

questions.q: Which spelling of the word for an unexpected event is correct?
questions.f: Both Rs belong: it comes from a French word meaning 'overtaken.'

questions.q: How many syllables are in the word 'temperature' when carefully spoken?
questions.f: Many speakers rush it into three, but 'tem-per-a-ture' is the full form.

questions.q: Which syllable is stressed in the word 'banana'?
questions.f: Stress means the beat you say loudest: ba-NA-na.

questions.q: Which word contains a prefix, a root, and a suffix all at once?
questions.f: 'Unhappiness' stacks three parts: un + happy + ness.

questions.q: The word 'alphabet' has more letters than the word 'letters.'
questions.f: 'Alphabet' has eight letters and 'letters' has seven.

questions.q: The plural of 'child' is formed by adding an S.
questions.f: 'Children' uses an old English plural ending, '-en,' instead.

questions.q: 'Bicycle' and 'binoculars' share a prefix that means two.
questions.f: Latin 'bi' also gives us 'biped,' a creature with two feet.

questions.q: An adjective describes a noun.
questions.f: 'Adjective' comes from Latin words meaning 'thrown next to,' since it sits beside the noun.

questions.q: The word 'queue' has four vowels in a row after the Q.
questions.f: Drop those four letters and 'queue' still sounds exactly the same.

questions.q: The word 'thesaurus' is a kind of dinosaur.
questions.f: It sounds like one because many dinosaur names end in '-saurus,' Greek for lizard.

questions.q: The root 'hydro' in 'hydroelectric' means...?
questions.f: A 'hydrant' delivers water and 'dehydrated' means dried out.

questions.q: The root 'phon' in 'symphony' means...?
questions.f: 'Symphony' means 'sounding together,' from Greek 'syn' plus 'phone.'

questions.q: The root 'graph' in 'autograph' means...?
questions.f: 'Auto' means self, so an autograph is literally self-writing.

questions.q: The root 'meter' in 'barometer' means...?
questions.f: 'Baro' means weight, so a barometer measures the weight of the air.

questions.q: The root 'scope' in 'periscope' means...?
questions.f: 'Peri' means around, so a periscope lets a submarine look around above the waves.

questions.q: The root 'psych' in 'psychology' means...?
questions.f: Psyche was a figure in Greek myth whose name came to mean soul or mind.

questions.q: The root 'derm' in 'dermatologist' means...?
questions.f: A 'pachyderm' like an elephant is named for its thick skin.

questions.q: The root 'cardi' in 'cardiologist' means...?
questions.f: 'Cardio' exercise gets your heart working harder.

questions.q: The root 'opt' in 'optician' means...?
questions.f: 'Optical illusion' and 'optometrist' come from the same seeing root.

questions.q: The root 'sol' in 'solar' means...?
questions.f: A 'solstice' is when the sun seems to stand still at its highest or lowest point.

questions.q: The root 'luna' in 'lunar' means...?
questions.f: A 'lunar month' is the time the moon takes to cycle through its phases.

questions.q: The root 'astro' in 'astronaut' means...?
questions.f: 'Astronaut' means star sailor, from 'astron' plus 'nautes.'

questions.q: The root 'mar' in 'maritime' means...?
questions.f: 'Marine,' 'submarine,' and 'mariner' all come from Latin 'mare,' the sea.

questions.q: The root 'vit' in 'vital' means...?
questions.f: 'Vitamin' was coined for substances thought vital for life.

questions.q: The root 'mort' in 'immortal' means...?
questions.f: With 'im-' meaning not, 'immortal' means not subject to death.

questions.q: The root 'gen' in 'generate' means...?
questions.f: 'Genesis,' 'genetics,' and 'generation' all share this root.

questions.q: The root 'nat' in 'native' means...?
questions.f: 'Nation,' 'natal,' and 'nature' all come from Latin 'nasci,' to be born.

questions.q: The root 'mater' in 'maternal' means...?
questions.f: 'Matrimony' and 'matriarch' come from the same Latin word, 'mater.'

questions.q: The root 'frater' in 'fraternal' means...?
questions.f: 'Fraternal twins' are simply siblings born together but not identical.

questions.q: The root 'magn' in 'magnify' means...?
questions.f: 'Magnificent,' 'magnitude,' and 'magnate' all mean something big.

questions.q: The root 'equi' in 'equilateral' means...?
questions.f: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, and 'equator' divides Earth equally.

questions.q: The root 'sect' in 'intersect' means...?
questions.f: An 'insect' is named because its body looks cut into sections.

questions.q: The root 'rupt' in 'erupt' means...?
questions.f: 'Interrupt' means to break in, and 'rupture' means a break.

questions.q: The root 'struct' in 'construct' means...?
questions.f: 'Structure,' 'instruct,' and 'destruction' all come from Latin 'struere.'

questions.q: The root 'spect' in 'spectator' means...?
questions.f: 'Inspect,' 'suspect,' and 'spectacles' all involve looking.

questions.q: The root 'vis' in 'visible' means...?
questions.f: 'Vision,' 'television,' and 'invisible' share this Latin seeing root.

questions.q: The root 'mit' or 'miss' in 'transmit' means...?
questions.f: A 'missile' is a thing sent, and a 'mission' is a sending out.

questions.q: The root 'tract' in 'tractor' means...?
questions.f: 'Attract,' 'subtract,' and 'retract' all involve pulling.

questions.q: The root 'duct' in 'conduct' means...?
questions.f: An 'aqueduct' leads water, and a 'duke' was a leader.

questions.q: The root 'ject' in 'reject' means...?
questions.f: 'Project' means thrown forward, and 'eject' means thrown out.

questions.q: The root 'flect' in 'reflect' means...?
questions.f: Light reflects by bending back; 'flexible' means easily bent.

questions.q: The root 'fract' in 'fracture' means...?
questions.f: A 'fraction' is a broken-off piece of a whole number.

questions.q: The root 'ver' in 'verify' means...?
questions.f: A 'verdict' is literally a 'true saying,' from 'verus' plus 'dictum.'

questions.q: The root 'voc' in 'vocal' means...?
questions.f: 'Vocabulary,' 'advocate,' and 'evoke' all grew from Latin 'vox.'

questions.q: The root 'ambul' in 'ambulance' means...?
questions.f: Early ambulances were walking field hospitals that moved with an army.

questions.q: The root 'migr' in 'migrate' means...?
questions.f: 'Immigrant' means one who moves in; 'emigrant' means one who moves out.

questions.q: The root 'urb' in 'urban' means...?
questions.f: 'Suburb' means just under or near the city.

questions.q: The root 'civ' in 'civilian' means...?
questions.f: 'Civic,' 'civilisation,' and 'city' all trace to Latin 'civis,' a citizen.

questions.q: The root 'dem' in 'democracy' means...?
questions.f: 'Demo' plus 'kratos' means 'people power.'

questions.q: The suffix '-cracy' in 'democracy' means...?
questions.f: 'Autocracy' is rule by one person; 'bureaucracy' is rule by desks!

questions.q: The root 'arch' in 'monarch' means...?
questions.f: 'Mono' plus 'arch' means one ruler; an 'anarchy' has no ruler at all.

questions.q: The root 'cosm' in 'cosmos' means...?
questions.f: 'Cosmonaut' means universe sailor, the Russian word for astronaut.

questions.q: The root 'chrom' in 'chromatic' means...?
questions.f: 'Monochrome' means one colour, and 'chromosome' means coloured body.

questions.q: The prefix 'hetero-' in 'heterogeneous' means...?
questions.f: Its partner 'homo-' means same, as in 'homogeneous milk.'

questions.q: The prefix 'neo-' in 'neon' means...?
questions.f: Neon was named 'the new one' in 1898 because it was a newly found gas.

questions.q: The prefix 'proto-' in 'prototype' means...?
questions.f: A 'protagonist' is literally the first actor in a play.

questions.q: The prefix 'syn-' in 'synchronise' means...?
questions.f: 'Synchronise' means to bring times together, from 'syn' plus 'chronos.'

questions.q: The prefix 'peri-' in 'perimeter' means...?
questions.f: A perimeter is the measure around a shape.

questions.q: The prefix 'hypo-' in 'hypothermia' means...?
questions.f: 'Hypo' under plus 'therm' heat: too little body heat.

questions.q: The prefix 'trans-' in 'transatlantic' means...?
questions.f: 'Transport,' 'translate,' and 'transparent' all mean crossing something.

questions.q: The prefix 'contra-' in 'contradict' means...?
questions.f: To contradict is literally to 'speak against.'

questions.q: The suffix '-cide' in 'insecticide' means...?
questions.f: It comes from Latin 'caedere,' to cut down or kill.

questions.q: The suffix '-vore' in 'herbivore' means...?
questions.f: 'Voracious' means very hungry, from the same Latin root 'vorare.'

questions.q: The suffix '-itis' in 'tonsillitis' means...?
questions.f: 'Appendicitis' and 'arthritis' use the same Greek medical ending.

questions.q: The suffix '-pod' in 'arthropod' means...?
questions.f: 'Arthropod' means jointed foot, covering insects, spiders, and crabs.

questions.q: The suffix '-arium' in 'terrarium' means...?
questions.f: 'Aquarium,' 'planetarium,' and 'terrarium' are all places built for something.

questions.q: The suffix '-esque' in 'picturesque' means...?
questions.f: 'Statuesque' means like a statue, tall and graceful.

questions.q: The prefix 'quad-' in 'quadrilateral' means...?
questions.f: 'Quadruped' means four-footed, and a quad bike has four wheels.

questions.q: The prefix 'hexa-' in 'hexagon' means...?
questions.f: Honeybees build hexagonal cells because six-sided shapes tile with no wasted wax.

questions.q: The prefix 'deca-' in 'decathlon' means...?
questions.f: A decathlon has ten events, and a decade lasts ten years.

questions.q: The prefix 'kilo-' in 'kilogram' means...?
questions.f: 'Kilo' comes from the Greek 'chilioi,' meaning a thousand.

questions.q: A person who studies birds is called an...?
questions.f: Greek 'ornis' means bird; the other three study insects, fish, and reptiles.

questions.q: A person who studies insects is an...?
questions.f: Do not mix it up with an etymologist, who studies word origins.

questions.q: A person who studies earthquakes is a...?
questions.f: Greek 'seismos' means shaking, which is why the machine is a seismograph.

questions.q: A person who makes maps is a...?
questions.f: 'Carta' means map or paper, and 'graph' means to write or draw.

questions.q: A person who collects stamps is a...?
questions.f: A numismatist collects coins, and a bibliophile loves books.

questions.q: A person who writes dictionaries is a...?
questions.f: 'Lexicon' means word list, so a lexicographer writes about words.

questions.q: A person who studies fossils and ancient life is a...?
questions.f: 'Palaeo' means ancient, so 'Palaeolithic' means the ancient stone age.

questions.q: The word 'photosynthesis' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Plants literally put things together using light.

questions.q: The word 'atmosphere' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Greek 'atmos' means vapour or steam.

questions.q: The word 'paragraph' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Ancient scribes drew a mark beside the text to show a new section.

questions.q: The word 'panorama' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: The word was coined in the 1790s for huge circular paintings that surrounded viewers.

questions.q: The word 'hippopotamus' is built from Greek parts meaning 'river horse.'
questions.f: 'Hippos' means horse and 'potamos' means river.

questions.q: The word 'rhinoceros' is built from Greek parts meaning 'nose horn.'
questions.f: 'Rhino' nose plus 'keras' horn describes the animal perfectly.

questions.q: 'As busy as a bee' compares two things using 'as.' What is this called?
questions.f: 'Simile' comes from Latin 'similis,' meaning alike.

questions.q: 'The classroom was a zoo' calls one thing another. What is this called?
questions.f: Greek 'metaphora' means a carrying across of meaning.

questions.q: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers' repeats a starting sound. That is...?
questions.f: Alliteration makes tongue twisters trip you up and makes headlines stick.

questions.q: Saying 'I have a million things to do' is a deliberate exaggeration called...?
questions.f: 'Hyperbole' comes from Greek meaning 'throwing beyond.'

questions.q: 'The wind whispered through the trees' gives the wind a human action. This is...?
questions.f: Poets use personification to make nature feel alive.

questions.q: A joke that plays on two meanings of a word is called a...?
questions.f: Shakespeare loved puns and packed hundreds of them into his plays.

questions.q: A poem where the first letters of each line spell a word is an...?
questions.f: 'Acrostic' comes from Greek words meaning 'at the tip of the line.'

questions.q: A short saying that passes on wisdom, like 'look before you leap,' is a...?
questions.f: Nearly every language has proverbs, and many share the same advice.

questions.q: A phrase so overused it has lost its power, like 'as old as time,' is a...?
questions.f: The word comes from a French printing term for a ready-made metal plate.

questions.q: Saying 'passed away' instead of a harsher word is using a...?
questions.f: 'Euphemism' comes from Greek words meaning 'speaking well.'

questions.q: Calling a huge storm 'a bit of weather' is an example of...?
questions.f: Understatement is a favourite of British humour.

questions.q: A group of lines that forms one block of a poem is called a...?
questions.f: 'Stanza' is Italian for room, so each stanza is a little room in a poem.

questions.q: A line or set of lines repeated in a song or poem is a...?
questions.f: 'Refrain' comes from an old French word meaning to break off and repeat.

questions.q: A three-line Japanese poem with a 5-7-5 syllable pattern is a...?
questions.f: Traditional haiku often name a season without saying its name outright.

questions.q: A funny five-line poem with an AABBA rhyme pattern is a...?
questions.f: It takes its name from Limerick in Ireland.

questions.q: A 14-line poem with a strict rhyme pattern is a...?
questions.f: 'Sonnet' comes from Italian 'sonetto,' a little song.

questions.q: NASA is said as a word, but FBI is spelled out letter by letter. FBI is an...?
questions.f: Acronyms are pronounced as words; initialisms are said letter by letter.

questions.q: 'Tear' the drop and 'tear' the rip are spelled alike but said differently. They are...?
questions.f: 'Homograph' means 'same writing' in Greek.

questions.q: Which word is spelled the same forward and backward?
questions.f: 'Rotator' joins 'racecar' and 'deified' in the palindrome club.

questions.q: Which pair are true synonyms?
questions.f: Even close look-alikes can mean very different things.

questions.q: In the word 'unbelievable,' what is the suffix?
questions.f: Prefixes go in front, suffixes go behind, and the root sits in the middle.

questions.q: What do we call the dictionary form of a verb, like 'to run'?
questions.f: In English the infinitive usually carries the little word 'to' in front.

questions.q: What is the correct plural of 'fungus'?
questions.f: Latin words ending in '-us' often switch to '-i,' like 'nucleus' to 'nuclei.'

questions.q: What is the plural of 'criterion'?
questions.f: Greek '-on' words switch to '-a,' like 'phenomenon' to 'phenomena.'

questions.q: What is the plural of 'phenomenon'?
questions.f: 'Phenomenon' comes from a Greek word meaning 'thing appearing.'

questions.q: What is the traditional plural of 'medium' when it means channels of news?
questions.f: 'Media' is now often treated as a single word, which annoys some grammarians.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'nucleus'?
questions.f: 'Nucleus' is Latin for a little nut or kernel.

questions.q: Which is the correct comparison: good, better, and...?
questions.f: 'Good, better, best' is irregular because it comes from three different old roots.

questions.q: Bad, worse, and...?
questions.f: 'Worse' comes from an Old English word unrelated to 'bad.'

questions.q: Which sentence avoids a double negative?
questions.f: Two negatives cancel out, so 'I did not see nothing' technically means you saw something.

questions.q: What do we call the word a pronoun refers back to?
questions.f: 'Antecedent' comes from Latin words meaning 'going before.'

questions.q: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly for a plural owner?
c: The dog's bowls were empty for six dogs.
questions.f: For plural words already ending in S, the apostrophe goes after the S.

questions.q: Which mark is longer and used to break up a sentence?
questions.f: Printers measure dashes in letter widths: the en dash and the wider em dash.

questions.q: What is the name of the '&' symbol's word meaning?
questions.f: The symbol began as a joined-up handwritten version of the Latin word 'et.'

questions.q: What is the star-shaped symbol '*' called?
questions.f: 'Asterisk' comes from a Greek word meaning 'little star.'

questions.q: Which of these is a proper noun?
questions.f: Proper nouns name one particular person, place, or thing, and always take a capital.

questions.q: What is a word like 'flock' or 'team,' naming a group as one unit, called?
questions.f: In British English a collective noun can take a plural verb: 'the team are winning.'

questions.q: Words like 'courage' and 'freedom,' which name ideas you cannot touch, are...?
questions.f: 'Abstract' comes from Latin meaning 'drawn away' from physical things.

questions.q: What do we call a whole list of the words a language or a person uses?
questions.f: An average adult English speaker recognises tens of thousands of words.

questions.q: What is the alphabetical list of topics with page numbers at the back of a book?
questions.f: 'Index' is Latin for a pointer or forefinger.

questions.q: What is the extra section of material added at the end of a book called?
questions.f: The body part has the same name because both are add-ons.

questions.q: What do we call a short introduction written by the author at the start of a book?
questions.f: 'Preface' comes from Latin meaning 'spoken before.'

questions.q: What is the small text under a picture, explaining it, called?
questions.f: 'Caption' comes from a Latin word meaning 'a taking,' once used for legal headings.

questions.q: A maze-like building in Greek myth gave us which word for a confusing network?
questions.f: The myth's labyrinth on Crete was built by the craftsman Daedalus.

questions.q: A task requiring enormous strength is called 'herculean' after a hero famous for...?
questions.f: Hercules is the Roman name for the Greek hero Heracles.

questions.q: Something enormous and grand is called 'titanic' after the Titans, who were...?
questions.f: The famous ship was named for them, and so is the element titanium.

questions.q: A sweet-sounding but dangerous temptation is a 'siren song.' Sirens were...?
questions.f: In the Odyssey, Odysseus had his crew plug their ears with beeswax.

questions.q: The word 'marathon' comes from a long run carrying news of a...?
questions.f: The modern 26.2-mile distance was fixed at the 1908 London Olympics.

questions.q: A very small change that copies a whole shape is 'fractal.' The root 'frac' means...?
questions.f: Mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot coined 'fractal' in 1975 from Latin 'fractus.'

questions.q: The word 'chameleon' is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: Chameleons change colour by shifting tiny crystals in their skin, not to match backgrounds.

questions.q: The word 'dinosaur' is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: Richard Owen coined the name in 1842, long before anyone knew about feathers.

questions.q: The word 'encyclopedia' is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: The idea was a complete circle of learning, from Greek 'enkyklios paideia.'

questions.q: The word 'helicopter' is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: 'Helix' spiral plus 'pteron' wing, the same 'pteron' in 'pterodactyl.'

questions.q: The word 'microscope' and the word 'microbe' share a part meaning...?
questions.f: 'Microbe' means small life, coined in 1878 by a French surgeon.

questions.q: A word that imitates a sound, like 'clatter,' is an example of...?
questions.f: The Greek word means 'name making,' because the sound makes the name.

questions.q: What do we call the pattern of stressed and unstressed beats in a poem?
questions.f: Shakespeare's favourite metre, iambic pentameter, has five beats per line.

questions.q: What is the repetition of vowel sounds, as in 'the rain in Spain,' called?
questions.f: 'Assonance' comes from Latin meaning 'to answer with the same sound.'

questions.q: 'Time flies' is an idiom because its meaning...?
c: Cannot be worked out from the separate words
questions.f: 'Idiom' comes from a Greek word meaning 'one's own,' since each language has its own.

questions.q: What kind of word is 'ouch' or 'wow'?
questions.f: 'Interjection' comes from Latin meaning 'thrown in between.'

questions.q: In 'Close the door,' the sentence gives an order. What mood is that called?
questions.f: 'Imperative' comes from Latin 'imperare,' to command.

questions.q: A sentence that asks a question is called...?
questions.f: 'Interrogative' shares its root with 'interrogate,' to question.

questions.q: Which of these is the most formal way to write 'kids'?
questions.f: Choosing words to fit the situation is called matching your register.

questions.q: What do we call a word or phrase borrowed unchanged from another language, like 'cafe'?
questions.f: English has borrowed from over 350 languages.

questions.q: What do we call words in two languages that share an ancestor, like 'night' and 'nacht'?
questions.f: 'Cognate' comes from Latin meaning 'born together.'

questions.q: 'Onomatopoeia' is itself a word that copies a sound.
questions.f: It is the NAME for such words; it does not imitate any sound of its own.

questions.q: A simile always uses the word 'like' or 'as.'
questions.f: A metaphor drops the comparison word and states the thing outright.

questions.q: The plural of 'appendix' can be written 'appendices.'
questions.f: 'Appendixes' is also accepted; doctors prefer it for the body part.

questions.q: An acronym and an abbreviation are exactly the same thing.
questions.f: An acronym is said as a word; abbreviation is the broad term for any shortening.

questions.q: 'Thesaurus' and 'treasure' both come from the same ancient root.
questions.f: Both trace to Greek 'thesauros,' a storehouse of valuables.

questions.q: The word 'alphabetical' describes putting words in the order they were invented.
questions.f: It means A to Z order, the system that makes dictionaries usable.

questions.q: The word 'curfew' comes from a French phrase meaning...?
questions.f: Medieval towns rang a bell telling everyone to bank their hearth fires for the night.

questions.q: 'Checkmate' comes from a Persian phrase meaning...?
questions.f: From 'shah mat'; the chess word 'rook' traces to a Persian word for chariot.

questions.q: 'Sarcophagus' is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: The name came from a limestone believed to consume the body placed in it.

questions.q: 'Assassin' traces to an Arabic word for a group named after...?
c: A plant they were said to use
questions.f: Marco Polo helped spread the tale of the 'hashishiyya' to Europe.

questions.q: The word 'algebra' comes from an Arabic word meaning...?
c: The restoring or reunion of broken parts
questions.f: It comes from al-Khwarizmi's 9th-century book title, and his own name gave us 'algorithm.'

questions.q: 'Magazine' first meant a...?
questions.f: An ammunition magazine and a paper magazine are both storehouses, one of shells and one of articles.

questions.q: The word 'admiral' comes from an Arabic phrase meaning...?
questions.f: From 'amir al-bahr'; European scribes stuck a D in it by linking it to Latin 'admirari.'

questions.q: 'Giraffe' reached English through Arabic 'zarafah,' but the animal was long called a...?
questions.f: Europeans thought it looked like a camel crossed with a leopard.

questions.q: 'Tarantula' is named after Taranto, a town in Italy known for...?
questions.f: The whirling tarantella dance was believed to cure the spider's bite.

questions.q: The word 'trophy' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Greeks raised monuments at the spot where the enemy turned and fled.

questions.q: The word 'pupil' means both a student and part of the eye because it once meant...?
questions.f: Latin 'pupilla' meant little doll, for the tiny reflected figure you see in someone's eye.

questions.q: The word 'museum' originally meant a place dedicated to...?
questions.f: The Muses were the nine Greek goddesses of the arts and sciences.

questions.q: 'Planet' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Unlike fixed stars, planets appeared to wander across the night sky.

questions.q: 'Comet' comes from a Greek phrase meaning...?
questions.f: The tail looked like flowing hair to ancient observers.

questions.q: 'Galaxy' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: That is why our own galaxy is called the Milky Way.

questions.q: 'Sarcasm' comes from a Greek verb meaning...?
questions.f: The word paints biting remarks as something that rips.

questions.q: 'Utopia' was coined by Thomas More from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: More published Utopia in 1516, and the joke is that the perfect place does not exist.

questions.q: 'Pandemonium' was coined by John Milton as the name of...?
c: A capital city in his poem
questions.f: In Paradise Lost it means 'place of all demons,' and it later came to mean wild uproar.

questions.q: 'Gargantuan' comes from Gargantua, a character created by which writer?
questions.f: Rabelais's 1530s giant had an appetite so vast his name became an adjective.

questions.q: The word 'avocado' traces to an Aztec word, 'ahuacatl,' whose other meaning was...?
questions.f: Spanish speakers reshaped it into 'aguacate,' and English turned that into 'avocado.'

questions.q: The word 'tuxedo' comes from...?
questions.f: Tuxedo Park, a wealthy resort, popularised the short dinner jacket in the 1880s.

questions.q: The word 'bikini' was named in 1946 after...?
questions.f: The designer expected his two-piece to cause an explosive reaction like the atoll's nuclear tests.

questions.q: 'Cappuccino' is named for its colour's likeness to the robes of...?
questions.f: The monkey called a capuchin got its name from the same brown hoods.

questions.q: 'Vanilla' comes from a Spanish word meaning...?
questions.f: Vanilla comes from an orchid, and each flower must often be pollinated by hand.

questions.q: The word 'bonfire' literally began as...?
questions.f: Old records really do describe open-air fires that burned bones.

questions.q: The word 'window' comes from an Old Norse word meaning...?
questions.f: Before glass was common, a window really was just an eye for the wind.

questions.q: The word 'husband' originally meant...?
questions.f: That old sense survives in 'husbandry,' meaning the careful management of a farm.

questions.q: The word 'lord' comes from an Old English compound meaning...?
questions.f: 'Lady' came from a matching word meaning loaf kneader.

questions.q: 'Sheriff' comes from an Old English compound meaning...?
questions.f: 'Shire' plus 'reeve,' a royal official, gave us the word centuries before Westerns.

questions.q: The word 'gymnasium' comes from a Greek word connected to...?
questions.f: Greek athletes trained bare, so 'gymnos,' naked, named the place.

questions.q: The word 'school' traces to a Greek word originally meaning...?
questions.f: Only people with free time could sit and study, so leisure became learning.

questions.q: Which word is an eponym taken from an army officer's name?
questions.f: The 7th Earl of Cardigan's troops wore knitted waistcoats in the Crimean War.

questions.q: The 'saxophone' is named after Adolphe Sax, who was a...?
questions.f: He patented it in 1846, and it is one of the few orchestral instruments with a known inventor.

questions.q: 'Pasteurize' honours Louis Pasteur, who showed that heating could...?
questions.f: His experiments also disproved the idea that life sprang spontaneously from broth.

questions.q: 'Galvanize' comes from Luigi Galvani, who experimented with...?
questions.f: His twitching-frog experiments inspired both the word and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein.

questions.q: The word 'silhouette' and the word 'guillotine' are both...?
questions.f: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin proposed the device as a humane reform, not as an invention of his own.

questions.q: 'Jumbo' entered English as a word for anything huge thanks to...?
questions.f: Jumbo was a London Zoo elephant bought by P. T. Barnum in 1882.

questions.q: The 'teddy bear' is named after Theodore Roosevelt because he...?
c: Refused to shoot a bear on a hunt
Kept a bear at the White House
Wrote a story about a bear
questions.f: A 1902 newspaper cartoon of the incident inspired toymakers on two continents.

questions.q: A 'dunce' cap takes its name from John Duns Scotus, who was actually a...?
questions.f: Rivals mocked his followers as 'Dunsmen,' and the insult outlived his reputation.

questions.q: The fabric 'chiffon' and the word 'tangerine' are alike because both...?
c: Come from a place or thing outside England
questions.f: Tangerines are named for Tangier in Morocco, from where they were shipped.

questions.q: 'Cantaloupe' is named after Cantalupo, a place near...?
questions.f: Papal gardens there are said to have grown the melon after seeds arrived from Armenia.

questions.q: The word 'badminton' comes from...?
questions.f: Guests at Badminton House played the game, which had come from British officers in India.

questions.q: The sport 'rugby' is named after...?
questions.f: By tradition a Rugby School pupil picked up the ball and ran with it in 1823.

questions.q: The colour 'magenta' was named after...?
questions.f: The new dye appeared the same year as the Battle of Magenta in northern Italy.

questions.q: The word 'bayonet' is thought to come from...?
questions.f: Bayonne in southwest France was known for its blades and knives.

questions.q: Seven hundred years ago, 'naughty' meant...?
questions.f: It came from 'naught,' zero, so a naughty person literally had nothing.

questions.q: In Middle English, 'pretty' first meant...?
questions.f: Its ancestor also gave us 'prat' senses of trickery before it settled on beauty.

questions.q: The word 'bully' originally meant...?
questions.f: That is why an approving old phrase is 'bully for you!'

questions.q: In Old English, 'starve' meant simply...?
questions.f: German 'sterben,' to die, is its close cousin.

questions.q: In Old English, 'deer' meant...?
questions.f: German 'Tier,' meaning animal, preserves the older, wider sense.

questions.q: The word 'egregious' originally meant...?
questions.f: Latin 'e grege' means 'out of the flock,' so it praised those who stood out.

questions.q: The word 'cute' began as a clipped form of which word?
questions.f: It first meant sharp-witted, and the apostrophe in 'cute was long printed.

questions.q: The word 'brave' shares an origin with which other English word?
questions.f: Both trace through Italian and Spanish to a word that could mean wild or bold.

questions.q: Trimming 'influenza' to 'flu' is an example of which word-formation process?
questions.f: 'Fridge,' 'gym,' and 'exam' were all made by clipping longer words.

questions.q: Words like 'chit-chat' and 'zigzag' are formed by which process?
questions.f: English usually shifts the vowel in the repeat: tick-tock, flip-flop, criss-cross.

questions.q: A brand-new word invented from nothing, like 'Kodak,' is a...?
questions.f: George Eastman said he simply liked the letter K and built a word around it.

questions.q: Rewriting 'hamburger' as if it contained 'ham' is an example of...?
questions.f: Folk etymology also turned Spanish 'cucaracha' into English 'cockroach.'

questions.q: A newly coined word not yet in general dictionaries is called a...?
questions.f: 'Neologism' itself is built from Greek parts meaning new word.

questions.q: The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of a Persian mathematician.
questions.f: Al-Khwarizmi's name was Latinised as 'Algoritmi' by medieval translators.

questions.q: The word 'orange' names the fruit before it named the colour in English.
questions.f: Before the fruit arrived, English called the colour 'geoluread,' or yellow-red.

questions.q: 'Zero' reached English through Arabic from a word meaning 'empty.'
questions.f: Arabic 'sifr' also gave us the word 'cipher.'

questions.q: Which word means to draw out a response?
questions.f: 'Illicit' means unlawful; the two words sound alike but share no meaning.

questions.q: Which spelling means 'separate and distinct'?
questions.f: 'Discreet' means tactful, and the two Es sit together like two people whispering.

questions.q: To 'censure' someone is to...?
questions.f: To 'censor' is to cut material out, a different job entirely.

questions.q: To 'flout' a rule means to...?
questions.f: 'Flaunt' means to display proudly, which is why the two are so often swapped.

questions.q: To 'proscribe' something means to...?
questions.f: A doctor prescribes medicine, but a law proscribes bad behaviour.

questions.q: If you are 'averse' to something, you...?
questions.f: 'Adverse' describes unfavourable conditions, like adverse weather.

questions.q: 'Continual' rain differs from 'continuous' rain because continual rain...?
questions.f: Careful writers save 'continuous' for something truly unbroken.

questions.q: A 'disinterested' judge is one who is...?
questions.f: 'Uninterested' is the word for bored, though the two are often confused.

questions.q: A 'credulous' person is someone who...?
questions.f: 'Credible' describes the story; 'credulous' describes the listener.

questions.q: An 'ingenuous' remark is one that is...?
questions.f: 'Ingenious' means brilliantly inventive, just two letters away.

questions.q: A 'venial' fault is one that is...?
questions.f: 'Venal' is the harsher word, describing someone open to bribery.

questions.q: To 'apprise' someone means to...?
questions.f: To 'appraise' is to estimate worth, as an appraiser does with a house.

questions.q: If an issue is 'moot,' it is...?
c: Open to debate or no longer relevant
questions.f: A 'moot' was an old English assembly for arguing matters out.

questions.q: The 'penultimate' item in a list is the...?
questions.f: Latin 'paene' means almost, so penultimate means almost last.

questions.q: To 'enervate' someone is to...?
questions.f: It looks like 'energise' but means the opposite: to remove strength.

questions.q: In its traditional sense, to 'peruse' a document is to...?
questions.f: So many people use it for skimming that dictionaries now list both senses.

questions.q: A 'biennial' event happens...?
questions.f: 'Biannual' means twice a year, which is why careful writers avoid both words.

questions.q: If someone is 'nonplussed,' they are...?
questions.f: Latin 'non plus' means 'no more,' as in no more can be said or done.

questions.q: A 'restive' horse is...?
questions.f: Despite looking like 'restful,' it means almost the opposite.

questions.q: 'Fulsome' praise is traditionally...?
questions.f: It once simply meant abundant before it soured into overdone.

questions.q: A 'laconic' reply is one that is...?
questions.f: It honours Laconia, the region of Sparta, whose people prized short speech.

questions.q: A 'garrulous' person is...?
questions.f: Latin 'garrire' means to chatter.

questions.q: Something 'ubiquitous' is...?
questions.f: Latin 'ubique' means everywhere.

questions.q: A 'taciturn' person tends to...?
questions.f: Latin 'tacere' means to be silent, the same root as 'tacit.'

questions.q: A 'gregarious' person...?
questions.f: Latin 'grex' means flock or herd, which is why 'egregious' means out of the flock.

questions.q: To 'rescind' a decision is to...?
questions.f: Latin 'rescindere' means to cut back or tear away.

questions.q: A 'cacophony' is...?
questions.f: Its opposite, 'euphony,' means pleasant sound, from Greek 'eu,' good.

questions.q: To quote someone 'verbatim' is to quote them...?
questions.f: Latin 'verbum' means word, the same root as 'verb' and 'proverb.'

questions.q: The 'vernacular' of a place is its...?
questions.f: Latin 'vernaculus' meant native or homegrown.

questions.q: 'Brevity' means...?
questions.f: Hamlet's Polonius declares that brevity is the soul of wit, then talks far too long.

questions.q: 'Tycoon' comes from a Japanese title meaning...?
questions.f: American sailors brought 'taikun' home, and it soon meant a business giant.

questions.q: 'Origami' is built from Japanese parts meaning...?
questions.f: 'Ori' fold plus 'kami' paper, and a single sheet can fold into thousands of designs.

questions.q: 'Safari' comes from a Swahili word meaning...?
questions.f: Swahili borrowed it from Arabic 'safar,' travel.

questions.q: The word 'bungalow' comes from a word meaning 'of Bengal,' describing a house that was...?
questions.f: British officials in India copied the style and carried the name home.

questions.q: The word 'jungle' comes from a Sanskrit-derived word originally meaning...?
questions.f: Rudyard Kipling's stories cemented the wet, leafy sense in English.

questions.q: The word 'loot' entered English from an Indian word meaning...?
questions.f: It arrived with British soldiers in the 18th century, from Hindi 'lut.'

questions.q: 'Alcohol' comes from an Arabic word first used for...?
questions.f: 'Al-kuhl' named kohl powder; alchemists borrowed the word for their distilled essences.

questions.q: The word 'kiosk' traces back to a Turkish and Persian word for a...?
questions.f: Elegant open pavilions in Ottoman gardens gave their name to today's newsstands.

questions.q: The word 'tariff' likely traces to an Arabic word meaning...?
questions.f: A tariff list notifies traders what they must pay.

questions.q: 'Confetti' comes from an Italian word originally meaning...?
questions.f: Italians once threw sugared almonds at celebrations before paper took over.

questions.q: 'Umbrella' comes from an Italian word meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'umbra,' shadow, because the first ones shielded people from sun.

questions.q: 'Graffiti' comes from an Italian word meaning...?
questions.f: Archaeologists first used it for scratched writing found on ancient Roman walls.

questions.q: 'Piano' is short for 'pianoforte,' a name meaning...?
questions.f: The name advertised the new instrument's ability to play both softly and loudly.

questions.q: 'Poltergeist' is built from German parts meaning...?
questions.f: 'Poltern' means to make a racket, and 'Geist' means ghost or spirit.

questions.q: 'Rucksack' is built from German parts meaning...?
questions.f: 'Rucken' relates to the back, the same idea as English 'backpack.'

questions.q: 'Delicatessen' comes from a German word meaning...?
questions.f: German borrowed it from French 'delicatesse,' fineness or daintiness.

questions.q: 'Waltz' comes from a German verb meaning...?
questions.f: The dance scandalised polite society in the early 1800s because partners held each other closely.

questions.q: The word 'klutz' comes from a word meaning...?
questions.f: Yiddish 'klots' means block or lump, and English 'glitch' came the same route from a word meaning to slip.

questions.q: What is the standard plural of 'matrix' in mathematics?
questions.f: 'Matrix' is Latin for womb, from 'mater,' mother.

questions.q: What is the singular of 'bacteria'?
questions.f: Greek 'bakterion' means little staff, because the first ones seen were rod-shaped.

questions.q: What is the singular of 'data' in strict traditional usage?
questions.f: Latin 'datum' means 'a thing given'; most scientists now treat 'data' as singular.

questions.q: What is the traditional plural of 'vertex'?
questions.f: 'Vertex' is Latin for the highest point or crown of the head.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'stimulus'?
questions.f: Latin 'stimulus' was a goad used to drive cattle forward.

questions.q: A moth pinned in a case, a Greek word for 'cut into,' and a scientist who studies beetles all point to which word?
questions.f: Insects look 'cut into' segments, which is why 'insect' and 'entomon' mean the same thing.

questions.q: A shepherd's rough shelter, a Latin word for hut, and the room where a captain sleeps all point to which word?
questions.f: Latin 'capanna' meant a humble hut long before ships had cabins.

questions.q: A cloth stall at a fair, a French word for booth, and a shop selling stylish clothes converge on which word?
questions.f: French took it from Greek 'apotheke,' a storehouse, which also gave German 'Apotheke,' pharmacy.

questions.q: Wool dyed a deep red, the Latin word for 'little worm,' and a royal robe converge on which colour word?
questions.f: 'Crimson' comes from the kermes insect, but 'scarlet' first named a fine cloth of any colour.

questions.q: The word 'nickname' began as 'an eke name,' meaning an additional name.
questions.f: The N slid over from 'an,' the same way 'a napron' became 'an apron.'

questions.q: 'Salary' and 'salad' both trace back to the Latin word for salt.
questions.f: Romans salted their greens, giving 'herba salata,' salted herb.

questions.q: The word 'sinister' originally meant 'left-handed' in Latin.
questions.f: Roman augurs treated omens on the left as unlucky, and the word darkened from there.

questions.q: Cheap lace sold at an Ely fair, a 7th-century abbess whose name English tongues wore down, and a word for gaudy trash converge on which adjective?
questions.f: 'St Audrey's lace' slurred into 'tawdry lace'; Audrey was the abbess Etheldreda.

questions.q: A Texas rancher who never branded his calves, ownerless cattle roaming the range, and a word for one who will not follow the herd point to which term?
questions.f: Samuel Maverick's stray calves were so famous that his surname entered politics.

questions.q: An 1880 land agent in County Mayo, shopkeepers who quietly refused to serve him, and a surname now used in dozens of languages give us which word?
questions.f: Charles Boycott's tenants invented a protest so effective it needed a new name.

questions.q: A Viennese physician's theory of 'animal magnetism', salons seated around a tub of iron filings, and a 1784 royal commission that debunked him give us which verb?
questions.f: Benjamin Franklin sat on the commission that tested Franz Mesmer's claims.

questions.q: An 1812 Massachusetts election map, a governor's surname, and a cartoonist who spotted a salamander in one district's outline created which word?
questions.f: Governor Elbridge Gerry signed the map; the beast in the cartoon did the rest.

questions.q: An English physician, an 1818 edition of Shakespeare with the awkward parts snipped out, and a verb for sanitising a text point to which word?
questions.f: Thomas Bowdler's 'Family Shakespeare' made his surname a synonym for prudish editing.

questions.q: An American Civil War general's spectacular whiskers, a word whose two halves later swapped places, and hair growing down the cheeks give us which term?
questions.f: General Ambrose Burnside gave us 'burnsides,' which flipped into 'sideburns.'

questions.q: Nottinghamshire weavers smashing frames in 1811, an apprentice named Ned who may never have existed, and a modern label for a technology-resister converge on which word?
questions.f: Letters signed by 'Ned Ludd' were sent from a mythical base in Sherwood Forest.

questions.q: A Napoleonic soldier of legend, French comedies that mocked his blind patriotism, and a word for excessive loyalty to one's own group point to which term?
questions.f: Nicolas Chauvin may be entirely fictional, but his name stuck to the attitude.

questions.q: An elderly reader of chivalric romances, a farm girl renamed Dulcinea, and an adjective meaning hopelessly idealistic converge on which word?
questions.f: Cervantes gave the world the windmill-charging knight in 1605.

questions.q: A 17th-century London linen draper, a cheap woollen cloth sold under his name, and the lace mat under a cake point to which word?
questions.f: The draper's name is recorded as Doiley or Doyley.

questions.q: A French marshal's cook, sugar-coated almonds, and a sweet now famous in New Orleans give us which word?
questions.f: The confection honours Marshal du Plessis-Praslin, whose cook devised it.

questions.q: A Glasgow chemist's rubber-and-cloth sandwich, an 1823 patent, and a raincoat spelled with a K its inventor never used point to which garment?
questions.f: Charles Macintosh spelled his name without the K; the coat gained one.

questions.q: A Hungarian village called Kocs, a 15th-century carriage design, and the person who trains a football team converge on which word?
questions.f: A tutor was said to carry students through exams like a carriage carries passengers.

questions.q: Atlantic islands that Rome named for their large dogs, a small yellow finch found there, and a bird kept in Victorian parlours point to which word?
questions.f: The bird is named after the islands, and the islands after 'canis,' dog.

questions.q: A Flemish town near Antwerp, its coarse woollen cloth, and a drawstring bag used by soldiers and students converge on which word?
questions.f: The town of Duffel also gave its name to the toggled duffel coat.

questions.q: A Belgian town with iron-rich springs, 16th-century visitors who came to 'take the waters', and a word on every modern hotel brochure point to which term?
questions.f: The town of Spa in the Ardennes lent its name to health resorts everywhere.

questions.q: A Libyan temple to a ram-headed god, a pungent salt gathered near it by ancient traders, and a household cleaner's sharp smell converge on which word?
questions.f: 'Sal ammoniac' was named for the temple of Amun, and the gas took the name later.

questions.q: A Greek colony in Cilicia whose settlers mangled their dialect, Athenian sneering at their grammar, and a word for a glaring blunder of usage point to which term?
questions.f: The town of Soloi gave its name to every grammatical slip since.

questions.q: An Athenian orator's furious speeches, a Macedonian king who was their target, and a word for a bitter public tirade converge on which term?
questions.f: Demosthenes attacked Philip II so fiercely that his speeches named the genre.

questions.q: A herald in the Iliad said to shout as loudly as fifty men, and an adjective for a voice that fills a hall, point to which word?
questions.f: Stentor's name is the reason a booming speaker is called stentorian.

questions.q: Athens' first written law code, a 7th-century BC lawgiver whose name means 'dragon', and an adjective for punishing rules converge on which word?
questions.f: Draco's laws were so severe that Athenians replaced them within a generation.

questions.q: A London priory of St Mary of Bethlehem, centuries of clipped local pronunciation, and a word for noisy chaos point to which term?
questions.f: 'Bethlehem' wore down to 'Bedlam' in the mouths of Londoners.

questions.q: A figure in Greek myth standing in water he could never sip, branches that drew back as he reached, and a verb meaning to tease with the unreachable point to which word?
questions.f: The metal tantalum is named after Tantalus because it resists absorbing acids.

questions.q: A daughter of the Greek god of medicine, a mythical remedy for every illness, and a word for a supposed cure-all converge on which term?
questions.f: Her sister Hygieia gave English the word 'hygiene.'

questions.q: A 4th-century BC ruler's tomb at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders, and a word for any grand burial building point to which term?
questions.f: King Mausolus's tomb was so admired that his name outlived his kingdom.

questions.q: A giant bronze harbour statue on a Greek island, another of the Seven Wonders, and an adjective meaning gigantic converge on which word?
questions.f: Rome's Colosseum was probably named for a colossal statue that stood nearby.

questions.q: A Germanic people who sacked Rome in 455, a French bishop's coinage during the 1790s, and a word for wilful destruction of property point to which term?
questions.f: Henri Gregoire coined 'vandalisme' to shame those wrecking art during the Revolution.

questions.q: An eastern capital renamed in 330, a court famous for layer upon layer of ceremony, and an adjective for maddening complexity point to which word?
questions.f: Constantinople's bureaucracy was so intricate its name became an insult.

questions.q: A region of the modern Czech Republic, mistaken French assumptions about where Roma travellers came from, and a word for an unconventional artist converge on which term?
questions.f: French 'bohemien' was applied to travellers, then to poor Parisian artists.

questions.q: A 16th-century French ambassador in Lisbon, seeds he posted to the French queen, and a chemical named in his honour converge on which word?
questions.f: Jean Nicot sent tobacco plants to Catherine de Medici, and botanists honoured him.

questions.q: A nonsense line in Finnegans Wake, a physicist hunting a name for a set of three, and a fundamental particle converge on which word?
questions.f: Murray Gell-Mann took it from Joyce's line 'Three quarks for Muster Mark.'

questions.q: A Greek word for a ship's steersman, Norbert Wiener's 1948 science of control systems, and a 1982 short story by William Gibson converge on which word?
questions.f: 'Kybernetes' gave us 'cybernetics,' which Gibson clipped into 'cyber-' everything.

questions.q: A humorist's joke dust jacket of 1907, an invented young lady pictured shouting praise, and the puff of praise on every book cover point to which word?
questions.f: Gelett Burgess put 'Miss Belinda Blurb' on a comic jacket and named a genre.

questions.q: An 1834 British review, a writer who needed a word to sit alongside 'artist', and a term that replaced 'natural philosopher' converge on which word?
questions.f: William Whewell coined both 'scientist' and 'physicist.'

questions.q: A Greek word for something imitated, a 1976 book about genes, and a name now attached to internet jokes converge on which word?
questions.f: Richard Dawkins clipped 'mimeme' to 'meme' in The Selfish Gene.

questions.q: A 17th-century Flemish physician, the Greek word 'chaos', and a state of matter converge on which one-syllable word?
questions.f: Jan Baptist van Helmont built the word from 'chaos' to describe wild, formless matter.

questions.q: A French chemist's mistaken belief that one element formed all acids, Greek roots meaning 'acid maker', and the gas we breathe converge on which word?
questions.f: Lavoisier was wrong: hydrogen, not oxygen, is the acid-maker.

questions.q: A blend of 'chuckle' and 'snort', a blend of 'gallop' and 'triumphant', and a boy with a sword: which poem gave English both words?
questions.f: 'Chortle' and 'galumph' both escaped Lewis Carroll's poem into ordinary English.

questions.q: An Oxford philologist who invented Elvish grammars, an essay called On Fairy-Stories, and his coinage for a story's sudden joyous turn point to which term?
questions.f: J.R.R. Tolkien built the word from Greek 'eu,' good, plus 'catastrophe.'

questions.q: The 1852 Bleak House, a novelist whose pages are the earliest record of the word, and the feeling of having nothing to do converge on which noun?
questions.f: Dickens is credited with the first known use of 'boredom' in print.

questions.q: An 1839 Boston newspaper joke spelling 'all correct', a New York politician nicknamed Old Kinderhook, and an 1840 campaign club converge on which expression?
questions.f: Martin Van Buren's Old Kinderhook clubs cemented the joke abbreviation forever.

questions.q: Clumsy walking in French dialect, a 19th-century word for botched work, and the deliberate wrecking of machinery converge on which word?
questions.f: The chain runs through 'sabot,' the wooden shoe that gave clumsiness its name.

questions.q: Walter Scott's Ivanhoe, medieval fighters pledged to no single lord, and a graphic designer with many clients converge on which word?
questions.f: Scott's 'free lances' were knights whose spears were available for hire.

questions.q: An immense festival chariot pulled through the streets of Puri, a Sanskrit title meaning 'lord of the world', and an unstoppable force converge on which word?
questions.f: European travellers turned 'Jagannatha' into a word for anything that cannot be stopped.

questions.q: Norse fighters said to wear animal pelts into battle, an Old Norse compound possibly meaning 'bear shirt', and a word for wild frenzy point to which term?
questions.f: 'Berserkr' may instead mean 'bare shirt,' meaning armourless: scholars still argue.

questions.q: A 12th-century Latin love poem copied across Europe, its hero's name shortened by English readers, and a thin unbound booklet converge on which word?
questions.f: The poem 'Pamphilus' was so widely passed around that its name meant any small text.

questions.q: A Persian word for a turban, the folded petals of an Ottoman garden flower, and 1630s Dutch speculation converge on which bloom?
questions.f: At the height of tulip mania a single rare bulb could cost as much as a house.

questions.q: A Latin word meaning 'not knowing', a medieval English sense of foolish, and a modern adjective used for almost anything pleasant converge on which word?
questions.f: Latin 'nescius' gave 'nice' its original sense of ignorant.

questions.q: An Old English word meaning blessed, a slide through 'innocent' and then 'helpless', and a word children now attach to jokes converge on which adjective?
questions.f: The same root gives German 'selig,' meaning blessed.

questions.q: A Latin word for a country estate, farm workers looked down on by nobles, and the bad character in every pantomime converge on which word?
questions.f: Latin 'villa' also gave us 'village' and 'villager,' with no insult attached.

questions.q: A Roman army punishment involving one man in ten, a Latin word for a tenth, and a verb people now use for near-total destruction converge on which word?
questions.f: Purists still insist it should mean reducing by a tenth, not wiping out.

questions.q: A mishearing of 'acorn', a term coined by linguists in 2003, and phrases like 'for all intensive purposes' point to which word?
questions.f: Unlike a plain mistake, an eggcorn makes its own strange kind of sense.
