questions.q: A 2004 coinage by an economics blogger, headline templates like 'X is the new Y', and a joke about Eskimo words for snow converge on which term?
questions.f: Glen Whitman coined it at the request of linguist Geoffrey Pullum.

questions.q: An Oxford college warden, a reported toast to 'our queer old dean', and slips that swap the opening sounds of words converge on which term?
questions.f: Reverend William Spooner denied most of the slips attributed to him.

questions.q: A 1775 comedy by Richard Brinsley Sheridan, a character who calls a man 'the very pineapple of politeness', and sound-alike word blunders converge on which term?
questions.f: Mrs Malaprop's name comes from French 'mal a propos,' inappropriate.

questions.q: A Scottish ballad's line 'laid him on the green', a 1954 magazine essay by Sylvia Wright, and a noblewoman who never existed converge on which term?
questions.f: Wright had heard 'and Lady Mondegreen' and mourned a character who was never there.

questions.q: A 1939 novel of about 50,000 words, an author who reportedly tied down one typewriter key, and a text missing English's commonest letter point to which form?
questions.f: Ernest Vincent Wright's 'Gadsby' never once uses the letter E.

questions.q: A slip of paper reading 'D or d', a 1934 Webster's entry that survived five years, and a word meaning density point to which famous mistake?
questions.f: An editor's abbreviation note was mistaken for a headword and printed as a real word.

questions.q: A word invented in 2001 to catch copiers, a hidden entry in the New Oxford American Dictionary, and a fake definition about shirking duties point to which term?
questions.f: The trap word was 'esquivalience,' and it was spotted in 2005.

questions.q: A 1604 book called A Table Alphabeticall, about 2,500 hard words explained for 'ladies and gentlewomen', and English's earliest such work point to whose dictionary?
questions.f: Cawdrey's slim volume is regarded as the first monolingual English dictionary.

questions.q: Nine years of labour with six assistants, an entry calling a dictionary-maker 'a harmless drudge', and a joke definition of oats aimed at Scotland point to whose work?
questions.f: Johnson's 1755 Dictionary held its authority in Britain for over a century.

questions.q: A corrugated-iron garden shed nicknamed the Scriptorium, millions of quotation slips from volunteer readers, and the word 'bondmaid' left out by accident point to which project?
c: The Dictionary of American Regional English
questions.f: Editor James Murray worked in that shed for decades; the first part appeared in 1884.

questions.q: In 2011 the OED's chief editor said this three-letter verb had overtaken 'set' as the entry with the most senses. Which verb?
questions.f: Editor John Simpson counted over 600 senses for 'run,' many of them modern.

questions.q: A physician who catalogued words as a hobby, an 1852 book arranging them by idea rather than alphabetically, and a writer's shelf staple point to whose work?
questions.f: Roget was a doctor and inventor who compiled his Thesaurus in retirement.

questions.q: A steel millionaire's funding, a 1906 board of reformers, and a president's order that government printers use 300 new spellings point to which failed campaign?
questions.f: Andrew Carnegie funded it and Theodore Roosevelt backed it, but Congress refused.

questions.q: A Warsaw eye doctor, a pen name meaning 'one who hopes', and a grammar of 16 rules with no irregular verbs converge on which invented tongue?
questions.f: L. L. Zamenhof published it in 1887 under the name Doktoro Esperanto.

questions.q: A 1930s simplified English, exactly 850 chosen words, and the scholar C. K. Ogden converge on which system?
questions.f: Ogden claimed almost any idea could be expressed with his 850 words.

questions.q: 'Posh' has been proven to stand for 'port out, starboard home'.
questions.f: No shipping ticket marked POSH has ever been found; the story is a later invention.

questions.q: 'Tip' for a gratuity is known to be an acronym of 'to insure promptness'.
questions.f: It comes from old slang meaning to give or pass something along.

questions.q: SOS was chosen as a distress signal because it stands for 'save our ship'.
questions.f: It was picked because three dots, three dashes, three dots is unmistakable in Morse.

questions.q: The word 'news' comes from the initials of north, east, west and south.
questions.f: It is simply the plural of 'new,' matching French 'nouvelles.'

questions.q: A slab found by French soldiers in 1799, a Englishman's partial breakthrough with royal cartouches, and a Frenchman's 1822 announcement converge on which decipherment?
questions.f: Thomas Young cracked the cartouches; Jean-Francois Champollion read the script.

questions.q: A London architect working in his spare time, clay tablets baked hard when a palace burned, and a 1952 proof that the script recorded early Greek point to which writing?
questions.f: Michael Ventris was an architect, not a professional linguist, when he solved it.

questions.q: A reed stylus pressed into damp clay, wedge-shaped strokes, and the earliest writing of Sumer converge on which script?
questions.f: 'Cuneiform' comes from Latin 'cuneus,' a wedge, describing the stylus marks.

questions.q: The word 'hieroglyph' is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: Egyptians themselves called their script 'the god's words.'

questions.q: Notches cut along the sharp edge of a standing stone, over 400 surviving Irish inscriptions, and an alphabet named after trees converge on which script?
questions.f: Ogham letters were read from the bottom of the stone upward.

questions.q: A row of runes named after its opening six letters, carvings on Scandinavian memorial stones, and the writing of the Vikings converge on which term?
questions.f: F, U, TH, A, R and K open the row, just as A, B and C open ours.

questions.q: A French army officer's raised-dot night writing, a blind teenager's improvement of it, and a system of six-dot cells converge on which invention?
questions.f: Louis Braille was only 15 when he reworked Charles Barbier's military code.

questions.q: In Morse code the letter E is a single dot because...?
c: It is the most frequent letter in English
It was the first letter tested
questions.f: Samuel Morse studied printers' type cases to work out which letters needed short codes.

questions.q: Early Greek inscriptions that switch direction line by line, a Greek phrase about ploughing, and an ox turning at the end of a furrow converge on which style?
questions.f: The name literally means 'as the ox turns,' which is exactly how the lines run.

questions.q: Ancient Latin and Greek manuscripts were often written in 'scriptio continua', meaning they had no...?
questions.f: Irish and Anglo-Saxon monks are credited with popularising word spaces.

questions.q: A writing system where each symbol stands for a consonant and the reader supplies vowels is called an...?
questions.f: Arabic and Hebrew are abjads; an abugida like Devanagari marks vowels on the consonant.

questions.q: Japanese kana and Cherokee writing are both examples of which kind of system?
questions.f: In a syllabary each character stands for a whole syllable, not a single sound.

questions.q: A Cherokee silversmith who could not read English, a set of 85 characters completed around 1821, and rapid literacy across a nation converge on which figure?
questions.f: The giant sequoia trees are believed to be named in his honour.

questions.q: A 15th-century king's project, a script whose original name means 'proper sounds to instruct the people', and letters shaped like the mouth that makes them converge on which alphabet?
questions.f: King Sejong promulgated Hangul in 1446 to make literacy possible for everyone.

questions.q: Two 9th-century missionary brothers, an older script called Glagolitic, and an alphabet used from Moscow to Belgrade converge on which writing system?
questions.f: Cyril and Methodius invented Glagolitic; their students built Cyrillic from Greek letters.

questions.q: Which language of Papua New Guinea is often cited as having one of the world's smallest alphabets, with about 12 letters?
questions.f: Twelve letters are enough because the language uses very few distinct sounds.

questions.q: A chant that once ended the alphabet, the Latin word 'et' written as a single joined stroke, and the symbol above the 7 key converge on which name?
questions.f: Children finished the alphabet with 'and per se and,' meaning 'and by itself, and.'

questions.q: In old printed books, a letter that looked like an f without a full crossbar was really...?
questions.f: The long s vanished from English printing in the early 1800s.

questions.q: Which of these was a genuine letter of the Old English alphabet, later dropped?
questions.f: Wynn stood for the W sound; eth, thorn, ash and yogh also disappeared.

questions.q: 'Ye Olde Shoppe' signs are misleading because that first word was originally spelled with...?
questions.f: Printers substituted Y for thorn, so 'ye' was always meant to be read as 'the.'

questions.q: A new telephone key of the 1960s, Bell Labs engineers hunting a name for it, and a symbol with eight points converge on which word?
questions.f: The 'octo' half is clear enough; nobody has ever explained the 'thorpe.'

questions.q: A reversed P inked in red, medieval scribes marking where a new thought began, and a symbol still hiding in word processors converge on which mark?
questions.f: Adding those red marks by hand was a specialist job called rubrication.

questions.q: Which mark's name comes from a Greek word for a roasting spit, once used to flag doubtful passages?
questions.f: The same mark, a bar with dots, became the division sign in arithmetic.

questions.q: A tiny hand drawn in a margin, Renaissance readers flagging their favourite lines, and the ancestor of the highlighter pen converge on which mark?
questions.f: Some scholars drew hundreds of manicules through a single book.

questions.q: A 16th-century French printer's name, brackets that point outward, and the marks around spoken words in a Paris novel converge on which term?
questions.f: They honour the printer Guillaume Le Be, whose name means 'little William.'

questions.q: A printer's ornament shaped like a leaf or flower, used to break up text, is a...?
questions.f: The ivy-leaf version is called a hedera, and it is one of the oldest text ornaments.

questions.q: Three asterisks arranged in a triangle to mark a break in a text form an...?
questions.f: Modern typesetters usually replace the asterism with three plain spaced asterisks.

questions.q: The dagger symbol used for a second footnote is also known as an...?
questions.f: Editors order footnote marks: asterisk, dagger, double dagger, then section sign.

questions.q: A gap that looks too wide between an A and a V, metal type filed down by hand, and a designer's fine tuning converge on which term?
questions.f: 'Leading' is the space between whole lines, named for the lead strips once slotted in.

questions.q: Two letters cast as one piece of type, like the joined f and i, form a...?
questions.f: The ampersand itself began as a ligature of the Latin letters E and T.

questions.q: In type design, the part of a letter like h or b that rises above the main body is the...?
questions.f: The tails of p and g are descenders, and the body height itself is the x-height.

questions.q: In careful typesetting, the dash used for a range of numbers such as 1914-18 is the...?
questions.f: The en dash is one 'n' wide and the em dash is one 'm' wide.

questions.q: The word 'serif' names which feature of a letter?
questions.f: 'Sans serif' is French for 'without serif,' describing plainer modern typefaces.

questions.q: A straight bar above a vowel, dictionary marks showing a long sound, and Maori spellings converge on which diacritic?
questions.f: Its curved partner the breve marks a short vowel; both come from Greek words for long and short.

questions.q: The small v-shaped mark above the c in Czech spellings is called a...?
questions.f: Czech speakers call it a hacek, meaning 'little hook.'

questions.q: The little tail hooked under a vowel in Polish spelling is called an...?
questions.f: 'Ogonek' is Polish for 'little tail,' and it marks a nasal vowel.

questions.q: The single difference between 'pat' and 'bat', a unit smaller than a syllable, and what linguists call a minimal pair converge on which term?
questions.f: English gets by on roughly 44 phonemes but spells them hundreds of ways.

questions.q: The slightly different ways one phoneme can be pronounced are called its...?
questions.f: The P in 'pin' and in 'spin' are allophones: try feeling the puff of air.

questions.q: In writing, the smallest unit that represents a sound, such as 'sh' or 'a', is a...?
questions.f: English has about 44 phonemes but hundreds of grapheme spellings for them.

questions.q: The catch in the middle of 'uh-oh', a consonant made by snapping the vocal folds shut, and the sound many accents use instead of the T in 'butter' point to which term?
questions.f: It is a full consonant in Arabic and Hawaiian, where it is written with its own mark.

questions.q: Sounds like F, S and V, made by forcing air through a narrow gap, are called...?
questions.f: 'Fricative' comes from Latin 'fricare,' to rub.

questions.q: Sounds like P, T and K, made by blocking then releasing air, are called...?
questions.f: They are also called stops, because the airflow really does stop.

questions.q: An accent that does not pronounce the R in 'car' or 'park' is described as...?
questions.f: Most English accents in England are non-rhotic; most American accents are rhotic.

questions.q: Which pair of English words are etymological doublets, entering from two related languages?
questions.f: 'Shirt' came down through Old English and 'skirt' through Old Norse.

questions.q: Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed. Such deceptive look-alikes are called...?
questions.f: Linguists call them 'faux amis,' borrowing the French term directly.

questions.q: Old English 'brid' became 'bird' and 'thridda' became 'third' through which sound change?
questions.f: Metathesis simply swaps two sounds; it is why some people say 'aks' for 'ask.'

questions.q: The reason 'bite' no longer rhymes with 'beet' and 'name' no longer sounds like 'nah-meh' is a change called the...?
questions.f: The shift ran roughly from 1400 to 1700, just as spelling was being frozen by printing.

questions.q: A German scholar who collected folk tales, a law explaining why Latin 'pater' matches English 'father', and the birth of comparative linguistics converge on which name?
questions.f: The same man behind Cinderella and Rapunzel founded the systematic study of sound change.

questions.q: 'Go' and 'went' come from two unrelated verbs mashed into one. Linguists call this...?
questions.f: 'Went' was once the past tense of 'wend,' which still survives on its own.

questions.q: The vowel change in sing, sang, sung is a Germanic pattern called...?
questions.f: Umlaut is the related change that gives us 'foot' and 'feet.'

questions.q: Using 'bank' for both a riverside and a place for money is an example of...?
questions.f: Those two 'banks' are unrelated in origin, which makes them homonyms rather than one word.

questions.q: Turning the noun 'email' into the verb 'to email' with no change of form is called...?
questions.f: It is also called conversion, and English does it constantly: to google, to text, to friend.

questions.q: Languages like Turkish and Finnish, which stack many endings onto one root, are described as...?
questions.f: A single Turkish word can carry the meaning of an entire English sentence.

questions.q: Words whose meaning depends on who is speaking and when, like 'here' and 'tomorrow', involve...?
questions.f: 'Deixis' comes from a Greek word meaning 'pointing.'

questions.q: The branch of linguistics dealing with how context changes meaning is...?
questions.f: Semantics asks what words mean; pragmatics asks what speakers mean by them.

questions.q: An asterisk before a reconstructed ancient form, as in *pater, tells a reader that the word...?
c: Is not recorded in any text
questions.f: Comparative linguists reconstruct Proto-Indo-European words from surviving descendants.

questions.q: The 'gl-' shared by glitter, gleam, glow and glisten is an example of a...?
questions.f: Phonesthemes are sound clusters that hint at meaning without being true prefixes.

questions.q: The International Phonetic Alphabet was first published in 1888 in order to...?
c: Give every speech sound one written symbol
questions.f: Language teachers created it so pronunciation could be written the same way worldwide.

questions.q: Two columns of a Linotype keyboard, keys laid out by letter frequency, and nonsense strings printed by accident in old newspapers converge on which phrase?
questions.f: A slip of the operator's hand would send the whole column into print unnoticed.

questions.q: In the NATO spelling alphabet, 'alfa' and 'juliett' are deliberately misspelled so that...?
c: Non-English speakers do not drop the sounds
questions.f: A French reader might silence the 'ph' in alpha, and 'juliet' could lose its final T.

questions.q: The QWERTY keyboard layout was devised in the 1870s by...?
questions.f: Sholes separated common letter pairs to keep early typebars from clashing.

questions.q: A puzzle society president's coinage of 1935, a chain of 45 letters, and fine dust breathed deep into the lungs converge on which record-holding word?
questions.f: It names a lung disease caused by inhaling very fine silica or volcanic dust.

questions.q: 'Antidisestablishmentarianism' describes opposition to removing official status from...?
questions.f: Peel apart anti, dis, establish, ment, arian and ism and the 28-letter word makes sense.

questions.q: Which word contains a, e, i, o, u and y in that exact order?
questions.f: 'Abstemious' has the five vowels in order but stops short of the Y.

questions.q: Which common word has no a, e, i, o or u at all?
questions.f: Seven letters, and the Y does all the vowel work.

questions.q: Which word packs three Ys into six letters?
questions.f: 'Syzygy' names the near-alignment of three bodies in space, like sun, earth and moon.

questions.q: 'Stressed' reversed spells 'desserts'. A word that spells a different word backwards is a...?
questions.f: 'Semordnilap' is itself 'palindromes' spelled backwards.

questions.q: A word containing no repeated letter, like 'dermatoglyphics', is called an...?
questions.f: A univocalic goes further and uses only one distinct vowel throughout.

questions.q: 'The old man the boat' baffles readers on the first pass. Such a sentence is called a...?
questions.f: Here 'man' is the verb: the old people are crewing the boat.

questions.q: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' was written in 1957 to show that a sentence can be...?
questions.f: Noam Chomsky used it in Syntactic Structures to separate grammar from meaning.

questions.q: A 2009 headline about a violinist 'linked to JAL crash blossoms' gave editors a name for...?
questions.f: 'Crash blossom' now labels any headline that reads two ways, usually comically.

questions.q: Zipf's law observes that in any long text, a word's frequency is roughly...?
questions.f: 'The' typically appears about twice as often as the second-place word.

questions.q: A river crossing in the Book of Judges, a password betrayed by one mispronounced sound, and a custom that marks who belongs converge on which word?
questions.f: The Hebrew word means 'ear of grain'; those who said 'sibboleth' were spotted as outsiders.

questions.q: A Scots word for enchantment, a spelling only one letter from a school subject, and a Hollywood magazine title converge on which doublet of 'grammar'?
questions.f: Old learning looked like magic, so 'grammar' shifted in Scots into 'glamour,' a spell.

questions.q: A Tongan word Captain Cook recorded in the 1770s, a Polynesian idea of things set apart, and a subject nobody will discuss converge on which word?
questions.f: Cook's journals also gave English 'tattoo,' from Tahitian 'tatau.'

questions.q: A Guugu Yimithirr word for a large grey species, Joseph Banks's 1770 notebook, and a persistent myth about a misunderstanding converge on which animal name?
questions.f: 'Gangurru' really did name the animal; the tale that it means 'I don't know' is false.

questions.q: A Taino word from the Caribbean, a storm god's name in Spanish ships' logs, and a spinning tropical storm converge on which word?
questions.f: Taino also gave English 'canoe,' 'barbecue,' 'hammock' and 'maize.'

questions.q: A Greenlandic word for a hooded skin jacket, Arctic hunting clothes, and a British word for a rain jacket converge on which garment name?
questions.f: 'Parka' came into English by a different Arctic route, from Nenets through Russian.

questions.q: A Japanese word for a squad leader, American servicemen stationed in Japan, and a slang term for the boss converge on which word?
questions.f: Japanese 'hancho' combines 'han,' squad, with 'cho,' chief.

questions.q: A Sanskrit word meaning gravel or grit, Arab traders carrying crystals westward, and the sweet stuff in your bowl converge on which word?
questions.f: Sanskrit 'sharkara' travelled through Arabic 'sukkar' into most European languages.

questions.q: A Sanskrit word for a lump or piece, Persian and Arabic traders, and a shop full of sweets converge on which word?
questions.f: 'Khanda' meant a piece of sugar; 'sherbet' arrived separately from Arabic 'sharbah,' a drink.

questions.q: A Tamil word for sauce or relish, Portuguese traders in south India, and a dish now called Britain's national favourite converge on which word?
questions.f: Tamil 'kari' named the sauce long before Britain adopted the dish.

questions.q: A Japanese word for picture, another for written character, and a set of symbols first designed for phone screens in 1999 converge on which word?
questions.f: 'Emoji' has nothing to do with 'emotion': the resemblance to 'emoticon' is pure coincidence.

questions.q: An older English plural mistaken for a plural of something smaller gave us which vegetable name?
questions.f: The old word was 'pease,' as in pease pudding; speakers assumed one of them was a 'pea.'

questions.q: A Norman French word 'cherise' misheard as a plural gave English which fruit name?
questions.f: Once 'cherise' looked plural, English quietly invented a singular: 'cherry.'

questions.q: 'A napron' and 'a nadder' lost their N to the word before them. Which everyday word gained an N the same way?
questions.f: 'An ewt' became 'a newt,' while 'a napron' became 'an apron': the N simply migrated.

questions.q: An umpire's title began as 'noumpere', a French word meaning...?
questions.f: 'A noumpere' slid into 'an oumpere,' so the referee lost a letter to the article.

questions.q: A word for a puzzle whose origin dictionaries still mark unknown, a Dublin theatre manager's alleged wager, and chalk marks appearing overnight converge on which word?
questions.f: The bet story is unproven, but 'quiz' really does have no confirmed etymology.

questions.q: A Latin word for hearth, an optical point where rays converge, and the centre of attention all point to which word?
questions.f: Latin 'focus' meant fireplace; Kepler borrowed it for optics in 1604.

questions.q: A Latin phrase meaning 'ripening before its time', fruit harvested early, and a child who reads at three converge on which adjective?
questions.f: 'Prae' before plus 'coquere' to cook or ripen: precocious fruit came first.

questions.q: A winter dusk over the reed beds, thousands of birds wheeling as a single body, and a collective noun that sounds like a whisper converge on which term?
questions.f: Each starling tracks only about seven neighbours, and the whole flock turns as one.

questions.q: Which is the traditional collective noun for a group of cats?
questions.f: 'Clowder' is a variant of 'clutter,' and a group of kittens is a kindle.

questions.q: A group of foxes is traditionally called a...?
questions.f: 'Sleuth' is the old collective noun for bears, not foxes.

questions.q: A group of squirrels is traditionally called a...?
questions.f: 'Dray' also names a squirrel's nest of twigs high in a tree.

questions.q: Which collective noun traditionally belongs to a group of apes?
questions.f: It comes from the same medieval lists that gave us an exaltation of larks.

questions.q: A group of turkeys is traditionally called a...?
questions.f: A 'rafter' may recall the beams where farmyard birds perched at night.

questions.q: A group of wild boar is traditionally called a...?
questions.f: 'Sett' is a badger's home, and badgers themselves gather in a cete.

questions.q: A group of herons is traditionally called a...?
questions.f: 'Siege' may come from the way a heron stands motionless as if besieging the water.

questions.q: A group of eagles is traditionally called a...?
questions.f: Many of these names come from the 1486 Book of St Albans, a gentleman's field guide.

questions.q: Which collective noun traditionally belongs to a group of crocodiles?
questions.f: 'Bale' belongs to turtles, and it fits the way they pile up to sunbathe.

questions.q: A group of flamingos is called a...?
questions.f: Their pink comes from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat.

questions.q: A group of ferrets is traditionally called a...?
questions.f: It may be a worn-down form of 'busyness,' which suits them perfectly.

questions.q: A group of moles is traditionally called a...?
questions.f: A single mole can shift several kilograms of soil in a night of digging.

questions.q: A word that appears exactly once in all of Homer, a Greek phrase meaning 'said once', and a translator's nightmare converge on which term?
questions.f: With no second example to compare, scholars sometimes can only guess at the meaning.

questions.q: Wedging a word inside another, as in 'a whole nother story', is called...?
questions.f: Greek 'tmesis' means a cutting, and it gives English one of its few TM words.

questions.q: The commonest vowel sound in spoken English, an upside-down e, and the lazy 'uh' at the start of 'about' converge on which name?
questions.f: The name was borrowed from Hebrew grammar, where 'shva' marks a reduced vowel.

questions.q: A term coined around 1980 for names invented only after a newer version arrived, like 'landline', is a...?
questions.f: Frank Mankiewicz coined it, and William Safire's column made it famous.

questions.q: 'Skyscraper' translated piece by piece into other languages, and 'flea market' from French, are both examples of a...?
questions.f: A calque copies the structure of a foreign phrase instead of its sound.

questions.q: The word 'cleave' can mean both to split apart and to cling tightly. Such a word is a...?
questions.f: 'Sanction' does the same trick: it can approve or punish.

questions.q: A design that reads the same when turned upside down is called an...?
questions.f: The term was popularised by writer Douglas Hofstadter.

questions.q: A surname that suits its owner's job, like a dentist named Dr Payne, is an...?
questions.f: The word was built by rearranging 'patronym,' a name taken from a father.

questions.q: A morpheme like '-ness' that cannot stand alone as a word is described as...?
questions.f: 'Dog' is a free morpheme; 'un-' and '-ing' are bound ones.

questions.q: The vowel sound in 'coin' or 'loud', which glides from one position to another, is a...?
questions.f: Greek 'di' two plus 'phthongos' sound; a single steady vowel is a monophthong.

questions.q: A verse-writing guide from about 19 BC, a warning against words 'a foot and a half long', and the ancestor of 'sesquipedalian' converge on which Roman poet?
questions.f: Horace's Ars Poetica mocked playwrights who padded their lines with monster words.

questions.q: The 29-letter 'floccinaucinihilipilification' was assembled by stringing together four Latin words that all mean...?
questions.f: Eighteenth-century Eton schoolboys are credited with stitching the joke word together.

questions.q: The 27-letter 'honorificabilitudinitatibus' appears in which Shakespeare play?
questions.f: It is his longest word, and it alternates consonant and vowel almost perfectly.

questions.q: Which 15-letter word is famous for using no letter twice?
questions.f: Words with no repeated letters are isograms, and 15 letters is close to the practical limit.

questions.q: Which word strings five vowels together with no consonant between them?
questions.f: Drop 'queue' to 'q' and it would still sound the same: four of its letters are silent.

questions.q: Sunday and Monday name the sky, Tuesday through Friday honour Norse gods, and one day breaks the pattern with a Roman god. Which day?
questions.f: Saturn's day survived in English while the other Roman names were replaced.

questions.q: Two centuries ago, 'terrific' meant...?
questions.f: Its cousin 'terrible' kept the fear while 'terrific' drifted into praise.

questions.q: The word 'meat' has narrowed over the centuries from an earlier sense meaning...?
questions.f: The old sense survives in 'sweetmeats,' an antique word for sugary treats.

questions.q: The joke spelling 'ghoti', supposedly pronounced 'fish', is meant to mock...?
questions.f: Take gh from 'tough,' o from 'women' and ti from 'nation'; the joke is often credited to Shaw without proof.

questions.q: Why do British and American English disagree over 'aluminium' and 'aluminum'?
c: Its discoverer used more than one name
questions.f: Humphry Davy tried 'alumium' and 'aluminum'; editors later preferred the classical '-ium.'

questions.q: A New Zealand hill carries one of the world's longest place names, an 85-letter Maori phrase describing...?
c: A chief who played a flute
questions.f: The name tells a story about Tamatea, and locals shorten it to Taumata.

questions.q: The 58-letter Welsh village name beginning 'Llanfairpwllgwyngyll' was lengthened in the 1860s in order to...?
c: Attract visitors to the railway station
questions.f: It reportedly worked: the platform sign became one of Wales's most photographed objects.

questions.q: Quilting gatherings, husking gatherings, and neighbours turning up to share a day's work converge on the origin of the 'bee' in 'spelling bee'. What did it mean?
c: A gathering of neighbours to help with work
A prize ribbon awarded to winners
questions.f: The insect link is a folk explanation; the dialect word came first.

questions.q: Noah Webster's 'Blue-Backed Speller' mattered because it...?
c: Taught generations of Americans a common spelling
Was the first book printed in America
questions.f: It sold in the tens of millions and helped standardise American spelling before his dictionary.

questions.q: In Through the Looking-Glass, Humpty Dumpty explains that 'slithy' blends which two words?
questions.f: He also unpacks 'mimsy' as flimsy and miserable.

questions.q: Which everyday English word for a rude or uncouth person was invented as the name of a race in Gulliver's Travels?
questions.f: Swift's book also gave English 'Lilliputian' for anything tiny.

questions.q: The study of language through its historical texts and origins is traditionally called...?
questions.f: Greek 'philologia' means love of words or learning.

questions.q: In etymology, the earliest known ancestor form of a word is called its...?
questions.f: So the etymon of English 'father' is a reconstructed Indo-European form written *pater.

questions.q: 'Burger', now a word on its own, was carved out of 'hamburger' by which process?
questions.f: Speakers wrongly split 'ham-burger' and set the second half free.

questions.q: The '-holic' in 'chocoholic' and the '-gate' in political scandals are both examples of...?
questions.f: 'Alcoholic' and 'Watergate' were never built from those pieces, but English took them anyway.

questions.q: Shakespeare is the earliest recorded user of well over a thousand English words, though many were probably already spoken.
questions.f: His plays are simply the oldest surviving writing to capture much everyday Elizabethan speech.

questions.q: The 1486 Book of St Albans is a major source of English collective nouns for animals.
questions.f: Its list of 'company terms' was partly a game of wit for gentlefolk, not strict zoology.

questions.q: The word 'thesaurus' and the word 'treasury' both descend from a Greek word for a storehouse.
questions.f: Greek 'thesauros' passed into Latin 'thesaurus' and then split into two English words.

questions.q: The International Phonetic Alphabet was designed so that each symbol stands for one specific speech sound.
questions.f: In practice, broad transcriptions still use one symbol, like r, for sounds that differ from language to language.

questions.q: 'Butterfly' in most European languages is a word borrowed from a shared ancient root.
questions.f: It is famously the opposite: papillon, mariposa, Schmetterling and farfalla are all unrelated.

questions.q: Aesop is famous for telling short animal stories called…?
questions.f: Aesop's fables, like 'The Tortoise and the Hare', are over 2,000 years old and each one teaches a lesson.

questions.q: In Aesop's famous race, who beats the speedy hare?
questions.f: The slow, steady tortoise keeps going while the hare naps — that is where 'slow and steady wins the race' comes from.

questions.q: Which author wrote 'The Cat in the Hat'?
questions.f: Dr. Seuss wrote 'The Cat in the Hat' using only about 236 different words.

questions.q: Alice falls into Wonderland while chasing which animal?
questions.f: In Lewis Carroll's story, the White Rabbit hurries past saying he is late, and curious Alice follows him down the hole.

questions.q: Peter Pan is famous as the boy who never wants to…?
questions.f: J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan lives in Neverland, where children never have to grow up.

questions.q: In 'The Jungle Book', the boy Mowgli is raised by which animals?
questions.f: Rudyard Kipling's Mowgli grows up in a wolf pack with friends like Baloo the bear.

questions.q: What happens to Pinocchio's nose when he tells a lie?
questions.f: Pinocchio is a wooden puppet who dreams of becoming a real boy in Carlo Collodi's classic tale.

questions.q: In the classic book 'Heidi', where does Heidi live with her grandfather?
questions.f: Heidi lives high in the Alps mountains and loves the goats, the meadows, and the fresh air.

questions.q: In the story 'Treasure Island', what are the pirates hunting for?
questions.f: Robert Louis Stevenson's pirates follow a map to an island where treasure is buried.

questions.q: In 'The Wizard of Oz', what kind of animal is Dorothy's pet Toto?
questions.f: Little dog Toto travels with Dorothy all the way down the yellow brick road.

questions.q: Robin Hood and his merry band live hidden in a…?
questions.f: The old tales say Robin Hood hid in Sherwood Forest in England.

questions.q: In the King Arthur legend, young Arthur pulls what out of a stone?
questions.f: Only the true king could pull the sword from the stone, and Arthur did it with ease.

questions.q: In 'Cinderella', what does Cinderella leave behind at the ball?
questions.f: The prince uses the lost glass slipper to search the whole kingdom for Cinderella.

questions.q: In 'The Ugly Duckling', the duckling grows up to be a beautiful…?
questions.f: Hans Christian Andersen's story reminds us not to judge anyone by how they look.

questions.q: William Shakespeare is famous for writing…?
questions.f: Shakespeare wrote his plays over 400 years ago, and people still perform them today.

questions.q: Which author wrote the happy line 'You're off to great places! Today is your day!'?
questions.f: It comes from Dr. Seuss's book 'Oh, the Places You'll Go!', a favorite gift for graduations.

questions.q: 'Curiouser and curiouser!' says Alice. Which author wrote that funny line?
questions.f: Lewis Carroll loved playing with words — 'curiouser' is not even a real word, but Alice says it anyway.

questions.q: In Roald Dahl's famous book, what does Willy Wonka's factory make?
questions.f: Charlie wins a golden ticket to visit Willy Wonka's amazing chocolate factory.

questions.q: Roald Dahl's Matilda loves to spend her time…?
questions.f: Matilda reads piles of library books before she is even five years old.

questions.q: In 'Jack and the Beanstalk', what does Jack find at the top of the beanstalk?
questions.f: The beanstalk grows from magic beans overnight, reaching up into the clouds.

questions.q: In the tales of Aladdin, what magical helper comes out of the lamp?
questions.f: Aladdin's story comes from the famous collection called 'The Arabian Nights'.

questions.q: Many fairy tales begin with the words 'Once upon a time'.
questions.f: Storytellers have used 'Once upon a time' as a magic doorway into stories for hundreds of years.

questions.q: A person who writes books is called an…?
questions.f: The word 'author' comes from a Latin word for someone who creates or begins something.

questions.q: A person who writes poems is called a…?
questions.f: Famous poets include Robert Frost, Emily Dickinson, and Maya Angelou.

questions.q: The person who draws the pictures in a storybook is the…?
questions.f: Illustrator Quentin Blake drew the funny pictures in many Roald Dahl books.

questions.q: The name of a book, printed on its cover, is called its…?
questions.f: 'Title' comes from the Latin word 'titulus', meaning a label or sign.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'cat' in a poem?
questions.f: Rhymes are words that end with the same sound — Dr. Seuss rhymed 'cat' and 'hat' in a famous title.

questions.q: A building where you can borrow books for free is a…?
questions.f: The word 'library' comes from 'liber', the Latin word for book.

questions.q: Someone who loves reading books all the time is called a…?
questions.f: 'Bookworm' is also the name for tiny insects that really do nibble old books.

questions.q: In 'Little Red Riding Hood', where is the girl going with her basket?
questions.f: Charles Perrault wrote down this tale in France over 300 years ago.

questions.q: How many little pigs are in the famous story about houses of straw, sticks and bricks?
questions.f: Only the brick house stands strong — a story about doing careful work.

questions.q: In 'Goldilocks', how many bears live in the little house in the woods?
questions.f: Goldilocks tries all three bowls of porridge, all three chairs, and all three beds.

questions.q: In 'Snow White', how many dwarfs share the little cottage?
questions.f: The Brothers Grimm collected this story in Germany; the dwarfs' names were added much later.

questions.q: In 'The Little Mermaid', where does the mermaid live?
questions.f: Hans Christian Andersen of Denmark wrote it; there is a famous Little Mermaid statue in Copenhagen.

questions.q: Which author wrote 'The Ugly Duckling' and 'The Little Mermaid'?
questions.f: Andersen's birthday, 2 April, is celebrated worldwide as International Children's Book Day.

questions.q: In 'The Emperor's New Clothes', who finally says out loud that the emperor is wearing nothing?
questions.f: A little child speaks the truth while all the grown-ups pretend — that is the point of the story.

questions.q: Which bear is Winnie-the-Pooh's gloomy donkey friend?
questions.f: Eeyore the donkey lives in the Hundred Acre Wood and often loses his tail.

questions.q: Winnie-the-Pooh's best human friend is a boy named…?
questions.f: A. A. Milne named the boy after his own son, Christopher Robin Milne.

questions.q: Which small pink animal is Pooh's nervous best friend?
questions.f: Piglet is small and easily scared, but he is brave when his friends need him.

questions.q: In 'The Tale of Peter Rabbit', whose garden does Peter sneak into?
questions.f: Beatrix Potter first told Peter's story in a letter to a sick little boy.

questions.q: In 'Charlotte's Web', what kind of animal is Charlotte?
questions.f: Charlotte the spider writes words in her web to save Wilbur the pig.

questions.q: In 'Charlotte's Web', what is the name of the pig?
questions.f: E. B. White also wrote 'Stuart Little' about a mouse-sized boy.

questions.q: In 'The Wind in the Willows', which animal loves driving motor-cars?
questions.f: Mr. Toad of Toad Hall gets carried away by every new craze, especially motor-cars.

questions.q: In 'The Wizard of Oz', what does the Scarecrow wish for?
questions.f: The Tin Woodman wants a heart and the Lion wants courage, so all three follow Dorothy.

questions.q: What colour is the famous road Dorothy follows in Oz?
questions.f: The yellow brick road leads all the way to the Emerald City.

questions.q: In 'The Jungle Book', Shere Khan is a fierce…?
questions.f: 'Shere' means tiger in several Indian languages, so his name really means 'Tiger King'.

questions.q: In 'Peter Pan', what is the name of the tiny fairy?
questions.f: Tinker Bell got her name because she mends pots and pans, like a tinker.

questions.q: What is the magical land where Peter Pan lives?
questions.f: To fly to Neverland you need fairy dust and happy thoughts.

questions.q: Who is Peter Pan's pirate enemy with a hook for a hand?
questions.f: Captain Hook is terrified of the ticking crocodile that swallowed a clock.

questions.q: Which children's classic is about a bear who loves marmalade sandwiches?
questions.f: Paddington Bear arrives at London's Paddington Station with a note: 'Please look after this bear.'

questions.q: In 'The Secret Garden', what does Mary Lennox discover behind a hidden door?
questions.f: A friendly robin helps Mary find the key to the locked garden.

questions.q: In 'Black Beauty', who tells the whole story?
questions.f: Anna Sewell wrote 'Black Beauty' to teach people to treat horses kindly.

questions.q: Anne of Green Gables is famous for her bright…?
questions.f: Anne Shirley lives on Prince Edward Island in Canada and talks a mile a minute.

questions.q: In 'A Christmas Carol', what is the grumpy old man's name?
questions.f: Ebenezer Scrooge learns to be kind after three spirits visit him one Christmas Eve.

questions.q: In 'Oliver Twist', hungry Oliver asks for more of what?
questions.f: 'Please, sir, I want some more' is one of the most famous lines Charles Dickens ever wrote.

questions.q: In 'The Little Prince', the prince comes from a tiny…?
questions.f: Antoine de Saint-Exupery, who wrote it, was a real airplane pilot.

questions.q: Which classic tells of a boy and a runaway raft on the Mississippi River?
questions.f: Mark Twain grew up beside the Mississippi and knew the river well.

questions.q: In 'Tom Sawyer', Tom tricks his friends into doing which chore?
questions.f: Tom makes whitewashing the fence look so fun that other boys pay him to let them try.

questions.q: Which sea creature is the giant white whale in a famous American novel?
questions.f: Herman Melville's 'Moby-Dick' begins with the three words 'Call me Ishmael.'

questions.q: Robinson Crusoe spends years living on a…?
questions.f: Daniel Defoe's hero makes tools, grows food, and meets a friend he calls Friday.

questions.q: In 'Gulliver's Travels', the tiny people of Lilliput are about the size of a…?
questions.f: Jonathan Swift's Gulliver is tied down with hundreds of tiny ropes while he sleeps.

questions.q: Which famous detective lives at 221B Baker Street in London?
questions.f: Arthur Conan Doyle gave Sherlock Holmes a helpful friend named Dr. Watson.

questions.q: In 'The Three Musketeers', the friends shout a motto about being…?
questions.f: 'All for one and one for all' is the musketeers' promise to stand together.

questions.q: Which poet wrote the line 'The woods are lovely, dark and deep'?
questions.f: It is from Frost's snowy poem 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening'.

questions.q: 'Hope is the thing with feathers' compares hope to which animal?
questions.f: Emily Dickinson pictured hope as a little bird singing inside your soul.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'The earth laughs in flowers'?
questions.f: Emerson loved walking in the woods near Concord, Massachusetts, and writing about nature.

questions.q: Complete Langston Hughes's line: 'Let the rain kiss you. Let the rain sing you a…'
questions.f: Langston Hughes wrote joyful poems about everyday things like rain and dreams.

questions.q: Which author wrote 'Those who don't believe in magic will never find it'?
questions.f: Roald Dahl wrote his stories in a little hut in his garden, using pencils.

questions.q: Which children's author wrote 'Don't cry because it's over, smile because it happened'?
questions.f: Dr. Seuss's real name was Theodor Seuss Geisel, and 'Seuss' was his mother's family name.

questions.q: A story that teaches a lesson at the end has a…?
questions.f: Aesop ends nearly every fable with a moral, such as 'slow and steady wins the race'.

questions.q: The people in a story are called its…?
questions.f: 'Character' comes from a Greek word for a stamped mark, like a mark that makes someone recognisable.

questions.q: Where and when a story happens is called the…?
questions.f: A setting can be a jungle, a spaceship, or a cosy cottage in the woods.

questions.q: The good main character of a story is often called the…?
questions.f: The word 'hero' comes straight from ancient Greek stories about brave warriors.

questions.q: The bad character who causes trouble in a story is the…?
questions.f: Surprisingly, 'villain' first meant a farm worker in Latin, long before it meant a baddie.

questions.q: Books are divided into parts called…?
questions.f: 'Chapter' comes from the Latin word 'caput', meaning head — each chapter is a little heading.

questions.q: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star' is an example of a…?
questions.f: Nursery rhymes are short rhyming songs passed from grown-ups to children for hundreds of years.

questions.q: 'She sells seashells by the seashore' is hard to say fast, so it is a…?
questions.f: Tongue twisters repeat similar sounds, which tangles up your tongue.

questions.q: A short puzzle in words that you must guess the answer to is a…?
questions.f: Riddles appear in very old stories, including the epic poem 'Beowulf' and Greek myths.

questions.q: Which pair of words would rhyme at the ends of two lines of a poem?
questions.f: Rhyming makes poems easy to remember, which is why old poems were sung aloud.

questions.q: A book that tells you what words mean is a…?
questions.f: 'Dictionary' comes from the Latin 'dictio', meaning a saying or a word.

questions.q: Writing about your own day in a private notebook makes it a…?
questions.f: 'Diary' comes from the Latin 'dies', meaning day — a day-by-day book.

questions.q: Long ago people wrote with feathers dipped in ink. Such a pen was called a…?
questions.f: That is why 'pen' comes from 'penna', the Latin word for feather.

questions.q: Which word means the front outside part of a book?
questions.f: The old saying 'don't judge a book by its cover' means look deeper than appearances.

questions.q: A poem does not have to rhyme.
questions.f: Poems without rhyme are called free verse; Walt Whitman wrote whole books of it.

questions.q: Shakespeare wrote his famous plays in English.
questions.f: He wrote in Early Modern English, which is why words like 'thou' and 'thee' appear.

questions.q: Which of these is a made-up story rather than a true one?
questions.f: Made-up stories are called fiction, from a Latin word meaning to shape or mould.

questions.q: In 'Aladdin', which famous story collection does he come from?
questions.f: In 'The Arabian Nights', clever Scheherazade tells a new story every night.

questions.q: Which classic story features a boy who cries wolf when there is no wolf?
questions.f: When a real wolf comes, nobody believes the boy — the fable warns against lying.

questions.q: Which classic story is about a wooden puppet who wants to be a real boy?
questions.f: Carlo Collodi wrote Pinocchio in Italy in the 1880s as a newspaper serial.

questions.q: In 'Sleeping Beauty', what wakes the princess after her long sleep?
questions.f: Charles Perrault and the Brothers Grimm both wrote versions of this old tale.

questions.q: In 'Rapunzel', what does the girl let down from the tower window?
questions.f: 'Rapunzel' is a German fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm.

questions.q: In 'Hansel and Gretel', what do the children follow to find their way home?
questions.f: Birds eat the breadcrumbs, which is how the children get lost in the forest.

questions.q: 'Puss in Boots' is a clever story about which animal?
questions.f: The talking cat wears boots and wins his master a castle by being clever.

questions.q: In 'The Tortoise and the Hare', which animal falls asleep during the race?
questions.f: The hare is so sure he will win that he takes a nap — and loses.

questions.q: In Aesop's fable, the fox says the grapes he cannot reach are…?
questions.f: That fable gave English the phrase 'sour grapes' for pretending you never wanted something.

questions.q: In Aesop's fable, which tiny animal helps a lion by pulling out a thorn?
questions.f: The lion had spared the mouse earlier, so the mouse repays the kindness.

questions.q: In 'The Ant and the Grasshopper', which insect works hard all summer?
questions.f: The busy ant stores food while the grasshopper sings, and winter proves the ant right.

questions.q: Aesop's fables usually star which kind of characters?
questions.f: Giving animals human speech and feelings is called personification.

questions.q: Which classic book features a girl named Alice and a grinning Cheshire Cat?
questions.f: The Cheshire Cat can vanish slowly, leaving only its grin behind.

questions.q: In Wonderland, which character shouts 'Off with their heads!'?
questions.f: The Queen of Hearts is a playing card come to life, and she is always cross.

questions.q: What kind of party do the Mad Hatter and March Hare hold in Wonderland?
questions.f: At their never-ending tea party it is always six o'clock, so it is always tea time.

questions.q: Which egg-shaped character sits on a wall in a famous nursery rhyme?
questions.f: Humpty Dumpty also appears in Lewis Carroll's 'Through the Looking-Glass', where he explains words.

questions.q: In 'Treasure Island', which pirate has a wooden leg and a parrot?
questions.f: His parrot is named Captain Flint, after a dead pirate captain in the story.

questions.q: On a treasure map, what shape usually marks the treasure spot?
questions.f: 'X marks the spot' became famous through pirate stories like 'Treasure Island'.

questions.q: Which author wrote 'Treasure Island'?
questions.f: Stevenson first drew the treasure map as a game to entertain his stepson.

questions.q: In 'Around the World in Eighty Days', how many days does the traveller have?
questions.f: Jules Verne's Phileas Fogg bets he can circle the globe in exactly eighty days.

questions.q: Captain Nemo travels the ocean in a submarine named the…?
questions.f: 'Nautilus' is also the name of a real sea creature with a spiral shell.

questions.q: In 'Heidi', which animals does Peter look after on the mountain?
questions.f: Peter the goatherd takes the village goats up the Alps every morning.

questions.q: In 'Little Women', how many March sisters are there?
questions.f: Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy are the four sisters; Jo dreams of being a writer.

questions.q: Which March sister in 'Little Women' wants to be a writer?
questions.f: Louisa May Alcott based Jo partly on herself.

questions.q: 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' is a story about a brave little…?
questions.f: Rudyard Kipling's mongoose protects an English family from cobras in India.

questions.q: Which classic children's poem begins 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat went to sea'?
c: a nursery rhyme by Mother Goose
questions.f: Edward Lear wrote wonderfully silly poems and also popularised the limerick.

questions.q: What does the word 'fiction' describe?
questions.f: 'Fiction' comes from a Latin word meaning to shape or mould, like shaping clay.

questions.q: Writing that is true and about real facts is called…?
questions.f: Non-fiction includes biographies, science books, and history books.

questions.q: A book that tells the true story of a real person's life is a…?
questions.f: 'Biography' is built from Greek words meaning 'life' and 'writing'.

questions.q: When two words start with the same sound, like 'silly snake', that is called…?
questions.f: Alliteration makes tongue twisters tricky and poems fun to say aloud.

questions.q: Words like 'bang', 'buzz' and 'splash' copy real sounds. Such words are…?
questions.f: The fancy name for these is onomatopoeia, from Greek words meaning 'name making'.

questions.q: A group of lines in a poem is called a…?
questions.f: 'Stanza' is the Italian word for room — each stanza is a little room in the poem.

questions.q: Who reads a story aloud to you in an audiobook?
questions.f: 'Narrator' comes from the Latin 'narrare', to tell a story.

questions.q: Which word means a very long story book?
questions.f: 'Novel' comes from an Italian word meaning 'new' — a new little story.

questions.q: A person who takes care of books in a library is a…?
questions.f: Librarians use catalogues to help you find any book in a huge collection.

questions.q: What do we call the very first sentence of a story?
questions.f: 'Call me Ishmael' from 'Moby-Dick' is one of the most famous opening lines ever.

questions.q: Which of these words means a short funny poem of five lines?
questions.f: The limerick is named after the Irish city of Limerick.

questions.q: 'Once upon a time' is usually the beginning. Which words often end a fairy tale?
questions.f: Old storytellers used the same beginnings and endings to signal magic was starting or stopping.

questions.q: Which classic tale features a big bad wolf and a girl in a red cloak?
questions.f: In the oldest versions, a woodcutter or huntsman rescues the girl and her grandmother.

questions.q: Thumbelina in Andersen's story is a girl no bigger than a…?
questions.f: Thumbelina is born inside a flower and rides on a swallow's back.

questions.q: In 'The Princess and the Pea', what proves the girl is a real princess?
c: she feels a pea under many mattresses
questions.f: Only someone very delicate could feel one tiny pea under twenty mattresses.

questions.q: Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet' is set in which Italian city?
questions.f: Verona is a real Italian city, and visitors still line up to see 'Juliet's balcony'.

questions.q: 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland' has a sequel called 'Through the Looking-Glass'.
questions.f: In the sequel Alice steps through a mirror into a world laid out like a giant chessboard.

questions.q: Aesop's fables were first told in ancient Greece.
questions.f: Aesop lived about 2,600 years ago, and the fables were passed on by word of mouth for centuries.

questions.q: A poem's rhythm is the pattern of beats you can clap along to.
questions.f: Poets choose rhythms the way drummers choose beats — it changes how a poem feels.

questions.q: Which classic character is a giant with a very kind heart in a Roald Dahl book?
questions.f: The BFG stands for Big Friendly Giant, and he collects dreams in jars.

questions.q: In Roald Dahl's 'James and the Giant Peach', James travels inside a giant…?
questions.f: James sails the Atlantic Ocean inside the peach with a team of friendly giant insects.

questions.q: In 'Charlie and the Chocolate Factory', what does Charlie find in a chocolate bar?
questions.f: Five golden tickets are hidden worldwide, and Charlie finds the last one.

questions.q: Which animal helps tell the story in Kipling's 'Just So Stories' about a trunk?
questions.f: 'The Elephant's Child' explains how the elephant supposedly got its long trunk.

questions.q: What is a picture book mostly made of?
questions.f: The Caldecott Medal is a famous prize given each year for the best picture-book art.

questions.q: Which of these is a poem you might sing to a baby at bedtime?
questions.f: Lullabies use slow, gentle rhythms on purpose to help babies drift off.

questions.q: Which classic book is about a mole, a rat, a badger and a toad by a river?
questions.f: Kenneth Grahame first told these river-bank stories to his young son.

questions.q: 'Pollyanna' is famous for a cheerful game called the…?
questions.f: In the glad game you look for something to be glad about in every situation.

questions.q: A word that means the opposite of another word is its…?
questions.f: 'Antonym' is built from Greek pieces meaning 'against' and 'name'.

questions.q: A word that means nearly the same as another word is its…?
questions.f: 'Synonym' is built from Greek pieces meaning 'together' and 'name'.

questions.q: 'Big' and 'large' are examples of what?
questions.f: Roget's Thesaurus is a whole book of synonyms, first published in 1852.

questions.q: The name of the letters A, B, C together is the…?
questions.f: 'Alphabet' comes from alpha and beta, the first two letters of the Greek alphabet.

questions.q: Which book of maps would you use to find countries?
questions.f: 'Atlas' is named after a giant in Greek myth who held up the sky.

questions.q: Which famous story features a boy raised by apes in the jungle?
questions.f: Edgar Rice Burroughs created Tarzan in 1912, a few years after Kipling's Mowgli.

questions.q: 'The Swiss Family Robinson' is about a family shipwrecked on a…?
questions.f: Johann David Wyss wrote it to teach his own sons about courage and cleverness.

questions.q: Which classic character says 'Bah! Humbug!' about Christmas?
questions.f: By the end of the book Scrooge is the most generous man in town.

questions.q: Which novel opens with the words 'Call me Ishmael'?
questions.f: Herman Melville's whaling novel sold poorly at first and only became famous decades later.

questions.q: Charles Dickens's 'A Tale of Two Cities' is set in London and which other city?
questions.f: Its opening line, 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times', is world famous.

questions.q: Which sisters wrote 'Jane Eyre' and 'Wuthering Heights'?
questions.f: Charlotte wrote 'Jane Eyre' and her sister Emily wrote 'Wuthering Heights', both published in 1847.

questions.q: Which author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
questions.f: Conan Doyle was a doctor, and he based Holmes on a sharp-eyed surgeon he studied under.

questions.q: Which author wrote 'Pride and Prejudice'?
questions.f: Austen published her novels anonymously; the title page just said 'By a Lady'.

questions.q: In 'Robinson Crusoe', what does Crusoe name the friend he meets on the island?
questions.f: He names him after the day of the week when they met.

questions.q: Shakespeare was born in which English town?
questions.f: That is why he is nicknamed 'the Bard of Avon' after the river running through his town.

questions.q: Which London theatre was Shakespeare's company famous for performing in?
questions.f: The original Globe was round and open to the sky, so plays were staged in daylight.

questions.q: Roughly how many sonnets did Shakespeare write?
questions.f: His sonnets were printed together in 1609, and each one is exactly fourteen lines long.

questions.q: 'To be, or not to be' is the start of a famous speech in which play?
questions.f: Prince Hamlet says it while wrestling with a huge decision, and it is Shakespeare's best-known line.

questions.q: In 'Macbeth', how many witches greet Macbeth on the heath?
questions.f: Their chant 'Double, double toil and trouble' is one of theatre's most quoted spells.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play features the fairy Puck and a weaver named Bottom?
questions.f: Puck magically gives Bottom the head of a donkey, and the fairy queen falls in love with him.

questions.q: 'All the world's a stage' comes from which Shakespeare comedy?
questions.f: The speech goes on to describe seven ages of a human life, from baby to old age.

questions.q: In 'Romeo and Juliet', the two feuding families are the Capulets and the…?
questions.f: Shakespeare calls Romeo and Juliet 'star-crossed lovers', meaning fate is against them.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'Two roads diverged in a wood, and I took the one less traveled by'?
questions.f: Frost's poem 'The Road Not Taken' is one of the most quoted poems in the English language.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'Hold fast to dreams, for if dreams die, life is a broken-winged bird'?
questions.f: Langston Hughes was a leading voice of the Harlem Renaissance in 1920s New York.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'There is no frigate like a book to take us lands away'?
questions.f: A frigate is a fast sailing ship, so Dickinson is saying a book carries you off like a voyage.

questions.q: Which writer said 'The secret of getting ahead is getting started'?
questions.f: Mark Twain's real name was Samuel Langhorne Clemens.

questions.q: Which Irish writer said 'Be yourself; everyone else is already taken'?
questions.f: Wilde was famous for witty one-liners as well as for the play 'The Importance of Being Earnest'.

questions.q: Which English Romantic poet wrote 'A thing of beauty is a joy forever'?
questions.f: Keats wrote his greatest poems in a single astonishing year and died aged just 25.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'To see a world in a grain of sand and a heaven in a wild flower'?
questions.f: Blake was also an artist who engraved and hand-coloured the pages of his own poetry books.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'Come forth into the light of things, let Nature be your teacher'?
questions.f: Wordsworth lived in England's Lake District and walked thousands of miles among its hills.

questions.q: Which Indian poet wrote 'You can't cross the sea merely by standing and staring at the water'?
questions.f: Tagore wrote the words to the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.

questions.q: Which French novelist wrote 'Even the darkest night will end and the sun will rise'?
questions.f: Victor Hugo wrote 'Les Miserables' and 'The Hunchback of Notre-Dame'.

questions.q: Which Russian novelist wrote 'Everyone thinks of changing the world, but no one thinks of changing himself'?
questions.f: Tolstoy wrote the enormous novels 'War and Peace' and 'Anna Karenina'.

questions.q: Who wrote the four March sisters into the novel 'Little Women'?
questions.f: Alcott wrote 'Little Women' quickly, at a publisher's suggestion, and it made her famous.

questions.q: Which novel features Jean Valjean and the policeman Javert?
questions.f: Victor Hugo's novel is so long that some editions run to well over 1,200 pages.

questions.q: Alexandre Dumas wrote about a wronged sailor named Edmond Dantes in which novel?
c: Around the World in Eighty Days
questions.f: Dantes escapes a prison island and returns with a new name and a fortune.

questions.q: Which of Jules Verne's novels is set aboard a submarine?
c: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas
Around the World in Eighty Days
Journey to the Center of the Earth
questions.f: Verne imagined electric submarines decades before real ones existed.

questions.q: H. G. Wells wrote about Martians invading Earth in which novel?
questions.f: A 1938 radio version was so realistic that some American listeners thought it was real news.

questions.q: Who wrote 'Frankenstein'?
questions.f: Mary Shelley began the story at 18, during a rainy summer holiday by a Swiss lake.

questions.q: In 'Frankenstein', what is Victor Frankenstein's job title in the story?
questions.f: The novel's full title is 'Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus'.

questions.q: Which novel by Bram Stoker is written as a collection of letters and diary entries?
questions.f: Telling a story through letters and diaries is called the epistolary style.

questions.q: Which Dickens character is a boy who grows up in a workhouse?
questions.f: Dickens knew hardship himself: at twelve he worked in a factory pasting labels on jars.

questions.q: In 'Great Expectations', what is the main character's name?
questions.f: Pip's real name is Philip Pirrip, but as a child he could only manage 'Pip'.

questions.q: Which American novel is about a runaway boy and Jim travelling by raft?
questions.f: Mark Twain wrote much of it at his home in Hartford, Connecticut.

questions.q: Jack London's 'The Call of the Wild' follows a dog named…?
questions.f: Buck is stolen from California and taken to pull sleds in the Yukon gold rush.

questions.q: Which Greek epic poem tells of Odysseus's ten-year journey home?
questions.f: 'Odyssey' has entered English as a word for any long, adventurous journey.

questions.q: Which Greek poet is credited with the 'Iliad' and the 'Odyssey'?
questions.f: Homer's epics were performed from memory by singers long before they were ever written down.

questions.q: In the 'Odyssey', the one-eyed giant Odysseus outwits is a…?
questions.f: Odysseus tells the Cyclops his name is 'Nobody', so nobody comes to help when the giant calls.

questions.q: Who wrote 'The Canterbury Tales'?
questions.f: Chaucer wrote in Middle English, which looks strange today but was ordinary speech in the 1300s.

questions.q: In 'The Canterbury Tales', where are the pilgrims travelling to?
questions.f: They set out from the Tabard Inn and each agrees to tell stories along the road.

questions.q: Which brothers collected German fairy tales like 'Rapunzel' and 'Hansel and Gretel'?
questions.f: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm were scholars of language who also worked on a huge German dictionary.

questions.q: Which writer's fairy tales include 'The Snow Queen' and 'The Steadfast Tin Soldier'?
questions.f: Unlike the Grimms, Andersen invented most of his tales rather than collecting them.

questions.q: A comparison using the words 'like' or 'as' is called a…?
questions.f: 'Simile' comes from the Latin 'similis', meaning like or similar.

questions.q: 'The classroom was a zoo' is an example of which literary device?
questions.f: A metaphor says one thing IS another; a simile only says it is LIKE another.

questions.q: When you give human feelings to the wind or the sun, that is…?
questions.f: 'The wind whispered' is personification, from the Latin 'persona', meaning a mask or character.

questions.q: The main character of a story is properly called the…?
questions.f: 'Protagonist' comes from Greek words meaning 'first' and 'actor' — the first actor on stage.

questions.q: The character who opposes the hero is called the…?
questions.f: The prefix 'anti-' means against, so an antagonist is the one who struggles against the hero.

questions.q: The word 'biography' is built from Greek pieces meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek bios (life) plus graphein (to write).

questions.q: The 'auto' in 'autobiography' means…?
questions.f: So an autobiography is a life story written by the person who lived it.

questions.q: 'Library' comes from a Latin word that means…?
questions.f: From Latin 'liber', meaning book — the same root as 'libretto' in opera.

questions.q: 'Poet' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek 'poietes', a maker — a poem was literally a made thing.

questions.q: The word 'chapter' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin 'caput' (head) — each chapter is topped by its own little heading.

questions.q: The word 'stanza' is Italian for…?
questions.f: Poets talk about stanzas as rooms because each one holds a complete thought.

questions.q: The word 'novel' comes from an Italian word meaning…?
questions.f: An Italian 'novella' was a new little story, and 'novel' kept that sense of newness.

questions.q: A collection of poems or stories by many different writers is called an…?
questions.f: 'Anthology' comes from Greek words meaning a gathering of flowers.

questions.q: The short section at the start of a book, before chapter one, is the…?
questions.f: 'Prologue' is Greek for 'before word'; an epilogue is the 'after word'.

questions.q: The word 'manuscript' literally means…?
questions.f: From Latin manus (hand) plus scriptus (written) — before printing, every book was one.

questions.q: A pen name that an author uses instead of their real name is a…?
questions.f: 'Pseudonym' means false name; George Eliot was really Mary Ann Evans.

questions.q: What was Mark Twain's real name?
questions.f: 'Mark twain' was a riverboat call meaning the water was two fathoms deep — safe to pass.

questions.q: What was Lewis Carroll's real name?
questions.f: Dodgson was an Oxford mathematics lecturer who wrote textbooks under his real name.

questions.q: Which novel's title character is a governess who works at Thornfield Hall?
questions.f: Charlotte Bronte published it under the pen name Currer Bell.

questions.q: 'Wuthering Heights' takes place on the wild Yorkshire…?
questions.f: 'Wuthering' is a Yorkshire word for wind roaring and rattling around a building.

questions.q: Which poet's collection is called 'Leaves of Grass'?
questions.f: Whitman kept rewriting and expanding it across nine editions over nearly forty years.

questions.q: Henry David Thoreau wrote a famous book about living simply beside which pond?
questions.f: He lived in a small cabin there for two years, two months, and two days.

questions.q: Which writer said 'I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately'?
questions.f: That line comes from 'Walden', Thoreau's book about his experiment in simple living.

questions.q: Edgar Allan Poe's most famous poem features which talking bird?
questions.f: The bird repeats a single word: 'Nevermore'.

questions.q: Edgar Allan Poe is credited with inventing which kind of story?
questions.f: His detective C. Auguste Dupin came decades before Sherlock Holmes.

questions.q: Which novel features Captain Ahab hunting a great white whale?
c: The Old Man and the Sea
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas
questions.f: Melville had really sailed on a whaling ship, which is why the details ring true.

questions.q: 'The Secret Garden' and 'A Little Princess' were both written by…?
questions.f: Burnett was born in England and later moved to the United States.

questions.q: Which writer created Winnie-the-Pooh?
questions.f: Pooh was named after a real black bear at London Zoo called Winnie, short for Winnipeg.

questions.q: Which children's author also studied and painted mushrooms and fungi?
questions.f: Potter's scientific drawings of fungi are still admired by mycologists today.

questions.q: Shakespeare wrote both comedies and tragedies.
questions.f: His plays are traditionally grouped as comedies, tragedies and histories in the First Folio of 1623.

questions.q: A sonnet has fourteen lines.
questions.f: 'Sonnet' comes from the Italian 'sonetto', meaning a little sound or little song.

questions.q: Emily Dickinson published most of her poems while she was alive.
questions.f: Fewer than a dozen of her nearly 1,800 poems appeared in print before she died.

questions.q: 'The Jungle Book' author Rudyard Kipling was born in India.
questions.f: Kipling was born in Bombay in 1865 and his Indian childhood shaped many of his stories.

questions.q: Which word describes a story with talking animals that teaches a lesson?
questions.f: 'Fable' comes from Latin 'fabula', a story, from 'fari', meaning to speak.

questions.q: A very long poem about heroes and great deeds is called an…?
questions.f: 'Epic' comes from Greek 'epos', meaning word or song.

questions.q: Which word means a short saying that gives advice, like 'Look before you leap'?
questions.f: Every language has its own proverbs, and many are hundreds of years old.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play is set on a magical island ruled by Prospero?
questions.f: Prospero's spirit helper is named Ariel, and the play ends with him giving up magic.

questions.q: In 'The Merchant of Venice', which character delivers the 'quality of mercy' speech?
questions.f: Portia argues the case disguised as a young male lawyer.

questions.q: 'Et tu, Brute?' is spoken in which Shakespeare play?
questions.f: The Latin means 'And you, Brutus?' — the shock of being betrayed by a friend.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare king divides his kingdom among his daughters?
questions.f: Lear's youngest daughter Cordelia refuses to flatter him, and he misjudges her badly.

questions.q: Which of these is a Shakespeare comedy about twins and mistaken identity?
questions.f: Viola disguises herself as a boy named Cesario, which tangles everything up beautifully.

questions.q: How many lines does a Shakespearean sonnet's final rhyming couplet have?
questions.f: Three quatrains plus a closing couplet make up the fourteen lines.

questions.q: 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?' opens which of Shakespeare's sonnets?
questions.f: It promises that the poem itself will keep its subject alive forever.

questions.q: Which classic poem describes an albatross and a cursed sea voyage?
c: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
The Charge of the Light Brigade
questions.f: Samuel Taylor Coleridge's poem gave us the phrase 'an albatross around your neck'.

questions.q: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' is a famous poem about which flowers?
questions.f: William Wordsworth wrote it after seeing a long band of daffodils beside a lake.

questions.q: Which poem begins 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright, in the forests of the night'?
questions.f: William Blake paired 'The Tyger' with a gentle poem called 'The Lamb'.

questions.q: 'Jabberwocky' is a nonsense poem from which book?
questions.f: Lewis Carroll invented words like 'slithy' and 'galumphing'; 'chortle' caught on for real.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'Listen, my children, and you shall hear of the midnight ride of Paul Revere'?
questions.f: Longfellow was the first American honoured with a bust in Westminster Abbey's Poets' Corner.

questions.q: Which Scottish poet wrote 'Auld Lang Syne'?
questions.f: Scotland celebrates Burns Night on 25 January, his birthday, with poems and haggis.

questions.q: Which poet wrote the line 'The best way out is always through'?
questions.f: Frost won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry four separate times.

questions.q: Which American poet wrote 'Nothing happens unless first we dream'?
questions.f: Sandburg also wrote a huge, prize-winning biography of Abraham Lincoln.

questions.q: Which American poet wrote 'The world is mud-luscious and puddle-wonderful'?
questions.f: Cummings loved inventing words and often skipped capital letters altogether.

questions.q: Which Irish poet wrote 'The world is full of magic things, patiently waiting for our senses to grow sharper'?
questions.f: Yeats won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923.

questions.q: Which English novelist wrote 'No one is useless in this world who lightens the burdens of another'?
questions.f: Dickens gave hugely popular public readings of his own books, acting out every character.

questions.q: Which novelist wrote 'The person who has not pleasure in a good novel must be intolerably stupid'?
questions.f: The line comes from Austen's novel 'Northanger Abbey', a playful defence of novel-reading.

questions.q: Which author of 'Little Women' wrote 'Far away there in the sunshine are my highest aspirations'?
questions.f: Alcott grew up in Concord, Massachusetts, among writers like Emerson and Thoreau.

questions.q: Which writer said 'Kindness is the language which the deaf can hear and the blind can see'?
questions.f: Twain travelled the world giving lectures and was one of the first global celebrity authors.

questions.q: Which author of 'Treasure Island' wrote 'A friend is a gift you give yourself'?
questions.f: Stevenson spent his last years in Samoa, where islanders called him 'Tusitala', the storyteller.

questions.q: Which Italian poet wrote that 'Nature is the art of God'?
questions.f: Dante's masterpiece 'The Divine Comedy' is written in Italian rather than Latin, which was daring.

questions.q: Which Roman poet wrote 'Fortune favors the bold'?
questions.f: Virgil's epic 'The Aeneid' follows the Trojan hero Aeneas to Italy.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek poet wrote 'Light is the task where many share the toil'?
questions.f: The line appears in the 'Iliad', Homer's epic about the Trojan War.

questions.q: Which Chinese thinker's sayings include 'The man who moves a mountain begins by carrying away small stones'?
questions.f: Confucius's sayings were gathered by his students into a book called the 'Analects'.

questions.q: Which writer said 'To learn to read is to light a fire; every syllable that is spelled out is a spark'?
questions.f: Hugo cared deeply about education for poor children, a theme all over 'Les Miserables'.

questions.q: Which writer wrote 'I keep six honest serving-men: What and Why and When and How and Where and Who'?
questions.f: Journalists still call those six question words the 'five Ws and an H'.

questions.q: 'Curiouser and curiouser' and 'Begin at the beginning' both come from which author?
questions.f: Carroll was also a pioneering photographer, one of the best amateurs of his day.

questions.q: Which author of 'Peter Pan' wrote 'The moment you doubt whether you can fly, you cease forever to be able to do it'?
questions.f: Barrie gave the rights to Peter Pan to a London children's hospital, which earns from it still.

questions.q: Which word describes exaggerating hugely for effect, like 'I've told you a million times'?
questions.f: 'Hyperbole' comes from Greek words meaning 'to throw beyond'.

questions.q: A three-line Japanese poem with 5, 7 and 5 syllables is a…?
questions.f: Haiku traditionally hint at a season, often with a single sharp image from nature.

questions.q: A poem written to praise or celebrate something is called an…?
questions.f: John Keats wrote famous odes to a nightingale, to autumn and to a Grecian urn.

questions.q: A sad poem written in memory of someone who has died is an…?
questions.f: 'Elegy' comes from a Greek word for a mournful song.

questions.q: The word 'theatre' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek 'theatron', from 'theasthai', to behold — audiences went to SEE a play.

questions.q: The word 'tragedy' comes from Greek words usually translated as…?
questions.f: From 'tragos' (goat) and 'oide' (song); the exact reason is debated but the roots are clear.

questions.q: The root 'graph' in 'autograph' and 'paragraph' means…?
questions.f: So an autograph is literally a self-writing — your own hand signing your name.

questions.q: The word 'alphabet' is made from the names of which two letters?
questions.f: The Greek alphabet begins alpha, beta, gamma, delta.

questions.q: The word 'paper' comes from the name of which plant?
questions.f: Ancient Egyptians pressed papyrus reeds into sheets thousands of years ago.

questions.q: The word 'pencil' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin 'penicillus', a little brush — the earliest 'pencils' were tiny paintbrushes.

questions.q: The word 'thesaurus' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Peter Mark Roget, a doctor, published his famous treasure house of words in 1852.

questions.q: An alphabetical list at the back of a book, showing where topics appear, is the…?
questions.f: 'Index' is Latin for a pointer, and also the name of your pointing finger.

questions.q: A list of hard words with their meanings at the back of a book is a…?
questions.f: 'Glossary' comes from Greek 'glossa', tongue — a word needing explanation.

questions.q: Which word means a story handed down for generations that may mix fact and legend?
questions.f: 'Legend' comes from the Latin 'legenda', meaning 'things to be read aloud'.

questions.q: In the King Arthur legends, what is the name of Arthur's sword?
questions.f: The Lady of the Lake gives Arthur Excalibur in many versions of the story.
