questions.q: Which wizard advises King Arthur in the classic legends?
questions.f: Thomas Malory gathered the Arthur stories into 'Le Morte d'Arthur', printed by Caxton in 1485.

questions.q: Robin Hood's famous companion is a very large man called…?
questions.f: 'Little John' is a joke name — in the ballads he is a giant of a man.

questions.q: 'Beowulf' is an epic poem written in which early form of English?
questions.f: Only one medieval manuscript of 'Beowulf' survives, and it was damaged in a fire in 1731.

questions.q: In 'Beowulf', what is the name of the monster who attacks the great hall?
questions.f: The hall is called Heorot, and Beowulf fights Grendel bare-handed.

questions.q: 'One Thousand and One Nights' is framed around a storyteller named…?
questions.f: She survives by ending each night on a cliffhanger so the king must hear more.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian collection is full of animal fables in Sanskrit?
questions.f: 'Panchatantra' means 'five treatises', and its stories travelled as far as Europe.

questions.q: Which Indian epic tells the story of Prince Rama and Sita?
questions.f: The 'Ramayana' is traditionally credited to the poet Valmiki.

questions.q: Which Spanish novel follows a knight who mistakes windmills for giants?
questions.f: Miguel de Cervantes's book is often called the first modern novel.

questions.q: Who is Don Quixote's loyal companion?
questions.f: Sancho rides a donkey while Quixote rides a bony old horse named Rocinante.

questions.q: Which novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe helped change American opinions about slavery?
questions.f: It was the best-selling novel of the 19th century in the United States.

questions.q: Which American author wrote 'The Scarlet Letter'?
questions.f: Hawthorne and Melville were friends, and Melville dedicated 'Moby-Dick' to him.

questions.q: Washington Irving wrote about a man who slept for twenty years. His name was…?
questions.f: Irving also wrote 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' with its Headless Horseman.

questions.q: Which of these novels is told entirely from an animal's point of view?
questions.f: Anna Sewell wrote it while ill, and it was her only book; it helped improve horse welfare.

questions.q: Which prize is given each year for the best American children's book?
questions.f: It is named after John Newbery, an English publisher called the father of children's books.

questions.q: Which is the world's most famous prize for a writer's whole body of work?
questions.f: Rudyard Kipling won it in 1907 at 41, the youngest literature laureate ever.

questions.q: Who invented the printing press with movable metal type in Europe?
questions.f: His famous Bible of the 1450s has 42 lines on most pages, so it is called the 42-line Bible.

questions.q: Who set up England's first printing press, in 1476?
questions.f: Caxton printed 'The Canterbury Tales' and helped fix which English spellings became standard.

questions.q: Which writer compiled a famous English dictionary published in 1755?
questions.f: Johnson worked about nine years with a handful of helpers, defining over 40,000 words.

questions.q: Which American simplified spellings like 'colour' to 'color' in his dictionary?
questions.f: Webster's American dictionary of 1828 is why US and British spellings differ today.

questions.q: 'Don Quixote' was written in Spanish.
questions.f: Cervantes published Part One in 1605 and Part Two ten years later.

questions.q: Charles Dickens published many of his novels in weekly or monthly instalments.
questions.f: Readers had to wait for the next part, exactly like waiting for the next episode of a series.

questions.q: The word 'poetry' and the word 'poem' share the same Greek root.
questions.f: Both trace to Greek 'poiein', to make — poems are made things.

questions.q: Which literary term means a hint about what will happen later in the story?
questions.f: A gun on the wall in act one, said Chekhov, should go off by act three.

questions.q: A scene that jumps back to an earlier time is called a…?
questions.f: Films borrowed the flashback from novels, where writers had used it for centuries.

questions.q: The most exciting turning point of a story is its…?
questions.f: 'Climax' comes from the Greek word for a ladder — the story climbs to it.

questions.q: Words spoken by characters to each other in a story are called…?
questions.f: 'Dialogue' is built from Greek pieces meaning 'across' and 'speech'.

questions.q: A long speech by one character alone on stage is a…?
questions.f: 'Mono' means one, so a monologue is one person speaking.

questions.q: Two lines of poetry that rhyme and sit together are called a…?
questions.f: Shakespeare ends each of his sonnets with a punchy rhyming couplet.

questions.q: A four-line group in a poem is called a…?
questions.f: 'Quatrain' comes from the Latin 'quattuor', meaning four.

questions.q: Which word means a repeated line or chorus in a song or poem?
questions.f: Frost repeats 'And miles to go before I sleep' as a haunting refrain.

questions.q: Which word describes the feeling or mood a writer creates in a scene?
questions.f: Writers build atmosphere with weather, light and sound — think of the moors in 'Wuthering Heights'.

questions.q: Which literary device repeats a consonant sound at the start of nearby words?
questions.f: 'Alliteration' traces to Latin 'ad litteram', meaning 'to the letter'.

questions.q: Repeating vowel sounds inside nearby words, as in 'fleet feet sweep', is called…?
questions.f: From Latin 'assonare', to answer with the same sound.

questions.q: The word 'metaphor' is built from Greek pieces meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek meta (across) plus pherein (to carry) — a metaphor carries meaning from one thing to another.

questions.q: The word 'protagonist' is built from Greek pieces meaning…?
questions.f: From protos (first) and agonistes (contestant); in Greek theatre it named the lead actor.

questions.q: 'Onomatopoeia' comes from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: From onoma (name) plus poiein (to make) — the word literally makes a name from a sound.

questions.q: The word 'oxymoron' joins Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: From oxys (sharp) and moros (dull) — the word is itself an oxymoron.

questions.q: 'Deafening silence' and 'bittersweet' are examples of which device?
questions.f: An oxymoron yokes two opposites together to make a fresh idea.

questions.q: The word 'paradox' comes from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: From para (beside, contrary to) plus doxa (opinion or belief).

questions.q: The word 'euphemism' is built from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: From eu (good) plus pheme (speaking) — saying 'passed away' instead of 'died'.

questions.q: 'Sarcasm' comes from a Greek verb that literally means…?
questions.f: From 'sarkazein', to tear flesh like dogs — a vivid picture of a cutting remark.

questions.q: The word 'satire' comes from a Latin word for…?
questions.f: From Latin 'satura', a medley or full plate — early satire mixed many targets together.

questions.q: The word 'parody' comes from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: From para (beside) plus oide (song) — a song sung alongside the original, mocking it.

questions.q: The word 'allegory' is built from Greek pieces meaning…?
questions.f: From allos (other) plus agoreuein (to speak in the marketplace) — saying one thing to mean another.

questions.q: The word 'catharsis', used by Aristotle about tragedy, means…?
questions.f: Aristotle argued that watching tragedy purges the audience's pity and fear.

questions.q: The word 'climax' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek 'klimax', a ladder — the story climbs rung by rung to its highest point.

questions.q: The French term 'denouement' literally means…?
questions.f: After the climax the plot's knots are untied and loose ends explained.

questions.q: The word 'verse' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin 'versus', a turn of the plough — the poet turns at the end of each line.

questions.q: The word 'prose' comes from a Latin phrase meaning…?
questions.f: From 'prosa oratio', speech going straight ahead — unlike verse, which keeps turning.

questions.q: Poetry with a regular rhythm but no rhyme is called…?
questions.f: Shakespeare's plays are largely in blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter.

questions.q: Poetry with no set rhyme and no set metre is called…?
questions.f: Walt Whitman's 'Leaves of Grass' is the great early monument of free verse in English.

questions.q: A rhythmic unit of one unstressed then one stressed syllable is called an…?
questions.f: 'Da-DUM' — the heartbeat of English poetry, and the basis of iambic pentameter.

questions.q: How many iambs are there in a line of iambic pentameter?
questions.f: 'Penta' means five, so the line has five beats and ten syllables.

questions.q: The metrical foot called a 'dactyl' is named after the Greek word for…?
questions.f: A finger has one long joint then two short ones, matching the dactyl's long-short-short pattern.

questions.q: Which term describes running a sentence past the end of a line of poetry?
questions.f: From French 'enjamber', to stride over — the sense strides over the line break.

questions.q: A deliberate pause in the middle of a line of poetry is called a…?
questions.f: 'Caesura' is Latin for a cutting; Old English verse used a strong one in every line.

questions.q: A poem in which the first letters of the lines spell a word is an…?
questions.f: From Greek akros (outermost) plus stichos (line of verse).

questions.q: A word or phrase that reads the same backwards, like 'level', is a…?
questions.f: 'Palindrome' comes from Greek words meaning 'running back again'.

questions.q: Lewis Carroll called blended words like 'slithy' (lithe + slimy) what?
questions.f: Humpty Dumpty explains the idea in 'Through the Looking-Glass': two meanings packed in one word.

questions.q: Which Lewis Carroll invention, meaning a gleeful chuckle, entered real dictionaries?
questions.f: 'Chortle' blends chuckle and snort, and it appeared first in 'Jabberwocky'.

questions.q: The word 'utopia', coined for a 1516 book, literally means…?
questions.f: Thomas More built it from Greek ou (not) and topos (place) for his imaginary island.

questions.q: 'Pandemonium', coined by John Milton, literally means…?
questions.f: Milton used it in 'Paradise Lost' as the name of the palace of the fallen angels.

questions.q: The adjective 'quixotic' comes from which literary character?
questions.f: It means wildly idealistic and impractical, exactly like the knight who charged windmills.

questions.q: Calling someone a 'Scrooge' comes from a novel by which author?
questions.f: 'A Christmas Carol' was written in about six weeks and published just before Christmas 1843.

questions.q: The word 'Lilliputian', meaning tiny, comes from which book?
questions.f: Jonathan Swift invented Lilliput, whose people are about six inches tall.

questions.q: Which word for a very old or ancient thing comes from a long-lived Bible figure?
questions.f: 'As old as Methuselah' is used because he is said to have lived 969 years.

questions.q: Someone who is 'stentorian' has a very loud voice, named after a herald in which epic?
questions.f: Homer says Stentor could shout as loudly as fifty men together.

questions.q: The word 'mentor', meaning a wise adviser, comes from a character in which poem?
questions.f: Mentor is the old friend Odysseus leaves in charge of his son Telemachus.

questions.q: An 'odyssey' now means a long adventurous journey. Whose journey gave us the word?
questions.f: His voyage home from Troy took ten years and filled twenty-four books of poetry.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play gives us the phrase 'green-eyed monster' for jealousy?
questions.f: Iago warns Othello to beware jealousy, 'the green-eyed monster which doth mock the meat it feeds on'.

questions.q: 'Brevity is the soul of wit' comes from which Shakespeare play?
questions.f: The long-winded Polonius says it, which is Shakespeare's joke on him.

questions.q: 'A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!' is cried in which Shakespeare play?
questions.f: The line comes at the battle of Bosworth Field, where Richard loses his crown.

questions.q: 'Once more unto the breach, dear friends' comes from which Shakespeare history play?
questions.f: Henry V also gives the famous St Crispin's Day speech before the battle of Agincourt.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play contains the stage direction 'Exit, pursued by a bear'?
questions.f: It is probably theatre's most famous stage direction, and scholars still argue over how it was staged.

questions.q: In Shakespeare's day, who played all the female roles on the London stage?
questions.f: Women did not act publicly on the English stage until after 1660.

questions.q: Which term describes a character speaking their private thoughts aloud on stage?
questions.f: From Latin solus (alone) plus loqui (to speak) — 'To be, or not to be' is the most famous one.

questions.q: A brief remark a character makes directly to the audience is called an…?
questions.f: The other characters on stage are supposed not to hear it.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'Hope is the thing with feathers' and lived quietly in Amherst?
questions.f: After her death her sister found nearly 1,800 poems, many sewn into little hand-made booklets.

questions.q: 'Because I could not stop for Death' was written by which poet?
questions.f: Dickinson wrote most poems in short hymn-like stanzas with her trademark dashes.

questions.q: 'Ozymandias', about a ruined statue in the desert, was written by which poet?
questions.f: The inscription reads 'Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!' — and nothing else remains.

questions.q: 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?' ends which poem by Shelley?
questions.f: Shelley wrote it in a wood near Florence during a wild autumn storm.

questions.q: 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty' comes from which Keats poem?
questions.f: The poem addresses figures painted on an ancient urn, frozen forever mid-story.

questions.q: 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness' opens which Keats ode?
questions.f: Keats wrote it in September 1819, during the most productive year of his short life.

questions.q: Which poet collaborated with Wordsworth on 'Lyrical Ballads' in 1798?
questions.f: That slim book is often taken to mark the start of English Romantic poetry.

questions.q: 'In Xanadu did Kubla Khan a stately pleasure-dome decree' opens which poem?
c: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
questions.f: Coleridge said the poem came to him in a dream and was interrupted before he could finish it.

questions.q: Which Tennyson poem describes a doomed cavalry charge in the Crimean War?
c: The Charge of the Light Brigade
questions.f: Tennyson wrote it within weeks of reading a newspaper report of the battle.

questions.q: 'To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield' ends which Tennyson poem?
questions.f: The ageing hero of the poem refuses to stay quietly at home.

questions.q: 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways' was written by which poet?
questions.f: It is Sonnet 43 of her collection 'Sonnets from the Portuguese'.

questions.q: 'The Pied Piper of Hamelin' was retold in verse by which poet?
questions.f: Browning wrote it for a sick young friend who wanted a poem he could illustrate.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'Goblin Market' and 'Who Has Seen the Wind?'
questions.f: Her brother Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a famous painter and poet too.

questions.q: 'The fog comes on little cat feet' is a whole short poem by which writer?
questions.f: Sandburg's poem 'Fog' is just six lines long.

questions.q: 'So much depends upon a red wheelbarrow' was written by which American poet?
questions.f: Williams was a working doctor who wrote poems between seeing patients.

questions.q: 'What happens to a dream deferred?' opens which Langston Hughes poem?
questions.f: Its image of a dream drying up 'like a raisin in the sun' gave a famous play its title.

questions.q: Which Maya Angelou book takes its title from a line about a caged bird singing?
c: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
questions.f: The title comes from a poem by Paul Laurence Dunbar.

questions.q: Which epic poem by Milton tells of Adam, Eve and a rebel angel?
questions.f: Milton was completely blind when he composed it, dictating the lines to helpers.

questions.q: In Dante's 'Divine Comedy', which poet guides Dante through the underworld?
questions.f: Later, Beatrice takes over as guide for the journey through paradise.

questions.q: Which Roman poet wrote the 'Aeneid' about the Trojan hero Aeneas?
questions.f: Virgil died before finishing it, and reportedly asked for the manuscript to be burned.

questions.q: Which Greek playwright wrote 'Oedipus Rex' and 'Antigone'?
questions.f: Only seven of his roughly 120 plays survive complete.

questions.q: The word 'thespian', meaning an actor, honours which ancient Greek?
questions.f: Thespis is said to be the first person to step out of the chorus and speak as a character.

questions.q: Which philosopher's book 'Poetics' set out the first great theory of drama?
questions.f: Aristotle introduced ideas we still use: plot, character, catharsis and the tragic flaw.

questions.q: Which term names a story's structure of beginning in the middle of the action?
questions.f: Latin for 'into the middle of things'; the 'Iliad' and 'Odyssey' both do it.

questions.q: 'Deus ex machina' describes a sudden rescue, and it literally means…?
questions.f: Greek theatres used a crane to lower an actor playing a god onto the stage.

questions.q: A novel told entirely through letters is called…?
questions.f: From Latin 'epistola', a letter; 'Dracula' and 'Frankenstein' both use the form.

questions.q: Which Dickens novel features the escaped convict Magwitch and Miss Havisham?
questions.f: Miss Havisham stopped all her clocks at twenty to nine on her wedding day.

questions.q: Which was Charles Dickens's first novel?
questions.f: It began in 1836 as monthly instalments and made the young Dickens instantly famous.

questions.q: Which novel by George Eliot is set in the town of Middlemarch?
questions.f: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, who used it to be taken seriously.

questions.q: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged…' opens which Jane Austen novel?
questions.f: Austen first drafted it under the title 'First Impressions'.

questions.q: Which Austen novel features the matchmaking heroine Emma Woodhouse?
questions.f: Austen said she was creating 'a heroine whom no one but myself will much like'.

questions.q: 'All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way' opens which novel?
questions.f: Leo Tolstoy revised 'Anna Karenina' obsessively; his wife copied the manuscript by hand many times.

questions.q: Which Russian novel by Tolstoy follows Russian families through the Napoleonic wars?
questions.f: It runs to well over half a million words and has hundreds of named characters.

questions.q: Which novel introduced the phrase 'Big Brother is watching you'?
questions.f: George Orwell's real name was Eric Arthur Blair.

questions.q: In Orwell's 'Animal Farm', which animals take charge of the farm?
questions.f: Orwell called the book 'a fairy story', but it is really a political allegory.

questions.q: Which novel features the Morlocks and the Eloi in a far future?
questions.f: H. G. Wells published it in 1895, and the phrase 'time machine' comes straight from the book.

questions.q: Which Sherlock Holmes story was the first, introducing Holmes and Watson?
questions.f: Conan Doyle was paid just 25 pounds for the whole story in 1887.

questions.q: Which Holmes novel is set on the foggy moors of Dartmoor?
questions.f: Conan Doyle had killed Holmes off years earlier, and this story brought him back.

questions.q: What is the name of the housekeeper at 221B Baker Street?
questions.f: Holmes's older, cleverer brother in the stories is named Mycroft.

questions.q: Which term describes a novel that follows a character's growth from youth to maturity?
questions.f: German for 'formation novel'; 'Jane Eyre' and 'David Copperfield' both fit.

questions.q: Which word describes a story shorter than a novel but longer than a short story?
questions.f: 'A Christmas Carol' is a novella, at roughly 30,000 words.

questions.q: Shakespeare's 'The Comedy of Errors' is his shortest surviving play.
questions.f: At around 1,800 lines it is less than half the length of 'Hamlet'.

questions.q: 'Robinson Crusoe' was partly inspired by a real castaway.
questions.f: The Scottish sailor Alexander Selkirk survived over four years alone on a Pacific island.

questions.q: The Brontë sisters first published under male-sounding pen names.
questions.f: They wrote as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, keeping their real initials.

questions.q: Which literary term names a recurring image or idea running through a work?
questions.f: 'Motif' comes from the same root as 'motive' — something that keeps moving through the work.

questions.q: The word 'symbol' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: A 'symbolon' was a token broken in two so two halves could later be matched.

questions.q: The word 'myth' comes from a Greek word meaning simply…?
questions.f: Greek 'mythos' meant word, speech or tale — with no suggestion of being untrue.

questions.q: The word 'irony' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: From 'eironeia', dissembling — Socrates was famous for pretending to know nothing.

questions.q: When the audience knows something a character does not, that is…?
questions.f: In 'Romeo and Juliet', the audience knows Juliet is only sleeping while Romeo does not.

questions.q: Which device gives an object a human quality, as in 'the sea grew angry'?
questions.f: Critic John Ruskin coined the term 'pathetic fallacy' for nature mirroring human feelings.

questions.q: Using a part to stand for the whole, as in 'all hands on deck', is called…?
questions.f: 'Synecdoche' comes from Greek meaning 'taken together with'.

questions.q: Saying 'the crown' to mean the monarchy is an example of…?
questions.f: 'Metonymy' comes from Greek roots meaning 'change of name'.

questions.q: A brief reference to another famous work or person is called an…?
questions.f: Calling a strong man 'a Hercules' is an allusion to Greek myth.

questions.q: Understatement such as 'not bad at all' for something excellent is called…?
questions.f: 'Litotes' comes from a Greek word meaning plainness or simplicity.

questions.q: Repeating the same word at the start of successive lines is called…?
questions.f: Greek for 'carrying back'; Dickens's 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' uses it.

questions.q: Which word means a newly invented word, like Carroll's 'chortle'?
questions.f: From Greek neos (new) plus logos (word).

questions.q: A word formed from a person's name, like 'sandwich', is called an…?
questions.f: From Greek epi (upon) plus onoma (name).

questions.q: The word 'malapropism', for a comically wrong word, comes from a character in…?
questions.f: Mrs. Malaprop in 'The Rivals' muddles her words; her name nods to French 'mal a propos'.

questions.q: A 'spoonerism' swaps the starting sounds of words, and is named after a…?
questions.f: The Reverend William Archibald Spooner supposedly muddled words like that constantly.

questions.q: In Old English poetry, a compound phrase like 'whale-road' for the sea is called a…?
questions.f: 'Beowulf' is packed with kennings such as 'ring-giver' for a king.

questions.q: Which term describes the repeated stress pattern of a line of poetry?
questions.f: 'Metre' comes from Greek 'metron', a measure.

questions.q: Homer's epics were composed in which metre?
questions.f: Six dactyls per line gave the long rolling sound that helped singers memorise thousands of lines.

questions.q: Repeated stock phrases like 'rosy-fingered dawn' in Homer are called…?
questions.f: They gave the reciting poet ready-made phrases that fitted the metre perfectly.

questions.q: Which term names the fatal flaw that brings down a tragic hero?
questions.f: Aristotle used the word in his 'Poetics'; it literally means 'missing the mark'.

questions.q: 'Hubris', the tragic hero's overreaching pride, is a word from which language?
questions.f: Greek tragedy warned again and again that hubris invites disaster.

questions.q: Which classic poem tells of a knight facing a challenge from a green-skinned foe?
c: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
questions.f: It survives in one manuscript alongside three other poems by the same unknown author.

questions.q: Which English poet wrote 'The Faerie Queene' and gave his name to a nine-line stanza?
questions.f: The Spenserian stanza has eight lines of one length and a longer ninth line.

questions.q: Which term names Petrarch's kind of sonnet, split into eight lines then six?
questions.f: The eight-line octave sets a problem; the six-line sestet answers it after the 'turn'.

questions.q: The 'volta' in a sonnet is the point where the poem…?
questions.f: 'Volta' is Italian for turn, and in a Petrarchan sonnet it usually arrives at line nine.

questions.q: Which classic novel gave English the word 'yahoo' for a rough, uncouth person?
questions.f: The Yahoos are filthy human-like creatures in the land of the horse-like Houyhnhnms.

questions.q: The word 'robot' entered English from a 1920 play, from a Czech word meaning…?
questions.f: Karel Capek's play 'R.U.R.' introduced it; Czech 'robota' means drudgery or forced work.

questions.q: The word 'serendipity' was coined by Horace Walpole from an old name for…?
questions.f: He built it from 'The Three Princes of Serendip', a tale set in Serendip, now Sri Lanka.

questions.q: The word 'gargantuan' comes from a giant created by which Renaissance writer?
questions.f: Rabelais's giant Gargantua has an appetite to match his enormous size.

questions.q: To 'bowdlerize' a book means to cut out parts thought improper, after a man who did that to…?
questions.f: Thomas Bowdler published a 'Family Shakespeare' with the awkward bits removed.

questions.q: Someone described as 'Panglossian' is absurdly optimistic, after a character in…?
questions.f: Voltaire's Dr Pangloss insists all is for the best, no matter what disaster strikes.

questions.q: Which word for a book-length work comes from a Greek word for a cut section of a scroll?
questions.f: Greek 'tomos' meant a slice, because a long work was split across several rolls.

questions.q: The word 'volume' for a book comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From 'volumen', a rolled-up scroll — the ancestor of every modern book.

questions.q: A 'codex' is an early book with pages, named from a Latin word meaning…?
c: tree trunk or block of wood
questions.f: Latin 'caudex' meant a wooden block; the earliest codices used wooden covers.

questions.q: 'Parchment' takes its name from which ancient city famous for its library?
questions.f: Legend says Pergamum developed parchment when Egypt cut off its papyrus supply.

questions.q: 'Vellum', the finest writing skin, takes its name from a Latin word for a…?
questions.f: From 'vitulus', calf — the same root as 'veal'.

questions.q: The word 'Bible' comes from a Greek word that simply means…?
questions.f: Greek 'biblia' meant books, from 'byblos', papyrus, named after the port city of Byblos.

questions.q: 'Italic' type is so named because it was first developed in…?
questions.f: The Venetian printer Aldus Manutius introduced slanted italic type around 1500.

questions.q: Why are capital letters called 'upper case'?
c: printers kept them in the upper type case
they sit higher on the line
questions.f: Hand-typesetters kept small letters in the lower case, within easier reach.

questions.q: The '&' symbol is called an ampersand, from a slurred phrase meaning…?
questions.f: Children reciting the alphabet ended with '...X, Y, Z, and per se and'.

questions.q: The word 'asterisk' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Ancient scribes used a little star in the margin to flag a line worth noting.

questions.q: The word 'comma' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Greek 'komma' meant a clause or a segment sliced out of a sentence.

questions.q: The word 'hyphen' comes from a Greek phrase meaning…?
questions.f: From 'hyph' hen', under one — the mark shows two words acting as one.

questions.q: The word 'ellipsis' for three dots comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: An ellipsis marks words left out, so the sentence falls short of complete.

questions.q: The word 'apostrophe' as a punctuation mark comes from a Greek sense of…?
questions.f: The same word names the poetic device of turning aside to address someone absent.

questions.q: The word 'cliche' comes from a French printing term for a…?
questions.f: 'Cliche' imitated the click of the metal plate used to print the same phrase again and again.

questions.q: The word 'blurb' for a book's promotional text was coined in 1907 by…?
questions.f: Burgess invented a fictional 'Miss Belinda Blurb' for a joke book jacket, and the word stuck.

questions.q: An 'anecdote' takes its name from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: A Byzantine writer titled his gossipy book 'Anekdota', literally 'unpublished things'.

questions.q: The word 'essay' comes from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: Montaigne titled his 1580 book 'Essais' — trials or attempts at thinking on paper.

questions.q: The word 'plagiarism' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Latin 'plagiarius' meant one who steals another person's slave or child.

questions.q: Which classic novel's hero is the hunchbacked bell-ringer Quasimodo?
questions.f: Hugo's original French title is simply 'Notre-Dame de Paris'; he wrote it partly to save the cathedral.

questions.q: In 'Les Miserables', what does Jean Valjean steal at the start of the story?
questions.f: He serves nineteen years for that theft and an attempted escape.

questions.q: Which novel's characters include Athos, Porthos and Aramis?
questions.f: The young hero d'Artagnan makes a fourth, so the title is a little joke.

questions.q: Which Scottish author wrote 'Ivanhoe' and 'Rob Roy'?
questions.f: Scott more or less invented the historical novel, and Europe copied him for a century.

questions.q: Which novel by Robert Louis Stevenson is about a man with two identities?
c: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
questions.f: Stevenson said the idea came to him in a nightmare, and he wrote the first draft in days.

questions.q: 'The Adventures of Pinocchio' was originally published in which language?
questions.f: Carlo Collodi wrote it as a serial for an Italian children's newspaper in 1881.

questions.q: Which novel is set in the Yorkshire moors and features Heathcliff?
questions.f: Emily Bronte published it in 1847 and died the following year, aged just 30.

questions.q: Which novelist wrote 'Far from the Madding Crowd' and 'Tess of the d'Urbervilles'?
questions.f: Hardy set his novels in a half-invented region of England he called Wessex.

questions.q: Which American short story about a poor couple's Christmas gifts is by O. Henry?
questions.f: O. Henry was the pen name of William Sydney Porter, famous for twist endings.

questions.q: Which novel features the runaway boy David Balfour being kidnapped at sea?
questions.f: Stevenson set it during real Scottish history, just after the Jacobite risings.

questions.q: 'The Last of the Mohicans' was written by which American novelist?
questions.f: Cooper's frontier scout Natty Bumppo is also called Hawkeye.

questions.q: Which Japanese work from around the year 1010 is often called the world's first novel?
questions.f: It was written by Murasaki Shikibu, a noblewoman at the Japanese imperial court.

questions.q: 'The Rubaiyat', famously translated by Edward FitzGerald, is by which Persian poet?
questions.f: Omar Khayyam was also a first-rate mathematician and astronomer.

questions.q: Which Japanese poet is the most famous master of the haiku?
questions.f: Basho's travel book 'The Narrow Road to the Deep North' mixes prose with haiku.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek poet from the island of Lesbos gave her name to a verse stanza?
questions.f: Only fragments of Sappho's poems survive, many recovered from scraps of papyrus.

questions.q: Which Persian poet's works include the long spiritual poem the 'Masnavi'?
questions.f: Rumi wrote in the 13th century and is among the best-selling poets in the world today.

questions.q: Which poet was the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.f: Tagore won in 1913 for 'Gitanjali', a collection of song-poems he translated himself.

questions.q: 'Gitanjali' by Rabindranath Tagore is a collection of what?
questions.f: The title means 'song offerings' in Bengali.

questions.q: Which poet's 'Songs of Innocence and of Experience' pairs 'The Lamb' with 'The Tyger'?
questions.f: Blake printed and coloured every copy himself, so no two are quite alike.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'The Lake Isle of Innisfree'?
questions.f: Innisfree is a real small island in Lough Gill in County Sligo, Ireland.

questions.q: Which Robert Frost poem contains the line 'Good fences make good neighbours'?
questions.f: The narrator actually questions the saying, even as his neighbour repeats it.

questions.q: Which poet read a poem at John F. Kennedy's 1961 inauguration?
questions.f: Sun glare stopped Frost reading his new poem, so he recited 'The Gift Outright' from memory.

questions.q: Which movement of 1920s Black American writers and artists centred on a New York district?
questions.f: Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston and Countee Cullen were leading figures.

questions.q: Which American author wrote 'Their Eyes Were Watching God'?
questions.f: Hurston trained as an anthropologist and collected folklore across the American South.

questions.q: Which group of English writers around 1800 was nicknamed the Lake Poets?
questions.f: They are called that because they lived in and wrote about England's Lake District.

questions.q: Which American writers led the 19th-century Transcendentalist movement?
questions.f: They believed nature and individual conscience were better guides than institutions.

questions.q: In Westminster Abbey, which poet was the first to be buried in Poets' Corner?
questions.f: Chaucer was buried there in 1400, at first because he had worked for the abbey, not for his poems.

questions.q: Which title is given to a poet officially appointed to write for the nation?
questions.f: 'Laureate' refers to the laurel wreath crown given to poets and victors in the ancient world.

questions.q: Which novelist's works include 'Heart of Darkness' and 'Lord Jim'?
questions.f: Conrad was born in Poland and English was his third language, learned as an adult sailor.

questions.q: Which novel by James Joyce takes place over a single day in Dublin?
c: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
questions.f: That day, 16 June 1904, is celebrated worldwide each year as Bloomsday.

questions.q: 'The Waste Land', which opens 'April is the cruellest month', is by which poet?
questions.f: Eliot's book of cat poems later became the basis of the musical 'Cats'.

questions.q: Which poet wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
questions.f: The poem is a villanelle, a strict French form built on two repeating lines.

questions.q: Which term names the 19-line poem with two repeating refrains and just two rhymes?
questions.f: The form began as an Italian and French song type before English poets adopted it.

questions.q: Which literary award is the most famous British prize for a single novel?
questions.f: It was first awarded in 1969 and is now known as the Booker Prize.

questions.q: Milton's 'Paradise Lost' is written in unrhymed iambic pentameter.
questions.f: Milton defended blank verse in a note, calling rhyme a needless jingling.

questions.q: A 'sestet' is the six-line part of a sonnet.
questions.f: In a Petrarchan sonnet the eight-line octave comes first, then the sestet answers it.

questions.q: Jules Verne wrote about a submarine before practical submarines existed.
questions.f: 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas' appeared in 1870, decades before real electric submarines.

questions.q: Homer's 'Iliad' covers the entire ten-year Trojan War from start to finish.
questions.f: It actually covers only a few weeks near the end, centred on the anger of Achilles.

questions.q: Which term describes a novel written about real people under invented names?
questions.f: French for 'novel with a key' — readers need the key to spot who is really who.

questions.q: Shakespeare's First Folio of 1623 was assembled by which two of his fellow actors?
questions.f: Without their volume, about eighteen plays including 'Macbeth' and 'The Tempest' might have vanished.

questions.q: Which poet supplied the dedicatory verse calling Shakespeare 'not of an age, but for all time'?
questions.f: Jonson also nicknamed him 'Sweet Swan of Avon' in the same First Folio poem.

questions.q: The longest word in all of Shakespeare, 'honorificabilitudinitatibus', appears in which play?
questions.f: It is 27 letters long and is spoken as a joke about long-winded scholarly language.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare comedy is based on the Roman play 'Menaechmi' by Plautus?
questions.f: Plautus gave Shakespeare one set of twins; Shakespeare doubled it to two sets.

questions.q: Shakespeare drew his Roman plays largely from Plutarch's 'Lives' in whose translation?
questions.f: North translated from a French version, so Plutarch reached Shakespeare third-hand.

questions.q: Which chronicle was Shakespeare's main source for 'Macbeth' and his English history plays?
questions.f: The real Macbeth ruled Scotland for about seventeen years, rather more calmly than the play suggests.

questions.q: Shakespeare's acting company changed its name in 1603 to the King's Men because…?
questions.f: Before that they were the Lord Chamberlain's Men, named for their earlier noble patron.

questions.q: During a performance of which play did the original Globe theatre burn down in 1613?
questions.f: A stage cannon set the thatched roof alight; remarkably, nobody was killed.

questions.q: Which is Shakespeare's longest play?
questions.f: At roughly 4,000 lines, an uncut 'Hamlet' runs well past four hours.

questions.q: Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 begins with which unromantic comparison?
c: My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day
Let me not to the marriage of true minds
questions.f: It is a deliberate joke on poets who compared their loves to suns, roses and coral.

questions.q: The term 'blank verse' entered English poetry through whose translation of Virgil?
questions.f: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, used unrhymed iambic pentameter for parts of the 'Aeneid' in the 1540s.

questions.q: Which two Tudor poets first brought the sonnet into English from Petrarch?
questions.f: Their versions were printed together in 1557 in the anthology now called 'Tottel's Miscellany'.

questions.q: Ben Jonson praised which rival playwright's 'mighty line'?
questions.f: Marlowe made blank verse thunder in 'Tamburlaine' and 'Doctor Faustus' before dying at 29.

questions.q: Which novel by Horace Walpole is generally credited as the first Gothic novel?
questions.f: The same Walpole also invented the word 'serendipity' in a letter to a friend.

questions.q: Which Gothic novelist's 'The Mysteries of Udolpho' is the book Jane Austen gently mocks?
questions.f: In 'Northanger Abbey', Catherine Morland reads too much Radcliffe and starts imagining horrors.

questions.q: A ghost-story contest at a villa on Lake Geneva in 1816 produced 'Frankenstein' and which other work?
questions.f: John Polidori's 'The Vampyre' shaped the aristocratic vampire long before Bram Stoker.

questions.q: Which writer's stated aim in 'Notre-Dame de Paris' was to save a neglected building?
questions.f: Public enthusiasm after the novel helped fund a major restoration of the cathedral.

questions.q: Which English novelist's heart is buried in Dorset while his ashes lie in Poets' Corner?
questions.f: Hardy wanted a village grave, the nation wanted the Abbey, so they compromised in a rather literal way.

questions.q: After hostile reviews of which novel did Thomas Hardy give up writing fiction altogether?
questions.f: He spent his last thirty years writing poetry instead, and much of it is superb.

questions.q: Hardy set most of his novels in a half-invented English region he called…?
questions.f: He revived the name of a real Anglo-Saxon kingdom and mapped his fictional towns onto it.

questions.q: Which American novelist invented the fictional Yoknapatawpha County?
questions.f: Faulkner even drew a map of it, describing himself as its 'sole owner and proprietor'.

questions.q: Which novel's title comes from a line in Macbeth's 'tomorrow and tomorrow' speech?
questions.f: Macbeth calls life 'a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing'.

questions.q: Aldous Huxley took the title 'Brave New World' from which Shakespeare play?
questions.f: Miranda exclaims 'O brave new world' on seeing other humans for the first time.

questions.q: Steinbeck's title 'Of Mice and Men' comes from a poem by which writer?
questions.f: Burns's 'To a Mouse' says the best-laid schemes of mice and men often go astray.

questions.q: Chinua Achebe took the title 'Things Fall Apart' from a poem by which writer?
questions.f: Yeats's 'The Second Coming' warns that 'the centre cannot hold'.

questions.q: Hemingway's title 'For Whom the Bell Tolls' comes from a meditation by which poet?
questions.f: Donne wrote that no man is an island, so every death diminishes us all.

questions.q: Which group of 17th-century English poets is known for elaborate extended metaphors called conceits?
questions.f: Samuel Johnson popularised the label, and Donne's compass and flea are the classic examples.

questions.q: Which poet coined the term 'negative capability' in an 1817 letter?
questions.f: He meant the power to sit with mystery and doubt without grabbing for easy answers.

questions.q: Which critic coined the phrase 'willing suspension of disbelief'?
questions.f: He used it in 'Biographia Literaria' to explain why readers accept the impossible in poetry.

questions.q: Which Victorian critic invented the term 'pathetic fallacy'?
questions.f: Ruskin used it disapprovingly for poets who made nature share their moods.

questions.q: Which poet invented the metrical system he called 'sprung rhythm'?
questions.f: Hopkins also coined 'inscape' and 'instress', and his poems appeared only in 1918, long after he died.

questions.q: Which literary term means a moment of sudden recognition, as when a hero learns the truth?
questions.f: Aristotle paired it with peripeteia, the reversal of fortune that usually comes at the same moment.

questions.q: The rhetorical figure that mirrors a phrase in reverse order is named after which Greek letter?
questions.f: Chiasmus is named for the X-shape of chi: 'Ask not what your country can do for you...'

questions.q: Which device uses one verb for two objects, as in 'He lost his coat and his temper'?
questions.f: 'Zeugma' is Greek for a yoking, as if two ideas were harnessed to one verb.

questions.q: 'Sound and fury' expresses one idea using two nouns. That device is called…?
questions.f: 'Hendiadys' comes from Greek meaning 'one through two', and Shakespeare loved it.

questions.q: Which device deliberately leaves a sentence unfinished for dramatic effect?
questions.f: Greek for 'becoming silent'; King Lear's broken threats are a famous example.

questions.q: Which device links clauses with repeated conjunctions, as in 'and... and... and'?
questions.f: Its opposite, asyndeton, drops conjunctions entirely: 'I came, I saw, I conquered'.

questions.q: In Greek drama, the second actor, supporting the lead, was called the…?
questions.f: Greek theatre added actors one at a time, and the third was the tritagonist.

questions.q: In literary criticism, a character who contrasts with the hero to highlight qualities is a…?
questions.f: The term borrows from jewellers, who set bright foil behind a gem to make it sparkle.

questions.q: Which term describes an object that drives a plot but hardly matters in itself?
questions.f: Alfred Hitchcock popularised the term for the secret plans or briefcase everyone chases.

questions.q: The word 'text' comes from a Latin verb meaning…?
questions.f: From 'texere', to weave — the same root as textile and texture; a text is woven words.

questions.q: The Old English word 'writan', the ancestor of 'write', originally meant…?
questions.f: Early writing was scratched into wood, stone or wax rather than flowing on paper.

questions.q: The Old English 'raedan', ancestor of 'read', first meant…?
questions.f: Reading meant working out a meaning, which is why we still 'read' someone's mood.

questions.q: The English word 'glamour' began as a Scots alteration of which other word?
questions.f: Learning, especially Latin grammar, looked like magic to outsiders, so 'grammar' bent into 'glamour'.

questions.q: A 'grimoire', a book of spells, is a French word that came from which ordinary word?
questions.f: Same source as glamour: a book of grammar was a book of mysterious learning.

questions.q: The Old English word 'spell' originally meant…?
questions.f: That is why 'gospel' is 'god spel' — good news, or good story.

questions.q: The word 'rhapsody' is built from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: A rhapsode stitched together episodes of epic poetry for an audience.

questions.q: The word 'ballad' shares its root with 'ballet' because both come from a word meaning…?
questions.f: From Late Latin 'ballare', to dance — early ballads were danced as well as sung.

questions.q: Which Muse of Greek myth presided over epic poetry?
questions.f: Her name means 'beautiful voice', and Homer calls on her at the start of the 'Odyssey'.

questions.q: The tragic and comic masks of theatre are traditionally linked to which two Muses?
questions.f: Melpomene holds the tragic mask; Thalia holds the comic one.

questions.q: The word 'museum' originally meant a place belonging to…?
questions.f: The great Museum of Alexandria was a research institute dedicated to the nine Muses.

questions.q: The word 'academy' comes from the name of…?
questions.f: Plato taught in a grove sacred to the hero Akademos, and the name stuck to schools forever.

questions.q: The Greek word 'skhole', the source of 'school', originally meant…?
questions.f: Free time to think turned into discussion, then into formal teaching.

questions.q: 'Encyclopedia' comes from a Greek phrase meaning…?
questions.f: From 'enkyklios paideia' — a rounded course of learning, not a big book.

questions.q: Books printed before 1501 are called 'incunabula', from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: They date from printing's infancy, and only a few tens of thousands of editions survive.

questions.q: A 'palimpsest' is a manuscript page that has been…?
questions.f: Greek for 'scraped again'; scholars have recovered lost works of Archimedes from one.

questions.q: In medieval manuscripts, a 'rubric' was so called because it was written in…?
questions.f: From Latin 'ruber', red — headings were rubbed in red to stand out from the text.

questions.q: The word 'miniature' for a small painting comes from a Latin word for…?
questions.f: From 'minium', the red pigment used in manuscripts; the link to 'small' came later by accident.

questions.q: The 'colophon' at the end of an old book takes its name from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: It told readers who printed the book, where and when — the ancestor of the copyright page.

questions.q: A cheap little pamphlet-book sold by travelling pedlars was called a…?
questions.f: 'Chap' comes from 'chapman', an old word for a trader — nothing to do with chapters.

questions.q: A 'hornbook', used to teach children their letters, was a tablet covered with…?
questions.f: The horn sheet protected the printed alphabet from sticky fingers, like early laminate.

questions.q: Which printer introduced italic type and pocket-sized editions around 1500?
questions.f: His Venetian press also gave the modern semicolon its first real workout.

questions.q: Which publisher launched cheap quality paperbacks in Britain in 1935?
questions.f: Allen Lane priced them at sixpence, the cost of a packet of cigarettes.

questions.q: Which library classification system was devised by Melvil Dewey in 1876?
questions.f: It splits all knowledge into ten main classes, each divided by tens again.

questions.q: The first editor of the Oxford English Dictionary worked from a corrugated iron shed he called the…?
questions.f: James Murray filled it with millions of quotation slips sent in by volunteer readers.

questions.q: Samuel Johnson's dictionary famously defined a 'lexicographer' as a harmless…?
questions.f: His full joke was 'a writer of dictionaries, a harmless drudge'.

questions.q: Which term describes writing that mixes prose with lines of verse?
questions.f: Basho's travel journals and Boethius's 'Consolation of Philosophy' both use the form.

questions.q: The Latin phrase 'in medias res', a standard epic technique, comes from whose 'Ars Poetica'?
questions.f: Horace praised Homer for plunging into the middle of the story rather than starting at the beginning.

questions.q: The word 'sesquipedalian', for very long words, comes from Horace's phrase meaning…?
c: a foot and a half long
questions.f: Horace mocked poets who used 'sesquipedalia verba' — words a foot and a half long.

questions.q: 'Carpe diem', much quoted in English poetry, comes from which Roman poet?
questions.f: It appears in his Odes and is better translated 'pluck the day' than 'seize' it.

questions.q: Which Roman poet's 'Metamorphoses' supplied the Pyramus and Thisbe story Shakespeare parodied?
questions.f: The 'rude mechanicals' of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' bungle it hilariously.

questions.q: Which Sanskrit poet and dramatist wrote the play 'Shakuntala'?
questions.f: Goethe was so struck by an early translation of 'Shakuntala' that he wrote a poem praising it.

questions.q: The Tamil classic 'Thirukkural' is made up of how many couplets?
questions.f: Thiruvalluvar packed each idea into just seven words, making it fiercely quotable.

questions.q: Which Chinese classic novel follows the Monkey King Sun Wukong on a pilgrimage west?
questions.f: It is loosely based on the real 7th-century monk Xuanzang, who travelled to India for scriptures.

questions.q: Which Finnish epic, compiled by Elias Lonnrot, inspired both Longfellow and Tolkien?
questions.f: Longfellow borrowed its chanting trochaic metre for 'The Song of Hiawatha'.

questions.q: Which epic is written on clay tablets and is the oldest great work of literature we still read?
questions.f: A young museum assistant, George Smith, stunned Victorian London by finding a flood story in it.

questions.q: Aladdin and Ali Baba are absent from Arabic manuscripts of the 'Nights' because they were added by…?
questions.f: Galland said he heard the tales from a Syrian storyteller, and they are now the best known of all.

questions.q: Which writer is generally recognised as the first Englishwoman to earn a living by her pen?
questions.f: Behn wrote plays, poems and the early novel 'Oroonoko' in the 1670s and 1680s.

questions.q: Which novel is often called the first English detective novel?
questions.f: Wilkie Collins published it in 1868, complete with a country-house theft and a patient detective.

questions.q: Conan Doyle based Sherlock Holmes largely on which real person?
questions.f: Dr Joseph Bell of Edinburgh could deduce a patient's trade and travels at a glance.

questions.q: Where did Conan Doyle apparently kill off Sherlock Holmes in 1893?
questions.f: Public outrage was so fierce that Doyle brought him back a decade later.

questions.q: Which magazine published most of the Sherlock Holmes short stories?
questions.f: Queues formed outside the publisher's office on the day each new issue appeared.

questions.q: Which pen name did Charles Dickens use for his earliest published sketches?
questions.f: 'Sketches by Boz' came out in 1836, just before 'The Pickwick Papers' made him famous.

questions.q: Which Dickens novel was left unfinished at his death, its mystery unsolved?
questions.f: He died in 1870 with only half the instalments written, so nobody knows the intended ending.

questions.q: Charles Dickens kept a pet raven named Grip who inspired a poem by which writer?
questions.f: Poe reviewed Dickens's novel featuring Grip, and 'The Raven' followed a few years later.

questions.q: In Poe's 'The Raven', the bird perches on a bust of which figure?
questions.f: Pallas Athena is the goddess of wisdom, which makes the bird's single word all the more chilling.

questions.q: Which detective did Edgar Allan Poe create, decades before Sherlock Holmes?
questions.f: Dupin appears in 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue', the first modern detective story.

questions.q: Which was Herman Melville's title for 'Moby-Dick' in its first British edition?
questions.f: The British edition also dropped the epilogue, so reviewers asked how the narrator could be telling the tale.

questions.q: After his novels stopped selling, Herman Melville spent nearly twenty years working as a…?
questions.f: His late short novel 'Billy Budd' was found in manuscript and only published in the 1920s.

questions.q: Which writer sent Walt Whitman a letter greeting him 'at the beginning of a great career'?
questions.f: Whitman promptly printed the private compliment on the spine of his next edition.

questions.q: How many poems were in the first 1855 edition of 'Leaves of Grass'?
questions.f: Whitman set some of the type himself, and the title page carried no author's name at all.

questions.q: Emily Dickinson gathered her poems into hand-sewn booklets known as…?
questions.f: She also pressed over 400 plant specimens into a herbarium as a teenager.

questions.q: Which of Shakespeare's works was NOT included in the 1623 First Folio?
questions.f: 'Pericles' and 'The Two Noble Kinsmen', both partly by other hands, were left out.

questions.q: A single-play pamphlet edition of a Shakespeare play is known as a…?
questions.f: 'Quarto' means the printing sheet was folded twice, giving four leaves and eight pages.

questions.q: Which term describes a book format where the printing sheet is folded just once?
questions.f: From Latin 'folium', a leaf — folios are big, which is why the Shakespeare collection is impressive.

questions.q: Which term names the poetic form Dante invented for 'The Divine Comedy'?
questions.f: Its interlocking aba-bcb-cdc chain pulls the reader forward for over 14,000 lines.

questions.q: Which seven-line stanza form did Chaucer use in 'Troilus and Criseyde'?
questions.f: It later became a favourite of Shakespeare in 'The Rape of Lucrece'.

questions.q: Roughly how many of the 120 tales Chaucer planned for 'The Canterbury Tales' did he finish?
questions.f: He planned four tales per pilgrim and got nowhere near, dying in 1400 with the work unfinished.

questions.q: Cervantes and Shakespeare both died in 1616.
questions.f: Their recorded death dates are a day apart, though England and Spain used different calendars.

questions.q: Jane Austen's gravestone in Winchester Cathedral does not mention that she wrote novels.
questions.f: It praises her character and mind; a later brass plaque finally noted her books.

questions.q: Emily Bronte published only one novel in her lifetime.
questions.f: 'Wuthering Heights' appeared in 1847 and she died the next year, aged 30.

questions.q: A hand-drawn map made to amuse a stepson on a rainy holiday grew into which novel?
questions.f: Robert Louis Stevenson said the whole story sprang from the map, not the other way round.

questions.q: Which author is buried on Mount Vaea in Samoa, where islanders called him 'Tusitala'?
questions.f: 'Tusitala' means teller of tales; he spent his last years there for his health.

questions.q: An Oxford mathematics lecturer who wrote a treatise on determinants is better known as…?
questions.f: Charles Dodgson published dry maths under his real name and wonderful nonsense under his pen name.

questions.q: The real Alice who inspired Wonderland was the daughter of a man famous for co-writing a…?
questions.f: Henry Liddell co-authored the Liddell and Scott Greek dictionary still used by students today.

questions.q: Who illustrated the first editions of 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland'?
questions.f: Tenniel was a political cartoonist for Punch, and he argued with Carroll over every detail.

questions.q: L. Frank Baum said the name 'Oz' came to him from…?
c: a filing cabinet drawer labelled O-Z
questions.f: His illustrator W. W. Denslow shaped the look of Oz almost as much as Baum's words did.

questions.q: Which author gave the copyright of one of his plays to a London children's hospital?
questions.f: Great Ormond Street Hospital still benefits from 'Peter Pan' more than a century later.

questions.q: The bear that inspired Winnie-the-Pooh was named after which Canadian city?
questions.f: A Canadian army officer bought the cub on his way to war and left it at London Zoo.

questions.q: Which children's author later bred prize-winning Herdwick sheep and gave land to the National Trust?
questions.f: Potter left over 4,000 acres of the Lake District to be preserved for the public.

questions.q: E. B. White, author of 'Charlotte's Web', also co-wrote which famous style guide?
questions.f: He revised the little book his own college professor, William Strunk Jr., had written.

questions.q: Anna Sewell's 'Black Beauty' was remarkable partly because it was…?
questions.f: She was ill for years while writing it and died only months after publication.

questions.q: Which author disappeared for eleven days in 1926, sparking a nationwide search?
questions.f: She was found at a Yorkshire hotel; she never publicly explained what had happened.

questions.q: Agatha Christie wrote romantic novels under which other name?
questions.f: She kept the secret for nearly twenty years.

questions.q: Which Belgian detective did Agatha Christie create?
questions.f: She grew tired of him decades before she stopped writing about him.

questions.q: Which children's author trained as a doctor before writing 'The Water-Babies'?
questions.f: Kingsley was actually a clergyman and naturalist; the book campaigned against child chimney sweeps.

questions.q: Which Oxford professor of Anglo-Saxon also produced a scholarly edition of 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight'?
questions.f: His day job was medieval languages; hobbits were, in his own phrase, a hobby that grew.

questions.q: Tolkien and C. S. Lewis both belonged to which Oxford writers' group?
questions.f: They read work aloud to each other in a pub called the Eagle and Child.

questions.q: Which author's tale-collecting brother also formulated a famous law of sound change in languages?
questions.f: Jacob Grimm's law describes how certain consonants shifted across the Germanic languages.

questions.q: Charles Perrault's 1697 fairy-tale collection carried a subtitle referring to which figure?
questions.f: That subtitle is how 'Mother Goose' became attached to fairy tales in English.

questions.q: Which French writer retold Aesop's fables as elegant verse in the 1600s?
questions.f: French schoolchildren still memorise 'The Crow and the Fox' from his collection.

questions.q: Which playwright, born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, collapsed while performing in his own comedy?
questions.f: He was playing the title role in 'The Imaginary Invalid' and died hours later.

questions.q: Which writer, born Francois-Marie Arouet, satirised blind optimism in 'Candide'?
questions.f: 'Candide' ends with the advice that we must cultivate our garden.

questions.q: Which German writer's early novel 'The Sorrows of Young Werther' made him famous across Europe?
questions.f: Young men copied Werther's blue coat and yellow waistcoat, an early case of book-driven fashion.

questions.q: Which Norwegian playwright wrote 'A Doll's House' and 'Peer Gynt'?
questions.f: The slammed door at the end of 'A Doll's House' was said to echo across Europe.

questions.q: Which Russian writer wrote 'The Gambler' in about a month to pay off a publishing debt?
questions.f: He dictated it to a young stenographer named Anna, and later married her.

questions.q: Which Russian author was a working doctor and gave his name to a rule about storytelling?
questions.f: 'Chekhov's gun' says a rifle shown in act one must be fired before the play ends.

questions.q: Which Russian novel in verse gave its name to a fourteen-line stanza form?
questions.f: Pushkin's stanza is a sonnet with its own strict, springy rhyme pattern.

questions.q: Which Italian poet's 100-tale collection is set during an outbreak of plague in Florence?
questions.f: In 'The Decameron', ten young people flee the city and tell ten stories a day for ten days.

questions.q: The word 'Divine' in 'The Divine Comedy' was added by which later writer?
questions.f: Dante himself simply called it 'Comedia', meaning a story that ends happily.

questions.q: Which Spanish novelist lost the use of a hand at the naval battle of Lepanto?
questions.f: His nickname was 'el manco de Lepanto', the one-handed man of Lepanto.

questions.q: Cervantes wrote Part Two of 'Don Quixote' partly to answer…?
c: a fake sequel by another writer
questions.f: A writer calling himself Avellaneda had published an unauthorised continuation, which infuriated him.

questions.q: Which novelist wrote 'Mrs Dalloway' and co-founded the Hogarth Press?
questions.f: She and her husband Leonard hand-printed early books themselves in their dining room.

questions.q: Which extended essay by Virginia Woolf argues a woman writer needs money and privacy?
questions.f: It grew out of two lectures she gave at Cambridge women's colleges in 1928.

questions.q: 'The Waste Land' is dedicated to Ezra Pound with a phrase Dante used, meaning…?
questions.f: Pound cut the poem down drastically, and Eliot never stopped acknowledging the debt.

questions.q: Which poetry movement, led by Ezra Pound, demanded hard clear images and no wasted words?
questions.f: Pound's two-line poem about faces in a Metro station is its perfect specimen.

questions.q: Whose phrase gave Hemingway's circle of expatriate writers the label the 'Lost Generation'?
questions.f: Hemingway put her remark as an epigraph to 'The Sun Also Rises'.

questions.q: Hemingway's spare style, leaving most meaning unstated, is often called his…?
questions.f: He argued that the dignity of a moving iceberg comes from the seven-eighths under water.

questions.q: Which novel's famous cover art was painted before the author had finished writing the book?
questions.f: Fitzgerald liked the eyes-over-a-fairground painting so much that he wrote it into the text.

questions.q: Harper Lee's childhood neighbour, the model for Dill in her novel, grew up to be which writer?
questions.f: Lee later helped Capote research 'In Cold Blood' in Kansas.

questions.q: Which novelist worked for years as a book editor at Random House before winning the Nobel Prize?
questions.f: She championed other Black writers as an editor while writing 'Song of Solomon' at night.

questions.q: Joseph Heller's 'Catch-22' was originally going to be called…?
questions.f: The number changed to avoid clashing with Leon Uris's novel 'Mila 18'.

questions.q: Ray Bradbury typed 'Fahrenheit 451' on a rented typewriter in the basement of a…?
questions.f: He paid ten cents per half hour, which he said kept him writing fast.

questions.q: Which Colombian novelist created the town of Macondo?
questions.f: 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' became the showcase of what critics call magic realism.

questions.q: Which Indian novelist set his stories in the invented town of Malgudi?
questions.f: Narayan wrote about Malgudi for over fifty years, mapping it in loving detail.

questions.q: Which writer is often called the greatest Hindi and Urdu novelist, author of 'Godan'?
questions.f: 'Godan' means 'the gift of a cow', and it follows a poor farmer's struggle for dignity.

questions.q: Which Urdu poet, famous for his ghazals, lived through the fall of Mughal Delhi?
questions.f: His letters are considered as great as his poems, and both are still quoted daily.

questions.q: Which literary form, common in Persian and Urdu, is built from independent rhyming couplets?
questions.f: Each couplet can stand alone, yet together they build one mood — often longing.

questions.q: The poet who wrote 'What you seek is seeking you' composed chiefly in which language?
questions.f: Rumi wrote mainly in Persian, though he lived in what is now Turkey.

questions.q: Which writer of 'The Prophet' wrote 'Progress lies not in enhancing what is, but in advancing toward what will be'?
questions.f: Gibran was born in Lebanon and wrote 'The Prophet' in English in the United States.

questions.q: Which writer of 'The Jungle Book' became, at 41, the youngest Nobel literature laureate?
questions.f: He won in 1907 and remains the youngest ever winner of that prize.

questions.q: Which writer holds both a Nobel Prize in Literature and an Academy Award?
questions.f: He won the Nobel in 1925 and an Oscar for the screenplay of 'Pygmalion' in 1939.

questions.q: Which Nobel-winning novel by Hemingway is about an old fisherman and a marlin?
c: The Old Man and the Sea
questions.f: It won the Pulitzer in 1953, and the Nobel followed the next year.

questions.q: Which term describes a narrator whose account the reader learns not to trust?
questions.f: The critic Wayne C. Booth gave the idea its name in 'The Rhetoric of Fiction' in 1961.

questions.q: Which narrative technique tries to render a character's unbroken flow of thought?
questions.f: The phrase came from the psychologist William James before critics borrowed it for Joyce and Woolf.

questions.q: Which term names the storytelling trick of one tale enclosing others inside it?
questions.f: 'The Canterbury Tales' and 'One Thousand and One Nights' are both frame narratives.

questions.q: Which term describes a plot device that misleads the reader on purpose?
questions.f: The phrase probably comes from a strong-smelling smoked fish used to throw hounds off a scent.

questions.q: Which term names the imaginary barrier between actors and audience?
questions.f: Breaking it means a character speaks directly to the audience, as Puck does at the end.

questions.q: The word 'catastrophe', now meaning disaster, first named which part of a Greek play?
c: the final turn of the plot
questions.f: From Greek 'kata' (down) plus 'strephein' (to turn) — the plot's downturn to its conclusion.

questions.q: The word 'epitaph' is built from Greek pieces meaning…?
questions.f: An epigram is written 'upon' anything; an epitaph specifically upon a grave.

questions.q: What is the exact difference between an 'elegy' and a 'eulogy'?
c: one is a mournful poem, the other a speech of praise
one is spoken, the other sung
one is long, the other short
one rhymes, the other does not
questions.f: 'Eulogy' comes from Greek for 'good speaking'; 'elegy' from a word for a lament.

questions.q: A poem or work about idealised shepherds and country life is called…?
questions.f: 'Bucolic' is its cousin, from a Greek word for a cowherd.

questions.q: Which term names a short pastoral poem, as used by Virgil?
questions.f: Virgil's 'Eclogues' set the pattern that English poets imitated for centuries.

questions.q: The word 'pastiche' comes from an Italian word for a…?
questions.f: From 'pasticcio', a pie — a pastiche mixes ingredients borrowed from other artists.

questions.q: The word 'bombast', for inflated language, originally referred to…?
questions.f: Padded doublets looked impressive but were mostly stuffing, exactly like bombastic writing.

questions.q: 'Doggerel' describes verse that is…?
questions.f: Chaucer himself used the word to mock bad rhyming in 'The Canterbury Tales'.

questions.q: A 'florilegium', an old term for an anthology, literally means…?
questions.f: It is a Latin translation of the Greek word 'anthology', which means exactly the same thing.

questions.q: 'Marginalia' are notes written…?
questions.f: Edgar Allan Poe published a whole magazine series of his own under that title.

questions.q: The Latin word 'incipit', used by scholars of old manuscripts, means…?
questions.f: Medieval books had no title pages, so scribes identified works by their opening words.

questions.q: In a book, the right-hand page is properly called the…?
questions.f: 'Recto' is Latin for right; the back of that leaf is the verso.

questions.q: The brown spots that appear on old book pages are called…?
questions.f: Nobody is entirely certain of the cause; iron impurities and mould are both blamed.

questions.q: The word 'anthology' and the word 'anther' in botany share a root meaning…?
questions.f: Greek 'anthos', flower — an anthology gathers the choicest blooms.

questions.q: Which word describes an extreme love of collecting books?
questions.f: An 1809 poem by Thomas Dibdin popularised the term among English collectors.

questions.q: The Latin phrase 'ex libris', found on bookplates, means…?
questions.f: Collectors have pasted decorated ex libris plates inside covers since the 1400s.

questions.q: Which word names the study of how poetry's rhythms and sounds work?
questions.f: From Greek 'prosoidia', a song sung to music — the tune under the words.

questions.q: Which word names the study of old handwriting in manuscripts?
questions.f: Epigraphy, its cousin, studies inscriptions carved in stone and metal.

questions.q: The 12-syllable line standard in classical French poetry is called an…?
questions.f: It is named after medieval French romances about Alexander the Great.

questions.q: Which eight-line stanza did Byron use for the comic epic 'Don Juan'?
questions.f: Its final couplet is perfect for a punchline, which is exactly how Byron uses it.

questions.q: Which strict poetic form repeats six end-words in shifting order across six stanzas?
questions.f: The troubadour Arnaut Daniel is credited with inventing it in the 12th century.

questions.q: A four-line comic verse about a named person is called a 'clerihew', after…?
questions.f: Edmund Clerihew Bentley invented the form as a schoolboy, reportedly during a science lesson.

questions.q: Longfellow's 'The Song of Hiawatha' uses which unusual metre for English?
questions.f: He borrowed the chanting rhythm from the Finnish epic 'Kalevala'.

questions.q: The word 'haiku' for the three-line form only became standard in which century?
questions.f: Basho's era called them 'hokku'; the poet Masaoka Shiki promoted the newer term.

questions.q: Which Japanese court lady wrote 'The Pillow Book', a collection of lists and observations?
questions.f: Her lists of 'things that make the heart beat faster' read astonishingly modern.

questions.q: Which poet's 'Pied Beauty' begins 'Glory be to God for dappled things'?
questions.f: Hopkins packed his lines with alliteration and hyphenated compounds unlike anyone else.

questions.q: Which poem by Emily Dickinson begins 'I'm Nobody! Who are you?'
questions.f: She compares public admiration to a bog full of croaking frogs.

questions.q: 'A word is dead when it is said, some say. I say it just begins to live that day' is by…?
questions.f: Dickinson often wrote about language itself, which suits a spelling champion perfectly.

questions.q: Which writer said 'A classic is a book which people praise and don't read'?
questions.f: Twain made a career of poking fun at literary self-importance, including his own.

questions.q: Which American writer said 'It is what you read when you don't have to that determines what you will be'?
questions.f: Wilde was Irish-born but the thought has been quoted at graduations worldwide.

questions.q: Which writer advised 'Read the best books first, or you may not have a chance to read them at all'?
questions.f: Thoreau kept a very short list of books he thought worth rereading.

questions.q: Which essayist wrote 'Knowledge is a city to the building of which every human being brought a stone'?
questions.f: Emerson's essays shaped American thinking about self-reliance and learning.

questions.q: Which author of 'The Old Curiosity Shop' had readers crowding a New York pier for news of Little Nell?
questions.f: Americans shouted to arriving ships to ask whether the character had survived.

questions.q: Which novel opens 'It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen'?
questions.f: Thirteen o'clock signals at once that the world has been rewired.

questions.q: Which novel begins 'All children, except one, grow up'?
questions.f: That is the novel version of 'Peter Pan', which Barrie wrote after the play succeeded.

questions.q: Which novel opens 'It is a truth universally acknowledged...' and was drafted as 'First Impressions'?
questions.f: A publisher rejected the first version unread, years before it became a classic.

questions.q: Which term names the opening section of a play or novel that supplies background?
questions.f: Greek drama often gave the job to a single speaker, which is why prologues exist.

questions.q: 'Ulysses' by James Joyce takes place on a single day, 16 June 1904.
questions.f: That date is now celebrated as Bloomsday, named after the character Leopold Bloom.

questions.q: Marcel Proust's 'In Search of Lost Time' is generally recognised as the longest novel ever published.
questions.f: It runs to roughly 1.2 million words across seven volumes.

questions.q: The semicolon was first used in printing by the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius.
questions.f: It appears in a book he printed in 1494, and it has divided writers ever since.

questions.q: George Orwell's real name was Eric Arthur Blair.
questions.f: He took his pen name partly from the River Orwell in Suffolk.

questions.q: Robert Frost won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry four times.
questions.f: No other poet has matched that record.

questions.q: An Indonesian volcano wrecking Europe's summer, a wager among houseguests beside Lake Geneva, and an 18-year-old's waking vision converge on which novel?
questions.f: Tambora's ash caused 1816's 'year without a summer', trapping the party indoors to invent ghost stories.

questions.q: A business manager for the actor Henry Irving, a borrowed library book about a Wallachian voivode, and a schooner driven ashore at Whitby converge on which novel?
questions.f: Stoker had planned to call his count 'Wampyr' until he found the name Dracula in that Whitby book.

questions.q: A riverboat sounding call meaning two fathoms, a patent for a self-pasting scrapbook, and a life bracketed by two passes of Halley's Comet point to which writer?
questions.f: He said he came in with the comet in 1835 and expected to go out with it — and did, in 1910.

questions.q: A cryptography column in a Philadelphia weekly, a review of a novel starring a talking raven, and the invention of the locked-room puzzle point to which writer?
questions.f: The raven was Dickens's own pet Grip; Poe met it on the page and 'Nevermore' followed.

questions.q: A published treatise on determinants, pioneering amateur photography, and a rowing trip to Godstow with a dean's daughters point to which author?
questions.f: Charles Dodgson kept his mathematics and his nonsense under strictly separate names.

questions.q: A herbarium of over 400 pressed plants, forty hand-sewn booklets found in a chest, and a lifetime tally of barely ten published poems point to which writer?
questions.f: Her sister Lavinia found nearly 1,800 poems after her death and refused to burn them.

questions.q: A volunteer in Washington's wartime hospitals, a private compliment from Emerson printed without permission, and a book that grew from twelve poems to hundreds point to which poet?
questions.f: He stamped Emerson's line about 'the beginning of a great career' on the spine of the next edition.

questions.q: The wreck of the whaleship Essex, nineteen years inspecting cargo on New York's docks, and a manuscript unpublished for over thirty years point to which writer?
questions.f: That late manuscript was 'Billy Budd', found among his papers long after his quiet death in 1891.

questions.q: An architect's apprenticeship, a county revived from the name of an Anglo-Saxon kingdom, and a heart buried separately from the ashes point to which writer?
questions.f: His heart lies in Dorset and his ashes in Poets' Corner — a compromise between village and nation.

questions.q: A Belgian boarding school, a first novel rejected and unpublished in her lifetime, and the pen name Currer Bell point to which novelist?
questions.f: That rejected first novel, 'The Professor', appeared only after her death.

questions.q: A publisher who bought a manuscript and shelved it for years, a title page reading only 'By a Lady', and a small twelve-sided writing table point to which novelist?
questions.f: The shelved book was 'Northanger Abbey'; her family eventually bought the rights back.

questions.q: A study of fungus spore germination, 250 privately printed copies of a rabbit story, and 4,000 acres left to the National Trust point to which author?
questions.f: Her fungi drawings were so accurate that mycologists still consult them.

questions.q: A girl's attempt at the word 'friend', five brothers met in Kensington Gardens, and a copyright signed over to a hospital point to which writer?
questions.f: That mangled word became the name Wendy, now an ordinary given name worldwide.

questions.q: A pamphlet against licensing printers, total blindness by the mid-forties, and 10,000 lines dictated to helpers point to which poet?
questions.f: That pamphlet, 'Areopagitica', is still quoted in free-speech arguments today.

questions.q: A controller of customs for the port of London, a plan for 120 tales that reached about 24, and the first grave in what became Poets' Corner point to which writer?
questions.f: He was buried in the Abbey in 1400 as a royal official; the poets clustered round him later.

questions.q: A hand crippled at Lepanto, five years as a captive in Algiers, and a second part written to spite an impostor point to which author?
questions.f: A rival's fake sequel appeared in 1614, so Cervantes hurried out the real Part Two in 1615.

questions.q: A permanent banishment from Florence, a chain of interlocking three-line stanzas, and a title to which Boccaccio added an adjective point to which poet?
questions.f: Florence offered him a humiliating pardon; he refused, and died in exile in Ravenna.

questions.q: Twelve books left unfinished, a deathbed request that the manuscript be burned, and a role as guide in a later poet's underworld point to which writer?
questions.f: Augustus overruled the request, which is why the 'Aeneid' survives at all.

questions.q: Fifteen books of transformations, banishment to a bleak Black Sea port, and the source Shakespeare's amateur actors mangle point to which poet?
questions.f: 'Metamorphoses' gave the mechanicals of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' their Pyramus and Thisbe.

questions.q: A jibe at 'words a foot and a half long', advice to plunge into the middle of things, and two words urging us to pluck the day point to which poet?
questions.f: 'Ars Poetica' and the 'Odes' between them gave criticism half its stock phrases.
