questions.q: A stanza form bearing her name, an island in the eastern Aegean, and poems surviving chiefly as papyrus scraps from a rubbish dump point to which poet?
questions.f: Many fragments came from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, recovered from ancient waste heaps.

questions.q: Clay tablets in the British Museum, a flood narrative announced to stunned Victorians in 1872, and a friendship with a wild man named Enkidu point to which work?
questions.f: George Smith, a former banknote engraver, deciphered the flood tablet and reportedly ran round the room.

questions.q: A spying trip for Charles II, a novel called 'Oroonoko', and a grave in the east cloister of Westminster Abbey point to which writer?
questions.f: Virginia Woolf held her up as proof a woman could live by her pen.

questions.q: A Gothic-revival villa at Strawberry Hill, a coinage taken from a Persian tale of three princes, and a novel passed off as a translation from Italian point to which writer?
questions.f: His 'Castle of Otranto' launched the Gothic novel, and his letter of 1754 launched 'serendipity'.

questions.q: Nine years' work with six copyists, a definition of 'oats' that offended Scotland, and a biographer who followed him about with a notebook point to which man?
questions.f: Boswell's 'Life of Johnson' is so thorough that a devoted biographer is still called a Boswell.

questions.q: A corrugated iron shed nicknamed the Scriptorium, millions of slips from volunteer readers, and a prolific contributor writing from Broadmoor point to which project?
questions.f: James Murray edited it for 36 years and still died with the letter T unfinished.

questions.q: Goldsmithing in Mainz, an oil-based ink thicker than any scribe's, and roughly 180 copies of a 42-line book point to which figure?
questions.f: About 49 copies of his Bible survive, making it among the most valuable books on earth.

questions.q: A cloth merchant in Bruges, a translation of Trojan histories, and a press set up beside Westminster Abbey in 1476 point to which figure?
questions.f: His choice of London-area spellings helped freeze English orthography where it stands today.

questions.q: A dolphin coiled round an anchor, pocket-sized classics for reading on horseback, and the first printed semicolon point to which printer?
questions.f: His slanted new typeface was imitated across Europe and is still called italic.

questions.q: A Jesuit who burned his early verses, the coinages 'inscape' and 'instress', and a friend who published him 29 years after his death point to which poet?
questions.f: Robert Bridges finally issued the poems in 1918, and readers thought them startlingly modern.

questions.q: A tower house in County Galway, a founding role at the Abbey Theatre, and a seat in the first Irish Senate point to which poet?
questions.f: He also wrote 'There are no strangers here; only friends you haven't yet met.'

questions.q: A verse translation of Dante, a chanting metre borrowed from Finland, and the first American commemorated in Poets' Corner point to which poet?
questions.f: He also wrote 'Perseverance is a great element of success' — and lived it, translating Dante while grieving.

questions.q: A failed poultry farm in New Hampshire, a first collection published in London, and four Pulitzer Prizes point to which poet?
questions.f: America ignored him until England printed 'A Boy's Will' in 1913 and the reviews came home.

questions.q: A busboy in a Washington hotel, a first major poem about rivers, and a line about a raisin that gave a famous play its title point to which writer?
questions.f: He wrote 'Hold fast to dreams' — and his poem 'Harlem' named Lorraine Hansberry's play.

questions.q: Years of childhood silence, work as San Francisco's first Black female cable car conductor, and a poem read at a 1993 inauguration point to which writer?
questions.f: She also wrote 'Nothing will work unless you do' — advice she plainly followed.

questions.q: Folklore fieldwork in Florida and Haiti, an unmarked grave located by Alice Walker in 1973, and a line about the agony of an untold story point to which writer?
questions.f: Walker's essay 'In Search of Zora Neale Hurston' rescued her books from thirty years of neglect.

questions.q: Nineteen years of exile on Guernsey, a lifelong campaign against the death penalty, and a novel written to shame a city into repairing a church point to which writer?
questions.f: He also wrote 'Even the darkest night will end and the sun will rise.'

questions.q: A general father born in Saint-Domingue, a collaborator named Auguste Maquet, and an island fortress off Marseille point to which novelist?
questions.f: His father was one of the first men of African descent to become a French general.

questions.q: A Paris stockbroker's desk, a publisher named Hetzel, and a series marketed as 'Extraordinary Voyages' point to which writer?
questions.f: Hetzel rejected his bleak 'Paris in the Twentieth Century'; it was finally published in 1994.

questions.q: A draper's apprenticeship, a 1903 story predicting armoured land battleships, and a 1914 novel using the phrase 'atomic bombs' point to which writer?
questions.f: Physicist Leo Szilard read that 1914 novel and later said it shaped his thinking about chain reactions.

questions.q: An airmail pilot over the Sahara, a 1935 crash in the Libyan desert, and a disappearance over the Mediterranean in 1944 point to which author?
questions.f: The desert crash, and the days without water that followed, fed straight into 'The Little Prince'.

questions.q: A cobbler's son from Odense, a boyhood job singing in a theatre, and an obsessive hobby of intricate paper-cutting point to which writer?
questions.f: He cut elaborate paper figures while telling stories aloud, then gave them to his listeners.

questions.q: A pen name borrowed from his mother's village, a serial for an Italian children's paper, and a hero the author first killed off point to which writer?
questions.f: Readers protested so loudly that Carlo Lorenzini revived his wooden puppet and continued the story.

questions.q: A German dictionary abandoned around the letter F, a law describing consonant shifts, and early editions far too grim for nurseries point to which pair?
questions.f: Jacob died in 1863 while working on the word for 'fruit'; the dictionary took another century to finish.

questions.q: A district doctor walking Karelia, thousands of lines of oral song taken down by hand, and a metre later borrowed by an American poet point to which epic?
questions.f: Tolkien also raided it, borrowing its tone and some names for his own invented languages.

questions.q: A lady-in-waiting at the Heian court, 54 chapters written around 1010, and a surviving personal diary point to which writer?
questions.f: 'The Tale of Genji' has a fair claim to be the world's first true novel.

questions.q: A pen name taken from a banana plant beside his hut, a 1,500-mile walk into Japan's far north, and a frog and an old pond point to which poet?
questions.f: 'Basho' means banana plant; a disciple gave him one and he named himself after it.

questions.q: Couplets of exactly seven words, a 133-foot statue at India's southern tip, and 1,330 verses claimed by every faith point to which work?
questions.f: The statue's height in feet matches the text's 133 chapters, a nice piece of literary arithmetic.

questions.q: A ring lost in a river, a cloud hired as a messenger, and a poet whom Goethe praised in a short German verse point to which writer?
questions.f: 'Shakuntala' reached Europe in 1789 and dazzled the Romantics.

questions.q: A knighthood renounced in 1919, the words of two national anthems, and a school founded at Santiniketan point to which writer?
questions.f: He wrote 'Faith is the bird that feels the light when the dawn is still dark.'

questions.q: A first story collection banned by British authorities, a career as a school inspector, and a novel titled 'the gift of a cow' point to which writer?
questions.f: Dhanpat Rai took the pen name Premchand after the ban and became Hindi's greatest novelist.

questions.q: A first novel championed by Graham Greene, stories about a schoolboy named Swami, and a small invented South Indian town point to which writer?
questions.f: Greene found him a publisher and even helped shorten his name for English readers.

questions.q: A protagonist named Okonkwo, a title lifted from an Irish poem, and a blistering essay against 'Heart of Darkness' point to which writer?
questions.f: 'Things Fall Apart' has been translated into more than fifty languages.

questions.q: A Colombian court reporter, household goods pawned to post a manuscript, and a town called Macondo point to which writer?
questions.f: He could afford postage for only half the manuscript, so he mailed the second half later.

questions.q: An imperial police posting in Burma, dishwashing in Paris kitchens, and a Suffolk river point to which writer?
questions.f: Eric Blair chose 'Orwell' from the river and 'George' as the plainest English name he could find.

questions.q: A hand press in a dining room, a mock biography whose hero lives 300 years, and two lectures at Cambridge women's colleges point to which writer?
questions.f: Those lectures became 'A Room of One's Own', with its demand for money and privacy.

questions.q: A Paris bookshop owner brave enough to publish it, a chapter written as a question-and-answer catechism, and a private schema mapping episodes onto Homer point to which novel?
questions.f: Sylvia Beach of Shakespeare and Company issued it in 1922 when nobody else would.

questions.q: A clerk at Lloyds Bank, a dedication borrowing Dante's praise of a troubadour, and a book of light verse about cats point to which poet?
questions.f: 'Il miglior fabbro' — the better craftsman — was his tribute to Pound's brutal editing.

questions.q: A Red Cross ambulance driver in Italy, a job on a Toronto newspaper, and a theory about icebergs point to which writer?
questions.f: He argued seven-eighths of a story should stay below the surface.

questions.q: A discarded title referring to a Roman banquet host, cover art commissioned before the text was finished, and an epigraph credited to an invented poet point to which novel?
questions.f: Fitzgerald nearly called it 'Trimalchio in West Egg', and the epigraph's 'poet' was his own earlier character.

questions.q: A university postmaster dismissed for reading on duty, a hand-drawn map of an invented county, and a title taken from Macbeth point to which writer?
questions.f: He called himself 'sole owner and proprietor' of Yoknapatawpha County on his own map.

questions.q: A childhood neighbour who became a famous journalist-novelist, a year's wages given by friends as a gift, and a single published novel for over half a century point to which author?
questions.f: The friends' gift let her quit her airline job and write full time for a year.

questions.q: A master's thesis on Woolf and Faulkner, years of editing other people's books at Random House, and a novel named for one word on a gravestone point to which writer?
questions.f: 'Beloved' won the Pulitzer in 1988; the Nobel followed in 1993.

questions.q: A dime-fed rented typewriter in a library basement, a title naming a paper's ignition point, and a lifelong refusal to drive a car point to which writer?
questions.f: He wrote the whole first draft in nine days at ten cents per half hour.

questions.q: A number changed to avoid clashing with a Leon Uris title, sixty bombing missions over Italy, and a rule that proves you sane for wanting out point to which novel?
questions.f: It was nearly 'Catch-18'; the phrase it invented is now in every dictionary.

questions.q: A ship's surgeon on an Arctic whaler, a campaign to clear a wrongly convicted solicitor, and a stubborn belief in photographs of fairies point to which writer?
questions.f: His work on the George Edalji case helped lead to England's Court of Criminal Appeal.

questions.q: A father's failed utopian farm, lurid thrillers written for cash under the name A. M. Barnard, and a family story dashed off at a publisher's suggestion point to which writer?
questions.f: She thought the family story dull; it made her the most successful American writer of her day.

questions.q: A pencil-making family firm, a night in jail over an unpaid poll tax, and a bean field beside a pond point to which writer?
questions.f: He improved his family's pencil formula, then wrote 'Books are the treasured wealth of the world.'

questions.q: A minister who resigned over communion, an 1836 essay simply called 'Nature', and a lecture titled 'The American Scholar' point to which writer?
questions.f: He also wrote 'The mind, once stretched by a new idea, never returns to its original dimensions.'

questions.q: A secretary of the Bank of England, bedtime tales for a son named Alastair, and a chapter titled 'The Piper at the Gates of Dawn' point to which author?
questions.f: He wrote in a bank by day, and Toad of Toad Hall came out of nursery storytelling.

questions.q: An assistant editor at Punch, a cricket team of literary men, and a toy bear bought at Harrods point to which writer?
questions.f: The real toys — bear, piglet, donkey and tiger — now live in a New York library.

questions.q: A move from Manchester to Tennessee, a landmark British copyright lawsuit, and a walled garden at Great Maytham Hall point to which author?
questions.f: She sued over an unauthorised stage version of her own novel and helped change dramatic copyright law.

questions.q: A manuscript rejected repeatedly and stored in a hat box, an upbringing by strict grandparents, and a clipping about a couple who wanted a boy point to which author?
questions.f: That clipping about an orphan sent by mistake became 'Anne of Green Gables'.

questions.q: A magazine about poultry breeding, a career advising shop-window dressers, and a pair of silver shoes point to which author?
questions.f: His first book was about Hamburg chickens; his second-most-famous was about a road of yellow brick.

questions.q: A wartime crash in the Libyan desert, a garden hut with a green baize board, and a co-invented medical valve for children point to which writer?
questions.f: The Wade-Dahl-Till valve helped children with hydrocephalus after his own son's injury.

questions.q: Advertising art for an insecticide, a publisher's bet about a fifty-word vocabulary, and the earliest known printed use of 'nerd' point to which author?
questions.f: 'Nerd' first appears in his 1950 book 'If I Ran the Zoo', years before it meant a bookish person.

questions.q: A Cambridge chair in medieval literature, a wartime radio series on belief, and Tuesday mornings at the Eagle and Child point to which writer?
questions.f: He wrote 'Hardships often prepare ordinary people for an extraordinary destiny.'

questions.q: A serial in an abolitionist newspaper, the best-selling American novel of its century, and the line about the tide turning point to which writer?
questions.f: She wrote 'Never give up, for that is just the place and time that the tide will turn.'

questions.q: Three separate autobiographies, a newspaper called The North Star, and the line 'if there is no struggle, there is no progress' point to which writer?
questions.f: He revised his life story across decades as his own view of America changed.

questions.q: The first African American to earn a Harvard doctorate, a 1903 essay collection on 'double consciousness', and the line that education must teach life point to which writer?
questions.f: 'The Souls of Black Folk' remains one of the most quoted works of American non-fiction.

questions.q: A degree earned with a teacher spelling into her palm, an autobiography written at 22, and the line about keeping your face to the sunshine point to which writer?
questions.f: She was the first deaf-blind person to earn a bachelor's degree, at Radcliffe in 1904.

questions.q: A novel pioneering multiple narrators, a close friendship with Dickens, and a stolen Indian diamond point to which book?
questions.f: T. S. Eliot called it the first and greatest of English detective novels.

questions.q: A masked player who answered the chorus, a Greek noun for one acting a part, and a modern word for feigned virtue all point to which term?
questions.f: The actor's word slid across into moral judgement, which is why 'hypocrite' still means playing a part.

questions.q: A Venetian nickname for Giovanni, a masked servant tumbling through improvised plays, and a modern word for silly antics point to which tradition?
questions.f: 'Zanni' was the standard name for the clownish servant, and English took it as 'zany'.

questions.q: A hinged wooden bat, an enormous crack made with almost no force, and a whole genre of silent film comedy point to which word?
questions.f: The Italian batacchio let comic actors 'beat' each other loudly and harmlessly on stage.

questions.q: The word 'farce' comes from a French word originally meaning…?
questions.f: Comic scenes were stuffed into serious religious plays, exactly like forcemeat into a bird.

questions.q: A tall thick-soled boot, a light slipper called a soccus, and a pair of nicknames for the two ancient dramatic genres point to which phrase?
questions.f: Tragic actors towered in buskins; comic actors padded about in socks, and the phrase survives in criticism.

questions.q: Which term names an exchange of single alternating lines between two characters in Greek drama?
questions.f: It produces the rapid-fire verbal duels that make Sophocles crackle.

questions.q: A blind poet's late tragedy, a Romantic's unstageable Prometheus, and Byron's mountain-top Manfred all belong to which category?
questions.f: Milton, Shelley and Byron all wrote plays meant for the reading chair, not the playhouse.

questions.q: A poet insisting words must rule, a designer insisting scenery must rule, and a grotesque opening act called an antimasque point to which form?
questions.f: Jonson and Inigo Jones fell out spectacularly over whose art mattered more at the Stuart court.

questions.q: An illiterate herdsman, a dream in a cattle byre, and a story preserved by the monk Bede point to which poem?
questions.f: Just nine lines long, it is the oldest English poem whose author we can name.

questions.q: A battered cathedral volume, scorch marks from rough handling, and riddles whose answers include an onion and a bookworm point to which book?
questions.f: It has sat in Exeter Cathedral's library for roughly a thousand years, riddles and all.

questions.q: A smoky hall, a harp passed along the benches, and an Old English word for the man who sang there point to which title?
questions.f: 'Skald' is his Norse cousin, 'bard' his Celtic one, and 'griot' his West African counterpart.

questions.q: An Icelandic lawspeaker, a handbook written so young poets could still decode kennings, and our main key to Norse myth point to which writer?
questions.f: Without his textbook for apprentice poets, most Norse mythology would be lost to us.

questions.q: An Occitan verb meaning 'to find', a courtly love song of southern France, and a northern cousin called the trouvere point to which kind of poet?
questions.f: They 'found' their songs rather than merely singing them, which is why the verb became the job title.

questions.q: A Latin word for a patchwork cloak, poems built wholly from Virgil's lines, and not one original phrase point to which form?
questions.f: Late Roman writers made whole Christian epics out of recycled pagan verse.

questions.q: The shield of Achilles, Keats's silent urn, and a Greek term for speaking a picture into words point to which device?
questions.f: Homer spends over 100 lines describing a shield that nobody can actually see.

questions.q: A lark mistaken for a nightingale, a lover complaining about the sunrise, and a Provencal dawn song point to which form?
questions.f: Romeo and Juliet argue about which bird is singing, which makes their parting scene an aubade.

questions.q: A Greek phrase meaning 'at the bridal chamber', 24 stanzas counting off a single day, and a poet celebrating his own marriage point to which form?
questions.f: Spenser's 'Epithalamion' times its stanzas to the hours of his wedding day.

questions.q: A French novel with no letter E, an English translation that pulled off the same trick, and a Greek term for missing letters point to which constraint?
questions.f: Georges Perec's 'La Disparition' avoided E entirely, and Gilbert Adair's translation did too.

questions.q: A word occurring exactly once in all of Homer, a translator's nightmare, and a Greek phrase meaning 'said once' point to which term?
questions.f: With no second example to compare, scholars can only guess what such words meant.

questions.q: Early Greek inscriptions, an ox turning at the end of each furrow, and lines that reverse direction point to which writing style?
questions.f: The reader's eye ploughs the stone exactly as an ox ploughs a field.

questions.q: No gaps between words, readers who had to murmur aloud to follow, and Latin for 'continuous writing' point to which practice?
questions.f: Silent reading was so unusual that Augustine remarked on seeing his teacher do it.

questions.q: A reversed P inked in red, a scribe's signal for a new turn of thought, and a symbol still hiding in word processors point to which mark?
questions.f: Its name probably wandered in from 'paragraph' by way of Old French 'pelagraphe'.

questions.q: A tiny drawn hand, a Renaissance reader marking a favourite line, and thousands of doodles down the margins point to which mark?
questions.f: Scholars study them to learn which passages readers actually cared about centuries ago.

questions.q: The dot over a lower-case i or j has its own name. It is a…?
questions.f: That is where the phrase 'to a T' — originally 'to a tittle' — probably comes from.

questions.q: A 1962 proposal by an advertising executive, a mark for astonished questions, and a name blending 'query' with printers' slang point to which symbol?
questions.f: Martin Speckter wanted one mark for lines like 'You did what'; a few typefaces still include it.

questions.q: In proofreading, the Latin word 'stet' instructs the printer to…?
questions.f: Its opposite is 'dele', from 'deleatur', let it be destroyed.

questions.q: A long metal tray of set type, a rough impression pulled before pages exist, and a writer's last chance to fix things point to which item?
questions.f: The tray was called a galley, so the proof pulled from it kept the name.

questions.q: In typesetting, a lone last line of a paragraph stranded at the top of a page is called a…?
questions.f: An orphan is the opposite: a lone first line left at the bottom of a page.

questions.q: The word 'font' in printing comes from a French verb meaning…?
questions.f: A font was one casting of metal type, poured from molten alloy.

questions.q: An Arabic word for a storehouse, a military depot for powder, and a bound collection of miscellaneous pieces point to which English word?
questions.f: From 'makhzan' — a magazine of writing stores articles as a magazine of arms stores cartridges.

questions.q: A small Venetian coin, hand-copied news-sheets sold in the 1500s, and the official journal of many governments point to which word?
questions.f: A 'gazetteer' later came to mean a geographical index, though it began as a journalist.

questions.q: The word 'pamphlet' is thought to derive from the title of a popular medieval…?
questions.f: 'Pamphilus', a much-copied 12th-century verse tale, circulated as loose unbound sheets.

questions.q: A small book meant to be carried about, such as a handbook, is called a…?
questions.f: Latin for 'go with me' — the ancestor of the pocket guide.

questions.q: An 'enchiridion', a term for a handbook, comes from a Greek phrase meaning…?
questions.f: Epictetus's 'Enchiridion' was meant to be held and consulted, like a manual.

questions.q: The word 'epitome' comes from a Greek verb meaning…?
questions.f: An epitome was a condensed version of a long work, which is why it means 'the essence'.

questions.q: The scholarly abbreviation 'ibid.' stands for a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From 'ibidem'; 'et al.' comes from 'et alii', and others.

questions.q: The abbreviation 'viz.' stands for a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From 'videlicet', it is permitted to see; the z is actually an old shorthand squiggle for -et.

questions.q: Which word describes a saying so compressed it becomes a general truth, as in Greek verse maxims?
questions.f: From Greek 'gnome', a maxim; the earliest Greek 'gnomic poets' wrote almost nothing else.

questions.q: A Greek colony in Asia Minor, Athenian sneering at provincial speech, and a modern word for a grammatical blunder point to which term?
questions.f: The people of Soloi spoke perfectly good Greek; Athens simply thought their accent funny.

questions.q: A river crossing, a pronunciation that betrayed the speaker's origin, and a modern word for a test of group membership point to which term?
questions.f: The word itself means an ear of grain; the sound at its start was the giveaway.

questions.q: A Macedonian king's expansion, a series of alarmed Athenian speeches, and a modern word for a blistering verbal attack point to which orator?
questions.f: Cicero later borrowed the label for his own attacks on Mark Antony.

questions.q: The word 'laconic', meaning terse, comes from the region around which Greek city?
questions.f: Sparta lay in Laconia, and Spartans were famed for one-word answers.

questions.q: A long, angry lament about the state of the world is called a…?
questions.f: Named after the prophet Jeremiah, whose book of Lamentations set the tone.

questions.q: Which adjective describes a plan that forces everything to fit one rigid standard, after a Greek villain's bed?
questions.f: Procrustes stretched or trimmed his guests to fit the bed exactly.

questions.q: Which mythical figure gave us the adjective for someone whose warnings are true but ignored?
questions.f: Apollo gave her true prophecy and the curse that no one would believe it.

questions.q: Keats's phrase 'the blushful Hippocrene' refers to a spring said to have been created by…?
questions.f: The winged horse struck Mount Helicon and the poets' spring gushed out.

questions.q: Alexander Pope warned readers to 'drink deep, or taste not' which spring of learning?
questions.f: The Pierian spring was sacred to the Muses, so a sip of learning was worse than none.

questions.q: A hat and a word for a manipulative mastermind both come from which Victorian novel?
questions.f: George du Maurier's 1894 novel gave English both 'Svengali' and the trilby hat worn on stage.

questions.q: The word 'namby-pamby' began as a mocking nickname for which poet?
questions.f: A rival made fun of his sugary verses for children and coined the insult from his first name.

questions.q: An umbrella was once slangily called a 'gamp', after a character created by which novelist?
questions.f: Mrs Sarah Gamp of 'Martin Chuzzlewit' carried an enormous cotton umbrella everywhere.

questions.q: 'Tweedledum and Tweedledee' were used by Lewis Carroll but first appeared in an epigram about…?
questions.f: John Byrom coined the pair in 1725 to mock the feud between Handel's supporters and Bononcini's.

questions.q: Which of these words was coined by Lewis Carroll in 'The Hunting of the Snark'?
questions.f: 'Chortle', 'galumph' and 'burble' come from 'Jabberwocky'; the boojum is the Snark's deadly variety.

questions.q: The word 'grok', for deep intuitive understanding, was coined in a novel by which writer?
questions.f: In 'Stranger in a Strange Land' it is a Martian word meaning to drink, and so to absorb entirely.

questions.q: The word 'cyberspace' was coined in the early 1980s by which novelist?
questions.f: He introduced it in a short story before using it in 'Neuromancer'.

questions.q: Which Orwell coinage names language designed to shrink the range of thinkable thoughts?
questions.f: Its whole purpose in the novel is that a shrinking vocabulary shrinks the mind.

questions.q: Which critic's essay on Hamlet popularised the term 'objective correlative'?
questions.f: He meant the exact set of objects and events that will reliably summon a particular emotion in a reader.

questions.q: A physician who was secretary of the Royal Society, a lifelong compulsion to make lists, and a book arranging words by idea rather than alphabet point to which work?
questions.f: Peter Mark Roget compiled it in retirement at 73, and it has never been out of print since 1852.

questions.q: A workshop accident at the age of three, a French army night-writing code, and a system finished before its inventor turned sixteen point to which invention?
questions.f: Louis Braille cut the army's clumsy twelve-dot cell down to six, and reading by touch became fluent.

questions.q: A banknote engraver turned museum assistant, a self-taught reading of cuneiform, and an 1872 lecture that astonished London point to which scholar?
questions.f: He had taught himself to read clay tablets in his lunch hours before deciphering the Babylonian flood story.

questions.q: Which term names the study of a text's transmission and the reconstruction of its lost original?
questions.f: Editors build family trees of manuscripts, called stemmata, to work out which readings came first.

questions.q: In editing old texts, a passage so corrupt that no reading makes sense is called a…?
questions.f: Latin for 'cross' — scholars mark hopeless spots with daggers and argue about them for centuries.

questions.q: A gap where text is missing from a manuscript is called a…?
questions.f: Latin for a pit or hollow — the same root as 'lake' and 'lagoon'.

questions.q: Which term names the first printed edition of a work previously known only in manuscript?
questions.f: For many Greek and Latin classics, the editio princeps came from Venice in the late 1400s.

questions.q: The Latin word 'imprimatur', once printed in books, literally means…?
questions.f: It was an official licence to print, the very thing Milton's 'Areopagitica' attacked.

questions.q: An ancient Greek reciter of Homer's poems for an audience was called a…?
questions.f: The older singer-composer was an aoidos; the later performer of fixed texts was a rhapsode.

questions.q: Marginal explanatory notes added by ancient and medieval scholars are called…?
questions.f: Much of what we know about lost Greek plays survives only in scholia.

questions.q: The scholarly question of whether one author composed both Homeric epics is called the…?
questions.f: Scholars still split over whether 'Homer' names a person, a tradition, or both.

questions.q: Which term names the repeated formulaic phrases that allowed oral poets to compose while performing?
questions.f: Milman Parry proved the theory by studying living Serbo-Croatian singers in the 1930s.

questions.q: How many books make up Homer's 'Odyssey'?
questions.f: The 'Iliad' also has 24, a division probably imposed by later Alexandrian editors.

questions.q: Which library's scholars first divided Homer into books and invented literary editing?
questions.f: Its head librarians included Callimachus, who also compiled the first great library catalogue.

questions.q: Which Alexandrian poet-librarian is credited with the first systematic library catalogue, the 'Pinakes'?
questions.f: He also famously argued that a big book was a big evil, preferring short polished poems.

questions.q: Which Greek play by Aristophanes stages a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides in the underworld?
questions.f: They literally weigh each other's verses on a set of scales.

questions.q: Roman comedy's two surviving playwrights, whose plots Shakespeare and Moliere both raided, were…?
questions.f: Plautus supplied the noisy farce; Terence supplied the neat plotting.

questions.q: Which Roman writer's bloody tragedies shaped Elizabethan revenge drama?
questions.f: 'Titus Andronicus' and 'The Spanish Tragedy' both descend from his ghost-haunted style.

questions.q: Which Elizabethan play established the revenge-tragedy formula that 'Hamlet' later perfected?
questions.f: Thomas Kyd's play was the biggest hit of the Elizabethan stage before Shakespeare arrived.

questions.q: Which theatre manager's diary is our best record of Elizabethan playhouse business?
questions.f: He recorded takings, costume costs and payments to playwrights, play by play.

questions.q: Which actor was the star of Shakespeare's company and the first Hamlet and Lear?
questions.f: The comic Will Kempe left the company around 1599, which changed the kind of clowns Shakespeare wrote.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play was written to be performed in a candlelit indoor theatre at Blackfriars?
questions.f: The indoor house allowed act breaks for trimming candles, which is why the late plays fall into five acts neatly.

questions.q: Shakespeare left his wife a famous item in his will, described as the…?
questions.f: Historians argue endlessly about whether that was an insult, a legal formality, or sentiment.

questions.q: Which two long narrative poems did Shakespeare dedicate to the Earl of Southampton?
c: Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece
The Sonnets and A Lover's Complaint
The Phoenix and the Turtle and Venus and Adonis
questions.f: They were the only works he seems to have overseen carefully through the press.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play contains the shortest scene in the canon and a queen named Cleopatra?
questions.f: Its 42 short scenes race around the Mediterranean in a way no earlier play attempted.

questions.q: Which word for a printed play text based on an actor's faulty memory is used by Shakespeare scholars?
questions.f: The 'bad quarto' of 'Hamlet' famously begins 'To be, or not to be, ay there's the point.'

questions.q: In Shakespeare studies, 'foul papers' means…?
questions.f: A neat version made from them was the 'fair copy', and the theatre's marked-up copy the prompt book.

questions.q: Which poet's 1598 list of English writers gives us the earliest praise of Shakespeare by name?
questions.f: 'Palladis Tamia' lists twelve of the plays, which helps scholars date the early works.

questions.q: Which 17th-century poet wrote 'To His Coy Mistress' with its chariot of hurrying time?
questions.f: He spent most of his life as a Member of Parliament and published almost no poetry while alive.

questions.q: Which poet shaped his devotional poems into patterns on the page, such as wings and an altar?
questions.f: 'Easter Wings' is printed so the stanzas taper and widen like a pair of wings.

questions.q: Which poet, having lost his sight, wrote a sonnet ending 'They also serve who only stand and wait'?
questions.f: He was writing about his blindness, decades before dictating 'Paradise Lost'.

questions.q: Which 18th-century poem set in a country churchyard ends with an epitaph for its own author?
questions.f: Thomas Gray reworked it for years; General Wolfe is said to have recited it before Quebec.

questions.q: Which mock-epic by Alexander Pope turns the theft of a lock of hair into a Homeric war?
questions.f: Pope wrote it to reconcile two real families who had fallen out over exactly that.

questions.q: Which verse form did Pope and Dryden use so relentlessly that it defined their age?
questions.f: Rhymed iambic pentameter pairs, tuned for wit and epigram.

questions.q: Which poet, a farm labourer's son who wrote about enclosure and birds' nests, spent his last years in an asylum?
questions.f: Once nearly forgotten, he is now ranked with the greatest English nature poets.

questions.q: Which novel is written as the digressive autobiography of a narrator who takes volumes to get born?
questions.f: Laurence Sterne included a black page, a blank page and a marbled page as jokes about book-making.

questions.q: Samuel Richardson's 'Pamela', a landmark of the English novel, is written entirely as…?
questions.f: Henry Fielding parodied it almost immediately, which helped launch his own novels.

questions.q: Which term names the picaresque novel's typical hero?
c: a roguish servant of low birth
questions.f: From Spanish 'picaro', a rogue; 'Lazarillo de Tormes' set the pattern in 1554.

questions.q: Which German literary movement's name translates as 'storm and stress'?
questions.f: Goethe's 'Werther' is its most famous product, all fierce feeling against cool reason.

questions.q: Which term names a novel about the growth of an artist specifically, rather than any young person?
questions.f: Joyce's 'A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man' is the textbook example.

questions.q: Which Russian critic's term 'dialogism' describes novels as a clash of many independent voices?
questions.f: He developed the idea largely from Dostoevsky, whose characters argue back at their author.

questions.q: Which Russian Formalist coined 'ostranenie', usually translated as 'defamiliarisation'?
questions.f: He argued art exists to make the stone feel stony again after habit has dulled it.

questions.q: Which scholar analysed Russian folktales into a fixed sequence of 31 narrative functions?
questions.f: His 1928 'Morphology of the Folktale' underlies a great deal of later storytelling theory.

questions.q: Which critic's 'Anatomy of Criticism' sorted literature into cycles matched to the four seasons?
questions.f: Comedy belongs to spring, romance to summer, tragedy to autumn and satire to winter.

questions.q: Which critical school insisted a poem's meaning lies in the text alone, warning against the 'intentional fallacy'?
questions.f: Wimsatt and Beardsley named both the intentional and the affective fallacies in the 1940s.

questions.q: Which term names a phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from its individual words?
questions.f: From Greek 'idios', one's own — an idiom is a language's private property.

questions.q: Which term names a word or phrase translated piece by piece from another language, like 'skyscraper' into other tongues?
questions.f: French for 'copy'; 'flea market' is itself a calque of the French 'marche aux puces'.

questions.q: Two English words descended from the same original word by different routes are called…?
questions.f: 'Guard' and 'ward', or 'chief' and 'chef', are doublets that took different roads into English.

questions.q: Which term names a word created by mistake from a misreading of an older text?
questions.f: 'Dord' famously appeared in a 1934 dictionary because a filing slip for 'D or d' was misread.

questions.q: The word 'syllabus' is widely traced to a misreading in printed editions of which author?
questions.f: A Greek word for a label, 'sittybas', was misprinted, and scholars have used the error ever since.

questions.q: Which word for a short pithy statement of principle comes from a Greek term used in medical writing?
questions.f: The Hippocratic 'Aphorisms' begin 'Life is short, art is long', and the form spread to every subject.

questions.q: Which figure of speech attaches an adjective to the wrong noun on purpose, as in 'a sleepless night'?
questions.f: Also called hypallage; the night is not sleepless, the person is.

questions.q: Which figure of speech describes one sense in terms of another, as in 'a loud shirt'?
questions.f: Keats and Baudelaire both built whole poems out of it.

questions.q: Which term names the repetition of a word at the end of one clause and the start of the next?
questions.f: Greek for 'doubling back'; it chains sentences together like links.

questions.q: Which device inserts a word into the middle of another word, as in 'abso-blooming-lutely'?
questions.f: Greek for 'a cutting'; ancient Greek poets did it constantly with prepositions.

questions.q: Which term names a self-contradictory phrase used to expose a deeper truth, distinct from mere wordplay?
questions.f: Wilde built a career on them: 'I can resist everything except temptation.'

questions.q: Which Old English poem, spoken by an exile, is a classic of the 'ubi sunt' lament?
questions.f: 'Ubi sunt' means 'where are they now', and the motif runs from Anglo-Saxon verse to modern song.

questions.q: Which allegorical Middle English poem features a dreamer, Lady Holy Church, and a ploughman?
questions.f: William Langland's poem survives in three quite different versions, all probably his own revisions.

questions.q: Which medieval play type dramatised Bible stories and was performed by town trade guilds?
questions.f: 'Mystery' here comes from a word for a craft or trade, not from anything mysterious.

questions.q: Which medieval English morality play sends its hero to death accompanied only by Good Deeds?
questions.f: Every companion — Beauty, Strength, Knowledge — abandons him at the grave's edge.

questions.q: Which term describes a printed book's arrangement in gatherings of folded sheets sewn together?
questions.f: Printers marked each gathering with a letter so binders could assemble the book in order.

questions.q: In old paper-making, a 'quire' traditionally meant how many sheets?
questions.f: Twenty quires made a ream, which is why reams still come in odd-looking round numbers.

questions.q: The rough uncut edge deliberately left on some fine books is called the…?
questions.f: It imitates the natural edge left by the deckle frame in hand paper-making.

questions.q: A painting hidden on the fanned-out edge of an antique book's pages is called a…?
questions.f: Closed, the book looks gilded; fan the pages and a landscape appears.

questions.q: Which term names a book's list of its own printing details, now usually on the copyright page?
questions.f: Publishers still call their logo a colophon, a memory of those old closing statements.

questions.q: Which poet's line 'Do not wait to strike till the iron is hot; but make it hot by striking' shows his taste for hammered proverbs?
questions.f: Yeats mixed Irish folklore, occult symbols and blunt practical advice throughout his career.

questions.q: Which writer, born in Lebanon, wrote 'Doubt is a pain too lonely to know that faith is his twin brother'?
questions.f: He wrote 'The Prophet' in English, and it has sold in the tens of millions.

questions.q: Which philosopher-writer said 'Patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet'?
questions.f: His 'Poetics' and 'Rhetoric' are still the foundation texts of literary and persuasive theory.

questions.q: Which Roman Stoic wrote 'It is not because things are difficult that we do not dare'?
questions.f: Seneca also wrote the blood-soaked tragedies that shaped Elizabethan revenge drama.

questions.q: The word 'novel' as a literary term is unrelated to the Italian word for 'new'.
questions.f: It comes straight from 'novella', a new little story, by way of French.

questions.q: Shakespeare's First Folio contains 36 plays.
questions.f: Only about 750 copies were printed and roughly 235 survive worldwide.

questions.q: Aristotle's 'Poetics' as we have it discusses comedy at the same length as tragedy.
questions.f: The section on comedy is lost, a gap that fascinated Umberto Eco enough to build a novel round it.

questions.q: Who shouts 'Action!' and guides everyone making a movie?
questions.f: The director is the boss of the film set and decides how every scene should look and sound.

questions.q: Walt Disney is famous for creating which cartoon mouse?
questions.f: Mickey Mouse first became a star in cartoons way back in 1928.

questions.q: What do we call a puppet that dangles and dances on strings?
questions.f: A marionette's strings run up to a wooden control bar that the puppeteer tilts and wiggles.

questions.q: Which puppet fits right over your hand like a glove?
questions.f: Your fingers make a hand puppet's head and arms move as you talk for it.

questions.q: A circus performer with a red nose, face paint, and giant shoes is called a…?
questions.f: Clowns have been making circus audiences laugh for more than 200 years.

questions.q: The giant tent where a traveling circus performs is called the…?
questions.f: The biggest circus tents could hold thousands of people under one huge roof of canvas.

questions.q: Keeping three balls flying through the air without dropping them is called…?
questions.f: Expert jugglers can keep five, seven, or even more balls in the air at once.

questions.q: In a theatre, the actors perform up on the…?
questions.f: The word 'stage' comes from an old word for a standing place or platform.

questions.q: The people who come to watch a show are called the…?
questions.f: 'Audience' comes from a Latin word about listening, because audiences listen as well as watch.

questions.q: All the actors in a play or movie together are called the…?
questions.f: A cast list tells you which actor plays each character in the show.

questions.q: What do people in the audience do with their hands when they love a show?
questions.f: Clapping to show joy is thousands of years old — even ancient Roman audiences applauded.

questions.q: A pretend sword, teapot, or wand that an actor uses on stage is called a…?
questions.f: 'Prop' is short for 'property', because these objects belong to the theatre.

questions.q: A practice session actors do before the real show is called a…?
questions.f: Big shows can rehearse for weeks or months before an audience ever sees them.

questions.q: A cartoon is made of many pictures shown one after another very quickly.
questions.f: When pictures flash by fast enough, your brain blends them into smooth movement.

questions.q: Kermit from The Muppets is what kind of animal?
questions.f: Kermit the Frog has starred on TV since the 1950s and even has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

questions.q: Elmo and Big Bird live on which famous TV street?
questions.f: Sesame Street has been teaching kids letters and numbers since 1969.

questions.q: In Toy Story, what is the name of the toy cowboy?
questions.f: Woody is a pull-string cowboy doll who becomes best friends with Buzz Lightyear.

questions.q: In Finding Nemo, what kind of fish is Nemo?
questions.f: Real clownfish live safely among the stinging arms of sea anemones.

questions.q: In The Lion King, what animal is Simba?
questions.f: 'Simba' is the Swahili word for lion.

questions.q: In Frozen, Elsa has magical powers over…?
questions.f: Elsa builds a whole sparkling palace out of ice while singing 'Let It Go'.

questions.q: Which crunchy snack made from corn do people love to eat at the movies?
questions.f: Movie theatres began selling popcorn in the 1930s, and it is still the favorite today.

questions.q: At the cinema, the movie is shown on a big white…?
questions.f: Some giant cinema screens are taller than a five-story building.

questions.q: In a silent film, you cannot hear the actors speak.
questions.f: Silent movies showed the words on cards on screen, while live music played in the theatre.

questions.q: Charlie Chaplin made people laugh in old movies that had no…?
questions.f: Chaplin was so funny with just his face and body that he never needed to say a word.

questions.q: 'Movie' is a short, friendly way of saying…?
questions.f: Early films amazed people simply because the pictures moved, so they called them moving pictures.

questions.q: The letters 'TV' are short for…?
questions.f: 'Television' is built from word parts that mean seeing things from far away.

questions.q: A person who performs in plays and movies is called an…?
questions.f: Actors pretend to be other people, which is one of the oldest jobs in show business.

questions.q: When fans shout 'Encore!' at the end of a concert, they want…?
questions.f: 'Encore' is a French word — shouting it asks the performer to come back and do more.

questions.q: A 'matinee' is a show that happens at what time of day?
questions.f: Matinee shows let families see plays and movies in the afternoon instead of late at night.

questions.q: A 'puppeteer' is a person who…?
questions.f: Some puppeteers hide below the stage and hold their arms up high through the whole show.

questions.q: A circus unicycle has how many wheels?
questions.f: 'Uni' means one — riding a unicycle takes amazing balance.

questions.q: The circus performer in a fancy coat who announces every act is the…?
questions.f: The ringmaster traditionally wears a bright red coat and a tall top hat.

questions.q: An 'acrobat' is a performer who…?
questions.f: Acrobats train for years to do flips and handstands high above the ground.

questions.q: The special clothes actors wear to look like their characters are called…?
questions.f: One big movie can use hundreds of costumes made by a whole team of sewers and designers.

questions.q: The written story of a movie, with all the words the actors will say, is the…?
questions.f: Actors study the script to memorize their lines before filming begins.

questions.q: What color is the cartoon character SpongeBob SquarePants?
questions.f: SpongeBob is a yellow sea sponge who lives in a pineapple under the sea.

questions.q: Scooby-Doo, who solves mysteries with his friends, is what kind of animal?
questions.f: Scooby-Doo is a Great Dane, one of the tallest dog breeds in the world.

questions.q: In Peter Pan, children fly off to which magical land?
questions.f: In Neverland, Peter Pan never has to grow up.

questions.q: What does Cinderella accidentally leave behind at the ball?
questions.f: The prince uses the lost glass slipper to search the kingdom for Cinderella.

questions.q: A movie that continues the story of an earlier movie, like Toy Story 2, is called a…?
questions.f: 'Sequel' comes from a word meaning 'to follow', because it follows the first story.

questions.q: The puppets on Sesame Street are called Muppets.
questions.f: Puppet maker Jim Henson created the Muppets, including Elmo, Grover, and Cookie Monster.

questions.q: Which tiny fairy is Peter Pan's friend?
questions.f: In stage plays, Tinker Bell is often shown as just a darting spot of light and a jingling bell.

questions.q: 'Lights, camera, …' — which word finishes the famous movie-set saying?
questions.f: Directors call 'Action!' so the actors know the camera is rolling and the scene has begun.

questions.q: Winnie the Pooh loves to eat which sweet treat?
questions.f: Pooh calls it 'hunny' and keeps it in big round pots.

questions.q: A 'trapeze' is a circus swing made of a bar hanging from…?
c: Two ropes high in the air
questions.f: Trapeze artists swing, let go, and get caught in midair by a partner.

questions.q: A movie that is full of jokes and makes you laugh is called a…?
questions.f: Comedy is one of the oldest kinds of show — ancient Greeks wrote funny plays too.

questions.q: A show where the performers sing lots of songs as part of the story is called a…?
questions.f: Famous musicals like The Lion King fill the stage with singing, dancing, and bright costumes.

questions.q: The audience is the group of people performing on stage.
questions.f: It is the other way around — performers are on stage, and the audience watches from their seats.

questions.q: Pinocchio's nose grows longer every time he…?
questions.f: Pinocchio is a wooden puppet who dreams of becoming a real boy.

questions.q: Dumbo the elephant can fly using his big…?
questions.f: Dumbo's giant ears work like wings and make him the star of the circus.

questions.q: In a shadow puppet show, the audience sees the puppets as…?
c: Dark shapes on a glowing screen
questions.f: A bright light behind the puppets throws their shadows onto a thin screen.

questions.q: Which machine shines the movie picture onto the cinema screen?
questions.f: The projector sits in a little room at the back of the theatre called the projection booth.

questions.q: What is the name of Mickey Mouse's pet dog?
questions.f: Pluto is one of the few classic Disney animal characters who doesn't talk.

questions.q: Donald Duck is usually dressed in what kind of outfit?
questions.f: Donald has worn his blue sailor jacket and cap since his very first cartoon in 1934.

questions.q: In Aladdin, the Genie whooshes out of a magic…?
questions.f: Rubbing the old oil lamp sets the joke-cracking Genie free.

questions.q: Which movie stars Totoro, a big cuddly forest spirit?
questions.f: My Neighbor Totoro comes from Japan's famous animation house, Studio Ghibli.

questions.q: Lightning McQueen from the movie Cars is a…?
questions.f: Lightning McQueen races with the number 95 painted on his sides.

questions.q: Shrek is what kind of storybook creature?
questions.f: Shrek is a green ogre who lives happily in a swamp.

questions.q: In Moana, the hero Maui carries a giant magical…?
questions.f: Maui's magic fishhook lets him change shape into animals like a giant hawk.

questions.q: The Minions from Despicable Me are mostly what color?
questions.f: The little yellow Minions speak a funny mixed-up language of their own.

questions.q: The long list of names that rolls up the screen after a movie ends is called the…?
questions.f: The credits thank everyone who helped make the movie — sometimes thousands of people.

questions.q: A short break in the middle of a long show is called an…?
questions.f: During intermission the audience can stretch, snack, and talk about the show.

questions.q: The helpful person who shows you to your seat in a theatre is the…?
questions.f: Ushers often carry little flashlights to guide people through the dark.

questions.q: A ventriloquist is a performer who makes it seem like their puppet can…?
questions.f: Ventriloquists speak without moving their lips, so the voice seems to come from the puppet.

questions.q: A 'trilogy' is a set of how many movies?
questions.f: 'Tri' means three — like the three wheels on a tricycle.

questions.q: Actors take a bow at the end of a play.
questions.f: Bowing is the traditional way performers say thank you for the audience's applause.

questions.q: In The Wizard of Oz, Dorothy follows a road made of bricks of what color?
questions.f: 'Follow the yellow brick road!' leads Dorothy toward the Emerald City.

questions.q: What is the name of Dorothy's little dog in The Wizard of Oz?
questions.f: Toto rides along in Dorothy's basket for much of the adventure.

questions.q: Painting an actor's face before a show is called putting on stage…?
questions.f: Stage makeup is extra bold so faces can be seen from the very back row.

questions.q: Wallace and Gromit are animated characters made from what squishy material?
questions.f: Animators gently reshape the clay figures between every single photograph.

questions.q: In stop-motion animation, you move a model a tiny bit and then take a…?
questions.f: Thousands of photos played quickly in a row make the model look alive.

questions.q: A 'duet' is a song performed by how many singers?
questions.f: 'Duet' comes from a word for two, just like 'duo'.

questions.q: Where does Ariel, The Little Mermaid, live?
questions.f: Ariel collects human treasures like forks in her secret underwater cave.

questions.q: A funny drawing in a newspaper and a funny animated film can both be called a…?
questions.f: The word 'cartoon' started out meaning a drawing on sturdy paper.

questions.q: The music that plays during a movie is called its…?
questions.f: Some movie soundtracks become so popular that people sing them everywhere.

questions.q: In Beauty and the Beast, what does Belle love to do most?
questions.f: Belle is thrilled when the Beast shows her his gigantic castle library.

questions.q: The big group of musicians who play instruments for a musical is called an…?
questions.f: A full orchestra can have strings, drums, trumpets, flutes, and many more instruments.

questions.q: A marionette is moved by strings from above.
questions.f: The puppeteer stands above the little stage and works the strings out of sight.

questions.q: The puppies in 101 Dalmatians are white with lots of black…?
questions.f: Real Dalmatian puppies are born pure white and grow their spots later.

questions.q: Olaf from Frozen is a talking…?
questions.f: Olaf dreams about summer even though he is made of snow.

questions.q: A story that actors perform live on a stage is called a…?
questions.f: People have been performing plays for more than 2,500 years.

questions.q: In a theatre, the big front curtain rises when the show…?
questions.f: The moment the curtain rises is the signal for the audience to go quiet and watch.

questions.q: Who carves the wooden puppet Pinocchio?
questions.f: The kind old woodcarver Geppetto wishes his puppet could become a real boy.

questions.q: The funny ending of a joke is called its…?
questions.f: Comedians practice their punch lines to get the biggest laugh at just the right moment.

questions.q: Circus performers who seem super tall are often secretly walking on…?
questions.f: Stilt walkers can be twice as tall as the crowd watching them.

questions.q: A 'solo' is a performance given by how many people?
questions.f: 'Solo' comes from a word meaning alone.

questions.q: In Tom and Jerry cartoons, Tom the cat is always chasing Jerry the…?
questions.f: Tom and Jerry cartoons have won seven Academy Awards.

questions.q: Bugs Bunny is famous for munching on…?
questions.f: Bugs asks 'What's up, Doc?' while crunching his carrot.

questions.q: The big room full of seats where the audience watches a show is the…?
questions.f: Some famous auditoriums have seats for more than 3,000 people.

questions.q: In the movie Up, the house floats away into the sky carried by thousands of…?
questions.f: Carl ties colorful balloons to his house to fly it to South America.

questions.q: WALL-E is a little robot whose job is collecting and squashing…?
questions.f: WALL-E spends his days tidying up an Earth covered in garbage — and collects treasures he finds.

questions.q: Popcorn is made by heating corn kernels until they pop.
questions.f: Steam builds up inside the kernel until it bursts and turns fluffy — at about 180 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: A person who stands on stage telling jokes to make people laugh is a…?
questions.f: Stand-up comedians write and practice their jokes just like actors learn lines.

questions.q: In Cinderella, the Fairy Godmother turns a pumpkin into a…?
questions.f: The magic wears off at midnight, when the coach turns back into a pumpkin.

questions.q: Snow White lives in the forest with how many dwarfs?
questions.f: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs was Disney's very first full-length animated movie.

questions.q: At a 'sing-along' movie, the audience is invited to…?
questions.f: Sing-along screenings show the song words on screen so everyone can join in.

questions.q: Which puppet maker created the Muppets?
questions.f: Jim Henson built his first Muppets when he was still a teenager.

questions.q: Mary Poppins flies through the sky holding her…?
questions.f: Mary Poppins floats down to the Banks family's house with her talking parrot-handle umbrella.

questions.q: The name of a movie, shown in big letters, is called its…?
questions.f: A movie's title is often chosen very carefully to make people curious.

questions.q: The area hidden behind the stage where actors get ready is called…?
questions.f: Backstage is full of costumes, props, and actors waiting for their turn to go on.

questions.q: In Kung Fu Panda, Po is a kung-fu-loving…?
questions.f: Po dreams of being a kung fu hero — and becomes the Dragon Warrior.

questions.q: The bright circle of light that follows a performer on stage is the…?
questions.f: A crew member called the spot operator moves the spotlight to follow the star.

questions.q: In Ratatouille, Remy the rat dreams of becoming a great…?
questions.f: Remy proves that a tiny rat can become a top chef in a fancy Paris restaurant.

questions.q: During a play, the audience sits up on the stage with the actors.
questions.f: The audience watches from seats facing the stage, so everyone can see the show.

questions.q: Goofy from the Disney cartoons is what kind of animal?
questions.f: Goofy is a tall, clumsy dog famous for his laugh — 'A-hyuck!'

questions.q: When a show is 'sold out', it means…?
questions.f: Popular shows can sell out months before opening night.

questions.q: In How to Train Your Dragon, Toothless is a…?
questions.f: Toothless is a rare Night Fury dragon who becomes Hiccup's best friend.

questions.q: The 'front row' of a theatre is the row of seats…?
questions.f: Front-row seats put you so close you can sometimes see the actors' makeup.

questions.q: If a trapeze artist lets go, what stretchy thing below catches them safely?
questions.f: The big safety net lets flyers practice daring tricks without getting hurt.

questions.q: What small piece of paper lets you into a movie or a show?
questions.f: Some people keep old tickets as souvenirs of their favorite shows.

questions.q: A person who teaches animals to do tricks for shows is an animal…?
questions.f: Movie animal trainers use treats and patience to teach dogs, horses, and even pigs their parts.

questions.q: At the 'curtain call', all the actors come back on stage to…?
questions.f: The stars usually bow last, when the clapping is loudest.

questions.q: A movie theater is also called a…?
questions.f: 'Cinema' comes from an old Greek word about movement — because the pictures move.

questions.q: A ventriloquist tries to speak without moving their lips.
questions.f: That trick makes the voice seem to come from the puppet instead of the performer.

questions.q: In Monsters, Inc., the monsters discover that laughter is more powerful than…?
questions.f: Mike and Sulley switch their whole city from scare power to laugh power.

questions.q: A 'cartoonist' is a person who…?
questions.f: Many famous animated characters started as a cartoonist's quick pencil doodle.

questions.q: The Cat in the Hat wears a tall striped hat colored white and…?
questions.f: His red-and-white hat is one of the most famous hats in any storybook or film.

questions.q: If a movie is 'animated', its pictures are…?
questions.f: Animated movies can show anything artists imagine — even talking teacups.

questions.q: A little desk lamp hops across the screen at the start of movies from which studio?
questions.f: The bouncy lamp squashes the letter I in the Pixar name.

questions.q: A 'movie star' is an actor who is very…?
questions.f: Some movie stars get their names set into golden stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

questions.q: In Frozen, Anna and Elsa are…?
questions.f: The love between the two royal sisters is what finally thaws the frozen kingdom.

questions.q: 'Stage fright' is the feeling of being…?
questions.f: Even famous performers get stage fright — deep breaths and practice help it fade.

questions.q: A carousel ride spins people around on beautiful wooden…?
questions.f: Some carousel horses are over 100 years old and carved entirely by hand.

questions.q: In a musical, the performers sing songs as part of the story.
questions.f: When feelings get too big for talking, characters in musicals burst into song.

questions.q: In Aladdin, what does Aladdin ride to fly through the sky?
questions.f: The magic carpet has no face, but its flips and waves show exactly how it feels.

questions.q: In the famous TV cartoon, Rudolph the reindeer has a shiny red…?
questions.f: Rudolph's glowing nose lights the way for Santa's sleigh on a foggy night.

questions.q: A microphone makes a singer's voice sound…?
questions.f: Microphones turn voices into electric signals that big speakers can boom out.

questions.q: On a movie set, the camera's job is to…?
questions.f: Big movie cameras can cost as much as a house.

questions.q: Baloo, who sings 'The Bare Necessities' in The Jungle Book, is a…?
questions.f: Baloo the bear teaches Mowgli to relax and enjoy the simple things.

questions.q: Stitch, Lilo's mischievous blue friend, is really a…?
questions.f: Stitch crash-lands in Hawaii and learns that 'ohana' means family.

questions.q: Puss in Boots is a clever cat famous for wearing…?
questions.f: Puss also wears a feathered hat and carries a tiny sword like a hero.

questions.q: A person who dances in shows and concerts is called a…?
questions.f: Show dancers may rehearse the same steps hundreds of times until they are perfect.

questions.q: 'Abracadabra!' is a word performers shout while doing a…?
questions.f: 'Abracadabra' is an ancient magic word that people once wore on charms.

questions.q: Your theatre ticket can tell you exactly which seat is yours.
questions.f: Tickets often show a row letter and seat number, like Row C, Seat 12.

questions.q: In the famous cartoon movie, the Grinch tries to steal which holiday?
questions.f: The Grinch's heart grows three sizes when he learns what the holiday really means.

questions.q: In a classic circus gag, a whole crowd of clowns squeezes out of one tiny…?
questions.f: The clown car trick works because the car is secretly empty inside — no seats at all!

questions.q: Sid from the Ice Age movies is a slow, silly…?
questions.f: Real sloths are just as slow as Sid — they can sleep 15 hours a day.

questions.q: In Madagascar, Alex the lion starts out living in a…?
questions.f: Alex is the star attraction of New York's Central Park Zoo before his big adventure.

questions.q: 'Applause' is the happy sound of many people…?
questions.f: The louder the applause, the more the audience loved the show.

questions.q: Bluey, the cartoon puppy from Australia, is what kind of animal?
questions.f: Bluey is a blue heeler, a real Australian dog breed that loves to work and play.

questions.q: A big colorful poster outside a cinema shows you…?
questions.f: Some old movie posters are so loved that collectors pay fortunes for them.

questions.q: In The Polar Express, the magical train carries children to…?
questions.f: The Polar Express was one of the first movies animated from actors' real movements.

questions.q: In a puppet show, the puppeteer often stays hidden from the audience.
questions.f: Puppeteers crouch behind screens or under the stage so only the puppets are seen.

questions.q: In Encanto, the Madrigal family lives in a magical…?
questions.f: Their house, called Casita, opens doors and waves its window shutters all by itself.

questions.q: A 'stage name' is…?
c: A special name a performer uses
A name written on the curtain
questions.f: Many stars pick a stage name that is easier to remember than their real one.

questions.q: Curious George, star of books and cartoons, is a very curious…?
questions.f: George's curiosity always gets him into — and out of — big trouble.

questions.q: The cartoon Pink Panther is a panther of what color?
questions.f: The Pink Panther first appeared in a movie's opening cartoon and became a star himself.

questions.q: The saying 'The show must go on' means performers should…?
c: Keep going even when things go wrong
questions.f: This old circus and theatre motto reminds performers never to give up mid-show.

questions.q: In Mulan, the hero disguises herself to take her father's place in the…?
questions.f: Mulan trains hard and becomes one of China's greatest legendary heroes.

questions.q: The word 'cinema' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek kinema, 'movement' — the same root gives us 'kinetic' energy.

questions.q: A 'matinee' takes its name from a French word meaning…?
questions.f: From French matin, 'morning' — though matinees are usually afternoon shows today.

questions.q: When an audience shouts 'Encore!', the word literally means…?
questions.f: 'Encore' is French for 'again' — the crowd is literally asking for one more.

questions.q: An 'understudy' in a theatre company is a performer who…?
c: Learns a role in case the star cannot perform
questions.f: Understudies rehearse in secret and sometimes become stars when they finally go on.

questions.q: The word 'theatre' comes from a Greek word meaning a place for…?
questions.f: From Greek theatron, 'a place for viewing' — the same root as 'theory'.

questions.q: The word 'animation' comes from a Latin root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin anima, 'breath, life' — animators literally bring drawings to life.

questions.q: Which company made Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first full-length cel-animated feature?
questions.f: Released in 1937, it took about four years and hundreds of artists to complete.

questions.q: Charlie Chaplin's most famous character was known as…?
questions.f: The Tramp's bowler hat, cane, and baggy trousers made him recognizable worldwide.

questions.q: Which Japanese studio made Spirited Away and My Neighbor Totoro?
questions.f: Studio Ghibli was co-founded by director Hayao Miyazaki in 1985.

questions.q: Which Pixar film was the first full-length movie animated entirely on computers?
questions.f: Toy Story arrived in 1995 and changed animation forever.

questions.q: Broadway, the world-famous theatre district, is in which city?
questions.f: Broadway is an actual long street in Manhattan lined with dozens of theatres.

questions.q: London's famous theatre district is nicknamed the…?
questions.f: Broadway and the West End are the two biggest theatre districts in the world.

questions.q: The golden statue given for the best films each year is called an…?
questions.f: 'Oscar' is the nickname of the Academy Award statuette, which stands about 34 cm tall.

questions.q: Which award honours the best of American theatre?
questions.f: Tony Awards go to Broadway shows; Oscars to films, Emmys to TV, Grammys to music.

questions.q: An award for outstanding television is called an…?
questions.f: Emmys have been awarded to TV shows since 1949.

questions.q: In stop-motion animation, the model must be photographed…?
questions.f: Twenty-four separate photos can make just one second of finished film.

questions.q: Cartoon animation works because your eyes and brain blend fast still pictures into motion.
questions.f: Films usually run at 24 pictures — called frames — every second.

questions.q: A single still picture in a strip of film is called a…?
questions.f: A two-hour movie contains roughly 170,000 individual frames.

questions.q: A short sample of a movie shown before its release is called a…?
questions.f: Trailers got their name because they once ran AFTER the main film — trailing it.

questions.q: The word 'puppet' comes from a Latin root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin pupa, 'doll' — the same root behind the 'pupil' in your eye.

questions.q: A 'ventriloquist' takes their name from words meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin venter (belly) + loqui (speak) — people once believed the voice came from the stomach.

questions.q: An 'acrobat' gets their name from a Greek word meaning to walk…?
questions.f: From Greek akrobatos, 'walking on tiptoe' — akros means highest, as in 'acrophobia'.

questions.q: The word 'circus' comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Roman chariot races ran in a circus — the same root gives us 'circle' and 'circular'.

questions.q: The word 'comedian' traces back to a Greek word for a…?
questions.f: From Greek komos, a joyful street procession with singing.

questions.q: A 'protagonist' in a movie or play is the…?
questions.f: From Greek protos (first) + agonistes (actor) — literally the first actor.

questions.q: The character who works against the hero in a story is the…?
questions.f: 'Anti' means against — the antagonist pushes against the protagonist.

questions.q: 'Television' is built from word parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek tele (far) + Latin videre (to see) — the same tele as in 'telescope'.

questions.q: The 'phone' part of 'microphone' means…?
questions.f: From Greek phone, 'sound' — micro + phone means 'small sound', because it picks up tiny sounds.

questions.q: A 'projector' gets its name from a Latin root meaning to…?
questions.f: From Latin proicere, 'to throw forth' — it throws the image onto the screen.

questions.q: Which of these describes a 'documentary'?
c: A film about real people and events
questions.f: Documentaries use real footage and interviews instead of invented stories.

questions.q: What does an animator do?
c: Creates the moving drawings or models
questions.f: Traditional animators sometimes drew thousands of pictures for a single scene.

questions.q: Who wrote plays like Romeo and Juliet, still performed on stages today?
questions.f: Shakespeare wrote about 38 plays, and they have been translated into over 100 languages.

questions.q: Shakespeare's own theatre in London was called the…?
questions.f: The round Globe Theatre was open to the sky, so shows happened in the afternoon light.

questions.q: In a musical, the singing group who back up the leads is called the…?
questions.f: 'Chorus' comes from ancient Greek plays, where a group sang and commented on the story.

questions.q: In old silent films, printed cards on screen showed the audience what characters said.
questions.f: Those cards were called intertitles, and some were beautifully decorated.

questions.q: 'Cel animation' is named after cels, which were sheets of…?
questions.f: Artists painted characters on transparent celluloid sheets laid over a background.

questions.q: The painted or built surroundings on a stage are called the…?
questions.f: Stage carpenters and painters can build a whole village on a single stage.

questions.q: What was Mickey Mouse's first cartoon released with synchronized sound, in 1928?
questions.f: Steamboat Willie thrilled audiences because Mickey's whistling matched the picture perfectly.

questions.q: A performer who spins plates, rides a unicycle and juggles is showing off their…?
questions.f: 'Versatile' comes from a Latin root meaning 'to turn' — a versatile performer can turn to any skill.

questions.q: 'Break a leg!' is something people say to performers to wish them…?
questions.f: Theatre people think saying 'good luck' is unlucky, so they say the opposite instead.

questions.q: The word 'audition' comes from a Latin root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin audire, 'to hear' — the same root as 'audio' and 'audience'.

questions.q: A 'rehearsal' comes from an old French word meaning to…?
questions.f: The old word meant dragging a rake over soil again — going over the same ground repeatedly.

questions.q: 'Costume' and 'custom' share a root meaning…?
questions.f: Costumes originally showed a character's customs — the habits of their time and place.

questions.q: Which of these is a 'genre' of film?
questions.f: 'Genre' is a French word for 'kind' or 'type' — comedy, horror, and western are all genres.

questions.q: In the theatre, 'blocking' means deciding…?
questions.f: Directors sometimes use tiny figures on a model stage to plan the blocking.

questions.q: The Muppet Show and Sesame Street puppets were created by…?
questions.f: Henson invented the word 'Muppet' himself, and it is now in dictionaries.

questions.q: Which animal roars in the famous opening logo of the MGM film studio?
questions.f: MGM's roaring lion has opened its films since the 1920s.

questions.q: Kabuki is a colourful traditional form of theatre from which country?
questions.f: Kabuki actors wear dramatic painted makeup called kumadori.

questions.q: Which country's shadow-puppet tradition is called wayang kulit?
questions.f: Wayang kulit puppets are cut from buffalo leather and moved with buffalo-horn sticks.

questions.q: An 'ovation' means the audience clapped enthusiastically, often while standing.
questions.f: A 'standing ovation' is the biggest compliment a live audience can give.

questions.q: The person who chooses which actors get which parts is the…?
questions.f: Casting directors may watch hundreds of auditions for one important role.

questions.q: The word 'scene' comes from a Greek word for the…?
questions.f: Greek skene was the hut behind the stage where actors changed costumes.

questions.q: 'Cartoon' originally meant a drawing on which surface?
questions.f: From Italian cartone, 'big paper' — artists drew full-size plans on it before painting.

questions.q: A film's 'score' is its…?
questions.f: Composers write the score to match the picture second by second.

questions.q: Which classic musical features the song 'Do-Re-Mi'?
questions.f: 'Do-Re-Mi' teaches the notes of the musical scale in a song.

questions.q: What is a 'flipbook'?
c: A book of drawings that animate when the pages are flicked
questions.f: Flipbooks from the 1860s were among the earliest animation toys.

questions.q: A 'zoetrope' creates moving pictures inside a spinning…?
questions.f: Peeking through the slits of the spinning drum makes the drawings inside gallop and run.

questions.q: What does a stunt performer do?
c: Performs dangerous action safely in place of an actor
questions.f: Stunt performers train for years in falling, driving, and fighting techniques.

questions.q: A 'double' on a film set is someone who…?
questions.f: Doubles can be filmed from behind or far away so the audience never notices.

questions.q: Ancient Greek actors wore large masks mainly to…?
c: Show the character's emotion to a huge crowd
questions.f: Some masks may also have helped project the actor's voice across huge stone theatres.

questions.q: In an old-fashioned theatre, the row of lights along the front edge of the stage were the…?
questions.f: Before electricity, footlights were oil lamps or candles — a real fire risk.

questions.q: A 'cameo' is a very small part played by a famous person.
questions.f: Directors sometimes give themselves quick cameo appearances in their own films.

questions.q: 'Slapstick' comedy is named after a stage prop that made a loud…?
questions.f: The slapstick was two thin boards that cracked loudly when an actor was gently tapped.

questions.q: What is a 'mime'?
c: A performer who acts without words
questions.f: Mimes use exact gestures to make invisible walls and objects feel real.

questions.q: Which colour is a 'green room' actually named for its purpose as a place to…?
c: Wait and relax before going on stage
questions.f: Nobody is certain why it is called green — one idea is that early ones really were painted green.

questions.q: A 'flea circus' was an old sideshow act featuring…?
questions.f: Showmen claimed their fleas pulled tiny carts — often with hidden springs helping out.

questions.q: Which pair of comedians starred together in classic films, one thin and one round, wearing bowler hats?
questions.f: Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy made over 100 films together.

questions.q: 'Punch and Judy' is a traditional British form of what kind of show?
questions.f: Punch and Judy shows are performed in a striped booth and are over 350 years old.

questions.q: What is a 'sound stage'?
c: A soundproof building where films are shot
The loudest seat in a theatre
questions.f: Sound stages block outside noise so microphones catch only the actors.

questions.q: A movie 'set' built to look like a street is usually made of…?
questions.f: Backlot streets are often just building fronts held up by wooden supports behind.

questions.q: 'Animatronics' combines animation with which other word?
questions.f: Animatronic creatures use motors and gears to blink, breathe, and roar.

questions.q: What is the job of a film 'editor'?
c: Choosing and joining the best shots together
questions.f: An editor may cut 100 hours of footage down to two.

questions.q: A 'close-up' shot shows…?
c: A face or object filling the screen
questions.f: Close-ups let audiences read tiny changes in an actor's expression.

questions.q: The word 'amphitheatre' begins with a Greek part meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek amphi, 'both' — seats curve around both sides of the performing space.

questions.q: A 'monologue' is a speech given by…?
questions.f: From Greek monos (single) + logos (speech).

questions.q: A 'dialogue' in a film script is…?
c: Words characters say to each other
