questions.f: From Greek dia (across) + logos (speech) — speech going back and forth.

questions.q: Studio Ghibli's Hayao Miyazaki is known for drawing much of his films' storyboards himself.
questions.f: Miyazaki often begins a film with drawings before the script is even finished.

questions.q: Which classic 1928 invention let cartoon characters be heard as well as seen?
questions.f: Matching sound to picture was so new that audiences gasped at Mickey's whistle.

questions.q: The word 'clown' is related to old words meaning a…?
questions.f: Early stage clowns played rustic characters who bumbled among city folk.

questions.q: 'Pantomime' is built from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek pantos (all) + mimos (imitator) — a performer who imitates everything.

questions.q: 'Hollywood' is a famous film-making neighbourhood in which US state?
questions.f: Film-makers moved to sunny Los Angeles because they could shoot outdoors nearly every day.

questions.q: India's huge Hindi-language film industry is nicknamed…?
questions.f: The name blends Bombay (now Mumbai) with Hollywood.

questions.q: What does a 'storyboard' show?
c: Sketches of each planned shot in order
questions.f: Storyboards let a film be 'watched' as drawings long before cameras roll.

questions.q: The 'clapperboard' snapped in front of the camera helps crews later match…?
questions.f: The sharp clap gives editors one loud noise and one clear picture to line up.

questions.q: 'Special effects' are often shortened in film credits to…?
questions.f: Computer-made effects are usually labelled VFX, for visual effects.

questions.q: A 'green screen' lets film-makers replace the green background with…?
questions.f: Green is used because human skin contains almost no green, so actors are easy to separate.

questions.q: A person who writes films is called a…?
questions.f: Screenwriters use a special layout so one page equals roughly one minute of screen time.

questions.q: What is a 'voice actor'?
c: A performer who speaks a character's lines without appearing on screen
questions.f: One voice actor can play a dozen different characters in a single cartoon.

questions.q: 'Dubbing' a film means…?
c: Replacing the speech with another language or take
questions.f: Skilled dubbing artists match the new words to the actor's lip movements.

questions.q: 'Subtitles' are words that appear…?
c: At the bottom of the screen
questions.f: Subtitles let you enjoy films made in languages you do not speak.

questions.q: An 'ensemble' cast means a group of actors sharing the spotlight rather than one lead star.
questions.f: 'Ensemble' is French for 'together'.

questions.q: Which classic Disney film features a wooden boy, a cricket, and the song 'When You Wish Upon a Star'?
questions.f: Jiminy Cricket serves as Pinocchio's conscience — the little voice telling right from wrong.

questions.q: Disney's 1940 film Fantasia set animation to what kind of music?
questions.f: In Fantasia, Mickey Mouse plays the Sorcerer's Apprentice with dancing brooms.

questions.q: Which animated Disney deer learns to walk on ice with the rabbit Thumper?
questions.f: Disney artists studied real fawns for months to get Bambi's wobbly steps right.

questions.q: A show performed live, as it happens, with no chance to redo a scene, is called…?
questions.f: Live performance means every night is slightly different — that is part of the magic.

questions.q: An 'aerialist' is a circus performer who works…?
questions.f: 'Aerial' comes from a Latin root for air, the same one in 'aeroplane'.

questions.q: 'Contortionist' comes from a root meaning to…?
questions.f: From Latin torquere, 'to twist' — the same root as 'torque' and 'tornado'.

questions.q: A tightrope walker's long pole helps them keep…?
questions.f: The heavy pole slows down wobbles, giving the walker time to correct.

questions.q: 'Cirque du Soleil' is a modern circus whose name means circus of the…?
questions.f: The French-Canadian company performs without any animal acts at all.

questions.q: The word 'audience' shares a root with which of these words?
questions.f: From Latin audire, 'to hear' — audience, audio, and 'audible' are all cousins.

questions.q: A 'debut' performance is a performer's…?
questions.f: 'Debut' comes from French and means the first move or beginning.

questions.q: 'Opening night' is the evening when a show…?
c: Is performed publicly for the first time
questions.f: Opening-night nerves are legendary, and casts often celebrate afterwards.

questions.q: A written opinion about whether a film is good is called a…?
questions.f: 'Review' literally means 'to see again' — the critic looks back over the film.

questions.q: A 'critic' is a person who…?
c: Judges and comments on films or plays
questions.f: From Greek kritikos, 'able to judge'.

questions.q: A 'premiere' is the…?
c: First public showing of a film
questions.f: From French premier, 'first' — the same word behind 'prime' and 'primary'.

questions.q: Which of these is a job in the film crew?
questions.f: The cinematographer decides how every shot is lit and framed.

questions.q: A 'choreographer' plans the…?
questions.f: From Greek khoreia (dance) + graphein (to write) — literally dance-writing.

questions.q: 'Bravo!' is a word shouted by audiences that means…?
questions.f: 'Bravo' is Italian for 'skilful' or 'excellent'.

questions.q: A 'flop' is a show or film that fails to attract an audience.
questions.f: Some famous flops later became beloved classics once people rediscovered them.

questions.q: Which invention let audiences see films in colour rather than black and white?
questions.f: Early Technicolor cameras exposed three separate strips of film at once.

questions.q: Which 1939 film is famous for switching from sepia tones to bright colour?
questions.f: Kansas is drab brown; the moment Dorothy steps into Oz, the screen bursts into colour.

questions.q: A movie shot 'on location' is filmed…?
questions.f: Location shooting can send crews to deserts, glaciers, or busy city streets.

questions.q: A film 'extra' is a person who…?
c: Appears in the background of scenes
questions.f: Big crowd scenes may need hundreds of extras in matching costumes.

questions.q: 'Silhouette' animation uses figures that appear as…?
questions.f: Lotte Reiniger's 1926 silhouette film is among the oldest surviving animated features.

questions.q: A 'squash and stretch' technique makes animated characters look…?
questions.f: A bouncing ball squashes when it lands and stretches as it flies — a core animation principle.

questions.q: 'Rotoscoping' means animators trace over…?
questions.f: Rotoscoping was patented in 1915 and gives animation lifelike motion.

questions.q: What is a 'cliffhanger' ending?
c: One that stops at a moment of suspense
questions.f: Old film serials literally left heroes dangling from cliffs until the next week's episode.

questions.q: A TV show broadcast in weekly parts telling one long story is a…?
questions.f: Each part is called an episode, from a Greek word meaning something coming in besides.

questions.q: 'Prime time' on television means the hours when…?
questions.f: Networks save their biggest shows for prime time, usually early evening.

questions.q: A 'sitcom' is short for…?
questions.f: Sitcoms put the same funny characters into a new situation each episode.

questions.q: Some television comedies are recorded in front of a live studio audience.
questions.f: The real laughter you hear can be the studio audience reacting in the moment.

questions.q: In television, a 'pilot' is…?
c: The person flying the camera drone
questions.f: Networks watch the pilot to decide whether to order a whole series.

questions.q: Which Jim Henson TV series was framed as a chaotic variety show hosted by Kermit the Frog?
c: Bear in the Big Blue House
questions.f: The Muppet Show framed each episode as a chaotic variety show hosted by Kermit.

questions.q: A 'variety show' features…?
questions.f: Variety shows might mix jugglers, singers, comedians, and magicians in one evening.

questions.q: 'Vaudeville' was a type of entertainment made up of…?
c: Many short live acts on one bill
questions.f: Many early film comedians, including Chaplin, learned their craft on vaudeville stages.

questions.q: An 'usherette' or usher's traditional job includes…?
c: Checking tickets and guiding people to seats
questions.f: In the golden age of cinema, ushers wore smart uniforms with brass buttons.

questions.q: The word 'gala', as in a gala performance, means an event that is…?
questions.f: 'Gala' comes through French and Italian from a word for showy finery.

questions.q: 'Trapeze' comes from a word meaning…?
questions.f: The bar and its two ropes make a trapezium shape — hence the name.

questions.q: Which of these is a real theatre superstition?
c: Never say the name 'Macbeth' inside a theatre
questions.f: Actors call it 'the Scottish play' instead, to avoid supposed bad luck.

questions.q: The 'wings' of a stage are…?
c: The sides where actors wait out of sight
questions.f: Actors 'waiting in the wings' are ready to make their entrance.

questions.q: A 'stage manager' is in charge of…?
c: Running the show smoothly each night
questions.f: The stage manager calls every lighting and sound cue over a headset.

questions.q: 'Props' is short for which longer word?
questions.f: A prop master keeps every teacup and sword organized backstage.

questions.q: The word 'gymnastics' and the circus word 'acrobatics' both describe…?
questions.f: Circus acrobatics and Olympic gymnastics share many of the same tumbling moves.

questions.q: 'Melodrama' combines Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek melos (song) + drama — early melodramas mixed spoken scenes with music.

questions.q: A 'tragedy' in theatre is a play that…?
c: Ends unhappily for the main character
questions.f: Greek tragedies were performed at festivals honouring the god Dionysus.

questions.q: The masks of comedy and tragedy are a symbol of…?
questions.f: One mask smiles and one frowns, representing the two oldest kinds of Greek drama.

questions.q: In ancient Greek theatre, all the performers were men.
questions.f: Male actors wore masks and costumes to play women's roles.

questions.q: An 'usher' shows you to your seat; a 'concessions' stand sells you…?
questions.f: Snack sales often earn a cinema more money than the tickets do.

questions.q: 'Widescreen' films are wider than they are…?
questions.f: Widescreen shapes were introduced in the 1950s to make cinema feel bigger than TV.

questions.q: 'IMAX' cinemas are famous for their…?
questions.f: The largest IMAX screens are over 30 metres wide.

questions.q: A '3D' film uses special glasses to give the picture a sense of…?
questions.f: Each eye sees a slightly different image, and your brain merges them into depth.

questions.q: An animation 'principle' called 'anticipation' means a character…?
c: Winds up before a big move
questions.f: A pitcher leaning back before throwing is anticipation — it makes the action readable.

questions.q: In animation, 'in-betweens' are the drawings that come…?
questions.f: Lead animators drew key poses while assistants filled in the in-betweens.

questions.q: 'Claymation' is stop-motion animation using figures made of…?
questions.f: Plasticine never dries out, so animators can reshape figures for months.

questions.q: Which of these films uses stop-motion puppets rather than drawings?
questions.f: Coraline's puppets had thousands of 3D-printed faces to give her expressions.

questions.q: A 'ringmaster' is to the circus what a…?
c: Host is to a variety show
questions.f: Both keep the evening flowing and introduce every act.

questions.q: A 'juggler' who keeps objects moving in a repeating loop is doing a pattern called a…?
questions.f: The three-ball cascade is the very first pattern almost every juggler learns.

questions.q: 'Sleight of hand' describes a magician's…?
questions.f: 'Sleight' is an old word meaning cunning or cleverness.

questions.q: A magician's assistant who helps hide the trick's secret is part of the trick's…?
questions.f: Misdirection means guiding the audience's attention away from the secret move.

questions.q: 'Illusionist' comes from a Latin root meaning to…?
questions.f: From Latin illudere, 'to play with, to trick' — related to 'ludicrous' and 'ludo'.

questions.q: Charlie Chaplin also composed music for some of his films.
questions.f: Chaplin wrote the tune 'Smile', which many singers have recorded since.

questions.q: Which silent-era comedian was famous for keeping a completely straight face?
questions.f: Keaton's nickname was 'The Great Stone Face'.

questions.q: 'Anime' is a style of animation strongly associated with which country?
questions.f: The word 'anime' is simply the Japanese shortening of 'animation'.

questions.q: 'Ghibli' in Studio Ghibli's name is a word for a…?
questions.f: Miyazaki, an aviation fan, took the name from an Italian aircraft named for that wind.

questions.q: Which theatre word means the whole group of people who work on a production, not the actors?
questions.f: 'Cast and crew' together can number in the hundreds for a big musical.

questions.q: A 'long-running' show is one that…?
questions.f: Some Broadway and West End musicals have run for over 30 years.

questions.q: Which classic musical about orphans includes the song 'Tomorrow'?
questions.f: Little Orphan Annie began as a newspaper comic strip in 1924.

questions.q: The 'proscenium' of a theatre is the…?
questions.f: From Greek pro (before) + skene (stage) — it stands in front of the stage.

questions.q: A show performed 'in the round' means the audience sits…?
questions.f: Theatre in the round has no scenery walls, so the actors' movement tells the story.

questions.q: The 'graph' in 'cinematograph' means…?
questions.f: Cinematograph literally means 'movement-writing' — the Lumiere brothers' 1895 camera-projector.

questions.q: 'Cinematography' combines roots meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek kinema (movement) + graphein (to write) — writing with movement.

questions.q: The word 'silhouette' is an eponym — it comes from the surname of a French…?
questions.f: Etienne de Silhouette's harsh 1759 budget cuts made cheap outline portraits a joke about him.

questions.q: The 'zoe' in 'zoetrope' means…?
questions.f: Zoetrope means 'wheel of life' — from Greek zoe (life) + tropos (turn).

questions.q: The 'phantasm' idea behind the 1790s 'phantasmagoria' shows referred to…?
questions.f: Showmen projected 'ghosts' onto smoke with hidden lanterns to thrill paying crowds.

questions.q: A 'magic lantern' was an early device that…?
c: Projected painted glass slides onto a wall
Lit up a stage from below
questions.f: Magic lanterns date to the 1600s — the ancestors of every film projector.

questions.q: 'Persistence of vision' describes how the eye and brain…?
c: Briefly hold an image after it disappears
questions.f: That lingering trace is part of why 24 separate frames per second look like smooth motion.

questions.q: The 'thaumatrope', an early animation toy, was a spinning…?
c: Disc with a picture on each side
questions.f: Spin a card with a bird on one side and a cage on the other, and the bird appears caged.

questions.q: The Lumiere brothers' first public film shows in 1895 took place in which city?
questions.f: Their programme included a train arriving at a station, which reportedly startled viewers.

questions.q: Georges Melies, an early film pioneer, was originally a…?
questions.f: Melies used his magic-show tricks to invent film effects like objects vanishing mid-shot.

questions.q: Melies's famous 1902 film A Trip to the Moon shows a rocket landing in the Moon's…?
questions.f: The hand-tinted versions of the film were coloured frame by frame with brushes.

questions.q: The 'stop trick', discovered accidentally by Melies, makes an object…?
questions.f: His camera jammed mid-shot; when he watched the film, a bus had turned into a hearse.

questions.q: The 'talkies' got their nickname because they were the first films with…?
questions.f: The Jazz Singer (1927) helped end the silent era with its spoken lines.

questions.q: In animation, a 'key frame' is a drawing that shows…?
c: An important pose in a movement
The final shot of a scene
questions.f: Key frames set the extremes of an action; the drawings between them create the flow.

questions.q: Disney's 'multiplane camera' created a sense of depth by filming…?
c: Several layers of artwork at different distances
questions.f: It won an Academy Award and made scenes in Bambi feel like real forests.

questions.q: 'Rendering' in computer animation means…?
c: Calculating the final image from the 3D scene data
questions.f: Some Pixar frames took many hours each to render, even on farms of computers.

questions.q: In 3D animation, a character's movable digital skeleton is called its…?
questions.f: Riggers build hundreds of controls so animators can move an eyebrow or a finger precisely.

questions.q: 'Motion capture' records an actor's movement using…?
c: Sensors or markers tracked by cameras
questions.f: Motion capture turns a performer's real walk into a digital creature's walk.

questions.q: A 'render farm' is a large collection of…?
questions.f: Big animated films need thousands of processors running for months.

questions.q: In traditional cel animation, backgrounds were painted separately from the characters.
questions.f: That let one painted background sit under hundreds of different character cels.

questions.q: The 'twelve principles of animation' were developed at which studio?
questions.f: Disney animators Ollie Johnston and Frank Thomas set them down in their book The Illusion of Life.

questions.q: In the animation principle 'follow through', a character's clothing or hair…?
c: Keeps moving after the body stops
questions.f: Follow through is why a cape swirls a moment after a hero halts.

questions.q: 'Exaggeration' as an animation principle means pushing an action to be…?
c: Clearer and more expressive than real life
questions.f: A cartoon character's jaw can drop to the floor — real surprise, exaggerated.

questions.q: 'Onion skinning' in animation software lets an artist see…?
questions.f: The name comes from the thin translucent paper animators once flipped through on a light box.

questions.q: The word 'proscenium' breaks down into parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek pro (before) + skene (stage building).

questions.q: In a theatre, the 'apron' is the part of the stage that…?
c: Juts out in front of the curtain
questions.f: Actors step onto the apron to speak directly to the audience.

questions.q: The 'orchestra pit' in a theatre is located…?
c: Below the front of the stage
questions.f: Sinking the musicians keeps sightlines clear so the audience sees the stage, not the trombones.

questions.q: A theatre's 'fly system' is used to…?
c: Raise and lower scenery from above
questions.f: Crew members called flymen haul counterweighted ropes to change scenes in seconds.

questions.q: A 'trapdoor' on a stage allows a performer to…?
c: Appear or vanish through the floor
questions.f: Shakespeare's Globe had a trapdoor its players called 'hell'.

questions.q: The 'ghost light' left burning on an empty stage overnight serves as a…?
questions.f: Superstition says it keeps theatre ghosts happy; practically, it stops people tripping.

questions.q: A play's 'denouement' is the part where…?
questions.f: 'Denouement' is French for 'untying' — the knot of the plot comes undone.

questions.q: A 'soliloquy' is a speech in which a character…?
questions.f: From Latin solus (alone) + loqui (to speak) — 'To be or not to be' is the most famous one.

questions.q: An 'aside' in a play is a remark made…?
c: To the audience, unheard by other characters
questions.f: Asides let the audience share a secret with one character.

questions.q: A 'prologue' comes at which point in a play?
questions.f: From Greek pro (before) + logos (word) — the words that come before the story.

questions.q: An 'epilogue' is the section that comes…?
questions.f: From Greek epi (upon, after) + logos (word).

questions.q: The Greek word 'skene' behind 'scene' and 'scenery' originally meant a…?
questions.f: The skene stood behind the Greek acting area, and its wall became the first backdrop.

questions.q: 'Deus ex machina' describes a plot solved by…?
c: A sudden unexpected rescue from outside
questions.f: It means 'god from the machine' — Greek theatres lowered gods in on a crane.

questions.q: In ancient Greek theatre, the flat circular dancing area was called the…?
questions.f: Modern orchestras are named after that space, where the chorus sang and danced.

questions.q: 'Thespian' is another word for an actor, named after Thespis, who is said to have been the first…?
c: Person to step out of the chorus and speak alone
questions.f: Thespis performed around 534 BCE, and actors have been 'thespians' ever since.

questions.q: Roman theatres were often built free-standing, while Greek ones usually leaned into a hillside.
questions.f: Greek builders used the natural slope for seating; Roman engineers raised their own with arches.

questions.q: 'Commedia dell'arte' was an Italian tradition of…?
c: Masked comedy with stock characters and improvising
questions.f: Its characters, like Harlequin and Pantalone, still shape clowns and cartoons today.

questions.q: Harlequin, from commedia dell'arte, is famous for a costume covered in…?
questions.f: Harlequin's diamond pattern began as patches on a poor servant's ragged clothes.

questions.q: 'Slapstick' comedy traces to a prop used in which tradition?
questions.f: The batacchio, or slap stick, cracked loudly while barely touching the other actor.

questions.q: In Japanese Bunraku puppet theatre, each large puppet is worked by…?
questions.f: The lead puppeteer works the head and right hand while assistants handle the left hand and feet.

questions.q: In Chinese opera, an actor's face paint colour signals the character's…?
questions.f: Red often marks loyalty and bravery, while white can suggest cunning.

questions.q: 'Kabuki' theatre began in Japan in about which century?
questions.f: Kabuki started with a dancer named Izumo no Okuni around 1603.

questions.q: In Kabuki, the raised walkway running into the audience is the…?
questions.f: 'Hanamichi' means 'flower path' — actors make grand entrances along it.

questions.q: Circus tradition credits Philip Astley, an English horseman, with inventing the…?
questions.f: His 1768 ring was about 13 metres across — still roughly the standard size today.

questions.q: A 'sideshow' at a travelling circus was…?
c: Extra attractions outside the main tent
questions.f: Sideshows featured jugglers, fortune tellers, and curiosities to draw in the crowd.

questions.q: The circus term 'clowning' includes a beginner clown role called the…?
questions.f: Classic circus clowning has three types: whiteface, auguste, and tramp.

questions.q: A 'diabolo' is a circus prop that is spun on…?
questions.f: Skilled players toss the diabolo metres into the air and catch it back on the string.

questions.q: A 'German wheel' is a circus apparatus that the performer…?
questions.f: The performer's own weight shifts steer the giant twin-hoop wheel across the floor.

questions.q: 'Equestrian' acts in a circus involve…?
questions.f: From Latin equus, 'horse' — trick riding was the very first circus act.

questions.q: A person who trains and cares for a circus's horses is a…?
questions.f: On a film set, by contrast, a 'grip' moves equipment and a 'gaffer' runs the lighting.

questions.q: On a film crew, the 'gaffer' is in charge of…?
questions.f: The gaffer's main assistant is called the best boy.

questions.q: A 'boom operator' on a film set holds a long pole carrying the…?
questions.f: The boom hovers just above the actors' heads, out of the camera's frame.

questions.q: 'Foley' artists in film-making create…?
c: Everyday sound effects performed in sync with picture
questions.f: Foley artists snap celery for breaking bones and shake gloves for bird wings.

questions.q: The 'Foley' in Foley sound is named after…?
questions.f: Jack Foley worked at Universal Studios in the early sound era, inventing the craft.

questions.q: A film's 'ADR' session brings actors back to…?
questions.f: ADR stands for automated dialogue replacement, sometimes called looping.

questions.q: On a film set, 'MOS' marks a shot filmed without recording sound.
questions.f: Crews joke it means 'mit out sound' — supposedly an early director's accented English.

questions.q: A 'dolly' on a film set is a wheeled platform for the…?
questions.f: A 'dolly zoom' moves the dolly while zooming the lens, warping the background eerily.

questions.q: A 'Steadicam' allows an operator to…?
c: Walk while keeping the shot smooth
questions.f: Its spring arm and vest absorb the operator's footsteps.

questions.q: A 'crane shot' lets the camera…?
questions.f: Crane shots often end a film by lifting away from the characters.

questions.q: A 'panning' shot moves the camera…?
c: Side to side on a fixed point
In a circle around the actor
questions.f: 'Pan' is short for 'panorama'; tilting up and down is called a tilt.

questions.q: 'Montage' in film-making means…?
c: A sequence of short shots compressing time
questions.f: 'Montage' is French for 'assembling' — training montages show months in a minute.

questions.q: A 'jump cut' produces the effect of…?
c: An abrupt leap forward in the same shot
questions.f: Jump cuts feel jarring on purpose, which is why online video creators love them.

questions.q: In a film script, 'INT.' at the start of a scene heading means the scene happens…?
questions.f: 'EXT.' means exterior — outdoors.

questions.q: A screenplay's 'logline' is…?
c: A one-sentence summary of the story
questions.f: Producers often decide whether to read a whole script based on its logline alone.

questions.q: 'Genre' entered English from French, where it means…?
questions.f: It shares an ancestor with 'genus' in biology and 'gender' in grammar.

questions.q: The word 'protagonist' contains 'agon', a Greek word for…?
questions.f: That same root gives us 'agony' — the struggle at a story's heart.

questions.q: 'Catastrophe', originally a term for a tragedy's final turn, literally means…?
questions.f: From Greek kata (down) + strephein (to turn) — the plot turns downward at the end.

questions.q: 'Improvisation' comes from a Latin root meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin improvisus, 'unforeseen' — improvisers cannot see what is coming.

questions.q: 'Repertoire' describes…?
c: The set of works a company can perform
questions.f: A repertory company rotates several plays instead of running just one.

questions.q: A 'troupe' is…?
questions.f: 'Troupe' and 'troop' are cousins — both mean an organized group.

questions.q: An 'impresario' is someone who…?
questions.f: 'Impresario' comes from Italian and is related to 'enterprise'.

questions.q: The word 'librettist' names the person who writes a musical work's…?
questions.f: 'Libretto' is Italian for 'little book' — the book of words.

questions.q: In musical theatre, the 'book' means the spoken script rather than the songs.
questions.f: A show's writing credits often list book, music, and lyrics as three separate jobs.

questions.q: An 'overture' is played…?
questions.f: 'Overture' comes from a word meaning 'opening' — it previews the show's best tunes.

questions.q: In a musical, the 'eleven o'clock number' is traditionally…?
questions.f: The name dates from when Broadway shows started at 8:30 and the big number landed near 11.

questions.q: Which long-running Broadway musical is based on T. S. Eliot's poems about felines?
questions.f: Cats ran on Broadway for 18 years, and the dancers wore intricate feline makeup.

questions.q: The Lion King stage musical is famous for its use of…?
questions.f: Director Julie Taymor let audiences see the puppeteers, making the artistry part of the magic.

questions.q: A theatre 'flat' is a piece of scenery that is…?
c: A light framed panel painted as a wall
questions.f: Flats are built of timber and canvas so two crew members can carry a whole wall.

questions.q: A 'cyclorama' in a theatre is a large…?
c: Curved backcloth lit to suggest sky
questions.f: Lighting a cyc in blue and orange can turn a bare stage into dawn.

questions.q: A 'gel' in stage lighting is a sheet used to…?
questions.f: They were once made from actual gelatine, which melted in the heat.

questions.q: A 'gobo' placed in a stage light projects…?
c: A pattern such as leaves or windows
questions.f: A leaf-pattern gobo is so common that lighting designers just call it 'breakup'.

questions.q: 'Blackout' in theatre terms means…?
c: All stage lights go out at once
questions.f: A snap blackout is one of the sharpest ways to end a scene.

questions.q: A 'quick change' in theatre is when a performer…?
questions.f: Dressers use velcro, magnets, and hidden zips to strip and redress an actor in 20 seconds.

questions.q: 'Pantomime', the British Christmas theatre tradition, typically includes a…?
c: Dame played comically by a man
questions.f: British panto also has audience shouting: 'He's behind you!'

questions.q: In animation, 'lip sync' means matching a character's mouth to the…?
questions.f: Animators break speech into mouth shapes called phonemes, or visemes.

questions.q: Which Studio Ghibli film won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature in 2003?
questions.f: It remains the only hand-drawn, non-English-language film to win that award.

questions.q: Studio Ghibli's Princess Mononoke is set in which period of Japanese history?
questions.f: Miyazaki set the film in an age when iron-working towns were pushing into ancient forests.

questions.q: Which Ghibli film features a girl working in a bathhouse for spirits?
questions.f: Chihiro must remember her own name to escape the spirit world.

questions.q: In Kiki's Delivery Service, Kiki starts a delivery business using her…?
questions.f: Kiki's black cat Jiji rides along on the broom handle.

questions.q: Which Pixar film features an elderly balloon salesman and a boy scout named Russell?
questions.f: The film's silent opening montage of Carl and Ellie's life is often called one of animation's finest scenes.

questions.q: Pixar's Coco is set during which Mexican celebration?
questions.f: Marigold petals form the bridge between the living world and the world of the ancestors.

questions.q: Which Pixar film's first 30 minutes contain almost no dialogue?
questions.f: WALL-E communicates almost entirely through beeps and body language, like a silent-film clown.

questions.q: Pixar's Inside Out takes place mostly inside a girl's…?
questions.f: Its emotion characters — Joy, Sadness, Fear, Anger, Disgust — were shaped with help from real psychologists.

questions.q: Which animation studio created Bugs Bunny and the Looney Tunes?
questions.f: Their animation building was jokingly nicknamed 'Termite Terrace'.

questions.q: The Flintstones, from 1960, was notable as the first…?
questions.f: It was made by Hanna-Barbera, who also gave us Scooby-Doo and Yogi Bear.

questions.q: Which animation technique did Ray Harryhausen make famous with creatures in adventure films?
questions.f: Harryhausen called his method 'Dynamation' — models moved frame by frame against live footage.

questions.q: The 1933 film King Kong brought its giant ape to life mainly using…?
questions.f: The main Kong model stood only about 46 cm tall.

questions.q: 'Aardman', the studio behind Wallace and Gromit, is based in which country?
questions.f: Aardman works in Bristol, and its animators leave tiny thumbprints in the plasticine.

questions.q: Wallace and Gromit's creator is which animator?
questions.f: Nick Park began Wallace and Gromit as a student film that took years to complete.

questions.q: A single day's shooting on a stop-motion film may produce only a few seconds of finished footage.
questions.f: Aardman animators average around two seconds per day.

questions.q: The word 'plasticine' describes modelling clay that is famous for…?
questions.f: Its oil base keeps it soft, which is exactly what stop-motion animators need.

questions.q: 'Pixilation' as an animation term means stop-motion using…?
c: Real people as the frame-by-frame subjects
questions.f: Actors hold still, get photographed, shift slightly, and appear to glide magically.

questions.q: In film production, 'pre-production' includes…?
questions.f: The three broad stages are pre-production, production, and post-production.

questions.q: 'Post-production' is when a film is…?
questions.f: Post can take longer than shooting, especially with heavy visual effects.

questions.q: A film's 'principal photography' is the period when…?
questions.f: Studios announce the start of principal photography as a milestone.

questions.q: A 'shooting schedule' groups scenes mainly by…?
questions.f: That is why actors often film a story's ending before its beginning.

questions.q: The 'continuity' supervisor's job is to make sure…?
questions.f: They track everything from a half-eaten sandwich to which hand held the umbrella.

questions.q: A film 'blooper' is…?
c: A mistake accidentally captured on film
questions.f: Some films run bloopers over the end credits as a treat.

questions.q: A hidden joke or reference tucked into a film for sharp-eyed viewers is called an…?
questions.f: Pixar hides the Pizza Planet truck from Toy Story in nearly all its films.

questions.q: A story that goes back to show events before the original is a…?
questions.f: 'Prequel' is a modern blend of 'pre' and 'sequel', coined in the 20th century.

questions.q: A 'spin-off' series takes a character from one show and gives them…?
c: A bigger part in the old show
questions.f: Frasier and Better Call Saul are two of the most successful spin-offs ever made.

questions.q: A 'reboot' of a film series means…?
c: Starting the story fresh with a new version
questions.f: The word borrows from computing — you restart the whole system.

questions.q: The word 'anthology' describes a series where each episode…?
questions.f: From Greek anthos (flower) + logia (collection) — literally a gathering of flowers.

questions.q: 'Adaptation' in film means turning a novel or play into…?
questions.f: Adapting a 400-page novel means choosing which scenes tell the story fastest.

questions.q: Shakespeare's plays have been adapted into films set in modern schools, gangs, and even outer space.
questions.f: West Side Story reworks Romeo and Juliet, and The Lion King echoes Hamlet.

questions.q: 'Auteur', used of directors with a strong personal style, is French for…?
questions.f: Critics argue an auteur's films are as personally written as a novel.

questions.q: The 'fourth wall' in theatre is the imaginary wall…?
c: Between the actors and the audience
At the back of the set
questions.f: 'Breaking the fourth wall' means a character speaks straight to the audience.

questions.q: A 'thrust stage' extends into the audience on how many sides?
questions.f: Shakespeare's Globe used a thrust stage, putting groundlings on three sides of the action.

questions.q: 'Groundlings' at Shakespeare's Globe were audience members who…?
questions.f: A standing ticket cost one penny, making theatre affordable to almost everyone.

questions.q: Shakespeare's acting company was known by which name during James I's reign?
questions.f: They were the Lord Chamberlain's Men until King James became their patron in 1603.

questions.q: The word 'melodrama' describes a story style that emphasises…?
c: Big emotions and clear heroes and villains
questions.f: Victorian melodramas came with sweeping music to cue the audience's feelings.

questions.q: 'Farce' is a comedy style built on…?
questions.f: 'Farce' comes from a word meaning 'stuffing' — comic bits stuffed into a serious play.

questions.q: 'Satire' uses humour mainly to…?
c: Criticise faults in people or society
questions.f: Satirists have poked fun at the powerful since ancient Rome.

questions.q: 'Parody' means a work that…?
c: Imitates another work for comic effect
questions.f: From Greek para (beside) + oide (song) — a song sung alongside another.

questions.q: 'Slapstick' and 'pratfall' both refer to comedy involving…?
questions.f: A pratfall is a deliberate, harmless-looking fall onto the backside.

questions.q: A 'double act' in comedy usually pairs a 'straight man' with a…?
questions.f: The straight man plays it seriously so the comic's nonsense lands harder.

questions.q: 'Timing' in comedy refers mainly to…?
c: The exact pause before a punch line
questions.f: Comedians say the pause is the joke — a half-second changes everything.

questions.q: Buster Keaton famously performed a stunt in which a house front fell around him, missing him through…?
questions.f: The clearance was only centimetres — Keaton designed and marked the spot himself.

questions.q: Harold Lloyd's most famous image shows him hanging from a giant…?
questions.f: The 1923 film Safety Last! used clever camera angles above a real Los Angeles street.

questions.q: Charlie Chaplin's film The Gold Rush includes a famous scene where the Tramp eats a…?
questions.f: The 'boot' was made of liquorice, and Chaplin reportedly needed dozens of takes.

questions.q: Chaplin, Douglas Fairbanks, Mary Pickford and D. W. Griffith founded which studio in 1919?
questions.f: They created it so artists, not executives, would control their own films.

questions.q: Charlie Chaplin kept making largely silent films for years after sound arrived.
questions.f: He believed the Tramp's magic lay in mime, and City Lights (1931) proved him right.

questions.q: The word 'kinetoscope', an early Edison device, let people watch films…?
c: One person at a time through a peephole
questions.f: Kinetoscope parlours charged a coin for a short peep-show film.

questions.q: 'Nickelodeon', the name of early American cinemas, referred to their…?
questions.f: 'Odeon' comes from a Greek word for a building for musical performances.

questions.q: The root 'ode' inside 'odeon' and 'melody' means…?
questions.f: From Greek oide, 'song' — the same root in 'parody' and 'rhapsody'.

questions.q: An 'opera' takes its name from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin opus, 'work' — the plural opera meant works of art.

questions.q: A 'diva' in performance originally meant a…?
questions.f: From Latin diva, 'goddess' — the highest praise for a leading soprano.

questions.q: 'Prima ballerina' means the…?
questions.f: The very top rank in some companies is prima ballerina assoluta — 'absolute first'.

questions.q: In ballet and stage dance, a 'pas de deux' is a dance for…?
questions.f: French 'pas' means step, so it is literally a step of two.

questions.q: 'Tap dancing' makes its sound from plates fitted to the dancer's…?
questions.f: Metal taps at the toe and heel turn the dancer into a percussion instrument.

questions.q: A 'vaudeville circuit' was…?
c: A chain of theatres a show toured
questions.f: Performers travelled the circuits by train, doing the same act in city after city.

questions.q: A 'headliner' on a show bill is the act that…?
c: Is most famous and best placed
questions.f: Being 'top of the bill' was the ambition of every vaudeville performer.

questions.q: In show business, being 'typecast' means an actor…?
c: Keeps getting the same kind of role
questions.f: Some actors deliberately take a wildly different role to break out of typecasting.

questions.q: An 'ingenue' role in theatre is traditionally a…?
questions.f: 'Ingenue' comes from a French word meaning naive or artless.

questions.q: A theatre 'dresser' is the person who…?
c: Helps actors in and out of costume
questions.f: During a big musical a dresser may handle 30 costume changes a night.

questions.q: 'Wardrobe' is the department in a theatre or film that handles costumes.
questions.f: Big productions keep costume 'bibles' with photos of every outfit for continuity.

questions.q: 'Prosthetic' makeup uses pieces made of…?
c: Silicone or foam latex glued to the skin
questions.f: A full prosthetic makeup can take four hours to apply before filming begins.

questions.q: The word 'prosthetic' comes from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Greek pros (toward) + thesis (placing) — placing something on.

questions.q: 'Animatronic' creatures in films are controlled by…?
questions.f: The Jurassic Park T-rex included a full-size animatronic weighing over five tonnes.

questions.q: 'Puppetry' using a rod attached to the puppet's arm is called…?
questions.f: Muppet arms are usually worked with thin rods the camera never sees.

questions.q: In Indonesian wayang kulit, the puppeteer who performs all the voices is the…?
questions.f: A dalang may perform for eight hours straight, voicing dozens of characters.

questions.q: Which instrument ensemble traditionally accompanies Indonesian shadow-puppet plays?
questions.f: A gamelan is built mostly of tuned metal gongs and metallophones.

questions.q: Turkish shadow theatre, featuring the characters Karagoz and Hacivat, uses puppets made of…?
questions.f: Light shines through the coloured leather, so the shadows appear in colour.

questions.q: The Italian puppet character Pulcinella is the ancestor of which British puppet?
questions.f: 'Punch' is short for Punchinello, the English version of Pulcinella's name.

questions.q: A 'swazzle' is a device a Punch and Judy performer holds…?
c: In the mouth to make Punch's voice
In the hand as a prop
questions.f: The reed device gives Punch his famous squawking voice.

questions.q: 'Marionette' comes from a French word that literally means…?
questions.f: Early European puppet plays often featured the Virgin Mary, giving 'little Marys' their name.

questions.q: A puppet's control bar or paddle held by the puppeteer is often called the…?
questions.f: An airplane control is one common design, with the puppet's strings tied at balanced points.

questions.q: 'Supermarionation', used in Thunderbirds, was a technique for…?
questions.f: Gerry Anderson's puppets had solenoids in their heads that moved their lips with the recorded dialogue.

questions.q: Sesame Street was created with the goal of helping children learn before starting school.
questions.f: Researchers tested episodes with real children and adjusted the show based on what held their attention.

questions.q: The circus term 'Greatest Show on Earth' was the slogan of which showman's circus?
questions.f: Barnum joined forces with James Bailey, and later the Ringling brothers, to tour America by train.

questions.q: Circus tents were nicknamed 'big tops' partly because the show ran…?
c: Under the highest section of canvas
questions.f: Crews raised the canvas on tall centre poles, some over 15 metres high.

questions.q: A circus 'roustabout' was a worker who…?
c: Set up and took down the tents
questions.f: A big circus could raise its entire tent city in a single morning.

questions.q: The 'human cannonball' act launches a performer using a…?
questions.f: The flash and boom are showmanship; the real push comes from air or springs.

questions.q: Circus performers who ride bicycles, spin plates and balance objects are doing acts of…?
questions.f: 'Equilibristics' is the formal circus word for balancing skills.

questions.q: 'Legerdemain', a word for conjuring, literally means…?
questions.f: From French leger de main — the polite old term for sleight of hand.

questions.q: 'Prestidigitation' is built from parts meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin roots for quick and finger — a fancy word for magic with the hands.

questions.q: Harry Houdini became world-famous as an…?
questions.f: Houdini escaped from handcuffs, packing crates, and a milk can filled with water.

questions.q: 'Vanishing' and 'levitation' are categories of…?
questions.f: Magicians classify effects into families like production, vanish, transformation and levitation.

questions.q: 'Pepper's ghost' is a stage illusion created using a large…?
questions.f: Named for John Henry Pepper, who demonstrated it in London in 1862 — theme parks still use it.

questions.q: In television, a 'teleprompter' displays…?
c: Words for the presenter to read
questions.f: The text scrolls over the lens, so a presenter can read and look straight at you.

questions.q: The word 'broadcast' originally described…?
questions.f: Radio engineers borrowed the farming word for scattering a signal in all directions.

questions.q: A television 'showrunner' is the person who…?
c: Leads the writing and overall creative direction
questions.f: The showrunner is usually the head writer and an executive producer at once.

questions.q: 'Syndication' means a TV show is…?
c: Sold to many separate stations or channels
questions.f: Syndication is why the same sitcom reruns can play in dozens of countries at once.

questions.q: The Muppets' name is said by Jim Henson to have blended which two words?
questions.f: Henson sometimes said he simply liked the sound of the word he had invented.

questions.q: A theatre 'programme' or 'playbill' typically lists the…?
questions.f: Collectors treasure playbills from famous opening nights.

questions.q: A 'dark' night in a theatre's schedule means the theatre is…?
questions.f: Most West End and Broadway houses are traditionally dark on Mondays.

questions.q: The word 'thespian' honours Thespis, but the word 'tragedy' itself literally means…?
questions.f: From Greek tragos (goat) + oide (song) — perhaps from goat-costumed choruses at Dionysian festivals.

questions.q: The Greek word 'hamartia', central to Aristotle's theory of tragedy, means…?
questions.f: It is an archery term — the tragic hero's error is an arrow that misses.

questions.q: Aristotle's term 'catharsis', describing tragedy's effect on an audience, literally means…?
questions.f: The same Greek root gives us 'cathartic' — tragedy purges pity and fear.

questions.q: Aristotle's 'peripeteia' in a tragic plot refers to a…?
questions.f: Its partner term is 'anagnorisis' — the moment of recognition, as when Oedipus learns the truth.

questions.q: The theatre term 'mise-en-scene' refers to…?
c: Everything arranged within the frame or on stage
questions.f: French for 'placing on stage' — critics use it for lighting, blocking, costume and set together.

questions.q: In film theory, 'diegetic' sound is sound that…?
c: Comes from within the story's world
questions.f: A car radio the characters hear is diegetic; the swelling score behind them is not.

questions.q: The Russian film-maker Sergei Eisenstein is most associated with theories of…?
questions.f: His 'Odessa Steps' sequence in Battleship Potemkin is the most studied edit in cinema.

questions.q: The 'Kuleshov effect' demonstrates that an audience's reading of a face depends on…?
c: The shot placed next to it
questions.f: Kuleshov cut the same neutral face against a coffin, a girl, and food — viewers saw grief, love, hunger.

questions.q: A 'MacGuffin', a term popularised by Alfred Hitchcock, is…?
c: An object that drives the plot but hardly matters in itself
questions.f: Hitchcock said the audience cares only that the characters care about it.

questions.q: Hitchcock pioneered a shot combining a zoom with a track in the opposite direction, now called the…?
questions.f: Also called the Vertigo effect, it makes the background rush while the subject stays fixed.

questions.q: 'Chiaroscuro' lighting, borrowed by film noir from painting, means strong contrast between…?
questions.f: From Italian chiaro (light) + oscuro (dark) — think of a single lamp cutting shadows across a face.

questions.q: 'Film noir' is French for…?
questions.f: French critics coined it in 1946 after seeing a wave of shadowy American thrillers at once.

questions.q: The 'German Expressionist' film The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) is famous for its…?
questions.f: Its crooked walls and slanted windows were painted flat onto canvas, tilting reality itself.

questions.q: The 1927 German film Metropolis is set in a…?
questions.f: Its robot Maria is one of the most copied designs in science-fiction history.

questions.q: 'Italian neorealism' films of the 1940s were known for using…?
questions.f: Post-war studios were damaged, so directors simply filmed in the streets.

questions.q: Akira Kurosawa's Seven Samurai directly inspired which American film genre remake?
questions.f: It became The Magnificent Seven — and its plot shape echoes through countless later films.

questions.q: The word 'benshi' describes a Japanese performer who, during silent films, provided…?
questions.f: Star benshi were sometimes bigger draws than the films themselves.

questions.q: The animation term 'xerography', adopted by Disney for One Hundred and One Dalmatians, replaced…?
questions.f: Photocopying the pencil lines saved enormous labour — and gave the film its sketchy look.

questions.q: Disney's Sleeping Beauty was made in an unusually wide format and cost so much it briefly hurt the studio's finances.
questions.f: Its angular, tapestry-inspired style came from artist Eyvind Earle.

questions.q: The 'nine old men' were a legendary group of…?
questions.f: Walt Disney borrowed the nickname from the US Supreme Court to describe his core animators.

questions.q: Ub Iwerks was the animator who, working with Walt Disney, largely drew the first…?
questions.f: Iwerks reportedly animated hundreds of drawings a day and later won Oscars for technical work.

questions.q: Before Mickey Mouse, Walt Disney's studio created a character named…?
questions.f: Disney lost the rights to Oswald in 1928 — and invented Mickey in response.

questions.q: 'Betty Boop' and 'Popeye' cartoons came from which pioneering studio?
questions.f: Max Fleischer also patented the rotoscope, tracing over live footage for lifelike motion.

questions.q: Winsor McCay's 1914 Gertie the Dinosaur was groundbreaking partly because McCay performed it…?
c: Live on stage, appearing to interact with the animation
questions.f: McCay 'fed' Gertie an apple by tossing a real one as the animated dinosaur caught a drawn one.

questions.q: Emile Cohl's Fantasmagorie (1908) is often cited as one of the first…?
questions.f: Its white-on-black look came from filming black ink drawings and printing the negative.

questions.q: Lotte Reiniger's The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926) was animated using…?
questions.f: Reiniger hand-cut every jointed figure from lead-weighted card — thousands of tiny moves.

questions.q: 'Norman McLaren', the animation pioneer, worked chiefly for the film board of which country?
questions.f: McLaren even drew sound directly onto the film's optical soundtrack to make music.

questions.q: A film shot at a higher frame rate and played at normal speed produces…?
questions.f: Shoot 120 frames a second, play back 24, and one second stretches to five.

questions.q: 'Undercranking' a camera makes the action look…?
questions.f: The word survives from hand-cranked cameras, whose speed depended on the operator's arm.

questions.q: 'Time-lapse' photography compresses hours into seconds by shooting frames…?
questions.f: One frame every 30 seconds turns a whole sunset into a few flowing seconds.

questions.q: The term 'aspect ratio' describes a picture's…?
questions.f: Classic Academy ratio was 1.37:1; modern widescreen films are often 2.39:1.

questions.q: 'Pan and scan', once used for showing films on old TVs, involved…?
c: Cropping the sides of a widescreen image
questions.f: Directors hated it — a two-person conversation could lose one of the faces entirely.

questions.q: 'Letterboxing' preserves a widescreen film on a narrower screen by adding…?
questions.f: The name comes from the shape of a letterbox slot.

questions.q: 'Cinerama' and 'CinemaScope' were 1950s systems invented largely to compete with…?
questions.f: Studios reasoned that a screen the size of a wall was something no home set could match.

questions.q: 'Anamorphic' lenses squeeze a wide image onto standard film and are then unsqueezed by…?
c: A matching lens on the projector
questions.f: Anamorphic lenses also create those long horizontal blue lens flares film-makers love.

questions.q: A 'long take' is a single unbroken shot, and some films are edited to appear as one continuous take.
questions.f: Hitchcock's Rope and the film 1917 both hide their cuts to feel seamless.

questions.q: Unlike a stunt double, a 'body double' on a film set is used for…?
c: Non-dangerous shots where the face is not seen
questions.f: Body doubles handle hands-on-piano close-ups or over-the-shoulder walks.

questions.q: A 'squib' on a film set is a small device used to…?
c: Create a tiny practical burst or spark
questions.f: Special-effects crews trigger squibs electrically, always under strict safety supervision.

questions.q: 'Breakaway' props on a film set are made from materials that…?
questions.f: Breakaway 'glass' is often sugar-based or resin, so it crumbles without sharp edges.

questions.q: 'Matte painting' in classic film-making added…?
c: Painted scenery blended with live footage
questions.f: Empire Strikes Back and countless epics used glass paintings for cities that never existed.

questions.q: 'Forced perspective' makes objects look bigger or smaller by exploiting…?
questions.f: The Lord of the Rings used it to make hobbits shorter while actors shared one shot.

questions.q: 'Bullet time', made famous by The Matrix, is created using…?
c: Many still cameras fired in sequence
questions.f: A ring of cameras fires in a wave, so the viewpoint moves while time nearly stops.

questions.q: 'Ray tracing' in computer animation simulates…?
questions.f: Tracing light paths gives realistic reflections and shadows — but costs enormous computing time.

questions.q: 'Subsurface scattering' is a rendering technique that makes which material look right?
questions.f: Light enters skin, scatters inside, and glows back out — that is why ears look red in sunlight.

questions.q: Pixar's software for lighting and rendering its films is called…?
questions.f: RenderMan has won Academy Awards for technical achievement and is used across the industry.

questions.q: Which computer-animated short won Pixar its first Academy Award, in 1989?
questions.f: Tin Toy's baby character led directly to the technology behind Toy Story.

questions.q: Before making features, Pixar's main business was selling…?
questions.f: Pixar started as a hardware division inside Lucasfilm before Steve Jobs bought it in 1986.

questions.q: The technical challenge that Pixar's Brave was built to solve was realistic…?
questions.f: Merida's hair uses about 1,500 individually simulated curls.

questions.q: Disney's Frozen required new simulation research into…?
questions.f: Engineers built a snow solver so drifts, powder and packed snow would all behave differently.

questions.q: Studio Ghibli's Hayao Miyazaki has said he prefers hand-drawn animation to computer imagery.
questions.f: Ghibli has used digital tools, but Miyazaki insists the drawing must lead.

questions.q: Isao Takahata, co-founder of Studio Ghibli, directed which film about a bamboo-cutter's daughter?
c: The Tale of the Princess Kaguya
questions.f: Its sketchy charcoal-and-watercolour look deliberately leaves the drawings unfinished at the edges.

questions.q: The Ghibli film Castle in the Sky features a floating island named…?
questions.f: Miyazaki took the name from Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels.

questions.q: A Broadway theatre must have at least how many seats to be officially considered 'Broadway'?
questions.f: Houses of 100 to 499 seats are 'Off-Broadway'; under 100 is 'Off-Off-Broadway'.

questions.q: Which musical, opening in 1943, is often credited with integrating song, story and dance into one whole?
questions.f: Rodgers and Hammerstein used a dream ballet to advance the plot — revolutionary at the time.

questions.q: Which musical holds the record as the longest-running show in Broadway history?
questions.f: It played over 13,000 performances across 35 years before closing in 2023.

questions.q: Lin-Manuel Miranda's Hamilton tells its story mainly through…?
questions.f: Miranda read a biography on holiday and thought the story sounded like a rap album.

questions.q: The musical Wicked reimagines the story of which earlier work?
questions.f: It follows Elphaba and Glinda before Dorothy ever arrives in Oz.

questions.q: 'Les Miserables' the musical is based on a novel by which author?
questions.f: Hugo's 1862 novel runs well over a thousand pages.

questions.q: In theatre lighting, a 'Fresnel' lantern is named after a French physicist whose lens design first improved…?
questions.f: Augustin-Jean Fresnel's stepped lens threw light far out to sea — and now across a stage.

questions.q: A theatre lantern with sharp-edged, shapeable beams is commonly called a…?
questions.f: Its internal shutters let a designer cut the beam into precise squares of light.

questions.q: 'Limelight' was a genuine Victorian stage light produced by heating…?
questions.f: Heating calcium oxide in a flame gives a brilliant white glow — hence 'in the limelight'.

questions.q: 'Upstage' originally referred to a raked stage's higher part, meaning the area…?
questions.f: Old stages sloped up toward the back, so 'upstage' really was uphill.

questions.q: In theatre directions, 'stage left' means the left as seen by…?
questions.f: The audience's left is 'stage right' — a classic source of rehearsal confusion.

questions.q: A 'raked' stage is one that is…?
questions.f: The rake is why 'upstage' and 'downstage' are vertical words for horizontal places.

questions.q: A revolving stage lets an entire set turn to reveal another scene already built behind it.
questions.f: Les Miserables famously used a huge revolve for its barricade scenes.

questions.q: 'Kabuki drop' describes a stage effect in which a cloth…?
c: Falls instantly to reveal what is behind
questions.f: Releasing pins at once drops the whole curtain in a heartbeat — hence the surprise.

questions.q: In Kabuki, the sudden dramatic pose an actor freezes into is called a…?
questions.f: The audience often shouts the actor's family name at exactly that moment.

questions.q: Japan's oldest surviving major theatre form, older than Kabuki and using carved wooden masks, is…?
questions.f: Noh dates to the 14th century, and some masks in use are centuries old.

questions.q: In Sanskrit drama theory, the ancient treatise on performance is called the…?
questions.f: It analyses dance, music and emotion, and is credited to the sage Bharata.

questions.q: Kathakali, a dramatic dance-theatre form with elaborate green face paint, comes from which Indian state?
questions.f: A Kathakali performer's makeup can take three hours and uses rice paste and mineral colours.

questions.q: The Chinese theatre form often called 'Peking opera' combines singing, acrobatics and…?
questions.f: Every hand position and sleeve flick carries a fixed meaning trained performers learn for years.

questions.q: A ring exactly 13 metres across, a former cavalry trick-rider, and a London riding school in 1768 point to the invention of the modern…?
questions.f: Philip Astley found that 13 metres was the perfect diameter for centrifugal force to help a standing rider.

questions.q: A jammed camera, a stage magician's day job, and a shot of a rocket in the Moon's eye all point to which film pioneer?
questions.f: Melies made over 500 films — and years later sold toys in a Paris railway station, forgotten.

questions.q: A lost rabbit named Oswald, a train journey back from New York in 1928, and a whistling steamboat pilot converge on the creation of…?
questions.f: Legend says Disney sketched the mouse on that train ride home after losing Oswald's rights.

questions.q: Liquorice boiled to look like leather, a Klondike setting, and a dance performed with two forks and bread rolls all come from which film?
questions.f: Chaplin's 1925 film is the one he said he most wanted to be remembered for.

questions.q: A word for a hot desert wind, an Italian reconnaissance aircraft, and a 1985 Tokyo studio founding all connect to which animation house?
questions.f: Miyazaki, an aircraft enthusiast, misremembered the pronunciation — it should be 'gibli'.

questions.q: Metal plates on shoes, minstrel and Irish step traditions, and Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson's stair dance all point to which dance form?
questions.f: Robinson's famous staircase dance made every step a different musical pitch.

questions.q: A block of quicklime, a Victorian gas flame, and the phrase for public attention all lead to which stage invention?
questions.f: Limelight was so intensely white that theatres used it to pick out a single leading actor.

questions.q: A milk can filled with water, a Hungarian-born rabbi's son, and a career debunking fake spirit mediums point to which performer?
questions.f: Houdini was born Erik Weisz in Budapest and took his stage name from the magician Robert-Houdin.

questions.q: A sheet of angled glass, a Royal Polytechnic lecture in 1862, and today's theme-park ghosts all descend from an illusion named after…?
questions.f: Pepper popularised it so successfully that his name stuck, though engineer Henry Dircks devised it.

questions.q: A trapdoor nicknamed 'hell', a thatched roof that burned in 1613, and standing spectators paying a penny describe which theatre?
questions.f: A cannon effect during Henry VIII set the thatch alight, burning the Globe to the ground in an hour.

questions.q: A jointed cardboard figure weighted with lead, three years of frame-by-frame work, and a 1926 German feature point to which animator?
questions.f: Reiniger's Prince Achmed is the oldest surviving animated feature film.

questions.q: A camera obscura, painted glass slides, and 17th-century Dutch lenses are the ancestors of which device?
questions.f: Christiaan Huygens is often credited with an early magic lantern around 1659.

questions.q: A row of trip-wired cameras, a bet about a galloping horse, and a Californian racetrack in 1878 point to which photographer?
questions.f: Muybridge proved a galloping horse lifts all four hooves at once — and inspired motion pictures.

questions.q: A solenoid in a puppet's head, a rescue organisation called International Rescue, and lip movements synced to tape point to which technique?
questions.f: Gerry and Sylvia Anderson's Thunderbirds made those electrically twitching puppet lips famous.

questions.q: 'Go-motion', developed for creature effects, improved stop-motion by adding…?
questions.f: Moving the model slightly while the shutter is open makes fast action look natural, not jerky.

questions.q: A film's 'negative cost' refers to…?
c: The cost of producing it, before marketing
The cost of the film stock
questions.f: Studios distinguish negative cost from prints-and-advertising, or P&A, spending.

questions.q: 'Box office' is thought to be named after the…?
c: Booth or box where tickets were sold
questions.f: Either way, box-office totals became the industry's scoreboard.

questions.q: The 'Hays Code', enforced in Hollywood from the 1930s, was a system of…?
questions.f: It was replaced in 1968 by the film ratings system used today.

questions.q: The film industry term 'blockbuster' is generally believed to come from…?
c: A cinema queue stretching around the block
questions.f: By the 1970s, Jaws and Star Wars had redefined what a blockbuster season looked like.

questions.q: 'Sleeper hit' describes a film that…?
questions.f: Word of mouth, rather than advertising, drives a sleeper's long run.

questions.q: The Academy Awards ceremony was first held in 1929 and lasted only about 15 minutes.
questions.f: Winners had been announced three months earlier, so there was no suspense to draw out.

questions.q: The Oscar statuette's official name is the…?
questions.f: It depicts a knight standing on a film reel with five spokes for the Academy's original branches.

questions.q: Walt Disney received a special Oscar for Snow White consisting of one full-size statuette plus…?
questions.f: Shirley Temple presented it to him in 1939 — one Oscar for each dwarf.

questions.q: Which film was the first animated feature nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture?
questions.f: Its 1991 nomination came before a separate Best Animated Feature category even existed.

questions.q: The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature was first presented in which year?
questions.f: Shrek won the first one, for films of 2001.

questions.q: The Palme d'Or is the top prize at which film festival?
questions.f: The palm design honours the palm trees along the Croisette in Cannes.

questions.q: The Golden Bear is the main award at the film festival held in which city?
questions.f: The bear has been Berlin's civic symbol for centuries.

questions.q: The Golden Lion is awarded at the world's oldest film festival, founded in 1932 in…?
questions.f: The lion is the emblem of Saint Mark, patron of Venice.

questions.q: 'EGOT' describes a performer who has won an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and…?
questions.f: Only a couple of dozen people have ever completed the set.

questions.q: The 'Method', taught by Lee Strasberg and others, asks actors to draw on…?
questions.f: It grew from the ideas of Russian director Konstantin Stanislavski.

questions.q: Konstantin Stanislavski's famous question for actors to ask about a character was…?
questions.f: Stanislavski called a character's goal their 'objective' — and the whole play's aim the 'superobjective'.

questions.q: Bertolt Brecht's 'Verfremdungseffekt' aimed to make an audience…?
c: Think critically rather than lose themselves in the story
questions.f: Often translated as the 'alienation effect', it used signs, songs and visible lights to break the illusion.

questions.q: 'Theatre of the Absurd' plays, such as Waiting for Godot, typically feature…?
c: Characters in situations without clear meaning
questions.f: Samuel Beckett's tramps wait for someone who never arrives — twice.

questions.q: A 'closet drama' is a play written…?
c: To be read rather than staged
questions.f: Some Romantic poets wrote grand dramas they never expected any theatre to attempt.

questions.q: A 'masque' in Renaissance courts combined poetry and music with…?
c: Elaborate costumes and dancing by courtiers
questions.f: Inigo Jones designed spectacular masque machinery for the English court.

questions.q: 'Kabuki' is written with characters often glossed as…?
questions.f: The word may also derive from 'kabuku', meaning to lean or be unconventional.

questions.q: Women were banned from the Kabuki stage in 1629, and male actors took over female roles.
questions.f: Those specialists are called onnagata, and the tradition continues today.

questions.q: The word 'circus' in 'Piccadilly Circus' preserves its original sense of a…?
questions.f: London's 'circuses' are road junctions that were originally designed as circles.

questions.q: 'Juggling' comes through Old French from a Latin word for one who…?
questions.f: From Latin joculari, 'to jest' — a medieval 'jongleur' told tales as well as tossing balls.

questions.q: The theatrical word 'clown' may share an origin with words for a…?
questions.f: Both trace to the idea of a coarse countryman — a rustic among sophisticates.

questions.q: 'Buffoon' derives from a word connected to…?
questions.f: From Italian buffare, 'to puff' — a comic's face-pulling gave us the word.

questions.q: 'Harlequin' likely descends from the name of a medieval…?
questions.f: 'Hellequin' led a troop of demons in old French drama before becoming a nimble comic servant.

questions.q: 'Pantaloons', the trousers, are named after Pantalone, a commedia character who was a…?
questions.f: His long tight breeches were so distinctive they named a garment — and gave us 'pants'.

questions.q: 'Zany', now meaning wildly funny, began as the name of a commedia…?
questions.f: 'Zanni' was a whole class of comic servants, including Harlequin himself.

questions.q: 'Scaramouche', a word for a boastful coward, came from a commedia character and later appeared in…?
questions.f: Queen's Bohemian Rhapsody asks 'Scaramouche, Scaramouche, will you do the Fandango?'

questions.q: The word 'vaudeville' may come from a French phrase referring to…?
c: Songs of the valley of the Vire
questions.f: Another theory traces it to 'voix de ville', voice of the town.

questions.q: 'Burlesque' originally meant a work that was…?
c: A comic imitation of something serious
questions.f: From Italian burla, 'a joke' — the earliest burlesques parodied grand opera.

questions.q: 'Revue' as a theatrical form is characterised by…?
c: Sketches and songs with no continuous plot
questions.f: French for 'review' — the show reviews topical fashions and follies.

questions.q: A 'jukebox musical' is one built around…?
questions.f: Mamma Mia! turned ABBA's back catalogue into a global stage hit.

questions.q: The 'ghost light' tradition has a practical cousin in film: the 'martini shot', which is the…?
questions.f: After the martini shot, crews say the next one is served in a glass.

questions.q: On film sets, 'golden hour' refers to the brief period after sunrise or before sunset with soft warm light.
questions.f: Terrence Malick's Days of Heaven was shot almost entirely in that narrow window.

questions.q: 'Day for night' shooting means filming in daylight and then…?
c: Darkening the footage to look like night
questions.f: The French call it 'la nuit americaine' — the American night.

questions.q: The camera term 'zoom' describes changing the lens's…?
questions.f: A dolly physically moves the camera; a zoom only changes the lens's magnification.

questions.q: 'Depth of field' describes how much of the image is…?
questions.f: Shallow depth of field isolates a face against a soft, creamy background.

questions.q: 'Rack focus' is the technique of…?
c: Shifting focus from one subject to another within a shot
questions.f: It steers the audience's eye without a single cut.

questions.q: A 'Dutch angle' shot tilts the camera to suggest…?
questions.f: Despite the name it comes from 'Deutsch' — German Expressionist film-makers loved it.

questions.q: 'Chroma key' compositing works by removing pixels of a chosen…?
questions.f: Blue screens once dominated, but digital sensors handle green more cleanly.

questions.q: A film's 'colour grade' is the process of…?
c: Adjusting colours and contrast to a final look
questions.f: Digital grading lets a colourist push a whole film cold blue or warm gold.

questions.q: 'Persistence of vision' is often paired with a related effect named…?
questions.f: Max Wertheimer's phi phenomenon explains how the brain constructs motion between still images.

questions.q: The 'praxinoscope', an improvement on the zoetrope, used what to view the strip?
questions.f: Emile Reynaud's mirrors gave a brighter, undistorted picture — and he later projected the images.

questions.q: Emile Reynaud's 'Theatre Optique' of 1892 is remarkable because it presented animation…?
questions.f: He hand-painted long perforated bands of images — three years before the Lumieres' film shows.

questions.q: 'Cinema verite' describes documentary film-making that…?
c: Observes real life with minimal interference
questions.f: French for 'cinema truth' — lightweight cameras in the 1960s made it possible.

questions.q: Robert Flaherty's Nanook of the North (1922) is often called the first feature-length…?
questions.f: Some scenes were staged for the camera, which is why scholars still debate its label.

questions.q: 'Mockumentary' films present fiction in the style of a…?
questions.f: This Is Spinal Tap made the form famous in 1984.

questions.q: The 'Voice of God' narration style in documentaries refers to a narrator who is…?
questions.f: Critics coined the phrase to describe the confident, invisible commentary of mid-century newsreels.

questions.q: Television's earliest regular electronic broadcasts began in the 1930s, well before World War II.
questions.f: The BBC launched a regular high-definition service in 1936, suspended during the war.

questions.q: A 405-line system, a north London transmitter, and a service switched off mid-cartoon in 1939 point to early television in which country?
questions.f: When the BBC resumed in 1946 it reportedly picked up the same Mickey Mouse cartoon.

questions.q: John Logie Baird's earliest television experiments produced pictures using a spinning…?
questions.f: The Nipkow disc scanned an image line by line — mechanical television before electronics took over.

questions.q: A 'kinescope' recording preserved early live TV by…?
questions.f: Before videotape, pointing a film camera at a monitor was the only way to keep a live show.

questions.q: 'Videotape' recording was introduced commercially in the 1950s by which company?
questions.f: Ampex's 1956 machine let networks time-shift programmes across US time zones for the first time.

questions.q: The television term 'interlaced' scanning means each frame is drawn as…?
questions.f: Interlacing halved the bandwidth needed while keeping motion looking smooth.

questions.q: 'Laugh track' technology was pioneered by engineer Charles Douglass, whose machine was nicknamed the…?
questions.f: Douglass kept the box locked and operated it himself for decades, guarding his recorded laughs.

questions.q: 'Three-camera setup' in sitcom production allows the show to be…?
c: Shot from several angles at once before a live audience
questions.f: Desi Arnaz and cinematographer Karl Freund helped standardise it on I Love Lucy.

questions.q: A television 'bottle episode' is one made cheaply by…?
c: Confining the action to existing sets
questions.f: Writers often love bottle episodes because the pressure forces sharper dialogue.

questions.q: The Muppet performer's technique of watching a monitor while working the puppet exists because…?
c: The performer cannot see the puppet directly
questions.f: Henson's performers learned to reverse their hand movements while watching themselves on the monitor.

questions.q: Jim Henson's fantasy film that used no human actors on screen at all was…?
questions.f: Every character was a puppet or creature, some operated by several performers at once.

questions.q: Frank Oz, a leading Muppet performer, also performed which famous film character?
questions.f: Oz performed Yoda as a hand puppet while also voicing him.

questions.q: The technique of building a puppet whose mouth is worked by the performer's hand is called a…?
questions.f: One hand works the mouth while the other, or an assistant, works rods on the arms.

questions.q: 'Audio-Animatronics' was a term coined by which company for its moving figures?
questions.f: Disney debuted them at the 1964 New York World's Fair with a talking Abraham Lincoln.

questions.q: 'It's a Small World', a ride full of singing dolls, first appeared at the 1964 World's Fair in which city?
questions.f: The Sherman brothers wrote its endlessly repeating song as a simple plea for world peace.

questions.q: Which pair of brothers wrote the songs for Mary Poppins and The Jungle Book?
questions.f: Richard and Robert Sherman won two Oscars for Mary Poppins alone.

questions.q: The invented word 'supercalifragilisticexpialidocious' comes from which film?
questions.f: The Shermans said they built it from nonsense syllables they had chanted as children at camp.

questions.q: 'Chim Chim Cher-ee' is a song about which occupation?
questions.f: It won the 1965 Academy Award for Best Original Song.

questions.q: The 1964 film Mary Poppins combined live action with animation in a sequence set…?
questions.f: Animated penguins waited on Dick Van Dyke's table in that sequence.

questions.q: Who Framed Roger Rabbit was groundbreaking because its cartoon characters…?
c: Interacted convincingly with live actors and real light
questions.f: Animators added painted shadows and highlights to every character so they sat inside real rooms.

questions.q: Who Framed Roger Rabbit featured characters licensed from both Disney and Warner Bros.
questions.f: Contract terms reportedly required Mickey and Bugs to have exactly equal screen time.

questions.q: The word 'toon', short for cartoon, was popularised as a noun for animated characters by which film?
questions.f: 'Toontown' in the film is where the animated characters live.

questions.q: 'Cel shading' in modern computer graphics is designed to make 3D images look…?
questions.f: Flat colours and bold outlines mimic the look of traditional cel animation.

questions.q: Disney's Tarzan used a technique called 'Deep Canvas' to create…?
c: Painterly 3D backgrounds the camera could move through
questions.f: It let the camera swoop through jungle that still looked hand-painted.

questions.q: 'Toon Boom' and 'TVPaint' are examples of software used for…?
questions.f: Digital ink and paint replaced physical cels almost entirely by the late 1990s.

questions.q: The last major Disney feature made with traditional hand-drawn animation was…?
questions.f: Disney's hand-drawn unit closed after it, though the art form thrives elsewhere.

questions.q: 'Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse' won acclaim for animation that imitated…?
questions.f: Animators even added misregistered colour dots, like old cheap comic printing.

questions.q: 'Animating on twos' means drawing a new image every…?
questions.f: Twelve drawings a second is often enough — but fast action needs 'ones'.

questions.q: An animation 'exposure sheet' or 'dope sheet' records…?
c: Which drawing appears on which frame
questions.f: It is the animator's musical score, mapping drawings against sound frame by frame.

questions.q: An animated film's 'animatic' is…?
c: A storyboard timed to a soundtrack
questions.f: Directors watch the animatic to feel a scene's rhythm before expensive animation begins.

questions.q: A 'model sheet' in animation shows a character…?
c: From several angles with proportions marked
questions.f: Model sheets keep a character on-model when dozens of artists draw them.

questions.q: 'Squash and stretch' preserves the illusion of weight best when the animator keeps the character's…?
questions.f: If a ball squashes flat, it must widen — otherwise it looks like it lost mass.

questions.q: 'Slow in and slow out' in animation refers to spacing drawings…?
c: Closer together at the ends of a move
questions.f: Almost nothing in nature starts or stops instantly — easing sells the physics.

questions.q: The animation principle 'secondary action' means adding a movement that…?
questions.f: A character walking angrily might also crumple a letter — the second action reveals the mood.

questions.q: A theatre's 'house' refers to…?
questions.f: 'Full house' means every seat sold, and the 'house manager' looks after the audience.

questions.q: 'Papering the house' means…?
c: Giving away free tickets to fill seats
questions.f: A full-looking house helps a nervous cast and generates better word of mouth.

questions.q: 'Corpsing' among British actors means…?
questions.f: One theory is that the giggling actor 'kills' the scene.

questions.q: 'Drying' on stage is theatre slang for…?
questions.f: That is why a prompter once sat with the script in a small box at the stage edge.

questions.q: The theatre role of 'prompter' involves…?
questions.f: Opera houses in some countries still keep a prompter in a hooded box downstage centre.

questions.q: 'Ad lib' comes from a Latin phrase meaning 'at pleasure' or 'as one wishes'.
questions.f: From Latin ad libitum — an ad-libbing performer invents freely.

questions.q: 'Sotto voce', a stage direction, instructs a performer to speak…?
questions.f: Italian for 'under the voice' — used in both music and theatre.

questions.q: The stage direction 'exeunt' means…?
