questions.f: It is Latin plural — 'exit' means one person leaves, 'exeunt' means several do.

questions.q: Shakespeare's most famous stage direction, from The Winter's Tale, reads 'Exit, pursued by a…'?
questions.f: Scholars still argue whether a real bear or a costumed actor appeared on stage.

questions.q: 'Iambic pentameter', the rhythm of much Shakespearean verse, has how many stressed beats per line?
questions.f: 'Penta' means five — each iamb is an unstressed then stressed syllable, like a heartbeat.

questions.q: In Shakespeare's day, boy actors played women's roles because…?
c: Women were not permitted on the English public stage
questions.f: English women appeared on the public stage only after the theatres reopened in 1660.

questions.q: Which of these Shakespeare plays contains a play-within-a-play performed by amateur actors?
questions.f: Bottom and his fellow 'mechanicals' stage the tragedy of Pyramus and Thisbe — badly.

questions.q: The word 'audition' and the theatre term 'call-back' relate because a call-back is a…?
questions.f: Final call-backs may pair actors together to test their chemistry.

questions.q: A 'cattle call' audition means…?
c: An open audition with very many hopefuls
questions.f: Producers of A Chorus Line built a whole musical about the audition process itself.

questions.q: 'Sides' given to an actor at an audition are…?
questions.f: The term dates from when actors received only their own lines and cues, not the whole play.

questions.q: The word 'cue' in theatre may derive from an abbreviation once written in scripts as…?
questions.f: 'Quando' means 'when' — marking when an actor should speak.

questions.q: The film term 'grip' for a crew member probably comes from the idea of…?
questions.f: The 'key grip' leads the department, and a 'dolly grip' pushes the camera platform.

questions.q: On a film crew, the 'best boy' assists which department head?
questions.f: The title survives from when a foreman would call for his 'best boy' to help.

questions.q: A 'craft service' table on a film set provides…?
questions.f: Crews joke that a production's mood can be measured by its craft service.

questions.q: The film term 'wrap' for finishing a shoot is popularly explained as standing for…?
questions.f: Historians think it is simply the everyday word 'wrap' — but the backronym persists.

questions.q: A film 'call sheet' tells the crew…?
c: Who is needed where and when tomorrow
The names of the cast's agents
questions.f: Call sheets go out the night before, listing sunrise, sunset and every scene planned.

questions.q: 'Dailies' or 'rushes' are…?
c: The previous day's footage viewed by the crew
questions.f: Directors watch them to check performance and technical faults while sets are still standing.

questions.q: A 'director's cut' is an edited version reflecting the director's preferences rather than the studio's.
questions.f: Blade Runner has been released in several distinct versions, including a Final Cut.

questions.q: 'Alan Smithee' was a name once used in Hollywood credits when a director…?
c: Was too young to be credited
questions.f: The pseudonym was officially retired after it became too widely recognised.

questions.q: 'Above the line' costs in a film budget cover…?
c: Key creative talent such as director and stars
questions.f: 'Below the line' covers the technical crew and physical production.

questions.q: 'Residuals' paid to performers are…?
c: Payments for reuse of their work
questions.f: Residuals are why a bit-part actor may still receive cheques decades later.

questions.q: 'Typage', a casting idea used by Soviet directors, meant choosing actors for…?
c: Their faces suiting a social type
questions.f: Eisenstein cast a non-actor as a general because the man simply looked the part.

questions.q: An 'ingenue' and a 'juvenile lead' differ mainly in the character's…?
questions.f: Old stock-company contracts listed such roles precisely, so actors knew what they would play.

questions.q: 'Panto dame', 'principal boy' and 'audience booing' all belong to which tradition?
questions.f: By convention the principal boy is played by a woman and the dame by a man.

questions.q: A 'clown alley' at a circus is…?
questions.f: Clowns traditionally guard their makeup designs, once even registering them on painted eggs.

questions.q: Hand-painted bands of images, a Paris waxworks called the Musee Grevin, and reels thrown into the Seine in 1910 point to which pioneer?
questions.f: Reynaud projected animation to paying crowds from 1892 — three years before the Lumieres' first film show.

questions.q: A newspaper strip about a boy whose bed walks away, roughly 10,000 rice-paper drawings, and a vaudeville act with a whip converge on which cartoonist?
questions.f: McCay's Little Nemo in Slumberland strip is still studied for its perspective; Gertie was his stage partner.

questions.q: A garden in Leeds in 1888, figures walking in a circle for about two seconds, and an inventor who vanished from a French train point to whom?
questions.f: Le Prince's Roundhay Garden Scene is often called the oldest surviving motion picture.

questions.q: A secretary at a Paris camera firm, an 1896 short about babies found in a cabbage patch, and a studio built in Fort Lee, New Jersey point to which director?
questions.f: Guy-Blache is widely regarded as the first woman to direct a fiction film, and she made hundreds more.

questions.q: Grains of potato starch dyed three colours, a photographic plate factory in Lyon, and one hand-cranked box that both filmed and projected point to which brothers?
questions.f: Their Autochrome plates used dyed potato starch to make the first practical colour photographs.

questions.q: An entomologist frustrated that his stag beetles would not perform, wires threaded into insect legs, and Moscow in 1912 point to which animator?
questions.f: Starevich built his puppets from real beetle shells and is a founding father of stop-motion.

questions.q: A 46-centimetre model, a Manhattan skyline miniature, and animator Willis O'Brien's rear-projection tricks point to which 1933 film?
questions.f: O'Brien mentored Ray Harryhausen, who carried stop-motion creatures on for another 50 years.

questions.q: Four months of work for about three minutes of screen time, seven fighters moved one frame at a time, and a Greek quest for a fleece point to which film?
questions.f: Harryhausen called that skeleton sequence the hardest thing he ever animated.

questions.q: Sound scratched directly onto the film's optical track, a Scottish-born animator, and Canada's National Film Board point to whom?
questions.f: McLaren also won an Oscar for Neighbours, animating live actors frame by frame.

questions.q: A qualified physician who chose comics instead, a 1963 television series about a robot boy, and the nickname 'god of manga' point to whom?
questions.f: Tezuka's Astro Boy set the template for Japanese TV animation, including the big expressive eyes.

questions.q: A Homeric princess, a Japanese folk tale about a girl who loved insects, and a 1982 manga serialised in Animage gave their names to which heroine?
questions.f: Miyazaki drew on both the Odyssey's Nausicaa and 'The Lady Who Loved Insects' for her.

questions.q: A child's mispronunciation of the word 'troll', a rural Tokyo suburb called Sayama Hills, and a bus with glowing eyes point to which film?
questions.f: In the story, little Mei's garbled attempt at 'totoro' is how the creature gets its name.

questions.q: A director who never learned to draw, a 1974 television series about a Swiss orphan girl, and Studio Ghibli's co-founding point to whom?
questions.f: Takahata directed Heidi, Girl of the Alps with Miyazaki laying out its scenes.

questions.q: A pseudo-Spanish verb invented to mean 'to make pictures', the word 'radar', and a Lucasfilm computer division point to the naming of which company?
questions.f: Alvy Ray Smith coined 'Pixar' from the fake verb 'pixer' plus the sound of 'radar'.

questions.q: A stray computer command in 1998, a rescue from a copy on an employee's home machine, and a film later rebuilt almost from scratch point to which sequel?
questions.f: An animator working from home had a backup — otherwise most of the film's files were gone.

questions.q: A CalArts classroom number appearing as a licence plate, a room code, and a train carriage is which recurring Pixar in-joke?
questions.f: A113 was the animation classroom at the California Institute of the Arts, and its alumni hide it everywhere.

questions.q: A stained-glass knight leaping from a window in 1985, a young detective's adventure, and Lucasfilm's computer group point to the first fully computer-generated…?
questions.f: The knight in Young Sherlock Holmes was made by the team that soon became Pixar.

questions.q: A chess-playing old man, a 1997 short film, and the debut of subdivision-surface skin point to which Oscar-winning Pixar short?
questions.f: The smooth-skinned technique developed for Geri went straight into Toy Story 2's human characters.

questions.q: A Chinese-American artist's misty watercolours, a studio strike in 1941, and a deer's forest home point to which film's celebrated visual style?
questions.f: Tyrus Wong's sparse paintings shaped Bambi's look; he later designed kites in Los Angeles.

questions.q: Multiple sound channels, specially built theatre speakers, and a 1940 Disney release point to the pioneering audio system called…?
questions.f: Fantasia's Fantasound was effectively the first commercial surround-sound system, decades early.

questions.q: A 1928 loss of a rabbit character, a 2006 trade involving a sports broadcaster, and Universal's archives point to which cartoon character's return to Disney?
questions.f: Disney reacquired Oswald in a deal that sent commentator Al Michaels to NBC.

questions.q: A concept artist's flat blocks of tropical colour, a 1941 South American research trip with Walt Disney, and a World's Fair boat ride point to whom?
questions.f: Blair designed the murals and dolls for 'It's a Small World' and coloured Cinderella and Peter Pan.

questions.q: Around 700 drawings a day, a partnership that broke apart in 1930, and an Oscar for optical printing later used on Hitchcock's The Birds point to whom?
questions.f: Iwerks drew most of Mickey's earliest cartoons almost single-handed, then became a technical genius.

questions.q: A digital ink-and-paint system built with Pixar, an Australian setting, and a 1990 sequel about mice point to the first Disney feature made entirely without cels?
questions.f: Disney's CAPS system won a technical Oscar and quietly ended a 60-year production method.

questions.q: Painted shadows added to every cartoon character, contractually equal screen time for two rival mice and rabbits, and 1988 point to which film?
questions.f: Animators added moving highlights and shadows so the toons appeared lit by the real set's lamps.

questions.q: A director often mistakenly credited to his producer, a stop-motion skeleton in a pinstripe suit, and 1993 point to which film-maker?
questions.f: Selick directed The Nightmare Before Christmas; Burton produced it and designed the characters.

questions.q: Recorded interviews with ordinary people, clay zoo animals lip-synced to their words, and a 1990 Oscar point to which short film?
questions.f: Nick Park interviewed real people about their homes, then gave the answers to a bored-sounding Brazilian lion.

questions.q: A terracotta-coloured clay figure, a BBC art programme presented by Tony Hart, and a Bristol studio's earliest fame point to which character?
questions.f: Morph launched Aardman years before Wallace and Gromit existed.

questions.q: A moon made of cheese, a rocket built in a cellar, and a Yorkshire dairy whose sales jumped afterwards point to which short film?
questions.f: Wallace's love of Wensleydale helped rescue the real Wensleydale Creamery from closure.

questions.q: A swimming pool in Toulouse used for practice, a garment still bearing a surname, and a music-hall song about a daring young man point to which performer?
questions.f: Leotard invented the flying trapeze in 1859 and the one-piece costume named after him.

questions.q: A rope stretched above Niagara, an omelette cooked halfway across, and a man carried on the performer's back point to which funambulist?
questions.f: 'Funambulist' means rope-walker; Blondin crossed Niagara many times, once on stilts.

questions.q: A soprano billed as the Swedish Nightingale, a performer known as General Tom Thumb, and an American Museum on Broadway point to which showman?
questions.f: Barnum's museum drew huge crowds long before he entered the circus business in his sixties.

questions.q: A London Zoo favourite sold in 1882 amid public protest, an English word for anything oversized, and an echo in a Disney elephant's name point to which animal?
questions.f: The African elephant Jumbo gave English the adjective; Dumbo's name plays on it.

questions.q: Stilt-walkers in the Quebec village of Baie-Saint-Paul, a 1984 anniversary of Jacques Cartier's voyage, and a company with no animal acts point to which troupe?
questions.f: The street performers who founded it were called Le Club des Talons Hauts — the High Heels Club.

questions.q: A large single hoop the performer stands inside, a Quebec inventor's surname, and a debut around 2003 point to which circus apparatus?
questions.f: Daniel Cyr's simple ring turned a novelty into a standard circus discipline within a decade.

questions.q: A crystal ball rolling over a goblin king's hands, a juggler crouched behind the actor working blind, and a technique later given a name point to whom?
questions.f: Moschen performed the ball manipulation in Labyrinth from behind David Bowie, unable to see it.

questions.q: A pantomime clown at Sadler's Wells, a nickname still given to circus clowns, and an autobiography edited by Charles Dickens point to whom?
questions.f: Clowns are called 'Joeys' after Grimaldi, who shaped the whiteface clown around 1800.

questions.q: A white-faced character named Bip in a battered opera hat, a Paris school of corporeal mime, and the only spoken word in a 1976 Mel Brooks film point to whom?
questions.f: In Silent Movie, Marceau says the single word 'Non!' — the film's only line of dialogue.

questions.q: A French playwright-actor, a comedy about an imaginary invalid, and a lasting superstition against green costumes in French theatre point to whom?
questions.f: Moliere fell ill while playing the hypochondriac in Le Malade imaginaire and died hours later.

questions.q: A hidden orchestra, a 'mystic gulf' between musicians and stage, and a Bavarian town's purpose-built festival house point to which composer's theatre?
questions.f: Wagner sank the Bayreuth orchestra out of sight so nothing broke the audience's illusion.

questions.q: A design by Andrea Palladio, painted street perspectives receding behind the stage, and a 1585 opening in Vicenza point to which surviving theatre?
questions.f: Its wooden trompe-l'oeil streets are the oldest surviving stage sets in the world.

questions.q: A whisper reportedly audible from the top row, a 4th-century BCE limestone bowl, and a Greek sanctuary of healing point to which ancient theatre?
questions.f: Researchers found the stone seats filter low-frequency crowd noise while passing voices through.

questions.q: A wheeled platform called an ekkyklema, a crane called a mechane, and a phrase now meaning a too-convenient rescue point to which theatre tradition?
questions.f: The mechane lowered gods to the stage, giving us 'deus ex machina'.

questions.q: The Greek word 'hypokrites', ancestor of the English word 'hypocrite', originally meant…?
questions.f: An actor answered the chorus from behind a mask — pretending was the job, not the insult.

questions.q: The Latin word 'persona', which gives us 'person' and 'personality', first named a…?
questions.f: One theory links it to 'per-sonare', to sound through — the mask's mouth amplified the voice.

questions.q: Thick-soled boots for tragedy, light slippers for comedy, and a phrase for drama's two faces converge on which pair of words?
questions.f: 'The sock and buskin' still means comedy and tragedy in old theatrical writing.

questions.q: A hired audience, a 'chef' who led their signals, and 19th-century Parisian opera houses point to which practice?
questions.f: Claqueurs were paid to laugh, weep, and demand encores exactly on cue.

questions.q: Cannonballs rolled down a long wooden trough, a Georgian playhouse's attic, and an effect no orchestra could match point to which stage device?
questions.f: Drury Lane's thunder run survives, and its rumble still shakes the building.

questions.q: Backstage whistling is traditionally unlucky because early theatre riggers were often sailors who used whistles as…?
questions.f: A stray whistle could drop a heavy backdrop on the wrong head — hence the ban.

questions.q: An 1820 melodrama, a hinged pair of spring-loaded flaps, and a vanishing through what looks like a solid wall point to which stage trap?
questions.f: Built for a play about a vampire, the flaps snap shut so fast the audience sees no opening.

questions.q: A loosely woven gauze, a wall that dissolves into a room behind it, and lighting shifted from front to back point to which piece of stage cloth?
questions.f: Light the scrim from the front and it is opaque; light behind it and the fabric seems to vanish.

questions.q: The theatre-lighting nickname 'Leko' is built from the surnames of…?
c: Its two inventors, Levy and Kook
A Greek god and a lens
A gel maker and a lamp maker
questions.f: Joseph Levy and Edward Kook founded Century Lighting, and their initials named the fixture.

questions.q: A Nipkow disc, a Selfridges department-store demonstration in 1925, and a ventriloquist's dummy head as the first televised face point to whom?
questions.f: Baird's first transmitted image was of a dummy he nicknamed 'Stooky Bill'.

questions.q: An image orthicon tube, an engineers' pet nickname 'immy', and a 1949 award ceremony point to the naming of which trophy?
questions.f: The winged statuette's name is a softened spelling of the tube's nickname.

questions.q: An actress-producer who died in 1946, the American Theatre Wing, and a medallion rather than a statuette point to which award?
questions.f: The Tony honours Antoinette Perry, and winners receive a swivelling medallion on a base.

questions.q: A 1962 Ron Grainer theme, tape loops cut and spliced by hand at the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, and no synthesizer at all point to which programme?
questions.f: Delia Derbyshire built the eerie theme from test-oscillator tones and painstaking tape edits.

questions.q: A swanee whistle for speech, a small blue planet, and a knitted creature called the Soup Dragon point to which stop-motion series?
questions.f: Oliver Postgate wrote real dialogue, then played it on the whistle so the rhythm matched.

questions.q: A saggy cloth cat, mice on a mouse organ, and only 13 episodes ever made point to which much-loved children's series?
questions.f: Despite its tiny run, Bagpuss has topped British polls of favourite children's programmes.

questions.q: An ordained minister, a 1969 appearance before a US Senate subcommittee, and a cardigan changed on camera point to which television presenter?
questions.f: Rogers' quiet six-minute testimony is credited with saving public television's funding.

questions.q: A performer who played both a towering yellow bird and a grouch in a bin points to which puppeteer?
questions.f: Spinney worked inside Big Bird with the script taped in front of him and a tiny monitor at his chest.

questions.q: A 1955 late-night show called Sam and Friends, a lizard-like character made from a coat, and two halves of a ping-pong ball point to which creation?
questions.f: Kermit only became a frog years later; his eyes began as ping-pong ball halves.

questions.q: A drawing of a family with every name borrowed except one, an anagram of 'brat', and shorts for The Tracey Ullman Show point to which series?
questions.f: Matt Groening named Homer, Marge, Lisa and Maggie after his own relatives; Bart he invented.

questions.q: A Great Dane designed by Iwao Takamoto, and a name borrowed from scat singing in 'Strangers in the Night', point to which character?
questions.f: A network executive is said to have plucked 'Scooby-dooby-doo' from the Sinatra recording.

questions.q: Nine written rules including 'the road runner must stay on the road' point to which animation director's cartoon series?
questions.f: Jones set self-imposed rules so the gags stayed inventive inside a rigid formula.

questions.q: A cartoon rabbit in Wagnerian armour, a plump horse, and inclusion in the US National Film Registry point to which 1957 short?
questions.f: Chuck Jones compressed Wagner's Ring cycle into about seven minutes.

questions.q: A film in which the animator's pencil torments the star, a duck stripped of his background, and a final reveal of the culprit point to which short?
questions.f: Daffy spends the film arguing with an unseen animator who turns out to be Bugs Bunny.

questions.q: A weekend shooting schedule, a crew of near-amateurs, and a Bengali village trilogy beginning in 1955 point to which director?
questions.f: Ray also wrote children's detective stories and designed his own film posters and title cards.

questions.q: A 1913 silent feature about a truthful king, a Nashik-born photographer, and an award now bearing his name point to which Indian pioneer?
questions.f: Phalke's Raja Harishchandra is regarded as India's first full-length feature film.

questions.q: A camera placed at the height of someone seated on a mat, a refusal to move it, and post-war Tokyo family dramas point to which director?
questions.f: Critics call it the 'tatami shot' — Ozu framed the world from a kneeling person's eyeline.

questions.q: Four contradictory accounts of one event, a 1950 Japanese film, and a term psychologists now borrow point to which effect?
questions.f: Kurosawa's Rashomon gave social science a name for irreconcilable eyewitness accounts.

questions.q: A 1927 Broadway show adapted from an Edna Ferber novel, a river setting, and the song 'Ol' Man River' point to which landmark musical?
questions.f: Show Boat is often called the first musical to weave serious drama fully into its songs.

questions.q: A 1932 Gershwin satire about a presidential campaign was the first musical to win which honour?
questions.f: Of Thee I Sing beat straight plays to the Pulitzer, decades before the Tonys existed.

questions.q: A Chagall painting, Sholem Aleichem's Tevye stories, and a 1964 Broadway opening point to which musical's title?
questions.f: Marc Chagall's floating fiddlers gave the show its image and its name.

questions.q: Taped late-night conversations with real dancers, a director-choreographer named Michael Bennett, and a 1975 Pulitzer point to which musical?
questions.f: Bennett built the show from workshop sessions in which dancers told their own stories.

questions.q: Puccini's La boheme, a 1996 East Village setting, and a composer who died the night before previews point to which musical?
questions.f: Jonathan Larson never saw his show performed publicly; it went on to win the Pulitzer Prize.

questions.q: A book of practical cats, a poem published in 1939, and a composer who set them almost verbatim point to which long-running musical?
questions.f: T. S. Eliot's widow supplied an unpublished fragment, "Grizabella the Glamour Cat", giving the show its central character; Trevor Nunn then wrote "Memory" from Eliot's "Rhapsody on a Windy Night".

questions.q: A murder-mystery play, a London run beginning in 1952, and a request that audiences keep the ending secret point to which production?
questions.f: Agatha Christie's play is the longest-running production of any kind in world theatre.

questions.q: A director who first trained in visual art, giant animal puppets whose operators stay visible, and a 1998 Tony for direction point to whom?
questions.f: Taymor was the first woman to win the Tony for directing a musical, for The Lion King.

questions.q: Roller skates, trains as characters, and a 1984 West End show requiring a rebuilt auditorium point to which musical?
questions.f: Skate ramps were built through the audience so the 'trains' could race around the crowd.

questions.q: A 1866 New York show that spliced a ballet troupe into a melodrama is often called the first American…?
questions.f: The Black Crook ran five and a half hours and was a sensation.

questions.q: Which musical holds the record for the most Tony Awards won by a single production, with 12?
questions.f: Hamilton earned more nominations, 16, but converted 11 of them.

questions.q: A dream ballet closing the first act, a Lynn Riggs play called Green Grow the Lilacs, and a 1943 opening point to which musical?
questions.f: Agnes de Mille's ballet let dance carry the plot — a first for Broadway.

questions.q: A Gregory Maguire novel, an unnamed green-skinned student, and a 2003 Broadway opening point to which musical?
questions.f: The novel imagines the Wicked Witch of the West's life before Dorothy's house ever lands.

questions.q: Damon Runyon's short stories, a floating crap game, and a 1950 Broadway hit point to which musical?
questions.f: Runyon's slangy New York characters gave the show its unmistakable voice.

questions.q: A 1957 musical transplanting Shakespeare to Manhattan, Jerome Robbins's choreography, and rival neighbourhood gangs point to which show?
questions.f: Leonard Bernstein's score and Stephen Sondheim's early lyrics made it an instant landmark.

questions.q: A 1936 crowd-scene technique of splitting film exposures, and Fred Astaire dancing with three of himself, point to which effect?
questions.f: Matting exposes different parts of the same negative separately so one actor meets themselves.

questions.q: A dance partner said to have done everything backwards and in high heels, a screen partnership of ten films, and 1930s RKO point to whom?
questions.f: The line about backwards and in heels comes from a 1982 comic strip, not from Rogers herself.

questions.q: A dance up a wall and across a ceiling, a hat-rack partner, and 1951's Royal Wedding point to which performer?
questions.f: The set was built inside a rotating drum, so Astaire stayed upright while the room turned.

questions.q: A choreographer known for bowler hats, turned-in knees and rolled shoulders, and shows including Chicago and Cabaret, points to whom?
questions.f: Fosse's signature style grew partly from hiding his own baldness and poor turnout.

questions.q: Milk mixed into water for visibility, a soaked suit, and a performer filming with a high fever in 1952 point to which musical number?
questions.f: Gene Kelly danced through the downpour with a temperature, and the crew mixed milk in so rain would read on camera.

questions.q: A 1927 Warner Bros. film, a disc-based sound system called Vitaphone, and an unscripted line about not having heard anything yet point to which milestone?
questions.f: Most of the film is silent; the ad-libbed spoken lines are what stunned audiences.

questions.q: Sound recorded on wax discs synchronised with the projector describes which early sound system?
questions.f: Rival systems put sound on the film itself, which soon won because reels could not drift out of sync.

questions.q: A three-strip camera, a colour consultant named Natalie Kalmus, and a company whose name honours MIT point to which process?
questions.f: Founder Herbert Kalmus named it for the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, his alma mater.

questions.q: A 1932 Silly Symphony called Flowers and Trees was historically significant as the first commercial cartoon in…?
questions.f: It also won the very first Academy Award for Animated Short Film.

questions.q: Which 1937 Disney short was the first film to use the multiplane camera, testing it before a feature did?
questions.f: The Old Mill won an Oscar and proved the depth effects that Snow White would need.

questions.q: An 18-year-old singer, a contract forbidding other screen work, and a 1937 Disney premiere point to the voice of which character?
questions.f: Adriana Caselotti's contract kept her voice off other screens to protect the illusion.

questions.q: A 1940 Disney feature that became the first animated film to win competitive Academy Awards did so for its score and…?
questions.f: Pinocchio's 'When You Wish Upon a Star' won Best Original Song.

questions.q: At about 64 minutes, which Disney animated feature is the studio's shortest?
questions.f: Dumbo was deliberately made cheaply and quickly after two costly features lost money.

questions.q: A Kansas City studio called Laugh-O-gram, a series of Alice Comedies, and a bankruptcy before the age of 22 point to whom?
questions.f: Disney's first company failed, and he left for California with almost nothing.

questions.q: Mickey Mouse's original proposed name, discarded before his debut, was…?
questions.f: Mortimer later became the name of a rival character courting Minnie.

questions.q: Walt Disney himself provided Mickey Mouse's voice until roughly which year?
questions.f: Sound-effects artist Jimmy MacDonald took over and voiced Mickey for nearly 30 years.

questions.q: Which Mickey Mouse cartoon entered the United States public domain in 2024?
questions.f: Its 95-year copyright term expired, letting anyone reuse that particular version of Mickey.

questions.q: A theatre in the Los Angeles district of Carthay Circle hosted the 1937 premiere of which film?
c: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.f: Audiences reportedly wept at the dwarfs' vigil — proof that a cartoon could move adults.

questions.q: A rejected list of dwarf names including Jumpy, Deafy and Awful survives from the making of which film?
c: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.f: Fifty candidate names were whittled down to Doc, Grumpy, Happy, Sleepy, Bashful, Sneezy and Dopey.

questions.q: An unnamed Academy Award nickname, a librarian named Margaret Herrick, and an uncle from Texas point to the naming of which trophy?
questions.f: Herrick reportedly said the statuette resembled her Uncle Oscar, and the newspapers ran with it.

questions.q: A knight on a reel of film with five spokes represents the Academy's five original…?
questions.f: The spokes stand for actors, directors, producers, technicians and writers.

questions.q: A performer's radio characters, a claimed 'man of a thousand voices', and Bugs Bunny's carrot crunch point to whom?
questions.f: Blanc voiced Bugs, Daffy, Porky, Tweety and Sylvester — often arguing with himself in one scene.

questions.q: A studio nickname 'Termite Terrace', a musical director named Carl Stalling, and a sound editor named Treg Brown point to which cartoon unit?
questions.f: Stalling quoted dozens of tunes per short, and Brown's crashes and boings became a shared language.

questions.q: A director who created Droopy, sharpened Daffy's mania, and later made cartoons at MGM points to whom?
questions.f: Avery's wild takes and impossible physics influenced nearly every cartoon that followed.

questions.q: An animation team that won seven Oscars for cat-and-mouse shorts before founding their own TV studio points to whom?
questions.f: After MGM closed its cartoon unit, William Hanna and Joseph Barbera reinvented animation for television.

questions.q: 'Limited animation', which made television cartoons affordable, saved money mainly by…?
c: Reusing drawings and moving only parts of a character
questions.f: Holding a body still and animating just a mouth cut the drawing count enormously.

questions.q: A Czech puppet-film director called by some the 'Walt Disney of the East', and films including The Hand, points to whom?
questions.f: Trnka's carved wooden puppets barely change expression, yet convey remarkable feeling.

questions.q: A Soviet animator, a hedgehog lost in mist, and a 1979 film often voted the greatest animated short ever point to whom?
questions.f: Norshteyn's Tale of Tales topped an international poll of animation professionals.

questions.q: Paint moved with fingertips on a lit glass sheet, then photographed frame by frame, describes which animation technique?
questions.f: Aleksandr Petrov won an Oscar using slow-drying oil paint pushed around by hand.

questions.q: Thousands of movable pins pushed through a board and lit from the side describe which animation technique?
questions.f: Alexandre Alexeieff invented the pinscreen, producing images like living charcoal drawings.

questions.q: A green clay figure from a 1953 short, a creator named Art Clokey, and a shape inspired by his father's hair point to whom?
questions.f: Clokey also made Davey and Goliath, and Gumby's shape was inspired by a bump in his father's hair.

questions.q: A television special using stop-motion its makers called 'Animagic', a 1964 broadcast, and a reindeer point to which studio?
questions.f: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer has aired every year since, making it one of TV's longest traditions.

questions.q: Wires inside real beetle shells, hand-carved wooden puppets, and pins pushed through a board are all techniques of…?
questions.f: Every one of them is photographed a single frame at a time — the defining trait of stop-motion.

questions.q: A 400-year-old family acting line, painted kumadori makeup, and shouted 'kakegoe' from the audience point to which theatre form?
questions.f: Fans shout an actor's hereditary stage name at his big freeze-frame pose, or mie.

questions.q: Black-clad assistants who move props in full view of a Japanese audience are called…?
questions.f: By convention the audience simply agrees not to see them.

questions.q: A treatise called Fushikaden, 14th-century patronage from a shogun, and carved masks worn slightly small point to which theatre form's founder?
questions.f: Zeami's writings on Noh acting are among the oldest theatre theory outside Greece.

questions.q: A chanter called a tayu, a three-stringed shamisen, and three puppeteers to one figure point to which theatre form?
questions.f: The lead puppeteer trains for a decade on the feet before he is trusted with the head.

questions.q: A playwright called 'the Shakespeare of Japan' who wrote for puppets before actors is…?
questions.f: Chikamatsu wrote around 130 plays, many first performed by Bunraku puppets.

questions.q: An oil lamp called a blencong, a stretched screen called a kelir, and a tree-shaped puppet called a gunungan point to which tradition?
questions.f: The gunungan opens and closes the performance and marks scene changes.

questions.q: A performer named after a black-eyed character, an Ottoman coffee-house tradition, and a bath-house legend point to which shadow theatre?
questions.f: 'Karagoz' means 'black eye' in Turkish; the shows were long a Ramadan evening favourite.

questions.q: A 1662 diary entry by Samuel Pepys, an Italian character called Pulcinella, and Covent Garden mark the English birthday of…?
questions.f: Pepys recorded seeing an Italian puppet play in Covent Garden on 9 May 1662.

questions.q: A glove puppet bear with a magic wand, a Bradford magician, and the catchphrase 'izzy wizzy, let's get busy' point to which character?
questions.f: Harry Corbett bought the bear on Blackpool pier in 1948 and inked its ears black for television.

questions.q: An American puppeteer who performed Lamb Chop, conducted orchestras, and won a dozen Emmys is…?
questions.f: Lewis performed Lamb Chop for four decades and also wrote Star Trek episodes.

questions.q: 'Kukla, Fran and Ollie', an early US television hit, was performed largely…?
questions.f: Burr Tillstrom improvised the puppet dialogue while Fran Allison responded live on air.

questions.q: A 1969 programme with a research team testing episodes on real children, and a title borrowed from a magic phrase, points to which show?
questions.f: 'Sesame' comes from 'open sesame' — the idea that learning opens doors.

questions.q: A 1957 April Fools' news film about Swiss farmers harvesting spaghetti from trees was broadcast by which organisation?
questions.f: Panorama's spaghetti-tree hoax fooled so many viewers that some asked how to grow their own.

questions.q: Long painted cloths wound between two rollers, letting scenery scroll past a static stage, were called a…?
questions.f: Victorian audiences watched whole river voyages unspool across the stage this way.

questions.q: A theatre 'angel' is best described as someone who…?
questions.f: Angels risk their money for a share of the profits — and most shows never repay them.

questions.q: A 'trunk song' in musical theatre is one that…?
c: Was written earlier and saved for a later show
Is sung inside a set piece
questions.f: Composers keep unused songs in a metaphorical trunk, ready for a show that finally fits.

questions.q: In musical theatre, an 'I want' song usually appears…?
c: Early, to state the hero's desire
questions.f: 'Part of Your World' and 'Wouldn't It Be Loverly' are textbook 'I want' songs.

questions.q: A musical's 'vamp' is a passage the band plays…?
questions.f: Vamping buys time when an actor is late or the audience is still applauding.

questions.q: The theatre expression 'in the wings' and the sailing term 'flies' both survive because early stage crews were largely…?
c: Sailors familiar with ropes and rigging
questions.f: Naval knots, blocks and belaying pins are still standard equipment above a stage.

questions.q: A safety device required in many theatres, made of metal and lowered between stage and audience, is called the…?
questions.f: It is often lowered once during a performance to prove that it still works.

questions.q: 'Deadpan' comedy takes its name from old slang in which 'pan' meant…?
questions.f: A 'deadpan' delivery is literally a motionless face — Buster Keaton's trademark.

questions.q: A 'ham actor' who overacts may owe the name to 19th-century performers who removed makeup with…?
questions.f: 'Hamfatter' appears in old theatrical slang for a cheap, overplaying performer.

questions.q: 'Barnstorming', now meaning a rousing performance, originally described troupes who played in…?
questions.f: Travelling companies really did set up in barns when no theatre was available.

questions.q: The theatre verb 'to upstage' someone originally described an actor…?
c: Moving nearer the back so others must turn away from the audience
questions.f: On a raked stage the upstage actor stood higher, forcing scene partners to face away from the crowd.

questions.q: The word 'robot' entered English from a 1920 stage play, where it was built from a Czech word meaning…?
questions.f: Karel Capek's play R.U.R. gave the world the word; his brother Josef suggested it.

questions.q: The Latin word 'larva', now a biology term for an insect's young stage, originally meant…?
questions.f: Roman actors wore the larva; naturalists later borrowed it for a creature 'masked' before adulthood.

questions.q: 'Somersault' is built from older words meaning…?
questions.f: From Latin supra (over) + saltus (a leap), by way of Old French sombresaut.

questions.q: 'Saltimbanco', an old word for a street performer, literally describes someone who…?
questions.f: Italian saltare in banco — mountebanks really did jump up on benches to gather a crowd.

questions.q: The word 'arena', used for circus and sports spaces, comes from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Roman arenas were spread with sand, which was easy to rake smooth between acts.

questions.q: The 'orama' shared by 'panorama', 'diorama' and 'cyclorama' means…?
questions.f: From Greek horama, 'that which is seen' — pan-orama is an all-round view.

questions.q: The circus prop name 'diabolo' comes from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: From dia (across) + ballein (to throw) — the same verb behind 'ballistic'.

questions.q: 'Villain', now a story's bad character, originally described a…?
questions.f: From Latin villanus, a worker at a villa — city-dwellers turned the word into an insult.

questions.q: 'Fiasco', meaning a spectacular failure, comes from an Italian phrase about making a…?
questions.f: Italian theatre slang 'far fiasco' meant to flop, though nobody is certain how bottles came into it.

questions.q: The word 'documentary' as a film term was coined in a 1926 review by which film-maker?
questions.f: Grierson called Flaherty's Moana material of 'documentary value', and the name stuck.

questions.q: 'Soap opera' got its name because early radio serials were sponsored by makers of…?
questions.f: Procter & Gamble sponsored so many daytime dramas that the genre took their product's name.

questions.q: 'Paparazzi' comes from the surname of a character in which director's film?
questions.f: A news photographer named Paparazzo appears in La Dolce Vita (1960).

questions.q: The word 'manga' is usually translated as…?
questions.f: The artist Hokusai popularised the term for his sketchbooks in the early 1800s.

questions.q: Japan's Bunraku puppet theatre is named after…?
c: A puppeteer whose stage name was Bunrakuken
questions.f: Uemura Bunrakuken's Osaka theatre gave the whole art form its modern name.

questions.q: 'Automaton' comes from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: 18th-century clockwork automata that wrote and drew were the ancestors of animatronics.

questions.q: In ancient Athens, a 'choregos' was a citizen who…?
c: Paid for a chorus's training and costumes
questions.f: Wealthy Athenians competed for the honour, and a winning choregos might erect a monument.

questions.q: The Greek theatre word 'didaskalos', used for the man who trained a chorus, literally means…?
questions.f: Playwrights taught their own choruses, so 'teaching a play' meant staging it.

questions.q: 'Theatre' and 'theory' share a Greek ancestor, a verb meaning to…?
questions.f: From theasthai, 'to view' — a theory was originally a way of seeing.

questions.q: 'Stichomythia' in Greek drama describes dialogue exchanged…?
questions.f: The rapid line-for-line duel makes arguments crackle — Shakespeare used it too.

questions.q: The 'parabasis' in an ancient Greek comedy was the moment when the chorus…?
questions.f: Aristophanes used it to poke fun at Athenian politics and even at his own audience.

questions.q: A 'dramaturg' in a modern theatre company is chiefly responsible for…?
c: Research and shaping of the text
questions.f: The role grew from Gotthold Lessing's work at a Hamburg theatre in the 1760s.

questions.q: 'Entr'acte' is French for…?
questions.f: An entr'acte can be music, a short scene, or a whole comic turn.

questions.q: 'Mimesis', a term from Aristotle used in theatre studies, means…?
questions.f: Aristotle argued that humans learn by imitating, which is why we enjoy drama at all.

questions.q: The Hollywood sign originally read…?
questions.f: It began in 1923 as an advertisement for a housing development; the last four letters were removed in 1949.

questions.q: MGM's Latin motto 'Ars Gratia Artis', encircling its lion, means…?
questions.f: The studio's founders wanted a motto that sounded loftier than the business really was.

questions.q: The drive-in cinema was patented in 1933 by Richard Hollingshead, who first tested it by…?
c: Propping a projector on his car bonnet in his driveway
questions.f: He nailed a screen to trees, put a radio behind it, and sprayed water to test rainy-night viewing.

questions.q: A three-projector system, a curved screen, and a 1952 roller-coaster sequence point to which widescreen process?
questions.f: Fred Waller's Cinerama used three synchronised films to wrap the picture around the audience.

questions.q: The cinema sound standard 'THX' takes its name partly from a George Lucas film and partly from…?
c: An engineer's initials and the word 'experiment'
questions.f: Tomlinson Holman's eXperiment — combined with Lucas's early film THX 1138.

questions.q: A gimmick called 'Percepto', which buzzed cinema seats during a 1959 film, was the work of which showman-director?
questions.f: Castle also insured audiences against death by fright — pure publicity, of course.

questions.q: A hand-coloured print discovered in Spain in 1993 restored the original look of which 1902 film?
questions.f: Restorers spent years digitally rebuilding Melies's frame-by-frame hand tinting.

questions.q: A 2008 discovery in a Buenos Aires archive restored roughly half an hour of which 1927 film?
questions.f: A near-complete print had sat mislabelled in Argentina for 80 years.

questions.q: Silent films often look comically fast today because they were commonly shot at about…?
questions.f: Projected at the modern 24 frames per second, everyone appears to scurry.

questions.q: Most surviving silent films are rare partly because early film stock was made of…?
questions.f: Nitrate decays and burns easily, so a large share of silent cinema is simply gone.

questions.q: A locomotive chase, a Civil War setting, and a 1926 comedy now in the National Film Registry point to which Keaton film?
questions.f: It flopped on release and is now regularly listed among the greatest films ever made.

questions.q: A brother who never spoke on screen but played the harp, and a stage family of five, point to which comedy team?
questions.f: Harpo Marx developed his silent character early and kept it for his whole career.

questions.q: A baseball-themed wordplay routine, a comedy duo of the 1940s, and a recording kept at the Baseball Hall of Fame point to which sketch?
questions.f: Abbott and Costello's routine turns players' names like 'Who' and 'What' into glorious confusion.

questions.q: A pipe-smoking character in a raincoat, a purpose-built city set nicknamed Tativille, and a near-wordless 1967 film point to whom?
questions.f: Tati built a whole modern district outside Paris for Playtime, and it nearly ruined him.

questions.q: An electrical engineering degree, a near-silent television character, and a small green car point to which British comedian?
questions.f: Atkinson studied electrical engineering at Newcastle and Oxford before Mr Bean made him famous worldwide.

questions.q: Which individual has won the most Academy Awards in history, with 22 competitive Oscars?
questions.f: Disney also received four honorary awards, and once won four Oscars in a single ceremony.

questions.q: Costume designer Edith Head holds the record for the most Academy Awards won by a woman, with…?
questions.f: Head worked on hundreds of films and was nominated 35 times.

questions.q: A miniature statuette presented in 1935 to a six-year-old star was a special award for…?
questions.f: Shirley Temple's small Oscar started a category for outstanding child performers.

questions.q: Tatum O'Neal became the youngest person to win a competitive Academy Award at the age of…?
questions.f: She won Best Supporting Actress for Paper Moon in 1974, acting alongside her own father.

questions.q: The first African American performer to win an Academy Award, in 1940, was…?
questions.f: McDaniel won Best Supporting Actress for Gone With the Wind.

questions.q: Charlie Chaplin's 1972 honorary Oscar is remembered for prompting…?
c: The longest standing ovation in Academy history
questions.f: The audience applauded for around 12 minutes when Chaplin returned to Hollywood after 20 years away.

questions.q: A Lyceum Theatre business manager who wrote a famous novel at night, and Britain's first knighted actor, point to which partnership?
c: Arthur Conan Doyle and Edmund Kean
H. G. Wells and Charles Kean
questions.f: Stoker managed Irving's theatre for 27 years and wrote Dracula in his spare hours.

questions.q: A French actress nicknamed 'the Divine', a celebrated Hamlet played by a woman, and nine American tours point to whom?
questions.f: Bernhardt played Hamlet in 1899 and became one of the first great stage stars to appear on film.

questions.q: A seagull emblem on a theatre curtain, a company founded in 1898, and a director who reshaped modern acting point to which theatre?
questions.f: The seagull honours Chekhov's play, whose success saved the young company.

questions.q: The writing principle known as 'Chekhov's gun' advises that any striking object shown early must…?
questions.f: Chekhov put it bluntly: do not hang a rifle on the wall unless someone will use it.

questions.q: France's national theatre company, founded in 1680 and nicknamed 'the House of Moliere', is the…?
questions.f: It is the oldest continuously active theatre company in the world.

questions.q: A South African company, life-size horse puppets visibly operated by performers, and a 2007 National Theatre hit point to which production?
questions.f: Handspring Puppet Company's horses breathe, twitch their ears, and carry riders on stage.

questions.q: A marionette sequence in The Sound of Music was created by which American puppeteer's studio?
questions.f: Baird's team built and performed the 'Lonely Goatherd' puppets for the film.

questions.q: Britain's first puppet television star, appearing on the BBC from 1946, was…?
questions.f: Muffin clattered about on top of a piano while Annette Mills played and sang.

questions.q: A precision dance line, a New York theatre opened in 1932, and identical eye-high kicks point to which troupe?
questions.f: Dancers are arranged by height to create the illusion that all are exactly the same size.

questions.q: A Broadway impresario whose lavish annual revues ran from 1907, celebrated for 'glorifying the American girl', was…?
questions.f: The Ziegfeld Follies launched careers including Fanny Brice's and W. C. Fields's.

questions.q: A songwriter-performer honoured with the only statue on Broadway, and the song 'Give My Regards to Broadway', point to whom?
questions.f: Cohan's statue stands in Times Square, looking down the street he helped define.

questions.q: 'Tin Pan Alley' was a New York street district famous for…?
questions.f: The nickname supposedly came from the clatter of dozens of cheap pianos being played at once.

questions.q: The practice of 'block booking', banned in Hollywood by a 1948 court ruling, forced cinemas to…?
c: Take a studio's weaker films to get its best ones
Show only one film a week
questions.f: The ruling also broke up studio ownership of cinema chains, ending the classic studio system.

questions.q: 'Poverty Row' referred to Hollywood's…?
questions.f: Some Poverty Row outfits, like Republic Pictures, turned out beloved serials and westerns.

questions.q: A 'chapter play' or serial ended each instalment with a peril precisely to…?
c: Bring the audience back next week
questions.f: The Perils of Pauline made the format famous in 1914.

questions.q: Pathe's early newsreels were identified worldwide by a logo featuring which animal?
questions.f: The Gallic rooster is a French national emblem, and Pathe's crowing bird opened newsreels for decades.

questions.q: A hand-cranked camera weighing about five kilograms that filmed, printed and projected was patented by…?
questions.f: One light box did all three jobs, which is why the Lumieres could tour the world so easily.

questions.q: Edison's first film studio, built on a track so it could turn to follow the sun, was nicknamed the…?
questions.f: Its tar-paper walls and cramped interior reminded workers of a police wagon.

questions.q: One of the earliest surviving copyrighted films, from 1894, shows a man doing what?
questions.f: Fred Ott's Sneeze was made for Edison as a series of photographs, then registered for copyright.

questions.q: A phenakistoscope, a Belgian physicist who studied how the eye is fooled, and 1832 point to whom?
questions.f: Plateau's spinning slotted disc was one of the very first true animation devices.

questions.q: The zoetrope's British inventor named his 1834 device the 'daedalum', meaning the wheel of…?
questions.f: William Horner's name referenced Daedalus; the friendlier 'zoetrope' replaced it decades later.

questions.q: A 'flip book' was patented in 1868 under which more formal name?
questions.f: From Greek roots for 'movement writing' — a whole animation studio in your thumb.

questions.q: Which pioneer built a 'chronophotographic gun' to record birds in flight on a single strip?
questions.f: Marey's camera shaped like a rifle took 12 frames a second onto one revolving plate.

questions.q: What does the toy company LEGO make?
questions.f: LEGO has made billions of little bricks in its factory in Denmark.

questions.q: The McDonald's 'golden arches' look like which big letter?
questions.f: The giant yellow M can be spotted from far away, which is exactly the idea.

questions.q: What fruit is on the Apple computer logo?
c: An apple with a bite taken out
questions.f: The bite helps people see it is an apple and not a cherry.

questions.q: The sports brand Puma shows which animal leaping on its logo?
questions.f: A puma is a real wild cat that can leap many times its body length.

questions.q: A person who thinks up brand-new machines and gadgets is called an...?
questions.f: The word 'inventor' comes from a Latin word meaning 'to find or come upon'.

questions.q: A company's special picture symbol is called its...?
questions.f: 'Logo' is short for 'logotype' - a picture that stands for a name.

questions.q: The little word 'ad' is short for...?
questions.f: Ads try to make you notice and remember a product.

questions.q: Thomas Edison is most famous for making which invention glow?
questions.f: Edison's team tested thousands of materials before finding a long-lasting bulb.

questions.q: The Wright brothers were the first people to fly a...?
questions.f: Their very first flight in 1903 lasted only about 12 seconds.

questions.q: What job does a zipper do on your jacket?
questions.f: A zipper's tiny teeth lock together one by one as you pull the slider.

questions.q: Velcro sticks together using thousands of tiny...?
questions.f: One side has little hooks, the other has fuzzy loops for them to grab.

questions.q: A thermos bottle is made to keep your drink...?
questions.f: A thermos has two walls with almost no air between them, so heat can barely escape.

questions.q: What do we call a staircase that moves by itself?
questions.f: 'Escalator' started out as a brand name before it became an everyday word.

questions.q: Which machine carries people straight up and down inside tall buildings?
questions.f: In many countries an elevator is called a 'lift' because it lifts you up.

questions.q: The name 'Facebook' joins the word 'face' with which other word?
questions.f: It was named after printed 'face books' - photo lists of students at schools.

questions.q: Google is a website that helps people...?
questions.f: People around the world ask Google billions of questions every day.

questions.q: The first LEGO toys were made of wood, not plastic.
questions.f: LEGO's founder was a carpenter who carved wooden toys like a famous little duck.

questions.q: Cheerios cereal pieces are shaped like which letter?
questions.f: The little oat rings even float in milk like tiny life rings.

questions.q: M&M's are small chocolates covered in a crunchy...?
questions.f: The hard shell keeps the chocolate from melting in your hand.

questions.q: A Band-Aid is used to cover a...?
questions.f: Band-Aids were invented by a man whose wife often nicked her fingers while cooking.

questions.q: Play-Doh is a soft dough used for...?
questions.f: Before it was a toy, the very same dough was sold for cleaning wallpaper.

questions.q: Which animal rears up on the yellow Ferrari badge?
questions.f: Ferrari's black horse is called the 'prancing horse'.

questions.q: Alexander Graham Bell is remembered for inventing the...?
questions.f: Bell's telephone let people talk to each other from far away for the first time.

questions.q: Barbie is a famous...?
questions.f: Barbie was named after Barbara, the daughter of the woman who created her.

questions.q: Hot Wheels are tiny toy...?
questions.f: Hot Wheels cars zoom down bright orange plastic tracks.

questions.q: A 'slogan' is a...?
c: Short catchy saying used by a brand
questions.f: 'Just Do It' is one of the most famous slogans in the world.

questions.q: A 'customer' is a person who...?
questions.f: Shops try hard to keep their customers happy so they come back.

questions.q: A factory is a place where...?
questions.f: 'Factory' comes from a Latin root meaning 'to make'.

questions.q: If your bike is 'brand-new', it is...?
questions.f: Long ago a 'brand' meant a burning mark - 'brand-new' meant fresh from the fire.

questions.q: Sneakers got their name because their soft soles let people walk quietly.
questions.f: Rubber soles made no noise, so you could 'sneak' around in them.

questions.q: What game piece is on the Domino's Pizza logo?
questions.f: The three dots stand for the company's first three pizza shops.

questions.q: Nintendo's hero Mario wears a cap of which color?
questions.f: Mario's brother Luigi wears green so players can tell them apart.

questions.q: A Frisbee is a toy that you...?
c: Throw so it glides through the air
questions.f: The first Frisbees were metal pie plates that students tossed for fun.

questions.q: A yo-yo rolls up and down on a...?
questions.f: Yo-yos are one of the oldest toys - ancient Greek children played with them.

questions.q: In the game Jenga, players pull wooden blocks out of a...?
questions.f: The name Jenga comes from a word that means 'to build' in the Swahili language.

questions.q: Scrabble is a game where players score points by...?
questions.f: In Scrabble the letter Q is worth 10 points because so few words use it.

questions.q: The teddy bear is named after a real American president.
questions.f: President Theodore 'Teddy' Roosevelt refused to harm a bear cub, and a toymaker honored him.

questions.q: Crayons are mostly made of colored...?
questions.f: The wax lets crayons glide smoothly and never needs sharpening ink or water.

questions.q: A 'label' on a product tells you...?
c: Its name and what is inside
questions.f: Reading labels helps shoppers compare things before buying.

questions.q: The company Cadbury is famous for making...?
questions.f: Cadbury started in England almost 200 years ago selling drinking chocolate.

questions.q: Maggi is a popular brand of...?
questions.f: Maggi is named after Julius Maggi, a food maker from Switzerland.

questions.q: Amul is an Indian brand best known for...?
questions.f: Amul's name comes from a Sanskrit word meaning 'priceless'.

questions.q: Bata shops mainly sell...?
questions.f: Bata began as a small family shoemaking shop more than 125 years ago.

questions.q: A Zamboni is a machine that smooths the ice at...?
questions.f: It is named after Frank Zamboni, the man who invented it.

questions.q: Nerf toys shoot darts and balls made of soft...?
questions.f: Nerf foam is so soft the first ads said you could play with it indoors.

questions.q: A Super Soaker is a toy that squirts...?
questions.f: The Super Soaker was invented by a real NASA rocket engineer.

questions.q: How do you erase a drawing on an Etch A Sketch?
questions.f: Shaking spreads shiny aluminum powder back over the screen like magic.

questions.q: A Rubik's Cube is solved when every side shows...?
questions.f: The cube's inventor took about a month to solve his very first cube.

questions.q: The word 'invent' means to...?
c: Make something for the very first time
questions.f: Inventions like the wheel and the zipper changed everyday life.

questions.q: A 'shoemaker' is a person who...?
questions.f: Big shoe brands like Bata and Nike all began with skilled shoemakers.

questions.q: A short catchy tune in an advertisement is called a...?
questions.f: Jingles get stuck in your head so you remember the product.

questions.q: A fun character that stands for a team or a brand is called a...?
questions.f: The word 'mascot' comes from a French word for a lucky charm.

questions.q: The name 'PlayStation' joins the word 'play' with which word?
questions.f: The PlayStation game console is made by the Japanese company Sony.

questions.q: The 'super' in 'supermarket' tells you the market is...?
questions.f: 'Super' comes from Latin and means 'above or more than usual'.

questions.q: Another word for a shop is a...?
questions.f: A store is where goods are 'stored' until someone buys them.

questions.q: When a shop holds a 'sale', the prices go...?
questions.f: Shops hold sales to invite more customers through the door.

questions.q: The 'price' of a toy tells you...?
questions.f: Price tags on goods only became common in shops about 150 years ago.

questions.q: The zipper got its name from the zippy 'zzzip' sound it makes.
questions.f: A boot company loved the sound so much it started calling the fastener a 'zipper'.

questions.q: Ping-pong is named after the sounds the ball makes as it bounces.
questions.f: 'Ping' and 'pong' copy the click-clack of the ball on paddle and table.

questions.q: Which toy's name is the same little sound said twice?
questions.f: Doubling a sound, like yo-yo, is a playful way languages build words.

questions.q: 'Cornflakes' is a word built from 'corn' and...?
questions.f: Corn flakes were first made by two brothers experimenting in their kitchen.

questions.q: A 'watchmaker' is someone who makes...?
questions.f: Many famous watch brands began in tiny workshops in Switzerland.

questions.q: 'Toothpaste' is a paste made for cleaning your...?
questions.f: Colgate once sold its toothpaste in little jars instead of tubes.

questions.q: The opposite of 'buy' is...?
questions.f: Every shop needs both buyers and sellers to do business.

questions.q: A person who sells things is called a...?
questions.f: 'Seller' and 'cellar' sound alike but a cellar is a room under a house.

questions.q: The money you get back when you pay too much is called...?
questions.f: Cash registers were invented to help shopkeepers count change correctly.

questions.q: A 'coupon' helps a shopper...?
questions.f: 'Coupon' comes from a French word meaning 'to cut' - you cut them out of papers.

questions.q: The paper or foil around a candy bar is called the...?
questions.f: Colorful wrappers help you spot your favorite treat on the shelf.

questions.q: A smiley face you send in a message is called an...?
questions.f: 'Emoji' comes from Japanese words meaning 'picture' and 'character'.

questions.q: In many countries, 'lift' is another name for an...?
questions.f: It is called a lift because it lifts people from floor to floor.

questions.q: A giant advertisement beside a road, big enough to read from a moving car, is a...?
questions.f: Some billboards are as long as a bus so drivers can take them in quickly.

questions.q: Many kids keep their coins at home in a...?
questions.f: Some of the oldest money boxes ever found were already shaped like little pigs.

questions.q: The 'phone' part of 'smartphone' means it can...?
questions.f: 'Phone' comes from a Greek word meaning 'sound' or 'voice'.

questions.q: The Shell fuel company's logo shows a...?
questions.f: The founder's family once really did sell pretty seashells in their shop.

questions.q: Tony the Tiger is the mascot of a brand of...?
questions.f: Tony has been roaring 'They're grrreat!' since the 1950s.

questions.q: Snap, Crackle and Pop are the three elf mascots of which cereal?
questions.f: They are named after the sounds the cereal makes when milk is poured on it.

questions.q: Mickey Mouse's famous ears are two big black...?
questions.f: The round ears make Mickey easy to recognize even as a shadow.

questions.q: Which company created Mickey Mouse?
questions.f: Walt Disney said everything his company built 'started with a mouse'.

questions.q: KFC restaurants are famous for serving...?
questions.f: The letters KFC stand for Kentucky Fried Chicken.

questions.q: Subway restaurants mainly sell long...?
questions.f: Subway's biggest sandwich size is called the footlong.

questions.q: Which drink brand's cans, cups and trucks are famous for being bright red?
questions.f: Coca-Cola has used its red-and-white look for well over a hundred years.

questions.q: The Pepsi circle logo uses red, white and...?
questions.f: The wavy stripe across the middle is nicknamed the Pepsi 'smile'.

questions.q: Lay's is a well-known brand of...?
questions.f: Potato chips are called 'crisps' in Britain.

questions.q: Nutella is a sweet spread made from chocolate and...?
questions.f: Nutella was created in Italy when chocolate was scarce and hazelnuts were plentiful.

questions.q: A Kit Kat bar is made to be...?
questions.f: Breaking off a crispy 'finger' is part of the fun of a Kit Kat.

questions.q: An Oreo has two dark cookies with a sweet white...?
questions.f: Many fans twist an Oreo open before eating it.

questions.q: The Michelin Man mascot looks like he is made of stacked...?
questions.f: He is white because tires were a pale color when he was drawn in 1898.

questions.q: Which brand has a friendly green giant as its mascot?
questions.f: The Jolly Green Giant stands for a valley where sweet corn and peas grow.

questions.q: The Amul mascot is a little...?
questions.f: The Amul girl has appeared in ads since 1966 - one of the longest-running campaigns ever.

questions.q: Air India's mascot is a bowing...?
questions.f: The Maharajah with his big moustache has welcomed flyers since 1946.

questions.q: Some famous inventions were created by children.
questions.f: The Popsicle was invented by an 11-year-old boy named Frank Epperson.

questions.q: The Popsicle was invented when a boy left his drink outside on a...?
questions.f: His fruit drink froze around its stirring stick and became the first ice pop.

questions.q: LEGO toys first came from which country?
questions.f: The first LEGOLAND park opened in Billund, the little Danish town where LEGO began.

questions.q: Nintendo, the maker of Mario games, comes from which country?
questions.f: Nintendo is based in Kyoto, one of Japan's oldest cities.

questions.q: What does the toy called a trampoline let you do?
questions.f: 'Trampoline' was once a brand name owned by its inventor, a gymnast.

questions.q: Chunky Duplo bricks for little kids are a bigger version of...?
questions.f: Duplo bricks are twice as big as LEGO bricks so small hands can grip them safely.

questions.q: A 'toymaker' spends the day making...?
questions.f: Ole Kirk Christiansen, LEGO's founder, began as a toymaker carving wood.

questions.q: The website Amazon shares its name with the world's biggest...?
questions.f: The Amazon River in South America carries more water than any other river.

questions.q: Colgate is best known for making which product?
questions.f: Colgate started out selling soap and candles before it made toothpaste.

questions.q: Heinz is world-famous for its tomato...?
questions.f: Heinz once gave out tiny pickle pins at a big fair to attract visitors.

questions.q: Nike is a famous brand of...?
questions.f: Nike's curvy 'swoosh' logo is one of the most recognized marks on Earth.

questions.q: Which car maker builds around 10 million vehicles a year and started out making looms?
questions.f: Its founder sold a loom patent, and the money started the car business.

questions.q: Boeing and Airbus are companies that build...?
questions.f: A Boeing 747 has about six million parts.

questions.q: Crayola is best known for making...?
questions.f: Crayola's very first crayon box had just eight colors and cost five cents.

questions.q: On YouTube, people mostly watch...?
questions.f: The very first YouTube video ever posted was filmed at a zoo.

questions.q: Which machine heats up food super fast with invisible waves?
questions.f: Microwave ovens can heat a cup of milk in about a minute.

questions.q: A refrigerator's job is to keep food...?
questions.f: Before fridges, people kept food cool with big blocks of ice.

questions.q: A vacuum cleaner is a machine that...?
questions.f: One of the first vacuum cleaners was so big it was pulled by horses.

questions.q: A 'saleswoman' is a woman whose job is to...?
questions.f: 'Sales' plus 'woman' - many job words are two words joined together.

questions.q: The word 'shopping' means...?
questions.f: 'Shop' once meant a small hut or stall where goods were sold.

questions.q: What do we call a small piece of a product given away so people can try it?
questions.f: Shops give free samples hoping you will love the product and buy it.

questions.q: A 'gift shop' is a store that sells...?
questions.f: Museums and zoos often have gift shops near the exit.

questions.q: 'Skateboard' is a word made from 'skate' and...?
questions.f: The first skateboards were roller-skate wheels nailed to wooden boards.

questions.q: The 'pop' in 'popcorn' describes...?
questions.f: Each kernel pops when the water inside turns to steam and bursts out.

questions.q: A 'brand' is the special name a company puts on the things it makes.
questions.f: Nike, LEGO and Amul are all brands - names that help you know who made something.

questions.q: The golden lady statue on a Rolls-Royce car is on the front of the...?
questions.f: The flying lady statue is called the Spirit of Ecstasy.

questions.q: Which toy 'walks' down the stairs coil by coil?
questions.f: The Slinky was invented by accident when an engineer knocked a spring off a shelf.

questions.q: Monopoly is a board game where players buy and sell...?
questions.f: Monopoly players pay each other with colorful pretend money.

questions.q: In the card game Uno, you shout 'Uno!' when you have how many cards left?
questions.f: 'Uno' means 'one' in Spanish and Italian.

questions.q: Which brand of little bandages do people often name when they get a scrape?
questions.f: Band-Aid is a brand name, but many people use it for any small bandage.

questions.q: A Sharpie is a pen that writes with...?
questions.f: Permanent ink stays put even when the paper gets wet.

questions.q: Post-it notes are small papers that can...?
questions.f: Post-it notes use a special weak glue that lets them peel off cleanly.

questions.q: What color are most classic Post-it notes?
questions.f: The bright yellow makes notes easy to spot on a desk or wall.

questions.q: Bubble wrap is fun to pop, but its real job is to...?
questions.f: Bubble wrap's little air pockets work like tiny cushions.

questions.q: The drink brand 7 Up has which number in its name?
questions.f: 7 Up is a clear, bubbly lemon-lime drink first sold in 1929.

questions.q: Pizza Hut, Domino's and Papa John's all mainly sell...?
questions.f: Pizza Hut got its name partly because its first building looked like a little hut.

questions.q: The word 'baker' names a person who makes...?
questions.f: Britannia, a big Indian brand, started as a small biscuit bakery.

questions.q: What is a 'shopping cart' for?
c: Carrying things you plan to buy
questions.f: The shopping cart was invented by a grocery store owner to help people buy more.

questions.q: Which of these is a famous brand of jeans?
questions.f: Levi's has been making tough denim jeans since the days of the gold miners.

questions.q: Crocs are comfy shoes covered in little...?
questions.f: The holes let air in and water out, and can hold charms called Jibbitz.

questions.q: The Google logo uses several different colors in its letters.
questions.f: The playful mix of blue, red, yellow and green shows Google likes to break rules.

questions.q: Which company's name do many people say when they mean 'search for it online'?
questions.f: 'Google it' has even been added to big dictionaries as a verb.

questions.q: Kellogg's is a famous name in which part of the day's food?
questions.f: The Kellogg brothers invented corn flakes while running a health resort.

questions.q: Parle-G is a much-loved Indian brand of...?
questions.f: Parle-G is one of the best-selling biscuit brands in the whole world.

questions.q: Which animal is on the Penguin Books logo?
questions.f: The little penguin has waddled on book covers since 1935.

questions.q: The name 'Hot Wheels' tells you the toy cars are meant to look...?
questions.f: 'Hot' in the name is slang for exciting, not warm to touch.

questions.q: A 'jeweler' is a person who sells...?
questions.f: Famous jewelry shops like Tiffany even have their own special blue color.

questions.q: The word 'open' on a shop door means...?
questions.f: Shops flip their sign to 'closed' when the day is done.

questions.q: What is a 'bookstore'?
questions.f: Amazon, now a giant store for almost everything, began by selling only books.

questions.q: Which toy brand's name sounds like the word 'leg' plus 'oh'?
questions.f: LEGO's name actually comes from Danish words - not from the word 'leg'!

questions.q: Cartoon character SpongeBob works at a burger restaurant called the Krusty...?
questions.f: Even pretend brands like the Krusty Krab have logos and slogans.

questions.q: McDonald's Happy Meal comes with food and a...?
questions.f: The Happy Meal with its little toy first appeared in 1979.

questions.q: Which of these keeps drinks cold in a lunch bag?
questions.f: Thermos flasks keep cold things cold and hot things hot with the same trick.

questions.q: A logo helps people recognize a company without reading any words.
questions.f: You can spot the golden arches or the Nike swoosh even from a moving car.

questions.q: Which of these would an inventor most likely use to protect a new idea?
questions.f: A patent is an official paper that says the invention belongs to its inventor.

questions.q: The 'tooth' in 'toothbrush' and the 'hair' in 'hairbrush' tell you...?
questions.f: English loves joining two words to make a new one that explains itself.

questions.q: A 'florist' runs a shop that sells...?
questions.f: 'Florist' comes from 'flora', a Latin word for flowers and plants.

questions.q: Which candy brand's name is just two letters and an 'and' sign: M&M's?
questions.f: The two M's stand for the last names of the two men who started the company.

questions.q: The Starbucks logo shows a smiling...?
questions.f: The two-tailed mermaid from old sea stories is called a siren.

questions.q: Which invention lets you write, erase and write again on paper?
questions.f: Rubber erasers got the name 'rubber' because they rub out pencil marks.

questions.q: The name 'LEGO' is built from Danish words meaning...?
questions.f: From Danish 'leg godt'; by luck, 'lego' also means 'I put together' in Latin.

questions.q: 'Google' comes from a misspelling of which huge number?
questions.f: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros - the founders wanted to suggest vast amounts of data.

questions.q: 'Adidas' was made from the founder's name. What was his nickname?
questions.f: Adolf 'Adi' Dassler shortened his own name into the brand Adidas.

questions.q: Nike is named after the Greek goddess of...?
questions.f: Nike's swoosh logo is often described as the wing of the winged goddess of victory.

questions.q: The word 'escalator' began life as a...?
questions.f: Otis owned 'Escalator' as a trademark until it became too common a word to protect.

questions.q: 'Trampoline' comes from a Spanish word meaning...?
questions.f: From Spanish 'trampolin'; gymnast George Nissen trademarked the English name in the 1930s.

questions.q: The word 'thermos' comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Greek 'thermos' means hot - the same root as in thermometer and thermal.

questions.q: Which everyday word for a moving stairway was once a protected brand name?
questions.f: When a brand name becomes the common word for the thing, it is called genericized.

questions.q: Volkswagen's name means 'the people's...' what?
questions.f: German 'Volk' means people and 'Wagen' means car or wagon.

questions.q: The Amazon logo's arrow points from the letter A to which letter?
questions.f: The a-to-z arrow means the store sells everything, and it doubles as a smile.

questions.q: Which fruit-named company was started by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak?
questions.f: Jobs had been working at an apple orchard and liked how friendly the word sounded.

questions.q: Coca-Cola's swirly written logo is an example of a...?
questions.f: A wordmark is a logo made only of letters, styled in a special way.

questions.q: Which brand's slogan is 'Just Do It'?
questions.f: The three-word slogan was chosen in 1988 and is now taught in marketing classes.

questions.q: Toblerone chocolate is shaped like a row of...?
questions.f: The peaks echo the Matterhorn, a famous pyramid-shaped mountain in Switzerland.

questions.q: Which animal is hidden inside the mountain on the Toblerone wrapper?
questions.f: The bear is the symbol of Bern, the Swiss city where Toblerone was created.

questions.q: The FedEx logo hides which shape between the E and the x?
questions.f: The white arrow suggests speed and moving forward - once you see it, you cannot unsee it.

questions.q: Post-it Notes were invented after a scientist created a glue that was...?
questions.f: A colleague used the 'failed' glue to keep bookmarks in his hymn book - and a hit was born.

questions.q: Velcro's name is a blend of two French words meaning velvet and...?
questions.f: From 'velours' and 'crochet' - the inventor got the idea from burrs stuck to his dog.

questions.q: George de Mestral invented Velcro after noticing burrs clinging to his...?
questions.f: Under a microscope he saw the burrs' tiny hooks - nature's own fastener.

questions.q: Which company makes the PlayStation game console?
questions.f: Sony's name was picked partly from the Latin word 'sonus', meaning sound.

questions.q: Which company makes the Xbox?
questions.f: The Xbox began as a project called 'DirectX Box', shortened to Xbox.

questions.q: 'Microsoft' is a blend of 'microcomputer' and which word?
questions.f: Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote software for the earliest small computers.

questions.q: Which video-game plumber was named after a landlord of the game company's warehouse?
questions.f: Nintendo of America rented a warehouse from a man named Mario Segale.

questions.q: The 'Pepsi Challenge' asked people to compare two colas while...?
questions.f: The blind taste test of 1975 is one of advertising's most copied ideas.

questions.q: Which drink was first sold as a medicine at a pharmacy soda fountain in 1886?
questions.f: Pharmacist John Pemberton mixed it in Atlanta, and it sold about nine glasses a day at first.

questions.q: The 'ade' in 'lemonade' and 'orangeade' tells you the drink is...?
questions.f: The ending '-ade' came into English from French for a drink made from something.

questions.q: Kleenex is a brand name people often use instead of the word...?
questions.f: Kleenex tissues were first sold in 1924 to remove make-up, not for sneezes.

questions.q: 'Xerox' became a verb meaning to...?
questions.f: The name comes from Greek roots meaning 'dry writing', because the process uses no wet ink.

questions.q: A trampoline, an escalator and a zipper are all examples of...?
questions.f: Companies lose the trademark when everyone uses the word for all such products.

questions.q: The name 'Pixar' was formed to sound like a Spanish-flavored word meaning...?
questions.f: The founders combined 'pixel' with an invented verb ending to sound like 'to make pictures'.

questions.q: Which Pixar lamp appears in the studio's logo?
questions.f: The lamp is named Luxo Jr. after a short film Pixar made in 1986.

questions.q: The word 'brand' originally meant a...?
questions.f: Makers burned marks into goods and cattle to show whose they were - the first branding.

questions.q: A 'trademark' is a mark that shows...?
questions.f: The little TM symbol tells others the name belongs to a company.

questions.q: A 'patent' protects an inventor's...?
