questions.f: Patents last only a set number of years, then anyone may copy the idea.

questions.q: Which brand of chocolate spread's name blends the English word for nut with a sweet ending?
questions.f: 'Nut' plus the soft Italian ending '-ella' makes a name that sounds friendly in any language.

questions.q: Who designed Apple's bitten-apple logo in 1977, adding the bite so it would not look like a cherry?
questions.f: Janoff added the bite mainly for scale, and liked the pun on the computer word 'byte'.

questions.q: Lego bricks made today still fit bricks from 1958 because the company keeps the...?
questions.f: LEGO moulds are accurate to within a fraction of a hair's width.

questions.q: 'Ferrari', 'Ford' and 'Honda' are all car brands named after...?
questions.f: A name taken from a person is called an eponym.

questions.q: A word or brand named after a real person is called an...?
questions.f: 'Eponym' comes from Greek roots meaning 'upon a name'.

questions.q: 'BMW' stands for German words meaning Bavarian Motor...?
questions.f: BMW built aircraft engines before cars, which is why its badge uses Bavarian blue and white.

questions.q: 'IKEA' is built from initials of its founder's name plus his...?
questions.f: Ingvar Kamprad added Elmtaryd, his family farm, and Agunnaryd, his home village.

questions.q: IKEA, the furniture company, comes from which country?
questions.f: IKEA's blue-and-yellow logo matches the colors of the Swedish flag.

questions.q: The 'Lego' company's motto is 'only the best is...'?
questions.f: The Danish phrase 'det bedste er ikke for godt' was carved in the founder's workshop.

questions.q: Who drew the Nike swoosh in 1971 for a fee of about 35 dollars?
questions.f: Nike later gave her shares in the company as thanks, worth far more than the fee.

questions.q: Before it was called Nike, the shoe company was named Blue Ribbon...?
questions.f: Blue Ribbon Sports began by importing Japanese running shoes in 1964.

questions.q: 'Sanitizer', 'moisturizer' and 'organizer' share an ending meaning...?
questions.f: The suffix '-izer' turns a verb into the name of the thing doing the job.

questions.q: The word 'aspirin' was a trademark of which German company?
questions.f: Bayer lost the aspirin trademark in several countries, so it became an everyday word.

questions.q: 'Nintendo' was founded in 1889 to make which kind of product?
questions.f: Nintendo made handmade Japanese hanafuda cards for decades before video games.

questions.q: Which everyday hook-and-loop fastener's name is a registered trademark?
questions.f: The company prefers you say 'hook and loop' for other brands' versions.

questions.q: The Starbucks logo's sea creature comes from stories of sailors and is called a...?
questions.f: A siren's song was said to lure sailors - just as coffee lures customers, said the founders.

questions.q: Which fast-food chain's founders were two brothers with the surname McDonald?
questions.f: Richard and Maurice McDonald opened their speedy burger stand in California in 1948.

questions.q: The 'Colonel' pictured on KFC buckets was a real man named Harland...?
questions.f: He was made an honorary Kentucky Colonel, a state title, not an army rank.

questions.q: Which brand's logo is three stripes that form a mountain shape?
questions.f: Adidas has used three stripes since the 1950s and calls itself 'the brand with the three stripes'.

questions.q: Instant noodles were invented in Japan by Momofuku...?
questions.f: He created them in a backyard shed in 1958 after seeing people queue for food.

questions.q: Bubble gum's pink color was chosen because pink dye was the...?
c: Only color the inventor had handy
questions.f: Dubble Bubble's inventor grabbed the pink dye in 1928, and pink gum stuck ever since.

questions.q: The word 'yo-yo' is thought to come from a language of which country?
questions.f: In Tagalog, 'yo-yo' suggests 'come back' - exactly what the toy does.

questions.q: 'Jenga' takes its name from a Swahili word meaning...?
questions.f: The game's creator grew up in East Africa, where Swahili is widely spoken.

questions.q: The Rubik's Cube is named after Erno Rubik, who worked as a...?
questions.f: He built it in 1974 to help students understand three-dimensional shapes.

questions.q: Play-Doh was originally sold as a product for cleaning...?
questions.f: When coal heating faded, sooty wallpaper cleaner found a second life as a toy.

questions.q: Which toy was invented when engineer Richard James knocked a spring off a shelf?
questions.f: He watched it 'walk' across the floor, and his wife found the name Slinky in a dictionary.

questions.q: The Frisbee's flying-disc name was inspired by a company that made...?
questions.f: Students tossed empty Frisbie Pie Company tins, and the name stuck with a spelling change.

questions.q: Barbie's full pretend name is Barbara Millicent...?
questions.f: Barbie was named after Barbara, the daughter of creator Ruth Handler.

questions.q: Ken, Barbie's companion doll, was named after the creator's...?
questions.f: Ruth Handler named both dolls after her own two children, Barbara and Kenneth.

questions.q: Which company makes Barbie and Hot Wheels?
questions.f: Mattel's name blends the founders' names Harold MATson and ELLiot Handler.

questions.q: Which company makes Monopoly, Play-Doh and Nerf toys?
questions.f: Hasbro's name is short for 'Hassenfeld Brothers', the family who founded it.

questions.q: The 'Hula Hoop' name borrowed the word 'hula' from a dance of which islands?
questions.f: Sailors said the hip-swaying hoop craze of 1958 looked like Hawaiian hula dancing.

questions.q: 'Bluetooth' technology is named after a medieval king of which country?
questions.f: King Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson united Denmark - just as the tech unites devices.

questions.q: The Bluetooth logo is made of two Viking runes standing for...?
questions.f: The runes are the initials of Harald Bluetooth himself.

questions.q: 'Wi-Fi' was invented as a catchy name; it does NOT officially stand for...?
questions.f: A branding firm coined Wi-Fi to echo 'hi-fi'; the 'wireless fidelity' meaning came later.

questions.q: The 'tele' in 'telephone' and 'television' means...?
questions.f: So a telephone is 'far sound' and a television is 'far seeing'.

questions.q: The word 'automobile' is built from roots meaning...?
questions.f: From Greek 'autos' (self) and Latin 'mobilis' (movable) - a thing that moves itself.

questions.q: The 'photo' in 'photograph' and 'photocopy' means...?
questions.f: A photograph is literally 'writing with light'.

questions.q: The 'micro' in 'microwave' and 'microscope' means...?
questions.f: Microwaves are radio waves with short - or 'micro' - wavelengths.

questions.q: Which company's name means 'people's car' in German?
questions.f: The famous Beetle was designed to be a car ordinary families could afford.

questions.q: 'Audi' is a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Founder August Horch's surname means 'listen' in German - so he used the Latin for it.

questions.q: 'Lego' is a company; but 'legos' is not the official plural. LEGO prefers you say LEGO...?
questions.f: The company asks fans to say 'LEGO bricks' to keep its trademark strong.

questions.q: Which brand name literally means 'good year' and honors a rubber pioneer?
questions.f: It honors Charles Goodyear, who discovered how to make rubber tough and springy.

questions.q: 'Bridgestone' tyres come from Japan; the name is a flipped translation of the founder's name...?
questions.f: Japanese 'ishi' means stone and 'bashi' means bridge - so 'Stonebridge' became Bridgestone.

questions.q: The Michelin Man mascot's real name is...?
questions.f: His name comes from a Latin toast, 'nunc est bibendum' - 'now is the time to drink'.

questions.q: Michelin, famous for tyres, also awards stars to...?
questions.f: Michelin printed guidebooks to give drivers reasons to travel - and wear out tyres.

questions.q: Mentos, Mars and Milka are all brands of...?
questions.f: The Mars bar is named after Frank Mars, who started making sweets in his kitchen.

questions.q: The car brand 'Volvo' is a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Fitting for a company that began by making ball bearings, which roll.

questions.q: Sony's Walkman got its name because it let people listen while they...?
questions.f: The 1979 Walkman was the first pocket cassette player with headphones.

questions.q: The 'i' in iPod and iPhone was first explained by Apple as standing for...?
questions.f: Steve Jobs introduced the iMac in 1998 with 'i' for internet, plus individual and inspire.

questions.q: Which brand sells shoes with a leaping cat and was founded by Rudolf Dassler?
questions.f: Rudolf and his brother Adi both made shoes - Adi founded Adidas, Rudolf founded Puma.

questions.q: Ballpoint pens are called 'Biros' in many countries after inventor Laszlo...?
questions.f: Hungarian journalist Laszlo Biro perfected the quick-drying ballpoint in the 1930s.

questions.q: The word 'crayon' comes from a French word meaning...?
questions.f: French 'craie' means chalk, so 'crayon' first meant a chalk pencil.

questions.q: 'Vaseline' blends the German word for water with the Greek word for...?
questions.f: From German 'Wasser' and Greek 'elaion' - water plus oil.

questions.q: The soft drink brand 'Fanta' takes its name from a German word meaning...?
questions.f: Staff were told to use their 'Fantasie' - imagination - to name the new orange drink.

questions.q: 'Nestle' is the founder's surname, and it also means 'little...' what in his dialect?
questions.f: That is why the Nestle logo shows a bird's nest with a mother feeding chicks.

questions.q: Which chocolate brand's name comes from the Swiss village of its founder's family?
questions.f: Henri Nestle was Swiss, and his family name became one of the world's biggest food brands.

questions.q: 'Toblerone' blends the founder's surname Tobler with the Italian word 'torrone', a kind of...?
questions.f: That honey-almond nougat is what makes Toblerone chewy in the middle.

questions.q: Coca-Cola's distinctive bottle shape is nicknamed the...?
questions.f: Designers wanted a bottle you could recognize in the dark or by touch alone.

questions.q: What does the 'Amul' in the butter brand mean in Sanskrit?
questions.f: From 'amulya'; the co-operative was built by dairy farmers in Gujarat, India.

questions.q: Which slogan belongs to Amul butter?
questions.f: The Amul girl in a polka-dot dress has starred in topical ads since 1966.

questions.q: The Indian company 'Tata' takes its name from...?
questions.f: Jamsetji Tata started the group in 1868; today it makes everything from salt to cars.

questions.q: 'Godrej', 'Bajaj' and 'Wipro' are Indian brands; Wipro's name shortens Western India...?
questions.f: Wipro began by making cooking oil before becoming a technology giant.

questions.q: Which soap brand's name is the English word for a bird's soft breast feathers?
questions.f: The dove is also a worldwide symbol of gentleness and peace.

questions.q: Lifebuoy soap's name refers to a floating ring that...?
questions.f: The name suggested the soap 'rescued' people from germs.

questions.q: The brand 'Pepsi' was named after a word for a digestion problem called...?
questions.f: Pharmacist Caleb Bradham first sold it as 'Brad's Drink' to soothe the stomach.

questions.q: Which soft drink was originally called 'Brad's Drink'?
questions.f: It was renamed Pepsi-Cola in 1898, five years after it was first mixed.

questions.q: The word 'cola' in drink names comes from a West African...?
questions.f: Kola nuts contain caffeine and were an early ingredient in cola drinks.

questions.q: Which two ingredients gave Coca-Cola the two halves of its name?
questions.f: Bookkeeper Frank Robinson thought two C's would look striking in advertising.

questions.q: Coca-Cola's animated winter mascots, first seen in a 1993 advert, are which animal?
questions.f: The bears were animated by the studio behind the film 'The Snowman'.

questions.q: Coca-Cola's advertising helped make the modern red-suited image of Santa Claus popular.
questions.f: Artist Haddon Sundblom painted the jolly Coke Santa from 1931 - though red Santas existed before.

questions.q: Which slogan, launched in 2003 with a five-note whistle, belongs to McDonald's?
questions.f: A German agency, Heye and Partner, won the internal contest to create it.

questions.q: A 'logotype', shortened to 'logo', originally meant a single block of...?
questions.f: Printers cast whole words as one metal block to save time - hence 'logotype'.

questions.q: The 'graph' in 'logogram' and 'autograph' means...?
questions.f: So an autograph is literally 'self-writing' - your own name in your own hand.

questions.q: Denim jeans were made tougher when Jacob Davis added metal...?
questions.f: He and Levi Strauss patented riveted work trousers in 1873.

questions.q: The word 'jeans' comes from the name of which Italian port city?
questions.f: Sailors from Genoa wore sturdy cotton trousers the French called 'bleu de Genes'.

questions.q: The word 'denim' comes from a French phrase meaning 'from...' which town?
questions.f: 'Serge de Nimes' - cloth from Nimes - shortened over time to denim.

questions.q: The Wright brothers ran which kind of shop before building aircraft?
questions.f: Their bicycle skills taught them about balance and steering - key to flying.

questions.q: Who is credited with inventing the telephone and patenting it in 1876?
questions.f: The unit of loudness, the decibel, is named in Bell's honor.

questions.q: The 'watt', a unit of power, is named after engineer James...?
questions.f: James Watt improved the steam engine so much that his name became a unit.

questions.q: The 'volt' is named after Italian scientist Alessandro...?
questions.f: Volta built the first true battery, a stack of metal discs called a voltaic pile.

questions.q: A pair of trousers held up by straps over the shoulders takes its name from 'dungri', a cloth from...?
questions.f: Dungarees are named after Dongri, a district of Mumbai where the cloth was made.

questions.q: The 'sandwich' is named after an earl who wanted to eat without leaving his...?
questions.f: The 4th Earl of Sandwich asked for meat between bread so he need not stop playing.

questions.q: Which biscuit-shaped word comes from a Dutch phrase meaning 'little cake'?
questions.f: From Dutch 'koekje' - brought to New York by Dutch settlers.

questions.q: The word 'biscuit' is built from roots meaning...?
questions.f: Baking twice dried biscuits out so they'd keep for long sea voyages.

questions.q: 'Cellophane' blends 'cellulose' with a Greek root meaning...?
questions.f: From 'diaphane', meaning transparent - the wrap you can see straight through.

questions.q: 'Linoleum' is named from Latin roots meaning oil and which plant fibre?
questions.f: From 'linum' (flax) and 'oleum' (oil) - the flooring is made with linseed oil.

questions.q: Which flying-disc, bouncy-toy and moving-stairway words were all once trademarks?
questions.f: Frisbee is still a trademark; trampoline and escalator became common nouns.

questions.q: 'Aspirin', 'heroin' and 'escalator' are examples of what happening to trademarks?
questions.f: Lawyers call it 'genericide' - the brand becomes the name of the whole category.

questions.q: Which brand of vacuum cleaner became a British verb, as in 'to ___ the carpet'?
questions.f: In Britain 'hoovering' means vacuuming, whatever brand you actually use.

questions.q: James Dyson's famous vacuum cleaners removed the need for a...?
questions.f: Dyson made over 5,000 prototypes before his bagless cyclone design worked.

questions.q: Which company's Android operating system is named after a word for...?
questions.f: Android versions were once named after sweets, from Cupcake to Oreo.

questions.q: The word 'jumbo', used for huge jets and drinks, came from the name of a famous...?
questions.f: Jumbo was a giant African elephant shown in London and America in the 1800s.

questions.q: The Boeing 747 nickname 'Jumbo Jet' pointed to the plane's...?
questions.f: The 747's upstairs deck gave it a distinctive hump behind the cockpit.

questions.q: Which brand's slogan promises 'Melts in your mouth, not in your hands'?
questions.f: The hard sugar shell really does keep the chocolate from smearing your fingers.

questions.q: Kit Kat's slogan invites you to 'Have a break, have a...'?
questions.f: The break-time idea matches a bar designed to snap into pieces.

questions.q: Which brand's slogan is 'Because You're Worth It'?
questions.f: It was written in 1971 by a young copywriter, Ilon Specht, and is still used today.

questions.q: 'The Happiest Place on Earth' is a slogan used by...?
questions.f: Disneyland opened in California in 1955 with just 18 attractions.

questions.q: Which slogan did Apple launch in 1997, showing portraits of famous thinkers?
questions.f: Steve Jobs defended the grammar, arguing 'different' was being used as a noun.

questions.q: 'A Diamond is Forever' is one of the most famous slogans in advertising, written for...?
questions.f: Copywriter Frances Gerety wrote it in 1947 - and it changed how people buy rings.

questions.q: Which brand's slogan was 'Betcha Can't Eat Just One'?
questions.f: Lay's built a whole campaign on how hard it is to stop after one chip.

questions.q: Pringles are packed in a tall tube so the chips can...?
questions.f: Their curved saddle shape lets them nest perfectly, chip on chip.

questions.q: The moustached man on the Pringles can is nicknamed Julius...?
questions.f: The name plays on Julius Caesar; the character has been redrawn several times.

questions.q: Which everyday product's name blends 'quick' with the sound of drying ink? Hint: it is a correction fluid.
questions.f: Liquid Paper was invented by Bette Nesmith Graham, a typist who used paint to fix mistakes.

questions.q: Bette Nesmith Graham invented correction fluid while working as a...?
questions.f: She mixed her first batch in a kitchen blender and later sold the company for millions.

questions.q: The chocolate chip cookie is said to have been created at the Toll House...?
questions.f: Ruth Wakefield's 1930s recipe is why some chocolate chips are still called Toll House.

questions.q: Which sticky sweet spread's brand name Marmite comes from a French word for a...?
questions.f: That is why the classic Marmite jar is shaped like a little round pot.

questions.q: Which cereal brand's name simply describes flattened corn?
questions.f: John Harvey Kellogg's brother added sugar and turned it into a breakfast empire.

questions.q: 'Granola' and 'Grape-Nuts' were invented as foods for people at...?
questions.f: Grape-Nuts contains neither grapes nor nuts - the name was pure marketing.

questions.q: Which fizzy drink brand's name contains a doctor's title?
questions.f: Dr Pepper was first served in 1885 in Waco, Texas - a year before Coca-Cola.

questions.q: Which Indian cola brand's logo shows a red thumbs-up hand?
questions.f: Thums Up was created in 1977 and is still hugely popular in India.

questions.q: The word 'soda' in 'soda pop' refers to the drink being...?
questions.f: Early fizzy drinks used sodium bicarbonate - washing soda's cousin - to make bubbles.

questions.q: A 'chain' of restaurants means many shops that...?
questions.f: McDonald's has more than 40,000 restaurants around the world.

questions.q: A company that lets others open shops using its brand is offering a...?
questions.f: 'Franchise' comes from a French word meaning 'freedom' - freedom to use the name.

questions.q: The stripey lines and numbers scanned at a checkout are called a...?
questions.f: The first product ever scanned with a barcode, in 1974, was a packet of chewing gum.

questions.q: Which chewing-gum brand was the first product ever scanned with a barcode?
questions.f: That 10-pack of gum is now kept in a museum in Washington, D.C.

questions.q: The 'super' in 'Super Glue' and 'superstore' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Super Glue's real name is cyanoacrylate, discovered while trying to make clear gun sights.

questions.q: Super Glue was discovered by accident by scientists trying to make...?
questions.f: It stuck to everything, which was a nuisance then and a fortune later.

questions.q: Which invention did Percy Spencer discover after a chocolate bar melted in his pocket?
questions.f: He was standing near a radar tube; the first commercial microwave was named the Radarange.

questions.q: The first microwave oven sold to restaurants was named the...?
questions.f: Early models were nearly six feet tall and weighed as much as a small piano.

questions.q: Which brand of building toy is a Danish company still owned by the founding family?
questions.f: LEGO has been run by three generations of the Kirk Christiansen family.

questions.q: The word 'stationery' with an 'e' means...?
questions.f: 'Stationary' with an 'a' means not moving - a classic spelling trap.

questions.q: A 'brand ambassador' is a person who...?
questions.f: Sports stars are often brand ambassadors for shoe and drink companies.

questions.q: When two brands work together on one product, it is called a...?
questions.f: Adidas and LEGO have released shoes designed to look like plastic bricks.

questions.q: A brand can lose its trademark if everyone starts using the name for all similar products.
questions.f: That is why companies write 'LEGO bricks' and 'Frisbee disc' instead of just the name.

questions.q: A trademark that has become the everyday word for a whole product type is called a...?
questions.f: Escalator, trampoline, zipper and aspirin all crossed that line into common speech.

questions.q: A brand name blended from two words, like 'Velcro' from velours and crochet, is a...?
questions.f: Lewis Carroll coined the term 'portmanteau word' for two meanings packed in one suitcase.

questions.q: The 'Nike' swoosh is meant to suggest the wing of which mythological figure?
questions.f: The Greek goddess Nike appears on ancient coins with wings spread wide.

questions.q: Adidas and Puma were founded by two brothers who fell out. Their surname was...?
questions.f: The feud split their German hometown of Herzogenaurach into two rival shoe camps.

questions.q: The German town where both Adidas and Puma have headquarters is...?
questions.f: Locals were once said to check a stranger's shoes before deciding to say hello.

questions.q: 'Kodak' was invented as a name because George Eastman wanted a word that was...?
questions.f: Eastman loved the letter K and built a word that sounded the same in every language.

questions.q: Kodak's early slogan was 'You press the button, we do the...'?
questions.f: Customers mailed the whole camera back to Kodak, which developed the film and reloaded it.

questions.q: 'Haagen-Dazs' is a made-up name invented in which country?
questions.f: Founders in the Bronx invented a Danish-sounding name; it means nothing in any language.

questions.q: 'Lego' happens to mean 'I assemble' or 'I read' in which ancient language?
questions.f: The company only discovered the Latin coincidence after choosing 'leg godt' in Danish.

questions.q: The 'zip' in 'zip code' stands for Zone Improvement...?
questions.f: The US Post Office picked initials that also suggested mail zipping along quickly.

questions.q: 'Spam' the tinned meat is thought to blend 'spiced' with which word?
questions.f: The email meaning came later, from a Monty Python sketch where the word repeats endlessly.

questions.q: 'Jacuzzi', now used for any whirlpool bath, is the surname of brothers who first built...?
questions.f: The Italian-American Jacuzzi brothers designed propellers before inventing the whirlpool pump.

questions.q: 'Ping-Pong' is a registered trademark; the official sport name is...?
questions.f: The trademark forced tournaments to use 'table tennis' in their official titles.

questions.q: Which word for a small motorized two-wheeler began as the brand name 'Vespa', Italian for...?
questions.f: The scooter's designer thought the narrow waist and buzzing engine resembled a wasp.

questions.q: 'Lamborghini' badges show a bull because the founder was born under which zodiac sign?
questions.f: Ferruccio Lamborghini also bred fighting bulls, and named many models after them.

questions.q: Ferrari's prancing horse badge is topped by the green, white and red of...?
questions.f: Enzo Ferrari added the tricolour stripe to mark the cars as proudly Italian.

questions.q: The Mercedes-Benz three-pointed star was meant to represent engines for land, sea and...?
questions.f: Gottlieb Daimler drew a star on a postcard of his house, promising it would shine over his factory.

questions.q: 'Mercedes' in Mercedes-Benz was the first name of the daughter of an early...?
questions.f: Emil Jellinek raced under his daughter Mercedes' name, and it became the brand.

questions.q: Audi's four interlocking rings stand for four companies that...?
questions.f: Audi, DKW, Horch and Wanderer joined as Auto Union in 1932.

questions.q: The word 'diesel' for a fuel and engine comes from inventor Rudolf Diesel's...?
questions.f: His engine ignites fuel by compression alone, needing no spark plug.

questions.q: 'Pasteurized' milk is named after Louis Pasteur, who showed that heating kills...?
questions.f: Pasteur first used gentle heating to save French wine from spoiling.

questions.q: The 'Braille' writing system for blind readers is named after Louis Braille, who was...?
c: A blind French teenager who invented it
questions.f: He devised his six-dot cells at just 15, adapting a military night-writing code.

questions.q: 'Silhouette' comes from the surname of a French finance minister known for...?
questions.f: Etienne de Silhouette's penny-pinching made cheap cut-paper outlines a joke named for him.

questions.q: The 'Segway' name blends 'segue' with which idea?
c: A smooth transition on the way
questions.f: 'Segue' means to move smoothly from one thing to the next - like gliding on two wheels.

questions.q: Which company's logo hides a 'bear' silhouette in the Swiss mountain design?
questions.f: Bern, Toblerone's home city, is nicknamed the city of bears and keeps bears in a park.

questions.q: The 'Baskin-Robbins' logo hides which number in its pink letters?
questions.f: Thirty-one stands for a different flavour for every day of the month.

questions.q: The arrow in the FedEx logo lives in the negative space between which two letters?
questions.f: Designer Lindon Leader built a custom letterform just to make the arrow appear naturally.

questions.q: Empty space in a logo that forms a hidden shape is called...?
questions.f: The FedEx arrow and the Amazon smile are the most-cited negative-space tricks in design.

questions.q: The little feet at the ends of letters in fonts like Times New Roman are called...?
questions.f: Brands often drop serifs for a modern look - Google did exactly that in 2015.

questions.q: Adjusting the space between two letters in a logo is called...?
questions.f: Bad kerning can turn a logo into an accidental joke, which designers dread.

questions.q: The Coca-Cola logo is written in a flowing 19th-century handwriting style called...?
questions.f: Bookkeeper Frank Robinson wrote it himself in the standard business hand of his day.

questions.q: The 'dynamic ribbon' is the name Coca-Cola gives to the white...?
questions.f: That swirling ribbon has curled beneath the wordmark since 1969.

questions.q: A logo that stays clear whether printed on a stamp or a stadium is said to have good...?
questions.f: Designers test marks at thumbnail size first; if it fails there, it fails everywhere.

questions.q: 'Pantone' is a company famous for standardizing...?
questions.f: Brands guard specific Pantone shades, like Tiffany Blue or UPS Brown, as part of identity.

questions.q: The specific shade 'Tiffany Blue' is protected as a...?
questions.f: Tiffany chose the robin's-egg blue in 1845, possibly because turquoise was fashionable.

questions.q: 'UPS Brown' and 'Cadbury Purple' show that companies can trademark a...?
questions.f: Courts sometimes allow color trademarks when shoppers strongly link the shade to one brand.

questions.q: The name 'Amazon' was chosen partly because it starts with 'A', helping it appear...?
questions.f: Jeff Bezos also liked that the Amazon is the world's largest river - suggesting huge scale.

questions.q: Amazon's original name, quickly abandoned, was...?
questions.f: A lawyer misheard 'Cadabra' as 'cadaver', so Bezos changed it fast.

questions.q: The word 'catalogue' comes from Greek roots meaning...?
questions.f: Mail-order catalogues were the internet of the 1890s, delivering brands to farms.

questions.q: 'Retail' comes from an old French word meaning to...?
questions.f: A retailer breaks bulk goods into small pieces to sell to individual shoppers.

questions.q: The word 'merchandise' shares a Latin root with 'merchant' and 'commerce' meaning...?
questions.f: From Latin 'merx', meaning goods for sale.

questions.q: 'Boycott', meaning to refuse to buy, comes from the surname of a...?
questions.f: Tenants shunned Captain Charles Boycott in 1880, and his name became a verb.

questions.q: 'Monopoly' is built from Greek roots meaning...?
questions.f: From 'monos' (single) and 'polein' (to sell) - one seller controls the market.

questions.q: The Monopoly board's streets in the original US edition are from which city?
questions.f: Boardwalk and Park Place are real Atlantic City locations.

questions.q: Monopoly grew out of an earlier game invented to teach about land ownership, called The...?
questions.f: Elizabeth Magie patented it in 1904 to criticize landlords - the opposite of its later reputation.

questions.q: Scrabble's inventor, Alfred Butts, chose letter values by counting letters in...?
questions.f: He tallied front pages of The New York Times to see which letters appeared most.

questions.q: Scrabble was originally called 'Lexiko' and then...?
questions.f: It was renamed Scrabble in 1948, from a word meaning to scratch or grope about.

questions.q: The word 'scrabble' itself means to...?
questions.f: It comes from a Dutch word 'schrabbelen', to scratch repeatedly.

questions.q: 'Lego Technic', 'Duplo' and 'Bionicle' are examples of a company's product...?
questions.f: A single brand often shelters many sub-brands aimed at different ages.

questions.q: The number of ways to combine just six standard 2x4 LEGO bricks is famously over...?
questions.f: LEGO's often-quoted figure is 915,103,765 combinations for six bricks of one colour.

questions.q: The Rubik's Cube has how many possible arrangements, roughly?
questions.f: Exactly 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 - yet any position can be solved in 20 moves or fewer.

questions.q: The proven maximum number of moves needed to solve any Rubik's Cube is nicknamed...?
questions.f: Computers proved in 2010 that 20 moves always suffice.

questions.q: Which invention did Hungarian Laszlo Biro improve by borrowing quick-drying ink from...?
questions.f: As a journalist he noticed newsprint ink dried instantly and smudge-free.

questions.q: The 'Post-it' inventor Spencer Silver made a glue that was too weak, and Art Fry used it for...?
questions.f: 3M sold the notes nationwide in 1980 after giving away samples in one test city.

questions.q: 3M's name stands for Minnesota Mining and ___ Company.
questions.f: 3M began by mining a mineral for sandpaper and now makes tens of thousands of products.

questions.q: Scotch Tape got its name from a jibe about the brand being...?
questions.f: Painters complained the tape had glue only at the edges, calling it 'Scotch' - meaning cheap.

questions.q: The word 'nylon' was a coined trade name from which company?
questions.f: DuPont chemists created the first fully synthetic fibre in 1935; nylon stockings sold out in hours.

questions.q: Which DuPont chemist discovered Teflon by accident in 1938?
questions.f: He found a slippery white powder left inside a frozen gas cylinder.

questions.q: 'Bakelite', an early plastic, is named after its Belgian-American inventor Leo...?
questions.f: Bakelite radios and telephones of the 1920s were the first true plastic consumer goods.

questions.q: 'Tupperware' is named after Earl Tupper, whose big idea was a lid that...?
questions.f: He copied the seal from a paint-can lid; sales took off through home 'Tupperware parties'.

questions.q: Brownie Wise made Tupperware famous by inventing a way of selling called the...?
questions.f: Tupperware sold better in living rooms than in shops, and Wise built a sales army.

questions.q: The Shell logo's scallop shell is technically the shell of a...?
questions.f: The founder's father genuinely imported seashells from the East before selling oil.

questions.q: 'Petroleum' is built from Latin roots meaning...?
questions.f: From 'petra' (rock) and 'oleum' (oil) - oil found in rock.

questions.q: The word 'gasoline' and the British word 'petrol' both refer to fuel refined from...?
questions.f: Standard Oil helped popularize 'gasoline' in America while Britain shortened 'petroleum spirit'.

questions.q: The Indian brand 'Godrej' first became famous for making which secure product?
questions.f: Ardeshir Godrej made springless locks in 1897, then India's first vegetable-oil soap.

questions.q: 'Dabur', the Indian brand, is a contraction of the founder's title 'Daktar' plus his name...?
questions.f: Dr S. K. Burman founded it in 1884 making Ayurvedic medicines in Kolkata.

questions.q: Which Indian detergent brand became a business-school case study for beating global rivals on price?
questions.f: Karsanbhai Patel mixed the first batches himself and sold them door to door by bicycle.

questions.q: 'Maruti', the Indian car brand, takes its name from another name for which figure?
questions.f: Maruti is a name for Hanuman, son of the wind - a fitting name for something fast.

questions.q: The Indian brand 'Britannia' takes its name from the Latin name for...?
questions.f: Britannia began in 1892 in Kolkata, baking biscuits in a small house.

questions.q: 'Haldiram's' and 'Bikaji' are Indian snack brands from which desert city?
questions.f: Bikaner's dry climate suited the crisp gram-flour snack called bhujia.

questions.q: The word 'shampoo' entered English from a Hindi word meaning to...?
questions.f: From 'champo'; Sake Dean Mahomed opened shampooing baths in England around 1814.

questions.q: 'Pyjamas' comes from Persian and Urdu words meaning leg...?
questions.f: From 'pai' (leg) and 'jama' (clothing) - loose trousers adopted by British colonists.

questions.q: 'Bungalow', used by builders and brands worldwide, comes from a word meaning 'of...' which region?
questions.f: From Hindi 'bangla' - a house in the Bengali style, with a wide veranda.

questions.q: The word 'khaki' for a dusty colour comes from an Urdu word meaning...?
questions.f: British soldiers in India dyed white uniforms with tea and mud to blend in.

questions.q: 'Cashmere', prized by clothing brands, is named after which region?
questions.f: The fine wool comes from the undercoat of goats bred in the Himalayan cold.

questions.q: 'Denim' and 'jeans' are both place-names; 'denim' points to which French city?
questions.f: 'Serge de Nimes' shortened to denim, while 'jeans' recalls Genoa in Italy.

questions.q: A word taken from a place name, like 'denim' or 'champagne', is called a...?
questions.f: From Greek 'topos' (place) and 'onoma' (name).

questions.q: Real 'champagne' may legally only come from a region of...?
questions.f: Sparkling wine made elsewhere must use another name - one of the strictest brand rules in food.

questions.q: Only cheese made in a certain Italian region may be called Parmigiano...?
questions.f: Its wheels are stamped with pin-dot lettering so fakes can be spotted instantly.

questions.q: 'Darjeeling tea' and 'Basmati rice' are protected by which kind of label?
questions.f: A GI tag ties a product's name to the place that made it famous.

questions.q: An 'acronym' brand like IBM or BMW is made from...?
questions.f: IBM stands for International Business Machines, a name adopted in 1924.

questions.q: IBM's nickname 'Big Blue' comes from its...?
questions.f: Its striped blue logo was designed by Paul Rand, one of the giants of logo design.

questions.q: Designer Paul Rand created famous logos for IBM, UPS and which television network?
questions.f: Rand's lowercase abc in a circle has survived almost unchanged since 1962.

questions.q: The CBS network's logo is famously known as the...?
questions.f: Designer William Golden drew it in 1951; it has barely changed in over 70 years.

questions.q: NBC's colourful logo is a stylized...?
questions.f: The peacock's feathers first appeared in 1956 to advertise colour television.

questions.q: 'Xerography', the process behind photocopiers, is built from Greek roots meaning...?
questions.f: Chester Carlson invented it in 1938; unlike earlier copiers, it used powder, not liquid.

questions.q: 'Polaroid' cameras were famous because the photo developed...?
questions.f: Edwin Land invented it after his daughter asked why she couldn't see a photo right away.

questions.q: The 'polar' in Polaroid refers to the founder's early work on...?
questions.f: Land's polarizing sheets cut glare in sunglasses and camera lenses first.

questions.q: 'Laser' is an acronym; the L stands for...?
questions.f: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation - a scientific mouthful turned everyday word.

questions.q: 'Radar' is an acronym for Radio Detection and...?
questions.f: The word was coined by the US Navy in 1940 and stuck worldwide.

questions.q: 'Scuba' gear's name stands for Self-Contained Underwater ___ Apparatus.
questions.f: Jacques Cousteau co-invented the aqualung that made recreational scuba possible.

questions.q: The name 'Nintendo' is often translated as 'leave luck to...'?
questions.f: Fitting for a company that started with gambling cards and now makes games.

questions.q: Which Nintendo character's Japanese name means 'donkey' plus 'kong' for a gorilla-like beast?
questions.f: Designer Shigeru Miyamoto reportedly wanted 'donkey' to suggest stubbornness.

questions.q: 'Pokemon' is a shortened blend of which two English words?
questions.f: The Japanese title 'Poketto Monsuta' was clipped to Pokemon for global release.

questions.q: 'Pikachu' blends Japanese words for a sparkle sound and a mouse's...?
questions.f: 'Pika' is the sound of a spark and 'chu' is the Japanese squeak of a mouse.

questions.q: The video game brand 'Sega' shortens the company's original name, ___ Games.
questions.f: Service Games began by supplying coin-operated machines to military bases in Japan.

questions.q: 'Atari' takes its name from a term used in which board game?
questions.f: In Go, 'atari' warns that stones are about to be captured - like saying 'check'.

questions.q: 'Canon', the camera brand, was renamed from 'Kwanon', the name of a Buddhist figure of...?
questions.f: The company softened the spelling to Canon, which also suggests a standard or rule.

questions.q: 'Nikon' shortens Nippon Kogaku, meaning Japan ___ Company.
questions.f: Nikon made microscope and binocular lenses long before it made cameras.

questions.q: 'Samsung' means 'three stars' in Korean, chosen to suggest something...?
questions.f: Samsung began in 1938 as a small grocery trading company selling dried fish and noodles.

questions.q: 'Hyundai' means which word in Korean?
questions.f: Its badge is a slanted H meant to look like two people shaking hands.

questions.q: 'LG' officially stands for Lucky and...?
questions.f: Two older Korean companies, Lucky and Goldstar, merged into LG in 1995.

questions.q: Which Japanese brand's name means 'three diamonds' and shows three rhombuses?
questions.f: 'Mitsu' means three and 'hishi' means water chestnut, used to mean a rhombus shape.

questions.q: Subaru's six-star logo refers to the star cluster known in English as the...?
questions.f: 'Subaru' is the Japanese name for the Pleiades, and six companies merged to form it.

questions.q: 'Mazda' is often linked to the ancient Persian god of light, Ahura...?
questions.f: The name also echoes the founder's surname, Matsuda.

questions.q: 'Sony' blends the Latin 'sonus' with the English word...?
questions.f: 'Sonus' means sound, and 'sonny' suggested a young, friendly company.

questions.q: 'Panasonic' is built from roots meaning 'all' plus...?
questions.f: From Greek 'pan' (all) and Latin 'sonus' (sound) - a name chosen for loudspeaker exports.

questions.q: 'Lenovo' combines 'Le' from an older name with a Latin root meaning...?
questions.f: From 'novo', as in 'novel' and 'innovation'.

questions.q: 'Verizon' blends the Latin 'veritas' with the word 'horizon'. 'Veritas' means...?
questions.f: Brand namers love Latin roots because they sound serious in many languages.

questions.q: 'Vodafone' blends voice, data and which word?
questions.f: The name signalled a network carrying both voice and data - unusual in 1985.

questions.q: 'Nokia' takes its name from a river and town in which country?
questions.f: Nokia began as a paper mill on the Nokianvirta river in 1865.

questions.q: 'Ericsson', 'Bosch' and 'Siemens' are all named after their...?
questions.f: European engineering firms often carried the founder's surname as a promise of quality.

questions.q: 'Haribo' is built from the founder's name Hans Riegel plus his home city...?
questions.f: HAns RIegel BOnn - and the company's gummy bears were first called 'dancing bears'.

questions.q: 'Nabisco' is a contraction of the National ___ Company.
questions.f: Nabisco created Oreo in 1912, and it is now the best-selling cookie in the world.

questions.q: The Oreo cookie's embossed pattern includes a circle with a two-bar cross, an old symbol of a...?
questions.f: Designers say the mark echoes an old European printer's or Templar-style emblem.

questions.q: The Oreo name's origin is uncertain; one theory says it comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Greek 'oros' means mountain - early Oreos were mound-shaped.

questions.q: 'Twinkie', 'Ding Dong' and 'Ho Ho' are examples of brand names built for...?
questions.f: Sound-based naming is called phonetic branding; short, punchy words stick in memory.

questions.q: 'Kodak', 'Xerox' and 'Exxon' were all invented words chosen partly because they contain...?
questions.f: Exxon was chosen after computer-testing thousands of nonsense words for global safety.

questions.q: When a company checks a new brand name in many languages, it is testing for...?
questions.f: Namers keep long lists of words that mean something rude or unlucky somewhere in the world.

questions.q: The 'mascot' in advertising comes from a French word meaning...?
questions.f: From Provencal 'masco', a sorceress - hence 'mascotte', a charm that brings luck.

questions.q: The Quaker Oats man is often described as a symbol of...?
questions.f: The Quakers themselves have no link to the company - the image was chosen for its reputation.

questions.q: The Pillsbury Doughboy mascot's proper name is Poppin'...?
questions.f: He giggles when poked in the tummy - a detail tested on audiences before launch.

questions.q: The Energizer bunny mascot is famous for a slogan about...?
questions.f: Energizer's rabbit was created partly to mock a rival battery's own drumming bunny ads.

questions.q: Which company's mascot is a stack of white tyres come to life?
questions.f: Bibendum debuted in 1898 holding a goblet of nails, showing tyres could swallow road hazards.

questions.q: 'Ronald McDonald' and 'the Burger King' are examples of a brand using a...?
questions.f: Characters give abstract companies a face children can recognize instantly.

questions.q: The Lacoste clothing brand's crocodile logo came from the nickname of a...?
questions.f: Rene Lacoste was called 'the Crocodile' for never letting go of a match.

questions.q: Which brand's polo shirt logo is a horse-riding player, not a real sport team badge?
questions.f: The polo player was chosen to suggest sporty elegance rather than any real club.

questions.q: Fred Perry's laurel-wreath logo honours a British champion in which sport?
questions.f: Perry won Wimbledon three times in the 1930s before starting the clothing brand.

questions.q: The 'Jumpman' logo on Air Jordan shoes shows the silhouette of which athlete?
questions.f: The pose comes from a 1984 photo shoot, and the shoe line still bears his name.

questions.q: Which shoe brand's name comes from a Japanese phrase about a sound mind in a sound body?
questions.f: Asics is an acronym of the Latin 'anima sana in corpore sano'.

questions.q: Converse's classic canvas basketball shoe is named after player Chuck...?
questions.f: Chuck Taylor was a salesman as well as a player, and his name is still on the ankle patch.

questions.q: The word 'sneaker' arose because rubber soles let wearers move...?
questions.f: Before that, shoes with hard leather soles announced every step.

questions.q: 'Plimsoll', a British word for a canvas shoe, comes from a line on the side of a...?
questions.f: The rubber band round the shoe resembles the Plimsoll line that shows a ship's safe load.

questions.q: 'Wellington boots' are named after a duke who won which famous battle?
questions.f: The Duke of Wellington asked his bootmaker for a shorter, softer riding boot.

questions.q: 'Cardigan' and 'raglan sleeve' are both clothing terms named after...?
questions.f: Both men served in the Crimean War, and both left their names in every wardrobe.

questions.q: 'Leotard' is named after Jules Leotard, who performed as a...?
questions.f: He invented the flying trapeze act and needed a garment that would not catch.

questions.q: John B. Stetson's famous wide-brimmed hat was sold under which name?
questions.f: His surname became a word for the hat itself across the American West.

questions.q: 'Bowler hat' is named after the London hatmakers who first made it - the ___ brothers.
questions.f: It was commissioned in 1849 to protect gamekeepers' heads from low branches.

questions.q: 'Mackintosh' raincoats are named after Charles Macintosh, who invented waterproof cloth using...?
questions.f: The garment gained a 'k' in spelling that the inventor's own name never had.

questions.q: The 'burberry' brand's gabardine fabric was invented to be breathable and...?
questions.f: Explorers wore Burberry gabardine to the South Pole and up Everest attempts.

questions.q: 'Trench coat' got its name from garments worn by soldiers in...?
questions.f: Its shoulder straps once held gloves and whistles; today they are pure style.

questions.q: 'Levi's 501' is an example of a product identified by a...?
questions.f: Levi Strauss & Co. used lot numbers in its catalogue; 501 has been used since about 1890.

questions.q: Levi's small red flag stitched onto a back pocket is called the...?
questions.f: It was added in 1936 so customers could spot genuine Levi's from a distance.

questions.q: Which everyday word for a soft drink container's pull-open lid was invented in 1975?
questions.f: Before it, detachable ring pulls were littered everywhere, so the tab was made to stay attached.

questions.q: 'Bic' shortens founder Marcel Bich's surname; which letter did he drop?
questions.f: He dropped the final 'h' so English speakers would not mispronounce the name.

questions.q: The tiny hole in a Bic pen's barrel exists to...?
questions.f: Without it, ink would not flow smoothly as the tube empties.

questions.q: 'Faber-Castell' and 'Staedtler' are old German brands famous for making...?
questions.f: Both families were making pencils in Nuremberg by the 1700s.

questions.q: The 'lead' in a pencil is really...?
questions.f: Graphite was called 'black lead' before chemists worked out it was a form of carbon.

questions.q: 'HB' on a pencil stands for hard and...?
questions.f: More B's mean softer and darker; more H's mean harder and lighter.

questions.q: Why are most classic pencils painted yellow?
questions.f: An 1890s Austrian brand used yellow to signal luxury Asian graphite, and rivals copied it.

questions.q: 'Crayola' is a coined name from French 'craie' plus 'oleaginous', meaning...?
questions.f: Alice Binney, a schoolteacher and the founder's wife, invented the name in 1903.

questions.q: Crayola retired the crayon colour 'dandelion' in 2017 and replaced it with a shade of...?
questions.f: The new colour was named Bluetiful after a public vote.

questions.q: 'Ludo', the board game, takes its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Ludo is a Victorian British version of the ancient Indian game Pachisi.

questions.q: 'Pachisi', the Indian ancestor of Ludo, means twenty-five, referring to the...?
questions.f: Emperor Akbar is said to have played it on a life-size courtyard board.

questions.q: 'Snakes and Ladders' descends from an Indian game about morality called...?
questions.f: Ladders were virtues and snakes were vices, teaching lessons through play.

questions.q: Chess descends from the ancient Indian game...?
questions.f: 'Chaturanga' means four divisions - elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry.

questions.q: 'Cluedo' was originally created during World War Two in Britain as...?
questions.f: Anthony Pratt, a musician, invented it while playing at English country-house parties.

questions.q: 'Trivial Pursuit' was invented by two Canadians after they realised a piece of their game was...?
questions.f: Scott Abbott and Chris Haney designed the whole game in one evening in 1979.

questions.q: The word 'trivia' comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: 'Trivium' was a crossroads where common gossip was exchanged.

questions.q: 'Meccano', the metal construction toy, was invented in Liverpool by Frank...?
questions.f: Hornby also gave his name to model railways still sold today.

questions.q: Frank Hornby first patented Meccano in 1901 under which name?
questions.f: Hornby later gave his name to the model railways still sold today.

questions.q: 'Airfix' model kits take their name from being fixed together with...?
questions.f: The company started making air-filled rubber toys, and the name stuck when it moved to plastic.

questions.q: 'Matchbox' toy cars got their name because each one was sold in a box the size of a...?
questions.f: The founder wanted a toy his daughter could carry to school, where only matchbox-sized toys were allowed.

questions.q: 'Tonka' trucks take their name from a lake in Minnesota; the word means 'great' in which language?
questions.f: Lake Minnetonka means 'great water' in the Dakota language.

questions.q: 'Fisher-Price' is famous for toys for which age group?
questions.f: Its founders wrote five rules in 1930, starting with 'intrinsic play value'.

questions.q: The 'Teddy bear' name arose after a US president refused to shoot a bear on a hunt in...?
questions.f: A newspaper cartoon of the 1902 incident inspired shopkeepers to sell 'Teddy's bears'.

questions.q: 'Steiff', the German company, is credited with making early teddy bears with...?
questions.f: Margarete Steiff, who used a wheelchair, built a toy empire from a felt elephant pincushion.

questions.q: 'Paddington' and 'Winnie-the-Pooh' show how a character can become a...?
questions.f: Licensing lets a story character appear on lunchboxes, films and shops worldwide.

questions.q: Winnie-the-Pooh was named after a real bear at London Zoo named after which city?
questions.f: A Canadian soldier from Winnipeg brought the cub to Britain in 1914.

questions.q: 'Hershey', 'Cadbury' and 'Lindt' are chocolate brands named after...?
questions.f: Rodolphe Lindt invented 'conching', the long stirring that makes chocolate melt smoothly.

questions.q: 'Conching', invented by Rodolphe Lindt, makes chocolate...?
questions.f: He supposedly left a mixer running all weekend by accident and returned to silky chocolate.

questions.q: Which brand invented the milk chocolate bar by adding condensed milk to cocoa in Switzerland?
questions.f: Daniel Peter used neighbour Henri Nestle's condensed milk to solve the water problem.

questions.q: 'Cadbury Dairy Milk' advertised itself with a phrase about a glass and a half of milk in every...?
questions.f: The slogan ran for a century and is one of Britain's most remembered lines.

questions.q: Cadbury built a whole village for its workers near Birmingham called...?
questions.f: The name blends the river Bourn with 'ville' to sound French and fancy.

questions.q: 'Hershey, Pennsylvania' is unusual because the town was built around a...?
questions.f: Its streetlights are shaped like Hershey's Kisses.

questions.q: The 'Kiss' in Hershey's Kisses may be named after the sound the machine makes as it...?
questions.f: Each Kiss is topped with a paper 'plume' printed with the brand name.

questions.q: 'Ferrero Rocher' uses the Italian and French word 'rocher', meaning...?
questions.f: The bumpy hazelnut coating was designed to resemble a small rock or grotto.

questions.q: 'Kinder' chocolate takes its name from the German word meaning...?
questions.f: Ferrero designed the bar in child-sized portions with extra milk.

questions.q: 'Milka' blends the German words for milk and...?
questions.f: 'Milch' and 'Kakao' - and the brand's lilac cow has appeared since 1973.

questions.q: 'Weetabix', 'Ovaltine' and 'Horlicks' are brands built by blending ingredient words with...?
questions.f: Ovaltine's original German name, Ovomaltine, mixed 'ovum' (egg) with malt.

questions.q: A wooden duck on wheels, a workshop motto against 'good enough', and a 1958 patent for hollow studs point to which company?
questions.f: The stud-and-tube coupling patented on 28 January 1958 is why bricks still clutch today.

questions.q: A soot-blackened wallpaper cleaner, a fading coal-heating market, and a teacher's nursery-school request produced which toy?
questions.f: Kay Zufall suggested her brother-in-law's cleaning compound be sold as modelling dough.

questions.q: A burr-covered trouser leg after an Alpine walk, a Swiss engineer's microscope, and a name mixing velvet with a crochet hook gave us...?
questions.f: George de Mestral spent eight years perfecting a loom that could weave tiny hooks.

questions.q: A 1975 blind taste test in shopping malls, unmarked cups, and sips that favoured the challenger name which campaign?
questions.f: Coca-Cola's response, New Coke, was withdrawn after 79 days of public revolt.

questions.q: What was the internal code name for the reformulated cola launched by Coca-Cola in 1985?
questions.f: It honoured Kansas editor William Allen White, photographed in the 1930s sipping a Coca-Cola.

questions.q: A pharmacist's headache syrup, a bookkeeper's flowing handwriting, and the year 1886 in Atlanta converge on which product's birth?
questions.f: Frank Robinson both named Coca-Cola and drew the script logo still used today.

questions.q: An Indiana glassworks designer studying an encyclopaedia entry for the wrong plant produced the shape of which container?
questions.f: Root Glass Company designers studied the ribbed cocoa pod, not the coca leaf, in 1915.

questions.q: Which brand's tagline 'The Ultimate Driving Machine' first ran in America in the 1970s?
questions.f: Ammirati and Puris wrote it in 1974 to sell a then little-known German import.

questions.q: A rejected Volkswagen ad style, a two-word headline in tiny type, and Julian Koenig's 1959 copy created which famous campaign?
questions.f: Doyle Dane Bernbach's Beetle ads are often voted the greatest advertising campaign ever.

questions.q: Which Volkswagen advertisement used the single word 'Lemon' as its headline?
c: A 1960 Beetle ad about quality control
questions.f: The ad explained that an inspector rejected the pictured car for a blemished glovebox strip.

questions.q: 'Serendipity' in brand history: a frozen gas cylinder, a slippery white residue, and a 1938 DuPont lab produced which material?
questions.f: Roy Plunkett's polytetrafluoroethylene later coated frying pans and space suits.

questions.q: A DuPont chemist's search for a stronger tyre cord led to a fibre five times stronger than steel by weight, named...?
questions.f: Stephanie Kwolek's 1965 discovery went on to line body armour and bicycle tyres.

questions.q: Which stretchy fibre, invented at DuPont in 1958, is known as elastane in Europe and spandex in America?
questions.f: 'Spandex' is an anagram-like rearrangement of the word 'expands'.

questions.q: The trade name 'Nylon' was chosen after DuPont rejected which earlier candidate?
questions.f: 'No-Run' was dropped because the stockings did, in fact, run; nylon itself means nothing at all.

questions.q: Which brand's early running shoes used a waffle-pattern sole first pressed in a kitchen appliance?
questions.f: Bill Bowerman ruined his wife's waffle iron in 1971; the Waffle Trainer arrived in 1974.

questions.q: Before founding Nike, Phil Knight imported shoes from which Japanese company?
questions.f: The split with Onitsuka pushed Blue Ribbon Sports to create its own brand in 1971.

questions.q: A Portland State accounting class, a Stanford paper about Japanese cameras, and a 35-dollar logo fee describe whose career?
questions.f: His graduate paper argued Japanese shoes could beat German ones on price, just as cameras had.

questions.q: A Bolton family shoe firm, a prize dictionary, and a small African antelope's name gave which brand?
questions.f: Joe Foster chose 'rhebok', a South African antelope, then registered the American spelling.

questions.q: The Adidas 'Trefoil' logo, used from 1971, was designed to represent...?
questions.f: The three petals stood for the world's landmasses, signalling global ambition.

questions.q: Which brand's slanted 'three-bar' mountain logo, drawn by Peter Moore for its 1991 Equipment line, became its Performance mark?
questions.f: Moore had designed the Air Jordan 1 and the Jumpman logo at Nike before joining Adidas.

questions.q: A 1968 glue that would not stick hard, a 1974 hymn-book bookmark, and a test city called Boise launched which office product?
questions.f: The 'Boise Blitz' of 1978 proved that people who tried the notes kept reordering them.

questions.q: Which 3M scientist spent years promoting a 'low-tack' adhesive before it became Post-it glue?
questions.f: 3M nicknamed him 'Mr Persistent'; he called it a solution waiting for a problem to solve.

questions.q: Which 3M engineer invented masking tape in 1925 after watching car painters struggle with two-tone finishes?
questions.f: Drew also invented cellophane tape, later branded Scotch, in 1930.

questions.q: A 'Boss of the Plains' hat, a Philadelphia hatter, and a mining camp in Colorado are all part of which brand's origin?
questions.f: John B. Stetson reportedly sold his first hat to a passing horseman for a five-dollar gold piece.

questions.q: A Bavarian immigrant's dry-goods store, a Reno tailor's copper rivets, and patent 139,121 of 1873 launched which product?
questions.f: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis shared the patent; the rivets stopped pockets tearing off.

questions.q: Which pen brand's 'Cristal' model has sold well over 100 billion units since 1950?
questions.f: Marcel Bich bought Laszlo Biro's patent rights and made the pen disposable and cheap.

questions.q: A Hungarian journalist, newspaper ink that dried instantly, and wartime RAF aircrew describe which invention?
questions.f: Laszlo Biro's design was licensed for British production because fountain pens leaked at altitude.

questions.q: Which company introduced the felt-tip marker known as the Sharpie in 1964?
questions.f: Sanford's Sharpie was the first pen-style permanent marker that wrote on almost anything.

questions.q: A typist's tempera paint, a kitchen blender, and a son who later joined a famous 1960s band belong to which invention story?
questions.f: Bette Nesmith Graham's son Michael was a member of The Monkees.

questions.q: Which company bought Liquid Paper in 1979 for around 47 million dollars?
questions.f: Graham had started with a bottle-filling operation in her own garage.

questions.q: An engineer standing beside a magnetron, a melted peanut cluster, and popcorn as the first deliberate test point to whom?
questions.f: Spencer held only a primary-school education yet earned 300 patents at Raytheon.

questions.q: The word 'magnetron', the tube behind microwave ovens, was coined by physicist Albert...?
questions.f: Hull's 1921 device was refined in Britain into the cavity magnetron that powered wartime radar.

questions.q: Which company sold the first domestic microwave oven, the 1955 Tappan RL-1, using Raytheon's technology?
questions.f: It cost about 1,295 dollars - roughly the price of a small car at the time.

questions.q: A second-floor fair booth, boys scattering free-gift cards, and a pickle-shaped pin for a million visitors made which brand famous?
questions.f: At the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, H. J. Heinz lured fairgoers upstairs with free souvenir pins.

questions.q: Heinz's famous '57 Varieties' slogan was chosen because the founder liked which two digits?
questions.f: Heinz already sold more than 60 products; he simply liked the sound of 57.

questions.q: The correct place to tap a glass Heinz ketchup bottle to make it pour is the...?
questions.f: Heinz says only about 11 percent of people know about the sweet spot.

questions.q: Which 1971 commercial showed young people on an Italian hillside singing about buying the world a Coke?
questions.f: The jingle was rewritten as the pop hit 'I'd Like to Teach the World to Sing'.

questions.q: A stranded advertising man at Shannon Airport, a napkin sketch, and a chorus about a hilltop produced which ad?
questions.f: Bill Backer watched fog-bound travellers sharing Cokes and laughing, and wrote the idea down.

questions.q: Which 1984 Super Bowl commercial for the Macintosh was directed by Ridley Scott?
questions.f: It aired nationally only once, and Apple's board had wanted to scrap it.

questions.q: The 'Think Different' campaign's grammar was defended by Steve Jobs on the grounds that 'different' was used as a...?
questions.f: He argued 'Think Different' worked like 'Think Victory' - and 'Think Differently' sounded weak.

questions.q: Which company's rainbow-striped apple logo was used from 1977 to 1998?
questions.f: The stripes were expensive to print, and Steve Jobs replaced them with monochrome on his return.

questions.q: The first Apple logo showed which scientist sitting under a tree?
questions.f: Ronald Wayne drew it in 1976, framed by a quotation about voyaging through strange seas of thought.

questions.q: Which typeface did Apple commission for its own products, replacing Helvetica Neue in 2015?
questions.f: Apple named it after the city near its old headquarters, reviving a 1980s Mac font name.

questions.q: Which font, designed by Susan Kare and others, appeared on the original 1984 Macintosh menus?
questions.f: Kare named early Mac fonts after cities, and also drew the smiling Mac and the trash can.

questions.q: Which designer created the Apple 'Command' key symbol, borrowing a Scandinavian sign for a place of interest?
questions.f: The looped square marks campsites and castles on Swedish road maps.

questions.q: Which designer created the 'I Heart NY' logo in 1977 on the back of an envelope in a taxi?
questions.f: Glaser was paid nothing for it and later said he never imagined its life beyond a short campaign.

questions.q: Which designer created title sequences and logos for AT&T, Continental Airlines and 'Vertigo'?
questions.f: Bass's AT&T 'globe' of 1983 replaced the Bell System bell after a century.

questions.q: The pictograms used at the 1972 Munich Olympics, later copied worldwide, were designed by Otl...?
questions.f: Aicher's stick figures are the ancestors of nearly every airport and toilet sign you see.

questions.q: Which system's 1972 diagram-style map, designed by Massimo Vignelli's team, drew complaints for showing Central Park as a square?
questions.f: Vignelli and Bob Noorda's 1970 standards manual had already fixed the system's signage.

questions.q: Which typeface, designed by Edward Johnston in 1916, still labels the London Underground?
questions.f: Johnston drew the lettering in 1916 and redrew the older roundel to match it in 1919.

questions.q: The London Underground's circle-and-bar symbol is officially called the...?
questions.f: It began in 1908 as a red disc behind a blue bar, to make station names readable.

questions.q: The trade name 'Escalator' lost its trademark in a 1950 US ruling because the owner had used it...?
c: As a generic word in its own ads
questions.f: Otis wrote 'escalator' in lowercase in its own advertising, undermining its claim.

questions.q: The legal term for a trademark destroyed by becoming an everyday word is...?
questions.f: Aspirin, cellophane, escalator and thermos all suffered genericide in the United States.

questions.q: Which company originally trademarked the word 'Thermos' for vacuum flasks?
questions.f: Physicist James Dewar invented the vacuum flask but never patented it; German firms named it Thermos.

questions.q: A Scottish physicist studying liquefied gases, a silvered double-walled glass vessel, and no patent at all describe whose invention?
questions.f: Dewar's 1892 flask kept gases cold in the lab before anyone thought of packed lunches.

questions.q: The generic term a hook-and-loop fastener company insists people use instead of its brand name is...?
questions.f: Velcro even released a music video begging people to stop using its name generically.

questions.q: Which company first used the name 'Zipper' as a trademark, for rubber galoshes in 1923?
questions.f: Goodrich lost exclusive rights to the word but kept it for the boots for a time.

questions.q: The zipper's modern interlocking design was perfected by Gideon Sundback, an engineer born in...?
questions.f: His 1917 'Separable Fastener' put more teeth per inch and finally worked reliably.

questions.q: Which trampoline pioneer coined the name from Spanish and toured with a kangaroo to publicize it?
questions.f: Nissen's 1960 photo shoot in Central Park with a kangaroo made newspapers worldwide.

questions.q: An Iowa gymnast, circus safety nets, and a garage rig of canvas and tyre inner tubes gave us which apparatus?
questions.f: Nissen and coach Larry Griswold built their first bouncing rig in the mid-1930s.

questions.q: Which flying-disc name did Wham-O adopt in 1958, echoing a Connecticut pie company?
questions.f: Wham-O also launched the Hula Hoop and the Slip 'N Slide.

questions.q: Walter Frederick Morrison, who invented the flying disc, originally marketed it as the...?
questions.f: He rode the 1950s saucer craze, selling discs at fairs with a gag about an invisible wire.

questions.q: Which brand's name is a portmanteau of 'Wham' and 'O' from the sound of a slingshot hitting a target?
questions.f: The company began in 1948 selling slingshots made from ash wood.

questions.q: The 'Nerf' ball's name is said to come from a term for the padding on...?
questions.f: 'Nerf bars' are foam-covered protective rails on off-road cars.

questions.q: Which NASA engineer invented the Super Soaker while testing a water-powered heat pump in his bathroom?
questions.f: Johnson worked on the Galileo probe's nuclear power source and holds over 100 patents.

questions.q: Which toy did Ohio Art license from a French inventor, renaming his 'L'Ecran Magique'?
questions.f: Andre Cassagnes, a French electrician, saw metal powder cling to a decal and hold pencil marks.

questions.q: Which powder inside an Etch A Sketch clings to the glass to make the drawing surface grey?
questions.f: A stylus scrapes the aluminium powder away from the inside of the glass, leaving a line.

questions.q: The Slinky's name was chosen by Betty James from a dictionary entry meaning...?
questions.f: She priced it at one dollar; Slinkys have used the same simple wire coil ever since 1945.

questions.q: Which toy launched at Gimbels in Philadelphia in 1945, selling 400 units in 90 minutes?
questions.f: Richard James demonstrated it on a makeshift ramp after nobody would stock it.

questions.q: Silly Putty was created during research into synthetic substitutes for which wartime shortage?
questions.f: It failed as rubber but bounced, stretched and lifted newspaper ink - and sold in plastic eggs.

questions.q: Which brand's toys travelled on Apollo 8 to help astronauts secure tools in zero gravity?
questions.f: Its stickiness kept small objects from drifting around the cabin.

questions.q: Which company released the first commercial home video game console, the Odyssey, in 1972?
questions.f: Ralph Baer's 'Brown Box' prototype became the Odyssey; it barely broke even, while Atari's Pong boomed.

questions.q: Atari's co-founder Nolan Bushnell went on to found which chain that put arcade games in a restaurant?
questions.f: Pizza Time Theatre paired animatronic characters with arcade cabinets, so games earned money while families ate.

questions.q: A playing-card maker, a taxi service, a vacuum cleaner and instant rice all appear in whose corporate history?
questions.f: Hiroshi Yamauchi tried many businesses before toys and video games finally saved the firm.

questions.q: Which Nintendo product line began as a calculator-chip experiment by Gunpei Yokoi and became a handheld hit?
questions.f: Yokoi got the idea watching a bored commuter fiddle with a calculator on a bullet train.

questions.q: Which design philosophy, credited to Gunpei Yokoi, favours 'lateral thinking with withered technology'?
c: Using cheap mature tech in new ways
questions.f: It explains the Game Boy's dot-matrix screen beating flashier colour rivals on battery life.

questions.q: Which Soviet-era puzzle game did Nintendo bundle with the Game Boy in 1989 to reach adult buyers?
questions.f: Alexey Pajitnov named it from the Greek 'tetra' plus his favourite sport, tennis.

questions.q: 'Tetris' blends the Greek prefix for four with the name of which sport?
questions.f: Every Tetris piece, or tetromino, is made of exactly four squares.

questions.q: LEGO lost a 2005 Canadian Supreme Court case trying to stop which rival copying its brick studs?
questions.f: The court held the stud pattern was purely functional, so it could not be protected as a trade mark for ever.

questions.q: LEGO's plastic bricks are moulded from which polymer, chosen in 1963 for colour and grip?
questions.f: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene replaced cellulose acetate, which warped and faded.

questions.q: Which toy company's smiling figure, with C-shaped hands and a cylindrical head, arrived in 1978?
questions.f: Playmobil's slightly earlier 1974 figures had a similar dot-eyed smile, but not the clip hands.

questions.q: Which German toy brand was invented in response to the 1970s oil crisis, to use less plastic?
questions.f: Hans Beck designed small figures with big heads, based on children's own drawings.

questions.q: Which company's 1959 doll was inspired by a German doll called Bild Lilli, bought on a European trip?
questions.f: Ruth Handler saw her daughter dressing paper dolls and wanted a three-dimensional teenager.

questions.q: Which brand did Hasbro create in 1964, coining the term 'action figure' to avoid calling it a doll?
questions.f: The phrase 'action figure' was pure marketing, and is now a standard toy category.

questions.q: Which Hasbro toy line was assembled from Takara's existing Diaclone and Microman ranges?
questions.f: Hasbro coined the English name Transformers; in Japan the same robots had belonged to unrelated toy lines.

questions.q: 'Tamagotchi' blends the Japanese word for egg with a clipped form of which English word?
questions.f: 'Tamago' plus 'wotchi' - an egg you wear and watch, released by Bandai in 1996.

questions.q: Which company's name comes from a Japanese phrase meaning 'eternally unchanging', and makes Beyblade and Tamagotchi?
questions.f: From 'bandai fueki'; Bandai and Namco merged in 2005, joining Pac-Man with Gundam.

questions.q: 'Pac-Man' was renamed from 'Puck Man' for Western release mainly because of...?
questions.f: Namco worried the P could be easily altered on arcade cabinets.

questions.q: Pac-Man's designer Toru Iwatani said the character's shape was inspired partly by a...?
questions.f: He also cited the Japanese character for 'mouth', kuchi, as an influence.

questions.q: Which soft drink was created by Coca-Cola's German branch from local ingredients when syrup imports stopped?
questions.f: Staff were told to use their 'Fantasie' - imagination - to name it, and the word was clipped to Fanta.

questions.q: 'Sprite' was originally the name of a Coca-Cola advertising character called Sprite...?
questions.f: The elf-like Sprite Boy appeared in 1940s Coke ads before the lemon-lime drink borrowed the name.

questions.q: Which brand's slogan 'Obey Your Thirst' launched in 1994?
questions.f: The campaign used hip-hop artists and marked a shift in soft-drink advertising.

questions.q: 'Gatorade' is named after the sports teams of which university, where it was developed in 1965?
questions.f: Researchers made it for the Florida Gators, whose players wilted in the heat.

questions.q: Which brand's name is the Western rendering of the Thai drink Krating Daeng, literally 'red gaur'?
questions.f: Krating is the gaur, a wild bison. Mateschitz tried the tonic for jet lag and brought a fizzy version to Europe.

questions.q: Which British brand was originally sold in 1927 as 'Glucozade' for hospital patients?
questions.f: A Newcastle chemist made it for the sick; it was rebranded as a sports drink in the 1980s.

questions.q: 'Vimto' is a contraction of 'Vim Tonic'; 'vim' means...?
questions.f: It was created in Manchester in 1908 and is hugely popular during Ramadan in the Middle East.

questions.q: Which brand of chewing gum did William Wrigley Jr. originally give away free with tins of...?
questions.f: He noticed the free gum was more popular than the product, so he switched businesses.

questions.q: Chicle, the original chewing-gum base, is sap tapped from which tree?
questions.f: Mexican general Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna brought chicle to New York, hoping to sell it as rubber.

questions.q: Which ice lolly, invented by a boy who left a drink outside overnight, was first sold as the Epsicle?
questions.f: Frank Epperson was 11 in 1905 but patented it only in 1924; his children called it 'Pop's sicle'.

questions.q: The Italian ice-cream brand name 'Cornetto' literally means...?
questions.f: Its wafer cone is shaped like a small horn, and the name is also a musical instrument.

questions.q: Whose 1901 espresso machine patent did Desiderio Pavoni buy, then mass-produce as the Ideale?
questions.f: Bezzera was a Milanese engineer; Pavoni added the steam wand and showed the machine in Milan in 1906.

questions.q: The name 'cappuccino' comes from the brown robes of which religious order?
questions.f: The coffee's colour matched the friars' hoods - and 'cappuccio' also means hood.

questions.q: Which brand's name is an acronym of a Latin motto meaning 'a sound mind in a sound body'?
questions.f: Anima Sana In Corpore Sano - founder Kihachiro Onitsuka chose it in 1977.

questions.q: 'Rolex' was invented by Hans Wilsdorf reportedly because the word could be...?
questions.f: He also claimed it sounded like a watch being wound - and it fitted neatly on a dial.

questions.q: Rolex proved its waterproof 'Oyster' case in 1927 when Mercedes Gleitze wore one round her neck while...?
questions.f: She wore it on her 21 October 'vindication' swim, abandoned after ten hours; it won Rolex its first front-page advert.

questions.q: Which watch brand's slogan is 'You never actually own a ___; you merely look after it for the next generation'?
questions.f: The Generations campaign began in 1996 and is one of luxury advertising's most quoted lines.

questions.q: 'Swatch' is a contraction of which two words?
questions.f: Founder Nicolas Hayek said it meant a second, casual watch - though 'Swiss watch' is often claimed.

questions.q: Which quartz movement, launched by Seiko on Christmas Day 1969, upended the Swiss watch industry?
questions.f: The resulting 'quartz crisis' cut Swiss watch employment by roughly two thirds.

questions.q: Which company, founded by Kintaro Hattori in 1881, took a name meaning 'exquisite' and made the first quartz watch?
questions.f: Hattori began with a Tokyo clock repair shop; the Seiko name was adopted for its watches in 1924.

questions.q: 'Casio' comes from founder Tadao Kashio's surname; the firm's 1957 breakthrough was the first all-electric...?
questions.f: The Casio 14-A used relays instead of gears, and did away with the hand crank of mechanical calculators.

questions.q: Which brand's G-Shock watch was developed after engineer Kikuo Ibe's own watch, a gift from his father,...?
questions.f: Ibe built 200 prototypes chasing the 'triple 10' goal: 10-year battery, 10-bar water resistance, 10-metre drop.

questions.q: The IKEA product names follow a system: beds and wardrobes are usually named after...?
questions.f: Founder Ingvar Kamprad was dyslexic, so names beat numbers for remembering products.

questions.q: IKEA's flat-pack idea reportedly began when an employee removed the legs from a table to...?
questions.f: Gillis Lundgren's 1956 improvisation became the company's whole logistics model.

questions.q: Which IKEA bookcase, launched in 1979 as 'Billy', is estimated to sell at a rate of roughly one every...?
questions.f: The Billy has become an informal economic indicator, the 'Billy Bookcase Index'.

questions.q: Which brand's founder wrote 'A Testament of a Furniture Dealer', a nine-point business creed?
questions.f: Kamprad's rules included 'simplicity is a virtue' and a warning against fear of mistakes.

questions.q: 'Muji' is short for a Japanese phrase meaning 'no brand, quality...'?
questions.f: Mujirushi Ryohin was launched in 1980 as a deliberately unbranded alternative.

questions.q: Which brand's designer, Dieter Rams, wrote ten principles including 'as little design as possible'?
questions.f: Rams's calculators and radios visibly influenced Apple's product design decades later.

questions.q: Which German design school's 1950s partnership with Braun carried Bauhaus ideas into consumer goods?
questions.f: Braun paired industrial designers with engineers, a rare practice at the time.

questions.q: 'Nivea' takes its name from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: From 'niveus'; the cream's white colour named it in 1911, and the blue tin arrived in 1925.

questions.q: 'Sensodyne', 'Aquafresh' and 'Sanatogen' show a naming style built from...?
questions.f: Health brands prefer scientific-sounding roots to signal expertise.

questions.q: 'Pepsodent' toothpaste's name blends pepsin, a digestive enzyme, with the Latin root for...?
questions.f: Advertising legend Claude Hopkins made it famous by highlighting the 'film' on teeth.

questions.q: Which brand's advertising is credited with making daily tooth-brushing a mass habit in America?
questions.f: Hopkins's 1920s campaign gave people a visible cue - the film they could feel with a tongue.

questions.q: Which 1955 Procter and Gamble toothpaste was the first to win the American Dental Association's seal?
questions.f: Crest with Fluoristan won the ADA seal in 1960, and its sales nearly tripled within two years.

questions.q: 'Listerine' is named after Joseph Lister, the surgeon who pioneered...?
questions.f: It was sold as a floor cleaner and surgical antiseptic before becoming a mouthwash.

questions.q: Listerine's sales exploded after advertisers popularized which medical-sounding word for bad breath?
