questions.f: The word existed in medicine but the 1920s campaign turned it into a social fear.

questions.q: 'Q-tips' cotton swabs were originally named 'Baby Gays'; the Q stands for...?
questions.f: Leo Gerstenzang invented them in the 1920s after watching his wife wrap cotton on a toothpick.

questions.q: 'Band-Aid' was invented by Earle Dickson, a cotton buyer at which company?
questions.f: His wife's kitchen cuts drove him to pre-stick gauze pads on strips of tape in 1920.

questions.q: Kleenex tissues were made from Cellucotton, a material developed in World War One to replace...?
questions.f: It was also used in gas-mask filters before becoming facial tissue.

questions.q: Which company's slogan warned customers 'Don't put a cold in your pocket'?
questions.f: The 1930 campaign successfully shifted Kleenex from make-up removal to handkerchief replacement.

questions.q: 'Cellophane' was invented by Swiss chemist Jacques Brandenberger after seeing wine spilled on a...?
questions.f: He wanted a clear waterproof coating; the film peeled off instead, and became packaging.

questions.q: Saran cling film was discovered when a Dow lab worker found a film he could not scrub off some...?
questions.f: Ralph Wiley found it in 1933; Dow chemist Jack Reilly named it Saran after his wife and daughter, Sarah and Ann.

questions.q: Bubble Wrap was invented in 1957 by two engineers who were trying to create...?
questions.f: Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes sealed two shower curtains together and got bubbles.

questions.q: Which computer company was Bubble Wrap's first big customer, for shipping its 1401 machines?
questions.f: Sealed Air's founders found their fortune in packaging, not decor.

questions.q: Which company began selling silk dental floss in 1896 and patented it in 1898?
questions.f: Dentist Levi Spear Parmly had urged flossing decades earlier, but nobody sold the thread commercially.

questions.q: Which cereal fortune was built by a former patient of the Battle Creek sanitarium who then competed with it?
questions.f: C. W. Post went to Battle Creek for his health, then launched Postum and Grape-Nuts against his hosts.

questions.q: 'Postum', a caffeine-free coffee substitute launched in 1895, was blended from molasses and which grain?
questions.f: Charles William Post sold it as a health drink before adding cereals to his range.

questions.q: The Kellogg brothers stumbled on their flaking process after leaving boiled wheat to sit, which made it...?
c: Temper, so it flaked when rolled
questions.f: Tempering spreads moisture evenly through the grain; corn flakes followed the original wheat flakes.

questions.q: Which cereal company was founded in 1906 by W. K. Kellogg to sell the flakes his brother's sanitarium had devised?
c: Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Company
questions.f: The brothers fell out over adding sugar; W. K. added it, and his firm became Kellogg's.

questions.q: Nestle's chocolate-drink mascot Quicky the bunny, who debuted in 1973, is known for wearing which prominent feature?
c: A large letter Q on a collar round his neck
questions.f: Nesquik joins Nestle with 'quick'; in the US the bunny's Q became an N when Quik was renamed in 1999.

questions.q: Which brand's ice cream is named after two real people who met in a school gym class?
questions.f: Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield opened their first shop in a converted petrol station in 1978.

questions.q: Baskin-Robbins was founded by two men who were...?
questions.f: Burt Baskin and Irv Robbins merged their separate shops, then chose the 31-flavours idea.

questions.q: Which brand's name was chosen because the founders wanted a Danish sound, even adding an umlaut Denmark does not use?
questions.f: Reuben Mattus put a map of Denmark on early cartons - pure invented heritage.

questions.q: Which coffee chain took its name from a first mate in the novel 'Moby-Dick'?
questions.f: The founders nearly called it Pequod, after the ship, before settling on Starbuck.

questions.q: Starbucks' original 1971 logo, adapted by Terry Heckler from an old Norse woodcut, showed a siren with how many tails?
questions.f: The twin-tailed mermaid, or melusine, came from a 16th-century woodcut Heckler found in a marine book.

questions.q: In 2011 Starbucks changed its logo by removing which element?
questions.f: Only brands confident of instant recognition dare drop the wordmark entirely.

questions.q: Ray Kroc's 1961 buyout of the McDonald brothers cost 2.7 million dollars and did NOT include the rights to...?
questions.f: They kept the first restaurant but lost the name, so it had to be renamed The Big M - and Kroc opened rival stores nearby.

questions.q: McDonald's founding brothers pioneered a kitchen layout they called the...?
questions.f: Speedee, a winking chef, was the chain's mascot before Ronald McDonald arrived in 1963.

questions.q: The golden arches began as a real architectural feature, sketched by Richard McDonald and refined by architect Stanley Meston, that was...?
c: Two yellow arches on the building
questions.f: Meston tapered Richard's crude half-circles into parabolas; seen at an angle they overlapped into the M logo of 1962.

questions.q: Which measure, coined by The Economist in 1986, compares currencies using a McDonald's product?
questions.f: It illustrates purchasing power parity in a way anyone who eats burgers can grasp.

questions.q: Which sandwich, invented by franchisee Jim Delligatti in 1967, has a name suggesting size and importance?
questions.f: A 21-year-old secretary, Esther Glickstein Rose, is credited with suggesting the name.

questions.q: The Filet-O-Fish was created to serve customers who avoided meat on which day?
questions.f: Catholic customers in Cincinnati drove the 1962 invention by franchisee Lou Groen.

questions.q: Which chain's 'Have It Your Way' slogan of 1974 was a direct attack on a rival's assembly-line uniformity?
questions.f: Burger King's flame-broiling and made-to-order pitch defined the burger wars of the 1970s.

questions.q: Wendy's 1984 campaign asked which three-word question that entered American slang?
questions.f: Clara Peller's line was even quoted in that year's US presidential campaign.

questions.q: A bookkeeper's flourish, a Spencerian penmanship craze, and the year 1886 explain the survival of which logo style?
questions.f: Spencerian script was standard in American business schools before typewriters replaced it.

questions.q: Ford's flowing script logo was designed by chief engineer and draughtsman Childe Harold...?
questions.f: Wills, a trained printer, drew the script with an old stencil set; the oval surround followed in 1907.

questions.q: The Model T was famously offered in 'any colour so long as it is...'?
questions.f: Black japan enamel dried fastest, which mattered on a moving assembly line.

questions.q: Ford's moving assembly line of 1913 cut Model T build time from about 12 hours to roughly...?
questions.f: Ford borrowed the idea from Chicago meatpacking plants, which disassembled rather than assembled.

questions.q: Which car company was named after a French explorer who founded Detroit?
questions.f: Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac's family crest inspired the marque's coat-of-arms badge.

questions.q: Which car brand carries the surname of a Swiss-born racing driver hired by General Motors' founder?
questions.f: Louis Chevrolet later left the company that bore his name and died relatively poor.

questions.q: 'Jeep' is widely thought to come from a slurred pronunciation of which military designation?
questions.f: Another theory credits Eugene the Jeep, a creature in the Popeye comic strip.

questions.q: Which brand's seven-slot grille is protected as a trademark shape?
questions.f: Trade-dress law can protect a shape when buyers treat it as a badge of origin.

questions.q: 'Toyota' was changed from the family name 'Toyoda' partly because the new spelling took how many brush strokes in Japanese?
questions.f: Eight is considered fortunate in Japan, and 'Toyota' also looked cleaner in print.

questions.q: Which manufacturing philosophy, developed at Toyota, uses the Japanese words 'kaizen' and 'kanban'?
questions.f: 'Kaizen' means continuous improvement; 'kanban' means signboard, used to signal restocking.

questions.q: The Japanese term 'kaizen', now used worldwide in business, means...?
questions.f: Toyota's system asks every worker to suggest small changes rather than await big reforms.

questions.q: Which term for stopping a production line when a fault appears comes from Japanese for 'automation with a human touch'?
questions.f: Sakichi Toyoda's loom stopped itself when a thread broke - the seed of the idea.

questions.q: Honda's founder began by making motorized bicycles using surplus engines designed to power...?
questions.f: Soichiro Honda bought 500 army surplus engines in 1946 to sell clip-on bicycle motors.

questions.q: Which Honda motorcycle, launched in 1958, became the best-selling motor vehicle in history?
questions.f: Over 100 million have been made - more than the Toyota Corolla or the Model T.

questions.q: Which brand's 'You Meet the Nicest People on a Honda' campaign of 1963 was designed to counter...?
questions.f: The campaign, by Grey Advertising, opened American suburbs to small motorcycles.

questions.q: 'Harley-Davidson' was founded in a wooden shed in which American city?
questions.f: The company even trademarked attempts at its engine sound, though it withdrew the claim.

questions.q: Harley-Davidson famously tried, then abandoned, a trademark application covering its...?
questions.f: Rivals argued a V-twin engine simply sounds that way, and the claim was dropped in 2000.

questions.q: Which sound trademark, registered by a film studio, features a roaring lion?
questions.f: Several different lions have played the role since 1916; the most famous was named Leo.

questions.q: Which company registered the three-note NBC chimes, one of the first sound trademarks ever granted?
questions.f: The G-E-C notes are often said to stand for General Electric, but that link is unproven; RCA owned NBC then.

questions.q: Which brand's five-note whistle accompanies the words 'I'm Lovin' It', composed with musician Pharrell Williams involved?
questions.f: German agency Heye created it; it launched in Munich in September 2003 and rolled out to over 100 countries.

questions.q: The five-note 'Intel Inside' bong was created in 1994 by Austrian musician Walter...?
questions.f: He layered synth, xylophone and marimba over a 'spark' of 20-plus sounds; recording took about ten days.

questions.q: 'Intel' is a contraction of Integrated...?
questions.f: The founders had to buy the rights to the name from a hotel chain already trading as Intelco.

questions.q: Which observation, named after an Intel co-founder, described transistor counts doubling roughly every two years?
questions.f: Moore's 1965 article predicted a yearly doubling; he revised the pace to every two years in 1975.

questions.q: 'Hewlett-Packard' decided the order of its founders' names by...?
questions.f: Bill Hewlett won the toss in 1939; their first product was an audio oscillator.

questions.q: The garage where Hewlett-Packard began is officially recognized as the birthplace of...?
questions.f: The Palo Alto garage is a California Historic Landmark, number 976.

questions.q: 'Adobe', the software company, is named after a...?
questions.f: Adobe Creek ran behind John Warnock's house in Los Altos, California.

questions.q: 'Oracle' took its name from a database project the founders had built for which client?
questions.f: The codename stuck when Larry Ellison and colleagues founded their own company.

questions.q: 'Cisco' is a shortened form of a city name; its logo depicts which landmark from that city?
questions.f: The stylized bars represent the bridge's towers, and the name drops the first syllables of San Francisco.

questions.q: Which company's name is a play on the phrase 'yet another hierarchical officious oracle'?
questions.f: Founders Jerry Yang and David Filo also liked the dictionary meaning of a rough, uncouth person.

questions.q: 'Skype' was shortened from 'Sky peer-to-peer', first contracted to...?
questions.f: The domain 'skyper.com' was taken, so the founders dropped the final letter.

questions.q: 'Spotify' was reportedly born when a founder mis-heard a word shouted across a room; it now blends 'spot' and...?
questions.f: Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon later invented the 'spot' plus 'identify' explanation.

questions.q: 'Twitter' was chosen from a dictionary; the founders liked its meaning of...?
questions.f: The bird logo was bought from a designer for about 15 dollars, then redrawn in-house.

questions.q: Which company's Android version names ran alphabetically through desserts, ending publicly with...?
questions.f: Google switched to plain numbers from Android 10, saying sweets didn't translate globally.

questions.q: Which brand's original 1996 name was 'BackRub', reflecting how it analysed links?
questions.f: PageRank counted the 'back links' pointing at a page; the name Google was adopted in 1997.

questions.q: Google's PageRank algorithm is named after which of its co-founders?
questions.f: The pun on 'web page' is a happy accident of his surname.

questions.q: Larry Page shortened a colleague's suggestion of 'googolplex' to which word, which was then mistyped as a domain?
questions.f: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros; the misspelling google.com happened to be free to register.

questions.q: 'eBay' was renamed from 'AuctionWeb' after the founder's consulting firm, Echo Bay Technology...?
questions.f: 'echobay.com' was already taken by a mining company, so the name was shortened.

questions.q: The first item famously sold on eBay was a broken...?
questions.f: The buyer explained he collected broken laser pointers - and Pierre Omidyar knew he had a market.

questions.q: Which brand's 'Frequently Bought Together' and one-click patents made it a pioneer of online retail?
questions.f: Amazon's 1-Click patent of 1999 was licensed even by Apple for its online store.

questions.q: Which Chinese company's name references a story from 'One Thousand and One Nights'?
questions.f: Jack Ma tested the name on waiters in San Francisco to check global recognition.

questions.q: 'Baidu' takes its name from a line of classical Chinese poetry about...?
questions.f: The phrase describes searching hundreds of times for an ideal, fitting a search engine.

questions.q: 'Xiaomi' means 'little rice'; the founder linked it to a Buddhist idea that a grain of rice equals...?
questions.f: Lei Jun also said MI stands for 'Mobile Internet' and 'Mission Impossible'.

questions.q: Which brand's logo is a rounded 'MI' and whose name literally translates as a small grain?
questions.f: Xiaomi sold its first phones only online, keeping prices low without shops.

questions.q: 'Nokia', 'Ericsson' and 'Motorola' all lost ground to smartphones; 'Motorola' blends 'motor' with which suffix from record players?
questions.f: The 1930 name announced a radio for cars, echoing 'Victrola'.

questions.q: Which brand made the first handheld mobile phone call in 1973, from a New York pavement?
questions.f: Martin Cooper rang a rival engineer at Bell Labs to say he was calling from a portable phone.

questions.q: 'Blackberry' was named because a branding firm thought the keyboard's keys resembled...?
questions.f: The firm also argued 'black' suggested seriousness while 'berry' sounded friendly.

questions.q: Which company began by making automatic looms, and its loom patent money funded a famous car division?
questions.f: Sakichi Toyoda sold his loom patent to a British firm; the cash launched Toyota Motor in 1937.

questions.q: A janitor with asthma, a soap-box motor and a broom handle in 1907 Ohio, and a leather-goods maker who bought the patent produced which household name?
questions.f: James Spangler sold his 'suction sweeper' to relative-by-marriage W. H. Hoover, whose name became a British verb.

questions.q: A Belfast veterinary surgeon, a son's jolting tricycle, and sheet rubber cut from a garden hose in 1887 lie behind which company?
questions.f: John Boyd Dunlop's pneumatic tyre patent was later invalidated - Robert Thomson had patented the idea in 1845.

questions.q: A cyclist's puncture repaired in three hours, Charles Terront's 1891 Paris-Brest-Paris win, and a goblet full of nails point to which brothers' firm?
questions.f: Andre and Edouard Michelin invented the detachable tyre; the nail-swallowing image became Bibendum.

questions.q: A Latin drinking toast, a stack of tyres seen at the 1894 Lyon exposition, and pale rubber before carbon black created which mascot?
questions.f: O'Galop reworked a beer poster a Munich brewery had rejected; Bibendum toasts rivals with a glass of road hazards.

questions.q: Free guidebooks until 1920, a stack of them propping up a workbench, and anonymous inspectors converge on which publication?
questions.f: Andre Michelin decided people value only what they pay for, so he set a price of seven francs.

questions.q: A cobbler in his mother's laundry room, spikes given to Jesse Owens in Berlin in 1936, and a post-war brothers' feud lie behind which brand?
questions.f: Adi Dassler persuaded Owens to wear his spikes; after the 1948 split brother Rudolf founded Puma across the river.

questions.q: A name spotted in a dictionary won as a boyhood sprint prize, a Bolton grandfather's spiked shoes, and an African antelope name which brand?
questions.f: Joe Foster found the grey rhebok in Webster's; grandfather Joseph Foster pioneered spiked running shoes in Bolton.

questions.q: A ruined waffle iron, a hand-cut rubber sole, and a 1972 shoe that sold for 437,500 dollars in 2019 belong to which company?
questions.f: Only about a dozen 'Moon Shoes' were made by hand for the US Olympic trials.

questions.q: An out-of-work architect, front pages of a newspaper tallied letter by letter, and a 1952 Macy's order converge on which game?
questions.f: Alfred Butts hand-made only a couple of hundred sets before James Brunot took over production in 1948.

questions.q: A rejection letter citing '52 fundamental errors', a Washington stenographer's 1904 patent, and Atlantic City street names describe which game?
questions.f: Parker Brothers rejected it in 1934, then bought it a year later when it sold out in Philadelphia shops.

questions.q: A 1951 shooting-party argument about Europe's fastest game bird, a Fleet Street pair of twins, and a brewery director produced which book?
questions.f: Sir Hugh Beaver could not settle whether golden plover or grouse was faster - so he commissioned a reference book.

questions.q: Which company's harp emblem is deliberately drawn facing the mirror-image direction of Ireland's official state harp?
questions.f: The company registered its harp first, so the Irish state had to flip its own emblem the other way.

questions.q: Britain's first registered trade mark, filed when the London registry opened on 1 January 1876, was a Bass red...?
questions.f: Legend says Bass sent an employee to sleep on the pavement so its mark would be number one.

questions.q: A tin design unchanged since 1885, a riddle about strength yielding sweetness, and green-and-gold Victorian lettering identify which product?
questions.f: Guinness World Records has recognized it as the world's oldest unchanged brand packaging.

questions.q: A Latin word for ox, a Victorian science-fiction novel's mysterious energy, and a beef extract for Napoleon III's troops name which spread?
questions.f: 'Bos' plus 'Vril', an all-powerful force in Bulwer-Lytton's novel 'The Coming Race'.

questions.q: A 1923 Australian naming competition judged by the founder's daughter, a brewer's yeast waste product, and a red-and-yellow label identify which spread?
questions.f: Fred Walker's chemist Cyril Callister made it; poor sales forced a 1928 rename to 'Parwill' before Vegemite returned.

questions.q: A New Zealand town called Oamaru, an Australian bootmaker's wife, and a flightless bird on a tin name which product?
questions.f: William Ramsay honoured his wife Annie's Oamaru homeland in 1906, before 'Kiwi' became the nickname for New Zealanders.

questions.q: A 1953 spray to stop rockets rusting, a formula numbered on the fortieth try, and letters standing for water displacement identify which product?
questions.f: It was first used on the outer skin of Atlas missiles, and sold to the public only in 1958.

questions.q: The English phrase 'for mica', an electrical insulator, and a 1913 Cincinnati workshop identify which surfacing material?
questions.f: Two ex-Westinghouse engineers made a cheap substitute for mica sheets - and accidentally invented the kitchen counter.

questions.q: Which product name is widely cited as the first trademark in history ruled generic, in an 1878 court decision?
questions.f: Frederick Walton's flax-oil flooring name became the common word in barely 15 years.

questions.q: A 1965 Houston stadium, a nylon-and-fibre carpet for baseball, and the loss of grass under a dome created which trademark?
questions.f: The Astrodome's roof panels were painted to cut glare, which killed the real grass; the carpet arrived in 1966.

questions.q: A metal called wolfram, the element osmium, and a 1906 German lamp filament give us which company name?
questions.f: 'Osram' welds osmium to wolfram - two metals once used for glowing filaments.

questions.q: A Scottish physicist's absolute temperature scale, an American refrigerator firm of 1914, and a name meaning 'the machine of Lord Kelvin' identify...?
questions.f: Naming a fridge after the man who defined absolute zero was a marketing masterstroke.

questions.q: A logbook page dated 1947, a moth taped beside a note, and a naval computing pioneer explain the popular origin of which term?
questions.f: Grace Hopper's team found a real moth in the Harvard Mark II; 'bug' for a flaw was already older.

questions.q: Which computing word did Werner Buchholz coin at IBM in 1956, deliberately misspelling an everyday word to avoid confusion?
questions.f: He replaced the 'i' with a 'y' so nobody would mistake it for 'bit' in a typed memo.

questions.q: The word 'bit', short for binary digit, was coined in a 1947 Bell Labs memo by which statistician?
questions.f: Claude Shannon's 1948 information theory paper made 'bit' famous and credited Tukey with the word.

questions.q: Which everyday electronics word blends 'transfer' with 'resistor', coined by engineer John R. Pierce in a 1948 office ballot?
questions.f: Bell Labs staff voted on a shortlist that also included 'iotatron' and 'semiconductor triode'.

questions.q: A 2004 newspaper article coining a word from a music player and 'broadcast' gave us which term?
questions.f: Journalist Ben Hammersley slipped it into a Guardian piece; it beat rivals like 'audioblogging'.

questions.q: A Honolulu airport shuttle bus, a Hawaiian word for quick, and a 1995 Portland software project named which kind of website?
questions.f: Ward Cunningham remembered the Wiki Wiki Shuttle and wanted a name shorter than 'quick web'.

questions.q: An advertising executive's 1958 headline about a clock at sixty miles an hour is credited to which copywriter?
questions.f: Ogilvy's Rolls-Royce ad is taught as proof that a specific detail outsells a vague boast.

questions.q: Which admen's term for the one claim a product alone can make was popularized by Rosser Reeves in 1961?
questions.f: Reeves also wrote 'melts in your mouth, not in your hands' for a sugar-shelled sweet.

questions.q: A 1962 campaign that boasted about being number two in car hire is remembered by which three-word slogan?
questions.f: Avis's admission of second place lifted it from losses to profit within a year.

questions.q: A 1965 airline repaint in seven solid colours, Alexander Girard's interiors and Emilio Pucci's uniforms belonged to which campaign?
c: The End of the Plain Plane
questions.f: Braniff International's campaign came from Mary Wells at Jack Tinker & Partners; a Calder-painted jet followed later.

questions.q: A 1957 bestseller by Vance Packard that alarmed readers about motivational research was called 'The Hidden...'?
questions.f: The book made 'subliminal advertising' a household fear and prompted broadcasting rules.

questions.q: A Vevey pharmacist's infant food, a mother bird feeding chicks, and a 1905 merger with an Anglo-Swiss milk firm describe which company?
questions.f: 'Nestle' means 'little nest' in his Swabian dialect - so the crest was literally his surname.

questions.q: A Bernese chocolatier's mixing machine left running for days, a trough named after a shell, and glossy melt-in-the-mouth texture describe which process?
questions.f: 'Conche' comes from the shell-shaped granite trough Rodolphe Lindt used in 1879.

questions.q: A Dutch chemist's alkali treatment that darkens cocoa and cuts its bitterness is named after which family?
questions.f: Coenraad van Houten's 1828 press and alkalizing gave us 'Dutch process' cocoa powder.

questions.q: A Piedmont hazelnut loaf called Giandujot, a post-war cocoa shortage, and a 1964 rename produced which spread?
questions.f: Pietro Ferrero's sliceable block became spreadable Supercrema in 1951, then Nutella.

questions.q: A 1969 request to a Surrealist painter, a lollipop wrapper redrawn as a daisy, and a Spanish verb meaning 'to suck' identify which brand?
questions.f: Salvador Dali sketched the logo in an hour and insisted it sit on top, not the side, of the wrapper.

questions.q: A Bib-Label drink of 1929 containing lithium citrate, a stock-market crash weeks later, and a name trimmed to two characters describe which soda?
questions.f: Charles Grigg's 'Bib-Label Lithiated Lemon-Lime Soda' had one of history's worst product names.

questions.q: A Waco drugstore in 1885, pharmacist Charles Alderton's mixing notes, and a blend older than its Atlanta rival identify which drink?
questions.f: Its recipe is often described as 23 flavours, and the company has never confirmed a single one.

questions.q: A Thai tonic called Krating Daeng, an Austrian toothpaste marketer's jet lag, and a 1987 Austrian launch describe which brand?
questions.f: Dietrich Mateschitz added bubbles, cut the sweetness and invented a whole drinks category.

questions.q: A backyard shed in Ikeda, tempura-inspired flash frying in 1958, and a 1971 polystyrene cup identify whose inventions?
questions.f: A 2000 Japanese poll named instant noodles the country's greatest 20th-century invention.

questions.q: A pressure fryer adopted in 1939, a Corbin service-station dining room, and an honorary state colonelcy describe whose brand?
questions.f: He was 62 when he began franchising in 1952, driving between states to cook chicken for restaurant owners.

questions.q: An Oklahoma grocer's folding chair on castors, a 1937 debut, and models hired to push them around identify which invention?
questions.f: Men thought the carts looked effeminate, so Sylvan Goldman hired models to push them round his stores.

questions.q: A 1946 Dallas store open from seven in the morning until eleven at night gave which chain its name?
questions.f: It had earlier been called Tote'm Stores, because customers 'toted' their purchases away.

questions.q: A 1974 packet of chewing gum in Troy, Ohio, a laser scanner, and a checkout clerk named Sharon Buchanan mark the debut of which technology?
questions.f: The Universal Product Code's inventor, George Laurer, chose a rectangular pattern over Woodland's bullseye.

questions.q: Who stretched Morse code into lines while dragging his fingers through Miami Beach sand, then patented a bullseye barcode?
questions.f: Woodland and Bernard Silver filed in 1949; the patent issued in 1952, decades before scanners could read it.

questions.q: A 1958 Diners Club rival, a Fresno mailing of 60,000 unsolicited cards, and a 1976 rename describe which card?
questions.f: BankAmericard became Visa because the word reads and sounds much the same in most languages.

questions.q: A 1949 restaurant bill left unpaid for want of cash, a New York lawyer, and a cardboard card for 27 restaurants describe which invention?
questions.f: Frank McNamara's 'first supper' story launched the modern charge card in 1950.

questions.q: A Yale term paper reportedly graded C, a rented Little Rock office, and 186 packages on the first night belong to which company?
questions.f: Fred Smith's hub-and-spoke idea meant every parcel flew via Memphis, even to a neighbouring state.

questions.q: Three surnames - Dalsey, Hillblom and Lynn - and a 1969 route between San Francisco and Honolulu created which company's initials?
questions.f: They flew shipping paperwork ahead of the cargo ships so port clearance was ready on arrival.

questions.q: An aircraft carrier a founder served on, a St Louis car-leasing desk in 1957, and a name borrowed from naval history identify which firm?
questions.f: Jack Taylor named it after USS Enterprise, the carrier on which he flew Hellcats.

questions.q: The unit of frequency and a famous car-hire firm share a surname but honour different people; the physicist was Heinrich and the businessman was...?
questions.f: John D. Hertz also founded the Yellow Cab Company, which is why the cars are yellow.

questions.q: The name 'aspirin' is built from an acetyl prefix plus a shortening of which plant genus?
questions.f: Meadowsweet, Spiraea ulmaria, yielded salicylic acid before willow bark took the credit.

questions.q: Under which 1919 treaty did a German company lose the exclusive right to the name 'Aspirin' in several countries?
questions.f: War reparations stripped Bayer of trademarks abroad - which is why aspirin is lowercase in the US.

questions.q: A cross-shaped wordmark registered in 1904, a Wuppertal dye works, and a company whose logo once glowed over Leverkusen identify...?
questions.f: The Bayer cross reads the same across and down, an early piece of clever logo geometry.

questions.q: 'BASF' stands for Badische Anilin und ___ Fabrik, revealing its origin in dyes.
questions.f: Aniline dyes made the fortunes that funded much of modern industrial chemistry.

questions.q: A Malay or Hokkien word for a fish sauce, an 18th-century English recipe using mushrooms, and a 1876 Pittsburgh bottling explain the history of which condiment name?
questions.f: 'Ke-tsiap' arrived with traders; tomatoes only became the standard base in the 1800s.

questions.q: A barrel left forgotten in a Worcester cellar, two chemists named Lea and Perrins, and a recipe said to come from a returning colonial official identify which sauce?
questions.f: The first batch was reportedly foul; only after months of accidental ageing did it taste right.

questions.q: A Mexican state's name, Avery Island salt domes, and a family called McIlhenny identify which sauce brand?
questions.f: The peppers ferment for up to three years in oak barrels topped with Avery Island salt.

questions.q: A Thai coastal town called Si Racha and a Vietnamese-American founder's rooster label identify which sauce brand?
questions.f: David Tran was born in the Year of the Rooster, hence the bird on the green-capped bottle.

questions.q: A restaurant manager in Piedras Negras, a 1943 improvised snack for officers' wives, and a nickname for Ignacio explain which food's name?
questions.f: Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya melted cheese on tortilla chips and named the dish after himself.

questions.q: A Tijuana restaurateur, a 1924 Fourth of July rush, and a salad tossed at the table are the true origin of which dish's name?
questions.f: Caesar Cardini, not the Roman general, gave the salad its name.

questions.q: An Australian orchardist named Maria Ann Smith and a chance seedling from discarded French crab apples gave the world which product name?
questions.f: She died in 1870, long before her tart green apple conquered the world's supermarkets.

questions.q: A California judge's garden cross, a berry named for him, and a rival berry named for Rudolph Boysen show which naming practice?
questions.f: Judge Logan's 1881 garden accident gave the loganberry; Walter Knott revived Boysen's dying vines.

questions.q: An American temperance preacher who campaigned for wholemeal flour in the 1830s lent his name to which food?
questions.f: Sylvester Graham's followers built a whole diet around unsifted flour and cold baths.

questions.q: An Australian soprano celebrated in Europe lent her name to both a thin toast and a peach dessert; she was Nellie...?
questions.f: Chef Auguste Escoffier created Peach Melba for her at the Savoy in London.

questions.q: A Russian ballerina's 1926 tour of Australia and New Zealand lies behind the disputed origin of which dessert name?
questions.f: Anna Pavlova's tutu inspired the meringue's name - though Australia and New Zealand still argue over which invented it.

questions.q: A 17th-century French marshal's cook and a sugared almond gave which sweet its name?
questions.f: The Marshal du Plessis-Praslin's confectioner coated almonds in caramelized sugar.

questions.q: A steward to Louis XIV named Louis de Bechameil lent his name to which kitchen staple?
questions.f: He probably never invented it - the sauce was renamed to flatter a powerful courtier.

questions.q: A Persian phrase meaning 'milk and sugar' describes the puckered texture of which fabric?
questions.f: 'Shir o shakar' captured the contrast of smooth and bumpy stripes in the cloth.

questions.q: The fabric name 'satin' is thought to derive from Zaytun, the Arabic name for which port?
questions.f: Silk shipped from Zaytun gave Europe both the fabric and, indirectly, the word.

questions.q: The word 'suede' comes from a French phrase for gloves made in which country?
questions.f: 'Gants de Suede' - Swedish gloves - were made from the soft flesh side of the skin.

questions.q: The popular claim that 'corduroy' comes from a French phrase meaning 'cord of the king' is...?
c: A folk etymology with no evidence
questions.f: Etymologists trace it to English 'cord' plus 'duroy', a coarse woollen cloth.

questions.q: Which word for a cylindrical bag comes from a Belgian town where its coarse cloth was woven?
questions.f: Duffel, near Antwerp, gave both the bag and the thick woollen duffel coat their names.

questions.q: A New York country-club suburb of the 1880s gave its name to which item of formal wear?
questions.f: Tuxedo Park's wealthy members popularized the tailless dinner jacket in the 1880s.

questions.q: Two hats, the trilby and the fedora, both take their names from...?
questions.f: 'Trilby' came from George du Maurier's novel and 'Fedora' from a Victorien Sardou play.

questions.q: A 1946 Pacific atoll test and a French designer's calculated shock explain the name of which garment?
questions.f: Louis Reard hoped his swimsuit would cause an 'explosive' reaction, and named it accordingly.

questions.q: The word 'jodhpurs' entered English after which sport spread from India to Britain?
questions.f: Sir Pratap Singh of Jodhpur's riding breeches were copied by British players in the 1890s.

questions.q: 'Badminton' takes its name from a stately home in which English county?
questions.f: The Duke of Beaufort's guests played the Indian game 'poona' in the hall at Badminton House.

questions.q: Which brand of racket sport equipment takes its name from a Japanese company founded to make wooden floats for fishing?
questions.f: Yonex switched to badminton rackets in 1957 when plastic floats destroyed its first market.

questions.q: A Nuremberg-area family firm founded in 1761, a green-and-white crest, and a pencil numbered 9000 identify which company?
questions.f: Faber-Castell dates from 1761, and its Castell 9000 drawing pencil launched in 1905.

questions.q: A French cartoonist's pen name, the Russian word for pencil, and a Geneva factory identify which brand?
questions.f: 'Karandash' is Russian for pencil; the artist Emmanuel Poire adopted it, and the brand borrowed it.

questions.q: Which pencil brand is named after a famous diamond, chosen to suggest the hardest possible lead?
questions.f: The Bohemian firm Hardtmuth adopted the name in 1889 for its yellow-lacquered pencils.

questions.q: A mountain's height in metres printed on a nib, a white six-pointed star, and a Hamburg stationer's shop identify which brand?
questions.f: 4810 is the height of Mont Blanc, and the star represents its snow-covered summit.

questions.q: Which pen took its name from the number of years its maker had been in business in 1939, the year its design was finished?
questions.f: Parker finished the design in its 51st year, 1939, but sold the pen only from 1941, and kept it to 1972.

questions.q: A 1932 Pennsylvania lighter maker liked the sound of a newly popular fastener, and named his product...?
questions.f: George Blaisdell borrowed the buzz of 'zipper' and guaranteed his lighter for life.

questions.q: A 1937 order from the US Army Air Corps for anti-glare glasses produced which brand name meaning to block rays?
questions.f: Bausch and Lomb's green G-15 lens cut glare for pilots flying above the clouds.

questions.q: 'Persol', the Italian eyewear brand, is a contraction of an Italian phrase meaning...?
questions.f: 'Per il sole' - the brand began in 1917 making protective glasses for pilots and drivers.

questions.q: A Turin optician, glasses made from 1917 for pilots and drivers, and flexible temples called Meflecto identify which brand?
questions.f: Ratti patented the Meflecto flexible temple in 1938 so glasses sat comfortably under a leather flying helmet.

questions.q: An Italian eyewear firm founded in Agordo in 1961, which bought Persol in 1995 and Ray-Ban in 1999, is called...?
questions.f: Leonardo Del Vecchio grew it from making spectacle parts in the Dolomites to owning the biggest brands.

questions.q: An 1894 utopian book called 'The Human Drift', a Boston bottle-cap salesman, and an 1901 patent application for a disposable blade identify whom?
questions.f: He applied in 1901 and won US patent 775,134 in 1904; boss William Painter urged him to invent a throwaway.

questions.q: The business strategy of selling a cheap device and expensive refills is commonly named after which product?
questions.f: Historians note Gillette actually kept razor prices high while its patent lasted.

questions.q: A candlemaker and a soapmaker who married sisters founded which company in 1837 Cincinnati?
questions.f: Their moon-and-stars mark began as a crude cross scratched on crates for illiterate dockworkers.

questions.q: Which soap brand advertised itself as '99 and 44 one-hundredths percent pure', a figure taken from a chemist's report?
questions.f: Harley Procter commissioned the analysis, then turned its leftover fraction into a slogan.

questions.q: A Procter & Gamble engineer's frustration with washable nappies while minding his grandchildren led to which 1961 product?
questions.f: Vic Mills also helped invent the machinery that made Pringles' saddle shape possible.

questions.q: Which 1946 product was the first heavy-duty synthetic laundry detergent, ending the reign of soap flakes?
questions.f: Its formula was so effective that Procter & Gamble launched it despite it undercutting its own soaps.

questions.q: A Dutch margarine firm and a British soap maker merged in 1929 to create which company?
questions.f: Margarine and soap both needed the same oils and fats, so a merger made industrial sense.

questions.q: A model village on the Wirral built for soap workers, and a name honouring sunlight, identify whose enterprise?
questions.f: Port Sunlight's houses were built for the workers who made Sunlight Soap.

questions.q: A Yorkshire mill owner's model village, named from his surname plus the river Aire, is called...?
questions.f: Titus Salt's village is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.q: A Quaker cocoa firm's Birmingham village with no public house, and a French-sounding suffix added to a stream's name, identify which place?
questions.f: George Cadbury added 'ville' because French chocolate was considered the finest.

questions.q: A 1935 bar launched as 'Chocolate Crisp', a 1937 rename echoing an 18th-century London club, and a slogan about breaks identify which sweet?
questions.f: The Kit-Cat Club of Whig politicians was itself named after pie-maker Christopher Catling.

questions.q: A 1909 Swiss patent filing on a chocolate-making process, a bear hidden in a peak, and a nougat named in Italian identify which bar?
questions.f: Theodor Tobler patented his chocolate-and-nougat process in Bern in 1909; the hidden bear stands for Bern.

questions.q: A Swiss chocolate firm's lilac cow, a name blending milk and cocoa in German, and an Alpine backdrop identify which brand?
questions.f: The brand's specific shade of lilac has been defended as a trademark colour in European courts.

questions.q: Which company won a long European battle to trademark the specific purple Pantone 2685C for chocolate?
questions.f: UK courts later narrowed the protection, showing how hard it is to own a colour.

questions.q: A 1946 milk-farmers' protest in Kaira district, a Sanskrit word for priceless, and Verghese Kurien's 'White Revolution' identify which brand?
questions.f: Amul pioneered making milk powder from buffalo milk, which experts had said was impossible.

questions.q: A 1966 debut, an advertising man named Sylvester daCunha, and a topical hoarding repainted every few days identify which mascot?
questions.f: The Amul girl holds the record as the longest-running advertising campaign of its kind.

questions.q: A 1946 creation by Bobby Kooka and Umesh Rao, a bow and a large moustache, and a striped turban identify which mascot?
questions.f: Commercial director Bobby Kooka and cartoonist Umesh Rao created him; he was never meant to be real royalty.

questions.q: A 1932 mail flight from Karachi via Ahmedabad, a Puss Moth aircraft, and a founder at the controls identify which airline's first day?
questions.f: J. R. D. Tata flew it himself; the airline was renamed Air India in 1946.

questions.q: An 1897 lock workshop, a 1918 soap made without animal fat, and ballot boxes for India's first general election identify which company?
questions.f: Godrej made about 12.8 lakh ballot boxes for the 1951-52 elections, and patented a springless lock in 1909.

questions.q: A Mumbai suburb's name clipped to two syllables, a 1929 factory, and a biscuit first sold as 'Gluco' identify which brand?
questions.f: Parle takes its name from Vile Parle; Parle-Gluco was renamed Parle-G in the 1980s.

questions.q: An honorific for 'doctor' clipped to two letters, an 1884 Kolkata practice, and Ayurvedic formulations identify which brand?
questions.f: 'Da' from Daktar plus 'bur' from Burman - one of the neatest brand contractions anywhere.

questions.q: An 1888 Belgaum bicycle shop, iron ploughs sold to sceptical farmers, and a 1910 factory town near Sangli identify which Indian group?
questions.f: Laxmanrao Kirloskar started with a bicycle shop in Belgaum, then built a whole company town round his plough factory.

questions.q: A 1945 steel-trading firm, a name joining two founders' surnames, and a later famous slogan about 'tough' vehicles identify which company?
questions.f: Mahindra & Mohammed became Mahindra & Mahindra after Partition, when Ghulam Mohammed left for Pakistan.

questions.q: A 1945 vegetable-oil mill in Maharashtra, a 1980 pivot into computing, and initials standing for Western India identify which company?
questions.f: After IBM left India in 1978, Wipro turned from cooking oil to computers, shipping its first minicomputer in 1981.

questions.q: A 1981 start-up funded with about 10,000 rupees, seven engineers in Pune, and a name blending 'information' with a Latin root identify which firm?
questions.f: 'Infosys' joins information with 'systems' - the founders wanted a name that travelled globally.

questions.q: A Wattens workshop in Tyrol, a secret glass-cutting machine, and a swan adopted as the logo in 1988 identify which company?
questions.f: Daniel Swarovski moved to Tyrol in 1895 for hydroelectric power to drive his machine in secret.

questions.q: A 1969 Christmas Day launch in Tokyo, a price equal to a small car, and a movement accurate to five seconds a month identify which watch?
questions.f: The Astron's quartz crystal ended two centuries of Swiss dominance almost overnight.

questions.q: A 1927 Channel swim, an early waterproof case named after a shellfish, and Britain's first front-page watch advertisement describe which company?
questions.f: Mercedes Gleitze's watch hung around her neck for over ten hours in cold water and kept time.

questions.q: A 1964 NASA request for a flight chronograph, three watches tested to destruction, and a 1969 lunar wrist identify which watch?
questions.f: Rolex and Longines-Wittnauer both failed the high-temperature test; only the Speedmaster came through all eleven.

questions.q: A 1983 Swiss counter-attack of plastic cases, 51 parts instead of 91, and a name explained as 'second watch' identify which brand?
questions.f: By welding the case shut, Swatch cut assembly costs enough to fight quartz imports head-on.

questions.q: A 1996 campaign promising you merely look after the watch for the next generation belongs to which brand?
questions.f: The 'Generations' campaign, launched in 1996, is credited to London agency Leagas Delaney.

questions.q: A 1775 Paris workshop on the quai de l'Horloge, a self-winding 'perpetuelle' pocket watch, and a tourbillon patent of 1801 identify which watchmaker?
questions.f: Breguet also invented the shock-absorbing pare-chute and the numerals still called by his name.

questions.q: A 1904 request from a Brazilian aviator who could not check a pocket watch mid-flight produced which named wristwatch?
questions.f: Alberto Santos-Dumont's friend Louis Cartier strapped a square watch to his wrist.

questions.q: A 1917 Paris design inspired by a military vehicle's tracks, first sold in 1919, gave which watch its name?
questions.f: Louis Cartier said the case's brancards echoed a tank seen from above.

questions.q: A leather-goods maker who began by packing trunks for European nobility, and flat-topped cases that could stack, identify which house?
questions.f: Flat lids replaced domed ones so trunks could pile in a ship's hold - a genuine engineering advance.

questions.q: A Paris harness-maker of 1837, a saddle-stitch by hand, and a scarf called a 'carre' identify which house?
questions.f: Hermes made harnesses for carriages before cars arrived, then moved to luggage and silk.

questions.q: A Florentine leatherworker who trained as a hotel porter, a bamboo handle bent over flame, and interlocking initials identify which house?
questions.f: Guccio Gucci noticed wealthy guests' luggage at the Savoy in London and copied its quality.

questions.q: A red-lacquered shoe sole, a bottle of nail varnish borrowed from an assistant, and Pantone 18-1663TP identify which designer's trademark?
questions.f: He painted a prototype's sole red in 1993 because the drawing looked flat without it.

questions.q: A 1837 New York stationery shop, a specific robin's-egg shade, and Pantone number 1837 identify which brand?
questions.f: The Pantone number was chosen to match the company's founding year.

questions.q: A 1947 slogan by copywriter Frances Gerety, written at three in the morning, ran 'A Diamond is...'?
questions.f: She wrote it for De Beers and later admitted she never married nor owned a diamond herself.

questions.q: An 1888 South African mining cartel, a slogan about permanence, and a new engagement-ring custom in Japan describe which company's marketing?
questions.f: Before the 1960s campaign, almost no Japanese brides received diamond rings; within 20 years most did.

questions.q: A San Francisco climbing-gear shop of 1966 named after the coldest, hardest-to-climb side of a mountain identifies which brand?
questions.f: Its logo outlines Yosemite's Half Dome, while the name points to the shaded northern side of any peak.

questions.q: A blacksmith making pitons in a tin shed, a switch to aluminium chocks in the early 1970s, and a Fitz Roy skyline logo identify which brand?
questions.f: Yvon Chouinard abandoned pitons because they scarred the rock, then argued for what he called clean climbing.

questions.q: Which zip component, made from one continuous coiled filament, is self-repairing when a tooth slips?
questions.f: Coil zips are lighter than metal-tooth zips and simply re-mesh when re-zipped.

questions.q: The world's largest zip manufacturer, founded in Japan in 1934, is known by which three letters?
questions.f: YKK stands for Yoshida Kogyo Kabushikigaisha, and the letters are stamped on billions of pulls.

questions.q: A 1958 Danish patent later copied worldwide, a Billund factory, and interlocking studs of exactly 8 millimetres pitch identify which system?
questions.f: LEGO moulds to a tolerance of about two thousandths of a millimetre, so any two bricks clutch.

questions.q: Which company's 1932 first products were wooden stepladders, ironing boards and pull-along ducks?
questions.f: Ole Kirk Christiansen made household goods and toys side by side until plastic changed everything.

questions.q: A 1949 toy called 'Automatic Binding Bricks', a British range called Kiddicraft, and hollow inner tubes trace whose path?
questions.f: LEGO's early bricks resembled Page's Kiddicraft Self-Locking Bricks; LEGO later bought the rights.

questions.q: A 1974 Budapest classroom aid, the Nuremberg Toy Fair of 1979, and a 1980 renaming of 'Magic Cube' identify which product?
questions.f: Ideal Toy renamed it after the inventor in 1980, partly because 'Magic Cube' was hard to trademark.

questions.q: A 1965 Florida research grant, a team nicknamed the Gators, and a formula of water, salt and sugar identify which product?
questions.f: Dr Robert Cade's team studied why players lost so much weight in one game and never rehydrated.

questions.q: A 1985 Nike 'banned' advertisement, a Chicago rookie's shoe outlawed for its colours, and a leaping silhouette identify which line?
questions.f: The NBA's ban on the black-and-red colourway became the campaign's own selling point.

questions.q: A visible air pocket in a shoe's heel, a former NASA aerospace engineer's idea, and a 1987 launch identify which product?
questions.f: Frank Rudy pitched pressurised gas cushions to Adidas first, and they turned him down.

questions.q: A 1982 aerobics shoe for women from a firm with Bolton roots, a soft garment leather upper, and a name from an antelope identify which hit?
questions.f: The Freestyle made Reebok briefly bigger than Nike in the United States.

questions.q: A Maryland footballer's sweat-soaked cotton shirt, a 1996 basement start-up, and moisture-wicking synthetics identify which brand?
questions.f: Kevin Plank sold from the boot of his car; his first big order came from Georgia Tech.

questions.q: A 1998 Vancouver yoga studio, a deliberately awkward name with three L's, and technical fabric called Luon identify which brand?
questions.f: Founder Chip Wilson said he chose the L's because the sound was hard for some markets to pronounce - and memorable.

questions.q: A 1917 canvas basketball shoe, a travelling player-salesman who ran clinics, and an ankle patch identify which product?
questions.f: Chuck Taylor's name went on the shoe in 1932, and it is among the best-selling shoes ever made.

questions.q: A 1966 Anaheim company that made shoes to order in a single day, on waffle-gum soles, is which brand?
questions.f: It began as the Van Doren Rubber Company; the checkerboard pattern only arrived in the late 1970s.

questions.q: A 1971 Oregon student's design drawn for 35 dollars, later rewarded with shares and a diamond ring, belongs to which logo?
questions.f: Carolyn Davidson's shares are reported to be worth well over a million dollars today.

questions.q: A spilled barrel of tar, waste furnace slag tipped over it by chance, and a 1902 patent named for a Scottish road engineer produced which trademark?
questions.f: 'Tarmac' compresses tar with the surname of John Loudon McAdam, who never used tar himself.

questions.q: Which building material is named after an English island whose limestone it was said to resemble when set?
questions.f: Joseph Aspdin patented the name in 1824, comparing the colour to Portland stone from Dorset.

questions.q: A 1930s Knoxville, Tennessee patent for hoisting standardized waste containers onto trucks gave English which everyday noun?
questions.f: Dempster Brothers blended their surname with 'dump' in 1936; the word soon outgrew the trademark.

questions.q: A snowmobile intended to be called 'Ski-Dog', altered by a sign painter's error, became which brand?
questions.f: Joseph-Armand Bombardier accepted the mistake, and the name stuck for good.

questions.q: A 1959 Mumbai firm, aluminium pressure cookers, and a brand name taken from a British licensor identify which Indian company?
questions.f: Hawkins Cookers began under licence from a British firm and now exports to dozens of countries.

questions.q: A 1938 Seattle co-operative formed by 23 climbers to import cheaper Austrian ice axes became which retailer?
questions.f: Members pooled their orders; Recreational Equipment Inc. still pays a yearly dividend back to them.

questions.q: An 1879 Cincinnati soap works and an over-whipped batch make up the long-told, company-doubted origin of which product's floating?
questions.f: A notebook kept by James N. Gamble suggests the aeration was deliberate - a rare case of a brand debunking its own legend.

questions.q: A 1908 patent for a paper drinking vessel, a shared tin dipper on trains, and the brand 'Health Kup' preceded which product?
questions.f: Lawrence Luellen's cup was renamed after a neighbouring doll company, Dixie Doll.

questions.q: A 1900 Rochester camera named after cartoon characters drawn by Palmer Cox sold for one dollar; it was the Kodak...?
questions.f: The original 1888 Kodak cost 25 dollars; the Brownie put photography in children's hands and created the family snapshot.

questions.q: A photocopying process rejected by more than twenty companies, a Battelle research contract, and a firm renamed from Haloid identify which company?
questions.f: Chester Carlson's first copy in 1938 read '10-22-38 Astoria' - the date and place he made it.

questions.q: The Xerox 914, the first plain-paper office copier, was named for its ability to copy paper up to...?
questions.f: The machine occasionally caught fire, so Xerox shipped it with a 'scorch eliminator'.

questions.q: A 1979 visit to a Palo Alto research centre, a three-button pointing device, and overlapping windows influenced which company's next products?
questions.f: Xerox did sell a GUI machine, the 1981 Star, but at over 16,000 dollars it flopped.

questions.q: Apple's 1983 computer 'Lisa' was publicly explained with a backronym standing for Local Integrated Software...?
questions.f: Insiders agree it was really named after Steve Jobs's daughter Lisa.

questions.q: Which term for a pocket digital organizer was coined by Apple's John Sculley in 1992?
questions.f: He used it to launch the Newton, whose handwriting recognition was famously mocked in comic strips.

questions.q: Steve Jobs often described the personal computer as 'a bicycle for the...'?
questions.f: He based it on a study finding the condor most efficient in nature - until a human on a bicycle was measured.

questions.q: The original 1998 iMac's translucent shell came in a single colour named after an Australian beach; it was called...?
questions.f: Later models added Tangerine, Lime, Strawberry, Grape and Blueberry - fruit names for a fruit company.

questions.q: A 1994 Bellevue garage, a bell rung for every order, and a first sale of a book about thinking machines describe which company's launch?
questions.f: They soon disconnected the bell because orders came too fast to keep ringing it.

questions.q: A 1997 late fee for a rented videotape is the founder's much-repeated origin story for which company?
questions.f: Reed Hastings told the tale often, though co-founder Marc Randolph has called it a useful simplification.

questions.q: A first Google Doodle in 1998 marked the founders' trip to which desert festival?
questions.f: They put the festival's stick-figure symbol behind the second 'o' so users knew nobody was on support duty.

questions.q: Which Google product launched on 1 April 2004 with a storage claim so large that many assumed it was a prank?
questions.f: One gigabyte was hundreds of times the free space Hotmail's 2 MB or Yahoo's 4 MB then offered.

questions.q: A colour named 'Pullman brown' after railway carriages was adopted by which company for its vehicles?
questions.f: The founder chose it in 1916 because the shade looked dignified and hid road dirt well.

questions.q: A 1907 Seattle bicycle-messenger service, started with a borrowed 100 dollars, was founded by which 19-year-old?
questions.f: His American Messenger Company grew into the brown-liveried giant UPS.

questions.q: A 1937 anti-glare lens for pilots, a 1952 acetate frame with upswept corners, and a name meaning 'traveller' identify which sunglasses?
questions.f: Designer Raymond Stegeman's Wayfarer used new moulded plastic, a break from wire frames.

questions.q: Which 1983 film's on-screen sunglasses turned a 1982 product-placement deal into a Wayfarer revival?
questions.f: Wayfarer sales had collapsed to about 18,000 pairs in 1981; by 1986 they passed 1.5 million.

questions.q: A 1934 British trademark whose name is shortened from the Latin for 'to see through' is...?
questions.f: 'Perspicere' means to look through; ICI registered Perspex for its clear acrylic sheet.

questions.q: Which product name for compressed hardboard honours William H. Mason, who worked as an assistant to Thomas Edison?
questions.f: He was trying to find a use for waste wood chips when a leaking press produced a dense board.

questions.q: A 1925 American company's trademark for solid carbon dioxide gave English which two-word noun?
questions.f: The DryIce Corporation's name became generic so fast that the trademark was worthless within years.

questions.q: 'Kerosene' began as a trademark coined by Abraham Gesner from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: From 'keros'; his coal-derived lamp fuel lit homes before petroleum kerosene took over.

questions.q: Which company lost its trademark on the word 'yo-yo' in a 1965 US ruling, and went bankrupt soon after?
questions.f: Duncan had spent so heavily promoting the word that rivals argued it had become the only word available.

questions.q: A London firm called J. Jaques & Son trademarked which sport's onomatopoeic name, selling the US rights to Parker Brothers?
questions.f: That is why tournaments must say 'table tennis' while 'Ping-Pong' remains someone's property.

questions.q: Which trademark for a personal watercraft belongs to Kawasaki, with 'personal watercraft' as the generic term?
questions.f: Yamaha's WaveRunner and Bombardier's Sea-Doo are rival trademarks for the same kind of machine.

questions.q: A 1943 letter to President Roosevelt urging a waterproof cloth tape for sealing ammunition boxes came from which factory worker?
questions.f: Stoudt, who inspected cartridges in Illinois, sketched her idea; the War Department passed it to Johnson and Johnson.

questions.q: Which brand's canary-yellow colour was chosen because a laboratory next door happened to have scrap paper of that shade?
questions.f: 3M has kept the colour ever since, and now defends 'canary yellow' as part of its trade dress.

questions.q: 'Sellotape' was deliberately misspelled when registered in 1937 because the correctly spelled word was...?
questions.f: 'Cellophane' was already trademarked, so Colin Kininmonth and George Grey swapped the C for an S in 1937.

questions.q: A door-to-door cheese seller with a horse named Paddy, a 1916 patent for processed cheese, and Chicago identify whose company?
questions.f: Kraft's heat-treated cheese kept without refrigeration, which made it a wartime ration staple.

questions.q: A 1928 sketch of a baby by artist Dorothy Hope Smith, submitted unfinished to a contest, became which company's logo?
questions.f: The company loved the charcoal sketch so much it declined her offer to finish it in oils.

questions.q: A 1937 macaroni-and-cheese kit was selling roughly 80 million boxes a year by 1943 thanks to which wartime rule?
questions.f: Two boxes cost one ration coupon and each fed four, making Kraft Dinner a wartime staple.

questions.q: A 1932 Texas cook's fried corn dough, a Frito name from Spanish, and a merger with a potato-crisp maker identify which company's roots?
questions.f: Elmer Doolin bought the recipe for 100 dollars from a Mexican-American cook in San Antonio.

questions.q: Which snack's name comes from a Spanish word meaning 'little golden things'?
questions.f: 'Doraditos' - the chips were created at Disneyland's Casa de Fritos restaurant from leftover tortillas.

questions.q: A saddle-shaped 'hyperbolic paraboloid', a tube instead of a bag, and a court ruling on whether it was really a crisp identify which snack?
questions.f: A UK court decided in 2009 that Pringles were potato crisps for tax purposes, reversing an earlier ruling.

questions.q: Who designed the Pringles tube, and asked to have some of his ashes buried in one?
questions.f: His family honoured the request in 2008; a food scientist named Alexander Liepa perfected the crisp itself.

questions.q: A Quaker Oats promotion in 1955 sold deeds to one square inch of land in which territory?
questions.f: Twenty-one million deeds went out with cereal as Sergeant Preston of the Yukon moved from radio to television.

questions.q: Which company registered the first trademark in the United States in 1870, for an eagle and ribbon?
questions.f: Registration No. 1 was issued on 25 October 1870; its mark paired an eagle and ribbon with 'Economical, Brilliant'.

questions.q: A logo in continuous use since 1787, a London shop on the Strand, and a golden lion between two Chinese figures identify which brand?
questions.f: It is often cited as the world's oldest commercial logo still in unchanged use.

questions.q: An insurance company's emblem chosen in 1896 to suggest permanence was which landmark?
questions.f: An advertising agent glimpsed a rocky outcrop from a train and pitched 'solid as the Rock' to Prudential.

questions.q: Three crossed tuning forks form the logo of which company, founded to repair a reed organ in 1887?
questions.f: Torakusu Yamaha's repair job led to Japan's first domestically built reed organs, then pianos and motorbikes.

questions.q: A search for a spray-on plaster cast produced which party novelty, patented in 1972?
questions.f: Leonard Fish ordered 500 nozzles; about the thirtieth shot a foam string thirty feet across the room.

questions.q: A 1976 Mattel toy of green goo in a plastic bin, sold under a one-word name, popularized which word for a toy texture?
questions.f: It was made from guar gum, and the smell alone is a core memory for a generation of children.

questions.q: The toy 'Spirograph' is built from roots meaning coil and...?
questions.f: Engineer Denys Fisher developed the gear-and-pen sets while designing bomb-detonator components.

questions.q: A 1966 Milton Bradley game criticized as scandalous by rivals, played on a mat of coloured circles, is called...?
questions.f: Sales took off after Johnny Carson played it with a guest on late-night television.

questions.q: Which board game's name comes from a Latin phrase meaning 'I play', and whose modern rules were patented in England in 1896?
questions.f: Ludo simplified Pachisi from India, replacing cowrie shells with a single cubic die.

questions.q: Which 1978 arcade game's runaway success is legendarily blamed for a shortage of 100-yen coins in Japan?
questions.f: The coin-shortage story is widely repeated; the Bank of Japan has cast some doubt on its scale.

questions.q: An 1865 Finnish paper mill turned electronics giant took its brand from a river whose name may derive from a word for which animal?
questions.f: 'Nois' is an old Finnish word for a dark-furred marten, giving the Nokianvirta river - and Nokia - its name.

questions.q: Which ringtone, adapted from a 1902 guitar piece by Francisco Tarrega, became one of the most-heard melodies on Earth?
questions.f: It comes from 'Gran Vals'; Nokia chose Tarrega partly because he was long dead and the music was copyright-free.

questions.q: Which industrialist built an Agordo spectacle-parts workshop into the world's largest eyewear group?
questions.f: Orphaned young, Del Vecchio trained as a tool and die maker before founding the firm in 1961.

questions.q: A Danish audio firm begun in a Jutland attic in 1925, named for its two founders, is...?
questions.f: Peter Bang and Svend Olufsen's first hit was the 1927 Eliminator, letting radios run off the mains, not batteries.

questions.q: Useless airline headphones on a 1978 transatlantic flight, and an MIT electrical engineering professor, identify which company?
questions.f: Amar Bose put on airline headphones, found them useless over engine roar, and started sketching.

questions.q: Which shipping term, from the Latin for 'according to value', names the declared value written on a bill of lading?
questions.f: An ad valorem duty is charged as a percentage of declared value, not per item or per tonne.

questions.q: Which company's name means 'three wells' in Japanese and appears on banks, ships and chemicals?
questions.f: 'Mitsu' is three and 'i' is a well; Mitsubishi by contrast means three water-chestnut leaves, or rhombuses.

questions.q: A 1907 'heat and pressure' patent, a Belgian-American chemist, and the first fully synthetic plastic identify which material?
questions.f: Leo Baekeland's phenol-formaldehyde resin was moulded into radios and telephones; the patent issued in 1909.

questions.q: Who said: 'Never, never, never give up'?
questions.f: Churchill led Britain through its hardest days in World War II and became famous for refusing to quit.

questions.q: 'Slow and steady wins the ___.' What completes Aesop's famous line?
questions.f: It comes from Aesop's fable of the tortoise who beat the speedy hare by never stopping.

questions.q: Who said: 'Reach for the stars'?
questions.f: Sally Ride was the first American woman to fly into space, in 1983.

questions.q: 'Practice makes ___.' What word completes this proverb?
questions.f: This old English saying reminds us that repeating something is how we get good at it.

questions.q: 'The early bird catches the ___.' What does the early bird catch?
questions.f: This proverb means people who start early get the best chances.

questions.q: What does the proverb 'Many hands make light work' mean?
c: A job is easier when everyone helps
You should work with a light on
questions.f: Teams get big jobs done faster because each person carries a little of the load.

questions.q: Who said: 'It's kind of fun to do the impossible'?
questions.f: Walt Disney was told cartoons could never be full movies, then made Snow White a giant hit.

questions.q: In the saying 'Look before you leap,' the word 'leap' means...?
questions.f: The proverb tells you to think carefully before you jump into action.

questions.q: 'A person's a person, no matter how ___.' What word did Dr. Seuss use?
questions.f: The line is spoken by Horton the elephant, who protects the tiny people of Whoville.

questions.q: The saying 'Cheaters never prosper' means cheating does not pay off in the end.
questions.f: To prosper means to do well, and this proverb warns that cheating never truly wins.

questions.q: Who said: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'?
questions.f: Armstrong said it in 1969 as he became the first person to step onto the Moon.

questions.q: In 'If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain,' the phrase 'put up with' means...?
questions.f: Singer Dolly Parton meant that good things often come after we get through tough times.

questions.q: 'Two heads are better than ___.' What completes this proverb?
questions.f: It means two people thinking together can solve problems better than one alone.

questions.q: 'Actions speak louder than ___.' What completes this proverb?
questions.f: What you actually do shows more about you than anything you say.

questions.q: What does the proverb 'Every cloud has a silver lining' mean?
c: Even hard times hold something good
Rainy days are the best days
You should always carry an umbrella
questions.f: The 'silver lining' is the bright edge of a dark cloud where the sun shines behind it.

questions.q: Who said: 'Whoever is happy will make others happy too'?
questions.f: Anne Frank wrote her famous diary while hiding as a young girl, yet still spread hope.

questions.q: 'Fall down seven times, stand up ___.' What number completes this Japanese proverb?
questions.f: It means no matter how many times you fall, you get up one more time than you fell.

questions.q: What is a 'proverb'?
c: A short wise saying passed down over time
questions.f: Proverbs like 'Look before you leap' carry old wisdom in just a few words.

questions.q: Who said: 'You're never too small to make a difference'?
questions.f: Greta Thunberg began speaking up for the planet when she was just a teenager.

questions.q: Confucius said, 'The man who moves a mountain begins by carrying away small stones.' What does he mean?
c: Big tasks get done one small piece at a time
Mountains are made of tiny stones
questions.f: Confucius was a wise teacher in ancient China about 2,500 years ago.

questions.q: Einstein said: 'Life is like riding a bicycle. To keep your balance, you must keep ___.' Keep what?
questions.f: Albert Einstein wrote this cheerful advice in a letter to his son.

questions.q: A quotation is the exact words that someone said or wrote.
questions.f: That is why quotations are wrapped in quotation marks, to show the words are exact.

questions.q: 'Rome was not built in a ___.' What completes this proverb?
questions.f: Great things take time, just like the mighty ancient city of Rome did.

questions.q: Walt Disney said the difference between winning and losing is most often not 'quitting.' What does 'quitting' mean?
c: Stopping before the job is done
questions.f: Disney kept going after his first cartoon studio failed, and then created Mickey Mouse.

questions.q: Who said: 'The mountains are calling and I must go'?
questions.f: Naturalist John Muir loved wild places so much he helped create America's national parks.

questions.q: 'You must be the change you wish to see in the ___.' What completes this line linked to Gandhi?
questions.f: Mahatma Gandhi taught that making things better starts with your own actions.

questions.q: Who said: 'Don't cry because it's over, smile because it happened'?
questions.f: Dr. Seuss, whose real name was Theodor Geisel, wrote more than 60 beloved books.

questions.q: The word 'impossible' starts with 'im-', which means...?
questions.f: From Latin: 'impossible' literally means 'not possible,' yet many quotes dare us to try anyway.

questions.q: Who said: 'Nothing will work unless you do'?
questions.f: Poet Maya Angelou meant that plans and dreams need our effort to come true.

questions.q: In 'Birds of a feather flock together,' the word 'flock' means...?
questions.f: The proverb means people who are alike tend to spend time together.

questions.q: Helen Keller said: 'Keep your face to the sunshine and you cannot see a ___.' See what?
questions.f: Helen Keller could not see or hear, yet she became a world-famous author full of hope.

questions.q: The saying 'Don't put all your eggs in one basket' means don't risk everything on a single plan.
questions.f: If the basket drops, every egg breaks, so wise people spread out their chances.

questions.q: Who said: 'Make each day your masterpiece'?
questions.f: Basketball coach John Wooden won 10 college championships with kind, wise teaching.

questions.q: A 'brave' person is someone who...?
questions.f: Many famous quotes say bravery is not having no fear, but acting in spite of it.

questions.q: What does the Chinese proverb 'Talk does not cook rice' mean?
c: Talking doesn't get things done; action does
You should not talk while eating
Quiet kitchens make the best food
questions.f: This proverb reminds us that words alone never finish a job.

questions.q: Martin Luther King Jr. said: 'If you can't fly then run, if you can't run then walk, if you can't walk then ___.' Then what?
questions.f: His full line ends, 'but whatever you do, you have to keep moving forward.'

questions.q: Who said: 'Look up at the stars and not down at your feet'?
questions.f: Scientist Stephen Hawking explored black holes and urged everyone to stay curious.

questions.q: What does the Japanese proverb 'Even monkeys fall from trees' mean?
questions.f: If even a tree-climbing champion like a monkey can slip, we shouldn't feel bad about our slips.

questions.q: Theodore Roosevelt said: 'Nothing worth having comes ___.' Comes how?
questions.f: Roosevelt believed the best things in life must be earned with real effort.

questions.q: 'Where there is a will, there is a ___.' What completes this proverb?
questions.f: A 'will' here means strong determination, which helps you find a path to your goal.

questions.q: A 'kind' person is someone who...?
questions.f: A Japanese proverb says one kind word can warm three winter months.

questions.q: Lao Tzu said: 'The journey of a thousand miles begins with a single ___.' A single what?
questions.f: Lao Tzu was an ancient Chinese thinker who taught that big goals start small.

questions.q: Who said: 'Well done is better than well said'?
questions.f: Franklin printed wise sayings like this in his famous almanac nearly 300 years ago.

questions.q: What does the Chinese proverb 'Dig the well before you are thirsty' mean?
c: Prepare ahead, before you need something
Wells are deeper than they look
questions.f: Getting ready early means you're never caught without what you need.

questions.q: Aesop said: 'United we stand, divided we ___.' What completes it?
questions.f: Aesop told fables in ancient Greece, and this one teaches that teams are strong together.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin is credited with the saying 'Honesty is the best policy.'
questions.f: Franklin loved short sayings, and this one means telling the truth is always the smartest choice.

questions.q: Who said: 'Whatever you are, be a good one'?
questions.f: President Lincoln meant that any job done with care and honesty is worth being proud of.

questions.q: 'A friend loves at all ___.' What completes this line from the Book of Proverbs?
questions.f: The Book of Proverbs is an ancient collection of wise sayings thousands of years old.

questions.q: In the line 'you're braver than you believe,' the word 'braver' means...?
questions.f: A. A. Milne, creator of Winnie-the-Pooh, wrote this gentle reminder for children.

questions.q: Who wrote: 'Would you like an adventure now, or shall we have tea first?'
questions.f: J. M. Barrie created Peter Pan, the boy who never grew up.

questions.q: What does 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch' mean?
c: Don't assume a good thing will happen before it does
questions.f: The idea comes from an old fable about counting riches from eggs that never hatched.

questions.q: 'A stitch in time saves ___.' What completes this proverb?
questions.f: One quick stitch now stops a small rip from becoming nine stitches later.

questions.q: Who said: 'The secret of getting ahead is getting started'?
questions.f: Author Mark Twain wrote Tom Sawyer and was famous for his clever, funny wisdom.

questions.q: Lincoln said: 'I am a slow walker, but I never walk back.' What did he mean?
c: Going slowly is fine if you never give up ground
questions.f: Lincoln lost several elections before becoming one of America's greatest presidents.

questions.q: Anne Frank wrote: 'No one has ever become poor by ___.' By what?
questions.f: She meant that sharing with others never truly leaves you with less.

questions.q: Astronaut Mae Jemison said: 'The best way to make dreams come true is to wake ___.' What completes it?
questions.f: Mae Jemison, the first African American woman in space, meant dreams need action.

questions.q: Who said the funny line: 'It ain't over till it's over'?
questions.f: Baseball star Yogi Berra was famous for sayings that sound silly but hold real truth.

questions.q: Yogi Berra, famous for his funny sayings, was a professional baseball player.
questions.f: Berra was a catcher for the New York Yankees and won 10 World Series titles.

questions.q: A 'champion' is someone who...?
questions.f: Boxer Jack Dempsey said a champion is someone who gets up when they can't.

questions.q: Michael Jordan said: 'I've failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I ___.' Why he what?
questions.f: Jordan was even cut from his high school varsity team before becoming a legend.

questions.q: What does 'A penny saved is a penny earned' mean?
c: Saving money is as good as making it
questions.f: This thrifty saying is linked to Benjamin Franklin's love of saving.

questions.q: Who said: 'You have to dream before your dreams can come true'?
questions.f: Abdul Kalam was a rocket scientist who became President of India and loved teaching kids.

questions.q: What does the Irish proverb 'Two shorten the road' mean?
c: A journey feels easier with a friend along
Two roads are shorter than one
questions.f: Good company makes a long trip, or a hard job, feel much quicker.

questions.q: Fred Rogers said: 'There are three ways to ultimate success: be kind, be kind, and be ___.' Be what?
questions.f: Mister Rogers taught millions of children that kindness matters most of all.

questions.q: Who wrote: 'Anything can happen, child. Anything can be'?
questions.f: Shel Silverstein wrote playful poems in books like Where the Sidewalk Ends.

questions.q: 'Wisdom' means...?
c: deep understanding of what is true or right
questions.f: Socrates said that wonder, or amazement at the world, is the beginning of wisdom.

questions.q: Who said: 'Where words fail, music speaks'?
questions.f: Andersen, the Danish author of The Little Mermaid, knew music can say what words cannot.

questions.q: 'Great oaks from little acorns ___.' What completes this proverb?
questions.f: Even a giant oak tree begins as a seed you can hold in one hand, just like big dreams.

questions.q: Who said: 'Those who don't believe in magic will never find it'?
questions.f: Roald Dahl wrote Matilda and Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, both full of wonder.

questions.q: Who said: 'The future depends on what you do today'?
questions.f: Gandhi led India to freedom using peaceful action instead of fighting.

questions.q: In 'Keep your eyes on the stars, and your feet on the ground,' keeping feet 'on the ground' means...?
questions.f: Theodore Roosevelt meant we should dream big while still working hard in real life.

questions.q: Who said: 'Life is either a daring adventure or nothing at all'?
questions.f: Though she was deaf and blind, Helen Keller traveled the world giving speeches.

questions.q: A fable is a short story that teaches a lesson, often using talking animals.
questions.f: Aesop's fables, like the tortoise and the hare, gave us many famous sayings.

questions.q: Will Rogers said: 'Don't let yesterday take up too much of ___.' Too much of what?
questions.f: The cheerful cowboy comedian meant we shouldn't let old mistakes spoil a new day.

questions.q: Who said: 'We are made of star-stuff'?
