questions.q: Over 500 books, a coined word for the study of robots, and 'That's funny...' as science's most exciting phrase name whom?
questions.f: Asimov coined 'robotics' in a 1941 story — and wrote or edited books in nine Dewey categories.

questions.q: A nickname earned in a famous Oxford debate, jellyfish anatomy, and 'Science is simply common sense at its best' point to whom?
questions.f: After the 1860 Oxford debate over evolution, Huxley was forever 'Darwin's Bulldog.'

questions.q: Which biologist said: 'The known is finite, the unknown infinite'?
questions.f: He compared human knowledge to an islet in an illimitable ocean of inexplicability.

questions.q: A telescope aimed at Jupiter, a trial before the Inquisition, and 'All truths are easy to understand once they are discovered' identify whom?
questions.f: Galileo spent his last nine years under house arrest — and wrote his best physics book there.

questions.q: A pulse used as a stopwatch, an inclined plane rolled with bronze balls, and 'Measure what is measurable' point to whom?
questions.f: Galileo timed rolling balls by pulse and by weighing water — the first quantitative physics experiments.

questions.q: A boy's playthings on a shore, a plague year spent at home inventing calculus, and 'Genius is patience' identify whom?
questions.f: Newton's 'year of wonders' came when Cambridge closed for plague and he went home to Woolsthorpe.

questions.q: 'If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants' appears in a letter Newton wrote to whom?
questions.f: Newton wrote it in 1675 to a rival he often clashed with — the phrase itself is far older, dating to medieval scholars.

questions.q: Which philosopher said: 'Science is built of facts as a house is built of stones; but a pile of facts is not a science'?
questions.f: Poincare wrote bestselling books explaining science to the public as well as founding whole fields of mathematics.

questions.q: Which physicist said: 'Science cannot solve the ultimate mystery of nature. We ourselves are part of the mystery'?
questions.f: Planck stayed in Germany through the war, losing a son, yet kept defending scientific integrity.

questions.q: Which physicist warned: 'If you thought that science was certain, that is just an error on your part'?
questions.f: Feynman insisted doubt is not a weakness of science but its engine.

questions.q: Which quoted physicist won the Nobel Prize in 1965 alongside Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga?
questions.f: They independently solved quantum electrodynamics — Feynman with the diagrams that bear his name.

questions.q: Which inventor said: 'Just because something doesn't do what you planned it to do doesn't mean it's useless'?
questions.f: Edison's failed telegraph experiment became the phonograph — the accident that made him world-famous.

questions.q: Which inventor said: 'The chief function of the body is to carry the brain around'?
questions.f: Edison slept in short naps at his lab bench so his brain could keep working nearly around the clock.

questions.q: Which astronomer said humanity 'explores the universe around him and calls the adventure science'?
questions.f: Hubble proved other galaxies exist beyond our own — and lobbied unsuccessfully to have astronomy count for the physics Nobel.

questions.q: Which mathematician said: 'There is geometry in the humming of the strings'?
questions.f: Pythagoreans discovered that string lengths in simple whole-number ratios make harmonious notes.

questions.q: Ada Lovelace, quoted on imagination as 'the discovering faculty', was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron.
questions.f: Her mother steered her toward mathematics specifically to suppress any inherited poetic wildness.

questions.q: A career spanning seven decades of nature broadcasting, a knighthood, and 'a source of not only great curiosity, but great fulfillment' point to whom?
questions.f: He joined the BBC in 1952, and more than 20 species and fossils have since been named in his honour.

questions.q: Chimpanzees given names instead of numbers, a study begun at 26 with no degree, and 'Only if we understand can we care' identify whom?
questions.f: Goodall's habit of naming her subjects broke scientific convention — and changed primatology forever.

questions.q: Which marine biologist wrote: 'Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts'?
questions.f: Carson wrote it in 1956, six years before Silent Spring led to the American ban on DDT.

questions.q: Which quoted explorer said: 'Curiosity is natural to the soul of man'?
questions.f: Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap in 1775.

questions.q: 'The world is a book and those who do not travel read only one page' is one of history's most repeated misattributions. Who actually wrote it?
questions.f: Lassels wrote it in his 1670 Voyage of Italy; later readers welded the sentence onto Augustine, who never said it.

questions.q: A monk-teacher who electrified Chicago in 1893, and 'Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man' — whose words?
questions.f: He was only 30 at that world congress and had arrived in America with almost no money.

questions.q: Which writer said: 'The capacity to learn is a gift; the ability to learn is a skill; the willingness to learn is a choice'?
questions.f: Brian Herbert continued the Dune saga begun by his father Frank.

questions.q: Which science fiction author said: 'I never learned from a man who agreed with me'?
questions.f: Heinlein also coined the word 'grok', now used by programmers worldwide.

questions.q: Which early American figure wrote: 'Learning is not attained by chance; it must be sought with ardor and diligence'?
questions.f: She wrote it to her son John Quincy — who became a president himself.

questions.q: In Abigail Adams's advice, 'ardor' means...?
questions.f: From Latin ardere, 'to burn' — the same root inside 'arson' and 'ardent.'

questions.q: Which French philosopher wrote: 'The more I read, the more I acquire, the more certain I am that I know nothing'?
questions.f: Voltaire read and wrote so relentlessly that his surviving letters alone number more than 20,000.

questions.q: Which historian wrote: 'They know enough who know how to learn'?
questions.f: Adams wrote his own life story in the third person, calling himself only 'Adams' throughout.

questions.q: Which author and professor said: 'Change is the end result of all true learning'?
questions.f: Buscaglia taught a famous non-credit university class simply called Love 1A.

questions.q: The saying 'What we learn with pleasure we never forget' is credited to American author Alfred Mercier.
questions.f: Mercier was a Louisiana physician and writer who wrote in French as well as English.

questions.q: Which blues musician said: 'The beautiful thing about learning is that nobody can take it away from you'?
questions.f: King played an estimated 15,000 concerts and named every guitar he owned Lucille.

questions.q: Which cellist said: 'The best thing about music is that it brings people together'?
questions.f: Ma founded the Silk Road Ensemble to blend musicians from dozens of traditions.

questions.q: Which composer urged: 'Don't only practice your art, but force your way into its secrets'?
questions.f: Beethoven completed his Ninth Symphony while almost totally deaf.

questions.q: Which Russian author said: 'Music is the shorthand of emotion'?
questions.f: Tolstoy played piano daily and wrote a whole novella about the effect of a violin sonata.

questions.q: Which American writer said: 'Art enables us to find ourselves and lose ourselves at the same time'?
questions.f: Merton was a Trappist monk whose autobiography became an unexpected bestseller.

questions.q: Which author said: 'To practice any art, no matter how well or badly, is a way to make your soul grow'?
questions.f: Vonnegut wrote it in a letter to a high-school class, telling them to write a poem and then tear it up.

questions.q: Which artist said: 'Every good painter paints what he is'?
questions.f: Pollock laid his canvases flat on the floor and dripped paint while walking around them.

questions.q: Which journalist said creativity is 'piercing the mundane to find the marvelous'?
questions.f: Moyers worked as a White House press secretary before becoming a broadcaster.

questions.q: 'Mundane', as in Moyers's definition, comes from a Latin root meaning...?
questions.f: From mundus, 'world' — mundane things are simply worldly and ordinary.

questions.q: Which German-American leader said: 'The desire to create is one of the deepest yearnings of the human soul'?
questions.f: Uchtdorf was an airline pilot for decades before becoming a religious leader.

questions.q: Which economist said: 'Creativity is thinking up new things. Innovation is doing new things'?
questions.f: Levitt also coined the business term 'globalization' in a famous 1983 article.

questions.q: Which advertising leader warned: 'A new idea is delicate. It can be killed by a sneer or a yawn'?
questions.f: Brower led one of Madison Avenue's biggest agencies through the 1950s and 60s.

questions.q: Which advertising pioneer said: 'Curiosity about life in all of its aspects is the secret of great creative people'?
questions.f: Burnett created the Jolly Green Giant and Tony the Tiger, and kept a bowl of apples in his lobby.

questions.q: Which filmmaker said: 'You can't do it unless you can imagine it'?
questions.f: Lucas used his Star Wars profits to found a company that reinvented film special effects.

questions.q: Which chef said: 'The more you know, the more you can create. There's no end to imagination in the kitchen'?
questions.f: Child worked in wartime intelligence before ever picking up a French cookbook.

questions.q: Which mythologist advised: 'Find a place inside where there's joy, and the joy will burn out the pain'?
questions.f: Campbell's 'hero's journey' shaped Star Wars, The Lion King, and countless other stories.

questions.q: Which poet said: 'The worst enemy to creativity is self-doubt'?
questions.f: Plath's only novel, The Bell Jar, was first published under the pen name Victoria Lucas.

questions.q: Which Chilean-American author advised: 'Write what should not be forgotten'?
questions.f: Allende begins every new book on January 8th, the date she started her first.

questions.q: Which American entrepreneur said: 'If you're not making mistakes, then you're not making decisions'?
questions.f: Cook co-founded a social network as a teenager with her brother.

questions.q: Which German writer observed that 'Doubt grows with knowledge'?
questions.f: Goethe collected the thought among his Maxims and Reflections, published near the end of his long life.

questions.q: Which comedian said: 'Creativity is a gift. It doesn't come through if the air is cluttered'?
questions.f: Cleese lectures seriously on creativity, arguing it needs an 'oasis' of protected quiet time.

questions.q: Which psychologist said: 'The greatest use of a life is to spend it on something that will outlast it'?
questions.f: James was trained as a physician and wrote the first great textbook of psychology.

questions.q: Which Canadian author said: 'The eye sees only what the mind is prepared to comprehend'?
questions.f: Davies was also an actor and newspaper editor before becoming a novelist.

questions.q: Which Nobel-quoted geneticist's famous 1973 essay title argued biology needs one unifying light?
questions.f: Dobzhansky wrote it for a teachers' magazine — and gave biology its most quoted sentence.

questions.q: Which computing pioneer said: 'We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done'?
questions.f: It closes his 1950 paper that proposed what we now call the Turing test.

questions.q: Which American humorist said: 'A classic is a book which people praise and don't read'?
questions.f: Twain delivered the line in a speech in 1900 — and the quip has outlived most of the classics he teased.

questions.q: Which US president said: 'My best friend is the person who will give me a book I have not read'?
questions.f: Lincoln had roughly a year of formal schooling and borrowed nearly every book he ever read as a boy.

questions.q: Which philosopher and scientist wrote: 'Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed'?
questions.f: Bacon died after an experiment stuffing a chicken with snow to test whether cold preserves meat.

questions.q: Which Renaissance scholar spent his money on books before food and clothes?
questions.f: Erasmus's Greek New Testament reshaped European scholarship — and he was often genuinely broke.

questions.q: Which American aphorist said: 'Reading gives us someplace to go when we have to stay where we are'?
questions.f: Cooley published five volumes of nothing but aphorisms — thousands of single sentences.

questions.q: An 'aphorist', like Mason Cooley, is a writer who specializes in short pointed sayings.
questions.f: From Greek aphorizein, 'to mark off' — Hippocrates' medical Aphorisms began the tradition.

questions.q: The Taj Mahal stands in which Indian city?
questions.f: Emperor Shah Jahan built it in Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

questions.q: The Taj Mahal is made mostly of which shiny white stone?
questions.f: Its white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, hauled to Agra by ox carts and elephants.

questions.q: The Qutub Minar in Delhi is a very tall what?
questions.f: At about 73 metres, it is the world's tallest tower built of bricks.

questions.q: India's oldest known civilization is named after which river?
questions.f: The Indus Valley people built cities of baked brick more than 4,000 years ago.

questions.q: Which animal sits on top of Emperor Ashoka's famous pillar at Sarnath?
questions.f: Four lions stand back to back; the design became India's national emblem.

questions.q: Ancient Indian mathematicians gave the world which very useful number?
questions.f: Without zero as a digit, writing a number like 105 would be almost impossible.

questions.q: Aryabhata, who lived long ago in India, was a famous what?
questions.f: He worked out that Earth spins on its own axis, centuries before telescopes existed.

questions.q: Sushruta of ancient India is remembered as an early what?
questions.f: His book describes over 100 surgical tools and even nose-repair operations.

questions.q: Which board game with kings, horses and elephants began in ancient India?
questions.f: It started as chaturanga, meaning four limbs of an army: foot, horse, chariot and elephant.

questions.q: The game Snakes and Ladders began as an old Indian game.
questions.f: It grew from Moksha Patam, where ladders were good deeds and snakes were bad ones.

questions.q: Mohenjo-daro was a city of which ancient people?
questions.f: Its streets were laid out in a neat grid, with covered drains running underneath.

questions.q: The Red Fort is a famous monument in which city?
questions.f: Every Independence Day, India's Prime Minister raises the flag on its walls.

questions.q: The Gateway of India, an arch by the sea, is in which city?
questions.f: Built facing the harbour, it welcomed ships arriving in what was then called Bombay.

questions.q: The Charminar, with four tall towers, stands in which city?
questions.f: Its name simply means four minarets, and it has stood since 1591.

questions.q: The Sun Temple at Konark is carved to look like a giant what?
questions.f: Twenty-four huge stone wheels line its base, and some work as sundials.

questions.q: Nalanda, in ancient India, was a famous what?
questions.f: Students travelled from China and Korea to study at Nalanda's giant library.

questions.q: The Chola kings of south India are most famous for building what?
questions.f: Their Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur still stands after a thousand years.

questions.q: The Great Bath, a huge brick pool, was found in which ancient city?
questions.f: It was lined with bricks and tar so the water would not leak away.

questions.q: Delhi's Iron Pillar is famous because it has hardly done what?
questions.f: Made about 1,600 years ago, its special iron still resists rust in the open air.

questions.q: The painted caves of Ajanta are best known for their what?
questions.f: Monks painted stories of the Buddha's life on the cave walls using natural colours.

questions.q: Which animal did Indian kings often ride into battle?
questions.f: War elephants were the tanks of the ancient world, and armies trained them for years.

questions.q: The Amber Fort sits just outside which pink-walled city?
questions.f: Jaipur was painted pink in 1876 to welcome a visiting prince.

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor ordered the Taj Mahal to be built?
questions.f: Shah Jahan's name means king of the world, and he loved white marble buildings.

questions.q: The stone chariot at Hampi is in which southern state?
questions.f: Hampi was once the rich capital of the Vijayanagara kingdom, full of markets and temples.

questions.q: Emperor Ashoka had rest houses built and trees planted for travellers.
questions.f: He carved these promises onto rocks and pillars so everyone could read them.

questions.q: The time of the Gupta kings is often called India's Golden what?
questions.f: During it, Indian artists, doctors and mathematicians made discoveries used worldwide.

questions.q: The huge Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved out of what?
questions.f: Workers chipped downwards from the top of a hill, removing enough rock to fill many pools.

questions.q: The Sanchi Stupa is shaped mostly like a huge what?
questions.f: Stupas are solid mounds built to hold holy relics, and Sanchi's is over 2,000 years old.

questions.q: Indus Valley people made their strong city walls from what?
questions.f: Their bricks were all the same shape and size, like a giant ancient LEGO set.

questions.q: Which white marble building is a famous landmark of Kolkata?
questions.f: It holds paintings and old objects, and its garden dome shines white in the sun.

questions.q: The Mysore Palace, lit up by thousands of bulbs, is in which state?
questions.f: Nearly 100,000 lamps switch on together to light the palace on special evenings.

questions.q: Ancient Indus Valley writing has been found carved on small stone seals.
questions.f: Nobody has managed to read that script yet, so it is still a real-life puzzle.

questions.q: Emperor Ashoka ruled which ancient Indian empire?
questions.f: His grandfather Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire from the city of Pataliputra.

questions.q: The Meenakshi Temple with tall colourful towers is in which city?
questions.f: Its gateway towers are covered with thousands of brightly painted stone figures.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian city was the Mauryan capital, near today's Patna?
questions.f: Greek visitors wrote that Pataliputra had a wooden wall with 570 towers.

questions.q: Hawa Mahal, the Palace of Winds, has hundreds of small what?
questions.f: Its 953 little windows let cool breezes blow right through the pink sandstone walls.

questions.q: Which very old Indian sport-like activity uses a chariot and horses on temple carvings?
questions.f: Stone carvings at Konark and Hampi show chariots, wheels and racing horses in action.

questions.q: The Taj Mahal looks a little different in colour at sunrise and sunset.
questions.f: Its marble catches the light, glowing pink at dawn and golden in the evening.

questions.q: Who is called the Father of the Nation in India?
questions.f: Millions called him Bapu, meaning father, because of the way he led without weapons.

questions.q: On his famous march to the sea, Gandhi went to make which everyday thing?
questions.f: Making salt from seawater was against the law then, so a pinch of salt became a protest.

questions.q: India celebrates Independence Day on which date?
questions.f: India became independent at midnight on 15 August 1947.

questions.q: India celebrates Republic Day on which date?
questions.f: That is the day in 1950 when India's Constitution came into force.

questions.q: Who was India's first Prime Minister?
questions.f: He gave a midnight speech in 1947 that began, Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny.

questions.q: Children in India fondly call Jawaharlal Nehru by which name?
questions.f: Chacha means uncle, and his birthday, 14 November, is celebrated as Children's Day.

questions.q: How many colours are there in India's national flag?
questions.f: Saffron, white and green, with a navy blue wheel in the middle.

questions.q: What sits in the middle of India's flag?
questions.f: The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes and stands for moving forward.

questions.q: Which is India's national animal?
questions.f: The Bengal tiger became the national animal in 1972 to help protect it.

questions.q: Which bird is India's national bird?
questions.f: The peacock's long train of feathers can be longer than the rest of its body.

questions.q: Which flower is India's national flower?
questions.f: Lotus leaves shed water so well that scientists copy the trick to make self-cleaning paint.

questions.q: Which fruit is India's national fruit?
questions.f: India grows more mangoes than any other country, in hundreds of different kinds.

questions.q: What is India's national anthem called?
questions.f: Sung properly, it takes about 52 seconds from start to finish.

questions.q: Who wrote the words of India's national anthem?
questions.f: Tagore also wrote the song that became Bangladesh's national anthem.

questions.q: Rani Lakshmibai was the brave queen of which place?
questions.f: She led her soldiers herself in 1858, riding on horseback, aged only about 29.

questions.q: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel is known as the Iron Man of India.
questions.f: He helped join hundreds of princely states into one country after 1947.

questions.q: Who was India's first President?
questions.f: He is the only person to have been elected President of India twice in a row.

questions.q: Who is called the chief architect of India's Constitution?
questions.f: He chaired the committee that wrote it, and pushed for equal rights for everyone.

questions.q: The written book of rules for how a country is run is called its what?
questions.f: India's is the longest written constitution of any country in the world.

questions.q: Subhas Chandra Bose was popularly known by which title?
questions.f: Netaji simply means respected leader, and his greeting Jai Hind is still used today.

questions.q: Gandhi's way of fighting unfairness without hurting anyone is called what?
questions.f: He called it satyagraha, or holding firmly to truth.

questions.q: Gandhi used a simple spinning wheel to make thread. What is it called?
questions.f: The charkha even appeared on an early version of the Indian flag.

questions.q: What colour is the top band of India's flag?
questions.f: Saffron stands for courage, white for truth and peace, green for growth.

questions.q: What colour is the bottom band of India's flag?
questions.f: Green was chosen to stand for the land, its plants and its harvests.

questions.q: Gandhi asked Indians to wear cloth spun at home. What is that cloth called?
questions.f: Every Indian flag by law must still be made of hand-spun khadi.

questions.q: What is India's currency called?
questions.f: The rupee's symbol, made in 2010, blends the Devanagari letter Ra with a Roman R.

questions.q: Which tree is India's national tree?
questions.f: A banyan drops roots from its branches, so one tree can spread like a small forest.

questions.q: Which river is India's national river?
questions.f: The Ganga starts as a glacier stream in the Himalayas at a place called Gaumukh.

questions.q: Bhagat Singh is remembered as a young Indian what?
questions.f: He was only 23, and he read books in jail right up to his last days.

questions.q: In which state was Mahatma Gandhi born?
questions.f: He was born in the seaside town of Porbandar on 2 October 1869.

questions.q: Netaji's famous greeting Jai Hind means Victory to India.
questions.f: It became India's official greeting in the army and in government after 1947.

questions.q: Gandhi's birthday, 2 October, is celebrated in India as what?
questions.f: The United Nations also marks it as the International Day of Non-Violence.

questions.q: Who leads India's government from day to day?
questions.f: The President is the head of state, while the Prime Minister heads the government.

questions.q: India's national emblem shows lions copied from a pillar of which emperor?
questions.f: The original stone lions still stand in a museum at Sarnath near Varanasi.

questions.q: Which everyday object did Gandhi always carry to help him walk?
questions.f: He walked about 24 kilometres a day on the Salt March, staff in hand, aged 61.

questions.q: Vande Mataram is India's national what?
questions.f: It is the national song, different from the national anthem Jana Gana Mana.

questions.q: Jawaharlal Nehru often wore a fresh rose pinned to his coat.
questions.f: The rose in his jacket became so famous that it is part of nearly every picture of him.

questions.q: India's Constitution promises the same rights to which people?
questions.f: Equality before the law is written into Article 14, one of its best-known lines.

questions.q: Which Indian space agency sent the Chandrayaan spacecraft to the Moon?
questions.f: ISRO stands for Indian Space Research Organisation, and it began work in 1969.

questions.q: The name Chandrayaan is built from Indian words meaning what?
questions.f: Chandra means moon and yaan means craft or vehicle, so the name says exactly what it does.

questions.q: India's Mangalyaan spacecraft travelled to which planet?
questions.f: Mangal is the Indian name for Mars, so Mangalyaan means Mars craft.

questions.q: Amul is an Indian brand best known for which food?
questions.f: The Amul butter girl has been drawn on billboards since 1966, making jokes about the news.

questions.q: The Amul girl on the billboards always wears a dress with what pattern?
questions.f: Her blue hair and polka-dot dress have barely changed in almost sixty years.

questions.q: Which Indian company built the steel town of Jamshedpur?
questions.f: Jamshedpur is named after Jamsetji Tata, who dreamed of an Indian-made steel industry.

questions.q: India's huge network of trains is run by Indian what?
questions.f: Indian Railways employs over a million people, making it one of the world's biggest employers.

questions.q: Bollywood films are made mainly in which Indian city?
questions.f: The name Bollywood mixes Bombay, Mumbai's old name, with Hollywood.

questions.q: Which sport is the most popular in India?
questions.f: India's first Test match was played in 1932, and the game is now watched by hundreds of millions.

questions.q: India won its first cricket World Cup in 1983.
questions.f: Kapil Dev's team beat the West Indies at Lord's in a match nobody expected them to win.

questions.q: Sachin Tendulkar became famous playing which sport?
questions.f: He is the only cricketer to score one hundred international centuries.

questions.q: In cricket, hitting the ball over the boundary without it bouncing scores how many runs?
questions.f: If it bounces first and then crosses the rope, it is four runs instead.

questions.q: Chandrayaan-3 landed near which part of the Moon in 2023?
questions.f: India became the first country ever to land softly so close to the Moon's south pole.

questions.q: Which state in India is Amul's dairy movement from?
questions.f: It began in the town of Anand, where farmers joined together to sell their own milk.

questions.q: India's very first satellite was named after which ancient scholar?
questions.f: Launched in 1975, it honoured the mathematician who described Earth's spin centuries ago.

questions.q: Amul's long-running slogan is The Taste of India.
questions.f: The line has appeared on Amul packs and posters since the 1990s.

questions.q: Besides cars, Tata is famous for making which strong metal?
questions.f: Tata Steel began making steel in 1912, before India was even independent.

questions.q: Which speedy modern Indian train shares its name with a patriotic song phrase?
questions.f: Vande Bharat trains were designed and built in India, at a factory in Chennai.

questions.q: India's Mangalyaan mission to Mars cost less than many big movies.
questions.f: It cost around 450 crore rupees, cheaper than several Hollywood space films.

questions.q: India is famous for growing which drink's leaves in Assam and Darjeeling?
questions.f: Assam alone grows more tea than most whole countries.

questions.q: Which Indian athlete won an Olympic gold medal in the javelin throw?
questions.f: His winning throw at the Tokyo Games flew 87.58 metres, about as long as a blue whale times four.

questions.q: Viswanathan Anand from Chennai became world champion in which game?
questions.f: He is nicknamed the Lightning Kid for how fast he used to play as a boy.

questions.q: ISRO launches its rockets from an island called Sriharikota.
questions.f: The island sits on India's east coast, so spent rocket stages fall safely into the sea.

questions.q: Tata's Nano was famous for being an extremely cheap what?
questions.f: It was launched in 2008 with a starting price of about one lakh rupees.

questions.q: Which fruit does India grow more of than any other country?
questions.f: India has over a thousand mango varieties, with names like Alphonso and Dasheri.

questions.q: What is a cricket bowler mainly trying to hit behind the batter?
questions.f: Three stumps and two small bails make up the wicket the bowler aims at.

questions.q: The word Bollywood comes from mixing Bombay with Hollywood.
questions.f: Other Indian film industries copied the idea, giving us Tollywood and Kollywood.

questions.q: Amul's billboards are famous for being full of what?
questions.f: The same advertising campaign has been running non-stop since 1966, a world record.

questions.q: Sachin Tendulkar's nickname was the Master what?
questions.f: He played his first international match at just 16 years old.

questions.q: Bollywood films are famous for including plenty of what?
questions.f: A typical Hindi film may have five or six full song sequences woven into the story.

questions.q: India's Chandrayaan-1 mission helped prove that the Moon has what?
questions.f: Its instruments found signs of water in the lunar soil, changing how we see the Moon.

questions.q: Which Indian brand of dairy is run as a cooperative owned by farmers?
questions.f: Millions of small farmers pour milk into village collection centres every morning.

questions.q: India's first woman in space-related fame, Kalpana Chawla, travelled aboard what?
questions.f: Born in Karnal, she flew on the shuttle Columbia and became a hero to young Indians.

questions.q: Which Indian city is known as the country's software and computer capital?
questions.f: So many software companies grew there that Bengaluru is called India's Silicon Valley.

questions.q: Indian Railways moves people using engines that mostly run on what today?
questions.f: India has electrified most of its huge railway network to cut smoke and cost.

questions.q: India's big rise in milk production was nicknamed the White what?
questions.f: Amul's model spread across India and helped it become the world's largest milk producer.

questions.q: Indian Railways carries millions of passengers every single day.
questions.f: On a busy day it moves more people than the whole population of Australia.

questions.q: The word jungle comes from an Indian word meaning what kind of land?
questions.f: From Sanskrit jangala through Hindi jangal; English later made it mean thick forest.

questions.q: The word shampoo comes from an Indian word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi champo, meaning knead the muscles, which is what a head massage does.

questions.q: A bungalow originally meant a house built in the style of which region?
questions.f: From Hindi bangla, a low house with a wide veranda, copied all over the world.

questions.q: The word pyjamas is built from words meaning what?
questions.f: From Persian pay, leg, plus jama, clothing, borrowed into English through Hindi and Urdu.

questions.q: The word guru means what?
questions.f: In Sanskrit it first meant heavy or weighty, then came to mean a weighty, wise teacher.

questions.q: The word chutney comes from an Indian word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi chatni, from chatna, to lick, because you lick this tasty paste off your fingers.

questions.q: The word cheetah comes from an Indian word meaning what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit chitra, meaning spotted or brightly patterned, which fits the cat perfectly.

questions.q: The word bandana comes from an Indian word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi bandhna, to tie, the same idea behind the knotted tie-dye patterns on old bandanas.

questions.q: The word loot comes from an Indian word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi lut, meaning plunder; English soldiers carried the word home in the 1700s.

questions.q: The word cot comes from an Indian word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi khat, a simple wooden bed frame, borrowed by the British in India.

questions.q: The word karma means what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit karman, action, the root idea that what you do comes back to you.

questions.q: The word avatar originally meant what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit avatara, a descent to earth; today it means your picture in an app.

questions.q: The word catamaran is built from Tamil words meaning what?
questions.f: From kattu, to tie, plus maram, wood: logs lashed together to make a steady boat.

questions.q: A dinghy is a small what?
questions.f: From Hindi and Bengali dingi, a little rowing boat used on rivers.

questions.q: The drink called punch takes its name from a word meaning which number?
questions.f: From Hindi panch, five, for its five ingredients including water, sugar and lemon.

questions.q: The soft wool called cashmere is named after which place?
questions.f: It comes from the fine underfur of goats reared high in the Himalayan cold.

questions.q: The word cummerbund is built from words meaning what?
questions.f: From Persian kamar, waist, plus band, tie, borrowed into English through India.

questions.q: Dungarees are named after Dongri, a place in Mumbai where the cloth was made.
questions.f: Sailors bought the tough cheap cotton there and the name stuck to the trousers.

questions.q: The word thug comes from an Indian word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi thag, a trickster; English later made it mean a rough bully.

questions.q: The word khaki comes from a word meaning what colour-source?
questions.f: From Urdu khaki, dust-coloured, chosen so uniforms would blend into dry Indian ground.

questions.q: A bangle is worn on which part of the body?
questions.f: From Hindi bangri, meaning a glass bracelet worn on the arm.

questions.q: The word curry comes from a Tamil word meaning what?
questions.f: From Tamil kari, a spiced sauce eaten with rice, which Europeans turned into curry.

questions.q: The word sugar traces back to a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit sharkara, gravel, because ground sugar looks like tiny grains.

questions.q: A veranda is what part of a house?
questions.f: The word came into English from Hindi varanda, a roofed open gallery along the wall.

questions.q: A juggernaut today means something huge and what?
questions.f: It comes from Jagannath, whose enormous temple chariot in Puri needs hundreds of people to pull it.

questions.q: A pundit is a person who is what?
questions.f: From Hindi pandit, a scholar; today a pundit is any expert who explains things on TV.

questions.q: The riding trousers called jodhpurs are named after the Indian city Jodhpur.
questions.f: Polo players from Jodhpur wore them to England, and the style caught on.

questions.q: A chit, meaning a small note, comes from an Indian word for what?
questions.f: From Hindi chitthi, a letter; British officials in India wrote chits for everything.

questions.q: The word mango came into English from which kind of language of south India?
questions.f: Portuguese traders turned Tamil mankay into manga, and English made it mango.

questions.q: The mongoose gets its English name from Indian words, not from which animal?
questions.f: From Marathi mungus; the goose part is just English ears mishearing the word.

questions.q: The strong furniture wood called teak takes its name from a language of which region?
questions.f: From Malayalam thekka; teak resists water so well it was used for ships.

questions.q: The word yoga comes from a Sanskrit root meaning what?
questions.f: The same ancient root gives English the word yoke, the bar joining two oxen.

questions.q: The word mantra comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit man, to think, plus tra, tool: a mantra is a tool for the mind.

questions.q: The word pepper travelled into English from an ancient Indian word, pippali.
questions.f: Pepper was so valuable that it was once weighed against silver.

questions.q: The word bungalow-style veranda house spread worldwide from India because of what?
questions.f: Officials liked the cool, low, wide-porch design and copied it from Bengal to Africa and America.

questions.q: Someone who is a guru of cooking is someone who is what at it?
questions.f: English borrowed guru from Sanskrit and now uses it for any master of a skill.

questions.q: The word bandana names a piece of cloth worn where?
questions.f: From Hindi bandhna, to tie: the cloth is knotted, and knot-dyeing gave it its patterns.

questions.q: The Indus Valley civilization is also called Harappan, after which site?
questions.f: Harappa in Punjab was the first of these cities to be dug up and studied, in the 1920s.

questions.q: Emperor Ashoka turned away from war after which battle?
questions.f: Kalinga is today's Odisha; after it Ashoka spent his reign spreading peace instead.

questions.q: Ashoka's messages carved on rocks and pillars are known as his what?
questions.f: They were written in everyday Prakrit so ordinary people, not just scholars, could read them.

questions.q: Which religion did Ashoka help spread far beyond India?
questions.f: He sent his own son and daughter as missionaries to Sri Lanka.

questions.q: Who founded the Mauryan Empire?
questions.f: He built the empire while still a young man, with help from his clever adviser Chanakya.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian thinker wrote the Arthashastra, a book on running a state?
questions.f: Also called Kautilya, he advised Chandragupta Maurya and wrote about spies, taxes and roads.

questions.q: Which Gupta-era poet wrote the play Shakuntala?
questions.f: Translated into German in 1791, his play amazed European writers like Goethe.

questions.q: Hampi's ruins were once the capital of which empire?
questions.f: Visitors in the 1500s said its markets sold diamonds by the basketful.

questions.q: Which king made the Vijayanagara empire famous for poetry and wealth?
questions.f: He wrote poetry himself and kept eight famous poets, the Ashtadiggajas, at his court.

questions.q: Which Chola king built the great Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur?
questions.f: Its tower rises 66 metres and its capstone weighs many tonnes, lifted without cranes.

questions.q: The Chola kings were unusual among Indian rulers for having a strong what?
questions.f: Chola ships sailed to Sri Lanka, Sumatra and Malaya, spreading Indian trade and art.

questions.q: Who founded the Mughal Empire in India?
questions.f: Babur wrote a lively diary, the Baburnama, describing India's fruits, birds and weather.

questions.q: Babur won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
questions.f: His small army used cannons and clever tactics against a much bigger force.

questions.q: Which grand Mughal city, built by Akbar, was abandoned soon after?
questions.f: Its red sandstone courts still stand nearly empty; water shortage is the likeliest reason it emptied.

questions.q: Which Delhi tomb is often called a first draft of the Taj Mahal?
questions.f: Built in the 1570s, its dome and garden plan were copied and improved at Agra.

questions.q: The Ajanta caves are in which Indian state?
questions.f: They were forgotten for centuries until a British hunting party spotted them in 1819.

questions.q: The Konark Sun Temple stands in which state?
questions.f: Sailors once used it as a landmark and called it the Black Pagoda.

questions.q: Nalanda's ruins are in which modern Indian state?
questions.f: A Chinese traveller wrote that Nalanda's library was so big it had three separate buildings.

questions.q: Which Indus Valley site in Gujarat had a large brick dockyard?
questions.f: Boats could be floated in and out of Lothal's basin, making it a very early port.

questions.q: The Indus Valley cities belonged to the Bronze Age, before iron was in use.
questions.f: Their tools were copper and bronze; iron reached India centuries later.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian mathematician wrote the first clear rules for using zero?
questions.f: In 628 CE he explained what happens when you add or subtract with zero and with negatives.

questions.q: Aryabhata calculated a value for pi very close to 3.1416.
questions.f: He even hinted the number could not be written exactly, long before that was proved.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian text is a famous handbook of medicine?
questions.f: It describes diet, exercise and hundreds of plant medicines, and is still studied today.

questions.q: Ancient Indian chess, chaturanga, took its name from words meaning what?
questions.f: The four limbs were foot soldiers, horses, chariots and elephants, matching pawn, knight, rook and bishop.

questions.q: India's counting digits spread to Europe through which people, giving them their common name?
questions.f: That is why 1, 2, 3 are called Hindu-Arabic numerals: invented in India, carried west by Arab scholars.

questions.q: The Ellora caves are special because they hold temples of how many religions?
questions.f: Hindu, Buddhist and Jain monuments sit side by side, carved over about 500 years.

questions.q: The Sanchi Stupa is in which Indian state?
questions.f: Its carved gateways show the Buddha only as symbols, such as a footprint or an empty seat.

questions.q: Golconda in south India was world-famous for mining what?
questions.f: The Koh-i-Noor and the Hope Diamond both came from the Golconda region.

questions.q: Chola craftsmen were masters at casting statues from which metal?
questions.f: Their dancing Shiva, Nataraja, is one of the most copied sculptures in the world.

questions.q: The Qutub Minar was begun by which ruler of Delhi?
questions.f: He built only the first storey; later sultans added the rest, so the styles change as you look up.

questions.q: Indus Valley children played with toy carts and whistles made of baked clay.
questions.f: Archaeologists have even found clay animals with heads that nod.

questions.q: Indus Valley traders measured goods using neat cubes made of stone. These were their what?
questions.f: The weights follow a strict pattern, so a trader in Harappa and one in Lothal used the same system.

questions.q: Which Indus city is famous for its huge stepped water reservoirs in Gujarat?
questions.f: Its builders cut rock channels to catch every drop of rain in a dry landscape.

questions.q: The marble for the Taj Mahal was quarried in which Rajasthan town?
questions.f: Makrana marble is still quarried today and was later used for many famous buildings.

questions.q: Which ancient centre of learning in the north-west taught medicine and grammar?
questions.f: Taxila attracted students from Persia and Greece, and Chanakya is said to have taught there.

questions.q: The Great Stupa, cave paintings and the Iron Pillar all show Indian skill in what?
questions.f: The Iron Pillar's rust-proof metal still puzzles engineers over 1,600 years later.

questions.q: Which Gupta ruler is nicknamed the Indian Napoleon for his many campaigns?
questions.f: His victories were praised in a long inscription carved on an older Ashokan pillar at Allahabad.

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor is remembered for discussing many religions at his court?
questions.f: He built a special hall, the Ibadat Khana, where scholars of different faiths debated.

questions.q: Which fort city in Rajasthan is famous for a hilltop fort you can see from far away?
questions.f: Jaisalmer's golden sandstone fort is one of very few forts in the world where people still live.

questions.q: Which Indian monument's four lions are shown on every Indian banknote and passport?
questions.f: Only three lions show at once in the emblem, because the fourth is hidden behind.

questions.q: Gandhi's Salt March started from which ashram?
questions.f: He set out from Ahmedabad on 12 March 1930 with 78 companions.

questions.q: The Salt March ended at which coastal village?
questions.f: There Gandhi picked up a lump of natural salt from the mud, breaking the salt law.

questions.q: Roughly how far did Gandhi and his followers walk on the Salt March?
questions.f: They covered it in 24 days, walking about 16 km a day while crowds grew along the road.

questions.q: The uprising of 1857 is often called India's First War of what?
questions.f: It began among soldiers at Meerut and spread across north and central India.

questions.q: The title Mahatma, given to Gandhi, means what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit maha, great, plus atma, soul; Gandhi himself was uncomfortable with the title.

questions.q: Which leader declared, Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it?
questions.f: Swaraj means self-rule; Tilak was called Lokmanya, meaning accepted by the people.

questions.q: The Hindi name of Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army, Azad Hind Fauj, means what?
questions.f: Azad means free, Hind means India and fauj means army; it even had its own stamps and currency plans.

questions.q: Which movement in 1942 demanded that British rule end at once?
questions.f: Its watchword, Do or die, asked Indians to work peacefully but without giving up.

questions.q: Which movement asked Indians to buy goods made in their own country?
questions.f: Swadeshi means of one's own country; people burned imported cloth and spun their own.

questions.q: Sarojini Naidu, poet and freedom fighter, was called the Nightingale of what?
questions.f: She also became India's first woman state governor, in Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: Who became India's first woman Prime Minister?
questions.f: She took office in 1966, nineteen years after Independence.

questions.q: The words below the lions in India's emblem, Satyameva Jayate, mean what?
questions.f: The line comes from an ancient text called the Mundaka Upanishad.

questions.q: How many spokes does the Ashoka Chakra on India's flag have?
questions.f: Each spoke is said to stand for a value, and together they mean life must keep moving.

questions.q: Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly that wrote India's Constitution?
questions.f: The assembly met for nearly three years, holding 11 long sessions before finishing.

questions.q: Which new country was created alongside India at Independence in 1947?
questions.f: Millions of families moved across the new borders, one of the largest migrations in history.

questions.q: Who was the last Viceroy of India?
questions.f: He announced the date of Independence, and later served as India's first Governor-General.

questions.q: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was independent India's first Deputy Prime Minister.
questions.f: He was also Home Minister, and persuaded over 500 princely states to join India.

questions.q: The Statue of Unity, the world's tallest statue, honours which leader?
questions.f: At 182 metres it stands beside the Narmada river in Gujarat, and opened in 2018.

questions.q: India's Parliament has how many houses?
questions.f: The Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha must both agree before most laws can pass.

questions.q: Lok Sabha means the House of the what?
questions.f: Rajya Sabha, the other house, means Council of States.

questions.q: Who was independent India's first Law Minister?
questions.f: He had earned doctorates in London and New York before returning to fight for equal rights.

questions.q: Who wrote the patriotic song Sare Jahan Se Achha?
questions.f: An Indian astronaut, Rakesh Sharma, quoted the line from orbit when asked how India looked.

questions.q: Who wrote the song Vande Mataram?
questions.f: He wrote it in the 1870s and later placed it inside his novel Anandamath.

questions.q: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, a follower of non-violence, was nicknamed which Gandhi?
questions.f: He led a peaceful movement in the north-west and spent decades in prison for it.

questions.q: In 1919 a peaceful gathering in a walled garden was fired upon in which city?
questions.f: The Jallianwala Bagh tragedy shocked India and turned many moderates into freedom fighters.

questions.q: After Jallianwala Bagh, which writer gave up his British knighthood in protest?
questions.f: He wrote that badges of honour felt shameful beside his people's suffering.

questions.q: Bhagat Singh's ringing slogan Inquilab Zindabad means what?
questions.f: He was only 23, and asked to be remembered for his ideas rather than his courage alone.

questions.q: Gandhi spent Independence Day in 1947 in Calcutta, working for peace rather than celebrating.
questions.f: He fasted and walked from house to house asking neighbours to look after one another.

questions.q: Nehru's Independence-eve speech is remembered by which phrase?
questions.f: He spoke just before midnight on 14 August 1947, as the clock ticked into 15 August.

questions.q: Which movement of 1920 asked Indians to stop cooperating with British offices and schools?
questions.f: Lawyers left courts and students left colleges, all without a single blow struck.

questions.q: Whose design was the main basis for India's national flag?
questions.f: He proposed a two-colour flag with a spinning wheel; the final design kept his idea with a chakra.

questions.q: Which freedom fighter led the women's regiment of the Indian National Army?
questions.f: A trained doctor, she commanded the Rani of Jhansi Regiment in Southeast Asia.

questions.q: Which day does India mark as Constitution Day, remembering its adoption in 1949?
questions.f: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 but came into force two months later.

questions.q: Which Indian leader was called Lokmanya, meaning respected by the people?
questions.f: He turned the Ganesh festival into a public celebration that helped bring people together.

questions.q: Lala Lajpat Rai was popularly known as the Lion of which region?
questions.f: With Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal, he formed the famous trio nicknamed Lal-Bal-Pal.

questions.q: India's national flag was officially adopted in which month and year?
questions.f: It was approved just three weeks before Independence Day.

questions.q: India's Constitution guarantees free schooling as a fundamental right for children.
questions.f: Added in 2002, Article 21A makes education a right for every child aged six to fourteen.

questions.q: Rani Lakshmibai fought in the uprising of which year?
questions.f: Her childhood name was Manikarnika, and she learned riding and swordplay as a girl.

questions.q: Who chairs the writing of new laws as head of the Indian state, signing bills into law?
questions.f: A bill passed by both houses becomes law only after the President signs it.

questions.q: Jamsetji Tata's first big industry was making which product?
questions.f: He named his Nagpur mill Empress Mills, opening it in 1877 before moving into steel.

questions.q: Which grand Mumbai hotel did Jamsetji Tata open in 1903?
questions.f: It was the first building in Bombay to be lit by electricity.

questions.q: Tata Airlines, started by JRD Tata, later became which airline?
questions.f: JRD flew the very first mail flight himself, from Karachi to Bombay in 1932.

questions.q: JRD Tata holds the record as India's first licensed what?
questions.f: He got licence number one in 1929, and was still flying planes in his seventies.

questions.q: The brand name Amul comes from a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: From amulya, priceless; it also fits Anand Milk Union Limited.

questions.q: Which man is called the Milkman of India for building the dairy cooperative movement?
questions.f: He turned a small farmers' union in Anand into a movement that made India the top milk producer.

questions.q: Amul's cheeky advertising slogan for its butter is Utterly Butterly what?
questions.f: The line was coined in 1966 and has outlasted almost every other Indian ad slogan.

questions.q: ISRO's most-used rocket, nicknamed its workhorse, is known by which short name?
questions.f: PSLV stands for Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, and it has flown dozens of successful missions.

questions.q: In 2017 a single Indian rocket launched a record how many satellites at once?
questions.f: One PSLV flight released 104 satellites, most of them tiny ones from other countries.

questions.q: India's Mars mission was remarkable because India succeeded on which attempt?
questions.f: No other country had reached Mars orbit on its first try.

questions.q: Who is called the father of India's space programme?
questions.f: Chandrayaan-3's lander was named Vikram in his honour.

questions.q: Parts of India's earliest rockets were once moved to the launch pad on a bicycle.
questions.f: Early ISRO teams worked from a church in Thumba and used bicycles and bullock carts.

questions.q: Chandrayaan-3's little six-wheeled rover was named what?
questions.f: Pragyan means wisdom; it rolled out of the Vikram lander to study the Moon's soil.

questions.q: India's first passenger train, in 1853, ran between Bombay and which town?
questions.f: The 34-kilometre trip took about an hour and fifteen minutes.

questions.q: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway toy train is famous for being what?
questions.f: Its narrow track loops and zigzags up steep hills, sometimes crossing the road.

questions.q: Which film is remembered as India's first full-length feature, made in 1913?
questions.f: Dadasaheb Phalke made it silent, and even played some roles with his own family.

questions.q: Alam Ara, released in 1931, was important because it was India's first film with what?
questions.f: Audiences queued for hours to hear actors speak and sing on screen for the first time.

questions.q: India's highest film honour is named after which pioneer?
questions.f: Phalke sold his wife's jewellery to buy a camera and start Indian film-making.

questions.q: Singers who record songs for actors to mime in Indian films are called what?
questions.f: Playback singing became so popular that singers grew as famous as the stars themselves.

questions.q: India makes more films each year than any other country.
questions.f: Films are made in dozens of Indian languages, not just Hindi.

questions.q: Who captained India to its first cricket World Cup win?
questions.f: His own catch running backwards to dismiss Viv Richards turned the 1983 final around.

questions.q: India won the very first men's T20 World Cup in which year?
questions.f: The final against Pakistan was decided in the last over by a young Joginder Sharma.

questions.q: Who captained India to the 2011 cricket World Cup title at home?
questions.f: He finished the final with a six, and India became the first host nation to win the trophy.

questions.q: Who was the first Indian to score a triple century in Test cricket?
questions.f: He did it twice, and reached the milestone the second time with a six.

questions.q: India's hockey team won how many Olympic gold medals in all?
questions.f: Six of those golds came in a row between 1928 and 1956.

questions.q: Which hockey player was nicknamed The Wizard for his stick skills?
questions.f: India's National Sports Day is held on his birthday, 29 August.

questions.q: Athlete Milkha Singh was nicknamed what?
questions.f: He missed an Olympic medal by a whisker in Rome in 1960, finishing fourth.

questions.q: Which sport did Abhinav Bindra win India's first individual Olympic gold in?
questions.f: His win in Beijing in 2008 came in the 10-metre air rifle event.

questions.q: The Indian Premier League cricket tournament began in which year?
questions.f: It mixed city teams, short matches and music, changing how cricket is watched worldwide.

questions.q: Sprinter P. T. Usha was nicknamed the Payyoli what?
questions.f: Payyoli is her home village in Kerala; she missed an Olympic medal by 1/100th of a second.

questions.q: India's postal system is famous for having the world's largest what?
questions.f: India even has a floating post office on Dal Lake in Srinagar.

questions.q: Chandrayaan-2's orbiter kept working around the Moon even though its lander did not land safely.
questions.f: The orbiter later helped Chandrayaan-3 by scouting and relaying signals.

questions.q: Which Indian company grew into the country's largest software services firm?
questions.f: Founded in 1968, it now employs hundreds of thousands of engineers worldwide.

questions.q: Which small car became a symbol of middle-class India in the 1980s?
questions.f: Its first buyer was picked by lottery and got the keys from the Prime Minister.

questions.q: India's Mars orbiter carried a camera that sent back famous full-disc pictures of what?
questions.f: Its wide orbit let it photograph the whole planet at once, which few missions could do.

questions.q: Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian to travel where?
questions.f: Asked in 1984 how India looked from orbit, he replied with a line from a patriotic song.

questions.q: Which Indian city is home to the film studios known as Film City?
questions.f: Its sets can become a palace, a temple or a village street in a single week.

questions.q: Amul's billboards are drawn fresh to comment on what?
questions.f: The team behind them has produced thousands of topical cartoons since 1966.

questions.q: India is the world's largest producer of milk.
questions.f: Most of it comes from tiny farms where families keep just one or two animals.

questions.q: The Tata group is unusual because most of it is owned by what?
questions.f: That means a large share of Tata's profits flows into schools, hospitals and research.

questions.q: The word juggernaut comes from a temple name meaning Lord of the what?
questions.f: From Jagannath at Puri, whose festival chariot is so huge it needs hundreds of pullers.

questions.q: The word guru comes from a Sanskrit adjective that literally means what?
questions.f: A guru was a person weighty with knowledge, so heavy came to mean wise.

questions.q: The word avatar breaks into parts meaning down plus what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit ava, down, plus tri, to cross: a god crossing down into the world.

questions.q: When shampoo first entered English it meant to massage the body, not to wash hair.
questions.f: From Hindi champo, press; hair-washing only became its main meaning in the 1800s.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word behind jungle first described dry, waste ground rather than thick forest.
questions.f: Jangala meant arid land; English speakers in India shifted it to mean dense wilderness.

questions.q: In catamaran, the Tamil part maram means what?
questions.f: Kattumaram means tied wood, exactly how the first catamarans were made.

questions.q: The name India itself comes from an old name for which river?
questions.f: Sanskrit Sindhu became Persian Hindu and Greek Indos, giving India, Hindu and Hindi.

questions.q: The word indigo comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.f: Greek indikon meant Indian dye, because the blue came from Indian plants.

questions.q: The word rupee comes from a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: From rupya, shaped or stamped silver; Sher Shah Suri made the rupiya a standard coin.

questions.q: The word pukka, meaning genuine or solid, comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi pakka; a pukka house was one of baked brick, not raw mud.

questions.q: The word chintz comes from an Indian word meaning what kind of cloth?
questions.f: From Hindi chint; the printed flowery cotton was so popular in Europe it was once banned to protect local weavers.

questions.q: The cloth called calico is named after which Indian port?
questions.f: Calicut, now Kozhikode in Kerala, sent shiploads of plain cotton cloth to Europe.

questions.q: The word ginger traces back to a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: From shringavera, because a ginger root looks like a set of antlers.

questions.q: The word sari comes from a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: From shati; the garment is one uncut length of fabric, wrapped without stitching.

questions.q: The word nirvana literally describes what happening?
questions.f: From Sanskrit nirvana, blown out: the calming of desire like a candle going quiet.

questions.q: The word gymkhana comes from words meaning ball plus what?
questions.f: From gend-khana, ball house, first a racquets court, later any sports meeting.

questions.q: The word bandicoot comes from Telugu words meaning what animal mash-up?
questions.f: From pandi-kokku, pig-rat; British settlers later stuck the name on an Australian marsupial.

questions.q: The word cushy, meaning easy and comfortable, comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi khush, pleased; soldiers in India brought the slang home.

questions.q: The sport of polo takes its name from a Himalayan word meaning what?
questions.f: From the Balti word pulu; British officers learned the game in Manipur and spread it worldwide.

questions.q: In polo, a period of play is called a chukker, from a word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi chakkar, a round; the same root as chakra, wheel.

questions.q: The word sandalwood traces to a Sanskrit word for the fragrant tree. What is it?
questions.f: Sandalwood oil keeps its scent for decades, which is why old carved boxes still smell sweet.

questions.q: The word camphor comes from a Sanskrit word for a white, sweet-smelling solid. Which?
questions.f: Camphor sublimes, turning straight from solid to vapour, which is why it seems to vanish.

questions.q: The word dacoit comes from an Indian word for what?
questions.f: From Hindi dakait; the word entered English law books written in colonial India.

questions.q: The coarse sacking called gunny gets its name from a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: From goni; gunny bags of Indian jute once carried much of the world's grain.

questions.q: The fibre called jute is grown mostly in which part of the subcontinent?
questions.f: Jute is called the golden fibre because of the shine of its dried strands.

questions.q: Which of these English words did NOT come from an Indian language?
questions.f: Igloo comes from Inuktitut in the Arctic; the other three all travelled from India.

questions.q: Which of these English words came from India rather than from Latin?
questions.f: Pyjamas reached English through Hindi and Urdu from a Persian phrase for leg garment.

questions.q: A veranda in India was usually built to give a house what?
questions.f: Deep verandas keep sun off the walls, an idea copied from Bengal to Australia.

questions.q: The word thug entered English in the 1800s from reports written where?
questions.f: From Hindi thag, cheat; the word later drifted to mean any rough bully.

questions.q: The word karma comes from a Sanskrit root meaning what?
questions.f: The root kri, to do, also lies behind Sanskrit words for work and ceremony.

questions.q: The English word cheetah and the Hindi word chitra, meaning picture, share a root about patterns.
questions.f: Sanskrit chitra meant variegated or bright, giving both a spotted cat and a painted image.

questions.q: The soft goat wool called pashmina takes its name from a word meaning what?
questions.f: From Persian pashm, wool; the finest pashmina fibres are far thinner than a human hair.

questions.q: The word cot, from Hindi khat, first described what?
questions.f: Woven-string khats are still used across rural India, cool and light to carry.

questions.q: The word bungalow keeps its Indian meaning best in which detail?
questions.f: From Hindi bangla, a Bengal-style low house; the design spread around the world.

questions.q: Which English word for a small boat came from Bengali and Hindi?
questions.f: From dingi; kayak is Inuit and canoe comes from the Caribbean.

questions.q: The word chutney describes a paste you would traditionally do what with?
c: Lick or taste in small amounts
questions.f: From Hindi chatni, from chatna, to lick, which is exactly how a tangy chutney is eaten.

questions.q: The word loot became common in English partly because of which activity?
c: Soldiers bringing back words from India
questions.f: From Hindi lut, plunder; by the 1800s English newspapers used loot freely.

questions.q: The word cummerbund names something worn around which part of the body?
questions.f: From kamar, waist, plus band, tie; Indian clerks and servants wore them long before dinner jackets did.

questions.q: The word bandana is linked to an Indian dyeing method in which cloth is first what?
questions.f: From bandhna, to tie; knotted spots resist the dye, leaving the pale rings you still see today.

questions.q: Which Indian city gave its name to a cotton cloth once hugely popular in Europe?
questions.f: Calico shipped out of Calicut by the millions of yards from the 1600s onwards.

questions.q: The word khaki was adopted for uniforms because the colour did what?
questions.f: From Hindi khaki, dust-coloured; soldiers in 1840s India dyed white cloth with mud and tea to hide better.

questions.q: The famous small bronze statue called the Dancing Girl was found at which Indus city?
questions.f: Cast around 2500 BCE using the lost-wax method, she stands just 10.5 cm tall.

questions.q: Most of Ashoka's edicts were carved in which ancient script?
questions.f: Nearly every modern Indian script, plus Thai and Tibetan writing, descends from Brahmi.

questions.q: Which Greek ambassador wrote an account of Mauryan India called Indica?
questions.f: He described Pataliputra's wooden walls, its moat and a court where the king heard cases daily.

questions.q: Aryabhata's famous book of mathematics and astronomy is called what?
questions.f: It packs trigonometry, planetary motion and square roots into just 121 verses.

questions.q: Lilavati, a classic Indian book written in verse, is about which subject?
questions.f: Bhaskara II wrote its problems as poems about bees, peacocks and lotus flowers.

questions.q: The Sushruta Samhita is best known for describing what?
questions.f: It explains how to rebuild a nose using skin from the forehead, an idea surgeons still use.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word for zero, shunya, literally means what?
questions.f: Arab scholars translated shunya as sifr, which became both cipher and zero in Europe.

questions.q: The name Vijayanagara means what?
questions.f: Its ruins at Hampi sprawl over 26 square kilometres beside the Tungabhadra river.

questions.q: Hampi's ruined city stands on the banks of which river?
questions.f: Huge granite boulders around the river gave builders stone right where they needed it.

questions.q: Kalidasa's poem Meghaduta is known in English as The what Messenger?
questions.f: In it a separated husband asks a passing monsoon cloud to carry a message to his wife.

questions.q: Panini's great work on Sanskrit grammar, the Ashtadhyayi, takes its name from meaning what?
questions.f: Its 4,000 short rules describe a whole language so tightly that computer scientists still study them.

questions.q: Which is considered the oldest of India's ancient Vedic texts?
questions.f: It was memorised and passed on by voice for centuries before being written down.

questions.q: Early Buddhist teachings were preserved mainly in which language?
questions.f: Pali was an everyday spoken language, chosen so ordinary people could understand the teachings.

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor had the great Jama Masjid of Delhi built?
questions.f: Its courtyard can hold tens of thousands of people at once.

questions.q: Akbar's group of nine outstanding courtiers was known as the what?
questions.f: Navaratna means nine gems, and the group included the musician Tansen and the witty Birbal.

questions.q: Roughly how long did the Taj Mahal take to complete?
questions.f: Records suggest around 20,000 workers and over 1,000 elephants were involved.

questions.q: The Khajuraho temples were built by which dynasty?
questions.f: About 25 of an original 85 temples survive, hidden by jungle until the 1830s.

questions.q: The stone observatory called Jantar Mantar in Jaipur was built by which ruler?
questions.f: Its giant instruments can measure the time and the positions of stars without any lens.

questions.q: The enormous Nandi bull at the Thanjavur temple is remarkable because it is what?
questions.f: It measures about 4 metres tall and weighs roughly 25 tonnes.

questions.q: The Indus Valley statue nicknamed the Priest-King was found where?
questions.f: Nobody knows if he really was a priest or a king, so the nickname is only a guess.

questions.q: Indus Valley houses often had their own bathrooms connected to covered street drains.
questions.f: Their drainage system was better than that of many cities built thousands of years later.

questions.q: Chandragupta Maurya made a treaty with which Greek general who ruled to India's west?
questions.f: The deal brought Chandragupta 500 war elephants' worth of bargaining power and a Greek envoy at court.

questions.q: Ancient Indian mathematicians of the Sulba Sutras worked out geometry mainly for what purpose?
questions.f: Baudhayana stated the right-triangle rule we call Pythagoras' theorem centuries before Pythagoras.

questions.q: Nalanda's long life as a university ended in the 1190s because of what?
questions.f: Legend says its libraries were so vast they smouldered for days; monks carried texts to Tibet for safety.

questions.q: Which travelling Chinese monk left a detailed description of Nalanda and Gupta India?
questions.f: He studied there for years and carried hundreds of manuscripts home by camel.

questions.q: Which Chola king led a daring naval expedition across the sea to Southeast Asia?
questions.f: His fleet reached the Srivijaya kingdom in today's Indonesia, an amazing distance for the 1000s.

questions.q: The Taj Mahal was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in which decade?
questions.f: It joined the list in 1983, along with Agra Fort in the same year.

questions.q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora is unusual because builders worked in which direction?
questions.f: They removed an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock, with no way to put a mistake back.

questions.q: Ancient Indian iron and steel were prized abroad, especially the type known as what?
questions.f: Wootz from south India was traded to the Middle East, where smiths used it for famous sword blades.

questions.q: India's oldest known stone stupas and pillars were mostly built during which empire?
questions.f: Ashoka's stonemasons polished granite so smoothly that early visitors thought it was metal.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian city name means the city of flowers, and is today's Patna?
questions.f: Patali refers to a flowering tree; Greek writers called the city Palibothra.

questions.q: The Ajanta caves were rediscovered in 1819 by a British party doing what?
questions.f: An officer spotted an arch above the trees while chasing a tiger across the Waghora valley.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian text on statecraft advises rulers on spies, taxes and treaties?
questions.f: Lost for centuries, it was rediscovered in 1905 when a scholar handed a palm-leaf copy to a library.

questions.q: India's ancient theatre handbook, the Natyashastra, covers dance, drama and what else?
questions.f: It also describes rasa, the emotional flavour a performance should leave in the audience.

questions.q: The Iron Pillar of Delhi resists rust because of a protective layer that formed on its surface.
questions.f: Scientists call the layer misawite; it grew from the pillar's unusually high phosphorus content.

questions.q: Fatehpur Sikri's name includes a word meaning what?
questions.f: Fateh means victory; Akbar named the city after campaigns in Gujarat.

questions.q: Which Indus Valley craft product was traded as far as Mesopotamia?
questions.f: Indus seals have turned up in Mesopotamian cities, proof of sea and land trade 4,000 years ago.

questions.q: Which Gupta-era astronomy text explains planetary positions and shadows?
questions.f: It contains sine tables that are surprisingly close to modern values.

questions.q: The Chola bronze of a dancing Shiva is known by which name?
questions.f: Nataraja means lord of the dance; a copy stands outside the CERN physics lab in Geneva.

questions.q: Which stepwell in Gujarat, carved like an upside-down temple, is a World Heritage Site?
questions.f: Built in the 1000s, it lay buried in silt for centuries and was dug out only in the 20th century.

questions.q: The rock-cut shore temples at Mahabalipuram were built by which dynasty?
questions.f: Their sculptors carved whole temples out of standing boulders, like giant models.

questions.q: Which Indus Valley site in Haryana is one of the largest yet found?
questions.f: Rakhigarhi's mounds spread over hundreds of hectares, rivalling Mohenjo-daro in size.

questions.q: Which Indian temple town's chariot festival gave English the word juggernaut?
questions.f: Puri's Jagannath temple chariots are rebuilt from scratch every single year.

questions.q: Ancient Indian surgeons described using ant heads as tiny clamps to close wounds.
questions.f: Similar tricks appear in old texts worldwide, but Indian works describe the tools in unusual detail.

questions.q: Which dynasty ruled from Badami and carved the early cave temples there?
questions.f: Their builders experimented with styles that later spread across the Deccan.

questions.q: The Indian National Congress was founded in which year?
questions.f: Its first session in Bombay had just 72 delegates.

questions.q: Who was the first president of the Indian National Congress?
questions.f: A Calcutta barrister, he presided over the very first session in December 1885.

questions.q: The Partition of Bengal in 1905, which sparked the Swadeshi movement, was ordered by whom?
questions.f: Protest was so strong that the partition was reversed in 1911.

questions.q: Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, at Champaran in 1917, helped farmers growing what?
questions.f: Farmers were forced to plant indigo instead of food; Gandhi's inquiry got the system changed.

questions.q: Gandhi returned to India for good from which country in 1915?
questions.f: He had spent 21 years there developing satyagraha before coming home aged 45.

questions.q: Who did Gandhi call his political mentor after returning to India?
questions.f: Gokhale advised him to travel India by third-class train for a year before speaking on politics.

questions.q: Gandhi's autobiography is titled The Story of My Experiments with what?
questions.f: He wrote it in weekly instalments for his own journal, admitting his mistakes as he went.

questions.q: Which 1919 law allowing arrest without trial triggered nationwide protest?
questions.f: Indians called it the black law, and Gandhi launched his first all-India satyagraha against it.

questions.q: Subhas Chandra Bose gave his soldiers which stirring two-word order in Hindi?
questions.f: Delhi Chalo means on to Delhi, the INA's goal as it advanced from the east.

questions.q: In 1941 Netaji left India secretly by doing what?
questions.f: He grew a beard, dressed as a Pathan gentleman and travelled overland through Afghanistan.

questions.q: The 1857 uprising is often said to have begun with a soldier's protest at which cantonment?
questions.f: Mangal Pandey's stand at Barrackpore in March 1857 came weeks before Meerut rose in May.

questions.q: Which last Mughal emperor was proclaimed leader by the rebels of 1857?
questions.f: He was also a fine Urdu poet, and his verses were written in exile far from Delhi.

questions.q: After 1857 the government of India passed from a trading company to whom?
questions.f: The East India Company lost its ruling powers in 1858 after nearly a century of them.

questions.q: India's Constitution begins with the words We, the people of what?
questions.f: That opening makes clear the Constitution's power comes from citizens, not from a ruler.

questions.q: How many Fundamental Rights does India's Constitution now guarantee?
questions.f: There were seven until the right to property was reclassified in 1978.

questions.q: India's Fundamental Rights were inspired largely by the constitution of which country?
questions.f: The framers studied dozens of constitutions and openly borrowed the best ideas from each.

questions.q: India's first general election was held over the winter of which years?
questions.f: About 173 million people could vote, most of whom had never voted before in their lives.

questions.q: On the national flag, the Ashoka Chakra replaced which earlier symbol?
questions.f: The charkha appeared on the Congress flag; in 1947 the chakra was chosen as a national emblem.

questions.q: Who administers the oath of office to India's President?
questions.f: If the Chief Justice is unavailable, the senior-most Supreme Court judge does it instead.

questions.q: Which leader was nicknamed the Grand Old Man of India?
questions.f: He was also the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons, in 1892.

questions.q: Which journal did Gandhi edit to spread his ideas in English?
questions.f: He also edited Navajivan in Gujarati and later Harijan, writing much of each issue himself.

questions.q: India's national anthem was first sung publicly in 1911, decades before Independence.
questions.f: It was performed at a Calcutta session of the Congress on 27 December 1911.

questions.q: Which tribal leader from the Chhotanagpur region led a movement for land rights in the 1890s?
questions.f: He died at just 25, and India now marks his birthday, 15 November, as a tribal pride day.

questions.q: The famous poem Jhansi ki Rani, learned by generations of Indian children, was written by whom?
questions.f: Its refrain, that she fought like a man, has become one of Hindi's best-known lines.

questions.q: Which queen of Karnataka resisted British annexation as early as 1824?
questions.f: Her stand came more than thirty years before the great uprising of 1857.

questions.q: India became a republic in 1950, meaning its head of state is what?
questions.f: Until 1950 the British monarch was still India's formal head of state.

questions.q: Which body of the Indian government makes the final decisions on what the Constitution means?
questions.f: India's Supreme Court began work on 28 January 1950, two days after the republic was born.

questions.q: Which movement's watchword was Do or die, spoken by Gandhi in 1942?
questions.f: Almost every senior leader was arrested within hours, so ordinary people led it themselves.

questions.q: The Indian National Army trials of 1945 to 1946 were held mainly at which fort?
questions.f: Public support for the accused soldiers was so huge that the sentences were quietly set aside.

questions.q: Sardar Patel's task of joining princely states to India involved persuading roughly how many?
questions.f: He and V. P. Menon completed most of it in the months around August 1947.
