questions.q: Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in 1913 for which collection of poems?
questions.f: He was the first person from Asia to win a Nobel Prize in Literature.

questions.q: The Kheda and Ahmedabad campaigns of 1918 showed Gandhi's method applied to whom?
questions.f: In Kheda he asked for tax relief after crops failed; in Ahmedabad he backed mill workers' pay.

questions.q: India's Constitution was written by an assembly that debated it for nearly three years.
questions.f: It met from December 1946 to November 1949, and every clause was argued in public.

questions.q: Which national symbol of India was formally adopted on 26 January 1950?
questions.f: The Lion Capital design became the State Emblem on the very day the republic began.

questions.q: Who was independent India's first and only Indian Governor-General?
questions.f: He held the post from 1948 until the office ended when India became a republic.

questions.q: Which pair of words did Lal Bahadur Shastri pair together in a famous slogan?
questions.f: It honoured soldiers and farmers together at a time when India needed both badly.

questions.q: Rani Lakshmibai's childhood name was what?
questions.f: Nicknamed Manu, she learned riding, shooting and swordplay alongside boys at the Peshwa's court.

questions.q: Which freedom fighter is remembered for the organisation abbreviated HSRA?
questions.f: The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association wanted complete independence and social equality.

questions.q: The Preamble describes India as sovereign, socialist, secular and what?
questions.f: The words socialist and secular were added later, by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

questions.q: India's Fundamental Duties for citizens were added to the Constitution in which decade?
questions.f: Added in 1976, they ask citizens to protect the environment, public property and the Constitution itself.

questions.q: Aruna Asaf Ali is remembered for raising the flag in 1942 at which city's park?
questions.f: With most leaders arrested, she hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank and became a symbol of Quit India.

questions.q: Which reformer campaigned for widow remarriage and girls' schooling in 19th-century Bengal?
questions.f: He also redesigned the Bengali alphabet primer that children used for over a century.

questions.q: Savitribai Phule is honoured as one of India's first what?
questions.f: With her husband Jyotirao she opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848.

questions.q: Jamshedpur, India's first planned steel city, is in which state today?
questions.f: Its original name was Sakchi; it was renamed in 1919 in honour of Jamsetji Tata.

questions.q: Which famous science institute in Bengaluru was founded with a Tata endowment?
questions.f: Jamsetji Tata planned it before he died in 1904; it opened in 1909 and still leads Indian research.

questions.q: In 2008 Tata Motors bought which pair of British car brands?
questions.f: An Indian company thus came to own two brands once seen as symbols of British luxury.

questions.q: Which British tea company did Tata buy in the year 2000?
questions.f: It made Tata one of the world's biggest tea businesses almost overnight.

questions.q: Air India's long-serving mascot is a moustached figure called the what?
questions.f: Created in 1946, the bowing Maharajah appeared in cartoons in airports around the world.

questions.q: India's great dairy development programme, led by Verghese Kurien, was called Operation what?
questions.f: Launched in 1970, it linked village milk producers straight to city markets.

questions.q: Amul's cooperative method became famous worldwide as the what pattern?
questions.f: Named after the town of Anand, the model puts farmers in charge of processing and selling.

questions.q: Which ISRO rocket, once called GSLV Mk III, launched Chandrayaan-3?
questions.f: Nicknamed Bahubali for its lifting power, it can carry about four tonnes to a high orbit.

questions.q: India's Aditya-L1 mission studies which object in space?
questions.f: It parked at a balance point about 1.5 million km from Earth so it can watch the Sun non-stop.

questions.q: India's Mars mission's official name was the Mars what Mission?
questions.f: Nicknamed Mangalyaan, the orbiter was designed for six months but worked for about eight years.

questions.q: ISRO's first rockets were launched from Thumba, in which state?
questions.f: Thumba was chosen because Earth's magnetic equator passes almost overhead there.

questions.q: The world's longest railway platform, opened in 2023, is at which Indian station?
questions.f: It stretches about 1,507 metres, longer than fifteen football pitches end to end.

questions.q: India's longest single train journey, the Vivek Express, runs from Dibrugarh to where?
questions.f: The trip covers roughly 4,200 km and takes about 80 hours.

questions.q: The Chenab Bridge in India set a world record as the highest what?
questions.f: Its arch rises about 359 metres above the river, higher than the Eiffel Tower.

questions.q: The Konkan Railway along India's west coast is famous for its many what?
questions.f: Engineers cut over 90 tunnels through soft rock and monsoon-soaked hills to build it.

questions.q: Which 1975 Hindi film ran in one Mumbai cinema for over five years?
questions.f: Its dialogue was released on records and became the first Indian film soundtrack of spoken lines.

questions.q: Who became the first Indian to win an Academy Award?
questions.f: She won for costume design in 1983 and later kept the statuette in a bank locker for safety.

questions.q: Which Indian film-maker received an honorary Oscar in 1992?
questions.f: Too ill to travel, he accepted it from his hospital bed in Kolkata by video link.

questions.q: Which Indian song won the Oscar for Best Original Song in 2023?
questions.f: It came from the Telugu film RRR, and its dance step became a global craze.

questions.q: The 2023 Oscar-winning short The Elephant Whisperers was filmed in which country?
questions.f: It follows a couple in Tamil Nadu raising an orphaned baby elephant named Raghu.

questions.q: Who was the first Indian to score a century in Test cricket?
questions.f: He made it on debut in 1933 at Bombay, and the crowd threw coins onto the field in delight.

questions.q: Which Indian bowler took all ten wickets in a Test innings in 1999?
questions.f: Only one other bowler in history had done it, England's Jim Laker in 1956.

questions.q: Who scored the first double century in men's one-day international cricket?
questions.f: He made 200 not out against South Africa in Gwalior in February 2010.

questions.q: Which Indian took the first hat-trick in cricket World Cup history?
questions.f: He did it against New Zealand in Nagpur in 1987, bowling three batters in a row.

questions.q: Which Indian became world chess champion in 2024, the youngest ever to do so?
questions.f: At 18 he beat a record set by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he first won the title.

questions.q: Mary Kom won world championship titles in which sport?
questions.f: She won six world titles, an achievement matched by very few boxers anywhere.

questions.q: P. V. Sindhu became the first Indian to win the world championship in which sport?
questions.f: She won gold in Basel in 2019 after finishing runner-up twice before.

questions.q: Which Indian company is the world's largest maker of vaccine doses?
questions.f: Based in Pune, it makes over a billion doses a year, many sold cheaply to poorer countries.

questions.q: India is often nicknamed the pharmacy of the world because it makes so many what?
questions.f: A large share of the world's low-cost medicines and vaccines is produced in India.

questions.q: Which Indian company is the world's largest maker of two-wheelers by numbers sold?
questions.f: It has sold well over 100 million motorcycles and scooters since 1984.

questions.q: Mumbai's dabbawalas are famous for delivering what with astonishing accuracy?
questions.f: Their coded lid markings are so effective that business schools study the system.

questions.q: India's UPI system, launched in 2016, is used for what?
questions.f: It now handles billions of transactions a month, many of them for just a few rupees.

questions.q: Which Indian company made the ballot boxes used in India's first general election?
questions.f: Godrej produced over a million steel boxes, having earlier been famous for locks and cupboards.

questions.q: Which Indian biscuit is often called the world's largest-selling biscuit brand?
questions.f: Its wrapper has barely changed in decades, and it is sold in tiny packs for a few rupees.

questions.q: Aadhaar is the world's largest system of what?
questions.f: Over a billion people are enrolled using fingerprints and iris scans.

questions.q: Titan, one of India's best-known watch brands, belongs to which business group?
questions.f: It began in 1984 and later grew into jewellery and eyewear as well.

questions.q: The rounded Ambassador car, once India's most common taxi, was made by which company?
questions.f: Based on a 1950s British design, it was built almost unchanged for over five decades.

questions.q: Which two team sports played worldwide today began in India?
questions.f: Kabaddi players must chant while raiding, which is why holding your breath is part of the game.

questions.q: Kapil Dev's famous innings of 175 not out in the 1983 World Cup was never filmed.
questions.f: A strike by BBC crews meant no cameras were at the ground for one of cricket's great innings.

questions.q: Which Indian city is called the tea capital because of the auctions held there?
questions.f: Kolkata and Guwahati hold huge tea auctions where buyers taste and bid on hundreds of lots.

questions.q: Indian Railways began in 1853 with a train pulled by how many locomotives?
questions.f: Sahib, Sindh and Sultan hauled 400 guests from Bori Bunder to Thane while a 21-gun salute sounded.

questions.q: The Chandrayaan-1 mission released a small craft to strike the Moon deliberately. It was the Moon what Probe?
questions.f: Its data on the way down helped confirm water molecules in the Moon's thin atmosphere.

questions.q: Which Indian steel or engineering feat used the phrase Make in India for locally built trains?
questions.f: Vande Bharat sets were designed and assembled at the Integral Coach Factory in Chennai.

questions.q: ISRO's Mars mission cost less per kilometre travelled than many city taxi rides.
questions.f: At about 450 crore rupees for a 650-million-km journey, the comparison genuinely works out.

questions.q: Which Indian film industry, based in Chennai, is nicknamed Kollywood?
questions.f: The name comes from Kodambakkam, the Chennai neighbourhood full of studios.

questions.q: The word veranda originally described what part of a building?
questions.f: Hindi varanda and Portuguese varanda both meant railing before the word meant the whole porch.

questions.q: The word charpoy is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: From char, four, plus pai, foot: the classic Indian bed is literally a four-footed frame.

questions.q: The place name Punjab is built from words meaning what?
questions.f: Panj, five, plus ab, water, for the five rivers that cross the region.

questions.q: The word candy traces back to a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: From khanda, a broken piece, via Persian qand for crystallised sugar.

questions.q: The word coir, the rope fibre from coconut husk, comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: From Malayalam kayar, cord; coir ropes resist salt water, so sailors loved them.

questions.q: The word orange can be traced back to which Sanskrit word?
questions.f: Naranga became Persian narang, Arabic naranj, then Spanish naranja; English dropped the n.

questions.q: In British English, a juggernaut is also the everyday word for what?
questions.f: From Jagannath's temple chariot; English first used the word for anything unstoppably heavy.

questions.q: The word chapati comes from a root meaning what action?
questions.f: From Hindi chapat, a slap: the dough is patted flat between the palms.

questions.q: The Indian English word bandobast means what?
questions.f: From Persian band-o-bast, tying and binding; it entered English as slang for organising things.

questions.q: The English word chakra means what?
questions.f: Its ancient root also gave English wheel and cycle, all from the same word for turning.

questions.q: In catamaran, the Tamil part kattu means what?
questions.f: Kattumaram, tied wood, is still the name of log rafts used off the Coromandel coast.

questions.q: The word raj, used in English for a period of rule, means what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit rajya; the same root gives raja, king, a cousin of Latin rex.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word danta, meaning tooth, is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: Sanskrit danta, Latin dens and English tooth all trace back to one ancient root.

questions.q: The word maharaja is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: Maha, great, plus raja, king; maha is a cousin of Latin magnus, as in magnify.

questions.q: The word Sanskrit itself means what?
questions.f: From samskrta, polished; its opposite, prakrta, gave the name Prakrit for everyday speech.

questions.q: Which English word shares an ancient root with the Sanskrit word veda, knowledge?
questions.f: Veda comes from vid, to know; the same root gives English wit and Latin videre, to see.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word agni, fire, is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: Agni and Latin ignis come from the same ancient word for fire.

questions.q: The Indian English word dekko, meaning a quick look, comes from which command?
questions.f: British soldiers in India picked it up, and it survives in British slang as have a dekko.

questions.q: The soup name mulligatawny comes from Tamil words meaning what?
questions.f: From milagu, pepper, plus tannir, water; British cooks added meat and turned it into a soup.

questions.q: The word dharma comes from a root meaning what?
questions.f: From dhri, to uphold; dharma is what holds life and society steady.

questions.q: The word thug in English shifted from meaning a cheat to meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi thag; English narrowed it to street toughs while Hindi kept the sense of trickster.

questions.q: The word punch for a party drink is linked to five of what?
questions.f: From panch, five: classically spirit, sugar, lemon, water and spice or tea.

questions.q: The fabric seersucker takes its name from a phrase meaning what?
questions.f: From Persian shir o shakar, describing the cloth's smooth and puckered stripes side by side.

questions.q: An English word for a very rich, grand person, nabob, comes from which Indian title?
questions.f: From Urdu nawwab, a deputy governor; British officials who came home wealthy were mocked as nabobs.

questions.q: The Indian word for tea, chai, did not begin in India but travelled there from China.
questions.f: Chinese cha became Persian cha and then Hindi chai; the leaf and the word arrived together.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word mantra is built from parts meaning think plus what?
questions.f: Man, think, plus tra, instrument; the tra ending also appears in yantra, a machine or device.

questions.q: Which pair of English words both came into English from Indian languages?
questions.f: Shampoo from Hindi champo, bungalow from bangla; kayak and igloo are Inuit words.

questions.q: The word pyjama's second part, jama, means what?
questions.f: Pay-jama, leg garment; Indian pyjamas were daytime trousers long before they meant nightwear.

questions.q: The dried coconut kernel called copra takes its name from a word in which language?
questions.f: From koppara; copra is pressed for the oil used in soaps and cooking.

questions.q: The word bangle's Hindi root, bangri, described a bracelet made of what?
questions.f: Glass bangles are still made by hand in Firozabad, where furnaces run day and night.

questions.q: The word cheroot, a kind of cigar, comes from a Tamil word meaning what?
questions.f: From shuruttu, a roll; the cheroot is simply rolled leaf cut straight at both ends.

questions.q: Which of these English words came from a Dravidian language of south India?
questions.f: Mango comes from Tamil mankay through Portuguese manga; the others are Latin or Greek.

questions.q: The word loot has a cousin in Hindi lutera, meaning what?
questions.f: From lut, plunder; English took the noun but not the person who does it.

questions.q: The word avatar is used in computing to mean what?
c: A picture standing for a person
questions.f: From Sanskrit avatara, descent: your avatar is you appearing in another world.

questions.q: The word karma is used loosely in English to mean what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit karman, action; the philosophical idea is far more careful than the slang.

questions.q: The English word guru is now used for anyone who is what?
questions.f: From Sanskrit guru, heavy; tech gurus and fitness gurus all borrow the same weighty idea.

questions.q: The word cheetah's Sanskrit root chitra also gives which sense in Indian languages?
questions.f: Chitra means bright or patterned, so a picture and a spotted cat share one root.

questions.q: The English word bungalow's Indian root also names which region's language?
questions.f: Bangla is both the name of the language and the root of bungalow.

questions.q: The Indian English word tiffin actually began as old English slang, not as an Indian word.
questions.f: It came from dialect tiffing, taking a sip; India kept it long after Britain forgot it.

questions.q: The word cot, from Hindi khat, is related in sense to which other borrowed bed word?
questions.f: A charpoy is a four-footed khat; both words came into English from India.

questions.q: Which English word for a spotted or printed cotton came from Indian cloth trade?
questions.f: From Hindi chint, spotted; denim comes from Nimes in France and tweed from Scotland.

questions.q: The Sanskrit number word sapta is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: Sapta, Latin septem and English seven all descend from one ancient number word.

questions.q: The word Bengaluru is traditionally explained as a town of what?
questions.f: The story says a lost king was fed boiled beans by an old woman, giving benda-kaalu-ooru.

questions.q: Which Indian metro city takes its name from a local goddess, Mumbadevi?
questions.f: The city was renamed in 1995; the older Bombay came from Portuguese Bom Bahia or bombaim.

questions.q: The word pashmina and the word pashm both point to which material?
questions.f: Pashmina goats grow their fine underfur at altitudes above 4,000 metres to survive the cold.

questions.q: The word yoga's ancient root also gave English which farming word?
questions.f: Sanskrit yuj, to join, is the same root as the wooden yoke that joins two oxen.

questions.q: The name Mohenjo-daro, given to the site long after it was abandoned, means what?
questions.f: It is a Sindhi nickname; nobody knows what the people who built it called their own city.

questions.q: Indus Valley writing is thought to have been read mainly in which direction?
questions.f: On cramped seals the signs squeeze up at the left end, as though the writer ran out of room there.

questions.q: Which Indus city is famous for a large open ground often described as a stadium?
questions.f: Dholavira also had a signboard of ten large Indus characters, the biggest known Indus inscription.

questions.q: The famous Indus seal showing a seated figure ringed by animals is nicknamed what?
questions.f: Some scholars link it to later ideas of Shiva as lord of animals, but the reading is still debated.

questions.q: Who cracked the ancient Brahmi script in 1837, unlocking Ashoka's edicts?
questions.f: He worked from bilingual coins, matching Greek letters against the unknown Indian ones.

questions.q: In his own edicts, Ashoka usually calls himself Devanampiya Piyadasi, meaning what?
c: Beloved of the gods, of gracious mien
questions.f: For decades scholars did not realise Piyadasi was Ashoka, until an edict at Maski used his real name.

questions.q: Ashoka's fifth pillar edict is striking as one of history's earliest laws protecting what?
questions.f: It lists creatures not to be harmed, from parrots and bats to river turtles, and bans burning forests carelessly.

questions.q: Gupta gold coins were known by a name borrowed from Roman currency. Which?
questions.f: Dinara comes from the Roman denarius, proof of how far trade carried both gold and words.

questions.q: A long inscription praising Samudragupta was carved onto a pillar that already bore whose words?
questions.f: His court poet Harisena added the praise to an older Ashokan pillar now kept in Prayagraj.

questions.q: Samudragupta's coins are unusual because they show him doing what?
questions.f: He also took the title Kaviraja, king of poets, which fits a warrior who wanted to be known for music.

questions.q: Aryabhata's value for pi works out to which decimal?
questions.f: He gave it as 62832 divided by 20000 and hinted the true value could never be written exactly.

questions.q: India's oldest firmly dated inscription using a zero symbol was found at which town?
questions.f: A temple inscription of 876 CE records a garden measurement of 270, complete with a small circle.

questions.q: A Chola inscription at Uttiramerur is famous for describing what unusual practice?
questions.f: Names were written on palm leaves, dropped in a pot, and a child drew out the winners.

questions.q: Rajaraja Chola's great Thanjavur temple was consecrated in which year?
questions.f: Its granite tower still holds the record as one of the tallest of its age anywhere in the world.

questions.q: Vijayanagara's power collapsed after which battle in 1565?
questions.f: A coalition of Deccan sultanates defeated it, and the great city at Hampi was never resettled.

questions.q: Which Portuguese traveller left a vivid description of Vijayanagara at its height?
questions.f: He compared the city's size to Rome and marvelled at its irrigation channels and market streets.

questions.q: Krishnadevaraya wrote the poem Amuktamalyada in which language?
questions.f: A king writing serious poetry in a regional language was unusual, and it helped Telugu literature flourish.

questions.q: Babur wrote his famous memoirs, the Baburnama, in which language?
questions.f: Akbar later had it translated into Persian, since few at his court could read his grandfather's Turkic.

questions.q: Akbar, who built a great library and loved learning, almost certainly could not read himself.
questions.f: Courtiers read aloud to him daily, and he could discuss philosophy in detail from memory.

questions.q: The Razmnama, made at Akbar's court, was a Persian version of which Indian epic?
questions.f: Its illustrated pages show Kurukshetra warriors in Mughal armour, a real blend of two worlds.

questions.q: The Taj Mahal's four minarets were deliberately built to do what?
questions.f: The tilt means that if one ever fell, it would fall away from the tomb rather than onto it.

questions.q: The only craftsman permitted to sign his work on the Taj Mahal was which specialist?
questions.f: Amanat Khan signed the Quranic inscriptions, and designed the lettering to look even from the ground up.

questions.q: The Taj Mahal's flower designs use tiny cut gemstones set into marble. This craft is called what?
questions.f: In India it is called parchin kari; a single flower can contain dozens of separate stone slivers.

questions.q: Shah Jahan's jewelled Peacock Throne was carried off to Persia in 1739 by whom?
questions.f: He also took the Koh-i-Noor; the throne was later broken up and its gems scattered.

questions.q: The diamond name Koh-i-Noor means what?
questions.f: It was mined in the Golconda region, probably at Kollur, and has changed hands for centuries.

questions.q: Hampi's Vittala temple is famous for stone pillars that do what?
questions.f: Struck gently, the slender granite columns give different pitches, so the hall works like an instrument.

questions.q: Chand Baori at Abhaneri, one of India's deepest stepwells, has roughly how many steps?
questions.f: Thirteen storeys of criss-crossing stairs keep the water cool even in the Rajasthan summer.

questions.q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was commissioned by a king of which dynasty?
questions.f: Krishna I ordered it in the 700s; an old inscription says even its builder wondered how it was done.

questions.q: The famous three-headed Trimurti sculpture is carved in the caves on which island?
questions.f: Locals call the island Gharapuri; Portuguese sailors named it after a stone elephant on the shore.

questions.q: Which Indian king hosted the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang and wrote Sanskrit plays himself?
questions.f: Harsha's plays Ratnavali and Nagananda are still performed, an unusual legacy for a conquering king.

questions.q: The great monastery-university of Vikramashila was founded by which dynasty of eastern India?
questions.f: The Palas also supported Nalanda, and their monks carried Buddhism into Tibet.

questions.q: Bhaskara II's masterwork combining arithmetic, algebra and astronomy is called what?
questions.f: Written in 1150, it contains an early idea of instantaneous motion, close to differential calculus.

questions.q: The Kerala school mathematician who found infinite series for pi and sine was who?
questions.f: His 14th-century series were rediscovered in Europe three centuries later by Newton and Leibniz's circle.

questions.q: Alongside Charaka and Sushruta, which writer completes Ayurveda's great classical trio?
questions.f: His Ashtanga Hridaya condensed the older works into verse that students could memorise.

questions.q: Indian crucible steel exported westwards became famous in Europe under which name?
questions.f: Called wootz in south India, its swirling patterns came from carbide bands formed as it cooled.

questions.q: An ancient carved pillar of pure iron, a Vishnu banner, and a courtyard added by Delhi's first sultan all belong to which monument complex?
questions.f: The Iron Pillar was moved there from elsewhere, probably from Udayagiri in central India.

questions.q: Sanchi's richly carved gateways are known by which architectural term?
questions.f: Toranas frame an entrance; the idea travelled with Buddhism and became Japan's torii gates.

questions.q: Which Odisha monument was known to European sailors as the Black Pagoda?
questions.f: Legend says a great lodestone at its top pulled ships' compasses off course, so sailors feared it.

questions.q: India's ancient blue dye, exported worldwide for centuries, came from which plant?
questions.f: European chemists only replaced it in the 1890s with a synthetic version made in a laboratory.

questions.q: Which Mughal-era tomb near Aurangabad is nicknamed the mini Taj?
questions.f: Azam Shah built it for his mother, but a tight budget meant much of it is plaster, not solid marble.

questions.q: Ashoka's rock edicts mention Greek-speaking kings ruling far to the west of India by name.
questions.f: Edict thirteen names rulers like Antiochus and Ptolemy, letting historians date Ashoka precisely.

questions.q: Harappa itself was first properly excavated in the 1920s by which archaeologist?
questions.f: His colleague R. D. Banerji uncovered Mohenjo-daro a year later, revealing a whole lost civilization.

questions.q: Buland Darwaza, one of the tallest gateways in the world, was built by which emperor?
questions.f: He raised it at Fatehpur Sikri around 1601 to mark his Gujarat campaign; it stands about 54 metres tall.

questions.q: A palm-leaf treaty tradition, a Jain hilltop, and an abdicated throne are linked to which ruler?
questions.f: Jain tradition says he gave up his empire, became a monk and ended his days at Shravanabelagola.

questions.q: Kalidasa's finest plays, Ajanta's later paintings and Aryabhata's sine tables all belong to which period?
questions.f: Historians call it classical India: three very different fields peaking within a couple of centuries.

questions.q: The Mauryan stone polish that still shines today is best seen on which objects?
questions.f: Some pillars are so glossy that early European visitors insisted they must be cast metal.

questions.q: India's earliest known stone inscriptions in a Dravidian language are found in which script?
questions.f: Cave inscriptions in Tamil Nadu adapted Brahmi letters to fit Tamil sounds over 2,000 years ago.

questions.q: Which Indian mathematician stated that dividing a number by zero gives an unbounded quantity?
questions.f: He compared it to a jar that never fills; Brahmagupta had earlier got this rule wrong.

questions.q: Which Indus Valley product line shows their skill in fired ceramics at industrial scale?
questions.f: Indus bricks kept a 4:2:1 ratio across hundreds of kilometres, an early example of standard sizing.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian text lists 64 arts a cultured person might learn, from music to gardening?
questions.f: Its lists of skills, games and manners are a rich source on everyday life in Gupta-era towns.

questions.q: Kalhana's Rajatarangini is a rare early Indian work of what kind?
questions.f: Written in Kashmir in the 1100s, it traces the region's kings with dates and even doubts its own sources.

questions.q: In 1943 Subhas Chandra Bose made the only known wartime transfer between submarines of two navies, near which island?
questions.f: He crossed by rubber dinghy from a German U-boat to a Japanese one, then sailed on to Asia.

questions.q: Bose broadcast to India from Europe over which radio service?
questions.f: His first broadcast in 1942 stunned Indians who had believed he was dead.

questions.q: Bhagat Singh wrote a famous essay in jail whose title begins Why I Am an what?
questions.f: He wrote it at 23, arguing that courage should come from conviction, not from fear of punishment.

questions.q: In 1929 Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt drew attention in the Assembly by throwing what?
questions.f: Their leaflet said it takes a loud voice to make the deaf hear, and they waited to be arrested.

questions.q: Chandra Shekhar Azad took his famous surname when he did what, aged fifteen?
questions.f: Asked his name in court, he answered Azad, meaning free, his father's name Swatantra, home Jail.

questions.q: The Simon Commission of 1928 was boycotted across India mainly because it had no what?
questions.f: Crowds met it with black flags and the chant Simon Go Back wherever it travelled.

questions.q: At its 1929 Lahore session the Congress adopted which demand?
questions.f: The tricolour was raised on the Ravi's bank at midnight, and 26 January 1930 was kept as Independence Day.

questions.q: India chose 26 January for Republic Day partly to honour which earlier event?
questions.f: Indians had marked 26 January as Independence Day for seventeen years before it became Republic Day.

questions.q: The Poona Pact of 1932 was an agreement between Gandhi and which leader?
questions.f: It replaced separate electorates with reserved seats, and was signed while Gandhi was fasting in prison.

questions.q: Ambedkar's first newspaper, Mooknayak, had a title meaning what?
questions.f: Launched in 1920, it gave a platform to communities whose concerns other papers ignored.

questions.q: Ambedkar earned degrees at Columbia University and which London institution?
questions.f: He also qualified as a barrister at Gray's Inn, an extraordinary record of study for his time.

questions.q: Which article of India's Constitution did Ambedkar call its heart and soul?
questions.f: It lets any citizen go straight to the Supreme Court when a fundamental right is broken.

questions.q: India's officially recognised languages are listed in which schedule of the Constitution?
questions.f: It began with 14 languages and now lists 22, the most recent additions coming in 2004.

questions.q: India's Directive Principles of State Policy were modelled largely on which country's constitution?
questions.f: The framers took the parliamentary system from Britain and the federal court idea from the United States.

questions.q: How many articles did India's Constitution contain when it was adopted?
questions.f: Amendments have since pushed the count past 470, kept tidy by numbers like 21A and 51A.

questions.q: Who illustrated and decorated the original handwritten Constitution of India?
questions.f: His Santiniketan team painted borders showing scenes from Indian history on every part's first page.

questions.q: The 1946 Cabinet Mission and the 1942 Cripps Mission both came to India to discuss what?
questions.f: Both failed to satisfy Indian leaders, but they shaped the path to the Constituent Assembly.

questions.q: Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit became the first woman to hold which international post?
c: President of the UN General Assembly
questions.f: Nehru's sister took the chair in 1953, and had earlier been India's ambassador to Moscow and Washington.

questions.q: How many companions set out with Gandhi at the start of the Salt March?
questions.f: He chose them carefully from his ashram; by the end, crowds of thousands walked behind them.

questions.q: After Gandhi's arrest in 1930, who led the salt protest at the Dharasana works?
questions.f: An American reporter's dispatch about the volunteers' discipline was printed in over a thousand newspapers.

questions.q: Gandhi's later ashram at Sevagram was near which town?
questions.f: He moved there in 1936 to live in a village at the geographic centre of India.

questions.q: Gandhi was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize several times but never received it.
questions.f: He was nominated five times; the Nobel committee later called the omission its greatest regret.

questions.q: Gandhi appeared as Time magazine's Man of the Year in which year?
questions.f: The Salt March had made him front-page news around the world within a single season.

questions.q: Which leader was widely known by the title Deshbandhu, friend of the nation?
questions.f: A hugely successful barrister, he gave away his house and wealth to the national movement.

questions.q: The Ghadar Party, formed in 1913 to work for Indian freedom, was based in which city?
questions.f: It published a newspaper in Punjabi and Urdu that was smuggled to Indian communities worldwide.

questions.q: Usha Mehta is remembered for secretly running what during the Quit India movement?
questions.f: Congress Radio moved from house to house in Bombay so its signal could not be traced.

questions.q: India's first state created on the basis of language, in 1953, was which one?
questions.f: It followed a long fast by Potti Sriramulu, and led to the States Reorganisation Act of 1956.

questions.q: Who was independent India's first Education Minister, honoured on National Education Day?
questions.f: India marks 11 November, his birthday, and he helped found the IITs and the UGC.

questions.q: Who served as India's first Chief Election Commissioner, organising the 1951 election?
questions.f: He had to build an electoral roll for 173 million mostly non-reading voters, so parties got picture symbols.

questions.q: The chief guest at India's first Republic Day in 1950 was the president of which country?
questions.f: President Sukarno's visit began a tradition of inviting a foreign guest of honour each 26 January.

questions.q: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the resistance of 1857 in which region?
questions.f: She held Lucknow for months after her husband was exiled, and later found refuge in Nepal.

questions.q: Which leader of 1857, aged around eighty, fought a mobile campaign in Bihar?
questions.f: Babu Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur used forest tracks and surprise marches against much larger forces.

questions.q: Which 1857 leader became famous for evading capture across central India for months?
questions.f: His long marches across the Deccan are still studied as an example of guerrilla mobility.

questions.q: A flag unfurled in Stuttgart in 1907, decades before Independence, was raised by whom?
questions.f: Madam Cama showed an early Indian tricolour to a socialist congress in Germany, calling it India's flag.

questions.q: Which official proportion is fixed for India's national flag?
questions.f: The chakra must exactly fill the width of the white band, and the flag must be hand-spun khadi.

questions.q: India's national anthem's music and words were formally adopted on which date?
questions.f: The Constituent Assembly settled the anthem question two days before India became a republic.

questions.q: Which body's constitutional adviser drafted the first outline text of India's Constitution?
questions.f: He toured other countries to study their constitutions, then produced the draft the committee worked from.

questions.q: Which Indian revolutionary organisation founded abroad later handed its army over to Subhas Chandra Bose?
questions.f: Rash Behari Bose, who had escaped India years earlier, passed the leadership to Netaji in 1943.

questions.q: India's Fundamental Duties were not part of the original 1950 Constitution.
questions.f: They were added as Article 51A in 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh committee.

questions.q: Ambedkar resigned from Nehru's cabinet in 1951 over a bill dealing with what?
questions.f: The Hindu Code Bill aimed to give women equal rights in marriage and property; it passed in pieces later.

questions.q: Matangini Hazra, remembered for leading a Quit India procession, was remarkable for her what?
questions.f: She kept walking at the head of the march in Tamluk, and became a symbol of ordinary people's courage.

questions.q: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931 led directly to Gandhi attending what in London?
questions.f: He travelled with a goat for milk and stayed in London's East End rather than a hotel.

questions.q: The Komagata Maru episode of 1914 involved Indian passengers being refused entry to which country?
questions.f: The ship waited two months off Vancouver before being turned back, hardening feeling against unjust laws.

questions.q: India's Constituent Assembly's final handwritten copies were made using what?
questions.f: Prem Behari Narain Raizada wrote every page by hand with a nib pen and asked for no fee at all.

questions.q: Sardar Patel's chief civil-service partner in integrating the princely states was who?
questions.f: Menon drafted the Instrument of Accession, a short document that states could sign quickly.

questions.q: Which slogan of the 1905 Swadeshi movement asked Indians to reject foreign cloth?
questions.f: Bonfires of imported cloth became a common sight in Bengal towns that year.

questions.q: Which woman scholar and reformer became the first woman president of the Indian National Congress?
questions.f: She presided in 1917; Sarojini Naidu became the first Indian woman to hold the post in 1925.

questions.q: Jamsetji Tata named his first cotton mill after a title Queen Victoria had just taken. Which?
questions.f: Empress Mills opened in Nagpur in 1877, the year Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India.

questions.q: Jamsetji Tata died before any of his three great dreams of steel, power and a science institute was finished.
questions.f: He died in 1904; the institute opened in 1909, the steel works in 1912 and the power plant in 1915.

questions.q: Tata's first hydroelectric power scheme, opened in 1915, was built in which hill range?
questions.f: Monsoon lakes above Khopoli were dammed to send water plunging down pipes to power Bombay's mills.

questions.q: JRD Tata flew India's first commercial mail flight in 1932 from Karachi to which city?
questions.f: He flew a single-engine Puss Moth, refuelling at Ahmedabad from cans carried by bullock cart.

questions.q: Air India was taken into government hands in 1953 and returned to Tata ownership in which year?
questions.f: Almost seventy years later, the airline JRD Tata founded came back to the group that started it.

questions.q: Amul's Utterly Butterly campaign holds a record for being the world's longest-running what?
questions.f: Running since 1966, its topical cartoons have commented on everything from moon landings to cricket.

questions.q: Verghese Kurien's team achieved a world first by making milk powder from what?
questions.f: Experts said it was impossible; solving it let India use the buffalo milk that most of its farmers produced.

questions.q: A metallurgy scholarship, an unwanted government posting to a small Gujarat town, and a repaired cream separator launched whose career?
questions.f: He had trained in metals, not milk, and only stayed at Anand because he had to work off a bond.

questions.q: India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975 using a rocket from which country?
questions.f: India built the satellite; the Soviets provided the ride, five years before India could launch its own.

questions.q: India's first satellite launched by an Indian rocket, in 1980, was called what?
questions.f: The SLV-3 that carried it had A. P. J. Abdul Kalam as project director.

questions.q: Which future President of India was project director of the SLV-3 launch vehicle?
questions.f: He famously wept after an earlier failure, then led the team to success in 1980.

questions.q: India's Mars Orbiter Mission cost roughly how much in rupees?
questions.f: About 74 million dollars, less than the budget of several Hollywood films set in space.

questions.q: Chandrayaan-3's landing spot on the Moon was officially named what?
questions.f: Chandrayaan-1's crash site had earlier been named Jawahar Sthal, on Nehru's birthday.

questions.q: The Nilgiri Mountain Railway is unique in India for using which system to climb?
questions.f: A toothed rail between the tracks grips a cogwheel under the engine, so the train cannot slip back.

questions.q: Three Indian lines together form the UNESCO-listed Mountain Railways of India: Darjeeling, Nilgiri and which other?
questions.f: The Kalka-Shimla line passes through more than a hundred tunnels on its climb into the Himalayas.

questions.q: Before Hubballi took the record, which Indian station had the world's longest platform?
questions.f: Kharagpur held it for decades, then Gorakhpur in 2013, then Hubballi in 2023: a very Indian record race.

questions.q: Which Indian film won a top prize at the very first Cannes Film Festival in 1946?
questions.f: Chetan Anand's film shared the Grand Prix, nearly a decade before Satyajit Ray's debut.

questions.q: Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali won a prize at Cannes in 1956 under which unusual category name?
questions.f: Ray had funded shooting by pawning his wife's jewellery and taking a loan from the Bengal government.

questions.q: A. R. Rahman won two Oscars in one night in 2009 for score and which song?
questions.f: On stage he quoted a Tamil line meaning all praise to God, then said he had a choice between hate and love.

questions.q: Resul Pookutty won an Academy Award in which technical field?
questions.f: He is from Kerala, and joked that his Oscar was for the sounds of a city he had never lived in.

questions.q: In India's first feature film, the female roles were played by male actors.
questions.f: In 1913 no actress would join the cast, so Phalke cast a young man as Queen Taramati.

questions.q: The Ranji Trophy, India's main domestic cricket competition, is named after a prince who played for whom?
questions.f: Ranjitsinhji dazzled English crowds with the late cut, and never played a Test for India.

questions.q: Who became the first batter in history to reach 10,000 runs in Test cricket?
questions.f: He got there in 1987, having faced the fearsome West Indies attack without a helmet.

questions.q: Who was named Player of the Match in both the semi-final and the final of the 1983 World Cup?
questions.f: He took three wickets and made runs in each, yet his father's 1933 century is often better remembered.

questions.q: The world's largest cricket stadium by capacity is in which Indian city?
questions.f: It seats about 132,000 people, more than any other cricket ground on Earth.

questions.q: Which is India's oldest cricket ground, in use since 1864?
questions.f: Kolkata's Eden Gardens has hosted Tests since 1934 and can hold over 65,000 spectators.

questions.q: In 2024 India won gold in both the open and women's sections of which team event?
questions.f: A country with almost no chess tradition in 1980 now leads the sport, thanks partly to Anand's example.

questions.q: Who became the first Indian woman to win two medals at a single Olympic Games?
questions.f: She took two shooting bronzes in Paris in 2024, one of them in a mixed team event.

questions.q: Infosys was famously founded in 1981 by seven engineers with capital of roughly how much?
questions.f: Legend has it much of the money was borrowed from a co-founder's wife's savings.

questions.q: India's Green Revolution in wheat is most associated with which Indian scientist?
questions.f: He adapted high-yield Mexican wheat to Indian fields, working with Norman Borlaug.

questions.q: C. V. Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering an effect involving what?
questions.f: He was inspired by the blue of the Mediterranean seen from a ship; India marks 28 February as Science Day.

questions.q: A whole class of fundamental particles is named after which Indian physicist?
questions.f: Bosons take his name after work he sent to Einstein, who translated and published it himself.

questions.q: A taxi number, two unsolicited letters to Cambridge, and a notebook found in 1976 point to which mathematician?
questions.f: Told 1729 was dull, he instantly named it the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes two ways.

questions.q: Which Indian scientist built the crescograph to record the growth and responses of plants?
questions.f: He also demonstrated radio waves in Kolkata in 1895, before Marconi's famous transmissions.

questions.q: Shakuntala Devi earned worldwide fame for her ability to do what?
c: Do huge sums in her head
questions.f: She once multiplied two 13-digit numbers mentally in 28 seconds, beating a computer of the day.

questions.q: E. Sreedharan earned the nickname Metro Man for building which system?
questions.f: He also rebuilt a cyclone-wrecked Pamban rail bridge in 46 days instead of the six months allowed.

questions.q: Homi Bhabha is remembered as the architect of India's programme in which field?
questions.f: He founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and pushed for research reactors in the 1950s.

questions.q: Which Indian company began life as a vegetable-oil maker before becoming a software giant?
questions.f: Its old name, Western India Palm Refined Oils, is where the short name Wipro comes from.

questions.q: Which Indian motorcycle brand claims the world's longest continuous production of any motorcycle?
questions.f: The Bullet has been made since 1932, and production moved fully to Chennai after the British factory closed.

questions.q: India's first colour feature film, Kisan Kanya, was released in which decade?
questions.f: It came out in 1937 using an Italian colour process, but colour did not become common in India for decades.

questions.q: Which Indian singer was once listed in the Guinness Book for recording the most songs?
questions.f: The entry was later disputed and revised, but her career still spanned about seven decades.

questions.q: India's first individual Olympic medal after Independence was won in which sport, in 1952?
questions.f: K. D. Jadhav's bronze came from a wrestler who had trained on village mud, not mats.

questions.q: Chandrayaan-2's lander did not land safely, but its orbiter later helped Chandrayaan-3 succeed.
questions.f: The orbiter relayed communications and had already mapped the terrain around the landing zone.

questions.q: Which joint India-United States satellite carries a giant radar to watch Earth's changing surface?
questions.f: Two space agencies each built half of the radar, then bolted them onto one spacecraft.

questions.q: Which Indian conglomerate grew from a young trader's small textile and polyester business?
questions.f: Dhirubhai Ambani started with yarn trading in Mumbai before building huge refineries.

questions.q: India's Vande Bharat trains are designed for a top speed of about what?
questions.f: Track conditions rather than the train limit real speeds; the sets have no separate locomotive at all.

questions.q: Which Indian scientist's ionisation equation is a standard tool for reading the spectra of stars?
questions.f: His 1920 equation let astronomers work out a star's temperature from the lines in its light.

questions.q: Which Indian-born astrophysicist has a NASA X-ray observatory named after him?
questions.f: He worked out the mass limit above which a white dwarf cannot survive, aged only nineteen.

questions.q: The maths word sine can be traced back to a Sanskrit term for a bowstring. Which?
questions.f: Jya was read in Arabic as jiba, mistaken for jaib meaning fold, then translated into Latin as sinus.

questions.q: The tree name banyan comes from a Gujarati word meaning what?
questions.f: European visitors saw Hindu traders, called banias, doing business under the tree and named the tree after them.

questions.q: The word tamarind is built from a phrase meaning what?
questions.f: From Arabic tamr hindi; the sticky pulp does look like a date but tastes sharply sour.

questions.q: The word jackfruit came into English from a word in which language?
questions.f: Malayalam chakka became Portuguese jaca and then English jack; the fruit can weigh over 30 kilograms.

questions.q: The word monsoon actually came into English from a word meaning what?
questions.f: From Arabic mawsim, season, via Portuguese; sailors named the sailing season, not the rain.

questions.q: The word cyclone was coined in the 1840s by a British observer living in which city?
questions.f: Henry Piddington built it from Greek kyklos, a coil, to describe the spiralling storms of the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: The dish name vindaloo actually comes from a Portuguese phrase meaning what?
questions.f: From carne de vinha d'alhos; Goan cooks swapped in palm vinegar and local spices.

questions.q: The checked cotton cloth called madras is named after what?
questions.f: Named after the port now called Chennai, the cloth is famous for bleeding colour in the wash.

questions.q: The word puttee, a long cloth strip wound round the leg, comes from a word meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi patti; soldiers in both world wars wore puttees copied from Indian hill regiments.

questions.q: The word punkah names an Indian version of what?
questions.f: From Hindi pankha; a punkah-wallah pulled a rope to swing a cloth fan across a hot room.

questions.q: The English suffix wallah, as in box-wallah, comes from an Indian ending meaning what?
questions.f: From Hindi -wala; English borrowed it for anyone defined by their job or gadget.

questions.q: The word durbar, an Indian royal court or reception, comes from words meaning what?
questions.f: From Persian dar, door, plus bar, audience; British Viceroys staged huge durbars to display power.

questions.q: The word sitar comes from a Persian phrase meaning what?
questions.f: From sih-tar; a modern sitar actually has around eighteen strings, most of them for resonance.

questions.q: The musical term raga comes from a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: A raga colours the mind, and traditionally each is linked to a season or a time of day.

questions.q: The word mahout, an elephant handler, descends from a Sanskrit title meaning what?
questions.f: From mahamatra, a high official; a mahout often works with the same elephant for decades.

questions.q: The word swami comes from a Sanskrit word meaning what?
questions.f: From svami; the same root gives svatva, ownership, and the polite Tamil ending -swami.

questions.q: The Indian number words lakh and crore come from roots meaning what?
questions.f: Sanskrit laksha meant a mark or 100,000, and koti a peak or heap; Indian English still counts this way.

questions.q: The sugar product called jaggery reached English through Portuguese from which Indian root?
questions.f: Malayalam chakkara from Sanskrit sharkara became Portuguese jagara, then English jaggery.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word sthana, as in Rajasthan, is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: From the ancient root for standing; the same root gives station, statue and stable.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word madhu, honey, is a cousin of which old English drink name?
questions.f: Both come from one ancient word for honey, showing how old honey-brewing must be.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word dvara, doorway, is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: Place names like Haridwar mean gateway, from the same root as English door.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word pada, foot, is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: Sanskrit pada, Latin pes and English foot all descend from the same ancient word.

questions.q: The Sanskrit number nava is a cousin of which English number?
questions.f: Sanskrit nava, Latin novem and English nine all come from one Indo-European root.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word manas is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: Manas means mind; Latin mens and English mind share the same distant ancestor.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word bhratr is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: Family words tend to survive longest, which is why brother sounds so similar across many languages.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word aksha, meaning axle or eye, is a cousin of which English word?
questions.f: The same root gives Latin axis; Sanskrit akshi for eye kept the sense of a pivot point.

questions.q: Which of these English words came from Persian by way of India rather than from Sanskrit?
questions.f: Bazaar came through Persian bazar; the other three are straight from Sanskrit.

questions.q: The word sepoy, an Indian soldier in colonial armies, came from a Persian word meaning what?
questions.f: From sipahi, from sipah, army; the same word gave the Turkish and North African spahi.

questions.q: The English word compound, meaning a walled enclosure, actually came from which language?
questions.f: From Malay kampung, a village; British Indian usage spread it worldwide as an enclosed set of buildings.

questions.q: In Indian English, a mugger is which animal?
questions.f: From Hindi magar; the marsh crocodile is still officially called the mugger crocodile.

questions.q: The word pariah, meaning an outcast, came from a Tamil word for a hereditary what?
questions.f: From paraiyar, from parai, a drum; English turned an occupation name into a word about exclusion.

questions.q: The British slang word Blighty, meaning home in Britain, came from a Hindi word meaning what?
questions.f: From bilayati, foreign; Indian speakers used it for European things, and soldiers flipped it to mean home.

questions.q: The word dhobi in Indian English names someone who does what?
questions.f: A dhobi mark is a tiny code inked on clothes so a washerman can sort hundreds of garments correctly.

questions.q: The word shawl came into English through India from a Persian word. What did it mean?
questions.f: From Persian shal; Kashmiri shawls were so prized that Europeans copied them at Paisley in Scotland.

questions.q: The word ashram comes from a Sanskrit root meaning what?
questions.f: From srama, exertion, with the prefix a: a place where one works hard at self-discipline.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word samsara, the cycle of rebirth, literally means what?
questions.f: From sam, together, plus sri, to flow: a continual flowing onwards from life to life.

questions.q: Which Sanskrit word for release gives the name of an old Indian board game that became Snakes and Ladders?
questions.f: Moksha Patam let a player climb by virtues and slide back by faults, ending at release.

questions.q: Jantar Mantar, the name of India's stone observatories, comes from words meaning what?
questions.f: From yantra, a device, and mantra, a formula: literally a place of calculating instruments.

questions.q: The word chit in Indian English derives from a Hindi word that also means what?
questions.f: From chitthi, a letter; the chit system let officers order goods on a signature rather than cash.

questions.q: The word gymkhana's khana element is also found in which other borrowed word?
questions.f: Khana means house or place; a gymkhana was literally a ball house before it meant a sports meeting.

questions.q: The word coolie is avoided today, but which neutral Indian English word for a porter is preferred?
questions.f: Language changes as attitudes do; railway signs in India now say porter or use the local word.

questions.q: Which spice name entered English from Sanskrit pippali?
questions.f: Long pepper was traded before black pepper, and both took the same name in Greek and Latin.

questions.q: The word betel, as in betel leaf, came into English from which language?
questions.f: From Malayalam vettila; the areca nut chewed with it also comes from a Malayalam word, adakka.

questions.q: The gemstone name beryl is thought to trace back to an Indian word linked to which place?
questions.f: Sanskrit vaidurya, probably from a southern town's name, became Greek beryllos and later gave us brilliant and spectacles.

questions.q: The Sanskrit word gau, meaning cow, is a distant cousin of the English word cow.
questions.f: Both come from one Indo-European word, as do Latin bos and Greek bous.

questions.q: Three of these words reached English from India. Which one did not?
questions.f: Kiosk came from Turkish kosk, a garden pavilion, by way of French.

questions.q: Which everyday English word for a small pattern of dots on cloth came from Indian trade?
questions.f: Gingham came from Malay, tartan from Scotland; chintz is from Hindi chint, spotted.

questions.q: An American geologist's survey, a forest clearing in 1907, and a village called Sakchi launched which Indian venture?
questions.f: Charles Page Perin's team found iron ore, coal and water close together, and a steel city was built there.

questions.q: Which Indian scientist shared the 1968 Nobel Prize for work on the genetic code?
questions.f: Born in a Punjab village with no electricity, he later helped build the first synthetic gene.

questions.q: Venkatraman Ramakrishnan won a Nobel Prize for mapping the structure of which cell part?
questions.f: Understanding the ribosome's shape helped explain how many antibiotics actually work.

questions.q: The number 6174, reached by a curious sorting trick, is named after which Indian mathematician?
questions.f: Take any four-digit number with different digits, subtract the smallest arrangement from the largest, repeat: you land on 6174.

questions.q: Salim Ali is known as the Birdman of India for pioneering what?
questions.f: A yellow-throated sparrow shot in his boyhood set him on a path that produced India's standard bird handbook.

questions.q: The Amul girl was first drawn in 1966 by an artist working with which advertising firm?
questions.f: Eustace Fernandes designed her, and the campaign has stayed with the same family firm ever since.

questions.q: Which Indian-American astronaut has held the record for the most spacewalk time by a woman?
questions.f: She also ran a marathon in orbit, strapped to a treadmill aboard the space station.

questions.q: A ten-character signboard, a bedrock reservoir and a stadium-sized ceremonial ground identify which Harappan city?
questions.f: Its water engineering was so advanced that sixteen reservoirs ring a city built in near-desert.

questions.q: A bilingual coin, a pillar standing in Firoz Shah's fort, and the year 1837 converge on which scholar?
questions.f: By matching Greek to unknown letters he cracked Brahmi, which unlocked every Ashokan edict at once.

questions.q: A minor rock edict at Maski settled a long argument about the identity of which ruler?
questions.f: Every other edict used only the title Piyadasi; the Maski text finally spelt out the personal name.

questions.q: An Aramaic and Greek bilingual edict of an Indian emperor was found near which modern city?
questions.f: It proves Ashoka expected Greek and Aramaic speakers inside his own empire's north-west.

questions.q: One rock at Junagadh carries inscriptions of Ashoka, Skandagupta and which other ruler?
questions.f: Rudradaman's text of about 150 CE is the earliest long inscription in polished Sanskrit anywhere.

questions.q: The Junagadh inscriptions repeatedly record repairs to what?
questions.f: Sudarshana lake's dam burst more than once, and each ruler proudly recorded rebuilding it.

questions.q: Coins of the Kushana ruler Kanishka are famous for showing the Buddha labelled in which script?
questions.f: The legend reads BODDO in Greek letters, among the earliest images of the Buddha in human form.

questions.q: Gandhara sculpture is distinctive for blending Indian subjects with which artistic tradition?
questions.f: Its Buddhas wear toga-like folds; sculptors in Mathura used Indian forms and red sandstone instead.

questions.q: Arab astronomers' Zij al-Sindhind took its name from which Sanskrit word?
questions.f: Indian astronomical siddhantas reached Baghdad in the 700s and reshaped mathematics across the Islamic world.

questions.q: The Malayalam text Yuktibhasa is remarkable as an early work containing what?
questions.f: Jyesthadeva set out the Kerala school's calculus-like reasoning about 1530, complete with justifications.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian astronomer wrote the wide-ranging Brihat Samhita?
questions.f: Besides astronomy it covers clouds, gemstones, perfumes and how to find groundwater by watching plants.

questions.q: A birch-bark manuscript found near Peshawar in 1881 is famous for containing early examples of what?
questions.f: The Bakhshali manuscript uses a dot to hold an empty place, one of the oldest such marks known.

questions.q: Rajendra Chola commemorated a northern campaign by filling a great tank with water from which river?
questions.f: He named the tank Cholagangam and built a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, beside it.

questions.q: Which temple at Darasuram completes the Great Living Chola Temples with Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram?
questions.f: Its stone steps were carved to give out musical notes when tapped.

questions.q: The vast open-air rock relief often called Arjuna's Penance is at which site?
questions.f: Nearly 30 metres long, it is one of the largest open-air rock reliefs anywhere in the world.

questions.q: Sculptors of the Hoysala temples were unusual in Indian art for doing what?
questions.f: Names like Malitamma appear beneath figures, so we know individual artists across generations.

questions.q: A temple named after its own sculptor, bricks light enough to float, and a Telangana village point to which monument?
questions.f: The Kakatiya-era Rudreshwara temple became a World Heritage Site in 2021.

questions.q: The Sun Temple at Modhera was built under which dynasty?
questions.f: Its stepped tank and sun-aligned sanctum were designed so light strikes the shrine at the equinox.

questions.q: Which Indian monument appears on the reverse of the 100-rupee note?
questions.f: Queen Udayamati's stepwell was buried in river silt for centuries before being excavated.

questions.q: Which monument appears on the reverse of India's 20-rupee note?
questions.f: The current note series pairs each denomination with a different heritage site.

questions.q: Sher Shah Suri's tomb at Sasaram is unusual because it stands where?
c: In the middle of a lake
questions.f: He also standardised the silver rupiya and rebuilt the road we now call the Grand Trunk Road.

questions.q: Which ruler set up a relay system of horse riders and rest houses that worked like a postal service?
questions.f: His dak chowkis let a message travel hundreds of kilometres in days rather than weeks.

questions.q: Which Mughal empress had silver coins struck bearing her own name?
questions.f: She also designed the tomb of her father, Itmad-ud-Daulah, now nicknamed the Baby Taj.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to rule from the throne of Delhi?
questions.f: She ruled from 1236, insisted on being addressed as Sultan rather than Sultana, and rode into court herself.

questions.q: Which Delhi sultan famously shifted his capital to Daulatabad and issued token coins?
questions.f: His brass and copper tokens were easy to forge, so the experiment in paper-style money collapsed.

questions.q: Which sultan is remembered for fixing market prices across his capital in detail?
questions.f: Officials checked grain, cloth and even horse prices, with separate markets for each type of goods.

questions.q: Amir Khusrau, a poet at several Delhi courts, is especially credited with shaping which musical form?
questions.f: He also wrote riddles and verses in early Hindavi, an ancestor of both Hindi and Urdu.

questions.q: Which French physician's travel account is a key source on Aurangzeb's India?
questions.f: His letters on Mughal courts, roads and famine circulated widely in Europe in the 1670s.

questions.q: Which Maratha admiral defended the Konkan coast against European fleets in the early 1700s?
questions.f: Shivaji had begun building a Maratha navy decades earlier, an unusual step for an inland power.

questions.q: Which 18th-century queen ruled Indore and funded temple rebuilding across India?
questions.f: She rebuilt the Kashi Vishwanath temple in 1780 and set up rest houses on pilgrim routes.

questions.q: Iron-cased rockets, a mechanical tiger now in a London museum, and an arsenal at Woolwich that studied Indian designs point to which ruler?
questions.f: Mysorean rockets were the first with iron casings, and British engineers built on them for years afterwards.

questions.q: The Battle of Plassey in 1757 was fought largely in and around what kind of place?
questions.f: Rain soaked the defenders' powder while the Company kept its own dry under tarpaulins.

questions.q: Which 1764 battle led directly to the Company gaining revenue rights over Bengal?
questions.f: The diwani rights granted in 1765 turned a trading company into a tax-collecting government.

questions.q: A survey begun in 1802, a Bengali mathematician's calculation in 1852, and a summit first labelled Peak XV produced what?
c: The first map of the Ganges
questions.f: Radhanath Sikdar's figures showed Peak XV was the world's highest before anyone had climbed near it.

questions.q: Indian surveyors who secretly mapped Tibet measured distance by doing what?
c: Counting paced steps on prayer beads
questions.f: Nain Singh Rawat walked with a fixed stride, clicking a bead every hundred paces, notes hidden in a prayer wheel.

questions.q: Which Indus Valley site, now in Balochistan, marks the civilization's far western edge?
questions.f: It sits near the Iranian border, suggesting a trade route running west along the coast.

questions.q: Rows of what have been found at the Harappan site of Kalibangan?
questions.f: The site also shows a ploughed field, among the oldest known anywhere in the world.

questions.q: Which ruler came between Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka on the Mauryan throne?
questions.f: Greek sources call him Amitrochates, probably from the title Amitraghata, slayer of foes.

questions.q: An inscription at Nashik praising Gautamiputra Satakarni was set up by whom?
questions.f: Queen Gautami Balashri's cave inscription is a rare royal record written in a mother's voice.

questions.q: Which Chinese pilgrim travelled to India before Xuanzang and described Gupta-era roads and rest houses?
questions.f: Travelling around 400 CE, he reported walking for weeks in safety and found charitable hospitals in cities.

questions.q: Which mathematician's Brahmasphutasiddhanta gave rules for arithmetic with negative numbers?
questions.f: He described positives as fortunes and negatives as debts, then set out how they combine.

questions.q: Ashoka's pillars were quarried mostly from sandstone found near which place?
questions.f: Single shafts weighing up to fifty tonnes were floated and dragged hundreds of kilometres.

questions.q: The Ajanta caves were carved in two separate bursts, several centuries apart.
questions.f: An early Satavahana-era phase was followed, after a long gap, by a burst of Vakataka-era work.

questions.q: The Indus Valley's most common seal animal is a one-horned creature usually called what?
questions.f: It may be a bull shown in profile, but the single horn appears on hundreds of seals.

questions.q: Which Vijayanagara-era ceiling paintings and hanging pillars are found at Lepakshi?
questions.f: One of its pillars hangs slightly clear of the floor, so a cloth can be slid underneath.

questions.q: Which Persian-language history of Akbar's reign was written by his court chronicler?
questions.f: Abul Fazl's third volume, the Ain-i-Akbari, lists everything from crop prices to elephant diets.

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor wrote his own memoirs, the Tuzuk, recording experiments on animals and plants?
questions.f: He had painters record rare birds and once had a turkey portrait made from life.

questions.q: Which Indian queen of Ullal is remembered for resisting Portuguese naval power in the 1500s?
questions.f: She held out for decades from a small Tulu-speaking kingdom on the Karnataka coast.

questions.q: India's oldest surviving cave paintings, at Bhimbetka, are in which state?
questions.f: Some shelters were used almost continuously for tens of thousands of years.

questions.q: Which South Indian dynasty's copper-plate grants are a major source for early Kerala history?
questions.f: Copper plates were durable, portable and hard to forge, so land grants were recorded on them.

questions.q: Which Gupta-era temple at Deogarh is an early example of the north Indian stone temple?
questions.f: Built about 500 CE, it shows the shift from wood and brick to fully carved stone shrines.

questions.q: India's earliest known stone image of a horse-drawn chariot in a temple wheel design appears at which site?
questions.f: Konark's wheels are precise enough that their spokes and axles work as sundials.

questions.q: Which Pallava king had the Kailasanathar temple at Kanchipuram built?
questions.f: Its sandstone walls still carry traces of the original painted plaster.

questions.q: An ICS exam passed in fourth place, a resignation letter, and the mayoralty of Calcutta precede which leader's later fame?
questions.f: He gave up a guaranteed elite career at 23, writing that he could not serve a government he opposed.

questions.q: At the 1939 Tripuri session, Bose won the Congress presidency by defeating which candidate?
questions.f: Gandhi called the result a defeat for himself, and Bose soon resigned and founded the Forward Bloc.

questions.q: The Provisional Government of Azad Hind issued its own what?
questions.f: It also set up a bank in Rangoon and was recognised by about nine governments.

questions.q: Who is generally credited with coining the greeting Jai Hind, later adopted nationwide?
questions.f: An INA officer proposed it as a neutral salute that soldiers of every faith could share.

questions.q: A 63-day hunger strike in 1929 demanding better treatment for political prisoners is linked to which young man?
questions.f: His long fast forced prison reforms into the newspapers and shocked opinion across India.

questions.q: Which nationalist made a famous escape from a ship at Marseilles harbour in 1910?
questions.f: He slipped through a porthole and swam ashore; the case went to an international tribunal at The Hague.

questions.q: Which nationalist editor of the paper Bande Mataram later withdrew to Pondicherry to write philosophy?
questions.f: He spent forty years there and became better known as a philosopher than as an agitator.

questions.q: Which British-born theosophist founded a Home Rule League in India in 1916?
questions.f: She later became the first woman to preside over the Indian National Congress.

questions.q: Who became the first Indian to enter the Indian Civil Service, in 1863?
questions.f: Rabindranath's elder brother sat the London examination and passed at the second attempt.

questions.q: Anandibai Joshi is honoured as one of the first Indian women to earn what?
questions.f: She graduated in Pennsylvania in 1886 after sailing alone to America as a teenager.

questions.q: Cornelia Sorabji is remembered as India's first woman to do what?
questions.f: She studied at Oxford in the 1890s, though rules kept her from full practice for years afterwards.

questions.q: Which reformer, founder of the Brahmo Sabha, died and was buried in Bristol in 1833?
questions.f: He had travelled to Britain to argue an Indian pension case and to observe Parliament.

questions.q: Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in 1909 in which unusual setting?
questions.f: He wrote it on the voyage from London to South Africa, using both hands as one tired.

questions.q: The word satyagraha was chosen after Gandhi ran what?
c: A naming competition in his newspaper
questions.f: A reader suggested sadagraha, firmness in a good cause, and Gandhi refined it to satyagraha.

questions.q: An admiral's daughter, a passion for Beethoven, and a new name meaning devotee describe which of Gandhi's associates?
questions.f: Madeleine Slade read a book about Gandhi, sailed to India in 1925 and stayed for decades.

questions.q: Which English clergyman and friend of Gandhi was called Deenabandhu, friend of the poor?
questions.f: He helped persuade Gandhi to return from South Africa, and Tagore called him a bridge between peoples.

questions.q: Sarojini Naidu's first poetry collection was titled The Golden what?
questions.f: Published in London in 1905, it made her a literary name before she became a political one.

questions.q: Vande Mataram was first sung at a Congress session in which year?
questions.f: Tagore himself sang it in Calcutta, twenty-two years before he sang Jana Gana Mana there.

questions.q: Tagore's own English rendering of Jana Gana Mana was titled what?
questions.f: He made the translation in 1919 at a school in Andhra Pradesh, where the tune was also set.

questions.q: The very first Bharat Ratna awards, in 1954, went to Raman, Radhakrishnan and who else?
questions.f: Patel and Ambedkar received the honour only decades later, in 1991 and 1990.

questions.q: Who received the first posthumous Bharat Ratna, in 1966?
questions.f: The rules were changed that year to allow awards after death.

questions.q: The lawyer who drew the 1947 boundary line had which striking disadvantage?
c: He had never seen a map
questions.f: Cyril Radcliffe was given roughly five weeks, outdated census data and no time to tour the districts.

questions.q: India's Constitution's original handwritten copies are preserved in cases filled with what?
questions.f: Helium-filled cases in the Parliament Library slow the ageing of the paper and ink.

questions.q: India's official national calendar, adopted in 1957, is based on which era?
questions.f: Its year one corresponds to 78 CE, and Chaitra 1 usually falls on 22 March.

questions.q: Which amendment to India's Constitution lowered the voting age to eighteen?
questions.f: Passed in 1988, it added tens of millions of young voters at a stroke.

questions.q: Which 1973 Supreme Court case established that Parliament cannot alter the Constitution's basic structure?
questions.f: Thirteen judges heard it over 68 days, the longest hearing in the court's history.

questions.q: Which amendment is so wide-ranging that it is nicknamed the mini-Constitution?
questions.f: Passed in 1976, it changed the Preamble and added the Fundamental Duties.

questions.q: Who became the first woman judge of India's Supreme Court?
questions.f: She was appointed in 1989, thirty-nine years after the court was founded.

questions.q: Anna Chandy is remembered as India's first woman to become what?
questions.f: She began practising in the 1920s, when women lawyers were still expected to sit apart in court.

questions.q: Anna Rajam Malhotra broke ground in 1951 as India's first woman what?
questions.f: Her interview board reportedly warned her the job was unsuitable for a woman; she took it anyway.

questions.q: Nehru moved which resolution in the Constituent Assembly in December 1946, setting out its aims?
questions.f: Its wording flowed almost directly into the Preamble we read today.

questions.q: India's first Republic Day parade in 1950 was held at which venue?
questions.f: The route we know today, along what was then Rajpath, was used from 1955 onwards.

questions.q: India's Flag Code was amended in 2002 to allow citizens to do what?
c: Use it as a table cloth
questions.f: Until then, private citizens could display the tricolour only on selected national days.

questions.q: Which princely state's accession to India was settled by a plebiscite in February 1948?
questions.f: Voters chose India overwhelmingly, and the vote is cited as an early exercise in self-determination.

questions.q: Which schedule of India's Constitution deals with disqualifying legislators who switch parties?
questions.f: Added in 1985, it is usually called the anti-defection law.

questions.q: Gandhi's first community experiments in South Africa included Phoenix Settlement and which farm?
questions.f: He named it after the Russian writer whose letters he treasured all his life.

questions.q: Which newspaper did Gandhi run during his South African years?
questions.f: It appeared in English and Gujarati, and Gandhi later said it kept the movement honest.

questions.q: Which committee of seven members was charged with drafting India's Constitution?
questions.f: Ambedkar chaired it, and by the end illness or absence left him doing much of the work himself.

questions.q: Article 1 of India's Constitution describes the country using which two names?
questions.f: The line reads India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.

questions.q: Which leader gave the Congress its 1929 midnight flag-raising on the bank of which river?
questions.f: Nehru raised the tricolour on the Ravi at Lahore as the Purna Swaraj resolution was adopted.

questions.q: Kadambini Ganguly and Chandramukhi Basu are honoured as India's first women to do what?
questions.f: They graduated in 1883; Ganguly went on to become one of India's earliest women physicians.

questions.q: Rukhmabai, the centre of a famous 1880s legal case, later became what?
questions.f: She trained in London and practised medicine in India for over thirty years.

questions.q: India's Constitution does not name any language as the national language.
questions.f: It names Hindi in Devanagari as an official language of the Union, with English alongside it.

questions.q: Which 1916 agreement between the Congress and the Muslim League was signed at Lucknow?
questions.f: Tilak and Jinnah were both central to it, a rare moment of joint demand for reform.

questions.q: Kiran Bedi became India's first woman to join which service, in 1972?
questions.f: She was also a national tennis champion before entering the police.

questions.q: Which of Gandhi's campaigns took its name from a district where farmers were forced to grow a dye crop?
questions.f: Farmers there had to plant indigo on part of their land under a system called tinkathia.

questions.q: The 1928 Bardoli satyagraha, over a tax rise, earned which leader his popular title?
questions.f: Grateful farmers called him Sardar, meaning chief, and the name stuck for life.
