questions.f: She wrote that the engine might weave 'elaborate and scientific pieces of music' — computers do exactly that now.

questions.q: Which weaving machine, controlled by punched cards, inspired the design of early computers?
questions.f: Jacquard's punched cards told the loom which threads to lift — the same trick later fed data to computers.

questions.q: During the Second World War, Alan Turing worked at Bletchley Park on…?
questions.f: Turing's code-breaking machines helped read enemy messages and are thought to have shortened the war.

questions.q: The German cipher machine that Turing's team worked against was called…?
questions.f: 'Enigma' means a puzzle or mystery — a fitting name for a machine with billions of settings.

questions.q: In the Turing test, how does the tester communicate with the hidden human and machine?
questions.f: Turing removed voices and faces on purpose, so only the quality of the answers could matter.

questions.q: The programmers of ENIAC who worked out how to set it up were mostly…?
questions.f: Six women became ENIAC's first programmers, rewiring it by hand for each new problem.

questions.q: Early computers like ENIAC used glass 'vacuum tubes' instead of…?
questions.f: Tubes glowed hot and burned out often; transistors replaced them and made computers small.

questions.q: Grace Hopper held a high rank in which service?
questions.f: She retired as a rear admiral and was nicknamed 'Amazing Grace' by fellow programmers.

questions.q: Grace Hopper helped create COBOL, an early language designed so that code would look more like…?
questions.f: COBOL programs use words like ADD, MOVE, and PERFORM so businesspeople could read them.

questions.q: Which came first: the internet or the World Wide Web?
questions.f: The internet's ancestor ARPANET started in 1969; the web arrived about twenty years later.

questions.q: The early network that grew into the internet was called…?
questions.f: ARPANET's first link, in 1969, connected computers in California — the message crashed halfway through.

questions.q: What is a 'browser' actually doing when it shows you a page?
c: Turning code it downloaded into pictures and text
questions.f: Every webpage arrives as instructions, and your browser paints the page from them in milliseconds.

questions.q: What does 'HTML', the language of webpages, describe?
questions.f: HTML marks up text with tags saying 'this is a heading' or 'this is a link'.

questions.q: The 'markup' in HTML borrows a word from which older trade?
questions.f: Editors once wrote marks on paper telling printers how text should look — HTML does the same digitally.

questions.q: Deep Blue's 1997 victory came after Kasparov had beaten an earlier version. What happened in 1996?
questions.f: Kasparov won in 1996, so IBM's engineers rebuilt the machine and returned a year later.

questions.q: AlphaGo's 2016 opponent was a champion from which country?
questions.f: Lee Sedol won one game out of five — and that single win became famous around the world.

questions.q: Go is played by placing stones on a grid. What is the aim?
c: To make five in a row
questions.f: Go's simple rules create such deep play that computers took twenty years longer to master it than chess.

questions.q: What did the winning program in the 2016 Go matches learn from?
c: Playing millions of games, including against itself
questions.f: Self-play let it discover moves that surprised professional players who had studied for decades.

questions.q: Nintendo, the company behind Mario, began in the 1880s by making…?
questions.f: Nintendo sold hand-painted Japanese cards for almost 80 years before it made a single video game.

questions.q: Why does Mario wear overalls and a cap with a brim?
c: Early screens had too few pixels for hair and arms
He was based on a farmer
It was a joke about hats
questions.f: With only a handful of pixels, a cap replaced hair and overalls made his arms easy to see.

questions.q: Pac-Man's designer said the game's shape was inspired by…?
c: A pizza with a slice removed
questions.f: The Japanese word 'paku' imitates the sound of a mouth snapping shut — hence Pac-Man.

questions.q: Which video game character came first?
questions.f: Pac-Man arrived in 1980, Mario in 1981, Link in 1986, and Sonic in 1991.

questions.q: An 'arcade' originally meant a…?
questions.f: Shops lined those arched passages, and later so did rows of glowing game machines.

questions.q: In coding, 'debugging' means…?
questions.f: Some programmers keep a rubber duck on the desk and explain their code to it to spot bugs.

questions.q: A 'crash' in computing happens when a program…?
questions.f: The word borrows from vehicles — everything stops suddenly and the work in progress can be lost.

questions.q: Which of these is measured in 'hertz'?
c: How many times per second something happens
questions.f: A 3-gigahertz processor ticks about three billion times every second.

questions.q: The unit 'hertz' is named after a scientist who studied…?
questions.f: Heinrich Hertz proved invisible electromagnetic waves exist — the same waves Wi-Fi uses today.

questions.q: What does a 'pixel art' picture deliberately show off?
questions.f: Artists still choose pixel art on purpose, placing each square by hand like tiny mosaic tiles.

questions.q: A screen described as '1920 by 1080' is telling you its…?
c: Number of pixels across and down
questions.f: Multiply them and you get about two million pixels lighting up at once.

questions.q: What is a 'byte' usually just big enough to store?
questions.f: That is why a page of text is a few thousand bytes, but a film is billions.

questions.q: Which counting system do people use every day, unlike a computer's binary?
questions.f: 'Decimal' comes from the Latin for ten — most likely because we have ten fingers.

questions.q: Programmers often use 'hexadecimal', which is a counting system based on…?
questions.f: Hex uses digits 0-9 then letters A-F, so the colour code for pure red is written FF0000.

questions.q: In web colour codes, what do the three pairs of digits stand for?
questions.f: Mixing red, green, and blue light in different amounts can make millions of screen colours.

questions.q: Why does a screen use red, green, and blue rather than red, yellow, and blue?
c: Because it mixes light, not paint
questions.f: Mixing light adds up to white; mixing paint takes light away and heads towards brown.

questions.q: A 'robotic' arm in a factory repeats its task using instructions that are…?
questions.f: Engineers 'teach' the arm a path once, then it can repeat it to within a fraction of a millimetre.

questions.q: The word 'android', used for a human-shaped robot, is built from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: From 'andros' (man) plus '-oid' (like) — so an android is something man-like.

questions.q: A machine that looks and moves like a person is also called a 'humanoid'. The suffix '-oid' means…?
questions.f: The same suffix gives us asteroid ('star-like') and spheroid ('sphere-like').

questions.q: The word 'cyborg' is a blend of which two words?
questions.f: Coined in 1960 for astronauts whose bodies might be helped by machines on long space trips.

questions.q: Isaac Asimov invented a famous word for the study and use of robots. What was it?
questions.f: Asimov thought he was using an existing word, but he had actually invented 'robotics' himself.

questions.q: The internet moves data without caring what the data means.
questions.f: That is exactly why email, games, and webpages can all share one network.

questions.q: A website's address like 'example.com' is called its…?
questions.f: Domain names exist because people remember words better than the long numbers computers use.

questions.q: Behind every domain name sits a number called an…?
questions.f: The Domain Name System works like a phone book, swapping names for those numbers instantly.

questions.q: What does 'Wi-Fi' let a device do?
questions.f: Despite the name, Wi-Fi is not short for anything — it was chosen because it sounded catchy.

questions.q: A 'firewall' protects a network by…?
questions.f: It works like a guard at a gate, checking what is allowed in and what must stay out.

questions.q: 'Phishing' emails try to trick people into giving away…?
questions.f: The spelling with 'ph' copies 'phreaking', an old nickname for tricks played on phone systems.

questions.q: Why is it wise to use a different password for each important account?
c: If one is stolen, the others stay safe
questions.f: Password managers exist precisely so people can have hundreds of different strong passwords.

questions.q: 'Encryption' protects a message by…?
c: Scrambling it so only the right person can read it
questions.f: From Greek 'kryptos', hidden — the same root as 'cryptic' and 'crypt'.

questions.q: Julius Caesar used a simple code where each letter was replaced by another a fixed number of places along. It is called a…?
questions.f: Shift every letter three places and CAT becomes FDW — kids still use it to pass secret notes.

questions.q: A 'cipher' is a system for…?
questions.f: The word travelled from Arabic 'sifr', meaning zero or empty — the same root as 'zero' itself.

questions.q: Morse code sends letters using combinations of…?
questions.f: SOS was chosen as a distress call because three dots, three dashes, three dots is easy to tap and hear.

questions.q: What does 'binary code' have in common with Morse code?
c: Both build messages from just a few symbols
questions.f: Morse uses two marks, binary uses two digits — proof that two symbols are enough for anything.

questions.q: A keyboard shortcut can replace several mouse clicks.
questions.f: Expert typists barely touch the mouse, because shortcuts are quicker than moving a hand.

questions.q: What is 'RAM' in a computer used for?
c: Holding work in progress while the computer runs
questions.f: RAM forgets everything when the power goes off — which is why unsaved work disappears.

questions.q: Which storage keeps your files even after the computer is switched off?
questions.f: An SSD has no moving parts, so it is faster and quieter than a spinning hard disk.

questions.q: What does the 'D' in 'SSD' stand for?
questions.f: Solid State Drive — 'solid state' means it stores data in chips with nothing spinning.

questions.q: A data centre is a building filled with computers that serve the internet.
questions.f: Big data centres use so much electricity that some are built beside rivers just for cooling.

questions.q: Most internet traffic between continents travels through…?
questions.f: Hundreds of thousands of kilometres of undersea fibre carry nearly all international data.

questions.q: 'Fibre optic' cables carry information as…?
questions.f: Light bounces along a glass thread thinner than a hair, carrying billions of bits a second.

questions.q: The 'optic' in 'fibre optic' relates to…?
questions.f: From Greek 'optikos', of sight — the same root as optician and optical illusion.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of 'input' to a computer?
questions.f: Input goes in, output comes out — a touchscreen is unusual because it does both.

questions.q: A printer is an example of an…?
questions.f: Output devices turn the computer's data back into things people can see, hear, or hold.

questions.q: A scanner turns a picture on paper into a computer file.
questions.f: A scanner shines a light along the page and measures the reflection line by line.

questions.q: 'OCR' software lets a computer do what with a scanned page?
questions.f: OCR stands for optical character recognition — it turns pictures of words into words you can edit.

questions.q: In programming, what is a 'function'?
c: A named block of code you can reuse
questions.f: Functions let programmers build big projects from small, tested pieces, like LEGO bricks.

questions.q: What is a 'syntax error' in code?
c: Code written in a way the computer cannot understand
A spelling mistake in an email
questions.f: Computers are fussy: one missing bracket or comma can stop an entire program.

questions.q: Sending an email is using the internet but not the World Wide Web.
questions.f: Email has its own rules and travels the internet directly — no webpages required.

questions.q: Every computer program is ultimately carried out as patterns of 0s and 1s.
questions.f: Whatever language a coder uses, it is translated down into binary before the chip runs it.

questions.q: The moth found in a computer in 1947 was the very first use of the word 'bug' for a fault.
questions.f: Engineers, including Thomas Edison, called faults 'bugs' decades earlier — the moth just made the word famous.

questions.q: A 'bit map' image stores a picture by recording…?
c: The colour of every single pixel
questions.f: That is why zooming into a photo too far turns it into visible blocks.

questions.q: 'Vector' graphics stay sharp at any size because they store…?
questions.f: Logos are usually vectors so they look crisp on a business card and a billboard alike.

questions.q: A file that has been 'compressed' takes up…?
questions.f: Compression finds repeated patterns and stores them once, with notes on where to repeat them.

questions.q: The 'zip' in a zip file suggests…?
questions.f: Its inventor picked the name to sound faster than the rival programs of the 1980s.

questions.q: What does an 'emulator' do?
c: Lets one computer pretend to be another
questions.f: Emulators let a modern laptop run games written for consoles that no longer exist.

questions.q: To 'emulate' someone means to…?
questions.f: From Latin 'aemulari', to rival — an emulator rivals the machine it copies.

questions.q: A 'platform game' gets its name from the way players must…?
questions.f: Mario and Sonic are platform games, or 'platformers', built around leaping from ledge to ledge.

questions.q: A 'sprite' in old video games is…?
c: A small moving image drawn over the background
questions.f: Sprites were named for the way they seemed to float freely above the scenery like fairies.

questions.q: 'Avatar' comes from Sanskrit, where it described a god…?
c: Coming down in a visible form
questions.f: Your game avatar is your descended form — the shape you take inside a virtual world.

questions.q: A game's 'AI' controls…?
questions.f: Pac-Man's four ghosts each follow different chase rules — one of the earliest famous game AIs.

questions.q: 'Frames per second' in a game measures how many…?
c: Pictures the screen shows each second
questions.f: Films run at 24 frames per second, while many games aim for 60 or more for smoothness.

questions.q: A hidden joke or secret tucked into software by its makers is called an…?
questions.f: The first famous one hid a programmer's name inside an Atari game in 1979.

questions.q: An 'open world' game is one where players can…?
c: Explore freely instead of following one path
questions.f: Open-world maps can be so large that walking across them takes real-world hours.

questions.q: The word 'joystick' came into gaming from which earlier machine?
questions.f: Early pilots called their control column the joystick, and gamers borrowed both name and shape.

questions.q: 'Latency' in an online game means the…?
c: Delay before your action reaches the server
questions.f: From Latin 'latens', hidden — latency is the hidden waiting time between action and response.

questions.q: What is 'bandwidth'?
c: How much data a connection can carry at once
questions.f: Think of a pipe: bandwidth is its width, while latency is how long the journey takes.

questions.q: A 'protocol' on the internet is a…?
c: Set of agreed rules for talking
questions.f: The word once meant the formal etiquette of diplomats — computers need manners too.

questions.q: What does 'HTTP' help move around the internet?
questions.f: HTTP stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol — the polite conversation between browser and server.

questions.q: 'Hypertext' means text that…?
questions.f: The word was coined in the 1960s, long before the web made hypertext an everyday thing.

questions.q: A 'download' speed of 100 megabits per second describes…?
questions.f: Notice bits, not bytes: divide by eight to guess how many megabytes arrive each second.

questions.q: Which of these best describes a 'database'?
questions.f: Libraries, schools, and shops all run on databases that can find one record among millions.

questions.q: The 'Cloud' in cloud computing was chosen because engineers used to draw the network as…?
questions.f: On old diagrams a fluffy cloud meant 'the network, details not important' — the name stuck.

questions.q: 'Streaming' a film instead of downloading it means the file…?
c: Plays as it arrives, without being kept
questions.f: Players keep a few seconds in a buffer so small hiccups in the connection go unnoticed.

questions.q: A 'buffer' in a video player is…?
c: A small store of data waiting to be played
questions.f: To buffer originally meant to cushion a shock — the data cushion smooths out a bumpy connection.

questions.q: What is a 'podcast', and where does the name come from?
c: An audio show, named after the iPod and broadcast
questions.f: The word was suggested by a journalist in 2004 and caught on within months.

questions.q: 'Blog' is a shortened form of which word?
questions.f: A weblog was literally a log kept on the web; people trimmed it to blog by 1999.

questions.q: A '#' used to label topics online is called a…?
questions.f: The symbol also has the wonderful old name 'octothorpe', though nobody agrees who coined it.

questions.q: The @ symbol was already used for centuries by merchants to mean…?
questions.f: A bookkeeper writing '5 crates @ 2 coins' inspired its use in email addresses in 1971.

questions.q: An email address has two parts joined by @: your name and the…?
questions.f: The engineer who chose @ needed a symbol that could never appear in someone's name.

questions.q: 'Netiquette' is a blend of 'network' and…?
questions.f: It covers online manners: no shouting in capitals, and read before you reply.

questions.q: Writing a whole online message in capital letters is usually read as shouting.
questions.f: This unwritten rule is older than the web itself, dating from early message boards.

questions.q: What does 'LOL' stand for in a message?
questions.f: It appeared on 1980s bulletin boards, long before phones had emoji to do the job.

questions.q: Which of these is a 'peripheral' device?
questions.f: From Greek for 'around the edge' — peripherals sit around the computer rather than inside it.

questions.q: The big board inside a computer that everything plugs into is called the…?
questions.f: Smaller boards plugged into it were nicknamed daughterboards, keeping the family theme.

questions.q: A 'graphics card' or GPU is especially good at…?
c: Doing many similar calculations at once
questions.f: That talent for parallel maths made GPUs the workhorses of modern artificial intelligence too.

questions.q: Parallel processing means a computer works on several things at the same time.
questions.f: Modern chips contain multiple cores, so they really can think about several jobs at once.

questions.q: A processor 'core' is…?
c: One complete calculating unit inside a chip
questions.f: A phone chip may have eight cores, sharing work the way a team shares chores.

questions.q: Moore's law, named after an engineer, described how chips would keep…?
questions.f: Gordon Moore noticed in 1965 that transistor counts roughly doubled every couple of years.

questions.q: A 'transistor' inside a chip works as a tiny…?
questions.f: A modern processor can hold tens of billions of these switches, each far thinner than a hair.

questions.q: 'Silicon Valley' in California is named after silicon because the area became famous for…?
questions.f: A journalist coined the nickname in 1971, and it outgrew every other name for the region.

questions.q: 'Bootstrap' code in a computer got its name from an impossible feat:…?
c: Lifting yourself by your own bootstraps
questions.f: Starting a computer really is a chain reaction where each small step loads a bigger one.

questions.q: A 'patch' for software is named after a patch on…?
questions.f: Early patches were literally strips of paper tape stuck over holes in the program tape.

questions.q: A software 'update' that fixes a security hole is best installed…?
questions.f: Many attacks target holes that were already fixed — the victims simply had not updated.

questions.q: 'Malware' is a blend of 'malicious' and 'software'. 'Malicious' means…?
questions.f: The Latin root 'malus' means bad, and it also hides inside words like malady and malfunction.

questions.q: A program that pretends to be helpful but hides something harmful is named after…?
questions.f: Like the wooden horse in the Greek legend, a Trojan gets invited in before it acts.

questions.q: A computer 'worm' differs from a virus because it can…?
c: Spread by itself without a host file
questions.f: The 1988 Morris worm spread so quickly it slowed down a large part of the early internet.

questions.q: 'Antivirus' software protects a computer by…?
questions.f: It compares files against a huge list of known threats, updated almost every day.

questions.q: The word 'hacker' originally described someone who was…?
questions.f: At MIT in the 1960s, a 'hack' meant an ingenious trick — the criminal meaning came later.

questions.q: In coding, a 'kilobyte' is closest to how many bytes?
questions.f: Strictly it is 1,024 in binary counting — a number that is exactly 2 multiplied by itself ten times.

questions.q: Put these in order from smallest to largest: gigabyte, kilobyte, megabyte.
questions.f: Each step is about a thousand times bigger, and after gigabyte comes terabyte.

questions.q: The prefix 'tera' in 'terabyte' comes from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: From 'teras', a monster or marvel — fitting for a trillion bytes.

questions.q: A 'CAPTCHA' on a website is there to check that you are…?
questions.f: The name is a squeezed-down phrase meaning a public test that tells computers and humans apart.

questions.q: Speech recognition turns your spoken words into…?
questions.f: Modern systems learn from thousands of hours of recorded speech in many accents.

questions.q: 'Synthesised' speech from a computer is speech that has been…?
questions.f: From Greek 'synthesis', a putting together — early synthesisers sounded charmingly robotic.

questions.q: Which of these did people use to store computer programs in the 1970s and 1980s at home?
questions.f: Loading a game from tape could take five minutes of screeching noise — and often failed.

questions.q: Punched cards stored information by having…?
questions.f: Drop a stack of unsorted cards and a whole program could be ruined — a real 1960s nightmare.

questions.q: What did the abacus, thousands of years old, help people do?
questions.f: Skilled abacus users can still beat someone with a calculator on simple sums.

questions.q: A slide rule, used by engineers before calculators, worked using…?
questions.f: Apollo astronauts carried slide rules to the Moon as a backup for the computers.

questions.q: Which came first: the pocket calculator or the personal computer?
questions.f: Pocket calculators arrived around 1970, several years before home computers reached shops.

questions.q: 'Portable' comes from a Latin verb meaning to…?
questions.f: The same root gives us porter, transport, and import — all about carrying things.

questions.q: The word 'gadget' is best defined as…?
c: A small clever mechanical or electronic device
questions.f: Nobody is sure where 'gadget' came from — sailors used it in the 1800s for any small fitting.

questions.q: 'Technology' comes from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: From 'techne' (craft) plus '-logia' (study) — technology is the study of how things are made.

questions.q: 'Electronic' devices are named after which particle?
questions.f: Electrons flowing through circuits are what make every computer work.

questions.q: A 'circuit' is named for a path that…?
questions.f: From Latin 'circuitus', a going around — electricity must complete the loop to flow.

questions.q: In binary, what is the largest number you can write with three digits?
questions.f: 111 in binary is 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, which is why three bits give eight values from 0 to 7.

questions.q: How many different characters can eight bits represent?
questions.f: That is exactly why the original ASCII and its extensions fitted in a single byte.

questions.q: A pixel on a colour screen is usually made of smaller red, green, and blue parts.
questions.f: Those parts are called subpixels — a magnifying glass reveals the tiny stripes.

questions.q: Charles Babbage finished building his Analytical Engine during his lifetime.
questions.f: He never completed it, but modern engineers have built his Difference Engine from his drawings and it works.

questions.q: The word 'computer' once described a person, not a machine.
questions.f: For centuries a 'computer' was someone employed to work out numbers by hand.

questions.q: Ada Lovelace's famous notes on the Analytical Engine are known by which set of labels?
questions.f: Note G contains her step-by-step method for computing Bernoulli numbers — widely called the first program.

questions.q: Ada Lovelace insisted the Analytical Engine could never truly 'originate' anything. Which objection is named after that idea?
questions.f: Alan Turing named and answered it directly in his 1950 paper on machine intelligence.

questions.q: Which Italian officer's lecture notes did Ada Lovelace translate before adding her own commentary?
questions.f: Menabrea later became Italy's prime minister, but his lasting fame rests on the paper Ada expanded.

questions.q: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 was finally built from his drawings and completed in 2002. Where?
questions.f: It has 8,000 parts, weighs five tonnes — and it works exactly as Babbage predicted it would.

questions.q: Alan Turing's 1936 paper introduced an imaginary device now named after him. What does it manipulate?
questions.f: That simple tape-and-rules machine defines what any computer can, and cannot, ever compute.

questions.q: Turing called his 1950 imitation game a test of whether a machine could do what?
c: Fool a human questioner about which player was human
questions.f: He predicted machines would pass it by around the year 2000 — that guess is still argued about.

questions.q: Which term describes a problem that no computer program can ever solve for all cases, proved by Turing?
questions.f: No program can always tell in advance whether another program will finish or loop forever.

questions.q: The code-breaking machines at Bletchley Park that helped attack Enigma settings were called…?
questions.f: Each bombe clattered through thousands of wheel settings an hour, doing weeks of hand work in minutes.

questions.q: Colossus, built at Bletchley Park in 1943, is regarded as the world's first…?
questions.f: It stayed an official secret for thirty years, so ENIAC got the glory Colossus had earned first.

questions.q: ENIAC was built at which university?
questions.f: Its 18,000 vacuum tubes drew so much power that legend claimed the lights of Philadelphia dimmed.

questions.q: Reprogramming ENIAC for a new problem originally required operators to…?
c: Rewire cables and set switches by hand
questions.f: A job that now takes seconds could take the ENIAC women several days of careful patching.

questions.q: The idea of storing a program in the same memory as its data is known as which architecture?
questions.f: It is why one machine can be a word processor, a game, and a calculator without any rewiring.

questions.q: Grace Hopper worked on the Harvard Mark I and later on which pioneering commercial computer?
questions.f: UNIVAC famously predicted the 1952 US election result correctly while broadcasters doubted it on air.

questions.q: Grace Hopper explained a nanosecond to audiences by handing them a piece of wire about how long?
questions.f: That is the distance light travels in a billionth of a second — she called them 'nanoseconds'.

questions.q: Which German engineer built the programmable Z3 computer in Berlin in 1941?
questions.f: The Z3 used telephone relays instead of tubes, and the original was destroyed in a wartime air raid.

questions.q: Hermann Hollerith's punched-card tabulating machines were first used at scale for what?
questions.f: His machines cut the 1890 US census from years to months, and his company grew into IBM.

questions.q: George Boole's algebra of true and false became the mathematical foundation of…?
questions.f: Boole died in 1864, decades before anyone could build a machine to use his AND, OR, and NOT.

questions.q: Which master's student showed in 1937 that electrical switches could carry out Boolean logic?
questions.f: Shannon's thesis is often called the most important master's thesis of the twentieth century.

questions.q: Claude Shannon also founded which field, giving the bit its formal definition?
questions.f: His 1948 paper measured information in bits and set the limits every modem still obeys.

questions.q: Who actually coined the short word 'bit' for a binary digit?
questions.f: Statistician John Tukey squeezed 'binary digit' into 'bit' — and later coined 'software' too.

questions.q: Tim Berners-Lee's original 1990 proposal called the web a system of…?
questions.f: He built the first browser on a NeXT computer that carried a note reading 'do not power down'.

questions.q: Which three inventions did Tim Berners-Lee create together to make the web work?
questions.f: CERN put them in the public domain in 1993, which is why nobody has to pay to use the web.

questions.q: Which pair developed TCP/IP, the rulebook that lets different networks join into one internet?
questions.f: Their protocol was designed so that no single point could control or break the whole network.

questions.q: The first message ever sent over ARPANET in 1969 was cut short after two letters. What were they?
questions.f: They were typing LOGIN when the system crashed — accidentally sending 'lo', as in 'lo and behold'.

questions.q: Which technique lets internet data travel as small chunks that can take different routes?
questions.f: Break a message into packets and even a damaged network can reassemble it perfectly at the far end.

questions.q: Deep Blue's 1997 rematch with Kasparov ended with which score?
questions.f: One buggy move in game two rattled Kasparov so much that he never recovered his confidence.

questions.q: Which company built Deep Blue?
questions.f: IBM dismantled the machine after the match, so there was never a rematch — one half is in a museum.

questions.q: AlphaGo's 2016 match is famous for 'move 37' in game two, which experts first thought was…?
questions.f: Professionals called it beautiful once they understood it — a move no human would have played.

questions.q: Lee Sedol's one victory over AlphaGo came from a brilliant move now nicknamed…?
questions.f: He found a wedge in game four that pushed the program into errors it could not recover from.

questions.q: Which company developed AlphaGo?
questions.f: A later version, AlphaGo Zero, learned Go entirely from self-play, with no human games at all.

questions.q: In 2011, an IBM computer named Watson beat human champions at which television quiz show?
questions.f: Watson had to untangle puns and wordplay, which is far harder for a machine than chess.

questions.q: The word 'algorithm' reached Europe through Latin translations of al-Khwarizmi's book on which system?
questions.f: 'Algorism' first meant doing arithmetic with those numerals, and later came to mean any method.

questions.q: Al-Khwarizmi's book title gave English another mathematical word besides 'algorithm'. Which one?
questions.f: 'Al-jabr' meant restoring or reuniting broken parts — exactly what you do when solving an equation.

questions.q: A modern web address begins with a 'scheme', then '://'. What is that pair of slashes formally part of?
questions.f: Berners-Lee later said he regretted the two slashes — they turned out to be completely unnecessary.

questions.q: In 'Bluetooth', the logo is a monogram of two runes standing for the initials of which king?
questions.f: The runes for H and B are combined, honouring the tenth-century Danish king who united tribes.

questions.q: Why was 'Bluetooth' originally only a code name?
c: The team expected to replace it with a marketing name later
It described the colour of the chip
It was chosen by a competition
questions.f: The proper names were not ready in time, so the placeholder became one of tech's best-known brands.

questions.q: The sketch that gave junk email the name 'spam' came from which comedy troupe?
questions.f: In the sketch a chorus of Vikings drowns out conversation by singing about spam — just like junk mail.

questions.q: The web 'cookie' takes its name from a programming term for a small token passed along. What was it called?
questions.f: Lou Montulli adapted the idea in 1994 so a shopping basket could survive between page loads.

questions.q: The 'daemon' processes running quietly on a computer take their name from a Greek word for a…?
questions.f: MIT programmers named them after Maxwell's imaginary demon, and they insist the spelling is deliberate.

questions.q: 'Patch Tuesday' and the term 'patch' both descend from the practice of fixing programs stored on…?
questions.f: You covered a wrong hole and punched a new one — a physical patch on a physical program.

questions.q: The verb 'to google' entered dictionaries from a company name that was itself a misspelling of…?
questions.f: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros — a hint at the huge number of pages the search engine indexes.

questions.q: A 'googol' was named in the 1930s by a mathematician's young…?
questions.f: Edward Kasner asked his nine-year-old nephew Milton for a name, and 'googol' was the answer.

questions.q: The programming term 'byte' was coined at IBM by an engineer working on which computer family?
questions.f: Werner Buchholz coined it in 1956, and the eight-bit byte became standard with System/360.

questions.q: 'Nibble', a genuine computing term, refers to how many bits?
questions.f: Half a byte is a nibble — and one nibble is exactly one hexadecimal digit.

questions.q: The word 'pixel' was popularised in the 1960s by researchers working with images from…?
questions.f: Engineers processing early lunar and planetary photographs needed a word for a single picture element.

questions.q: Which term describes the smallest unit of a three-dimensional computer image?
questions.f: Voxel means volume element — medical scanners build the body from millions of them.

questions.q: In graphics, a 'texel' is the smallest unit of a…?
questions.f: Texture element — game engines stretch textures over 3D shapes texel by texel.

questions.q: 'Sprite' as a graphics term was coined at Texas Instruments, but the word originally meant a…?
questions.f: From Latin 'spiritus' via old French — game sprites hover over the background like little spirits.

questions.q: The 'Konami code' is a legendary cheat sequence beginning with which inputs?
questions.f: Up up down down left right left right B A — a programmer added it to help himself test a game.

questions.q: Which 1972 machine was the first home video game console?
questions.f: It used plastic overlays taped to the TV screen because it could not draw colours or scores.

questions.q: Ralph Baer, who created the first home console, is often called the father of…?
questions.f: He sketched the idea in 1966 while waiting for a bus, on the back of a notepad.

questions.q: The 1983 collapse of the American video game market is known as the video game…?
questions.f: Unsold cartridges were famously buried in a New Mexico landfill — and dug up again in 2014.

questions.q: Tetris reached the West largely because it was bundled with which handheld console?
questions.f: Nintendo's decision to pack Tetris with the Game Boy sold the console to adults as well as kids.

questions.q: For years Alexey Pajitnov earned nothing from Tetris because the rights belonged to…?
c: The Soviet state institute where he worked
questions.f: He finally began receiving royalties in 1996, twelve years after inventing the game.

questions.q: The seven Tetris pieces are known by which set of names?
c: Letter names like I, O, T, S, Z, J, L
questions.f: Each name matches the shape's outline, and the pieces are formally called tetrominoes.

questions.q: A shape made of four squares joined edge to edge is called a…?
questions.f: There are exactly seven of them when you allow rotations — hence Tetris's seven pieces.

questions.q: Mario is named after a real person: a…?
questions.f: Nintendo of America's staff thought their landlord, Mario Segale, resembled the little character.

questions.q: Which designer created both Donkey Kong and The Legend of Zelda?
questions.f: Miyamoto based Zelda's world on childhood memories of exploring caves and hillsides near Kyoto.

questions.q: Zelda's designer named the princess after the wife of which American author?
questions.f: Zelda Fitzgerald was famous and glamorous, and Miyamoto thought the name sounded pleasant and significant.

questions.q: The Atari game 'Breakout' was designed with help from which future computer company founders?
questions.f: Wozniak cut the chip count so far that Atari's engineers could barely understand the design.

questions.q: In Pac-Man, the ghost that chases most directly is nicknamed…?
questions.f: Each ghost uses a different rule: Blinky targets you, Pinky aims ahead, and Clyde wanders off.

questions.q: Pac-Man ends abruptly at level 256 because of an error involving…?
c: A byte that could not count higher
questions.f: With only eight bits for the level counter, 256 rolls over to zero and the screen fills with garbage.

questions.q: Which was the best-selling home computer of the 1980s, with tens of millions sold?
questions.f: Its sound chip was so beloved that musicians still compose with it today.

questions.q: The 1984 advertisement that introduced the Apple Macintosh was directed by Ridley Scott and referenced which novel?
questions.f: It aired only once during the Super Bowl and is still studied as the most famous advert ever made.

questions.q: The mouse and windows style of computing was pioneered at which research centre?
questions.f: PARC invented the graphical desktop, laser printing, and ethernet — but Xerox sold almost none of it.

questions.q: Douglas Engelbart's 1968 demonstration of the mouse, video calls, and hypertext is nicknamed…?
questions.f: In ninety minutes he showed almost every idea personal computing would spend thirty years catching up with.

questions.q: Which programming language, created in 1972, underlies much of the Unix operating system?
questions.f: C was so influential that C++, C#, Java, and JavaScript all borrow its curly-brace style.

questions.q: Which language shares almost nothing with Java despite the similar name?
questions.f: JavaScript was renamed from LiveScript purely as a marketing move while Java was fashionable.

questions.q: FORTRAN's name is a contraction of which two words?
questions.f: Released in 1957, it let scientists write mathematics instead of raw machine codes.

questions.q: BASIC, designed to teach beginners, has a name standing for Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction…?
questions.f: It was created at Dartmouth College in 1964 so that any student, not just engineers, could program.

questions.q: The 'GNU' project's name is a recursive joke meaning…?
questions.f: Richard Stallman loved recursive acronyms — the name explains itself by referring to itself.

questions.q: Which student released the first version of the Linux kernel in 1991?
questions.f: He announced it as 'just a hobby, won't be big' — it now runs most of the world's servers and phones.

questions.q: Linux's mascot is a penguin named…?
questions.f: Torvalds chose a penguin after, he joked, being nipped by one at an Australian zoo.

questions.q: 'Unix' and 'Linux' both end in a syllable coming from…?
c: Multics, the system Unix reacted against
questions.f: Multics was huge and complex; Unix was named as a deliberately simple, single-user answer to it.

questions.q: The abbreviation 'CPU' stands for Central Processing…?
questions.f: Modern CPUs cram their circuitry into features measured in single-digit nanometres.

questions.q: A 'kernel' in an operating system is named after the…?
questions.f: The kernel is the essential core, wrapped in layers of other software like a nut in its shell.

questions.q: A 'shell' in computing is so called because it…?
questions.f: You type into the shell, and it passes your commands inward to the kernel.

questions.q: The term 'firmware' describes software that is…?
questions.f: It sits between hardware and software in firmness — hence the deliberately in-between name.

questions.q: Which unit describes how many instructions a processor can retire per clock cycle?
questions.f: Instructions per cycle explains why a slower-clocked chip can still beat a faster-clocked rival.

questions.q: A 'blockchain' keeps records secure mainly by…?
c: Linking each record to a fingerprint of the one before
questions.f: Change one old record and every fingerprint after it stops matching, exposing the tampering.

questions.q: A 'hash function' takes any input and produces…?
c: A longer version of the input
questions.f: Tiny changes to the input scramble the whole output, which is what makes hashes useful for checking files.

questions.q: What does 'GPU' stand for?
questions.f: GPUs were built for games, but their parallel maths now trains almost every large AI model.

questions.q: 'Ray tracing' in graphics simulates the paths of…?
questions.f: It follows light backwards from the eye into the scene, which is why reflections look so convincing.

questions.q: The 'uncanny valley' describes the discomfort people feel when a robot or animation looks…?
questions.f: The idea was named by Japanese roboticist Masahiro Mori in 1970, and animators still design around it.

questions.q: Asimov's famous Three Laws govern how robots must treat…?
questions.f: He later added a 'Zeroth Law' about humanity as a whole, placed above all three original laws.

questions.q: 'Telepresence' robots let a person do what?
c: Be present somewhere far away through a machine
questions.f: Combining 'tele' (far) with presence, they let hospital patients attend school from their beds.

questions.q: Which spacecraft carried the first robot rover to successfully drive on Mars, in 1997?
questions.f: Its little rover Sojourner was the size of a microwave oven and travelled about 100 metres in total.

questions.q: The Soviet Lunokhod machines of the 1970s were the first successful rovers on…?
questions.f: Lunokhod 1 was driven remotely from Earth, with operators coping with a several-second signal delay.

questions.q: Shakey, built at Stanford in the late 1960s, was the first robot able to…?
questions.f: Researchers named it Shakey because it wobbled so much when it moved.

questions.q: The word 'automaton' describes a machine that moves by itself. Its plural is…?
questions.f: Eighteenth-century automata could write, draw, and play instruments using cams and springs.

questions.q: Jacques de Vaucanson's most famous eighteenth-century automaton was a mechanical…?
questions.f: His duck appeared to eat grain and digest it — a trick so clever that Voltaire wrote about it.

questions.q: 'The Turk', an eighteenth-century chess-playing machine, was actually…?
questions.f: It fooled audiences for decades — and inspired a modern service named 'Mechanical Turk'.

questions.q: Which everyday web feature did the term 'surfing the internet' come from?
questions.f: Jean Armour Polly coined it because riding a surfboard captured the feel of hopping from site to site.

questions.q: Vannevar Bush's 1945 essay imagined a desk-sized machine of linked documents called the…?
questions.f: His memex predicted hyperlinks half a century before the web existed.

questions.q: Who coined the words 'hypertext' and 'hypermedia' in the 1960s?
questions.f: His unfinished Project Xanadu aimed for links that worked in both directions, which the web still cannot do.

questions.q: Alan Kay's 1970s 'Dynabook' concept anticipated which modern device?
questions.f: He also coined the saying that the best way to predict the future is to invent it.

questions.q: What does 'ASCII' stand for?
c: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
questions.f: Its 1963 table fixed the numbers for letters and symbols — capital A has been 65 ever since.

questions.q: Unicode replaced ASCII's small table so computers could handle…?
c: Writing systems from around the world
questions.f: Unicode now covers well over 100,000 characters, from Chinese and Cherokee to emoji.

questions.q: Which body decides which new emoji are officially added?
questions.f: Anyone may submit a proposal, but it must argue that people will genuinely use the new symbol.

questions.q: Colossus, not ENIAC, was the first programmable electronic digital computer to operate.
questions.f: Colossus ran in 1944, but wartime secrecy hid it, so ENIAC was long credited as the first.

questions.q: The World Wide Web was released so that anyone could use it without paying royalties.
questions.f: CERN's 1993 decision to place the web in the public domain is why it grew so explosively.

questions.q: A moth taped into a Harvard logbook, a rear admiral's uniform, and a language full of English verbs all point to which computing pioneer?
questions.f: Hopper's team logged that moth in 1947 — and she went on to make COBOL readable by ordinary people.

questions.q: A poet's daughter, a translated Italian lecture, and a table for computing Bernoulli numbers converge on which figure?
questions.f: Her Note G is widely called the first published computer program — written before any computer existed.

questions.q: An unfinished engine of brass gears, a quarrel with a stubborn engineer named Clement, and a rebuilt machine in a London museum all point to whom?
questions.f: Babbage never finished a full engine, yet his drawings were good enough to build from 150 years later.

questions.q: An imitation game, a wartime hut in Buckinghamshire, and a proof that some questions have no computable answer all belong to which mathematician?
questions.f: Turing invented his abstract machine in 1936 purely to settle a question in pure logic.

questions.q: Punched cards for a national headcount, a company later renamed in 1924, and the ancestor of the modern data centre point to which inventor?
questions.f: Hollerith's company merged and was renamed International Business Machines — IBM.

questions.q: A master's thesis about switches, a wartime paper about secrecy, and a juggling unicyclist in the halls of Bell Labs describe which thinker?
questions.f: Shannon built a juggling machine and a mouse that solved mazes — and invented information theory.

questions.q: Six women, a room of 18,000 glowing tubes, and firing tables for artillery converge on which historic machine?
questions.f: Its programmers had to learn the machine from wiring diagrams because no manual existed.

questions.q: A shuttle bus in Honolulu, a programmer wanting the fastest possible page edits, and a word repeated for emphasis gave us which term?
questions.f: Ward Cunningham launched WikiWikiWeb in 1995, and Wikipedia borrowed the idea six years later.

questions.q: A tenth-century Danish king, a monogram of two runes, and a code name nobody bothered to replace gave us which technology's name?
questions.f: Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson united warring tribes — the technology unites squabbling devices.

questions.q: A cafe menu, a chorus of Vikings, and a tin of pressed meat explain the nickname for which modern nuisance?
questions.f: The Monty Python sketch buried conversation under one repeated word — exactly what junk email does.

questions.q: A ninth-century scholar in Baghdad, a Latin mistranslation of his name, and every recipe your phone follows converge on which word?
questions.f: 'Algorismus' was medieval Latin for al-Khwarizmi — his name became the word for method itself.

questions.q: A 1920 Czech play, a word for compulsory peasant work, and a warning about artificial workers gave English which word?
questions.f: Karel Capek credited his brother Josef with suggesting 'robota' — the play's workers were flesh, not metal.

questions.q: Ninety minutes in San Francisco in 1968, a wooden block with wheels, and the first public demonstration of video conferencing belong to whom?
questions.f: Engelbart showed the mouse, hyperlinks, and screen sharing while most computers still used punched cards.

questions.q: A level counter that overflows, four ghosts with different chase rules, and a pizza missing one slice all describe which arcade classic?
questions.f: Level 256 breaks because a single byte cannot hold a number higher than 255.

questions.q: A Moscow computing institute, the Greek word for four, and a handheld console bundle converge on which game?
questions.f: Alexey Pajitnov's puzzle escaped the Soviet Union by being copied from friend to friend on floppy disks.

questions.q: A warehouse landlord, a character first called Jumpman, and a cap invented because pixels could not show hair point to whom?
questions.f: Nintendo's American staff renamed Jumpman after Mario Segale, who rented them their warehouse.

questions.q: A rattling wooden cabinet in a California bar, a coin box stuffed too full, and two paddles with a square ball describe which machine?
questions.f: Atari got a call saying the machine was broken — it had simply jammed solid with quarters.

questions.q: A crashed login attempt, a laboratory in California, and two letters that arrived before the system failed describe which network's debut?
questions.f: Only 'LO' got through in 1969 — the operators had to reboot and try again.

questions.q: A physics laboratory near Geneva, a NeXT machine with a warning sticker, and three inventions given away free converge on whose work?
questions.f: His sticker read 'This machine is a server — do not power it down', because it hosted the entire web.

questions.q: A move numbered 37, a Korean champion's single brilliant win, and a program that later learned entirely by playing itself point to which match?
questions.f: Lee Sedol's win in game four is the last time a human beat a top Go program in a serious match.

questions.q: A rematch in New York, a puzzling computer move caused by a bug, and a machine dismantled before it could be challenged again describe which contest?
questions.f: IBM retired Deep Blue in 1997, leaving Kasparov permanently without the rematch he wanted.

questions.q: A hobby announcement to a newsgroup, a Finnish student, and a penguin mascot converge on which project?
questions.f: His 1991 post modestly said the project would never be anything 'big and professional like GNU'.

questions.q: A television comedy troupe, a language whose tutorials joke about spam and eggs, and a Dutch programmer point to which language?
questions.f: Guido van Rossum named Python after Monty Python, which is why example code says 'spam' instead of 'foo'.

questions.q: An imaginary demon of physics, a spelling that looks like a misprint, and a program running quietly in the background describe which term?
questions.f: MIT's programmers borrowed Maxwell's demon, a thought experiment about sorting molecules.

questions.q: A number named by a nine-year-old, a deliberate misspelling, and a company that indexes the web converge on which word?
questions.f: The founders wanted 'googol' — 1 followed by 100 zeros — but registered the misspelling instead.

questions.q: A shopping basket that had to survive between pages, a term borrowed from magic tokens, and a 1994 browser engineer describe which invention?
questions.f: Without cookies, every webpage would forget you the instant you clicked to the next one.

questions.q: Paper tape, a hole punched in the wrong place, and a strip stuck over the mistake explain which computing word?
questions.f: The word survived the tape era — now a patch is a file, but the metaphor is unchanged.

questions.q: A missing manual, a machine that thought 1900 was the same as 2000, and worldwide panic on New Year's Eve describe which problem?
questions.f: Programs saving years as two digits had to be checked worldwide — the enormous clean-up mostly worked.

questions.q: Which storage unit follows the terabyte?
questions.f: The full ladder runs kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta, exa, zetta, yotta — each about a thousand times bigger.

questions.q: 'Peta' as a prefix was coined to suggest which number of thousands multiplied together?
questions.f: It echoes the Greek for five, since a petabyte is a thousand to the fifth power.

questions.q: 'Sudo', typed by system administrators, is short for…?
questions.f: It temporarily grants full powers, which is why the command is treated with such respect.

questions.q: In computing, 'foo' and 'bar' are traditional placeholder names collectively called…?
questions.f: They appear in textbooks worldwide, and their use is documented in a formal internet standards document.

questions.q: 'Grok', meaning to understand deeply, entered programmer slang from which novel?
questions.f: Robert Heinlein invented it as a Martian word meaning to drink — and so to absorb completely.

questions.q: The term 'cyberspace' was coined by which science-fiction author?
questions.f: Gibson used it in 1982, before he had ever owned a computer — he wrote on a manual typewriter.

questions.q: 'Meme', now inseparable from the internet, was coined in 1976 by which scientist?
questions.f: He shortened Greek 'mimema', a thing imitated, to rhyme with 'gene' — ideas that copy themselves.

questions.q: 'Emoji' comes from Japanese elements meaning…?
questions.f: Its resemblance to 'emotion' is pure coincidence — 'e' means picture and 'moji' means character.

questions.q: 'Avatar' entered computing through which 1985 online role-playing world?
questions.f: Lucasfilm's Habitat gave every player a graphical body and borrowed the Sanskrit word for it.

questions.q: The 'Turing Award', computing's highest honour, is often described as the field's equivalent of which prize?
questions.f: There is no computing Nobel, so the Turing Award, first given in 1966, fills the gap.

questions.q: Which of these was the first widely popular graphical web browser, released in 1993?
questions.f: Mosaic showed pictures alongside text, and web traffic exploded within a year of its release.

questions.q: The competition between browsers in the late 1990s is known as the browser…?
questions.f: Netscape and Internet Explorer added features so fast that webpages of the era broke in both.

questions.q: What does 'DNS' do on the internet?
questions.f: Before DNS, one person maintained a single text file of every host name on the entire network.

questions.q: An IP address like 192.168.1.1 belongs to which version of the internet protocol?
questions.f: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out — IPv6 has enough for every grain of sand.

questions.q: 'Ping', used to test a connection, borrows its name from which technology?
questions.f: Its author explicitly compared it to a submarine's sonar pulse waiting for an echo.

questions.q: 'Ethernet' was named partly after 'luminiferous ether', a substance nineteenth-century physicists believed…?
questions.f: The ether was disproved, but Robert Metcalfe liked the image of a medium carrying signals everywhere.

questions.q: 'Wi-Fi' is not officially short for anything at all.
questions.f: A naming firm invented it; the tagline 'The Standard for Wireless Fidelity' came later and was dropped.

questions.q: 'Hi-fi', the model for Wi-Fi's name, was short for high…?
questions.f: Fidelity means faithfulness — hi-fi promised sound faithful to the original performance.

questions.q: Which storage technology is named for the way data is written and erased in whole blocks 'in a flash'?
questions.f: Its Toshiba inventors said block erasure reminded them of a camera flash going off.

questions.q: Before silicon chips, computer memory was often woven by hand from tiny magnetic rings called…?
questions.f: Apollo's guidance computer used core memory hand-woven by skilled workers — nicknamed 'LOL memory'.

questions.q: Margaret Hamilton led software engineering for which historic programme?
questions.f: She is credited with popularising the very phrase 'software engineering' — colleagues thought it was a joke.

questions.q: Katherine Johnson's calculations were so trusted that John Glenn asked her to check the work of…?
questions.f: Glenn would not fly until Johnson had verified the machine's numbers by hand.

questions.q: The Apollo Guidance Computer's famous 1202 alarm during the first Moon landing meant the computer was…?
questions.f: Its designers had built in priority scheduling, so it shed low-priority jobs and kept flying.

questions.q: 'Spaghetti code' describes a program that is…?
questions.f: The cure was structured programming, which replaced wild jumps with loops and functions.

questions.q: Edsger Dijkstra's famous 1968 letter argued against which programming statement?
questions.f: His note, titled 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful', changed how programs are written everywhere.

questions.q: 'Refactoring' code means changing it to…?
c: Improve its structure without changing what it does
questions.f: Like tidying a workshop, refactoring makes the next change easier without altering the output.

questions.q: 'Big O notation' describes how a program's running time grows as…?
questions.f: An algorithm can look fast on ten items and be hopeless on ten million — Big O predicts that.

questions.q: A 'binary search' can find an item in a sorted list of a million entries in roughly how many steps?
questions.f: Halving repeatedly is astonishingly powerful: each step throws away half of everything left.

questions.q: 'Recursion' in programming means a function that…?
questions.f: Every recursion needs a base case, or it keeps calling itself until the computer runs out of room.

questions.q: A 'stack' data structure works on which principle?
questions.f: Like a pile of plates, you can only take the one you put down most recently.

questions.q: A 'queue' data structure works on which principle?
questions.f: Printers use queues so documents come out in the order people sent them.

questions.q: The 'garbage collector' in many languages automatically…?
c: Frees memory no longer in use
questions.f: John McCarthy invented it for the language Lisp in 1959, sparing programmers a whole class of bugs.

questions.q: John McCarthy is credited with coining which term in 1955?
questions.f: He used it in the proposal for a summer workshop at Dartmouth that founded the whole field.

questions.q: A 'neural network' is loosely modelled on…?
questions.f: Artificial neurons pass numbers, not chemicals, but the idea of weighted connections is the same.

questions.q: 'Deep' in 'deep learning' refers to the number of…?
questions.f: Modern networks can stack dozens or hundreds of layers, each spotting more abstract patterns.

questions.q: 'Training data' is what a machine learning model uses to…?
c: Learn patterns before it is used
questions.f: The old warning 'garbage in, garbage out' matters more than ever with training data.

questions.q: The term 'GIGO' in computing stands for…?
questions.f: Coined in the 1950s, it reminds programmers that a computer cannot rescue bad information.

questions.q: The 'QWERTY' layout is usually said to have been arranged to…?
questions.f: Rival layouts like Dvorak claim to be faster, but QWERTY's head start has never been overcome.

questions.q: Which alternative keyboard layout was patented in 1936 to reduce finger travel?
questions.f: August Dvorak put the most common letters on the home row, where fingers already rest.

questions.q: 'Kerning' and 'font' come from typesetting. What does 'font' originally describe?
questions.f: From French 'fonte', a casting — printers once bought a whole font of metal letters at one size.

questions.q: 'Upper case' and 'lower case' letters got their names from the position of…?
c: Trays of metal type in a printing shop
questions.f: Capitals lived in the upper case above the compositor's bench, small letters in the lower one.

questions.q: The 'em dash' and 'em space' are named after the width of which letter?
questions.f: An 'en' is half that width, named after the letter N — typographers have used these units for centuries.

questions.q: 'Boilerplate' text, reused in documents and code, was named after which industry's practice?
questions.f: Syndicated columns arrived as ready-made steel plates that small papers dropped straight into the press.

questions.q: The 'clipboard' on a computer is named after a real clipboard because it…?
questions.f: Most systems hold only the latest copied item, which is why copying twice loses the first.

questions.q: A software 'beta' version is named because it comes after which stage?
questions.f: IBM used alpha for internal tests and beta for outside testers, and the labels spread everywhere.

questions.q: 'Vaporware' is software that is announced but never actually released.
questions.f: The word appeared in the 1980s for products that evaporated between press release and shop.

questions.q: 'Killer app' means a program so useful that people buy…?
c: The hardware just to run it
questions.f: The spreadsheet VisiCalc sold Apple IIs to businesses that had no other reason to want a computer.

questions.q: VisiCalc, released in 1979, was the first widely used…?
questions.f: Accountants queued to buy computers purely to escape recalculating columns by hand.

questions.q: 'WYSIWYG', a mouthful from the 1970s, stands for what you see is what you…?
questions.f: Before WYSIWYG editors, you typed formatting codes and only discovered your mistakes after printing.

questions.q: 'Rubber duck debugging' means explaining your code to…?
questions.f: Saying the logic aloud forces you to notice the step you skipped in your head.

questions.q: A 'Heisenbug' is a bug that…?
c: Disappears when you try to observe it
questions.f: Named after Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, because measuring it changes the behaviour.

questions.q: 'Yak shaving' in programming describes…?
c: A chain of small tasks needed before the real one
questions.f: You want to fix one line, and four detours later you are updating a tool you had never heard of.

questions.q: 'Technical debt' describes the future work created by taking shortcuts today.
questions.f: Like a loan, quick fixes charge interest — every later change becomes a little harder.

questions.q: 'Open source' licences such as the GPL are built on the idea of…?
questions.f: The GPL's 'copyleft' rule means anyone who distributes changes must share the source too.

questions.q: 'Copyleft' was coined as a deliberate pun, with the slogan 'All rights reversed'.
questions.f: The licence requires anyone distributing changed code to share their source too.

questions.q: 'Version control' systems like Git let programmers…?
c: Track and undo every change over time
questions.f: Git was written by Linus Torvalds in about two weeks after the Linux team lost its previous tool.

questions.q: In Git, a 'commit' is best described as…?
questions.f: Each commit records who changed what and when, building a complete history of a project.

questions.q: A 'pull request' asks other developers to…?
questions.f: It turned code review into a conversation, and helped open-source projects scale to thousands of contributors.

questions.q: 'Agile' software development favours…?
c: One huge plan at the start
questions.f: Seventeen developers wrote the Agile Manifesto at a ski lodge in Utah in 2001.

questions.q: 'Scrum', a term used in software teams, is borrowed from which sport?
questions.f: The name suggests the whole team moving down the field together, passing the ball among themselves.

questions.q: Browsers put each tab in a sandbox so one bad page cannot reach the rest of your computer.
questions.f: The name borrows from a play sandbox: a contained place where any mess stays put.

questions.q: A honeypot is a system set up deliberately to attract attackers.
questions.f: Researchers learn attackers' tricks by watching them break into a system holding nothing real.

questions.q: 'Two-factor authentication' adds a second check that is usually…?
questions.f: Something you know, something you have, something you are — mixing two makes stolen passwords far less useful.

questions.q: 'Biometric' security uses measurements of…?
questions.f: From Greek 'bios' (life) and 'metron' (measure) — fingerprints, irises, and faces are all biometrics.

questions.q: A 'zero-day' vulnerability is dangerous because…?
c: It is exploited before a fix exists
questions.f: Defenders have had zero days of warning, which is exactly what makes these flaws so valuable to attackers.

questions.q: 'Quantum computing' uses units of information called…?
questions.f: A qubit can hold a blend of 0 and 1 at once, which lets certain problems be attacked in parallel.

questions.q: The word 'robot' was invented by a novelist's brother, not the playwright himself.
questions.f: Karel Capek said Josef, a painter, suggested 'robot' when Karel was stuck for a word.

questions.q: Alan Turing's abstract machine was described in a paper about pure mathematics, not about building computers.
questions.f: His 1936 paper answered a logic puzzle — the computer age was an unintended side effect.

questions.q: 'Emoji' and 'emotion' are unrelated words that only look similar.
questions.f: Emoji is Japanese for picture-character; the resemblance to 'emotion' is a lucky coincidence.

questions.q: Grace Hopper's team invented the very first compiler for a programming language.
questions.f: She led the work on the A-0 system around 1952, when many insisted computers could only do arithmetic.

questions.q: A quarrel over street musicians, a scheme to number every London house, and a plan for a mechanical postal system all belong to which inventor?
questions.f: Babbage campaigned furiously against organ-grinders — and his engines are what the world remembers.

questions.q: A treatise on cracking the Vigenere cipher, a study of lighthouse signalling, and a table of the cost of glassmaking all came from whose restless pen?
questions.f: Babbage broke the 'unbreakable' Vigenere cipher years before Friedrich Kasiski published the same method.

questions.q: A childhood illness that left her bedridden, a scheme for a flying machine drawn at twelve, and a fascination with the Jacquard loom describe whose youth?
questions.f: Young Ada wrote a book she called Flyology, illustrating wings she hoped to build herself.

questions.q: Ada Lovelace signed her published notes with initials only. What were they?
questions.f: Augusta Ada Lovelace hid behind initials because a woman's name on a scientific paper invited dismissal.

questions.q: A cryptographic study of naval Enigma, a silver ingot buried in a wood, and a habit of chaining a mug to a radiator all describe which figure?
questions.f: Turing buried silver against wartime inflation and never found it again — the maps he drew were too clever.

questions.q: A Post Office engineer who trusted thousands of glass valves, a machine partly paid for from his own pocket, and a wartime secret kept for three decades point to whom?
questions.f: Flowers was a Post Office engineer who trusted valves because he had already used thousands in telephone exchanges.

questions.q: A German cipher machine never captured intact, a mathematician who deduced its wiring from intercepts alone, and the codename 'Tunny' point to whom?
questions.f: Tutte reconstructed the Lorenz machine's internal structure without ever seeing one — perhaps the war's greatest intellectual feat.

questions.q: A 1900 lecture in Paris listing 23 problems, a programme to mechanise all of mathematics, and the challenge Turing demolished in 1936 point to which mathematician?
questions.f: Hilbert asked for a mechanical decision procedure for mathematics; Turing proved none can exist.

questions.q: A calculus written with the Greek letter lambda, a doctoral student from Cambridge named Turing, and a thesis now carrying two surnames point to which logician?
questions.f: The result is now called the Church-Turing thesis, honouring both approaches to the same deep truth.

questions.q: A chess-playing algorithm worked out on paper called Turochamp, a pilot ACE machine at the National Physical Laboratory, and a paper on how spots form on animals belong to whom?
questions.f: Turing designed Turochamp before any machine could run it, so he played out its moves by hand.

questions.q: A 1952 paper on how a leopard could get its spots, two chemicals spreading at different speeds, and a Greek compound meaning shape-maker describe which term?
questions.f: From Greek for 'shape-makers' — biologists confirmed his prediction decades after his death.

questions.q: A woman who learned ENIAC from its wiring diagrams, later helped standardise Fortran and COBOL, and worked at the Ballistic Research Laboratory is who?
questions.f: Holberton later helped design COBOL and Fortran standards — and invented the numeric keypad's layout ideas.

questions.q: A young engineer at Pennsylvania, a 1946 partnership that built America's first commercial computer, and a patent struck down in 1973 point to whom?
questions.f: A 1973 court ruling declared their ENIAC patent invalid, crediting John Atanasoff's earlier machine.

questions.q: A court case in 1973, a professor's basement machine at Iowa State, and a lost prototype converge on which claimed 'first' computer?
questions.f: The judge ruled ENIAC derived from Atanasoff's ideas, quietly rewriting who invented the computer.

questions.q: A cathode-ray tube pressed into service as memory, a 52-minute hunt for the factors of a large number, and a 1948 machine in northern England describe which computer?
questions.f: Its first program searched for factors of a large number and took 52 minutes to finish.

questions.q: A chain of tea shops, a bakery delivery payroll, and the first computer put to work on ordinary office paperwork describe which 1951 machine?
questions.f: LEO stood for Lyons Electronic Office — a tea-shop company built its own computer.

questions.q: A moth, a logbook page now in a museum, and the phrase 'first actual case of bug being found' converge on which machine?
questions.f: The note's wording proves 'bug' already meant a fault — the joke was finding a literal one.

questions.q: Statements that read like English sentences, a direct ancestor of COBOL, and Grace Hopper's insistence that machines could handle words describe which system?
questions.f: She had to prove computers could handle words at all — critics insisted they were only for numbers.

questions.q: Which of Grace Hopper's sayings became a favourite motto of engineers everywhere?
c: It is easier to ask forgiveness than permission
Perfect is the enemy of good
Make it work, then make it fast
questions.f: She kept a clock on her wall that ran backwards, to prove that things can be done differently.

questions.q: A gambler's card-counting scheme, a paper on juggling, and the mathematical definition of entropy in messages belong to which Bell Labs figure?
questions.f: Shannon and Ed Thorp built a wearable computer for roulette — arguably the first wearable computer ever.

questions.q: The statistician behind the box plot, the coiner of the word software, and the man who squeezed binary digit into three letters is who?
questions.f: Tukey's knack for naming things may be the finest record in the whole history of computing.

questions.q: Weekend crashes that infuriated a Bell Labs mathematician, parity checks hidden inside memory chips, and codes that repair themselves describe which family?
questions.f: Richard Hamming was so annoyed by weekend machine crashes that he invented codes that fix their own errors.

questions.q: An MIT thesis about relay circuits, a boat with a rope, and the coining of the word 'cybernetics' belong to which mathematician?
questions.f: Wiener took 'kybernetes', a helmsman, because control means constant small corrections of course.

questions.q: An unfinished draft circulated in 1945, a Hungarian-born polymath who also founded game theory, and an architecture credited to one man though many built it point to whom?
questions.f: Because his name appeared first on an unfinished circulated draft, the whole architecture became his.

questions.q: A chip sitting idle while it waits, a crowded road between processor and memory, and a limit named after a Hungarian-born mathematician describe which phenomenon?
questions.f: No matter how fast a chip thinks, it waits on the road between itself and its memory.

questions.q: A stubborn fraction of a task that cannot be split, a warning against simply buying more processors, and a rule named for an IBM mainframe architect describe which law?
questions.f: If a tenth of a job cannot be divided, no number of processors can make it more than ten times faster.

questions.q: A cheque promised for every error found, volumes still unfinished after sixty years, and rewards paid in hexadecimal dollars point to which work?
questions.f: Knuth offers a small cheque to anyone who finds an error, and collectors keep the cheques uncashed.

questions.q: A ten-year detour from finishing one book, version numbers creeping ever closer to pi, and the typesetting beloved of mathematicians describe which system?
questions.f: He set out to fix one book's typography and spent ten years building the system mathematicians still use.

questions.q: A monthly essay collection, a warning that adding people to a late project makes it later, and the management of IBM's System/360 point to which author?
questions.f: His book The Mythical Man-Month is still handed to new project managers half a century later.

questions.q: A paper rejected by a journal in 1968, an observation that org charts leak into software, and the reason company reshuffles reshape code describe which law?
questions.f: Melvin Conway noticed a system's design mirrors the communication structure of whoever built it.

questions.q: An essay contrasting a cathedral with a bazaar, a Linux kernel, and the phrase 'given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow' belong to whom?
questions.f: He named that principle Linus's law, after Linus Torvalds's habit of releasing early and often.

questions.q: A broken printer at MIT, a refused request for source code, and a manifesto typed in 1985 launched which movement?
questions.f: Richard Stallman could not fix a jammed Xerox printer because the code was secret — so he built GNU.

questions.q: An acronym that contains itself, a wildebeest mascot, and a 1983 plan to rebuild Unix as free software describe which project?
questions.f: GNU's Not Unix — a joke that keeps unfolding forever, exactly as he intended.

questions.q: An unfinished kernel called Hurd, a student's hobby posted to a newsgroup, and a licence written years earlier combined to produce which system?
questions.f: Stallman had every piece but the kernel; Torvalds had only a kernel — together they completed the puzzle.

questions.q: A system small enough to print inside a textbook, a Dutch professor's teaching tool, and the software a Finnish student outgrew describe which operating system?
questions.f: Minix was small enough to study line by line, and it shipped in a textbook rather than a box.

questions.q: A wager over a beer, a rule about doubling components, and a 1965 magazine article converge on which observation?
questions.f: Gordon Moore's original article predicted only ten years ahead — the trend then held for half a century.

questions.q: Two telephones allowing one call, a thousand allowing half a million, and a rule named by Ethernet's co-inventor describe which law?
questions.f: Value rising with the square of the users is why networks snowball once they pass a tipping point.

questions.q: A Hawaiian radio experiment, a rule of talk and try again after a collision, and the direct ancestor of Ethernet point to which network?
questions.f: ALOHAnet's simple 'talk and retry if you collide' idea became the heart of Ethernet.

questions.q: An algorithm written in a week and explained in a poem, a protocol that stops networks looping forever, and the nickname mother of the internet point to whom?
questions.f: She wrote the algorithm in a week and explained it in a poem — she is called the mother of the internet.

questions.q: A demand that a square work wherever a shape works, a Turing Award, and the L in the acronym SOLID describe which principle?
questions.f: If code works with a shape, it must work with a square — that simple demand reshaped software design.

questions.q: A language in which absolutely everything is an object, a Xerox PARC team led by Alan Kay, and ideas borrowed from Norwegian ship simulations describe which language?
questions.f: Kay borrowed ideas from the earlier Norwegian language Simula, then built a whole interactive world around them.

questions.q: Two Norwegians modelling ships and queues, the invention of the class in the 1960s, and the language Stroustrup later borrowed from point to which pair?
questions.f: They were modelling ships and queues, and needed a way to describe many similar things at once.

questions.q: A young researcher translating Russian, a dictionary tape that had to be sorted first, and a 1959 divide-and-conquer idea describe which algorithm?
questions.f: He needed to sort words to look them up in a dictionary tape, and invented one of computing's fastest sorts.

questions.q: A feature added in 1965 simply because it was easy, a public apology forty years later, and a phrase about a billion dollars describe which invention?
questions.f: He added it in 1965 simply because it was easy — and apologised publicly forty years later.

questions.q: Twenty minutes at an Amsterdam cafe, no pencil and no paper, and the route your map app quietly computes point to which algorithm?
questions.f: Dijkstra devised it without pencil or paper while having coffee with his fiancee in Amsterdam.

questions.q: The Ackermann function is famous among computer scientists because it…?
c: Grows faster than any simple loop can compute
questions.f: It proved that some computable functions need recursion, not just counting loops — a foundational result.

questions.q: A million-dollar Clay Institute prize, a gap between checking an answer and finding one, and the question most researchers expect to answer no is called…?
questions.f: If the two turned out equal, almost every hard search problem in the world would suddenly become easy.

questions.q: A 1971 paper by Stephen Cook, the first problem shown to be as hard as any in its class, and a puzzle about making a logic formula come out true describe which problem?
questions.f: Once one problem was pinned down, hundreds of others were shown to be secretly the same difficulty.

questions.q: A mathematician's 1936 lambda calculus, a 1958 language for symbol manipulation, and a mountain of parentheses converge on which language?
questions.f: John McCarthy's Lisp is the second-oldest high-level language still in use, after Fortran.

questions.q: A 1972 creation in Marseille, code that states facts and rules instead of steps, and a machine left to find its own path describe which language?
