questions.f: In Prolog you describe what is true and let the machine work out how to reach a conclusion.

questions.q: A language that needed a keyboard of its own, the Game of Life written on a single line, and Kenneth Iverson's notation describe which language?
questions.f: APL needed its own keyboard, and its Game of Life implementation famously fits in one line.

questions.q: Grace Hopper's colleague Jean Sammet co-designed COBOL and wrote which influential 1969 survey?
questions.f: Sammet catalogued hundreds of languages when most people assumed there were only a handful.

questions.q: A language named after a nineteenth-century countess, a 1970s drive to replace hundreds of languages at once, and code still flying aircraft point to which sponsor?
c: The United States Department of Defense
questions.f: They wanted one reliable language to replace hundreds in use — and Ada still flies aircraft and trains.

questions.q: A joke about being called by value or by reference, a teaching language named for a French mathematician, and successors called Modula-2 and Oberon point to whom?
questions.f: Wirth joked that Americans pronounced his name by value while Europeans pronounced it by reference.

questions.q: A notation that defined Algol 60, two surnames from America and Denmark, and the grammar rules printed in language manuals describe which form?
questions.f: John Backus and Peter Naur's notation defined Algol 60, and it still specifies languages today.

questions.q: Algol 60 is remembered as the language that introduced which structuring idea now taken for granted?
questions.f: Hoare said it was so far ahead of its time that it improved on nearly all its successors.

questions.q: One month alone while his wife was away, a week each for shell, editor, and assembler, and the very first Unix point to which computer?
questions.f: He allotted one week each for the operating system, shell, editor, and assembler — and finished on time.

questions.q: A famously slim manual co-written with Kernighan, a language named with a single letter, and the reason Unix could move between machines point to whom?
questions.f: C was designed so Unix could be rewritten to run on any machine — a revolutionary idea in 1972.

questions.q: A two-word greeting typed by beginners everywhere, a slim 1978 manual, and a ritual copied by every language since point to which book?
questions.f: Brian Kernighan used it earlier in a tutorial, and every language since has copied the ritual.

questions.q: A skiing accident, a language named for two plus signs, and the wish to add Simula's classes to C converge on whose work?
questions.f: Stroustrup first called it 'C with Classes'; the ++ operator gave it a wittier name in 1983.

questions.q: A tree outside an office window, a language first aimed at interactive television, and a name dropped for trademark reasons describe which original title?
questions.f: James Gosling named it after a tree outside his office, then the team switched to a coffee theme.

questions.q: Ten days of work in May 1995, a language renamed from LiveScript purely for marketing, and quirks the whole web still lives with point to whom?
questions.f: A ten-day language now runs almost every webpage on earth — and its quirks come from that hurry.

questions.q: 'Node.js', 'V8', and 'JIT compilation' all relate to making which language run fast?
questions.f: Just-in-time compilers translate code while it runs, which made browsers hundreds of times faster.

questions.q: A name chosen deliberately as one step up from Perl, a Japanese creator seeking programmer happiness, and a colleague's July birthstone point to which language?
questions.f: Yukihiro Matsumoto wanted a name a step up from Perl, and picked the gem that follows pearl in lists.

questions.q: Perl's mascot is a camel because of the cover of…?
questions.f: O'Reilly's animal covers became so iconic that the books are known by their creatures, not their titles.

questions.q: An accent on a Brazilian keyboard, a language for making web pages dynamic in 1995, and a recursive acronym describe which language?
questions.f: PHP now stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor — another acronym that contains itself.

questions.q: A gopher's portrait, three Google engineers frustrated by slow compiles, and a language released in 2009 point to which project?
questions.f: The team began sketching Go while waiting for a huge C++ program to finish compiling.

questions.q: A creator who admired a fungus over-engineered for survival, a crab mascot named Ferris, and a language built to stop memory bugs point to which language?
questions.f: Graydon Hoare named it after rust fungi; the community adopted the crab entirely on its own.

questions.q: A man who wore his own computer daily for decades, the coinage sousveillance, and spectacles used as a display anticipated which product category?
questions.f: Mann wore his rigs daily for decades, calling the practice 'sousveillance' — watching from below.

questions.q: A pot in a room named after Troy, researchers tired of pointless walks down a corridor, and the world's first webcam point to which university?
questions.f: Researchers in the Trojan Room were tired of walking to an empty pot, so they watched it online instead.

questions.q: A broken gadget, a buyer who collected broken ones on purpose, and the first sale on the site that became eBay describe which item?
questions.f: The buyer explained he collected broken laser pointers — the founder decided the internet would be fine.

questions.q: Which was the first banner advertisement on the web, in 1994, and what did it ask?
c: An AT&T ad asking 'Have you ever clicked your mouse right here?'
questions.f: Astonishingly, 44 percent of viewers clicked it — a rate no advert has come close to since.

questions.q: A book bought by a friend of the engineers, an order shipped from a Seattle garage in 1995, and the very first item Amazon ever sold point to which subject?
questions.f: It was a technical book on machine learning — bought by a friend of the company's engineers.

questions.q: A vending machine, a Carnegie Mellon corridor, and programmers who hated wasted trips describe which early internet-connected appliance?
questions.f: Students wired sensors to the machine in the 1980s so they could check stock before walking over.

questions.q: A pitch about radio tags on lipstick shelves, a 1999 presentation to sceptical bosses, and a phrase that outgrew supply chains entirely point to whom?
questions.f: He was trying to sell his bosses on radio tags for lipstick shelves — the phrase outgrew the pitch.

questions.q: A 1991 magazine essay, a claim that the deepest technologies disappear from notice, and a vision its author called calm computing described computing as…?
questions.f: He argued the deepest technologies disappear into the background, like writing or electric motors.

questions.q: Star charts added purely out of pride, a PDP-1 at MIT in 1962, and the game that inspired the first arcade cabinet describe which title?
questions.f: Its authors added accurate star charts for background scenery, purely out of pride.

questions.q: A laboratory open day in 1958, an oscilloscope wired to an analogue computer, and an invention its maker never bothered to patent describe which game?
questions.f: William Higinbotham built it to entertain visitors at Brookhaven, then dismantled it and never patented it.

questions.q: Instructions that baffled customers in bars, Nolan Bushnell's very first product, and a 1971 flop that came before Pong describe which machine?
questions.f: Its failure taught Bushnell that an arcade game must be understood in about three seconds flat.

questions.q: Nolan Bushnell famously said the whole instruction set for Pong had to fit in one line. What did it say?
c: Avoid missing ball for high score
Hit the ball with the bat
Move the paddle up and down
questions.f: He wanted an arcade game a slightly tipsy stranger could understand in three seconds.

questions.q: A monster invented for one game and later borrowed by fantasy dictionaries, a flooded underground empire, and MIT students' mainframe project describe which title?
questions.f: Grues were invented for Zork and have since crept into fantasy dictionaries as a real-sounding monster.

questions.q: A real cave mapped by a surveyor, a game written to amuse two daughters, and a maze of twisty little passages point to which state's cavern?
questions.f: Will Crowther mapped Mammoth Cave in real life, then turned his survey notes into the first adventure game.

questions.q: A cave surveyor, a router engineer at the birth of ARPANET, and a father writing a game for his daughters describe whom?
questions.f: Crowther helped build the first ARPANET routers by day and invented interactive fiction by night.

questions.q: A programmer denied a credit on the box, a hidden room reached through a single grey dot, and 1979's best-kept secret describe which Atari game?
questions.f: Warren Robinett hid his name because Atari refused to credit programmers on its boxes.

questions.q: Donkey Kong's level 22, a bonus timer that allots too little time, and a barrier no amount of skill can pass describe which term?
c: A programming limit makes further play impossible
questions.f: At stage 22-1 the timer routine leaves Mario too few seconds to survive, so every run ends there.

questions.q: Aliens that speed up as their ranks thin, chips ordered specially because none were fast enough, and a Japanese coin shortage in 1978 point to whom?
questions.f: He noticed the aliens sped up as fewer remained — a hardware limitation he kept because it felt exciting.

questions.q: A philosophy of using cheap, proven parts on purpose, the Game and Watch series, and a grey handheld that outsold every rival point to whom?
questions.f: His design philosophy was 'lateral thinking with withered technology' — cheap old parts used cleverly.

questions.q: A Soviet institute's Elektronika 60, a game with no graphics chip, and brackets typed as blocks converge on which title's first version?
questions.f: Pajitnov's first Tetris drew its pieces from text characters because the terminal had no graphics.

questions.q: A Dutch-born businessman flying to Moscow, handheld rights nobody had thought to claim, and a courtroom defeat that cost a rival its cartridges point to which company?
questions.f: A young Nintendo lawyer named Henk Rogers flew to Moscow and discovered the handheld rights were still free.

questions.q: A nineteenth-century pedlar's song, a Nintendo arrangement, and a tune millions hum while stacking blocks describe which piece of music?
questions.f: It is a nineteenth-century pedlar's song, and Nintendo's arrangement made it globally famous.

questions.q: A robot accessory whose real job was disguise, shops refusing to stock anything called a video game, and the 1985 rescue of an industry point to which company?
questions.f: Nintendo sold it partly as a toy with a robot accessory, because shops refused to stock 'video games'.

questions.q: The robot accessory sold with the Nintendo Entertainment System was called…?
questions.f: R.O.B. stood for Robotic Operating Buddy, and it existed mainly to make the console look like a toy.

questions.q: A first episode given away free, university networks buckling under downloads, and an engine now running on cash machines and calculators describe which game?
questions.f: Its makers gave away the first episode, and university networks buckled under the downloads.

questions.q: Quake III Arena's engine used a trick nicknamed the fast inverse square root. It traded accuracy for…?
questions.f: Its released source code held the constant 0x5f3759df beside a baffled comment that programmers still quote.

questions.q: Old engine source code released to the public, a later career in rockets, and the coder behind 1993's shareware phenomenon point to whom?
questions.f: He released the source code to his old engines, so Doom now runs on calculators, cameras, and cash machines.

questions.q: Minecraft's creator originally released it under which name for its earliest builds?
questions.f: Markus Persson's early test builds were literally called Cave Game before he settled on Minecraft.

questions.q: Minecraft's Creeper mob exists because of a coding accident while making which animal?
questions.f: The height and length values were swapped, producing a tall green thing too good to delete.

questions.q: A Japanese word meaning warehouse keeper, crates that can only ever be pushed, and a 1984 puzzle whose hardest levels defeat computers describe which game?
questions.f: Sokoban means 'warehouse keeper', and solving its hardest levels is provably very difficult for computers.

questions.q: A machine that plays perfect checkers, a 1994 world championship, and a program named for a First Nations term converge on which milestone?
questions.f: By 2007 Chinook's successors had proved checkers is a draw if both sides play perfectly.

questions.q: A name lifted from the Hitchhiker's Guide, the first tournament win over a grandmaster in 1988, and a team IBM promptly hired point to which machine?
questions.f: Its name was a Hitchhiker's Guide joke, and IBM hired the team that built it.

questions.q: In 2017, a poker-playing program called Libratus beat top professionals at which variant?
questions.f: Poker was harder than chess for machines because players must reason about hidden cards and bluffing.

questions.q: Nine hours of playing against itself, three ancient board games mastered from the rules alone, and not one human game studied point to which program?
questions.f: After nine hours of self-play it beat the strongest conventional chess engine in the world.

questions.q: A fifty-year grand challenge in biology, a laboratory better known for board games, and a free public database of predicted molecular shapes point to which program?
questions.f: It predicts how protein chains fold into shapes, a puzzle biologists had wrestled with for decades.

questions.q: The 'algo' spelling in 'algorithm' was reshaped in medieval Europe by confusion with a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: Scribes blended al-Khwarizmi's name with 'arithmos' — which is why we spell it with 'rithm', not 'rism'.

questions.q: The word 'cipher' travelled into Europe from an Arabic word for zero, which literally meant…?
questions.f: From 'sifr' (empty) came both 'zero' and 'cipher' — and 'decipher' means emptying out the secret.

questions.q: 'Cybernetics' was built from a Greek word describing a person who…?
questions.f: Norbert Wiener chose 'kybernetes' because steering means constant correction — the essence of feedback.

questions.q: 'Governor', both the political title and the mechanical device on an engine, shares a root with which computing term?
questions.f: Latin 'gubernare' came from the same Greek helmsman — governing and steering are the same idea.

questions.q: The '-ware' in 'software', 'hardware', and 'firmware' originally meant…?
questions.f: The same '-ware' appears in hardware shops and silverware — things made and sold.

questions.q: A word coined by analogy with hardware and software, the one component that cannot be upgraded, and a jokey name for grey matter describe which term?
questions.f: Programmers use it to distinguish the machine's limits from the limits of the person using it.

questions.q: The word 'protocol' comes from Greek roots meaning the…?
questions.f: 'Protokollon' was the first sheet glued to a scroll, carrying its summary — hence rules and formalities.

questions.q: 'Modem' compresses two verbs describing what it does to a signal. The second of them means to…?
questions.f: Modulate then demodulate: shape the signal for the line, then strip that shaping off at the far end.

questions.q: 'Codec', a word used for video and audio formats, is a blend of which two words?
questions.f: Like modem, it names both directions of the same journey in a single tidy word.

questions.q: 'Pixel' and 'voxel' both end in a shortened form of which word?
questions.f: Picture element and volume element — the '-el' is doing quiet work in both words.

questions.q: 'Bitmap' and 'bitrate' both use 'bit', a word coined by shortening…?
questions.f: John Tukey's contraction was so natural that few people notice it is a portmanteau at all.

questions.q: The verb 'to boot' a computer comes from a saying about lifting yourself by your own…?
questions.f: The image is deliberately impossible, which is why the trick of loading a loader felt so clever.

questions.q: 'Kernel' and 'corn' are related words, both descending from a root meaning…?
questions.f: A kernel is a little grain — the diminutive form gave English the name for a system's essential core.

questions.q: 'Robotics', 'positronic', and the Three Laws all trace to which author's coinages?
questions.f: Asimov invented 'robotics' by accident in 1941, assuming the word must already exist.

questions.q: Capek's play used 'robot' for artificial workers made of what material?
questions.f: His robots were grown in vats, closer to today's clones than to metal machines.

questions.q: 'Golem', a legendary artificial servant that influenced robot stories, comes from a Hebrew word meaning…?
questions.f: The Prague golem legend is often called the ancestor of every runaway-machine story since.

questions.q: 'Automaton' descends from Greek roots meaning acting…?
questions.f: 'Autos' (self) plus 'matos' (thinking or willing) — a machine that appears to want to move.

questions.q: 'Servomechanism', shortened to servo, takes its first part from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: The same root gives 'serve' and 'servant' — a servo obediently follows its command signal.

questions.q: 'Gyroscope', vital in robot balance, is built from Greek parts meaning…?
questions.f: Foucault coined it in 1852 for a device that let you watch the Earth's rotation.

questions.q: 'Actuator', the part that makes a robot move, comes from a Latin verb meaning to…?
questions.f: From 'agere', to act or drive — the same root as agent, agile, and agenda.

questions.q: 'Telemetry' combines Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: Mars rovers send telemetry home, letting engineers measure a machine hundreds of millions of kilometres away.

questions.q: 'Haptic' feedback, the buzz in a controller, comes from a Greek word meaning to…?
questions.f: From 'haptesthai', to grasp — haptic engineers design sensations you feel rather than see.

questions.q: 'Stereoscopic', as in VR displays, uses a Greek root meaning…?
questions.f: From 'stereos' (solid): two flat images give the brain a solid-looking world.

questions.q: 'Holography' is built from Greek roots meaning…?
questions.f: Dennis Gabor coined it because a hologram records the whole wavefront, not just brightness.

questions.q: 'Laser' is an acronym in which the final letter stands for…?
questions.f: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation — an acronym so smooth it became a verb.

questions.q: 'Modem', 'codec', and 'pixel' are all examples of which kind of word formation?
questions.f: Lewis Carroll named portmanteau words after a suitcase that opens into two halves.

questions.q: A Latin phrase meaning by itself, a chant recited just after the letter Z, and a symbol formed by joining E and T describe which character's name?
questions.f: Children chanted X, Y, Z, and per se and — which slurred together into a single word.

questions.q: The 'octothorpe' name for # is one theory's product; another traces the symbol to a squeezed abbreviation of which Latin word?
questions.f: 'lb' for pounds weight, written with a bar across it, collapsed into the hash we type today.

questions.q: The 'asterisk' used as a wildcard in searches gets its name from a Greek word meaning…?
questions.f: From 'asteriskos' — the same 'aster' that names the flower and the word disaster ('bad star').

questions.q: 'Tilde', the ~ used in file paths, reached English from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: Scribes drew a little 'titulus' above letters to mark omissions, and it survives in Spanish and Unix.

questions.q: 'Caret', the ^ symbol, is Latin for…?
questions.f: Proofreaders wrote it to show that something was missing — a word 'lacking' from the line.

questions.q: 'Slash' and 'solidus' both name the / character, and 'solidus' was originally a Roman…?
questions.f: The coin's name lived on in accounting, where the stroke separated shillings from pence.

questions.q: 'Backslash', a symbol invented in the ASCII era, was originally added to write which logic symbols?
questions.f: Bob Bemer proposed it in 1961 so Algol's logical operators could be typed as /\ and \/.

questions.q: The father of the escape character, an early and ignored warning about two-digit years, and the man who proposed the backslash point to which engineer?
questions.f: He proposed the backslash in 1961 and spent decades warning anyone who would listen about Y2K.

questions.q: An 'escape sequence' in code is so named because it lets a character…?
c: Break out of its normal meaning
questions.f: A backslash tells the computer 'the next character escapes the usual rules' — hence \n for a new line.

questions.q: The mysterious 'foobar' of programming examples is often traced to a wartime military abbreviation meaning…?
questions.f: Engineers had used 'foo' in comics and cartoons even earlier, so the trail is delightfully tangled.

questions.q: A 1962 humour piece about an absurd fictional computer, a definition about poorly matching parts, and a word for a fix that works anyway describe which term?
questions.f: Jackson Granholm's definition was so apt that programmers adopted the word almost immediately.

questions.q: 'Cruft', meaning leftover useless code, is believed to come from a building nickname at which university?
questions.f: Harvard's Cruft Laboratory reputedly accumulated junk, and the name became a programmer's insult.

questions.q: 'Bogosort', a joke algorithm, sorts a list by…?
c: Shuffling randomly until it happens to be sorted
questions.f: On average it takes longer than the age of the universe for even a modest list — hence the name.

questions.q: A logician fascinated by self-reference, a program whose only output is its own source code, and a puzzle Hofstadter loved describe which term?
questions.f: Willard Van Orman Quine studied self-reference; Douglas Hofstadter borrowed his name for the stunt.

questions.q: A committee that waved a nuclear plant through in minutes, an hour lost to a shed for bicycles, and Parkinson's law of triviality describe which habit?
questions.f: Everyone had strong opinions about the shed, because everyone understood sheds.

questions.q: 'Hofstadter's law' states that a project always takes longer than expected, even when…?
questions.f: The law is deliberately self-referential — its author wrote a whole book celebrating such loops.

questions.q: 'Cargo cult programming' means copying code without understanding why it works.
questions.f: Richard Feynman's cargo cult image describes going through the motions and expecting results anyway.

questions.q: A team's 'bus factor' counts how many people could vanish before the project stalls.
questions.f: A bus factor of one is the nightmare: a single person holds knowledge nobody else has.

questions.q: 'Dogfooding' means a company uses its own product internally before customers do.
questions.f: The phrase spread at Microsoft in 1988, from an advert where a boss ate his own brand's dog food.

questions.q: 'Bit rot' describes software breaking over time even though its code never changed.
questions.f: Everything around it moved on — libraries, systems, and assumptions all quietly drifted.

questions.q: 'Rubber ducking', 'yak shaving', and 'bikeshedding' all belong to which category of language?
questions.f: Programmers coin metaphors relentlessly, because the work is invisible and needs pictures to discuss.

questions.q: A whimsical file format signature, a word meaning 'magic', and the first bytes that identify a file type describe which concept?
questions.f: Every PNG file starts with the same eight bytes, so a program can recognise it without trusting the filename.

questions.q: The PDF, PNG, and ZIP formats all begin with a fixed signature so software can identify them. What is this called?
questions.f: ZIP files begin with the letters PK — the initials of their inventor, Phil Katz.

questions.q: The GIF format's compression method, LZW, is named after three researchers, the last being…?
questions.f: Lempel, Ziv, and Welch — a patent on their method once caused a web-wide campaign to switch to PNG.

questions.q: A patent dispute over a compression method, a recursive name declaring what it is not, and a format built as a free replacement describe which image type?
questions.f: PNG's Not GIF — the joke echoes GNU, and the web-wide campaign of 1995 made the format a standard.

questions.q: JPEG compression works by throwing away detail the human eye…?
questions.f: That is why saving a JPEG repeatedly slowly smears it — each save discards a little more.

questions.q: MP3's compression relies on 'psychoacoustics', the study of…?
questions.f: It deletes sounds masked by louder ones, because your ear would never have heard them anyway.

questions.q: A German research institute, an a cappella song called Tom's Diner used for tuning, and a format that discards sounds you could never hear point to whose laboratory?
questions.f: Its developers famously tuned the codec using Suzanne Vega's a cappella song 'Tom's Diner'.

questions.q: 'Lossless' compression differs from 'lossy' because it…?
questions.f: Text and program files must be lossless — a single wrong bit can break a program completely.

questions.q: A student who chose a term paper over sitting the final exam, a professor whose own method was beaten, and an optimal code taught everywhere point to whom?
questions.f: Huffman's homework beat the scheme devised by his own professor, Robert Fano.

questions.q: 'Checksum' and 'parity bit' both help a computer detect…?
c: Errors in stored or sent data
questions.f: A single parity bit can reveal that something went wrong, though not exactly where.

questions.q: A 'race condition' in a program happens when the result depends on…?
c: The unpredictable timing of separate tasks
questions.f: The Therac-25 medical accidents in the 1980s were traced partly to a race condition in the software.

questions.q: 'Deadlock' between two programs occurs when each is…?
c: Waiting for a resource the other holds
questions.f: The classic illustration is the dining philosophers problem, posed by Dijkstra in 1965.

questions.q: 'Thrashing' in an operating system means the machine spends most of its time…?
c: Moving data between memory and disk
questions.f: The computer works furiously and achieves almost nothing — a state every user recognises.

questions.q: 'Buffer overflow', a classic security flaw, happens when data is written…?
c: Past the end of its allotted space
questions.f: The 1988 Morris worm used one, and the same class of bug still causes serious breaches today.

questions.q: 'Off-by-one errors' are so common that programmers joke there are only three hard problems in computing:…?
c: Naming things, cache invalidation, and off-by-one errors
questions.f: The joke itself is usually delivered as a list of two — because the third is an off-by-one error.

questions.q: Which naming convention writes variables like 'myVariableName'?
questions.f: The humps give it away — and the version starting with a capital is called Pascal case.

questions.q: Writing identifiers as 'my_variable_name' is known as…?
questions.f: Hyphenated 'my-variable-name' is kebab case, because the words look skewered.

questions.q: A Budapest-born programmer at Xerox PARC, letters glued to the front of variable names, and a convention Microsoft adopted wholesale describe which style?
questions.f: Charles Simonyi invented it, and it is named for his nationality rather than for any language.

questions.q: A 'regular expression', or regex, is a compact way to describe…?
questions.f: Ken Thompson built them into Unix tools, and the mathematics behind them dates to the 1950s.

questions.q: 'Grep', a Unix command for searching text, takes its name from an editor instruction meaning…?
questions.f: Programmers now use 'grep' as an everyday verb, even away from computers.

questions.q: Years of arguing for a single idea, an overnight implementation that made the lab cheer, and the vertical bar joining Unix commands point to whom?
questions.f: McIlroy pushed for it for years; when Thompson finally implemented it overnight, the lab cheered.

questions.q: The Unix philosophy is often summed up as 'do one thing and…'?
questions.f: Doug McIlroy's summary explains why tiny tools joined by pipes outlived enormous monolithic programs.

questions.q: A 'shebang' at the top of a script, written #!, tells the system…?
questions.f: The name blends 'sharp' and 'bang', old nicknames for the two characters.

questions.q: 'Bang', 'splat', 'twiddle', and 'sharp' are all informal names for computing…?
questions.f: Programmers needed to read symbols aloud fast, so a whole spoken vocabulary grew up around them.

questions.q: 'Vi' and 'Emacs', two legendary editors, are the subject of a long-running…?
c: Friendly rivalry called an editor war
questions.f: The joke religion 'Church of Emacs' has Richard Stallman as its self-declared Saint IGNUcius.

questions.q: A 300-baud connection that made every keystroke precious, a name short for visual, and commands so terse they baffle newcomers describe which editor?
questions.f: Bill Joy wrote it over a 300-baud line, which is why its commands are so terse — every keystroke hurt.

questions.q: A five-bit telegraph code older than ASCII, a unit of signalling speed, and a nineteenth-century French engineer's surname point to whom?
questions.f: Baudot's five-bit telegraph code predates ASCII by decades and still influences character encoding.

questions.q: 'Teletype' machines gave Unix the abbreviation 'tty', which still appears when you…?
questions.f: Modern Linux still calls its consoles tty, honouring machines that clattered like typewriters.

questions.q: The 'carriage return' and 'line feed' characters are named after two separate actions of a…?
questions.f: That old split is why Windows uses both characters for a new line while Unix uses just one.

questions.q: 'Daemon', 'zombie', and 'orphan' are all technical names for kinds of…?
questions.f: A zombie process has finished but lingers in the table until its parent reads its exit status.

questions.q: 'Fork', in Unix and in open-source projects, means to…?
questions.f: The word works for both a process copying itself and a community splitting a codebase.

questions.q: A 'semaphore' in programming borrows its name from a signalling system using…?
questions.f: From Greek 'sema' (sign) and 'phoros' (bearing) — a semaphore signals whether it is safe to proceed.

questions.q: 'Mutex', a programming lock, is a contraction of which phrase?
questions.f: Only one thread may hold it at a time — mutual exclusion is exactly the guarantee it provides.

questions.q: A fault that vanishes when observed, one that is reliably repeatable, and one whose causes seem fractal are all named after which sort of people?
questions.f: A mandelbug's causes are so complex they seem fractal — named after Benoit Mandelbrot.

questions.q: The 'Mandelbrot set', often rendered as glowing computer art, is an example of a…?
questions.f: Zoom in forever and new detail keeps appearing — a shape only computers could reveal.

questions.q: 'Fractal' was coined by Mandelbrot from a Latin word meaning…?
questions.f: From 'fractus' — the same root as fracture, describing shapes too rough for ordinary geometry.

questions.q: Conway's 'Game of Life' is a famous example of which kind of system?
questions.f: Its four simple rules produce gliders, guns, and even a working computer built inside the game.

questions.q: A five-cell pattern found in 1970, a shape that walks diagonally across the grid forever, and an emblem adopted by hacker culture in 2003 describe what?
questions.f: The glider became the unofficial emblem of hacker culture, adopted as a symbol in 2003.

questions.q: 'Turing complete' describes a system powerful enough to…?
c: Compute anything a Turing machine can
questions.f: Surprising things are Turing complete, including some spreadsheet formulas and certain card games.

questions.q: A 'quantum' advantage claim rests on a machine solving in minutes a task a classical computer would need…?
questions.f: Every such claim gets fiercely rechecked, because clever classical algorithms sometimes catch up.

questions.q: Shor's algorithm, a landmark in quantum computing, would threaten today's encryption by quickly…?
questions.f: Peter Shor's 1994 result is why cryptographers are already designing post-quantum systems.

questions.q: Public-key cryptography's famous RSA algorithm is named after…?
c: The initials of its three inventors
questions.f: Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman published in 1977 — and British cryptographers had found it secretly earlier.

questions.q: A 1973 idea locked away for over twenty years, a mathematician at GCHQ, and three Americans who received all the credit point to whom?
questions.f: His 1973 work was classified until 1997, so three Americans got the fame and the algorithm's name.

questions.q: 'Diffie-Hellman key exchange' lets two people agree a secret while…?
questions.f: It sounds impossible, which is why its 1976 publication astonished the cryptography world.

questions.q: A 'one-time pad' is the only cipher proved unbreakable, provided the key is…?
questions.f: Shannon proved its perfect secrecy mathematically — its weakness is entirely practical, not theoretical.

questions.q: 'Steganography' differs from cryptography because it…?
c: Hides that a message exists at all
questions.f: From Greek for 'covered writing' — a message can hide in the least significant bits of a photo.

questions.q: 'Kerckhoffs's principle' in security says a system should stay secure even if…?
c: Everything but the key is public
questions.f: That is why serious cryptography is published openly — secrecy of design is not a defence.

questions.q: 'Security through obscurity' relies on attackers never discovering how a system works.
questions.f: Once the trick leaks the whole defence evaporates — which history shows happens reliably.

questions.q: A graduate student's 1988 experiment, an internet brought to its knees overnight, and an organisation founded within days describe which kind of body?
questions.f: CERT was created within days, because nobody had a plan for an internet-wide incident.

questions.q: 'Ransomware' attacks work by encrypting files and demanding payment for the…?
questions.f: The best defence is dull: keep offline backups, and the attacker's leverage disappears.

questions.q: A 'botnet' is a network of…?
questions.f: Their controllers call the infected machines 'zombies', and a single botnet can span millions of them.

questions.q: An air-gapped computer is one kept physically disconnected from every network.
questions.f: Even air-gapped systems have been reached — famously by malware carried in on USB sticks.

questions.q: The 'CIA triad' in information security stands for confidentiality, integrity, and…?
questions.f: A system nobody can reach is not secure either — availability is as much a goal as secrecy.

questions.q: 'Latency' and 'throughput' can be traded off. Which does a satellite link typically suffer from?
questions.f: Signals to geostationary orbit and back travel about 70,000 kilometres — you can hear the delay.

questions.q: A hierarchy of comp, sci, rec, and talk, an upheaval of 1987 called the Great Renaming, and discussion groups older than the web describe which system?
questions.f: It created the familiar hierarchy of comp, sci, rec, and talk groups that shaped online conversation.

questions.q: A lawyer's deliberate 1990 coinage, a countermeasure designed to fight a meme with a meme, and an inevitability in long arguments predict what?
questions.f: Mike Godwin invented it deliberately as a memetic countermeasure — a meme designed to fight a meme.

questions.q: A missing tone of voice, the reason the /s tag was invented, and a warning about satire nobody can distinguish describe which law's claim?
questions.f: It is why the winking emoji and '/s' tag exist — text strips away the tone of voice.

questions.q: The word 'algorithm' and the word 'algebra' both trace back to the same ninth-century mathematician.
questions.f: Al-Khwarizmi gave his name to one and his book's title to the other — a rare double.

questions.q: Public-key cryptography was invented in secret by British government researchers before it was published in America.
questions.f: Clifford Cocks worked it out in 1973, but the discovery stayed classified for over twenty years.

questions.q: The Game Boy's designer built his career on deliberately using cheap, outdated components.
questions.f: Gunpei Yokoi called it 'lateral thinking with withered technology' — reliable, cheap, and endlessly inventive.

questions.q: "Hola" is a cheerful hello in which language?
questions.f: Spanish is spoken in Spain, Mexico and most of South America.

questions.q: In France, people greet each other with...?
questions.f: "Bonjour" literally means "good day" in French.

questions.q: What is the dot at the end of a sentence called?
questions.f: In Britain the very same dot is called a "full stop."

questions.q: Which mark goes at the end of a question?
questions.f: The curly question mark tells your voice to go up at the end.

questions.q: Which mark shows excitement, as in "Wow!"?
questions.f: Writers try not to use too many — one "!" is plenty of excitement.

questions.q: What is the first letter of the alphabet?
questions.f: The letter A began long ago as a picture of an ox's head.

questions.q: Sign language is a way of talking with your...?
questions.f: Sign languages are full languages with their own words and grammar.

questions.q: Braille lets people read by touching raised...?
questions.f: Readers slide their fingertips across the bumps to feel each letter.

questions.q: A book that explains what words mean is called a...?
questions.f: Big dictionaries explain hundreds of thousands of words.

questions.q: Words like "cat" and "hat" that end with the same sound are said to...?
questions.f: Rhymes make poems and songs fun to remember.

questions.q: In Japan, "konnichiwa" is a way to say hello.
questions.f: It is used in the daytime — Japanese has different greetings for morning and evening.

questions.q: To make "dog" mean more than one dog, which letter do you add?
questions.f: Adding -s is the most common way to make English words plural.

questions.q: "Ciao" can mean both hello and goodbye in which country?
questions.f: Italians use "ciao" coming and going, just like "aloha" in Hawaii.

questions.q: Which language do most people speak in Mexico?
questions.f: Mexico has more Spanish speakers than any other country — even more than Spain!

questions.q: English words are read from left to right.
questions.f: Some languages, like Arabic and Hebrew, are read from right to left instead.

questions.q: Big letters like A, B and C are called...?
questions.f: The small ones — a, b, c — are called lowercase letters.

questions.q: "Namaste" is a friendly greeting from India.
questions.f: It is often said with the palms pressed together in front of the chest.

questions.q: Which letter comes right after B?
questions.f: A, B, C — the first three letters gave the alphabet its nickname, the ABCs.

questions.q: Which letter sits between L and N?
questions.f: M makes the humming sound you can say with your lips closed.

questions.q: How many vowel letters does English have?
questions.f: A, E, I, O, U — and the letter Y sometimes acts like a vowel too.

questions.q: The word "pizza" came into English from Italy.
questions.f: English borrows tasty words from everywhere — pizza and spaghetti are both Italian.

questions.q: What do we leave between two written words?
questions.f: Long ago some people wrote with no spaces at all — itwasveryhardtoread!

questions.q: Which word means the opposite of "big"?
questions.f: Opposite words like big and small are called antonyms.

questions.q: Which word means almost the same as "happy"?
questions.f: Words with almost the same meaning are called synonyms.

questions.q: Which word is the sound a cat makes?
questions.f: In Japan, people say cats go "nyan" — animal sounds change between languages!

questions.q: Where do people greet each other with "aloha"?
questions.f: "Aloha" can mean hello, goodbye and love, all in one little word.

questions.q: Which of these is a letter, not a number?
questions.f: Letters build words, and numbers count things — B is a letter.

questions.q: "Taco" is a word English borrowed from Spanish.
questions.f: English is full of borrowed food words, like taco, sushi and croissant.

questions.q: Which language do people speak in France?
questions.f: French is spoken in many countries, including Canada and Senegal.

questions.q: What is the main language of China?
questions.f: Mandarin Chinese has more native speakers than any other language on Earth.

questions.q: In many languages around the world, the word for mother sounds like "mama."
questions.f: "Ma" is one of the easiest sounds for babies to make, so it became mom's name.

questions.q: The word "buzz" sounds like the noise it names.
questions.f: Sound-copying words like buzz, pop and splash are called onomatopoeia.

questions.q: Which letter makes a hissing sound like a snake?
questions.f: S is one of the most common starting letters for English words.

questions.q: What goes at the start of every written sentence?
questions.f: A capital letter at the start and a mark at the end frame every sentence.

questions.q: "Adios" means what in English?
questions.f: It is Spanish, and cowboys in old movies love to say it.

questions.q: In French, "merci" means...?
questions.f: Say "merci beaucoup" to mean "thank you very much."

questions.q: "Gracias" is the Spanish word for...?
questions.f: It comes from an old Latin word meaning thanks and grace.

questions.q: Which of these is a question?
questions.f: Questions in English often start with words like what, who, where and why.

questions.q: Cat, bat and hat all...?
questions.f: They share the same "-at" ending, which makes them a rhyming family.

questions.q: All the letters from A to Z together are called the...?
questions.f: The word "alphabet" comes from alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters.

questions.q: Which word starts with the same sound as "ball"?
questions.f: Words that repeat a starting sound make tongue twisters like "big blue balloons."

questions.q: "Arigato" means thank you in which country?
questions.f: For extra politeness, Japanese speakers say "arigato gozaimasu."

questions.q: Which letter looks like a circle?
questions.f: O has kept its round shape for about 3,000 years of alphabet history.

questions.q: How do you say "yes" in Spanish?
questions.f: The other three choices all mean "no" — in French, German and Russian!

questions.q: How many letters are in the word "bee"?
questions.f: "Bee" is also the name of a spelling contest — a spelling bee!

questions.q: More than one mouse are called...?
questions.f: English has funny plurals — one mouse, two mice, but one house, two houses!

questions.q: What is the plural of "foot"?
questions.f: Foot/feet and tooth/teeth follow the same old vowel-swapping pattern.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of "hot"?
questions.f: Hot and cold are antonyms — words with opposite meanings.

questions.q: Which word means the same as "small"?
questions.f: English often has two words for one idea because it borrowed from many languages.

questions.q: In Germany, people speak...?
questions.f: German is famous for long words built by gluing smaller words together.

questions.q: What language do people speak in Italy?
questions.f: Italian grew out of Latin, the language of ancient Rome.

questions.q: Which word is a Japanese way to say goodbye?
questions.f: "Sayonara" became so famous that English speakers use it for goodbye too.

questions.q: A group of words that tells a complete idea is a...?
questions.f: Even one word can be a sentence — like "Stop!"

questions.q: Which of these words names an action?
questions.f: Action words are called verbs — every sentence needs one.

questions.q: On a door, the word "EXIT" shows you the way...?
questions.f: "Exit" comes from Latin and literally means "he goes out."

questions.q: Which word rhymes with "dog"?
questions.f: Dog, frog, log and jog all belong to the "-og" rhyme family.

questions.q: Which letter comes just before Z?
questions.f: Y is the only letter that works as both a consonant and a vowel.

questions.q: "Uno, dos, tres" is counting in which language?
questions.f: Spanish numbers come from Latin — Roman soldiers counted almost the same way.

questions.q: "Un, deux, trois" is one, two, three in...?
questions.f: French counting gets tricky later — their word for 80 means "four twenties"!

questions.q: The word "wow" reads the same backward as forward.
questions.f: Flip "wow" upside down and it even turns into "mom"!

questions.q: Spelling a word with hand shapes, one letter at a time, is called...?
questions.f: Signers use finger spelling for names and new words.

questions.q: In English, what do many people say when someone sneezes?
questions.f: In Germany people say "Gesundheit," which means "health."

questions.q: Which word starts with the same sound as "cheese"?
questions.f: The letters c and h team up to make the "ch" sound — two letters, one sound.

questions.q: Which of these words has exactly four letters?
questions.f: Counting letters carefully is a spelling champion's first skill.

questions.q: Short rhyming poems for young children are called nursery...?
questions.f: Some nursery rhymes, like "Humpty Dumpty," are hundreds of years old.

questions.q: In which puzzle do you hunt for words hidden in a grid of letters?
questions.f: Words in a word search can hide sideways, downward and even diagonally.

questions.q: Which puzzle has numbered word clues going across and down?
questions.f: The first crossword puzzle appeared in a New York newspaper in 1913.

questions.q: Scrabble is a game where you build words from letter tiles.
questions.f: In Scrabble, rare letters like Q and Z are worth ten points each.

questions.q: A spelling bee is a contest where you spell words out loud.
questions.f: The biggest one, the Scripps National Spelling Bee, has run since 1925.

questions.q: How many letters come before D in the alphabet?
questions.f: A, B, C — then D, whose ancient shape began as a picture of a door.

questions.q: Which spelling of the word for a pal is right?
questions.f: A trick to remember it: a friend is there to the END — f-r-i-END.

questions.q: How do you spell the place where you learn?
questions.f: "School" keeps a quiet h from its Greek great-grandparent word.

questions.q: Pick the correct spelling of the word for a home.
questions.f: "House" is one of English's oldest words, over a thousand years old.

questions.q: "Buenas noches" is Spanish for...?
questions.f: "Buenos dias" is the morning version — good day!

questions.q: "Danke" is thank you in which language?
questions.f: "Danke" and English "thanks" are cousins from the same old word family.

questions.q: "Please" and "thank you" are often called...?
questions.f: "Please" is a short way of saying the older phrase "if you please."

questions.q: What is this mark called: , ?
questions.f: A comma tells the reader to take a tiny pause.

questions.q: Which mark is used in the word "don't"?
questions.f: The apostrophe shows where the missing letter of "do not" used to be.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of "up"?
questions.f: Little direction words like up, down, in and out are among English's oldest.

questions.q: Adding "-er" to "sing" makes "singer," which means...?
questions.f: The -er ending turns actions into people: sing-singer, teach-teacher.

questions.q: Which word means a person who paints pictures?
questions.f: Add -er to a job action and you name the person who does it.

questions.q: Which of these words is made of two smaller words?
questions.f: Rain + bow — words glued together like this are called compound words.

questions.q: "Cupcake" is made from the words "cup" and "cake."
questions.f: Cupcakes got the name because they were first baked in little cups.

questions.q: Which compound word means a box for letters and mail?
questions.f: Compound words pack two ideas into one: mail + box.

questions.q: Star + fish makes the word...?
questions.f: Scientists now prefer "sea star," since a starfish is not really a fish.

questions.q: Your own name should start with a capital letter.
questions.f: Names of people, places and pets all get capital letters in English.

questions.q: In English, days of the week start with capital letters.
questions.f: In Spanish and French, day names are written with small letters!

questions.q: Which day of the week has "sun" in its name?
questions.f: Sunday was named the day of the sun nearly two thousand years ago.

questions.q: "Monday" began as the day of the...?
questions.f: Old English "monandaeg" meant moon's day — Monday!

questions.q: The name of a book printed on its cover is called the...?
questions.f: "Title" comes from a Latin word for a label or sign.

questions.q: The person who draws the pictures in a picture book is the...?
questions.f: "Illustrate" comes from a Latin word meaning to light up or make bright.

questions.q: "Don't" is a short way of writing...?
questions.f: Squeezed-together words like don't and can't are called contractions.

questions.q: "I'm" is short for...?
questions.f: The apostrophe stands in for the missing letter a.

questions.q: "Can't" is a short way of saying...?
questions.f: "Cannot" is one of the few English words made of two words stuck together with no space.

questions.q: When you write about yourself, the word "I" is always a capital letter.
questions.f: English is unusual — most languages do not capitalize their word for "I."

questions.q: Which word means very, very big?
questions.f: English piles up size words: big, huge, giant, enormous, gigantic!

questions.q: "Ni hao" is hello in which language?
questions.f: "Ni hao" literally means "you good" in Mandarin Chinese.

questions.q: In Korea, "annyeong" is a friendly way to say...?
questions.f: The longer, extra-polite version is "annyeonghaseyo."

questions.q: How do you spell the number 2?
questions.f: To, too and two all sound the same — English loves sound-alike words!

questions.q: Which number word rhymes with "gate"?
questions.f: "Eight" hides a silent g and h — you write them but never say them.

questions.q: Which word is the opposite of "open"?
questions.f: Signs use opposite pairs all day: open/closed, push/pull, on/off.

questions.q: "Oui" means yes in which language?
questions.f: It sounds like "wee" — French for yes is just one tiny syllable.

questions.q: A building where you can borrow books is a...?
questions.f: "Library" comes from "liber," the Latin word for book.

questions.q: A person who helps you find books in a library is a...?
questions.f: The -ian ending often names a person, like librarian and musician.

questions.q: What do most English speakers say when they answer the phone?
questions.f: In Italy people answer "pronto," which means "ready!"

questions.q: Waving your hand can mean either hello or goodbye.
questions.f: Gestures are a kind of language too, but they differ from country to country.

questions.q: Nodding your head up and down usually means...?
questions.f: In a few countries, like Bulgaria, the head signals for yes and no are swapped!

questions.q: Which spelling answers the question "why"?
questions.f: A silly memory trick: Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants.

questions.q: How do you spell the word for what you drink?
questions.f: "Water" is such an old word that German still says almost the same: Wasser.

questions.q: Which greeting would you hear in Kenya?
questions.f: "Jambo" is Swahili, a language spoken across East Africa.

questions.q: Which sport word came to English from Japan?
questions.f: Karate literally means "empty hand" in Japanese.

questions.q: Which dance word came to English from France?
questions.f: Ballet began in royal courts, so many ballet words are French.

questions.q: Which food word came to English from Italy?
questions.f: Spaghetti is Italian for "little strings" — which is just what it looks like!

questions.q: Which word is a greeting?
questions.f: "Hello" only became the favorite English greeting after telephones arrived.

questions.q: A, B and C are all...?
questions.f: Letters stand for sounds, and together they build every word you know.

questions.q: Which word names the meal you eat in the morning?
questions.f: In France it is "petit dejeuner" and in Spain "desayuno."

questions.q: Which word rhymes with "mouse"?
questions.f: Mouse and house rhyme, but their plurals don't — mice and houses!

questions.q: Letters that are not capitals are called...?
questions.f: Printers once kept small letters in a lower drawer, or "case" — that's the name!

questions.q: A made-up story is called...?
questions.f: Its opposite, nonfiction, means writing about real things.

questions.q: How many letters does the word "moon" have?
questions.f: The double o in "moon" makes a long "oo" sound, like in "soon."

questions.q: You read an English book from the front cover to the back.
questions.f: Japanese books often open the other way, with the spine on the right.

questions.q: In Spanish, "amigo" means...?
questions.f: "Amigo" comes from "amicus," the Latin word for friend.

questions.q: "Bon appetit!" is said in France before...?
questions.f: It means "good appetite" — a wish to enjoy your meal.

questions.q: You say "goodbye" when someone is...?
questions.f: "Goodbye" started long ago as the blessing "God be with ye."

questions.q: Which spelling of the word meaning "small" is correct?
questions.f: Many English words end in -le: little, apple, purple, table.

questions.q: "Salut!" is a casual hello in which language?
questions.f: French friends say "salut" for both hi and bye.

questions.q: The two words inside "snowman" are snow and...?
questions.f: Compound words are like word LEGO — snap two together to build a new one.

questions.q: Letters make words, and words make...?
questions.f: Sentences then build paragraphs, stories and whole books.

questions.q: "Shalom" is a Hebrew word used as a greeting that also means peace.
questions.f: Arabic has a matching greeting, "salaam," which also means peace.

questions.q: Which language do many people in India speak?
questions.f: India has hundreds of languages — Hindi is the most widely spoken.

questions.q: A person enjoying a book is called a...?
questions.f: Reading silently in your head was once rare — most people read out loud!

questions.q: When you speak the printed words of a book, you read...?
questions.f: "Aloud" and "allowed" sound exactly alike but mean different things.

questions.q: "Guten Tag" means good day in which language?
questions.f: "Tag" means day in German — and "Guten Morgen" is good morning.

questions.q: Which spelling of the word for lots of persons is right?
questions.f: Remember: PEOple — the o hides quietly in the middle.

questions.q: The word "hi" is a short, friendly...?
questions.f: "Hi" is one of the shortest words in English — just two letters.

questions.q: Some children grow up speaking two languages at home.
questions.f: Being able to speak two languages is called being bilingual.

questions.q: "Konnichiwa," "hola" and "bonjour" are all ways to say...?
questions.f: There are thousands of languages, so there are thousands of ways to say hi!

questions.q: What is the last letter of the word "fox"?
questions.f: X is one of the rarest letters — very few English words use it.

questions.q: Which word gets a capital letter because it is a place's name?
questions.f: Names of cities, countries and rivers always start with capitals in English.

questions.q: The alphabet has more letters than you have fingers and toes.
questions.f: 26 letters beats 20 fingers and toes — by exactly six!

questions.q: Letters that are not vowels are called...?
questions.f: English has 21 consonant letters, and some, like C, can make more than one sound.

questions.q: How many syllables does "banana" have?
questions.f: Clap as you say it — ba-na-na — each clap is one syllable.

questions.q: A word that names a person, place or thing is a...?
questions.f: "Noun" comes from the Latin word "nomen," meaning name.

questions.q: A describing word, like "shiny" or "tall," is called an...?
questions.f: In French and Spanish, adjectives usually come after the noun instead of before.

questions.q: "Won't" is the tricky short form of...?
questions.f: It kept an old form of "will" — that's why it isn't spelled "willn't."

questions.q: Which word sounds exactly like "sea"?
questions.f: Sound-alike words with different meanings are called homophones.

questions.q: Words like "their," "there" and "they're" that sound alike are called...?
questions.f: "Homophone" is built from Greek parts meaning "same sound."

questions.q: The ending "-ful" in "careful" means...?
questions.f: Careful literally means "full of care."

questions.q: A person who speaks two languages is called...?
questions.f: "Bi" means two and "lingua" means tongue — two-tongued!

questions.q: What language do most people in Brazil speak?
questions.f: Brazil has more Portuguese speakers than Portugal — about 20 times more!

questions.q: Canada has two official languages: English and...?
questions.f: That's why Canadian cereal boxes are printed in both languages.

questions.q: Arabic is written from right to left.
questions.f: Arabic books open from what English readers would call the back cover.

questions.q: Chinese is written with characters that stand for words and ideas, not letters.
questions.f: A well-read person in China knows several thousand characters.

questions.q: Ancient Egyptians wrote with picture symbols called...?
questions.f: Some hieroglyphs stand for sounds, so they could spell out names too.

questions.q: Paper was invented about 2,000 years ago in which country?
questions.f: Before paper, Egyptians wrote on papyrus — the plant that gave paper its name.

questions.q: Long ago, pens were made from what?
questions.f: A feather pen is called a quill — "pen" itself comes from Latin "penna," feather!

questions.q: A single Braille letter is built from up to how many raised dots?
questions.f: Those six dots can be arranged into 63 different patterns.

questions.q: "Kindergarten" literally means...?
questions.f: The word came from German — the first kindergartens opened in Germany in the 1830s.

questions.q: The hamburger is named after Hamburg, a city in Germany.
questions.f: No ham needed — the name comes from "Hamburg steak."

questions.q: Karaoke singing first became popular in which country?
questions.f: The word "karaoke" itself is Japanese, and machines spread worldwide from there.

questions.q: The croissant is named after its shape. What does "croissant" mean?
questions.f: It is the French word for a crescent moon shape.

questions.q: Which word comes first in a dictionary?
questions.f: Dictionaries have used alphabetical order for about 400 years.

questions.q: Words in a dictionary are arranged in which order?
questions.f: Early word lists were sometimes sorted by topic instead — much harder to search!

questions.q: Which letter appears most often in English writing?
questions.f: E is so common that some writers have tried writing whole books without it!

questions.q: In English words, which letter almost always follows Q?
questions.f: Queen, quick, quiet — the Q-U team came to English from Latin spelling habits.

questions.q: In the sentence "I read a book," which word is the verb?
questions.f: "Read" is odd — present and past are spelled the same but said differently!

questions.q: How many syllables does "elephant" have?
questions.f: El-e-phant — long words break into syllable chunks that make spelling easier.

questions.q: Which of these words imitates a real sound?
questions.f: Splash, bang and hiss are onomatopoeia — words that echo the noises they name.

questions.q: Antonyms are pairs of words that...?
questions.f: "Anti" means against or opposite — antonyms pull in opposite directions.

questions.q: Synonyms are words that...?
questions.f: English is rich in synonyms because it borrowed from so many languages.

questions.q: Which pair of words are synonyms?
questions.f: "Quick" is an old English word, while "rapid," its fancier cousin, came from Latin.

questions.q: Which pair of words are antonyms?
questions.f: The other three pairs are all synonyms — near twins in meaning.

questions.q: What is the plural of "child"?
questions.f: "Children" keeps a very old plural ending that most English words lost.

questions.q: What is the plural of "sheep"?
questions.f: Sheep, deer and fish usually stay the same whether there is one or a hundred.

questions.q: What is the plural of "tooth"?
questions.f: Goose becomes geese the same way — but moose never becomes meese!

questions.q: What is the main language of Egypt today?
questions.f: Arabic is spoken across more than 20 countries, from Morocco to Iraq.

questions.q: Spell "no" backward and you get which word?
questions.f: Word pairs like this — no/on, pot/top, was/saw — are fun little mirror words.

questions.q: Which word begins with a silent K?
questions.f: Long ago English speakers really did pronounce the k in knee and knight!

questions.q: Which word ends with a silent B?
questions.f: Lamb, comb and thumb all end in a b that went silent centuries ago.

questions.q: Which word begins with a silent W?
questions.f: Write, wrong and wrist keep a w that English mouths stopped saying long ago.

questions.q: A group of sentences about one main idea forms a...?
questions.f: "Paragraph" comes from a Greek mark scribes drew beside a new section.

questions.q: Cursive is a style of writing where the letters are...?
questions.f: "Cursive" comes from a Latin word meaning running — the pen runs along!

questions.q: A person who turns spoken words from one language into another is an...?
questions.f: Interpreters at the United Nations translate speeches while they are still being spoken!

questions.q: The first language you learn at home is called your mother...?
questions.f: "Tongue" has meant "language" in English for over a thousand years.

questions.q: Emoji are small pictures used in text messages.
questions.f: The word "emoji" is Japanese for "picture character."

questions.q: How is the symbol @ read aloud?
questions.f: In Italian the @ sign is called "chiocciola" — the snail!

questions.q: In a social media tag like #spelling, the # symbol is called a...?
questions.f: Before social media, # was mostly called the pound or number sign.

questions.q: What does it mean to "translate" something?
c: Change it from one language to another
questions.f: "Translate" comes from Latin for "carried across" — meaning carried between languages.

questions.q: Sign languages are exactly the same in every country.
questions.f: American and British Sign Language are so different that signers can't fully understand each other.

questions.q: Which day of the week hides a silent D in its spelling?
questions.f: Say it "Wed-nes-day" in your head and the spelling becomes easy.

questions.q: Which month is often misspelled because of a quiet first R?
questions.f: Feb-RU-ary — the sneaky r hides right after the b.

questions.q: All the words a person knows make up their...?
questions.f: "Vocabulary" grows from Latin "vox," meaning voice.

questions.q: The root "tele" in "telephone" means...?
questions.f: Telephone means "far sound" — and television means "far seeing."

questions.q: The root "phon" in "microphone" means...?
questions.f: Microphone means "small sound" — it catches sounds too faint to hear far away.

questions.q: The prefix "tri-" in "tricycle" means...?
questions.f: Triangle, tripod and triplets all carry that same "three."

questions.q: The prefix "re-" in "rewrite" means...?
questions.f: Rewrite, replay, return — re- sends you back for another go.

questions.q: "Alphabet" is built from the names of which two letters?
questions.f: Alpha and beta are the first two letters of the Greek alphabet.

questions.q: The word "dinosaur" is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: From deinos and sauros — the name was coined in 1841 by Richard Owen.

questions.q: The word "hippopotamus" literally means...?
questions.f: From Greek hippos (horse) and potamos (river) — a horse of the river.

questions.q: "Astronaut" is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: Russia's version, "cosmonaut," means "universe sailor."

questions.q: "Bicycle" is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Bi (two) plus cycle (wheel or circle) — two wheels!

questions.q: "Volcano" is named after Vulcan, who in Roman stories was god of...?
questions.f: Vulcano, an Italian island, was thought to be Vulcan's chimney.

questions.q: The word "museum" originally meant a place for the...?
questions.f: The Muses were the Greek goddesses of art and learning.

questions.q: "Sandwich" got its name from a...?
questions.f: The Earl of Sandwich liked meat between bread so he could keep playing cards.

questions.q: The word "chocolate" travelled into English from a language of...?
questions.f: It came from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, then through Spanish.

questions.q: "Ketchup" reached English through trade with which part of the world?
questions.f: The first ketchups were fish or mushroom sauces — tomatoes came much later!

questions.q: "Shampoo" came into English from India. It first meant to...?
questions.f: From Hindi "champo" — British traders brought both the word and the head massage home.

questions.q: "Bungalow" is a house word English borrowed from India. It meant a house from...?
questions.f: A "bangla" was a low house with a wide veranda — perfect for hot afternoons.

questions.q: "Safari" came into English from Swahili and means...?
questions.f: Swahili took the word from Arabic "safar," travel.

questions.q: "Tsunami" is built from Japanese words meaning...?
questions.f: Tsu (harbour) plus nami (wave) — the wave that swamps the harbour.

questions.q: "Kangaroo" came into English from an Aboriginal Australian language.
questions.f: It comes from Guugu Yimithirr "gangurru," a name for a large grey kangaroo.

questions.q: "Boomerang" is a word English borrowed from...?
questions.f: It comes from the Dharug language spoken near Sydney.

questions.q: "Igloo" came from Inuit languages, where it means...?
questions.f: An igloo does not have to be made of snow — the word covers any dwelling.

questions.q: Which of these English words came from Arabic?
questions.f: Arabic gave English many science words: algebra, algorithm, alcohol, zero.

questions.q: Latin was the everyday language of which ancient people?
questions.f: Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian all grew out of Latin.

questions.q: Languages that grew out of Latin, like Spanish and French, are called...?
questions.f: The name has nothing to do with love — it means "in the Roman style."

questions.q: Which country's language is Mandarin?
questions.f: Mandarin is a tonal language — the same syllable said at a different pitch means something else.

questions.q: There are more than 6,000 languages spoken in the world today.
questions.f: Roughly 7,000 — but nearly half have very few speakers left.

questions.q: Which continent has the most languages?
questions.f: Asia and Africa each have well over 2,000 living languages.

questions.q: Which country is famous for having over 800 languages?
questions.f: Steep mountains kept villages apart, so each valley developed its own language.

questions.q: Esperanto is unusual because it was...?
questions.f: A Polish eye doctor published it in 1887, hoping it would help nations get along.

questions.q: A language nobody speaks any more is called...?
questions.f: A language with only a few elderly speakers left is called endangered.

questions.q: The words "aquarium" and "terrain" both come from the language of which ancient people?
questions.f: Latin "aqua" means water and "terra" means land — both hide inside dozens of English words.

questions.q: The root "aqua" means...?
questions.f: Aquarium, aqueduct and aquatic all trace back to it.

questions.q: The root "terra" means...?
questions.f: Territory, terrain and terrace all grow from that same root.

questions.q: A word ending in "-ology" always names...?
questions.f: From Greek "logos" — word or reason. Zoology, geology and biology all follow the rule.

questions.q: A person who studies animals is a...?
questions.f: "Zoo" is Greek for animal — that's why the animal park is a zoo!

questions.q: "Autograph" is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Auto (self) plus graph (write) — you write it yourself.

questions.q: The root "graph" in "photograph" means...?
questions.f: Photograph means "light writing" — a picture drawn by light.

questions.q: The root "scrib" or "script" means...?
questions.f: Scribble, describe, manuscript and script all come from Latin "scribere."

questions.q: The Rosetta Stone helped scholars finally read...?
questions.f: It carried the same text in three scripts, so the known Greek unlocked the rest.

questions.q: Vikings carved letters called...?
questions.f: Runes have straight lines because they were easiest to carve into wood and stone.

questions.q: The world's oldest known writing was pressed into what?
questions.f: Cuneiform scribes in Mesopotamia poked wedge shapes into clay with a reed.

questions.q: Hindi is written in a script called...?
questions.f: Devanagari letters hang from a horizontal line drawn across the top.

questions.q: Russian is written in which alphabet?
questions.f: Cyrillic was inspired by the Greek alphabet, which is why some letters look familiar.

questions.q: Korean writing, called Hangul, was deliberately designed to be easy to learn.
questions.f: King Sejong announced it in the 1440s so ordinary people could read and write.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a real writing system?
questions.f: The other three are used daily by hundreds of millions of people.

questions.q: The word "alphabetical" describes putting things in the order of the...?
questions.f: Phone books, dictionaries and class lists all rely on it.

questions.q: Which spelling of the word for a beat pattern is correct?
questions.f: "Rhythm" is famous for having almost no vowels — the y does all the work.

questions.q: Which spelling of the word meaning "apart" is correct?
questions.f: Remember there's "a rat" in sepARATe.

questions.q: A word that means the opposite of "ancient" is...?
questions.f: "Modern" comes from a Latin word meaning "just now."

questions.q: The ampersand (&) is a squashed-together version of which Latin word?
questions.f: "Et" means "and" — squint at & and you can still see the e and t.

questions.q: Which punctuation mark is made of two dots stacked up?
questions.f: A colon says "here it comes" — a list or an explanation follows.

questions.q: Three dots in a row (...) are called an...?
questions.f: "Ellipsis" is Greek for "leaving out" — the dots mark missing words.

questions.q: The little star symbol (*) is called an...?
questions.f: "Asterisk" comes from the Greek word for "little star."

questions.q: Marks like " " that show someone is speaking are called...?
questions.f: In French, speech is marked with pointed guillemets that look like arrows.

questions.q: A short line joining words, as in "twenty-one," is a...?
questions.f: A hyphen is short; the longer dash used for pauses is called an em dash.

questions.q: In Spanish, a question can begin with an upside-down question mark.
questions.f: Spanish puts one at the start and one at the end, so you know to raise your voice early.

questions.q: In Chinese and Japanese writing, a sentence often ends with a small...?
questions.f: That little circle does the same job as an English period.

questions.q: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is...?
questions.f: "It's raining cats and dogs" means heavy rain — no pets fall from the sky!

questions.q: If someone says "break a leg," they are wishing you...?
questions.f: Actors thought saying "good luck" was unlucky, so they said the opposite.

questions.q: "Piece of cake" is an idiom meaning something is...?
questions.f: In Italian the same idea is "easy as drinking a glass of water."

questions.q: A tongue twister is a phrase that is hard to...?
questions.f: "She sells seashells" is about a real fossil hunter, Mary Anning.

questions.q: An acronym is a word made from the first...?
questions.f: NASA and scuba are acronyms — scuba means "self-contained underwater breathing apparatus."

questions.q: The word "laser" started life as an acronym. It describes a beam of...?
questions.f: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation — quite a mouthful!

questions.q: A palindrome is a word or phrase that reads the same...?
questions.f: "Racecar" and "level" are palindromes; so is the phrase "never odd or even."

questions.q: An anagram is made by...?
questions.f: "Listen" and "silent" are anagrams of each other.

questions.q: A word or phrase like "hiss" that copies a sound is an example of...?
questions.f: Comic books are full of it: BAM, POW, ZAP!

questions.q: Repeating the same starting sound, as in "big brown bear," is called...?
questions.f: Tongue twisters and newspaper headlines both love alliteration.

questions.q: Which word describes a nickname made shorter, like "Ben" from "Benjamin"?
questions.f: Short forms are called clippings — like "phone" from "telephone."

questions.q: The word "pupil" can mean a student and also a part of the...?
questions.f: Both come from Latin for "little doll" — you see a tiny you in someone's pupil!

questions.q: A word with more than one meaning, like "bat," makes English...?
questions.f: Words spelled alike but different in meaning are called homonyms.

questions.q: Which language is spoken by the most people as a first language?
questions.f: English wins if you count second-language speakers too — over a billion learners.

questions.q: Which language has the most words borrowed into English?
questions.f: After 1066, French words flooded in — beef, castle, judge, music, royal.

questions.q: English is officially the national language of the United States by law.
questions.f: The US has no single law-declared national language, though English is used everywhere.

questions.q: Which of these is a sign language used in the United States?
questions.f: American Sign Language actually grew partly from French Sign Language.

questions.q: When you use sign language, your face and eyebrows help show...?
questions.f: Raised eyebrows can turn a signed statement into a question.

questions.q: Which country's people speak Swahili?
questions.f: Swahili is used across East Africa as a shared trade language.

questions.q: The word "hakuna matata" comes from Swahili and means...?
questions.f: It became world-famous through a song, but it is everyday Swahili.

questions.q: The letters SOS in Morse code are used to signal...?
questions.f: SOS was chosen because three dots, three dashes, three dots is easy to tap and hear.

questions.q: Morse code sends letters as patterns of...?
questions.f: The letter E, the commonest in English, is just one quick dot.

questions.q: Which word means the small marks above letters in words like "cafe"?
questions.f: French, Spanish and Vietnamese all use accent marks to guide pronunciation.

questions.q: The two dots above the u in German "uber" are called an...?
questions.f: An umlaut changes the vowel sound — and can change a word's meaning entirely.

questions.q: In Spanish, the squiggle in the letter n of "manana" is called a...?
questions.f: With the tilde, that n sounds like the "ny" in canyon.

questions.q: German is known for very long words made by joining shorter words together.
questions.f: German dictionaries have entries over 30 letters long — no spaces needed!

questions.q: The German word "Handschuh" literally means...?
questions.f: It means glove — German builds words out of plain ingredients.

questions.q: In Welsh, the word "araf" painted on roads means...?
questions.f: Welsh road signs are bilingual — Welsh on top, English below.

questions.q: Which country uses Gaelic alongside English on its road signs?
questions.f: Irish is a Celtic language, related to Scottish Gaelic and Welsh.

questions.q: Iceland has a committee whose job is to...?
c: Invent Icelandic words for new things
questions.f: Instead of borrowing "computer," Icelandic coined a word meaning "number prophetess."

questions.q: Which word entered English from the Dutch language of sailors?
questions.f: Dutch sailors gave English yacht, deck, skipper and cruise.

questions.q: "Robot" came into English in the 1920s from a play written in which language?
questions.f: It comes from a Czech word for forced labour, in a play by Karel Capek.

questions.q: "Jungle" travelled into English from India. It first meant...?
questions.f: From Hindi and Sanskrit "jangala" — it did not have to be leafy at all.

questions.q: "Pyjamas" came to English from India, where the word meant...?
questions.f: From Persian and Urdu "pai jama" — loose trousers tied at the waist.

questions.q: How does a brand-new word usually get into a dictionary?
c: Many people use it for a while
questions.f: Editors track real usage in books, news and online before adding a word.

questions.q: Dictionary editors read and collect examples of how people really use words.
questions.f: They keep huge collections of quotations, called a corpus, as evidence.

questions.q: A word that has fallen out of use is described as...?
questions.f: Dictionaries still list obsolete words so we can read old books.

questions.q: A book of synonyms, used to find a better word, is a...?
questions.f: "Thesaurus" is Greek for treasure house — a treasury of words.

questions.q: Which word describes the study of where words come from?
questions.f: Careful: entomology with an n is the study of insects!

questions.q: American English writes "color" where British English writes...?
questions.f: An American dictionary maker, Noah Webster, deliberately simplified many spellings.

questions.q: British "lorry" is called what in American English?
questions.f: Boot/trunk, lift/elevator, biscuit/cookie — the same language, two vocabularies.

questions.q: English belongs to which branch of the Indo-European family?
questions.f: That is why English "water" and German "Wasser" are near twins, but French "eau" is not.

questions.q: Which of these languages is NOT part of the Indo-European family?
questions.f: Finnish belongs to the Uralic family, alongside Estonian and Hungarian.

questions.q: Spanish, French, Italian and Romanian are all descended from...?
questions.f: They evolved from the everyday Latin of soldiers and traders, not the fancy written kind.

questions.q: The Devanagari script is used to write which language?
questions.f: Sanskrit, Marathi and Nepali use Devanagari too — and its name means "of the divine city."
