questions.q: Which ancient script was pressed into clay with a wedge-shaped reed?
questions.f: "Cuneiform" comes from Latin "cuneus," a wedge — the marks are literally wedge-writing.

questions.q: Cuneiform was first developed by which ancient people?
questions.f: Sumerian scribes in Mesopotamia were keeping written accounts over 5,000 years ago.

questions.q: Our alphabet's earliest ancestor is credited to which trading people?
questions.f: Phoenician sailors carried their letters around the Mediterranean along with their cargo.

questions.q: What important thing did the Greeks add to the Phoenician alphabet?
questions.f: Phoenician wrote only consonants; Greek vowels made reading far less guesswork.

questions.q: The Latin alphabet reached the Romans mainly through which people?
questions.f: Etruscans in Italy adapted Greek letters, and Rome adapted theirs.

questions.q: The Greek letter "alpha" grew from a Phoenician letter named after which animal?
questions.f: "Aleph" meant ox — turn a capital A upside down and you can still see the horns.

questions.q: Korean Hangul was created during the reign of which king?
questions.f: He wanted a script so simple that, as the announcement said, a wise man could learn it in a morning.

questions.q: Hangul letters were designed to show the shape of the...?
questions.f: The letter for "k" pictures the tongue humped at the back of the mouth.

questions.q: The Cyrillic alphabet is traditionally linked to two missionary brothers named...?
questions.f: Cyril is credited with Glagolitic; his followers shaped Cyrillic and named it for him.

questions.q: Japanese writing uses Chinese-derived characters called...?
questions.f: Japanese mixes kanji with two syllable scripts, hiragana and katakana.

questions.q: Roughly how many characters does a Chinese newspaper reader need to know?
questions.f: Dictionaries list tens of thousands, but a few thousand cover almost all everyday reading.

questions.q: The Danish word "hygge" describes a feeling of...?
questions.f: Think candles, blankets and friends — Danes treat hygge as a national art.

questions.q: The Japanese word "komorebi" names...?
questions.f: Japanese has a whole family of such words, including one for dappled light on water.

questions.q: The Portuguese word "saudade" describes...?
c: A deep longing for something absent
questions.f: Brazilians and Portuguese both claim it as the hardest word to translate.

questions.q: The German word "Schadenfreude" means pleasure at...?
questions.f: English borrowed it whole because it had no single word of its own for the feeling.

questions.q: The German word "Wanderlust" means a strong desire to...?
questions.f: Literally "wander-desire" — English took it in the early 1900s.

questions.q: The Japanese word "tsundoku" describes the habit of...?
c: Buying books and not reading them
questions.f: It combines the ideas of "piling up" and "reading" — a very familiar bookshelf problem.

questions.q: Esperanto was created by a doctor from which country?
questions.f: L. L. Zamenhof published it in 1887 under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, "one who hopes."

questions.q: The name "Esperanto" itself means...?
questions.f: It was the author's pen name before it became the language's name.

questions.q: In Esperanto, all nouns end with which letter?
questions.f: Adjectives all end in -a, so the grammar has almost no exceptions to memorise.

questions.q: A language invented on purpose, like Esperanto, is called a...?
questions.f: Fans call them conlangs — Klingon and Elvish are famous fictional examples.

questions.q: Which author invented Elvish languages for his novels?
questions.f: Tolkien was a professional philologist — he built the languages first and the stories after.

questions.q: A simplified mixed language used so traders can understand each other is a...?
questions.f: When children grow up speaking a pidgin as their first language, it becomes a creole.

questions.q: The Great Vowel Shift changed English by altering how people said its...?
questions.f: It hit between about 1400 and 1700 — which is why our spelling no longer matches our speech.

questions.q: English spelling was partly frozen by the printing press before pronunciation stopped changing.
questions.f: Printers standardised spellings in the 1400s, then the Great Vowel Shift moved the sounds anyway.

questions.q: The joke spelling "ghoti" is supposed to be pronounced...?
questions.f: gh as in tough, o as in women, ti as in nation — a jab at English spelling.

questions.q: Words like "knight" and "gnome" keep silent letters because those letters were once...?
questions.f: Chaucer's audience really did say the k in knight — the sound faded, the spelling stayed.

questions.q: Why does English "debt" contain a silent B?
c: Scholars added it to show the Latin root
A printer ran out of vowels
It rhymed with an older word
questions.f: Latin "debitum" inspired the b — and "doubt" got one for the same reason.

questions.q: The letters "gh" in "night" once stood for a sound made in the...?
questions.f: Scots still keep a version of that raspy sound in words like "loch."

questions.q: Which pair shows English's split personality, with an Old English animal and a French meat word?
questions.f: Anglo-Saxon farmers raised the cow; Norman nobles ate the boeuf.

questions.q: The Norman Conquest of 1066 flooded English with words from which language?
questions.f: For 300 years England's rulers spoke French — that's why law and cooking words sound French.

questions.q: Viking settlers gave English everyday words including...?
questions.f: Old Norse also handed English the pronouns they, them and their.

questions.q: The root "lingua" or "lingu" means...?
questions.f: Language, linguist and bilingual all come from Latin "lingua."

questions.q: A scientist who studies how language works is a...?
questions.f: A lexicographer is the specialist who actually writes dictionaries.

questions.q: A person whose job is compiling dictionaries is called a...?
questions.f: Samuel Johnson defined "lexicographer" in his own dictionary as "a harmless drudge."

questions.q: The word "lexicon" means a...?
questions.f: From Greek "lexis," a word or phrase.

questions.q: The word "grammar" comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: "Gramma" meant a written letter — grammar began as the art of letters.

questions.q: "Calligraphy" is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: Kallos (beauty) plus graphein (to write).

questions.q: "Hieroglyph" is built from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: Greeks assumed the symbols were priests' sacred writing — hieros plus glyphein.

questions.q: Who was the French scholar who cracked hieroglyphs in the 1820s?
questions.f: He noticed royal names ringed in ovals called cartouches and worked outward from there.

questions.q: The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in how many scripts?
questions.f: Hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek — the Greek was the key that unlocked the others.

questions.q: An oval ring drawn around a royal name in hieroglyphs is called a...?
questions.f: Spotting Ptolemy's name inside one gave Champollion his first foothold.

questions.q: The phrase "the alpha and the omega" means...?
questions.f: Alpha opens the Greek alphabet and omega closes it — omega even means "big O."

questions.q: Hebrew and Arabic scripts mainly write which sounds?
questions.f: Vowels can be shown with small dots and dashes, often left out for skilled readers.

questions.q: A writing system where each symbol stands for a syllable is called a...?
questions.f: Japanese hiragana and Cherokee writing are both syllabaries.

questions.q: Who created the Cherokee syllabary in the 1820s?
questions.f: He could not read English, yet designed a script so learnable that Cherokee literacy soared.

questions.q: Louis Braille invented his reading system as a...?
questions.f: He was blinded as a toddler and finished his six-dot system before he turned 16.

questions.q: Braille was inspired by a military system of raised marks used for reading in the...?
questions.f: A French army captain's "night writing" let soldiers read messages without a lamp.

questions.q: A language with very few remaining speakers is described as...?
questions.f: Experts warn that a language dies roughly every two weeks somewhere in the world.

questions.q: Hebrew is remarkable because it was successfully...?
questions.f: After centuries as mainly a written and prayer language, it became Israel's spoken tongue.

questions.q: Which language is spoken in Wales and had to be actively revived in schools?
questions.f: Welsh is now taught to every schoolchild in Wales, and speaker numbers are rising.

questions.q: Which language is Basque's closest known relative?
questions.f: Basque is a language isolate, spoken in the Pyrenees long before Latin arrived.

questions.q: The Maori language belongs to which country?
questions.f: Maori is an official language of New Zealand, and "kia ora" is its everyday greeting.

questions.q: A tonal language uses changes in pitch to change a word's...?
questions.f: In Mandarin, "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or scold depending on the tone.

questions.q: Which of these languages is famous for its click consonants?
questions.f: Xhosa and Zulu speakers make clicks with the tongue as ordinary letters of their alphabet.

questions.q: Whistled languages, used to talk across valleys, really exist.
questions.f: Silbo Gomero in the Canary Islands whistles Spanish, and carries for kilometres.

questions.q: The question mark is thought to have grown from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Medieval scribes may have stacked the q above the o, curling it into the mark we use.

questions.q: The word "ampersand" grew out of schoolchildren chanting "and per se and." What does "per se" mean?
questions.f: They recited "& by itself: and" — the mumbled phrase fused into one word.

questions.q: The exclamation mark may come from the Latin word "io," meaning an expression of...?
questions.f: Writing the i above the o gives you a stroke over a dot — an exclamation mark.

questions.q: Which Italian printer helped standardise the comma and semicolon in printed books?
questions.f: His Venetian press also invented italic type and the pocket-sized book.

questions.q: Ancient Greek and Roman texts were often written with no...?
questions.f: Readers voiced the words aloud to work out where each one ended.

questions.q: The word "punctuation" comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Early marks really were just points placed high, middle or low to guide the voice.

questions.q: The mark called the interrobang combines a question mark with a...?
questions.f: An advertising man invented it in 1962 for questions shouted in disbelief.

questions.q: The tiny dot over a lowercase i or j is called a...?
questions.f: That is the "tittle" in the phrase "every jot and tittle."

questions.q: The small decorative strokes on letters in fonts like Times are called...?
questions.f: Fonts without them are "sans serif" — French "sans" means without.

questions.q: When two letters are joined into one shape, like the ae in some fonts, it is called a...?
questions.f: The ampersand itself began as a ligature of the letters e and t.

questions.q: Johannes Gutenberg's great contribution to writing was...?
questions.f: Korea and China had movable type earlier, but his 1450s press transformed Europe.

questions.q: A medieval book copied by hand, often with gold decoration, is called an illuminated...?
questions.f: "Illuminated" meant lit up — real gold leaf caught the candlelight.

questions.q: The word "paper" traces back to which plant?
questions.f: Egyptians sliced papyrus stems, layered them crosswise and pressed them flat.

questions.q: Parchment for writing was traditionally made from...?
questions.f: The finest grade, vellum, was so smooth that ink hardly ever feathered.

questions.q: A book with pages bound along one edge, rather than a rolled scroll, is called a...?
questions.f: The codex won out because you can flip straight to a page instead of unrolling metres.

questions.q: "Palindrome" is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: Palin (again) plus dromos (running) — the same word running back at you.

questions.q: A sentence using every letter of the alphabet, like the quick brown fox one, is a...?
questions.f: "Pan" means all, "gramma" means letter — all the letters.

questions.q: A book written on purpose without using one particular letter is called a...?
questions.f: Ernest Vincent Wright's novel "Gadsby" runs over 50,000 words with no letter e.

questions.q: A word formed by shortening a phrase to its initials, then said as a word, is an...?
questions.f: If you say each letter instead, like FBI, that is strictly an initialism.

questions.q: A word made from someone's name, like "sandwich," is called an...?
questions.f: Boycott, cardigan and diesel are all named after real people.

questions.q: The word "boycott" comes from the name of a land agent in which country?
questions.f: In 1880 Irish tenants refused all dealings with Captain Charles Boycott.

questions.q: The "cardigan" sweater is named after a British...?
questions.f: The 7th Earl of Cardigan's officers wore knitted waistcoats in the Crimean War.

questions.q: The word "denim" comes from cloth "de Nimes," meaning from a town in...?
questions.f: And "jeans" comes from Genoa, in Italy — one garment, two city names.

questions.q: The word "salary" comes from a Latin word for...?
questions.f: Roman soldiers received a salt allowance — hence "worth your salt."

questions.q: The word "companion" literally means someone you share...?
questions.f: Com (with) plus panis (bread) — a fellow bread-eater.

questions.q: "Alphabet soup" aside, the word "lunatic" once linked odd behaviour to the...?
questions.f: From Latin "luna" — people believed the moon's phases affected the mind.

questions.q: "Disaster" is built from parts meaning...?
questions.f: Ancient astrologers blamed calamities on an unlucky alignment of the stars.

questions.q: The word "nice" originally meant...?
questions.f: From Latin "nescius," not knowing — its meaning drifted for centuries into a compliment.

questions.q: The word "silly" originally meant...?
questions.f: It slid from blessed to innocent to simple to foolish — a classic meaning drift.

questions.q: When a word's meaning becomes more positive over time, linguists call it...?
questions.f: The opposite, a slide toward the negative, is called pejoration.

questions.q: The root "dict" in "dictionary" and "predict" means...?
questions.f: A dictionary is a book of sayings; a verdict is a truth spoken.

questions.q: The root "loqu" in "eloquent" and "soliloquy" means...?
questions.f: A soliloquy is a character speaking alone on stage — solus plus loqui.

questions.q: A person who speaks many languages is a...?
questions.f: "Poly" means many and "glotta" means tongue — many-tongued.

questions.q: "Monolingual" describes someone who speaks how many languages?
questions.f: Worldwide, being bilingual is more common than being monolingual.

questions.q: A shared language used between people with different mother tongues is called a lingua...?
questions.f: The original lingua franca was a trade mix used around medieval Mediterranean ports.

questions.q: The word "vernacular" refers to the language...?
questions.f: Dante shocked scholars by writing his great poem in vernacular Italian, not Latin.

questions.q: A word borrowed unchanged from another language is called a...?
questions.f: English never gives them back — kindergarten and karaoke are here to stay.

questions.q: A phrase translated piece by piece, like "skyscraper" into other languages, is a...?
questions.f: A calque is also called a loan translation — the idea is borrowed, the words are local.

questions.q: Words in different languages that share an ancestor, like English "night" and German "Nacht," are...?
questions.f: Spot enough cognates and you can sketch a whole family tree of languages.

questions.q: Which word pair are true cognates?
questions.f: English and German both descend from Germanic, so their core words still rhyme.

questions.q: A "false friend" between two languages is a word that...?
c: Looks familiar but means something else
questions.f: Spanish "embarazada" means pregnant, not embarrassed — a classic trap.

questions.q: The Spanish word "librería" is a false friend: it actually means a...?
questions.f: The Spanish word for library is "biblioteca," from Greek for book-container.

questions.q: American Sign Language is historically related to the sign language of...?
questions.f: Laurent Clerc, a French teacher, helped found the first US deaf school in 1817.

questions.q: In sign language, the space in front of the signer is used to show...?
c: Grammar such as who did what
questions.f: Signers place people in that space, then point back to them like pronouns.

questions.q: Which country's sign language is called Auslan?
questions.f: Auslan is related to British Sign Language, not American.

questions.q: Nicaraguan Sign Language is famous among linguists because it...?
c: Was created by deaf children themselves
questions.f: When a school brought deaf children together in the 1980s, they built a full language from scratch.

questions.q: The word "onomatopoeia" is built from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: Onoma (name) plus poiein (to make) — the word makes a name from a noise.

questions.q: In Japanese, the sound a dog makes is written as...?
questions.f: Italian dogs say "bau bau" and Korean dogs "meong meong" — same dog, different ears.

questions.q: Which language uses the word "kia ora" as a greeting?
questions.f: It literally wishes you life and health.

questions.q: Which language family includes Hawaiian, Maori and Malagasy?
questions.f: Austronesian sailors spread from Taiwan to Madagascar and Easter Island.

questions.q: Arabic and Hebrew both belong to which language family?
questions.f: That is why their word for peace, salaam and shalom, sounds so similar.

questions.q: Tamil, Telugu and Kannada belong to which language family?
questions.f: Dravidian languages of South India are unrelated to Hindi, despite sharing a country.

questions.q: Swahili belongs to which large African language group?
questions.f: Bantu languages spread across half of Africa over several thousand years.

questions.q: Which language is written in a script created for it in the 5th century and used only there?
questions.f: Mesrop Mashtots designed the Armenian alphabet around 405 CE, and it is still in use.

questions.q: Turkey switched from Arabic script to the Latin alphabet in which decade?
questions.f: Ataturk toured the country with a blackboard, teaching the new letters himself.

questions.q: Vietnamese is written today using which alphabet?
questions.f: Missionaries devised it, and stacked marks show both vowel quality and tone.

questions.q: Some languages have no words for left and right, using compass directions instead.
questions.f: Guugu Yimithirr speakers in Australia say things like "the cup north of you."

questions.q: The Sapir-Whorf idea suggests that your language may shape how you...?
questions.f: Strong versions are disputed, but colour and direction words really do affect memory tests.

questions.q: Which language famously has many distinct words in its vocabulary for reindeer?
questions.f: Sami herders in Lapland need precise words for age, antlers and coat colour.

questions.q: How is a language usually classified as "official" in a country?
questions.f: South Africa's constitution recognises twelve official languages, including sign language.

questions.q: Samuel Johnson's famous 1755 achievement was a...?
questions.f: He worked with a handful of assistants and defined over 40,000 words.

questions.q: Noah Webster changed American spellings such as "centre" to...?
questions.f: He also dropped the u from colour and honour, wanting a distinctly American spelling.

questions.q: The Oxford English Dictionary was built largely from slips mailed in by...?
questions.f: Thousands of volunteers copied out sentences showing each word in real use.

questions.q: The first edition of the Oxford English Dictionary took roughly how long to finish?
questions.f: Begun in 1857, it was completed in 1928 — far past its planned ten years.

questions.q: For a new word to enter a major dictionary, editors mainly look for...?
questions.f: Editors want evidence a word is used by many people in many places over time.

questions.q: A huge searchable collection of real texts used by dictionary editors is called a...?
questions.f: "Corpus" is Latin for body — a body of language evidence.

questions.q: A word or phrase used mostly by one group, like gamers or doctors, is called...?
questions.f: Jargon speeds up talk between experts but can shut outsiders out.

questions.q: Very informal words that come and go quickly are called...?
questions.f: Some slang survives — "cool" has been fashionable for nearly a century.

questions.q: A polite word used in place of a blunt one is a...?
questions.f: "Passed away" for died is the classic example — from Greek for "speaking well."

questions.q: The study of what words mean and how meaning changes is called...?
questions.f: Syntax handles word order; semantics handles sense.

questions.q: The branch of linguistics that studies speech sounds is...?
questions.f: Phoneticians use a special alphabet, the IPA, to write any sound in any language.

questions.q: What does IPA stand for in language study?
questions.f: With about 100 symbols it can capture sounds English spelling could never show.

questions.q: The study of word structure — roots, prefixes and endings — is called...?
questions.f: "Morph" means shape, so morphology studies the shapes words take.

questions.q: The smallest meaningful part of a word, like the "un" in "unkind," is a...?
questions.f: A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound; a morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning.

questions.q: A single distinct sound unit in a language is called a...?
questions.f: English has around 44 phonemes but only 26 letters — hence our spelling headaches.

questions.q: Two vowel sounds gliding together in one syllable, as in "coin," form a...?
questions.f: "Di" means two and "phthongos" means sound — a two-sound vowel.

questions.q: Two letters that together spell one sound, like "sh," form a...?
questions.f: English leans on digraphs — ch, th, ph, sh — because it ran short of letters.

questions.q: The "ph" in "physics" spells an F sound because the word came through...?
questions.f: Greek had a letter phi, which Romans wrote as ph — and English inherited the habit.

questions.q: Which letter did English once have, written like a thorn, for the "th" sound?
questions.f: Printers lacking thorn substituted a y — that is why old signs read "Ye Olde Shoppe."

questions.q: The old letter "wynn" was replaced in English by which modern letter?
questions.f: Scribes doubled the u into a "double u" — you can still hear the name today.

questions.q: The letters J and V were the last additions to which alphabet?
c: The Latin alphabet used for English
questions.f: They split off from I and U, and were not fully separate letters until the 1600s.

questions.q: The ampersand once appeared where in the recited English alphabet?
questions.f: Children chanted "...X, Y, Z, and per se and" — so & was practically the 27th letter.

questions.q: The word "quiz" is unusual because its origin is...?
questions.f: A popular tale credits a Dublin theatre bet, but etymologists cannot confirm it.

questions.q: The name "OK" is most often traced to a joking abbreviation of...?
questions.f: Boston newspapers in 1839 loved comic misspellings — "oll korrect" became OK.

questions.q: "OK" is understood in nearly every country on Earth.
questions.f: It is often called the most widely recognised word on the planet.

questions.q: The word "alphabet soup" style term "emoji" is built from Japanese parts meaning...?
questions.f: E (picture) plus moji (character) — the resemblance to "emotion" is a coincidence.

questions.q: Emoji were first designed in the 1990s for use on which devices?
questions.f: Shigetaka Kurita's 176 tiny images were only 12 pixels across.

questions.q: The system that gives every character in every script its own code number is called...?
questions.f: Unicode covers over 150 scripts, including ancient cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs.

questions.q: The root "poly" in "polysyllabic" means...?
questions.f: A polysyllabic word has many syllables — like "polysyllabic" itself.

questions.q: A word made by blending two others, like "brunch," is called a...?
questions.f: Lewis Carroll coined the term, comparing such words to a suitcase with two compartments.

questions.q: Which word is a portmanteau of "smoke" and "fog"?
questions.f: It was coined around 1905 to describe London's murky air.

questions.q: Lewis Carroll's poem "Jabberwocky" is famous for its...?
questions.f: "Chortle" and "galumph" escaped the poem and joined real dictionaries.

questions.q: Which everyday word did Lewis Carroll invent in "Jabberwocky"?
questions.f: He blended chuckle and snort — and now it is in every dictionary.

questions.q: A limerick is a short comic poem with how many lines?
questions.f: Its bouncing rhythm and AABBA rhyme scheme make it instantly recognisable.

questions.q: A haiku traditionally has how many syllables in total?
questions.f: Five, seven, five — and classical Japanese haiku usually name a season.

questions.q: The word "thesaurus" literally means...?
questions.f: Peter Mark Roget, a doctor, published his famous one in 1852.

questions.q: Which word means the exact dictionary meaning of a word?
questions.f: Connotation is the feeling around a word — "home" and "house" denote the same thing but feel different.

questions.q: The extra emotional colour a word carries is its...?
questions.f: "Thrifty" and "stingy" mean much the same, but only one is a compliment.

questions.q: The root "chron" in "chronology" means...?
questions.f: A chronometer measures time; something anachronistic sits in the wrong time.

questions.q: The root "anthrop" in "anthropology" means...?
questions.f: Philanthropy literally means love of humankind.

questions.q: "Philology" literally means love of...?
questions.f: Philologists study old texts closely — Tolkien's day job was exactly this.

questions.q: The prefix "proto-" in "Proto-Indo-European" means...?
questions.f: Nobody wrote Proto-Indo-European down — scholars reconstructed it by comparing its descendants.

questions.q: Proto-Indo-European was probably spoken about how long ago?
questions.f: From that one ancestor grew English, Hindi, Greek, Russian, Persian and hundreds more.

questions.q: Sanskrit's close resemblance to Greek and Latin was famously noted in 1786 by...?
questions.f: A judge in Calcutta, he sparked the whole science of comparative linguistics.

questions.q: Jacob Grimm, of fairy-tale fame, also discovered a law about shifting...?
questions.f: Grimm's Law explains why Latin "pater" matches English "father."

questions.q: Which language is the sacred and classical language of ancient India?
questions.f: Its grammar was analysed so precisely by Panini that computer scientists still study his rules.

questions.q: The English word "avatar" came from Sanskrit, where it meant a...?
questions.f: Computers borrowed it in the 1980s for the form you take in a virtual world.

questions.q: The English word "karma" comes from Sanskrit for...?
questions.f: The idea is that deeds, not luck, shape what comes back to you.

questions.q: The word "guru" came into English from Sanskrit, where it means...?
questions.f: It also carries the sense of "weighty" — a person of substance.

questions.q: The word "loot" entered English from Hindi, meaning...?
questions.f: British soldiers in India brought it home along with pyjamas and shampoo.

questions.q: Which Chinese-derived word for a strong storm entered English through several languages?
questions.f: Its path likely ran through Chinese, Arabic and Portuguese before reaching English.

questions.q: The word "tea" spread around the world in two forms, "tea" and...?
questions.f: Sea traders spread "te" from a coastal dialect; overland routes spread "cha."

questions.q: Which sport's vocabulary gave English "checkmate," from a Persian phrase meaning "the king is helpless"?
questions.f: Shah mat travelled from Persian through Arabic and French into English.

questions.q: The word "admiral" traces back to an Arabic phrase meaning...?
questions.f: From "amir al-bahr" — the extra d crept in via medieval Latin.

questions.q: Which English word for a number came from Arabic "sifr," meaning empty?
questions.f: The same root gave us "cipher" — a code, or a nothing.

questions.q: The word "algorithm" comes from the name of a...?
questions.f: Al-Khwarizmi wrote a maths book so influential his name became a word.

questions.q: "Alcove," "alcohol" and "algebra" share an Arabic element "al-," which means...?
questions.f: English swallowed the article whole, so we effectively say "the-the-gebra."

questions.q: Which of these words came into English from Persian?
questions.f: Persian also gave English caravan, paradise and pistachio.

questions.q: Which script, used for Amharic and Tigrinya, is written in Ethiopia?
questions.f: Ge'ez is a syllabary of over 200 shapes, each a consonant fused with a vowel.

questions.q: Ogham, an early Irish script, was written as notches along the...?
questions.f: Over 400 ogham stones survive, most in Ireland, and they read from the bottom up.

questions.q: Michael Ventris astonished scholars in 1952 by proving Linear B recorded an early form of...?
questions.f: He was an architect, not a professional linguist, and he was only 30 years old.

questions.q: Which ancient Italian language is still largely unread despite its alphabet being understood?
questions.f: We can pronounce Etruscan words but rarely translate them — the language has no known relatives.

questions.q: The undeciphered Indus Valley script survives mostly on small carved...?
questions.f: Most inscriptions are only five signs long — far too short to crack by statistics alone.

questions.q: Rongorongo, an undeciphered script carved on wooden tablets, comes from which island?
questions.f: Its lines alternate direction, so readers had to rotate the tablet after every row.

questions.q: The Cherokee syllabary designed by Sequoyah contains roughly how many characters?
questions.f: Within a few years the Cherokee Nation had its own newspaper printed in the script.

questions.q: Hangul's original 1446 name, Hunminjeongeum, means...?
c: Proper sounds to instruct the people
questions.f: Scholars who preferred Chinese characters mocked it as vulgar — it took centuries to win out.

questions.q: Nushu, a script used secretly for centuries in Hunan, China, was written and read almost only by...?
questions.f: It was often embroidered onto cloth and fans, and passed between sworn sisters.

questions.q: Inuktitut in Canada is often written in a syllabic script adapted from one first made for which language?
questions.f: Missionary James Evans devised Cree syllabics in the 1840s using shapes that rotate for each vowel.

questions.q: Which language holds the record for the largest alphabet, with over 70 letters?
questions.f: Cambodian schoolchildren learn 33 consonants plus dozens of vowel signs.

questions.q: Rotokas, spoken in Papua New Guinea, is famous for having one of the world's smallest...?
questions.f: Just twelve letters do the whole job: A, E, G, I, K, O, P, R, S, T, U, V.

questions.q: Maltese is remarkable as the only Semitic language that is...?
questions.f: It grew from Arabic, absorbed Italian and English, and is an official EU language.

questions.q: Afrikaans developed mainly from which European language?
questions.f: It simplified Dutch grammar sharply — no verb conjugation by person at all.

questions.q: Yiddish is a Germanic language traditionally written in which script?
questions.f: English owes Yiddish words like bagel, glitch, klutz and schlep.

questions.q: The Romani language, spoken across Europe, originated in which region?
questions.f: Comparing its vocabulary to Sanskrit revealed the Roma people's Indian origins.

questions.q: Haitian Creole is largely built on the vocabulary of which language?
questions.f: It became an official language of Haiti alongside French in 1987.

questions.q: Tok Pisin, an official language of Papua New Guinea, is a creole based mainly on...?
questions.f: Its name literally means "talk pidgin," and "gras bilong het" means hair.

questions.q: Which constructed language, published in 1879 by a German priest, briefly rivalled Esperanto?
questions.f: Its name means "world speech," but bitter arguments among its supporters sank it.

questions.q: Toki Pona, a constructed language created by Sonja Lang, is famous for having only about...?
questions.f: Speakers combine those few words into phrases — "telo nasa" is roughly "strange liquid."

questions.q: Klingon, spoken in Star Trek, was developed into a full language by linguist...?
questions.f: He deliberately used sounds and word orders rare in human languages to make it feel alien.

questions.q: George Bernard Shaw left money in his will to promote a new...?
questions.f: The resulting Shavian alphabet has 48 letters and no capital letters at all.

questions.q: Solresol, a 19th-century constructed language, could be sung or played because it was based on...?
questions.f: Seven syllables — do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si — combined into every word.

questions.q: The word "nostalgia" was coined in 1688 by a Swiss doctor to describe...?
questions.f: Johannes Hofer built it from Greek nostos (homecoming) and algos (pain).

questions.q: The word "quarantine" comes from an Italian word meaning...?
questions.f: Venice made arriving ships wait forty days before anyone could come ashore.

questions.q: The word "influenza" originally referred to the supposed influence of the...?
questions.f: Italians blamed epidemics on unlucky astrological influence — "influenza di stelle."

questions.q: "Malaria" is built from Italian words meaning...?
questions.f: People blamed swamp vapours until mosquitoes were identified as the carrier.

questions.q: The word "vaccine" traces back to a Latin word for which animal?
questions.f: Edward Jenner used cowpox — vacca is Latin for cow.

questions.q: The English word "lord" comes from an Old English compound meaning...?
questions.f: And "lady" came from hlaefdige — the loaf kneader. Power began at the bread table.

questions.q: The word "window" came from an Old Norse compound meaning...?
questions.f: Vindauga — before glass, a window really was just an eye for the wind.

questions.q: The word "daisy" comes from an Old English phrase meaning...?
questions.f: The flower opens its yellow centre at dawn and closes it at dusk.

questions.q: The word "tragedy" comes from Greek words apparently meaning...?
questions.f: Tragos means goat — the link may be to goat-costumed choruses at festivals of Dionysus.

questions.q: An "orchestra" in ancient Greek theatre was the...?
questions.f: Only much later did the word shift to mean the musicians who sat there.

questions.q: The Greek word behind "school" originally meant...?
questions.f: Skhole was free time — the leisure in which philosophers could think and teach.

questions.q: A "candidate" in ancient Rome was so called because he wore...?
questions.f: Candidus means shining white — the same root gives us candle and incandescent.

questions.q: The word "clue" comes from an older word "clew," meaning a ball of...?
questions.f: Theseus followed thread out of the labyrinth — that is literally where a clue leads.

questions.q: The word "sheriff" is a squashed form of an Old English title meaning...?
questions.f: Shire plus reeve — a reeve was the king's local administrator.

questions.q: The word "marshal" originally meant a servant who looked after...?
questions.f: Constable has a similar past: it comes from "count of the stable."

questions.q: A "chancellor" was originally an official who stood beside a...?
questions.f: Latin cancelli meant a barrier or grating — and it also gave us the word "cancel."

questions.q: The English word "orange" lost its initial N because speakers reanalysed "a naranj" as...?
questions.f: This shuffling of word boundaries is called rebracketing — "apron" was once "napron."

questions.q: The word "adder" was once "nadder." What caused the change?
c: The N migrated to the article
questions.f: "A nadder" became "an adder" — the same slip that turned "a numpire" into "an umpire."

questions.q: The word "nickname" grew from the Middle English phrase "an eke name," where "eke" meant...?
questions.f: "An eke name" became "a nickname" — rebracketing running the other direction.

questions.q: Making a shorter verb from a longer noun, as in "edit" from "editor," is called...?
questions.f: "Burgle" was back-formed from "burglar," and "donate" from "donation."

questions.q: The word "bird" was once "brid." Swapping neighbouring sounds like this is called...?
questions.f: The same process turned "thridda" into "third" and gives us the common slip "nucular."

questions.q: A misheard song lyric, like "a girl with colitis goes by," is called a...?
questions.f: Sylvia Wright coined the term in 1954 after mishearing "laid him on the green."

questions.q: Swapping the opening sounds of two words, as in "blushing crow" for "crushing blow," is a...?
questions.f: It is named for William Spooner, an Oxford don famous for such slips.

questions.q: Using a similar-sounding wrong word, like "dance a flamingo," is called a...?
questions.f: It is named after Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's 1775 play "The Rivals."

questions.q: A word accidentally created by a dictionary error, like the famous "dord," is called a...?
questions.f: "Dord" appeared in Webster's in 1934 after a filing slip reading "D or d" was misread.

questions.q: A word that is its own opposite, like "cleave" or "sanction," is called a...?
questions.f: They are also called Janus words, after the Roman god with two faces.

questions.q: A word appearing only once in an entire body of writing is called a hapax...?
questions.f: Homer's poems contain hundreds — words we can only guess the meaning of.

questions.q: The word "serendipity" was invented in 1754 by Horace Walpole from an old name for...?
questions.f: Serendip came from Arabic Sarandib; he coined it after a fairy tale about lucky discoveries.

questions.q: Thomas More built the word "utopia" from Greek parts meaning...?
questions.f: He was punning: "eutopia" would mean good place, and the two sound alike in English.

questions.q: Which word for a tiny particle did Murray Gell-Mann take from a line in "Finnegans Wake"?
questions.f: The line reads "Three quarks for Muster Mark" — and quarks do come in threes.

questions.q: The word "meme" was coined in 1976 by which scientist?
questions.f: He clipped Greek "mimeme" so it would echo "gene" — an idea that copies itself.

questions.q: The word "scientist" was coined in the 1830s by which English polymath?
questions.f: Before that, researchers were called natural philosophers — Faraday disliked the new word.

questions.q: The word "nerd" first appeared in print in a 1950 book by which author?
questions.f: A Nerd is one of the imaginary creatures listed in "If I Ran the Zoo."

questions.q: The word "pandemonium," meaning uproar, was invented by John Milton as the name of a...?
questions.f: He built it from Greek pan (all) and daimon (spirit) — literally the place of all the spirits.

questions.q: The word "blurb" was coined in 1907 by humorist Gelett Burgess to mock...?
questions.f: He invented a fictional Miss Belinda Blurb and printed her gushing praise on a cover.

questions.q: The word "cyberspace" was coined in the 1980s by which novelist?
questions.f: He later admitted the word was chosen mainly because it sounded evocative and meant nothing yet.

questions.q: Jonathan Swift's "Gulliver's Travels" gave English which word meaning very small?
questions.f: The same book also gave us "yahoo" for a crude, noisy person.

questions.q: The word "gas" was coined in the 1600s by which Flemish chemist?
questions.f: He seems to have based it on Greek "chaos" — matter without shape.

questions.q: The word "gerrymander" blends a politician's name with which animal?
questions.f: An 1812 Massachusetts voting district drawn under Elbridge Gerry looked like a salamander.

questions.q: The word "silhouette" comes from the name of an 18th-century French...?
questions.f: Etienne de Silhouette's harsh money-saving cuts made his name a byword for the cheapest portrait.

questions.q: "Mesmerize" comes from the surname of an 18th-century...?
questions.f: Franz Anton Mesmer's dramatic healing sessions were an early ancestor of hypnotism.

questions.q: "Galvanize" is named after Luigi Galvani, who experimented with electricity and...?
questions.f: His twitching frog legs also inspired Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein."

questions.q: The word "dunce" comes from the name of a medieval...?
questions.f: Followers of John Duns Scotus were mocked by rivals — an unfair fate for a brilliant thinker.

questions.q: To "bowdlerize" a book means to...?
questions.f: Thomas Bowdler published a "Family Shakespeare" in 1807 with the awkward bits removed.

questions.q: "Sideburns" comes from the name of an American general whose surname was...?
questions.f: Ambrose Burnside's spectacular whiskers had his name flipped around to make the word.

questions.q: "Leotard" is named after a 19th-century French...?
questions.f: Jules Leotard also popularised the flying trapeze act.

questions.q: The word "khaki" came into English from Urdu, where it means...?
questions.f: British troops in India dyed white uniforms with tea and mud to blend in.

questions.q: The word "juggernaut" comes from a Sanskrit title meaning...?
questions.f: Jagannath's huge temple chariot at Puri impressed British visitors into a new English word.

questions.q: The English word "cheetah" comes from a Sanskrit-derived word meaning...?
questions.f: From Hindi "cita," from Sanskrit "citra," meaning variegated or marked.

questions.q: The word "veranda" reached English through India, but likely began in which language?
questions.f: Portuguese traders in India used "varanda" for a railing — the word bounced back to Europe.

questions.q: "Kowtow" comes from a Chinese expression meaning to...?
questions.f: It described touching the forehead to the ground before the emperor.

questions.q: The word "tycoon" came into English from a Japanese title meaning...?
questions.f: Americans applied "taikun" to the shogun in the 1850s, then to business bosses.

questions.q: The Japanese word "umami," now used in English, names a taste often described as...?
questions.f: Kikunae Ikeda identified it in 1908 while studying seaweed broth.

questions.q: "Bonsai" is built from Japanese parts meaning...?
questions.f: The art came to Japan from Chinese penjing, which means much the same thing.

questions.q: "Sudoku" is short for a Japanese phrase meaning...?
questions.f: It was first published in America in 1979 as Number Place, but only became a craze after Japanese puzzlers renamed it.

questions.q: "Manga" is built from Japanese parts usually translated as...?
questions.f: The artist Hokusai used the word for his sketchbooks back in 1814.

questions.q: The word "hurricane" came into English through Spanish from which language family of the Caribbean?
questions.f: Taino also gave English canoe, hammock, barbecue and potato.

questions.q: "Avocado" traces back to a word in which language of ancient Mexico?
questions.f: Nahuatl also gave English tomato, chocolate, chili and coyote.

questions.q: "Alligator" came into English from a Spanish phrase meaning...?
questions.f: "El lagarto" was blurred into one English word by early sailors.

questions.q: "Orangutan" comes from Malay words meaning...?
questions.f: Malay speakers may originally have used it for forest-dwelling people, not the ape.

questions.q: Words like "moose," "raccoon" and "skunk" entered English from which language family?
questions.f: Early English colonists in New England had no words for these animals at all.

questions.q: "Anorak" is a word English borrowed from...?
questions.f: Kayak came from Inuit "qajaq," and both words travelled with Arctic explorers.

questions.q: "Tundra" reached English through Russian from which northern European language?
questions.f: The Sami word described treeless high ground — exactly what the term means today.

questions.q: The Russian word "sputnik" literally means...?
questions.f: It was already an ordinary Russian word for companion before 1957.

questions.q: The Russian word "vodka" is a diminutive meaning...?
questions.f: Its root, "voda," is a cousin of English "water" through Proto-Indo-European.

questions.q: The titles "tsar" and "kaiser" both descend from the name of...?
questions.f: Two thousand years on, one Roman family name still echoed in two imperial titles.

questions.q: A test word or phrase used to identify who belongs to a group is called a...?
questions.f: The term comes from a Hebrew word used in a biblical episode as a pronunciation test.

questions.q: Which coarse-cloth name came to mean pompous, overblown language?
questions.f: A cheap cotton-and-flax fabric became the perfect insult for writing that puffs itself up.

questions.q: The Hungarian language is famous among learners for having roughly how many noun cases?
questions.f: Finnish, its distant cousin, gets by with about fifteen.

questions.q: Turkish grammar builds long words by stacking endings — this is described as...?
questions.f: One Turkish word can carry what English needs a whole sentence to say.

questions.q: Turkish, Finnish and Hungarian all use a rule called vowel...?
questions.f: Endings change their vowels to match the word they attach to, so the word sounds even.

questions.q: Swahili nouns are sorted into about fifteen groups linguists call noun...?
questions.f: Prefixes ripple through the whole sentence to agree with the noun's class.

questions.q: Some languages, like Quechua and Turkish, use grammatical endings to show...?
questions.f: This feature is called evidentiality — you must mark whether you saw it or merely heard it.

questions.q: Languages such as Tagalog distinguish two forms of "we" — this feature is called...?
questions.f: One "we" includes the listener, the other pointedly leaves them out.

questions.q: The most common vowel sound in spoken English is the unstressed...?
questions.f: It is the lazy "uh" in the middle of "sofa" and "about" — and it has no letter of its own.

questions.q: An accent in which the R is pronounced after a vowel, as in most American speech, is called...?
questions.f: Shakespeare's London was rhotic — dropping the R came later, and America kept the old way.

questions.q: A ball of thread in a Cretan maze, a Latin word for white clothing, and a Roman salt allowance explain the origins of clue, candidate and which other word?
questions.f: Roman soldiers were partly paid in salt money — sal became salary, and "worth his salt."

questions.q: A Dublin bet, an Irish land agent boycotted by tenants, and a mocked medieval scholar all gave English words. Which one has an origin still unproven?
questions.f: The tale that a theatre manager won a bet by chalking "quiz" on walls has never been verified.

questions.q: A 1440s Korean royal decree, an 1820s Cherokee silversmith and a teenage blind Frenchman all did what?
questions.f: Sejong, Sequoyah and Louis Braille each built a script from scratch for people shut out of reading.

questions.q: A misfiled slip reading "D or d", a ghost word that survived years in print, and editors who plant fake entries to catch copycats relate to errors in which reference work?
questions.f: The ghost word "dord" sat in Webster's Second from 1934; fake entries are named after Lillian Mountweazel of a 1975 encyclopedia.

questions.q: Three thousand slips of paper a month, a murderer contributing from an asylum, and 70 years of work produced which book?
questions.f: Dr W. C. Minor sent thousands of quotations from Broadmoor — his story became a bestseller.

questions.q: A twitching frog's leg, a Viennese healer's dramatic sessions, and a general's magnificent whiskers all became English...?
questions.f: Galvanize, mesmerize and sideburns — three eponyms with very different pedigrees.

questions.q: An Oxford don's tangled tongue, a Sheridan character's borrowed vocabulary, and a misheard Scottish ballad each named a kind of...?
questions.f: Spoonerism, malapropism and mondegreen — English names its mistakes beautifully.

questions.q: A 1957 satellite, a Roman family name behind two imperial titles, and a diminutive meaning "little water" all came into English from which language?
questions.f: Sputnik, tsar and vodka — three very different borrowings from one source.

questions.q: A city that made ships wait, air blamed on the stars, and swamp vapours named as "bad air" gave English three words about...?
questions.f: Quarantine, influenza and malaria all record beliefs about illness that turned out wrong.

questions.q: A 1786 speech in Calcutta, a fairy-tale brother's sound law, and a language nobody ever wrote down founded which field of study?
questions.f: William Jones, Jacob Grimm and reconstructed Proto-Indo-European built a family tree of tongues.

questions.q: Loose trousers, a low house in Bengal, and a head massage all became English words during the era of...?
questions.f: Pyjamas, bungalow and shampoo — Britain imported vocabulary along with everything else.

questions.q: An architect who was not a linguist, clay tablets baked hard by a palace fire, and lists of sheep and chariots led to reading which script?
questions.f: The tablets survived because a fire that destroyed the palace fired the clay like pottery.

questions.q: Embroidered fans, sworn sisterhoods in rural Hunan, and a script men mostly ignored describe which writing tradition?
questions.f: When its last fluent traditional writers died, scholars raced to record it.

questions.q: A Polish eye doctor, a pen name meaning "one who hopes," and nouns that all end in O describe which language?
questions.f: Zamenhof grew up in a town where four languages jostled daily — he wanted a neutral fifth.

questions.q: A children's school in Managua in the 1980s, teachers puzzled by their pupils, and a language born in a generation describe...?
questions.f: Linguists had never before watched a full language appear from scratch in real time.

questions.q: A fabric from Nimes, trousers from Genoa, and a dust-coloured Urdu word all describe the history of...?
questions.f: Denim, jeans and khaki — three garments named for a place or a shade.

questions.q: On mock-old shop signs, the Y in "Ye Olde Shoppe" is really a printer's substitute for which lost letter?
questions.f: So it was always meant to be read "The Olde Shoppe" — nobody ever said "ye."

questions.q: Old English poets called the sea a "whale-road." Such riddling compounds are called...?
questions.f: Beowulf also calls the body a bone-house and a ship a wave-floater.

questions.q: Old English poetry's main sound device was not rhyme but...?
questions.f: Each line hinged on repeated opening consonants across a central pause called a caesura.

questions.q: Which English text is generally called the first great work in Middle English by a named poet?
questions.f: Chaucer wrote in the London dialect, helping decide which English became standard.

questions.q: Which invention did most to standardise English spelling?
questions.f: Caxton's press in 1476 had to pick one spelling per word — and the choices stuck.

questions.q: About how many words is Shakespeare credited with first using in print?
questions.f: Eyeball, lonely and swagger all first appear in his plays — though he may have heard some spoken.

questions.q: Which pair of everyday English words were both first recorded in Shakespeare?
questions.f: He needed vivid new words fast, and audiences apparently kept up.

questions.q: The Grimm brothers are best known for fairy tales, but their scholarly life's work was a German...?
questions.f: They began it in 1838; it was finally completed in 1961, over a century later.

questions.q: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda is celebrated for his part in reviving which language as an everyday tongue?
questions.f: He raised his son speaking only Hebrew — reportedly the first such child in centuries.

questions.q: Which language of the Isle of Man lost its last traditional native speaker in 1974 but is now taught in schools?
questions.f: Children now attend a Manx-medium primary school — a language brought back from the brink.

questions.q: Ubykh, a Caucasian language with an extraordinary number of consonants, went extinct in 1992 with the death of...?
questions.f: Tevfik Esenc worked with linguists for years so his language would be documented.

questions.q: Which language holds records for having one of the largest consonant inventories, including many clicks?
questions.f: Taa, spoken in Botswana and Namibia, may use over a hundred distinct consonants.

questions.q: Pirahã, an Amazonian language, became famous for linguists' claims that it lacks...?
questions.f: Its speakers reportedly use terms like "few" and "many" rather than one, two, three.

questions.q: The Guugu Yimithirr language of Australia is famous for describing position using...?
questions.f: Speakers say "the ant north of your foot" — and stay oriented even indoors.

questions.q: Silbo Gomero, a whistled language, is used on which island group?
questions.f: It whistles Spanish across ravines and was named a UNESCO cultural treasure in 2009.

questions.q: Basque marks the doer of an action with a special ending — a grammatical feature called...?
questions.f: Ergative languages treat the subject of a transitive verb differently from other subjects.

questions.q: Georgian is the main language of which language family?
questions.f: Georgian's rounded alphabet, Mkhedruli, has no capital letters at all.

questions.q: Which script did the Mongol Empire adopt, written vertically in columns?
questions.f: It descends from Aramaic by way of Uyghur, and Inner Mongolia still uses it today.

questions.q: Chinese characters were first written on which surfaces during the Shang dynasty?
questions.f: Farmers dug up these "oracle bones" and sold them as medicine before scholars recognised them.

questions.q: Pinyin, the official system for spelling Chinese in Latin letters, was adopted in which decade?
questions.f: It replaced Wade-Giles — which is why Peking became Beijing on maps.

questions.q: Simplified Chinese characters were introduced mainly to...?
questions.f: Taiwan and Hong Kong kept the traditional forms, so both systems remain in use.

questions.q: Small kana printed beside kanji in Japanese to show pronunciation are called...?
questions.f: Children's manga uses furigana heavily so young readers can tackle hard characters.

questions.q: Which Japanese script is used mainly for foreign loanwords?
questions.f: So "television" appears in katakana as terebi — instantly flagged as a borrowing.

questions.q: Vietnamese was once written with Chinese-style characters in a system called...?
questions.f: It was gradually replaced by the Latin-based quoc ngu during the colonial era.

questions.q: Korean uses some Chinese characters, known in Korean as...?
questions.f: They appear mostly in newspapers and formal names, to tell similar-sounding words apart.

questions.q: Grimm's Law describes regular sound changes that separated Germanic languages from...?
questions.f: It explains why Latin "pater" and "pisces" match English "father" and "fish."

questions.q: Verner's Law solved exceptions to Grimm's Law by pointing to the position of the...?
questions.f: Karl Verner published it in 1875 and rescued the whole theory in a single stroke.

questions.q: The English word "knight" once meant simply a...?
questions.f: German "Knecht" still means servant — English promoted the word to armour and honour.

questions.q: The word "villain" originally described someone who...?
questions.f: A villein was a peasant tied to a villa — snobbery slowly turned the word into an insult.

questions.q: When a word's meaning worsens over time, as with "villain," linguists call it...?
questions.f: The reverse happened to "knight" and "nice" — words can climb as well as fall.

questions.q: The word "decimate" comes from a Roman practice involving which fraction?
questions.f: Purists still argue whether it should only mean reducing something by a tenth.

questions.q: The word "sinister" comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Roman augurs read omens by direction, and left-hand signs were the unlucky ones.

questions.q: The word "dexterity" comes from a Latin word meaning...?
questions.f: Language has long favoured the right hand — and "ambidextrous" means right-handed twice over.

questions.q: The word "person" traces back to a Latin word for a theatrical...?
questions.f: Persona was the mask an actor spoke through — and it still means the face we present.

questions.q: The word "companion" and "pantry" both descend from a Latin word for...?
questions.f: Panis fed both words — a companion shares bread, a pantry stores it.

questions.q: The word "pen" and the word "pinnate" both go back to a Latin word for...?
questions.f: Penna meant feather or wing — quills wrote for over a thousand years.

questions.q: Which word shares its Latin root with "annual" and "anniversary"?
questions.f: Annus means year — a perennial plant lives right through the years.

questions.q: Which word shares its root with "aquarium" and "aqueduct"?
questions.f: Aquiline is the false friend — it comes from aquila, an eagle.

questions.q: The root "vid" or "vis" in "video" and "vision" means...?
questions.f: Latin "video" literally means "I see" — the machine was named with a verb.

questions.q: The root "greg" in "gregarious" and "segregate" means...?
questions.f: To segregate is to pull out of the flock; to congregate is to gather into one.

questions.q: The root "cede" or "ceed" in "precede" and "recede" means...?
questions.f: So an antecedent is something that has gone before.

questions.q: The root "tract" in "tractor" and "attract" means...?
questions.f: A tractor pulls, a distraction pulls your mind away, a contract draws terms together.

questions.q: The root "ject" in "eject" and "projectile" means...?
questions.f: An interjection is a word thrown between others — like "oh!" or "wow!"

questions.q: The root "nym" or "onym" in "synonym" and "pseudonym" means...?
questions.f: An anonymous author is literally "without a name."

questions.q: An "exonym" is a place name used by...?
questions.f: Germany calls itself Deutschland — "Germany" is an English exonym.

questions.q: A word for a broad category that includes narrower ones, like "animal" over "dog," is a...?
questions.f: Flip it and "dog" is a hyponym of "animal" — linguistics has a word for every direction.

questions.q: A word for a part of a whole, like "wheel" to "car," is called a...?
questions.f: Meronymy maps how words nest inside each other, part within whole.

questions.q: Words spelled alike but pronounced differently, like "lead" the metal and "lead" the verb, are...?
questions.f: They are a spelling bee's nightmare — you must ask for the word in a sentence.

questions.q: Calling the British monarchy "the Crown" is an example of...?
questions.f: Metonymy swaps in a closely linked thing — "the White House said" works the same way.

questions.q: Deliberate understatement, such as "not bad" for excellent, is called...?
questions.f: Old English poetry loved it — Beowulf's foes are described as "not friendly."

questions.q: An oxymoron joins two words that...?
questions.f: "Deafening silence" and "bittersweet" are oxymorons — and the word itself is Greek for sharp-dull.

questions.q: A word or phrase like "the more the merrier" that everyone repeats unchanged is called a...?
questions.f: "Cliche" was a French printer's word for a stereotype plate — reused endlessly.

questions.q: In printing, a "stereotype" was originally a...?
questions.f: Because the plate reproduced the same image forever, the word came to mean a fixed idea.

questions.q: The word "cliche" and the word "stereotype" both came into English from the world of...?
questions.f: Print shops gave English many metaphors: upper case, out of sorts, mind your p's and q's.

questions.q: The keyboard layout QWERTY was designed in the 1870s for the...?
questions.f: Christopher Latham Sholes's arrangement spread the commonest letters apart to reduce jamming.

questions.q: The alternative Dvorak keyboard was designed mainly to...?
questions.f: It puts all the vowels on the home row — but QWERTY's head start proved unbeatable.

questions.q: French keyboards are called AZERTY because of...?
questions.f: German keyboards are QWERTZ, swapping Y and Z to suit German spelling.

questions.q: Which body famously guards the French language and its dictionary?
questions.f: Founded in 1635, its 40 members are known as "the immortals."

questions.q: Spain's equivalent language academy uses the motto "cleans, fixes and gives..."?
questions.f: The Real Academia Espanola has coordinated Spanish spelling across two dozen countries since 1713.

questions.q: Germany carried out a significant official spelling reform in which decade?
questions.f: The 1996 reform changed how the sharp s, called Eszett, was used — and caused years of arguments.

questions.q: The German letter that looks like a B and represents a double s is called...?
questions.f: Switzerland dropped it entirely and writes "ss" instead.

questions.q: Norway is unusual because it has two official written standards of its language, one being...?
questions.f: Bokmal grew from Danish-influenced writing; Nynorsk was built from rural dialects.

questions.q: Serbian is notable for being routinely written in how many alphabets?
questions.f: Cyrillic and Latin sit side by side — signs and newspapers may use either.

questions.q: Using two writing systems for the same language is called...?
questions.f: Diglossia is the related idea of a high formal variety alongside an everyday one.

questions.q: Arabic speakers commonly use a formal written variety alongside local speech — this situation is called...?
questions.f: Newsreaders use Modern Standard Arabic; families at home use their own dialect.

questions.q: Switching between two languages within a single conversation is called code...?
questions.f: Far from sloppiness, it follows precise grammatical rules that bilinguals obey instinctively.

questions.q: Which century saw the great flood of Latin and Greek words into English called the "inkhorn" controversy?
questions.f: Critics mocked showy new words as poured from an inkhorn — yet many, like "describe," survived.

questions.q: Which royally sponsored English Bible of 1611 shaped countless English phrases?
questions.f: It gave English "the salt of the earth," "a labour of love" and "the writing on the wall."

questions.q: William Tyndale is remembered for the first printed English translation of the...?
questions.f: He coined "scapegoat" and "atonement" — words English had lacked entirely.

questions.q: The word "scapegoat" was coined in the 1500s by which translator?
questions.f: He needed an English word for a Hebrew term and built one from "escape" and "goat."

questions.q: Which Italian poet's decision to write in his local speech helped make it Italy's standard language?
questions.f: His Tuscan became the model for modern Italian, centuries before Italy was a country.

questions.q: Martin Luther's German Bible translation is credited with helping to standardise...?
questions.f: He said he listened to how mothers in the marketplace spoke, then wrote that way.

questions.q: The Cyrillic alphabet was reformed and simplified under which Russian ruler?
questions.f: His "civil script" of 1708 made Russian books look far more like Western European ones.

questions.q: The Ugaritic tablets are prized because they preserve one of the oldest known...?
questions.f: A schoolroom tablet lists letters in an order strikingly close to our own A-B-C.

questions.q: An ancient list of letters in their fixed order is called an...?
questions.f: Abecedaries from around 1200 BCE show the alphabet's order is over three thousand years old.

questions.q: Why do English and many other alphabets keep A-B-C order at all?
c: It was inherited unchanged from Phoenician
It was chosen for ease of typing
It was set by the Romans by vote
questions.f: Hebrew and Greek preserve the same basic run — aleph-bet-gimel, alpha-beta-gamma.

questions.q: The Phoenician letter behind our M was named after which natural thing?
questions.f: "Mem" meant water — you can still see the wave in the letter's zigzag shape.

questions.q: Which Greek letter name literally referred to a camel in its Semitic original?
questions.f: From "gimel" — a camel's hump, flattened over the centuries into an angular letter.

questions.q: The Greek letter "delta" gave its name to which geographical feature?
questions.f: Herodotus noticed the Nile's mouth was shaped like a triangular capital delta.

questions.q: The word "omega" literally means...?
questions.f: And omicron means "little o" — Greek labelled its two O letters by size.

questions.q: Which letter did the Romans borrow from Greek but keep only for Greek loanwords?
questions.f: They called it "i graeca" — Greek i — and French still calls it "i grec."

questions.q: The letter W is called "double u" because it began as two written...?
questions.f: French and Spanish still describe it as double v — same letter, different eyes.

questions.q: A Czech scholar working in wartime 1915, a clay tablet mentioning bread, and the word "watar" revealed that which ancient language was Indo-European?
questions.f: Bedrich Hrozny spotted that a line about eating bread and drinking water used words like our own.

questions.q: A Soviet scholar who never visited the ruins, a 16th-century bishop's flawed alphabet, and a cat he named as co-author advanced the reading of which script?
questions.f: Yuri Knorozov trusted Diego de Landa's much-mocked list, and it turned out to be the key.

questions.q: A cliff face 100 metres up in Iran, a British officer dangling on ropes, and three languages in wedge-shaped signs unlocked which writing system?
questions.f: Henry Rawlinson copied the Behistun inscription of Darius, and its Old Persian cracked the rest.

questions.q: A British official in Calcutta, coins bearing two scripts, and the edicts of an emperor led to the 1837 reading of which ancient Indian script?
questions.f: James Prinsep's breakthrough revealed the pillar edicts of Ashoka, unread for 1,500 years.

questions.q: A German schoolteacher, a bet with friends in 1802, and the repeated phrase "king of kings" began the decipherment of which script?
questions.f: Georg Grotefend guessed royal names correctly without knowing a word of Persian.

questions.q: A 12th-century abbess, 1,011 invented words, and a glossary written beside her music make her the author of the earliest known...?
questions.f: Hildegard of Bingen's Lingua Ignota predates Esperanto by seven centuries.

questions.q: Two teenage brothers in Guinea in 1989, a language written awkwardly in Arabic letters, and a script now in Unicode describe the invention of...?
questions.f: Ibrahima and Abdoulaye Barry built Adlam for Fulani — and lived to see it on smartphones.

questions.q: A Guinean writer in 1949, a bet about whether African languages could be written properly, and a right-to-left alphabet produced which script?
questions.f: Solomana Kante created N'Ko for the Manding languages, and it spread through informal schools.

questions.q: A West African sultan, a dream, and a script that shrank from hundreds of pictures to a tidy syllabary describe which writing system?
questions.f: Sultan Ibrahim Njoya of Cameroon revised his script through six versions in about 20 years.

questions.q: A Liberian man's dream in the 1830s, a syllabary of over 200 signs, and one of Africa's oldest indigenous scripts point to...?
questions.f: Momolu Duwalu Bukele's Vai script was in use before most European colonisation of the region.

questions.q: A group in Utah in the 1850s, a schoolbook printed in strange letters, and a 38-character alphabet describe which failed reform?
questions.f: Brigham Young backed it to spell English phonetically; only a few books ever appeared.

questions.q: A 1907 schism among idealists, a reform that angered its parent movement, and a name meaning "offspring" describe which constructed language?
questions.f: Ido means "derived from" in Esperanto — the split badly weakened both camps.

questions.q: An American sociologist, a language designed to test whether thought could be reshaped, and a logic-based grammar describe which conlang?
questions.f: James Cooke Brown built Loglan in 1955 to test the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis experimentally.

questions.q: A science-fiction author, a language designed to express women's perceptions precisely, and a 1984 novel introduced which conlang?
questions.f: Suzette Haden Elgin created Laadan and wrote "Native Tongue" around it as a thought experiment.

questions.q: A ceremonial vocabulary with only about 200 words, an Australian language called Lardil, and initiation rites describe which restricted register?
questions.f: Damin used sounds found in no ordinary human language, including a click on an inward breath.

questions.q: An Australian language, a special vocabulary used only near certain in-laws, and a full parallel word list describe Dyirbal's...?
questions.f: Jalnguy, or mother-in-law language, shared Dyirbal's grammar but almost none of its words.

questions.q: A parchment full of unknown script, plants nobody can identify, and a 15th-century radiocarbon date describe which famous puzzle?
questions.f: Yale keeps it, statisticians insist its text behaves like a real language, and nobody can read it.

questions.q: A Cretan clay disc, 45 distinct stamped signs, and a spiral of symbols pressed with punches describe which undeciphered object?
questions.f: It may be the earliest known example of movable type — used just once, around 1700 BCE.

questions.q: Gold sheets found in an Italian sanctuary, a text in two languages, and a Phoenician version supplied the best bilingual key to which language?
questions.f: The Pyrgi Tablets of about 500 BCE still have not made Etruscan fully readable.

questions.q: A script we can pronounce perfectly, a Sudanese kingdom, and a language with no known relatives describe which frustrating case?
questions.f: Francis Llewellyn Griffith cracked the Meroitic alphabet by 1909 — the language itself stays opaque.

questions.q: Manuscripts in a Silk Road cave, a language written in an Indian-derived script, and vocabulary related to English describe which extinct family branch?
questions.f: Tocharian was Indo-European yet spoken in western China — its discovery redrew the family map.

questions.q: A Sanskrit grammarian of roughly the 5th century BCE, about 4,000 terse rules, and a system compared to computer code describe...?
questions.f: Leonard Bloomfield called Panini's grammar one of the greatest monuments of human intelligence.

questions.q: A Swiss professor, lectures published only after his death in 1916, and the pairing of signifier with signified founded which approach?
questions.f: Ferdinand de Saussure's students reconstructed his "Course in General Linguistics" from notes.

questions.q: A 1957 book, a sentence about colourless green ideas, and the claim that grammar can be studied apart from meaning describe whose work?
questions.f: "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously" is grammatical nonsense — his point exactly.

questions.q: A 1958 experiment, cartoon birds, and children inventing a plural they had never heard tested what about young minds?
c: That they learn grammar rules, not just words
questions.f: Jean Berko Gleason's wug test showed toddlers apply rules to words that do not exist.

questions.q: A French surgeon in 1861, a patient known as Tan, and a preserved brain in a Paris museum identified which region?
questions.f: Leborgne could understand speech but say almost nothing — his brain is still on display.

questions.q: Fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension, and damage behind the ear rather than in front characterise which condition?
questions.f: Patients may talk smoothly for minutes without conveying anything — and often not notice.

questions.q: A 1960 monograph, a notation for hand shape and movement, and a fight for academic respect proved what about American Sign Language?
c: That it is a full language
That it is a code for English
questions.f: William Stokoe's work overturned a century of dismissal of signing as mere gesture.

questions.q: An 1880 international congress in Milan resolved to promote speech and to discourage the use of...?
questions.f: Its effects lasted a century, and deaf communities kept signing anyway — often in secret.

questions.q: A New England island, high hereditary deafness, and a village where hearing people signed too describe which vanished language?
questions.f: For generations in Chilmark, signing was simply a normal part of everyday village life.

questions.q: A shared signing system used across the Great Plains for trade and diplomacy between many nations is called...?
questions.f: It let speakers of completely unrelated languages negotiate without an interpreter.

questions.q: A 1988 student protest, a university in Washington DC, and the appointment of I. King Jordan are remembered as which movement?
questions.f: Gallaudet University had never had a deaf president in 124 years — students shut the campus until it did.

questions.q: A 45-letter lung disease name is often cited as the longest word in major English dictionaries. It ends in which element?
questions.f: Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis was coined in 1935, some say as a stunt.

questions.q: Which 29-letter word, meaning the habit of dismissing things as worthless, is often called the longest non-technical word in the OED?
questions.f: It stitches together four Latin words that all mean "of little value."

questions.q: A Welsh village name of 58 letters, a railway platform sign, and a 19th-century plan to attract tourists point to...?
questions.f: A local tailor reportedly lengthened the name on purpose — the ploy worked and still works.

questions.q: A New Zealand hill of 85 letters holds a record for the longest official...?
questions.f: Taumatawhakatangihangakoauau... describes a chief playing his flute to a lost love.

questions.q: Which 17-letter word is usually cited as the longest English word with no repeated letter?
questions.f: Words with no repeated letter are isograms; this one describes the skin layer beneath your fingerprints.

questions.q: Which word contains all five vowels in alphabetical order?
questions.f: "Abstemious" and "arsenious" manage it too — and "facetiously" throws in a Y for luck.

questions.q: Which word famously contains three consecutive pairs of double letters?
questions.f: OO, KK, EE in a row — its cousin "bookkeeping" pulls off the same trick.

questions.q: Which nine-letter English word is often cited as the longest with just one vowel letter?
questions.f: Only the E is a vowel — the R does surprising work holding the word together.

questions.q: The letter sequence "ough" is notorious because in English it can be pronounced in about how many ways?
questions.f: Though, through, thought, tough, cough, plough, thorough, hiccough and lough.

questions.q: The odd spelling of "colonel" reflects a tug-of-war between Italian and French forms of the word for a...?
questions.f: Italian gave the L in the spelling; French gave the R we actually say.

questions.q: A word appearing exactly once in a whole corpus is a hapax legomenon. Homer's poems contain many because...?
c: Their vocabulary is archaic and formulaic
questions.f: Some Homeric words baffled even ancient Greek scholars, who guessed at their meaning.

questions.q: Zipf's law describes the striking relationship in any language between a word's frequency and its...?
questions.f: The second-commonest word appears about half as often as the first — across every language tested.

questions.q: A Swadesh list is a short list of basic words used to...?
questions.f: Morris Swadesh picked words like "eye" and "water" that languages rarely borrow.

questions.q: Glottochronology attempts to estimate how long ago two languages...?
questions.f: It assumes core vocabulary is replaced at a roughly steady rate — a claim still hotly debated.

questions.q: Berlin and Kay's 1969 study argued that basic colour terms enter languages in a...?
questions.f: Black and white come first, then red — a pattern found across dozens of unrelated languages.

questions.q: Russian speakers beat English speakers on some colour tests because Russian has separate basic words for...?
questions.f: Goluboy and siniy are as distinct to Russians as pink and red are to English speakers.

questions.q: Languages that use a single basic word covering both green and blue are described by linguists as having...?
questions.f: Japanese "ao" traditionally spanned both — which is why a green traffic light is still called blue.

questions.q: Which document is generally recorded as the most translated in the world?
c: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
questions.f: It exists in well over 500 languages, and the count keeps climbing.

questions.q: Which novel is usually named the most translated work of fiction?
questions.f: Saint-Exupery's story has appeared in more than 500 languages and dialects, including Sami.

questions.q: A 1969 French novel written entirely without the letter E was matched by an English translation titled...?
questions.f: Gilbert Adair rendered Georges Perec's "La Disparition" in 1995, keeping the same impossible rule.

questions.q: The French writers' group Oulipo is known for creating literature under...?
questions.f: Members swapped nouns by dictionary position, banned letters, and wrote poems as machines.

questions.q: A Chinese linguist, a poem of over 90 syllables all written "shi," and a romanisation system he designed point to which scholar?
questions.f: His "Lion-Eating Poet in the Stone Den" is readable on paper but unintelligible aloud.

questions.q: A city in New York State, a verb meaning to bully, and an animal name combine in a famous eight-word sentence built from one repeated...?
questions.f: "Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo" is grammatically valid English.

questions.q: "The horse raced past the barn fell" is the classic example of which kind of sentence?
questions.f: Your brain commits to a reading, hits the last word, and has to reverse — hence the name.

questions.q: A word that fills a slot in a joke about a bird, a made-up creature, and a plural test — Jean Berko Gleason's creature was called a...?
questions.f: Shown two, children said "wugs" — proving they had internalised a rule, not memorised a word.

questions.q: A French teacher of English, an association founded in 1886, and about a hundred symbols able to write any human sound produced whose creation?
questions.f: He wanted a fair, spelling-proof way to teach pronunciation to learners anywhere.
