questions.q: The phonetician Henry Sweet is widely thought to have inspired which fictional character?
questions.f: Shaw admitted in his preface to "Pygmalion" that Sweet was partly the model.

questions.q: Daniel Jones's "cardinal vowels" gave phoneticians a reference set of...?
questions.f: His vowel quadrilateral still appears in phonetics textbooks nearly a century later.

questions.q: "Use your loaf" for head, market traders wanting privacy, and a rhyme that vanishes once everyone knows it describe which slang's key trick?
questions.f: Loaf of bread rhymes with head — then "bread" disappears, leaving outsiders stranded.

questions.q: Words like naff and zhoosh, a blend of Italian, Yiddish and Romani, and a 1960s BBC radio comedy popularised which secret vocabulary?
questions.f: It thrived in theatre, circus and merchant-ship life, where privacy mattered.

questions.q: Cod boats meeting on Arctic water, a vocabulary of roughly 400 words, and 150 years of bartering describe a pidgin mixing Russian with which language?
questions.f: Russenorsk split its words almost evenly between the two sides — a rare mark of equal footing.

questions.q: Cree verbs, buffalo-hunting communities on the Canadian plains, and nouns imported wholesale from Europe describe which mixed language?
questions.f: Michif borrowed two entire grammatical systems, which is why linguists call it a true mixed language.

questions.q: The words potlatch and high muck-a-muck, fur traders bargaining with many nations, and a vocabulary drawn from several tongues describe a jargon of which coast?
questions.f: At its height it was understood from Oregon to Alaska by tens of thousands of people.

questions.q: Jesuit missions that printed books in it, a national radio audience, and more household speakers than Spanish describe Guarani's status in Paraguay as...?
questions.f: Paraguay is one of very few American countries where an indigenous language is genuinely national.

questions.q: The Inca kept records not in writing but with knotted cords called...?
questions.f: Some researchers argue quipus encode narrative, not just numbers — the debate is unresolved.

questions.q: Which language, spoken in Alaska, lost its last fluent speaker in 2008?
questions.f: Marie Smith Jones spent her final years working with a linguist to record everything she knew.

questions.q: The death of Boa Sr in 2010 ended which ancient Andaman Islands language?
questions.f: She said the loneliest part was having nobody left who could laugh at her jokes.

questions.q: Seven years of hunt-and-peck typing, a grandmother in the Central Valley, and a finished dictionary of Wukchumni belong to which US state?
questions.f: Marie Wilcox recorded the whole language letter by letter after learning to type in her seventies.

questions.q: Preschools where adults may speak only one tongue, a 1980s change to a state's school law, and a language once down to a few hundred child speakers describe the revival of...?
questions.f: Punana Leo means "language nest" — and thousands of children now grow up speaking Hawaiian.

questions.q: Kohanga Reo language nests were pioneered in New Zealand to revitalise...?
questions.f: The model was so successful that Hawaii and Wales studied and copied it.

questions.q: Which living language is generally considered English's closest relative?
questions.f: An old rhyme runs "bread, butter and green cheese is good English and good Fries."

questions.q: Icelandic speakers can read medieval sagas fairly easily because the language has been unusually...?
questions.f: Icelandic still keeps four cases and coins new words rather than borrowing them.

questions.q: The Icelandic word for computer, "tolva," was built from words meaning number and...?
questions.f: Rather than importing "computer," Icelanders reached back into Norse mythology for a name.

questions.q: Bilingual road signs in Lusatia, elaborate painted Easter eggs, and a Slavic island inside Germany describe which minority language?
questions.f: Upper and Lower Sorbian have survived over a thousand years surrounded entirely by German.

questions.q: Romansh is one of the four official languages of which country?
questions.f: It descends from the Latin of Roman soldiers and is spoken by well under one percent of Swiss.

questions.q: A windswept fishing coast, a Uralic language ringed by Baltic neighbours, and a final native speaker who died in 2013 describe Livonian, once spoken in...?
questions.f: Livonian was closer to Estonian than to the Latvian spoken all around it.

questions.q: The word "seersucker" comes from a Persian phrase meaning...?
questions.f: The alternating smooth and puckered stripes really do look like poured milk beside sugar.

questions.q: "Tulip" and "turban" are thought to share an origin in a Persian word for a...?
questions.f: European visitors reportedly thought the flower resembled an Ottoman turban.

questions.q: The word "magazine" comes through Arabic from a word meaning...?
questions.f: A gun's magazine stores ammunition; a printed magazine stores articles.

questions.q: "Mattress" comes from an Arabic word meaning a place where something is...?
questions.f: Crusaders brought home the Arab habit of sleeping on cushions thrown on the floor.

questions.q: A word for gravel or grit, another for a broken lump, and a sweet carried west through Persia and Arabia gave English sugar and which companion word?
questions.f: Sanskrit sharkara meant grit; khanda meant a piece — both describe the crystals exactly.

questions.q: A Sanskrit word about antlers, a knobbly underground stem, and a spice traded west before Rome fell gave English which name?
questions.f: Srngaveram means roughly "horn body" — one look at the rhizome explains it.

questions.q: The word "peach" comes from a Latin phrase meaning...?
questions.f: Romans thought peaches came from Persia, though they actually began in China.

questions.q: The word "currant" comes from the name of which city?
questions.f: They were sold as "raisins of Corinth" — the place name shrank into the fruit's name.

questions.q: "Damask," "muslin" and "calico" are all fabrics named after...?
questions.f: Damascus, Mosul and Calicut — the trade routes are stitched into English vocabulary.

questions.q: A blue stone mined in Persia, Ottoman merchants who carried it to Europe, and a name crediting the wrong country produced which word?
questions.f: It simply means "Turkish" — Europeans named the gem after the traders, not the mine.

questions.q: A 1756 siege, a French commander's kitchen, and a harbour called Mahon gave a sauce its name — on which island?
questions.f: The story is disputed, but the Menorcan port remains the leading candidate.

questions.q: A bird native to North America, called "peru" in Portuguese and "d'Inde" in French, is named in Turkish after which country?
questions.f: Almost every language blames a different distant place — English blames Turkish merchants.

questions.q: A Persian word for pitch, powders sold in European apothecaries, and a mistaken idea about black coatings gave English which word?
questions.f: Europeans believed embalmed bodies were tar-coated, and even ground them up as medicine.

questions.q: "Zenith" and "nadir" both entered English from which language of medieval science?
questions.f: "Zenith" is a garbled reading of Arabic script by European copyists — a scribal accident that stuck.

questions.q: The word "giraffe" came into European languages from Arabic "zarafa," replacing an earlier name meaning...?
questions.f: Greek "camelopardalis" survives in the giraffe's scientific name today.

questions.q: "Check," "chess" and "exchequer" all descend from a Persian word for a...?
questions.f: Shah gave English checkmate, cheque and the chequered cloth of a treasury table.

questions.q: "Satin" is thought to be named after a Chinese port Arab traders called...?
questions.f: Zaitun is generally identified with Quanzhou, a great medieval silk-trading harbour.

questions.q: The word "silk" is thought to descend ultimately from an ancient name for...?
questions.f: Latin "sericus" came from Seres, the silk people — Greek and Roman geographers' name for China.

questions.q: "Coconut" comes from a Portuguese word for a...?
questions.f: Sailors thought the three marks on the nut looked like a face — "coco" was a bogeyman grin.

questions.q: The word "apricot" travelled into English through Arabic and Latin, from a word meaning...?
questions.f: Latin "praecoquum" — the same root as "precocious."

questions.q: Which English word for a fruit began as Arabic "al-kharshuf"?
questions.f: It passed through Spanish and Italian, collecting a folk-etymology "choke" on the way.

questions.q: When speakers reshape a strange borrowed word into familiar parts, as with "artichoke," it is called...?
questions.f: "Shamefaced" was once "shamefast," and "cockroach" reshaped Spanish "cucaracha."

questions.q: The term "Hobson-Jobson" describes both a famous glossary and the process of...?
c: Reshaping foreign words into familiar sounds
questions.f: Yule and Burnell's 1886 glossary of Anglo-Indian words gave its own name to the phenomenon.

questions.q: The word "tattarrattat," coined by James Joyce in "Ulysses," is notable as the longest English...?
questions.f: Twelve letters, and it means a knock at the door.

questions.q: The famous palindrome "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" was devised in 1948 by...?
questions.f: He was a British wordplay enthusiast who also produced palindromes hundreds of letters long.

questions.q: The Latin word square containing SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS reads the same...?
questions.f: Found scratched on Roman walls, it can be read across and down, forwards and back.

questions.q: A word that spells a different word backwards, like "stressed" and "desserts," is playfully called a...?
questions.f: "Semordnilap" is "palindromes" spelled backwards — the name demonstrates itself.

questions.q: A design that reads as the same or another word when rotated is called an...?
questions.f: Book covers love them — the word "NOON" rotated 180 degrees still reads NOON.

questions.q: A Finnish flavour for one tongue and a Welsh one for another, a professor's private hobby begun in his teens, and a mythology built to house them describe whose invented languages?
questions.f: Quenya echoes Finnish and Sindarin echoes Welsh — he said the stories existed to give the languages a home.

questions.q: A vocabulary of Russian-derived teen slang, a 1962 British novel, and words like "horrorshow" and "droog" describe which invented argot?
questions.f: Anthony Burgess built Nadsat from Russian — "nadsat" itself is the Russian ending for teen numbers.

questions.q: A shrinking dictionary, the deliberate destruction of synonyms, and a word like "doubleplusgood" describe which fictional language?
questions.f: Orwell's appendix explains the aim: to make unapproved thoughts literally unsayable.

questions.q: A linguist hired for a film about blue aliens, a real phonetic system, and songs written to be singable describe the creation of...?
questions.f: Paul Frommer gave Na'vi ejective consonants and a rare grammatical marking system.

questions.q: An applicant who won a competition, a language for horse-riding warriors, and thousands of words invented for television describe whose work?
questions.f: He beat dozens of rivals for the job and went on to build languages for many series.

questions.q: An illustrated book of imaginary plants and machines, an unreadable script, and an Italian architect describe which famous volume?
questions.f: Luigi Serafini has said the writing means nothing — it is designed to feel like reading a child does.

questions.q: A Cambridge examiner's Greek, an African grey parrot, and over a hundred spoken labels describe which research subject?
questions.f: Irene Pepperberg's Alex could identify colours and shapes, and reportedly asked what colour he was.

questions.q: A bonobo, a keyboard of abstract symbols, and comprehension of spoken English sentences describe which primate?
questions.f: Kanzi learned by watching his mother's lessons rather than being trained directly.

questions.q: A chimpanzee named as a pun on a famous linguist was part of a 1970s project to test...?
c: Whether apes can learn sign language
questions.f: Nim Chimpsky's name teased Noam Chomsky, who insisted grammar was uniquely human.

questions.q: Charles Hockett's list of "design features" was an attempt to define what makes...?
questions.f: His features include displacement — talking about things not present — and productivity.

questions.q: Hockett's term "duality of patterning" describes how meaningless sounds combine into...?
questions.f: A few dozen phonemes produce unlimited words — the trick no animal call system manages.

questions.q: A Scottish word for a magic spell, medieval suspicion of book-learning, and a modern word for allure link "glamour" to which other English word?
questions.f: Grammar meant learning, then occult learning, then enchantment — and finally star quality.

questions.q: A Greek antidote for venomous bites, a medieval apothecary's sweet paste, and a modern tin of syrup explain which word?
questions.f: "Theriake" was the antidote; only the sugary carrier survived into modern kitchens.

questions.q: The word "tragedy" pairs with "comedy," which comes from Greek words meaning...?
questions.f: "Komos" was a boisterous festive procession — comedy began as party music.

questions.q: A "sycophant" in ancient Greek literally meant a...?
questions.f: Nobody is sure what the gesture meant, but the accusation of informing stuck to the word.

questions.q: The word "laconic" comes from a region of Greece whose people were famed for...?
questions.f: Laconia contained Sparta — legend says they replied to a threat with the single word "if."

questions.q: The word "stoic" comes from a Greek word for a...?
questions.f: Zeno taught under the painted colonnade in Athens — a school named after its architecture.

questions.q: The word "academy" comes from the name of a...?
questions.f: Plato taught in a grove sacred to a hero named Akademos.

questions.q: The word "cynic" comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Ancient Cynics were mocked for living rough like dogs — and rather enjoyed the label.

questions.q: The word "barbarian" originally described people whose speech sounded to Greek ears like...?
questions.f: Sanskrit has a similar formation, suggesting the joke is thousands of years old.

questions.q: The word "idiot" originally meant a...?
questions.f: In Athens it meant someone with no public role — a citizen who kept to himself.

questions.q: The word "enthusiasm" originally described being filled with a...?
questions.f: En plus theos — for centuries English writers used it to mean religious fanaticism, not keenness.

questions.q: The word "hazard" is thought to come through Arabic from a word for a...?
questions.f: Chance at dice became chance in general, then danger — a word that gambled its way into English.

questions.q: The word "tennis" is generally traced to a French word shouted by the server, meaning...?
questions.f: "Tenez!" — the old indoor game also gave us "deuce" and, arguably, "love."

questions.q: The word "canter" is a shortening of a phrase describing the pace of pilgrims riding to...?
questions.f: "Canterbury gallop" was an easy trot — Chaucer's pilgrims travelled in the word's ancestor.

questions.q: The word "tawdry" comes from cheap lace once sold at a fair honouring...?
questions.f: "Saint Audrey's lace" slurred into "tawdry lace" — and then into an insult.

questions.q: The word "maudlin" comes from artistic depictions of which biblical figure weeping?
questions.f: Her name, pronounced the English way, became a word for tearful sentimentality.

questions.q: The word "bedlam" is a worn-down form of the name of a London...?
questions.f: St Mary of Bethlehem's name collapsed to Bedlam, and the noise inside gave us the word.

questions.q: The word "jovial" comes from the belief that people born under which planet were cheerful?
questions.f: Astrology also gave English "saturnine," "mercurial" and "lunatic" — a whole mood chart in the sky.

questions.q: The word "quintessence" originally meant the fifth...?
questions.f: Beyond earth, water, air and fire, philosophers imagined a purer fifth substance filling the heavens.

questions.q: The word "humour" originally referred to bodily...?
questions.f: Ancient medicine blamed moods on the balance of four humours — hence "in a good humour."

questions.q: The word "melancholy" literally means...?
questions.f: One of the four humours — the very word carries a discarded medical theory inside it.

questions.q: "Sanguine," meaning cheerfully optimistic, comes from a word for...?
questions.f: A blood-dominant humour was thought to produce a warm, hopeful temperament.

questions.q: Two Australian scientists, a 1964 paper in Nature, and the fluid said to run in gods' veins produced which coined word?
questions.f: Petrichor blends stone with ichor — the smell is oils from rocks released by rain.

questions.q: The word "philtrum," the groove above the upper lip, comes from a Greek word meaning...?
questions.f: Ancient writers thought the dip was one of the body's most attractive features.

questions.q: The metal or plastic tip on a shoelace is properly called an...?
questions.f: From French for needle — before buttons were common, laces were the main way to fasten clothes.

questions.q: "Defenestration" means throwing someone or something out of a...?
questions.f: Latin "fenestra" is window; the word became famous through the Defenestrations of Prague.

questions.q: The word "susurrus" describes a...?
questions.f: The word itself whispers — Latin built it by imitating the noise of soft rustling.

questions.q: A word wrongly reanalysed as sensible parts, like "eggcorn" for "acorn," is named after...?
questions.f: Linguists needed a name for the phenomenon, so they used one of its best examples.

questions.q: Inserting a word inside another, as in "abso-blooming-lutely," is called...?
questions.f: Greek for cutting — Eliza Doolittle uses one of English's most famous examples.

questions.q: A cliche phrase pattern reused with swapped words, like "X is the new Y," is nicknamed a...?
questions.f: The name mocks the tired claim that Eskimo languages have countless words for snow.

questions.q: Which claim about Eskimo languages and snow words is widely considered a linguistic myth?
c: That they have hundreds of unrelated snow words
That they have no snow words
questions.f: They do have rich snow vocabulary, but the numbers were inflated in retellings for a century.

questions.q: A capitonym is a word whose meaning changes when you...?
questions.f: March the month and march the walk; Polish the nationality and polish the shine.

questions.q: A word or phrase whose letters are all in alphabetical order, like "almost," is sometimes called an...?
questions.f: "Spoonfeed" is often cited as the longest word running in reverse alphabetical order.

questions.q: A poem in which the first letters of each line spell a word is an...?
questions.f: Lewis Carroll hid a girl's name down the first letters of a poem closing "Through the Looking-Glass."

questions.q: Which musical term is often cited as an English word made entirely of vowels?
questions.f: It marked a chant cadence in medieval music books — six letters, not a consonant in sight.

questions.q: The word "queueing" is often cited for having how many consecutive vowels?
questions.f: Q-U-E-U-E-I-N-G — the U's, E's and I line up in an unbroken run.

questions.q: Which word is often named the longest that can be typed using only the top row of a QWERTY keyboard?
questions.f: A tidy coincidence, and a favourite piece of typing-class trivia.

questions.q: The NATO phonetic alphabet spells one letter's word as "Alfa" rather than "Alpha" because...?
c: Not all speakers pronounce PH as F
questions.f: For the same reason Juliet is spelled "Juliett" — French speakers would drop a final single T.

questions.q: Alfred Vail is credited by many historians with shaping Morse code by studying the contents of a...?
questions.f: Counting how many of each letter printers kept revealed which letters deserved the shortest signals.

questions.q: Contracted or "Grade 2" braille uses shortcuts mainly to...?
questions.f: Uncontracted braille books are enormous — the contractions are what make them portable.

questions.q: The Nemeth Code is a braille system designed for writing...?
questions.f: Abraham Nemeth devised it because he was studying maths and existing braille could not cope.

questions.q: A word for cheap lace sold at a saint's fair, a London hospital's slurred name, and a weeping figure in old paintings all became English words describing...?
questions.f: Tawdry, bedlam and maudlin — three insults that began as perfectly respectable names.

questions.q: A pace suited to pilgrims, a shout from a server, and a dice game borrowed through Arabic gave English three words connected with...?
questions.f: Canter, tennis and hazard — sport has quietly stocked the dictionary for centuries.

questions.q: Black bile, a blood-warm temperament, and four fluids in ancient medicine explain the origins of melancholy, sanguine and which other word?
questions.f: A whole discarded medical theory survives inside English words for mood.

questions.q: A grove sacred to a hero, a painted porch in Athens, and men mocked for living like dogs gave their names to three...?
questions.f: Academy, Stoic and Cynic — the buildings and the insults outlasted the arguments.

questions.q: A region whose people answered a threat with one word, a private citizen with no public role, and being filled with a god gave English laconic, idiot and...?
questions.f: For centuries "enthusiasm" was a criticism, meaning wild religious excitement.

questions.q: A grinning bogeyman's face, a fruit thought to come from Persia, and dried grapes sold as "of Corinth" describe the naming of...?
questions.f: Coconut, peach and currant — a snack shelf full of accidental geography.

questions.q: Damascus, Mosul and Calicut all gave English the names of...?
questions.f: Damask, muslin and calico — the medieval textile trade left its map inside our wardrobes.

questions.q: A Persian word for a headwrap, an Arabic word for a storehouse, and a place where cushions were thrown down gave English tulip, magazine and...?
questions.f: Three borrowings, three utterly different destinations in modern English.

questions.q: A misread Arabic manuscript, a Persian word for king behind a treasury's cloth, and a camel-leopard renamed by traders describe how English gained zenith, exchequer and...?
questions.f: Arabic "zarafa" replaced the Greek name that survives only in scientific Latin.

questions.q: Milk and sugar in Persian, an early-ripening Latin fruit, and a thistle reshaped into a "choke" describe the arrival of seersucker, apricot and...?
questions.f: Folk etymology reshapes strange words into familiar ones — even when it makes no sense.

questions.q: A Silk Road port Arabs called Zaitun, an ancient Greek name for the silk people, and Kashmir's goats explain how English got satin, silk and...?
questions.f: Three luxury fabrics, three place names buried in plain sight.

questions.q: An 1886 glossary by Yule and Burnell, British soldiers in India, and words reshaped to sound English gave its own name to which phenomenon?
questions.f: The glossary's title was itself a garbled English version of an Arabic ritual cry.

questions.q: A knock at the door in "Ulysses," a 1948 canal-building sentence, and a Roman word square scratched on walls all celebrate which wordplay form?
questions.f: Tattarrattat, "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama," and SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS.

questions.q: A word that is "palindromes" spelled backwards, rotating book-cover art, and stressed desserts all describe games with a word's...?
questions.f: Semordnilaps and ambigrams both play with reading the same marks another way.

questions.q: A Sudanese kingdom's readable alphabet, a Cretan spiral of stamped signs, and a Yale library's mysterious herbal share which frustrating quality?
questions.f: Meroitic, the Phaistos Disc and the Voynich manuscript remain linguistics' great cold cases.

questions.q: An abbess's 1,011 invented words, a Polish eye doctor's pen name, and a language of only 120 roots are all examples of...?
questions.f: Lingua Ignota, Esperanto and Toki Pona — eight centuries of building languages on purpose.

questions.q: A Cameroonian sultan's dream, two Guinean teenagers in 1989, and a Liberian syllabary of 200 signs all record Africans inventing...?
questions.f: Bamum, Adlam and Vai — each created so a spoken language could finally be written well.

questions.q: A hillside chief playing a flute in New Zealand, a Welsh tailor's marketing idea, and a 45-letter lung disease share what distinction?
questions.f: The Welsh station name was reportedly stretched on purpose to lure Victorian tourists.

questions.q: A frog's twitching leg, a Viennese healer, and an 1812 voting district shaped like a salamander all produced English words called...?
questions.f: Galvanize, mesmerize and gerrymander — names that escaped their owners.

questions.q: A mocked medieval theologian, an 1807 family edition of Shakespeare, and an Oxford don's tangled sentences gave English three words about...?
questions.f: Dunce, bowdlerize and spoonerism — English immortalises embarrassment.

questions.q: A murderer in Broadmoor, slips of paper by the thousand, and seventy years of editing produced which reference work's first edition?
questions.f: Dr Minor's asylum cell became one of the project's most productive reading rooms.

questions.q: A misfiled slip reading "D or d," a fake fountain designer, and copyright traps describe the accidental and deliberate errors inside...?
questions.f: Ghost words and mountweazels are two very different kinds of dictionary phantom.

questions.q: A 1957 book of sleeping green ideas, cartoon birds tested on toddlers, and a chimpanzee with a punning name all belong to debates about...?
questions.f: Chomsky, the wug test and Nim Chimpsky all circled the same enormous question.

questions.q: A brain preserved in Paris, fluent speech that means nothing, and damage behind the ear are landmarks in the study of...?
questions.f: Broca's and Wernicke's patients mapped language onto the brain long before scanners existed.

questions.q: A 1960 notation for hand shapes, an 1880 congress in Milan, and a 1988 campus shutdown are turning points in the history of...?
questions.f: Stokoe's research, the Milan ban and Deaf President Now bracket a century of struggle.

questions.q: A Massachusetts island with hereditary deafness, Bedouin villages in the Negev, and Managua schoolchildren in the 1980s all produced...?
questions.f: Communities create full sign languages spontaneously whenever enough deaf people live together.

questions.q: Ravines in the Canary Islands, drums in West Africa, and hand signs across the Great Plains all solved which problem?
questions.f: Whistled Silbo, talking drums and Plains Sign Talk each carried messages speech could not.

questions.q: A woman in Alaska in 2008, an Andaman islander in 2010, and a Turkish villager in 1992 all shared the sad distinction of being...?
c: The last speaker of a language
questions.f: Marie Smith Jones, Boa Sr and Tevfik Esenc each worked with linguists to leave a record behind.

questions.q: Hawaiian toddlers in "language nests," Welsh schoolchildren after a 1993 act, and Manx pupils in a new primary school illustrate...?
questions.f: Immersion for the very young turned out to be the single most effective tool.

questions.q: Fishermen bartering in the Arctic, Metis families in Canada, and traders on the Pacific Northwest coast all developed...?
questions.f: Russenorsk, Michif and Chinook Jargon each grew where two peoples needed one tongue.

questions.q: Knotted cords in the Andes, notches on the edge of Irish stones, and wedge marks in Mesopotamian clay were all used to...?
questions.f: Quipu, ogham and cuneiform show how differently "writing" can be imagined.

questions.q: Oracle bones sold as medicine, a spiral-stamped disc, and gold sheets in an Italian sanctuary all became crucial evidence about...?
questions.f: Shang China, Minoan Crete and Etruscan Italy each left records archaeologists nearly missed.

questions.q: A word meaning "number prophetess," a committee in Reykjavik, and sagas readable after 800 years describe which language's approach to new words?
questions.f: Rather than borrow, Icelandic builds — and its grammar has barely budged since the Viking age.

questions.q: A phrase about bread, butter and green cheese, a North Sea coast, and grammar startlingly close to English point to which language?
questions.f: Frisian is English's closest living relative, and the old rhyme was a party trick to prove it.

questions.q: Four official languages, a Latin descendant spoken by well under one percent, and Alpine valleys describe which country's language map?
questions.f: Romansh survives in Graubunden, protected by mountains and by federal law.

questions.q: Two written standards, one built from rural dialects and one from Danish-influenced writing, describe which national language?
questions.f: Norwegians choose between Bokmal and Nynorsk in school — and argue about it constantly.

questions.q: A newsreader's formal variety, a family's everyday speech, and one language living two lives describe which situation, common in Arabic?
questions.f: Children often meet the formal written variety only when they start school.

questions.q: Eighteen noun cases in one language, vowels that must match across a word in another, and endings stacked like beads describe grammar found in...?
questions.f: Agglutinative languages let one word do a sentence's work — and keep the vowels in harmony.

questions.q: An ending that shows whether you saw something yourself, two different words for "we," and fifteen noun classes are all grammatical features...?
questions.f: Evidentiality, clusivity and noun classes are ordinary elsewhere and unthinkable in English.

questions.q: Speakers who say "the ant north of your foot," a language with no exact number words, and clicks made on an inward breath all challenge assumptions about...?
questions.f: Guugu Yimithirr, Piraha and Damin each broke a rule linguists thought was universal.

questions.q: Basque in the Pyrenees, Sumerian in Mesopotamia, and Ainu in northern Japan share which classification?
questions.f: An isolate has no demonstrated relatives — a family tree with a single branch.

questions.q: Manuscripts in a Chinese desert cave, a clay tablet about drinking water, and a judge's 1786 lecture in Calcutta all expanded knowledge of which family?
questions.f: Tocharian, Hittite and Sanskrit each stretched the family further than anyone had expected.

questions.q: Latin "pater" beside English "father," a fairy-tale collector's sound law, and a Dane's 1875 rescue of that law all concern...?
questions.f: Grimm found the pattern; Verner explained the exceptions by looking at where the stress fell.

questions.q: A word ranked second appearing half as often as the first, lists of words languages rarely borrow, and a clock ticking in vocabulary all belong to...?
questions.f: Zipf's law, Swadesh lists and glottochronology try to make language measurable.

questions.q: Two Russian words for blue, a 1969 study of colour terms, and a Japanese traffic light called blue all illustrate...?
questions.f: Berlin and Kay found order in colour naming; later experiments found real effects on the eye.

questions.q: A 1969 novel without the letter E, its English translation titled "A Void," and a Paris group writing under rules describe which literary game?
questions.f: Georges Perec later wrote a companion piece, "Les Revenentes," using E as its only vowel.

questions.q: A Chinese poem of ninety syllables all pronounced "shi," a New York city name used as a verb, and a horse racing past a barn all demonstrate that a sentence can be...?
questions.f: Chao's poem, the Buffalo sentence and the garden-path sentence are linguistics' favourite showpieces.

questions.q: An African grey parrot asking about colours, a bonobo at a symbol keyboard, and a chimpanzee named as a pun all featured in research on...?
questions.f: Alex, Kanzi and Nim Chimpsky each pushed the argument about what only humans can do.

questions.q: Russian-flavoured teen slang, a dictionary designed to shrink, and words for horse-riding warriors were all invented for...?
questions.f: Nadsat, Newspeak and Dothraki each served a story before anyone tried speaking them.

questions.q: A language modelled on Finnish, another on Welsh, and a mythology written to house them both are the achievement of...?
questions.f: He called the stories a background for the languages, not the other way round.

questions.q: An Italian printer's italic type, a Latin word for a point, and Greek and Roman texts written with no gaps all belong to the story of...?
questions.f: Readers once had to voice a text aloud to find where each word ended.

questions.q: What is the name of the tallest mountain on Earth?
questions.f: Everest rises 8,849 metres above sea level on the border of Nepal and Tibet.

questions.q: Which two brothers flew the first powered airplane?
questions.f: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew for 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk in 1903.

questions.q: Which icy continent sits at the very bottom of the world?
questions.f: Antarctica has no towns or cities, only research stations run by scientists.

questions.q: A person who travels to unknown places to find out about them is called an...?
questions.f: The word explore comes from Latin explorare, meaning to search out.

questions.q: Which animals pulled the sleds of explorers crossing the polar snow?
questions.f: Amundsen took 52 sled dogs on his race to the South Pole in 1911.

questions.q: What do we call the very top of a mountain?
questions.f: Summit comes from the Latin word summus, meaning highest.

questions.q: How many astronauts flew on the Apollo 11 mission to the Moon?
questions.f: Armstrong and Aldrin landed while Michael Collins circled the Moon alone.

questions.q: What is the deepest part of the ocean called?
questions.f: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is nearly 11 kilometres deep.

questions.q: Mount Everest is taller than any building people have ever built.
questions.f: Everest is about ten times taller than the Burj Khalifa, the tallest building.

questions.q: Which bird waddles on ice in Antarctica and cannot fly?
questions.f: Emperor penguins huddle in groups of thousands to stay warm in the polar winter.

questions.q: What do we call a long journey made by explorers with a team and supplies?
questions.f: Expedition comes from Latin words that mean to free the feet for marching.

questions.q: Which flat picture shows roads, rivers and towns from above?
questions.f: The oldest known maps were scratched onto clay tablets thousands of years ago.

questions.q: Amelia Earhart became famous for flying which kind of machine?
questions.f: In 1932 Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.q: Which ocean did sailors cross to sail from Europe to America?
questions.f: Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 in about five weeks.

questions.q: What do you call the person who steers a ship and finds its way?
questions.f: Navigate comes from Latin navis, a ship, plus agere, to drive.

questions.q: Yuri Gagarin was the first person to do what?
questions.f: Gagarin circled Earth once in 1961 in a flight lasting 108 minutes.

questions.q: Which vehicle takes people down to explore the bottom of the sea?
questions.f: A submersible has thick walls because deep water squeezes with enormous force.

questions.q: What is the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth called?
questions.f: Equator comes from a Latin word meaning to make equal, since it splits Earth in half.

questions.q: Explorers of the freezing Arctic have to watch out for which large white animal?
questions.f: Polar bears live only in the Arctic; there are no bears at all in Antarctica.

questions.q: What word means to sail or fly all the way around the world?
questions.f: Circum means around, so circumnavigate is simply to sail around.

questions.q: Which sea creature helped early sailors know that land might be near?
questions.f: Columbus's crew took heart when birds and floating branches appeared near land.

questions.q: A traveller who climbs mountains is called a...?
questions.f: Mountaineers use ropes, spikes and helmets to climb safely on rock and ice.

questions.q: Astronauts must carry their own air with them in space.
questions.f: There is no air in space, so spacesuits and spacecraft supply oxygen to breathe.

questions.q: Which country's flag did Apollo 11's astronauts plant on the Moon?
questions.f: Six American flags were planted on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

questions.q: The North Pole sits in the middle of which frozen place?
questions.f: Unlike Antarctica, the North Pole has no land underneath, only floating sea ice.

questions.q: What do we call a very big ship that carries explorers on long voyages?
questions.f: Magellan set out with five wooden vessels in 1519 to sail around the world.

questions.q: Which shape is the Earth?
questions.f: Earth bulges slightly at the equator, so it is not a perfect ball.

questions.q: What are the four main directions on a compass?
questions.f: These four are called the cardinal directions, from a Latin word for hinge.

questions.q: Which vehicle carried astronauts down onto the Moon's surface?
questions.f: Apollo 11's lunar module was nicknamed Eagle, giving us the words The Eagle has landed.

questions.q: What is a globe?
c: A round model of the Earth
questions.f: The oldest globe still around today was made in Germany in 1492.

questions.q: Which drink-making animal carried goods across the deserts of the Silk Road?
questions.f: Bactrian camels of Central Asia have two humps and thick winter coats.

questions.q: A group of travellers crossing a desert together is called a...?
questions.f: Caravan comes from a Persian word for a company of desert travellers.

questions.q: What precious cloth gave the Silk Road its name?
questions.f: Silk thread is spun by silkworms, and China kept the secret for centuries.

questions.q: Which frozen water floats in the sea and can be dangerous to ships?
questions.f: Only about one tenth of an iceberg shows above the water.

questions.q: What do we call people who travel into space?
questions.f: Astronaut is built from Greek words meaning star and sailor.

questions.q: Which large land was reached by Polynesian sailors travelling in canoes?
questions.f: Polynesian voyagers crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific in double canoes.

questions.q: How did old sailors travel across the ocean before engines were invented?
questions.f: Sailors learned the ocean's steady winds and named them the trade winds.

questions.q: There is no wind or weather on the Moon.
questions.f: With no air, the Moon has no wind, so Apollo footprints may last millions of years.

questions.q: Which word means the height of something above the sea?
questions.f: Altitude comes from the Latin word altus, meaning high.

questions.q: What did explorers use to see far-off ships and coastlines?
questions.f: Telescope is built from Greek words meaning far and to look.

questions.q: Which cold place is home to research stations but no towns?
questions.f: About 1,000 to 5,000 scientists live in Antarctica, depending on the season.

questions.q: Who was the first woman in space?
questions.f: Tereshkova flew in 1963 and orbited Earth 48 times in three days.

questions.q: What did the Wright brothers repair and sell before they built airplanes?
questions.f: Their bicycle shop taught them about balance and light, strong frames.

questions.q: Which piece of clothing keeps a polar explorer warmest?
questions.f: Parka comes from a word used by Arctic peoples for a hooded skin coat.

questions.q: What is a record?
c: The best or biggest ever measured
questions.f: Guinness World Records began in 1955 to settle arguments about the best and biggest.

questions.q: What do sailors call the front of a ship?
questions.f: The back of a ship is called the stern, and its kitchen is the galley.

questions.q: Which helper animal carried messages and mail for early travellers?
questions.f: Homing pigeons can find their way back over hundreds of kilometres.

questions.q: Which mountain range holds Mount Everest?
questions.f: The Himalayas are still rising a few millimetres every year.

questions.q: What is a rocket used for?
questions.f: A rocket works by throwing hot gas downwards very fast, pushing itself up.

questions.q: Which word describes the ice-covered regions at the top and bottom of Earth?
questions.f: Polar comes from a Greek word for the axis that the Earth spins around.

questions.q: Antarctica is colder than the Arctic.
questions.f: Antarctica is a high, dry continent, so it gets far colder than the Arctic sea ice.

questions.q: What does a lighthouse do for sailors?
questions.f: Lighthouse beams can be seen from more than 30 kilometres out at sea.

questions.q: Which sport-like activity means walking a long way through wild country?
questions.f: Trek comes from a Dutch word for pulling a wagon on a long journey.

questions.q: Who reached the South Pole first, in 1911?
questions.f: Amundsen's team arrived on 14 December 1911 and left a tent called Polheim.

questions.q: What is the name of the ship Ernest Shackleton took towards Antarctica in 1914?
questions.f: The ship was crushed by ice, yet every one of Shackleton's 28 men survived.

questions.q: Which two men first reached the top of Mount Everest?
questions.f: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the summit on 29 May 1953.

questions.q: Charles Lindbergh became famous for flying alone across which ocean?
questions.f: His 1927 flight from New York to Paris took 33 and a half hours without sleep.

questions.q: What is a spacesuit for?
c: Keeping an astronaut safe and supplied with air
questions.f: A spacesuit is really a tiny spacecraft with its own air, water and cooling.

questions.q: Which word means a journey by sea?
questions.f: Voyage comes from a Latin word for the food and supplies packed for a road trip.

questions.q: What do we call a small boat carried on a bigger ship for emergencies?
questions.f: Shackleton's crew sailed a lifeboat called the James Caird to fetch help.

questions.q: Which line on a map divides north from south?
questions.f: Countries on the equator have days and nights that stay nearly equal all year.

questions.q: What is the Moon's surface covered in?
questions.f: Moon dust is sharp and sticky, and it clung to every Apollo spacesuit.

questions.q: Which machine takes off straight upwards using spinning blades?
questions.f: Helicopter is built from Greek words meaning spiral and wing.

questions.q: An explorer who studies plants on a journey is called a...?
questions.f: Botanists on old sailing ships filled thousands of notebooks with new plants.

questions.q: What are footprints good for when tracking a route?
questions.f: Explorers often followed animal tracks to find water and safe paths.

questions.q: Which is the longest river in the world?
questions.f: The Nile flows about 6,650 kilometres north through eleven countries.

questions.q: What is a canoe?
c: A narrow boat moved by paddles
questions.f: Pacific voyagers lashed two canoes together to make them steady in big waves.

questions.q: The first airplane flight by the Wright brothers lasted less than one minute.
questions.f: It lasted just 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres, shorter than a jet's wing today.

questions.q: Which star helped sailors in the north find their direction at night?
questions.f: The North Star, Polaris, sits almost exactly above Earth's north axis.

questions.q: What do we call the wide sandy places explorers cross with very little water?
questions.f: Antarctica counts as a desert too, because so little snow actually falls there.

questions.q: Which piece of gear keeps a mountain climber from slipping on ice?
questions.f: Crampons are metal spikes that strap under boots and bite into hard ice.

questions.q: What is the name of the pushed-along vehicle astronauts drove on the Moon?
questions.f: Apollo 15, 16 and 17 crews drove electric rovers across the Moon's dust.

questions.q: The word 'map' first meant a cloth or sheet. What was drawn on it?
questions.f: Mappa was the Latin word for a napkin or cloth, the sheet a map was drawn on.

questions.q: Someone who makes maps for a living is called a...?
questions.f: The ending -grapher means one who writes or draws.

questions.q: Which word means a person who arrives somewhere first, before others follow?
questions.f: Pioneer once meant a foot soldier who went ahead to clear the way.

questions.q: What does the word 'discover' literally describe doing?
questions.f: Dis- undoes a word, so discover is to take the cover off something hidden.

questions.q: A traveller's plan of stops and places is called an...?
questions.f: Itinerary comes from the Latin word iter, meaning a journey.

questions.q: Which word means a boat's diary of everything that happens each day?
questions.f: Sailors once measured speed with a wooden log on a rope, and wrote it in the log.

questions.q: Which of these means 'half a ball' and is used for halves of Earth?
questions.f: Hemi means half, and sphere means ball, so a hemisphere is half the globe.

questions.q: What is the opposite direction from north?
questions.f: On most modern maps north is at the top, but that was not always the rule.

questions.q: Which word names a chain of many islands close together?
questions.f: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelago, with over 17,000 islands.

questions.q: What word means a piece of land with water on nearly every side?
questions.f: Peninsula comes from Latin words meaning almost an island.

questions.q: A person who sails a boat is a...?
questions.f: The word sail is one of the oldest English words still in everyday use.

questions.q: Which word means to go around something?
questions.f: The same circ- beginning shows up in circus, circuit and circumnavigate.

questions.q: An 'astronaut' and a 'cosmonaut' both mean a space traveller.
questions.f: Astronaut means star sailor and cosmonaut means universe sailor; both end in sailor.

questions.q: What is a 'record breaker'?
c: Someone who does better than anyone before
questions.f: Guinness World Records checks each claim carefully before printing it.

questions.q: Which land animal is the fastest runner?
questions.f: A cheetah can sprint about 100 kilometres an hour, but only for short bursts.

questions.q: Which bird can dive faster than any other animal on Earth?
questions.f: A diving peregrine can pass 300 kilometres an hour, folding its wings like an arrow.

questions.q: Which is the biggest animal that has ever lived?
questions.f: A blue whale can grow to 30 metres, longer than three buses in a row.

questions.q: How long does light from the Sun take to reach Earth?
questions.f: Sunlight travels 150 million kilometres to reach us, at 300,000 km per second.

questions.q: Which planet did the Voyager spacecraft visit on its way out of the solar system?
questions.f: Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter in 1979 and photographed its Great Red Spot.

questions.q: Which vehicle floats up into the sky using hot air?
questions.f: The first passengers in a hot air balloon were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.

questions.q: What did explorers use to measure how deep the water was under their ship?
questions.f: Sailors called this sounding, and the knotted rope was called a lead line.

questions.q: What are the frozen rivers that flow slowly down mountains called?
questions.f: Everest climbers must cross the Khumbu Glacier's icefall, which cracks and shifts daily.

questions.q: Which explorer's crew was the first to sail all the way around the world?
questions.f: Magellan died along the way, and Juan Sebastian Elcano brought the last ship home.

questions.q: What is the name for a boat that travels under the water?
questions.f: Sub means under and marine means of the sea.

questions.q: Which word describes very high up in the air, where planes fly?
questions.f: Pilots also say airborne, which simply means carried by the air.

questions.q: Explorers on long sea voyages long ago often ran out of fresh fruit.
questions.f: Without fruit sailors fell ill with scurvy, until limes and lemons became standard supplies.

questions.q: Which of these did sailors of long ago NOT have to help them find their way?
questions.f: Today's GPS uses more than 24 satellites circling high above the Earth.

questions.q: What is the name of the mountain climber's helper and guide in the Himalayas?
questions.f: The Sherpa people live high in Nepal, and their name means people of the east.

questions.q: Which sea creature can dive deeper than any other mammal?
questions.f: Cuvier's beaked whales have been tracked diving nearly three kilometres down.

questions.q: What do we call a place where a ship stops to load and unload?
questions.f: The left side of a ship is also called port, because that side faced the dock.

questions.q: Which giant ice sheet covers most of Greenland?
questions.f: Greenland's ice is up to three kilometres thick in the middle.

questions.q: What kind of hat or hood protects a climber's head from falling ice?
questions.f: Modern climbing helmets weigh less than a large apple.

questions.q: Which country did Tenzing Norgay, the Everest climber, come from?
questions.f: His climbing partner Edmund Hillary was from New Zealand and kept bees for a living.

questions.q: What do we call it when a spacecraft touches down gently on another world?
questions.f: The first soft landing on the Moon was by the robot Luna 9 in 1966.

questions.q: Which explorer travelled from Italy to China and wrote a famous book about it?
questions.f: Marco Polo spent about 24 years travelling before returning to Venice.

questions.q: How do you find out how far a trip is on a map?
questions.f: A scale bar shows how many real kilometres fit into one centimetre of map.

questions.q: Which vehicle needs a runway to take off?
questions.f: The Wright brothers used a wooden rail on the sand instead of a runway.

questions.q: Which of these keeps explorers dry in a storm?
questions.f: Early explorers waxed or oiled their coats to keep the rain out.

questions.q: What is the special word for a tent camp high on a mountain?
questions.f: Everest Base Camp sits at 5,364 metres, higher than most of Europe's mountains.

questions.q: Nobody owns Antarctica; countries agreed to share it for science.
questions.f: The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 set the whole continent aside for peaceful research.

questions.q: Which is the coldest place on Earth?
questions.f: A Russian station in Antarctica once recorded minus 89.2 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What do we call the sound-based tool ships use to find the seafloor?
questions.f: Sonar sends a ping of sound down and times how long the echo takes to return.

questions.q: Which is heavier to carry up a mountain?
questions.f: A full climbing oxygen bottle weighs several kilograms, and climbers often take two.

questions.q: What did the astronauts leave behind on the Moon that scientists still use today?
questions.f: Lasers fired at those mirrors measure the Moon's distance to within centimetres.

questions.q: Which word means finding your way using the stars, sun and sea?
questions.f: Pacific wayfinders read stars, swells and birds instead of using instruments.

questions.q: What sort of animal is a husky?
questions.f: Huskies have double coats and can curl up and sleep in the snow.

questions.q: Which of these can an explorer use at night to see?
questions.f: Climbers often set off at 2am by headlamp so they can be down before afternoon storms.

questions.q: What does a flag on a summit or pole show?
questions.f: Amundsen left a note in his tent at the South Pole in case he never got home.

questions.q: Which of these words means very brave?
questions.f: Courage comes from the Latin word cor, meaning heart.

questions.q: What did explorers do with new plants and animals they found?
questions.f: Ships often carried an artist to draw creatures long before cameras existed.

questions.q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
questions.f: Lake Baikal in Siberia is over 1,600 metres deep and holds a fifth of Earth's fresh water.

questions.q: Which is the world's highest waterfall?
questions.f: Angel Falls in Venezuela drops 979 metres, so far that much of it turns to mist.

questions.q: How does a hot air balloon go higher?
questions.f: Hot air is lighter than cold air, so a heated balloon rises like a bubble.

questions.q: Astronauts float inside a spacecraft because there is no gravity anywhere in space.
questions.f: Gravity is still there; astronauts float because they and the spacecraft are falling together.

questions.q: What is a crater?
questions.f: Moon craters were mostly punched out by rocks smashing into the surface.

questions.q: Which is the biggest island in the world?
questions.f: Australia is bigger, but it counts as a continent rather than an island.

questions.q: What did Chinese admiral Zheng He command on his great voyages?
questions.f: His treasure fleets carried tens of thousands of people to Africa and back.

questions.q: Which word means a very long walk or march to somewhere far away?
questions.f: Journey comes from a French word for a day, since it meant one day's travel.

questions.q: What is the name for a wide, treeless plain of frozen ground in the Arctic?
questions.f: Under the tundra lies permafrost, ground that stays frozen all year round.

questions.q: What do we call the moment a rocket leaves the ground?
questions.f: Apollo astronauts returned by splashdown, parachuting into the ocean.

questions.q: What kind of picture does a satellite take of Earth?
questions.f: Satellite photos let mapmakers check coastlines without ever visiting them.

questions.q: What is the highest point in a country or region called?
questions.f: Nepal and China share Everest, so both can claim the world's highest point.

questions.q: Which of these do sailors use to catch the wind?
questions.f: A modern racing yacht can sail faster than the wind that pushes it.

questions.q: Which of these is a real world record kept by Guinness World Records?
questions.f: Usain Bolt's 9.58 seconds for 100 metres has stood since 2009.

questions.q: What does a knot measure on a ship?
questions.f: One knot is one nautical mile per hour, measured long ago with a knotted rope.

questions.q: Which weather made polar expeditions hardest?
questions.f: In a whiteout blizzard the ground and sky look the same, so up and down blur.

questions.q: Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly alone across the Atlantic Ocean.
questions.f: She flew from Canada to Northern Ireland in 1932 in about 15 hours.

questions.q: What is a 'first' in exploring?
questions.f: Explorers often kept careful records so their firsts could be proved later.

questions.q: Which of these helps a traveller carry everything on their back?
questions.f: Rucksack comes from German words meaning back sack.

questions.q: Which sea is famous for having water so salty that people float easily?
questions.f: The Dead Sea shore is the lowest dry land on Earth, over 400 metres below sea level.

questions.q: What did old sailors sometimes draw in the empty corners of maps?
questions.f: One 1510 globe carries the Latin words meaning here are dragons.

questions.q: Which team reached the South Pole first, beating Robert Scott's group by five weeks?
questions.f: Amundsen arrived on 14 December 1911; Scott's party reached the Pole in January 1912.

questions.q: What is the deepest place in the ocean called?
questions.f: It lies in the Mariana Trench and is about 10,900 metres deep.

questions.q: Which spacecraft carried the first human into orbit around Earth?
questions.f: Yuri Gagarin flew in Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961 and shouted the Russian for Let's go!

questions.q: Which airplane did Charles Lindbergh fly alone from New York to Paris?
questions.f: He had no front window, using a periscope and side windows to see out.

questions.q: The Silk Road carried goods between which two regions?
questions.f: It carried more than goods: paper, printing and religions travelled along it too.

questions.q: Ibn Battuta spent nearly 30 years doing what?
questions.f: He set out from Tangier in Morocco in 1325 and covered roughly 117,000 kilometres.

questions.q: The root 'geo' in the word 'geography' means what?
questions.f: Geography joins geo, earth, with graphein, to write, so it means earth-writing.

questions.q: The root 'naut' in 'astronaut' and 'nautical' means what?
questions.f: From Greek nautes, a sailor, related to naus, a ship.

questions.q: The prefix 'circum' in 'circumnavigate' means what?
questions.f: Circumnavigate is literally to sail around, from circum plus navigare.

questions.q: The root 'aero' in 'aeroplane' and 'aerodynamic' means what?
questions.f: So an aeroplane is really an air-plane, a flat surface moving through air.

questions.q: Which explorer's expedition ship was called the Fram?
questions.f: Fram means forward in Norwegian, and the ship was designed to be lifted by ice, not crushed.

questions.q: How long did Yuri Gagarin's first spaceflight last?
questions.f: One lap of the Earth was enough to make him the most famous man alive.

questions.q: What is a sextant used for?
c: Measuring the angle of the sun or a star
questions.f: With that angle and a clock, a sailor can work out where on Earth they are.

questions.q: Which Chinese admiral led seven great treasure-fleet voyages in the 1400s?
questions.f: He sailed as far as East Africa and brought a giraffe back to the emperor's court.

questions.q: Polynesian navigators crossed the Pacific mainly by reading what?
questions.f: Skilled wayfinders memorised a star compass of rising and setting points.

questions.q: On a map, lines of latitude run in which direction?
questions.f: Latitude comes from Latin latus, wide, since these lines measure width from the equator.

questions.q: What do lines of longitude measure?
questions.f: Longitude comes from longus, long, because these lines run the long way round the globe.

questions.q: A map can never show the round Earth perfectly on flat paper.
questions.f: Flattening a sphere always stretches something, so every map distorts shape, size or distance.

questions.q: Which mapmaker's famous 1569 projection is still used for sea charts and phone maps?
questions.f: His grid lets a sailor draw a straight compass course as a straight line.

questions.q: On a Mercator map, which place looks far bigger than it really is?
questions.f: Greenland looks the size of Africa, but Africa is about 14 times larger.

questions.q: Which two people first reached the summit of Mount Everest in 1953?
questions.f: News of their climb reached London on the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.

questions.q: Which vessel took two men to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 1960?
questions.f: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh spent about 20 minutes on the deepest seafloor.

questions.q: What is on the golden record carried by the Voyager spacecraft?
c: Sounds, music and pictures from Earth
questions.f: It holds greetings in 55 languages, whale song, thunder and Chuck Berry's guitar.

questions.q: Which word means the study and making of maps?
questions.f: From Greek khartes, a sheet of papyrus, plus graphein, to write.

questions.q: The word 'expedition' comes from Latin words meaning what?
questions.f: Its opposite, impede, means to shackle the feet, so expedite means to speed things up.

questions.q: The word 'navigate' is built from Latin words meaning what?
questions.f: From navis, a ship, and agere, to drive or lead.

questions.q: Which planet's moon did the first humans ever set foot on?
questions.f: Twelve people have walked on the Moon, all of them between 1969 and 1972.

questions.q: Where did the Wright brothers make their first powered flights?
questions.f: They chose the spot for its steady sea breezes and soft sand for landing.

questions.q: Which sea ice trapped and finally crushed Shackleton's ship Endurance?
questions.f: The crew camped on the floes for months, then rowed to Elephant Island.

questions.q: How many of Shackleton's 28 crew members survived the Endurance expedition?
questions.f: Shackleton's rescue voyage in a lifeboat is still studied as a masterclass in leadership.

questions.q: Which word means to travel to a high place and get used to thin air?
questions.f: Climbers go up and back down repeatedly so their blood can make more red cells.

questions.q: Which is the largest desert in the world?
questions.f: A desert is defined by how little falls from the sky, not by heat or sand.

questions.q: Sailors once needed an accurate clock to work out their longitude at sea.
questions.f: Comparing local noon with home time gives longitude, so clockmaker John Harrison became a hero.

questions.q: The word 'atlas' for a book of maps comes from what?
questions.f: Mercator put the Titan Atlas on his map book's cover, and the name stuck.

questions.q: What is the imaginary line through Greenwich, London, called?
questions.f: Countries agreed on it in 1884, which is why world time is measured from London.

questions.q: The word 'meridian' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Along one meridian, noon happens at the same moment everywhere.

questions.q: Which explorer named the Pacific Ocean, calling it the peaceful sea?
questions.f: After the stormy strait at South America's tip, the calm water seemed peaceful indeed.

questions.q: Which spacecraft's astronauts first orbited the Moon and saw its far side?
questions.f: Their photo of Earth rising over the Moon in 1968 is called Earthrise.

questions.q: Which large bird can glide for hours over the Southern Ocean without flapping?
questions.f: A wandering albatross wingspan can stretch beyond three metres, the widest of any bird.

questions.q: What did the first mountain climbers use before oxygen bottles were invented?
c: Nothing at all, they stayed low
questions.f: Above 8,000 metres the air holds only about a third of the oxygen found at sea level.

questions.q: Which continent did Vasco da Gama sail around to reach India by sea?
questions.f: He rounded the Cape of Good Hope and reached India in 1498.

questions.q: The word 'arctic' comes from a Greek word for which animal?
questions.f: It points to the Great Bear constellation overhead in the far north.

questions.q: If arctic points to the bear, what does 'antarctic' mean?
questions.f: The name is a clue: there really are no bears in Antarctica.

questions.q: Which is the fastest passenger plane ever to carry people across the Atlantic?
questions.f: Concorde crossed from New York to London in under three hours, faster than sound.

questions.q: Which pair made the first non-stop flight across the Atlantic, in 1919?
questions.f: They flew from Newfoundland to Ireland and landed in a bog, eight years before Lindbergh.

questions.q: Voyager 1 has now travelled beyond the edge of the Sun's bubble of particles.
questions.f: It crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and still sends faint signals home.

questions.q: Which word describes a very deep, narrow valley in the seafloor?
questions.f: Trenches form where one slab of the Earth's crust slides beneath another.

questions.q: What is the 'death zone' that Everest climbers talk about?
c: Above 8,000 metres, where air is too thin to live long
questions.f: Bodies slowly weaken up there no matter how fit the climber, so speed matters.

questions.q: Which was the first animal to orbit the Earth?
questions.f: Laika the dog flew in Sputnik 2 in 1957, paving the way for human flight.

questions.q: What does the Russian word 'sputnik' mean?
questions.f: A fitting name for a small object that keeps company with the Earth.

questions.q: What does the root 'bathy' mean in words like 'bathysphere'?
questions.f: A bathysphere is a deep ball; a bathyscaphe is literally a deep boat.

questions.q: The word 'submarine' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: Marine comes from Latin mare, the sea, also found in maritime and mariner.

questions.q: Which explorer sailed alone around the world in the small sloop Spray?
questions.f: Slocum finished in 1898 after three years at sea, and he never learned to swim.

questions.q: How did old sailors keep track of speed and distance without instruments?
questions.f: Dead reckoning means adding up your speed, heading and time from a known starting point.

questions.q: Which mountain is the second highest in the world?
questions.f: K2 got its plain name from a survey list of Karakoram peaks, and the label stuck.

questions.q: What is a caravanserai?
c: A roadside inn for desert travellers
questions.f: These walled courtyards along the Silk Road offered water, safety and news.

questions.q: The word 'safari' means what in Swahili?
questions.f: Swahili borrowed it from the Arabic word safar, meaning travel.

questions.q: Which ocean current pattern did sailing ships rely on to cross the Atlantic?
questions.f: The word trade here comes from an old sense meaning a steady track or path.

questions.q: The Moon has less gravity than Earth, so astronauts could jump higher there.
questions.f: Moon gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, though bulky suits limited Apollo hops.

questions.q: Which Antarctic mountain is an active volcano?
questions.f: Erebus holds a rare lake of molten lava, bubbling in the middle of an ice continent.

questions.q: Which word means an unmapped or unknown region?
questions.f: A chart is a sea map, so uncharted water is water no one has mapped.

questions.q: Which is the highest capital city in the world?
questions.f: La Paz sits about 3,600 metres up, where visitors often feel breathless at first.

questions.q: Roughly how fast does a spacecraft have to travel to stay in orbit around Earth?
questions.f: At that speed the International Space Station circles the Earth every 90 minutes.

questions.q: Which ship carried Charles Darwin on his famous voyage of discovery?
questions.f: The five-year voyage gave Darwin the notes that later shaped his ideas on evolution.

questions.q: Which explorer captained HMS Endeavour on a voyage to the Pacific in 1768?
questions.f: Cook's crew mapped New Zealand's coast so accurately that the charts served for 150 years.

questions.q: What is a 'first ascent'?
c: The first time anyone reaches a summit
The first step of a ladder
questions.f: Climbers also record firsts for new routes and for climbs without extra oxygen.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to reach the summit of Mount Everest?
questions.f: Tabei summited in 1975 after her team was buried by an avalanche and dug itself out.

questions.q: Which sea creature's name literally means 'sea nettle' in some languages?
questions.f: French calls it meduse, after the Greek Medusa's snaky hair.

questions.q: Which is the world's longest mountain range on land?
questions.f: The Andes run about 7,000 kilometres down the western edge of South America.

questions.q: What did the word 'travel' originally mean?
questions.f: It shares a root with travail, so a journey once meant a genuine struggle.

questions.q: What does the word 'journey' originally come from?
questions.f: From Old French jornee, a day's travel, from Latin diurnus, daily.

questions.q: Which instrument did ancient and medieval astronomers use to measure star heights?
questions.f: Astrolabe is built from Greek words meaning star taker.

questions.q: Antarctica is officially counted as a desert.
questions.f: Some inland areas get less moisture each year than the Sahara does.

questions.q: Which explorer led the first expedition to sail through the Northwest Passage?
questions.f: Amundsen's little ship Gjoa took three winters to work through the Arctic maze.

questions.q: What did explorer Thor Heyerdahl sail across the Pacific on in 1947?
questions.f: His raft Kon-Tiki drifted 6,900 kilometres in 101 days to prove such trips were possible.

questions.q: Which word means the point directly overhead in the sky?
questions.f: Its opposite, nadir, means the point straight down; both words came through Arabic.

questions.q: What is 'permafrost'?
questions.f: In parts of Siberia permafrost reaches more than a kilometre deep.

questions.q: Which record-keeping book was first published in 1955 to settle pub arguments?
questions.f: The founder's own unsettled question was which game bird flies fastest.

questions.q: Which is the tallest mountain measured from its base rather than sea level?
questions.f: Mauna Kea rises over 10,000 metres from the seafloor, but most of it is underwater.

questions.q: Which word means a person who walks, from the Latin for foot?
questions.f: The same root gives pedal, pedicure and expedition.

questions.q: The 'graph' in 'cartography' and 'photograph' means what?
questions.f: So a photograph is light-writing and cartography is chart-writing.

questions.q: Which word means the science of measuring water depth?
questions.f: Bathymetric maps use colour bands to show underwater mountains and trenches.

questions.q: What is an 'archipelago' made of?
questions.f: The word originally described the island-dotted Aegean Sea.

questions.q: Which word means the flat land at a river's mouth, shaped like a triangle?
questions.f: It is named after the Greek letter delta, which is triangular.

questions.q: Which explorer's name is on the strait at the southern tip of South America?
questions.f: The Strait of Magellan gave ships a stormy shortcut between two oceans.

questions.q: About how many of Magellan's original 270 crew made it home in 1522?
questions.f: They came back on one battered ship, the Victoria, after three years at sea.

questions.q: Which mountain in Alaska is North America's highest peak?
questions.f: Denali means the tall one in the local Koyukon language.

questions.q: Which desert is the driest non-polar place on Earth?
questions.f: Some Atacama weather stations have never recorded a drop of rain.

questions.q: The Wright brothers' first flight was shorter than the length of a modern jumbo jet.
questions.f: Their 37-metre hop would fit inside the 76-metre wingspan of a Boeing 747.

questions.q: Which explorer disappeared over the Pacific in 1937 while trying to fly around the world?
questions.f: She and navigator Fred Noonan had already flown about 35,000 kilometres.

questions.q: What made Bessie Coleman a record breaker in 1921?
c: First African American woman to earn a pilot's licence
First to break the sound barrier
questions.f: Refused training in the United States, she learned French and studied in France instead.

questions.q: What is a 'nautical mile' based on?
c: One minute of latitude on the Earth
questions.f: That neat link means a degree of latitude is exactly 60 nautical miles.

questions.q: Which word describes a ship's right-hand side when facing forward?
questions.f: It comes from steer-board, the side where the old steering oar was fixed.

questions.q: What is a 'fathom' a measure of?
questions.f: A fathom is six feet, about the span of a sailor's outstretched arms.

questions.q: What did Edmund Hillary do for a living before climbing Everest?
questions.f: He said the mountain was climbed by an ordinary beekeeper with extraordinary friends.

questions.q: Which spacecraft first photographed the far side of the Moon?
questions.f: Luna 3 sent back blurry but historic pictures in 1959 of a face no one had seen.

questions.q: Which is the world's largest lake by area?
questions.f: It is called a sea because it is salty, but it is completely surrounded by land.

questions.q: What did Auguste Piccard invent that let people reach the deep ocean?
questions.f: He also flew a balloon into the stratosphere, so he explored both up and down.

questions.q: Which word means the outer part of the atmosphere pilots and balloonists reach?
questions.f: Strato- comes from a word for a layer, and airliners cruise at its lower edge.

questions.q: Which is the world's longest river system in South America?
questions.f: The Amazon carries more water than the next seven biggest rivers combined.

questions.q: What is a 'monsoon'?
c: A seasonal wind that brings heavy rain
questions.f: The word comes from Arabic mawsim, meaning a season.

questions.q: Which sailing ships used the monsoon winds to trade across the Indian Ocean?
questions.f: Sailors timed voyages to the wind's yearly switch, going out one season and back the next.

questions.q: Where does the word 'catamaran' come from?
questions.f: It comes from Tamil kattumaram, and describes hulls lashed together for stability.

questions.q: What does the name 'Polynesia' mean?
questions.f: Compare Micronesia, small islands, and Melanesia, dark islands.

questions.q: Pacific voyagers reached Hawaii and New Zealand centuries before Europeans arrived.
questions.f: They settled thousands of islands across an ocean covering a third of the planet.

questions.q: What was the Hokulea, launched in Hawaii in 1975?
questions.f: Its 1976 voyage to Tahiti without instruments revived Pacific wayfinding.

questions.q: Which is the world's longest tunnel for trains?
questions.f: Its 57 kilometres run straight through the Swiss Alps.

questions.q: What does 'altitude sickness' come from?
c: Too little oxygen in thin air
questions.f: It can start above about 2,500 metres, which is why climbers go up slowly.

questions.q: Which of these words does NOT share a root with 'aquarium'?
questions.f: Aqua means water in Latin, and an aqueduct is a water-duct or water-leader.

questions.q: Which word describes an animal or plant found only in one place?
questions.f: Explorers prized endemic species, like the finches Darwin studied in the Galapagos.

questions.q: Which explorer's crew ate ship's biscuit so hard it was nicknamed hardtack?
questions.f: Hardtack lasted for years because it contained almost no moisture at all.

questions.q: Which illness struck sailors who went months without fresh fruit and vegetables?
questions.f: Vitamin C from lemons and limes fixed it, and British sailors became known as limeys.

questions.q: Which mountain range did the Silk Road caravans have to cross in Central Asia?
questions.f: Traders called the high Pamir passes the roof of the world.

questions.q: Who reached the North Pole area by ship-and-sledge in 1909 and claimed a first?
questions.f: Later measurements left the claim disputed, but Henson's skill on the ice was never in doubt.

questions.q: Which word means a wide flat area of floating sea ice?
questions.f: Shackleton's men camped on drifting floes for months after their ship was lost.

questions.q: What do we call a huge crack in a glacier that climbers must bridge?
questions.f: Crevasses can be dozens of metres deep and hidden by a thin lid of snow.

questions.q: Explorers use ropes to tie themselves together when crossing hidden crevasses.
questions.f: If one climber breaks through, the others can hold the rope and haul them out.

questions.q: Which word means the lowest point, opposite of the highest?
questions.f: Nadir came into English through Arabic nazir, meaning opposite.

questions.q: What is a 'compass rose' on a map?
questions.f: Its points once carried the names of winds rather than of directions.

questions.q: Which is the world's tallest building?
questions.f: At 828 metres it is still less than a tenth the height of Mount Everest.

questions.q: How fast is the world record for the 100 metres sprint?
questions.f: Usain Bolt set it in Berlin in 2009 and it still stands.

questions.q: Which animal makes the longest migration of any on Earth?
questions.f: Arctic terns fly pole to pole each year, seeing more daylight than any other animal.

questions.q: Which word means to break a record by doing better than before?
questions.f: Sur- comes from a word meaning over or above, as in surface and surplus.

questions.q: Which ocean zone is named after the Greek underworld?
questions.f: Below 6,000 metres, the hadal zone is named for Hades and includes all the deep trenches.

questions.q: What is a 'glacier calving'?
c: Ice breaking off to form icebergs
questions.f: Greenland's glaciers calve enough ice each year to fill millions of swimming pools.

questions.q: Which spacecraft was the first to land softly on another planet's surface?
questions.f: Venera 7 reached Venus in 1970 and survived about 23 minutes in the furnace-like heat.

questions.q: Which was the first spacecraft to fly past Mars and send back pictures?
questions.f: Its 21 grainy photos in 1965 showed a cratered world, surprising many scientists.

questions.q: Which astronaut stayed in orbit alone while his crewmates walked on the Moon?
questions.f: When his craft passed behind the Moon, he was cut off from every other human alive.

questions.q: Which word means a plan to be first at something?
questions.f: Ambition originally described walking around to seek votes, from Latin ambire.

questions.q: How did explorers preserve food before refrigerators?
questions.f: Salt beef and dried peas kept crews going for years at sea.

questions.q: The International Space Station has had people living aboard continuously since 2000.
questions.f: Crews have handed over to each other without a break since November 2000.

questions.q: Which word means the layer of an old map that shows heights of land?
questions.f: Shaded relief maps use fake shadows so mountains seem to pop off the page.

questions.q: What do the closely spaced lines on a hiking map show?
questions.f: These are contour lines; the closer they are, the harder the climb.

questions.q: Which word means to face the right way, and comes from a word for the rising sun?
questions.f: Old maps put east at the top, so orienting a map once literally meant facing east.

questions.q: Which sport uses a map and compass to race between checkpoints?
questions.f: It began in Scandinavia as military training and is now a world championship sport.

questions.q: Which of these did explorers use as a portable shelter?
questions.f: Amundsen's team left a spare tent at the South Pole with a letter inside.

questions.q: Which is the world's highest volcano that people climb?
questions.f: On the Chile-Argentina border, it tops 6,800 metres, higher than any other volcano.

questions.q: Which word describes a route across a mountain range between two peaks?
questions.f: Silk Road caravans, armies and pilgrims all funnelled through the same few high passes.

questions.q: Which Italian city was Marco Polo from?
questions.f: He dictated his travel stories while a prisoner of war in Genoa.

questions.q: Which continent did Ibn Battuta NOT visit?
questions.f: He crossed the Sahara to Mali and reached India, the Maldives and possibly China.

questions.q: Which African city on the Niger became a famous centre of books and learning?
questions.f: Its libraries held tens of thousands of handwritten manuscripts.

questions.q: What is a 'trade route'?
c: A regular path used to carry goods
questions.f: Some Silk Road stretches were used for well over a thousand years.

questions.q: Which word means someone who studies old objects and ruins?
