questions.f: Archaeology comes from Greek words meaning the study of ancient things.

questions.q: What kind of place did explorers call an 'oasis'?
c: A watered spot in a desert
questions.f: Silk Road cities like Kashgar grew where meltwater met the desert's edge.

questions.q: A compass needle points to the magnetic pole, not exactly to the true North Pole.
questions.f: The difference is called magnetic declination, and navigators must correct for it.

questions.q: Which word means a scientist who studies the weather on an expedition?
questions.f: Meteor once meant anything high in the air, not just a shooting star.

questions.q: Which explorer's rowboat journey covered 1,300 kilometres of stormy Southern Ocean?
questions.f: Six men in the lifeboat James Caird reached South Georgia after 16 days at sea.

questions.q: Which spacecraft has travelled farther from Earth than any other?
questions.f: It is now over 24 billion kilometres away, and its signals take more than 22 hours to arrive.

questions.q: Which explorer flew over the North Pole in an airship in 1926?
questions.f: He had already reached the South Pole, making him the first person to see both.

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk in space, outside a spacecraft?
questions.f: In 1965 his suit ballooned so much he had to let out air to squeeze back inside.

questions.q: Which word describes something that has never been done before?
questions.f: A precedent is an earlier example, so unprecedented means there is no earlier example.

questions.q: Which piece of equipment tells a diver how deep they are?
questions.f: Pressure rises by about one atmosphere for every ten metres of water.

questions.q: What is the name for the whole set of maps and charts a ship carries?
questions.f: Ships once guarded their charts jealously, since good ones were worth a fortune.

questions.q: Which record does the peregrine falcon hold?
questions.f: Its name means wandering, because falconers took young birds while they were migrating.

questions.q: Which word means measuring how high land rises, used in mapmaking?
questions.f: India's Great Trigonometrical Survey measured a whole subcontinent triangle by triangle.

questions.q: Which flight record did Chuck Yeager set in 1947?
c: First to fly faster than sound
questions.f: He flew the Bell X-1 with two broken ribs, using a broom handle to shut the hatch.

questions.q: Which is the world's largest coral reef system?
questions.f: It stretches over 2,300 kilometres and is visible from space.

questions.q: What does the word 'discovery' describe when a new island is named?
c: Finding something previously unknown to the finder
questions.f: Many so-called discoveries were places where people already lived, sometimes for millennia.

questions.q: Which word means the art of finding your way at sea?
questions.f: Before satellites, navigation combined stars, clocks, charts and careful arithmetic.

questions.q: Which mountaineer pair made the first ascent of Everest without bottled oxygen?
questions.f: Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler proved it possible in 1978; Messner then did it solo in 1980.

questions.q: The word 'cartography' is built from parts meaning what?
questions.f: From Greek khartes, a papyrus leaf, plus graphein, to write.

questions.q: Which projection keeps every compass bearing as a straight line, helping sailors?
questions.f: Such a line is called a rhumb line, and it is why the 1569 map won over navigators.

questions.q: What does the Mercator projection sacrifice in order to keep shapes correct locally?
questions.f: Land near the poles is stretched enormously, which is why Greenland looks vast.

questions.q: Which name did Ibn Battuta give the book describing his travels?
questions.f: Rihla simply means journey; the full title praises the marvels of cities and travelling.

questions.q: Roughly how far did Ibn Battuta travel in his lifetime?
questions.f: That is close to three times around the equator, all before 1355.

questions.q: In which years did Zheng He lead his seven great voyages?
questions.f: His largest fleets carried over 27,000 people, decades before Columbus set sail.

questions.q: Which term did German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen coin in 1877?
questions.f: The ancient traders themselves never called it that; the romantic name is modern.

questions.q: The word 'meridian' traces to a Latin phrase for which part of the day?
questions.f: Related words include ante meridiem and post meridiem, the a.m. and p.m. on clocks.

questions.q: The word 'sextant' refers to which fraction of a circle?
questions.f: Its arc spans 60 degrees, one sixth of 360; an octant spans one eighth.

questions.q: Which invention finally solved the problem of measuring longitude at sea?
questions.f: John Harrison's H4 watch lost only seconds on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761.

questions.q: Which ship carried Shackleton's crew across 1,300 km of open ocean for rescue?
questions.f: Navigator Frank Worsley got only four sextant sights in 16 days of storm.

questions.q: What did Shackleton's men name their camp after the Endurance sank?
questions.f: Patience Camp was well named; they waited on drifting ice for over three months.

questions.q: Which Norwegian ship was purposely built to be squeezed upward by pack ice?
questions.f: Its rounded hull let the ice lift it instead of crushing it, and it drifted for three years.

questions.q: Which word describes the point on Earth's surface farthest from any ocean?
questions.f: The Eurasian pole of inaccessibility lies in northwestern China, some 2,500 km from any sea.

questions.q: What does the root 'hypso' mean in 'hypsometric' maps of land height?
questions.f: Hypsometric tints colour low land green and high land brown or white.

questions.q: The word 'altitude' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: The same root altus gives us exalt, altar and the musical alto.

questions.q: What are the Nepali and Tibetan names for Mount Everest?
questions.f: Sagarmatha suggests forehead of the sky; Chomolungma means goddess mother of the world.

questions.q: Everest was named in 1865 after George Everest, who held which job?
questions.f: Everest himself objected, partly because locals could not easily pronounce his name.

questions.q: What was Everest called on survey lists before it was named?
questions.f: Calculations by Radhanath Sikdar in 1852 first showed Peak XV was the world's highest.

questions.q: Which dangerous section must Everest climbers cross just above Base Camp?
questions.f: The icefall shifts daily, so a team of Sherpas re-fixes ladders across it each season.

questions.q: Which two men vanished near Everest's summit in 1924?
questions.f: George Mallory's body was found in 1999, but whether they reached the top is unknown.

questions.q: Whose famous answer to 'Why climb Everest?' was 'Because it's there'?
questions.f: He gave the line to a New York reporter in 1923, and it became mountaineering's motto.

questions.q: Which mountain is nicknamed the Savage Mountain?
questions.f: K2's first winter ascent came only in January 2021, by a team of ten Nepali climbers.

questions.q: Mount Chimborazo's summit is farther from Earth's centre than Everest's is.
questions.f: Earth bulges at the equator, so this Ecuadorian volcano wins on distance from the core.

questions.q: Who piloted the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of the Challenger Deep?
questions.f: Their descent in 1960 took nearly five hours, and a window cracked on the way down.

questions.q: After whom is the Challenger Deep named?
c: A British survey ship of the 1870s
questions.f: HMS Challenger's crew first sounded the trench with a weighted rope in 1875.

questions.q: Which film director made a solo dive to the Challenger Deep in 2012?
questions.f: His submersible Deepsea Challenger descended vertically like a green torpedo.

questions.q: The word 'bathyscaphe' is built from Greek words meaning what?
questions.f: Compare bathysphere, a deep ball, which Beebe and Barton rode to 923 metres in 1934.

questions.q: Which submersible discovered deep-sea hydrothermal vents in 1977?
questions.f: Whole ecosystems living without sunlight were found around those hot chimneys.

questions.q: The word 'abyss' comes from Greek parts meaning what?
questions.f: The abyssal zone spans roughly 4,000 to 6,000 metres deep.

questions.q: Which Latin root in 'submersible' means to dip or plunge?
questions.f: The same root gives us immerse, emerge and merger.

questions.q: Which spacecraft first carried a human, and what did its name mean?
questions.f: Gagarin's callsign was Kedr, the Russian word for cedar.

questions.q: What was Valentina Tereshkova's radio callsign on her 1963 flight?
questions.f: She had been a textile worker and amateur parachutist before being chosen.

questions.q: On which lunar plain did Apollo 11 land?
questions.f: These dark lunar seas are ancient lava plains, not water, and never held a drop.

questions.q: What was the name of Apollo 11's lunar module?
questions.f: The command ship was Columbia, so the famous words were Eagle has landed.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission carried the only professional geologist to walk on the Moon?
questions.f: Harrison Schmitt found orange soil at Taurus-Littrow, evidence of ancient volcanic glass.

questions.q: Which languages are represented by greetings on the Voyager golden record?
questions.f: The record also carries whale song, a mother's kiss and a heartbeat.

questions.q: What is the Voyager golden record physically made of?
questions.f: A uranium sample on the cover acts as a clock, letting finders date the launch.

questions.q: Which rock and roll song was placed on the Voyager golden record?
questions.f: Chuck Berry's guitar is now the farthest-travelled music in history.

questions.q: Voyager 2 was launched before Voyager 1.
questions.f: Voyager 2 left on 20 August 1977; Voyager 1 followed on 5 September but took a faster route.

questions.q: Which Voyager 1 photograph is known as the Pale Blue Dot?
c: Earth seen from 6 billion km away
questions.f: Carl Sagan pushed for the shot; Earth fills less than a single pixel.

questions.q: The word 'satellite' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: Kepler borrowed satelles for Jupiter's moons, and the sense stuck for Sputnik too.

questions.q: What do the words 'apogee' and 'perigee' both refer to?
c: Points of an orbit around Earth
questions.f: The gee comes from Greek gaia, Earth; apo means away and peri means near.

questions.q: Which navigator sailed with Captain Cook and drew a chart of over 70 Pacific islands?
questions.f: Tupaia, a Tahitian priest-navigator, could name islands across thousands of kilometres.

questions.q: Which master navigator from Satawal taught Hawaiians traditional wayfinding?
questions.f: He guided Hokulea to Tahiti in 1976 with no instruments at all.

questions.q: What is a 'star compass' in Pacific wayfinding?
c: A memorised circle of star rising and setting points
A map of constellations on cloth
questions.f: Navigators memorised over 30 star houses and steered from one to the next all night.

questions.q: Which star does the name Hokulea refer to?
questions.f: Arcturus passes directly over Hawaii, so it guided canoes home; the name means star of gladness.

questions.q: How did Polynesian navigators use ocean swells to steer?
c: By feeling the pattern of waves from distant storms
By listening to the wind only
questions.f: Some navigators lay in the hull to feel swell patterns through the canoe itself.

questions.q: The Marshall Islands' stick charts were used to teach what?
c: Wave and swell patterns between islands
questions.f: Curved sticks showed how islands bend passing swells, a lesson learned by hand not by eye.

questions.q: Which crop's spread across the Pacific hints at ancient contact with South America?
questions.f: Sweet potatoes were grown in Polynesia long before Europeans arrived.

questions.q: Which word for a body marking came into English from Polynesian languages?
questions.f: From Tahitian and Samoan tatau; Cook's sailors brought both the word and the practice home.

questions.q: Which everyday English word comes from Tongan 'tapu', meaning forbidden?
questions.f: Captain Cook recorded it in 1777, and it entered English almost unchanged.

questions.q: Juan Sebastian Elcano, not Magellan, completed the first voyage around the world.
questions.f: Magellan died in the Philippines in 1521; Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522.

questions.q: Who wrote the eyewitness journal of Magellan's circumnavigation?
questions.f: Pigafetta also compiled word lists of languages met along the way.

questions.q: Which ship was the only one of Magellan's five to complete the voyage?
questions.f: She returned so leaky that her cargo of cloves barely paid for the whole expedition.

questions.q: Who was the first person to sail alone around the world?
questions.f: Slocum rebuilt an abandoned oyster sloop, the Spray, and covered 46,000 miles.

questions.q: Who made the first solo non-stop sailing voyage around the world?
questions.f: He finished the 1968-69 Golden Globe Race in Suhaili, the only entrant to complete it.

questions.q: Which journalist raced around the world in 72 days in 1889?
questions.f: She beat the fictional record of Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days.

questions.q: Which botanist became the first woman known to circumnavigate the globe?
questions.f: She joined Bougainville's 1766 voyage disguised as a young man named Jean.

questions.q: Which explorer was the second to lead a voyage around the world, in the Golden Hind?
questions.f: He returned in 1580 with treasure worth more than a year of England's income.

questions.q: The Latin root of 'voyage' originally meant what?
questions.f: From viaticum, the food and money packed for a journey, from via, a road.

questions.q: What does the word 'peregrination' mean?
questions.f: From peregrinus, a foreigner abroad, which also named the peregrine falcon.

questions.q: Which word means a route that goes around an obstacle rather than through it?
questions.f: Ships avoiding Cape Horn's storms took circuitous routes through calmer waters.

questions.q: What does the Latin prefix 'trans' add to words like 'transatlantic'?
questions.f: So a transpolar flight crosses the pole and transcontinental crosses a continent.

questions.q: What did the Wright brothers build to test wing shapes before flying?
questions.f: Their tunnel let them correct published tables that had been leading inventors astray.

questions.q: How long was Charles Lindbergh's 1927 solo flight from New York to Paris?
questions.f: He carried sandwiches but no radio or parachute, saving weight for extra fuel.

questions.q: Which prize did Lindbergh win for his transatlantic flight?
questions.f: The 25,000 dollar prize had gone unclaimed for eight years.

questions.q: Which aircraft did Amelia Earhart fly solo across the Atlantic in 1932?
c: A Spirit of St. Louis replica
questions.f: Ice, a leaking fuel line and a broken altimeter did not stop her reaching Ireland.

questions.q: Which pilot flew solo from England to Australia in 1930, a first for a woman?
questions.f: She bought a second-hand plane named Jason and learned navigation on the way.

questions.q: Which aviator first flew across the English Channel, in 1909?
questions.f: He crash-landed near Dover with a burnt engine and won a newspaper's 1,000 pound prize.

questions.q: Which balloonist first crossed the Atlantic non-stop by balloon, in 1978?
questions.f: Their helium balloon drifted from Maine to France in about 137 hours.

questions.q: What is the term for flying by instruments alone, without seeing the ground?
questions.f: Jimmy Doolittle made the first entirely blind flight, takeoff to landing, in 1929.

questions.q: Which word means the science of moving through air, from Greek roots?
questions.f: Aeronautics literally means air-sailing; astronautics means star-sailing.

questions.q: The first hot air balloon passengers were animals, not people.
questions.f: In 1783 a sheep, a duck and a rooster flew before King Louis XVI, and all landed safely.

questions.q: Which is the lowest exposed land surface on Earth?
questions.f: It lies more than 430 metres below sea level and keeps dropping as the lake shrinks.

questions.q: Which place recorded the world's lowest natural temperature at ground level?
questions.f: On 21 July 1983 the thermometer there read minus 89.2 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Which valley holds the record for the highest reliably measured air temperature?
questions.f: Furnace Creek hit 56.7 degrees Celsius in 1913, a figure still debated but still official.

questions.q: Which waterfall drops farther than any other in the world?
questions.f: Its local name Kerepakupai Meru means waterfall of the deepest place.

questions.q: The word 'summit' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: The same root gives us sum, the highest total, and summary.

questions.q: What does 'hypoxia', a danger for high climbers, mean?
c: Too little oxygen in the body
questions.f: Hypo means under, and oxy comes from the same root as oxygen.

questions.q: Which word describes camping overnight on a mountain with minimal shelter?
questions.f: It came from a Swiss German word for an extra night watch.

questions.q: What does the Beaufort scale measure?
questions.f: Admiral Francis Beaufort standardised it in 1805 by describing what sails could carry.

questions.q: Which belt of calm near the equator once trapped sailing ships for weeks?
questions.f: Its name may come from an old word for dull, related to dolt.

questions.q: What do sailors call the stormy westerly winds between 40 and 50 degrees south?
questions.f: Clipper captains rode them eastward, and modern round-the-world racers still do.

questions.q: Which word means the shortest path between two points on a globe?
questions.f: That is why flights from London to Tokyo curve north over the Arctic.

questions.q: On a map, what is a 'projection'?
c: A method of flattening the round Earth
questions.f: Every projection is a compromise, so mapmakers choose one to suit the job.

questions.q: Which projection is used by National Geographic for world maps since 1998?
questions.f: Its name means triple, because it balances area, direction and distance errors.

questions.q: What is special about an equal-area projection like the Gall-Peters?
c: Countries' true sizes are compared correctly
questions.f: The trade-off is stretched shapes, which is why Africa looks tall and narrow.

questions.q: Which 1507 map was the first to use the name America?
questions.f: It honoured Amerigo Vespucci, who argued the new lands were a separate continent.

questions.q: Which Latin phrase found on an old globe means 'here are dragons'?
questions.f: It appears on the Hunt-Lenox Globe of about 1510, near eastern Asia.

questions.q: What does 'terra incognita' mean on old maps?
questions.f: Mapmakers filled such gaps with guesswork, sea monsters or honest blank space.

questions.q: The imagined southern continent on old maps was called what?
questions.f: When Antarctica was finally found, the guessed name survived in Australia's.

questions.q: Which ancient scholar wrote the Geographia, mapping the known world with coordinates?
questions.f: His grid of latitude and longitude was rediscovered in Europe around 1400 and changed mapmaking.

questions.q: Which Greek scholar first measured the Earth's size using shadows?
questions.f: Comparing noon shadows in two Egyptian cities, he came within a few percent of the true figure.

questions.q: The oldest surviving globe was made before Europeans knew about the Americas.
questions.f: Martin Behaim's 1492 Erdapfel, or earth apple, shows no American continent at all.

questions.q: Which giant survey measured India triangle by triangle for nearly 70 years?
questions.f: Its measurements of Himalayan peaks revealed that Everest was the world's highest.

questions.q: What is 'triangulation' in surveying?
c: Fixing positions using angles from known points
questions.f: One carefully measured baseline can anchor thousands of kilometres of triangles.

questions.q: Which two words describe places exactly opposite on the globe?
questions.f: From Greek for opposite feet, since people there would stand sole to sole with you.

questions.q: Which line on the map do travellers cross to change calendar day?
questions.f: Magellan's crew came home one day 'behind' their calendar, the first to notice the effect.

questions.q: Why is the Tropic of Cancer named after a crab?
c: The Sun once stood in the constellation Cancer there at solstice
It curves like a crab's claw
A ship named Cancer charted it
questions.f: Tropic itself comes from a Greek word for turning, where the Sun turns back.

questions.q: The Latin word 'insula' in 'peninsula' and 'insular' means what?
questions.f: Paene means almost, so peninsula is almost-an-island.

questions.q: Which word names a narrow strip of land joining two larger masses?
questions.f: The Isthmus of Panama was cut by a canal in 1914, saving ships the trip round Cape Horn.

questions.q: What did explorers hope the Northwest Passage would provide?
c: A shortcut from Europe to Asia
A route to the South Pole
questions.f: Centuries of attempts failed until Amundsen finally sailed it between 1903 and 1906.

questions.q: Whose 1845 Arctic expedition vanished with the ships Erebus and Terror?
questions.f: Both wrecks were finally located in Canadian waters in 2014 and 2016.

questions.q: Which explorer let his ship freeze into the Arctic ice on purpose to drift with it?
questions.f: Nansen's Fram drifted for three years, testing his theory of a trans-polar current.

questions.q: Which explorer walked hundreds of kilometres back alone after losing his companions?
questions.f: Mawson's 1913 solo trek across Antarctic ice is one of survival's greatest feats.

questions.q: On Shackleton's Nimrod expedition, what record did his party set in 1909?
c: Closest anyone had come to the South Pole
questions.f: They turned back at 88 degrees 23 minutes south, only 180 km short, to stay alive.

questions.q: Which Antarctic volcano did Shackleton's Nimrod team first climb?
questions.f: They hauled sledges up 3,794 metres and looked into its steaming crater.

questions.q: Amundsen used skis and dogs while Scott relied partly on ponies and man-hauling.
questions.f: Amundsen had learned polar travel from Inuit methods, and his choices proved decisive.

questions.q: What did Amundsen name the tent he left at the South Pole?
questions.f: Framheim was his base camp, and heim means home in Norwegian.

questions.q: Which Antarctic ice shelf is the largest in the world?
questions.f: It is about the size of France, and its cliff edge blocked early ships from sailing farther.

questions.q: Which animal can dive deepest of all the birds?
questions.f: Emperors have been tracked below 500 metres and can hold their breath over 20 minutes.

questions.q: Which word describes the long polar night when the Sun never rises?
questions.f: At the poles it lasts for months, and early expeditions wintered through it in darkness.

questions.q: What causes the aurora borealis that polar explorers described in their diaries?
c: Particles from the Sun hitting the upper atmosphere
questions.f: Borealis comes from Boreas, Greek god of the north wind, so it means northern dawn.

questions.q: What is the southern version of the aurora called?
questions.f: Australis means southern, from the same root as Australia.

questions.q: Which word means a fierce polar wind that blows dry snow horizontally?
questions.f: In a whiteout, the horizon disappears and explorers can lose all sense of direction.

questions.q: How did Shackleton advertise for crew, according to a famous legend?
c: With a notice promising hardship and danger
questions.f: Historians have never found the advert, but over 5,000 people really did apply.

questions.q: Which record does the Arctic tern hold among all animals?
questions.f: Some terns fly over 70,000 kilometres a year, chasing summer from pole to pole.

questions.q: What does the term 'first ascent without supplementary oxygen' mean?
c: Climbing using only the air on the mountain
questions.f: Doctors had once argued the human body simply could not survive Everest's summit air.

questions.q: What is the modern official height of Mount Everest?
questions.f: Nepal and China announced the joint figure together in December 2020.

questions.q: What are 'the seven summits' that mountaineers try to collect?
c: The highest peak on each continent
questions.f: Richard Bass completed the set in 1985, launching a whole new kind of record chase.

questions.q: Which term means climbing light and fast with no fixed ropes or camps?
questions.f: It is faster but riskier, and Messner championed it on the highest peaks.

questions.q: Kami Rita Sherpa holds the record for most ascents of Mount Everest.
questions.f: He has summited more than 30 times, working as a guide since the 1990s.

questions.q: Which word means the tools and supplies carried on an expedition?
questions.f: Provision comes from Latin providere, to see ahead, the same root as provide.

questions.q: Which word describes a member of a crew who is not officially on board?
questions.f: Perce Blackborow stowed away on Endurance and ended up part of Shackleton's legendary crew.

questions.q: Which explorer named the Cape of Good Hope's stormy predecessor Cape of Storms?
questions.f: Portugal's king renamed it Good Hope to encourage more voyages to India.

questions.q: Which Portuguese prince sponsored the school of navigation that opened the Atlantic?
questions.f: He never sailed far himself, but his charts and caravels reshaped world travel.

questions.q: What kind of ship was a caravel, favoured by Portuguese explorers?
questions.f: Its lateen sails let it beat back against the wind, essential for returning home.

questions.q: Which spice was so valuable that whole voyages were launched to reach its islands?
questions.f: Cloves grew almost only in a handful of Indonesian islands known as the Moluccas.

questions.q: Which trading city in Central Asia became a great Silk Road crossroads?
questions.f: Its markets mixed Chinese silk, Indian spices, Persian glass and Mediterranean coins.

questions.q: Which cave complex on the Silk Road holds thousands of ancient paintings?
questions.f: Near Dunhuang, they also hid a sealed library of manuscripts for nearly 900 years.

questions.q: Which Chinese envoy's journey west in the 2nd century BC opened the Silk Road?
questions.f: He was held captive for a decade, escaped, and still completed his mission.

questions.q: Which Buddhist monk travelled from China to India and back, writing a famous account?
questions.f: His 17-year journey inspired the classic novel Journey to the West.

questions.q: Which ruler's 1324 pilgrimage across the Sahara became famous for its scale?
questions.f: Chroniclers wrote that his caravan's gifts of gold unsettled Cairo's markets for years.

questions.q: Bactrian camels have two humps and were the main pack animal of the eastern Silk Road.
questions.f: Their thick coats and wide feet handled both freezing passes and hot sand.

questions.q: Which word for a market on a trade route came into English from Persian?
questions.f: Caravanserai, another Persian-rooted word, meant the inn beside the bazaar.

questions.q: Which everyday English word comes from an Arabic word meaning 'the directions'?
questions.f: Azimuth is the compass angle to an object, still used by surveyors and astronomers.

questions.q: Which navigation word came into English from Arabic 'samt', a path or direction?
questions.f: Nadir and azimuth came from the same family of Arabic direction words.

questions.q: Which explorer's title 'Il Milione' was the nickname of his famous travel book?
questions.f: The nickname may mock his million tall tales, or come from a family name.

questions.q: Which emperor did Marco Polo claim to serve in China?
questions.f: Polo said he spent 17 years in the Khan's service, travelling as far as Yunnan.

questions.q: What did Zheng He's fleet famously bring back to the Chinese court from Africa?
questions.f: Court artists painted it as a qilin, a mythical creature of good fortune.

questions.q: How did the Chinese treasure-fleet voyages end?
questions.f: After 1433 China turned inward, and the vast shipyards fell silent within decades.

questions.q: Which Chinese invention helped ships steer a steady course centuries before Europe had it?
questions.f: Chinese texts describe magnetic direction-finding by the 11th century.

questions.q: Which ship design feature, used in Chinese junks, stopped one leak sinking the whole hull?
questions.f: Marco Polo described the idea, and European shipbuilders adopted it much later.

questions.q: Which word for a spacecraft's return through the atmosphere means to enter again?
questions.f: Friction heats a capsule's shield to thousands of degrees during those minutes.

questions.q: What is a 'splashdown'?
c: A spacecraft landing in the sea
questions.f: All Apollo crews splashed down under three parachutes and were picked up by ships.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission's crew survived an explosion by looping around the Moon?
questions.f: They used the lunar module as a lifeboat and returned safely after four tense days.

questions.q: Which astronaut hit two golf balls on the Moon?
questions.f: He used a club head taped to a sample-collection tool during Apollo 14.

questions.q: The last people to walk on the Moon did so in 1972.
questions.f: Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt of Apollo 17 were the last, in December 1972.

questions.q: Which spacecraft became the first to visit Pluto, in 2015?
questions.f: It flew past at over 49,000 km/h after a nine-year journey, revealing icy mountains.

questions.q: Which cosmonaut holds the record for the longest single stay in space?
questions.f: He spent 437 days aboard the Mir station in the 1990s, a mission longer than a Mars trip.

questions.q: Which was the first space station ever put in orbit?
questions.f: Launched in 1971, it proved humans could live and work in orbit for weeks.

questions.q: What does the Russian word 'mir', the name of a space station, mean?
questions.f: Soyuz means union and Vostok means east, so Soviet craft carried meaningful names.

questions.q: Which American woman first flew in space, in 1983?
questions.f: She was 32, and later founded a science education company for young students.

questions.q: Which explorer was the first person to reach both the North and South Poles?
questions.f: He stood at the South Pole in 1911 and flew over the North Pole in 1926.

questions.q: Which word describes the plants and animals a naturalist records in one place?
questions.f: Flora comes from a Roman goddess of flowers and Fauna from a woodland god.

questions.q: Which islands' unique animals shaped Charles Darwin's thinking?
questions.f: Different finch beaks on nearby islands hinted at how species change over time.

questions.q: Which naturalist explored the Amazon and Malay islands and reached ideas like Darwin's?
questions.f: A line named after him still marks the boundary between Asian and Australian wildlife.

questions.q: Which German naturalist's 1799 voyage measured mountains, currents and climate in the Americas?
questions.f: More places are named after Humboldt than after almost any other person.

questions.q: Which explorer of Africa searched for the source of the Nile and vanished for years?
questions.f: When Henry Morton Stanley finally found him, the meeting became a legendary greeting.

questions.q: Which Victorian traveller wrote Travels in West Africa after canoeing its rivers?
questions.f: She travelled in ordinary Victorian dress and credited her thick skirt with saving her from a fall.

questions.q: Which desert explorer wrote Arabian Sands about crossing the Empty Quarter?
questions.f: He crossed with Bedu companions who could recognise a camel's tracks like a signature.

questions.q: The Empty Quarter of Arabia is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth.
questions.f: Its dunes can rise 250 metres, taller than most skyscrapers.

questions.q: Which word means a person travelling on foot over long distances for religion?
questions.f: Pilgrim comes from peregrinus, a traveller abroad, the same root as peregrine.

questions.q: Which word means a written record of a voyage kept day by day?
questions.f: Journal shares its root with journey and diurnal, all from the Latin for day.

questions.q: Which word means the study of place names?
questions.f: Topos means place and onyma means name, so explorers' maps are full of toponyms.

questions.q: What does the root 'topo' mean in 'topography'?
questions.f: So topography is place-writing: the shape and features of the land.

questions.q: Which word means an instrument for measuring how far a walker has gone?
questions.f: Leonardo da Vinci sketched a pedometer centuries before fitness trackers existed.

questions.q: Which word describes crossing a river or shallow water on foot?
questions.f: Many old towns grew at fords, which is why Oxford and Frankfurt carry the word.

questions.q: Which term describes the practice of leaving marked stone piles as trail signs?
questions.f: Cairn comes from Gaelic, and Arctic explorers hid messages under them for rescuers.

questions.q: Which record is held by the Mariana Trench?
c: Deepest known point in the ocean
questions.f: Everest could sit inside it with more than two kilometres of water still above the summit.

questions.q: Which explorer completed the Five Deeps Expedition, diving to all five ocean floors?
questions.f: He finished in 2019 in a submersible aptly named Limiting Factor.

questions.q: Which pioneering oceanographer is nicknamed Her Deepness?
questions.f: She set a solo untethered dive record and has logged thousands of hours underwater.

questions.q: Which scientist mapped the Atlantic seafloor and revealed the mid-ocean ridge?
questions.f: Her maps helped convince doubters that continents really do drift apart.

questions.q: Which word means an animal or person able to survive extreme cold?
questions.f: Polar explorers bred hardy dogs and grew hardy vegetables in ship-board boxes.

questions.q: What does the root 'therm' contribute to the word 'thermos', vital on polar trips?
questions.f: A vacuum flask keeps heat in by removing the air that would carry it away.

questions.q: Which word describes a ship built to break through sea ice?
questions.f: Modern icebreakers ride up onto the ice so their weight cracks it downward.

questions.q: An explorer's 'chronometer' measures time, from a Greek root meaning time.
questions.f: Chronos gives us chronology, chronicle and synchronise as well.

questions.q: At what depth was the wreck of Shackleton's Endurance found in 2022?
questions.f: Freezing Weddell Sea water and no wood-eating worms left the ship astonishingly intact.

questions.q: Whose century-old navigation notes guided searchers to the Endurance wreck?
questions.f: Worsley's sextant readings, taken in gales, put the search box within a few miles.

questions.q: Which photographer saved glass plate negatives from the sinking Endurance?
questions.f: Shackleton made him smash the ones they could not carry, so temptation would not slow them.

questions.q: Which term describes Mercator's projection because it preserves local angles?
questions.f: Conformal means the shapes of tiny regions stay true, even as their sizes explode.

questions.q: What is the technical name for a course of constant compass bearing?
questions.f: Loxodrome means slanting run; it spirals toward the pole rather than reaching it.

questions.q: What is Tissot's indicatrix used to show on a map?
c: How much a projection distorts shape and area
questions.f: Small circles are drawn across the map; where they turn into ellipses, distortion is at work.

questions.q: Gerardus Mercator's family name was originally which Flemish word?
questions.f: He latinised it to Mercator, which also means merchant, as scholars often did.

questions.q: Which projection distorts so that Antarctica cannot be shown at all?
questions.f: The poles sit at infinity on a Mercator grid, so charts simply cut off near 85 degrees.

questions.q: Which 1513 map by an Ottoman admiral shows Atlantic coasts from many sources?
questions.f: Piri Reis noted on it which older charts and captains' reports he had combined.

questions.q: Which medieval world map, kept in an English cathedral, puts Jerusalem at its centre?
questions.f: It is drawn on a single calfskin and packs in over 500 places and creatures.

questions.q: Which Arab geographer made the Tabula Rogeriana for a Sicilian king in 1154?
questions.f: His map was drawn with south at the top, the convention in much Islamic cartography.

questions.q: The convention of putting north at the top of maps is a choice, not a scientific rule.
questions.f: Medieval European maps often put east at the top, which is why we speak of orienting a map.

questions.q: Which word describes the angle between magnetic north and true north?
questions.f: It changes with place and slowly with time, so charts print the year of measurement.

questions.q: Which method of finding longitude relied on measuring the Moon against stars?
questions.f: It worked but demanded hours of arithmetic, so Harrison's clock eventually won out.

questions.q: How much prize money did Britain's 1714 Longitude Act offer for a solution?
questions.f: That was a fortune, and clockmaker John Harrison fought for decades to collect it.

questions.q: Which Astronomer Royal was Harrison's chief rival in the longitude contest?
questions.f: Maskelyne championed the lunar-distance method and published tables sailors used for a century.

questions.q: Which sea creature's absence helped preserve wooden shipwrecks in Antarctic water?
questions.f: Wood-boring molluscs cannot survive there, which is why Endurance still looks like a ship.

questions.q: A frozen sea that would not release a ship, a stowaway who became a crewman, and an 800-mile lifeboat crossing all belong to which expedition?
questions.f: Shackleton failed to cross Antarctica yet brought all 28 men home alive.

questions.q: A carpenter's cat named Mrs Chippy, a hut roofed with a lifeboat, and a rescue tug from Chile point to which leader?
questions.f: After four attempts, Shackleton reached Elephant Island aboard the Chilean tug Yelcho in 1916.

questions.q: Which crew member of Shackleton's rescue party had also served with Scott?
questions.f: Crean once walked 35 miles alone across the ice with three biscuits to save a companion.

questions.q: What did Shackleton's carpenter do to the James Caird before the rescue voyage?
c: Raised its sides and added a deck
questions.f: Harry McNish used sledge runners and canvas, and the little boat survived hurricane seas.

questions.q: Which mountain range did Shackleton's party cross unroped to reach a whaling station?
questions.f: They crossed in 36 hours with 50 feet of rope and screws in their boots for grip.

questions.q: Which polar explorer wrote 'The Worst Journey in the World' about a winter egg-collecting trip?
questions.f: They hauled sledges in total darkness at minus 60 to fetch emperor penguin eggs for science.

questions.q: Which of Scott's ships gave its name to his final expedition?
questions.f: Terra Nova means new land, and the ship had begun life as a Newfoundland whaler.

questions.q: What did Amundsen leave for Scott inside the tent at the South Pole?
c: A letter asking him to forward news to Norway's king
questions.f: It was insurance: if Amundsen never got home, Scott would carry the news.

questions.q: Amundsen originally planned to attack the North Pole, and changed target in secret.
questions.f: Hearing the North Pole was claimed, he turned south and cabled Scott only once at sea.

questions.q: Which explorer made the first verified surface crossing to the North Pole, in 1969?
questions.f: His British team crossed the entire Arctic Ocean by dog sledge, some 6,000 kilometres.

questions.q: Which polar record did Borge Ousland set in 1994?
c: First solo unsupported trek to the North Pole
questions.f: He skied and swam through leads of open water, hauling everything he needed.

questions.q: Which vessel carried the 2022 expedition that located the Endurance wreck?
questions.f: Autonomous submarines flew search patterns beneath the ice for days at a time.

questions.q: In which year did Ernest Shackleton die, on his way south for one last expedition?
questions.f: The Endurance wreck was found exactly 100 years later, almost to the day.

questions.q: A survey number instead of a name, a Bengali mathematician's calculations, and a British officer's objection all lie behind the naming of what?
questions.f: Radhanath Sikdar's 1852 sums identified Peak XV; George Everest himself disliked the honour.

questions.q: Which climber's ice axe was found high on Everest in 1933, hinting at the 1924 mystery?
questions.f: Mallory's body appeared in 1999; his camera, which might settle everything, has never been found.

questions.q: What did the 1953 Everest team use to reduce weight in their oxygen sets?
c: Closed-circuit and open-circuit systems tested side by side
questions.f: Hillary and Tenzing summited on the heavier open-circuit sets, which proved more reliable.

questions.q: Who led the 1953 British expedition on which Everest was first climbed?
questions.f: Hunt planned the whole logistical pyramid; Hillary and Tenzing were his final pair.

questions.q: Which rock step near Everest's summit was named after Edmund Hillary?
questions.f: Its shape changed after the 2015 earthquake, and climbers now debate what remains.

questions.q: Which mountaineer completed all fourteen 8,000-metre peaks first?
questions.f: He finished in 1986, and every climb was without bottled oxygen.

questions.q: Which Nepali climber led the 2021 first winter ascent of K2?
questions.f: The ten-man team paused below the summit so they could step onto it together, singing.

questions.q: What is the 'Death Zone' threshold height that mountaineers use?
questions.f: Only 14 mountains on Earth reach it, and all of them are in Asia.

questions.q: Everest's height changed slightly after the 2015 Nepal earthquake shifted the region.
questions.f: Surveys detected small shifts, which is one reason Nepal and China re-measured in 2020.

questions.q: Which term describes the shallow saddle between Everest and Lhotse?
questions.f: Col comes from the Latin for neck, and Cwm is a Welsh word for a bowl-shaped valley.

questions.q: Who named the Western Cwm on Everest, borrowing a Welsh word?
questions.f: Mallory knew Welsh hills well; cwm is pronounced coom and means valley.

questions.q: Which term describes a plume of snow blowing off a summit, used to judge wind?
questions.f: Everest's banner can stream for kilometres when the jet stream touches the summit.

questions.q: What is a 'cornice' on a mountain ridge?
c: An overhanging lip of wind-blown snow
questions.f: It can look like solid ground and collapse under a climber's weight.

questions.q: Which condition, named for its whiteness, can blind climbers who lose their goggles?
questions.f: It is sunburn of the eye's surface; Inuit carved slitted goggles from bone to prevent it.

questions.q: Which vessel first reached the Challenger Deep, and what powered its float?
questions.f: Petrol is lighter than water and does not compress, making it a perfect deep-sea float.

questions.q: How did the Trieste control its descent and ascent?
questions.f: Electromagnets held the shot; a power failure would simply drop it and float them up.

questions.q: Which fish was famously seen from Trieste's window, later thought to be a sea cucumber?
questions.f: The 1960 sighting sparked decades of argument about what can live at 11 kilometres down.

questions.q: Which Japanese robotic vehicle reached the Challenger Deep in 1995?
questions.f: It later mapped the trench in detail before being lost in a typhoon in 2003.

questions.q: Which woman was the first to reach the Challenger Deep, in 2020?
questions.f: She had also been the first American woman to walk in space, in 1984.

questions.q: A stratospheric balloon in 1931, a deep-sea float filled with petrol, and a grandson flying non-stop around the world belong to which family?
questions.f: Auguste, Jacques and Bertrand Piccard explored the sky, the deep, and the globe by balloon.

questions.q: Which balloon carried Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones around the world non-stop in 1999?
questions.f: They landed in Egypt with only a little propane left after nearly 20 days aloft.

questions.q: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world using no fuel at all.
questions.f: Its 17,000 solar cells charged batteries for night flying; one leg lasted almost five days.

questions.q: Which aviator made the first solo non-stop balloon flight around the world, in 2002?
questions.f: It was his sixth attempt, and he flew the whole way in a tiny unheated capsule.

questions.q: Which record did Felix Baumgartner set in 2012 over New Mexico?
c: First person to break the sound barrier in freefall
questions.f: He leapt from about 39 kilometres up; Alan Eustace later jumped from even higher.

questions.q: Which pilot's aircraft was called Glamorous Glennis when the sound barrier fell in 1947?
questions.f: He named it after his wife, and flew with taped-up ribs from a horse-riding fall.

questions.q: Which aircraft holds the record as the fastest air-breathing crewed plane?
questions.f: It could cross the Atlantic in under two hours and leaked fuel until heat sealed its skin.

questions.q: Which rocket plane still holds the crewed winged-aircraft speed record?
questions.f: It reached about Mach 6.7 in 1967 and flew high enough to earn astronaut wings for some pilots.

questions.q: What was unusual about the Wright brothers' 1903 controls?
c: The pilot lay down and steered by shifting a cradle
It was steered by a wheel
questions.f: Wing warping twisted the wings themselves, a system that predates ailerons.

questions.q: Which key aerodynamic insight did the Wright brothers get from watching birds?
c: Banking to turn, not just rudder steering
questions.f: They combined roll and yaw, solving the control problem others had ignored.

questions.q: Who won the Wright brothers' coin toss and made the first attempt on 14 December 1903?
questions.f: Wilbur stalled and damaged the machine; Orville flew successfully three days later.

questions.q: Who built the lightweight engine for the Wright Flyer?
questions.f: Their bicycle-shop mechanic made a 12-horsepower engine in six weeks from scratch.

questions.q: A leaky fuel line, a broken altimeter, and a farmer's field in Northern Ireland ended whose record flight?
questions.f: She had aimed for Paris, landed in a cow pasture, and became the first woman to fly the Atlantic alone.

questions.q: Which aviator made the first solo east-to-west flight across the Atlantic in 1936?
questions.f: Flying against the wind is far harder; she ran out of fuel and crash-landed in Nova Scotia.

questions.q: Lindbergh flew without a radio to save weight for extra fuel.
questions.f: He also skipped a parachute and used a wicker chair to keep the plane light.

questions.q: Which of Lindbergh's design choices meant he could not see straight ahead?
c: A fuel tank in front of the cockpit
questions.f: He used a periscope and leaned out the side window to see when landing.

questions.q: Which airline first offered scheduled transatlantic passenger flights by flying boat?
questions.f: Its Boeing 314 Clippers landed on water, since long runways were still rare.

questions.q: Which term describes the loss of an aircraft's lift when the wing's angle grows too steep?
questions.f: Understanding stalls turned early gliding accidents into a solvable engineering problem.

questions.q: The word 'aviation' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.f: From avis, which also gives us aviary and the science of birds, ornithology's Latin cousin.

questions.q: The word 'helicopter' is built from Greek roots meaning what?
questions.f: From helix and pteron; the same pteron appears in pterodactyl, wing-finger.

questions.q: Which Greek root in 'astronaut' also appears in 'Argonaut'?
questions.f: Jason's Argonauts were sailors of the ship Argo, so astronauts are sailors of the stars.

questions.q: Which word for a Chinese space traveller blends a Chinese word with a Greek one?
questions.f: Taikong means outer space, joined to nautes, sailor.

questions.q: A callsign meaning cedar, a shout of 'Let's go!', and a landing by parachute away from the capsule belong to which flight?
questions.f: Gagarin ejected and parachuted separately, a detail kept quiet for years to protect the record claim.

questions.q: Why did Gagarin's separate parachute landing nearly complicate his record?
c: Rules then required landing inside the craft
questions.f: Officials described the flight carefully so the first-orbit record would stand.

questions.q: Which cosmonaut's spacewalk suit swelled so much he had to vent air to re-enter the airlock?
questions.f: Leonov's 1965 walk lasted 12 minutes and nearly ended in a jammed hatch.

questions.q: Which was the first spacecraft to make a controlled landing on the Moon and send pictures?
questions.f: In 1966 it proved the surface was firm, calming fears of a deep dust ocean.

questions.q: Which spacecraft was the first human-made object to reach the surface of another world?
questions.f: It struck the Moon in 1959 after Luna 1 had missed and sailed into orbit around the Sun.

questions.q: Venera 7 survived on the surface of Venus for less than half an hour.
questions.f: About 460 degrees Celsius and crushing pressure ended its transmissions in roughly 23 minutes.

questions.q: What is the 'grand tour' trajectory that Voyager 2 uniquely completed?
c: Flybys of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune
questions.f: A once-in-176-year planetary alignment made the four-planet route possible.

questions.q: Which technique let Voyager gain speed without using fuel?
questions.f: Each planet flyby stole a little orbital momentum, flinging the craft onward faster.

questions.q: Who chaired the committee that chose the contents of the Voyager golden record?
questions.f: The record includes the brainwaves of Ann Druyan, recorded while she thought about love.

questions.q: What does the pulsar map etched on the Voyager record cover show?
c: A map of the solar system
questions.f: Because pulsars slow at known rates, the diagram also acts as a cosmic date stamp.

questions.q: Which speed is the Voyager record meant to be played at?
questions.f: A diagram of a hydrogen atom's transition explains the timing unit to any finder.

questions.q: Which plaque preceded the golden record, carried on Pioneer 10 and 11?
c: A gold-anodised aluminium plaque with human figures
questions.f: Sagan and Drake designed it in three weeks, complete with the same pulsar map idea.

questions.q: What is the heliopause that Voyager 1 crossed in 2012?
c: The boundary where the solar wind meets interstellar space
The edge of the asteroid belt
questions.f: Instruments saw the charged-particle count flip, proof the craft had truly left the bubble.

questions.q: What powers the Voyager spacecraft nearly fifty years after launch?
questions.f: Heat from radioactive decay becomes electricity, dropping about four watts a year.

questions.q: Which record does the Parker Solar Probe hold?
c: First to leave the solar system
questions.f: Sun-diving speeds have passed 690,000 kilometres an hour, fast enough to cross the US in half a minute.

questions.q: Apollo 8's crew were the first humans to see the far side of the Moon with their own eyes.
questions.f: They orbited ten times in December 1968 and read from Genesis on live television.

questions.q: Who took the famous Earthrise photograph on Apollo 8?
questions.f: The crew had no plan to shoot it, and scrambled for colour film as Earth appeared.

questions.q: Which piece of Apollo 11 equipment is still used by scientists on Earth today?
questions.f: Bouncing lasers off it shows the Moon drifting away about 3.8 centimetres each year.

questions.q: How much lunar material did the Apollo missions bring back in total?
questions.f: Some of it is still sealed, saved deliberately for future instruments to study.

questions.q: Which Apollo 11 alarm nearly forced a landing abort?
questions.f: A 24-year-old engineer, Steve Bales, called go because he knew the computer was only overloaded.

questions.q: Roughly how much landing fuel did Apollo 11's Eagle have left at touchdown?
questions.f: Armstrong had flown long to avoid a boulder field, spending precious seconds.

questions.q: Which mission first tested the lunar module in space, in Earth orbit?
questions.f: Apollo 10 then flew it around the Moon, stopping just 15 kilometres above the surface.

questions.q: Which navigation aid did Apollo crews use as a backup for aligning their guidance system?
questions.f: Space sextants read known stars, tying spaceflight straight back to sailing tradition.

questions.q: Which record does Valeri Polyakov's 1994-95 mission still hold?
questions.f: He spent 437 days in orbit, then insisted on walking from his capsule to prove he could.

questions.q: Which craft carried the first crew to the International Space Station in 2000?
questions.f: Expedition 1 began an unbroken human presence in orbit that continues today.

questions.q: A Tahitian priest, a chart of seventy islands, and a sailing memory stretching 4,000 kilometres describe which navigator?
questions.f: Tupaia joined Cook in 1769 and astonished the British by naming islands they had never charted.

questions.q: What is 'etak' in Micronesian navigation?
c: A mental system of moving reference islands
questions.f: Navigators imagine islands sliding past under the stars, tracking progress without instruments.

questions.q: Micronesian navigators could locate an island by reading how it bends ocean swells.
questions.f: Islands reflect and refract swells, creating a signature detectable dozens of kilometres away.

questions.q: Which archaeological culture is linked to the first great Pacific island expansions?
questions.f: Their distinctive stamped pottery traces a voyaging trail from Melanesia into Polynesia.

questions.q: How does a Pacific navigator use a 'zenith star' to find an island?
c: The star passes directly overhead at that island's latitude
questions.f: Arcturus stands over Hawaii, and Sirius over Tahiti, so the sky itself becomes a latitude gauge.

questions.q: Which bird did Pacific voyagers watch because it returns to land each evening?
questions.f: Frigatebirds will not land on water, so seeing one meant land lay within reach.

questions.q: Which Polynesian settlement was the last major landmass reached by voyaging canoes?
questions.f: Maori tradition remembers named canoes; archaeology dates arrival to around 1300.

questions.q: Which term describes the double-hulled canoe design used for long Pacific voyages?
questions.f: Two hulls bridged by a deck made a platform stable enough for months at sea.

questions.q: Which theory did Thor Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki voyage try to support?
c: That Polynesians came from South America
questions.f: He proved the raft could drift there, but DNA and language show settlement came from the west.

questions.q: Which language family links Madagascar with Hawaii and New Zealand?
questions.f: It is a record of its own: the widest ocean-going language spread before modern ships.

questions.q: A cargo of cloves worth more than the whole voyage, a captain buried in the Philippines, and a Basque officer's homecoming describe which expedition?
questions.f: Only 18 of about 270 men returned in 1522, aboard the leaking Victoria.

questions.q: Which surprising discrepancy did Magellan's returning crew notice in their records?
c: They had lost a day compared with home
questions.f: Sailing west against the Sun cost them a calendar day, the first practical proof of the effect.

questions.q: What did Magellan's crew call the stormy passage at South America's tip?
questions.f: It was later renamed the Strait of Magellan, and takes 38 winding sea-miles at its narrowest.

questions.q: Which coat of arms did Spain grant Elcano, featuring a globe and spices?
c: One with cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg
One with a lion and anchor
questions.f: His motto meant you were the first to encircle me, spoken as if by the Earth.

questions.q: Francis Drake's Golden Hind was renamed mid-voyage from the Pelican.
questions.f: He honoured a patron whose crest featured a golden hind, a female red deer.

questions.q: An oyster sloop rebuilt from a rotting hull, a captain who could not swim, and 46,000 miles alone point to whom?
questions.f: Slocum finished the first solo circumnavigation in 1898 and wrote a bestseller about it.

questions.q: Which trick did Joshua Slocum use to keep intruders off his deck at night?
questions.f: He wrote that a barefoot visitor discovered them and departed at remarkable speed.

questions.q: Which race, run in 1968-69, produced the first solo non-stop circumnavigation?
questions.f: Robin Knox-Johnston was the only one of nine starters to finish.

questions.q: Which sailor abandoned a likely race victory in 1969 to keep sailing on toward the Pacific?
questions.f: He slingshotted a message onto a passing ship saying he was carrying on to save his soul.

questions.q: Which sailor became the first woman to sail solo non-stop around the world?
questions.f: The Australian completed the voyage in 1988 in 189 days aboard Blackmores First Lady.

questions.q: Which British sailor set a solo round-the-world record in 2005 in a trimaran?
questions.f: She trimmed the record to 71 days, sleeping in short bursts to keep the boat flying.

questions.q: Which route do round-the-world sailing records traditionally follow?
c: Eastward past the three great capes
questions.f: Good Hope, Leeuwin and Horn are the three capes, all in the roaring southern winds.

questions.q: Which cape do sailors call the Everest of the sea?
questions.f: Its waves pile up where the Andes funnel wind into a narrowing seabed.

questions.q: What is a 'clipper route' in sailing history?
c: A fast trade route running east in the southern ocean
questions.f: Wool and tea clippers raced home along it, sometimes covering 400 miles in a day.

questions.q: Which term describes the practice of throwing a knotted line to measure a ship's speed?
questions.f: Knots per half-minute gave the unit sailors still use today.

questions.q: What does 'swinging the compass' mean on a ship?
c: Spinning it to test the needle
questions.f: Iron hulls deflect needles, so compasses must be corrected in every new ship.

questions.q: The Plimsoll line on a ship's hull shows how heavily it may safely be loaded.
questions.f: Samuel Plimsoll's campaign saved countless sailors from dangerously overloaded ships.

questions.q: Which Latin root gives us both 'navy' and 'nave', the central hall of a church?
questions.f: A nave's high ceiling reminded builders of an upturned hull.

questions.q: Which word for a captain's log came from a Dutch word for a rough day-book?
questions.f: Ships also kept a 'waste book' of rough notes, tidied into the official log later.

questions.q: What did the word 'trade' originally mean, as in 'trade winds'?
questions.f: They were winds that blew in a steady track, and only later became linked with commerce.

questions.q: Which belt of calm at about 30 degrees latitude is called the horse latitudes?
questions.f: Sailing legend links the name to horses lost when becalmed ships ran short of water.

questions.q: Which term describes a ship's failure to move because there is no wind at all?
questions.f: Doldrums crossings could strand a sailing ship for weeks within sight of the equator.

questions.q: Which term describes an unmapped hazard marked on charts as 'position doubtful'?
questions.f: Charts still carry vigias reported by old captains that nobody has been able to confirm.

questions.q: Which phantom island appeared on maps of the South Pacific for over a century?
questions.f: Sandy Island was finally 'undiscovered' in 2012 when a research ship sailed straight through it.

questions.q: Which Arctic phantom land appeared on charts after a 1906 sighting near Alaska?
questions.f: An expedition spent years searching before concluding it was a mirage on the ice.

questions.q: Which optical effect made distant ice look like cliffs and misled polar explorers?
questions.f: Layers of cold and warm air bend light, lifting whole coastlines into the sky.

questions.q: Which Silk Road manuscript hoard was sealed in a cave for nearly 900 years?
questions.f: It held the world's oldest dated printed book, a Diamond Sutra from 868.

questions.q: Which desert did Silk Road caravans skirt rather than cross, calling it a sea of death?
questions.f: Its name is often read as 'you can go in but not come out'.

questions.q: Paper-making technology travelled from China to the Islamic world along the Silk Road.
questions.f: Papermakers reached Samarkand in the 8th century, and Europe followed centuries later.

questions.q: A judge from Tangier, a shipwreck in the Maldives, and a book called simply 'The Journey' point to whom?
questions.f: He travelled some 117,000 kilometres, further than any known traveller before the steam age.

questions.q: Which job did Ibn Battuta hold in several of the lands he visited?
questions.f: His legal training let him find work and welcome from Delhi to the Maldives.

questions.q: Who actually wrote down Ibn Battuta's travels at a sultan's request?
questions.f: The scholar shaped the dictated memories into the flowing book we read today.

questions.q: Which North African traveller wrote a description of Africa that shaped European maps?
questions.f: Born al-Hasan al-Wazzan, he wrote his geography while living in Italy in the 1520s.

questions.q: Which trans-Saharan trade good was exchanged nearly pound for pound with gold?
questions.f: Salt slabs were mined at Taghaza and carried south by camel to the gold lands.

questions.q: Which 1375 atlas shows Mansa Musa holding a golden nugget?
questions.f: That single illustration drew European eyes toward West African gold for generations.

questions.q: Which term describes Zheng He's largest vessels?
questions.f: Chronicles give lengths so large that historians still argue about the true figures.

questions.q: Which emperor sponsored Zheng He's first six voyages?
questions.f: He also moved the capital to Beijing and ordered the Forbidden City built.

questions.q: Which stone tablet records Zheng He's voyages and his thanks to a sea goddess?
questions.f: The inscriptions list the countries visited, our best contemporary record of the fleets.

questions.q: Which term describes the Chinese practice of exchanging gifts with distant rulers?
questions.f: Zheng He's fleets carried porcelain and silk out, and returned with giraffes, zebras and envoys.

questions.q: Zheng He's voyages reached the east coast of Africa.
questions.f: Fleets called at Malindi and Mogadishu decades before Portuguese ships rounded the Cape.

questions.q: Which record is held by Angel Falls in Venezuela?
questions.f: Pilot Jimmie Angel spotted it in 1933 while hunting for a rumoured river of gold.

questions.q: Which flat-topped mountains of Venezuela and Guyana are called tepuis?
questions.f: Their isolated summits host plants found nowhere else, like islands in the sky.

questions.q: Which explorer's 1913 river journey in Brazil nearly killed him and mapped an unknown river?
questions.f: The River of Doubt was renamed Rio Roosevelt after the punishing descent.

questions.q: Which American brought Machu Picchu to world attention in 1911?
questions.f: Local farmers already knew the ruins; a boy guided him up the ridge to them.

questions.q: Which record does Lake Baikal hold besides being the deepest lake?
c: It holds the most liquid fresh water
questions.f: Roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water sits in that one Siberian rift.

questions.q: Which Andean lake is the world's highest large navigable lake?
questions.f: Reed boats have crossed its 3,800-metre-high water for many centuries.

questions.q: Which place holds the record for the greatest average yearly rainfall?
questions.f: Monsoon air rammed against the Meghalaya hills dumps over eleven metres of rain a year.

questions.q: Which Chilean weather station is famous for having recorded essentially no rainfall?
c: Stations in the Atacama's Yungay area
questions.f: Some Atacama river beds have been dry for many thousands of years.

questions.q: Which mountain holds the record for the greatest rise from base to summit on land?
questions.f: Its base-to-peak rise of about 5,500 metres beats Everest's, which starts on a high plateau.

questions.q: Which Guinness World Records question started the whole book in 1951?
c: Which is Europe's fastest game bird
Which is the world's tallest man
How long can a person hold their breath
questions.f: Sir Hugh Beaver could not settle a shooting-party argument, so he commissioned a book of facts.

questions.q: Guinness World Records itself holds a record as the best-selling copyrighted book series.
questions.f: More than 150 million copies have sold since 1955, in dozens of languages.

questions.q: Which unit measures a mountain's prominence?
c: Height above the lowest connecting saddle
questions.f: By prominence, Everest is first and Aconcagua second, since it stands clear of any higher link.

questions.q: Which term describes a peak that is the highest point for a great distance around?
questions.f: A nunatak, by contrast, is a peak poking through an ice sheet, from a Greenlandic word.

questions.q: Which word describes a rocky peak poking through an ice sheet?
questions.f: It comes from Greenlandic Kalaallisut, one of several polar words English borrowed whole.

questions.q: Which Inuit-derived word names a light paddling boat with a sealed deck?
questions.f: From Inuktitut qajaq; canoe by contrast came from the Caribbean Taino word canoa.

questions.q: Which everyday word for a hooded waterproof jacket comes from Greenlandic?
questions.f: From annoraaq; parka arrived instead through Russian from a Nenets word.

questions.q: The word 'tundra' entered English from which language family?
questions.f: From a Kildin Sami word meaning treeless heights, borrowed via Russian.

questions.q: Which word literally means 'ice mountain' in Dutch?
questions.f: Berg means mountain, which is why only the tip shows and the mountain lies below.

questions.q: Which word means the science of measuring Earth's exact shape and size?
questions.f: From Greek for dividing the earth; geodesists discovered our planet is slightly pear-shaped.

questions.q: What is a 'graticule' on a map?
c: The network of latitude and longitude lines
questions.f: From Latin for a little grating, the same image as a grill or grid.

questions.q: What is a 'cartouche' on an old map?
c: The decorated panel holding the title
questions.f: From Italian cartoccio, a paper cone, because the frames were drawn like curling paper.

questions.q: What do 'isobath' lines join on a chart?
questions.f: Iso means equal, so isotherms join equal temperatures and isohyets equal rainfall.

questions.q: Which medieval sea chart type is named from the Italian word for harbours?
questions.f: Portolan charts covered coastlines with radiating compass lines but ignored inland detail.

questions.q: What is a 'binnacle' on a ship?
questions.f: From Latin habitaculum, a dwelling place, because it is the compass's little house.

questions.q: The word 'mile' comes from a Latin phrase meaning a thousand paces.
questions.f: Mille passus counted double steps of a marching Roman soldier.

questions.q: Which word for a hot desert wind came into English from Arabic?
questions.f: Simoom traces to a root meaning poison, describing the choking dust it carries.

questions.q: Which word did Sanskrit give English, originally meaning dry uncultivated land?
questions.f: Jangala meant arid waste; English flipped it to mean thick green forest.

questions.q: Which Caribbean language gave English 'hurricane', 'hammock' and 'canoe'?
questions.f: Those words crossed the Atlantic on the earliest Spanish ships and never left.

questions.q: Which Australian language gave the word 'kangaroo' to English?
questions.f: Cook's crew recorded gangurru in 1770 on the Endeavour River in Queensland.

questions.q: Which Dutch-derived Afrikaans word for a long ox-wagon journey is now used for hiking?
questions.f: The Great Trek of the 1830s gave the word its epic flavour.

questions.q: Which word means the mapping of coastlines and harbours for navigation?
questions.f: Naval hydrographic offices still publish the charts that keep shipping safe.

questions.q: Which 1570 book by Abraham Ortelius is called the first modern atlas?
questions.f: Ortelius also noticed that continents look as if they once fitted together.

questions.q: Which French family spent four generations mapping their country by triangulation?
questions.f: Their survey shrank France on paper, prompting a king's joke that they had cost him territory.

questions.q: Which military campaign prompted the founding of Britain's Ordnance Survey?
questions.f: Ordnance meant artillery, so the maps were first drawn for guns, not for hikers.

questions.q: How was the original metre defined in the 1790s?
c: A fraction of the distance from pole to equator
The length of a pendulum second
questions.f: Delambre and Mechain surveyed the Paris meridian for seven years to fix it.

questions.q: Which nations' 1884 conference chose Greenwich as the prime meridian?
questions.f: France abstained and kept using the Paris meridian on its maps for decades.

questions.q: Ptolemy's underestimate of the Earth's size encouraged Columbus to sail west.
questions.f: If Asia really were that close, his little fleet could have reached it in weeks.

questions.q: Which explorer first crossed the Antarctic Circle, in 1773?
questions.f: He circled the continent without seeing it, and concluded any land there was worthless ice.

questions.q: Which naval officer located the North Magnetic Pole in 1831?
questions.f: He later commanded Erebus and Terror in Antarctica, where an ice shelf now bears his name.

questions.q: Which captain of HMS Beagle later founded Britain's first weather forecast service?
questions.f: He coined the word forecast and published storm warnings that saved fishing fleets.

questions.q: Which expedition of 1872-76 made the first global survey of the deep ocean?
questions.f: Its crew sounded, dredged and catalogued about 4,700 new species in four years.

questions.q: Which idea about deep water did the Challenger expedition disprove?
c: That nothing could live below 550 metres
That the sea floor was flat
That the deep was fresh water
questions.f: The azoic theory collapsed as dredges came up wriggling with life from kilometres down.

questions.q: Which diver invented the Aqua-Lung with engineer Emile Gagnan?
questions.f: Their demand valve let divers breathe compressed air freely, opening the sea to everyone.

questions.q: Which record did Sylvia Earle set in 1979 off Hawaii?
c: Deepest untethered walk on the sea floor
First woman to dive the Titanic
questions.f: She walked at 381 metres in an armoured suit connected to nothing but a small submersible.

questions.q: Which submersible drifted along the Gulf Stream for a month in 1969?
questions.f: Jacques Piccard's mesoscaphe carried six men and helped NASA study crews in confined spaces.

questions.q: Which trench holds the Atlantic Ocean's deepest point?
questions.f: The Milwaukee Deep there reaches over 8,300 metres, far shallower than the Pacific's best.

questions.q: Which deep is the Arctic Ocean's lowest point?
questions.f: At about 5,550 metres it was the final target of the Five Deeps Expedition.

questions.q: Which trench contains the second deepest point in any ocean?
questions.f: Horizon Deep there is only about 100 metres shallower than Challenger Deep.

questions.q: The deepest hole ever drilled into the Earth did not even pierce the crust.
questions.f: The Kola Superdeep Borehole reached 12,262 metres, still inside the continental crust.

questions.q: Which spot is known as the oceanic pole of inaccessibility?
questions.f: The nearest land is 2,688 kilometres away, so the closest humans are often on the space station.

questions.q: Which inhabited island group is the most remote in the world?
questions.f: Its few hundred residents live over 2,000 kilometres from the nearest other settlement.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain never officially climbed?
questions.f: Bhutan closed its high peaks to climbing out of respect for local beliefs.

questions.q: Which record does the Trans-Siberian Railway hold?
c: Longest railway line in the world
questions.f: Its 9,289 kilometres cross eight time zones and take about a week end to end.

questions.q: Which railway crosses the world's highest railway pass, above 5,000 metres?
questions.f: Carriages carry extra oxygen for passengers over the Tanggula Pass.

questions.q: A ship's cat named Mrs Chippy, a stowaway who became a crewman, and a carpenter denied the Polar Medal all belong to which vessel's story?
questions.f: Four of Shackleton's men, including carpenter Harry McNish, were never given the medal despite his lifesaving boat work.

questions.q: A terse telegram reading 'Beg leave to inform you Fram proceeding Antarctic', a hut named Fram-home, and a plan that counted on eating sled dogs identify which leader?
questions.f: He had told the world he was heading north, then swung south, reaching the Pole in 1911.

questions.q: A coded telegram about abandoning advance base, a beekeeper's winter hobby, and a Sherpa's seventh attempt converge on which day's news?
c: The first winter ascent of K2
questions.f: The cipher hid the triumph so a newspaper could break the story on coronation morning, 2 June 1953.

questions.q: A refugee travel document, a Nobel Peace Prize, and a hull built to be squeezed upward by ice all belong to which explorer?
questions.f: The Nansen passport let stateless people travel after the First World War.

questions.q: An American who learned Inuktitut, twenty-two years as an Arctic partner, and belated Explorers Club membership in 1937 describe whom?
questions.f: Henson was Peary's most skilled companion on the ice, driving dogs and building sledges.

questions.q: A woman barred from research ships, hand-drawn ocean-floor profiles dismissed as 'girl talk', and a rift valley down the Atlantic's spine point to whom?
questions.f: Her maps with Bruce Heezen helped prove the sea floor is spreading apart.

questions.q: Prayer beads used as a counting machine, paces measured to 33 inches, and a disguise as a pilgrim describe which 19th-century surveyor of Tibet?
questions.f: He and the other Pundits mapped forbidden Himalayan country step by careful step.

questions.q: A valet called Jean, a flowering vine named for the ship's commander, and the first woman known to circle the globe identify whom?
questions.f: Bougainvillea honours her captain; a plant genus, Baretia, was named for her.

questions.q: A Newfoundland dog named Seaman, a live prairie dog shipped east as a gift, and a Shoshone interpreter belong to which expedition?
questions.f: Their Corps of Discovery crossed the continent and back between 1804 and 1806.

questions.q: A cat called Trim, a shipwreck on a coral reef, and the campaign to popularise the name 'Australia' point to which navigator?
questions.f: Flinders circumnavigated the continent and argued its name should replace New Holland.

questions.q: Seven months in prison for heresy, a Latin surname meaning 'merchant', and a grid that turns compass courses into straight lines identify whom?
questions.f: Born Gerard de Kremer, he published his world-changing projection in 1569.

questions.q: A Danish captain in Russian service, a naturalist who described a now-extinct sea cow, and a shipwreck on a treeless island identify which expedition's leader?
questions.f: Georg Steller sailed with him; Steller's sea cow was hunted to extinction within 27 years.

questions.q: A carpenter's son from Yorkshire, wooden gears that needed no oil, and a sea trial to Jamaica that lost only seconds point to whom?
questions.f: His H4 watch solved the longitude problem that had wrecked fleets for centuries.

questions.q: A piece of muslin from a 1903 wing, a helicopter weighing under two kilograms, and a flight in air one percent as thick as Earth's converge on what?
questions.f: NASA taped Wright Flyer fabric to the little rotorcraft that first flew on Mars in 2021.

questions.q: A hammer and a falcon feather dropped together, a small statuette left in the dust, and the first wheels driven on another world belong to which mission?
questions.f: Dave Scott's feather-and-hammer drop proved Galileo right on live television.

questions.q: A family photograph left on the surface, a leaping high-jump that nearly toppled a spacesuit, and rocks from the lunar highlands belong to which mission?
questions.f: Charlie Duke left a photo of his family in the dust, where it presumably still lies.

questions.q: Which crew travelled farther from Earth than any humans before or since?
questions.f: Their crippled craft swung around the Moon's far side at 400,171 kilometres from home.

questions.q: Which Apollo crew holds the record for the fastest speed ever reached by humans?
questions.f: On re-entry in 1969 they touched about 39,900 kilometres an hour.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission landed close enough to an earlier robotic probe to bring pieces home?
questions.f: Pete Conrad's crew cut parts from Surveyor 3 to see how three years on the Moon had aged them.

questions.q: A stowaway packet of seeds, a command module pilot who never landed, and trees now growing on four continents describe which flight?
questions.f: Stuart Roosa's orbiting seeds became the Moon Trees, planted around the world in the 1970s.

questions.q: Which cosmonaut was the first person to sleep in space and to suffer space sickness?
questions.f: At 25 he is also still the youngest person ever to fly in orbit.

questions.q: Which two dogs became the first animals to orbit Earth and return alive?
questions.f: One of Strelka's puppies was later given to President Kennedy's family as a gift.

questions.q: Which country launched a cat named Felicette into space in 1963?
questions.f: She is still the only cat known to have flown, on a suborbital hop from Algeria.

questions.q: Vanguard 1, launched in 1958, is the oldest human-made object still in orbit.
questions.f: Sputnik and Explorer 1 both fell back long ago; the grapefruit-sized Vanguard is still circling.

questions.q: Which woman made the first spacewalk, in 1984?
questions.f: She welded metal outside the Salyut 7 station, three months before Kathryn Sullivan's walk.

questions.q: Which probe made the most distant landing ever achieved by a human-made craft?
questions.f: In 2005 it parachuted onto Saturn's moon and found pebbles of water ice in a methane river bed.

questions.q: Which lander bounced twice and came to rest in shadow on a comet in 2014?
questions.f: Its harpoons failed to fire, so it drifted for two hours before settling on comet 67P.

questions.q: Which spacecraft first returned samples from an asteroid to Earth?
