questions.f: Despite engine failures and a lost lander, it limped home from Itokawa in 2010 with dust grains.

questions.q: Which rover broke the off-world driving distance record held for decades by Lunokhod 2?
questions.f: Opportunity passed a marathon's distance on Mars, having been designed to last 90 days.

questions.q: A one-year mission that stretched into fifteen, a marathon distance driven at walking pace, and a final message about batteries and darkness belong to which explorer?
questions.f: A planet-wide dust storm ended it in 2018 after 45 kilometres of driving.

questions.q: Two toy black cats as mascots, a landing in an Irish bog, and a Daily Mail prize of 10,000 pounds belong to which flight?
questions.f: They flew a converted bomber from Newfoundland to Clifden in under 16 hours.

questions.q: Which aircraft made the first aerial crossing of the Atlantic, with stops, in 1919?
questions.f: It took 19 days with island hops, weeks before Alcock and Brown's non-stop dash.

questions.q: Jettisoned landing gear, a belly landing on a beach, and a 1931 Pacific first identify whose flight?
questions.f: They dropped the wheels to cut drag, then slid Miss Veedol onto sand in Washington state.

questions.q: Which pilot made the first solo flight around the world, in 1933?
questions.f: He flew the Winnie Mae in under eight days, aided by a new autopilot and radio compass.

questions.q: Which woman first flew solo around the world, in 1964?
questions.f: The Ohio housewife flew a single-engined Cessna called the Spirit of Columbus for 29 days.

questions.q: Which woman was the first to fly across the English Channel, in 1912?
questions.f: Her achievement was almost lost in the news because the Titanic had sunk days earlier.

questions.q: Which aircraft made the first non-stop unrefuelled flight around the world, in 1986?
questions.f: Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager flew nine days in a cockpit the size of a bathtub.

questions.q: Concorde's record New York to London crossing took under three hours.
questions.f: In 1996 it flew the route in 2 hours 52 minutes, faster than the Earth turns beneath it at that latitude.

questions.q: After whom is the Mach number, used for supersonic speeds, named?
questions.f: The Austrian physicist photographed shock waves decades before any aircraft made one.

questions.q: What is the Karman line, the usual boundary of space?
questions.f: Above it, a wing would need orbital speed to generate lift, so flying becomes orbiting.

questions.q: Which Brazilian aviation pioneer's need to time flights hands-free popularised the wristwatch?
questions.f: Cartier made him a leather-strapped watch, and pilots everywhere copied the idea.

questions.q: Which glider pioneer made about 2,000 flights in the 1890s and inspired the Wright brothers?
questions.f: The Wrights studied his data closely, then rebuilt it after finding errors in his tables.

questions.q: How many witnesses saw the Wright brothers' first powered flight?
questions.f: Three lifesavers, a businessman and a teenage boy, plus a camera Orville had preset.

questions.q: What did the Wright brothers' telegram home on 17 December 1903 announce?
questions.f: The telegraph operator misspelled Orville's name, and a newspaper garbled the story entirely.

questions.q: A rebuilt oyster sloop, carpet tacks on a night deck, and a captain who never learned to swim identify whom?
questions.f: His book Sailing Alone Around the World has never been out of print.

questions.q: A slingshot message onto a passing ship's deck, an abandoned certain victory, and a course set for Tahiti describe which sailor?
questions.f: He simply kept sailing past the finish, writing that he wanted to save his soul.

questions.q: A Basque commander, a coat of arms of cloves and nutmeg, and a motto meaning 'you first encircled me' identify whom?
questions.f: He brought the Victoria home in 1522, completing the first circumnavigation.

questions.q: Which navigator worked out the return route across the Pacific that made Spanish trade possible?
questions.f: His northern loop, found in 1565, powered the Manila galleon route for 250 years.

questions.q: Which expedition vanished in 1788, its wrecks found much later at Vanikoro?
questions.f: Louis XVI is said to have asked on his last morning whether any news had come of him.

questions.q: Sauerkraut served daily, the second voyage's chronometer trial, and a crossing of the Antarctic Circle belong to which captain?
questions.f: His insistence on fresh and pickled food kept scurvy from crippling his crews.

questions.q: James Cook carried a copy of Harrison's chronometer on his second voyage.
questions.f: Larcum Kendall's K1 copy proved so accurate that Cook called it his never-failing guide.

questions.q: A birth name of Ma He, a giraffe presented at court as a mythical qilin, and a stone stele at Changle identify whom?
questions.f: His seven fleets sailed from 1405 to 1433, reaching Africa decades before Portuguese ships.

questions.q: A shipwreck in the Maldives, an appointment as an envoy for Muhammad bin Tughluq, and a book dictated to Ibn Juzayy identify whom?
questions.f: His Rihla records nearly 30 years of travel across Africa, Asia and Europe.

questions.q: Which 10th-century traveller's account of a Viking funeral on the Volga is a key historical source?
questions.f: An Abbasid envoy, he described the Rus in vivid detail few other writers matched.

questions.q: Which Chinese pilgrim's 5th-century journey to India produced one of the earliest travel books?
questions.f: He walked out across the Taklamakan and sailed home through a typhoon, saving the Sanskrit manuscripts he later helped translate.

questions.q: Which sealed cave near Dunhuang yielded the world's oldest dated printed book?
questions.f: A Diamond Sutra printed in 868 lay bricked up there for around nine centuries.

questions.q: Which Swedish explorer mapped Central Asia and searched for the wandering lake Lop Nur?
questions.f: He showed the lake shifts position over centuries as its feeding rivers change course.

questions.q: Which French traveller reached Lhasa in 1924 disguised as a beggar pilgrim?
questions.f: She was in her mid-fifties, spoke Tibetan, and walked in over the winter passes.

questions.q: Which Austrian climber's escape from an Indian internment camp led to years in Tibet?
questions.f: He had been on the first ascent of the Eiger's north face before the war stranded him in Asia.

questions.q: Which mountain was the first 8,000-metre peak ever climbed, in 1950?
questions.f: Maurice Herzog's French team found it almost by accident after failing to locate another peak.

questions.q: Which climber made a 41-hour solo push to the summit of Nanga Parbat in 1953?
questions.f: He carried on alone after his companions turned back, and survived a standing bivouac.

questions.q: Which climbing club's motto 'Let's go on an overseas expedition by ourselves' preceded a 1975 first?
c: The Ladies Climbing Club of Japan
questions.f: Junko Tabei's club took her to Everest, where she was dug out of an avalanche and carried on.

questions.q: Edmund Hillary later reached both the South Pole and the North Pole as well as Everest's summit.
questions.f: He drove tractors to the South Pole in 1958 and flew to the North Pole in 1985 with Neil Armstrong.

questions.q: Who led the first overland crossing of Antarctica, completed in 1958?
questions.f: Hillary laid depots from the other side, and the two parties met near the Pole.

questions.q: Which explorer led the Transglobe Expedition, circling Earth through both poles?
questions.f: The 1979-82 journey followed the prime meridian as closely as ice and land allowed.

questions.q: A name borrowed from Jules Verne, a voyage under the polar ice cap, and a 1958 message reading 'Nautilus ninety north' identify which vessel?
questions.f: She crossed from the Pacific to the Atlantic entirely submerged, passing under the Pole.

questions.q: A lone woman on Wrangel Island, two years of Arctic survival, and skills learned from her Inupiat upbringing describe whom?
questions.f: She was the only survivor of a failed 1921 colonising expedition and was rescued in 1923.

questions.q: Which airship crash near the North Pole in 1928 led to a famous rescue involving a red tent?
questions.f: Roald Amundsen died flying to search for the survivors, his aircraft never found.

questions.q: Three national flags dropped from a gondola, an Italian designer flying with a Norwegian leader, and a 1926 Arctic crossing identify which airship?
questions.f: The two men later quarrelled bitterly over who deserved the credit.

questions.q: Which German airship completed a circumnavigation of the globe in 1929?
questions.f: It crossed Siberia in one hop and took 21 days for the entire journey.

questions.q: A quartz window, a cable to a barge above, and 923 metres in 1934 describe which craft?
questions.f: William Beebe and Otis Barton described glowing creatures nobody had ever seen alive.

questions.q: Which submersible's name honours a science-fiction spacecraft in an Iain Banks novel?
questions.f: Victor Vescovo used it to reach the deepest point of all five oceans in 2018 and 2019.

questions.q: Which deep-sea vehicle imploded in 2014 while exploring the Kermadec Trench?
questions.f: It had been designed to switch between free-swimming and tethered modes at ten kilometres deep.

questions.q: Antarctic ice hides a subglacial lake, sealed for millions of years, called Lake Vostok.
questions.f: It sits under nearly four kilometres of ice and is one of the largest lakes on Earth by volume.

questions.q: Alpine-sized peaks no human eye has seen, radar echoes from four kilometres down, and a Soviet geophysicist's name identify which range?
questions.f: The ice sheet may have started growing on these very summits millions of years ago.

questions.q: A bed lying 3,500 metres below sea level, radar flown across East Antarctica, and the lowest point of land on the planet identify which glacier?
questions.f: Its rock floor is far deeper than the Dead Sea shore, but buried under kilometres of ice.

questions.q: A submarine ledge between Greenland and Iceland, dense cold water sliding over it, and the biggest waterfall on Earth identify which strait?
questions.f: The cataract drops around 3,500 metres, dwarfing every waterfall in the open air.

questions.q: A Kentucky ridge of limestone, saltpetre mined for gunpowder in 1812, and over 680 kilometres of mapped passage identify which cave?
questions.f: Surveyors add new kilometres almost every year, so its record keeps stretching.

questions.q: Which cave holds the record for the greatest known depth below its entrance?
questions.f: Both record-holders lie in the same Abkhazian mountains, over two kilometres deep.

questions.q: A pair of dividers walking across a chart, a Latin phrase meaning 'to step together', and a needle that never rests point to which instrument?
questions.f: Com plus passus gave both the drawing compass and the magnetic one their shared name.

questions.q: A Greek word for slanting, a course that crosses every meridian at one angle, and a track that spirals forever toward the pole describe what?
questions.f: Mercator's grid turns these spirals into straight lines, which is why sailors adopted it.

questions.q: A sundial's pointer whose Greek name means 'one who knows', a projection drawn as if from Earth's core, and great circles that come out straight identify what?
questions.f: Radio operators and pilots use it because the shortest path really is a straight line on it.

questions.q: A German word meaning 'of last year', snow that has survived one summer, and the halfway stage between a flake and glacier ice all name what?
questions.f: Squeeze firn long enough and the air is driven out, turning it to blue glacier ice.

questions.q: A crumbly Swiss cheese, a leaning white tower above a climber's helmet, and the worst hazard of the Khumbu Icefall share which name?
questions.f: Seracs can topple without warning, which is why teams cross the icefall before dawn.

questions.q: A Greenlandic loanword, a summit with an ice sheet lapping its flanks, and an island surrounded by something other than water describe what?
questions.f: Nunataks poking through Antarctic ice are often the only bare rock for hundreds of kilometres.

questions.q: A Kildin Sami word for treeless heights, ground frozen a kilometre deep, and summer reindeer pasture converge on which landscape?
questions.f: Russian carried the Sami word into every European language.

questions.q: A Dutch compound meaning 'ice mountain', a bulk nine-tenths hidden, and an ocean patrol founded in 1914 all concern what?
questions.f: The International Ice Patrol still tracks bergs drifting into the North Atlantic shipping lanes.

questions.q: A Nenets word borrowed through Russian, a hood that saved faces from frostbite, and the standard coat of Arctic expeditions point to which garment?
questions.f: Anorak took a different route into English, straight from Greenlandic annoraaq.

questions.q: An Arabic word for travel, a Swahili word for a journey, and an English word now meaning a wildlife trip trace which single origin?
questions.f: The word crossed the Indian Ocean with traders long before it reached Europe.

questions.q: A Persian word for a company of travellers, a walled courtyard with water and news, and a night's safety on the Silk Road name what?
questions.f: Serai means palace or lodging, so the word is literally the travellers' company's palace.

questions.q: A Sanskrit word for dry waste ground, a meaning that flipped completely in English, and a word now used for dense rainforest identify what?
questions.f: Jangala meant arid and uncultivated; English speakers in India reversed the sense entirely.

questions.q: A Taino word from the Caribbean, an early Spanish sailor's notebook, and a storm season named for a native spirit point to which word?
questions.f: Canoe, hammock and savanna reached English by exactly the same route.

questions.q: A word recorded on a Queensland riverbank in 1770, a language called Guugu Yimithirr, and a ship under repair converge on which animal name?
questions.f: Cook's Endeavour was beached for repairs when his crew wrote gangurru in their notebooks.

questions.q: A Latin phrase meaning 'to free the feet', a word whose opposite means to shackle them, and a march with porters and mules point to which word?
questions.f: Ex plus pes explains why expedite means to hurry and impede means to slow down.

questions.q: A Latin word for midday, the letters that follow clock times, and a line where noon arrives everywhere at once identify what?
questions.f: Ante meridiem and post meridiem are the a.m. and p.m. of every timetable.

questions.q: A sixth of a circle in polished brass, a pair of mirrors that double an angle, and 120 degrees of readable arc describe which instrument?
questions.f: Because the mirrors double the angle, a 60-degree arc can measure right up to 120 degrees.

questions.q: A Latin word for a wheel rut, the bony socket around an eye, and Kepler's term for a moon's path all share which word?
questions.f: Orbita described the track a cart leaves, an image of a path already worn.

questions.q: A Latin word for a bodyguard, Kepler's name for the moons of Jupiter, and a beeping metal ball of 1957 identify which term?
questions.f: Satelles meant an attendant who follows a great person everywhere.

questions.q: A Greek phrase meaning 'star taker', centuries of Islamic refinement, and a brass disc that models the whole sky point to what?
questions.f: A skilled user could tell the time, find north and even work out prayer directions with one.

questions.q: A Latin word meaning 'little dwelling', a lamp for night reading, and a compass shielded from iron describe which ship's fitting?
questions.f: Correcting magnets tucked inside the binnacle cancel the pull of an iron hull.

questions.q: An Italian word for harbours, radiating rose lines across the sea, and coasts drawn superbly while inland stays blank identify which chart type?
questions.f: Their accuracy is still unexplained, since no one knows what surveys they were built from.

questions.q: A Latin word for a little grating, a mesh of parallels and meridians, and the one thing every projection must bend describe what?
questions.f: Compare grate and grill: all three picture the same crossing bars.

questions.q: An Italian word for a paper curl, a framed panel of curling edges, and the space where a mapmaker signs their name point to what?
questions.f: The fancier the cartouche, the richer the patron who paid for the map.

questions.q: A Greek word for equal, a line joining points of the same depth, and a chart that reveals a drowned river canyon identify what?
questions.f: Iso lines let flat paper carry information about a third dimension.

questions.q: Halley's 1701 Atlantic chart, curved lines joining equal compass error, and a correction every navigator must apply describe what?
questions.f: His voyage in the Paramore may have been the first ever made purely for science.

questions.q: Edmond Halley commanded a ship of his own to map magnetic variation at sea.
questions.f: He sailed the Paramore in 1698, mixing astronomy with the messy business of command.

questions.q: A Latin superlative of 'above', the total written at the foot of a column, and the last step of a climb all share which root?
questions.f: Summit, sum, summary and consummate all grow from the same small word.

questions.q: A Greek phrase meaning 'without a bottom', a zone from four to six kilometres down, and the plains covering most of the sea floor name what?
questions.f: Abyssal plains are the flattest large surfaces anywhere on Earth.

questions.q: The Greek underworld, everything below six kilometres of water, and snailfish stuffed with a protective molecule describe which zone?
questions.f: Named for Hades, it exists only inside the ocean's deep trenches.

questions.q: Greek words for deep and boat, a hull floated on petrol, and iron shot released to rise identify which vehicle?
questions.f: Auguste Piccard reasoned that if a balloon works in air, a float would work in water.

questions.q: A thousand paces, a Roman soldier's double step, and a unit that outlived the empire that invented it identify what?
questions.f: Mille passus is why the abbreviation for a thousand still hides inside the word.

questions.q: Outstretched arms, six feet of knotted line, and a depth called out by a leadsman in the bows describe which unit?
questions.f: From Old English faethm, an embrace, since the rope was measured arm to arm.

questions.q: A chip of wood tossed overboard, a half-minute sand glass, and knots counted as the line runs out identify which measurement?
questions.f: That is why speed at sea is still given in knots rather than miles per hour.

questions.q: A steering board mounted on the right, a dock reached with the other side, and two words still shouted on modern bridges identify which pair?
questions.f: Port replaced the older larboard because it sounded too much like starboard in a gale.

questions.q: A Greek phrase for 'opposite feet', medieval arguments about people standing sole to sole with us, and a word for the far side of the globe identify what?
questions.f: Some scholars insisted nobody could live there, since they thought no one could cross the tropics.

questions.q: A Greek word for turning, the latitude where the Sun reverses direction, and a crab and a goat drawn on globes identify what?
questions.f: The Sun stood in Cancer and Capricorn at the solstices when the names were fixed.

questions.q: Boreas the north wind, a Latin word for dawn, and shimmering green curtains over Tromso identify what?
questions.f: Galileo is often credited with coining the aurora part of the name.

questions.q: A Latin phrase meaning 'almost an island', a cousin of the word insulate, and Italy's familiar shape identify what?
questions.f: Paene plus insula; the same insula gives insulate, insular and even isle.

questions.q: A Greek phrase meaning 'chief sea', the island-strewn Aegean, and a word that shifted from water to land identify what?
questions.f: Because the Aegean was full of islands, the name for the sea became the word for the islands.

questions.q: An ancient root meaning 'to cross over', a deep Norwegian inlet, and a shallow river crossing in England share which family?
questions.f: Both words name places where people got across, one by boat and one on foot.

questions.q: A Welsh word for a bowl-shaped hollow, a naming by George Mallory, and the great basin above the Khumbu Icefall identify what?
questions.f: Mallory knew Snowdonia's cwms well, and the spelling survives on Himalayan maps.

questions.q: A Latin word for a neck, the dip between two summits, and the last camp before Everest's final push identify what?
questions.f: At 7,900 metres it is one of the highest places people regularly sleep.

questions.q: The syllables shar and pa, a migration out of eastern Tibet, and the word 'east people' identify which name?
questions.f: The name records where the community came from long before mountaineering existed.

questions.q: A Koyukon phrase for 'the tall one', an official name change in 2015, and North America's highest summit identify what?
questions.f: Its base-to-summit rise beats Everest's, since it starts from low ground rather than a plateau.

questions.q: A Greek word for darkness, one of James Clark Ross's two ships, and a lava lake in a land of ice identify what?
questions.f: Its sister ship gave its name to neighbouring Mount Terror.

questions.q: Mount Erebus contains one of the world's few long-lived lakes of molten lava.
questions.f: It has bubbled away inside an Antarctic crater since at least the 1970s.

questions.q: A German compound meaning 'mountain crack', the gap where moving ice pulls away from rock, and a hazard at the head of a glacier identify what?
questions.f: Climbers often must cross it on a fragile snow bridge to reach the wall above.

questions.q: A French dialect verb meaning 'to go down', a wall of snow released by a footstep, and a hazard that ends most expeditions identify what?
questions.f: Avaler still means to swallow in modern French, another kind of going down.

questions.q: A Latin word for ice, a slow river that carves valleys, and a French dessert served cold share which root?
questions.f: Glacier, glacial and glace all trace back to the same chilly Latin noun.

questions.q: A Latin word for a journey, a word meaning to repeat, and a traveller's list of stops all share which root?
questions.f: Itinerary and reiterate both hold the idea of going over ground again.

questions.q: A Latin word for a foreigner abroad, a falcon taken while migrating, and a word for long wandering travel identify which family?
questions.f: Pilgrim, peregrine and peregrination all come from the same Latin stranger.

questions.q: A word for provisions packed for the road, a Latin noun for a road, and a modern word for a long sea trip identify what?
questions.f: Via gives us viaduct and deviate as well as the food money for the road.

questions.q: A Latin word for a day, a French word for a day's travel, and a modern word for any long trip identify what?
questions.f: Journal, journalism and diurnal all grew from the same daily root.

questions.q: An Old French word for a foot soldier sent ahead, a cousin of the words pawn and pedestrian, and a name for the first to arrive identify what?
questions.f: The military sense of clearing the way survives in engineer units called pioneers.

questions.q: A Latin verb meaning 'to spy out', a small party sent ahead of the main group, and a cousin of the word recognise identify which word?
questions.f: Polar leaders sent reconnaissance parties to lay depots before the main march.

questions.q: A shooting party argument, twin brothers with encyclopaedic memories, and a brewery director's frustration produced which book?
questions.f: Norris and Ross McWhirter compiled the first edition for Sir Hugh Beaver in 1955.

questions.q: Which bird was at the centre of the argument that inspired Guinness World Records?
questions.f: Nobody at the shoot could settle whether the plover or the grouse flew faster.

questions.q: What is the record height of Robert Wadlow, the tallest man ever measured?
questions.f: He was still growing when he died in 1940, aged just 22.

questions.q: A Baffin Island wall that leans out at fifteen degrees, a 1,250-metre drop, and a Norse thunder god's name identify which peak?
questions.f: It holds the record for the greatest purely vertical rock face on Earth.

questions.q: A river that loops between two 7,000-metre peaks, a gorge over five kilometres deep, and a Tibetan name meaning 'purifier' identify which canyon?
questions.f: The Yarlung Tsangpo becomes the Brahmaputra once it escapes onto the plains.

questions.q: An arc of 265 survey stations, ten modern countries, and a nineteenth-century measurement of the planet's curve identify what?
questions.f: It runs from the Arctic Ocean to the Black Sea and is now a World Heritage site.

questions.q: A theodolite needing twelve men to lift, towers built above the treetops, and fifty years of triangles identify which project?
c: The Great Trigonometrical Survey of India
questions.f: Its final triangles delivered the height of Peak XV, later named Mount Everest.

questions.q: A geodesic net of 96 triangles, an award-winning Japanese design, and a rectangle where areas stay nearly honest identify which projection?
questions.f: Hajime Narukawa's map can be tiled edge to edge without an obvious top or bottom.

questions.q: An architect who loved triangles, a map that folds into a solid, and an argument that the world is one island in one ocean identify which projection?
questions.f: Buckminster Fuller unfolded the globe onto an icosahedron to avoid choosing a centre.

questions.q: Eleven volumes, an Amsterdam workshop, and the most expensive printed book of the seventeenth century identify which atlas?
questions.f: Buying one cost roughly as much as a modest Amsterdam house.

questions.q: A cracked outer window at nine kilometres down, a hull floated on petrol, and twenty minutes on the deepest floor describe which craft's 1960 dive?
questions.f: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh saw the silt cloud they raised hide everything outside.

questions.q: A green vertical torpedo, a 3D camera rig, and a solo pilot folded into a metal sphere describe which 2012 dive?
questions.f: James Cameron spent about three hours alone on the floor of the Challenger Deep.

questions.q: Which peak on Guam is sometimes called the world's tallest mountain measured from the ocean's deepest floor?
questions.f: It rises modestly above sea level but sits close to the Mariana Trench's abyss.

questions.q: Which fish holds the record for the deepest one ever filmed alive?
questions.f: A hadal snailfish was recorded over 8,300 metres down in a Japanese trench in 2022.

questions.q: Which chemical adaptation lets hadal fish survive crushing pressure?
c: High levels of the molecule TMAO
questions.f: Because TMAO can only be packed so densely, there may be an absolute depth limit for fish.

questions.q: An inscription naming Richard of Haldingham, a cathedral archive, and a calfskin map with Jerusalem at its centre point to which object?
questions.f: Drawn about 1300, it crowds some 500 drawings, from towns and rivers to Bible scenes and marvels, onto a single hide.

questions.q: Which map of Britain, from about 1360, is the oldest to show roads and recognisable coastlines?
questions.f: It is drawn with east at the top, and its coast of Scotland is oddly stretched.

questions.q: Which Roman road map survives only as a medieval copy on a long strip of parchment?
questions.f: It squashes the empire into a ribbon nearly seven metres long but only 34 centimetres tall.

questions.q: A globe called an 'earth apple', a Nuremberg cloth merchant, and a world without America identify which artefact?
questions.f: Made in 1492, it is the oldest surviving terrestrial globe on Earth.

questions.q: Which globe of about 1510 bears the Latin words often translated 'here are dragons'?
questions.f: The phrase appears only on a couple of surviving objects, despite its legendary reputation.

questions.q: Which feature did Marie Tharp's sea-floor profiles reveal running down the middle of the Atlantic?
c: A deep rift valley along the ridge crest
questions.f: The rift was the smoking gun for sea-floor spreading, and she spotted it in the numbers.

questions.q: A drifting station on ice, a Soviet-era research programme, and rescue flights each spring describe which kind of Arctic base?
c: A North Pole drifting ice station
questions.f: The first, in 1937, drifted 2,500 kilometres before its floe finally broke apart.

questions.q: Which Norwegian's balloon flight toward the North Pole in 1897 ended on the ice at Kvitoya?
questions.f: He was Swedish; his party's diaries and undeveloped film were found 33 years later.

questions.q: Which explorer's crew survived by wintering in a stone hut and eating walrus, then met a rescuer by chance?
questions.f: Nansen's chance meeting with Frederick Jackson in 1896 has been called history's luckiest handshake.

questions.q: Which polar explorer is remembered for the phrase 'For God's sake look after our people'?
questions.f: Those were among the last lines of his diary, found with his tent eight months later.

questions.q: Antarctica was the last continent on Earth to be sighted by human beings.
questions.f: The first confirmed sightings came only in 1820, thousands of years after every other continent was settled.

questions.q: Leaves in stone hauled to the very last camp, proof of forests at the bottom of the world, and 14 kilograms never abandoned identify which fossil?
questions.f: The same fossil in Africa, India and Australia helped show the southern continents were joined.

questions.q: Which sledging journey did Douglas Mawson survive alone in 1913 after losing both companions?
questions.f: He crawled the last stretch to Cape Denison only to watch his relief ship sail away.

questions.q: Which Antarctic base recorded winds fierce enough to earn it the name 'home of the blizzard'?
questions.f: Mawson's men measured average yearly winds near 80 kilometres an hour there.

questions.q: Which record does the Antarctic katabatic wind belong to?
c: Windiest place on Earth at sea level
questions.f: Katabatic means going down: dense cold air pours off the ice plateau under gravity alone.

questions.q: Which explorer's ship Gjoa was small enough to slip through shallow Arctic channels?
questions.f: Its shallow draught was the very reason he finally solved the Northwest Passage in 1906.

questions.q: Which Inuit skills did Amundsen deliberately study before his polar attempts?
questions.f: He wintered near Netsilik communities and learned to dress in loose caribou skins.

questions.q: Which Franklin expedition ship was found in 2014 in Canadian Arctic waters?
questions.f: Inuit oral testimony passed down for generations helped searchers narrow the area.

questions.q: Which Arctic explorer's abandoned ship drifted free and was found years later off Greenland?
questions.f: HMS Resolute's timbers later became the desk used in the American president's office.

questions.q: A wrecked ship, a cook who became a hero, and a rescue from Wrangel Island in 1914 describe which vessel's crew?
questions.f: Captain Robert Bartlett walked over 1,100 kilometres across ice and Siberia to fetch help.

questions.q: A star that stands over Hawaii, a canoe rebuilt from tradition, and a Satawalese teacher converge on which 1976 voyage?
questions.f: Mau Piailug navigated the 4,000-kilometre crossing without a single instrument.

questions.q: Which navigator became the first Hawaiian in centuries to guide a canoe by traditional wayfinding?
questions.f: He learned from Mau Piailug and later sailed Hokulea right around the world.

questions.q: Which Micronesian island's navigators preserved wayfinding knowledge into the 20th century?
questions.f: Its master navigators held the rank of palu, with knowledge passed on in chanted lessons.

questions.q: Which term describes the Marshall Islands navigational devices made of sticks and shells?
questions.f: They were memory aids studied ashore, never carried on the canoe itself.

questions.q: Which distinctive pottery style traces the first Pacific voyaging expansion?
questions.f: Its stamped patterns appear from the Bismarck Archipelago to Tonga within a few centuries.

questions.q: Polynesian voyagers carried plants and animals with them to settle new islands.
questions.f: Taro, breadfruit, chickens, pigs and dogs travelled as a portable farm on the canoes.

questions.q: Which is the standard name for the double-hulled voyaging canoe in Hawaiian?
questions.f: Different Polynesian languages keep recognisably related names for the same design.

questions.q: Which balsa raft crossed from Peru to Polynesia in 1947, and after whom was it named?
c: Kon-Tiki, after an Inca sun deity name
questions.f: Heyerdahl's later Ra voyages tested Atlantic crossings in reed boats.

questions.q: Which Portuguese explorer first rounded Africa's southern tip, in 1488?
questions.f: He was blown around it by storms and only saw the cape on his way back north.

questions.q: Which pilot is said to have guided Vasco da Gama across the Indian Ocean to Calicut?
c: A local pilot hired at Malindi
questions.f: Monsoon knowledge built up over centuries let the fleet cross in just 23 days.

questions.q: Which Ottoman admiral wrote the Kitab-i Bahriye, a great book of Mediterranean sailing directions?
questions.f: He also drew the surviving 1513 world map fragment named after him.

questions.q: Which explorer of the Amazon in 1541 gave the river its name after a legendary encounter?
questions.f: He made the first descent of the whole river, drifting 4,000 kilometres to the Atlantic.

questions.q: A veteran who had lost an arm in war, four wooden boats, and uncharted rapids run in 1869 identify which explorer?
questions.f: He later served as director of the US Geological Survey and argued the arid West needed careful planning.

questions.q: Which explorer of Australia's interior gave his name to a desert after nearly dying in it?
questions.f: Giles named the Gibson Desert for a companion lost there in 1874.

questions.q: A dig tree with a message carved on it, a return to camp hours too late, and a crossing of Australia describe which expedition?
questions.f: They reached the northern tidal waters in 1861, then missed their relief party by nine hours.

questions.q: The Dig Tree in Queensland still stands as a monument to the Burke and Wills expedition.
questions.f: Carved instructions told the returning party where buried supplies had been left.

questions.q: Which explorer's search for a city he called only 'Z' ended in the Mato Grosso in 1925?
questions.f: Later archaeology found large ancient settlements in the region he was seeking.

questions.q: Four years on the Rio Negro, a ship fire that swallowed a life's collection, and a letter from Ternate that forced Darwin to publish identify whom?
questions.f: He went straight back out east and there worked out natural selection independently.

questions.q: Which line, named after a naturalist, divides Asian from Australian animal life?
questions.f: On one side of a narrow strait there are tigers, on the other, marsupials.

questions.q: A diagram of plant belts stacked like latitudes, an Ecuadorian volcano, and an altitude record unbroken for thirty years identify which mountain?
questions.f: Its summit is also the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre.

questions.q: Which insight about mountain plants did Humboldt's Andean climbs produce?
c: Vegetation zones stack by altitude like latitudes
questions.f: His diagram of Chimborazo's plant belts founded the science of biogeography.

questions.q: Which ocean current is named after Humboldt?
c: The cold current along Peru and Chile
questions.f: He measured its temperature and noted the extraordinary fish life it supports.

questions.q: A ship named for a small hunting dog, a captain who invented weather forecasts, and a passenger who was nearly rejected for the shape of his nose describe which voyage?
c: The second voyage of the Beagle
questions.f: FitzRoy doubted Darwin's nose showed enough determination, then took him anyway.

questions.q: Which record does the Beagle's second voyage hold in navigation history?
c: Among the first to fix longitudes worldwide with many chronometers
questions.f: She carried 22 chronometers, building a chain of accurate longitudes right around the globe.

questions.q: Which sea creature's name honours the naturalist who sailed with Vitus Bering?
questions.f: Georg Steller described the sea cow, jay and eider now bearing his name in one brief stay.

questions.q: Which explorer gave his name to a passage, a strait and a group of clouds in the southern sky?
questions.f: The Magellanic Clouds are two dwarf galaxies visible only from southern latitudes.

questions.q: The Drake Passage is named after Francis Drake, though he probably never sailed through it.
questions.f: His ship was blown south of Cape Horn, proving open water lay there, but he sailed on north.

questions.q: Which Dutch navigator's name survives in a sea, an island and a glowing plankton phenomenon?
questions.f: The Tasman Sea, Tasmania and the Tasman Glacier all carry his name.

questions.q: Which Dutch explorer's winter camp on Novaya Zemlya was found preserved three centuries later?
questions.f: Visitors in 1871 found clothes, clocks and books just as the crew had left them in 1597.

questions.q: Which explorer's name is on a bay, a river and a strait in North America?
questions.f: He sailed for both England and the Netherlands, searching for a passage to Asia.

questions.q: A Dutch fleet in 1722, a Christian feast day used as a name, and an island its own people call Rapa Nui identify which explorer?
questions.f: He was searching for a great southern continent and found stone giants instead.

questions.q: Which record belongs to the Vostok Station in Antarctica besides extreme cold?
c: It sits above a huge subglacial lake
It is the highest base on Earth
questions.f: Its ice cores also gave scientists a climate record stretching back over 400,000 years.

questions.q: What do the deepest Antarctic ice cores let scientists read?
questions.f: Each bubble is a sample of the atmosphere from the year the snow fell.

questions.q: Which record does the Weddell seal hold among mammals?
c: It lives farther south than any other mammal
questions.f: Weddell seals keep breathing holes open in the fast ice by rasping them with their teeth.

questions.q: Which record does the wandering albatross hold among all birds?
questions.f: Spans of about 3.5 metres let it glide for hours, barely flapping, on wind shear over waves.

questions.q: Which bird holds the record for the longest non-stop flight ever tracked?
questions.f: One flew from Alaska to New Zealand, over 13,000 kilometres, without landing once.

questions.q: A bird that cannot perch, ten months of flight without landing, and sleep taken on the wing identify which record-holder?
questions.f: Its scientific name Apus means 'without feet', a nod to how rarely it touches down.

questions.q: Emperor penguins are the only birds that breed through the Antarctic winter.
questions.f: Males balance a single egg on their feet for around two months in the darkness.

questions.q: A shout of 'Poyekhali!', a pilot only 1.57 metres tall, and an ejection seat used over farmland describe which flight?
questions.f: Gagarin's small stature helped him fit the cramped capsule that made him the first human in orbit.

questions.q: Which group of women trained for American spaceflight in the early 1960s but never flew?
questions.f: They passed the same tests as the male astronauts before the programme was cancelled.

questions.q: There was an English physician. Clinical syndrome sharing features of Parkinson's disease. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: James Parkinson called it the shaking palsy in 1817 and noted he had studied some of his cases only by watching them in the street. His name was attached decades later by a French neurologist who thought he deserved it.

questions.q: There was a German neurologist. First described progressive dementia in 1906. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Alois Alzheimer's first case was a woman named Auguste Deter, who told him: I have lost myself. He kept her file, and when he examined her brain after death he found the plaques and tangles that still define the disease.

questions.q: There was an English physician. Identified a unique lymphatic cancer. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Thomas Hodgkin described seven cases in 1832 and nobody noticed for thirty years. Another doctor read the paper later, confirmed it, and insisted the disease carry Hodgkin's name — a rare act of credit in medical history.

questions.q: There was an English physician. Lymphomas other than Hodgkin's disease. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An entire family of cancers defined by what they are not. Once Hodgkin's type could be identified under a microscope, every other lymphoma had to be grouped somewhere — and got a name built out of a negative.

questions.q: There was an American physician. Chronic inflammatory bowel disease described in 1932. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Burrill Crohn published with two colleagues in 1932, and the paper listed authors alphabetically. Crohn came first. His two co-authors, Ginzburg and Oppenheimer, did the same work and are remembered by almost nobody.

questions.q: There was an American neurosurgeon. Described symptoms of excess cortisol. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Harvey Cushing essentially invented brain surgery as a survivable procedure, cutting mortality from around 90 per cent to under 10. The hormone disorder named after him is a footnote in a career mostly spent elsewhere.

questions.q: "Down Syndrome" is named after a place.
questions.f: John Langdon Down wrote the first careful clinical description in 1866. His original name for it was withdrawn in the 1960s as both inaccurate and offensive, and the condition was renamed for the doctor instead.

questions.q: There was an American physician. Described inherited neurodegenerative disease. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: George Huntington described the disease at twenty-two, in the only medical paper he ever published. He had seen it in families on Long Island, where his father and grandfather had also practised — three generations of doctors watching the same households.

questions.q: There was an Irish physician. Autoimmune hyperthyroidism. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Robert Graves was an Irish physician who also introduced the radical idea that feverish patients should be given food and water rather than starved. He suggested his epitaph should read: he fed fevers.

questions.q: There was a Japanese physician. Autoimmune thyroiditis first described in 1912. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Hakaru Hashimoto published his findings in German in 1912, as a young doctor, and then returned to rural Japan to run a country practice. His work was overlooked for twenty years before anyone realised what he had found.

questions.q: There was an English physician. Adrenal insufficiency described in 1855. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Thomas Addison worked out that the small glands sitting on top of the kidneys were essential to life — before anyone knew what hormones were. Colleagues found him difficult; patients found him extraordinary.

questions.q: There was an English physician. Early term for kidney disease. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Richard Bright discovered he could detect kidney disease by heating a patient's urine over a candle and watching for a cloud of albumin. It was one of the first bedside chemical tests in medicine.

questions.q: There was an English surgeon. Bone remodeling disorder. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: James Paget has two different diseases named after him, plus a professorship and a hospital ward. He also worked out, as a student, that the tiny specks in bad pork were a parasite — a finding his professors ignored.

questions.q: "Ménière Disease" is named after a person.
questions.f: Prosper Meniere showed that vertigo could come from the inner ear rather than the brain, which overturned the standard view. He published it in 1861 and died the following year, before the profession accepted it.

questions.q: There was a british neurologist. Copper metabolism disorder. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Kinnier Wilson described a disease in which copper builds up in the body until it damages the liver and brain. It is one of the few inherited neurological disorders that can be treated — if it is caught in time.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "facial paralysis" comes from a Scottish surgeon?
questions.f: Charles Bell mapped which nerves carry movement and which carry sensation, work so foundational that a whole law of neurology carries his name too. The sudden facial paralysis is what most people know him for.

questions.q: There was an English physician. Clinical sign named after him. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Thomas Hodgkin's name attaches to a lymphoma, a clinical sign, and a form of anaemia. He was also a Quaker campaigner who lost a hospital post partly for his outspoken views on the treatment of indigenous peoples.

questions.q: There was a French neurologist. Reflex indicating upper motor neuron lesion. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Stroke the sole of an adult's foot and the toes curl down. If they fan upward instead, something is wrong with the pathway from the brain. Babinski found a whole diagnosis hiding in one reflex.

questions.q: There was a German neurologist. Test for proprioception and balance. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Stand with your feet together and close your eyes. If you sway, you were relying on sight to stay upright rather than on your body's own position sense. Romberg turned that into a test in the 1840s.

questions.q: There was a Polish physician. Sign of meningeal irritation. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Jozef Brudzinski found that lifting the head of a patient with meningitis makes the knees pull up involuntarily — the body protecting inflamed membranes. He described several such signs; this is the one that kept his name.

questions.q: "Kernig Sign" is named after a place.
questions.f: Vladimir Kernig noticed that patients with meningitis could not have their leg straightened once the hip was bent. Paired with Brudzinski's sign, it gave doctors a bedside test decades before spinal taps were routine.

questions.q: There was an American surgeon. Pain on inspiration suggesting gallbladder inflammation. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Press under the ribs on the right and ask the patient to breathe in. If they stop short from the pain, the gallbladder is inflamed. John Murphy was a Chicago surgeon known for tests that needed no equipment at all.

questions.q: There was an American surgeon. Point of tenderness in appendicitis. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Charles McBurney worked out that appendicitis pain settles at one specific spot, about two-thirds of the way from the navel to the hip bone. Surgeons still press exactly there, and still call it McBurney's point.

questions.q: There was an American anesthesiologist. Rapid assessment of newborn health. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Virginia Apgar sketched five checks on a scrap of paper in a hospital cafeteria after a student asked how to judge a newborn quickly. It is now done on virtually every baby born in a hospital.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "first-aid procedure" comes from an American surgeon?
questions.f: Henry Heimlich published the technique in 1974 and it was saving lives within weeks. He was ninety-six when he reportedly used it in a real emergency for the first time, on a fellow resident of his retirement home.

questions.q: There was an American urologist. Inflatable urinary catheter. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Frederic Foley's design added a small balloon that inflates once the catheter is in place, so it stays put without strapping. He lost the patent fight to a rival, but kept the name.

questions.q: There was a Greek physician. Cervical cancer screening test. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: George Papanicolaou spent twenty years being ignored. His test could catch cervical cancer before symptoms appeared, and the profession did not want it. Once adopted, deaths from the disease fell by around seventy per cent.

questions.q: "Koch's Postulates" is named after a person.
questions.f: Robert Koch set out four conditions that must all hold before you can blame a specific microbe for a specific disease. It is a rule for not fooling yourself, and it ended centuries of guesswork about contagion.

questions.q: There was a Danish bacteriologist. Differential staining technique for bacteria. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Hans Christian Gram published his staining method in 1884 and wrote that it was imperfect and would surely be improved by others. It has not been. Bacteria are still sorted into Gram-positive and Gram-negative today.

questions.q: There was a German scientists. Acid-fast staining for tuberculosis bacteria. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Tuberculosis bacteria have a waxy coat that shrugs off ordinary dyes. Ziehl and Neelsen worked out how to force the stain in with heat and acid, making the bacteria visible as bright red rods under the microscope.

questions.q: There was a German chemist. Stain used for blood cells and parasites. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Gustav Giemsa refined a dye mixture that colours the nucleus and cytoplasm of blood cells differently. It is still the standard way of finding malaria parasites in a drop of blood.

questions.q: There was a Swedish scientists. Immunological assay developed in 1971. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Engvall and Perlmann built a test that uses an enzyme to make an invisible immune reaction visible as a colour change. It underpins pregnancy tests, HIV screening, and most rapid tests you have ever used.

questions.q: There was a british scientist. Device for studying cell migration. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Stephen Boyden put a porous membrane between two fluid compartments so he could watch cells crawl through it toward a chemical signal. It is a simple piece of equipment that turned cell migration into something measurable.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "laboratory dish" comes from a German bacteriologist?
questions.f: Before Petri, cultures were grown under bell jars that had to be lifted, letting in whatever was floating past. His two-part dish with an overlapping lid solved contamination with no moving parts at all.

questions.q: "Erlenmeyer Flask" is named after a place.
questions.f: Emil Erlenmeyer gave the flask sloping sides and a narrow neck, so it can be swirled hard without spilling and stoppered easily. It is the shape everyone draws when asked to draw a chemistry flask.

questions.q: There was a German chemist. Funnel for vacuum filtration. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Ernst Buchner's funnel has a flat perforated plate instead of a cone, so suction can pull liquid through a filter fast. It is the difference between filtering in minutes and filtering overnight.

questions.q: There was a Scottish chemist. Double-walled vacuum flask. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: James Dewar built a double-walled vessel with a vacuum between the layers to hold liquid gases. He never patented it. A German glassware firm did, sold it as the Thermos, and made the fortune.

questions.q: There was a French scientist. Glass pipette associated with microbiology. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A glass tube drawn to a fine point, plugged with cotton, sterilised by flame — Pasteur's answer to moving liquid without carrying microbes along with it. The plastic version in every lab still carries his name.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "radiation detector" comes from a German physicist?
questions.f: Geiger's early detectors had to be watched, hour after hour, counting faint flashes on a screen in a darkened room. He built the clicking tube partly so physicists could stop staring and start listening.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "wave frequency phenomenon" comes from an Austrian physicist?
questions.f: Christian Doppler predicted the effect in 1842 using starlight. Three years later a Dutch scientist tested it by hiring a train, filling an open carriage with trumpeters, and having musicians on the platform write down what they heard.

questions.q: There was an American physicist. Voltage produced across a conductor in a magnetic field. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Edwin Hall found that a magnetic field pushes a current sideways inside a conductor, producing a small voltage across it. He was a graduate student at the time, testing something Maxwell had said was impossible.

questions.q: "Coriolis Effect" is named after a person.
questions.f: On a spinning planet, anything moving in a straight line appears to curve. It steers hurricanes and long-range artillery. It does not steer water down a plughole — that scale is far too small, whatever you have been told.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. Spinning object experiences sideways force. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A spinning ball drags air around with it, and the uneven airflow pushes it sideways. Heinrich Magnus was investigating why cannonballs curved off target; footballers have been exploiting the same physics ever since.

questions.q: There was a Swiss mathematician. Pressure decreases as fluid speed increases. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Daniel Bernoulli found that fast-moving fluid exerts less pressure than slow-moving fluid. He came from a family of mathematicians so competitive that his own father, jealous of a prize, threw him out of the house.

questions.q: There was an Austrian physicist. Radar using the Doppler effect to measure velocity. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Bounce a radio wave off something moving and it comes back at a shifted frequency — so you can measure speed, not just position. It is why forecasters can see a storm rotating before a tornado forms.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "temperature scale" comes from a william Thomson?
questions.f: William Thomson worked out there is a coldest possible temperature, where molecular motion stops, and built a scale starting there. He was made Lord Kelvin after the river running past his Glasgow laboratory.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "temperature scale" comes from a Swedish astronomer?
questions.f: Anders Celsius put 0 at boiling and 100 at freezing — the exact reverse of today's scale. It was flipped after his death, and the version everyone now uses is upside down from the one he actually proposed.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "temperature scale" comes from a German physicist?
questions.f: Fahrenheit set his zero at the coldest temperature he could reliably reproduce: a mixture of ice, water and salt. That is why the scale's landmarks look so arbitrary — they were pinned to what he could make in a bucket.

questions.q: "Beaufort Scale" is named after a place.
questions.f: Beaufort's scale needs no instruments — each step is defined by what the sea and the sails are doing. Force 12 was originally described as that which no canvas could withstand.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "famous periodic comet" comes from an English astronomer?
questions.f: Halley noticed that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 followed the same path, decided they were one object, and predicted its return in 1758. He died in 1742. It arrived on Christmas night, sixteen years after his death.

questions.q: There was an American astronomer. Discovered that galaxies recede from each other, leading to the expanding universe model. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Hubble measured how fast galaxies are moving away and found the farther ones move faster — which means the universe is expanding. Astronomers still cannot agree on the exact number, and the disagreement has a name: the Hubble tension.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "orbiting space telescope" comes from an astronomer?
questions.f: Launched in 1990 with a mirror ground to the wrong shape by an amount thinner than a human hair. Astronauts flew up in 1993 and fitted it with corrective optics — effectively giving a telescope a pair of spectacles.

questions.q: There was a German astronomer. Three laws describing planetary motion around the Sun. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Kepler spent years trying to fit Mars's orbit to a circle and failing by an eight-minute discrepancy he refused to ignore. Those eight minutes broke two thousand years of circular astronomy and gave him the ellipse.

questions.q: There was a Polish astronomer. Shift from geocentric to heliocentric worldview. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Copernicus reportedly received the first printed copy of his book on the day he died. Moving the Sun to the centre was not just astronomy — it was the moment humanity stopped being the centre of anything.

questions.q: There was an Italian astronomer. Large gap separating Saturn's rings. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Giovanni Cassini spotted a dark gap in Saturn's rings in 1675 — the first hint that the rings were not one solid sheet. The spacecraft sent to Saturn three centuries later was named after him.

questions.q: "Oort Cloud" is named after a person.
questions.f: Jan Oort proposed an enormous shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system, a thousand times farther out than Pluto, purely from the way long-period comets arrive. Nobody has ever seen it.

questions.q: There was a Dutch-American astronomer. Region of icy bodies beyond Neptune. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, and the reason Pluto was reclassified — once astronomers found Pluto had thousands of neighbours out there, it looked less like a planet and more like the largest of a crowd.

questions.q: There was an astronomers. Classifies stars by luminosity and temperature. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Two astronomers independently plotted stars by brightness against temperature and found they do not scatter randomly — they fall into a narrow band. That band is the life story of a star, drawn on one chart.

questions.q: There was an Indian-American astrophysicist. Maximum mass of a stable white dwarf (~1.4 solar masses). Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Chandrasekhar calculated the limit at nineteen, on the boat to England. Eddington, the most famous astronomer alive, publicly ridiculed it. He was right and Eddington was wrong, and he received the Nobel Prize fifty-three years later.

questions.q: There was an astronomer. Classification system for galaxies. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Hubble sorted galaxies by shape into a diagram shaped like a tuning fork — ellipticals on the handle, spirals branching into two prongs. He thought it showed how galaxies evolve. It does not, but the classification stuck.

questions.q: There was a French astronomer. Catalog of nebulae, clusters, and galaxies to avoid confusing them with comets. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Charles Messier was hunting comets and kept being fooled by fuzzy things that turned out not to be comets. He catalogued them as a list of objects to ignore — and that list of annoyances is now the most-used catalogue in amateur astronomy.

questions.q: There was a british astronomer. Companion catalog to Messier objects. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Patrick Moore noticed Messier's catalogue missed many fine objects, so he made a companion list. He could not use M for Moore, since Messier had it — so he used the other half of his surname, Caldwell.

questions.q: "Roche Limit" is named after a place.
questions.f: Get close enough to a planet and its gravity pulls harder on your near side than your far side, until the difference tears you apart. Saturn's rings sit inside Saturn's Roche limit, which is very likely how they formed.

questions.q: There was an astronomer. Region around a star where orbiting matter remains gravitationally bound. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Around each star in a close pair is a teardrop-shaped region where its gravity still wins. Fill that region and matter spills across to the companion — which is how some stars slowly eat each other.

questions.q: There was a German astronomer. Empirical rule approximating planetary distances. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A numerical pattern that seemed to predict planetary distances, and even pointed to a gap where the asteroid belt was later found. Then Neptune was discovered in the wrong place and the whole thing collapsed. It was never a law.

questions.q: There was a German engineer. Most fuel-efficient orbital transfer between two circular orbits. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Walter Hohmann worked out the cheapest route between two orbits in 1925 — two engine burns and a long coast. Every mission to Mars still uses it, which is why launch windows come round only every twenty-six months.

questions.q: There was a French mathematician. Positions where gravitational forces balance. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Five spots where the pull of two large bodies balances so a small object can sit still relative to both. The James Webb telescope parks at one of them, a million miles out, permanently shaded from the Sun.

questions.q: There was an American astronomer. Gaps in the asteroid belt caused by Jupiter's gravity. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Daniel Kirkwood noticed empty lanes in the asteroid belt and worked out why: any asteroid orbiting in a simple ratio with Jupiter gets a repeated nudge at the same point until it is flung out. Resonance clears the road.

questions.q: There was a british physicist. Criterion for collapse of gas clouds into stars. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A gas cloud is a contest between gravity pulling in and pressure pushing out. James Jeans worked out the mass at which gravity wins — and that threshold is where every star in the universe begins.

questions.q: "Eddington Limit" is named after a person.
questions.f: A star can only be so bright before its own light blows its outer layers off. Eddington calculated the ceiling — the same Eddington who told the young Chandrasekhar his white-dwarf limit was nonsense.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. Radius defining the event horizon of a non-rotating black hole. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein's equations while serving in the trenches of the First World War, and posted the result to Einstein from the front. He died of illness months later, before anyone understood he had described a black hole.

questions.q: There was a new Zealand mathematician. Solution describing rotating black holes. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Schwarzschild described a black hole that does not spin, in 1916. It took until 1963 for Roy Kerr to solve the far harder case of one that does. Every real black hole spins, so Kerr's is the solution the universe actually uses.

questions.q: There was a british physicist. Theoretical radiation emitted by black holes due to quantum effects. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Hawking showed black holes are not entirely black — they leak, very slowly, and eventually evaporate. He set out to disprove the idea and ended up proving it, which he described as the most surprising result of his life.

questions.q: There was a british mathematician. Method of extracting energy from a rotating black hole. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Roger Penrose worked out that you could throw an object at a spinning black hole, split it in two, and have one half come back with more energy than you sent in. The black hole pays, by spinning slightly slower.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "optical illusion" comes from a mathematician?
questions.f: A triangle that looks perfectly solid and cannot exist. Penrose called it impossibility in its purest form and showed it to the artist Escher, who built entire staircases and waterfalls out of the same trick.

questions.q: There was a Dutch physicist. Mathematical basis of special relativity. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Lorentz wrote down the equations before Einstein did, but treated them as a mathematical fix. Einstein took the same equations and said they meant time and space themselves change with speed — which is why relativity is his.

questions.q: "Lorentz Force" is named after a place.
questions.f: A charged particle moving through a magnetic field gets pushed sideways, at right angles to both its motion and the field. It is the reason electric motors turn and the reason the aurora glows near the poles.

questions.q: There was a Scottish physicist. Unified electricity, magnetism, and light. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Four equations that between them describe every electric motor, radio wave and beam of light in existence. Feynman said that from a long enough view of history, the nineteenth century would be remembered for these.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "electromagnetic shield" comes from an English scientist?
questions.f: A metal shell keeps electric fields out, which is why you are safe inside a car in a lightning storm — the charge runs around the bodywork, not through you. Faraday tested it by sitting in a foil-lined room while assistants zapped it.

questions.q: There was a scientist. Rotation of polarized light by a magnetic field. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Faraday showed that a magnetic field can twist a beam of polarised light. It was the first hard evidence that light and magnetism were connected at all, and it pointed straight at Maxwell's equations twenty years later.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "sETI paradox" comes from an Italian physicist?
questions.f: Over lunch at Los Alamos in 1950, Enrico Fermi interrupted a conversation about aliens with one question: where is everybody? The galaxy is old and vast and should be crowded. It looks empty. Nobody has answered him yet.

questions.q: There was a physicist. Highest occupied energy level at absolute zero. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Even at absolute zero, electrons in a metal are not still — the rules of quantum mechanics forbid them all sitting in the lowest state. The Fermi energy is the level the topmost ones are stuck at.

questions.q: There was a physicist. Calculates quantum transition probabilities. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Fermi called it golden rule number two in his lectures, and the name stuck. He did not discover it — Dirac did — which makes it one of physics' more cheerfully misattributed results.

questions.q: "Feynman Diagram" is named after a person.
questions.f: Feynman replaced pages of algebra with little pictures of particles meeting, scattering and moving on. Older physicists were suspicious of anything so easy to draw. Within a decade nobody could work without them.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "study technique" comes from a physicist?
questions.f: Explain the thing to a child. Wherever you stumble is exactly where you do not understand it. Feynman used this on himself constantly, and it remains the cheapest study method ever devised.

questions.q: There was a british physicist. Relativistic equation describing electrons. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Dirac's equation had two solutions, and one of them described a particle with negative energy. Rather than discard it he suggested it was a real particle nobody had found yet. Four years later someone found the positron.

questions.q: There was a physicists. Predicted fifth state of matter at extremely low temperatures. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Bose's paper was rejected by a journal. He posted it to Einstein, who translated it into German himself, added his own extension, and got it published. Seventy years later the state of matter they predicted was finally made in a lab.

questions.q: There was an Indian physicist. Gas composed of bosons obeying Bose-Einstein statistics. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Satyendra Nath Bose worked out a new way of counting identical particles that behaves nothing like counting ordinary objects. Swap two of them and nothing changes at all — because there is no way even in principle to tell which is which.

questions.q: There was an Indian physicist. Family of particles named in Bose's honor. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Every particle in the universe is either a boson or a fermion, and the bosons are named after Bose. Dirac chose the name. Bose himself never received a Nobel Prize, though at least ten have been awarded for work built on his.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "elementary particle" comes from a british physicist?
questions.f: Peter Higgs's paper was rejected in 1964 as being of no obvious relevance to physics. The particle it predicted was found in 2012, and he got the Nobel the following year — forty-eight years after the rejection.

questions.q: "Higgs Field" is named after a place.
questions.f: An invisible field filling all of space, which particles drag through like walking in water. The dragging is what we call mass. A writer nicknamed it the God particle; Higgs, an atheist, disliked the name intensely.

questions.q: There was an Indian physicist. Inelastic scattering of light by molecules. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: C. V. Raman started wondering why the sea is blue on a voyage home from England, and ended up discovering that molecules shift the colour of light that bounces off them. It won him the Nobel Prize in 1930.

questions.q: There was a physicist. Analytical technique based on Raman scattering. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Shine a laser at a substance and the light that scatters back carries a fingerprint of exactly which molecules are present. It identifies paint on a masterpiece or a pill in a packet without touching either.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. Recoil-free emission and absorption of gamma rays. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Rudolf Mossbauer found that atoms locked in a crystal can emit gamma rays without recoiling, giving a beam of extraordinary precision. He was a doctoral student, and had a Nobel Prize by the age of thirty-two.

questions.q: There was a Dutch physicist. Splitting of spectral lines in magnetic fields. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Put an atom in a magnetic field and its spectral lines split apart. Zeeman was reprimanded for wasting laboratory time on the experiment. He won a Nobel Prize for it six years later.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. Splitting of spectral lines in electric fields. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: The electric-field twin of the Zeeman effect — spectral lines splitting under voltage rather than magnetism. Johannes Stark won a Nobel for it, then spent his later career attacking the physics of Einstein on political grounds.

questions.q: There was an American physicist. X-ray scattering demonstrating particle nature of light. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Compton bounced X-rays off electrons and found the light lost energy, exactly as if it were made of particles colliding. It was the experiment that made physicists accept the photon as real rather than a bookkeeping trick.

questions.q: "Hall–Petch Relationship" is named after a person.
questions.f: Metals are made of tiny crystal grains, and cracks travel easily inside a grain but struggle to cross a boundary. Make the grains smaller and the metal gets stronger — which is why smiths have hammered steel for three thousand years.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of electric potential" comes from an Italian physicist?
questions.f: Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked cloth between them and made electricity flow steadily for the first time. He demonstrated it to Napoleon, who made him a count and put him on the currency.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of electrical resistance" comes from a German physicist?
questions.f: Ohm published his law in 1827 and German academics dismissed it as a web of naked fancies. He resigned his teaching post in disgust. Recognition came fifteen years later, from England, and eventually the unit.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of pressure" comes from a French mathematician?
questions.f: Pascal built a working mechanical calculator at nineteen to help his father, a tax official, with endless sums. He also founded probability theory, largely by answering a gambler's question about how to split an interrupted bet.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of force" comes from an English physicist?
questions.f: A newton is roughly the weight of a medium apple in your hand — a coincidence physicists enjoy rather too much given the story about the tree. Newton himself told that story late in life, and only about seeing an apple fall.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of energy" comes from an English physicist?
questions.f: James Joule was a brewer who did physics on the side, and he measured heat with the precision of someone used to controlling fermentation. On his honeymoon he reportedly took a thermometer to a waterfall to see if the falling water warmed up.

questions.q: There was an English scientist. Pioneer of electromagnetism and electrochemistry. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Michael Faraday left school at thirteen and worked as a bookbinder, reading the books he was binding. He became the finest experimentalist of the century and turned down both a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society.

questions.q: "Henry" is named after a place.
questions.f: Joseph Henry discovered electromagnetic induction before Faraday did, but he was teaching a full timetable at a small American academy and published late. Faraday got the credit; Henry got the unit.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of frequency" comes from a German physicist?
questions.f: Hertz proved radio waves exist. Asked what use they might be, he said none whatsoever — it is just an experiment that proves Maxwell was right. Within fifteen years Marconi was sending signals across the Atlantic.

questions.q: There was a French physicist. Discovered natural radioactivity. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Becquerel expected sunlight to make uranium salts glow, so when the weather turned cloudy he shut everything in a drawer with a photographic plate. Days later the plate was fogged anyway. He had found radioactivity by being rained off.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of radioactivity (historical)" comes from a scientists?
questions.f: Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes; anyone wanting to read them must sign a waiver.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. Discovered X-rays in 1895. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Roentgen called them X-rays because he did not know what they were. The first radiograph was of his wife's hand; she looked at her own skeleton and said she had seen her death. He refused to patent any of it.

questions.q: There was a German mathematician. Major contributions to mathematics and magnetism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Told as a schoolboy to add the numbers from 1 to 100, Gauss saw that they pair up into fifty sums of 101 and answered almost immediately. He went on to contribute to nearly every branch of mathematics there was.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. Collaborated with Gauss on electromagnetism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Wilhelm Weber built a working telegraph line across Gottingen with Gauss in 1833, years before commercial telegraphy. He was later dismissed from his professorship for refusing to swear an oath to the king.

questions.q: "Siemens" is named after a person.
questions.f: Werner von Siemens built his first telegraph business on a loan from a cousin and turned it into one of the largest electrical firms in the world. The unit of conductance is the reciprocal of the ohm — and it used to be called the mho.

questions.q: What does "Diesel" mean?
questions.f: Rudolf Diesel designed an engine that ignites fuel by compression alone, with no spark. In 1913 he boarded a ferry across the English Channel and was never seen again; his body was found floating ten days later.

questions.q: Which word meaning "elevator brand that became synonymous with elevators" comes from an American inventor?
questions.f: Elisha Otis did not invent the elevator — he invented the brake that catches it. At the 1854 World's Fair he had himself hoisted up, then ordered the rope cut. The platform dropped a few inches and stopped.

questions.q: There was an American inventor. Developed rapid-fire mechanical gun. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Richard Gatling wrote that he built it hoping one man could do the work of a hundred, so armies would need fewer soldiers and fewer would die. It is among the worst predictions anyone has ever made about a weapon.

questions.q: Which word meaning "revolver" comes from an American inventor?
questions.f: Samuel Colt is said to have got the idea for the revolving cylinder watching a ship's wheel lock into position as it turned. He carved his first model out of wood on that voyage, aged sixteen.

questions.q: There was an industrialist. Company popularized repeating rifles. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The rifle made the family fortune. Sarah Winchester, the widowed heir, spent decades adding rooms to a California mansion — stairs to nowhere, doors opening onto walls — in a house that still stands and can still be visited.

questions.q: There was a gunsmith. Small concealable pistol named after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Henry Deringer spelled his name with one r. Rival manufacturers copying his pocket pistol added a second to dodge the trademark, and the misspelling is the version that survived into the dictionary.

questions.q: "Bowdlerize" is named after a place.
questions.f: The Family Shakespeare removed everything Thomas Bowdler thought unsuitable to read aloud. His sister Henrietta did most of the editing but published anonymously, so the brother's name became the word for censoring a text.
