questions.q: Which word meaning "hypnotize" comes from an Austrian physician?
questions.f: Franz Mesmer claimed to heal patients by redirecting an invisible fluid he called animal magnetism. A royal commission including Benjamin Franklin investigated and found no fluid — but noticed the patients often got better anyway.

questions.q: Which word meaning "tobacco alkaloid" comes from a French diplomat?
questions.f: Jean Nicot was a French ambassador who sent tobacco seeds to the queen as a headache remedy. The plant, the genus and the addictive chemical inside it all ended up carrying the name of a diplomat who never smoked.

questions.q: There was a diplomat. Tobacco genus named after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Linnaeus named the whole tobacco genus after Jean Nicot. It is a large family — tobacco's relatives include the tomato, the potato, the aubergine and deadly nightshade, all in the same botanical clan.

questions.q: Which word meaning "flower" comes from a Swedish botanist?
questions.f: Named for Anders Dahl, a Swedish student of Linnaeus. The tubers were brought from Mexico to Europe partly as a possible food crop to replace the potato. Nobody liked the taste, so it was kept for the flowers.

questions.q: Which word meaning "flower" comes from a German botanist?
questions.f: Leonhart Fuchs died in 1566, nearly two centuries before the flower was found and named for him. The colour is named after the flower, so a sixteenth-century German doctor is the reason a shade of pink has that spelling.

questions.q: Which word meaning "flowering tree" comes from a French botanist?
questions.f: Pierre Magnol invented the idea of the plant family — grouping species by shared structure rather than listing them alphabetically. Magnolias themselves are older than bees, and are pollinated by beetles instead.

questions.q: "Gardenia" is named after a person.
questions.f: Alexander Garden was a Scottish-born naturalist working in Charleston who sent specimens back to Europe for years. He was rewarded with a flower he had nothing to do with discovering — and which does not grow where he lived.

questions.q: There was a jesuit botanist. Missionary who studied Asian flora. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Georg Kamel was a Jesuit missionary and pharmacist in the Philippines. Linnaeus latinised his name to Camellus for the flower. Tea comes from the same genus, so every cup you drink is technically a camellia.

questions.q: There was a French governor. Patron of botany. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Michel Begon was a French colonial governor who collected plants and sponsored botanists. He never saw the flower named after him — it was named by a monk he had once employed, years after Begon's death.

questions.q: Which word meaning "christmas flower" comes from an American diplomat?
questions.f: Joel Poinsett was the first United States minister to Mexico and sent cuttings home in 1828. The Mexican name is flor de nochebuena, Christmas Eve flower — rather better than naming it after a visiting diplomat.

questions.q: There was a Scottish horticulturist. Royal gardener. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: William Forsyth was royal head gardener at Kensington and a founder of what became the Royal Horticultural Society. He also sold the government a tree-wound plaster that turned out not to work, which caused a considerable scandal.

questions.q: There was a German botanist. Described many flowering plants. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Johann Gottfried Zinn was an anatomist who mapped the structures of the human eye, and died at thirty-two having also written on Mexican plants. There is a zone of the eye named after him as well as the flower.

questions.q: There was an American physician. Anatomist and educator. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Named for Caspar Wistar — with an a. The botanist who named it spelled it with an e, nobody corrected him, and two centuries later we all still misspell an anatomist's surname every time we mention the flower.

questions.q: There was a Greek roots. Often mistaken for an eponym but derived from Greek words. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: This one is a trap. It looks like somebody called Philo Dendron, but it is plain Greek: philo-dendron, tree-loving, because the plant climbs. Not every scientific-sounding plant name hides a person.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "whole-wheat cracker" comes from an American minister?
questions.f: Sylvester Graham was a minister who preached that bland food calmed the passions and that spices were dangerous. His cracker was designed to be dull on purpose. Modern versions are sweetened, which would have appalled him.

questions.q: There was a health reformer. Developed coarse whole-wheat flour. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Graham insisted flour should keep the whole grain, bran and all, against the fashion for fine white flour. He was wrong about the moral effects and right about the nutrition, which is a better record than most food reformers manage.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "salad" comes from an Italian-American restaurateur?
questions.f: Caesar Cardini ran a restaurant in Tijuana and was overwhelmed on the Fourth of July, 1924. Running short of ingredients, he threw what was left into a bowl and tossed it at the table for show. No Roman emperor was involved.

questions.q: There was a british general. Dish allegedly named in his honor. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Nobody can prove the Duke of Wellington ever ate it. The name may simply be patriotic, or may come from the dish's resemblance to a brown boot. The duke has better claims to fame elsewhere.

questions.q: Which word meaning "tortilla chips with toppings" comes from a Mexican chef?
questions.f: In 1943 Ignacio Anaya was closing up when a group of American army wives arrived hungry. He fried some tortilla, added cheese and jalapeno, and served it. Ignacio's nickname was Nacho.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "pizza variety" comes from a queen of Italy?
questions.f: In 1889 a Naples pizzaiolo made three pizzas for the visiting queen. She preferred the one in the colours of the new Italian flag — red tomato, white mozzarella, green basil — and he named it after her.

questions.q: "Pavlova" is named after a person.
questions.f: Created for the ballerina Anna Pavlova during a tour, and claimed by both Australia and New Zealand ever since. A researcher combing old cookbooks found the earliest recipe in New Zealand, which has settled nothing.

questions.q: There was an Austrian chef. Invented Vienna's famous chocolate cake. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Franz Sacher invented it at sixteen, standing in for a sick head chef. A later dispute between two Viennese firms over who could call theirs the original ran for seven years in court and is still called the Sweet Seven Years.

questions.q: There was a Russian nobleman. Dish created for his household. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Named for the Stroganovs, one of the wealthiest families in imperial Russia. Their chef is credited with the dish, possibly designed so that beef could be cut thin and cooked fast in a Russian winter kitchen.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "flavored tea" comes from a british Prime Minister?
questions.f: Bergamot-scented tea named for a British prime minister who almost certainly never blended anything. The likeliest explanation is that a merchant used his name to sell it, which worked so well it outlasted his politics.

questions.q: Which word meaning "coffee drink" comes from a WWII Italy?
questions.f: American soldiers in Italy found espresso too strong and added hot water. Italian baristas named the result after them, not entirely as a compliment. It is now on the menu in Italy too.

questions.q: There was a cocktail origin debated. One theory traces it to Martinez, California. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Every origin story for the martini is contested: a town called Martinez in California, a vermouth brand called Martini and Rossi, a bartender of the same name. The drink is older than any reliable record of it.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "waterproof boot" comes from a military commander?
questions.f: The duke asked his shoemaker for a boot that was tough enough for the battlefield and neat enough for the evening. It became so fashionable that gentlemen wore them everywhere. The rubber version came decades later.

questions.q: "Raglan Sleeve" is named after a place.
questions.f: Lord Raglan lost his right arm at Waterloo and had his coats cut with the sleeve running in one piece to the collar, so he could dress himself more easily. The design turned out to be better for movement and became standard sportswear.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "laboratory burner" comes from a German chemist?
questions.f: Peter Desaga, Bunsen's instrument maker, actually built it to Bunsen's specification. Bunsen lost the sight in one eye to an explosion and twice nearly died of arsenic poisoning — chemistry was a rougher trade then.

questions.q: There was an Italian physicist. Proposed that equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Avogadro's idea was ignored for nearly fifty years, and he died before it was accepted. The number itself — about six hundred thousand billion billion — was calculated by others and named in his honour afterwards.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "gas law" comes from an anglo-Irish chemist?
questions.f: Squeeze a gas into half the space and its pressure doubles. Boyle worked it out with a J-shaped glass tube and a quantity of mercury, and published it in 1662 while helping to invent the whole idea of the experiment.

questions.q: There was a French physicist. Demonstrated relationship between gas volume and temperature. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Jacques Charles worked out that gases expand as they warm — and he was also a balloonist, making the first hydrogen balloon flight in 1783. Villagers where it landed attacked it with pitchforks, believing it was a monster.

questions.q: There was an English chemist. Developed modern atomic theory. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: John Dalton was colour blind and wrote the first scientific description of the condition, using himself as the subject. He asked for his eyes to be examined after his death; they are still preserved in Manchester.

questions.q: There was a scientist. Mineral named in his honor. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A rare potassium mineral found near volcanic vents on Vesuvius, named for Avogadro. It is one of the quieter honours in science — a man who waited fifty years for recognition, given a mineral almost nobody has seen.

questions.q: "Mohs Scale" is named after a person.
questions.f: Friedrich Mohs ranked minerals one to ten by which scratches which — talc at one, diamond at ten. It measures nothing absolute, only the order. A fingernail is about 2.5, which is why it will mark gypsum but not glass.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "earthquake magnitude" comes from an American seismologist?
questions.f: Each whole step is about thirty-two times more energy, so a magnitude 7 is not slightly worse than a 6 — it is thirty-two times worse. Richter built the scale for southern California and it was adopted worldwide.

questions.q: There was an Italian volcanologist. Developed earthquake intensity scale based on observed effects. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Mercalli measured what an earthquake does rather than how much energy it releases — from barely felt up to total destruction. Two places at the same Richter magnitude can be far apart on Mercalli, depending on what was built there.

questions.q: There was an engineer & Meteorologist. Categorized hurricanes by destructive potential. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An engineer and a meteorologist built it together: Saffir was studying how buildings fail in high wind, Simpson ran the National Hurricane Center. Categories 1 to 5 describe damage, not just wind speed.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "space observatory" comes from an astronomer?
questions.f: Launched in 1990 with a mirror ground to the wrong shape by less than the width of a hair. Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993 — effectively giving a telescope spectacles — and it has been working ever since.

questions.q: There was a Polish astronomer. Proposed heliocentric model of the Solar System. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Copernicus is said to have received the first printed copy of his book on the day he died. Moving the Sun to the centre was not only astronomy; it was the moment humanity stopped being at the centre of anything.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "movement disorder" comes from an English physician?
questions.f: James Parkinson called it the shaking palsy in 1817, in an essay of sixty-six pages based on six patients — some of whom he had only observed walking past in the street. His name was attached decades after his death.

questions.q: "Asperger Syndrome*" is named after a place.
questions.f: Hans Asperger described the pattern in 1944. The term is being retired from clinical use in favour of the wider autism spectrum, both because the boundary proved hard to draw and because later research into his wartime conduct raised serious concerns.

questions.q: There was a French neurologist. Identified neurological tic disorder. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Georges Gilles de la Tourette described nine patients in 1885 whose tics came with involuntary sounds. He was later shot in the head by a former patient who believed he had hypnotised her, and survived.

questions.q: Which word meaning "heat treatment of food" comes from a French chemist?
questions.f: Pasteur was asked why French wine kept going sour. He found living organisms in it and showed that a short spell at moderate heat killed them without ruining the taste. Applied to milk, it saved a great many children.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "surgical childbirth" comes from a Roman leader?
questions.f: Probably not named after Caesar at all. Roman law required the operation on a dying mother — and Caesar's mother lived for decades after his birth. The likelier root is caedere, Latin for to cut.

questions.q: Which word meaning "loose undergarments/trousers" comes from an American women's rights advocate?
questions.f: Amelia Bloomer did not invent them — she promoted them in her newspaper, and the press attached her name. Women wearing them were mocked in the street, and the campaign was dropped as a distraction from the vote.

questions.q: Which word meaning "soft felt hat" comes from a fictional character?
questions.f: Named after a play. Sarah Bernhardt played Princess Fedora in 1882 wearing a soft centre-creased hat, and women adopted it as a symbol of the movement for women's rights before men took it over entirely.

questions.q: Which word meaning "wide-brimmed hat" comes from an American hatmaker?
questions.f: John Stetson made a wide-brimmed hat on a prospecting trip to keep sun and rain off, and sold it off his own head for five dollars. He called the design the Boss of the Plains and built a factory on it.

questions.q: "Mackintosh" is named after a person.
questions.f: Charles Macintosh spelled his name without the k. He glued two layers of cloth together with rubber dissolved in naphtha — a by-product of the gasworks — and made the first genuinely waterproof coat. The k crept in later.

questions.q: Which word meaning "woolen face covering" comes from a crimean War battle?
questions.f: Named for a battle, not a person. British troops at Balaclava in the Crimean winter of 1854 were sent knitted headgear from home because the army had not equipped them for the cold.

questions.q: Which word meaning "two-piece swimsuit" comes from a pacific atoll?
questions.f: Louis Reard named his 1946 swimsuit after Bikini Atoll, where an atomic bomb had been tested four days earlier — he wanted a name that suggested an explosion. No Paris model would wear it, so he hired a dancer.

questions.q: There was a british statesman. Sofa style associated with aristocratic taste. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The fourth Earl of Chesterfield is said to have commissioned a sofa that would let a gentleman sit upright without creasing his suit. He is better remembered for letters of advice to his son that Samuel Johnson called immoral.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "folding bed" comes from an American inventor?
questions.f: William Murphy was courting a singer while living in a one-room San Francisco apartment, and etiquette forbade a woman entering a bedroom. He designed a bed that folded into the wall, turning his bedroom into a parlour.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "glass preserving jar" comes from an American tinsmith?
questions.f: John Mason patented the screw-thread glass jar with a rubber-sealed lid in 1858, making home preserving safe and reliable. His patent expired, competitors flooded in, and he died poor while everyone else got rich.

questions.q: Which word meaning "ballpoint pen" comes from a Hungarian journalist?
questions.f: Laszlo Biro was a journalist who noticed newspaper ink dried almost instantly while his fountain pen smudged. He built a pen that used the thicker ink with a rolling ball to feed it. Britain still calls every ballpoint a biro.

questions.q: "Tupperware" is named after a place.
questions.f: Earl Tupper's airtight seal sold badly in shops because nobody could see why it mattered. Brownie Wise worked out you had to demonstrate the burp in someone's living room, and invented the Tupperware party.

questions.q: There was a mythical king of Corinth. Condemned by the gods to roll a boulder uphill forever, only for it to roll back each time. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Sisyphus cheated death twice — once by chaining up Death himself, so that for a while nobody on earth could die. His punishment was a boulder that always rolls back. Camus argued we must imagine him happy.

questions.q: Which word meaning "to tease with something unattainable" comes from a king punished in Hades?
questions.f: Tantalus stood in water that drained whenever he bent to drink, under fruit that swung away whenever he reached. English took his name for the very specific cruelty of something being just out of reach.

questions.q: Which word meaning "excessive self-love" comes from a beautiful youth?
questions.f: Narcissus saw his reflection in a pool, did not realise it was himself, and could not leave. The flower that grew where he died still bends its head toward water.

questions.q: There was a king of Thebes. Unknowingly killed his father and married his mother, inspiring Freud's psychological theory. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Oedipus was abandoned as a baby precisely so the prophecy could not come true, and it came true because he was abandoned. Freud borrowed the name in 1899 for a theory the play itself does not require.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "source of unforeseen troubles" comes from first woman in Greek mythology?
questions.f: It was a jar, not a box. Erasmus mistranslated the Greek pithos as pyxis in the sixteenth century and the mistake stuck. Pandora shut the lid with one thing still inside: hope.

questions.q: "Procrustean" is named after a person.
questions.f: Procrustes offered travellers a bed and guaranteed a perfect fit — by stretching anyone too short and cutting down anyone too tall. Theseus eventually gave him the same treatment on his own bed.

questions.q: There was a cypriot sculptor. His statue came to life after Aphrodite answered his prayers; later adapted in psychology to describe self-fulfilling expectations. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A teacher told that certain pupils are gifted will, without meaning to, treat them differently — and those pupils improve. Named after the sculptor who loved his statue into life, because expectation does the shaping.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "ability to generate wealth or success" comes from a phrygian king?
questions.f: Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold, and it did — including his food, his drink, and in some versions his daughter. He begged to have the gift taken back, and washed it off in a river.

questions.q: Which word meaning "trusted adviser or guide" comes from a friend of Odysseus?
questions.f: When Odysseus sailed for Troy he left his son with a friend named Mentor. Athena kept borrowing that shape to deliver advice — so the word for a trusted guide is really the name of a goddess's disguise.

questions.q: The word "Odyssey" is named after…?
questions.f: Ten years to sail home from a war that itself took ten years. Odysseus survives by lying, hiding and outthinking everything he meets, which makes him a strange sort of hero and a very durable one.

questions.q: Which word meaning "requiring immense effort" comes from a Greek hero?
questions.f: Twelve labours, each supposedly impossible: the lion, the hydra, the stables, the golden apples. He was given them as punishment, completed all twelve, and the word for an enormous task has been his ever since.

questions.q: There was a fire-breathing monster. Composite creature with lion, goat, and serpent parts. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A lion at the front, a goat rising from the back, a snake for a tail. Even the Greeks found it absurd, which is why chimera came to mean a wild impossible idea rather than an actual monster.

questions.q: "Cerberus" is named after a place.
questions.f: Three heads, so one is always awake. The way past was music — Orpheus played him to sleep — or cake, since Romans buried honey cakes with their dead specifically as a bribe. Hence a sop to Cerberus.

questions.q: Which word meaning "two-faced" comes from a Roman god of beginnings?
questions.f: Janus guarded doorways, with one face looking back and one forward. His temple doors in Rome stood open in wartime and shut in peace. In roughly seven hundred years they were recorded as closed only a handful of times.

questions.q: There was a Roman god of fire. Charles Goodyear named the rubber-hardening process after the god associated with fire and metalworking. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Charles Goodyear spent years and several fortunes trying to make rubber stable, and found the answer by accidentally dropping a rubber-and-sulphur mixture on a hot stove. He named it for the Roman god of the forge, and died in debt.

questions.q: Which word meaning "planet or chemical element" comes from a Roman messenger god?
questions.f: The fastest-moving planet took the name of the fastest god. The liquid metal got it too, for rolling away the moment you touch it — and gave English mercurial for anyone whose mood does the same.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to war or the military" comes from a Roman god of war?
questions.f: Everything military traces to Mars: martial arts, martial law, court-martial. March is his month too, because it was when the campaigning season opened and Roman armies could move again.

questions.q: Which word meaning "cheerful and good-humored" comes from a king of the Roman gods?
questions.f: Medieval doctors believed the planet overhead at your birth set your temperament. Jupiter — Jove — produced the cheerful sort. Saturn produced the gloomy sort, which is why saturnine still means what it does.

questions.q: Which word meaning "sudden overwhelming fear" comes from a Greek god of shepherds?
questions.f: Pan was the goat-legged god of wild places, and travellers who heard an unexplained noise in an empty wood blamed him. That particular fear — sudden, irrational, contagious — is the one that kept his name.

questions.q: "Echo" is named after a person.
questions.f: Echo was a nymph who talked too much, and Hera cursed her to repeat only other people's last words. She fell in love with Narcissus and could never say so — only give him his own words back.

questions.q: Which word meaning "flower" comes from a goddess of the rainbow?
questions.f: Iris was the rainbow, and the messenger who ran along it between gods and mortals. The coloured ring of your eye is named after her, and so is the flower, and so is the word iridescent.

questions.q: Which word meaning "plant life of a region" comes from a Roman goddess of flowers?
questions.f: Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and spring, and her festival involved so much noise and colour that stricter Romans disapproved. Biologists took her name for all the plant life of a place.

questions.q: Which word meaning "animal life of a region" comes from a Roman god of forests?
questions.f: Faunus was the Roman god of forests and wild animals, and his female counterpart Fauna gave her name to all animal life. Flora and fauna are a goddess and a goddess, still working as a pair.

questions.q: There was a Greek god of marriage. Wedding songs invoked Hymen for blessings. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hymen was the Greek god of weddings, and a hymeneal is a wedding song. Greek marriage processions called his name aloud on the way to the bride's house, which is where the word comes from.

questions.q: Which word meaning "symbol of romantic love" comes from a god of love?
questions.f: The Romans made him a chubby child with a bow. The Greeks knew him as Eros and took him rather more seriously — a primordial force older than most of the gods, not a decoration for a card.

questions.q: There was a primordial deity. Personification of darkness in Greek cosmology. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Erebus was darkness itself, born near the beginning of things. A British polar ship took the name, and after it was lost in the Arctic, a volcano in Antarctica was named after the ship — darkness, twice removed.

questions.q: "Morpheus" is named after a place.
questions.f: Morpheus did not bring sleep; he supplied the people who appear in your dreams, taking their shapes himself. His name comes from morphe, the Greek for form.

questions.q: Which word meaning "powerful opioid analgesic" comes from a god of dreams?
questions.f: A German pharmacist isolated it from opium in 1804 and named it after the god of dreams. He tested it on himself and on three boys, nearly killing all four, then spent much of his life addicted to it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "artificially induced trance" comes from a Greek god of sleep?
questions.f: Hypnos was the Greek god of sleep, brother of Death and son of Night. Hypnosis is not really sleep at all — the name was chosen before anyone understood what was happening — and its coiner later regretted it.

questions.q: There was a Greek personification of death. Named after the god of peaceful death. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Thanatos was the gentle personification of death, as distinct from the violent kind. Thanatology — the study of dying, grief and how people face the end — took his name rather than a harsher one deliberately.

questions.q: There was a goddess of youth. Early psychiatric term derived from the youthful goddess. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: From Hebe, goddess of youth, because the condition was first described in adolescents. Like several psychiatric terms built from Greek gods, it has largely been retired in favour of plainer clinical language.

questions.q: Which word meaning "memory aid" comes from a goddess of memory?
questions.f: Mnemosyne was memory, and the mother of all nine Muses — which makes memory, in Greek thinking, the parent of every art. Sensible, for a culture that recited Homer for centuries before writing it down.

questions.q: Which word meaning "institution preserving knowledge and art" comes from a nine daughters of Mnemosyne?
questions.f: A museum was originally a place belonging to the Muses — a shrine to the nine goddesses of the arts. The greatest of them, at Alexandria, was a research institute with the famous library attached.

questions.q: "Music" is named after a person.
questions.f: Music means, literally, the art of the Muses. It covered poetry and dance as well as sound, because the Greeks did not separate them — a performance was all three at once.

questions.q: Which word meaning "cleanliness promoting health" comes from a goddess of health?
questions.f: Hygieia was the daughter of the god of medicine, and her job was keeping people well rather than curing them once sick. Her sister Panacea handled cures — and gave English a word for a remedy for everything.

questions.q: There was a Greek god of medicine. Ancient physicians claimed descent from Asclepius. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Ancient physicians claimed descent from Asclepius, god of medicine, and called themselves Asclepiads. His snake-wound staff is still the symbol of medicine — though it is often confused with a different, two-snake staff belonging to Hermes.

questions.q: There was a Roman equivalent of Asclepius. Used to describe doctors or medicine. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Roman spelling of Asclepius. When plague struck Rome in 293 BC the Senate sent for the god, and a snake from his temple reportedly boarded the ship and slid off onto an island in the Tiber, where they built him a temple.

questions.q: There was a legendary sage. Secret writings attributed to him gave rise to the idea of being tightly sealed or esoteric. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hermes Trismegistus was a legendary sage credited with secret writings. Alchemists working in that tradition developed a way of fusing glass to seal a vessel completely — so a hermetic seal is named after a wizard.

questions.q: There was a titan. First cervical vertebra supports the skull just as Atlas supported the heavens. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Atlas was condemned to hold up the sky forever. The top vertebra of your spine, which holds up your skull, carries his name — and the book of maps does too, from a picture of Atlas on the cover of an early collection.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "largest tendon in the body" comes from a Greek hero?
questions.f: His mother dipped him in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel — the one spot the water never touched. The largest tendon in your body is named after the one weak point in a legend.

questions.q: "Caesarian (historical adjective)" is named after a place.
questions.f: Caesar's name outlived his empire twice over: German emperors were Kaisers and Russian ones Tsars, both worn-down forms of the same word. Caesarian, meaning imperial, is the direct English adjective.

questions.q: Which word meaning "eighth month of the year" comes from first Roman Emperor?
questions.f: Renamed for Augustus in 8 BC. The story that he stole a day from February so his month would match Julius Caesar's is a medieval invention — but the Senate really did rename it for him.

questions.q: Which word meaning "seventh month of the year" comes from a Roman dictator?
questions.f: Renamed for Julius Caesar after his death, in the month he was born. He had just reformed the calendar into something close to the one we use, so the honour was at least on topic.

questions.q: There was a French diplomat. Historical term referring to nicotine poisoning or dependence. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An old medical term for nicotine poisoning, built from the name of the French diplomat who introduced tobacco to his queen as a headache cure. He would probably not have chosen this particular memorial.

questions.q: Which word meaning "oppressively authoritarian" comes from an English novelist?
questions.f: Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four in 1948 and swapped the last two digits for the title. The word now gets used for any surveillance at all, which slightly misses the point — his real subject was the corruption of language.

questions.q: Which word meaning "theory of biological evolution" comes from an English naturalist?
questions.f: Darwin sat on his theory for twenty years, worried about the reaction. He only published when a letter arrived from Alfred Russel Wallace describing the same idea — and their work was presented jointly.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to evolution or competitive selection" comes from a naturalist?
questions.f: Darwin never wrote survival of the fittest — Herbert Spencer coined it, and Darwin adopted it reluctantly in a later edition. Fittest means best-suited to the surroundings, not strongest, which is the misunderstanding that persists.

questions.q: "Mendelian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Gregor Mendel grew about 28,000 pea plants in a monastery garden and worked out the rules of inheritance. His paper was almost entirely ignored for thirty-four years, until three separate scientists rediscovered it at once.

questions.q: There was a French biologist. Early evolutionary theory proposing inheritance of acquired characteristics. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Lamarck thought a giraffe that stretched for high leaves would pass longer necks to its young. He was wrong about the mechanism, but he was arguing that species change at all, decades before Darwin — which took some courage.

questions.q: There was a French chemist. Refers to principles or methods associated with Pasteur's work. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Pasteur's germ theory met fierce resistance from doctors who resented being told they carried disease on their hands. He was also a chemist, not a physician, which the medical establishment mentioned frequently.

questions.q: There was a German microbiologist. Pertaining to Koch's work on bacteriology. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Koch identified the bacteria behind anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera, and set out the rules for proving any such link. He and Pasteur were bitter rivals, and their national newspapers cheered them on.

questions.q: There was a geneticist. Classical inheritance principles. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Mendel's laws describe how traits pass on in neat ratios — but he chose pea characteristics that happened to be unusually simple. Most inheritance is far messier, which is partly why his results looked almost too tidy.

questions.q: There was a Swedish botanist. Creator of binomial nomenclature. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Linnaeus gave every living thing a two-word name, genus then species, replacing descriptions that ran to whole sentences. He also named himself: born Carl Nilsson, he took Linnaeus from a lime tree on the family farm.

questions.q: There was a French naturalist. Founder of comparative anatomy and paleontology. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Cuvier could reconstruct an entire animal from a few bones, and proved that species go extinct — an idea many found impossible, since it implied the creation was not perfect. He rejected evolution to his last day.

questions.q: "Buffonian" is named after a place.
questions.f: Buffon estimated the Earth was at least 75,000 years old by heating iron spheres and timing how long they took to cool. The Church objected. He apologised in print and went on believing it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to psychoanalysis" comes from an Austrian neurologist?
questions.f: A Freudian slip is a mistake that supposedly reveals a hidden thought. Freud's own term was Fehlleistung — faulty achievement — and he collected examples obsessively, including a great many of his own.

questions.q: There was a Swiss psychiatrist. Based on archetypes and the collective unconscious. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Jung was Freud's chosen successor until they fell out permanently over how much of the mind is sexual. He went on to argue that certain images recur across all cultures, and called them archetypes.

questions.q: There was an Austrian psychologist. Focuses on inferiority, social interest, and striving. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Adler broke with Freud over the same question and built a psychology around the drive to overcome feelings of inferiority. He gave us inferiority complex, one of the few psychiatric terms everyone uses correctly.

questions.q: Which word meaning "automatic conditioned response" comes from a Russian physiologist?
questions.f: Pavlov was studying digestion, not learning, and the dogs' drooling was ruining his measurements. He investigated the nuisance instead of eliminating it, and found conditioning. He was not, incidentally, ringing a bell — usually a metronome.

questions.q: There was an American psychologist. Developed operant conditioning and behaviorism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Skinner trained pigeons to guide missiles during the Second World War, and the system worked — the military just could not bring itself to trust it. He also raised his daughter's early months in a heated, filtered climate-controlled crib.

questions.q: There was a Swiss psychologist. Theory of cognitive development in children. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Piaget worked out his stages of child development largely by watching his own three children very closely and writing down everything. He published his first scientific paper, on an albino sparrow, at the age of eleven.

questions.q: "Maslowian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Maslow never drew his hierarchy as a pyramid — someone else added that later, and the shape implies a rigidity he did not intend. He was interested in what healthy people do, when psychology mostly studied illness.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to Descartes" comes from a French philosopher?
questions.f: Descartes is supposed to have thought of coordinates while lying in bed watching a fly on the ceiling and wondering how to describe its position with numbers. Every graph you have ever drawn descends from that fly.

questions.q: Which word meaning "ideal or non-romantic" comes from a Greek philosopher?
questions.f: Platonic love, in Plato, meant a love that climbs from a particular person toward beauty and truth themselves. English flattened it into love without romance, which Plato would have considered the least interesting part.

questions.q: There was a Greek philosopher. Based on Aristotle's philosophy and logic. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great, dissected sea creatures on Lesbos, and wrote the first surviving works on logic, physics and drama. For much of the Middle Ages, scholars simply called him The Philosopher.

questions.q: Which word meaning "using guided questioning" comes from a Greek philosopher?
questions.f: Socrates wrote nothing. Everything we have comes from students, chiefly Plato. His method was to ask questions until the other person discovered their own answer had a hole in it — which made him popular with the young and not with anyone else.

questions.q: There was a Greek philosopher. Advocated rational pleasure and freedom from fear, later popularly associated with refined enjoyment. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Epicurus taught that the greatest pleasure is freedom from pain and anxiety, and lived on bread, water and the occasional pot of cheese. English turned his name into a word for a gourmet, which reverses him completely.

questions.q: Which word meaning "enduring hardship without complaint" comes from a Greek philosophy?
questions.f: Named after a building. Zeno taught on a painted porch — a stoa — in Athens, and his followers were called the porch people. Their doctrine was that you control your judgements and nothing else.

questions.q: "Cynic" is named after a place.
questions.f: From the Greek for dog-like. The Cynics lived rough on purpose, and Diogenes is supposed to have accepted the insult and adopted it. Modern cynicism — assuming bad motives — is a long way from the original.

questions.q: There was a Greek philosopher. Modern medical term referring to severe self-neglect and hoarding; the association with Diogenes is debated. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A modern term for extreme self-neglect and hoarding. It is arguably misnamed: Diogenes chose poverty deliberately and owned almost nothing, which is close to the opposite of hoarding.

questions.q: There was a Greek mathematician. Father of geometry. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Euclid's Elements ran as a school textbook for over two thousand years — the longest run of any book but the Bible. Asked by a king for a shortcut, he replied that there is no royal road to geometry.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to right triangles" comes from a Greek mathematician?
questions.f: Pythagoras ran what was half a school and half a secret society, with rules against eating beans. The theorem was known to Babylonian mathematicians a thousand years earlier; his followers may have supplied the first proof.

questions.q: There was a Greek mathematician. Discoveries in geometry, mechanics, and buoyancy. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Archimedes worked out how to measure the volume of a crown in the bath and, the story goes, ran into the street shouting. He was killed by a Roman soldier while drawing diagrams in the sand, reportedly telling him not to disturb them.

questions.q: Which word meaning "normally distributed" comes from a German mathematician?
questions.f: The bell curve turns up everywhere — heights, errors, exam marks — because adding up enough small independent effects produces it almost regardless of what those effects are. Gauss found it while analysing astronomical errors.

questions.q: Which word meaning "binary logic" comes from an English mathematician?
questions.f: George Boole reduced logic to algebra with two values, true and false, in 1854. He thought he was studying the laws of thought. Ninety years later it turned out he had written the mathematics of every computer ever built.

questions.q: "Turing Machine" is named after a person.
questions.f: An imaginary device with an infinite paper tape that reads, writes and moves one square at a time. Turing invented it to prove something impossible, and accidentally defined what a computer is.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "aI benchmark" comes from a computer scientist?
questions.f: Turing called it the imitation game: if you cannot tell from a conversation whether you are talking to a person or a machine, he argued, asking whether the machine thinks is the wrong question.

questions.q: There was a Hungarian-American mathematician. Stored-program computer architecture. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: The idea that a computer should keep its instructions in the same memory as its data — so a program can be changed without rewiring the machine. Von Neumann's name went on the report; several colleagues who helped were left off it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "number sequence" comes from an Italian mathematician?
questions.f: Fibonacci's real service to Europe was not the sequence but the digits: he brought Hindu-Arabic numerals west in 1202, and argued they beat Roman numerals for arithmetic. The rabbits were a small example in a long book.

questions.q: There was a Greek mathematician. Method for finding the greatest common divisor. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A method for finding the largest number that divides two others, written down around 300 BC. It is the oldest algorithm still in everyday use — your web browser runs a version of it during encryption.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "non-orientable surface" comes from a German mathematician?
questions.f: Give a strip of paper a half twist and join the ends: it now has one side and one edge. Mobius and another mathematician, Listing, both found it in 1858, independently, within months of each other.

questions.q: There was a German mathematician. Closed non-orientable surface. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Klein called it a Kleinsche Flache — a Klein surface. Someone misread Flache as Flasche, which means bottle, and the mistranslation was too good to correct. It is a surface with no inside and no outside.

questions.q: "Banach Space" is named after a place.
questions.f: Banach and his colleagues did much of their mathematics in the Scottish Cafe in Lwow, writing problems in a notebook the waiters kept behind the bar. Prizes for solutions included a bottle of wine and, once, a live goose.

questions.q: There was a German mathematician. Generalized geometry underlying Einstein's relativity. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Riemann described geometry on curved surfaces in a lecture in 1854, with no application in mind. Gauss, in the audience and hard to impress, was reportedly astonished. Sixty years later Einstein needed exactly that mathematics.

questions.q: There was a Swiss mathematician. Major contributions across mathematics and mechanics. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Euler went blind in his sixties and his output actually increased — he dictated to his sons. He produced so much that a project to publish his complete works has been running since 1911 and is still not finished.

questions.q: There was a French mathematician. Differential operator central to physics. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Asked by Napoleon why his book on the heavens never mentioned God, Laplace is said to have replied that he had no need of that hypothesis. The operator named after him turns up in heat flow, waves and quantum mechanics.

questions.q: There was a French mathematician. Represented periodic functions as sums of sine and cosine waves. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Fourier showed any repeating wave can be built from simple sines added together — which is how audio compression works. He also worked out that the atmosphere warms the planet, describing the greenhouse effect in the 1820s.

questions.q: There was a Swiss mathematician. Relationship between fluid speed and pressure. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Faster fluid means lower pressure. It is often used to explain how wings lift, which is only part of the story — the fuller answer involves the wing pushing air downwards, and physicists still argue about the best way to teach it.

questions.q: There was an English statistician. Foundation of Bayesian probability. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Thomas Bayes never published it. A friend found the paper among his effects after his death and sent it to the Royal Society. It is now the mathematics behind spam filters, medical testing and most machine learning.

questions.q: "Pareto Principle" is named after a person.
questions.f: Pareto noticed that a fifth of Italy's population owned four-fifths of the land — then found the same lopsided split in his garden, where a fifth of the pea pods held most of the peas.

questions.q: There was an American mathematician. Stable outcome in game theory where no player benefits from changing strategy alone. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A situation where nobody can do better by changing their own move alone. Nash wrote it up in a doctoral thesis of twenty-seven pages, won a Nobel Prize for it forty-four years later, and had a film made about his life.

questions.q: There was a british economist. Advocated government intervention to stabilize economies. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Keynes argued governments should spend in a downturn rather than tighten their belts. Told that markets would correct themselves eventually, he replied that in the long run we are all dead.

questions.q: There was a british economist. Comparative advantage in international trade. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Ricardo showed two countries both gain from trade even when one is better at making everything — each should do what it gives up least to make. It is counterintuitive enough that people still argue against it two centuries on.

questions.q: There was an English economist. Predicted population growth would outstrip food supply. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Malthus predicted population would outrun the food supply and reasoned it could only end in famine. He did not foresee fertiliser, mechanised farming or falling birth rates — so he was wrong, and influential anyway.

questions.q: There was a German philosopher. Pertaining specifically to Marx's original economic and philosophical writings. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Marxian points at the analysis; Marxist points at the politics. Economists who use his tools to study capitalism without wanting to overthrow it tend to insist on the first word.

questions.q: There was a German philosopher. Political and economic ideology derived from Marx's theories. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Marx spent his most productive years in the Reading Room of the British Museum, in poverty, supported largely by Engels. He is buried in Highgate Cemetery in London, a short walk from where he wrote.

questions.q: "Leninism" is named after a place.
questions.f: Lenin argued a revolution needed a small disciplined party to lead it rather than waiting for the workers to rise on their own. He returned to Russia in 1917 in a sealed train, permitted through Germany by an enemy hoping to destabilise Russia.

questions.q: There was a Soviet leader. Characterized by centralized authority, forced collectivization, and extensive state control. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Stalin was a name he chose — it means man of steel. He was born Ioseb Jughashvili in Georgia and trained briefly as a priest. His rule is associated with forced collectivisation and mass political repression.

questions.q: There was a Chinese revolutionary. Adapted Marxism-Leninism with emphasis on the peasantry and prolonged revolutionary struggle. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Mao adapted a theory built for industrial workers to a country that was overwhelmingly rural, arguing revolution would come from the peasantry. It was a substantial departure from what Marx had written.

questions.q: There was a Russian revolutionary. Advocated "permanent revolution" and opposed Stalin's policies. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Trotsky organised the Red Army, lost the power struggle after Lenin's death, and was exiled. He was killed in Mexico in 1940 by an assassin with an ice axe, while his followers argued for permanent revolution.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to Gandhi's philosophy" comes from an Indian independence leader?
questions.f: Gandhi's satyagraha meant refusing to cooperate with injustice while refusing to answer it with violence. In 1930 he walked 240 miles to the sea to make salt, breaking a British monopoly with a handful of mud.

questions.q: There was a british Prime Minister. Associated with privatization, deregulation, and free-market reforms. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Britain's first woman prime minister and its longest-serving of the twentieth century. Her programme of privatisation and deregulation still divides the country, which is why the word gets used as praise and insult in equal measure.

questions.q: There was an u.S. President. Popular term for supply-side economics pursued during the 1980s. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The argument that cutting taxes at the top increases total revenue by growing the economy. A journalist coined the word on air; the administration disliked it at first and then adopted it.

questions.q: "Bonapartism" is named after a person.
questions.f: Rule by a strong leader who claims to speak directly for the people, over the heads of parliaments. Napoleon held plebiscites to confirm his power, which made his authority look popular and left nobody able to challenge it.

questions.q: There was a German chancellor. Associated with Realpolitik, German unification, and the modern welfare state. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Bismarck unified Germany through what he called blood and iron, then introduced the world's first national health insurance and old-age pensions — partly to undercut the socialists. Ruthlessness and welfare, from the same man.

questions.q: There was a Czech writer. His fiction portrays bewildering bureaucracy and existential anxiety. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Not merely bureaucratic — Kafkaesque means the system is impossible to argue with because nobody in it will admit to being in charge. Kafka asked his friend to burn all his manuscripts. His friend published them instead.

questions.q: Which word meaning "harsh, impoverished conditions" comes from an English novelist?
questions.f: Dickens was twelve when his father went to debtors' prison and he was sent to paste labels on bottles in a factory. He told almost nobody for the rest of his life, and wrote about it in every book he produced.

questions.q: Which word meaning "dramatic" comes from an English playwright?
questions.f: Shakespeare is the first recorded user of something like 1,700 English words — though first recorded often means only that his plays survived and the pamphlets did not. Either way, he was not shy about inventing one.

questions.q: There was an ancient Greek poet. Refers to the style or epic grandeur of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: We do not know whether Homer was one person, several, or a tradition. The poems were composed to be recited from memory, and their repeated phrases — swift-footed Achilles, the wine-dark sea — are the scaffolding that made that possible.

questions.q: There was an English poet. Style associated with *Paradise Lost* and elevated blank verse. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Milton went completely blind in his forties and composed Paradise Lost at night in his head, dictating each morning to whoever was available. Twelve books of epic verse, and he never saw a line of it written down.

questions.q: "Chaucerian" is named after a place.
questions.f: Chaucer wrote in English when serious writers used Latin or French, and largely settled which English would become standard. He also held a day job as a customs official on the London docks.

questions.q: There was an Irish satirist. Sharp political and social satire modeled on *Gulliver's Travels*. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: In A Modest Proposal, Swift suggested in flat reasonable prose that the Irish poor should sell their children as food. Readers who missed the satire were exactly the point — he was mimicking the economists of his day.

questions.q: There was an English poet. Romantic, rebellious, melancholic hero archetype. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Brooding, brilliant, self-destructive and impossible to advise. Byron largely invented the type by living it; a former lover called him mad, bad and dangerous to know, and the phrase has followed him for two centuries.

questions.q: There was a writer. Modern expression describing situations where denial itself is treated as evidence of guilt. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An accusation built so that denying it counts as proof — your protest shows how deep the problem goes. Named for Kafka's Trial, where the accused is never told the charge and cannot therefore answer it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "impractically idealistic" comes from a cervantes' fictional knight?
questions.f: Curiously, the word is pronounced quick-SOT-ic in English while the character is Key-HO-tay in Spanish — the adjective went one way and the name the other. Both mean chasing something noble and impossible.

questions.q: Which word meaning "miserly person" comes from a dickens character?
questions.f: Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in six weeks because he needed money, and published it himself. It has never been out of print, and Scrooge's name became the word for a miser within a few years.

questions.q: Which word meaning "excessively optimistic person" comes from an eleanor H. Porter's heroine?
questions.f: Pollyanna plays the glad game: find something to be pleased about in any disaster. The book was a bestseller in 1913, and her name turned into a mild insult for optimism that refuses to look at facts.

questions.q: "Lothario" is named after a person.
questions.f: From a 1703 play, The Fair Penitent, where Lothario seduces and abandons the heroine. He is on stage for a fraction of the play and is the only thing anybody remembers about it.

questions.q: There was a Venetian adventurer. Famous for numerous romantic affairs documented in his memoirs. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Casanova was a soldier, spy, violinist, and briefly a librarian at a Bohemian castle, which is where he wrote his memoirs out of boredom. They run to twelve volumes, and the romance is a small part of them.

questions.q: Which word meaning "romantic male lover" comes from a shakespeare character?
questions.f: Romeo is in love with a different girl, Rosaline, when the play opens, and forgets her the instant he sees Juliet. The whole tragedy takes place in about four days.

questions.q: There was a Spanish literary character. Became the universal symbol of a seducer. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: He first appears in a Spanish play of 1630 and has been rewritten ever since — by Moliere, Mozart, Byron and Shaw. Almost every version ends with him dragged off to hell, which has not dented his popularity.

questions.q: There was a character in *Trilby*. Manipulated others through psychological domination. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: In the 1894 novel Trilby, Svengali hypnotises a tone-deaf girl into a great singer who cannot perform without him. The book was a sensation, and gave English both a word and, from a character's hat, the trilby.

questions.q: Which word meaning "enormous" comes from a giant in Rabelais' novels?
questions.f: Rabelais's giant Gargantua was born calling for a drink, and in one episode a whole army shelters from the rain under his tongue. He is also, in the same book, sent to school and taught rather well.

questions.q: There was a voltaire's *Candide*. Absurdly optimistic philosopher believing everything happens for the best. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Dr Pangloss insists this is the best of all possible worlds while being hanged, dissected and enslaved in succession. Voltaire was mocking a real philosophical position, and did such a thorough job that the name became the argument against it.

questions.q: "Rip Van Winkle" is named after a place.
questions.f: He falls asleep in the Catskills, wakes twenty years later, and wanders into town still cheering for a king who has been gone since the Revolution. Washington Irving wrote it in England, homesick, in 1819.

questions.q: Which word meaning "highly analytical" comes from a conan Doyle detective?
questions.f: Conan Doyle modelled Holmes on his medical teacher Joseph Bell, who could deduce a patient's trade and travels before they spoke. Doyle killed Holmes off at a waterfall and public outrage forced him to bring him back.

questions.q: There was a holmes' companion. Explanation from within a fictional universe. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Watsonian explanation stays inside the story — Watson made a mistake in his notes. A Doylist one steps outside it — Conan Doyle forgot. Fans of every fictional world now use both terms.

questions.q: There was a holmes' adversary. Criminal mastermind opposing the detective. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Moriarty appears properly in one story and is mentioned in a handful of others. Conan Doyle invented him specifically as someone impressive enough to kill Holmes off with, and he has loomed over the canon ever since.

questions.q: There was an English philosopher. Belief in strong centralized authority to prevent chaos. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Without a strong state, Hobbes wrote, life would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. He was writing during the English Civil War, which rather explains the mood.

questions.q: There was an English philosopher. Emphasized natural rights and government by consent. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Locke argued government is legitimate only by the consent of the governed, and that people may replace one that fails them. Jefferson borrowed the structure of that argument almost directly for the Declaration of Independence.

questions.q: There was a French philosopher. Advocated the "general will" and natural human goodness. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Rousseau opened his most famous book with man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains. He also wrote a celebrated treatise on educating children while placing all five of his own in a foundling hospital.

questions.q: "Confucian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Confucius held only minor office and considered himself a failure. His students wrote down his conversations after his death, and those notes shaped Chinese government, family life and education for two thousand years.

questions.q: There was a Chinese philosopher. Based on harmony with the Tao ("the Way"). Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Tao Te Ching opens by saying that the Way which can be named is not the true Way — a book that begins by warning you it cannot do its job. It is one of the most translated texts in the world.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to Buddhism" comes from a religious teacher?
questions.f: Buddha is not a name but a title meaning the awakened one. Siddhartha Gautama was a prince who left the palace, saw sickness, age and death for the first time, and spent the rest of his life on what to do about them.

questions.q: The word "Christian" is named after…?
questions.f: The book of Acts records that followers were first called Christians at Antioch — and it was probably a nickname given by outsiders rather than one they chose. They adopted it anyway.

questions.q: There was a historical English term. Former English term for Muslims; now considered outdated because Muslims worship God, not Muhammad. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An outdated English term for Muslims, formed by analogy with Christian. It was dropped because it misdescribes the faith: Muhammad is regarded as a prophet, not an object of worship. Muslim is the correct word.

questions.q: Which word meaning "protestant denomination" comes from a German reformer?
questions.f: Luther set out ninety-five points for debate in 1517 and, thanks to the new printing press, they were all over Germany within weeks. He was arguing for reform, not a new church — the split happened anyway.

questions.q: There was a French theologian. Emphasized predestination and divine sovereignty. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Calvin turned Geneva into a model reformed city, strictly governed. The doctrine that God has already chosen the saved gave rise, oddly, to a famously hard-working culture — since worldly success might be a sign of it.

questions.q: "Wesleyan" is named after a place.
questions.f: John Wesley and his Oxford friends were mocked as Methodists for the methodical way they organised their prayer and study. They adopted the insult. Wesley rode an estimated 250,000 miles on horseback preaching.

questions.q: There was a christian monk. Monastic order following the Rule of St. Benedict. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Benedict's sixth-century Rule set out how a monastery should divide the day between prayer, work and reading. It is also a liqueur — made to a recipe a wine merchant claimed to have found in an old monastic manuscript.

questions.q: There was a Spanish priest. Founded the Order of Preachers. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Dominic founded an order of travelling preachers. Latin-speaking wits nicknamed them Domini canes — the hounds of the Lord — a pun the order seems to have enjoyed, since dogs turn up in their art.

questions.q: Which word meaning "religious order" comes from an Italian saint?
questions.f: Francis of Assisi gave away his inheritance, including the clothes he was wearing, and founded an order on absolute poverty. He is said to have preached to birds, and is now the patron saint of animals and ecology.

questions.q: There was a Spanish priest. Society of Jesus devoted to education and missionary work. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Ignatius Loyola was a soldier until a cannonball shattered his leg and he read the only books available during a long recovery. The order he founded became the great educational network of the Catholic world.

questions.q: There was a christian theologian. Philosophy and theology derived from Augustine's writings. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Augustine's Confessions is arguably the first autobiography in the Western tradition — a man examining his own mind in public. He prayed, famously, for chastity, but not yet.

questions.q: There was a medieval philosopher. Scholastic philosophy integrating Aristotle with Christian theology. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aquinas set out to reconcile Aristotle with Christian theology and produced a work of immense length. Near the end of his life he had an experience after which he stopped writing, saying everything he had written seemed like straw.

questions.q: "Machiavellian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Machiavelli wrote The Prince while out of a job, partly hoping to be hired again. Within decades English playwrights had turned his name into a stock villain who smiles while calculating exactly how to use you.

questions.q: There was a Norwegian politician. Collaborated with Nazi Germany during WWII. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Vidkun Quisling helped Germany occupy Norway in 1940, and his name became the English word for a traitor within about a week — while he was still alive to read it. He was executed in 1945.

questions.q: Which word meaning "organized refusal to deal with someone" comes from an Irish land agent?
questions.f: Captain Boycott was a land agent in Ireland who evicted tenants in 1880. The community simply stopped dealing with him — no worker, no shop, no post. He had to import labour under police guard to save his harvest, and left.

questions.q: There was a virginia landowner. The term likely derives from extrajudicial punishment associated with "Lynch's Law.". Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Probably from Charles Lynch, a Virginia judge whose unofficial wartime court handed out floggings. Lynch law began as a phrase for rough frontier justice and became the name for one of America's darkest habits.

questions.q: Which word meaning "manipulation of electoral boundaries" comes from a governor of Massachusetts?
questions.f: In 1812 Governor Elbridge Gerry approved a district shaped so oddly that a newspaper drew wings on it and called it a salamander. His name was hard-G — so strictly it should be gerrymander with a hard sound, which nobody says.

questions.q: Which word meaning "outline profile image" comes from a French finance minister?
questions.f: Etienne de Silhouette was finance minister for eight months and imposed such harsh economies that anything cheap was mocked as being a la Silhouette. Cut-paper profiles were the cheapest portraits going, and the insult stuck to them.

questions.q: Which word meaning "independent-minded person" comes from a texas rancher?
questions.f: Samuel Maverick was a Texas rancher who did not brand his cattle. Neighbours took to calling any unbranded animal a maverick — and then any person who refuses to carry anybody's mark.

questions.q: "Guillotine" is named after a place.
questions.f: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin opposed the death penalty and proposed the machine as a humane step toward abolishing it. He was appalled to have it named after him, and his family later petitioned unsuccessfully to have the name changed.

questions.q: Which word meaning "one-piece athletic garment" comes from a French trapeze artist?
questions.f: Jules Leotard invented the flying trapeze and performed in a knitted one-piece that let the audience see the body work. He also inspired the song about the daring young man on the flying trapeze.

questions.q: Which word meaning "knitted sweater" comes from a british general?
questions.f: The seventh Earl of Cardigan led the Charge of the Light Brigade — a catastrophic order, gallantly obeyed. He came home a celebrity, and the knitted waistcoat his officers wore in the Crimea took his name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "waterproof boot" comes from a british general?
questions.f: The duke asked his shoemaker for a boot tough enough for the field and neat enough for the evening. It became so fashionable that gentlemen wore them everywhere; the rubber version arrived decades later.

questions.q: There was a british field marshal. Sleeve style designed to accommodate his amputated arm. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Lord Raglan lost his right arm at Waterloo, and asked for his sleeve to be cut in one piece running to the collar so he could dress unaided. The design turned out to allow better movement and is now standard on sportswear.

questions.q: Which word meaning "vacuum cleaner" comes from an American businessman?
questions.f: William Hoover made leather goods. A department-store janitor named Murray Spangler built the vacuum cleaner out of a fan, a pillowcase and a broom handle — then sold the patent to Hoover, his wife's cousin.

questions.q: Which word meaning "photocopy" comes from a company?
questions.f: From Greek xeros graphos, dry writing, because the process needed no liquid ink. The inventor was turned down by more than twenty companies before one took it on. Xerox now sends letters asking people not to use it as a verb.

questions.q: Which word meaning "facial tissue" comes from a company?
questions.f: Launched in 1924 as a disposable cloth for removing cold cream. Customers kept writing in to say they were blowing their noses on it instead, so the company changed the advertising and the market.

questions.q: Which word meaning "vacuum flask" comes from a company?
questions.f: James Dewar invented the vacuum flask and never patented it. A German glassware firm did, ran a public competition to name it, and a resident of Munich won with thermos — Greek for hot.

questions.q: Which word meaning "moving staircase" comes from a company?
questions.f: Otis owned the trademark and lost it by using the word generically in its own advertising. A court ruled in 1950 that the company had turned its own brand into an ordinary noun.

questions.q: Which word meaning "acetylsalicylic acid" comes from a company?
questions.f: Bayer's trademark, lost as a war reparation — the Treaty of Versailles handed the name to the Allies in 1919. It is still a Bayer trademark in Germany and generic in Britain and America.

questions.q: Which word meaning "toy" comes from a company?
questions.f: The toy is thousands of years old, but the name is Filipino. Pedro Flores brought it to America in the 1920s; Donald Duncan bought his company, trademarked the word, and eventually lost the trademark for being too successful.

questions.q: Which word meaning "flying disc" comes from a company?
questions.f: Students at Yale threw empty pie tins from the Frisbie Pie Company. When Wham-O started selling a plastic flying disc they heard the students shouting Frisbie, respelled it, and used it as the brand.

questions.q: Which word meaning "table tennis" comes from a company?
questions.f: An English firm trademarked the sound the game makes. Everyone else had to call it table tennis, which is why the sport's governing body uses the duller name and the rest of us do not.

questions.q: "Velcro" is named after a place.
questions.f: George de Mestral came back from a walk and looked at the burrs stuck to his dog under a microscope — tiny hooks catching in loops. He spent eight years reproducing it, and named it from velours and crochet.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "search the internet" comes from a technology company?
questions.f: The company itself lobbied against this, worried that a brand which becomes a verb can lose its trademark. A court disagreed in 2017, ruling the name still identified the company. The verb had already won.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "digitally alter an image" comes from a software?
questions.f: Written by two brothers, one a PhD student and one working at Industrial Light and Magic. Adobe's style guide insists it is a proper adjective and asks people not to say photoshopped, which nobody has ever obeyed.

questions.q: There was an inventor. Whirlpool technology became associated with relaxation and hydrotherapy. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Candido Jacuzzi built the first pump so his young son could have arthritis hydrotherapy at home. The company only realised it had a leisure product years later, when customers started asking for the pump without the illness.

questions.q: There was a mythological king. Alternate adjective occasionally used instead of *Sisyphean*. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An occasional variant of Sisyphean. Both describe the same boulder rolling back down the same hill forever — and the fact that English cannot settle on one spelling is itself faintly Sisyphean.

questions.q: Which word meaning "excessively harsh" comes from an Athenian lawgiver?
questions.f: Asked why the penalty for petty theft was death, Draco reportedly said small crimes deserved it and he could think of nothing worse for the large ones. Athenians said his laws were written in blood rather than ink.

questions.q: There was a biblical king. Celebrated for wisdom and fair judgment. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Two women each claimed the same baby. Solomon called for a sword and offered them half each. One agreed; the other begged him to give the child away instead — and he handed the baby to her.

questions.q: "Judaic" is named after a person.
questions.f: From Judah, one of the twelve tribes, whose emblem was a lion. The name travelled from the tribe to a kingdom to a Roman province, and from there into the words Judaism and Jewish.

questions.q: There was a brother of Moses. Pertains to the hereditary priesthood descended from Aaron. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aaron was Moses's brother and did the talking, because Moses said he was slow of speech. The priesthood descended from him, so the family that spoke for Moses ended up speaking for everybody.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to Moses" comes from a biblical prophet?
questions.f: Careful — this is the Moses word, meaning of his law. The mosaic made of coloured tiles is unrelated: that one comes from the Muses, via rooms decorated in their honour. Two identical English words, two different origins.

questions.q: There was a biblical king. Refers to the royal lineage of David. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: David was a shepherd boy who became king, and the line descending from him mattered enormously to later writers — both Gospel genealogies take care to route Jesus back to him.

questions.q: Which word meaning "giant opponent" comes from a philistine giant?
questions.f: The giant loses because David refuses to fight the way giants fight. He turns down armour, keeps his sling, and wins at a distance — which makes the story less about size than about choosing your own contest.

questions.q: There was a biblical figure. Endured immense suffering while remaining faithful. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Job loses his family, his wealth and his health, and keeps asking why. The book never really answers him. The patience of Job is proverbial, though anyone who reads it notices he complains a great deal.

questions.q: Which word meaning "betrayer" comes from a disciple of Jesus?
questions.f: Judas gave up his teacher for thirty silver coins and marked him with a kiss so the soldiers would know which man to take. Two thousand years later, almost nobody names a child Judas.

questions.q: "Samaritan" is named after a place.
questions.f: The point of the parable is who the helper was: Samaritans and Judeans despised each other. A modern retelling would have to pick whichever group the listener likes least, which is uncomfortable, and deliberate.

questions.q: There was an American general. Defected to the British during the American Revolution. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Arnold was one of the ablest American generals of the Revolution before he changed sides. There is a monument at Saratoga to his wounded leg — a boot, with no name on it, honouring the part of him that stayed loyal.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "romantic balcony" comes from a shakespeare character?
questions.f: There is no balcony in Shakespeare's text. Juliet appears at a window; the word never occurs in the play. The balcony was added by an eighteenth-century adaptation and has been there ever since.

questions.q: Which word meaning "creator of something dangerous" comes from a mary Shelley's scientist?
questions.f: Frankenstein is the scientist, not the creature — the monster has no name at all. Mary Shelley was eighteen when she wrote it, during a wet summer holiday where the group agreed to each write a ghost story.

questions.q: Which word meaning "book of maps" comes from a titan?
questions.f: Mercator put a picture of Atlas holding up the world on the front of his collection of maps in 1595, and the name transferred from the picture to the book. Atlas himself held up the sky, not the Earth.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "fatal weakness" comes from a Greek warrior?
questions.f: His mother dipped him in the river Styx holding him by the heel, and that one patch stayed dry. Homer never mentions this — the heel appears in later versions, long after the Iliad.

questions.q: There was a goddess of health. Associated with disease prevention and cleanliness. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Daughter of the god of medicine, and her job was keeping people well rather than curing them. Her sister Panacea handled cures. Prevention and treatment, split between two sisters, which is roughly how medicine still divides.

questions.q: "Thanatos" is named after a person.
questions.f: The gentle death, as opposed to violent death, who was his brother. Freud later borrowed the name for a supposed drive toward destruction — a use the Greeks would not have recognised at all.

questions.q: Which word meaning "massive" comes from a Greek primordial gods?
questions.f: The Titans were the generation of gods before the Olympians, and they lost. Naming the largest ship afloat after a family famous chiefly for being overthrown was, in hindsight, an odd choice.

questions.q: Which word meaning "majestic" comes from a home of Greek gods?
questions.f: Mount Olympus was where the gods lived; Olympia, where the games were held, is a different place about two hundred miles away. English uses Olympian for both the majestic sense and the athletic one.

questions.q: Which word meaning "powerful female warrior" comes from a mythical warrior women?
questions.f: The river was named by a Spanish explorer who reported being attacked by women warriors. The bookshop was named after the river, because its founder wanted something that suggested enormous scale and started with A.

questions.q: Which word meaning "austere" comes from a Greek city-state?
