questions.f: Spartan boys left home at seven for military training and were underfed on purpose, so they would learn to steal food. A boy caught stealing was punished — not for the theft, but for being caught.

questions.q: There was an ancient Greek city. Renowned for ornate architecture and capitals. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Corinth was rich, and its architecture showed it. In Victorian England a Corinthian also meant a wealthy amateur sportsman — which is why an English football club founded by gentlemen amateurs is called Corinthian.

questions.q: There was an ancient Greek region. One of the classical Greek architectural orders. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The order with the scrolls at the top, like a ram's horns or a rolled scroll. Greek writers considered it the feminine order to the Doric's masculine — slimmer, more decorated, and set on a base.

questions.q: "Doric" is named after a place.
questions.f: The plain one — no base, no scrolls, just fluting and a flat top. The Parthenon is Doric. It is the oldest of the three orders and the one that looks most like a stone version of a wooden post.

questions.q: There was a Greek city. Most elaborate classical architectural order. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: The most decorated of the three, with carved acanthus leaves. The story goes that a sculptor saw a basket left on a girl's grave with an acanthus plant growing up around it, and built a column out of the image.

questions.q: Which word meaning "intricate or excessively complex" comes from an ancient city?
questions.f: The Eastern Roman Empire ran for a thousand years after Rome fell, with a court so layered in ceremony and intrigue that its name became the English word for anything needlessly complicated.

questions.q: Which word meaning "uncultured person" comes from an ancient people?
questions.f: The Philistines were a real people with cities, pottery and trade. Matthew Arnold popularised the cultural insult in the 1860s, aiming it at the English middle classes — so an ancient nation is now a synonym for bad taste.

questions.q: There was a Greek city-state. Reflects austere Spartan lifestyle. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: The famous dish was black broth — pork boiled in blood and vinegar. A visitor from another city tried it and said he now understood why Spartans were so willing to die in battle.

questions.q: There was a Greek sanctuary. Home of Apollo's oracle known for ambiguous prophecies. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The oracle told Croesus that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire. He attacked. The empire he destroyed was his own. Delphic answers were always true and almost never useful.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "costly victory" comes from a king of Epirus?
questions.f: Pyrrhus beat the Romans twice and lost so many men doing it that he reportedly said one more such victory and we are undone. Rome could replace its losses; he could not.

questions.q: "Laconic" is named after a person.
questions.f: Philip of Macedon warned Sparta that if he entered Laconia he would raze it to the ground. The Spartans sent back a one-word reply: If. He did not invade.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "laryngeal prominence" comes from a biblical first man?
questions.f: A medieval story held that a piece of the forbidden fruit stuck in Adam's throat and left a lump in every man since. The Bible never says the fruit was an apple either — that came from a Latin pun.

questions.q: There was a biblical figure. Pertaining to mankind's earliest state. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Adam simply means man or earth in Hebrew — he is named after the ground he was made from. Adamic language means the supposed original speech of humanity, before Babel scattered it.

questions.q: There was a biblical patriarch. Pertaining to the Flood or Noah's covenant. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: After the flood, the covenant with Noah is made with all humanity rather than one people, and the rainbow is its sign. Flood stories appear across Mesopotamian literature, including one a thousand years older.

questions.q: Which word meaning "relating to Abraham" comes from a biblical patriarch?
questions.f: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all trace themselves to Abraham, which is why they are grouped under his name. It is one of the few labels all three traditions accept.

questions.q: Which word meaning "one restored from apparent death" comes from a biblical figure?
questions.f: Raised after four days in the tomb. The name is now used for anything that comes back when it should not: Lazarus taxa in biology are species that reappear in the fossil record long after apparently going extinct.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "skeptic" comes from a disciple of Jesus?
questions.f: Thomas said he would not believe without putting his hand in the wounds. He is remembered for the doubt rather than for what he did next, which was to believe immediately once he was shown.

questions.q: "Prodigal" is named after a place.
questions.f: Prodigal means wastefully extravagant, not returning — the son is prodigal in the first half of the parable, before he comes home. People use it to mean the coming back, which is exactly backwards.

questions.q: There was a biblical follower of Jesus. Historically associated (incorrectly in tradition) with penitence. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Mary Magdalene was identified with a penitent sinner by a pope in 591, on no textual basis, and the Church formally separated them again in 1969. Her name also gave English maudlin — from paintings of her weeping.

questions.q: There was a jewish religious sect. New Testament portrayal emphasized legalism and hypocrisy. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Pharisees were a reform movement that made scripture accessible outside the Temple, and rabbinic Judaism descends from them. The English insult comes entirely from how the Gospels portray their arguments.

questions.q: There was a jewish priestly sect. Influential group in Second Temple Judaism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, and they rejected any belief in resurrection. When the Temple was destroyed in AD 70 they vanished with it, leaving the Pharisees to shape everything that came after.

questions.q: There was an ancient Mesopotamian city. Symbol of grandeur, decadence, and exile in biblical tradition. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Babylon really did have the scale the legends suggest — walls, ziggurats, and possibly gardens. Its reputation for decadence comes mostly from the people it conquered, who had every reason to be unkind.

questions.q: Which word meaning "confused mixture of voices or languages" comes from a biblical story?
questions.f: The Babylonians called their city bab-ilu, gate of the god. Hebrew writers heard it as balal, to confuse, and built the story of the scattered languages around the pun. The tower was probably a real ziggurat.

questions.q: Which word meaning "emperor or absolute ruler" comes from a Roman ruler?
questions.f: One family name became the word for supreme ruler in half of Europe, and outlasted the empire by fifteen centuries. Caesar himself was never emperor — the title did not exist yet when he was killed.

questions.q: "Kaiser" is named after a person.
questions.f: German emperors were Kaisers right up to 1918, and the word is Caesar worn down by two thousand years of German mouths. The pronunciation is actually closer to the original Latin than the English Caesar is.

questions.q: Which word meaning "russian emperor" comes from a via Latin *Caesar*?
questions.f: Russian rulers took the same Roman title, arguing that after Constantinople fell Moscow was the third Rome. English still uses it for anyone put in charge of a problem — a drugs tsar, a productivity tsar.

questions.q: There was a Roman dictator. Introduced sweeping calendar reform in 45 BC. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Caesar's reform in 45 BC required one transitional year of 445 days to drag the calendar back into line with the seasons. Romans called it the year of confusion.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "modern civil calendar" comes from a pope?
questions.f: By 1582 the Julian year was ten days out of step, so October simply lost ten days — people went to sleep on the 4th and woke on the 15th. Britain held out until 1752 and had to skip eleven.

questions.q: There was a Roman general. Avoided pitched battles to wear Hannibal down gradually. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Rome nicknamed Fabius the Delayer as an insult. After Hannibal destroyed a Roman army that did attack him head-on, it became a compliment, and Fabian has meant winning by patience ever since.

questions.q: There was a Roman statesman. Returned to farming after serving as dictator. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Given absolute power to save Rome, Cincinnatus won the war in about a fortnight, resigned, and went back to his farm. George Washington was compared to him constantly — and an American city is named for the society that admired him.

questions.q: There was a Greek philosopher. Founded the school of philosophical skepticism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Pyrrho argued you should suspend judgement about everything, since certainty is not available. Sceptics after him used his name. He is not the Pyrrhus of the costly victory — two different Greeks, frequently confused.

questions.q: "Stoicism" is named after a place.
questions.f: Named after a painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught. The core claim is that you control your own judgements and nothing else — and two of its greatest writers were an enslaved man and a Roman emperor.

questions.q: There was a Greek philosophers. Rejected wealth and social convention. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: From the Greek for dog-like, meant as an insult about living rough in public. The Cynics accepted it. Their point was that convention is arbitrary; modern cynicism, assuming everyone is selfish, is a much later invention.

questions.q: There was a Greek teachers. Known for persuasive rhetoric, sometimes regardless of truth. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Sophists were paid teachers of rhetoric in a city where winning an argument in court could save your life. Plato disliked them intensely, wrote the dialogues that survived, and their name has been an insult ever since.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "question-based teaching" comes from a Greek philosopher?
questions.f: Socrates claimed to know nothing and asked questions until the other person found the hole in their own answer. Athens executed him for it, which suggests the method works better than it is welcomed.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "plane geometry" comes from a Greek mathematician?
questions.f: Euclid's fifth postulate, about parallel lines, bothered mathematicians for two thousand years because it looked like it should be provable. It is not — and dropping it produces the curved geometries relativity needs.

questions.q: There was a Greek inventor. Device for raising water. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A spiral inside a tube: turn it and water climbs uphill. It is still used to move water and grain today, and versions have been found that predate Archimedes — he may have described it rather than invented it.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "fundamental geometry theorem" comes from a Greek mathematician?
questions.f: Babylonian tablets show the relationship a thousand years before Pythagoras. What his followers may have supplied is the proof — the argument that it must hold for every right triangle, not just the ones anyone measured.

questions.q: "Eratosthenes Sieve" is named after a person.
questions.f: Cross out every multiple of two, then of three, and keep going; what survives are the primes. The same man measured the circumference of the Earth using shadows in two cities and got within a few per cent.

questions.q: There was a Greek mathematician. Ancient algorithm for finding the greatest common divisor. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Keep replacing the larger number with the remainder until nothing is left over. It is the oldest algorithm still in daily use, and a version of it runs every time your browser sets up an encrypted connection.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "medical ethical oath" comes from a Greek physician?
questions.f: First, do no harm is not in it. That phrase comes from another of his works entirely. The actual oath swears by Apollo and includes clauses about not using a knife, which modern surgeons have quietly set aside.

questions.q: There was a Greek physician. Classical description of facial appearance before death. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Hippocrates described the sunken, drawn appearance of a face in the last stage of illness so precisely that the description was still being used two thousand years later, before machines could measure anything.

questions.q: There was a Greek physician. Medical practices based on Galen's teachings. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Galen dissected pigs and apes because Roman law forbade human dissection, then described human anatomy from what he found. His errors went uncorrected for fourteen hundred years, because questioning Galen was unthinkable.

questions.q: There was a Persian physician. Based on the influential *Canon of Medicine*. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was the standard European medical textbook for six centuries — longer than it was used in the world that produced it. He wrote it in Persia around 1025.

questions.q: There was a Flemish anatomist. Founder of modern human anatomy. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Vesalius dissected human bodies himself rather than lecturing while an assistant did the cutting, and found more than two hundred places where Galen was wrong. He published at twenty-eight and was attacked for it immediately.

questions.q: "Harveyan" is named after a place.
questions.f: Harvey proved blood circulates by simple arithmetic: the heart pumps more blood in an hour than the whole body contains, so it cannot be constantly made and consumed. It must go round. His practice suffered for saying so.

questions.q: There was a british surgeon. Introduced antiseptic surgical techniques. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Lister sprayed carbolic acid in operating theatres and death rates collapsed. Surgeons resented the implication that they carried infection on their own hands, and adoption took years longer than the evidence warranted.

questions.q: There was an English physician. Exhibiting features of Parkinson's disease. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The tremor Parkinson described is at its worst at rest and eases when the hand does something — the reverse of most tremors. That detail is still one of the first things a neurologist looks for.

questions.q: Which word meaning "exceptionally handsome man" comes from a beautiful youth loved by Aphrodite?
questions.f: The name is not Greek but Semitic — adon means lord, and the story travelled west from Phoenicia. So calling a handsome man an Adonis is a compliment in a language almost nobody using it knows.

questions.q: Which word meaning "step-by-step computational procedure" comes from a Persian mathematician?
questions.f: From al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician of the ninth century. His name latinised to Algoritmi. Another of his book titles gave English a second word — al-jabr became algebra.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of electric current" comes from a French physicist?
questions.f: Ampere founded the study of electromagnetism in a few weeks of intense work after hearing that a current deflects a compass needle. His father had been guillotined during the Revolution when he was eighteen.

questions.q: Which word meaning "tactile writing system" comes from a French educator?
questions.f: Louis Braille was blinded at three by an accident in his father's workshop. At fifteen he adapted a military code for reading messages in the dark into a six-dot alphabet. His school did not adopt it until after his death.

questions.q: "Chauvinism" is named after a person.
questions.f: Nicolas Chauvin was supposedly a soldier so devoted to Napoleon that he stayed loyal after everyone else gave up. Historians have never found evidence he existed. The word may be named after a man who was never born.

questions.q: Which word meaning "stimulate into action" comes from an Italian physician?
questions.f: Galvani made a dead frog's leg twitch with electricity and concluded animals carry their own vital force. Volta disagreed, and invented the battery to prove it. Galvani was wrong, and English kept his name anyway.

questions.q: There was a Scottish engineer. Revolutionized road-building with compacted crushed stone. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: McAdam worked out that a road needs no heavy stone foundation if it is raised, drained, and surfaced with small angular stones that lock together under traffic. Add tar to keep the dust down and you get tarmac.

questions.q: There was a French military officer. Known for relentless drilling and strict discipline. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Jean Martinet drilled Louis XIV's infantry into the best in Europe and was loathed for it. He was killed at the siege of Duisburg in 1672 by his own side's artillery, which some of his troops are said to have found fitting.

questions.q: Which word meaning "grand tomb" comes from a ruler of Caria?
questions.f: Mausolus ruled a small kingdom and his widow built him a tomb so vast it became one of the Seven Wonders. It stood for sixteen centuries, was destroyed by earthquakes, and its stone was carted off to build a castle.

questions.q: Which word meaning "arch-rival" comes from a Greek goddess of retribution?
questions.f: Nemesis did not punish crime — she punished excess. Too much luck, too much boasting, and she arrived to restore the balance. Her name now means an unbeatable rival, which is a demotion from goddess of cosmic accounting.

questions.q: There was a daughter of Asclepius. Represented universal healing in Greek mythology. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Panacea and Hygieia were sisters, daughters of the god of medicine — one the cure for everything, the other the prevention. English kept both, and uses panacea almost entirely to say that no such thing exists.

questions.q: "Sandwich" is named after a place.
questions.f: The Earl of Sandwich asked for meat between bread so he could keep working — or keep gambling, depending on who is telling it. The gambling version comes from a political opponent, so it may be an insult that stuck.

questions.q: Which word meaning "musical instrument" comes from a Belgian instrument maker?
questions.f: Adolphe Sax survived falling from a third floor, swallowing a pin, drinking acid by mistake and a gunpowder explosion, all before adulthood. His mother said he was a child doomed to misfortune. He invented the saxophone at thirty.

questions.q: There was a Greek herald. His voice was said by Homer to equal that of fifty ordinary men. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Homer says the herald Stentor could shout as loudly as fifty men together. In one version he challenges a god to a shouting match, loses, and dies of it — which is a very specific way to go.

questions.q: There was a wealthy Greek colony. Celebrated for luxury, pleasure, and extravagance. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Sybaris was so wealthy that its citizens were said to have banned noisy trades from the city so nobody's sleep was disturbed. A rival city destroyed it in 510 BC and diverted a river over the ruins.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of magnetic field strength" comes from a serbian-American inventor?
questions.f: Tesla claimed to see detailed visions of his inventions before building them, and tested some purely in his head. He died in a New York hotel room, owing money, having given away most of the patents that made others rich.

questions.q: Which word meaning "unit of power" comes from a Scottish engineer?
questions.f: Watt did not invent the steam engine — he made an existing one three times more efficient by adding a separate condenser. He also coined horsepower, as a sales device to explain his engines to people who owned horses.

questions.q: Which word meaning "rigid airship" comes from a German airship pioneer?
questions.f: Count Zeppelin was fifty-two and retired when he started building airships. The Hindenburg disaster ended the industry in thirty-seven seconds of newsreel — and a British rock band took the name a generation later.

questions.q: "Babbitt" is named after a person.
questions.f: Sinclair Lewis invented a realtor named George Babbitt who bought whatever his neighbours bought and believed whatever his club believed. Readers recognised him instantly — and within a year Americans were calling any such man a Babbitt.

questions.q: There was an anti-heroine of Thackeray's Vanity Fair. Born poor, she charmed and schemed her way up through English society without ever quite being caught. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Thackeray refused to give his novel a hero, so he gave it Becky Sharp instead: penniless, brilliant, and willing to flatter anyone who might raise her a rung. Readers were supposed to disapprove. Most of them rooted for her anyway.

questions.q: There was an English philosopher. He judged every law and custom by one test: does it increase happiness for the greatest number. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Jeremy Bentham thought morality should be arithmetic — add up the happiness, subtract the suffering, keep whatever comes out positive. He left his body to University College London, where his preserved skeleton, dressed in his own clothes, still sits in a cabinet.

questions.q: There was a heroine of Flaubert's Madame Bovary. She read romantic novels until she could no longer see her ordinary life clearly. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Emma Bovary read so many romances that her real life — a country doctor, a quiet village — became unbearable by comparison. The French coined bovarysme for that exact ache: mistaking the daydream for the life you were owed.

questions.q: There was a land of giants in Swift's Gulliver's Travels. Gulliver, a normal man, reached a country where wasps were the size of birds and he could be carried in a pocket. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Swift sent Gulliver first to Lilliput, where he was a giant, then to Brobdingnag, where he was a toy. English kept both: lilliputian for the tiny, Brobdingnagian for the colossal. Only one of them is hard to spell.

questions.q: There was an English preacher and author of The Pilgrim's Progress. He wrote his allegory in plain, forceful English while imprisoned for preaching without a licence. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: John Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress in Bedford jail, turning a Christian's life into a journey past the Slough of Despond and Vanity Fair. He had almost no schooling, and his plain thundering English outsold nearly every book in the language.

questions.q: There was a naive hero of Voltaire's 1759 satire. He was taught that this is the best of all possible worlds, then survived earthquake, war, and shipwreck still half-believing it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Voltaire wrote Candide in three days to mock philosophers who insisted everything happens for the best. His hero endures catastrophe after catastrophe, and ends up concluding only this: we must cultivate our garden.

questions.q: "Cassandra" is named after a place.
questions.f: Cassandra saw Troy burn years before it happened. She warned everyone. Apollo's curse meant her family heard her perfectly and dismissed her every time — the cruellest gift in Greek myth, and now the word for any warning nobody heeds.

questions.q: There was an enchantress in Homer's Odyssey. She fed Odysseus's crew a drugged feast and turned them into pigs. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Circe welcomed Odysseus's sailors with wine and cheese, then touched them with her wand and watched them drop to all fours as swine. Odysseus, protected by a herb from Hermes, was the one guest she could not transform.

questions.q: There was a Roman statesman and orator. His speeches set the standard for balanced, rhythmic Latin prose for the next two thousand years. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Cicero could hold the Roman Senate for hours with sentences built like architecture. Renaissance scholars admired him so much that some refused to use any Latin word he had not used first — a fussiness their rivals mocked as Ciceronian.

questions.q: There was a florentine poet. His Inferno mapped hell in nine descending circles with terrible precision. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Exiled from Florence on pain of burning, Dante spent his banishment writing a tour of the afterlife — and quietly placed several of his political enemies in hell. A Dantesque scene is one of infernal, orderly horror.

questions.q: There was an Athenian orator. He overcame a speech impediment to become the most forceful public speaker in Greece. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Demosthenes is said to have practised with pebbles in his mouth and shouted over the surf to strengthen his voice. He turned that hard-won delivery on Philip of Macedon in speeches so fierce that attacks on any leader are still called philippics.

questions.q: There was a Greek god of wine and theatre. His festivals celebrated ecstasy and loss of self, the opposite of calm reason. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Nietzsche split art in two: Apollonian for order and clarity, Dionysian for ecstasy and abandon. Both named for gods — Apollo the composed archer, Dionysus the god whose worshippers danced themselves out of their own minds.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a place of fabulous, unattainable wealth" comes from a legendary golden king of a South American tribe?
questions.f: El Dorado means 'the gilded one' — originally a person, not a place. A Muisca chief really did coat himself in gold dust for a ritual on Lake Guatavita. Spanish rumour inflated one man into a city, and expeditions died searching for it.

questions.q: "Euhemerism" is named after a person.
questions.f: Euhemerus claimed to have found an inscription on a distant island proving Zeus had been an ordinary king. Nobody has ever located the island, but the idea stuck: euhemerism is the theory that every god started out as somebody's grandfather.

questions.q: There was a comic knight in Shakespeare's Henry IV. Fat, cowardly, boastful and irresistibly funny, he stole every scene he appeared in. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Falstaff lies about his own bravery so extravagantly that his friends count the exaggerations for sport. Legend says Queen Elizabeth enjoyed him so much she asked Shakespeare for a play showing the fat knight in love.

questions.q: There was a scholar of German legend who traded his soul to the devil. He wanted unlimited knowledge and pleasure, and signed away eternity to get them. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The real Johann Faust was a wandering German magician. Legend gave him a contract with the devil, Marlowe and Goethe gave him great plays, and English gained the Faustian bargain — a deal that pays now and ruins you later.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a person of flawless nobility and purity" comes from a knight of Arthur's Round Table?
questions.f: Every knight at the Round Table went looking for the Grail. Only Galahad, so pure he could sit in the one chair that killed all other occupants, was permitted to find it — and having found it, he was taken straight to heaven.

questions.q: There was a legendary king of Phrygia. His ox-cart was tied with a knot so intricate that an oracle promised Asia to whoever loosed it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: For centuries nobody untied the Gordian knot. Alexander the Great arrived, considered it briefly, and cut it in half with his sword. He went on to conquer Asia, which suggests the oracle accepted his method.

questions.q: There was a title character of Shakespeare's tragedy. Told to avenge his father, he spends four acts examining the question from every angle. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hamlet has the proof, the motive, and the opportunity by act three — and still stops to ask whether being is better than not being. Shakespeare made indecision so gripping that the prince's name became the word for it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a greedy snatcher" comes from a winged snatchers in Greek myth?
questions.f: The Harpies were storm spirits with women's faces and birds' bodies, sent to snatch the food from Phineus's table again and again. Their name comes from the Greek for 'snatchers', and it is still what we call anything that will not stop grabbing.

questions.q: "Hectoring" is named after a place.
questions.f: This one is unfair to Hector. In the Iliad he is the most decent man in the war — a devoted father defending his city. Later English writers recast him as a swaggerer, and to hector has meant to bully ever since.

questions.q: There was a Greek arsonist. He burned down the Temple of Artemis purely so that history would remember his name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Herostratus torched one of the Seven Wonders of the World and freely confessed his motive: fame. Ephesus made it a capital crime to speak his name, hoping to erase him. You are reading it now, which tells you how well that worked.

questions.q: Which word meaning "keenly observant and deductive" comes from a detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle?
questions.f: Conan Doyle based Holmes on his medical teacher Joseph Bell, who could diagnose a patient's trade and travels before they spoke. Doyle killed Holmes off at a waterfall; public outrage was so fierce he had to bring him back.

questions.q: There was a titan of light in Greek myth. Father of the sun, moon and dawn, his name means 'he who goes above'. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hyperion fathered Helios the sun, Selene the moon, and Eos the dawn. Hamlet uses him as the measure of magnificence — comparing his noble father to Hyperion and his uncle to a satyr. The tallest living tree on Earth carries the name.

questions.q: There was a son of Daedalus in Greek myth. Given wings of wax and feathers, he ignored his father's warning and flew too near the sun. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Daedalus warned his son twice: not too low, or the sea will soak the feathers; not too high, or the sun will melt the wax. Icarus flew high anyway. The stretch of water where he fell is still called the Icarian Sea.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a traitor, especially one who betrays a friend" comes from the disciple who betrayed Jesus?
questions.f: Judas gave up his teacher for thirty silver coins and marked him with a kiss so the soldiers would know which man to take. Two thousand years later the name is still a synonym for betrayal, and almost nobody names a child Judas.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a person with two violently opposed personalities" comes from a twin identities in Stevenson's 1886 novella?
questions.f: Stevenson is said to have written the first draft in three days, burned it after his wife's criticism, and rewritten the whole thing in three more. The result gave English its standard phrase for anyone who is two different people.

questions.q: "Jezebel" is named after a person.
questions.f: Jezebel painted her face and dressed her hair before meeting the men who came to overthrow her — defiant to the last minute. The Bible meant it as a portrait of vanity; her name has been an insult in English for four hundred years.

questions.q: There was a Czech-German writer. His characters are trapped by rules nobody will explain, in systems with no visible person in charge. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Kafka wrote about a man arrested for a crime the court refuses to name, and a surveyor who can never reach the castle that employs him. He asked his friend to burn all of it after his death. His friend published everything instead.

questions.q: There was a Roman general and famous host. He retired from war to throw banquets so extravagant they became proverbial. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Asked why he had ordered a magnificent dinner when he was eating alone, Lucullus is said to have replied that tonight Lucullus dines with Lucullus. He also brought the cherry tree to Italy, which may be his more useful legacy.

questions.q: There was a florentine diplomat and writer. The Prince advised rulers that keeping power sometimes requires setting honesty aside. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Machiavelli wrote The Prince while out of a job, partly hoping to be hired again. Within decades English playwrights had turned his name into a stock villain — the Machiavel — who smiles at you while planning exactly how to use you.

questions.q: There was a character in Sheridan's play The Rivals. She reached for grand words and grabbed the wrong ones, calling someone the very pineapple of politeness. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Sheridan named her from the French mal a propos, 'badly suited'. She meant to call a man the pinnacle of politeness and called him the pineapple instead — and every mixed-up word since has carried her name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "lacking a wise guide or adviser" comes from an odysseus's old friend in the Odyssey?
questions.f: When Odysseus sailed for Troy he left his son in the care of a friend named Mentor. The goddess Athena kept borrowing that shape to deliver advice — so the word for a trusted guide is really the name of a disguise.

questions.q: "Merlinic" is named after a place.
questions.f: Merlin appears first in a twelfth-century history that presented him as fact. He is said to have aged backwards, remembering the future and forgetting the past — which is one way to explain a prophet who always knows what happens next.

questions.q: There was an English poet. Paradise Lost set the standard for grand, sweeping epic in English. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Milton went completely blind in his forties and composed Paradise Lost in his head at night, dictating each morning to whoever was available — often his daughters. Twelve books of epic poetry, and he never saw a line of it written down.

questions.q: There was an American writer who coined the term in 1942. Wylie attacked what he saw as smothering sentimentality about American mothers. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Philip Wylie coined momism in Generation of Vipers, a book so scathing that it made him famous and disliked in equal measure. It is one of the rare eponyms built not from a person's name but from what a whole country called its mothers.

questions.q: There was a Greek god of dreams. He shaped the human figures that appear in dreams — his name comes from morphe, 'form'. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Morpheus did not bring sleep; he supplied the people in your dreams, taking their shapes himself. When a chemist isolated a powerful sleep-bringing drug from opium in 1804 he named it morphine after the same god.

questions.q: There was a Greek hero of Homer's Odyssey. He took ten years to sail home from Troy, surviving by cunning rather than strength. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Odysseus escaped a cyclops by telling it his name was Nobody, so that its cries for help made no sense to the neighbours. Ten years of that kind of thinking got him home, and gave English both odyssey and Odyssean.

questions.q: There was a wife of Odysseus in the Odyssey. Besieged by suitors, she promised to choose one when her weaving was done, then unpicked it every night. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Penelope told a hall full of suitors she would remarry once she finished weaving a shroud. Each night she quietly unravelled the day's work. She held them off for three years before a servant gave her away.

questions.q: Which word meaning "cheerfully naive" comes from a genial hero of Dickens's The Pickwick Papers?
questions.f: The Pickwick Papers made the twenty-four-year-old Dickens famous in monthly instalments. It also gave English a strange, useful phrase: to mean something in a Pickwickian sense is to insist your insult does not count.

questions.q: "Protean" is named after a person.
questions.f: Proteus knew everything but hated being asked. Grab him and he becomes a lion, then a snake, then running water, then a tree — and only when you have held on through all of it does he give up and tell you the truth.

questions.q: There was a French monk, physician and writer. His giant heroes Gargantua and Pantagruel eat, drink and joke on an enormous scale. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Rabelais wrote about giants so large that a whole army once sheltered under one's tongue. His books were banned by the theologians of the Sorbonne, which did nothing to slow their sales and gave French a word for cheerful excess.

questions.q: There was an Israelite king renowned for wisdom. Faced with two women claiming one baby, he proposed dividing it and identified the true mother by who refused. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Two women each swore the baby was hers. Solomon called for a sword and offered to give each of them half. One agreed; the other begged him to give the child away instead — and he handed the baby to her.

questions.q: There was a moneylender in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice. He held a debtor to a contract promising a pound of the man's own flesh. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Shylock's bond entitles him to a pound of flesh, and the court agrees it is valid — then rules he may take flesh but not one drop of blood, because the contract never mentioned blood. He loses on the same literal reading he demanded.

questions.q: Which word meaning "idealistic" comes from an ideal island in Thomas More's 1516 book?
questions.f: Thomas More described a perfect island republic and named it, in Greek, No Place. Everyone since has used utopia to mean a paradise, missing the pun. More was beheaded by Henry VIII, which was not utopian at all.

questions.q: There was an Italian physicist. He built the first battery, a stack of zinc and copper discs that produced steady current. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked cloth between them and made electricity flow steadily for the first time. Napoleon made him a count. The volt is named for him too, so he is one of very few people who are twice a unit.

questions.q: There was an Athenian general and politician. Brilliant, beautiful and completely unreliable, he changed sides between Athens, Sparta and Persia. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Alcibiades led Athens, defected to Sparta, advised Persia, then came home to cheering crowds. Socrates taught him and could not steady him. He is the ancient world's model for the dazzling person you should probably not trust.

questions.q: "Antigonean" is named after a place.
questions.f: Creon forbade the burial of Antigone's brother on pain of death. She scattered earth over his body anyway and told the king to his face that no decree of his could overrule the unwritten laws. She was walled up alive for it.

questions.q: There was a hundred-eyed giant in Greek myth. Hera set him to guard a prisoner because some of his hundred eyes stayed open while the rest slept. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hermes eventually bored Argus to sleep with stories and killed him. Hera gathered his hundred eyes and set them into the tail of her peacock, which is why the bird still looks like it is watching you from every direction.

questions.q: There was a Cretan princess in Greek myth. She gave Theseus a ball of thread to unwind so he could find his way back out of the Labyrinth. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Theseus could kill the Minotaur; the harder problem was leaving. Ariadne handed him thread to unspool on the way in. Mathematicians still call the technique of solving a maze by exhaustive tracking an Ariadne's thread.

questions.q: There was a Roman god of wine. His festivals were famous for wild dancing and drinking. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Rome so distrusted the Bacchanalia that the Senate banned them in 186 BC and executed thousands of participants. The god survived the crackdown, and English kept bacchic and bacchanal for any party that goes well past sensible.

questions.q: There was a Byzantine general. He won back much of the Roman west for Justinian and was repaid with suspicion and disgrace. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Belisarius reconquered North Africa and Italy for an emperor who never quite trusted him, and was twice stripped of command. A later legend, probably false, had him blinded and begging in the streets — a story too good for painters to resist.

questions.q: There was a Greek hero who rode Pegasus. He was sent to a king carrying a sealed letter that requested his own execution. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Bellerophon delivered his own death warrant, unaware, because he could not read the sealed tablet he carried. The king who received it sent him to fight the Chimera instead — and he survived that too, on the back of the winged horse Pegasus.

questions.q: There was a hundred-handed giant in Greek myth. One of three brothers with fifty heads and a hundred arms apiece who fought for Zeus against the Titans. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Zeus was losing the war against the Titans until he freed three hundred-handed giants from the underworld. Briareus and his brothers hurled three hundred boulders at once, and the Titans broke. Some jobs need more hands than others.

questions.q: "Burkean" is named after a person.
questions.f: Burke supported the American colonists and opposed the French revolutionaries, which sounds inconsistent until you notice his rule: mend what exists, do not tear it down and start fresh. His prediction that France would end under a general came true.

questions.q: Which word meaning "imperial" comes from a Roman general and dictator?
questions.f: Caesar's name outlived his empire twice over: German emperors were Kaisers and Russian ones Tsars, both worn-down forms of Caesar. The surgical caesarean also carries it, though the old story that he was born that way is almost certainly untrue.

questions.q: There was a Roman emperor. Ancient historians recorded him as cruel and unhinged, and said he planned to make his horse a consul. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Caligula was a soldiers' nickname meaning 'little boot' — he wore a miniature army uniform as a child on campaign with his father. The cuddly nickname stuck to one of the most feared names in Roman history.

questions.q: There was a nymph in Homer's Odyssey. She kept Odysseus on her island for seven years, offering immortality if he would stay. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Calypso offered Odysseus eternal youth and a beautiful island forever. He sat on the shore and wept because he wanted to go home to a middle-aged wife on a rocky one. The gods eventually made her let him go.

questions.q: There was a Roman statesman. Famously austere and moralising, he ended every speech by demanding the destruction of Carthage. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Whatever the Senate was debating — roads, taxes, anything — Cato finished his speech with the same line: and furthermore, Carthage must be destroyed. He kept it up for years. Eventually Rome destroyed Carthage.

questions.q: There was three-headed dog guarding the Greek underworld. He let the dead in and let nobody back out. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Cerberus had three heads so at least one was always awake. The trick was music — Orpheus played him to sleep — or cake, since the Romans buried honey cakes with the dead specifically as a bribe. Hence a sop to Cerberus.

questions.q: There was a whirlpool monster in the Odyssey. She swallowed the sea three times a day, facing the six-headed Scylla across a narrow strait. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Odysseus had to steer between Scylla's six heads and Charybdis's whirlpool. Choosing Scylla cost him six men; Charybdis would have cost the ship. Between Scylla and Charybdis still means a choice between two disasters.

questions.q: "Clytemnestran" is named after a place.
questions.f: Agamemnon sacrificed their daughter to get his fleet to Troy. Clytemnestra waited ten years, welcomed him home across a purple carpet, and killed him in his bath. Greek tragedy rarely takes a clear side on which of them was worse.

questions.q: There was a king of Lydia. His kingdom's gold-rich rivers made him a byword for wealth while he still lived. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Croesus asked an oracle whether to attack Persia and was told he would destroy a great empire. He attacked. The empire he destroyed was his own. Rich as Croesus survived him by two and a half thousand years.

questions.q: There was a master craftsman of Greek myth. He built the Labyrinth on Crete, then wings to escape from the island he had made inescapable. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Daedalus designed the Labyrinth so cunningly that he could barely find his own way out of it. King Minos imprisoned him to keep the secret, so he built wings. His son Icarus did not follow the flight instructions.

questions.q: There was a Greek hero at Troy. In the Iliad he fights so boldly he wounds two gods, Aphrodite and Ares, in a single day. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Diomedes is the only mortal in the Iliad to wound two gods in one afternoon. Athena lends him the sight to tell gods from men on the battlefield, and he uses it immediately to pick a fight with the god of war.

questions.q: There was a daughter of Agamemnon in Greek tragedy. She urged her brother to kill their mother in revenge for their father's murder. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Jung named it in 1913 as the daughters' counterpart to Freud's Oedipus complex. Freud disliked the term and never really used it. The Electra of the plays is less a case study than a study in how long a person can hold a grudge.

questions.q: There was a Dutch humanist scholar. He argued for reform through scholarship and gentle satire rather than schism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Erasmus produced the Greek New Testament that Luther translated from, then spent the Reformation refusing to join either side. Both sides attacked him. He said he would rather be a spectator than a soldier in a war of words.

questions.q: There was a Greek mathematician. His Elements built all of geometry from five plain postulates and became the model of rigorous proof. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Euclid's Elements was a school textbook for over two thousand years — the longest run of any book but the Bible. Asked by a king for a shortcut, he is supposed to have replied that there is no royal road to geometry.

questions.q: "Fabian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Rome nicknamed Fabius the Delayer as an insult; after Hannibal destroyed a Roman army that did attack, it became a compliment. Britain's Fabian Society took the name in 1884 to signal socialism by patience rather than revolution.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Florence" comes from a city in Tuscany, Italy?
questions.f: Catherine de' Medici left Florence in 1533 to marry the future king of France, reportedly bringing her own cooks and a fondness for spinach. Whether or not the story is true, French menus have called spinach dishes a la florentine ever since.

questions.q: There was an Italian astronomer and physicist. He discovered Jupiter's four largest moons and framed the principle that motion looks the same to all steadily moving observers. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: In January 1610 Galileo pointed a homemade telescope at Jupiter and saw three little stars beside it. Four nights later they had moved. They were moons, orbiting something other than Earth — and the sky was never the same shape again.

questions.q: There was a statue brought to life in Greek myth. The sculptor Pygmalion fell in love with his own ivory carving and Aphrodite made her real. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Pygmalion carved a woman more perfect than any living one and then could not stop loving her. Aphrodite took pity and warmed the ivory to skin. Shaw reused the plot in Pygmalion, which became My Fair Lady.

questions.q: There was three snake-haired sisters of Greek myth. Anyone who met the gaze of a Gorgon turned instantly to stone. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: There were three Gorgons, but only Medusa could be killed. Perseus managed it by never looking at her directly — he watched her reflection in his polished shield and struck at what he saw there.

questions.q: There was a tree nymphs of Greek myth. Each was bound to one particular tree and died when it died. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A dryad could wander the forest. A hamadryad could not: she lived inside a single tree and her life ended with it, so cutting one down was murder. Naturalists later borrowed the name for the king cobra.

questions.q: There was a Roman poet. His satires teased human folly with a smile rather than attacking it with a knife. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Roman satire came in two flavours: Horatian, which laughs at you, and Juvenalian, which wants you punished. Horace also gave us carpe diem — seize the day — from a poem about opening the wine now rather than later.

questions.q: "Irenic" is named after a place.
questions.f: Eirene was one of three sisters who kept the seasons and the social order. Athens raised a statue of her holding the infant god of wealth, making the point plainly: peace is what makes prosperity possible.

questions.q: There was a river and river-god of Thebes. The Ismenus ran through Thebes, so poets used the name to mean Theban. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Greek poets rarely said Thebes when they could say something more ornate. Ismenean, after the river running past the city, was the elegant option — the kind of word that tells you the writer had a classical education.

questions.q: Which word meaning "majestic and genial" comes from a Roman king of the gods, also called Jupiter?
questions.f: Jove gave English two words with opposite moods. Jovial means cheerful, because Jupiter's influence was thought lucky. Saturnine means gloomy, from Saturn. Your temperament, medieval doctors believed, depended on which planet was up when you were born.

questions.q: There was a Greek satirist. He wrote mocking dialogues, including a voyage to the moon presented as a straight-faced travel report. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Lucian wrote A True Story, about sailing to the moon and meeting its army — and opened by announcing that everything in it was a lie. Scholars call it the first science fiction, written eighteen centuries before the rockets.

questions.q: There was a legendary lawgiver of Sparta. He is credited with the harsh code that turned Sparta into a permanent military camp. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Lycurgus supposedly made the Spartans swear to keep his laws until he returned, then left and never came back — binding them forever by a technicality. Whether he existed at all is still argued over.

questions.q: There was the mortal Gorgon of Greek myth. Her hair was a mass of living snakes and her gaze turned men to stone. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Perseus cut off Medusa's head and the winged horse Pegasus sprang from her neck. He kept the head as a weapon — it worked just as well detached — and eventually gave it to Athena, who mounted it on her shield.

questions.q: There was a Roman goddess of wisdom and crafts. She sprang fully armed from Jupiter's head, and became the patron of thought and skill. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Minerva was born from her father's skull, fully grown and already in armour, after he swallowed her mother. The owl on her shoulder is why owls have stood for wisdom in Western art for two thousand years.

questions.q: "Myrmidon" is named after a person.
questions.f: Myrmex is Greek for ant. When a plague emptied the island of Aegina, Zeus turned its ants into people — and they kept the ant temperament: tireless, obedient, and utterly without independent opinions.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a sea nymph" comes from an old man of the sea in Greek myth?
questions.f: Nereus had fifty daughters and they were the good sort of sea spirit — they helped sailors rather than drowning them. Neptune's second-largest moon is called Nereid, and so is a whole class of bristly marine worms.

questions.q: There was a queen of Thebes in Greek myth. She boasted of her fourteen children, the gods killed them all, and she wept until she turned to stone. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Niobe said she was luckier than a goddess who had only two children. Apollo and Artemis — the two children in question — killed all fourteen of hers. She wept until she became a rock, and the rock kept weeping.

questions.q: There was a legendary musician of Greek myth. His playing moved stones and trees, and persuaded the lord of the dead to release his wife. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Orpheus played so beautifully that Hades agreed to release Eurydice — on one condition: do not look back until you are both in daylight. He was almost out when he turned around to check she was following.

questions.q: There was a Greek name for Pharaoh Ramesses II. Shelley's 1818 sonnet describes his shattered statue boasting in a desert where nothing else remains. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Shelley wrote the sonnet as a bet with a friend over who could write the better poem about Egypt. The inscription in it — look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair — sits on a broken statue in an empty desert.

questions.q: There was an Athenian statesman. He led Athens through the decades that built the Parthenon and produced its greatest drama. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Pericles spent the treasury of an alliance on rebuilding his own city, which the allies noticed. The Parthenon was the result. He died of plague three years into the war that ended the age named after him.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Phoenicia" comes from an ancient seafaring civilisation of the Levant?
questions.f: The Phoenicians were merchants, not conquerors, and their greatest export was not cloth or cedar but the alphabet. Every letter you are reading descends from marks made by traders who needed a quick way to keep accounts.

questions.q: "Plutonian" is named after a place.
questions.f: Poe's raven comes from the Night's Plutonian shore. When an eleven-year-old girl suggested Pluto for the new planet in 1930, the underworld god fit — it was the coldest, darkest, farthest thing anyone had found.

questions.q: There was a titan of Greek myth. He stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity, and was chained to a rock for it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Zeus chained Prometheus to a mountain and sent an eagle to eat his liver each day; it grew back each night. Mary Shelley subtitled Frankenstein 'The Modern Prometheus' — a warning about the cost of stealing fire.

questions.q: There was a Greek poet of Lesbos. She wrote in a distinctive four-line stanza that now carries her name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Sappho was so admired that Plato called her the tenth Muse, yet almost all of her nine books are lost — we have one complete poem and a drift of fragments, some recovered from ancient rubbish dumps in Egypt.

questions.q: There was a Roman god and the slowest visible planet. Astrologers blamed Saturn's cold, sluggish influence for gloomy temperaments. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Medieval doctors believed the planet overhead at your birth set your personality for life. Saturn, slow and cold and distant, produced the melancholy sort. The planet has moved on; the word has not.

questions.q: There was an Athenian hero of Greek myth. He entered the Cretan Labyrinth, killed the Minotaur, and found his way back out. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Athens had been sending fourteen young people into the Labyrinth every nine years as tribute. Theseus volunteered to be one of them, killed the monster at the centre, and ended the tribute — which is how you get a city named after you.

questions.q: There was an ancient Greek city in Boeotia. Home of Oedipus, Antigone and Cadmus, it supplied Greek tragedy with its darkest family. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Thebes was where Greek tragedy went for its worst stories: a king who married his mother, a daughter buried alive, brothers who killed each other at the gates. Alexander the Great later flattened the city, sparing only the poet Pindar's house.

questions.q: There was a Greek keeper of the winds. He gave Odysseus a bag holding every wind but the one he needed. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aeolus bagged up the contrary winds so Odysseus could sail straight home. In sight of Ithaca the crew opened the bag, assuming it held treasure, and blew themselves all the way back. Geologists still call wind-blown sand aeolian.

questions.q: "Agamemnonian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Agamemnon won the ten-year war and survived the whole of it, only to be killed in his own bathroom within hours of arriving home. Schliemann dug up a gold funeral mask at Mycenae and cabled that he had gazed on the face of Agamemnon. It was three centuries too old.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a figure of great strength brought down by wounded pride" comes from a Greek warrior at Troy?
questions.f: Ajax was the wall of the Greek army — the man who never lost a duel. He killed himself over a prize he did not win. A cleaning powder now carries his name, on the reasoning that it is stronger than dirt.

questions.q: There was a princess chained to a rock in Greek myth. She was offered to a sea monster to pay for her mother's boasting, and Perseus rescued her. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Andromeda's mother said her daughter was lovelier than the sea nymphs, and a monster was sent to collect the difference. Perseus saved her mid-flight. The whole family — mother, father, hero, monster — was put in the sky as constellations.

questions.q: There was a giant of Greek myth. He was invincible while touching the earth, his mother, and lost all strength when lifted from it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Antaeus beat every wrestler who came at him, because every time he was thrown down he got up stronger. Heracles worked out the trick, hoisted him off the ground, and held him in the air until he weakened.

questions.q: There was a Greek god of light, music and prophecy. He stood for clarity, proportion and reason. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Nietzsche paired Apollonian order against Dionysian ecstasy and argued great art needs both — the clear shape and the wild energy inside it. The Apollo space programme took the name of the god who drove the sun across the sky.

questions.q: There was a mortal weaver of Greek myth. She out-wove Athena in a contest and was turned into a spider for the insult. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Arachne's tapestry was better than the goddess's — that was the problem. Athena tore it up and struck her, and when Arachne despaired, turned her into a creature that could weave forever. Spiders are still classed as arachnids.

questions.q: There was an athens's ancient council, meeting on the Hill of Ares. It served as the city's highest court for the gravest crimes. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Areopagus tried murder cases, and myth says its first defendant was the war god Ares himself. Milton borrowed the name in 1644 for Areopagitica, his argument against censorship — a speech to a court that no longer existed.

questions.q: "Argonaut" is named after a place.
questions.f: The Argonauts were named for their ship, not their leader — argonaut simply means Argo-sailor. Prospectors racing to California in 1849 called themselves Argonauts too, which was optimistic about the fleece.

questions.q: There was an Athenian comic playwright. He put living politicians on stage and mocked them by name in front of the whole city. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aristophanes wrote a comedy attacking Socrates as a fraud who taught students to dodge debts. Twenty-four years later, at his trial, Socrates complained that the play had poisoned the jury against him long before he arrived.

questions.q: There was a Greek philosopher. He classified everything from tragedy to squid and set the framework for European thought for centuries. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great, dissected sea creatures on Lesbos, and wrote the first surviving works on logic, physics and drama. For much of the Middle Ages, European scholars simply called him The Philosopher.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a wild, drunken celebration" comes from a Roman god of wine?
questions.f: The Roman Senate banned the Bacchanalia in 186 BC, calling them a conspiracy. Thousands were arrested. The festivals had grown from a small women's rite into all-night gatherings the state could neither see into nor control.

questions.q: There was a Roman senator. He joined the plot to kill Julius Caesar, who had treated him as a friend. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Shakespeare gives the dying Caesar the line Et tu, Brute — you too, Brutus. The real Caesar probably said nothing at all. Brutus insisted he acted for the Republic, not against the man, and killed himself two years later.

questions.q: There was a founder of Thebes in Greek myth. He sowed a dragon's teeth and armed men sprang up and killed each other until only five were left. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Cadmean victory costs more than losing would have. Cadmus also, according to the Greeks, brought them the alphabet from Phoenicia — so the man behind the ruinous win is also the reason they could write about it.

questions.q: There was Greek Muse of epic poetry. Chief of the nine Muses, she inspired Homer and the grand heroic style. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Calliope was the eldest Muse and the mother of Orpheus. In 1855 an American inventor attached her name to a steam whistle organ so loud it could be heard for miles — the calliope that still shrieks over fairgrounds.

questions.q: "Caryatid" is named after a person.
questions.f: Six caryatids hold up a porch of the Erechtheion in Athens. One was removed by Lord Elgin and taken to London; the Athenians said for years that the remaining five could be heard at night, crying for their missing sister.

questions.q: There was a ferryman of the dead in Greek myth. He rowed souls across the Styx, and only for those buried with the fare. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Greeks buried their dead with a coin in the mouth to pay Charon. Anyone unburied waited a hundred years on the wrong bank. Pluto's largest moon is named Charon, still ferrying alongside the underworld.

questions.q: There was Greek Muse of history. She carried a scroll and was invoked at the opening of historical works. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Clio's name comes from the Greek for 'to make famous' — the historian's actual job, as the Greeks saw it. Herodotus's nine books of history were each named after one of the nine Muses, and Clio got book one.

questions.q: There was one of the three Fates in Greek myth. She spun the thread of each human life while her sisters measured and cut it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Three sisters ran every life: Clotho spun the thread, Lachesis measured it, Atropos cut. Even Zeus could not overrule them. Engineers borrowed the name for the clothoid, the spiralling curve that eases a road into a bend.

questions.q: There was a titan father of Zeus. He ruled the Golden Age, and the Romans identified him with Saturn. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Cronus swallowed each of his children at birth to stop the prophecy that one would overthrow him. His wife handed him a stone in swaddling clothes instead of the sixth. The sixth was Zeus, and the prophecy held.

questions.q: There was a town near Athens. Its secret initiation rites promised a better afterlife and were never written down. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: For nearly two thousand years, thousands of Greeks were initiated at Eleusis — and not one of them ever recorded what happened inside. The penalty for telling was death. It remains the best-kept secret in the ancient world.

questions.q: There was a paradise of the blessed dead in Greek myth. Heroes were sent there instead of the grey underworld, to fields of perpetual ease. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Elysium was the good afterlife — sunlight, meadows, no work. Paris named a boulevard after it: the Champs-Elysees, the Elysian Fields. Anyone stuck in its traffic may question the comparison.

questions.q: "Eumenidean" is named after a place.
questions.f: The Furies hunted murderers without rest. Calling them the Eumenides — the Kindly Ones — was pure superstition: you did not want to attract their attention by using the real name. It is the oldest recorded nickname made out of fear.

questions.q: There was a wife of Orpheus in Greek myth. Orpheus won her back from the dead and lost her again by glancing behind him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: One rule: do not look back until you are both out. Orpheus walked the whole way up in silence, heard nothing behind him, and turned at the last step to check. She was there, and then she was not.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of the Hebrew language, people or tradition" comes from an ancient people of the Levant?
questions.f: Hebrew stopped being an everyday spoken language for roughly seventeen centuries, surviving only in prayer and study — then was deliberately revived, and is now the first language of millions. No other language has managed that.

questions.q: There was a Greek goddess of witchcraft and crossroads. She was worshipped at night where three roads met, with offerings left in the dark. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hecate is often shown with three faces, watching all three roads at once. Greeks left food for her at junctions on the night of the new moon, and did not look too closely at who collected it.

questions.q: There was a queen whose flight to Troy began the Trojan War. Marlowe called hers the face that launched a thousand ships. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Careful with the spelling: Helenic is Helen of Troy, Hellenic is Greek in general. Both trace to Greece, but only one of them started a ten-year war by leaving with a visiting prince.

questions.q: There was a Greek god of the forge. Lame and cast out of Olympus, he made the finest armour and machines of the gods. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hephaestus was thrown off Olympus as an infant and walked with difficulty afterwards — the only Greek god with a disability. He was also the only one who actually made things, including golden servants that moved on their own.

questions.q: There was a youth of Greek myth loved by Apollo. Killed by a discus throw, and from his blood Apollo raised a flower. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Apollo threw the discus, the wind blew it off course, and his friend died. The flower that grew where the blood fell carried the boy's name. Homer uses hyacinthine for hair, meaning dark and tightly curled.

questions.q: "Iliadic" is named after a person.
questions.f: The Iliad is not about the whole war — it covers about seven weeks near the end, and never reaches the wooden horse. Its actual subject, announced in the first word, is the anger of one man.

questions.q: There was a daughter of Agamemnon in Greek myth. Her father sacrificed her to obtain a favourable wind for the fleet sailing to Troy. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Agamemnon summoned his daughter to the coast on the pretext of a wedding. In some versions Artemis snatched her away at the last instant and left a deer on the altar — a rescue the Greeks invented later, when the original proved unbearable.

questions.q: There was a river of forgetfulness in the Greek underworld. Souls drank from it to erase their memories before being reborn. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The dead drank from Lethe so they could start again with nothing. Its opposite, Mnemosyne, ran alongside — and initiates of some mystery cults were told to refuse the first river and ask for the second.

questions.q: There was an ancient region of southwest Anatolia. Its people carved elaborate tombs into cliff faces and kept their own language and alphabet. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Lycians cut house-shaped tombs high into sheer rock so the dead would be closer to the sky. Their alphabet borrowed from Greek but kept extra letters for sounds Greek did not have, and nobody could read it for two thousand years.

questions.q: There was a sorceress of Greek myth. Betrayed by Jason, she took a revenge so extreme that Greek audiences were shocked by it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Medea gave up her home and her family to help Jason steal the Golden Fleece. When he left her for a princess, she destroyed everything he loved and escaped in a chariot drawn by dragons. Euripides gave her the last word.

questions.q: There was Greek Muse of tragedy. She is shown holding a tragic mask and wearing the raised boot of the tragic actor. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Melpomene started as the Muse of singing — her name means 'to celebrate with song'. She was reassigned to tragedy later. The two masks hanging outside theatres are hers and her sister Thalia's, comedy and tragedy together.

questions.q: There was a Greek goddess of memory. She was the mother of all nine Muses, making memory the parent of every art. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Greeks made memory the mother of the arts, which is exactly right for a culture that recited Homer from memory for centuries before writing it down. Mnemonic — a memory trick — comes from the same root.

questions.q: "Nemesian" is named after a place.
questions.f: Nemesis did not punish crime — she punished excess. Too much luck, too much boasting, and she arrived to restore the balance. Her name now means an unbeatable rival, which is a demotion from goddess of cosmic accounting.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of the ocean" comes from a titan of the great river encircling the world?
questions.f: For the earliest Greeks the Ocean was not water everywhere — it was one enormous river running in a circle around the rim of a flat world, and Oceanus was the Titan who was that river.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a four-year period" comes from a sanctuary in southern Greece?
questions.f: An Olympiad is properly the four-year gap, not the festival — the Greeks dated events by counting them. The ancient games ran for roughly twelve centuries before a Roman emperor shut them down as a pagan rite.

questions.q: There was a Greek hero who killed Medusa. He beheaded the Gorgon, rescued Andromeda, and was placed in the sky as a constellation. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Perseus borrowed winged sandals, a cap of invisibility and a mirrored shield, which is a lot of equipment for one monster. The Perseid meteor shower every August appears to come from his constellation.

questions.q: There was an Athenian princess of Greek myth. After a brutal wrong she was turned into a nightingale, whose song poets treated as beautiful grief. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Philomela was silenced and wove her story into a tapestry instead, because nobody thought to take away her loom. The gods turned her into a nightingale — the bird that sings most beautifully after dark.

questions.q: There was a judge of the dead in Greek myth. A son of Zeus so famously just that he was made a judge in the underworld. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Rhadamanthus was one of three judges deciding where each soul went, and he had the reputation of being unbribable. His name is now the strongest word English has for a judge who will not bend, not even slightly.

questions.q: There was a Greek goddess of the moon. She drove the moon across the night sky in a silver chariot. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Selene fell in love with a shepherd and asked Zeus to keep him young forever; he granted it by putting the man into eternal sleep. The element selenium is named after her, because it was found alongside one named for the earth.

questions.q: "Terpsichorean" is named after a person.
questions.f: Terpsichore is the reason a dancer can be called a terpsichorean — a nine-letter way of saying it. Of the nine Muses she is the one whose job survives most recognisably: she is usually shown mid-step, holding a lyre.

questions.q: There was a Roman god of fire and the forge. His workshop was said to lie under Mount Etna, which explained the smoke. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Romans thought the rumble of Etna was Vulcan hammering underground. The island of Vulcano off Sicily was his chimney, and it gave every volcano on Earth its name — including the ones nowhere near Italy.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Hadria or the Adriatic" comes from an ancient town in northern Italy?
questions.f: A small Roman town called Hadria named the whole Adriatic Sea, then lent its adjective to the emperor Hadrian, then to popes and a great many children. The town itself is now several miles inland, left behind by the silt.

questions.q: There was a Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid. He carried his father out of burning Troy and sailed on to found the line that led to Rome. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Virgil's stock epithet for him is pius Aeneas — not pious exactly, but dutiful. He escapes Troy with his father on his back and his household gods under his arm, and spends the rest of the poem doing what he is told by fate.

questions.q: There was a Greek word for selfless love. Early Christian writers chose it over other Greek words for love to mean unconditional goodwill. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Greek had at least four words for love, and early Christian writers deliberately picked the least romantic one. Agape is not affection or desire — it is the kind you extend to someone who has done nothing to earn it.

questions.q: There was a queen of Greek myth. She agreed to die in her husband's place when no one else would. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Admetus was allowed to escape death if someone would go instead. He asked his parents, who declined. His wife Alcestis volunteered. Heracles turned up, heard the story, and went to wrestle Death at the graveside to get her back.

questions.q: There was a Theban general of Greek myth. In Moliere's play the true host is identified as the one who provides the dinner. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Zeus disguised himself as Amphitryon to visit his wife, producing two identical husbands and a very confused household. Moliere's version settles the question with a line the French adopted: the real Amphitryon is the one who serves the meal.

questions.q: "Anchisean" is named after a place.
questions.f: The image of Aeneas escaping Troy with his father on his back and his son by the hand became Rome's picture of duty itself — carrying the past out and leading the future forward at the same time.

questions.q: There was a Greek lyric poet. He wrote light verse in praise of wine, music and good company. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A London gentlemen's club sang a drinking song called To Anacreon in Heaven. An American lawyer later set his poem about a flag to that same tune, and the United States ended up with a national anthem built on a Greek wine poet.

questions.q: There was a Greek term for one who withdraws. Early Christian hermits withdrew to the desert to live alone in prayer. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Anchorites went further than monks: some were sealed into a small cell attached to a church wall, with one window to the altar and one to the street, and stayed there for the rest of their lives.

questions.q: There was first Roman emperor. Virgil, Horace and Ovid all wrote under him, making his reign the peak of Latin literature. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Augustus boasted he found Rome brick and left it marble. Eighteenth-century English writers admired the period so much that they called their own era Augustan and set out to imitate it deliberately.

questions.q: There was a region of central Greece. Athenians mocked their rural neighbours as slow-witted, and the slur stuck to the region's name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: This is an ancient insult that outlived its target. Athens sneered at Boeotia as farmland full of dullards — conveniently forgetting that Hesiod, Pindar and Plutarch all came from there.

questions.q: There was a Spanish novelist. Don Quixote mixes comedy and idealism so closely that neither wins. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Cervantes lost the use of his left hand at the battle of Lepanto and spent five years as a captive in Algiers before writing what is often called the first modern novel. He died in the same week as Shakespeare.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of the Americas or of Columbus" comes from a Genoese navigator?
questions.f: America was named for Amerigo Vespucci, not Columbus — but Columbian survived as the poetic alternative. It is why the United States has a District of Columbia and Canada a British Columbia.

questions.q: "Coriolanian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Coriolanus could not bring himself to show his battle scars to voters, which was the custom. Exiled for the insult, he marched on Rome and was stopped only when his mother walked out to meet the army.

questions.q: There was a Trojan woman in medieval and Shakespearean versions of the Troy story. She swore constancy to Troilus and transferred her affections once she reached the Greek camp. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Cressida does not appear in Homer at all — she was invented in the Middle Ages and handed down through Boccaccio and Chaucer to Shakespeare, each of whom made her a little less sympathetic than the last.

questions.q: There was a French soldier-poet, immortalised in Rostand's 1897 play. In the play he lends his eloquence to a handsome friend, wooing the woman he loves on someone else's behalf. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The real Cyrano wrote science fiction about travelling to the moon. Rostand gave him an enormous nose, a duelling sword, and the finest words in French theatre — all spent under a balcony, for another man.

questions.q: There was a florentine poet. His descent through the nine circles of hell set the standard for infernal imagery. Which word grew out of it?
