questions.f: Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in Italian rather than Latin, which scholars considered a waste of a good poem. It is the reason modern Italian sounds the way it does.

questions.q: There was Greek Cynic philosopher. He lived in a large ceramic jar and owned almost nothing on principle. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Diogenes walked Athens in daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for an honest man. When Alexander the Great offered him anything he wanted, he asked him to move slightly — he was blocking the sun.

questions.q: There was a hero of Cervantes's novel. He read so many chivalric romances that he set out as a knight and charged windmills believing them giants. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Don Quixote's windmills are the most famous mistake in literature. Cervantes meant to mock outdated romances, but readers kept siding with the old man who insisted the world should be nobler than it is.

questions.q: There was a Greek people who settled the Peloponnese. Their name attached to a musical mode and to the plainest of the classical column orders. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Doric column is the plain one — no scrolls, no leaves, just fluting and a flat top. Greeks thought of it as the masculine, unfussy order, and used it for the Parthenon.

questions.q: "Euclidian" is named after a place.
questions.f: Euclid's fifth postulate — about parallel lines — bothered mathematicians for centuries because it seemed like it should be provable. It is not. Dropping it produced curved, non-Euclidean geometries, and eventually general relativity.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of the Gospel" comes from a Greek word meaning 'good news'?
questions.f: Euangelion literally means good message — in classical Greek it was the reward you gave the runner who brought good news from a battle. English kept the messenger sense in evangelist and the enthusiasm in evangelical.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of the modern calendar or of plainsong chant" comes from a pope who reformed the calendar in 1582?
questions.f: To fix the drift, October 1582 simply lost ten days — people went to sleep on the 4th and woke on the 15th. Britain held out until 1752, by which time it had to skip eleven.

questions.q: There was a narrator of Swift's Gulliver's Travels. He is a giant in one land and a doll in the next, and reports both with the same flat calm. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Swift wrote Gulliver's Travels as savage political satire. It was so successful as an adventure story that it turned into a children's book, which is the fate of a surprising number of angry books.

questions.q: There was a cambridge stable owner. He rented horses strictly in rotation: you took the one nearest the door, or none at all. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hobson had forty horses and a rule that stopped customers from wearing out the best ones. Students grumbled about Hobson's choice, and the phrase outlived every horse in the stable.

questions.q: There was an English writer and lexicographer. He wrote a dictionary almost single-handedly and spoke in weighty, balanced sentences. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Johnson spent nine years on his dictionary and slipped jokes into it — he defined lexicographer as a harmless drudge. His friend Boswell wrote down his conversation for years, producing the most famous biography in English.

questions.q: There was a German philosopher. He argued morality means acting only on rules you could will everyone to follow. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Kant kept to a schedule so exact that neighbours in Konigsberg were said to set their clocks by his afternoon walk. He never travelled more than a hundred miles from his birthplace, and rearranged Western philosophy from there.

questions.q: "Lilliputian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Lilliput's great political dispute is whether to crack a boiled egg at the big end or the little end — a war that has killed thousands. Swift was writing about religious conflict, and he was not being subtle.

questions.q: There was a name meaning 'light-bringer', applied to the fallen angel. Pride made him rebel against heaven and fall from it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Lucifer is Latin for light-bringer and was originally the morning star, Venus. A verse in Isaiah about a fallen Babylonian king was read as being about Satan, and the planet's name transferred to the devil.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Newton's classical physics" comes from an English physicist and mathematician?
questions.f: Newton did his best work during a plague year when Cambridge closed and he went home to the farm. In eighteen months he laid out calculus, optics and gravitation. He later called it his year of wonders.

questions.q: There was an Italian poet. He wrote hundreds of sonnets to a woman named Laura, in a form now named after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Petrarch saw Laura in a church in Avignon in 1327 and wrote poems about her for the next forty years, including twenty-one after her death. There is no evidence they ever had a conversation.

questions.q: There was a castaway hero of Defoe's 1719 novel. His story of surviving alone on an island spawned an entire genre of imitations. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Defoe based Crusoe partly on Alexander Selkirk, a Scottish sailor marooned for four years on a Pacific island. Germans coined Robinsonade for the flood of imitations, and the genre now includes Swiss Family Robinson and Lord of the Flies.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Victoria's reign" comes from a british monarch?
questions.f: Victoria came to the throne at eighteen and reigned longer than any British monarch before her. The word Victorian now suggests prudishness, though the queen herself wrote frankly in her diaries about how much she adored her husband.

questions.q: There was a Greek town, home of Democritus. Democritus was known as the laughing philosopher for his amusement at human folly. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Abdera produced Democritus, who worked out that matter is made of atoms twenty-three centuries early, and who reportedly could not stop laughing at people. The town's neighbours took the laughter personally.

questions.q: "Acadian" is named after a place.
questions.f: Deported Acadians who reached Louisiana were called Acadiens, then Cadiens, then Cajuns. The whole of Cajun food, music and dialect traces back to one forced expulsion from the far north.

questions.q: There was a beautiful youth of Greek myth. Aphrodite loved him; a boar killed him, and anemones grew where his blood fell. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The name is not Greek but Semitic — adon means lord, and the story came west from Phoenicia. Calling a handsome man an Adonis is therefore a compliment in a language most people using it do not know.

questions.q: There was a Greek keeper of the winds. An aeolian harp is played by nothing but the breeze passing over its strings. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An aeolian harp is left in an open window and plays itself. Romantic poets loved the idea — an instrument with no performer — and used it as an image for inspiration arriving from somewhere outside you.

questions.q: There was a Greek fabulist. His animal fables carried their real meaning underneath the surface story. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aesop was said to be an enslaved man who won his freedom through cleverness. In Soviet Russia, Aesopian language meant writing your real point in code — because the fable was still the safest way to criticise power.

questions.q: There was a king of the Phaeacians in the Odyssey. He gave the shipwrecked Odysseus a feast, gifts and a ship home, asking nothing first. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Alcinous had a garden where fruit ripened all year round and never failed. He also had the good manners to feed his exhausted guest for two days before asking him who he was.

questions.q: There was an English scholar at Charlemagne's court. He led the palace school and drove the revival of learning across the Frankish empire. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Alcuin's scribes developed a clear rounded script called Carolingian minuscule to replace the tangle scribes had been using. Renaissance printers copied it, and the lower-case letters you are reading now descend directly from it.

questions.q: There was a goat who nursed the infant Zeus. One of her horns broke off and filled forever with whatever its holder wished for. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Amalthea's broken horn became the cornucopia — the horn of plenty still drawn overflowing with fruit at harvest festivals. Zeus later set her among the stars in gratitude for the milk.

questions.q: "Ammonian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Camel caravans camped at the temple of Amun, and a white salt crusted the ground where they did. Romans called it sal ammoniac, salt of Amun. Every bottle of ammonia is named after an Egyptian god by way of camel dung.

questions.q: There was a Roman emperor. His reign was the calm centre of what Gibbon called the happiest period in human history. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Antonine Wall was built across Scotland under him, north of Hadrian's, and abandoned within about twenty years. Rome kept the older wall — the one named after the emperor who did less building.

questions.q: There was a Roman gourmet of the first century AD. The oldest surviving cookbook in the West carries his name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The recipes attributed to Apicius include flamingo and dormice stuffed with pork. Legend says he poisoned himself on discovering he had only a modest fortune left and could no longer eat as he wished.

questions.q: There was a French poet. He coined the word surrealism and wrote poems shaped like the objects they described. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Apollinaire wrote calligrammes — poems typeset in the shape of a horse, the Eiffel Tower, falling rain. He also invented the word surrealism, three years before the movement that took it existed.

questions.q: There was a Greek scholar and critic. As librarian at Alexandria he marked doubtful lines of Homer with a severity that became proverbial. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aristarchus went through Homer marking every line he thought was a later addition, using a small horizontal stroke in the margin. That stroke is the ancestor of the obelus, and the dagger symbol still used in footnotes.

questions.q: There was an English poet and critic. He defined culture as the best which has been thought and said in the world. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Arnold spent his working life as a school inspector, travelling England examining classrooms, and wrote criticism in the gaps. He argued that culture was the antidote to what he called anarchy, by which he mostly meant the middle classes.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Athens or Athena" comes from a Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare?
questions.f: Athena and Poseidon competed for the city. He struck the rock and produced a salt spring; she planted an olive tree. The citizens chose the olive, and the city took her name.

questions.q: "Attic" is named after a place.
questions.f: Attic salt means dry Athenian wit. The attic in your house is the same word: architects called a small decorative upper storey in the Athenian manner an attic storey, and the name slid up into the roof space.

questions.q: There was a prince in a tale from the Arabian Nights. He served a starving beggar a magnificent banquet of entirely empty dishes. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Barmecide describes each imaginary course in loving detail while the beggar mimes eating it. The beggar plays along, then pretends to be drunk on imaginary wine and punches him — at which the prince laughs and serves a real dinner.

questions.q: There was a dante's idealised love. She guides him through Paradise in the Divine Comedy after Virgil can go no further. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Dante met Beatrice when they were both about nine and spoke to her only a handful of times. She married someone else and died at twenty-four. He put her in charge of heaven.

questions.q: There was an English philosopher. He proposed judging every action by how much happiness it produced overall. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Bentham also designed the panopticon, a prison where one unseen guard could watch every cell. It was never built to his plan, but the idea has been borrowed by everyone writing about surveillance since.

questions.q: There was a Roman philosopher. Awaiting execution, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy and its image of Fortune's turning wheel. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Boethius wrote his masterpiece in a cell while waiting to be executed for treason. The wheel of fortune he described — lifting people up only to drop them — became the standard medieval image for how luck works.

questions.q: There was a Flemish painter. He filled his canvases with crowds of peasants at work, at play and at their worst. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Bruegel painted a hundred children's games in a single picture and a village wedding where you can count the pies. In his Icarus, the boy falls out of the sky and every farmer in the painting keeps working.

questions.q: There was a Scottish physician. He taught that all disease came from too much or too little excitement in the body. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Brown reduced medicine to one dial: too stimulated or not stimulated enough. Treatment was opium or alcohol accordingly. It was wrong, wildly popular across Europe, and probably killed more patients than it saved.

questions.q: "Carolingian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Charlemagne ruled most of western Europe and worked at learning to write late in life, keeping a tablet under his pillow to practise. He never quite managed it, but he made sure his empire's scribes could.

questions.q: There was a Trojan prophetess of Greek myth. Her prophecies were always right and never believed. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Apollo gave Cassandra prophecy hoping to win her affection. When she refused him he could not take the gift back, so he added a condition: she would always be right, and nobody would ever act on it.

questions.q: There was a Roman poet. He wrote short, direct, intensely personal poems about love and hatred. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Catullus survives by luck — a single manuscript turned up in Verona around 1300 and vanished again after being copied. His most famous poem is two lines long and begins by saying he hates and loves at the same time.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Chaldea" comes from a region of southern Babylonia?
questions.f: Chaldean astronomers kept night-sky records for centuries and could predict eclipses. Greeks and Romans used Chaldean to mean fortune-teller, which was rather like calling an astronomer a horoscope writer.

questions.q: There was a Roman orator. Italian guides who talked at length about the sights were nicknamed after the most talkative Roman. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Eighteenth-century travellers on the Grand Tour hired local guides and named them ciceroni — after Cicero, whose reputation for eloquence had by then drifted into a reputation for not stopping.

questions.q: There was a Roman emperor. Dismissed as a stammering fool, he proved a capable administrator who conquered Britain. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Claudius survived the purges that killed the rest of his family precisely because nobody thought him worth killing. The Praetorian Guard found him hiding behind a curtain after Caligula's murder and made him emperor.

questions.q: There was an English poet. His dreamlike Kubla Khan and Ancient Mariner defined the visionary side of Romanticism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Coleridge said Kubla Khan came to him complete in a dream, and that he was writing it down when a person from Porlock knocked on the door about business. By the time he got rid of the visitor, the rest of the poem was gone.

questions.q: "Corneillean" is named after a place.
questions.f: Corneille's Le Cid was so popular that the French Academy was pushed to condemn it for breaking the rules of classical drama. Audiences kept going anyway, and the phrase beau comme le Cid entered the language.

questions.q: There was an English soldier and Lord Protector. He led Parliament's army, signed a king's death warrant, and ruled without a crown. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Cromwell told his portrait painter to include everything, warts and all, or he would not pay for it. Two years after his death the restored monarchy dug up his body and executed it anyway.

questions.q: There was a small Greek island, birthplace of Apollo. It was the sacred centre of an Athenian-led alliance whose treasury was kept there. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Delos was so sacred that no one was allowed to be born or to die on it. There is also the Delian problem: an oracle demanded the islanders double a cube-shaped altar, which turns out to be impossible with compass and straightedge.

questions.q: There was a Greek god of wine and theatre. His festivals combined drinking, masks and the first performances of Greek drama. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Western theatre started as a religious festival for Dionysus. The plays of Sophocles and Euripides were competition entries, performed once, in an open-air theatre, at a party for the god of wine.

questions.q: There was an Athenian lawgiver. His code prescribed death for almost every offence, including stealing a cabbage. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Asked why the penalty for minor theft was death, Draco reportedly said small crimes deserved it and he could find nothing worse for the large ones. The laws were said to be written in blood rather than ink.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of the 1900s in Britain" comes from a british king?
questions.f: Edward waited fifty-nine years to become king — the longest apprenticeship in British history — and reigned nine. The decade named after him is remembered as one long garden party, mainly because of what came next.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Elizabeth I's reign" comes from a queen of England?
questions.f: Elizabeth reigned forty-four years and refused to marry throughout, telling Parliament she was already married to England. The theatre, the language and the navy all took their modern shape while she was on the throne.

questions.q: "Fabianism" is named after a person.
questions.f: The Fabian Society, founded in 1884, chose the name deliberately: change by patience, not revolution. Its members included George Bernard Shaw and H. G. Wells, and it helped found the British Labour Party.

questions.q: There was a legendary warrior band of Irish myth led by Finn MacCool. Nineteenth-century Irish republicans took the ancient warriors' name for their movement. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Fianna were mythical hunter-warriors who roamed Ireland in the old stories. When republicans organised in 1858 they reached back two thousand years for a name, which tells you how they wanted to be seen.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of France, especially its church" comes from a Roman name for the region that became France?
questions.f: Gaul gave French a great deal: Gallic wit, Gallicanism, and the rooster that is still France's unofficial emblem — because gallus is Latin for both a Gaul and a cockerel, and someone enjoyed the pun enough to keep it.

questions.q: There was a paris building where the radical revolutionary club met. The club took its nickname from the address, and the name came to mean political extremism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Jacobins were named after a building, not a person — the Paris convent where they met. Under Robespierre the club drove the Terror, and Jacobin has meant dangerous radicalism in English ever since.

questions.q: There was a king of England. Jacobus is Latin for James, and his reign named a style of drama, furniture and Bible. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The King James Bible was produced under him by six committees of scholars, and its cadences shaped English prose for four centuries. Jacobean drama went the other way entirely — revenge, poison and skulls.

questions.q: There was an ancient region around Jerusalem. The name of the kingdom of Judah gave us both Judaea and Jew. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Judaea is named for Judah, one of the twelve tribes, whose emblem was a lion. The name travelled: from the tribe to the kingdom to the Roman province, and from there into the word Jewish.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of Napoleon" comes from a French emperor?
questions.f: Napoleon's civil code is still the backbone of the legal system in dozens of countries. He was of perfectly ordinary height for his time — the short-Napoleon story comes from British cartoons and a confusion between French and English inches.

questions.q: "Pauline" is named after a place.
questions.f: Paul began as Saul, a persecutor of Christians, and changed course after a blinding experience on the road to Damascus. A Damascene conversion — a sudden complete reversal — is named from that same journey.

questions.q: There was a French artist and inventor. He fixed an image on a silvered copper plate, producing the first practical photograph. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The French government bought Daguerre's process in 1839 and gave it to the world free — except in England, where he patented it. Each daguerreotype was unique: there was no negative, so no copies could be made.

questions.q: There was a French architect. He popularised a roof with two slopes, the lower one steep, creating a usable extra floor. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Paris property was once taxed by the number of floors below the roofline, so a mansard roof added a whole storey the tax collector did not count. Good architecture and good accounting at the same time.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the dot-and-dash telegraph code" comes from an American painter and inventor?
questions.f: Morse was a portrait painter first. Away from home on a commission, he received a letter saying his wife was ill; by the time he got back she was already buried. He spent the rest of his life on faster messages.

questions.q: There was a French weaver and inventor. His loom used punched cards to control the pattern automatically. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Jacquard's loom read its pattern from a chain of punched cards. Charles Babbage saw one and borrowed the idea for his calculating engine, and punched cards ran computers into the 1970s. Modern computing starts with a French silk loom.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a large short-haired guard dog" comes from a German tax collector?
questions.f: Dobermann collected taxes in a rough district and also ran the local dog pound, which gave him unusual access to breeding stock. He set out to build the perfect bodyguard, and the breed still carries his name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a hairstyle with the hair swept up from the forehead" comes from a mistress of Louis XV of France?
questions.f: Madame de Pompadour was the most powerful woman at Versailles without being queen, and set fashion for two decades. Two centuries later Elvis Presley wore a version of her hairstyle, which she would probably have enjoyed.

questions.q: "bechamel" is named after a person.
questions.f: Bechameil was a wealthy court official, not a cook. Another courtier complained that the man was lucky — he himself had been serving the same sauce for years before Bechameil was born, and nobody had named it after him.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a soft creamy cheese with a white rind" comes from a village in Normandy, France?
questions.f: The story goes that Marie Harel sheltered a priest fleeing the French Revolution, and he taught her a cheesemaking method from Brie. The round wooden box came later, and is why Camembert could travel.

questions.q: There was a village in southern France. The blue cheese must be aged in the natural limestone caves beneath the village. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Only cheese ripened in the caves of one specific village may be called Roquefort — a protection first granted by royal charter in 1411, making it one of the oldest brand protections in the world.

questions.q: There was a town in western France. Brandy distilled from grapes grown around the town takes its name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: All cognac is brandy, but only brandy from around this one town may be called cognac. The rule is strict enough that even neighbouring Armagnac, made a hundred miles away, has to use its own name.

questions.q: What does "champagne" mean?
c: Sparkling wine from the Champagne region
questions.f: The region's name comes from the Latin campania, meaning open country. The bubbles were originally an accident and considered a fault — the cold Champagne winters stopped fermentation, which restarted in spring inside the sealed bottle.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a deep purplish red" comes from a region in eastern France?
questions.f: Burgundy is one of a small group of colours named after drinks — along with claret and port. The region itself is named for the Burgundians, a Germanic people who settled there around 1,500 years ago.

questions.q: Which word meaning "porcelain tableware" comes from the country?
questions.f: Europeans spent centuries trying to work out how the Chinese made porcelain so thin that light passed through it. The recipe was finally cracked in Saxony in 1708, but by then the tableware was permanently called china.

questions.q: "damask" is named after a place.
questions.f: Damascus gave English three words: damask for the cloth, damascene for patterned steel and inlaid metal, and damson for the plum. All three arrived along the same trade routes.

questions.q: Which word meaning "hard-wearing cotton twill fabric" comes from a city in southern France?
questions.f: Your jeans are named after two European cities at once. The fabric is de Nimes, from Nimes in France. The trousers are from Genoa in Italy, which the French called Genes — which English turned into jeans.

questions.q: What does "cashmere" mean?
c: Very fine soft wool from the cashmere goat
Confused mixture of voices or languages
questions.f: Cashmere is not the goat's outer coat but the soft underlayer it grows for winter, combed out by hand in spring. One goat yields a few ounces a year, which is why a cashmere jumper costs what it does.

questions.q: What does "angora" mean?
c: Wool from the angora goat or rabbit
Confused mixture of voices or languages
questions.f: Angora names three different animals — a goat, a rabbit and a cat — all long-haired, all from around Ankara. Confusingly, the goat's wool is sold as mohair, and only the rabbit's is sold as angora.

questions.q: There was a city in northern Iraq. European traders first met the fine cotton cloth there and named it for the city. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The finest muslin actually came from Bengal, where weavers produced cloth so sheer it was nicknamed woven air. Europeans met it in Mosul first, so the Iraqi city got the credit and the name.

questions.q: There was a port city in Kerala, India, now Kozhikode. Printed cotton shipped from the port took its name across Europe. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Calico was so popular in England that in 1721 Parliament banned it outright to protect the wool trade. The ban lasted thirty-three years and made smuggling printed cotton genuinely profitable.

questions.q: There was a country in North Africa. The ribbed crepe fabric took the French name for Moroccan. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Marocain is simply French for Moroccan. It is one of several fabrics that arrived in Europe with a nationality attached and kept it, alongside morocco leather from the same country.

questions.q: "cordovan" is named after a person.
questions.f: Cordoba's leather was so famous that the workers who made shoes from it were called cordwainers — a word still used for shoemakers in Britain, six centuries after the trade with Spain dried up.

questions.q: Which word meaning "leather with a soft napped finish" comes from the country?
questions.f: Suede is just the French word for Sweden. Parisians bought Swedish gloves made from the underside of the skin rather than the smooth outer face, and English took the country's name for the texture.

questions.q: There was last king of Illyria. He was said to have discovered the medicinal value of the plant's bitter root. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Gentius lost his kingdom to Rome and was paraded through the streets as a captive. His one lasting monument is a small blue alpine flower, named because he supposedly found a use for its extraordinarily bitter root.

questions.q: There was a Flemish botanist. He was physician to James I of England, and the plant was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: De l'Obel tried to classify plants by the shape of their leaves, which was wrong but useful — it was one of the first attempts to sort plants by their structure rather than by whether they were edible.

questions.q: There was a Greek phrase meaning 'of good name'. The shrub is poisonous to livestock, so the flattering name was a superstitious precaution. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The name means good name or lucky name — given precisely because the plant is poisonous to cattle. Farmers named it something pleasant in the hope of not attracting bad luck. It is also called the spindle tree.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a garden plant with funnel-shaped flowers" comes from a Tupi word for tobacco?
questions.f: Petunia is not named after a person or a place but after a plant it merely resembles. Petun is the Tupi word for tobacco, and petunias and tobacco really are close relatives — both in the nightshade family.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a knitted garment" comes from a channel Island between England and France?
questions.f: Jersey knitting was originally what fishermen wore. The island also gave its name to a small fawn-coloured cow prized for creamy milk, and to a large American state that needed a name in 1664.

questions.q: "holland" is named after a place.
questions.f: Holland cloth was the standard lining and window-blind fabric for centuries. The region also gave English the Dutch oven, Dutch courage and going Dutch — mostly coined by the English during periods of naval rivalry.

questions.q: There was a French dressmaker. The sheer crinkled silk she popularised took her first name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Georgette is one of very few fabrics named after a woman, and one of fewer still named by first name rather than surname. The crinkle comes from twisting the yarn hard in opposite directions before weaving.

questions.q: There was a town in northern France. Its lacemakers produced a fine bobbin lace with a distinctive diamond mesh. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Valenciennes lace was so slow to make that a skilled worker might produce an inch and a half in a day, and only in a cool damp cellar — dry air made the linen thread snap.

questions.q: There was a town in northern France. It was the leading medieval centre for woven wall tapestries. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An arras hung a little away from the wall, which made it useful for eavesdropping. Polonius hides behind one in Hamlet to listen in, and Hamlet stabs straight through the cloth.

questions.q: There was a capital of Syria. Its smiths inlaid steel with gold and silver in flowing patterns; also the site of Paul's conversion. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Damascene carries two unrelated senses from the same city: watered patterns in steel, and a Damascene conversion — a sudden reversal of belief, from the apostle Paul's experience on the road there.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small dark purple plum" comes from a capital of Syria?
questions.f: Damson is Damascus worn down by centuries of English mouths: damascenum, damascene, damson. The Romans carried the tree west, and it grows in English hedgerows now as if it had always been there.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a thick cold sauce of egg yolk and oil" comes from a port on the island of Menorca?
questions.f: The usual story credits the Duke of Richelieu's cook, improvising a sauce after taking Port Mahon in 1756. Rival theories point to the town of Bayonne or to the French word for egg yolk. Nobody can settle it.

questions.q: "bologna" is named after a person.
questions.f: Bologna's own mortadella is studded with pistachios and cubes of fat. The American version dropped nearly all of that, kept the name, and pronounced it baloney — which then became a word for nonsense.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a hard, sharp, aged Italian cheese" comes from a city in northern Italy?
questions.f: Real Parmigiano-Reggiano ages at least a year, and each wheel is tested by a man who taps it with a small hammer and listens. Wheels that sound wrong inside are marked and sold under a different name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a firm smooth Italian cheese, often smoked" comes from a southern Italian cheese name, from a word meaning a round shape?
questions.f: Provolone means big provola. It is a pasta filata cheese — the curd is heated and stretched like dough until it turns glossy, the same technique that makes mozzarella, then hung in ropes to age.

questions.q: There was a Portuguese island in the Atlantic. Its fortified wine survived long sea voyages and improved in the heat. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Madeira was discovered to taste better after crossing the tropics twice in a hot ship's hold. Producers began heating it deliberately. American revolutionaries toasted the Declaration of Independence with it.

questions.q: There was a Portuguese island in the Atlantic. The plain butter sponge was named not for its ingredients but for the wine served alongside it. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: There is no Madeira in Madeira cake. Nineteenth-century English hosts served the plain sponge with a glass of Madeira wine in the middle of the morning, and the cake ended up named after the drink.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a cigar made in Cuba" comes from a capital of Cuba?
questions.f: Havana cigars are rolled from tobacco grown in the Vuelta Abajo valley, where the soil and humidity are considered impossible to reproduce. Rollers traditionally worked while a reader read novels aloud to the room.

questions.q: There was a German for 'sea foam'. The soft white mineral is so light that it floats, and was imagined to be foam turned to stone. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Not named for a person or a place but for what sailors thought it was: lumps of white mineral washing up light enough to float, so obviously sea foam gone solid. It carves beautifully, which is why pipes were made of it.

questions.q: "frankfurter" is named after a place.
questions.f: Frankfurt has been making this sausage since the 1400s. German emigrants brought it to America, where it met a bread roll — and the frankfurter became the hot dog, named by someone who thought the shape looked like a dachshund.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small smoked sausage" comes from a capital of Austria, Wien in German?
questions.f: Vienna and Frankfurt both claim the sausage, and each named it after the other city: Austrians call it a Frankfurter, Germans call it a Wiener. The man who first made it had trained in Frankfurt and moved to Vienna.

questions.q: There was a city in Bohemia, now the Czech Republic. The world's first pale golden lager was brewed there in 1842. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Before 1842 nearly all beer was dark and cloudy. Plzen's brewers dumped thirty-six barrels of bad beer in the street, hired a Bavarian brewer, and produced a clear golden lager. Most beer in the world today is a copy of it.

questions.q: There was a town in Alsace, France. Monks at the town's monastery made the strong-smelling cheese; the name comes from monasterium. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Munster is a worn-down form of monasterium, the Latin for monastery — so the cheese is really called monastery cheese. Irish Munster is a different word entirely, from an old Irish tribal name.

questions.q: There was a historic duchy now split between Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. The cheese was first made by monks in the region. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Limburger's smell comes from a bacterium that also lives on human skin. Researchers have shown that mosquitoes attracted to human feet are equally attracted to a piece of Limburger, which says something about both.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a mild Dutch cheese in a red wax coating" comes from a town in the Netherlands?
questions.f: Edam ages slowly and barely spoils, which made it the standard cheese for long sea voyages. Dutch ships carried it worldwide, and its red wax shell is really just very effective packaging.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a mild yellow Dutch cheese" comes from a town in the Netherlands?
questions.f: Gouda is named for a marketplace, not a dairy. The town held the sole right to trade cheese in the region, so every wheel that passed through took the town's name regardless of which farm made it.

questions.q: "cheddar" is named after a person.
questions.f: Cheddar Gorge's caves stay at a steady cool temperature all year, which is exactly what the cheese needs. Cheddar is now the most-eaten cheese in the world, and almost none of it comes from Cheddar.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a strong English blue cheese" comes from a village in Cambridgeshire, England?
questions.f: Stilton is named after a village where it was never produced. Coaches on the Great North Road stopped at the Bell Inn there, the landlord sold cheese from Leicestershire to passengers, and they named it after the stop.

questions.q: There was a city in England. Two chemists in Worcester made the fermented sauce in 1837, from a recipe they found unpleasant at first. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Lea and Perrill mixed the first batch, tasted it, hated it, and left the barrel in the cellar. Eighteen months later they tried it again out of curiosity. Fermentation had transformed it, and they started selling it immediately.

questions.q: What does "tabasco" mean?
c: A very hot sauce made from tabasco peppers
questions.f: Tabasco sauce has been made on the same Louisiana island since 1868, aged three years in oak barrels with salt from the salt dome beneath. The pepper — and therefore the name — came from Mexico.

questions.q: There was a town in Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolivar. A German army surgeon there developed the bitters in 1824 as a stomach remedy for soldiers. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Dr Siegert made his bitters as medicine for Simon Bolivar's troops. The town changed its name to Ciudad Bolivar in 1846 and the company later moved to Trinidad, so the bottle now names a place that no longer exists.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a light scented perfume" comes from a city in Germany, Koln in German?
questions.f: Giovanni Maria Farina created his scent in Cologne and wrote that it reminded him of an Italian spring morning after rain. His company still exists — arguably the oldest perfume house in the world.

questions.q: There was a city in Germany. Literally 'water of Cologne', the original name of Farina's 1709 scent. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: Napoleon's soldiers took eau de Cologne home in such quantities that it became the standard word for light perfume across Europe. Napoleon himself is said to have used a bottle a day.

questions.q: "magenta" is named after a place.
questions.f: The dye was discovered in the same year as the Battle of Magenta and named to ride the news. It is one of the four printing inks — every colour photo ever printed uses a colour named after a battlefield.

questions.q: There was a village in northern Italy. Another 1859 battle in the same campaign gave its name to a second new dye colour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Solferino's real legacy is not the colour. A Swiss traveller named Henry Dunant saw forty thousand casualties left untended after the battle, wrote a book about it, and founded the Red Cross.

questions.q: Which word meaning "knee-length shorts" comes from a british island territory in the Atlantic?
questions.f: Bermuda shorts began as British army tropical kit and became ordinary office wear on the island — worn with a jacket, tie and knee socks. It is still normal business dress in Bermuda.

questions.q: Which word meaning "heavy cotton twill" comes from a port city in Italy, Genes in French?
questions.f: Genoese sailors wore trousers of this hard-wearing cloth, and the French called the city Genes. English heard jean. The cloth in modern jeans is denim, from Nimes, so the garment is named after two cities at once.

questions.q: Which word meaning "printed glazed cotton with a floral pattern" comes from a hindi word meaning variegated or speckled?
questions.f: Chintz is a rare case of an English singular made from a foreign plural — chints was the plural of chint. It was so fashionable, then so common, that chintzy came to mean cheap and gaudy.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a checked or striped cotton cloth" comes from a Malay word meaning striped?
questions.f: Gingham was originally striped, not checked — the checks arrived later in Manchester mills. The name is Malay, one of a handful of everyday English words that came by ship from Southeast Asia.

questions.q: There was a village in Suffolk, England. A coarse ribbed woollen cloth was woven there from the fourteenth century. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Kersey is a village of a few hundred people that named a cloth traded across medieval Europe. Along with worsted from Norfolk, it is a reminder that English wool towns once set the standard for the continent.

questions.q: "worsted" is named after a person.
questions.f: Worstead is now a quiet village, but in the Middle Ages its cloth funded the enormous churches that still stand across Norfolk — buildings far too large for the parishes that own them.

questions.q: There was an Arabic word meaning 'choice' or 'select'. The Arabic name for the fine goat-hair cloth was reshaped in English as if it contained the word hair. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Mohair only looks like it contains the word hair. It is Arabic mukhayyar, meaning select cloth, which English speakers reshaped into something that sounded like it made sense. That process is called folk etymology.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a fine goatskin leather" comes from a country in North Africa?
questions.f: Morocco leather was the standard for fine bookbinding for centuries — soft enough to work, strong enough to last. The best grade is still called levant morocco, after another region entirely.

questions.q: There was a town in central France. A fine silk net for veils and gowns was first made there. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Tulle is the stuff of every ballet skirt and wedding veil. The town that named it is a quiet place in the Correze that most French people associate with something else entirely — it is also a former presidential hometown.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a thin transparent fabric" comes from a city on the eastern Mediterranean?
questions.f: The Gaza origin is the traditional explanation, though some scholars trace gauze to an Arabic word for raw silk instead. Either way it arrived in Europe along Mediterranean trade routes with its name attached.

questions.q: There was a city in present-day Uzbekistan. The crisp sheer cotton is thought to be named for the Silk Road city that traded it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Organdy is the crispest cotton made — the stiffness comes from treating the woven cloth with acid. Its name most likely travelled the Silk Road from Urgench, a city few English speakers have ever heard of.

questions.q: There was a city in the Netherlands. Its potters imitated Chinese porcelain in blue on white tin-glazed earthenware. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Delft potters were copying Chinese porcelain they could not chemically reproduce, so they faked it: white tin glaze over ordinary clay, painted blue. The imitation became famous in its own right and outlived the thing it imitated.

questions.q: "majolica" is named after a place.
questions.f: Majolica is named for a stopover, not a source. The pottery was Spanish, but it reached Italian buyers through Majorca, and Italians named it after the island the ships came from.

questions.q: There was a city in northern Italy. French buyers named the tin-glazed pottery after the Italian city that supplied it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Faience and majolica are nearly the same pottery named by two different countries after two different middlemen — the French said Faenza, the Italians said Majorca. Both were describing tin-glazed earthenware.

questions.q: There was a london street and market carriers of the eighteenth century. The strong dark beer was popular with the men who hauled goods around the city. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Porter is named after its drinkers rather than a person or place — the porters who carried loads through London markets. Extra-strong porter was called stout porter, which is where stout comes from.

questions.q: There was a port town in western Sicily. An English merchant began fortifying the local wine in 1773 so it would survive shipping. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: John Woodhouse's ship sheltered at Marsala, he tasted the local wine, and he added spirit so it would survive the voyage to England. Sicily got an export industry out of one storm.

questions.q: There was a town in Andalusia, Spain. English traders pronounced Jerez as sherris, then took it for a plural and made a singular from it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: English merchants heard Jerez, said sherris, assumed the s meant plural, and invented sherry as the singular. The same mistake gave English pea from pease and cherry from cerise.

questions.q: There was an old French word meaning 'pale' or 'clear'. Medieval Bordeaux wine was lighter in colour than modern red, so the English called it clairet. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Claret describes a colour, not a place — the pale red of medieval Bordeaux, which was closer to today's rose. English drinkers kept the word even after the wine got much darker.

questions.q: There was a region of Gascony in southwest France. Brandy distilled there predates cognac by about two centuries. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Armagnac is older than cognac and distilled only once rather than twice, which leaves more flavour and less polish. It is made in far smaller quantities, largely because Armagnac has no river to the sea.

questions.q: "panama" is named after a person.
questions.f: Panama hats are Ecuadorian. They were shipped through Panama, and when Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the canal works in 1906, the wrong name stuck permanently to a hat from another country.

questions.q: Which word meaning "to heat a liquid briefly to destroy harmful microbes" comes from a French chemist and microbiologist?
questions.f: Pasteur was asked to find out why French wine kept going sour. He found living organisms in it, and that a short spell at moderate heat killed them without ruining the taste. Milk got the same treatment, and childhood deaths dropped.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a grain crop" comes from a Roman goddess of grain and harvest?
questions.f: Your breakfast is named after a Roman goddess. Ceres governed grain and the harvest, and the Romans called the crops themselves cerealia — her things. Four thousand years later it is written on a cardboard box.

questions.q: Which word meaning "quick-changing and unpredictable in mood" comes from a Roman messenger god?
questions.f: Mercury had winged sandals and never stayed anywhere long. The only liquid metal was named after him for the same reason — it rolls away the moment you touch it. A mercurial person is just as hard to hold.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a mountain that erupts molten rock" comes from a Roman god of fire and the forge?
questions.f: There is a small Italian island called Vulcano, named for the god the Romans thought was hammering away beneath it. Every volcano on Earth — and on Mars — is named after one god's forge.

questions.q: Which word meaning "fragments scattered by an exploding shell" comes from a british artillery officer?
questions.f: Shrapnel spent his own money developing the shell and worked on it for years before the army adopted it in 1803. He got a pension and a word in every language. It is not the legacy most people would choose.

questions.q: Which word meaning "strips of facial hair grown down the sides of the face" comes from American Civil War general?
questions.f: They were called burnsides first, after the general who wore an enormous pair. Somewhere along the way English swapped the two halves and produced sideburns — which now sounds like it describes the sides, purely by accident.

questions.q: "dunce" is named after a place.
questions.f: Duns Scotus was one of the sharpest minds of the Middle Ages. When fashions in learning changed, his stubborn followers were mocked as Dunses — and one of the cleverest men of his age ended up meaning the opposite.

questions.q: There was a French writer and aristocrat. He wrote about cruelty at length and spent much of his life imprisoned. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: De Sade spent roughly thirty-two years locked up, and wrote much of his work in prison — including one novel on a continuous roll of paper hidden in his cell wall. A psychiatrist coined sadism from his name in 1886.

questions.q: There was an Austrian writer. His novel Venus in Furs described a man who found pleasure in being dominated. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Sacher-Masoch was a respected historian and novelist who deeply resented having his name turned into a clinical term. The psychiatrist Krafft-Ebing coined it anyway, and paired it with sadism in the same book.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a slip in which the first sounds of words are swapped" comes from an oxford don and clergyman?
questions.f: Spooner is supposed to have toasted our queer old dean instead of our dear old queen. Most of the famous examples were probably invented by students, but he really did make the slips — and only ever admitted to one.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a large dark berry crossed from several species" comes from an American horticulturist?
questions.f: Boysen gave up and left his experimental vines to die. Walter Knott tracked down the last few survivors on the abandoned farm, nursed them back, and named the berry after the man who had quit.

questions.q: There was a French nobleman. His cook coated almonds in caramelised sugar and named the sweet after his employer. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The cook, Clement Lassagne, is said to have invented the sweet after watching a kitchen boy eat spilled caramel and almonds. He named it for his employer, opened a shop, and the shop still exists in Montargis.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a pizza of tomato, mozzarella and basil" comes from a queen of Italy?
questions.f: In 1889 Raffaele Esposito made three pizzas for the visiting queen. She preferred the patriotic one, and he named it after her. Whether the story is strictly true is argued over, but the pizza is definitely named for a queen.

questions.q: "salmonella" is named after a person.
questions.f: Theobald Smith actually identified the organism. Salmon was his supervisor, and the naming followed the rank rather than the work — an old habit in science. Salmon was the first person in America to earn a veterinary doctorate.

questions.q: There was a british surgeon. He pioneered antiseptic surgery, and the bacterium was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Lister worked out that infection came from invisible organisms and started spraying carbolic acid in operating theatres. Death rates collapsed. He has a bacterium named after him and, less flatteringly, a mouthwash.

questions.q: There was a Soviet foreign minister. Finns mocked his claim that Soviet bombs were food parcels, and named their petrol bombs a drink to go with the bread. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Molotov said Soviet aircraft were dropping food to starving Finns. The Finns called the cluster bombs Molotov bread baskets — and named their own petrol bombs Molotov cocktails, a drink to go with the meal.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a unit of loudness" comes from a Scottish-American inventor?
questions.f: The bel turned out to be too big for everyday use, so almost nobody uses it — we use tenths. Bell's mother and wife were both deaf, and his work on sound began as work on teaching deaf children to speak.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a gas burner giving a hot clean flame" comes from a German chemist?
questions.f: Peter Desaga, Bunsen's instrument maker, actually built the burner to Bunsen's specification. Bunsen also lost the sight in one eye to an explosion and nearly died twice of arsenic poisoning. Chemistry was more dangerous then.

questions.q: Which word meaning "to punish without lawful trial" comes from a virginia planter and judge?
questions.f: Lynch's court handed out floggings, not hangings — the killing sense came later and much worse. Lynch law began as a phrase for rough frontier justice and turned into a word for one of America's darkest habits.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the first month of the year" comes from a Roman god of doorways and beginnings?
questions.f: Janus guarded doorways and had a face on each side, so he could see where you had been and where you were going at the same time. That is exactly what people do on the first of January.

questions.q: "march" is named after a place.
questions.f: March was once the first month of the Roman year — the point where winter ended and armies could move again. That is also why September, October, November and December mean seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the fifth month of the year" comes from a Roman goddess of growth and spring?
questions.f: Maia was a goddess of growing things, and her month is when growth is at its fastest. She was also the mother of Mercury, which makes May and mercurial distant relatives.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the sixth month of the year" comes from a Roman queen of the gods, protector of marriage?
questions.f: Juno looked after marriage, so Romans thought June the luckiest month for a wedding. Two thousand years later June is still the most popular wedding month in much of the world, for a reason almost nobody remembers.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the seventh day of the week" comes from a Roman god of agriculture and time?
questions.f: Saturday is the odd one out. The Anglo-Saxons swapped most Roman gods for their own — Mars became Tiw, Jupiter became Thor — but nobody found a match for Saturn, so he kept his day.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the fifth day of the week" comes from a Norse god of thunder?
questions.f: The Romans called it Jupiter's day; the Anglo-Saxons had their own thunder god and swapped him in. In French it is still jeudi, from Jove — so the same day is named after two different thunder gods in two languages.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the sixth day of the week" comes from a Norse goddess, wife of Odin?
questions.f: Friday matches Frigg to Venus — love goddess for love goddess. French kept the Roman version as vendredi. English took the Norse one, which is why our week is a mixture of two different mythologies.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the third day of the week" comes from a Norse and Germanic god of war, also called Tyr?
questions.f: Tyr lost his hand feeding it to a giant wolf as a pledge, knowing the pledge was a lie — the bravest act in Norse myth. His day is the plain-sounding Tuesday, which does not hint at any of that.

questions.q: "wednesday" is named after a person.
questions.f: Wednesday is Woden's day, and the silent d is the fossil of the missing name. Odin gave an eye for wisdom and hung from a tree for nine nights to learn the runes — none of which survives in the spelling except that d.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a man's formal dinner jacket" comes from a wealthy village in New York State?
questions.f: Tuxedo Park is named from a Lenape word, probably meaning something like crooked river. So the most formal jacket in English is named after a New York country club named after a Native American place name.

questions.q: What does "ottoman" mean?
c: A low padded seat or footstool without a back
Of Phoenicia; relating to its traders and alphabet
Boldly original and defiant of limits
questions.f: An empire that lasted six hundred years is now best known in English homes as a padded footstool. Osman's dynasty ruled from the Balkans to Arabia, and the furniture is what English kept of the name.

questions.q: What does "spencer" mean?
questions.f: One story says his coat-tails caught fire at a fireplace and he simply had them cut off. Another says he lost a bet. Either way the cropped jacket became fashionable and has come back roughly once a century since.

questions.q: There was an elizabethan executioner at Tyburn. His hoisting gallows design gave its name first to the gallows and then to any lifting crane. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Derrick was a convicted criminal pardoned on condition that he become the hangman. His gallows used a pivoting beam and pulley, and oil rigs use the same shape and the same name four hundred years later.

questions.q: Which word meaning "ostentatiously luxurious" comes from a Swiss hotelier?
questions.f: Ritz was fired from his first restaurant job for being unsuited to the trade. He went on to run the Savoy, open the Paris Ritz, and put his name into English twice — as ritzy and in putting on the Ritz.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a giant redwood tree of California" comes from a Cherokee scholar?
questions.f: Sequoyah could not read any language when he began, and worked for twelve years to build a writing system from scratch. Within a few years most of the Cherokee nation was literate. The largest trees on Earth carry his name.

questions.q: "bougainvillea" is named after a place.
questions.f: The plant was probably first described by Jeanne Baret, the expedition's botanist's assistant, who sailed disguised as a man and became the first woman to circumnavigate the globe. The plant is named after the captain.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small brightly coloured freshwater fish" comes from a trinidad clergyman and naturalist?
questions.f: The guppy had already been described and named twice before Guppy sent his specimens, so his name is not the official scientific one. It is the one everybody actually uses, which he probably would have settled for.

questions.q: There was an American judge and amateur breeder. He crossed a blackberry with a raspberry in his garden, by accident. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Logan was trying to breed better blackberries and planted his varieties too close to a raspberry. The bees did the rest. He was a judge by profession and got a fruit named after him for a gardening mistake.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small sweet seedless citrus fruit" comes from a French missionary in Algeria?
questions.f: Brother Clement ran an orphanage outside Oran and noticed one tree in the garden producing unusually sweet, seedless fruit. It was a chance hybrid. Every clementine sold today descends from that single accidental tree.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a seedless variety of mandarin orange" comes from a former province in southern Japan?
questions.f: The wife of an American ambassador sent trees home from Satsuma province in 1878 and the name travelled with them. In Japan the same fruit is called mikan — nobody there calls it a satsuma.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small loose-skinned orange" comes from a port city in Morocco?
questions.f: Tangerines are named for the port they were shipped from, not where they grew — the fruit is originally Chinese. It is the same pattern as the Panama hat: the name records the harbour, not the home.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a sweet orange-fleshed melon" comes from a papal country estate near Rome?
questions.f: Cantalupo means something like wolf-song. The melon came from Armenia by way of a papal garden, and the sweet orange fruit in your fruit salad is named after a place where wolves were once heard howling.

questions.q: "sousaphone" is named after a person.
questions.f: Sousa wanted a bass instrument that would carry sound over a marching band rather than up into the sky. He wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever too, so he is one of very few people who named both an instrument and an anthem.

questions.q: There was a Russian inventor. He built an instrument played by moving the hands near two antennas, without touching it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Theremin invented his instrument by accident while building a proximity sensor. He later designed a Soviet listening device that hung inside the American embassy for seven years, powered by nothing but the radio beam aimed at it.

questions.q: There was an Italian violin maker. His instruments have never been convincingly matched, and his Latinised name marks them. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Stradivari made about 1,100 instruments and around 650 survive. Scientists have tested the varnish, the wood density, even the effect of a colder climate on the trees, and still cannot agree on why they sound the way they do.

questions.q: What does "steinway" mean?
c: A piano made by Steinway and Sons
questions.f: Steinweg built his first piano in his kitchen in Germany as a wedding gift for his wife. He emigrated in 1850, changed the name to Steinway because it sounded better in English, and the firm holds well over a hundred patents.

questions.q: There was an American engineer. He built the first widely used voltage-controlled music synthesizer. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Moog started out building theremin kits as a teenager. His synthesizer reached the public through a 1968 album of Bach played entirely on it, which went platinum and put an electronic instrument in ordinary living rooms.

questions.q: There was a French physicist. He measured the force between electric charges and the unit of charge took his name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Coulomb measured forces far too small to feel by hanging a rod from a fine thread and watching how far it twisted. The same delicate trick was later used to weigh the Earth.

questions.q: There was a Scottish physicist. His equations unified electricity, magnetism and light; a unit of magnetic flux bears his name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Maxwell's four equations showed that light is an electromagnetic wave — arguably the single greatest leap in physics between Newton and Einstein. Einstein kept a photograph of him on his study wall.

questions.q: "gray" is named after a place.
questions.f: Gray worked out how to measure exactly how much radiation a tissue absorbs — the difference between a useful cancer treatment and a lethal exposure. It is a rare unit that is genuinely a matter of life and death.

questions.q: There was a Swedish physicist. He mapped the solar spectrum in units of one ten-billionth of a metre. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An angstrom is about the width of a hydrogen atom, which makes it the natural ruler for anything atomic. Angstrom also found hydrogen in the Sun, using nothing but the colours in its light.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the ratio of speed to the speed of sound" comes from an Austrian physicist and philosopher?
questions.f: Mach photographed a bullet in flight in 1887 and captured the shock wave coming off it — the first evidence anyone had seen. Mach 1 is not a fixed speed: sound travels slower in cold air, so it changes with altitude.

questions.q: There was an American virologist. He developed the first effective polio vaccine and refused to patent it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Asked who owned the patent, Salk said the people did — could you patent the sun? Forgoing the patent may have cost him billions. Polio cases in the United States fell from around 58,000 a year to almost none.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a diagram of overlapping circles showing set relations" comes from an English logician?
questions.f: Venn called them Eulerian circles and never claimed to have invented them — versions appear centuries earlier. He did build a cricket bowling machine that clean bowled a visiting Australian team, which he may have preferred to be known for.

questions.q: The word "nobel" is named after…?
questions.f: A French paper mistakenly printed Nobel's obituary while he was alive, under the headline The Merchant of Death Is Dead. He read his own reputation, disliked it, and rewrote his will to fund the prizes.

questions.q: There was a Hungarian-American newspaper publisher. He endowed prizes for journalism and letters in his will. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Pulitzer arrived in America as a penniless immigrant recruited into the Union army, and ended up owning New York's biggest paper. He also helped pay for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal by shaming his readers into donating.

questions.q: "oscar" is named after a person.
questions.f: Three people claimed to have named it, all saying the statuette reminded them of someone called Oscar. The Academy could not settle the argument, gave up, and made the nickname official.

questions.q: There was a Belgian-American chemist. He created the first fully synthetic plastic and named it after himself. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Bakelite was the first plastic made from nothing that had ever been alive — no plant, no insect, entirely synthetic. Baekeland had already made a fortune inventing photographic paper, and could afford to experiment.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a long-distance race of about 42 kilometres" comes from a plain in Greece, site of a battle in 490 BC?
questions.f: The modern distance was set at the 1908 London Olympics so the race could start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box — which is why every marathon since has been an oddly specific 42.195 kilometres.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a place of learning or a society of scholars" comes from a Greek hero whose sacred grove stood outside Athens?
questions.f: Plato's school met in an olive grove sacred to a half-forgotten hero named Akademos. It ran for nearly nine hundred years, and every academy, academic and academia traces back to that one patch of ground.

questions.q: Which word meaning "tearfully and excessively sentimental" comes from a follower of Jesus in the Gospels?
questions.f: Medieval English pronounced Magdalene as maudlin, which is why two Oxford and Cambridge colleges spelled Magdalen are still said that way. Centuries of paintings of her in tears did the rest.

questions.q: There was a physician to the Greek gods. Hymns of thanksgiving sung to him became the word for any song of praise. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Paean was the doctor who patched the gods up when they were wounded in battle. The hymns sung to him in gratitude gave English the word for any outburst of praise.

questions.q: There was an American engineer. His luxurious railway sleeping cars set the standard for comfortable long-distance travel. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Pullman built a whole company town for his workers, then cut wages without cutting rents. The strike that followed in 1894 shut down railways nationwide. He was buried under concrete to stop anyone digging him up.

questions.q: "hansom" is named after a place.
questions.f: Hansom was an architect who designed a cab as a sideline, sold the patent for £10,000 and was never paid. The cab made London's streets fast; he went back to designing churches.

questions.q: There was a Scottish statesman. He commissioned a small enclosed carriage that could turn in a narrow street. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Brougham was a lawyer, a Lord Chancellor and a campaigner against slavery, and he is remembered for a carriage. He also popularised Cannes as a resort, more or less by accident, after being stranded there.

questions.q: There was a town in Germany. A four-wheeled carriage with a folding two-part roof was first built there. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The landau's roof splits in the middle and folds both ways, so passengers could be seen in fine weather and covered in bad. British royal processions still use them for exactly that reason.

questions.q: There was a son of the sun god in Greek myth. He begged to drive the sun chariot, lost control, and scorched the earth. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Phaethon took the reins of the sun for one day and nearly destroyed the world before Zeus shot him down. Naming a fast, unstable, open carriage after him was a joke that everyone at the time understood.

questions.q: There was a spa town in Germany. Edward VII took to wearing the local stiff felt hat and made it fashionable in Britain. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The future Edward VII visited the spa, liked the hat, and brought it home. Churchill wore one, and so did nearly every diplomat photographed between the wars.

questions.q: There was a title character of George du Maurier's 1894 novel. The hat worn in the London stage version took the character's name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The novel that gave us the word Svengali also gave us the trilby — named not for the villain but for the heroine, from the hat worn onstage in the first London production.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a hard felt hat with a rounded crown" comes from a london hatmakers?
questions.f: It was commissioned to stop gamekeepers being knocked off their horses by branches. The customer tested the prototype by putting it on the floor and stamping on it. It held, and he paid twelve shillings.

questions.q: "slinky" is named after a person.
questions.f: James was designing springs to steady instruments on rough seas when he knocked one off a shelf and watched it step end over end to the floor. His wife found the word slinky in a dictionary.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a twisting cube puzzle" comes from a Hungarian architecture professor?
questions.f: Rubik built it as a teaching aid and only realised he had made a puzzle when he scrambled it and could not put it back. It took him a month to solve his own invention.

questions.q: Which word meaning "interlocking plastic building bricks" comes from a Danish phrase meaning 'play well'?
questions.f: Lego is short for leg godt, Danish for play well. By coincidence it also means I put together in Latin, which the company only discovered later and has been enjoying ever since.

questions.q: There was an Australian opera singer. The chef Escoffier created a peach dessert and a thin dry toast in her honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Escoffier served peach Melba in a swan carved from ice. The toast came later, when the singer was ill and could only manage something very thin and very dry. She got a dessert and a diet food.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "poached eggs and ham on muffin with hollandaise" comes from a new York stockbroker?
questions.f: Benedict wandered into the Waldorf with a hangover and asked for buttered toast, bacon, poached eggs and hollandaise. The maitre d' was impressed enough to add it to the menu, swapping in muffin and ham.

questions.q: There was a Venetian painter. A Venice barman named his peach-and-prosecco drink after a shade of pink in one of the painter's works. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Giuseppe Cipriani mixed white peach purée with prosecco at Harry's Bar and thought the colour matched a saint's toga in a Bellini painting. A fifteenth-century artist therefore named a twentieth-century drink.

questions.q: There was an Italian aristocrat. He asked a Florence barman to strengthen his Americano by replacing the soda with gin. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The count had reportedly spent time in America as a rodeo rider and came back wanting something stronger than the drink named after his adopted country. The barman swapped soda for gin, and added an orange slice to mark the difference.

questions.q: "garibaldi" is named after a place.
questions.f: Garibaldi unified Italy and was mobbed by crowds on a visit to England. Britain honoured the liberator of a nation by naming a flat currant biscuit after him, universally known in playgrounds as squashed-fly.

questions.q: There was a French writer and diplomat. His chef is credited with the thick centre-cut steak served with a reduction sauce. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Chateaubriand was a novelist, ambassador and foreign minister, and is now mostly a steak. His cook grilled the fillet between two lesser cuts so the outer meat burned and the middle stayed perfect, then threw the outer pieces away.

questions.q: There was French Protestant writer. The cheese-enriched white sauce is traditionally credited to him or to his household. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Mornay was a Huguenot leader nicknamed the Pope of the Protestants, who spent his life on theological argument. The attribution of the sauce is shaky, which puts it in good company among French sauces.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a smooth sharp mustard" comes from a city in Burgundy, France?
questions.f: Dijon mustard is a recipe, not a place of origin — the name is not protected, so most of it is made elsewhere. The seeds mostly come from Canada, which would surprise a fourteenth-century Burgundian.

questions.q: There was a town in Switzerland. The hard alpine cheese has been made in the district since at least the twelfth century. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Gruyere famously has no holes, despite being the cheese most cartoons draw with them. The holes belong to Emmental, which comes from a different Swiss valley entirely.

questions.q: There was a valley of the river Emme in Switzerland. The cheese with large holes was made in the valley's dairies. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The holes are bubbles of carbon dioxide from bacteria, and dairies can control their size by adjusting the temperature. For years the holes got smaller because the milk got cleaner — fewer hay particles for bubbles to form around.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a soft cheese with a white rind" comes from a region east of Paris?
questions.f: At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, with Europe being carved up, the delegates held a competition to name the finest cheese. Brie won, and was dubbed the king of cheeses — the only crown that congress awarded.

questions.q: "gorgonzola" is named after a person.
questions.f: Legend says a distracted cheesemaker left curd overnight to chase a girl, added fresh curd in the morning to hide the lapse, and invented a blue cheese. Every blue cheese has a version of this story.

questions.q: There was an Italian word for sheep. Any Italian cheese made from sheep's milk carries the name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Not a place or a person — pecorino just means sheepish, in the literal sense. Roman legionaries were issued a daily ration of it, which makes it one of the oldest recorded packed lunches.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a soft fresh Italian cheese" comes from an Italian verb meaning 'to cut off'?
questions.f: Mozzarella is named after the action that makes it: the curd is heated, stretched like dough, and pinched off in lumps. The name means the cutting-off, which is exactly what the cheesemaker's hands are doing.

questions.q: Which word meaning "country in South America" comes from a venezuelan revolutionary leader?
questions.f: Bolivia is one of very few countries named after a real person. Bolivar liberated six nations and died poor and disillusioned, writing that he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.

questions.q: Which word meaning "country in South America" comes from a Genoese navigator?
questions.f: Columbus never set foot in Colombia. The name was chosen by a revolutionary who wanted a title for the whole of Spanish America, and it ended up attached to one country.

questions.q: Which word meaning "country in Southeast Asia" comes from a king of Spain?
questions.f: Named in 1543 for a Spanish prince who never visited. There have been serious proposals to change it since independence, on the grounds that the country is named after a foreign monarch who colonised it.

questions.q: There was a Dutch navigator. He was the first European to reach the island, and it was renamed in his honour in 1856. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Tasman called it Van Diemen's Land after his sponsor. The name was changed in 1856 partly to shake off its association with convict transportation — so the island is named after the navigator instead of the governor.

questions.q: "seychelles" is named after a place.
questions.f: A hundred and fifteen islands in the Indian Ocean are named after a French finance minister who never saw them. He was in office for two years and is remembered nowhere else.

questions.q: The word "america" is named after…?
questions.f: Martin Waldseemuller printed the name on a map in 1507 because Vespucci had argued it was a new continent rather than Asia. He later changed his mind and removed it — but a thousand copies were already out.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small yellow songbird" comes from a latin for 'islands of the dogs'?
questions.f: The bird is named after the islands, and the islands are named after dogs — canis in Latin. So a small yellow songbird is, at two removes, named after a pack of large dogs.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a large game bird" comes from the country?
questions.f: The bird is American and the name is a mistake. English traders met a similar African bird sold by Turkish merchants and called it turkey; when the American bird arrived it inherited the wrong name. The Turkish for it is hindi, meaning Indian.

questions.q: There was a Swiss mathematician. His notation and results run through almost every branch of mathematics. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Euler gave us the symbols e, i, f(x) and the sigma for sums. He also wrote the equation many mathematicians call the most beautiful there is, tying together five fundamental constants in seven characters.

questions.q: There was a Russian mathematician. He studied processes where the next step depends only on the current state, not the history. Which word grew out of it?
