questions.f: Markov developed his chains partly to win an argument, analysing the vowels and consonants in a Pushkin poem to prove a rival wrong about probability. The maths now runs speech recognition and page ranking.

questions.q: There was a Polish-French-American mathematician. He coined the word fractal and found the set that carries his name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Mandelbrot asked how long the coast of Britain is, and answered: it depends on the length of your ruler. Measure in smaller steps and it gets longer without limit. That question opened up fractal geometry.

questions.q: "hamiltonian" is named after a person.
questions.f: Hamilton solved a problem he had wrestled with for years while walking along a Dublin canal, and carved the formula into the stone of Broom Bridge with a penknife. A plaque marks the spot; mathematicians still visit.

questions.q: There was a Norwegian mathematician. Groups where order does not matter are named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Abel proved that no formula can solve every fifth-degree equation, settling a question three centuries old. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-six, two days before a letter arrived offering him a professorship.

questions.q: There was a Swedish physicist. The unit measures the biological effect of radiation, not merely the energy absorbed. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A gray measures energy absorbed; a sievert measures how much harm it does, which depends on the kind of radiation. The difference matters: the same energy from alpha particles is twenty times more damaging.

questions.q: There was a Danish physicist. He noticed a compass needle twitch near a current-carrying wire, linking electricity and magnetism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Orsted spotted it during a lecture, in front of students, when a compass on the bench moved as he switched on a current. He said nothing at the time and spent three months checking before publishing.

questions.q: There was an Italian physicist. He invented the barometer and proved that air has weight. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Torricelli filled a tube with mercury, upended it in a dish, and found the column always fell to about the same height — leaving a vacuum above it. Philosophers had insisted for two thousand years that a vacuum was impossible.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a violent troublemaker" comes from a disputed — probably a rowdy London family of Irish origin in the 1890s?
questions.f: The word appears suddenly in London newspapers in the summer of 1898, already meaning street rowdy. Whether the Houlihans were a real family, a music-hall joke, or both, nobody has ever settled.

questions.q: There was a probably legendary English weaver. Textile workers destroying machinery in 1811 signed their threats as followers of General Ludd. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Luddites were not against machines in principle — they were skilled workers whose trade was being destroyed and who had no vote to object with. Ned Ludd, in whose name they wrote, probably never existed.

questions.q: "munchausen" is named after a place.
questions.f: The real baron told entertaining war stories. A writer published a wildly embroidered version without asking, making him a laughing stock across Europe — he spent his last years trying to sue, and hated the book.

questions.q: There was a queen of England. The drink is generally held to be named for the queen whose reign saw Protestant executions. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: The naming is disputed — rival theories point to a Chicago bar and a Hollywood actress. The queen's own nickname is not disputed: roughly 280 people were burned during her five-year reign.

questions.q: There was a village and beach in eastern Cuba. An American engineer working at the nearby iron mines mixed rum, lime and sugar and named it for the place. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Jennings Cox ran out of gin while entertaining guests near the Daiquiri mines and improvised with local rum. Hemingway later drank them in Havana by the dozen, and had a variant named after him in turn.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a cocktail of whiskey and vermouth" comes from an island borough of New York City?
questions.f: The island's own name comes from a Lenape word usually translated as place where we get bows, after the wood that grew there. So the drink is named after an island named after a bow-making forest.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a tequila, lime and orange-liqueur cocktail" comes from a Spanish for 'daisy' — and a common given name?
questions.f: At least six people have claimed to have invented it for a woman named Margarita. The likelier answer is dull: daisy was already a category of cocktail, and margarita is simply the Spanish for daisy.

questions.q: What does "tarmac" mean?
c: Of a classical golden age in literature
questions.f: Hooley noticed a stretch of road outside an ironworks that was smooth and dustless, and learned a tar barrel had burst there and been covered with slag. He patented the accident and named it after McAdam.

questions.q: There was a latin for 'flax oil'. Frederick Walton made the floor covering from oxidised linseed oil, and built the name from Latin. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Walton got the idea from the rubbery skin that forms on a tin of old paint. He never trademarked the name, and a court ruled in 1878 that it had already become generic — the first product ever to lose a name that way.

questions.q: "plimsoll" is named after a person.
questions.f: Plimsoll campaigned against coffin ships — overloaded and over-insured vessels worth more sunk than afloat. The shoe is named after the line too: the rubber band round the sole looks just like a ship's load mark.

questions.q: There was a Polish-American virologist. He developed the oral polio vaccine given on a sugar cube. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Sabin's vaccine could be swallowed rather than injected, which made mass campaigns possible in places with few doctors. Like Salk, he refused to patent it. The two men disliked each other for decades.

questions.q: There was a capital of Sweden. Hostages in a 1973 bank siege there defended their captors afterwards. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: After six days in a bank vault, the hostages refused to testify against the robbers and some raised money for their defence. The psychiatrist who coined the term was himself part of the police negotiation.

questions.q: There was a German-American instrument dealer. His firm made the theatre organs and jukeboxes that carried the name into everyday speech. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Wurlitzer organs were built to replace whole orchestras in silent-film theatres — one player, hundreds of pipes, plus drums, cymbals, birdsong and a car horn. Sound film arrived and the market vanished almost overnight.

questions.q: There was an American luthier. He carved mandolin and guitar tops like violin tops, and the company kept his name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Gibson had no formal training and carved instrument tops from a single piece of wood, arched like a violin, when everyone else bent flat sheets. He sold the patent and the company outgrew him entirely.

questions.q: There was an American inventor. He designed the first mass-produced solid-body electric guitar and bass. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Fender never learned to play the guitar. He was a radio repairman who approached the instrument as an engineering problem — bolt the neck on so it can be replaced, and the whole thing can be built on a production line.

questions.q: There was an American actor. He was rarely filmed without a cigarette, and the slang came from his habit of letting it hang from his lip. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: To bogart something is to hog it, from the way Bogart kept a cigarette clamped in his mouth without ever seeming to smoke it. The word entered wide use through a 1968 song.

questions.q: "tradescantia" is named after a place.
questions.f: The Tradescants kept a museum of curiosities in Lambeth called the Ark, open to anyone who paid sixpence — the first public museum in England. Its collection became the founding core of Oxford's Ashmolean.

questions.q: There was a Swedish scientist. Linnaeus named the genus after his patron and predecessor at Uppsala. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Rudbeck discovered the lymphatic system as a student, and later spent decades trying to prove that Sweden was the lost Atlantis. Linnaeus named the flower for him regardless.

questions.q: There was an American statesman and scientist. Two botanists found the tree in Georgia and named it for their friend. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Bartrams found this tree growing in one small patch in Georgia in 1765 and collected seeds. It has not been seen in the wild since 1803. Every franklinia alive today descends from those seeds.

questions.q: There was a German botanist. The genus was named for the head gardener of the Vienna palace gardens. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Its other name is dumb cane: the sap contains needle-shaped crystals that make the mouth and throat swell, temporarily robbing anyone who chews it of speech. It remains a popular office plant.

questions.q: There was an Austrian botanist and physician. The genus was named for the emperor's physician, who was also a botanist. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Hostas are grown for foliage rather than flowers, thrive in shade, and are eaten enthusiastically by slugs. Host himself was physician to the Austrian emperor and ran the imperial botanical garden.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a word-building board game" comes from an English word meaning to scratch or grope about?
questions.f: Alfred Butts, an out-of-work architect, counted letter frequencies on the front page of the New York Times to set the tile values. The game failed twice under other names before Scrabble stuck.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a tower-stacking block game" comes from a swahili verb meaning 'to build'?
questions.f: Leslie Scott's family played it with wooden blocks from a sawmill in Ghana. She named it from the Swahili kujenga, to build — which is slightly ironic for a game everyone plays in order to watch it fall over.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a property trading board game" comes from an economic term for exclusive control of a market?
questions.f: Elizabeth Magie invented the original in 1904 as a protest against landlords hoarding property. Decades later a man sold a version to Parker Brothers as his own invention. She was paid five hundred dollars.

questions.q: There was an American bandmaster. He composed the marches that defined American band music and asked for a tuba to be redesigned for marching. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Sousa wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever, the official national march of the United States. He also campaigned against recorded music, warning it would stop people learning instruments — a prediction with some merit.

questions.q: There was an Italian hatmaker. His Alessandria workshop became the most famous felt hat maker in the world. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Borsalino takes around seven weeks and dozens of separate operations to make, mostly from rabbit felt. The firm was still going after more than 160 years, which very few hat companies can say.

questions.q: There was a british surgeon. An American doctor named his antiseptic after the pioneer of antiseptic surgery. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Listerine was sold first as a surgical antiseptic, then as a floor cleaner and a cure for gonorrhoea. It only became a mouthwash when the makers popularised the word halitosis to convince people they had a problem.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a patty of minced beef served in a bun" comes from a great German port city?
questions.f: Sailors leaving one busy German port ate a minced beef steak served flat on a plate. They carried the habit across the Atlantic, cooks there slid the patty into a bun, and the sandwich kept the port city's name.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a soft stuffed toy bear" comes from an American president and keen hunter?
questions.f: On a hunting trip a president refused to shoot a bear that had been tied to a tree, calling it unsporting. A newspaper cartoon spread the story, a shopkeeper sewed a plush bear in tribute, and the toy carried his nickname ever after.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a team sport played with an oval ball that players may carry" comes from an English boarding school?
questions.f: At one English school the football rules allowed a player to pick the ball up and run with it. Old boys carried the handling version to clubs everywhere, and to tell it apart from the kicking game people simply called it by the school's name.

questions.q: "dalmatian" is named after a place.
questions.f: A tall spotted dog that loved to trot beside horses became fashionable as a carriage escort. Early writers linked the breed to one stretch of Adriatic coastline, and although the connection is thin, the region's name stuck to the dog for good.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a strong, friendly retriever with a short water-shedding coat" comes from a rugged region of eastern Canada?
questions.f: Fishermen on a cold Canadian coast kept short-haired dogs that dived into freezing water after nets and fish. English gentlemen brought the dogs home, bred them for the shooting field, and named them after the coast they came from.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a very small dog with large upright ears" comes from the largest state in Mexico?
questions.f: American visitors to a northern Mexican state in the 1800s bought tiny dogs from villagers near the border. Nobody recorded a breed name, so the buyers simply used the name of the state, and the smallest dog in the world has answered to it since.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a soft round fruit with fuzzy skin and a large stone" comes from the ancient empire of modern Iran?
questions.f: The fruit really began in China, but it reached Rome along the road from Persia. Roman growers called it the Persian apple, persicum, and centuries of shortening in French wore that long name down to a single soft syllable.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a hot drink brewed from roasted ground beans" comes from a highland region of Ethiopia?
questions.f: Wild bushes with red berries still grow in one Ethiopian highland. Traders carried the beans to Arabia, where the brewed drink became qahwa, and every European name for it -- cafe, kaffee and the English word -- goes back to that first green hillside.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a very large expanse of salt water" comes from the Greek titan of the world-encircling river?
questions.f: Greeks imagined the earth as a flat disc ringed by one endless river, and gave that river the name of a titan, the eldest son of sky and earth. When sailors learned the water went on much further than they thought, the titan's name went with it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a device that makes a loud wailing warning sound" comes from a sea creatures in Greek myth whose singing lured sailors onto rocks?
questions.f: In the old story, singers on a rocky island sang so beautifully that crews steered towards them and were wrecked. Odysseus tied himself to the mast to hear them safely. Centuries later an inventor gave the name to a machine whose wail means danger.

questions.q: "cinderella" is named after a person.
questions.f: A girl who slept beside the fireplace and was named for the cinders in her clothes went to the ball and left one slipper behind. Now any unfancied team that reaches the final, or any ignored talent that shines, gets called by her name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "neither too much nor too little" comes from the girl in the tale of the three bears?
questions.f: A girl in a fairy tale tried porridge too hot, then too cold, then just right. Astronomers borrowed her fussiness: a planet in the narrow band that is neither too hot nor too cold for water now sits in the zone named for her.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "an adult who refuses to grow up" comes from the boy who would not grow up, created by J. M. Barrie?
questions.f: A playwright invented a boy who flew, fought pirates, and flatly refused to get any older. Psychologists later borrowed him: someone who dodges every adult responsibility and stays a delighted child is said to have his syndrome.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a person who behaves in a wildly eccentric way" comes from the tea-party host in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
questions.f: At a tea party that never ended, a hat-maker asked a riddle he could not answer and poured tea on a dormouse. Real hat-makers of the day were poisoned by the mercury they used, which is why madness and hat-making went together in the joke.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a broad fixed grin" comes from the grinning cat in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
questions.f: A cat in a wonderland book sat in a tree, gave unhelpful directions, and vanished slowly from the tail forwards until nothing was left but its grin. Anyone smiling that widely for no clear reason is now said to be grinning like it.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "something so broken it cannot be mended" comes from the egg who sat on a wall in the nursery rhyme?
questions.f: An egg sat on a wall, fell off, and all the king's horses and men could do nothing about it. Writers now reach for his name whenever a treaty, a company or a friendship has shattered in a way no committee is going to fix.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a resort with mineral springs or health treatments" comes from a small town in eastern Belgium?
questions.f: A Belgian town with bubbling iron-rich springs became the fashionable place to take the waters in the 1500s. Visitors came home saying they had been to the town by name, and soon every mineral bath in Europe was borrowing it.

questions.q: "sardine" is named after a place.
questions.f: Fishing boats around one large Mediterranean island hauled in silver shoals of a small oily fish by the tonne. The catch was salted, shipped and eventually tinned, and it carried the island's name to breakfast tables everywhere.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a racket game played with a shuttlecock over a high net" comes from a stately home in Gloucestershire, England?
questions.f: Officers home from India brought back a shuttlecock game and played it in the hall of an English duke's country house on a wet afternoon. When people asked what the game was called, they answered with the name of the house.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a giant upright rotating wheel with passenger cars" comes from an American bridge engineer?
questions.f: Chicago wanted something to outdo the Eiffel Tower. A bridge engineer proposed a wheel two hundred and fifty feet across, carrying two thousand people at once. Everyone said it would collapse; it did not, and every big wheel since has borne his name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a blue-green mineral" comes from the land the stone was traded through?
questions.f: The blue-green stone was mined in Persia, but it reached Venice and Paris in the packs of Turkish merchants. French buyers called it pierre turquoise, the Turkish stone, and the shortened word now names the colour as much as the mineral.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a Mexican spirit distilled from blue agave" comes from a town in the Mexican state of Jalisco?
questions.f: In the red volcanic soil around one Mexican town, blue agave plants grow for years before their hearts are roasted and distilled. Mexican law now says the spirit may only carry the town's name if it comes from that region.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a very small long-haired dog with a plumed tail" comes from a historic region on the Baltic coast?
questions.f: Big white spitz dogs pulled sleds along a cold Baltic coast. Breeders shrank them generation by generation until Queen Victoria fell for an eleven-pound one and made the miniature fashionable, and the region's name shrank onto the little dog.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a large powerful black-and-tan guard dog" comes from a town in south-west Germany?
questions.f: Butchers in a German market town used heavy dogs to drive cattle to market, then tied the purse of takings round the dog's neck for the walk home. Nobody robbed them. The town's name went onto the breed and stayed.

questions.q: "siamese" is named after a person.
questions.f: A pair of pale blue-eyed cats with sooty faces was given to a British consul by a royal court in South East Asia in 1884. They were shown in London the next year, astonished everybody, and took the kingdom's old name as their own.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a small tailless rodent kept as a pet or used in experiments" comes from a stretch of West African coast?
questions.f: The animal is not a pig and has never been near West Africa: it comes from the Andes. But it arrived in Europe aboard ships working the Guinea trade route, sailors named it after the last coast they had seen, and the mistake stuck.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a rich coffee" comes from a port on the Red Sea coast of Yemen?
questions.f: For two hundred years almost every coffee bean that reached Europe left through one Yemeni harbour. The beans had a chocolatey edge, so when cooks later stirred cocoa into coffee they reached for the harbour's name to describe it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "coffee" comes from the main island of Indonesia?
questions.f: Dutch growers planted coffee across one Indonesian island until it supplied much of the world. American sailors and soldiers took to calling any cup of coffee by the island's name, and a programming language later borrowed it as a nod to the coders' fuel.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a flat pale edible bean" comes from the capital of Peru?
questions.f: Crates of a broad flat bean left a Peruvian port stamped with the city of origin. Buyers in North America read the stamp rather than any botanical label, and started ordering the beans by the name of the city instead.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a hard, tart, bright green apple" comes from an Australian orchardist?
questions.f: An Australian orchardist threw some French crab apple cores onto a creek bank. A seedling came up, and its fruit turned out hard, sharp and green, and kept for months. Neighbours called it by her nickname and the apple never lost it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a hard-shelled Australian nut with rich creamy flesh" comes from a Scottish-Australian chemist and doctor?
questions.f: A botanist studying rainforest trees in Queensland found one with a nut so hard you needed a hammer. He named the genus after a chemist friend who, as it happens, never tasted the nut that would carry his name around the world.

questions.q: "reuben" is named after a place.
questions.f: A grocer playing his weekly poker game in an Omaha hotel asked the kitchen for corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese and dressing between rye bread, grilled. The hotel owner put it on the menu under the player's first name, and it never came off.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a layered pastry of puff pastry and cream" comes from the French emperor?
questions.f: The layered cream slice began as a Naples pastry, napolitain in French. English speakers heard the more famous name in it and rewrote the word, so the dessert now honours an emperor who had nothing whatever to do with inventing it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a slow-cooked Italian meat and tomato sauce" comes from a city in northern Italy famous for its cooking?
questions.f: Cooks in one wealthy northern Italian city simmered minced meat with a little tomato, milk and wine for hours, and served it with wide flat pasta. The city's name travelled with the recipe, though what most countries make of it would horrify the locals.

questions.q: Which word meaning "ice cream in three coloured layers" comes from a southern Italian port city?
questions.f: Ice cream makers from a southern Italian port emigrated in the 1800s and sold moulded ice cream in coloured stripes, in imitation of their national flag. Abroad the layers became chocolate, vanilla and strawberry, and kept the city's name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a red wine from the region around one French port" comes from a port city in south-west France?
questions.f: For centuries English merchants bought red wine at one French Atlantic port and shipped it home in barrels. They called it by the harbour rather than the vineyard, and even now the region's most famous wines answer to the port's name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a deep blue-violet dye or colour" comes from the country the dye was traded from?
questions.f: Greek traders met a deep blue dye that came in hard cakes from the East, and called it indikon, simply the Indian thing. The name outlasted the trade: the colour between blue and violet in the rainbow still carries the country's name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a soft reddish metal that conducts heat and electricity well" comes from the Mediterranean island whose mines supplied Rome?
questions.f: Rome got most of its reddish metal from mines on one Mediterranean island, and called it the Cyprus metal. Latin wore aes cyprium down to cuprum, and English wore that down again, so an island's name now sits in every electrical cable.

questions.q: "alsatian" is named after a person.
questions.f: During the First World War British owners could not bring themselves to call the breed a German shepherd. They renamed it after a border region that had changed hands between the two countries, and in Britain the wartime alias lasted for decades.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small flat-faced dog with a long flowing coat" comes from the old English name for Beijing?
questions.f: Only the Chinese imperial family could keep the little lion dogs of the palace. When British and French troops looted the Summer Palace in 1860 five were carried off, one was given to Queen Victoria, and the capital's old name went with them.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a horse breed with a dished face, high tail and great stamina" comes from the peninsula where the breed was developed?
questions.f: Desert tribes bred horses that could go far on little water and live close to the family tent. The line is one of the oldest kept anywhere, and almost every modern racing breed carries some of its blood along with the peninsula's name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a problem that grows worse each time you attack it" comes from the many-headed water serpent of Greek myth?
questions.f: Heracles found that every head he sliced off the marsh serpent was replaced by two more, and only fire could stop the regrowth. Ever since, a difficulty that spawns two new difficulties each time you solve it has been called by the monster's name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a large snake that kills by constriction" comes from the great serpent of Delphi killed by Apollo?
questions.f: A monstrous serpent guarded the spring at Delphi until Apollo shot it, and the oracle's priestess took her title from it. When naturalists needed a name for enormous constricting snakes, they reached back into the myth for the serpent's own.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the coloured lights that glow in polar skies" comes from the Roman goddess of the dawn?
questions.f: Romans said a goddess rose each morning to paint the eastern sky before the sun came up. When Galileo needed a name for the green and red curtains that hang over the far north, he gave them hers, adding the northern dawn.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a person behaving wildly or foolishly" comes from the Roman goddess and personification of the moon?
questions.f: Doctors from Rome to the Middle Ages believed that fits of madness rose and fell with the phases of the moon, and English law once separated the permanently ill from those thought to change with it. The moon goddess's name is still inside the word.

questions.q: "big brother" is named after a place.
questions.f: In a novel published in 1949 every wall carried a poster of a moustached face and the line that he was watching you. Nobody in the book ever meets him. Seventy years on, his name is the fastest way to say a state is watching too closely.

questions.q: Which word meaning "american whiskey distilled mainly from corn and aged in charred oak" comes from a county in Kentucky named for a French royal house?
questions.f: Barrels of corn whiskey floated down the Ohio and Mississippi from one Kentucky county, whose name was stencilled on the staves. By the time they reached New Orleans the oak had mellowed the spirit, and buyers asked for it by the county on the barrel.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a cylindrical canvas bag closed with a drawstring" comes from a town in Belgium?
questions.f: A Belgian town wove a thick coarse wool that soldiers and sailors trusted to keep out weather. Coats and kitbags cut from it carried the town's name across every navy in Europe, and the bag kept the name long after the cloth changed.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a machine that shaves and resurfaces ice" comes from an American ice-rink owner and inventor?
questions.f: Resurfacing a rink took five men over an hour. A rink owner in California spent nine years bolting a shaving blade, a water tank and a squeegee onto an army surplus chassis until one driver could do it in ten minutes. His name is now on the machine everywhere.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a German luxury car marque" comes from the daughter of an Austrian car dealer?
questions.f: An Austrian businessman raced Daimler cars under his young daughter's name because a foreign entrant needed a pseudonym. The cars won, dealers demanded that model by that name, and the factory quietly made a ten-year-old girl's name its own.

questions.q: Which word meaning "an American luxury car" comes from the French officer who founded Detroit in 1701?
questions.f: A French officer built a fort on a narrow strait and called it the place of the strait, which became Detroit. Two centuries later a carmaker in that city borrowed his name and his family crest, and the word came to mean the best of anything.

questions.q: Which word meaning "an American car marque" comes from a Swiss racing driver and engineer?
questions.f: A Swiss racing driver went into partnership with an ousted car executive, lending his famous name to a new company. He fell out with his partner over building cheap cars, sold his shares early, and watched his surname become one of the biggest in America.

questions.q: "bowie knife" is named after a person.
questions.f: A frontiersman was shot and stabbed in a duel-turned-brawl on a Mississippi sandbar and still killed two men with a heavy butcher's knife. Newspapers described the blade in detail, smiths were flooded with orders, and the knife took his name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a blade fixed to the muzzle of a rifle" comes from a fortified city in south-west France?
questions.f: The story goes that soldiers besieged in a French border city ran out of powder and jammed their hunting knives into their musket barrels. Whether or not that happened, the city's forges made the blades, and its name went onto them.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a hard glossy black lacquer finish" comes from the island nation?
questions.f: Lacquered boxes arriving from East Asia in the 1600s astonished Europe with a black finish nothing local could match. Workshops in England and France tried to copy it, sold the results as the country's own name, and turned a nation into a verb.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a close-fitting knitted woollen jumper" comes from one of the Channel Islands?
questions.f: Fishermen on a small Channel Island knitted jumpers so tightly that seawater ran off them. Naval crews adopted the pattern, Australian footballers borrowed the word for their shirts, and the island's dairy cattle carried the same name to farms worldwide.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a very large draught horse with feathered legs" comes from a valley in southern Scotland?
questions.f: Farmers in one Scottish river valley crossed local mares with imported Flemish stallions to get a horse that could haul coal and plough heavy clay. The breed grew to a tonne, kept its white feathered legs, and carried the valley's name to the world.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small dried grape used in baking" comes from a Greek city and port?
questions.f: Medieval traders bought tiny seedless dried grapes at a Greek port and sold them in England as raisins of that city. The phrase wore down over centuries until only a mangled version of the city's name was left on the packet.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a small mild onion that grows in clusters" comes from an ancient port in the Levant, now Ashkelon?
questions.f: Returning crusaders brought back a small onion that grew in clusters and tasted milder than the ones at home. They said it came from one Levantine port, called it the onion of that place, and French cooks wore the phrase down to a single word.

questions.q: "pheasant" is named after a place.
questions.f: Greek sailors returning from the Black Sea brought back a spectacular long-tailed bird and said it lived along one particular river. They called it the bird of the Phasis, and every European language still carries a worn-down version of that river's name.

questions.q: Which name or term meaning "a knobbly edible tuber from a sunflower relative" comes from the Italian word for sunflower, misheard as a city name?
questions.f: The knobbly tuber is a North American sunflower and has never grown near the Middle East. Italians called the plant girasole, turning to the sun; English ears heard a famous city in that word, and the wrong name has stuck for four hundred years.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a warm sauce of egg yolk, butter and lemon" comes from the Dutch region?
questions.f: French cooks named several sauces after foreign countries to suggest a style rather than an origin. This one, whisked from yolks and warm butter until it thickens, was labelled Dutch, possibly because the Netherlands supplied the butter.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a warm sauce of egg yolk, butter, tarragon and shallot" comes from a region in the French Pyrenees?
questions.f: A chef outside Paris invented a herbed butter sauce at a restaurant named for Henry IV, who was born in a Pyrenean region and nicknamed for it. The sauce took the region's name, though nobody there had ever made it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a dry red Italian wine" comes from a hilly wine region in Tuscany?
questions.f: A grand duke drew a boundary round some Tuscan hills in 1716 and declared that only wine from inside it could carry the region's name. It was one of the first protected wine areas anywhere, three centuries before such rules became normal.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a light fruity red wine" comes from a wine region north of Lyon in France?
questions.f: Growers in a French region north of Lyon make a light red from gamay grapes and release the newest vintage on the third Thursday of November. Bottles race to Paris and beyond overnight, and the region's name goes with every cork.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a white wine grape" comes from a village in the Maconnais, Burgundy?
questions.f: A small Burgundy village gave its name to a green-skinned grape that turned out to grow almost anywhere, from Champagne to California to Australia. It is now the most planted white wine grape on earth, still carrying one village's name.

questions.q: "rioja" is named after a person.
questions.f: When disease wrecked French vineyards in the 1800s, Bordeaux winemakers crossed the Pyrenees and taught growers in a northern Spanish valley to age wine in oak barrels. The region kept the technique, and its name now means oak-aged Spanish red.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a loud musical instrument of steam whistles" comes from the Greek Muse of epic poetry?
questions.f: An inventor in 1855 mounted a keyboard on a row of steam whistles loud enough to be heard eight miles away. He named it for the Muse of epic poetry, whose name means beautiful-voiced, which anyone who has stood near a circus one may dispute.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a crude, loud, uncultivated person" comes from the brutish human-like creatures in Gulliver's Travels?
questions.f: On his last voyage Gulliver meets talking horses ruling over filthy, howling creatures that look uncomfortably like humans. Swift meant it as a mirror. The creatures' name became an insult, and much later a search engine picked it up as a joke.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a problem whose only solution is blocked by the problem itself" comes from the impossible rule in Joseph Heller's 1961 novel?
questions.f: A bomber pilot could be grounded for insanity, but asking to be grounded proved he was sane enough to fly. Heller's invented regulation was so exact a picture of bureaucratic traps that its number entered the dictionary within a decade.

questions.q: Which word meaning "deliberately ambiguous or misleading official language" comes from the shrinking official language in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four?
questions.f: In Orwell's novel the state shrinks the dictionary every year, on the theory that a thought you have no word for cannot be thought at all. The invented language's name is now used for any official wording designed to blur rather than explain.

questions.q: Which word meaning "holding two contradictory beliefs at the same time" comes from the mental habit demanded by the Party in Nineteen Eighty-Four?
questions.f: Orwell's Party required citizens to believe two opposite things at once and to be sincere about both, forgetting the contradiction and then forgetting the forgetting. The coined word escaped the novel and is now used of real politics every week.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a pattern of coloured diamonds" comes from the acrobatic trickster servant of Italian commedia dell'arte?
questions.f: A masked servant character in Italian street comedy wore a patched costume that hardened over time into neat coloured diamonds. He tumbled, schemed and chased Columbine through two centuries of theatre, and left his name on the pattern itself.

questions.q: "zany" is named after a place.
questions.f: In Italian street comedy the servant clowns, named from a dialect form of Giovanni, copied their masters' gestures badly on purpose. English audiences took the troupe's name for the behaviour, and it now describes any cheerfully absurd person.

questions.q: Which word meaning "the lightest inert gas, used to fill balloons" comes from the Greek sun god?
questions.f: During an eclipse in 1868 astronomers saw a yellow line in the sun's spectrum that matched no known element. They named the unknown gas after the Greek sun god. Twenty-seven years passed before anyone found any of it on earth.

questions.q: There was an English baronet. He imported the plum from France, and the labels were lost in transit. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English baronet imported plum trees from a French monastery, and the labels were lost on the way. His gardener, needing something to call the green ones, combined the colour with his employer's surname, and the plum has answered to it since.

questions.q: There was a Massachusetts merchant. He distributed the English Williams pear in America under his own name. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An English variety called the Williams pear was already growing on a Massachusetts farm when a merchant bought the land. Not knowing the name, he propagated and sold it under his own. The same fruit still has two names on two sides of the Atlantic.

questions.q: There was a Soviet tank sergeant turned weapons designer. He designed the rifle while recovering from wounds in 1942. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A wounded Soviet tank sergeant lay in hospital listening to comrades complain that German troops had better automatic weapons. He sketched a design built to work when filled with mud or sand. Over a hundred million have been made, all carrying his name.

questions.q: There was a German firearms designer. His bolt-action rifle became the pattern copied by most armies. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German designer perfected a bolt action so reliable that armies from Spain to Japan bought or copied it, and hunting rifles still use his locking system a century later. His surname is stamped on more military rifles than almost any other.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. He found that energy comes in fixed packets set by one small number. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A German physicist trying to explain the colour of hot glowing objects found the maths only worked if energy came in indivisible packets. He called the idea a desperate act. It founded quantum theory, and the tiny number in it carries his name.

questions.q: "bohr model" is named after a person.
questions.f: A Danish physicist proposed that electrons could only sit in certain orbits and jumped between them by swallowing or spitting out exact packets of light. It explained hydrogen's spectrum precisely, was wrong in detail, and is still the first atom every student draws.

questions.q: There was a French physicist. He hung a heavy pendulum in the Pantheon to show the earth turning beneath it. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: In 1851 a French physicist hung a sixty-seven-metre wire from the dome of the Pantheon with a heavy iron ball on the end. As it swung, its path slowly rotated. Paris could watch the planet turning for the first time, in a public hall.

questions.q: There was an Italian physicist and priest. He showed that fluid speeds up and its pressure drops in a narrowing pipe. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian priest and physicist showed that squeezing a pipe makes the fluid inside run faster and press outwards less. Carburettors, atomisers, aircraft instruments and hospital suction all use the trick, and all carry his name for it.

questions.q: There was an Irish-born engineer. He found a single number that predicts whether flow will be smooth or turbulent. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An engineer injected a thread of dye into water flowing down a glass pipe. Below a certain speed the thread stayed straight; above it, the dye burst into swirls. He reduced the whole question to one dimensionless ratio that now bears his name.

questions.q: There was a Japanese-American meteorologist. He rated tornado strength by the damage left behind. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A meteorologist who had surveyed the blast damage at Nagasaki applied the same eye to tornado wreckage, working backwards from broken buildings to wind speed. His damage-based scale, from a snapped branch to a house swept clean off its slab, still rates every twister.

questions.q: There was an English mathematician. He showed how to rebuild a function from its derivatives at a single point. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An English mathematician showed that if you know a curve's height, slope, curvature and every higher rate of change at just one point, you can rebuild the entire curve as an endless sum. Almost all of numerical computing rests on that trick.

questions.q: There was a German mathematician. He generalised ordinary geometry to spaces with infinitely many dimensions. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A German mathematician extended ordinary distance and angle into spaces with endlessly many directions. It sounded like pure abstraction until quantum mechanics arrived and turned out to need exactly that geometry to describe the state of a particle.

questions.q: "jacobian" is named after a place.
questions.f: A German mathematician studied the grid of partial derivatives that says how much a change of coordinates stretches or twists each direction. Its determinant is the factor by which volume changes, which is why it appears in every multiple integral.

questions.q: There was a German mathematician. He studied the square array of second derivatives that describes curvature. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A German mathematician assembled all the second derivatives of a function into one square array. Its signs tell you whether a flat point is a peak, a valley or a saddle, which is why every optimisation algorithm reaches for it.

questions.q: There was a plateau town in the Veneto, northern Italy. The cow's-milk cheese has been made on that plateau for centuries. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Shepherds on a high plateau in northern Italy once made this cheese from sheep's milk. When cattle replaced the flocks the recipe changed but the name did not, and European law now protects it for that plateau alone.

questions.q: There was a small town in Wisconsin. A cheesemaker's son invented the washed-curd cheese there in 1885. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Wisconsin cheesemaker's teenage son washed the curds in cold water instead of letting them cook dry, and got a softer, milder, moister cheese than cheddar. It was the first cheese invented in America, and it took the little town's name.

questions.q: There was an experimental farm outside Copenhagen. A Danish cheesemaker developed the cheese at that farm in the 1800s. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Danish woman toured European dairies, came home to an experimental farm outside Copenhagen, and worked out a semi-soft cheese full of tiny irregular holes. The farm's name went onto it, and Denmark's best-known cheese was born on a research plot.

questions.q: There was the northern Italian city. The city's cooks breadcrumb and fry veal, and saffron their risotto. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A northern Italian city gave its name to two very different dishes: a veal cutlet beaten thin, breadcrumbed and fried in butter, and a risotto turned gold with saffron. Vienna's schnitzel is very probably the same cutlet under another flag.

questions.q: There was a French city famous for its cooking. Dishes finished with sliced onions are named for the city's style. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: One French city is so serious about food that its small restaurants have their own name, bouchons. Any dish labelled with the city's adjective on a French menu comes with sliced onions browned in butter, whatever else is on the plate.

questions.q: "provencal" is named after a person.
questions.f: The name of a southern French region on a menu promises the same three things every time: tomato, garlic and olive oil, usually with herbs from the dry hills. The region's Roman name simply meant the province, the first one Rome held outside Italy.

questions.q: There was the miserly old Venetian merchant of commedia dell'arte. His tight leg-covering costume gave its name to trousers. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A stock character in Italian street comedy played a mean old Venetian merchant in tight full-length hose, unusual when other men wore breeches. Audiences named the garment after him, French shortened it, and the word ended up as plain pants.

questions.q: There was the boastful cowardly soldier of commedia dell'arte. His swagger and swift retreat made his name a word for a boastful rogue. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A stock character in Italian comedy strutted in black with a sword, boasted of battles he had not fought, and ran at the first real threat. His name, from a word meaning skirmish, became the English word for exactly that sort of man.

questions.q: There was the hypocritical architect in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit. He preached morality endlessly while behaving badly, so his name means smug hypocrisy. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Dickens created an architect who never designed a building, lived off his pupils' work, and lectured everyone he met about virtue while cheating them. His name became the exact English word for moralising that the moraliser has no intention of following.

questions.q: There was an Austrian physicist. He wrote the wave equation that governs how a quantum state evolves. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An Austrian physicist on a winter holiday in the Alps wrote down a wave equation that predicted the hydrogen spectrum exactly. He later invented a thought experiment about a cat to show how absurd he found the standard reading of his own equation.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. He showed that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A young German physicist working alone on Helgoland realised that the sharper you pin down where a particle is, the vaguer its momentum must become, and not because your instruments are poor. The limit is built into nature, and it carries his name.

questions.q: There was an Austrian physicist. He showed that no two electrons can share the same quantum state. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An Austrian physicist, famous for a scathing tongue and for equipment that broke when he entered the room, showed that two electrons can never sit in exactly the same state. That single refusal is why atoms have shells and why matter takes up space.

questions.q: "rydberg constant" is named after a place.
questions.f: A Swedish physicist hunting for pattern in the coloured lines of glowing gases found one formula that fitted them all, with a single number in it. He had no idea why it worked; Bohr's atom explained it thirty years later.

questions.q: There was an Austrian physicist. He linked the temperature of matter to the statistics of its moving particles. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An Austrian physicist argued that heat is just particles jostling and that entropy counts the ways they can be arranged. Colleagues mocked the idea for decades. His formula is carved on his gravestone, and the constant in it carries his name.

questions.q: There was a German mathematician. He built a set by repeatedly deleting middle thirds, and founded set theory. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A German mathematician took a line, cut out the middle third, cut the middle third from each remaining piece, and kept going forever. What is left has no length at all yet contains uncountably many points, which is the sort of thing that made his colleagues furious.

questions.q: There was a French mathematician killed in a duel at twenty. He linked the solvability of equations to the symmetry group of their roots. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A French student twice failed his entrance exams, was expelled for politics, and spent the night before a duel writing out his mathematics with a note in the margin saying he had no time. He died at twenty. The theory reshaped algebra.

questions.q: There was a French lawyer and mathematician. He claimed a proof in a book margin and never wrote it down. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A French lawyer scribbled in the margin of a book that he had a proof but the margin was too small to hold it. Three and a half centuries and thousands of failed attempts later, Andrew Wiles finally proved it, using mathematics that did not exist in the margin-writer's lifetime.

questions.q: There was a Scottish mathematician. He invented both logarithms and a set of numbered rods for multiplying. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: A Scottish laird who also invented logarithms cut multiplication tables onto strips of ivory. Line the rods up beside a number and the products can simply be read off and added. It was the pocket calculator of the seventeenth century.

questions.q: There was an American pathologist. He identified the tick-borne bacteria and died of the fever he was studying. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An American pathologist traced spotted fever to ticks, then went to Mexico to study typhus. He caught it from the lice he was working with and died at thirty-nine. The genus was named for him a few years later.

questions.q: "shigella" is named after a person.
questions.f: During a dysentery epidemic that killed a fifth of those infected, a young Japanese bacteriologist isolated the organism from patients' stools and proved it was the cause. He was twenty-six. Both the genus and the toxin it makes carry his name.

questions.q: There was a German-Swiss microbiologist. The genus of pneumonia-causing bacteria was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German microbiologist who also spotted the diphtheria organism under his microscope gave his name to a genus of rod-shaped bacteria wrapped in a thick slimy capsule. That capsule is exactly what makes them so hard for the immune system to grip.

questions.q: There was a Swiss-French bacteriologist. He identified the plague bacterium in Hong Kong in 1894. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Two researchers found the plague organism in Hong Kong within days of each other in 1894, and for decades the credit was muddled. The genus now carries the name of the one whose samples were clean, who also worked out that rats and their fleas carried it.

questions.q: There was a German-Austrian paediatrician. He first described the gut bacterium in infants in 1885. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A paediatrician studying infant digestion described a rod-shaped bacterium living harmlessly in the gut. It was renamed in his honour after his death, and the species is now the most studied organism on earth after ourselves.

questions.q: There was a Scottish microbiologist and army surgeon. He identified the organism behind Malta fever in 1887. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Scottish army surgeon posted to Malta traced the fever wrecking the garrison to an organism in goats' milk. Stopping the milk ration ended the epidemic almost overnight, and the genus was named after him.

questions.q: There was a spa town in central France. A chef named the chilled leek and potato soup after the region of his childhood. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French chef working at a New York hotel served the leek and potato soup of his childhood cold instead of hot, on a hot summer day. He named it after the spa town near his home, and a Manhattan invention now sounds thoroughly French.

questions.q: There was a Greek colony in Cilicia whose settlers spoke poor Attic Greek. Athenians mocked the colonists' broken grammar and named the fault after their town. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Athenian visitors to a distant Greek colony were appalled by the dialect the settlers had drifted into, and turned the town's name into an insult for any mangled sentence. The word later widened to cover social blunders as well as grammatical ones.

questions.q: "meander" is named after a place.
questions.f: One river in Asia Minor looped so extravagantly across its flat valley that Greek writers used its name as a byword for anything that would not go straight. Geographers still use it as the technical term for a river bend.

questions.q: There was the king of Macedon and father of Alexander. Demosthenes delivered a famous series of attacking speeches against him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Athenian orator spent years warning his city about the ambitions of a northern king, in speeches so fierce that the king's name became the word for any blistering public attack. Cicero later borrowed the form to go after Mark Antony.

questions.q: There was the Hebrew prophet of the Book of Lamentations. His long laments over Jerusalem's fall gave the name for any prolonged complaint. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Hebrew prophet warned his city for forty years that disaster was coming, was thrown into a cistern for saying so, and then watched it happen. The book of laments that followed gave English a word for any lengthy, gloomy tirade.

questions.q: There was a sorcerer in the Acts of the Apostles. He offered money for the power to give the Holy Spirit. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A sorcerer watched the apostles lay hands on people and offered them cash for the same power. Peter's refusal was blistering. His name became the church's legal term for buying office, and a serious offence for the next eighteen centuries.

questions.q: There was the river of the Greek underworld. Its dark waters gave the word for gloom that is total. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Souls were ferried across one black river to reach the land of the dead, and the gods swore their most binding oaths on its water. Anything gloomy enough to suggest that crossing is described with the river's name.

questions.q: There was the Roman queen of the gods. Her stately imposing figure became the compliment for a tall commanding woman. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Roman queen of the gods was pictured as tall, broad-browed and unmistakably in charge, never girlish. Painters and novelists borrowed her name as a compliment for a woman built on the same commanding scale.

questions.q: There was the Athenian grove sacred to Apollo Lykeios where Aristotle taught. Aristotle's school met in that grove, so its name came to mean a place of learning. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Aristotle taught in a grove outside Athens sacred to Apollo under one of his titles, walking as he lectured. The grove's name became the word for a lecture hall, and in France it still names the secondary school itself.

questions.q: "gradgrind" is named after a person.
questions.f: Dickens opened a novel with a schoolmaster demanding facts, nothing but facts, and a girl punished for defining a horse poetically instead of anatomically. His name is now the English word for anyone who measures everything and understands nothing.

questions.q: There was the cheerfully insolvent optimist in Dickens's David Copperfield. He waited endlessly for something to turn up, so his name means hopeful improvidence. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Dickens created a man permanently one letter away from ruin who assured everyone that something would turn up. Economists borrowed his budgeting advice, and his name became the word for waiting for rescue instead of arranging one.

questions.q: There was an American-British inventor. He built the first fully automatic machine gun, recoil-operated. Which name or term grew out of it?
questions.f: An American inventor in London decided that the surest way to make money in Europe was to help Europeans kill each other more efficiently. He used the recoil of each shot to load the next, and one man could suddenly do the work of a hundred riflemen.

questions.q: There was an American firearms designer. He designed the pistols and machine guns that armies bought for a century. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A gunsmith's son in Utah filed his first patent at twenty-four and ended with a hundred and twenty-eight. He designed the pistol the US Army carried for seventy-four years, and died at his workbench in Belgium with a design half finished.

questions.q: There was an Italian anatomist. He described the tube linking the middle ear to the throat. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian anatomist working before the printing of good anatomical plates described the narrow tube that lets the middle ear equalise pressure. It is why your ears pop in a lift, and it has carried his name for four centuries.

questions.q: There was an Italian anatomist and surgeon. He described the tubes running from ovary to womb. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian anatomist who died at thirty-nine described the delicate tubes running from ovary to womb, comparing their flared ends to trumpets. He got the function wrong but the anatomy right, and the tubes still bear his name.

questions.q: There was an English physician. He described the microscopic canals running through compact bone. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English physician put thin slices of bone under an early microscope and found it was not solid at all but drilled through with a network of tiny tunnels carrying blood vessels. Bone turned out to be plumbing, and the canals took his name.

questions.q: "pacinian" is named after a place.
questions.f: An Italian anatomist found onion-layered capsules buried deep in the skin and joints that fire when pressed or vibrated. He also saw the cholera bacterium thirty years before Koch, and got credit for neither in his lifetime.

questions.q: There was a Dutch physician and anatomist. He described the fluid-filled follicle that releases an egg. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Dutch physician described the fluid-filled blisters on the ovary and argued they held the egg. He was nearly right: they hold the follicle that releases it. He died at thirty-two, embittered by a priority quarrel with a colleague.

questions.q: There was an Italian physician and microscopist. He gave his name to structures in the kidney, spleen and insect gut. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian microscopist was the first to see capillaries, red blood cells and the filtering knots of the kidney. So much of the invisible body was his discovery that his name now attaches to structures in three separate organ systems.

questions.q: There was a German physician. He described the oil glands along the rim of the eyelid. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German physician described rows of tiny oil glands along the eyelid margin. Their oil stops tears evaporating too fast; when they clog, eyes feel gritty and dry. Modern eye clinics still name the condition after him.

questions.q: There was a Danish physician and antiquary. He described the small extra bones found in skull sutures. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Danish physician described the small irregular islands of bone that sometimes form inside the wavy joints of the skull. They are harmless in most people but crowd in on certain bone diseases, which is why radiologists still count them.

questions.q: There was a Dutch physician and anatomist. He described the deep cleft dividing the temporal lobe from the rest of the brain. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Dutch physician traced the deep cleft that separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. It is the most obvious landmark on the side of the human brain, and the artery running along it carries his name too.

questions.q: There was an Italian anatomist. He described the central furrow dividing motor from sensory cortex. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian anatomist mapped the deep furrow running down the top of the brain. In front of it lies the strip that commands movement; behind it, the strip that receives touch. A whole class of childhood epilepsy is named from that furrow.

questions.q: "purkinje" is named after a person.
questions.f: A Czech physiologist who founded the world's first independent physiology department described both the fibres that carry the heart's electrical signal and the huge fan-shaped neurons of the cerebellum. Two entirely different cells carry the same name.

questions.q: There was a German physiologist. He described the cells that wrap nerve fibres in insulating sheaths. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German physiologist proposed that all animal tissue is built from cells, then found the ones that spiral around nerve fibres like insulation on wire. Without them a nerve signal would crawl instead of race.

questions.q: There was an Italian physician and Nobel laureate. His silver staining method revealed a stack of membranes inside the cell. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian physician invented a silver stain that made single nerve cells stand out black against pale tissue. It won him a Nobel Prize shared with a rival he publicly disagreed with, and it revealed the cell's packaging depot, now named for him.

questions.q: There was a Baltic German anatomist. He described the scavenging cells lining the liver's blood channels. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Baltic German anatomist described star-shaped cells stationed in the liver's blood channels. They swallow bacteria and worn-out red cells as blood filters past, making the liver a checkpoint as well as a chemical works.

questions.q: There was an Italian physiologist. He described the nurse cells that support developing sperm. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian physiologist, still a student when he made the discovery, described tall cells in the testis that cradle developing sperm and feed them through their whole maturation. They are among the few true nurse cells in the body.

questions.q: There was a German zoologist and anatomist. He described the testosterone-producing cells of the testis. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German zoologist described clusters of cells sitting between the sperm-making tubes rather than inside them. Their job turned out to be chemical, not reproductive: they make the hormone that drives male development.

questions.q: There was a German anatomist. He described the touch receptor cells at the base of the epidermis. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German anatomist described cells sitting at the base of the outer skin layer that report steady pressure and fine texture. They are why you can feel the difference between paper and silk with a fingertip.

questions.q: "meissner" is named after a place.
questions.f: A German anatomist described egg-shaped bundles of nerve endings packed just under hairless skin. They fire on the lightest brush and go quiet if the touch holds still, which is why you stop noticing your own clothes.

questions.q: There was an Italian anatomist and embryologist. He described the stretch-sensing endings in skin and joint capsules. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian anatomist described spindle-shaped nerve endings that report sustained stretch rather than momentary touch. They tell your brain where your fingers are without your having to look, which is how you can type in the dark.

questions.q: There was an English surgeon and histologist. He described the capsule that collects filtrate in the kidney. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English surgeon showed that the kidney works by filtering blood through a knot of capillaries into a cup, rather than by secreting urine directly. The cup is named after him and the filtering knot after Malpighi.

questions.q: There was a German physician and anatomist. He described the hairpin loop in the kidney tubule that concentrates urine. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German anatomist traced a hairpin bend in the kidney's tubules that dips down into the organ and back. The bend lets the kidney pull water back out of urine, which is why land animals can survive on so little of it.

questions.q: There was a Swiss anatomist. He described the patches of lymph tissue in the wall of the small intestine. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Swiss anatomist described oval patches of immune tissue studding the lining of the small intestine. They sample everything passing through, which makes them the gut's border control and the first place typhoid attacks.

questions.q: There was a Swiss anatomist. He described the alkaline-secreting glands of the duodenum. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Swiss anatomist described glands in the first stretch of intestine that pump out alkaline mucus. Their job is defensive: they neutralise the flood of stomach acid before it can burn the gut wall downstream.

questions.q: There was a German anatomist and neuropathologist. He described the nerve network in the gut wall that drives its muscle waves. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German neuropathologist found a full nerve network woven between the muscle layers of the gut. It runs the waves that push food along without asking the brain, which is why the gut is sometimes called a second nervous system.

questions.q: "wernicke" is named after a person.
questions.f: A German neurologist found patients who spoke fluently in complete nonsense and could not understand a word said to them. The damage sat behind the ear, in a region that turns sound into meaning, and it carries his name.

questions.q: There was a French physician and anthropologist. He located the brain region whose damage destroys fluent speech. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French physician examined a patient who understood everything but could say only one syllable. The autopsy showed a lesion in the left frontal lobe. It was the first hard evidence that a single mental function lives in one patch of brain.

questions.q: There was an Italian anatomist. He described the sensory organ of the inner ear that converts sound to nerve signals. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian anatomist dissected the spiral of the inner ear and found a ribbon of hair cells sitting on a membrane. Each responds to a different pitch, so the ear separates a chord into notes before the brain hears anything.

questions.q: There was a Danish surgeon and anatomist. He described the accessory smell organ in the nasal cavity. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Danish surgeon described a second smell organ tucked into the nasal cavity. In snakes and cats it reads chemical signals from other animals, which is why a snake flicks its tongue into the roof of its mouth.

questions.q: There was a Danish anatomist. He described the pair of lubricating glands at the vaginal opening. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Danish anatomist from a family of three generations of anatomists described a pair of pea-sized lubricating glands. His father named the lymphatic system's thoracic duct; the family put its surname on a remarkable amount of the body.

questions.q: There was an English surgeon and anatomist. He described the pair of glands that secrete pre-ejaculatory fluid. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English surgeon described a pair of pea-sized glands below the prostate. He also republished another anatomist's plates under his own name, causing one of the ugliest plagiarism rows in the history of anatomy.

questions.q: There was an English physician and anatomist. He named the submandibular salivary duct and the jelly inside the umbilical cord. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English physician who stayed in London through the plague of 1665 while most doctors fled described the duct draining the salivary gland under the jaw. The jelly that cushions the vessels inside an umbilical cord also carries his name.

questions.q: "stensen" is named after a place.
questions.f: A Danish anatomist found the duct draining the big salivary gland in front of the ear when he was twenty-two. He then left medicine, worked out how fossils form and how rock layers stack, and ended his life as a bishop.

questions.q: There was a German pathologist. He described the hormone-producing islands scattered through the pancreas. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German medical student described strange islands of cells scattered through the pancreas and admitted he had no idea what they did. Forty years later they turned out to make insulin. He died of tuberculosis at forty-one.

questions.q: There was an English physician and pioneer of neurology. He described the ring of arteries supplying the base of the brain. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English physician traced a ring of arteries at the base of the brain that lets blood reach it from more than one direction. If one vessel blocks, the ring can reroute around it, which is why some strokes cause far less damage than expected.

questions.q: There was an Italian anatomist and surgeon. He described the deep membranous layer of the abdominal wall. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An Italian anatomist described the deep membranous sheet in the abdominal wall that limits how far leaked fluid can spread. He was so disliked that after his death a colleague kept his severed head on display in the university museum.

questions.q: There was a French surgeon and naturalist. He described the thickened band of tissue running to the groin. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French surgeon described the thickened cord of tissue running from the hip bone to the pubic bone. Every hernia repair works around it, and the two kinds of groin hernia are distinguished by which side of it they emerge.

questions.q: There was a German anatomist. He described the ring of lymphoid tissue guarding the throat. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German anatomist described the ring of tonsils and lymph tissue circling the entrance to the throat, catching whatever is breathed or swallowed. He also coined the words neuron and chromosome, which outlasted the ring in fame.

questions.q: There was a Baltic German anatomist. He described the thin membrane dividing chambers of the inner ear. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Baltic German anatomist described a membrane just two cells thick separating two fluid chambers of the cochlear spiral. The fluids on either side carry different salts, and that difference is what powers hearing.

questions.q: "bruch" is named after a person.
questions.f: A German anatomist described the thin layered membrane between the retina and its blood supply. It thickens with age and cracks, and those cracks are where the blood vessels of macular degeneration break through.

questions.q: There was an English physician and microscopist. He described the whorled bodies found in the thymus. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English microscopist described onion-like whorls of flattened cells buried in the thymus. He also used his microscope on London's drinking water, and his drawings of what lived in it helped force the city to build proper sewers.

questions.q: There was a German neuropathologist. His stain revealed granular bodies in the nerve cell body. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German neuropathologist invented a dye that turned the protein factories inside nerve cell bodies deep blue. When a nerve is injured the granules scatter and fade, so the stain became a way of reading damage directly.

questions.q: There was a Ukrainian anatomist. He described the giant motor neurons of the cerebral cortex. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Ukrainian anatomist described the largest cells in the human cortex, giant neurons whose fibres run all the way down the spinal cord. Each one commands muscle directly, and a single cell can be a metre long.

questions.q: There was a French pathologist and histologist. He described the gaps in a nerve's insulating sheath where the signal jumps. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French histologist noticed that the insulation around a nerve fibre is not continuous but broken by regular tiny gaps. The signal leaps from gap to gap instead of crawling along, which makes a nerve impulse fifty times faster.

questions.q: There was a Romanian surgeon and anatomist. He described the fibrous envelope around the kidney. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Romanian surgeon described the fibrous envelope wrapping each kidney in its bed of fat. Surgeons still name the plane by him, because a tumour contained inside that envelope is a far better prospect than one that has broken out.

questions.q: There was a French surgeon and anatomist. He described the fascial layer between rectum and prostate. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French surgeon described a thin sheet of fascia separating the rectum from the prostate. Two centuries later it decides the outcome of prostate surgery: staying on the right side of that sheet is what spares the nerves.

questions.q: "banksia" is named after a place.
questions.f: A wealthy young botanist paid his own way onto Cook's Endeavour and came home with fourteen hundred plants nobody in Europe had seen. He later ran Kew Gardens for four decades, and the bottlebrush-flowered shrub carries his name.

questions.q: There was an English botanist and rector. A botanist named the butterfly bush in his memory. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English country rector spent his spare hours cataloguing mosses and grasses so carefully that Linnaeus later used his work. He never saw the shrub named for him: it came from China decades after his death, and now colonises railway sidings everywhere.

questions.q: There was a Spanish vicereine of Peru said to have been cured by the bark. The malaria-treating bark took her title, though the story may be legend. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The bark of a Peruvian tree was the only cure for malaria for three centuries. Linnaeus named the genus after a vicereine said to have been saved by it, then misspelled her title. The story is probably invented; the spelling error certainly was not.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a scented South African flower grown from a corm" comes from a German physician?
questions.f: A German botanist collecting in South Africa found a small scented flower on a one-sided spike and named it after a doctor friend back home. It became one of the most popular cut flowers in the world on the strength of its smell alone.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a large brightly coloured daisy from South Africa" comes from a German naturalist and physician?
questions.f: A German doctor ran a botanical garden in Moscow and explored the Volga collecting plants before dying at thirty-three. A colleague named a South African daisy after him, and it is now the fifth most sold cut flower on earth.

questions.q: There was a German botanist and physician. The bell-flowered houseplant was named for him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German botanist writing in the 1780s had a genus of velvet-flowered tropical plants named after him. Confusingly, the plant sold in shops under his name today belongs to a different genus entirely, which botanists have given up trying to correct.

questions.q: There was a British collector and founder of the Royal Horticultural Society. A botanist named the Australian genus after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A British collector who helped found the Royal Horticultural Society had a large Australian genus named after him. There are over three hundred and fifty species, from ground creepers to trees, and almost all of them are pollinated by birds rather than insects.

questions.q: "rafflesia" is named after a person.
questions.f: The plant has no leaves, no stem and no roots. It lives inside a vine and erupts as a metre-wide reddish flower that smells of rotting meat to draw flies. It was named for the colonial official who founded Singapore.

questions.q: There was a Russian grand duchess who became Queen of the Netherlands. A Dutch-funded expedition named the tree after their queen. Which word grew out of it?
