questions.f: A German botanist working for the Dutch named a Japanese tree after the Russian grand duchess who had become Queen of the Netherlands. It grows faster than almost any hardwood, up to five metres in a single season.

questions.q: There was the American explorer of the Lewis and Clark expedition. A botanist named the alpine flower from specimens he collected. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An American explorer crossing the Rockies collected a low plant with fleshy leaves whose root the local tribes ate. It survived being pressed, dried and carried across a continent, and then sprouted in a Philadelphia garden.

questions.q: There was the American explorer of the Lewis and Clark expedition. The wildflower was named for the second leader of the expedition. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The other leader of the great American overland expedition got his name on a genus of showy pink wildflowers found along the route. His companion got a different plant, so the two men who crossed the continent together are commemorated in separate genera.

questions.q: There was the Swedish botanist who invented modern biological naming. He chose a small modest twinflower to carry his own name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The man who named tens of thousands of species reserved one for himself, and pointedly chose a tiny creeping woodland plant with two nodding pink bells. A colleague wrote that it was lowly, insignificant and flowered only briefly, like its namesake.

questions.q: There was a German chemist and botanist. The flowering shrub was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German chemistry professor who also taught botany had an East Asian flowering shrub named after him. Robert Fortune brought it out of China in the 1840s on the same journeys that smuggled tea plants to India.

questions.q: There was an English horticulturist and orchid collector. He coaxed a discarded orchid into flower and it was named for him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English collector was sent a crate of Brazilian mosses packed in what looked like dead stems. He planted the packing material anyway. It flowered into an orchid nobody had seen, and the genus took his name.

questions.q: "kalmia" is named after a place.
questions.f: Linnaeus sent a student to North America to find plants that might survive Swedish winters. He came back with an evergreen shrub whose stamens are spring-loaded and fling pollen at visiting bees. Linnaeus named it after him.

questions.q: There was a Scottish physician and patron of Linnaeus. Linnaeus named the henna plant after the man who funded his great work. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Scottish army physician paid the printing costs of the book in which Linnaeus first laid out his system of classification. In return Linnaeus named the henna shrub after him, so the dye on a thousand years of hands carries a Scot's surname.

questions.q: There was a French-Canadian surgeon and naturalist. The pitcher plant genus was named after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French surgeon in Quebec sent European botanists a plant whose leaves form tall tubes half full of liquid. Insects walk in on downward-pointing hairs and cannot climb out. The genus was named after him.

questions.q: There was a French royal gardener. The false acacia was named after the gardener who first grew it in Europe. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A gardener to three French kings planted a North American tree in Paris around 1601. One of the specimens he or his son planted is still alive, propped on crutches, making it the oldest tree in the city.

questions.q: There was a Finnish physician and botanist. Linnaeus named the air plants after him as a joke about water. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Finnish botanist was so violently seasick on one voyage that he walked home round the Gulf of Bothnia instead. Linnaeus, who found this funny, gave his name to a genus of plants that seem to repel water and live on air.

questions.q: There was a Baltic German naturalist and ship's surgeon. A shipmate named the California poppy after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Baltic German ship's surgeon sailed round the world twice on Russian expeditions. His friend and shipmate named the golden poppy of the Californian hills after him, saddling the state flower with one of the hardest genus names in botany.

questions.q: There was a French botanical illustrator. The trailing rock plant was named after the artist. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French botanical artist who drew plants on expeditions to the Levant had a low cushion-forming rock plant named after him. It is the sheet of purple that spills over garden walls in April.

questions.q: "gunnera" is named after a person.
questions.f: A Norwegian bishop who catalogued his country's flora between sermons had a genus named after him whose largest species carries leaves three metres across, big enough to shelter under. Nothing in Norway grows remotely like it.

questions.q: There was a German physician and botanist. The red hot poker plant was named after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German physician published books illustrated by pressing inked plants straight onto the page. A South African plant whose flower spike burns from red at the top to yellow at the bottom was later named after him.

questions.q: There was a Spanish physician and botanist. Linnaeus named the aromatic herb after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Spanish physician in Seville wrote the first European account of the plants coming back from the Americas, including tobacco and sunflowers, without ever crossing the Atlantic himself. Linnaeus named a fragrant mint-family herb after him.

questions.q: There was a German colonial administrator. He sent the African violet's seed to his botanist father. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German administrator in East Africa found a small purple flower growing in the shade of a rock and posted seed home to his father. It became one of the most popular houseplants in the world, and the genus took the family name.

questions.q: There was a British sealing captain and navigator. He sailed further south than anyone had and both a sea and a seal took his name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A British sealing captain pushed his ship further south than anyone before him through an unusually ice-free summer. The sea he found and the seal that lives in it both took his name; the seal can hold its breath for eighty minutes.

questions.q: There was a Russian explorer of Central Asia. He described the last truly wild horse. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Russian explorer brought back a skull and hide from the Mongolian steppe that proved a genuinely wild horse still existed, never domesticated. It went extinct in the wild in the 1960s and was brought back from twelve captive animals.

questions.q: There was a German naturalist on the Russian Bering expedition. He described a sea cow, a jay, a sea eagle and a sea lion in a few weeks. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German naturalist got ten hours ashore in Alaska and used them so well that six species now carry his name. He described a nine-metre sea cow that was hunted to extinction within twenty-seven years of his sighting it.

questions.q: "adelie" is named after a place.
questions.f: A French explorer charting the Antarctic coast named the land he found after his wife, waiting at home in France. The small penguins nesting on it took the same name, so the commonest penguin in Antarctica is called after a Frenchwoman who never went there.

questions.q: There was a German city and grand duchy. The grand duke's court bred the grey hunting dog. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The court of a German grand duchy bred a grey gundog for hunting big game, then kept the bloodline closed to outsiders for a century. When Americans finally got some in the 1920s, the breed carried the duchy's name.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a very large gentle dog bred for water rescue" comes from a large island off eastern Canada?
questions.f: Fishermen on a cold Canadian island bred an enormous dog with webbed feet and a waterproof coat to haul nets and pull drowning men out of the surf. One is recorded as having saved twenty people from a single wreck.

questions.q: There was an ancient city in southern Arabia. The desert hunting hound is thought to take its name from the town. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A slender hound bred to run down gazelle across open desert appears in Egyptian tomb paintings four thousand years old. Bedouin tribes let them sleep in the tent, an honour no other dog received, and their name traces to an Arabian town.

questions.q: There was a valley in Yorkshire, England. Mill workers in the valley bred the large terrier. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Mill workers in a Yorkshire river valley crossed terriers with otterhounds to get a dog that could hunt on land and in water. It grew into the largest terrier of all, and served as a messenger dog in the trenches of the First World War.

questions.q: Which word meaning "a short-haired cat with a distinctive ticked coat" comes from the historic name of Ethiopia?
questions.f: A cat shown in London in 1871 was billed as having been brought back from an Ethiopian campaign. The claim is doubtful and the breed's real origins are probably Indian Ocean coastal, but the country's old name stuck to it.

questions.q: There was the French chemist and microbiologist. The genus of animal-borne bacteria was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The Frenchman who proved germs cause disease had a whole genus named after him: rod-shaped bacteria that live harmlessly in cats' and dogs' mouths and cause fast, angry infections in bitten humans.

questions.q: "bordetella" is named after a person.
questions.f: A Belgian immunologist grew the whooping cough organism from his own infant son's cough in 1906. He won a Nobel Prize for separate work on how blood destroys bacteria, and the genus carries his name.

questions.q: There was a German physician and bacteriologist. He identified the bacterium causing gonorrhoea. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German bacteriologist aged twenty-four identified the coffee-bean-shaped paired bacteria behind one venereal disease, staining them from patients own samples. The same genus includes the organism that causes the most feared and fastest-moving form of bacterial meningitis.

questions.q: There was a French bacteriologist. The corkscrew-shaped bacteria were named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French bacteriologist gave his name to a genus of loosely coiled corkscrew bacteria. One species, carried by ticks that feed on deer and mice, causes Lyme disease and can hide in the body for years.

questions.q: There was a United States veterans' organisation. An outbreak at their 1976 convention revealed the organism. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: In 1976 a hundred and eighty delegates at a veterans' convention in Philadelphia fell ill and thirty-four died. It took six months to trace it to bacteria breeding in the hotel's cooling tower, and the organism took the delegates' name.

questions.q: There was a French zoologist. The intestinal parasite was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French zoologist had a pear-shaped single-celled parasite named after him. It clamps onto the lining of the small intestine with a sucking disc, and hikers who drink from clear mountain streams have been discovering it ever since.

questions.q: There was a Scottish pathologist and army officer. He identified the parasite behind a fatal tropical fever. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Scottish army pathologist found tiny bodies in the spleen of a soldier dead of a wasting Indian fever. The parasite is spread by sandflies, and in its worst form it destroys the liver and spleen and kills within two years.

questions.q: There was an American pathologist. The insect-infecting bacteria were named after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An American pathologist gave his name to bacteria living inside the cells of most insect species on earth. They manipulate their hosts' reproduction so thoroughly that scientists now use them deliberately to stop mosquitoes carrying dengue.

questions.q: "serratia" is named after a place.
questions.f: An Italian pharmacist investigating why polenta turned blood-red overnight found a bacterium making a scarlet pigment, and named it after a countryman he thought had been cheated of credit for the steamboat. It is now a serious hospital infection.

questions.q: There was a German physician and Nobel laureate. The tick-borne bacteria were named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The German who invented chemotherapy and the first cure for syphilis had a genus of tick-borne bacteria named after him. They hide inside the very white blood cells sent to destroy them, which is why the infection is so hard to spot.

questions.q: There was a French veterinarian and microbiologist. He isolated the branching bacteria from cattle disease. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French veterinarian isolated a branching, thread-like bacterium from cattle on Guadeloupe. It lives in soil and dust and mostly troubles people whose immune systems are already failing, which is why it became far better known after 1980.

questions.q: There was a Romanian bacteriologist. He identified the blood parasite in cattle. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Romanian bacteriologist found parasites inside the red blood cells of cattle with a wasting fever. It was the first proof that a tick could carry disease, and the discovery reshaped how doctors thought about insects entirely.

questions.q: There was a Swiss-South African veterinary scientist. The cattle blood parasite was named after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Swiss veterinarian who lost an arm in an accident became the founding figure of South African veterinary science. The tick-borne parasite named after him kills cattle across east and southern Africa, and shaped the whole continent's livestock trade.

questions.q: There was a Brazilian-German physician. He found the worm larvae behind elephantiasis. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German physician working in Brazil found thread-like worm larvae in the urine of patients with grotesquely swollen limbs. The adult worms clog the lymph vessels, and the disease they cause still affects tens of millions of people.

questions.q: There was the husband-and-wife pioneers of radioactivity. The element was named for the couple who founded the study of radioactivity. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element ninety-six was made by bombarding plutonium with helium nuclei in 1944 and kept secret until the war ended. It was named for the husband-and-wife team who discovered radium, the only element honouring two people at once.

questions.q: "einsteinium" is named after a person.
questions.f: Element ninety-nine was first found in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952. Its discovery stayed classified for three years, and it was named after the physicist whose equation had made such bombs conceivable.

questions.q: There was an Italian-American physicist. The element was named after the builder of the first nuclear reactor. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element one hundred appeared in the same hydrogen bomb debris as its neighbour. It was named after the physicist who built the first nuclear reactor under a Chicago squash court, and who had died the year before the name was announced.

questions.q: There was the Russian chemist who devised the periodic table. The element honours the man whose table predicted where elements would fall. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element one hundred and one was made one atom at a time, seventeen atoms in the first experiment. Naming it after the Russian who invented the periodic table was a deliberate Cold War gesture from an American team.

questions.q: There was a New Zealand-born physicist. The element honours the man who split the atom and found the nucleus. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element one hundred and four was claimed by both Soviet and American labs, and the two names fought it out for nearly thirty years. The winner honours the New Zealander who discovered that atoms have a dense nucleus at all.

questions.q: There was an American nuclear chemist. The element was named for him while he was still alive, which broke precedent. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element one hundred and six was named after a living chemist, which caused a formal objection: no element had ever honoured someone still breathing. He had co-discovered ten elements himself, so the rule bent rather than held.

questions.q: There was an Austrian-Swedish physicist. The element honours the physicist who explained nuclear fission. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: She worked out the theory of nuclear fission in exile after fleeing Nazi Germany, and her collaborator took the Nobel Prize alone. Element one hundred and nine was named for her decades later, an apology written into the periodic table.

questions.q: There was the Polish astronomer who put the sun at the centre. The element honours the man who displaced the earth from the centre of the cosmos. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element one hundred and twelve was announced on the five hundred and thirty-seventh anniversary of the astronomer's birth. The team chose him to honour a scientist whose ideas took a century to be accepted and then changed everything.

questions.q: "gadolinium" is named after a place.
questions.f: A Finnish chemist analysed a black stone from a Swedish quarry and found an entirely new kind of earth in it. That single quarry eventually yielded eight elements, and both a mineral and this metal carry his name.

questions.q: There was a Russian mining official. The mineral named after him yielded the element. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Russian mining official who supplied specimens to chemists had a mineral named after him, and the element later teased out of that mineral inherited the name. He is the first person ever to have a chemical element named after him.

questions.q: There was the Swedish inventor of dynamite and founder of the prizes. The element honours the man whose fortune funds the science prizes. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element one hundred and two was claimed first by a Stockholm team whose result nobody could reproduce. The name they had chosen, honouring the founder of the prizes, survived even though their discovery did not.

questions.q: There was an American physicist and inventor of the cyclotron. The element honours the inventor of the particle accelerator that made such elements possible. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element one hundred and three was named for the physicist who invented the cyclotron, the machine that hurls particles fast enough to build new elements at all. Nearly every element past uranium exists because of his machine.

questions.q: There was the Danish physicist who modelled the atom. The element honours the architect of the quantum atom. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element one hundred and seven honours the Dane who worked out that electrons sit in fixed shells. The team originally proposed a form of the name that would have been confused with boron, and had to be talked out of it.

questions.q: There was the continent, itself named after a navigator. The element was named for the Americas, by analogy with europium. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element ninety-five was named after a continent to mirror the element named for Europe directly above it in the table. It is the only synthetic element sitting in ordinary homes: a speck of it makes smoke detectors work.

questions.q: There was the American state and its university. The element was named for the state and university where it was made. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Element ninety-eight was named for the state and the university where it was created. The team joked that they had skipped the tradition of honouring a person because getting to California had been hard enough for the pioneers.

questions.q: "berkelium" is named after a person.
questions.f: Element ninety-seven was named for the university town where it was made, following the pattern of the element above it in the table, which had been named for a Swedish village. Both sit in the same column by design.

questions.q: There was the continent. The rare earth element was named after the continent. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French chemist separated a new rare earth in 1901 and named it after his continent. It glows a distinctive red under ultraviolet light, which is why euro banknotes carry a trace of it as an anti-forgery mark.

questions.q: There was the country. Its German discoverer named it after his homeland. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German chemist found a new element in a silver ore in 1886 and named it for his country. It filled a gap Mendeleev had predicted almost exactly, and its properties matched the prediction so closely that the periodic table was suddenly beyond argument.

questions.q: There was a marie Curie's homeland. She named her first new element after the country of her birth. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Polish-born chemist working in Paris isolated a new element and named it after her homeland, which at the time did not exist as an independent state. It was a deliberate political act disguised as a chemical one.

questions.q: There was the country. Its French discoverer named it after her homeland. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French chemist found the last naturally occurring element to be discovered in 1939 and named it after her country. There is thought to be less than thirty grams of it in the entire earth's crust at any moment.

questions.q: There was the northern European region. Its Swedish discoverer named it after the region. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Swedish chemist separated a new element from a Scandinavian mineral in 1879 and named it for the region. It turned out to be one of the elements Mendeleev had predicted and left a blank space for a decade earlier.

questions.q: There was a village and quarry near Stockholm. The quarry's black mineral yielded four elements named after the village. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: One small quarry on a Swedish island produced a black mineral that turned out to contain eight new elements. Four of them were named after the village itself, which makes it the most honoured place name in the periodic table.

questions.q: "strontium" is named after a place.
questions.f: A mineral dug from lead mines in a Highland village turned out to contain a new element that burns crimson. It is the only chemical element named after a place in Scotland, and it is why fireworks can be red.

questions.q: There was a French geologist and mineralogist. He described the rock, and both it and a mountain range took his name. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French geologist noticed that some Alpine limestone did not fizz in acid the way limestone should. It proved to be a different mineral entirely. Both the rock and the spectacular Italian mountain range made of it now carry his name.

questions.q: There was the German poet, playwright and naturalist. A mineralogist named the iron oxide after the poet, who collected minerals. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Germany's greatest poet was also a serious mineral collector with eighteen thousand specimens. A mineralogist named the commonest iron oxide after him, so the substance that rust is mostly made of is named for the author of Faust.

questions.q: There was an English chemist and mineralogist. He distinguished the zinc carbonate mineral, and his fortune founded the Smithsonian. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English chemist showed that two minerals long lumped together were chemically different. He never visited America, but left his entire fortune to found an institution there, and both the mineral and that institution carry his name.

questions.q: There was a Swedish-German pharmacist and chemist. He identified the acid in the tungsten ore now named after him. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Swedish apothecary discovered oxygen, chlorine and several other elements, then largely lost the credit for each by publishing late. He had a habit of tasting his compounds, which probably killed him at forty-three.

questions.q: There was an English chemist and physicist. The calcium silicate mineral was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An English chemist discovered palladium and rhodium, and made a fortune quietly selling purified platinum. A needle-crystalled calcium silicate was named after him, and the dark lines he first noticed in sunlight became the science of spectroscopy.

questions.q: There was a Russian mineralogist and statesman. The mineral was named after him, and now names a whole class of crystal structures. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Russian mineralogist had one obscure titanium mineral named after him. Its crystal arrangement turned out to be shared by hundreds of compounds, and materials built on that pattern are now the great hope of cheap solar power.

questions.q: "alexandrite" is named after a person.
questions.f: A green gem found in the Urals was presented on the day the future tsar came of age. Under candlelight it turned raspberry red. Since those were the Russian imperial military colours, the stone became instantly fashionable.

questions.q: There was the American banker and gem collector. A gemmologist named the pink beryl after his greatest patron. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A New York gemmologist persuaded a banker to fund the assembly of two of the finest gem collections in the world, both later given to museums. He named a newly recognised pink beryl after his patron.

questions.q: There was an American mineralogist and gem expert. The pink spodumene was named after its describer. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A self-taught mineralogist joined Tiffany at twenty-three and became the most influential gem buyer alive. He described a pale lilac stone from California that fades in sunlight, and colleagues named it after him.

questions.q: There was a French chemist and Nobel laureate. He found the silicon carbide crystals in a meteorite crater. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French chemist picking through fragments from a meteorite crater found crystals he first took for diamond. They were silicon carbide, almost unknown in nature. Grown in laboratories, they now outsparkle diamond and cost a tenth as much.

questions.q: There was an American chemist and founder of a leading science journal. The aluminium silicate mineral was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: An American chemist founded the journal that became the backbone of nineteenth-century American science and analysed the first meteorite fall studied in the United States. A high-temperature aluminium silicate was named after him.

questions.q: There was a diamond-mining city in South Africa. The diamond-bearing volcanic rock was first identified there. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: Diggers at a South African hill found diamonds in a strange bluish rock filling an ancient volcanic pipe. The rock had come up from a hundred and fifty kilometres down, fast enough that the carbon stayed diamond, and it took the town's name.

questions.q: There was the South American mountain range. The volcanic rock is characteristic of the range's volcanoes. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: The volcanoes running down the spine of South America erupt a rock midway between basalt and granite in composition. It was named for the range, and the boundary where that rock type appears around the Pacific carries the same name.

questions.q: "bauxite" is named after a place.
questions.f: A French geologist described a reddish rock near a Provencal village in 1821. It turned out to be the world's only economic source of aluminium, so every drinks can and aeroplane wing traces back to a name from southern France.

questions.q: Which word meaning "magnesium sulphate, used dissolved in baths" comes from a town in Surrey, England?
questions.f: A farmer noticed his cattle would not drink from one spring on a Surrey common. The water was bitter with magnesium sulphate. Boiled down it became a famous purgative, and the town grew into a spa on the strength of it.

questions.q: Which word meaning "of the random jittering motion of tiny particles suspended in a fluid" comes from a Scottish botanist?
questions.f: A Scottish botanist watching pollen grains in water saw them jitter endlessly and could not explain it. Eighty years later Einstein showed the jittering was invisible water molecules knocking them about, which finally proved atoms are real.

questions.q: There was a Soviet physicist and Nobel laureate. He explained the blue glow given off by particles moving faster than light in water. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Soviet physicist explained the eerie blue glow around nuclear reactor cores. Light slows down in water, so a particle can outrun it there, and the glow is the optical equivalent of a sonic boom.

questions.q: There was a Welsh physicist and Nobel laureate. He predicted current tunnelling between superconductors separated by a barrier. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Cambridge graduate student predicted that a supercurrent would tunnel straight through an insulating gap between two superconductors. Senior physicists doubted it. He was twenty-two, was proved right, and the effect now defines the standard volt.

questions.q: There was a Baltic German physicist. He found that a temperature difference across joined metals produces a voltage. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Baltic German physicist joined two different metals, heated one junction, and found a compass needle nearby swung. He had made electricity out of a temperature difference. Every thermocouple in every industrial furnace uses the effect.

questions.q: There was a French watchmaker turned physicist. He found that passing current across joined metals moves heat. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French watchmaker who retired at thirty to do physics found the reverse of the thermoelectric effect: run a current through joined metals and one junction gets cold. Camping fridges and chip coolers run on it.

questions.q: "lenz" is named after a person.
questions.f: A Baltic German physicist established that nature pushes back: a current induced by a changing magnetic field always flows so as to oppose that change. Drop a magnet down a copper pipe and it floats down slowly because of it.

questions.q: There was a German physicist. He formulated the rules for current and voltage in electrical circuits. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German physicist stated his two circuit rules while still a student: charge in equals charge out at any junction, and voltages round any loop sum to zero. He also co-founded spectroscopy and named the black body.

questions.q: There was a German chemist and Nobel laureate. His equation links a cell's voltage to the concentrations inside it. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A German chemist derived the equation linking an electrochemical cell's voltage to what is dissolved in it, then went on to state the third law of thermodynamics. Every nerve impulse in your body obeys his equation.

questions.q: There was a Swedish chemist and Nobel laureate. His equation describes how reaction rate rises with temperature. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Swedish chemist nearly failed his doctorate for proposing that salts split into charged particles in water. He later won a Nobel Prize for it, and was the first person to calculate how carbon dioxide warms the planet.

questions.q: There was a French chemist. His law relates a solution's vapour pressure to its composition. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French chemist found that dissolving something in a liquid lowers how readily that liquid evaporates, in exact proportion to how much is dissolved. It is why the sea freezes later than a pond and why antifreeze works.

questions.q: There was a French chemist. His principle predicts how a system at equilibrium answers a disturbance. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A French chemist stated that a chemical system at balance always shifts to undo whatever you do to it: squeeze it and it shrinks its own pressure, heat it and it absorbs heat. Industrial chemistry is largely the art of exploiting this.

questions.q: There was a Swiss mathematics teacher. He found the formula fitting hydrogen's visible spectral lines. Which word grew out of it?
questions.f: A Swiss schoolteacher with a taste for numerical puzzles found, at fifty-nine, a simple formula that fitted the four visible lines of glowing hydrogen exactly. He had no physical explanation. Bohr supplied one thirty years later.

questions.q: "waals" is named after a place.
questions.f: A Dutch schoolteacher who taught himself physics at night wrote an equation for real gases that accounted for molecules taking up space and pulling faintly on each other. Those faint pulls are why geckos can walk up glass.
